### Series Title Page

**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR A UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL THE MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION WHICH HAVE SURVIVED THROUGH THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, CAREFULLY CORRECTED BY COMPARISON WITH THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS, DISCOVERED AFTER THE COMPLETION OF THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS PRODUCED DURING THE THREE MOST RECENT CENTURIES; FURNISHED WITH INDIVIDUAL ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING THE SEVERAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF ANY IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY SET WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AS WELL AS WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT MATTER BELOW; ENLARGED WITH WORKS BOTH DUBIOUS AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH NEVERTHELESS POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY WITH RESPECT TO ECCLESIASTICAL TRADITION; ENRICHED WITH TWO COPIOUS GENERAL INDEXES: ONE, NAMELY, OF SUBJECTS, BY CONSULTING WHICH WHATEVER EACH Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY LEARN WHICH FATHERS HAVE COMMENTED ON EACH SCRIPTURAL TEXT OF EACH BOOK, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS.**

**A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to every other, if one weighs: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the completeness of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the course of the whole work, the modest price, and, above all, this one methodical and chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES, in which are published the Latin Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.** Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the *Universal Clerical Library*, or of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred francs. The strictly Latin edition embraces all authors, Western and Eastern alike; the latter, however, are supplied there in Latin translation alone.

## [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF RUPERT OF DEUTZ]

# Prolegomena

[Col. 0009]

### Michael Pleunich Sends Greetings in the Lord to the Most Illustrious and Highly Esteemed First Associates of This Recent Edition

As I was undertaking this new edition of all the works of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, a man esteemed in every respect, I immediately began to consider whom I should choose as patron: a person distinguished by rank, learning, or piety, under whose protection and powerful guardianship the edition might appear with success and greater security. For I judged that these outstanding studies should be dedicated only to men of the highest distinction.

While I was turning these matters over in my mind, I did not have long to hesitate before deciding. At once I observed that not one person, but all of you—the first associates enrolled for bringing such an edition to completion, men indeed most select—had presented themselves to my mind. Accordingly, because you are marked by excellent gifts, I wished these works, now to be newly printed, to be dedicated to you.

For among you there shine especially certain patricians of this most august Venetian republic, who join to the distinction of their lineage every virtue worthy of a nobleman and learning of every kind. There are likewise men of another rank, to be held in especial honour and esteem, highly skilled in both laws and deservedly awarded the doctoral laurel; they not only devote industrious effort to ensuring that each person receives what is his in an equal balance, but also apply themselves to the finest literary pursuits. Finally, and perhaps not undeservedly to be named first, I see enrolled among the associates men devoted to sacred things, whose approved piety and learning are unknown to no one; indeed, as defenders of ecclesiastical discipline and more serious studies, they commend themselves to every discerning person.

Let it suffice to have indicated these matters merely with a brief pen. For if I had to recount at greater length the merits and illustrious distinctions of each of you, I should both offend the great modesty with which you are adorned and allow my discourse to become excessively long, if not less welcome. If, therefore, I am compelled to yield to your disposition and to brevity, fame nevertheless will not be prevented from making public what you have done so commendably with regard to this edition.

For when Rupert’s works had for many years been desired in Italy, so that they could scarcely, indeed hardly at all, be obtained even at great cost, it was chiefly through your care that they now stand available for anyone to acquire at a more convenient expense, in these our first Venetian—and indeed Italian—impressions. I shall add, moreover, how readily and willingly you gave me assistance, so that the Rupertian volumes might be reprinted as swiftly as possible. This being so, who does not see that you have rendered the commonwealth of letters, and especially myself, the greatest service, and have thereby acquired for yourselves a most honourable name?

These, certainly, were the reasons why I recognized that I was equally obliged to dedicate to you yourselves this new edition, as though claimed by you in a particular right. It remains only, men undoubtedly most illustrious whether collectively or individually, that you receive this dedication—as I earnestly request of you—with that exceptional kindness which is yours, as the surest token of my respect; and that you continue to support me and my labour with your patronage, so that I may increasingly devote myself to the usefulness and advantage of students. Meanwhile, I implore the supreme Divinity to preserve you unharmed unto Nestor’s years.

Given at Venice, from my printing-house, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, 1748.

[Col. 0009]

### The Printer to the Benevolent Reader

[Col. 0009]

Here, most gracious reader, I present to you not an *anticomarita* or an *anagyris*, by whose touch or foul smell you might stain your hands or bring about some deadly result for yourself, but, so to speak, wonderfully fragrant cinnamon: namely, the studies of that most excellent Rupert, Abbot of Deutz. The more you engage in their attentive handling, the more you will perceive yourself inhaling the fragrance of Christian thoughts, and indeed extracting from them the sweetest and most beneficial liquid of holy deeds.

Enjoy, therefore, my labour under favourable auspices. For I restored these works to the press, and shall restore the rest, with no other intention than to provide for your convenience and benefit. As to the publication of Rupert’s complete corpus, I have spoken more than sufficiently in the notice prefixed to this edition concerning its supplement and division, and concerning every other matter required for its skillful completion in my press. Therefore, lest I seem to boil over boiled cabbage, I pass over the recent casting of the type, the choice of paper, and the vigilance of the corrector. It will be for you, friendly reader, to consider whether I have thus far fulfilled the pledge I gave. For my part, I have omitted nothing, nor shall I omit anything, that may make the accomplishment answer to the promises.

I would nevertheless have you know that I have taken our Rupert’s *Dialogue between a Christian and a Jew* from the works of St Anselm, Venetian edition of 1745, at the end of which it is printed; likewise the two books *On the Truly Apostolic Life* and the *History of the Distinguished Monastery of St Lawrence at Liège*, which I have excerpted from the *Anecdota* of the most illustrious Edmond Martène. I have also wished to add his prologues respectively to these studies, since they establish that these are genuine offspring of our Rupert.

All these things, together with the *Apology against the Opponents of Rupert’s Teaching*, composed by Gerberon, a man of the same order, and published at Paris in 1669—since I have at last spoken of the addition of works of this sort, and since I would scruple to deprive anyone of his due praise—I frankly acknowledge, most gracious reader, that, if you consider the supplement and all the other features which render this edition superior to all those already published, the Reverend Father Gregory Cannoni, an Augustinian Hermit, has been my chief author and helper. By the diligence which he possesses, he most willingly gave his service both to enriching it with the aforesaid works and to completing it in every respect. Let this suffice concerning our effort in the matter. Farewell.

[Col. 0011]

# Life of the Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, by John Trithemius

[Col. 0011]

Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne, of the Order of St Benedict, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures through the illumination of the Holy Spirit in a vision, and not ignorant of secular literature, was a monk of St Lawrence’s at Liège. Because of his incredible learning, Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, took him from there and elevated him to be abbot of the monastery of Deutz. He composed many distinguished works.

For from the time when he entered the monastery in his youth, he had exercised himself so much in the sacred Scriptures that even in sleep he seemed unable to rest from meditating upon them, but his tongue and lips moved as though he were reading. Of his works, I have at present found only the following:

To Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, afterwards Bishop of Regensburg:

*On the Victory of the Word of God*, thirteen books: “Recently, when you were a guest …”  
*On Genesis*, nine books: “Whoever, with a faithful soul, while …”  
*On the Song of Songs*, seven books: “He who against a man like himself …”  
*On the Book of Holy Job*, ten books.  
*On the Books of Kings, concerning David*, fifteen books.  
*On the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament*, forty-two books.  
*On the Apocalypse of John*, twelve books: “That you also, O venerable one …”  
*On the Divine Offices*, twelve books: “Those things which through the cycle of the year …”  
*Meditations on the Fire at Deutz*, three books: “See how the accuser …”  
*On the Twelve Minor Prophets*, thirty books.  
*On the Gospel of John*, fourteen books.  
*An Apology of the Same Work*, one book.  
*On the Gospel of Matthew*, eight books.  
*On the Rule of St Benedict*, one book.  
*A Book of Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

Finally, he is reported also to have written many other works, and to have expounded most of the New and Old Testament in many books. Of these, up to the present, we have seen nothing except the works we have listed. He flourished, resplendent in great holiness, learning, and miracles, under Henry V, in the year of the Lord 1124; and he died under Lothair III.

### Epitaph Carved on the Stone of the Monument at Deutz

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1135, ON THE FOURTH DAY BEFORE THE NONES OF MARCH, DIED THE VENERABLE FATHER AND LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF THIS MONASTERY, A MAN MOST LEARNED AND MOST RELIGIOUS, AS IS MOST CLEARLY EVIDENT IN THE BOOKS WHICH HE PUBLISHED.**

[Col. 0011]

# Oration of John, Abbot of Sponheim

Composed at the request of Lord Gerlach of Breitbach, Abbot of Deutz, in praise and commendation of Rupert, formerly Abbot of Deutz, a man most illustrious, devout, and learned.

[Col. 0011A] Most devout brethren, I would most earnestly wish that power of speech had been bestowed upon me from above by which I might celebrate with fitting praises the outstanding merits, most admirable character, and overflowing virtues of your Rupert, former illustrious abbot of this monastery of Deutz. For such and so great a man was he that not merely my eloquence but that of any orator whatsoever must be judged far inferior to his merits.

For if you inquire into holiness of life, he was a most devout man; if into learning, most learned in every field; if into conduct, remarkable for every kind of honourableness. Born of distinguished parents, he shone with a more distinguished faith when, despising the world for the love of God, he subjected himself with great fervour to monastic observances. He preferred, with our lawgiver Benedict, to be wearied by labours for God [Col. 0012A] rather than to be vainly exalted by the favours of this world. For “he could have transgressed, and did not transgress; he could have done evil, and did not do it.” Rather, humbling himself, he followed the Lord; despising worldly pomp, he happily attained, as we trust, the heavenly kingdoms.

Placed in the monastery, he regarded himself as lower than all, though he proved the equal of the holy Fathers. For to those who looked upon him he was an example of honourable conduct, a model of life, and a rule of devotion. When elected abbot of the monastery of Deutz, what sort of man he showed himself to his subjects—how pious, how solicitous, and, where necessary, how stern—what speech could explain? His bearing was dignified, his voice elevated, his speech eloquent, his expression serene, and every movement or action of his body becoming.

With regard to the inward person, however, he was firm in faith, secure in hope, filled with the twofold love, illustrious in wisdom, and strong in courage. He possessed honourableness in action, moderation in habitual conduct, humility in prosperity, and patient constancy in adversity. He was a thoroughly capable shepherd of Christ’s sheep, knowing how appropriately to show himself to all as their ruler. He was gentle and affable, terrible to the proud, a companion through humility to the devout, and formidable through authority to the unruly.

As to himself, he was devout in prayer, profound in meditation, diligent in reading, and exceptional in contemplation of divine things. No one ever found him idle, for his study of the Scriptures was unfailing. He always read, always wrote, always prayed, so that, like a second Origen or Jerome, he had established this order of life for himself: reading should take up prayer, and prayer should conclude reading. So constant indeed was he that he allowed no time, whether by day or by night, to pass for him slothfully or as a holiday, whether in vigils or in study by lamplight [Col. 0013B]; he deprived himself by day of food, sleep, and other bodily necessities in order that he might apply himself more freely to the study of Scripture.

The careful works which he wrote prove this, works in which every kind of learned knowledge is commended. Under him great religious discipline flourished in the monastery of Deutz; the brethren burned with the greatest devotion; zeal for saving knowledge prospered; and twofold love shone forth among them. Under a holy and learned shepherd, integrity triumphed securely.

With incredible fervour he used to kindle his brethren’s zeal for the study of Scripture. He untangled for them questions proposed to him, and gladly encouraged them to pose such questions more frequently. For the wise man knew that a double benefit lay in this: by answering them skillfully, he both showed himself learned and made them eager to learn. Hence, in his daily and familiar conversation, no shameful or useless speech was ever heard, nor was slander ever mixed in; rather, his discourse concerned the salvation of the soul, progress in religious life, and the majesty of the holy Scriptures.

The fellowship of wisdom contained in the sacred writings was most delightful to him. He learned it without pretence and shared it without envy with those who desired it. When he was still less learned both in secular letters and in the divine Scriptures, he continually sought from God, by prayer and reading, the gift of wisdom with Solomon; nor did he cease from the prayer he had begun until, with the Holy Spirit inspiring him through a vision, he received in fullest abundance, beyond all his contemporaries, that which he had desired.

He was a most ardent lover of the blessed Mary ever-Virgin, through whose intercession he is believed to have obtained so great a gift of wisdom. Later, lest he be ungrateful for the benefit, he expounded the Song of Songs in seven books in her praise, referring the whole work to her honour in such a way that it seems especially written with her in view. I myself have found no one else to have laboured over this kind of exposition on the Song of Songs. It is indeed a wonderful and plainly commendable work [Col. 0013D], which, without precedent, rose to so lofty a summit in praise of the virgin Mother of God.

What Rupert was like in observing regular discipline, the book which he composed on the Rule of St Benedict will show when read. For he lived in no other way than that in which, in his exposition of our law, he stated monks ought to live. He was a devout doer of holy speech and a fruitful teacher.

How far he advanced through reading in the divine Scriptures is clearly shown by the thirteen books which he published to Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, *On the Victory of the Word of God*. In these, while traversing the whole of Scripture and subtly opening up the victory of the divine Word, he declared that the rationale of our salvation consists therein. He also wrote the noted excellent work on the Holy Trinity in the Old Testament. If you wish to read it, you will readily see what he could accomplish in the holy Scriptures. For, as we have already said, enlightened by divine mercy, he was so powerful in expounding the Scriptures that, held in the greatest admiration of all, he was publicly recognized in his own day as the teacher of teachers.

Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, repeatedly experienced this in him and cherished the man with great affection. Accordingly, he earnestly urged him to expound the Scriptures. And indeed, with good reason, that man is to be held by all in honour and reverence whom the Holy Spirit deigns to instruct in the knowledge of the Scriptures.

Finally, not only did our sacred interpreter deserve to be enlightened in the divine Scriptures, but he was also found so learned in secular letters that whatever he himself did not know another person might readily be ignorant of. How sweet, ornate, and eloquent he was in speech is confessed by the almost countless books he wrote, when they are consulted. You will readily establish the powers of his intellect and the depth of his learning if you linger even a little in reading what he wrote.

For the force of divine love which burned within him also fashioned words burning outwardly; since, when the mouth speaks from the abundance of a fervent heart, speech rises above ordinary human usage [Col. 0014B] to the heights. The love of God which was aflame in the teacher’s breast allowed no idle or useless word to fall from his mouth. His words, therefore, were fervent, full of reason and usefulness, mature, and worthy of reverence with a certain majestic authority. At times he was pleasant, but never frivolous, since the greatest propriety was apparent in his conduct. He was highly able to persuade, so that even Hortensius would fail by comparison with him; for by his honeyed exhortations he preserved the minds of many brethren in the unity of peace.

His brethren looked upon him as upon an angel living among them, in whom shone the mirror and norm of all religious life. For he presented himself to them in every respect as one to be imitated, knowing that he had undertaken care for them all. He loved and cultivated purity of heart to such an extent that he lamented even the slightest negligences of thought as though they were great ones. Every negligence seemed blameworthy to him, because he aspired to purity of mind. Therefore, to wipe away the stains of sin devoutly, he persisted in earnest prayers, almost with tears.

Mystical sleep was sweet to him in his activity, for, dwelling among the flowers of paradise, he gathered most sweet fruits in prayer. O holy devotion of the man, which never allowed him to be idle! For that he might apply himself more quietly to sacred reading, he shrank from the care of household affairs; he loved seclusion and avoided the tumult of men. He entrusted the management of temporal matters, without which spiritual things cannot endure, to capable brethren, while he himself devoted his time to prayer and study.

For care for temporal things and love of the Scriptures cannot dwell in one breast. Wisdom fills a mind that is tranquil and free from cares, and it will be the guest of a peaceful heart. He himself was serene and gentle, not quickly moved to anger, but mild in heart and well able to overcome wrath. He “sat solitary and lifted himself above himself,” when, fleeing the world, he composed many varied treatises in the field of Scripture. Of his works, so far as our recollection extended, we have already made mention in the second book *On the Illustrious Men of Our Order*.

For, as we have said, he was a man most learned in every respect, subtle in intellect, illustrious in knowledge, sweet in eloquence, and adorned with polished grace. He taught the ignorant, corrected those in error, confuted heretics, and humbled the proud. He was a most admirable lover of virtues and an enemy of vices. In his own conduct he made clear what he loved in others. He detested pride, trampled down avarice, overcame lust, subdued anger, banished hatred, expelled envy, and threw down gluttony. He fixed his heart’s desire in the paradise of the Scriptures, and therefore no access to him was open to vices. For his frequent fasts, repeated mortifications of the flesh, continual prayers, and persistence in vigils extinguished in him the powers of vice.

There was no virtue of which Rupert’s way of life was ignorant. The love of God poured out in him burned; faith flourished; uplifted hope was vigorous; holy prudence shone; and discerning temperance triumphed. [Col. 0015A] He was humble in heart, sweet in speech, loving in affection, vigorous in work, zealous for discipline, chaste in body, peaceful in spirit, constant in prayer, fervent in study, cautious in prudence, exceptional in devotion, and discerning in zeal.

And what need is there for me to run through many things? The day would surely fail me if I wished to enumerate his individual virtues. For his merits exceed my eloquence and easily surpass the powers of my pen. Therefore, although the Church has not enrolled him among the holy Fathers, we nevertheless believe that he celebrates with the saints in heavenly blessedness. Nor are we much troubled by this neglect, because we know that the rewards of holiness are to be granted not in this life but in the life to come. Feasts of saints do not make saints, but demonstrate them. Honours bestowed upon the righteous add nothing to them; they are directed to the benefit of the living. But who could doubt that innumerable saints reign with Christ whose feasts are not celebrated among the living? Their eternal happiness, now possessed, is sufficient for them. Our neglect diminishes it in no way, and bestowed honour increases it in no way.

If, then, a religious life makes saints, Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, should rightly be regarded as a saint: learning made him illustrious and his way of life made him venerable. It is a mark of holiness if he who is honoured is proved righteous by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. Just as of old the blessed Syrian deacon and monk Ephrem was, by a vision of the Holy Spirit, established as a fervent teacher, so our Rupert, priest and abbot, was enlightened by the same gift. Equal virtue deserves equal reward.

We do not say that knowledge of the Scriptures suffices for holiness, for good and evil persons may possess it alike. Rather, we speak of that virtue of love which alone distinguishes the good from the evil. This made Rupert venerable on earth and glorious in heaven. Therefore he is rightly believed holy, since, filled with the twofold love, he both worshipped God with a pure mind and loved his neighbour as himself. He did not labour for himself alone, as many do, but for all who sought truth.

[Col. 0015C] A saint labours when, intent on prayer and contemplation, he does not refuse to teach and form his neighbour. But our Rupert provided for all: he attended both to himself through prayer and to others through teaching. Accordingly, he must be held worthy of double honour, since he took care to rule well. He trained the brethren of this monastery of Deutz so diligently to live in regular observance that, even after his death, the praiseworthy life of the monks there remained for many years.

But as time passed, the devotion of the monks again grew cold, and worldly pomp utterly destroyed holy observance. In that disfigurement many perished miserably for many years, until at last in our own days you arose, venerable Father Gerlach. Setting yourself as a wall before the house of God, you revived the ancient footsteps of the most illustrious Rupert, your predecessor, and brought reform of the order into this place by your ever-watchful care.

Therefore I exhort you and your brethren with all the earnestness I can command: continue laudably the observance that has been introduced, for you shall receive the reward of your labours from him who grants increase to good works. Look upon your Rupert, of whom we speak. So far as possible, hasten to imitate him, who was such and so great a man that by his life he offers examples of virtues to all. What virtue could he lack, when he lived in such a way that not even inquisitive eyes were afforded occasion for detraction? Supreme prudence, supreme religious devotion, and supreme piety shone in him, so that he seemed set before all as an example of how to live.

O venerable man, whose entire way of life was teaching, whose conduct promoted piety no less than his words! The Lord set him over his household and, having entrusted talents to him for holy increase, commanded him to be diligent. Faithfully caring for those committed to him, he invested his Lord’s mystical money for great profit: purified in affection, he extended to the benefit of many the gift of understanding which he had received. For the love of God which he bore in his breast always stirred him to works of mercy.

Love of God is never idle; it accomplishes great things. Burning inwardly in the mind, it gives light outwardly in action. Hence Rupert was never idle from work, because he burned within from love. Great love produced a great fire; with all his desires he thirsted for the salvation of souls. For the prudent man knew that, above all sacrifices, zeal for souls pleased God. He therefore instructed many in righteousness and turned very many away from iniquity. Now, rejoicing in heaven, he receives the reward of his labours. If we desire to attain his glory, we must follow in his footsteps.

[Col. 0015]

# Declamation on Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, Compiled from His Own Books, by Matthias Agricola Witlich

[Col. 0015D] Most gracious hearers, it is an ancient custom to celebrate in speech the praises of illustrious men. For the wise have observed that the proclamation of such praises and the nobility of the persons praised give steadfastness to the high-born and a spur to the sluggish, just as we see that the sound of trumpets makes the minds of valiant soldiers more resolute and rouses the degenerate.

Although, when I recall the most ancient custom of the Greeks, it occurs to me that funeral speeches, or *monodies*, embraced the praises of many brave men who had fallen in battle fighting for altars and hearths; later, by transferred custom, this came to be applied both to others and especially to those who surpassed many persons of their time in the praise of intellect and learning. The Greek orator Lysias, and Cato in his *Origines*, mention this. Certainly, among all nations which extreme barbarism has not divided and turned away from it, the glory of letters has always been noblest in every respect.

There survives an encomium of a certain king of Jerusalem, who said that he would rather lack a diadem than letters; and this has hitherto been an everlasting honour to him. As I was, for particular reasons, rapidly reading some works of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, I confess that the intellect, learning, and piety of so great a man—whose illustrious traces he impressed upon his writings—produced in my mind great, though pleasant, admiration. Therefore I wished in this declamation to trace the course of his life as he himself, by far its most reliable witness, has transmitted it to memory in scattered passages.

Nor shall I here summon your attention, since I know beforehand that all of you will gladly receive with attentive ears the praises of so noble a teacher. I shall proceed, therefore, to the narrative of his history.

What Rupert’s native country was, and what his birth, is equally unknown to me. Trithemius and Cochlaeus, learned men, testify that he was German by nationality. Yet I judge it of little consequence whether you are an Athenian or a Seriphian, provided that you equal your ancestors in virtues, or, if born in an undistinguished position, you illuminate the obscurity of your ancestors by the ornaments of intellect and right actions. For virtue is bounded neither by ancestral portraits nor by the greatness of one’s wealth; it does not disdain the lowly and sordid, but shares the fruit of its splendour equally with all in whom love of labour is discerned.

More persons of obscure birth, it seems to me, have emerged through divine inspiration and the striving of a noble spirit to such glory that no antiquity of time can overwhelm its memory, than persons born of illustrious lineage. Intellectual gifts are judged not by condition of blood and family, but by love of virtue. Well known is that saying of Ausonius concerning the Emperor Severus:

> His origin was Punic, but by his virtue he proved  
> That birthplace does not hinder where talent has strength.

Rupert, then, from his very boyhood was trained in every form of duty and piety in the monastery of St Lawrence near Liège, upon which an impious band of sectarians laid torches two years ago. Under Abbot Berengar he had as instructor Heribrand, a faithful and prudent man. Under him he advanced both in years and in the reception of boyish instruction, as one who pondered that saying of the ancient comic poet:

> “Virtue is the greatest weapon for mortals.”

[Note: [Col. 0017D] See Rupert’s preface to the book *On the Works of the Trinity*.]

Nor could he act otherwise than did those with whom he was joined in the habits of life: they made it their continual concern, in imitation of that heavenly fellowship, to praise God with everlasting praises and to occupy themselves in meditation upon every form of piety. Basil puts it elegantly: “Ascetic practice (*askēsis*) of piety warms the soul with divine thoughts.”

[Col. 0017C] In those times, as in certain earlier ones, it was customary for childhood to be educated in monasteries, especially among those belonging to the Order of St Benedict. From this practice came many men of illustrious memory, among whom are reckoned Boniface, the first Archbishop of Mainz, and Bede, the priest venerable in every respect. Let someone now compare the morals of our youth with that age.

How negligently—not to say impiously—is the education of children conducted in many places! Is not youth infected by the contagion of domestic luxuries? Is it not corrupted by the sweetness of licence and depraved by perversity of character—indeed, I might say, by errors—before it attains either to any maturity of virtue or to maturity of judgment? Who, I ask, could deny that there are just grounds for grief when in our age he has before his eyes, almost everywhere on earth, very many examples of this?

The difficulty later encountered by men of letters in remoulding certain distorted and corrupted minds teaches us this. Of such minds we rightly recall the saying of the most wise poet:

> “A bent piece of wood is never straight.”

For just as white wool never wholly regains its natural colour if it has once been dyed with a foreign colour, so a child’s mind, once corrupted either by depraved habits or by errors, can with the greatest difficulty—or rather can never—be restored to its former innocence. Through all subsequent years there remain marks and certain lineaments impressed upon the unformed tablet.

What shall I say of our Rupert’s youth? Very many things indeed present themselves to be said; but, pressed for time, I must touch upon the more important heads. In no single kind of praise did he flourish. For, as I have said, he embraced piety above all, being led to it by the habits of his household; [Col. 0018A] and by its daily increase he became most devout, for piety, like all other good things, desires to grow through continued progress. Apart from piety, however, there is nothing that can truly satisfy a human being with sweet delight, fortify him with security and the consciousness of an excellent will, or fill him with the abundance and fullness of every good. Piety alone is rightly regarded as the nourishment of the Christian soul, not merely by reason of study and learning; and it alone is truly the life that is lived chiefly in the cultivation of piety and uprightness. This may be seen most beautifully of all in Rupert himself, in the book he entitled *On Piety*.

Thus advancing at a full pace, as the saying goes, he daily equaled the expectation formed of him by the singular praise of an ever more abundant learning joined with piety; and he gladly accepted this refrain sung to him:

> Go, good man, go where your virtue calls you, with propitious step,  
> destined to bear the great rewards of your merits.

[Col. 0018B] That Pauline saying never escaped his eager-to-learn mind: “Attend to yourself and to reading.” He exercised himself in every kind of literature then in use, now turning verse into free prose in order to moderate his style, now binding free prose within the laws of verse. There were also certain small works of poetry, and likewise various odes, which I suspect have perished through the injuries of time. Among these, besides several others, was a poem *On the Holy Spirit*, of which a fragment survives; a *Life of St. Augustine*; a *Life of St. Odilia the Virgin*; and ecclesiastical chants concerning St. Severus the Confessor. In the same work, chapter 26 on Matthew, he testifies that this habit of mind had been so prepared and, as it were, cultivated beforehand for undertaking the exposition of the sacred Scriptures.

Although endowed with the highest intelligence and the strongest memory, he cultivated eloquence more correctly than the others—who were very few, neither devoted to good studies nor sufficiently Latin-speaking. The study of Greek lay wholly neglected; indeed scarcely even its name remained in the schools—an unhappy condition of that age even among Italians. [Col. 0018C] Eloquence had withered away; filth had replaced the native purity of the Roman tongue; and people had ceased to shape discourse according to any settled manner of speaking. What was foul pleased those accustomed to it. And just as, in Cicero’s age, the same brilliant polish, purity, and propriety, everywhere consistent with themselves, shone forth in that rich abundance of writers, so, when Latin had become obsolete, coarseness came to be approved.

Indeed, barbarism was often exchanged for another barbarism. For just as before Tully’s age Latin gradually attained its splendor and native perfection, while in Tully’s flourishing lifetime it was said, by the consensus of the greatest men, to have attained elegance and perfect richness, so from his death onward we find it to have withdrawn and degenerated from its highest brightness into another mode of expression. This happened, as the good writers Tacitus and Suetonius relate, through the idleness of youth, the negligence of parents, and the ignorance of teachers.

Rupert lived in an age wholly barbarous [Col. 0018D] and almost estranged from humane letters. All the more I admire that Rupert’s style is not more corrupted, but rather possesses that praise of gravity and grace to which many in that age did not even dare aspire. Yet I cannot but grieve when I see that, though the finest and most highly praised writers in every kind of learning and language have revived, the industry of many of our people languishes through perversity of judgment.

How few are there who, in this most fortunate age, emulate Rupert’s diligence; who unite poetry with oratorical power through such exertion of talent and labor—and this in an age in which every worthy branch of learning has received its light. In a great multitude of young people, scarcely one or two sufficiently industrious persons are found in both fields.

Rupert struggled with the darkness and gloom of barbarism; [Col. 0019A] with how little sharpness, with how little vigilance, do we behold the light set before us! How few season their speech with native propriety, content merely to have dyed their discourse with any sort of color. Christian poetry is even distasteful to some who ought to enjoy a reputation not only for piety but also for learning. Of some such persons I suspect that they frequently use this verse of the Greek sage—a verse unworthy of a wise man:

> “The works of the Cyprian-born goddess are now dear to me, and those of Dionysus.”

For my part, I judge that the most ancient, holy, and learned Fathers alike drew incredible delight—indeed, a certain blood and vital sap of piety—from poetry, while by no means rejecting the color and brilliance of words. They tasted secular poetry, certainly, but cultivated sacred poetry, whose delight filled their minds. In that age poetry, as it were a torch of inflamed piety, was widely practiced, while ecclesiastical hymns filled the churches with words both meaningful [Col. 0019B] and artfully figured, composed for piety.

Nor should meter be thought to strike the ears with an empty sound alone; for, soothing them by the sweetness of composition, it also generates delight in the soul. As the Greek Theologian says: “The consolations of hymns bestow upon the soul a cheerful and painless condition.” Rupert likewise says beautifully in Book V on the Books of Kings, chapter 23:

> “Music, by a certain natural force and power, moves the human spirit inwardly; and when it fittingly accords with the word or meaning of divine praise, it shakes the inner chambers of the heart and revives within a person that grace of the Spirit of God which he has received.”

The Psalmist, the illustrious chief singer, experienced this most fully when he said: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit.” Augustine too, as Rabanus reports, approves the custom of singing in the Church, so that through the delight of the ears the weaker mind may rise to an affection for piety. Those who can bring to this kind of exercise ears and judgment not untrained know that this is so. The others, as they are remote from the knowledge of poetry, are likewise farther from this spirit. [Col. 0019C] Bede alone, if consulted, will give full confirmation to my words: he was not content merely to compose excellent verses, but also left us useful books on meter.

To this class must be summoned Prudentius, Ambrose, Prosper, Paulinus, Sedulius, Arator, Bede, and the other men surpassing every praise, whose thoughts, devoutly and chastely occupied in this kind of labor, have hitherto brought the richest fruits into Christian society. I shall say nothing of more recent writers, since among them we do not lack persons who have expressed equal grace together with simplicity and piety. Nothing is sweeter, nothing more powerful, than sacred poetry, which every excellent person always prizes as highly as he ought.

There follows manhood, which reminded him of weightier matters. Therefore, leaving behind the studies of the arts and poetry, as though the sinews of his intellect had been exercised, he raised the keenness of his mind to the treatment of the greatest subjects and to the innermost hidden things of heavenly philosophy [Col. 0019D] drawn forth from their depths. Wisely smelling and tasting the lights of the flowers that most sweetly give fragrance and shine in the open, most holy field of theology, and happily delighting the eyes not of bodies but of souls, he was especially accustomed to devote himself to morning vigils and prayers. Bathed in the brightness of light poured down from above, he was wholly fixed upon God, and at times wholly radiant.

When Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, whom he revered as a parent and pursued with every mark of veneration, adjured him, Rupert himself wrote that at night the Holy Spirit had entered him like a fiery globe, surrounded his whole breast with marvelous sweetness, and taken possession of the whole man. Thereafter, in expounding the sacred writings—the wisdom of God—he labored by the shining of a wonderful torch, with both skill and profit. Such, it is said, was his ardor in sacred reading that even his living body could scarcely take rest; his lips too seemed to move, as the day’s studies often recur at night while the limbs rest from labor.

[Col. 0020A] Whenever he observed in others greater gifts of intellect and grace, he mingled the constancy of his prayers with tears, continuing thus until he perceived that a more abundant grace of God had been added to the advancement of his intellect. Returning from prayer, his breast overflowed with such abundance of learning as two or three men could scarcely take down with the swiftest movements of their fingers. Late in life he attained the rank of priest, because of the dissensions of the Roman see, which subsided somewhat after their authors had died, so that it was not sufficiently certain to whom one should adhere in ecclesiastical authority.

Nevertheless Rupert was never seen to rest from the labors he had undertaken, although the arms of Henry IV ranged through Germany. Bound by the pope’s curses, Henry burned with violent hatred of the ecclesiastical order, and at that time no dwelling anywhere was safe either for religion or for the Muses. Yet God willed to deal graciously with Rupert, upon whom the task of writing had been divinely imposed and whom the Spirit of the Lord so often deemed worthy of his inspiration, even when [Col. 0020B] things did not go at all well for others.

Who does not know that it rests in the Lord’s will and goodwill under what condition of life or fortune he wishes each person to live? For to one, even amid the storm and darkness of wars or other calamities, Halcyon days breathe; while upon another the storm itself rushes down upon his head and all his fortunes with great ruin. Most ecclesiastics at that time were in nearly the same cause, though not in the same condition. For it is likely that, just as they differed in counsel and judgment, they also separated into camps and arms, especially when the emperor was attacking ecclesiastical rights.

It happened very advantageously for Rupert that Archbishop Frederick of Cologne, having previously brought him to Deutz because of the outstanding reputation of his name and learning, appointed him, as I find, the tenth abbot of that place. There, amid the disturbance of all things, he himself enjoyed the tranquillity of literary and sweet leisure; and he offered hospitality and shelter to certain others who feared the emperor’s arms resounding everywhere around them. [Col. 0020C] That industrious man (*philoponos*) never rested from the activity of his mind; he always needed time. While he presided over that abbey—and he presided for very many years—he achieved something by reflection, as is characteristic of a learned man, having transferred the management of household affairs to suitable persons. For a mind not equally hindered by external cares offers, or preserves, a resting-place for its guest, the Spirit, when calm, self-possessed, and wholly consistent with itself.

He himself relates that, after deliberation, he resolved to lay aside the anxiety of domestic administration, partly because of the importunity of certain inhabitants who contended against him in litigation and judgment, and partly because he was wearied by those who lived near the monastery on the bank of the Rhine, in dark caves and subterranean corners. They were held to be of insufficient honesty and reputation, because, having leased towers, they disturbed the solitude and leisure both of his literary work and of the whole monastery. It is plain, moreover, that solitude is a sweet and welcome refuge for devout souls, outside which one does not altogether live sufficiently tranquilly and holily.

In a lengthy account, he explained in his writings the whole matter of his grief: first, the very severe grief he drew from a disastrous fire, and then the troubles caused him by these less-than-honest neighbors. [Col. 0020D] Rupert built, lest he should wholly lack a memorial of such events, a chapel dedicated to St. Lawrence at the gate of the castle of Deutz; he regarded that saint’s feast as altogether glorious. Moreover, he left completed with marvelous beauty the choir of the sacred building, raised in vaulting.

Nor was he free from calumniators, by whose attacks he was often assailed. Yet he broke them by greatness of spirit and checked them with the aid of the Holy Spirit, consoling and raising his mind with hope for a more equitable posterity, when, setting aside the dignity or condition of the person, people would judge severely not who had said or written something, but what each had said or written. For he did not fail to know that death hangs over the whole human race at every hour; that the living judge the writings of the living and weigh particulars at times according to favorable or unfavorable standards; yet that judgment will one day be more correct, when, after both parties have died, the generation of descendants has succeeded and, the first leaves having fallen, the green forest has grown up, as St. Jerome says. He himself speaks fully and clearly on these matters in chapters 7 and 26 on Matthew.

[Col. 0021A] His detractors, “boasting grandly and absurdly self-loving” (*megapoiountes kai atopōs philautoi*), gloried magnificently in the excellence of their masters. Conversely, they held Rupert’s teachers in great contempt, looking down upon them with immense arrogance, as men endowed neither with knowledge of sacred Scripture and the liberal arts nor with any celebrated reputation. They implicitly taunted Rupert with either ignorance or ambition: he had received no instruction from any famous academy, but had been bound from childhood in the bonds of monastic discipline; therefore he could not have acquired so great a cultivation of intellect and learning. Yet, besides teachers who were not unlearned, he had the Holy Spirit as witness and encourager of his labors, and he perceived that the presence of that grace [Col. 0021B] could in a single moment breathe into him marvelous and wholly divine gifts both of intellect and learning.

They further cried that he was a heretic, because he had somewhere departed from the determinations of the Catholic Church and twisted or perverted sacred Scripture to suit his own meaning. Then they said that everything was already full of good books and that there was no need for new ones. But he passed by with deaf ears voices that were surely contemptible. [Note: [Col. 0021D] See the preface to the commentary on John.] His conscience, he felt, was unstained by any blemish of such suspicion. He boldly opposed the heretics of that age, especially the Colitians, who proclaimed that God was the author of evil no less than of good; and he taught that such an opinion had long ago been condemned in Augustine’s time, having written booklets on this subject containing a *Panoply* (*Panoplian*) of most powerful arguments. The book *On the Fire* and the preface to the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* mention this.

To his adversaries he gives nearly the same answer that Jerome gave the detractors of his own age: namely, that books written by learned men were certainly abundant [Col. 0021C] and had been, and continued to be, of singular benefit to the use of the Church; but that each person’s gifts—whether gifts of wisdom, knowledge, kinds of tongues, or interpretation of utterances—must, according to the Apostle’s command, be brought forth and communicated with great zeal. The offering of the Old Testament has indeed ceased in the work of the heavenly sanctuary; but it is by no means pious to cease from exercising the graces or charisms which the Holy Spirit distributes to individuals as he wills. He writes this to the Roman pontiff in the letter prefixed to the work *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*.

He himself acknowledges that, in some places, when the violence of his calumniators was raging, he had fully resolved in his mind to stop henceforth writing books, yielding with a hardened mind to the tongues of certain men devoted not so much to eloquence as to slander. Yet his mind remained restless until he turned his thoughts back to his interrupted studies. For it happened at one time that, while he had ceased writing, various colors came over his face; sitting and silently, anxiously pondering many things, he trembled in all his limbs like a pupil under his master’s upraised rod. [Note: [Col. 0021D] See *On the Fire*.] Thus, struck by a divine prompting in a marvelous but terrifying way, he returned to his abandoned writings, recalling the task of writing imposed upon him from heaven and that the saving good of learning, if not made public, could no more be contained in the recesses of his soul than fire shut up in the bones, as the prophet Jeremiah testifies.

Nor was he ignorant that the present grace of the Holy Spirit, which sometimes insinuates itself into our breasts by a perceptible infusion, is by the highest right to be preferred even to the instruction of the most illustrious teachers. Meanwhile, through the providence of God, he was not without powerful men, as it were defensive bulwarks, [Note: [Col. 0022D] See Rupert’s preface to the Twelve Minor Prophets and his commentary on Matthew.] whose authority protected those who esteemed him [Col. 0022A] most illustrious, who were wonderfully captivated by all his words and writings, and who urged him toward the course of most devout studies he had undertaken.

Among these were Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, who had enrolled him among his dependents, and Cuno, abbot and later bishop of Regensburg; while Berengar was still alive, Rupert was, as I find, entrusted to Cuno’s protection. He was certainly one to be revered and embraced, whom the Holy Spirit deemed worthy of so familiar an illumination. Great intellects have scarcely ever lacked patrons; yet we see that great envy has also lain in wait for them after their birth. We ought to be ashamed of our own times, in which nothing is more common than those beasts and monsters seemingly born to revile.

> “We are struck, and with as many blows we wear down the enemy.”  
> —Horace, *Epistles*

Thus it happens that while some sate themselves upon hatred of others, others in turn rob others of the benefit of literary pleasure, which the foremost Roman orator in his *Tusculan Disputations* calls sweetest, and at another point supreme. [Col. 0022B] Yet it is some consolation that savage and brutal envy, moved by a natural sense of shame, generally spares the dead. Beautiful are these verses of Callimachus:

> “All men are terrible toward a man of good repute while he lives, in envying him; but when he has died, then they praise him.”

The hyena knows that it is a foul beast, exercising its cruelty upon corpses buried in the earth. Rupert therefore lives, whose books are in people’s hands. He lives, I say, illustrious in the judgment of posterity, destined to extend his praises to the bounds of the world so long as the Catholic Church stands. We gladly receive his name from pulpits, academies, and every assembly of the devout: he alone most splendidly ennobled the domain of the Church of Agrippina [Cologne]; in his writings nothing appears but what is weighty, holy, and solid; aided by divine grace, he investigated and handed down many things worthy in themselves of being known; he treats the articles [Col. 0022C] of Christian faith sincerely and acutely; and he sets forth ecclesiastical ceremonies with the light of truth placed before them and their veil, as it were, removed, in an explanation that is bare, plain, graceful, and remarkable.

In short, he fulfills every qualification of the perfect theologian; and, like the much-desired Neptune alone when heard, he could calm the storms of opinions raised within the Christian religion. There is no need to speak of secular letters, for we know that he was most devoted to them in youth. In his book *On Knowledge* he calls their fruit now “the arts,” a precious gift of God, now servants or handmaids of theology; and he teaches that other studies, soberly and cautiously employed to assist in expounding the heavenly word, are wonderfully useful.

It remains now to add something concerning his last years and, within the same compass of discourse, to include the kind of illness by which so great a man was extinguished. He attained, indeed, the full age of human life, since he died in extreme old age, his strength exhausted by manifold cares and labors by day and night. When he appeared about to bring the course of his life to an end, in his final year—for he had previously learned through a divine prediction that he would survive another eight years, a prediction of the kind he remembered as having happened to Cassius, bishop of Narnia, according to Pope Gregory in *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 56—he began more earnestly to recall the memory of his past life, to give himself more frequently to tears, and to ask the Lord for pardon of his errors and forgiveness for the sins of his earlier years. In short, he did everything that seemed conducive to wiping away the stains of his soul.

This certainly increased his suspicion of approaching death and at the same time increased his concern for repentance. Nor did the outcome disappoint this expectation. For, in the depth of winter, that excellent old man fell into a most violent fever, which gradually drained the remnants [Col. 0023A] of his strength. Whatever either the long duration of his labors or the weakness of extreme old age had left, the force of illness almost claimed and consumed as its own by right. Thus he most devoutly and peacefully met his day, having acquired the immortal splendor of piety and every praiseworthy virtue. Thereafter he would rest from labors from which he had never been free, and would enjoy through everlasting ages the one he most dearly loved, whom he had longed for both living and dying, whom his writings breathe forth most sweetly, and whose memory no posterity will ever allow to perish from human society, as he deserves.

You have heard in brief, most candid hearers, the life of Lord Rupert, formerly abbot of Deutz. Whoever strives to imitate it to the extent of his powers may, through the cultivation of learning and piety—the most fitting arms of the Christian person—become more fruitful and produce fruits of maturity such as never abandon one, whether living or dead. Some are stimulated by examples from their own household, which we are accustomed gladly to prefer, even when equal in virtue, to those of outsiders; others are summoned to love and cultivate the native splendor of the honorable—a quality belonging especially to gifted minds; [Col. 0023B–0024A] still others are moved by other causes. Fear moves some; the pursuit of ambition moves others; emulation too adds much vigor and ardor to most.

But that learning joined with piety is the noblest distinction has been celebrated in the languages of all peoples, so that there is no one who has not either believed it or observed it. In Rupert we have a supreme example of both learning and piety. His life, once consonant with his learning, was a living image of praiseworthy character. Look again and again upon this model, as painters repeatedly look upon the image they seek to depict with their brush. Strive to imitate him, to represent him; remembering the Apostle exhorting his Timothy to the love of learning and piety in these words: “Attend to yourself and to reading.” And again: “Exercise yourself unto piety. For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but piety is useful for all things, having the promise [Col. 0024B] of the present life and of that which is to come.” I have spoken.

[Col. 0023]

# APOLOGY FOR THE RIGHT REVEREND LORD RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ

In which the defender, Brother Gabriel Gerberon, a Benedictine ascetic in the Congregation of Saint-Maur, demonstrates that Rupert held and wrote concerning eucharistic truth in a Catholic manner. He shows those to be liars who defamed him (Wisdom 10).

[Col. 0023]

# PREFACE

[Col. 0023C] It is the lot of writers to be subjected to the criticism of readers. Very many of these, judging from partiality, do violence to authors by dragging their words into meanings of their own; more read in order to tear them apart with an envious tooth; others are not even sufficiently capable of understanding what they read, yet nevertheless do not dismiss the author without passing judgment.

That lot is indeed harsh; but harsher is the one that often misrepresents a Catholic teacher, so that one who thinks nothing but what is Catholic is called a heretic, and one who has always pursued truth is regarded as a teacher of error.

Most harsh is the lot by which someone, even unwillingly, is dragged over to the party of heretics, so that he is believed to have favored heretics or adopted their opinions; and, as though he had defected from his own side and passed over to strangers, he is deserted by his own people, so that he cannot find among his brethren either patron or defender.

[Col. 0023D] This is Rupert’s most harsh lot. Even while he lived, he could not escape envy, which pursues him all the more fiercely because he is praiseworthy. In his letter to Cuno, abbot of St. Michael at Siegburg, he complains that many people envied his reputation, who, as he says, raged against him not only in word but also in deed. Had every other protection failed, Christ himself would have been present to him and, through Berengar, abbot of St. Lawrence on the public hill of Liège, would have entrusted him to the care of Abbot Cuno [Col. 0024C] as an orphan to a guardian.

For, as Rupert himself writes to that same man, then already bishop, in the prologue to the book *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, many read his works in such a way as to lie in wait for him.

Would you know, then, what reproaches were brought against Rupert by both learned and unlearned people? Learn it from him himself. In order to defend himself and his writings against their calumnies, and to refute their falsehoods and heresies, he wrote an *Apology*, which is the first book of the four he composed on certain chapters of the Rule of St. Benedict. In that book he explains as follows who his adversaries were and what traps they laid for him:

> “The Florinians, named from Florinus, said that God created evils, including the things contrary to virtue. [Col. 0024D] But the men called great masters and teachers, the illustrious lights of all France, to whose lectures swarms of disciples hurried from almost every province, were said to have put forth and steadfastly defended that opinion concerning the will of God. Therefore whatever I said was not merely unheard but was also despised as foolish. [Col. 0025A] So secure were the adversaries—or seemed to be—of the authority of those men, which they thought unanswerable, as though an angel from heaven had spoken to them.
>
> “The wiser among them may in some fashion have been tolerable in speech; but what shall I say of the unlearned rabble of the schools, supporting the adversaries as clerics against a monk, as masters against an unlearned man? I became the subject of their song and a proverb among them. Yet, despising with a hard brow all their song and all their contempt, I went alone in France, riding upon a humble ass, accompanied by only one boy, to contend against such men as I knew would have both speech and intellect at their disposal and great dignity both of office and of teaching. Nor was it lacking—as indeed happened—that a considerable host of masters and disciples assembled to hear me and to convict me.
>
> “But this seems remarkable: when I entered the city, one of the aforesaid men, and the chief of the masters, drawing his last breath, died immediately after my arrival. The other, with whom I had a bitter conflict, I do not know whether he survived a full year. From that time the poison of that dispute ceased; but those against whom I first fought long retained the former hatred they had conceived against me, so that I may say truly: ‘They hated him and could not speak peacefully to him,’” etc.

Let these statements by Rupert suffice, so that everyone may know what adversaries he endured in his earlier studies. But how dishonestly, and with how much envy or ignorance, those who examined Rupert’s writings while he was still alive twisted them into alien meanings and condemned what they did not understand, may be learned from three charges which certain persons dared, with great rashness of their own opinion, to bring against Rupert’s teaching.

First, Rupert says in his *Apology*:

> “One man of good conscience but newly converted, of great name but doubtful reputation; already a prelate and preacher, but almost never a subject or a hearer, familiarly asked me, as if for the sake of reading, to lend him something from my little works. I lent him the little work *On the Divine Offices*. He received it, went away, read as much and for as long as he wished, and after many days returned the book, saying and asking nothing good or bad.
>
> “But then, after several days, I heard—and many reported to me, while learned brethren were even sent to me from foreign cities to ask—whether the report widely spread far and near about me was true: namely, that I had said and written that the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary. I shuddered, I confess, and, fortified by the shield of conscience, diligently sought who could be the author of such a rumor. Why say more? After a long search, I finally learned through certain of our companions that the author of this accusation—indeed, this false accusation—was the man whom I have mentioned, and that he had wickedly seized upon these words from the book I had lent him, in the Office for the fourth Sunday of the Lord’s Advent:
>
> ‘For who can investigate how the Word is embodied, how [Col. 0026A] the supreme and life-giving Spirit is animated within the womb of the Mother, how he who has no beginning both comes into being and is conceived?’
>
> “But what did that man bring forth from the face of this Word? How did he believe that he had exposed it as poor? How did he wish to overturn it? He proclaimed the book heretical and deserving to be burned in flames. He did this among the unlearned, who followed and listened to him; and, as men of this sort commonly do in divine and secular matters, showing almost greater zeal than learned people, they became excessively hostile to the book and hurried even to seize it for burning.”

Who would not cry out at this: O blind envy, O envious blindness, which proclaims not Rupert but Gregory the Great in Rupert a heretic, and which condemns as heretical words that are Gregory’s, though it regards them as Rupert’s! He who writes that the Word, the supreme and life-giving Spirit, is animated—what, I ask, does he either write or teach that is heretical? He who worships the Word as the supreme Spirit, what does he think except what is Catholic? But one who reads, “the Word, the supreme and life-giving Spirit, is animated,” and says that he has read that the third Person of the supreme Trinity was incarnate—what has he said but a calumny, and what has he revealed but either his ignorance or his envy?

The second charge by which they wished to stain Rupert as with a heretical blot was that he had said angels were created out of darkness. Yet Rupert fearlessly defended this as consonant with the canonical Scriptures and with Book II of St. Augustine’s *City of God*. Thirdly, they dared with still bolder spirit to criticize Rupert because, as it seemed to them, he had written in a novel sense that Christ did not offer his body to Judas at the Supper, since Judas had departed before the consecration of this sacrament. They had Augustine’s authority readily at hand for asserting that Christ gave his body to Judas the traitor.

The necessity of this argument compelled Rupert to say that Augustine should not be accepted in every respect as the canonical books are accepted. Thus, where holy teachers—although certainly agreeing in the faith—differ in some opinion, one may not lend a consenting ear to that teacher whose opinion one knows to be less strongly confirmed by the testimony of canonical Scripture. And, as he says near the end of his *Apology*, they then began to defame him as a heretic for this very reason. But the authority of St. Hilary raised up the man whom the judgment of St. Augustine seemed to have crushed; for that judgment of Rupert’s is Hilary’s, though when Rupert wrote it, he did not know that he agreed with St. Hilary in this matter.

From these three instances, I think, you have more than sufficiently demonstrated how violently hostile they were to Rupert through envy: they rashly condemned in his writings whatever did not please them, so far as not to hesitate to misrepresent his meaning, even when plain and plainly Catholic, and to judge it heretical.

Rupert endured these things and yet did not yield to them. But after death he suffers harsher things, while the Sacramentarian heretics violently drag him over to their side. Not only is he not defended by his own people; he is more unjustly condemned as though he had held heretical views.

[Col. 0027A] But I, though least of all, when I recognized that my master in doctrine and father by profession was enduring these most harsh wrongs unjustly and without redress, have firmly resolved to exert whatever strength is in me for his most just defense.

> Nor will God fail this cause: charity urges us to undertake it; truth gives us arms to defend it; and justice promises aid.

Therefore, God giving courage—for he is charity—Christ favoring—for he is truth—and he himself presiding who is justice, I shall endeavor according to my strength to defend Rupert, master of much learning, profound humility, and supreme piety; glory of Germany and honor of the Benedictine Order; and above all champion of eucharistic truth, from those errors against the Eucharist which some say he anticipated in advance of the Wycliffites, Lutherans, and Calvinists. [Col. 0027B]

I know well that very many people who believe errors are defended when those to whom they are attributed are heard to be vindicated will receive this sort of dissertation with a more hostile mind, as though it served not so much to defend the writer as the error.

Yet let anyone who has learned wisdom in good time rather than late judge how unjust that objection is. Such a person knows that the vindication of a Catholic writer from error is the highest condemnation of the error itself, and that consequently error is not affirmed but most strongly condemned when the defense of a Catholic writer from error is undertaken.

Moreover, anyone of sound judgment understands that he shares responsibility for a calumny who, hearing an accusation brought against the reputation of a brother whom he knows innocent, remains cowardly silent. Such a person will deem this complaint wholly unjust—the complaint, perhaps, of one who has zeal but not knowledge. And whoever has learned that it is the more humane duty to ward off another’s injury will regard the murmurings of such objectors as entirely lacking in duty. They not only violate equity and offend against duty, but also suppress truth by tearing its defenders away from it; or at least they divide the unity of faith, by not preventing Catholic Fathers from being torn away from the mind, and therefore the bosom, of the Church.

Would not the purer innocence of Christians have been sullied, shaken by the taunts of unbelievers, had it not been vindicated by the Apologies of Justin, Minucius, Tertullian, and others? Would not Dionysius of Alexandria, fighting for the Catholic faith against the heresies of the Sabellians, have been drawn over to Arius’s side, unless Athanasius, holding his see and faith [Col. 0027D], had stoutly defended him as nowhere deviating from the Catholic faith? Would not Gregory Thaumaturgus likewise have borne the reputation of Arian perfidy, had Basil not erased that false designation through his vindication of him? Would not [Col. 0028A] the faith of Cyril of Alexandria likewise have been condemned along with Eutychian dogmas, unless those who condemned Nestorius’s inventions had defended him? Would not Augustine himself have been charged by otherwise pious and learned men with founding the predestinarian heresy and, by establishing Christ’s grace, with destroying human freedom, unless Prosper, acting as patron of his own master, had refuted the charges made against this holy doctor by the Semi-Pelagians? Thus truth, no less than virtue, as it either lies hidden or withers away without an adversary, so fails without a defender—who himself often needs another’s defense, lest he who stood for truth be believed to have fought against truth.

Therefore, disregarding this complaint of those less devoted to truth, I approach to defend the faith of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, concerning the body and blood of Christ in the sacrament of the altar—a faith of which he was a most vigorous champion—with that zeal for truth, that consideration of duty, and that rule of equity by which Prosper defended Augustine, very many defended Cyril, [Col. 0028B] Basil defended Gregory, Athanasius Dionysius, and Tertullian, Minucius, and Justin defended the conduct of the faithful. And, lest I proceed rashly and without order, in the first part I shall set forth the works composed by Rupert, the spirit in which he wrote them, and the manner in which he interpreted Holy Scripture. In the second part I shall expound the four errors attributed to him: namely, the merely figurative presence of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament, taught by the Wycliffites; eating by faith, which the Calvinists teach in some sense; impanation, maintained by the Lutherans; and the hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word, for which scarcely [Col. 0028C] anyone has argued. Thereafter I shall clear Rupert of the first of these errors, then vindicate him from the second, afterward defend him from the third, and finally demonstrate that he was wholly free from the fourth.

But if anyone is less pleased by historical than by dogmatic controversies, and finds burdensome or unsuitable the critical examination of Rupert’s works introduced here—which we nevertheless judged it necessary to preface because of the celebrated controversy among theologians themselves concerning the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*, on whose testimony Rupert’s cause chiefly rests—let him readily pass it over.

I would also have the reader warned here that I sometimes designate Rupert in this work [Col. 0028D] by the title of sanctity, not in my own voice but in that of the whole order, or rather of the Church; for approved writers record him in catalogues of saints as illustrious for the merit of holiness and the power of miracles. [Note: [Col. 0027D] Molanus, in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Belgium*; and Surius, under 3 March; the *Memorial of Benedictine Martyrs*, with Menard’s observations, on the same day, 3 March. Likewise the Benedictine *Menologium*, where it reads: [Col. 0028D] “On the same day, the heavenly birthday of St Rupert, Abbot of Deutz,” etc., for 3 March; and Arnaldus of Wion, Book V of the *Tree of Life*.] Let envy, then, be far from the name.

## SYNOPSIS OF THE APOLOGY FOR RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ

[Col. 0029]

[Col. 0029A] This Rupert, or Robert, whose Apology I write, devoted himself to the Rule of our holy father Benedict under Berengar, abbot, in the monastery of St Lawrence on the Public Mount of Liège, or, as others prefer, Leodium. There, devoting his whole self religiously to exercises of piety and to the study of sacred doctrine, he was chosen as abbot of the monastery of Deutz, or Divitia, on the Rhine opposite Cologne. He flourished until the year of restored salvation 1135, when, full of merits, he attained the eternal fruits of blessed life. I divide the Apology of that holy abbot into two parts.

The first part contains a critical examination of Rupert’s works. The second vindicates him from the errors imputed to him.

In Part I I show students which books Rupert wrote, in what order, and at what age; [Col. 0029B] and I provide a complete catalogue of his writings.

Accordingly, the various catalogues of that holy doctor’s works, published by several persons and by himself, are corrected: namely, the three which Rupert himself compiled; one supplied by Trithemius; one composed by Reynerus; one constructed by Sixtus of Siena; one cited by Bellarmine; one set down by the Centuriators; and one found in the latest Paris edition. To these may be added the lists of Rupert’s books published by Possevino in the *Apparatus*, Valerius Andreas in the *Bibliotheca Belgica*, Fr Labbe in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and others; these too must be corrected from the most accurate catalogue which we provide there.

There also we lament that certain books of venerable Rupert [Col. 0029C] are missing from the printed editions: namely, the little book *On the Diverse Meanings of Scripture*; the little book *Of Unrhymed Discourse*; *On the Condition of the Monastery of St Lawrence on the Mount of Liège*; and so forth; a Sapphic poem on the same subject; a *Life of St Augustine*; a *Life of St Odila the Virgin*; songs concerning St Theobald the Martyr, and the confessors Goar and Severus; *On the Books of Kings, concerning King David*; *The Ring*, or *Dialogue of a Christian and a Jew*; and the letter beginning *Meditatus* (“Having reflected”), which in the Cologne edition is prefixed to the Commentaries on John’s Gospel, and which we there advise should be restored in the other editions.

There also I demonstrate briefly but certainly that Bellarmine spoke less than truthfully when he said that Rupert’s works had lain for about four hundred years, without honor and light, in the darkness of oblivion, and that [Col. 0029D] Rupert’s errors had caused them to remain hidden during that period.

After this I address the celebrated controversy concerning the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*. I exclude Valeramnus—whether of Attenberg or of Naumburg—to whom Waldensis, [Col. 0030A] Alanus, Vasquez, and certain others attributed that work, from every claim; and I establish it with several titles as certainly belonging to Rupert alone, Abbot of Deutz.

For we do not judge that the letter “I read and reread,” etc., was proved by John Picard and Theophilus Raynaud to have been written by Anselm; rather, we hold that it was sent by William of St Thierry—not to any one of the several Valeramni whom we have identified around the times of Anselm and Rupert, but to Rupert, then a monk of St Lawrence at Liège. Nor does John of Paris, of the Order of Preachers, who about 1304 wrote a determination concerning the manner in which Christ’s body is in the sacrament—a work which I have read in its entirety—make any mention of any Valeramnus, as Vasquez invented; he merely sets before himself the aforesaid letter under Anselm’s name.

We close this first part of the Apology with the divine illuminations [Col. 0030B] through which Rupert obtained an understanding of Holy Scripture infused from above. Yet we do not thereby imply that his natural talent was duller; we show that this is an unfounded fiction of those who wrote less carefully about Rupert.

I begin the second part of the Apology with an enumeration of the errors which critics have more unfairly attached to Rupert of Deutz: among heterodox writers, M. Claudius, Albertinus, and others; among Catholics, Bellarmine, Vasquez, and others. These are: a shadowy or merely figurative presence of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar; the true eating of Christ’s body at the Lord’s table only by faith; [Col. 0030C] impanation of Christ’s body; and, lastly, the hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father.

Having set these out, I prove that our man of Deutz was generally free from every error against the truths of the Eucharist: first, from the testimonies of distinguished writers who praised Rupert’s faith and learning while removing every suspicion of any error whatsoever; and above all from John Cochlaeus, a most vigorous opponent of the Lutherans, who would neither have published nor praised in these times—when they were attacking the mystery of the Eucharist more violently—those works of Rupert which had anticipated Lutheran or Calvinist errors.

Then I argue from the fact that his enemies, raging against Rupert and reading his writings in order to catch him in his speech, [Col. 0030D] never accused him anywhere of any of these errors. Yet in that period more ardent and inquisitive disputes concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist were being stirred up, disputes which would have carefully examined even the slightest shadow of error had any been discovered in Rupert’s writings.

Afterward I vindicate Rupert more explicitly from each of these errors. Hence, in the following dissertation: [Col. 0031A]

I demonstrate most conclusively that Rupert nowhere thought or taught that in the Eucharist there is nothing but a figure of Christ’s body and blood; indeed, that he opposed this error and championed, against the Berengarians, the real existence of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine.

First, from Rupert’s own works, namely the books *On the Divine Offices*, in which his opponents themselves seem to find this error. For in that work, explaining the words “he was carried in his own hands,” Rupert affirms the reality of the body and blood in the sacrament of the altar, which he there calls, with great piety, a testimony of humility [Col. 0031B] and charity.
