There he also distinguishes the truth of the thing from the figures of the Old Testament, as a thing from its sign; and the man of Deutz states most expressly that Christ, promised and prefigured in the Old Testament, is here presented in His presence, **NOT IN SHADOW, BUT IN TRUTH; NOT IN FIGURE, BUT IN REALITY**. There he also rebukes those who, murmuring against the reality of Christ’s body and blood on the altar, said: “How can this be?”

There he teaches that by that Testament Christ assigns to his heirs the treasure of his body and blood, and so forth.

He teaches that, when the priest says, “The peace of the Lord,” etc., he immerses a particle of the victim in the sacred blood. [Col. 0031C] He teaches that, after the cross has been saluted, two priests carry to the altar the Lord’s body, the body of the Lord. He teaches that the blood which we receive cries to God from our mouth. He teaches that through the food of his body and the drink of his blood Christ procures life and preservation for the souls of his children. Certainly neither Berengarians, Wycliffites, nor Calvinists would say these things.

Second, from Rupert’s other books I vindicate his Catholic faith concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine.

From Book VI on John, chapter 6, where Rupert explains the error of the Shadow-men (*Umbratici*), who maintained that bread and wine are no more Christ’s body and blood on the altar than the manna which the Jewish people ate, or the water drawn from the rock, which [Col. 0031D] not only the people but also the beasts drank.

There the man of Deutz explains the Apostle’s words, “They all ate the same spiritual food, and they all drank the same spiritual drink”; he declares that all these things happened as figures, and at the same time determines that a figure is nowhere equivalent to the very thing which it figures, just as a shadow is not the same as the substance of the thing or body itself.

There he shows how Augustine’s statement that Christ’s words, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” etc., are figurative language, must be understood—namely, in such a manner that nothing whatsoever is detracted from the reality of Christ’s flesh and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

There he firmly establishes the real and true existence of Christ’s body and blood under the outward species of bread and wine [Col. 0032A] from Christ’s words, who expressly says: “This is my body, which shall be delivered up for you. And do you dare to say that it is something other than Christ’s body? If this is not the body that is delivered up for you, Truth has lied to itself.”

In the same place our man of Deutz states that the carnal and merely natural person cannot receive Christ’s flesh and blood, because nothing changes in the outward species of bread and wine. He playfully refutes this by the analogy of a certain Moor who, through the power of baptism, is made from a son of the devil into a son of God, though the outward blackness of his body is not changed. Amid these remarks Rupert says that the mass of the damned is the body of the devil, and the Church Christ’s body—but not that body which is made on the altar.

Again, in the same place, [Col. 0032B] the man of Deutz explains the Apostolic words “they all eat the same food,” on which the Shadow-men thought they rested their error, in a sense wholly different from that of the Berengarians, Wycliffites, and Calvinists: that is, according to the Catholic reality of Christ’s body on the altar.

Against them he sets Blessed Ambrose, teaching that what we make is the body from the Virgin, etc., and that the flesh which we receive is true flesh. He also sets against them Blessed Augustine, who interpreted the Psalmist’s words, “he was carried in his own hands,” as referring to Christ’s own body, which Christ gave to his disciples at the supper.

Finally, Rupert judges that nothing is to be added to or taken away from Christ’s words, “This is my body; this is my blood.”

And although Christ’s words, “I am the vine,” are understood as spoken by way of comparison [Col. 0032C], the holy doctor shows that these words, “This is my body; this is my blood,” must be understood literally. In accordance with this, he sincerely and Catholicly professes that bread and wine, after the Father has marked them through the hands of the Church, are Christ’s body and blood.

Rupert also elucidates from the mystery of the divine Word in flesh the manner in which bread becomes Christ’s body which hung on the cross, and wine becomes that blood which Christ poured forth from his side. After much discussion he says that the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, so that that which then hung on the cross and that which the faith of the Church makes with a sacred mouth are one body—one flesh, I say, and one blood.

[Col. 0032D] Moreover, the proposition drawn from Augustine’s statements—namely, that to eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood is to remain in the unity of faith—Rupert accepted in such a way that he would by no means allow the real eating of that body to be excluded. Indeed, he affirms more firmly that bread once consecrated never afterward ceases to be Christ’s flesh, and that, in order to give eternal life to the living persons who eat it, Christ transforms bread into his flesh.

Finally, from the words added by Christ himself—“This is my body, which shall be delivered up for you; this is my blood, which shall be shed for many”—he unhesitatingly confesses in that book that we eat not just any body, nor Christ’s body which is the Church, but the Lord’s body which was delivered up for us; [Col. 0033A] and that we drink that blood which was poured out for us.

In the following little book, Rupert restrains those same objectors who say: “If this bread is Christ not figuratively but in reality, then Christ suffers daily and dies as often as this bread is broken in commemoration,” by the example of Abraham sacrificing Isaac in the ram, while nevertheless preserving the distinction between figure and truth.

Furthermore, the man of Deutz interprets these words objected by the Shadow-men from the Apostle—“the flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life”—so that Christ’s flesh is eaten not alone, or dead, after the manner of the flesh of beasts, but together with his Spirit; nor should we suppose that the flesh or blood in the bread or cup is lifeless.

[Col. 0033B] Having scattered these objections of the Shadow-men, Rupert boldly declares that the true body of Christ is sacrificed, broken, and eaten on the altar. And he concludes this book, which he had undertaken in defense of Eucharistic truth against heretics, with this confession: “So far as we were able, with God’s help, we have taken care to demonstrate, from the Lamb’s own bleating—that is, from Christ’s own words—that he is the true and living Lamb of God.”

After adducing these statements of Rupert from his books on John, from which it is clear how Catholicly he maintained and taught the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist, I produce the same author’s letter beginning *Meditatus* (“Having reflected”), which is found in the Cologne edition.

In it he declares that the heresy of the Berengarians was the belief that in the mystery of the altar there is only a figure, sign, or image of Christ’s body and blood. [Col. 0033C] He declares that in his own age scarcely anyone dared openly to profess or defend this error.

He declares that the whole Church knew that in this sacrament there are Christ’s true body and true blood, and that he had exerted himself wholly for this truth in his books on John, to which this letter is customarily prefixed.

In it he expressly teaches that the Eucharistic sacrament is Christ’s body and blood in three ways: in name, in reality, and in effect; but that it differs in a fourth respect, namely in outward appearance.

From the book *On the Works of the Holy Spirit* [Col. 0033D] I have brought forward precisely the same distinction, by which I convict as false M. Claudius’s invention that the holy Fathers, according to Rupert, understood in the sacrament of the Eucharist only the name and the effect or power of Christ’s body and blood. Furthermore, our man of Deutz contrasts the devil’s deceitful promise, “If you eat, you will be like gods,” with Christ’s promise, “He who eats this bread shall live for ever”; and he calls that food the food of life, the food and drink by which divinity is truly communicated, the effective flesh and blood of Christ.

He further writes that this gift which is offered is a true, holy, and immaculate sacrifice, a life-giving body, and the true blood of the brother to whom you have been reconciled.

He also writes that, since Judas went out before Christ instituted the supper of the New [Col. 0034A] Testament, Christ gave him not his body but a morsel of bread dipped in liquid.

He writes that the mystery of the Eucharist is a great trial of faith.

He writes that, in order that God might test faith, the outward appearance of bread and wine remains.

He writes that Christ gives not something merely his own, but his flesh and his blood.

He writes that at the Supper Christ took ordinary bread, but by blessing transformed it far into something other than it had been, so that he could truly say: “This is my body, which shall be delivered up for you.” Likewise, he took the substance of wine, but there, by giving thanks or blessing—giving thanks and blessing being the same—he changed it into something else, [Col. 0034B] so that Truth, which does not lie, could say: “This is my blood, which shall be shed for many.”

Finally, he writes that for our salvation it suffices, and accords with our use, that Christ’s flesh and blood in the sacrament of the altar be neither seen by the eyes of the flesh nor perceived by the taste of the mouth.

There he also teaches that Christ worked remission of sins and eternal life on the cross for all the elect who came before; and that in the sacrament of the altar he undoubtedly grants remission of sins and eternal life also to all the elect who come to faith in him after that same Passion.

In another chapter of the same book Rupert explains what is sacrament and what is the reality of the sacrament, and what understanding Augustine’s distinction should have.

[Col. 0034C] And there again he opposes Christ’s words, truly promising, to the devil’s words, wickedly equivocating.

Therefore, as Rupert says, this sacrament must be believed to contain what is not seen: namely, the reality of flesh and blood capable of making us one body with the only-begotten Son of God.

We seal this faith of Rupert with three miracles of Christ’s body, which we recount from him. Thus we defend Rupert’s doctrine from the figures of the Shadow-men.

The second error, namely the eating of Christ’s body by faith, is excluded from venerable Rupert.

At the outset we state who have accused our [Col. 0034D] man of Deutz of this error.

And we distinguish a fourfold eating of Christ’s body by faith. The Church approves the first and fourth; it condemns the second and third: both in the sense of those who said that Christ’s body is not in the sacrament except when it is actually contemplated; and in the sense of those who maintained that indeed the whole bread is changed into Christ’s body by the mystical prayer, but withdraws from its species when the sacrament is received by the unworthy; and in the sense of those who impiously taught that the portion of bread which God foreknew would be distributed to sacrilegious persons is not changed into Christ’s body.

To repel these errors from venerable Rupert, we make it plain that this holy doctor truly [Col. 0035A] thought and Catholicly taught that Christ’s body is eaten even by the unworthy.

As an invincible argument for this Catholic faith of the Abbot of Deutz, I adduce the most explicit words of this Catholic writer.

For Rupert expressed most distinctly:

> “No one can eat unworthily, but no one ought to eat unworthily.
>
> “Bread once consecrated never afterward loses the power of sanctification or ceases to be Christ’s flesh; but it profits the unworthy person nothing.
>
> “A person whose faith without works is dead does not possess the life-giving Spirit by whom he may receive with his mouth; but earth eats earth—that is, Christ’s flesh which is from our earth—without the life-giving Spirit of divinity [Col. 0035B].
>
> “Christ’s body is received by the unworthy in such a way that it is nevertheless not subject to excretion, contrary to the stercoranists.
>
> “The worthy person has more than the unworthy: to the former it profits for salvation, to the latter for judgment; and the fatness of divine power withdraws from the latter because of his sins.”

Rupert likewise explains Augustine’s distinction between sacrament and the reality of the sacrament so that Christ’s true flesh is truly received orally, even by the unworthy, however sacrilegious the mouth may be, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “He shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.”

“For,” Rupert says, “his unworthiness could not evacuate the dignity of so great a consecration. But [Col. 0035C] because in mind, and by faith working through love—who here does not tremble?—he does not regard Christ’s Passion, he therefore does not obtain the effect of that sacrament.”

With Rupert’s faith thus immovably established, we refute by answering the one point objected by Bellarmine.

Our man of Deutz did indeed say that “to one in whom faith is absent, nothing of the sacrifice comes except the visible species of bread and wine,” etc.

But I show that Rupert says the same thing as Augustine, when he says that one who is at discord with Christ does not eat his flesh or drink his blood, even though he daily receives the sacrament of so great a thing to the judgment of his own destruction.

Thus the manifest meaning of Augustine and Rupert [Col. 0035D] is that one who is at discord with Christ, or in whom faith is absent, receives no fruit of Christ’s flesh, and is not nourished by Christ’s flesh.

Indeed, at this point the holy doctor of Deutz teaches with great piety of faith that, for one who does not possess faith working through love, Christ’s body in the sacrament is neither sanctification, nor truth, nor peace, but death, destruction, condemnation, and judgment.

With the same faith and piety I have set forth Rupert’s statement that one who, by not believing, drives away invisible bread from his heart kills Christ, because he separates life from life-giving power. As it were dead, lacking the life-giving Spirit, he tears with his teeth the body of the sacrifice. [Col. 0036A] He grinds Christ’s body, lean—that is, without the fatness of power—with his teeth; and thereby becomes guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

I further give another interpretation of such words of Rupert: namely, that for one who does not believe Christ’s body to be in the sacrament, there is certainly nothing other than bread and wine at the Lord’s table; and that person receives from the altar only bread and wine in that faith—or rather, in that error.

Thus Rupert emerges free from the error of eating by faith.

I now undertake the third dissertation of the Apology, in which:

## I Vindicate Rupert of Deutz from the Error of Impanation

I demonstrate that he thought and taught a true conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s [Col. 0036B] body and blood, which we now call transubstantiation. I establish this Catholic doctrine of Rupert from three considerations:

1. From Rupert’s most explicit words and statements by which he expresses it.
2. From Rupert’s complete agreement with ecclesiastical writers.
3. From the genuine, clear, and Catholic exposition of passages which appear somewhat obscure in Rupert.

To proceed to the first: I candidly set forth the very explicit words of the Abbot of Deutz by which he declares this faith of his and defends this doctrine.

First, from the dedicatory letter to the books on John’s Gospel, which he testifies that he wrote against the Berengarians in defense of Eucharistic truth. There he says: “Let us believe the faithful Savior God concerning that which we do not see: namely, that bread and wine have passed into the true substance of body and blood.”

Then, from Book VI itself on John, where, rejecting figuration, he says that bread is converted by divine power into the true substance of Christ’s body; that this visible bread and wine, although nothing has changed in their outward appearance, have passed into something else and have been converted into that food and drink which is the sustenance of angels.

He says that bread becomes that flesh of Christ which was fastened to the cross, and wine becomes that blood of Christ which was shed for many; that the Word changes earthly bread into his flesh. [Col. 0036D]

Then, from Rupert’s Commentaries on Exodus, where in several places he again teaches that bread and wine become, their outward appearance remaining unchanged, transferred into the true substance of Christ’s body and blood.

Finally, there he teaches that God, the creator of substances and species, does not effect this merely on the surface, but efficaciously converts bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood, although the outward species remains.

Then, from that Catholic writer’s books *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*. There he openly declares that Christ took ordinary bread, but by blessing transformed it far into something other than it had been, so that [Col. 0037A] he could truly say: “This is my body, which shall be delivered up for you”; that the bread became Christ’s flesh and the wine was changed into blood. Whoever doubts this is charged with Jewish unbelief.

From these passages we refute M. Claudius’s assertion that no testimony of that author can be produced from which it must necessarily be understood that he taught transubstantiation—as though transubstantiation were anything other than the transformation of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood. How many times our man of Deutz expressed this in the most distinct terms will be judged by a reader who loves fairness and truth.

The second basis by which we clear this holy doctor of the error of impanation is his complete harmony with Eucharistic truth.

[Col. 0037B] For concerning this conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, which we believe from ecclesiastical tradition, I show that Rupert spoke precisely as Tertullian, Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Cyril of Alexandria, Hesychius, Euthymius, Isidore, Bede, and others discussed it; indeed, precisely as Paschasius, Lanfranc, Guitmund, Alger, and the other defenders of that truth spoke after disputes had arisen concerning this Eucharistic transformation.

Third and finally, I set forth this rule of Christian justice, by which anyone ought to interpret Scriptures and writers otherwise Catholic:

What seem harsher must be tempered by what is milder; and what is obscure must be explained from what is evident.

According to this rule of Catholic truth, I illuminate by a clear and Catholic explanation those words of Rupert which, if understood too harshly or obscurely, have seemed to some to contain the error of impanation.

1. I show in what sound sense our man of Deutz said that in this mystery the Word is in the bread: namely, because the sacrament of the Eucharist, as we learn from the Apostle and Christ himself, retains the name “bread” as well as its outward appearance; and because it comes from bread. Thus a woman, formed from bone, is called “bone” in the Scriptures; even elementary dialecticians know that words or names sometimes stand in a transferred sense.

2. I make clear, with an intervening explanation, in what sound sense the holy abbot wrote [Col. 0037D] that the Word joins bread with his flesh and wine with his blood, and that, intervening between bread and wine, he makes one sacrifice.

For it is made altogether plain there that Rupert, in this and many other passages, taught nothing other than that the Word joins bread and wine with that flesh and blood which he assumed from the Virgin’s womb—by changing them into that flesh and blood which, together with the flesh and blood to which he was hypostatically united in the Virgin’s womb, are one flesh and one blood. And from the unity of the divine Word, who assumes bread and wine on the altar in such a way that he converts them into the substance of flesh and blood, Rupert manifestly demonstrates [Col. 0038A] the unity of the flesh and blood which the operation of the Holy Spirit makes from bread and wine with that flesh and blood which, when the Holy Spirit overshadowed her, the same Word of the Father formed for himself from the most pure blood of blessed Mary. For that divine Word has only one flesh and only one blood.

Therefore, in this sense he says that the Word, intervening between bread and wine to be changed into flesh and blood, makes one sacrifice; that is, as he explains himself elsewhere several times, the unity of the Word makes the sacrifice one, by making the flesh offered on the altar, the flesh consecrated on the altar, and the flesh immolated on the cross the flesh of the divine Word, whose flesh is one only.

[Col. 0038B] Whoever grasps this meaning of Rupert discovers no trace of impanation in his entire doctrine.

Moreover, I show that in that place Rupert in no way thought that the substance of bread remains in the sacrament, from his words there declaring that nothing of the sacrifice reaches one who receives the sacrament with a sacrilegious mouth except the visible species of bread.

3. Rupert is proved to have said Catholicly that after consecration the fivefold sign of the cross is impressed on the substance of bread and wine—namely, as he says, on that which has been made one body with Christ sitting at the Father’s right hand; that is, changed into the flesh of Christ which is one flesh with that flesh of Christ that sits at God’s right hand.

4. Our man of Deutz, who in so many pages [Col. 0038C] wrote that bread and wine are turned, converted, transformed, and changed into that flesh of Christ which was suspended on the cross, and into that blood of Christ which was shed for us, while the outward appearance of bread and wine remains, must be understood in a correct and Catholic sense when he says that the substance of bread and wine is not changed or destroyed—not, indeed, in itself, but, as he himself explains, according to its outward appearance as apprehended by the five senses.

Furthermore, from this holy doctor’s statement we rightly infer, from the very phrase “or destroyed,” that he denies only a destructive change, not a perfective change.

Thus we convict M. Claudius of falsehood when he says that Rupert [Col. 0038D] overthrew the mystery of transubstantiation.

After this I present Gregory of Valencia’s judgment, by which he declares that the Abbot of Deutz erred in principles of philosophy, not of theology or faith.

To correct this singular judgment of Gregory, I show that Rupert investigated and attained the deeper secrets of natural science. There I briefly explain what that most learned abbot knew concerning the first cause, the first subject, the first principles of things, transformations, accidental and substantial properties, configurations, modes, and so forth.

Since critics violently twist into the sense of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father the statements which we have adduced in Rupert’s vindication, statements by which this holy doctor sincerely [Col. 0039A] professed that bread and wine truly become and are transformed into Christ’s body and blood, and attribute this corrupt meaning to Rupert, I therefore defend, in the final dissertation of this Apology:

## I Defend Rupert from the Error of the Hypostatic Union of Bread and Wine with the Divine Word in the Sacrament of the Altar

In the preliminaries of this dissertation I propose these two points, in which rests the sum of our faith concerning the venerable sacrament of Christ’s body and blood:

1. That under the outward species of bread and wine there is truly not merely a figure of the Lord’s body and blood, but the reality itself.
2. That the substance of bread and wine is converted and transformed into Christ’s flesh and [Col. 0039B] blood.

Then I explain the meaning, date, origin, and course of that error, namely hypostatic impanation.

I plainly convict as false the tale of Albertinus and others who trace this error back to earlier centuries. Since I prove from the clearest testimonies of Guitmund and Alger that the impiety of this error arose only at the end of the eleventh or the beginning of the twelfth century, I incidentally vindicate Anastasius of Sinai, Germanus of Constantinople, Nicephorus, and others of an earlier age from the accusation of hypostatic impanation, against the inventions of Albertinus and others of the same stamp. After these preliminaries I clear our Rupert of Deutz from the absurd [Col. 0039C] novelty of that perversity by the force of multiple arguments.

The complete argument concerning Rupert’s faith which I offer is this: no Catholic writer, from the more ancient down to the later centuries, marked Rupert’s faith with this error, although from Rupert’s own time—and indeed in the age of that holy doctor himself—many Catholics defended the Catholic truths concerning the Eucharist against every novelty of error.

Here Alger, while attacking this new—as he himself calls it—and absurd heresy of hypostatic companation, is plainly shown, against Bellarmine’s observation, to be describing not Rupert but other authors of that error. Moreover, Bellarmine has nothing [Col. 0039D] from which he can reasonably infer that Alger is indicating an ecclesiastical writer.

Especially because the opinions by which Alger writes that the innovators explain and defend this impiety are found in none of Rupert’s works; nor does Alger adduce any of those propositions which we read in Rupert’s books and which critics now mark out.

Here too one must note the falsehood of what Vasquez reports from Waldensis: that this error of Rupert’s was refuted by John of Paris, theologian of the Order of Preachers. For although John of Paris attempts to defend the common opinion of the Church—that the substance of bread and wine so passes over and is converted into Christ’s flesh and blood that the substance of bread and wine does not remain—he holds that this is not a matter of faith; instead, he maintains as probable another mode, namely, that bread is so united to Christ’s body and, through that body, to the Word of God, that it is called Christ’s body. But nowhere does he mention Rupert, nor anywhere refute a hypostatic union, without any intermediary, of the divine Word with the substance of bread and wine, as though that had been Rupert’s position. Indeed, although that John of Paris draws into his own meaning all those who expressed the mode of transmutation through an assumption or union of the Word, nevertheless he nowhere adduces Rupert’s words or opinions. Let the reader observe this and judge by what right our man of Tuitiensis is accused, and even condemned, of this error by Vasquez and others.

Nor can M. Claude infer from the determination of John of Paris, Master in Theology, [Col. 0040A] that even in the fourteenth century—namely in the year 1304 from the restoration of salvation, when that determination is noted by the continuator of Nangis as written or at least published—doctors had not yet held as an article of faith that the substance of bread and wine remains in the sacrament.

For this very determination of John of Paris utterly destroys M. Claude’s argument. It holds and defends as of faith the real and true existence of Christ’s flesh in the Eucharist; and its title expressly declares that it introduces a mode by which Christ’s body exists in the sacrament of the altar, other than the one held by the Church. This heading, to speak with the canonists, conforms to the text.

Nor is M. Claude helped by the fact that Masters in Theology are said to have approved the mode of this determination as probable. For the continuator of Nangis, whose History I have before me and who was writing it in that same year, expressly relates that the other doctors of theology, apart from John of Paris, maintained the contrary: first, they asserted that the first mode—the one held by the Church—must necessarily be maintained as determined by the Church, especially through the decretal *Extra, De summa Trinitate et fide catholica*, chapter *Firmiter credimus*; secondly, they deservedly rejected the other mode introduced by John as discordant with the truth of faith. Hence, when Brother John would not retract what he had said, but seemed rather to maintain it obstinately, perpetual silence was imposed upon him under penalty of excommunication by William, bishop of Paris, [Col. 0040D] on the advice of Brother Giles, bishop of Bourges, an eminent theologian; Master Bertrand of Saint-Denis, an outstanding doctor; the bishop of Orléans; William, bishop of Albi; doctors of canon law; and lords specially summoned for this purpose. He himself was deprived of lecturing and preaching.

I have set these things down in summary, lest I omit what, because I had not yet read it in the manuscripts, I omitted in the *Apology*. I return to its arguments.

The second argument by which I most strongly maintain Rupert’s doctrine to be free from hypostatic impanation is this: his ardent opponents, who carefully read his writings in order to proclaim heretical, with an unjuster censure, whatever might offer even a shadow of any error, conceived from Rupert’s works not even the slightest suspicion of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word. [Col. 0041A]

Those understand the weight of this argument who know whom envy spares, and who have learned from our earlier discourse what zeal Rupert’s rivals displayed at the time when questions concerning the sacrament of the Eucharist were being raised.

The third argument by which I judge Rupert’s doctrine should be defended from the blasphemy of hypostatic companation is this: the abbot of Tuitiensis dedicated all his works, with congratulations, to the bishop of Regensburg, the archbishop of Cologne, the legate of the Apostolic See, and even the Roman pontiff himself. With what face could even the most imprudent man have done this if he had previously taught, in so many passages censured by the critics, this new and absurd heresy of hypostatic impanation, at a time [Col. 0041B] when the Apostolic See watched with the greatest concern for the eradication of errors opposed to Eucharistic truths and the suppression of novelties? The Church never accepts such blasphemies; rather, it refutes every novelty as soon as it arises, as we observe from Facundus.

The fourth defence of Rupert from this perversity is that the perpetual sense of the Church forbids those words of the Tuitiensis—by which he declares that bread and wine, through the mystical prayer, become and are, in name, reality, and effect, Christ’s flesh and blood; and that bread and wine are turned, converted, changed, and transmuted into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, not into a person or hypostasis—to be understood in the sense of hypostatic union [Col. 0041C] or communication of properties. Otherwise the whole tradition would collapse, since he always expressed that sacrament in the same words as Scripture and Catholic writers. The rules of grammar forbid it; the laws of dialectic forbid it, as I plainly demonstrate.

The fifth clearing of Rupert from this error is that, in all the passages from which they freely condemn the Tuitiensis for that hypostatic companation, he nowhere expresses it; indeed, he illustrates and explains Eucharistic truth in precisely the same words, propositions, and comparisons by which the holy Fathers clearly expounded and constantly affirmed it.

And lest I seem to deceive, I set forth all these passages of Rupert [Col. 0041D] in full and with sincere fidelity.

For their explanation—since some are difficult—I here set down two chief doctrines handed on to us by the holy Fathers for establishing the truth of that sacrament.

1. Christ’s flesh and blood, which are made upon the altar from bread and wine through the Church’s consecration, are that very flesh which was fastened to the cross, and that blood of Christ which was poured out for many on the altar of the cross; so that Christ’s flesh is one and his blood is one, and the ground of that indivisible unity is the very unity of the Word. This is taught by Gregory of Nyssa, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Damascene, Remigius, and Alcuin.

Accordingly, I show that the Tuitiensis follows their words and thought: in the passages adduced against him, from the unity of the divine [Col. 0042A] Word he does not argue that Christ’s body has a severed existence in the sacrament of the altar, but more expressly proves that the flesh made from bread and wine and that which the Word assumed from the Virgin are one flesh of Christ. Whoever observes this has the clearest understanding of all Rupert’s passages.

There also I note the differing statements of Catholic Fathers concerning Christ’s body in the sacrament, though their sense of faith is one.

Some say that Christ’s body on the altar differs in appearance from that which sits in glory; others say that it is the very body formed from the Virgin’s blood, and yet is not the same according to appearance and certain qualities; others call it the type, likeness, image, and figure of that body, namely in remembrance of the bloody sacrifice; others say that this body is visible and seen, tangible and touched, broken and ground by the teeth; while others say that Christ’s body is one and the same, not one thing and another. And this body which is in the sacrament is invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, by reason of its manner of existence under mystical species. Though these expressions differ in sound, I reconcile them briefly in one understanding of one faith.

The second point which I offer from the holy Fathers for a fuller and clearer understanding of Rupert is this: I observe that the unbloody sacrifice of the altar and the dread sacrament are compared by the holy Doctors in many respects with the ineffable and adorable mystery of the Incarnation; especially in this: that, just as the unity of the Word constitutes the unity [Col. 0042C] of Christ, who is a divine mixture from two natures, so the unity of the Word makes the sacrifice one, so that the body pierced on the wood and that daily offered on the altar are one.

Above all, I show that our Tuitiensis, in the testimonies alleged against his faith, thought and taught this with Catholic writers, even against their will.

And indeed, in the first of the passages objected, taken from book II of *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 2, I show Rupert, in accordance with the mind of the holy Fathers, to have taught three things:

1. That the Word of God, by the same divine power by which he assumed our flesh from the Virgin, undertakes to transform bread and wine into his body and blood.

2. That Christ’s body which individual priests make, whether at different times or at the same time, is one; and that the flesh offered on the altar and that hung upon the cross are one flesh of Christ.

3. That the ground of that indivisible unity of Christ’s flesh is the very unity of the divine Word, since one divine Word has only one body or one flesh.

In the second, third, and fourth passages likewise Rupert is shown to have understood nothing else than that the unity of the divine Word makes the sacrifice one. And it is evident from other Fathers that the words “is joined,” “is joined together,” and “is united,” which Rupert sometimes says of the body on the altar, do not at all harm this interpretation of the Tuitiensis.

[Col. 0043A] There also I prove, even against the obstinate by rules of dialectic, that these words of Rupert and of other holy Fathers—“bread becomes and is Christ’s body,” “bread is transmuted into Christ’s flesh,” and similar expressions—cannot bear the sense of hypostatic union.

I then explain Rupert’s fifth passage in such a way that no one can fail to see that there the Tuitiensis defends the reality of Christ’s body in the Eucharist and explains the manner in which Christ’s body is broken on the altar without suffering or dying. I acknowledge that this may be understood in a twofold sense, but both senses are Catholic.

There also I maintain, from Chrysostom’s teaching and Berengar’s own Catholic confession, that the statements “Christ’s body is broken on the altar” contain nothing foreign to the faith. [Col. 0043B]

Finally, I explain again here that, in the sixth passage, Rupert understood the substance of bread and wine to remain unchanged in the sacrament not in itself, but according to its outward appearance, apprehended by the five senses; and that our Tuitiensis denied only a destructive, not a perfective, change to the operation of the Holy Spirit.

Why Rupert so often teaches and proves that Christ’s body—the one which the faith of the Church brings about through the sacred utterance—is the same body delivered to death for us, or that bread and wine are converted into that very flesh fastened to the cross, I infer from two considerations:

1. In Rupert’s time some said that bread and wine were changed into the body indeed of the Son of Man, of some just and holy person, but not of Christ—thus in some manner reviving Nestorius’s doctrine.

2. Some Catholic writers, even doctors, as has already been observed, had sometimes stated that the body consecrated on the altar by mystical prayer was, in certain respects, not that very same body which once hung upon the cross. Rupert could not tolerate these expressions as insufficiently consonant with Eucharistic truth.

[Col. 0044B] Thus I present the venerable Rupert as cleared of every charge of error against the Catholic truths of the Eucharistic sacrament: namely, of the merely shadowy figure of the Umbratici; of the Calvinists’ eating by faith; of the Lutherans’ impanation; and of the mediated or immediate hypostatic union of bread and wine defended by John of Paris, who alone is known by name to have defended it as not at all contrary to Catholic faith. I show them to be liars who have stained him (Wisdom 10).

## FIRST PART OF THE APOLOGY FOR RUPERT, ABBOT OF TUITIENSIS, WHOSE WORKS THE DEFENDER ENUMERATES

[Col. 0043C] Rupert, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict in the monastery of Saint Lawrence on the Public Mount of Liège, born not so much for his own benefit as for that of the Christian commonwealth, wrote very many works which instruct faith, advance hope, and kindle charity. While not yet a priest but still young, Rupert wrote a little book of hymns in praise of the Holy Spirit. The first was Sapphic and began: “To the great river”; he himself transcribes it in full in book XII on Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. The other was iambic and is printed in full at the end of book XIII on Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*; it begins: “My God and Lord, you are, O Holy Spirit.” Whether this little book contained other hymns, I neither know nor have been able to discover. One thing I know: this little book was the first [Col. 0043D] utterance Rupert sent forth after the inundation, but not yet full of the river of the Holy Spirit; for he did not obtain its fullness until he received the grace of the priesthood. He says these things of himself in the cited twelfth book.

At the same age he wrote a book *On Various Opinions of Scripture*, which I take to have been merely a collection of various opinions drawn from Holy Scripture, since he did not apply himself to expounding Holy Scripture [Col. 0044C] until, after becoming a priest of Christ—whose mouth is sought for wisdom—he himself received the lawful opening of his mouth for treating the sacred Scriptures according to ecclesiastical custom. He says this in the cited twelfth book on Matthew. Reiner, in his book *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Saint Lawrence*, where he relates Rupert’s life and works, agrees.

Rupert added to this little book a heroic poem *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, as Reiner writes in the passage cited. Hence I too should judge that this poem was published by Rupert when, still young and wishing to gird himself, he proposed to undertake a work bearing that title, invited by a heavenly voice, as he himself relates in the prologue to his books on the *Song of Songs*:

> “This purpose,” he says, of writing on the Incarnation of the Lord, “has not now newly come upon me. [Col. 0044D] Some years ago, when I was young, I wished to gird myself and undertake a work bearing that title, namely, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, on this occasion: I speak before the Queen of Heaven; I ought not to be mocked by any fellow-servant of mine saying, ‘Behold, a dreamer.’ I sat as though alone in a vision by night, and behold, something like the whisper of a gentle breeze, passing through both ears more swiftly than could be told, placed these verses within me:

> [Col. 0045A] A woman conceived God in her mind, Christ in her body.  
> Whole and inviolate, she brought him forth, with no man acting.

> “When I returned to myself and pondered in my mind the verses thus received, and told certain persons privately, not without amazement, whence or how I had received them; and when the verses had come to the knowledge of many, although they did not know whence I had received them, then among the many diverse things I heard an occasion was afforded me to desire to write something on the Incarnation of the Lord, undertaking a great burden upon weak shoulders.”

These are Rupert’s words in the prologue to the book on the *Song of Songs*.

Since, therefore, this occasion gave Rupert the intention of writing on the Incarnation of the Lord, it is not unreasonable to think that this heroic poem was composed by him on the same occasion—especially since it can be thought to have been written at no other age or on any other occasion more suitably.

While young Rupert was engaged in these pursuits, he described in one little book the condition of his monastery of Saint Lawrence, from the episcopal seat of Heraclius of Liège to Ogbert. He also wrote a *Life of Saint Augustine* and a *Life of Saint Odilia, Virgin*. Since none of these works now survives and nothing concerning them is found in Rupert, I report them solely on Reiner’s authority.

Meanwhile Rupert, knowing that in the house of God no one takes honour to himself unless called by God, did not dare approach the sacred order of priesthood. Both out of reverence for the priesthood and because of the grave discord of the schism—namely, between Paschal, Roman pontiff, and Guibert, the antipope, whom certain German bishops and Emperor Henry III himself [Col. 0045C] favoured—he humbly and peaceably withdrew from it. He did so until at length that long discord which vexed Christ’s Church had somewhat subsided through the death of its authors, namely Guibert the antipope, who relinquished both pontificate and life in the year 1100, and Emperor Henry III, who laid down sceptre and life in 1106.

Then, one night, as Rupert was contemplating eternal day, Christ crucified infused into his innermost mouth, by a kiss, such love for the priestly office that, as soon as day came, Rupert told his spiritual Father that he no longer wished to resist but wished, as soon as he should be commanded, to take up the Lord’s yoke—though he kept silent about the vision which had occurred. And so, when the time for ordination first arrived, Rupert received this sacred order.

But scarcely thirty days had passed after receiving the order when, behold, so great a flooding force of divine love suddenly entered Rupert’s mind that thereafter he opened his mouth and, when writing, could not cease; nor, even if he wished, could he keep silence. Rupert himself relates all this of himself, having been adjured by Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, in book XII *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.

The first word which Rupert’s heart, full of the divine Spirit, poured forth, and which his mouth opened by the Lord [Col. 0046A] uttered, expounded the divine offices and produced chants concerning the saints. For under Abbot Berengar, in the year 1111 from the restoration of salvation—when Henry IV entered Rome peaceably—he published twelve books *On the Divine Offices*, which he himself calls the first-fruits of the produce of his land, to which the Lord has given blessing.

> **Note:** [Col. 0045D] See book VIII, *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 4.  
> **Note:** [Col. 0045D] Baronius, under this year.  
> **Note:** [Col. 0045D] Book I *On the Rule*, and in the letter to Bishop Cuno, [Col. 0046D] beginning “First-fruits.”

A serious controversy concerning the author of these books *On the Divine Offices*, raised by many writers of distinction, should be decided here. But lest this dispute disturb the sequence of Rupert’s works, I shall more suitably state my opinion on this matter after Rupert’s works have been enumerated; that opinion will readily be understood from what has already been set down in Rupert’s favour.

What dispute is there concerning Rupert’s chants, which I have heard attributed to no one and which, so far as I know, Reiner alone heard? For he writes that Rupert, already anointed priest of the Lord, composed chants concerning Saint Theobald the martyr and Saints Goar and Severus, confessors. Yet I neither despise nor reject them.

After this Rupert compiled a *Commentariolum*, [Note: [Col. 0046D] Rupert, bishop, in the cited “First-fruits.”] abridged into ten books on Job from the abundance of thought and language in Saint Gregory. I think this is none other than Rupert’s own Commentary on the forty-two chapters of Job, which now survives in the editions divided likewise into forty-two chapters. Thus I judge that only the division of this Commentary was changed by copyists, who thought it more convenient to fit the chapters of those books severally to the chapters of the Book of Job, [Col. 0046C] abandoning the division into books.

I am moved to this judgment, first, because no other Commentaries on Job by Rupert appear either in the editions or in catalogues of his works. Secondly and especially, because this Commentary now divided into forty-two chapters can most aptly be called an abridgment of the thoughts and statements of Saint Gregory. Whoever compares this work of Rupert with Saint Gregory’s *Morals on Job* will discover it to be composed from Gregory’s words and opinions.

I judge that this Commentary was arranged after the books *On the Divine Offices*. Since I could neither learn nor infer its order from any source, I could not justly deny it the first place after the books *On the Divine Offices*, which Rupert assigned it among his works.

> **Note:** [Col. 0046D] See the cited letter.

If this place belongs to another work, I gladly yield it. Let us proceed with the rest.

Rupert, still under Abbot Berengar, not yet entrusted to the care of Cuno or Conon, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael at Siegburg, and not yet known to him, applied himself to the books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works* about the year 1114. Since, however, he completed that work only after three years had elapsed, I shall speak of it below. It is sufficient here to note that they were begun [Col. 0047A] under Abbot Berengar, indeed about the year 1114.

I infer the first point because Rupert himself asserts that he undertook this work before he was known to Cuno, to whose protection, he writes in his letter to Abbot Cuno beginning “To Every Faithful Soul,” he was entrusted after Berengar’s death. This letter is prefixed to the books *On the Trinity*. I infer the second because he spent three years on them and, in 1117, offered them when completed to Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, now under obedience to Abbot Heribrand, Berengar’s successor, as he testifies in the same letter.

I judge that Rupert’s work *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works* extended over three years because it was interrupted by various controversies which diverted Rupert’s studies elsewhere. [Col. 0047B]

First, Rupert heard one of his own brethren professing that he had learned in the schools of William, bishop of Châlons, and Anselm, dean of Laon—who were then flourishing in Gaul—that God so wills evil opposed to virtue that Adam’s transgression resulted from the divine will. Inflamed with zeal for the faith, Rupert wrote to William of Châlons and Anselm of Laon a little book *On the Will of God*. In it, having very keenly explained the distinction between God’s permitting and approving will, he wisely demonstrates that God does not will evil contrary to virtue.

Yet with this little book Rupert did not restrain the minds of those holding the opposite view; rather, he stirred up their hostility against himself so greatly that, raging against Rupert as though he diminished God’s omnipotence, they freely judged, more insolently accused, and more unjustly condemned him as one too wise in his own eyes and departing from the opinions of the holy Fathers, especially Saint Augustine.

To repel this calumny, Rupert wrote to G. and A. another little book, *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, in which he proves more fully that God does not will what is evil, and that many things therefore happen which God does not will, yet without any detriment to God’s omnipotence. These matters may be learned from the prologues to those books. From them it is also established, first, that these books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God* were not published by Rupert before 1113; [Col. 0047D] for William of Châlons, to whom he first wrote, was not made bishop before that year, when his predecessor died.

Secondly, they were not issued until after 1114 and after the work *On the Holy Trinity* had been begun. For the prologue to the book *On Omnipotence* proves that at least the second book was published under Abbot Heribrand. Heribrand succeeded Berengar, as Rupert himself relates in his letter to Abbot Cuno beginning “To Every Faithful Soul.” But Berengar did not die until after Rupert had undertaken the work *On the Holy Trinity*, toward the end of 1114. For, as I have already noted above, three years before 1117, when Rupert completed the books *On the Holy Trinity*, and while he was still under Abbot Berengar—that is, before Rupert came to Cuno’s notice through Berengar’s recommendation—Rupert had girded himself for this work *On the Holy Trinity*.

Thirdly, finally, Rupert expressly declares in the dedicatory letter to his Commentary on John, beginning “Having Meditated,” that these books appeared before Rupert’s Commentary on John. The letter is found in the Cologne edition but absent from the Paris edition. In it he says that he had already written the apologetic books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*. [Col. 0048A]

At this time, after publishing the books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, but before completing the work *On the Holy Trinity*, and therefore before 1117, Rupert completed fourteen books of Commentary on John. Their principal purpose was to defend the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar against those who, following Berengar’s errors, contended that the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is merely a figure of a sacred reality, wresting Saint Augustine’s words into a bad sense. This is stated in the cited letter beginning “Having Meditated,” which expressly declares that Rupert had already written the apologetic books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, and plainly indicates that these Commentaries on John are later than those books.

But you may be certain that they are earlier than the completed forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, both from Rupert’s own catalogues in book I on the Rule of Saint Benedict and in the letter to Bishop Cuno, “First-fruits”; from Reiner’s aforementioned book; from Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Rupert; and especially from Rupert’s third book *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, which is the thirty-sixth of the forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity*, chapter 25 at the end. There Rupert compares the serpent’s words deceiving our first parents, “You shall not die, but shall be as gods,” with Christ’s promises, “Whoever eats this bread shall live for ever,” and says: [Col. 0048C]

> “But we have spoken more fully concerning these things in another work; therefore we refrain from saying more now.”

By these words he plainly indicates the sixth book of the Commentary on John, since in no work other than that sixth book does Rupert more fully expound the serpent’s promises and Christ’s promises concerning Christ’s body and its eating, as anyone may easily discover through attentive and repeated reading of Rupert. Moreover, whoever notices there the three modes of being according to which Rupert, in chapter 21 of that third book *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, asserts that the sacrament of the altar is truly Christ’s body and blood—namely in name, reality, and effect—and finds them distinctly expounded there, will judge it a most welcome and useful repetition of what he wrote in the dedicatory letter of these Commentaries.

In book I and book IV on the *Song of Songs*, Rupert compares at sufficient length Christ’s true promises with the serpent’s deceitful promises and applies them to eating Christ’s body. But, as we shall say below, the books on the *Song of Songs* had not yet appeared when he composed this third book *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*. [Col. 0049A]

Having completed these Commentaries on John, Rupert in the year of salvation 1117, in the seventh indiction, completed the work *On the Holy Trinity*, begun three years earlier, in forty-two books. Bringing it before the public, he dedicated and offered it to Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, by the letter “To Every Faithful Soul,” from which we too have obtained these details. Thus, in these three years, Rupert composed, with an understanding of Holy Scripture wholly divine: two apologetic little books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*; fourteen books of Commentary on the Gospel of John; and forty-two books *On the Trinity [Col. 0049B] and Its Works*, in which all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden.

In this same year 1117, when disputes in Gaul about the will and omnipotence of God were at their height, Rupert, riding a paltry little ass, as he himself relates in book I on the Rule of Saint Benedict, accompanied by one boy, went to France to enter into a disputational battle against the most renowned masters of sacred theology. One was at once master and bishop, William of Châlons; the other, Anselm of Laon, was more famous than any bishop though he was not a bishop.

Rupert came; and when he came, he conquered. From that time the dispute, extinguished or suppressed, fell silent, and the masters yielded sufficiently. One, namely William, died in that same year 1117, as soon as Rupert arrived; the other, with whom Rupert had a bitter conflict, scarcely survived an entire year. All marvel that Rupert, sitting upon an ass, entered the city with a boy to subdue doctors and confound the wise and learned in the law; and all proclaim him triumphant with the applause due to truth.

Yet to pursue the glory of this triumph belongs not to a defender but to one acting as historian. It is enough to observe that these events occurred in this year: William, bishop of Châlons—whom Rupert undoubtedly designates in the cited passage on the Rule of Saint Benedict by the title “master and bishop”—entered the way of all flesh in 1117.

> **Note:** [Col. 0049D] *Gallia Christiana.*

And Anselm of Laon—whom Rupert there calls not a bishop but more famous than any bishop—is reported by the very writers of *Gallia Christiana* to have died in 1119, namely one year, as Rupert says, after the conflict.

> **Note:** [Col. 0050D] The cited book on the Rule.

Those writers therefore should, without any qualification of doubt, have assigned his death to 1119.

After this, Rupert became known to Frederick, who, according to the *Chronicon Magnum*, was made archbishop of Cologne in 1099 and governed that church for thirty-three years. This occurred through the efforts of Abbot Cuno [Col. 0050A] of Siegburg, who, while Frederick listened, proposed certain chapters of the Apocalypse to Rupert, so that from Rupert’s ready exposition it might become evident to Frederick that Rupert could usefully add something beyond what the earlier Fathers had thought and said in expounding this book.

Moreover, Cuno strongly urged Rupert to undertake an exposition of this book and did not cease his persuasion until, pressing Rupert’s reluctant mind with earnest prayers, he brought him to write twelve books on the Apocalypse, which he dedicated to Frederick, primate of Cologne. Rupert relates these things in the prologue to those books and in the prologue to the second book, though with much humility concerning himself and gratitude of heart toward Cuno, “who,” he says, “thought more highly of me.”

John Cochlaeus offers no less celebrated a judgment concerning these books of Rupert. In his letter to Henry, abbot of Tuitiensis, in 1526, after praising Rupert’s works in these terms:

> “This author is such and so great that he not only instructs the reader by knowledge but also kindles him to piety and prepares him for holiness of life: an ornament of Germany, a truly solid doctor, who may not undeservedly be compared with every one of the ancients, both Greek and Latin, in the elucidation of the sacred writings,”

he especially commends him for his exposition of the Apocalypse:

> “For who,” Cochlaeus adds, “among all writers has written more diligently, lucidly, and copiously on the Gospel and Apocalypse of John? Who has weighed every word thus? Who has so explained and fortified all things from the Scriptures?”

Finally, he concludes the praise of this exposition in few words:

> “On the Apocalypse he far surpassed all the commentaries of everyone.”

After accomplishing these works, Rupert, now almost asleep, was roused by Cuno, Father of the monastery of Siegburg, who began to press him opportunely and importunately to expound the *Song of Songs* concerning the Incarnation of the Lord. At Cuno’s insistent wishes, Rupert’s mind recalled the purpose of writing on the Incarnation of the Lord which he had conceived while young, on the occasion when he composed, as we said above, the heroic poem *On the Incarnation of the Lord*.

A further circumstance occurring about the same time also moved him: a certain brother, of innocent, pure, and simple understanding, told him that he had seen the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, sitting upon his altar, with a company of saints about him, and Rupert standing near in peace, holding the *Song of Songs*. Encouraged by all this, Rupert undertook the task of such magnitude and successfully completed it in seven books. Rupert’s prologue to those books has taught me all these things.

But at what time these books were written I find nowhere, hear from no one, and infer from no source. Therefore, not daring to determine that point, I shall offer only my conjectures, drawn from certain indications.

First, that these books were composed by Rupert after the books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works* is suggested by the fact that, in their prologue, and especially at the beginning of Book Four, Rupert confesses that the Blessed Virgin spoke with him concerning the glory of the Trinity. This most likely occurred while he was describing the glory of the Holy Trinity and its works in those twenty-four books.

Second, it is beyond all doubt that Rupert wrote on the *Song of Songs* before he put the finishing hand to the books on Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. This is clear both from Book Twelve of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, near its end, where he mentions the books on the *Song of Songs*; and from Rupert’s letter to Bishop Cuno, beginning *Firstfruits*, where he counts among the works dedicated to him his books on the *Song of Songs*. Yet there he declares that he had brought the work *On the Glory of the Son of Man* only as far as Book Eight, though he later completed it in Book Thirteen. It is also clear because, while he was explaining the *Song of Songs*, he had not yet disclosed his secret concerning the heavenly gift, except privately to Cuno; nevertheless, when Cuno adjured him, he openly revealed it in that Book Twelve of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.

Third, no one will deny that Rupert published these books on the *Song of Songs* before he had even set his first hand to the books on Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. For in the prologue to the *Song of Songs*, Cuno—at whose urging this work was undertaken—is designated only as “Father of the monastery of Siegburg” (*Cuno pater coenobii Sigebergensis*). But in the prologue even to the first books on Matthew, this same Cuno is described as “the venerable former abbot of the monastery of Siegburg, but now bishop of the church of Regensburg.” From this it is entirely evident that Rupert explained the *Song of Songs* while Cuno was still abbot; whereas he began and completed Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, after Cuno had become bishop, and thus after the year 1126, in which, according to Dodechin in the appendix to Marianus Scotus, he was placed at the head of the Church of Regensburg.

Nor should you be troubled by the fact that Rupert writes in Book Eight on Matthew that Cuno, the head of the household of the monastery of Siegburg, was indeed the first to urge this work *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. For what does this prove except that Cuno, while he governed the monastery of Siegburg, had already induced Rupert to write on the glory of the Son of Man—a task which he did not undertake until Cuno was bishop, as the prologue to these books plainly testifies. There is therefore no reason to doubt that the books *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, on the *Song of Songs*, are earlier in date than the books on Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, since they appeared before even the plan of the latter had been conceived.

It is useful to add that, if the books on the *Song of Songs* had interrupted the work on Matthew, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, once it had already begun, Rupert would not have been silent about this in the chapter of Book Eight in which he endeavours to set forth the reasons why, at Cuno’s prompting, he had left the work begun at Book Seven. Yet he makes no mention at all of books of this sort. Finally, that Rupert was induced by Cuno, while the latter was still abbot, to treat the Incarnation in the *Song of Songs*, and that Rupert composed this work before beginning the books *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, is evident even from the fact that Rupert himself, in Book Eight of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, indicates quite plainly that up to that point—namely, while he had elaborated those seven books, and until Frederick compelled him to write the history of David from the Books of Kings—he had applied himself to one work alone and had been debtor for one obligation only. This would surely seem less than true if, during that very period, Cuno had urgently and inopportunely demanded from Rupert that work on the *Song of Songs*. Rupert had therefore already discharged that obligation—namely, to show human nature betrothed, in the chaste kisses of love, to God the Word, the Son, in the Virgin’s womb—when he undertook to expound the glory of that very Son of Man.

Indeed, in Book One on the Rule of Saint Benedict, when Rupert enumerates the works which he had hitherto issued, he does not list these books on the *Song of Songs*. Yet in the same place he says that the work *On the Glory of the Son of Man* had most recently been begun by him at Cuno’s request; and while he was wholly occupied with it, he was interrupted by the same man. He therefore ends this catalogue with that work, as though it were the goal of his labours. From this it is easy to infer that the work *On the Incarnation* on the *Song of Songs* is not to be counted among Rupert’s works issued before these books on the Rule, and hence before the books on Matthew had been begun, which are enumerated there.

Considering this, I confess that I hesitated in suspense. But, weighing that negative argument, I judge that it does not outweigh the much weightier arguments set forth above, but is of less force than they, especially since there exists no catalogue of Rupert’s books, even one published by Rupert himself, which does not omit some one of his works, as is clear to anyone who attends to them. I therefore conclude that the work on the *Song of Songs* was omitted from this catalogue, just as were the work on Job and the books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, which I maintain were nevertheless composed by the younger Rupert before this index. And if, in the final enumeration which he addressed to the Roman pontiff, he kept silent concerning these works, and moreover concerning the *Ring*, consisting of three books, and the books on the Rule already issued, that omission is only an indication of humility: in listing his own works Rupert was extremely sparing and careless.

There can therefore now be no reason for transferring these books *On the Incarnation* on the *Song of Songs* to a position after the work *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, or after the other works which followed it. It is not, however, equally certain that Rupert’s commentaries on the Twelve Prophets are later than these books. Yet I infer this from the prologue to the last six prophets, which suggests that Rupert wrote all the more ardently on the first six because he felt a more fervent love for the incarnate Word—a love which he undoubtedly conceived while writing on the *Song of Songs* concerning the Incarnation of the Lord. Let, then, this work of Rupert, *On the Incarnation of the Lord* on the *Song of Songs*, arranged in seven books, occupy its place between the exposition of the Apocalypse and the commentaries on the Twelve Prophets.

After completing this work, Archbishop Frederick of Cologne and Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, applied spurs to Rupert, as he himself says [Note: [Col. 0053D] In the Prologue to the books on the Twelve Prophets.], that he might interpret the prophecies of the Twelve Prophets. He undertook this task fervently and readily, not so much stirred by them as by love for the Son whom God had promised through His prophets. But when, over two years, he had spread out the threshing-floors of the first six and reached the end of Micah, who is sixth in this order, he paused with the work unfinished, his zeal having cooled because Nahum, who follows seventh, says scarcely anything about Christ’s coming in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0053D] Rupert, in the prologue to the last six prophets.].

Meanwhile Cuno, supposing that Rupert had completed this work, stayed with him in his monastery and, as though at leisure, spoke about the contests and triumphs of the saints even of the former Testament. Rupert declared that in them the Word of God had conquered [Note: [Col. 0053D] Rupert, in the prologue to Nahum and in the prologue to the books *On the Victory of the Word*.]. Cuno, still an abbot and not yet a bishop, was so delighted by Rupert’s saying that he suddenly burst out with the words: “Write me a book *On the Victory of the Word of God*.” Repeating this request often, he did not desist until Rupert, yielding to his wishes, undertook the little work *On the Victory of the Word*, which he completed in thirteen books, as he himself declares in the prologue to the last six prophets.

This little work was admired and cherished by the learned, who consequently studied it with great diligence, as he relates in Book Twelve of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*; although only twelve books *On the Victory of the Word* are counted. But below we shall show that this is an error of copyists.

Rupert had scarcely put an end to this work [Note: [Col. 0053D] Rupert, in the prologue to the last six prophets.] when Eckembert, venerable abbot of Corvey, urged him to treat the later prophets with the same zeal with which he had treated the first six. Nor did he alone press him. At the same time Eginhard, prior of the monastery of Burscheid, sent Rupert a letter through two brothers, in which, among other things, he addressed him thus:

> “You still owe it to love; you owe it to honour and service, beloved of Christ—and through Him and for His sake, to our desire—that you should unfold to the end, as you have begun, the words of His mouth. Otherwise, if, on account of their difficulties—those who were jealous of Rupert—we have perhaps followed too lukewarmly and have not run strongly in the fragrance of His ointments, it may be imputed to you, because, having been brought into the king’s cellar, you concealed the bridegroom’s riches which you beheld there. I mean your exposition of the Twelve Prophets, a portion of which I once copied with such eagerness that I seemed only now for the first time to have devoted myself to such a study. And the more I delight in the part, the more vehemently I burn in expectation of the whole.”

Thus he wrote to Rupert. Rupert yielded to this exhortation—or rather, to the command of Cuno, still abbot, who instructed him in these words: “By the command of the Holy Spirit I command you”—and humbly obeying, he devoted himself constantly to completing this work, which he finished in thirty-two books.

When he had completed these thirty-two books on the Twelve Minor Prophets and had published thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word*, Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, demanded from Rupert, now abbot of the monastery of Deutz, that he write *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. Rupert heard Cuno’s demand impatiently, because, as he himself states, “the care of the house of the Lord entrusted to him already oppressed him, and many read his writings so as to lay snares for him” [Note: [Col. 0054D] Rupert, in the prologue to the book *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.].

That this happened while Cuno was not yet bishop, and thus before 1126, is made clear from Book Eight of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. There, near the beginning, Rupert writes that Cuno, head of the household of the monastery of Siegburg, had urged him to undertake this work [Note: [Col. 0054D] Book X of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.].

But amid these wishes of Cuno concerning the glory of the Son of Man—who blesses those who bless Him and confesses those who confess Him not only before His Father but also before men—the Son of Man Himself chose and raised Cuno to be bishop of the Church of Regensburg in 1126, at the time of His own glorification. For in the year of salvation 1126, if Dodechin in the appendix to Marianus Scotus is to be trusted, when clergy and people, as Rupert says [Note: [Col. 0054D] Book XII of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.], divided into parties over the election of their shepherd and the contest of factions became dangerous—some shouting for this man, others for that—and when, as sedition increased, they were nearly taking up arms, one man wiser than the rest, whose heart God had touched, suddenly put forward Cuno’s name. Thus Cuno, chosen by the voice of all, but especially by the voice of the eternal Father, was installed on the very Rogation Days, for the feast of the Lord’s glorious Ascension, in the see of the Church of Regensburg, amid the immense applause of all clergy and people.

Therefore, lest anything be lacking to that glory, and lest Rupert deny to the bishop the service which others eagerly desired either to promise or render, he undertook this work *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, by which he might diligently fulfil the wishes of Cuno, formerly abbot of Siegburg and now bishop of the Church of Regensburg, in the hope of heavenly consolation and with an effort not in vain [Note: [Col. 0054D] Rupert, in the prologue to the books *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.].

But after he had completed the seventh book of this work, before he had turned mind, hand, and pen to the eighth, Frederick demanded another work from Rupert still more urgently [Note: [Col. 0054D] Rupert, Book VIII of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.]: namely, that he turn his studies to the Books of Kings and write the history of the kings, and especially of David. Thus Rupert, anxious as though caught in a narrow pass between the commands of Cuno, who while not yet bishop had said to him, “Write for me *On the Glory of the Son of Man*,” and those of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, determined within himself to divide his heart in two, as he himself says in Book Eight: giving one half to the one and the other half to the other, he would complete *On the Glory of the Son of Man* and write the histories of the Kings, and thus fulfil the wishes and commands of both.

But at that time certain religious men among the servants of God, professing the monastic life, raised questions of no small importance concerning some chapters of the Rule of Saint Benedict [Note: [Col. 0055D] Rupert, Book I on the Rule.]. Cuno, now bishop, diverted Rupert from the work *On the Glory of the Son of Man* which he had begun, so that he might offer arguments concerning them. For almost a whole year Cuno pressed him, though he resisted, until at last Rupert yielded and wrote four books on the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The first is Rupert’s brief apology, in which he complains that Cuno interrupted him, refutes the calumnies of his rivals, and enumerates his works. The second explains the order of the Sunday night vigil. The third concerns the service of the altar, and therein he sharply rebukes monks who,

> “although distinguished by sacred orders and consequently wholly dedicated to sacred altars, nevertheless, being entirely occupied in the works of their hands, neglect the most holy offices of the altar. They take little or no care for the daily celebration of the dreadful mysteries and the continual contemplation of the heavenly sacraments, as though idleness, which is hostile to the soul, could be avoided by manual labour alone. Yet in well-ordered monasteries scarcely do the summer days suffice to complete the course of the office, especially if the community is large or numerous. And if they undertake something in manual work, going out together to work, because of the brief time expended, I would call it not so much work as the semblance of work; almost the whole daily exercise of spiritual work is made insipid, hindered, and deprived of some part of itself.”

Rupert intends this statement not as an excuse for idleness or an injury to poverty, but as a just defence of those who devote themselves to the divine leisures of sacred things.

Afterward Rupert discusses the usefulness and colour of garments, and finally, after considering the use of breeches, this third book ends. The fourth, with great wisdom, restrains the contention of clerics who, saying, “I am of Augustine,” excluded monks from orders, and of monks who, saying, “I am of Benedict,” shut monasteries against clerics. It both opens the cloisters to clerics and does not prohibit monks from receiving orders.

While occupied with these matters, Rupert did not proceed to Book Eight of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. Yet, out of the greater reverence due to Frederick, the archbishop, he proceeded as far as Book Eleven of *On the Glorious King David*. There too he paused for a little [Note: [Col. 0055D] See the letter beginning *Firstfruits*.], in order to present all his works to Cuno, now bishop, humbly offering them to him as fruits of a land blessed by the Lord, as though placed in a basket. Having made this offering, he immediately returned his attention to the work *On the Glory of the Son of Man* and to the history of King David from the Books of Kings.

That this letter, in which Rupert dedicates his works to Bishop Cuno, was written while he was still occupied with those books is beyond all doubt. For he expressly states in it that, in one work—that is, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*—he had proceeded as far as Book Eight, and in the other, namely *On King David*, as far as Book Eleven; and that he was at that time, when he wrote this letter, still occupied with them. Moreover, this letter declares that Cuno, judging that Rupert’s private simplicity in having disclosed to him three years earlier how he had received the gift of heavenly understanding from Christ and His Mother was not enough for his love of Rupert, for Rupert’s own glory, and also for the good of the Christian commonwealth, adjured him by the dread name of the adorable Trinity to commit to writing what he had privately narrated.

Rupert had not yet dared to obey Cuno’s adjuration by so adorable a name. “Why,” he says [Note: [Col. 0056D] The letter cited.], “I have not yet dared to obey that adjuration, God knows, and you know in part, being privy to it.” Until finally, humbly yielding to the sacred terror of this divine name, he made his secret public in Book Twelve of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*. Finally, in this letter Rupert promises that, if life remains with him, he will complete these works, so that through Cuno’s hand he may present them also in the sight of the Lord. And indeed, distracted by all these concerns, he at last happily completed these works: *On the Glory of the Son of Man* in thirteen books, and *On King David* in fifteen. He himself gives this number of books in the letter by which, shortly afterward, he dedicated all his works to the Roman pontiff.

All this did not quench Cuno’s thirst; rather, the more he drank the waters springing up into eternal life, the more he thirsted. Thus he earnestly requested that Rupert explain the mysteries of faith in the form of a *Dialogue between a Jew and a Christian*. Rupert assented and published in three books the little work which, according to its subject or its own character, he chose to call the *Ring*, as Rupert himself tells Cuno in the prologue to the books *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. It follows with certainty that this little work appeared before those books.

When Rupert had added even this, Cuno, “as though his palate had been stimulated by the taste of good savour,” as Rupert says in that prologue, urgently asked him to add a discussion against Jewish unbelief: first, concerning the three persons of the one supreme Godhead, and to show the Jew, however unwilling, that the glory of the Trinity is attested by the Law and the Prophets, whose Scriptures he reads and accepts; secondly, why or how the assumption of flesh pertained especially to the person of the Son; and finally, to show that the time in which Jesus Christ—whom we confess and know to be the Messiah—was born is the very time which the holy Fathers awaited as near to themselves. This does not differ from the truth; indeed, it accords very closely with the prophecy which the patriarch Jacob uttered beforehand:

> “The sceptre shall not be removed from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent.”
