When Rupert proposed to undertake this treatise *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity*, he remembered that long before, Lord William, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Apostolic See, had asked Cuno—when Cuno had presented him with certain works of Rupert and handed him a copy of his exposition on the first six prophets—whether Rupert had published any work on the procession of the Holy Spirit. Cuno regretted that Rupert had nothing to bring to the footsteps of the Apostolic See. Rupert therefore thought that some benefit would accrue to this work if, “in the sweetness of its course,” as he says in the cited prologue, he intermingled some discussion of the procession of the Holy Spirit. Moved by these considerations, he composed nine books not only on the glorification of the Holy Trinity but at the same time on the procession of the Holy Spirit.

He had scarcely finished this work [Note: [Col. 0057D] Rupert, chapter 19, *On the Burning of the Town of Deutz*.] when, in the year 1128 from the Virgin’s childbirth, the town of Deutz was consumed by fire. From its flames he rescued unharmed that work which he had written most recently and of which he had no other copy remaining. “I was almost as concerned for it,” he says himself [Note: [Col. 0057D] Ibid.], “as a merchant who, having lost everything else and despairing of all, would wish at least to preserve one pearl which perhaps he had recently bought.”

In that same year he described this fire in a book divided into twenty-three chapters, entitled *On the Burning of the Town of Deutz*. This dreadful conflagration, sparing not even sacred things and bringing utter desolation upon all, gave Rupert occasion to write two other books, which he wished to call *Meditations on Death* [Note: [Col. 0057D] See Book I, chapter 2.].

He offered to the Roman pontiff, along with his other works which he enumerates in his letter to him, this work *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, rescued from the flames.

Finally, near the end of his life, though I cannot determine the time with such certainty, Rupert wrote five books on Ecclesiastes, preceded by a letter to Gregory, doubtless a monk, since he calls him “dearest brother.” Whoever knows Gregory’s years will be able more easily to identify the date of this work.

Last, if the printed editions are to be trusted, Rupert wrote the *Life of Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne*, with a prologue to Macuward, who had been transferred from the monastery of Siegburg to the church of that saint. He also wrote the *Passion of Blessed Eliphius, Martyr*, with a prefatory prologue to Albanus, abbot of Saint Martin. He also composed the *Disputation of the Cleric and the Monk*, in which he argues that it is lawful for a monk to preach. He also wrote a letter to Evehard, abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler, in which he demonstrates that it is lawful to place brethren in charge of churches.

There is also a lengthy response of Rupert to a certain person who had written to him, *On the Violation of Virginity and Whether a Defiled Woman May Be Consecrated*. Reiner also says [Note: [Col. 0057D] The work cited.] that Rupert wrote something against certain religious persons, one of whom, a priest—indeed, a concubinary priest—had falsely asserted that priests may freely use concubines. At what period these works were written you may perhaps learn if catalogues of such abbots are available to you. Since they are lacking to me, it will suffice, lest I fail you altogether, to have indicated their names.

Having supplied this brief and carefully ordered sequence of Rupert’s literary labours, let there now follow this very brief, yet most accurate, catalogue of all Rupert’s works, which may set all his writings before the eye at once.

## WORKS OF RUPERT WHILE STILL A YOUNG MAN AND NOT YET A PRIEST

Sapphic hymn on the Holy Spirit.  
[Col. 0058B] Iambic hymn on the Holy Spirit.  
Little book on various interpretations of Scripture [Note: [Col. 0058D] It does not survive.].  
Heroic poem on the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0058D] Missing.].  
A prose treatise on the condition of the monastery of Saint Lawrence on Mount Liège, from Eraclus, bishop of Liège, to Ogbert [Note: [Col. 0058D] It does not survive.].  
Sapphic poem on the same subject.  
Life of Saint Augustine.  
Life of Saint Odilia, virgin.

## WORKS OF RUPERT THE PRIEST

Chants concerning Saint Theobald, martyr, and Goar and Severus, confessors.  
*On the Divine Offices*, twelve books (A.D. 1111). A dedicatory letter to Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, written much later (after 1126), is prefixed to it.  
[Col. 0058C] Commentaries on Job, ten books [Note: [Col. 0058D] It survives divided into twelve chapters.].  
*On the Will of God*, one book (after 1114), with a prologue to William, bishop of Châlons, and Anselm, dean of Laon.  
*On the Omnipotence of God*, one book, with a prologue to G. and A.  
Commentaries on the Gospel of John, fourteen books, with a letter to Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, beginning *Meditated*.  
*On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, forty-two books (begun three years earlier and completed in 1117), with a prologue to Abbot Cuno.  
Commentary on the Apocalypse, twelve books, with a prologue to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.  
[Col. 0058D] Commentary on the *Song of Songs*, seven books, with a prologue.  
Commentary on the first six Minor Prophets, seventeen books, with a prologue to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne.  
*On the Victory of the Word of God*, thirteen books, with a prefatory discourse to Abbot Cuno.  
Commentary on the last six prophets, seventeen books, with a prologue to Eckembert, abbot of Corvey.

## WORKS OF RUPERT AS ABBOT

Commentary on Matthew (*On the Glory of the Son*), thirteen books (begun in 1126 but completed after the books on the Rule), with a prologue to Cuno, now bishop.  
[Col. 0059A] Commentary on the Books of Kings (*On the Glorious King David*), fifteen books, addressed to Frederick, archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0059D] It does not survive.].  
Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, addressed to Cuno, four books [Note: [Col. 0059D] The first of these is an apology.].  
*The Ring, or Dialogue of the Christian and the Jew*, three books.  
*On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, nine books, with a prologue to Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, and with a letter to the Roman pontiff.  
*On the Burning of the Town of Deutz*, one book (A.D. 1128).  
*Meditations on Death*, two books.  
Commentary on Ecclesiastes, five books, with a letter to Gregory.  
*Life of Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne*, one book, with a prologue to Macuward.  
*Passion of Blessed Eliphius, Martyr*, one book, with a prologue  
[Col. 0059B] to Albanus, abbot of Saint Martin.  
*Disputation of the Cleric and the Monk*, one book.  
Rupert’s letter to Evehard, abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler.  
Rupert’s response on the violation of virginity and whether a defiled woman may be consecrated.  
Against certain religious persons, one of whom, a concubinary priest, had shamelessly maintained that priests are permitted to use concubines.

This most faithful index of all Rupert’s works indicates to readers not only how great and blessed was the fertility of that holy teacher, who produced so many offspring worthy of their parent, but also what is lacking in other catalogues or arranged in a less exact order. It is therefore useful here to correct all other catalogues of Rupert’s books by restoring from this one what they omit, or by returning to their proper position what they have placed out of order.

I possess three short catalogues of his works from Rupert himself. The first occurs in Book One on the Rule of Saint Benedict, addressed to Abbot Cuno. The second is read in the letter to Cuno, now bishop, which is usually prefixed to the books *On the Divine Offices*. The third is written in Rupert’s letter to the Roman pontiff.

Although these catalogues were drawn up by the author himself, they differ greatly in the listing, numbering, and ordering of Rupert’s works. Therefore, unless you collect with much care from the evidence set out above which works Rupert composed, how many they were, and in what order, you will fall into the same error as Bellarmine and others, who, following one of Rupert’s catalogues, have given a part for the whole. To avoid this error, it is best briefly to note here what is lacking in them and what is arranged less accurately.

## FIRST CATALOGUE OF RUPERT’S WORKS, BY RUPERT HIMSELF

“I have spoken first,” says Rupert [Note: [Col. 0059D] Book on the Rule of Saint Benedict.], “of the little work on the divine offices, or sacraments, arranged through the cycle of the year, in twelve books. Then of fourteen books on the Gospel according to John. [Col. 0060A] And after this, forty-two books on the Holy Trinity and its works. Then twelve books on the Apocalypse of John. Then thirty-one books on the Twelve Prophets. Then twelve books on the victory of the Word of God. And now, most recently, on the glory and honour of the Son of Man according to the Gospel of Matthew; and you interrupted me while I was wholly occupied with this.”

## SECOND CATALOGUE OF RUPERT’S WORKS, FROM RUPERT HIMSELF

“There are, moreover, twelve books of the present ‘Firstfruits’”—thus he calls the work *On the Divine Offices* [Note: [Col. 0060D] Letter to Bishop Cuno.]. Ten books of commentaries on Job, abridged from the abundance of the thoughts and sayings of Blessed Gregory. [Col. 0060B] A treatise on the Gospel of John, fourteen books. A work on the works of the holy and undivided Trinity, forty-two books. A work on the Apocalypse of John, twelve books. A work on the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty books. A little work on the victory of the Word of God, twelve books. A work on the glory and honour of the Son of Man according to the Gospel of Matthew. And a work from the Books of Kings on the glorious King David. In the former I have proceeded as far as Book Eight, and in the latter as far as Book Eleven; I am now occupied with these works, which, if life remains with me, I shall complete and send on, these too, through your hand into the sight of the Lord. I have also expounded the *Song of Songs* in seven books.”

## THIRD CATALOGUE OF RUPERT’S WORKS, FROM RUPERT HIMSELF

[Note: [Col. 0060D] Rupert, letter to the Roman pontiff.]

“Receive, therefore, first of all this present work, divided into nine books, *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. There are other works which I have not yet been able to present. A certain work in thirteen books, *On the Victory of the Word of God*. Likewise a work *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man* in the same number of books. Thirty books on the Twelve Prophets. Fourteen books on the Gospel of John. Forty-three [Col. 0060D] books on the Holy Trinity and its works. Fifteen books on Samuel and David. Seven books in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, on the *Song of Songs*. Before all these I had also written a little work on the sacraments, or divine offices, arranged through the cycle of the year, in twelve books or volumes.”

These are Rupert’s catalogues in which he lists his own works. Yet several observations must be made concerning them.

First, Rupert does not preserve the exact order of composition in any of these enumerations of his works, as becomes evident from the evidence produced above. For the order is more nearly preserved in the first and second catalogues, while in the third it is completely reversed.

Second, none of these lists of his works contains all Rupert’s books. The productions of his younger years, as well as the books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, the *Ring*, and the books on the Rule of Saint Benedict, occur in none of them—not even in the third catalogue, which was issued after those works.

Third, not all the works counted in one catalogue are numbered in another, even when the latter is later. For in the third he does not mention the commentary on Job, though it is included in the second.

Fourth, Rupert’s works do not have in one catalogue the same number of books that is written in others. For in the third catalogue forty-three books are counted *On the Works of the Holy Trinity*, although in the first and second only forty-two books are listed. This latter number is certainly the correct one, since Rupert himself expresses it more distinctly in his letter to Abbot Cuno, in which he distributes that work as follows:

> “Thus we made three books on the proper work of the Father, from the first creation to the expulsion of Adam from paradise; then thirty books on the proper work of the Son, by which, through figures, He advanced from Abel’s righteousness or death to the assumption of flesh and the death of the cross; then nine books on the proper work of the Holy Spirit, namely from the incarnation of that same Christ to the end of the age. Together these make forty-two books.”

Rupert says this there, from which the printers’ error in the third catalogue, counting forty-three books of this work, is easily recognized and readily corrected.

A greater difficulty confronts me concerning the number of books on the Twelve Prophets. For in the first catalogue thirty-one books are noted; but in the second and third I find only thirty described. Yet in the actual sequence of books thirty-two are counted. Amid such a variety of numbers, I think we must abide by the sequence itself, in which a complete set of thirty-two books on the Twelve Minor Prophets is found to have been composed, among which we have none superfluous and none lacking. Accordingly, I judge that the thirty books which occur in the printed editions are the same works that are counted in other indexes as either thirty-one or only thirty. Thus the whole discrepancy between these catalogues lies in the numerical notations, which undoubtedly arose from the multiplication of copies or from scribal carelessness. Nor would I deny that this same cause also resulted in only five books on Hosea being noted even in the printed editions, although six books on that prophet are found there.

The number of books *On the Victory of the Word* is likewise variable in these catalogues of Rupert. The first and second divide this work into twelve books, but the third into thirteen. Indeed, in the prologue to the books on the last six prophets, Rupert says: “Behold, with God’s help I have completed that little work *On the Victory of the Word of God* in thirteen books.” But later, at the end of chapter fourteen of Book Seven of *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, he says otherwise: “That work of ours entitled *On the Victory of the Word of God* consists of twelve books.” In the printed editions themselves, twelve and thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word* are counted in different places.

Nevertheless, in all printed copies thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word* are found, and this number is written in Rupert’s third and final catalogue, as also in the prologue to the books on the last six prophets. Moreover, Meingoh’s letter to Rupert calls Book Twelve of *On the Glory of the Son of Man* the penultimate book of that work; while, in the letter to the supreme pontiff, this work is said to have as many books as the work *On the Victory of the Word*. It consequently follows that Book Twelve of the work *On the Victory of the Word* is likewise penultimate, and that this work *On the Victory of the Word* was likewise completed in Book Thirteen.

Since it has now been established, with this error corrected, that the work *On the Victory of the Word* was completed in thirteen little books, no difficulty remains concerning the number of books of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, a number not specified in either the first or the second catalogue of Rupert’s works. For in the third catalogue, contained in the letter to the Roman pontiff, he assigns to *On the Glory of the Son of Man* the same number of books as to *On the Victory of the Word*: “A certain work,” he says, “of thirteen books, *On the Victory of the Word of God*. Likewise, a work *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*, in the same number of little books.” It is therefore absolutely certain that this work *On the Glory [Col. 0062C] of the Son of Man* consists of thirteen books, as is also found in every printed edition. Rupert did not specify this number of books in the two earlier catalogues because the work was not yet complete, as he himself states in the same places. [Note: [Col. 0061D] Book I on the Rule, in the letter to Bishop Cuno.]

Let us now consider other catalogues of Rupert’s works. Trithemius, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, under Rupert, lists the following works of Rupert.

## TO CUNO, ABBOT OF SIEGBURG, AFTERWARDS BISHOP OF RATISBON

*On the Victory of the Word of God*, thirteen books: “Recently, when you were a guest.”  
*On Genesis*, nine books: “To every faithful soul.”  
*On the Song of Songs*, seven books: “He who against man.” [Col. 0062D]  
*On the Book of Saint Job*, ten books.  
*On the Books of Kings, concerning David*, fifteen books.  
*On the Holy Trinity, on the Old Testament*, forty-two books.  
*On the Apocalypse of John*, twelve books: “That you also.”  
*On the Divine Offices*, twelve books: “Those things which.”  
*Meditations on the Fire at Deutz*, three books: “Behold how.”  
*On the Twelve Minor Prophets*, thirty books.  
*On the Gospel of Matthew*, eight books.  
*On the Gospel of John*, fourteen books.  
*On the Rule of Saint Benedict*, one book; an apologetic book of the same work, one book. [Col. 0063A]  
*Letters to Various Persons*, one book.

He is also said to have written many other works, and to have expounded the New and Old Testaments for the greater part in many books; of these we have seen nothing down to the present.

Such is Trithemius’s account of Rupert’s works. Since, however, several difficulties may be raised regarding it, I have thought it necessary to make certain observations on this catalogue.

First, not all Rupert’s works are shown in this list, as Trithemius himself expressly stated at its end; and this is already evident from what has been set out above. He passed over the books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*. He omitted the *Ring*. He said nothing of the books *On the Glorification of the Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. Nor did he include the books on Ecclesiastes. I do not mention the youthful works, which he did not intend to mention either.

[Col. 0063B] Second, nevertheless, this catalogue presents the greater part of Rupert’s works. Hence we shall observe below that Bellarmine was mistaken in saying that they lay hidden for five hundred years.

Third, it preserves neither the order of subject matter nor that of composition, which must be recovered from the matters set out above.

Fourth, the heading of dedication which Trithemius prefixed to this list does not apply to all the works placed beneath it, as though Rupert had dedicated them all to Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg and later Bishop of Ratisbon. For some of them—for example, the books on the Apocalypse, the books on the six former prophets, and the books on David from the Books of Kings—he wrote under the name of Frederick, Bishop of Cologne, and in response to his wishes. Others, such as *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, *On the Victory of the Word*, and so forth, [Col. 0063C] he entitled in Cuno’s name, as he himself writes in his letter to Cuno, Bishop of Ratisbon. Finally, he left others without the distinction of any such title. Therefore Rupert’s works bear this heading in Trithemius not as though all had been dedicated to Cuno, but as belonging properly to the books *On the Victory of the Word*, which Trithemius placed at the head of his list and which Rupert himself, in his letter to Bishop Cuno, says are almost Cuno’s own.

Yet Trithemius could also have prefixed this heading to each of Rupert’s works without injustice: both because Rupert himself more than once professes in various letters to Cuno that, through the protection and concern of affection, all his works belong more to Cuno than to himself; [Col. 0063D] and because Rupert brought his works, as it were, in a basket to Cuno, now bishop, so that Cuno, receiving them from his hand, might place them before the altar of the Lord God. Rupert writes this in the letter “Firstfruits,” to Bishop Cuno, which customarily precedes the books *On the Divine Offices*.

Fifth, Trithemius’s enumeration of nine books on Genesis as distinct from the forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works in the Old Testament* is an error, refuted by the very opening words by which Trithemius indicates that those books on Genesis begin. For it is established that the words “To every faithful soul” are the beginning of the prologue to the forty-two books *On the Trinity*, among which that very prologue also reckons [Col. 0064A] the books on Genesis. Furthermore, if those nine little books on Genesis were counted separately, not forty-two but only thirty-three would be counted.

Sixth, the printed editions contain one book, called the *Golden Book*, entitled *On the Fire of the Town of Deutz*, followed by two other books *On Meditation upon Death*. Trithemius, however, joins the first, which begins “Behold how,” to those two and lists three books of meditations on the fire at Deutz. Nor is this without reason. For the occasion of writing this little work, which, Rupert says, [Note: [Col. 0063D] *Meditation on Death*, book I, ch. 2.] he chooses to call a meditation on death, was the danger of fire which he narrated in the preceding little book.

Seventh, he incorrectly counts only thirty books on the twelve prophets, whereas, according to the printed editions and what has been proved above, thirty-two must be counted.

Eighth, Trithemius lists only eight of Rupert’s books on Matthew, though thirteen are found both in the printed editions and in the matters noted above. Rupert indeed writes to Cuno, now bishop, that he had proceeded as far as the eighth book of *On the Glory of the Son of Man* on Matthew; and it is permissible to believe that this is why Trithemius counted only eight books on Matthew. But had he consulted what we have set out above, he would have learned that the work was completed in thirteen books.

Ninth, he assigns one book on the Rule of Saint Benedict and one apologetic book, although the apologetic book is the first of the four books on the Rule. But since that first book of Rupert’s contains [Col. 0064C] an *Apology*, and the prologue to the following books is called by Rupert himself, in Book II on the Rule, chapter 13, the second book on the Rule: while the second, at Cuno’s request, expounds the order of the night watches on the Lord’s Night; the third, entitled *On the Office of the Altar*, resolves various difficulties about manual labour and the colour and number of monks’ garments; and the fourth, suppressing with much charity and wisdom the contention of the cleric who says, “I belong to Augustine,” and the monk who says, “I belong to Benedict,” teaches that a cleric can become a monk and a monk can become a cleric. Trithemius regarded only the one which is second in the aforementioned order as an exposition of the Rule of our most holy Father, attending more to the title of the third than to its subject matter [Col. 0064D] and judging that the fourth pertained less to elucidation of the holy Rule. Thus Trithemius listed one little book on the Rule. Nothing prevents us from believing that the two later books, namely the third and fourth, which he omitted, were entirely unknown to him.

Finally, Trithemius lists one book of Rupert’s letters to various persons. Yet scarcely any letters of Rupert now survive, apart from those prefixed to his various works in place of prologues or attached to prologues. The book which Trithemius indicates here is not a collection of those serving as prologues; for he counted those among Rupert’s works, as anyone may readily observe from the opening words by which Trithemius denotes these works as though by their beginnings. [Col. 0065A] For example: *On the Victory of the Word*, thirteen books: “Recently, when you were a guest.” Yet these words are not the beginning of the books but of the prologue: “Recently, when you were a guest” begins not the work *On the Victory of the Word* but Rupert’s prefatory letter to Cuno for that work.

Apart from those which Trithemius counted among Rupert’s works and which serve as prologues, we now possess no other letters of Rupert, except his letter to Cuno beginning “Having reflected,” in which Rupert dedicates his books to Cuno; another to the same Cuno, now Bishop of Ratisbon, “The firstfruits of the fruits of the earth,” by which Rupert concludes his works; his letter to the prelate of the Apostolic See, the Roman pontiff, “Before your face,” by which he dedicates all his works to him; the letter [Col. 0065B] to Evehard, seventh abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler, “An old and long complaint”; and the letter to the abbots, in the form of a little treatise, *On the Violation of Virginity, and Whether a Virgin Secretly Defiled May Be Consecrated*.

## CATALOGUE OF RUPERT’S WORKS FROM REINER, MONK OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT LAWRENCE ON MOUNT LIÈGE, IN HIS BOOK *ON THE ILLUSTRIOUS MEN OF THAT MONASTERY*, UNDER RUPERT

Rupert the Younger wrote: a little work in metre in praise of the Holy Spirit; likewise another on various meanings of Scripture; likewise another in heroic verse on the Incarnation of the Lord; a little work on the condition, goods, and evils of the monastery of Saint Lawrence from Eraclus, Bishop of Liège, down to Ogbert. [Col. 0065C] Likewise, a little work on the same subject in Sapphic metre; a *Life of Saint Augustine*; and a *Life of Saint Odilia the Virgin*.

Having become a priest, he composed chants on the holy martyr Theobald, and on Goar and Severus, confessors. He published twelve little books *On the Divine Offices, or Sacraments, Celebrated in the Church through the Cycle of the Year*. Then fourteen books on the Gospel of John; forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*; twelve books on the Apocalypse; thirty-one books on the Twelve Prophets; thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word*; thirteen books on the Gospel of Matthew; [Col. 0065D] seven books on the Song of Songs; fifteen books on Samuel, concerning David; nine books *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*; five books of the *Ring*; four books on the Rule of Saint Benedict; an apologetic book *On the Will of God*; one book *On the Fire at Deutz*; one book *On Meditation upon Death*; a work against certain religious persons, one of whom was a priest—indeed, a concubinary priest—who had maintained in disgraceful pages that priests might lawfully have intercourse with menstruating concubines; another concerning a monk who, having become a cleric, left [Col. 0066A] the monastery and defended his error with shameless arguments.

Of all the enumerations of the venerable Rupert’s works which I have read, this one made by Reiner is the fullest and most accurate; yet it too is defective in some respects.

First, it omits the commentary on Job, the one book *On the Omnipotence of God*, the *Life of Saint Heribert*, the Passion of Saint Eliphius, the book *On the Violation of Virginity*, and the commentaries on Ecclesiastes.

Second, it counts thirty-one books on the twelve prophets, although we have seen that thirty-two must be counted. I regard this as a copying error, which readily and often occurs in setting down numerical characters, commonly called ciphers. By a similar error, the *Ring* is divided into five books: [Col. 0066B] for Rupert, in the prologue to *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, writes out in full, rather than in numerals, that he published this little work in three books. And this number of three books rightly corresponds to the proposed disputation against the Jews: first, that the glory of the Holy Trinity has testimony in the Law and the Prophets; second, that the assumption of flesh belonged more particularly to the person of the Son; third, that the time when Jesus Christ was born is the one foretold by the patriarch Jacob in this prophecy: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent.” Finally, through the same slip he noted only one book *On Meditation upon Death*.

The book *On the Monk Who*, etc., I take to be the very work which we read entitled [Col. 0066C] *The Disputation of Cleric and Monk*.

## CATALOGUE OF THE VENERABLE RUPERT’S WORKS, PUBLISHED BY SIXTUS OF SIENA IN 1566, IN BOOK IV OF THE *SACRED LIBRARY*, UNDER RUPERT OF DEUTZ

[Note: [Col. 0065D] As is gathered from the dedicatory letter to Pius V, 1566.]

*On the Holy Trinity and Its Works in Both Testaments*, addressed to Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg, forty-two books; the following is the division of those forty-two books, noted together:

**Part I.** *On the Holy Trinity and the Works of the Father*: three books of commentary on the first three chapters of Genesis, the first of which begins, “Of all the Scriptures.”

**Part II.** *On the Trinity and the Works of the Son*: thirty books of commentary, namely:

On the remainder of Genesis, [Col. 0066D] six books of commentary: “Of the human creature.”  
On Exodus, four books of commentary: “For what cause, or in what order.”  
On Leviticus, two books: “This book.”  
On Numbers, two books of commentary: “It is clear in the Apocalypse.”  
On Deuteronomy, two books: “This book.”  
On Joshua, one book: “Seven sections.”  
On Judges and Ruth, one book: “After the death of Joshua.”  
On the four Books of Kings and the Book of Psalms, one book: “After the broad green.”  
On Isaiah, one book: “Every soul which.”  
On Jeremiah, one book: “Of the fifth age.”  
On Ezekiel, one book: “In this age of the world.” [Col. 0067A]  
On Daniel, Zechariah, and Malachi together, two books: “When Christ opens.”  
On Maccabees, one book.  
On the volume of the four Evangelists, one book: “In the sixth age of the world.”

**Part III.** *On the Works of the Holy Spirit from Christ’s Coming to the End of the Age*: nine books: “The wrath of the Almighty.”

Besides these he wrote: *On the Incarnation of the Lord*; seven books on the Song of Songs: “He who against man”; thirty books on the Twelve Minor Prophets, addressed to Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne: “To the Holy Spirit”; thirteen books *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man* on Matthew, addressed to [Col. 0067B] Cuno, Abbot: “You demand of me”; twelve books on the Gospel of John: “The disciple whom”; and twelve books on the Apocalypse, addressed to Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne: “That you also.”

From all this Sixtus of Siena set down Rupert’s death, as though it were the finishing-point of his labours, as follows: “He died in the year of the Lord 1124.”

How mutilated this catalogue is becomes evident to everyone from what has already been set out above; as does the grave negligence of Sixtus of Siena in investigating matters on which he wrote. For in his own time many of Rupert’s works, published chiefly through the efforts of John Cochlaeus, had appeared in print; and Trithemius had already discovered many others, which he described when treating of Rupert in his catalogue in the book *On [Col. 0067C] Ecclesiastical Writers*. He is guilty not only of these omissions, since he passes over in silence the twelve books *On the Divine Offices*, the two books *On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, the thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word*, the fifteen books *On King David*, the nine books *On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, and other works of Rupert mentioned above; but even in those which he does list he made very many errors which he should not have allowed.

First, although he counted forty-two books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, and did so correctly, he distributed the individual books in such a way that only thirty-eight can be collected from them. While dividing them, without noticing, [Col. 0067D] he lost four. If he had assigned not one book only but five books to the Books of Kings together with the Book of Psalms, the distributed total would have equalled the total gathered. Therefore not one book but five must be written for the Books of Kings and the Book of Psalms. If anyone wishes to attribute this error to the printer, let it be so; but Sixtus of Siena makes other mistakes. For, secondly, he counts one book on Isaiah, one on Ezekiel, and two on Daniel; whereas Daniel has one, Isaiah two, and Ezekiel two. He also indicates one book on Maccabees, which is spurious: it is found nowhere, [Col. 0068A] and therefore Sixtus gives no opening words for it, as he does for the others.

Third, he is deficient in counting only thirty books on the Twelve Minor Prophets, rejecting the additional two.

Fourth, although he writes that the books *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man* were dedicated to Cuno as abbot, the opening words which he gives—“You demand of me”—plainly contradict him. For in that prologue Rupert expressly declares that Cuno, the venerable former abbot of the monastery of Siegburg, is now bishop of the Church of Ratisbon. Hence we have concluded that *On the Glory of the Son of Man* could not have been begun before the year 1126, when Cuno was made bishop.

[Col. 0068B] Finally, Sixtus committed a most disgraceful blunder when he asserted that Rupert died in the year of the Lord 1124, although Rupert provides the most certain evidence that in the year 1128 he described the fire of the town of Deutz in this very book. How true is that saying of the Psalmist: “The sons of men are deceitful in measures and weights.” With scarcely any sound judgment of truth and equity weighing what they transmit, they present falsehoods as truths. Let scholars therefore learn that writers are not to be believed lightly—a lesson I have often experienced myself, and for which Sixtus of Siena is here an example. Let us now consider whether Bellarmine deserves greater confidence in the case of Rupert.

## EXAMINATION OF THE CATALOGUE OF THE VENERABLE RUPERT’S WORKS FROM BELLARMINE’S BOOK *ON ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS*, UNDER THE YEAR 1119, ON RUPERT

[Note: [Col. 0067D] This work was revised, polished, and enlarged by Bellarmine himself in 1612, as he states in his preface to the reader in the Cologne edition of 1613.]

[Col. 0068C] *On the Divine Offices*, twelve books.  
A brief commentary on Job, ten books.  
On the Gospel of John, fourteen books.  
*On the Works of the Holy Trinity*, forty-two books.  
On the Apocalypse, twelve books.  
On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty books.  
*On the Victory of the Word*, thirteen books.  
*On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man according to the Gospel of Matthew*, eight books.  
*On the Glorious King David, from the Books of Kings*, eleven books.  
On the Song of Songs, seven books.

Bellarmine here admits that he is copying only the catalogue composed by Rupert himself in the letter to Bishop Cuno. [Col. 0068D] This is indeed a sincere and commendable admission. But it is no slight error for so eminent an author to present it as a catalogue of all the works Rupert wrote. Since he had undertaken to catalogue the works of ecclesiastical writers in a book which, as he says in his preface to the reader, he revised, polished, and enlarged in old age for the common benefit, he ought to have known that quite a few works were lacking from Rupert’s own catalogue, both works published before it and works published after it. Had he consulted, with the diligence or fidelity demanded of one treating ecclesiastical writers, Rupert’s works already published at Cologne, or at least Trithemius’s catalogue in the book [Col. 0069A] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, or even the defective list of Sixtus of Siena, he would not have presented this mutilated catalogue as complete—a catalogue which reveals a few things but suppresses many, all of which he ought to have disclosed if he wished to speak truthfully.

Finally, had he investigated Rupert’s works with the attention incumbent upon a critic of books, or even glanced through them, he would not have fixed the number of the books *On the Glory of the Son of Man* and *On King David*. For he would have learned that the catalogue of Rupert which he chose to follow had been written before Rupert completed these little works, which he afterwards finished: the latter in fifteen books and the former in thirteen little books, as has been demonstrated above from Rupert himself.

Perhaps, however, those works of Rupert were not at hand for Bellarmine. He does indeed correctly count thirteen books *On the Victory of the Word*; [Col. 0069B] and had he learned from Rupert’s letter to the Roman pontiff that *On the Glory of the Son of Man* must likewise be counted as thirteen books and *On the Glorious King David* as fifteen, he would have had less error and therefore less fault. If only he had more successfully counted Rupert’s already published books on the Twelve Minor Prophets in his own time: he would have given not thirty only but thirty-two, correcting rather than following the typographical error. Yet he prudently preferred to follow the catalogue’s error caused by printing than to correct what he did not know. But lest he be thought to have added nothing of his own concerning Rupert, he appends to this mutilated catalogue of Rupert’s works two observations: the first contains a censure of the books *On the Divine Offices*; the second identifies Rupert’s errors. We shall give a critique of these observations of Bellarmine below: of the first, shortly after the catalogues of Rupert’s works, when we submit the censure of the twelve books *On the Divine Offices* to a fresh examination; of the second, when we have vindicated Rupert from every error and from Bellarmine’s censure.

## LIST OF THE VENERABLE RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, PUBLISHED BY THE CENTURIATORS, CENTURY XII, CHAPTER 10

*On the Victory of the Word of God*, thirteen books.  
On Genesis, nine books.  
On Exodus, four books.  
On Leviticus, two books.  
On Numbers, two books.  
On Deuteronomy, two books.  
On Joshua, one book. [Col. 0069D]  
On Judges, one book.  
On the Books of Kings, five books.  
On Isaiah, two books.  
On Jeremiah, two books.  
On Ezekiel, two books.  
On Daniel, one book.  
On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty-two books.  
On Job, ten books.  
On the Song of Songs, seven books.  
On Matthew, thirteen books.  
On the Gospel of John, fourteen books.  
An apologetic work for that same work, one book.  
On the Apocalypse of John, twelve books.  
On the Procession of the Holy Spirit, nine books.  
On the Divine Offices, twelve books. [Col. 0070A]  
Meditations, three books.  
A disputation between a Christian and a Jew, one book.  
On the Rule of Saint Benedict, one book.  
On the Four Most Difficult Questions, one book.  
Sermons, one book.  
Letters, one book.  
He died in the year 1124, according to Trithemius.

This list of the Centuriators is deficient in some respects and excessive in others. Of the forty-two books *On the Works of the Holy Trinity*, it lists only thirty-three, omitting the nine books *On the Works of the Holy Spirit* and one book on the volume of the four Gospels. To make up the number, it counts two books on Jeremiah, where there is only one. [Col. 0070B] It also omits all the works composed by Rupert the Younger. It absurdly presents the apologetic work as being for the work on the Gospel of John, although the apologetic work, which is the first book on the Rule of Saint Benedict, was not written by Rupert for that work alone, as any reader can easily understand.

It reduces the disputation between Christian and Jew to one book, although Rupert himself testifies that he expounded it in three little books.

It gives one book on the Rule of Saint Benedict, although four exist. It further assigns one book to the Four Most Difficult Questions and attributes one book of Sermons to Rupert, as also one book of Letters. From this it seems to me somewhat likely that the single book on the Rule in the Centuriators is [Col. 0070C] the one which is second in the printed editions and deals with the vigil of the Lord’s Night according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. The book which they ascribe to the Four Most Difficult Questions I take to be the third and fourth books on the Rule; thus the Centuriators have compressed two into one. Concerning the book of Letters, I hold the same opinion as I noted above on Trithemius’s catalogue. But the book of Sermons—which no one knows, no one has seen, and no one mentions—I call an invention of the Centuriators. Nor shall I pass over their error, no greater than that of Sixtus, when they state, on Trithemius’s authority, that Rupert died in 1124. They did not notice that Trithemius says he flourished under Henry in 1124, but died [Col. 0070D] under Lothair, who obtained the empire in 1126, according to Dodechin in the Appendix to Marianus Scotus.

## INDEX OF THE VENERABLE RUPERT’S WORKS NOW EXTANT IN PRINT, DISTRIBUTED IN TWO VOLUMES IN THE PARIS EDITION

**First volume.** *On the Works of the Holy Trinity*, with a prologue and Rupert’s letter to Cuno, Abbot, “To every faithful soul”: forty-two books.

On the Twelve Minor Prophets, thirty-two books, with a prologue to this work, another to the books on Hosea, and a third to the commentaries on the six latter prophets.

On the Song of Songs, seven books, with a prologue.

On Job, one book, with a prologue.

[Col. 0071A] On Ecclesiastes, five books, with a prologue to Gregory.

**Second volume.** *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man* on Matthew, thirteen books, with a prologue to Cuno, Bishop of Ratisbon; and a Sapphic hymn *On the Holy Spirit*, found in book twelve; and an iambic hymn on the same subject, which concludes book thirteen.

*On the Glorification of the Holy Trinity and the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, nine books, preceded by Rupert’s letter to the Roman pontiff and additionally furnished with a prologue to Cuno, Bishop of Ratisbon.

On the Gospel of John, fourteen books, with a prologue, and, in the Cologne edition, with the dedicatory letter to Cuno, Abbot, beginning “Having reflected,” which [Col. 0071B] must by every right be restored to this Paris edition.

On the Apocalypse, thirteen books, with a prologue to Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, and others to particular books.

*On the Victory of the Word*, twelve books, with prefaces to Cuno, Abbot.

*On the Divine Offices*, twelve books, preceded by a letter to Bishop Cuno, besides a brief prologue. This prologue, under the title “Prologue of Robert in the Book on the Divine Offices,” is prefixed to this same work in a manuscript codex of Saint-Germain which divides it into only ten books, though omitting no chapter.

*On the Fire of the Town of Deutz*, one book.

*On Meditation upon Death*, two books.

[Col. 0071C] *Life of Saint Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne*, one book, with a preface to Macward, formerly abbot and then chief prelate of that church.

*Passion of Blessed Eliphius the Martyr*, one book, with a prologue to Albanus, Abbot of Saint Martin.

*On the Will of God*, addressed to William, Bishop of Châlons, and Anselm, schoolmaster of Laon.

*On the Will and Omnipotence of God*, one book, with a preface to S.; one should write G., that is William, and A., that is Anselm.

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, four books.

The first of these is Rupert’s *Apologetic Work*; the second, *On the Vigils of the Lord’s Night*; the third, *On Manual Work and the Garments of Monks*; the fourth, *On the Contention of Those Saying, “I Belong to Augustine; I to Benedict.”*

[Col. 0071D] *Disputation of Monk and Cleric on Whether a Monk May Preach*, one book.

Rupert’s letter to Evehard, Abbot of the monastery of Brauweiler: *Whether It Is Lawful to Put Brethren in Charge of Churches*.

A certain person’s letter to Rupert, and Rupert’s reply to the same: *On the Violation of Virginity, and Whether One Defiled May Be Consecrated*.

From this index, which assigns Rupert’s commentaries on the Old Testament to the first volume and commits his other works now extant to the second, you may mourn the loss of the fifteen books *On King David* and the *Ring*, distinguished by three books like so many gems, whereby the Jews might acknowledge the Church of Christ as bride [Col. 0072A] and desire to have her as mother; and, finally, the loss of Rupert’s other little works, stolen from us by the malice of time and perhaps one day to be restored through the care of some scholar. Trithemius testifies that he found certain works, which he included in his catalogue, and that he heard of many others but saw nothing of them. John Cochlaeus, renowned for his disputations against the Lutherans, brought many works of Rupert out of the repositories of libraries into public view through great effort in the years 1526, 1528, and 1532. At last, not a few more were added in the Paris edition. A more just age will supply the rest.

Meanwhile, let the reader who loves fairness judge with what zeal for truth Bellarmine, in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, revised and enlarged in 1612, declared that Rupert’s works [Col. 0072B] first began to see the light in our own age, and that the error of impanation which he attributes to Rupert was the reason why the works of Rupert of Deutz—otherwise, he says, not bad or unlearned—lay without light and honour in the darkness of oblivion for about four hundred years.

This twofold fiction of Bellarmine is overthrown by Honorius, priest of Autun, who, according to Bellarmine himself, lived about the year 1220, that is, in the century immediately following Rupert. In a few words he says much of Rupert of Deutz: that, enlightened by the Holy Spirit through a vision, he composed nearly the whole of Scripture in an excellent style.

Who could have testified this concerning Rupert if Rupert’s works had lain without light, in darkness, and without honour for [Col. 0072C] about four hundred years? How could he have said around the year 1220 that works had been composed which, according to Bellarmine, did not begin to see the light until our own time, namely the present seventeenth century? Did a man lie without light for so many ages whose splendour was such that four hundred years ago he was proclaimed to have been enlightened by the Holy Spirit and to have expounded nearly all Scripture in an excellent style? Did he first begin to see the light in our age when he himself was the light of every age after him? Finally, did he lie hidden, dishonoured, in darkness for five hundred years, when, born in the twelfth century, he illuminated with a purer light the thirteenth century, in which his name is celebrated with such high praise, and the fifteenth, sixteenth, [Col. 0072D] and seventeenth centuries, through works published before Trithemius’s time and which Trithemius himself credibly attests that he saw?

Therefore, on no trustworthy basis, because on the authority of no witness; with no right, because on no testimony; but with great injustice contrary to these testimonies of established credibility, Bellarmine [Note: [Col. 0071D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book III, ch. 11.] pronounced that Rupert’s works had lain without honour and light for about four hundred years. I know, indeed, that Bellarmine is mistaken in placing Honorius of Autun in the year 1220 on the authority of Trithemius, who nevertheless writes that he flourished under Henry V in 1120, that is, in Rupert’s own age. But it is enough here to reveal from this chronology that Bellarmine is inconsistent with himself even in a work however [Col. 0073A] polished.

The other assertion which Bellarmine made against Rupert in this same note is grievous to me: namely, that he brands Rupert with a charge of error that so stains his glory as to condemn his works, most worthy of eternal ages, to four hundred years of darkness. By what law of fairness, I ask, can Bellarmine infer from the fact that Rupert’s works lay hidden that Rupert erred; or, from the fact that Rupert erred, as he supposes without sufficient learning, infer that his works lay hidden for four hundred years?

As though an author’s error were the reason that his works remain hidden. Was Bellarmine unaware that professed teachers of error among the deceitful sons of men are heard more readily [Col. 0073B] than teachers of truth? Was Bellarmine unaware that countless inventions of error readily come forth into the light while very many works of truth lie in darkness? Did Augustine err because his work once called *The Unfinished Work* lay hidden for a long time and is now complete? Did so many eminent writers err because we still mourn the loss of their works? Bellarmine ought rather to have judged that falsehood, the rival of truth, and the envious malice of times and men had stolen these treasures of wisdom and knowledge from us. But if this seemed to Bellarmine the cause, then the work because of which the others especially lay without light ought itself to have appeared especially hidden; yet he testifies that it lay hidden nowhere. For Bellarmine, quite inconsistent with himself, signifies that the work *On the Divine Offices*, [Col. 0073C] which he assigns to Rupert and in which he says he has found Rupert’s errors most conspicuously, enjoyed public circulation before the present times. He admits, on the testimony of Thomas Waldensis, who flourished around 1430, that before these times Rupert’s work appeared publicly now under the name of Fulgentius, now under that of Ambrose, now under that of Isidore. Perhaps, however, Bellarmine judges that this work lay hidden because it did not bear its author’s own name. Then the book *On the Imitation of Christ* must likewise be judged to have lain hidden until now, since it bears the name of no author, or most often that of another. But if it is unbecoming for Bellarmine to advance such claims and not recognize as public the work from which he chiefly charges Rupert with errors, [Col. 0073D] it is no less unbecoming for him to say that Rupert’s works lay without light for four hundred years because of Rupert’s error and remained hidden in darkness, as though they had failed through some lapse of Rupert’s faith.

Think, then, that the matter happened otherwise: not every work of Rupert was published at every time, but different works at different times; and thus, in cataloguing them, you find writers who are either few or late, and indeed widely divergent concerning their number and order. Nothing has happened to our Rupert in this respect which you will not find to have happened very commonly to other writers, whose works, through the injury of time, human neglect, or the excessive difficulty of copying and transmitting books, appeared in different places and at different times, while very many perished. [Col. 0074A] Rupert himself complains, near the end of his life, that he had lost copies of his own works. [Note: [Col. 0073D] Prologue to the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, addressed to Bishop Cuno.] Therefore there is now no reason to wonder that, once even the copies of Rupert’s works themselves had been dispersed in different directions, Rupert’s works were made public only after scholars had sought them out with great labour, and that some are still missing—which person will provide them? Meanwhile,

*The Defender of Rupert of Deutz* maintains that he is the author of the work

*On the Divine Offices*, divided into twelve little books.

The celebrated dispute concerning the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*, which are counted among Rupert’s works, we judged should be deferred to this place, in order to disentangle it from the complications of the catalogues [Col. 0074B]. Therefore the pledge I have given compels me to raise the question here, and my subject requires it; for they commonly attribute the error of impanation—which I have undertaken to vindicate Rupert against—to the man to whom they assign this work *On the Divine Offices*.

But lest I pronounce, contrary to legal order, whose work this is before the case has even been stated and before both sides have been heard, I shall first set out the case; then weigh the arguments of each side; then dispossess Valeramnus of every claim to this work; and finally demonstrate most conclusively that it must be assigned to Rupert alone, and so pronounce by every right.

This is the case. Wyclif, holding that in the sacrament of the altar there is nothing but bread, in order that he might support this error of his under the name of some Catholic doctor [Col. 0074C], and more easily impose the belief that he was advancing nothing alien to the mind of the Church, produced a certain work *On the Divine Offices*, divided into twelve books, claiming that his opinion was taught beforehand by its Catholic author [Note: [Col. 0073D] Waldensis says this in *On the Sacraments*, chapters 47, 67, and 93.], sometimes under the fabricated name of Isidore, sometimes under that of Fulgentius, and sometimes under other names.

Hence the various names prefixed to this work made its author uncertain, so that the fact that several persons were indicated made none of them identifiable. Hence ecclesiastical writers adopted divergent opinions concerning the author of this work; hence some judged it to be the work of one author, others of another. All detected the impersonated Fulgentius, the impersonated Isidore or Ambrose; so that no one now inscribes this work under their names [Col. 0074D]. Yet some assign it to a certain Valramnus, while the rest assign it to Rupert. Waldensis, Domingo de Soto, Alanus, Sanctius, the Oxford doctors, and Vasquez attribute books of this kind to Valramnus, and consequently establish him as the author of impanation; but Bellarmine [Note: [Col. 0073D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and bk. III, ch. 11, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*.], together with others [Note: [Col. 0074D] Possevino in the *Apparatus*; Raynaldus in the *Syntax of the First Part of the Minor Works of St Anselm*.], vindicates the work for Rupert.

Here, then, are the claims and arguments of each side; examine them attentively, with no zeal save for truth and equity.

Vasquez [Note: [Col. 0074D] *In 3*, disputation 180, ch. 1, no. 5 ff.], who undertakes Valeramnus’s cause and claims against Rupert [Col. 0075A], chiefly argues as follows in maintaining that *On the Divine Offices* ought to be assigned not to Rupert but to Valeramnus, bishop of Attemberg. First, Anselm writes thus at the beginning of his letter and book *On the Body and Blood of Christ*, addressed to Valeramnus:

> “I read and reread, dearest friend, your work *On the Offices*, and its reading gives me great delight, both because of its usefulness and because of my most sweet affection for its author. But since the truth of charity and the charity of truth hate the disguise of flattery, I seem to see upon the face of this beautiful work one blemish. Even if it may for the present be concealed between us by a kindly dissimulation, should the work come into the hands of those who love to criticize even the good sayings of others, you will become a sign against whom many will speak.”

He then adds what he had noted in that work [Col. 0075B]:

> “Why, namely, when you were proposing to treat, in the order of sacrifice, those three matters—the material, the intention, and the final cause—you said, after much discussion concerning the material: ‘But my opponent will say to me: Christ, living and sentient in his body, is movable, both as God and man; but the body of the sacrifice has no life, has no sensation, is not movable. Therefore it is not the body of the Lord.’”

Finally, Anselm writes thus in response to the words just cited from the work itself:

> “First, I do not at all understand what body of the sacrifice you call this. For at the mystical blessing, when the Word of God works invisibly, body is changed into body and substance into substance. Just as at the wedding feast, after water was changed into wine, only the wine into which the water had been changed was present; so at the table of the altar only the body of the Lord is present [Col. 0075C], into which the true substance of bread has truly been changed. Except that, in that transformation, nothing of the water remained, whereas in the transformed bread, for the accomplishment of the instituted sacred mystery, only the visible appearance remains. Hence blessed Ambrose says: ‘Lest there be horror at flesh, we receive the sacrament in a likeness.’ For Christian piety has always recoiled from the survival of the substance of bread upon the altar after the consecration of the Lord’s body, and recently condemned it in Berengar of Tours and his followers. For, if this were admitted, the Word might now be said to have been not only incarnate but also impanate; as that man said: ‘If bread were changed into the body of the Lord, it would nevertheless not cease to be bread.’”

From these words of St Anselm, Vasquez [Note: [Col. 0075D] Passage cited.], following the Oxford doctors and Waldensis, concludes on behalf of Valeramnus [Col. 0075D]:

> “Since these things are so, and since all the words cited by Wyclif are contained in the book found among Rupert’s works, there can be no doubt that the book *On the Divine Offices* was written by Valeramnus, not by Rupert. For Valeramnus and Anselm were earlier than Rupert: Rupert flourished under Henry V and died under Lothair III; but they flourished under Henry III.”

Here Vasquez seems to me to argue thus: The book *On the Divine Offices* now circulated among Rupert’s works [Col. 0076A] contains the words, and under the same words the error, which Anselm lovingly rebuked in Valeramnus’s book *On the Divine Offices*, by a letter addressed to him. Therefore this work now published among Rupert’s books must still be assigned to Valeramnus, not Rupert, who, being younger than Anselm and Valeramnus, could not have written what Anselm criticized.

The second ground upon which Vasquez declares without doubt that *On the Divine Offices* is not Rupert’s but Valeramnus’s is that John of Paris attributes to Valeramnus words that are read in book II, chapter 9, of *On the Divine Offices*.

Finally, the third ground is that Waldensis infers from Anselm’s book *On Leavened and Unleavened Bread*, at its beginning, that this Valeramnus was suspect regarding matters of our faith [Col. 0076B], because Anselm offers him no greeting, on the ground that he favored the emperor against the pope.

With this argument, as with a threefold cord, Vasquez thinks that he has torn *On the Divine Offices* away from Rupert and bound it to Valeramnus of Attemberg alone. But a cord, however threefold, whose strands are unfastened and do not cohere at all, is easily broken; and once it is broken, the work tied to Valeramnus quickly slips from his grasp.

Vasquez could indeed have assigned to Valeramnus some work *On the Divine Offices* in which the aforementioned words occur, assuming these premises. But if anyone denies that this letter was written by Anselm to Valeramnus, how will Vasquez prove it?

For it is wholly uncertain, first, whether this letter and this treatise are by St Anselm. Neither Eadmer [Col. 0076C] nor Robert of Monte [Note: [Col. 0075D] In the German Appendix to Sigebert, under the year 1109 (*Patrologia*, vol. CL).], in their lists of St Anselm’s works, nor Trithemius among Anselm’s works, reckoned this letter or any such treatise among them. Moreover, manuscript codices preserve the letter under no name of Anselm. It exists by itself, without the treatise and without an author’s name, in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in a very ancient manuscript codex. There the work *On the Divine Offices* differs from printed copies only in its division of chapters and books, being divided into only ten books. It is preceded by the prologue, “All things which throughout the course of the year,” under this title: “Here begins the prologue of Robert”—the same name in German as Rupert—“in the book *On the Divine Offices*.” The entire work is followed by this rubric: “Here ends the book *On the Divine Offices* of Lord Robert [Col. 0076D], monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège.” Finally, after these books the letter is appended, under the title of greeting: “To the dearest brother in Christ. Enlightened are the eyes of the heart”; and it begins: “I read and reread, dearest friend, your work *On the Offices*.” But the treatise *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, or *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, is not found in that codex.

The same letter, however, together with such a treatise, is preserved in the library of Saint-Victor at Paris, likewise without naming its author.

If these negative arguments do not suffice, consider that in both manuscripts of Signy this title [Note: [Col. 0075D] All this is attested by the Rev. Fr Bertrand Tissier, vol. III of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*, in the preface to the works of Blessed William of Saint-Thierry, and at the end of this letter.] is found prefixed to the letter [Col. 0077A]: “Letter of Lord William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, to a certain monk who had written on the body and blood of the Lord.”

And it is concluded by these words: “Here ends the letter of Lord William, formerly abbot of Saint-Thierry,” etc. Moreover, in the monastery of Igny, a manuscript codex of the books *On the Divine Offices* prefixed the letter, inscribed with the name of this William.

Picard [Note: [Col. 0077D] Note 3 on the first chapter of that treatise.], indeed, who first attributed these materials to Anselm, produced one copy bearing Anselm’s name, communicated to him by Nicolas Fabri; and he further supports his opinion by the testimony of Vincent of Beauvais, St Antoninus, and Peter of Aquila. He might have added Waldensis, and Vasquez himself may now be added. But what do all these persons, holding diverse opinions [Col. 0077B], testify except this one thing: namely, that it is uncertain whether Anselm wrote this letter? And where anything is doubtful, what certain conclusion can be established? What firm structure can be built upon it—especially one intended to shake and overthrow what is certain and firm: namely, as will later be shown, that Rupert composed the books *On the Divine Offices*?

Secondly, it is uncertain that this letter was written to Valeramnus. For if St Anselm wrote a book *On Unleavened and Leavened Bread* to Valeramnus, what follows from this? That the books *On the Divine Offices*, in which Anselm read material which the envious might criticize, were published by Valeramnus; and, for that reason, that the letter together with the treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was directed by Anselm to Valeramnus?

Thirdly [Col. 0077C], it seems entirely uncertain who this Valeramnus was, since I find several Valeramni, Valerami, or Valeranni around the times of Anselm and Rupert.

The first is Valeranus, abbot of Saint-Vitton at Verdun, brother of Hugh, bishop of Langres. He is said to have died in the year of the Lord 1060 or 1066 [Note: [Col. 0077D] Vol. IV of the *Chronicle of the Order of St Benedict*, under the year of Christ 852, in the catalogue of abbots of the monastery of Saint-Vitton; and at the end of Lanfranc’s works, published through the labors of the Rev. Fr Dom Luc d’Achery (*Patrologia*, CL).].

The second, Valeramus or Vileramus, according to Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0078D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*.], was abbot of Mersburg, of the Order of St Benedict, a German by nation, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, skilled in verse and prose. Having devoted himself for some time to study at the University of Paris, he returned to his homeland [Col. 0077D], obtained the office of scholasticus of the Church of Bamberg, and then, considering that the glory of the world passes with time, despised the world and assumed the monastic habit in the monastery of Fulda for Christ’s sake. Finally, as his merits increased, he was consecrated abbot of the monastery of St Peter at Mersburg, and made his name known to posterity by writing. “Of his little works,” says Trithemius, “I have seen only a volume composed in a beautiful variety of metre, verse, and mingled prose, *On the Marriage of Christ and the Church*: three books on the *Song of Songs*, beginning, *cum studia intu…* He flourished [Col. 0078A] under Henry III, in the year of the Lord 1070.”

Trithemius relates these things in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* concerning Vileramus or Valeramus of Mersburg, who alone among all these Valerami is reported to have composed any works.

The third is Valerannus, formerly cantor of the Church of Paris. He had entered the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs under Ursio, or Urso, who was appointed its first prior by St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, in the year of restored salvation 1079. Anselm wrote a letter to this Walerannus, urging him by no means to abandon the holy purpose of monastic life, even if the bishop of Paris should violently draw him out of the monastery [Col. 0078B]. In that letter Anselm also commends this Valerannus’s learning and ability. I infer that this letter of Anselm was written between 1079 and 1090, because Ursio, under whose obedience Walerannus lived, was appointed prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs in 1079, and Theobald succeeded him around 1090. This may be learned both from Anselm’s letter, which is the thirteenth in book III of his letters, and from the *History of the Royal Monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs*, and from the book entitled *Martiniana*.

The fourth Valeramus is bishop of Kitzingen, who, when Emperor Henry IV rejected Abbot Frederick, was substituted for Gunther around the year of the Lord 1089 [Col. 0078C]. Paul Langius records this in the *Chronicle of Kitzingen* for that year.

Dodechinus, in his appendix to Marianus Scotus under the year 1100, records a fifth, Waltram, bishop of the Church of Magdeburg. A letter which he wrote to Count Louis testifies that he favored King Henry against the Roman pontiff, urging the count to submit to King Henry and defend his cause, lest he perish with those who resisted God’s ordinance—Rudolf, Hildebrand, Ekbert, and many others. That letter, with Louis’s reply, may be seen in Dodechinus’s appendix to the *Chronicle* of Marianus Scotus under the year 1090.

The same Dodechinus introduces a sixth Valeramus under the year 1094 [Col. 0078D], bishop of Naumburg. St Anselm wrote to him a letter on the procession of the Holy Spirit, at the head of which he vehemently rebukes Valramus as a supporter of Henry against Urban, Roman pontiff. The letter begins: “Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury, speaks briefly to Valramus, bishop of Naumburg: ‘If I were certain,’” etc. For in the year 1109 Valramus had published a treatise on the investiture of bishops, declaring it to belong by right to the emperor rather than the supreme pontiff. But [Col. 0079A] after the death of Urban II, he followed the party of Paschal II, Urban’s successor, and had peace and communion with the Church. Accordingly Anselm subsequently honors him with a friendly greeting in the letter entitled: “To Lord and friend Valramus, venerable bishop, Anselm, servant of the Church of Canterbury and archbishop, gives greeting, serves,” etc. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Stephen or Herrand, Trithemius calls this bishop of Naumburg Valtram.

The Centuriators [Note: [Col. 0079D] Century XI, ch. 10, p. 605.] indeed report concerning this Valramus, bishop of Naumburg, all the things which Dodechinus distinctly related of both Waltram of Magdeburg and Valramus, bishop of Naumburg. But they should have observed that this Valramus, bishop of Naumburg, to whom St Anselm wrote, is not the same Valramus whom Dodechinus, shortly before, called bishop of Magdeburg in his appendix [Col. 0079B]. Rather, for Dodechinus there is one Valramus and another Valramus: the former bishop of Magdeburg, the latter bishop of Naumburg; the former the man to whom Count Louis wrote, the latter the man to whom Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote.

The seventh Valeramus, as the Centuriators call him—or Valerannus, as Robert of Monte’s Appendix to Sigebert calls him in the second appendix to the Benedictine Martyrology—was a monk of Clairvaux. Summoned by Simon, bishop of Noyon, together with several monks, in 1129 he became the first abbot and governed the monastery of Ourscamp, commonly Orcamp, as the *Chronicle of Flanders* testifies in book V [Col. 0079C]. Having founded three other abbeys there, he died in 1142, as the continuator of Sigebert attests for that year, and as the Centuriators report in Century X, p. 1692, along with the second appendix to the Benedictine Martyrology.

The eighth, Galeranus or Valeranus, was son of Robert, count of Meulan. Succeeding his father, he became count of Meulan in Normandy in 1118 and took the cross in 1145, according to Robert of Monte in the German Appendix to Sigebert under the years 1118 and 1145.

Finally [Col. 0079D], a ninth who lived in Rupert’s century may be counted: Valeramnus, archdeacon of Bayeux, who succeeded Walter, bishop of Rochester, and died in 1182, as Robert of Monte has in his appendix to Sigebert.

Since, therefore, so many Valeramni, Waltrams, and Valranni occur in the age of St Anselm and Rupert, it cannot at all be established which of them was the author of *On the Divine Offices*, or to which of them the letter was directed that censures some blemish in such a work.

It is certainly established that it was not written to Valeramus of Attemberg, since no bishop Valeramus of Attemberg is known [Col. 0080A]. Vasquez therefore erred in writing that Anselm directed this letter to Valeramus of Attemberg, in order to assert that this Valeramus of Attemberg was the author of *On the Divine Offices*.

Nothing suggests that the letter was directed to Waltram of Magdeburg. Nor have I any basis for prudently conjecturing that it was sent to Valramus of Naumburg. For what follows if St Anselm sent his book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit* to Valramus of Nuremberg? Are all the works of one author spoken to one person, or are they all directed to a single recipient?

Indeed, two considerations prove to me that the letter was written neither to the bishop of Naumburg, nor to the bishop of Kitzingen, nor to the bishop of Magdeburg [Col. 0080B]. First, none of these Valerami, except Naumburg’s, is found to have published any work or to be numbered among ecclesiastical writers. Second, if St Anselm is the author of this letter, he calls the Valeramnus to whom he directs it simply “dearest friend.” St Anselm nowhere greets a bishop in that fashion, without any added designation of honor and reverence, or at least of episcopal dignity. For even if in his first letter to Valeramnus of Naumburg he denied him greeting because he stood outside communion with the Church, he nevertheless did not omit the title of episcopal rank; and in the other letter to the same man, after his reconciliation, he greets him as “lord and friend,” as the inscriptions of such letters show [Col. 0080C].

Nor would anyone attribute this work to Valerannus, chamberlain of King Philip I, who concerned himself not with the sacraments of the Church but with service to his prince; nor to Count Valeranus, who devoted his mind not to divine offices but to military affairs. Therefore this letter was written neither to Valeramnus, bishop of Naumburg, nor to the bishop of Kitzingen, nor to the count of Meulan; and *On the Divine Offices* should not be attributed to any of them.

To which Valeramnus, then, should this work be attributed? To which Valeramus was this letter directed? To which Valramus was it sent? Either to Valeramnus, abbot of Saint-Vitton; or to Valramus or Vileramus [Col. 0080D], abbot of Mersburg; or to Valerannus, formerly cantor of the Church of Paris; or to Valeramus or Valeramnus, monk of Clairvaux and later first abbot of Ourscamp; or to Valerannus, archdeacon of Bayeux. But if this book was published by Anselm, chronology appears to prevent us from asserting that it was sent to the first or the last. The first died in 1060 or 1066, when Anselm was still young. The last died in 1182; and thus Anselm, who died in 1109, had died before this Valeramnus could have composed the book *On the Divine Offices*.

Thus the whole matter now lies between the Mersburg man, the Parisian, and the man of Ourscamp: which of them authored the work *On the Divine Offices* attributed to Valeranus, and to which of them was written this letter said to be Anselm’s [Col. 0081A].

The claim of the man of Mersburg seems stronger because he published several works and thereby deserved to be numbered among ecclesiastical writers, among whom none of the others obtained a place. But since, so far as I know, no one has assigned *On the Divine Offices* to this Vileramus of Mersburg, nor said that the letter regarded as Anselm’s was written to him; and since Anselm was very much later in age than he, it is certainly utterly untrustworthy that Anselm wrote this letter, and therefore utterly untrustworthy that *On the Divine Offices* was published by that Valramus to whom Waldensis, the Oxford men, Vasquez [Col. 0081B], and others wished to assign it without any right or any substantiated testimony worthy of belief.

Yet lest I appear to establish the claims of Rupert of Deutz by doing injustice to Anselm, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, or any other author, there is one judgment, whether of those who contend for Anselm or for William, pronounced in favor of the abbot of Deutz: namely, that the books *On the Divine Offices* were composed by Rupert. John Picard [Note: [Col. 0081D] Notes on this letter and on the book *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*.] maintains that the letter was sent by Anselm of Canterbury to Rupert, thereby establishing him as author of this work. He nevertheless says, on a rather slight conjecture, that Rupert undertook the work while Anselm lived but completed it after Anselm’s death, which he does not deny occurred in 1109. Theophilus Raynaldus [Note: [Col. 0081D] In the *Syntax of the First Part of the Minor Works of St Anselm*.], unconcerned about chronology, likewise attributes the letter to Anselm and the books *On the Divine Offices* to Rupert of Deutz. Finally, the Rev. Fr Bertrand Tissier [Note: [Col. 0082D] In the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*.] maintains that this letter was written not by Anselm but by William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, to Rupert the monk; and he thereby establishes without any opponent that *On the Divine Offices* is Rupert’s work [Col. 0081C].

From this one may see how slight is the first argument by which Waldensis, Vasquez, and others seek, on the basis of this letter—which some call Anselm’s, others William’s, and others the work of an unknown author—to take the books *On the Divine Offices* away from our Rupert. For whether the letter was written by Anselm, by William, or by some other unknown author, Rupert is nevertheless undeniably proclaimed the author of this work by the critics of both sides [Col. 0081D].

Nor does it aid them much that John of Paris, who lived more than a hundred years after Rupert, attributes to Valramus words read in chapter 7 of book II of *On the Divine Offices*. I would say that John of Paris wrote Valramus in place of Rupert because he had heard that an abbot of the Order of St Benedict, German by nation, very learned in sacred letters, and flourishing in Germany, had composed, among other works, one *On the Divine Offices*. He had heard that a certain Vileramus—a German by nation, a Benedictine monk by profession, an abbot highly practiced in sacred letters—had studied at the University of Paris and had published several books; and from these facts he judged him to be the author of the work. But he took a German for the German, monk for monk [Col. 0082A], German abbot for German abbot: that is, Vileramus of Mersburg for Rupert of Deutz. He passed this man off as the other to the Oxford doctors, Waldensis, and others, who, failing to distinguish Valeramnus from Vileramus, supposed him to be bishop of Naumburg. Vasquez and others thought it preferable to ascribe the work—in which they thought they found something not inconsiderably contrary to Eucharistic truth—to a schismatic rather than to a Catholic writer whose name the Lutherans invoked in defense of their error.

This, in my judgment, was the origin and course of the error that substitutes Valeramnus for Rupert [Col. 0082B]. It is enough to have indicated it, so that the one testimony brought against Rupert’s most solid claims may be judged too untrustworthy either to overthrow what is most certain or to establish most firmly what is wholly uncertain.

Yet if anyone, like Vasquez, should contend too stubbornly on the authority of this one writer, or should more readily concede, like Monsieur de Lestoq, professor of sacred theology at the Sorbonne, that one work *On the Divine Offices* proceeded from Valeramnus, he still ought not, with the Oxford men, Waldensis, Vasquez, and others, to deny that the particular work about which we are contending was written by Rupert. Did not Isidore, Alcuin, Amalarius, and others also compose books *On the Divine Offices*? “But,” they will say, “in the books circulated among Rupert’s works, there are passages also found in Valeramnus’s work” [Col. 0082C]. Must passages borrowed in this way be taken from the child and assigned to the parent? Who that has even a slight acquaintance with Rupert has not observed that he sometimes produces passages without naming their author, as if they were his own? Does Rupert not himself declare that this happened to him in this work *On the Divine Offices* [Note: [Col. 0082D] Book I, *On Kings*.], in his *Apology*, when he simultaneously rebukes the ignorance and envy of an opponent who rashly condemned St Gregory in that work?

More wisely, then, whoever understands with Monsieur de Lestoq that nothing against Rupert’s work follows from the alleged work of Valeramnus will know that these two propositions can stand together: Valeramnus published a work *On the Divine Offices* [Col. 0082D]; Rupert composed books *On the Divine Offices*, and in one chapter of them the same words occur. How are these propositions incompatible, so that allowing one requires the denial of the other? Therefore the second argument of the Oxford men, Waldensis, and Vasquez, derived from the testimony of John of Paris, proves nothing against Rupert’s claims.

The third argument, based on Valeramnus’s suspected faith, is still weaker. Valeramnus was indeed schismatically separated from the Roman pontiff: therefore is he to be regarded as the author of a work in which there is not only nothing against the authority of the Roman pontiff, but rather very much in commendation of the Roman See and Church [Col. 0083A], and in praise of the Church’s unity?
