Would a rebel and schismatic, in chapter 27 of book I of *On the Divine Offices*, establish Peter as prince of the apostles, and hold that, because of Peter’s pre-eminence, Peter’s successors stand above the other patriarchs, whom alone he says are called apostolic princes? Would he teach that the beginning of faith proceeds from that See, and consequently that this rule is observed in the churches: that they have no bishop except one sent from that same See from which their first preacher of faith was sent; and would he call that sending the grant of the pallium? Would a man outside communion with the Roman See commend the ordinances of the Roman See and undertake their defense against the Greeks, as the author of this work praises and defends them [Note: [Col. 0083D] Book II, *On the Divine Offices*, chs. 21 and 22.]? Would one severed from the head declare, as this author does [Col. 0083B; Note: [Col. 0083D] Book III, *On the Divine Offices*, ch. 10.], that the Church, by the authority of Peter himself, whose office the Roman pontiff exercises, distributes the divisions of spiritual gifts; that it belongs to this prince to appoint shepherds over Christ’s sheep; and so forth?

Therefore the man who infers wrongly from the schism of Valeramnus of Naumburg that this work could have proceeded from no one but him has not read this work. From Valeramnus’s suspected faith and his own rebellion against the Apostolic See, he ought rather to have inferred that books of this kind were never published by him: books which, whenever the occasion arises, profess the highest observance of due reverence toward the Apostolic See. What claim, then, remains to Valeramnus of Naumburg, by which the Oxford men, Waldensis, Vasquez, and others may assert that he is the author of *On the Divine Offices*? What injury is this but to steal a child from its lawful parent, in order to substitute it for another [Col. 0083C]? Valeramnus is the stranger; our Rupert of Deutz alone is the lawful parent.

One who substitutes a child, just as one who steals a child from its father, commits a crime to be punished with the full severity of every law. Lest I seem liable to this charge—as though I had taken from Valeramnus a work properly his in order to assign it to Rupert as another’s—I undertake to prove most conclusively by what titles and by what right it belongs to Rupert himself.

That child ought not to be judged supposititious whose rightful parentage is attested by all who make it their business to understand offspring of this kind; much less one which the parent himself acknowledges as his own, preserves as his own, and defends as his own. What stronger indications of legitimate offspring are there than the sure testimony of such judges, than the parent’s embraces, love, and protection? Yet all these proclaim Rupert the author of *On the Divine Offices* [Col. 0083D]. For which compiler of catalogues of ecclesiastical writers did not assign this work to Rupert?

The continuator of Henry of Ghent, in chapter 5 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, testifies that Rupert composed especially such books *On the Divine Offices*:

> “Rupert, abbot of Deutz, wrote for Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, a book full of mysteries of the Scriptures, which he entitled *On the Victory of the Word of God*. He wrote another, *On the Divine Offices*.”

Trithemius does likewise in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Rupert, in the catalogue cited above. Baronius, under the year 1111, acknowledges that Rupert published *On the Divine Offices* in that year. Bellarmine does so in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Rupert. The Centuriators, Century XII, and Sixtus of Siena in the *Bibliotheca*, count this work *On the Divine Offices* among Rupert’s works [Col. 0084A].

Cochlaeus, a most ardent defender of the Catholic faith against the Lutherans, to whom nothing could seem right that did not accord with the Church’s sound doctrine, and a most devoted student of Rupert, enumerates among Rupert’s principal works—which, he writes in a letter to Henry, abbot of Deutz, had been entrusted to his care and which he arranged to have printed at Cologne for public circulation—his twelve books *On the Divine Offices*:

> “Three of his principal works are being published,” he says, “to be issued on the coming Kalends of April: namely, fourteen books of commentaries on the Gospel of John, twelve books on its Apocalypse, and the same number of books *On the Divine Offices*. Since he entrusted all these to my care,” etc. [Col. 0084B]

Nicholas Sander, in book VII of the works which he wrote *On the Visible Monarchy of the Church against Heretics* [Note: [Col. 0083D] Book VII, nos. 806 and 812, and under the years of Christ 1124–1145.], declares in several places that Rupert was the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*. Gualter also counts it among Rupert’s works in his *Chronology*. Sirmond himself, as also another Jesuit called Floridus, in the *Sponge* [Note: [Col. 0083D] Fifth assertion on the third proposition, title 2.], under the assumed name Leomellus, commends and defends the authority of this work as Rupert’s [Col. 0084C].

Peter Aurelius likewise, to whom Sirmond and Floridus object this work as worthy of Rupert [Note: [Col. 0084D] In the *Vindications of the Censure of the Sorbonne*, p. 41; and in part I of the *Orthodox Reply against Jacques Sirmond’s Antirrhetic II*, p. 561; and in part II of the *Antirrhetic*, pp. 619–620.], accepts it in diverse places. Had it been of doubtful authority and reliability, he should by no means have accepted it so often, but ought rather to have made an exception, instead of repeatedly trying to dispose by exposition of the testimony objected from chapter 16 of book V of *On the Divine Offices*.

But John Picard, of the Augustinian Canons, by a more careful investigation, maintains that the letter *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* was directed by Anselm to Rupert, not [Col. 0084D] to Valeramnus. He thus tries to demonstrate that Rupert completed this work *On the Divine Offices* after Anselm’s death, namely in 1111, but began it while Anselm lived, that is, before 1109.

Since every writer who made a point of listing ecclesiastical authors and, above all, Rupert’s books—and Aurelius himself, against whom the authority of so great a man was urged from the books *On the Divine Offices*—testifies that this work is Rupert’s [Col. 0085A], who would refuse to assign it to him, when so many judges unanimously award it to him?

It would be too little merely to vindicate this double offspring of Rupert from strangers by the testimony that suffices for others, especially that of those who compiled catalogues of Rupert’s works or enumerated his books. Who would deny as conceived in his bosom the child whom he lovingly received as his own, cherished as his own, and protected as his own? Who would not judge with certainty that this work was conceived in Rupert’s bosom and brought forth by Rupert’s fruitful mind, when he observes Rupert declaring it his own, commending it as his own, calling it his own, and defending it as his own?

Rupert himself declares that this work, *On the Divine Offices*, is his own; he commends it as his own, and in several passages of his other works dedicates it to God as the fruits of his own land. Most especially, in his letter to Cuno, bishop of the Church of Regensburg, he names this work, *On the Divine Offices*, first among his writings; accordingly, he offers it to Cuno as the firstfruits of the produce of his land—or rather, in his own words, sends it through Cuno’s hands into the presence of the Lord. “The firstfruits of the produce of the land,” says Rupert, “which the Lord has given me, I now offer according to the commandment of the holy and mystical law, when I send you the present little work, which I wrote on the divine offices, long desired by you, Father Cuno—hitherto abbot of the monastery of Siegburg, but now bishop of the Church of Regensburg. For these are the firstfruits of all the works which, to my joy, have come to me from the Lord,” etc. “But this work *On the Divine Offices*, which was the first,” etc. Moreover, in the same letter, when he himself enumerates his works, he describes this one first: “There are,” he says, “twelve little books of these present firstfruits.” He then appends his other works, as we set them out above in his catalogue taken from that letter.

How highly Rupert commended this book and made it his own may be learned from chapter thirteen of the second book which he wrote on the Rule of St Benedict. There he speaks of this work as follows: “In the book which I wrote on the sacraments, or offices, I set forth the reasons for this observance—why a tract is sung in place of Alleluia—which I have long since learned are eagerly read by many; and their height, or depth, is so great and such that they cannot here be briefly repeated.”

Does not this single fact bring crashing down all the foundations of the Oxford men, Valdensis, Vasquez, and others who exerted themselves on the contrary side? Does it not establish Rupert’s claim to the work *On the Divine Offices* so firmly that it can be taken away from him only by grievous injustice—he who affirms it to be his own and sends it, as his own, through the hands of a bishop into the presence of the Lord? Will they call the most religious Rupert a plagiarist, faithless, or sacrilegious? Far be it.

Rupert humbly offered this work as his own not merely to one bishop, but to the supreme pontiff, head of all the Churches. For in his letter to the supreme pontiff, among his other compositions which he there enumerates, he again dedicates this work as the firstfruits of his labour and the chief of all the works he wrote: “Before all these things,” he says, “I had also written a little work *On the Sacraments, or Divine Offices, through the Course of the Year*, divided into twelve little books or volumes.”

Therefore, if Rupert did not write this little work, he lied more shamefully and damnably than Sapphira, to his own ruin—not to say, against the Holy Spirit—bringing another’s goods as his own to the feet of St Peter’s successor, and thus adding theft to falsehood. If a devout mind recoils from entertaining such thoughts about most holy Rupert, a sound mind should likewise shrink from depriving him of this work.

He is himself the defender of this work in the first book on the Rule, also called Rupert’s *Apology*. For when the envious mind of his rivals had condemned one proposition from his book *On the Divine Offices*—a book which, free of any suspicion of fraud, he had entrusted to one person who earnestly requested it for study—as altogether contrary to the faith and to the economy of the Word, and when learned brethren, as he himself relates [Note: [Col. 0085D] Book I on the Rule], were being sent to investigate whether the report widely spread concerning him were true, namely, that he had said and written that the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary: where did Rupert turn? To what did he flee? Did he disdain the book from which the suspicion arose?

Moreover, when one of Rupert’s opponents proclaimed this book heretical, and even the ignorant rabble demanded it and hastened to seize it for burning, what did Rupert do? Did he deny that the work was his? Did he call it another’s? If this work is not Rupert’s, do you suppose Rupert would assert as his own something seized as heretical and to be committed to the flames? If it is not Rupert’s, this accusation has nothing to do with Rupert. Let Rupert leave the book to its own author, and every slander against himself is repelled.

Nevertheless Rupert asserted that this work was his own, defending at once his work and his faith. Nor did he pass over in silence either the ignorance or envy of his opponent; rather, he mocked the man’s ignorance and scorned his envy, as we stated in advance at the beginning of this work. But when he sees his adversary, among the little works that had sown the seeds of this hatred against him, he counts this work first: “I have spoken,” he says [Note: [Col. 0086D] Book I on the Rule], “first of the little work *On the Divine Offices, or Sacraments, through the Course of the Year*, divided into twelve little books; and I compressed a very extensive subject into a work briefer than it ought to have been.” He then adds his other works.

Indeed, the book itself reveals its author: the offspring its parent, the fruit its tree. For in chapter twenty-three of the second book the author professes himself a monk in these words: “The subject requires that I should not pass over something proper to our order, that is, the monks.”

And in chapter twenty-five of the seventh book: “These things have rightly and laudably been handed down by the elders of our—that is, the monastic—order.” More explicitly still, in chapter four of the eighth book, the author of this work is declared to be a monk under Abbot Berenger, or Berengarius, in the monastery of St Lawrence, in the year 1111 [Col. 0087A]. It is established that Rupert lived in that monastery under that abbot, from his letter to Abbot Cuno, *To Every Faithful Soul*; from Reiner’s *Life of Rupert*; and from the sequence of Rupert’s works set out above by us.

Let the doctors of Oxford, Valdensis, Vasquez, and the others hear these things, and strip their Valeramnus of every claim to this work. Let them hear that a monk composed what they maintained was produced by the bishop of Naumburg. Let them read that it was written in the year 1111, which they contend Valeramnus issued in the period after St Anselm was removed from their midst in 1109. Finally, overwhelmingly convicted by so many testimonies of Rupert himself concerning this his own work—to which full faith is due—let them restore the work to Rupert by every right, since they assigned it to Valeramnus under no title of right, but merely on the uncertainty of a slight conjecture.

Nor should it be passed over that John Picard of Beauvais, a regular canon of St Augustine, in order to claim the letter and treatise *On the Sacrament of the Altar* for Anselm without any objection, and to prove that it was transmitted by him to Rupert in 1079 or the following year, is compelled to say that at least the earlier books *On the Divine Offices*—in which the author of that letter found something to criticize—had been written by Rupert before this time, though with a ruder Muse, and sent to Anselm, until with advancing age Rupert perfected them and dedicated them to Cuno, now bishop of Regensburg.

This whole fiction of John Picard collapses of itself. It cannot in any way stand that Rupert, scarcely born—if indeed he was born before the year 1079—wrote *On the Divine Offices*. It cannot stand that Rupert sent an unfinished work to Anselm, who congratulates Rupert in his letter not on a work begun, but on a labour completed. It cannot stand that for thirty-two years—from 1079 to 1111, which is recorded in the eighth of these books—Rupert left aside the work he had undertaken, while no concern pressed upon him. [Col. 0087D] It cannot stand that Rupert treated of the divine offices at that age, when he was anointed priest of the Lord only after the schism of Paschal II and Guibert had been extinguished, that is, after its instigators Henry III and Guibert had died; and when the Lord, as he himself relates, then opened his mouth, he began to speak the divine sacraments and to write that first work, *On the Divine Offices*, divided into twelve little books—hence he calls it the *Firstfruits of the Produce of the Land which the Lord Blessed*. Finally, it cannot stand that, when Rupert put the finishing hand to that work, he refused voluntarily to correct or explain more clearly those matters which Anselm—if he is the author of the letter on the sacrament of the altar—had noted as requiring correction or explanation in the work. It must therefore stand [Col. 0088A] that this work was composed by Rupert only at the age which he himself described as marked in the Paschal candle, namely, in the year 1111 of restored salvation.

## Rupert’s Understanding of Sacred Scripture

No one reaches truth except through truth; and the person governed by the Spirit of God, who leads humankind only to himself—the supreme and first Truth—never departs from truth. It greatly assists the defender of Rupert’s faith against errors that Rupert obtained his understanding of sacred Scripture not from his own judgment but from a heavenly gift. Therefore I shall not pass over this heavenly gift, to which all who have written about Rupert bear witness.

[Col. 0088B] Reiner, monk of the monastery of St Lawrence, where Rupert was brought up from childhood, particularly commends this gift poured down upon Rupert from above in his book *On the Illustrious Men of that Monastery*: “The Wisdom of God opened his understanding, so that he might understand the Scriptures and treat of them with the greatest ease and the greatest usefulness.” And a little later: “He had this most praiseworthy custom: whenever he felt grace to be less present to him, he would cast himself cruciform upon the ground before the Lord, and ask of the Holy and True One, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens, that what was closed might be opened. To his humble seeking and faithful knocking, it was immediately opened, when, by a light wonderfully poured upon his understanding, he heard what the Lord God was speaking within him. For he had so enriched the man who loved him, so filled the treasury of his breast, that scarcely two or three scribes together could take down what he dictated. Once, in a vision of the night, he had seen the Wisdom of God—the Word of God—kissing him; its whole body, that is, seemed formed as if of the purest gold, and from it there projected on every side many pipes, which poured living waters violently into him.” With these words Reiner recounts Rupert’s grace.

But lest you suppose that Reiner, a fellow-monk, flattered his own man, hear how the most learned John Cochlaeus celebrates Rupert’s gift in his letter to Henry, abbot of Deutz: “Such and so great is that author Rupert,” whose works he was taking pains to publish [Col. 0088D], “that he not only instructs the reader with knowledge, makes him practiced in sacred letters, and makes him a scribe learned in the kingdom of heaven, but also kindles him to piety, prepares him for holiness of life, inflames him with divine love; he teaches him to think humbly, agree with the Church, and reverence prelates. He is truly the glory of Germany, a doctor genuinely substantial, an eminent ecclesiastical writer, who might not undeservedly be compared with the ancients, both Greek and Latin, in the exposition of sacred letters. For who among all writers has written more diligently, more clearly, and more abundantly on the Gospel and Apocalypse of John? Who has weighed every word so carefully? Who so explains and fortifies all things by the Scriptures? Splendid monuments of Chrysostom, Cyril, and Augustine on the Gospel of John indeed survive; yet our Rupert, aided by divine illumination, discovered after them many things worthy of being known—because he was a German. In his commentary on the Apocalypse he far surpassed all commentaries of all writers.”

Trithemius would have failed his native country, his order, and his own office, had he not presented our Rupert, his and ours, among ecclesiastical writers as especially rich beyond the rest in that singular gift. Thus in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he writes of Rupert: “Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne, of the Order of St Benedict, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit enlightening him through a vision, and not ignorant of secular letters; a monk of St Lawrence at Liège, from which he was taken by Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, because of his incredible learning [Col. 0089B], and raised to be abbot of the monastery of Deutz—he composed many outstanding little works. For from the time when he entered the monastery in his youth, he had so exercised himself in the sacred Scriptures that even while asleep he seemed unable to rest from meditating upon them, but his tongue and lips moved as though reading. He flourished in great holiness, resplendent in learning and miracles.”

In these words Trithemius portrayed Rupert, as if on a small panel. He adorns Rupert’s learning, faith, and holiness more fully in the oration he delivered, at the request of Dom Gerlac of Breitbach, abbot of Deutz, concerning Rupert. Because it is longer and is now prefixed to Rupert’s works [Col. 0089C], I shall transcribe only a few passages which more clearly reveal his heavenly understanding. “He always read,” says Trithemius of Rupert, “always wrote, always prayed, so that reading might take up prayer and prayer might conclude reading. The carefully composed little works which he wrote prove this, works in which instruction in every kind of knowledge is praised. While he was still less learned both in secular letters and in divine Scripture, through continual prayer and reading he asked God, with Solomon, for the gift of Wisdom; nor did he cease from the prayer he had begun [supply: *until*], until, the Holy Spirit inspiring him through a vision, he received most abundantly, beyond all his contemporaries, what he had desired. He was a most ardent lover of the ever-Virgin blessed Mary, through whose intercession he is believed to have obtained [Col. 0089D] so great a gift of wisdom. How greatly he advanced in reading the divine Scriptures is plainly shown by the thirteen books which he published *On the Victory of the Word of God* for Cuno, abbot of Siegburg. He also wrote on the Old Testament an outstanding work *On the Holy Trinity*; if you wish to read it, you will readily see what power he possessed in the sacred Scriptures. For enlightened by divine mercy, he was so powerful in expounding the sacred Scriptures that, held in the highest admiration by all, he was publicly acknowledged in his time to be a doctor of doctors. He taught the ignorant [Col. 0090A], corrected those in error, confounded heretics, and cast down the proud. Just as of old among the Syrians the blessed deacon and monk Ephrem was, through a vision of the Holy Spirit, established as an ardent teacher, so our Rupert, priest and abbot, was enlightened with the same faculty.” Thus Trithemius, in his oration in praise of Rupert of Deutz.

Sixtus of Siena, in the fourth book of the *Sacred Library*, also bears striking testimony concerning Rupert’s heavenly gift: “Rupert, abbot of Deutz near Cologne, Benedictine by profession, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, the Holy Spirit enlightening him through a vision.”

Yepes, in the *Chronicles of the Order of St Benedict*, under the year of Christ 536, says that Rupert, abbot of Deutz and distinguished doctor in the Church [Col. 0090B], flourished so greatly that he could have said with Paul in Galatians 1: “Neither did I receive it from men, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.”

Walter, in his *Chronology* under the year 1111, and Hugh Menard in the *Benedictine Martyrology* under 5 March, report of that holy doctor that, because he had an intellect too dull to advance in learning by any labour or study, he fled to the Mother of God. Granting Rupert’s prayers and appearing to him, she illuminated his understanding with such light that Germany was astonished, having no other man equal to him in searching out the secrets of Scripture.

Before all these, Honorius, priest and scholastic of Autun, had already summed up Rupert’s entire praise in fewer [Col. 0090C] but weightier words. In his book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the year 1124, he exalts Rupert in these few but lofty terms: “Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz, enlightened by the Holy Spirit through a vision, expounded almost all Scripture in an excellent style.”

Thus every age speaks of Rupert’s divinely infused understanding of sacred Scripture. Bellarmine alone, writing on ecclesiastical writers, passed it over in silence. He ought not to extol with praise one whom he wished to charge with error. The Centuriators [Note: [Col. 0089D] cited century] do indeed report it, but in order to ridicule it; for they regard as trifles the gift believed to have been granted by God to Rupert. [Col. 0090D] But who except one either ignorant or impious can ridicule the gift of heavenly understanding which all recognize and admire in Rupert, and of which his own writings speak? Fools blaspheme whatever they do not understand.

Yet I would not readily agree with Walter [Note: [Col. 0089D] place cited] and some others [Note: [Col. 0089D] Hugh Menard, place cited; Bucelinus in the *Menologium*; and Lanne, Benedictine, *In the Life of the Venerable Rupert*] that Rupert’s intellect was so dull that he was altogether incapable of learning. For what these writers, following Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0090D] in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and in the *Hirsau Chronicle*], put forward without warrant, I reject with ample justification and disprove by Rupert’s own testimony concerning himself.

[Col. 0091A] For in the twelfth book, after the middle, of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, in order more forcefully to restrain his rivals, who especially boasted of their teachers and of their knowledge of the liberal arts, as though this alone had been granted to them, Rupert speaks highly of his own study of the books of the liberal arts and of scholastic disciplines. Yet above all these he places the gift of the Most High, which he calls a visitation: “Although I too,” he says, “have had certain fathers in scholastic disciplines and have been no idle student in the books of the liberal arts, I confess this: a visitation from the Most High is better for me than ten such fathers,” etc.

To this testimony of Rupert speaking on his own behalf, I add this one point: Rupert is regarded as having been granted only an understanding of sacred Scripture. Were all other things, then, unknown to Rupert? Whence, therefore, did he possess an excellent command of Greek and Hebrew, such that he produced commentaries on the Book of Ecclesiasticus according to the Hebrew truth, and, from repeated reading of Jerome’s work according to the Seventy Interpreters, recognized it to be mutilated and misshapen—as he himself declares in the prologue to those commentaries?

Reiner therefore judged Rupert more correctly in his book *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of St Lawrence*, where he writes of Rupert while still young that, memory strengthening his intellect, he added labour as he added learning. Trithemius, too, thought more soundly of him when, speaking in Rupert’s praise, he declared him so learned in secular letters that whatever Rupert [Col. 0091C] did not know, another could readily be ignorant of: “For,” he says, “he was a man most learned in every respect, subtle in intellect, distinguished in knowledge,” etc. Finally, Matthias Agricius Witlichius also spoke more correctly and soundly in his *Declamation on Rupert*, saying “that he was endowed with the highest intellect and the greatest memory, and cultivated the studies of eloquence in an age plainly barbarous and removed from humane letters.”

But do not suppose that this commendation of Rupert’s intellect and memory detracts in any way from the divine gift. For that gift was not granted for liberal studies, but for an easy, ready, pure, and full understanding of sacred Scripture. Since this was the sign against which his opponents spoke, let Rupert himself speak for it; let him openly declare this gift of a more hidden grace, which one who does not possess it does not comprehend. Praise indeed becomes tarnished in one’s own mouth, and one who speaks of himself is readily believed false. But shall that which the one who received it can disclose to others remain hidden for ever? Shall John be judged a liar because he bears witness concerning himself, in order to bear witness to the Truth? Will you convict Paul of falsehood because he reveals the greatness of his revelations in order to strike down the mouths of gainsayers? Praise does not become worthless even in one’s own mouth if it is just and tends to the glory of him from whom all good comes. Nor can testimony be refuted or rejected which is true and which is borne [Col. 0092A] not so much to oneself as to the first and supreme Truth; rather, it ought to be admitted.

Therefore, although revelations made to the man of Deutz are not owed the same faith as the testimonies of Paul and John, let Rupert speak confidently of himself, and let the testimony of one speaking of himself be heard: testimony which he brought forth not voluntarily but reluctantly; not of his own accord but at the command of a priest of Christ, indeed under adjuration by the dread name of God; not for his own praise but for the correction of gainsayers; and finally not for his own glory but for the glory of truth. He committed it to writing for posterity, though he had entrusted it only to Cuno’s secrecy and fidelity.

Cuno, bishop of Regensburg [Note: [Col. 0091D] These are Rupert’s words in Book XII, chapter 26, *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, vol. III, p. 680], as Rupert himself relates, repeatedly required Rupert to write whence he had acquired that facility through which Cuno knew him [Col. 0092B] to expound the Scriptures almost without those preparations of the holy Fathers by which those intending to labour in scriptural study happily prepared themselves—as ministers of God—through vigils, fasts, and other good works. By the use of these, the human understanding is customarily made clear, so that we may deserve to walk with right sight through the holy and venerable Scriptures of Truth. But when Cuno obtained nothing from Rupert by bare request, he put around his neck a very great and strong bond by which to draw him, as Robert says: namely, the adjuration by the holy and dread Name, commanding him through the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to write these things.

Out of reverence for so great a Name, Rupert confesses this ability to interpret the Scriptures to be the consolation of God’s mercy, according to the good pleasure of his wisdom [Col. 0092C], and recounts it thus:

“For I was sorrowful, and as a boy or young man I went about bitter in spirit because of the tyranny of the devil, who had made his yoke heavy upon the children of the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. Having seized all of them in Adam, he led them captive to Babylon, in this wicked world, subject to original sin and liable to death. Lamenting, I praised the dead more than the living; not with just any lament, but with groaning lamentation, as though I already feared that what is said in the Gospel had happened to me: ‘Two shall be in one bed; one shall be taken and the other left’ [Matthew 24]. ‘I alone am left,’ I said, ‘and they seek my soul’; and with words of this kind I often sang the mournful song, ‘By the rivers of Babylon.’ While I was [Col. 0092D] in the midst of the captives beside the river Chebar, the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God. Awake, I saw the Son of Man himself living upon the cross. I did not see with bodily sight; rather, that I might see, the eyes of the body suddenly vanished, and better eyes—that is, inward eyes—were opened. I was holding and embracing a wooden cross, with the image of the same Saviour upon it, while I sat hidden behind the holy altar in a certain oratory of the ever-Virgin blessed Mary, at clear dawn. I fixed my eyes many times upon that same image and moved round it, adoring, as I was accustomed, with frequent bowing of my head. I was accustomed to do the same thing [Col. 0093A], but at that dawn I did it with greater contrition, that is, humility of mind. What his appearance was like, no human tongue can comprehend in words. I shall say only this: there I briefly felt how truly he himself says, ‘Learn of me, for I am meek and humble of heart’ [Matthew 11]; how truly the Apostle says of him that ‘he was heard because of his reverence’ [Hebrews 5]. In a wonderful and ineffable way his countenance inclined itself, signifying how favourably he received the kisses of one reverently looking upon him, and the adoration of one kissing him. There was no delay; and, returned to ordinary sight, I restored the cross to its place upon the altar. Yet a certain taste of his ineffable sweetness remained in the mouth of my soul for some time that day; gradually receding and finally failing, it nevertheless still makes me mindful of this verse: ‘Taste and see how sweet the Lord is’ [Psalm 33]. And what wonder if Truth speaks truly: ‘Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted’ [Matthew 5], and if the Paraclete—that is, the consoling Spirit—deigns to give his children the firstfruits of consolation already in this world? I shall therefore, in thanksgiving, say what consolation he afterward gave me as I persevered in that assembly of captives who said: ‘By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion’ [Psalm 136].”

This was Rupert’s first vision. While he was held in these afflictions, to the point of desiring, with the Apostle, to be dissolved and to be with Christ, he underwent a second vision, which he there relates as follows:

[Col. 0093C] “About the same time, after seeing a memorable vision full of modest sweetness, I was sorrowful and gave myself to sleep at the hour customary for prayer. The cause of my sorrow was that peace from the malicious persons rising against me had not come to me as quickly, nor in as great a measure, as I wished—as though we could ever be safe or secure while we live. Thus sorrowing like a child whose will is not immediately done, I gave myself to sleep at the usual hour of prayer. And behold, half awake in my very bed, I saw a great light like the sun resting upon me, and I heard the signal sounding in the church, as usually happens when we are called at the appointed time to prayer. I seemed to rise and run to prayer. Let it happen to me according to the voices or words which I heard: [Col. 0093D] one company of many persons unknown to me sang in one part of the church Psalm 50, ‘Have mercy on me, O God’; another company in another part of the church sang Psalm 26, ‘The Lord is my light.’ A malignant adversary stood against me in the corner at the entrance of the oratory. When I saw him, I reproached him, as we are accustomed to reproach some phantom appearance, rather by the gesture of my whole face than with words. Because of this he rushed at me in anger, and I was awakened from that light sleep. I could understand that these things were happening for my consolation. Nevertheless I spent that whole day also in sorrow; and at the dawn, or pre-dawn hour, of the next day—here Rupert begins to recount the Lord’s third visitation, by which the understanding of Scripture was given him and the office of writing entrusted to him—I omitted my accustomed prayer and, sorrowing, surrendered myself to sleep. And behold, while lightly asleep, it seemed to me, as on the preceding day, that the signal for prayer was sounded. I rose and ran to the church; and behold, as if for the Lord’s solemn feast, a great crowd of diverse orders filled the church, while a bishop of venerable white hair celebrated the solemn rites of the Mass. A great procession of venerable persons of both sexes went up to make offerings, as if after the Gospel, when the holy sacrifice is customarily offered. I too ran as though to ask alms from those offerings; and behold, beside the right wing of the altar stood three persons of most reverend bearing and dignity, such as no tongue can attain in words. [Col. 0094B] Two of the persons were very old—that is, very white-haired; the third stood there as a handsome young man, recognizable from his clothing as possessing royal dignity. One of the persons, as I said, of venerable white hair, with most gracious condescension and a serene countenance took my hand, kissed me, and spoke a few words. I did not retain them in memory, though I know they concerned the office or ministry of writing. Those three persons, equal in great and matching stature, stood around me, a little one; and, opening a very great book, they raised me aloft as I stood upon that book. When this had been done, he who had first kissed me, strengthening me graciously and familiarly, said: ‘Do not fear.’ Then, pointing out upon the holy altar certain reliquaries [Col. 0094C] of saints worked in gold, which we commonly call shrines, he said: ‘For you shall yet be better than these are.’

“This vision was so manifest that I may truly say: ‘Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows’ [2 Corinthians 12]. For when I was led to see, I know that I left my bed and ran to the church by the usual direct route, awake and alert. When the vision was complete and I wished to follow those departing persons, but was not allowed to do so, I saw that I was naked and without any clothing. For that reason, running back more quickly to the place from which I had come, the moment I touched my bed, I immediately awoke.

“Concerning the opening of the book and the statement made by that person while showing the golden memorials or reliquaries [Col. 0094D] of the saints, there is no need for me to give an interpretation to your charity, whose judgment concerning me many have often heard and followed: namely, that God truly opened his book—that is, sacred Scripture—to me, and that I have said things somewhat better than many sayings of the holy Fathers, whose memory is honourably celebrated in the holy Church and gleams like gold.”

Finally, he describes thus how he received the overflowing Holy Spirit through a vision: “It was the night before the day which Christian religion calls the Beginning of the Fast, on which it is customary solemnly to sprinkle heads with ashes. Lightly asleep, I seemed to be speaking with a friend who asked why I was so earnestly concerned to seek or discover [Col. 0095A] such a thing: namely, whether I would depart this life in that year. I replied that it was, as indeed it is, a great matter. Although I desired it because of the many perils of sins which occur here, I knew that greater expenditures were necessary if I were in any measure to prepare for departure. When I had said such things, suddenly, having moved a little away from the person to whom I was speaking, I saw the heavens above seem to open slightly; and from there something like a luminous talent of ineffable, living substance was swiftly sent down, more swiftly than speech. Falling into my breast, it immediately shook me out of sleep by its greatness or weight—heavier than gold, sweeter than honey. In a wonderful and ineffable manner floods came round me, one after another, and poured themselves in, until [Col. 0095B] at last the final infusion, like some great overflowing river, gave me to understand and made me feel that the whole receptacle of my soul or heart was full and could receive no more.

“Behold, in this I have obeyed the name of the Lord by which you adjured me, venerable bishop: I have written to you how I received this faculty in the sacred Scriptures, concerning which you never wished to doubt that it was from the grace or Spirit of God. I was so consoled, and the hope which he gave me in his Word so consoled me in my humility, that I do not doubt that the saying of Christ, Son of God, giver of that same hope, occurred to me: ‘From his belly shall flow rivers of living water.’ . . . . ‘Let your spring be blessed; rejoice with the wife of your youth’; find consolation in every study or exercise of sacred Scripture. For this is that woman, Wisdom; this is the woman whom, in dreams, you saw me take as my wife, and whose sons you embraced as born to me from her—which you surely do when you gladly read my writings. I shall not pass over what beginning I made, what first voice I uttered after that overflowing of the river which I have described: when I wrote a little book of hymns in praise of the Holy Spirit. Listen attentively, as is your custom: ‘To the great river,’ etc.”

These are the firstfruits of gifts which the Holy Spirit poured out upon Rupert while he was still young. Yet in him the saying, “Let your spring be blessed,” was not yet fulfilled; for he had not yet received [Col. 0095D] the order of priesthood, nor, as he says, had he yet received the lawful opening of his mouth. Meanwhile, as he fearfully reflected in his heart how he might anticipate the day of the Lord and kept the eternal days in mind, sweet sleep came upon him as he slept; in it he felt the inward meanings of the Word opened to him through a vision, which I learn from him.

> “I saw,” he says, “as I stood before the altar, the Lord’s cross standing upon it in the middle, and upon it the image of the Lord and Savior. When I looked upon him more attentively, I recognized the Lord Jesus himself there, crucified and living, with his eyes open and fixed upon me. When I perceived this, immediately bowing my face, I said to him: ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Matt. XI) [lacuna]. This was not enough for me, unless I might take him in my hands [Col. 0096A] and embrace and kiss him; but what could I do? The altar was too high for me to reach him. Therefore, when he saw such a thought or desire in me, he also willed it; for I felt that he willed it, and by the nod of his will the altar itself opened in the middle, and received me as I ran within. When I had hastened inside, I took hold of him whom my soul loves; I held him, I embraced him, I embraced him for a long time. I felt how profoundly he admitted this taste of love, when, while I was kissing him, he himself opened his mouth so that I might kiss more deeply [lacuna]. When I had returned to myself, and in the night watches most sweetly reconsidered such a vision, and thus interpreted that opening of the altar and of the very mouth of the Lord Jesus to mean that I ought thereafter to understand more clearly the depths of his sacraments, meanwhile love of that priestly office gradually poured itself into me and grew so greatly that, when day had come, I told my spiritual Father that I was no longer willing to resist, but wished to go as soon as he should command and to receive the Lord’s yoke—while keeping silent the reason for what had occurred. He rejoiced; and when the time for ordination first arrived, I received this sacred order, though unworthy.”

But the mercy of God which had preceded Rupert in order to advance him to the sacred order of the priesthood followed him even more abundantly once he had been placed in Christ’s priesthood. I speak from his own testimony:

> “Nor,” says Rupert, “did my God, my mercy, follow me [Col. 0096C] in this office with a lesser sign than that by which he had preceded me.”

He himself explains what that more abundant mercy was:

> “For scarcely thirty days had passed when, behold, as I lay in bed, the day being almost ended, and when I had scarcely closed my eyes in sleep, there came down from above something like the likeness of a man bent forward and stretched out evenly, concealing only his face most completely. Descending into me, it filled the whole substance of my soul, being impressed upon me in a manner which I cannot at all express in words—far more swiftly and deeply than any softest wax can receive a strongly impressed seal. Yet it may truly be said that, unless that sudden flood of holy delight had quickly restrained itself, it would swiftly have drawn the soul from the body in the manner of a torrent [Col. 0096D] into its own being. But, as I said, that inundating force of love quickly stopped and gradually withdrew. From that time I opened my mouth, and I have never been able to cease writing; and even now, if I wished, I cannot be silent.”

Whoever hears Rupert thus speaking of himself and of the gift of heavenly understanding granted to him may perhaps think that he is boasting of himself too insolently. But he who forbids glorying in oneself wills that glorying be in the Lord. Rupert commends not his own goods, nor himself, but God’s goods. Should he conceal this heavenly gift entrusted to him, which he alone knows? Is not a gift given in vain to one who denies from whom it was given? And what human boasting is there in matters which Rupert kept secret for a long time and disclosed only when commanded, only when adjured under the dreadful [Col. 0097A] name of God, out of reverence for that adorable name and from the great necessity of defending truth and repelling calumny?

You may marvel at Rupert’s restraint and religious scruple in concealing this gift: to his spiritual Father he declared himself ready to receive the Lord’s yoke in sacred orders, while keeping silent the grace of the Holy Spirit overflowing upon him; and even when, writing on the Song of Songs, he interpreted the words, “My beloved put forth his hand,” etc., as referring to that overflowing sweetness of divine consolation, he did so not under his own name but as though in the person of another.

> [Note: As he relates in *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, book XII, chapter 26.]

Such was Rupert’s modesty in revealing his secret that he scarcely whispered it even to Cuno, who often urged him to write; and, as to a friend, he disclosed only sparingly what he had learned by experience concerning the manner of speech by which the Beloved is accustomed to speak to holy and beloved souls.

> “Truly I would not dare,” he says, “but I have not feared to say this into your ear, O my friend Cuno, you who yourself often urge me to write; and let it be enough to have said this: that indeed, even if I should wish to be silent or to cease from the pursuit of writing, I am unable; and I know and clearly perceive that this is not granted to me. I have learned that he is true.”

> [Note: Book VII of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.]

You might therefore say that Rupert’s whole art and study consisted in concealing this one thing granted him by God, and in keeping silent concerning the one thing which others proclaimed about him.

Up to this point he wished it to remain a secret to himself, which he made public only when commanded, only when adjured by Cuno, and only when compelled by the necessity of defending truth and faith and repelling calumny.

> [Note: Book XII, chapter 26, of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.]

> “Some people,” says Rupert, [Col. 0097C] “thinking that they properly do what is said in Job: ‘The wise confess and do not conceal their fathers, to whom alone the land was given; no stranger shall pass among them’ (Job XV), once afflicted my soul, crushed me with words, and pierced me no fewer than ten times (Job XIX). Nor were they ashamed to oppress me because I resisted certain opinions which they advanced, opinions diverging from the true and sound sense, though they seemed to have received them from their great and highly renowned fathers—that is, their masters. These fathers [Col. 0097D] they thought it glorious to confess and not conceal. When I would not yield to the authority of those fathers, who were men, however wise, but dared to speak better and more soundly according to the authority of the Scriptures—oh, what indignation, what reproach followed, after this fashion! ‘Why does your spirit swell against God, that you utter such words from your mouth? The wise confess and do not conceal their fathers’ (Job XV). ‘Where are your fathers? What or what sort of masters taught you?’ By such things and others like them they pierced and oppressed me with words, not once or for a few days, but many times and for several years, until, supported by the strength of perseverance and the authority of the Scriptures, I gained the palm of victory—with your very great assistance, however, and your testimony that this had not come to me from swelling of spirit or presumption of my own heart, but from the gift of the Lord’s grace and the condescension of the Holy Spirit: namely, that I should have such confidence in treating the mysteries of the holy Scriptures, and that I could by no means have attained this ability except through the good Spirit, from whom, or through whom, all good things proceed.”

> [Note: Against these men Rupert wrote *On the Will and Omnipotence of God* and the *Apologeticus*, which is the first book in the *Rule of St. Benedict*.]

Thus Rupert sets the divine gift of understanding against his detractors, who were said to speak from human judgment; [Col. 0098B] thus he glories in having God as his teacher, in order more forcefully to restrain opponents who contemptuously assailed his writings as though they possessed no authority and foolishly swore by the words of their own masters.

> “How do you know?” his rivals reproached him, “that you conceived from the presence of the Lord, so that you speak as one in labor of the things you have written?”

> [Note: As he relates near the end of book I on the Rule of our holy Father Benedict.]

By what could Rupert have more forcefully crushed their mouths than by the gift of heavenly understanding, before which earthly, animal, and devilish wisdom must necessarily yield? Yet he still did not wish to disclose his secret; by the modesty of silence he wished to restrain their insolence:

> “But this—my secret—is mine, my secret is mine.”

Does this silence do injury to his faith and truth, and indeed to this divine gift? Against so many enemies raging [Col. 0098C] against him, he proves the truth of his faith and teaching by these words:

> “Tamar was defended by fitting evidences, saying: ‘By the man to whom these things belong I have conceived; recognize whose are the signet, bracelet, and staff’ (Gen. XXXVIII). You too, if you wish, recognize whether or not there are in my writings the ring of faith, the staff of hope, and the bracelet of charity; and hear my soul saying: ‘By the man to whom these things belong I have conceived.’ For I recall something also as having been sensibly done within me, so that I may say without doubt that this endowment or gift descends from above, from the Father of lights.”

By this single authority of a divine gift those who murmured against Rupert could have been restrained.

Finally, lest that heavenly gift, which ought to have restrained envy, should provoke it, Rupert, after recounting his visions, entreats that

> “whoever reads these things may not mock me as a fool, but may consider them with compassion, as the cause of a sorrowful little child.”

> [Note: Book XII of *On the Glory of the Son of Man*.]

For if Rupert wished to glory in the Lord, he was not a fool; for he spoke the truth, which he confirmed even by this oath:

> “If I have spoken truth, if I have invented none of these things from my heart, may the name of the Lord—by which you have adjured me, my Father and lord—be a most strong tower to me.”

As though he were saying: “It is so; and may God so help me.” These words have the force of the oath by which Berengar had abjured his errors.

Let, therefore, that testimony of Rupert concerning this heavenly gift of divine wisdom and perfect understanding of the sacred Scriptures stand firm: a testimony which Rupert disclosed, wrote down, and confirmed by an oath—not through the vanity of human boasting, but from obedience, because he was righteous; from religious duty, because he had been adjured by a bishop; and from observance of faith and Scripture, because he had been compelled by the need to defend truth and faith.

Let stand firm, I say, what so many aforementioned authors have testified with much faith and reason concerning Rupert: namely, that, enlightened by the divine light, instructed by the anointing of the Holy Spirit, and furnished with the wisdom of the word of God, he expounded the sacred Scriptures. [Col. 0099B] But if these things stand firm, who can maintain that Rupert not only failed to attain understanding of Scripture, but even dragged Scripture into erroneous senses and taught heretical doctrines contrary to Scripture? What fellowship has light with darkness, truth with falsehood, or the Spirit of God with error?

From that understanding of sacred Scripture thus poured out upon Rupert, who would not conclude beforehand how pure Rupert’s faith was, how sound his teaching, and how foreign to him were the errors which not a few attribute to Rupert? Perhaps you are surprised that I have said that errors are attributed to Rupert, to whom God opened the understanding that he might understand the Scriptures, and whom I undertake to vindicate from them.

Lest, therefore, I seem to be one who invents wars in order to gain the palm of a fictitious contest, without any wound, by easily defeating enemies who in fact do not exist, I shall set before you several persons who attacked Rupert’s faith by forcibly twisting his words into diverse errors; I shall set forth those errors attributed to Rupert, [Col. 0100B] and shall then vindicate him from them.

## Second Part of the Apologies for Rupert, Abbot of Deutz: Rupert Vindicated from Errors

[Col. 0099]

The first is that in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood there is nothing but a figure and shadow of the body and blood. Wyclif attributes this opinion [Col. 0099C] to the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*, which we have established to be Rupert’s.

The second is that Christ’s true body is eaten only by worthy persons, or those possessing faith. Our man of Deutz is accused of this error by Bellarmine in book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Rupert, second observation:

> “Bellarmine says that he understands the Virgin’s childbirth to remain in human beings through faith, not in reality.”

And by Vásquez, in III, distinction 80, chapter 1, where, among other things, he writes of Rupert:

> “Finally, the author of the books *On the Divine Offices* teaches that ungodly men in communion receive only the *corpus panaceum*—that is, the substance of bread—whereas the godly receive both, that is, bread and Christ’s human body.”

[Col. 0099D] The third error attributed to Rupert is the one now followed by the Lutherans: namely, that the substance of bread and wine is not converted into Christ’s body and blood, but that Christ’s true body and blood are in the sacrament together with bread and wine. Bellarmine, Vásquez, and other recent writers attribute this error of impanation to Rupert; before them, Waldensis did so; and John of Paris himself, if we believe Waldensis, thought that the author of the books *On the Divine Offices* held the opinion which asserted

> “that after consecration several bodies and hypostases remain in the Eucharist: [Col. 0100B] one of bread, the other of Christ; and that Christ is thus impanated, being joined to bread merely by relation, as to a garment.”

Claude also wrote most recently concerning Rupert’s faith:

> “Neither Anastasius, nor Damascene, nor Rupert ever taught a change of substance,” etc.

> [Note: *Response to the First Treatise on the Perpetuity of Faith concerning the Eucharist*, pp. 28–29.]

The fourth and final error is that bread and wine remain in the sacrament together with Christ’s body and blood in such a way that bread and wine are hypostatically united to the Word, and by the power of this union become one body with Christ’s flesh and blood. Bellarmine identifies this error of hypostatic impanation as Rupert’s own in these words:

> “Rupert’s error consists in this: that he thought that bread is not converted into Christ’s body when the Eucharist is made, but assumed by the Lord Word, just as humanity was assumed.”

> [Note: This judgment of Bellarmine was imprudently followed by Valerius Andreas in his *Bibliotheca Belgica*, under Rupert; Possevinus in the *Apparatus*; Theophilus Raynaud in the *Syntaxis* of the first part of the opuscula of St. Anselm; and other recent writers.]

And Vásquez, setting forth various errors against the truth of the eucharistic sacrament, gives the opinion

> “which, as he says, recent scholastics commonly attribute to Rupert, abbot of Deutz, as its first author: namely, that bread remains in the Eucharist together with Christ’s body, hypostatically united to the Lord Word, just as humanity itself is.”

He adds that this is held to be an error in Rupert’s Commentary on John; and that there can be no doubt that Rupert was the first author of this error, if it is established that the work *On the Divine Offices* came from him. Finally, Claude held it certain that Rupert thought this:

> “It is evident,” says Claude, “that Rupert, who seems to have followed Damascene, holds this opinion—of the assumption of bread—and clearly taught it.”

> [Note: The cited book, and below, in the *Response to the Second Treatise*, p. 284.]

Thus four errors are enumerated: figurative presence of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament; their eating by faith; impanation; and the hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word. By a hasty and blind judgment, the crowd of theologians has stained the most pure faith of holy Rupert with these errors; and from them we shall clear him by a more equitable judgment.

## Rupert of Deutz Vindicated from Every Error

Against this crowd of theologians, from whom we have seen Rupert’s supposed errors rashly denounced, it should be enough to set the many cited testimonies of celebrated writers and eminent theologians—namely Honorius of Autun, Trithemius, Reynerius, John Cochlaeus, Sixtus of Siena, Nicholas Sander, and others of this sort—concerning Rupert’s uncorrupted faith, sound teaching, and heavenly understanding in expounding the sacred Scriptures.

For which of these men notes even a blemish in the works of most learned Rupert? Indeed, which does not commend the learning and writings of that holy doctor, and especially the books *On the Divine Offices*, from which Rupert’s opponents chiefly try to extract his supposed errors? Alberic praises them highly in this single expression:

> “Rupert, or Rubert, prior of St. Lawrence at [Col. 0101C] Liège, who wrote the famous book *On the Divine Offices throughout the Year* and many other works.”

> [Note: In the *Great Chronicle*.]

I know indeed that the word “famous” is often taken in a bad sense; but I also know that it should be taken in a good sense when an author is celebrated.

Cochlaeus himself, the most vigorous defender of Catholic truth against the Lutherans, restored to light those works of Rupert, *On the Divine Offices* and the commentaries on John’s Gospel, in which unfair critics claim that Rupert anticipated Lutheran errors. Yet from these very works Cochlaeus adorns Rupert’s faith and teaching with the most ample praises in his letter to Henry, abbot of Deutz, in the year 1526, as we cited above. How could the strongest defender of the faith against Luther’s impious novelties be believed to have published, under the name of a Catholic doctor, works which proclaimed and defended Luther’s errors, to the utter ruin of the Catholic faith?

You would therefore have to say either that Cochlaeus was wholly blind—which the acuity of both his eyes, namely of faith and doctrine, forbids us to say—or that he cruelly raged against the Church in publishing these works of Rupert, which anticipated Luther’s errors. The sincere faith of so great a doctor and his burning zeal for the faith against Luther do not permit us even to think this of Cochlaeus. More truly, therefore, and more fairly, you will judge that no error is found in these works of Rupert, and that nothing but Catholic doctrine was written by Rupert, whom Cochlaeus thinks he has sufficiently praised by calling him an ecclesiastical writer.

Add to these the great diligence of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, and Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, in studying Rupert’s works, without any suspicion of error ever arising; so much so that they not only devoted themselves wholly to Rupert’s writings, but also earnestly urged him to write, as may be seen from the prologues to the book on the Apocalypse, the book *On the Glory of the Son of Man*, the book *On the Victory of the Word*, the book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*, and others.

Add what Rupert was called even while alive: the man who asked him about the violation of virginity calls him outstanding in every wisdom of morals and doctrine.

> [Note: Rupert, in the book *On the Violation of Virginity*.]

Add that Rupert offered to Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, [Col. 0102B] the work *On the Divine Offices*—where, if there is any error, it is found—as the first-fruits of the land which the Lord had given him, together with his other works on Exodus, John, and so forth. He presented them against eloquent rivals as testimony to his sincere faith.

> [Note: Letter to Bishop Cuno, and in the *Apologeticus*.]

Indeed, he himself dedicates this little work *On the Sacraments*, or *On the Divine Offices*, divided into twelve books, to the supreme pontiff, together with his Commentaries on Exodus and John and his other works, “thinking and wishing them to be thought,” he says,

> “like wood by which the fire of charity or love may be fed on the altar of the Lord—in the heart of any reader or hearer who, by reading or hearing, desires to make progress in love of the Lord’s name.”

And in his letter to the Roman pontiff he writes freely [Col. 0102C] that

> “it has always been lawful, and always will be lawful, for anyone to say, without prejudice to the faith, what he thinks.”

With what face would Rupert have uttered these things to the Roman pontiff? With what faith would he have asserted as his own, and dedicated to the Roman pontiff as incentives to divine charity, works which taught throughout so many books and pages the heresy of Berengar, recently condemned and destroyed by the Apostolic See—namely, the works on Exodus, John’s Gospel, and *On the Divine Offices*, from which Bellarmine and Vásquez attribute to the man of Deutz the errors stated above? Let someone other than I, and other than any prudent Catholic, believe that most devout Rupert had cast off all shame in order to say these things, and had abandoned all faith [Col. 0102D] in order to renew Berengar’s heresy, which he knew to have been condemned, and to present it most shamelessly to the Roman pontiff.

Are these not enough—indeed, more than enough—to refute the attacks of recent theologians against Rupert’s faith and teaching? His raging opponents could not discover even in his work *On the Divine Offices* anything concerning the most august sacrament of Christ’s body and blood which their biting envy could censure. Yet they openly condemned everything which seemed to them to have been said less than Catholicly, proclaiming Rupert’s doctrine heretical.

[Col. 0103A] By this single fact Rupert’s sincere faith is established and vindicated from the errors imputed to him: the very envy which attacked Rupert’s faith becomes its defender. I shall make the matter clearer. When Rupert had most sharply refuted the error of those who taught that God wills the evil of guilt just as much as the good of virtue, they searched Rupert’s writings more eagerly, wishing to find something which they might cast at him so as to stain him with some heretical blemish, in revenge for the reproach which, in the controversy over the will of God, they complained had been cast upon them by him.

> [Note: Rupert’s words in the *Apologeticus*.]

At last they thought they had found something in their search and began for a time to rejoice like enemies because he had said that angels were created from darkness—a statement which they called manifest heresy. Yet Rupert shows it to be altogether consonant with the sacred Scriptures. One prelate and preacher too, but, as Rupert says, almost never a subject or hearer, amiably requested from Rupert, ostensibly out of zeal for reading, that he be given some of Rupert’s works; Rupert gave him the little work *On the Divine Offices*. He received it, went away, and read as much and as long as he wished; and behold, he proclaimed the book heretical and fit to be burned in flames. On what grounds, do you suppose? Because it denied transubstantiation? Because it taught that Christ’s body is not eaten by the ungodly? Because it called Christ *panaceus*, that is, impanated? Because it taught that bread is hypostatically united to the Word? The book was not proclaimed heretical on any of these grounds; it was not said to deserve burning on any of them. This rival put one chapter of this book before a more ignorant populace, and whispered to each person, as if groaning, [Col. 0103C] that Rupert had set forth a heretical proposition in it. Which proposition? That Christ’s body and blood are in the sacrament only shadowily and figuratively? That Christ’s body and blood are received not by real eating but by eating of faith alone? That bread and wine remain there together with Christ’s body and blood? That bread and wine are hypostatically united to the Word in the sacrament? He attributed none of such heretical propositions to Rupert; but only this one: that the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary. From this alone an envious mind could malign Rupert’s faith, crying out

> “that therefore the world would perish, because such things were being written.”

> [Note: As Rupert complains in the *Apologeticus*.]

[Col. 0103D] But how great the malice or ignorance of this calumny was became clear to all from Rupert’s own words, so that this commentator, convicted of the manifest wickedness of falsehood, withdrew. Would that, by the argument drawn from this calumny, those who think Rupert anticipated the Lutherans—especially in the very work *On the Divine Offices*—might be convicted and covered with shame for their unjust judgment, and might think more truly and more Catholicly concerning Rupert, once they observe that the clamorous envy of his rivals found nothing in Rupert’s works, not even in that book *On the Divine Offices*, against the truth of the eucharistic sacrament upon which it could rush.

If Rupert had errors, they did not escape those who, in order to ensnare him in his speech, weighed his words on a deceitful balance. Sparing Rupert’s name was not the intention of those who, burning against him, fabricated a new error and proclaimed him a heretic. Why, then, did they not summon Rupert to judgment concerning these errors against the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, if his writings display even the faintest shadow of any one of them? That age undoubtedly had a clearer understanding of sound faith in those very passages which later criticism twisted toward heretical senses.

Thus recent writers argue errors in Rupert’s works with greater envy, or at least greater rashness, than the more biting envy could find there; but more discerning understanding knows them to be wholly foreign to Rupert’s mind, [Col. 0104B] teaching, and faith. Since, however, to have shown indefinitely that our man of Deutz was free from every error is insufficient for his complete defense, we shall vindicate Rupert separately from each of the errors attributed to him.

## Rupert Defended against the Error of the Shadow-Theorists

It is shown that he neither believed nor taught anywhere that the Eucharist is a figure of Christ’s body and blood; rather, that he attacked this error and asserted and defended the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine.

Wyclif, in order to put a mask upon his error, falsely invented that the orthodox author of the books *On the Divine Offices*, whom we have established to be Rupert, denied the presence of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine, and held that in the sacrament of the Eucharist there is nothing but bread and wine; so that for him it was nothing else than a type and figure of Christ’s body and blood.

It is a religious duty to refute this impious lie of Wyclif, lest, transferring his heretical dogmas to Catholic doctors, he deceive the unwary under a Catholic name; and Christian justice commands us to dispel this first calumny against Rupert’s faith, for it does not permit one who defended the Church’s truth and meaning to be torn away from her unity and bosom.

From the very source from which Rupert’s faith is condemned, it is acquitted; and from that work which was corrupted against it, sincere testimonies are brought forth in its favor. They accuse Rupert of this first error from the work *On the Divine Offices*; from [Col. 0104D] that same work Rupert’s Catholic faith concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine is established.

In chapter 6 of book I, Christ is said to have written his Testament while borne in his own hands:

> “In the evening the Lord, taking bread and wine and representing the reality of his body and blood, writes his Testament while borne in his own hands, for his heirs: namely, humility and charity.”

And in chapter 17, discussing the ministry of the altar and distinguishing reality from sign, he says:

> “What was promised, prefigured, and saluted from afar in the Old Testament, but in the New was given, revealed, and made manifest, is here presented in its presence—not [Col. 0105A] in shadow but in reality, not in figure but in the thing itself. Here that is enacted in which our David seemed mad before King Achish, when he beat the drum while hanging on the cross and struck against the gates of the city—that is, against the closed hearts of those not believing in him—when he was borne in his own hands, holding bread and wine and saying: ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD, the New Testament,’” etc.

He treats this more fully in chapter 19 of book V of *On the Divine Offices*, where he elucidates by this interpretation the words of Psalm 33, “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord”:

> “This is taken from Psalm 33, whose title reads: ‘A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and was borne in his own hands, and dismissed [Col. 0105B] him, and departed.’ It is well known in the sacred Scriptures, and has already been said by us, that David—that is, ‘strong of hand’ and ‘beloved’—who fled Saul’s persecution and came to Achish, here called Abimelech, and changed his countenance before him and was borne in his own hands, signified the Lord Jesus. Before Abimelech, which means ‘the kingdom of my father,’ that is, before the Jews, he changed his countenance, that is, the rite of sacrifice, when, after the lamb of the old Passover had already been sacrificed, he took bread and wine and was borne in his own hands, saying: ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.’ This was done on this day of remission and grace—Thursday, at the Lord’s Supper, when penitents are reconciled to the Church. Therefore, when so great a High Priest stands before God the Father, [Col. 0105C] holding bread and wine and inviting all to the banquet of his BODY and BLOOD,” etc.

But when was Christ borne in his own hands, except when, taking bread and wine, he changed them into his true body and his blood, made bread his own flesh and wine his true blood, transforming these elements by the power of the word by which he said, “THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD,” as Rupert himself states in several passages to be produced below?

When is Christ borne in his own hands, except—as Augustine, with the same mind as Rupert, explains the same words of Psalm 33—when, commending his own body, he says, “THIS IS MY BODY”?

> “For he bore that body in his own hands. And he was borne in his own hands. How was he borne in his own hands? Because, when he commended his own body and blood, he took into his own hands what the faithful know; and in some manner he bore himself when he said: ‘THIS IS MY BODY.’”

> [Note: Augustine, sermon on Psalm LXIII.]

> [Note: Augustine, Sermon 2, section 3, on the same Psalm.]

What then? Does he deny the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament who separates the thing or reality of that body and blood from the figures and shadows of the former Testament? Does he divide Christ’s true body and blood from the sacrament who, with Augustine, adores in Christ’s hands the true body and blood of Christ, as the faithful know? Christ, bearing himself in his own hands, [Col. 0106A] bore and offered to his disciples not a figure, not a shadow, but the reality of his body and blood, saying: “THIS IS MY BODY.”

If this one testimony from such a work should not suffice to establish his faith—though it is indeed a proof of faith—another is produced from book II, chapter 2. There, explaining the offering of the Mass, or, as they call it, the offertory, he expressly professes that

> “bread and wine are changed into the TRUE BODY and BLOOD of the Lord.”

He also condemns as unbelievers those who, seeing in this sacrifice nothing beyond bread and wine, murmur when it is said to them, “This is the body and blood of the Lord,” asking, “How is this so?” He suppresses their murmur by teaching them that

> “if [Col. 0106B] the priest pours out the river of the Word over bread and wine, the Word of God immediately receives bread and wine from the holy altar so as to change them into his BODY and BLOOD.”

The one and same body is received from the Virgin Mary and from the altar. Finally:

> “It is one body: that which, born of Mary, hung on the cross, and that which, offered daily on the holy altar, renews for us the Lord’s passion itself.”

These statements surely possess a meaning too evident to be subject to any doubtful interpretation. They are proofs of faith that admit not even the shadow of the error of the Shadow-Theorists.

No less established and no less explicit are the words read in chapter 5 of the same book:

> “On Thursday, when the agony was now near, he writes his Testament for his heirs, entrusting to them the treasure [Col. 0106C] of his body and blood. By the truly living stream of the divine Word flowing upon bread and wine, we receive as true a divinity and as true a humanity of Christ, seated and reigning in heaven, as truly as we can almost daily change the true substance of fire by placing a small crystal sphere beneath the sun.”

These are Rupert’s words. But Christ does not entrust to us the treasure of his body—rather, he deceives us—if he hands over only a figure and shadow of the body. Far be this from the Truth, which, since it can neither lie nor deceive anywhere, must be believed, when it says that it entrusts to us the treasure of the body, to have entrusted to its Church the very reality of the body, by which we are enriched, not a shadow by which we are deceived. If we receive in the sacrament the humanity of Christ which is in heaven as truly [Col. 0106D] as we receive the substance of fire in crystal, what doubt is there, in Rupert’s own judgment, that Rupert believed and taught that Christ’s true humanity—the very humanity which sits and reigns in heaven—is present in the sacrament in reality?

Add to these the words of chapter 16 of book II, in which Rupert explains the rite of breaking the host, performed by the priest while saying, “The peace of the Lord be always with you”:

> “Meanwhile the priest, holding the body of the Lord—because he is recognized in the breaking of bread—by a threefold breaking assigns his offering to the holy Trinity; and he plunges into the sacred blood one particle, signifying the person of the Son.”

Who, upon hearing this, would not voluntarily abandon every suspicion concerning Rupert’s faith which he may have conceived from false rumor? Who, hearing that the Lord’s body is held in the priest’s hands and that a particle of the host is dipped and plunged into the sacred blood, would judge that not the body but a shadow, not blood but a figure, is shown in the sacrament? He therefore deceives himself and others who imputes to Rupert the error of a mere figure.

Even if the injury of this calumny has not yielded to these considerations, let Rupert himself be heard attacking this invention of a merely figurative presence of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrament, and overthrowing the theory of a sign alone from the very words of the Lord. In chapter twenty-two of the same second book he says:

> “In that which is consecrated, not even the very individual body of the Lord is signified; for the Lord does not signify this, but says: [Col. 0107B] THIS IS MY BODY.”

What have these statements in common with Wyclif, Calvin, and the rest who teach that in the sacrament there is only a figure of Christ’s body? What could be stronger or more explicit against that impious doctrine in favour of the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament? What could be more consonant with the Holy Fathers—Cyril of Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 0107D] In the Catechesis.] and others—who teach us this truth from these words of Christ? What, then, more completely overturns sign and figure and more firmly establishes the truth of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament than that no one born for falsehood, calumny, or error who reads these things could say or think that the author of this work *On the Divine Offices* not only failed to affirm but denied that truth?

[Col. 0107C] I would consider it superfluous to add more, unless another rule taught me that an abundance of proof does no harm. Accordingly, while turning over the sixth book of *On the Divine Offices*, in chapter twenty-three, “On Good Friday,” I find these words:

> “After the cross has been saluted, two priests carry the Lord’s body to the altar; when the chalice is elevated with the Lord’s body, it is said: ‘Through all ages,’” etc.

He interprets this rite mystically as follows:

> “Now it must be said that the two priests who carry the Lord’s body to the altar signify Joseph,” etc.

And:

> “But we have communicated in silence; yet that blood which we receive cries to God from our mouth,” etc.

Finally, in chapter sixteen of the last book, he says that “through the food of his body and the drink of his blood, Christ procures life and preservation for the souls [Col. 0107D] of his spiritual children.”

Did Wyclif, Calvin, and the other advocates of shadows ever speak in this way about Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament? Does one who denies the reality of Christ’s body and blood on the altar, and acknowledges only a shadow of body and blood, speak thus?

He who writes that the Lord’s body is carried to the altar; who notes that the chalice is elevated with the Lord’s body; who reminds us that the blood which we receive at the altar cries to God from our mouths, alluding to the words concerning Abel’s blood, “The blood of your brother cries out to me from the ground”; who, furthermore, says that through the food of Christ’s body and the drink of his blood, Christ provides life and preservation for souls—how could such a man fail to have held and affirmed [Col. 0108A] the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar? In what more forceful words have the Holy Fathers handed down to us the truth of this sacrament? Let the slanderer therefore be ashamed of his slander, and no longer assail the sound teaching of this work *On the Divine Offices* or its author’s Catholic faith.
