From this work *On the Divine Offices*—the work on whose basis Rupert’s critics most particularly complain against Rupert’s faith—it is sufficiently demonstrated that he upheld the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar, and consequently defended Rupert’s Catholic faith. Yet, since there are those who attribute the twelve books *On the Divine Offices* to another author, as we noted above, lest I seem to have vindicated someone other than Rupert from the error of the advocates of shadows, I shall show, from works which are regarded as Rupert’s without any dissent, [Col. 0108B] that he consistently affirmed and vigorously defended the reality of Christ’s body and blood.

## Rupert’s Catholic Faith concerning the Reality of Christ’s Body and Blood Is Vindicated from His Other Books

Throughout his whole life Rupert stood firm and fought courageously for the reality of Christ’s body and blood, which the Berengarians had shortly before attacked with greater obstinacy. If you consider the first encounters of this youthful athlete, you marvel that he fought for this truth with such strength of faith against a scholastic and monk of great name and high esteem that his adversary, unable to withstand his force, cited Augustine against him, teaching that this sacrament had been offered by the Lord to Judas himself. From this he inferred [Col. 0108C] that the reality, or true substance, of Christ’s body and blood was by no means contained in the sacrament delivered to the sacrilegious traitor.

Though pressed by the weight of so great an authority, Rupert, although young, did not yield. Rather, with the discernment and firmness of mind appropriate to a man of mature learning, he examined the force of so great an authority and replied that Augustine was not to be trusted in every respect as the canonical books are. Thus, in religious freedom, following the meaning which he judged more consonant with the Gospel reading—and later found to be that of Saint Hilary—he denied that Christ had given Judas a morsel of his body and blood, and maintained that Christ had given him another morsel, dipped in the dish. By overthrowing this foundation of his adversary, he deprived the latter’s entire argument of strength. [Col. 0108D] Rupert himself recounts this dispute with that celebrated scholastic and monk, concerning the reality of Christ’s body, near the end of the first book of his *Commentary on the Rule*, called the *Apologeticus*. He says that it happened when he was not yet known to Cuno, but had only seen him once and exchanged a few words with him.

He who gave Rupert the contest so that he might conquer offered him, after these preliminaries of war, further struggles for the crown. In these, contending more vigorously for the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar against those who proclaimed that the sacrament was no more than a figure, he published commentaries on the Gospel of John. [Col. 0109A] In the sixth book, expounding John chapter six, concerning Christ’s body and the eating of it, he explains more fully its true and real presence under the mystical species of bread and wine; and he more powerfully refutes the arguments most commonly adduced against it from Saint Augustine, interpreting with acuteness the testimonies drawn from that same writer.

The whole of that book ought to be transcribed here; but lest our little apologetic work grow too large, I shall draw out only some passages, both from this book of the *Commentaries on John* and from Rupert’s dedicatory epistle to Cuno, which express this faith and teaching of Rupert more clearly.

[Col. 0109B] In book VI on John, chapter 6, Rupert establishes with all his force the Catholic truth of the real presence of Christ’s body and blood under mystical species against the advocates of shadows, or Berengarians, vigorously shaking and utterly overthrowing their foundations. First he states their error thus:

> “At this point it must not be passed over in silence that certain unknown men of obscure name wrongly suppose, and defend in their speeches and writings, that the true bread and drink which we receive at the holy altar were nevertheless eaten and drunk by those fathers at that time; and that this is no more the true body and blood of Christ than was the manna which that people ate, or the water brought forth from the rock, which not only the people but also the beasts drank.”

[Col. 0109C] Rupert of Deutz then sets out the argument of this stated error, which they regard as weighty because they derive it from the Apostle:

> “For their chief argument in support of this error,” Rupert says, “they employ the authority of the Apostle, who says: ‘They all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock which followed them, and the rock was Christ’ [1 Cor. 10].”

To this detestable presumption, in his own words, he replies briefly, setting forth the Apostle’s genuine meaning:

> “First it must be said that the Apostle did not say, ‘They all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink,’ in the sense in which these men understand it.”

Nor did he use the relative expression “the same food” or “the same drink” in order that it should refer to that food and drink of which the Lord himself said, “THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.” Rather:

> “Dathan and Abiram ate the same food and drank the same drink as Moses and Aaron; Korah ate the same food, certainly, as Caleb or Joshua.”

He confirms this to be the Apostle’s meaning as follows:

> “For the Apostle’s intention in that passage is to make every person cautious, lest he suppose that he has already attained the goal because he has received the sacraments of the Christian faith. For ‘all these things,’ says the Apostle, ‘happened to them in figure’—that is, so that from ancient examples we may learn that, although we have all been baptized [Col. 0110A] in the same name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and all eat the same body and blood of Christ, we must not suppose that God is equally pleased with all of us, however we live or whatever we do after baptism. For just as all those people were honoured by the same signs—the evil, I say, along with the good—and nevertheless God was not pleased with most of them so as to bring them into the promised land; so likewise he will not be pleased to bring us into the kingdom of God if we become desirers of evil things, as they desired them; if we commit fornication, as some of them committed fornication,” etc.

[Col. 0110B] Having most acutely explained the Apostle’s meaning, he concludes that the argument drawn from this passage against the reality of Christ’s body and blood has no force:

> “Therefore the text of the apostolic writing helps no one who wishes ‘the same food’ and ‘the same drink’ to be understood as meaning an identity with the life-giving food and drink which we receive in commemoration of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Since, however, an adversary might press the point that the Apostle did not say merely “food,” but “spiritual food,” Rupert shows that this too cannot be twisted into the adversary’s meaning:

> “Nor does the fact that he calls the food and drink spiritual constrain you—however much you resist—because the food and drink occurred in a spiritual figure and therefore arose not by the natural order of things but by spiritual power. For a little later [Col. 0110C] he says: ‘All these things happened in figures.’”

Having thus dispersed these mists and driven away these shadows, Rupert brings forth the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament, pure and resplendent in its own light:

> “Therefore that manna was no more this true bread, nor was that drink more the life-giving drink—which we truly believe and confess to be Christ’s blood—than that rock was Christ: namely, an inanimate and insensible rock which Moses struck with his rod.”

He builds this truth upon the foundation which he immediately adds:

> “For all things, as has already been said, happened in figure; and a figure is certainly nowhere the same thing as the reality which it figures, just as a shadow is not the same thing as the reality itself or the substance of a body.”

[Col. 0110D] So firmly did Rupert hold the reality of the Lord’s body and blood that he opposed it to figure—although other Holy Fathers taught us that truth and figure coexist in this mystery; reconciling their meaning belongs elsewhere.

But the adversary still insists, saying that this bread which we consecrate at the altar is a figure of the living bread which came down from heaven, not the living bread itself. Rupert rebukes this opinion, as one resting on no canonical authority:

> “By what Catholic authority, I ask, do you introduce this into Catholic ears? When he himself, the living bread, said of the bread which he held in his hands, ‘THIS IS MY BODY [Col. 0111A],’ was anything said such as Paul said when, having said, ‘the rock was Christ,’ he added, ‘all these things happened to them in figure’? Surely, if Christ himself, or an Evangelist or Apostle, were the author of this expression, you would not be rebuked.”

Thus the Abbot of Deutz rejects as unsupported by any legitimate authority—and dismisses as an invention—the adversary’s interpretation of Christ’s words about the bread held in his hands, “THIS IS MY BODY,” as figurative.

[Col. 0111B] Yet because they boasted that they were supported by Augustine’s authority where he says that the words, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,” are figurative speech, Rupert, lest yielding to the misused authority of so great a teacher should also mean yielding to error, most subtly expounds Augustine’s meaning without naming him, and shows most wisely and devoutly that Augustine in no way detracts from the reality of Christ’s body and blood:

> “Even if someone says that the statement which is made later—‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves’—is figurative speech, he does not oppose us. For that figurative quality of expression does not destroy the reality of the thing, just as the parabolic words in the parable of the sower do not destroy the reality of the one who truly sows. For what is the definition of figurative speech? Surely, when one thing sounds in the utterance and another is to be understood, it is figurative speech. Clearly, therefore, even if the aforesaid saying is figurative—for it sounded one way to the Jews and Christ meant it another way—[Col. 0111C] the figure itself does not destroy the reality. Rather, the figure itself is destroyed while the reality remains, when it is said emphatically of bread and wine: ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.’ For there the Jewish understanding is destroyed, because it is clearer than light that Christ is not to be eaten as they understood it. For they thought that he wished his flesh to be cut up and eaten, as the flesh of a lamb is cut up and eaten. There, I say, this figurative understanding is destroyed, and the meaning consonant with the words remains: namely, that by divine power bread is changed into the true substance of his body.”

Therefore, according to Rupert, Augustine rightly understood Christ’s words, “Unless you eat,” etc., as figurative, yet with no loss to the Catholic truth concerning Christ’s body. When “you eat” is said, it is figurative for the Jews, who, thinking that Christ’s flesh had to be cut up, understood something other than the words expressed. But when “the flesh of the Son of Man” is said, there is no figure but reality. For when it is said emphatically of bread and wine, “THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD,” the meaning consonant with the words remains: namely, that by divine power bread and wine are changed into the substance of body and blood.

If Rupert with such zeal refuted or explained those grounds by which the advocates of shadows established nothing more in the sacrament than a figure of Christ’s body, in order to establish more firmly the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar, who—unless he speaks ignorantly from another’s [Col. 0112A] error, eagerly seeks to malign his neighbour out of envy, or raves in madness—would say that Rupert denied the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the mystical species of bread and wine?

Rupert is so wholly engaged, especially throughout this book, in defending this truth that, when some said the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood was impossible, he demolished the walls of that impossibility. He proved that the body received at the altar is Christ’s very body which hung on the cross, and that the blood offered is his very blood which was shed there. For this purpose he offers various comparisons drawn from nature, by which he explains the true conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood:

> “[Col. 0112B] When, therefore, the word of Christ’s cross and passion is added to wine, what reason prevents us from believing it to be that same blood which was shed for many for the remission of sins?”

After he had added how close a kinship bread has with the body, he again, and indeed more vehemently, concludes this reality of Christ’s body and blood from Christ’s own words:

> “When, therefore, that living bread which came down from heaven says emphatically, ‘THIS IS MY BODY WHICH SHALL BE GIVEN UP FOR YOU,’ do you dare to say that it is something other than Christ’s body? Truth says, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ and adds, ‘WHICH SHALL BE GIVEN UP FOR YOU.’ And do you say that it is not the same body?”

Rupert rebukes this with a deeper understanding:

> “If it is not the same body—if the living bread which came down from heaven is not the same—then this is not the body which shall be given up for you, and Truth has lied to itself.”

[Col. 0112C] For this appended phrase cannot belong to a figure, but only to the substance of the body. It proves most invincibly that what is in the sacrament of the altar is not a figure of Christ’s body but the reality; and therefore that Rupert is not a teacher of shadows, but an invincible defender of the truth of Christ’s body.

Thus far the struggle for this truth had been waged, but victory had not yet been won, because the adversary had not yet laid down his arms. Now entirely carnal and animal-minded, he objects that nothing in the outward appearance of bread and wine is changed; Rupert pursues him more sharply:

> “But it has long been plain to everyone,” says Rupert, “where your carnal and wholly animal-minded understanding clings, and therefore fails to perceive the things of God: namely, because neither bread nor wine has changed anything of its outward appearance, you cannot and will not understand how THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD HAVE TRULY COME TO BE.”

[Col. 0112D] He playfully breaks the whole force of this duller argument, insofar as it has force among those who judge everything:

> “It follows, then, that if a white bishop happens to baptize you, a black man, you will not believe that before God you have become what he who baptized you is—namely, that from a son of the devil you have become a son of God,” etc., “because your black hair did not become fair again and your Ethiopian face and the skin of your whole body did not shine according to the colour of him who baptized you. [Col. 0113A] But if you do not shrink from admitting this, lest you be worse than an unbeliever, and prefer to confess that, although you have changed nothing of the outward appearance of your body, you have truly passed from another body of the devil, which is the whole mass of the lost, into another body of Christ, which is the Church: believe this also, that this visible bread and wine, by which you live temporally, although nothing of their outward appearance has been changed, have passed into another state and have been changed into that food and drink which is the nourishment of angels,” etc.

He therefore blinks in midday light who does not clearly see Rupert refuting with every resource, or even playfully rejecting, everything opposed to the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine, in order to demonstrate by an effective argument *ad hominem* that bread and wine have been changed by the power of the divine Word into the true substance of body and blood, [Col. 0113B] although their outward appearance remains unchanged; and that he unquestionably held and affirmed that the true substance of body and blood is present in the sacrament of the altar.

Yet Rupert does not cease here from defending this truth. Again he attacks those who, in order to destroy the reality of Christ’s body and blood, press more insistently the Apostle’s words, “They all ate the same spiritual food,” and heap up testimonies of holy teachers teaching that manna signified this bread; that the altar of God signifies this bread; that those were sacraments and these are sacraments; that they differ in signs but are equal in the reality signified; that they ate one thing and we another under visible species, [Col. 0113C] though the same thing is signified by spiritual power.

Rupert, taking all these statements in his adversaries’ sense, reduces them to the absurdity that the sacrifices of lambs and rams were holier than the new sacrifice of bread and wine. For those sacrifices were far holier than manna or water flowing from the rock, from which they are willing to distinguish the bread and wine in the sacrament of the altar only in signs; whereas this bread and this drink are consecrated only with much blessing and are received only by those who have been sanctified: “For he who eats and drinks unworthily,” etc. Yet men and beasts alike used manna and the water of the rock without distinction: “Water came forth most abundantly, so that the people drank, and the beasts.”

[Col. 0113D] And lest anyone be moved by the authority of teachers of this sort, Rupert sets Saint Ambrose against them, who says among other things:

> “The Virgin gave birth outside the order of nature; and that which we make is the body from the Virgin,” etc.

Likewise:

> “Just as our Lord Jesus Christ is truly the Son of God, as Son from the substance of the Father, so the flesh which we receive, as he himself said, is true flesh, and the drink is true drink.”

He also adduces Augustine, whom they regarded as patron of the opposing view, dragging his sayings into a foreign sense. Rupert proves the reality of Christ’s body in the sacrament from Augustine’s words on Psalm 33, “He was carried in his own hands,” interpreting them concerning Christ so as to affirm that the true David, that is, Christ, without doubt carried nothing other than himself in his own hands when, holding bread and wine, [Col. 0114A] he said: “THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.”

Here Rupert especially insists that nothing is to be added to or taken away from these words of Christ, so as to exclude from them the understanding of figure and sign and defend the bare truth which they set forth:

> “If anyone adds to these things, may God add upon him the plagues written in this book [Rev. 22]; and if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, may God take away his portion from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book. Is that curse any less to be feared here, so that we should take away from or add anything to the words of him who says: ‘THIS IS MY BODY, which shall be given up for you; THIS IS MY BLOOD, the new covenant, which shall be poured out for [Col. 0114B] many for the remission of sins’? For when, as he says, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ we add an implied qualification, saying that it is spoken figuratively or by resemblance; when, I say, though he says, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ we say, ‘this signifies body,’ do we not add much, or by a perverse alteration take much away, and generate a meaning which so great an author—God and man—never spoke and which never entered his heart?”

Who, I ask, either among the ancients or even among the moderns, has taught more expressly, explained more clearly, or defended more strongly the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist?

Therefore, if anyone handed down this Catholic truth expressly, Rupert did so most expressly; if anyone explained it purely, Rupert did so most purely; if anyone ever affirmed it consistently, the man of Deutz did so most consistently; if anyone defended it courageously, Rupert did so most courageously; if anyone, finally, held and wrote Catholic doctrine concerning this truth, Rupert did so in the fullest Catholic sense. Thus no faith concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine is stronger, more constant, purer, more explicit, or more Catholic than Rupert’s.

[Col. 0114D] Nevertheless, so that nothing may be lacking from the dispute undertaken for this truth, Rupert rebuts every objection usually constructed against the plain and proper understanding of Christ’s words:

> “When someone objects that it was written in little notes that the same Truth likewise said, ‘I am the vine,’ he drags this into his erroneous argument as boldly as ignorantly. For the immediately following words, ‘As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me,’ compel us to understand the saying as spoken by comparison—especially since he did not say emphatically, ‘I am this vine,’ as he did emphatically say, ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD,’ immediately adding a description of true propriety: of the body, he says, ‘which shall be given up for you’; and of the blood, ‘which shall be poured out for many.’”

Having thus repelled this objection, distinguished between these words of the Lord Christ, “THIS IS MY BODY,” and those words, “I am the vine,” and most wisely differentiated their meanings by the added properties of the body [Col. 0115A] “which shall be given up” and the blood “which shall be poured out,” Rupert firmly professes in the Word of God:

> “This bodily bread, after the Father has signed it, and this wine pressed from grapes now present, as soon as it has been signed with the same sign through the hands of the Church saying, ‘That it may become for us the body and blood of your most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ,’ etc., ‘Do this in remembrance of me,’ IS HIS BODY AND BLOOD—the body and blood of him who is the author of this handing-over—and this sacrifice is Christ himself,” etc.

After this profession of sincere faith concerning the reality of Christ’s body, no one can complain against Rupert’s Catholic faith except with great injustice. But if anyone is doubtful about the manner in which bread becomes the body that hung on the cross and wine becomes the blood of Christ shed on the cross, he may ask Rupert; nor will Rupert dismiss him unanswered:

> “[Col. 0115B] But if someone asks us how bread which grew from the earth this year becomes the body of Christ which hung on the cross, and wine which was pressed from grapes now present becomes the blood which he poured from his side, let us ask him how the Son of Man, who was certainly conceived from a woman and born from the earth, descended from heaven; or how, before he ascended into heaven, he could already be in heaven, according to the truth of his own saying: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.’ If anyone understands these things, he will be able to answer that this was most rightly said on account of the unity of God and man in Christ. Therefore, [Col. 0115C] altering the words slightly, let us say to him: the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, both that which then hung on the cross and that which the faith of the Church now makes by the sacred mouth; it is one body, one flesh, and one blood.”

Would one who denied Christ’s body in the sacrament have replied thus? Would one who did not admit the reality itself have taken such pains to explain its mode?

One testimony of Augustine, which the Berengarians drew to their own side, remained for Rupert to explain: namely, that to eat the Lord’s flesh and drink his blood is to remain in the unity of faith. Rupert readily accepts this, but only so that the truth of the Lord’s definition always remains firm, by which Christ said: “THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.” So fully did Rupert judge that these words of the Lord demonstrate not a figure of his body and blood, or something else, but reality:

> “[Col. 0115D] Whatever such things they may discover aptly and put forward profitably, provided that the foundation remains which was laid by him himself when he said of the bread and the cup of wine: ‘THIS IS MY BODY which shall be given up for you; THIS IS THE CUP OF MY BLOOD which shall be poured out for you.’ That is, that remaining in the unity of faith is eating Christ’s flesh and drinking his blood, so that bodily eating at the Lord’s table is not necessary for salvation—Christ did not teach this. Rather: ‘He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood,’ namely in the manner in which I shall hand myself over, believing in his heart unto righteousness and eating and drinking with his mouth unto salvation, ‘he remains in me and I in him.’”

[Col. 0116A] Rupert adds that “bread once consecrated never afterward ceases to be Christ’s flesh.” And below, concerning the words, “And the bread which I will give is my flesh for the life of the world,” he says:

> “Then I shall give bread to these who remain, in which the reality of that same flesh or body of mine is not lacking—the body which, brought forth from the belly of the whale, will sit safe and whole eternally at the right hand of the Father.”

[Col. 0116B] And a little later:

> “He gives us earthly bread, which he changes into his own flesh so that, by being eaten by the living, it may give them eternal life. Therefore, just as we truly confess of our flesh, which the Virgin Mary bore, that it is God because of the unity of person, so likewise we truly and Catholicly confess concerning this visible bread, which the invisible divinity of the same Word takes up and transfers into his flesh, that it is Christ’s body.”

And lest any evasive ambiguity remain in Christ’s words, “THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD,” Rupert most wisely observes:

> “Just as dialecticians, in order to avoid the troublesome ambiguities of sophistical arguments, add a particular property to a common name—so that, when it is said, ‘Alexander carried off Helen,’ lest Alexander, the Macedonian king Philip’s son, be understood, ‘the Trojan, Priam’s son,’ is added—so, when Christ said, ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD,’ lest anything other than the very body which hung on the cross and the very blood shed upon the cross should be believed, he wisely added: ‘which shall be given up for you,’ and ‘which shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins.’”

[Col. 0116C] From these points he finally concludes:

> “Therefore, once every mist of figures or likenesses has been removed, we undoubtedly believe that we eat not just any body, nor the body of Christ which is the Church, but that body of the Lord which was given up for us; and that we drink that blood which was shed for us for the remission of sins. And we know—and know well—that what he did, we do likewise in remembrance of him: that is, we eat HIS FLESH and drink HIS BLOOD.”

What could be more explicit or purer than so open and sincere a profession of faith concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist?

[Col. 0116D] Finally, expressions of this kind occur throughout this book: “food of the Lord’s body and drink of his blood”; “to receive, eat, from the altar the Lord’s body, and to drink his blood”; “those eating Christ’s body and drinking his blood.” Rupert certainly would never have written these words had he thought that the Lord’s body and blood were not on the altar.

Nor is this faith of Rupert found in this book alone. It shines forth especially also in book VII, where, briefly expounding the words “This saying is hard,” he admits that the saying is hard, but for those who thought the flesh was to be cut up, and for those who think that Christ suffers and dies as often as he is offered and eaten:

> “[Col. 0117A] To those,” says Rupert in book VII on John, “who still murmur and argue today when we defend the reality of the Lord’s body and blood, we seem to speak an intolerable hardness for other reasons. For when, by reasoned faith constrained through evangelical authority, they have been brought to where it cannot be denied that this body of the Lord is that which was given up for us and that this blood of his is that which was shed for us; when, I say, we have established this firmly for them, then they say: ‘Therefore, if this bread is called and is Christ not figuratively but in reality, Christ suffers daily and dies as often as this bread is broken in remembrance of him’; and, he says, ‘this saying is hard.’”

[Col. 0117B] Rupert suppresses their murmuring thus:

> “Our faith has not judged so, nor have its eyes been so darkened that it cannot see itself breaking the bread of God and preserving the Son of God whole, just as old Abraham could see himself strike the ram and not harm the son laid upon the altar.”

Yet with this distinction:

> “There Isaac was sacrificed in the ram in figure; here the Son of God is sacrificed in bread and wine in the reality of flesh and blood.”

Here Rupert openly professes that he defends the reality of the Lord’s body and blood, and that he has so constrained his opponents by evangelical authority that they cannot deny that this body of the Lord which is on the altar is that which was given up for us, and that this blood of his which is consecrated is that which was shed for us. Finally, the Son of God is sacrificed in the sacrament of the altar in the reality of flesh and blood.

[Col. 0117C] Yet not even by these arguments did the heresy of the advocates of shadows fall silent. Rather, against Rupert’s faith concerning the reality of body and blood, it more insolently brandished Christ’s words as though they supported its error beyond all understanding:, “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” Rupert, explaining nothing that even apparently favoured this error and leaving no escape through which this heresy could flee, opens the meaning of these words of Christ and fittingly reconciles it with the reality of the Lord’s body and blood:

> “[Col. 0117D] This statement,” says Rupert, “in no way destroys or weakens the earlier one in which Christ said, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,’ etc.; rather, it corrects the carnal understanding of those who misunderstand, detracting nothing from the reality of his flesh which is to be eaten, but adding to that same flesh the Spirit of that same flesh, who must be eaten together with it: ‘It is the Spirit,’ he says, ‘who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.’ As though he were saying: In the way in which you understand what I said above, ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves,’ the flesh of no living creature can be eaten together with its life, nor can its blood be drunk. In order that this may be done by man or beast, it is known that the living creature must be killed. Therefore, I shall not give my flesh to be eaten in this manner. For my flesh, unless it is eaten living and with its Spirit, profits nothing. Flesh alone, flesh without Spirit, profits nothing; for it is the Spirit [Col. 0118A] who gives life. By saying, ‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing,’ he forbids us to suppose that such flesh and blood—namely, lifeless flesh and blood—are in his bread and cup.”

How, however, with the outward appearance of bread and wine remaining unchanged, bread and wine are transformed into Christ’s body and blood, he himself explains there as follows: “But what is the spirit which gives life to this flesh, so that it may benefit those who eat it? He says: ‘The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.’ These words work invisibly in the bread of which I am about to say, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ and in the wine of which I am about to say, ‘THIS IS MY BLOOD,’ so that it is truly my flesh and my blood, although the outward appearance remains unchanged. Therefore we too, because we have not understood, believe in order that we may understand, because [Col. 0118B] truly, as Christ is one God and man, so this consecrated visible bread is one flesh with that flesh which hung upon the cross: it is one body of Christ. Upon the altar the true body of Christ is offered, broken, and eaten. So far as we could, with God’s help, we have taken care to prove from its own bleating that the holy bread and the cup which we receive from the altar are the true and living Lamb of God.”

By this profession of his faith—that he believes, not because he understands, but in order that he may understand, that beneath the visible appearance of bread and wine is that very flesh of Christ which hung on the cross, and that very blood of Christ which was shed on the cross, this being effected by the word by which he said, “THIS IS MY BODY,” and “THIS IS MY BLOOD,” so that the flesh which, without the Spirit, profits nothing is not without life [Col. 0118C]—Rupert dispels every stain of calumny. For who could now think that Rupert sided with the “shadow-men,” when he refutes all their arguments; that he held the errors which he opposes; or that he attacked the reality of the body and blood which he tirelessly defends?

That Rupert’s Commentaries on John were published with the same mind and faith is attested not only by the passages which we have cited from them, but also by his letter in which Rupert dedicates these books to Abbot Cuno. For there, in dealing with the envy of his rivals, who took Rupert’s writing on John’s Gospel more ill, after laying their errors before Cuno as before a father, and especially that error whereby they wished the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood to be merely a sign of a sacred reality—as Berengar of Tours had formerly held in error—he states: “But what do they say, what do they advance as an argument? They have nothing, except that some among them, wishing the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood to be merely a sign of a sacred reality, according to a certain error of Berengar of Tours, suppose that blessed Augustine also held this view; which is utterly false.” Rupert wholly sets himself against this error. “But I,” he says, “hold, as the Catholic Church holds, that the body of Christ which was given for us is truly his body, and that the blood which was shed for us is certainly truly his blood.” He indicates in a few words that scarcely anyone in his time maintained Berengar’s error, but that the whole Catholic Church held with one mind the reality of Christ’s body and blood: “By now scarcely anyone dares openly to profess or defend this, since the whole Church knows that the true body and the true blood of Christ are [Note: [Col. 0119D] The whole Catholic Church holds that in the Eucharist the true body and true blood of Christ are present. Christ’s body and blood are upon the altar in three ways: by name, in reality, and in effect. The body which hung upon the cross differs from that which is in the sacrament only in its outward appearance. Had the minister Claude heard this most explicit profession of Rupert’s faith—by which bread is said to be Christ’s flesh and wine his blood not only in effect, but also in reality—he would undoubtedly not have cited Rupert in so many places (pp. 104, 125, 198) as though Rupert had unhesitatingly taught only that bread is called and is Christ’s body, and wine called and is his blood, in effect alone and not in reality.].”

Do you suppose that Rupert dissented from the Church? That in his published Commentaries on John and in the twelve books *On the Divine Offices* he asserted what no one now dares openly to profess or defend? That Rupert denied what he knew and declares the whole Catholic Church to profess and defend—namely, that in the sacrament of the altar there are the true body and true blood of Christ?

He himself sets forth his faith where he sincerely opens to his Cuno this reality of the body and blood: “I now briefly disclose to you what, and in what manner, I thought when I treated [Col. 0119B] those words of the Lord himself by which he commends the life-giving sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Christ’s body and blood are present in three modes of essence, and differ in a fourth: they are present by name, in reality, and in effect; but they differ in appearance. They are present, I say, by name, because the supreme Priest of heaven, who is Truth itself, is not accustomed to attach empty names to things. He impressed this name so strongly that he did not merely say, ‘I CALL THIS MY BODY; THIS is called MY BLOOD,’ but, ‘THIS IS,’ he says, ‘MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.’ They are present also in reality, because assuredly he is the Holy of holies: as truly in that appearance in which he was handed over and pierced with a lance, he himself is the Holy of holies. They are present no less in effect, because, as truly as in that appearance in which he hung upon the cross [Col. 0119C] he effected remission of sins for all who had awaited it from the beginning of the world with faith, without the legal sacraments of faith—for all from righteous Abel to the thief whom he received as confessing him on the cross—so truly in these appearances of bread and wine he effects the same remission of sins for all who have entered, or are entering, into that same faith, after that appearance departed from here and ascended into heaven. In a fourth respect he differs in appearance; and this is most beneficial, not only lest the colour or taste of human blood cause any horror to those who receive it, but also that the excessive credulity of our first parents may be cured by an appropriate antidote. For they believed the deceiver, the devil, in what they saw—namely, that the tree possessed an efficacious power for attaining divinity [Col. 0119D]—and, eating, they died. Let us, on the contrary, believe the faithful Saviour God in what we do not see—namely, that bread and wine have passed into the true substance of body and blood—and, eating and drinking, let us live for ever.”

What faith concerning the life-giving sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood could be more Catholic than that which professes that the body of Christ which hung upon the cross and the blood which was shed upon the cross are present beneath the appearances of bread and wine, not merely by name and in effect, but in reality itself? What faith could be more Catholic than that which teaches that the BODY and BLOOD which are in the sacrament differ from Christ’s true flesh and true blood in this alone: that in the sacrament they display the appearance not of flesh and blood, but of bread and wine? Or, finally, than that which believes bread and wine to have passed into the true substance of body and blood? Let even the shameless be ashamed, then, to charge Rupert with denying the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament, when he taught it Catholicly everywhere and in so many places.

Nor did Rupert think and write these things about the reality of the body and blood only while young, as though merely rehearsing in these works; he held them also when, advancing in age, he turned his mind to greater matters [Col. 0120B]. For, describing the victory of the Word of God (*Book XII*, ch. 12), by which the Word of the Father overcame the unbelief of the first parents, who believed the devil saying, “If you eat, you shall be as gods,” more than God, he demonstrates it thus: “Against that food—the food of death, beautiful to the sight—in which they believed there was an effect of divinity, another food had to be given, a food of life: so that the mind might believe that there is in it food and drink, truly the efficacious flesh and blood of Christ for communicating divinity—something which the senses of flesh and blood cannot perceive. By this faith God judges that satisfaction has been made to him by man, when man believes him no less than he had believed the devil.”

He establishes this reality at greater length in writing *On the Glory and Honour of the Son of Man*. Expounding, in the fourth book on Matthew, the words in chapter five, “If you offer your gift,” etc., he says: “Then, when you come, you shall offer your gift: a holy gift, a true sacrifice—not the flesh of bulls, nor the blood of cattle or calves, but the very BODY of that brother to whom you have been reconciled, life-giving, true BLOOD, a holy and immaculate sacrifice.” And in the fifth book, explaining the fourth petition of the Lord’s Prayer, “Our bread,” etc., he says briefly: “The third bread is Christ’s flesh, which he gives us from the holy altar, as he says: ‘And the bread [Col. 0120C] which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.’”

Finally, in the tenth book, raising the question whether the Lord communicated his body and blood to Judas, he adduces differing opinions of the holy Fathers: namely, Augustine’s, who, following Luke’s account literally, judged that Christ had handed Judas a morsel of his own body; and Hilary’s, who, in accordance with the histories of Matthew and Mark, held that the Passover was celebrated without Judas—that is, after his departure—when the cup had been received and the bread broken, because Judas had not been worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments [Col. 0121A]. Rupert follows and firmly maintains Saint Hilary’s opinion as more conformable to the sacred text, although he did not know it to be Hilary’s.

While Rupert treats this difficulty from both sides, he offers many statements expressly testifying to the reality of Christ’s body and blood beneath the appearances of bread and wine, but especially near the end, where he says that in this sacrament there is a great testing of God, a testing that seeks faith: “Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing. Therefore the reality had to be invisible, in order that this substance might have its place; the reality, I say—that is, the FLESH and BLOOD—had to be invisible, not only lest it offend our senses as eaters and drinkers by a natural repugnance, since to eat or grind with the teeth human flesh and to drink human blood is not congenial to nature, but also that this substance of things hoped for, this evidence of things not appearing—namely, faith—might have its place.” And shortly afterward: “But he who says, ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me,’ gives not just any thing of his, but his own flesh and his own blood.”

To subject Rupert’s faith concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood, so abundantly established by testimonies, and yet with the outward appearance of bread and wine unchanged, to even the slightest suspicion of any error would be counted no slight injury. Therefore, that it may remain inviolate in the future, let it be sealed with these words of Rupert, by which in chapters twenty-one, twenty-two, and twenty-three [Col. 0121C] of the third book *On the Works of the Holy Spirit* he explains clearly this sacrament of Christ’s body and blood:

“While they were dining—that is, still sitting at the supper in which they ate the flesh of the Lamb, the flesh of the old Passover—he took bread and blessed it. He took common bread, but by blessing transformed it into something far different from what it had been, so that he could truly say: ‘THIS IS MY BODY, which shall be given for you.’ Likewise he took the substance of wine; but there, by giving thanks or blessing, he changed it into something else, so that Truth, who does not lie, might say: ‘THIS IS MY BLOOD of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many.’ ‘This,’ he says—that is, this bread—is my body, or my flesh. For elsewhere he also says: ‘And the bread [Col. 0121D] which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world.’ But it is not seen by the eyes of the flesh, nor felt by the taste of the mouth, that this bread has become Christ’s flesh, that this wine has been changed into blood; for if the colour or taste of human flesh and blood were perceived, it would bring not more salvation but much horror. Thus it is Christ’s body or flesh and blood in the manner fitting for its existence and for our use, and sufficient for our salvation. In what manner, or in what modes of essence? Assuredly by name, in reality, and in effect. We understand it to be present by name in him who says, ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD.’ As nowhere else, so neither in this matter—indeed, most emphatically not in this matter—may we take the Lord’s name in vain. For if in all consecrations performed by the Lord’s ministers upon invocation of his name [Col. 0122A] we do not dare take the Lord’s name in vain, how much more in this consecration, in which the Lord himself placed with his own mouth the name of his body and blood, should we not take that very name in vain? We understand Christ’s body and blood also to be present in reality from his saying that the body will be given and the blood will be shed. We understand them to be present in effect from his adding, after saying that the body will be given and the blood shed, ‘for you, for the remission of sins.’ Therefore, although in that appearance in which he hung on the cross he is the Holy of holies, and in that appearance wrought remission of sins and eternal life for all the elect who had gone before, so also in this appearance of bread and wine he is no less the Holy of holies, and without doubt confers remission of sins and eternal life upon all the elect who come to faith in him after that same passion [Col. 0122B]. For elsewhere he also said: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.’”

These are Rupert’s words in chapter 21. If anyone finds Rupert’s faith doubtful or obscure in them, then surely the earth itself shakes beneath him and the sun is dark to him!

Again, more distinctly, in chapter 22 of Book III *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, he explains what the sacrament is and what the reality of the sacrament is, at once expounding Saint Augustine’s meaning and the reality of Christ’s body and blood in this sacrament:

“Thus, as Father Augustine also says, in this sacrament, which worthy and unworthy persons receive, there is a reality of the sacrament which only worthy persons can receive. But not as his words have been understood by some. For they thought that he had said [Col. 0122C] that what any unworthy person receives is not Christ’s body or blood; and that, according to the meaning of so great a teacher, what we visibly receive from the Lord’s table is not Christ’s body or blood, but only a figure or sign of Christ’s body and blood. He did not say this; indeed, he did not think it. For he was not accustomed to oppose Christ. Now Christ speaks, both in his own person, saying, ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD’; and through his Apostle, of whom we have proof that Christ speaks in him, saying: ‘Therefore whoever eats the bread of the Lord or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person test himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup; for whoever eats and drinks unworthily [Col. 0122D] eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’ He did not say that whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats ordinary or common bread and drinks wine such as it was before the consecration had been celebrated; but he says, ‘shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord,’ and, ‘eats and drinks judgment upon himself,’ not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore let us seek the understanding by which the aforesaid teacher Augustine distinguished the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament not from someone’s contentious disputation, but from the Apostle’s truth. Christ himself said that this reality is the mystery of his passion, as we have already said: holding this visible sacrament in his hands, when he said, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ he added, ‘which shall be given’; when he said, ‘THIS IS MY BLOOD,’ he added [Col. 0123A], ‘which shall be shed.’ But the person who approaches unworthily does not share in Christ’s sufferings; with the mouth of the mind he does not touch what he receives with the mouth of the body. Therefore this visible sacrament, which he receives with his mouth, is indeed Christ’s body and blood. For his unworthiness could not annul the dignity of so great a consecration,” etc.

Finally, in chapter 23, setting the serpent’s fraud and lie—when it deceitfully promised the first parents, “If you eat, you shall be as gods”—against the faithfulness and truth of Christ, who faithfully promises, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me,” he exhorts readers in these few words to faith in Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament: “Let it be believed,” he says, “that in this sacrament there is what is not seen, namely, the reality of flesh and blood, able to make us fellow-members of the [Col. 0123B] only-begotten Son of God,” etc.

Let these things, then, be the seal of Rupert’s faith—a seal than which none could surely be applied more firmly or impressed more expressly—so that whoever corrupts Rupert’s sound teaching concerning the Lord’s body and blood, or translates his meaning into the errors of the shadow-men, may be held guilty of violating the faith.

And in order that Rupert’s faith, sealed by these testimonies, may shine more brightly, and that, as it does not depart without attestation, so neither may it depart without glory, it will not be irrelevant to add some miracles from Rupert by which no little glory accrued both to this venerable sacrament and to Rupert’s faith.

Rupert, now elderly and near death, describes the fire of the town of Deutz in the book which he entitled from the event. He recounts three miracles which occurred in this conflagration [Col. 0123C] in praise and commendation of the sacrament of the Lord’s body, by whose power they were accomplished. In the first chapter he relates the first miracle thus: “I wish to narrate the event as it occurred, with this intention: that our descendants too may know, and that no antiquity of time may be able to erase from our hearts the memory of the glorification by which the sacrament of the Lord’s body was glorified throughout the whole fire, as our eyes saw; and of the deliverance by which the church in which we invoke the Lord’s name was delivered from the pressure of the flames: in such a manner that many saw the presence of divine protection, namely, as though the form of a most beautiful man were bending over it from above and repelling with his outstretched hand the assault of the surrounding flames [Col. 0123D],” etc. Here Rupert attributes the rescue of the monastery church at Deutz from the dreadful fire to Christ’s body which was kept there.

He writes of the second miracle in chapter three: namely, that the Lord’s corporal cloth, cast amid the globes of flame, was preserved unharmed from injury by the fire, since reverence for Christ’s body made the flames stop before it. The fire itself, though most ravenous, left only a singed line as a sign of the Lord’s power, which resisted the flames but did not extinguish them, so that it might be believed that, unharmed amid their fury, it had overcome and inspected all their force—and had overcome because it visited.

He gives the third in chapter five: namely, that the Lord’s body itself, kept beside the altar of the parish church [Col. 0124A] under the invocation of Saint Urban, situated before the gates of the monastery of Deutz, remained untouched while flames devoured the entire basilica. Although the fire utterly consumed even the window made fast with wooden boards, in which a wooden pyx along with the Lord’s body was stored; another pyx containing unconsecrated hosts; a pewter vessel of wine; a little vessel of incense; and other things enclosed together with the pyx and the Lord’s body in that window—yet the flames raging all around, with beams ablaze and burning stones falling on every side, so revered that wooden pyx containing the Lord’s body that they did not even dare touch it. “These indeed,” Rupert exclaims in chapter 6, “are your miracles, Christ, of glory not unlike that by which you were glorified with your three youths in the midst of the Babylonian furnace: namely, your body, with its vessel and corporal cloth, remained unchanged, just as the garments of those youths were neither changed nor burned [Col. 0124B].”

Rupert again mentions these matters in chapter nineteen of the same book.

But this fire proved not only the reality and power of the Lord’s body, but also the firmness of Rupert’s faith in that reality, consuming every suspicion of error; so that by these very miracles of Christ’s body Rupert’s faith may shine forth more brilliantly. Let every adversary’s envy, then, and every malicious misrepresentation yield to the purity of so great a faith. Let unjust calumny concerning perverse error yield to the praise deserved for his defence of the reality of the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 0124C], and for his confirmed faith in that venerable sacrament.

Rupert truly held and taught in a Catholic manner that Christ’s true body and his true blood are truly present beneath the appearances of bread and wine. Wycliffe therefore had no warrant for fastening his lies upon him. And the other biting rivals or unjust critics did great wrong to the teaching of so great a man by accusing him of denying this Catholic truth, which he taught more purely, expounded more fully, and defended more vigorously.

**The error of eating Christ’s body by faith is rejected by Rupert. Indeed, it is proved that he held and wrote that the Lord’s body is received and eaten in the sacrament even by the unworthy.**

[Col. 0124D] Bellarmine, excessively ready to attribute errors, and Vasquez, sharp in intellect but without inquiry into the truth or examination of proofs, declared the author of *On the Divine Offices*, which we have assigned to Rupert, guilty of the error of eating Christ’s body by faith—as though he had taught, erroneously, that Christ’s body is received and eaten only by the merit of faith and only by worthy persons. I have therefore not erased every calumny by which our man of Deutz is said to have anticipated the Calvinists unless I also convict as false this opinion concerning Rupert’s faith, rashly preconceived by Bellarmine and Vasquez.

That this may not be thought a dispute about words, I set out at the outset a fourfold eating of Christ’s body by faith [Col. 0125A]. One is that in which the faithful mind communicates in the Lord’s body only with the mouth of the heart: that is, it shares in that holy bread with the fervour of devotion alone, not by the act of reception. This eating by faith is approved not only by all Catholics but also frequently celebrated by all who devote themselves to Christian piety.

A second eating by faith [Note: [Col. 0125D] Article 36 of the Calvinists’ confession of faith.] is said to be that by which a person, certainly believing bread and wine to be the mystery, figure, sacrament, or sign of Christ’s body and blood unto eternal life, receives, eats, and drinks them with the mouth in such a way that at the same time his soul, through the merit of this faith, is truly refreshed from the very substance of Christ’s body and blood, while his body is nourished from the substance of bread and wine. The Church rejects this eating by faith as heterodox.

[Col. 0125B] A third eating by faith is that by which a person eats this sacrament with the mouth, firmly believing that the true body of the Lord is in it; yet the body is placed there only through the faith of the recipient. Those who followed this view did not keep to one and the same path. Some thought that the Lord’s body is not constituted under the appearances of bread and wine unless it is actually received with that faith. Others, as Guitmund [Note: [Col. 0125D] Books I and III, *On the Eucharist*.] and Alger [Note: [Col. 0125D] In the prologue to the book *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Body and Blood* [Col. 0126D].] testify, said that one part of the bread and wine is truly changed into the Lord’s flesh and blood at the priest’s words, while the other part remains unchanged and is reserved for worthy recipients. Still others wished the whole substance of bread and the whole substance of wine to be converted into Christ’s flesh and blood; yet, when an unworthy person approaches the [Col. 0125C] table, they revert to the nature of bread and wine.

All these agree in one point: namely, that Christ’s body and blood cannot be partaken of by the unworthy. The Church struck this error with an anathema at the Council of Trent [Note: [Col. 0126D] Session 13, chapter 7, and canons 4 and 8.].

The fourth eating of Christ’s body by faith, and indeed the perfect one, is that by which the Lord’s true body is received with the mouth and with that purity of faith which obtains the benefits of divine grace communicated to worthy recipients. This is that holy participation in the Lord’s body and blood with the charity of faith. This is Christian communion in the body, by which we are one with Christ. This is the perfect eating of the heavenly bread, to which eternal life is owed by Christ’s promises: “Whoever eats this bread shall live for ever.”

[Col. 0125D] It must now be distinguished which eating by faith the Abbot of Deutz admitted and which he excluded. All readily concede that he accepted the first and fourth; the dispute therefore remains concerning the second or third. Bellarmine and Vasquez, on one side, contend that Rupert taught either that Christ’s body and blood are never established beneath the appearances of bread and wine, but are received by faith alone when its sacrament—which is in reality only bread and wine—is taken by the mouth; or that Christ’s body and blood do indeed remain in the sacrament and are truly eaten by believers, [Col. 0126A] but are in no way received by the unworthy—whether they cease to be under the sacrament and, as it were, withdraw from it when a person approaches it without faith, or whether they were never placed in that portion of the sacrament which God foreknew would be distributed to an impious person. We, on the contrary, maintain that Rupert’s teaching is so pure that it cannot be stained even by this aspersion of Bellarmine and Vasquez. Since it is fairer here to make this plain in the presence of an impartial judge, I shall fulfil the task I have undertaken by proving most conclusively that neither of these errors was in Rupert’s teaching.

**Rupert held and expressly taught that Christ’s body is eaten even by the unworthy.**

Rupert’s words are so explicit that merely to produce them is to drive from the Abbot of Deutz Bellarmine’s and Vasquez’s judgment—or the imputed error of eating by faith [Col. 0126B]. Therefore listen attentively to what that holy doctor says [Note: [Col. 0126D] Book VI on John.]: “Someone may eat unworthily, but no one ought to eat unworthily.” Are not these words more than sufficient to dispel the calumny?

It was not enough for Rupert merely to say this unless he also proved it more forcefully in defence of faith in so great a sacrament, against those who, as we observed from Guitmund and Alger, maintained that Christ’s body withdraws from the appearances of bread if someone lacking the wedding garment should approach, even when invited, the sacred banquet of the immaculate Lamb.

Let one devoted even to Bellarmine be astonished here, on hearing Rupert explicitly assert and establish strongly what Bellarmine’s observation claimed that he denied [Col. 0126C]. Yet who is astonished if he knows that this man, though most eminent not merely in rank but also in learning and piety, is not beyond all need of proof? Too much is often attributed to a name. If you do not wish to err, believe no one quickly—and never believe merely a name; for the judgment of what is fair and true depends not upon a name but upon the force of proofs. And what proof of Rupert’s teaching and faith could be more certain than his own most open words? Receive these, then, and judge.

When this Eucharistic doctor had plainly declared (*Book VI on John*) that “someone may eat unworthily, but no one ought to eat unworthily,” he immediately adds in confirmation of this truth: “For bread once consecrated never afterwards loses the power of sanctification or ceases to be Christ’s flesh; but it profits the unworthy person nothing, since his faith without works is dead, and therefore he does not have the Spirit who gives life, whom he might receive by the mouth. For what is surprising if earth should eat?” But that by the name “earth” the man of Deutz means Christ’s flesh, taken from our earth, he himself explains thus: “But what is Christ’s flesh apart from divinity, if not our earth?” Thus he does not wish it to be thought surprising that any person, however unworthy, eats the Lord’s flesh which he assumed from us. “Accordingly,” he says (*Book [Col. 0127A] VII on John*), “we are not alarmed when anyone eats Christ’s flesh, being certain what the Son of God has taken from what is ours, and what belongs to himself.”

Then the man of Deutz asks where what is eaten and drunk by the unworthy goes; and he briefly resolves this difficult question against the Stercoranists: “Certainly, as has been said before us, it is pious and salutary to believe that it is distributed through the limbs, so that it is not subject to evacuation.”

Finally, he concisely teaches how eating Christ’s body with the religion of faith and the piety of religion differs from that eating which has neither piety nor religion (*Book VI on John*): “But the worthy person has this more than the unworthy: to the former it profits unto salvation; to the latter, unto judgment.”

[Col. 0127B] Who, after hearing these manifest testimonies to Rupert’s teaching, would not regard Bellarmine’s and Vasquez’s criticism as less than fair? Who would not judge more fairly that Rupert truly held and expressly taught that the Lord’s body is received and eaten even by the unworthy? For who could believe that Rupert uttered such words, on a matter of such importance, rashly or casually? But perhaps someone may suggest that the man of Deutz expressed something different elsewhere. To whom shall faith be given? I produce other passages from other books of Rupert which demonstrate most fully how firm the teaching of that holy abbot was in this faith.

Writing on Matthew (*Book X*), on Christ’s words, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him,” after explaining them thus—“he gives not just any thing of his, but his own flesh and his own blood”—he openly declares, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “that in those who do not believe and yet, though unbelieving, receive the sacrament with the mouth, this food and drink—undoubtedly of his own flesh and blood—works judgment.” For the one who, as Rupert explains elsewhere (*Book IV on Genesis*, ch. 5), “because of his sins shuns the fatness of divine power, and himself grinds with his teeth only the lean body of the sacrifice, is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” Let those hear this and tremble who defile the sacraments of the Lord’s table, or rather eat and drink judgment upon themselves, not discerning the Lord’s body [Col. 0127C].

But let Rupert’s critics hear these things and learn that, in Rupert’s teaching, even unbelievers receive with the mouth the sacrament which is food and drink of Christ’s flesh and blood; let them learn that, in Rupert’s teaching, even one whom divine power does not fatten with its richness because of his sins grinds with his teeth the body of the sacrifice, which is certainly Christ’s body.

In still more explicit words the man of Deutz sets forth the meaning of his faith (*Book III, On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, ch. 22), where he directly refutes this error of eating by faith. He undertakes to prove that Christ’s body is truly eaten even by the unworthy, so that he shows that those who think Augustine’s statement—“only worthy persons can receive the reality of the sacrament” [Note: [Col. 0127D] *Book of Sentences of Prosper*, in which this statement is no longer found.]—means that what is received by the unworthy is not Christ’s body or blood, do not understand Augustine’s meaning [Col. 0128A].

Rupert states the terms of this difficulty in Augustine’s words: “Thus, as Father Augustine also says, in this sacrament, which worthy and unworthy persons receive, there is a reality of the sacrament which only worthy persons can receive. But not as his words have been judged by some. For they thought that he had said that what any unworthy person receives is not Christ’s body or blood; and that, according to the meaning of so great a teacher, what we visibly receive from the Lord’s table is not Christ’s body or blood, but only a figure or sign of Christ’s body and blood.”

Rupert shows that this erroneous interpretation of eating by faith—because it plainly contradicts the words of the Apostle and of Christ himself—is entirely foreign to Saint Augustine’s mind: “He did not say this; indeed, he did not think it. For he was not accustomed to oppose Christ. But Christ speaks, both in his own person, saying, ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD’; and through his Apostle, of whom we have proof that Christ speaks in him, saying: ‘Therefore whoever eats the bread of the Lord and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person test himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup; for whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.’” The man of Deutz interprets the Apostle’s statement as concerning not ordinary bread but Christ’s body and blood: “He did not say: ‘Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats ordinary or common bread and drinks wine such as it was before the consecration had been celebrated’; but: ‘shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord’; and: ‘eats and drinks judgment upon himself,’ not discerning the body of the Lord [Col. 0128C].”

From this most plain meaning of the Apostle concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood even in the sacrilegious reception of that dreadful sacrament, Rupert derives Augustine’s meaning. “Therefore,” he says, “let us seek the understanding by which the aforesaid doctor, Augustine, distinguished the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament not from someone’s contentious disputation, but from the Apostle’s truth.”

[Col. 0128D] Then our doctor of Deutz continues the explanation of this distinction: “Christ himself said that the reality of the sacrament is the mystery of his passion, as we have already said: holding this visible sacrament in his hands, when he said, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ he added, ‘which shall be given’; when he said, ‘THIS IS MY BLOOD,’ he added, ‘which shall be shed.’”

And thus, in accordance with this explanation of the distinction, Rupert himself, together with Augustine, teaches that profane eating indeed receives with the mouth Christ’s body and blood, or the sacrament, but not the reality of the sacrament, since unworthy eating of the sacrament in no way shares in Christ’s death and its benefits. [Col. 0129A] “But he,” adds the Tuitian, “who approaches unworthily does not share in Christ’s sufferings; he does not touch with the mouth of the mind what he receives with the mouth of the body, and hence is himself unworthy.”

From these points he finally concludes as follows: “Therefore this visible sacrament, which the ungodly person receives with his mouth, is indeed Christ’s body and blood; for his unworthiness could not nullify the dignity of so great a consecration. But he does not attain the reality of the sacrament, because with mind and faith working through love he does not look to Christ’s passion; and therefore he does not receive the effect of this same sacrament—namely, that this body was given and this blood shed for him. Rather, he receives that which is contrary to this effect: that is, he becomes guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, and has eaten and drunk judgment upon himself.” [Col. 0129B]

This is Rupert’s most evident teaching. Whoever detects even the faintest shadow of an eating merely by faith in it sees spots in the sun. Does he say that what every unworthy person receives is not Christ’s body and blood, when he expressly concludes that what one receives with the mouth, however unworthy one may be, is Christ’s body and blood? Does he hold that the Lord’s body is eaten not in the reality of the thing, but only through faith, when Augustine rejects this view as contrary to the Apostle and to Christ himself? Does he teach that Christ’s body and blood are not received orally, in the invisible sacrament, by an unworthy person, when he clearly defines that “he who approaches unworthily receives with the mouth of the body what he does not touch with the mouth of the mind”? Finally, from the Apostle’s threatening words—not to say Christ’s—what does he charge against those who do not have the faith that works through love? That they eat Christ’s flesh and drink his blood, but unto judgment and death. He grants the sacrament, which is Christ’s body and blood, to the unworthy, but not the reality of the sacrament, which is participation in Christ’s passion and death. He believes that not even the recipient’s unworthiness “could nullify the dignity of so great a consecration,” by which bread and wine are changed, through the wondrous operation of the Holy Spirit, into that very body of Christ which was given for us, and that very blood of Christ which was shed for us. From all these points he concludes against certain persons who eat by faith alone that this very body of Christ, given for us, and this blood, shed for many, are received and eaten truly—not by faith alone, but in reality—not only by those who possess the piety of faith, but also by the ungodly, with the mouth of the body. What, then, does he think concerning the eating of Christ’s body that does not accord with the Catholic faith? What does he teach that is not handed down by the Church’s doctrine? [Col. 0129C–D]

What can the critic oppose to arguments stronger than every proof? What testimony does he bring forward against this faith of Rupert? I hear one. Rupert said, Bellarmine observes, “that to one in whom there is no faith, nothing from the sacrifice comes except the visible species of bread and wine.” [Col. 0130A] But if Rupert’s faith is condemned on this basis, whose interpretation of St Augustine will not be condemned? For Augustine writes most expressly [Note: [Col. 0129D] *Book of Sentences of Prosper*, sentence 339; and it is read in chapter *Qui discordat*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2.] that “he who is at variance with Christ does not eat his flesh or drink his blood, even though daily he receives, unto the judgment of his own destruction, the sacrament of so great a thing.”

Is Augustine made guilty by Rupert, or Rupert by Augustine? Shall we reject the teaching of Augustine together with Rupert? For “to one in whom there is no faith, nothing from the sacrifice comes except the visible species of bread and wine” does not sound harsher than this: “he who is at variance with Christ does not eat his flesh or drink his blood, even though daily he receives, unto the judgment of his own destruction, the sacrament of so great a thing.” [Col. 0130B]

Therefore, lest anyone presume to correct Augustine together with Rupert by a more severe censure—and thereby deserve punishment himself—let him observe that the eating of Christ’s body, even when performed with the very mouth, does not produce in the unworthy those fruits in which worthy communicants share through Christ’s merits. Accordingly, one manner of eating Christ’s body is fruitful; another is a manner in which Christ’s flesh is eaten, but without the fruit of salvation—indeed, with the judgment of destruction.

Thus, one who gains no fruits from his reading is said to have read nothing, as our French idiom expresses it most aptly: *il n’a rien fait* (“he has done nothing”); not because he did nothing, but because what he did was of no benefit to him. So too, one who communicates in Christ’s body but does not receive the gifts of sanctifying grace is not judged, in the full sense, to eat or receive Christ’s flesh. Only the person who eats Christ’s flesh in such a way as to receive the spirit of its life—that is, who eats it so as to be refreshed by it—is so judged. [Col. 0130C]

“For the flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life.” Augustine himself gives us this understanding [Note: [Col. 0129D] Sermon 2, *On the Words of the Apostle*; and it is read in chapter *Qui manducat*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2.], where he says: “To eat Christ is to be refreshed,” that is, to be nourished by the Spirit of sanctification; or, according to Rupert, to be filled with the richness of divine power.

But to whom is it not utterly certain that one who lacks Christ’s faith and Spirit, and is not a member of Christ’s body, does not eat Christ’s flesh in such a manner as to be refreshed by it, or filled with its goods, but is sent away empty? [Col. 0130D] To whom, then, did Augustine not speak most wisely [Note: [Col. 0129D] Place cited.] when he said: “He who is at variance with Christ does not eat his flesh or drink his blood, even though daily he has received, unto the judgment of his own destruction, the sacrament of so great a thing”? That is, in the sense in which [Note: [Col. 0130D] Augustine, Tractate 26 on John; and it is read in chapter *Credere*, *On Consecration*, distinction 2, and in chapter *Ut qui*, the same distinction.] “to eat Christ is to be refreshed”; in which to believe in Jesus Christ is to eat the living bread; and in which to communicate in the Lord’s body and blood is to abide in Christ, or to be a member of Christ’s body and have one spirit with him. What, then, did Rupert write less Catholicly when he said that “to one in whom there is no faith, nothing—that is, no fruit of spiritual life or blessing—from the sacrifice comes except the visible species of bread and wine”? [Col. 0131A]

For no prudent person will deny that this is Rupert’s meaning in the very passage (*On the Divine Offices*, book II, chapter 9) from which Bellarmine copied words sufficient to undermine, rather than explain, Rupert’s faith. There Rupert introduces a certain piece of Berengarian chaff, who, because he could perceive neither sensation nor movement in the body of the sacrifice, argued, entirely carnally from the sensation of flesh, that Christ and the Lord’s body were not present in the sacrifice of the altar. To demonstrate to him the reality of the Lord’s body, or Christ’s flesh, in the sacrament of the Eucharist, and to cut off this shoot of Berengarian impiety, Rupert distinguishes two lives: one animal life, which functions through the five senses; the other heavenly and spiritual, which is “the Word of life, or the Spirit of sanctification and blessing, of mercy and peace.” Rupert rightly allows that no movement of animal life, which functions through the senses, is present in the body of the sacrifice; but he does not allow the heavenly life to be absent from it—though it “does not come to the one in whom there is no faith.” [Col. 0131B]

For who would say that, for one who lacks the faith that works through love, Christ’s body in the sacrament is life, sanctification, mercy, truth, or peace, rather than, more truly with the Apostle, Augustine, and Rupert, death, destruction, condemnation, and judgment?

[Col. 0131C] But how one who truly, though unworthily, eats that flesh in which the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, and truly, though impiously, drinks that blood which is the fountain of water springing up into eternal life, does not receive this spiritual life—which remains indivisibly with the Word of life in Christ’s body—Rupert explains there by a comparison and an example.

The comparison is that of an ass pricking up its ears at the sound of a lyre: just as it hears the sound but by no means grasps the modes of the melody, though they are in the sound, because it is not rational and cannot understand the principles or modes; so the carnal person receives the visible species of bread and wine and the body of the sacrament, but does not attain the spiritual life that is in it, because he is animal, because he does not at all perceive the things of God.

As an example or figure he brings forward the Jews: because they ate manna without faith and died, so one who communicates in Christ’s body and blood without the righteousness of faith eats and drinks for himself the judgment of condemnation, guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

But how is he guilty of the Lord’s death? Does one who approaches Christ’s table unworthily kill Christ? Hear Rupert answer there with as much piety as subtlety: “He who eats the visible bread of the sacrifice and, by unbelief, rejects from his heart the invisible, kills Christ. How does he kill him? Because he separates the heavenly and spiritual life from the one made alive, and with his teeth rends the body of the sacrifice as dead”—[Col. 0132A] that is, without the Spirit of sanctification—“and by this he is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” Whom would these words not terrify: that those who impiously eat Christ’s flesh without Christ’s Spirit kill Christ and tear apart his body?

But to whom do these matters not testify that, in Rupert’s words, “to one in whom there is no faith, nothing from the sacrifice comes except the species,” not the body of the sacrifice, which is Christ’s flesh itself, but the fruit of the sacrifice—the merits of Christ’s passion and death—is excluded? Thus San-Bovius, a most acute investigator and teacher of theological truth, worthy of all praise for wisdom, replied that this passage means: “Nothing comes, beyond the species, that is useful to the recipient.” By an answer of the same kind, and with the same regard for Rupert’s faith, Monsieur de Lestocque resolves the entire difficulty of this passage. [Col. 0132B]

Yet, if one asks, another interpretation of these words is available, no less consonant with Rupert’s mind and no less with the sense of Catholic faith: namely, that one who does not hold with certain faith the reality of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, or in whom “there is no faith” in that body, receives in his own faith—or rather in his own error—not the Lord’s body but only the species of bread and wine. That is, he believes that he receives these, not discerning the Lord’s body, which he regards as common food; just as the ass pricks up its ears at the sound of the lyre, yet by no means discerns its modes.

Therefore Rupert nowhere declared that Christ’s body and blood are absent from sacrilegious communions, or received by faith alone.
