On the contrary, by constant and manifest teaching he deliberately demonstrated that this very body of Christ, which was given for us, and this very blood of Christ, which was shed for us, are truly contained under the species of bread and wine after consecration has been accomplished; and that they are in the reality of the thing eaten and drunk, even by the ungodly, with the very mouth of the body. Such is the faith of that holy doctor. [Col. 0132C]

The *Vindicator* defends Rupert from the error of impanation, and proves that he held and taught transubstantiation, or the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood.

What is there to marvel at here? What do his rivals prattle here? What vain things do they devise? Could anyone fabricate, or can anyone suspect, that Rupert did not hold the conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood at the prayers or words of the priest, when in countless passages he teaches and writes with the greatest explicitness that bread is “changed, turned, converted, passes over, and is transferred” into Christ’s body, and wine into blood; that bread is made and becomes Christ’s body, and wine his blood?

And should Rupert be refuted from the very works by which he is accused? His faith must especially be vindicated from his Commentaries on John and on Exodus, from which he is chiefly condemned.

In the dedicatory epistle of his books on John’s Gospel, addressed to Abbot Cuno, he gives a brilliant testimony to his faith. For after declaring that he was proclaiming war against the Berengarians and writing these Commentaries on John’s Gospel for the glory of Christ’s body and blood, he closes and seals them with words worthy of a golden seal: “Let us believe God, the faithful Saviour, concerning what we see: namely, that bread and wine have passed into the true substance of body and blood.” [Col. 0133A]

Nor does he fail to fulfil his promise. For in book VI on John’s Gospel, expounding the words, “My Father gives you the true bread from heaven,” he says: “The Jews thought that Christ intended his flesh to be cut up and eaten,” etc. “There this figurative interpretation is destroyed and the sense consonant with the word remains: namely, that bread is converted by divine power into the true substance of his body. But if this appears impossible to anyone—namely, that bread which grew from the earth this year should become Christ’s body, and that wine pressed from grapes now present should be turned into the Lord’s blood,” etc. “Because neither bread nor wine has changed anything of its outward appearance, you cannot and will not understand that the Lord’s body and blood have truly been made.” Etc. “Believe this also: that this visible bread and wine, though nothing has been changed in their outward appearance, have passed into another thing and have been converted into that food and drink which is the nourishment of angels,” etc. “Not so much from fear of punishments as from love of truth, we confess that this bread and this wine, pressed from grapes now present, as soon as it has been marked with the same sign through the hands of the Church saying, ‘That it may become for us body and blood, beloved,’ etc., ‘you shall do unto my remembrance,’ is the body and blood of him who is the author of this institution,” etc. “But if anyone asks how bread created from the earth this year becomes Christ’s body which hung on the cross, and wine pressed from grapes now present becomes that blood which he poured out from his side, let us ask him how the Son of Man, who was indeed conceived from a woman and born of the earth, came down from heaven,” etc. “He changes earthly bread into his flesh.” [Col. 0133B–C]

Rupert wrote these things on John chapter 6 in order to declare most fully, against the Berengarians, that Christ’s body and blood are truly contained under the outward species of bread and wine; that bread and wine are converted, turned, passed over, and changed into Christ’s body and blood; and that bread and wine thus become and are Christ’s body which hung on the cross, and Christ’s blood which was shed for us. [Col. 0133D]

Therefore no credence is due to anyone for whom Rupert’s faith, so clear and certain, still remains doubtful. Rather, anyone who, having heard this profession of Rupert’s faith, does not judge Rupert to be wholly Catholic even in the books he wrote on John, must be considered altogether unjust.

He had already given no less sincere testimony of his faith in the books in which he expounded Exodus. For in chapter 6 of book II he says: “With his own hands he offered himself to God the Father, taking bread and wine and, by the wondrous and ineffable power of sanctification, transferring them into the sacrament of his body and blood.”

And lest body and blood seem to you insufficiently expressed under the name “sacrament,” hear the matter itself explained more fully in chapter 10, where it is said that “by the operation of the Holy Spirit bread and wine become Christ’s body.” Again, in book III, chapter 7: “The substance of bread and wine,” he says, “is converted for us into the reality of body and blood.” In chapter 10: “Let everyone believe that through the words of consecration bread and wine, without change in outward appearance, are transferred into the true substance of Christ’s living body and blood.” [Col. 0134A]

Do you demand ampler proof? Receive this from book IV on Exodus, chapter 7: “Both species, bread and wine, are taken from the earth. But God, the creator of substances and species, approaches … He does not act merely upon the surface, but efficaciously converts these into the flesh and blood of Christ, although the outward species remains.”

But perhaps Rupert’s faith is different in his books *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, which have also troubled some persons? Learn from these words which Rupert sets forth most clearly in chapter 2 of book III: “He took common bread, but by blessing changed it far into something other than it had been, so that he could truthfully say, ‘THIS IS MY BODY, WHICH SHALL BE GIVEN FOR YOU.’ Likewise, he took the substance of wine, but in the same way, by giving thanks or blessing, turned it into something else, so that the Truth who does not lie could say: ‘This is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many.’ Yet it is not seen by the eyes of flesh, nor perceived by the taste of the mouth, that that bread has become Christ’s flesh, that that wine has been turned into blood.” In what more explicit words, I ask, could transubstantiation have been taught and explained? [Col. 0134B]

In the same book II of *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 2—where an eye of clay looks askance at something—he professes in these words the ineffable change of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, which takes place by the power of the divine Word: “Bread and wine are transferred into the true body and blood.” And a little later: “If you pour the stream of this Word over bread and wine, and in the order established by Christ himself utter the truth of this Word, immediately, by transferring the bread itself and wine into his body and blood, he receives them from the holy altar.” [Col. 0134C]

He who in his youth held such thoroughly Catholic views concerning the transformation of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, when he had become not only older in years but also more mature and great in faith, sharply rebuked those who attacked the truth of this conversion and tempted the Lord by saying: “For he struck the rock and waters flowed, and torrents overflowed; can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” [Col. 0134D]

For, applying these words in an allegorical sense, the Tuitian introduces, in book X on Matthew, persons who murmur and who, in order to deny this conversion of bread into Christ’s body, say with Jewish perfidy: “Because God was able, when the side of the crucified Jesus Christ was opened—which was to strike the rock—to cause water with blood to flow, so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled and our minds might have enough to drink: because he could do that, will he also be able to convert bread made by human hands into his body, and wine from these vines into his blood?”

Since, then, it was for Rupert an utterance of Jewish unbelief to deny, or to believe less than certainly, that almighty God can convert bread made by human hands into his body and wine into his blood, do you suppose Rupert denied what, in his view, only Jewish impiety denies? [Col. 0135A]

When Rupert explicitly teaches that bread and wine are transferred, changed, turned, converted, and pass over into Christ’s true body and into his blood, which of the holy Fathers and doctors of the Church ever explained the transformation of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood in more forceful words?

And yet with what face did Monsieur Claude [Note: [Col. 0135D] *The Reply to the First Treatise on the Perpetuity of Faith concerning the Eucharist*, p. 29.] not blush to say “that one cannot produce any passage from these authors (Anastasius, Damascene, and Rupert) which necessarily gives ground for transubstantiation”? [Col. 0135B] As though the name transubstantiation could mean anything other than that the substance of one body is transferred, changed, turned, and converted into another.

For although Rupert did not use this name “transubstantiation,” which Stephen of Autun [Note: [Col. 0135D] Flourished from 1104 to 1130.] was the first, in Rupert’s age, to write [Note: [Col. 0135D] *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, chapter 14.], he nevertheless expresses, professes, and defends the reality denoted by that name—namely, the true conversion of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s flesh and blood—by the same words with which the holy Fathers and ecclesiastical writers before Rupert, his contemporaries and peers, and those after him, expressed, professed, and defended it. If we believe them, why should we deny faith to Rupert as holding and teaching the same thing? If in them we understand a transformation of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood, why should we not understand the same in Rupert, who speaks in the same manner? [Col. 0135C]

Irenaeus [Note: [Col. 0135D] *Against the Valentinian Heretics*, p. 34.] is believed to have held this transubstantiation when he says that “when the mixed cup and the broken bread receive the Word of God, they become the Eucharist of the Lord’s blood and body.”

Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0135D] Tertullian, book IV *Against Marcion*.] is judged to have handed it down to us where he speaks thus: “Having taken the bread and distributed it to the disciples, he made it his body by saying, ‘THIS IS MY BODY.’”

Origen [Note: [Col. 0135D] Origen, book VIII *Against Celsus*.] declared the mystery of this not obscure conversion when he said that “we eat the offered loaves, which indeed through prayer are made a holy and sanctifying body.”

[Col. 0135D] Gregory of Nyssa says [Note: [Col. 0135D] Gregory of Nyssa, Catechetical Sermon, *On the Divine Sacraments*.]: “We believe that bread sanctified by God’s Word is changed into the body of God’s Word”; and below: “It is changed into the body by the Word, as soon as it has been said by the Word, ‘THIS IS MY BODY.’”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0135D] Ambrose, book *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 9; and [Col. 0136D] book IV, *On the Sacraments*, chapters 4 and 5.] explains this conversion in no other terms than as a change effected by the divine word, changing things that were into what they were not, so that Christ’s body is made from bread and blood is made from wine through consecration by the Word. [Col. 0136A]

Hesychius [Note: [Col. 0136D] Hesychius, book VI on Leviticus, chapter 22.] expounded it under the names of transfer and change. And Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 0136D] Chrysostom, Homily 83 on Matthew.] says: “He himself is the one who sanctifies and changes these things.”

In Cyril of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0136D] Cyril of Alexandria, Letter to Calosyrius.] one reads: “God converts the offerings into the reality of his own flesh.”

Euthymius [Note: [Col. 0136D] Euthymius on Matthew.] says: “He ineffably changes these into his own life-giving body and into his own precious blood.”

Isidore [Note: [Col. 0136D] Isidore, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 18.] expressed this transformation in these words: “These two, bread and wine, are visible; yet, sanctified through the Holy Spirit, they pass into the sacrament of the divine body.”

[Col. 0136B] The Venerable Bede [Note: [Col. 0136D] Bede, homily on the Johannine text, “John saw Jesus coming toward him.”] says the same: “The creature of bread and wine is transferred, by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit, into the sacrament of his flesh and blood.”

Such are the expressions concerning bread and wine offered on the altar: they pass over, are transferred, changed, and converted into body and blood; they become and are made Christ’s body and blood. When in the holy Fathers we read of the transformation of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood—or, as we now call it, transubstantiation—if we are Catholic, we immediately understand it. For from such open and constant tradition we hold the faith of this conversion; and it is consequently lost if these expressions are forcibly drawn to alien meanings or judged equivocal. Therefore, when we hear the same words in Rupert’s many passages and books, we must surely understand from them this same truth of transubstantiation in him also, unless we are envious or stupid. [Col. 0136C]

And do not say that the holy Fathers indeed expressed the sacrament of that ineffable divine conversion in these words before disputes had arisen in the Church concerning it—disputes stirred up in the time of Charles the Bald. But once the controversy arose, and Berengar’s heresy was condemned in the Councils of Vercelli and Rome, ecclesiastical writers explained the conversion which we call transubstantiation in words of this kind. I shall cite some writers of no insignificant standing who, defending this transformation against heretics, expressed it in precisely the same words as Rupert and no others.

[Col. 0136D] Paschasius, abbot of Corbie in Gaul, is set at the head of this sacred band—which I may rightly call Benedictine—contending with learned and noble faith in defence of the Lord’s body. In his age an irreligious dispute was already being stirred up concerning the truth of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar. In his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, he writes: “Let the priest observe how a sensible thing is intelligibly transferred by the power of God through Christ’s word into his flesh and blood.” And at the end of chapter 3 he says: “The Holy Spirit, by the sanctification of his sacrament, effects through invisible power that the substance of bread and wine is Christ’s flesh and blood, although it is apprehended neither outwardly by sight nor by the taste of flavour.” And in chapter 4 he concludes: “Thus the truth, while Christ’s body and blood are made, by the power of the Spirit, in his Word, from the substance of bread and wine.” In chapter 8 he says: “The substance of bread and wine is effectively changed inwardly into Christ’s flesh and blood.” In chapter 2 he had already said: “Although bread is converted into flesh and wine into blood,” etc. [Col. 0137A–B]

With these words Paschasius, worthy of much praise for his faith and teaching, expounded the astonishing conversion of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood against certain persons who held less correct views concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood than did the faith of the whole world, though they had not yet stubbornly attacked its truth.

With these words Paschasius opened up that adorable mystery of Christ’s body and blood under the species of bread and wine alone. What lesser glory is due to Rupert, who, in order to explain this truth of Christ’s body and blood genuinely, tirelessly wrote and taught in many passages and books that bread and wine become and are made Christ’s body and blood; that the substance of the fruits of the earth passes over, is transferred, turned, converted, and changed into Christ’s true body which hung on the cross, and into that blood which was shed for many? [Col. 0137B–C]

Lanfranc, abbot of Bec, fighting with armed hand for the truth of the Lord’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 0137D] *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, throughout.], asserts that the substance of bread and wine is converted into Christ’s flesh and blood; and, from Ambrose, that the body is made from bread and Christ’s blood, which redeemed the people, is made from wine. What less illustrious thing did our Rupert do, contending for the same truth, when he maintains and says more strongly that bread and wine have become Christ’s body and blood, and have been converted and changed into Christ’s flesh and blood? By what words could a Catholic doctor speak more plainly and openly in affirming transubstantiation? [Col. 0137C–D]

Guitmund [Note: [Col. 0137D] Flourished about the year 1080.], Lanfranc’s disciple, comes to his master’s aid. Having already attacked with the greatest force the rising heresy of impanation, he professes the faith of transubstantiation in these words in the first of the books he wrote *On the Truth of the Eucharist*: “We believe that bread and wine are changed by divine power, through a singular power, into Christ’s own body”; and below: “What is changed passes into divine flesh.” Nor does he speak less explicitly in the other book: “We necessarily believe that bread and wine pass into the Lord’s flesh and blood. We necessarily believe that this change takes place through Christ’s words; we say that bread is here converted into flesh …” [Col. 0138A] If these words overthrow the error of impanation in Guitmund and declare and at the same time establish the faith of transubstantiation, why should they not do so also in Rupert, who over so many pages professes and demonstrates that bread and wine pass over, are transferred, converted, and changed into Christ’s body and blood?

Nor should Bellarmine’s censorious error in his enlarged and corrected book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* be passed over: he falsely imagined Rupert to be the author of impanation, as though he had first poured forth that monstrosity. The falsity of this invention is demonstrated even by Guitmund alone; for Guitmund, who was older than Rupert, describes and attacks various heresies concerning impanation that had already arisen in his own time. [Col. 0138A–B]

Finally Alger [Note: [Col. 0138D] Flourished about the year 1130.], sustaining the part of that Benedictine sacred line, explains and defends the Church’s faith against the Shadowy Ones and the Impanators, in defence of the truth of transubstantiation, in no words other than Rupert’s: namely, that “the Word of God converts the substance of bread into the coexisting substance of his flesh, into which substance—that is, of Christ’s body and blood—the substance of bread and wine has been converted and transferred, since bread is converted into Christ’s body and becomes Christ’s body.”

If Alger’s faith, and that of the others, concerning the truth of transubstantiation is sincere in these words, in what respect did Rupert think less Catholicly concerning it? He wrote no less explicitly or Catholicly of it. He so often firmly asserted that bread is converted by divine power into the true substance of Christ’s body; that bread which grew from the earth this year becomes Christ’s body; that wine pressed from grapes now present is turned into the Lord’s blood; that bread and wine, while their outward appearance has not changed at all, have truly become the Lord’s body and blood; that they have been converted into that food and drink which is the nourishment of angels; that bread and wine are transferred and pass into Christ’s true body and blood. [Col. 0138B–C]

Nor should you say that under an equivocal sense of such words there lay hidden, like a snake in grass, in Rupert’s age, the heresy of those who said that the substance of bread and wine remains together with the Lord’s body and blood and is hypostatically united with them, so that on account of that hypostatic union bread and wine are said to become, be made, pass into, be transferred into, be converted into, and be changed into Christ’s body. Alger knew this heresy and all its artifices, for he sets them forth in the prologue to his books *On the Sacraments of the Lord’s Body and Blood*. Yet he did not in any way suspect that the poison of this heresy lay hidden under such expressions, by which he himself asserts the Catholic truth concerning this sacrament. [Col. 0138C–D]

Therefore whoever entertains even a slight scruple of suspicion concerning Rupert’s faith about that fearful mystery must necessarily doubt Alger’s understanding, and indeed that of all the holy Fathers, concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body. Or, if the certain and constant faith of the Catholic Fathers is accepted, as it ought in every right to be accepted, no legitimate suspicion whatever can arise concerning the soundness and rectitude of Rupert’s faith and teaching, concerning the true transformation of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood, with only the outward species of bread and wine remaining. Yet, to satisfy some who are troubled by a slight matter, we shall examine the words by which Rupert has seemed to some to deny transubstantiation and hold impanation. [Col. 0139A]

All admit that this one rule must be maintained in expounding the statements of a writer otherwise Catholic: that passages which seem harsher are to be moderated by gentler ones, so that neither excess is charged in the more severe statements nor deficiency in the milder. Whoever does not follow this rule will scarcely, if at all, attain any writer’s meaning, but will wrongly judge him either to have gone too far, fallen short, or spoken contradictions. Let the many testimonies of Holy Scripture serve as an example: if you attach to them the sense demanded by the strictness of the words, you will wholly depart from the truth and consequently from their understanding. Let us therefore weigh Rupert’s words by this rule of Christian prudence, so that we may attain their certain meaning. [Col. 0139B]

Rupert says in chapter 2 of book II, *On the Divine Offices*: “The Word, one and the same God, is above in flesh. Here”—that is, in the sacrament—“he is in bread.” These words appear to imply that in the sacrament of the altar the Word of the eternal Father is in the substance of bread, and that bread accordingly remains, so that the Word may be “impanated,” so to speak; for impanation is understood to mean nothing other than being in the substance of bread. [Col. 0139C]

I admit that Rupert uttered these words.

Yet Rupert could no more Catholicly express this sacrament than the Apostle, who, handing down to us what he received from the Lord, calls Christ’s body placed in the sacrament of the altar “bread”: “The bread which we break, is it not a communion of Christ’s body? Let him eat of that bread,” etc.

Nor could Rupert write or speak more wisely or profoundly concerning this ineffable mystery than the Son himself, the Wisdom of the Father, who called his body in the sacrament bread: “He who eats this bread shall live for ever,” etc. [Col. 0139D]

Thus the word “bread” contains no error; and, without any injury to so great a mystery or to transubstantiation, Rupert could say that the Word of the eternal Father is above in the flesh, here in the bread—distinguishing the flesh of the Word which is in heaven from the flesh of the Word which is under the species of bread, in such a way that it is one in name, reality, and effect, according to what he himself expressed in the letter to Cuno and elsewhere, and differs only in its outward species. See, then, lest, while you condemn Rupert on account of the word “bread,” you refute the Apostle’s words and even reject the very Word of the eternal Father.

In this same chapter 2 Rupert writes that in that unbloody sacrifice—which nevertheless is not without blood [Col. 0140A]—“the holy Catholic Church offers to her Creator the true Word of God, the true Son of God, offering likewise with her hands bread and wine, as the Savior himself handed down to the Church. Finally, the holy Church offers not only the bread and wine which are seen bodily, but also that Word of God, Son of God, whom only the eyes of faith behold, sacrificing a new and true sacrifice.”

From this someone might imagine that bread and wine are simultaneously present with Christ’s body and blood in that new and true sacrifice, by which the Church offers to her Creator not bread and wine alone, but something besides bread and wine, namely the Word of God.

And indeed it is no wonder that one who wishes to mock should play with words. Nor is it surprising if one who wishes to mock [Col. 0140B] is mocked. The sense of this chapter and of these words of Rupert is plain. Why do you wrap it up? Do you play the boy in order to make a doll? Naked things please when they are pure. Therefore, lest you either mock or be mocked, Rupert’s plain and pure meaning is set forth.

The holy Catholic Church, through the hands of priests, offers bread and wine, as the Savior handed it down when he took bread in his hands and blessed it amid thanksgiving. What could be truer? But what could be purer? Do not priests still offer bread and wine to God the Father, though immediately to be changed and transformed by heavenly power into Christ’s body and blood—as Rupert himself explains in that chapter, declaring this to be the work of Truth, by which bread and wine are transformed into the true body and blood of the Lord? Do we not still offer bread and wine in the offertory, which is sung after the Gospel [Col. 0140C] and which Rupert expounds in that chapter, in order that we may prepare the sacrifice of the body and blood of the divine Word?

Rightly, therefore, Rupert, explaining in this and the following chapter the mysteries of the offertory or offering, said that bread and wine are offered by the Church. Rightly he said that, besides this bread and wine, the true Son of God is offered and sacrificed in that new and true sacrifice. Finally, wisely he said that those do not possess the eyes of faith who, seeing nothing further in this sacrifice beyond bread and wine, when told, “It is the body and blood of the Lord,” murmur, “How can it be?”

There is therefore no reason why a suspicion of error, wrongly preconceived, should twist into perverse meanings what is more correct in Rupert; or wrest into distorted errors what is read in him as more Catholic [Col. 0140D].

Therefore, from Rupert’s having said that bread and wine—and not bread and wine alone, but also the true Son of God—are offered, no one should infer that Rupert thought the substance of bread and wine remained in the adorable sacrament of the Eucharist, and that the divine Word was thus “impanated” by Rupert.

The censors of Rupert bring against him chapter 9 of the same book as though it were the chief source of his errors. For in this chapter, treating of the matter of the sacrifice, Rupert wrote:

“The Word, which had assumed human nature—that is, remaining in the flesh—received the substance of bread and wine by means of life; he joined bread with his flesh, wine [Col. 0141A] with his blood.” And, after a few intervening words: “The Word of the Father, intervening as a mediator between the flesh and blood which he had assumed from the Virgin’s womb, and the bread and wine which he assumed from the altar, makes one sacrifice. When he distributes it into the mouths of the faithful, the bread and wine are consumed and pass away; but the offspring of the Virgin, together with the Word of the Father united to it, remains whole and unconsumed both in heaven and in human beings. But to the one in whom there is no faith, nothing of the sacrifice comes, beyond the visible species of bread and wine.” And later: “The invisible bread which descended from heaven is the life of the visible bread which grew from the earth. Yet it is one bread; just as he who descended from heaven and he who was conceived and born from the Virgin’s womb are one Christ. Therefore, whoever eats the visible bread of the sacrifice [Col. 0141B] and repels from his heart through unbelief the invisible bread, kills Christ.” And at the end of the chapter: “From these things the supreme Priest constructs for us a sacrifice, by which the whole human being is nourished: that is, from the Word of God, in whom the human being lives, and from the fruits of the earth, by which the body alone lives. For bread is foremost among things pertaining to food, wine among things pertaining to drink.”

From this one chapter of Rupert they accuse him of three errors: namely, real eating through faith; impanation; and the hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word. The first of these errors we have already disposed of above. We shall vindicate Rupert from the third below. But, to show how far he is here from the second, we shall provide a clearer and truer understanding of this somewhat obscure chapter, with an explanatory interpolation [Col. 0141C].

The divine Word, which in the mystery of the Incarnation “assumed human nature, remaining in the flesh,” receives in the sacrament of the altar “the substance of bread and wine,” transforming it into his own body and blood, “by means of life”—that is, through the life of the Word, in whom Christ’s body subsists; or “by means of life,” namely sacramental life, which is intermediate between the merely spiritual and the sensible. The bread which he received and converted into his body, and which retains the name of bread as well as its species, he joined “with his flesh,” in which the Word remains; the wine, which likewise he received and changed into his blood, and which consequently is now wine only in outward species, “with his blood” [Col. 0141D] which the Word assumed. He joined them so completely that there is not two bodies but one body of the one Christ, through the Word: namely, that which is in the sacrament of the altar, in which it has intermediate life, and that which is in heaven, in which the Word always dwells.

Hence this statement: “The Word of the Father,” who never abandoned “the flesh and blood which he had assumed from the Virgin’s womb,” and who “assumed the bread and wine from the altar,” but changed them in the sacrament into body and blood—intervening as mediator between this flesh and this blood of Christ according to the species which it has in heaven, and that same flesh and blood according to the species of bread and wine which it has in the sacrament—makes “one sacrifice,” or one victim, one Christ, and one body of Christ. This body is not one thing in reality in heaven and another thing in the sacrament, since whether in the sacrament or in heaven it is the true and one body of Christ subsisting in the Word. When it “is distributed into the mouths of the faithful” in communion, “the bread and wine”—the species of each, which remain in the sacrament—“are consumed and pass away.” But the offspring of the Virgin, Christ’s body, together with the Word of the Father united to it, remaining united to the Word of the Father, “remains whole and unconsumed, both in heaven,” according to its proper species, “and in human beings,” in the sacrament under the species of bread and wine.

But to the person in whom faith is absent, beyond the visible species of bread and wine—which alone consequently remain after their substance has been changed into Christ’s body and blood—nothing of the sacrifice comes that confers anything of spiritual life upon the recipient [Col. 0142B]. That is, Christ’s body does not come to such persons in the reality or fruit of the sacrament, which is for them judgment, condemnation, and death; nor indeed does even the substance of bread remain, as is sufficiently indicated when it is said that nothing of the sacrifice reaches them beyond the species.

“The invisible bread,” therefore—the Word of the Father, who is that bread which descended from heaven—“is the life of the visible bread which grew from the earth.” For in that Word Christ’s body, which in the sacrament was made from visible bread, retaining its name and external species, subsists by means of intermediate, namely sacramental, life. “Yet it is one bread”: the Word of the Father and Christ’s body, which under the outward species of bread nevertheless lives and subsists in the Word. “Just as he who descended from heaven and he who was conceived and born from the Virgin’s womb are one Christ.” For just as he who descended from heaven and he who was conceived and born from the Virgin’s womb are one Christ, because of the unity of the Word in whom both he who came from heaven and he who was born from the Virgin subsist, so there is one bread, or one body, both that which is in heaven and that which is in the sacrament, because of the unity of the Word in whom both the body which is in the sacrament and that same body which is in heaven subsist and live.

“Therefore, whoever eats the visible bread” [Col. 0142C]—which under the species of bread is the flesh of the Word—“of the sacrifice,” in the real eating of Christ’s body, “and repels the invisible,” namely the Word, “from his heart through unbelief,” refusing to believe that it is in Christ’s body or flesh under the mystical species, “kills Christ” [Col. 0142D], separating through his unbelief from the flesh, or life-giving body, the Word which is life and in whom that flesh has its subsisting life. “From these things the supreme Priest constructs for us a sacrifice, by which the whole human being is nourished: that is, from the Word of God, in whom the human being lives, and from the fruits of the earth”—bread and wine, which truly are fruits of the earth, but are to be changed by the consecration of the divine Word into Christ’s body and blood—“by which, insofar as they are fruits of the earth, the body alone lives,” etc.

From this brief, plain, and easy explanation of such a chapter according to Rupert’s meaning, it becomes evident to anyone who pays even slight attention that Rupert teaches nothing else in this chapter than that bread is assumed by the divine Word in order to be transformed and changed into his own flesh [Col. 0143A]; and that this bread, thus assumed and changed by the Word in the sacrifice, is not flesh other than that which the Word has in heaven, but is one flesh, because it is the flesh of that one Word, whether it is in heaven or in the sacrifice. Let anyone who understands Christ’s flesh not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit judge what error these statements contain, and how far they are removed from the heresy of impanation.

Nor should anyone be disturbed because Rupert, in the following chapters of the same book, calls that awe-inspiring mystery the sacrament of bread and wine. For the holy Fathers do not hesitate, following the Apostle and Christ himself, to call it bread or the sacrament of bread; yet by these expressions they not only do not deny the true conversion of the substance of bread into Christ’s body, but clearly establish it by their interpretations. Rupert, therefore, must not be thought to have denied it by these words. Although he sometimes calls this mystery the sacrament of bread and wine, in many other places he also calls it the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. Does he not, writing on Exodus, say that Christ, by the marvelous and ineffable power of sanctification, transforms bread and wine into the sacrament of his body and blood [Col. 0143B]? Is not this sacrament of body and blood the Lord’s body and blood, which Christ himself offered in his hands under the species of bread? It was therefore not inappropriate, and did no injury to Eucharistic truth, for Rupert to call this mystery of the Lord’s body and blood the sacrament of bread and wine.

And if, in book 12, chapter 2, of this work *On the Divine Offices*, Rupert says: “After consecration, the fivefold sign of the cross is impressed upon the substance of bread and wine,” hear what follows, and from it discern Rupert’s meaning. For he does not say that the fivefold sign of the cross is impressed upon the substance of bread and wine while it remains in its own being, but upon that which is truly incorporated with Christ seated at the right hand of the Father. That is, according to Rupert’s understanding, what had been the substance of bread has, by divine power through an ineffable conversion, become the one true body of Christ, that very body which sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven—as we have already explained above and shall explain more fully below from Rupert himself. Let us proceed to resolve other matters.

[Col. 0143D] Rupert interprets the words of Exodus, “You shall not eat any of it raw, nor boiled with water, but only roasted with fire,” concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, as follows: “You will attribute everything to the operation of the Holy Spirit, whose effect is not to destroy or corrupt the substance, whatever it assumes for its own purposes, but to preserve the good of the substance.”

These are the words most noted by the critics, in which they claim that Rupert plainly expresses the error of impanation: “To add invisibly what was not there, without destroying what was; just as God does not destroy human nature when, by his operation, he joined it from the Virgin’s womb to the Word in the power of personhood, so he does not change or destroy the substance of bread and wine, subject in its outward species to the five senses, when he joins it to that same Word in the unity of the same body [Col. 0144A] which hung upon the cross, and to the blood of that same body which he poured forth from his side. Likewise, just as the Word sent down from on high became flesh, not by being changed into flesh, but by assuming flesh, so bread and wine, both lifted up from below, become Christ’s body and blood, not by being changed into the taste of flesh or the horror of blood, but by invisibly assuming the truth of the immortal substance—both divine and human—which is in Christ,” etc.

To this Rupert’s censors cry out: How could transubstantiation be more explicitly denied, or impanation more explicitly taught? For if the operation of the Holy Spirit does not destroy the substance, but invisibly adds to what remains in the good of its substance what was not there; if, finally, it does not change or destroy the substance of bread, how can it be true that the entire substance of bread and wine is destroyed by the invisible operation of the Holy Spirit, that nothing of the substance of bread and wine remains, but that it is entirely changed into Christ’s body and blood? What could be more contrary to this?

Nevertheless, those who have accepted Rupert’s faith as established by the testimonies cited—who have heard him say that bread and wine pass, are transferred, changed, altered, and converted into Christ’s flesh, which hung for us on the cross, and into the blood poured out for us; who have moreover observed that in that chapter Rupert especially teaches this one point, “that to every person consecrated through baptism and cleansed from the stain of the old food by which the human race perished, Christ’s body and blood are delivered; that in the sacrament we eat the Lord’s body” [Col. 0144C]; and finally that “by the operation of the Holy Spirit bread becomes Christ’s body and wine becomes his blood,” etc.—will recognize that these claims cannot stand in the Church’s perpetual understanding except on the basis of that conversion of the substance of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood which has received the name transubstantiation.

Such persons will not yield to the words advanced, which are of more obscure meaning, and abandon Rupert’s doctrine as though it were less Catholic. Rather, examining his thought more deeply, they will find that he does not deny that transmutation of substance by which, through the power of the Holy Spirit, a thing ceases to be what it was and begins to be something more perfect which it was not; indeed, they will find that he defines this very change more than once [Col. 0144D].

For Rupert, explaining Christ’s first miracle, says (*Book II on John*, after the middle): “God made wine from water; and every year, by the same power, he causes water received into the bosom of the earth to pass into wine in the vines. But here, where the entire order of nature is lacking, he testifies that wine was made from water, because he is the Lord of nature. And below it should be noted that the Lord did not make from nothing the wine by which he gladdened the guests, nor the bread by which he satisfied the hungry crowds, nor indeed did he make anything at all in the whole course of his signs from non-existent things; rather, he advanced things already existing into something greater and better, making wine from water,” etc.

These words plainly declare that Rupert in no way removes from the operation of the Holy Spirit those changes [Col. 0145A] by which a thing ceases to be what it was in order to advance into something greater and better; rather, he refuses to attribute to the Holy Spirit only those changes by which a thing is brought back into its original nothingness, so that nothing of it remains.

Therefore, when Rupert says that, while the good of the substance remains, what was not there is invisibly added to what was there, he by no means understands that in those transformations of things which the power of the Holy Spirit effects, things begin to be what they were not without ceasing to be what they were—that they are simultaneously what they were and begin to be what they were not. Otherwise, wine made from water would, for Rupert, be not wine alone but at once water and wine—a view which no one could refrain from laughing either to hold or to ascribe to Rupert. Who, then, would not marvel or be astonished that the censors fail to understand in what correct sense [Col. 0145B] Rupert said that the Holy Spirit does not change or destroy the substance of bread and wine according to its outward species, which is subject to the five senses—namely, by a destructive change, as Rupert plainly indicates by adding the word “destroy”—but rather by a perfective change, when he joins it to that same Word in the unity of the very body which hung upon the cross? That is, as Rupert says in countless places, when he changes and converts bread and wine into the body of Christ, the Son of God, who says: “THIS IS MY BODY, WHICH WILL BE GIVEN FOR YOU; THIS IS MY BLOOD, WHICH WILL BE POURED OUT FOR MANY,” he makes them now the flesh and blood of the Word, and therefore one body with that which hung on the cross—or rather, that very body which was fastened to the cross, since the Word of God has but one and the same body.

Who, then, does not see that from Rupert’s statement, “while the good of the substance remains, what was not there is invisibly added to what was there,” the censors infer that Rupert thought that bread, which is changed and passes into Christ’s body, nevertheless remains bread—just as though they inferred from the same statement that water changed into wine by the marvelous power of the Holy Spirit always retains its nature as water, so that wine is simultaneously water? Let them therefore not provoke such laughter; if they have sense, let them understand Rupert’s words to concern not every sort of change, but one that is utterly destructive.

Moreover, let them observe that Rupert by no means says that the Holy Spirit does not change or destroy the substance of bread and wine considered in itself and simply—necessity compels us to make a distinction, without shrinking from the vocabulary of the schools—but says that he does not change or destroy it “according to its outward species, subject to the five senses” [Col. 0145D]. What else does this mean except that the operation of the Holy Spirit, by which bread and wine are changed into Christ’s body and blood, does not change the sensible species of bread and wine, although bread and wine are now no longer under them, but the body and blood of the Lord? And that this is Rupert’s meaning is made persuasive by all those passages in which he repeatedly teaches that “bread is seen, but Christ’s body is present; Christ’s body and blood are under the species of bread and wine,” and similar statements.

[Col. 0146A] If these things do not overcome the wrongly assumed suspicion, let the critics themselves read what Rupert wrote in chapter 6, book II, on Exodus: “With his own hands the supreme Priest offered his body and blood under the species of bread.” And in chapter 7 of book IV: “The two species of bread and wine,” Rupert says, “are taken from the earth; but God, the creator of substances and species, comes to them and converts these not superficially but effectively into his flesh and blood, although the outward species remains.” Earlier, in chapter 32, book VII, on Genesis, he had written “that bread brought near and immersed in the terrible mystery of Christ’s passion still appears to be bread, what it was; and yet in truth it is Christ, what it was not.”

One who expressly says that bread and wine are converted into Christ’s body and blood while the outward species remains, undoubtedly did not think that the substance of bread and wine remains, but unquestionably affirmed that conversion of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood which we commonly call transubstantiation. One who writes so openly that bread immersed in the terrible mystery of Christ’s passion appears to be what it was—

Claude the minister, therefore, falsely maintained [Note: [Col. 0145D] *In the place cited above*, p. 29.] that in that chapter of book II on Exodus Rupert overthrew the mystery of Eucharistic transubstantiation. Let Rupert’s other censors also consider with what religious regard for faith and what fairness in law—which requires judgment in doubtful as well as obscure matters to favor the possessor—they condemned Rupert, as though he had either introduced or at least approved the error of impanation, and had anticipated for the Lutherans this new fiction of error [Col. 0146C], on the basis of obscure, uncertain, and weaker statements, without attending to the clearest, firmest, and weightiest testimonies which irrefutably prove Rupert’s sound faith.

Only Gregory of Valencia remains here to be refuted. Thinking differently about Rupert from the others, he says not that Rupert denied transubstantiation, but that he placed the change of substances in accidents alone; so that, if one believes Gregory, in Rupert’s mind substances differ only by accidents, and one passes into another solely through a change of accidents.

Gregory of Valencia himself explains this singular opinion concerning Rupert as follows, in *Third Part*, disputation 6, question 3, point 2, part VII. Having objected to himself that Abbot Rupert, in chapter VII on John [Col. 0146D], denies that the substance is changed in the sacrament, he responds to the objection:

“As regards Abbot Rupert, this author intended to teach nothing distinctive here concerning this transformation, but likewise adapted to it, as also to other changes of things, a certain error of his own which conflicts even with philosophy. For he supposed that the substance of bread, wine, body, blood, and other such things is one and the same, and that they differ only in accidents. Consequently, he judged that, when bread and wine are truly changed into body and blood, the substance of the thing is not changed. Therefore this testimony of Rupert is in one respect rather for us: for he thought that bread is in reality changed here into Christ’s body, just as one thing is ordinarily changed into another when, according to true philosophy, it is changed substantially” [Col. 0147A].

Here Gregory of Valencia does not charge Rupert with error against the faith of transubstantiation, but only with error against the human doctrine of changes in things; and he rebukes Rupert as having sinned more against philosophy than against Catholic truth. Yet the force of this Peripatetic censure must be weighed. And against it I first maintain that Rupert perfectly understood the principles, causes, alterations, and transformations of things.

For, first, he knew that God created one common principle from which created things arise: namely, unformed matter, called *hyle*, which is properly called substance, since it is the first subject from which and in which everything created in the lower world has its being, except the rational soul [Col. 0147B].

Second, he knew that this first substance is variously shaped through different modes, qualities, and properties, and that, clothed in different forms of this kind, it displays different species. Thus the elements are formed, drawing their being from *hyle*, or created unformed matter, and receiving their form and name from their various modes, qualities, and properties. Thus earth, which has its being from *hyle*, is called earth because it is heavy and dry.

Third, he knew that other things consist of the substances of the elements, whose differing configuration under different modes, properties, and qualities defines the different natures of the things composed from them. Thus earth, configured under the species of bronze, is called bronze; and bronze itself, configured under the species of a king, is called a king. And all these things, whether works of art or of nature, consist of matter and form together, and are mutable.

Rupert describes this entire teaching of the truer philosophy in these words (*Book II, On the Divine Offices*, chapter 6): “When an artisan fashions a statue by the craft of the smith, the formed matter is bronze in species, namely an image of the emperor, or, if he prefers, an idol of Jupiter. Thus what we call a statue is not what it is, because it is not one or simple thing. Nor is even the bronze itself, before it is fashioned in it, something simple, since its matter is earth, greatly different from what is seen in the species of bronze [Col. 0147D]. If you consider earth itself, it is not what it is—for example, it receives its name from its form; for it is called earth because it is heavy and dry. But it derives its being from *hyle*, which they call created unformed matter. Likewise, a human being is not simply this or that, because he consists of parts, namely soul and body, which death undoubtedly separates though they are joined by a dissoluble bond. So also are all other things which consist, as stated, of matter and form; and for that reason they are subject to a multitude of accidents and are mutable. But God’s substance is simple, not formed, but form alone—form, I say, lacking matter.” From these few words, learn the lion from the claw.

Fourth, he knew that there are two kinds of modes and qualities: some substantial, others accidental. The former constitute a thing’s species and therefore, as philosophers say, cannot be separated from a thing while its being remains. The latter, whether they are merely accidents in themselves or substances in their own right, come to a thing already established in its nature in such a way that they do not alter its species; or they may be absent while the thing nevertheless preserves its *entelechy*.

Rupert states this as follows (*Book X, On the Divine Offices*, chapter 6): “Every human or angelic creature, and all substantial qualities without which no substance can anywhere be thought to exist—namely, to be, to live, to perceive, and to discern—which are naturally present and therefore cannot be absent from it, were created through the Son together with the substance itself. But to fare well, to live holily, to perceive rightly, to discern prudently, or to understand wisely are accidental qualities added through the Holy Spirit. It is clear that these are accidental because they are present in a good human being or angel and absent in an evil one, while nature or substance remains [Col. 0148B]. And lest any room for calumny should appear to remain, these qualities have been called accidental even though the Holy Spirit himself, whose gifts these are, is substance; just as being pregnant is undoubtedly an accident to a woman, although the seed by which she is impregnated, or that from which and through which the seed was transferred into her, is substance. Let the philosopher illustrate this by familiar examples; that is not the role I am playing here.”

Fifth, Rupert knew that different species of things are defined not by accidents but by substantial qualities, so that between different natures there is a distinction not merely accidental but also substantial. Although one thing is not distinguished from others by a form which is in itself and in reality a distinct substance, it is not therefore separated from others only by accidental qualities, but principally by the substantial qualities by which it itself is constituted. And although substantial qualities, considered in themselves and in reality, are accidents of the first subject or primary substance to which they accrue, they are not accidents of the nature which they constitute and by reason of which they are called substantial. These points follow from what precedes [Col. 0148C].

Sixth, he knew that transformations and generations of one and the same substance occur through the appearance of new modes, the accession of new qualities, and also through differing stages of maturation. Rupert discusses this in another work (*Book II on John*, after the middle), where he describes the conversion of water into wine—an operation of nature alone in the vines—as follows: “With all the other elements cooperating, this comes about, that water becomes wine in the vines. For first water is received into the bosom of the earth, without whose help it could provide no richness to the roots of vines, herbs, or trees.” Here Rupert most wisely teaches that water is nature’s first principle, as Helmont also successfully demonstrated in this century. “Then, by the gentle tempering of the air, it is prompted to break forth in the shoots; and, with the further aid of heat, the shoot puts forth leaves, blossoms, and the grape is gradually ripened.”

[Col. 0149A] Among the more penetrating investigators of nature, whom, I ask, do you find who has expounded this wonderful work of nature more eloquently, or explained more clearly, briefly, and learnedly than our Rupert the various stages of maturation by which the internal efficient cause, with the aid of the external, produces the entire course of the thing?

Far be it, therefore, that Rupert sinned against the principles of sounder philosophy, since he investigated its deeper matters with the greatest acuteness and reached its higher truths with the utmost subtlety. Rupert never thought or taught that things differ from one another through accidental qualities alone, or what he calls accidental qualities—qualities which happen to a thing already possessing the essential perfection of its own nature. He never said that transformations of things from one species into another are effected by the accidents of that species alone. Even if Rupert sometimes wrote that water passes into wine by the addition of an accident, he understood by the name “accident” not only accidental qualities, which can be absent from a thing’s nature, but also substances and substantial qualities, insofar as they happen to matter or the first subject [Col. 0149B].

The Peripatetic theologian therefore falsely answered that Rupert supposed the substance of bread, wine, body, blood, and other such things to be identical, differing only by accidents. But he said most falsely that Rupert held that in this sacrament of Christ’s body and blood the substance of the thing—that is, of bread and wine—is not changed, when all the many testimonies adduced prove that Rupert thought and taught that the substance of bread and wine passes, is converted, and is changed into Christ’s body and blood [Col. 0149C]. How could this be true if the substance of bread were the same as the substance of Christ’s blood? How, I ask, could one truthfully say that he taught bread and wine to be changed into Christ’s body and blood if he ever denied that they are changed into another substance?

I therefore convict this theological philosopher of falsehood by this single brief argument. Rupert admits the transformation of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood. Valencia himself concedes this, and cannot deny it. Therefore the transformation is either of substance or of accident, since in a thing there is and can be nothing else, according to Gregory’s own school. Is it not of accident? For Valencia would not dare attribute to Rupert the claim that he ever said that the species, or accidents, of bread and wine themselves and alone are changed in the sacrament; for it is universally admitted that Rupert teaches in almost countless passages that the outward species of bread and wine alone remain in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 0149D]. It remains, therefore, that Gregory, admitting that Rupert teaches the transformation of bread and wine, must acknowledge that in Rupert’s doctrine it is not a conversion of accident but of substance.

And so Gregory ought rather to correct his own understanding than amend Rupert’s doctrine. That doctrine has been assailed and struck out by so many censures only in order that, more powerfully vindicated, it might emerge more illustrious [Col. 0150A] and, more fully proved, shine forth more pure—every shadow of impanation, as Guitmund calls it, and of “invination” having been banished.

But if anyone wishes to object to Rupert’s very pure faith the error of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father in the sacrament of the altar, by transferring to this charge Rupert’s words cited above, so as either to obscure or utterly erase the glory of so great a doctor, we shall readily dispel this cloud by the light of truth.

The *Defender* defends the venerable Rupert from the error of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father in the sacrament of the altar, and first explains the meaning of that error.

The Catholic faith believes and professes concerning this awe-inspiring sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood:

[Col. 0150B]

1. That it contains not merely a figure of Christ’s body and blood, but that very body of Christ which, taken from the Virgin, hung upon the cross, and that very blood of Christ which was poured out for many.

2. That bread and wine pass or are transferred, changed, altered, and converted into Christ’s true body and blood, while the outward species of bread and wine alone remains.

Upon these two points rests the sum of our faith concerning this sacrament. To overthrow it, the heretics of our time leave no effort untried. When they discovered that we hold it immovably, established by the uninterrupted tradition of Catholic writers, they strove with every effort to pervert the meaning and intention of those writers’ words—that is, to turn them to their own errors—thinking that by this means alone [Col. 0150C] our faith could be shaken.

Albertinus above all (book III, p. 902), when he heard Anastasius of Sinai [Note: [Col. 0149D] Around A.D. 635.], Germanus of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0149D] Around A.D. 720.], John Damascene [Note: [Col. 0149D] Around A.D. 740.], bishops, the Second Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0150D] Around A.D. 787.], and Nicephorus of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0150D] 806] openly denying that that which is in the sacrament of the Eucharist is a figure and image of the Lord’s body and blood—in the sense, namely, in which a figure and image exclude the presence of the thing and are substituted for it while it is absent—and clearly professing that this is that very body which was born of the Virgin, and that very blood which flowed from the side of Christ hanging upon the cross; finally, that by the operation of the Holy Spirit bread and wine pass over, are transferred, changed, and converted into the true body of Christ which was fastened to the cross for us, and into his true blood, which was shed for the wiping away of the sins of many [Col. 0150D]: lest the force of these most explicit testimonies should prevail, he imposes upon them a sense wholly foreign to them. What sense do you suppose? One which neither favors his own error nor supports our faith—so that, if it is not his, neither is it ours, but is altogether different.

But this innovator, like the false mother crying in vain, “Neither mine nor yours; let it be divided,” betrays his falsehood by that very cry. What sense, then, does Albertinus attribute, most evidently, to this teaching of the holy Fathers, which he strives to tear away from our side? [Col. 0151A] A sense which no one but a subtle master and servant of error could have devised.

For he has imagined that the faith of the Church was changed by the aforesaid Doctors—a faith which, if we believe him, God forbid, had until then professed nothing but a figure of the Lord’s body and blood in the sacrament of the altar. And lest, even unwillingly, he should acknowledge that they teach a true conversion of the substance of bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, Albertinus wishes the following words of theirs—by which they expressly profess that bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood, pass over, are transferred, and are converted into the Lord’s body and blood, and other such things—to be understood only of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the divine Word. That is, bread and wine, joined to the Word in unity of person, and consequently also to his body and blood, may truly be called, in Albertinus’s sense, the Lord’s body and blood; just as the manhood in Christ, because of the hypostatic union of human nature with the Word of God, is truly and catholicly called God.

This novel invention of Albertinus was most learnedly refuted by a book worthy of eternal light, entitled *The Perpetuity of Faith in the True Presence of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ in the Holy Sacrament of the Altar*. I know indeed that a very acute refutation of that book has appeared—if it ought to be called a refutation rather than a repeated heap of errors. [Note: [Col. 0151D] The author had issued this defence of Rupert before the final book of the most steadfast defender of the Catholic faith, the most learned Dr. D. Arnauld, had appeared.] Yet it too will be more powerfully demolished, by a renewed refutation, by the tireless champions of Catholic truth. This task [Col. 0151C] does not belong to the cause which I am defending here.

Yet I can readily say this one thing without departing from our subject: namely, that this heresy of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the divine Word did not even arise in the age of Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, who flourished in the eleventh century down to the year 1080. Three facts establish this with certainty for anyone who does not reject all faith.

1. Guitmund himself, while more carefully explaining [Note: [Col. 0152D] Book III, *On the Truth of Christ’s Body and Blood in the Eucharist*.] and more forcefully refuting the newly born heresy of the Impanators, plainly declares that no one dared defend it after the fashion of the hypostatic union of the divine Word with human nature; or assert that the Word was “impanated,” as we believe that the Word became flesh; [Col. 0151D] or say that bread and wine are one Christ, as we confess God and man to be one Christ. “Whence, then,” says this Eucharistic champion, “has this evil error of impanation invaded them? The whole world sings with one voice: as a rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ. No one dares to say: so God and man and bread and wine are one Christ. Whence, then, comes this new combination to these men?”

2. Although this new heresy taught that Christ was impanated and “invinated,” it nevertheless did not believe that bread and wine were turned by the Savior’s words into his flesh and blood [Col. 0152A]; rather, it held that bread and wine were mixed with Christ’s body and blood, or that Christ’s body and blood lay hidden beneath bread and wine, as Guitmund testifies in the same book.

3. Guitmund, who diligently investigated and examined with precision everything upon which this heresy seemed to rely, nowhere advanced this hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word. Yet he would neither have feigned nor passed it over, but would have attacked it vigorously, if this new heresy of combination had then consisted in it.

Indeed, in that place he is wholly occupied with the statements of the holy Fathers, from which he demonstrates against these impanators that bread and wine, by the wondrous operation of the Holy Spirit, become Christ’s body and blood, pass over, [Col. 0152B] are changed, and are converted into Christ’s body and blood. He would certainly have uttered these things ridiculously if his opponents, freely admitting them, had expounded them in the sense of hypostatic union—a sense which Guitmund did not even dare to touch. More ridiculous, therefore, is the man who has boldly asserted that this heresy of the all-healing hypostatic union was born many centuries earlier and was more freely handed down by many writers of no obscure name, whom we have cited above.

It appeared later than Guitmund himself, only in the following century, about the time of Alger. Alger, flourishing at the beginning of the twelfth century, around the year 1130, describes this heresy as novel and absurd in these words:

> “Certain persons, led astray by some sayings of the saints, say that Christ is personally impanated in bread just as God is personally incarnate in human flesh. Since this heresy is novel and absurd, it must, insofar as God inspires, be uprooted from the foundations by arguments and authorities.”

After this Alger sets out the foundation upon which they built this new error:

> “For from a certain comparison of blessed Augustine in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*, they derive and defend their heresy, which says that the sacrifice of the Church is made of two things and consists of two things, just as Christ’s person consists and is made of God and man. For, by wrongly supplying what is unstated, they say that the sacrifice of the Church—that is, Christ sacrificed on the altar—consists personally of two things in the same person, just as Christ’s person consists of God and man.” [Col. 0152D]

This vigorous defender of the Eucharistic sacrament also does not pass over what they themselves answer to objections raised against this perverse doctrine:

> “But if it is objected to them,” he says, “that that appearance of the elements is not one person with Christ, but only his sacrament, mystery, and figure, they do not even thus desist. They say that blessed Ambrose says to Gratian: ‘as the sacrament of the assumed man is spoken of, so the sacrament of the Lord’s body is spoken of’; and blessed Maximus speaks of God coming under the mystery of flesh; [Col. 0153A] and in many Scriptures God is said to be covered by a human form or figure, just as Christ is on the altar by the form or figure of bread.”

And, after inserting a few words, he again explains this absurd error from the objections which they raised:

> “But again they object that Christ is said to assume the species or form of bread on the altar just as the Word of God assumes the species or form of flesh in the virginal womb; and as the Word becomes flesh, so bread becomes that same flesh.”

All these inventions of this new heresy Alger most forcefully shakes and utterly overturns by the weight of arguments and authorities. I shall pursue what pertains to our subject.

By these testimonies of Alger and Guitmund it is most certainly and plainly proved what was the meaning of that new and absurd [Col. 0153B] heresy which hypostatically impanated and invinated the Word; what was the foul origin of this error; and finally what were the developments of this pernicious monster.

1. The Berengarians placed in the sacrament nothing but a figure and sign of Christ’s body and blood.

2. But when constrained by the authority and arguments of the Church, and driven from that perversity, they fled, as Guitmund relates, to the impiety by which, while believing in Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament of the Eucharist, they wickedly imagined Christ’s body together with bread so that it might be eaten, and his blood together with wine so that it might be drunk. This was in Guitmund’s age, and he calls this heresy the new “combination.”

3. Since they had nothing by which either to defend or in any way persuade others of this [Col. 0153C] impanation of Christ, and since no one had yet dared to say that Christ was impanated in the manner in which we profess the Word to have been incarnate, as Guitmund himself testifies, they finally gave free rein to their error. About Alger’s time they rushed headlong into such blasphemy that, with sacrilegious mouth, they declared bread and wine to be hypostatically united to the Word and assumed by him, with flesh and blood, into unity of person, as Alger testifies—just as, by the Catholic faith, we believe human nature to have been assumed by the Word.

This is the first and true origin of hypostatic impanation: it must be traced not to Anastasius, Damascene, or other orthodox writers, but to the Berengarian heretics [Col. 0153D]; it belongs not to the seventh but to the twelfth century; nor did this heresy alter the Church’s faith by its novelty, since it was almost extinguished as soon as it was born, and, so far as I know, no one except John of Paris [Note: [Col. 0153D] In the treatise which he entitled: *Determination of Brother John of Paris, Preacher, concerning a mode of the existence of Christ’s body in the sacrament of the altar other than that held by the Church*; as I myself read in a manuscript codex, in which he recognizes the letter beginning “I read and reread,” etc.—concerning which we noted more above—to be Anselm’s, but in no way says that it was addressed to Valramnus. Vasquez, following Valesius, asserted this ineptly.] ever favored it. Who, then, will not now laugh at Albertinus’s fable? In order to evade the faith and doctrine of Catholic writers, and more readily deceive those too ready to believe, he invented the claim that, when they expressly taught that bread and wine become and are Christ’s body and blood, and that by the Church’s mystical consecrations bread and wine pass over, are transferred, changed, and converted into the Lord’s body [Col. 0154A] and blood, and other such things, they had introduced the new and absurd heresy of a hypostatic combination or union of bread and wine with the divine Word.

Let, then, the whole machine of Albertinus collapse, by which he wished to shake the firmness of our faith in the adorable sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, attempting—but in vain—to break the unbroken succession of that Catholic tradition.

Yet the censure of both Bellarmine [Note: [Col. 0154D] Book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Rupert, first observation.] and Vasquez must likewise be corrected here. That distinguished cardinal, in order to embellish Rupert with his observations, pronounced as if from a tripod that all the material which we have set forth above from Alger concerning the novel and absurd error of hypostatic impanation describes a new heresy of Rupert [Col. 0154B] and points to him by an unspoken name. So far did he go that this new heresy of Rupert is said by him to be the reason why the works of that abbot of Tuitiensis, though otherwise not unlearned, as he says, lay without recognition and honor in the darkness of oblivion for about four hundred years. By what fairness toward truth Bellarmine formed this judgment concerning Rupert’s works, we have already shown above; below we shall refute the graver calumny concerning the heresy of impanation through hypostasis.

Vasquez, a man of equally subtler and readier intellect, traces the beginnings of this error back to the year 1060, believing it to have come from Valramnus, whom he supposes to be the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*. He moderates Bellarmine’s judgment by maintaining that Rupert [Col. 0154C] was not the parent of this heresy, but its defender.

We have already sufficiently exposed Vasquez’s first error concerning the beginnings of this heresy: both when we proved that it had not yet arisen in Guitmund’s age, and when we deprived Valramnus of Attenberg, by every right, of the work *On the Divine Offices*. We shall shortly reduce the excess of that moderated censure to its proper measure, when we demonstrate more fully and plainly that the man of Tuitiensis was in no way a patron of this error.

Therefore I undertake to defend Rupert’s faith—him whom I venerate as a father for his wisdom and holiness, love as a brother by profession, and hear as a Catholic teacher—with all the devotion proper to a son, all the charity proper to a brother, and all the reverence and zeal proper to a disciple, from the impious novelty and novel impiety of this hypostatic union of bread and wine with the divine Word. [Col. 0154D]

## The Defender maintains that Rupert is free from the error of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word

The following considerations especially establish and declare that Rupert’s teaching is free from the absurd impiety of this error.

[Col. 0155A]

1. No Catholic among the earlier writers stained Rupert’s faith with this blemish.

2. None of that holy doctor’s enemies—who read his writings in order to lay snares for him and catch him in speech—accused him of this blasphemous perversity.

3. Catholic writers received Rupert’s works, including those in which Bellarmine and Vasquez allege that he taught this heresy, with no suspicion of any error, but with great praise for his doctrine and faith.

4. Our Tuitiensis nowhere set down this profane and sacrilegious novelty in a single book; rather, in many places he expressly stated the opinion contrary to this error.

[Col. 0155B]

5. If he ever discussed Eucharistic truth somewhat obscurely, he nevertheless said nothing concerning it that in any way opposes the faith, doctrine, or even words of the holy Fathers, or that cannot readily be reconciled with their opinions.

### To the first point

Whoever has Christ’s Spirit ought not only to walk as Christ walked, but also to judge as Christ judged, and thus not condemn one whom no one condemns.

By what justice of Christian piety, then, have they dared condemn our Rupert as though, with adulterous faith, he had brought forth this monstrous error? What witnesses of the error do they have? What judges? They produce no witness who charges this error upon the Tuitiensis. They hear no judge who condemned Rupert for this impiety. Why, then, do they deliver such a judgment?

Bellarmine does indeed have Alger pursuing this new heresy most sharply. But whose heresy was it? Was it Rupert’s? Is it Rupert’s because it is not Alger’s heresy, but is attacked by Alger? Why Rupert rather than another? By what mark does Alger identify the Tuitiensis? How, then, does Bellarmine discern that Alger identifies the Tuitiensis rather than someone else? “Because,” he says, “Rupert was a little older than Alger.” Could this heresy not have belonged to Alger’s contemporaries? But if it belonged to someone a little older, was Rupert alone a little older than Alger? Were not so many men distinguished for learning, who flourished at the opening of the twelfth century, a little older than Alger, according to Bellarmine’s own *Chronicles*? Why, then, will Rupert alone be held guilty of this perversity at that time? But if the Tuitiensis was not even older than Alger himself, since he flourished about 1135 while Alger flourished about 1130, what evidence remains to Bellarmine for this error in Rupert? What if Rupert is cleared, by Alger’s own testimony, of the charge of that absurd and novel hypostatic combination? On the testimony of that very man, by what right is Rupert declared by Bellarmine guilty and author of this most impious union of bread and wine with the divine Word? [Col. 0155D]

From Alger’s own words it becomes evident to me that Rupert was by no means designated by him as one of those who introduced this heresy. For Alger, describing this new heresy—against which he inveighs with all the ardor of Catholic zeal—states that “certain persons, led astray by sayings of certain saints, say [Col. 0156A] that Christ is personally impanated in bread, just as God is personally incarnate in human flesh.”

In this portrayal of the error, I observe three points in Rupert’s defense.

1. Alger indicates not one person but several defenders of this union. Hence this heresy cannot be ascribed to Rupert alone on the basis of Alger’s description.

2. Rupert was of an independent and free spirit, as he himself testifies about himself and as his writings consistently demonstrate; he did not serve the opinions of others. Hence, even in the places where he is accused of teaching this error, Rupert adduces no testimonies from the saints by which he endeavors to establish this novel hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word [Col. 0156B] of the Father. Rupert, then, is not one of those who said, from certain sayings of the saints, that “Christ is personally impanated,” and so forth.

3. I have read neither in wording nor in any sense this proposition in the works of the Tuitiensis: “Christ is personally impanated in bread just as God is personally incarnate in human flesh.” In what book did Rupert say that Christ is personally impanated in the Eucharist? On what page did he write that bread and wine are one person with the divine Word in the sacrament? In what line did he state that bread and wine are personally assumed by the Word and joined to him in unity of person? You will read none of these things in the works of the Tuitiensis. Therefore Rupert is not among those whom Alger recounts as saying that Christ is personally impanated in bread just as God is personally incarnate in human flesh.

Another point by which Rupert is vindicated from the calumny of this error on Alger’s own testimony is this. In presenting the arguments for that hypostatic impanation, Alger says that “from a certain comparison of blessed Augustine in Prosper’s book of *Sentences*, they derive and defend their heresy, which says that the sacrifice of the Church is made of two things and consists of two things, just as Christ’s person consists and is made of God and man.”

But what has this to do against the Tuitiensis, who nowhere even mentions that proposition—which is not found among Augustine’s writings—and who nowhere writes that “the sacrifice of the Mass, that is, Christ sacrificed on [Col. 0156D] the altar, consists personally of two things in the same person, just as Christ’s person consists of God and man”? This, Alger says, those innovators claimed to infer from the cited proposition by wrongly supplying what is unstated. How, then, does Alger’s censure weigh upon Rupert?
