On the contrary, it acquits our Tuitiensis, who nowhere expounded any of those things which Alger himself condemns.

Moreover, Alger here attacks only those who, when it was objected that the appearance of the elements was not one person with Christ but only his sacrament, mystery, and figure, objected in turn from Ambrose “that, as the sacrament of the assumed man is spoken of, so the sacrament of the Lord’s body is spoken of”; and from Maximus, “that God is said to come under the mystery of flesh” [Col. 0157A]; and finally from many Scriptures, “that God is said to be covered by a human form or figure, just as Christ is on the altar by the form or figure of bread.” But which of these objections will you find in Rupert’s books either raised or proposed? The words cited from blessed Ambrose and blessed Maximus occur nowhere in them, even for a constant reader.

Nor does the Tuitiensis allow bread and wine, or the appearances of bread and wine, to be called in any way a figure, sacrament, or mystery of the Lord’s body. Although some Catholic expositors of the divine Word have sometimes called bread and wine, or bread and the cup, or the appearance of bread and wine, a type, figure, sign, sacrament, and mystery of the Lord’s body and blood—yet in such a manner that they did not exclude from the Eucharist the reality of that body and blood—many others, and Rupert especially, judged that these terms should be avoided. Far, therefore, from Rupert’s mind was the production of those testimonies by which the appearances of bread and wine might be called a figure, sign, or mystery of the Lord’s body and blood. Far, therefore, is Rupert from Alger’s designation. [Col. 0157B]

But if the abbot of Tuitiensis raises none of the objections raised by the hypostatic impanators whom Alger pursues; if Rupert infers none of the things which they infer; if he assumes none of the things which they assume: by what fairness of judgment could this man be reckoned among them—this Catholic among innovators, Rupert among hypostatic impanators, and their leader? By what judgment of equity shall the just be condemned with the impious? If the laws require that those who are in the same cause of condemnation should be subjected to the same punishment of condemnation, the same laws forbid the same condemnation to be imposed on those whom no cause renders liable to it. [Note: [Col. 0157D] To this argument may be added that John of Paris, of the Order of Preachers, in the cited *Determination*, collecting those statements of ecclesiastical writers by which the mode of Christ’s body’s existence in the sacrament of the altar through a hypostatic union of bread [Col. 0158D] and wine with the Word, mediated by Christ’s body, might in any way be proved, produced nothing concerning Rupert’s opinion and no words from his works—words which he certainly would not have passed over if he had understood such a hypostatic union of bread with the Word to be openly taught in them.]

But the laws especially forbid a judgment to be rendered against one whom no accuser denounces and whom no witness proves guilty. Therefore, if Rupert is acquitted by Alger’s own testimony—the sole testimony on the basis of which Bellarmine proceeded to condemn him—what must be pronounced about Rupert’s teaching except that it is most pure from the error of hypostatic impanation and breathes nothing but Catholic doctrine? Let this be the first argument for its purity.

I offer another. The doctrine of the Tuitiensis was so sound and so foreign to hypostatic inventions that not even the sharper eyes of envy could discover in Rupert’s works the shadow of that fiction [Col. 0157D]. In the preface to these defenses we stated what enemies Rupert endured; yet they never charged him with this novel and absurd heresy of hypostatic impanation.

If the burning envy of his enemies could not endure Rupert’s having written, as it seemed to them, on no authority that Christ had not handed his body to Judas, who could endure the Tuitiensis teaching, against so many testimonies of the holy Fathers and the faith of the whole Church itself, the impious novelty that the substance of bread remains in the Eucharist hypostatically united to the Word—that bread and wine, by mystical consecrations, become one person with the divine Word? [Col. 0158A]

With what fidelity to faith, then, do you attack one whom not even envy bites? With what reverence for the laws do you condemn for a new heresy one whom not even an envious person accuses? You will read nothing in Rupert which the envy of his opponents has not more diligently searched through. Yet you perceive an error in order to condemn one whom envy itself could not discover in order to ensnare him. Thus zeal not directed by knowledge is sometimes more biting than envy itself.

Let this be the third and more powerful proof of that holy doctor’s sound faith. Rupert’s enemies were not only silent about this perverse impiety, but the chief princes [Col. 0158B] of the Church commend the heavenly gift of understanding in him; they urge him with every wish to write, and celebrate his writings with many praises: namely, Cuno or Cono, who, after presiding with great piety over the monastery of St. Michael at Siegburg, was made bishop of the Church of Regensburg; the most illustrious Frederick, archbishop of Cologne; and William, bishop of Palestrina and then legate of the Apostolic See in Germany. Rupert has these men, illustrious in every splendor of rank, piety, and learning, as witnesses to his faith, to say nothing of the others about whom enough has already been said above.

Christ’s vicar himself also received Rupert’s books with joy. For our Tuitiensis, now close to death—after the fire at Tuitiensis—brought to the feet of the supreme pontiff his books [Col. 0158C] which he had written *On the Divine Offices*, on John, and on Exodus, and all his other books. With what face would an otherwise Catholic doctor have done this if in them he had taught a heresy worse than the Berengarian one, as Alger notes, by an absurd and impious novelty?

Finally, with what love of piety did Cuno, bishop of Regensburg, with what zeal for learning did Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, with what fervor for faith did William, legate of the Holy See, and others continually urge Rupert to new works? Why did they diligently peruse his writings, including those most exposed to suspicion of error, with all the zeal due to purer teaching; and rejoice that they appeared dedicated to their own names and that of the supreme pontiff? Let someone other than I suspect that books marked with such great names taught the heresy of the utmost impiety: namely, the impanation of the divine Word in the sacrament of the altar by hypostasis. [Col. 0158D]

If I repeated here the testimonies of all those who declared Rupert’s most pure faith and his heavenly understanding of the sacred Scriptures—testimonies which I set forth above, both when I defended Rupert from every error and when I displayed that singular gift of Rupert—I would again weave the crown of that holy abbot’s faith and doctrine. Lest this be burdensome to anyone, let whoever is not wholly foolish judge, from the opinions already adduced of Catholic doctors concerning Rupert’s doctrine, what right we have against his censors. They, “thinking lofty thoughts,” to use Facundus’s words, book IX, chapter 5, reject and esteem as nothing the opinions of the holy Fathers by whom our Tuitiensis was approved and praised. We, agreeing with the humble, obediently receive them with due reverence. They rashly attribute authority to heretical errors, asserting that the heretics taught doctrines like the preaching of honored men, and above all of Rupert. We, granting the heretics no such occasion, accordingly answer that the Church [Col. 0159B] of Christ never received such blasphemies—namely, hypostatic impanation—but refuted every novelty as soon as it arose.

Let this be the brief and effective fourth proof of Rupert’s uncorrupted faith. He who has professed, in express words and in almost innumerable places, as we have shown of the Tuitiensis, that bread and wine are changed, turned, and converted into Christ’s body and blood, certainly cannot be believed to have thought that the substance of bread and wine was joined to the Word by hypostatic union—unless the entire faith of the Fathers concerning transubstantiation is empty, for they too, as we have already observed, handed it down to us in no other words.

What other sense can be understood from these words than that bread and wine, by ceasing to be what they were, begin to be Christ’s body and blood, which they were not; that bread and wine put off their own nature [Col. 0159C] in order to put on the substance of Christ’s flesh and blood; finally, that bread and wine, changed and converted by the ineffable operation of the Holy Spirit into the Lord’s body and blood, are no longer bread and wine but solely Christ’s body and blood? By what rule of grammar, trope, or figure of speech does saying that bread and wine are changed and converted into the Lord’s body and blood mean the same as saying that bread and wine are hypostatically united either to the Word or to the Lord’s body and blood? What Catholic has ever expressed, or understood when expressed, the hypostatic union of flesh with the Word, which he believes in Christ by divine faith, in these words: “Flesh is changed, turned, and converted into the Word”? Who would not hear an Eutychian heretic if he proclaimed the ineffable economy of the divine Word in these terms: “Flesh was changed, turned, and converted into the Word”? Conversely, who would not at least be considered Catholic in expression if he professed that human flesh is joined to the divine Word in unity of person? By what right could anyone suspect him, when he says, “Human flesh subsists joined to the divine Word in unity of person,” of thinking or meaning that flesh is changed and converted into the Word of God? [Col. 0159D]

Since, therefore, Rupert in whole books and page after page expresses and demonstrates the astonishing conversion and change of bread and wine into the Lord’s body and blood in these words and in words no different from them, it is impious to believe that he held the altogether opposite opinion: namely, that the substance of bread and wine remains joined to the divine Word by the bond of hypostatic union. [Col. 0160A]

“Granted,” someone will object, “these words of Rupert may not be drawn into that sense. But if in many other places he set forth his opinion concerning the hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father and disseminated the error, what wrong is there in condemning what sound faith rejects?” Yet Rupert must not be judged, even from his own mouth in those very places, to have said anything which does not perfectly accord with the doctrine and faith of the holy Fathers. This is the final argument for the Tuitiensis’s integral faith and unstained doctrine; and to pursue it:

## The more difficult passages of the venerable Rupert are explained, and the more obscure clarified

If Rupert ever spoke somewhat obscurely, nevertheless he said nothing which is not entirely in conformity with the opinions of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0160B] The first passage occurs in chapter 2 of book II of *On the Divine Offices*, where Rupert writes:

> “For the unity of the Word produces the unity of the sacrifice. For the one Word both formerly took flesh from the Virgin Mary and now receives from the altar the saving victim.”

A second passage is produced from chapter 9 of the same book, where we read:

> “The Word which had taken human nature—that is, remaining in flesh—received the substance of bread and wine. As a mediating life, he joined bread with his flesh and wine with his blood. As in bodily senses the intervening tongue mediates between the mind and the material air, joining both and making one thing, so the Word of the Father, intervening as physician between the flesh and blood which he had assumed from the Virgin’s womb and the bread and wine which he assumed from the altar, makes one sacrifice.” [Col. 0160C]

Here the critic leaps up, but he will quickly recoil when a genuine exposition gives Rupert’s meaning.

The third passage is in book VI on John:

> “But if anyone,” says Rupert, “asks us how bread which is created from the earth this year becomes the body of Christ which hung upon the cross, and wine which has been pressed from grapes now present becomes that blood [Col. 0160D] which he poured out from his side, let us ask him how the Son of Man, who certainly was conceived of a woman and born from the earth, descended from heaven; or how, before ascending into heaven, he could already be in heaven, according to the truth of him who says: ‘And no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.’ If anyone understands this, he can answer that this was most rightly said because of the unity of God and man in Christ: namely, because Christ, the Son of Man together with the Son of God who descended from heaven, is one; and, while he was on earth, was nonetheless also in heaven and everywhere. For no place contains him, because the nature of divinity is uncircumscribed. Therefore, changing the words slightly, I shall say to him: ‘No one raises you into [Col. 0161A] heaven except this bread which descended from heaven, this body of the Lord which hung upon the wood, and this blood of his which was shed for the whole world.’ Certainly, if he has perceived the former statement, I do not see what he can doubt about this one. For the unity of the Word makes Christ’s body one, so that that which then hung upon the cross and that which the faith of the Church now makes by the sacred mouth are one body—one flesh, I say, and one blood.”

The fourth passage is taken further on from the same chapter, where Rupert says:

> “The Word, which is the bread of angels, became flesh—not changed into flesh, but by assuming flesh. So that same Word, long since made flesh, becomes visible bread—not changed into bread, but by assuming bread [Col. 0161B] and transferring it into the unity of his person. Therefore, just as we truly confess concerning our flesh which the Virgin Mary bore that, because of unity of person, it is God, so likewise concerning this visible bread, which the divinity of that same invisible Word assumes and transfers into his flesh, we truly and catholicly judge that it is Christ’s body.”

A fifth passage is adduced from book VII on John:

> “Our faith,” says Rupert, “has not grown so old that it cannot see itself break the bread of God and preserve the Son of God whole, just as old Abraham could see both strike the ram and not harm the son laid upon the altar. Although this visible bread has become one with the invisible Son of God, that ram could not be or become one with Isaac, for whom it was placed upon the same altar. For the Son of God—that is, God and man—has within himself the effective power by which he unites this visible bread to himself; but Isaac could not incorporate that ram into himself while preserving both substances. . . . For truly, as God and man are one Christ, so this consecrated visible bread, together with that flesh which hung upon the cross, is one flesh, one body of Christ. And as in the true death of the flesh the divinity suffered nothing, so where Christ’s true body is offered, broken, and eaten on the altar, that same humanity of Christ which once suffered and rose again suffers nothing; for it no longer dies.” [Col. 0161C]

The sixth passage is from chapter 10 of book II on Exodus, where Rupert speaks thus:

[Col. 0161D] “Just as God the Word did not destroy human nature when, by his operation, he united it from the Virgin’s womb to the unity of his person, so he does not change or destroy the substance of bread and wine according to their outward appearance, subject to the five senses, when he joins them to that same Word in the unity of the very body which hung upon the cross, and of the very blood which he poured out from his side. Likewise, just as the Word, sent down from on high, became flesh—not by being changed into flesh, but by assuming flesh—so bread and wine, both raised up from below, become Christ’s body and blood, not by being changed into the taste of flesh [Col. 0162A] or into the horror of blood, but by invisibly assuming the reality of each immortal substance, namely the divine and the human, which is in Christ. Therefore, just as we rightly and catholically confess as God the man taken from the Virgin who hung upon the cross, so we truthfully call that which we receive from the holy altar Christ, and proclaim it the Lamb of God.”

Who, from such manifest testimonies of Rupert himself, would not condemn Rupert? Yet a hasty judgment is often unjust. Learn from Facundus (book X, chapter 4) that “we both express many things as we think them, and many things are received by others otherwise than as we utter them.” Learn that (in the same book, chapter 5) “what is said must be judged not from the superficial sound of words, but from the speaker’s intention.”

[Col. 0162B] These are all the passages of the man of Deutz that I have been able to discover, in which less equitable critics judge that he scattered seeds, or laid foundations, for a new and absurd hypostatic impanation. It is now the task I have undertaken to weigh these more carefully, so that, once Rupert’s legitimate meaning has been established, it may become clear to all how fully Rupert always agreed with sound faith, with the holy Fathers, and with himself in every respect.

In order to attain this more successfully, I set down here two principal points handed down to us by the holy Fathers concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body and its unity: first, that Christ’s body, made upon the altar by divine power, is that very body which was joined to the Word of God in the unity of person—or, as they speak, hypostatically—and consequently is the very body of the Word which was formed in the Virgin’s womb, born from her, hung upon the cross, rose from death, and sits at the right hand of God’s power.

So much so that the first and chief reason for this unity—by which the body upon the altar and that in heaven are not two bodies but one body—is the unity of the Word. For since there is only one Christ subsisting in the divine Word, and only one body of the Word, it follows that there is only one body of Christ: both that which sits in heaven and that which lies hidden in the sacrament.

Certainly, I know that some Catholic teachers have distinguished, in a certain respect, the body consecrated upon the altar [Col. 0162D] from the body born of the Virgin and fastened to the cross for the sins of the whole world.

Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0161D] *In Anch.*] says: “This is mine, this and this we see, which is neither equal nor like the image in the flesh, nor the invisible Godhead, nor the outlines of the limbs.” And Rabanus says more expressly against Paschasius: “Christ’s body that suffered is one thing; that in the sacrament, another.”

Lanfranc himself [Note: [Col. 0162D] *Book on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 18] admits that we receive the very body taken from the Virgin, and yet not the very body. “The very same, namely in substance,” as he there explains both his own and others’ opinion; “not the very same in its qualities and outward appearance or form.”

Others, however, forbade one to say that Christ’s body on the cross and that on the altar were different bodies; and above all our man of Deutz, who, adducing every passage bearing upon this single point, proves that the body fastened to the cross or born of the Virgin and that consecrated upon the altar are not different, but one and the same body.

According to the account of the Catholic meaning expounded by Lanfranc, this sacrament—or Christ’s body in the sacrament—could sometimes be called, and indeed was called, in a Catholic sense, a type, likeness, and figure of the body which hung upon the wood and of the blood poured out on the cross, especially by ancient writers. Yet others wished to refrain from such expressions at another time, lest they cause [Col. 0163B] scandal; among them is numbered the abbot of Deutz.

In the same sense, some did not hesitate to say that this body under the outward appearance of bread is visible and seen, tangible and handled, and even broken, as one reads in Chrysostom. This did not seem right to others, who described the body in the sacrament as invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, but that in heaven as visible and tangible. “Flesh,” says Lanfranc, “is the sacrament of flesh and blood. By flesh and blood, both invisible and intelligible, is signified the Redeemer’s body—visible, tangible, manifest, full of the grace of every virtue.”

Although the language of all Catholic Fathers does not sound in one identical voice, their meaning is one; [Col. 0163C] nor has this diversity of expressions introduced any discord in faith or doctrine, but has expressed in different modes one and the same faith in the adoration of this sacrament.

For those who said that Christ’s body made by the Church’s prayers was, namely in respect of the outward appearance of bread, other than that which hung upon the cross and now sits at the Father’s right hand; those who called the Eucharist a type and figure of Christ dying upon the cross; those who described the body in the sacrament as invisible and intelligible but that in heaven as tangible and visible; and those who called Christ’s body on the altar hidden but that in heaven manifest—all of these professed with one mind and one faith that there are not two bodies of the divine Word, [Col. 0163D] but one body: whether that born from the Virgin, suffering on the cross, and now glorious in heaven; or that offered upon the altar through mystical consecrations and invisibly adored under the perceptible appearance of the elements, as remaining indivisibly united to the divine Word.

Justin thus presents this comparison between the body and blood in the mystery of the altar and the Incarnation, or the union of the Word with flesh [Note: [Col. 0163D] *Apology* II, near the end]:

“We receive these things, which the priest has blessed by thanksgiving, not as common bread or common drink; but just as Jesus Christ our Savior became flesh through the Word of God and possessed flesh and blood for our salvation, so too we have been taught that the food over which thanksgiving has been offered through prayers of his word, and from which by change our blood and flesh are nourished, is the flesh and blood of that incarnate Jesus. For the apostles, in the memoirs composed by them, which are called Gospels, thus taught that Jesus commanded them: taking bread and giving thanks, he said, ‘Do this in remembrance of me. This is my body.’ And likewise, taking the cup and giving thanks, he said, ‘This is my blood,’” etc.

Receive what a golden stream Chrysostom poured out concerning the truth and unity of the Lord’s body [Note: [Col. 0163D] Homily 24 on First Corinthians]:

“That body”—that is, the body in the sacrament—“is united [Col. 0164B] to Christ. This body, which is broken in the sacrifice of the altar, was nailed up and scourged. This same body was bloodied and wounded by the lance. What is in the cup is that which flowed from his side.”

And in another homily he says [Note: [Col. 0163D] Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Ephesians] that the body of which we become partakers at the table and the blood which we taste at the altar are the body and blood of him who sits above the heavens, whom angels reverently adore, who stands nearest to the immortal power of God.

Brief, but how powerful and sweet, is Ambrose’s utterance [Note: [Col. 0164D] *On Those Who Are Initiated*, chapter 9]: “What we make is the body from the Virgin.” Hesychius explains this more fully [Note: [Col. 0164D] Book VI on Leviticus, chapter 22]: “The holy of holies are Christ’s own mysteries, because it is his body, concerning which Gabriel said to the Virgin: ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power [Col. 0164C] of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore the holy thing born from you shall be called the Son of God.’”

Gregory of Nyssa, in his catechetical discourse [Note: [Col. 0164D] Oration 237, vol. III] on the divine sacraments, mentioned by Euthymius, Bessarion, and Garetius, teaches more explicitly than all these that bread and wine become and are in the sacrament one body of Christ hypostatically united to the divine Word, just as the bread and wine upon which Christ fed became his divine body, united to the Word in the unity of person.

Accordingly, he resolves the difficulty of this question—how that one body of Christ is thus made from many loaves and distributed to each person seated at this heavenly table without undergoing multiplication [Col. 0164D] or diminution—by the reasoning which the Sacramentarians should consider. Namely: just as, by eating bread and drinking wine, the Word made them his body and blood, so now, by speaking, the Word makes bread and wine upon any altar the same flesh, or the same body, and the same blood of his own; since from each bread and each wine one and the same body of Christ is made. Yet the person who receives this flesh of Christ under one species of bread does not receive it under another, in which it nevertheless remains whole. Thus, without diminution of himself, the divine Word imparts himself to all believers [Col. 0165A] through the flesh which is made from bread upon the altar for his manifold distribution and the manifold nourishment of the faithful.

Cyril on John [Note: [Col. 0165D] Book IV, chapter 2, especially verses 54, 55, 56, 57, 58, 59, 62, 63, 64, etc.] declares this unity of Christ’s body briefly indeed, but clearly, when he says that the flesh we eat is that which, because it is joined to the Word, who is life by nature, is life-giving.

But Remigius [Note: [Col. 0165D] Remigius, either of Rheims, as Villalpandus maintains; or bishop of Lyons, as others entitle him; or a monk of Auxerre, as Albertinus and others more soundly judged. He wrote this on [Col. 0166D] chapter X of the First Epistle to the Corinthians. He writes similar things on chapter XI of the same Epistle] explains it to us at greater length:

“The flesh which the Word of God the Father assumed in the Virgin’s womb into the unity of his person, and the bread consecrated in the Church, are one body of Christ. For just as that flesh is Christ’s body, so this bread passes into Christ’s body; nor are they two bodies, but one body. For the fullness of the Godhead which was in that flesh fills this bread also; and the very Godhead of the Word, which fills heaven and earth and all that is in them, fills the body of Christ which is sanctified by many priests throughout the world, and has made it one body of Christ.”

I cannot remain silent here: if the words cited from Rupert teach hypostatic impanation, although they say and mean nothing other than these words of Remigius, then Remigius, not Rupert, is the inventor of hypostatic impanation.

Let Damascene be added to these [Note: [Col. 0166D] Book IV, *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 14]. Although he is called an innovator by an innovator, he is Catholic in the judgment of a Catholic. Deriving the unity of the Lord’s body from the unity of the divine Word, he explains the whole rationale of our argument in these terms:

“If God the Word himself, willing it, became [Col. 0165C] flesh and sustained in himself flesh from the most pure blood of the holy Virgin without seed, is he not able to make bread his own body and wine and water his blood? The holy Virgin says, ‘How shall this be to me, since I know not a man?’ The archangel Gabriel answers, ‘The Holy Spirit shall come upon you and overshadow you.’ And now you ask how bread becomes Christ’s body, and wine and water his blood? I too answer you: the Holy Spirit overshadows and performs these things above reason and understanding; but bread and wine are changed. Since it is customary for human beings to eat bread and drink wine and water, he joined his Godhead to these very things and made them his body and blood. For the body truly united [Col. 0165D] to the Godhead is the body from the holy Virgin; not that the very body assumed from heaven descended, but that this bread and wine are changed into the body and blood of God. If you inquire into the manner in which this occurs, let it suffice you to hear that it is through the Holy Spirit, just as the Lord sustained flesh from the holy Mother of God by himself and in himself. Just as bread by natural eating, and wine by drinking, are changed into the body and blood of the eater [Col. 0166A] and drinker, and do not become another body besides what was previously his own, so too the bread of the offering, wine, and water are supernaturally changed through the invocation and coming of the Holy Spirit into Christ’s body and blood; and they are not two, but one and the same.”

After omitting a few words: “Bread and wine are not a figure of Christ’s body and blood. Far be it! Rather, they are the deified body of the Lord itself, as the Lord himself said: ‘THIS IS MY BODY’; not a figure of the body, but body; and not a figure of the blood, but blood.”

These passages clear Rupert of every charge—or else they first accuse and condemn Damascene of the same hypostatic error. For in exactly the same terms as Rupert, he professes not only the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the sacrament, rejecting figure, but also explains most clearly how that which is in the sacrament is not another body of Christ from that which, taken from the Virgin, now sits in heaven; and how they are not two bodies but one body of God, from the union of this body with the Word—that is, because the divine Word assumes to himself this very body which is in the sacrament, and therefore it becomes the body itself of the Word, of whom we believe and profess there are not two bodies but one body.

Peter Damian [Note: [Col. 0166D] *The Lord Be with You*, chapter 8], departing in no respect from these writers, derives from this unity of the divine Word alone the reason why Christ’s flesh is consecrated at distant places and different times, although it is one:

“For such is the Church’s unity in Christ [Col. 0166C] that throughout the whole world there is everywhere one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood. For the Godhead of the Word is one, filling the whole world. Thus, although that body is consecrated in many places and upon many days, there are nevertheless not many bodies, but one body of Christ.”

You might have said that these were Alcuin’s words, for he had already expounded this unity of Christ’s body—assumed by the Word in the Virgin’s womb and daily assumed by the same Word on different altars—in identical words and with no different meaning [Note: [Col. 0166D] *On the Divine Offices*]:

“Such is the Church’s unity in Christ that everywhere there is one bread of Christ’s body and one cup of his blood. ‘Taking this glorious cup’: he says that he took this cup because the cup which the Catholic priest offers in sacrifice [Col. 0166D] is none other than the very cup which the Lord delivered to the apostles. For just as the divinity of the Word of God is one and fills the whole world, so, although that body is consecrated in many places and on innumerable days, there are nevertheless not many bodies of Christ, nor many cups, but one body of Christ and one blood, together with that which he assumed in the Virgin’s womb and gave to the apostles. For the Godhead fills that which is everywhere, on each altar throughout the whole world [Col. 0167A] of the Church, and joins it and brings it about that, just as the Godhead itself is one, so it is joined to Christ’s body and is truly one body of his.”

Remigius of Auxerre [Note: [Col. 0167D] In the treatise *On the Celebration of the Mass*], following Alcuin’s thought, virtually transcribed the very words by which to express it: “Such is the Church’s unity in Christ, that everywhere there is one bread of Christ’s body,” etc., as in Alcuin.

Thus it is clearer than noonday light that this is the one doctrine of all the Catholic Fathers: that the body made from bread upon the altar is that very body of Christ which was formed from the most pure blood of the undefiled Virgin and joined by an indissoluble bond to God the Word of the Father in the unity of person; that the body sanctified in the sacrament at different places and times, and that which was glorified upon the cross, are not several bodies but one and the same body of Christ; finally, that the singular reason for this indivisible unity is the very unity of the divine Word, which assumed and possesses not several bodies but one, in which it subsists and lives, whether it be in the mystery or in heaven. This, first of all, will most powerfully vindicate Rupert’s faith, by demonstrating most clearly the Catholic meaning of that holy teacher.

The second point which I set before the clearer understanding of Rupert’s teaching and a fuller appreciation of his agreement with Catholic writers is that the most holy and awe-inspiring sacrifice and sacrament of the altar is compared by the holy Fathers in many respects to the wondrous and ineffable mystery of the Incarnation, or economy [Col. 0167C] of the divine Word.

1. As we have already set forth, just as the unity of the Word establishes Christ’s unity, so the unity of that same divine Word also makes the sacrifice one.

2. Just as Christ is composed of two things, namely the Word and flesh, so the sacrament consists of two things: the outward appearance of bread and wine and Christ’s body, called the reality (*res*) of the sacrament. Thus the comparison between the sacramental body of Christ and the economy of the divine Word is established not in a personal unity, but solely in their composition from two things. Alger interpreted the judgment which he thought Augustine’s in this sense [Note: [Col. 0167D] Cited book, chapter 5].

3. Just as God came veiled in human form, [Col. 0167D] so Christ assumes the form of bread upon the altar, though not in such a way as to possess the reality of bread. And just as the Incarnation of the assumed man is called a mystery or sacrament, so the consecration of the Lord’s body is called a sacrament, yet not in such a way as to exclude the reality of the Lord’s body.

These are statements of St Ambrose and Blessed Maximus in Alger [Note: [Col. 0167D] Cited book, chapter 6].

4. Just as God became flesh in the Father’s Word, so in the Word of God we Catholicly confess bread and wine to become and be the flesh and blood of the incarnate God [Col. 0168A]. So teaches St Justin [Note: [Col. 0167D] In *Apology* II], echoed by St Gregory of Nyssa [Note: [Col. 0168D] Cited discourse *On the Divine Sacraments*]:

“The body, because God the Word dwelt in it, acquired divine dignity. Hence we also rightly believe that bread sanctified by the Word of God is changed into the body of the Word of God. For just as there the grace of the Word of God makes that body, whose sustenance consisted of bread—and was itself, in some manner, bread—so here also bread is sanctified through the Word of God and prayer, not because it progresses by being eaten so as to become the Word’s body, as other foods do, but because it is immediately changed into the body through the word, as the Word said: ‘This is my body.’”

5. Just as Christ is born of a Virgin by wondrous power outside the order of nature, so it is above the natural order of divine power and operation that Christ’s body is made from bread upon the altar. So Ambrose teaches in the passages cited above [Note: [Col. 0168D] *On Those Who Are Initiated*, chapter 9; and Book IV, *On the Sacraments*, chapter 9].

From these comparisons by which Catholic teachers have connected both mysteries of the divine Word in flesh, Rupert’s meaning, the purity of his doctrine, and the Catholic character of his faith are made entirely plain by the very passages we have cited. For when Rupert, in chapter 2 of book II of *On the Divine Offices*, says that the unity of the Word makes the sacrifice one, he thinks nothing that the aforementioned writers did not think; he says nothing which ecclesiastical commentators have not professed, whom we heard above explaining from the unity of this Word the unity of the body assumed by the Word of the Father from the Virgin’s womb with that consecrated upon the altar.

To make your understanding of this first passage from Rupert easier and readier, note that the man of Deutz teaches three things there:

1. The Word of the eternal Father, by the same operation of divine power, assumes bread and wine from the holy altar by changing them into his body and blood, by which he united our flesh from the Virgin Mary to himself.

2. The bread which we sacrificed yesterday, and that which we shall sanctify today or tomorrow, are not two bodies. Thus it is impious to believe or say that bodies of Christ are offered in the Church—as many, namely, as the loaves consecrated daily, that is, almost as many as the priests ministering in the Church.

3. That which is made from bread and immolated in the unbloody sacrifice, and that which was made from a woman and hung upon the cross, are neither called nor are two bodies, but are one and the same, because of the indivisible unity of the divine Word, in which both alike subsist and live.

And lest I seem to impose upon the uninstructed and careless, I produce Rupert’s own words, by which he teaches this, firmly establishing in that chapter the truth of this sacrament for some who still waver in its faith:

“Therefore do not say in your heart, ‘Who shall ascend into heaven?’—that is, to bring Christ down—so that he who, having risen from the dead in himself, [Col. 0169A] now dies no more, may yet be immolated again for us in his mystery through the victim of the sacred altar. ‘For the Word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; this is the word of faith which we preach,’ says the Apostle. Therefore, because the Word of God—the Word of the cross, Christ the Lord—is near in your mouth and heart, if you pour the flood of this Word over bread and wine, and utter in the order established by him the truth of this Word, immediately, by changing into his body and blood the very bread and wine from the holy altar, he assumes them by the same strength, power, or grace by which he was able, as he willed, to assume our flesh from the Virgin Mary.”

After this he immediately adds the second and third points against those who said that the body upon the altar was not that which was born from the Virgin and fastened to the cross:

“Nor are there, or are called, two bodies: this one from the altar and that taken from the Virgin’s womb. For one and the same Word, one and the same God, is above in flesh and here in bread. Otherwise, both the bread which we sacrificed yesterday and that which we shall sacrifice today or tomorrow are several bodies; nor do we rightly say that the Church offers the body of Christ, and we would better say ‘bodies,’ because almost as many loaves are offered daily”—here he identifies the matter of the sacrifice—“as there are priests in the Church. But the cause forbids this, reason refutes it, religion rejects it. For the unity of the Word makes the sacrifice one. In like manner, the one Word both formerly took flesh from the Virgin Mary and now receives the saving victim from the altar.”

From this he concludes: “Therefore, both the body born from Mary which hung upon the cross and that offered upon the holy altar are one body; daily it renews for us the Lord’s very passion.”

What error, I ask, is there in these three things which Rupert sets forth in the challenged chapter? Is it error that Catholic faith believes Christ’s body to be made from bread upon the altar by the same divine power and the same operation of the Holy Spirit by which it was formed in the Virgin’s womb? Is it error that Catholic faith professes that the consecrated bodies of Christ are not many, but one, and that at one and the same time the Church offers the body of the divine Word in however distant places? Is it error that we hold as certain by divine faith that what is immolated in the mystery—the Lord’s body—is that very body which [Col. 0169D] suffered for us upon the cross and reconciled the lowest things with the highest? Is it error, I say, to reason—as every Catholic recognizes—that this is one body, the body of the one divine Word, from the unity itself of that divine Word, so that the unity of the Word makes the sacrifice one?

This is the teaching and faith of the ancients. What, then, did Rupert write in that chapter which accords less than fully with the teaching and faith of the holy Fathers? What did he say which does not wholly recoil from the impious error of hypostatic impanation?

Nor did Rupert think less Catholicly in chapter 9 of the same book, *On the Divine Offices*. Inquiring there into the matter of that dread sacrifice, he compares it most acutely with the priest who offered himself, so that by this art of comparison he may show the matter of this sacrifice, like that of the supreme priest, not as simple but as composite:

“The matter or substance of the sacrifice, which then existed when Christ, taking bread into his holy and venerable hands, said, ‘THIS IS MY BODY,’ and which now is in the hands of our priest, is not simple; just as the priest himself is not of divine substance alone or human substance alone.”

He explains what this twofold substance of sacrifice, as also of priest or sacrificer, is:

“For in both the priest and the sacrifice there is a divine substance and an earthly substance. The earthly element in both is that which can be seen bodily or locally. The divine element in both is the invisible Word, which in the beginning was God with God.”

[Col. 0170B] In order to make known from Christ’s words that in both sacrifice and priest that divine substance is the Word of God, and that in the sacrifice the body itself of that Word or priest is offered, the man of Deutz adds:

“For when that same great priest, holding bread and wine, said, ‘THIS IS MY BODY; THIS IS MY BLOOD,’ it was the voice of the incarnate Word, the voice of the eternal beginning, the voice of the ancient counsel.”

But how are the bread and wine that are offered changed by the power of the divine Word into the body and blood of the divine Word, so that the sacrifice truly is one—both that consummated on the cross and that performed upon the altar? Just as the Word, having assumed human nature—that is, remaining in flesh—received the substance of bread and wine, so during the course of his life he joined bread with his flesh and wine with his blood.

Understand this manner, which exceeds every manner, from Rupert, where he reasons as follows from the unity of the divine Word concerning the ineffable unity of the body joined to God the Word in the Virgin’s womb and that made from bread and wine by mystical prayer:

“The Word of the Father, intervening as a middle, makes one sacrifice from the flesh and blood which he had assumed from the Virgin’s womb, and from the bread and wine which he has assumed from the altar.”

What else do these words mean except that the divine Word, to whom both the body assumed from the Virgin and that placed upon the altar remain united in the unity of person, is, as it were, a middle between these seemingly two bodies of Christ, bringing it about by its own unity that they are no longer two, but one body and one sacrifice, since the one divine Word and Christ have only one body and one sacrifice?

What, therefore, does the man of Deutz teach in that chapter which he had not taught, in accordance with the Fathers’ meaning, in the chapter explained above? There, in accordance both with the meaning and the words of Catholic commentators, he had said that the unity of the Word makes the sacrifice one. Here he says that the Word, intervening as a middle, makes one sacrifice. What, then, did Rupert produce in that chapter for which he might justly be condemned for the blasphemous impanation through hypostasis?

Nor should Rupert’s critics object that one reads in him, “The Word joins bread with flesh and wine with his blood”; for union is only of two things. Rather, let them hear Blessed Gregory teaching that “this sacrifice which is seen upon the altar before the priest’s eyes is caught up on high and associated with Christ’s body.” Is joining more an action of two things than association?

Let them also hear Chrysostom expressly saying that this body, set before the table of the faithful, “is united to Christ.” Finally, let them know that the most perfect of all unions is that by which one thing so passes into another that it becomes that very same thing. Once they have understood this, they will judge more fairly that the man of Deutz is not heterodox, but agrees in every respect with the holy doctors of the Church and with orthodox faith.

[Col. 0171B] But perhaps it is still difficult and harsh for them that Rupert, in that chapter (chapter 9, book II, *On the Divine Offices*), says that the visible bread grown from the earth is present in the sacrifice; that visible sacrificial bread is eaten; and that the sacrifice is constructed from God’s Word and the fruits of the earth, by which the body alone lives.

But why force in these objections, whose Catholic and genuine meaning we have already given where we defended this holy doctor against the error of impanation? There we saw that by “bread” Rupert, like the Apostle and Christ himself, understands nothing other than Christ’s body under the outward appearance of bread; or bread and wine, which are the material from which the sacrifice is made and are to be changed by Christ’s Word into his body and blood.

“Believe this also,” says the man of Deutz (*Book VI on John*), “that this visible bread and wine, although nothing in their outward appearance has changed, have passed into another food, which is the food of angels. The heavenly bread”—he who says, ‘I am the bread who came down from heaven,’ namely, the Father’s Word—“gives us earthly bread, which he changes into his flesh. And thus the Word, who is the bread of angels and long ago became flesh, becomes visible bread; and nevertheless we truly and Catholicly confess concerning this visible bread that it is Christ’s body.” — “Bread appears to be what it was,” he says elsewhere (*Book VII on Genesis*, chapter 32), “and yet in truth it is Christ.” — “For although bread and wine remain in outward appearance,” as he writes later (*Book IV on Genesis*, chapter 4), “in truth it is the Lamb of God.” Or, as he says elsewhere: “We proclaim the Lamb of God.” — “Not common bread,” says Rupert, explaining Exodus (*Book IV*, chapter 16), “but the bread of eternal life, which is Christ’s body, is set forth.”

What forbids one, in this sense, from saying that visible bread is in the sacrifice and is eaten, and that the sacrifice is constructed from it? When these things are said, what disturbs a mind that understands the things of faith? Is it not of divine faith that bread is in the sacrifice, concerning which Truth says: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world”? Is it not of divine faith that bread in the sacrifice is eaten, concerning which Truth says: “He who eats this bread shall live for ever”? What, then, has Rupert uttered contrary to divine faith, when he has spoken only the words of primal Truth?

[Col. 0172A] And lest Rupert appear to some to have indicated his opinion concerning hypostatic impanation more plainly in the third and fourth passages, we shall explain both passages together, so that nothing obscure, harsh, or difficult for the slower reader may give offense.

In the sixth book of the commentaries which Rupert published on John, he proposes this difficulty: “How does bread created from the earth this year become the body of Christ which hung upon the cross, and how does wine pressed from grapes now present become that blood which he poured out from his side?”

He judges that a sufficient answer is given if one answers, as he himself does, “that because of the unity of Christ as God and man, it is most rightly said that there is one Christ, the Son of Man with the Son [Col. 0172B] of God who descended from heaven.”

With this single answer he resolves the whole knot of the question previously proposed:

“For the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, so that that which then hung upon the cross and that which the Church’s faith then makes by its sacred mouth are one body—one flesh, I say, and one blood.”

Thus, even in that place, Rupert demonstrates nothing other than the indivisible unity of the body which hung upon the cross and that made upon the altar.

For Rupert does not ask there—and this must especially be observed—how bread becomes or is called Christ’s body, but how bread becomes that body of Christ “which hung upon the cross”; nor does he ask how wine becomes or is called Christ’s blood, but how wine becomes [Col. 0172C] and is that blood which Christ “poured out from his side.” Thus the question should be understood as concerning not a proposed union of the substance of bread with Christ’s body, but the perfect identity—to use that term—of the body consecrated from bread with that which was fastened to the cross.

Accordingly, in resolving the question posed—and this too should be noted—Rupert by no means states that the unity of the Word makes bread be called, or be, Christ’s body and wine his blood. Though this might be forced into the sense of hypostatic union, he instead says that the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, so that that which hung upon the cross and that which the Church’s faith then makes by its sacred mouth are one body and one blood. These words cannot in any way sustain an interpretation of hypostatic union.

For hypostatic union in no way causes two things which, in one suppositum, are joined only in the unity of person, to become, be, or be called one substance or nature. Rather, just as in Christ two substances remain unaltered and distinct, joined in the one substance of the divine Word—namely, the divine essence and human nature—and no one thing is made or said to be from these two: so too in Christ there are two bodies and they remain unaltered, if that which is reckoned as bread is joined to that which hung on the cross only by hypostatic union in the Word.

For who, even granting what no one would deny can occur—namely, that the Word of the eternal Father should assume at once a body of bread [Col. 0173A] and a human body into the unity of that divine person—who, I say, could either understand or dare to say that there is one body of the divine Word, rather than two bodies? Who could understand or dare to say that this body of bread is itself that body which is a human body, because of the indivisible unity of the Word?

Therefore, since our man of Deutz teaches here and in many other places that the body which the Church makes by the sacred mouth, and that which obedience fastened to the cross, are one body, one flesh, one blood, and one sacrifice; and everywhere demonstrates this unity of Christ’s body and blood from the adduced unity of the divine Word, it is more certain than anything certain that the unity of this body, which Rupert proves in so many places, is not understood by that holy doctor as personal [Col. 0173B] or hypostatic unity. For just as hypostatic unity cannot constitute one nature out of two substances, so neither can it make one body out of two bodies. Let the critics therefore now be silent, who, deceived by a false understanding, have dared to charge Rupert with a false doctrine. Yet if they do not feel the force and weight of this one argument, by which alone their false interpretation is refuted, I press them with this second argument.

If the doctor and abbot of Deutz intended, from the repeatedly introduced unity of the Word, only to show that bread and wine are united with the divine Word in unity of person, and for that reason become Christ’s flesh and blood without any transmutation of bread and wine according to substance—so that, on account of that hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word which [Col. 0173C] became flesh, this bread might truly be called Christ’s flesh and this wine truly Christ’s blood, just as in Christ, because of the unity of the same divine Word, the man is truly and catholicly called God—if, I say, this alone is what the man of Deutz seeks to establish by so many proofs, and if this sense which his critics ascribe to him could stand, then by precisely the same principle of interpretation bread and wine could truly be called Christ’s soul; bread could rightly be called Christ’s blood, and wine could lawfully be called Christ’s body. Moreover, bread could properly be called wine, and conversely wine could properly be called bread.

Finally, one could truly say that in the sacrament bread is truly God, and that in the sacrifice of the altar wine is truly the Word of the eternal Father, just as in Christ [Col. 0173D] man is truly God. Likewise, one could catholicly declare that the Word became bread, that the Word became wine in the mystery of the sacred table, that God is wine, and that God is bread in the sacrament of the Church—just as we truly and catholicly believe and confess that the Word became flesh and that in Christ God is man. For once a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word is granted, all these things are true, if, once that premise is admitted, bread and wine can truly be called the flesh and blood of Christ and of the divine Word.

Do you suppose that Rupert held these impious and dreadful things—things which neither a fool would invent nor a blasphemer or impious person utter? Say where Rupert, who in so many books and on so many pages expounded this mystery of Christ’s body and blood, ever said by reciprocal predication [Col. 0174A] that God is bread, that God is wine; or that bread is wine and wine bread; or that bread or wine is Christ’s soul. Nor did he merely say that bread and wine are the body and blood of Christ and of the Word, as the Catholic Fathers who explained to us the divine economy of the Word did not merely hand down to us that, in that ineffable union, man is God, but also taught us that God is man. Since, therefore, the man of Deutz wrote none of these things concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; indeed, since in so many places he said that bread is transmuted only into Christ’s body and wine only into his blood, why do you imagine that Rupert thought things which he neither uttered nor wrote? Why do you charge him with an error by which he proved, from the unity of the divine Word, neither that bread is more wonderfully converted by the operation [Col. 0174B] of the Holy Spirit into the body than into the divine substance, nor that the Church by its sacred mouth makes from bread Christ’s body rather than God?

If he who introduced this new heresy of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word is unquestionably to be judged to have introduced these impious and sacrilegious consequences, then, by no dissimilar equity of judgment, he who cannot endure so many blasphemies of such great impiety must himself be judged to have recoiled from the heresy from which they would flow no less necessarily and plainly than that the substance of bread and wine, without any transmutation of itself, truly is and is catholicly called the body and blood of Christ, or of the divine Word.

From what, then, will you now [Col. 0174C] accuse Rupert of hypostatic impanation? “From the unity of the Word,” you say, “by which he seeks to prove that bread becomes Christ’s body in the sacrament, and wine his blood.” But what follows from that? “Therefore,” you will infer, “the man of Deutz believed that bread and wine remain hypostatically united to the Word?”

Your reasoning, then, is this: “Bread and wine remain hypostatically united to the Word in the mystery of the altar. Therefore, through the unity of the Word, the bread sanctified on the altar, or the body made on the altar, becomes the very body of Christ which hung on the cross.” And from this you argue against Rupert: “Rupert teaches that, through the unity of the Word, bread becomes the very body of Christ affixed to the cross; therefore he too believed that bread and wine remain joined to the Word in unity of person in the sacrament of the altar.” You would reason badly against [Col. 0174D] the man of Deutz unless you judged that this hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father, which you attribute to Rupert, must necessarily be presupposed, so that the other point which Rupert truly teaches could lawfully follow from it.

But you may now see from this reasoning that the error is not Rupert’s but yours. From Rupert against Rupert you argue a posteriori, as dialecticians speak: “Bread becomes and is Christ’s flesh, and wine is his blood, because of the unity of the Word; therefore bread and wine are joined to Christ’s flesh and blood in unity of person, or hypostatically.”

And I, on your terms, argue from Rupert on Rupert’s behalf and against you a priori: “Bread and wine [Col. 0175A] are hypostatically united to the divine Word; therefore bread is Christ’s flesh and wine is his blood.”

If, from that antecedent hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word, the consequent—that unity of Christ’s body—follows correctly, why should it not follow most aptly from the same Word’s hypostatic union with human nature that God is blood, or that God is the flesh which is a part of man? Why, too, could it not rightly be inferred from that incomprehensible union of the divine Word that Christ’s blood is flesh or Christ’s very soul, or, by reciprocal predication, that Christ’s soul is flesh and his flesh blood?

For nowhere will you establish a difference between the one and the other, since the subsistence of God in Christ is no different from that [Col. 0175B] of the flesh and blood of that divine composite; and since soul, flesh, and blood in Christ are equally hypostatically joined to the one and same Word, just as, according to your assumption drawn from Rupert, bread, wine, Christ’s flesh, and Christ’s blood in the sacrament are united without confusion and hypostatically to the one and same suppositum of the divine Word.

If any difference is discerned in these cases, it is this: flesh and blood are parts of one perfect body composed from them; bread and wine, however, do not so concur in forming the substance of one whole, but are complete natures. Since in the concrete they imply a suppositum—pardon logical terminology where we are examining subtleties of reasoning—they may be made the subject of a proposition, so that something else may be predicated of them, if not according to nature, [Col. 0175C] at least according to suppositum.

But this ground of disparity does not help you; it destroys you. For if that which has the character of a part and is not complete cannot bear what is said of a suppositum, and therefore it cannot at all be said that Christ’s blood is bread, just as neither can it be said that Christ’s body is the Word of the Father, then by exactly the same argument that which belongs to the order of parts and has no subsisting nature in itself cannot be predicated of another, however subsisting, merely idiomatically and not formally—as the barbarism of the schools disputes—that is, only according to suppositum and not according to nature. For how can that which is not perfected by the completion of a suppositum be predicated of another according to the perfection of that completion which it does not possess?

[Col. 0175D] Therefore, since Catholic utterance recoils from saying that blood is bread, or that flesh, which is a part of man, is the Word of the eternal Father, even though bread and blood subsist in the same person of the divine Word and the suppositum of flesh and Word is the same, by precisely the same reasoning Catholic doctrine refuses to declare that bread is Christ’s flesh or that wine is Christ’s blood—even if it be granted that bread and wine are hypostatically joined to the one and same Word to whom Christ’s flesh and blood are joined.

For it is no less contrary to the rules of dialectic for some nature, or a part of a nature, abstracted from its suppositum, to be spoken of another according to the character of the suppositum [Col. 0176A] than for such a nature, or its incomplete part, to be made the subject of something whole and complete, not formally but merely idiomatically.

See, then, how shamefully you sin against the laws of dialectic, and how gravely against the rules of faith, when from the proposition which you falsely invent as Rupert’s—that bread and wine in the sacrament of the altar are hypostatically united to the divine Word—you think it lawfully follows that bread is Christ’s flesh and wine Christ’s blood.

See into what monstrous and execrable blasphemies of impiety the inference which you yourself have drawn compels you. For if bread in the sacrament is Christ’s flesh and wine is Christ’s blood because bread subsists in the same eternal Word in whom Christ’s flesh subsists, and wine is joined in the unity of the same person with Christ’s blood [Col. 0176B], then whoever professes the hypostatic union of the divine Word with human nature must, by precisely the same dialectical law, consequently confess that in Christ the Word is blood, and that the Word is Christ’s soul. And by mutual reciprocal predication, he must confess that in Christ blood is the Word of eternal counsel, and that the rational soul is the Wisdom of the Father, the Son of God, since that divine Word is itself the suppositum in Christ in which Christ’s blood and soul subsist by a power no one can sufficiently comprehend.

Could it not, I ask, also be said catholicly that Christ’s blood is flesh and Christ’s soul, or conversely that Christ’s soul is flesh and flesh Christ’s blood, since Christ’s blood, flesh, and soul are completely perfected in the one person of God the Word? [Col. 0176C]

What prevents one from uttering or thinking these impious things? Is it that, as I have shown above, Christ’s blood and soul are not wholes but parts, and, because they do not in themselves imply a suppositum, cannot be made subjects of idiomatic predication? But, as I also replied above, in your inference do not flesh and blood stand for parts, which, since they too are incomplete, cannot at all be attributed to a subject according to the complete character of a suppositum?

Either, then, admit these dreadful things, which a faithful mind recoils even from hearing; or, as you detest these dreadful and impious things with the piety of Catholic faith, reject with the knowledge and zeal of that same faith the ill-drawn consequence based on the falsely assumed hypostatic [Col. 0176D] union of bread and wine with the Word of the Father. And thus at last acknowledge that, even if it were granted as true that bread and wine remain hypostatically united with the Word of God in the wondrous sacrament of the Eucharist, it nevertheless would not follow that in these terrible and adorable mysteries bread is Christ’s flesh, or wine Christ’s blood.

You may thus see by what justice of judgment one who said that, at the priest’s prayer, bread on the altar becomes Christ’s flesh which hung on the wood, and wine his blood poured out for the sins of the whole world, would immediately be accused of a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word—although no necessity of legitimate consequence connects these things.

[Col. 0177A] Who, then, can now be such an unjust judge as to arraign Rupert for this personal union of bread and wine with the Word, and undertake to prove it from the fact that this Catholic writer Catholicly taught that, in mystical consecrations, bread becomes Christ’s flesh and wine Christ’s blood?

“But,” another will object, “this error of the man of Deutz is drawn not from that proposition, which is Catholic, but rather from the reason which he constantly adduces from the unity of the divine Word in support of his proposition, and from the comparison which he makes in that place: namely, that just as Truth itself says of Christ that he ascended into heaven, though he was in heaven, because the one and same person of the eternal Word in Christ, while filling heaven with the glory of his majesty, ascended above the heavens in the pomp of triumph, leading captive [Col. 0177B] captivity; so the unity of the Word—that is, the hypostatic union of the Word of God with bread—causes bread, even while it is bread, nevertheless truly to be able to be called, and truly to be called, Christ’s flesh.”

But wherever you attempt to escape and wherever you flee, our objection presses you. For if, from these words of Rupert’s, in which he says that the unity of the Word causes the bread offered in the unbloody sacrifice to be that body of Christ which was offered in the punishment of the cross, you understand him to have thought that bread is Christ’s flesh in the sacrament of the altar just as man is and is called God in the mystery of the Incarnation, with what fidelity as interpreter do you attribute to the author a sense which these words not only do not contain, as I shall shortly prove, [Col. 0177C] but cannot even admit? For, as we have already made plain, the union of bread and wine in unity of person with the Word cannot cause bread to be, or to be called, one flesh of Christ and wine one blood of his.

Therefore, since the abbot of Deutz here and in many other places demonstrated nothing else from the adduced unity of the Word and the assumed comparison with the Incarnation than that the body which the Church makes from bread by its sacred mouth, and that which, born of the Virgin, hung upon the wood, are one flesh, one body of Christ, and one sacrifice: who does not now see and judge that Rupert’s mind is wholly free from the impious heresy of hypostatic impanation, and that his teaching, in its very language, reasons, and comparisons, [Col. 0177D] perfectly agrees with the faith of the holy Fathers—so that this concord of Rupert with the Catholic Fathers, even in this respect, utterly erases every mark of hypostatic impanation?

Above I have adduced in good faith many testimonies of the holy Fathers in which, by the same unity of the divine Word and the same comparison with the Incarnation as Rupert uses, they unanimously explain the indivisible unity of the body set forth in the sacrament and that fixed upon the wood. Yet no one has hitherto charged them with hypostatic impanation, except one Albertine, whom it would be easy, from the authorities already adduced, to refute here more forcefully as alien to the faith of the Church [Col. 0178A]—but that would be beside the point.

What shadow of error, then, has in Rupert a reason or comparison which occurs not infrequently among Catholic writers, yet without any stain or injury to their teaching or faith?

Rupert, in the place at issue and elsewhere, expounded nothing which Peter Damian, Remigius of Auxerre—or of Rheims, as Sanctius and others think—Alcuin, or Damascene had not expressly said many centuries earlier. What, then, in Rupert savours of the new and absurd heresy of hypostatic impanation?

Rupert, in the cited place, when asked how bread becomes the body of Christ which hung on the cross, and how wine [Col. 0178B] becomes his blood which he poured out from his side, raises another question no less difficult: namely, how the Son of Man, who was born from the earth, descended from heaven. “If anyone can solve this,” he says, “I shall answer that, because of the unity of Christ’s Godhood and manhood, it is most rightly said that the Son of Man and the Son of God are one Christ, who was both in heaven and everywhere.”

“Concerning the proposed question,” says the man of Deutz (*Book VI on John*), “I do not see what is doubtful. For the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, so that that which then hung on the cross and that which then the faith of the Church makes by its sacred mouth may be one body—one flesh, I say, and one blood.” These are Rupert’s words. Do you not read the same thing in Remigius [Note: [Col. 0177D] On 1 Corinthians, ch. X.], where he resolves and explains the same question by the same reason and the same [Col. 0178C] comparison? “The flesh,” he says, “which the Word of God the Father assumed in the Virgin’s womb into the unity of his person, and the bread consecrated in the Church, are one body of Christ.” Is this not Rupert’s proposition?

Attend to the comparison: “For just as,” Remigius adds, “that flesh is Christ’s body, so this bread passes into Christ’s body; and there are not two bodies, but one.” Is this not the comparison introduced by Rupert? Is this not the conclusion which Rupert too gives? Listen to Remigius’s reason, by which he proves the truth of the proposition and explains the sense of the comparison: “For the fullness of the divinity,” says Remigius, “which was in that flesh, fills this bread also; and the very divinity of the Word, which fills heaven and earth and all [Col. 0178D] things in them, itself fills the body of Christ sanctified by many priests throughout the whole world, and makes it one body of Christ.” What other reason is Rupert’s? What other conclusion is Rupert’s?

Therefore, if the comparison made by Remigius between the economy of the divine Word and the Eucharistic sacrament [Col. 0179A]—“just as that flesh which the Word of God the Father assumed in the Virgin’s womb into the unity of his person is Christ’s body, so this bread passes into Christ’s body; and there are not two bodies, but one”—never had the sense of an impanated hypostasis, why, when you meet this same comparison in Rupert, do you understand it thus: just as he who was formed from the Virgin and born from the earth descended from heaven because of the unity of Christ’s Godhood and manhood, so bread created from the earth becomes Christ’s body which hung on the cross, and wine becomes that blood which he poured out from his side?

If Remigius’s reasoning—“for the divinity itself of the Word, which fills heaven and earth, itself fills the body of Christ sanctified by many priests throughout the world and makes it one body of Christ”—did not hand down to believers hypostatic impanation but the perfect unity or identity of Christ’s body made by the Church and that which the divinity of the Word clothed in the Virgin’s womb, why should Rupert’s identical reasoning—“for the unity of the Word makes one body of Christ, so that that which hung on the cross and that which [Col. 0179B] the faith of the Church then makes by its sacred mouth may be one body, one flesh, I say, and one blood”—introduce the new impiety of hypostatic impanation? The sole difference between Remigius’s teaching and Rupert’s is that our man of Deutz, as you see, sets forth for us much more clearly the Catholic faith and meaning of this sacrament, opposed to every heretical depravity.

Finally, do you wish to see the pattern of Rupert’s teaching in Damascene, Alcuin, Peter Damian, and again in Remigius? Behold: examine the words of these authors which we gave above, and carefully compare them point by point with the passages objected against Rupert. When you discover one faith, one teaching, and one voice in Rupert and in them, let every shadow of the error of impanation flee from Rupert’s mind and words; and let this one doubt remain for you: whether Rupert spoke beforehand in Remigius, Damascene, Alcuin, and the others, or whether Alcuin, Damascene, Remigius, and the others spoke afterward again in Rupert.

Let no one, then, condemn Rupert’s teaching as hypostatic impanation without himself deserving condemnation, since, while forcing Rupert’s words into the error of hypostatic impanation, he also slanders the Catholic faith of the Church, violently and wrongfully dragging the doctrine of Catholic writers together with Rupert into the heresy of this impiety.

But which Catholic, together with that holy doctor and the other holy Fathers, would not freely profess what was wrongly advanced in the fourth place against the faith of the man of Deutz? Who, I say, with him, and according to their mind, would not profess in free and upright faith that “just as we truly confess that our flesh, which the Virgin Mary bore, is God because of the unity of person, so likewise we truly and catholicly judge that this visible bread, which the invisible divinity of that same Word assumes and transforms into his flesh, is Christ’s body”?

Moreover, who, with the man of Deutz in the very place from which he is charged, would not confess in Catholic language that “just as the Word became flesh, not by being changed into flesh, as the Eutychians dreamed, but by assuming flesh; so that same Word, long since made flesh, is now visible bread, not by being changed into bread but by assuming [Col. 0180A] and transferring bread into the unity of his person”?

Does not the one who assumes that flesh become “visible bread,” of which Truth itself says: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world”? Does not he assume bread and transfer it into the unity of his person who assumes that flesh—which Christ himself calls bread—in such a way that it is truly the flesh of the Word, the very same flesh which that same Word ineffably joined to himself in the Virgin’s womb in unity of person? This is the faith of venerable Rupert. Is it not ours too?

Why, then, do critics rashly condemn in the teaching of that holy abbot what all who are sound in faith profess with one voice? Why did Claude himself [Note: [Col. 0179D] *Réponse au traité De la Perp.*, p. 28.] dare to say that those words of Rupert plainly assert an assumption of bread by the divine Word, an assumption which we have shown, from the very words of the man of Deutz and from the rules of dialectic, cannot at all [Col. 0180B] cohere with his teaching?

They adduce a fifth passage from Rupert against Rupert; but its sound faith is so certain from what has been said and repeated so often that, without the reader’s leave, I hardly dare to examine it here. For who now doubts that he did not hold our faith in such a way that he failed to see himself, as Rupert says after Chrysostom (*Book VI on John*), “breaking the bread of God, concerning which we truly and catholicly confess that it is Christ’s body, and preserving the Son of God whole, although this visible bread has become one with the invisible Son of God,” since it is the true flesh of the Word which became flesh?

Who now doubts that “the Son of God—that is, God and man—has in himself effective power by which [Col. 0180C] he unites this visible bread to himself, namely by causing this consecrated visible bread and the flesh which hung on the cross to be one flesh, one body of Christ”?

Finally, who, when the bread of God is broken, does not hold with Rupert that the Son of God nevertheless remains whole? This is true, first, because “just as God and man are one Christ, so this consecrated visible bread and that flesh which hung on the cross are one flesh, one body of Christ”; and second, because “just as in the true death of the flesh the divinity suffered nothing, so, where the true body of Christ is offered, broken, and eaten on the altar, the same humanity of Christ, which suffered once and rose again, suffers nothing; for it no longer dies.”

[Col. 0180D] What faith has ever professed more clearly than Rupert’s that not bread, not a figure of Christ’s body, but Christ’s very true body is offered, broken, and eaten on the altar? What confession of faith can deny hypostatic impanation more expressly and more catholicly than this confession of Rupert, in whose sense bread, as we have established above, can neither be called nor be one flesh of Christ or one body of Christ? To avoid weariness, then, I shall make one observation concerning this fifth passage of Rupert.

Some, whom the Father did not draw, refusing with stiff neck to approach the Eucharistic truth of Christ’s body, objected that the Apostle says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more.” For they thought Christ [Col. 0181A] died as many times as this bread is broken, if this bread is Christ in truth. Rupert, altogether steadfast in defending this truth, thus explains this contention of unbelieving impiety: “To those who today murmur and contend when we defend the truth of the Lord’s body and blood, we seem to maintain great harshness. For when they have been constrained by argumentative faith through evangelical authority so that they cannot deny that this body of the Lord is that body which was given for us, and that this blood is that which was shed for us—when, I say, we have firmly established this for them—then they say: ‘Therefore, if this bread is called or is Christ not figuratively but truly, Christ suffers daily and dies as often as this bread is broken in commemoration of him.’ This is contrary to the Apostle’s declaration: ‘Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him.’” [Col. 0181B]

To resolve this objection of the Shadowy Ones by the light of truth, Rupert firmly asserts these two points: first, that the body offered, broken, and eaten on the altar is Christ’s true body, which was given for us; second, that nevertheless the same humanity of Christ, which suffered once and rose again, now suffers nothing, for it no longer dies.

To defend at once both this apostolic declaration and the truth of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, the man of Deutz adduces not the weight of arguments—which in matters of faith is slight or nonexistent—but various comparisons drawn from faith. By these he restrains carnal understanding and [Col. 0181C] in some measure explains to believers how the true flesh, which is Christ’s one and true flesh, or his true body, is here offered, broken, and eaten, yet Christ suffers nothing and remains in glory.

For by these likenesses he shows more clearly that it does not at all conflict with faith for diverse, even apparently opposed, things to belong to one reality, provided it is considered under different aspects, according to which that which is one in itself is regarded as if it were two, because it differs from itself in these different ways.

With this in mind, Rupert in the passage at issue sets forth Isaac and the ram. Although these two stood for one thing, namely Isaac, Abraham nevertheless struck the ram in such a way as not to injure the son placed upon the altar. [Col. 0181D] Yet he himself observes this difference: Isaac and the ram were one not in substance but only by a freely chosen sign; whereas in the Eucharist this visible bread has become one with the invisible Son of God, namely because the substance of the body which is on the altar has been united in one body with him.
