Accordingly, the man of Deutz adduces other examples better suited to the purpose, in which Catholic faith believes and proclaims diverse things of the same subject: for example, of the one Son of God, that he was born from the earth and yet descended from heaven; that, though immortal and Lord of death, he nevertheless underwent death; and that he who was already in heaven nevertheless ascended into heaven.

From these things, which animal perception does not grasp but which the faith of Christ alone acknowledges, [Col. 0182A] Rupert in some measure unfolds that hidden sacrament of divine mercy, in which the Church believes that beneath the outward appearance of bread there is the true and one body of Christ: that very body which hung on the cross and rose from the dead is daily offered, broken, and eaten in mystical consecrations; and yet that Christ does not thereby suffer anything or die in any way, but sits in heavenly glory as victor over death and hell.

It is as if our man of Deutz, in explaining so great a mystery to the faithful people, were saying: “He who reads the holy Scriptures has learned that the ram was struck while Isaac remained unharmed, although they were one thing in sign. But he who believes understands that, in the harshest torture and bitterest death of Christ’s flesh, Christ’s divine nature felt no [Col. 0182B] pain of suffering, although the person of that divine nature and of that flesh was one in Christ; there was one Son of God, one Christ, God and man, who, while dying on the cross according to the flesh, reigns immortal according to divinity.”

Thus, why should not one who believes also understand that, while Christ’s true flesh is offered, broken, and eaten in the unbloody sacrifice of the altar, Christ suffers nothing and no longer dies, although the flesh which is offered, broken, and eaten here under the appearance of bread is one flesh of Christ and one body of Christ, while under its own proper appearance it lives in heaven as Lord of death?

Who would reject this genuine meaning of Rupert unless he favoured the Shadowy Ones, whom the man of Deutz vigorously [Col. 0182C] pursues with zeal for Eucharistic truth? If another sense of this fifth passage is sought—a sense which not only instructs our faith but kindles the piety of our faith—you may say that Rupert teaches there that just as the divinity of the Word, because it is life and spirit, could not be separated from its life and spirit even when his flesh was cruelly fixed to the cross, so, while Christ’s body is broken and eaten in the sacrament, Christ’s humanity nevertheless suffers nothing, because in this breaking and eating of Christ’s body the spirit is not separated from Christ’s body; “but,” says the man of Deutz, “the flesh is eaten together with the spirit, and the spirit together with the flesh.”

But lest anyone be troubled by the holy abbot’s saying [Col. 0182D] that Christ’s body is broken in the sacrifice of the altar, where only the outer appearance of bread seems to be broken, let Chrysostom be heard [Note: [Col. 0181D] Homily 42 on 1 Corinthians.], who explains these words of the Apostle, “and the bread which we break,” in this freer interpretation: “Why does the Apostle add, ‘which we break’? This can be seen in the Eucharist, but by no means on the cross—rather, the opposite occurred: ‘A bone,’ he says, ‘shall not be broken.’ But what he did not suffer on the cross, he suffers in the offering for your sake: he submits to being broken.”

Berengar himself, abjuring his heresy, professed the Catholic faith in these very words and on apostolic authority [Note: [Col. 0182D] C. *Ego Berengarius*, dist. 2, *De consecr.*]: “I profess with mouth and heart that I hold concerning the sacraments of the Lord’s table the same faith which the lord and venerable Pope Nicholas [Col. 0183A] and this holy synod, by evangelical and apostolic authority, handed down as to be held and confirmed for me: namely, that the bread and wine placed upon the altar, after consecration, are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; and that Christ’s body is sensibly—not only sacramentally, but in truth—handled by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful; swearing by the holy and homoousian Trinity.”

If, by these words “broken” and “ground,” you understand not that Christ’s flesh is torn into parts or pulverized, but that the true flesh of Christ—not merely a figure of the Lord’s body—remains in every particle formed by the division of the species of bread and is received by those who eat, [Col. 0183B] there is nothing objectionable in these words of Berengar, Chrysostom, and Rupert.

Having thus explained this fifth passage of Rupert, I hasten to the sixth, against which certain Catholics, hastily turning over the writings of this doctor, dash themselves less happily. They imagine that they have read in the man of Deutz (*Book II on Exodus*, ch. 10) that the substance of bread and wine is not changed or destroyed by the Holy Spirit, but assumed by the Word of the Father. Therefore they pronounce without any doubt that Rupert both held and taught a hypostatic union of bread and wine with the Word of eternal counsel.

But how can one who wrote on so many pages that bread and wine are turned, converted, changed, and transmuted into Christ’s body and blood; who even in that place distinctly and expressly confesses that bread on the altar becomes Christ’s body [Col. 0183C]; who proclaims that what we receive on the altar is Christ and the Lamb of God—how can such a person be judged to have thought or taught that the substance of bread and wine is not changed in the sacrament of the Eucharist?

Rupert did indeed there state that the substance of bread and wine, namely insofar as it is subject to the five senses under the outward appearance, is not changed or destroyed. What carnal perception would not judge this? Or understand him to say that bread and wine are not changed by a destructive change—that is, one which does not introduce a nobler substance. What Catholic would not profess this, who believes that bread is changed by the divine operation of the Holy Spirit into that one true body of Christ which the Word assumed and fastened to the cross?

Or understand the bread and wine to become Christ’s body and [Col. 0183D] blood in such a way that they are nevertheless not changed into the appearance of Christ’s body and blood—that is, as he himself explains it, into the taste of flesh and the horror of blood. Let a more mature judgment, I say, understand and judge these things; it will not condemn the faith of St. Rupert, but will praise it as following, in all respects, the opinions and words of the holy Fathers.

“But why,” you will say, “did he labor, from the comparison so often repeated with the Lord’s Incarnation and from the unity of the divine Word, to demonstrate in so many places that the flesh which is in the sacrament is the very same flesh which was conceived in the womb of the Virgin, [Col. 0184A] assumed by the Word of God, and pierced upon the cross; although in the sacrifice of the altar neither the taste of flesh nor the horror of blood alarms us, but the pleasing appearance of bread and wine invites us to the table?”

He did so fittingly and wisely, indeed, against those who, in Rupert’s age, as Alger notes [Note: [Col. 0183D] In the prologue.], said that bread and wine were changed into flesh and blood—not of Christ, but of some Son of Man, holy and acceptable to God; or even against certain Catholic writers who, as we noted above, maintained that the flesh of Christ offered by the Church in the consecrated bread was one thing, while that which was born of the Virgin and hung upon the cross was another.

Therefore, not irrelevantly, nor contrary to the mind and language of the Fathers, Rupert sought especially in these passages to establish this one point [Col. 0184B]: that this body which is consecrated on the altar by the mystical prayer is that very body of Christ which, in obedience of love, through love’s obedience to the Word of God, was made fit for death. And he proves the indivisible unity of that flesh—which is one true flesh of the Word both on the altar and on the cross—most forcefully from the unity of the divine Word. Nor, departing from the faith of the eucharistic sacrament, did Rupert explain from the wondrous dispensation of incarnate Wisdom the astonishing and terrible mystery of Christ’s body; he followed in this also the illustrious lights of the Church.

It is therefore contrary to right, and a grave wrong not only to the Tuitiensian but also to the faith and piety of the whole Church, when some persons divert these most pure streams of Rupert’s teaching, which flowed continuously from the Church’s clearest springs, [Col. 0184C] toward the unheard-of novelties of hypostatic impanation.

Let, then, the slanderous insolence of certain persons now be silent, lest, while it falsely disgraces Rupert’s faith with the name of error, it insultingly dishonor the teaching of the Catholic Fathers. Let this zeal, burning more from impulse than knowledge, restrain itself, lest it rashly proscribe in Rupert the faith which the Church has always held [Note: [Col. 0183D] This eloquence, book IX and final book.].

Or, if they delight in reopening the tombs of those now resting in peace and gnawing the bones of the dead, let them test their teeth upon this adamantine man; they will learn that they will be broken in their mouths, so that hereafter they may bite no one under this guise of piety.

Far from Rupert’s teaching, therefore, be the claim that he set forth at the Lord’s table merely [Col. 0184D] a figure or sign of Christ’s body and blood. For everywhere he contends that the true body and blood of Christ are made by the Church’s sacred utterance beneath the outward appearance of bread and wine—wholly, not in shadow but in truth; not in figure but in reality, name, and effect [Note: [Col. 0184D] Book I, *On the Divine Offices*, ch. 17; and the letter to Cuno, beginning *Meditatus*, and elsewhere.].

Far from Rupert’s glory be the claim that Christ’s body is not eaten by the unworthy; for with him: “Someone may eat unworthily, but no one ought to eat unworthily. For bread once consecrated never afterwards loses the power of sanctification or ceases to be Christ’s [Col. 0185A] flesh; but, as he says in book VI on John, it profits the unworthy person nothing, whose faith without works is dead.”

Far from Rupert’s name be the sacrilegious folly of impanation. Rather, as he himself exhorts [Note: [Col. 0185B] Dedicatory letter to Cuno, beginning *Meditatus*, and book III on Exodus, ch. 10.]: “Let us believe the faithful Savior God concerning what we do not see: namely, that bread and wine, though their outward appearance is unchanged, are transferred into the true substance of the living body and blood of Christ.” — “For God, creator of substances and appearances, effectively converts these into Christ’s flesh and blood, although the outward appearance remains” (*On Exodus*, book IV, ch. 7).

And finally, let the new and absurd impiety of hypostatic impanation be far from Rupert’s faith and piety. In full pages he wrote and taught in express terms [Col. 0185B] that the substance of bread and wine is turned, converted, changed, and transmuted into that very body of Christ which hung upon the cross for us, and into that blood of his which was poured out for the blotting out of the sins of many; that bread becomes and is that flesh which the Word of the Father assumed from the Virgin and offered to God, bloodied, upon the altar of the cross; and that wine becomes and is that blood which Christ poured forth from his side. These are things which, [Col. 0186A] as we have shown, the blasphemous impiety of hypostatic impanation could neither tolerate nor assert.

Since, therefore, Rupert has openly taught all these Catholic truths concerning Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist, with all the faith fitting a son of the Church, all the learning fitting an interpreter of the divine Word, all the glory fitting a defender of the faith, every title that makes a man renowned among saints and learned men, and indeed all the devout faith befitting one who is at once Catholic and holy; and since he firmly opposed them to profane and sacrilegious errors: what is purer than the faith of the venerable Rupert? What is surer than Rupert’s teaching? What more illustrious than Rupert’s glory? What more celebrated than Rupert’s name? Finally, what is holier [Col. 0186B] than Rupert’s faithful piety toward the adorable sacrament of Christ’s body and blood? Therefore, with every mark of any error erased, I have freely presented, faithfully displayed, steadfastly defended, and happily vindicated Rupert, Father of the monastery of Tuiti, as pure in faith, certain in doctrine, illustrious in glory, celebrated in name, and at once faithful and holy in Catholic piety toward the eucharistic mystery of Christ’s body and blood—showing false those who defamed him (Wisdom 10).

## APPENDIX

The unjust and unlearned criticism of Simplicius Verinus concerning Rupert, Abbot of Tuiti, in the book *On Transubstantiation*.

[Col. 0185]

[Col. 0185C] After every page of our *Apology for Rupert, Abbot of Tuiti*, had gone to press, I came upon Simplicius Verinus’s book *On Transubstantiation*. In it this bitter writer of the Protestant sect—namely, the celebrated Salmasius—draws Rupert of Tuiti into every error against the sacrament of the Eucharist: namely, the presence of a mere sign or power, eating by faith, impanation, and a hypostatic union of bread with the Word. He makes many claims requiring notice, which the defender of that holy doctor ought not to have passed over, but should add and correct here by way of an appendix.

### I.

Concerning the author of the books *On the Divine Offices*, Verinus doubts [Note: [Col. 0185D] *On Transubstantiation*, pp. 184, 185, 197.] in such a way that he is more inclined to agree with those [Col. 0185D] who deny that they were composed by Rupert of Tuiti.

The first part of the *Apology* corrects this first error of Verinus, where, by a careful dissertation, we assigned this work *On the Divine Offices* to Rupert of Tuiti alone, with certain right.

Indeed, it is read under this name in the manuscript codices kept in the more distinguished libraries of Belgium: in the library of Alne Monastery, in the Liège edition; in the library of Saint-Amand [Elnone], [Col. 0186C] in whose codex chapter twenty-five and the final chapter of book ten are missing, though they are found in printed copies; in the library of Saint Martin at Tournai, where another work *On the Divine Offices*, written by Master Robert—who is someone other than the Tuitiensian—is also found, with a prologue beginning, “I remember that he wrote certain brief things concerning the ecclesiastical offices,” etc.; in the library of Villers; in the library of Bonne-Espérance Monastery; in the library of Utrecht; and in the library of Cambron, as Anthony Sanderus reports to us in his *Belgian Library*.

Nor is there any weight in the reason by which Verinus calls into question the author of books of this sort, since it proceeds only from a preconceived error and a false understanding of Rupert. Verinus thinks that the author of this [Col. 0186D] work did not hold the real presence of Christ’s true body in the sacrament of the altar, but taught that divinity or grace alone was joined with the bread in the Eucharist. Yet he judges Rupert of Tuiti—who undoubtedly wrote the Commentaries on Exodus—to have held that not only divinity but also Christ’s humanity was hypostatically united to bread.

From this conflict of opinions Verinus wished it to be denied that the books *On the Divine [Col. 0187A] Offices* were published by the same Rupert who issued the Commentaries on Exodus. Error drags Verinus into error. This first mistaken notion concerning Rupert’s work plainly reveals Simplicius Verinus’s carelessness in turning over Rupert’s books; for they consistently reckon this work among Rupert’s other writings and everywhere declare it to be the first fruits of Rupert’s labors.

What wonder, then, if Verinus, who either never read Rupert’s books or did so most superficially, failed to grasp the mind of that most learned writer and attributed alien opinions to him?

### II.

Verinus asserts from the words found in book II, chapter 9, of *On the Divine Offices* that Rupert—who is unquestionably the author of those books—understood the sacrament of the Eucharist to consist only of the substance of visible things, namely [Col. 0187B] bread and wine, and of the divine power by which the souls of the righteous are fed and sanctified [Note: [Col. 0187D] pp. 316, 318.]:

> “There is in both the priest and the sacrifice a divine substance; there is also an earthly one. In each, the earthly is that which can be seen bodily or locally; in each, the divine is the invisible Word, which in the beginning was God with God,” etc.

How foolish this exposition of Verinus is becomes evident to anyone who observes: first, that for Rupert the earthly substance includes not only the substance of bread and wine, from which the sacrifice is indeed made, but of which the sacrament does not consist; it includes also Christ’s very flesh, which, as Rupert says, is from our earth and is seen on the altar beneath [Col. 0187C] the appearance of bread. Second, in that very work Rupert expressly professes that the Eucharist contains not merely divinity, as Verinus imagined, but at the same time Christ’s humanity itself—Christ’s true body and his true blood—not in shadow but in truth, as the Tuitiensian says; not in figure but in reality. We demonstrated this in detail in the *Apology* by producing testimonies from book I, chapter 17, and book II, chapters 2, 5, 16, and 22, of *On the Divine Offices*. Third, the genuine explanation, given in the *Apology*, of the passage adduced by Verinus plainly shows that Rupert there means and teaches nothing other than that, in the sacrifice of the altar, the divine Word assumes bread so as to transfer and transmute it into that [Col. 0187D] very flesh which he put on in the Virgin’s womb; and thus, from visible bread assumed by the Word and transmuted into his true flesh, and from the invisible Word of God itself, a visible sacrifice is constituted.

There is therefore no reason why Verinus or any other defender of a shadowy body should claim Rupert as patron of his error; rather, there is reason for him, casting off these figures of his own faith, to adhere firmly to the Catholic truth of Christ’s body.

### III.

Anyone who believes that the sacrament contains nothing but the substance of bread and wine and a divine power or grace must necessarily conclude that, in communion in [Col. 0188A] that sacrament, the unworthy receive only the substance of bread and wine.

Thus Verinus argues [Note: [Col. 0187D] p. 225.] that one who eats unworthily, in his own sense and Rupert’s, eats bread alone; that the wicked receive indeed the sacrament, but not Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 0187D] p. 247.], according to these words of Rupert: “Into the person in whom faith is absent, nothing of the sacrifice comes except the visible appearances of bread and wine.”

Our *Apology* corrects this unjust judgment of Verinus concerning Rupert’s teaching: first, where it proves from Rupert’s most certain testimonies that he held and expressly taught that Christ’s body is eaten even by the sacrilegious mouth of the unworthy; and second, where it offers a twofold Catholic understanding of these words, “into the person in whom faith is absent,” etc.: namely, that nothing from the sacrifice which is useful to the recipient comes into one in whom faith is absent; or, that into one who does not believe Christ to be present in this sacrifice, nothing from the sacrifice comes—according to that faith which recognizes only the appearances of bread and wine in the sacrifice—except the visible appearances. Who does not see how far this differs from Verinus’s judgment?

### IV.

As Verinus proceeds in his disputation against transubstantiation, he dares to say of Rupert [Note: [Col. 0188D] pp. 317 and 318.] that Rupert did not think bread really changed into Christ’s body; and that, by the words, “when the Word of the cross comes to the wine, it becomes that blood which was poured out for the remission of sins,” Rupert nevertheless did not intend to confirm the transubstantiation [Col. 0188C] of bread into body and wine into blood. Finally Verinus concludes [Note: [Col. 0188D] p. 320.] that Rupert, like the older Fathers themselves, denied that any change of the substance of bread, wine, and water intervenes in these sacraments.

Let anyone who has heard Rupert everywhere teaching that bread and wine, by the mystical prayer, become and truly are Christ’s true flesh—the very flesh pierced for us—and Christ’s true blood, the blood poured out for the remission of sins; that bread and wine are turned and converted, changed and transmuted into the substance of Christ’s flesh and blood, even though the outward appearance of bread and wine remains—judge how truthfully this was said. These points were established in the *Apology* by Rupert’s most evident testimonies [Col. 0188D].

For no legitimate method of interpretation allows these words to be subjected to equivocal explanations or drawn off toward the power or figure of Christ’s divinity or body, or toward the notions of hypostatic impanation. Who, unless he does Rupert’s faith the greatest wrong, would suspect him to have concealed an alien doctrine under these words? To think one thing and say or write another concerning the divine sacraments is a grave impiety; far be that from a Catholic teacher.

Nor is Verinus’s violent interpretation [Note: [Col. 0188D] p. 319.] at all supported by the fact that the Tuitiensian expressly wrote that the water [Col. 0189A] with which believers are washed in baptism is the very water which flowed from Christ’s opened side—although Rupert did not think its substance changed [Col. 0189A].

For nowhere did Rupert either think or write that baptismal water was converted and transmuted into the water which flowed with blood from Christ’s side; whereas in almost countless passages he wrote that bread and wine are converted into Christ’s body and blood. Here Verinus is compelled to admit that such words express transubstantiation, since, in order not to admit its truth, he allows no one to say that “the water of baptism is converted into the water which flowed from Christ’s side.”

But Rupert did not define the water of regeneration to be that which the soldier’s lance drew forth from Christ’s side in the sense [Col. 0189B] in which he asserted, without any ambiguity of language or meaning, that bread in the Eucharist becomes and is that flesh of Christ which was affixed to the cross.

For since Rupert rightly judged that all water—whether in the Rhine, the Tiber, sacred fonts, or flowing from Christ’s side upon the cross—has one substance; and since he held that the power in the washing of regeneration flows from Christ’s blood, which came forth from Christ’s body together with water, he very wisely said that the water of baptism is that water which, both in substance and in power, flowed mixed with Christ’s blood from his side.

But what, I ask, does this teaching of Rupert prove against the transubstantiation of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood [Col. 0189C]?

Rupert calls baptismal water the very same water “by reason of substance, which is one in kind among all waters, and by reason of the power which flows from Christ’s blood into each,” as that which came forth with blood from Christ’s pierced side. Therefore, when Rupert calls bread consecrated by the Church’s utterance that very flesh of Christ which, suspended upon the cross, redeemed the world, is no transmutation of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood to be understood? Why, then, did he commit to writing on so many pages that bread and wine are converted and transmuted into the very substance of Christ’s flesh and blood?

If Christ’s flesh and bread are one substance, how can one be transmuted into the other? If the latter merely possesses [Col. 0189D] the power of the former, how is bread said by Rupert, not merely in effect but in name and in reality itself, to become and be Christ’s flesh? This he states in the express words we brought forward in the *Apology*. “Indeed,” the critic’s client will protest, “Rupert argues that bread and wine are Christ’s flesh and blood because wine differs from blood, and bread from the human body, only in accidents.” Salmasius considers this claim as remote from the truth of transubstantiation as it is foolish and contrary to physics.

I do not deny that no transubstantiation can be understood where one substance is identical with another. But if the celebrated Salmasius understands Rupert to posit bread [Col. 0190A] and wine in the Eucharist in such a manner that, in this sacrament, there is at the same time the substance of body and blood, which is the same as bread and wine only by a substantial, not an individual, unity, he must confess that Rupert asserted in the mystery of the altar not the individual substance of Christ’s flesh and blood any more than that of any other human being. Who could think this of Rupert, when he expressly declares that bread and wine become that individual body of Christ which was affixed to the cross, so that Christ may be believed to have spoken truly: “This is my body, which shall be given for you”?

Nor did Rupert there depart from the truth of transubstantiation, since he nowhere sought to demonstrate that bread and wine become and are Christ’s blood from the fact [Col. 0190B] that the substance of bread and flesh, or wine and blood, is of one and the same kind. This is clear from several considerations against Salmasius and the other critics of Rupert.

1. Even if the substance of bread and flesh, or wine and blood, were granted to be one in genus, no fool could infer from this that bread and wine become and are Christ’s flesh and blood rather than the flesh or blood of any other person. So too the Word, in assuming the nature common to all human beings, did not join to himself the nature of one man rather than another.

2. Even if bread and the human body had one substance, it would nevertheless be true that several loaves are several bodies; even a beginner in logic would allow that several loaves are several substances. And even on that assumption, it could not stand [Col. 0190C] that one numerically identical body should be made from several loaves.

3. If bread by its own nature is of the same substance as human flesh, or wine by its innate properties has the same nature as blood, such that under this consideration bread and wine are truly called and are Christ’s flesh and his blood, it would be entirely false and foolish to say that, by divine operation and the ineffable power of the Holy Spirit, bread and wine become Christ’s flesh and blood during the mystical prayers.

4. Nor would it be any less foolish to teach that the unity of the Word causes bread and wine to become and truly be that very flesh which was nailed to the cross and that very blood which was shed upon the cross.

5. Finally, there would not be two substances in the Eucharist: those of bread [Col. 0190D] and flesh.

Since, then, Rupert, according to Verinus’s criticism [Note: [Col. 0189D] p. 385.], admitted in these books two substances besides the divine in the sacrament of the Eucharist—namely, bread and Christ’s flesh; since he expressly said in several places that the unity of the Word produces the unity of the sacrifice, not merely substantial, as Verinus imagines [Note: [Col. 0190D] p. 319.], but individual, such that bread is that one flesh of Christ which hung upon the cross, and wine that one blood which was poured out for many; since he plainly wrote that, by divine operation and the power of the Holy Spirit, bread and wine pass into Christ’s flesh and blood; that the many breads offered daily [Col. 0191A] by priests are not many bodies, but that one body which was an offering for sins; and finally that Christ gives human beings not merely some flesh and some blood, but his own flesh and his own blood, so that it is not the flesh of just anyone but of the one Christ—

Who could suppose that Rupert meant bread and wine to be of the same substance as a human body and blood in such a way as to prove from this that, without any transmutation of substance, bread and wine become, are, and are truly called Christ’s flesh and blood?

Who, guided by human reason, would not judge more soundly that Rupert there explains, from a certain analogy of bread and wine with flesh and blood, or even from some substantial similarity, how it is not contrary to all reason nor [Col. 0191B] beyond all power that bread and wine should pass and be converted into Christ’s flesh and blood?

For although Rupert sometimes said that water and wine, wine and blood, are of the same substance, since wine and blood are constituted from the one common principle of water, our Tuitiensian nowhere judged that water, wine, and blood have substance of the same definition, species, or nature. He thought that in wine and blood there is not water alone, but fire joined with water; and he understood different essences, definitions, and natures in things.

The features by which things differ from one another and receive distinct definitions in essence Rupert therefore calls accidents, because they supervene upon primary substances already established in their being; not because they happen to things—or [Col. 0191C] ultimate substances, such as wine or blood—in such a way that, when they depart, an incorruptible substance nevertheless always remains, preserving every *entelechy* and essence of wine and blood. We discussed this more fully in the *Apology* against Gregory of Valencia.

If anyone wishes to bring these matters under the doctrines of Descartes, which recognize no substance distinct from the subject in forms, except the rational soul, I willingly grant it—provided that, in accordance with Rupert’s doctrine and faith, he professes in Catholic fashion, firmly holds, and vigorously defends that the whole substance of bread and wine is converted and transmuted into the individual flesh of Christ which suffered on the cross, and into his individual blood which he poured out for the ungodly, with only the outward appearance of bread and wine remaining.

[Col. 0191D] Nor should Verinus’s opinion be heard. In order to pronounce Rupert alien to the faith of transubstantiation, it seeks to prove from Rupert’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0191D] p. 320.] that no corruption of the visible appearances of the sacrament occurs. In that testimony the Tuitiensian sincerely declares that by the operation of the Holy Spirit bread becomes Christ’s body and wine his blood; yet the good of the substance is not destroyed or lost, but remains in its being as regards its visible or outward appearance, while in reality it is advanced to the truth and dignity of Christ’s body and blood.

[Col. 0192A] As though, according to Verinus’s invention, substance were the same thing for our Tuitiensian as outward appearance, and a thing did not undergo a change which its visible appearance does not undergo—although Rupert most distinctly declares that in the Eucharist bread and wine become and are Christ’s body and blood in reality, name, and effect, but not in outward appearance.

Thus Verinus is caught by the wisdom which does not understand these things. Thus Salmasius is blind in those matters from which he boasts that he clearly demonstrates to all that Rupert, like the Fathers older than himself, denied that any change occurs in these sacraments in the substance of visible and bodily things—that is, bread, wine, and water.

[Col. 0192B] What does the celebrated Salmasius not distort in order to twist everything toward his own errors? He translates this word of Theophylact, εἶδος, as “substance” [Note: [Col. 0191D] p. 342.], assigning to the very words, by what right one can scarcely see, meanings never heard before, that they may serve his faith.

At last Verinus is judged out of his own mouth [Note: [Col. 0192D] p. 345.], when he himself firmly declares that it is utterly impossible for the substance of bread to remain and at the same time to be Christ’s true body.

What truer thing could Verinus have said? But with what fidelity as an interpreter does Verinus interpret Rupert, when Rupert says that bread is Christ’s true body, in a sense which he himself is certain cannot stand—namely, that bread is Christ’s true body in such a way that it is simultaneously the substance of bread? Or does he think the substance of bread remains because the word “bread” is retained [Col. 0192C]? When Christ says, “The blind see,” does Salmasius suppose that those who now see are still blind? Surely the person who thinks such things is foolish and must be handed over to the rudiments of dialectic, since he has not yet learned that in statements of changes the thing which is changed is expressed by the name of its former state, so that the proposition may indicate more clearly, by its proper terms, both the state from which the thing passes and that into which it is transferred. What credibility, therefore, does one deserve who bends writers to meanings that can neither stand nor be admitted in the schools of dialectic?

Indeed, I know that Rupert said that the Word does not change or destroy the substance of bread in the sacrament of the Eucharist. But I also know two kinds of change: one, by which a thing so ceases to be what [Col. 0192D] it was that it passes into nothing; and another, by which a thing so begins to be what it was not that it is raised to higher things. Of these two kinds of change, who does not see which Rupert means, unless he invents darkness or falsehood for himself? For the Tuitiensian, by adding the phrase “or destroys it,” plainly signifies only that no change of substance occurs in bread by which bread is so destroyed as to become nothing; he does not deny that change by which it so loses its own being as to be transferred into the dignity and reality of the flesh of the divine Word. We observed this in the *Apology*, [Col. 0193A] where we explained Rupert’s harsher passages and brought clearer light to the more obscure ones.

### V.

Certainly Verinus—or Salmasius under that assumed name—is no wiser than Grotius, whom he attacks, nor more successful in his criticism. For he concludes [Note: [Col. 0193C] p. 383.] that a hypostatic union of bread with the Word of God, though not with Christ’s humanity, in the sacrament of the altar is most ancient and was believed and handed down by the ancient Fathers. Yet, quite inconsistent with himself, after some discussion [Note: [Col. 0193C] pp. 394, 395.], he says that the ancient Fathers neither held nor taught a hypostatic conjunction of bread with divinity.

With the same shifting mind, after inventing that, among the more recent writers, Rupert of Tuiti, in book II, chapter 9, of *On the Divine [Col. 0193B] Offices*, taught this hypostatic unity of the divine Word with bread in such a way as to posit only Christ’s divinity [Note: [Col. 0193C] p. 184.] as adhering to the mystical bread in the same manner in which divinity is joined with humanity in Christ’s person and true body, Verinus shortly afterward [Note: [Col. 0194C] *Ibid.*] drags our Tuitiensian into the opposite error by a new fiction. He writes that Rupert, in his Commentaries on Exodus, held that not only Christ’s divinity but also his humanity is joined with sacramental bread, because Rupert says in his commentary on Exodus: “Just as the Word sent down from on high became flesh, not by being changed into flesh, but by assuming flesh, so also bread and wine.”

But these passages of Rupert, which we produced in full [Col. 0193C] and explained with a sincere mind in the *Apology*, establish no belief in that hypostatic impanation, whether of Christ’s divinity or humanity, but introduce only a comparison with the Incarnation [Col. 0194A]. From this comparison, as Verinus himself admits [Note: [Col. 0194C] p. 395.], one would too inconsequently infer that the holy Fathers understood a hypostatic union of the divine Word with bread in the Eucharist, since a likeness must never be fitted to every individual point.

Moreover, Salmasius, under the false name of Verinus, casts this error not only upon Rupert but also upon Haimo of Halberstadt, Remigius of Rheims, Valeram [Valeramnus], and certain others, as though they believed that the Divinity which fills heaven and earth, and remains united with Christ’s body in heaven, is joined to the substance of bread in the sacrament of the altar by that same hypostatic union, such that the substance of bread, without any transmutation of itself, became, was, and was truly called Christ’s body, one with that body which sits [Col. 0194B] at God’s right hand.

Thus the liar overthrows what he constructs. We have seen in the *Apology* that Rupert said and thought things similar to Remigius. But how Catholic the doctrine of both is, and how remote from hypostatic impanation, we demonstrated there at greater length from their words and from the very rules of dialectic.

Sound criticism would have identified this Remigius not as the man of Rheims, but rather as the man of Auxerre. Nor would it have supposed that Valeramnus wrote these things, since either he never existed or, if the Valeramnus set forth in the first part of the *Apology* is indeed the person intended, he at least nowhere committed anything of the sort to writing, as we noted in that dissertation.

Therefore, in every respect, the judgment of Simplicius Verinus concerning Rupert of Tuiti in the book *On Transubstantiation* is unjust and wholly unlearned.

[Col. 0193]

## Letter of R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Tuiti, to Cuno, Abbot of Siegburg

[Col. 0193]

[Col. 0193D] The authority of the same Word—truthful as it is gentle—judges that no faithful soul is to be reproached when it renders any office of devotion to the incarnate Word, when He says: “Why do you trouble this woman? For she has performed a good work upon me. For you always have the poor with you,” He says, “but you do not always have me” (Matt. 26). For because He said, “You do not always have me,” and after saying this ascended into heaven, does no one now anoint His head and feet with precious ointment? But You, the same One whose greatness has no end, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth [Col. 0194D] (Isa. 66), said with the same mouth: “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Therefore, in one sense, He says, “You do not always have me”: namely, in bodily and visible presence; but in another sense He says, “I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age”: namely, by the incorporeal presence of uncircumscribed divinity, an invisible presence.

It is clear, moreover, that those things which were then done concerning that bodily and visible presence were prefigurative of the things to be done under this incorporeal [Col. 0195A] and invisible presence. The woman who had been a sinner, when she poured out precious ointment upon the head and also, as John relates, upon the feet of Him reclining in the Pharisee’s house (Luke 7; John 12), prefigured the Church from the Gentiles. She now performs this act spiritually, having been admitted into that house of the Jewish people, concerning which the Apostle says: “To them belong adoption as sons, glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9).

Having been admitted there, I say, so that the same Apostle may say: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow-citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (Eph. 2), she spiritually renders this renowned office [Col. 0195B] of devotion to the Lord Jesus Christ. Yet she does so in one way in the active life and in another in the contemplative life. For in the active life she anoints only His feet, while she supplies bodily aid to the poor or needy in His name, since they are, as it were, the lowest members of the Head. But in the contemplative life she anoints His head and feet more graciously, when, from the faithful root or marrow of the holy Scriptures, she fashions a devout discourse and sweetly expounds, as far as she is able, how “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God; all things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made” (John 1); and likewise how “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

When, therefore, we do something of this kind, let not the Lord’s disciples be indignant [Col. 0195C], remembering that He Himself said: “Let her alone. Why do you trouble her? She has done what she could; she has anticipated anointing my body for burial” (Mark 14). She was defended by that Defender who knew her heart better; and He made her more confident concerning what had pleased her in her own possession: she spent where she wished, and upon whom she wished, what she had bought with her own means. How much better did she spend it thus than Judas, the thief of the Lord’s money-bag, would have done had he sold it, as he wished, for three hundred denarii! For now the house has been filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John 12), because wherever the Gospel is preached, what she did is also told in remembrance of her (Matt. 26); but the stench of that theft and envy will never be erased.

You know these things, my Father Cuno, venerable abbot and most zealous student of venerable letters; and, what is greater still, pillar of monastic religion. On Mount Siegburg, at the memorial shrine of the holy archangel Michael, now in the twelfth year from your ordination—that is, the year 1117 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the tenth indiction—you have thus far faithfully served Christ and filled the Lord’s house with a good fragrance [Col. 0195D]. You know these things, I say, because unless you—or rather Christ through you—had come to my aid and protection, those who have been troublesome to this work merely in words would doubtless have raged against me in deeds also. You have become for me “a peg fixed in a sure place” (Isa. 22), upon which the little vessel of my hope may be hung.

Accordingly, I believe it was brought about through the providence of God the Father, without whom not even one sparrow falls to the ground (Matt. 10), [Col. 0196A] that I should come to the knowledge of your charity and faith; and that thereafter, when my father was about to depart from this world—Berengar, abbot of Saint Lawrence, a man venerable in life and memorable for wisdom—I should be entrusted to your faith on the public hill of Liège, like an orphan to a guardian. For the only man who has now succeeded him, the faithful and prudent Heribrand—who was himself learned in letters and had been the master of my boyhood—could not protect me as far as that point to which, as you know, envy of my name had reached.

I shall therefore now recall my cry and my dream, rightly to be reckoned among serious matters, since I do not doubt that it was a forewarning of what has now happened: namely, that the man just mentioned, when about to die, left me in your hand, enduring the enmities of those who hated me without cause (Ps. 34). [Col. 0196B] I shall recall, I say, my cry in a nocturnal vision, when I cried out—as I had learned to sing in a responsory—that great and final cry of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite: “Now, Lord, receive me through the crown of martyrdom with my brethren, Your servants.”

Something was being sung in antiphon, I do not know what; and around me, in the midst as it were of a great church, while choirs thundered loudly and most high, the reproaches of those reproaching and contending—which have now fallen upon me (Ps. 68)—were prophesied in reverse by that image of singing. Meanwhile I stood silent and gentle, because I was joined to the side and held hand in hand with my aforesaid abbot. Then, behold, in a wonderful fashion that I can scarcely express, he placed my hand into what seemed another hand, as though [Col. 0196C] into a glove, each of my fingers being inserted into a corresponding finger of that hand.

What did that hand signify for me, my Father, if not the protection of your charity? For he departed from human affairs and left me in your hand, as you yourself know, against men by whom very many had already been stirred up. Thus the singing went on, as I have said, and as the crowd multiplied the chant, the vocal tumult grew stronger. At last I broke forth into a great and high voice, wonderfully pleasing even to my own hearing for its beauty and arrangement. With every eye turned upon me, I now sang that aforesaid responsory of blessed Dionysius, while the hand already mentioned—representing your hand, as the event itself has now proved—led me by the hand.

For, especially safe through your help after God and relying on your testimony, behold, I answer those who reproach [Col. 0196D] me with a word (Ps. 118). And while you act and grant the authority to write to the heavenly gift which, you freely testify, inspired me, this work—begun with your knowledge—now comes before public hearing, to the glory and honor of the holy and indivisible Trinity.

For I had intended to make it threefold, from the beginning of the first creation to the end of the age: the first part from the rising of the first light to the fall of the first man; the second from that fall of the first man to the incarnation or passion of the second man, Jesus Christ the Son of God; the third from then until the consummation of the age, that is, the general resurrection of the dead. The first belongs properly to the Father, [Col. 0197A] the second to the Son, and the third to the Holy Spirit.

Thus we have made three books concerning the work proper to the Father, from the first creation—that is, from the beginning in which God created heaven and earth—to Adam’s expulsion from paradise. Then, concerning the work proper to the Son, by which the Word of the Lord, drawing near to us gradually from Abel’s righteousness or death through prophetic figures and visions, came as far as the assumption of flesh and death on the cross, we have made thirty books. Then, concerning the work proper to the Holy Spirit, namely from the incarnation of the same Christ, Son of the living God, whom the undefiled Virgin conceived by the Holy Spirit, until the end of the age, we have made nine books. Together they amount to forty-two books.

The very words, therefore, which run thus—“Now, Lord, receive me through the crown of martyrdom with my brethren, [Col. 0197B] Your servants”—help me, I confess, and make this vessel of my hope sweet to me. For “through the crown of martyrdom” is the same as saying “through the victory [Col. 0198A] of testimony,” though it has pleased men to call testimony carried as far as the shedding of blood “martyrdom,” by the Greek name, in order to heighten the distinction of its meaning. Now all who bear testimony to Truth will most certainly be crowned by Truth itself. May that Truth deign to receive and number me among my brethren, His servants, as one bearing testimony to Him in voice and writing.

May you and all others have a share among them, in this and in every good and faithful word of the Lord. With Christ’s help through you, it was permitted and possible for me somehow and wherever I could to complete within three years the work I had begun, as though my soul were saying: “She has performed a good work upon me; for she has anticipated anointing my body for burial” (Mark 14)—not now my burial, but His. May the holy [Col. 0198B] Trinity, to whom I dedicated it, deign to accept it as an odor of sweetness.

[Col. 0197]

# Prologue of Rupert to the Books *On the Holy Trinity and His Works*

[Col. 0197B] Although Moses’ face is radiant everywhere from his conversation with God, and therefore, when he had to veil his meaning—which is understood by “face”—with figurative words [Col. 0197C], yet in the creation of the world it has such splendor that all the children of Israel could in no way have endured it unless he had wrapped it in the coarser fabric of the letter, as though in the swaddling-clothes of infancy.

For he relates to us, insofar as a human being could learn from the aforesaid conversation with God, that ineffable begetting of the Son of God, concerning which God the Father Himself says in David: “My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44). Likewise he enumerates those seven Spirits of God, whom the holy Catholic Church today knows to have been sent into all the earth: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord.

Without [Col. 0197D] doubt, if he had openly written these things for all, without a veil, as they are now preached everywhere throughout the whole world, since Jesus has now been glorified and the Spirit given, and it is permitted us with unveiled face to behold the glory of the Lord (2 Cor. 3), he would surely have set an excessively horned face, an excessive splendor of God, before eyes too weak and bleary to endure it. But he wisely spread the veil of such language over his face: “God said: Let there be, and it was so” (Gen. 1). Seven times He spoke; seven times the goodness of His utterance pleased Him; and on the seventh day He rested (ibid.).

Beneath this veil of such language you will find that what He says, “God said: Let there be,” is the very thing which the Father says in David, “My heart has uttered a good word”; or which [Col. 0198B] the Evangelist John says of the Word, that in the beginning God was with God, and all things were made through Him [Col. 0198C] (John 1). Further, the seven forms of His good work are the seven days of God, because it was on account of His goodness—which is the sevenfold Holy Spirit—that the Father begot this Word from His heart: for He spoke seven times, and by speaking made seven works very good (Gen. 1).

Although an eighth day is yet to come, nevertheless God’s work has seven days, because man—whose universal resurrection is the eighth day—will rise again not in another form but in that very form in which he was created.

Each of these days consists of evening and morning, because certainly everything that was made existed in the Word of God before it was made. For, says the Evangelist, “What was made in Him was life” (John 1). It was evening when that which was made was still only [Col. 0198D] life in Him, because the luminous power or foreknowledge of making all these things lay hidden in the secret counsel of God. But then bright morning came, when this life which was in Him shone forth openly in the act or forms of things. All these matters must be discussed more fully in their proper places.

Therefore, seeking in this pilgrimage the glory of the Holy Trinity that is to be adored, we set before our minds the mirror of His works, so that, since in the condition of mortality we still cannot fix weak eyes upon the splendor of His majesty, we may at least, beholding His works in some small measure of His light, walk without error.

The work of the same [Col. 0199A] Trinity, from the creation of the world to its end, is threefold. The first is from the rising of the first light to the fall of the first man. The second is from that fall of the first man to the passion of the second man, Jesus Christ the Son of God. The third is from His resurrection to the consummation of the age, that is, the general resurrection of the dead. The first is properly the work of the Father, the second of the Son, and the third of the Holy Spirit.

Certainly the inseparable Trinity, one God, works inseparably. Nevertheless, for each of these—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—as each has a property of person, so also in the perfection of the world a proper action must be considered: namely, creation as the Father’s, redemption as the Son’s, and the renewal of the creature as the proper work of the Holy Spirit. Finally, [Col. 0199B] when the Father makes all things through the Word and the Holy Spirit is borne over the waters, the two Persons indeed cooperate with the one acting; nevertheless, the utterance of the Word itself, or the sending forth of the Spirit, is the proper action of the Father.

Likewise, when the Son—that is, the Word of the Father—enters in order to save the world, the Father indeed brings Him forth from His heart into the Virgin’s womb, and the Holy Spirit fashions for Him a small body from maternal substance; and thus two Persons cooperate with the one acting. Nevertheless, the Person of the Son alone is clothed in flesh and dies as well. Again, when, through the passion of that same Son, the Holy Spirit is given for the remission [Col. 0199C] of sins, the Father mercifully relaxes what had hitherto justly contained His bowels, so that He may stretch them out over us; and the risen Son breathes upon human beings. Thus two Persons cooperate with the one acting; nevertheless, the proper Person of the Holy Spirit is the gift or grace of the Father and Son, and is the whole adornment of the rational creature [Col. 0200A].

This work, then, shall be threefold in honor of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The first part concerns the week of the first days; the second, the week of the succeeding ages of the world; the third, the twofold resurrection of the dead. By these both weeks are completed and brought to their fulfillment in the eighth day. For by the first resurrection of souls, which is the remission of sins, the death of sin—which was admitted after seven days—is abolished; by the second resurrection of bodies, the death of all flesh that has died through the seven ages of the world is swallowed up.

Having set forth these matters, we must now look to the door opened in heaven, to the throne set there, and to Him seated upon the throne, who created all things; and we must entreat Him through the seven burning lamps which He has placed before His throne, and through the seven horns and equally many eyes of the Lamb who is in the midst of His throne, that He may grant us worthily to expound the aforesaid adornment of creation, three times sevenfold, according to the truth of the great book which that same Lamb received from His right hand and, as the only one worthy, opened by loosing its seven [Col. 0200C] seals (Rev. 4–5).

[Col. 0199]

# The Forty-Two Books of Dom Rupert, Abbot of Tuitz, *On the Trinity and His Works*

## Commentaries on Genesis

### Book One  
*(Genesis, chapter 1, verses 1–23)*

[Col. 0199]

## Chapter One. That the Holy Trinity had no model outside itself by which to create these three things: heaven, earth, and all their adornment.

**(Chapter 1.)** The lofty summit of all Scriptures, the book of Genesis, begins thus: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” To these two, namely heaven and earth, it later adds a third, saying: “Thus heaven and earth were completed, and all their adornment.” Certainly, by the name “heaven” is signified that invisible homeland of the holy angels; by the term “earth,” this visible world. The adornment of heaven is the angelic creature; that of earth is, along with the other things which grow or exist in it, especially the human race.

What model did the one God, who is Trinity, have in making these three things, except Himself? Certainly not the Ideas—that is, the forms—which secular philosophers devised, but God the Father Himself; Himself, I say, the one God, Father and Son, together with the Holy Spirit, with whom both alike are naturally adorned. He created not only the incorporeal heaven but also the bodily substance of earth, and adorned each with a corresponding adornment: heaven, namely, with angelic spirits; earth, by filling it with human beings, whom He was to make equal to angels.

For when heaven and earth were created, it was already then the purpose of the Creator—whose purpose admits no new counsel—that the Son of God should put on earthly substance. Accordingly, we rightly understand heaven to have been created according to the Person of the Father, and earth according to the Person of the Son. That the adornment of both, namely of heaven and earth, was made according to the proper Person of the Holy Spirit is especially clear from the fact that before the creation of the world began to be adorned, “the Spirit of God,” Scripture says, “was borne over the waters”; and then, when the sevenfold adornment was completed, “God rested from all His work”: that is, because in the work of His art He had effectually brought forth a creature upon which His Spirit might rest, the kind He had been eager to make or find and for which He had beforehand been borne over the waters.

Therefore do not seek or suppose that there was a model outside God, or the Ideas which the wise men of this age called helpers of creatures [Note: [Col. 0201D] He means Plato’s Ideas.], because, assuredly, when nothing existed besides God, the Trinity alone was its own model for making these three things.

## Chapter II. Why it is called Genesis.

Before entering upon the words of Scripture themselves, we must ask whence, or why, this book is called *Genesis*. For this title, properly understood, truly illumines the lofty head of this book in accordance with its name. A title (*titulus*) is so called from Titan, that is, the sun, by which this world is illuminated, because through the superscription which we call a title, as by a light sent beforehand, the entrance of the following book is opened.

Why, then, is this book called *Genesis*? From the generations of heaven and earth—or rather from the generation of that Day in which these generations were created before they came to be, as it is written in this book: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day in which God made heaven and earth [Col. 0201D], and every shrub of the field before it sprang up in the earth, and every herb of the region before it germinated.” What is this day in which these things were created before they sprang up or germinated, except Him whom we proclaim as “Day from Day”—Day, I say, from Day—that is, the Word from the Father, in whom, as the Evangelist says, “was life” (John 1): that which was made before it was made?

For this book contains a twofold generation of this Word: one belonging to divinity, the other to humanity. It touches upon the begetting of divinity, as was said already in the preface, where it says of each thing: “God said: Let there be. And it was so.” But it openly expresses the generation of humanity where God, speaking to Abraham, says: “I will bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven; and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22). Therefore this book is rightly and nobly called *Genesis*, because together with the generations of heaven and earth it declares both generations of one and the same God and man, Christ the Son of God. Now at last let us hear the very words of the book. It says:

## Chapter III. That the Son, or Word, through whom heaven and earth were created, is the Beginning.

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Since creation itself is the beginning of the world, why is it said thus: “In the beginning He created”? It is the same as if it were said: “In the beginning He made the beginning.” But if here “beginning” is understood in the ordinary sense when it is said, “In the beginning He created,” there is a fault of superfluity in the expression [Col. 0202B]. Therefore “beginning” is rightly understood here as a certain proper title of the Son, because He Himself so willed it, who, when questioned by the Jews, “Who are you?”, said: “The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

For God truly created heaven and earth in this Beginning, because “all things were made through Him” (John 1). Another Scripture also acknowledges this when it says: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103). This wisdom is nothing other than the Word of God, God the Word, who, as has already been said, called Himself the Beginning. It is not that the native language of this Scripture, namely Hebrew, denotes “son” and “beginning” by the same word: in that language “son” is *ben*, while “beginning” is *bereshith* [Col. 0202C]. Yet we say this too: even if not by word, still by meaning the Son is Beginning. He is Son because He was born from God; He is Beginning because He is shown to be the first and efficient cause of all creatures.

Thus in the Beginning—that is, in His Son, in His Word, in His wisdom—God created heaven and earth. He created, I say: that is, not as the philosophers of the Gentiles vainly imagined, that He had matter (*hyle*) coeval with Himself, but that He made the substance of heaven and earth from nothing. If anyone objects that man also, though made not from nothing but from earth, is called created, as Scripture says: “God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him”; or likewise: “And God created the great sea-creatures,” we reply that this is rightly said only in the respect that the matter from which these forms were produced or taken had itself already been created. By the names “heaven” and “earth,” as has been said above, the whole visible and invisible creation together is signified.

That nothing is excepted is also confirmed by the Apostles’ Creed, in which we say: “I believe in God, the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.” Since we add no creatures, we do not doubt that by these names we have included all things visible and invisible. Likewise, in another Catholic creed of faith, when we say, “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth,” we immediately explain what we have called heaven and earth by adding: “of all things visible [Col. 0203A] and invisible.” Therefore, the statement, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” is the same as saying: Through His Son God the Father created the entire substance of all visible and invisible things—still such as the subsequent description of earth expresses: “But the earth was empty and void.”

## Chapter IV. Why He did not say, “Let heaven be, and let earth be,” as He said, “Let there be light.”

Why was it not said, “In the beginning God said: Let heaven be, and let earth be; and it was so,” as is later said: “Let there be light, and there was light,” and so forth? This must be answered in three ways.

First, because, as has already been said, the Beginning itself is the Word of God; thus it would have been superfluous or unsuitable to say, “In the Beginning God said,” as if one said, “In His Word God said.” Next, because an imperative word such as *fiat* (“let there be”) is improperly introduced where there is as yet nothing to which an order can be given or a command imposed. Yet nothing as yet existed, if, as we truly believe and the present Scripture testifies, God created heaven and earth—that is, made them from nothing. Therefore, lest God be said to have given a command to nothing, which would be unsuitable, Scripture rightly first records that He created some confused or formless matter, and then gave a command to a thing already existing, that it might receive or bring forth the distinct and beautiful forms which it did not possess.

Third, it must likewise be understood that the writer of matters so great ought to have spoken in this way, so that no one might be free to suppose, as stated above, what certain philosophers devised from their own hearts: namely, that God indeed made the world’s form, or the very diverse forms of things in the world, but that *hyle*, that is matter from which all these things were made, was not made by God but had always been coeternal with God. Therefore it was said as it ought to have been said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

## Chapter V. That God’s making of the world is not to be ascribed to mutability, against those who say that the world is coeternal with God.

But certain persons—those, namely, who wish the world to be coeternal with God—attributed it to God’s mutability that He made this world which had not existed. They said: “Either the world is coeternal with God, or God is mutable. For if He at last made something which He had not made throughout such vast stretches of His eternity, He surely adopted a new counsel and is therefore mutable.”

To this I say: “Most truly, God is neither mutable nor is the world coeternal with God. Does a man exhibit mutability when, not wishing his wisdom to remain hidden, he writes down upon paper with ink and pen a fine discourse or some similar thing which he certainly holds concealed in his mind, and invites many to hear wisdom and understand useful knowledge? Is he to be said to suffer from the fault of a changeable mind because he has usefully made public what he held hidden, so that it might be known by an audience? Certainly he is not to be blamed for mutability, but [Col. 0204A] praised for benevolence.

“But the world and all things contained in heaven and earth are very bright signs of God’s wisdom. This wisdom, or Word, was in God’s heart before these things were made, just as wisdom or art is in your heart before you signify it by visible marks or by any work. Hence, when the Evangelist had said, ‘All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made’ (John 1), he immediately added: ‘What was made in Him was life’ (ibid.). Therefore God created heaven and earth so that His wisdom might be known, so that there might be those by whom it could be known; and He set angels in heaven and human beings on earth, that from themselves and the other things made they might profitably know so great an artificer.

“Therefore, unless you are excessively ungrateful, do not accuse God in this of mutability; rather praise Him for great benevolence, and render humble thanks to Him because, on account of His gratuitous goodness, ‘in the beginning God created heaven and earth.’”

## Chapter VI. Why heaven must be understood in that beginning.

Now, when we hear “heaven and earth,” the natural man, who has never dwelt in heaven and cannot say with the Apostle, “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3)—such a person cannot even imagine what kind of dwelling heaven is or was immediately upon its creation. For not even the spiritual man, however greatly he contemplates heavenly things while he lives, can adequately judge it, except that it is a great and boundless place, the great and spiritual house of the Father [Col. 0204C], in which from the beginning many dwelling places have been prepared for blessed angels and holy human beings; and there, locally and in a local manner according to His true human body, sits the High Priest who penetrated the heavens, Jesus Christ the Son of God.

In comparison with that spiritual dwelling, whatever is seen by fleshly eyes is earth. Thus the Psalmist rightly calls it “heaven of heaven,” for after saying, “You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 113), he immediately adds: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but He has given the earth to the children of men” (ibid.). He gave the heaven of heaven, because in comparison with it this visible firmament, made on the second day, is no longer heaven but earth—or, at most, a certain adornment of earth—because the former is invisible while the latter is visible to earthly creatures.

What that heaven of heaven was like when made, the natural man cannot even imagine. But perhaps earth immediately occurs to his mind in the form in which it is seen: clothed with green grass, trees, and fruit-bearing trees, and filled with different kinds of living creatures. Therefore it immediately follows: “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep.”

## Chapter VII. How “the earth was empty and void,” and what kind of “darkness was upon the face of the deep.”

When heaven and earth had been created, he says, heaven was not empty or void of every adornment, since it shone with the light of the divine majesty, just as this visible heaven and the air shine with the light of this sun in likeness of it. But earth—that is, bodily substance—was empty and void [Col. 0205A]. Not that it was removed from divine greatness, since the Seraphim most truly cry of Him: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory” (Isa. 6). But that same Majesty had not yet filled or adorned it in act, though it may be understood prophetically that this was said concerning the preaching of Christ’s Gospel, by which it came about that not only the one nation of the Jews but the whole earth was filled with the knowledge of divinity.

In the sense already stated, however, earth was empty and void because the Creator had not yet separated it dry from the waters, had not yet made it firm, had not yet clothed it with the mantle of the stars of this heaven, and had not yet adorned it with so many kinds of creatures. Therefore, if you consider the letter carefully, earth was not created in the beginning with the visible form which then appears as its own; rather, it was empty—empty, namely, of every shoot now rooted in it—and void, namely, of all the living creatures which now move in it.

Moreover, darkness was upon the face of the deep: that is, upon the depth of the waters, which had not yet been divided or gathered together into one place so that dry land might appear. These were bodily darknesses around the undifferentiated body of the world, because there was not yet a firmament in the midst of the waters; nor had those things which shine bodily therein and illuminate the earth—the sun, moon, and stars, which were made on the fourth day—yet been made [Col. 0205C].

Thus, briefly and in summary, the whole formlessness of creation is set forth: so poor and void that it would have been created in vain in the Beginning, that is, in the Son, unless the Spirit of God, who is the third Person in the Trinity, was borne over the waters. Thus it immediately adds: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

## Chapter VIII. How “the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.”

Thereupon follows the forming or adornment of that same creation; and, through the attention of the Spirit of God, it receives as great an improvement and so great a supply for its former lack as, in its own measure, an egg receives when it is quickened by the warmth of a bird and produces a chick. But what are we to suppose this Spirit to be, if not the goodness and love of God—not a love of emotions, but substantial love: love, I say, and life, and a living power abiding in the Son and the Father, or proceeding from both, consubstantial with Father and Son? This Spirit, indeed, was borne over the waters, and likewise over the dry land hidden beneath the waters, because the Creator was borne along by great affection toward His creation, so that—despite a problematic negative construction in the text—He who had created it might make from it such forms as could be joined to the Creator, live with Him, and reign with Him. This love, this goodness of the Creator, is the Holy Spirit.

Plato, not knowing Him, when he had read this Scripture, supposed Him to be the spirit of the world—that is, the air—which, according to the order of the elements, rises above the waters as lighter than they. And because he also suspected that by “heaven,” of which it was already said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” fire was meant, he believed that only the four elements—fire, earth, air, and water—were enumerated here. For he did not recognize this Spirit, who plainly is not the spirit of the world but the Spirit of God—especially since, by the darkness that was upon the face of the abyss, the air may more nearly be understood: it was not yet irradiated from above by any lights and is therefore rightly denoted by the name of darkness.

Why, then, when there are four elements of the world, did the writer of this sacred history express only these two, earth and water, by their own names, and signify air not by its proper name but by the name “darkness”? [Col. 0206B] Plainly because it belonged to his purpose to state from what source arose those kinds of things which, in the adornment of creation then still unformed, were so diverse and so numerous. It is clear, moreover, that light shone forth from this darkness which was upon the face of the abyss, Paul bearing witness when he says: “For God, who said that light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts” [II Cor. 4]. He does not say “in darkness,” but that God said light should shine “out of darkness.”

Now from earth and water were produced all the kinds of things we know. Fire alone, although it cooperates with earth and water in generating things, yet produces nothing from itself; and therefore this element is not improperly passed over in silence, until the fourth day, when its source—the sun—is set in the firmament. For the more careful natural philosophers also testify that the sun is the source of ethereal fire. [Col. 0206C]

## CHAPTER IX. That the Trinity Is Shown Forth at the Beginning of the Book

Thus at the beginning of the book the presence of the creating Trinity is splendidly shown forth. For in the name of God the Father is understood; in the name of the Beginning, the Son; and He who is borne over the waters is the Holy Spirit. Let us now hear what so attentive a presence of majesty is about to do or say. It follows:

## CHAPTER X. That the Light Which Was Made Is the Angelic Creation

“And God said, Let there be light; and there was light.” The strength and wisdom of God are great and terrible. His Spirit is intent [Col. 0206D] over the waters; He cries aloud and speaks ineffably in power and magnificence [Ps. 28]. Yet this is conveyed briefly and sweetly to our understanding when it is said, “God said”—briefly, I say. For what do we gather from this most concise utterance except the certain truth that God worked all things through His Word?

Nor are we so childish in understanding as to suppose that God, using teeth, palate, lips, and the instrument of the tongue, uttered “Let there be light” in an articulated sound; any more than, when it is said that the Spirit of God was borne over the waters, do we accept the fantasy that God, standing or sitting somewhere, blew forth His mighty breath over all the waters. No: we do not think so childishly or carnally concerning God, the Creator of spirits. Nor do we ascribe to the immutable and impassible God those mental movements by which we send forth through the air words that pass onward, in the manner described.

What then? What ought we to understand in the words, “God said,” except the generation of the eternal Word, the Word consubstantial with God, through whose effect both we and the angels are rational beings? For the Word, truly born without a voice and containing all things potentially, was then actually generated by the Father when He created heaven and earth, when He made light and the rest. Therefore the Father’s heart “uttered a good Word” [Ps. 44]; and “from the womb,” that is, from the hidden recess of His own substance, He begot it “before the morning star” [Ps. 109], when He said, “Let there be light.”

But what is this very thing which He said: “Let there be light”? What is this light? Some suppose that the light then made was merely the illumination of the air, and that the darkness which was upon the face of the abyss was divided into alternating night and day; so that, when the period of day—namely twelve hours—had elapsed, the light was extinguished and darkness succeeded it; and likewise, when the period of night had passed, the light shone again. Thus for three days night and day, without those corporeal lights—the sun, moon, and stars—gave way to and succeeded one another of themselves.

But on this interpretation this first day is the poorest of all days. Every other day was distinguished by the creation or formation of substances, whereas this day was left with nothing but a transitory accidental quality applied to it when “Let there be light” was said. For whatever was made on the other days is substantial and enduring; but that accidental light, rekindled on the third day, afterwards wholly perished. Consider whether it is fitting for so great a Majesty that He should establish forever and ever the works of the other days—for example, the sun, moon, and stars made on the fourth day, and the division of the waters made on the second day—and appoint for them a commandment that shall not pass away [Ps. 148], but make the work of the first light such that, after a brief three days, He should completely extinguish it upon a change of plan.

What then? Was the Spirit of God borne over the waters, and did He say, “Let there be,” that, when it was spoken—as the holy Scripture wonders at and celebrates it as the utterance of a truly good Word—there might be made only such a light, accidental to the air, soon to perish, and no substance might be created? The great and most renowned Fathers understood better: they understood the angelic nature to be signified by the name “light.” We approve and follow their more reasonable view: the angelic creation is rightly called light—intellectual light, light, I say, not only because it possesses the power of discernment, but also because it shines by the grace of the true and unbounded Light.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Angelic Creation Is Called Light Not by Metaphor but in Reality

Nor do we say it is called light by metaphor, but in reality—that is, not because it resembles this visible light. Rather, this visible light and these visible stars were made after the likeness of that light, so that the spiritual person may understand that holy angels, though in the same blessedness, differ in rank and glory, just as “star differs from star in brightness” [I Cor. 15]; and that, in comparison with the eternal Sun, namely their Creator, they are not the true light, just as stars throughout the whole hemisphere cannot display their own light in the presence of the sun.

Once this is observed, we no longer wonder, uncertainly asking what the Spirit of God intended over the waters, what the voice of the Lord was over the waters, what, I say, God, the Lord of majesty, thundered over the waters. This effect is worthy indeed, since it followed from the working of the whole Trinity: the Holy Spirit breathing over the waters, the Father thundering, and the thunder itself—that is, the Word by which He said, “Let there be.” For such a creation is a worthy reason why that Word was thundered forth, which, shaking the abysses or waters [Ps. 28] and the darkness that was over the waters, caused companies of such light to flash forth.

What then? Are we to suppose that angels came from heaven, rather than that they were made here and transferred to heaven? [I Cor. 15.] For angels were no more made in heaven than man was formed in paradise.
