Man was formed outside paradise and placed in paradise, as it is written: “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which He placed the man whom He had formed.” Thus likewise the angels, created outside paradise and transferred into heaven, inhabit heaven not by nature but by grace.

For no one came from heaven except He who is above all, and who is therefore above all because He is a simple spirit, composed of nothing; hence He could clothe Himself in a human spirit together with a body, which none of the angelic spirits could do. Although angels are called, and are, spirits in comparison with us, yet in comparison with God they are corporeal. For, as learned and eminent men also attest, they have bodies composed of this dense and moist air, which is felt to be driven when the wind blows—especially such air as it was when darkness was still upon the face of the abyss, from which, as the Apostle says, God commanded light to shine [II Cor. 4].

Evidence for their condition may be drawn from those who fell. Just as a dead man, returning to the earth, openly shows that he was taken from earth [Gen. 3], so those who, having abandoned the perennial fountain of light, were extinguished in their darkness, openly show that, although they were from darkness, they were made shining not by nature but by grace. The same Apostle, clearly perceiving this, does not say, “God who said that light should shine in darkness,” but “who said that light should shine out of darkness has shone upon the face of our heart, unto the illumination of the brightness in the face of Jesus Christ.” For there is no small difference between the two expressions. The true light, God, shines in darkness when He deigns to enlighten us who sit in darkness. We shine out of darkness when, leaving unbelief behind, we look upon His face through faith.

Thus, since it is evident that angels, though they possess subtle bodies, nevertheless have them from their origin, it is also clear from this that they are localized and, when they wish, appear to human beings. If they are thought not to retain a body but to assume one from the air for a time, because they do not always appear and, when they do appear, suddenly vanish, we on the contrary say that our Lord after the resurrection displayed His own body—certainly an earthly one—so that, when He wished, He suddenly appeared to people and, when He wished, immediately disappeared.

Therefore angels have bodies, composed of that air and moisture over which, when the Spirit of the Lord was borne, He said, “Let there be light.” “Why,” you ask, “did God not make angels from heaven, so that they might be heavenly by nature?” Plainly because God had not made heaven in order to create them from it, but in order to raise them, once created, into heaven by grace alone. But we shall speak more fully on this later.

## CHAPTER XII. That That Light Confesses Its Creator, According to the Verse of Psalm 103: “You Have Put On Confession and Beauty, Clothed with Light as with a Garment”

Therefore God employs no new design toward us when, in order to restore us to the dignity of our first origin and make us equal to angels, He sets before us this necessity: that we be born again of water and the Spirit of God [John 3], baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For in the creation of angels also God spoke—that is, He uttered His Word, which is His Son—and the third Person, the Holy Spirit, was borne over the waters.

Likewise, their very creation is no less a reminder of humility to them than ours is to us: for as earth or dust was the principle or material of our existence, so the dark abyss was theirs. For, at God’s command, this light shone forth from darkness, as has been said above. Hence they are not ungrateful, but without ceasing praise, confess, love, and adore their Creator.

The Psalmist wonderfully seeks to express the constancy of this praise or confession and their unceasing devotion in these words: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment” [Ps. 103]. Without doubt he said this concerning the formation of this light. For he continues: “Stretching out heaven like a skin, who covers its upper parts with waters” [ibid.], and so forth. First, indeed, He said, “Let there be light, and there was light”; then He stretched out the firmament, which He also called heaven. Therefore he said concerning the beauty of angelic praise, “You have put on confession and beauty,” adding, “clothed with light as with a garment.”

He could not have expressed more magnificently either the dignity of Him who is praised or the earnestness of those who praise. For each person rightly puts on his own garment, because it belongs to him and not to another; and it does not dishonor him if it is suitably fitted to the condition of his body. Therefore, when he says, “You have put on confession and beauty,” he offers the fullest praise and rightly declares God worthy of the praises of so many confessing angels, and declares it fitting that they should proclaim or know whatever good they can, because He made the very organs of their substance and voice, and in great honor happily established or arranged them around His exalted throne.

But when he adds, “clothed with light as with a garment,” he also magnificently distinguishes this created light from the Light that made it. A garment adorns or honors a body, but it is not itself of the body. Thus, in saying this, he confesses that the blessed spirits are indeed light, but that they differ from that unbounded Light by whom they were created as much as a garment differs from a body: they have the true Light, God, within themselves, but are not of His substance.

It follows: “And God saw the light, that it was good; and He divided the light from the darkness.”

## CHAPTER XIII. That That Light Is Called “Good,” Not as It Is Said of the Other Works: “And God Saw That It Was Good”

First, it should be noted that it is said: “God saw the light, that it was good.” For “none is good except the one God” [Matt. 10]. Whoever is called good, whether human or angel, is rightly called good only in relation to the good God; for since none is good except the one God, whoever is good, or is said to be good, is good only insofar as he partakes of the good God.

Accordingly, it is not said, “God saw the earth, that it was good,” or “the lights, that they were good,” because they are not capable of goodness. But of each it is said: “God saw that it was good,” that is, a good thing—good, I say, in the sense of a useful thing. For only the rational creation is capable of divine goodness, that is, of the Spirit of God. Therefore only a human being or an angel can be called good absolutely, insofar as that human being or angel has become a partaker of the good God.

Thus this very judgment—“God saw the light, that it was good”—compels us to understand that light which is capable of divine goodness: rational light, intellectual light, the splendid dignity of the angelic creation. But how is it said: “God saw the light, that it was good”? Did He not see, before He made it, that it was good to make it? Does not the Evangelist likewise say of this Word through which He said “Let there be,” that “what was made in Him was life” [John 1]? Therefore, “He saw” means that He weighed it in just judgment and deemed it worthy of His regard.

It follows: “And He divided the light from the darkness.” This division of light and darkness suggests that a terrible judgment of God was passed upon the devil. Of Him the Psalmist says: “You are terrible, and who shall resist You? From that time, Your wrath” [Ps. 75]. It is as though he said: Who can resist You, since from the moment anyone resists You, Your terrible wrath blazes forth? For from the time the devil resists—that is, wished to resist—You, You were angry, and he could not resist; for the angel fell and became the devil.

This terrible judgment is intimated by the division of light and darkness. For what is this darkness except all Satan’s angels together with their prince? God divided this darkness and the light because He separated evil angels from good ones. He divided them, I say, by an immutable separation, so that neither those who fell can rise again, nor those who, though able to sin, refused to fall by sinning, may ever again have—or be able—to fall by sinning.

“For by the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their strength by the Spirit of His mouth” [Ps. 32]. This light—these are the heavens. The light, I say, which God divided from darkness; and the heavens which God established by His Word, by His Spirit—that is, by His love—so that they can no longer be darkened or dissolved; “gathering the waters of the sea as in a skin-bag, laying up the abysses in storehouses” [ibid.]. All these things, according to the letter, were undoubtedly made in that beginning.

“Let all the earth fear the Lord; let all the inhabitants of the world be moved by Him” [ibid.]. For certainly, as He then destroyed the counsels of proud spirits, so even to the end the Lord frustrates the counsels of nations; He rejects the thoughts of peoples and rejects the counsels of princes [ibid.]. But whence came this darkness? It has already been said: from where the light mentioned above came, from there also came this darkness. For they were shining angels and, by their own fault, became dark demons.

## CHAPTER XIV. That the Angelic Creation Had Progress as Well as a Beginning

Here it is commonly asked with amazement: how could vice steal into a good substance, and light be changed into darkness? The chief reason for this amazement is that most people do not reflect that angels, like human beings, were indeed innocent immediately after their creation, but were not instantly supreme; and that nothing but God rests at the summit, or attains immovable stability, without progress.

Most people, I say, do not reflect upon this. They are so preoccupied with the greatness of the angelic name that they have no opportunity to know that spiritual creation, as it had a beginning, also had to have progress: it has existence by necessity, but by will it began to tend toward the likeness of the good Essence. A brief answer must therefore be given concerning this.

## CHAPTER XV. That, by the Will of the Creator, a Certain Part of This Creation Became Corrupted

First of all, we must think devoutly of God the Creator: namely, that neither angel nor human being perished by His will, and that ice did not come forth from His womb, nor did He beget frost from heaven in such a way that He either created an evil creation or Himself first abandoned a good nature and changed it into evil.

“What then?” you ask. “If He wished His creation to be safe, why did He not create it so that it would be wholly incapable of receiving or undergoing any fault?” To this, I say, an illustration must be taken from the well-known image of God, namely, the human being. See: a human being can generate by nature and make by choice. What he generates can be nothing other than what he himself is; what he makes cannot in any way be what he himself is. For a human being begets nothing but a human being. He makes, for example, a house in which to live, or a beautiful garment to wear. None of these is the very thing that he himself is. Yet he is praised if he makes these skillfully and fittingly, as befits him.

So likewise God indeed begets that very thing which He Himself is: God from God, impassible from impassible, immutable from immutable, true Light likewise from true Light—namely, His only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, the firstborn before every creature, indeed the only-begotten. But He made His garment, of which it was said above according to the Psalm: “Clothed with light as with a garment” [Ps. 103]—namely, the angelic creation—by saying, “Let there be light”; and He made this fabric of the world, in which He made the human being in His image and likeness. None of these either had to be or could be the very thing which He who made them is, or equal to Him whom the same Maker begot—just as a building or painting can in no way be the same thing as its builder or painter, or as the one whom he begot from his flesh.

It is worthy of praise, and should suffice for our inquiry, that the Almighty could make such a creation as could be capable of its Maker and could attain by effort the divinity which it does not possess by nature. Therefore angel and human had to be mutable, as created from nothing; for that from which they were made was created from nothing. Each was indeed created pure and innocent, yet so that from this very innocence each could either advance to the highest things or decline to the lowest.

For that holy angels have advanced—indeed, still advance—the Apostle also bears witness, writing to the Ephesians: “That the manifold wisdom of God may be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” [Eph. 3]. Therefore, since all angels were made in such a state that they might be perfected by advancing in God, or be cast out by declining into that very thing from which they had been made, that is, into darkness, some received love for the Creator, clothed Him with confession and beauty, and thus the Creator was clothed by them as with a garment, while they continually cried: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” [Isa. 6]. And so, because they were not ungrateful, God saw the light, that it was good, and rejoiced in His works.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Envy or Pride of the Devil

One great prince among the princes of the great court envied. We have heard of his pride: “He is very proud, and his pride and his indignation are greater than his strength” [Isa. 16]. For the beginning of his sin was pride. Swollen with it, he appeared exceedingly great, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty, and needing nothing of God’s wisdom, since he took pleasure in himself in his splendor.

Hence in Ezekiel he is improperly called a *Cherub*, that is, “the fullness of God’s wisdom,” because he dared to compare himself with God’s wisdom, saying: “I am God; I have sat in the seat of God; and he gave his heart as the heart of God” [Ezek. 28]. A little later the same prophet says, with reproach and irony: “You, the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, were in the delights of God’s paradise. Every precious stone was your covering: sard, topaz, and jasper; chrysolite, onyx, and beryl; sardonyx, carbuncle, and emerald. Gold—the work of your adornment—and your sockets were prepared on the day on which you were created. You were an outstretched and sheltering Cherub” [Ezek. 28], and so forth.

This, I say, was said ironically—namely, that in truth every precious stone was his ornament. For the nine orders of angels, signified by those stones, are the ornament of the Creator alone; and He is clothed with this light as with a garment, He who created them for His own praise and glory. But the devil thought that such adornment belonged to himself, and in this he was false.

That this was said ironically is clear from another prophet, who reproaches him thus: “You said in your heart: I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne; I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” [Isa. 14]. For by the stars of God are signified the same orders of angels which are denoted by the nine stones. Therefore, just as he never truly set his throne above the stars of God or was like the Most High, so neither was every precious stone ever truly his covering; rather, he arrogated it to himself, said it, and thought it. He was not truly light, but a rebel against the Light.

Perhaps this interpretation seems to conflict with the statement on the same prophetic authority that he was perfect in his ways: “You walked perfect in your ways amid fiery stones from the day of your creation until iniquity was found in you” [Ezek. 28]. It is hard here to maintain that he was not perfect; but it is harder to affirm that he ever possessed in himself love for the Creator, without which there is no perfection of ways.

For although the prophet mentioned above said, “Gold—the work of your adornment—and your sockets were prepared on the day on which you were created,” he does not say or in any way signify that he received into those same sockets the binding of gold. Since he was a rational creation, he certainly had natural capacity, understanding, and memory—like sockets into which he ought to have received the spirit of God’s love, which is the finest gold—but he proudly refused it.

Therefore the statement that he was perfect in his ways strikes at his hypocrisy. Though he could entice substantial spirits and deceive many, he could not remain hidden from God, whose terrible judgment is indicated in the words, “until iniquity was found in you.” Therefore we must not complain against the Creator because He did not make His creation such that it would be unchangeable by nature or incapable of any fault. That would be like complaining of a potter because not every vessel he makes is such as he himself is, or such as the son whom he begot from himself.

## CHAPTER XVII. That the Good and Merciful Creator Nevertheless Justly Made One Whom He Foreknew Would Be Evil, and Concerning His Fall

But it is still asked: Why did the good and merciful Creator make him whom He foreknew would perish? This is a strange and importunate—indeed, violent—question, and so foolish that there is no rationality in its meaning. For what could He foreknow except what was going to happen? Or how could what was foreknown as going to happen in this or that way fail to happen?

It would be closer to reason if someone said: Why does God permit the substance of evil spirits or wicked human beings to continue, since it continues wickedly, instead of causing it wholly to perish, as the spirit of a beast perishes and ceases to be? For one could answer that it is just that one should always be in punishment who, because of his own fault, lacks the condition of always being in glory. Is God’s justice, then, milder than His foreknowledge?

Thus, just as it is not unjust that He does not now wholly destroy the substance of a corrupted creation, so it was not unjust that He condemned foreknown wickedness and yet did not omit to create a good nature. But since nothing is enough for a contentious inquirer, let us now say to him with the Apostle: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does not the potter have power to make from the same clay one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” [Rom. 9].

Setting him aside, let us confess that, when God saw the light, that it was good, He justly divided light and darkness, forming beautiful light in heaven and casting away deformed darkness. For He established holy angels, whom He had clothed with confession and beauty, in perpetual stability, and rejoiced in His works on their account; but Satan fell from heaven with his attendants like lightning [Luke 10].

Like lightning, I say: for just as lightning, struck with the crash of thunder and clouds in motion, shines briefly and suddenly vanishes, so he, cast out of heaven while all the angelic orders trembled terribly at God’s indignation, fell miserably into this air, extinguished from every light and nevermore to see God’s light eternally. Scripture frequently teaches that he and all his attendants, whom we call aerial companies, have now been cast down into this air—for example, in the Apostle’s words: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” [Eph. 6].

But it will come to pass that, before the eyes of all, he will be hurled into the lower hell, into the eternal fire prepared for him and his angels [Matt. 25]. For just as, because of the first sin, man was expelled from paradise—in which he had by no means been created—in order to cultivate this earth from which he had been taken, so he was cast from heaven, into which he had been received by grace with the other spirits, back into this dark air from which he had been created. It had not yet been illuminated by the sun, moon, and stars when he was created; nor can this sun now avail him to receive light. From there, with his angels and evil human beings, because of persistent sins, he is to be cast down on the day of judgment.

The Apostle Peter expresses both judgments: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, drawing them down with the cords of hell, delivered them into Tartarus to be kept for torments on the day of judgment” [II Pet. 2]. He called this air “hell” or “Tartarus” in comparison with the heaven from whose height they fell; it is nevertheless then also called heaven, whence we speak of “birds of heaven,” in comparison with that hell of which the Psalmist says: “You have delivered my soul from the lowest hell” [Ps. 85].

Likewise the prophet Isaiah, after speaking of the first judgment in the words, “How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who arose in the morning?” [Isa. 14], immediately adds concerning the second: “Yet you shall be drawn down to hell, into the depth of the pit. Those who see you shall bend toward you and look upon you” [ibid.].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Naming of Day and Night, and What That Day and That Night Are

“And He called the light Day, and the darkness Night.” He called the light which He saw was good, Day; and He called the darkness, whose being is not good, Night. This must be carefully observed. First He saw the light, that it was good; then, dividing light and darkness, He assigned to each suitable names.

If the order of the text had been arranged thus: “God said, Let there be light; and there was light; and He divided the light from the darkness; and He called the light Day and the darkness Night; and God saw that it was good,” we would suppose that darkness or night is spoken of here in the same manner as it is on the fourth day: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night”; or as it is likewise said below, “light and darkness.” Their division is certainly good, so that, according to the Psalmist [Ps. 103], when darkness is appointed and night comes, all the beasts of the forest go about in it; but when the sun rises, a person goes out to his work, refreshed by nocturnal rest.

But now darkness is excluded from the praise of goodness. First, as has already been said, He said that God saw the light, that it was good; and then He divided, and gave them mutually desired names, calling the light Day and the darkness Night. Therefore this darkness is of the kind in which nothing good is understood.

Indeed, the darkness from which He commanded this light to shine was something good in God’s providence, just as wood or iron is good in the hand of a skilled craftsman. Therefore, ascribing even it to His praise, He says: “I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness” [Isa. 45]. For it was good that He created the darkness from which formed light might shine, as has been said—the darkness that was borne over the face of the abyss. But that formed light should return to darkness is, beyond doubt, most evil and apostate.

Therefore, to avoid making a long circuit of discussion about the naming of day and night, day and night must be understood according to the nature of spiritual eyes, such as alone then existed: namely, spiritual night and spiritual day—the beauty of good angels and the dreadful, gloomy ugliness of evil spirits. Spiritual persons still call these realities by these names; for example, Paul says: “You are all children of light and children of day; we are not of night or darkness” [I Thess. 5], and much else of the same kind.

But someone says: “These and similar statements are made by likenesses rather than according to the nature of things; that is, not because that heavenly city Jerusalem, whose children we are, truly is day, or because that city of the devil, whose inhabitants we once were, truly is night, but because in them there is some likeness of day and night, and whatever Scripture says of this kind is spoken metaphorically.”

To this I say: those invisible things are not images and likenesses of these visible things; rather, these visible things are images and likenesses of those invisible things. For those were not made for the sake of these, but these for the sake of those. In them is truth; in these is shadow, indeed vanity. “I have seen,” says Ecclesiastes, “all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity” [Eccl. 1].

But because, for the understanding of those who are instructed concerning the invisible things, these visible things come first, and because we exiles come to know them before that first homeland which we have lost, those realities are called like these. Thus our weak-sighted eyes, unable to behold the brightness of heavenly things, may contemplate their images in these mirrors.

Therefore God, as has been said, called light—that is, the beauty of good angels—Day; and darkness—that is, the foulness of evil spirits—Night.

## CHAPTER XIX. Likewise, How God Established Those Names
God is said to have called them day and night, not because he spoke either Hebrew, Greek, or Latin—for he had neither a tongue nor lips to move, since he is neither bodily nor spatial—but because he assigned to each part a fixed determination that can no longer be changed. This naming of day is the establishment of blessedness, the firm foundation of grace and honor, so that that light which once received this name from the mouth of God and deserved to be called day may no longer be turned into darkness, may no longer be removed from the source of eternal light. When the apostatizing, light-fleeing spirits fell away, it preferred to remain in the light; and therefore it will now advance eternally as the light of this beauty and loveliness, until it is perfected in the likeness of the Father of lights, “with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (James 1).

Conversely, the naming of night is the firm and stable condemnation of darkness, once pronounced from the mouth of that same unchangeable God: because the foot of pride came upon them, they were moved from their place, fell of their own accord, and wrought iniquity; once expelled, they can no longer stand as apostates incapable of conversion. Yet the foolish compassion of certain heretics has dared to promise them some sort of time for repentance. It is therefore a very weighty saying, and should be understood wisely: God, “who is not a man that he should change, nor a son of man that he should lie” (Num. 23), once called such light day and such darkness night, and thus on either side set a judgment that shall not pass away. Whoever therefore agrees with him should truly say that that light is day, and that darkness is night.

For one who considers this, many things shine forth in the Scriptures. For example, blessed Job says: “Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night on which it was said: A man has been conceived. Let a dark tempest possess that night; let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months. Let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise” (Job 3). This is plainly the same as if he had said: “Let him perish—let him, I say, deservedly perish, as he has truly perished,” [Col. 0217A] that is, let the devil, in whom I was born according to Adam, cease to be light or day; he is now day not truly but deceptively, and truly night. He shall no longer be counted among the days of the year or numbered among the months, because he has once for all been darkened and made night. By no change whatsoever will he be restored to the beauty of that light which God, judging it worthy of praise, called day. Finally it is added:

## CHAPTER XX. Why it was not said, “Darkness and night were made, the first day,” but “there was evening and morning, one day.”

“And there was evening and morning, one day.” Here it must first be noted that he did not say: “And darkness and light were made, one day.” This was rightly and wisely observed by the sacred writer. For what God divided, how could it be joined together or make one thing? He divided light from darkness, and called the light day—day, I say, whole and complete, without fellowship with darkness. It would therefore have been well said: “Darkness and light were made, one day,” because, as has already been said, things separated by God’s division cannot be united or make one thing.

Accordingly, we must ask what was made evening and what morning, from which one day may soundly be reckoned. To make this clearer at last, we must first know why it was said, “the first day.” What then? Is this day of angelic brightness, however beautiful and splendid, the first day? By no means. Far be it! For it is far inferior to that sanctified and blessed day in which God rests, concerning which this book writes, after the other days:

> “These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, in the day when God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it sprang up in the earth, and every green herb before it germinated.”

What day do you suppose this is, in which every shrub and every herb was created before the earth caused it to spring up or germinate? What, I say, do you suppose this day to be but that Word in which everything that was made was life before it came to be? This day, therefore, was rightly called not the first but one day, because that other day is the first day—indeed, the day of days.

You say in response: “If that is the first, why was this not called the second?” Plainly because that day is not of the order or nature of the other days, but is the original cause of days, and of those who, knowing the Creator from the other days, glorify him and give thanks. This day, I say, is their everlasting reward: that, after the labor of these days, they may rest in it and breathe again. It was therefore rightly not placed beneath the other days in their order, but set above them. But we shall speak more fully of this in its proper place. Now, since the meaning is clear, let us see how evening and morning made one day.

Certainly, when God said, “Let there be light,” it was evening, because the sun of this utterance lay hidden in the heart of the Father; this light had not yet been brought forth in act in his Word, but was life hidden in the contemplation of that sun. But when the light was made, [Col. 0218A] then morning came to be; in it that light-bearer who fell before day first shone forth, and thence the day is full and shines in the sight of us all. For we all know—and it is a terrifying example to us—the division of light and darkness which was made there. Therefore, there was evening and morning: evening and morning, I say, not darkness and light; and from this one day endures.

## CHAPTER XXI. Who and what that “one day” is.

This one day is the original reason why the Spirit of God, who was borne over the waters so that this light might be made, is rightly called the Spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). For from this event the creature, first made subject to God, learned that the Creator is truly to be feared. Hence the Psalmist says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110).

Why then, you ask, does another prophet place fear last, saying:

> “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11)?

Plainly because he of whom these things are said, though not only man but also God, “increased in wisdom, age, and grace” according to his humanity (Luke 2), yet according to that whereby he is and was God had no increase. Rather, being wisdom itself, he descended from his heavenly heights to our low estate. But the creature, not merely human but angelic also, has advanced—as was already said above, the Apostle testifying—and advances; and the beginning of its progress is to possess the fear of the Lord, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

And from this beginning of its knowledge, namely fear, God is called in Greek *theos* (θεός), a name altered slightly and rendered in Latin *Deus*, because he is rightly feared. A certain pagan, though in his vanity, nevertheless knowing this, said:

> “Fear first made gods in the world.”  
> (Statius, *Thebaid* III.661)

But foolish fear caused those who were not to be feared to be called gods; whereas the Creator, because he alone is rightly to be feared, is called God by rational fear.

## CHAPTER XXII. On God’s saying, “Let there be a firmament.”

God also said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters. And God made the firmament, and divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament. And it was so.”

Already clothed with confession and beauty, already, as was said above, “clothed with intellectual light as with a garment” (Ps. 103), the magnificent Lord of heaven, containing the thrones and seated over the cherubim in dreadful majesty, looked upon the depths with compassion joined to his terror. In order to repair the losses of heaven from the depths of the abyss, he worked more vigorously and thus began his work:

> “Stretching out heaven like a skin, and covering its upper parts with waters; making the cloud his ascent, and walking upon the wings [Col. 0219A] of the winds; making his angels spirits, and his ministers burning fire” (Ps. 103).

For the Psalmist clearly indicates that all these things are the work of the second day, immediately adding the work of the third day: “You founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for ever and ever” (ibid.).

First, for the simpler reader, it must be said what the firmament is and whence it comes. The firmament is not something solid or hard, as the common people suppose, but expanded air, so refined that, although it can be seen, it may more properly be called spirit than body. Ecclesiastes testifies to this when he says concerning the heavenly lights visibly borne through it: “The spirit goes round and round, and returns to its circuits” (Eccl. 1). Therefore, although it is not solid, nor yet as dense as this lower region of air, Scripture nevertheless called it a firmament, because it divides waters from waters.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What are the waters “above the firmament”?

The writings of great and distinguished men also disagree in this chapter, namely concerning the statement: “Let it divide waters from waters; and it divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that were above the firmament.”

Some understand the words, “you cover its upper parts with waters” (Ps. 103), in such a way that they say: the upper parts of heaven, according to Genesis, are covered by waters—that is, the waters placed above the firmament—which we understand as multitudes of angels, according to: “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148).

But if the harper, that leader of praises, intended this—praising God from the heavens, praising him “in the highest”—why, when about to say, “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord,” did he first say, “Praise him, all his angels”? For by saying universally, “Praise him, all,” he excluded none of his angels; and he would therefore have repeated himself superfluously by saying, “Let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord,” if by the name waters he intended the multitudes of angels.

Likewise, in the hymn of the three children, when it first says, “Bless the Lord, angels of the Lord” (Dan. 3), and then, “Bless the Lord, heavens; bless the Lord, all waters above the heavens” (ibid.), Scripture plainly compels us to understand something other than angels by the name waters. Moreover, if angels must be understood by the name of the waters above the firmament, how or in what respect were waters of this sort divided from those beneath the firmament? Surely these are the waters of which God afterwards says: “Let the waters beneath the firmament be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear,” and so forth. How, then, were angels divided from these waters? They were rather divided from those spirits who became reprobate: angels of light from angels of darkness, as has already been said concerning the division of light and that same darkness.

Other teachers, however, wish to understand by the name of the waters above the firmament nothing other than waters simply. Their opinion undoubtedly seems the more just and safer, so that the meaning may not depart from the letter of the sacred history. Yet we do not agree so completely that waters are above the firmament as to grant that they are frozen, as some have thought more conjecturally than rationally.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What kind of form should be attributed to those waters?

If we are asked in what form those waters are above the firmament, if they are not frozen, let us ask them in what form they were before the firmament was made. But they cannot answer, because there was chaos and a confused mass, of such a kind as human senses cannot determine.

Therefore, since we can scarcely, even by philosophizing as much as we wish, attend to the small vault of this world which God, the wondrous craftsman, made by hollowing it out in the midst of the great abyss—the place in which we were born—let us be silent about the nature or form of the surrounding waters. For we cannot plausibly determine that they are altogether like these remnants of waters which later received their form or appearance; nor do we think it proper to invent anything, for example to suppose, as already said, that they are frozen.

Let us hold this one thing as certain: the vault of this world is situated in the midst of waters. For the firmament, which is as it were the roof of this vault and surrounds it on every side, was made “in the midst of waters,” on the authority of sacred Scripture. For God said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of waters.” And what then? “Let it divide,” he says, “waters from waters.” So that its firmness might be unquestioned, Scripture, having said this once, repeated the same thing: “And God made the firmament, and divided the waters beneath the firmament from those above the firmament.” Again, because “every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19), it adds: “And it was so.”

This threefold repetition is observed in each of God’s works: according to evening, morning, and the whole day. Hence it has already been said, and must still be said: since the Spirit of God, who was borne over the waters, is the Spirit of piety, he made for himself a work truly worthy of him: that he should penetrate the needy bottom of the abyss and illuminate the inner parts of its womb with such great adornments, the last and best of which is Christ, God and man, [followed in the text by the defective phrase:] “the administration of principalities and powers in the heavenly places, so that his manifold wisdom might gradually become known to them” (Eph. 3).

Truly the merciful Lord, after the fall of the perishing spirits, instructed the adoring dominions and trembling powers in the true wisdom of humility by the restoring work of his mercy, while preparing to bring forth from the inner depths of the abyss—over whose face darkness lay—their King and Lord. In this manner he began such a fabric. This order applies to us even now: every soul is first pierced by fear, then by the piety of love. For just as we are first distressed in fearing hell and afterwards, according to our measure, delighted in loving eternal life, so they too first knew God as terrible in the fall of the condemned angels, and then as lovable from the works that followed.

Do you think that it profited them little toward piety that they saw in such a firmament an image of their own steadfastness? For as the waters above the firmament do not fall down, and those below the firmament do not rise upon it, so neither can those blessed spirits fall further, nor can those reprobates be restored to their proper state by any change.

## CHAPTER XXV. Again, on the not-impossible placement of waters “above the firmament.”

As was said above, the Lord our God was greatly magnified: first clothed with light as with a garment, then stretching out heaven like a skin [Col. 0221B] and covering its upper parts with waters (Ps. 103). It is indeed a marvelous work of the magnificent God that the subtle nature of the firmament supports the mass of waters poured over it. Yet this very wonder becomes more bearable through a present example, lest it seem unbelievable to anyone. For what supports the very heavy earth, of which we shall speak later, except air poured around it on every side—though denser—and waters partly flowing around it? The Psalmist, marveling at this, says: “Give thanks to the Lord, who alone does great wonders, who made the heavens in understanding, who established the earth upon the waters” (Ps. 135).

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the words written in the aforementioned Psalm: “Who makes the cloud your ascent.”

[Col. 0221C] What, then, is meant by the same Prophet’s saying, “Who coverest its upper parts with waters,” and immediately adding: “Who makest the cloud thy ascent; who walkest upon the wings of the winds; who makest thy angels spirits, and thy ministers burning fire” (Ps. 103)?

Mystically, indeed, it is prophecy concerning the very Word of God, God most magnificent, who stretches out heaven: because he became man, died, and after his resurrection ascended into heaven. Then he made the cloud his ascent and walked upon the wings of the winds; for, as his apostles watched, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes (Acts 1).

But here we seek the literal sense, so that we may retain the sure foundation of history. What then does “Who makest the cloud thy ascent,” and so forth, mean except that, beneath the same firmament of this heaven—that is, the air—various motions necessary to this habitation are brought about by the Creator’s beneficence? For he then makes the cloud his ascent and again walks upon the wings of the winds, when waters evaporated from sea, rivers, pools, and marshes are gathered to moderate the heat of heaven; driven by gusts of wind, they are then carried back to earth in condensed drops of rain.

In this way he plainly makes the cloud his ascent and walks upon the wings of the winds—not by wandering about in his circumscribed substance, but by providing fitting help, when and as he wills, for governing the things he has made, which always need his providence. In this manner, I say, “he makes his angels spirits and his ministers burning fire.” If you understand this rightly in accordance with the subject of the present passage, nothing could be said more magnificently.

For here we must understand storm-winds, which perform his word with such certain effects and depart no more from his will or determination than rational spirits, whom we call angels, that is, messengers. Therefore, “who makes his angels spirits and his ministers burning fire” means: he who uses the spirits of storms or tempests as his angels or messengers, and burning fire as his ministers.

Although this seems to admit another meaning—namely, that rational angels are said to become spirits according to their proper life, and burning fire according to their bodies, as has appeared doubtful to some—this is nevertheless true and certain: these things serve the Lord of the world in such a way that, by their habitual announcing, they make the seasons known to us, and by their continual service they nourish his creation up to the present.

And note that he did not say in the past tense: “Who made the cloud your ascent, who walked upon the wings of the winds, who made your angels spirits,” as he later says: “Who founded the earth upon its stability, and set a boundary to the waters which they shall not pass; and made the moon for seasons; and set darkness, and night came to be.” Rather he said in the present tense: “Who makes the cloud your ascent, who walks upon the wings of the winds, who makes your angels spirits.” For he is not dealing here with the establishment of any creature, but with the incidental movement of creation—namely, of this heaven—because these spirits, that is, winds, are not creatures in themselves but are rather certain breaths of a breathing nature, or motions of creation.

Since creation is always moved by the same nod of the Creator—by which the upper firmament always revolves and the lower flowing waters always run—it is not always driven equally or with constant motion, but now more vigorously and now more quietly. The firmament alone revolves always at the same unchanging speed, just as, conversely, the earth always remains unmoved, except that every year it changes according to its upper appearance. The middle elements, however—water and the air nearest the earth—are carried now more slowly and now more swiftly, God acting, whose gaze permits no nature in his commonwealth to be idle.

There are twelve such spirits: four principal and eight lateral, two attached to each chief, on the right and left. Through the long continuance of their service, they are already known by fixed regions and names to many, especially to seafarers. In the vast house of this world they are like the great brooms of a great householder, each eagerly sweeping away all corruptions of the air in its own season.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Again, on burning fire, thunder, and lightning.

Sometimes also, if burning fire—which itself is a necessary minister in its own part—becomes too troublesome, not one but several winds leap upon it from different directions and vigorously compress it by forces turned against one another. When they struggle, a crash occurs which we call thunder; the fire, confined among them, is scattered and leaps down in flashes as sparks, or, when too violently enraged, strikes the earth as lightning. The frightened populace thinks that the firmament is being broken or heaven is falling. But it stands firmly in accordance with its name and is touched by no force of tempest; indeed, this disturbance does not surpass even the lowest circle of the moon.

Therefore it was rightly said in the past tense: “God made the firmament,” stretching it out like a skin; but in the present: “Who makes the cloud his ascent, who walks upon the wings of the winds, who makes his angels spirits and his ministers burning fire” (Ps. 103).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the statement: “And he called the firmament heaven.”

[Col. 0223B] “And God called the firmament heaven.” Where or when did God call the firmament heaven? Certainly when, speaking to Noah, he said: “I will place my bow in the clouds of heaven” (Gen. 9); or, more certainly, to Abraham: “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you can” (Gen. 15). For stars are seen not in just any heaven, but in the firmament; therefore he undoubtedly then called the firmament heaven.

Yet what does it mean that the writer affirms that God himself called the firmament heaven? It should not be thought to be without reason that, speaking of the living creatures which undoubtedly pass away, he says: “He brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. For whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name” (Gen. 2). But God himself assigned the name of light—that is, day—and of darkness—that is, night; and it is surely beyond doubt that these cannot pass away or be changed.

Does the same writer also imply the perpetuity of heaven and earth from the fact that God himself assigned names, calling the firmament heaven and the dry land earth? Perhaps you respond: “Heaven and earth will pass away also.” For the same Lord says: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24). But another Scripture again says: “A generation passes away and a generation comes, but the earth stands forever” (Eccl. 1).

We must therefore distinguish which heaven and which earth, or in what manner, are to pass away, since both Scriptures must be true: both the one which says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away,” and that which says, “But the earth stands forever.”

When the Apostle Peter said in his Epistle: “For, because they will it, this escapes them: that heavens existed of old, and earth, standing out of water and through water by God’s word, by which the world then was, being flooded with water, perished,” he immediately added: “But the heavens which now are, and the earth, by the same word are stored up, reserved for fire unto the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (2 Pet. 3). The meaning is clear: he declares that the earth and heavens which perished in the Flood and were restored after the Flood are to be destroyed by the final fire.

Therefore, when the Lord says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away,” he affirms not that the substance of earth will pass away, but its present condition. The Apostle says this concerning a time when it is certain that its substance did not perish: “by which the world then was, being flooded with water, perished.” Still less, because the Psalmist says: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands; they shall perish, but you remain” (Ps. 101), should it be thought that the firmament will perish—especially since, when the heavens perished in respect of the extent and appearance of this air, which the rising water occupied, the firmament nevertheless stood.

There are, moreover, higher heavens in the firmament, through which the sun and moon are borne, and besides these the five stars called planets, that is, wandering stars. But whether these too will perish in fire, or only those which also perished in the Flood, is a somewhat more difficult dispute among learned men. Yet since Truth says, speaking of the resurrection of the dead: “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13), what will the sun and moon do there, where there will be, as it were, as many suns as bodies of the righteous? Even if they remain, they will be unable to shine, their light being overpowered by the brightness reflected from so many bodies. John also says: “And night shall be no more; and they shall need neither the light of a lamp nor the light of the sun” (Rev. 22).

Therefore, as has been said, there is a difficult dispute among learned men whether the heavenly lights themselves, together with the heavens or circles through which they are borne, will perish. Accordingly, this distinction must be observed between those things whose names God himself assigned and those to which man gave names: the former remain, though changed; the latter are transitory.

Concerning the sea alone, because it is said in the Apocalypse, “And the sea is no more” (Rev. 22), whether it will be dried up in that great conflagration, when the age is judged by fire, or changed for the better, no one can easily say. Yet it may be understood that he spoke of the turbulent present age when he said, “And the sea is no more,” since, as above, when he says, “And the sea gave up its dead” (Rev. 20), the present age must be understood under that same name.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Again, why he called the firmament heaven.

Why did God call the firmament heaven when, following what he had begun, he could have called the firmament “firmament”? Plainly because “firmament” is said in relation to something else and is a relative name. Every firmament is the firmament of something. And when one says “this firmament,” one must say or understand “the divisions of the waters,” since God made it for this purpose: to divide waters from waters. But the common people do not know this.

“Heaven,” however, is an absolute name. When you say “heaven,” there is no need to ask whose heaven it is; just as, when earth or sea is spoken of, you need not ask whose earth or whose sea. Therefore, because common speech finds it more convenient to use one word rather than many for the same thing, God rightly called the firmament heaven. “Heaven” is thus a more absolute term than “firmament,” just as “man” and “Adam” are more absolute than “creature” or “thing formed.”

The word *caelum* (“heaven”) is said to derive from *cernere* (“to behold”), for an appropriate reason: it escapes none who have eyes. Hence it is also called in Greek *ouranos* (οὐρανός).

## CHAPTER XXX. That there was evening and morning, the second day; and what the second day is.

“And there was evening and morning, the second day.” This day is the revelation of the Creator; this day, I say, made God manifest even to the eyes of the Gentiles. For the Apostle says: “His invisible things, understood through the things that are made from the creation of the world, are clearly seen” (Rom. 1). This is one of the greatest grounds for the charge that, “when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (ibid.).

“And there was evening and morning,” because it did not happen by chance, but was arranged in evening—that is, in the hidden wisdom of God—and came to be before it emerged into visible actuality; and morning came to be, so that what was in the sight of God might emerge publicly through an evident work, as has already been said concerning the preceding day.

In this second day it should be noted that, according to the Hebrew truth, the commendation of the work is absent, which was added on the other days: “And God saw that it was good”; but it is added in the Septuagint. Why this pleased the writer—or rather the Holy Spirit, who wrote through him—is rightly asked. The first answer must be that one thing ought to be whole if it is rightly called well made.

Now the firmament is one beautiful form, but in relation to the intention of the worker it is not one complete thing. For what did God the architect intend when he said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of waters, and let it divide waters from waters”? Certainly this: that he might make the spacious house of this world, a beautiful house, whose roof, as it were, is this firmament. As the roof of a house may indeed be a beautiful work, but is not yet a house unless it has been placed upon foundation and walls—and is not itself a complete whole—so the firmament was indeed a beautiful part of the world, but was not yet the world before earth and sea possessed their own forms, over which the firmament stands.

It would therefore have been too hasty already to praise it, already to say, “God saw that it was good.” Why then, you ask, did he not, as in this case, postpone saying also: “There was evening and morning, the second day”? Why did he assign not one day only but two to one world? To this I reply: Did he arrange only two days, and not also three, in the formation of the world, according to its three parts? For earlier he said: “And darkness was upon the face of the abyss.” That abyss, of course, must be understood as the confused multitude and depth of waters. On this second day he said that “God divided waters from waters.” Yet he did not say that either this or that was good until, on the third day, God said: “Let the waters beneath the firmament be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear”; then he was to say: “And God saw that it was good.”

Add that the following belongs to the same day: after he said, “Let the earth bring forth green herb,” and so forth, it is added, “And God saw that it was good.” And behold: just as there are three parts of the world and three days, so you likewise have three goods—the formation of good light, the ordered work of the world, and the planting of paradise. Note also that, although there are twice three days, apart from the seventh, which is the rest of the day, both the third of the first group and the third of the following group are adorned with a double commendation of goodness. Thus, as there are seven days, so there are seven forms of goodness, wonderfully bearing witness from themselves to the sevenfold Spirit of God.

Let us now enter upon the work of that day, namely the third.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the third day, and why it is said there, “God saw that it was good.”

But God said: “Let the waters beneath the firmament be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear.” And it was so. And God called the dry land earth, and called the gatherings of waters seas. And God saw that it was good.

Here at last the writer of God—or rather, the hearer of the Trinity—having on the third day the world completed in its three parts, heaven, earth, and sea, rightly and fittingly said that God saw that it was good. For we must note the threefold exercise of creative power over the waters. First, darkness was upon the abyss created in the beginning, and it was not said to be good. Next, when the firmament had intervened, the waters were divided, and again it was not said to be good. Third, the waters were gathered into one place; and so, when the dry land appeared, it was said that God saw that it was good. For this is truly good: it is a most effective work for the Trinity seeking the treasures of its grace beneath the abyss.

But now let us examine the words of him who searches the abyss. “Let the waters beneath the firmament,” he says, “be gathered into one place, and let the dry land appear.” The waters beneath the firmament are certainly the remainder or a part of the waters above the firmament. For it was said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of waters, and let it divide waters from waters,” and so forth. Therefore the division of waters mentioned above must be understood simply and literally: not that division which philosophers call the division of a word into several meanings, [Col. 0226D] but that which they call the division of a whole into parts.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How it was said: “Let the waters be gathered into one place.”

“Let the waters,” he says, “be gathered into one place.” How did he say that they should be gathered “into one place,” when there is not one gathering of the waters? For it was not said, “and he called the gathering of the waters seas,” but, “and he called the gatherings of the waters seas.” How then did he say, “Let them be gathered into one place,” unless it were as if he said: “Let the waters withdraw from here and there, and flow together separately here and separately there, and let them create no obstacle to the work proposed”? For toward what did the supreme skill of the Craftsman tend, if not to what he says: “And let the dry land appear”? He had long been seeking the dry land, hidden in the depths of the abyss, before he divided the waters from the waters—dry land which he alone knew to be there, because he alone had created it. He sought, I say, the dry land, the material of a great and most beautiful work, which by a wondrous and ineffable counsel he was devising within himself: with which he would adorn the golden palaces of his higher heaven, out of that lowest and ignoble mass. Having found this, therefore, God saw that it was good; he saw it, I say, and his sight did not deceive him. For as he saw then, so it has now come to pass, since truth has sprung up from the dry land (Ps. 84), a rising that surpasses the rising in heaven. “And God,” he says, “called the dry land Earth, and called the gatherings of the waters Seas.” It has already been said above what force is implied by the placement of the divine naming: namely, that no one can readily say that the substance of those things to which God himself assigned names will pass away.

And indeed, according to the nature which he himself created, the earth is plainly dry. For in truth it is naturally dry; and unless it were compacted by an admixture of moisture, it would be dust and would yield lightly to every wind. Therefore, since it is aided from elsewhere and is never wholly left in its own poverty, its name too was rightly changed, so that it is now called not “dry land” but “earth.” Likewise, what is now customarily called “sea” is by nature a gathering of waters.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Again, concerning the gathering of the waters, the dry land, and the saying in the Psalm: “You founded the earth upon its stability.”

The wondrous God spoke this wondrously; the begetter of the eternal Word uttered this command. He spoke it in an ancient, secret, and incomprehensible utterance, and so it came to pass. Marveling at this, the illustrious psalmist David, God’s organ-player, says: “You founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for ever and ever. The abyss, like a garment, is its covering; the waters shall stand above the mountains. At your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid. The mountains ascend and the plains descend to the place which you founded for them. You set a boundary which they shall not pass over, nor shall they return to cover the earth” (Ps. 103).

What more marvelous thing could be said than this: “You founded the earth upon its stability”? Yet similar to this is what he says in another Psalm, while singing a confession of this divine goodness: “He who made the heavens in understanding”—and immediately he adds—“who established the earth upon the waters” (Ps. 135). For which is the more marvelous saying: “You founded the earth upon its stability,” or “You established the earth upon the waters”? Indeed, although these differ in words, they are equal in meaning. For who does not know that the earth is not supported by the waters, but rather that the waters are supported by the earth? The globe of the earth is surrounded everywhere by waters and enclosed everywhere by the air poured around it. And if our antipodes stood beneath the earth with their feet turned toward ours, as the philosophers of the Gentiles supposed, they would have no more reason to fear falling downward than we have to fear plunging into heaven. For all weights are borne by their tendency toward the earth, and waters are supported everywhere by the earth.

What then is meant by, “Who established the earth upon the waters,” unless it is as though he said: “Who established the earth, which has no support except the waters that it itself, rather, bears”? Therefore he established the earth upon itself; therefore he founded the earth upon its stability. Yet the petty learned men, the philosophers of this world, knowing this very thing—that the earth hangs like a center in the midst of the empty world—formerly mocked Holy Scripture as ignorant and childish because it said that the earth was established upon the waters. True wisdom and philosophy ought rather to marvel that the Creator’s command has firmly and immovably established heavy earth upon nothing but moist air.

Further, when he says concerning the gathering of the waters: “The abyss, like a garment, is its covering; above the mountains the waters shall stand; at your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid,” he expressed, as fittingly as a man could, by the figure called metaphor, the strength of the word and the majesty of the command by which this was done. For are waters animate or sentient, so that he should say, “At your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid”? At the same time, it should be noted that, while he strives to amplify or adorn the matter, wise indeed but childish in proportion to the greatness of the thing, he also used a solecism: he put the future for the past, “they shall flee” and “they shall be afraid,” where he meant to say, “they fled” and “they were afraid.”

Finally, when he says, “You set a boundary which they shall not pass over, nor shall they return to cover the earth,” this is so true that even in the Flood the sea did not cross its own boundary in order to cover the earth. Rather, Scripture says, “All the fountains of the great abyss were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened; and rain came upon the earth for forty days and forty nights” (Gen. 7). How much more, then, will the seas not now cross their boundary, after the Lord swore by himself, saying: “I will no longer add the waters of a flood upon the earth; I will place my bow in the clouds of heaven; I will remember my covenant, that I may not destroy all flesh by the waters of a flood” (Gen. 9).

Therefore, “the upheavings of the sea are wonderful,” but “wonderful on high is the Lord,” who surrounded it with its boundaries, set bar and doors, and said: “Thus far shall you come, and here shall you break your swelling waves” (Job 38). “Let the sea be moved, and its fullness” (Ps. 95), because this is expedient. Otherwise its waters would become putrid and would not be fit to nourish the fish that feed their ruler, humankind. Let it be moved, I say: now by the force of winds, now by its natural advance and retreat; thus the waters are kept alive, which would die in idleness or stillness. For God rendered the dry land secure by ensuring that they would not cross the boundary set for them, nor return to cover the earth.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Why it was necessary for the dry land that mountains should rise and plains descend.

Moreover, why was it necessary for that same dry land—that is, the earth—that “mountains should rise and plains descend to the place,” he says, “which you founded for them” (Ps. 103)? Here it must certainly be understood that, if the earth lay level everywhere, no less a storm of winds would rage upon it than upon the sea. Even now, in those regions which lack mountains—especially Libya—a tempest is accustomed to trouble all whom it catches outdoors, whether on foot or riding horseback, no less than on the open sea. For where, over level and bare places that produce nothing, a rising wind lifts the sand from the ground and drives it with great force, it fills mouths and eyes and thus impedes progress and walking, so that there is no greater shipwreck on any sea. What if no mountains anywhere had risen, if the whole earth had descended into a plain? If, where winds are permitted to run even a little way, they gather such force in a short time, what could they do if throughout the whole world they had no barrier at all?

Therefore this too ought not to be absent from the praises of the magnificent God: that mountains rise and plains descend to the place which he founded for them. He founded them, I say, so that the mountains, once commanded to rise, should not descend, nor the plains, once depressed, rise again. When the founder of the earth drove away the abyss, which covered it like a garment, by that same fitting power he abundantly diffused a supply of waters through its innermost veins. For the waters did not flee at his rebuke and gather into one place in such a way that the dry land which appeared was cast out from the womb of the abyss like an untimely birth. Rather, continually drawing waters through all its veins, it draws from the abundant breast of the abyss; and, rising through clouds and falling again, it receives from heaven the early and latter rain. It is nourished inwardly by waters made sweet and watered outwardly from its heights. Springs also gush forth and rivers flow.

The Psalmist likewise praises this: “You send forth springs in the valleys; waters pass between the midst of the mountains” (ibid.). Accordingly Ecclesiastes, considering the source of flowing waters, says: “All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow” (Eccl. 1). Why? Clearly because nothing flows there except what is drawn from it by the modes already mentioned. But now let us hear the command of the mighty Word sent forth over the earth.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the saying, “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation,” and the threefold repetition of each utterance.

“Let the earth bring forth green vegetation, bearing seed, and fruit-bearing wood making fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.” And it was so. “And the earth brought forth living vegetation, bearing seed according to its kind, and wood making fruit, each having seed according to its own species. And God saw that it was good. And evening and morning came: the third day.”

Because these are works of the creating Trinity, Holy Scripture fittingly repeats its testimony everywhere three times. Three things are said—indeed, one and the same thing is said three times. God spoke, whose speaking is doing. “And it was so,” and “the earth brought forth.” The first corresponds to evening, that is, to the secret counsel of the Word of God, in whom was life; the second, “and it was so,” corresponds to morning, that is, to the substantial production of things; the third corresponds to the continuous day of a creature somehow persisting.

You will find this in all the works of the six days: “God said, Let there be lights,” and “it was so,” and “God made two great lights.” Likewise: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” and “God created great sea-creatures,” and “God blessed them,” and so forth. But in the creation of light, God said: “Let there be light,” and light was made, and he divided the light and darkness. Everywhere three words of witness accord, because the Trinity creates everywhere throughout the whole evening, morning, and day. This is also the original ground of the holy and just law by which the same writer ordained that no judicial case should require more than three witnesses.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Again, concerning green vegetation, seed-bearing vegetation, fruit-bearing wood, and wood whose seed alone is in itself.

“Let the earth,” he says, “bring forth living vegetation,” and so forth. Every herb and every tree is first divided in two ways. There is vegetation that is merely green, such as the grass which the earth produces for beasts of burden. And there is vegetation bearing its own seed, such as wheat or celery, and the other kinds which it produces for the service of human beings. Likewise, there is wood bearing no fruit but only its own seed, such as beech or holm-oak, the other trees of the open country, and the cedars of Lebanon, where, according to the Psalmist, “sparrows make their nests” (Ps. 103); these cannot properly be called fruit trees. And there is fruit-bearing wood, which we call a tree, such as an apple tree or pear tree, or anything of that sort, bearing fruit and seed in the fruit according to its kind.

God’s command omits absolutely none of these in this Scripture. For he did not say merely “vegetation bearing seed,” but first set forth the more universal expression, “green vegetation.” Likewise, he did not say merely, “and the earth produced fruit-bearing wood making fruit,” but added, “and bearing seed, each according to its kind.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the planting of Paradise, and the saying: “He who lives for ever created all things together.”

From this beginning of the earth’s adornment, as is written below, the Lord God had planted the Paradise of delight, in which he placed the formed human being. He had planted it, I say, not by seeking shoots from elsewhere, but by once impressing the power of this command of his, from which the earth’s inborn nature or power of germination arose.

Since mention of that planting has now presented itself, although it should be discussed more fully in its proper place, we must nevertheless now ask those who maintain that all creation was sudden and confused how they understand what is said: “He had planted the Paradise of delight from the beginning.” For because it is written elsewhere, “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18), they wish vegetation already mature and trees already strong, with their fruits and seeds, to have existed suddenly and without any stages of growth; likewise lights in the firmament; likewise the creeping things of the sea and birds of heaven to have teemed forth; likewise the animals of the earth; and human beings themselves to have walked at once upon their feet.

This plainly conflicts with reason, and the text of the present reading does not permit such an interpretation. For from the beginning it has already been said that the Lord God had planted the Paradise of delight, and that there was no human being to cultivate the ground, but a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth. As for the saying, “He who lives for ever created all things together,” we shall say more suitably how it should be understood, without violating the order of this reading, when we come to that conclusion of the creation in which it is said: “These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created,” and so forth.

For now it was necessary to say that, from this beginning of the earth’s adornment, the Lord God planted the Paradise of delights. For certainly in its planting that gracious command of the Lord—“Let the earth bring forth green vegetation, bearing seed, and fruit-bearing wood”—was poured forth far more gloriously than in this impoverished exile of the human race, where the earth very often does not give its fruits to a human being laboring in the sweat of his face. In that delightful place of earth, close to heaven, all seeds of herbs and trees are healthful. But in this earth, from which the human being was taken and to which he was cast back on account of sin, very many things are born harmful to that same human being. Nor is this surprising. For he says: “Cursed is the earth in your work; when you cultivate it, it will not give its fruits, but will bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” If it belongs to the curse to bring forth piercing thorns and thistles, how much more does it belong to the curse to bring forth herbs and juices that kill?

Does it not follow that, just as a woman was made to bear superfluous offspring, not belonging to the blessing given in Paradise, when the Lord said to her, “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions,” so it should be believed that this also befell her earth: that it should pour forth varied and harmful juices not belonging to the words of blessing, “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation,” and so forth?

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Again, concerning the saying, “each according to its kind,” and that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father.

“Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor” (Isa. 40) and shown him? Who, I say, showed him, or from what exemplar was he instructed, to command the earth to bring forth every herb and tree with the seed of its own kind? We ask this of the Jews and likewise of heretics, whoever, in an impious understanding, wish God the Father to be altogether barren, denying that he brought forth the Word consubstantial with himself and not believing that he begot a Son equal to himself.

You Jews say that he has no Son; you Arians say that he has a dissimilar Son. Whence, then, did he grant not only to living creatures but even to the herbs of the earth that each should have within itself the seed of its own kind, if he possessed in himself nothing of such nature or power? Therefore, may you be grass, which Behemoth—that is, the beast, namely the devil—eats like an ox (Job 40); may you, I say, be like forest trees which bear no fruit and are useful for nothing except to be cut down and cast into the fire (Matt. 7), whoever blasphemously say that God, the creator of all, begot either no Son or a Son unlike himself.

For the nature of God is neither barren—he who gave fertility to his creature—nor did his begetting degenerate, so that God begot something other than God: he who spoke and it was done, so that every tree or herb should bear in itself seed not other than according to its own kind.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Again, concerning the third day.

On this third day that aspect of divine goodness shines forth from which the holy sevenfold Spirit, in the third place for those ascending after fear and piety, is called the spirit of knowledge (Isa. 11). For it belongs to most beautiful knowledge that such and so great a gardener planted that Paradise of delights. It was in hope of this knowledge that the human being was puffed up, when the devil said: “Eat, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). For, miserable as he was, inspired by the devil, he resented guarding another’s garden under another’s authority, while some tree was forbidden to him; and therefore sought it as though it were a remedy, so that he himself might have knowledge of planting paradises for himself. But of this elsewhere.

Certainly, in the other works of the seven days too, God did nothing without knowledge. Nevertheless, according to their proper distinctions, the several names of the sevenfold power are more properly assigned to particular things. For example, he also made the fish of the sea and birds of heaven with the greatest knowledge. Yet in their nature there is already recognized that power of creative might which is called the spirit of counsel (Isa. 11). For they possess a certain natural counsel of mutual love, by which they are united with one another, which joins male and female, so that lovers come together, make nests together, and feed their young.

So too, in each of the works of the other days, besides God’s knowledge, some other attribute is more properly considered and proclaimed. But from the work of this third day nothing better than God’s manifold knowledge is proclaimed, because as yet nothing external cooperates besides its own being, except that it signifies the knowledge of so great a planter. Therefore evening and morning came, the third day, as was said above. This work of God’s knowledge is followed by another work displaying great strength with manifest clarity.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning the fourth day, the lights, and the power of the greater light.

Then God said: “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night; and let them serve as signs, and seasons, and days, and years, that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth.” And it was so. And God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.

God certainly spoke and made this in the spirit of strength. For, to say nothing of the moon and the stars, whose powers scarcely any but natural philosophers know in some measure, what country-dweller does not know concerning the sun that without it the fabric of the world is not merely weak and destitute, but is uninhabitable by any living thing? When it is somewhat farther away from this habitable region, the soil is fit for no seed of tree or herb. Fields grow sluggish, rivers freeze, leafy groves die, and the idle farmer drags out harmful leisure beside the hearth.

What if that same sun remained at a distance longer, or did not exist at all? Accordingly, when it visits us more closely by its ascent and begins with strengthening rays to break up the hardness of the fields, it is compared to a ram.
