When, ascending higher, it causes the labors of oxen to appear, it is said to resemble a bull; and when, with heat pressing down from above, it ripens the crops, it is compared to a lion.

## CHAPTER XLI. Again, concerning the same matter: that the Paradise of delights flourished before it, and that it is the land of promise.

Here we must not pass over what natural philosophers elegantly customarily say of this great ruler of our heaven: that it is the source of ethereal fire, the heart or mind of heaven, and the tempering power of the world. For, they say, it is evident to reason that it truly tempers the world. It is certain that the sun tempers not only the earth but even heaven itself, so that those extremities which lie farthest from the sun’s path lack every benefit of heat and grow numb in perpetual cold. It is difficult to disregard their reasoning.

For the Psalmist too seems to have touched on this very point when he says: “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains” (Ps. 74). By “desert mountains” he means the lands lying beneath the southern and northern poles, stiff with perpetual frost because of their remoteness from the sun. Between these and the middle zone, which they call the burnt zone, they say there are two zones, tempered by cold on one side and heat on the other, so as to be habitable.

The question then arises: how could the earth, before the sun was made, bring forth fruit-bearing wood and green, seed-bearing vegetation, when even now, though the sun burns in heaven, the regions mentioned remain barren in perpetual cold solely because they are farther removed from it? To this ecclesiastical ears readily answer that what was not known or believed by those inquisitive investigators of the world’s creation is this: that Paradise which the Lord God planted in the beginning by saying, “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation, bearing seed, and fruit-bearing wood,” and so forth—for this was the beginning of all things commanded to come into being in the world—that Paradise, I say, which the Lord God planted by this utterance of his Word, is the Paradise of pleasure, the Paradise of delights, of another heaven and another climate. It is not subject to the alternations of summer and winter, spring and autumn, but is a Paradise of perpetual pleasure and enduring delights, always blooming, always bright, delightful to sight and taste in everlasting sweetness.

This same writer commends its unending delights, under the name of that land of promise into which the Lord was leading an untaught people, in such gracious descriptions: “For the Lord your God will bring you into a good land, a land of streams, waters, and springs, in whose plains and mountains the abysses of rivers burst forth; a land of wheat, barley, and vineyards, in which figs, pomegranates, and olive groves grow; a land of oil and honey” (Deut. 8), and so forth. Likewise: “For the land which you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you came out, where, after seed is cast, waters are led for irrigation after the manner of gardens. Rather, it is mountainous and level country, awaiting rains from heaven, which the Lord God always visits, and upon which his eyes rest from the beginning of the year until its end” (Deut. 11).

These matters have been said now so that it may be certain that the earth brought forth at the Lord’s command before this sun existed. For that land, the fullness of which cannot be expressed by such shadowy descriptions, does not need to bloom anew at the sun’s visitation: the Lord God always visits it, and his eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year until its end. But now let us consider the power of the same sun and moon according to the Creator’s own words.

## CHAPTER XLII. Again, concerning the lights and their magnitudes.

“Let lights be made,” he says, “in the firmament of heaven,” and so forth. By “lights” he means the sun and moon. For he continues: “And God made two great lights, the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night.” Both lights are great in relation to the stars, which are certainly of lesser power. But in relation or comparison to one another, the greater light is the sun and the lesser light is the moon.

For, as the inquisitive philosophers of this world have discovered, the earth is indeed greater than the moon; but the sun—which, because of the height of its course and the smallness of our eyes, appears as though small—is, they say, eight times greater than the earth in size. Moreover, the sun is the greater light than the moon because it shines by its own light; for the moon shines back from it, by a light not its own but another’s. The sun’s light is poured into the body of the moon, and from it, shining brightly, the moon returns brightness alone, not heat. So also a mirror, when from itself it emits the splendor of a fire set at a distance opposite it, displays only the likeness of fire, devoid of the sensation of heat.

Others, however, say that the moon has its own light, but that one half of its globe is bright and the other dark; and that, as it moves in its orbit, the same part by which it shines gradually turns toward us so that it may be seen by us, and for this reason it first appears, as it were, horned. Whichever opinion is true, the sun is indeed the greater light both in the size of its sphere and in brightness; but these two are great lights in comparison with the stars, which illuminate the world far less and are of lesser power.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning the differing position of the lights and stars in the firmament.

It should be known that, although after saying, “Let lights be made,” he added, “in the firmament of heaven,” and likewise concerning the stars, “and he placed them in the firmament of heaven,” nevertheless, although the wording is not different, their position is different. For, according to what astronomers have better observed, all stars except the five planets—that is, the wandering stars—and except these two great lights, are fixed in the firmament and are carried along with the firmament.

Indeed, these lights and the five stars just mentioned, which they consecrated under the names of their idols—namely Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, and Mercury—have their own circuits, which are carried in a contrary motion. For they revolve against the firmament. Saturn’s circuit is reckoned the highest, the moon’s the lowest. “Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven,” he says well: that is, each in its own firmament of heaven. For the circuits of these lights and of the other planets are also called heavens, which praise the Lord, according to the Psalmist saying: “Praise him, heavens of heavens” (Ps. 148), that is, the heavens or greater circuits enclosing the complex of lesser circuits.

For the firmament is no small subject of divine praise: their course, which they never exceed, as they run without ceasing and return into their circuits by a twofold motion—namely, the motion of the higher firmament, which they call the *aplanēs* (“unwandering”), and their own motion, by which they are continually carried against it. Ecclesiastes expresses both motions when speaking of the sun in these words: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; there, rising again, it circles toward the south and turns toward the north. The spirit proceeds, surveying all things in a circuit, and returns to its circuits” (Eccl. 1). The same must be understood concerning the moon and the other bodies: the greater or smaller their circuits, the more or less time they spend revolving and revolving again.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning the division of day and night, and the power of the lights.

For what purpose were these lights made? “And let them divide,” he says, “day and night,” and so forth. This is the chief reason why the lights were made. Hence it is repeated a third time when it is said: “The greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night.” And later: “Let them shine upon the earth and divide light from darkness.”

If God had already divided light and darkness by himself, what need was there for the lights to divide day and night, or light and darkness? Indeed, how could they divide what God had already divided, and what no one had again confused? Therefore there the statement concerned intellectual light and spiritual darkness; here the discourse concerns the light and darkness of bodily vision.

God rightly established this darkness, since by his ordinance and command, which will not pass away, the sun descends below and then, from the shadow of the earth, the upper hemisphere is darkened and night comes. Thus “all the beasts of the forest pass through it, the young lions roaring to seize prey and seek their food from God; when the sun rises, they gather in their dens, but human beings go forth to their work and to their labor until evening” (Ps. 103). This too, I say, belongs among those works which are most magnificent: “Lord, you have made all your works in wisdom” (ibid.).

Accordingly, the writer first introduced this darkness when he said, “that they may divide light and darkness,” and then added, “and God saw that it was good.” But he excluded the earlier darkness from the praise of goodness by first saying, “And God saw the light, that it was good,” and only then, “he divided,” he says, “the light and darkness.” “Let them divide day and night,” he says, so that the greater light may rule the day and the lesser light rule the night.

The Psalmist also records this among his confessions of the Lord: “Give thanks to the Lord who made the great lights: the sun to rule the day, the moon and stars to rule the night” (Ps. 135). And in the Psalm mentioned above: “He made the moon for seasons; the sun knew its setting” (Ps. 103). If, therefore, you ask how the greater light rules the day, it rules by setting and rising. For “the sun knew its setting” is a metaphorical statement: it sets at a fixed time and, as though knowing what it does, likewise returns to its rising at a fixed hour. In accordance with that same setting, for definite reasons, the length and shortness of days alternately vary, now earlier and now later. For, advancing higher toward the north, because it sets later for us, it lengthens the day; and descending again toward the south, because it is hidden from us sooner, it makes the day shorter.

For day comes from nothing else than the sun’s being above the earth, just as, conversely, night comes from nothing else than the sun’s being lowered beneath the earth and the earth’s shadow, cast against the sun, being raised over us. And if, before the sun’s globe rises above the horizon, the morning shines with illuminated air and it is day, this occurs through the sun’s proximity; just as, conversely, in the evening, once it is hidden from us, the remaining traces of light do not disappear immediately but gradually. Thus the greater light always rules the day.

But the moon rules the night only temporarily. Hence the Psalmist fittingly says: “He made the moon for seasons.” For it does not rule every night, nor the whole night; it is absent on many nights and for most of the night. It increases temporarily and likewise decreases temporarily. Further, it rules the night differently from the way the sun rules the day. The sun rules the day because it makes the day from itself; the moon rules the night because it somewhat overcomes its darkness through the aid of light borrowed from the sun. Therefore, “let them divide day and night”: that is, let the sun make the whole day by its own light, while the moon illuminates certain nights, or some portion of the night.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the saying, “And let them serve as signs, seasons, days, and years.”

“And let them,” he says, “serve as signs, seasons, days, and years.” Four things are named: signs, seasons, days, and years. Of these, three—signs, seasons, and days—belong to the sun. For these are perceived from it, especially the signs of the hours. Though even rustic common people observe them, the Church of Christ considers them more religiously for the service of God. According to the sun, the seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter also vary. Further, it is plainly evident to all eyes that this light serves for days: by each rising it makes a separate day.

Years, together with their parts—that is, the twelve months—are assigned to the moon. For the Hebrews, to whom this Scripture was given or from whom it came to us, know only lunar months and years. A month is twenty-nine and a half days. A common year, that is, one of twelve months, has 354 days; but an embolismic year, that is, one of thirteen months, has 384 days.

For the Romans, however, the greater light serves for the year. They calculate a solar year of 365 days, with an additional quarter-day. But this year is not so natural, because its parts, namely the months, do not run according to nature but are arranged at pleasure. The lunar year, on the other hand, is natural, because its parts, namely the lunar months, likewise come from nature. Thus they are all of the same length, except that the half-day remaining beyond twenty-nine days, since it cannot be counted as a whole day, must be preserved, so that one month is of twenty-nine days and another of thirty.

Before the faith of Christ the Roman world did not observe these years or months of this sort, and even now the uneducated multitude does not know them. Accordingly, in ordinary use the Church of Christ calculates the year as the pagan world, ignorant of this Scripture, established it; but for the lawful observance of the Paschal feast, it reasonably observes the Hebrews’ lunar months and years, both common and embolismic.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Why “and let them illuminate the earth” was said last.

Why, after all this, did he immediately add, “and let them give light upon the earth”? Clearly, lest you suppose that before these luminaries the earth had been illuminated by some bodily light. For perhaps you would say: “The earth had already been illuminated before this, but that light was not marked out in signs and seasons, days and years, by a distinguishable alternation.” Therefore these luminaries were made in order that those distinctions might be added. The wording of the text wholly excludes this sense, when it adds also, “and let them give light upon the earth.” For from this likewise it is plainly understood that there had previously been no visible light upon this earth.

Nevertheless, concerning that land of Paradise, it should be known that as soon as God said, “Let the waters which are under the firmament be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear,” it so appeared that afterward it never disappeared; just as, no less, as soon as God said, “Let the earth bring forth green herb,” etc., it so sprouted, flowered, put forth leaves, and bore fruit [Col. 0237D] that it can no longer cease from flowering. For, to say nothing of the light of the angelic forms, which are never absent there: if, in this exile, certain portions of this earth—namely precious stones, especially carbuncles—appear such that they can serve as lamps at night, how splendidly do you suppose that land appeared, where nothing of such stones, nor of any good thing delightful to behold, can be lacking?

These luminaries, therefore, illuminate this world only. Nor should this point concerning them be passed over: chiefly for their sake the firmament needed to be revolving—namely, so that the sun, which has such heat that, as was said above, it has been called the fountain of ethereal fire, being made for this purpose, might provide not only illumination but also frequent moderation of the world [Col. 0238A], be present to all regions, and make the observable order of the stars, returning so often in its course, better known. For it is far better now, when the burning sun is present briefly indeed but frequently, than if, scorching the lands above for six months, it then hid beneath the earth for the space of another six months, leaving us a long night accompanied by an equally prolonged cold.

For in twelve months it traverses the zodiac; and if the motion of the firmament ceased, it would be carried round by that course alone. Consequently, what is now a year would then be a single day with its night.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
Why, in saying “and the stars,” he did not add “and let them be for signs and seasons”; and concerning the same fourth day, and what the fourth day is

“And God made,” he says, “two great luminaries: the greater luminary to rule the day, and the lesser luminary to rule the night, and the stars.” It should be noted in this repetition that, when he says, “And God made two great luminaries, and the stars,” he did not add, “for signs,” lest he give occasion to those who suppose that fatal signs exist in the stars. Such people, imitators of the creature rather than of the Creator, knowing God from the creation of the world but not glorifying him as God or giving thanks, and professing themselves wise, became foolish in this also (Rom. 1), while they ascribed to the stars almost all the power of the Creator, so that they said the fatal necessity of their life and death depended upon the stars’ movements.

No such suspicion could arise from this Scripture [Col. 0238C]. For, having said, “And God made two luminaries,” he then added, “and the stars,” in such a way that one may not supply “for signs.” Yet stars do serve for certain signs and certain seasons, which a Christian may accept or observe without injury to piety—for example, such matters as Scripture speaks of: “Who made Arcturus, the Hyades, and Orion?” (Job 9). Again: “Can you bind together the glittering Pleiades, or can you loosen the circuit of Arcturus? Can you bring forth Lucifer in his season, or cause Vesper to rise over the children of the earth?” (Job 38).

It is not harmful to accept such things and to take from them indications of fair weather or storms; indeed, it is especially useful for fearful sailors. Further, it is praiseworthy to derive a spiritual sense from such positions or significations of the stars by fitting comparisons. Likewise, to ascertain the hours of the night from the altitude of any star—using the fixed stars that move with the firmament, with an horoscopium applied—is a pleasant art and harmless exercise; indeed, it is a beautiful sight to determine at what hours the nightly praise of God is performed. But this does not belong to the present subject.

For one who truly seeks wisdom and desires to know the Creator from the creation of the world, to glorify him and give thanks, is content to know this alone concerning it: that, as sacred Scripture testifies, the divine Creator established the aforesaid things—namely, the luminaries and the stars—in the firmament of heaven in order to shine upon the earth [Col. 0239A] and to rule day and night. “And God saw that it was good”: he saw, I say, and saw truly; nor is there falsehood in his sight. For this is truly a good effect of his goodness: this fourth form, I say, of his good and beautiful work is good. And evening and morning came to be, because it was previously in a hidden and invisible ordering, and now in this visible form is the glorious day of the eternal Word, the beautiful and radiant glorification of the only-begotten Son.

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
Concerning the fifth day, and what the fifth day is

God also said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul, and winged creatures above the earth under the firmament of heaven.” And God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and every creeping thing according to its kind.

As has already been said above, in this form of creature—namely, the creeping creatures of the sea and the birds of heaven—there is a certain natural or affective counsel. That is, under the prompting of generative love, male and female come together and devote as much care to propagating their offspring as is sufficient to ensure and accomplish the continuance of their desired posterity. Therefore it may unquestionably be declared that this form of God’s good work belongs to the Spirit of counsel, just as the preceding work was shown above to belong to the Spirit of fortitude.

Why the writer excluded cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth from the fifth day of this work, though their nature is no higher than that of these creatures [Col. 0239C]—for both alike employ the five bodily senses—will more fittingly be discussed in its place.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
Concerning the words, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul”

“Let the waters,” he says, “bring forth creeping things of living soul.” It is indeed remarkable that solid bodies should be born or produced from the fluid element of waters; yet more remarkable is the fact that the mighty Creator had already made the very element of waters from nothing.

But when he says, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” why add “of living soul,” since the very name “creeping things” sufficiently expresses a living soul? For everything that creeps lives and senses, although not everything that lives creeps or can creep. The herb lives which the earth brings forth, green and bearing seed. Every fruit-bearing tree lives, or every tree having its seed within itself which the earth produces. But life of this sort is without sensation and likewise without movement. Yet everything that creeps, as has already been said, also lives.

Why then, after saying, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” did he add, “of living soul”? Clearly, in order to distinguish the soul of creeping creatures from the soul of human beings. For when he says, “of living soul,” he intends us to understand: living, but not also discerning. The life of creeping things surpasses the life of herbs and trees in that it is sentient; those indeed live, but do not sense. Yet it is far inferior to human life, because a human being does not merely live so as to sense; rather, he lives, senses, and—what is most worthy—discerns.

Therefore, when it is said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” he immediately fittingly adds, “of living soul”: living only, I say, and not also discerning. Likewise, concerning the birds, it is understood: “Let the waters bring forth creatures of living soul,” likewise not discerning. For birds sense more acutely than creeping things, yet nonetheless lack discernment or reason. That they sense more acutely is beyond doubt. Indeed, evil spirits so abused the sharpness of their senses to increase the error of the Gentiles that augurs and diviners were appointed because people believed that the cries or appearance of birds foretold future good or evil.

Against this, their distinguished poet, thinking somewhat more rightly, says:

> I do not indeed believe that they possess  
> A more divine intelligence, or a greater knowledge  
> Of the fate of things. But when storm and the shifting moisture  
> Of the sky have changed their courses,  
> The beasts are changed, and the ravens, joyful in their throats, give voice.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* I.415)

He says that birds do not consciously divine, but, according to conditions in the sky, experience diverse movements. For, despising the heavier earth, they range aloft and are borne in lighter air; and with their mobile bodies, less weighed down, they lead an agile life above. On the contrary, a heavier nature presses down creeping things; and they yield to the aforesaid birds in sharpness of sense by as much as the watery element is denser than the nature of air.

Thus, when he had said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul” [Col. 0240C], it should be noted that he added nothing further. But concerning winged creatures he says, “Let the waters bring forth winged creatures,” and adds, “above the earth.” Yet even this would not have been sufficient, for creeping things also lie beneath the waters of the earth; they do not always swim, but seek sustenance from land or sand. Therefore he fittingly adds this too: “under the firmament of heaven.”

This is a full and sufficient definition of the production of birds: namely, the waters brought forth creeping things of living soul; they brought them forth, I say, but did not also send them out, although some of them, such as dolphins and seals, venture for a time to come forth outside, nature permitting. But they brought forth winged creatures and sent them out above the earth under the firmament of heaven. For this one class of living beings delights in nothing more than the freedom of flying, swimming beneath the firmament of heaven and ranging with its little wings, unlike the other creeping things which the waters retained within themselves, in the depths of those same waters and especially in river waves.

Moreover, each species of bird, according as it has denser feathers and a smaller body, flies higher and more swiftly beneath the firmament of heaven—for example, the hawk, heron, or eagle. Conversely, those whose bodies are heavy and whose feathers are sparse or small rise more slowly and fly less, such as the vulture or the ostrich, which, though it has feathers, is nevertheless wholly unable to fly.

## CHAPTER L  
Why, although the waters brought forth all birds, they cannot also live under the waters

It may now be asked why, although the waters brought forth all birds, those same birds cannot also live beneath their native waters. There are indeed birds called sea-birds, such as coots, or the small but noble halcyon, which is said to nest on the shores while the sea awaits her, so that for twice seven days, until she rears her young, its reliable calm is in no way stirred or disturbed. Yet these and the others, though produced from the waters, cannot live by the waters.

Why, then, does nature succeed them as though from a maternal womb so unlike their origin? Why can they not retain life there whence they received life? This question is indeed more difficult to solve if by “waters” we understand only the pools of a single element. But now air can rightly be called water also, since it subsists from water or through water. Hence it is said in the Epistle of the apostle Peter: “For this escapes their notice willingly: that the heavens were of old, and the earth out of water and subsisting through water by the word of God” (2 Pet. 3). Another version has: “The heavens were formerly out of water and constituted through water.” But it signifies this moist and cloudy air; and Scripture is accustomed to call this heaven. Thus it is written: “The kite knew its season in heaven” (Jer. 8).

Air, therefore, can also be understood together with the element of waters. But perhaps the contrary will be said: “In this sense it can be said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul and birds, and likewise cattle and beasts. For, as was said above, the earth too subsists out of water and through water: out of water, namely, because God said, ‘Let the waters be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear,’ and it was so; and through water because, by divine ordering, it is wholly filled within with veins of water, as the body of an animal abounds in veins of blood, lest it fail through dryness if the watering of waters ceased.”

To this I reply: after God commanded the dry land to appear and called it earth, it is no longer permissible to designate it by the name of water. But the name of air was not assigned by the same authority; it was given by human beings, who named air from its height. For Greek αἴρω (*airō*) is said in Latin *sursum tollo*, “I raise upward.” Through this air are borne masses of water raised by the sea’s exhalation. Therefore do not suppose that this region is designated by the name “firmament,” since the firmament divides waters from waters; whereas through this air, it is manifest that dense volumes of water are carried, so that clouds are almost rivers.

Therefore, when it is said, “Let the waters bring forth,” air also may be understood with them, because, when waters ascending through the spaces of air are changed into snow by the force of cold, by the same capacity and by the power of the command they could be changed into birds. Thus they were produced from waters, and yet cannot live under waters, perhaps because they did not receive life beneath dense waves, but the little bodies of flying birds were made from masses of thinner water flying through clouds.

But however they were produced, this is certain: the waters brought forth creeping things of living soul and winged creatures above the earth under the firmament of heaven [Col. 0241D], their natural limits being there established in threefold fashion by him whose command, once given, shall not pass away (Ps. 148). For it follows:

## CHAPTER LI  
Concerning the threefold distinction of the creatures which the waters brought forth

“And God created the great sea-creatures and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and winged creatures according to their kind.” Why did he distinguish them thus: “And God created the great sea-creatures and every living and moving soul,” when the great sea-creatures could have been included or jointly signified had he merely said, “And God created every living and moving soul”? For by saying this, he would have excluded neither great sea-creatures nor little fishes.

Why, then, did he distinguish them so? Clearly, in order to indicate that this creative work of the Trinity also is divided into three forms. Of living or moving beings, some come by offspring—that is, they bear young, and the sea-creatures are the largest among them; others come by egg, of which there are far more kinds. To these add every winged creature according to its kind. And behold, you have this work of creation also divided into three parts.

Further, after saying, “And God created the great sea-creatures and every living and moving soul,” he added, “which the waters had brought forth.” This could fittingly have been said in each individual work: “He created the luminaries which he had made,” and so forth. God distinctly made at once all the things he had made, in this respect: because, as has already been said, “whatever was made in him was life” (John 1). Therefore at the end of these generations it is said of all things: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day when God created heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it sprang up,” etc. In the same way as one must understand that God had created every shrub before it sprang up, so must one understand the statement now made that the waters had already brought forth every living and moving soul while God was creating them.

## CHAPTER LII  
Again, concerning the same passage: the words, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea”

“And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea; and let birds multiply above the earth.” Here it shines forth more clearly why, in these works of God, the making of each work is repeated three times. Since “what was made in him was life,” God first said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things of living soul, and winged creatures above the earth under the firmament of heaven.” Then, because what was life in him was manifested in action through visible essences, “God created,” he says, “the great sea-creatures and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their kinds, and winged creatures according to their kind.” And because each was required to subsist by its succession through that same power of the Creator, “God blessed them,” he says, saying, “Increase and multiply,” etc.

There are three words of blessing: “Increase,” “multiply,” and “fill the waters of the sea”; but the sense is one and the same, since it is again expressed by one word when it is added: “and let birds multiply above the earth.” Nor is this surprising. For there are three names, or three persons, of him who blessed; yet he is one and the same God.

But why did he who commanded the multiplication of these creatures to occur by blessing not likewise bless the green herb bearing seed, and the fruit-bearing tree, each having its seed within itself, when he commanded them to be produced from the earth, saying, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth”? Or whence comes to them such an abundance of growth or blessing in multiplication, when God did not also bless them?

For they too grow and multiply. According to the kind of each, new plants rise everywhere beside the old, tender shoots beside sturdy ones; for example, saplings grow from a small seed into beeches or oaks, and their lofty crowns gradually rise into the air. What, then, did the blessing accomplish more for the creeping things of the sea or the birds of heaven than for the shrubs of the earth in their own kind? Or in what will its effect be more certainly known?

To this I reply: the green herb and each fruit-bearing tree do indeed grow and multiply in their kind, but the manner of their growth differs according to the differing quality of their essences. For the same earth which sprouts or produces the green herb and fruit-bearing tree also multiplies them; it supplies them with seed and receives what falls, even if the hand of a sower should perhaps be absent. Thus soil alone suffices for the multiplication of their offspring.

But if creeping things and birds had no appetite, they themselves would neither grow nor multiply, and their species would not endure. Therefore, once they had received the beginning of existence, it was necessary that, by command of the same Creator, a natural love or appetite be implanted deep within them: that the male might burn with desire to impart seed, and the female likewise be eager to receive it. This blessing granted them that, and for this reason it was necessary. Thus creeping things increased and multiplied and filled the waters of the sea, and birds multiplied from them.

The great power of this blessing holds these living things in the bond of love. So long as springs are sent forth into the valleys and waters pass between the mountains, so long shall birds of heaven dwell above them and give voice from among the rocks (Ps. 103). And so long as the trees of the plain and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted are filled with the upper waters and the richness of the earth, so long shall sparrows nest there (ibid.).

By the same love or desire, the languishing hen changes her voice; and the joyful nightingale, sitting upon her little eggs, sings throughout the wakeful night with such sweetness of song that you might suppose her highest purpose to be to animate her young not less by sweet melodies than by bodily incubation. The offspring brought forth from this will, in a manner, declare evening, morning, and noon, and nature, not ungrateful, will announce the praise of the Creator (Ps. 54). The birds of heaven praise God, who gives food to all flesh (Ps. 136), with such harmony that a rational human being ought to blush if ever he has received the Creator’s gifts as food in silence, without praising him.

Likewise, so long as this great and broad sea remains, in which ships pass through (Ps. 103)—how it shall pass away is known by him who said, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24)—so long, with the power of this blessing enduring, there shall be creeping things there without number [Col. 0244A], little animals with great; and all, not created in vain, shall await him to give them food in due season. When he gives to them, they gather; when he opens his hand, all are filled with goodness (Ps. 103): whale no less than frog, crocodile no less than moray eel.

## CHAPTER LIII  
Why it was not said, “God saw that the birds or creeping things were good,” but “he saw that it was good”

“And God saw that it was good; and evening and morning came to be, the fifth day.” If human beings lived in justice as steadfastly as the things aforesaid observe their appointed order under the command of blessing, then, concerning the rightly formed human being, it could appropriately be said individually, just as it is said, “And God saw the light, that it was good”: “And God saw the human being, that he was good.”

Nevertheless, Scripture neither said nor ought to have said, “And God saw the birds of heaven or the creeping things of the sea, that they were good.” Rather, “God saw,” it says, “that it was good”—meaning, that it had thus been made. Here it is not the merit of this creature—which is nonexistent—that is praised, but the good design of the Creator is weighed. Likewise, when it is said, “And God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good,” the merits of creatures are not extolled, but—what is quite different—the wisdom of the Creator is commended.

Light alone, because it could have a will and voluntarily directed its essence toward God, was called good, as capable of the good God. Because it received him with love, it rightly received a share in the praise of divine goodness.

## CHAPTER LIV  
Why cattle and animals of the earth are assigned with humanity to the work of the sixth day

The sixth form of God’s creature is the human being, in whose essence the understanding that is sixth from fear shines forth manifestly. This is clear, for the human creature is rational and has not only understanding but also intelligence and memory; hence it can attain to the knowledge of spiritual things and to the wisdom of God.

But why are cattle, though irrational, assigned with humanity to the sixth day? For cattle surpass the five bodily senses no more than the creeping things of the sea or birds of heaven; nor are these creatures less or more devoid of reason than those. To this I reply: even if cattle are on the same level of essence as birds and creeping things of the waters, since all alike are animate and sentient bodies and can do no more, nevertheless they are rightly counted with humanity on the sixth day. For the species of cattle is also an ornament of that same part of the world to which humanity belongs—namely, the earth—and is especially appointed to humanity’s service, as we see: not birds or the creeping things produced by the waters, but cattle alone cooperate and labor with human beings.

Therefore, because the species of cattle is contiguous with those creatures—birds and fishes—by equality of condition, but contiguous with humanity by its material origin [Col. 0245A], it rightly yielded to the superior, that is, to humanity, so that it shares one day of divine operation with the one whose part of the world—namely, the earth—it ornaments. But let us now consider the very words of the Creator’s command.

## CHAPTER LV  
Concerning the threefold species of cattle, creeping things, and beasts

“Let the earth,” he says, “bring forth living soul according to its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their kinds. And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and cattle, and every creeping thing according to its kind.”

Under the one genus of living soul which the earth brings forth, Scripture plainly distinguishes three species: cattle, creeping things, and beasts. Observe carefully the providence of God’s unsearchable judgments. For it was by one of these species—that is, by a creeping thing—that humanity was deceived; by another—that is, by beasts of the earth—the same sinful human being is justly assailed; and by another—that is, cattle—the weakness of that same wretched human being is helped, God’s mercy bringing relief.

They are called *jumenta* (“beasts of burden”) because they are certain aids (*adjumenta*) to humanity; *reptilia* truly because they creep or crawl; and *bestiae* (“beasts”) are, as it were, *festiae* by antiphrasis, because they are hostile. Here the question arises how it is said to the serpent as a curse, “Upon your breast you shall go” (Gen. 3), when it had previously possessed by nature this very trait, that it crept—that is, went upon its breast. For, just as cattle, so creeping things too had already been commanded to be produced. But this will be more fittingly discussed in its proper place.

## CHAPTER LVI  
That every kind of serpent is corrupted, or venomous, because the devil used it for the death of humanity

Now it should be known that the serpent crept before, just as every animal of this species or kind now creeps; but its creeping would inspire no horror if the devil had not used it for the death of its lord, humanity. Still more, it would neither vomit deadly venom nor have it within itself if that same poisonous adulterer of God’s creation had not polluted it with the venom of his own malice and, through its mouth, as has already been said, hissed death into the human being.

Even today—to say nothing of the fact that we read that serpents were not merely harmless but even obedient to many holy servants of Christ—an entire people is reported to live safely among serpents. Hence a most distinguished Roman author says:

> … A single people inhabits the lands,  
> Unharmed by the savage bite of serpents:  
> The Marmaridan Psylli, whose tongue is a match for potent herbs.  
> Their very blood is safe and cannot admit any poison,  
> Even when the chant has ceased.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX.892 ff.)

How much more would humanity then, ruler and lord of all living creatures, have exercised lawful dominion over the creeping things of the earth, if either the devil had never hissed through the serpent’s mouth, or if humanity itself, while in honor, had understood in such a way that it did not receive the poison of his persuasion?

Therefore, the creation of all things was good; but for humanity, because it became opposed to God and burdensome to itself, those things which had been well made were justly turned to evil. Moreover, because the foreknowledge of him who made the things that were to come was not ignorant of what another—namely humanity or the devil—would do, it is not surprising that he had prepared fierce beasts and venomous animals for sinful humanity, he who had also prepared hell for the future sins of demons and human beings.

Of these, as of the others, there is no doubt that in the evening of his secret counsel God said [Col. 0246B], “Let the earth bring forth living soul according to its kind”; and in the morning—that is, in the first creation of this species—it was so. And through successive generations God now continues to make the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, cattle, and every creeping thing according to its kind.

## CHAPTER LVII  
Concerning the adulterous intermixture of cattle

This law of nature, once established, endures: each propagates its offspring according to its kind. Thus donkeys are not born from the equine species; bears are not generated from lions; stags from cattle; elephants from camels; or wild asses from buffaloes.

Yet certain adulterous products of natures arise from unequal intermixture: for example, a mule is born from a mare and an ass, and a *tityrus* [a goat-sheep hybrid] from a he-goat and a ewe. The Law forbids this to be done by human prompting, when it says: “You shall not cause your cattle to mate with animals of another kind” (Lev. 19).

Ana, son of Sebeon, son of Esau, is reported to have been the first to do this: he first caused herds of mares in the wilderness to be mounted by asses, so that new animals, mules, might be born from them contrary to nature. Yet even beasts which are not under human control intermix contrary to nature from diverse species: thus, when a lion mates with a leopard, a leopard-lion is born; and when a wolf mates with a hind, lynxes are generated.

Irregular intermixture is also found among creeping things. For natural philosophers report that the viper, a most wicked kind of creeping creature and craftier than all things of the serpent kind, when it takes up the desire to mate, seeks union with the sea-moray. Going out to the shore, it testifies to its presence by hissing and summons her to a marital embrace. The invited moray does not fail to come, and grants the poisonous serpent the desired use of her union. But enough has now been said concerning these matters. Let us proceed to the account of humanity’s creation—which is our sinful and laborious day.

# THE SECOND BOOK ON GENESIS  
(Genesis, chapter 1, verses 25–31; chapter 2, verses 1–25)

[Col. 0247]

## CHAPTER I  
[Col. 0247A] Concerning the dignity of the human creature, and that humanity was made with the counsel of the provident Trinity

**CHAPTER 1 CONTINUES.** “And God saw that it was good, and said: Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.”

Behold, having pursued from afar the wisdom of God, the maker of all things, who alone traverses the circuit of heaven and walks alone upon the waves of the sea, we have at length come to the cause which is the culmination of this purpose and work: namely, to ourselves, human beings, whom our Creator deigned to make in his own image and likeness.

For what is proposed except to contemplate the glory of the Holy Trinity, as in a mirror, through its works, and to recognize the property of each person from the character of that person’s own work? This human creature is plainly the preeminent work which the blessed Trinity in its great condescension apportioned to itself: the Father to create it, the Son to redeem it, and the Holy Spirit to set it aflame.

Let us therefore reverently hear, as is fitting, the dignity of this creation, carefully expressed not by any ordinary judge but by the finger of God, whose this Scripture is. He says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” He changed his manner of speech. For up to this point he had said concerning individual things: “Let it be,” and it was; “Let the earth bring forth”; “Let the waters bring forth,” and it was. But now, as though he had sat down weary after making the circuit of earth, heaven, and sea, and while catching his breath it occurred to him that one thing still remained which it was fitting or necessary to make, he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

“Lord,” says the prophet, “let your ancient, true counsel be fulfilled.” Do you think it a small counsel to be signified by these few little words of the Holy Trinity? It was surely a great counsel: a venerable deliberation—indeed, not so much a council as a soliloquy—of such persons as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, held concerning us sinners in the counsel of Wisdom.

Do you suppose that anything of those things done or yet to be done concerning us was absent there? Certainly the whole of our cause was set forth there in their midst; our future death or destruction was foreseen there; and from that proceeded the whole counsel, so that each person might undertake that person’s share of the work: namely, that, as has already been said, the Father might then create; the Son might later, in the fullness of time, redeem what had perished; and the Holy Spirit might accomplish the remission of sins and the resurrection of the flesh. Thus, by the common counsel of the Trinity, the desolate places of the ages might be rebuilt in humanity [Col. 0248A], and the foundations of generation upon generation raised up.

Praise to the wisdom of the Creator; honor to the grace of the Deliverer; thanksgiving to the loving-kindness of the Enlightener; worship to the one, undivided Trinity, creator, deliverer, and governor of all things. Let our mouth be filled with praise, that we may sing all day of his great glory and greatness (Ps. 70).

## CHAPTER II  
What difference there is between image and likeness, in the words: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

First, it is worth asking what difference there is between image and likeness; then it will become clear that the wording was arranged not accidentally, but with rational design, so that it was not said, “Let us make man [Col. 0248B] according to our likeness and image,” but “according to our image and likeness.” Image and likeness differ in this: an image is the image of one; likeness, however, is never the likeness of fewer than two. Now the image of God is the Son of God the Father. Thus the Apostle says of him: “who,” he says, “is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1). The Son, equally invisible, is, I say, the image of the invisible God.

Yet “image” is said in many ways: a painting on a wall or a carving in wood or stone is the image of a man or a horse; the image of the sun or moon is seen in a well. The Son is not called the image of God in that way, but in such a way that, as the Apostle says elsewhere, he is “the express figure of his substance” (Heb. 1). For just as any substance is recognized from its visible form, so God the Father is known through [Col. 0248C] his Word, which is the Son. Yet the distinctive character of a man’s substance is also called his image; in this sense the saying concerning the first man must be understood: “Adam lived one hundred and thirty years, and begot a son according to his likeness and image, and called his name Seth” (Gen. 5). Thus the son is the image of the father.

But the Holy Spirit is the likeness of the Father and the Son, for he is the common goodness or love of Father and Son. Therefore you should not suppose that it could rightly have been said, “Let us make man according to our likeness and image”; for certainly, just as the Son is not the Son of the Father and the Holy Spirit together, but of the Father alone, so he is the image not of the Father and that same Holy Spirit, but of the Father alone. Conversely, it was most rightly said, “according to our image and likeness,” because [Col. 0248D] the Holy Spirit, just as he is the common goodness or love of Father and Son, is likewise their common likeness.

## CHAPTER III. Again, on the same subject.

What, then, is meant by “Let us make man according to [Col. 0249A] our image and likeness,” except: Let us make a man who bears in himself the evident marks of our threefold operation? Consider some well-ordered man—for example, such as the one now writing these things is, or rather such as all the elect were, by whom this same blessed Trinity is to be seen in its glory. They certainly live, which they share with beasts; they discern, which they share with reprobate human beings and even with evil spirits; and they are holy or righteous, which belongs especially to the children of God. Therefore, to say, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” is to say: Let us make a living, rational man, like God.

A little earlier, speaking of brute animals, he said: “Let the earth bring forth the living creature according to its kind.” The condition of man surpasses such [Col. 0249B] a living creature by a twofold honor when it is said, “according to our image and likeness”: according to the image, namely, that he may be rational; according to our likeness, that he may be upright by following God’s righteousness. Of the first of these, namely rationality, he cannot be deprived; the second, that is, likeness to divine uprightness or righteousness, he cannot attain except through grace. But the capacity for rationality, which a human being cannot lack, is an instrument or, as it were, an eye for seeking God’s likeness. Thus he is without excuse when he has not attained the likeness of God, because he refused to use a good instrument for the purpose for which it was given him.

But when God first made man, he made him not only rational but also endowed with the honor [Col. 0249C] of his likeness. For Scripture says: “God made man upright; but he entangled himself in many inquiries” (Eccl. 7). Now, however, having been deceived, he has indeed lost the honor of God’s likeness; but the capacity of reason remains in him, by which he may hear the one who calls him back and may follow him as guide and teacher toward his restoration.

## CHAPTER IV. Why it was not said, “according to our likeness and image,” but “according to our image and likeness.”

Therefore, God, wishing this creature to be rational and a participant in his holiness, said: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” Scripture did not say that God said, “Let man be made according to [Col. 0249D] our image and likeness,” and man was made, as he said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. Why? Clearly because it was necessary that the completed man should stand in the image and likeness of his Creator, not all at once, but through labor.

For the angelic creature, once made, will neither be moved among those who stood nor restored to its former state among those who fell. But man, after his first creation, was to fall and was to be renewed by the merciful One’s re-creation. Therefore the three Persons encourage one another, as it were, saying: “Let us make.” Yet it should be known that both the fewer words in which it was said, “Let there be light,” and these fuller words, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” signify the equal dignity or glory of the elect [Col. 0250A] angels and human beings. For the elect angel, because he is light, was made and perfected according to God’s image and likeness; and the human being who was made and restored according to God’s image and likeness is light. Since each is rational, each was made according to God’s image; and since each is rightly ordered and subject to God, each was made according to God’s likeness. Thus, just as the former is light, or an angel of light, so the latter too is called light and a child of light.

Likewise, just as the words “Let there be light” indicate that only the elect angels are the Creator’s concern and exclude the angels of darkness, although he also created them, so this expression, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” embraces only those whom he predestined to life and does not admit those who were to be born superfluously [Col. 0250B] beyond the number from the root later corrupted. Thus, if it is asked why Scripture represents God as saying, “Let there be light,” when he could have said, “Let angels be made,” or “Let spirits be made,” we ask why the same God said all this: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” when he could simply have said, “Let us make man,” and this could have sufficed ordinary understanding to indicate that he meant the substance which we are.

The cases are parallel, so that to each you may rightly answer that it did not belong to the mouth of the Lord to command concerning those whom he himself does not know. By no name, however, could he better express the angels who belong to him alone than by the name of light; nor, likewise, could he better designate the human beings whom he had ordained to eternal life than by this definition: “Let us make man according to [Col. 0250C] our image and likeness.” Thus here and there God, through this his interpreter, expressed in fitting words in his Scripture his own angels and his own human beings, and distinguished them with sufficient economy of language from others who do not belong to him. Let us now proceed with the order of the text.

## CHAPTER V. On human dominion: “And let him rule over the birds of the air, the fish of the sea, and the beasts of the earth.”

After God had said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” he immediately added: “And let him rule over the birds of the air, the fish of the sea, all the beasts of the earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon [Col. 0250D] the earth.” This part of the divine utterance extends more broadly than the preceding words, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.” For it embraces every human being. Why does man rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the beasts, and the creeping things of the earth, except because he himself is rational while they are irrational? This difference indeed sets man far above all of them, because he rules over them not merely in such a way as to be more worthy, but also so as to be able to tame the natures of them all. Therefore, for a human being to rule over them, it is enough that he be rational.

But it is altogether certain that the greater part of humankind, though endowed with reason, is empty of God’s likeness; and although all, as already said, being made in God’s image, rule over all living creatures, very many are rebellious against God and not subject to him, and are therefore far from God’s likeness. Thus the words, “And let them rule over the birds of the air,” and the rest, extend more broadly than the saying, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” because all human beings rule over beasts, whereas only the elect have been made—indeed, perfected—according both to the image and likeness of God.

Let human beings, then, rule over beasts by nature; but let God’s human beings rule over human beings by grace. Or rather, because “when they were in honor, they did not understand,” human beings are, through their fault, compared with beasts (Ps. 48 [49]); but those who glorified God or gave thanks to him in the dignity of their nature should be like God and should be called, and be, children of God, as the Apostle John says (1 John 3). It follows:

## CHAPTER VI. Why the writer who followed did not say, “And God created man according to his image and likeness,” but only “according to his image.”

“And God created man according to his image; according to the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.” What does it mean that this writer, after reporting that God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” omitted one of the two when he said: “And God created man according to his image; according to the image of God he created him”? Did he by accident or forgetfulness diminish in his own account, by so great a part, the human condition which in God’s utterance he had so nobly exalted by both parts? [Col. 0251C] Certainly not. Rather, he knowingly expressed in God’s words what God intended, and carefully observed in his own account what had been received.

For when God said, “Let us make man,” he certainly intended to make him according to his image and likeness. But when this writer wrote it, man had lost God’s likeness through sin. He indeed knew that no one could turn aside that divine purpose; and in this faith or knowledge, when the Lord looked upon him, his face shone (Exod. 34). Nevertheless, no certain person had yet arisen in whom the recovered glory of that divine likeness, which had perished in the person of the first man, could be displayed without any contradiction. There were saints, there were righteous persons—among the foremost of whom was Moses himself—but only through faith and hope in the man to come, who would be made according to God’s image and likeness by being born of a virgin, so as to pour God’s likeness, lost in the children of Adam, back into them, making them like himself and his own children, abolishing the old and restoring a new origin.

Therefore, after writing that God said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” he wrote only this: “God created man according to his image,” so that you may understand: he would someday re-create him according to his likeness. For he had not yet, in a sense, made according to his image and likeness the one who had become vain and lost the glory of that likeness [Col. 0252A]; he had made him only according to his image.

It should be noted that whatever God is said to have made endures, and whatever he is written to have named is stable. It is said that God made the firmament and called it heaven, and it remains; it is said that he planted paradise, and it remains; and so on. Conversely, things that move on the earth and in the sea do not remain, but some continually replace others. Therefore Scripture carefully did not say, “God said: Let the creeping things of the sea and the beasts of the earth be made,” whose existence swiftly passes away; rather, God said, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things; let the earth bring forth cattle or beasts.” And rightly so, for the very nature of bringing forth remains.

Thus, following a fixed consistency, it is said that “God created man according to his image,” because this had been so made that it could neither be lacking nor fail: for man is rational and eternal, because he was made according to God’s image. It did not say the whole thing, “God created man according to his image and likeness,” because that had not yet been done in such a way that it could not be changed.

## CHAPTER VII. That woman, equally with man, was made according to God’s image.

Further, why did he repeat this very point a second time, saying: “And God created man according to his image; according to the image of God he created him”? He immediately made it clear by adding: “Male and female he created them.” For “man” is the name not of one sex only but of both, and each sex was created according to God’s image, because each is rational and eternal. Therefore, on account of the two sexes, he appropriately gave a double statement of creation according to God’s image.

Accordingly, as the Apostle says with great caution, “A man ought not to cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11); and the same Apostle immediately adds: “But woman is the glory of man” (ibid.). He did not say, “Woman is the image and glory of man,” but says, “Woman is the glory of man.” Giving the reason, he says: “For man is not from woman, but woman from man” (ibid.). For woman, equally with man, is the image of God; yet, on account of the condition or material of her origin, woman is in a certain respect the glory of man.

Thus he repeated for the second time, “According to the image of God he created him,” and immediately added, “Male and female [Col. 0252D] he created them,” plainly indicating that God made both male and female according to his image, or that he made the male no more than the female according to his image; because there, as the same Apostle says—there, I say, where man was made according to God’s image—“there is neither male nor female,” for example, in ruling more over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and every living creature of the earth, as male rather than female.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the blessing expressed in the words, “Increase and multiply.”

“And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subject it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, and all living creatures that move upon the earth.” In the grace of this blessing, the purpose of God surely resounds—the purpose which the Apostle has in view when, after saying, “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” [Col. 0253A] (Rom. 8), he immediately adds, “to those who are called saints according to his purpose” (ibid.).

Because this purpose could in no way be turned aside by intervening evils, he then attaches the sequence of its outcomes in a beautiful gradation: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (ibid.). This blessing, I say, commends that purpose of God, by which, having before his eyes only those belonging to his grace, foreknown and predestined before the ages, he then blessed them in the first roots of our race, male and female; and at the fullness of time he will glorify the two who have been called and justified, saying to them when assembled and placed at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

But the excess number of the lost, not unknown but already condemned, is designated where, after sin, the same God says to the woman: “I will multiply your sufferings and your conceptions” (Gen. 3).

## CHAPTER IX. Again, what “Increase and multiply” means, and to what extent human beings ought to have multiplied had they not sinned.

“Increase,” he says, “and multiply” (Gen. 3). Increase, namely, in the dignity of virtues, and multiply in numerical quantity. “Increase,” I say, “and multiply”—that is, up to the kingdom of heaven and to the fixed number, which surely is known only to him to whom even all the hairs of our head are numbered (Matt. 10).

Moreover, what follows—“and fill the earth”—is common to elect and reprobate alike, since all alike fill the earth by being born and living in the same way. But they are distinguished in what follows: “and subject it.” For the elect alone, whose land is the land of the living, subject to themselves by the freedom of their minds this earth which they have filled with their bodies; for, setting God alone before themselves, they steadfastly despise all earthly things.

Do the reprobate also subject the earth to themselves when they turn it with the plow or seize it by arms? Yes, certainly, in some manner they subject the earth. But this or that mode of subjection is not from God’s blessing, since, on the contrary, because of sin it was said to man: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). Nor did savagery discover weapons through the grace of blessing, but through covetousness. Therefore these words also—“Subject it, and rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, the beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth”—are the fruit of blessing, manifest in the elect. Earthly things or brute animals cannot subject them, nor will they be able to do so, through covetousness, as they do the reprobate, of whom it is written: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48 [49]).

Yet those also rule over all living creatures by the dignity of reason; they rule, I say, merely in that respect. But these do not rule merely in any fashion: they also exercise dominion in that honor by which they are devoutly subject to God. This blessing, given to the first human beings, is effective for increase and multiplication.

There have, however, been some who thought that those human beings would not have begotten children unless, after committing sin, they had been expelled from paradise. Such people, beyond doubt, hold the highly absurd opinion that human sin was necessary to God, who wished human beings to be born—as if he could not have made human nature such that it would generate unless sin had assisted it. But a lengthy argument against this is unnecessary, since God says, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” and his utterance is the constitution of nature: not only of human nature for generating, but also of the earth’s nature for bringing forth plants.

It is more pleasing to think that, if man had not sinned, such a great and vicious progeny would not have sprung from his flesh; rather, he would have produced only the fruit of the blessing already mentioned, that is, all and only the elect—not rushing into lust after the manner of beasts, but, under the governance of reason and through the pure nature of the flesh, building up the predestined progeny of heaven. For sin did not bring in the power of generating; it corrupted the instruments of generation and took honor from the race.

Let us consider why it was necessary for the burning heat of lust to be implanted deeply in beasts, and we shall undoubtedly recognize that it did not belong to man to receive that same heat as a monitor in his flesh for generating. For when God said to the other living creatures, “Increase and multiply, fill the waters of the sea, and let birds multiply from them,” they themselves did not understand what God wished, or that the race of each could be propagated from the union of male and female. Therefore they necessarily received a monitor, the burning spur of their flesh, so that the male may leap upon the female in the raging storm of lust, with no awareness of propagating offspring; and thus the brute ignorance of the creature serves the Creator who knows.

But man is rational. Therefore, if he had loved his Creator and wished to build his household in devout love, he would have needed no other monitor. Knowing and prudent, he would have begotten citizens for the heavenly commonwealth, and would have devoted the service of his flesh to that work with the same piety with which a priest or bishop now devotes his tongue or voice to the work of regenerating well through God’s grace in Christ those who have been born badly into this world.

But he, corrupted by a diabolical spirit, desired not to beget for God but to be like God himself; he was carried away by such perversity that he preferred to produce children for his own honor or name rather than for the glory of his Creator. For the serpent’s promise, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3), must not be understood as though it meant, “You shall be like angels,” since God, striking that presumption and vain hope with the gravest irony, said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us,” thereby indicating in himself the same plurality of persons which he had indicated above when he said, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness.”

Would one who desired to generate for God’s honor not rather have wished to be free from the work of generation, when he himself desired to be like God? God the avenger therefore rightly rose against the contumacious man and hurled against his adversary the beastly weapons of lust, so that he who could have begotten for God in honor and the delights of love might generate, bound and chained as a slave, in punishment and shame.

Whenever any cultivated person feels the barbarous tumult of this lust, he rightly cries out and says with the Psalmist: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger; for your arrows are fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand upon me. There is no health in my flesh because of your wrath” (Ps. 37 [38]), and so forth. But a more suitable occasion for speaking of these and similar matters will come later. For now it is enough to say that the use of generation was given to man not through sin but through God’s blessing, and that by this blessing only the elect were sent forth to be generated or born, so that someday, without passing through death, they may be transferred into the ethereal paradise and joined in glory to the blessed angels—a glory which the transgressing angel lost.

## CHAPTER X. On the words: “Behold, I have given you every herb,” and so forth, “that they may be food for you.”

“And God said: Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed upon the earth, and every tree that has within itself the seed of its own kind, that they may be food for you; and for all living creatures of the earth, every bird of the air, and all things that move upon the earth and in which there is a living soul, that they may have them for food. And it was so.”

Just as, in speaking of the man whom God created according to his image, Scripture said that he created them male [Col. 0255C] and female, without saying how or in what order he first made the man and then made the woman from the man, so now Scripture similarly recounts in general that God said to man and all living creatures of the earth: “Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing herb upon the earth and every tree having within itself the seed of its kind, that they may be food for you.” It says that he had given man for food not trees of any sort, but the trees of paradise, which far surpass all the riches of this age; and that he forbade him one of them all.

For the history is not yet complete; rather, this is the division of the days, in which the kinds of God’s work are certainly and very clearly distinguished. When these have been completed, then at last—setting aside the rest—the history concerning man is to begin. “Behold,” he says, “I have given you”: this gift of God is the placing or constitution of nature. For not human reason alone knows taste; the throat also, and the appetitive nature of all living creatures, perceives that these things have been given it for food. They desire them by a natural motion, so that in gluttonous birds especially you may see even their stomachs leap up to their open throats as they hurry to snatch the food set before them, given to them, with nature itself bearing witness.

Thus, by saying, “Behold, I have given,” he did not point with his finger to every herb and tree; rather, he founded in the stomachs of these living creatures their natural appetite for them. And this applies not only to creatures which are known to be, or called, animate beings or animals, but also to little worms, which ordinary usage disdains to call animate beings or animals. Therefore Scripture was not content to say “for all living creatures of the earth,” but added, “and for all things that move upon the earth.” Still further, lest anything be lacking, it added, “and in which there is a living soul.” For there are some things which live indeed but are immobile, possessing sense alone and lacking all other powers of thought, such as sea-shells and other things which, clinging to rocks, are nourished.

Scripture indicates that not even these were excluded from divine providence, when, not content with saying “for all living creatures of the earth” and “for all things that move upon the earth,” it added further, “and in which there is a living soul.” And this utterance of the Creator, as has already been said, is the establishment of natural appetite. Hence it significantly says at once: “And it was so.” For what came to be so, except that the nature of things which are born and live endures according to the command of him who spoke, producing, as the Psalmist says, “grass for cattle, and herb for the service of human beings, that he may bring bread from the earth, and wine that gladdens the heart of man; that he may make his face cheerful with oil, and bread may strengthen the heart of man; that the trees of the field may be filled, and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted” (Ps. 103 [104])?

Otherwise they would not live, just as the herb itself, or any tree whatever, would neither be green nor fruit-bearing unless, competing as though sucking with a mouth, it drew by its roots the earth’s moisture. This is the common yet wonderful banquet prepared by God for everything that grows from the earth: its shoots drink the maternal moisture of the earth through their roots, and gradually convey that same moisture, grown and thickened in the grain of herbs and the fruit of trees, into the mouths and teeth of all living creatures.

Nature would be content with these foods, if an unrestrained greediness had not increased through the habit of gluttony in human beings and even in beasts. A distinguished pagan author also declaims thus:

> … O lavish extravagance of things,  
> Never content with scant provisions,  
> And earth- and sea-searcher for food;  
> Ambitious hunger, and the glory of a sumptuous table:  
> Learn with how little life may be sustained.  
> They do not drink from gold and myrrh; rather, from a small stream  
> Life returns. For peoples, a river and Ceres are enough.  
> (LUC. an. lib. IV, *Phars.* 373).

“Yet every creature of God is good,” says the Apostle, “and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4). For the authority of the same God came to the aid of wretched human beings, now weaker than they would have been in paradise. For God says to Noah: “I have delivered all the fish of the sea into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you. As the green herb, I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood” (Gen. 9), and so forth.

## CHAPTER XI. That God saw “all things which he had made, and they were very good”; and why it was not said, “God saw that man was good.”

“And God saw all things which he had made, and they were very good.” In man, ruler of all earthly things, all the things that had hitherto been made and had separately pleased him were at last adorned with a universal praise of goodness, Scripture saying: “And God saw all things which he had made, and they were very good.”

It should be noted that, although man is capable of divine goodness, being rational, it was nevertheless not said: “And God saw man, that he was good,” as it had been said: “And God saw the light, that it was good.” This was because the human being who did not understand that it was good for him to cleave to God had not yet deserved singular praise. Yet both he and the other things which so great a Maker had made according to his wisdom are called very good. And rightly, at the final creation of man, all things were praised together: for all these things beneath the firmament of heaven were made for man; man contains in himself the essences of all things; and, by the one privilege of rationality, which is best, he surpasses them all.

For a clearer manifestation of the degrees of being, we must return to the beginning of this worldly creation. The firmament dividing the waters from the waters exists indeed, but its existence is subject, among all the senses, to sight alone. The earth exists, and its existence is apprehended both by sight and touch. The heavenly lights exist, and their existence is known both by our sight and by their heat; moreover, they are always in motion. In motion, I say, locally—not simply, as the firmament is; nor as the earth is, in the motion of changing qualities; but in local motion in a twofold manner. For they are carried around daily by the movement of the firmament, and, besides this, as has already been said above, they unceasingly run and return by their own motions into their circuits.

The being of living creatures surpasses the being of these things, since they are not only subject to our senses but themselves employ the five senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Finally, above all these things and above the five bodily senses, man has also the use of reason. Therefore, in him to whom all these things are subject, and who presides over all in dignity, all things rightly please God and are judged very good.

## CHAPTER XII. Again, on the sixth day, and what the sixth day is.

“And evening and morning were the sixth day.” Rightly, as has already been said, the spirit of understanding is placed by the prophet in the sixth place after the spirit of fear (Isa. 11), because here, after the judgment of the proud and condemned angels, in the sixth place—that is, on the sixth day—man was found to be created, in whom understanding plainly flourishes.

This great day presents a great and long spectacle to the world, angels, and human beings. For through the work of this creation the manifold wisdom of God is made known especially to principalities and powers in the heavenly places (Eph. 3). In this work hitherto, and from it now and forever, God is wonderful—wonderful and glorious, terrible and praiseworthy, performing marvels at which we wonder.
