But let us first look upon the seventh day set above this sixth day, concerning which he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XIII. On the seventh day, and what the seventh day is.

**(CHAPTER II)** “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had accomplished. And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make. These are the generations of heaven and earth when they were created, in the day when God created heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose in the earth, and every herb of the region before it sprouted.”

All this text commends the seventh day. And what that day is has already been said above at the beginning of the days: namely, that it is the first day, and that it is set above the other days, not as lesser and subsequent to them, but as far more worthy. For this day is the splendor of the Father’s glory, light from light and the fountain of light, the day of days enlightening the days, the true and unfailing sun itself: a day not made, but making every day.

The particular character [Col. 0258B] or proper dignity of this day must be carefully considered here. First, it differs from the other days in that it has neither evening nor morning. For Scripture did not say, “And evening and morning were the seventh day,” as it had said, “And evening and morning were the sixth day,” “And evening and morning were the fifth day,” and similarly of all the others. Nor did it even say, “And the seventh day was made.” Catholic faith agrees that it ought altogether to be said as has been stated. For this day was born, not made; begotten, not created. How, then, could it have evening and morning, or how could it rightly be called made?

For of each of the other days you rightly say, “There was a time when it was not,” since there was evening when it was not, and morning came to be when each began to exist. But to say of this day, “There was a time when it was not,” or to suppose that any evening preceded it, or that a new morning was ever essential to it, belongs to heretics. For Catholic faith knows nothing else concerning this day except that it is. Thus there is this great difference between it and all the other days: of them it is said, “And evening and morning were one day,” or “the sixth day”; but this day, because it was not made but was and is before all things, is abruptly introduced thus: “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and he rested,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XIV. Again, on the difference between the seventh day and the other days.

Then this differs from the other days as well: the work of the other days was completed in it. For thus [Col. 0258D] he says: “And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and he rested from all his work which he had accomplished.” And it must be carefully noted that it was not said, “And God completed on the seventh day all his work which he had made,” as it is immediately said, “and he rested from all his work which he had accomplished”; but, “God,” he says, “completed his work which he had made.” For not every work of God which he had made is completed on this blessed and glorious day; rather, only the work of rational creation—its glory—is brought to fulfillment.

Accordingly, not this firmament or heaven, not sea and dry land, not the earth’s shoots or plants, not sun and moon, not the creeping things of the sea or birds of heaven, not cattle, beasts, or creeping things of the earth, but rational creation alone—namely, angelic [Col. 0259A] light, and man made in the image and likeness of God—behold the holy brightness of this day. Thus it was rightly not said, “God completed on the seventh day all his work,” but, “He completed on the seventh day his work which he had made”: a certain work of his, a certain creature of his—his rational creature, which he had made. Yet he rested from all his work which he had accomplished. He rested, I say, from all his work, because thereafter he made no new kind of creature. But a certain work, that is, the angelic creature, he then completed in this seventh day, in which he himself rested; and on that same day he was at some time to complete, in the same blessedness of wisdom, the multitude of the human race, forechosen and to be born from those two, male and female.

For what is the completion of rational [Col. 0259B] creation except eternally, or immortally, to behold the brightness of this day? For to this end tends the whole predestination of God concerning those whom he foreknew, both human beings and angels—“all who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8)—that he might make them conformed to the image of his Son. Yet with this distinction: he, because he is the only-begotten, is therefore also the first-born among many brethren. There the work of God is indeed completed, where those who were made through him are re-formed to him. This is the beginning and this is the end of the work. Hence he himself says: “I am A, and the first and the last, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1).

In his own day God, so great a worker, rests, having long had the holy angels as participants in his rest. For in that day they were made steadfast, in that day rewarded, and each in his own rank glorified [Col. 0259C].

## CHAPTER XV. On the Nine Orders of Angels

For nine orders of them are named in authoritative Scriptures: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim. Since it is agreed that chosen human beings are gathered into their fellowship, each into his own order, and that they will be like those same holy angels—some higher than others according to the differing ranks of their order and degrees of brightness, which are understood from the names of the orders set down above—many suppose as a consequence that sinful angels fell from all the angelic orders. Yet no Scripture reports this.

As though it were one thing for holy [Col. 0259D] angels to be made steadfast and another for them to be divided into nine orders. For example: if, before the chosen spirits were made steadfast, some were already thrones, others cherubim, and others seraphim, what did they afterward receive through being made steadfast? For what can be added to this steadfastness or firmament which is the burning of divine love, understood by the name *seraphim*? Or in what can a creature be established more highly than in being the throne of God? Therefore the orders were not already distinct before the apostate angels fell; rather, after they fell, those who remained were ordered, and distinguished into nine orders, in the reward in which they were made steadfast.

Otherwise the evangelical woman (Luke 15) would have had not merely ten but eleven drachmas [Col. 0260A]; not one drachma only, but two, would have been lost; and the others also would have been diminished, if one order of already ordered angels fell and carried off with it portions from the other orders. But far be this. For the Wisdom of God had only ten drachmas; and this one which is sought, before it was lost—indeed, before it was created—was, according to God’s foreknowledge or predestination, both the tenth and one of those ten.

Therefore the orders of holy angels belong to the Sabbath; and from the time when they rested, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues, cherubim, and seraphim are what they are. On the same day on which God rested, they too were fulfilled with blessed rest; and whoever has once entered that rest shall never toil eternally.

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 0260B] On What Was Said: “He Blessed the Seventh Day and Sanctified It”

“And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make.” Is it doubtful that the Father blessed and sanctified this day of eternity? The one who is himself first blessed and sanctified says to the Jews: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10).

Did he say this without the authority or testimony of Scripture? Certainly not. Just as, when the same Jews asked him, “Who are you?”, he looked to this Scripture and said: “The Beginning, who also speak to you” [Col. 0260C] (John 8); for in the beginning God created heaven and earth in no one other than his Word. So likewise, after he had said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and they said that he blasphemed, looking to this Scripture he said: “Do you say of him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?”

For he did not say, “whom the Father sent into the world and sanctified,” lest you suppose this referred to the blessing of his assumed flesh or to the sanctification of the human nature he assumed; rather, he said, “sanctified,” and then “sent into the world.” And the Prophet in the psalm speaks of this day as one that would come and illuminate the whole world: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.” And immediately: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity. Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117 [118]).

He called blessed this day which the Lord made, and said that the same day would come in the name of the Lord—of whom it is clear and certain that he has now come. Then, rejoicing, he says: “God and Lord”—understand, “is this day”—“and he has shone upon us. Establish a solemn day amid dense boughs, as far as the horn of the altar” [Col. 0260D] (ibid.). That is: cease from the servile work of sin; in contemplation amid “dense boughs,” that is, amid a multiplicity of good works, see that this day is the prince of the altar, who, since he is God and Lord, ought rightly to be worshipped.

“But what then?” you ask. “Did not the same Lord make all the days already described before this seventh day?” For unless he made the others in one manner and this one in another, how could he say of this one alone, “This is the day which the Lord has made,” plainly intending this as its distinctive property, that the Lord made it? He did indeed make it, but he made this one differently and the others differently. For he made the others by creating them, but he made this day from himself by begetting it—just as this visible sun makes the visible day. It does not make it by working outside itself, but by sending forth brightness from itself.

Therefore this day which the Lord made—who, when the Prophet wrote the things just predicted about him, was still to come, but who now has come, blessed in the name of the Lord—is he whom we confess as the Father’s Son, blessed before the ages, who is, as the Apostle says, “Christ, God over all, blessed for ever” [Col. 0261A] (Rom. 9). Blessed, I say, and sanctified: for the Father, as has already been said, sanctified him and sent him into the world.

## CHAPTER XVII. What That Rest of the Day Is

But what need was there to say or write that the Father blessed and sanctified him in whom the sum of all blessing and holiness consists? What need, I say, was there for this to be written, except to signify that the cursed and unsanctified—whoever misuse earthly and evil days—are not to rest in such a day? For of such people he says: “But they have not known my ways; therefore I swore in my wrath: if they shall enter into my rest” (Ps. 94 [95]).

This day of rest, joy, and exultation is blessed and sanctified, because it has been prepared from the foundation of the world for those blessed by God the Father who keep the sanctification of the Spirit 29 [Col. 0261C] (Matt. 25). Yet it should be known that in that day, so good and so blessed, we rest in one way and God in another. We, truly weary, truly pilgrims and captives, when our present captivity has been released, shall there breathe freely as those comforted; and after labours and burdens here, we shall be refreshed, finding rest for our souls. But God rests in that day in such a way that he has never laboured, since he merely spoke and all things were made (Ps. 148).

What, then, is meant by “God rested on this day,” except that this day is compared with the others? For weigh all the days written above: apart from two—namely angel and human being—there is nothing capable in itself of preparing a place for God. God indeed dwells in these; but first God himself must prepare a dwelling for himself in them, so that he may work through the arm of his strength and build the grace in which the glory of his name may be worthily established for rest [Col. 0261D]. For no angel or human being becomes fit for his habitation except through the laborious working of his grace.

Thus he himself first works in them; and before his house or dwelling is completed, he as it were labours. Hence, uttering the complaint of one weary, he says: “I have laboured while enduring” (Isa. 1). But this day alone—his only Son—just as he did not create but beget him, so he did not make him good through an accidental gift, but always possessed him good through essential goodness. This alone is he in whom God did no labour at all in making him righteous, nor ever exercised patience while awaiting his progress.

For the creation of angels and human beings he expended the resources of his wisdom; and for saving or separating them he built up mercy and judgment at great expense on both sides, so that the whole world marvels and the entire court of heaven has long magnified it. In this one alone there was never anything that resisted him, whether he rested in his bosom or, about to serve at his command, put on the nature of our flesh [Col. 0262A]. Therefore this is the one in whom God rested; and he rests over us only insofar as we are conformed to him. Thus this most holy Scripture—not of a human being, but of the finger of God—says: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had accomplished; and he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why It Was Not Said, “From All His Work Which God Created and Made,” but “Which He Created in Order to Make”

Here a great and wonderful statement is pressed upon us, even if we are unwilling or pretend not to see it: “because on it he ceased from all his work which God created in order to make.” He did not say, “from all his work which he created or made,” but, “which he created in order to make,” because before he made all things in those days in their distinct essences described above, he created them in this seventh day. He created, I say, heaven and earth before he made them; he created every shrub of the field before it sprang up [Col. 0262C].

“Then,” you ask, “did he first create what he afterward made?” Certainly it is so. For the letter conveys this sense and compels the hearer to it. If you have not heard it—if perhaps you have dozed—the writer himself immediately pulls and strikes you with the hand of his own question, asking what you ought to have asked: “When were these generations of heaven and earth created?” And immediately he answers: “In the day when God created heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it sprang up, and every green herb before it germinated.”

Thus it was well and excellently said: “which God created in order to make.” For, as has often already been said, “what was made in him was life.” Therefore, when it is said, “He who lives for ever created all things together” [Col. 0262D] (Sir. 18), let us understand: before he made them. For here we have, “he created in order to make”: he created all things together in his wisdom, in order that he might make each of them in its own proper essence.

For you must not suppose that “he created all things together” means that everything at once existed in its proper species or forms, so that neither green herb nor fruit-bearing trees were even a moment younger than heaven and earth. The text continues, as it says: “For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground; but a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Gen. 2). Therefore, when heaven and earth already existed, every shrub of the field and every green herb did not yet immediately exist; but those shrubs of the field which grow of themselves grew gradually, and the soil, cultivated by man, brought forth many things which the earth of his exile would not produce of itself [Col. 0263A].

Therefore this blessed and sanctified day is he in whom God created all things together, seeing all things simultaneously present in him which he was to make separately; and he rested in him in whom he created, through whom he made all things. This seventh day is called and is Wisdom. Hence, in the often-mentioned prophet, the Spirit of wisdom is placed seventh, after fear (Isa. 11).

Accordingly Wisdom itself speaks thus: “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything; from the beginning, from eternity, I was ordained, and before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the fountains of the deep had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood in their massive weight; before the hills I was brought forth” (Sir. 24). And shortly afterward: “I was with him arranging all things, and I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the circle of the earth; and my delights were to be with the children of men.”

Therefore God did not first rest in his day after all things had been made; rather, before he made anything, he rested in him in that kind of rest which is rightly called the play and delight of Wisdom. This Wisdom played through each day; and through each act of play God, seeing and delighting, said, “It is good.” For it is written, and has already been said above, that God saw that it was good, and that he saw all things which he had made, and they were very good. God, the craftsman, greatly delighted in himself in this Wisdom.

Hence, when this same incarnate Wisdom was baptized [Col. 0263C], he declared her by this witnessing voice: “You are my beloved Son; in you I have been well pleased” (Matt. 3). He did not say, “In you I am well pleased,” lest you think that only what he was beginning to do—saving the world through him—pleased him, though that work is highly praiseworthy. Rather, “In you,” he says, “I have been well pleased,” affirming that this is he through whom, while he made all things, the good worker delighted in himself in each thing, seeing that it was good.

He who was incarnate, who came blessed in the name of the Lord—he, I say, is the seventh day in whom God rested, in whom, before making all things, he created: none other than the Word of God, God the Word, the only-begotten Son of God.

## 30 CHAPTER XIX. On the Law of the Carnal Sabbath

[Col. 0263D] Therefore even the law of the carnal Sabbath was holy, just, and good (Rom. 7). For just as the sign of circumcision foretold the incarnation, and the sacrifice of the paschal lamb foretold the future passion, of the same only-begotten Son of God, so that Sabbath observance announced the rest laid up after this life for the saints and elect, where God rests in the light of his wisdom, and where he has prepared that rest itself for them as a reward.

But the spiritual person strives to keep Sabbath not on one day of the week but at all times, always attentive to the Word of God, according to the Psalmist, who speaks of this Sabbath—or rather, according to the Lord of Sabbaths himself, who speaks through him: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45 [46]). Be still from the activities of the world, and in holy, quiet study see that the Lord is God: this is the beginning of that Sabbath, which we also call the contemplative life. Truth himself testifies that it is the better part: “Mary,” he says, “has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from her” [Col. 0264A] (Luke 10).

Knowing that its sweetness already breathes gently upon its lovers in the present life, the same Lord elsewhere says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. I).

Having thus counted the six days of the generations of heaven and earth, together with the seventh, which is God’s rest, Scripture now at last returns to the sixth, that is, to man, and begins the history from that creation of the same man which it had already touched upon above. For it continues:

## CHAPTER XX. That God Made Man from the Mud of the Earth; and on the Apostle’s Saying, “O Man, Who Are You to Answer Back to God?”

“Therefore the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth, breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” It had already said above that God created man, but it had not said how or from what he made him. It had said that he created them male and female, but it had not said that he made the female from the male.

If, concerning the creation of male and female, it had said nothing more than it had said above—“he created them male and female”—perhaps we would similarly suppose that God created male and female simultaneously, so that neither was created before the other, but they suddenly appeared and first beheld one another. So, for example, even today there is disagreement among learned persons concerning the sun and moon: some say that when God created the moon he immediately showed it full, setting it opposite the sun and separated from it by half the heaven; others, conversely, maintain that, as he made them together, so he set them in conjunction, so that the moon gradually emerged from beneath the sun’s side as it increased in borrowed light [Col. 0264C].

This kind of doubt is removed by the historical narrative, which begins thus: “Therefore the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth.” The male alone must be understood here, because afterward the female was formed from the male. “He formed,” it says, “from the mud of the earth.” Two things are said, and it is worthwhile to attend carefully to them: namely, that he formed, and that he formed not from just anywhere, but from the mud of the earth.

Holy persons, reflecting on this as was fitting, called their Creator himself the potter and called themselves clay—though beautiful works prepared for glory and honour—in an elegant confession and tearful declaration. “And now, O Lord,” Isaiah says, “you are our Father, and we are clay; you are our potter, and all of us are the work of your hands” (Isa. 64). And our same Potter, God, says to Jeremiah: “Shall I not be able to do with you, house of Israel, as this potter does? Behold, as clay is in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel” [Col. 0265A] (Jer. 18), etc.

For he had shown him a potter making his work upon the wheel. “And,” it says, “the vessel which he himself was making from clay with his hands was spoiled; and he turned and made it into another vessel, as it pleased him in his eyes to make it” (Isa. 45). Hence the same Isaiah, who says above: “Woe to him who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among earthen potsherds” (ibid.).

Knowing these and similar passages, the heavenly lawyer Paul says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Can what is formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have authority from the same clay to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” (Rom. 9). Thus, when we read that the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth, we should not investigate why he did it in this way. Rather, each of us should fear this for himself: lest the vessel he made be spoiled in his hands, and, after casting it aside, he make another vessel as it pleased him in his eyes to make it [Col. 0265B].

Yet we may soberly inquire—that is, wonder—why God was able to rebuild the ruins of angels with new angels, and to create as many at once as had fallen and raise them into heaven, so that all the people and all the nobility of the heavenly country might be of one kind; but made human beings of another nature or condition, to restore them in place of angels; and why he did not create all, or many, at once, but formed only one, from whom the rest should be propagated. It is not improper for us, as has been said, to inquire soberly into this and similar questions; and the Apostle’s rebuke, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”, was not made on our account, nor was that saying of the Lord, spoken because of mockers, addressed to the apostles: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7).

For we do not seek high things in order to answer back to God or presume to comprehend his judgments, but so that, drawing near to his feet, we may receive from his teaching. Thus we receive also the answer presently given, with which it is fitting that we be content: God, the maker of all things, brought forth from the treasury of his heart what he possessed. The Evangelist says to us concerning his Word: “What was made in him was life” (John 1). Must not, therefore, works such as that life was in him be made outwardly? Lift up your eyes, if you have them, and see the Wisdom of God playing not in a narrow theatre but in the world, and delighting with the children of men [Col. 0265D] (Sir. 24). Consider what and how great things she has made, what and how great things she has said, while thus playing with the children of men. Have the inhabitants of heaven been instructed by contemplating this play—or these delights—which he had with the children of men, and does some little man disdain it as though it were a superfluous game? Indeed, from this spectacle, as the Apostle says, the manifold wisdom of God became known to principalities and powers (Eph. 3).

## 31 CHAPTER XXI. On the Same Earlier Statement, “He Breathed into His Face the Breath of Life”

Therefore, because he so willed and Wisdom so ordained, he formed from the mud of the earth one man from whom the rest would be propagated. From the mud, I say, of the earth. It is clear that, according to the body, man is earth. “For you are earth,” says the Lord, “and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3); and from this it is sufficiently proved that what returns to earth is earth.

But Scripture does not likewise plainly indicate what substance or material the soul is [Eccles. 3]. It says only: “and he breathed into his face the breath of life.” Likewise, when it says above, “Let the earth bring forth cattle of living soul,” it sufficiently expresses that earth is the material of the bodies of cattle; but it does not define the material of their living soul. Yet there is no doubt that this soul is taken from the air and is again dispersed into thin breezes, and thus dies so as no longer to exist.

Ecclesiastes says: “Therefore there is one destruction for man and beast, and the condition of both is equal. As man dies, so they also die. All breathe alike, and man has nothing more than a beast. All lie subject to vanity, and all go to one place. They were made from earth and return to earth. Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam rises upward, and whether the spirit of beasts descends downward?” [Col. 0266B] (Eccl. 3).

Therefore human souls have not fallen from heaven, as the Platonists hold; rather, Ecclesiastes says, “the condition of both is equal”—equal, I say, for man and beast—and all breathe alike. Their condition is equal, they breathe alike, and there is one destruction for both; but their end is not one and the same. For the spirit of beasts comes to an end: it descends downward, that is, extinguished, it returns into this lowest air. But there is no end to the human spirit, for it returns to him who made it.

By saying, “Who knows?”, he does not himself doubt, but as a preacher marvels at how few care to attend to this. “Man has nothing more than a beast,” he says; “for their condition is equal, and there is one destruction.” What, then, is the reason why man alone is distinguished? A certain gift, a certain talent entrusted by the Creator. Perceiving this, one of the secular authors also said: “Below the moon there is nothing except what is mortal and perishable, apart from the souls given to humankind by the gift of the gods.”

The talent of reason [Col. 0266C] has been entrusted to man (Luke 19). If he spends it well, he himself will be rewarded; but if he buries it in the earth, it will be taken away from him, and he himself will be punished. For will there be reason in the lower world? “Whatever your hand can do,” says the same Ecclesiastes mentioned above, “do earnestly; for there shall be neither work, nor reason, nor knowledge in the lower world to which you are hastening” (Eccl. 9). This is not because human rationality can fail, but because madness shall be perpetually tormented there.

Thus the spirit of man differs from the spirit of beasts in that the former received rationality as God’s gift, while the latter remained brute. This, I say, is the difference: the former is marked with the image of God, as wax is marked with the image of the testator’s seal, while the latter is not marked. Scripture indicated this marking above when it said: “And God created man in his own image; in the image of God he created him.” And now, after saying, “Therefore the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth,” it immediately adds: “and he breathed into his face the breath of life” [Col. 0267A].

For what does “he breathed” mean, except—as another version has it—that “he breathed into his face the breath of life”? Is God a body, so that he might be thought to have inflated the collected air from pursed lips into the face of his formed creature? This is plainly absurd. But “he breathed” is said because, by the command of the same Word by which he commanded light to shine out of darkness—by which angels are understood—he summoned a substance subject to himself, caused it to take on or open the eyes of reason, and swiftly inserted it into the hidden inward parts of the formed human being.

Likewise, when we read that the Lord brought sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, and built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, it must be understood that he breathed into her face the breath of life. For “he created them both, male,” I say, “and female.” These are properly called created; the others born from them are properly called begotten. That their souls do not flow by propagation is the unanimous judgment of all orthodox persons, lest—as would be absurd—as many souls perish every day as seeds perish.

“But why,” you ask, “do all die in Adam if souls are not derived by propagation, that is, transferred with seed from the man?” To this I say: by God’s authority, is the male alone called Adam, and not the female too? For it is written thus: “This is the book of the generation of Adam. In the day when God created man, he created them male and female, blessed them, and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created” [Col. 0267B] (Gen. 5).

For just as *homo* in Latin denotes both sexes, so *Adam* in that language denotes both sexes. Moreover, what is called *vir* in Latin is called *Ish* in Hebrew, in which there is a distinction of the male sex; while what is called *mulier* in Latin is called *Ishah* in Hebrew. Therefore, when Eve conceives, she receives the inanimate seed of the transgressing male; yet she herself is likewise a transgressor, and from her living body that seed is made alive in its kind through the blessing in which it was said: “Increase and multiply.” Thus Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all living beings: that is, because the life of those born should take its beginning from her. For *Eve* is rendered “life.”

But because each, namely male and female, is a transgressor, and each is Adam, the one who is born and dies in Adam is rightly said to die in Adam. For the child is rightly deprived of the inheritance of life which each parent justly lost [Col. 0267D].

## CHAPTER XXII. Why Only This Was Said: “And Man Became a Living Soul”

Therefore, when it has been said that the Lord formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life, the dignity of the human condition is beautifully expressed: it differs greatly from every animal, both in the formation of the body and in the quickening wrought by God who breathes. Both are clear. In this animal alone the bodily form raises its head upward, looks to heaven, treads the earth beneath its feet, walks with upright breast, and is moved to contemplate the stars or heavenly realms above with eyes set aloft [Col. 0268A]. The mind or breath which God breathed into his face is, by the gift of reason bestowed upon it, the discoverer of many good and useful arts.

But all the more attention must be paid to what is implied by the words, “and man became a living soul.” For this expression is far inferior to the thing described above. Even a beast became a living soul, when God said: “Let the earth bring forth cattle of living soul.” But when God said, “Let us make man,” he added, “in our image and likeness; and let him rule over the fish of the sea, birds of heaven, beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing which moves on the earth.” Why, then, is so much taken away from the honour of this creation, when Scripture says only: “And man became a living soul”?

Plainly because the man who was made did not use the gift of reason well and did not understand his honour, but was compared with beasts. It was therefore proper that the Writer should, as it were, withdraw from the man already formed that by which he is superior to beasts. Perceiving this, the Apostle says: “The first man became a living soul; but the last, a life-giving spirit” [Col. 0268B] (1 Cor. 15). Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear the beautiful harmony of this music—that is, the concord of the Scriptures—when here one precentor says, “The first man became a living soul,” and another responds, “but the last, a life-giving spirit.”

Therefore the first did not utter an imperfect song by chance, but by holy and prudent design, to be sung until those should come who knew how to complete it and bring it to its final sound. So today, when it is already in frequent and familiar use, we say: “The first man became a living soul; the last Adam, a life-giving spirit,” adding further: “The first man is earthly, from the earth; the second man is heavenly, from heaven. As is the earthly man, such also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly man, such also are the heavenly” (ibid.). It follows.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Planting of Paradise; and That Man Was Not Formed in Paradise but Placed There

“Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight in the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed.” Scripture beautifully safeguards God’s right of possession [Col. 0268D] by using these words: “Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight.” It also suggests the frail legal claim or standing of man by saying: “in which he placed the man whom he had formed.” By these words it in some manner declares that God alone—as is true—is the lawful Lord of paradise, while man in that paradise was an outsider and a tenant of the Lord God.

The same Lord plainly impresses this upon his people under the image of the land of Canaan, speaking of this paradise of delight, which is certainly a land flowing with milk and honey: “The land is mine; but you are my strangers and tenants” (Lev. 25). Therefore it was grace that placed in paradise the man formed outside it; but justice that took back what had been given when he sinned. Why he placed him in paradise Scripture says afterward: namely, that he might cultivate and guard it.

Moreover, *paradisus* is Greek, and in Latin means “garden”; and Scripture immediately makes clear how great its pleasure or how abundant its delights are—what is called *Eden* in Hebrew—when it says: “And God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food, and also the tree of life in the midst of paradise” [Col. 0269A].

## CHAPTER XXIV. Again on Paradise: That It Truly Is a Place on Earth
But now, before our discourse proceeds into this paradise, we must by no means pass over the fact that great and illustrious men have also discussed with scrupulous care this most beautiful garden of the Lord’s delights, though with widely differing understandings. For some, following an entirely spiritual interpretation, seem to have neglected the historical narrative of this sacred Scripture, as though those visible and bodily things had not existed, but had been spoken or written in this manner only to signify intelligible realities; and they turn these trees, fruit-bearing or fruitful woods, into virtues of life and moral dispositions—as if a bodily paradise could not have existed because it can also be understood spiritually. Others, however, adhering more prudently to the truth of Scripture, say: let these things, and whatever may fittingly be said concerning the understanding of a spiritual paradise, be said without anyone’s prohibition, provided that the utterly trustworthy truth of that history, commended by the narrative of events, is also believed. For it was not therefore the case that there were not two women, Hagar and Sarah, and from them two sons of Abraham, one [Col. 0269C] by a slave-woman and one by a free woman, because the Apostle says that two Testaments are prefigured in them; nor did water therefore fail to flow from any rock when Moses struck it because Christ can also be understood there by figurative signification, as the same Apostle says: “Now the rock was Christ” (Gal. IV).

Moreover, those who wish here to pass over the letter or history are especially troubled by the fact that, of the four rivers flowing from paradise, two are written to be the Tigris and the Euphrates. For, they say, Sallust, a most trustworthy author, asserts that the sources both of the Tigris and of the Euphrates are shown in Armenia; from which we perceive that paradise and its rivers must be understood otherwise. But let it be so. Even if Sallust is that most trustworthy author and speaks the truth—that the sources of these rivers are shown in Armenia—the truth of the letter is nevertheless not weakened, which says that the river of paradise is divided into four heads, of which these two are among them. For all drinkable and healthful waters, wherever they flow or whencesoever they appear, derive their origin through hidden channels from the fountain of paradise; and from its sweetness they possess the quality of being drinkable and healthful. For above it was said in this manner: “But a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth”—the surface, I say, because surely the effect or fruit of irrigation is evident on the surface, in green herbs and fruit-bearing trees.

Finally, this must be noted: it was not said, “A river went out of paradise and was thereafter divided into four rivers,” but, “which was thereafter [Col. 0270A] divided into four heads.” For that fountain waters the whole earth, as has already been said; and just as the liver in an animal’s body—which physicians call the source of the blood—supplies blood to all the veins and sustains the animal’s life by this service, so that fountain vivifies the whole earth through hidden veins and overflows into many springs and rivers; but these four are the heads, that is, the principal rivers, of them all. Therefore let the sources of the Tigris and Euphrates, if anyone pleases, be shown in Armenia; yet let them nevertheless be believed, by the way known to God, the author of rivers, to flow from paradise according to the truth of this Scripture.

## CHAPTER XXV. Again, concerning paradise: that God planted it from the beginning.

[Col. 0270B] But how is the Lord God said to have planted this paradise “from the beginning”? For if we were to say that “from the beginning” was so said because He planted paradise before making heaven and earth, human reason cannot conceive this, since paradise is a local and earthly place—indeed, an adornment of the earth. “From the beginning” may indeed be understood thus: because, as has already been said above, the Lord created every shrub of the field and every herb of the region before it arose or germinated, on the day when He created heaven and earth—that is, in the manner of which it is written: “What was made in him was life” (John I). Yet this may likewise be said of heaven and earth, and of all things made: that the Lord God thus made all things from the beginning, because “he who lives forever created all things together.”

This, then, may more readily be understood: that the Lord God planted paradise from the beginning means the same as if it were said, “From the beginning of the world’s adornment,” when, at His command, the earth brought forth herb and tree. For when the three parts of the world—heaven, earth, and sea—had been distinguished, the first adornment was the planting of paradise, God saying: “Let the earth bring forth green herb,” and so forth. He briefly describes that delightful planting thus: “And God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food, the tree of life also in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” It is plainly evident to the understanding that such a planting is paradise—that is, a garden of great delight—in which Scripture, or the finger of God who wrote these things, took such care to commend, as it were, the artistry of the maker. For almost every word is so placed that it depicts God before the readers’ eyes as a diligent and careful workman, planting and rooting, and with utmost care seeking out everything that He judged would be beautiful to see and pleasant for food, and devising such instruments of delight that, once planted, the knowledge of Him who planted them deservedly ought to be praised.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Again, concerning the same: that God planted it for man’s sake.

Indeed, what Scripture said—“The Lord [Col. 0271A] God had planted paradise”—it repeated in saying, “God brought forth from the ground every tree”; and what it had called “a paradise of delight,” it explained somewhat when it said, “every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food, the tree of life also in the midst of paradise.” Nevertheless, in saying, “The Lord God had planted a paradise of delight,” it proclaimed the dignity of the matter more exaltedly. For “God brought forth from the ground every tree,” and so forth, is the modest language of narrative; but by the word *planting* it signifies the enduring character of this blessed reality, and by the name *delight* it elegantly expresses its pleasantness.

For the word “planting” suggests the care of its planter or gardener, who never gave attention to transitory things, such that he should be concerned about them—as the Apostle testifies when he says, “Is God concerned about oxen?” (1 Cor. IX). But the name “delight” excludes every notion of need, because there food will not be eaten from necessity as it is here. For in man’s pilgrimage here, food is a consolation for mortality; there, it is a delight of immortality.

And this must be understood: the Lord God planted this earthly paradise for man alone; but He planted that heavenly paradise both for angels and for human beings. For an angel, who does not possess an earthly body, is content with the delights of one spiritual paradise; but man, who consists of body and spirit, will delight in a twofold paradise. There, blessed by eternal resurrection, according to the soul alone he will be nourished by the happy vision of divinity; but according to the body he will eat of every tree beautiful and most pleasant, not from necessity [Col. 0271C] but for great and ineffable delight. Did our Lord, after His resurrection, eat before His disciples from necessity? Certainly not, but by power; and then, because He could, He ate as immortal for the benefit of mortals. Now, however, and forever, He can eat the fruits of His paradise for His own delight.

Yet because the holy angels—as has already been said elsewhere—whatever bodies they may possess, were sometimes so delighted by the hospitable charity of holy human beings that they are recorded to have eaten food set before them, it may be believed that by the same power they will much more delight with us in our banquet then, when they see us gathered together and fed upon the inheritance of our Father—those whom, when they saw them condemned in the first parent to exile, they compassionately mourned with friendly love through the wide enclosures of empty paradise. If the Lord thus ordered His commonwealth, if God, the wise householder, thus arranged His household, may we also will it.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the earthly paradise was planted after the pattern of the heavenly paradise; and likewise concerning the tree in the midst of paradise.

It must be known that this earthly paradise was fashioned after the pattern of the heavenly paradise, in which angelic powers were like most beautiful trees, and the tree of life was God Himself, by whose blessed vision the happy angels live continually. The prophet Ezekiel especially commends this in these words, speaking against the devil, prince of darkness, under the name of King Pharaoh, among other things:

> “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his height, and the plane trees were not equal to his branches. No tree in the paradise of God was like him or his beauty, because I made him beautiful; and all the trees of delight which were in the paradise of God envied him.”

And shortly afterward:

> “To whom are you likened, O renowned and lofty one among the trees of delight? Behold, you have been brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest earth” (Ezek. XXXI).

When the prophet says these and similar things, he certainly does not undermine the truth of this historical narrative, but makes the most beautiful rationale of the divine counsel shine forth to our minds in this paradise.

Therefore we first inquire in what respect this earthly paradise is especially like the heavenly one, and only then shall we follow the traces of the written text. Two trees of this paradise, having contrary effects, most especially bear the likeness of the heavenly paradise: namely, the tree of life in the midst of paradise and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. I rightly say that these have contrary effects, because, if you weigh the matter rightly, just as this is called the tree of life, so that other ought truly to be called the tree of death. For it will be clear that it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil ironically. God said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death”; and He spoke the truth. The serpent, on the contrary, said: “Eat, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil”; and he spoke falsely. God, I say, spoke truth, and the serpent falsehood. For by eating they were not made gods, nor did they receive fuller knowledge so as to know good and evil in every respect; [Col. 0272C] rather, according to God’s truth, they immediately died in soul and became mortal in body.

Therefore that tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil ironically, so that its very name might present to readers a memorial of the devilish lie. For it is indeed evident that through the disobedience of the eater it became for man a tree of death—though that death arose not from the nature of the tree but from the fault of the eater. Thus the most beautiful, yet no less terrible than beautiful, rationale of the divine counsel shines forth to us through these things: just as God placed the devil in heaven with the elect angels in order to test every angelic creature, so He willed in this paradise, together with the tree of life, to plant a forbidden tree in order to test man. He made both especially beautiful beyond the rest: that tree and that angel.

Indeed, because of its appearance, that forbidden tree pleased the first human beings more than the unf​​orbidden tree of life; just as, because of his appearance, that angel pleased the vain and proud angels more than God. For concerning the tree’s desired beauty, Scripture says: “The woman therefore saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate” (Gen. III). Concerning that prince of vanity, the aforesaid prophet, drawing a likeness from the trees of this paradise, says:

> “No tree in the paradise of God was like him or his beauty, because I made him beautiful, with many thick branches; and all the trees of delight which were in the paradise of God envied him” (Ezek. XXXI).

“The trees of delight,” he says—not those that are, but those that *were* in the paradise of God—“envied him,” because those spirits who envied the form of his pride when he said, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIII), and admired or followed his vanity more than God’s wisdom, were indeed in the paradise of God, but are there no longer.

Therefore, just as in that heavenly paradise God, the true tree of life, who feeds the holy angels with His sweetness, took the holy angels up with Himself into heaven, so the same great and terrible God, terrible in counsels above the children of men, planted in this paradise, together with the tree of life, that rebel king of pride, along with this tree through which defiant man might be exposed by the fault of disobedience—just as all those spirits who were children of pride might be convicted and judged in their king, the rebel against God. There also were all the princes of heaven, none of whom is found to have been given a proper name except the one who wished to be as God and was named “great.” The others are called by the common name “light”; but he, though he is the bearer of darkness, is by contrast called Lucifer.

Likewise here the Lord brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food around the tree of life, and none of them is designated by a proper name except this one alone, which truly, as has already been said, became the tree of death, yet by contrast was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For, as some have supposed, “every tree” is not the proper designation of a single tree, so that in the phrase, “God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food,” one tree must be understood, just as one and only one must be understood by “the tree of life” and likewise by “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

For below, when the cunning serpent said, “Why did God command you not to eat of every tree of paradise?” the woman, mixing falsehood into her answer to his question, said: “We eat of the fruit of the trees which are in paradise; but of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise God commanded us not to eat.” Therefore, since she says “of the fruit of the trees,” many things must be understood in what is called “every tree.” And note that not only the tree of life, but also this forbidden tree, is said to be in the midst of paradise, because in this too there is a certain likeness of God and His adversary the devil. For while God ought rightly to rule in the midst of His creation, that rival of majesty, that adversary, could not endure that He should rule there alone; but presumed that he too should rule, should eat in the midst as though the Most High, and that thousands of thousands should stand or minister around his throne.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That “a fountain rose from the earth, which is then divided into heads”; and concerning the threefold meaning of paradise.

What, then, does it mean that “a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth,” and that it is also divided from there, as must later be learned, into four heads? Clearly the wondrous Creator contemplated no less a mystery in this fountain than in that tree of life. For does not the aforementioned prophet, deriving a comparison from the waters of this fountain, say concerning the same one of whom he spoke above: “He was most beautiful in his greatness, for his branches were beside many waters” (Ezek. XXXI)? And concerning those spirits humble in mind, who, when he had grown proud and been cast down, were established and strengthened: “And,” he says, “all the noble and excellent trees of delight in Lebanon, which are watered by waters, were comforted in the lower world.”

But what are those waters by which these trees—weak indeed, yet splendid; weak indeed, yet nevertheless excellent—are watered? Their weakness, because it is humility, is true strength; just as, conversely, the strength of that mighty one is, in contrast to these, true weakness. What, I say, are those waters by which these trees were watered and comforted, except the floods of charity, except the outpourings of the Holy Spirit, who so filled them with His sweetness that they are rightly called trees of delight?

Therefore, when the Lord God planted such a paradise in the earth and caused a fountain to rise from it, to be divided among all lands, He contemplated a great mystery and poured forth an image of great grace. We shall speak more fittingly of this matter when we come to the glorification of the Lord Jesus and the gift of the Holy Spirit, which, according to the plan, will be the third part of this work.

For the present, it must be understood that the rational creature has two paradises: one, namely, the society of holy angels; the other, the Church of chosen human beings. And this earthly paradise of which we speak is the image or likeness of both. For just as in this paradise the tree of life was planted, and the tree through which death entered the world, so in heaven the devil became the author of death in opposition to God, author of life. Likewise, among humankind, Christ is the tree of life, and his opposite, Antichrist, will be the tree of death, who long ago works the ministry of iniquity through his members.

Again, just as a fountain rises from this earthly paradise, watering the whole surface of the earth and then dividing into four heads, and rendering the whole earth fit for nourishing crops, so from that heavenly paradise a fountain deigned to flow: that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, watering the mass of the human race in such abundance that, amid the cedars, olives, and vines of all the saints and elect, it caused the tree of life also—that is, Christ, God and man—to spring from the earth of virginal flesh. Around this tree it divided the streams of Scripture into four heads, which the prophet distinguishes in the diverse faces of the four living creatures: namely, a human being, a lion, a calf, and a flying eagle.

For not only the four Gospels, but all divinely inspired Scripture has this certain fourfold aspect of its intention: to show our one Lord as gentle toward us, as truly human; powerful against the devil, as a lion (Ezek. I), that is, as almighty God; sacrificed for us as a chosen and fattened calf; and risen and ascended into heaven as a flying eagle. But these matters must be discussed elsewhere. Having briefly reviewed these things concerning paradise according to the truth of history, let us now at last pursue the order of the text begun.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Again, concerning the same fountain and river which went forth from paradise.

“And a river went out of paradise, which from there is divided into four heads.” As has already been said above, it did not say that it is divided there into four rivers, but into four heads—that is, principal rivers. For the fountain which, as Scripture said above, rose from the earth watering the whole surface of the earth, is not dispersed at the outlet of paradise into four rivers. Rather, while watering the whole surface of the earth, it produces many springs and many rivers flow from it, of which these are the heads.

And this intends to commend the wondrous sweetness of paradisal earth, because the nature of waters is corrupt and unfit for drinking, as the sea demonstrates in itself. But rising from the abyss into that breast, as it were, of the earth’s great body—that is, into the fountain of paradise—it takes on a kind of milky sweetness, and waters the whole surface of the earth, so that, in the Psalmist’s words, “all the beasts of the forest may drink, and the wild asses may await it in their thirst” (Ps. CIII); indeed, so that the whole earth might become sweet for nourishing the green herb and fruit-bearing tree which it had been commanded to produce.

This is especially evident in eastern lands, fertile not only in bread and wine but also in precious aromatics. For the land of Sodom and Gomorrah was once among the best, and before the Lord overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, as this Scripture itself testifies (Gen. X), it was watered like the paradise of the Lord. “The name,” it says, “of the one is Physon; it is that which surrounds the whole land of Evilat, where gold is produced; and the gold of that land is excellent; bdellium and the onyx-stone are also produced there.” Physon is the river which our people, changing its name, call the Ganges. Evilat, moreover, is a region of India, having its name from Evila the son, where, it says, gold is produced. Gold is indeed produced elsewhere too, but “the gold of that land is excellent”; bdellium is found there, and the onyx-stone.

Bdellium is an aromatic tree, concerning whose nature Pliny writes at greatest length (PLIN., book XII, ch. 9). Onyx is a gem so called because it has whiteness mingled in it in the likeness of a human fingernail; for the Greeks call a fingernail *onyx*. Moreover, many other most precious gems are produced there, including the carbuncle and emerald. “And the name of the second river is Gyon,” which is also called the Nile, the river of Ethiopia. “It is,” Scripture says, “that which surrounds the whole land of Ethiopia”: a river of such great benefit that Egypt once worshipped it as its greatest god, since, watered by its streams and filled thence with every abundance, it never needed rains poured down from above. For during the greatest heat of the summer sun, as its waters rise, it spreads out; nor, by falling, is it again confined within its banks before the autumnal equinox. Hence Lucan:

> … The Nile neither raises its waters  
> before the rays of the Dog-star,  
> nor binds the river within its banks  
> before Libra, equal to the night, brings Phoebus under its sign.  
> (LUCAN, *Pharsalia*, book X)

And concerning these rivers, no opinion can contradict this truthful history, that they rise from paradise.

For no one has anything else to say. Accordingly, the same author cited above says of the Nile, also called Gyon:

> No generation has failed to desire  
> to pass knowledge of it on to future ages;  
> but nature still prevails in concealing it.

And of the Ganges, also called Physon:

> The fame of war stirred even the eastern recesses,  
> where the Ganges is worshipped—the only river in all the world  
> that dares to open mouths opposite the rising Phoebus  
> and drive its waves against the east wind.  
> (LUCAN, same work, book III)

That the sources of the others—that is, of the Tigris and Euphrates—are shown in Armenia or Persia, and that this Scripture or history is nonetheless true, has already been said above. Certainly, the Tigris takes its name from the swiftest beast, the tiger, because of the speed of its course. Euphrates, however, means “fertility,” being so named because, in the manner of the Nile, it spreads through fields and makes the lands fertile. The same writer cited above says concerning their nature:

> Where great Euphrates lifts its head beside swift Tigris—  
> rivers which Persia produces not from separate sources—  
> and it is uncertain whether the land mingles their streams.  
> Which of them rather retains the water’s name; but Euphrates,  
> scattered through the fields, fruitful, performs the office  
> of the Pharian flood.  
> Yet the earth swallows Tigris in a sudden chasm  
> and gathers up its hidden course; then, reborn  
> from a new source, the river does not refuse itself to the sea’s waters.  
> (LUCAN, same work, book VII)

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the command given to man not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

“The Lord therefore took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it. And He commanded him, saying: ‘Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat. For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.’”

After the Apostle had said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments, and unsearchable His ways!” he immediately added: “For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counsellor and has shown Him? Or who has first given to Him, and shall be repaid? For from Him, and through Him, and in Him are all things. To Him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.”

See those to whom God gave: angel and man. With His other creatures God had no reckoning of giving or receiving, since to them He gave nothing beyond natural existence. He gave heaven to angels and paradise to man. To the one and the other He gave, and to the one and the other He gave first. For what had either one first given to Him? Therefore He first gave, yet on a prescribed condition, so that He might be repaid. But what repayment did He require from [Col. 0277A] the angel except love, and from man except faith working through love?

For Scripture says: “The Lord therefore took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work it and guard it.” What was he to work, or from whom was he to guard it? He was surely to work the work of God, which is nothing other than the work of faith, the service of hope, and the obedience of charity. Someone may say: Why did He not place him in paradise without any condition, without any command? Would it not have been better to give no command than, by giving a command, to make room for transgression? For where there is no command, there is no transgression.

To this I say: How, then, would man have been joined to God, if he had not been bound beneath the yoke of obedience, if he had not received a charge in which he ought to prove faithful to God? For where nothing is entrusted, no faith appears. Moreover, without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI). As though God now acts otherwise, or accepts anyone otherwise than through faith. Therefore He took man into paradise so that he might work through faith; and so that he might guard it, namely, lest, abandoning faith or love for the Creator, he should at the same time lose the excellent gift bestowed upon him.

Thus God, truly good and wise, both gave first and gave paradise to man on a rational condition. Yet people, curious about God but negligent of themselves, continue to inquire, wishing to know the mind of the Lord and daring to give Him counsel. “If,” they say, “God wished man to be safe or blessed, why did He not make him incapable of turning? Why did He not make him unchangeable? Why did He not establish for him a nature incapable of any change?”

Against objections of this sort we have already responded briefly above, when speaking of the firstborn of perdition, or the devil, prince of death: namely, that nothing besides God is by nature incapable of turning or change; and that no creature can attain an unchangeable state of virtue except by making progress or applying effort with God’s grace. Now, with our eyes opened not by the serpent’s persuasion but in the Holy Spirit, let us consider the Creator’s command which that man unhappily transgressed. He says: “Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.” Great is the generosity of the gifts, and not burdensome the command of the giver: “Eat,” He says, “from every tree of paradise; but from one tree do not eat.” In such abundance, self-restraint would have been easy, had goodwill, the guide of self-restraint, not been lacking.

This must certainly be known: the tree is here called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil by anticipation—a figure called *prolepsis* in Greek. For the origin of this name did not flow from the mouth of God, present Truth, saying, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death,” but from the devil’s later deceit, as has already been said above; for, persuading them to eat, he said: “You shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.” The sorrowful remembrance of the Writer marked that tree as though saying: “He gave permission to eat from every tree of paradise; He forbade only that tree which, from its outcome and by contrast, is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. That man owed God faith, hope, and charity, but did not render them because he was ungrateful.

“Eat from every tree of paradise,” He says, and so forth. The majesty of the Trinity deemed three things worthy to command: “Eat from every tree”; “do not eat from this one”; and “on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” By these three propositions He required three virtues from man: charity, hope, and faith. The same Trinity, one God, now requires from us these virtues in reverse order: faith, hope, and charity, because man descended by falling, while we, rising from faith, ascend through hope to the charity of God.

For in making man freely, and then freely placing him in that place of delight, in such a paradise overflowing with delights, as the future father of a multitude of saints, He plainly made that same man His debtor for great charity and strongly bound him by His benefits. But the ungrateful man did not repay the debt of charity owed for such great grace—a debt whose magnitude no one can estimate because of the greatness of his wickedness.

Likewise, in the command saying, “But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat,” he ought to have displayed outstanding hope. He ought, I say, to have had hope and hoped in the good God that He who had already freely bestowed such great goods upon him would surely someday grant greater things, which He promised—namely, the heavenly paradise and the fellowship of holy angels—to one who observed submission and obedience in the command. But undoubtedly he did not possess this virtue of hope concerning future things because, as has already been said, lacking charity, he was first ungrateful for present goods.

Likewise, in the warning that said, “For on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” he ought to have had faith—firmly to have faith and to believe that God had not forbidden such a tree out of envy for human divinity, but had truthfully foretold the unavoidable penalty of transgression. But that unhappy woman, companion of an unhappy man both in punishment and guilt, believed the serpent more than God: the serpent, I say, who said, “By no means shall you die by death; for God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes shall be opened and you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil.” She believed him more than God and thought that he was truthful, while God—an outrage even to hear—had lied through envy.

Thus God, good, wise, and just, preserved His nature, regarded His divinity, and maintained His purpose, when in His one command He rightly required from His creature three virtues resembling Himself—faith, hope, and charity—which it was fitting to offer Him. Let us therefore, who speak one thing and do another—having lost these virtues in that old parent of ours and wretchedly neglecting them in the grace of our new parent, the second man Jesus Christ—not continue to speak what is most wicked, disputing our Lord God: why He did this or that; why He gave man such a command; or why He did not instead permit him to be born free, like a colt of a wild ass.

“What then?” you ask. “Does not Scripture say: ‘He has done all things whatsoever He willed, in heaven and on earth’” (Ps. CXIII)? How then did the Lord do all that He willed, if He was unable to bring to effect what He commanded—which, surely, unless He had willed it to be done, He would not have commanded? For in this creature whom He fashioned, He found faith, hope, and charity according to His command.

To this I say: God’s counsel or purpose was by no means frustrated, for He made those virtues blossom again from that trunk. For that man proved disabled for this work of God and, contrary to God’s work or command, stretched out unrestrained hands through desire; but from his race there was found a man after God’s heart, who, content against every desire, stretched out His hands upon the wood of the cross in obedience that brought Him suffering; and, trampling sin beneath His feet, set before many thousands who followed Him examples of virtue worthy to be read.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the saying, “It is not good for man to be alone”; and that the woman was not made in paradise.

And the Lord God also said: “It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.” If indeed the order of events is supposed to be such as is the order of the words—namely, that the Lord first brought the man into the paradise of delight and gave him a commandment, before He said this: “It is not good for the man to be alone; let us make [Col. 0279C] for him a helper like himself”—then it must likewise be supposed that He gave no commandment to the woman; and consequently, absurdly, it could be said that she was not guilty of transgression, since she had received no commandment. But she herself plainly shows that the commandment had also been given to her, in answering the serpent thus: “We eat of the fruit of the trees which are in paradise; but concerning the tree which is in the midst of paradise, God commanded us not to eat.”

Moreover, if God had already placed the man in paradise before He said these things, then asses, horses, and the other animals of the earth, clean and unclean, were also in that place of delight—a place which a rational human being counts it a great benefit of God’s grace if he can attain. For immediately after these words of God Scripture continues: “Therefore the Lord God, having formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and the birds of heaven, brought them to Adam,” etc.

Therefore this saying of the Lord God, “Let us make for him a helper like himself,” is better connected with the earlier passage where it was said: “Therefore the Lord formed man from the clay of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life”; indeed, with the still earlier passage: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” “Why then,” you ask, “did Scripture so long defer its account of the making of the woman?” Clearly, so that it might arrange the individual parts of the history reasonably according to their proper causes. For it is established that man was not made for the sake of woman, but woman for the sake of man (1 Tim. 2); and she was placed with him [Col. 0280A] in paradise.

Accordingly, it properly first set out, together with the formation of the man, the account that the Lord God brought him and placed him in paradise, and it described paradise itself. Again, the man was not deceived, but the woman. For the devil did not deceive the woman through the man, but the man through the woman. Therefore it has deferred the formation of the woman until now, so that it might continue the history of the calamity which came to the man through the woman.

Tichomus calls this manner of narration “recapitulation,” when he wrote seven highly useful rules for understanding the difficulties of Scripture. To this method belongs the fact that this same Scripture, after saying, “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to his language and families in their nations” [Col. 0280B], says some time later: “But the earth was of one speech and of the same words.” Then it tells how the languages were divided, though it had already said that they had been divided. “And when they journeyed,” it says, “from the east, they came into a plain in the land of Sennaar and dwelt there. And one said to his neighbor: ‘Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire’” (Gen. 10), and the rest.

Thus, when man had been formed, the Lord God also said this—said it, I mean, by that utterance of His own wisdom in which He said all things and in which He made all things: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself” (Gen. 11). It is not good, I say; it is not useful; it does not conduce to our purpose that man should be alone. For we have purposed to propagate from the first [Col. 0280C] man those foreknown and predestined persons who shall be holy and conformed to our image and likeness. Therefore, that this purpose may be fulfilled: “Let us make for him a helper like himself”—a helper, I say, for multiplying the predestined offspring of the saints.

It should be noted that, in making such a helper, the same plurality of persons speaks as spoke in making the man. The same Trinity, one God, now says: “Let us make for him a helper.” By adding “like himself,” He includes everything He said in making the man: “in our image and likeness,” and “let him rule over the fish of the sea, the beasts of the whole earth, and every creeping thing which moves upon the earth.” Except for sex, the substance of woman differs in nothing from the substance of man [Col. 0280D]; that is, woman does not preside over all living creatures by the dignity of her creation less than man does, because she is no less rational, nor is she less able to aspire to the likeness of the Creator, as was said above, where Scripture speaks of this creation on the sixth day: “Male,” it says, “and female He created them.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the saying: “But for Adam there was not found one like him.”

When the Lord God had said these things, Scripture immediately set before us a great spectacle, so that with minds rightly aroused we may ask: What is the Lord doing? What does He will? What does He intend? “The Lord God,” it says, “having formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and the birds of heaven, brought them to Adam.” And shortly afterward: “But for Adam [Col. 0281A] there was not found a helper like him.”

Did the Lord God then not know that among all the animals of the earth or birds of heaven none could be found like the man, one that might suitably be joined to him as a helper for propagating the human race as He willed or purposed? Did He not know this, I say, unless, as it were, taking up a threatening rod, He marshaled all things before Adam, so that God might seem to deliberate with man in a common inquiry, asking whether perhaps something like him might be found among all these things? For it is as though, labor having ceased, God had failed: “But for Adam,” Scripture says, “there was not found a helper like him.”

What then does the Lord intend by this great concern, except to show the man, that he might understand the honor of his creation: namely, that nothing among beasts or other living creatures of any kind was his equal? For this ought to have contributed to a rational man’s love of his Creator: when all were gathered before him, he undoubtedly excelled in singular honor, not only by the privilege of reason but also by bodily form. Seeing all the others bowed down to the ground, four-footed, dragging their tails, or even creeping with their whole bodies, he alone, upright in stature and with breast held free, could glory that he held primacy over all—if he had wished to glory in the Lord his God.

God therefore intended that His creature should render Him a gratitude worthy of Him, which would surely have been profitable to that creature. Scripture fittingly indicates His concern: “The Lord God,” it says, “having formed from the ground all [Col. 0281C] the animals of the earth and the birds of heaven, brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them”; that is, to see that none of them had a nature worthy to receive a name derived or altered from the name of man because of any likeness. “For whatever Adam called each living creature, that was its name.” And it adds further: “And Adam gave names to all animals, to all birds, and to all beasts of the earth. But for Adam there was not found a helper like him.”

That is, he considered the natures of each and, from their differing qualities, formed differing names. Thus, for example, the Latin calls a horse *caballus* from digging, because it digs the earth with its hoof; an ass from sitting; a pig as though from *spurcus*, “filthy,” because it is filthy [Col. 0281D]; and a dog because in hunting it produces a melodious bark. And many such examples might be given.

So likewise he, in the primitive language—which, after the division of languages, remained among the Hebrew people—formed names for individual things by considering the properties of their natures; and he saw that the nature of none was such that he could rightly give it a name related to his own, as he later rightly said of the woman: “She shall be called *virago*, because,” he says, “she was taken from man.” And this, as has already been said, ought truly to have had great power to move man to love of the Creator and to thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Adam’s rib and the union of a man with his wife

“Therefore the Lord cast a deep sleep upon Adam. And when [Col. 0282A] he had fallen asleep, He took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place. And the Lord built the rib which He had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam.”

Therefore, it says, because it was not good for man to be alone, and because, when all the animals had been brought to Adam, he himself perceived that no helper like him was found, the Creator, as it were, returned to the laborious word of His omnipotence, saying: “Let us make for him a helper.” The sleep which the Lord God cast upon Adam certainly ought not to have closed the wakefulness of reason; rather, with the five bodily senses shut off, it left the mind’s perception free, so that he might know what the wisdom of God, the artificer of all things, was doing to him. Hence, when the woman was afterward brought to him, he could say: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”

Perhaps for this reason the Seventy translated by “ecstasy,” that is, “a departure of mind,” the word *ardema*, which among the Hebrews signifies a deep sleep.

But what does it mean that, although He could form the woman from the clay of the earth just as He formed the man, He chose rather to take a rib from the man and build it into a woman? What did He intend by this, I ask, except to show that the love of a single marriage ought to be firm and indissoluble?
