Therefore, when the Lord was tested by the Pharisees concerning putting away one’s wife, who said, “Moses commanded us to give a bill of divorce,” He answered: “Have you not read that He who made man from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Thus they are no longer [Col. 0282C] two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matt. 19). And again He said to His disciples: “Whoever puts away his wife and takes another commits adultery against her. And if a wife puts away her husband and marries another, she commits adultery” (Mark 10).

Therefore, O spouses, it was not a new commandment written for you when the Lord or His apostle commanded (1 Cor. 7) that a woman not depart from her husband. No, I say, it was not a new commandment written for you, but an old commandment which you heard from the beginning. For behold the reasonable—indeed, natural—ground of this commandment was established from the beginning of marriage. Behold, I say, the God who instituted marriage made such a helper for the man, not from just anywhere, but from the man’s rib.

Can a man cast away his own rib without injury to its Maker? If one who is blind, lame, of small, large, or crooked nose, with a broken foot or hand, hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, or bearing any such blemish, may not approach the ministry of the Lord according to the commandment of the Law (Lev. 21), how much more ought one who has violently removed or cast away a whole rib from his body deservedly to be barred from the altar—indeed, from the communion of the whole Church of God?

For as soon as any man takes any woman as such a helper, through the faith and testimony of Him who brought this woman to this man, she is his rib, bone of his bones, and flesh of his flesh. Therefore, if he abandons her of his own accord for any cause whatever, except the cause of fornication, he will no longer be a man before God [Col. 0283A], nor will he be accounted a whole body, because one rib has been mutilated: a rib, I say, not just any rib, but one well built; the body has been diminished. Likewise, if a woman leaves her husband, she will no longer be counted before God, because by the law of creation she is shown to be not a whole body or all flesh, but a part, since she is proved to have been taken from man.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Again, on the saying: “What God has joined together, let no man separate.”

The single cause of fornication can excuse either party, because in fornicators and adulterers every ground of marriage perishes. For what reason did God make woman for man? Clearly, that she might be a helper [Col. 0283B] to him. A helper, I ask, in what thing or work? Certainly, a helper in propagating offspring, according to the blessing which the same God gave upon male and female, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” etc.

But whoever, man or woman, violates the lawful marriage-bed is shown not to pursue this end, but rather to seek his or her own lust. For a woman subjected to many men becomes not more fruitful, but more shameful. A man lavished upon many women may indeed be able to beget more children; but the world, long since full of the thorns and thistles of our race, has no need of such effort.

Formerly, among holy men, there was a liberty not merely pardonable but even blameless, as, for example, in the patriarch Jacob, from whose seed was to come Christ—God blessed above all—author of the blessing. As He was to destroy Adam’s sin, so He also had to restore honorable marriage and the undefiled marriage-bed; indeed, from the sowing of spouses He had to reap the early and late harvest of virgins.

Therefore only on the ground of fornication are the divorces of those rightly married excused, yet in such a way that those who have separated from one another for such a cause must either remain as they are or be reconciled (1 Cor. 7). In this manner, however, it is lawful to observe the saying which Wisdom itself—through whom, or in whom, this was made—uttered with as much strength as sweetness: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matt. 19). For man separates what God has joined when divorce takes place through hatred, for new sexual indulgence, or for any similar cause.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Whether God—and how God alone—lawfully separates what He Himself has joined

What if He who joined them should Himself separate them? This is plainly lawful. For it is not separation or divorce, but an honorable alteration of marriage, when chaste spouses withdraw from one another for God’s cause in order to devote themselves to prayer, preferring love of the spirit to carnal intercourse. When this is agreed between both in harmony, whether they have been stirred to it by any person exhorting them and speaking outward words [Col. 0284A], it is not man who separates what God has joined; rather, God, who joined them well in the flesh, joins them better in the spirit.

This proceeds rightly only when one will and the same purpose are present in both spouses. For if one tends toward holy leisure in order to devote himself or herself to prayer, and the other consents, it proceeds rightly. But if the other has a different intention and does not wish to profess the faith of the same warfare, or the purpose of that warfare, then it is certainly not God’s counsel but man’s; and therefore the protest must immediately be raised: “What God has joined together, let no man separate.”

But if someone thus divided or mutilated should receive even the ecclesiastical tonsure and proceed already girded with the belt of Christ’s sacred warfare, while that part of his body which has been left in the world protests, he could not serve according to his vow, being restrained by the authority of the sacred canons, lest his holiness become a cause of adultery for his spouse [Col. 0284B]—so forcefully was it said: “What God has joined together, let no man separate.”

The Apostle agrees with this saying: “Are you bound to a wife?” he says. “Do not seek release” (1 Cor. 7)—that is, release through a human being. For unless God, by whose witness and lawgiving you are bound, releases you by preparing your wife’s mind so that she has the same vow or purpose of chastity, you cannot find release in any way.

Nature itself first set forth this law, and the first-created man immediately ratified it by his declaration. For he says: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Col. 0284C] How or whence Adam could know: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”

Although Adam had been put to sleep, his words plainly prove that what was done had not been hidden from him. “This now,” he says, “is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” It is as though he said: “This, which shortly before was only bone of my bones—that is, a rib from my ribs—is now also flesh. Therefore, as it was formerly my bone, so now, after the rib has been built up, it is rightly my flesh: flesh, I say, from my flesh.”

Therefore the Lord cast sleep upon Adam not so that he should not know what was being done, but so that a great sacrament might be prefigured in him. The Apostle, perceiving this, says: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). He does not say that this is a sacrament in that man and that woman—in the woman’s being taken from the man, in the Lord’s casting sleep upon Adam, taking one of his ribs, building the rib taken from Adam into a woman, and in Adam’s saying, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” etc. For these were carnal events, and they were spoken carnally by that Adam, namely, without awareness of future spiritual things.

But this is a great sacrament in Christ and the Church, because Christ thus admitted into Himself the sleep of death, having undertaken obedience according to the Father’s will; and God took blood and water from His side—from the side, I say, of Him sleeping, that is, already dead—and drew out blood and water through the wound of the spear. From that time until the end of the age He does not cease to build [Col. 0285A], so that He may present to Himself a glorious Church without spot or wrinkle (ibid.).

Therefore, from one point of view it is rightly written in another edition: “The Lord cast ecstasy upon Adam,” because, though the bodily senses were closed, reason nonetheless remained awake, so that he did not fail to know that bone had been taken from his bones and flesh built from his flesh. Yet from another point of view it is no less rightly said that “the Lord cast sleep upon Adam”: sleep, I say, that is, a heavy and profound slumber, which in Hebrew is called *tardema*; namely, because the new bride, the Church, was to be regenerated from the deep sleep of death of the new Adam.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. [Col. 0285B] On the saying: “A man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife”

“This,” he says, “shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from man.” This looks back to what was said above: “The Lord God, having formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and the birds of heaven, brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them,” namely, while seeking a helper for him, as is afterward added: “But for Adam there was not found a helper like him.” “And Adam gave names to all animals, to all birds of heaven, and to all beasts of the earth,” and he gave none of them a name related to the name of man, because he saw that none was like himself.

But when he recognized in this woman his own likeness, he saw what he should call her; and he called her *virago*, saying [Col. 0285C] that she was taken from man. For since she was taken from man, the name given to her was suitably derived from the word for man. It should be understood, however, that in Hebrew literature the etymology or derivation of the name is clearly expressed. For man is called *ish* in Hebrew, and woman *isha*. But in Latin *vir* (“man”) and *mulier* (“woman”) have nothing in common either in sound or in their literal letters; instead of *mulier*, therefore, *virago* is used, a name derived from *vir*.

Thus the man, rightly recognizing his own substance in the woman, says: “This shall be called *virago*, because she was taken from man.” And he added: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.”

This is held as a law: a man may leave father and mother when a fitting cause demands it; but neither human nor divine law permits a wife to be left except willingly, and only for the cause of fornication, as was said above. Therefore when the Law says: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brothers, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and did not acknowledge his sons: these kept Your word and observed Your covenant” (Deut. 33), when, I say, the holy and just Law says this, it should be noted that it passes over the wife alone. For one who desires to keep His word and covenant may disregard father and mother, brothers, and sons, and may lawfully leave them even protesting and unwilling; but the wife alone may not lawfully be left unless she is willing and embraces the same purpose.

Therefore, in saying: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” it declares that the bond of marriage is the greatest and strongest of all carnal relationships, so that once joined they are no longer two, but one flesh.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On human ingratitude, by which man remained mute in all things concerning the praise of the Creator

Here at last it must be observed how persistently the first man, the earthly man, remained mute with respect to the Creator’s praise; with what stubborn lips he refrained from all thanksgiving and rendered the Lord God an ungrateful silence. When God formed him and breathed into him the breath of life, and he became a living soul, he did not breathe forth in response, with the same breath of life he had received, toward the face of his Maker, so as to worship, glorify, and thank Him [Col. 0286B].

Again, when the same Lord God placed him in the paradise of delight, he gave Him no thanks; and with silent ingratitude he took possession of that place of God’s delights, so great and so easily granted, as though it were a plunder. Behold, now for a third time he has been enriched by the gift of divine condescension, in that God made for him a helper like himself: a helper, I say, so that he might increase and multiply, and, from himself alone, propagate a fortunate offspring and fill the land of the living.

Whether this was the third or the second benefit of God, as was said above, though enlarged by three gifts of divine generosity, he is still silent and speaks nothing that resounds in praise of the Lord. Scripture bears witness that no word of love or gratitude was in his mouth (Eccl. 7) [Col. 0286C]. Therefore it is not surprising that one who did not acknowledge God’s grace should sin and not acknowledge his sin, since the two matters are close. For by the same inward sight man recognizes both his own evil deed and God’s benefit toward him.

## CHAPTER XL. On the saying that they were not ashamed of their nakedness

“And they were both naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.” Their nakedness was not a disgrace but an honor; their lack of shame at their nakedness was not folly but security. For what? Did they receive from their Maker the notion that God’s creation is shameful and to be hidden? Or does nature produce such shame, rather than conscience?

This torment of shame has indeed become almost natural; nevertheless, its origin sprang not from the original creation but from a later fault. For we are ashamed of our nakedness because we are conscious how great a weakness—indeed, how great a rebellion of our flesh against us—we bear. But at that time the conscience of the heart was sound, since no lust of the eyes troubled it. For the lust of the flesh is the punishment of sin, by which the preceding pride of the mind is punished. “God,” Scripture says, “made man upright.”

This testimony is surely true, because the God who is most upright is believed to have made man only upright. Human uprightness consists in this: that the spirit, as the superior, should preside over and rule the flesh, which is inferior, and that the flesh should be at the spirit’s command and obey it. For the rational spirit of man is placed between God and his flesh, so that he may obey God and command his flesh. Because that first man disturbed and broke this order by rejecting God’s commandment, the spirit which had been superior was made subject to the lowest flesh, so that he who despised being rightly subject to the superior might, by just punishment, be subject to the inferior.

From this arose that shame of face, breaking forth from the hidden recesses of conscience into public sight and forcing penal disgrace to seek the strange relief of coverings. This weakness, I say, or rebellion of the flesh against the spirit, did not yet exist. Therefore they were both rightly naked and were not ashamed, because they had nothing of which to be ashamed.

Having lost that security of nakedness, we groan because, stripped of glory and honor, we are wrapped in little rags. For [Col. 0287B] while thus clothed we truly walk naked, even if—what is impossible—we should be clothed as the lilies of the field are clothed. “Not even Solomon in all his glory,” says the Lord, “was clothed like one of these” (Matt. 6). Even if, I say, we could be clothed as they are, we would still be stripped and naked. Hence, the Apostle says, “We await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of His glory” (Phil. 3).

For when the righteous shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. 13), will they be covered with tunics and cloaks? Certainly not. Rather, whatever vessels of mercy are there will stand for the glory of their Potter or Maker, beholding one another with mutual glory: bright outwardly and joyful inwardly; whole in body and glad in mind; blessed, I say, in both [Col. 0288B] body and soul.

# THE THIRD BOOK ON GENESIS  
*(Genesis, chapter 3, verses 1–24)*

## CHAPTER I. On the serpent’s cunning, and on the fact that man first swelled inwardly through pride before he was outwardly tempted by the serpent

That saying in David is the voice of the human race: “Before I was humbled, I sinned” (Ps. 118). He said this truly, not because, according to certain heretics, each of our souls was exalted in the height of heaven before it was humbled in a body, sinned there, and on account of its sin was humbled—that is, shut up in the prison of its own body. That is a perverse interpretation.

Rather, “Before I was humbled, I sinned” is to be understood according to Adam: that is, before I was compared to beasts and made like them, I, being set in honor, “did not understand” (Ps. 48); I did not glorify God, the author of my honor, nor give thanks, but I also transgressed His commandment and sinned in this. Concerning this sin, it must be carefully observed how Scripture began the narrative (chapter 3). It says: “But the serpent also was more cunning than all the animals of the earth which the Lord God had made.”

It had first stated the glory, honor, and security of man, saying: “And they were both naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.” Then it immediately adds: “But the serpent also was more cunning than all the animals of the earth.” What does this mean: that it did not simply say, “But the serpent was more cunning,” but inserted the conjunction *also*, saying, “But the serpent also was more cunning than all the animals of the earth”? This is what it intends, and toward this it directs the reader: that he should not think that the beginning of Adam’s sin or temptation—or that of his wife—began with the serpent’s outward persuasion.

For the spirit of the devil first spoke inwardly, by itself, to the human heart, so that man might become proud and might hold God his commander in contempt, or disdain to bear His commandment. For unless he had first swollen inwardly through pride, he would not have yielded so easily when tempted outwardly. Therefore, so that the creature of two substances, namely man, who consists of body and soul, might be drawn by a twofold death—of body and soul—he was first corrupted spiritually in his soul by the vice of pride, and then defiled bodily by food contrary to God’s commandment.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, the restorer of our substance, also beautifully indicates this by a parabolic allusion when He says: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke 18). He did not simply say, “A certain man fell among robbers”; rather, He says that he was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and only then fell among robbers. For unless he had gone down, he would not have fallen among them; that is, unless he had been proud in mind, he would not have incurred transgression of the commandment given to him.

He was going down because his mind was swelling; for to ascend in swelling is truly to descend, because where the mind is lifted up, it is cast down by that very lifting up. Hence the Psalmist says: “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 27). Therefore, when it was said, “And they were both naked and were not ashamed,” it should immediately have been understood that, ungrateful for such great benefits, they disdained to be subject to God and, conscious that they were the parents and rulers of so great a race, already wished to be regarded as gods—that is, truly as gods.

For *sicut* (“as,” “like”) is used not always for resemblance, but sometimes to affirm reality, as there: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we became like those consoled” (Ps. 125). “Like those consoled,” he says—that is, truly consoled. This, I say, should be understood and immediately joined: “But the serpent also was more cunning than all the animals of the earth.” The meaning is: the devil corrupted man inwardly by himself, and not only inwardly by himself [Col. 0289A], but also outwardly deceived him through the serpent.

## CHAPTER II. Whether the serpent could have been in paradise

The question is asked how the serpent could have been in paradise, if paradise is to be believed to be solely the dwelling-place of man, given to him as a great grace of the Creator on condition that he perform good works and guard it with the utmost diligence, as was said above. For if paradise was common to serpents, it follows that that place of delight was not without wolves, lions, and other beasts as well; and therefore it would not be thought to possess so great a blessedness that it could rightly be called the paradise of delight, or said to have been planted by the Lord God Himself.

Indeed, such an objection would be more difficult to solve if Scripture had expressly said that the serpent spoke to the woman within the enclosure of paradise. But now, since it says: “But the serpent also was more cunning than all the animals of the earth which the Lord God had made,” and afterward adds, “who said to the woman,” etc., we are left free to maintain that the serpent—especially while possessed bodily by the invading devil—was not in paradise. Rather, while the woman wandered bodily and with her eyes, walking about without restraint and perhaps looking out to see what the world outside paradise was like, and while the serpent, being crafty, pressed nearer to the sweetness of the earth or was eager for it, an opening was given to the devil and an occasion presented for temptation.

It should be understood that before the serpent became the devil’s instrument for man’s destruction, it could be called wise or prudent. Hence another edition reads: “But the serpent also was wiser than all the animals of the earth.” But after its prudence was joined to the devil’s malice and it furnished an opportune instrument of death, it can more rightly be called cunning, wicked, or deceitful [Col. 0289C].

For its prudence, before it rendered service to that father of lies, was such that Christ Himself testifies that it remains a model for Christ’s disciples, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10): prudent, He says, but not harmful, as those serpents became when they possessed venom through the devil’s subsequent corruption; rather, on the contrary, simple as doves.

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 0289D] Again, whether man did not know that the serpent, which appeared to speak, was irrational by nature.

The same question is also raised: whether the woman did not know that the serpent, like the other animals, was irrational and could not speak by its own power. If she did not know this, then—absurdly—she possessed less understanding in that bright paradise of God than she now possesses in this darkness of a life full of miseries, where, although “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9), she nevertheless knows that no life except her own is rational. But if (as is true) she knew that the serpent could speak only through an alien spirit, then the enormity of the deception is indeed astonishing: the woman marvelled, as though at that spirit’s omnipotence, that it could form human words through an irrational animal. And if this is so—indeed, because it is so—there no longer remains any doubt from what root that vast and bitter tree of idolatry, springing up, spread itself among all nations; or whence miserable human beings acquired the inborn habit of seeking, with such persistence and such mad and foolish reverence, articulated voices fashioned by the cunning of demons through innumerable images, worshipping the devil as God and falsehood in place of truth. There is no longer any doubt, I say, whence the fault of so great an error has clung so tenaciously to humankind: namely, because our mother Eve, the mother of all the living, was first inwardly embittered with the gall of this wickedness, when she marvelled at the eloquence of the serpent, wickedly skilled in speech, as though it were the divine wisdom of a diabolical spirit, and was foolishly poisoned.

Therefore the devil, or Satan, is himself [Col. 0290B] the great dragon and the ancient serpent. Yet he did not deceive unhappy humanity alone, but riding upon another serpent—that is, an earthly animal—he deceived it in two ways: infecting both its mind with the poison of suggestion and its flesh with forbidden food, and thus bringing upon it the double death of soul and body. For the letter of Scripture compels us to understand an earthly animal, when it says that “the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth.” And because of this deception the devil is called in the Holy Scriptures not a lion but a serpent or dragon, since he obtained the effect of our death not by force but by cunning. For he had as yet no claim upon the human being and could not drag anyone unwillingly into sin; for that which the groaning Apostle says did not yet exist: “I see another law in [Col. 0290C] my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7). Still less did that exist which he now sometimes roars through open persecution. Therefore, because he did not compel by assaulting, but first enticed the first human being into sin by flattery, he has since been called the ancient serpent, or the winding serpent. But because, once admitted, he thereafter tyrannized cruelly and furiously over the human race, he has been called a lion, bearing both names—of malice and of savagery—as the Psalmist says: “You shall tread upon the asp and basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90 [91]). But now let us consider the ensuing sequence of our betrayal.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 0290D] On the serpent’s question to the woman: “Why did the Lord command you not to eat?”

He said to the woman: “Why did God command you not to eat of every tree of paradise?” Why, unless because, being a most wicked huckster, he polluted his question with a lie when he said: “Why did God command you not to eat of every tree of paradise?” For although what is uttered as a question is neither true nor false, the serpent nevertheless plainly hissed a lie here, pretending not to know the matter as it was, so that he might gradually poison the poor hearer’s soul with his gall. He did not say, “Why did God command you not to eat of that one tree?” but, “of every tree of paradise?” Why, then, except so that, as has already been said, by creeping gradually he might inject into the human being more and more of the venom of the hatred with which he himself burned against the Creator; and, by exaggerating the supposedly unfair command, might kindle indignation and arouse the boldness of rebellion?

See how great is the deceiver’s subtlety in deception. The Lord God had said three things. “Eat of every tree of paradise”: that is one. Another was: “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat.” A third was: “For on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death.” This last statement—“On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death”—he passes over, as though unaware of it, saying: “Why did God command you?” But the first two—“Eat of every tree of paradise” and “Of that tree do not eat”—he confounds and mingles, and from two truths constructs one falsehood, saying: “that you should not eat [Col. 0291B] of every tree of paradise.”

Truth spoke truly (John 8): “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth; when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own resources, because he is a liar and its father”—understand, the father of the lie which he speaks. For when Christ, who is Truth, spoke everything according to the authority of the Scriptures, in this saying of Scripture too he undoubtedly had the present chapter in mind when he said that the devil had been a murderer from the beginning. It is as though he said: “From the beginning of his conversation with humanity the devil is a murderer and a liar; for behold, at the beginning of his speech he is found to be a liar and to intend murder.” O ancient sinner and long-standing murderer, truly a serpent, truly deceitful and wicked! But before we pursue his wickedly witty malice, let us hear the woman’s folly in replying.

## CHAPTER V. On the woman’s faulty answer.

The woman answers him: “We eat of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but of the tree which is in the midst of paradise God commanded us not to eat of it, nor even touch it, lest perhaps we die.” These words are already signs of a corrupted mind. For, so far as lay in her power, the woman distorted the words of the Lord’s command in three ways—addition, subtraction, and alteration—by which everyone who belongs to the devil still strives to distort Holy Scripture to this day.

She added by saying, “nor even touch it,” since the Lord God had said only: “But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, do not eat.” [Col. 0291D] She subtracted, because, although God had spoken with a certain and affirmative declaration—“For on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death”—she, wishing to make it doubtful or trivial, says: “lest perhaps we die.” She altered it because, whereas the Lord had said, “Eat of every tree of paradise,” and had forbidden one tree only, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, she says: “Of the tree which is in the midst of paradise he commanded us,” and thus she lied. For the tree of life was also in the midst of paradise, and the Lord God had not forbidden it. Therefore she was already bearing the matter impatiently and murmuring because God, as though miserly or greedy, reserved the precious things in the middle of paradise and allowed the human being to gather the more worthless things around its circumference for food.

Thus, I say, in three ways—addition, subtraction, and alteration—the foolish woman attempted to corrupt the holy command of God. Moreover, John testifies in the Apocalypse how great a condemnation it is to add anything to, or subtract anything from, the word of God, when he says: “If anyone adds to these things, God shall add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God shall take away his share from the tree of life, and from the holy city, and from the things written in this book” (Rev. 22).

Therefore, truly—as has already been said above—before the devil began to speak through the bodily or visible serpent, he had already spoken inwardly, by himself, to the ear of the heart, and had foreseen a willing inclination or consent to perform outwardly the work of sin. Consequently, the remaining events [Col. 0292B] must be understood as though the work of diabolical fornication or adultery had been consummated; for before this, certain preliminaries had occurred through secret inspiration or suggestion, delighting the mind. It follows:

## CHAPTER VI. On the devil’s blasphemy, by which he wished the Lord to be judged a liar, saying: “You shall by no means die.”

But the serpent said to the woman: “You shall by no means die the death. For God knows that on whatever day you eat of it your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” What intention could be more deadly, speech more malicious, or presumption more atrocious? For consider: we had detested the devil’s pride, by which, swelling with arrogance, he had said: “I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall place my throne; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). This, I say, we had detested: that this rebel against the Most High Light said he would be like him. What shall we say when, conversely, he strives to make the Most High like himself?

For he himself is a liar; he himself is envious. As a liar, he wants to make God like himself—that is, a liar—when he says: “You shall by no means die the death.” For what else does this mean except: “He who said, ‘You shall die the death,’ lied”? Again, being truly envious, he dares to assert that the reason for God’s command was envy, when he says: “For God knows that on whatever day you eat of it your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods.” For after saying, “You shall by no means die the death,” as though someone asked why then God had forbidden it so severely and prohibited it so threateningly, he says: “For he knows that your eyes shall be opened and you shall be like gods.”

What, then, is more horrible than this blasphemy of the dragon? What more criminal than this presumption of the most wicked impostor? As though it were not enough that through pride he lost the likeness of God, he still presumes, by slander, to assert that God is like himself. Indeed, he persuades wretched humanity that God must be regarded as a liar and he himself as truthful. Therefore let not the Lord’s hand be content with the simple vengeance by which it cast him down from the height of heaven; let it be raised still further and strengthened against this enemy, so that it may cast him into the hell of fire (Matt. 25). But now let us pursue each of the serpent’s words.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 0293A] How, as a wicked liar, he mocked them in saying: “Your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods.”

“You shall by no means die the death.” He is now a mocker and gives an ambiguous answer, so that, when God’s truth has been fulfilled, he may nevertheless confirm with an enemy’s laugh that he himself spoke truly. For there are two deaths, one of the soul and the other of the body. They were not immediately to die one kind of death—namely, that which separates the soul from the body. For because they ate, they did not therefore die bodily on that very day. But because by eating they incurred for themselves the death of the soul on that day, God’s mercy made them mortal in body, lest, like the devil himself, they should be beyond recovery by living wickedly and miserably forever.

Therefore, just as Apollo of Delphi is said to have been accustomed to play with ambiguous riddles, so now this same mimic of God and humankind was playing, wickedly abusing the equivocation of “death,” the greatest of hateful sophists. “He who speaks sophistically is hateful,” as a certain wise man says (Ecclus. 37). Likewise, by equivocation he confounds and disturbs everything that follows, speaking in one sense while wishing his words to be understood in another. “For God knows,” he says, “that on whatever day you eat of it your eyes shall be opened,” and so forth. He wished it to be understood that, envying humanity the brightness of all wisdom, divinity itself, and the knowledge of all things, God had forbidden them such a tree. This, I say, he wished to be understood from his speech, though he himself perceived that the outcome would be otherwise; yet his own meaning concerning these very words involved an almost inexpressible reversal.

“Your eyes shall be opened,” he says—namely, to the knowledge of your own shame. For there is an unhappy opening of eyes, by which the eyes of the ungodly shall be unveiled when, as the Book of Wisdom testifies, “seeing, they shall be troubled with horrible fear, and shall marvel at the suddenness of an unexpected salvation; and, groaning for anguish of spirit, they shall say within themselves, repenting: ‘These are those whom we once held in derision and as a likeness of reproach’” (Wisdom 5), and so forth. And the eminent poet speaks of this operation of the eyes when the tyrant of the underworld taunts amid torments:

> Learn righteousness from this warning, and do not despise the gods.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 9)

Likewise, when he said, “And you shall be like gods,” he intended to make them like false gods—that is, like himself and his followers, the apostate angels—though he wished, as has already been said, something else to be understood in this promise. To this promise, sweet-sounding as it was, he had mixed the poison of death as though with wine. Further, in adding, “knowing good and evil,” he sought to bring it about that they should possess both the memory of good lost and the experience of evil found, though he wished something else to be understood: that through that food they would acquire all knowledge and that nothing would be hidden from them—a knowledge which indeed belongs to God alone.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0294A] How the devil deceived humanity by the same fault through which he himself fell from heaven.

Consider now how great an exaltation there is here, according to the understanding of the one deceived, and how great a downfall according to the understanding of the deceiver. Under the same promise, when it is said, “Your eyes shall be opened,” she thinks of the height of wisdom, while he thinks of the shame of conscience. Under the same expression, when it is said, “And you shall be like gods,” she thinks of seizing God’s loftiness, while he thinks of finding a condemnation like his own. Again, under the same promise of the knowledge of good and evil, she thinks of fullness of knowledge, while he thinks of the experience of misery.

This is a most troublesome kind of deceit, in which the deceiver both gains the prize of falsehood and boasts that he has spoken truly and told the truth. But the deceived person has no basis on which to accuse the taunting deceiver of falsehood, however utterly deceitful he may be. Our understanding struggles here in the abyss of so great an evil, for it is of such darkness and depth that it is scarcely visible even to the eyes of the wise. For who can accuse the deceiver here in such a way as to excuse the deceived? God, who considers the deceiver’s intention and the deceived person’s hope, “knows both the deceiver and the deceived” (Job 12). Could he, without prejudice to justice and without being appeased by any satisfaction, hold one more excused than the other? For why had he cast the devil down from heaven, except because in pride he said: “I shall be like the Most High”? Surely the woman, swollen by the same breath, said the same thing—said it, I mean, because she thought that by eating she would become like the Most High. Who then could call upon, or summon as judge or defender, God on behalf of either party, when both were evidently made enemies of God?

Indeed, according to the true rule of justice, the deceived person first had to be reconciled; only then could judgment be sought concerning the impious, cruel, and bloodthirsty crime of the deceiver. O how truly necessary for humanity was the coming of the Mediator between God and human beings, who alone could both restore peace between God and humanity and bring the deceitful presumption of humanity’s deceiver to judgment! But of this elsewhere; for now let us proceed with the present matter.

## CHAPTER IX. How the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and how she gave it to her husband; and why she was punished with a double penalty, while her husband was not.

Therefore the woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes and delightful in appearance; and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband, who ate, and the eyes of both were opened. It cannot be adequately expressed how weighty the statement is: “Therefore the woman saw.” It is as though she had not seen before, just as she is said not to have seen. And indeed she had not yet seen in that manner, because she had not yet considered it with the presumption by which she now looked upon it.

For it should be noted that Scripture did not say, “Therefore the woman saw the tree and took of its fruit and ate,” but: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes and delightful in appearance, and she took of its fruit and ate.” Therefore she saw—that is, she considered it, looked at it attentively, examined it more curiously, and wished herself to be judge of the things she had heard. She had heard God say: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death”; she had heard the serpent say the opposite: “You shall by no means die.” Suspended between the two, she wished to judge the nature of the tree by her own senses, in order to know to whom she should chiefly award the palm of truth—to God, that is, or to the serpent.

But the inner eyes, which ought to have judged this, were already impeded by the concupiscence of the outer eyes, so that they did not see that it was not the nature of the tree, but the transgression of the command, which would bring not merely bodily death but a double death. Thus she considered the tree’s nature with outward eyes alone and discovered, through her misguided caution, that no poison of death was in the fruit of the tree; for it was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance. She judged these things to be contrary to everything God had said and to agree more with the serpent’s speech, proving its assertion true. Thus she saw; and thus, with sacrilegious rashness, she believed the devil rather than God, the serpent rather than the Creator; and she took of the fruit of the tree and ate.

Nor was it enough for her that she ate; she also gave it to her husband. But how did she give it, except now by feminine misuse of authority or by importunity? For she did not persuade him to believe her in that in which she herself had believed the serpent. “For,” says the Apostle, “the man was not deceived, but the woman” (1 Tim. 2). And how great or what kind of feminine importunity is, examples everywhere testify—not only divine examples but human ones as well. Therefore, she achieved this more by compelling than by deceiving, more by commanding than by inventing anything: the man obeyed her voice more than God’s. Hence the Lord God says to him: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat: cursed is the earth in your work.” The penalty of disordered rule is also repaid to the woman, when the same God says: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

Therefore the woman was afflicted with the penalty of a double shame, but the man with a single disgrace. For the man is ashamed only in the genital parts of his body; but for the woman, who presumed not only to offend God but also to rule over her husband, it is shameful not only to leave those parts uncovered, but almost equally shameful not to cover the head. And nature itself teaches that this is altogether to be considered shameful, because it was imposed by God as judge. Hence, after the Apostle said, “Therefore a woman ought to have a covering over her head because of the angels,” he immediately adds: “Judge for yourselves: is it fitting for a woman to pray to God with her head uncovered?” Nature itself, he says, teaches us this: for our natural judgment is that a woman who does not cover her head is the same as if she were shorn. “For if a woman is not covered, let her also be shorn”—understand: which is most shameful. “But if it is shameful for a woman to be shorn or shaved, let her cover her head.” Conversely, if a man lets his hair grow, it is a disgrace to him; and if he prays with his head covered, he dishonours his head (1 Cor. 11).

Thus there is no longer any need for a question whether man ought to rule woman or woman man; for nature itself teaches that the woman is so much the lesser head than the man that he dishonours his head by covering it, while she dishonours hers by not covering it. Therefore, the diminution of the woman’s head itself teaches that, in imperious rashness, she gave her husband the fruit of the forbidden tree, as God says: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.”

## CHAPTER X. How it is said, “The eyes of both were opened,” and how the shame of lust is the penalty of that sin.

How, then, is it said: “The eyes of both were opened”? Were they blind before they ate, and enlightened by eating? Certainly not. For the woman had already seen that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and delightful in appearance. And the Lord had already brought all the animals to Adam, so that he might see what he would call them. Therefore it was not their outer but their inner eyes, which they had closed against God, that were opened—their eyes were opened because they recognized God as truthful and the serpent as utterly false in their misery.

For it immediately follows: “And when they knew that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves and made for themselves coverings.” Therefore the statement “The eyes of both were opened” clearly has a double sense. If you look to the expectation they had conceived from the serpent’s promise—“Your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil”—it is a most bitter irony and the writer’s mournful complaint when he says, “And the eyes of both were opened”; which is the same as saying, “The eyes of both were opened, but not as the serpent had promised.” Yet it is stated more bitterly now in the form of ironic affirmation, as though openly denied.

But if you look to what actually happened, it is the manifestation or recognition of great shame; and this is immediately added, as has already been said: “And when they knew that they were naked,” and so forth. “When they knew that they were naked,” he says—that is, when they perceived that they were stripped of the honour in which they had been placed and created, made comparable to beasts, and left naked without all God’s protection. For similar is the statement which this truthful Scripture also makes, Scripture which calls things by their true names and appropriately declares events in fitting words: “Moses, therefore, saw that the people had been stripped naked—for Aaron had stripped them for the shame of their filth and had set them naked among their enemies” (Exod. 32), and so forth.

Thus the statement, “The eyes of both were opened,” has a double sense, but in both cases the true result was born: on every side the great reproach of mutual shame; God angry; the devil enlarged with mocking laughter; both sexes struck with disgrace; and amid all this the souls and eyes of the guilty were tormented and ashamed. For immediately the genital part of the body began similarly to buffet each sinner with unsolicited movements, as the due reward of pride (cf. 2 Cor. 12 [the citation is printed as XIII]). Nature spontaneously recognizes the shamefulness of this passion; it understands without a teacher and confesses it by its unprompted flight. Why is this so? Because this ought not to have existed in a rational creature, but was imposed by the offended God upon one who did not understand his own honour, so that he might be compared to beasts.

For whatever has been established for humanity by God, whether gracious or wrathful, human nature cannot altogether fail to know. Therefore, just as it cannot lack the reason given by a gracious God, so it cannot fail to know that this passion of lust is shameful. Even among spouses it blushes and avoids the mutual sight of one another’s nakedness, just as these first spouses did: having no one yet before whom they might blush except themselves—though they were one flesh—they sewed fig leaves and made for themselves *perizomata*, that is, loin-coverings.

## CHAPTER XI. How from then on we have been children of wrath, because we are born from sin and the just penalty of sin.

Yet few are those who willingly wish to be without this punishment. For in a wonderful way it is sweet as punishment and punishable as sweetness, so that very many cannot even recognize that it is a wound, an insult to rational nature, and the shame of the proud. Hence few are those who knowingly say under this scourge: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath; for your arrows are fixed in me” (Ps. 37 [38]), and so forth.

Yet the few who grieve under this blow and humbly pray to God for the remedy of healing eventually, after their labour, experience in their peace the glory of his mercy. To them it is beyond doubt that this passion of the flesh is God’s fury or wrath, because the more they advance in love for the Creator, the more they seek to restrain the movement of lust; and the more the soul is subject to God, the more the body itself is subject to the soul.

Therefore, because we are all born from such a nature against which God is angry, both Gentiles and Jews were rightly called children of wrath, as the Apostle testifies: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2). Who, then, may glory according to the flesh that he belongs to God? For how many of our carnal fathers beget children in order to multiply servants for the Lord God and cultivators for his paradise? Surely scarcely anyone does; one whose chief intention is desire merely to produce children for himself and enlarge the number of his kindred is rare. Almost all are drawn by one cause: the ardour of satisfying lust, which overwhelms not only regard for God but even remembrance of posterity itself.

Therefore, since we who are born are not begotten for God under such a condition, it is not something owed but a matter of grace that we have God as Father, that we are called and are children of God. For by nature we were children of wrath. But how justly this wrath was brought upon the human race will become clearer from what follows.

## CHAPTER XII. How the very fact that they hid themselves from the Lord’s face was an act of unbelief and impenitence.

“And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the breeze after midday, Adam and his wife hid themselves from the face of the Lord God in the midst of the tree of paradise.” By hiding, each thought wrongly about God and foolishly provided for himself or herself, like one impenitent and unbelieving. By contrast, the faithful person says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me and your right hand shall hold me” (Ps. 138 [139]).

Here the person trusts that God is present everywhere, and that one becomes far from him not by a place but by iniquity. And when, a little earlier, he says: “You understood my thoughts from afar; you investigated my path and my line” (Ps. 87 [88]), this new person, the faithful person, plainly confesses that God looks upon the good and the evil in every place and understands all the thoughts of minds. And as one truly penitent says elsewhere: “For I shall declare my iniquity, and I shall be anxious concerning my sin” (Ps. 37 [38]). Again: “But I shall cry to you, O Lord, and in the morning my prayer shall come before you” (Ps. 87 [88]). These are the voices of the new person.

But this old person hid himself from the face of the Lord in an altogether different frame of mind: as an unbeliever, thinking wrongly about the eyes that see all things; and as impenitent, not merely failing to declare his iniquity and failing to come before the Lord God by his prayer, but, even upon hearing his voice, still wishing to remain hidden. Indeed, when God came first and rebuked him as a transgressor, he accused God by defending himself.

Therefore it is no wonder that corrupt fruits sprang from so corrupt a root of the tree, carrying in themselves the evil sap of the root: when they incline their hearts to words of wickedness in order to make excuses for sins; or when workers of iniquity seek hiding places as though they could deceive God’s eye. Thus, for example, according to blessed Job, “the eye of the adulterer watches for darkness, saying, ‘No eye shall see me’; and covering his face, he breaks through in darkness, as they had agreed together in the daytime” (Job 24).

But where did they hide themselves? “In the midst,” he says, “of the tree of paradise.” This seems improperly said, since he did not say “in the midst of paradise” or “in the midst of the trees of paradise,” but “in the midst of the tree of paradise.” For what one tree has a middle in which the bodies of two people can hide? Therefore we must understand here a hiding not so much of the body as of the soul, which God principally seeks. How did they hide themselves in the midst of the tree according to the soul? Namely, by loving the vice of concupiscence which they had contracted through the fruit of the tree.

For as long as the sinner loves a pleasing vice, so long the enclosed and hidden mind keeps the door of the mouth shut tight and does not come out to meet God who calls through the straightforward approach of confession. Hence the Lord himself says: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved” (John 3). This is truly to hide from the face of the Lord God: not that such a person escapes the Lord’s eyes, since it is written, “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 58 [59]), but because such a person does not deserve to see the Lord’s face, since he hides himself from him so far as lies within himself.

And each person is rightly said to be hidden in the vice in which, held by delight, he does not come forth anywhere through the doors of confession, while his deceiver the devil lies with him, as the Lord says to blessed Job: “He sleeps under the shadow, in the secrecy of his chamber, in marshy places” (Job 40). Thus Adam and his wife hid themselves in the midst of the tree of paradise because they preferred to keep the usurpation of the tree which was in the midst of paradise to themselves rather than confess it to the Lord God.

## CHAPTER XIII. How God is said to have walked in paradise in the breeze after midday.

What, finally, does the writer mean by inserting the words: “walking in paradise in the breeze after midday”? These expressions seem lowly in relation to God’s majesty, as though, like a human being, he sleeps after eating because of cares or labour and has the midday hours allotted to his sleep or rest; then, after sleep, refreshes his heavy little body by walking and revives it with a pleasant breeze. But do not be surprised: for God had indeed slept excessively long for humanity at that time. For if he of whom it is now said, “Behold, he who guards Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. 120 [121]), had not then slept, so great an evil would never have happened, and the thief, the devil, would never have inflicted such great loss on the household.

Therefore the statement, “when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the breeze after midday,” is not the superfluity of empty speech but a most grave complaint uttered at the appropriate time. Following this example, we may say with the prophet: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up” (Ps. 63 [44]). For if the same Psalmist could rightly say, “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome by wine” (Ps. 77 [78]), because he came to help rather slowly—for the ark of God had already been captured and his priests, Hophni and Phinehas, had fallen by the sword (1 Sam. 4)—how much more should he then be said to have slept through the whole midday like one overcome by wine, when, while he was silent, so great an evil was brought forth for the whole human race.

It should be noted that the Lord God is said to have awakened and walked not after night, but after midday. For the Lord is light and there are no darknesses in him. Therefore, whether he watches or sleeps in relation to us, he never has night but always midday, because he himself is always light. “What then,” you ask, “is God to be blamed because he slept through the whole midday and, while he slept, the wolf carried off the hundredth sheep?” Certainly not; rather, the entire fault belongs to the one who allowed his guardian to sleep. For it lies within the human being’s power that he should not sleep: the human being must always stir him up, lest he slumber or sleep.

Hence through the prophet his Spirit says: “You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence” (Isa. 62; printed “VI”). How are we not to give him silence? Namely, by not ceasing, day and night, to praise the name of the Lord. But Adam and his wife, each with equal obstinacy, kept silence, because, as has already been said, neither because God formed the human being, nor because he placed him in paradise, nor because he united the two—male and female—for the propagation of the human race, did either render any thanksgiving; nor did any word of devout confession from either of their mouths sound in God’s ears.

Thus the fault belongs not to him who slept, but to the one who offered him so ungrateful a silence that he might deservedly sleep. Therefore, by the magnitude of human negligence and the justice of God, Scripture has expressed the matter powerfully and quite fittingly in likening the Lord God to a person sleeping so quietly and freely at midday that, after completing his sleep, he even has leisure to walk in the breeze and take a stroll, with no one interrupting him or bringing him concern about any business.

## CHAPTER XIV. [Col. 0300B] How Adam did not call upon God first, but God called Adam first.

And the Lord God called Adam and said: “Adam, where are you?” And Adam said: “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I was naked, and I hid myself.” It was not Adam, the guilty transgressor, who first called upon God; rather God the judge first called the transgressor. Yet it would have been more advantageous for Adam to forestall his presence by confession, and at least after sin to strive to offer worthy satisfaction. He is rightly asked: “Where are you?” For clearly he has moved his foot and is no longer in his place. For God is the place of man, apart from whom nowhere is well.

Thus blessed Job, after saying, “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends to the underworld shall not rise [Col. 0300C]; nor shall he return any longer to his house,” immediately adds: “Nor shall his place know him any more” (Job 7). He did not say, “Nor shall he know his place any more,” but, “Nor shall his place know him any more”; because surely, once God has said, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25), he will know none of the condemned, nor seek again any [47] of the lost. Well, therefore, does his place after the Fall—that is, God himself, his place—seek the man and say: “Adam, where are you?” Certainly, he who of his own accord did not wish to recognize where he was—that is, how far into evil he had fallen—ought at least, struck by this questioning of God, to have awakened and seen where he was. For this was the purpose of the seeker’s kindness: that he who was sought might find himself and know [Col. 0300D] what he had lost and what he had deserved.

But he did not answer what was being asked. For he said: “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid, and I hid myself.” He did not say: “Behold, I am here.” For he was not present to God, nor did he wish obediently to be present, since after disobedience he had hidden himself. And it should be noted that he was silent about his fault, which was the cause of his shameful nakedness; and he so complained that he was naked as rather to accuse God for having fashioned such a human creature. For he did not say: “I heard your voice in paradise, and I was afraid because I had transgressed your command”; but, he says, “I was afraid because I was naked.” Therefore he censures not his own deed, but God’s workmanship in himself.

And how perverse is this fear, in which he confesses not repentance for his deed, but only shame at his punishment [Col. 0301A]. This perversity persists to the present day among Adam’s children: when they are afflicted with some punishment for their evil deeds, they accuse not what they themselves have done, but always what has been done to them by their judges, until the rebellious spirit is utterly crushed and humbled by an intolerable wound; they do not recognize their folly. As it is written: “Affliction alone shall give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28). Indeed, when caught and convicted, since they cannot deny their guilt, they insolently defend it, and therefore are without excuse. Hear, then, how these persons, once caught, defended their guilt. It follows:

## CHAPTER XV. That both Adam and Eve defended their sin.

[Col. 0301B] To him he said: “Who told you that you were naked, unless because you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” And Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave to me, and I ate.” And the Lord God said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” She replied: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

Because the man was silent, as was said above, about his nakedness, it was necessary for God to speak and to charge against the man that very cause. Now this is the rule of divine equity: if a man wishes to be justified—that is, if he accuses himself, for “the righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18)—then God’s mercy deals more mildly and gently with him. But if, because the man delays, God must speak first and recount what the man has done, then he rebukes and corrects him more sternly [Col. 0301C], not in gentleness and mercy but in his fury and wrath.

Therefore he did not gently say: “You ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat”; rather, he sharply assailed him, questioning in judicial fashion and pressing the evasive culprit with a severe inquiry: “Who told you that you were naked, unless because you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” As though he said: This very knowledge by which you perceived yourself to be naked is guilt, because it is theft. For whence were your eyes opened in such a way that both desire stirred them and conscience struck them back, so that you could no longer bear to walk naked? Whence, I ask, did you receive this sight [Col. 0301D], by whose report you discovered your nakedness, unless because you ate from that tree of which I commanded you not to eat, and received in yourself the fitting wage of iniquity: that you should desire your shame and, from your desire, be ashamed?

What did he say to this? “The woman,” he says, “whom you gave me as a companion, gave to me, and I ate.” Before saying “I ate,” he seized the shield of defense, saying, “The woman gave to me”; and immediately, by inserting “whom you gave me as a companion,” he insolently struck God with the sharpness of his tongue. Would that he who had sinned, and knew that his sin had been reproved and made known by God’s declaration, had at least said only this: “I ate”; and, falling down as a great debtor for his offense—that is, as one greatly guilty of sin—had begged him, saying: “Have patience with me, and I will repay you all” [Col. 0302A]. But, as has already been said, he held forth the shield of defense, saying: “The woman gave to me,” as though this defense had any firmness or reason in it, and were not accusation rather than excuse, since he confessed that he preferred the woman’s gift to God’s command.

Thus, with the salt of reason rendered tasteless, he wished even to turn the blame back upon God because he had given him the woman as a companion. And he did not say, “The woman whom you gave me as a help,” though God had said, “Let us make him a help like himself” (Matt. 18 [an erroneous citation in the source]); but, since he was wholly in the gall of bitterness, avoiding the sweeter names and words, instead of saying, “whom you made as a help for me,” he says, “whom you gave me as a companion.”

With the same obstinacy the woman does not simply say, “I ate,” but, [Col. 0302B] holding out a shield “to excuse excuses in sins,” says: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” but, holding out a shield “to excuse excuses in sins,” says: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” As though the Lord God had asked who persuaded her, rather than why she had done it. He knew indeed that she had done it with a sacrilegious mind, by believing the serpent when it said: “You shall be as gods.” For, in saying, “Why have you done this?” he wished to summon the woman to conscience, so that she might reflect and say: “What have I done?” But she, unwilling to understand, answered one thing for another. She did not say, “Deceived by hope of this sort, I did it”; rather: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On the four stages of this same sin.

Meanwhile mercy labored, flying around the accused, but corrupted creation resisted it on every side, blocking its approach. For by the fourth increase of sin [Col. 0302C] it comes about that there is no place for pardon: namely, when deed is added to thought, habit to deed, and defense to habit. Hence the same Lord now says through the prophet Amos: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn him back” (Amos 1), and so forth. Clearly, under the names of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, and the other nations, he signifies that God can grant pardon to any sinner who sins for the third time; but he declares that to those who sin for the fourth time he will give neither repentance nor pardon.

Blessed Job, mystically lamenting these four stages of sin as fulfilled in these first human beings, speaks in the person of the human race: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish immediately when I came forth from the womb? Why was I received upon the knees? [Col. 0302D] Why was I nursed at the breasts? For now I should lie sleeping in silence” (Job 3), and so forth. For the sin of the first humans, before it gave birth in the effective deed—that is, in their presumptuous taking of the forbidden tree—lay hidden in the secret of a proud and ungrateful mind, just as a child before birth into the world grows together within the swelling womb of its mother. For unless it had first swelled within, as has [48] already been said elsewhere, it would not so easily have yielded when tempted without.

Again, just as an infant, once born, is received upon the knees and gathered up, and then, that it may live, is nursed at the tender breasts of its nurse, so those same sinners embraced their sin and the punishment of their flesh for which they blushed at their nakedness; they delighted in lust, and then, reproved by God, flattered themselves and dared [Col. 0303A] to defend their deed. Therefore, when pardon had been repelled, judgment was at last justly pronounced against them, first upon the very author of sin, from whom the beginning of all evil had flowed. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XVII. On the enmities established between the woman and the serpent, and why God did not ask concerning the serpent’s sin, “Why have you done these things?”

And the Lord God said to the serpent: “Because you have done this, you shall be cursed among all living creatures and beasts of the earth.” The Lord God questioned the man, toward whom, even when angry, he remembers mercy, and deigned to reason with him concerning the deed. But with the serpent there is no such reckoning. For it is written: “According to the multitude of his wrath, he will not inquire” [Col. 0303B] (Ps. 9). We know that God’s wrath against the ancient serpent, the devil, is great and unending. But the serpent through which that dragon spoke—that is, the earthly animal—will render no account at all to God, since it is an irrational creature.

Therefore God the judge rightly pronounces sentence against the serpent without investigating cause or deed, and spreads it with a clear and explicit declaration over both serpents thus: “Because you have done this, you are cursed among all living creatures and beasts of the earth. I will place enmity between you and the woman,” and so forth. He did not say, in the spirit of one uttering an imprecation, “May you be cursed,” but by declarative designation, “You are cursed.” This, indeed, should be observed concerning the manner of the Lord: he who made all things very good corrupts no creature by a curse [Col. 0303C] proceeding from himself.

Therefore, when he says to the serpent, “You are cursed among all living creatures and beasts of the earth,” he announces by judicial equity its evil desert in such a judgment. He declares that this hateful kind of animal has become hateful above all living creatures and beasts of the earth because it served the devil for the destruction of him who was so made as to rule over all living creatures and beasts of the earth. The serpent is not malicious and venomous because God said, “You are cursed”; rather, because it had been wholly rendered hateful through the devil’s defilement, this was therefore pronounced by the Lord God.

For Pythagoras says that a serpent is created from the marrow of a dead human being, which is in the spine; and another writer also recalls this in his book, saying:

[Col. 0303D]

> There are those who believe that, when the spine has decayed in a closed tomb,  
> human marrow is changed into a serpent.

If this is believed, it fittingly comes about that, just as human death came through the serpent, so also a serpent should be born from a human being’s death. It is also reported that it has not dared to touch a naked human being.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How it was said: “You shall go upon your breast.”

But what does what follows mean, when it says: “You shall go upon your breast”? Before the devil had spoken through its mouth, did it walk on feet or legs with its breast lifted from the earth, and afterward, when its feet had been removed, did it begin to go upon its breast, using its scales and ribs for feet and legs, and crawling with a pressed-down movement [Col. 0304A]? Did not God say even before he made man: “Let the earth bring forth cattle, creeping things, and beasts according to their kind”? How then is imposed now as punishment that which we cannot deny it had previously possessed by nature?

Therefore, under the name of the serpent which the devil invaded, he himself is struck; and he who in his pride imagined that he would be like the Most High is judicially made, as a punishment for his malice, like the lowest creature which he himself corrupted. “You shall go upon your breast,” he says, as though to say: Just as this creeping thing, whose cunning you employed, goes upon its breast and presses itself to the earth, so you, devil, although you are a rational spirit, will always burden your rational faculty with heavy folly; wherever you turn, you will always direct your intention [Col. 0304B] downward and weigh it down with contrary deeds.

For example: by envying, you emptied out the merit of man; but by that act you opened a place for God’s grace, which you will envy still more when man becomes so much higher than himself as the grace of God surpasses the merits of every creature. From this point to the end, while willingly opposing God you unwillingly cooperate with God; and so, having “a ring in your nostrils” (Job 40), you go upon your breast, because in a wonderful way you intend evil and do good, while in persecuting you pursue precisely that which you seek to destroy; while, like a little hammer, you wickedly strike God’s gold and, by striking it, stretch it forth to glory.

Meanwhile, “you shall eat earth all the days of your life.” You shall eat earth, I say, and not heaven: that is, not those “whose manner of life is in heaven” (Phil. 2), but those who savor earthly things [Col. 0304C]; they shall be your food. Though an evil worker and worthless servant, you are nevertheless useful to God: by devouring such people you will console the weariness of your wrath.

## CHAPTER XIX. Again on what was said: “I will place enmities between you and the woman.”

“I will place enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed. She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel.” Enmities differ from deceits in this: deceits display a peaceful outward appearance, whether in speech or in anything else; enmities, however, have an openly contrary intention. It is clear that the crafty devil in the serpent did not meet the woman as an armed adversary [Col. 0304D], but joined himself to her side on the way as a faithful counselor.

Therefore, when God says, “I will place enmities between you and the woman,” he surely promises a great work of his grace: that the woman, now conquered, should someday conquer by strength the devil, who had conquered by deceit. Yet these enmities are to be exercised not through the woman herself, but through her seed, and are to be carried through to victory. Accordingly, after saying, “I will place enmities between you and the woman,” he immediately adds, “and between your seed and her seed.” Of what seed are these things said, except of the one who is Christ? For he alone is so the seed of woman that he is not also the seed of man.

Therefore this addition is right: when the Lord God says, “I will place enmities between you and the woman,” her seed—that is, [Col. 0305A] Christ—is understood. For he plainly contended mightily with that ancient serpent and was never in any respect in agreement with him. Therefore, freer and more unencumbered, “girded with his sword upon his thigh,” most mighty, fair, and beautiful, “he aimed prosperously, went forth, and reigned” (Ps. 44); and he crushed and wounded the public enemy brought beneath his feet, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “You humbled the proud one as though wounded, in the strength of your arm” (Ps. 138). Then was fulfilled for the woman, in this her seed, what had here been foretold: “She shall crush your head.”

Hence in another psalm the Prophet says: “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters; you broke the heads of the dragon” (Ps. 73). Which of us, all of whom are seed mixed from man and woman [Col. 0305B], will boast that we maintain unbroken enmity against this deceiver? Were we not rather all enemies of God, except that through this unique seed of one woman we have been reconciled? Therefore, according to his grace, we are now children or friends of God and have enmity against that dragon; but according to ourselves, or according to our first parents, we were partners and accomplices in his rebellion, and, with faith not yet perfected, have rejected his adulterous flatteries.

For whenever we are drawn into some sin, he first flatters our head, then delights our belly, and finally binds us with his tail; for every temptation of his is accomplished in three ways: suggestion, delight, consent. In such circumstances we assuredly have no true [Col. 0305C] enmity against him. Most certainly, therefore, that seed of the woman is here promised which is Christ, through whom the very sex that was deceived wholly crushed the deceiver’s head, when, for the destruction of sin, the blessed Virgin, without sin, gave this new and heavenly man to the world.

“And you,” he says, “shall lie in wait for her heel”: that is, you shall thrust yourself into the final stages of his life; “you shall lie in wait,” he says, but you will not be able to bite. This indeed may be understood, since in other words the same son of the woman plainly affirms it when, soon to be led to his Passion, he says: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 0305D] Again on what was said: “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait,” etc.

Furthermore, great enmities have been placed between the woman and her seed, and this kind of animal through which the woman was seduced. On either side perpetual hatred is maintained not so much by rational judgment as by natural instinct. For the woman, although not always in act, nevertheless always by a certain power crushes its head; but the serpent, being pressed to the ground and lowly, lies in wait for her heel. For if the bare sole of a woman’s foot gets ahead of the serpent’s tooth and even lightly presses its very vigorous head, immediately the whole body suddenly dies together with its head, so that absolutely no movement or sensation remains in any part. Certainly this cannot quickly or lightly be accomplished even by hammers or crowbars [Col. 0306A], nor by swords cutting it to pieces. Indeed, its severed head, together with two or three little finger-lengths of body, is said to live and move away.

We have also learned from the trustworthy report of those who have investigated it experimentally that what was said above is so. Hence it is also reported that it has not dared to touch its naked body. Conversely, however small it may be, if it inserts its little tooth even into the tip of the sole, it kills. For the pestilence injected by its bite runs through the veins, increased by the living activity of the body, and takes away the soul. So grave are the enmities placed between the two natures, displaying a memorial of the ancient evil over the new. As soon as the poison injected by the bite has touched human blood, it gradually creeps on and kills the animal hostile to its nature. Hence a certain writer says:

[Col. 0306B]

> The noxious plague of serpents is mingled with blood.  
> They possess poison in their bite and threaten death in their tooth.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book IX)

For every poison is cold; therefore the soul, which is fiery, flees cold poison. As many kinds of serpents as there are, so many poisons; as many species, so many destructions; as many colors, so many pains are found. For it is a cursed animal, because by its own cunning it assisted the devil in the service of death, and thereafter it is naturally hostile to human beings.

But why should it seem strange that God permits this evil to humans, when human beings themselves arm themselves with serpents’ poisons for the killing of their neighbor, and by obstinacy acquire, and by money purchase, a venom which nature does not possess? For the same author cited above cries out in such execration:

[Col. 0306C]

> But what shame will profit bring us? From there  
> Libyan deaths are sought here, and we have made the asp an article of trade.  
> (Id., ibid.)

Accordingly, because human beings themselves in some fashion become serpents, while they endure not only spiritually “the poison of asps beneath their lips,” but also literally the poison of asps in their *sistarcia* [uncertain term], they too should not murmur that they hunt and perish—so many human beings—by the plagues of serpents.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the three, as it were, strokes of God’s sentence upon the woman.

He also said to the woman: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear your children; and you shall be under [Col. 0306D] the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.” These three strokes of the divine sentence continually torture the female sex with grievously familiar afflictions. Finally, death is added to these as the punishment of her sin. Yet this evil is common to her with the man. Why, then, does the woman, besides this, have a threefold punishment in her own sex? Clearly because the quantity of sin in the woman is three times greater than in the man.
