First, because she was deceived by believing the serpent more than God. Second, because she delightfully desired the beauty and sweetness of the tree. Third, because, not content with her own transgression, after she had eaten she also gave to the man. Concerning this it should be observed that, when God asked her, saying, “Why have you done this?”—that is, why did you give it to your husband?—having nothing she could offer even as a vain [Col. 0307A] defense, she answered one thing for another, saying: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.”

Thus, for a threefold sin, a threefold punishment was rendered besides the death she shares with the man. For because she believed the serpent saying, “You shall be as gods,” she deserved, in just opposition to this—for God is the God of the living, not of the dead—to be mother not of the living but of the dead, God saying: “I will multiply your conceptions.” For every one of her conceptions dies, in soul and body, in her sin; and none of them lives to God unless made alive in Christ.

Again, because she saw that the tree was good for food and beautiful to the eyes and delightful to behold, pain of the womb was given as a contrary return for the delight of her sight: “In pain,” he says, “you shall bear your children.” Third, because she gave to her husband [Col. 0307B] and enticed him to eat through feminine importunity, “you shall be,” he says, “under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.” Thus, for deception—for “the man,” says the Apostle, “was not deceived, but the woman” (2 Tim. 2)—for deception, I say, because she was deceived, multiplication of conceptions was returned; for the pleasure of gluttony, pain of the womb; for rash command, the punishment of that servitude.

Concerning the woman’s subjection to her husband, by which she is subject to him, and his dominion by which he rules her, enough has already been said above. But it may still rightly be asked what it means for a woman to be under the husband’s power and for the husband to be the woman’s lord, since he said both: “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you.” To this one must answer that for a woman to be under a lord is a stronger form of domination than to be under the power [Col. 0307C] of a husband.

For even according to Roman laws, a woman is under her husband’s power before she comes into the husband’s *manus*; under the husband’s power, that is, yet not as under a lord but as under a guardian, so that she may not make a will without his authorization. But she who comes into the husband’s *manus* may still less make a will without her husband as long as he lives; hence a woman who comes into the husband’s *manus* is said to undergo diminution of legal status. So greatly did this law, which the Lord of nature imposed when he said to the woman, “You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you,” prevail naturally even among the Gentiles, who had not read this Scripture or observed the commands of this true God.

Yet certain barbarian nations, like other things, confused this order of nature as well, so that a woman without a head—that is, without her husband—exercised power and dominion over men. Hence, in the Roman poet, a woman pleads her own cause, saying among other things:

[Col. 0307D]

> Shall I, a woman, first possess the cities of the Nile?  
> Pharos knows how to bear a queen,  
> with no distinction of sex.  
> (Lucan, Book X)

But this should be called not so much a right or law as a usurpation. Therefore he rightly said not merely, “You shall be under the power of your husband”—for even a little male child is under the power of a man, that is, of a guardian—but added: “And he shall rule over you.” That is, a woman shall never be free from the husband’s yoke: both her age and condition shall be first under the power of a male [Col. 0308A] guardian, and then, when through the lawful documents of marriage she has come into the husband’s *manus*, under her husband’s lordship.

Yet for chaste and faithful women goodwill makes this third punishment either none at all or very light. It not only does no harm but even brings praise. For this reason the apostle Peter, exhorting women to voluntary subjection, says: “Likewise, let women be subject to their husbands” (1 Pet. 3). “For thus formerly holy women also, hoping in God, adorned themselves for their own husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord,” and so forth. Having said these things, something further must be said concerning the multiplication of conceptions.

## CHAPTER XXII. Again on what was said: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions.”

[Col. 0308B] “I will multiply,” he says, “your afflictions and your conceptions”—that is understood as, beyond the number. For the number of the elect is indeed multiple, but all their multiplication comes from the blessing of God who said, as has already been stated above: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” and so forth. But this multiplication is not one of blessing but of condemnation; not of grace but of wrath; not of mercy but of vengeance. Hence he did not say merely, “I will multiply your conceptions,” but: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions.”

For the more fertile a woman is, the more afflicted she is. After each conception, pain tortures her in each childbirth; her own blood exhausts her, since even when she seems healthy she suffers from menstrual flows. For woman is the one and only menstruating animal. How great, do you suppose, is this wrath [Col. 0308C], how great this vengeance: that so many human beings should be conceived or born beyond the number who do not belong to the Lord or to eternal life, and for whom it would therefore have been better had they not been born?

Surely, if the soil of our nature had remained uncorrupted and had not added the pestilence of the cursed serpent to God’s blessings, it would have produced only good trees—that is, only good human beings—and the abundance of its sap would have brought forth none of the wild trees, which are born in order to be cut down and cast into the fire because they bear no fruit. This is a severity of divine judgment mighty and exceedingly terrible, more to be feared than examined.

## CHAPTER XXIII. [Col. 0308D] Again on the multiplicity of conceptions, and how Rebecca also conceived Esau and Jacob thereby.

Exceedingly pious people, who with tasteless piety criticize this very severity of God, would prefer that human beings so unhappily born as to be deprived of divine blessing should not be born and should not exist at all. Why, then, do these people beget children? Why do they—or rather their parents—sow in their flesh rather than in God’s blessing, carrying out the work of generation more for satisfying lust than for multiplying the household of the Lord God?

Surely, as was said long above, bodily incontinence proceeds from pride of mind, and from bodily incontinence the multiplicity of conceptions springs up. But someone says: “Is there not offspring, produced beyond the number, even among holy and continent people [Col. 0309A]? Did not Rebecca, for example, by one intercourse with Isaac our father bring forth one elect and one reprobate, as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Gen. 25)?”

To this I say: Do not all women even those called holy—apart from the one Mother of the Son of God—conceive or have conceived in iniquities and sins? Nothing is here detracted from the blessed mothers of the saints, who by great faith built up the blessed offspring from whom Christ, God and man, was born. Nevertheless, just as they bore their children in pain, so they conceived in iniquity—not only original iniquity, but also the sin of their own lust.

That Rebecca herself also gave birth in great pain is testified by Scripture, which says [Col. 0309B]: “Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. He heard him and gave Rebecca conception; but the little ones struggled together in her womb. She said: ‘If it was to be so with me, why was it necessary to conceive?’” (ibid.). Therefore she did not conceive without the sin of lust, since she gave birth in such pain that she almost preferred not to have conceived.

Lest you think there remains any doubt about this very young woman, Sarah herself speaks—the first mother of our faith, now an old woman, for whom womanly functions, that is, menstruation, had already ceased because of old age: “After I have grown old, and my lord is old, shall I give myself to pleasure?” (Gen. 18). Therefore, when people criticize God for multiplying the unhappy conceptions of women, let them rather accuse themselves or their parents, because they multiply their sexual unions [Col. 0309C], not in order to beget offspring for the honor of God, but in pursuit rather of their own lust.

For nature did not become prone to superfluous conceptions because God said: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions.” Rather, because the woman sinned and was corrupted by her sin, God therefore foretold what would come to her from her vice. Even if Rebecca had twins, Jacob and Esau, by one intercourse [51], as was said above—although “by one intercourse” may not inappropriately be understood as meaning “from a single act of intercourse”—one should not debate why God did not love both. Rather, thanks should be given to him because, from two little worms springing from one sinful mass, he made at least one of them worthy of his love: he who [Col. 0309D] could justly have left both, mercifully chose one in love and justly left the other in hatred.

But something has already been said elsewhere concerning such matters: namely, that one foolishly asks why God either created those angels or permits those human beings to be born whom he knows will act wickedly or perish.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the sentence pronounced upon the man, and how it was beneficial for man, after labor, to return to ashes in order to subdue his pride.

To Adam also he said: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree of which I commanded you, ‘You shall not eat from it,’ cursed is the earth because of your work. In labours you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles [Col. 0310A] it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the earth; by the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

“Because you listened,” he says, “to the voice of your wife.” It is as though he said: “Because the woman whom I gave you as a companion gave it to you, and you ate: cursed is the earth because of your work,” and so forth. A form of expression of this kind is read in the book of Numbers as follows: “Because the Amalekite and the Canaanite dwell in the valleys, tomorrow move camp and return into the wilderness by the way of the Red Sea” (Num. XIV). A judgment uttered with such a turn of phrase has the most manifest justice. For in this way the guilty person is judged from his own mouth; and, by the very answer through which he supposes himself to be defended, he is held fast before his judge. For what of it? Was the woman [Col. 0310B] greater than the Lord God?

“Cursed, therefore, is the earth because of your work.” He does not say, “Cursed is the earth in itself,” since, being an inanimate and insensible thing, it is neither worthy nor capable, in itself, of blessing or curse. But, he says, cursed “because of your work,” that is, on account of your deed. Or “cursed in your work,” that is, let it be laborious for you, its worker or cultivator. For the following verse plainly suggests this, when, explaining what he has said, he declares: “In labours you shall eat from it all the days of your life.”

For what does it yield if you do not labour, if you do not cultivate it? Certainly, “it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you,” and so forth—such things as it produces of itself—“and you shall eat the herbs of the earth,” that is, the grass which it likewise produces of itself for beasts of burden. Thus, “by the sweat of your face you shall eat [Col. 0310C] your bread”: that is, if you sweat, if you labour by ploughing and sowing, then at last it will give you your bread, that is, what is necessary for you.

According to the Hebrew truth, it was not said thus: “When you have cultivated the earth, it will not give its fruits, but will bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” Rather, the sequence of the wording is this: “In labours you shall eat from it all the days of your life.” And then this is added: “It shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you,” so that one must understand: if you do not labour, if you do not cultivate it. Thus, “by the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” But that bread of yours will by no means perpetuate your life; rather, it will sustain for some time the frailty of your mortality, “until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

Behold: the final [Col. 0310D] blow is the death of the flesh. At least this wound was capable, at some point, of taming the pride of ashes and bending necks that must be brought down into mud. Even before this, indeed, the wretched man was truly dead, because he was dead to God—namely, by the death of sin, which separates the soul from God. For God said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” But, anointed with the fresh wantonness of the flesh, he did not feel the bitterness of that death. So too we today: although we see so many people daily dying in the flesh as well, while our blood is still wanton we jest and laugh; already deprived of eternal joys and soon to be deprived of temporal ones also, nevertheless we are cheerful.

What if we were never to die in the flesh? How should we pass by with deaf [Col. 0311A] ears the death of the soul and the judgment to come at the end of the age—we who, though due to die tomorrow, are proud today? What, I say, if meanwhile, while we live, every person ate his bread without labours and without the sweat of his face? Though we are always troubled by hunger and alternating scarcity of goods, and although we are never certain about approaching death, nevertheless our flesh still does not know itself on account of pride and pours itself out into lusts.

Therefore the good God rightly acted so that man should not fail to know the evil death of his soul, nor sleep securely in his pleasures until the dawn of the last judgment: he forestalled him with the death of the flesh, so that at least someone might awaken through fear of its approach. And meanwhile, because an abundance of bread and idleness might also erase this concern, he willed that man should not eat his bread without labour and the sweat of his face; indeed, he willed that, even while labouring vigorously, he should sometimes, in barren years, be deprived in large measure of his fruit.

That this is by no means useless to man is so true that even the outstanding poet of the Gentiles says:

> The Father himself willed that the path of cultivation  
> should not be easy; and first, through skill,  
> he stirred the fields, sharpening mortal hearts with cares,  
> nor did he allow his realms to grow torpid in heavy lethargy.  
> (VIRGIL, *Georgics*, I)

He testified that torpor or idleness was useless to the realm of the Father whom he called Jupiter, although, as a Gentile, he passes over the fact that sin arises from idleness. Yet, vauntingly, elsewhere, indulging the flattering caresses of a certain little child, he promises spontaneous riches, among other things, as a great happiness:

> Gradually the field shall grow yellow with soft ears of grain;  
> red grapes shall hang upon uncultivated brambles;  
> and hard oaks shall sweat dewy honey.  
> (VIRGIL, *Eclogues*, IV)

And so forth. But this is no wonder in a heathen man professing no good doctrine, since even very many professing the Christian name, though not unaware that abundance of bread and idleness were the sin of the Sodomites, proclaimed that Christ would reign for a thousand years, saying: “Then a hundredfold of all the things which we have carnally left behind shall be restored to us”—without considering that, if recompense is fitting in other matters, indecency becomes apparent in the case of wives: so that one who has left one [Col. 0311D] wife for the Lord may receive a hundred in the future (Matt. XIX).

## CHAPTER XXV. That it was a grace of compassion, not of wrath, that God willed man to be mortal.

Therefore it belongs not to wrathful justice, but to compassionate grace, that God willed corrupted man to be mortal and, while he lived, to eat his bread in labours: so that, before the day of judgment comes, in which all the wicked are to be condemned with the devil, the ancient sinner (Matt. XXV), some might come to their senses through labours and pains, and finally through death itself be instructed, so that “affliction alone may give understanding to hearing” (Isa. XXVIII).

A certain philosopher of the Gentiles, Plotinus, likewise perceived this and judged mortality to be rationally useful [Col. 0312A] to human beings: “Then,” he says, “the merciful Father fashioned mortal bodies for them.” He understood so fully that this was expedient that he declared God compassionate precisely because he willed human beings to be mortal.

But the condemnation of those who do not come to their senses even when afflicted by so many blows of paternal discipline is just, because their guilt is inexcusable. For what more should God do to restrain them from evils? “Why should I strike you any more,” he says, “when you add transgression?” And immediately thereafter: “Your land is desolate, and your cities burned with fire. Foreigners devour your region before your eyes, and it shall be desolated as in an enemy’s devastation” (Isa. I), and so forth.

When he says these things through the prophet, he plainly indicates, assuredly, that he has struck the entire human race even with death itself, so that they might not, like the immortal [Col. 0312B] devil, add transgression, but rather flee from the pride of the ancient transgression through the humility of repentance.

The fact that he willed the day or hour of that death to be unknown to man serves the same purpose: because, while its time is unknown, though it will undoubtedly come, it always renders him anxious and does not permit him to be confidently proud. For he said without qualification: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken”; and he did not say, “Until so many years or so many days have passed, after which you will immediately return to the earth from which you were taken.” Thus he willed man to live as though he were to be judged the next day and render an account of his own deeds.

And see how terribly he reproves the man who thought wickedly that he was like God, and sets him before his own face (Ps. XLIX), saying: “For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Nature feels the force of this judgment so deeply that it was anciently customary for people in utmost affliction to sprinkle their heads with ashes as a chief instrument of grief. Yet this recollection of one’s proper condition manifests itself usefully when it proceeds from wise humility, according to the example of father Abraham, who says: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII). For when we humbly remember this, he too remembers it mercifully, as it is written: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear him; for he himself knew our formation, and remembered that we are dust” (Ps. CII). It follows.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Adam’s calling his wife Eve.

“And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living.” A remarkable digression by the narrator. The judgment of so great a calamity has not yet been completed, and yet there is leisure to turn aside and tell us by what name the man now convicted and hanging beneath the judge’s hand called his wife.

He had related that God said: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return”; and immediately God was about to say: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us.” What place was there here for the insertion that Adam called his wife Eve? Or perhaps it is not a digression, but this is the sequence of events as [Col. 0313A] the narrative itself presents it? If so—indeed, because it is so, for this interpreter of God must be believed to have pursued his narrative here not carelessly but with the greatest wisdom—the astonishing deafness of the sinner and contemner, together with the hardness of his proud mind, is briefly displayed.

For what could be more insane than to call Eve, in such a moment, one who does not have life? For *Eva* is translated “life.” But God had said: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death.” And she had eaten, had given it to her husband, and by giving it had killed him; and now he was saying, in the present moment: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Thus, by both deaths—the death of body and of soul—both he and his wife were already dead and yet still destined to die. What, then, could be more insane than, in the judgment of such a cause, to call her Eve—that is, Life—who did not even possess life; to call “the mother of all the living” her who is rather the mother of all the dying? For all die in her sin, and none of her children lives except those given life through the one man, Christ.

Indeed, if he had said this elsewhere—for example, above, where he said, “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man”—if, I say, he had then said, “She shall be called Eve because she is the mother of all the living,” it would have caused us no amazement. For she is mother, according to this sense as well, of all the living—that is, of those entering upon this unhappy life. But now the marvel lies in this: where the sentence of bodily death was being pronounced, while he was already dead by spiritual death, he called his wife Eve—that is, Life. Similarly, this too is to be noted: nowhere does Sacred Scripture mention this name, Eve, except in this place and a little further below, where it says: “Adam knew his wife.” There, as here, if you examine rightly, there is the astonishing hardness of an unrepentant heart; and the pride of the flesh is also suggested, still glorying in its very punishment because of a future posterity.

The difference between the placing of the two names, Adam and Eve, is manifest: the name Eve was devised by presumptuous man in proud estimation; but the name Adam was given by the Lord God to both sexes, as is later written: “Male and female he made them, and he called their name Adam on the day on which they were created” (Gen. V).

Therefore, after God had said, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” the immediate addition, “And Adam called the name of his wife Eve, because she was the mother of all the living,” is the same as if it had been said: Just as, when God had said above, “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death,” he did not believe, but ate, because he did not see the woman, who had eaten first, die bodily at once; so now too, when God says, “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return,” he does not believe so thoroughly that, on the contrary, he calls his wife Eve—that is, Life—because she was to be the mother of all the living.

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 0314A] On the garments of skin which God made for them.

“The Lord God also made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them; and he said: ‘Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil.’”

This statement—that the Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife—seems casually said and almost laughable. For it is not an action of the same dignity to sew together skins stripped from dead animals and make garments as are the things hitherto said of the Lord God: for example, stretching out the heaven like a skin, founding the earth, placing sun, moon, and stars in the firmament (Ps. CIII), and finally creating the natures of those very animals [Col. 0314B] whose skins they are.

Accordingly, some so shrank from attributing this work to God that they said that bodies were first made for them at that point; and that garments of skin were therefore spoken of in place of bodies, because, just as bodies are now clothed with garments, so then God clothed souls with bodies on account of sin. But this error, more truly worthy of every kind of mockery, has long since been refuted.

We ought to understand better that earthly bodies are indeed certain garments of souls, yet that they were made before the souls. For it was written above that the Lord God first formed man from the mud of the earth, and afterwards breathed into his face the breath of life.

“What then,” you ask, “was the Lord God a cobbler or a tanner, making garments of skin through the costly work of an art?” He did indeed make garments of skin, because the present Scripture so testifies; yet it does not compel us to confess that he made them in the manner which people may laugh at, rather than in the manner which all who wear garments ought to weep over. For he made them—that is, he imposed upon them the necessity of making them. Since he willed that, on account of sin, their bodies should be such and so wretched that they could not endure without garments of skin.

And it should be noted that he made for them not garments of any sort, but garments of skin. This is excellently said. For the naked bodies of both sexes are weak not only for the sake of covering shameful or private parts because of lust, but also for enduring cold. Therefore the Lord God is rightly said to have made for them not merely garments, but garments of skin, because he justly willed their bodies to be such that they needed not only covering because of shame but also warming [Col. 0314D] because of weakness.

You have, then, two consolations for misery set before man amid labour and need: sustenance and clothing—sustenance, where a little earlier he said, “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”; clothing, where it is now said, “The Lord God also made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the saying: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us.”

Thus, when man had at last died spiritually and was to die bodily, and had become needy of sustenance and clothing alike, the same Lord God exclaims: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us, knowing good and evil.” When the Lord God says “Behold”—an adverb of pointing—he strikes a great crash into the ears of all who have ears to hear.

What does he point out? “Adam,” he says, “has become as one of us.” In Adam, which is interpreted “earthly,” understand both man and woman, because, as has already been said, it is a name common to man and woman alike. What is meant by “has become as one of us”? He has become as God. For the same Trinity speaks here that spoke above in the plural to itself, saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” The same Trinity, I say, here shows what Adam has become through his fault, which above had set forth what it willed to make him.

Therefore he says, “as one of us.” Clearly, among the three persons of the Trinity, one is the Father, one the Son, one the Holy Spirit. And these three are one, indeed, but not one person. For the Father is one, the Son another, the Holy Spirit another. Thus the Lord God says: “Adam has become as one of us,” so that we are now not a Trinity but a quaternity—although he sought to be God not God with God, but God against God.

This is, in the manner of the Lord God, a most severe and exceedingly bitter irony. For who or what is Adam? Adam, already dead in soul and soon to die in body as well; needy of sustenance and covered, and necessarily to be covered, with clothing. Yet any one of us—the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit—neither is dead nor will die, and needs neither sustenance because of hunger nor clothing because of shame or cold. Therefore it is not truly but ironically said, or to be said, [Col. 0315C] that such a man has become as one of us.

And why should he be mocked by such irony? Certainly because he foolishly and proudly believed the utterly deceitful devil saying: “You shall be as gods.” Behold how he has become as God, or as one of us; behold how he has become one knowing good and evil. It did not happen as he hoped, but it happened as the deceiver intended. He does not know good and evil as God does, who foresees all things; rather, having experienced good, he now experiences evil, as God does not.

Thus, by an apparently affirmative statement, aided by the perversity of the speaker, it is denied much more bitterly than if he had exclaimed in negative terms, saying: “Behold, Adam has by no means become, as he was permitted to become, like one of us.” Indeed, he had become not merely by no means like God, but almost like the devil. But the merciful Lord God hastened and intervened, lest man, dead to God, should remain immortal like the devil.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the saying: “See lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand and take also from the tree of life.”

“Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever, the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight, to cultivate the earth from which he was taken.”

The writer uses, in the person of God, an elliptical—that is, defective—expression concerning the matter and time. When the gravity of the speaker supports this mode of expression, what it seems to lack is expressed all the more forcefully. For where he said, “Now therefore, lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever,” the statement is indeed incomplete, but gravely incomplete; and it is readily understood: “Let us send him out from the paradise of delight.”

For the writer continues in his own person where the Lord God leaves his utterance incomplete, and immediately says: “The Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight.” Therefore, he says, because he has become as one of us—or rather, because he has been deprived of the grace of our likeness—because he ate and died, and thereafter his eyes were opened and he knew that he was naked, it is now necessary that he be sent out of this paradise of delight; and, because he has become such a person, it is expedient for him, since abundance and idleness will no longer benefit him.

Why must this be done with such urgency? Certainly lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand and take also from the tree of life, eat, and, having done so, Adam—made such a wretched being—live forever. For what if, having become such, he should live forever? Surely nothing but eternal evil. For, having become wretched, if he should also be eternal, what would he have but eternal misery?

Let us spare him, lest in this way he be badly “as one of us”; lest, as each one of us is eternal—for the Father is eternal, the Son eternal, the Holy Spirit eternal—so he too should be eternal, and the wicked eye of the devil, who promised him likeness to God, should laugh that it had proved truthful. For it is indeed an evil for him to be temporal, but it is worst for him to be eternal. This likeness to God is exceedingly evil and false; it is far better for him to be wholly unlike God.

How so? Namely, because, since he is wretched, let him also be temporal. This is to be wholly unlike God. For God is both eternal and happy, and his happiness is eternal: a happy eternity. The devil lost one of these, namely happiness, but did not lose eternity; and his unhappiness is eternal: an unhappy eternity. Let us spare man, I say, and because he has lost happiness, let us also take eternity away beforehand from the unhappy man, so that in neither respect may he be as one of us. Ours is eternal happiness, happy eternity; let his be temporal misery, or miserable temporality, so that eternity may then be restored to him more advantageously when happiness has been recovered.

Therefore, amid great wrath, the Lord God remembered great mercy in this very thing—that he did not grant the tree of life to wretched man. For he willed man to be like himself in such a way that he might in both respects be unlike the devil: that is, lest man live, as the devil does, until the last judgment, and, like him, pass without temporal death into eternal fire. We have already spoken of this above, where, according to the same mercy, he says: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

## CHAPTER XXX. Again on the same tree of life, and that Adam did not know it to be the tree of life.

Now this should be noted: he did not say merely, “lest he stretch forth his hand,” but “lest perhaps,” he says, “he stretch forth his hand.” From this it is quite clear that the tree of life was not a tree in the manner of some herb that is a remedy for health. For if a medicinal herb is perhaps taken, it does not confer perpetual health; rather, it is kept by careful provision against an illness that may perhaps return. But concerning this tree he says: “Lest perhaps he eat and live forever.” Therefore the tree was by no means, as some suppose, necessarily to be used repeatedly as a passing remedy for perpetuating life; rather, once this had been taken, the body would live forever.

No less is it understood from this that Adam up to that point did not know that tree to be the tree of life, when it is said, “lest perhaps.” For someone is said perhaps to have done or found something when he did not know in his mind that the very thing which follows was in that place or object. For example, someone who turns over the earth, intending to sow and intending nothing else, finds a treasure.

God therefore said, “Lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand,” while nevertheless being certain that Adam would not stretch it forth knowingly, though he spoke, as it were, doubting or anxious, like a man, lest it happen by chance. Thus neither Adam knew, nor did the serpent, the devil himself, know that the Lord God had also planted the tree of life in the midst of paradise. For if either had known, the devil would never have so divided the counsel of his malice in half. Rather, as he persuaded man to violate that tree so as to make him wretched, so he would have advised him to seize this one so as to make him eternally wretched, or wretchedly eternal.

Nor should it be wondered at as though incredible that an inanimate and insensible tree could bear fruit of eternal life-giving power. Do not many things grow even in this exile of our poverty which are proved, by natural power, to change the nature of our mortality into a somewhat better state? Is not medicine, which is administered only by God, especially concerned with those things that are rooted in the earth? To say nothing of other things: was not the barren womb of Rachel so improved by the powerful aid of mandrakes that she conceived and bore first Joseph and then Benjamin, though she gave birth with danger of death?

Even to this day physicians, in praise of their art, maintain that what is read in books of the Gentiles was not fabulous but true: that Asclepius restored a dead man to life by medicines made from herbs, and was therefore struck by lightning, namely lest human beings become accustomed to an art by which they might escape the decree of death that was beneficial to them.

Why, then, should it seem incredible to anyone that in that paradise of delight, which the Lord God planted, there could have been a material tree of life which, by its own power, would defend a man who ate from it against bodily death, until, having earned his reward through obedience, he might enjoy the vision of the divine majesty in complete joy with the blessed angels? But let us now pursue the order we have begun.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That many doubt Adam’s salvation, and that, after being sent out of paradise, he was buried in Hebron.

“The Lord God,” he says, “sent him out from the paradise of delight, to cultivate the earth from which he was taken. And he cast out Adam.” The repetition of the statement is confirmation. For what had been said in this way, “The Lord God sent him out,” is repeated in the words, “And he cast out Adam.”

Some still dispute whether he ever obtained through Christ the mercy by which we have been saved and delivered, because canonical Scripture nowhere testifies that he performed repentance. Only in the book entitled Wisdom is this written concerning him: “She”—wisdom is understood—“guarded him who was first formed by God, the father of the world, when he alone had been created; she brought him out of his transgression and gave him power to hold all things together” (Wis. X).

But this Scripture is neither part of the canon, nor is this statement drawn from canonical Scripture, as are the other things which are commemorated in that book concerning the fathers in praise of wisdom; for example: “She did not abandon the righteous man sold”—Joseph is understood—and so forth. Therefore, the words spoken there, “she brought him out of his transgression and gave him power to rule all things,” are received with less confidence than they are discounted, because it is not shown when or where he acknowledged his sin or offered satisfaction through repentance.

Moreover, the statement, “she gave him power to hold all things together,” presents no certain meaning, because, apart from the one man Jesus Christ, no human being has the power to hold all things together. Therefore, because no good work is found anywhere concerning that old Adam, and because the new Adam is set in opposition to him—“For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV)—his salvation is freely denied by many and is adequately defended by none.

Yet lest anyone define the matter rashly, it is established also—as Ecclesiastical History reports (book IV, ch. 26)—that this assertion was invented by the Encratite heretics, whose author was Tatian.

Certainly, although Adam includes man and woman together, and both were cast out or sent away, yet the statement “to cultivate the earth from which he was taken” is better understood of the man alone, who was taken from the earth; for woman was taken from the flesh or bones of the man. Nature itself also teaches that it is fitting for the man to cultivate the earth, whereas it is more suitable for the woman to be occupied in servile work concerning the man’s body, in whatever task it may be. Therefore, when it is said, “to cultivate the earth from which he was taken,” one suitably understands also: and the woman was to work in the service of the man from whom she was taken.

But we do not read where or in what part of the lands this unhappy labourer lived, except that Sacred Scripture testifies that he was buried in the city of Hebron, fourteen miles distant from Jerusalem. For it is written thus in the book of Joshua: “The name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba; but Adam the greatest was buried there among the Anakim” (Josh. XIV), and so forth.

Moreover, *Kiriath-arba* is translated “city of four,” so called because the three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—and before them Adam the greatest were buried there. It follows.

## CHAPTER XXXII. [Col. 0319A] Who is the flaming and turning sword placed before the paradise of delight.

“And he placed before the paradise of delight Cherubim, and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life.”

Here too great wrath does not abandon its association with mercy necessary for us. For it belongs to the wrath of the just God that he placed a flaming sword before paradise; but it belongs to mercy that he willed that same sword to be turning. The turning sword is the sentence of divine judgment, which is such that it can turn—that is, it does not always close the entrance to paradise against human beings with the same severity.

It is called flaming because the judgment of the Lord is truly a judgment of fiery flame, according to the Apostle, “rendering vengeance to those who have done evil” (II Thess. I). Moreover, *cherubim* is the name of angelic powers. When we read that these were placed before paradise to guard access to the tree of life, we are astonished; yet we publicly hold and confess that we shall pass through fire (I Cor. III) and enter paradise only after examination through the ministry of angels.

What is conceived by comparing this passage with other passages of Scripture is exceedingly terrible—for example, with what the Apostle says: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each person’s work shall be made manifest. For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work which he built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (ibid.).

For what do we infer from sayings of this kind except that this flaming and turning sword was placed before paradise so that all who are henceforth to be admitted there may pass through a testing fire? It is as though he said: Because Eve’s conceptions were to be multiplied, and a confused or mingled multitude of good and evil persons would arise, but the Lord God wished to admit none except those whom he knew by name and who had been so examined that they could say, “For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us with fire as silver is examined” (Ps. LXV), and so forth, therefore he placed before [Col. 0319D] paradise Cherubim and a flaming and turning sword.

And rightly the angels who preside in matters of this kind are called Cherubim, that is, “fullness of knowledge.” For they possess full knowledge for judging. They know what is written in the book of each one of us—that is, they hold in faithful memory what good or evil each of us has done. Daily they read these books individually, and at the last day they will recite them universally—the books concerning which it is written in Daniel: “The court sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII).

Cherubim are therefore rightly named not so much for their own praise as for our terror, because our hidden things are to be made public to them. It should be known that this fire is most grievous to both souls and bodies, and inaccessible to all mortals. But for the dead—that is, the souls of the faithful dead—it has been surmountable from the time of the Lord’s Passion; and in the resurrection it will be passable for their bodies as well.

Before that Passion of our Lord, however, it was passable to no child of Adam at all, until the blood poured from his body together with water overcame that fire—not because they extinguished the substance of that fire, but because they conferred upon those who had awaited him the power that the fire could not harm them. Immediately thereafter came that venerable thief (Luke XXIII), whom, after he confessed upon the cross, faith in Christ’s blood at once endowed against that fire, so that it might not hinder him.

All of us also attain this, having Christ as our foundation: some bearing gold or silver, some precious stones, some wood, hay, straw—that is, sins of five different weights or measures. And just as some of these are consumed by fire more easily and others with greater difficulty, so each of us, according to the diversity of sins, after being purified more quickly or more slowly, will enter the happiness of paradise.

This fire is called a sword not only in this passage but also in very many places in Scripture, as there: “For the whole earth shall be devoured in the fire of the Lord, and all flesh by his sword” (Zeph. III). Therefore, when this divine writer says, “And he placed before the paradise of delight Cherubim, and a flaming and turning sword, to guard the way to the tree of life,” he indeed touches more briefly and covertly upon the matter—the judgment of fire through which we must pass—than it is found in many passages of Scripture; yet, for those who examine carefully, he proclaims more terribly the difficulty of return by which the children of blessing, begotten in this exile, are recalled there through God’s grace.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Why God is said to have placed not only the flaming sword but Cherubim also.

What is placed at the end—“to guard the way to the tree of life”—seems to say less than the matters already discussed. For it is clear that the same thing could have been said if no one were to be kept away from that tree of life except while living in this body, for the reasons already given above. For that purpose the flaming sword would certainly suffice; there would be no need for Cherubim also to be placed before paradise.

For that fire is inaccessible to all living persons, and its very blast is intolerable before anyone can by any means know where paradise is. For it is known by all who, following the Nile upstream in order to find its source, were able to drink it warm but could not reach its origin. Thus the Roman poet says:

> Those, scorched by the ruddy [—]…

A zone of the pole held [it], to see the hot Nile. (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book X.) It does not concern us here what such people say about the five zones of heaven, since they have no foundation in the Scriptures of truth, their statements being merely opinions or conjectures of secular writers. Yet, even by their own admission, we establish as certain that, because of the unbearable heat of the fire, no mortal has ever been able to reach the source of the River Nile, whose origin, according to this Scripture, is known to flow forth from Paradise. Therefore, as has already been said, even if the cherubim had not been stationed before Paradise, the flaming sword would have sufficed to drive human beings away.

If it is objected to this that Enoch and Elijah, still living, were translated into Paradise, we say that the Lord God could indeed have conveyed them unharmed through the fire already mentioned—he who, in translating Elijah, lifted him up in a fiery chariot (4 Kings 2). Yet Scripture nowhere gives us to understand that he took them into Paradise itself, there to eat from the tree of life and live for ever. Rather, they were taken away in such a manner as to be led into a certain hidden region of the earth, where they might live in great repose of flesh and spirit, until they return at the end of the world and pay the debt of death.

Thus, by saying “to guard the way of the tree of life,” the very name of “guarding” signifies not merely the exclusion of human beings—which is all that the letter seems to convey—but also judgments to be made, through rational discernment, concerning those to be admitted and those not to be admitted. For this reason not the flaming sword alone but the cherubim also are said to keep watch. But this has already been discussed above. Some teachers distinguish the matter in this way: they understand the flaming sword, that is, the wall of fire, to have been placed around Paradise because of human beings, while the guardianship of angels was placed there because of evil spirits. We agree with this only insofar as we do not deny that bodily, punitive fire also exists for evil spirits. For according to evangelical truth, eternal fire has been prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25). Fire, however, does not harm the holy angels, since righteousness has made them incapable of suffering; nor does it harm righteous souls, which, as has already been said above, faith in the blood of the righteous God-and-man Jesus Christ has cleansed and fortified.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the two succeeding generations of humankind, and why the generation of Cain is traced only as far as Lamech, who was sixth from Cain and seventh from Adam

Up to this point we have traversed the lofty summit of this holy Scripture more by creeping than by walking; henceforth bright and pleasant plains open themselves to our weary feet and present themselves to our gaze. Up to this point, I say, we have explained, as far as possible, how God the Father, through his Word, who is his Son, and because of his goodness, which is the holy sevenfold Spirit, created all things in six days and rested on the seventh day; and how he struck with a judicial sentence the sin of the man whom he placed in Paradise, and expelled him from Paradise.

Next it must be explained how, and in what order, the very Word through whom all things were made gradually made himself known, through the same number of ages of the world, to that expelled and captive human being; drawing so near to his creature that he took flesh from our flesh, and offered it to God his Father as a true sacrifice for the salvation of the world. Having done this, he himself entered into his rest and caused humanity to rest freely with him.

But before we enter upon contemplation of so great a condescension, a few things must be said concerning the two most familiar generations. From one come the children of this age; from the other, the children of God, to be saved through the already mentioned only Son of God. They are reckoned by successions of faith rather than of flesh. Just as the works of these generations are opposed and perpetually hostile to one another, so their original or principal causes arose in opposition. For the cause of the generation of the elect is the grace of God, who says: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1), and so forth. But the generation of the reprobate arises from the wrath of the same God, who says to the woman: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions” (Gen. 3).

The generation which was first commanded to be born grew more slowly, hindered by the course of sins. For first it is written thus: “Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, ‘I have acquired a man through God.’ And again she bore his brother Abel” (Gen. 4). The former is reckoned first in the generation of the wicked; the latter first in the generation of the righteous. Yet Cain was received with such exultation by his mother that, in the astonishment of her joy, she declared, as though under oath: “I have acquired a man through God”; and for that reason she called his name Cain, for *Cain* means “possession.”

He, I say—the first miracle of human generation, the false happiness and empty joy of the unhappy—killed his brother Abel, whose name means “mourning.” This name suits Abel not only because he was the cause of the first mourning for his parents, but also because he was the first of those of whom it was said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

Meanwhile Cain was already able to beget children, and the generation of sinners was burgeoning; yet not one shoot was counted from which fruit might be hoped for the good generation. At last, among many conceptions and many sons and daughters, one was born who was called Seth, that is, “placing,” because he had been set in Abel’s place, so that he might be the beginning of the chosen generation. For thus it is written below: “Adam again knew his wife, saying, ‘God has set for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed’” (Gen. 4). Therefore, as has already been said, they called his name Seth.

From him the ninth, but from Adam the tenth, Noah is born, his father Lamech speaking by the prophetic Spirit: “This one will comfort us and cause us to rest from the works and labours of our hands upon the earth which God cursed” (Gen. 5). For this reason he called him Noah, which means “rest.” Conversely, Lamech, sixth from Cain and seventh from Adam, is born—not because no further generations came from that line, but because it did not serve the author’s purpose to trace their succession as far as the Flood. His intention was to show in what generation Cain, who killed Abel, was himself killed.

That there were other generations after Lamech and before the Flood is evident from the letter itself: “Lamech,” it says, “took two wives, the name of one Adah and the name of the other Zillah. Adah bore Jabal, who was the father of those dwelling in tents and of shepherds; and the name of his brother was Tubal, who was the father of those who play the harp and the organ” (Gen. 4), and so forth.

It should be understood that, after Abel’s death, this generation in which Noah is found as the tenth began to propagate more slowly. For Seth was born in Adam’s one hundred and thirtieth year. “Adam,” Scripture says, “lived one hundred and thirty years and begot a son in his likeness and image, and called his name Seth” (Gen. 5). How then could there be more generations through Seth down to the Flood, but fewer through Cain? As has already been said, the author’s purpose regarding the generation that began earlier was to identify the generation by which Cain was killed; therefore, passing over the succeeding generations rather carelessly, he left them unmentioned.

At last Noah, the survivor from that mass which perished in the Flood, and called righteous because of his faith, begot Shem, Ham, and Japheth; through them the world was filled again, and good and evil persons were born. From Shem, Noah’s firstborn, Abraham was born in the tenth place according to the Hebrew truth. For the fact that he is found in the eleventh place in the Evangelist Luke (Luke 3) derives from the common edition of the Seventy translators, among whom Cainan is placed between Arphaxad and Eber—a name not found in the Hebrew.

Thus, according to the Hebrew truth, Abraham is born as the tenth from Shem, Noah’s firstborn. With Abraham’s seed the Lord his God made a covenant, while abandoning all the nations to walk in their own ways. The outcome itself bears witness that God’s sentence was exceedingly true when he said to the woman deceived by the devil: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. Again, on the joining of the two generations, and how God’s purpose could not perish in that generation

Who, amid these matters, can adequately estimate the steadfastness of God’s purpose toward those whom he foreknew and predestined, whom he had already purposed to call holy, when he said to the first two whom he had created, male and female: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1)? How could the race of the elect anywhere retain strength or even survive amid so great a multiplication of the opposing generation, both before and after the Flood, except through the great power of his blessing and good will?

God’s goodness conquered our wickedness, and speaking to this Abram promised him that all nations would be blessed in his seed, which is Christ. “And Abraham,” Scripture says, “believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15). Yet even in his one seed according to the flesh through Sarah, namely Isaac, the generation of the elect was neither simple nor pure. For when Isaac had begotten those two, one belonged to Cain and the other to Abel. “Jacob,” says the Lord, “I loved; but Esau I hated” (Gen. 25; Mal. 1).

As the offspring of faithful Abraham thereafter increased, the conceptions of women multiplied more and more even within that nation; and such an Israel was propagated according to the flesh that God rightly said to it through the Prophet: “Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Gen. 22). Meanwhile David was reached, and something further was said to him concerning the seed of heavenly blessing. For whereas in the promise to Abraham Christ had been designated only as man, when it was said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed,” the Lord swore truth to David and said to that same king and prophet: “From the fruit of your womb I will set [one] upon his throne” (Ps. 131). Christ was now designated as king.

Then, at the Babylonian captivity, when the old Temple had been destroyed, permission was given for a new one to be rebuilt, as a type of the new priesthood which was to succeed when the old priesthood passed away. Zechariah the prophet was shown (Zech. 3) Jesus the high priest clothed in filthy garments, by which our sins are signified; the great high priest Jesus Christ took these upon himself. The filthy garments of our mortality are removed from him, and he is clothed with changes of raiment—that is, with the new glory of resurrection and immortality. Thus the Son of God, man, king, and priest, having been prefigured, the seed of blessing is at last born, conceived by the Holy Spirit from the Virgin’s womb, through whom every curse is overcome.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Again, the divisions or distinctions of the six ages of the world, which have a certain likeness to the first six days of the age

These are the six ages of the world, distinguished by definite boundaries and definite increases of grace: the first from Adam; the second from Noah; the third from Abram; the fourth from David; the fifth from the Babylonian captivity; the sixth from the incarnation of the Lord.

In the first, Christ himself is prefigured only in deeds. In the second, he too is signified by deeds, and in addition the Lord God makes a covenant with human beings through familiar speech. In the third, he in whom we are to be blessed is promised as about to be born. In the fourth, he is already [shown as] king. In the fifth, he is also prefigured as about to be priest. In the sixth, at last, he enters the world itself through the mystery of the Incarnation.

These six ages correspond to the first six days, of which we have spoken up to this point; but what was made in those days was natural, whereas what occurs in these ages is instructional. For no new natures are formed here; rather, the deformed nature of humankind is prepared for reformation. Accordingly, the works of those days, as was said at the beginning of this work, pertain to the person of the Father; but these works properly pertain to the person of the Son.

Therefore, just as the Father is in no respect unlike the Son, and the Son in no respect unlike the Father, so it must be shown that, in the same order in which it was displayed in those days, the Spirit of fear, piety, knowledge, strength, counsel, understanding, and wisdom was communicated in these ages.

For in the expulsion of humankind from the Paradise of delight, the placement before Paradise of the cherubim and the flaming, turning sword, and then the bringing of the Flood upon the world: fear. In Noah’s preservation through the ark with the few companions of his righteousness, and in God’s establishing his covenant with human beings: piety. In the promise made to Abraham concerning Christ’s incarnation, and in the Law given to his descendants: knowledge. In Christ the same king being promised to the victorious kings of God’s people: strength. In the faithful and merciful high priest being prefigured, according to the prophet Zechariah, at the restoration of the Temple: counsel. In the incarnate and suffering one opening the understanding of human beings so that they might understand the Scriptures: understanding. In his entering into his glory and filling all heavenly things with the vision of his majesty: wisdom is rightly commended.

For the seventh age and the seventh day are one and the same rest of the divine festival. Now, as we are about to enter upon this contemplation of the Word of God, manifested to the world through so many stages of growth, let us ask the very Word of the Father to be a lamp for our feet and a light for our paths.

[Column 0325] [End of the first part of this book on the Holy Trinity and the works, concerning the works of the Father, the first person of that same Trinity.]

# FOURTH BOOK ON GENESIS  
(Gen. ch. 3, v. 24; 4–10)

## CHAPTER I. On what all the saints of old lacked before Christ’s coming

The preparation of salvation for the human creature is to be instructed by the same Word through whom it was made, so that it may first believe in the heart unto righteousness and afterwards confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10), receiving through the sacrament of his Passion the necessary remission of sins.

We indeed, who live now—whose blessedness he sighed for with open eyes as he fell, when he said, “Alas, who shall live when God does these things?” (Num. 24)—we, I say, are instructed and instruct others when we wish; and likewise we receive and administer the sacrament of perfect salvation when we wish. For we live in the time when God performed these things, when the Son of God underwent death for the whole world, so that all of us might be baptized in his death (Rom. 6).

But the earlier saints or righteous persons did not possess the same fullness. They had faith in what was to come, but they did not possess the present sacrament of regeneration. Hence the Apostle says: “All these died in faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth” (Heb. 11), and so forth.

Therefore, having died, they were still detained among the lower regions, not to be admitted into that heavenly Church until the great priest, Jesus Christ, should come and cleanse them by the sacrament of his Passion. For just as catechumens, however complete and well-instructed their faith may be, do not partake of the holy altars of the present Church until they have first been baptized, so all the saints of old ought not to have been admitted among the heavenly saints until Christ, through his death, expiated in them the stain of the first transgression.

Thus the entire earlier people of the saints or elect—the whole body of the Church which preceded the Lord’s Passion—must be treated by us in the present inquiry as one catechumen. We shall now begin to say in part how that catechumen was instructed, that is, taught, through sayings or deeds occurring as figures; for we cannot comprehend everything.

## CHAPTER II. On Abel: that he was the first witness of the only-begotten Son of God

(Chapter 4.) Once the human being had been chosen in the Paradise of delight, Scripture immediately added what concerns the expectation of the Son of God, saying: “And he placed before Paradise cherubim and a flaming and turning sword” (Gen. 3). By calling the sword flaming and turning, it aroused the hearer to remember the mercy and judgment to come, so that he might await in fear and hope the one who would extinguish that flaming sword for his faithful people and turn the turning sword.

Then it prefigured—or rather, showed as prefigured—by such a narrative the order in which he would extinguish the flame of that sword. “Now Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a cultivator. And it came to pass after many days that Cain offered gifts to the Lord from the fruits of the earth. Abel likewise offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts; but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (Gen. 2).

Abel, the first witness of the only-begotten Son of God, offered to God a voluntary sacrifice from the firstborn of his flock, through faith in the Passion of that same only and beloved Son of God, whom it was fitting that such a sacrifice should prefigure. For the Apostle Paul says: “By faith Abel offered to God a more abundant sacrifice than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts; and through it, though dead, he still speaks” (Heb. 11).

“By faith,” he says, “a more abundant [sacrifice],” for each offered an equal sacrifice in outward worship or religious observance. Each offered to whom he owed it, and therefore each offered rightly; but they did not both divide rightly. For Cain, when he offered his possessions to God, retained himself for himself, being stored up in earthly desire. God does not receive such a portion, but says: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23). Yet Cain, as has been said, retained his heart for himself and offered to God the fruits of the earth.

Abel, however, first offered his heart and then his possession; and thus, as has been said, he offered by faith a more abundant sacrifice. He believed, namely, that the sword which the Lord God had placed before Paradise to guard the way of the tree of life would be turned; he believed that the seed of the woman would come which would crush the head of the ancient serpent. Through this faith, there can be no doubt that he also received the Spirit of prophecy, so as to know that the seed of which he had heard spoken to the serpent—“I will put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed”—would be not only the woman’s seed but also the Son of God: the true Lamb of God, who through his innocence would trample the serpent’s malice and through his own blood quench the flaming sword.

Thus, after first offering himself, as has been said, he also offered gifts from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. In this manner he offered a more abundant sacrifice than Cain. Consequently, he obtained testimony that he was righteous, God bearing witness to his gifts. For it is immediately added: “And the Lord looked upon Abel and his gifts” (Gen. 4); that is, by God’s looking upon his gifts, it was openly made known that God looked upon Abel himself. “But upon Cain and his gifts he did not look” (ibid.). Clearly, because the offerer was not worthy of God’s regard, neither were his gifts in consequence.

It should be understood, moreover, that this regard of God was made manifest by a visible sign, as the faithful sacred history also testifies of other righteous persons (Lev. 9): their burnt offerings were consumed by fire granted from God.

## CHAPTER III. On Cain’s shame, the meaning of “Why has his countenance fallen?”, and how he was rebuked by God

“Cain was exceedingly angry, and his countenance fell. And the Lord said to him: ‘Why are you angry? And why has your face fallen? If you do well, will you not receive? But if you do evil, sin will at once be present at the door; and its desire will be under you, and you will rule over it.’”

He was, it says, exceedingly angry; this became apparent at once from the result, because his countenance fell. That is, anger turned into hatred weighed down his face and eyes to the earth with beam-like heaviness. For those who devise cruel things look at the earth. Hence the Psalm says: “Those who now cast me down surrounded me; they fixed their eyes to turn toward the earth” (Ps. 16).

God asks both things of him. He said, “Why are you angry?” and added, “Why has your face fallen?” Even if Cain had not intended to kill, it was already wicked to be angry for such a reason; it was a devilish sin, because he imitates the devil, who envies another’s righteousness. At other times, however, to be stirred or angered is human, provided that anger subsides before it gives birth to the deed of sin. Therefore the Psalm says: “Be angry, and do not sin; be pierced with compunction in the things you say in your hearts and upon your beds” (Ps. 4). It is as though it said: Even if for an hour you are stirred as human beings are, nevertheless do nothing through anger, and quickly repent even of the very fact that you were stirred or angry.

But Scripture nowhere allows the anger with which Cain was angry, for it is the envy of the devil himself. Rightly, therefore, does God ask both matters, saying, “Why are you angry, and why has your face fallen?” Cain had been angry through envy, and his face had fallen because he was plotting fratricide. By questioning him in this way, the gentle one calls him to mercy and to his own conscience; he invites him to his heart, that he may see for himself whether what he is thinking is good or evil.

Moreover, by adding, “If you do well, will you not receive?” and so forth, he strikes him with a forceful admonition, so that he may lift his face from the earth and raise the eyes of his mind from the earth: that is, cast the beam from his own eye, look far ahead, and prudently see what is more advantageous, what will happen, and what end and fruit will follow if he completes in deed the evil which he is deliberating in thought.

“Will you not,” he says, “if you do well, receive? But if you do evil”—and the rest is understood: you will receive that also. For sin will at once be at the door, so that wherever you turn and whatever you wish to do, it may be with you as a companion on the journey and ruler in the act. At that point it will indeed be above you and rule over you, because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). But now, before you do it, while it still exists only in desire, its desire will be under you and you will rule over it.

For example, just as one who has not yet been made king is subject to the people and the people rule over him, so that they may receive him if they wish.

## CHAPTER IV. On the voice of Abel’s blood, and how his life and death speak of Christ in the same way as prophetic writings and the Gospels speak

“And Cain said to Abel his brother, ‘Let us go out.’ And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him.”

Since these things and the rest that follows concerning Abel are clear, let us hear what the life or death of this righteous man says, and what his blood cries out to God. For the Apostle says, as mentioned above, that “though dead, he still speaks” (Heb. 11). And now the Lord himself says to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth.” Therefore the voice of blood crying to God must not be supposed to be inarticulate, that is, without meaning.

For what else do Abel’s life and death speak to us concerning Christ than what the prophetic writings and the Gospels speak? Everything that Abel did and suffered is certainly a parable or figure of our Lord Jesus Christ. First, the fact that he was a shepherd of sheep is not empty of mystery in relation to him who says: “I am the good shepherd; I am the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10).

Certainly those who despised this good shepherd, this great shepherd—especially Annas and Caiaphas, and the other thieves and robbers who killed this shepherd of sheep—were altogether one body with Cain. They were different members, but one body was formed from them and from all who persecute innocence or righteousness; and their one spirit and one head is the devil. Indeed, in respect of different offices or persons, they were many evil and wickedly doomed tenants, according to the Gospel parable (Matt. 21); but in their united purpose of cruelty their whole assembly was one Cain and one cultivator, wickedly gathering the fruits of the Lord’s vineyard not for the Lord himself but for themselves.

The lawful hour of sacrifice came, and this Cain offered to the Lord gifts from the fruits of the earth, while Abel offered from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat. The hour in which the sacrifice of this Abel stood opposed to the sacrifice of that Cain, and in which the latter was rejected while the former pleased God, is rightly understood as the evening of the old Passover. At that time, while the Jews according to their solemn rite ate their Passover, this shepherd, who was also the true Lamb of God, performed his priestly office, taking bread and wine and blessing them: “Take,” he said, “and drink from this, all of you; for this is my body, which will be delivered up for you. This is the cup of my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Matt. 25).

Thus Cain then offered to the Lord gifts from the fruits of the earth, namely, an inanimate and faithless sacrifice. For the sacrifice of the cruel was dead. And even if that Jewish sacrifice had previously possessed a certain life or meaning, insofar as it prefigured or preceded Christ’s true sacrifice, nevertheless from that time and for ever it is dead, and can confer no good. It was offered without God’s love, amid great hatred of the Son of God; indeed, because the time of figures has passed and the day of truth now shines.

Hence it was rightly said: “It came to pass after many days,” and so forth. For that sacrifice had been celebrated and not rejected during many preceding days; it was rejected at the end of the ages. Conversely, Abel then offered from the firstfruits of his flock and from their fat, because the sacrifice which our high priest Jesus Christ instituted that night, though in its outward appearance bread and wine, is in truth the Lamb of God, the firstborn of all lambs or sheep belonging to the folds of heaven, to the Passover of Paradise.

## CHAPTER V. On Abel’s sacrifice: that, according to the mystery, God truly looks upon Abel—that is, Christ—and his gifts, and no longer looks upon Cain—that is, the Jewish people—and his gifts

It should be noted that it was not said merely, “from the firstborn of his flock,” but was added, “and from their fat.” For this true sacrifice of bread and wine is not only flesh and blood but spirit and life, because the true Word who was incarnate and true divinity are in the bread and wine. Hence we truly believe and confess that it is the bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation.

This fat in this firstborn of rams or sheep is true divinity and the true Word of God in his flesh and blood. Therefore even today we say to him with the Prophet: “May the Lord remember all your sacrifice, and may your burnt offering become fat” (Ps. 19), so that, just as then, when through himself he instituted this sacrament, so now, wherever he himself accomplishes it through the hands of the Church, the richness of spirit and life may be present. May the fatness of divine power not withdraw from any of us because of his sins, lest, unworthily grinding with his teeth the sacrificial body alone, stripped of that richness, he become guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.

“And the Lord,” Scripture says, “looked upon Abel and his gifts; but upon Cain and his gifts he did not look.” It is openly established also by prophetic testimony that the Lord no longer looks upon this Cain and his gifts. For through the Psalmist he says to him: “I will not take calves from your house nor he-goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49). And afterwards: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (ibid.). Then immediately, concerning the sacrifice of this true Abel, upon which God looks: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and render your vows to the Most High” (ibid.).

And in Isaiah: “‘What is the multitude of your victims to me?’ says God. ‘I am full; I have not desired the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened beasts, and the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. Who has required these things from your hands?’” (Isa. 1). And soon after: “Your new moons and your solemnities my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me” (ibid.). And there are many such statements in the other prophets.

Likewise, it is clear also by prophetic testimony that God looks upon this Abel and these his gifts—namely, the gifts of bread and wine. For the Holy Spirit says of this one in David: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: ‘You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Ps. 105).

That the whole likeness may be completed: after that sacrifice of righteousness, the pious priest Abel is called outside by his evil brother and killed. Thus, on the evening of that most sacred supper, our Lord God Jesus Christ, both priest and sacrifice, offered by his own hands and accepted as an odour of sweetness, was betrayed by an ungodly disciple, seized by the Jewish people—his brother according to the flesh—and led out beyond the city gate to be crucified.

These are the things which Abel, though dead, still speaks; and beneath God’s altar, among all the souls of those slain because of the word of his testimony (Rev. 6), he is the first to give voice. By that voice he condemns in heaven the evil and adulterous generation of Cain, and on earth builds the holy Church of the chosen generation.

## CHAPTER VI. What is the earth which opened its mouth and received the blood of this Abel, upon which that Cain—that is, the Jewish people—is a wanderer and fugitive
At this outcry, the Lord, as though roused in displeasure, said to Cain: “Where is Abel your brother?” He answered: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?” And He said to him: “What have you done? The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground. [Col. 0330D] Therefore now you are cursed upon the ground, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. And when you cultivate it, it shall not yield its fruits to you; you shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth.” Both the folly and the insolence of him of whom this history is woven are thereby denounced—so great that no one could fully convey them in words—and the crime of fratricide is struck with a fitting punishment. Moreover, the mystery now made manifest to the whole world is prefigured in the Jews who killed Christ.

For truly, what was then said to the one lost Cain—“The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the ground”—is now rightly said to that people, as no one can fail to know. For what is this ground of which it may now, in a figurative yet proper expression, rightly be said that it opened its mouth and received from the hands of the Jews the blood [Col. 0331A] of their brother? It is plainly the holy Church of Christ: surely a good ground, a fruitful ground, which, according to the Apostle, “drinking in the rain which often comes upon it, brings forth vegetation suitable for those by whom it is cultivated, and therefore receives blessing from God”; whereas ground which brings forth thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse, “whose end is for burning” (Heb. 6).

Since this ground is rational, it surpasses inanimate and senseless ground by as much as the blood of this Abel, which it received when it opened its mouth in a cry of exultation and confession, cries better than the blood of that Abel could cry. Thus the same Apostle quoted above says: “But you have come,” he says, “to Jesus, the mediator of the New Testament, to the sprinkling of blood crying much better [Col. 0331B] than Abel” (Heb. 12). For that blood, by crying out, accused only the wicked crime of one man; and if—as is true—it announced something else yet to come, it was then audible or intelligible to God alone. But this blood, from the mouth of the faithful ground—which we are—intercedes for the whole world and pleads for the sins of all. It even invites to repentance those who shed it, and openly announces the coming judgment to those who remain unrepentant.

Upon this ground, subjected to a curse, this Cain is a wanderer and fugitive, more grievously than that former Cain was upon the earth, where he even first built a city and called it Enoch after the name of his firstborn son. Nor is it sufficiently clear, according to the literal sense, that the ground did not yield its fruits to that Cain when he cultivated it, but instead produced thorns and thistles [Col. 0331C] for him.
