But in the case of this Cain it is well known: though he thinks himself to cultivate the Church of the patriarchs and prophets by repeatedly reading the same Law and observing the same ceremonies as they did, she does not give him her fruits—that is, the benefit which, though incomplete, she conferred before the Lord’s Passion and which can now be conferred upon no one. On the contrary, she produces thorns and thistles, since a person is not merely left unjustified but even accumulates his own condemnation from this source.

Furthermore, that he is a wanderer and fugitive upon this ground—that is, on account of Christ’s Church—is manifest in the fulfilment of what Christ Himself said concerning that people: “They shall fall by the edge of the sword, and shall be led captive into all nations” (Luke 21). This, I say, occurred upon the ground, that is, on account of Christ’s Church. For [Col. 0331D] the blood itself demanded that this should happen in the Psalm, where, after God had said, “He showed me concerning my enemies” (Ps. 58), He immediately added: “Do not kill them, lest at any time my people forget. But what? Scatter them,” He says, “in Your power.” Therefore Christ Himself willed this people to be wandering and fugitive, so that this might serve to increase His remembrance or recognition among the peoples. For both their scattered captivity and the Scripture held captive with them bear witness that this brother of theirs whom they killed was righteous, and that Christian faith has not fabricated any of the things we proclaim.

Thus the letter itself also plainly treats this matter and strikes this Cain no less evidently than it struck the former one. For that Cain was not so much a wanderer [Col. 0332A] or fugitive upon the earth that he lacked a city of his own; nor did the ground so refuse its fruits to him when he cultivated it, or so produce thorns and thistles for him, that he could not find resources to build a city.

## CHAPTER VII. How the words “Whoever kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold” are to be understood

Cain said to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for. Behold, You drive me today from the face of the ground; and I shall be hidden from Your face, and shall be a wanderer and fugitive on the earth. Therefore everyone who finds me will kill me.” And the Lord said to him: “It shall not be so; rather, everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

It is the language of one in despair and holding a mistaken view of God’s mercy when he says, “My iniquity is greater than I can [Col. 0332B] deserve forgiveness for.” But what does this uncultivated farmer fear now that he has been caught? “Behold,” he says, “You drive me today from the face of the ground,” and so forth. He fears that he may no longer be permitted to farm; that, because of his crime, he may lose the ground which alone he loves, or his present life; and that the Lord may establish a law against him, by which anyone who finds him will kill him.

Accordingly, answering him concerning precisely what he alone feared, the Lord says: “It shall not be so.” But what then? “Everyone,” He says, “who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.” Different interpreters translated this passage differently. For where the Hebrew truth here reads, “But everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold,” Symmachus rendered it, “He shall be avenged seven times”; Aquila and Theodotion rendered it, “He shall pay seven acts of vengeance.” Thus the diverse translation [Col. 0332C] produced a diverse interpretation.

There is one explanation which I do not wish to pass over. Cain sinned sevenfold: first, because in the Lord’s sacrifice, as has already been said above, he did not divide rightly; second, because he envied his brother who divided rightly; third, because when corrected by the Lord he did not heed Him; fourth, because he deceitfully entrapped his brother by saying, “Let us go outside”; fifth, because he killed him; sixth, because, when questioned by the Lord, who said, “Where is Abel your brother?”, he answered insolently: “I do not know. Am I my brother’s keeper?”; seventh, because, convicted, he despaired, saying: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for.”

Therefore, because for a sevenfold sin he lay under a curse, as a wanderer, fugitive, and trembling person—as some report—“Whoever kills him,” He says, “shall pay seven acts of vengeance”; that is, he shall end through a brief death the long punishment due to Cain’s sevenfold [Col. 0332D] sin. For they maintain that Cain’s sin was erased by bodily death, concerning which it is written: “God will not take vengeance twice for the same thing” (Nah. 1).

But both faith itself knows how weak this reasoning is, and the more careful judgment of the holy Fathers plainly establishes it. For this saying should be understood of those whose confession God accepts in their punishment or before their punishment, and who therefore do not receive eternal punishment in addition after the same temporal punishment. Thus, for example, the Lord rightly opened Paradise to the thief who confessed upon the cross, because “God will not take vengeance twice for the same thing.” But the other thief passed from temporal punishment to eternal punishment. Of him too one may rightly say that God did not take vengeance twice for the same thing: for the punishment which begins here and is completed forever is rightly called one vengeance.

Therefore, since the present letter does not even permit the inference that Cain lived with a trembling body, one must nevertheless consider the fact that according to the Hebrew truth it is said very differently: “But everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the saying: “Vengeance shall be exacted seven times for Cain, but seventy-seven times for Lamech”

What then does “he shall be punished sevenfold” mean? Certainly, just as a murderer shall be punished eternally—unless, it is understood, he repents. Likewise, where it is said, “All who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26), the sword is plainly that of which David, in fear, said in the Psalm: “You who redeemed David Your servant, rescue me from the evil sword” (Ps. 143). Unless one understands “unless they repent,” the statement will not stand according to the faith.

And so elsewhere, wherever such a saying is written—for example, in the prophet, “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18), or in the Gospel, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to the hell of fire” (Matt. 5)—one must understand, “unless he repents”; otherwise the statement does not accord with faith. Thus here also, when it is said, “But everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold,” the qualification already mentioned must be understood, and eternal punishment is intended.

For the number seven signifies universality, not only among ecclesiastical writers but also among pagan philosophers. Therefore “sevenfold” means that he shall be punished with full and complete [Col. 0333C] vengeance, unless he repents. It is established, however, that the one who killed Cain, namely Lamech, repented. For he said to his wives Adah and Zillah: “Hear my speech, wives of Lamech; listen to my words, for I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise.” Therefore he immediately pronounced very differently concerning his own punishment, saying: “Vengeance shall be exacted seven times for Cain, but seventy-seven times for Lamech.”

The Lord had said: “Whoever kills shall be punished sevenfold”; but this man who killed says: “Vengeance shall be exacted seventy-seven times.” In the quantity of the number, “vengeance shall be exacted seventy-seven times” appears greater than “he shall be punished sevenfold”; but it is certainly less. For one must attend here not to the quantity of the two numbers, but to their nature. Both seven and seventy-seven are odd numbers, but not all odd numbers have the same nature. Some odd numbers are simple or non-composite; others are composite; others are intermediate. Here only composite and non-composite numbers concern the matter.

A non-composite odd number is one for which no divisor is found except unity: such are three, five, eleven, and others of this kind, for which no measuring number is found besides unity. A composite number is one which is measured by another number besides unity: such are nine, fifteen, and twenty-one. For three times three is nine; five times three, or three times five, is fifteen; seven times three, or three times seven, is twenty-one. [Col. 0334A]

Seven and seventy-seven differ, then, in this: seven is non-composite and therefore is regarded as indivisible; whereas seventy-seven is composite and therefore more readily divisible. For no number besides unity measures seven, whereas both seven and eleven measure seventy-seven. For eleven times seven, or seven times eleven, makes seventy-seven.

Thus, when God says, “But everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold,” an indivisible punishment must be understood; and it must be understood as qualified by this: unless prior repentance has made the sin soluble—that is, remissible. But when Lamech says, “Vengeance shall be exacted seven times for Cain, but seventy-seven times for Lamech,” Cain’s vengeance must be understood as indivisible and Lamech’s as soluble. And rightly so: Cain did not repent, but Lamech repented because he confesses his sin.

Observe that Scripture plainly contradicts those who suppose Cain’s sin was erased by final death, since it says of him when already dead: “Vengeance shall be exacted seven times for Cain.” Relevant to this passage is what occurred when Peter said to the Lord: “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” (Matt. 18). He, because He speaks everything according to the Scriptures, replied: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy-seven times” (ibid.). To sin up to seven times is to sin incessantly and indivisibly—that is, without repentance—as Cain did; but to sin seventy-seven times is indeed to commit sin, yet to dissolve it through repentance, as Lamech did.

But what the same Lord says in Luke—“If your brother sins against you seven times in a day, and seven times in a day turns to you saying, ‘I repent,’ forgive him” (Luke 17)—must be understood of personal injuries, which we must forgive seven times, that is, whenever they are committed, lest we hear from the Lord: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you begged me. Ought you not therefore also to have had mercy upon your fellow servant?” (Matt. 18). But concerning sins committed against God, one must understand what was stated from Matthew’s Gospel, and what the same Luke had said before this: “If your brother sins, rebuke him. And if he repents, forgive him.”

## CHAPTER IX. Why the Lord set Cain as a sign so that everyone who found him should not kill him, although in the Law He says: “The kinsman of the slain man, as soon as he finds the murderer, shall kill him”

“And the Lord set Cain as a sign, so that everyone who found him should not kill him. And Cain went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt as a fugitive in the land toward the eastern region of Eden,” and the rest.

Someone may say: In the Law this same Lord God commands, saying: “If anyone, through hatred, has pushed a man, or thrown anything at him by ambush, or struck him with his hand while he was an enemy, and he dies, the striker shall be guilty of murder. The kinsman of the slain man, as soon as he finds him, shall kill him” (Num. 35). Since Cain killed not merely any man but his brother born of the same womb, through hatred, striking him by hand while he was an enemy, so that he died, why did this same God so strongly forbid his execution, saying, “Everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold”? Moreover, the Lord set him as a sign, so that everyone who found him should not kill him.

A brief answer is this: that Law has force by the right of kinship. For the kinsman is permitted to kill one who has slain through hatred. But who could kill Cain by right of kinship? For who could have been nearer to him than Abel? Abel begot no children and had no kinsmen except Cain’s own kinsmen. In this also he was like our Lord, who, when delivered to Pontius Pilate the governor, said: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, [Col. 0335B] My servants would surely fight so that I should not be delivered to the Jews. But now My kingdom is not from here” (John 18).

Therefore, just as the legal right was that which the Lord God later commanded or permitted—namely, that the kinsman of the slain man should kill the striker—so the natural right was that by which He forbade Cain to be killed by any man. Since no kinsman survived, the case of the killer concerned no human being but the Lord God. Lamech himself, who killed him, belonged more closely to Cain than to Abel, since he descended from Cain in the sixth generation. For Cain begot Enoch; Enoch begot Irad; Irad begot Maviael; Maviael begot Mathusael; Mathusael begot Lamech.

The Lord therefore rightly set Cain as a sign, so that everyone who found him should not kill him. It should be observed that Scripture does not say, “And the Lord placed a sign in Cain,” as if, for example, he lived with a trembling body, bore a horn upon his forehead, or something of that kind. Such notions derive not from Scripture’s authority but from Jewish fables. Rather, “He set Cain as a sign,” that is, as though he himself were a sign, so that no one would dare to touch him in revenge, just as no one ought to remove the standard of a king or emperor.

Who could reproach the giver of the Law, before the Law was given, for this decision of His, when a man living under the Law, though a king, did nearly the same? A woman of Tekoa came to King David and said: “Alas, I am a widow; my husband is dead, and your maidservant had two sons. They quarrelled with one another, and one struck [Col. 0335D] the other and killed him. And behold, the whole family has risen against your maidservant and says, ‘Hand over him who struck his brother’” (2 Kings 14), and so forth. Then subsequently she says: “Let the king remember the Lord his God, lest the blood-avengers multiply in taking vengeance, and lest they kill my son.” He replied: “As the Lord lives, not a hair of your son shall fall to the ground. Whoever opposes you, bring him to me, and he shall no longer continue to touch you” (ibid.).

That case resembles this one. In this way the king set as a sign the man who had killed; anyone among the relatives who avenged the blood of the slain man would be held guilty, as though he had rashly violated the royal sign of an edict. And this was wise, since through vengeance of this kind the blood-avengers multiply; therefore no one rightly censures it. How much more, when God Himself does this in His own person, should it be ascribed to wisdom, and how guilty should one be held who violated such an edict of His?

But Lamech confessed this wound of his and recognized the bruise of his soul when he said: “For I have killed a man for my wound, and a young man for my bruise”; and therefore, as has already been said, his sin was placed under the number of remission. It should be known, however, that some understand “the man” as Cain himself and “the young man” as his leader, but this is vain: one and the same Cain can rightly be understood as both man and young man—man, namely, in age; young man, however, in his vigour.

## CHAPTER X. That homicide was the origin of the first earthly cities

[Col. 0336B] Finally, it must be observed that homicide was the origin of the first earthly cities. For because Cain had killed his brother and on that account was hateful to all, and a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, he therefore built a city in which he might protect himself. He went out—that is, departed—from the face of the Lord, having no share in His heavenly city. He called his firstborn Enoch, which is interpreted “dedication,” and named the city he founded from his name.

All who hasten toward the festivity of earthly happiness and do not await the future dedication of the kingdom of the Son of God imitate him. Therefore, just as Cain did not see the seventh generation—for Lamech, the sixth from him, killed him—although, given that longevity, some could have seen even the eighth generation; for example, Seth could see Methuselah already more than a hundred years old: so they themselves do not attain to the Sabbath, that is, the seventh day of eternal rest. Hence also the saying of the wise man: “An inheritance hastily gained at the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20).

On the other hand, in the generation of the righteous, the seventh to be born is called Enoch; and he, walking with God, was not found because God took him. For the righteous, through faith, hope for the rest dedicated to them in the seventh age of the world, and their hope proceeds toward that which is not seen in the present. “For,” they say, “we do not have here an abiding city, but seek the one that is to come” (Heb. 13).

Thus far has been said concerning three men: Abel, Cain, and Lamech—one righteous, another sinful and unrepentant, [Col. 0336D] the third indeed sinful but confessing. By these divisions all human beings have been distinguished from that time until today. For the third part, which is that of the unrepentant, is assigned to burning, according to the Apocalypse of John, which says: “And the third part of the earth was burned up, and the third part of the trees was burned up, and the third part of the sea became blood, and the third part of the ships perished” (Rev. 8). The righteous—that is, irreproachable teachers—and hearers also—that is, penitents—are saved; the third part, that is, the mass of the unrepentant, is burned with fire after the death of the flesh, receiving sevenfold punishment for all its sins, as it was said of Cain already dead: “Vengeance shall be exacted seven times for Cain.”

## CHAPTER XI. How the words “God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed” are to be understood

[Col. 0337A] After Abel’s death, therefore, another beginning is taken in this manner: “And Adam knew his wife again, and she bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying: ‘God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed.’” From him, I say, begins the tracing of the generations through which were descended the fathers of our faith, from whom Christ came according to the flesh. For this reason it immediately adds: “(CHAPTER V.) This is the book of the generations of Adam,” and so forth. And a little later: “Adam lived one hundred and thirty years, and begot a son according to his likeness and image, and called his name Seth.”

Seth is interpreted “resurrection” or “appointment”: resurrection, namely, because the generation of the righteous which had fallen asleep in Abel in some way rose again in this man; or appointment, because she says, “God has appointed for me another seed in place of Abel.” For why did Scripture distinguish his begetting with such splendid language, adding, “and he begot according to his likeness and image”—that is, a rational man begot one rational, a mortal one mortal—when the same might rightly be said of all the sons and daughters he begot, unless it intended that this man should be recognized as set at the head of the generations, Cain having been rejected as though an untimely birth?

Accordingly, it also states here the year of his father in which he was begotten: “Adam lived one hundred and thirty years and begot Seth.” In this sequence the times or years of births are counted not according to firstborn sons but according to the righteous, as is plainly gathered from the inclusion of this one hundred and thirtieth year, as has already been said. Cain begets a firstborn, and no year is stated; nor would any mention have been made of his descendants, except that the fifth of them, namely Lamech, killed Cain.

So also in the other cases Scripture traces the generations of individuals in this holy manner, not according to firstborns but according to merits: Adam begot Seth; Seth begot Enos. This man began to call upon the name of the Lord, either because, in accordance with his own name, which is interpreted “man,” he worshipped God perfectly; or because he was the first to call upon God the Creator by the very name “Lord.” Enos begot Cainan; Cainan begot Malaleel; Malaleel begot Jared; Jared begot Enoch; Enoch begot Methuselah; Methuselah begot Lamech; Lamech [Col. 0337D] begot Noah, in whose time the flood occurred, in the one thousand six hundred and fifth year from Adam.

## CHAPTER XII. What it means that, when human beings had multiplied, the sons of God took the daughters of men as wives

CHAPTER VI. “And when human beings began to multiply upon the earth,” and the rest. How great a multiplication of human beings could occur even within the lifespan of one person in that age cannot be estimated. From Abraham alone, whose wife was barren until old age, within nearly four hundred years and not many more, such a multitude arose that—apart from the line of Esau, indeed apart from the lines of the concubines whom Abraham took from Hagar and Keturah, whose respective descendants spread into Abraham’s own nations—the stock that proceeded through Jacob alone, his grandson, was so great that at the exodus from Egypt six hundred thousand fighting men were counted, besides women and children (Exod. 12).

Therefore it is not surprising that Cain, Adam’s firstborn, built a city, when the longevity of human beings was such that forefathers or great-grandfathers, living nine hundred or at least fewer than seven hundred years, could see children down to great-great-grandchildren or even more remote descendants, through the seventh or eighth generation, while begetting sons and daughters as well. Thus there could be enough citizens not for one city only but for several. Nor should those be heard who wish the years of that age to be calculated as short years, for example monthly years or years of four months; for Moses did not reckon years in contradiction to the Law, but counted the very sort of years that he himself required to be observed for feasts, sacrifices, and other sacred rites: namely, lunar years, ordinary years indeed of twelve months, but intercalary years of thirteen months.

Therefore, when human beings had now multiplied: “Seeing,” it says, “that the daughters of men were beautiful, the sons of God took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.” “Sons of God” and “sons of men” differ here because the sons of God are from Seth’s line, whereas the sons of men are from Cain’s line. How destructive such mingling was to good morals may readily be inferred from later examples. Solomon, for instance, although he was a son of David and a son of Abraham and thus belonged to the sons of God, took wives for himself from the daughters of men. For he “loved many foreign women,” including Pharaoh’s daughter, Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women, from nations concerning whom the Lord said to the children of Israel: “You shall not go in to them, nor shall they come in to you” (3 Kings 11). By this, I say, he was corrupted, because the women turned his heart so that he worshipped their gods and built shrines for idols.

Therefore, wisely, even before the Law prohibited marriages of this sort, holy men took precautions for themselves or their sons. Thus Abraham said to the oldest servant of his house, who was over all that he possessed: “Put your hand under my thigh, that I may adjure you by the Lord, God of heaven and earth, that you shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell; but you shall go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac” (Gen. 24). Rebecca likewise said: “If my son Jacob takes a wife from the stock of this land, I do not wish to live” (Gen. 27). It is therefore clear that it was no small evil for the sons of God that, seeing the daughters of men were beautiful, they took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.

## CHAPTER XIII. What it means that it was said: “My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, and his days shall be one hundred and twenty years”

God said: “My spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh; and his days shall be one hundred and twenty years.” Formerly it was thought that the Hebrew read: “My spirit shall not judge these human beings forever.” The meaning was: because the human condition is frail, I shall not preserve them for eternal torments, but shall repay them here for what they deserve. For concerning the text, “God will not take vengeance twice for the same thing,” great and illustrious men, as has already been said above, held differing opinions.

But now, according to the Hebrew truth, we read: “My Spirit shall not remain in human beings forever because they are flesh.” The meaning is this: behold, all human beings are flesh, and in following the flesh they have all corrupted their way. Was it not therefore for this reason that He said: “Behold, Adam has become as one of Us. Now therefore see lest perhaps he stretch out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever”; and He sent him out [Col. 0339B] of the paradise of delight? For what would have happened if man had lived forever, when, though certain to die and dying daily, he has nevertheless now utterly corrupted his way?

Therefore, as I then said in foresight, so now, with My sentence confirmed, I say that My spirit—that is, the spirit made by Me according to My image—shall not remain in human beings forever. For though they ought to be spiritual human beings, they are flesh and savour only the things of the flesh. I shall persist in My sentence to such an extent that man shall not only fail to live forever, but shall also have a shorter lifespan, and the years of individual persons shall be fewer. “And their days,” He says, “shall be one hundred and twenty years.”

Some lived a little more and some a little fewer years after the flood: Jacob lived one hundred and forty-seven years, Joseph one hundred and ten. But the days of him who writes these things, namely Moses, were one hundred and twenty years. For it is written of him: “Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died” (Deut. 34). And in a remarkable and almost ineffable way, the gentlest man of all men who dwelt upon the earth opportunely and inopportunely inserts himself into that mass of people dying, and living for a shorter time because of the corruption of their life; in some way he laments that he himself had been struck there according to God’s foreknowledge, so that, though destined to die, he could not even attain Methuselah’s lifespan in order to enter the promised land, but his days were few—that is, only one hundred and twenty years.

Alternatively: “But their days shall be one hundred and twenty years”; that is, they will have one hundred and twenty years in which to perform repentance. But because they scorned to repent, God would not wait for the appointed time, but, cutting off a period of twenty years, brought on the flood in the hundredth year assigned for performing repentance. This is the older interpretation.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the saying: “Giants were upon the earth”

“Giants were upon the earth in those days. For after the sons of God went in to the daughters of men and they bore children, these were mighty men of old, men of renown.” For “giants,” some translators, interpreting from Hebrew, rendered “fallen ones,” others “violent men.” “Fallen ones” are rightly so called—that is, proud persons—whoever are mighty men of old or men of renown. For pride itself is falling, according to that Psalm: “But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81).

Otherwise, if giants are here understood in reference to greatness of stature, did the union of the sons of God and daughters of men produce another nature, so that men of astonishing height were born? Therefore “giants” means proud persons, proud, namely, because they were nobly born from both lines, both that of Seth and that of Cain. From this also Absalom had material for pride, because his blood was derived from two kingdoms: his mother Maacah was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.

Ishmael too, although he was illegitimate—that is, unequal in human lineage—was nevertheless mighty in the world and a man of renown, that is, a wild man (Gen. 16), or proud, because he drew kinship from two nations: Hebrew by his father’s line and Egyptian by his mother’s line.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the saying, “He repented that He had made man upon the earth”

But the Lord, seeing that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth and that every thought of their heart was intent upon evil continually, repented that He had made man upon the earth. And, foreseeing the future and touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, He said: “I shall destroy man, whom I created, from the face of the earth—from man even to animals, from creeping things even to birds of heaven. For I repent that I made them.”

This divine utterance labours here and, as though struggling to turn a burden of excessive magnitude, almost breaks down, while striving to make plain to our understanding that which no discourse suffices adequately to explain: namely, how God may rage without movement and kill without cruelty; how, with compassion preserved, He may exact vengeance and, in tranquillity, act in or possess wrath.

“For He repented,” it says, “that He had made man upon the earth; and, foreseeing the future and touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, He said: ‘I shall destroy man; for I repent that I made man.’” He who was to say through His prophet, “I shall speak as a woman in labour” (Isa. 42), had indeed already spoken as one in labour. For just as a woman in labour does not bring forth what she has conceived without feeling pain, yet prefers to suffer pain rather than not bring forth what she has conceived, so God does not pronounce the sentence of judgment without the feeling of compassion; yet, compassion overcome, He prefers to see the miseries of the wicked rather than not pronounce what He has conceived at justice’s command.

Why? Because it is more beneficial to press the surgeon’s instrument deeply into the diseased part than, by gentle handling, to foster the corruption. Therefore, the statement that He repented of making man upon the earth and was touched inwardly with sorrow of heart belongs to compassion. But the decree, “I shall destroy man whom I created from the face of the earth,” although He says it not overcome by that same sorrow, belongs to severe judgment or judicial severity. After it has been said, “I repent that I made them,” no stronger declaration could be made.

He says something similar elsewhere: “I repent that I have made Saul king over Israel” (1 Kings 15). Certainly, a saying of this kind indicates not changeableness in the impassible God, but His fixed purpose either to destroy the former work or to bring about its very necessary improvement.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Noah, the cause of the flood, and the threefold judgment of God
Noah, however, found favor before God. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous and perfect man; he walked with God and begot three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, etc. It is a testimony to this man’s great virtue that, amid such an abundance of sins, he walked with God; it is a proclamation of his great merit that, amid such an abundance or multitude of heavenly wrath, he found favor, because he was righteous and perfect among [Col. 0341B] generations such as his, as though they were corrupt. It is altogether a great matter that a flood was brought upon the entire world; and first one rightly asks the purpose or benefit of so great a deed. For what did God chiefly intend by this? Clearly, that future ages might know how greatly he opposes sins. Indeed, he had undertaken to instruct the whole world as though it were one man.

We know that, while a person is still a child, one must act so that he may fear, lest, left to his own will, headlong and unbridled in evil—to which human nature is always prone—he rush with unguarded neck into ruin: “Strike your son with the rod,” Scripture says, “and you will deliver his soul from death” (Prov. 23). Rightly, therefore, and beneficially, as befitted the wisdom of God, he corrected the young world, wanton and reveling in flesh and blood [Col. 0341C], like a foolish little child, striking it with such a blow that throughout all its lifetime it could not forget it. We all know the history; let us seek the mysteries.

First, it must be known that the judgment of the one Trinity is threefold. The first is that by which the devil was cast down from heaven; the last, that by which the same devil, at the end of the age, is to be sent with his angels and wicked human beings into eternal fire; the middle judgment is this one, by which the flood was brought upon the world. Nor should this point be passed over: as it is intermediate in time or order, so also is it intermediate in character. For in the first and the last, the reprobate alone are struck and the elect alone are preserved; but in this one, neither are the elect alone preserved nor the reprobate alone drowned. For it must be believed [Col. 0341D] that some perished in this flood whose sin was erased by that very peril of death, according to what is written: “God will not take vengeance twice for the same thing”; but that very many of them, being impious, passed from that temporal flood of waters into eternal fire, according to the same written saying: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Jer. 15).

Among those who survived, preserved by so great a grace of God, though Noah had only three sons, one proved reprobate, and from all of them there grew up a vast forest of reprobates. This judgment, therefore, properly proclaims the person of the Son of God, who alone, by assuming our nature, tempered the strength of his divinity to the condition of our humanity; and, before he came, prefigured the work of his coming [Col. 0342A] in this kind of cataclysm. First, Noah himself signified this same mediator of God and human beings both by name and by deed. By name, because the very name Noah is interpreted “rest.” Our true rest, moreover, is he himself, who says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). How, by his deeds, Noah signified Christ must be explained more fully below.

Therefore, not without divine foreknowledge, his father called him Noah, saying: “This one shall console us,” or, “shall cause us to rest from our labors in the ground which the Lord has cursed.”

## CHAPTER XVII. What rest Noah signifies by his name; concerning the ark and the mystery of the ark

[Col. 0342B]

What, then, is the rest or consolation by which this true Noah, namely the Son of God, consoles us, except the forgiveness of sins which he grants us in his baptism, in likeness to that Noah who, by his faith, preserved with himself a few souls in that flood? For the Apostle Peter also testifies that that flood was a figure of baptism when he says: “Those who had once been unbelieving, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah while the ark was being built, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved through water. Baptism, corresponding to this, now also saves us” (1 Pet. 3), and what follows.

Thus the flood signifies baptism; those who perished in the flood prefigured our sins, which are wiped away in baptism. [Col. 0342C] In this way the mystical prophecy of the saying is fulfilled: “This one shall console us,” or, “shall cause us to rest from our labors.” Noah was one, and in him one seed was saved for the restoration of the earth, because Christ is one, in whom is our salvation; and salvation is in no other. “For no other name under heaven has been given to human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4).

Because the ark signified the holy Church, which indeed consists of human beings, it too was commanded to be made after a certain likeness of the human body: namely, it was to be three hundred cubits long, fifty broad, and thirty high. Thus its length contained its breadth six times and its height ten times. For the body of a man lying prone or supine contains, in its length, six times its breadth and ten times its own height.

Moreover, the ark itself signifies the ancient Church of all the elect. The smoothed timbers—that is, timbers coated with bitumen—signify holy men, patriarchs and prophets, from whose faith that Church itself is most firmly joined together. For bitumen is a most hot and tenacious glue, also called asphalt, from Lake Asphaltites. It therefore signifies the most steadfast concord of the saints in faith. Our Noah, namely Christ the Son of God, built this ark before he came into this world, as Paul testifies when he says: “He is faithful to him who made him, as Moses also was in all his house. For this man was deemed worthy of greater glory than Moses, inasmuch as he who built the house has greater honor than the house itself. Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony to the things that were to be spoken; but Christ as a Son over his own house, whose house we are” (Heb. 3). [Col. 0343A]

Thus the ark, as has already been said, signifies the ancient Church; Noah, who both built it and entered it, signifies Christ the Son of God, who both founded that same Church from his elect as God and entered under its law as man. The seven souls who enter with him signify the first election of evangelical grace: namely, all the apostles and disciples of Christ who walked with him and received from him the holy sevenfold Spirit sent from heaven. Finally, the clean and unclean animals signify the multitude of the elect whom they received, coming both from Jews and from Gentiles, at the command of the Spirit of Christ.

This is made clearer from another passage of Scripture. Thus we read in the Acts of the Apostles: when Peter was hungry and wanted to eat, he fell into a trance and saw heaven opened and a certain vessel descending, like a great sheet lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners. In it were all kinds of quadrupeds, creeping things of the earth, and birds of heaven. And a voice came to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). And again: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.” Having seen this, Peter immediately explained what he had understood to the Gentiles who came to him, saying among other things: [Col. 0343C] “But God has shown me that I should call no human being common or unclean.” And afterward: “In truth I have learned that God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (ibid.).

Thus here also, where male and female from both clean and unclean animals are commanded to be admitted into the ark, God already prefigured what he afterward showed Peter: namely, that no race of human beings is rejected from God’s grace, but that the faith or conversion of all will be acceptable to the Creator of all. It should be noted that the admission of those animals is repeated four times in this reading, so that the future gathering from the four quarters of the world might be prefigured.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 0343D] Concerning the compartments and form of the same ark

“You shall make compartments in the ark,” he says, “and you shall finish its top within a cubit.” Thus it was constructed in such a shape: three hundred cubits in extent at the bottom, and, narrowing gradually as it rose, it was completed within a cubit, so that where its curve was higher it was narrower, and conversely, where it was lower it was broader.

In this way, surely, the holy Church is distinguished by different orders: each order, the more confined it is, is also the higher; or conversely, the more spacious an order is, the lower it is; the higher, the narrower. Thus, for example, the state of widowhood, the more restrained in chastity than the married state, has also higher merit; and the beauty of the virginal state, the higher it is, [Col. 0344A] the fewer people in whom it is found. Because this order pursues more freely the one thing necessary, its dignity is fittingly signified by the one cubit at the summit. In such orders is mystically fulfilled more plainly what was said: “You shall make upper chambers and three stories,” that is, three-tiered chambers, in the ark.

Nor should anyone find it incredible that an ark of such capacity could be made of bitumen-coated timber, since it is plain that immense cities are built from mortared stones—especially since the work was completed not in one or two years, but throughout a full hundred years. Further, lest you complain of the small number of cubits, geometers have larger cubits, such that one of theirs contains six ordinary cubits. And Moses, who was trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, must surely be believed to have reckoned geometrical cubits. If so, it cannot be estimated how great the capacity of that ark was, extending through so many and such large cubits in length, breadth, and height, so that it could provide ample spaces for animals of every kind, two by two and seven by seven.

What, finally, is the door set low in the side of this ark? Surely it is the saving sacrament of Christ’s baptism, which flowed from his opened side; without it no one can enter the Church or be freed from sins.

## CHAPTER XIX. How long the patience of God waited while the ark was being built

(CH. VII.) Noah was six hundred years old when the waters of the flood overflowed the earth. From this is gathered how long God waited for them to repent, according to the Apostle Peter in his Epistle: “Those who were once unbelieving in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built” (1 Pet. 3). For when Noah was five hundred years old, God gave the command: “Make yourself an ark.” But he was six hundred years old when, as the waters overflowed, he entered it. Therefore for approximately one hundred years they were unbelieving, while the public construction of the ark preached to them, and the patience of God waited for them for so long. But they, according to their hardness and impenitent heart, “stored up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath” (Rom. 2).

“And rain fell,” it says, “upon the earth for forty days and forty nights.” By the forty days [Col. 0344D] and forty nights is signified all the remaining time of this age from the incarnation or passion of the Lord, during which the waters of baptism continually overflow and drown the sins left outside by those entering the Church. For just as, in the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea, the drowned Egyptians signify evil spirits or sins, so the ungodly who perish in the flood, while the ark survives with a few, fittingly signify sins that perish.

## CHAPTER XX. Again concerning the flood, and the saying, “the floodgates of heaven were opened”

“All the fountains of the great deep were broken up,” it says, “and the floodgates of heaven were opened.” The statement, “the floodgates of heaven were opened,” must be understood hyperbolically, [Col. 0345A] as spoken to convey the magnitude of the inundation, so great that the firmament made by God in the midst of the waters, to divide waters from waters, seemed, in popular opinion, to have been shattered.

We do indeed say that the floodgates of heaven are hidden channels through which rain descends from the aerial heaven. Yet in saying this we speak more according to popular usage than the meaning of Scripture. For heaven is not something solid or hard, so that it may rightly be understood as cut through with floodgates—that is, windows—as a wall is pierced, so that when they are opened waters are poured downward that were held above when those same gates were closed. Otherwise, if it must truly be thought to have been dissolved because it is said that “the floodgates of heaven were opened,” consider how true can be what the Psalmist sings of the heavens: “He established them for age and for age of age; he gave a command, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 143).

But if you ask whence came such masses of water, covering everything so that they stood fifteen cubits higher than the mountains they covered, the answer is readily apparent: they came from where they had gone, when God said: “Let the waters under the firmament be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear” (Gen. 1). It is clear that the firmament had already been made, dividing waters from waters, and that so many waters remained beneath the firmament that dry land could nowhere appear. Hence, after saying, “You founded the earth upon its stability; it shall not be moved for age upon age” (Ps. 103), the Psalmist immediately adds, so that you may know that not even the mountain summits rose above the waters: [Col. 0345C] “The waters shall stand; at your rebuke they shall flee; at the voice of your thunder they shall be afraid” (ibid.), using the future tense for the past, which grammarians call a solecism.

Again, if you ask where they withdrew after repose was granted, it is known, according to Ecclesiastes, that all waters and streams return through hidden channels to the womb of the deep (Eccles. 1).

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the fear of the Lord, and that the Lord truly ought to be feared according to these acts

Almost everything said thus far, from the beginning of judgment upon the transgressing human being, is full of fear; and from it every creature plainly sees that God is truly, as the Psalmist says, “terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 65). [Col. 0345D] Hence the very name *Deus* (“God”) is derived by Greek etymology. For in Greek *theos* is said in Latin to mean “fear”; and from this our Creator is called *Deus*, because he is truly to be feared.

Hence the saying of the Wise Man: “My son, do not be without fear; do not add sin upon sin and say, ‘God’s mercy is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins.’ For mercy and wrath swiftly draw near from him, and his wrath looks upon sinners” (Ecclus. 5).

Now at last we must enter inwardly—that is, to Noah himself and his wife, his sons and his sons’ wives—and, from this beginning of the world’s second age, consider from what God said and did with them the reason why, as we ascend, the holy prophet rightly placed after the spirit of fear the spirit of piety (Isa. 11). For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110), while piety is the second step of ascent, already calling forth love, which, when perfect, casts fear out (John 4).

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the piety of the same Lord, according to which he remembered Noah, as Scripture says; and concerning the true Noah, Christ, whom God the Father remembered after the waters of tribulation, raising him from the dead; and concerning the dove he sent forth, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit which he gave

(CH. VIII.) “But the Lord remembered Noah, and all the animals and all the cattle [Col. 0346B] that were with him in the ark; and he brought a wind upon the earth, and the waters diminished,” etc.

First, it must not be passed over that whatever a pious feeling touches cannot be unaware how much Noah, a righteous and perfect man, suffered in such a storm. For, to say nothing of the fact that that ark was for him a storm-tossed and restless prison through a whole year—for then especially “the stormy wind stood still, and its waves were lifted up; they went up to the heavens and went down to the depths; their soul melted away in evils” (Ps. 106)—to omit this, I say, Noah would not truly have been righteous or perfect if, amid that multitude of common human misery, he had been able to laugh at his own safety, especially when Scripture did not hesitate to say of the impassible God that at that time he “was touched inwardly with grief of heart” (Gen. 6).

One may confidently say that Jeremiah did not endure so many inward crosses over the burning of the city or the captivity of the people that he saw, nor, in foretelling the coming Babylonian army, hear so many insults or terrors as Noah heard—unless it was because the mighty and renowned men of old who existed at that time were no less [formidable] (ibid.). Thus, even if he suffered nothing in body, he was tossed by great suffering in his mind; and the voice of his Head, speaking in the Prophet according to the truth of his passion, fits him especially well: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul. I am sunk in deep mire, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 68). [Col. 0346D]

For those waters by which sinners were then destroyed in some manner truly entered even into his soul; and these waters of baptism, by which our sins are now destroyed, almost went forth with the very soul of the Lord Jesus from his body. Therefore, in the fact that the Lord remembered Noah, all the animals, and all the cattle that were with him in the ark, brought a wind upon the earth, and diminished the waters; and in the fact that Noah, after long waiting, sent out a raven that did not return to him, and also sent out a dove that returned the first and second times but, when sent out the third time, did not return—there is indeed a great and beautiful work of piety, but far greater [Col. 0347A] and more beautiful is what is mystically prefigured in it.

For God the Father remembered Christ his Son after waters had entered even to his soul, after the tribulations of death had passed through his soul, while he was held enclosed in the tomb. He brought a spirit upon the earth—by “spirit,” I mean returning life—upon the earth, that is, his lifeless body: for he raised him from the dead. And over all the earth, through the resurrection of one, God brought a spirit: from that time he gave human beings the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. He disperses the mists of hearts and dries up the waves of temptations just as the spirit that God then brought upon the earth diminished the waters and gradually drove them away unto dry ground, by warming the air that had until then been damp and cold.

For here, according to the letter, we understand “spirit” as a warm wind, or even the sun itself, which until then had lain hidden beneath thick clouds. Of it Ecclesiastes says: “The wind goes around, circling through all things, and returns to its circuits” (Eccles. 1).

But truthful Scripture says that, when the waters had already diminished and the mountain summits were already visible, Noah waited forty days and then released the raven; when it did not return, he sent out the dove. A great mystery, and a great proclamation of the true Truth. For after our Lord rose from the dead and raised his mountains, covered with sorrow, into joy, the Christian faith knows that he quietly waited forty days; then at last, ascending into heaven, he caused the former service of the old Law to pass away and commanded the new grace of baptism to be preached, sending the Holy Spirit from heaven. [Col. 0347C]

The raven was sent out and no longer returns, because the unbelieving people of the Jews, cast out from the Church of patriarchs and prophets, wander outside; craving the corpses of ancient sacrifices, they boast in empty talk of the carnal stock of the ancient fathers. But the holy apostolic Church, having received the Holy Spirit, is sent forth and returns, according to what is said of the holy preachers of the Gospel through the wondering prophet: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). For they fly like clouds, bringing the rain of peace to the world, and like doves return to the windows of him who sent them for the ministry of our salvation, eagerly beholding his glory.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Again concerning the same dove, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit, and how it was sent forth the third time

Those individuals are indeed like doves, but the one dove is the grace of the Holy Spirit; because of it they are called doves. That dove which the holy Noah sent from the ark signified the Holy Spirit especially in his own person. But why was it sent out three times, unless because from the sacraments of Christ or of the Church the threefold grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon each believing soul? The first grace is the forgiveness of sins; the second, the distribution of diverse gifts [Col. 0348A]; the third, recompense in the resurrection of the dead.

Moreover, Christ himself, who is the head of the Church, was anointed three times: first, when he was conceived of the Holy Spirit; second, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him at the Jordan in the form of a dove; third, when he rose from the dead. In his figure David, who bore the type both of Christ and of the Church, was anointed king three times: first, when Samuel anointed him in his father’s house (1 Sam. 16); second, when he was anointed at Hebron over Judah alone (2 Sam. 2); third, when he was anointed over all Israel (2 Sam. 5).

Thus the first sending of the dove is the forgiveness of sins, which the true Noah—that is, Christ our rest—sent forth immediately after his resurrection, breathing on them and saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). But they did not yet dare to go out publicly and announce such grace to people, because of fear of the Jews. Therefore it was aptly said of that dove that, “when it found no place where its foot might rest, it returned to him in the ark.” For the waters, Scripture says, were over the whole earth: namely, those waters which, according to the Psalmist (Ps. 68), entered even unto the soul of the Lord Jesus and which the apostles, still weak, feared.

Nor is it surprising that the raven, which according to the letter did not return, could find what the dove could not find—a place where its foot might rest—even though, as the waters diminished, the mountain summits had already appeared. For the raven could more easily find rest because it found corpses in abundance; but the dove, because it does not feed on corpses, even if it could find some mountain ridge on which to perch, could not rest without food. [Col. 0348C]

After waiting another seven days, Noah again sent the dove out from the ark. But it came to him at evening, carrying in its beak a branch of green olive. Sent forth the second time, the dove returned at evening and brought back a branch of green olive, because the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles a second time on the day of Pentecost and summoned each of them, at the end of life, to the rest of the heavenly Church with the eternal reward of perfect peace.

Sent out a third time, it did not return, because when they rise from the dead—which, as has already been said above, will be the third outpouring of the Holy Spirit—they will be sent nowhere from which to return; for they shall go forth not to labor but to reign immortally. So too, the same dove comes three times to each of the elect: first, when one is baptized for the forgiveness of sins; second, when one receives the laying on of hands through bishops; third, as has been said, in the resurrection of the dead (Eph. 2).

Behold how truly it was said that Noah found favor before God. For this other Noah truly found favor: he reconciled us to God and, abolishing enmities in his flesh, made children of wrath into children of grace, and children of Gehenna into children of eternal life.

## CHAPTER XXIV. [Col. 0349A] Concerning the obedience of Noah, a righteous man: as he entered at God’s command, so he left at the same command

Thus, in the six hundred and first year, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters diminished from the earth; and Noah, opening the covering of the ark, looked all around and saw that the surface of the earth was dry. In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dried. Then God spoke to Noah, saying: “Go out of the ark, you and your wife,” etc.

It should be carefully noted that it is said Noah looked on the first day of the first month and saw that the earth was dry, and then it is added: “In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the earth was dried.” For when Noah had already seen on the first day of the first month that the earth was dry, what does it mean that Scripture again says that in the second month, on the twenty-seventh [Col. 0349B] day of the month—after so long an interval, namely fifty-four days from the day on which Noah saw the earth dry—the earth was dried? Clearly, so that what follows might more suitably be added: “God spoke to Noah, saying: Go out of the ark.” It is as though it said: The earth had been dry for so many days before Noah at last went out of the ark at God’s command.

Thus, in this also, the great righteousness or perfection of a righteous and perfect man is commended as worthy of praise: though imprisoned for so long, he did not break out as soon as he saw land, but as he faithfully received the command to enter, so he obediently waited for permission to leave.

Now one must investigate the times of the flood itself: at what season of the year it began to overflow; how long the waters possessed the earth without abatement; when the ark came to rest upon the mountains of Armenia; likewise at what time the mountain summits appeared, when the earth dried, and when Noah himself went out of the ark with all the others—following the order of the preceding passage.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the year of the flood and the season of the year when its waters began to overflow

“In the second month,” it says, “on the seventeenth day of the month, all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the floodgates of heaven were opened” (Gen. 7). The second month according to the Law is the same month which Romans call May; and it is called, by the law or nature of the seasons, the month in which days are lengthened and extended in fair and serene weather, while the earth is clothed with the beauty of all things in the world that pertain to the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes.

The month called April by the Romans is the first month of the year for this Moses. Thus, when he was about to give, by God’s authority, the Law concerning eating the paschal lamb, he says: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exod. 12). And lest the difficulty arise that the beginnings or ends of the years or months may here be reckoned according to Noah’s birth, recall that, before the year of the flood had been completed by about a full month, [Col. 0350A] the dove Noah sent out returned carrying in its beak an olive branch with green leaves. Thus, whatever season Noah’s birth occurred in, this too is an indication that the year was completed in springtime.

Therefore that sudden snare of judgment did not catch those people unawares at all lightly, since it came upon them in the more fervent season of pleasure. Hence the Lord rightly says: “As it happened in the days of Noah, so it shall be in the days of the Son of Man: they were eating and drinking, taking wives and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all” (Matt. 24).

From that day rain fell upon the earth for forty days and forty nights. Thereafter the overflowing waters, rising fifteen cubits above all the mountains, possessed the earth for one hundred and fifty days. For as soon as that number of days had elapsed, evidence of their decrease appeared. Indeed, Scripture says: “In the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, the ark rested upon the mountains of Armenia” (Gen. 8). Forty days of rain added to one hundred and fifty days make six lunar months, with a little more than ten days remaining, because one month exceeds another by a day. But the seventeenth day of the month was the day when the rains first overflowed. Therefore the ark rested not on the tenth but on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, because the fountains of the deep were broken up and the floodgates of heaven opened not on the first but, as has already been said, on the seventeenth day of the month. [Col. 0350C]

Let one carefully follow this year, which was one among Noah’s nine hundred and fifty years, so that it may be clearer than light that the years of those people who lived for so many years in the still-new world were not shorter, as some have supposed, but of the same length as years are now. Now the seventh month from the beginning of the flood is the same month that the Romans call November. Hence the storm of that judgment is all the more astonishing: it was aided by no seasonal condition, but, on the contrary, the force of rains burst forth in May, the month in which, as already said, the sun advances higher and the sky naturally grows bright; and around wintertime, that is, in November, when the waters had diminished, the ark came to rest, after so great and prolonged a scattering of storms.

Finally, in the tenth month of the flood, which is February for us, the mountain summits appeared on the first day of the month. Then, after waiting forty days and twice seven days—nearly two months, namely February and March—the year of twelve months was completed with that April in which the waters of the flood first overflowed, and which had already elapsed. Therefore, since it was said above that in the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, in the second month, all the fountains of the deep were broken up; and now, after such a careful calculation of days and months, it is said that in the six hundred and first year Noah opened the covering of the ark and saw that the earth was dry, it is plainly evident that those people of so many years reckoned individual years as twelve lunar months, some months of thirty and others of twenty-nine days; and the eleven extra days of the solar year accumulated over twelve lunar months were assigned to intercalations. [Col. 0351A]

## CHAPTER XXVI. What it means mystically that the Lord commanded Noah to leave the ark

“In the second month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month”—that is, ten days beyond the completion of the year since the waters of the flood began to overflow—God spoke to Noah, saying: “Go out of the ark, you and your wife,” etc. God was not content to say: “Go out of the ark, you and your wife, your sons and your sons’ wives,” but was also concerned for all the animals: “Bring out with you,” he says, “all the animals that are with you, both birds and beasts and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth.”

Even if God had commanded Noah to bring out all the animals, Noah would have known that this had to be done, and we would know that it had been done even if Scripture had not narrated it. Yet Scripture relates both that God gave such a command and that it was thus carried out, adding: “Therefore Noah went out, and his sons, and his sons’ wives with him. And all the animals, cattle, and creeping things that creep upon the earth, according to their kinds, went out of the ark.” What is the point of this—that the finger of God, which knows how to write or speak nothing except what is fitting, spends so much time on things of this kind? Certainly, if you receive here nothing but the letter, it was superfluous to write this.

Thus let what has already been said above now return to mind: that ark, which Noah both built and entered with his own household, signified the ancient Church of patriarchs and prophets. Our Lord both founded it before coming into this world and, when he came made man, endured within it the tribulations of death, with the few who remained with him, to whom he also says: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 23). [Col. 0351C]

All the animals, clean and unclean, entered this same Church with Noah, because whoever are gathered to Christ, whether from the clean Jews or the unclean Gentiles, are grafted into the faith of the ancient fathers and belong to Christ in no other way than by being incorporated into that Church. Yet they are not permitted to remain in its carnal ceremonies—that is, to be circumcised carnally, observe sabbaths, sacrifice a lamb, or in any manner practise Judaism in the other such rites, which were shadows of things to come.

Therefore, while that seemingly superfluous point is so carefully repeated so many times, this highly necessary point is prophetically set forth in figure: all Gentiles who wished to be saved would necessarily enter into the expectation of the ancients, but would not remain within their carnal religion. The saying here, “You shall go forth upon the earth; increase and multiply upon it,” has the same mystical meaning as if it said: Cast aside carnal things, which were once gain to you and are now counted as loss, and sow in the Spirit, that from the Spirit you may reap eternal life (Col. 2).

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 0352A] How fittingly Noah offered a sacrifice from all the animals that had been preserved, as a figure of us, from whom Christ offers living victims to God the Father
Noah built an altar to the Lord; and taking of all the clean cattle and birds, he offered burnt offerings upon the altar. The altar which Noah built, and the burnt offerings which he offered to the Lord, were thanksgivings: they acknowledged, as was fitting, the remembrance of past benefits by their very presentation. For he who had commanded a man to make an ark in which he might be saved is worthily honoured when man builds him an altar upon which that same Saviour is worshipped. And he who had preserved in that same ark not only man, but also, for man’s sake, the remnants of beasts and of all living creatures, rightly receives from man burnt offerings upon the altar from all clean cattle and birds. This natural law, not a written one, taught this to be just; for reason itself naturally judges it fitting and right that he who gave should first be honoured from his own gifts.

Moreover, in this also the mystery of our Lord Jesus Christ shone forth: having gone out from that ark of the Synagogue, in which through his Passion he won salvation for the world, he instituted a new rite of sacrifice; and what was preserved there he does not cease to offer henceforth as a burnt offering to God the Father, both through himself and through the hands of his priests. That very body which hung there upon the wood, that very blood which was shed there, we offer with honourable thanksgiving to him who saved him from death. Furthermore, from all clean living creatures—and all things are clean, for whatever had hitherto been unclean he cleansed by his blood, in accordance with what was said to the apostle Peter: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10)—from all living creatures, that is, from human beings, he offers burnt offerings to God and Father when, by his grace, we do what he commands us, or what he himself entreats us through his Apostle, saying: “I beseech you, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. 12). And in doing this we are all priests, as in the Apocalypse we say in thanksgiving to him: “For you were slain, and redeemed us to God by your blood, and made us a kingdom to our God and priests” (Rev. 5).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the saying: “I will no longer curse the earth because of human beings.”

And the Lord smelled an odour of sweetness, and said to him: “I will no longer curse the earth because of human beings. For the disposition and thought of the human heart are inclined to evil from its youth; therefore I will not again strike down every living creature as I have done.”

It is as though he said: “Behold, I have now cursed the earth because of human beings. For because of human beings he brought the flood upon it; and it, which had been filled with their wickedness, was almost destroyed along with them, and lost its own form when the waters prevailed over it. Yet it had committed no sin. For the disposition and thought of man—the disposition, I say, and thought of transgressing man, not of the senseless earth itself—are inclined to evil from youth. Therefore I will no longer do as I have done; that is, in a punishment thus indiscriminately mingled, I will not destroy along with the human being, who alone sins, the senseless earth also, or beasts, which have neither righteousness nor sin, as I have now destroyed them.

“But what then? ‘All the days of the earth, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease.’ Such a year as this has been shall not occur again: one lacking the succession of seasons, spent wholly in stormy rains, tempered by no benefit of heat or moderation of winter, in which the nature of seedtime everywhere fails and no harvest is gathered. Rather, nature shall have its fitting alternations, with heat and cold in turn ripening the lands or crops. Never again shall the face of nature or the constitution of the world be so confused, throughout all the days of the earth—that is, until the end of the age.”

Therefore this belongs to the Spirit of mercy: that the Lord smelled an odour of sweetness—not because he delights in the fumes of flesh; for he is not flesh or body, to be drawn by the smell of such things—but because he is spirit, and in bodily sacrifices looks upon the heart of the offerer. If it is devout, the gracious Lord delights in its contrition more than a human being is pleased by any bodily fragrance, however sweet, as it is written: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50).

This, I say, belongs to mercy: that he received the sacrifice of the righteous man as an odour of sweetness and, as though soothed by a great gift, said: “I will no longer curse the earth because of human beings.” Yet this same mercy is not lax or indulgent, nor has it laid aside the rod of discipline for its children, even though it promises impunity to the offender; for immediately it adds this reason: “For the disposition and thought of the human heart are inclined to evil from its youth.” By the singular term *sensus* (“sense” or “perception”), it signifies the five bodily senses, which are inclined to evil—especially when the thought of the heart, by which they ought to be restrained or governed, itself inclines to evil and uses those very senses as weapons for evil work.

Henceforth, indeed, let the earth be secure, and let whoever walks upon it in such a way that his senses and thought are not inclined to evil be secure. But let that human being alone fear whose senses or thought are inclined to evil. For henceforth the earth stands for ever; indeed, perhaps even the waters which then destroyed humankind together with the earth will wholly fail, according to what is said in the Apocalypse: “And the sea is no more” (Rev. 21). But human beings, distinguished by another judgment, shall each receive recompense according to their own merits.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the addition, after he had said, “The disposition and thought of man are inclined to evil”: “from his youth.”

Certainly, after he had said, “the disposition and thought of the human heart are inclined to evil,” he fittingly added, “from its youth.” For youth is the first age capable of understanding. Hence what precedes it in human life is freer, both by natural and by written law. But what is added from that time onward has lawful judgment of good and evil.

Accordingly, certain sages of the age said that human life resembles the Greek letter Y, which, beginning from a single stroke, divides into two paths. Thus in infancy or childhood a person walks a single path, not weighing the difference between good and evil; but when one has reached the bounds of youth, one perceives the distinction between the two, with reason as guide. Therefore, if one chooses the right hand, one receives the reward of virtue; but if the left, one incurs the punishments of evils. Hence the greatest of poets also says:

> Here lies for us the way to Elysium; but the left-hand path  
> inflicts the punishment of the wicked and sends them to impious Tartarus.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book VI

## CHAPTER XXX. On the blessing in which it is said: “Let your terror be upon every living creature of the earth.”

(Chapter 9.) And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth; and let your terror and fear be upon all the animals of the earth, and upon all the birds of heaven, together with everything that moves upon the earth.”

God now blesses these remnants of creation for the second time. For shortly before he had blessed them, saying: “Enter upon the earth; increase and multiply upon it.” This is fitting and faithful. For because of our Lord Jesus Christ, after he rose from the dead, the abundance of heavenly blessing was poured out twice upon human beings: the grace of the Holy Spirit was given to the Apostles by a twofold gift. First, when it was given by him as he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). Secondly, when that same Holy Spirit came from heaven, appearing to them in fire and sitting upon each of them (Acts 2), and so kindled them inwardly that he made the unlearned learned, the untrained wise, and the fearful strong.

Therefore it is noteworthy that in this second blessing it is said: “Let your terror be upon all living creatures.” From that point, thundering with threats, flashing with miracles, and raining with words, they became terrible to every person living beastlike. It must be noted that he did not say, “Let your terror be upon other human beings,” but, “upon all living creatures of the earth, and upon all birds of heaven.” Perceiving this well, these sons of our Noah, or men of his household, wished to exercise their terror only over those who live beastlike. For insofar as others live rationally, they count them their equals as subjects, or even set them above themselves. Thus that vessel of election, Paul, says to some: “We do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ our Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake” (2 Cor. 4).

According to the letter, nearly these same words had been spoken to the first human beings, Adam and his wife: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, and all living creatures which move upon the earth.” But here, through God’s generosity, this has been added: “All fish of the sea have been delivered into your hand, and everything which moves and lives shall be food for you.” For then it was said only: “Behold, I have given you every green herb bearing seed upon the earth, and every tree which has in itself the seed of its own kind; they shall be food for you.”

Yet for a human being still happy and inexperienced in weakness, that light fare was more sufficient than the eating of flesh can now be for one infirm and dying. But this power over all living creatures has now justly increased for humanity. For, both when they were created for humanity and now when they are preserved for humanity, they owe humanity this very fact—that they exist—for a twofold reason. Therefore, although previously humanity presumed to take these for food without any authority from God commanding it, yet now, having received authority first before the Law and afterwards through the Law, humanity rightly claims them for food; so that the person who tries to prohibit this rather acts against God’s command, as the Apostle testifies when he says of certain people:

> Giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, having their conscience seared; forbidding marriage, and abstaining from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving.  
> —1 Timothy 4

It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the addition, after he had said, “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you”: “As green herbs I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood.”

“As green herbs I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood. For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast; and from the hand of man, and from the hand of a man’s brother, I will require the life of man. Whoever has shed the blood of man, his blood shall be shed. For man was made in the image of God.”

The exception is good and honourable: “Except that you shall not eat flesh with blood,” unless the blood has first been poured out. But why shall you not eat flesh with blood? “For,” he says, “I will require the blood of your lives.” A striking argument, yet not empty but most weighty. Having set forth a command concerning the blood of cattle—“You shall not eat flesh with blood”—he immediately adds the reason concerning human blood. For it serves to increase the estimation of human blood, so that no one may judge it a light matter to harbour human blood within the conscience, when it is not permitted even to put the blood of a beast into one’s mouth outwardly.

For this reason he again commanded through the Law that, when the sanctuary was far away, the blood of victims should be poured out upon the ground (Lev. 17)—that is, of those animals which they prepared for their own food. But when the sanctuary was present, it should be poured upon the altar, as is written in Deuteronomy: “You shall pour the blood of your sacrifices upon the altar, but you yourself shall eat the flesh” (Deut. 12). Hence comes that passage in the Book of Kings: “Turning to the spoil, they took sheep, oxen, and calves, slaughtered them on the ground, and the people ate with the blood. And Saul said: ‘You have transgressed’” (1 Sam. 14), and so forth.

If, therefore, it is a transgression to put brute blood into one’s mouth, how much more ought it to be abominable for one professing true purity to store human blood in the conscience? Thus, so that the greatness of the guilt in the sin of homicide might become clear from comparison with the lesser matter, he rightly added immediately after saying, “You shall not eat flesh with blood”: “For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast and from the hand of man.”

But how does God require human blood from the hand of beasts? For he requires it from the hand of a man, even a stranger, and from the hand of his brother, just as he required Abel’s blood from Cain’s hand—a crime because of which, as some report, he especially brought the flood upon the world. But how does he require human blood from the hand of a beast—for example, of a wolf perhaps killing a person? Either this must be understood to mean that beasts themselves often pay the penalty when caught by human beings; or, what seems more reasonable, malicious spirits are to be understood under the name of beasts, who will receive eternal judgment for the death of human souls.
