Therefore, “whoever has shed the blood of man, his blood shall be shed,” because every murderer will be punished—unless he has repented. For this qualification must be understood in divine pronouncements of this kind, such as: “The soul that sins, it shall die,” and similar statements.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Again on the same subject.

With this exception preserved, “As green herbs,” he says, “I have given you all things”; that is, you shall kill and eat all things without penalty, as green herbs, which indeed live, but are insensible. For herbs and all such things live by their greenness; but this is not the life which one could rightly call a soul. Yet the Epicureans—and even the most filthy Manichaeans who followed them—said that when a person dies, his soul is transformed by degeneration into a pig or dog, then into a tree, shrub, or whatever herb; and consequently, in their judgment, even herbs have souls.

The celebrated satirist Flaccus [Horace], ridiculing their folly, says to someone:

> But whether you slaughter fish, or leek and onion,  
> make use of Pompey.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* 1.12.21

He said “you slaughter” instead of “you eat,” because, according to that school, one slaughtered as many souls as one ate leeks, onions, or other things each day.

Thus there is no injustice in eating flesh. Indeed, in not eating it—unless this is done for a religious vow—there is an unjust superstition. Pythagoras is reported to have practised this excessively: he abstained not only from every animal but even from every legume, especially beans, calling them his kindred, because he said either that when cooked they assume the colour of human blood, or that, if green beans are kept for a long time in a bronze vessel, they turn into blood.

The same poet quoted above, likewise mocking him, says:

> O when will beans, Pythagoras’ kinsfolk, and vegetables  
> well anointed with rich bacon, be served together?  
> —Horace, *Satires* 2.6

Indeed, Pythagoras is said to have regarded the bean as kindred for the reason already given to such an extent that, one day when he had no escape, he preferred to pass through the midst of robbers rather than through a field of beans.

But such absurdities have now been exploded by the wisdom of God, and the serious declarations of divine authority prevail, according to which the Apostle also says: “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4). “I have given you all things,” he says, “and everything which moves upon the earth and lives shall be food for you.” Here he would appear to have made no distinction between clean and unclean things, unless above he had already said that Noah, taking from all clean birds, offered a burnt offering upon the altar. But Moses himself will give a law concerning such discrimination in its proper place.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What is signified by the third saying also: “Increase and multiply.”

“But you, increase and multiply, enter upon the earth, and fill it.” At last, these words of one and the same blessing have been pronounced for the third time over the remnants of humankind. Just as Noah himself sent out the dove a third time, so likewise for a third time the word of blessing was poured out upon him and his sons. And rightly so, because, as has already been said above, the dove signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, and God’s blessing is nothing other than the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore one and the same Noah receives a blessing also for the third time, because one and the same Christ, since he is God, sends and bestows the Holy Spirit; and, since he is human, receives blessing both in himself and in his members. In himself: when he is conceived by the Holy Spirit from the womb of the Virgin; when he is baptized and the Holy Spirit descends upon him in visible form; when he rises from the dead and thus enters into the glory of his kingdom—as David the king was anointed a third time in prefiguration of him, as was said above. In his members: when each one of us receives remission of sins through faith in him in baptism; then through the laying on of hands; and finally in the resurrection receives eternal reward for the same faith.

It should be noted that these same stages in the growth of the grace of the Holy Spirit are beautifully marked in the threefold wording of the blessing itself. For first it was said: “Enter upon the earth; increase and multiply upon it.” Secondly it was said: “Increase and multiply”; and it was added: “Let your terror be upon all living creatures of the earth.” Thirdly: “Increase and multiply, and enter upon the earth, and fill it.”

This final saying is almost identical with the first. For at first it was said, “Enter upon the earth; increase and multiply upon it”; while here it says, “Increase and multiply, and enter upon the earth and fill it.” These appear to be one and the same, but they differ in the order of the words. There first it was said, “Enter upon the earth,” and then, “Increase and multiply upon it”; but here first, “Increase and multiply,” and then, “Enter upon the earth and fill it.”

There, therefore, “Enter upon the earth” means implicitly, in order to labour; but here “enter” means implicitly, in order to reign. For there are two callings of the predestined: one by which we are called to faith, concerning which the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called” (Rom. 8); the other by which we are to be called to the kingdom, according to the Gospel’s faith, when the king says to those at his right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25).

Thus in the first blessing it is right that entering the earth comes first and increasing and multiplying follows; for we who enter the present Church ought to increase and multiply by calling others, in accordance with: “Let the one who hears say: Come” (Rev. 22). But in the last blessing increasing and multiplying comes first, and entering upon the earth and filling it follows; because certainly after every increase and multiplication there will be that entrance into the kingdom of God, after which there is no longer increase or multiplication; then, I say, there is no longer hearing and saying, “Come.”

Between these is the middle blessing, where, after saying “Increase and multiply,” it immediately adds: “Let your terror be upon all living creatures of the earth.” By this is signified the second outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by which, as has already been said above, the holy Apostles, made strong and fervent, not only did not fear, but deserved to be feared and dreadful to all who live beastlike.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On God’s saying: “Behold, I will establish my covenant with you.”

God also said these things to Noah and his sons: “Behold, I will establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you. And no longer shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of a flood; nor shall there thereafter be a flood destroying the earth.” And God said: “This is the sign of the covenant between me and you: I will place my bow in the clouds, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.”

One thing which we must first inquire into here is the covenant: what it is, or of what kind it is, concerning which he says, “Behold, I will establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you.” For it is not sufficiently clear from the present passage itself where or when he established this covenant, or what were the respective things given and received in constituting the covenant. For a covenant is not customarily established without something given and received; nor is it made with fewer than two parties—for example, between Abraham and Abimelech, king of the Philistines. For the latter restored the well which his servants had forcibly taken away; and the former gave sheep and oxen, and besides, seven ewe-lambs of the flock set apart as a witness.

But here there is no gift. God indeed says: “No longer shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of a flood”; but this is not the covenant or its establishment itself, but the tenor of the covenant, just like what the aforesaid Abimelech required of Abraham, saying: “Do not harm me, or my descendants, or my stock” (Gen. 21). Again, God says: “I will place my bow in the clouds”; but this is not the covenant itself, but the sign of the covenant. For, he says, it “shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth.”

Moreover, it must be understood that he did not say in the present tense, “Behold, I establish,” but in the future: “Behold,” he says, “I will establish my covenant with you.” Nor did he only say “with you,” but added “with your seed after you.” Indeed, he says later: “It shall be the sign of the covenant which I have established between God and all flesh upon the earth.” Yet there too the past rightly stands for the future, according to the words written: “He made the things that are to be” (Eccl. 3).

We must therefore seek this covenant; and then it will be clear how great is the force of the other words which now proceed from God’s mouth. We say, then, that the covenant is not one merely promised many times, but one made once and for all—the one covenant, I say, by which the enmities that existed between God and human beings are dissolved: the incarnation or Passion of Christ, the Son of God. There, without any contradiction, the establishment of peace is certain, with its rationale of giving and receiving: God, receiving the faith of human beings, gives them that same Christ his Son, that they may be saved through him.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the covenant, or the sign of the covenant.

Only two chief signs of this covenant exist, though many promises or significations preceded them. The first is the sign now given, God saying: “This is the sign of the covenant between me and you: I will place my bow in the clouds.” The second is given to Abraham by the same speaker: “You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Gen. 17).

Here one should note that the sign of the covenant is sometimes rightly called the covenant, because, after he had said, “This is the covenant which you shall keep: every male among you shall be circumcised,” he immediately added: “And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (ibid.). But this must be discussed more fully in its proper place. Now we must consider this bow of God, and how it is a sign of that one covenant or treaty.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On how God made his covenant with human beings in Christ; how that which he made with Noah was a sign of his covenant; and on the bow, which in Greek is called *iris*, that is, “peace.”

God made a covenant with human beings through Christ his Son in this: reconciling us to himself through Christ’s death on the cross, he washed us from our sins in Christ’s blood and gave us through him the holy Spirit of his love, consecrating the baptism of water and the Holy Spirit, by which we are reborn.

This bow which appears in the clouds is a sign of such a Christ, Son of God. In it many, indeed almost countless, colours are seen; but the chief and most conspicuous are these two: blue and fiery-red. The blue signifies the baptismal water by which we are visibly washed; the fiery-red, the Holy Spirit, by whom our sins are invisibly consumed. Thus we may be separated from both those who perished in the former flood of water and those who will perish in the future judgment of fire.

Therefore this bow in the clouds of heaven is the sign of the covenant—that is, the sign of the Son of God, judged on account of the elect and about to judge the reprobate. And this sign in the clouds means that God will no longer destroy all flesh by the waters of a flood. But God himself, whom the cloud received, who is beyond the clouds and exalted above all heavens, is a sign of eternal remembrance in the eyes of God the Father and an everlasting memorial of our peace, so that, after he has dissolved enmities in his flesh (Eph. 2), the friendship of God and human beings may be firm: no longer the friendship of servants, but of friends and children of God.

Thus, after saying, “No longer shall all flesh be destroyed by the waters of a flood,” he rightly adds: “Nor shall there thereafter be a flood destroying the earth,” because neither shall the earth again be destroyed by a flood of waters, nor shall our flesh after the resurrection be disturbed by any flood of miseries or overwhelming sufferings.

“This,” he says, “is the sign between me and you and every living soul which is with you, for everlasting generations.” For this sign itself will pass away with the clouds; but the covenant of which it is the sign—that is, the memorial of our redemption—will remain for ever before the Father in the flesh of his Son, in the scars of the wounds of his hands, feet, and side. Hence, because he himself is our peace, this sign of the covenant is fittingly called in Greek *iris*, that is, “peace.” Ignorant of its causes, the inquisitive philosophers of this world say that it is produced causally when the sun, shining its rays upon a hollow cloud, casts them into it; but however it comes to be, it is God’s work, not by chance but by reason, presenting itself as a sign of divine remembrance.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Noah’s three sons, and why he did not say, “Cursed be Ham,” but “Cursed be Canaan.”

There were, therefore, three sons of Noah who came out of the ark: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Now Ham himself was the father of Canaan. “He himself,” it says, “was the father of Canaan”—that is, of the inhabitant of this land which you, O Israel, will enter to possess. The writer did not say, “He was the father of Canaan,” because Canaan was either Ham’s only son or his firstborn, but because Israel needed to know this people especially, since it had a great concern with them.

The writer immediately hastens to set down the ancient stain of that people, so that it may not seem so astonishing or incredible that the land ought to vomit it out at Israel’s entry. Thus he says: “And Noah, a husbandman, began to cultivate the ground and planted a vineyard. Drinking wine, he became drunk and lay naked in his tent. When Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s naked private parts, he told his two brothers outside,” and so forth.

For it greatly advances the disgrace of the nation that, owing to its father’s slavish wickedness, it inherited from him the penalty of a curse. Accordingly, once, twice, and three times he strikes that same nation here by saying: “Now Ham himself was the father of Canaan”; and then: “When Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s naked private parts, he told his two brothers outside.” For naming the hostile people in the report of such an action by its father is a grave reproach.

Then, when Noah awoke and learned what his younger son had done to him, he said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a slave of slaves to his brothers.” He said, “Cursed be Canaan,” although Canaan had not yet been born, or was not Ham’s only son. So greatly does he detest Canaan’s descendants that he declares the whole disgrace or penalty of that curse will fall upon them. He also calls him “younger,” though he who had disclosed his father’s private parts was middle-born: younger, I say, not so much in age as because of his vice and unworthiness of character.

“He shall be a slave of slaves to his brothers.” He did not merely say, “He shall be a slave,” a term by which even good or voluntary service is sometimes signified; but he said, “He shall be a slave of slaves.” By this addition the most extreme slavery, indeed slavish worthlessness, is usually expressed—except where there is subjection to God, when through outstanding humility someone calls himself the servant of the servants of God.

This narrative, as it is now written, serves those for whom it is written: namely, to strengthen them, knowing that God has long hated their enemy Canaan. It is as though he said: “Be strengthened and be brave. For just as God has already dealt with Ham in his son Mizraim, that is, the Egyptians—for the Egyptians were born from Mizraim, the second of Ham’s sons—whom God afflicted on our account with various plagues and finally overwhelmed in the Red Sea, so much more will he deal with this same Ham in his son Canaan, that is, in these peoples against whom you proceed with God as your leader and who were born from him” (Gen. 14).

For before your father Abraham came to be, this Canaan was pronounced accursed and destined to be your slave, when that same father [Noah] still said, concerning him through whom he foresaw your father Abraham in the prophetic Spirit: “Blessed be the Lord God of Shem”—that is, the God of Abraham, for Abraham was born from Shem—“let Canaan be his slave.” Therefore do not say: “We cannot go up against this people, because it is stronger than we are,” or “because it is of lofty stature” (Num. 13). Do not say these or such things, for the people is truly cursed and will be your slave and tributary, as was prophesied through father Noah.

For one must understand that all this belongs to the Spirit of prophecy. Since one worshipping people of Hebrews was to be born from Shem, he said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Shem.” Since the islands of the nations were to be divided among Japheth’s descendants, and their fullness was to come through faith and dwell in the house of the God of the Jews, he did not say “the Lord God of Japheth,” because they worshipped false and many gods; but, “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.” Having said these things according to the letter, let us set forth a higher sense, according to which Canaan is likewise the slave of Japheth, for it was said of Japheth: “Let Canaan be his slave.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Again, mystically, on Noah’s drunkenness and nakedness: how through this is signified the humility of Christ’s Passion, which Ham—that is, any heretic—despises.

The vineyard which the Lord our God—who, as has often already been said, is prefigured by Noah—planted, Holy Scripture does not allow to remain unknown, for example when it says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You went before it on the way, and planted its roots, and it filled the land” (Ps. 79). And in Isaiah: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil; and he fenced it, removed stones from it, and planted it with a chosen vine; and he built a tower in its midst and constructed a winepress in it; and he expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (Isa. [Col. 0362B] 5), etc.

Likewise, it cannot be hidden that this vineyard, well planted and formerly beautiful, afterwards turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine, gave its very planter the bitter cup of death to drink, and, when the bitterness had been completed, made him drunk, so that he fell asleep in the sleep of death, stripped naked—that is, found weak or capable of suffering—since he was made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2). To him who literally said, “I thirst,” it offered wine mingled with myrrh, wine—or vinegar—mixed with gall (John 19; Matt. 27). Therefore Noah, drunk from the vineyard which he himself planted and stripped naked in his own tent, is Christ himself: put to death by the people to whom he gave the Law, and held in contempt among that same nation of his. Hence Isaiah speaks mournfully: “He has neither form nor beauty; [Col. 0362C] and we saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” (Isa. 53), etc.

Any heretic who, under the Christian name, because of weaknesses of this kind denies that Christ—the power of God and the wisdom of God—is true God from true God, born before the ages, is Ham, whose name means “hot”: namely, impatient, ever heated for quarrelling and contentiousness. Such a one publishes abroad the father’s weakness, according to what John says of persons of this sort: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2), while they deny in Christ what belongs to power. He preaches only what belongs to weakness and creates turmoil.

By contrast, those who worthily venerate our weakness assumed by the power of God, knowing that “the weakness of God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1), are Shem and Japheth—that is, the renowned and the enlarged. For Shem means “renowned” or “named,” while Japheth means “breadth.” The greater persons—that is, teachers and prelates—in the house of this Noah, that is, in Christ’s Church, are named and renowned; but the hearers or subjects are very numerous, and therefore are rightly to be understood under the name Japheth, that is, “breadth.” The third is Ham, that is, the company of false brethren. Beyond these divisions of men none is found among the sons of Noah—that is, among those who are designated by the Christian name. Two indeed are saved; for the third perishes, as we have in the Apocalypse: either because they are cast down by the dragon’s tail, which drew after it a third part of the stars of heaven (Rev. 12), or because, at the sounding of the angelic trumpet, [Col. 0363A] a third part of creation perished (Rev. 8).

How do those designated by Shem and Japheth honour that weakness which heretics despise in Christ? With their backs turned, placing a cloak over it, they cover the father’s weaknesses: that is, reverently recalling the Lord’s past sufferings, they clothe them in the venerable order of the sacraments—such things as it is holy to perform and devout to understand in God’s house. The apostles did this first, then apostolic men; and together with them, and after all of them, religious observers and faithful Christians do so.

Therefore Canaan—that is, every heretic—is rightly the servant of servants to them, because, while he blasphemes and disputes, indeed even persecutes bodily (as Arian madness especially did), he serves their glory and ministers to the completion of their crowns. And it was fittingly said, “Canaan is cursed,” rather than “Ham is cursed,” because, while their punishment is reserved for the age to come, they are punished, as it were, not in themselves but in their descendants. Canaan, moreover, means “their movement.” This interpretation suits such persons, because they were cursed on account of the movement—that is, the deed—of their father.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. What, mystically, are the tents of Shem in which Japheth dwelt.

“May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem.” Since it is already known, and has already been stated above, that Shem signifies the Jews and Japheth the Gentiles who were to obtain the promises of the Jews, blessed by the father’s prophetic Spirit, we may now know more certainly what the tents of Shem are and by what entrance Japheth was admitted to begin dwelling [Col. 0363C] in them.

The tents of Shem are the privileges of the Jews, which the Apostle enumerates in these words: “Theirs,” he says, “is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9). That people once dwelt alone in these things; for we Gentiles were outside. “At that time,” says the same Apostle, “you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants, without hope of the promise, and without God in this world” (Eph. 5:2).

For all these things were enclosed within the single boundary of the Hebrew language, which, in the days when the division or confusion of languages occurred, remained in the house or family of Heber; hence this language was called Hebrew. (CHAPTER X.) Thus the things mentioned above are here plainly called the tents of Shem: not because all Shem’s generations dwelt in them, but a part—namely, the part of the people of Israel which descended through Abraham from Heber, Shem’s great-grandson.

Now Greeks and Latins were born from Japheth. For Japheth had seven sons: Gomer, from whom came the Galatians; Magog, from whom the Scythians; Madai, from whom the Medes; Javan, from whom came the Ionians, who are Greeks, and from whom the Ionian Sea is named; Tubal, from whom came the Italians and Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom the Celtiberians; Meshech, from whom came the Cappadocians, whence a city among them was called Mazaca; and Tiras, from whom came the Thracians, whose name is not greatly altered. Among these and almost all nations, [Col. 0364A] the Greek and Latin languages hold pre-eminence: the one because of Greek wisdom, the other because of Roman power. Through them the tents of Shem were opened for all Gentiles to inhabit, since by means of them, through the efforts of many translators, they obtained knowledge of the Scriptures and thus knowledge of the one God. Jews indeed, for whom those tents had first been built, and also some persons from the other nations, entered the tents of Shem; but the generations of Japheth, by whom Europe was especially occupied, prevailed in inhabiting them.

## CHAPTER XL. Again concerning Noah’s three sons: their generations filled the three parts of the world.

[Col. 0364B] The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Cush is called Ethiopia by the Hebrews even to this day; Mizraim, Egypt; Put, Libya, from whom the river of Mauretania is still called Put at the present day, and every region around it Putian. Canaan, as has already been said, occupied the land which the Jews afterwards possessed after the Canaanites had been driven out.

The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. These occupy the part of Asia from the Euphrates River to the Indian Ocean. Elam is the source of the Elamites, the chief people of Persia; Asshur founded the city of Nineveh; Arphaxad is the source of the Chaldeans; Lud, of Lydia; Aram, of the Syrians, whose metropolis is Damascus.

It would be long to follow individually all the nations scattered from these three sons of Noah. Let this be said briefly in summary: Shem, in his sons, occupied Asia; Ham, chiefly Libya; and Japheth, Europe, so that the three parts of the world were filled from the generations of the three, in which also the Church of Christ was prefigured as set forth in the faith of the Holy Trinity.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the building of the tower of Babel.

“The earth was of one lip and of the same speech. And when they journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar and dwelt there. And each said to his neighbour: ‘Come, let us make bricks and bake them with fire,’” etc.

Above, when Scripture arranged the seven sons of Japheth in order, it added: “From these the islands of the Gentiles were divided in their regions, each according to his language and families.” This must be gathered or continued by the rule which Tyconius calls recapitulation: there it was not stated how they had been divided, and therefore it is found here, so that it may be related how and for what reason such a division or confusion occurred.

“The earth,” it says, “was of one lip”—that is, one language—“and of the same speech,” namely because all expressions and individual words throughout the whole earth signified the same thing. “They found,” it says, “a plain in the land of Shinar.” Scripture now calls the very plain they found Shinar, namely from the event, indicating the place by a fitting name. For Shinar means “the knocking out of teeth,” or “their stench”: “the knocking out of teeth,” that is, of expressions or words which are not made without teeth. Teeth contribute greatly to speech; and in a sense their teeth were knocked out when those toothed ones—that is, those proud or powerful men—lost their accustomed capacity for speaking. Likewise it is rightly called “their stench,” because by such an undertaking they sent forth the stench of their pride even to the nostrils of God. Just as humility, or a contrite spirit, is a sacrifice of sweet savour, so, conversely, pride is a horrible stench.

Scripture, indicating the astonishing greatness of their pride, introduces God as descending to see the city and tower which, it says, the sons of Adam were building, and as saying: “Behold, one people, and one lip for them all. They have begun to do this, [Col. 0365B] and they will not desist from their designs until they complete them in deed. Come, therefore, let us descend and confuse their language there, so that no one may hear his neighbour’s speech,” etc.

Scripture says that he descended to see, concerning him who knows all things before they occur and is absent nowhere, because the case was such that heavenly judgment ought by no means to leave it unexamined; and Scripture had to speak in this way in order to signify that nothing should be believed to occur rashly. For if he who knows all things is said here to descend in order to see, and elsewhere says, “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous; I will descend and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18), how much more must a human being, who can be deceived, investigate a matter carefully before pronouncing judgment?

And it should be noted that he here calls them sons of Adam. When it says, “which the sons of Adam were building,” this may indeed mean the same as “sons of men,” since among the Hebrews *adam* is the common word for “man”; yet in this place it ought, both in wording and meaning, to be referred to the same Adam who was first created. For in this way he strikes them much more sharply, those who said, “Let us make our name famous,” and began to build a tower of pride by which they might reach heaven. In this respect they were especially imitating Adam’s transgression, by which he followed the devil saying, “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3); and in this way they wished, just as the devil did, to ascend above the height of the clouds [Col. 0365D] and be like the Most High (Isa. 14).

## CHAPTER XLII. On the confusion of languages, and how, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, all languages were again united in the mouths of the apostles.

“Behold,” he says, “one people, and one lip for them all. They have begun to do this, and they will not desist from their designs until they complete them in deed.” Then if the capacity of their single language had not been removed, could they have fulfilled their designs in deed—that is, could they have constructed a tower of such height that its summit reached heaven? Certainly not the ethereal heaven, whose height geometers cannot calculate even by their conjectures, but perhaps the aerial heaven, from which birds are customarily called birds of heaven.

Therefore, when God says in response to their foolish presumption, “They will not desist from their designs until they complete them in deed,” one must understand: so far as lies in their power. For they sufficiently imitate the devil saying, “I will ascend above the height of the clouds” (Isa. 14), who, as far as he can, exalts himself against the most high God.

“Come, therefore,” says the Lord, “let us descend and confuse their speech there, so that no one may hear his neighbour’s voice.” It is as though he said: “I have found how to repay them worthily, according to the measure of their fault, with what they deserve. Since they are tending toward heaven by a perverse way, let us hide from them the true way by which one truly goes to heaven.”

For when God said this, it was yet to come that he would establish Holy Scripture through his servant Moses, containing the knowledge of the one God, by which alone one truly goes to [Col. 0366B] heaven. There was only one language of writing, which was then surely common to all and which is still called Hebrew. Therefore, lest, when those pearls of heavenly teaching had been given, they should be trampled by swine of this kind, “Come,” he says, “let us confuse their speech there.”

God alone could bring about this punishment of such astonishing severity, by which human beings are especially divided from one another. Accordingly, when he says in the plural, “Come, let us descend, let us confuse,” he is not summoning multitudes of angels to aid him, but testifies that the whole Trinity and the one God are present to strike down pride. This is clearer from the remedy which stands opposed to it. For where all kinds of languages are restored in the apostles’ mouths (Acts 2), the same Trinity reveals itself to humankind, and on that day the humble are first baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This is the true structure of the highest tower, by which a human being may flee to heaven to reign with God.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Nimrod, whom Josephus asserts to have been the leader of those who built the tower.

Josephus asserts that their leader was Nimrod, of whom Scripture says above: “Cush begot Nimrod. He began to be mighty on the earth, and he was a mighty hunter before the Lord” (Gen. 10). He began, I say, to be mighty on earth and was a mighty hunter, because he first seized an unfamiliar tyranny over the people, as it were by hunting. And he reigned in Babylon, which was called Babel because there the languages of those building the tower were confused. For Babel means “confusion.”

He also reigned in Arach, that is, Edissa; in Achad, now called Nisibis; and in Chalamue, which afterwards, with its name changed, was called Seleucia after King Seleucus. From that land Asshur went out and built Nineveh and the city Rehoboth. Here we should not suppose that two cities are indicated; rather, because *Rehoboth* means “street” or “broad place,” it should be read: “He built Nineveh and the streets of the city.” Nineveh was named after Ninus, son of Belus.

Nimrod means “tyrant” or “transgressor,” and signifies the devil, who seized tyranny in this world and even dared to devise it in heaven, saying: “I will ascend above the height of the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). And for this reason the proverb truly arose: “Like Nimrod, a mighty [Col. 0367A] hunter before the Lord.” The meaning understood is: such is everyone who exalts his horn on high, who speaks iniquity against God (Ps. 74). While he imagines that he makes his own name famous by celebrating Nimrod as an example, he instead acquires, conversely, everlasting reproach.

That city or tower itself—Babel, that is, “Confusion”—of whose construction that man was the leader, everywhere in Scripture signifies the spiritual city of the devil, contrary to the city of God. It is called and is Babylon, the harlot who drinks the blood of the saints. Conversely, the city of God is Jerusalem, that is, “vision of peace,” in which all peaceful persons will reign for ever and beyond with the peaceful and true King: truly blessed, because they will be called and will be sons of God (Matt. 5).

# FIFTH BOOK ON GENESIS  
*(Genesis, chapters 12–18)*

[Col. 0367]

## CHAPTER I. That in Abraham began the third age of the world.

“Search the Scriptures,” Christ, the Son of the living God, who is himself the life we have in the Scriptures, says to the Jews: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have life” (John 5). What follows? “And they,” he says, “are those which bear witness concerning me” (ibid.). This is what we have undertaken to do in the present work.

And behold, in searching we have come to that part of the field of which one may rightly say: “It has veins which are the sources of silver” (Job 28), in which is situated a heap of many of his testimonies—silver, indeed—concerning Abraham, the father of believers and, according to his name, the father of many nations, to whom the promise of that same blessed seed was first made. Therefore he is also the beginning of another—that is, the third—age of the world, in which Christ was promised and the Law was given through Moses. “If you believed him,” Christ himself says, “perhaps you would also believe me; for he wrote about me” (John 5).

Here is knowledge; and consequently the spirit of knowledge is placed third after the spirit of fear, because in the third age of the world God gave human beings knowledge of great salvation and of the promise, through the word and the written Law. Therefore, as we are about to enter this age, we invoke the holy Spirit of knowledge, that in this sense he may enable us to find and bring forth the treasure of testimonies concerning Christ, the Son of God, laid up in this field.

## CHAPTER II. On Abraham: that, as many say, he was delivered by God’s help from Ur of the Chaldeans—that is, from fire.

[Col. 0367D] (CHAPTER XII.) The Lord said to Abram: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house; and go into the land which I shall show you. I shall make you into a great nation, bless you, make your name great, and you shall be blessed. I shall bless those who bless you and curse those who curse you; and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

Abram, whose name means “exalted father,” was a Hebrew descended from Heber, in whose house or family the original language had remained and from that time was called Hebrew after him. He was born in the one hundred and ninety-first year from the birth of Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided; two hundred and ninety-two years after the Flood; and was born in the tenth generation from Shem, Noah’s son. For Shem begot Arphaxad; Arphaxad begot Shelah; Shelah begot [Col. 0368B] Heber; Heber begot Peleg; Peleg begot Reu; Reu begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor; Nahor begot Terah; Terah begot Abram. Cainan, who is placed in Luke the Evangelist between Arphaxad and Shelah (Luke 3), is not found in the Hebrew.

The Hebrews hand down the following reason why his own land, namely the land of the Chaldeans, was not worthy of such a man; and distinguished ecclesiastical writers defend it as true. Abram, they say, was thrown into the fire because he refused to worship the fire which the Chaldeans worship. Delivered by God’s help, he fled from the fire of idolatry. This, they say, is the meaning of the statement: “Abram died before Terah his father in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldeans”: namely, that he was consumed because he refused to worship the fire. For, they say, Abram, surrounded by that very conflagration, [Col. 0368C] was delivered by God’s help. Hence the Lord later says to him: “I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans” (Gen. 11).

Otherwise, they say, an insoluble question arises from the later statement that Abraham was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran (Gen. 12). For if Terah, Abram’s father, begot Abram when he was seventy years old, while he was still in the region of the Chaldeans (Gen. 11), and later died in Haran at the age of two hundred and five, how is Abram said to have been seventy-five years old when he left Haran after Terah’s death, when a hundred and thirty-five years are shown to have elapsed from Abram’s birth to his father’s death? Therefore the Hebrew tradition is true: Terah went out from the fire of the Chaldeans with his sons, Abram was delivered by God’s help, and from that time the days of his life and the period of his age are reckoned.

Yet it may rightly be understood that Terah, with all his household, came to Haran immediately after the persecution and, although he had intended to go into the land of Canaan, remained there. Abram, however, at God’s command to go out from his land and kindred, departed. For thus the order of the narrative stands.

## CHAPTER III. Why God did not say only, “Go out from your land,” but added, “and from your kindred.”

Terah therefore took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of Abram his son; they came into Haran and dwelt there. And Terah’s days were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran [Col. 0369A] (Gen. 11).

Then the Lord said to Abram—understand, when he had come to Haran, while his father Terah was still alive—“Go out from your land and from your kindred,” etc. (Gen. 12). For why did he not say only, “Go out from your land,” but add, “and from your kindred,” unless his land was in one place and his kindred in another? His land was Chaldea; but his kindred had now, in fleeing, arrived in Haran, that is, Syria.

Thus, when God said “go out from your land” and added “and from your kindred,” it is as if he said: “Just as you have bodily departed from the land of the Chaldeans, so depart in mind, never to return there; and furthermore go out from this place where you now dwell, away from your kindred.” For Abram’s kindred remained in Haran, that is, Syria, after he departed and multiplied there. This is sufficiently indicated by Abraham’s servant, whom Abraham adjured, saying: “Do not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell, but go to my land and my kindred, and take from there a wife for my son Isaac” (Gen. 24). Scripture says: “He went to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the city of Nahor.” “Go to my land and my kindred,” he said, because when he said this, his kindred had already mixed with the Syrian people and already regarded that land as their own. Hence the Syrian language is even now akin to Hebrew—that is, in large part similar to it. But let us now hear the word of promise.

## CHAPTER IV. Whence and in what respect Abram was a prophet.

[Col. 0369C] “I will make you,” he says, “into a great nation, and in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12). From this point Abram, the exalted father, is a prophet. For all holy men whom the house of God honours with the prophetic name are called and are prophets because they were granted foreknowledge of the incarnation of the Son of God. Behold, God first reveals to this man that secret of his counsel when he says: “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” Without doubt he refers to no other blessing than that by which the grace of the Holy Spirit was poured out through Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, upon all nations.

Abraham, therefore, is now a prophet; Isaac is a prophet; Jacob is a prophet. Yet under the title “patriarchs,” this same name is almost hidden in them. But God says to Abimelech, king of Gerar, concerning Abram: “Now restore the man’s wife, because he is a prophet, and he shall pray for you, and you shall live” (Gen. 20). And in the Psalm, concerning both this man and the other patriarchs, his descendants: “He rebuked kings for their sake,” the words understood being: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets” (Ps. 104).

Therefore, because the statement is brief, let us not suppose that what was revealed to him was of little account; but opening the small casket of this saying, let us consider more carefully what is contained within.

## CHAPTER V. What reward or recompense God set before him when commanding him to depart.

Like a chosen labourer whom God hires for work, after saying, “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” he immediately sets out, as though appraising it, the reward to be hoped for. First he says, “I will make you into a great nation”; then, “I will bless you”; he also adds, “I will make your name great, and you shall be blessed”; and finally, “In you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.”

Let us firmly judge that in all these words not one iota or one stroke is empty or lacking in weight of meaning. “I will make you,” he says, “into a great nation.” He did not say “a numerous nation.” For that nation which is promised, which is now offered as the blessing, was not to be very numerous in comparison with other nations. “The Lord has joined himself to you and chosen you,” says Moses, “not because you surpassed all nations in number, for you are fewer than all peoples, but because the Lord loved you and kept the oath which he swore to your fathers” (Deut. 7).

Thus he appropriately says not, “I will make you into a numerous nation,” but “into a great nation.” For truly great is the nation whose Lord is its God, which the great Lord magnified and honoured, and from which we have great patriarchs, prophets, learned scribes, and great men of diverse merits, through whom the world came to know the true greatness of God. “And I will bless you,” he says. The order of the words should be observed. If he had first said, “I will bless you,” and then added, “I will make you into a great nation,” perhaps we should suppose that the blessing promised only that a bodily lineage would be propagated from him. But now he first promises that he shall become a great nation and then be blessed, so that you may understand that blessing of which the Prophet sings in the Psalm: “For the lawgiver will give a blessing” (Ps. 83). Since this is given after the giving of the Law, it must certainly be understood as the grace of the Holy Spirit, of which John says: “For the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

But this grace of blessing was promised or given commonly to all followers of his faith. Therefore there follows and is added what is more particularly his own: “And I will make your name great,” he says, “and you shall be blessed.” For Abraham’s name has today been made great, when it is proclaimed throughout the world together with the great and fearful name of God in this designation of God’s name: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3; Matt. 22). This is the true magnificence of Abraham’s name. Hence the Apostle says: “Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God” (Heb. 11).

Thus, “I will make your name great, and you shall be blessed”: namely, your name will be magnificently commemorated in the very invocation of my name; and so you will be blessed, so that whoever curses you will instead himself be cursed. “For,” he says, “I will curse those who curse you and bless those who bless you.” Nevertheless, since this promise ends thus, “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed,” and since “in you” must be understood as “in your seed,” just as he will finally say in the promise, “Your seed shall possess the gates of your enemies, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22), it is rightly understood thus: “I will make your name great, and you shall be blessed,” means, “I will make great the name of your seed,” by giving him the name which is above every name (Phil. 2). The Apostle confesses this when he says: “Who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9).

For just as Levi, while still in the loins of this father, is rightly said to have paid tithes—as the same Apostle says, “And, so to speak, through Abraham Levi also, who receives tithes, paid tithes”—why should not Christ likewise rightly be said to have received the promises in the one in whose loins he too was according to the flesh? (Heb. 7.) Therefore, when it is said to Abraham, “And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed,” it is rightly understood as spoken to Christ, as though it were said: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2).

## CHAPTER VI. How he went out, according to the Apostle, “not knowing where he was going.”

Abram therefore went out as the Lord had commanded him, and Lot went with him (Gen. 12). “He went out,” it says—understand: not knowing where he was going. “For by faith,” says the Apostle, “Abraham, who was called, obeyed by going out to a place which he was to receive as an inheritance; and he went out, not knowing where he was going” (Heb. 11).

For God said only this: “Come into the land which I shall show you,” and had not yet shown him the land itself. He therefore commanded him to go without knowing where he was going; and, in a remarkable manner—which is true pilgrimage—he commanded him both to travel while waiting and, while travelling, to wait for where rest would be given him. And so he acted. For Scripture says: “When they had come into the land of Canaan, Abram passed through the land as far as the place of Shechem, as far as the renowned valley. Now the Canaanite was then in the land.” It immediately adds: “And the Lord appeared to Abram and said to him: ‘To your seed I shall give this land.’”

It is as though it said: because he had gone out not knowing where he was going, he passed through this place and that as a wanderer without shelter, until the Lord appeared to him and, according to his promise, showed him the land he would give him. The Apostle therefore rightly says that he went out by faith, not knowing where he was going.

But there was another respect in which his faith was to be considered. For it has already been said above: “Sarai was barren and had no children” (Gen. 11). Thus, in one command, he courageously showed obedience and faith in two matters that were in a sense opposed: although the Canaanite was then in the land, he believed God’s promise that that land would be given to him; and although his wife was barren, he believed that it would be inherited by his seed. In both matters he was strengthened in faith, as the same Apostle says, giving glory to God and knowing most fully that whatever God has promised, he is also able to perform (Rom. 4).

At last, when the land which God had promised him had been shown to him, reckoning him faithful who had promised, he dwelt confidently, having Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. Bethel means “house of God,” Ai “festival.” Bethel is called so here by anticipation, since Jacob gave it the name Bethel, whereas it had formerly been called Luz. Thus, facing the western region of spiritual darkness, with the house of God, and celebrating toward the east of the true light the festival of great hope, he built an altar to the Lord who had appeared to him. Not ungrateful for the benefits of so great a grace, he anticipated and consecrated with the sacred title of his God the future possession of his rightful inheritance.

“And he went farther, proceeding and advancing toward the south.” The south signifies perfection. Therefore he is rightly said to advance toward the south who, going farther from the dawn of his faith already mentioned and advancing from virtue to virtue, undoubtedly comes to the full and eternal day of perfection.

## CHAPTER VII. On his journey into Egypt, and what is signified by the statement, “God struck Pharaoh’s house on account of Sarai.”

A famine arose in the land, and Abram went down into Egypt to live there as a sojourner; for the famine had become severe in the land. And when he was near to entering Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: “I know that you are a beautiful woman, and when the Egyptians see you they will say, ‘She is his wife’; then they will kill me and preserve you. Say, therefore, I beg you, that you are my sister, so that it may go well with me because of you, and my life may be spared for your sake,” etc.

He did not make his wife’s chastity saleable by making light of it, so that it might go well with him through her; rather, he removed himself from the danger of dying on her account, being most certain that He who had brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans was able to preserve her from the fire—that is, from the Egyptians’ lust.

“Why,” someone asks, “did he not, trusting in the same faith that the Lord could deliver her from the hand of the Egyptians so that he would not die on her account, confidently say that she was his wife?” Plainly because he feared the Lord, because he was unwilling to put the Lord his God to the test. For that person tests God who, insofar as he can, does not extricate himself from danger, and asks for God’s miracle where the help of human reason, ready to hand, can accomplish something. Thus the prudent man, properly concerned on both sides—lest they kill him and subjugate her, once preserved, to their lust—removed such part of the danger as he could [Col. 0372C], and faithfully left the rest to God’s care.

Indeed, even on the plain level of the letter, the victorious perseverance of the obedient man is evident: when famine came upon the land of his sojourning, he preferred still to seek foreign relief by living as a stranger in the land of Ham, which is Egypt, rather than in any degree look back toward the land or kindred from which he had departed at God’s command. Yet the very face of the present history already smiles upon us with clear light and offers us the mysteries shining through it, with which it is full.

For it is not without purpose that Abram, when famine arose, went down into Egypt and Pharaoh was scourged because of him, whose offspring were later likewise to go down into Egypt from the same land of Canaan when famine arose (Gen. XLVI), and Pharaoh was to be scourged with the well-known plagues because of them. It is not, I say, without God’s design that, having returned wealthy from Egypt, Abram later arms himself against kings, frees Lot his brother’s son, and is then blessed by Melchizedek, priest of the Most High. For his people, namely Israel, later to depart from Egypt with a mighty hand and uplifted arm, had to fight against many very powerful kings: the faith and arms of its leaders protected those among the people who were carnal and repeatedly delivered the whole nation from the slavery of its enemies, until there came forth the King and Priest of the Most High, born of the Virgin—Christ, the Son of God—to bestow upon Abraham and his seed blessing, that is, remission of sins, through the true sacrifice of his body and blood.

Therefore, under the guidance of apostolic authority—he who, taking an allegorical comparison from the slave woman and the free woman, says, “For these are the two covenants” (Gal. IV)—let us understand in Abraham the company of all the righteous living in those times by faith; in Sarai his wife, God’s covenant; and in Lot, the multitude of Israelites who were Israelites only according to the flesh.

## CHAPTER VIII. Again concerning the same matter, and what it signifies that Pharaoh took Sarai into his house.

“Abram entered Egypt, and,” it says, “the Egyptians saw that the woman was exceedingly beautiful; and Pharaoh’s princes reported her and praised her before him, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house. But God scourged Pharaoh with many plagues and [Col. 0373C] his house,” etc.

This event truly is a prophecy of another event to be accomplished. For Israel later went down into Egypt with God’s covenant, which He had established with Abraham his grandfather and Isaac his father, with all that he had, with sons and grandsons, because God had called famine upon the land, broken every staff of bread, and sent Joseph before them (Ps. CIV).

And when Israel was near to entering Egypt, Abram in some manner sought help from Sarai his wife. Israel too sought, and readily found, the consolation of God’s covenant, so that it might go well with him because of it and his life might be preserved for its favor. For God appeared to him in a vision, saying: “I am the most mighty God of your father. Do not fear, and go down into Egypt, for there I shall make you into a great nation” (Gen. XLVII), etc.

He went down with this promise, and the Egyptians treated him well because of the beauty of God’s grace which was with him. He had sheep, cattle, asses, male and female servants, and camels; indeed, he possessed land in Egypt, in the best part of the land, in Rameses, and there he increased greatly (Gen. XLVII). Then another Pharaoh arose who did not know Joseph (Exod. I), and this one undoubtedly took Sarai into his house. For he took God’s covenant away from Israel, since under him Israel did not worship the God of his fathers. “You are idle,” he says, “and therefore you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord’” (Exod. V).

But the Lord God scourged him and [Col. 0374A] his house with the greatest plagues: “For I,” He says, “have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, that I might perform these my signs among them, and that you may recount in the hearing of your son and your grandson how often I crushed the Egyptians and performed my signs among them” (Exod. X). Then indeed he restored the wife to her husband. “Now therefore,” he says, “behold your wife; take her and go.” For that Pharaoh rose by night, and all his servants and all Egypt; and a great cry arose in Egypt. Calling Moses and Aaron by night, he said: “Rise and depart from among my people, both you and your sons. Go, sacrifice to the Lord as you say” (Exod. XII).

—[CHAPTER XIII.] “And Abram went up out of Egypt, he and his wife and all that he had, and Lot with him, toward the south. And he was very rich in possessions of gold and silver.” Likewise, the people permitted to worship their God went up from Egypt with all that they had, Pharaoh saying: “Take your sheep and your herds, as you requested” (ibid.). And they were rich in possessions of gold and silver, for at the Lord’s command through Moses they had despoiled the Egyptians: a man was to ask his neighbor, and a woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold and garments.

## CHAPTER IX. On the return of Abram and Lot from Egypt, and what it signifies that Lot was separated from him.

When Abram and Lot had departed from Egypt, “the land,” Scripture says, “was unable to contain them so that they might dwell together. For their substance was great, and they could not live in common. Abram therefore said to Lot: ‘Let there not, I pray, be strife between you and me, [Col. 0374C] and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers’” (Gen. XIII), etc.

As regards the moral sense of this passage, it is a condemnation of riches: because of their wealth, those whom the love of God and the fraternal bond of kinship had joined while they were poor could not live together. Indeed, that bond had held them joined together, so that they departed together from their land and kindred.

At the same time, the gentleness and fairness of the elder Abram are shown when he says: “Let there not, I pray, be strife between me and you, and between my shepherds and your shepherds, for we are brothers. Behold, the whole land lies before you. Depart from me, I pray. If you go to the left, I shall take the right; if you choose the right, I shall go to the left.” This kind of fairness is rightly observed among heirs even to this day: in order to end disputes, the elder divides and the younger chooses.

But let us now direct our course according to the order already begun. We know well the disputes that occurred, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, between those who were Abraham’s offspring according to faith and those who were so only according to the flesh; and why, truly, the land could not contain them so that they might dwell together. For they quarrelled so long that they wished to stone Moses and Aaron, appoint a leader for themselves, and return to Egypt. Finally they were separated from one another; for the Lord God swore in His wrath that they would not see the land concerning which He had sworn to their fathers. “As I live,” says the Lord, “you shall not enter the land over which I lifted up my hand to make you dwell: all of you who were numbered from twenty years old and upward, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun” (Num. XIV).

Therefore, appropriately, after Lot was separated from him, the Lord speaks to Abram: “Lift up your eyes and see, from the place where you now are, north and south, east and west. All the land that you see I shall give to you and to your seed.” For after the generation of those who quarrelled had been consumed, the Lord at last brought their children into the land which He had promised Abram.

And after they entered that land, they were separated from one another. Among the few was Abram, dwelling between Bethel and Hai, at the place of the altar that he had made, there calling upon the name of the Lord. Among the many, however, was Lot, dwelling in Sodom [Col. 0375B]. For few perseveringly worshipped the God of heaven, the God of Abraham their father; most served foreign gods, mingled with the nations, learned their works, and served their graven images (Ps. CV).

Nor is it inappropriate that Lot, although righteous in his own person, nevertheless bears the type of a corrupt multitude. For in the Gospel Lazarus is the Lord’s friend, as the Lord himself testifies: “Our friend Lazarus sleeps” (John XI); yet by that same sleep, or by his four-day burial, he bears the type of the sinner already hardened by the habit of wickedness and already foul with an evil reputation.

## CHAPTER X. On the saying, “I shall make your seed like the dust of the earth,” and by what right his seed ought to possess that land.

“I shall make your seed like the dust of the earth” (Gen. XIII). “If any person can number the dust, he shall also be able to number your seed.” This must be understood only of that seed to which the Lord was to give the land that He was then showing, although other nations also sprang from Abraham’s flesh—the Hagarites, Midian, and the Edomites. Balaam too confirms this in his prophecy: “Who can count the dust of Jacob, and know the number of Israel’s stock?” (Num. XXXIII).

But why is this people compared, because of its multitude, to the innumerable dust of the earth, when, as Moses testifies and as was said above, they were fewer than all peoples (Deut. VII)? This must therefore be referred not to a comparison with other nations, but to the number of the elect who were to come from that nation. For since only the elect belong to the number, while that nation, for the most part rejected, has made an empty place for us, they are rightly compared with the dust of the earth: we cannot number it, but in God’s judgment it is superfluous, with Him to whom the elect alone are known.

“Rise,” He says, “and walk through the land in its length and breadth, for I shall give it to you.” Therefore Abraham moved his tent and came and dwelt by the valley of Mamre, which is in Hebron; and there he built an altar to the Lord (Gen. XIII). Not by chance, but by God’s most ordered providence, he was commanded to walk through the land and came to Hebron. He not only dwelt there as a stranger, but later bought from the sons of Heth, inhabitants of the land, a field with the double cave as a burial possession (Gen. XXIII).

For Adam the greatest was buried there among the Anakim, as is read in the book of Joshua (Josh. XIV). Hence it was later called Kiriath-arba, that is, “city of four,” because first Adam, and then the three patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, were buried there. Thus, while he builds an altar to the Lord’s name in the place where the first parent of the earthly world was buried, he already proclaims himself, by this title, heir of the whole world. And when he acquires that same place as a burial possession, he establishes a certain legal claim for his seed, so that the sons of Abraham might demand that land not only by heavenly judgment, because the Canaanites were sinners, but also by a kind of secular justice: its inhabitants had sold it to their father as a burial possession [Col. 0376B].

Moreover, Mamre, from whom the valley of Mamre is now named, is himself the brother of Aner and Eshcol, who, as is later said, were allied with Abraham.

## CHAPTER XI. On Abraham’s delivering his kinsman Lot.

—[CHAPTER XIV.] “Now it came to pass at that time that Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Pontus, Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites, and Tidal king of the nations made war against Bera king of Sodom, and against Birsha king of Gomorrah, and against Shinab king of Admah, and against Shemeber king of Zeboiim, and against the king of Bela, which is Zoar. All these assembled in the woodland valley, which is now the Salt Sea,” etc.

After Lot was separated from Abraham and dwelt in Sodom, wars arose and Lot was led captive. So too, because Abraham’s offspring was to mingle among the nations, because the land was defiled by their works and they committed fornication with foreign gods, the Lord raised enemies against them: for example, Moab, Ammon, Midian, and other nations. And, as the Psalmist says, the Lord was angry in wrath against His people, abhorred His inheritance, handed them over to the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them; their enemies afflicted them, and they were humbled under their hands (Ps. CV).

All this land of the five cities—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela or Zoar—was formerly watered like the Paradise of the Lord. But now this same Pentapolis, as a testimony to wickedness, has left behind a smoking land consumed by fire. The Woodland Valley, which is now the Salt Sea or Valley of Salt-pits, where there had formerly been bitumen wells, was from that time—that is, after God’s wrath and the rain of sulphur—turned into the Dead Sea, also called the Bituminous Lake.

Bela, which is also Zoar (Isa. XV; Jer. XLVIII), is called in the Hebrew language “devouring.” The Hebrews report that this same place is elsewhere in Scripture called Salissa, and again called “the calf that tramples three times,” because, that is, it was swallowed up in the third earthquake. From the time when Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim, were overthrown by divine fire, that place has been called Zoar, that is, “little.” For Zoar is translated “a small [city].”

“And,” it says, “they struck the Rephaim at Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim with them, and the Emim at Shaveh-kiriathaim, that is, at Shaveh, the city.” *Rephaim* means “giants” or “strong men”; *Zuzim* and *Emim* mean “terrible” and “fearsome.” These names indicate that the peoples whom they struck were very powerful.

“Then they returned and came to the spring of Mishpat,” that is, “Judgment,” which is Kadesh. It is called the Spring of Judgment here by anticipation, since it received that name later from the event. The place by the rock called the Spring of Judgment signifies that God judged the people there (Num. XX). “And they struck all the country of the Amalekites at Hazazon-tamar.” This town was afterward called Engedi, fertile in balm and palms. Hazazon-tamar, moreover, in our language means “city of palms”; for *tamar* means “palm.” The country of the Amalekites is likewise called so here by anticipation, for Amalek was one of Esau’s later descendants.

“Behold, one who escaped came and told Abram the Hebrew, who dwelt in the valley of Mamre the Amorite, brother of Eshcol and brother of Aner,” etc. *Hebrew* means “one who crosses over” or “sojourner.” He dwelt in the valley of Mamre, that is, in Hebron, as was said above. But why, when Abram has already been named so many times and is still to be called Abram in this Scripture, so that nowhere else is he called “the Hebrew,” did it please the text to call him here “the Hebrew,” that is, the sojourner?

Plainly, it was to commend the greatness of the deed and of his courage: a sojourner and foreigner, under God’s protection, did what five native kings were unable to do, and inflicted a single retaliation upon the four victorious kings and gained a complete victory. “And he pursued them as far as Dan,” to a Phoenician town later called Paneas. Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan; the other is called Jor, which means “stream.” When these two springs, not far from one another, unite into one small river, it is thereafter called the Jordan.

But let us return to the meaning begun above. When Lot was captured by enemies, Abram took his forces and divided his allies—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre are understood—and rushed upon the enemy. Victorious, he brought back his kinsman free. So too, when Abraham’s offspring was handed over to the nations, Abraham’s faith would not fail, though it remained among few; that faith would often deliver them, God remembering His covenant which He made with Abraham and raising up saviors for them—for example, Ehud against Moab (Judg. III), Barak against Jabin king of Canaan, Gideon against the king of Midian, and other leaders or saviors in their times, and finally glorious kings, warriors victorious over hostile nations.

## CHAPTER XII. On the king of Sodom, who went out to meet him; and on Melchizedek, who blessed him while bringing forth bread and wine.

“The king of Sodom went out to meet him after he returned from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him, in the valley of Shaveh, which is the King’s Valley. But Melchizedek king of Salem, bringing forth [Col. 0378A] bread and wine—for he was priest of the Most High—blessed him and said: ‘Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection the enemies are in your hands.’”

The ranks or merits of the king of Sodom—whose people were exceedingly wicked and sinners before the Lord—and of Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of the Most High, are very contrary to one another; yet both met Abram the victor.

Concerning Melchizedek, however, no one doubts or is ignorant that he signifies Christ, of whom, as the Holy Spirit says through David: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). What, on the other hand, does the king of Sodom signify except the people of the Jews, such as they were at the time when Christ, King and High Priest, was born of the Virgin and came to meet our father Abraham?

Isaiah, looking upon the Jews of that time, says: “Woe to the sinful nation, the people burdened with iniquity, the evil seed, the criminal sons” (Isa. I). And then: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah” (ibid.). Again: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (ibid.).

O great and wonderful mystery of this present narrative! The king of Sodom, that is, of men most wicked and exceedingly sinful, celebrates Abraham’s victorious encounter. For in the last time, very wicked men and grievous sinners—namely the scribes, Pharisees, and other Jews, rulers of Sodom not by birth but truly by their conduct—were to celebrate the victorious faith of the patriarchs and prophets. They were like whitewashed tombs outwardly, precisely because they celebrated the works of the fathers, while within they were full of dead men’s bones (Matt. XXIII), living secretly according to the sulphurous flesh of the Sodomites.

But Christ, King of righteousness, King of Salem—that is, of peace—King, I say, and also great High Priest, born in the days of such men, exercised his priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek. For He brought forth bread and wine, saying: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. XXVI); and thus He offered himself as the true sacrifice for faithful Abraham and blessed him. Through His blood He obtained for him blessing, that is, forgiveness of sins—indeed, for all the elect who awaited Him from the beginning of the world.

## CHAPTER XIII. Again concerning Melchizedek, and the Hebrew tradition that he was Shem son of Noah.

The Apostle, recalling the present passage, says: “For this Melchizedek, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, to whom Abraham apportioned tithes of all things—first, indeed, because his name is interpreted ‘king of righteousness,’ and then also king of Salem, which is ‘king of peace’—without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, made like the Son of God, remains a priest forever” (Heb. VII).

These words and the other things which the same Apostle adds gave an occasion of error to those who misunderstood them, so that they thought Melchizedek was not a human being but an angel, or even—more foolishly—that he was the Holy Spirit himself, appearing in human form.

But many others agreed in saying that he was a Canaanite man, king of Jerusalem, a city called first Salem, later Jebus, and finally Jerusalem. “It is not surprising,” they say, “if he is described as priest of God Most High without circumcision, legal ceremonies, or Aaronic descent, since Abel, Enoch, and Noah also pleased God and offered sacrifices; and in the book of Job we read that Job himself both offered gifts and was a priest, and daily sacrificed victims for his sons” (Job I).

Nevertheless, the Hebrews maintain something else. They state that he was Noah’s first son, and that at the time Abraham was born he was three hundred and ninety years old. Indeed, if you calculate the number of years in each generation, you will find three hundred and ninety years from Shem’s birth to Abraham’s generation. Abraham died in the one hundred and seventy-fifth year of his life. Thus, by calculation, Shem is found to have outlived Abraham, his descendant in the tenth degree, by thirty-five years.

They also state that, until Aaron’s priesthood, all the firstborn in Noah’s line, whose succession and order are described, were priests and offered sacrifices to God; and that these are the birthrights which Esau sold to his brother Jacob.

They say that Salem was not Jerusalem, as Josephus thinks, but a town near Scythopolis, which is still called Salem. It is mentioned in the Gospel: “John was baptizing in Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there” (John III). It makes no difference whether it is called Salem or Salim, since according to readers’ preference and regional diversity the same words are pronounced with differing sounds and accents.

In this same book of Genesis it is written that Jacob came to Succoth, built houses and tents there, and passed on to Salem, a city of the region of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan (Gen. XXXIII). It should also be considered that, as Abraham was returning from the slaughter of enemies whom he had pursued as far as Dan, Jerusalem was not on his route, but the town of Salem, the metropolis of Shechem, was.

It is therefore foolish that what is said typologically—that Christ’s priesthood has no end—should be referred by some to an anagogical meaning in such a way as to remove the truth of the history. For when the Apostle says “without father, without mother, without genealogy,” he did not mean that Melchizedek literally lacked father and mother. He said it because Melchizedek is suddenly introduced in Genesis as meeting Abraham returning from the slaughter of enemies, and neither before nor after is his name recorded.

And in saying, “he remains priest forever,” the Apostle affirms that Aaron’s priesthood—that is, the priesthood of the Jewish people—had both a beginning and an end; but Melchizedek’s priesthood—that is, Christ’s, who has neither beginning of days nor end of life—is eternal both in the past and in the future [Col. 0380A].

## CHAPTER XIV. Again: that it was not Melchizedek who gave Abraham tithes, as the Hebrews think, but Abraham who, as the Apostle says, gave tithes of all to Melchizedek the priest.

Thus Melchizedek, blessing Abram, says: “Blessed be Abram by God Most High, who created heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, by whose protection the enemies are in his hand. And he gave him tithes of all.”

“He gave him” is said ambiguously. Neither in the wording nor in the expression is it distinguished who gave to whom: whether Abram gave tithes to Melchizedek the priest, or Melchizedek the priest himself gave tithes to Abraham. The Hebrews indeed judge that Melchizedek, that is, Shem, owed this to his descendant; that he did not receive from Abraham tithes of the spoil and victory, but himself gave Abraham tithes of his own property and showed due generosity toward his kinsman.

Both interpretations are possible because of the ambiguity of the expression: both that he himself received tithes of the spoils and that he gave Abraham tithes of his own substance. But the Apostle in the aforesaid Epistle to the Hebrews defines most clearly that Abraham did not receive from Melchizedek tithes of wealth; rather, the high priest received portions from the spoils of the enemies (Heb. VII).

## CHAPTER XV. On Abraham’s refusal to receive anything from all the goods, and on the mystical number of his three hundred and eighteen household servants.

Then the king of Sodom said to Abram: “Give me the persons; take the rest for yourself.” He answered: “I lift up my hand to the Lord God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, that from a thread of the warp to a shoe-strap I shall take nothing of all that is yours, lest you say: ‘I made Abram rich’; except what the young men have eaten, and the shares of the men who came with me—Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre. Let them receive their shares.”

Spiritually, this passage also instructs the Gospel man. Whoever raises the banner of the cross and preaches Christ’s name, and thus contends lawfully, conquers fanatical error or heretical barbarism, and thereafter seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ—he is in a sense Abram, who with his three hundred and eighteen household servants defeated four kings, despoiled those who had despoiled, freed his kinsman, and, after doing this, refused to be enriched by a man or through a man. He says to the king of Sodom: “From a thread of the warp to a shoe-strap I shall take nothing of all that is yours.”

For the number mentioned is entirely sacred: the holy Council of Nicaea rejoiced in it, not through human contrivance or any arrangement, but through divine providence at work. There Arius, the devastator of Christianity, was defeated and condemned. The distinction of this number shone there: three hundred and eighteen bishops were present when they were convened; and this number, as has been said, is entirely sacred.

For if you wish to use the Greek method of reckoning, *tau*, T, signifies three hundred, while I and H signify eighteen. Tau, T, signifies the cross; I and H, with a line drawn above them, signify the name “of Jesus.” Observe that here the name “Jesus” is expressed in the genitive, not nominative, case; therefore the letter sigma, S, is not added, but it is written IH with a line above, by which the number eighteen is completed. Moreover, the letter tau, T, lacks the line across its top; if this were added, it would no longer have merely the appearance of a cross, but would be the cross itself.

When such warriors, therefore, in fighting seek not earthly gain but only the fruit of human salvation, and say with the Apostle, “For I do not seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (Phil. IV), they rightly imitate father Abram, saying: “I lift up my hand to the Lord God Most High, that I shall take nothing of all that is yours.”

“They,” he says—namely Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre—“shall receive their shares.” Those who imitate this, namely by using the authority which they have from the Lord, who ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel (I Cor. IX), act justly; but they possess less glory than those who refuse to use this same authority.

## CHAPTER XVI. What it morally signifies that four kings conquered five kings.

We may likewise draw a pleasing moral meaning from this passage. The four kings gaining victory over five kings are the four passions of the soul, capturing the five bodily senses.
