These passions are often mentioned in the books of pagan philosophers: joy, grief, hope, and fear. The outstanding poet expressed them in a single little verse:

> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice . . .  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid*, VI

Where faith working through love (Gal. V) has overcome these passions of the soul and freed the inner person from their captivity, it has truly triumphed praiseworthily after the example of father Abraham. Therefore the Priest of the Most High—and likewise the Most High himself, Christ the Lord—meets him with the saving sacrifice. For He judges him worthy to share in His heavenly sacraments.

For it is great and victorious neither to rejoice in this world’s prosperity nor grieve at its adversity, neither to hope for prosperity nor fear this world’s adversities. Proclaiming this victory to a certain man, Philosophy sings:

> Drive away joys;  
> drive away fear;  
> banish hope,  
> nor let grief be present.  
> The mind is clouded  
> where these things reign.  
> —Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, I, at the end

Whoever he may be, let him disdain to receive anything from the king of Sodom, and let it not be said that the latter made him rich. That is, let him beware of doing his righteousness before men in order to be seen by them, and so incur the sentence: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI).

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 0382A] On the word of the Lord which came to Abraham after that victory.

After these things had taken place, the word of the Lord came to Abram in a vision, saying: “Do not fear, Abram. I am your protector, and your reward exceedingly great.” Abram said: “Lord God, what will you give me? I shall depart childless, and this Damascus Eliezer, the son of the steward of my house, will be my heir.” And Abram added: “But you have not given me seed; and behold, my household servant will be my heir.”

What the events thus far narrated signify is declared by the words of this subsequent vision, especially when it says: “Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; they shall subject them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years. Yet I shall judge the nation whom they shall serve.” The truth of God confirms beyond doubt, by a twofold prophecy—of deeds promised and of words which follow—that one and the same thing will come to pass.

“Do not fear,” He says, “Abram. I am your protector.” As though He said: “You have already received a taste of my protection: first, because for your wife Sarai I scourged Pharaoh and his house with the greatest plagues, and caused you to go up from there wealthy; then also because, under my protection, your enemies—the five kings—were in your hand. Therefore henceforth be more confident that I am the protector both of you and of your offspring, and that your reward is exceedingly great: so that, made a stranger for my sake, you may rejoice in both respects—now in my protection, by which your very sojourning may be bearable to you, and in the future in your exceedingly great reward.”

Nor does his saying, “Lord God, what will you give me? I shall depart childless,” etc., arise from an unbelieving mind, but from a contrite and humbled heart, consulting the Lord with the greatest humility. By his mournful complaint God is, as it were, importuned, so that He may answer more certainly concerning the earlier promise of the seed for which he hopes.

For it had been said to him above: “I shall make you into a great nation,” and, “If any person can number the dust, your seed too shall be able to be numbered” (Gen. XIII). But this was not enough, since adopted sons or heirs could be denoted by the equivocal term “seed.” Therefore, as though demanding a definition of his own seed, when he had said, “I shall depart childless, and this Damascus Eliezer, the son of the steward of my house, will be my heir,” he added, still knocking earnestly: “You have not given me seed; behold, my household servant will be my heir.”

*Eliezer* means “my God is helper”; *Damascus* means “drinking blood.” They say that the city Damascus was founded by him, and that the proto-martyr Abel was killed in that place.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Again concerning the same matter, and the saying: “Look up to heaven and count its stars, if you can.”

Immediately the word of the Lord came to him, saying: “This man shall not be your heir; rather, he who shall come forth from your womb—you shall have him as your heir.” And He led him outside and said to him: “Look up at heaven and count its stars, if you can.” [Col. 0383A] “So shall your seed be.” Abram believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. XV).

Here God promises two things concerning one and the same seed: namely, its nature and its grace. For by saying, “He who shall come forth from your womb—you shall have him as your heir,” He defines the seed Abram is to have: that is, not by adoption but by the propriety of nature. By adding, “Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be,” He prefigures the heavenly grace or glory by which that same seed is to be glorified.

Earlier, when He had said, “Lift up your eyes and look from the place where you now are, northward and southward, eastward and westward: all the land which you see I will give to you and to your seed” (Gen. XIII), He did not say, “So shall your seed be, like the stars of heaven,” but, “I will make your seed like [Col. 0383B] the dust of the earth.” For not all who were to possess that land on Abram’s account were to be compared with stars, nor were they to be numbered like the stars of heaven by Him of whom it is truly said: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names” (Ps. CXLVI); rather, they were to be multiplied beyond the number of the dust, and to love earth rather than heaven.

But here, where He led him outside, He says, “Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can”; and because he could not, He says, “So shall your seed be.” For assuredly, because Abram obeyed Him who led him outside and said to him, “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” heaven is prepared for him as an exceedingly great reward, and for all who follow his example by obeying Him who leads them outside and says to each individual: “Forget your people and [Col. 0383C] your father’s house” (Ps. LXIV). For all shall be as the stars of heaven: many indeed, yet counted in a definite multitude, or multiplied according to a definite number; and all called and known by their own names.

Nor did He say, “So shall your seed be,” merely because of multitude or number, but also because of differing brightness. For just as not only is there one brightness of the sun, another of the moon, and another of the stars, but also star differs from star in brightness (I Cor. XV), so there is not only one glory of God and another glory of the holy children of Abraham, but they themselves shall have differing glory from one another according to their various merits.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the words: “Abraham believed God, and [Col. 0383D] it was reckoned to him as righteousness.”

“Abram believed God,” he says, “and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Of this the Apostle says: “We say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How was it reckoned? In circumcision, or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision” (Rom. IV), and so forth.

For these words avail to undermine confidence in Jewish righteousness, concerning which he had also said above: “Where, then, is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? Of works? No, but by the law of faith” (Rom. III). Abram had not pursued or devoted himself to the works in whose law the Jew boasts—namely, foods and drinks, various baptisms, and righteousnesses of the flesh—for he was not even circumcised when he was justified. Rather, “Abraham believed God,” and faith alone was reckoned to the believer [Col. 0384A] as righteousness.

And rightly does faith possess the merit of righteousness; for conversely, to be without faith is the height of unrighteousness. Indeed, the first man’s unbelief was reckoned to him as unrighteousness, because he did not believe God when He said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II). For if he had believed, he would not so readily have eaten of that sign.

Therefore our father here took the antidote required against the death of unrighteousness: he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body now dead, or Sarah’s womb dead; but, strengthened, giving glory to God, he knew most fully that whatever God had promised, He was also able to perform (Rom. IV).

## CHAPTER XX. On the words: “On that day the Lord made [Col. 0384B] a covenant with Abram.”

And He said to him: “I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land that you may possess it.” But he said: “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?”

He does not ask in disbelief, he who prefaces such devout words of goodwill: “Lord, what will You give me?” “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?” But why, when he now says, “Lord God, how can I know that I shall possess it?” did he not shortly before say, “Lord God, how can I know that I shall have as my heir him who comes forth from my womb?” Rather, he believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. For which is greater: to possess an inheritance that already existed, or to receive as an heir a great nation that did not yet exist? [Col. 0384C]

Thus he did not doubt as an unbeliever with weakened faith; rather, as a pious father he provided for his future children, lest perhaps, when they sinned, God should repent of this promise of His. Therefore, in the promise he wished that some support of fixed and stable truth should be given him, as it were an interposition of an oath.

And the Lord God did not delay: what His faithful friend desired, though he did not dare to ask it, He freely offered. For He immediately answered: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, and a ram three years old, together with a turtledove and a dove.” Taking all these, he divided them through the middle and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not divide. And birds of prey came down upon the carcasses, and Abram drove them away, and so forth.

This vision ends thus: “On that day the Lord [Col. 0384D] made a covenant with Abram, saying: ‘To your seed I will give this land.’” This covenant is a kind of oath, by which the Lord bound Himself according to the human manner, so that He might lawfully be held as a debtor if, should some occasion of sin intervene, He wished to withdraw His hand and do something contrary to what He had promised.

Mindful of this oath, Moses, when God had said that He would destroy them, stood in the breach before Him; and when God said, “Let me alone, that I may destroy them,” the man held Him firmly, saying: “Why, Lord, are You angry with Your people? Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom You swore, saying: ‘I will give all this land of which I have spoken to your seed, and you shall possess it’” (Exod. XXXIII).

Therefore, whenever in this Scripture we find “covenant” or “compact,” it is not yet the covenant of human reconciliation, but the firm promise of the future covenant and a prophetic image of the one covenant by which, in Christ alone, God reconciled human beings to Himself. [Col. 0385A]

## CHAPTER XXI. What is meant by the words: “Take for me a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old goat, and a ram three years old, together with a turtledove and a dove.”

“Take for me a three-year-old heifer,” he says, and so forth. This whole taking is prophetic. The heifer, goat, and ram—animals plainly suited to servitude, since they feed their masters with their milk and clothe them with their wool—signify the three generations during which Abraham’s seed was to serve in a land not its own. “In the fourth generation,” says the Lord, “they shall return here.”

Now the heifer is three years old, the goat three years old, and the ram three years old. Why? Because the first fathers or patriarchs, through whom the name of the Lord was invoked over them, are three in number; and the Lord God deigned to receive from them a designation, so that He might be called “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. III). Under these names the Trinity, one God, willed to be proclaimed in those ages, because people could not yet receive the manifest names of that Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 0385B]

The birds of prey which descended upon the carcasses of these animals, and which Abraham drove away, signified the rapacious and troublesome Egyptian masters. On account of Abraham’s merit, they were eventually to be driven off from devouring that race. Their return in the fourth generation is signified by the free nature of the birds—namely, by the turtledove and the dove—not only because of the freedom of that return, but also because of the spiritual grace of prophets and priests, whose first or chief representatives in that return were Moses and Aaron.

Accordingly, Scripture says that he took all these things and divided them through the middle—understand: the four-footed animals—and set each half opposite the other; but the birds he did not divide. For the carnal persons signified by the quadrupeds were to make disputes and seditions by murmuring against the Lord; but the spiritual were to preserve unanimous concord, indeed to call even the seditious back to peace. [Col. 0385C]

## CHAPTER XXII. [Col. 0385D] What was signified by the words: “A deep sleep fell upon Abraham, and a great dark horror seized him.”

As the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great dark horror seized him; and it was said to him: “Know with certainty that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own,” and so forth.

In this vision the setting of the sun and the mention of darkness occur twice. First, when it is said: “As the sun was setting, a deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great dark horror seized him.” Secondly, when likewise it is said: “When the sun had set, a dark gloom came to be, and there appeared a smoking furnace and a lamp of fire passing between those divisions.”

This repetition of darkness signifies a double adversity of Abraham’s seed. The first was that by which they sold their brother Joseph (Gen. XXXVII), the cause of their sojourning and servitude. The second was that by which, after Joseph’s death, they were troubled and afflicted by Pharaoh (Exod. I). The former adversity was indeed an act of wickedness; therefore it is pointedly said: “A deep sleep fell upon Abram, and a great dark horror seized him.” The subsequent adversity, however, was an affliction; hence, with no mention of horror, it says: “A dark gloom came to be, and a smoking furnace appeared.” [Col. 0386A]

And because that seed of Abraham was to be visited and delivered amid that very affliction by a strong hand, with many great miracles preceding and following, a lamp of fire also appeared between those divisions. [Col. 0386B] For the smoking furnace was an image of the Egyptian furnace, in which they were to serve in mud and baked brick. But the lamp of fire passing through those divisions was a sign of divine love, by which they were to be illumined through many miracles, of which the Psalmist also says: “Your lightnings shone forth upon the world; the earth was moved and trembled; your way was in the sea, and your paths in many waters” (Ps. LXXVI).

If you follow the simple letter, that lamp passing between those divisions—that is, amid Jewish seditions—was indeed most bright; but by its very passage it declared that it would migrate elsewhere. For behold, glory has been transferred from them and passed to the nations.

Therefore, because when God said, “To your seed I will give this land,” Abram in return said, “Lord God, how can I know [Col. 0386C] that I shall possess it?” such an image was fittingly shown beforehand: it was to serve as an oath that the promise of God which he had heard would be fulfilled without repentance and without doubt.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the words: “In the fourth generation they shall return here.”

It is asked, finally, how Exodus can say: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went out from the land of Egypt” (Exod. XIII), whereas God here foretold: “In the fourth generation they shall return here.” The short answer is that according to one genealogy they went out in the fourth generation, but according to another in the fifth.

For according to the genealogy of Levi, from whom came Moses and Aaron, who led the children [Col. 0386D] of Israel out of Egypt, they are found to have gone out in the fourth generation, as follows: Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; Amram begot Aaron; Aaron begot Eleazar. Kohath entered Egypt with his father; again, Eleazar went out of Egypt with his father Aaron. From Kohath to Eleazar are four generations.

But according to the genealogy of Judah, they are found to have gone out in the fifth generation, as follows: Judah begot Perez; Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon (Ruth IV; Matt. I). Perez entered Egypt with his father Judah. Nahshon is recorded as leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, and his son Salmon entered the land of promise. From Perez to [Col. 0387A] Nahshon are five generations.

Thus both are true: according to the priestly tribe they went out in the fourth generation, and according to the royal tribe in the fifth. Nevertheless, according to the Hebrew truth, as the most learned man Jerome testifies, where the Septuagint has, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt,” it is better read, as Aquila also translated it: “And the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt” (Exod. XIII).

Furthermore, in the reason which the Lord gave—“for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time”—it should be noted that the children of Israel obtained that land not because of their own righteousness, but because those nations were destroyed on account of their iniquities. Hence this same Moses says in Deuteronomy: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Because of my righteousness God brought me in to possess this land,’ whereas these nations have been destroyed because of their iniquities. For you do not enter because of your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart; but because they acted impiously, they are destroyed as you enter, that the Lord may fulfill His word which He swore to your fathers, though you are a people of most stiff neck” (Deut. IX). [Col. 0387B]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the words: “Go in to my maidservant.” What mystery they contain according to the Apostle.

**Chapter XVI.**—Thus Sarai had no children; but having an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar, she said to her husband: “Behold, the Lord has shut me up, so that I cannot bear. Go in to my maidservant; perhaps at least through her I may receive children,” [Col. 0387C] and so forth.

At this point let us cite the Apostle Paul as witness that what is written here is not a merely popular history but mysteries related to heavenly things. “It is written,” he says, “that Abraham had two sons, one by a maidservant and one by a free woman. But he who was of the maidservant was born according to the flesh; whereas he who was of the free woman was born through promise. These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants” (Gal. IV), and so forth.

Following this author, since we have long had experience of Him who speaks in him—Christ (II Cor. XIII)—we understand Sarai as the testament or covenant which God established with Abraham, and Hagar as the law made four hundred and thirty years later. To put it more plainly: in Sarai we recognize the law of faith by which Abraham was justified [Col. 0387D] (Rom. IV); in Hagar, mystically, the law of works, which brought nothing to perfection (Heb. VII).

“Behold,” she says, “God has shut me up so that I cannot bear. Go in to my maidservant; perhaps at least through her I may receive children.” It is as if that free woman which is above, the mother of us all, said: “Behold, the time has not yet come when, with the grace of the Gospel revealed, human beings may receive through Christ the Spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom. VIII). Meanwhile Israel receives the spirit of slavery in fear (ibid.), so that at least from carnal ceremonies and figurative ordinances you may perform some small sort of works of righteousness.

For Abraham first received from the maidservant a son according to the flesh, and only afterward from the free woman through promise. In the same way, God’s people worked under the carnal law, [Col. 0388A] serving only in foods and drinks, various baptisms, and righteousnesses of the flesh (Heb. IX), before the faith of the fathers brought forth evangelical grace and the whole world found true righteousness—that is, eternal redemption—through the blood of Christ.

And it should be noted that Abram took his maidservant not at God’s command but only with His permission, so that Sarah might at least receive a son through her. For God permitted the ancient ceremonies but did not command them to Israel, as He testifies through the prophet Jeremiah when He says: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this word I commanded them, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people’” (Jer. VII), and so forth. [Col. 0388B]

But the ten commandments of the law, which depend upon these two: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind,” and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII), plainly belong rather to the tablets of lawful marriage. Although first written on Mount Sinai, they nevertheless had force naturally before the law, and have still greater force after the servile law in the freedom of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXV. What was signified by the pride of the maidservant who despised her mistress.

But when she saw that she had conceived, she despised her mistress. And Sarai said to Abram: “You act unjustly toward me. I gave my maidservant into your bosom; she, seeing that she has conceived, holds me in contempt,” [Col. 0388C] and so forth.

It is known to all that the Synagogue, though a maidservant, is proud and despises her mistress; that is, it glories in Abraham’s flesh and makes little of his faith. “Desiring,” says the Apostle, “to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X).

Before Sarai, who had been barren, gave birth—that is, before the promises of God’s covenant were fulfilled in the birth of Christ—the maidservant had leisure to be proud (Rom. IV), yet not without punishment. For the tablets cried out: that is, the ten commandments, which are a holy law (Rom. VII), righteous and good. By the voices of this protesting Sarah, the carnal law (Heb. VII), like Hagar, was convicted: either because she could not despise Sarah with impunity, or because she vainly imagined herself free.

For example, when God speaks against Eli on account of his sons: “Therefore I have sworn to the house of Eli that the iniquity of the house of Eli shall not be expiated by sacrifices and offerings for ever” (I Reg. III). But Sarai strikes the swelling pride of the maidservant still more when the Spirit of the true and holy law says through David: “God, the Lord of gods, has spoken. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX), and many similar things in the prophets. [Col. 0388D]

“Therefore,” it says, “when Sarai afflicted her, she fled. And when the angel of the Lord found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, which is on the way to Shur, he said to her in the desert: [Col. 0389A] ‘Hagar, Sarai’s maidservant, where have you come from, and where are you going? Return to your mistress, and humble yourself under her hand.’”

Whatever the holy law commands in saying, “You shall not covet; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX), and so forth—whatever, I say, is written by the finger of God on the two tablets—is a punishment to the servile multitude of carnal Israelites, desiring to commit adultery and loving their own desires. And if they restrained themselves through fear of punishment, that very restraint was an affliction, because fear has punishment.

Therefore this carnal people, unable to endure commands of this kind, often fled to the idols of the nations, under whose worship they thought it lawful to covet, fornicate, and commit adultery. Thus the maidservant more safely took flight when afflicted by her mistress and wandered in the wilderness of Shur, which lies on the way to Egypt, whenever the carnal multitude, unable to bear the spiritual commands of the holy law, fled to nations abandoned by God so that, freed after their manner from the bit and bridle of righteousness, it might follow its own desires. [Col. 0389B]

And fittingly the Egyptian maidservant fled by the way of Egypt, thereby also clearly signifying that same servile people; for it often said: “Let us appoint a leader for ourselves and return to Egypt” (Num. XIV). Shur means “wall.” By this name the vain hope of that people is well expressed: by mingling with the nations, it thought it had escaped the hand of the Lord and was safe from His law.

Likewise, as often as the angel of the Lord called the maidservant back, saying, “Hagar, Sarai’s maidservant, [87] where have you come from, and where are you going? Return to your mistress and humble yourself under her hand,” God heard them when they cried out in tribulation and raised up deliverers for them, sometimes sending His angel—as when He met Gideon (Judg. VI), or when He foretold Samson (Judg. XIII). [Col. 0389C]

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the words: “His hand against all, and the hand of all against him”; and on why the maidservant saw not the face but the back parts of the One who saw her.

“This man,” he says, “shall be a wild man. His hand shall be against all, and the hand of all against him; and he shall pitch his tents opposite all his brothers.”

That this is openly understood of the one whom Hagar then carried in her womb is clear, because these words signify that his seed would dwell in the desert: that is, as wandering Saracens with uncertain settlements, who raid all the nations adjoining the desert on its side and are attacked by all.

Moreover, how savage that previously mentioned carnal people is—the people empty of Abraham’s faith, yet glorying in Abraham’s flesh; savage with a savagery by which it may be compared not so much to the noble lion as to the foolish wild ass—the whole world has heard. For truly its hand is against all, and the hand of all is against it, especially from the time when it was said—or at least fulfilled—what had been said: “Cast out the maidservant and her son.” From that time it has especially hated all nations, and from that time has raged still more fiercely because of the free woman’s son, the firstborn—namely, Christ—who set the Gentile people free with the same freedom by which He Himself is free.

Hence the Apostle says: “But as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now” (Gal. IV). As long as it could, and to the extent it could, it persecuted; now, though unable to do so, it still dares to blaspheme. [Col. 0390A]

And she called upon the name of the Lord who spoke to her, saying: “You are the God who saw me.” For she said: “Truly here I have seen the back parts of Him who sees me.” Therefore she called that well “the Well of the Living One and of the One who sees me.”

Because the Lord was speaking in the angel, it is therefore said: “She called upon the name of the Lord who spoke to her.” But why did she see not the face but the back parts of Him who saw her? Because she desired to rejoice not in the face but in the back parts of Him who saw her. By the back parts of the Lord, earthly or transitory things are meant; by His face, heavenly or eternal things are rightly understood.

And indeed she had heard no heavenly promises—for example, such as those spoken concerning the free woman: “And I will give you a son from her, whom I shall bless, and I will establish my covenant with him,” and the like. She had heard none, I say, of such things, by which she knew herself to have been heard; hence she was to give her son the name Ishmael, meaning “God’s hearing.” Everything she had heard was earthly: namely, “I will multiply your seed, and it shall not be numbered because of its multitude,” and “This man shall be a wild man,” and so forth. Thus the maidservant rightly saw not the face but the back parts of Him who saw her. [Col. 0390B]

So too the Synagogue of that people which was born according to the flesh saw not the face of the Lord but His back parts. It was unable at all to endure the inner things of the holy law, where the face shines—that is, the knowledge of God—where the face of Moses is radiant; but, being animal rather than spiritual, it looked only upon the outward letter and did not receive the things of the Spirit of God (I Cor. II).

Furthermore, even now, after the maidservant and her son have been cast out, it will come to see the back parts of Him who sees it; for the grace of God which it would not see when present, it shall one day see as past. For when the fullness of the nations has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved (Rom. XI). In accordance with this, Moses also was told as a type of the same people: “You shall see my back parts, but you shall not be able to see my face” (Exod. XXXIII).

“It is between Kadesh and Bered.” Kadesh and Bered are regions of the wilderness, between which lies also the wilderness of Shur, where, as already stated, the angel found Hagar. Then too she will be found in the wilderness of Shur, that is, within a wall. For Shur means “wall”: within the wall, I say, which she built in unbelief against God, concerning which the Psalmist says: “And in my God I shall cross over a wall” (Ps. XVII). [Col. 0390D]

She will be found between Kadesh and Bered—that is, wavering and wandering between the life-giving Spirit and the killing letter. For Kadesh means “holy,” and Bered means “hail.” And truly the law of the Lord, according to the life-giving Spirit, is holy; according to the killing letter, it is hail.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Again, on Ishmael’s birth and on the words, “born according to the flesh”; also on his father’s age when he was born.

And she bore Abram a son, and he called his name Ishmael. Ishmael means “God’s hearing,” as has already been said. [Col. 0391A] Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore him Ishmael.

When Ishmael is born, his father is eighty-six years old; when Isaac is born, he is one hundred. Isaac was born when his father was that age. Now the number eighty-six is arranged by two limits: it is eight in the tens place and six in the units. Conversely, the number one hundred is simple—that is, contained in one limit; and it is the third unity, and likewise square. For ten times ten expands into one hundred.

Therefore what the Apostle says—“He who was of the maidservant was born according to the flesh, but he who was of the free woman through promise” (Gal. IV)—is also beautifully signified in these two births by the differing number of years. Ishmael was born from the naturally corresponding flesh or blood of man and woman, since nature permits a young woman, such as Hagar was, to conceive by a man, even an old man. Conversely, nature does not ordinarily permit an old woman, such as Sarai was, to conceive by an old man. [Col. 0391B]

Accordingly, when Ishmael is born, the compound number of the father’s age is fitting. The number six, a perfect number in the units place, is in a manner Abram himself: a man perfect in works, yet of scant and cold blood. The number eight, which philosophers also call feminine, is in the tens place in a manner Hagar: weaker indeed because female, yet more fruitful than the man because young.

They call the number six perfect because it consists of its own parts: its half, which is three; its third, which is two; and its sixth, which is one. For three, two, and one make up six. They call eight feminine because it is evenly even—that is, divisible all the way down to its final units. For it is divided into two fours; four, its half, into two twos; and two into two indivisible units. Thus it is called feminine, just as, conversely, an odd number—for example, seven—is called masculine because it is indivisible: for it cannot be divided into two equal parts. [Col. 0391C]

Under these numbers, then, Ishmael’s natural generation according to the flesh is fittingly found. Conversely, when Isaac is born, whose generation the one grace of God accomplished, the number of the father’s age is full and whole, one and simple: that is, contained under the single hundred-place limit. [Col. 0391D] [88] For among those same philosophers unity is called neither masculine nor feminine; and therefore Isaac fittingly is born under the hundred-unit of his father’s years, since neither male nor female nature, but the truth of divine promise alone, accomplished his generation.

The preparatory conversations concerning this birth between God and man begin as follows.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Isaac, or his promise.

After he had begun to be ninety-nine years old, the Lord appeared to him and said: “I am the Almighty Lord; walk before me and be perfect. I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly greatly.” Abram fell prostrate upon his face.

Abram’s ninety-ninth year is Ishmael’s thirteenth. Therefore Abram’s hundredth year, when Isaac was born, is [Col. 0392A] Ishmael’s fourteenth year. O the great and wonderful beauty of the divine ordering! When Abram the father is already cold with age, and conversely the maidservant’s son Ishmael warmly enters the bounds of adolescence, then Isaac, the fruit of faith, is born from the free woman. For it was to come about that, when God’s people had already grown old, faith was vigorous in a very few, and servile iniquity abounded everywhere, the Christ promised to Abraham would be born.

What does the Lord say at that age? “I,” He says, “am the Almighty Lord; walk before me and be perfect.” This is no longer a command to make progress, but a gift of perfection. Therefore He rightly prefaces it: “I am the Almighty Lord,” because for Abram—or anyone else—to walk before the Lord and be perfect is the work of the Lord’s omnipotence, the work of almighty God. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (Jas. I). [Col. 0392B]

But why had He not said this up to this point, though He had appeared and spoken to him many times? Why, unless this too belonged to the mystery? For just as Isaac’s birth was a type of Christ’s incarnation, through which the people of the saints attained the perfection they had awaited, so it was then at last fitting for the words to be spoken: “Walk before me and be perfect,” when the generation of Isaac was being prepared by the gift of the almighty Lord.

Therefore He immediately added the bond of perfection: “And I will establish my covenant between me and you; I will multiply you exceedingly greatly.” What covenant did He then promise, except the sacrament of Christ’s incarnation and passion, which He has now bestowed in His covenant of human reconciliation? For what was said earlier—“On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram”—was the oath by which He swore to him, saying: “To your seed I will give this land” (Gen. XV).

But what He here promises with emphasis, saying, “between me and you,” is the promise and coming of the mediator between God and human beings. And because, through the establishment of this covenant, the propagation of Abraham’s spiritual race was to be enlarged, He immediately added: “And I will multiply you exceedingly greatly.” He was not content to say “exceedingly,” but added “greatly,” because such multiplication is promised as no human being can comprehend in quantity or estimate in dignity, and which belongs to Abraham more in spirit than in flesh. [Col. 0392D]

Fit to hear these things, Abram fell prostrate upon his face—understand: giving thanks.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That in the true Isaac, that is, Christ, the promise spoken in the words “I will multiply you exceedingly greatly” was fulfilled; and on the enlargement of Abraham’s name.

And God said to him: “I am, and my covenant is with you; and you shall be the father of many nations.” This is surely what he said: “I will multiply you exceedingly, beyond measure.” Clearly this multiplication is mighty and beyond measure: to be father of many nations, father of all who believe, whether they are of the circumcision or of the uncircumcision. For it is in Christ that this covenant exists, of which he now says: “And my covenant is with you.” For it is not merely any covenant, but a uniquely great one [Col. 0393A]; and, being about to declare it, he prefaced it with “I am.” This covenant, I say, is in Christ, the mediator between God and men, through whom alone Abram was made father of many nations—indeed, as it is most holy and most fitting to say, father of all God’s children. For all who are called and are children of God received such grace only through Christ, by whom they were redeemed and reborn to God. And that Christ, according to the reality of the flesh assumed, is Abraham’s seed.

Therefore, all those whose Father is God—of all those, I say, Abraham too is father. Rightly, then, he fell upon his face, worshipping and giving thanks, when he received the abundance of so great a gift. God places the distinction of this same multiplication in the very title of his name: “Your name,” he says, “shall no longer be Abram, but you shall be called Abraham; because I have made you father of many nations, and I will cause you to increase most exceedingly; and I will set you among nations, and kings shall come forth from you.”

The Hebrews say that God added to Abraham and Sarah the letter *h* from his own name, which among them is called the Tetragrammaton. For at first he was called Abram, which is interpreted “exalted father,” and afterwards he was called Abraham, which is rendered “father of many”; “of nations,” which follows, is not contained in the name but is understood. Nor is it surprising that, although among the Greeks and ourselves an *a* seems to have been added, we say that the Hebrew letter *he* was added. For it is an idiom of that language to write with *e* but pronounce with *a*, just as, conversely, they often pronounce the letter *a* as *e*.

[Col. 0393C] This also strongly accords with the rationale of the promise: that in the name of this father, whose son according to the flesh is the Lord Christ Jesus, the Son of God, one letter of the Lord’s name already shines forth. Why indeed should the father of him in whom is the whole name of the Lord not have even one letter of the Lord’s name? Thus Moses was told concerning him: “And my name is in him” (Exod. XXIX). He did not say, “upon him,” which is common to all those, drawn from many believing nations, of whom this man is father, in accordance with what is said in the Apocalypse concerning each believer: “I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, and my new name” (Apoc. III). Rather: “My name is in him,” which belongs properly to the only-begotten Son, who, being God and Lord, is in every respect—both in name and in reality—like and equal to God and Lord the Father.

“And I will set you among nations, and kings shall come forth from you.” The kings here are rightly understood as those known to him by the merit of faith, concerning whom he himself says in the Gospel: “For I tell you,” he says, “many kings and righteous persons desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Luke X). Yet it may also, not improperly, be understood universally of both wicked and righteous kings. For speaking also of Ishmael, he says: “He shall beget twelve princes.”

## Chapter XXX

Concerning the words: “And I will establish my covenant between me and you, and between your seed after you.”

“And I will establish my covenant,” he says, “between me and you, and [Col. 0394A] between your seed after you in their generations, as an everlasting covenant: that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you. And I will give to you and to your seed the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession; and I will be their God.”

Since it has already been said that Abraham bears the type of the ancient people of the saints, the distinction now made by God in saying, “between me and you, and your seed after you,” and likewise, “that I may be your God and the God of your seed, by an everlasting covenant,” should properly be understood thus: in the name of Abraham, all the elect who are both of his flesh and of his faith are understood; in the name of his seed after him, all the elect from among the nations are understood—those who are not Abraham’s flesh and blood, but who are Abraham’s seed through faith in his seed, which is Christ (Rom. II): the later seed, I say, just as the wild olive, which is grafted in, is later than the natural branches which were broken off.

Likewise, under the name of the land of Canaan is rightly understood that land of the living which cast out that accursed Canaan, who is truly accursed from ancient times—that is, the devil. That entire land the aforesaid seed of Abraham will possess forever through faith. Otherwise, if you understand here only the land then inhabited by the Canaanite people, how will what was said stand: “I will give it to you as an everlasting possession”? Canaan, moreover, is interpreted “their motion.” By this name the motion of the proud angels is rightly signified: to them came the foot of pride; by the hand of their sin they were moved, fell, were expelled, and could not stand (Ps. XXXV).

[Col. 0394C] Not only in this place, but in almost all divine utterances of this kind, that land is to be understood—the land truly flowing with milk and honey, upon which the Lord our God looks from the beginning of the year to its end, that is, always.

And the Lord said again to Abraham: “You therefore shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you in their generations.” It is as though he said: “It belongs to my grace to enter freely into covenant with humanity; it belongs to man not to neglect so great a grace nor render the covenant of his God void. For I indeed ‘will not profane my covenant, nor make void what proceeds from my lips’ (Ps. LXXXVIII); nevertheless, whoever makes it void, I shall appear as avenger. You therefore, since you are human—and a human being can hold fast to the truth, which is natural in God, only by laborious effort—you, I say, by applying diligence, keep my covenant, you and your seed after you.”

## Chapter XXXI

Concerning circumcision: that it was a sign of the righteousness of faith; why it had to be placed in that part of the body; and why, after the coming of the promised seed, which is Christ, circumcision ought properly to cease.

“This is my covenant which you shall keep between me and you, and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin.” In this place “covenant” must be understood equivocally for the sign of the covenant. For it immediately follows: “that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you.” The Apostle Paul confirms this also. After saying, “How then was faith reckoned to Abraham as righteousness: in circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision,” he immediately adds: “And he received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith which is in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision” (Rom. IV).

Thus, since Scripture here explains how it calls circumcision “covenant,” saying that it is “a sign of the covenant,” and since the Apostle calls the same circumcision a sign or seal of the righteousness of faith which is in uncircumcision, it is plain that circumcision of the flesh was not the covenant itself but the sign of the covenant; not righteousness itself but the seal of the righteousness of faith.

Here the question arises: Why did our father Abraham receive the seal of the righteousness of faith in such a place, in such a part of the body? “For,” says the Jew [Col. 0395B], “if the mark of circumcision was given as a sign of righteousness, why was it not given rather upon a visible part or limb of the body, so that it might always be exposed?” To this foolish objection I answer, somewhat childishly: if God had placed the sign of circumcision upon the nose, lip, ear, or eye, a damaging blemish would certainly have disfigured the human face.

Yet the matter requires a more serious answer. We have already said that circumcision is, according to Moses, the sign of the covenant and, according to the Apostle, the seal of the righteousness of faith—a fact which neither Jew nor the heretic Ebionite can deny. It is established that the covenant itself, or the faith reckoned to Abraham as righteousness, lay in the promise of the seed in whom all nations would be blessed. This, indeed, is what Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. In what part of the body, then, could the seal of this faith be more fittingly given than in that through which the seed itself naturally passes?

There the guarantor and debtor of his promise, God, fittingly placed the seal, so that both he himself might always be reminded of the promise and man of his expectation. For he wished emphatically to hold himself as debtor, who placed the sign of the promised seed in the very outlet of the seed upon the believing man. At the same time, it must be understood that just as the sign of Noah’s faith was rightly placed in the clouds—God saying, “When I cover the sky with clouds, my bow shall appear in the clouds, and I shall remember my covenant which I made with you” (Gen. II)—because Noah had believed God’s prediction that a flood of waters would overflow from the clouds, so likewise the sign of Abraham’s faith was rightly placed in the place of the seed, that is, in the generative part of the body, because he had believed God when he said that all nations would be blessed in his seed.

[Col. 0395D] Now see how great a sacrilege it is, after the coming of that same seed, still to apply to one’s flesh the seal of that same circumcision. For, according to the stated meaning of circumcision, receiving circumcision is a profession of awaiting that seed. Whoever is circumcised professes, if not in consciousness, yet by that sign, that he awaits the future coming of the seed promised to Abraham. But that one—namely Christ—has already come, has already been born, and, once he was given as a blessing to all nations, the truth of God was fulfilled. Therefore whoever is still circumcised denies that he has come, whom by such a sign he declares himself to await as coming; and accordingly he denies that the one who has already come is Christ. Thus the Apostle rightly and truly says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. VI).

## Chapter XXXII

Again concerning circumcision, and why an infant was commanded to be circumcised on the eighth day.

“An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you.” Beyond the fact that the sign of circumcision testified to that people that it possessed faith in the coming seed of Abraham, namely Christ, there is also a mystery in the fact that the infant is to be circumcised not on any day whatsoever, but on the eighth day [Col. 0396B]. For the eighth day of the infant signifies the eighth age of the world, in which the infant—that is, the world—will be circumcised, stripped of every corruption of mortality; and the world, renewed by the universal resurrection, will be new. For those deemed worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead “neither marry nor are given in marriage; for neither can they die any more, since they shall be equal to the angels and are children of God, being children of the resurrection” (Matt. XXII). Therefore an infant eight days old is rightly commanded to be circumcised, because what circumcision signifies will be accomplished in the eighth age of the world.

“Every male in your generations, both a resident alien and one bought, shall be circumcised; and anyone not of your stock”—understood: if he should wish to enter your settlement. Thus in Exodus, after saying, “This is the ordinance of the Passover: a foreigner and hired servant shall not eat of it” (Exod. XII), it immediately adds: “But if any of the strangers wishes to enter your settlement and keep the Passover to the Lord, every male of his shall first be circumcised, and he shall be as a native of the land” (ibid.).

The Pharisees sought such converts most eagerly in order to glory in their flesh; to them the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who travel sea and land to make one proselyte; and when he has become one, you make him twice as much a son of perdition as yourselves” (Matt. XXIII). For, roaming the entire world for trade and various profits, which they pursued from native disciples as much as from foreigners, under the appearance of zeal for holiness [Col. 0396D], they made it their aim to make a proselyte from the nations—that is, to join a circumcised foreigner to God’s people. But one who, while still a heathen, had erred simply and had been once a son of perdition, when he saw his teachers’ vices and understood that they destroyed in deed what they taught in word, returned to his vomit (2 Pet. II); and, becoming a Gentile again, he deserved a greater punishment.

“My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant.” By these words the Jews strive to defend the circumcision of the flesh, because it is said, “as an everlasting covenant,” as though this meant: “You shall observe the rite of circumcision forever.” But it has already been said that circumcision is not the covenant but the sign of the covenant: “You shall circumcise,” he says, “the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me [Col. 0397A] and you.” Otherwise, how can the rite of circumcision be everlasting, when the succession of birth and generation will undoubtedly have an end?

Therefore, when he says, “My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant,” in the meaning already given the statement refers to Christ, the mediator of God and men, who is true flesh from their flesh. In him the covenant is truly everlasting, because “he is our peace, who made both one” (Eph. II); in him all hostilities have been dissolved, and heavenly things have been reconciled with earthly.

## Chapter XXXIII

Concerning the words, “The male whose foreskin’s flesh,” etc.; and what circumcision effected before Christ’s coming.

“The male whose foreskin’s flesh has not been circumcised [Col. 0397B]—that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has made my covenant void.” It is as though he said: “The male who has not received the above-mentioned sign of my covenant—that is, who has not circumcised the flesh of his foreskin—has denied faith in your seed. But without faith in your seed, which is Christ, salvation is impossible. Therefore that soul shall be cut off from his peoples: that is, he shall not be numbered among the peoples of whom I made you father. Why? Because he made my covenant void: that is, because he transgressed in Adam, in whose loins he then was; and, having arisen from him, he preferred to follow Adam’s transgression rather than your faith, and to embrace imitation of sin rather than expectation of your seed.”

For whence came the hostilities between God and human beings, except because the first man transgressed God’s covenant in paradise? Therefore, one who does not receive the testimony of him through whom alone those hostilities are resolved—one, I say, who before his coming was not marked with the seal then instituted, and after his coming is not marked with his own seal now instituted—rightly perishes for the same fault of the first transgression.

Someone may now ask: Why then did the holy fathers before Christ’s coming not enter the kingdom of God, if they too had been justified through faith in Christ under circumcision? We answer in another way: Why are our catechumens not admitted to the sacraments of the holy Church—for example, to communion in the Lord’s body and blood? Do they not believe Christ’s faith in their hearts and confess it with their mouths? “Because,” you say, [Col. 0397D] “they have not yet been regenerated in the sacred font.” Precisely so: the saints of old likewise ought not to have been received into communion with the glory and vision of divine brightness, into that heavenly glory; nor was it lawful for any righteousness of the human race to be received among the brightness of innocence or angelic splendor, since all such righteousness, as Isaiah testifies, was “like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. LXIV), unless it had first been washed by the flood of blood and water flowing from Christ’s side.

## Chapter XXXIV

Concerning the words: “You shall not call your wife Sarai, but Sarah.”

And he said to Abram: “You shall not call your wife Sarai, but Sarah; and I will bless her, and from her I will give you a son, whom I shall bless; and he shall become nations, and kings of peoples shall arise from him.” One letter, namely *i*, having been removed, the letter *e*, pronounced as *a*, was added, and she was called *Saraa*. For, as has already been said, it is an idiom of the Hebrew language to write with *e* but pronounce with *a*, just as conversely they often pronounce the letter *a* as *e*.

Sarai, moreover, is interpreted “my princess”; Sarah, “princess” absolutely. The reason for changing her name is the same as for Abraham’s. For that Jerusalem which is above, which is free (Gal. IV), and is the mother of us all, before the true Isaac—that is, “laughter,” namely our Lord Jesus Christ, our laughter and joy—was born, was princess of one people, the Jews. For we Gentiles, as the Apostle says, “were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants [Col. 0398B] of promise, having no hope, and without God in this world” (Eph. II). But now we are no longer strangers and foreigners; rather, we are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets (ibid.).

Therefore, just as he is no longer Abram but Abraham, that is, father of many nations, so she is no longer called Sarai, that is, “my princess,” an expression belonging to the Jewish people alone, but Sarah, that is, “princess”—understood, of many nations. For just as Abraham is father, so Sarah, our mother, is mother of the same faith.

“And from her,” he says, “I will give you a son, whom I shall bless; and he shall become nations”—understood, through that one seed, in whom you too will be, as I have already said, father of many nations. For he foretells Christ in Isaac, who indeed becomes nations because through faith in him the grace of the Holy Spirit has also been poured out upon the nations. Accordingly, when he says, “whom I shall bless,” it must likewise be understood that his blessing overflows to all nations, just as I foretold you: “In you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. II, 12).

“Kings of peoples shall arise from him,” he says—understood, through faith. For according to the flesh, kings of the peoples of Israel and Edom indeed descended from Isaac. Yet this is greater and more praiseworthy, and more relevant to the promises of the Lord’s magnificent utterance: that from Abraham’s seed according to Isaac, through faith in Christ, kings of the nations were reborn, or very many worthy rulers of churches.

## Chapter XXXV

[Col. 0398D] Concerning Abraham’s laughter when he said in his heart: “Shall a son be born to a man a hundred years old?”

Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: “Shall a son be born to one a hundred years old, and shall Sarah, ninety years old, give birth?” And he said to the Lord: “Would that Ishmael might live before you!” O man truly worthy of eternal laughter and well prepared for everlasting joy: for he so fell upon his face that he laughed, and so laughed that he fell upon his face, worshipping the omnipotence of him whose singular grace he had heard in the promise.

“Shall a son,” he says, “be born to a hundred-year-old man?”—understood, a son of such a kind; “and shall he be born of Sarah, ninety years old?” She had been barren when, by age, she should have borne children. This indeed is to be understood, especially since, after Sarah’s death, and after Isaac had taken a wife and was already grown, Abraham himself did not hesitate to take a wife named Keturah, and not without result, since by her he received a multitude of sons.

Therefore, what he said in his heart—“Shall it be?”—was not said in doubt, but in inexpressible wonder at his own happiness. But what he said aloud to the Lord, “Would that Ishmael might live before you,” clearly belongs to a reverent and modest mind, confessing that what was granted was far more abundant than he himself dared request.

And the Lord said to Abraham: “Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac,” and so forth. This forceful repetition of God’s speech is meant to awaken the man’s recognized faith, so that he may have ears to hear and not, through excessive humility, dissemble that he has heard such great things. “Sarah your wife,” he says, “shall bear you a son, as I have already said. Because you laughed”—this is to be understood—“his name shall be called Isaac, because truly your offspring shall laugh in the end.” For Isaac is interpreted “laughter.”

By this name the blessed birth of Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, is rightly signified. He is, for the whole company of saints—whose true flesh and true man he himself is from the flesh—the cause of everlasting laughter and unending joy. Of him he himself says: “I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John XVI). One of them beautifully tasted beforehand this joy or laughter of all, while still enclosed in the womb, when his mother said to Mary: “For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the infant leaped for joy in my womb” (Luke I).

[Col. 0399C] This is mystically the voice of all those who are one body and one spirit: “Shall a son be born to one a hundred years old, and shall Sarah, ninety years old, give birth?” Its meaning is: “Until now, when the state of affairs flourished in the times of noble kings, Christ did not come. Now a certain old age has come upon Abraham’s race; for ‘the sceptre has been removed from Judah, and the ruler from between his thighs’ (Gen. XLIX). Shall he therefore now come who is to be sent? Shall I, do you think, see him? Shall I, do you think, endure? Will that birth find me here?” Simeon’s expectation sufficiently shows the sighs of such people: in his heart’s desire he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before first seeing the Lord’s Christ (Luke II).

Thus he marks Christ as Isaac both by name and by office, because he was given to aged parents and received his name from laughter.

## Chapter XXXVI

Concerning the words: “I have heard you also concerning Ishmael,” and how “But I will establish my covenant with Isaac” must be understood.

“I have heard you also concerning Ishmael: behold, I will bless him, increase him, and multiply him greatly. He shall beget twelve princes, and I will make him into a great nation. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year.”

Whether Ishmael himself belongs to the lot of the elect and lives before the Lord, in accordance with his father’s petition, “Would that Ishmael might live before you,” especially because the Lord answered, “I have heard you also concerning Ishmael; behold, I will bless him,” etc. [Col. 0400A], is not certain to us on the authority of another Scripture. For Scripture nowhere plainly declares anything concerning Isaac and Ishmael like this: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Matt. I).

Although this same Scripture says: “When Sarah saw the son of the Egyptian Hagar playing with Isaac her son, she said to Abraham: ‘Cast out this maidservant and her son; for the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac’” (Gen. XXI). And the Apostle calls that same playing persecution, saying: “But as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now” (Gal. IV). Still, it does not necessarily follow that he was rejected or cast out by God, especially since shortly afterward it is written there: “God heard the voice of the boy from the place where he was.”

The Hebrews indeed relate that his play was of this sort: he made idols out of clay, according to what is written elsewhere: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII). Others, however, say conversely that he jokingly and playfully claimed the birthright against Isaac, as being the elder. But of this elsewhere. Let this now be said: although he bore the type of the reprobate, it is not wholly consequent or certain that he himself was rejected by God in his own person, since God said, “I have heard you also concerning Ishmael,” because Abraham had said, “Would that Ishmael might live before you.”

“He shall beget twelve princes” (Gen. XXV). These princes, that is, his sons, are described below: the firstborn Nebaioth; then Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, [Col. 0400C] Hadar, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.

“But I will establish my covenant with Isaac.” In this place too “covenant” is not meant as circumcision, which, as already said, is rather the sign of the covenant. For Ishmael too was circumcised. It follows: “When he had finished speaking with him, God went up from Abraham. And Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his household, and circumcised them,” and so forth. Therefore the covenant properly belonging to Isaac is the redemption or reconciliation of the human race, which God who promised determined should occur in Isaac through Christ—determined, I say, because he is faithful and his purpose cannot be weakened.

## Chapter XXXVII

[Col. 0400D] Concerning Abraham’s hundredth year, in which Isaac was born; and that, when he was now to be born, the mystery of the Trinity deigned to manifest itself to a human being in the form of angels.

(Chapter XVIII.) The Lord appeared to him again in the valley of Mamre, while he sat at the door of his tent in the very heat of the day. This hundredth year of Abraham’s age points, according to the divine plan, to that fullness of time of which the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. IV).

Accordingly, the whole year was festive and solemn for him, and marked by divine revelations, especially because at this time he was granted to see the form of the Holy Trinity, which hitherto he is not recorded to have seen. For behold, Scripture says, “God appeared to him again in the valley of Mamre, while he sat at the door of his tent in the very heat of the day. And when he lifted up his eyes, three men appeared standing near him. When he saw them, he ran from the door of his tent to meet them, bowed to the ground, and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant,’” and so forth.

When Isaac, now to be born, is not merely promised as before but actually given, the mystery of the Trinity deigns to reveal itself to humanity in the form of three angels. For where Christ is born from Abraham’s seed, the whole Trinity, by the presence of its majesty, effects the incarnation of that same Christ, the Son of God, in the lodging of the virginal womb. From that point the name of this same Trinity—the name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is proclaimed publicly throughout the world.

For the Father is he who impregnates the Virgin; the Son is he who assumes human nature; and the Holy Spirit is he through whose operation the Virgin, who knew no man, conceives. But let us now follow the very course of the text. “He appeared,” it says, “again.” It leaves uncertain how long after the events narrated above this took place; but it is certain that the interval was very brief. For in the preceding vision, after God said, “But I will establish my covenant with Isaac,” he immediately added, “whom Sarah shall bear to you at this time next year”; and in this vision he again says: “Returning, I will come to you at this same time, with life accompanying me, and Sarah shall have a son.”

Yet “in the very heat of the day” may be understood as though it said, “in the heat of that very day”—understood, the day whose preceding night he had appeared to Abraham and given him the command concerning circumcision.

## Chapter XXXVIII

What is signified by the fact that angels—or God in angels—then lodged so familiarly with a man, and that their reception differed scarcely at all from customary hospitality.

“In the very heat of the day,” it says. The quality and particular character of the vision which now appeared could not have been expressed more aptly. It is the same as if it had been said: not now in the custom of the night, nor in some merely spiritual vision, but before a human being, in the sight of the eyes and common perception under this sun. For truly all the things recounted in this vision belong to common sensory experience.

[Col. 0401D] “And when he lifted up his eyes, three men appeared standing near him,” and so forth, down to the words: “Therefore the Lord rained fire and sulphur upon Sodom and Gomorrah” (Gen. XIX). In what respect do these actions or words of the heavenly guests differ, in ordinary appearance or in every kind of gesture, from human beings lodging with their friends?

That hospitable father of the household runs to meet them as though they were men in need of shelter and refreshment because of fatigue. “Let me bring,” he says, “a little water, that your feet may be washed, and rest under the tree. I will set before you a morsel of bread; strengthen your hearts, and afterwards you may go on.” What could one say more humanly to a person whom weak and broken breathing showed to be nearly failing from the exertion of travel and emptiness of stomach?

And what more ready answer could weary travelers give, delighted by a good and courteous host? “Do as you have said.” He hastens to Sarah as though for hungry friends: “Hurry,” he says, “and mix together three measures of flour and make hearth-cakes.” He himself runs to the herd, takes a very tender calf and kills it, giving it to a servant, who hastens and cooks it. At last he sets before them a rich meal: butter, milk, and the calf he had cooked; while he himself stands before them as they eat and drink, according to the custom or duty of attendants.

Then they, as well-fed guests are accustomed to be, cheerful and joyful, ask: “Where is Sarah your wife?” And thereafter one among them, who in these matters was the Lord God, says: “Returning, I will come to you at this time, with life accompanying me, and Sarah shall have a son.” This is altogether how a human being speaks, who is always uncertain about future events because of the contingency of his own life: “I will come to you, with life accompanying me”—that is, “I will come to you if life accompanies me.”

[Col. 0402B] Sarah laughed, as a modest woman, apparently blushing before venerable men. “After I have grown old,” she says, “and my lord is aged, shall I give myself to pleasure?” For the things proper to women—that is, menstruation—had ceased for her, naturally on account of her age and the scarcity of blood. Hence the difficulty of conceiving or bearing seemed twofold for her, since she had been barren even when her blood had been abundant.

When she was frightened and said, “I did not laugh,” the Lord, still pressing her, says: “It is not so; you did laugh.” With Lot also, angels called to lodge with him say almost exactly what men say and do: “No, we will remain in the street”; and only with difficulty, under compulsion, do they turn aside to him. Lot too, when they had entered, made them a feast, baked unleavened bread, and they ate. What, I ask, is there here that differs from human conversation or ordinary deliberation?

For these are not trivial or playful matters, but true and holy proclamations concerning the true Son of God and true Son of Man. What then was being prepared except that Isaac should be born as a type of him who, after making the earth in everlasting time and filling it with cattle—for indeed “all things that exist were made through him” (John I)—was afterwards to be seen upon earth and dwell among human beings (Baruch III)?

But he was not merely to be seen, nor merely to live among human beings in any fashion; rather, in the truth of human substance, truly conceived and born of a woman, true man and true flesh, he was to dwell among us. Among us, I say, in every respect: coming forth from his invisible things into our visible condition. For he dwelt among us when, in that secret place of female nature from which each of us proceeds not without sin, he lodged for ten months—not nine—without contagion of sin; and then, coming forth as a bridegroom from his chamber, “he set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII), clothed in tender flesh as an infant and uttering infant cries. Made under the law and subject to Joseph and Mary, circumcised, and cleansed by the legal sacrifice as though a sinner, he suffered hunger, endured the deceiver’s fraud, bore human persecutions, was sorrowful unto death [Col. 0403A], fled from place to place, and finally became obedient unto death.

Therefore, rightly and beautifully, when this was prefigured, heavenly things were already joined with earthly: so that in no way did the heavenly spirits present themselves unlike human beings in speech, table fellowship, or every kind of gesture and manner, both of word and deed.

It should be noted in this passage that the words vary in number: some things are said in the singular and others in the plural. The reason for this variation is as follows. Where things belonging to God are said or done, everything is said in the singular; where, among the guests, almost exclusively human things are heard, everything is said in the plural.

To make this clearer: when Abraham worships, he does not say in the plural, “My lords, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant”; but in the singular: “Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes, do not pass by your servant,” because one Lord or God in three persons is alone and singularly to be worshipped. But when he offers what belongs not to God but to guests, he speaks in the plural: “Let me bring a little water, that your feet may be washed; rest under the tree, strengthen your hearts, and afterwards you may go on.” Likewise, when they, cheerful and well refreshed, ask about Sarah, it is written in the plural: “They said, ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’” But where there immediately follows a promise whose giving or doing belongs to God alone, it is written in the singular: “Returning, I will come to you, and Sarah shall have a son.”

# Sixth Book on Genesis

(Genesis, chapters XVIII–XXV.)

[Col. 0403]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0403B] Concerning the gentleness and wrath of God, who lodged so familiarly with the righteous man and turned aside so terribly against Sodom.

Promise or coming of Christ, the Son of God, brings to the elect an abundance of mercy, but to the reprobate an abundance of wrath and vengeance. “Wrath,” says the Apostle, “and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of man that does evil, of the Jew first, and also of the Greek. But glory and honour and peace to every one that does good, to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom. 2). Thus it is fitting that he whose Gospel was simultaneously to reveal wrath and grace should, already in the prefiguration of his coming—while he is prefigured in Isaac—set before the whole world examples of both realities.

[Col. 0403C] Beside the very tents of the godly he grants chaste delights; and, almost smiling upon those who laugh and rejoicing with them, he multiplies the occasion and confirms the cause of eternal laughter. Then, turning aside to Sodom, he rains upon the wicked and sinners a most dreadful wrath, as an example of eternal fire. There God displays gentleness; here, the truth and justice of his Son. The Prophet, singing beforehand of him in the bridal song, after saying, “Ride prosperously, go forth and reign” (Ps. 45), immediately adds: “Because of truth and gentleness and justice; and your right hand shall lead you wonderfully” (ibid.). But let us now enter upon the very signs of that truth and justice.

## CHAPTER II. [Col. 0403D] On the sin of the Sodomites, and how it prefigured the Jews who crucified the Lord after mocking him.

**CHAPTER 18.**—“And when the men rose up from there, they turned their eyes toward Sodom, and Abraham walked with them, accompanying them.” The men of Sodom, as was said above, were exceedingly wicked and sinners before the Lord [Col. 0404B]. Their sin is known—indeed, notorious and infamous throughout the whole world—namely, fullness of bread and idleness (Ezek. 16), in which they abused themselves most shamefully: exchanging the natural use for that which is against nature, males committing disgraceful acts with males, and thus receiving in themselves the recompense fitting for their error (Rom. 1). For this sin is utterly foul, and also the punishment for preceding sins. Therefore, from that time and forever, the memory of them stinks even to tax collectors and heathens—not to mention wholly chaste nostrils.

They plainly bore the type of the false Jerusalemites, those who crucified our Lord, the Son of God. Isaiah testifies to this when, speaking of them in the prophetic voice, he says: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1) [Col. 0404C]. Thus the Lord, delighted by the hospitality of father Abraham, turns his eyes toward Sodom, Abraham accompanying him; he is almost to suffer violence from sinners. That is, gladdened by teaching and miracles, amid the goodwill of the disciples—in whom Abraham existed according to faith—and accompanied by those same apostles, he ascended to that Jerusalem which is spiritually called Sodom (Rev. 11), to be crucified by the chief priests, Pharisees, elders, and scribes of the people.

## CHAPTER III. On the words: “Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?”

And the Lord said: “Can I hide from Abraham [Col. 0404D] what I am about to do, seeing that he shall become a great and exceedingly mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him? For I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord and to do righteousness and judgment, so that the Lord may bring upon Abraham all that he has spoken [Col. 0405A] to him.”

Wonderful is the condescension of one beginning to speak, by which God seeks both to stir a man’s attention and, as it were, to win his goodwill. For he begins his discourse from certain praises of this very hearer: “Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?” The sense understood is: despite such strong reasons against it. First, because he is to become a great nation—great, I say, more according to faith than according to flesh—and an exceedingly mighty nation. Concerning the wondrous strength of that nation I may rightly say: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11).

Then he says: “For I know that he will command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the Lord.” This he did, first by his own good example, and afterward through the writing and teaching [Col. 0405B] of the Law, by means of his descendants. How great, do you suppose, are these praises or attestations spoken to a man from God’s own mouth? Abraham, therefore, is not lightly esteemed before God, since God testifies that, for reasons so great and many, he cannot hide his counsel from him.

These things were indeed fittingly said to Abraham in accordance with his own person, for he has received even today his great and exceedingly mighty nation, that they may keep judgment and righteousness, knowing that sinners must fear God’s severe sentence, as demonstrated by the example of Sodom. Yet, according to the mystery already described, when the Lord was about to suffer and fixed his eyes upon that Sodom—that is, Jerusalem—he did not hide from Abraham, that is, from his apostles, Abraham’s children in flesh and faith, what he himself was about to do. He knew that they would become a great and exceedingly mighty nation [Col. 0405C], namely, that Church which we see, from that time onward, spread throughout the whole world, “terrible as an army set in array” (Song 6); that through their ministry all nations of the earth would be blessed in Abraham’s seed; and that he would command his children, that is, his hearers, to keep righteousness and judgment, believing in the resurrection to come and the universal judgment of the living and the dead.

## CHAPTER IV. On the outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abraham’s prayer.

“The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has increased, and their sin is exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.” And they turned away from there and went to Sodom.

As regards the immediate historical passage, people are forbidden rash judgment, lest they readily believe reports they have heard or judge matters they have not tested. For God, who cannot be deceived and knows all things even before they occur, deigned to say: “The outcry of Sodom has increased; I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me.”

Mystically, however, it must be said that the outcry of the Sodomites—that is, of the Jerusalemites—had frequently risen to the Lord. The Gospel parable testifies to this: the wicked and doomed tenants of the vineyard cast out the servants of the master of the vineyard, sent to them once, twice, and a third time; indeed, after insulting them, they killed them (Matt. 21) [Col. 0406A]. Therefore, when at last the only son was sent, the father supposing and saying, “They will respect my son” (ibid.), he rightly said: “The outcry of Sodom has increased; I will go down and see,” and so forth.
