For he went down and saw whether they had fulfilled in deed the outcry that had risen up; and he saw—that is, he experienced—how utterly wicked they were. In himself he learned how cruelly and hatefully they had killed the holy prophets and righteous men.

“And they turned,” he says, “and went to Sodom. But Abraham still stood before the Lord, and, drawing near, said: ‘Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked?’” and so forth. It is plainly clear from the character of the prayer itself that Abraham truly stood before the Lord and drew near to the Lord, because in prayer he sought not his own glory but God’s; he asked not for his own will but for God’s will to be done [Col. 0406B]. For he said: “Far be it from you to do this thing and kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be like the wicked! This is not yours; you who judge all the earth will by no means perform this judgment.”

Thus the faithful servant advised the Lord to act and judge in such a way that he himself might worthily be praised for his judgments. Accordingly, the Lord God did not disdain a man who admonished him and, as it were, reproved him, but granted each of his requests in turn: “I will spare the entire place for the sake of fifty; I will not destroy it if I find forty-five there; I will not strike it for forty; I will not do it if I find thirty there; I will not kill it for twenty; I will not destroy it for ten.”

For the man was strong with true strength, who held fast the all-powerful Lord [Col. 0406C]. Strong, I say, and powerfully breaking himself, he who said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes”; and: “Do not, I beg you, be angry, Lord, if I speak yet further”; and: “Since I have begun once, I will speak to my Lord”; and: “I beseech you, Lord, do not be angry if I speak just once more.” For this is true strength: the spirit of humility and a mind subject to God’s righteousness.

The same prophet who, at the beginning of his book, said, “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1), lamenting that this strength had failed among human beings, says near the end of the same book in mournful complaint: “There is none who calls upon your name; there is none who rises up [Col. 0406D] to hold fast to you” (Isa. 64). In the Spirit he saw the Lord turned toward that Sodom and saw that there was no one to hold him back because of its abundant wickedness. What he mourned, he made clear in what followed: “Jerusalem has become deserted; the house of our sanctification and our glory, where our fathers praised you, has become a burning with fire” (ibid.). This occurred irreparably under Vespasian and Titus.

## CHAPTER V. Again on the same matter, and why the wise man did not by chance reduce the number in this way—first fifty, then forty, and finally ten.

But what is the meaning of this descent in the numbers? Did a man speaking with God, by chance and without knowledge or understanding, pour out inserted numerical reductions just as they came to his lips? Certainly not. Rather, he spoke with a rationale which, although it is not wholly clear to us, nevertheless causes some gleam of beauty to shine upon our minds.

For we observe this excellent provision made by God in these numbers: they are so arranged not only by ordinary arithmetical ratios but also by musical proportions that they encompass the harmonies of every musical consonance, except the number fifty, which is consecrated for other reasons. For forty-five compared with forty yields the *epogdoon*, that is, the ratio of nine to eight, which musicians call a tone. Forty compared with thirty produces the *epitrite*, that is, the ratio of four to three [Col. 0407B], which they call the consonance *diatessaron* (a fourth). Thirty compared with twenty establishes the *hemiole*, that is, the ratio of three to two, which they call the consonance *diapente* (a fifth). Twenty compared with ten is double, which they call the greatest consonance, namely *diapason* (an octave). Again, thirty in relation to ten makes a triple ratio, and forty in relation to ten a quadruple ratio; one yields an octave with a fifth, the other a double octave.

What, then, do these numbers indicate except the true worthiness of so great an intercessor? Namely, that he desires the Lord his God to spare sinners only in such a way as advances the praise and honour of God’s name. For it is fitting that he enact a mercy fit for song, that is, one which does not depart from the truth of judgment, as the Psalmist testifies: “I will sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100) [Col. 0407C]. Therefore, because in the numbers already mentioned the force of every consonance is contained, Scripture says: “The Lord departed after he had ceased speaking with Abraham, and Abraham returned to his own place.” For the wise person neither wishes nor ought to ask anything of God outside the praise of God’s righteous judgment. So far was Abraham from seeking his own will that, although he had concern for his nephew Lot, his mouth made no mention of him.

## CHAPTER VI. Why two came to Sodom, and why they came in the evening.

**(CHAPTER 19.)** “Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot sat at the gate of the city” [Col. 0407D]. It was fitting that two angels should come, so that righteous judgment might stand on the testimony of two. This refers to what the Lord had said above: “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.” Just as those words were spoken so that no one might rashly pronounce judgment concerning an untested accusation, so two came to Sodom, so that no condemnation might decide the case of the accused on fewer than two witnesses.

And fittingly, not three as came to Abraham, but only two came to Sodom. For although the mystery of the Trinity is not revealed to the hearts of the impious, yet the Son of God was seen on earth among sinners and conversed with ungodly people (Bar. 3); and the Holy Spirit appeared visibly among those same people—upon the Lord himself in the form of a dove (Matt. 3), and upon the disciples in the form of fire (Acts 2) [Col. 0408A]. Thus not three but two angels fittingly came to the city of the wicked, because, at the time of visitation, the two Persons—the Son and the Holy Spirit—were made known to humanity in such a way that all sinners and ungodly persons are without excuse.

“They came in the evening,” he says. The very time or hour accords with the most sorrowful cause of sinners’ visitation. Abraham was visited at midday. For God appeared to him above, while he sat at the entrance of his tent, in the very heat of the day. The righteous person is also visited in the morning, according to: “In the morning I will stand before you and see” (Ps. 5). Again: “In the morning I put to death all the sinners of the earth” (Ps. 100). And elsewhere: “In the mornings I will meditate on you” (Ps. 62).

But the phrase “while he sat at the gate of the city” suits one who in spirit did not sit among the crimes of the city. Hence the apostle Peter says: “For by sight and hearing that righteous man, dwelling among those who day by day tormented that righteous soul with their wicked deeds” (2 Pet. 2) [Col. 0408B].

## CHAPTER VII. On the fact that they turned aside to Lot’s lodging only when he had strongly compelled them.

“When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them; and he bowed himself to the ground and said, ‘I beg you, my lords, turn aside to the house of your servant and remain there. Wash your feet; in the morning you will proceed on your way.’ They said: ‘No; we shall remain in the street.’ He strongly compelled them to turn aside to him.”

Their first saying, “No; we shall remain in the street,” and then, when he compelled them, their turning aside to him, though seemingly unwillingly, does not signify changeability, as though with the Lord or his holy angels there were yes and no. Rather, because of different causes, different things were said and done. For Lot’s cause was different—indeed contrary—to the cause of the Sodomites. Thus, when they say, “No; we shall remain in the street,” this is a rejection of the city, in which the bonds of friendship and hospitality were in no way to be shared with heavenly or holy beings [Col. 0408C]. But when, compelled and as if unwilling, they turn aside to Lot in rejection of the entire city, this is grace set apart and peculiar to the merits of his righteousness.

Moreover, this image accords well with the truth of the future reality. For when the Lord was about to be crucified in that city which, as stated, is spiritually called Sodom, he so flattered no one that in the great city he found neither host nor lodging, but stayed in a small rural place with Lazarus and his sisters. Yet on the evening when he was to be betrayed, he turned aside to a certain person and ate the Passover with his disciples (Matt. 26) [Col. 0408D]. What follows fittingly corresponds to that supper: “Having entered, he made a feast, baked unleavened bread, and they ate.” For our Lord ate unleavened bread with the Paschal lamb in the city that night.

Lot, indeed, represents the type of those few who did not consent to the crime of the Jews (Matt. 27). Though pious, they fell short of the apostles’ faith by as much as Lot’s righteousness fell short of Abraham’s perfection.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0409A] How the Sodomites surrounded the house before they went to bed, and how at a like hour the Jews seized the Lord.

“But before they went to bed, the men of the city surrounded the house, from youth to old age, all the people together; and they called Lot and said to him: ‘Where are the men who entered your house tonight? Bring them out to us, that we may know them,’” and so forth.

Likewise, before they went to bed, “behold, a crowd came, and he who was called Judas” (Luke 22). For he had said to his followers: “Why do you sleep? Rise and pray, lest you enter into temptation.” Again, reproving them: “Sleep now and rest; behold, he who will betray me is drawing near” (Matt. 26). Thus, according to the prophet already cited, they were truly rulers of Sodom and truly people of Gomorrah (Isa. 1) [Col. 0409B]. The former sought, in mockery, to violate unknown men against nature; the latter sought, by a lie—that is, by the accusation of falsehood—to stain before every creature the Lord God, of whom they said: “We do not know where he comes from” (John 9).

See how closely God saw, and how painfully he experienced here and there, that the outcry of Sodom which had risen to him had truly been fulfilled in deeds. “Here,” he says, “the men of the city, all from youth to old age, surrounded the house. ‘Bring out to us,’ they say, ‘the men who entered your house tonight, that we may know them.’” Although Lot begged them and said, “Do not, I beseech you, my brothers, do this evil,” and so forth, they answered instead: “Get back there!” And again: “You entered as a stranger; are you now to be a judge? We will afflict you more than these” [Col. 0409C]. O unrighteous freedom and free unrighteousness, which had struck heaven with so grievous an outcry!

What of those other Sodomites, that people of Gomorrah? When the crowd that had come for the feast impeded their plans—for they feared the people—they hired a traitor and brought in an exceedingly violent force, namely, a military band of Romans. Rushing out with clubs and swords (John 8), they judged the visiting crowd that had come up from the country before Passover unworthy of a hearing, saying: “This crowd that does not know the Law is accursed.”

## CHAPTER IX. What it signifies that they shut the door and struck those outside with blindness.

“And they pressed Lot most violently, and were now near breaking down the doors. And behold, the men stretched out their hand, brought Lot inside, shut the door, and struck with blindness those who were outside, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door.”

Concerning those other rulers of Sodom and that other people of Gomorrah, it was afterward prophesied: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn, and I heal them” (Isa. 6) [Col. 0409D]. Therefore, rightly were they first struck with blindness, since afterward they were to be consumed from heaven by sulphurous fire, so that they could not find the door. For those people, who are to be tormented in eternal fires, are meanwhile blinded in mind, so that they cannot find him who says: “I am the door” (John 10) [Col. 0410A].

But because the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation and to reserve the wicked for torment in eternal fires (2 Pet. 2), after Lot had been brought in and those outside struck with blindness, they said: “Have you here anyone of your own—sons-in-law, sons, or daughters? Bring out of this city all who are yours. For we shall destroy this place.” Thus the Lord indeed brought into himself, by the hand of his mercy and grace, some from the Jewish people who had not consented to their crime or who had repented. And after those others had been struck with the inward blindness already described, he commanded these not to remain in their city—that is, not to share their religion or their carnal sacrifices [Col. 0410B], which from then on he himself hates.

The prophet Isaiah testifies to this. After crying out the words already quoted—“Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1)—he immediately added what they ought to hear: “‘What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?’ says the Lord. ‘I am full.’” And shortly afterward: “I will not endure new moon, Sabbath, and other solemnities. Your assemblies are wicked; my soul hates your calends and your solemnities. They have become burdensome to me” (ibid.), and so forth.

Therefore, he says, “Bring out of this city all who are yours,” because after they filled their hands with Christ’s blood, as the same prophet immediately says, “Your hands are full of blood” (ibid.), that synagogue—that assembly of evildoers—must be wholly fled by those who desire to be saved [Col. 0410C].

## CHAPTER X. On the words: “Do not look behind you,” and so forth, according to the moral and anagogical sense.

“But while he delayed, they seized his hand, because the Lord spared him; and they brought him out and set him outside the city. There they spoke to him, saying: ‘Save your life; do not look behind you, nor remain anywhere in all the surrounding region, but save yourself on the mountain.’”

Up to the words, “The sun had risen upon the earth, and Lot entered Zoar,” the moral sense is more prominent. “While he delayed,” he says. That is, although he was righteous in comparison with the Sodomites, he still fell short of perfect righteousness and had less faith than Abraham. He was held by the pleasantness of Sodom and its fields, almost watered like Paradise; therefore, as though he did not sufficiently understand what was said, when he was alarmed by the announcement of imminent danger, he turned away his sleepy eyes, weighed down by love of riches, from the present light [Col. 0410D].

So too, very often, one who now knows heavenly things, to whom the wrath of God has been revealed through Christ’s Gospel, and who has been permitted to receive instruction in spiritual matters, is nevertheless still ensnared by a ruinous love of the world. Enticed by his own desire, he disregards the threats of future judgment and the sulphurous punishments of eternal fire which he has heard and well understood, intent upon somehow enjoying the fulfillment of his desire.

While he thus delays, if God, sparing him, seizes his hand, leads him out before the accomplishment of sin, and sets him outside the city—that is, outside the enclosure of temptation—then, at last returning to himself, he says: “I beg you, my lord, because your servant has found grace before you, and you have magnified the mercy which you have shown me, to save my life,” and so forth [Col. 0411A]. For when God swiftly comes to the aid of one willing to perish—that is, willing to carry out a sinful act—and by whatever means hinders his will in its moment of madness, he truly seizes that person’s hand and leads him out from the midst of the Sodomites, because he spares him. Once this has happened, sensing at once that he has been liberated by God’s grace, he is indeed ashamed within himself that he had for a moment entertained an evil will; yet he gives thanks with joy because the Lord has truly magnified his mercy toward him [Col. 0411B].

What, then, is meant by his saying: “I cannot be saved on the mountain, lest evil overtake me and I die. Here is a city nearby to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved there. Is it not a little one? And my life shall live”? This is precisely what we see in many persons too conscious of their own weakness. With little faith, they do not dare undertake a higher commitment, lest they perhaps fail under the burden. They think it better to be content with moderation, not hearing Scripture say: “Those who trust in the Lord shall renew their strength” (Isa. 40); and again: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 26).

For the mountain of which it is rightly said, “Save yourself on the mountain,” is that perfection concerning which our Lord says in the Gospel to the rich young man: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have [Col. 0411C], give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). This perfection of life is the mountain of righteousness. Therefore, the words “Do not look behind you, and do not remain anywhere in all the surrounding region,” in this sense, are a necessary command, because “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9).

But what he added—“Save yourself on the mountain”—is familiar counsel, like that concerning the preservation of virginity, about which the Apostle says: “I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7). For to possess nothing and to be without a wife belong to the same commitment. Thus the Lord’s permission to Lot—“See, I have granted this request also, not to overthrow the city for which you have spoken; hurry and save yourself there” [Col. 0411D]—corresponds to the Apostle’s statement, proposed as a remedy or concession to those who cannot be saved on the mountain described above: “If they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn.” Again: “Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.”

For this moderate course requires the aid of intercessory prayers if it is to be saved. Such people are not among those who shall judge, but among those who shall stand before judgment and yet be saved by mercy triumphing over judgment. Hence, after the Lord said, “See, I have granted this request also, not to overthrow the city for which you have spoken,” it is afterward added: “For this reason the name of the city was called Zoar,” which means “little one.” The sense understood is that Lot had said: “Is it not a little one? And my life shall live?” For formerly it was called Bela [Col. 0412A].

Indeed, the life of worldly people is small; for it is necessary that the Lord receive the prayers of intercessors on its behalf. But the life of spiritual people is great, its praise being from God; like a mountain, it rises above the former and can assist them. “The sun had risen upon the earth, and Lot entered Zoar”: that is, with the sun rising—which, when it had risen, brought the destruction of the Sodomites—Lot entered Zoar. This is in likeness of the future, when Christ, the Sun of righteousness, appears for judgment: the destruction of sinners will be completed, while mercy will receive those whom he deems worthy to spare as they flee from wrath.

## CHAPTER XI. Why the Lord rained not merely any fire, but sulphurous fire; and on the words: “The Lord from the Lord.”

[Col. 0412B] “Then the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven; and he overthrew these cities and the whole surrounding region, all the inhabitants of the cities, and every green thing of the earth.”

Because, he says, the outcry of the Sodomites had risen to the Lord, while he himself said, “I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know,” he found by his own experience that a most dreadful injury had been done to him. Therefore [as was fitting] the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire, that is, sulphurous fire or fiery sulphur.

Why did he rain not merely any fire, but sulphurous fire? Because their flesh had burned not with any ordinary lust, but with the fire of that desire which is against nature. Therefore, because they had sent up to heaven such a stench of flesh against nature, they rightly received from heaven a fiery stench, or a fetid fire [Col. 0412C]. Such fire, such a conflagration, was an example, as already stated, of the judgment to come and of eternal fire.

Thus it was rightly said: “The Lord rained from the Lord,” because the Son, the Lord, received from the Father, the Lord, the office of carrying out that judgment. As he himself says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).

## CHAPTER XII. What it signifies that Lot’s wife looked back and was changed into a pillar of salt.

“And his wife looked back, and was changed into a pillar of salt. But Abraham, rising early in the morning, went to the place where he had previously stood with the Lord; and he looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah [Col. 0412D] and over all the land of that region, and saw ashes rising from the earth like the smoke of a furnace. For when God overthrew the cities of that region, he remembered Abraham and delivered Lot from the overthrow of the cities in which he had lived.”

The literal sense is this: Lot’s wife looked back because she transgressed the command that said, “Save your life; do not look behind you,” and so forth. She was punished in such a way that she stiffened and was changed into a pillar of salt. But lest something similar should happen to Lot himself, Abraham rose early in the morning. At the very hour, namely, when the angels compelled Lot to leave and, as he delayed, seized his hand—at that hour, I say—Abraham rose and stood where he had previously stood with the Lord: that is, he remained in the same intention of heart, fulfilling the worthy and vigorous office of an intercessor [Col. 0413A]. This was immediately made clear by the result. For when God overthrew the cities of that region, he remembered Abraham and delivered Lot.

This is as though it were said: Abraham’s standing before the Lord proved effective because the Lord remembered Abraham and delivered Lot from the destruction of the cities in which he had lived. Moreover, in accordance with the evident force of the allegory already set forth, what this example of Lot’s wife teaches had long ago occurred from apostolic times onward, and there is no doubt that it still occurs today in its moral sense. For a portion of those who had departed from the sacrileges of the Sodomites—that is, from the bloody ceremonies of the Jews—looked back, seeking to impose circumcision again in addition to Christ’s Gospel and asserting that Jewish observances were necessary together with faith in Christ [Col. 0413B].

The Apostle, condemning those who looked back in this way, says: “If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the Law, a Pharisee; according to zeal, persecuting the Church of God; according to the righteousness which is in the Law, living without reproach. But whatever things were gain to me, these I counted loss for Christ. Indeed, I count all things to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Jesus Christ my Lord, for whose sake I have made all things loss and count them as dung.” And shortly afterward: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have attained; but one thing: forgetting those things which are behind and stretching myself toward those things which are before, I press toward the mark, toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Phil. 3) [Col. 0413C].

In the moral sense also, whenever a fool returns to his folly, as a dog to its vomit (2 Pet. 2), whatever his rank or profession, he is changed, after the example of Lot’s wife, into a pillar of salt. That is, he becomes senseless and useless to himself, yet benefits others, as those who consider his end are corrected—just as the palate of animals licking a rock of salt is made savoury and their appetite for eating is restored. Therefore, after the Lord said in the Gospel, “In that hour, whoever is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, let him not come down to take them away” (Matt. 24), and, “Likewise, whoever is in the field, let him not turn back,” he immediately added: “Remember Lot’s wife. Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, and whoever loses it will make it live” (Luke 17), and so forth [Col. 0413D].

Thus she was fittingly changed not into just any pillar, but into a pillar of salt, whose remembrance promotes wisdom according to Christ’s Gospel.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the daughters of Lot, who slept with their father.

Ascended Lot from Zoar and dwelt on the mountain, with his two daughters also with him. For he had feared to remain in Zoar, and he dwelt in a cave, he and his two daughters. And the elder said to the younger: “Our father is old,” etc. The question arises why, when at first in his flight he preferred Zoar to the mountain, and desired to be delivered there as into his dwelling-place, he now moves again from Zoar to the mountain. We shall answer that the Hebrews’ conjecture concerning Zoar is true: that it was overthrown by a frequent earthquake, was first called Bela, and afterwards Salissa; and that Lot was afraid, saying: “If, while the other cities were still standing, this one has been overthrown, how much less will it now be able to escape the common ruin?” And his daughters also gave this occasion of unbelief as the beginning of their intercourse. For one who had seen the other cities overthrown, while this one remained standing, and had himself been rescued by God’s aid, certainly ought not to have doubted about what he had heard was granted to him.

Moreover, that which is said in excuse of the daughters—that they thought the human race had perished and therefore lay with their father—does not excuse the father. Finally, the Hebrews add to the following words, “And he did not know when she lay down with him, nor when she rose from him,” the observation that this is almost incredible, because the nature of things does not admit that anyone should have intercourse unknowingly. Yet it should be noted that it is not said, “He did not perceive when they had intercourse,” but that he did not know when the daughter lay down, nor when she rose.

But let us now pursue the mystical meaning. “Lot ascended from Zoar and dwelt on the mountain,” etc. Thus indeed, very often, those who through scant faith do not dare to seize the height of a holier calling, as was said above, and confess themselves weak and in a sense unworthy for it, each saying those words of the Gospel, “I beg you, hold me excused” (Luke 14), are strong—indeed rash—in seizing an undertaking of holy honour. Unbidden, they do not fear to preside over others in the honour of government, though, when commanded or admonished, they distrusted their ability to rule themselves in holiness of life.

From this unbelief it consequently happens to them that they defile themselves by nefarious incest with their daughters. For what are the little populations subject to them but certain daughters, whom they ought to have betrothed, not to themselves, but in order to present a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ? (III Cor. II.) But they, seeking not Christ’s glory but their own, drink their daughters’ wine while receiving from them the praises they love. Drunk with turbulent overthrow, they adulterate the word of God; asleep, they preach every evil incestuously and no good chastely.

From this were born Moab, interpreted “from the father”—that is, with the devil understood—and Ammon, that is, “the son of my people,” or “a turbulent people”: namely, all the sects of heresies. Concerning them the Lord speaks in Deuteronomy: “The Ammonites and Moabites, even after the tenth [the phrase ‘of the said little populace’ is textually corrupt]” (Deut. 23).

“Our father is old, and no man remains in the land who can come in to us according to the custom of the whole earth.” This is to say: “Our apostle or bishop is great and wise, and besides him there is none among all who call themselves apostles, ministers of Christ, or stewards of God’s mysteries, who can worthily preach the word of God.” Any such heresiarch, because he is an apostle beyond measure, while he delights in such favour, is certainly intoxicated by the evil wine of his daughters; and thus he begets sons who may never enter the Church of the Lord. And of one drunk in this manner you may rightly say that he did not know when the daughter lay down with him or when she rose. For the fool does not know that his spiritual work is adultery and nefarious intercourse. “Priest and prophet,” says Isaiah, “have not known because of drunkenness; they have been swallowed up by wine” (Isa. 28).

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Abraham’s sojourn in Gerar.

(CHAPTER 20.)—“Abraham departed from there into the southern land; he dwelt between Kadesh and Shur, and sojourned in Gerar. And he said of Sarah his wife, ‘She is my sister.’ Therefore Abimelech king of Gerar sent and took her.”

When Isaac was about to be born—when he had been promised and foretold by name—Abraham sojourns for a second time, so that Sarah is taken from him, while he says, “She is my sister,” and does not dare to confess that she is his wife. What does this prefigure except that, when Christ’s birth was near, after he had already been foretold by name through the prophets—for example, when they said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7)—the seed of Abraham would again sojourn in a land not its own, namely in the Babylonian captivity?

For after their Egyptian sojourn they were subjected to slavery for seventy years, and Sarah was almost taken by a foreigner. For apart from Daniel and his three companions, no one there dared to confess the nuptial covenant of God’s holy law, while Nebuchadnezzar raged and the furnace was kindled.

Gerar, moreover, was the metropolitan city of Palestine, on the southern boundary of the Canaanites, between Kadesh and Shur—that is, between the two wildernesses mentioned above. Gerar is interpreted “sojourning” or “approaching strangers”; Abimelech, “my father is king,” or “my father’s kingdom.” By these names strangers—that is, Gentiles—are rightly understood as future inhabitants of God’s kingdom, of whom the seed of Abraham, namely Christ, would say: “My Father’s kingdom,” or “My Father is king”—understand, “is their king.”

## CHAPTER XV. How God rebuked Abimelech differently from Pharaoh on account of Sarah, Abraham’s wife.

“But God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: ‘Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.’ But Abimelech had not touched her. And he said: ‘Lord, will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation?’” etc.

God rebuked this man differently from Pharaoh on Abraham’s account. He scourged Pharaoh and his household with very great plagues. But from this man he accepted the excuse when he said: “Did he not himself say to me, ‘She is my sister’? And she said to me, ‘He is my brother.’ I did this in the simplicity of my heart and the cleanness of my hands.” And God says: “I also know that you did it through ignorance, and therefore I did not permit you to touch her.”

Thus, in order that Abraham’s seed might be delivered from Egyptian slavery, God smote Egypt with very great plagues. But in order that it might be released from Babylonian captivity, Cyrus king of Persia was not smitten with plagues but anticipated by divine prompting, so as to send forth a proclamation throughout his whole kingdom, even speaking by an edict: “Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is among you of all his people? May his God be with him” (2 Chron. 36). “Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the Lord God of Israel; he is the God who is in Jerusalem” (1 Ezra 1).

“I thought with myself, saying: ‘Perhaps there is no fear of the Lord in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife. Yet she is indeed also my sister, the daughter of my father,’” etc. Of this fear of his, by which he also feared Pharaoh, enough has already been said above. What was remarkable in Sarah was that, although she was an old woman at that age, she still seemed desirable. She signifies the beauty of divine religion, which even at the time when the Jews were led captive seemed worthy of imitation amid the errors of the Gentiles; the surrounding nations emulated it, although not chastely.

Hence it is written in the First Book of Maccabees: “And they fasted on that day, put on sackcloth, placed ashes upon their heads, and rent their garments; and they spread out the book of the law, concerning which the Gentiles had searched for the likeness of their idols” (1 Macc. 3)—namely, so that they might offer to their idols a rite or order of sacrifices after the manner of the divine law.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the words, “Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother,” etc.; and what it signifies that, when Abraham prayed, Abimelech’s household was healed.

But he said to Sarah: “Behold, I have given a thousand pieces of silver to your brother. This shall be for you a covering of the eyes before all who are with you. Wherever you go, remember that you have been discovered.”

He played upon the designation, saying, “I have given [them] to your brother.” Then, mocking the shame of one exposed, he said: “This shall be for you a covering of the eyes before all who are with you,” as though he meant: “Since he really is your brother, the son of your father and not of your mother, you will be able truthfully to say to all, ‘He is my brother’; and by that name it will be veiled and concealed that he is your husband and that you are his wife.”

After saying this jokingly, he immediately added in earnest: “Wherever you go, remember that you have vainly covered your eyes with such a name, saying that he is your brother. For you could not and will not conceal that you are his wife, since God reproves kings for your sake, as he reproved me, and has removed the covering of your eyes by saying, ‘She has a husband.’”

“But when Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his maidservant, and they bore children. For the Lord had closed every womb in Abimelech’s household because of Sarah Abraham’s wife.”

The present mystery also concerns this: that when Abraham prayed, the sterility of the foreign household was healed. For it was to come to pass that, when the seed of Abraham—namely Christ—prayed or interceded, he who, as the Apostle says, also intercedes for us (Rom. 2 [as printed]), the sterility of the Gentiles would be healed, and that saying from the song of the prophetess Hannah would be fulfilled: “Until the barren woman bore many, and she who had many children became weak” (1 Sam. 2).

For Abimelech’s household—that is, the household of the Gentiles, whose Father is God today—is the Church. In that house one is the wife, namely whatever soul is united to the Lord God; another is the maidservant, who serves faith or the word of doctrine through fear or for a temporal cause. Yet all bear children: whether they are united to God through love or serve the word of faith through fear or a temporal cause, because, in whatever manner Christ is proclaimed, the hearers become children of God by believing.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Isaac’s birth.

(CHAPTER 21.) “And the Lord visited Sarah as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken. And she conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time that God had foretold to her. And Abraham called the name of his son, whom Sarah bore to him, Isaac; and he circumcised him on the eighth day, as God had commanded him, when he was a hundred years old.” For Isaac was born when his father was of this age.

This was done for the praise and glory of God’s truth: that Sarah conceived and bore a son—the reward of faith, the joy of his parents, the splendour of the household, the glory of the family, the hope of posterity. Therefore it was rightly prefaced: “The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised, and fulfilled what he had spoken.” For God’s visitation is the abundant bestowal of his grace.

But, to pursue the mystery begun: God then visited Sarah, that noble princess who is above, who is truly free and the mother of us all (Gal. 4), when the true Isaac, our true joy, namely Christ the Son of God, was born from her according to the flesh. Then, I say, the Lord God visited her as he had promised and fulfilled what he had spoken.

Thus Zechariah says in the Gospel canticle: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people, as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from the beginning” (Luke 1). And the Apostle says: “For however many promises of God there are, in him is the ‘Yes’; therefore through him is also the ‘Amen’ to God for our glory” (2 Cor. 1).

And that Sarah bore him at the time God had foretold. For God foretold it through one person, saying: “The sceptre shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler’s staff from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the Gentiles” (Gen. 49). And so it happened. For the sceptre had scarcely been taken from Judah, Herod the foreigner reigning, when he was born of the Virgin Mary.

“And Abraham called his son Isaac.” Concerning the name Isaac, interpreted “laughter,” its suitability to Christ, the eighth day of circumcision, and Abraham’s hundredth year, enough has already been said above.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Sarah’s words, “God has made laughter for me”; and how Christ is the laughter and joy of the heavenly mother Jerusalem and of God the Father.

Sarah said: “God has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me.” And again she said: “Who would have believed, on hearing it, that Sarah would nurse a son for Abraham, whom she bore to him in his old age?”

The statements “Whoever hears will laugh with me” and “Who would have believed, on hearing it, [that Sarah would nurse a son for Abraham]?” seem contrary or mutually inconsistent. For whoever laughs on hearing, surely believes what is heard and rejoices in it; conversely, whoever does not believe on hearing certainly does not laugh with, or rejoice with, what is heard. Yet she says both: “Whoever hears will laugh with me,” and “Who would have believed, on hearing it, [that Sarah would nurse a son for Abraham]?”

Therefore these words must be understood as prophetic concerning the birth of the future Isaac, of whom this Isaac is a figure; and they correspond to Simeon’s prophecy when he held him in his arms: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and the rising again of many in Israel” (Luke 2). For the one who hears and does not believe is set for falling, according to the prophet’s words: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53). But the one who hears and laughs with her is set for rising.

Therefore, just as the saying is divided—“Sarah said, ‘God has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me’; and again she said, ‘Who would have believed, on hearing it, [that Sarah would nurse a son for Abraham]?’”—so it must be understood of the division between good and evil, faithful and unbelieving persons.

Let that woman, then, who, as has been said, is understood through Sarah—the free Jerusalem above, the mother of us all (Gal. 4)—say, when the true Isaac has been born to her: “God has made laughter for me; whoever hears will laugh with me.” For behold, the whole world truly laughs with her, because her only Son has brought great and true joy to the whole world.

Let the maidservant, then, who is “from Mount Sinai, bearing children into slavery” (ibid.), weep—let her, I say, and her daughter weep—because she hates this laughter of the Father and of the free mother, since she will no longer be an heir. O loving desire, devout hope, and long sighs of the holy people, bent down and panting as if already advanced in long old age: how has it been raised into joy and enlarged into laughter? How has every tear been wiped from its eyes? How did that mother Jerusalem laugh when such a son was born to her?

For Isaiah testifies how great an occasion for laughter she then possessed, when he says: “Shake yourself from the dust; sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds from your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says God: Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who spoke—behold, I am present” (Isa. 52).

## CHAPTER XIX. On Isaac’s weaning and the great feast on the day of his weaning.

“The child therefore grew and was weaned; and Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.” What need was there for this to be done or written unless a sure beauty of mystery underlies it, able to invite little children still nursing to solid food? For there is a certain milk and a certain infancy which the true Isaac, namely Christ, quickly outgrew; and every worthy imitator of Christ ought likewise to surpass it.

Those who are too slow in this are rebuked by the Apostle, who says: “For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you need to be taught again what are the elements of the beginning of God’s words; and you have become such as need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unacquainted with the word of righteousness, for he is a little child. But solid food belongs to the perfect, those who through use have their senses trained to discern good and evil.”

The boy Jesus spiritually outgrew this infancy, as Luke testifies when he says: “And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age before God and men” (Luke 2). This does not mean that he previously knew anything less, since he is the very wisdom of God, but that, gradually setting aside discourse concerning the fleshly ceremonies of the law, he led little children toward perfection.

There is indeed a great feast when, leaving milkly—that is, infantile—rites, such as the sacrifices of brute animals, he brings his own to the true and sole sacrifice of his body and blood. For this is the great feast of which the prophet says: “The Lord of hosts will make for all peoples upon this mountain a feast of rich things, a feast of vintage wine, rich things full of marrow, wine refined” (Isa. 25). And because sins are loosed by this feast, he immediately continues: “And he shall cast down upon this mountain the face of the bond binding all peoples, and the web which he has woven over all nations; and he shall cast down death for ever” (ibid.). And because this host of the feast is the true Isaac, that is, true laughter and true joy, he adds shortly afterwards: “This is the Lord; we have waited for him; we shall exult and rejoice in his salvation” (ibid.).

Therefore, if you follow the plain letter, these things are slight; but if you perceive the inward spirit, it was highly relevant to relate that the child grew and was weaned, and that Abraham made a great feast on the day of his weaning.

## CHAPTER XX. On Ishmael’s playing with Isaac, and the words, “Cast out the maidservant,” etc.

“When Sarah saw the son of Hagar the Egyptian playing with her son Isaac, she said to Abraham: ‘Cast out this maidservant and her son; for the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with my son Isaac.’”

The Apostle’s exposition in writing to the Galatians has made this passage well known and famous: “It is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the maidservant and one by the free woman. But he who was of the maidservant was born according to the flesh; while he who was of the free woman was born through promise” (Gal. 4). And shortly afterwards: “But as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now. But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the maidservant and her son,’” etc. (ibid.).

Certainly, according to the letter, what the Hebrews thought concerning this playing has already been related above: either that Ishmael fashioned idols from mud with his hands, or that, being the older, he jocularly claimed the birthright for himself. But according to the mystical sense already stated, the Apostle calls this playing persecution. In its likeness, at that time fleshly Jews and fleshly circumcision were attacking spiritual Judaism and spiritual circumcision.

Therefore, when Isaac was weaned, Sarah could not bear Ishmael playing with him. That is, when the dispensation of his ministry for humankind had passed, in which the Son of God, made under the law, had served, and when the fleshly people, remaining in the oldness of the letter, mocked the new and spiritual sons—namely Christ’s disciples—the holy Spirit of the new grace could not bear it, and said: “Cast out this maidservant and her son. For the son of the maidservant shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.”

How the maidservant and her son are cast out, the same Apostle immediately explained: “Behold,” he says, “I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5), etc.

Furthermore, the maidservant and her son are cast out so that he may not play with Isaac when that Jerusalem which was in slavery with her children, and that most famous temple of God, are destroyed; when that people is led captive among all nations; and when the entire order of servile ceremonies is thus scattered. This happened under Vespasian and Titus, Roman rulers, so that the old Synagogue might no longer more violently insult the Church of the new law while continuing in its former standing—though, even now, thus cast out, it dares proudly to claim the birthright for itself or its son.

That son of the maidservant suffered this casting out because he played: because he mocked, scourged, crucified, and killed Christ, the son of the free woman, the king and prince of all liberty; and afterwards persecuted his household servants, his freed people, in a wickedly stubborn game.

## CHAPTER XXI. Again on the same matter, and what is signified by the casting out of the maidservant’s son.

“Abraham took this harshly because of his son. But the Lord said to him: ‘Let it not seem harsh to you concerning your son and your maidservant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac your seed shall be called. But I will also make the son of the maidservant into a great nation, because he is your seed.’”

By Abraham, as has often been said, we understand the holy Fathers—heirs of Abraham not only according to the flesh but also according to faith—such as Peter, Paul, and the other apostles were at the time when this maidservant and her son were cast out. For they truly took harshly the command: “Cast out this maidservant and her son.”

For one of them, the apostle Paul, says: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, whose are the adoption as sons, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9).

Nevertheless, however Abraham takes it here, this maidservant with her son had to be cast out. For the Lord said to him: “Let it not seem harsh to you concerning your son and your maidservant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, because in Isaac your seed shall be called.”

Is it legitimate according to the letter that a man should obey his wife’s voice, rather than that the wife should obey her husband’s? Therefore Abraham must rather, according to the mystical meaning, listen to the voice of Sarah in all that she says—that is, the chorus of preachers or apostles must listen to the voice of holy and prophetic Scripture in all that it says concerning Jews and Gentiles.

And this it does when, wearied by the obstinacy of that player, namely the Jewish people, it says: “To you it was necessary that the word of God should first be preached; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). “For thus the Lord commanded us: ‘I have set you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the end of the earth’” (Isa. 49).

Therefore, at Sarah’s voice, the maidservant and her son are cast out when, by the authority of Scripture, the fleshly people is left outside because of its unbelief. “For in Isaac,” he says, “your seed shall be called.” Even if there are many sons of concubines or of the flesh, in Isaac—who was born not according to the flesh but through promise—your seed shall be called. For from him will be born the one who shall be called your seed, namely that seed in whom, as I promised you, all nations shall be blessed and shall be called your seed.

For all are Isaac who are born to you not according to the flesh but according to faith, just as Isaac was born not according to the flesh but through promise. The Apostle expounds it thus, when, after saying, “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor because they are Abraham’s seed are they all children,” he immediately introduces this testimony: “But in Isaac your seed shall be called.” Explaining this very point, he adds: “That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are called children of God, but the children of the promise are reckoned as seed” (Rom. 9).

“And I will make the son of the maidservant into a great nation, because he is your seed.” “He is your seed,” he says; nevertheless he did not say, “In him your seed shall be called,” for it is not such seed as is called that which is known by name before God. Yet this son of the maidservant also, who has been cast out in the manner described, will become a great nation, worthy to be called and named Abraham’s seed: namely, “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11).

## CHAPTER XXII. What is mystically signified by the words, “Abraham took bread and a skin of water and placed them on her shoulder.”

“So Abraham rose early in the morning, and taking bread and a skin of water placed them on her shoulder; he gave her the boy and dismissed her. When she had gone away, she wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba. And when the water in the skin was used up, she cast the boy under one tree that was there and went away. She sat opposite, at a distance, as far as a bow can shoot. For she said, ‘I shall not see the boy die’; and sitting opposite, she raised her voice and wept. But God heard the voice of the boy.”

After the son of the maidservant had played with the son of the free woman, Abraham rose in the morning and sent out the maidservant and her son. For after, as said above, the servile wickedness of the Jewish people had mocked Christ, after the morning resurrection had been celebrated, the Synagogue was cast out, together with its pupils, from the house and inheritance of father Abraham.

But how did he send out that maidservant? “He placed bread and a skin of water on her shoulder, gave her the boy, and dismissed her.” Was that rich conqueror of kings, master of three hundred and eighteen household servants, so miserly that he gave nothing besides bread and a skin of water to the son whom he sadly cast out? Did he not even lend him a single little donkey, but put these things on the mother’s shoulder?

Or did the boy himself—indeed the young man, whom it is beyond doubt was already, or had been, no less than eighteen years old—also sit upon his mother’s neck along with the skin of water? For it is said: “When the water in the skin was used up, she cast the boy under one tree and went away.”

Therefore, in things which seem so ridiculous, the letter serves the spirit and under the lowly texture of its language foretells things to come which the whole world now sees present. For the cast-out maidservant carries on her shoulder not just any bread but barley bread, and a skin not of wine but of water, bowed under the burden, because the Synagogue, having lost the inheritance of father Abraham, carries only the literal sense of the law and pants beneath an unbearable burden.

Peter the Apostle also testifies that the burden of the killing letter is unbearable, saying: “Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15). Therefore he rightly placed on her shoulder a skin not of wine but of water, and gave her neither even a little donkey nor any other conveyance, but the boy, whom, when the water failed, she would cast down as dying beneath a tree while wandering through the wilderness. For it was to come to pass that the cast-out and God-forsaken Synagogue would proceed, more burdened than refreshed by the fleshly knowledge of the law; and would cast down her children, dying in their sin, beneath the tree of the cross, while the sentence persisted over them which that most cruel mother pronounced: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

## CHAPTER XXIII. Again: what is signified by the angel of the Lord calling Hagar, and by God opening her eyes so that she saw a well of water.

“And the angel of the Lord called to Hagar from heaven, saying: ‘What are you doing, Hagar? Do not fear. For God has heard the voice of the boy from the place where he is. Rise, take the boy, and hold his hand, for I will make him into a great nation.’ And God opened her eyes. Seeing a well of water, she went and filled the skin and gave the boy a drink; and God was with him.”

This will finally happen when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in (Rom. 11). Then the angel of great counsel will call the Synagogue, saying: “What are you doing, Hagar?”—that is, “adverse” or “turned away”—“do not fear,” etc. He will open her eyes, removing the veil that is now laid over their heart (2 Cor. 3); and with true understanding she will see the well of Scriptures, the well of living waters, and will give her son drink—that is, she will offer the true understanding of the Scriptures to her hearers.

It should be noted that it is not said, “God heard Hagar’s voice,” although she herself had raised her voice and wept, but “God heard the boy’s voice.” For the mother herself was mourning not her own death but her son’s. Therefore God spared him for whom the weeping had occurred.

From the words, “Rise, take the boy, and hold his hand,” it is clear that he was not a burden to his mother but her companion. That he is held by the parent’s hand shows her anxious affection. Yet above Scripture wisely says, “She cast down the boy,” as though he had sat upon his mother’s neck, because, for the present, until the angel of the Lord calls the Synagogue as foretold, the unlearned people are a burden to the Synagogue of the Pharisees and their scribes; and for the destruction of those whom it supposes itself to instruct, it is weighed down by a greater condemnation.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the covenant made between Abraham and Abimelech, and what it mystically signifies.

“At that time Abimelech and Phicol, commander of his army, said to Abraham: ‘God is with you in all that you do. Swear therefore by God that you will not harm me, my descendants, or my stock. But according to the mercy which I have shown you, you shall show it to me and to the land in which you have sojourned as a stranger.’”

First, it should be noted from both the preceding and present passage that Isaac was not born in the land of promise but in Gerar, the metropolitan city of the Palestinians, where the town of Beersheba was also situated. This too is not without mystery. For Christ was born under the Roman Empire, and God’s people were subject to foreign rulers and served by paying tribute.

Thus he was born in Gerar, which was the metropolitan city of the Palestinians—that is, of “the falling”—and signifies Rome, which was to become the mother and queen of those who perish. Nor should it trouble us that, having said above that Abraham’s sojourn in Gerar was a sign of the Babylonian captivity, we now say that Isaac’s birth in Gerar signified that Christ would be born under the service of the Roman Empire. For Rome was a second Babylon.

Hence Peter says in his Epistle: “The Church which is gathered in Babylon greets you” (1 Pet. 5), figuratively designating Rome. For it should be known that when that Babylon was overthrown by the Medes and Persians, Rome was founded or born; and from that captivity until Christ, the Jews’ slavery was almost one and unbroken. For from the time when they were taken captive there with their king, they never possessed a king lawfully, nor were they free from the yoke of the Gentiles. Rather, as the condition of the leaders and priests contending with one another weakened and gradually declined, they finally received the foreign king Herod, under whom Christ was born.

Therefore Abraham, from the time Isaac was promised to him by name until Isaac’s birth or weaning, sojourned under Abimelech in Gerar, because from the times of the prophets through whom Christ was foretold until his birth, the temporal kingdom of the Jews was almost continually worn down beneath the yoke of the Gentiles.

But after Isaac was weaned and the son of the maidservant was cast out, Abimelech and Phicol, commander of his army, come to Abraham, confessing that God is with him in all that he does and asking him: “Swear by the Lord that you will not harm us,” etc. For after the Synagogue, to which the word of God had first to be spoken, rejected it and judged itself unworthy of eternal life, the apostles turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13); indeed, some of the Gentiles themselves voluntarily came to them, in a manner saying: “God is with you in all that you do. Swear to us by God that you will not harm us, our descendants, or our stock.”

For when the Gentiles offered the confession of faith to the holy apostles and asked those Fathers for counsel as to how they might receive forgiveness of sins in the present and escape the final judgment in the future, they said things similar and nearly identical to these.

By Abimelech, whose name means “my father is king” or “my father’s kingdom,” is understood the multitude of the Gentiles whom Christ made the kingdom of his Father. But by Phicol, commander of the army, whose name means “mouth of all,” are understood the leaders of military forces—that is, commanders, kings, emperors, and other authorities—who also embraced Christ’s faith and, by their licence or authority, opened more widely the mouth of all to confess the true God.

## CHAPTER XXV. What the well which Abimelech’s servants had forcibly taken signifies mystically.

Abraham said, “I will swear.” And he rebuked Abimelech concerning the well of water which his servants had seized by force. Abimelech answered, “I did not know who had done this thing; but neither did you inform me, nor had I heard of it before today.” Before swearing, he settles the whole matter of their dispute, lest any spark of former disturbance remain; and, concerning a well of water, so great a man rebukes the king, because it was certainly no insignificant matter, especially in those regions, where there is naturally a great scarcity of living water. Mystically, moreover, the well of water which Abimelech’s servants had seized by force is Holy Scripture, [Col. 0424C] which the philosophers of the Gentiles had violently seized—that is, had plundered by reading it with an incorrect understanding, without a preacher and without the Spirit of God. For example, Plato, in the *Timaeus*, having stolen the creation of the world from the beginning of this book of Genesis, deceitfully and perversely substituted one thing for another.

Accordingly Abraham rebuked Abimelech over such a well, for example when the Apostle Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I see that in every respect you are exceedingly religious. For as I passed by and observed your images, I found an altar bearing the inscription: ‘To an Unknown God.’ What therefore you worship in ignorance, this I proclaim to you” (Acts 17). And shortly afterward: “For in him we live and move and are, as certain also of your poets have said: ‘For we too are his offspring’” (ibid.). “I did not know,” he says, [Col. 0424D] “who had done this thing; but neither did you inform me, nor had I heard of it before today.” This is a complete and sufficient defence, perfect in three respects. For in every inquiry concerning an act, it is insufficient for purity of conscience merely not to know by whom it was done, if one knows whether it was done or what was done—especially if one appears to have consented by silence. Thus he reasonably clears himself of every element of guilt when, finally, he says: “Nor had I heard of it before today.” The aforementioned Athenians and the other nations could say the same: “We do not know this matter; no patriarch or prophet informed us of it; and we had not heard of it before today.” For they likewise said to the Apostle: “You bring strange things to our ears” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXVI. What the seven ewe-lambs which Abraham caused to stand apart mystically signify

Abraham therefore took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech, and the two made a covenant. Abraham set apart seven ewe-lambs of the flock. Abimelech said to him, “What do these seven ewe-lambs mean, which you have caused to stand apart?” He answered, “You shall receive seven ewe-lambs from my hand, that they may serve as a testimony for me that I dug this well.”

The sheep which Abraham gave Abimelech bear lambs and nourish their tender young with sweet milk; the oxen, meanwhile, now thresh upon the floor, now labour by turning the earth, and bring forth bread to strengthen the human heart. For we know that the apostolic Fathers appointed greater and lesser teachers and rulers for individual peoples or cities, [Col. 0425B] so that, like sheep, they might instruct immature hearers with milk—that is, with elementary teaching—and, like oxen, of whom, as the Apostle testifies, the Law says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (1 Cor. 9; Deut. 25), they might feed with solid bread those whose faculties, trained by practice, are borne toward perfection.

In this manner Abraham and Abimelech—that is, the Fathers who were from the Jews and the Gentiles—made a covenant and were joined into one household through Christ, the cornerstone, who makes both one, “that he might create in himself the two into one new human being, making peace, and might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, destroying enmity in himself” (Eph. 2). [Col. 0425C] The seven ewe-lambs, however, which are set apart at the making of the covenant, signify the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, whose gifts are distributed to us in baptism, by which we are joined in covenant with Christ. These ewe-lambs are set apart because the gifts of the Holy Spirit are certainly not within human power. For we all equally administer baptism in water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit through the office of the Church; but we neither give nor receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit in such kinds or measures as we wish. Rather, “the same Holy Spirit works all things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Whatever this sevenfold Spirit speaks or works through us is true testimony that Father Abraham dug this well: that is, that according to his seed, which is Christ, he established and fulfilled the whole truth of the Scriptures. Well, therefore, was it said: “That they may serve as a testimony for me that I dug this well.” Therefore that place was called Beersheba, because there both men swore. And they entered into a covenant concerning the well of the oath. Then Abimelech arose, with Phicol, the commander of his army, and they returned to the land of the Philistines. Where “well of the oath” is read here, the Hebrew has *Bersabee* [Beersheba]. There are two reasons why it was so named: either because Abimelech received seven ewe-lambs from Abraham’s hand—for seven is called *sabee*—or because he swore there, since an oath is likewise called *sabee*. If we read this name above before this occasion, we should know that it was used by anticipation, as also Bethel and Gilgal, which were certainly called otherwise until the time when they received those names. [Col. 0426A]

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Abraham’s planting a grove at Beersheba pertains to the mystery

But Abraham planted a grove at Beersheba, and there invoked the name of the Lord, the eternal God. And he was a resident in the land of the Philistines for many days. This too certainly pertains to the mystery. For Abraham’s faith, transferred from the Jews and planted among the Gentiles, produced a great grove from diverse persons, as from diverse trees, in order that there the name of the Lord, the eternal God, might be invoked. God himself, promising such a grove to the abandoned Gentile world through the prophet Isaiah, distinguished the different merits of different persons in this way: “I will give in the wilderness the cedar, the thorn, the myrtle, and the olive tree. I will set in the desert the fir tree, the elm, and the box tree together, that they may see, know, and consider together” (Isa. 41). [Col. 0426B]

In such a grove the name of the eternal Lord is invoked, according to Abraham’s faith, even to this day. Thus, having left the land of his Jewish people, Abraham is a resident in the land of the Philistines, a name interpreted as “the drinking of those who fall”—such as we formerly were. But now we are the Lord’s planted things, firmly established and beautiful, according to the Apostle, who, after touching on our former vices, says: “And such indeed you were; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus, in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. [Col. 0426C] Concerning the trial by which God tested Abraham, saying, “Take your son,” etc.

(Chapter 22.) After these things had happened, God tested Abraham and said to him, “Abraham, Abraham.” He answered, “Here I am.” And he said to him, “Take your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Vision; there offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you.”

God, the examiner of hearts, did not wish the treasure of faith and of the fear of the Lord, which this father of many nations stored up here as a good example for us his children, to remain concealed. Rather, though it had already been sufficiently tested by long wandering and prolonged expectation of his offspring, he ensured that it should blaze forth with the utmost strength in one further fire of trial. For from this most severe trial [Col. 0426D] Abraham’s faith shines with greatest splendour, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, and he who had received the promises was offering his only son, to whom it had been said: ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called,’ considering that God was able even to raise him from the dead” (Heb. 11).

Likewise, “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18). This fear, which descends from love, shone forth more clearly from this event, as the Lord himself testifies when he later says: “Now I know that you fear God, and have not spared your only son for my sake.” Rightly, therefore, did this writer preface the account by saying: “God tested Abraham”—not, of course, that he himself might know, since no thought is hidden from him, but lest we, his future children, remain ignorant what kind of father he was, [Col. 0427A] whose faith is set before us for imitation. Thus, when a merchant seeks costly things, a diligent seller tests whatever he pleases, not so that he himself may know what he sells, but so that the buyer may not hesitate to give all that he has and buy them.

These are the words of the one testing him: “Take your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Vision; there offer him as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I shall show you.” Here he calls him his only son, adds “whom you love,” and expressly names Isaac, so that the father’s present affections might not be too slight at the very crisis of so great a trial. Where it now says “in the land of Vision,” the Hebrew has *Moriah*. The Hebrews say that this is the mountain on which the Temple was later built, on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite, as it is written in Chronicles: “They began to build the Temple on the second day of the month, on Mount Moriah” (2 Chron. 3). [Col. 0427B] It is therefore interpreted “illuminating” and “shining,” because there is *Dabir*, that is, the oracle of God, and the Law, and the Holy Spirit, who teaches people the truth and inspires the prophets.

Yet what need is there to seek from the Hebrews a doubtful etymology of this name—that is, of the land or mountain of Vision—or to investigate a merely conjectural one, when the present passage of Scripture plainly establishes that Abraham called that place by this same name because of the presence or regard of God’s grace? For because he inwardly felt that the eyes of God who was testing him were opened and fixed upon him, while the angel of the Lord cried out, as he had seized the sword, “Abraham, do not stretch out [Col. 0427C] your hand over the boy,” and, “Now I know that you fear God,” it is then added: “And he called the name of that place, ‘The Lord sees’; whence it is said to this day, ‘On the mountain the Lord will see.’” It is clear, therefore, that Abraham, rejoicing and exulting beyond expression for the reason already stated, marked the place of his joy by the name Vision, since there he could truly confess that he had been seen by the Lord. Accordingly, as with many other things, this too was said shortly beforehand by anticipation: “Go into the land,” with the addition of this name, Vision.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Again on the same matter, and that the mountain on which the Temple was later founded was that to which Isaac was led for sacrifice

Accordingly Abraham, rising in the night, saddled his ass, taking with him two young servants and Isaac his son. Having cut wood for the burnt offering, he went to the place which God had commanded him. On the third day, raising his eyes, he saw the place from afar; and he said to his servants: “Wait here with the ass. The boy and I will go on there; after we have worshipped, we shall return to you.”

Because he had set the fear of the Lord before his eyes, as soon as he heard the command of the One commanding, he knew no delay in carrying it out, with obedience close at hand. He rose in the night and saddled his ass. The ass does not, however, reveal either the rusticity or lowly poverty of so great a man, whom we know to have been great and renowned, and wealthy—for above we read that he was conqueror of so many kings. [Col. 0428A] Rather, the single name “ass” suitably signifies every kind of subjection, not only because of the Latin etymology of the word—for *asinus* is said to come from *assidere*, “to sit beside”—but also because of the nature of the animal itself, which is especially servile and burden-bearing.

“On the third day,” it says, “he saw the place from afar.” It should be noted that the journey from Gerar to Mount Moriah—that is, the site of the Temple—is three days’ travel, and accordingly he is said to have arrived there on the third day. Some therefore wrongly say that Abraham was then living by the oak of Mamre, that is, at Hebron, since from there to Mount Moriah there is scarcely a full day’s journey. Nor did he say falsely but faithfully: “Wait here with the ass. After we have worshipped, we shall return to you,” believing, namely, that God could even raise to himself from the dead that boy whom he had sacrificed.

Since the matters that follow are clear in their literal sense, let us now, if you would understand to the marrow, look more deeply at what God chiefly intended in the action of this celebrated trial, and at what was prefigured both in Abraham, whose command it was, and in Isaac, whose obedience it was. For it is not enough to say that God tested him thus in order to know—that is, to make us know—how great Abraham’s fear of the Lord was, especially since immediately after saying, “Now I know that you fear God,” he at once added, “By myself I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son: I will bless you,” etc. [Col. 0428B]

## CHAPTER XXX. [Col. 0428C] Again, why God tested Abraham; and that it was not without justice that “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son,” because a human being so loved God that he gave his only son

Did God, against his will, encounter that human fortitude, so that he was compelled to interpose an oath, and reason forced God to swear to man by himself because he knew no one greater than himself? “For men,” says the Apostle, “swear by one greater than themselves, and an oath is for them the end of every dispute for confirmation. But when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself” (Heb. 6). Could God, I ask, have been driven unwillingly or imprudently [Col. 0428D] to an oath of this kind? Certainly not. Rather, by testing him willingly and providently, God prepared for man a great victory in a grave cause—a victory for which holy Job, sighing, spoke to the same God: “Hear my desire, O Almighty One, and grant me an adversary who may set forth equity against me, and let my judgment attain victory” (Job 31).

For God had indeed purposed, through abundant mercy, to bring to victory through Christ the case of the human race prejudged in Adam; but to show mercy without judgment or justice is incompatible with God. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100). Again: “Mercy and truth shall go before your face” (Ps. 88). And elsewhere: “God is merciful and just” (Ps. [Col. 0429A] 114). And there are many similar passages testifying that mercy and judgment, or truth and gentleness, are not separated in God.

Therefore, so that human salvation might rest wholly upon mercy, yet mercy and truth might meet each other, the merciful God sought in humanity a ground upon which he himself might justly be held as debtor. He sought, I say, that a human being should offer to him his only son in sacrifice, so that in just reciprocity he ought to give his own Son to humanity. Thus, when that same Son says in his Gospel: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son” (John 3), this is not an indulgent love or a mercy devoid of justice. For a human being likewise so feared God that he did not hesitate to offer him his only son.

Accordingly, in this deed above all, the boy Isaac is rightly believed to bear the figure of the only-begotten Son of God. The exalted Father had him as his only son; and in him he became the father of many nations. Though he loved him, he did not spare him for God’s sake; he offered him in a wondrous manner, and yet did not touch him with the sword. But seeing a ram caught by its horns among the briars, he took it and offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son. Thus God the Father “did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). Yet according to the nature in which he is God, he could not die; while that nature remained immortal and incapable of suffering, according to the human nature which he assumed, caught among briars—that is, among the crimes of the Jews—with the horns of the cross fastened by nails, he truly suffered, truly died, and was truly buried. [Col. 0429B]

## CHAPTER XXXI. [Col. 0429C] What it signifies that the father led Isaac to be sacrificed; what are understood by the fire, the sword, the wood carried by Isaac, and the father’s binding of his son

Isaac’s father, having two servants, leads him to be sacrificed, because God the Father delivered his aforementioned Son to suffering for the salvation of all with the harmonious proclamations of both the New and the Old Testament. “Wait here,” he says, “until we return to you,” because at that hour the voices of all the Scriptures were silent, so that no one bore witness to him; nor did he himself even resist, by any Scriptural testimonies whatsoever, with his own voice—so that the benefit of the cross might not be delayed.

What then is signified by the father’s taking the wood of the burnt offering and placing it upon Isaac his son, while he himself carried the fire and the sword? What indeed, except that our Lord himself, according to John’s Gospel, carried his cross? For it says: “Jesus went out, carrying his cross himself” (John 19). Thus Isaac appropriately carries the wood of his burnt offering, because Christ himself was to carry the wood of his passion. The father himself carried the fire and the sword. Fire rightly signifies the Holy Spirit, through whom the Son of God offered himself, as the Apostle testifies: “The blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself to God, cleansed our conscience from dead works” (Heb. 9). The sword signifies not only death but also sovereign power. Thus the Father himself carried the sword, [Col. 0430A] because the sword—that is, the authority governing the Lord’s death—was in the hand not of the Jews but of God the Father: where, when, or by what manner of death he ought to be slain. He also carried the fire of the burnt offering because, just as the Son offered himself through the Holy Spirit, so too the Father delivered up his own Son for us all through that same Spirit of love.

When he had bound Isaac his son, he placed him on the altar upon the pile of wood, with marvellous patience submitting and enduring, for his father’s will, the torment of death that was intended for him. Did God the Father then also bind his Son? He did indeed bind him, but not with a bond of weakness: with the command of great love, lest he defend himself, lest, scorning to die, he reject the cup of suffering offered to him. For this is what he himself sings in the Psalm: “You held my right hand, and guided me according to your will” (Ps. 72).
