After enduring all these things, Isaac is at last withdrawn from the single stroke of the sword, and the ram, as has already been said, is sacrificed in his place. For he who is the laughter of heaven, he into whom the angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1), according to the nature in which he is the Father’s joy and the gladness of the holy angels, did not admit death at all, though according to the nature in which he is like us he truly died. [Col. 0430B]

## CHAPTER XXXII. How, even today, on the mountain of Vision—that is, in the holy Church—the true Isaac, Christ, is sacrificed in the sacrament

It is most beautiful and holy to perceive how, even today, upon the mountain of Vision—that is, in the holy Catholic Church, outside which no one shall ever see God—the same Son is continually offered to God the Father, yet remains immortal and incapable of suffering. The sacrifice of the pious and faithful patriarch is rightly compared with this offering, since, just as there, so here, the blood of a son slain by cruel hands is not shed. Rather, the same Son, remaining alive and whole, is both presented to God the Father by the hands and received by the mouths of the faithful.

Therefore in this holy sacrifice the priestly order itself is Father Abraham—father, I say, of many nations—because through its ministry of fatherhood many nations have been regenerated for God. Whomever divine grace calls to the holy altar, and whose faith the election of the Holy Spirit rewards with priestly dignity, by the very fact that he is called and elected to such an office, is certainly commanded to take his beloved son Isaac and offer him to the Lord as a burnt offering in the land of Vision. For no one doubts that this was truly said: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12). Why, then, should a priest or bishop, in whose heart Christ dwells through faith and from whose preaching mouth Christ is conceived in the soul of the hearer, hesitate to call this same Christ his son?

Thus Abraham rises in the night and saddles his ass, because the priest of God, casting away every shameful thing, restrains and subdues every irrational movement of his flesh, lest, as he says, “after I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified” (1 Cor. 9). [Col. 0431A] He also takes with him two servants: that is, he receives alike the Old and New Testament. For “every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13). He also carries fire and sword, because no one is worthy to approach so great a mystery without the fire of the Holy Spirit, and this burnt offering of salvation is not sacrificed without the sword of the word.

Christ is present as Isaac, according to his own truth, by which he says: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18). The two servants are commanded to halt. For at the hour of sacrifice the voices of both Testaments, which had accompanied it in singing and reading, fall silent together. The greatest silence must be observed, so that the passion of Christ our Lord may be celebrated by the priest alone, just as Christ himself, with all his own fleeing, was left alone: “I have trodden the winepress alone,” he says (Isa. 63).

But if, as has been said, he is present wherever two or three are gathered in his name, how is he absent in an assembly gathered for such a purpose? Indeed, he is wholly present; he wholly attends upon the holy altar, not that he may suffer again, but that his passion may be recalled and made present in memory by faith, for which all past things are present. Thus Christ is sacrificed again, and yet remains incapable of suffering and alive, just as Isaac there was sacrificed, yet was not touched by the sword. Bread is broken in his place and eaten; but although that bread is now Christ himself, Christ nevertheless remains whole and alive. [Col. 0431C]

“How,” you ask, “is the bread which is seen Christ?” To this I reply:

> [Note: [Col. 0431D] This comparison must be read cautiously. For when metal is melted and dissolved by the power of fire, it may truly be called ignited, but by no means fire itself—as we truthfully say [Col. 0432D] of the mystical bread of the holy altar that it is the body of Christ.]

Just as any kind of metal—for example, gold or silver—when melted and dissolved by powerful fire, is truly both gold and is called, and is, fire. For the gold is seen and is what it was, yet it is most truly called, and is, fire—what it was not. Thus, in precisely this manner, bread brought into contact with or immersed in the fearful and ineffable mystery of Christ’s passion still appears to be bread, what it was; yet in truth it is Christ, what it was not.

Therefore, just as fire, though divided into parts, nevertheless suffers no diminution of its imparted light, so this bread, divided in the customary breaking, possesses no less of the sacrament or power in each portion than in the whole, so that it consumes all sins if it has the fuel of faith—just as even a small spark of fire, if fuel is not lacking, burns a great forest. And since a *holocaust* means a wholly burned offering, and this sacrifice of the Lord’s passion is a holocaust, of which the Psalmist says, “May your burnt offering be rich” (Ps. 19), the comparison has fittingly been taken here, and nearby, from corporeal fire to incorporeal and invisible fire. But this is not the place to treat the matter at length. This alone concerns the present argument: as Isaac was sacrificed but not killed, so Christ is indeed sacrificed here, but is sacrificed without suffering and immortally. [Col. 0432A]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning God’s promise, and the words, “Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies”

When the angel of the Lord had cried from heaven and, as has already been said above, had sworn by himself, because he had no one greater by whom he could swear, and had said, “I will bless you and multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the shore of the sea”—of which stars of heaven and sand of the sea we have already spoken elsewhere—he also added: “Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you obeyed my voice.”

The Lord has now spoken this word of promise concerning the blessing of the nations in Abraham’s seed for a second time. For at the beginning, when he said to him, “Go out from your land and from your kindred,” he promised this, saying: “And in you all families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12). Since God promised this once and again, it is rightly now called a promise; yet there is some difference. Where no merit of Abraham had yet preceded, he simply promised; but where Abraham had now earned merit through obedience, he renewed the promise with the interposition of an oath, so that, as the Apostle says, “by two immutable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us may have strong consolation” (Heb. 6). [Col. 0432C]

For this too concerns us: that Abraham called the name of that place, “The Lord sees”; whence it is said to this day, “On the mountain the Lord will see.” Among the Hebrews this became a proverb, so that whenever they find themselves in distress and wish to be relieved by the Lord’s help, they say, “On the mountain the Lord will see”—that is, as he had mercy on Abraham, so he will have mercy on us. Hence, in remembrance of the ram given as a sign, they are accustomed even now to sound a horn.

Having interposed an oath, therefore, he also enlarged the blessing thus: “Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies.” The gates of their enemies are the powers of darkness, which Abraham’s seed, Christ, now possesses, according to what he himself foretold: “When a strong man, armed, guards his courtyard, all that he possesses is in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his armour in which he trusted and distribute his spoils” (Matt. 12; Luke 11). This was accomplished through Christ’s suffering and death. For God raised him from the dead, “having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2).

Thus it is fitting that in this place, where Isaac was sacrificed, he first says, “Your seed shall possess the gates of their enemies,” and then, “And in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed.” For after Christ had been sacrificed, the victor was first to take possession of the gates of his enemies—the gates, I say, [Col. 0433A] of hell—and afterward, once the Holy Spirit had been given, blessing—that is, repentance and forgiveness of sins—was to be preached among all nations.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That Saint Job and Balaam descended from the stock of Nahor, Abraham’s brother

After these things had taken place, Abraham was informed that Milcah too had borne sons to his brother Nahor: Uz, the first-born; and Buz his brother; Kemuel, father of the Syrians; Chesed; Hazo; Pildash; Jidlaph; and Bethuel, from whom Rebekah was born, etc. Abraham was informed of this, it is understood, because he was unwilling to take a wife for his son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom he lived, and was concerned from where a daughter-in-law worthy of his son might be hoped for. This concern, or occasion, is a suitable reason why Holy Scripture relates that this was reported to him.

“Uz, the first-born,” it says, etc. Uz, from whose stock Job descended, was the first-born of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, by his wife Milcah, the daughter of Haran, as it is written at the beginning of Job’s book: “There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job” (Job 1). Therefore some are wrong to think that Job was of Esau’s line. For the statement found at the end of the book in certain manuscripts—that he was translated from the Syriac language and was the fourth from Esau, along with the other material contained there—is not found in the Hebrew books.

The second son of Milcah was Buz; from his stock came Balaam, that diviner, whom the Hebrews maintain is called Elihu in the book of Job (Job 32). At first he was a holy man and prophet of God; afterward, through disobedience and desire for gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, he was denounced by a divine utterance. In the same book it is said: “Then Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite was angry,” [Col. 0433C] descending, of course, from the line of this Buz. Kemuel, moreover, was father of Damascus, which is also called Aram or Syria. Chesed was the fourth, and from him the Chasdim—that is, the Chaldeans—were afterward named.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning Sarah’s death and the purchase of her burial-place

(Chapter 23.) Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years, and died in the city of Arba, which is Hebron in the land of Canaan. And Abraham came to mourn and weep for her. *Arba* means “four.” The city is called Arba, or Kiriath-arba, because the four celebrated persons were buried there: namely, the greatest, Adam, as it is written in the book of Joshua (Josh. 14); then Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Sarah’s death signifies the end of the Law and the Prophets, concerning which the Lord says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16). And the Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10), because once he had been given, the prophecies and promises—which we said above were signified by Sarah—fell silent. Hence it should be noted that God is no longer read to have appeared to Abraham. Yet this end of the Law and the Prophets is not harmful, just as Sarah’s death was not evil. For the death of the righteous is precious and a desirable rest; and that end is perfection or consummation, signified by him who is himself the End, when, as we have said, [Col. 0434A] he received the vinegar and said: “It is finished” (John 19).

“And when he had risen from the office of mourning, he spoke to the sons of Heth, saying, ‘I am a stranger and a sojourner among you. Give me a right of burial among you, that I may bury my dead,’” etc., as far as the statement that he weighed out the money Ephron had demanded, in the hearing of the sons of Heth: four hundred shekels of silver, of current public coinage.

In Hebrew his name is first written *Ephron*, and then *Ephran*. For after he had been overcome by the price to sell the burial-place and receive the silver, although Abraham compelled him, the letter *waw*, which among them is read as *o*, was removed from his name; and instead of Ephron he was called Ephran. Scripture thereby signifies that he was not a man of complete and perfect virtue, since he was able to sell memorials of the dead. Let those therefore who sell graves, and are not compelled to take payment but even extort it from unwilling persons, know that their name is changed and that something of their merit perishes, when even the man who accepted payment unwillingly is rebuked. [Col. 0434B]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Again, concerning the field and the double cave in which she was buried

Thus the field formerly belonging to Ephron, in which was the double cave facing Mamre, was confirmed to Abraham as a possession—both the field itself, the cave, and all its trees within all its surrounding boundaries—in the sight of the sons of Heth and of all who entered through the gate of that city. Because this is no small matter, what has already been said once is repeated a second and third time, so that the entire confirmation may be accomplished by three testimonies. For it continues: “And so Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the double cave of the field facing Mamre—that is, Hebron in the land of Canaan.” And immediately: “And the field and the cave that was in it were confirmed to Abraham as a burial possession from the sons of Heth.”

What is said the third time, “the field and the cave,” is the same as what had been said the second time: “the field and the double cave,” or “the cave of the double field.” Thus confirmation was made by three witnesses or testimonies. For the number of witnesses is customarily counted not only in persons, but also in repeated words or deeds, as Paul testifies when he says to the Corinthians: “Behold, this third time I am ready to come to you”; then he immediately adds: “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (2 Cor. 13). [Col. 0434D]

What was accomplished by this purchase, if not the granting to Abraham’s seed of a lawful right, so that it ought to reclaim that same land not only by the judgment of God, who would justly exterminate sinners from that land, but also by human judgment, since their father had purchased it for four hundred shekels of silver and current public coinage? What if Father Abraham did not purchase that whole land? A part ought to establish a more just claim to the whole, especially where the adversaries would not concede what could lawfully be demanded for the part. Thus also in a renowned Roman author, a certain disputant declaims among other things: “He gives everything who denies what is just.” But now I do not wish to pass over the mystical sense of this matter either.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Col. 0435A] On the same matter, according to the mystical sense
“Then the field that had once belonged to Ephron was confirmed,” it says, etc. Mystically, this is as though it were said: the whole world was confirmed, through Christ’s passion, in the faith of Abraham and his seed—Christ, of whom Isaac had shortly before been offered as a type—as an inheritance for him; and in it Sarah, that is, the holy scriptural Law and Prophets, rested in a venerable tomb. She was indeed dead to the unbelieving Jews, but fulfilled and brought to completion among the Gentiles through faith in the coming of Christ, the Son of God.

For the field of Ephron with the double cave—Ephron, I say, being interpreted “useless dust”—signifies sinners, both of the former and of the latter [Col. 0435B] people, who were formerly like “dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1), but were made firm by the dew of the Holy Spirit, according to the Psalmist’s words: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created; and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103). This field faces Mamre, interpreted “division” or “clear-sighted”; for it understands how great will be the division of good and evil on that day which it faces and attentively considers—the day of the Last Judgment. Thus in the double cave of this field, that is, in the conscience of both peoples, Sarah—that is, God’s covenant, confirmed in Christ—rests.

The taller trees around this field are persons who can bear fruit for the lesser by word and example—that is, enable them to make progress. “In the sight of,” it says, “the sons of Heth” [Col. 0435C], that is, while all fear the word that has been spoken or the judgment that is to come; for Heth is interpreted “fear” or “astonishment.” Such a field, therefore, in which Sarah was to be buried, first had to be purchased at a price and confirmed to Abraham as a burial possession. For we had to be bought at a great price and cease to be slaves of sin, so that God’s utterances and the promises to the fathers, fulfilled in the heart of Christ, might then at last be laid up among us. This was prefigured by Isaac’s sacrifice, which preceded Sarah’s death. Finally, since, as has already been said, Adam, the first man and father of the world, was buried there, we rightly understand the purchase of that field as the acquisition of the whole world.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
[Col. 0435D] On the words, “Put your hand under my thigh,” etc., and on what Isaac’s marriage signifies mystically.

“CHAPTER 24.” Now Abraham was old and advanced in days, and the Lord had blessed him in all things. This phrase, “he was old and advanced in days,” was not said in the ordinary way merely because of his great age. For although some who lived before him had lived three times, others four times, indeed some even seven times, as many days as he had, nothing of the sort is said about them. Therefore, “old and advanced in days” means perfect in faith and abundant in good works. “And the Lord had blessed him in all things”: that is, God had foretold in his seed all the good things that He would do for all nations, and had confirmed them to him with an oath [Col. 0436A].

A narrative worthy of such a preface follows: “And he said to the eldest servant of his household, who had charge of all that he possessed: Put your hand under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the Lord God of heaven that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell, but will go to my land and my kindred and take from there a wife for my son Isaac.”

This event commends both faith and chaste marriage. The aged Abraham did not seek a daughter-in-law from among the Canaanites, from whom she might offer some consolation for his exile. Nor did the young Isaac seek a wife whom he might desire with his eyes; rather, he waited in accordance with his father’s will for one whom he had never seen. It is no small merit of faith in Abraham [Col. 0436B], nor does it lack in Isaac a true testimony to chastity, that the former embraced his pilgrimage for the sake of the God in whom he trusted, so as to admit neither himself nor his descendants into any kinship with those who did not please God; and that the latter so overcame youthful impetuosity as to await the wife whom God would give him, rather than seize one for himself with a great dowry through lustful eyes.

In this also, therefore, he is likened to the Son of God, who of His own will—that is, by human judgment—neither receives nor rejects any soul, as He Himself says: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of my Father” (John 5). For if one considers the natural affection of the flesh, He ought to have cherished His own country with the same tenderness with which, seeing the city of Jerusalem, He wept real tears over it [Col. 0436C] (Luke 19). “But I came down from heaven,” He says, “not to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me” (John 6).

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
Who Abraham’s servant is, mystically.

“Put your hand,” he says, “under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the Lord God of heaven.” The Hebrews maintain that he commanded him to swear by his sanctification—that is, by his circumcision. But we say that he adjured him by his seed, that is, by Christ, who was to be born from him, according to Matthew: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1).

Moreover, it should be noted that the father neither adjures Isaac himself, whom he had been commanded to offer to God [Col. 0436D], nor sends him himself to seek a wife so that he may take whichever one pleases him. For Christ Himself, after His suffering, was not to gather the Church to Himself from this world by His own bodily presence.

“Do not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, but go to my land and kindred, and take from there a wife for my son Isaac.” The Canaanites, among whom the father dwelt, were the Jews, whose God He was only in name; hence He says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). This applies, of course, to that portion rightly called Ishmael, which was born according to the flesh. For they are rightly called Canaanites for the same reason for which the prophet reproached that people: “Your father,” he says, “was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” [Col. 0437A] (Ezek. 16).

The many daughters of that people, that is, their many heresies or sects, were the traditions of the Pharisees, Sadducees, and those called Samaritans, together with, as is said, nearly nine other schismatic heresies. “Do not take a wife for my son Isaac from their daughters,” he says, because God the Father does not deign to establish the one new bride of His Son—the Church, “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5)—according to any of their sects.

“But go to my land and kindred.” To go to the father’s land and kindred is, for the faithful and prudent servant, to attend to the faith by which those were justified who were truly God’s people [Col. 0437B] and, through love of righteousness, in a certain manner kindred to God; and to establish the holy Church according to their meaning. For example, they say: “Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 42). The answer is understood: No. But what then? “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (ibid.). To observe, and to hand down for observance, these and innumerable similar teachings is precisely to form a true bride worthy of the Son of God.

But when did God the Father thus adjure His servant? Certainly when He sent the Holy Spirit to the apostles, through whom He so possessed their hearts that they could speak or do absolutely nothing except what God willed concerning such matters. “If the woman is unwilling to come with me,” he says, “must I bring your son back there from which he came?” [Col. 0437C] This means: if no Jew wishes, after abandoning the righteousness of circumcision and fleshly ceremonies, to receive the one necessary righteousness that comes from faith, must it be permitted or endured that we communicate or intermingle evangelical faith with fleshly Judaism, from which Christ, circumcised or minister of circumcision, came forth, establishing another way when He says: “Baptize all nations” (Matt. 28)?

“Beware,” he says, “that you do not bring my son back there.” And immediately, strengthened in his accustomed faith: “The Lord, the God of heaven, who took me from my father’s house, will Himself send His angel before you, and you shall take from there a wife for my son.” And immediately: “But if the woman is unwilling to follow you, you shall not be bound by the oath.” [Col. 0437D] The evangelical man is enjoined under every condition to preserve the same freedom and purity of conscience: “If they will not receive you, shake the dust of your feet upon them” (Matt. 10). The vehement repetition shows that a serious and strong man spoke: “Only do not bring my son back there—do not, I say, bring him back there; rather say: ‘You are severed from Christ, you who are justified by the Law; you have fallen from grace’” (cf. Gal. 5). Likewise: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5), and similar sayings.

## CHAPTER XL  
What the camels signify, and what are the goods of his master which he took with him.

So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master, and swore to him concerning this matter. This servant also, understood as the company of apostolic preachers [Col. 0438A], put his hand under Abraham’s thigh by professing faith in Christ’s incarnation, and swore concerning this matter. He swore, I say—that is, he bound himself under a grave necessity to dispense this mystery. Hence one of them says: “If I preach the Gospel, it is no ground for glory to me; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore, he truly swore who would be under woe if he did not preach the Gospel, because he would be guilty of perjury.

“And he took ten camels from his master’s herd and departed, carrying with him goods of every kind.” That senior servant departed wisely in accordance with the occasion and time: namely, with ten camels, carrying with him goods of every kind belonging to his master [Col. 0438B]. For the girl had to be instructed by the gifts at hand, so that she might know and hope for no small riches from her husband and father-in-law. Thus the servant already mentioned—that is, the evangelical preacher—was sent with great gifts, those of which it was said: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. 6). And: “He gave some to be apostles, some prophets, others evangelists, others pastors and teachers” [Col. 0438B] (Eph. 4). Thus grace was given to each of the faithful servants according to the measure of Christ’s gift (ibid.).

They carried with them from these goods of their master Jesus Christ, or of His Father God, so that the bride sought for Christ might recognize from the glorious present testimony of miracles [Col. 0438C] that He is truly great, rich, and powerful in heaven and on earth. What, then, do the ten camels which he took from his master’s herd signify? Surely the weightier matters of the Law, such as those neglected by the tithers of mint and dill, who were rightly rebuked in these words: “Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matt. 23). The camels are therefore rightly ten, because all the true righteousness of the Law is contained in the ten commandments written upon the tablets by God’s finger (Exod. 31). This alone must be observed in Christ’s Gospel, all fleshly righteousnesses being rejected, which the Apostle counts as loss for Christ and considers as dung (Phil. 3).

## CHAPTER XLI  
[Col. 0438D] On Mesopotamia, to which the servant went, and on his prudence in seeking Rebekah.

“And he journeyed to Mesopotamia, to the city of Nahor.” The native country of Abraham was the land of the Chaldeans; but, driven by persecution, Terah had gone out with his people, as was said above, to go into the land of Canaan (Gen. 12). They had settled in Haran, that is, Syria, which is called Mesopotamia from *meso*, “middle,” and *potamo*, “river,” because it is enclosed by the two rivers Tigris and Euphrates.

The servant, therefore, commanded to go to the land and kindred of his master, went to Mesopotamia, because his master’s kindred inhabited and had grown established in that land, in which Terah also died. “To the city,” it says, “of Nahor.” From this and other testimonies of this sacred history [Col. 0439A], it is shown that Nahor, Abraham’s brother, also left the region of the Chaldeans and established his dwelling in Mesopotamia, where Abraham had lived with his father.

Why then did Scripture not mention him when Terah went out from the Chaldean people with his household and dwelt in Mesopotamia, where it records that he took not only Abraham his son, but also Sarah his daughter-in-law and Lot his grandson? Why, unless perhaps Nahor had departed from the piety of his father and brother and attached himself to Chaldean superstition; and later either repenting of this, or suffering persecution because he was regarded with suspicion, he too migrated?

“And when he had made the camels kneel outside the town beside a well of water, in the evening, at the time when women usually go out to draw water [Col. 0439B], he said: ‘Lord, God of my master Abraham, meet me today, I pray, and show mercy to my master Abraham,’” etc. Scripture truly called this man “the eldest” above. For what was worthy of an elder is this: he did not entrust the judgment of the maiden to be sought to his own eyes, which could discern only the face, not character or virtue; rather, trusting in his master’s faith that God cared for his master, he placed all hope of selection in Him.

“Therefore,” he says, “the girl to whom I say, ‘Give me water from your pitcher that I may drink,’” etc. For he believed that frugality tested and discovered by this examination, corresponding to his master’s character, would be worthy to receive golden earrings and bracelets. This he did immediately, worshiping and blessing God and saying: “Blessed be the Lord God of my master Abraham, who has not withdrawn His mercy and truth from my master, and has led me by a straight way to the house of my master’s brother.”

“And bread was set before him. But he said: ‘I will not eat until I have spoken my words.’ They answered him: ‘Speak.’ And he said: ‘I am Abraham’s servant,’” etc. Therefore Wisdom rightly and truly says: “Like the coolness of snow in the day of harvest, so is a faithful messenger, who refreshes the soul of him who sent him” [Col. 0439C] (Prov. 25). In what way could a faithful messenger better strive to refresh the soul of him who sent him? He first offered a suppliant prayer to the God of his master; with gifts he endeavored to awaken the girl’s favorable disposition more fully; he waited excellently for the right opportunity to speak [Col. 0439D]; and, though welcome to his hosts, he was still silent until bread was set before him. Then at last, amid the highest pledges of hospitality—that is, in the presence of the bread set before him—he began his address, starting with true praises of God and of Abraham his master.

Since these silvered wings of the dove are sufficiently evident—that is, the plain surface of the letter—let us now, as we began above, pursue by inquiry the inward beauty of the allegory.

## CHAPTER XLII  
On the same matter in the mystical sense.

“When,” he says, “he had made the camels kneel outside the town beside the well.” Thus undoubtedly the prudent servant—that is, the evangelical preacher, for example the Apostle Paul—knelt beside the well and there encountered a very beautiful girl: that is, he fixed spiritual eyes upon Holy Scripture and found sound doctrine and beautiful speech to ascribe to Christ’s glory. Therefore Wisdom, the well-adorned sister and friend, rightly says as she looks upon him: “Those who make me clear shall have eternal life” [Col. 0440A] (Ecclus. 24).

For the beautiful girl Rebekah is mystically Holy Scripture itself, the Scripture of God’s covenant [Col. 0440C]. She was also signified above by Sarah, according to the Apostle’s testimony (Gal. 4), with this one difference: through Sarah Scripture is figured as yet to be fulfilled; through Rebekah, as already fulfilled. Hence the diligence of the letter should be noted: when it had been said, “a most beautiful virgin,” it was added, “and unknown to a man.” “Unknown to a man,” that is, hidden—what is called in Hebrew *aalma*. This is indeed found in Isaiah: for where our manuscripts read, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear” (Isa. 7), the Hebrew has, “Behold, an *aalma* shall conceive and bear.”

Therefore *aalma*, interpreted “hidden”—that is, a virgin guarded with the greatest care—seems a greater praise than “virgin.” For a virgin, according to the Apostle, may be one in body and not in spirit (1 Cor. 7). But she who is a hidden virgin has an epithet of virginity and the etymology of hidden wisdom. For it is written in Job: “Whence then is wisdom found? And where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living beings” [Col. 0440B] (Job 28).

The names themselves also suit the matter well. “I am Rebekah,” she says, “daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor.” Rebekah means “patience”; Bethuel, “virgin of God”; Milcah, “queen”; Nahor, “rest of light.” For the teaching of Holy Scripture is patience: “Whatever was written,” says the Apostle, “was written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15). And she is the daughter of Bethuel, that is, of the virgin of God; for she was born or composed from those whose virgin souls God joined to Himself, so that good speech might be born from them.

Milcah—that is, the queen—bore this Bethuel: the queen, I say, namely that free Jerusalem which is above, which is truly the mother of all belonging to this Isaac (Gal. 4). And she bore him from Nahor, that is, from the rest of light, in which that queen Jerusalem rests.

[Col. 0440D] The servant who sought and found her not for himself but for his master represents those who truly say: “We do not preach ourselves, but the Lord Jesus Christ; and ourselves as your servants through Jesus” (2 Cor. 4). Likewise: “We are not like the many who adulterate the word of God” (2 Cor. 2), and similar sayings. Thus the servant adorns the maiden’s household with royal earrings and bracelets whenever any minister of Christ and steward of God’s ministries supplies Holy Scripture with necessary testimonies concerning the true Isaac, that is, the Son of God incarnate and sacrificed for the whole world.

“Earrings weighing two shekels, and bracelets weighing ten shekels.” Because the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon two commandments (Matt. 22), the earrings are rightly of two shekels; and because one must work according to the ten commandments [Col. 0441A], the bracelets weighed ten shekels. In Hebrew a shekel is called *secel*; in Latin, through corruption, it is called *siclus*. It has the weight of an ounce.

Therefore, because there are many daughters whose charm is deceitful and whose beauty vain (Prov. 31), he says: “The girl to whom I say, ‘Give me water from your pitcher that I may drink,’ and who says, ‘Drink, and I will give your camels drink also,’ is she whom you have prepared, Lord, for my master’s son.” For truly, whatever Scripture is fitted with living waters to refresh the soul lest anyone perish from thirst, that Scripture is prepared for the Son of God as sister and friend: through grace giving birth, she tenderly and powerfully nourishes with milk and wine the children born to Him.

Nor did that faithful servant wish, or ought, to eat in the house until he had spoken his words and obtained the consent of the whole household. For as long as anyone denies to Christ the testimonies of Holy Scripture, the evangelical man has no fellowship with him; indeed, he should shake upon them the dust clinging to him from the city of those who are such (Matt. 10). For first, according to the command of Him who sends them, in whatever house they enter they must first say, “Peace to this house” (Luke 10); and if a son of peace is there, and evangelical peace rests upon it, then at last, “remain in that same house, eating and drinking what they have” [Col. 0441B] (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XLIII  
On Laban, Rebekah’s brother, and the gifts given mystically to Rebekah.

[Col. 0441C] Now Rebekah had a brother named Laban, who hurried out to the man where the spring was. And he said to him: “Come in, blessed of the Lord. Why are you standing outside?” etc. Laban means “white,” and by that name signifies the world made bright by temporal glory.

Now, when he sees the earrings and bracelets on his sister’s hand, he runs out and says, “Come in, blessed of the Lord. Why are you standing outside?” And afterward, when he says, “The word has come forth from the Lord, and we cannot speak anything else with you apart from His pleasure,” he signifies the world in a favorable sense: namely, those whom evangelical grace delighted immediately upon first hearing, and who, with fraternal affection, seeing and understanding from the adornment—that is, the sweetness and elucidation of the Scriptures—that God’s truth had been fulfilled and the promises to the fathers confirmed [Col. 0441D], hastened to be baptized and made white through remission of sins.

But when he changed Jacob’s wages, though he served well, ten times (Gen. 31), and pursued him as he fled but was at last reconciled with him by covenant, he signifies the world in the persons of those who at first opposed the good works of believers, but could finally be satisfied and, conquered by reason, came to their senses. Thus, when the grace of the Gospel was revealed, those who are represented by Laban shone forth as white.

“If you sleep,” says the Psalmist, “between the midst of the lots, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” [Col. 0441D] (Ps. 67). There he calls Scripture itself the dove, whom we understand here as the girl; by the silvered wings he signifies the sacred utterances, beautiful and outwardly luminous even in the letter; by the pallor of gold, the most precious mysteries of Christ and the Church that lie within.

At once, too, he identifies those who are here understood by Laban, that is, the white or whitened: “While he distinguishes kings over her”—that is, while He appoints apostles, prophets, teachers, and pastors to administer Holy Scripture—“they are made white as snow in Zalmon” [Col. 0442A] (ibid.). Zalmon is interpreted “shadow of stumbling” or “image of strength,” and signifies Christ, who is “a stone of stumbling” to unbelievers (1 Pet. 2), but to believers is the image of the most mighty One, namely God the Father.

The praises which this servant here proclaims before the Lord or the Son of his master, saying, “I am Abraham’s servant, and the Lord has greatly blessed my master and made him great; and Sarah, my master’s wife, bore a son to my master in his old age, and he has given him all that he had,” the Prophet there likewise continues concerning that Son of God the Father: “The mountain of God is a rich mountain, a curdled mountain, a rich mountain. Why do you look with suspicion upon curdled mountains? The mountain in which God has been pleased to dwell—for the Lord shall dwell there unto the end” (Ps. 67), etc.

And as this servant bows in worship, blessing God, and brings out vessels of silver and gold and garments, giving them to Rebekah as gifts, offering gifts also to her brothers and mother, and saying, “Send me away, that I may go to my master. Do not detain me, because the Lord has directed my way,” so in the same Psalm the kings whom the heavenly King distinguishes over that dove proclaim His gifts in song: “You ascended on high; you led captivity captive; you received gifts among men” [Col. 0442C] (ibid.). Immediately afterward, rejoicing, they say: “Blessed be the Lord day by day; the God of our salvation will make our journey prosperous” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XLIV  
What is signified by the girl’s ready answer to those who inquire, “I will go”; and on Isaac’s meditation after going out into the field.

“Let us call the girl and ask her own will.” When she had come at their summons, they asked her: “Will you go with this man?” She answered: “I will go.” Laban and Bethuel had already answered, saying: “The word has come forth from the Lord, and we cannot say anything else with you apart from His pleasure.” Why, then, do the brother and mother now hesitate and say, “Let us call the girl”? This is surely a sign of apostolic judgment or testing.

For Rebekah’s household represents the primitive Church that was formed from the Jews under the apostles. Some murmured against the Apostle Peter, saying: “Why did you go in to men who have uncircumcised flesh?” And they said: “Unless you are circumcised according to the law of Moses, you cannot be saved” [Col. 0442D] (Acts 11). They were then trying to bring it about not that Rebekah should go to Isaac, but that Isaac should return for Rebekah’s sake—a thing Abraham the father had rejected, saying, “Beware that you do not bring my son back there.”

When the girl was called and asked, “Will you go with this man?” she replied swiftly and briefly: “I will go.” For when Holy Scripture was consulted whether it wished God’s grace to be directed with Christ toward the Gentiles, it quickly answered, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, with these words: “After these things I will return, and I will rebuild the tabernacle of David that has fallen; and I will rebuild its ruins and raise it up, that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles upon whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does these things” (Acts 15).

“Then Rebekah and her maidens mounted the camels and followed the man.” What Rebekah and the girl are here, the silvered and golden dove and the young maidens playing timbrels are in the Psalm mentioned above; and what the servant is here, Benjamin the young man is especially there: “There is Benjamin, a young man, in ecstasy of mind” [Col. 0443A] (Ps. 67), that is, the Apostle Paul of the tribe of Benjamin, caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12).

These maidens, I say, are the young women playing timbrels who accompany Rebekah and honor the golden dove with burning zeal by their timbrel-playing: that is, by sweetly sounding forth Christ’s testimonies and crying in harmonious timbrel-music against beasts and bulls—that is, against proud heresies and heresiarchs: “Rebuke the beasts of the reeds, the herd of bulls among the cows of the peoples, that they may exclude those tested by silver” (Ps. 67).

Thus the virginal beauty of the Scriptures goes out to the Gentiles in order to bear children for Christ; for Christ had already gone there before it. This is indicated by the statement: “Isaac dwelt in the southern land, and had gone out to meditate in the field.” In the literal sense, the southern land signifies Gerar, from which he had once been led by his father to be offered in sacrifice. And the devotion of a good man is commended, as he meditates upon the covenant of God, his father Abraham, and therefore loves solitude. Scripture commends such a man when it says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and lift himself above himself” [Col. 0443C] (Lam. 7).

Mystically, however, this signifies that the Lord Jesus, praying alone, meditated according to the Father’s will on leaving the ceremonies of the Jews and going out into the wilderness of the uncultivated Gentiles. And this was in the southern land—that is, in the dispensation of the Holy Spirit—when the day was already declining, that is, in the last age of the world. [Col. 0443D] “At that time,” it says, “he was walking to the well whose name is ‘of Seeing and Living.’” Hagar had given that name to the well, as was said above. It is wonderful and very beautiful that Rebekah was found at a well and that Isaac, likewise going toward a well, was found; for although the water of God’s wisdom or knowledge is one, yet one is the well of the Law and another the well of the Gospel, toward which the holy and life-giving Spirit of Scripture strives at Christ’s summons.

## CHAPTER XLV  
On Rebekah’s chaste modesty: on seeing Isaac, she covered herself with a veil; and what is mystically signified by Isaac’s bringing her into Sarah’s tent.

“And when he lifted up his eyes, he saw camels coming from afar. But Rebekah, seeing Isaac, dismounted from the camel and said to the servant: ‘Who is that man coming through the field to meet us?’ He said to her: ‘It is my master.’ Then she quickly took up a veil and covered herself. And the servant told Isaac all that he had done.”

[Col. 0444A] No one doubts that this girl was prepared for the faithful man not by flesh and blood, but by God Himself; and that, in accordance with faithful Abraham’s hope, when he had said, “The Lord God of heaven Himself will send His angel before you, that you may take from there a wife for my son,” so it came to pass.

Certainly she did not hasten to a man’s embrace from the ardor of youthful love, though when asked above, “Will you go with this man?” she so quickly answered, “I will go.” For the prophet denounces women of that sort in these words: “Because the daughters of Zion were exalted and walked with outstretched necks, went with gestures of their eyes, clapped their hands, and walked with affected steps, the Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will lay bare their hair” [Col. 0444B] (Isa. 3).

But Rebekah, when she saw Isaac, dismounted from the camel and quickly took up a veil and covered herself. Did she then, when she said, “I will go,” burn with youthful desire to be desired or to desire, she who so hastily covered her beauty when she saw Isaac? Certainly not. Rather, forestalled by a heavenly prompting, she preferred to make pilgrimage with the faith of Abraham and Isaac and seek the city that was to come rather than possess the present one.

Thus every sound doctrine and evangelical religion walks modestly and presents itself in service under the honorable and humble veil of its mysteries to Christ, its lover. But the daughters of deceitful charm and vain beauty (Prov. 31)—that is, all heresies—walk with outstretched necks, go with gestures of their eyes and clap their hands, and, like shameless little prostitutes, seek to be seen and desired. Hence in another place the same prophet says to such a prostitute under the name of Tyre: “Take a lyre; go around the city, prostitute forgotten; sing well, repeat your song often, that you may be remembered” [Col. 0444C] (Isa. 23).

“But the servant told Isaac all that he had done.” Truly a prudent and faithful servant, as a great testimony to his faith, told all that he had done for the praise and glory of God, who had directed his way for the sake of Isaac himself; and he was worthy to receive the great reward of freedom. This is sufficient commendation of a good servant: to stand before the Son of God with joyful confession and recount—that is, confess—what had diligently been accomplished through his service. For everyone who confesses the Son has the Father also; just as, conversely, everyone who denies the Son has neither the Father (1 John 2).

[Col. 0444D] “And he brought her into Sarah’s tent and took her as his wife. And he loved her so greatly that she tempered the sorrow caused by his mother’s death.” What great thing was it, according to the outer bark of the letter, that a young man so loved his youthful wife that she eased the grief caused by his mother’s death? Therefore the spiritual kernel of meaning must not be absent. For Christ the Lord truly grieved, according to human affection, over His mother, the Synagogue; indeed, when He saw the city, He wept over it [Col. 0444D] (Luke 12). But having gained the new queen, from whom a new people would be born for Him [Col. 0445A], He rightly moderated His grief and was delightfully consoled.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
On Abraham’s other sons, and on his death and that of Ishmael.

(CAP. XXV.) Abraham, however, took another wife named Keturah, who bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. *Keturah* in the Hebrew language means “bound” or “joined.” For this reason the Hebrews suppose that, after her name had been changed, she was the same as Hagar, who, after Sarah’s death, passed from concubine to wife. But since it is immediately written: “Abraham gave all that he had to Isaac; but to the sons of the concubines he gave gifts, and while he was still alive he separated them from Isaac his son,” it is clear that Keturah was not Hagar. For Scripture would have said not “sons of the concubines,” [Col. 0445B] but “sons of the concubine.” Leaving aside what is uncertain, we state on reliable authorities that Abraham’s sons by Keturah, according to Hebrew historians, occupied Troglodytis and Arabia as far as the borders of the Red Sea.

It has also been handed down by those who composed barbarian histories in Greek that one of Abraham’s descendants, called Asher, led an army against Libya, settled there after defeating the enemy, and that his descendants named Africa after the name of their great-grandfather. “And the sons of Dedan,” it says, “were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.” They think that *Asshurim* should be rendered “traders”; *Letushim*, those who work metals, copper and iron; and *Leummim*, “tribal chiefs,” that is, rulers of many tribes and peoples. Others maintain that the Syrians were called after this Asshurim, [Col. 0445C] and that regions of India were occupied by the numerous sons of Abraham through Keturah.

Now the days of Abraham’s life were one hundred and seventy-five years; and, failing, he died in a good old age, advanced in years and full of days, and was gathered to his people. Our copies add from the Seventy Interpreters: “and failing he died.” This is unsuitable, for it does not belong to a righteous man to fail and diminish. [Col. 0446A] What we read also, “full,” with the addition “of days,” has been taken from Greek copies. Although this seems to explain the sense—that he set having been full of light and deeds of the day—yet it lends itself more to anagogical interpretation if it is simply written “full.”

Moreover, the words “and he was gathered to his people” should be understood figuratively: just as ripe grain is gathered from the fields into the barn, so the elect are gathered from the common field of this life, each in his own time, into the hidden dwellings of those at rest.

These are the generations of Ishmael son of Abraham, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to him; and these are all his sons according to their names and generations. Ishmael’s firstborn was Nebaioth; then Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam; also Mishma, Dumah, and Massa, [Col. 0446B] Hadar and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. Nebaioth was the firstborn of the twelve sons. From him the entire region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is still called Nabathene; it is Abraham’s portion. Their clans, towns, villages, small fortresses, and tribes are likewise known by the name of each one of them: Kedar in the wilderness; Dumah, another region; Tema in the south; and Kedemah in the eastern quarter.

But what we read at the end of this chapter according to the Septuagint, “He shall dwell opposite all his brothers,” is less accurate than what we have given: “He died in the presence of all his brothers,” that is, he died in the hands of all his sons, his children surviving and none having previously been taken away by death. “Brothers,” moreover, may be used for sons, as Jacob also shows in speaking to Laban: “What is my sin, that you have pursued me and searched through all my goods? What have you found among all the goods of your house? Set it before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us” (Gen. XXXI). [Col. 0446C] For we cannot believe, as Scripture records, that Jacob had any brothers with him apart from his children.

# Seventh Book on Genesis  
*(Genesis XXV–XXVIII)*

[Col. 0445]

## Chapter I. On the generations of Isaac: how the generations of Isaac differ from the generations of Christ.

(CAP. XXV.) “These also are the generations of Isaac son of Abraham: Abraham begot Isaac.” The generations which Moses here calls those of Isaac, and proceeds to set out down to his own time, the Evangelist Matthew calls the generations of Jesus Christ, Son of God, and continues them almost down to Christ himself. For, after placing the heading at the front, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. I), he immediately begins the sacred genealogy from the present chapter: “Abraham begot Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob.”

But the generations of the one and of the other are different. [Col. 0446D] Those of Jesus Christ are arranged more according to faith than according to flesh; conversely, those of Isaac are arranged as succeeding more according to flesh than according to faith. Thus there the bodily genealogy comes to an end at its summit: it was not said, nor ought it to have been said, “Joseph begot Jesus, who is called Christ”; rather, “Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (ibid.). Conversely, here the generation of corruptible flesh proceeds: when Rebecca’s conception had been granted, the little ones struggled in her womb, concerning whom God rightly says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” [Col. 0447A] (Mal. I).

Therefore, since the generations of Isaac, whom Abraham begot, are the generations of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, let us pursue them both as the generation of the Jews according to the flesh, by which they are Abraham’s children, and as the generations of the Gentiles according to faith, by which that same Abraham, through Christ, is the father of many nations.

## Chapter II. On Isaac’s taking a wife at forty years of age and bringing her into Sarah’s tent.

Isaac, when he was forty years old, took as wife Rebecca, daughter of Bethuel the Syrian of Mesopotamia, sister of Laban. Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. The Lord heard him and gave Rebecca conception; but the little ones struggled in [Col. 0447B] her womb.

Sarah bore Isaac when she was ninety years old. She lived one hundred and twenty-seven years and died; Isaac, however, took Rebecca as wife when he was forty years old. Therefore Sarah died three years before Rebecca’s marriage. Thus, without doubt, three years before Christ’s Passion—by which he united to himself the grace of evangelical preaching—from the days, or baptism, of John, the Law and prophecy died: not for themselves, but for the Jews. Christ himself bears witness when he says: “The Law and the prophets prophesied until John” (Matt. XIII).

For from the time when they began to blaspheme Christ, present among them and declared by John’s testimony to be the Son of the living God, all holiness and all life left their wicked assemblies, because they were a council of vanity and a congregation of evildoers—except for the few who retained Abraham’s faith and deserved to be Sarah’s tent. Of such persons the Psalm says: “His tent is round about him” (Ps. XVII). Into this tent Isaac brought Rebecca and took her as wife: that is, Christ opened their understanding, imparted to them the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures, and founded for himself a new Church.

“And Isaac prayed to the Lord for his wife, because she was barren. The Lord heard him and gave Rebecca conception. But the little ones struggled in her womb.” She said: “If this was to happen to me, what need was there for me to conceive?”

## Chapter III. Why the Lord prepared a barren woman for Abraham’s son.

Because it was God’s gift, and not from human beings, that all nations should be blessed in Abraham’s seed, it was fitting [Col. 0447D] that God’s hand should be so stretched out in giving that human ingratitude might not sleep in recognizing it. What, in such a matter, could better instruct faith or shut every mouth than the barrenness of women?

God’s providence therefore prepared Rebecca well; nor was Abraham’s servant wrong when he said, “She is the one whom you have prepared, Lord, for my master’s son.” Yet he prepared her such that no flesh could glory before God, but faith alone. He provided a barren womb. And lest you think that this occurred by chance, consider further that not Isaac alone, nor Abraham alone, but three patriarchs of peoples in unbroken succession—the pillars of the Fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—received barren wives: Abraham, Sarah; Isaac, Rebecca; Jacob, Rachel, for whom he served and whom he calls virtually his only wife. [Col. 0448A]

Thus, because their offspring—Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph—are sons not of flesh but of promise, it is rightly demonstrated that in them the figure of Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, shines forth most clearly. In him rests the whole sum of promise; for as a type of him Isaac was offered up, Jacob served, and Joseph was sold and, after prison, called saviour of the world, delivering Egypt from the peril of famine.

The Lord therefore heard Isaac praying for his wife, because he himself had so provided and so prepared matters that faith might be aided by prayer and the predestination of the seed fulfilled through prayer concerning barrenness. Having said this, Scripture immediately adds in contrast: [Col. 0448B] “But the little ones struggled in her womb.” This is to say: conception indeed was matter for joy, but the joy of conception was troubled by the pain of the mother’s womb.

The little ones struggled, not in contention, nor with awareness of combat, nor from a desire to conquer; rather, they were moved by the same nod of God by which not only irrational cattle but even inanimate elements are accustomed to be moved or altered in forewarning of future events. Such things have often already happened, and still greater things will happen, as the Lord testifies when he says: “There will be signs in sun, moon, and stars, and on earth distress among the nations because of the confusion of the sea and its waves” (Luke XXI). But according to the mystical sense, the little ones struggled in their mother’s womb in the event recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: for the Jews strove to drive away the admitted Gentiles, begrudging their salvation [Col. 0448C] (Acts XI).

## Chapter IV. On the words, “Two nations are in your womb,” and the rest; and what they signify spiritually.

She went to consult the Lord. He answered and said: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall prevail over another people, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

The Apostle declares that this passage must inspire fear and be handled reverently, when he says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” (Rom. IX.) For he had said [Col. 0448D]: “When they were not yet born and had done neither good nor evil, so that the purpose of God according to election might remain—not from works, but from him who calls—it was said to her, ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (ibid.).

What, then, was the Apostle discussing when he said these things? Certainly the division and struggle of the children of flesh and the children of promise: namely, that not all who are of Israel are Israelites, nor are all Abraham’s seed his children. Hence, adding the testimony of Scripture, he says: “But in Isaac shall seed be called to you”; that is, not the children of flesh are God’s children, but the children of promise are reckoned as seed.

Therefore, with the Apostle’s authority, we understand in this struggle of the little ones [Col. 0449A] a prefiguration of the struggle of the children of flesh and the children of promise. It immediately became evident when the true Isaac, the Lord Jesus Christ, took the mother of us all, holy Scripture, by which we are reborn to God, into his marriage—that is, into the practice of evangelical preaching. Then *Aalma*, that is, “the hidden virgin,” the most beautiful woman who had been barren—namely, wisdom, or the teaching of the Law and prophets, which had brought nothing to perfection so long as it did not have Christ as husband—conceived twins. That is, once the killing letter had been removed, through the life-giving Spirit she embraced every human soul, Jews first and Greeks. She conceived twins, I say: she called Jews and Gentiles alike to life, making no distinction between them. This is that Rebecca whose name means “patience.” For the Apostle also says of this womb of evangelical grace: “God’s patience leads you to repentance” (Rom. II). [Col. 0449B]

Of these it was most truly said: “One people shall prevail over another, and the elder shall serve the younger.” For the people who came from the Gentiles is rightly called younger than the Jewish people according to the order of calling, since it was a stranger to the covenants and promise and without God in this world. For the elder is that people to which, as the same Apostle says, belong adoption as sons, glory, the covenant, the giving of the Law, worship, and promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever (Rom. IX).

How the younger prevailed over and supplanted the elder, and the elder served the younger, is evident even in the historical sense: David struck Edom and made it tributary (I Kings VIII; I Chron. XVIII). In the spiritual sense the Apostle beautifully demonstrates this in the same epistle by the comparison of the olive tree and the wild olive: “The natural branches,” he says, “were broken off; and you, though you were a wild olive, were grafted in among them contrary to nature and became a partaker of the root and richness of the olive tree. They were broken off because of unbelief; but stand firm by faith” (Rom. XI). Therefore the elder, broken off through unbelief, was overcome by the younger standing in faith; and the elder serves the younger when the branch of the natural olive yields to the wild olive a share in the olive root and its richness.

## Chapter V. On the birth of the twins, and what it signifies that the younger [Col. 0449D] held the elder’s heel.

The time for giving birth had come, and behold, twins were found in her womb. He who came out first was red and wholly hairy like a skin, and his name was called Esau. Immediately afterward the other came out, holding his brother’s heel in his hand, and therefore he called him Jacob.

Because he was red, his name was called Esau, which means “red.” Since he was wholly like a hairy skin, he was called Seir, that is, “hairy.” The appearance or condition of each disclosed who had been the leader in the struggle even in the womb, who would become after the womb the instigator of hostility or hatred, and who had conquered in the womb and would thereafter rightly claim the palm of victory.

For just as the red and hairy one first came out, so he first struggled with his brother in the womb, and after the womb he would plot death against his peaceable brother. And just as this one was gentle, so from the womb onward he followed his brother’s heel with gentleness and modesty, without force or injustice, as Scripture itself will subsequently make clear.

According to allegory, however, the time of giving birth is the time for professing the faith conceived by hearing the word. Hence the Apostle, who had already laboured in birth for the Galatians to the point that they believed well and ran well, but who had been subverted by false apostles and bewitched so as not to obey the truth—so that Jesus Christ had rightly been portrayed before their eyes as crucified among them—felt a mother’s pain and said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. IV). [Col. 0450A]

Then he who came out first [Col. 0450B]—that is, he who contended for precedence and to whom God’s word ought first to have been spoken—came out red and hairy: polluted by Christ’s blood and untameable through harsh ways. Such a one did not come out well but badly, as is written in the Psalm—and as must also be understood of heretics—“Sinners were estranged from the womb; they went astray from the belly; they spoke falsehood” (Ps. LVII), and so forth.

But the people of the Gentiles that followed did indeed come out from the heart’s belief into the mouth’s confession: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth one confesses unto salvation” (Rom. X). Yet it did not come out from its mother’s affections, just as that gentle and simple man did not. For Rebecca loved Jacob.

## Chapter VI. [Col. 0450C] On Isaac’s love for Esau and Rebecca’s love for Jacob; and on Esau’s sale of the birthright.

Isaac was sixty years old when the little ones were born to him. When they grew up, Esau became a man skilled in hunting, but Jacob was simple and lived in tents. Since the younger had held the heel of the elder, already a victor in the sight of God, who alone had been spectator and judge of the hidden contest, it was necessary immediately to recount how he had supplanted him. Thus it might be known that the one who supplanted was not unjustly judged victorious, but that the one who could be so supplanted was justly judged defeated in the sight of him who said: “One people shall prevail over another, and the elder shall serve the younger.”

“Esau,” it says, “became a man skilled in hunting and a man of the field; but Jacob was simple and lived in tents.” [Col. 0450D] Behold already in their occupations a difference as great as that between the unlike occupations of Cain and Abel. For Jacob was simple like Abel and, as what follows will show, a shepherd of sheep; Esau, like Cain, was a man of the field and, as the following narrative will teach, through envy toward his brother was fratricidal in will, though not in deed. For he said: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I will kill Jacob my brother” (Gen. XXVII).

Should a holy father, then, have loved such a son? Or could he forget or make light of the fact that heavenly judgment had preferred the younger brother to him? But it should be observed that the statement of each one’s love differs. Scripture says simply: “Rebecca loved Jacob.” But it says in a qualified way, “Isaac loved Esau,” adding the reason: because he ate of his hunting. [Col. 0451A] Therefore it is the same as though only this had been said: Isaac gladly ate of Esau’s hunting. From this it does not follow that he also delighted in Esau’s character, as must necessarily be granted concerning Jacob, whom Rebecca is said simply to have loved.

Now Jacob cooked a stew. When Esau came to him from the field, weary, he said: “Give me some of this red cooking, for I am exceedingly weary.” For this reason his name was called Edom. Jacob said to him: “Sell me your birthright.” He answered: “Behold, I am dying; what good will the birthright do me?” Jacob said: “Swear to me, then.” Esau swore and sold the birthright; and so, having received bread and a meal of lentils, he ate and drank and went away, making light of the fact that he had sold the birthright.

Therefore Jacob rightly grants the palm of victory, by the whole counsel of heaven and earth, [Col. 0451B] to the supplanter. For he did not deceive his brother by fraud, since he was simple; rather, possessing with the simplicity of the dove the prudence of the serpent, he wisely set before the glutton the price he asked for, and openly demanded in return, without deceit and without force, what the other possessed—a just and lawful sale.

The Hebrews say that from Shem, Noah’s firstborn, whom they also affirm to have been Melchizedek, all firstborn were priests; and that these were the birthrights Esau sold to Jacob. Let us now pursue the allegorical sense.

## Chapter VII. What these things signify spiritually.

“Behold, I am dying,” he says; “what good will the birthright do me?” In the Epistle to the Hebrews, where it says, “See to it [Col. 0451C] that no one falls short of the grace of God; that no root of bitterness springing up may hinder, and through it many be defiled; that there be no fornicator or profane person,” it immediately adds: “like Esau, who for one morsel of food sold his birthright. For know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears” (Heb. XII).

Therefore the Jew who falls short of God’s grace, in whom is the root of bitterness, is that Edom who sold his birthright for one morsel of food. But what was that red cooking which this Edom so eagerly sought and ate at such cost? Or when did this Jacob—that is, “supplanter,” namely the Gentile people—cook such a stew? O wondrous and great spectacle [Col. 0451D] of this food, of this red cooking! For the bloody death of Christ was red cooking for the Jews. Hence it was prophetically said: “The children have been filled and have left their remnants to their little ones” (Ps. XVI). For striving to be filled with the sufferings of the innocent man, they cried to Pilate: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

They cried this, I say, against the declaration of the Gentile who washed his hands and said: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; see to it yourselves” (ibid.). He did not know what he was saying or doing, just as Caiaphas did not know when he prophesied and said that it was expedient for one man to die for the people (John XVIII). The hands of the Gentiles cooked that red cooking of the Lord’s death, while this Edom pressed to be filled, as has been said, and to leave his remnants to his little ones (Ps. XVI); but the cleanness of hands he yielded to the people of the Gentiles, which is the true birthright. [Col. 0452A]

For from that time the birthright passed to the Roman empire—whose official and voice Pilate was when he said, “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man; see to it yourselves.” To the Roman empire, I say, the birthright passed: that is, the primacy of priesthood passed there by such a transaction, transferred from Edom, that is, from the bloodthirsty Jews.

The Apostle therefore rightly says: “Like Esau, who for one morsel of food sold his birthright,” adding also: “And he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears” (Heb. XII). For tears that seek a heavenly gift for the sake of temporal glory have no power: such were Esau’s tears, or rather [Col. 0452B] the Jews’ tears when they wailed over the ruin of the temple or city but did not weep for their sins.

“But then,” you ask, “did that Isaac—that is, ‘laughter,’ in whom, when we see him, we shall then truly be blessed—love such an Esau and eat of his hunting? And did that Rebecca, the holy and life-giving Spirit of the Scriptures, love such a Jacob, who had cooked the flesh of the Lamb of God on the altar of the cross?” Indeed, yes; no lengthy proof is necessary.

For Christ the Lord loved that hunter even according to human affection so greatly that, foretelling the destruction of the place of his hunting—that is, the city or temple from which he had received hunts of so many victims—he shed true tears (Luke XIX). And the Spirit of the holy Scriptures loved the Gentile people so greatly that, as though hastening toward it, [Col. 0452C] he said: “Behold me, behold me, to a nation that did not call upon my name” (Isa. LXV), and many similar things.

Individually too, this Rebecca loves each of us all the more the more simply one lives in tents. Conversely, the more Esau there is in anyone, the less Rebecca loves that person: that is, the more one roams abroad, the less one is nourished at the breasts of holy Scripture and fed by the bread stored within. And if one is even a hunter in the presence of father Isaac—that is, accustomed to preach Christ—yet if by this he seeks what is his own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ, he sells his birthright and is like Esau. But Rebecca loves the quiet and simple person, as has been said; for holy Scripture is very much reconciled to a heart at rest. Hence the saying: “The wisdom of the scribe comes in a time of leisure, and he whose activity is reduced shall gain it” (Ecclus. XXXII). [Col. 0452D]

## Chapter VIII. What it signifies that, when famine arose, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines.

Now when famine arose over the land after the barrenness which had occurred in Abraham’s days, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar. The Lord appeared to him and said: “Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land which I shall tell you,” and so forth.

The order is inverted. For God would not appear to someone already living in Gerar, the metropolis of the Philistines, and say: “To your seed I will give all these regions” (Gen. XII). [Col. 0453A] Therefore it was said first, out of order, that Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar; and afterwards that, when the Lord God appeared and commanded him, he turned aside there rather than elsewhere. In due course it will become clear that this inversion has not been made without purpose.

Now that the literal surface of the reading is plain, the sequence of mysteries must be continued. “When famine arose,” it says, “after the barrenness which had occurred in Abraham’s days, Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, at Gerar.” After Edom—that is, the Jewish people—had sold its birthright in the manner described above, famine came upon Isaac and his household, that is, upon Christ and his apostles. It was the famine of which the Prophet speaks in the Psalm: “They shall return at evening, suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city” (Ps. XCVII). “But they themselves shall be scattered to eat” (Ps. LVIII).

For the dogs—the distinguished apostles, of whom the same Prophet says elsewhere, “The tongue of your dogs [shall receive its portion] from enemies through him” (Ps. LXVII)—did not find an abundance of food among Christ’s Jewish enemies, from whom they themselves were also descended according to the flesh. For they could eat—that is, convert and incorporate into themselves—only a few of them. [Col. 0453B] Therefore, when Peter was hungry because he had eaten little from Judaism, he was shown and commanded to seize and eat the Gentiles. For he saw a kind of vessel, like a sheet, lowered from heaven to earth by its four corners; in it were every kind of quadruped, creeping thing of the earth, and bird of heaven. It was said to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts X). Again: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (ibid.).

From that time, those who until then had suffered hunger were scattered to eat, murmuring because they had not been satisfied, and saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

Isaac therefore went to Gerar—that is, Christ to King Abimelech, and so forth. He went, I say, on these horses of his, upon which he had mounted: that is, on his preachers, whom he sent, of whom it is also written elsewhere: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. III). And he began to live as a stranger in Gerar, that is, among the Gentiles whom he had not formerly known. Gerar was the metropolis of the Philistines, which means “those falling,” and signifies Rome or the Roman empire, once the head of those perishing. Abimelech, “my father is king,” or “the kingdom of my father,” aptly signifies the multitude of the Gentiles—not because they had formerly been so, but because from that time onward it came about that Christ could rightly call them by such a name. [Col. 0453D]

## Chapter IX. On Isaac’s fear to confess that Rebecca was united to him in marriage.

The Lord appeared to him and said: “Do not go down into Egypt, but remain in the land which I shall tell you; live there as a stranger, and I shall be with you and bless you,” and so forth.

According to this mystical sense, the order of the letter has been inverted, as we have already said. For after [Col. 0454A] Christ’s apostles turned to the Gentiles, they did not go where they themselves wished, but where the Holy Spirit called them. For example, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, “having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia, they attempted to go to Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. When they had come down to Troas, a vision appeared to Paul by night: a certain Macedonian man stood and pleaded with him, saying, ‘Cross over into Macedonia and help us’” (Acts XVI). And they went to Macedonia, being assured that God had called them to preach the Gospel to them.

Isaac, therefore, being forbidden to go down into Egypt, lived in Gerar. But when the men of that place asked him about his wife, he said: “She is my sister.” For he feared to declare that she was united to him in marriage, thinking that they might kill him [Col. 0454B] because of her beauty. Thus, when persecution was pressing, believers feared openly to celebrate evangelical grace; while keeping themselves hidden away, they nevertheless practised Christian religion as they could—“needy, distressed, afflicted, wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and holes of the earth” (Heb. XI). Yet they were searched out even there, because the world was not worthy of them (ibid.).

The narrative continues: “When many days had passed and he remained there, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looking through a window, saw him playing with Rebecca his wife. Calling him, he said: ‘It is evident that she is your wife.’” For while they baptised secretly in crypts and the cemeteries of martyrs, and celebrated the other sacraments of faith as best they could—things that were play to the wise of this world, whose wisdom God made foolish (I Cor. I)—they were very often discovered and dragged before public tribunals. At length even earthly rulers accepted Christ’s yoke and began to become defenders of the evangelical faith or Christian religion which they had previously attacked. Hence it immediately adds: “And he commanded the people, saying: ‘Whoever touches this man’s wife shall die.’” [Col. 0454C] Indeed, Constantine was the first to establish by law what anyone should suffer who harassed a Christian; and thereafter Christian religion has been defended both by the swords of kings and by the word of priests.

## Chapter X. [Col. 0454D] On the words “Isaac sowed,” and the rest; and on the envious Philistines stopping up his wells.

Isaac sowed in that land and found a hundredfold in that year. The Lord blessed him; the man became rich, and he went on prospering and increasing until he became exceedingly great. He also had possessions of flocks and herds, and a very great household.

Sowing belongs to a time of peace and quiet. For scarcely, if ever, is land well cultivated and sown in wartime, especially so that the seed should return a hundredfold at harvest. Therefore, by Isaac’s sowing—through whose finding of a hundredfold the man became rich, prospering and increasing until he became exceedingly great—we rightly understand that magnificence of Christ’s name by which, in the peace of the Church, the seed of God’s Word was enlarged and multiplied.
