Priestly authority was joined with imperial power, so that workers of the Gospel might be permitted to go out to sow, while Christ’s opponents were not permitted to claim the broad field of the whole world for their errors. [Col. 0455A]

For this reason the envious Philistines stopped up all the wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug, filling them with earth, so that Abimelech himself said to Isaac: “Depart from us, for you have become far more powerful than we.” After the magnificence of Christ’s name had also taken possession of the Roman empire and idols had been despised, envy arose among heretics. Through them the devil, unable to uproot the Gospel by the force of persecution, attempted to corrupt the truth of the Scriptures.

Thus, after he had become exceedingly great, [Col. 0455B] the envious Palaestini, or Philisthiim—an expression interpreted “those falling by position”—stopped up all the wells which the servants of his father Abraham had dug in that time, filling them with earth. For the wells which the servants of Christ’s father, God, dug are all the holy Scriptures, composed by Moses, the prophets, and all the apostles, servants of God. These wells—that is, these Scriptures—the heretics stopped up, as far as they were able, in that time, so that it could not easily be found where the doctrine of truth was. This went so far that Abimelech himself said: “Depart from us, for you have become far more powerful than we.”

For the envious power of heretics grew so great that it gained possession even of the hearts of kings and emperors, and, using their swords, raged against Christians almost more cruelly than the error of the Gentiles had done. But Abimelech’s statement, “You have become far more powerful than we,” is consistent with this same sense. For the heavenly empire became more powerful among the Gentiles than the earthly empire, so much so that the tongue of priests bound fierce rulers and barbarous nations whom the sword of emperors could not reach; and the pontiffs of the Roman Church exercised dominion more widely than the Caesars of the Roman empire. For although Rome, enlarged by many victories, extended the right of its empire over land and sea, what martial labour subjected to it was less than what Christian peace brought under its sway. [Col. 0455C]

## Chapter XI. What it signifies that the shepherds of Gerar contended over two wells but not over the third, and [Col. 0455D] that Abimelech and his friends made a covenant with Isaac.

And he departed, so that they came to the torrent-bed of Gerar, etc. Christ departs from heretics; for they work nothing with God, nothing with Christ or with the Holy Spirit, but everything that is theirs is left to the devil. Christ himself, however, proceeds to the torrent-bed—that is, to the authors of the Scriptures, to those who await rain from heaven and, receiving it, swell into a great torrent.

“Again,” it says, “he dug other wells, which the servants of his father Abraham had dug and which, after his death, the Philistines had formerly stopped up.” For whatever heresy may arise, Christ is always present and ready; and he prepares some of his own, adorned by his gift with knowledge [Col. 0456A] and speech, able to stand against loquacious heretics and to give thirsty little ones pure truth from the Scriptures to drink. “And he called them by the same names by which his father had called them before”: that is, by the same truth and the same Spirit of truth he made them understand the Scriptures by which those authors whom the Father had sent before the Son’s coming—and whom the Father himself had given to the Son—wrote them.

“And they dug in the torrent-bed and found living water. But there too there was a dispute between the shepherds of Gerar and Isaac’s shepherds; they said, ‘The water is ours.’” The wells which his father’s servants had dug, those men filled up and stopped; but those which his servants dug they did not stop up, though they disputed and contended over them. Thus indeed the heretics stopped up with their earthly interpretations the sacred Scriptures [Col. 0456B] that were for the most part written before Christ’s coming. But they did not stop up the sacraments of living water—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—which were given from the coming, or the Passion, or the Resurrection of the Son; rather, they contended over them, saying, “The water is ours.” That is to say: “Our sacraments are the true sacraments; what we confer is holy, life-giving, and quickening; the Church is with us alone.”

In saying this the shepherds lie. For the Church must be believed to be not confined or constricted within one corner of the earth or within the portion belonging to any heresiarch, but spread among all nations, according to what God the Father promised to the Son when speaking in the Prophet: “Ask of me, and I will give [Col. 0456C] you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2).

There are, moreover, three wells which the servants of this Isaac dug. For there are three gifts of the Holy Spirit: baptism, the laying on of hands, and the renewal of all in the general resurrection of the dead. In accordance with these, David, as a type of Christ and the Church, as we have already said elsewhere, was anointed king for the third time. The shepherds contend over two of them, but not over the third, because heretics now quarrel over baptism and the laying on of hands, contending as they claim them for themselves. But when they are changed by universal regeneration, they will be unable to quarrel and will not dare to contend.

Therefore [Col. 0456D] he called its name “Breadth,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and made us increase upon the earth.” Thus amid accusations and hostilities Christ and his Church are enlarged, and the splendour of his name increases over the whole earth.

He went up from that place to Beersheba, where the Lord appeared to him that same night, saying: “I am the God of Abraham your father,” etc. This will take place at the end of the age: when all disputes, both those of Jews and of heretics, have been stilled, Christ will go up and build his altar where it is not now, and will dig a well of abundance or satiety for the remnant of Israel, so that they may drink the living water of the Scriptures. At the same time Abimelech and Ahuzzath his friend, and Phicol the commander of his army—kings and princes alike, Jews [Col. 0457A] and Gentiles alike—will enter into covenant with Christ.

Ahuzzath, for whom the Hebrew has “the company of his friends,” signifies not so much an individual as the crowd of friends who had come with the king, among whom was Phicol, the commander of his forces. “So he made them a feast. And after food and drink, they rose in the morning and swore an oath to one another; and Isaac dismissed them peacefully to their home.” When they make their covenant, Christ will give them a final banquet in the kingdom of their Father, and will dismiss each one to his own place: that is, he will render to each according to his own work and merit, a fitting place or dwelling; for there are many dwellings in the Father’s house (John 14).

“Then on that very day Isaac’s servants came and said: ‘We have found water.’” The end of all [Col. 0457B] that concerns Isaac is the rejoicing of those who say, “We have found water.” And rightly so. For on the very day when all that concerns Christ is fulfilled, praise and thanksgiving will resound, saying: “Through you, Christ, we have found the fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4).

Therefore he called it “Abundance,” and the city was named Beersheba to the present day. In this passage the city’s name Beersheba is interpreted as “well of abundance” or “well of satiety.” Although above we maintained that Beersheba was so named from the word for an oath, or from the number seven of the sheep, called *sabee*, nevertheless Isaac now, because water was found, makes an allusion to the city’s name. He slightly altered the letter: instead of the hissing Hebrew *sin*, with which *sabee* begins, he used the Greek sigma—that is, the Hebrew *samech* [Col. 0457C].

Thus the city of living waters, that is, the blessed fellowship of all the elect, is called the well of satiety or abundance, fulfilling what the Psalmist now prays for it: “Let peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121).

## CHAPTER XII. On Esau’s wives, both of whom offended Isaac and Rebekah.

Now Esau, at forty years of age, took as wives Judith, daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon of the same place; both offended the mind of Isaac and Rebekah.

The discussion must be continued from what was said above [Col. 0457D]: “And he went away, holding cheap the fact that he had sold his birthright” (Gen. 25). And behold, at the beginning of the account of the sons, the degeneration of Esau—the supplanter and one yet to be supplanted—is indicated. By declining more and more, he made room for his younger brother to hold his heel ever more closely. For just as above he sold his birthright for food, so now, by taking foreign wives in pursuit of his desires, he offended Isaac and Rebekah, because he despised the blessing of Abraham’s seed. For if he had desired to beget children within that blessing, he would never have taken a wife from the daughters of those whom both his father had rejected, his grandfather Abraham had judged to be avoided, and on whose account his mother Rebekah was weary of her life.

But he despised both their judgment [Col. 0458A] and God’s promises, evidently supposing that kinship with the inhabitants of the land could make him praiseworthy and renowned more than God’s help or grace could. For this reason the present Scripture did not omit the notable names of the family: “Judith,” it says, “daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, daughter of Elon of the same place.” Judith is interpreted “praising”; Beeri, “of my well”; Basemath, “in names”; Elon, “strong” or “oak.” By these names he seems manifestly rebuked for immersing himself in sinful alliances while desiring to be praised, enriched without God, made famous, and strengthened upon earth. Upon such people fear and terror rightly fall (Exod. 16), according to the name “Hittite,” which means “fear” or “terror.” Therefore he who fell away inwardly from God’s grace was deservedly rejected outwardly also, as the narrative immediately following will show.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Isaac’s old age, and why he had only one blessing.

(CHAPTER 27.) [Col. 0458B] Now Isaac grew old, his eyes grew dim, and he could not see. He called Esau his son and said to him, “My son.” He answered, “Here I am.” His father said to him: “You see that I have grown old, and I do not know the day of my death. Take your weapons, your quiver and bow, [Col. 0458C] and go out. When you have caught something by hunting, make me from it a dish, as you know that I like, and bring it that I may eat, and that my soul may bless you before I die.”

Here we must not pass over why Isaac had only one blessing. Esau cried out in lamentation: “Have you only one blessing, father? Bless me too, I beg you.” For the father had said: “I have made him your lord and subjected all his brothers to his service. I have established him with grain and wine; and after this, my son, what more can I do for you?” We must therefore inquire why he had only one blessing, what the grain and wine are that cannot be shared when divided, and thus make clear why Jacob ought more rightly than Esau to possess that same blessing as his inheritance.

First we say that there are not many seeds but one seed (Gal. 3), which is Christ, concerning whom Abraham had been promised that in him all nations would be blessed. What blessing could the father have had besides that seed [Col. 0458D]? Necessarily, then, he had only one. But there were two brothers, and from them two peoples were to be divided against one another, according to the truth of the saying: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly” (Gen. 25). How, then, could the one seed, which is Christ, be shared with them once divided? For he is one, and he is found not in division but in unity. Therefore one had to be preferred to the other; and the one preferred was he whom God commended, not he whom flesh and blood wished to commend by the right of primogeniture.

The present reading is, according to the simple letter, an open account of that supplanting. But the Hebrews maintain that the birthright itself was the inheritance or succession of the priesthood, or else those priestly garments mentioned here: “And [Col. 0459A] she clothed him in Esau’s very fine garments, which he had at home.” By the right of the firstborn, they say, Esau should have exercised the priestly office, and therefore already had the priestly garment in which he offered sacrifices to God, as did all firstborn sons before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Rebekah’s example, in preparing Jacob rather than Esau for the blessing, should be imitated in the Church.

Here, then, the further question arises: how could a priesthood so fraudulently usurped be valid, when the law remains to this day that whoever comes when summoned to receive the blessing of ordination and seizes it by climbing up from elsewhere ought to have his blessing judged not merely void [Col. 0459B], but rightly turned into a curse for him?

The answer to this is plainly easy: he did not usurp the blessing in a blameworthy manner. Indeed, whoever today is promoted not according to his example, we say, speaking according to the Gospel, has not entered through the door but has climbed up some other way (John 10). For the law is that no one should ordain someone for any gift, service, or eloquence, but the person whom the testimony of the Church present chooses on account of merit in life.

What then? Does Isaac not, according to the anagogical sense, bear the role of those who strive to ordain favourably for advantage or for a pastry? For when he says, “Take your weapons, your quiver [Col. 0459C] and bow; and when you have caught something by hunting, make me from it a dish,” and then adds, “that my soul may bless you before I die,” does he not plainly demand an advantage in exchange for a blessing? Yet this does not detract from this holy man; rather, what the Holy Spirit, the foreknower of future things, works in him for our edification is pleasing.

Thus in the present passage Isaac bears the role of any high priest; Rebekah, that of the Church, which is subject to him; and the two sons, Jacob and Esau, represent those who, in the household of the Church, are proposed for training in a holy calling despite contrary characters and a different end. The high priest indeed presides over the Church entrusted to him, as a husband over his wife or a head over the body. Nevertheless [Col. 0459D], the choice of those to be ordained belongs not to him alone but to the Church: for while he grows old amid many concerns, and his eyes are at times dimmed by the dust of external cares, she sees her sons more clearly and more readily; she knows their conduct, observes their purpose, and considers each person’s progress or decline.

When, therefore, she hears that a bishop, won over by the services of some unworthy man, intends to promote him and prefer him over one better, she ought to follow Rebekah’s example. Rebekah neither reproved her husband’s desire nor failed to act prudently, so that the father, delighted by the elder son’s hunting, might not prefer him to the better man—mindful of what God had said to her: “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25). Therefore Jacob did not seize the blessing by blameworthy theft; rather, with the order of justice preserved, he who was worthy [Col. 0460A] approached by God’s will and by the election of her who knew his merit.

## CHAPTER XV. Why God allowed the holy man to turn in affection toward the reprobate; and what the two kids and Esau’s garments signify.

Again it is asked why God allowed the holy man to turn in affection toward the reprobate, and why he wished one who had not been called to be blessed by a man who did not know and could not see him.

Here we first say that the Lord came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and did not wish to take the children’s bread and give it to dogs (Matt. 15), and that he brought the first blessing to the Jewish people, to whom were entrusted the oracles of God, the promise, the giving of the law, and the confession of the covenant [Col. 0460B] (Rom. 9). But because they refused to believe, the blessing was transferred to Jacob—that is, to the younger people. Yet the elder son was not entirely despised, because when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

Thus the allegorical meaning begun above lies ready to hand, long ago handed down by the holy Fathers and now celebrated by the mouth of the whole Church. For the true Isaac, namely the Son of God, grew old and his eyes grew dim when, clothed in the old age and senescence of our nature, he was also darkened by bodily death. In that dimness of old age he commanded Esau, his firstborn: “Take,” he said, “your weapons, your quiver and bow; and when you have caught something by hunting, make [Col. 0460C] me from it a dish.”

For throughout his life and even in his death, he invited the former people to repentance, through himself and through his apostles after the glory of his resurrection, so that by believing they might offer him the food of which he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). But Esau delayed and still wanders abroad. Meanwhile Rebekah—that is, the mother of grace, whose affection had turned from the human affection of this father toward another son—urged the younger son, namely the people of the Gentiles, to enter and obtain beforehand the inheritance of blessing, not empty-handed but with two kids. For the law says: “You shall not appear empty-handed before the Lord your God” (Deut. 16).

One kid could indeed have sufficed for food; for not even one person [Col. 0460D] could have consumed a kid (Exod. 12). But this too happened figuratively: the one who approaches the grace of Christ’s blessing must profess both the New and the Old Testament, and such confession is food for Christ, the Son of God.

“And she clothed him,” it says, “in Esau’s very fine garments, which he had at home.” The father of the household in the Gospel identifies these garments by their names when the son who had been lost and is found, who had been dead and has come to life, returns to him: “Quickly,” he says, “bring out the first robe and clothe him; put a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet” (Luke 15). The elder son—that is, the former people—lost these through his fault. “And she put the skins of the kids around his hands and covered the bare part of his neck.”

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 0461A] It is not surprising that Isaac was deceived, so as to say: “The voice indeed is Jacob’s voice, but the hands,” etc.

In these matters Isaac was so deceived that he said: “The voice indeed is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.” Nor is it surprising that a righteous man should have been ignorant of something and done something contrary to his will. No human being, except him who for our salvation put on human flesh, possessed complete knowledge and most certain truth.

Paul, accordingly, knows in part and prophesies in part, and now sees through a mirror in an enigma (1 Cor. 13). He also says that we do not know how to pray as we ought (Rom. 8), because when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial will be abolished (1 Cor. 13). Samuel the prophet, numbered with Moses in God’s priesthood (Ps. 98), was sent to anoint a king. When he saw Eliab, the eldest of Jesse’s sons, he said: “Behold, his anointed is before the Lord.” And the Lord said to Samuel: “Do not look upon his face or the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For God does not see as man sees: man sees the face, but God looks upon the heart” (1 Sam. 16). And, as he remained ignorant concerning each son in turn, he is described as not knowing until David.

Elisha also, glorified with a double spirit, whose bones restored life to a lifeless corpse (2 Kgs. 13), when the Shunammite came to him on the mountain and fell weeping at his feet, said—when Gehazi tried to prevent her—“Let her alone, for her soul is bitterly distressed; the Lord has hidden it [Col. 0461C] from me and has not told me” (2 Kgs. 4). There are more examples than need be offered to show that holy men dear to God knew only what was revealed to them by the Lord, while they did not know what had not been revealed to them; and that Zechariah and Daniel, at individual visions, asked the angel and humbly begged him to explain what the things were that they had seen.

## CHAPTER XVII. On his blessing, and how it is to be understood concerning Christ.

As soon as he perceived the fragrance of his garments, he blessed him and said: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed.”

The aforesaid garments—namely, the first robe which we have in the washing [Col. 0461D], the shoes upon the feet, which are the examples of the ancient saints, and the ring, that is, the seal of faith—together with the remaining virtues or the prayers of penitents, have a great and most pleasing fragrance. Delighted by such things, therefore, the author of the blessing says: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field which God has blessed”—with “may it be” understood.

For it follows: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth an abundance of grain and wine.” For it belongs to a field which God has blessed to receive from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth an abundance of grain and wine, and to be filled with such abundance; that indeed is to be blessed by God.

For a rational creature, the dew of heaven is nothing other than the grace of the Holy Spirit that remits sins; while the richness of the earth, or the abundance of grain and wine, is the opening of the mind [Col. 0462A] to understand the mysteries of the kingdom of God hidden in the Scriptures. For there lies hidden the grain of wheat which, falling into the earth, died and brought forth much fruit (John 12); and the wine that gladdens the heart of man, and the oil by which the face is made cheerful (Ps. 103).

Therefore, when he says, “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which God has blessed,” and immediately adds, “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth an abundance of grain and wine,” he both prophesies and desires what has now taken place and continues until the end of the age: namely, that through faith Abraham’s seed is like one field, the breadth of the whole world, made fruitful by the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit. One gift is for remission of sins, by which the face of the world is renewed through heavenly dew; the other is the distribution of diverse graces of the same Holy Spirit, by which we are enriched in every respect, according to the Apostle, so that we lack nothing in any grace (1 Cor. 1).

Having said these things [Col. 0462B], he turns his words, as it were, from the whole body to its head: “Let peoples serve you and tribes adore you. Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you.” For who is he whom peoples serve and tribes adore except the head of the seed of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—namely Christ, who is not only man, but is God and man, the one Jesus Christ? He is indeed the Lord of his brothers, and before him all the sons of his mother—that is, all citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all—rightly bow down. For all his brothers are sons of God by adoption, and all [Col. 0462C] the adopted are his brothers. He alone, however, is the natural Son, both Son of Man and Son of God: in one respect their brother, in the other respect the God of his worshipping brothers and the Lord of his serving brothers.

“May he who curses you be cursed, and he who blesses you be filled with blessings.” He curses Christ who blasphemes Christ, as, for example, the poisonous tongues of the scribes and Pharisees saying, “He has a demon” (John 10), “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 12), and the like. Conversely, he blesses Christ who confesses and praises Christ, who says in heart and lips: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21). The Apostle says that no one speaking in the Spirit of God says [Col. 0462D] “Jesus be accursed,” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). Therefore, because whoever curses Christ lacks the Holy Spirit, which truly is to be cursed, and whoever blesses him speaks in the Holy Spirit, which truly is to be blessed, the Holy Spirit is God’s true and only blessing. Rightly, then, he says: “May he who curses you be cursed, and he who blesses you be filled with blessings.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. That carnal Jews are like Esau, who did not seek the spiritual blessing; and on Esau’s hatred.

Isaac had scarcely finished speaking, and Jacob had gone out, when Esau came. He brought to his father food cooked from his hunting, saying: “Rise, my father, and eat of your son’s hunting, that your soul may bless me,” etc.

It is clear [Col. 0463A] that Esau, just as he lacked faith, so also lacked knowledge and hope of that seed which is Christ, in whom the whole substance of the paternal blessing consisted. For among other things he says: “Have you only one blessing, father?” But we have already said above why Isaac had only one blessing, and why one and the same blessing ought not to have been shared by the two brothers: namely, because they were divided and were to be divided, according to the answer: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly” (Gen. 25).

Therefore, since in these twin brothers that which was to happen until the end of the age is plainly evident—that, once divided against each other, those who are Abraham’s according to the flesh only and those who are Abraham’s by faith, Christ would be the inheritance only of those who were by faith, whatever their descent according to the flesh from a human being—let us hear the final utterance, that is, the remnants of the blessing.

He who sought not one but many blessings, saying, “Have you only one blessing, father?” and who wept with loud lamentation—Isaac, moved, said to him: “Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above.” This richness of earth and this dew of heaven differ from those written above in Jacob’s blessing. For that blessing is such that service of peoples, adoration of tribes, the bowing of brothers, and the blessing of all who are worthy of God’s blessing follow it. But earthly things follow this one: “You shall live by the sword, and you shall serve your brother.”

This also happened according to the historical account. For David placed garrisons in Idumea and established a military post, and all Idumea became subject to David (1 Chron. 18). More rightly, however, the servitude is understood here of which Wisdom says: “Free men shall serve a prudent servant” (Sir. 10). In this place the richness of earth and the dew of heaven are a temporal filling of the belly. This final blessing suits him who did not know hunger for spiritual grace, since he sold his birthright for one meal.

In the days of Titus and Vespasian the Jewish people sought this blessing with loud lamentation, holding food in their hands—not food from their hunt, cooked in a manner Isaac gladly ate, but rather, with incredible obstinacy more than endurance, offering unwelcome [Col. 0463D] sacrifices amid the swords of their enemies and their own blood. Thus, before the altar, in a spectacle astonishing to their enemies, they offered as they fell and fell while offering. But the dignity of the priesthood had already passed to the younger son. The Father, filled with that son’s offerings, was now declaring in facts what he had foretold through the prophet: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

Certainly, what is finally said here—“And the time shall come when you shake yourself free and loosen his yoke from your neck”—has happened according to history and will happen according to allegory. For in the time of Joram son of Jehoshaphat, Edom rebelled so as not to be under Judah’s dominion (2 Chron. 21). And near the end of the age, he who is now [Col. 0464A] Esau will no longer be a servant in the letter, as he now is, having the liberty of malice as a veil; rather, he will be like the servants of God (1 Pet. 2), whom he now serves by carrying about his books for their use. He too, I say, will be like God’s servants: a servant of righteousness indeed, but free from sin (Rom. 6).

The reading makes plain what his weeping and lamentation were like, when it immediately adds: “The days of mourning for my father will come, and I shall kill Jacob my brother.” Rightly, therefore, as the Apostle says, “he found no place for repentance, though he sought it with tears” (Heb. 12). For the disposition of his heart in that very weeping and lamentation was like Cain’s when his face fell because of Abel (Gen. 4).

## CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 0464B] What it signifies that Isaac calmly endured the obtaining of the blessing, and that, at Rebekah’s urging, he sent Jacob to take a wife.

These things were reported to Rebekah. If Esau said them in his heart, how were they reported to Rebekah? But it should be understood that a man speaks something in his heart when he does not wish what he says to be publicly heard. Conversely, one is rightly said to speak openly when he wishes what he says, wherever he says it, to be publicly heard. Therefore the Lord, though he had said many things privately to his disciples, nevertheless says to the high priest: “I have spoken openly to the world, and in secret I have said nothing” (John 18).

She sent for and summoned Jacob her son, and said to him: “Behold, Esau your brother threatens to kill you. Therefore now [Col. 0464C], my son, obey my voice; rise, flee to Laban my brother in Haran, and stay with him a few days,” etc.

All counsel on Jacob’s behalf begins with Rebekah. She sent him to obtain the blessing; she first offers the counsel of flight; and then, anxious also about his marriage, she says to Isaac: “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the stock of this land, I do not wish to live.” Isaac calmly endures the obtaining of the blessing and approves her counsel or wish as excellent, so that by their shared consent Jacob is sent to take a wife from the daughters of Laban.

Thus all the counsel for the salvation of the Gentiles proceeded, before our Lord Jesus Christ, from the authority of Scripture. For he himself wished, through human [Col. 0464D] affection, to cherish the Jewish people as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings (Matt. 23). Yet, because the truth of the Scriptures required that their house be left desolate to them (ibid.), he neither opposed this nor turned back—just as Isaac spoke no word against Rebekah or Jacob concerning Esau’s being deprived or Jacob’s being put forward.

Rebekah shows what religion we Gentiles ought to hold: namely, one grounded upon the faith of the Fathers, not upon Jewish ceremonies, as in the Acts of the Apostles we read that it pleased the Holy Spirit and the apostles (Acts 15). Although Christ had given no command on this matter while he was with them, but had rather said, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10), he nevertheless calls this decision a judgment and regards it as valid.

## CHAPTER XX. Again on the same matter, and that Esau, as a type of the Jews, increased his sin.

(CHAPTER 28.) Therefore Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, and commanded him: “Do not take a wife from the race of Canaan; but go and proceed to Mesopotamia of Syria, to the house of Bethuel, [Col. 0465A] your mother’s father, and take for yourself from there a wife from the daughters of Laban, your uncle.”

The one whom Isaac had unknowingly—or rather, whom God had blessed through Isaac’s unknowing—he now calls by name and knowingly blesses: that is, he confirms in him the blessing that had been obtained. Esau, however, as was said above, by attaching himself to foreign wives to the offence of his father’s and mother’s feelings, was no longer [Col. 0465B] a son of Abraham, Isaac, or Rebekah. For he had begun to beget offspring in his own flesh and in his own name, not in the blessing of Abraham’s seed, and to build a household other than God’s.

Therefore Isaac blessed his son. But the expected end of that blessing was none other than Abraham’s seed itself, which is Christ. Rightly, then, these are the words of the one blessing: “May God Almighty bless you, make you increase and multiply, so that you become a multitude of peoples; may he give you the blessings of Abraham and to your seed after you, that you may possess the land of your pilgrimage which he promised to your grandfather.”

Esau, seeing that his father had blessed Jacob and recognizing that his father did not willingly look upon the daughters of Canaan, went to Ishmael and took, besides the wives he had previously had, [Col. 0465C] Mahelet, daughter of Ishmael son of Abraham and sister of Nebaioth.

Esau acted either as a fool or, indeed, as truly stupid. For if he wished to lessen his mother’s weariness or soften the offence to his father’s feelings, it was foolish to attempt this in such a manner and with such an intention—to turn, without consulting his parents, whom he had already offended through his other wives, toward the tents of slaves, which was to go out with the expelled. Thus Sarah had said: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21), and so it had been done.

But if, as is more likely, he was angry with his parents on Jacob’s account, like Cain whose face had fallen, and acted thus in order to offend them further, he was undoubtedly stupid. In either case, by tripling his marriages to the offence of his parents [Col. 0465D] he has no excuse, “for fool and stupid alike shall perish” (Ps. 48). So also the Jews, who first abandoned God’s traditions for human traditions (Matt. 15), and afterward, persecuting Christ and his disciples, degenerated further into Ishmael, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also now” (Gal. 4). Whether they do this through foolishness or through stupidity, they will have no excuse for their sin (John 15).

## CHAPTER XXI. On Jacob’s journeying and his vision.

Thus Jacob, having departed from Beersheba, was making his way to Haran [Col. 0466A]. When he came to a certain place and wished to rest there after sunset, he took some of the stones lying there, placed one beneath his head, and slept in that same place. It is therefore not without reason that the Apostle calls our fathers strangers and sojourners. For after he had said, “All these died in faith, not having received the promises, but seeing them from afar and greeting them,” he immediately added: “And confessing that they are strangers and pilgrims upon the earth. For those who say such things make it clear that they seek a homeland. And if indeed they had remembered that country from which they had gone out, they surely had opportunity to return. But now they desire a better, that is, a heavenly country” (Heb. 11).

Behold: it is easy to recognize in Jacob such a confession or expectation as theirs. Was he really so destitute and poor [Col. 0466B] that necessity compelled him to leave his land with only his staff, as he himself later confesses when he says: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies” (Gen. 32)? For his having gone forth so completely alone is also shown by the fact that he had nowhere to lay his head except by taking stones that lay there, putting one beneath his head, and sleeping in that place.

Was not his father exceedingly great? For it was written shortly before: “The man grew rich and went on prospering and increasing, until he became exceedingly great,” so that Abimelech himself said: “Depart from us, for you have become far more powerful than we” (Gen. 26). And Abraham, Jacob’s grandfather—the conqueror of kings—was doubtless rich and renowned. What, then, except a great poverty of spirit, worthy [Col. 0466C] of imitation, is set before us for contemplation in this departure of our father Jacob, when he went to receive a wife, waiting in his father’s faith for Christ—the salvation of the world and blessing of all nations—to be born from his seed?

O flight worthy of the protection of the heavenly sanctuary! By faith alone, without the reading of the Scriptures, he had learned that, in order to possess the inheritance of blessing and to sow the expectation of the blessed seed, one must set out not pompously, but humbly and with a supplicant conscience. Moreover, how truly it was said, “The Lord is near to those who are broken of heart” (Ps. 33), is clear from what immediately follows: “And he saw in a dream a ladder [Col. 0466D] standing upon the earth, its top touching heaven; and angels ascending and descending by it; and the Lord leaning upon the ladder, saying to him: ‘I am the Lord God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac.’”

All who, sent with the blessing of God the Father and of his Son Jesus Christ, together with the grace of the Holy Spirit, lay aside the burdens of the world in order to sow spiritual seed and press, naked and unencumbered, toward their appointed goal, imitate him. They keep watch, labour in all things, and are sober, judging themselves to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2); and with the Apostle they say: “We have here no abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13). To them the gate of heaven is opened, and this ladder which appeared to him is raised up for those who ascend; upon it angels are shown ascending and descending [Col. 0467A].

That descent and ascent undoubtedly mean for us nothing other than descending by exaltation and ascending by humility. The upright ladder itself is our life in this world, raised by the Lord toward heaven when the heart has been humbled. We call the two sides of this ladder our body and soul; into these sides the divine summons has inserted various rungs of humility or discipline, which must be climbed.

## CHAPTER XXII. A mystical interpretation of the same vision

Nevertheless, in order to treat the present matter and the traveller’s own person, it must be said allegorically what this ladder signifies, touching the heavens by its height [Col. 0467B] and having the Lord leaning upon it, while the gate stands open. This is indeed a great condescension of heavenly mercy: it could not restrain its compassion toward this pilgrim or fugitive, but hastened to show him what a secure refuge it was preparing in the height of heaven for him and for his seed.

For what was this ladder of such height to him, if not that line of descent which we all know from the Gospel book of the generation of Jesus Christ, Son of God? The highest rung of its ladder, upon which the Lord leaned, was none other than Joseph, the one hundred and twenty-second and last man in that genealogy, husband of Mary, from whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ (Matt. 1). Was the Lord not leaning upon the ladder when, having become man, he made use of Joseph’s fatherly help and pious conveyance, needing it as he fled from place to place while Herod pursued him? He was fatherless in this world—that is, begotten without a carnal father [Col. 0467C].

Jacob therefore saw the ladder, having the Lord leaning upon its summit, touching the heavens and opening heaven’s gate. In this figure he foresaw the Lord leaning upon it, and that his own lineage would have the Lord incarnate from himself, through whom he would reach the heavens and enter the gate of heaven, hitherto closed to humankind. This dream suits both the event and the time, according to the person and undertaking of him who saw it. For he was then travelling with God’s blessing and at his father’s command in order to take a wife from among the daughters of his uncle Laban, with faith and hope in the promise made to his own grandfather.

He also saw angels ascending [Col. 0467D] and descending by it. The angels of God—that is, the holy messengers—are preachers of the truth, heralds or witnesses alike of the divine and human generation of Jesus Christ. They never stand fixed solely above or below: they never proclaim Jesus Christ, the seed of Abraham, to be merely God or merely man. Rather, running upward and downward with unimpeded foot, as they ascend they say, “In the beginning was the Word”; as they descend they say, “The Word became flesh” (John 1). In descending, they confess God made man; in ascending, they confess man united to God.

Therefore the two preachers of this genealogy, Matthew and Luke, fittingly divided between themselves this ascent and descent: the former descended from Abraham as far as the Virgin’s womb (Matt. 1); [Col. 0468A] the latter ascended from the one “who was supposed to be the son of Joseph” to God himself (Luke 3).

“The land in which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed.” This was said of the seed according to the flesh. But what follows—“You shall spread abroad to the west and east, north and south”—was said of the seed of faith; for he concluded thus: “And in you and in your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed.” The former occurred before, the latter after the coming of Christ, his seed. For in his twelve tribes he then gave him the land in which he slept; in Christ he blessed the whole world in its four regions.

Likewise, what he added—“And I will be your guardian wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land; nor will I leave you until I have completed all that I have said”—was both spoken and fulfilled concerning Jacob himself and his seed. He did not leave him until he brought him back to say: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies” (Gen. 32). He did not leave his seed until he led them from Egypt into this land, with silver and gold, so that there was none feeble among their tribes (Ps. 104). Nor did he cease to spread his seed, which is Christ, into the four regions of the world, as it is written: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit unto its height; and none is hidden from his heat” (Ps. 18) [Col. 0468B].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the words, “Truly the Lord is in this place,” and on what that place is

When Jacob awoke from sleep, he said: “Truly [Col. 0468C] the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.” And, afraid, he said: “How terrible is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.”

When he says, “The Lord is in this place,” “by the presence of grace” must be understood; for he is in this place and in every place by the magnitude of his presence. For of the immensity of his majesty it is most truly said: “Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). Likewise: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Isa. 6).

And, afraid, he says: “How terrible is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.” Notice that he fears not the Lord himself but the place, which he calls terrible. What ground for fear or terror could this place have in itself? Was it because he saw the Lord in that place in a dream? Yet the same God often appeared elsewhere both to Jacob and to his fathers Abraham and Isaac. There is therefore no doubt that he was a prophet, as it is likewise written in the Psalm concerning him and his aforementioned fathers: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not deal wickedly with my prophets” (Ps. 104). Here, with his heart enlarged by the spirit of prophecy, he foresaw what was signified by such a dream and was struck with awe at the place of which this was a figure [Col. 0468D].

That place, namely, is the Church of God. Hence the Psalmist says: “God in his holy place; God who makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (Ps. 68). He marvelled and was awestruck at the future Church of God and at the fearful works of God in it, through which, as the Apostle says, “the manifold wisdom of God has been made known to principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3) [Col. 0469A]. Likewise Habakkuk had been awestruck by the prophetic Spirit when he said: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was awestruck” (Hab. 3).

The sum of those works is this: as was said shortly before, through Christ’s humanity the gate of heaven was opened and heavenly things were joined to earthly things.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Why, rising in the morning, he took the stone which he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil upon it

Rising therefore in the morning, he took the stone which he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil upon it. And he called the name of the city Bethel, which had formerly been called Luz.

What cause or reason was there that, rising [Col. 0469B] in the morning, he took the stone which he had placed beneath his head, set it up as a pillar, poured oil upon it, and named the city Bethel, which means “house of God”? The same reason should govern every person in every place of his dominion: to build a house for the name of the Lord.

The first thing is that, following Jacob’s example and confessing that he is a stranger and sojourner upon earth, a person should place a stone beneath his head—that is, establish his conscience in Christ—so that in sleep he may rest in him, according to his precept or counsel: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11).

Sleeping in that rest, he should dream—that is, by believing, he should now see through a mirror and in an enigma, since he cannot yet see face to face (1 Cor. 13)—what Jacob saw as future: namely, the ladder upon which the Lord leaned, that is, the evangelical genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham, of which we have spoken above. It reaches heaven and opened heaven’s gate to us; having destroyed the dividing wall of hostility (Eph. 2), it joined earthly things to heavenly. Thus was fulfilled what Christ himself foretold: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you shall see the heavens opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man” (John 1) [Col. 0469C].

These things, I say, should be dreamed throughout the whole night by one who sleeps and says, “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5): that is, throughout his entire life he should meditate upon them in the peace and quiet of his heart. Whoever in this faith erects an altar to invoke the Lord’s name is Jacob by unity of faith, with this difference: Jacob dreamed and believed things future; the present person reads or hears things past or present, and nevertheless believes.

These words, therefore, of Jacob waking and crying, “Truly the Lord is in this place,” and the rest that follows, the Catholic Church of Christ fittingly took from his mouth; and from every place in which the name of the Lord is invoked, she truthfully declares and most steadfastly says: “This place is terrible; this is the house of God and the gate of heaven.” For where the holy baptismal rite is celebrated and the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood is performed—whence faithful souls are reborn for heaven and borne to heaven by the hands of angels descending and ascending—what is it but the gate of heaven and a place terrible to the gates of hell?

There the stone of the pillar, and here the stone of the altar [Col. 0470A], solemnly anointed with the oil of blessing, signifies Christ, “whom God anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44). What the individual stones are in the walls of the visible structure, individual persons are in the spiritual building. Thus it is not in vain that the dedication of a temple or altar is customarily celebrated year after year with festal praises. For as the altar signifies Christ, and each stone of the walls signifies each chosen person—living stones (1 Pet. 2), built upon the foundation of apostles and prophets for the construction of the temple of the one Church (Eph. 2)—so all that we sing under the names of altar, stones, foundations, and walls are fitting thanksgivings both for the chief anointing of Christ, the Holy of Holies [Col. 0470B], and for the regeneration of every believer.

For it could not be done that each of us should celebrate annually the day of his own regeneration; yet neither was the joy of so great a grace, bestowed upon each one of us from the house of the Church, to be omitted without a commemorative festival. Therefore, although we were born at different times and were likewise reborn at different times through the Church’s sacraments performed in their respective places, we fittingly celebrate, under particular festivals, the universal festivals of the places in which we received God’s life-giving gifts.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Jacob’s vow

He also made a vow, saying: “If the Lord is with me and guards me on the way by which I walk, and [Col. 0470C] gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear.”

This must be done both bodily by those who possess such resources and spiritually by all—both by those who use this world and by those who have nothing in this world. For the Psalmist says: “The thought of man shall give thanks to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep festival for you” (Ps. 75). And afterward: “Vow and render to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him—to the Terrible One, to him who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth” (ibid.).

Nor ought we to pass over the conditional prayer of the one making the vow. For after he had said, “If the Lord is with me and guards me on the way by which I walk,” this son of a powerful man, as was said above, a man exceedingly great and rich, also added: “And gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear” [Col. 0470D]. He said this as a poor man, indeed as one truly begging from God. Nor is this surprising, since even the greatest and strongest king confesses in the Psalm that he is needy and poor: “But I am needy,” or, “But I am a beggar and poor” (Ps. 69). Likewise: “For I am poor and needy” (Ps. 85).

The fathers, therefore, provided their children with a good example: however rich we may be, let us all say, as beggars before the doors of heavenly grace, “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11). We should ask God, the Father of all, not only for the bread of spiritual nourishment but also for the bread necessary for life (John 6), so that we may confess that this too is ours by his gift—he alone both could and deigned to create it—and that it is no less necessary for a king shining upon his throne than for a widow sitting at the millstone.

Therefore, as true poor people, let us ask the Father under one name for a threefold bread: the bread of eternal life, of which he said, “And the bread which I shall give you is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid.) [Col. 0471A]; the bread of understanding, of which he said, “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8; Matt. 4); and the bread which he alone brings forth from the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, together with the clothing by which we may be covered—namely, the clothing of holiness and righteousness.

Having received these things, we shall not ungratefully offer him tithes and sacrifices from all that we possess: tithes, that the labourer who serves at the altar may have his reward, since he is worthy of it; and peace-offerings—that is, “the sacrifice of lips confessing his name”—so that we may have peace toward him and do all things in charity.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On how, coming into the eastern land, he saw a well in the field and three flocks around it

**(CHAP. 29.)** Jacob therefore set out and came into the eastern land. He saw a well in the field, and three flocks of sheep lying beside it. For the cattle were watered from that well, whose mouth was closed by a great stone. It was customary, when all the sheep had been gathered, to roll away the stone; and, after the flocks had been refreshed, to replace it over the mouth of the well.

The literal sense of this narrative is plain and open [Col. 0471C]; yet in its very plainness it would produce great astonishment in the attentive reader, unless the authority of the preceding Fathers had already opened its meanings. For who would suppose that this freeborn son of such great Fathers was without divine reasons when he served in so laborious a bondage, for wages repeatedly changed, tending sheep for the sake of wives—especially under the protection of God, who had said to him, “I will be your guardian wherever you go” (Gen. 28)?

But no: with the eyes of faith let us contemplate in this mirror also the shining image of the Sun from above—that is, the beautiful and true allegorical likeness of the Son of God—and at the same time, according to anagoge, a pattern worthy of imitation by any faithful minister of his.

Thus Esau having been rejected, Jacob was chosen and consecrated with his father’s blessing; at his father’s command he went abroad to receive a wife. That is: Jesus Christ, God and man, chosen from among thousands, having grace poured out upon his lips and blessed for ever, girds himself in the exile of this world with the office of holy preaching, in order to unite the Church to himself. He came to the well, whose mouth was closed by a great stone and from which the cattle were watered, where it was customary, once all the sheep had been gathered, to roll away the stone and, after the flocks had been refreshed, to replace it over the well’s mouth.

The wise of this world would certainly judge these things, and what follows, ridiculous, empty, and unworthy of public ears, unless stewards of God’s mysteries were accustomed to disclose openly beneath the coarse veil of the letter the splendid majesty of the meanings [Col. 0472A]. What, then? It is indeed a great and admirable mystery.

This man came into the eastern land, he whose name, according to the prophet, is “the East” or “Rising” (*Oriens*) (Zech. 6). By his very coming he made his land eastern, which, according to the Psalmist, he blessed, illuminating those who sat in darkness and the shadow of death (Ps. 84). He came to the well whose mouth was closed by a great stone, beside which three flocks of sheep lay—that is, he came to open the Scripture, which Jews, Samaritans, and Gentiles, though divided from one another in every way, sought out (John 4).

For Jews and Samaritans alike possessed among themselves the Scripture of the holy Law; yet they were so divided from one another that, as the Evangelist testifies, Jews would not even associate with Samaritans in drawing water from a well (John 4)—that is, in the elemental water [Col. 0472B]. The Gentiles, moreover, were more remote from both, since they did not worship the God of heaven, yet sought to know the same Scripture translated by the seventy interpreters.

Yet these and the others lay there in vain. The scribes and Pharisees had closed the well of sacred Scripture with a great stone: having abandoned God’s traditions for their own traditions, they had obstructed it with a perverse interpretation. Hence they are openly rebuked in the Gospel, when the Lord says: “Woe to you lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who were entering” (Luke 11). Again: “Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your traditions? For God says: ‘Honour your father and your mother’; but you say: ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, Whatever gift there is from me will profit you’” (Matt. 15) [Col. 0472C]. And things like these.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Who the shepherds were mystically, to whom he spoke concerning the watering of the sheep, and who Rachel herself was

And he said to the shepherds: “Brothers, where are you from?” They answered: “From Haran.” *Haran* is interpreted “angry” or “ornament.” This name suitably fits those shepherds who fed themselves. He calls them brothers, as though they were known to him; yet he says to them, as to strangers, “Where are you from?” For according to the flesh they were indeed his brothers, but according to the Spirit he did not know them—nor did he know whence they were.

For they were angry and ornamental: within they were full of robbery and murder, while outwardly they were religious and severe, like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to human eyes but within are full of dead men’s bones (Matt. 23) [Col. 0472D]. Questioning them, he said: “Do you know Laban, son of Bethuel?” They replied: “We know him.” “Is he well?” he asked. They said: “He is well; and behold, his daughter Rachel is coming with his flock.”

*Laban* means “white”; *Nahor*, “rest of light”; *Rachel*, “sheep” or “one seeing God.” This comes about through differences of accents or letters, so that names are often altered into different meanings. Laban signifies the whole world, in respect of that part of it which belongs, through Christ’s redemption, to the rest of eternal light: he whitened it by that baptism, through faith in his passion, as the Prophet says in the Psalm: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50).

Rachel, his daughter, signifies that part of the elect which is from the Jews; for the other daughter, Leah—whose name means “laborious”—holds the type of the Church which is among the Gentiles [Col. 0473A]. Therefore, through the indications received from those whom he asked, “Brothers, where are you from?” Jacob came to the house for which he was seeking. That is, through the election or teaching of those seated on Moses’ chair, there is testimony and a sure distinction as to who belongs to Christ and who is his.

Jacob said: “There is still much of the day left, and it is not time for the flocks to be brought back to the folds. First give the sheep water, and then lead them back to pasture.” They answered: “We cannot, until all the cattle are gathered and we remove the stone from the mouth of the well, so that we may water the flocks.”

Why did this stranger know the sheep’s proper time better than the native shepherds, unless because Christ the good shepherd knew better than the scribes and Pharisees how to care for souls? And what does it mean to say, “First give the sheep water, and then lead them back to pasture,” except to command shepherds to speak in such a way that they first do—that is, that what they preach in words they should teach beforehand by the example of their deeds?

Those who do not do this still have much of the day—that is, of the divine work—remaining for them; nor is it time for such hirelings to bring the sheep back to the folds, where they may receive their supposedly due reward. Such were those shepherds of Israel to whom woe was proclaimed through Ezekiel: they were able not to lead the sheep back to pasture but to feed themselves (Ezek. 34) [Col. 0473B]. Therefore they say, “We cannot until all the cattle are gathered,” and so forth.

For it was their custom to refrain from instructing all souls until people had assembled at Jerusalem from every district and even from the nations for a feast day—for example, Passover or the Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*)—in order to worship. Then, at their own discretion, as though the stone had been removed, they poured out for them a scant, shallow water of doctrine: teaching them to tithe mint, cumin, and dill, while offering no example of life, and neglecting the weightier matters of the Law—judgment, righteousness, and faith (Matt. 23).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the same subject, and on why he kissed her and wept with a raised voice

While they were still speaking, behold, Rachel came with [Col. 0473D] the sheep of her father; for she herself was tending the flock. When Jacob saw her and knew her to be his kinswoman, together with the sheep of his uncle Laban, he removed the stone by which the well was closed; and, having watered the flock, he kissed her. Then he raised his voice and wept, and so forth.

How much better did he remove the stone and water the flock than did those shepherds: he who, condemning Pharisaic traditions, preached the truth of Scripture without respect of persons (Matt. 22). He did not require the flocks of the people to be gathered to himself, though they pressed upon him of their own accord and hurried to him from the cities (Luke 8); rather, he went around through cities and villages (Matt. 9), saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). This was to weep with a raised voice. Hence in another place he says to those who did not repent: “We lamented, and you did not weep” (Luke 7).

Thus, having watered the flock, he kissed her. This was clearly already a certain, though slight, betrothal of his future bride, because by his preaching he joined to himself not very many from among the Jews. He kissed her because he knew her to be his kinswoman. Kinsfolk (*consobrini*) are so called, as it were, from “together-sisters” (*consorores*), because they are born from sisters, or from a brother and sister. All Jews according to the flesh were related to the Lord; but he did not know this of all—that is, he did not draw near to the kinship of all, for in his case to know is to draw near and approve.

Those whom he knew in his own manner, he kissed in their small number—that is, joined them to himself and revealed his secrets to them as to friends [Col. 0474A]. But she hurried and announced it to her father. This is fitting: through those few disciples whom he had from the Synagogue, Christ the Lord became known to the whole world, whose entirety is represented in Laban, and its parts in his daughters, as we said above, according to election.

How warmly he received him after hearing the reasons for his journey is immediately stated in a brief utterance: “You are my bone and my flesh.” It is the same as if he said: “Behold, what is mine is yours; for you are my bone and my flesh.” In turn, the following makes clear how kindly Jacob submitted himself to service, and how moderately he awaited marriage: “After the days of one month had been completed, he said to him: ‘Because you are my brother, will you serve me for nothing? Tell me what wages you will receive.’ Now he had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the younger was called Rachel. Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was beautiful in face and comely in appearance.”

The Church from the Gentiles, which is figured by Leah, as was said above, had weak eyes. For it had been defiled by the fault of idolatry; the faculty of reason had been corrupted in the vices of its mind, and it could not see the brightness of the one true deity which is in heaven. Conversely, the Synagogue, signified by Rachel, was beautiful in face and comely in appearance, because “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75) [Col. 0474B].

## CHAPTER XXIX. What it signifies that Jacob served for marriage to her, and that Laban substituted Leah for Rachel

Jacob said: “I will serve you for your younger daughter Rachel for seven years.” Laban replied: “It is better that I give her to you than to another man,” and so forth.

This is distinctive of this patriarch: while abroad in order to take a wife, he gave himself to voluntary service and became subject. We read nowhere of this concerning any of the others, just as it was distinctive of his father that he was led by his own father to be sacrificed (Gen. 22), and of his son Joseph that, sold by his brothers (Gen. 37), he came before his purchasers in the famine. In all these cases each one, born by God’s gift from mothers who were barren, bore beforehand a distinctive likeness of Christ, Son of God, who was to be born from a Virgin.

What was the service by which Jacob served for Rachel—that is, for the Synagogue? Surely it was that of which the Apostle says: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2) [Col. 0475A]. Was it not service to the world to perform repentance—indeed, to be baptized with the baptism of repentance because of the sins of the world—in order, according to the prophet, to cast them into the depths of the sea (Mic. 7), and finally, by ascending the cross, to bear the servile burdens of the age, that is, to take upon himself the sins of the world by which it was burdened?

The reward of this service ought to have been Rachel—that is, the Synagogue. Christ loved her because of the fathers, and testifies that he came into service for her when he says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). But Laban introduced Leah in Rachel’s place, because, while the Synagogue remained in being, the Church of the Gentiles from the whole world entered, as though unawares, into Christ’s bridal chamber; while the people whom, according to the Psalmist, he did not know (Ps. 17), or the nation which, according to Isaiah, did not call upon his name (Isa. 55), hastened to his service and to the delights of his love—that is, to the grace of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0475B].

## CHAPTER XXX. Again on the same matter: what it signifies that after Leah Jacob also obtained marriage with the younger woman, and concerning their handmaids

“What is this that you have done? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?” Laban replied: “It is not the custom in our place to give the younger in marriage first. Complete the week [Col. 0475C] of days of this union, and I will give you this one also,” and so forth.

For Christ or his apostles are moved by no small human feeling for that nation; this is especially known from the groaning of the teacher of the Gentiles, when he says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart” (Rom. 9), and so forth.

To this the whole world—indeed, the Creator of the world, who sent this same Son or servant—replies with the authority of the Scriptures and says: “It is not the custom in our place to give the younger in marriage first. Complete the week of days of this union, and I will give you this one also.” That is to say: “It is not the counsel or purpose of God, O Christ, Son of God, that he should set your nation before the people of the Gentiles—who are both older and more numerous—in the grace of the Gospel, as though he were God of Jews only and not also of Gentiles. For the present, carry through the marriage you have begun with the Church of the Gentiles until the end of the age; and when their fullness has entered in (Rom. 11), then the Synagogue too shall be united to you.”

Certainly, one handmaid is given to each wife, to bear children by the same husband; because in each Church there are some who serve Christ’s Gospel out of love, others out of fear, or for some reason other than Christ. Indeed, some, wholly professing the Catholic faith, beget spiritual offspring for Christ; while others, as the Apostle says, “having an appearance of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3) [Col. 0476A], preach and baptize outside the Catholic Church. Their sects are like concubines. Nevertheless, those who have been born among them, if they return to the Catholic mother, shall not lack their inheritance from the Father among the children.

The baseness of such concubines is denoted also by the meanings of their names. For *Zelpha* means “flowing mouth,” from *mouth* (*os*), not from *bone* (*os*); *Bala* means “aged.” These names fittingly apply to the sects of heretics: for they flow from the mouth through talkativeness or contentiousness, and retain the oldness of their former life.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Again on the same matter according to anagoge
Further, according to the anagogical sense, there is another interpretation of the present passage [Col. 0476B]. For the fact which an ecclesiastical man striving after perfection ought to know—namely, that there are two lives, the active and the contemplative, which even the pagan philosophers, corrupting them, called the one πρακτική (*praktikē*, practical) and the other θεωρητική (*theōrikē*, theoretical), and that one can rightly arrive at the contemplative through the active—is most certainly exemplified by this narrative. Jacob, then, leaving his own land, came to a well; and there he found Rachel, beautiful in face and lovely in appearance, and immediately fell in love with her. So whenever any supplanter of vices, wishing to follow Christ, devotes himself to the study of sacred Scripture and thereby discovers the beauty of the contemplative life to be delightful, he immediately longs to rush into its embrace. He desires to choose the best part, which shall not be taken away: namely, to sit [Col. 0476C] at the Lord’s feet and continually hear his word (Luke 10), according to the counsel that says: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. 45 [46]). But the other, which comes first, is anxious and troubled about many things (Luke 10). For it is exercised in the six works of mercy, which are enumerated by the evangelist Matthew in this way: “For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in; naked, and you clothed me; sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25). One trained in these works of the active life can at last advance to the contemplative, and that this is the rightful order of life the prophet also testifies when he says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone [Col. 0476D] and raise himself above himself” (Lam. 3). And in Job: “You shall enter the grave in abundance” (Job 5), that is, when you have been enriched by the revenues of the active life, only then will you be able, without failure, to rest within the hidden retreat of contemplation.

This is rightly figured by Leah, whose name means “laborious”: fruitful indeed, but seeing less clearly. For, as though with bleared eyes, she contemplates spiritual things less fully while she is anxious and troubled about many things. Rachel, on the other hand, beautiful indeed but barren, signifies the contemplative life. Since it attends to the one thing necessary, it sees more with lovely vision; and, devoted to holy leisure, it as though bears less fruit. Therefore, when someone suddenly, omitting the stages, hastens to seize Rachel by striving for the height of contemplation, it is often well for him [Col. 0477A] that he should first be bound in marriage to Leah—that is, drawn outward to the laborious actions of frequent ministry. If he murmurs against this, or grinds his teeth with a complaining gesture, sacred Scripture says to him: “It is not the custom in our place to give the younger in marriage first.” That is, the order is not such that anyone should leap first to the contemplative life, which is “younger” because it does less outward work, before experiencing the active life. “Complete the week of days of this union, and you too shall be able to obtain the other.”

For just as God worked all things in six days and rested on the seventh, so each person must first be exercised in the aforesaid six works of mercy, that then at last he may lawfully keep Sabbath in the contemplative life. “But when the Lord saw that he despised Leah, he opened her womb, while her sister remained barren” [Col. 0477B] (Gen. 29). That he despised Leah means that he loved her less. For this was said beforehand because, once he had finally obtained the marriage he desired, he preferred the love of the latter to the former. Nor was this without reason: the one had been rightly given or received, whereas the other had been introduced to his bed by fraud. It should be noted that, seeing that he despised Leah, the Lord did not have compassion on her by making her lovely in appearance instead of bleary-eyed; rather, he had compassion by opening her womb while her sister remained barren.

For the active life always sees less, persists with bleared eyes, and is such as the Apostle does not permit a woman to teach in the Church. “But she shall be saved,” he says, “through childbearing” (1 Tim. 2): that is, through the performance of works of mercy. For what reason will the King sitting on the throne of his majesty give when he says: [Col. 0477C] “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: for I was hungry and you gave me food; and whatever you did to one of these least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25)? Therefore she who has not attained to manly perfection shall be saved through childbearing (1 Tim. 2), that is, the life of those who have not remained in outward actions alone and have never advanced to the grace of the contemplative life shall be justified through the practice of good works.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the names of Jacob’s sons

The names of all the patriarchs, together with their brief reading, display the etymology of the names. “And she called,” he says, “his name Reuben, saying: ‘Because God has seen my affliction.’” Reuben is interpreted “son of vision.” And she conceived another son and said: “Because the Lord has heard that I am held in contempt, he has given me this one also”; and she called his name Simeon. From the fact that she was heard, she gave him the name Simeon. Simeon, indeed, means “hearing” or “being heard.”

Of the third it follows: “And she conceived again and bore a son, and said: ‘Now also my husband will be joined to me.’” That is, he will be my companion in this life, and his love will lead me as far as death. And she continues: “Because I have borne him three sons.” Therefore she called his name Levi, which means “added.” She conceived a fourth time and bore a son, and said: “Now I shall confess to the Lord.” And for this reason she called him Judah. Judah [Col. 0478A] is called “confession”; thus his name is derived from the confession of the confessor. Yet here “confession” is understood as thanksgiving or praise, as frequently in the Psalms and in the Gospel: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11), that is, “I give you thanks” or “I glorify you.”

(Chapter 30.) Bilhah conceived and bore a son. Rachel said: “The Lord has judged me and given me a son.” Therefore she called his name Dan. She gave the reason for the name, so that because the Lord had judged her, she gave the son of her handmaid a name meaning judgment. Dan, indeed, means “judgment.” Again Bilhah conceived and bore another. Concerning him Rachel said: “The Lord has compared me with my sister, and I have prevailed.” She called his name Naphtali, which means “expansion.” Zilpah [Col. 0478B], Leah’s handmaid, bore a son. Leah said: “Happily!” and called his name Gad. For Gad means “outcome” or “a troop prepared for battle.” From the favourable outcome, or the fortunate mustering of her forces, she gave such a name to the son of her handmaid.

Zilpah bore another. Leah said: “This is for my blessedness; for women will call me blessed.” And because she would be called blessed by people, she called her son “blessed.” Asher means “blessed,” at least in the present passage. Elsewhere, according to the ambiguity of the word, it can also mean “riches.” God heard Leah’s prayers; she conceived and bore a fifth son, and said: “God has given me my reward, because I gave my handmaid to my husband.” And she called his name Issachar. The etymology of this name is taken from what she says: “God has given my [Col. 0478C] reward.” For Issachar means “reward.” *Is* means “he is,” and *sachar*, “reward.” This was because, with her son Reuben’s mandrakes, she had bought for herself her husband’s entry, which was owed to Rachel.

Again Leah conceived, bore a sixth son, and said: “God has endowed me with a good dowry.” For she needed a dowry to commend herself, since, though not sought in marriage, she had been secretly given to her husband in addition, and without a dowry. Zebulun means “dwelling of strength,” from the word she used when she said: “My husband will dwell with me,” because she had borne him six sons. The meaning is: “Therefore I am now secure, and fear neither future divorce nor repudiation, because I have borne six sons to Jacob.” After this she bore a daughter and called her Dinah. This name is transferred to a “cause,” for she was the cause of the quarrel at Shechem (Gen. 34). After the names of the children, the names of their parents must be set down: Leah means “labouring,” Rachel “ewe,” and her son Joseph is called “increase,” because his mother desired that another might be added to her.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Reuben the firstborn, and how his birthright was reckoned to Joseph

Reuben, therefore, was the firstborn. But when he violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to Joseph, as is read in Chronicles, and he was not reckoned as firstborn. But Judah, who was strongest among his brothers, produced rulers from his line; while the birthright was reckoned to Joseph (1 Chron. 5). Therefore the birthright was not given to Joseph because Leah was hated [Col. 0479A] and Rachel loved, but because the one to whom it belonged lost it through his own fault; afterwards the father gave it to whom he wished.

For the law forbids such a transfer for precisely this reason: “If a man has two wives, one loved and the other hated, and has children by them, and the son of the hated wife is the firstborn, then, when he wishes to divide his property among his sons, he may not make the son of the loved wife the firstborn and prefer him to the son of the hated wife. Rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn and give him a double share of all that he has; for he is the beginning of his children, and to him belongs the birthright” (Deut. 21). Thus, when Reuben lost the birthright, it was lawfully transferred, and Joseph received a double portion from his father, where he said: “Behold, I die, and the Lord will be with you and will bring you back to the land of your fathers; and I will give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow” (Gen. 48 [printed “IV”]). The priesthood also, which the Hebrews hand down as having likewise belonged until then to the firstborn, was given to Levi. Thus the birthright which one man lost was divided into three parts: Judah received the leadership, Joseph the double portion, and Levi the priesthood. Why Judah is placed first in the Apocalypse (Rev. 7), and thereafter no order of this genealogy is observed, is another question not relevant to the present passage.
