## CHAPTER XXXIV. Which wives in Christ are spiritually free, and which are handmaidens

The present reading lashes ears that are excessively modest; they are greatly wearied by hearing the rivalries of four women contending over one man. But let such people have prudence together with their simplicity, and know that everything said or done breathes an immense desire for children. Let prudent souls therefore hasten with as much eagerness to conceive or bear spiritual offspring from Christ their husband as they hear those women eagerly seizing their husband and receiving their children in childbirth with such joy.

For this one man, our Christ, has free wives and handmaid-concubines. “There are sixty queens,” he says, “and eighty concubines” (Song 6). Every queen, or free woman, truly groans and labours in childbirth through love; for example, when she says: “My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed [Col. 0479D] in you” (Gal. 4). But she should not be content with this. Let her be enlarged by so great a longing to multiply blessed offspring that she also permits handmaids to this husband, and says: “What then? Only that, in every way, whether from pretext or from truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, yes, and I shall rejoice” (Phil. 1).

For it can happen—and often has happened—that one conceived by a handmaid or concubine is born upon the knees of a free woman: that is, one who heard the word through the proclamation of an envious person may confess and hold within the Catholic mother Church the perfection of the true and only faith, and thus differ in nothing from legitimate sons in receiving the Father’s inheritance. For when the Lord drove the nations from before the children of Israel and divided the land to them by lot with the measuring-line of distribution (Ps. 77 [78]), did Gad, Asher, Dan, and Naphtali [Col. 0480A] receive anything less or later because they were born of concubines or handmaids? Thus, in the harsh outer husk of such matters, the understanding of the simple is indeed offended; but the more perfect, whose food is solid, are by no means less delighted by the inner grain.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How, after Joseph was born, he said to his father-in-law, “Let me go back”

After Joseph was born, Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Let me go back to my homeland and to my own land. Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served you, that I may depart. You know the service by which I have served you.” The words “after Joseph was born” were set beforehand, so that you may undoubtedly understand that Jacob would have declined to say these things before Joseph’s birth [Col. 0480B]. For if even then he feared that Laban would take away his daughters, and for this reason left him secretly, as he says, “I departed without your knowledge because I feared that you would take your daughters away by force,” how much more could he have feared that Rachel, whom he loved, would be taken from him if he wished to leave while he had not yet received any son by her?

Therefore, because through Joseph’s birth he believed his wife’s wish had been confirmed for him, he rightly spoke these words after Joseph’s birth; or Scripture, recounting these words of his, placed “after Joseph was born” beforehand. It also does so to emphasize his right to dismissal, that he might be allowed to depart with his wives: “You know,” he says, “the service by which I have served you.” Nor should that be passed over which he says: “That I may return to my land and my homeland,” calling the land of his fathers’ sojourning his homeland and his land because of God; and, conversely, calling the land of his fathers his place of sojourning when he says: “I have sojourned with Laban” (Gen. 32).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. What it spiritually means that Jacob partly peeled the rods, and set them before the sheep at the time of conception

Laban said: “May I find favour in your sight. I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you. Fix the wage that I should give you.” He answered: “You know how I have served you and how great your possession has become in my hands. You had little before I came to you, and now you have become rich; the Lord has blessed you at my coming. It is therefore just that I should at some time provide also for my own household.”

In the present reading we have that Jacob took green poplar rods, almond rods, and plane-tree rods, and partly peeled them; and, when the bark had been stripped away, whiteness appeared in the parts that had been stripped, while those left whole remained green [Col. 0480D]. What is it to place green rods of poplar, almond, and plane tree before the faces of the flocks, except to offer the lives and sayings of the ancient Fathers, through the sequence of sacred Scripture, as an example to the peoples? In these, whenever we avoid the literal understanding, we as it were remove the bark; and whenever we follow the literal understanding, we as it were preserve the bark.

First, therefore, we must consider the present passage under this comparison. This life of our father Jacob is rightly called a rod, because, according to the judgment of reason, it is straight. Accordingly, when the bark of the letter has been partly removed, let the whiteness of allegory appear in that which has been stripped; and, when the bark has been partly preserved, let the deed as it occurred remain to be drawn into an example. How? Namely, we must never carnally proclaim in Christ’s Gospel, by the example of our patriarch Jacob, that it is lawful to multiply marriages fourfold. Indeed, we should advise abstinence even from one marriage, the only one that is lawful; for such old things have passed away, and behold all things have become new (2 Cor. 5). After the law was given, this example had no force for taking two sisters in marriage to one man; how much less force should it have after the law, under the presence of evangelical grace? Then [Col. 0481B] there was a time for sowing or scattering stones; now is a time for reaping and gathering stones (Eccl. 3). Therefore, after stripping away the bark of the letter in matters of this kind, let the inner whiteness of allegory be sought, as has already been said.

But when Jacob goes on to say, “It is therefore just that I should at some time provide also for my own household,” namely by demanding a suitable reward, this should be taken as an example in Christ’s Gospel in such a way that the outer bark of the letter is not removed at all, but that the deed as performed is held as law, in harmony with the authority of the Gospel, where it is said: “The worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Laban’s words: “I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you”

[Col. 0481C] Let us therefore say to this world, of which we said above that Laban bears the type, since it itself confesses and says, “I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you”—let us say, I say, to it in the person of Christ our Head, on whose account the Lord blessed it: “You know how I have served you and how great your possession has become in my hands. You had little before I came, and now you have become rich; and the Lord has blessed you at my coming.”

For what did this world have before Christ came? What but a little knowledge of the law, known only to a few; and a little of the carnal ceremonies, through whose shadowy rite very few somehow worshipped the one God? But now, Christ says, you have become rich, and God has blessed you at my coming. Truly the whole world has become rich through the exceedingly glorious knowledge of the true God; and God blessed it at the coming of Christ his Son with every spiritual blessing: first, by forgiving it all sins, although very many turn back and are converted to Satan; and then by bestowing the manifold gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“It is therefore just,” he says, “that I should at some time provide also for my own household.” What is Christ’s household except his domestic family, which serves at the altar and feeds the rational flocks of peoples with spiritual sacraments? This is the apostolic, priestly, and Levitical order, which first served without payment, proclaiming the Gospel of the kingdom of God not only freely, but even at its peril, receiving evil in return for good, until [Col. 0482A] Leah and Rachel alike were joined to Christ—that is, until the respective varieties of the active and contemplative life were multiplied throughout the world in their orders.

At last the abundance of grace reached Laban himself—that is, the kings of the world, emperors, and other rulers and great men. It was therefore just that Christ should at some time provide for his household: that is, enrich his churches from royal palaces, the treasuries and estates of rulers, so that there might be sufficient resources for the necessary expenses of those who serve at the altar, for the needs of the poor and pilgrims, and for the restoration of churches or cemeteries.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Whether Jacob’s righteousness answered for him in this, when he devised a novel trick and contended by art against the nature of white and black livestock

Laban said: “What shall I give you?” He replied: “I want nothing. But if you do what I ask, I will again pasture and guard your flocks. Go through all your flocks, and separate all the variegated sheep, those with scattered fleece, and whatever is tawny, reddish, or spotted, among both sheep and goats; these shall be my wages. And tomorrow my righteousness shall answer for me, when the time of agreement comes before you.”

Here the question is raised whether his righteousness truly answered for him in this, or how, according to his action, it could be called or be righteousness. For what did he do? Did he not devise a new trick [Col. 0482C] and contend by natural art against the nature of white and black livestock? Taking poplar, almond, and plane-tree rods and partly peeling them, he made the colour of the rods variegated, so that wherever he left bark on a rod the old colour remained, but where he removed the bark a white colour remained and was revealed in brightness.

He watched for the time when the livestock were mating, and, after the heat of day, eagerly went to drink. He set the multicoloured rods in the watering-troughs; and, introducing the rams and he-goats, he made the sheep and goats mate in the very eagerness of drinking, so that through a double desire—while they drank eagerly and were mounted by males—they might conceive such offspring as the reflections of the rams and he-goats mounting above them, which they beheld in the mirror of the waters. For from the rods set in the troughs the colour of the reflected images also became variegated.

Nor is it surprising that this should be the nature of women at conception: that whatever they have looked upon or conceived in mind at the final heat of pleasure in which they conceive, they should bear offspring like it. For this same thing is said to occur even among herds of mares in Spain. And Quintilian, in the controversy in which a matron was accused of having borne an Ethiopian child, argues in her defence that this is the nature of conception which we have described above. The question, then, is whether in such an act one may rightly expect righteousness to answer for him, when fraud or deception is plainly established.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Again on the same matter, and how he may be excused in that device

To this we reply that, even before this device, Jacob had long had a claim of justice against Laban. If a time of hearing had been granted him before Laban with lawful defence, he ought by right to have taken Laban’s property. For Laban had imposed upon him by fraud another daughter as well, though he had asked for one daughter in marriage and undertaken service for one: namely, the one whose marriage he knew would be difficult to arrange because she was unattractive. For no capable man would accept her without a large dowry, since the beauty of face, which counts for much in such matters, had not made her desirable.

If, I say, a time of hearing had been granted him, Laban was liable to legal action because he had imposed his daughters upon Jacob to support without a dowry; and, in addition, because for the one [Col. 0483B] whom he thrust upon him by fraud he had extorted seven years’ service. But Jacob was a stranger and a foreigner, and therefore could not bring the violent and stronger native to court. Thus he necessarily employed art against the father on account of the daughter, so that some of the father’s goods might come to the daughter, to whom they belonged. And concerning this, at every time of hearing, a vindication of justice is ready for him.

Therefore, when the sheep first mated, Jacob put the rods in the water-troughs before the eyes of the rams and sheep, so that they might conceive while gazing upon them. But when it was the later mating season, he did not put them there. Thus the later-born belonged to Laban, and those of the first season to Jacob. In this too there is a most evident regard for justice. For, as has already been said, in the marriages of the first period there was on Laban’s part a cause of injustice; but concerning the later marriage to Rachel he had no ground for complaint and could claim no dowry by right. He therefore regulated all things justly, so that he himself might receive the fruit of his labour and Laban might not be wholly despoiled.

## CHAPTER XL. On what was said, “The man became exceedingly rich,” and what it signifies mystically

“The man became exceedingly rich, and had many flocks, female and male servants, camels, and donkeys.” Here he is strikingly called “the man,” when he who had arrived poor is said [Col. 0483D] to have become exceedingly rich. If this is remarkable and worthy of admiration in this man, how much more is it so in that Man of whom he is a type? For that one is truly and uniquely Man because he is God and man, and because he had been poor: “For though he was rich,” says the Apostle, “for our sake he became poor” (2 Cor. 8). And behold, he has become rich—not only in himself, where he was crowned with glory and honour and set over the works of the Father’s hands (Ps. 8), but also in his present household, that is, the Church, where the dignity already mentioned is maintained for his ministers, a dignity which Gospel authority rightly claims for them in saying: “The worker is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10).

In many places Christ’s household has been made equal to royal palaces. Bodily, it has many flocks, female and male servants, camels, and donkeys [Col. 0484A], in such abundance that it can amply supply not only spiritual but also material things to those in need. Not that we glory in these things, for “our glory is this, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1), but that we should have cause for thanksgiving because we hold in abundance the religion which our Father Christ acquired through his poverty and beggary.

His righteousness will answer for him concerning all these things tomorrow—that is, in the future judgment, when the time of hearing comes. What will it answer? Namely, what the Apostle indicated ought to be answered when he said: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9). Did not he and the other apostles or apostolic men, though they could and knew how to enjoy Rachel’s embraces—that is, to feed upon the sweetness of the contemplative life—turn aside to Leah, that is, to the active life, because of this wretched world? Did not those who both wished and were able, by God’s grace, to dwell in heaven in mind descend even to arranging marriages, for example when saying: “Let the husband render the due to the wife, and likewise the wife to the husband” (1 Cor. 7)?

Surely this is the complaint of every such person: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” Therefore Christ, who speaks in us, should rightly partly peel the rods and partly leave bark upon them, and set them in the channels before the sheep, so that they may conceive varied offspring in beholding them; and thus he takes away Laban’s wealth in order to become rich. That is, by setting forth teaching from the Scriptures that is partly allegorical and partly historical [Col. 0484C], he encourages his hearers to furnish the ministers of the altar cheerfully with goods, because no one feeds a flock without eating of its milk, or plants a vineyard without having the right to eat of its fruit (1 Cor. 9), even though the children of this age envy them, like those sons of Laban of whom the account immediately continues.

## CHAPTER XLI. How it was beneficial for Jacob to hear Laban’s sons’ words; how their father regarded and sold his daughters as strangers; and how these carnal matters happened as types of spiritual realities

(Chapter 31.) After Jacob heard the words of Laban’s sons saying, “Jacob has taken all that belonged to our father, and from his wealth he has become glorious,” and also observed Laban’s face, that it was not toward him as yesterday and the day before yesterday—especially as the Lord said to him, “Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred”—these words of Laban’s sons worked for Jacob’s good, as did that severity in Laban’s countenance concerning which he said, after calling Rachel and Leah to him: “I see that your father’s face is not toward me as yesterday and the day before yesterday.”

For it was good for him to hear the voice of the Lord God saying, “Return to the land of your fathers and to your kindred, and I will be with you,” and to remain a continual imitator of obedience and pilgrimage, so that he too might remain forever heir of the blessing of Abraham his grandfather and Isaac his father. It was a matter of no small concern to them never to return to that place from which God had commanded them to depart. Hence: “Take care not to bring my son back there.” And again: “Do not bring my only son back there” (Gen. 24).

Thus both these things already mentioned and what he later says to Rachel and Leah—“But your father deceived me and changed my wages ten times,” and so forth—work together for the holy man’s good, so that, driven by adversity itself, he might more quickly follow where God called him. Likewise, the unkindness of their unloving father worked together for the same good for the wives themselves; they immediately complain of it and say: “Have we any remaining share in the goods and inheritance of our father’s house? Has he not treated us as strangers and sold us, and consumed our price?” With this adverse wind happily driving their vessel, they freely sight the harbour and say: “But God has taken our father’s riches and given them to us and to our children. Therefore do everything that the Lord has commanded you.”

These things, I say, also worked for their good, so that they might more quickly follow such a husband, receive with fathers of such merit the promises of those same fathers, and become examples of spiritual realities for the instruction of souls. Of such souls we have heard the Holy Spirit—or God the Father of Christ—saying in the Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty” (Ps. 44 [45]). For just as these adversities drove Jacob’s wives to leave the father who had consumed their price and to follow such a husband, so the adversities of the world often help the soul beloved by God to strive more eagerly toward God. Therefore God also says to it through the prophet: “Behold, I will hedge up your way with thorns; I will fence it with a wall, and she shall not find her paths. She shall pursue her lovers and not overtake them; she shall seek them and not find them. Then she shall say: ‘I will go and return to my former husband, for it was better with me then than now’” (Hos. 2).

Before Jacob had been hurt by thorns of this kind, when he was still gently received and Laban said, “May I find favour in your sight; I have learned by experience that God has blessed me because of you,” and so forth, he delayed returning and said: “If you do what I ask, I will again pasture and guard your flocks.” But now, once he had been injured, “Jacob arose,” Scripture says, “and, placing his children and wives upon camels, departed to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan” [Col. 0485D]. Thus also in other cases it is plain that the Apostle’s statement is true: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8).

Moreover, where Jacob says, “I lifted my eyes and saw in a dream males mounting females, striped, spotted, and of various colours; and the angel of the Lord said to me: ‘Lift your eyes and see all the males mounting the females, striped, speckled, and spotted, for I have seen all that Laban has done,’” he makes clear that he performed that device involving the rods by heavenly authority [Col. 0486A], because, for the reason stated above, it was just for God to take Laban’s wealth and give it to Jacob.

## CHAPTER XLII. How Rachel stole her father’s idols

At that time Laban had gone to shear his sheep, and Rachel stole her father’s idols. Even if from nowhere else, Jacob could at least have sufficiently perceived from this that Laban’s face was not toward him as yesterday and the day before yesterday: for what among the ancients was an occasion of a large gathering of friends and festive joy—namely, shearing sheep—Laban was undertaking without Jacob, the keeper of the flocks. For, leaving Jacob and all who belonged to him, both wives and children, he had gone to shear his sheep. Jacob’s departure is therefore rightly called a flight, when it immediately follows: “Jacob did not wish to tell his father-in-law that he was fleeing.”

“And Rachel,” it says, “stole her father’s idols.” In this place the authority of Scripture first presents the name or worship of idols. Therefore, in that Gospel passage in which a woman is read to have been healed of a twelve-year flow of blood (Matt. 9), and a twelve-year-old girl raised (Mark 5; Luke 8), the Fathers rightly observed this divine point: when the woman was healed, the girl died; and just when the woman began to be ill, the girl was born. This is a type of the Gentiles and the Synagogue: for when the Gentiles began to flow into idolatry, the Synagogue was born in the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and when the Gentile world was healed through faith in Christ, the Synagogue died through envy and unbelief.

But Rachel, who stole the idols, plainly was not yet of perfect faith [Col. 0486C]. Yet before she died, Jacob was most appropriately told: “Cast away the foreign gods that are among you; cleanse yourselves and change your garments.” So they gave them to him, and he buried them beneath the terebinth tree (Gen. 35). Not long afterward it is written: “Rachel died and was buried on the way that leads to Ephrath; this is Bethlehem” (ibid.). Therefore it was no small good for her that she obtained or followed a faithful husband, by whose faith she was saved. For “the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the faithful husband” (1 Cor. 7). Accordingly the Apostle rightly and reasonably says: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, let her not dismiss her husband” (ibid.). And a little later: “For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?” (ibid.).

But where we now read “idols,” the Hebrew has *teraphim*, which is translated “figures” or “images.” This is stated so that we may know what *teraphim* means in the book of Judges (Judg. 18).

## CHAPTER XLIII. How the wicked man saw God in a dream rebuking him not to speak harshly against Jacob
When he had departed, both he himself and all that was his by right, and, having crossed the river, was proceeding toward Mount Gilead, Laban was told that Jacob was fleeing. Taking his kinsmen with him, he pursued him for seven days [Col. 0487A] and overtook him on Mount Gilead. Not that at that time Gilead was called a mountain; it is so called by anticipation, by the name later given to it. It lies behind Phoenicia and Arabia, joined to the hills of Lebanon, and extends through the desert as far as the place where Sihon, king of the Amorites, once lived beyond the Jordan. The aforesaid mountain fell by lot to the sons of Reuben and Gad and to the half-tribe of Manasseh.

And in a dream he saw God saying to him: “Take care not to say anything harsh against Jacob.” Here he did not hear God calling him by name, as God was accustomed to call Jacob; for he was not of such merit that God should know him by name. He merely saw him—that is, angry, threatening, and saying: “Take care.” Indeed, even this vision [Col. 0487B] was granted not for his own sake but for another’s, so that the latter might know how great was God’s care for him: for his sake God deemed it worthy to appear to one unworthy, or to be seen by one unworthy.

Thus also, because of Isaac, he rebuked Abimelech (Gen. XXVI); and because of Abraham he scourged Pharaoh (Gen. XII, 20), in accordance with the Psalm that says: “He did not permit a man”—understand, Laban—“to harm them; and he rebuked kings for their sake” (Ps. CIV)—understand, Pharaoh and Abimelech.

And he said to Jacob: “Why have you acted thus, secretly carrying off my daughters as though they were captives taken by the sword? Why did you wish to flee without my knowledge, rather than inform me, so that I might send you away with joy, songs, timbrels, and lyres?” etc. In saying these things he did indeed take heed, in accordance with God’s threat, not to speak anything too severe against Jacob; but he made that very caution foolish by lying [Col. 0487C], so that he must plainly be reproved out of his own mouth. For if he was truly troubled by this concern—that Jacob had not allowed him to send him away with joy, songs, timbrels, and lyres—why, as he himself admits, did God rebuke him lest he speak too harshly? He would therefore have taken better heed for himself if, confessing the truth, he had promptly offered fitting satisfaction to God and to his deserving dependant.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That although Jacob was a prophet, he nevertheless did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.

“You have acted foolishly,” he says. “Even if you wished to go to your own people, and longed for your father’s house, why did you steal my gods?”

This was the time for a wise man to speak, [Col. 0487D] one who was certainly wise not only in this matter but also in others, although Scripture called him simple, saying: “But Jacob, a simple man, dwelt in tents” (Gen. XXV). For he had joined the prudence of the serpent to the simplicity of the dove, and out of both had fashioned for himself one wisdom. He who had outwitted Laban was returning rich, with justice as his protector. Therefore, when he was charged with foolishness by Laban, who said, “You have acted foolishly,” he still remained patiently silent. But when he was asked by the same man, “Why have you stolen my gods?” he gave such an answer to the question that he first drove away the imputation of foolishness.

For he said: “I departed without your knowledge because I feared that you would violently take away your daughters. But as for your charge of theft: with whomever you find your gods, let that person die before our kinsmen.” As though [Col. 0488A] he said: “My departure without your knowledge is not only no proof of injustice; it is rather an act of wisdom and reason opposed to foolishness. For in law he is to be called foolish who, knowing that evil threatens him from someone, does not take precautions. But I knew without doubt that I had to guard against you, since you changed my wages ten times. If, therefore, I had not guarded myself by departing without your knowledge, committing myself to heavenly protection and trusting in the guardianship promised me, then I would more rightly have been found foolish, condemned by my losses.

“But concerning the theft of which you accuse me—come now, let justice be done. With whomever you find your gods, let that person die before our kinsmen.”

By “kinsmen” he here means his sons, though it may also be understood that some relatives came with Laban, whom he would properly call brothers according to common usage. [Col. 0488B] In saying this, he did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols. Thus Jacob was a prophet, and Isaac too was a prophet, as in the Psalm, where after the words, “Do not touch my anointed ones,” it immediately adds: “and do not act wickedly against my prophets” (Ps. CIV). Yet neither this man, who did not know of a theft within his own household, nor that man, who could be deceived in blessing his son, nor any human being ever knew everything or always had the Spirit of prophecy subject to him, except him who, though man, is also God, and knows all things because he is the very wisdom of God.

Jacob therefore sinned not a little in speaking against himself so quickly, though the sentence itself was not unjust. For if one who worships idols is worthy of death, how much more one who commits theft out of love of idolatry? [Col. 0488C] how much more one who commits theft out of love of idolatry? Indeed, if some Jews justly fell, as is read in the Book of Maccabees (II Macc. XII), because they had under their tunics objects dedicated to idols, how much more justly ought one to have been killed who had stolen the idols themselves? Yet God spared Jacob, causing the theft to remain hidden by his providence, and likewise the cunning of her who had committed it. For she hastened to hide the idols beneath the camel’s trappings and sat upon them. When he searched the whole tent and found nothing, she said: “Let not my lord be angry that I cannot rise before you, because the customary condition of women has now come upon me.” Thus the searcher’s diligence was deceived: he readily believed the excuse of one who seemed afflicted, and knew with difficulty how to approach female impurity.

## CHAPTER XLV. [Col. 0488D] How aptly it is said that Jacob, swelling with quarrelsomeness, recalled his past servitude.

And Jacob, swelling with quarrelsomeness, said: “For what fault of mine, and for what sin of mine, have you so burned with anger in pursuit of me and searched all my belongings?”

The phrase is remarkably apt here: “Jacob, swelling with quarrelsomeness.” Swelling or quarrelsomeness is the disposition of a slave; no one could rightly or properly say this of the anger of a freeborn or noble man. But in this case Jacob was certainly not free. Although he did not know it, the cause of servitude—that is, guilt and theft—was nevertheless in his possession. And now, as though his household goods were wholly clean because Laban had found nothing, he vigorously presses his case in judgment [Col. 0489A] and says with quarrelsomeness: “What have you found among all the possessions of your house? Set it here before my kinsmen and your kinsmen, and let them judge between me and you.”

How swollen and contentious is the irony with which he immediately adds: “For this reason I have been with you twenty years: your sheep and goats were not barren.” “For this reason,” he says—that you might burn with anger after me and search all my belongings, a great indignity indeed—“for this reason, I say, in hope of such a return I have been with you twenty years: with such faithfulness, such honesty, and with the Lord’s blessing, which, as you also confessed, entered your house with me. How great this blessing was may be demonstrated from the things I now say. Your sheep and goats were not barren”—understand: “nor did I allege that they had years of barrenness because I withheld their offspring.”

“I did not eat the rams [Col. 0489B] of your flock.” This is what hired men and those who are not shepherds commonly do, those who feed not the flocks but themselves. “I did not show you an animal seized by a beast”—that is, as an excuse for myself, so that I might not be compelled to make up the number to you. “I made good every loss; whatever was lost by theft, you demanded from me,” although the excuse would have been legitimate. “By day and by night I was consumed by heat and frost,” namely, in a land where, according to the nature of its climate, there is intense heat by day and equally intense frost by night.

Recounting these and other works of faithfulness, he finally brings forward the strongest argument for his justice. Having first said, “God regarded my affliction and the labor of my hands,” he immediately adds: “and rebuked you yesterday.” For it is a sure proclamation of righteousness to have God as witness or defender. Accordingly, at once granting the palm of victory to the righteous man over Laban, he turns to another matter: “My daughters,” he says, “and the sons and your flocks, and everything you see, are mine.” What can I do to my sons and grandsons? Come then, let us make a covenant.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. What it spiritually signifies that Laban pursued Jacob, and that Rachel said: “The customary condition of women has come upon me.”

And behold, even to this day [Col. 0489D] the world pursues Christ, or Christ’s disciples, as they flee from the world—that is, as they desire to possess nothing in this world—while it continually strives to conform them to itself, sometimes by evil examples and sometimes even by force. Even to this day, I say, the world pursues those who flee in this way; and even to this day Rachel steals the idols of the world, her persecutor.

For whenever those who, by religious habit or order, promise a contemplative life look toward avarice, which is “the service of idols” (Eph. V), so that they sometimes commit fraud in ecclesiastical property or—as most often happens—bestow God’s spiritual gifts for money, Rachel steals the idols of her sluggish old father. What could be more contemptible or more abject than that she hides them beneath camel-trappings and sits upon them, pretending that the customary condition of women has come upon her?

For Laban searches Rachel’s tent to see whether he may perhaps find his idols there when worldly people point out that the service of idols which they think lawful only for themselves—that is, such avarice—is secretly present in the conduct of religious people. For it is now commonly known that Jesus, angry and severe, drives sellers and buyers out of his temple with a whip [Col. 0490A] (Matt. XXI). But they put forward some pretext which may indeed appear reasonable, yet lacks the truth of reason; just as the camel appears to possess something of cleanliness because it chews the cud, but is not truly a clean animal because it does not divide the hoof.

Perhaps she did lie in saying, “The customary condition of women has now come upon me”; but in truth the prophet rightly says of the soul of every such person who commits theft through the aforesaid service of idols: “All who seek her shall not fail; in her monthly impurity they shall find her” (Jer. II). [Col. 0490B]

Meanwhile, however, for the sake of those who belong to Christ, and who will not be lacking in his holy Church until the end of the age, God continually rebukes the world; and his rebukes gradually overcome worldly hearts. “When,” Christ says, “the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will rebuke the world” (John XVI).

Thus he who was rebuked by God says: “Come, let us make a covenant.” These are the words of the covenant: “May the Lord look upon us and judge between us when we have departed from one another. If you afflict my daughters, or introduce other wives over them, there is no witness to our words except God, who is present and watches.”

In saying this, he was especially concerned for Leah, whom he had secretly imposed upon the unsuspecting Jacob—unasked for, without dowry, and unattractive in appearance. For Jacob could almost, without opposition from justice, have repudiated her [Col. 0490C] as a concubine, since he had not given her marital faith, nor had Laban celebrated her marriage before witnesses or friends before Jacob had gone in to her according to custom. But Jacob had intended not only not to repudiate her; he had even, as was said above (Gen. XXX), employed ingenuity for her legal right, so that she should not depart without a dowry—namely, when, by the variegated rods placed in the channels before the sheep, the nature of the conceptions was altered.

## CHAPTER XLVII. What it signifies that Jacob and Laban made a heap of witness for their covenant, and ate upon it.

Jacob therefore took a stone and set it up as a pillar, and said [Col. 0490D] to his kinsmen: “Bring stones.” They gathered them, made a heap, and ate upon it.

Here Jacob clearly knew that the vow he had made at Bethel had been accepted. He perceived that the Lord had been with him, had kept him on the way by which he had travelled, had given him bread to eat and clothing to wear, and had enabled him to return safely to his father’s house, because Laban had been pacified (Gen. XXVIII). Thus here too he took a stone and set it up as a pillar, and they made a heap: in both places the mystery is almost the same. For there too the stone set up as a pillar, to be called the house of God, signifies Christ, the head of the body—the Church, which is God’s house. And here the first stone in the heap of witness similarly signifies Christ, the chief of martyrs—that is, of God’s witnesses.

For what is it that Laban and Jacob, in making a covenant, set up a stone as a pillar and pile stones into a heap of witness, and eat upon it as the ratification of the covenant they seek? What, I say, except what we see almost continually: after long swelling passions and savage quarrels, worldly authorities are reconciled with churches or priests through reverence for the martyrs and for Christ, their Lord and King?

Indeed, after hostilities, to eat together upon the heap of witness means this: after any injustices, once satisfaction has been given or received in the basilicas of the martyrs, then, for the confirmation of peace, to eat and drink together the body and blood of Christ. It is therefore rightly said that Jacob “swore by the fear,” that is, by the God, of his father Isaac. For God is named from fear, and in Greek is called *theos*. What did he swear? Namely, that he would devise no evil against Laban nor pass over to him with evil intent, being warned by the witness of the present heap.

It is rightly said. For all of us who are priests or ministers of Christ, after reconciliation at the altar has been granted to our adversaries, must bring forward no complaint before God, the common judge, concerning past grievances.

“Laban called it the Heap of Witness, and Jacob the Heap of Testimony,” each according to the property of his own language. In Hebrew, a heap is called *Gal*, while *Aad* means “testimony.” Again, in the Syrian language, a heap is called *Igar*, and *Seduth* means “testimony.” Jacob called the heap of testimony *Galaad* in the Hebrew language; Laban, however, called the same thing—the heap of testimony—*Igarseduth*, in the speech of his own people. For he was a Syrian, and had changed the ancient language of his parents for the language of the province in which he lived.

# EIGHTH BOOK ON GENESIS  
*(Genesis XXXII–XL)*

[Col. 0491]

## 133 CHAPTER I. That Esau, being natural, did not understand what the paternal blessing had bestowed upon the spiritual Jacob.

“The natural man,” says the Apostle, “does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are examined spiritually. But the spiritual man judges all things, and is himself judged by no one” (I Cor. II).

We must not therefore suppose that Esau perceived or understood either what his brother Jacob had less than he, or what more the paternal blessing had bestowed upon Jacob. For he was a natural man, wise only in matters belonging to humankind; and whatever belonged to the Spirit of God was foolishness to him. Thus he regarded his brother’s exile and servitude not as the benefit of wisdom but as the misery of folly.

But Jacob, because he was spiritual [Col. 0491C], understood all things—human things, of course, but divine things as well. Comparing spiritual things with spiritual, and making little of his brother’s earthly exaltation, he instead consoled himself inwardly, amid his own affliction and labor, with glorious knowledge. Being judged by no one, he himself judged all things.

Since these things stand before us, we too must now examine spiritually what Jacob had in greater measure and Esau in lesser: wherein the former increased through his father’s blessing, and wherein the latter was diminished, because, having sold his birthright, he also justly lost the blessing. For if matters are examined carnally, he who was supplanted will undoubtedly, for the present, be judged stronger than he who supplanted him.

## CHAPTER II. That angels met Jacob as he returned, like a victor, when he said: “These are the camps of God.”

*(Chapter XXXII.)* First, then, we understand from the greatness of the man what is said: “Jacob also went on the journey he had begun, and angels of God met him.” [Col. 0492B] When he saw them, he said: “These are the camps of God.” And he called that place Mahanaim, that is, “camps.”

It is not said that an angel appeared to him, or that angels appeared to him—which has happened to many—but that angels of God met him. This has the distinction of a victor and one who has completed his service: for the glory of his triumph, a heavenly procession came forth to meet him and, in festive reception, rendered joyful service. Nor did he see only a few, he who said, “These are the camps of God,” and therefore called that place Mahanaim, that is, “camps”; for the camps of angels are many. Hence also in the Prophets, who because of visions of this kind are called Seers (I Kings IX), the customary expression is “the Lord God of hosts,” which in Hebrew is called *Sabaoth*.

And rightly did he receive such a meeting, since under obedience he had served [Col. 0492C] as a soldier in a foreign land, had fought in faith, had accomplished victory in hope, and, with his soul enlarged in charity, rendered profound thanks for God’s benefits. “I am less,” he says, “than all your mercies, O God of my father Abraham: with my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I go forth with two companies,” etc.

Moreover, what is added a little later: “After he had conveyed all that belonged to him, he remained alone, and behold, a man wrestled with him until morning. When he saw that he could not overcome him,” etc. This reveals in Jacob a greatness beyond the measure of man and a strength not of flesh but of spirit. Esau, the natural man, who was coming with four hundred men and glorying only in this strength of his, could not judge this.

[Col. 0492D] But Jacob, before he could spiritually judge Esau, who was unworthy of such glory, and know in himself through these things that the blessing which had been spoken to him—“May my Lord make you increase,” by which he had been established as lord of his brothers (Gen. XXVII)—had been, or would be, far from lightly fulfilled, [Col. 0493A] had indeed already begun to abound even in the kinds of wealth in which Esau took pride. Yet, making little of these in comparison with better things, he rather gloried in his humility and other virtues, which he rightly counted as true riches.

Knowing full well, as a spiritual man—as has already been said, such a man judges all things—his brother’s vanity, he hastened to satisfy that vanity by excessive acts of submission. He sent gifts ahead to his lord Esau and instructed his servants: “You shall say this and this; speak thus and thus to my lord Esau.” Then he himself went forward, bowing to the ground, and caused all his people, instructed and carefully taught, to bow—that is, to incline—before Esau.

And he says: “Thus I have seen your face [Col. 0493B] as though I had seen the face of God.” That is, because from Esau’s face he perceived that his hatred had been calmed and that he would not strike mother and children, he received this joyfully as though he had seen the face of God, whose presence is truly known from his benefits bestowed in the present.

The carefulness of his fear should be noted: he arranged that Rachel and Joseph should stand last and bow last, because, miserable as the hope was, if Esau struck those who met him, perhaps before he reached these last, his cruelty would have spent itself, and in these who stood last he would preserve the greatest part of Jacob’s life. Conversely, he placed each maidservant and her children first, and Leah and her children in the second [Col. 0493C] place, so that each group might stand farther from the striking sword in proportion as it was less deeply rooted in the father’s affections. But something should now be said briefly concerning this chapter also according to the anagogical sense.

## CHAPTER III. That in this Jacob bore the type of Christ ascending into heaven, received as a victorious conqueror by angels.

Therefore, after Jacob carried out his father’s command, angels of God met him as he returned. Thus we may know that, after the labor of obedience, every faithful man remains to be glorified by heavenly revelations and, already in this life, rewarded by frequent visitation from heavenly spirits. So Christ himself, after overcoming temptations, was received as a victor by angels: “The tempter left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV).

[Col. 0493D] In their own measure, the more the elect rise above human beings, the nearer to God they become, and the more they enjoy the ministry of angels. For they all, as the Apostle says, are “ministering spirits sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation” (Heb. I).

The place where this visitation is revealed is the mystery of the Church, rightly called Mahanaim, “camps.” For the Church herself is “terrible as an army with banners” (Song VI). Yet this victor still has within him that which he must fear: namely, Seir or Edom, he who under the name of a brother performs every hostile deed. He must fear him, I say, if not for himself—because perhaps he may die sooner than be corrupted by imitating him—then at least for his little ones, lest he strike mother together with children.

For such an Esau is within: he is also called Seir, [Col. 0494A] that is, “hairy,” or Edom, that is, “earthly” or “bloody.” By his examples he sometimes destroys the tender nourishment of the Church worse than an outward enemy does by the sword. Therefore any prelate or father of this kind, when Esau threatens, divides his people into two companies—that is, he assigns stronger guards to those who are weaker.

Meanwhile, remaining watchful, as one who must render an account for their souls (Heb. XIII), he says to the Lord: “I am less than all the mercies and truth which you have fulfilled toward your servant; rescue me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I greatly fear him, lest he come and strike mother with children.” To this prayer corresponds, almost in the same words, the Prophet’s voice in the Psalm: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation’” [Col. 0494B] (Ps. CXXXVI).

For a father must fear for his children what they say concerning Jerusalem—that is, concerning Christ’s Church. Though they profess its name, they hate its religion. For what do they mean by saying, “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation”? They urge one another to empty out and abolish every discipline and religious observance, even to its foundation: that is, down to the bare Christian name, which alone they consent to retain, so that in name they may be Jacob—that is, Christ’s—but in works Edom, and may live without a yoke.

[Col. 0494C] “Remember, therefore, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem”:  that is, repay their recompense to the imitators of Edom, for the consolation of Jerusalem, which desires to see peace in the time of tribulation. When such people have been exalted so that they cannot be corrected by the apostolic rod, they must not only be endured in a spirit of gentleness but even soothed with anticipatory honors, so that the hatred they bear against spiritual persons because they are carnal may be moderated or softened.

## CHAPTER IV. That the words, “With my staff I crossed,” etc., apply both to Christ the Lord and to every faithful Christian.

That part of his prayer in which he says to God, “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies,” applies both to Christ the Lord and to every perfect Christian, whether prelate or subject, provided [Col. 0494D] that person has deserved to follow the faith or righteousness of this patriarch.

It applies to Christ because, abandoned by all in his passion and death, which he passed through “with a staff,” that is, by his own will, he instituted for us the sacrament of baptism, commonly understood through the name Jordan. And now he returns with two companies, namely Jews and Gentiles, because he rules alike over those who came before and those who followed, whose salvation he accomplished.

It applies to the Christian set over Christ’s household because, with only the single and simple word of Christian confession or faith, he passed through the sacrament of regeneration. But now, enriched with the gifts of the Holy Spirit and set over God’s Church, he has received two companies to nourish: one of little children, who still need milk; [Col. 0495A] the other of those already perfect, whose food is solid (Heb. V).

Likewise, any subject who has reached the goal of perfection may say with Jacob: “With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I return with two companies.” For each of us comes naked to baptism, possessing nothing except the staff of Christian confession that supports him. Now he returns with two companies because he has received both the remission of sins, which all receive equally in baptism, and, besides this, the divided grace of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. “To each one of us,” says the Apostle, “grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV). Let us now continue the sequence of the history.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 0495B] On Jacob’s wrestling with a man until morning after he had brought all his household across the ford, and on the change of Jacob’s name to Israel.

When he rose early in the morning, he took his two wives, his two maidservants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of Jabbok. After he had brought across all that belonged to him, he remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him until morning.

Jabbok is the name of a river and means “wrestling” or “sand.” It flows between Arene—that is, Philadelphia—and Gerasa, at its fourth milestone, and then flows onward into the Jordan.

[Col. 0495C] “A man,” it says, “wrestled with him until morning.” He had risen early in the morning and wrestled until morning: that is, he rose before daylight to celebrate the sacred vigils, according to the Psalmist’s words: “If I remembered you upon my bed, I will meditate on you in the mornings, because you have been my helper” (Ps. LXII). And he wrestled with the man until morning—that is, until dawn. For the man said, when he could not overcome him: “Let me go, for dawn has now risen.”

“What is your name?” he asked. He replied: “Jacob.” But he said: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel.” The meaning is this: “Your name shall not be ‘supplanter,’ that is, Jacob; but your name shall be ‘prince with God,’ that is, Israel. For just as I am a prince, so you who have been able to wrestle with me [Col. 0495D] shall also be called a prince. And if you have been able to contend with me, who am God or an angel of God, how much more with human beings—that is, with Esau, whom you need not fear?”

The interpretation, repeated in almost everyone’s speech, that Israel means “a man seeing God” or “a mind seeing God,” seems to Blessed Jerome less true than forced.

## CHAPTER VI. What that famous wrestling between God and man signifies.

The famous wrestling, celebrated throughout the world by the mouth of the whole Church, in which a human being wrestled with God and held him fast until the defeated one blessed the victor who had defeated him—saying, “I will not let you go unless you bless me”—and, having received the blessing, the victor began to limp: the event of which this is a foreshadowing extended from the departure of the children of Israel out of Egypt to the incarnation and passion of Christ, the Son of God.

[Col. 0496A] So long was the wrestling between Jacob, the strongest victor, and God, the defeated one, although he is the strongest spirit of all flesh. First, then, it must be carefully understood that this kind of wrestling occurred in such a way that God struggled to depart and Jacob strove to hold the departing Lord. Thus the man says: “Let me go, for dawn has risen.” Jacob, on the other hand: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”

Thus Jacob wrestles with God and, as victor, extorts a blessing from one who is, as it were, unwilling and says, “Let me go.” For it was to happen that God would threaten to depart from Jacob’s seed because of the sins of that rebellious and unbelieving people. When he first spoke thus, Moses rose and himself held the reluctant God by wrestling, so that he should not do it.

[Col. 0496B] “I see,” God says, “that this people is stiff-necked; let me go, that my wrath may be angry against them and destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation” (Exod. XXXII). Moses, stirred by the greatness of the danger and, as it were, clasping him more tightly in a wrestler’s arms, says: “I will not let you go. ‘Why,’ he says, ‘O Lord, is your wrath angry against your people? Do not, I pray, let the Egyptians say: He brought them out deceitfully, to kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth. Let your anger cease, and be merciful concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your faithful servants, to whom you swore by yourself’” (ibid.), etc.

There already—that is, at the making of the calf, before which they danced while singing and saying, “These are your gods, Israel” (ibid.)—there, I say, the fierce wrestling began [Col. 0496C]. From that time God began to attempt to depart from Jacob; and as often as the children of Israel sinned by serving foreign gods, so often the Lord, angry and turned away from them, as though wrestling, shook himself free in order to go away when released.

But Jacob’s strength endured through all the days. For at no time were faithful people lacking among that people, in whom Jacob was father both according to faith and according to flesh. This was so much the case that Elijah thought himself the only one left, saying: “Lord, they have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” And the Lord said to him: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men in Israel whose knees have not been bent before Baal” (III Kings XIX).

[Col. 0496D] Thus God was held by long wrestling and was not released until he blessed Jacob, until the lawgiver fulfilled his blessings by giving that blessing in which all nations were to be blessed, as he had first spoken to Abraham, the father of many nations. For then God truly blessed Jacob, when Christ, taking flesh from his seed, removed the ancient curse and, after his passion, poured out both blessings—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER VII. On the withering of Jacob’s thigh-sinew, and why the Jews do not eat any sinew.

But when giving the blessing, he touched the sinew of Jacob’s thigh, and it immediately withered. Jacob himself limped on his foot. “Therefore the children of Israel do not eat the sinew [Col. 0497A] that withered in Jacob’s thigh unto this present day.”

The sinew of the thigh signifies the propagation of the flesh. Before Christ came and gave the blessing described above, Israel’s carnal race flourished and was vigorous. It was lawful and holy carefully to distinguish the individual tribes by families, households, and men until this fruit of blessing came forth, lest it be uncertain from which tribe and which family he should arise—the one foretold to be born from the tribe of Judah, from the house and family of David.

But once he came—the one who was the sole reason for weaving genealogies—we, with the Apostle, despise and avoid all genealogies, or “fables of genealogies” (I Tim. I; Tit. III), which the Jews thereafter attempt to weave; indeed, we count them as dung (Phil. III). Therefore that man touched the sinew of Jacob’s thigh; therefore Jacob’s thigh-sinew withered. “Therefore,” it says, “the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that withered in his thigh.” They eat no sinew [Col. 0497B] because of that one sinew of the thigh, which is the head and, as it were, the source of all the body’s sinews. Nor were they burdened with such a law without cause: namely, because what is now the case was to come to pass—because they themselves especially withered in Jacob’s thigh; indeed, they themselves are that withered thigh of Jacob.

## VIII. That Jacob limped in respect of the reprobate, and in respect of the elect saw the face of God.

Thereafter Jacob limps in respect of the reprobate, according to the words: “Alien children have lied to me; alien children have grown old and have limped from their paths” [Col. 0497C] (Ps. XVII). But in respect of the elect, the same Jacob says: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved.”

For truly, before the lawgiver gave the blessing already described, so that “the God of gods might be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII), “no one had ever seen God” (John I). But through that blessing it has been brought about that now “we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII), when we have completed our present pilgrimage.

Therefore it was not without reason that it was said: “And immediately the sun rose for him after he had crossed Phanuel,” which is interpreted “the face of God.” For, once the blessing had been poured out, the sun of righteousness rose for the people of the saints, both dead and living, bringing salvation, as Zechariah says, “in the remission of sins, through the tender mercies of our God, by which the Dayspring from on high has visited us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” [Col. 0497D] (Luke I).

He said “sit” in the present tense; for when he said these things, all were still in darkness, and, as has already been said, no one had ever seen God.

### Chapter XXXIII

Likewise, in the person of the reprobate, Jacob bows down to Esau and offers gifts; for his race is weak, weaker than all peoples today, scattered everywhere, and pays many tributes to its lords and kings. But in the person of the elect—for example, such as the apostles were—he does not allow them even to proceed with him for a little way. “For,” he says, “I have tender little children, and pregnant sheep and cattle with me; if I make them labour too much in travelling, all the flocks will die in one day” [Gen. 33:13; col. 0498A].

Here is an example of great discernment. For he is a little child and tender who is not yet perfect in faith and wisdom; and like a pregnant sheep is one whose beginning or purpose has not yet been tested by the practice of works. Such persons are easily corrupted by the company of carnal people, whose whole joy and gladness, according to the prophet, is “to kill calves and slaughter rams, to eat flesh and drink wine: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” [Isa. 22:13]. Hence also the Apostle: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” [1 Cor. 15:33].

Therefore the father Jacob rightly avoids such heedless travellers or runners: “I have tender little children, and pregnant sheep and cattle with me; if I make them labour too much in travelling, all the flocks will die in one day” [col. 0498B]. Yet this example ought also to be applied in good works, so that the shepherd may discern and moderate everything in such a way that the strong may have what they desire, while the weak do not draw back.

## Chapter IX. That everyone who applies himself diligently to the study of Holy Scripture, striving to grasp the meaning of God’s word, wrestles with God after the pattern of Jacob.

Moreover, Jacob—that Jacob who wrestled with God—rightly limps according to the anagogical sense. Having engaged in a long and unremitting struggle, he happily obtained from Him the palm of victory. For a person wrestles with God as long as he applies himself diligently to the study of Holy Scripture and strives to hold fast the elusive meaning of God’s word.

Why does the word of God so greatly flee from the beloved and diligent soul which desires to hold it? Among many reasons, this is one: that it may stir up ever more strongly the eagerness of the seeker, so that, through desire for Him whom she seeks, she may strike against the resistance offered to her intention and bring into bondage the impulses of unruly flesh [col. 0498C].

Thus, stretching out her arms as though for wrestling, such a soul says: “My beloved, I will seize you and lead you into my mother’s house; there you will teach me” [Song 8:2]. But He, in the manner of one resisting, almost turning away, says: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee” [Song 6:5].

A sweet wrestling, more delightful than all peace. At last the victorious conscience of Jacob says: “I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me” [Song 3:4].

But he conquered with great profit to the spirit, though also with great loss to his flesh. Indeed, the one who conquered limps, because the one who was conquered touched the sinew of his thigh, and it withered. How does he limp? Clearly, by resting one foot upon the earth and lifting the other from the earth: that is, not altogether abandoning the active life because of care for those subject to him, while with all his strength he clings to the contemplative life because of its sweetness. This lame man leaps or ascends like a stag and scarcely deigns to touch the ground, “for his citizenship is in heaven” [Phil. 3:20]. Nevertheless, this is only in part: for now he is suspended there, as it were, by one foot only, until that which is perfect comes.

## X. Why, after pitching tents, he called that place Succoth, that is, “Tents.”

“And Jacob came to Succoth. There, after building a house and pitching tents, he called the name of the place Succoth,” that is, “Tents” [Gen. 33:17; col. 0499A].

Because he still breathed the fresh air of the vision in which he had seen the citizens of that city—of which he did not wish to possess here an abiding city [Heb. 13:14], but only its hope—or in which vision he had wrestled with God, the maker of that city, he fittingly called the first place to which he came afterwards Succoth, that is, “Tents”: namely, with reference to the face of God, from which he had named Peniel, and from whose glory he was a pilgrim.

For tents belong to soldiers on campaign. Hence soldiers who dwell beneath the same tent are called *contubernales*, “tent-companions.”

“And he crossed over to Salem, a city of the Shechemites, which is in the land of Canaan, after he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria” [Gen. 33:18; col. 0499B]. Salem is the very same city as Shechem. For it was formerly called Shechem, an older name which has continued until now, except that, through corruption of the name, it is read Sychar, as in the Gospel: “Jesus came to a city called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph” [John 4:5].

Concerning that estate it is immediately added: “And he bought a portion of the field in which he had pitched his tents from the sons of Hamor, Shechem’s father, for a hundred lambs.” But Jacob called it Succoth.

A difficulty arises: how can Salem be called the city of Shechem, when Jerusalem, where Melchizedek reigned, is called Salem? Either both cities bear one name—which we may also find in many places of Judaea, where the same name of city or place occurs in different tribes—or else this Salem, which we now say is named for Shechem, is to be interpreted here as “completed” and “perfected,” while that which was afterwards called Jerusalem is rendered in our language as “peaceful.” For with the accent shifted slightly, this word conveys both meanings.

The Hebrews relate that Jacob’s limping thigh recovered and was healed there; and that for this reason the city received the name of one healed and made perfect. “After he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria.” Here it must be understood that, according to the vow which he had vowed at Bethel, he ought to have gone there and done what he later did there: namely, to build an altar, or a house, for God. For thus he vowed, pouring oil upon the stone which he set up as a pillar: “If I return safely, the Lord shall be my God, and this stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be called the house of God” [Gen. 28:20–22; col. 0499C–D].

Therefore, after he had returned, he ought promptly to have gone up to Bethel and paid his vows. This he did shortly afterwards, being admonished by adversities, God Himself thus requiring the vows: “Arise, go up to Bethel, and dwell there; and make an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau” [Gen. 35:1].

## Chapter XI. That Dinah, Leah’s daughter, became the cause of her own defilement when Shechem, prince of that land, violated her by force.

### Chapter XXXIV

“Dinah, daughter of Leah, went out to see the women of that region. And when Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of that land, saw her, he loved her, seized her, and lay with her, violating the virgin by force,” etc. [Gen. 34:1–2; col. 0500A].

Dinah, whose name means “cause,” in accordance with her name became a serious cause both of her own corruption and of conflicts for others. In what respect? Namely, because she went out to see the daughters of that land: a wandering daughter, undisciplined in her gaze, beautiful in face.

Since the surface meaning of the history is clear, this alone should briefly be said concerning her: the example of such a girl must be avoided by every soul professing religion. For if such a soul is found outside, the devil, the corrupter, will violate her; and he is rightly signified by Shechem, son of Hamor. For Shechem means “broad-shouldered,” while Hamor means “ass.” The devil is broad-shouldered or strong as a lion or bear, but foolish as an ass.

And he will ensnare her not only spiritually but also bodily; not only by himself, but by those like him—that is, by asinine men—whose flesh, according to the prophet, is “like the flesh of asses, and whose emission is like the emission of horses” [Ezek. 23:20; col. 0500B]. Thus it often happens: “The virgin Israel has fallen, and there was none to raise her up” [Amos 5:2].

Furthermore, Philo asserts that this Dinah was Job’s wife, and that she was the woman by whom he fathered fourteen sons and six daughters: namely, seven sons and three daughters before his affliction, and the same number of sons and daughters after it.

“The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father deceitfully, enraged by the violation of their sister.” That Jacob was neither privy nor party to this deceit is also indicated by his own words: “Simeon and Levi, instruments of iniquity in warfare: let not my soul enter into their counsel” [Gen. 49:5–6], etc. Their deceit consisted in this: they spoke holy and useful things, not in order to make proselytes for salvation, but in order that, on the third day, when the pain of wounds is naturally most severe, they might more easily kill men who were equally unsuspecting and wounded, and thus unprepared.

## Chapter XII. That Jacob was commanded to build an altar at Bethel, and that therefore he inquired about the foreign gods among his household.

### Chapter XXXV

“The Lord spoke to Jacob: Arise, go up to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar to God, who appeared to you when you fled from Esau your brother” [Gen. 35:1].

By this same vision Jacob could at last be taught that there was in his house the sin of idolatry, and that he could neither stand against his enemies nor drive them away so long as his household was polluted by that sin. For it is immediately added: “Then Jacob, having summoned all his household, said: Cast away the foreign gods that are among you; purify yourselves and change your garments” [Gen. 35:2; col. 0500D].

Plainly, by this order and these stages of progress one must ascend to Bethel, that is, to the house of God, which is none other than the Church of Christ. First comes the renunciation of former errors and the confession of faith in the one true God: this is to remove the foreign gods from our midst. Then comes baptism in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: this is purification. Thereafter comes walking in newness of life: this is changing garments.

“So they all gave him the foreign gods which they had, and the earrings which were in their ears” [Gen. 35:4]. Men wore earrings, according to the custom of other Eastern peoples: an ornament of a soft and effeminate disposition. Earrings signify the ornaments of false teaching, brilliant in expression but empty of the sense of truth. When we were Gentiles, its fabulous eloquence drew us toward mute idols [cf. 1 Cor. 12:2], like the songs of the Sirens.

“But he buried them beneath the terebinth which is behind the city of Shechem.” The terebinth, a tree producing a most precious resin, signifies the wood of the cross, which possesses supreme power; beneath it all our sins are buried, so that no trace of them may thereafter be found [col. 0501A].

“And when they departed, the terror of the Lord came upon all the surrounding cities, and they did not dare pursue those who withdrew” [Gen. 35:5]. Therefore it was not without purpose, but necessary, that the blessed Jacob was divinely prompted to say: “Remove the foreign gods from among you.” For previously he had been fearful and travelled in danger, bowing down to Esau, while his household was troubled by slaughter and bloodshed. But now the terror of the Lord came upon all the surrounding cities, and they did not dare pursue those who withdrew.

## Chapter XIII. That, having built an altar at Bethel, Jacob paid his vows; and why Deborah’s death is mentioned, while that of Rebecca, whom she had nursed, is passed over in silence.

So Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, surnamed Bethel, he and all the people with him. There he built an altar and called the name of the place “House of God” [Gen. 35:6–7]. Luz was the city’s former name [col. 0501C], meaning “nut” or “almond,” that is, “long nut”; but now it is called Bethel, that is, “House of God.”

There he paid his vows, and he is an example to every person not to delay rendering to God what he has vowed.

At that same time Deborah, Rebecca’s nurse, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel beneath an oak. The name of that place was called “Oak of Weeping” [Gen. 35:8]. What is this—that the death of Deborah the nurse is here committed to memory, while the death of the one whom she had nursed, namely Rebecca, is nowhere found? Was the nurse thought worthier than the one she had reared, so that the nurse’s death was made known because of her worthiness, while Rebecca’s remained unknown because of unworthiness?

Here, then, we must seek the grain beneath the chaff. For as Rebecca signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, so her nurse Deborah signifies the holy, just, and good law of Moses. It further pleases us to infer this from her very name: for Deborah means “bees.” We know that the bee has sweet-flowing honey in its mouth and carries a troublesome sting in its tail.

So indeed the holy law has in its face—the face veiled to the Jews—the life-giving Spirit; in its latter part, which the holy Apostle forgets [Phil. 3:13], it has the killing letter [col. 0501D]. Thus Deborah’s death, though she nourished Rebecca, is recorded because, for those ascending to Bethel, that is, to the house of God, the killing letter of the law is left behind, while the life-giving Spirit remains and is glorified everywhere.

“And she was buried,” he says, “at the foot of Bethel”: that is, at the first entrance of the house of God. Deborah is buried beneath an oak because, at the beginning of the rising Church, in the first stages of Christian religion, which is wholly spiritual, the carnal interpretation of the law and all carnal ceremonies are covered over beneath the wood of the cross [col. 0502A]. And because this is mourned to this day by the Jews, who sit without priest and without temple, the place was rightly called “Oak of Weeping.”

## Chapter XIV. That Jacob, after paying his vows, receives the blessing; and concerning the distinction among the three changes of the names Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.

“God appeared again to Jacob after he had returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and blessed him, saying: You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name. And he called him Israel” [Gen. 35:9–10].

When Jacob paid his vow, he received the blessing by which both what he had seen in a dream when he made his vow while fleeing Esau and what he had most recently heard while wrestling with God were confirmed by repetition [col. 0502B]. “You shall no longer,” He says, “be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.” And the writer added, reporting His very words: “And he called him Israel.” By this statement he showed that the authority of the name must be regarded as most certain, because God’s calling is assuredly not changeable.

What He added—“I am God Almighty; grow and multiply; nations and peoples of nations shall come from you”—has already been explained, because the same promise was made on many occasions. Therefore we rightly call them God’s repeated promises, not merely a promise renewed once, because of their frequent repetition.

Here, in view of the dignity of Him who gave the name, the name Israel must not be passed over. There is a threefold manner in the conferring or designation of names in these three figures of ours: Abraham, Isaac, and Israel [col. 0502C]. God Himself named Abraham in one way, Jacob in another, and Israel in another. He merely enlarged Abraham’s name; He wholly fixed Isaac’s name, unchangeably, before he was born; and He exchanged the whole name Israel for the whole name Jacob.

The cause or rationale of these differences becomes clearer if we first hold in mind that Abraham bore the figure of the former people, Jacob that of the latter people, and Isaac, between them, that of Christ, who joined both peoples in Himself as two walls, being the cornerstone [Eph. 2:14, 20]. The former people, before Christ came, also possessed something of life or righteousness; for “God was known in Judah, and his name was great in Israel” [Ps. 75:1]. But the latter people, coming from the Gentiles, possessed nothing good while it served demons and was truthfully called by the prophet “not my people” or “not my nation” [Hos. 1:9; col. 0502D].

Once these points are observed, it is readily understood how fittingly Abraham’s name was enlarged by only one syllable, while Jacob’s name was wholly changed into Israel. The former people, the Hebrews, were indeed justified by faith in the patriarchs, yet were kept from entrance into Paradise; they needed only one addition, so that they might be perfected in Christ. But the latter people of the Gentiles received from Christ’s coming both the beginning and the perfection of life or righteousness.

Isaac’s name, however, was neither enlarged nor changed; indeed, it was not bestowed by human beings, but named by God’s own mouth before he was born. For Christ’s righteousness never needed to be increased and could not be diminished. It is not by an added gift: before righteousness itself appeared on earth, He was Himself righteousness, Himself life, Himself God and Son of God [col. 0503A].

After the words of this vision alone, the writer added: “And he departed from him.” How did He depart from a holy and righteous man? Namely, by permitting him to be tested or afflicted, so that, when great adversities came upon him, he might be pressed toward an increase of merit. These adversities continue from this place until his descent into Egypt. The first is that which immediately follows.

## Chapter XV. That Rachel died, and why her death is described while Leah’s is passed over in silence.

Leaving there, he came in the springtime to the land leading toward Ephrath. While Rachel was giving birth there, she began to be endangered by the difficulty of her labour. And afterwards: “Rachel died on the way which leads to Ephrath; that is Bethlehem” [Gen. 35:16, 19; col. 0503B].

Springtime signifies the time when all things burst into bloom; it is the season of the elect, or the time when those travelling along the way pluck and choose from neighbouring fields whatever comes to hand, invited by diverse flowers. Ephrath and Bethlehem are two names for one city and have a similar interpretation. For they are rendered “fruitful” and “house of bread,” because of Him who says that He descended from heaven as bread [John 6:41].

“Rachel died,” he says. As was said above, the fact that Deborah the nurse’s death is recorded while Rebecca’s death is silent is not without mystery. So now we must understand that Rachel’s death is not recorded without reason when Leah’s death is not written. For what does Rachel signify except the Church first gathered from the Hebrews? And what does Leah signify except the Church gathered from the Gentiles?

Rachel therefore dies, while Leah’s death is suppressed in silence: because the Synagogue openly fell from the grace of life through unbelief, whereas the Church of the Gentiles lives through faith to the end of the age [col. 0503C]. Notice that Rachel died in childbirth. For the Synagogue died when it brought forth Christ and His apostles. “For what is their receiving,” except “life from the dead”? [Rom. 11:15.]

Hence Rachel, “as her soul was departing because of pain,” calls her son Benoni, which means “son of my sorrow.” For she grieved—that is, she envied—and died by a sorrowful fate because life was taken from her. But the father called that son Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” For he is indeed the choir of apostles, whom God made to sit with Christ at His right hand in the heavenly places [Eph. 2:6; col. 0503D].

## Chapter XVI. On the phrase “beyond the Tower of the Flock”: what place it is.

Leaving there, he pitched his tent beyond the Tower of the Flock [Gen. 35:21]. The ambiguity of this place or name has led some into error.
