Some have supposed this to be the place where the temple was later built, and that the Tower of Eder, the “Tower of the Flock,” signifies the congregation and assembly, as the prophet Micah also attests: “And you, misty Tower of the Flock, daughter of Zion” [Mic. 4:8], etc. They suppose that at that time Jacob had his tents beyond the place where the temple was later built [col. 0504A].

But if we follow the course of the shepherds’ journey, the place lies near Bethlehem: there either the host of angels sang at the Lord’s birth [Luke 2:13–14], or Jacob fed his livestock, giving the place its name, or—what is truer—the mystery that was yet to come was already being shown by a certain prophecy.

“And while he lived in that region, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine.” This did not escape Jacob’s notice. Thus Reuben, though the firstborn, deserved to hear: “You have poured yourself out like water; you shall not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch” [Gen. 49:4].

All heretics resemble him, for they defile Christ’s people with the adulterous seed of evil doctrine. Therefore Bilhah, whose name means “aged” or “worn old,” is rightly here called a concubine. For none but a worn-out concubine prostitutes herself to the lust of heretics. But she who is a lawful wife—that is, one who acknowledges Christ as her husband—can neither fail to know herself nor admit adulterous intercourse [col. 0504B].

## Chapter XVII. On the descendants of Esau, father of Edom.

### Chapter XXXVI

“These are the descendants of Esau, father of Edom, in Mount Seir, and these are the names of his sons” [Gen. 36:1–2]. Esau, Edom, and Seir are names of one man, and why he is called by different names has been explained above.

“Eliphaz, son of Adah, Esau’s wife”: this is the Eliphaz whom Scripture remembers in the book of Job [Job 2:11].

What follows—“These are the chiefs of the Horites who ruled in the land of Seir”—goes farther back. For it had already enumerated Esau’s sons, and now explains who were the Horite chiefs before Esau. In our language *Horites* means “free men.” In Deuteronomy it is more plainly read how the sons of Esau came, killed the Horites, and possessed their land as an inheritance [Deut. 2:12; col. 0504C].

The Horites are mentioned because the firstborn among Esau’s sons had taken Theman, a concubine from their daughters, and Amalek was born from her. As for the names Theman, Kenaz, Amalek, and so forth, we should know that names were afterwards given from these persons to regions of Idumaea.

“This is Anah who found the *haimim* in the wilderness while he fed the asses of Zibeon his father” [Gen. 36:24]. In the Hebrew it is written: “This is he who found *haimim*.” Many think that while feeding his father’s asses in the desert he discovered pools of water, a discovery difficult in the wilderness. Some think that the word signifies hot waters, because of the affinity of the Punic language, which borders upon Hebrew. Others suppose that he introduced wild asses to female asses and discovered this kind of mating, so that very swift asses, called *haimim*, might be born from them. Most think that he was the first to have herds of mares mounted by asses in the desert, so that new animals, mules, contrary to nature, might be born from them [col. 0504D].

## Chapter XVIII. Why, when he was about to speak of Joseph’s age—Joseph who bore the type of Christ, the Sun of Righteousness—the writer prefaced it with “These are his descendants.”

### Chapter XXXVII

“Jacob lived in the land of Canaan, in which his father had lived as a stranger. And these are his descendants: Joseph, when he was sixteen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers, still a boy” [Gen. 37:1–2; col. 0505A].

Thereafter the most holy Joseph, a great and shining star, begins to give forth his light from the lofty heaven of Holy Scripture. Almost alone, in the bright course of his life, he foreshadows how Christ, the Sun of Righteousness, would proceed from the beginning to the end of the day—that is, from His incarnation to the consummation of the age.

The account of his life begins thus: “These are the descendants of Jacob. Joseph, when he was sixteen years old,” etc. Earlier Scripture had said: “The sons of Jacob were twelve,” and had given their catalogue. But now, being about to say, “Joseph, when he was sixteen years old,” it prefaces the statement: “These are the descendants of Jacob” [col. 0505B].

The sense is this: he had twelve sons, certainly; but in the one Joseph he poured out the beauty of his own offspring—that is, the beauty of his own likeness or his fatherly likeness. For just as Jacob himself was begotten from barren Rebecca, from impoverished nature, with divine grace helping him, and was endowed with divine blessing [Gen. 35:11], so Joseph likewise was received as a gift of God from barren Rachel and was to be heir of the same blessing.

## Chapter XIX. That Joseph, still a boy, accused his older brothers—his rivals—of a very grievous crime.

“Joseph,” he says, “when he was sixteen years old, was feeding the flock with his brothers, still a boy” [Gen. 37:2]. The speech of God is not so superfluous that He merely intends to teach us that a person is still a boy at this age, when, after saying “when he was sixteen years old,” He adds “still a boy.” Rather, both expressions—“sixteen years old” and “still a boy”—are carefully used so that you may marvel at the swift perfection of righteousness or merit which is immediately set forth [col. 0505C].

“And he was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. And he accused his brothers to his father of a very grievous crime” [Gen. 37:2]. This deserves careful consideration: though still a boy, he accused his older brothers. He certainly would not have done so unless he already possessed love of purity and zeal for righteousness—something especially praiseworthy in a boy or youth.

But since Scripture did not state what crime he charged his brothers with, room has been given to uncertain opinion, for there are many vices whose completed act is very wicked. Distinguished men nevertheless say that the crime was Sodomitic wickedness. Moreover, the fact that it is specifically said, “He was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives,” already suggests the rivalry of the brothers who were born of Leah. He did not dare be with them because, being born of the free woman and having loftier spirits, they did not willingly look upon the son of beloved Rachel [col. 0505D].

The cause of their envy is immediately added. Scripture says: “But Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had begotten him in his old age. And he made him a many-coloured tunic. And immediately: When his brothers saw that he was loved by his father more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him” [Gen. 37:3–4].

The stated reason for his father’s love must be noted: “because he had begotten him in his old age.” Was Jacob physically old when he begot Joseph, but young when the others were born? For, apart from Benjamin, he begot all of them within fourteen years. It remains, therefore, that the old age meant here is that of which Wisdom says: “Venerable old age is not that which is prolonged, nor measured by the number of years. For the understanding of a man is gray hair, and an unstained life is old age” [Wis. 4:8–9; col. 0506A].

Israel truly begot Joseph in that old age because, through that old age of his righteousness, he deserved to possess such an heir. For a righteous man does not rejoice in a multitude of sons if they are evil; he recognizes himself as a father only if he leaves after himself a son who obtains the inheritance of righteousness. Hence the saying of the Wise Man: “His father has died, and yet he is as though not dead, for he leaves one like himself after him. In his life he saw him and rejoiced in him; in his death he was not grieved” [Sir. 30:4–5].

For a worthy reason, therefore, he loved Joseph and, as one already perfect and full of days—that is, full of virtues—made for him a many-coloured tunic, distinguished by the marvellous variety produced by the craftsman’s hands and reaching down to the ankles: namely, because of the multiplicity of virtues or the perfection of righteousness [col. 0506B].

“Thus, when his brothers saw him, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.” He carefully expressed the greatness of their hatred by saying that they could not speak anything peaceably to him. For hatred is indeed great and most troublesome when the tongue cannot conceal the poison of the mind.

These things have been said according to the literal sense. But now we must say, or behold, how beautifully the image of Christ, Son of God and true Sun, shines forth in this mirror of His [col. 0506C].

## Chapter XX. How Jacob bore the type of Christ the Father, and Joseph that of Christ the Son.

Therefore, in the mystery, Joseph—that is, “increased”—is Christ, the Son of God, full of all the Holy Spirit, “in whom dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” [Col. 2:9].

Though He is sixteen years old—for He both accomplished the six works of the whole creation and wrote the Decalogue of the law with the finger of God—He nevertheless, still a boy, fed the flock of His Father: that is, having taken the form of a servant, He assumed the care of the rational sheep of God the Father.

“And he was with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives” [Gen. 37:2; col. 0506D]. Bilhah means “aged”; Zilpah, “flowing mouth.” By these names are understood the Scribes and Pharisees, grown old in evil days and flowing in speech, who corrupted the teaching of the law through their traditions. He was with them, hearing and questioning them; and not indeed He Himself, but Moses because of Him [John 5:45–47], in whom they hoped, accused them before the Father of a very grievous crime.

“For if I had not come,” He says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin. If I had not done among them the works which no other has done, they would not have sin; but now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father” [John 15:22, 24].

Who doubts that the Father loves this Joseph? For John says: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” [John 13:3], because He begot Him in old age [col. 0507A]. In what old age did that Father beget such a Son? In the old age of eternity, according to which He Himself is called and is the Ancient of Days [Dan. 7:9].

In that old age, in that ancientness of nature, without number of years, without beginning of days, without change of times, that old and ancient Father begot that equally old and equally ancient Son. Therefore He loves Him and made Him a many-coloured tunic.

What is this Son’s tunic except the holy scriptural garment of law and prophecy? For for whose sake, for whose testimony or glory, except that of this Son, did the fingers of God weave all Scripture, which we rightly confess to be divinely inspired? Therefore the Father made for His Son a many-coloured tunic, variously beautiful and beautifully various [col. 0507B].

This like begetting, this many-coloured tunic, and this paternal love—“Let him who has ears to hear, hear” [Matt. 13:9]—are proclaimed by the Father through the Psalmist when He says: “My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king” [Ps. 44:2], etc., to the end of the psalm.

“But when his brothers saw him, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.” It is known that those wicked brothers hated this beloved son exceedingly, with such hatred that they could not speak anything peaceful to Him. Therefore He says in David: “With those who hated peace, I was peaceful; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” [Ps. 119:7]. Again: “They surrounded me with words of hatred and attacked me without cause” [Ps. 108:3; col. 0507C].

They spoke nothing but hostile things: “He casts out demons by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” [Matt. 12:24]; “He has a demon and is mad. Why do you listen to him?” [John 10:20]; and things like these.

But did they see that the Father loved Him, or that He was the Son of God the Father? Certainly. “If you were blind,” He says, “you would not have sin; but now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains” [John 9:41]. They truly saw, and therefore they have no excuse for their sin.

## Chapter XXI. On Joseph’s dream, which he related to his brothers.

Accidentally, too, he related a dream he had seen to his brothers—a thing that became the seedbed of greater hatred. Besides the cause mentioned above, this too happened as an increase of hatred. It is said in this way as if one said: “It happened that his speech became the seedbed of greater hatred.” And this is rightly said to have happened, for he said none of these things deliberately; that is, it was not in his awareness that the report of this dream would become the seedbed of greater hatred. Indeed, it would not have been the mind of a simple or innocent person to wish further to inflame the souls of those who hated him by the prospect of his future happiness.

“I thought,” he says, “that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as it were, rose and stood, while your sheaves stood round about and bowed down to my sheaf.” Again: “I saw,” he says, “in a dream, as it were, the sun and moon and eleven stars bowing down to me.”

Since we all know how the subsequent outcome of events was fulfilled in that Joseph, it remains now for us to understand how these dreams, according to the same causes or results, accord with the Gospel parables of our Lord Jesus Christ. For as in a dream, so also in a parable, one thing is said and another understood; just as the shadow is one thing and the body another, though the body is sometimes recognized from the shadow. And no one can doubt that, just as the cause of Joseph’s dreams became for him a seedbed of greater hatred, so the cause of parables became for our Lord a seedbed of greater hatred and supplied fuel for greater envy.

For example, this parable is set forth: “There was a householder who dug a vineyard, enclosed it with a hedge, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, leased it to tenants, and went abroad” (Matt. 21), etc. For just as Joseph’s eminence was prefigured by the vision in which his sheaf rose and stood, while the sheaves of his brothers stood round it and bowed down, so too our Lord indicated his own exaltation at the conclusion of the parable, saying: “Have you never read in the Scriptures: ‘The stone rejected by the builders has become the head of the corner; this was done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes’?” (Matt. 21).

And just as they, conjecturing what the dream meant for them, said with increased envy, “Will you really be our king, or shall we be subjected to your rule?” so these men, understanding the intention of the parables, became more jealous; and, seeking to seize him, says the evangelist, “they feared the crowds, because they regarded him as a prophet” (ibid.).

Moreover, less was seen in the dream than was said in the parable. For the dream does not state how Joseph’s sheaf ought to rise and stand and be worshipped by the surrounding sheaves of his brothers; whereas this parable declares that the Jews would cast the Son of God the Father outside the city gate in order to kill him, and then, by adding the testimony of the Psalm which says, “The stone rejected by the builders has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117), openly confirms that, having thus been cast away or rejected, he was to be established as the head of the nations. Therefore, insofar as Joseph bore the type of Christ, these dreams of his are likewise similar to the parables of that same Christ.

There were indeed two dreams, but they were, or should be, regarded as one, just as he himself said to Pharaoh: “The king’s dream is one; and that you saw the dream a second time, pertaining to the same matter, is an indication of certainty, because the word of God will be done, or will be fulfilled more swiftly” (Gen. 41). One dream was from the earth or field, the other from heaven, because the happiness of Joseph, to be worshipped by his brothers, was to receive worship not only from earth but also from heaven—not only from human beings but also from God; indeed, it was to receive its first and greatest praise from God.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the interpretation of the dream from Jacob’s saying: “Shall I, etc., bow down to you upon the earth?”

But why did the father attempt to interpret the dream thus: “Shall I and your mother and your brothers bow down to you upon the earth?” Since he knew that Rachel, Joseph’s mother, had died, how did he suppose that she who had departed could bow down? Or does he here call his surviving wife his mother by custom rather than by nature? For since an aunt is called *matertera*, “another mother,” he could rightly call Leah his mother here.

Nevertheless, it is not openly read that even his father bowed down, except when Joseph had sworn that he would take his father out of Egypt and bury him in the tomb of his ancestors: according to the Septuagint, “Israel his father worshipped the top of his staff.” But according to the Hebrew truth it is better read: “He worshipped God, turning toward the head of the bed” (Gen. 41). Thus the whole is put for a part; or it is to be understood that the father truly worshipped heavenly grace, giving thanks for his son, and that the mother too would undoubtedly have done so had she still lived.

And even if the letter may seem weak to anyone in this respect, it must firmly be known that, according to the spiritual sense, every truth is fulfilled in Christ. For who is his father here, if not the earlier people from whom he was incarnate, which, from the day of the passion or resurrection of that same Son, shines in the heavenly kingdom, in the portion of the elect, like the sun? And what is the moon, if not the present Church, subject to change and shining less brightly so long as it is a pilgrim in this life? The individual elect are stars—imperfect in themselves, as it were in the number eleven; but their perfection is the twelfth star, the perfect and morning star, namely Christ himself, their brother.

All things bow down: sun and moon, all stars, all heavenly things, all earthly things, greater and lesser alike; they venerate and worship him. “To me every knee shall bend, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 45). For what is his sheaf, if not the evangelical faith sown by him and brought, and yet to be brought, to harvest? The sheaves of his brothers, moreover, are the readings of the Law and the Prophets, which the Jews, as they read them, bind or gather as sheaves. Behold: Christ’s sheaf is plainly visible to all, standing in the whole field of the world; and the sheaves of his brothers stand around it and bow down—that is, the Gospel, the faithful harvest and finest grain, asserts Christ’s sole and unique dominion, while all readings of the Law and Prophets render to it the service of testimony and the homage of due worship. Let the envious brothers therefore imitate their sheaves: they will one day do this, worshipping him whose sheaf their own sheaves already worship.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That Joseph, obedient to his father and sent to his brothers at Shechem, bore the type of Christ obedient to his Father unto death

When his brothers were staying in Shechem to feed the flocks, Israel said to him: “Your brothers are feeding the flocks at Shechem; come, I will send you to them.” This was the cause of the father’s anxiety: his sons were feeding his sheep at Shechem, where previously their stubborn fury and fierce indignation had made them hateful to the people of that land. Under the same anxiety he had earlier said: “You have troubled me and made me hateful to the Canaanites and Perizzites, inhabitants of this land. We are few; they will gather together, strike me, and I and my household shall be destroyed” (Gen. 34).

Thus he was not without reason anxious: “Your brothers are feeding the flocks at Shechem; come, I will send you to them.” The father thought the visit would be welcome to his sons, since he was sending them not just any man, but the son whom he loved. “Go,” he said, “and see whether all is well with your brothers and the livestock, and report to me what is happening.” Scripture inserted a brief but distinguished word of the obedient son, saying that he answered: “Here I am.” The perseverance of his goodwill and attentiveness is likewise indicated by the fact that, when he did not find them in Shechem, he continued searching while wandering, needing a guide or informant, until he found them in Dothan.

This plainly signifies the thing which the Apostle proclaims in Christ the Son of God as admirable and worthy of imitation: that “he became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). His brothers according to the flesh—the scribes and Pharisees—were feeding sheep at Shechem; that is, after the example of the Shechemites, they were teaching, indeed deceiving, the foolish. Of such people the Psalmist says: “Like sheep, they are placed in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48).

In what way after the example of the Shechemites? Namely, because they traversed sea and land to make one proselyte and, once he had been made, made him a child of perdition, twice as much as themselves (Matt. 23). For their fathers did this to the Shechemites, deceitfully deceiving them so that they were circumcised: they made them proselytes and killed the unsuspecting (Gen. 34). And when the Son was sent by God the Father to such shepherds in order to suffer, he said: “Here I am.” For, he says, “The Lord opened my ear; but I do not resist; I did not turn back” (Isa. 50).

Therefore he came to the tents of the shepherds; he went up to Jerusalem for the feast day (John 7), to report to the Father what was being done—not by a local return or backward steps, but by the loud cry of his blood (Heb. 5), through which the most cruel crime of those brothers is continually proclaimed to heaven.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That Joseph, surrounded by the anguish of death, figured the likeness of Christ’s death and his passion

He went on after his brothers and found them at Dothan. When they saw him from afar, before he came near them, they planned to kill him, and said to one another: “Behold, the dreamer comes. Come, let us kill him,” etc.

It was not necessary that, for the sake of likeness to his Son, God should permit Joseph to be killed and then raise him from the dead—although this too was possible to him, since he is almighty. For to be killed is no longer a likeness of death, but death itself. “For if,” says the Apostle, “we have been made conformed to the likeness of his death, we shall also be conformed to his resurrection” (Rom. 6). Does he, in saying this, urge us to be physically extinguished? Therefore, for the likeness it was sufficient that, while still living and without loss of life, he should be surrounded by the anguish of death and thus share beforehand in Christ’s future sufferings.

But in order that he might escape death when they said, “Behold, the dreamer comes. Come, let us kill him and see whether his dreams will profit him,” the division among the wicked became a safeguard to the righteous man. For Reuben said: “Let us not kill him; do not shed blood, but cast him into this cistern in the wilderness, and keep your hands innocent.” He said this because he wanted to rescue him from their hands and restore him to his father. Perhaps Reuben thought that he himself would be more suspected and that the whole weight of the crime would be laid upon him, since he had lost the birthright which the father had begun to transfer to Joseph, the firstborn by the other wife. He was certainly separated from the others in this matter; and they had to beware of offending him, since, if offended, he could report the affair to his father.

Accordingly, yielding to one man, as soon as Joseph came to them they stripped him of the long, many-coloured tunic and cast him into a cistern that had no water. But on this arrangement, if he were left there he would not escape death; while if Reuben, as he intended, rescued him from their hands and restored him to his father, the dreams divinely provided for him would not be fulfilled. Thus another division arose, and they were divided into three parties, so that God’s purpose might more swiftly run its appointed course. For it follows: “As they sat down to eat bread, they saw Ishmaelite travelers.” Then Judah said to his brothers: “What profit is there for us if we kill our brother? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites,” etc.

Certainly he did not say this from himself; but just as Caiaphas prophesied when he said, “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people, and not the whole nation perish” (John 18), so this man too, by God’s prompting, prophesied that it would be better for Joseph to be sold than killed, and more profitable for themselves to sell him to the Ishmaelites than to kill him and conceal his blood. This rather was God’s will; yet Joseph’s brothers intended evil against him, while God knew how to turn it into good. Joseph himself says: “Can we reject God’s will? You intended evil against me, but God turned it into good” (Gen. 50). The Psalmist also testifies to this, saying: “He sent a man before them,” and immediately adding, “Joseph was sold as a slave” (Ps. 104).

They, I say, intended evil against their brother whom they sold as a slave; but God turned it to good by sending a man before them. This was to be compared with Christ: truly, to be pierced through by the iron of the passion. Thus he who had said above, “They humbled his feet in fetters,” immediately added, “Iron passed through his soul” (ibid.). By iron passing through the soul he means the soul’s distress. How violent it was, the brothers testify as they speak to one another: “We suffer these things deservedly, because we sinned against our brother, seeing the distress of his soul when he begged us and we would not listen” (Gen. 42).

## CHAPTER XXV. That Joseph’s brothers sent his tunic dyed with a kid’s blood and announced his death to their father; and on the father’s mourning

They took his tunic and dipped it in the blood of a kid which they had killed. They sent persons to carry it to their father and say: “We found this; see whether it is your son’s tunic or not.” They deliberated this way and did not wish to say themselves, “We found this”; rather, they sent others to carry it and say that they themselves had found it. Thus they could more safely appear innocent, lessen for themselves the labor of dissimulation, and turn their father’s mind further away from suspicion of their crime.

But could they deceive so watchful a man even in this way? Even if that holy man had nothing beyond human conjecture, could they envelop his whole spirit in the darkness of their deceit? For in one place he says: “You know that my wife bore me two sons. One went out, and you said: ‘A beast devoured him’” (Gen. 44). What did you say, unless you also sent those who were to say it? Therefore that most evil wild animal, that most savage beast, which, so far as it lay in itself, had devoured him, could not be wholly unknown to the father.

But what could he do? How could he bind that beast? How could he think that his son, whom he believed devoured, could be drawn out from the belly of that beast? It was rather a time for silence and concealment of what he could conjecture, lest, if he provoked with open complaints that beast known to him—that is, the bold and violent envy of his sons—he should whet its teeth to greater frenzy. Therefore, in his most bitter grief, forcing himself and restraining his words, he said: “It is my son’s tunic. A most evil beast has eaten him; a beast has devoured Joseph.” In saying this he was neither false nor lying. Such cruelty may most rightly be denoted figuratively by the name of a wild animal or beast, such as a lion or bear.

After tearing his garments, he put on sackcloth and mourned for his son a long time. What rest, then, from their envy or what cooling of their jealousy did Joseph’s abductors obtain? If their brother was burdensome to see because he was loved, their father could be much more burdensome, because the whole household before their eyes was perpetually tormented by his sickness and sorrow and worn away by excessive grief.

When all his children had gathered to soften their father’s grief, he refused to receive consolation and said: “I shall go down mourning to my son into hell.” Because he believed his son dead—and all the dead, even the righteous, descended into hell before Christ’s coming—he said, “I shall go down to hell to my son,” meaning: “When I end my present mourning together with my life, I shall cease mourning for my son only by dying.”

But with what disposition did his assembled children come to alleviate their father’s grief? For who could mitigate his sorrow except one whom that sorrow itself bit to the marrow? Such is the nature of genuine sorrow. “For if,” says the Apostle, “I make you sorrowful, who is there to make me glad except the one who is made sorrowful by me?” (2 Cor. 2). Yet they could not weep in truth or be sincerely grieved, since, as a means of their own sorrow and a relief from their tormenting envy, they had carried their brother away. With what face, then, did they assemble and stand by? For one of the secular writers says:

> Alas, how difficult it is not to betray guilt by one’s face!  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 2.447

The father’s tears, because they had found the wounded vein of his heart, ran without restraint as far as they wished; nor could they be checked by tightened reins, because they had shaken themselves free with violent force. But the brothers’ tears were shut in; however sharply they might urge them with spurs, they would not break forth. Therefore, though they wished to soothe the father’s genuine sorrow, he would not receive consolation; he would not hear them; he would not even invite them to mourning; he did not care even to stir their voices to weeping with him—which is the final consolation.

For those bereft of every joy and nourished only by their own tears, struck only by their own groans, are accustomed to do this. Thus, for example, the prophet Jeremiah says: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1).

## CHAPTER XXVI. Again on the same subject; and that, like Isaac, Joseph was attacked for killing but did not die, and thus prefigured Christ’s passion

Therefore, just as the boy Isaac, led to be sacrificed, bound and placed upon the altar, was nevertheless not struck by the sword, so Joseph too was attacked by his brothers for killing, cast into the cistern, and sold, yet not actually killed. He is therefore rightly said to have suffered, and in his suffering to have been made like the Son of God.

Likewise, just as the ram offered as a burnt offering in Isaac’s place accomplished the mystery of the likeness of the Son of God—whose divine nature remained impassible, while his human nature alone suffered or died—so too the slaughtered kid, by whose blood Joseph’s long and many-coloured tunic was dyed, is recognized as having displayed the same figure or likeness.

We have already said above that Christ’s many-coloured tunic is Holy Scripture: that tunic of which the envious brothers, the Jews, so far as lay in them, stripped the Father’s beloved Son when they rejected him and denied that he was the one written of by Moses in the Law and by the Prophets. Behold Christ’s tunic in Jewish hands—that is, the legal and prophetic Scripture. It has been stained with that blood, with the blood of the kid: that is, with the blood of Christ himself, who bore sins not his own but others’, and was therefore signified by the kid. It is defiled in Jewish hands. Whatever they strive to read, whatever Sabbath observance they pursue, all that they think they possess as holy is full of blood; and the hands of the Jews themselves are full of blood.

Who are those whom they sent, upon whom they laid the task of bringing this tunic to the father? Surely we are they: we neither sold this son nor killed the kid—who is the same according to his human nature—bearing our sins. But we heard where it occurred, and, coming afterward, received the tunic already dyed. They themselves did not send us; rather, they expelled, cast out, and anathematized both us and our fathers, the apostles. Yet they could not prevent us from carrying off these spoils.

Whenever, then, we stand before the Father, whenever in singing, chanting psalms, or reading we expound Holy Scripture, let us familiarly say to God: “We found this; see whether it is the tunic of your Son or not.” And he answers us: “It is my Son’s tunic; a most evil beast ate him; a beast devoured Joseph.” For that nation, once the Father’s household or inheritance, is now called and is a most evil wild animal or beast, and is called a hyena. Thus the Son himself says in the prophet: “My dwelling has become to me like a hyena’s den” (Jer. 12).

Long ago this father tore his garments and put on sackcloth; that is, after tearing and casting away from himself the adornments of former ceremonies, scorning the rite of the priests and the adornment of sacrifices, he admitted and joined to himself a multitude of penitent idolaters. Certainly, when all such children of his gather in order to soothe his grief—that is, to flatter him with sacrifices and Mosaic readings—he utterly refuses to hear them and says: “When you stretch forth your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

But what then? “I shall go down,” he says, “mourning to my son into hell.” Mourning, I say—that is, making them mourn with unutterable groans—I shall go down to those who, though they are in hell or in tombs, hear the voice of my Son; and I shall go down for this purpose: that whoever hears may live (John 5).

## CHAPTER XXVII. How Joseph, once sold by his brothers for twenty denarii, was sold a second time in Egypt by the Midianites to Potiphar the eunuch

While he persisted in weeping, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, a eunuch and commander of the guard. A question is raised concerning this man, who is now said to be a eunuch: how is he later said to have had a wife? The Hebrews relate that Potiphar bought Joseph, because of his exceptional beauty, for shameful service; that the Lord afterward caused Potiphar’s male organs to wither; and that he was then chosen, according to the custom of the hierophants, for the priesthood of Heliopolis. Aseneth, whom Joseph later took, is said to have been Potiphar’s daughter.

Behold, Joseph was sold as a slave a second time (Ps. 104). It should be noted that Scripture did not conceal the price of the first sale: his brothers sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. But it neglected to say for how much he was sold the second time. Rightly so: for the Ishmaelite or Midianite merchants, mixed together, lawfully sold what was theirs and what they had bought. But the brothers, in doing this evil, sold themselves; and therefore it was necessary to know at what price they sold themselves—that is, for how trifling a price they became slaves of so immense a sin. For in such a transaction, what are twenty silver pieces among so many? Since ten brothers were sellers of one person, their individual shares were two good silver pieces. They therefore sold themselves cheaply, except that they cared not so much to enrich their purses as to satisfy their envy.

The Midianites who bought Joseph and sold him again are comparable to the wicked brothers—namely, the chief priests, who both sold Christ and promised money to the disciple in order that he might sell him. They sold him, I say, because, to serve their own purpose of preserving their place and nation, they delivered him to Pilate as though selling him again. For if, according to the Apostle, all who persecute those born according to the Spirit or who are children of promise are from Ishmael (Gal. 4), how much more rightly may those be called Ishmaelites who pursued unto death this one born not merely according to the Spirit, but conceived from the Holy Spirit, to whom God gives the Spirit not by measure (John 3), and in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2).

This was their astonishing sale: for the sake of their place and nation they delivered up their king, the sole defense both of their place and of their nation, saying: “Otherwise the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). The price of their purchase was likewise reckoned: they gave thirty pieces of silver to the betraying disciple. Here the divinely ordained difference of prices, corresponding to the difference of persons, must be carefully noted. In the limit of ten, twice ten makes twenty and thrice ten thirty. Thus the amount of the price for which Joseph was sold is twofold; the price for which Christ was bought is threefold. And rightly so. Joseph, being merely human, consists only of soul and body; but Christ consists of soul and body together with the reality of the divine nature. Thus there is fittingly a twofold amount there, but here a threefold amount of price.

Moreover, both there, where Joseph was sold in Egypt, and here, where our Lord was handed over to the Gentiles, the price or profit of those selling or handing him over is not specified. Nevertheless, in the prophet’s words, “Let them be afraid, and not I; bring upon them the day of affliction, and crush them with a double destruction, O Lord my God” (Jer. 17), a just recompense was allotted to their wickedness. For because, fearing—or rather pretending fear—they said, “The Romans will come and take away our place,” they were crushed not merely by this single destruction, but their destruction was doubled: they lost both their place and incurred the eternal death of the soul.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Judah’s marriage and his sons; and that Tamar, a foreign woman, and Judah’s adulterous intercourse shut the mouths of Jews who glory in the flesh

**(CHAPTER 38.)** At that time Judah went down from his brothers and turned aside to a man of Adullam named Hiram. There he saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua; and, having taken her as wife, he went in to her. She conceived and bore a son, and called his name Er. Conceiving again, she called the son who was born Onan. She also bore a third, whom she called Shelah. After he was born she ceased bearing further children. Judah gave a wife named Tamar to his firstborn Er. But Er, Judah’s firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord, and he killed him, etc.

Everywhere God dispenses and governs the gifts of his grace among his elect in such a way that there may be a righteousness of faith to proclaim, and presumption of the flesh in which not to glory; so that, according to the Apostle, “every mouth may be stopped and the whole world become subject to God” (Rom. 3), and “no flesh may glory before him” (1 Cor. 1).

For the carnal Jews, glorying in the flesh, had great confidence in the fact that their fathers were called holy and that they themselves had holy wives, abominating foreign women—that is, daughters of the Canaanites among whom they lived. But behold: Tamar, a foreign woman, and Judah’s adulterous intercourse stop their mouths, since, if they wish to conceal it, they are plainly shamed by the fact that their leaders, princes, kings, prophets, and they themselves descended from it. All the glory of the nation and all the nobility of this people flowed from this adultery, so that, as has already been said, every mouth may be stopped, no one may glory in personal merits, and God alone may be righteous and the justifier of the one who is of faith (Rom. 3).

Since the surface of the literal text is plainly unlovely, let us seek inwardly the beauty of the Spirit, to the honor of him who came to call not the righteous but all sinners and the ungodly (Matt. 9). For we must not suppose that he wished in vain to have the fathers from whom he himself was to be born according to the flesh arise from such beginnings (Rom. 9)—he who is God over all, blessed for ever.

## CHAPTER XXIX. What Tamar the adulteress signifies mystically

Tamar—whose name means “bitterness”—signifies repentance, necessary for every human being ever since the first Adam sinned, in whom all die. Er and Onan, of whom one means “skin-like” and the other “their sorrow,” were commanded to take Tamar as wife but did not father children by her, and died because of their wickedness. They signify those who lived before the Law and under the Law, who, though commanded to practice repentance, neglected it; indeed, they wickedly abused God’s forbearance and squandered the time for repentance.

Judah, who at last went in to her and fathered two sons by her in one intercourse, signifies Christ, who at last undertook the repentance to be performed for the whole world and, through the single experience of death, as though giving birth in the pains of death, bore fruit in the salvation and eternal life of two peoples. Let us explain this meaning more fully in the order of the letter.

After the death of Shua’s daughter, Judah’s wife, he, having received consolation after mourning, was going up to the sheep-shearers of his flock—he and Hiras, the Adullamite shepherd of the flock—to Timnah. Judah means “confession”; Hiras, “I have seen my brother”; Adullamite, “testimony in water”; Timnah, “forbidding” or “failing.” Therefore in Judah we recognize Christ, whom the Apostle also calls “the high priest of our confession” (Heb. 3); in Hiras, John the Baptist, who says: “And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1). In his being called an Adullamite, we understand the very testimony for which he came baptizing in water. In Timnah, the Jews, who forbid and, by forbidding, fail. In the death of Shua’s daughter—whose name means “speaking” or “song”—we understand the silence of the Law and Prophets, who prophesied until John.

Then Judah was going up to shear his sheep, and Hiras with him; for Christ then came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15), and with him, or before him, John the Baptist, baptizing in water and preaching the washing necessary for shearing the sheep: that is, repentance and fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. 3), necessary for laying aside the burdens of sins.

## CHAPTER XXX. What it mystically signifies that Tamar received a pledge until the kid should be sent

This was announced to Tamar, that is, to bitterness; and, putting on the dress of a prostitute, she sat at the crossroads. For the voice of that shepherd of the Lord’s flock had been heard, crying and saying: “Repent, and bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3). From that time everyone who feared for his or her sins became bitter; and so every soul showed itself a sinner through public confession, just as the dress Tamar had taken testified her to be a prostitute. For she had put on a *theristrum*, that is, a light, thin summer mantle. She sat at the crossroads, by which is understood the boundary between the Law and grace.

Our Judah saw her—that is, he had compassion; he loved her—that is, he accepted her satisfaction. For how did he wish to enjoy intercourse with her except by deigning to share repentance with bitterness? So far was he from disdaining this that, among penitents, he himself received from his servant the baptism of repentance.

But what was the agreement between them, and upon what payment did they agree? “I will send you a kid from the flock,” he says. What does it mean that a kid is given to Tamar as payment except that Christ is sacrificed for penitents? For according to his own innocence he is the Lamb of God; according to the sins of others, which he undertook to expiate in himself, he was a kid. “What,” he says, “do you wish to be given as a pledge?” She answered: “Your ring, bracelet, and staff which you hold in your hand.” The ring signifies faith; the bracelet, the working of love; the staff, the strength of hope. Tamar rightly asks for these as a pledge until she receives the kid. For the penitent soul is pledged by faith, hope, and charity until it sees Christ, sacrificed for its sins, face to face.

She is also defended from accusation of having committed fornication through the pursuit of wandering disgrace by the testimony of these three things: she conceived from Judah. That is, on the day of judgment, summoned by faith, hope, and charity, she will be justified and glorified, because she conceived from no spirit other than Christ’s Spirit, saying with the prophet: “From fear of you, Lord, we conceived and bore spirit; we did not bring about salvations upon the earth” (Isa. 26).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Tamar’s childbirth and what the twins in her womb signify: that one first put out his hand and the other broke down the wall
When her delivery was imminent, twins appeared in her womb [Col. 0518A]. In the very birth of the children, one put out his hand; the midwife tied a scarlet thread upon it, saying, “This one will come out first.” But when he drew back his hand, the other came out. And the woman said, “Why has the wall been divided because of you?” For this reason she called his name Perez. Afterwards the other came out, with the scarlet thread on his hand, and she called him Zerah.

The season, or day, of this birth is “the acceptable time” and “the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6): it begins from the hour of Christ’s passion, whose bitterness—that is, death—brought forth every human being, both Jew and Greek, into eternal life. For these are the two twins found contending in Tamar’s womb, as though disputing over the privilege of being born first. The Apostle, desiring to make them equal and to form them into the harmony of peace, [Col. 0518B] frightens them with threats and soothes them with promises: “Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress, upon every soul of a human being who does evil—of the Jew first and also of the Greek. But glory and honour and peace to everyone who does good—to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2), and so forth.

“In the very birth of the children,” he says, “one put out his hand.” The one who first put out his hand is the Jew, who first received the Law and to whom it was necessary first to speak the word of God (Acts 13). But he rejected it and judged himself unworthy of eternal life. Thus he quickly drew back the hand bound with scarlet: that is, he turned away a conscience stained by Christ’s blood. Immediately the other came forth—the Greek, that is, the Gentile people, came into the light and was born to God. “Why,” she says, “has the wall been divided because of you?” [Col. 0518C] Certainly she did not say this of herself, but truly prophesied what has now openly occurred: namely, that a partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. 11). This interruption of Israel is the division of the wall, which the name Perez also signifies; for it is interpreted “division.” The other she called Zerah. By this name the blindness that happened to Israel is indicated as destined to be driven away, so that, after the present night of unbelief, it may see the true light, looking toward the east. For Zerah is interpreted “rising” or “east.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. That Joseph, sold to a eunuch, was delivered by the Lord [Col. 0518D] lest he be taken for disgraceful service.

**(Chapter 39.)** Therefore Joseph was brought down into Egypt, and Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian man, bought him from the Ishmaelites, who had brought him there. The Scripture, having interrupted the sequence of the previous narrative, resumes it through this repetition: “Therefore,” it says, “Joseph was brought down into Egypt,” and so forth.

And immediately, in accordance with the Psalmist, who says concerning the blessings of the righteous: “A person’s steps shall be directed by the Lord, and He shall will his way; when he falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord supports him with His hand” (Ps. 33 [34]). “And the Lord was with him, and he was a man prospering in all things.” Where had he fallen by being sold in this manner? Or against what collision did the Lord support him with His hand, lest he should be dashed down? Clearly, according to the Hebrew tradition mentioned above, [Col. 0519A] he had fallen into evil slavery: that Egyptian man had bought him for shameful service. But, as the Lord supported him with His hand, he was not dashed down; for, they say, that same master of his withered and became a eunuch. Perhaps for this very reason it is said with such emphasis that he knew very well that the Lord was with him: namely, because he had learned it through such an experience concerning himself.

The Lord therefore supported him with His hand, not so as to raise him entirely up, but only so that he should not be dashed down—that is, so that he should not be defiled by another’s sin or broken by adversity. For the furnace of temptation had not yet sufficiently tested this receptive man, as “the furnace tests the potter’s vessels” (Sir. 27). Nor had it yet been sufficiently seen [Col. 0519B] how great he was inwardly, though he was already pleasing outwardly.

Let Joseph therefore be increased, according to his name. For he was not so named without cause, nor did his mother speak of herself; rather, divine foreknowledge preceding her, she prophesied that his growth in virtues would be great, although, when she imposed this name, she did not know the future. Let him be increased, I say; and let him, on whose account God wonderfully deprived a man of strength lest Joseph suffer violence, show himself worthy of that miracle by conquering, through virtue, the woman. It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That four virtues are discerned in Joseph because he despised his lustful mistress.

Now Joseph was handsome in face and beautiful in appearance. After many days his mistress cast her eyes upon [Col. 0519C] Joseph and said, “Sleep with me.” But he in no way consented to the wicked deed, and so forth.

In this tribulation, in this hidden danger of the storm (Ps. 80 [81]), where Joseph was heard and tested, we recognize four virtues: temperance, justice, courage, and prudence. What could be more temperate than that the young man did not incline his mind to the one who said, not merely anyone, but his own mistress, “Sleep with me”? What more just than his saying: “Behold, my master, having entrusted all things to me, does not know what he possesses in his house; nor is there anything that is not in my power, or that he has not entrusted to me, except you, because you are his wife. How, then, can I commit this evil and sin against my master?” What more courageous than this perseverance: she spoke words of this kind [Col. 0519D] to him day after day; the woman troubled the young man, and he refused the sexual violation. What more prudent than that, when she seized the hem of his garment and said, “Sleep with me,” he left his cloak in her hand, fled, and went outside?

Indeed, he judged it safer to shake off his clothing at a temporal loss and cast the fire far from himself than, by long suppressing it in silence, to bind the woman’s flame in his bosom at the danger of his soul. Rightly, therefore, the Psalmist called him a man, saying: “He sent a man before them” (Ps. 104 [105]). Yet women sought to capture in body the man whose mind was unconquered by such great virtues. For it follows: “When the woman saw the garment in her hands and that she had been despised, she called the people of her house and said to them: ‘Behold, [Col. 0520A] my master has brought in a Hebrew man to mock us,’” and so forth.

When he heard this, the master, far too ready to believe his wife’s words, became very angry and delivered Joseph into the prison where the king’s prisoners were kept. Thus, although he was free from sin and a servant of righteousness, he—a man—was put in fetters by a woman; but only in body, not in mind. Thus “they humbled his feet in fetters, and iron passed through his soul,” as he endured God as his judge and witness, “until his word came” (Ps. 104 [105]).

In this manner, what Israel’s father said was not far from the truth: “A most evil beast has eaten him; a wild beast has devoured Joseph” (Gen. 37). For that woman was truly a beast, indeed a most evil wild beast, wounded by lust and made savage by the pain of her own contempt. Although she did not devour his soul through consent to sin, she nevertheless bit it and pierced it with sharp pain as with an iron tooth. This concerns the literal sense.

But, as a type of the Lord the Saviour, that tragedy of the woman is the madness of the Synagogue. According to the historical account the periods are divided: for “after many days” the mistress cast her eyes upon Joseph. But according to the mystical sense the event is joined together and its order continuous. For after our Lord had been seized by the Jews, his brothers, and had suffered mockery and reproaches throughout the whole night, daylight followed, and he was brought before the governor and accused with false witnesses. We must therefore say what the Synagogue desired in Christ and why, grieving that it had not obtained it, it handed Christ over to its governor.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. [Col. 0520C] Again, concerning the same matter in a mystical sense.

Now Joseph was handsome in face and beautiful in appearance. Everything that Holy Scripture proclaims of Christ is beautiful and comely, yet not apart from what lies hidden within (Song 4). For example: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth; Ethiopians shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust; the kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of Arabia and Sheba shall bring presents” (Ps. 71 [72]). Whatever of this sort is sung or read concerning Christ is beautiful; yet the same beauty was contemplated in one way by the carnal Synagogue and in another by the spiritual Church.

The former, pleased only by what is in the world—by the lust [Col. 0520D] of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, the ambition of the spirit, and the pride of life (1 John 2)—when it read that the Messiah was to come, that is, Christ the great king, “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44 [45]), hoped that everything would happen carnally. It expected that, according to his humanity, he would sit on David’s throne in that Jerusalem which killed the prophets, in that Zion which stoned those sent to it; that thence he would rule from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth; that Ethiopians and the kings of islands would come before him; that the kings of Arabia and the kings of Sheba would offer gifts and bring presents to that golden, jewelled Jerusalem (Matt. 2); that absolutely everyone would worship that king and city; [Col. 0521A] and that all nations would serve Jewish greed under so great a king.

To think thus carnally about Christ and to hope according to the human being was to have the wanton woman cast incestuous eyes upon the beautiful Joseph. But Christ does not accept such an understanding; indeed, he hates and rejects one who understands in this fashion. Long ago he rejected the Synagogue which read and thought in this way; fleeing with his life-giving Spirit, he left it only the letter that kills (2 Cor. 3). Thus Joseph rightly fled, leaving his cloak in the adulteress’s hand, and went outside. For he fled who also said, “Behold, your house shall be left desolate to you” (Matt. 23). He fled, I say, and went outside; and he prefigured this also by his action, when the Jews took up stones [Col. 0521B] to throw at him, but he hid himself and went out of the Temple (John 8).

Therefore, as evidence for her belief, she showed the retained cloak to her husband when he returned home and said, “He came in to me to mock me.” She showed the retained cloak to her husband—that is, before her governor she produced vain testimonies from the Scriptures as evidence for the claim that the Lord Jesus was either a deceiver or a mocker. For example: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19). Again: “He stirs up all Judaea, teaching from Galilee as far as this place and saying that he is Christ the king” (Luke 23).

Pilate—or rather Caesar—was then the husband of such a synagogue, one whom it was fitting should here be signified through the Egyptian eunuch. For just as she who has a eunuch as her husband [Col. 0521C] neither truly has a husband nor is free from the law of a husband so as to marry whomever she wishes, so Judaea neither then had her husband—namely God, who speaks in the prophet, “From now on call me ‘my husband’” (Jer. 3)—nor was she like a widow or virgin. For, having neither her king nor her Lord, she courted Caesar with flattery, saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19).

When he heard these things, he handed him over to death, and iron passed through his soul—not only his soul, but also his flesh. For his hands and feet were pierced with nails, and his side was pierced by a spear.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How Joseph, cast into prison, [Col. 0521D] was not abandoned by the Lord.

Thus he became “like a man without help,” indeed insofar as concerned human judgment or opinion; nevertheless, he was “free among the dead” (Ps. 87 [88]). This is the true likeness of his freedom. “The Lord,” it says, “gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison, who handed over into his hand all the prisoners held in custody; and whatever was done was under his direction.”

It was rightly said of that righteous man, with praise worthy of Wisdom: “She did not forsake the righteous man when he was sold, but delivered him from sinners; she descended with him into the pit and did not abandon him in his chains” (Wis. 10). For he suffered adverse judgment, having no human helper to plead his cause for him, nor any protector in whose confidence a solitary slave could demand judgment. He could rightly say, “I became like a man,” or certainly, “I am a man without help.”

But because Wisdom had descended with him into the pit—that is, into the cistern into which his brothers lowered him—and had not abandoned him in chains—that is, in the Egyptians’ prison—[Col. 0522A] he could nevertheless rightly say not merely “free among the dead,” but “free among the king’s prisoners.” For, with a free spirit, he was delivered into the prison where the king’s prisoners were held; and while confined there, with Wisdom accompanying him, he found favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison, who handed over into his hand all the prisoners held in custody, and whatever was done was under his direction.

[Col. 0522B] Perhaps because, with all the prisoners entrusted to his hand, he showed partiality to no one but served all with the same diligence, it is therefore said: “He knew nothing of all that had been entrusted to him.” For if he showed partiality, he would know something. But here let us also speak of the One to whom belongs that prophetic lament: “I became like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87 [88]).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That, as with Joseph, so also with Christ, when he was sent into prison, all things were in his power.

[Col. 0522C] We know that God the Father gave favour to him who descended into the prison of death because of our sins. For John says: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). To him, I say, God gave favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison—that is, in His own sight, since He alone has the power of life and death.

[Col. 0522D] For, according to the truth of the historical account, Pharaoh sitting in the royal place was one man, and the keeper of the prison subject to him was another. But according to this spiritual meaning, the king of the highest throne and the keeper of hell’s prison are one and the same. The devil can indeed be called the keeper of the prison, because he is also called the ruler of the world. Yet he is not keeper of the prison in such a way as to be free from prison punishment or chains, as was the one in whose sight innocent Joseph found favour. Rather, he is keeper of the prison, or overseer of death, in such a way as to receive the chief sentence of condemnation.

Therefore, in the sight of the keeper of the prison—that is, in His own sight—God the Father gave grace to the man Jesus Christ. For by the Father’s command he descended into that prison in order to find grace and obtain timely mercy for the captives, and so say, according to the prophet, to those who were bound, “Go forth,” and to those who were in darkness, “Be revealed” (Isa. 49). Hence it immediately adds: “He handed over into his hand all the prisoners held in custody, and whatever was done was under his direction.”

This is surely what he himself said before he was handed over: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12). All things, I say: heavenly things, earthly things, and things under the earth, so that, according to the Apostle, at the name of Jesus our Lord every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2); first those under the earth, then those in heaven, and after these those on earth. For he first descended to the lower regions and gave life to the dead and release to the bound; [Col. 0523A] then he ascended to heaven, to be worshipped by all who were already in heaven—the spirits of human beings and the holy angels. After this his name was preached to the nations, that all kings might worship him and all nations serve him (Ps. 71 [72]).

It is therefore clear that the keeper of the prison handed all the prisoners into his hand. But he “knows nothing,” though all are entrusted to him: that is, with all judgment given to him, he shows partiality to no one, but judges in equity and renders to each according to his deeds.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That, as Pharaoh hanged one of two accused persons and restored the other to his former position, so God has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills.

[Col. 0523B] **(Chapter 40.)** After these things had happened, it came to pass that two eunuchs sinned—the cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the baker—against their lord. Pharaoh was angry with them—for one was over the cupbearers and the other over the bakers—and sent them into the prison of the captain of the guard, where Joseph too was confined. But the keeper of the prison entrusted them to Joseph, who also ministered to them.

There is no need to linger over what is plain. Yet those who dare to investigate and criticize God’s judgments ought, in connection with the saying to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me” (Exod. 33), and who say, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. 9), to be asked whether they wish here to criticize Pharaoh.

For what is it? “It came to pass,” Scripture says, “that two eunuchs sinned [Col. 0523C] against their lord.” Both sinned against him; he was angry with both; he put both into prison. Afterwards, remembering both, he restored one of them to his former rank and hanged the other upon the gallows. Behold: here too he had mercy on whom he wished and was gracious to the one with whom he was pleased. He could have punished both, because both had sinned; he could have pardoned both, because both had sinned against him. For justice permits a judge to pardon an injury committed against himself to whomever he wishes; and such pardon is not merely beyond reproach, but even praiseworthy.

But in another person’s cause or accusation, the order of judgment or the assumed duty of office does not allow the same liberty to those who administer punishments. “For he does not bear the sword without cause,” says the Apostle (Rom. 13). [Col. 0523D] Scripture plainly stated, moreover, that both had sinned against Pharaoh himself. For after saying, “It came to pass that two eunuchs sinned, the king’s cupbearer and baker,” it adds, “against their lord.” Thus he could display either shared anger or shared clemency toward them both. Yet he did not choose, by his power, to do either the one or the other, but taking a middle course, he showed wrath toward one and clemency toward the other. Does anyone criticize him for this? Certainly not, if he has sound judgment. For just as mercy is an honour to a ruler, so “the honour of a king loves judgment” (Ps. 98 [99]). Where all are punished, royal severity is stained by cruelty; where all are forgiven, the face of majesty is despised without the fear of discipline.

[Col. 0524A] Who, moreover, does not know that the whole world, the entire mass of the human race, is or was in God’s hand like two accused persons or two prisoners in the hand of a king or judge? For from the time when Adam, the first-created father of all, sinned, all of us were guilty according to him and bound because of him. Therefore there are two accused persons, but one is taken and the other left. Indeed, the Lord indicates this division of the whole race in three ways, because of the three classes of the bound, when he says: “Two shall be in the field: one shall be taken and one shall be left. Two women grinding together: one shall be taken and one shall be left” (Matt. 24). “Two shall be in a bed: one shall be taken and one shall be left” (Luke 17).

But who are you, O human being, to answer back to God (Rom. 9), when you cannot answer back even to Pharaoh? Since all are guilty and all are bound, does not God, against whom the offense was committed, have at least as much authority as Pharaoh—to pardon one and exact punishment from another? [Col. 0524B] Indeed, since the human being who had been made through grace unto the glory of God’s image and likeness (Gen. 1) became clay through his own fault, does not the potter, says the Apostle, have authority to make from the same clay one vessel for honour and another for dishonour? (Rom. 9).

He did not say, “Does not the goldsmith or silversmith have authority to make from the same gold or silver one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?”—which might be judged unworthy. Rather, he fittingly drew the illustrative argument from a potter and clay. A potter takes nothing from clay by making of it a vessel for dishonour, since the clay itself is dishonourable; but he confers much upon it when he makes from it a vessel for honour. “And now, O Lord,” says the prophet, “you are our Father; we are clay, and you are our maker, and we are all the work of your hands” (Isa. 64).

[Col. 0524C] We are clay not merely because we were made of clay—which does not concern our complaint—but also because, though we ought to shine with the silver reason or golden likeness of our Maker, when our father sinned we all fell back with him into clay and became mortal. The holy man lamented both points: “I have been compared to clay and made like ashes and cinders” (Job 30). Therefore every mouth is stopped. God takes nothing from those whom he permits to be vessels of dishonour, because by their own fault they have become clay. But he freely does what he did not owe when [Col. 0524D] he forms some of them into vessels of honour.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That, as Pharaoh through Joseph took one accused person, so God through Christ took one thief from the cross.

A little time passed, and they were held in custody. Both saw a dream in one night, each according to an interpretation suited to himself, and so forth. Behold, he who had been a dreamer, though his dreams had profited him nothing, begins to become the interpreter of other persons’ dreams, so that his envious brothers may see that his dreams greatly benefit him.

[Col. 0525A] How beautifully, too, Joseph, standing between two prisoners in prison and giving each an interpretation fitting to his dream, is also in this a figure or shadow of our Saviour, who stood between two thieves on the cross and gave each, according to his faith or merit, a fitting sentence. For what is the difference? There Pharaoh, through Joseph, takes one from prison; here God, through Christ, takes one from the cross and leaves the other. There is the figure; here, the example. The aforementioned division of the whole race, there only prefigured, is here displayed in actuality. As two are in the field, two grinding, and two in a bed, and one of them is taken while the other is left, as was said above, so there are two in prison, one of whom was taken by Pharaoh and one left; likewise two on the cross, one of whom was taken by God and one left.

[Col. 0525B] Yet in both cases there is a mystery. For as Pharaoh restored the cupbearer to his former rank but hung the chief baker upon the gallows, and as one of the thieves, confessing, entered Paradise with the Lord, while the other died in his sins, so through Christ’s passion the Gentile people are received into grace and the Jewish people are sent into wrath. Hence the Apostle says to the former, as to a cupbearer offering his king a cup of praise, or as to a thief entering Paradise: “See therefore the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward the one who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you remain in goodness” (Rom. 11), and so forth.

Moreover, the utterance of the Lord which kindled Joseph so that he opened the dark matters of dreams which no one else could disclose, and prophesied according to them, belongs to the mystery or type of the same [Col. 0525C] Son of God, upon whom the sevenfold Spirit rested so fully that he fulfilled all the prophets and opened his apostles’ minds to understand the Scriptures. Let us proceed through what follows, marvelling also in this at the depth of the divine counsel: when prosperity followed, the chief cupbearer forgot his interpreter. For it follows:

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning Pharaoh’s dream, and that no one except Joseph was able to interpret it.

[Col. 0525C] **(Chapter 41.)** After two years Pharaoh saw a dream. He thought that he was standing beside the river, from which seven cows, beautiful and exceedingly fat, came up and fed in marshy places. Then another seven emerged from the river, ugly and worn away by leanness, and fed [Col. 0525D] on the riverbank itself, in green places. And they devoured those whose appearance and bodily condition were remarkable, and so forth.

God showed Pharaoh what He was going to do. For who was going to do these things? Who, I say, except He of whom it is most truly said, “Making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45)? For the Psalmist, understanding this well, says: “He called a famine upon the land and broke every support of bread” (Ps. 104 [105]). He therefore showed that He would call a famine upon the land: a harsh executioner and a grim minister, by whose severity He would constrain those who had eaten the price of their brother. Should not those who had sold their brother into slavery themselves become slaves? Should not those who had carried off a human being as though he were prey themselves go as prey to men?

[Col. 0526A] This must surely be firmly committed to memory: the children of Israel were justly handed over into Egyptian slavery and deservedly served others, since Joseph had been sold into slavery through their crime (ibid.). They were visited solely by God’s grace and delivered from that house of slavery solely by mercy, not by their own merit. God therefore rightly showed Pharaoh what He was going to do, and showed it so that the magnitude of the danger, foreseen, might be alleviated for many peoples, while the greatest hardship might thereby come upon those who ought, under the punishment and avenging famine, to worship the brother whom they had sold.

[Col. 0526B] But how is it said that God showed Pharaoh these things, when Pharaoh did not understand the dreams he had seen, nor could any of the Egyptian interpreters or all the wise men to whom he had sent interpret them? Yet this was rightly said by him with whom the certain interpretation already rested, which God would soon show Pharaoh through him. Further, just as no one could interpret the king’s dream except Joseph alone, so no one was found worthy to disclose the counsel of God the Father, hidden in the Scriptures under the veil of the letter, except the Lord Jesus Christ. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “No one in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth, was able to open the book or look upon it. And I wept much, because no one was found worthy to open the book or see it. And one of the elders said to me: ‘Do not weep. Behold, the lion from the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered to open the book and loose its seven seals’” (Rev. 5).

## CHAPTER XL. That, as Joseph triumphs in royal adornment after being brought from prison, so Christ, having conquered the ruler of the world, was crowned with glory and honour and appointed by his Father over the works of His hands.

Therefore Joseph, brought from prison at the king’s command, with the hair grown during his long confinement cut off and his garment changed, clothed in a linen robe, wearing the king’s ring and a golden chain around his neck, and seated upon the king’s chariot—he who made him lord of his house and ruler of all his possessions, “to instruct his princes as himself and teach wisdom to his elders” (Ps. 104 [105])—was called, I say, in the Egyptian tongue “Saviour of the world,” because he delivered the earth from the coming destruction by famine.

Such a Joseph, proceeding in this manner while the herald cried out [Col. 0526D] that all should bend the knee before him, is a beautiful likeness and most illustrious mirror of Jesus Christ, Son of God, raised from the dead and clothed in the robe of incorruption and immortality. The Father, after previously making him a little lower than the angels, crowned him with glory and honour, set him over all the works of His hands, and subjected all things beneath his feet (Ps. 8).

In place of the fetters in which they humbled his feet, he received a golden chain; in place of the cloak which he left in the adulteress’s hand and escaped naked, he was clothed, God being judge, in a linen robe; instead of a slave’s name, he bears a royal ring; and instead of prison humiliation, he sits upon the lofty chariot of dominion. In the victor and triumpher, humility and lowliness of mind persist together with the height of glory and honour.

[Col. 0527A] What then? Could he not, once exalted, have sent royal chariots ahead to meet the camels or donkeys of his brothers coming to him, with a great trumpet sounding before him, both to mock his hostile brothers and to invite his holy father, worn out by prolonged mourning, to the festivity of his joy? Certainly he could. But presuming nothing from his own spirit and depending wholly upon the divine will, he entrusted the remainder of his time to the hands of Him whose care for him he had thus far experienced.

Thus whatever praiseworthy thing the Apostle says of the fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—“They remained by faith in the land of promise as in a foreign land, dwelling in tents, and confessing that they are strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” (Heb. 11). “For those who say these things show that they seek a homeland; and if indeed [Col. 0527B] they had remembered the one from which they had gone out, they certainly had opportunity to return”—all this man’s patience, or rather passion, not now in pilgrimage but in captivity, surpasses it. For to be sold as a slave was more than voluntarily to be a pilgrim; to live in prison more than in a foreign land; to be humbled in fetters more than to dwell in tents.

For unless he embraced this captivity because of the same hope for which his fathers embraced their pilgrimage, he surely had opportunity, once free, to summon his father—as, if they had remembered their own city, the Apostle says, they had opportunity to return. But now, just as they seek a better city, so he seeks a better father, although he rightly hoped also for consolation from that father through God.

[Col. 0527C] Moreover, because Joseph was sold as a slave, by human law as well he acknowledged himself to belong to those to whom he had been sold. Therefore, with fitting and praiseworthy faith, he served as humbly as he served faithfully—in the house, in prison, and even in Pharaoh’s chariot—always considering that he was a purchased slave, not that through his prudence he had become Pharaoh’s father. So also Christ, since he was denied by his Jewish brothers and handed over to the Gentiles, although in human affection he loves that people, who are, as the Apostle says, “most beloved for the fathers’ sake” (Rom. 11), is nevertheless held among those to whom he was handed over by a certain right; and he rightly does not know those by whom he was not known, and denies those by whom he was denied.

## CHAPTER XLI. That, as Joseph fed Egypt, so our Saviour has nourished us, once barren, with the food of evangelical grace.

[Col. 0527D] Behold, as though forgetting them, he travelled through the land of Egypt in the royal chariot—that is, in the beautiful chariots of evangelical grace, of which Habakkuk says: “You ride upon your horses, and your chariots are salvation” (Hab. 3). Certainly, when Pharaoh changed his name and called him in the Egyptian tongue “Saviour of the world,” he did not speak of himself, but truly prophesied this salvation.

He travelled, I say, through the land of Egypt and undertook the whole care of feeding the Egyptians. Egypt—for the name means “darkness”—was once ourselves, the Gentiles, upon whom the Lord then shone, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5; the source prints “IX”). [Col. 0528A] Nor were we merely Egypt, but Egypt suffering hunger and barrenness. Once we were so; now, however, we are both light in the Lord and filled with bread in our Saviour, while Christ’s brothers according to the flesh—that is, the Jews—perish through famine.

According to the historical account, the periods of abundance were divided; but according to this mystical sense, it is one and the same period in which we Egyptians eat and Christ’s Jewish brothers hunger. As soon as Christ ascended into his chariot and went out through this Egypt, at the same time seven beautiful and exceedingly fat cows came up from the river on one side, and seven others, equally numerous, ugly and wasted by leanness, on the other; at the same time seven full and beautiful ears of grain sprang up on one side, and seven others, thin and blasted by scorching wind, on the other.

[Col. 0528B] The beautiful and exceedingly fat cows, or the full and beautiful ears, are Christians who follow the life-giving Spirit of the Scriptures during the seven years—that is, throughout all days until the consummation of the age, for the number seven customarily signifies universality.
