But the ugly cows wasted by leanness, or the thin ears blasted by scorching wind, are the Jews, who devote themselves to the letter that kills and, always reading and always pursuing by their reading only the chaff of Scripture, are unable to show any sign of fullness. [Col. 0528C] Foretelling this abundance for the Egyptians and this famine for the Jews, the Lord says: “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall thirst” (Isa. 65).

## CHAPTER XLII. That Joseph, because of his two sons, forgot his labours together with his father’s house, and how in this he bore a type of Christ.

Joseph had two sons before the famine came, borne to him by Aseneth, daughter of Putiphar, priest of Heliopolis. It should be noted that he took as wife the daughter of his former master and purchaser, who at that time was high priest of Heliopolis. For it is not lawful for any but eunuchs of that idol to be its priests, so that the Hebrews’ true suspicion, concerning what we have already said, is confirmed. He called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, saying: “God has made me forget [Col. 0528D] all my labours and my father’s house.” And he called the name of the second Ephraim, saying: “God has made me increase in the land of my poverty.”

We should understand this also as mystically applicable to our Lord: that by his example we too may first become forgetful and then fruitful, in accordance with the names Manasseh and Ephraim, of whom the one is interpreted “forgetfulness,” the other “fruitful.” For he, on our account, forgot the house of his Father—that is, that people among whom God his Father had the synagogue and the Temple, and many sons, that is, worshippers of his name. And on our account he was likened to the grain of wheat which fell into the earth and died, that it might bear much fruit (John 12). By his example, I say, let us also forget our own house—that is, every kinship [Col. 0529A] of the flesh—wherever it strives to call us away from that same Lord Jesus Christ, according to what the Holy Spirit says in David to every faithful soul: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44 [45]).

For Christ himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother, and wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own life besides, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). What fruit this produces, so that according to the name Ephraim one may say, “God has made me increase in the land of my poverty,” he declares elsewhere when he says: “And everyone who has left house, or brothers, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or [Col. 0530A] children, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

When at last the Egyptians came to Pharaoh seeking food, and the king said, “Go to Joseph, and do whatever he tells you,” let us recognize from his utterance the power belonging to that one, and likewise understand that no one can obtain from God the food of eternal life except through the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. For, as the apostle Peter says, “There is salvation in no one else; for no other name under heaven has been given to human beings in which we must be saved” (Acts 4). And he himself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14). And John the Baptist [the Evangelist]: “The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3).

## Ninth Book on Genesis  
*(Gen. 42–49)*

[Col. 0529]

### Chapter I. On what was said to blessed Job: “Will he make a covenant with you,” etc.; and how, as fulfilled in Christ, it was prefigured in Joseph.

Speaking to blessed Job about the devil, the Lord says among other things: “Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as an everlasting servant?” (Job 40)—with “as I do” understood. How truly he says this is attested by the present passage of Scripture, in which what the goodness of God had inwardly intended concerning blessed Joseph as a type of Christ his Son was outwardly brought to fulfilment through the devil’s envy at work by means of Joseph’s brothers.

For he who was sold precisely so that he might not, as he had dreamed, be worshipped by his brothers, was worshipped precisely because he had been sold. And the Son of God, who was rejected by the builders precisely lest he should, as he had foretold in the Gospel parable, [Col. 0529C] become the cornerstone (Matt. 21), precisely because he was rejected and crucified—“this was done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes” (Ps. 117 [118]).

Thus the devil opposes by will, and is therefore called in Greek *Satanas*, that is, “adversary”; but in deed he is an everlasting servant. He serves as though he were faithful; he so cooperates and advances good things as though he wished to assist the Spirit of the Lord; and he proceeds with such watchfulness as though he were eager to give counsel and reveal it to him. We must therefore speak henceforth in praise of God’s wisdom, showing how, through the assistance of the brothers’ envy, Joseph’s dreams were fulfilled: with what eagerness their sheaves stood around and worshipped his standing sheaf, and likewise the sun and moon with [Col. 0529D] the eleven stars.

### Chapter II. How Joseph’s brothers, by worshipping him, fulfilled his dream.

**(Chapter 42.)** When Jacob heard that provisions were being sold in Egypt, he said to his sons: “Why are you negligent? I have heard that grain is for sale in Egypt. Go down and buy necessities for us, that we may live [Col. 0530B] and not be consumed by want.”

The first words of the father reveal how great the severity of the scarcity was: “Why are you negligent?” and so forth. First, to rouse and make them attentive, he strikes them with the hand of rebuke; then he tells them what he has heard. Third, he thunders what he wishes: “Go down into Egypt”; and, finally, he concludes this brief speech with terrifying force: “lest we be consumed by want.”

Joseph’s brothers therefore went down to buy grain in Egypt, while Benjamin was kept at home by Jacob, because he had said to his brothers: “Perhaps he may suffer some harm on the journey.” In Benjamin, Joseph’s brother by the same mother, the father’s heart was comforted, worn out by frequent and almost unceasing sobs for Joseph, concerning whom, as has already been said above, the father could have had no slight suspicion that he had perished through his brothers’ [Col. 0530C] malice. Benjamin was therefore kept at home by him, who said: “Perhaps he may suffer some harm on the journey.”

When his brothers had worshipped him, and he recognized them, he spoke harshly to them as though they were strangers, asking: “Where have you come from?” and so forth. At their first entrance, seeking the goodwill of the ruler, they worshipped him—that is, they greeted him in royal fashion. But why did they worship him? Clearly, in order that they might have permission to buy what they wanted. For they had come with their sacks in order to purchase food; yet they could not do this without Joseph’s command or assent. Pharaoh had decreed and established this law, saying: “I am Pharaoh: without your command no one shall move hand or foot” (Gen. 41): namely, hand to take [Col. 0530D] or foot to go forth, throughout all Egypt.

This act of worship was therefore fittingly prefigured for him in his own imagination of the future through the dream, when he told his brothers: “I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf as it were rose and stood, while your sheaves stood around and worshipped my sheaf” (Gen. 41 [probably 37]). For indeed their sheaves in a sense truly worship his sheaf, since they worship the ruler of Egypt, unknown to them, for no other reason than that their own sheaves had failed, whereas he had a granary full from his sheaves.

And, to speak also in terms of Pharaoh’s dream, they worship because their thin ears, blighted by rust, had devoured the abundance of the preceding years; whereas he, through wisdom, had saved ears that were full and beautiful from their devouring power, at least in part, and stored them in granaries. Joseph’s sheaf stood tall and exalted; the lowly sheaves of his brothers, standing round about it, worshipped his sheaf.

### Chapter III. In what manner, and with how much prudence, he afflicted them.

Remembering the dreams which he had once seen, [Col. 0531B] he said to them: “You are spies; you have come to see the weak parts of the land,” and so forth.

Even in recognizing his brothers Joseph retains the image of the gentle and true Son of God, to whom David says through the mouth of the bridal song: “Aim prosperously, go forth and reign because of truth, gentleness, and righteousness” (Ps. 44 [45]). It was an act of justice and fitting severity that he scourges sinners for so long and rebukes them with the goads of his words, and finally pierces them with sharp nails, until they acknowledge their sin and say: “We deservedly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother, seeing the anguish of his soul when he pleaded with us and we did not listen.”

He also touched upon their crime by a sufficiently close, though not its proper, name when he said: “You are spies,” instead of saying: “You are thieves.” For they had committed theft—indeed sacrilege—when they stole and sold their son and brother from their holy father. Accordingly, when they said, “It is not so, my lord. Your twelve servants are brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan; the youngest is with our father, and the other is no more,” then, as soon as they said, “the other is no more,” he immediately replied: “This is what I said: you are spies.” Because one is no more, you are spies; because of that, you are thieves.

His shrewdness must be noticed. For, when he had said, “You are spies,” he immediately altered the expression: he did not say, “You have come to spy out,” but “You have come to see the weak parts of the land.” They had come to see the weakness of the land—namely, whether it was not so weak, even during famine, that it could not by its own resources help other lands. But in another sense, and truly, when, seeing their brother deprived of their father’s presence and of every witness, they said, “Come, let us kill him” (Gen. 32 [probably 37]), they observed and inspected the unprotected parts of the land. Therefore, turning the finger back upon themselves, he could say without falsehood: “You have come to inspect the unprotected parts of this land.”

Truth and justice, then, account for his harsh speech to them as strangers: “You are spies; you have come to inspect the unprotected parts of this land.” And he swore by Pharaoh’s life: “You shall not leave here until I test you”; and he put them in custody for three days. Again he said: “Let one of your brothers be bound in prison, and bring your youngest brother to me, so that I may test your words, and [Col. 0532A] you may not die.”

But who can explain the works of his gentleness? Amid the very deeds and words of severity he wept, and in the end repaid every evil with whatever good he could. He knew that bringing their youngest brother would be difficult for them. Indeed, this was why he demanded it of them: that, troubled by the difficulty of the matter, they might weigh their deserts, as they had already begun to do, saying: “We deservedly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother.” Later they would say: “God has found out the iniquity of your servants” (Gen. 44).

For as they tortured both his soul and body—“they humbled his feet in fetters, and iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104 [105])—so this compassionate torturer also humbled their feet in fetters for three days and, because of that youngest brother, as what follows makes clear, pierced their souls with iron, until, overcome by compassion, he judged that satisfaction had been made to divine judgment. Had he not aimed at this, he could certainly have revealed himself to his brothers at first sight.

### Chapter IV. That, following Joseph’s example, Christian rulers ought to act in this manner toward the Jews, the enemies of Christians.

Following this example, Christian rulers ought even today to deal in a fitting manner with Christ’s brothers, the Jews: that is, not to kill them. The Holy Spirit, through the Psalmist speaking in the person of Christ himself, declares: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest at any time my people forget” (Ps. 58 [59]). But what then? “Scatter them in your strength” (ibid.).

They should therefore not be killed, but should by this example be brought to knowledge of their guilt. For as then they worshipped the ruler of Egypt, not knowing that he was Joseph whom they had sold, so today the Jews are subject to Christian rulers, not knowing that in this manner they are subject to the feet of Christ, whom their fathers crucified when they denied him.

Therefore, just as Joseph did not kill them in vengeance for himself but compelled them by compassionate torture toward repentance, so that they said, “We deservedly suffer these things, because we sinned against our brother,” and so forth, so today it is not fitting that Christ—that is, we, or all those in whom Christ speaks—should kill the Jews, captives and prisoners of Christ; rather, they should compel them greatly toward repentance.

This has at times been done profitably and beneficially by holy Fathers: namely, they burdened Jewish peasants on their estates, who refused altogether to come to Christ, with so heavy a charge of rent [Col. 0532D] that by the punishment of their own conduct they were compelled to hasten to the faith; conversely, once they had been brought to Christ’s grace, they lightened the burdens of rent. For even if they themselves come with too little faith, those born from them are nevertheless baptized more faithfully. “Thus,” they say, “they will gain either the persons themselves or their children.”

### Chapter V. That Jacob feared to send his son Benjamin with them.

But they, carrying grain on their asses, departed, and so forth. The brothers, having been dismissed, return as though not dismissed. Their feet indeed have been released from fetters, but their hearts remain bound with Simeon. They did not know [Col. 0533A] that the lord of the land loved them, and that for this reason, lest terrified they should not return to him, he had kept one of them in chains.

Having returned, they report as though bringing evil news: “The lord of the land spoke harshly to us and thought us to be spies,” and so forth. Their astonishment and terror alike were increased when, as each emptied out his grain, they found their money tied in the mouths of their sacks. They thought that a subtle scheme was being mounted against them, and that, by carefully prepared devices, occasions for accusations against them were being sought.

Hence later in Egypt they said to the steward: “We pray, my lord, hear us. We previously came down to buy food, and, when we had bought it and came to the lodging-place, we opened our sacks and found in their mouths the money, which we have now brought back in the same weight. [Col. 0533B] We do not know who put it in our purses” (Gen. 43).

To the terror of them all is added the torment of their minds and the father’s mournful complaint: “You have made me childless.” He almost said what he felt. For when he says, “You have made me childless,” and immediately adds, “Joseph is no more,” what else does he say except: “You have made me without Joseph”? Moreover, because he immediately continues: “Simeon is held in chains, and you are taking Benjamin away,” while their consciences tortured them as guilty with regard to Joseph, they could fear that their father suspected they had sold Simeon for grain and thus brought back the money, and likewise that they intended maliciously to take Benjamin away.

Then, when he says: “My son shall not go down with you. His brother is dead, [Col. 0533C] and he alone remains. If any adversity happens to him in the land to which you are going, you will bring my grey hairs down to the underworld,” it is plainly understood that, if he dared, he would wish to say more. Especially since, after saying, “If any adversity happens to him,” he does not say, “My grey hairs will go down,” but, “You will bring my grey hairs down to the underworld in sorrow.” With the sequence of the speech standing thus, “If any adversity happens to him” is the same as though he said: “If you do any harm to him.” But he spares his mouth and does not give his grief free rein, lest, as belongs to an angry man, he himself further disturb his already greatly troubled household.

### Chapter VI. On Judah’s pledge, when he said, “If I do not bring him back to you,” etc.; and how the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipped Joseph.

**(Chapter 43.)** Meanwhile the famine pressed heavily upon the whole land. When the food which they had brought from Egypt was consumed, Jacob said to his sons: “Return and buy us a little food.” Judah answered: “That man solemnly warned us under oath, saying: ‘You shall not see my face unless you bring your youngest brother with you,’” and so forth.

Great was the difficulty of the affair; great the anguish of the father’s mind; great the penalty of the brothers’ conscience. But why is the father, as though lulled into sleep, held down in the depths of sorrow when joy awaits him outside? The other dream also must be fulfilled, since one has already been fulfilled. It must be fulfilled, I say, because the brothers’ sheaves have already worshipped Joseph’s sheaf, as stated above, [Col. 0534A] and it is time for the sun, moon, and eleven stars to worship Joseph.

At length Benjamin is handed over and entrusted to Judah, who says: “If I do not bring him back to you, I shall be guilty of sin against you for all time.” The wise father accepted this pledge more willingly. For what Reuben had earlier said to him—“Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you”—the father neither accepted nor ought to have accepted or approved.

The eleven stars therefore set out for Egypt—that is, all the brothers—and worship Joseph, holding gifts in their hands: a little resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth, and almonds. But the sun—that is, the father himself, and in him the maternal affection of the moon, that is, of Rachel—the sun, I say, remaining behind and absent in body, nevertheless worships when he says concerning Benjamin: “May my God Almighty make him favourable to you, and send back with you your brother whom he holds, and this Benjamin.”

Or certainly this sun too, Jacob the father, worshipped Joseph when, after his brothers had greeted him again respectfully, Joseph said at once: “Is your aged father well, of whom you spoke to me? Is he still alive?” They answered: “Your servant, our father, is safe and still lives”; and they bowed down and worshipped on his behalf, earnestly [reading uncertain: *nimis nomine*] pleading by his name that Joseph might be merciful to them in consideration of the old man, whom Joseph himself had deigned to mention.

For nowhere is it found that the father himself worshipped in his own person, as was said much earlier above. It should be noticed how lofty Joseph’s honour was, how great his maturity and dignity amid a spirit of gentleness: for one word of his graciousness—when he said, “Is your father well? Is he still alive?”—they again bowed down and worshipped. Well, then, brothers, you were about to see what profit his dreams would bring him.

### Chapter VII. On Joseph’s compassion: when he saw Benjamin, he could not restrain himself.

Joseph lifted up his eyes and saw Benjamin, his brother by the same mother, and said: “Is this your little brother, of whom you spoke to me?” Again he said: “May God have mercy on you, my son.” And he hastened away, because his heart was moved for his brother and tears burst forth; entering his chamber, he wept, and so forth.

Joseph “lifted up his eyes.” It had already been said that [Col. 0534D] they stood before Joseph. When he saw them, with Benjamin among them, he commanded the steward of his house, saying: “Bring the men into the house, kill victims, and prepare a feast, because they are to eat with me at noon.” Why then, as though he had not yet seen him, is it now said: “Joseph lifted up his eyes and saw Benjamin, his brother by the same mother,” except because at first he saw him in such a way as to conceal it, while now he saw him in such a way that the sight seemed to recall his own warning: “You shall not see my face without your youngest brother”? For those who worshipped him did not yet deserve to know that, amid the supreme affairs of the kingdom, the ruler of Egypt and lord of the land could have remembered such matters.

But while he fixed upon them with assumed severity as strangers, compassion burst forth unbidden, freely and excessively overcoming the prepared strength [Col. 0535A] of his heart. He no longer had the power to conceal himself; and so, as though taking flight, he hurried into his chamber and wept, because tears burst forth and he could not restrain himself. Overcome by the stirring of his heart and the tumult of tears, he yielded, allowing them to flow as far as they wished.

Then, after washing his face, he came out again, restrained himself, and said: “Set out bread,” and so forth. This feast, to speak of it also in accordance with its mystery, was rightly celebrated with Benjamin—that is, with the “son of the right hand.” Thus, at the end of the world, when the fullness of the Egyptians—that is, of the Gentiles—has entered in (Rom. 11), the brothers of Jesus Christ, namely the Jews, together with the son of the right hand—that is, apostolic faith—will be joined in the feast of the body and blood of Christ, their brother; and then, truly drinking with their wealthy brother, they will be filled to overflowing.

There is only this difference: here the feast took place before they recognized their brother saying, “I am Joseph” (Gen. 45); there, however, Christ must first be recognized, and only then will they share in his foretold feast.

### Chapter VIII. On the feast Joseph gave his brothers, and on the order of the firstborn according to their birthright.

When the food had been set before them, Joseph sat separately, his brothers separately, and the Egyptians who ate with them separately—for it is forbidden for Egyptians to eat with Hebrews, and they consider such a feast unclean. They sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his age.

“The firstborn according to his birthright and the youngest according to his age” means that the older each was by birth, the higher he sat; and conversely, the younger each was by birth, the lower he sat. Undoubtedly the highest and greatest of all, as lord of the house and ruler of the feast, was Joseph himself. All sat before him as far inferior persons.

What, then, is the purpose of this careful detail in Scripture, when, after stating that they sat before him, it added, “the firstborn according to his birthright,” unless to indicate that from that time onward Joseph possessed the birthright in actual practice? For so it is read in the Book of Chronicles: “Because Reuben had violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, son of Israel; and he was not reckoned as the firstborn. But Judah, who was strongest among his brothers, produced rulers from his stock; the birthright, however, was reckoned to Joseph” (1 Chron. 5).

For he received what belonged to the firstborn, namely a double portion, Jacob the father saying: “I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow” (Gen. 48). Thus Joseph, after prison, is in this also likened to Christ, who is “the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1), “the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom. 8), and, according to the renewal of the world, “the beginning of the creation of God”—that is, of the new creation, which must be understood.

Luke the Evangelist also had this in view when, speaking of the Virgin Mary, who was never afterward to bear another child, he said, “She bore her son,” and immediately added, “her firstborn” [Col. 0536A] (Luke 2). Yet even according to the divine generation he should rightly be called firstborn, for the Father begot him before creating anything.

The Egyptians and Hebrews, for whom eating together was forbidden and unclean, yet feast in the same house and at the same banquet—though these separately and those separately—with Joseph as author and ruler of the feast. They are the two walls, namely Gentiles and Jews, whom Christ, hitherto discordant, joins together in himself (Eph. 2) and will one day bring to the harmony of one faith.

The statement, “They were intoxicated with him,” is an idiom of the Hebrew language, which uses intoxication to mean fullness, as there: “By watering its streams, multiply its growth; in its falling drops it shall rejoice—or be made drunken—when it springs forth” (Ps. 64 [65]); plainly referring to the earth watered with rains.

### Chapter IX. On his saying, “Put my cup,” etc.; and on Judah’s plea for Benjamin.

**(Chapter 44.)** Joseph commanded the steward of his house, saying: “Fill their sacks with grain, as much as they can carry, and put each man’s money in the mouth of his sack. But put my silver cup, and the price he gave for the grain, in the mouth of the youngest one’s sack,” and so forth.

Perhaps someone may suppose that Joseph wished, by this occasion, to retain his brother by the same mother, Benjamin, as though by right—especially because he would later say: “He who stole the cup shall be my servant; but you, go free to your father.” But who would not judge this unworthy of a holy man? For the sale of a brother and such deception of brothers differ little in guilt.

We should therefore suppose that he intended rather what in fact occurred. For the Lord was with Joseph and directed all his works (Gen. 39); and reason denies that, under such direction, he could have acted with the aforesaid intention, because it conflicts with justice and does not approach truth.

What then happened? When Joseph had said, “He who stole the cup shall be my servant; but you, go free to your father,” Judah came nearer and, before many bystanders, disclosed the private affairs of his father’s house—which greatly served as testimony for Joseph himself—in such a narrative that, because of two brothers, [Col. 0536D] one of whom was Joseph himself and the other Benjamin, he would have drawn tears and groans even from hearts of stone. At length he concluded his plea thus:

“I myself shall properly be your servant, for I received this boy under my own pledge and promised, saying: ‘Unless I bring him back, I shall be guilty before my father for all time.’ I shall therefore remain as a servant in place of the boy, in the service of my lord; and let the boy go up with his brothers. For I cannot return to my father without the boy, lest I stand by as witness to the calamity that will overwhelm my father.”

What could be more beautiful according to the order of justice? The one who here devotes himself to slavery is the very one at whose counsel Joseph was sold as a slave. For above we have that Judah said to his brothers: “Behold, the Ishmaelites are passing by; come, let him be sold” (Gen. 37). Thus even in this corresponding stratagem the glorious man deserves praise: through the occasion of his silver he compelled the counsellor of the sale into such necessity that he wished to become a slave; and so, distributing through the brothers’ purses the silver coins which he had received when his brother was sold, he pursued them in such a way that the money, though one kind in place of another, might shake their consciences, while such punishment might nevertheless somewhat free those guilty persons from that stain.

### Chapter X. On his saying: “Do you not know that no one is like me in the knowledge of augury?”

Nevertheless, beyond the matters already stated, there is another reason both for this and for his placing them in custody for three days. For did he say falsely, or with deceit, “Do you not know that no one is like me in the knowledge of augury?” Augury is indeed a practice of the Gentiles and forbidden by God’s law; nevertheless, there is no doubt that by the word *augurari*, “to practise augury,” he correctly signified divine knowledge—that is, understanding of future things—the grace by which he was also the trustworthy interpreter of dreams.

Whatever he had thus far done to his brothers was indeed a small present punishment for them; but in truth he acted not as an augur but as a prophet of God, performing those present actions with an eye to future events. For he knew that, because of the guilt of selling him, their descendants would serve the Egyptians for three generations, but would return in the fourth generation. Therefore, when he was about to die, he said to his brothers: “After my death God will visit you and bring you up from this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Carry my bones with you from this place” [Col. 0537C] (Gen. 50).

He could also have foreknown that they would be led out with gold and silver, as it is written: “Tell the children of Israel that each man should ask his neighbour, and each woman her neighbour, for vessels of silver and gold” (Exod. 11), and so forth. For God had foretold both things to Abraham: “In the fourth generation they shall return here; and the nation whom they shall serve I will judge; and afterwards they shall depart with great possessions” (Gen. 15).

Fittingly, therefore, in prophetic representation of the three generations that would serve in Egypt and of Egypt’s despoiling, he held them in custody for three days and placed his silver cup upon them as they departed. Likewise, as a foreshadowing of the Egyptians who would pursue fleeing Israel, he sent an officer after them to bring them back, as though for judgment, in extreme agitation. And as the children of Israel would finally sing, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. 15), so he also fittingly ended his brothers’ sorrow in unexpected joy by saying: “I am Joseph.”

### Chapter XI. On their mutual recognition, where he said to his brothers: “I am Joseph.”

**(Chapter 45.)** Joseph could no longer restrain himself before the many people standing by. Therefore he commanded everyone to go outside and that no outsider should be present at their mutual recognition. He raised his voice in weeping, and the Egyptians heard it, as did all Pharaoh’s household. He said to his brothers: “I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?”

[Col. 0538A] When he had rightly understood how great the father’s calamity for his sake was, or had been, and that the brothers were greatly concerned lest the same calamity should be renewed or grow worse, Scripture says that Joseph “could no longer restrain himself.” Pain had come as it were to childbirth, and the woman in labour had no strength. For just as a pregnant woman, having sorrow when her hour is at hand (John 16), remains silent and quiet, enduring as much as she can, but, at the very hour when she gives birth, speaks, bursts forth, and cries aloud, unable to restrain herself from satisfying the growing pain by crying out: so Joseph, who had thus far restrained himself somehow, swallowing and concealing his interrupted groans and dividing the streams of tears by force, at the moment when he opened his mouth to say, “I am Joseph,” was more swiftly and violently overtaken by an ungoverned tempest of grief. He raised his voice in weeping, so that the Egyptians outside, and all Pharaoh’s household, heard it.

At last he said: “I am Joseph,” and, as though struck by a great bolt of terror, his brothers were stunned and rendered almost senseless. “For they could not answer him, being exceedingly terrified.” He had therefore fittingly commanded everyone to go outside, so that no outsider should be present at their mutual recognition. Knowledge of a crime within the household was no longer to be shared with outsiders; nor did the compassionate brother wish to recount, before them, a matter so shameful that the brothers could not bear it even after every witness had been removed.

“I am Joseph,” he said; and immediately: “Is my father still alive?” He did not say this as a question in order to learn it, for he had already asked and heard that his father lived. Rather, he said it with sorrowful wonder that he was still alive and with deep compassion that he had grown old in mourning on Joseph’s account, overwhelmed by so great a calamity as Joseph could infer even from Judah’s most recent account, which concluded: “Lest I stand by as witness to the calamity that will overwhelm my father.”

To those terrified by such great fear he said: “Come near to me.” When they came close, he said: “I am Joseph, your brother, whom you sold into Egypt,” and so forth. Great was his restraint when he said, “I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?” Since they were exceedingly terrified, he briefly held back, as it were, the force of the tempest; and, interposing consolation in the words “Come near to me,” he somewhat revived them, repeated what he had said, and continued the course of his explanation.

With such sweetness and gentleness did he overcome his former severity that he may deservedly be thought similar in this respect also to the Samaritan who truly poured wine and oil upon the wounds—that is, the sins—of human beings, in order that they might be healed.

### Chapter XII. How he said, “Do not fear,” and how he could have endured so many delays when he said, “Hasten; bring him to me.”

“Do not be afraid,” he says, “nor let it seem hard to you that you sold me into these regions.” When he says, “Do not be afraid,” “of me” must be understood; [Col. 0539A] for fear and dread of God, especially after such a crime, ought not to have been absent from them. For when he says, “I was sent here not by your design but by God’s will, who made me as a father to Pharaoh and lord of his whole house,” it is as though Christ said to the Jews: “I was to die not by your design”—you who said, “Lest perhaps the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John 11)—“but by God’s will, for the nation; and not for the nation only, but that I might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad.”

For your design was, for example, that you should say, “When will he die and his name perish?” (Psalm 40 [41]). But God’s will was that, through the suffering of death, He should crown me with glory and honour and set me over the works of His hands [Col. 0539B] (Hebrews 2; Psalm 8). Thus Joseph says, “I was sent here not by your design but by God’s will.” Your plan indeed was that my dreams should profit me nothing; but God’s will was to make me as a father to Pharaoh, lord of his whole house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

Therefore, when he says, “Do not be afraid, nor let it seem hard to you that you sold me into these regions. For God sent me before you into Egypt for your preservation. It is now two years since famine began in the land, and five years still remain in which neither ploughing nor reaping will be possible; and God sent me beforehand so that you might be preserved upon the earth. I was sent here not by your design but by God’s will”—when, I say, he says these things, [Col. 0539C] he does not declare them guiltless. Rather, seeing that they were struck with fear in their consciences and did not dare speak, he strives, like a wise physician, temporarily to cover over the greatness of their crime.

“Make haste,” he says, “go up to my father, and say this and this to him.” And below: “Make haste,” he says, “and bring him to me.” How could one who now hastens so eagerly in the just longing for his father have endured so long a delay until then? Clearly, if he had invited his father before he had settled all his brothers together with him in the firmest assurance, he would have stirred up too great a disturbance in his father’s house.

But once all had been comforted, after he had kissed them all and wept upon the neck of each one, and had thus given them assurance, for the sake of true forgiveness, that they might be certain of his peace and favour—after they had been confirmed by his tearful kiss and then dared to speak to him, after he had brought out two garments for each of them—he was nevertheless still concerned for them and urged them: “Do not be angry on the way.” “Do not,” he says, “be angry; do not quarrel; do not, while one wishes to seem more righteous or more innocent than another and strives to shift the blame from himself onto someone else, provoke one another and become divided against one another.”

At the fitting time, therefore, Joseph hastens: “Tell my father,” he says, “that five years of famine remain; report to my father all my glory and everything that you have seen”—so that he may have in me or in my glory something to invite him, and in the dreadful danger of famine something to impel him, and thus he may hurry. “Behold your eyes!” That is, “Behold: your own eyes, by which you ought to make my father certain, see that [Col. 0540A] my mouth speaks to you.”

And it was heard and widely reported in the king’s court: “Joseph’s brothers have come.” Pharaoh adds his own invitations; the riches of Egypt are brought forth, and greater things are promised. Royal conveyances are also sent to transport the little children and wives, lest father Jacob be insufficiently encouraged or doubt in any respect.

## CHAPTER XIII. What is signified by his ordering two garments to be brought out for each of his brothers

He ordered two garments to be brought out for each of them. But to Benjamin he gave three hundred silver shekels with five excellent garments; and he sent his father the same amount of money and clothing.

Let us first judge that the saying of the Wise Man, which the Apostle Paul also uses, has here attained its fulfilment as an example of perfect love: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink. For in doing this you shall heap coals of fire upon his head. Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12). For he gave food and drink to his enemies, who had sold him while eating. It was said above that, while sitting down to eat bread, they saw Ishmaelite travellers coming from Gilead and said, “It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites” (Genesis 37). To these enemies of his, I say, who had sold a hungry man while they were eating, he gave food and drink; indeed, as was said above, they became drunk with him. And behold, to those by whom he had been stripped of the long-sleeved and many-coloured robe, he gave two garments to each.

Moreover, it is easy to recognize the culmination of all Christ’s mysteries, which the finger of God prefigured in Joseph, [Col. 0540C] in this: that he bestowed not merely one garment, but two upon each. For now the souls of the elect, happily rejoicing after the burden of the flesh has been laid aside, enjoy one garment—that is, their blessedness alone. But when we have all risen again, all of us who are changed will receive two garments apiece: the double glory of soul and body together.

Accordingly, from the beginning of the narrative of this blessed Joseph down to this descent into Egypt, let the mysteries of Christ be regarded according to his likeness. For from this point another beginning is taken and another sequence of wonderful sacraments is woven, which, now frequently celebrated and well known in the public teaching of Christ’s Church, we shall endeavour to contemplate, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, according to the order of the history to which we return in a fresh treatment.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the report brought to Jacob that Joseph was still alive

They told Jacob, saying: “Joseph is alive and rules over all the land of Egypt.” On hearing this, Jacob, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, nevertheless did not believe them. Scripture beautifully expressed in brief how a father received news of so great a matter, in terms which could not more effectively have been explained with any circumlocution of words: “As though awakening from a heavy sleep,” it says.

For what is one like who, suddenly startled, wakes from a heavy sleep? Surely bewildered and stupefied, slow and dull in understanding or answering because his senses are as though dead. Hence, when they immediately recounted to the still-unbelieving man the whole sequence of events, and he saw the wagons and everything Joseph had sent, Scripture uses the same expression: “His spirit revived,” [Col. 0541A] and he said: “It is enough for me if Joseph my son is still alive; I shall go and see him before I die.”

“His spirit revived”—that is, he recovered the capacity for discernment, so that he could receive the multitude of his joys and converse rationally with those whose sudden arrival had overwhelmed, like a great flood, a mind to which nothing of the kind had been commanded and which had expected nothing of the sort.

## CHAPTER XV. What Jacob feared, so that God said to him: “Do not be afraid; go down into Egypt”

(Chapter 46.) Israel set out with all that he possessed and came to the Well of the Oath. Having sacrificed victims there to the God of his father Isaac, he heard Him in a night vision calling him and saying: “Do not be afraid; go down into Egypt,” and so forth.

We have already stated why the Well of the Oath was so named: namely, because Abraham and Abimelech made a covenant there. For that place was called Beersheba because each swore there (Genesis 21). “Do not be afraid,” He says, “but go down into Egypt.” It is clear from this that Jacob was afraid to go down into Egypt; otherwise God would vainly have said to him, “Do not be afraid.” Perhaps he feared for this reason: he did not fail to know that return would be difficult.

For, besides being a prophet—as the Psalm says of him and his fathers in the person of God, “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do no evil to my prophets” [Col. 0541C] (Psalm 104 [105])—that saying also could have instilled this fear in him, when God spoke to Abraham, oppressed by deep, dark sleep and great terror: “Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall reduce them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years” (Genesis 15). He knew that this had been said, and believed that the Egyptians would be that nation—especially since the great and dark terror of domestic wickedness had already preceded it.

Therefore divine consolation supplies confidence to one who is afraid, saying: “Do not be afraid; go down into Egypt, for there I shall make you into a great nation. I shall go down with you there, and I shall also bring you back from there.” This is the height of the consolation: “Joseph too shall place his hand [Col. 0541D] upon your eyes.” For, holding this to be of the greatest value, Jacob later says: “Now I shall die gladly, because I have seen your face and leave you surviving.”

## CHAPTER XVI. How Scripture here says, “All the souls of Jacob’s house were seventy,” while Luke says “seventy-five”

Jacob rose from the Well of the Oath and came into Egypt with all his seed: his sons and grandsons, daughters, and all his offspring together. Although he had feared for his descendants, yet, strengthened by God, he judged this preferable and more desirable for himself: that Joseph should place his hand upon his eyes. Hence he said: “It is enough for me if Joseph my son is alive.”

When the names of the sons who entered Egypt have been counted in their order, the sequence finally concludes thus: “All the souls of Jacob’s house who entered Egypt were seventy.” There is no doubt that, apart from Joseph and his sons, seventy-six souls who came forth from Jacob’s thigh entered Egypt. For the total, counted gradually person by person, proves this. They found three souls in Egypt—Joseph, namely, with his two sons. Jacob himself was the seventieth.

But if, conversely, this is objected to us—how in the Acts of the Apostles, in Stephen’s address to the people, seventy-five souls are said to have entered Egypt (Acts 7)—we should know that Stephen took this from the seventy translators, where it is written: “The sons of Joseph who were born in Egypt were nine souls.” [Col. 0542B] But in the Hebrew there are two, not nine. Ephraim and Manasseh were born in Egypt to Aseneth, daughter of Potiphar, before Jacob entered Egypt and before the time of famine came on; and it is clear that, when Jacob entered Egypt, they were not of an age to have begotten sons.

If it is asked why St Luke, the author of the aforesaid history, in sending out the volume of the Acts of the Apostles among the nations, said not that seventy souls had entered Egypt according to Hebrew truth, but seventy-five according to the edition of the seventy translators, the excuse is easy. He ought not to have written anything contrary to that Scripture which had already been circulated among the Gentiles. And, at least at that time, the authority of the seventy translators was held in higher repute than that of Luke, who was spoken of among the nations as unknown, insignificant, and not highly credible.

This should be observed generally: wherever the holy Apostles or apostolic men speak to peoples, they generally employ those testimonies which had already been circulated among the Gentiles. Although many maintain that Luke the Evangelist, being a proselyte, was ignorant of Hebrew letters.

## CHAPTER XVII. How each of us ought, by this example, to act in love for Christ, saying: “Now I shall die gladly, because I have seen your face”

Joseph yoked his chariot and went up to meet his father. On seeing him, he threw himself upon his neck and wept in his embrace. And the father said to Joseph: “Now I shall die gladly, because I have seen your face and leave you surviving.”

Taking up this saying of wonderful filial affection from this father’s mouth, let us all say—and each one of us say—to the true Joseph, that is, to our Lord, the Son of God, who is truly the Saviour of the world: “Now I shall die gladly, because I have seen your face and leave you surviving.” When, Christian, you die—or rather, even while you live, because you are going to die—say to the only Son of God the Father, your Saviour: “Now I shall die gladly, because I have seen your face and leave you surviving.”

For now we see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Corinthians 13); and at the hour in which each of us dies, we leave Him surviving—the One who alone is able, where we cannot and where we fail, after our bodies have been laid aside, to care for our souls. [Col. 0543A] He remains alive for us in order to set our cause right, He who died in order to give life to our souls and rose again in order to raise our bodies and set each of us at His right hand in the heavenly places, in body and soul. “For I know,” says blessed Job, “that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise again from the earth; and I shall again be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job 19).

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the humility of the fathers, by which they professed themselves shepherds of sheep and strangers before Pharaoh

And he spoke to his brothers and to all his father’s household: “I shall go up and report to Pharaoh, and shall say to him: My brothers and my father’s household have come to me, [Col. 0543B] and they are shepherds of sheep,” and so forth.

This passage of Scripture sets forth the holy pursuit of strangers who are strangers for God: namely, that they sought not merely not to please men, but even to displease them; and that, truly having no abiding city here, they endeavoured to seek one that is to come and endures (Hebrews 13).

(Chapter 47.) Joseph entered first and told Pharaoh, saying: “My father and brothers, their sheep, their herds, and all that they possess, have come from the land of Canaan, and behold, they are stationed in the land of Goshen.” He also set five men from among the least prominent of his brothers before the king—the firstborn—and, when the king questioned them, saying, “What is your occupation?” they answered, “Your servants are shepherds of sheep, both we and our fathers.”

Why? “Because,” it says, “the Egyptians detest all shepherds of sheep”: that is, because they pride themselves in horses and chariots more than other nations and therefore despise and detest the humble work of shepherds as a disgrace.

Afterward the father was brought before the king and questioned by him: “How many are the days of your life?” Did the wise king say nothing else to the venerable old man except ask him, “How many are the days of your life?” Surely this alone was worthy of being written because of the memorable answer: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life are one hundred and thirty years; they are few and evil, and they have not attained to the days of my fathers, during which they were strangers.”

Of his own accord he confessed himself a stranger and preferred to call this miserable life a pilgrimage, as a citizen of a better life or homeland—that is, of the heavenly one. In this sense he completed the king’s question by a true correction. When the king said, “How many are the days of your life?” he answered: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life are few and evil.” He called his days few because of humble self-awareness, and evil because tribulation had continued. And it seemed too little to him merely to have confessed himself a stranger unless he also asserted that his fathers had been strangers. For he immediately adds: “And they have not attained to the days of my fathers, during which they were strangers.”

Thus both father and son disdained to please men or to exalt themselves for the pageantry of worldly things. Therefore, in praise of the faith of these fathers, the Apostle says among other things: “Confessing that they are guests and strangers upon the earth” (Hebrews 11). Their confession is nowhere found clearer or more certain than in this passage, where this stranger, in the king’s court, not forgetting his heavenly homeland, voluntarily confesses himself a stranger.

Thus an ancient example has been set before spiritual shepherds and all who seek the heavenly homeland: content with glorious humility, let them despise the vain and impoverished exaltation of the world, and wherever they see Egyptians riding, let them say: “These in chariots and these on horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Psalm 19 [20]); before citizens or kings of an earthly homeland, let them say: “We have no abiding city here, but seek the one to come” (Hebrews 13).

## CHAPTER XIX. In what year of his father’s life Joseph was born

Moreover, the statement, “The days of my pilgrimage are one hundred and thirty years,” opens an easy path for discovering in what year of Jacob’s life Joseph was born; indeed, also in what year of his life he took Leah and her sister Rachel as wives.

For Scripture previously said of his brother Esau that he took wives at forty years old (Genesis 26), and of his father Isaac that he took Rebecca as his wife when he was forty years old, and that he was sixty when the children were born (Genesis 25). But of this man it is not stated at what age he took a wife.

Therefore, since Jacob said that he was one hundred and thirty years old, while Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh king—and since seven years of abundance and the following two years of famine had passed, making Joseph thirty-nine years old altogether—it is beyond doubt that Jacob was ninety when Joseph was born. Subtract fourteen years from that age, during which he served Laban for his daughters, and it clearly follows that he was already seventy-six when, by his father’s command, he set out as a stranger and took wives.

For he served twenty years. Anyone who reads understands that Joseph was born before the final six of these. Indeed, when Joseph was born, Jacob said to his father-in-law: “Dismiss me, that I may return to my land and my homeland” (Genesis 30). Then, when the agreement was renewed, he who had served fourteen years for the daughters added that he would serve six further years.

## CHAPTER XX. On Joseph’s subjecting the whole land of Egypt when its inhabitants sold it because of the severity of famine

Israel therefore entered Egypt, and Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham (Psalm 104 [105]), that is, in Egypt itself. For the Egyptians arose from one of Ham’s descendants, namely Mizraim.

Let us consider what happened next. After Jacob had blessed the king and gone out, and Joseph had given him a possession in the best part of the land, Ramesses, where Pharaoh had ordered it, all Egypt came, Scripture says, to Joseph, declaring: “Give us bread. Why should we die before you because our money has failed?” He answered them: “Bring your livestock, if you have no price,” and he sustained them that year in exchange for livestock.

They came also in the second year and said: “Why [Col. 0545A] should we die while you look on? Buy us into royal servitude, and supply seed, lest the land be reduced to wilderness when the cultivator perishes,” and so forth.

These were the effects of what is said, that the Lord “called for famine upon the land”; and His summons achieved this: Israel entered Egypt, and the pride of the Egyptians was reduced to servitude. Scripture had just above marked this pride by saying that the Egyptians detested all shepherds of sheep (Genesis 46). Therefore let even those wise persons who delight in polished language approve what the Psalmist said by metonymy: “He called for famine” (Psalm 104 [105]).

Accordingly, like a vigorous lictor, famine stood ready at the command of Him who called it and performed the will of Him who ordered it, when it confined two culprits as though in one prison. One, namely Israel, who had sold his brother, was to be released in the fourth generation, chastened, unto glory; the other, the Egyptian people who prided themselves in chariots and horses, was brought forth unto punishment.

Joseph therefore bought all the land of Egypt, while its inhabitants sold their possessions because of the severity of famine. He subjected it to Pharaoh, together with all its peoples, from the furthest boundaries of Egypt to its utmost limits, except the land of the priests, which the king had granted them.

Joseph then said: “Behold, as you see, Pharaoh possesses both you and your land. Receive seed and sow the fields, so that you may have crops. You shall give a fifth part to the king; I leave the other four for you, for seed and food, for your households and children.” It was as though he said: “Since you sold your possessions and said, ‘Buy us into royal servitude,’ I shall impose no other burden upon you. Nevertheless, retain on equitable terms what you have begun. A fifth of the produce from every region was stored under Pharaoh’s care and protection during the seven years of abundance for your preservation. Therefore henceforth you shall give a fifth to the king, to whose servitude you sell yourselves.”

From that time until the present day, a fifth part is paid to kings throughout the whole land of Egypt. And indeed, because victorious famine had then settled upon the necks of the proud, they gladly accepted the terms of slavery, saying: “Our salvation is in your hand; only let our lord look favourably upon us, and we shall gladly serve the king.” But when returning abundance drove famine away, pride revived along with it. Perhaps for that reason they became enemies to the children of Israel, and for that reason their heart was turned so that they hated the Lord’s people [Col. 0545D] and dealt deceitfully with His servants: because the remembrance of him who, in the time of famine, received, fed, and subjected them to royal servitude, and was called the saviour of the world, began in the time of abundance to be hated by the descendants of those who had sold themselves, as though he had been a betrayer of liberty.

## CHAPTER XXI. Why Joseph had to be put under oath concerning the transfer of his father’s body, and why the holy man did not wish to be buried in that land

When Israel saw that the day of his death was drawing near, he called his son Joseph and said to him: “If I have found favour in your sight, put your hand under my thigh, and you shall show me mercy and truth: do not bury me in Egypt, but let me sleep with my fathers; take me away from this land and bury me in the tomb of my ancestors.”

Was the father then distrustful of his son’s obedience, and could he not be secure otherwise? Certainly not. Rather, he wished to place in his son’s mouth the reason he should give Pharaoh and his servants for transferring his father, saying briefly: “For my father put me under oath.” Thus he would remove suspicion that he bore a mind estranged from love for Egypt.

But why did so great a patriarch, a citizen of heaven, for whom the entire world was exile while he lived, take such care for his body and earnestly wish to know in what place dust would return to dust and ashes to ashes? Clearly because it was the land of the Lord’s promise, of God who said, for example: “The land in which you sleep I shall give to you and to your seed” [Col. 0546B] (Genesis 28), and other similar things which God had spoken and promised to him and his fathers concerning that land.

Whatever God’s gift may be—great or small, heavenly or earthly—it is and ought to be precious in the eyes of a wise person because of the honour or love of the Giver. Therefore, if at his death he revered with such thanksgiving the promises of the land he had received that he desired at least to possess it in his dead body, how much more ought living possessors to have taken care to live in it so that God, not angered, would not again take His gift away from the ungrateful?

For in dying he gave the living an example: that in hope of the heavenly homeland they might love the pledge, the resting-place of the eternal inheritance. When Joseph had sworn, Israel worshipped God, turning toward the head of the bed. That is, after his son had sworn, he was now secure concerning the fulfilment of his request. “Toward the head of the bed,” it says. For the holy man devoted to God, oppressed by old age, had his bed so placed that his very posture as he lay was prepared for prayer without any difficulty.

158

## CHAPTER XXII. On Joseph’s hastening to his sick father with his two sons, and on that father’s blessings

Joseph was told that his father was ill. Taking his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, he went on his way—that is, he hastened to go—and devoted himself wholly to receiving shares in his father’s riches, to seeing the treasures of blessing which the father had stored up [Col. 0546D] for his sons. Therefore he took with him his sons Manasseh and Ephraim.

And it was said to the old man: “Behold, your son Joseph is coming to you.” Strengthened, he sat upon the bed. Although it may rightly be understood that he was strengthened with joy at the arrival of the son whom he loved—as he had formerly said, “Now I shall die gladly, because I have seen your face and leave you surviving” (Genesis 46)—nevertheless it should also be known that he was strengthened when the holy spirit of prophecy rushed upon him.

For from where could he have had confidence or authority to say, “This one also shall become peoples and shall multiply, but his younger brother shall be greater than he,” and similar things, unless he had been strengthened by the power of the prophetic Spirit? Thus he who was sick in body was so strengthened in mind that the weary body itself was relieved by the mind’s cheerfulness; and he whose bodily eyes had grown dim through extreme old age and could not see clearly had the vision of his inner person enlightened, so that he foretold things to come and bestowed the inheritance to be possessed by blessing.

Thus he begins: “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz, which is in the land of Canaan, blessed me, and said: ‘I shall increase you and multiply you and make you into multitudes of peoples; and I shall give this land to you and your seed as an everlasting possession.’” He first stated the source of his right or office to confer blessing. He did not say, “My father Isaac blessed me,” though this had also occurred; but rather, “God Almighty blessed me.” For blessing belongs not to a human being but to God, and a human blessing has force when it proceeds from God or is confirmed by God’s testimony.

Someone may say: Why did Abraham, at his death, not bless Isaac in the same manner in which Isaac blessed Jacob and Jacob blessed his sons? Clearly because Isaac, from the time he was offered to God as a whole burnt offering, possessed blessing as an inheritance. It was unnecessary that he be consecrated by a spoken word, since in reality he deserved, as a type of the Saviour, to be a holy sacrifice and living victim.

Likewise, if anyone asks why Isaac, though he had only two sons, did not bless each of them, whereas Israel, having more, blessed each one with particular blessings, the answer is easy: Isaac’s two sons were to be divided into two peoples, as the divine oracle had foretold to him (Genesis 25), or to his mother Rebecca. But Jacob’s many sons were to possess as an inheritance—or rather, to be possessed by—the true and living God as one nation and one people in the unity of their father’s faith.

After these three patriarchs, in whom the almighty Trinity is to be invoked—God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob—we no longer find blessing conferred on fleshly sons in this same succession and with authority. Rather, from the law of Moses onward, it was prayed for generally upon the people through the ministry of priests, though its effect did not always or everywhere follow.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Why he said, “Your two sons shall be mine: Manasseh and Ephraim shall be reckoned to me”

“God Almighty,” he says, “appeared to me and blessed me,” and so forth, as above. Why this? Clearly, so that you may reflect and know that this came about through the merits of paternal faith, enabling you to say: “God has made me forget [Col. 0547D] all my labours and my father’s house,” and for this reason to call your firstborn Manasseh. Likewise: “God has made me increase in the land of my poverty,” and for this reason to call the second Ephraim.

For because God blessed me when I voluntarily became a stranger and said, “I shall increase you and multiply you and make you into multitudes of peoples,” therefore you also, though an exile against your will and sold into slavery, grew in your labours and in the land of your poverty. For it was not you sons who stored up heavenly help for us parents; rather, we parents—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—stored it up for you sons.

“Therefore your two sons, born to you in Egypt before I came here to you, shall be mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be reckoned to me as Reuben and Simeon.” It is as though he said: “Because, before I came here, I advanced you while absent; for paternal faith contended for you amid great sorrows and brought forth your salvation, in which you also begot two sons. By right, therefore, they shall be my sons.”

“As Reuben and Simeon shall be reckoned to me,” and so forth, means this: just as Reuben and Simeon shall be two tribes and produce two peoples, and thus inherit the land of promise, so also shall your sons. But the remaining sons whom you shall beget after my death—thereby showing that they had not yet been born at that time—shall be yours and shall be called by the name of their brothers in their inheritances. “They shall not,” he says, “receive land separately or have their own allotted portions like the other tribes; but they shall be mingled into the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh as subsidiary parts of the people.”

But for what reason shall they be reckoned to me and be mine? “For me,” he says, “when I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel died in the land of Canaan on the journey itself; it was springtime. And I was entering Ephrath, and I buried her beside the road to Ephrath.”

“For me,” he says—that is, to my loss, or while she was bearing me a son—your mother Rachel died, whom I loved and from whom I still hoped to receive sons. “It was springtime”—for me, we must understand—and I was entering Ephrath, which means “fruitful”: namely, when, after the winter of barrenness, she was blossoming in desired childbirth and beginning to be fruitful for me. Therefore these two sons of yours shall be mine, so that by adoption I may raise up and supply offspring for my dead wife, which I lacked through natural generation.

Joseph’s taking this as a great honour—namely, that his two sons should become princes and heads of tribes in Israel—is shown by this: when he had taken those same sons from the lap of their father who was kissing and embracing them, he bowed down to the ground in worship.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How Jacob, in blessing Joseph’s sons, prefigured Christ’s cross by crossing his hands

Joseph placed Ephraim at his right hand—that is, at Israel’s left—and Manasseh at his left hand, that is, at his father’s right, and brought both of them near him. Jacob stretched out his right hand and placed it upon the head of Ephraim, the younger brother, but his left upon the head of Manasseh, who was the elder, crossing his hands.

He himself gives the reason why he did this when Joseph took it badly and said, “It is not fitting, father, for this is the firstborn; place your right hand upon his head.” Refusing, Jacob said: “I know, my son, I know. This one also shall become peoples and shall multiply, but his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall grow into nations.”

Without doubt, the crossing of the hands expressed the figure of the cross. Did he, by crossing his hands in this way, happen by chance to represent the cross? Could he not, while giving the same blessing, have put Manasseh at his right and Ephraim at his left? Certainly he could; but he was a prophet, and by the prophetic Spirit he knew that the blessing which the coming Lawgiver would give, or by which all nations would be blessed in that seed of Abraham, was to be arranged through the cross.

For could he who later said concerning the one who was to be sent and was to be the expectation of the nations—that is, concerning Christ—“He shall wash his garment in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes” (Genesis 49), have been ignorant under what kind of winepress that grape was to be pressed, or how that wine itself was to be pressed out? Therefore, as both prophet and patriarch, just as he could truly prophesy in words, saying, “This one also shall become peoples and shall multiply, but his younger brother shall be greater than he,” so he knew how, by the placement of his hands, to prefigure the cross of Christ, through which the younger, that is, the Gentile people, was to be preferred to the elder Jewish people.

He says to Joseph himself: “I give you one portion beyond your brothers, which I took from the hand of the Amorite by my sword and my bow.” He means Shechem, or Sichem, which in John the Evangelist is incorrectly called Sychar—a corruption that has become established—and it is now the metropolitan city of the Samaritans.

But when he says that he possessed it by bow and sword, he calls the bow and sword here “justice,” through which he deserved, as a stranger and foreign resident, to be delivered from danger after Shechem and Hamor had been killed. Or certainly, “I took it by my sword and bow” means “I bought it by my strength,” namely with money which I acquired through much labour and sweat.

## CHAPTER XXV. On his calling his sons: “Gather together, that I may tell you,” and so forth
(CAP. XLIX.) Now Jacob called his sons and said to them: “Gather together, that I may declare to you what will come to pass in the last days. Gather together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear Israel, your father.” This calling does not mean merely what the plain letter sounds like, nor does it summon only twelve men, [Col. 0549C] but it convenes and gathers all who recognize or profess themselves to be sons of Jacob. And indeed, all of us who belong to the faith of this Father, who truly confess and worship the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, faithfully acknowledge and truthfully call ourselves sons of Jacob.

Therefore Father Jacob invites us with the trumpet of prophecy when he says, “Gather together, that I may declare to you what shall happen to you in the last days”; and again he sounds forth and says, “Gather together”—that is, both that we may assemble bodily within the same walls, in the same house of God, in the same school of Christ, and, what is more necessary, that we may be gathered in mind, in the unity of faith, in the fellowship of the Spirit, in the bond of peace. Finally, he repeats himself in order to make the hearer attentive: [Col. 0549D] “Hear,” he says, “sons of Jacob; hear Israel, your father.” For the single hearing of the body is not enough; another hearing also must be applied, namely that of the inner person, where the Spirit speaks and declares the things to come.

Thus, as sons trained in the Father’s house under the instruction of faith and the discipline of conduct, let us hear, in these last days, those things which were then to come, but which have now already come and been accomplished in these days—indeed, the last days—as Paul testifies: “upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10); and as John says: “Little children, it is now the last hour” (1 John 2).

## CHAPTER XXVI. [Col. 0550A] On the blessings of Reuben, and whom he prefigured

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow; first in gifts, greater in authority. You have been poured out like water: do not increase, because you went up to your father’s bed and defiled his couch.”

This is the meaning: You are my firstborn, eldest among my children; according to the order of your birth you occupied the place in which you hoped to receive the inheritance lawfully due to firstborn sons—that is, the priesthood and the kingdom. For this is indicated by “bearing the burden” and by surpassing strength. But because you sinned and, like water which is not retained in a vessel, were poured out in the rush of lust, I command you not to sin further, but to remain [Col. 0550B] among the number of your brothers, paying the penalty of sin in having lost the rank of firstborn.

Thus the two following clauses answer to the two preceding: “You are my strength; you are the beginning of my sorrow.” Why are you “my strength”? Namely because you are “first in gifts, greater in authority.” Why “the beginning of my sorrow”? Because “you have been poured out like water,” in going up to your father’s bed. For this became the beginning of his sorrow—not because he had never previously grieved in any matter, but because the first true sorrow arising from the wound of sin occurred in his household through this son; afterward it increased through the sale of his son.

Like this Reuben is whoever ascends the bed of God the Father—that is, the rule over His people—by an adulterous entrance: namely, seeking not the salvation or advancement of those who hear him, but the pleasure of his own glory. So Reuben, in ascending his father’s bed, sought not to beget offspring from it, but to satisfy the lust of his own body. Thus, before Christ’s coming, the Pharisees, Sadducees, Samaritans, and other heretics of that time, or founders of heresies, violently ascended the bed of God the Father—that is, the Scripture of the holy Law—and corrupted His people with unlawful seed. After Christ’s coming, Cerinthus, Marcion, Ebion, and the other heresiarchs, uncalled, ascended the bed of that same Christ—that is, the teaching of the Gospel—and each in his own place or time defiled His people with perverse doctrine.

Hence it should be known that the woman whom Reuben violated was not free, but a slave; not a lawful wife; and she was called Bilhah, a name interpreted “aged” or “grown old.” [Col. 0550D] In short, every people or soul that is free, or is Christ’s lawful wife, truly loving Christ, admits neither adultery nor incest. But one that is a slave, not possessing the Spirit of the Lord, “where there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3), one that has grown old and walks in the oldness of sin, quickly yields to adultery and readily assents to a heretic.

To the wicked assembly of such persons the Spirit says, “You are my firstborn; you are my strength.” This is rightly understood as a most severe irony directed against its arrogance or presumption, because this is how it sees itself, proclaims itself, and judges itself. For it says: “What I give is holy; that in which I baptize, and what I consecrate, is full and perfect; with me alone is the strength of truth.” But what is added in opposition—“and the beginning of my sorrow” [Col. 0551A]—is the Father’s genuine complaint, because truly “under his tongue are labor and sorrow” (Ps. 10), because “he conceived sorrow and brought forth iniquity” (Ps. 7). Why should the Father not call such people the leaders of His sorrow or labor? For through the prophet He says to them: “Will a man crucify God, that you crucify me? And you said: ‘In what have we crucified you?’ In tithes and firstfruits; in poverty you are accursed, and you crucify me, the whole nation” (Mal. 3). Again: “You have made the Lord labor by your words. And you said: ‘In what have we made him labor?’” (Mal. 2), and so forth.

Thus the adulterous heretic seems to say to the Father: “In what way am I the beginning of your sorrow?” “You have been poured out,” He says, “like water”—that is, through the incontinence of your mouth. For heretics flow forth without restraint and without discernment in watery words. [Col. 0551B] “For they are old cisterns which cannot hold water” (Jer. 2).

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the blessings of Simeon and Levi, and whom they prefigured

“Simeon and Levi, brothers, weapons of iniquity for warfare. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly. For in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they dug down a wall. Cursed be their fury, for it is obstinate; and their indignation, for it is harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.”

By these words he plainly indicates that it was not according to his counsel that they killed the allied men of Shechem and Hamor, shedding innocent blood contrary to the law of peace and friendship, and that, as though in a certain frenzy, they ranged in cruelty and overthrew the walls of the hospitable city (Gen. 34). Therefore he says: “Cursed be their fury, for it is obstinate; and their indignation, for it is harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Levi did not receive a proper inheritance, but received a few cities to inhabit among all the allotments. Concerning Simeon, however, it is written in the Book of Joshua that he too did not receive his own proper territory, but received something from the tribe of Judah (Josh. 14). In the Book of Chronicles it is written more plainly that, when he had multiplied and had no place of possession, he went out into the wilderness (1 Chron. 4).

But since Jacob says that he prophesies concerning the last days—“Gather together and I will declare to you what shall happen to you in the last days”—the passage is rightly understood as spoken prophetically concerning the Pharisees. In accordance with Simeon and Levi, they killed their first proselytes to circumcision, namely the Shechemites; they were “weapons of iniquity for warfare,” because, after traversing sea and land to make proselytes, they finally, in their fury, killed the Man and in their self-will undermined the wall. For they killed Christ and pierced with nails and a lance the wall of the temple—which is His body—and by doing this made their proselytes and all their hearers with themselves children of perdition.

But that Man, “a prophet mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24), just as He had prophesied concerning the temple of His body, saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2), did so; and in vengeance for their fury [Col. 0552A] and harsh indignation He said: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” For they themselves ceased to be Jacob or Israel, while the Gentiles through faith inherited this name. Why He did not wish to kill them but to divide and scatter them, the Psalmist declares in His person. Having first said, “God has shown me concerning my enemies,” he immediately adds, “Do not kill them, lest my people ever forget”; and he says, “Scatter them in your power” (Ps. 58).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What is meant in the blessings of Judah

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hands are upon the necks of your enemies. The sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness.”

Here he opened his mouth more widely, drew breath, and declared more clearly what the whole world would joyfully hear: “Judah,” he says, “your brothers shall praise you.” It is indeed agreed that kings came from the tribe of Judah; but, apart from David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, they all sinned, nor were they so strong that so great a patriarch ought, on account of the praise of their strength, to have opened his mouth so expansively. Therefore, from among all these, Christ the King alone is chosen, of whom these words may rightly be spoken.

Judah, whose name means “confession,” is Himself the prince and author of our confession. Without Him we could not confess, and without Him what is written would not occur: “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121); nor would anyone pass into [Col. 0552C] “the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 41).

Therefore, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you.” You, Christ, I say, your brothers shall confess, praise, and proclaim; all the sons of God shall praise you, and for this very reason shall praise you—that they are your brothers, that they are named and are sons of the living God. For unless they had been received through you and adopted through you, they would always, as they once were, be enemies, sons of death, sons of wrath, sons of the devil. Rightly, therefore, shall they praise you.

How shall they praise you? What shall they cry out in praise? “Your hands are upon the necks of your enemies.” This is truly praiseworthy, truly worthy of melodious praise, because it is true strength and glorious victory. Why are your hands upon the necks of your enemies? Namely, so that, bowed down and bent, [Col. 0552D] they may either worship you or be expelled from your borders, to be shut in prisons in everlasting bonds. He immediately adds the better part of the victory: “The sons of your father shall worship you.” Those who are your enemies are themselves the sons of your Father—first enemies according to their deserts, afterward, through your grace, sons of your Father.
