Your hand is upon the necks of your enemies so that they may worship you, be reconciled to you, and from enemies become your brothers, becoming sons of your Father.

Thus your right hand, set upon the necks of your enemies, will guide you wonderfully; thus peoples will fall beneath you; [the text is corrupt, but appears to read: “into the hearts of the king’s enemies”]; “your throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Ps. 44). Since you are God, it was too little merely to say, “Your brothers shall praise you”; therefore it was completed by saying, [Col. 0553A] “The sons of your Father shall worship you.” But what is the ground or matter of praise, or whence comes the dignity of your worshipful majesty? He says: “Judah, lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up.” Because you are a lion’s cub—that is, the Son of the most mighty God and prince of all strengths or powers—the sons of your Father shall worship you. And because you, my son, have gone up to the prey and vanquished hell, your brothers shall rightly praise you.

Although they are called and are your brothers or sons of your Father, nevertheless they cannot, as you are the cub, be called or be lion’s cubs. For they are sons of God, your Father, by adoption, not by nature; therefore, apart from you, my son, no one could go up to the prey and despoil hell. You alone, plunderer of death, “resting, have lain down like a lion and like a lioness.”

This is marvelous: “resting”—that is, dying—you lay down like a lion, for in dying you did not fail, nor was your strength diminished. Nor did you merely lie down like a lion with open eyes, but also like a lioness, whom great love drives to fierceness and whose great affection for her hungry young stirs her to prey. [Col. 0553B] For you hastened to strip off spoils; you hurried to seize prey (Isa. 8), so that you might bring to your cubs—that is, your apostles—the joy of great spoil and the great triumph of resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the saying, “Who shall raise him up?” and “The sceptre shall not be taken away,” etc.

“Who shall raise him up?” Up to this point the father had spoken in the tender inclination of an affectionate mind to that prince of strength, his son according to the flesh. Now, overwhelmed by admiration, he looks about, as it were, upon the whole world standing by and asks, in order by asking to stir the whole human race to wonder: “Who shall raise him up?”

And we too rightly say concerning what is past: “Who raised him up?” Elijah raised the widow’s son (3 Kings 17). He Himself raised Lazarus (John 11). “Who helped His Spirit?” (Isa. 40). He Himself, needing no one, awoke by His own roar, for He had power to lay down His life and power to take it again (John 10).

Then, as though someone asked when He would come and what would be the sign of the time of His advent, there immediately follows: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, [Col. 0553D] until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.” This is certain and clear to every person possessing eyes. For when, or from what time, was the sceptre taken away from Judah and a ruler from his thigh? Evidently from the time when Herod, a foreigner, the son of an Idumaean father and an Arabian mother, obtained the kingdom of the Jews by Roman grant.

Kings indeed had long failed from the time of the Babylonian captivity; nevertheless leaders descended from that nation continued until the disputes of Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. Born from intermixed tribes, namely the priestly and royal, they divided kingdom and priesthood between themselves in discordant spirits; by contention and mutual warfare, they finally gave an opportunity to Roman power and opened a place for the foreigner Herod. Thus, as Judah’s thigh gradually failed and became lame, all power was finally taken away from him. Therefore it was wisely said not only, “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah,” but also added, “nor a ruler from his thigh.” The sceptre was first taken away from Judah, then, when Herod took it (Matt. 2), who certainly was not a Jew.

And who does not know that then came He who was to be sent? For then Jesus Christ, the Son of God, deigned to be born of a Virgin in Bethlehem of Judah (Luke 2). When, therefore, he says, “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent,” the most holy one raises up the sure prophetic word of the prophets as “a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1), so that the seeker of the kingdom of God may know when and from what point he ought to be certain of the advent of Him whom all His brothers and all the sons of His Father ought to praise and worship.

The aged Simeon, a righteous and devout man, attending in the Holy Spirit to this lamp and prophetic word, knew and saw that, with a foreigner reigning, the sceptre had been removed from Judah and a ruler from his thighs. He understood that it was time for Him who was to be sent to come; therefore he knocked with prayer, long suspended, at the gates of heaven from which he expected Him to come, until he received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death before he saw the Lord’s Christ (Luke 2). And he saw Him; and just as he read in this passage of Scripture, “He shall be the expectation of the nations,” so he believed and confessed Him to be “a light for the revelation of the nations” (ibid.).

But how could Israel himself, the father, know so as to say, “He shall be the expectation of the nations”? From God, certainly—not only because he was a prophet, but because God had also spoken thus to Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

## CHAPTER XXX. What that expectation of the nations is, according to the words, “Binding his foal to the vine,” etc.

What this expectation of the nations is, this prophetic oracle subsequently declares through familiar names and a clear comparison: “Binding his foal to the vine, and to the vine-stock, O my son, his she-ass.” No tongue can follow in words the depth of affection with which, though speaking in the third person, he turns to the second in saying, “O my son”; scarcely can the mind perceive it, even with the gracious indulgence of love.

“Binding,” he says, “his foal to the vine, and to the vine-stock, O my son, his she-ass.” We know the colt of the she-ass upon which the Lord Jesus sat: this is the people of the Gentiles, whom He has now bound to His vine when, by His grace, He joined that people to the apostolic Church which is from the Jews. What is signified by the foal is also signified by the she-ass; what is signified by the vine-stock is also meant by the vine. One vine, or one vineyard, is the Church of all the elect from the beginning of the world to the apostolic faith, together with Christ its head. Christ the head says of Himself: “I am the vine, and my Father is the husbandman” (John 15). Of the Church, which is His body, the prophet says: “I will sing to my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard. A vineyard was made for my beloved [Col. 0555A] on a horn, the son of oil” (Isa. 5), and so forth.

To this vine, to this vineyard, we Gentiles, awaiting Christ until we see Him face to face, are meanwhile bound as a foal or she-ass—an animal to which the Gentile world is rightly compared because of its former burdens of folly. We are bound, I say, to such a vine so that, after straw, the fodder of asses, we may eat the sweetest cluster and drink, in the Holy Spirit, the excellent wine of the Scriptures. Of this it immediately adds: “He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes.” Therefore He shall bind His foal to the vine and His she-ass to the vine-stock in order to wash His robe in wine and His cloak in the blood of grapes.

Nothing is truer. What is signified by the foal and she-ass is likewise signified by the cloak and robe: understand one and the same Church. For the same Gentile people, before being reborn through this washing, was a wanton she-ass or foal; but after Christ washed it, it is His robe or cloak, of which the Psalm says: “Like ointment upon the head, which comes down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which comes down upon the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132).

Therefore, “He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes”: that is, He shall cleanse His Church by the Holy Spirit and His faithful people by the blood of His passion. For He is the grape of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna” (*botrus cypri*) (Song 1). This grape, or cluster, pressed in the winepress of the cross, poured out His blood and gave the Holy Spirit; thus He washed His robe—that is, cleansed His Church—[Col. 0555C] “that he might present to himself a glorious bride, having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. 5).

The Holy Spirit concludes the beauty of this prophetic praise thus: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.” We read both in the prophet Zechariah (Zech. 3) and in the Apocalypse of John that these most beautiful eyes are seven: “They are,” he says, “the seven spirits of God, sent into all the earth” (Rev. 5). First, in this passage we understand wine to signify the old severity of the Law, just as in other places of Scripture new wine signifies the new doctrine of evangelical grace. It is evident that the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which we have received through the grace of the Gospel, is more beautiful and sweeter than the oldness of the Law.

The teeth also are those who, in His body—which is the Church—are strong enough to take solid food. And these are indeed whiter than milk: that is, holier and more beautiful than those who, because of the infancy of their understanding, need the milk of the letter. Let him therefore say: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the blessings of Zebulun and Issachar

“Zebulun shall dwell by the shore of the sea, and at a station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon. Issachar is a strong ass lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear and became a servant under tribute.”

According to the letter, after saying of Zebulun that he would possess the shores of the great sea and reach Sidon and the other cities of Phoenicia, he now returns to the inland province and, because Issachar was to possess a most beautiful region in Galilee near Naphtali, makes him through his blessing its inhabitant. He calls him a strong, or bony, ass, and says that his shoulder was devoted to bearing, because he would labor greatly in cultivating the land and in carrying to the sea the goods produced within his borders, also bringing tribute to kings.

The Hebrews say that this is metaphorically meant to signify that, meditating day and night upon the holy Scriptures, he devoted himself to labor, and that therefore every tribe served him, bringing gifts as to a teacher. But let us rather refer these matters, together with the later statement concerning Naphtali—“Naphtali, a stag let loose, giving words of beauty”—to the teaching of the Savior, because it was especially there that He taught, as is written in the Gospel: “And he dwelt in maritime Capernaum, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee’” (Matt. 4), and so forth.

Therefore, according to the anagogical sense, Zebulun and Naphtali, and Issachar possessing the inland province, are the apostles or apostolic men. Dwelling by the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, because they became fishers of men, they were always intent upon drawing multitudes of rational fish out of the deep and deceptive waves. “He saw,” he says, “that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he bent his shoulder to bear and became a servant under tribute.” This, I say, Issachar—whose name means “reward”—saw; or Zebulun, that is, “dwelling-place of strength”: namely, whoever heard Him proclaiming the giver of eternal reward and bestower of the most strong dwelling-place: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). Therefore Issachar, according to his name, bent his shoulder under the light burden for a good reward, because he saw and found rest for his soul.

## CHAPTER XXXII. [Col. 0556D] On the blessings of Dan, and what they contain in the literal and allegorical senses

“Dan shall judge his people, as also another tribe of Israel. Let Dan become a serpent in the way and a *cerastes* on the path, biting the horse’s hoofs, so that its rider falls backward. I shall await your salvation, O Lord.”

Samson, a judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan. Therefore he says: “Now I see in the Spirit your Nazirite Samson nourishing his hair and triumphing after his enemies have been slain; like a serpent and a basilisk lying in wait upon the roads, he permits no one to pass through the land of Israel. Even if some reckless person, trusting in his own strength as in a horse’s swiftness, should wish to flee through it like a plunderer devastating the people, he will not be able.” He speaks wholly through the metaphor of serpent and rider.

Seeing, therefore, so mighty a Nazirite of yours, who himself also died because of a prostitute and, dying, killed our enemies, I thought, O God, that he was Christ, your Son. But because he died and did not rise again, and Israel was once more led captive, another Savior of the world and of my race must be awaited by me: He must come to whom it is assigned, “He shall be the expectation of the nations.”

Alternatively: “Let Dan become a serpent in the way and a *cerastes* on the path, biting the horse’s hoofs, so that its rider falls backward.” Some maintain that Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because Dan is here said to be a serpent and a biting *cerastes*. Hence, too, when the Israelite people received lands in the division of their camp, Dan first pitched camp to the north, signifying him who said in his heart: “I will sit on the mount of the covenant, upon the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Of him the prophet says: “From Dan was heard the snorting of his horses” (Jer. 8).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*. In Greek, *cerastes* means “horns.” This serpent is said to be horned, and through it the advent of Antichrist is fittingly declared, because against the life of the faithful he is armed both with the bite of pestilential preaching and with the horns of power. Who does not know that a path is narrower than a way? Therefore Dan becomes a serpent in the way, because he invites people to walk in the breadth of this present life, flattering them as though sparing them; but he bites in the way because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants liberty.

He becomes a *cerastes* on the path because those whom he finds faithful and constraining themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly command, he attacks not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion, but also oppresses with the terror of power; in the pressure of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he employs the horns of power. In this place the horse also signifies, or suggests, this world, foaming through its pride in the course of passing times. And because Antichrist is said to seize the ends of the world, the *cerastes* is said to bite this horse’s hoofs. To bite the hoofs of the horse is to strike at the end of the age, “so that its rider falls backward.”

The rider of the horse is whoever is exalted in the dignities of the world. He is said to fall backward, not upon his face, as Saul is recorded to have fallen (Acts 9). To fall upon one’s face is for each person in this life to acknowledge his own sins and bewail them in repentance. But to fall backward, where one does not see, is to depart suddenly from this life and not know to what punishments one is being led. And because Judaea, caught in the snares of its error, awaits Antichrist, Jacob appropriately, suddenly turning in the voice of the elect, says: “I shall await your salvation, O Lord” [Col. 0557D]—that is, not Antichrist as the unbelievers do, but I faithfully believe in Christ, who is to come for our redemption.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the blessings of Gad, and what they contain in each sense

“Gad, armed, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be armed from behind.”

The Hebrews maintain that this entirely refers to Gad’s return after fourteen years to his sons, whom he had left in possession beyond the Jordan, before his people—that is, before Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh. He then found a great war against them from neighboring nations and, fighting bravely, defeated the enemies. You may gather this partly from the Book of Joshua son of Nun (Josh. 22), and especially from Chronicles (1 Chron. 5).

But this Jewish sense is excessively dry and slight, and does not concern these last days, concerning which, as Father Israel declares at the beginning, this whole pronouncement is made. Therefore the meaning must be investigated more deeply. It can indeed be understood in two further ways.

“Gad, an armed fighter before his people, who fights indeed before him beyond the Jordan,” is mystically the Jewish people; but we are the people before whom he, armed, fights. His weapons are the sacred books. He is armed with them, indeed, but only from behind, not in front; for he himself does not see his weapons—that is, he does not understand the Scriptures themselves—by which he fights before us for the truth and helps us, while he carries books throughout the world from which we prove that the testimonies of the prophets concerning Christ which we preach are true and not fabricated by ourselves. But this must be discussed more fully elsewhere.

Alternatively, since these are not merely prophetic announcements of future things but also paternal instructions concerning both the present and the future, Scripture later says: “And when he had finished the commands by which he instructed his sons, he gathered his feet upon the bed and died.” It may also be taken in a good sense, as though it said: Gad will then rightly observe his name if, armed, he fights before his people, armed from behind—that is, cautious and provident concerning the future. The kind of warfare for which it is fitting that a holy man should train his sons must be such as the warfare for which, for example, the Maccabean brothers fought; or rather, to ascend to evangelical perfection, the battles of those truly armed must be like those whose victories we honor in persons who gave their bodies for God’s covenant and preferred to conquer by dying rather than by killing.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. [Col. 0558D] On the blessings of Asher

“Asher, his bread is rich, and he shall provide delights for kings.”

Asher means “blessed” or “happy.” He therefore aptly plays upon his name by saying, “His bread is rich.” For richness or abundance of bread is, in popular judgment, a kind of happiness. Hence the Psalmist says: “They called blessed the people to whom these things belong”—namely, storehouses full and overflowing from one thing into another, fruitful sheep abundant in their offspring, and fat cattle (Ps. 143). “And in this happiness,” he says, “he shall provide delights for kings,” for the service of a people is delightful to kings where its bread is rich.

But in those last days, concerning which he promised to make his declaration, Asher—that is, “Blessed is the people whose Lord is God” (ibid.)—has as his own rich bread Him who says: [Col. 0559A] “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” Truly this bread of God, which came down from heaven, is rich, because it gives life to this world. Therefore Asher, who enjoys the richness of this bread, shall provide delights for kings: that is, for those who strive to govern themselves, so that they may be worthy of the royal court’s table. He shall offer them the delights of life-giving nourishment, either by administering the Eucharist or by expounding the rich marrow of the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the blessings of Naphtali

“Naphtali, a stag let loose, giving words of beauty.”

The Hebrews think that Naphtali is called “a stag let loose” because of early crops and the swiftness of a more fertile land, and that “words of beauty” are prophesied because of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law. But this interpretation, concerned with early crops and the swiftness of a more fertile land, carries little weight.

Therefore it is better to refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, because, as has already been said above, He preached there especially, “giving words of beauty.” For to Him it was most truly said: “You are beautiful in form above the sons of men; grace is poured out upon your lips” (Ps. 44). And, like a stag let loose, by running He accomplished the whole matter in a short time. Therefore the bride says to Him in the Song of Songs: “Return; be like a gazelle, my beloved, or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song 2).

Alternatively: “Naphtali, a stag let loose, giving words of beauty.” [Col. 0559C] It is as if he said: Whoever is worthy to be called by this name, which means “breadth,” must, with heart enlarged, run like a stag let loose in the way of God’s commandments and give words of beauty—just as that stag who, running in his release and unable to endure remaining at a station, says: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not constrained in us” (2 Cor. 6). These and similar words of love are words of beauty. Whoever gives such words is rightly called Naphtali, because love has indeed enlarged his heart, and love shines with the true beauty of speech.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the blessings of Joseph
Joseph, an increasing son, an increasing son and fair in appearance. Daughters ran about upon the wall, but they embittered him, quarrelled with him, and envied him, being armed with darts. Again, as in the case of Judah, so also in this case the father more fully unfolds his affections toward his own, especially on account of Christ, whom by the spirit of prophecy he saw both to be born from the one and prefigured by the other. “Joseph,” he says, “is an increasing son”—understood by his name. For Joseph is interpreted “increasing” or “augmented”; he is also understood to be increasing in effect, for the land of his poverty increased, and he became exceedingly great. “And fair,” he says, “in appearance.” Who reported this, or whence was it made known to the holy patriarch that his son was fair in appearance? He says: “Daughters ran about upon the wall.” Unless wandering and wanton daughters, running about upon the wall, had cast [Col. 0560A] their eyes upon him and said, “Sleep with us,” it would not so have been remembered that he was fair in appearance. But now, because the beauty of his appearance became for him the occasion of conflict, chains, and a great victory, he is rightly known and proclaimed to have been fair in appearance.

In saying “daughters ran about,” he used the plural for the singular, a frequent and customary usage in Scripture, so that more may be expressed for amplification of the matter; this figure is called synecdoche. For one woman only—namely, his mistress, who should rather be called a daughter than mistress of the household—is recorded to have cast her eyes upon him (Gen. XXXIX): a foolish and unguarded daughter, whose incontinence is also indicated by the phrase, “they ran about upon the wall.” She is such as Solomon describes: talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet, [Col. 0560B] unable to keep her feet in her own house, now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners; she seizes and kisses a young man and flatters him with an impudent face, saying: “I have woven my bed with cords; I have spread it with embroidered coverings from Egypt; I have sprinkled my couch with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. My husband is not at home; he has gone on a very long journey” (Prov. VII).

These and similar things she said; but the increasing son, fair in appearance, did not heed the words of her mouth; his mind was not drawn away into her paths, nor was he deceived by her tracks. Such is the son of Joseph. “But they embittered him, quarrelled with him, and envied him, being armed with darts”—understood, his brothers. In what did they embitter him, or in what did they quarrel with him? Clearly in this: seeing that he was loved by his father more than all his brothers, they hated him [Col. 0560C] and could not speak peacefully to him (Gen. XXXVII). Thus they quarrelled, and by quarrelling embittered him, because, prompted by hatred, they could speak nothing peacefully, nothing without contention. They had darts, therefore—namely, in their mouths. For their teeth were weapons and arrows (Ps. LVI), as they said: “Come, let us kill him” (Gen. XXXVII); “come, let us sell him.” They envied him and carried their envy into effect.

But what follows? “His bow sits in strength, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosed by the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there came forth the shepherd, the stone of Israel.” They envied him, having arrows of jealousy, and were themselves wounded by the darts of their own zeal. But he placed his bow and his weapons of warfare in God, [Col. 0560D] who is a mighty warrior; and his bonds, with which his brothers had bound him, were loosened and broken by God, so that from his seed Ephraim’s tribe might arise—strong, steadfast, invincible like a harder stone—and might rule the ten tribes of Israel. This is what he says: “From there came forth the shepherd”: that is, Ephraim, father of the royal tribe, was born from Joseph. “Stone,” that is, the strength of Israel.

Otherwise: Joseph himself was a shepherd when he said, “I will feed you and your little ones” (Gen. L). In the time of famine he fed many peoples with the most watchful care of a shepherd. Thus, from the bonds upon his arms and hands he came forth through the hand of the Mighty One of Jacob, and he himself was the stone—that is, the support—of Israel. This interpretation comes closer to the mystery, because the good shepherd, whom Joseph [Col. 0561A] here preceded as a type, came forth from the bonds of death through the hand of God the mighty Father, who is the God of Jacob; and, having come forth from his bonds, became the stone of Israel, made the head of the corner (Matt. XXI), whom God raised up, loosening the pains of hell, since it was impossible that he should be held by it (Acts II). The stone of Israel, I say—the cornerstone rejected by the builders (Ps. CXVII). It follows:

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Why he said, “The blessings of your father have been strengthened,” and why he called Joseph a Nazarite.

“The God of your father shall be your helper, and the Almighty shall bless you with blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep lying beneath, blessings of breasts and womb. The blessings of your father have been strengthened [Col. 0561B] by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the eternal hills should come. Let them be upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazarite among his brothers.”

“Blessings of heaven above and blessings of the deep”: that is, the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth. “Blessings of breasts and womb”: that is, the populous multitude of Ephraim and Manasseh. As though one should ask him whence he knew, so as to say, “God Almighty shall bless you with these and those blessings,” he immediately added: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of his father.” As if he said: By the blessings of Isaac my father, or of Abraham, these blessings by which I, Israel, now bless you as your father have indeed been so strengthened that their end cannot be doubtful or their effect uncertain.

By the blessings, I say, of Abraham or Isaac—through whom, by hereditary grace from God, the right and power of blessing flowed down to me, your father—my blessings have been commanded to remain strong, to remain in force, until the desire of the eternal hills comes: that is, Christ, the desirable expectation of all the righteous. They are so powerful and strong that, according to them, not only must your descendants increase, but that desire of all the saints must also come and be fulfilled—the one in whom all nations are to be blessed according to the blessings of my father Abraham. Therefore, strengthened and supported by the foundation of truth, let them be upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazarite [Col. 0561D] among his brothers.

What he had said, “upon the head of Joseph,” he repeated in saying, “upon the crown of the Nazarite among his brothers,” alluding, of course, to his once uncut hair, which a long imprisonment allowed to grow. For it belongs to Nazarites to preserve their hair by vow (Num. VI), and this rightly counts in his case as being a Nazarite—that is, consecrated—because he endured it for sacred chastity.

But our Lord Jesus Christ is in truth the Nazarite among his brothers. For he is the Holy of holies, and upon his crown all the blessings of his Father are fulfilled: blessings of heaven above, blessings of the deep lying beneath, blessings of breasts and womb—that is, of the Church continually bearing and nursing children—so that at the name of Jesus every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth may bow (Phil. II). Concerning him, or his head, the Prophet says in the psalm: “For thou hast gone before him with blessings [Col. 0562A] of sweetness; thou hast placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Ps. XX).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Benjamin’s blessings.

“Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he shall devour the prey, and in the evening divide the spoils.” This is an exceptionally elegant correspondence of figures. Judah is a lion’s cub; Benjamin, however, is a ravening wolf. The one is king; the other his armour-bearer. The one is the expectation of the nations; the other their devourer. For this is plainly a prophecy concerning the Apostle Paul. As Judah is Christ, because he was to be born from the tribe of Judah, so Benjamin is Paul, because he was to be taken from the tribe of Benjamin. For he himself says: “For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Rom. XI). Again: “If anyone else seems to have confidence in the flesh, I more: circumcised on the eighth day, of the stock of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin” (Phil. III).

“Benjamin is a ravening wolf.” This was certainly evil. But hear what follows: “In the morning he shall devour the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils.” If being a ravening wolf and devouring prey in the morning was evil, dividing spoils in the evening is good. In the morning the ravening wolf devoured prey; for in youth he was a persecutor, blasphemer, and violent man (I Tim. I), bringing bound to the rulers whatever men and women of this Way he could find (Acts IX). But in the evening—that is, until the end of his life—he shall divide his spoils, namely, the sacred words of evangelical preaching. Of these the Psalmist says: “I shall rejoice over thy words, as one who finds great spoils” (Ps. CXVIII).

The Hebrews, because they do not know Paul and are far from the truth, explain it thus: The altar, upon which victims were sacrificed and the blood of offerings was poured at its base, lay within Benjamin’s portion. This, therefore, they say, signifies that the priests sacrifice victims in the morning and in the evening divide what has been supplied to them by the people according to the Law. They assign the bloody, devouring wolf to the interpretation of the altar, and the division of spoils to the priests, who, serving at the altar, live from the altar.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Why it is said, “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel,” although Joseph’s two sons were added.

“And all these are the twelve tribes of Israel”—understood, fathers and princes; that is, from each of these arose and was named a tribe, and there are twelve tribes. Yet Ephraim and Manasseh were added to these, the father saying to Joseph: “Therefore your two sons, who were born to you in the land of Egypt before I came here to you, shall be mine: Ephraim and Manasseh shall be counted to me as Reuben and Simeon” (Gen. XLVIII). Why, then, are not fourteen tribes now counted, but only twelve tribes of Israel?

One must know that where Simeon and Levi are counted in their own natural generation, Ephraim and Manasseh, who are adopted sons, cannot be counted. Conversely, where Ephraim and Manasseh are included—namely, in inheritances and the individual land-allotments of the tribes—Simeon and Levi are omitted. For these did not receive their own allotments, as has already been said above, but had a few cities in all the territories, in accordance with their father’s prophecy: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” Therefore, whichever way one looks, whether to the apportioned territories or to the natural descent, there are only twelve tribes of Israel.

In the Apocalypse of John, Dan, who was born a son of Israel, is omitted, and Manasseh, who was adopted, is included (Apoc. VII). Likewise Reuben, who was born, though lesser, is included in the number, while Ephraim, though numerous, is omitted (ibid.). This indicates that, for attaining the inheritance for which we are sealed on our foreheads with the seal of the living God, neither only natural sons nor only adopted sons of Israel—that is, neither only those from the Jews nor only those from the Greeks—are chosen or rejected; rather, from both alike are chosen or rejected those whom faith has commended or unbelief has made reprobate.

## CHAPTER XL. Why he makes no mention of Aaron and Levi’s priesthood.

“And he blessed each one with his proper blessings, and commanded him, saying: ‘I am being gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers in the double cave,’” etc. Here again the question arises: since he blessed each one with his proper blessings, why did he make no mention of Aaron’s priesthood in the tribe of Levi, which was most holy and renowned among that people? For even if he rightly says, “Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of iniquity in warfare; let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly, because in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall,” etc., nevertheless the sons of Levi later laudably took up arms for vengeance concerning the calf; and therefore it was said to them: “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each against his son and brother, so that a blessing may be given to you” (Exod. XXXII).

Why, then, did the father omit that priesthood in his blessings and proclaim no praise of the Levitical ministry? To this one must first reply that he professed himself to announce the last days; but that priesthood, or that Levitical order, does not belong to these last days, to these ends of the ages. Secondly, one must know that Aaron’s priesthood was granted not as the blessing itself but as a sign of the blessing. Nor were those sacrifices of bulls, calves, rams, and goats commanded by God, but permitted, as the prophets testify (Heb. VII; Pss. XXXIX, XLIX); this will be discussed more fully in its proper place.

But the true priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek was reserved for Christ in the tribe of Judah, David saying: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). And if you look rightly, this same father did not keep silence about this in Judah’s blessings, saying: “He shall wash his garment in wine and his cloak in the blood of grapes.” For to wash one’s garment in wine and one’s cloak in the blood of grapes—that is, to grant repentance and remission of sins through his own blood—is the office of the true and only priest.

Certainly, when he says, “I am being gathered to my people,” that is, “I descend to the underworld,” where the whole people of saints await the Saviour who is to be sent and who shall be the expectation of the nations, until he comes. Concerning the care he took for the burial of his body, enough has already been said above.

## CHAPTER XLI. How Joseph buried his dead father in the land of Canaan with great mourning.

When he had finished the commands by which he instructed his sons, he drew up his feet upon the bed and died, and was gathered to his people. (CH. L.) Seeing this, Joseph fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him, etc. All this care bestowed upon the dead—his son’s pious tears for his father; his command to his physician-servants to embalm his father with spices; and, after the funeral rites had been performed, his burial of him with great and vehement mourning in the land of Canaan, in the double cave that Abraham had bought, together with the field, as a burial possession from Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre—all these offices of filial devotion, I say, the divine oracle had promised Jacob in a brief response of consolation, saying: “Joseph also shall put his hand upon your eyes” (Gen. XLVI). Taking this as a great thing, Jacob said: “Now I shall die joyful, because I have seen your face and leave you alive” (ibid.).

But the fact that Egypt mourned for him seventy days and seven more is not an example to be imitated by those who confess themselves strangers and pilgrims upon the earth, who have here no abiding city but seek the city to come (Heb. XIII). For when the Scriptures say that the children of Israel likewise mourned Moses and Aaron for thirty days (Num. XX; Deut. XXXIV), this was a remnant of Egyptian custom among a people not yet instructed. Later, gradually accustomed to better things, they departed from that superstition, as Scripture says: “Weep a little over the dead, knowing that he has entered into rest” (Ecclus. XXII).

Moreover, mourning or weeping in such accounts is not always meant literally; for there are also funeral games, which are denoted by the name of mourning. True mourning and true tears, however, are allowed only in moderation to worthy men. Hence the Wise Man says: “My son, shed tears over the dead, and begin to lament as though you had suffered terrible things; cover his body according to the rite, and do not neglect his burial; make mourning according to his worth, for one day or two” (Ecclus. XXXVIII). Nor is it surprising that the Egyptians mourned so with great and vehement lamentation that the place was even named from it: it was called “the Mourning of Egypt.” For Flaccus also says:

> . . . those hired to weep at a funeral say  
> And do . . . . . more than those who grieve sincerely . . . . .  
> (HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, v. 431.)

Joseph, the wise man, did not hire or request the Egyptians to weep; but while he intended something else, he allowed this too to occur of its own accord as an additional matter. What, then, did he intend in saying to Pharaoh’s household: “If I have found favour in your sight, speak in the ears of Pharaoh, because my father made me swear, saying: ‘Behold, I die; in my tomb which I dug in the land of Canaan you shall bury me. Therefore I shall go up and bury my father, and I shall return’”? He certainly intended, in transporting his father, to avoid jealousy by closing the mouths of detractors, who might perhaps say, “He does not love our land.” Nor did the prudence of this humility fail: not only did he escape this jealousy and Pharaoh’s anger, but all spoke so favourably of him that all the elders of Pharaoh’s house and all the chief men went with him; he had chariots and horsemen in his escort, and there was a very great company. Therefore, as he prudently sought goodwill, so he ought wisely to admit the Egyptian funeral observances, since they would not harm the holy purpose of pilgrimage. In that pilgrimage the proper object of weeping is rather this: that their sojourning is prolonged (Ps. CXIX), though they await a better country and a better city.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Joseph’s clemency, by which he forgave his brothers, and on his own command concerning the removal of his bones.

After Jacob’s death, his brothers, fearing and speaking among themselves, said: “Perhaps he remembers the injury he suffered and will repay us for all the evil we did.” They sent to him: “Your father commanded us before he died that we should say these things to you in his words: ‘I beg you to forget the crime of your brothers,’” etc. It is a praise of inborn clemency that, when he heard his brothers say, “We too pray that you forgive this iniquity to the servants of the God of your father,” Joseph wept. This is the holiest and best kind of granting or remitting forgiveness: when those who have sinned do not weep but merely confess, the one offended alone weeps as he pardons, and to those who bow down for forgiveness he returns pious tears together with pardon.

Yet where mercy soothes, truth also pierces, lest the brothers rejoice so in the forgiveness of the one injured that they close the eyes of their minds to concern for God’s judgment. “Do not fear,” he says. “Can we resist the will of God?” This surely belongs to mercy. “You intended evil against me, but God turned it into good, so as to exalt me as you now see and to preserve many peoples alive.” This belongs to stern truth. All rulers should take from this a useful example: they should quickly forgive those who sin against them, and indeed repay good for evil, but should not allow sinners to become excessively secure concerning God’s judgment.

He lived one hundred and ten years and saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. This should be referred to the strength of the paternal blessings, among which he pronounced blessings of breasts and womb, and of which he said: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened” (Gen. XLIX): namely, that he saw Ephraim’s offspring to the third generation, and that the children of Machir, son of Manasseh, were born upon Joseph’s knees—that is, that their great-grandfather Joseph held Machir’s newborn children upon his knees with nurturing affection. So also should be understood the saying of his mother Rachel: “Go in to my maidservant, that she may bear upon my knees” (Gen. XXX): that is, what she bears I may hold as adopted upon my knees like a mother.

Here also he commanded concerning the removal of his bones: “After my death,” he said, “God will visit you and bring you up from this land; carry my bones with you from this place.” Moses did this, as is written in Exodus (Exod. XIII). Yet Joseph was not buried in the same tomb with his fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob at Hebron, but at Shechem, which, as was said above, Jacob gave without a lot to the tribe of Joseph; and his mausoleum is seen there to this day.

# The Forty-Two Books of the Reverend Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, *On the Trinity and Its Works*: Commentaries on Exodus

## Book I. (Exodus, chapters I–XI.)

[Col. 0565]

## CHAPTER I. Continuation of the preceding book of Genesis and of the following book of Exodus; and how Pharaoh prefigured the devil, while the Paschal lamb prefigured Christ.

For what cause, or in what manner, Israel entered [Col. 0566C] Egypt and Jacob became a resident in the land of Ham has been narrated in the final part of the preceding book of Genesis: namely, because “the Lord called a famine upon the land and broke all the sustenance of bread; but he sent a man before them”—not for their own merits, [Col. 0567A] for “Joseph was sold as a slave; they humbled his feet in fetters, and iron passed through his soul”—while he patiently endured and placed his hope in God, “until his word came.” At length it came, and “the word of the Lord kindled him,” like a lamp worthy of a lofty lampstand; and his light began to shine from the interpretation of dreams. Accordingly, “the king sent and loosed him; the ruler of peoples sent and released him from prison” (Ps. CIV). He freed him from his chains and said: “Could we find a man filled with the Spirit of God?” He “appointed him lord of his house and ruler of all his possession, that he might instruct his princes as himself and teach wisdom to his elders.” Then, according to the truth of the interpreter, “the Lord called,” as has already been said, “a famine upon the land; and because of this Israel entered Egypt” (ibid.), and “dwelt in the land of Goshen, possessed it, and increased and multiplied exceedingly” (Gen. XLVII).

These things, I say, were narrated in the final part of the preceding book. Thereafter the first portions of this following book of Exodus contain this: “He turned their heart that they might hate his people and deal deceitfully with his servants; and he sent Moses his servant, Aaron whom he had chosen; he placed in them the words of his signs” (Ps. CIV). In these matters and the rest, as arranged and begun, we shall touch briefly upon the letter, and, as far as we can with his help, shall diligently endeavour to bring forth in uncorrupted faith the mysteries of Christ, the Son of God, hidden within.

First of all, scarcely anyone is unaware that Pharaoh, the new king “who did not know Joseph,” bore the type of the devil; that the Paschal lamb commanded to be sacrificed prefigured Christ, the Son of God; that Egypt signifies this world; and that the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea prefigures Christ’s baptism. Therefore, that we may proceed to these things in a proper order, let us look further back and inquire what the entry of the children of Israel into Egypt signifies, so that we may know that, just as their departure, so also their entry occurred as a figure of all pilgrims awaiting the heavenly country amid their present sojourn.

## CHAPTER II. How that Israel signified all the elect, and that Egypt signified this world, in which all the elect are pilgrims.

[Col. 0567D] For the whole Israel, the blessed nation and people “whom the Lord chose as his inheritance” (Ps. XXXII), the first instrument of righteousness and salvation is to know and confess that through its own fault it was cast into this exile, far from the face of God and far from the land of the living, in which it ought to have seen the good things of the Lord (Ps. XXVI); and that it is solely through grace that it is at last rescued from this present evil age and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love.

Yet Israel would not have attained knowledge of this confession unless, through the introduction of an outwardly occurring likeness, it had advanced to an understanding of righteousness. Therefore, lest a suitable likeness for instructing children should be absent, it came about that the particular, or carnal, Israel entered [Col. 0568A] Egypt for such a cause and in such an order that its entry was owing to its own fault, while its liberated departure thence was owing to God’s grace. For if, in answer to one who asks why Israel entered Egypt, you reply, “Because God willed it,” what you say is true, but your answer embraces less than the whole truth. It still remains to ask why God willed it so. God is just, and there is nothing that he wills or commands to happen without reason. Pursuing the inquiry into the reason, therefore, one must answer that God willed this because the house of Israel sinned: it sold its brother as a slave. For this reason God justly willed it; for this reason he called a famine and justly handed over his guilty ones, as to a harsh taskmaster, that they might go into Egypt, into that prison to which they had sent their brother before them.

The patriarch Israel himself was free from guilt; therefore he entered with consolation preceding and following him. For he heard the God of his father Isaac calling to him in a vision by night and saying: “I am the mighty God of your father. Do not fear; go down into Egypt, for there I shall make you into a great nation. Joseph also shall put his hand upon your eyes” (Gen. XLVI). Thus, since he was without guilt, he entered with grace; but his household, because it had incurred guilt, went unknowingly under the rod of strict correction to the prison where it was justly to be restrained. God’s justice, therefore, caused that people to enter Egypt in order to serve; but it was grace, as said before, that God brought it out.

Thus an event was enacted in part that might become a parable of the whole: that is, by whose likeness the whole “generation of those who seek God, who seek the face of the God of Jacob” (Ps. XXIII), more fully instructed, might at the beginning of its justification accuse itself and with a clear harmony sing a confession, on the one hand of its own guilt and on the other of divine justice.

For Israel received in promise the land flowing with milk when “God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight,” on this condition, “that he should work”—understood, by obeying God’s command—and thus “keep it” for himself (Gen. II). But while eating, this same Israel sold its brother into Egypt when the one “in whom all sinned” (Rom. V), through tasting the forbidden food, sold himself to the devil. God cries out concerning this sale through the prophet: “You were sold for nothing”; and immediately promising a gratuitous deliverance, he adds: “You shall be redeemed without silver” (Isa. LII).

Thus “the Lord called a famine upon the land, that Israel might enter Egypt” (Ps. CIV), when he said to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labours you shall eat of it all the days of your life; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III), and, having prescribed this sentence, sent him into the exile of this world. This habitation is rightly called Egypt, a name which is interpreted as “darkness,” because here there is darkness, where God is not seen. There Pharaoh was the new king of Egypt; here the devil is the new usurper of a royal name—indeed, the old tyrant, prince of darkness. There the Egyptians hated Israel; here are “the principalities and powers of the world, the rulers of this darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, against whom, according to the Apostle, is our struggle” (Eph. VI). With these matters thus set forth, the following mysteries of liberating grace must now be treated according to the order of this Scripture.

## CHAPTER III. On the names of the sons of Israel, and why they are rightly written at the beginning of this book.

(CH. I.) “These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob; each entered with his household and wives: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin; Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. Thus all the souls who came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy. [Col. 0569B] Joseph, however, was in Egypt.”

This beginning of the book, even if you consider only the literal sense, possesses the remarkable merit of a skilled historian, who judged it fitting briefly to repeat here what he had said more fully in the preceding book. For he could have begun with what immediately follows, thus: “When Joseph and all his brothers and all his kindred had died, the children of Israel increased; multiplying as though sprouting, they became exceedingly strong and filled the land.” Such a beginning would have been sufficiently connected and continuous with the end of the preceding book. But he wished to present the body of this book as complete. Therefore he prefixed an excellent head, illuminated, as it were, by the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt, like a number of stars. This adornment of the head is of great value, both for the history and for the allegory, because it is proper that, at the beginning, there should be presented the entry of those whose departure from Egypt, whether according to the letter or according to the spirit, is contained in this book. Therefore, having duly praised the architect of this structure at its doors, let us now go inside and examine this house of most extensive Scripture, which he built and filled with heavenly treasures.

## CHAPTER IV. How Pharaoh was also like the devil in his perverse concern when he said, “Behold, the people,” etc.

Meanwhile a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph, and he said to his people: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel has multiplied and is stronger than we are. Come, let us oppress it wisely, lest perhaps it multiply; and if war should arise against us, it may join our enemies and, when we have been overcome, depart from the land.”

Here, if you read intelligently, you necessarily understand that the children of Israel were accustomed to sigh for the land promised to their fathers. This, heard from the fathers by their sons as they came and listened to the oft-repeated hope, stirred angry jealousy in the Egyptians. Therefore the writer aptly makes the matter clear when, after saying, “lest war should arise against us,” he does not add, “when we are overcome, it may take possession of the land,” but, “it may depart from the land.”

Spiritually, the new king of Egypt, who is so anxious and speaks thus, is the devil: king of Egypt—that is, prince of darkness; king, I say, of the Egyptians—that is, of all the proud, since the Lord says to blessed Job that “he is king over all the children of pride” (Job XLI). “Behold,” he says, “the people has multiplied and is stronger than we are,” etc. He said this in anger because he saw and grieved that, through his fraud, the Creator’s blessing could not perish. For, in the predestination of the elect, God blessed our first parents, saying: “Increase and multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it” (Gen. I). But later he said to the deceived woman concerning the luxuriant offspring of the reprobate: “I will multiply your miseries and your conceptions” (Gen. III).

But however enviously you may speak, O devil, you have spoken truth here; and all your Egyptian attendants have spoken without falsehood: for we are a people multiplied and stronger than you. And if war should arise—indeed, it has long since arisen—against you, with Christ, the Son of God, commander of the war, raising the standard of his cross, we are joined to your enemies, namely the holy and blessed angels. Before those stronger beings you turn your faltering backs in flight; and, when you have been overcome, we depart from the land, because heaven awaits us.

## CHAPTER V. On the same matter, and how the children of Israel increased amid Pharaoh’s oppressions, just as God’s elect advance amid the devil’s assaults.

“Come,” he says, “let us wisely oppress him.” This is what he said: “And he set taskmasters over them, to afflict them with burdens.” It is to be understood that this was so that labor and abuse, producing forgetfulness of pleasure, would not allow them to enter into marital embraces and beget children [Col. 0570C]. “And they built for Pharaoh the store-cities Pithom and Rameses.” The enemy of nature, mad and ineffectual, was doing this as though, in summer heat, he strove to burn up the roots of trees lest they burst forth into flowers or fruit. For the root of nature does not wither in the heat of exhausting work; rather, after labor it becomes more eager for food, drink, and sleep. By such things pleasure is not ordinarily extinguished, but, revived, strives to grow and break forth. Thus envy fought in vain in this manner, especially where the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth—that is, the blessing of God and of the fathers—did not permit Israel to be barren. Therefore it follows: “And the more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied and increased.” And immediately: “And the Egyptians hated the children of Israel [Col. 0570D] and afflicted them with mockery,” etc.

It is especially worth observing what the Psalmist thought concerning this. For, having said, “And He increased His people exceedingly, and made them stronger than their enemies,” he added: “He turned their heart so that they hated His people and dealt deceitfully with His servants” (Ps. 104). What then? In saying this, does he justify the Egyptians in their hatred or excuse their hatred? Certainly not. Rather, he indicates that they were exceedingly sinful: God found them such that, at the sight of His benefits, their heart turned to hatred of His servants. This must not be understood as though He turned their heart from good to evil, making an evil heart out of a good heart; but in this way: “He turned their heart into hatred,” just as the sun turns soft mud [Col. 0571A] hard. But on this matter elsewhere, where God says: “I will harden the heart of Pharaoh and of his servants” (Exod. 17:9).

For the present, let it suffice to say this: the splendor of the prosperous newcomers so burned their muddy favor—in which they had formerly received Israel because of Joseph—that it turned into the hardness of hatred. And God repaid them with a single and deserved punishment: because they afflicted them not merely without compassion but even with mockery, therefore, just as those works of mud and brick, first soft and then hardened by baking fire, so their hearts were gradually hardened in eternal impenitence.

Now let the discourse return to that Pharaoh and those Egyptians from whom Christ’s grace has delivered us. “Come,” he says, “let us wisely oppress him,” etc. We began long ago to perceive how grievous are the burdens of this wise oppressor, with which he afflicted the human race, when we heard the Liberator saying in His Gospel: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take My yoke,” etc., down to, “My burden is light” (Matt. 11). For before He said this, we did not know our own labor; indeed, we delighted in the burdens of sin, beneath which both the living perception of our souls had expired and our bodies languished under impending mortality. The yokes of that slavery are as numerous as its vices, and its burdens as numerous as its sins—things whose pursuit in detail would be too long and difficult, indeed impossible.

I shall say only this: from the time Israel entered Egypt until the evening sacrifice of the lamb—that is, from Adam’s fall from Paradise until the Passion of Christ the Son of God—“that exactor did not cease, the tribute did not rest, the yoke of the rulers was not broken” (Isa. 14) [Col. 0571C]. From that time peace was made and freedom restored. For he no longer acts as he did before by sovereign rule; nevertheless, like a treacherous robber he follows behind us and pursues in envy those who have been set free, lamenting that the cities we built for him lie empty: Pithom, interpreted “mouth of the abyss,” from which Christ brought us out; and Rameses, interpreted “from the moth,” from which that Physician cleansed our heads.

## CHAPTER VI. That Pharaoh is most rightly proclaimed similar to the devil also in what he says: “If it is a male, kill him,” etc.

[Col. 0571D] “Now the king of Egypt said to the midwives of the Hebrews, one of whom was called Sephora and the other Phua, commanding them: When you act as midwives for the Hebrew women and the time of birth comes, if it is a male, kill him; if it is a female, preserve her. But the midwives feared God and did not do according to the command of the king of Egypt, but preserved the males,” etc.

Even if Holy Scripture rightly employs the names of whatever visible enemies of Israel whenever it attacks the spiritual powers of wickedness—for example, when the Psalmist says, “For they devised with one mind; together they formed a covenant against You—the tents,” etc., down to, “to help the sons of Lot” (Ps. 82)—all the more rightly does it thus disgrace Egyptian wickedness, transforming into Pharaoh king of Egypt and his servants the pride of the devil [Col. 0572A]. For example, the Lord says this in Ezekiel: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say, ‘The river is mine, and I made myself.’ And I will put a bridle in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers cling to your scales; and I will draw you out from the midst of your rivers, and all your fish shall cling to your scales; and I will cast you into the wilderness, you and all the fish of your river” (Ezek. 29), etc.

For Pharaoh, or Egypt, in the first place imitates the devil against Israel in three—indeed, in four—of his crimes, corresponding to the crimes on account of which, according to the prophet Amos, God declares that He will not revoke His sentence against Damascus, Gaza, Ashdod, Tyre, and the other neighboring enemies of Israel (Amos 1) [Col. 0572B]. Pharaoh’s first crime is that, by oppressing the children of Israel, he intends that the pleasure of generation might die and children might not be begotten. The second is that he attempts to act by the deceit of the midwives, so that newborn infants may secretly be killed. The third is that, raging in open persecution, he commanded all his people: “Whatever male child is born, cast into the river; whatever is female, preserve.” The fourth is that, when the Lord commanded him, saying, “Israel is My firstborn son; let My son go, that he may serve Me” (Exod. 4), he proudly replied: “Who is the Lord, that I should hear 170 His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5), and things of that sort.

Therefore Pharaoh is rightly sung of throughout the Scriptures and in the mouth of the whole Church as a figure of the devil; and through Pharaoh the devil is understood, to the glory of Christ, by whose victory we have been delivered from such a Pharaoh. For he is the one who did this from the beginning, insofar as lay in his power: first, that no true Israelite should beget spiritual children for God through the word of preaching; then, that he should kill such newly born little ones through the midwifery of heretical malice; and finally, when his devices had failed, he armed himself with open persecution so as to cast the children of grace into those rivers of which the Psalmist says: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord; the rivers have lifted up their voice” (Ps. 92), etc. [Col. 0572C] By this he signifies the great and manifest storms raised by persecuting enemies.

Observe that here too the spiritual Pharaoh hates the male sex more than the female, according to the distinction kept by the wise man when he says: “The wickedness of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42). For “man” stands for strength: one who presides or is able to rule. “Woman,” however, stands for any soul which, because of the softness of its imperfection, is susceptible to deception, needs a ruler, and, if without discipline, becomes a reproach in Israel. Wickedness occurring in such a man becomes an occasion for increasing virtue, as with David (2 Kings 12). But if such a woman’s good deed shines before men, the slight wind of human glory quickly carries it away; and if a man as admonisher is absent, even that whatever-it-may-be ceases to be done and turns into apostasy [Col. 0573A]. Thus this wise Pharaoh hates such a man and orders him killed, being certain that he can corrupt in adultery such a woman, deprived of a man and consenting to him.

## CHAPTER VII. On the lie of the midwives, and how God dealt well with them because they feared God

“The midwives,” he says, “feared God and did not do according to the command of the king of Egypt, but preserved the males,” etc. Here there is an excessively inopportune dispute about lying, asserting that the midwives could not be justified in lying when they said: “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. For they themselves have skill in midwifery, and before we come to them they give birth.” For they were present at the time of birth, yet it was said of them that “they preserved the males” [Col. 0573B].

Whoever objects to this as a fault must consequently rebuke Rahab the harlot for lying. Taking the two spies whom Joshua had sent, she hid them and said to those seeking them: “I admit they came to me, but I did not know where they were from. And when the gate was being shut in the darkness, they went out together; I do not know where they went. Pursue them quickly, and you will catch them” (Josh. 2). Therefore those who accuse the midwives of lying in order to save so many infants must, all the more, refuse to justify Rahab, who lied in order to free two men—Rahab whom both prophetic and evangelical authority justify.

For in the Gospel she is received as mother and parent of Christ, who is Truth itself, because Rahab so lied: “For Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab” (Matt. 1) [Col. 0573C]. And the Prophet foretells concerning her, as a type of the Church from the Gentiles: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon” (Ps. 80). The Apostle, moreover, so completely prefers no truth at all to charity that he wishes himself to be anathema from Christ—who, it is understood, is Truth—for charity, that is, for his brothers, his kinsmen “according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (Rom. 9). For he had said: “Neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities nor powers nor virtues, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor strength nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God” (Rom. 8).

Let us therefore ascribe no supposed darkness of lying to the bright work of charity, where they so deceived an impious murderer as to preserve human lives—especially since God judged this very act worthy of praise and reward. Scripture immediately says: “Therefore God dealt well with the midwives; and because the midwives feared God, He built them houses”—that is to say, eternal ones; for what God builds is eternal [Col. 0573D].

## CHAPTER VIII. On the birth and beauty of Moses

(Chap. 2.) “After these things a man went out from the house of Levi, taking a wife of his own stock. She conceived and bore a son; and seeing him beautiful, she hid him for three months. And when she could no longer conceal him, she took a little basket of reeds and smeared it with bitumen and pitch, and placed the infant inside it,” etc.

First it must be said that the impious command of the king—“Whatever male child is born, cast into the river; whatever is female, preserve”—was not carried out in every case. Otherwise, how did Aaron, who was born three years before this beautiful infant, escape? Indeed, since it is said that after these things—that is, after the edicts of the impious king—that man went out from the house of Levi and took a wife, Aaron too was undoubtedly born after these same events. For the same wife, as Scripture testifies elsewhere, “bore Aaron, Moses, and Miriam to him” (Exod. 6) [Col. 0574A]. That Aaron was three years older than Moses is written more plainly later: “Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7).

Moreover, when they departed, the children of Israel had both little children and young men of twenty years of age. It is therefore clear that the whole wicked command of the king was not fulfilled. Otherwise there would have been no man among Israel at the Exodus younger than eighty years; Aaron would not have escaped before Moses, nor after the king’s command. Accordingly, the present letter must be examined more carefully. It appears to signify that, while all the infants were being cast away, this child’s mother, made more diligent because of his beauty, hid him for three months, so that at least this one might be saved while the others perished. But the very clear argument already stated opposes this sense.

Rather, it is certain that she did so lest envy, already beginning to burn because of his beauty, should become more inflamed. Moses, speaking briefly and sparingly about himself, said that he was a beautiful infant (Exod. 2); but in truth his beauty was as great as befitted a foreshadowing of that divine splendor by which his face was later made radiant through converse with God (Exod. 34) [Col. 0574C]. For a beauty deliberately cultivated could not belong to an infant newly born.

Next, observe that where Holy Scripture rightly wished the midwives who feared God to be named because they preferred useful charity to useless truth—for it immediately said, “one of whom was called Sephora,” interpreted “beauty” or “pleasing,” “the other Phua,” that is, “perfection”—there it did not express the father’s and mother’s names, being content to say: “After these things a man went out from the house of Levi, taking a wife of his own stock.” Elsewhere, however, without setting aside this humility but observing the law of history, it gives both the name of his father, Amram, interpreted “exalted people,” and the name of his mother, Jochebed, interpreted “Where is my glory?” or “She is weighty”: “She bore Aaron, Moses, and Miriam to him” (Exod. 6) [Col. 0574D].

Aaron means “mountain of strength,” or “strong mountain”—a name certainly suited to the dignity of the priesthood. Moses means “drawn from water,” or “drawing up,” which does not differ from the meaning of the law given through him, for it was drawn from the abundance of divine Wisdom. Miriam means “illuminatrix,” like “star of the sea”; for the prophecy signified through her both enlightens us and is a star for our sea, that is, this age, in which we attend to it “as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawn and the morning star rise in our hearts” (2 Pet. 1) [Col. 0575A].

## CHAPTER IX. What was foreshadowed by the infant’s being placed in a basket, found by Pharaoh’s daughter, and entrusted to his mother to be nursed

“He took,” he says, “a little basket of reeds and smeared it with bitumen and pitch, and placed the infant within it”—that is, in the papyrus. For Scripture subsequently says of Pharaoh’s daughter: “When she saw the basket in the papyrus,” etc. According to the letter, the fugitive affection of the mother and her sorrowful diligence are suggested; yet this was not without faith and hope, by which she entrusted her orphaned child to God his guardian—the child in whom the beauty of His grace shone forth: a great citizen indeed of heaven, but excessively a stranger upon earth [Col. 0575B].

The reed is a kind of watery broom, without a knot; papyrus is a light reed. Lucan says of it:

> When the Nile holds all things,
> 
> Memphis’ boat is woven from thirsty papyrus.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, IV.135.)

Bitumen is a most tenacious safeguard against water entering the bilge. She therefore took such care as she could: though the infant lay gently in a reed basket, and the boat woven from light papyrus floated on the surface without weight, and though bitumen excluded every ingress of water.

Mystically, however, the whole event is a foreshadowing of the Scripture to be administered through him. The beautiful infant is placed in lowly reeds because it was to come about, through his writing, that the beauty of the Spirit should be veiled by the lowliness of the letter. The papyrus itself foreshadows the pen of the same future writer, proceeding with the rush of “the river which makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45), against those vessels of papyrus—that is, the vessels of writers of falsehood—of which the Prophet says: “Woe to the land of the clamor of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends its messengers by sea in vessels of papyrus upon the waters!” (Isa. 18) [Col. 0575C].

For that land, namely the devil or Antichrist to come in an earthly body—who on account of pride is called “the clamor of wings,” that is, the sound of blasphemies—sends nothing but falsehood through his messengers, his pagans and his heretics, into the sea of this age, in his vessels of papyrus, that is, the writers of his own party by whom he stands against God. In opposition to this, God was to send through this beautiful infant the beauty of truth.

“Do you wish,” she says, “that I should go and call you a Hebrew woman who can nurse the infant? She answered her: Go. The girl went and called his mother,” etc. This too foreshadowed the future: Pharaoh’s daughter found the infant, nourished him through such a nurse, and adopted him as her own son. It was indeed to come about that the beauty of the holy Scriptures should please the schools of the Gentiles—for example, Ptolemy Philadelphus. Burning with eagerness for the study of every useful writing, he earnestly requested that the laws of God, written by this man, also be translated into Greek for him. He received from Eleazar, high priest of the Jews, seventy elders; when they translated these laws and he read them again, he rejoiced exceedingly [Col. 0576A].

For what he did here was in some manner like what the sister of the child—Miriam—did when she stood at a distance awaiting the outcome and called his mother, who “nursed the infant and, when he was grown, handed him over to Pharaoh’s daughter.” The mother of this Holy Scripture is the Hebrew language itself. As was said, true philosophy persuaded her to call that language forth for interpretation or translation into Greek. Further, the beautiful infant, looking graciously from heaven upon beauty, was received by an encounter of compassion, so that he should not perish to the mother of whom he had been born, but should find another, exceedingly powerful mother to adopt him. By her authority, “he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians,” as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 7) [Col. 0576B].

## CHAPTER X. That Moses rebuked an Egyptian striking one of his brethren, and knew beforehand that he would be the deliverer of his people

“In those days, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his brethren and saw their affliction, and an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brethren,” etc. “After he had grown up,” that is, for forty years. For Stephen the first martyr, speaking in an address to the Jews, says: “When the time of forty years had been fulfilled for him, it came into his heart to visit his brethren, the children of Israel; and when he saw a certain man suffering injustice, he defended him and took vengeance for the one suffering injustice by striking the Egyptian” (Acts 7) [Col. 0576C]. Immediately afterward, he states on what authority Moses did this: “For he supposed that his brethren understood how God would give them salvation through his hand” (ibid.). In saying this, he plainly signifies that Moses knew beforehand that he would be the deliverer of his people.

“But,” he says, “they did not understand”; that is, they were unwilling to understand. For immediately it follows: “On the following day he appeared to them while they were quarrelling and sought to reconcile them in peace, saying: ‘Men, you are brethren; why do you harm one another?’ But he who was doing the injustice thrust him away, saying: ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you wish to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’” (ibid.). Later he attributes this one man’s denial to all, saying: “This is the Moses whom they denied, saying: ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge?’” (ibid.) And rightly so. If all had professed him, one man could not have been permitted to deny him, especially on behalf of all, since he did not say “over me” but “over us” [Col. 0576D].

Moreover, emphasizing the unjust denial, he presses and repeats the description of him as “ruler and judge”: “This man,” he says, “God sent as ruler and redeemer; this man led them out; this is Moses, who said to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren; you shall hear him as myself.’ This is he who was in the Church in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him” (Deut. 18), etc. Why he brought forward these and similar things before them he makes clear in his final exclamation: “You stiff-necked men, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so also do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?”

That is, they denied Moses, rejected Samuel, drove David from the kingdom, stoned some, sawed others asunder, and killed others by the sword (Heb. 11) [Col. 0577A]. Finally he concludes thus: “And they killed those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers” (Acts 7). Moses, therefore, was denied as a figure of Him by those saying, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?”—just as the Just One was to be denied by those saying, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). Just as this One, denied by His own, went to acquire for Himself a Church from the Gentiles, so Moses, denied by his own, fled and took a foreign wife from the daughters of the priest of Midian [Col. 0577B].

Moreover, Moses’ going out to his brethren to see their affliction, and that denial, are rightly referred to by the Apostle in his catalogue of fathers renowned for faith. Thus he says: “By faith Moses, when he had become great, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the passing pleasure of sin; accounting the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians. For he looked to the reward. By faith he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king” (Heb. 11).

Whence did he not fear the wrath of the king? Clearly, because, though fleeing from the king’s wrath, he did not lay aside the armor of zeal. With the same justice and piety by which he had struck the Egyptian for striking one of his Hebrew brethren, he defended the seven daughters of the priest of Midian from the shepherds and watered their sheep. And when on the following day he saw Hebrews quarrelling, he rebuked the one doing wrong. Thus, in this manner and order, he deserved to see “the Invisible One, as though seeing Him, he endured” (ibid.) [Col. 0577C].

## CHAPTER XI. On the cry of the children of Israel to the Lord, and why they cried out not while Pharaoh lived but after Pharaoh died

[Col. 0577D] “After a long time, the king of Egypt died; and the children of Israel groaning because of their works cried out to the Lord. Their cry because of their works ascended, and He heard their groaning,” etc.

Why, while Pharaoh lived, did the children of Israel not groan or cry out to the Lord? Clearly because the excess of oppression did not permit them to groan or cry aloud. Such is the violent force of tyrants: for those whom they oppress, even to desire liberation is counted a crime of audacity or defiance. They had indeed previously groaned while the Egyptians mocked them and made their life bitter; but it makes a difference whether one groans secretly and consumes sorrow within one’s breast in silent groaning, or publicly, in an assembly and in anyone’s hearing, sends a loud complaint upward [Col. 0578A].

Thus, speaking sympathetically to one conquered beneath the conqueror’s power, it was said:

> O wretched ones, whose groans gave voice to grief!
> 
> You did not mourn for you together in a full theatre.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, VII.43.)

Thus the children of Israel had groaned before, but did not dare to groan openly.
