Now, however, because Pharaoh king of Egypt had died, they groaned in public assemblies and raised their groaning to heaven, so that their cry might ascend to the Lord. He heard their groaning and remembered—that is, showed that He had not forgotten—the covenant which He had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

According to the anagogical sense, moreover, the moral lesson is what Scripture intends in the present passage. As long as Pharaoh lives—that is, as long as sin reigns in the mortal body—the soul does not groan nor cry aloud to the Lord. Rather, willingly feeling the labor of its most wretched slavery and its opposing burdens, it is subjected to the hard works of mud and brick and to every service by which it is oppressed in earthly works [Col. 0578B]. It does groan somehow and sigh, and sometimes even weep. But there is a difference between groaning and weeping while washing mud, and, after casting away the works of mud, taking up a better purpose and crying strongly to heaven for God’s help.

If the wicked king of Egypt dies, if, according to the Prophet, “the yoke decays because of the oil” (Isa. 10), and the love of sin ceases through the true confession of the Holy Spirit, then Israel will groan and freely cry out; its cry will ascend to the Lord, and the Deliverer will hear its groaning.

## CHAPTER XII. Why God appeared to Moses in a flame of fire rather than in another elemental form, and what is signified by the burning bush that was not consumed

(Chap. 3.) “Now Moses was feeding the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, the priest of Midian. And when he had driven the flock into the inner desert, he came to the mountain of God. And the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush,” etc.

The order of the words is this: the children of Israel, groaning because of their works, cried out to the Lord. The Lord, hearing their groaning, appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush, where he fed the sheep of Jethro, his father-in-law, priest of Midian. “Moses therefore said: I will go and see this great vision, why the bush is not consumed” [Col. 0578D].

“I will see,” he says, “a great vision.” Truly that vision was great, and it is proclaimed to this day throughout the whole world in the voices of all who see by faith. If, with God’s illumination, the cause of this vision is understood, it explains the work that follows; and it itself “gives understanding to little ones” (Ps. 118). We first ask, therefore, why at that time, for such a purpose, God appearing to a man wished to be seen in a flame of fire rather than in any other elemental form. Then, why was the bush not consumed while burning?

The invisible God, who is neither circumscribed by place nor apprehended by any bodily senses, whenever He visibly appears to men assumes a form suited to the matters for which He deigns to appear. And who does not know that the subsequent effects of this great vision were most strong and clear? Though we were not present then, the great brightness of God’s power or strength, which He made known at that time, shines upon us, and the memory of His terrible miracles is marvelous in our eyes. Hence today too, in wonder, we say: “Who is like You among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like You—magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders?” (Exod. 15). Again: “Your right hand, O Lord, has been magnified in strength” (ibid.), and similar words [Col. 0579A].

Rightly, therefore, God appeared here in fire, a strong and bright element, in some manner preparing His strength when He says: “I know that Pharaoh king of Egypt will not let you go unless by a mighty hand” (Exod. 3). Again, to Pharaoh: “For this reason I have set you up: that I may show My strength in you, and that My name may be proclaimed in all the earth” (Exod. 9).

But why is the bush not consumed, while Moses is forbidden to approach as though he would be consumed unless he removes the sandals from his feet? “For when the Lord saw that he was going to see, He called to him from the midst of the bush and said: ‘Moses, Moses.’ And when he answered, ‘Here I am,’ He said: ‘Do not come near here.’” And immediately: “Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place in which you stand is holy ground.” This was certainly said as though he could immediately have been burned by approaching unless he removed the sandals from his feet. Yet the bush was not burned, and the holy fire shining from the midst of its shrubs did them no harm [Col. 0579B].

What, then, does this mean? It means that “our God is indeed a consuming fire” (Deut. 4), yet this fire is very unlike elemental fire. Bodily fire, which we use in bodily operations and call the fourth element of the world, burns the things that contain it and does no harm to things far away. But our God, the true and eternal fire, manifests His nature and power in the contrary way. To those in whom He dwells He is not merely harmless, but even saving and most merciful; but to those far away, unwilling to approach worthily, He is exceedingly harmful. Of such people the Psalmist says: “As wax melts before the fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67) [Col. 0579C].

This is clearer and more manifest in the blessed Virgin Mary. This entire fire—that is, Christ, God and man—dwelt in her womb for nine months. He not only did not burn the light straw or hay of her flesh or soul, but perpetually illumined it with the greater honor of virginity and with the grace of the man whom He there formed and assumed. And the nearer anyone approaches in faith to that temple of eternal fire, the more worthily that person shines with that fire. Conversely, the farther away Jew, pagan, or heretic stands, the sooner that person melts like wax when that fire appears.

Meanwhile, we who approach must see to it that we do not have sandals upon our feet, which are made from the skins of dead animals. That is, we must not imitate the deadly examples of those dead and dying in their sins. He was indeed commanded physically to approach barefoot, which is the customary instrument of humility. But we must do this spiritually in the way already stated, knowing that our God, whom we approach, “is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 12) [Col. 0580A].

## CHAPTER XIII. On Moses’ humility, by which he repeatedly declined when commanded to go to Pharaoh

“The cry of the children of Israel has come to Me from every side, and I have seen their affliction, by which they are oppressed by the Egyptians. But come: I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring My people out of Egypt.”

Observe that after saying, “The cry of the children of Israel has come to Me,” He added “from every side,” so that you may understand it both from the Egyptians who oppressed them and from the children of Israel who groaned. For a cry came from both sides, but in very different ways. The cry of the children of Israel ascended to the Lord as though provoking a defender and judge to anger.

“Come,” He says, “I will send you.” He said first “Come,” then “I will send you.” It is no slight matter that God said “Come” to one bodily present and standing before Him. It is no slight matter, I say, nor was it subsequently done lightly: the man bodily present before God was to be present also in mind, ready to obey. It is clear from what follows that he had not yet come to the place to which he was so often commanded to go [Col. 0580B]. At the first command, “Come,” he immediately answered: “Who am I, that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?”

It is indeed a good and worthy example of humility, when God calls one to so great and glorious a ministry, to say, “Who am I?”—that is, according to one’s own consciousness or estimation, “no one.” Therefore the Lord God received this question of his, as if it leaped suddenly from a precipice, with a calm countenance: “I,” He says, “will be with you, and this shall be the sign that I have sent you.” As though He said: Although you are no one, I am the Lord, who am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. “I,” He says, “will be with you,” speaking words in your mouth and working signs through your hand. By this, I say, it will be shown to all that I have sent you, without whom man can do nothing.

Therefore, “when you have brought My people out of Egypt,” you, not ungrateful for the present vision but mindful of the thanks to be given, “will sacrifice to God upon this mountain” [Col. 0580C]. This is, I say, a good and imitable example of gentle humility. Yet neither should we despise the fact that a man of the same order—that is, the prophetic order—also seeing a great vision, namely God seated upon a high and exalted throne, with what was beneath Him filling the temple, immediately and eagerly offered himself when that Lord asked, “Whom shall I send?” He said: “Behold, here I am; send me” (Isa. 6).

Therefore when anyone is called by the Holy Spirit to be sent against Pharaoh—that is, against the devil—to perform some ministry for the salvation of souls, that person should keep the royal road between these two, neither turning to the right nor to the left. He should neither be excessive in saying, “Who am I, that I should go?” nor importunate in crying, “Here I am; send me.” For on the one side the vice of obstinacy, and on the other that of presumption, must be avoided.

Meanwhile, “Moses had hidden his face,” that is, he stood with bowed head; but, hidden in this way and cast down, he deserved all the more to be lifted up by the Lord. For as confidence in grace gradually increased, he said to the Lord:

## CHAPTER XIV. On His saying: “I am who I am. He who is has sent,” etc.

“Behold, I shall go to the children of Israel and say to them: ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you.’ If they say to me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” [Col. 0581B] Since the deluded error of paganism had made the name of God common to many, he therefore sought the distinctive name of this God who was speaking with him. “For, although,” says the Apostle, “there are those called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father” (1 Cor. 8).

“God said to Moses: ‘I am who I am.’ And he said: ‘Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you. This is my name for ever, and this is my memorial from generation to generation.’” To one inquiry he gave two answers, because mighty was the questioner who knocked—mighty, I say, with that true might which is the strength of humility. Through the practice or exercise of divine conversation this grew into such strength that later he could restrain the mighty and angry God, standing before him in the breaking of the heart. He declared, I say, two names of himself: one, namely “I am who I am,” belongs to nature; the other to grace or condescension (Exod. 32), namely, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—this,” he says, “is my name for ever.”

And because this latter name belongs to grace, he had already voluntarily uttered it above, without being asked, saying: “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground. I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” But here he added what he had not said there: “This is my name for ever”—namely, because of their faith, worthy to be named, or because of their obedience, in which they confessed themselves strangers and pilgrims upon the earth, awaiting a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb. 11). “For this reason,” says the Apostle, “God is not ashamed to be called their God” (ibid.). Therefore, he says, “this is my name for ever, and this is my memorial”—that is, according to the things which I have done or shall do in those worshippers of mine and in their seed.

Having taken these two statements—“I am who I am”; “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you”—he says again: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.” It follows, then, that those whom Abraham did not know, Isaac ignored, and Jacob did not acknowledge are not gods. And this was a fitting answer here, for the time and circumstance: the children of Israel were to cease, as though because of a multitude of gods, from seeking a distinctive title for their God; they were to be content with knowing only this, that he who sends Moses to them is—not falsely called God, as the rest are, but truly is. [Col. 0582A]

Moreover, the Creator excludes himself not only from the multitude of those who are not, but also from every multitude of creatures, when he says, “I am.” For what? Is anything created to be called, simply and absolutely, “being”? Certainly not, because none of these things is simple or uncompounded. Everything apart from God is said, as is evident, to consist of matter together with form. For example, a statue has bronze as its matter, while its form is whatever likeness the craftsman has shaped—say, that of Jupiter or Serapis. Accordingly, what we call a statue is not what it is: it is neither one and the same thing nor simple.

Nor indeed is bronze itself something simple, since its matter is earth, from which it differs greatly in its appearance as bronze. The name “earth,” too, is derived from form: it is called earth because it is heavy and dry, and it has received its slight being, although its matter is known to have been created without form. But God’s substance is simple form, without any matter at all; accordingly, he is what he is. Nothing can be present in him besides that which he is substantially. He cannot be a subject, nor can he receive from any accident any motion or change; for, being form devoid of matter, from what source could he suffer accidents?

Finally, the reason why formed things—human beings, beasts, and all the rest—change in successive turns is that their matter bears this in them. Hence “a man comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same state” (Job 14). Hence it is that “like grass he passes away in the morning; in the morning he flourishes, in the evening he falls, hardens, and withers” (Ps. 89 [90]). Therefore God, who is not formed but is form alone, rightly declares his own distinctive name, excluding himself alone both from gods which are indeed called gods but are not, and from all creatures, whose formations or natures are most diverse: “I am who I am. And thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you.”

Concerning the land which he promises when he says, “I have surely visited you, that I may bring you up from the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanite, [Col. 0582D] and the Hittite, and the Amorite,” and so forth: it has already been said elsewhere that this land bore the figure of the land of the living, which truly flows with streams of milk and honey. For just as the Lord brought that people, delivered from Pharaoh’s slavery, into that land, so he restores the whole multitude of the elect, released from the yoke of the devil, to their heavenly homeland, expelling from it the malignant spirits understood beneath these peoples. For Canaanite means “possessing”; Amorite, “bitter”; Girgashite, “driving out the inhabitant”; Jebusite, “trodden down”; Hittite, “fearing”; Perizzite, “separating”; Hivite, “wild.” All these may rightly be understood in an evil sense and usefully assigned to malignant spirits.

## CHAPTER XV. On the statement, “The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us”; on why it was rightly said, “You shall despoil Egypt”; and on how we despoil it after their example.

“And you and the elders of Israel shall go in to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: ‘The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us. We shall go by the way of the wilderness for three days, that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God,’” and so forth.

This happened in precisely this way. For, after crossing the Red Sea, when Moses and the children of Israel had sung this song to the Lord, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted; horse and rider he has cast into the sea,” they entered, it says, the wilderness of Shur; and they journeyed for three days through the wilderness and found no water, and came to Marah (Exod. 15). [Col. 0583B] Behold what sort of journey the Lord their God commands the Hebrews to profess before Pharaoh when they are departing from Egypt and going to the land of promise. For this purpose he stretches forth his mighty hand: “I shall stretch forth,” he says, “my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders, which I shall perform in their midst”—for this purpose, I say, “that they may go, not by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is near” (Exod. 13), but through the wilderness, solely that they may sacrifice to the Lord their God.

Therefore whoever professes himself to be a Hebrew—that is, a passer-over—and to have departed from Egypt, in order, according to the name of the Hebrews, whose Lord and God he is, to pass over to the heavenly homeland, having “no abiding city here but seeking the one to come” (Heb. 13), should hold to this manner of life and walk in solitude: that is, he should remain removed both from Egyptians and from Philistines. Egyptians are interpreted “dark”; Philistines, “falling through drink.” The fellowship of such people must certainly be avoided by one who desires to attain God’s inheritance and to offer sacrifices of righteousness to the Lord his God.

“And I shall give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. And when you go out, you shall not go out empty; but a woman shall ask of her neighbor and of the woman lodging in her house vessels of silver and gold, and garments; and you shall put them upon your sons and daughters, and you shall despoil Egypt.” This is not an unjust command. The Egyptians had violently subjected Israel, who was neither native-born nor purchased, mocking him and afflicting him with works of clay and brick. It was therefore just that they should despoil their oppressors in return—not as plunderers of masters, [Col. 0583D] but as true victors over enemies—so that, exceedingly stirred by grief over their gold and silver, they would pursue those who were departing and thus perish in the sea while Israel passed through to salvation.

But we, according to the anagogical sense, departing as has been said, ought to despoil Egypt of all gold and silver and every precious garment. Whether these be the golden circles of dialecticians, the silver ornaments of rhetoricians, or the fabrics and garments of whatever philosophical arts, by which the Egyptian, using them wrongly, adorns and clothes falsehood: none of these things should remain without passing with Hebrews of this kind into the service of the true God, for the adornment of truth and the service of our lady, heavenly Wisdom.

Moses himself, at the time these words were spoken, was the first to despoil Egypt in this fashion. For, as has already been said above, he was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians; yet he brought those same spoils, as this Scripture testifies, into the treasury of the Lord his God. “You shall put these,” he says, “upon your sons and daughters”: that is, you shall teach them to take up spoils of Egypt of such a kind, so that they may know how to test all things, hold fast what is good, and abstain from every form of evil (1 Thess. 5). [Col. 0584A]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the signs shown to Moses as testimony.

**(Chapter 4.)** “Moses answered and said: ‘They will not believe me or listen to my voice, but will say: “The Lord has not appeared to you.”’ The Lord therefore said to him: ‘What is that which you hold in your hand?’ He answered: ‘A rod.’ The Lord said: ‘Throw it upon the ground.’ He threw it down, and it was changed into a serpent, so that Moses fled.”

God’s expectation was just; for this objection of the man is truthful and sound. “They will not believe me,” he says—that is, unless they see signs. For even to this day “the Jews seek signs and the Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. 1). Therefore the Lord patiently bears this objection and says: “Throw down the rod which you hold upon the ground.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent. And the Lord said: “Stretch forth your hand and grasp its tail.” He stretched it out and took hold of it, and it became a rod again. And again: “Put your hand into your bosom,” and so forth.

Since reason agrees that “every word may stand in the mouth of two—or at most three—witnesses” (Deut. 19), he arranged these two signs as witnesses on the right and left. “That they may believe,” he says, “that the Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.” Again: “If they do not believe you or heed the message of the first sign, they will believe the word of the following sign.” [Col. 0584C] He adds a third witness, as though following behind, condemning those who have not believed the two testimonies to the bloody punishment of death: “Take water from the river,” he says, “and pour it upon dry ground, and whatever you draw from the river shall become blood.”

We all acknowledge the literal truth, or firm witness, of these signs; let us seek their mystical authority. For just as the people serving in Egypt undoubtedly signified the whole multitude of the elect who are pilgrims in this world, so these signs, by which it ought or could have recognized the time of its visitation, had to signify other and better signs, by which it ought or could have known the time of its redemption—which took place through Christ.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the mystical causes of the same signs.

What then does this rod signify, if not the humanity of Christ, the Son of God, taken from the root of Jesse? For it was truly cast upon the earth and changed into a serpent, so that Moses fled, when the only-begotten Son of God deigned, by assuming humanity, to come into this world and undergo death—so that carnal Israel flees from believing in him.

After this had taken place, he says, “Stretch forth your hand and grasp its tail,” so that it may again become a rod. For after all things had been completed, he who had died returned to life. And Christ’s death was fittingly prefigured by a serpent, because death came to the human race through the serpent’s cunning, and Christ truly received that death in his body. Moses therefore grasped the serpent’s tail, and the serpent returned to a rod, because the faith of the elect followed Christ’s passion or death: “for, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). [Col. 0585A]

But after this sign the greater part of the Jewish nation recoiled and refused belief. To what, then, shall it be compared? “Put your hand,” he says, “into your bosom.” When he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out leprous, white as snow. Surely the hand drawn out leprous from the bosom is the Synagogue cast away from God’s grace. From the time that it pierced the side of its Savior with a lance, that hand was withdrawn from his bosom, soaked in the burning leprosy of its sins. Foreseeing this long beforehand, the Prophet mournfully says: “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom unto the end?” (Ps. 73 [74]).

Behold, we see that people separated from the camp of God and, unquestionably at the judgment of the high priest, condemned for leprosy: its garments torn, its head uncovered, its mouth covered with a garment, crying out—that is, unable to deny—that it is unclean and defiled (Lev. 13). Its leprosy is exposed; its face, however, is covered by the veil of unbelief.

Whoever, with these two signs bearing witness, does not believe that he who was to be sent has already come, and that he is Jesus Christ, who alone was able to free us from spiritual Pharaoh, namely the devil—there remains for him the fulfillment of the third sign against him: namely, “whatever he draws from the river shall become blood.” That is, whatever he attempts to touch from the streams of the Scriptures, he must necessarily understand wrongly, to his own condemnation. At last the same hand, drawn back into the bosom of grace and brought forth, will again be like the rest of the flesh. “For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11). [Col. 0585C]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the words, “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send,” and so forth.

“Moses said: ‘I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent. From yesterday and the day before yesterday, since you began speaking to your servant, I am slow and halting of tongue.’”

It is clear from this that all these things were not said or done in a single day, namely from his saying, “From yesterday and the day before yesterday,” and so forth. For *nudiustertius* means the same as if you were to say: “It is now the third day since,” he says, “you began speaking to your servant.” It is as though he said: Before you spoke to your servant, I appeared to myself eloquent, quick-tongued, and fluent; but now, since you began to speak and reveal to me the hidden things of your wisdom, I have learned and felt this about myself: that I am not eloquent, nor of speech sufficiently fluent worthily to declare before people the things which I now understand must be done.

For Moses, beginning to be a prophet and illumined inwardly by that flame which he had seen outwardly, perceived that mysteries so great were being entrusted to him that he could rightly and praiseworthily judge himself unworthy and unequal to administer them. Thus the Lord, accepting his objection also as reasonable, said to him: “Who made the mouth of man? Or who fashioned the mute, the deaf, the hearing, the seeing, and the blind?” [Col. 0586A] Undoubtedly it must be understood that he who made all these things can quickly sharpen a tongue which was shortly before dull. “Go, therefore,” he says, “and I shall be in your mouth and teach you what you are to say.” But he said: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you will send.”

At last Moses disclosed to us what he wished and toward what end all his repeated excuses tended. “Send,” he says, “Lord, whom you will send.” For whom was the Lord going to send when he said these things, except him who has now been sent—the one whom the patriarch Jacob had announced as the expectation of the nations, the desire of the everlasting hills? (Gen. 49). Therefore Moses did not refuse to perform the saving command out of distrust; but, knowing that his ministry would bring nothing to perfection (Heb. 7), he dared to press the Lord to send him who was to be sent and was to accomplish perfect salvation.

“The Lord, angry with Moses, said: ‘Aaron your brother, the Levite—I know that he is eloquent.’” “The Lord,” he says, “was angry with Moses.” He seemed greatly angered, because he sorely afflicted the tender desire of piety by not answering the request. In anger, he says, deferring his Christ, who was owed to the human race, he was silent about him and said these things and other things in place of others. He commanded these twins to go: Moses as the law, Aaron as the priesthood. But both were human, and neither was both God and man; consequently, nothing could be brought to perfection through their ministry. [Col. 0586B]

For what great thing was it to lead a people from place to place, from Egypt into the land of Canaan; to write the killing letter and not confer life-giving grace (2 Cor. 6 [3]); to offer for the people the blood of goats or calves and not save the people from their sins? (Heb. 9). Surely the one thing necessary for it was to be led or pass over from sin to righteousness, from death to life, from darkness to light, from the enemy to the Lord, from the devil to God. This was to be accomplished by the only one capable of accomplishing it, and has now been accomplished: the only-begotten Son of God, God and man, Jesus Christ.

“Therefore he was angry with Moses,” he says: that is, he was not so favorable to Moses as not to delay fulfilling the desire of the one entreating him, so as at least to say to the words, “Send whom you will send,” “I shall send him after so many years,” or “at that time.” He judged Moses unworthy to know the times or seasons which he had placed in his own power (Acts 1). [Col. 0586D]

## CHAPTER XIX. On Moses’ request for leave from his kinsman, and his keeping secret what he had heard.

“Moses went away and returned to Jethro his kinsman,” and so forth.

He calls him his kinsman here because of his daughter, whom Moses had taken as wife—that is, he means his father-in-law. He did not say, “I shall go to lead my brothers out of Egypt according to the command of my God, who appeared to me because he saw their affliction and heard their cry”; rather, he kept this secret. “I shall go,” he said, “to my brothers in Egypt, to see whether they are still alive.” For he sought not his own glory but God’s glory, which God himself would reveal at a most fitting time, without any prior announcement from Moses.

Jethro is interpreted “his superfluity.” Therefore, whoever is such a person, whoever imitates him, should regard it as superfluous to disclose before people the grace bestowed upon him, so as to be seen by them. He should instead await the fitting time, until God’s secret becomes manifest of itself and his light shines fittingly before people, so that they may see and glorify God the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 9). “And Jethro said to him: ‘Go in peace.’”

## CHAPTER XX. On the Lord’s wish to kill Moses; on Zipporah’s touching his feet after circumcising her sons; and on their mystical meaning.

“Then the Lord said to Moses in Midian: ‘Go, return to Egypt, for those who sought your life are dead.’”

For that Pharaoh was dead who had heard that Moses killed the Egyptian and sought to kill Moses; and this one, after a long time—as said above, that is, after another forty years, as Stephen the proto-martyr testifies in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 7)—was also dead. “Moses took his wife and his sons,” and so forth.

Before proceeding, we must explain what occurred concerning this wife and Moses’ sons. “When he was,” it says, “at a lodging-place on the way, the Lord met him and wished to kill him. Zipporah immediately took a very sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son,” and so forth. “He wished,” it says, “to kill him.” Why? Because he had not circumcised his sons. Yet he had been unable to do this because his foreign wife opposed it, in a foreign land, a land not his own. Therefore, when Zipporah saw that the Lord wished to kill him, she recognized through the presence of danger what reason had not persuaded her of: that it was salutary for every male of Abraham’s seed to be circumcised. [Col. 0587C]

Without hesitation as to which she should prefer—the death of her husband or the circumcision of her sons—she “immediately took a very sharp stone and circumcised the foreskin of her son. And she touched his feet, saying: ‘You are a bridegroom of blood to me.’” Why did she touch his feet? Namely, that he might let her go. For it immediately follows: “And he let him go, after she had said: ‘You are a bridegroom of blood to me because of the circumcision.’” For this reason she “touched his feet,” that is, she urgently entreated that she should not be compelled to follow him farther, terrified or unprepared for visions so great, since, living as a Gentile, she was not yet worthy to take part in them.

Touching his feet, therefore, she said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me.” She did not say “a man of blood,” nor “of marriage,” but “bridegroom,” lest she should be thought to have said this with cruelty in view. For “man of blood,” in ordinary usage, signifies the grim work of cruelty and homicide. It was therefore better, though improper, to say “bridegroom of blood,” although a bridegroom is not usually called such except during the celebration of the wedding. Afterwards she returned to him, Scripture saying: “When Jethro, priest of Midian, the kinsman of Moses, heard all that the Lord had done for Moses and for Israel his people, and that the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt, he took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, whom he had sent away, and her two sons” (Exod. 18), and so forth. [Col. 0588A]

This too is not devoid of mystery. Moses’ foreign wife Zipporah, whose name means “beauty” or “pleasing,” signifies, as said above, the Church of the Gentiles, which was foreign. But she did not take part in the victory which her husband, Christ, completed by dying over the prince of darkness, the devil. That man fought alone; he triumphed alone. After he had rescued the people of the saints of old from the darkness of hell through his blood, then she too approached; then she was brought in evangelical horses and chariots and received in baptism the sacrament of victory.

Moreover, every day Mother Church circumcises her sons with spiritual circumcision, lest Christ’s faith die in them. She touches his feet and says to her sons during their circumcision: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2), and similar things.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Lord’s words: “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart.”

“And the Lord said to him as he returned to Egypt: ‘See that you perform before Pharaoh all the signs which I have put in your hand. I shall harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.’”

For a man such as the Apostle does not know—or rather, in whom Christ, speaking in the Apostle, says, “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’” (Rom. 9), and so forth—for the person, I say, wise according to the flesh, this passage has created a difficulty and aroused suspicion. For after God said, “See that you perform before Pharaoh all the signs which I have put in your hand,” he immediately added, “I shall harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.” For he says: “Why then does he still find fault? For who resists his will?” (ibid.).

But a person is offended in this way because he does not attend to the divine light of that same flame which appeared there to Moses, so as to know what he lacks. [Col. 0588D] For what he lacks is that he should inquire, before voicing the complaint just mentioned, how Pharaoh was hardened when God says, “I shall harden”—that is, what action of God hardened Pharaoh.

For what? “Is there injustice with God?” (ibid.). Is God, seeking his own glory, to be thought to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart, though it was previously gentle, so that he himself might be glorified by performing wonders on the occasion of Pharaoh’s hardness? Far be it! A person must not understand God’s words, “I shall harden,” in this sense.

Rather, Pharaoh hated the children of Israel, and so did all the Egyptians, as was said above. That hatred itself arose from envy, as they said: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel is many and stronger than we” (Exod. 1), and so forth. Nor did he otherwise, according to the Psalmist, “turn their heart so that they hated his people” (Ps. 104 [105]), except that, while he blessed and multiplied his people, their envious heart increased—or rather, was turned into bitter hatred. It is a property of envy or hatred that the greater the benefits bestowed upon those envied, the more that envy or hatred is strengthened. For the more brightly the one envied shines, the more the envious person is hardened and inflamed. The books are full of examples of this kind; nevertheless, let us produce even one example.

God is challenged by the prophet, who says: “Why, O Lord, have you made us stray from your ways, and hardened our heart so that we do not fear you?” (Isa. 63). First he answers that prophet in this way: “Those who did not formerly ask sought me; those who did not seek me found me” (Isa. 65). Then the Son of God also says to the Father: “Behold me, behold me, to a nation that did not call upon my name” (ibid.). [Col. 0589B]

Surely this is the same as saying: In this way I caused you, O Jews, to stray from my ways, and in this way I hardened your heart so that you would not fear me: namely, because I willed to be found by Gentile nations who did not seek me, whose salvation you hate. For because of your hatred of them you have been hardened, and, unable to endure having them as companions on the way, you have turned aside. Thus, although intending something else, I caused you to stray from my ways and hardened your heart.

Therefore, when God says, “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart,” it must be understood that he does so not by corrupting Pharaoh, but by visiting in compassionate love the children of Israel, whom Pharaoh unjustly hates. For I do this indeed with the intention of love, but it will result in the envious man’s hardening of heart and increase of hatred. Thus, by one and the same pleasant light of the sun, hard ice melts and soft mud hardens. Hence in what follows it is often said: “And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the people go.” But sometimes it is also said that Pharaoh himself “hardened his heart.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the statement: “Israel is my firstborn son.”

“And you shall say to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Let my people go, that he may serve me; and you refused to let him go. Behold, I shall kill your firstborn son.’”

When, he says, you have performed before Pharaoh all the signs which I put in your hand and he, with hardened heart, has not let the people go, then at last you shall say to him: “Israel is my firstborn son,” and so forth. Even if that Israel were God’s only people, it could nevertheless be called “firstborn”; but conversely, not every firstborn is only-begotten. We must understand the phrase, “Israel is my firstborn son,” to be said in relation to a younger son, namely the people of the Gentiles.

And rightly indeed, in regard to the elect among that people, we grant it every privilege of the firstborn. As the Apostle says: “To them were entrusted the oracles of God; theirs is the adoption as sons, the glory, the covenant, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9). [Col. 0590A] But when this firstborn envies his younger brother and, blinded by hatred for him, stumbles at the stone of stumbling and rock of offense (1 Pet. 2), and refuses to enter his father’s house because his brother has come and the rejoicing father has killed the fatted calf for him (Luke 15)—when, I say, the firstborn behaves thus, we acknowledge him to be such a firstborn as Cain was, as Ishmael was, as Esau was.

It should be noted that, apart from Shem, Noah’s firstborn, almost all the firstborn sons of the patriarchs were either ruined by their own wickedness or set behind their younger brothers by divine authority. Concerning the statement, “When Moses was at a lodging-place on the way, God met him and wished to kill him,” enough has already been said above.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Moses and Aaron speaking against Pharaoh as signifying the law and the old priesthood; and on the meaning of “Pharaoh became more cruel.”

“And the Lord said to Aaron: ‘Go to meet Moses in the wilderness.’ He went to meet him at the mountain of God and kissed him. Moses told Aaron all the words of the Lord for which he had sent him, and the signs which he had commanded. And they came together and assembled all the elders of the children of Israel,” and so forth.

**(Chapter 5.)** The historical surface of this whole chapter is plain: Pharaoh answered proudly, “Who is the Lord, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I shall not let Israel go.” Not only did he fail to let Israel go; he even increased their affliction. “You shall by no means any longer,” he says, “give the people straw for making bricks, as before; let them go and gather stubble themselves. And you shall impose upon them the same number of bricks which they previously made, and you shall not lessen anything.” When they cried out to Pharaoh and said, “Why do you treat your servants in this way?” he replied, “You are idle, and therefore you say: ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord.’” These things, I say, are plain according to the letter.

But beneath the letter shines here the brilliant sense of allegory. Pharaoh, whose name means “scattering,” is the devil, and his kingdom is death. “Death,” says the Apostle, “reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5). [Col. 0590D] “Until Moses,” he says, “death reigned”: that is, sin, through which death entered this world, had before the law no opposing voice from the precepts of righteousness, while all were dead in soul and dying in body.

Moses and Aaron, acting against Pharaoh, signify the law and the priesthood of the law, through which righteousness began to have a voice against the devil for the destruction of sin and death. But when the commandment of the law came, reigning sin and death roared. “What then shall we say?” the same Apostle says. “Is the law sin? Far be it! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetousness. For without the law sin was dead” (Rom. 7).

Because these things are better understood from individual persons, he immediately continues: “But I was once alive without the law. Yet when the commandment came, sin revived” (ibid.), and so forth. For when does a person live without the law? Surely when he still sins without fear, when he has not yet formed any resolve to resist sin—for example, an ungoverned young man or girl. But when does the commandment come? Certainly when, from fear of future punishment, one resolves to leave an old habit and, because of the commandment, to hold to righteousness. There is then a struggle: “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; and these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish” (Gal. 5). [Col. 0591B]

Such a person later says, in the same Apostle: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7).

When does this grace of God deliver? Surely when the militant mind, still remaining in the body after the temptations of the flesh, is soothed by the Spirit’s consolation, and, after the blows of the goading Satan, is granted the golden torque of liberty. As it is with one person, so the whole world advances through three states. Before the law entered, death indeed reigned, and that strong man armed guarded his court, and all that he possessed was in peace (Luke 11). Yet sin was not so imputed as to be called transgression: “where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4). Therefore that tyrant advanced more slowly against his subjects.

But when the law entered and came to investigate that strong man’s fortifications, he perceived this; snarling, he raged, and at last struck down the necks of captives sighing for freedom, until one stronger came, overcame him, and plundered his goods (Luke 11). Then those whom he freed sang: “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). [Col. 0591D]

Therefore, “from the day,” says Moses, “when I went in to Pharaoh to speak in your name, O Lord, he has afflicted your people.” They groan and say, “You have made our smell foul before Pharaoh and his servants, and have given him a sword to kill us.” For, as the Apostle says, “when the commandment came, sin revived, but I died; and the commandment which was for life was found to be for death to me. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me” (Rom. 7).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the statement: “And I did not make my name Adonai known to them.”

(CAP. VI.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; and I did not make known to them my name Adonai. And I made a covenant with them,’” etc. Of the ten names by which he is called among the Hebrews, the seventh is *Adonai*, which we generally render “Lord.” “And I did not make known to them my name Adonai,” he says; that is, it is understood: *which I make known to you.* But how does he assert that he did not reveal this name to those to whom he appeared as God Almighty? First, he says to Abraham: “I am the Lord Almighty; walk before me and be perfect” (Gen. XVII). Behold, here [Col. 0592B] he openly called himself both Lord and God Almighty—which is *Adonai*. Therefore, when he says here, “I did not make known,” it must be understood as referring to how great his power or might was.

For, being about to perform great and terrible deeds, he says these things in order to display the glory of his name—deeds such as he did not perform in the days of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom nevertheless he appeared as God Almighty, and who did not seek to test by miracles the very fact that he was almighty, being content with reason. Hence their faith is judged more glorious and of greater merit. Conversely, Pharaoh’s hardness, which was the reason that the signs were performed, was more detestable; and the more things were done, the more justly did the despiser incur eternal destruction.

Thus, I say, when he says, “And I did not make known to them my name Adonai,” it is to be understood [Col. 0592C] that now, since the occasion requires it, “I shall make known to you how glorious and how terrible it is.” For shortly before he said, “Now you shall see what I shall do to Pharaoh,” and afterward he was to say to Pharaoh himself: “For this very reason I have set you up, that I may show my power in you” (Exod. IX).

Certainly, it should be known that wherever the tetragrammaton, the name of the Lord which is called ineffable, is written, the Hebrew says *Adonai* and the Latin says “Lord”; as, for example: “Give thanks to the Lord, and call upon his name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice; seek the Lord and be strengthened” (Ps. CIV).

“And I made a covenant with them,” he says, “that I might give them the land of Canaan, the land of their sojourning, in which they lived as strangers.” [Col. 0592D] The order of the words is: “I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, and I made a covenant with them that I might give them the land of Canaan.” Moreover, it should be known that giving them the land of Canaan is not the whole covenant, nor the reason for the covenant; rather, he has put a part of the covenant for the whole. For the substance of the covenant is in this saying: “And in you shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed” (Gen. XII), in which the incarnation of Christ, the Son of God, is plainly promised.

Having made this declaration—“And I made a covenant with them, that I might give them the land of Canaan”—he now acknowledges that he is rightly bound as debtor of the promise, and says: “I have heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians oppressed, and I have remembered my covenant.” “I have remembered,” he says; that is, “I have shown that I have not forgotten,” it being understood [Col. 0593A] when I sent you, my servant, and Aaron, and placed in you the words of my signs. And immediately he concluded thus: “Therefore say to the children of Israel: I am the Lord who will bring you out from the prison-house of the Egyptians,” etc.

By saying, “over which I lifted up my hand, that I might give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,” he made plain why he had said, “And I did not make known to them my name Adonai”: namely, because now, in lifting up his hand, he intends it to be made known in an outstretched arm and great judgments.

“Moses therefore told all these things to the children of Israel, who did not heed him because of anguish of spirit and grievous labor.” These things, plainly, had been spoken or commanded by the Lord for their consolation. But they, not having the firm hope of perfect faith, groaned under the affliction of their enemies and therefore did not heed him. Thus indeed, according to the anagogical sense, when the kingdom of sin, aggravated through opposition to the law, as was said above, brought the people of God under its service, as often happened, so that they said, “Let us go and serve foreign gods” (Deut. XIII), the law and the prophets spoke in vain; for they did not hear them. Likewise, sometimes rebuke is made in vain for a time to a person who indeed delights in the law of God according to the inward man, but suffers another law in his members, warring against the law of his mind (Rom. VII); for he is near to despair.

## CHAPTER XXV. How it is proved that what had been said was fulfilled in Moses and Aaron: “But in the fourth generation they shall return here.”

[Col. 0593C] “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Go in and speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt, that he may let the children of Israel go out of his land.’ Moses answered before the Lord: ‘Behold, the children of Israel will not listen to me; and how will Pharaoh listen to me, especially since I am uncircumcised in lips?’”

Having scarcely begun this little account of his excuse, in which he says that he is uncircumcised in lips, he suddenly makes this digression: “These are the heads of the houses according to their families.” Why so? Plainly, in order to establish the truth of God: for God had spoken beforehand to Abraham concerning this servitude and the subsequent liberation of the children of Israel, saying: “Know beforehand that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall reduce them to servitude and [Col. 0593D] afflict them for four hundred years”; and he further fixed the limit by saying: “But in the fourth generation they shall return here” (Gen. XV).

This, then, is what he says: “And these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their kindreds: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. And Amram took Jochebed, his father’s sister, as wife; and she bore him Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.” It is therefore clear that this was the fourth generation. For Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; and Amram begot Moses and Miriam. Thus, by repeating it a second and third time, he points this out when he says: “This is Aaron and Moses; these are they who speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt; this is Moses and Aaron on the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt”—so that you understand: those who are fourth in their generation [Col. 0594A] from Levi.

And it should be noted that first he says, “These are Aaron and Moses,” and then reverses the order: “This is Moses and Aaron.” For Aaron was first by the order of birth, but Moses by calling or the privilege of administration before God. Moreover, so that he might begin above, that is, with Reuben, the digression made on his own account and therefore ending in himself, this was prudently done out of humility, lest among the twelve tribes he should seem to make mention of his own alone—that is, the Levitical tribe.

Nor should this be passed over: Aaron, the first priest of the law, took a wife from that tribe to which the true priesthood in Christ was owed. “For Aaron,” he says, “took as wife Elizabeth, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon”—namely, from the tribe of Judah.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On what was said to Moses: “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh.”

[Col. 0594B] “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘I am the Lord. Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I speak to you.’ And Moses said before the Lord: ‘Behold, I am uncircumcised in lips; how will Pharaoh listen to me?’” (CHAP. VII.) “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you; he shall speak to Pharaoh, that he may let the children of Israel go from his land.’”

After the foregoing digression, he continues what he had begun to say above. For what he had said there, “especially since I am uncircumcised in lips,” he repeats here in order to add [Col. 0594C] what the Lord answered to this. “Behold,” he says, “I have made you a god to Pharaoh.” Humility, the glorious queen of virtues, which is accustomed to fly heavenward, spoke in him when he called himself uncircumcised in lips; and therefore he received a worthy and, in proportion to his reverence, magnificent answer: that a private man should hear that he was a god to a reigning man.

And God, the author of gods, did not say, “Behold, I shall make you,” but “Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh”—understand, from the foundation of the world. For that God of gods establishes or removes nothing by a new plan. It is as though he said: Since you, the gentlest of men, consider yourself unworthy to contend with Pharaoh and to struggle with kings in so glorious a cause, and in this way humble yourself even to the farthest ends [Col. 0594D] of the earth, behold, I shall raise you above the height of the clouds and make you a god: not one whom he will faithfully worship, but one whom he will servilely fear. You shall command the waters by God’s power; you shall create frogs; you shall command the earth and ashes, and make gnats and blisters upon the king and his army; you shall command the air, that it may produce a very grievous pestilence; you shall command fire, that mingled with hail it may be borne upon sinners. Thus, by commanding the elements, you shall be Pharaoh’s god.

And because Pharaoh is not worthy even to speak with such a god, Aaron your brother shall be your prophet, announcing the plagues which you will perform, or bringing them on as a minister. Therefore there are gods in whose assembly, according to the Psalmist, God stood, whom he judges in their midst, to whom he says: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons [Col. 0595A] of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI). For this is not the only man of whom Pharaoh was unworthy; there were many others also. After the Apostle had mentioned such men, he concluded: “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. XI).

“You,” he says, “shall speak all that I command you; he shall speak to Pharaoh, that he may let the children of Israel go out of his land.” Again, above he had said: “He shall speak to the people for you, and he shall be your mouth; but you shall be to him in those things which pertain to God” (Exod. IV). The sense is as if it were said: You, established as Pharaoh’s god, to whom I, God of gods, speak “face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend” (Exod. XXXIII), will not deign to say much, to prolong discourse with the king of Egypt, or to uncover your face to unlearned common people. Rather, you will speak to Aaron, your prophet; and he will speak against Pharaoh and to your people, after my example. For I neither conduct my business with the prince of darkness by indications of words, nor indiscriminately appear visibly to mortal children of men; but through my prophets I command what they ought to hear, or what judgment I shall execute.

Moreover, “you shall be to him in those things which pertain to God.” For, as you speak and he hears, he will receive what he is to say. And these two men acted thus for a short time: one possessing authority in speech, the other obeying that authority in performing signs before Pharaoh, until the sacrifice of the paschal lamb.

But the law, given through Moses, and the priesthood in which Aaron first ministered, acted likewise with the same distinction [Col. 0595C] until the sacrifice of the true paschal Lamb, Christ the Son of God (John V). For afterward Moses no longer stands for that people against the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, the devil; rather, he accuses that same people. And Aaron’s priesthood has been removed from the midst, no longer possessing altar or temple. Formerly, when Moses was read, he presided over the priests of Aaron’s race in matters pertaining to the Lord. For they feared Moses in their reading, so as to offer sacrifices according to the pattern which he had seen on the mountain; and they spoke for the people against Pharaoh—that is, the devil. But now, with those priests removed and a priest established according to the order of Melchizedek, Moses has shut his mouth and veiled his face to that people, turning to this one.

“But I,” he says, “will harden [Col. 0595D] his heart,” etc. The hardening has been discussed above; now let us continue with the rest.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the age of Moses and Aaron, and how it is clear that the wicked king’s edict was not carried out.

“Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh.” Stephen the protomartyr distinguishes this eighty-year age of Moses in the Acts of the Apostles as follows: “When the period of forty years was fulfilled for him, it arose in his heart to visit his brethren, the children of Israel. And when he saw someone suffering wrong, he defended him” (Acts VII). And shortly afterward: “And when forty years had been completed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in a fire [Col. 0596A] of flame in a bush” (ibid.).

Moreover, it is evident that both Aaron and Moses were born after that edict of the impious Pharaoh, which said: “Whatever is born of the male sex, cast into the river; whatever is female, 180 preserve” (Exod. I). “For after this,” Scripture says—that is, after these words and actions of Pharaoh—“a man went out from the house of Levi, having taken a wife of his own stock” (Exod. II), etc. Therefore, since Aaron, who was born of that wife three years before Moses, was preserved; and since, at Israel’s departure from Egypt, little children and youths under twenty years old were present, it is clear that such a wicked king’s edict did not prevail. And the reason Moses was feared when he was born was rather his beauty, of which mention was made above.

“When Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh,” he says, “Moses was eighty years old.” Moreover, after he had presided over the people in the wilderness for forty years, he died. He was therefore no more than one hundred and twenty years old. Thus no place is left for conjectural license, even to doubt whether they stood before Pharaoh performing prodigies for a long or a short time. For, lest anyone imagine that he left Egypt before the fortieth year had elapsed, Moses himself, about to die, says in Deuteronomy: “Behold, it is the fortieth year, that you may consider in your heart: as a man disciplines his son, so the Lord has disciplined you” (Deut. VIII), etc. When the latter forty years are added to the former eighty, the whole number of Moses’ years is beyond doubt one hundred and twenty, as is written in Deuteronomy: “For Moses was one hundred and twenty years old [Col. 0596C] when he died” (Deut. XXXIV). Therefore, in the eighty-first year of his age, at the beginning of the year—that is, in spring—Moses stood before Pharaoh; and, after the signs had been performed, at the same time of year he led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the mystical meaning of the signs performed before Pharaoh.

“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: ‘When Pharaoh says to you, “Show signs,” you shall say to Aaron: “Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, and let it become a serpent,”’” etc. Since the account of the signs seems plain upon the surface of the letter, let us rather seek their mystical meanings, with the help of the Lord’s Spirit; and then the letter itself, appearing more worthy, will follow the sound interpretation that proceeds well.

First, then, we must ask what mystical rationale there is in this divine arrangement: that before the sacrifice of the paschal lamb, by which the entire matter was accomplished, it pleased God that ten signs should be performed—by which he knew Pharaoh could not be overcome—before he himself, who brought it about, should act. The first sign was when Aaron’s staff, turned into a serpent, devoured the staffs of the enchanters. The second was when the water of the river was turned into blood. The third, when frogs came up from the waters and covered the land. The fourth, when the dust of the earth was turned into gnats. The fifth, when God sent every kind of fly. The sixth, when the animals of the Egyptians died by pestilence. The seventh, when, after ashes had been scattered into the sky, wounds of swelling [Col. 0597A] blisters arose. The eighth, when God gave thunder and hail and lightning running over the earth, and hail and fire mingled together were borne along. The ninth, when God spoke and locust and *bruchus* came, without number. The tenth, when dreadful darkness came upon all the land of Egypt.

Although Pharaoh was afflicted by these ten signs or plagues, and Egypt was worn down, Israel was not thereby released by the Egyptians. After these things, at last the lamb is commanded to be taken into the houses of the children of Israel, to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening; and in it the whole matter was accomplished. That same night all the firstborn of Egypt died, and Pharaoh, overcome, spoke mildly, saying: “Go out quickly, and as you depart bless me” (Exod. XII). And when the children of Israel passed through, Pharaoh was again hardened, and all the Egyptians who pursued them were drowned in the Red Sea (Exod. XIV). We rightly ask, therefore, of whom these things were figures.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the ten commandments, which depend upon love of God and neighbor.

We said above—as everyone knows—that Pharaoh signifies the devil; Moses, the law; Aaron, the old priesthood; and that through those things the kingdom of the devil, the kingdom of sin and death, was not destroyed but was stirred up and aggravated on account of the commandment. Now the law has ten precepts, all of which depend upon love of God and neighbor.

The first is: You shall have no foreign gods before me. The second: You shall not make for yourself a carved image. The third: You shall not take the name of your God in vain. The fourth: Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. These four belong to love of God. Then come those that belong to love of neighbor, in their proper order: the fifth is, Honor your father and mother. The sixth: You shall not kill. The seventh: You shall not commit adultery. The eighth: You shall not steal. The ninth: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. The tenth: You shall not covet.

By these ten precepts of righteousness, the ancient saints who observed them before Christ’s coming did indeed harass the spiritual Pharaoh—that is, the devil—resisting and opposing him so as to leave the kingdom of death; but they did not prevail. “For the law brought nothing to perfection,” says the Apostle (Heb. VII), each one of the ancients, namely the prophet Isaiah, likewise proclaiming: “All our righteousnesses are as the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV). At last, Christ the Son of God enters this world, to be sacrificed as the true Lamb and to become the sacrifice of righteousness; and what could not be done through human righteousness, however vigorously people fulfilled the precepts of the law, he alone accomplished through his own blood. “For what was impossible for the law,” says the Apostle, “because it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh because of sin, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom. VIII).

Therefore, just as the evening sacrifice of that lamb, through which Pharaoh was overcome and Israel freed, signified the Lamb of God, Christ, and his passion—through which in the last days the devil was overcome and the world was freed and saved—so those ten signs, or plagues, by which Pharaoh could be scourged but not overcome, signified the ten precepts of the law, by whose observance the kingdom of death could be disturbed but not destroyed. Now it must be said how each of these signs, performed by the finger of God in the plagues of Pharaoh, corresponds to each of the precepts which were written by that same finger of God on tablets of stone.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the signs of Aaron and the magicians before Pharaoh.

“Aaron took the staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it was turned into a serpent. But Pharaoh summoned wise men and sorcerers, and they likewise did the same by Egyptian incantations and certain secret arts. Each cast down his staff, and they were turned into dragons; but Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs. And Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had commanded.”

Moses did this as Pharaoh’s god, because he turned an inanimate staff into a true living creature, which belongs to divine power alone: namely, he transformed it into a serpent. “For Aaron’s staff,” he says, “devoured their staffs.” And rightly so: their staffs remained what they had been, but by Egyptian incantations and certain secret arts the magicians had bewitched human eyes, so that the staffs seemed to have the appearance of dragons. Therefore, those which seemed devourers but were not could be devoured, and could not devour.

Mystically, here the finger of God plainly foreshadowed the first commandment which he himself was to write upon tablets of stone: “You shall have no foreign gods before me” (Exod. XX). For Moses’ staff turned into a serpent is, in mystery, the almighty Word of God, sent into the earth in the likeness of sinful flesh. The staffs of the magicians, however, are the deceptions of demons, who caused themselves to be worshipped as gods. But he—the Word of God, clothed in flesh—by proving that the gods of the nations are demons, so that he alone might be worshipped, devoured all false gods, declaring in public preaching with supreme authority: “You shall have no foreign gods before me.” The workers of deceit wished, but were unable, [Col. 0598D] to stand against the truth; those magicians of Pharaoh were their first fathers or prototypes.

“For just as,” says the Apostle, “Jannes and Mambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth: men corrupted in mind, reprobate concerning the faith. But they shall progress no further, for their folly shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (II Tim. III).

## CHAPTER XXXI. What is signified by the waters being turned into blood.

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Pharaoh’s heart is weighed down; he is unwilling to let the people go.’” And shortly afterward: “Say to Aaron: ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers and marshes and all pools of water, that they may be turned into blood; and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in wooden vessels and in stone vessels’” [Col. 0599A]

This second plague signifies the punishment owed to transgressors of the second commandment, which was spoken or written on the tablets: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness; you shall not worship them or serve them” (Exod. XX). For it follows: “I am the Lord your God, a mighty and jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation” (ibid.).

Accordingly, once this was heard and began to be observed, all the waters of the Egyptians—that is, the consciences of idolaters—became bloody; for they shed much blood of the saints, like these Egyptians who, because the children of Israel said, “Let us go and sacrifice to our God” (Exod. V), raged against them more cruelly. Therefore, because they cast their males into the water, their waters were deservedly also literally turned into blood, so that they might suffer while drinking the water of the river; and afterward, while pursuing them, they were drowned in the Red Sea.

Thus the mighty and jealous Lord repaid blood to all their imitators, who worship carved images, glory in their idols, and shed blood because of them: he gave it to them to drink, and to suffer while drinking—not for one or two, but for all seven days, as it is written: “Seven days were completed after the Lord struck the river.” This number signifies the totality of ages. For unto ages of ages the springs of waters—that is, the depths of those wise in making carved images and persecuting the worshippers of the true God for their sake—shall remain turned into blood. Hence in the Apocalypse an angel is heard saying: “You are just, who are and who were holy, because you have judged these things; for they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink, for they are worthy” (Apoc. XVI).

## CHAPTER XXXII. What is signified by the rivers’ teeming with frogs.

(CHAP. VIII.) “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Go in to Pharaoh and say to him: “Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will strike all your borders with frogs, and the river shall teem with frogs,”’” etc.

And the third commandment of the law is: “You shall not take the name [Col. 0599D] of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. XX). For transgressors of this commandment, the reproach of foulness is prefigured in frogs. Who are these empty talkers who take the name of God in vain, if not especially the talkative poets, telling tales and croaking not only in the rivers of Egypt but in the marshes of other nations? Or who more rightly may be compared with the foulness of frogs than poets clamoring in theaters with the ridiculous inventions of fables? These plainly take the name of God in vain when, for example, they ascribe the name of deity to adulterous Jupiter and to the little harlot Venus.

Those frogs were indeed exceedingly troublesome, ascending and entering the king’s house, his bedchamber, and upon his bed, into his servants’ houses, among his people, into his ovens, [Col. 0600A] and into the remnants of his food. These frogs, however—that is, fabulous poets—delight bodily ears by their recitations and eyes by their gestures, but prove deadly to souls.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On why gnats were throughout the land of Egypt, which the sorcerers, unable to produce, said: “This is the finger of God.”

“The Lord said to Moses: ‘Speak to Aaron: Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and let there be gnats throughout all the land of Egypt.’ And they did so,” etc. Gnats are very tiny flies, exceedingly troublesome in their stings. Here Pharaoh’s sorcerers failed. “For the sorcerers,” he says, “did likewise, in order to produce gnats, and they could not.” Above it was said that they did likewise by their incantations so as to turn waters into blood; “they did likewise and brought up frogs over the land of Egypt.” In this they failed. “And they said to Pharaoh: ‘This is the finger of God.’” They said this as defeated men, plainly to console their shame. It is as if they said: “If a man were fighting against us, we would have prevailed; but now the one who fights is not a human finger but God’s finger. Therefore we must be excused for being defeated.”

What then is this: that by their incantations the sorcerers could turn waters into blood and bring forth frogs, but could not produce gnats? Could gnats also have been made to appear, but, because they did not inflict troublesome stings upon anyone, were they convicted of having acted deceptively? Surely the horror of blood and the foulness of frogs are perceived by sight alone; and so the tricksters displayed utterly false frogs and deceptive blood to bewitched eyes. But gnats are plainly identified also by their painful sting; therefore they did not produce them, because humans without God could not create what was real and could be truly felt.

Moreover, according to the anagogical sense, to strike the dust of the earth and make gnats is, in condemnation of the pride of man—who is indeed dust—to make such utterances in the Scriptures as repel from truth the minds of hearers, who are not worthy to understand; just as gnats are troublesome and importunate to eyes, preventing them from seeing, and to ears, preventing them from hearing freely.

For example, the fourth commandment of the law is: [Col. 0600D] “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX). Preoccupied by such a saying, the Egyptian, 182 who calls himself a Jew and is not, judges that nothing else is commanded here except the Sabbath which the Lord hates, as he himself testifies through the prophet when he says: “The new moon and Sabbath, and other feasts, I will not endure; your calends and solemnities my soul hates” (Isa. I). Thus preoccupied, he does not deserve to understand that Sabbath, that seventh day, on which “God completed the work which he had made, in which he rested, which he blessed and sanctified” (Gen. II), as he himself says: “Do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John X).

Without reverence for this Sabbath, concerning which the Psalmist also says: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. CXVII), what are Sabbaths and other feasts in the judgment of the Jews except importunate gnats in the eyes of Egyptians, hindering the free sight of light? Therefore, in turning waters into blood and bringing forth frogs—that is, in preaching the future punishments of evil persons and in despising the verbose fables of poets—enemies may in some fashion compare themselves to the preachers of truth, “but they shall progress no further” (II Tim. III). For they shall not be able, by their sophisms, like wandering and flying gnats, to ensnare the disciples of truth in return as they themselves were blinded.

“This is the finger of God,” they say. It is well known and most celebrated in the faithful Church of God that the Holy Spirit is, or is called, the finger of God. For the Son himself, speaking of the Holy Spirit’s power, says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has indeed come upon you” (Matt. XII; Luke II). Yet several fingers are also spoken of to signify the same Spirit; just as there is one Spirit, and yet we read of seven spirits before the throne. Hence the Psalmist says: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. VIII). He said “fingers” in the plural because of the plurality of gifts of the one and same Holy Spirit.

But were those men of corrupted mind—that is, those enchanters and sorcerers—so close to the Spirit that they knowingly said, “This is the finger of God,” considering the distinctive property of his person and the reason why he was called the finger of God? Therefore they too did not speak from themselves: that is, without knowing what they said, they confessed to us the distinctive property of the Holy Spirit, intending nothing else than to say, “The power or operation of God is here.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. What is signified by the sending of every kind of fly, and by Moses’ saying: “We shall sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians.”

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Rise early and stand before Pharaoh, for he will go out to the waters, and say to him: “Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. For if [Col. 0601D] you do not let them go, behold, I shall send upon you, your servants, your people, and your houses every kind of fly,”’” etc.

God offered a great spectacle to the entire world when he subdued the pride of the Egyptians not by lions and bears, but by frogs and flies. “He spoke,” says the Psalmist, “and the *coenomyia* came” (Ps. CIV), that is, the dog-fly. He inflicted upon them a fitting disgrace: dog-like filth, and their insolent pride subdued by every kind of fly. This is the fifth plague.

Now the fifth commandment of the law says: “Honor your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. XX). These correspond beautifully in contrast. On the one hand, those who honor their parents are long-lived in the land of the living; on the other, all the contemptuous perish swiftly, deprived of honor, as unworthy of the favor of God the Father and Creator, as is written of such persons: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccles. X). Thus Pharaoh, the powerful and great king of Egypt, was nearly overcome by flies.

For it follows: “Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: ‘Go, sacrifice to your God in this land.’ And Moses said: ‘It cannot be done so. For we shall sacrifice to our God the abominations of the Egyptians. If we slaughter before them those things which the Egyptians worship, will they not stone us?’” This is a serious denunciation of the Egyptians, and a fine instruction for those who truly desire to be worshippers of the one God.

First, it must be known that no cattle are meant here which Egyptians either abominate or worship, to be slaughtered or sacrificed to the true Lord God. For he himself speaks through the prophet: “Add your burnt offerings to your victims and eat flesh; for I did not speak to your fathers or command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and victims. But this I commanded them, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people’” (Jer. VII), etc.

What then are the abominations of the Egyptians except faith and all virtues of the soul? Or what do Egyptians worship except all vices? For humility is abominable to the proud, and all righteousness to the unjust. Scripture says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. X). Conversely, Egyptians worship a swollen neck and a fat heart. But true Israel must first slaughter these things, and only then offer a contrite spirit and a contrite and humbled heart, so that the sacrifice may be lawful and rightly ordered.

Therefore, “we shall sacrifice,” he says, “the abominations of the Egyptians”—that is, truth and holiness. “And those things which the Egyptians worship”—namely, every falsehood and every perversity—we shall sacrifice within ourselves by worshipping the one true God. But all who wish to sacrifice in this order suffer persecution. Therefore he says: “If we slaughter before them the things which the Egyptians worship, they will stone us.”

According to the anagogical sense, Pharaoh is not heard saying, “Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God,” but only, “in this land”; whereas the apostolic trumpet of true sacrifice says: “Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What consent has the temple of God with idols?” (II Cor. VI).

## CHAPTER XXXV. What is signified by the grievous pestilence that came upon the fields and cattle.
