(CAP. IX.) “And the Lord said to Moses: Enter in to Pharaoh, and speak to him. Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. But if you still refuse, behold, my hand shall be upon your fields, and upon your horses, camels, asses, sheep, and oxen—a very grievous pestilence [Col. 0603A],” etc. This sixth plague of sinners announces its scourge to transgressors of the sixth commandment. For there too it is said: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX). And here death in their waters is drawing near to the murderers of the children of Israel, whom they cast into the river. Vengeance first ranges through the animals, not rushing upon them suddenly, but advancing gradually even to the people themselves and overtaking sinners step by step, so that they may be without excuse. For concerning such delay in God’s vengeance the Apostle says: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that the patience of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. II).

183 Therefore, when he says these things, one must understand [Col. 0603B] how Pharaoh stored up wrath for himself. From the authority of the present Scripture, his example must be heeded by every person against whom vengeance seems to come slowly, lest, when it comes, it fall upon one who is hard and impenitent with a force all the greater because it was delayed—as it did upon this man, whose heart became more and more hardened, until at last the whole treasury of eternal wrath which he had amassed descended upon him in the Red Sea.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. What is signified by the dust being spread over all the land of Egypt

“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Take handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh; and they shall become dust [Col. 0603C] over all the land of Egypt, and there shall be sores and swelling blisters upon men and beasts throughout all the land of Egypt.” This seventh plague foreshadows the deserved punishment of the transgressor of the seventh commandment—or rather, of him who transgresses the seventh commandment. For the seventh commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX). What, indeed, is the adulterer burned by the sulphurous fire of lust, if not ash from a furnace? “For all adulterers,” says the prophet, “are like an oven heated by the baker” (Hos. VII).

The ash from the furnace is therefore taken up and scattered toward heaven, and sores of swelling blisters arise upon men and beasts, because the adulterer is snatched from the fire of his committed adultery to the heavenly judgment; swollen with eternal punishment and wholly ulcerated, he bears in soul and body an everlasting [Col. 0603D] fire. “And the magicians,” he says, “could not stand before Moses because of the sores which were upon them and throughout all the land of Egypt.” Behold, they were defeated for the third time; consequently, no further mention is made of the magicians, for their memory perished. First, they were disarmed by their rods, not without disgrace, because Aaron’s rod devoured their rods. Second, they were confounded because, when they could not produce gnats, they said: “This is the finger of God.” Now, for the third time, they were so thoroughly overcome that they could breathe no hope of any victory. For they too were ulcerated and could no longer stand before Moses.

All who resist the truth may be certain of a similar disgrace. “For their folly,” says the Apostle, “shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (II Tim. III).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That hail and fire were borne mingled together, and concerning God’s words: “For this reason I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you”

“And the Lord said to Moses: Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh, and you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me,” etc. And immediately afterward: “For this reason I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed among all nations throughout the earth,” etc. The Apostle recalls this formidable declaration in these terms: “Therefore it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy. For Scripture says to Pharaoh: For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, that my name might be proclaimed [Col. 0604B] throughout all the earth” (Rom. IX).

At once, whoever is a presumptuous investigator of God’s judgments, saying, “Why then does he still complain? For who has resisted his will?” (ibid.), rightly hears the same Apostle’s indignant reply: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does not the potter have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (ibid.). Thus the man who, owing to his presumption, is unworthy of knowledge of the secrets of God is repelled far from the Apostle’s audience. The Apostle turns to him who, with a submissive mind in the fear of the Lord, asks heavenly teaching even for a small drop of understanding, and says to him: “But what if God, willing to show wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to show the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (ibid.), etc.

In saying this, he surely defends God against human suspicion, so that no one may suppose that Pharaoh, or anyone else, stored up unjust wrath for himself because God raised him up for this very purpose. Rather, God raised Pharaoh up—understand, to royal power—and bestowed supreme authority upon him because he was a vessel of wrath and had long since been fitted for destruction. Therefore he was set over the children of mercy for their correction, that he might be “the rod of fury and the staff in the Lord’s hand against them” (Isa. X), whom God had prepared to bring through tribulation into glory.

Therefore, when he says, “For this reason I raised you up,” one must understand: to a kingdom—namely, by permitting, not by causing, you to ascend to supreme rule and to have authority according to the wickedness or hardness of your heart, cruelly persecuting my people. “Behold,” he says, “at this very hour tomorrow I shall rain a very great hail, such as has not been in Egypt from the day it was founded.” And afterward: “The Lord rained hail upon the land of Egypt, and hail and fire were borne mingled together.”

This is the eighth plague, now nearer than all those before it to accomplishing their destruction. “For the hail struck throughout all the land of Egypt everything that was in the fields, from man even to beast.” As yet no human being had died, but by this plague their firstfruits are already struck. Now the eighth commandment of the law is: “You shall not steal” (Exod. XX). Certainly, although there are several kinds of theft, it is established that the worst theft is to hold the truth of God in unrighteousness. This plague declares the deserved penalty for that sin; it came from heaven, where “hail and fire were borne mingled together.” “For,” says the Apostle, “the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and unrighteousness of those people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what may be known of God is manifest among them; for God has revealed it to them” (Rom. I).

Then he explains what he had said, “who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness”: “Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened [Col. 0605B]; and they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed creatures, and serpents” (ibid.). Likewise, he expresses terribly what the wrath of God is which is revealed from heaven against impiety, and which here is signified by hail and fire, when he immediately adds: “Therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that they dishonor their bodies among themselves” (ibid.), etc.

This hail and this fire “struck,” he says, “every herb of the field and broke every tree of the country,” because this shame, of which the Apostle spoke, defiles by heavenly wrath cast into vessels of wrath all the beauty of human nature and utterly destroys every dignity of rational creation [Col. 0605C]. Many things which follow are sufficiently clear in themselves, and we pass them over in our eagerness to proceed.

184 ## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That locusts were brought up over the whole land of Egypt

(CAP. X.) “And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locust, that it may come up over it and devour every herb which remained after the hail. And Moses stretched out his rod over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought in a scorching wind throughout that day and night. And when morning came, the scorching wind carried up the locusts, which came up over all the land of Egypt,” etc.

See what battle lines the Lord arrayed, with what ranks he filled his camp while fighting for Israel: frogs, gnats, flies, and locusts were the battle lines of his camp; from such cohorts he composed whole legions against the mighty Egyptians. Individually, the soldiers were indeed small and weak in themselves, yet under God’s commanding leadership they were sufficiently strong against Pharaoh’s armies. What a great human army could not have done, these phalanxes of locusts accomplished through vigorous military service. “For they covered the entire surface of the earth, laying everything waste. Therefore Pharaoh, in haste,” as though to surrender, “called Moses and Aaron,” the leaders of so great an army and chief officers of their commander, God. “I have sinned,” he says, “against the Lord your God and against you. But now forgive [Col. 0606A] my sin, even this once, and pray to the Lord your God that he may take this death away from me.”

He had said this also above: “I have sinned yet again. The Lord is righteous; I and my people are wicked” (Exod. IX). He said both this and the other as a man surrendering; but once relief was granted, he hardened his heart like a deserter and did not let the children of Israel go. Therefore it is not enough for anyone to have said, “I have sinned,” nor can confession profit when it is not joined to faith. Nevertheless, the mighty king was defeated by the locust.

Accordingly, when God had said somewhere through the prophet, “And I will restore to you the years which the locust, beetle, and caterpillar have eaten” (Joel II), he immediately added: “My great strength which I sent among you” (ibid.). “My great strength,” he says—the locust, beetle, and caterpillar—understand, not in comparison with heavenly powers and strengths, but with weak and feeble human beings who pride themselves on their weakness, who raise their neck against God, though they submit it to fleas.

This plague of locusts is the ninth. Now the ninth commandment of the law is this: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exod. XX). This, of course, is especially done by heretics and by all who speak falsehood. But in the Apocalypse of John, the force of heretics’ falsehood is signified under the likeness of locusts in this manner: “And smoke,” he says, “ascended from the pit like the smoke of a great furnace, and the sun and air were darkened. From the smoke locusts came out upon the earth” (Apoc. IX). There, where locusts came out from the smoke upon the earth, and here, where the scorching wind carried up the locust, the same thing must be understood mystically: namely, that just as locusts do not possess flight of their own but were carried by the wind for the destruction of the Egyptians, so all false witnesses—whether in court or in an ecclesiastical council—who bring forward false testimony from the Scriptures against their neighbor’s blood or against the faith of Christ imagine that they fly with the wings of knowledge; but without doubt they are carried aloft by the empty wind of diabolical pride, to the overthrow of their hearers and the destruction of those who consent to them.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That “horrible darkness came over the land of Egypt”

“And the Lord said to Moses: Stretch out your hand toward heaven, and let darkness come over the land of Egypt, so dense that it can be felt. Moses stretched out [Col. 0606D] his hand toward heaven, and horrible darkness came over all the land of Egypt. For three days no one saw his brother, nor did anyone move from the place where he was. But wherever the children of Israel lived, there was light.”

This density of horrible darkness was rightly inflicted on the Egyptians according to both their name and their merit. For they are called Egyptians by name and in reality, because their eyes had been darkened by envy and hatred of the children of Israel. Now, if you would free yourself from the Egyptians’ darkness—which is the tenth plague—you must hear the tenth commandment of the law: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; nor shall you desire his wife, his servant, his maidservant, his ass, his ox, or anything that is his” (Exod. XX). This commandment, I say, must be observed by you, so that you may not remain with the Egyptians in darkness [Col. 0607A], but may dwell with Israel in light.

For what more than the eye of covetousness darkens the whole person? “The lamp of your body,” says the Lord, “is your eye. If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. But if it is evil, your body too will be dark. Therefore see to it that the light which is in you is not darkness” (Matt. V). What, I ask, is darker than an evil eye—for example, when it looks upon a woman in order to desire her, or regards some possession of its neighbor in order to seize it? Certainly, such a person recognizes no one as a neighbor. For if he recognized a neighbor, he would do none of those things to him which “covetousness, the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI), persuades him to do.

Therefore it is pointedly said of the Egyptians that “for three days no one saw his brother” [Col. 0607B]. A mind preoccupied by covetousness does not see its brother and does not recognize its neighbor, attending only to giving false testimony against him, to stealing because it coveted what was his, and to committing adultery with his wife because it coveted her. Such things are far from seeing one’s brother or recognizing one’s neighbor.

“And Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: Go, sacrifice to the Lord.” A little later follows: “But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not let them go.” Indeed, he even said: “Depart [Col. 0608A] from me; take care that you see my face no more,” etc.

## CHAPTER XL. Conclusion of the same signs, and a preliminary consideration of the mystery: why Pharaoh, not overcome by these signs, was finally defeated by the sacrifice of the Paschal Lamb

Therefore, as was said above, the ten plagues of Egypt, by which Moses and Aaron were able indeed to afflict Pharaoh, but not so to conquer him that he would let the people go, mystically represent the ten commandments of the law. By observing them, every righteous person could indeed fight the devil, but could not so overcome him as utterly to destroy within himself the kingdom of sin or death.

But the sacrifice of the lamb, followed that same night by the death of Egypt’s firstborn, when “a great cry arose, for there was no house in which no dead person lay” (Exod. XII)—what this signifies is long known to the whole Israel of God. It has likewise already been said above that it signified the passion of Christ, the Son of God, through which both original sin and all the sins of the world were blotted out. Therefore the account of so great a work of God must now be continued in praise and glory of that same holy and spotless Lamb of God, who alone bore the sins of the world, striking the spiritual Pharaoh with the single plague of his cross in order to accomplish the salvation of his people, which the law, with the decrees of its ten commandments, could not bring to perfection.

# SECOND BOOK ON EXODUS  
*(Exodus, chapters XII–XV)*

[Col. 0607]

185 ## CHAPTER I. A renewed consideration of the third age of the world, in which Holy Scripture was first composed, according to the likeness of the third day

Let us recall that from Abraham we reckon the third age of the world, corresponding by a certain likeness to the third day of the world’s creation and to the third spirit, the spirit of knowledge, which again proceeds from the spirit of fear and possesses true riches.

For on the third day, when God said, “Let the earth bring forth green herb yielding seed, and fruit-bearing tree yielding fruit according to its kind” (Gen. I), we learn that the paradise of delight was planted. And in this third age of the world, when the same God spoke and wrote through Moses, we know that Holy Scripture was composed: truly a paradise of delight, truly a garden of pleasures, “a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Cant. IV), whose shoots are a paradise of pomegranates. For from this all the other Scriptures have their beginning.

In that paradise, “the Lord God had planted every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food, and also the tree of life in its midst” (Gen. II). In this paradise of Scripture he planted beautiful and pleasant things—the plantings of the patriarchs—and in their midst the lovely mysteries of the tree of life, that is, of Christ. Therefore we linger longer in this [Col. 0608C] age, delighted by the fruit of its trees, while we desire to pluck something from each tree: ever-new beauty invites our eyes, and thus the eagerness of the mind is never satisfied with the treasures laid up. For all are beautiful to behold; all are pleasant for food. The tree of life is in their midst, for all things said or done look to Christ, the author of life.

Therefore, since we have reached this center—that is, the Paschal Lamb—we gladly linger longer; for it is sweet to be more abundantly nourished by the mystical fruits of life. After inserting a few matters sufficiently clear in themselves, the text continues as follows.

## CHAPTER II. On the Paschal month, which Scripture calls the first among the months of the year

[Col. 0608D] “And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: On the tenth day of this month let every one take a lamb according to their families and houses,” etc.

“This month,” he says. Which month is this? Evidently that which they call Nisan and we call April. But the month and year are not reckoned among them as they are among us—that is, among the Romans. For the Romans divided the solar year into conventional months by the Kalends. The Hebrews, according to the law, recognized only lunar months and years. Therefore, whenever this Holy Scripture, whether in the law or before the law, indicates on what numbered day of a month something was done or said, it signifies nothing other than the age of the moon.

One month has thirty days and another thirty-one, because the moon’s course is completed in twenty-nine and a half days—that is, twelve hours [materially uncertain: the Latin OCR reads “20 diebus ac semisse,” evidently for “29 diebus ac semisse”]. Therefore this “month,” which we call the April moon, “shall be for you,” he says, “the beginning of months.” He significantly says, “for you.” For the Egyptians’ beginning of months was the month which the Romans call September and which they call Thoth. And not content merely to say “the beginning of months,” he added, “it shall be the first among the months of the year.”

“Beginning of months,” that is, according to the natural order of the spring season; “first among the months of the year,” according to the Paschal festival of divine authority. For “first,” that is, chief, and the festive glory of the other months, “it shall be for you,” he says. The lawful rule for this beginning of months, or first month, is that after the moon of March, which they call Adar, the following moon, if it becomes full even one day too early before the equinox, is not to count as “the beginning” or “the first month among the months of the year,” but is to be added to the preceding twelve months, making the year a thirteen-month year.

Hence it is also called in Greek *embolismos*, that is, an intercalation or addition. For the year of twelve lunar months is called the common year, and it is shorter than the solar year by eleven days. Consequently, the moon’s wandering course cannot remain fixed in any certain place; and the moon of April, which we seek for calculating Pascha, sometimes falls in March, sometimes in April, and sometimes occupies several days of May, though it is more properly reckoned as April. Yet in this wandering we are guided by a certain rule: wherever the first full moon occurs after the spring equinox, it is undoubtedly the Paschal boundary.

## CHAPTER III. On the tenth day and the fourteenth day of the same month, and on the mystery of the lamb

“On the tenth day,” he says, “of this month, let each one take a lamb according to their families and houses.” In this place, “families” differs from “house” only in this: the house consists of its walls, the family of its inhabitants. “According to houses,” he says, that is, within domestic walls, “and according to your families”—that is, each of you shall take a lamb for your family’s meal.

But perhaps some small household may be so scanty that it cannot consume a lamb at one meal. He therefore says: “But if the number is too small to be sufficient for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor who is joined to his house, according to the number of persons who can be sufficient to eat the lamb.” And immediately: “The lamb shall be without blemish, male, one year old.” It shall not be lawful, he says, for each person to take a larger or smaller lamb according to the size of his household; but it shall be according to equality [Col. 0610A]—that is, everywhere “male,” and with all persons “one year old,” that is, of one year.

And in order that there may be no lack of eaters, the master of the little house shall provide by taking from the neighboring house. “According to this rite you shall also take a kid.” This was said by anticipation. For he had not yet stated the actual rite for taking the lamb, yet already says, “According to this rite you shall also take a kid.” The meaning is: Whether anyone takes a lamb or a kid, it will be acceptable for the purpose, provided that in taking, sacrificing, and eating it you observe the same rite.

He immediately adds that same rite: “And you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month.” Why take it so long beforehand, to keep it for such a time? Clearly, so that, while it is present, its purpose may also stir your hearts, lest you be forgetful or unprepared because you must depart, while it reminds you so many days beforehand to prepare for departure. For as often as it gives its bleating cry, so often it rouses the battle lines that are to leave camp as though with the sound of a trumpet.

“And the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening.” There were, of course, as many lambs or kids as there could be houses or families among the entire multitude of the children of Israel. Yet he rightly said, in the singular, “you shall sacrifice it,” not only because several lambs, or several human beings, are, as philosophers maintain, one lamb or one human being through participation in the species, but, more relevantly, because in all there was unity of the sacrament: in all, the sacrament was of the one who was to come, of whom something must later be said.

“And they shall take of the lamb’s blood and put it on both doorposts and upon the lintels [Col. 0610C] of the houses in which they shall eat it.” Why he commands this is first made clear when he says: “The blood shall be for you a sign in the houses in which you are. And I shall see the blood and pass over you, and there shall be no destroying plague among you when I strike the land of Egypt.” And a little later: “For the Lord shall pass through, striking the Egyptians.”

Moses says to the elders of Israel: “And when he sees the blood upon the lintel and upon both doorposts, he will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter.” He does not strike by himself, but grants authority to the striking angel—the evil angel—as the Psalmist also testifies, saying: “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation, indignation and wrath and tribulation, a sending forth through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII). Therefore it is not God’s own sudden wrath but the wrath of his indignation sent upon them that passes through. And they are rightly handed over to the striking evil angel after they refused to submit to God himself, who was correcting them and inviting them to repentance through the ten plagues.

Furthermore, when he says, “I shall see,” this means: I shall approve the faith or the attentive expectation of believers. For God is neither forgetful nor wandering about, so that unless he sees the sign of blood on the doorposts, he does not know in which houses the lamb has or has not been eaten, and, deceived by error, strikes the righteous together with sinners.

Thus the lamb’s blood was certainly not drunk, for Scripture says elsewhere: “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood” [Col. 0611A] (Gen. IX). Yet nevertheless it is efficacious when, on seeing it, the destroyer is not permitted to enter the house. “And they shall eat,” he says, “the flesh that night, roasted with fire, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces,” etc.

What literal reason or benefit these things have—namely, that the lamb is commanded to be eaten with unleavened bread and wild lettuces—we cannot know. But as for the words, “Nothing of it shall remain until morning; if anything remains, you shall burn it with fire,” this should be understood literally, because no Hebrew would be eating this sacred meal in the morning, since the Egyptians would compel them to leave at midnight. And was that people accustomed to eat raw flesh, that they should be told, “You shall not eat anything of it raw”?

Further, when he says, “You shall eat it in this manner: you shall gird your loins, have shoes on your feet, hold staffs in your hands, and eat in haste,” this can be understood as done or said so that, when the cry occurred in Egypt—which was soon to happen after all the firstborn had died—they would be ready, the Egyptians urging and compelling them to depart and allowing no delay whatsoever in setting out.

Therefore let us now also depart, namely from this literal glory “which is passing away” to the abiding glory of the life-giving Spirit in the face of Christ (II Cor. III).

## CHAPTER IV. Mystically concerning the same lamb: in that lamb there was a figure, but in ours there is the truth of Pascha

[Col. 0611C] We now know that *phase* or *pascha* means our passage, as the Apostle says: “For Christ our Pascha has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V). There was the figure; here is the truth. There was the shadow; here is the body.

“But,” you say, “they were saved through the same faith by which we are saved.” We agree: through the same faith, but not through the same knowledge of faith, nor through the same confession of faith. Today it is openly required that you believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X): that Christ, the Son of God, is the true Lamb, who by his death redeemed us from death, consecrated us by his blood, and restored us to life by his resurrection.

That this was prefigured in the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, in the passage of the children of Israel, and in the drowning of Pharaoh’s chariots and army while the children of Israel passed through the Red Sea, is evident. Did they already possess knowledge of faith or confession? Moses and the prophets certainly had knowledge of this sacrament, some more and some less, according to the good pleasure of the Holy Spirit, who distributes “to each as he wills” (I Cor. XII). But in Moses alone it was signified to all how they ought to conceal this from the people.

For when he received knowledge of heavenly secrets, his face shone according to the likeness of his mind; but because the children of Israel could not endure that brightness, he covered it with a veil (Exod. XXXIV). Did he cover only his shining face, while openly proclaiming to all the cause of its brightness—namely, knowledge of the sacraments of Christ, the Son of God? Certainly not. Rather, as he covered his face beneath a veil, so he concealed the secret of the Spirit beneath the covering of the letter.

The prophets too were forbidden to proclaim openly. Thus one of them is told: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. VIII). Another is told: “Therefore seal the vision, for it is for many days hence” (Dan. VIII). Again: “Go, Daniel, for the words are closed and sealed until the appointed time” (Dan. XII).

Therefore faith was indeed required of the people Israel: namely, that they should believe that the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, was one and the only true God, and that all nations were to be blessed in Abraham’s seed. But they could not be required to believe what had not been announced to them: namely, that those blessings were to be fulfilled in Christ in this manner or order. “For if they had known,” says the Apostle, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II).

What had they “known”? “The wisdom,” he says, “which we speak among the perfect; yet not the wisdom of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are passing away. But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which has been hidden, which God predestined before the ages for his glory, and which none of the rulers of this age knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (ibid.).

Thus we receive and read both this sacrifice of the Paschal lamb and all the other things which, as the Apostle says, “happened to them as figures” (I Cor. X), as actual prophecies or promises of the Christ who was to come, closed beneath seals which only that same Lamb of God could open (Apoc. V). This he did after he rose from the dead, as the Evangelist says: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke XXIV). The mystery of his passion was prefigured in such figures because the world could not have contained it if it had then been foretold in plain words, nor would such a manifestation of the Spirit have been given beneficially at that time.

## CHAPTER V. On John’s testimony, “Behold the Lamb of God,” and what is signified by the command that the lamb be sacrificed at the full moon

In this figure of the lamb, the nature of the reality contained within it is most clearly displayed by John, who, pointing to Christ with his finger, says: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). For when he says this, he surely—as the “burning and shining lamp” (John V)—illuminates for us that evening on which the whole multitude of the children of Israel sacrificed in this rite the lamb of which we have spoken; and he declares openly in the true light all that was done there in darkness. All things are splendid; all things are full of divine meaning.

First, the full moon itself at which the lamb is sacrificed mystically signifies that fullness of time of which the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of children” (Gal. IV). For in the fullness of time—that is, when the number of the elect, awaiting their redemption in infernal Egypt, had already been largely completed—the Son of God came; then the Lamb of God came to take away the sins of the world.

What of the fact that it is sacrificed not before but after the spring equinox? Certainly from the spring equinox onward the day begins to overcome the night, for before that time we have longer darkness and shorter light. Thus this too is a mystery: from the sacrifice of Christ, the unstained and spotless Lamb, the light of righteousness began to overcome the darkness of sins; for previously the night of sins was long and deep, while the light of legal righteousness was brief and clouded.

And does not the spring mildness of the month Nisan, that is, April—when the earth flowers anew and the whole world, after winter as though after old age, grows young again—teach a rational person that, renewed in the spirit of the mind, green with faith, joyful in hope, and flowering with charity, he ought to participate in the spiritual feast of the Paschal Lamb?

## CHAPTER VI. That Christ, the true Lamb, according to the mystery of the law, entered the city on the tenth day and instituted the sacrament of eating his body and drinking his blood on the evening of the fourteenth day
Accordingly, this true Lamb carefully fulfilled in every respect the very time of his sacrifice which he had prescribed for the figurative lamb. In the first month, on the tenth day of the month—when, according to the Law, the lamb was taken into the houses of the Jews—he entered the holy city of Jerusalem, [Col. 0613C] led along by crowds; and for as long as, again according to the Law, it was to be kept, so long did he remain about that same city and its Temple: that is, until the fourteenth day of the same month, chewing over the herb of holy Scripture and meanwhile, with unceasing bleating, inviting his hearers to the pastures of eternal life. At last, on the fourteenth day, toward evening, when he had eaten that lamb of the old Passover with his disciples, then he himself, the Lamb of the new sacrifice, immediately to be seized and led away to be sacrificed, already agonizing in the anguish of his Passion, first sacrificed himself to God the Father with his own hands, taking bread and wine and, by a wondrous and ineffable power of sanctification, transforming them into the sacrament of his body and blood. [Col. 0613D]

For when he was afterwards crucified and died by the hands of sinners, that same Lamb at once became the salvation of all, past and present. He descended also to those who were held in the lower Egypt—that is, in the darkness of hell—and who had been gathered there through the five preceding ages of the world. Thus it is rightly established that the lamb was kept for five days, namely from the tenth to the fourteenth day of the month, because from the time when the first Abel offered a lamb as a type of this same Son of God, five ages of the world elapsed, at whose end this true Lamb of God was to be sacrificed.

Immediately, I say, when the Son of God was killed by the hands of the ungodly, the kingdom of death was destroyed and the captivity of God’s people was loosed. The Egyptians could not hold them, [Col. 0614A] because the power of Christ’s blood overwhelmed those Egyptians, together with their prince the devil, ruler of death, just as the deep of the sea engulfed the Egyptian men and their king Pharaoh with his chariots.

But the fact that the supreme High Priest himself offered his body and blood with his own hands under the appearance of bread, as has been said, and said, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22), is the salvation of those held in this life, for whom Egypt is this world and true captivity is ignorance of God under the devil, prince of the world. For unless he had instituted this sacrament of his body and blood together with the mystery of baptism, in which there is a likeness of his death, his death would have profited none of us who did not yet exist, nor any of the Gentiles who then existed and were going after dumb idols, as they were then led (1 Cor. 12), when Christ died once for our sins. For in that hour he washed from sins only those whom his death found faithful, whether dead or alive.

Therefore let us spiritually measure the lawful rite of eating the body and drinking the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ by the rite of that figurative lamb, to the glory and honor of this true Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world.

## CHAPTER VII. What is meant by: “Let each one take a lamb for his families and households”; how the Church celebrates this yearly and daily.

“On the tenth day of this month,” he says, “let each one take a lamb for his families and households, and you shall keep [Col. 0614C] it until the fourteenth day, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening.”

All Israel—that is, the Church of God—does this in a solemn rite, when, upon the return of the season of the year in which Christ suffered, five days beforehand it imitates, with a reverent procession or reception and with sung praises, his entrance into the holy city and the meeting of the children with palm branches (Matt. 21). The only difference is that, whatever weekday the tenth moon may fall on—which according to the Hebrews is the tenth day of the month—or the fourteenth moon, which is the fourteenth day of the month, it nevertheless always celebrates this meeting in procession on the first day of the week, that is, the Lord’s Day; his death on the sixth day; and likewise his resurrection on the first day. Thus the day once consecrated by his death and resurrection may remain holy through all years as the memorial of his death and resurrection.

But for the sacrifice or eating of the Lamb, not one evening but the whole year is acceptable to the holy Church. On whatever day, in whatever house of Israel one wishes to sacrifice or eat, the mystery of this Scripture must be observed. “But if the number is too small,” he says, “so that it is not sufficient to eat the lamb, he shall take his neighbor, who is joined to his household,” and so forth.

Here “number” must almost certainly be understood mystically, as in the Psalm where the Prophet says: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that [Col. 0615A] I may know what is lacking to me” (Ps. 38). For, to speak in terms of the present subject, a person’s number is sufficient when the one who eats the Lamb is able to penetrate its mysteries. But who is so qualified for this? Who has advanced so far beyond infancy and gathered so great a multitude of good days that he lacks nothing for receiving such wholly solid food? Therefore, whenever we sacrifice this Lamb, rightly confessing our own insufficiency because we cannot grasp his whole mystery, we take a neighbor joined to our household: namely, the choir of apostles and martyrs, who through the same faith are near to the Christian family.

Indeed, we never presume to eat without inviting them. For we say: “United in communion with and venerating the memory, first, of the glorious ever-Virgin Mary, Mother of God, and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs.” [Col. 0615B] This is as though we said: We sacrifice and eat the Lamb of God in the same faith in which the Virgin conceived and bore him, which the holy apostles preached, and for which the blessed martyrs suffered. Thus, having taken our neighbors with us, through God’s grace we are sufficient for eating the Lamb; for even if we cannot comprehend his whole mystery, it is enough that we hold no view concerning him contrary to the apostolic faith.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the statement: “The lamb shall be without blemish, a male of one year.” And what it means to take a kid.

[Col. 0615C] “It shall be,” he says, “without blemish, a male of one year.” Blemish is sin. But he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. 53; 1 Pet. 2). Therefore it shall be “without blemish,” that is, “holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners” (Heb. 7), one in whom there is no iniquity.

Yet innocence alone would have little glory if there were not also strength for performing the works of perfect righteousness. Therefore it shall also be “male.” For “male” means strong, because he admits nothing feminine—that is, soft or unstable. Thus in the Apocalypse it is said of the great woman that “she bore a male son who was to rule the nations with a rod of iron” (Rev. 12).

It is further added that it shall be “of one year.” Of one year means perfect; for we receive perfection from him, as he himself testifies in the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the broken-hearted, and to preach forgiveness to captives and opening to those who are shut in; to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God” (Isa. 61; Luke 4). [Col. 0615D] He says “the acceptable year” for those whom he has prepared for glory, and “the day of vengeance” for those whom he has appointed for wrath. For by “acceptable” or “pleasing year” he means full acceptance, which the Apostle also proclaims in these words: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6), and so forth.

Of the fullness of that year—indeed, of our year as well—it is said to him through the Psalmist’s mouth: “You will bless the crown of the year [Col. 0616A] of your goodness” (Ps. 64); that is, when all flesh comes to you to be rewarded in that length of eternal days. And because he who had no sins of his own bore the sins of others, the Law continues and says: “According to the same rite you shall take also a kid.” For just as he is rightly prefigured by the lamb because of his own innocence, so he is rightly prefigured by the kid because of the iniquities of us all which God laid upon him.

Whether it is a lamb or a kid that is sacrificed in either case, it is one and the same Christ in mystery: clean from sins of his own, because he has none, but to be offered for the sins of others. Or he is a kid—that is, a sinner—in the false estimation of men; but in the true and most genuine likeness of innocence, he is a lamb. Considering both, the prophet says: “And we thought him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled; but he was wounded for our transgressions and crushed for our crimes” (Isa. 53). “And you shall keep him until the fourteenth day of this month.” This has already been discussed.

## CHAPTER IX. What it means to sacrifice the lamb at evening, first to mark the doorposts with its blood, and then to eat its flesh.

“The whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening.” Evening is rightly called the present age of the world, in which we are, “upon whom,” as the Apostle says, “the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10). The “whole multitude of the children of Israel” is the whole body [Col. 0616C] of believers. Wherever it may be spread throughout the world, it is one Lamb that it sacrifices in so many places, one bread that it breaks, one Christ whose flesh it eats and whose blood it drinks—provided that, in a spiritual sense, it bears the testimony of catholic faith which follows:

“They shall take,” he says, “of the blood, and put it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels of the houses in which they shall eat him.” What the blood of the Lamb is, we have learned not merely by hearing but by drinking. This blood is put upon both doorposts when it is drawn not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart. For the blood of the Lamb is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his Passion is received by the mouth for redemption and is also considered with an attentive mind for imitation. Whoever receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he is not yet willing to imitate his Passion has put the blood on only one doorpost. [Col. 0616D]

It must also be put upon the lintels of the houses. For what do we understand spiritually by houses but our minds, in which we dwell by thought? The lintel of such a house is the intention itself, which presides over action. Therefore, one who directs the intention of his thought toward imitation of the Lord’s Passion puts the Lamb’s blood upon the lintel of his house. Or, indeed, our houses are our bodies themselves, in which we dwell as long as we live. And we put the Lamb’s blood on the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of his Passion on our forehead.

Another interpretation: “They shall take of the blood of the lamb,” and so forth. It should be noted that the house must first be marked with the Lamb’s blood, and only then may its flesh be eaten in it. This is truly lawful and necessary, and it cannot be done worthily otherwise. For each person must first be baptized into the death of the Lamb, that is, of Christ; first, I say, be planted together in the likeness of his death, so that he may also be in that of his resurrection (Rom. 6). Thus, after the house has been consecrated, one may at last partake within of the life-giving table.

There are three marks of the blood: two on the two doorposts and a third on the lintel. For we are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: three names, or three persons, but one God. And when confession of this threefold name is adorned by faith in Christ’s Passion, the two doorposts of one entrance together with the lintel are inscribed with the Lamb’s blood. [Col. 0617A]

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 0617B] How the statement, “You shall not eat of it anything raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire,” is to be observed in the sacrament of the altar.

“And they shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with fire. You shall not eat of it anything raw or boiled in water, but only roasted with fire.” We eat after the house has been marked: that is, after each person has been consecrated through baptism and cleansed from the stain of the old food by which the human race perished, the body and blood of Christ are given, so that by this food one may not wish proudly to become as God but may humbly deserve to be adopted into the grace of God’s children.

For we eat the lamb at night—we who now receive the Lord’s body in the sacrament—because we still do not see one another’s consciences. “The flesh,” he says, [Col. 0617C] “roasted with fire”: that is, cooked through by the suffering of the Passion. Since the very force of the Passion makes him stronger for resurrection, the Psalmist says in his person: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. 21). For what is a potsherd before fire but soft clay? But fire acts upon it so that it may be hardened. Thus the strength of his humanity dried up like a potsherd, because from the fire of Passion it grew into the strength of incorruption.

Moreover, because the Virgin conceived him by the Holy Spirit, who is eternal fire, and he himself through the same Holy Spirit, as the Apostle says, offered himself as a living sacrifice to the living God (Eph. 5), he is roasted on the altar by that same fire: for by the operation of the Holy Spirit the bread becomes Christ’s body and the wine becomes his blood. But human wisdom does not grasp this. Therefore that which is not so much wisdom as curiosity is repelled when the text reiterates: “You shall not eat of it anything raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted with fire.” [Col. 0617D]

To eat it “raw” is nothing other than to judge it according to what appears; and to eat it “boiled in water” is to wish to determine carnally how it comes about. But “you shall eat,” it says, “only roasted with fire”: that is, you shall attribute everything to the operation of the Holy Spirit, whose effect is not to destroy or corrupt the substance that he takes for his purposes, but, while the good of the substance remains what it was, invisibly to add what it was not.

> **Note:** [Col. 0617D] This opinion was later rejected at the Lateran Council under Innocent III. For the substance of bread and [Col. 0618D] wine does not remain, but is converted into the body and blood of Christ. Therefore the comparison cited is not accepted.

Just as God the Word did not destroy human nature when, by his operation, he joined it from the Virgin’s womb to the unity of his person, so he does not change or destroy the substance of bread and wine, as regards their outward appearance subject to the five senses, when he joins them to the unity of the same body that hung upon the cross and of the same blood that he poured out from his side. [Col. 0618A]

Likewise, as the Word sent down from on high became flesh, not by being changed into flesh but by assuming flesh, so bread and wine, both raised up from below, become Christ’s body and blood—not by being changed into the taste of flesh or the horror of blood, but by invisibly assuming the reality of both immortal substances, namely the divine and the human, which are in Christ. Therefore, just as we rightly and catholically confess as God the man taken from the Virgin who hung upon the cross, so we truly call that which we receive from the holy [Col. 0618B] altar Christ, and proclaim it the Lamb of God.

## CHAPTER XI. What unleavened breads with wild lettuces signify.

“And unleavened breads with wild lettuces.” One of these requirements, namely that concerning unleavened bread, we observe both in reality and in mystery: we use unleavened bread to make Christ’s body, and mystically purge out from ourselves the old leaven—the leaven of malice and wickedness—according to the Apostle’s command (1 Cor. 5). But the other requirement, concerning wild lettuces, we consider only spiritually, since the author of this sacrament did not use them bodily, but merely blessed bread and wine [Col. 0618C] and gave them to his disciples.

It is therefore remarkable by what authority the custom of the Greeks has become established: they demand leavened bread and reject unleavened bread from Christ’s sacrament, although no one should doubt that our Lord originally performed it only with unleavened bread. For on that night, by the decree of the Law, leavened bread could be found in none of the houses of Israel; nor, if he had kept leavened bread with him, ought he to have supplied his enemies a lawful ground for accusation, when the Law said: “Whoever eats leavened bread, that person shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether from the sojourners or from the natives of the land” (Exod. 12). But long ago the Roman See argued this matter abundantly against them.

Yet we have an evident example from the apostles themselves, who first did this, for eating unleavened bread and wild lettuces spiritually. For they purged out the old leaven and were a new lump, feasting upon the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5), because Christ’s present Passion cleansed them from all the sins by which the corrupt first human being had leavened the whole mass of his race. For in that most holy supper this true Lamb of God said to them: “You are already clean because of the word that I have spoken [Col. 0618D] to you” (John 15). Unless you had heard and believed my word, you would certainly not be cleansed through this Passion of mine.

He said “you are clean” as if it were already past, in the same manner as he later said there to the Father, “And now I am no longer in the world” (John 17), although he had not yet accomplished, but had begun to accomplish, his passing from this world. [Col. 0619A]

They also ate the wild lettuces, which are very bitter, because they were certainly already in the greatest sorrow on account of what was being said, and throughout the whole three days they shared very painfully in the bitterness of his Passion. Following their example, we eat the Lamb’s flesh with wild lettuces when, receiving the Redeemer’s body, we afflict ourselves for our sins, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe away from the stomach of the mind the unhealthy moisture of a perverse life.

## CHAPTER XII. What it is to consume the whole lamb, its head together with its feet and entrails.

[Col. 0619B] “You shall consume the head together with the feet and entrails.” All may do this together, but no one can fulfil it individually. For in both great and small households there are the perfect, for whom solid food such as the bony head is suitable; and there are also little ones, whose weak teeth can scarcely chew even the soft entrails.

To consume the lamb’s head is manfully to receive the lofty words concerning Christ’s divinity—for example: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). To consume the feet is not to be ignorant also that “the Word became flesh.” To consume the entrails with the feet is eagerly to receive his hidden and mystical commands, or indeed to turn each of his acts or sufferings of weakness to the use of virtue—for example, that he hungered, wept, was sorrowful, and, above all, was tempted, “in every respect similarly, yet without sin” (Heb. 5). [Col. 0619C]

When it says “consume,” what else does it do but rebuke the sluggishness of our laziness? We neither investigate his mysteries and words ourselves nor willingly hear them when spoken by others. Therefore the whole must be consumed while we have time. For it says: “Nothing of it shall remain until morning.” His sayings must be examined with great care, so that, before the day of resurrection appears, all his commandments may be penetrated by understanding and practice during this night of the present life.

But because it is very difficult for nothing to remain of it—that is, for every saying of the Lamb to be understood and every one of his mysteries to be penetrated—it rightly adds: “But if anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.” We burn with fire what remains of the Lamb when we humbly reserve to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand or penetrate concerning the mystery of his Incarnation, so that no one may presumptuously dare either to despise or to declare definitively what he does not understand. He hands it over to fire when he reserves it to the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0619D]

## CHAPTER XIII. What it is to have loins girded, shoes on the feet, and staffs in the hands.

Since, then, we have learned how the Passover is to be eaten, let us now recognize by what sort of persons it should be eaten. “Thus you shall eat it: You shall gird your loins.” What is understood by the loins except carnal pleasure? [Col. 0620A] Hence the Psalmist asks, saying: “Burn my loins” (Ps. 25). For if he did not know that sensual pleasure is in the loins—that is, that lust is in his loins—he would never have asked that they be burned. Since the devil’s power prevailed most strongly over the human race through lust, the Lord says of him to Job: “His power is in his loins” (Job 40).

Therefore whoever eats the Passover must have girded loins, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through any vices, but may subdue pleasures and restrain fleshly lust. For one who is still subject to corruption through lack of self-control does not know what the solemnity of incorruption is. These things are hard for some, but narrow is the gate that leads to life (Matt. 7). Yet we already have many examples of the continent. [Col. 0620B]

Hence it is well further added: “You shall have shoes on your feet.” For what are our feet but our deeds? And what are shoes but the skins of dead animals? Shoes protect the feet. But what are the dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected, except the ancient Fathers who preceded us to the eternal homeland? When we look upon their examples, we protect the feet of our deeds. To have shoes on one’s feet is to look to the lives of the dead and to guard one’s steps from the wound of sin.

“Holding staffs in your hands.” What does the Law signify by staffs except pastoral care? It should be noted that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterwards to hold staffs, because those who undertake pastoral care ought already to know how to subdue the inconstancy of lust in their own body, lest, while preaching strong things to others, they themselves feebly yield to soft desires. [Col. 0620C]

It is therefore well added: “And you shall eat in haste.” Note also the word “in haste.” God’s commandments, the mysteries of the Redeemer, and the joys of the heavenly homeland must be known with haste; and the commandments of life must be fulfilled with haste. For although we know that today it is still permitted to do good, we do not know whether it will be permitted tomorrow.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the statement: “For it is the Passover, that is, the passing-over of the Lord,” and the striking down of the firstborn.

He then gives the reason for doing all that has here been commanded: “For it is the Passover, that is, the passing-over [Col. 0620D] of the Lord; and I shall pass through the land of Egypt that night, and shall strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man even to beast; and I shall execute judgments upon all the gods of Egypt: I am the Lord. But the blood shall be a sign for you in the houses where you are; and I shall see the blood and pass over you, and no destroying plague shall be upon you when I strike the land of Egypt.”

Therefore, he says, you shall mark your doorposts with the lamb’s blood and eat its flesh in haste in this manner. It is, indeed, the lamb’s flesh; for it adds that “it is the Passover, that is, the passing-over of the Lord.” “Of the Lord” is not in the word *phase* [Passover], but has been added to the interpretation because it must necessarily be understood. For the Lord himself goes on and says: “I shall pass through the land of Egypt that night.”

What is meant by “I shall see the blood” has already been discussed above. But movement from place to place does not belong to God, since he is confined by no place but is everywhere. Thus when he says, “I shall pass through,” it is spoken figuratively in accordance with the events of that time: that is, I shall go forth like a giant, rushing in strength against the enemy and, after my departure, leaving behind the traces of my victory full of lamentations.

Hence the Book of Wisdom says: “For while all things kept quiet silence and the night in its course had reached the middle of its way, your almighty word, leaping down from heaven from the royal thrones, came as a stern warrior into the midst of the land of destruction; bearing your sharp sword, your unfeigned command, [Col. 0621A] and standing, he filled all things with death” (Wis. 18).

But the holy Evangelist says of that passing-over which is prefigured by this one: “Before the feast day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John 13). For that is truly the passing-over of the Lord—indeed, the passing-over of us all. For when he passed from this world to the Father, we too, by the grace of that same Father, passed from bonds to freedom and from darkness to the opening of our eyes.

He passed from this world, which itself is in a certain sense called Egypt; he passed through lower Egypt, that is, hell, which, according to the name of Egypt, is truly a dark and dreadful place. And all whom he found there worthy children of Israel, marked by faith in his blood—from righteous Abel, who first offered a lamb as a type of him, to Iatron, whom he marked with his own blood in the very hour of his passing-over—he delivered them all, destroying Pharaoh’s firstborn: that is, the sin of the first transgression, called original sin, which the devil’s persuasion generated. [Col. 0621C]

Therefore the doorposts must be marked eagerly and the lamb’s flesh eaten speedily, for the Lord has passed beyond and will not return. For, having died once, he rose again, and “he dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom. 6). Be content with this passing-over of his, and mark the doorposts, all children of Israel; for it is not permitted to hope for another passing-over. The same Lord will indeed come, but he will no longer pass through the Egypt of hell; he will not again die for those who are now commanded to depart in darkness.

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 0621D] What it means mystically to eat unleavened bread for seven days, and what is the first day on which leaven must not be found in the houses.

“But you shall have this day as a memorial, and you shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, with perpetual observance. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread.” A splendid memorial, a great and magnificent instrument of remembrance: not to eat leavened bread for seven days. That this must be guarded against with the utmost diligence is confirmed by what follows: “On the first day there shall be no leavened bread in your houses”—so that, while it is present, one may not the more easily fall into transgression.

The first day of unleavened bread is the fourteenth of the month. What then? Does God care about leaven in breads? Or does he speak because of the sin of diabolical pride, by which the human race was leavened in the transgression of its first parent? Therefore, for seven days—that is, throughout our whole life—let us beware of this leaven. By grace it comes about that it is not found on the first day; thereafter it is our responsibility that it not be corrupted again.

For on the first day of our solemnity, that is, as soon as each of us is marked with Christ’s blood—that is, baptized—into his death, all the leaven of old sin has been emptied out; none of its traces remains and it cannot be found. Therefore, with a great threat, he repeats the prohibition again and again: “Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall perish from Israel, from the first day to the seventh day.” [Col. 0622B] The order of the words is: Whatever soul eats leavened bread from the first day to the seventh day shall perish from Israel.

And immediately it adds: “The first day and the eighth day of this feast shall be equally venerable.” For the eighth day divided itself into the first day and seven days. For it says afterwards: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month at evening.” Clearly, in saying this it has included eight days.

Immediately applying a still stronger bond, it declares: “For seven days leaven shall not be found in your houses.” It immediately adds: “Whoever eats leavened bread, that person shall perish from the assembly of Israel, whether from the sojourner or from the native of the land.” Without delay, as if running under a single breath, it concludes: “You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread.”

What is that first day, except the one of which the Psalmist says, “This is the day which the Lord has made”—understood: made to dawn upon us—adding: “Let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Ps. 117). This day is plainly Christ, the great and splendid day in whom we came out of Egypt, in whom we were called out of darkness and led into marvelous light (1 Pet. 2). Therefore he says: “The first day shall be holy and solemn.”

Likewise the Psalmist says of the same day: “Appoint the day in the dense throng, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117): that is, being established in the density and abundance of good works, be free from sins in accordance with the day that has dawned upon us, until you come to the knowledge of his divinity, in whose faith, as upon an altar, we offer to God whatever good is in us. [Col. 0622D]

Therefore, he says, the first day shall be holy and solemn. He who was like a lamb slain through the weakness of man is himself the true day, shining with eternal brightness through the power of God. Our seven days follow this day in uninterrupted celebration, so that the seventh too may be venerable with the same festivity; for our whole life must be conducted so that it may be completed in him from whom it began.

He gives the reason why so great a feast must be carefully observed: “For on that same day,” he says, “I shall lead your army out of the land of Egypt.” He significantly says “your army,” because we leave the land of Egypt, the house of ancient slavery, not for leisure or amusements but to fight against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. 2); for it is the time when the kingdom of God suffers violence and we seize it by forceful action (Matt. 11).

Therefore he adds: “You shall do no work in it except those things that concern eating, and you shall observe unleavened bread.” For those who fight for the kingdom of God must care for nothing of the whole world; but, according to the Apostle, having food and clothing, they should be content with these (1 Tim. 6), though preferring and seeking first the bread of God’s word, and meanwhile observing without any forgetfulness the unleavened bread of which much has been said.

## CHAPTER XVI. What it means to mark the doorposts with blood by means of a bundle of hyssop, and not to go outside until morning; and how it is one thing to keep this word and another to observe these ceremonies.

“Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them: Go, take an animal for each of your families, and sacrifice the Passover; dip a bundle of hyssop in the blood which is on the threshold, and sprinkle from it the lintel and both doorposts.” He used the general term “animal,” meaning either kid or lamb; whichever a person took, as stated above, he would fulfill the command by observing the prescribed rite: “Dip,” he says, “a bundle of hyssop in the blood which is in the basin.” He spoke as though the blood were already on the threshold [Col. 0623C], and did not say, “which you shall put on the threshold.” Thus he left uncertain where and how the blood was to be placed on the threshold: whether the lamb ought to be slaughtered there, or whether it ought to be poured out there in some other way.

But concerning the blood of the true Lamb, Christ the Son of God, it is certain that it was not hidden away or kept within, but set openly before the whole world, 192 so that whoever wishes to mark his house, in order to be delivered from the hand of the destroying devil, may find it at once and that salvation may swiftly come to him—provided that he does this: let him take a bundle of hyssop and dip it in the blood; that is, let him recite the Creed, placing his entire hope in the saving passion of Christ alone, and from it make three marks on the two doorposts [Col. 0623D] and on the lintel—being baptized, namely, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

For hyssop is a lowly herb: it grows in rocky places and reduces swelling of the lungs. It signifies faith and the humility of Christ’s passion, through which the swelling of pride is reduced—the pride by which the first human being, corrupted, swelled up against his Creator. Hoping for this, the Psalmist said: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [51]). Therefore hyssop dipped in the blood of the lamb, by which the house is marked, is humility of mind joined with faith in Christ’s passion, in which every believer is baptized.

“Let none of you,” he says, “go out of the door of his house until morning.” Why? “For the Lord will pass through, striking [Col. 0624A] the Egyptians.” This too we must observe with the greatest vigilance: that until morning—that is, until the end of this nocturnal life of ours—we remain within the bounds of the Catholic Church, and that no one be found to have burst tumultuously outside through heresies or schisms. For whoever is found outside will be reckoned an Egyptian, and will be struck together with the Egyptians by the scourge of the Lord as he passes through.

“And when he sees the blood on the lintel, he will pass over the door and will not permit the destroyer to enter your houses and harm you.” This has already been discussed above: as this passage shows, although the Lord is said to strike the Egyptians, he does not strike them himself, but gives the destroying angel—the evil angel—the power to strike.

Finally he concludes thus: “Keep this ordinance as a statute for yourself and your children forever. And when you enter the land which the Lord will give you, as he has promised you, you shall observe these ceremonies,” etc. It may perhaps seem that in saying, “Keep this ordinance,” he repeated the same thing when he said, “You shall observe these ceremonies”; but this is not so. For in this place *verbum*, “word,” that is, rational meaning, differs from ceremonies as much as what is signified, or the meaning, differs from signs and letters. Ceremonies are indeed signs—that is, figures or shadows of things to come; but the word is the rational meaning or truth of the sacrament, fulfilled in Christ, as we have already said to the extent possible.

Rightly, therefore, when he said, “Keep this ordinance as a statute,” he added, “forever.” But where [Col. 0624B] he said, “You shall observe these ceremonies,” he did not add, “forever.” For all carnal ceremonies that were given had a temporary status: they were imposed because of transgressions until the appointed time, until that should come which was promised under them—the word of the Lord, which remains forever. But how the statement spoken through the prophet Jeremiah, “For I did not speak to your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices” (Jer. 7), is not contrary to their institution, must be explained more fully elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XVII. What is suggested by the fact that the firstborn were not slain at midday, [Col. 0624D] but at midnight.

“And it came to pass in the middle of the night that the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat upon his throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, and every firstborn of cattle. And Pharaoh rose in the night, and all his servants, and all Egypt; and there arose a great cry in Egypt. For there was no house in which there did not lie a dead person.”

A great scourge and a remarkable continuity of the striking are indicated when Scripture says, “from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat upon his throne, to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison.” Thus neither kings escape the wrath of God because of the height of their towers, nor proud poor people because of the obscurity of their huts [Col. 0625A].

It has already been said above that the Lord’s striking of every firstborn through the sacrifice of the lamb signifies that God destroyed the original sin of the world in the passion of Christ his Son. Yet, while preserving this same signification, it could have occurred at midday, while all were awake. Why, then, did it please him rather to kill them at midnight while they slept? Clearly, so that the historical example might also benefit sleepers and arouse them to vigilance, knowing that whoever, after the example of the Egyptians, stores up wrath for himself, will likewise receive unforeseen vengeance after their example.

Thus the universal judgment will also come unexpectedly upon the hard-hearted and unrepentant, like a snare and like a thief. Therefore the Lord compared his coming, by which the wicked are to perish, to midnight; for example, when in the parable of the wise and foolish virgins he says: “At midnight a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25).

He himself also rose at midnight, and, as an example of the distinction between the godly and the ungodly, he soothed the devout women by an angelic vision and address, but terrified the impious and foolish guards and rendered them as dead, preceded by a great earthquake (Matt. 28). Accordingly, through the mouth of the Psalmist the holy Church says: “At midnight I rose to confess you” (Ps. 118 [119]). That time has been assigned to sacred vigils and to most salutary confession, so that, confessing the Lord in the deep night, we may remind ourselves not to be unprepared for that hour which cannot be foreseen [Col. 0625B].

That great cry which arose in Egypt therefore beneficially troubles our inward hearing, so that we may not sleep like the Egyptians, but may keep watch and be sober. “For those who sleep,” says the Apostle, “sleep at night; and those who get drunk are drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5).

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Pharaoh’s saying, “As you depart, bless me,” and on the fact that those who went out by night transgressed the literal law.

“Having summoned Moses and Aaron by night, he said: Rise, go out from among my people, you and your children. Go, sacrifice to the Lord, as you say. Take your sheep and [Col. 0625D] your herds, as you asked, and as you depart bless me.”

If he said these things after summoning Moses and Aaron by night, how can the earlier statement, “Let none of you go out of the door of his house until morning,” stand according to the letter? Yet it was morning for them when, after midnight had already 193 passed, they were summoned and compelled to go out, and the light of present joy was dawning.

But those plainly transgressed this law who, on the night when they had sacrificed the lamb according to the same rite, went out to seize the Lord Jesus. Therefore prophetic Scripture, in the one traitor—who, having received the morsel, immediately went out, though it was night (John 13)—thus secretly but gravely accuses them: “His heart gathered iniquity to itself, and he was going out” (Ps. 40 [41]).

“Your sheep and your herds,” he says—understand, lest there be any further reason for delay, as before—“take, as you asked, and as you depart bless me.” At last the Egyptian king of hard heart spoke something gentle. Indeed, above he had once and twice said, “I have sinned,” but he did not say, “As you depart, forgive me”; now, however, he even says, “As you depart, bless me.”

Was not this also to come to pass: that the proud one, of whom Pharaoh here bore the type, should speak gentle words? Certainly the Lord speaks thus of him to blessed Job: “Will he multiply supplications to you, or speak soft words to you?” (Job 40 [41]). For who doubts that he spoke soft words to him who plundered hell, when, while Christ was still living in the body, he cried out: “What have you to do with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy [Col. 0626A] us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God” (Luke 4).

Nor does the Prophet say of him without reason: “You have humbled the proud one like one wounded” (Ps. 88 [89]). For just as a proud man, however rigidly he may stand before the blow, nevertheless descends from his swelling under the stroke of a wound, lays aside his words, and lowers his neck, so the king of pride, the devil, however confidently he had formerly spoken as a strong man armed, when he felt one stronger, laid down his weapons, gave back his spoils (Matt. 12), and spoke soft words not from compassion but from pain. And at the final judgment, he himself—the head of the wicked—will speak still softer words with his whole body.

“But I will not spare him,” says the Lord, “his mighty words and those composed for supplication” (Job 41 [41]), because repentance is late and unworthy when torment extorts it [Col. 0626B].

These things have been said so that, in the fitting admiration of those who praise the Lord, that most beautiful miracle may not be lacking: that a little lamb conquered and crushed the greatest lion, and pressed the mouth of the proud one so that it uttered gentle speech.

Moreover, the statement here, “And the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded; and they asked the Egyptians for silver and gold vessels and very many garments, and they despoiled the Egyptians,” must not be understood as though they first asked for these things when they were being compelled to leave. For the Egyptians would not have lent them to people departing. Rather it should be understood as if it said: “They asked,” that is, they carried away what they had asked for. The just cause of this spoil, to be imitated spiritually by us, has also been discussed above.

## CHAPTER XIX. What it means that a mixed and innumerable multitude went up with them.

“And the children of Israel set out from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men, besides little children. And also a mixed and innumerable multitude went up with them, sheep and herds, and very many animals of diverse kinds.”

Although God was not well pleased with many of them, since their bodies were strewn in the wilderness (1 Cor. 10), nevertheless the name “children of Israel” and the perfect number, namely a hundredfold six—that is, six hundred—signify only those who come to Christ by fleeing this world in such a way that they are worthy both of the grace or adoption of the children of God and of being all numbered with the Father [Col. 0627A].

But the “mixed and innumerable multitude” that went up with them, precisely in being innumerable, bore the type of those very many who come to the faith only in name and confess in word alone that they know Christ. Of such persons the Prophet says in the Psalm: “I proclaimed and spoke; they were multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39 [40]).

Further, what follows—“They baked the dough which they had brought from Egypt, having previously kneaded it, and made unleavened cakes baked under ashes; for they could not allow it to be leavened, since the Egyptians were compelling them to leave and allowing them no delay”—means the same as if it said: Even if they had not been forbidden leaven, the urgency of those compelling them to leave was so great that they could not have let it rise.

This manner of speech accords with the frequently stated mystery of unleavened bread: namely, that our coming forth unleavened, that is, sincere, from the darkness of our sins must be ascribed not to our own effort but to divine grace, which compelled the spiritual Egyptians swiftly to withdraw with their leaven [Col. 0627B].

## CHAPTER XX. On the four hundred and thirty years during which the children of Israel dwelt in Egypt, and from what point they should be reckoned.

“Now the dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they remained in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years. When these were completed, on the same day all the army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.”

If one looks only to the four generations, this cannot stand, since the children of Israel went out from Egypt in the fourth generation [Col. 0627C]—even if Levi, Kohath, and Amram had not begotten sons before reaching one hundred years, and Moses, the fourth from Levi, had already stood before Pharaoh as a centenarian. This is especially so because Levi and the other sons of Jacob were already grown men, and each entered Egypt with his wife and children.

From what beginning, then, should we reckon these four hundred and thirty years? We have the testimony of the Apostle. After saying to the Galatians, “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.
