He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though to many, but as though to one: ‘And to your seed,’ who is Christ” (Gal. 3), he immediately adds: “This is what I mean: the covenant confirmed by God, the law which came four hundred and thirty years later does not invalidate, so as to nullify the promise” (ibid.).

Therefore these years must be counted from the promise of God, spoken to Abraham when he was seventy-five years old: “I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you; and in you”—or, as he says elsewhere, “in your seed all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22; Gen. 12). The Apostle calls this word “the covenant confirmed by God” (Gal. 3). We must know that, together with this servitude of the children of Israel, the sojourning of the fathers is also included within the four hundred and thirty years.

And rightly so, for father Abraham himself first sojourned in Egypt after that same promise. On his return it was said to him: “Know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall subject them to servitude and afflict them for four hundred years; for the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet complete up to the present time” (Gen. 15).

Here it should be noted that he did not say, “and they shall afflict them for four hundred and thirty years,” but only “for four hundred years,” since something had already been subtracted from this total from the aforesaid confirmation of the covenant. Thus, from the total of four hundred and thirty years, subtract first the twenty-four years between God’s speaking to Abraham and Isaac’s birth, and the forty years of Isaac before Jacob’s birth. Then subtract the ninety years of Jacob, after which he begot 194 Joseph, and then the one hundred and twenty years of Joseph, during whose life all things prospered; and there remain no more than one hundred and forty-four years for the servitude of the children of Israel, as historians of chronology before us have carefully recorded.

And note carefully that, for the crime which the sons of Jacob committed against their brother, the punishment was repaid to their children tenfold in the third and fourth generation, according to the period of time. For Joseph, sold by them, served fourteen years: he was sixteen years old when sold, while he was thirty when he was brought out of prison and stood before Pharaoh. Fourteen multiplied by ten makes one hundred and forty. Therefore, as stated, the penalty of servitude was returned to them tenfold.

“When these were completed,” he says, “on the same day all the army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.” By this statement Scripture plainly indicates that they did not remain even one day beyond the four hundred and thirty years [Col. 0628B].

## CHAPTER XXI. On the statement, “This night is to be observed for the Lord,” etc., and on the Paschal night of Christians.

“This night is to be observed for the Lord, when he brought them out of the land of Egypt. All the children of Israel must observe it throughout their generations.”—“This night,” understand, when the lamb was sacrificed and the firstborn of Egypt were slain. Certainly, another was the night in whose morning watch the Lord looked upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, destroyed their army, overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were borne into the deep (Exod. 14).

Yet one night, on account of the events of two nights, was commanded to be observed for the Lord. And rightly so: for it was one and the same deliverance of Israel, begun in the death of the firstborn and completed in the drowning of all the Egyptians. Therefore the holy Roman Church, neither by novel nor presumptuous authority, established that the deeds of two likewise nights should be celebrated in one and the same night: namely, of the one in which Christ was seized and led to death, piercing by his cross Pharaoh’s firstborn—that is, the pride of the devil; and of the other in which, rising from the dead, he brought complete joy to the whole world, both from the redemption of souls, which he obtained by dying, and from the resurrection of bodies, which he obtained by rising [Col. 0628C].

These, I say, are the deeds of two nights which it established should be celebrated in one night, to the praise and glory of the true Lamb, who took away the sins of the world, conquered our death by dying, and restored life by rising. “All the children of Israel,” he says, “must observe it.” Indeed, they do so. All the children of Israel—rather, all the children of God, who had been scattered abroad and gathered into one—after the sacrament of this night, in which Christ the Son of God was slain as a lamb for his children and rose as a lion, celebrate this night everywhere with harmonious rejoicing. They do not doubt that this is the night of which it is written: “Night shall be illumined as day, and night is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. 138 [139]).

Therefore the holy Church celebrates the night equally with the following day as fully as it can: for it rejoices in the evening with the same service of the victorious resurrection as on the following day. It first offers the evening sacrifice, then the morning sacrifice, of so great a solemnity. Why is this? Clearly because there is a first resurrection which illuminates the night, and a second resurrection which illuminates the day.

The first resurrection is the remission of sins, which those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit receive on that Paschal evening, and thus already rise in soul. The second resurrection is the raising of bodies, which has already taken place in Christ and will finally take place in all. But the present Church, which was once night, becomes light through this first resurrection and is illumined like day [Col. 0629A]. Through it each of us, even now while in the body, shines with truth; and after the body’s dissolution, throughout the whole evening of the Sabbath until dawn on the first day of the week (Matt. 28)—which will itself be the eighth day—will be illumined as day, while in the meantime the soul alone keeps Sabbath because it is at rest.

Rightly, therefore, before the dawn of the first day of the week, that Sabbath evening is illumined by the joy of the Paschal sacrifice, with Christ as its leading singer, saying: “Night shall be illumined as day, and night is illumination in my delights.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Lord’s statement: “This is the ordinance of the Passover.”

“And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: This is the ordinance of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it. But every purchased slave shall be circumcised, and then shall eat. A resident alien and a hired servant shall not eat of it. It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not carry any of its flesh outside, nor break one of its bones.”—“This,” he says, “is the ordinance of the Passover.” Truly, it is a holy, just, and good ordinance.

What then? Does it reject the foreigner because of a lowly condition? Certainly this conflicts with the statement, “But every purchased slave shall be circumcised, and then shall eat.” Thus, while the foreigner is free, he shall not eat; but once he has been bought as a slave, he himself shall eat of it. Why? Clearly because, while he is free, after eating the Passover today, a foreigner may tomorrow—or immediately, if he wishes—participate in Egyptian superstition, making no distinction between the two. The same is true of the hired servant, because he has not professed constancy in the Israelite house; therefore he has nothing by which he is bound after having once tasted the Passover [Col. 0629B].

God, then, rejects the foreigner and hired servant not because he is God only of carnal Israel and not of the nations, but because of the wandering license of instability; yet he admits the purchased slave. But it is certain that the ordinance of the spiritual Passover admits no one except the purchased slave—that is, only one who has received through baptism the sacrament of Christ’s purchase. Even if he is already a catechumen, he shall not eat; but, like a hired servant, he shall be separated from the gathering of those who eat, so that he may not even remain in the house while this Passover is sacrificed, while it is eaten by the members of the household of faith.

Likewise, it is unlawful to divide this Passover among persons belonging to another sect—to any heretics or schismatics—even if they say that they have the doorposts of their foreheads marked with the blood of the Lamb. For he says: “It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not carry any of its flesh outside.” This command, according to the letter, necessarily requires what was said above: “But if the number is too small to suffice for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor who is joined to his household,” etc.

But according to the spirit, the unity of the holy Church is more earnestly commended: those who are to eat the Lord’s table must be one house—that is, we must all say the same thing, and there must be no heresies or schisms among us. For then the Lamb is not eaten in one house, but his flesh is carried outside, when it is indiscriminately given to those who rend the unity of faith; for God is not in the division of minds. Therefore, on the present testimony of Scripture, one may confidently say that there is no true sacrifice outside the unity of the Church [Col. 0630A].

“And you shall not break one of its bones.” The holy Evangelist used this testimony thus: “But when they came to Jesus and saw 195 that he was already dead, they did not break his legs” (John 19). And immediately afterward: “For these things happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of it’” (ibid.). Thus the prophecy is manifest even according to the proper meanings of the words.

Nevertheless, we must also observe this mystically every day, so that we do not break the bone of this sacrament of food and drink—that is, the Word by which he subsists—but preserve it whole and unviolated. For whoever thinks anything perverse concerning the divinity of this Lamb breaks his bone for himself.

Having prescribed that it must be eaten inside and that nothing of its bones is to be carried outside, he finally gives instruction concerning those outside: “And if any of the strangers wishes to enter your settlement and keep the Passover for the Lord, all his males must first be circumcised, and then he shall celebrate it lawfully, and he shall be as a native of the land. But if anyone is not circumcised, he shall not eat of it. The same law shall be for the native and for the resident alien who sojourns among you.”

Therefore whoever is still a stranger and not yet a member of the household of faith—whether pagan, heretic, or even falsely a Jew—must be circumcised for the Lord by the circumcision of heart and ears. This is to enter the Israelite settlement; then he shall eat the flesh of the Lamb, which must not be carried outside the one Catholic Church.

By the native and the resident alien, for whom the law is the same, we may understand the people from the circumcision and the people from the foreskin. The former, from circumcision, is rightly called the native; the latter, from foreskin, the resident alien, for he was formerly “a stranger to the covenants and alien from the commonwealth of Israel” (Eph. 2) [Col. 0630B]. The law is the same for both peoples: both, laying aside every superstition and every righteousness of the flesh, must seek Christ’s grace alone and, through this cornerstone, come together like two walls into one house.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Succoth, that is, tabernacles, and on the two feasts of Passover and Tabernacles.

“All the children of Israel did as the Lord commanded, and on the same day the Lord brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.” In saying, “on the same day the Lord brought them out,” he seeks to recall to memory where these commands, and those which follow, were given: namely, at Succoth, where they first pitched their tents after setting out from Rameses.

For, gathered at Rameses—which is interpreted “the stirring of the moth,” or “thunders of joy,” namely, the place where they put off the moth of servitude and went out into joy—they first pitched their tents there, as stated. Thus the place also received its name from that event. For *Succoth* is interpreted in our language as “tabernacles” or “tents.”

For this reason the Feast of Tabernacles was instituted in the seventh month—not because they came there in the seventh month, but because the one and same joy of the exodus was divided into two feasts: at the beginning of the year, that is, in the first month, the feast of Passover or Unleavened Bread was observed; and in the middle of the year, that is, in the seventh month, the feast of Tabernacles, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, corresponding to the day of the first month on which they came to Succoth and, after the Egyptian workhouses, pitched the tents of their own liberty [Col. 0631A].

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Lord’s statement, “Sanctify to me every firstborn,” etc., and why he added, “that opens the womb.”

(Chapter 13.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of human beings and of cattle. For all things are mine.” And a little later Moses says: “When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanite, you shall set apart for the Lord every firstborn that opens the womb, and whatever is firstborn among your livestock. But every firstborn of your sons you shall redeem with a price.”

This law belongs specifically to firstborn children. But the law which applies alike to firstborn and to those born later is the common law written in Leviticus as follows: “When the days of her purification are completed”—namely, of the woman who has borne a son or a daughter—“for a son or a daughter she shall bring a one-year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin, to the door of the tabernacle of testimony,” etc. “But if her hand cannot find or she cannot afford to offer a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for sin; and the priest shall pray for her, and so she shall be cleansed” (Lev. 12).

Thus the firstborn human being was doubly indebted to the law: first, to be presented to the Lord and redeemed; second, for an offering to be given for him as for the others. In the presentation of the Lord, the Evangelist declares both points in this way: “They took him to Jerusalem,” he says, “to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of Moses: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’” (Luke 2). This concerns the law of the firstborn, because our Lord, being the only-begotten of his mother, is consequently also firstborn—although, conversely, not every firstborn is also only-begotten.

The Evangelist continues: “And to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons” (ibid.). This concerns the law common to mothers, because the law commanded this to be done, without any exception, for a daughter as well as for a son—not for the redemption of the child, but for the cleansing of the mother who had given birth [Col. 0631B].

Moreover, where he says, “But every firstborn of your sons”—understand, not of foreigners or hired servants—“you shall redeem with a price,” this is not so much a command as a permission. For one who redeemed with a price did well indeed. Nevertheless Hannah, who resolved by vow not to redeem Samuel, did better.

Why, then, when he said, “Sanctify to me every firstborn,” did he add, “that opens the womb”? Clearly, so that his intention should not be uncertain. He intends the firstborn of every womb, which is more than the firstborn of a man. For it has often happened, and does happen, that one man has several wives. Therefore, lest anyone suppose that from however many wives a man should owe only one firstborn, he rightly defined his claim by saying, “every firstborn,” and adding, “that opens the womb.”

Moreover, when he says “sanctify,” he means: claim for me by a legal enactment which may not be violated or passed over. What he then says, “You shall redeem the firstborn of an ass with a sheep; but if you do not redeem it, you shall kill it,” contains, together with literal correctness, a pleasing moral sense: namely, that each person should overcome the preceding works of the flesh by the later correction of the spirit. The sin of the flesh is the firstborn of the ass; but almsgiving, by which the preceding sin is redeemed, is rightly called a sheep. “But if you do not redeem it,” 196 he says, “you shall kill it,” because whoever refuses to redeem his sins consigns himself to everlasting death [Col. 0631C].

## CHAPTER XXV. On the law of ceremonies, and on the fact that it did not possess the same authority and permanence as Christ’s commandments, which alone are said to have been written by the finger of God.

“Sanctify to me,” he says, “every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of human beings and cattle; for all are mine. And Moses said to the people: Remember this day on which you went out from Egypt, from the house of bondage,” etc.

It should be noted that, although the Lord said, “Sanctify to me every firstborn,” this messenger of the Lord first speaks other things to the people. He tells them to remember this day when the Lord brings them into the land of the Canaanite, and to keep its worship at the appointed time from days to days: today, in the month of new produce, that is, on the fifteenth day of April, when, according to the mildness of the climate, the first fruits may already be eaten among them. His purpose is that they should carefully observe throughout all years the use of the lamb and unleavened bread, which they had received once.

We say this so that we may know what to answer the Jews who suppose that their carnal ceremonies ought to possess the same authority or permanence as the ten commandments of life written upon the stone tablets. But the Lawgiver himself declared this as the chief distinction regarding those commandments: they were written by the finger of God. He nowhere said this, nor ought he to have said it, concerning ceremonies of this sort, which he knew would be transitory.

And the Apostle, after saying, “This is what I mean: the covenant confirmed by God, the law which came four hundred and thirty years later does not invalidate, so as to nullify the promises” (Gal. 3), immediately says: “Why then the law? It was imposed because of transgressors, until the seed should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (ibid.).

He says that the law of ceremonies was ordained not by the hand or finger of God, but by the hand of Moses the mediator; whereas he declares the covenant confirmed by God. Conversely, Moses says that the commandments of life were written by the finger of God, while he says nothing of the kind concerning the observance of sacrifices or solemnities [Col. 0631D].

Therefore not only here, where Moses, without being commanded, repeats the matter of unleavened bread and gives a law concerning annual feasts, but wherever such institutions are established for that people through the hand of the same mediator—institutions without which the covenant confirmed by God with Abraham stood firm—they must be understood not as commands but as permissions, namely, because of transgressions.

For, as the Apostle most truly says, they were certain bonds imposed because of transgressions, so that, while the people were occupied with the rite of such sacrifices and feasts, they would have no leisure to stray from their God into their own inventions and unlawful idol worship. Therefore God speaks through the prophet to those who trust in them: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But I commanded them this word, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in the way which I commanded you, that it may be well with you’” (Jer. 7).

“I did not speak,” he says, that is, “I did not command.” For whatever Moses commanded concerning such matters as though from my mouth, he commanded not because I ordered it, but because I permitted it. And in David: “Will I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 46 [50]); and many similar passages.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the firstborn sanctified to the Lord, and on the fact that the sons of Levi were reckoned in the carnal priesthood until Christ.

The basis on which He exacts every firstborn He makes clear by adding the reason:

> “When, he says, your son asks you tomorrow, saying, ‘What is this?’ you shall answer him: ‘Because by a strong hand He brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. For when Pharaoh was hardened and would not let us go, the Lord slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of cattle. Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb, and I redeem every firstborn of my sons.’”

All of us who stand as legal experts in this audience of holy laws—or who possess an understanding of truth—agree with the justice of this: it is right that those for whose deliverance the bodily firstborn were slain should owe every firstborn to their Deliverer.

But in the book of Numbers the Lord speaks to Moses, saying:

> “I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel. And the Levites shall be mine, for every firstborn is mine” (Num. 3).

And again:

> “Number the firstborn males, from a month old and upward, and you shall have their total. And you shall take the Levites for me in place of every firstborn of the children of Israel” (ibid.).

The question, therefore, arises: if every firstborn among the children of Israel was redeemed by a price, by what right are the Levites taken for the Lord in place of every firstborn of the children of Israel? Or, if He was to take the Levites in place of the firstborn, with what justice did He command a price to be given or received for the firstborn?

To this I say: the true priesthood belongs to the firstborn. For one of them all was to become a priest [Col. 0634C] forever according to the order of Melchizedek; Holy Scripture in many places calls Him the firstborn, namely in relation to all the children of Israel—that is, to all the children of God—as the Apostle says:

> “For those whom He foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of the Son of God, so that He might be the firstborn among many brethren” (Rom. 8).

Moreover, Luke, intending to say, “They took Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’” (Luke 2), first said of the Virgin:

> “And she bore her firstborn son” (ibid.),

so that one acquainted with the law of the Lord may understand that He was called holy to the Lord, He for whom the highest and true priesthood was reserved.

Now the carnal priesthood of the law was a substitute for this true priesthood. It was not established as necessary, or as sufficient for salvation, but as a kind of pedagogue because of transgressions, until He should come to whom He had promised the priesthood—He in whom, God testifies, all nations would be blessed (Gal. 3). Therefore, because, as has now been said, the priesthood of the firstborn was reserved in Christ, while the carnal priesthood was its substitute, it was right that the sons of Levi, who acted in the place of those firstborn, should also receive their price for necessary sustenance. They were not to possess their own portions among their brethren, the children of Israel, according to the pronouncement of their father Jacob:

> “Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of iniquity in warfare; I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. 49).

Therefore, because the substitute priesthood was appointed because of transgressions until the true priesthood should come—the priesthood which belongs by right to the Firstborn—the vacant firstborn places were redeemed, and their 197 substitute priests and ministers were hired by their price to minister in their stead, until the Firstborn should come: He who would not redeem Himself, but, standing before the Lord through His own blood, would immediately remove the substitute and take up His priesthood according to the order of Melchizedek.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the statement: “The Lord did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines,” etc.

[Col. 0635B]

> “Therefore, when Pharaoh had dismissed the people, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is nearby, lest perhaps the people should repent if they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt; but He led them around by the way of the wilderness, which is near the Red Sea.”

A little later Moses says in his song:

> “The peoples went up and were enraged; pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Then the princes of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew stiff with fear” (Exod. 15).

Having said, “The peoples went up and were enraged,” one might ask: which peoples, and how were they enraged? “Pains,” he says, “seized the inhabitants of Philistia,” and so forth. He says that the princes of Edom were troubled, the mighty men of Moab trembled, all the inhabitants of Canaan grew stiff with fear, but that the inhabitants of Philistia suffered pain—that is, they were envious.

Thus the inhabitants of Philistia especially had to be avoided, and not without reason: while the others were afraid, they alone were already nursing hostile envy against Israel. But was the Lord able to fight for Israel against Pharaoh and the Egyptians, yet unable to do so against the Philistines? Certainly He could fight against these also. But in this, as in the other deeds contained on the historical surface, He rationally provided a spiritual instrument.

For spiritually He does this in all His elect: at the exodus from Egypt—that is, at the beginning of conversion, while the mind of the convert is still new and has not wholly emerged from former errors—He makes sin yield a path away from vices, so that those who are called may depart peacefully and gladly, lest, assailed by sudden temptations, they be frightened away from their holy purpose scarcely begun.

Moreover, this was a people whom the Lord had beneficially determined to leave for Israel, so that Israel might be exercised through them and chastised, as by a nearby scourge, whenever it should abandon the law of its God—as it was often to do. Therefore, not as one afraid, as the plain wording seems to suggest, but as one who provided wisely, “He did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, but led them around by the way of the wilderness, which is near the Red Sea.”

“He led him around,” and by leading him around He taught him, as Moses himself says here in the song of Deuteronomy:

> “He led him around, taught him, and guarded him as the apple of His eye” (Deut. 32).

“And they went up armed,” he says: namely, as an example for us, who have been called out of the Egypt of this world not to ease, but to warfare—against the barbarian battle-lines of vices and against the phalanxes of evil spirits. Yet they themselves were not fit for battle before their crossing of the Red Sea; just as we too could do nothing bravely before receiving the saving sacrament of Christ’s baptism.

> “Moses also took Joseph’s bones with him, because Joseph had bound the children of Israel by an oath, saying, ‘God will visit you; carry my bones hence with you’” (Gen. 50).

Admirable is the order of divine judgment. God made the sellers of their brother descend after him into Egypt; and they did not bring him back alive while he was living. Rather, after they had died and remained there, their sons brought him back dead; those men were buried in a foreign land, but he was laid away here in the land and inheritance of his fathers.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the statement: “The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never failed before the people.”

> “Setting out from Succoth, they encamped at Etham, on the outer borders of the wilderness.”

Etham means “strength.” By the phrase, “on the outer borders of the wilderness,” it is shown that the place lay on the boundary between the desert and Egypt.

> “And the Lord went before them, to show the way, by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire, that He might be the guide of their journey at both times. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by [Col. 0636C] night never failed before the people.”

Everywhere in this heaven of Holy Scripture bright stars meet us, all looking toward the fountain of their light, namely Christ the true Sun; and no place is empty. Behold: a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, the guide of the journey at both times, before the eyes of the children of Israel—adapted, that is, to the nature of their eyes, so that they might be able to follow: under the sun they readily recognize a cloud, and in the night, fire.

Who is this guide of the journey but Jesus Christ the Son of God, who is both guide and way for us? He is the pillar of fire, because He is true God; He is likewise the pillar of cloud, because He is true man. Hence Scripture speaks pointedly and properly: it does not say, “The Lord went before them” *in a pillar* of cloud and *in a pillar* of fire, but, in the case which grammarians call the accusative, “into a pillar of cloud and into a pillar of fire”—that is, like a pillar of cloud and like a pillar of fire.

While it was still night, there was only fire. But when the day of grace, or the time of mercy, arrived, He who was fire became cloud—that is, He became man or flesh, by putting on flesh though He was God. The fiery sun, the Sun of righteousness by day, is greater than the bright fire, the fire of the prophetic word, in the night. In order that the sun might be endured, it came in a cloud: that is, God came in the flesh so that He might dwell among human beings.

Here, appropriately, we take up prophetic testimony. Isaiah says:

> “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter into Egypt” (Isa. 19), etc.

Let that prophecy be compared with the present history; for the mysteries here marked by deeds are the same as those there marked by words. Egypt signifies this world, while the children of Israel signify Christ’s chosen people—now in the part of those who follow His coming until the end of the age.

For above, where the lamb was slain and Egypt’s firstborn were killed, Egypt signified hell and the children of Israel Christ’s chosen people, in the part of those who preceded His coming or passion and, being placed in the lower regions, awaited His coming there.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the mystical meaning of the same pillar.

Therefore we know the mysteries of this pillar: in the night—that is, before the light of grace had been revealed—it was fire and shone only a little, that is, to very few in prophetic grace. Little, I say, compared with the present day, when the whole source of fire, the true Sun and entire fountain of light, came with the cloud of His flesh. Although the sun is in a cloud, it nevertheless shines more brightly than the fire formerly did in the night.

For what purpose did such a pillar go before us? Clearly, to show us the way of fleeing Pharaoh, king of Egypt—that is, the devil, prince of this world—and to open for us the way through the Red Sea, that is, the grace of baptism made red by His blood. Thus, when Pharaoh and the Egyptians enter the sea after us—that is, when the idolatrous nations persecute us who have been baptized into Christ’s death—they may perish from our memory along with their gods, or rather their demons; and “all who worship carved images, who glory in their idols,” may be confounded [Col. 0637C] (Ps. 69).

What else did the prophet just mentioned declare in the chapter cited above? After saying, “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. 19)—that is, He will take pure flesh, understood here as a white cloud—“and enter Egypt,” he immediately added the following effects:

> “The idols of Egypt shall be moved at His presence, and the heart of Egypt shall melt within it; and I will set Egyptians against Egyptians” (ibid.).

And after some intervening words:

> “The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of dizziness, and they caused Egypt to err in all its work, as a drunken man staggers and vomits” (ibid.), etc.

The sole difference in the comparison is this: here all the reprobate are signified by the Egyptians, and all the elect by the children of Israel. In that prophecy, however, Egyptians are divided against Egyptians—that is, the elect against the reprobate—because all human beings, whether those taken from among us or those left behind, all of us, I say, “were Gentiles, led away to mute idols as we were led” (1 Cor. 12).

On behalf of the reprobate, who were left with their gods and their prince the devil, he says:

> “The foolish princes of Zoan; Pharaoh’s wise counselors gave foolish counsel. How will you say to Pharaoh, ‘I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings’? Where now are your wise men?” (Isa. 19), etc.

But on behalf of the elect, who withdrew from the devil, he continues:

> “In that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a monument of the Lord near its boundary. And it shall be a sign and testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and He shall send them a savior and defender, who will deliver them. And the Lord shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the Lord” (ibid.).

To pursue all these matters now would be burdensome. Accordingly, it must be explained how the Lord was the leader of His people in the pillar of cloud and drowned their pursuers in the depths.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the mystical positioning of the camp.

(Chapter 14.)

> “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Return and encamp opposite Pihahiroth, which lies between Migdol and opposite Baal-zephon. You shall set the camp before it, by the sea.’”

Pihahiroth means “mouth of the nobles”; Migdol, or Magdol, as it appears in many manuscripts, means “greatness” or “tower”; Baal-zephon means “lord of the north.”

“Return,” he says—understand, from Etham—so that they should not go, as was already said, through the land of the Philistines. Etham means “strength.” The Psalmist says:

> “You dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Ps. 73),

that is, You brought the wisdom of the strong to nothing.

Therefore, fleeing the contrary strength both of the Egyptians and of the Philistines—that is, both of demons and of those who worship them, and also of Jews or heretics, according to the name Philistines, “those who fall through drinking,” because “the Lord mingled for them a spirit of dizziness,” as was said above from the prophet (Isa. 19)—fleeing, I say, these contrary strengths, they are to encamp opposite Pihahiroth. This, as has been said, means “mouth of the nobles,” and signifies the noble teaching or faith of the apostles.

“Between Migdol and the sea”: that is, between the great tower of strength, namely Christ, and His holy baptism. “Opposite Baal-zephon”: that is, opposite the devil, lord of the north, who, lifted up in prideful boldness, says:

> “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14),

that is, I will possess those who remain cold toward love of the Creator.

In such a position our catechumens spiritually encamp when, fleeing the Egypt of this world, where they worshiped mute idols, and rejecting all sects of heretics who in their own estimation are *Ethan*, that is, strong, they come to the sea: namely, to the sacrament of the one true baptism, which must be sought and confessed in the one holy catholic and apostolic Church.

The Lord makes clear what He intends by this command, adding:

> “Pharaoh will say concerning Israel, ‘They are hemmed in by the land; the wilderness has shut them in.’ And I shall harden his heart, and he will pursue you.”

The order is inverted. In sense, “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart” comes first, and “Pharaoh will say concerning the children of Israel” afterward. But so that the speech might proceed more fittingly in accordance with the person speaking—“I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart and he will pursue you, and I shall be glorified in Pharaoh and in all his army”—the order was rightly changed.

Concerning the word “I shall harden,” it has been said above that this means: I shall torment his hatred and envy by the prosperity of those departing. “He will say,” He says, “They are hemmed in by the land; the wilderness has shut them in”: that is, Egypt lies on one side, the land of the Philistines on another, the wilderness again on another, and the Red Sea on the fourth quarter; therefore they will not be able to escape.

“And I shall be glorified,” He says, “in Pharaoh and in all his army.” This is stated properly both according to history and according to allegory. Although He performed many great works in Egypt, He was glorified in none more than in having so terribly drowned Pharaoh and his army in the Red Sea. And although He has done numberless great works in heaven and on earth, He is proclaimed glorious in none more than in casting down the devil and overthrowing his counsel through the humility of Christ His Son.

Finally, when He says, “And the Egyptians shall know”—that is, the Egyptians will not be able not to know—“that I am the Lord,” this is illustrated by their saying, when the waters meet them:

> “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the hardening of the same Pharaoh, who bears the type of the devil.

> “And it was reported to the king of the Egyptians that the people had fled,” etc.

Is this not the Pharaoh who said above:

> “Arise, go out, and, when you depart, bless me” (Exod. 12)?

How then is it now said, “It was reported to the king that the people had fled”? Was it because the children of Israel had requested from the Egyptians articles of silver and gold and abundant clothing, had despoiled the Egyptians, and a mixed and innumerable multitude—perhaps slaves of the Egyptians fleeing their masters—had gone up with them? For this reason, it is thus said: “It was reported that the people had fled.”

Indeed, that same reason also strongly suggests why, once the children of Israel had obtained the spoils of Egypt, the more eagerly they were laden, the more gladly and quickly they would go at the Lord’s command; while Pharaoh’s army would be readier to pursue, the more madly they believed themselves despoiled of their gold and silver by those whom they had formerly despoiled of liberty. Therefore inflamed, and inflaming one another with blind fury, they say:

> “What have we chosen to do, that we should let Israel go, so that it should no longer serve us?”

Then Pharaoh yoked his chariot and took all his people with him. He took six hundred chosen chariots, every chariot there was in Egypt, and the leaders of the whole army. And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the children of Israel. But they had gone out with an uplifted hand, etc.

Holy Scripture has often used—and now for the final time uses—that terrible expression: “And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” not fearing that the clay or creature might speak against its maker and say:

> “Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and hardens whom He wills. Why then does He still find fault? For who resists His will?” (Rom. 9).

For if it dare mutter anything of that kind, it will be told:

> “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (ibid.), etc.

But this has already been discussed more fully elsewhere.

Spiritually, “then it was reported to the king of Egypt that the people had fled” when the devil perceived that, Christ having been exalted above all heavens and all nations called to faith in Him, his temples were being abandoned and the filth of his images cast away. For concerning those whom he lost from hell, whom Christ the conqueror restored to paradise and placed within the walls of heavenly peace, he afterward received no report, nor could any hope remain for the envy that panted after them.

Therefore, when the glory of Christ’s resurrection began to be preached and the sign of His victory shone forth, so that all nations might hear that the prince of this world had already been judged (John 16), and might therefore desert to the kingdom of the Victor and receive His title upon their foreheads—then, I say, having heard the grievous report, he took chosen chariots, every chariot there was in Egypt: for example, Nero, Trajan, Decius, Diocletian, or Maximian.

These, and others of that sort, were Pharaoh’s chariots, the devil’s chosen chariots; and his horses, according to the Apocalypse, were red (Rev. 6), that is, bloody. Upon these he mounted and pursued the children of Israel—that is, he stirred up public persecution against all who believed in Christ.

“But they,” he says, “had gone out with an uplifted hand.” An exceedingly elegant contrast. The chariots of Pharaoh just named, and the leaders of the devilish army, appeared exalted; but in truth the Lord’s hand is exalted, in which we have gone out—the exalted hand of the Lord, and the exalted Lamb of God, by whose blood we have been redeemed and have departed.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the statement that the children of Israel, lifting up their eyes, saw the Egyptians behind them and were afraid, according to the mystical sense.

> “And when Pharaoh drew near, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes, saw the Egyptians behind them, and were greatly afraid,” etc.

According to the historical sense, the faith of those who said to Moses, “Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, so you brought us out to die in the wilderness,” was altogether too feeble and untrained by the works of God they had seen.

But according to the higher sense, the children of Israel “lifted up their eyes and saw the Egyptians behind them” when hearers of the Gospel, with the eyes of their heart already enlightened by the preceding pillar, look back upon the former errors in which they had been. Comparing them with the truth which they have heard through the new proclamation, they were greatly “astonished, troubled, shaken, and trembling seized them; yet there were pains as of a woman in labor” (Ps. 47): pains not empty, but bringing forth the fruit of everlasting joy. So a woman in labor, after she has given birth, remembers her pains or suffering no longer because of joy that a human being has been born (John 16).

> “And Moses said to the people: ‘Do not fear. Stand firm and see the great works of God which He will do today. For the Egyptians whom you now see, you shall never see again forever. The Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent.’”

As this occurred in the truth of history, so it has truly occurred hitherto, and continually occurs, in the abundance of spiritual grace through Christ. Whatever Egyptians, whatever works of darkness, the catechumens of the Church see behind them as they come to the baptism of catholic faith, they will never see again; nor will their remembrance endure forever. For there, through Christ’s blood, every handwriting of sin is blotted out, when the Holy Spirit is given for the remission of sins. Christ bore the sins of many: without doubt, of those who through baptism share in the likeness of His death and resurrection (Rom. 6).

Therefore He rightly and faithfully says:

> “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent,”

not because Christ fights again or dies again, but because in His past struggle or death He bore the sins of all who were to believe.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. [Col. 0641B] On the Lord’s saying to Moses, “Why do you cry to me?” and on what the rod lifted over the earth signifies.

> “And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Why do you cry to me? Speak to the children of Israel, that they may go forward. But you, lift up your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, that the children of Israel may enter through the midst of the sea on dry ground,’” etc.

“Why,” He says, “do you cry to me?” Certainly it was a mark of great grace and of worthy, gracious acceptance for the Lord to say to Moses alone at such a time, “Why do you cry to me?” For what of it? Were not the Egyptians also crying out? Was it not said shortly before that “they lifted up their eyes, saw the Egyptians behind them, were greatly afraid, and cried out to the Lord”?

Certainly these too cried out, and made a great uproar with confused voices. But what follows?

> “Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, so you brought us out to die in the wilderness.”

Thus they did cry out, but not worthily, so that God might rightly say to them, “Why do you cry to me?” For they cried without faith; and such crying is regarded as vain and unworthy of God’s ears.

But what did Moses cry? “Do not fear,” he says; “stand firm and see the great works of God; the Lord will fight for you; you shall be silent.” He said this to the people with his bodily voice; he said it to the Lord by the mighty outcry of faith. Rightly, therefore, did that pillar of cloud, that pillar of fire, hear this man alone.

Thus, indeed, the same pillar—now truly a pillar of cloud, that is, the same God now clothed in the cloud of flesh—while walking with crowds and pressed by crowds, suddenly cried out:

> “Who touched me?”

When all wondered and said, “The crowds press and afflict you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” (Matt. 9), He persisted in His judgment and said:

> “Someone touched me” (ibid.).

So here Moses, because the children of Israel cried without faith while he alone spoke with faith, alone could be heard by a great cry; just as there the woman, while the crowds pressed upon the Lord irreverently, herself touched the fringe of His garment with most reverent faith and alone deserved to be perceived.

“But you,” He says, “lift up your rod,” etc. According to the higher sense which we have pursued thus far, Moses’ rod, which the Lord commands to be raised over the sea so that the sea may be divided and the children of Israel may enter dry-shod through its midst, is the power of Christ the Son of God and the one rule of baptism. After He rose from the dead, He commanded the leaders of His people, namely the apostles, to stretch it over the waters:

> “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

For at this rod—as it were, at this authoritative word—the waters divide so that the children of Israel, the children of acquisition and salvation, may enter. That is, the grace of the Holy Spirit opens itself, receiving children of the devil to be reborn as children of God, children of wrath to be regenerated as children of grace.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. [Col. 0642B] On the statement, “Who divided the sea into divisions,” according to the Psalmist.

The Hebrews say that the sea was divided not once but into twelve divisions, according to the number of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, so that each tribe might proceed through its own division; and that this is what is said in the Psalm in the plural:

> “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Ps. 135).

If this is so, it too is not devoid of mystery: many divisions of graces are opened in the one Spirit to those baptized in Christ. They are not all bestowed upon one person, but some more or less upon different persons, according to the good pleasure of the one and same Spirit, who distributes to each as He wills (1 Cor. 12).

Yet it must be known that the first gift and chief benefit of baptism, namely the remission of sins, is not distributed in portions, nor is more given to one and less to another. Rather, it is granted equally to all by equal grace, though the abundance of bestowed gifts differs. The sins of all, I say, are swallowed up, and in the waves of baptism all Egyptians—all liabilities both of original fault and of actual crimes—are immediately overwhelmed.

But the spiritual gifts mentioned by the Apostle, when he says:

> “To each of us is given the manifestation of the Spirit for profit: to one indeed wisdom is given through the Spirit, to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit” (ibid.), etc.,

are undoubtedly not all conferred upon anyone except the one head of the body of the Church, which is Christ (Eph. 5), “in whom dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2).

Therefore, if anyone wishes to hold that several divisions were made, he cannot compel us to accept it, since he has no certain authority for it from the Holy Scriptures. Nevertheless, once he has adopted this literal sense, he has something he may profitably understand mystically.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the statement: “The angel of the Lord, and likewise the pillar of fire, leaving the front, went behind them,” and on its mystical meaning.

> “And the angel of the Lord, who went before the camp of Israel, moved away and went behind them; and together with him the pillar of cloud, leaving the front, stood behind them between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel. And the cloud was dark, yet illumined the night, so that they could not approach one another throughout the whole night.”

From the movement of the pillar, leaving the front and standing behind them, it could be known or foreseen that the angel of God who went before the camp of Israel had gone behind them. For the angel—whether He was the Angel of Great Counsel, or one of the angelic spirits in whom the power of the delivering God was present—did not appear to everyone in His own person. Nor does the text compel this interpretation; otherwise, it would not have been necessary for the pillar of cloud to appear before the people by day, or the pillar of fire by night, as the guide of their journey.

But how could one and the same pillar be both a dark cloud and one illuminating the night, unless one and the same power, according to differing—indeed, contrary—deserts, shone for the godly and blinded the ungodly? Here too, then, is a most beautiful mystery: for “we preach,” says the Apostle, “one and the same Christ—to Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1), which is very obscure; “but to those called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (ibid.), which is very luminous.

Further, what does it mean that this pillar, such as it was, left the front and stood behind Israel, between the camp of the Egyptians and the camp of Israel? Mystically, it signifies what the Church rightly believes and firmly holds: our Lord Jesus Christ, who went before us, who before we knew Him went, passed through, and entered heaven as our forerunner for us, is nevertheless present at the hour of holy baptism. For immediately after saying:

> “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28),

He concluded:

> “Behold, I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (ibid.).

Let us go securely where He went before through His passion. For when we approach baptism, through the sacrament of that same passion He begins to stand behind us; enclosing us within the walls of His grace, He excludes our sins from us, so that throughout the whole night—that is, throughout this present life—they cannot overtake or approach us.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the entry of the children of Israel through the midst of the Red Sea, and on the sacrament of baptism.

“Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord drove it back by a mighty, scorching wind [Col. 0643D], and turned it into dry land; the water was divided, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea,” etc. The deed is plainly one of the Lord’s glorious majesty: “the water was divided, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea”; and “the Lord destroyed Pharaoh’s army, overturned the wheels of the chariots, and they were borne into the depths.” Thus the Egyptians themselves learned that the Lord is God, so that they said: “Let us flee from Israel, for the Lord fights for them against us.” But as they fled, the Lord enveloped them amid the waves, “looking down upon their camp in the morning watch,” that is, the fourth watch. For four watches of the night were counted, each watch comprising three hours.

In the mystical sense, however, “the morning watch” is the very resurrection to the Lord’s life. For in the morning an angel sat at the Lord’s tomb and, after the deep night of grief, announced to the women—and through them to the mourning apostles—the day of great joy. Hence the Psalm says: “From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord” (Ps. 129). By the morning watch he means the guard of soldiers terrified at dawn, as an example to all the ungodly; whereas the women were made joyful as an example to all the godly. What is Israel to hope in the Lord from that morning watch? Namely, that what was then made known to have occurred in him will occur in itself: he rose from the dead, “for with the Lord is mercy, and with him abundant redemption; and he himself will redeem Israel from all its iniquities” (ibid.). It is understood: just as [Col. 0644B] he redeemed those children of Israel from all the Egyptians.

Thus, the morning watch in which the children of Israel passed through while the Egyptians remained behind is mystically, for us, the joy of the Lord’s resurrection, in which, putting off the old man, we were reborn, while the devil—the one whom we renounced, together with all his pomps—remained behind. For the Apostle says: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death; we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been made united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall also be [united with him] in that of his resurrection” (Rom. IX).

Therefore we must no longer be silent concerning the most celebrated mystery of this glorious deed, since we possess [Col. 0644C] the song of Moses which follows: “For this is wisdom, which opened the mouth of the dumb and made the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. 10), so that we may together praise your victorious hand, O Lord our God. For that this song ought not to be absent from the mouths of all who have received this grace is indicated by that passage in the Apocalypse: “And I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, standing upon the sea of glass, holding harps of God and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying: Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God Almighty” (Rev. 15), etc.

Behold, we stand upon the sea of glass—that is, striving to preserve the innocence which [Col. 0644D] we received through baptism: “the sea, I say, of glass,” because of the pure confession there made of sins to be left behind; but also “mixed with fire,” that is, enlivened by the Holy Spirit, by whom those sins themselves were consumed. He too is mystically signified here by the scorching wind, when it is said that “when Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord drove it back by a mighty and scorching wind blowing all night.”

“Having therefore harps of God,” that is, the mortification of the flesh which God commanded, “singing this song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb,” rejoicing in both: both for the deed accomplished through the hand of Moses, and for the mystery of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, Christ, which Moses prophetically understood in that very deed.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The song of Moses in praise of Christ the Lord, who drowned our sins in the Red Sea, that is, in baptism.

**(Chapter XV.)** “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he cast into the sea.”

The first utterance of the precentor is an exhortation, urging all who are in the Shulamite’s choirs of camps to raise their harmony according to the greatness of the festival, according to the quantity or quality of the divine works. “Let us sing,” he says, “to the Lord.” Let us sing with the spirit; let us sing also with the mind. For the Apostle too says: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. IV). To sing or make melody with the spirit, then, is to keep the deed in memory and to make it alone [Col. 0645B] the subject of song. To sing with the mind is to perceive the inward mystery in the outward deed.

Let us therefore sing to the Lord. Why? “For he has been gloriously magnified.” In what? “Horse and rider he cast into the sea.” Truly this is glorious majesty, even if you consider only the outward deed. But if you also discern the inward mystery, there is a more glorious abundance of majesty there. For by the horse this world is signified, and by the rider the devil. When did he cast down that rider and such a horse? Surely when he said: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world shall be cast out” (John 12); and immediately thereafter, explaining in deed what he had said, he received “the horns of the cross in his hands, and there his strength was hidden; and death, having dared to creep up, thereafter went conquered before his face, [Col. 0645C] and the devil went forth before his feet” (Hab. 3).

Then he cast him down, and from that time he does not cease casting him down into the sea: a sea of glass, mixed with the fire of the Holy Spirit for us; but pitchy, fiery, and sulphurous for him. For that sea through which the children of Israel passed cast out the former and swallowed the latter; but our sea, in which we are baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, by no means admits this horse and his rider. Rather, while we pass through that sea of glass, he is cast into the depth of hell.

It is most glorious that the Lord has done this. Long ago he dragged down and cast into this darksome air that rider who said, “I will ascend into heaven, and above the stars of God I will exalt my throne” [Col. 0645D] (Isa. 14). But now, sitting upon the horse—that is, upon the unbridled folly of proud people deceived by him—he has cast him into the depth of the pit, into the abyss of burning hell. “Yet,” says the prophet, “you shall be brought down to hell, into the depth of the pit; those who see you shall bend toward you and gaze upon you” (ibid.), etc. Behold, we see him, and we shall see him still on the day of judgment; for then “he shall be cast down before the eyes of all” (Job 40).

“Let us therefore sing to the Lord,” says this learned and melodious precentor: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.” Having received this exhortation, the whole choir—one body made of many members—begins this delightful song with such an opening: “The Lord is [Col. 0646A] my strength and my praise.” What follows? “And he has become my salvation.” Is he therefore your strength because he has become your salvation? Certainly: “my strength,” for the strength of my head is my strength; indeed, if my head is strong, it is my strength. And who does not know that the Lord himself, the glorious one, is my head, since “the Word became flesh” (John 1), and I, the one Church called to this song, am his one body?

Therefore both the whole body together and every individual member may glory, while preserving the grace of the head, and say: “He is my strength; he has become my salvation”; and this is my praise, nor does the praise of the head dishonor the whole body. Otherwise, if I did not have this most mighty head, as hitherto, from the time when I drank the cup of his wrath from the Lord’s hand and drank it to the dregs because of Adam’s transgression—as hitherto, he says, “there was none of all my sons whom I bore to raise me up” (Isa. 51)—so I should sleep for ever, like that beast ensnared and full of the Lord’s indignation.

“This is my God, and I will glorify him; the God of my father, and I will exalt him.” This one, I say—once despised, the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness (Isa. 53)—who by dying cast down such a horse and such a rider, is my God. He is man, and he is my God. “I will glorify him”: I shall not be ashamed of him. But the hostile peoples who went up and were enraged say to me—namely, the synagogue of the Jews and the assemblies of heretics—whose pains seized them: If this one is your God, then a recent God, a foreign God, is within you; and you do not act according to the precept of Scripture, but against Scripture, which says: “Israel, if you will listen to me, there shall be no recent god in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” [Col. 0646C] (Ps. 80).

To these charges I shall answer and confidently sing: “This is my God, and I will glorify him, the God of my father” Abraham, “and I will exalt him.” “Your father Abraham,” he says, “rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). Again: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am” (ibid.). Therefore there is no recent God in me, nor do I worship a foreign God, but the God of my father, the ancient God. For though he is Son, though begotten or born, yet he is not younger than his Father, the Ancient of Days, by a single instant or atom. I shall glorify him, I shall exalt him, and I shall say:

“The Lord is like a warrior (**Almighty is his name**); he cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea. His chosen princes were drowned in the Red Sea; the depths covered them; they descended into the deep like a stone.”

Read “Almighty is his name” parenthetically, so that in the midst of the sentence the adversary may be rebuked, to whom it seemed excessive for the Lord to be named (Exod. 5). “Like a warrior,” he says: that is, he did these things in the manner of a warrior. For as a warrior adapts and arms himself according to the kind or quality of his enemy, so he had to arrange war in new and wonderful ways according to the nature of his enemy. His enemy was not flesh and blood, but a certain aerial principality and power, the ruler of this world of darkness, spiritual wickedness in heavenly places [Col. 0647A] (Eph. 6).

Therefore the Almighty did not gird a material sword upon his thigh; he did not put on a breastplate or helmet woven of iron. Rather, against such a principality or power of pride, he put on humility and obedience; against spiritual wickedness, he put on and girded himself with the strength of charity. Thus, like a warrior, he cast into the sea Pharaoh’s aerial chariot, upon which he believed he would ride above the height of the clouds so as to be like the Most High (Isa. 14), and his army, both of vices and of demons, whom he had stationed in the temples and shrines of the Gentiles. For by dying he received authority in heaven and on earth, and drew all things to himself (John 12).

From then on his chosen [Col. 0647B] princes were drowned in the Red Sea. For his billowing tribulation, of which he says in the Psalm, “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. 68), flooded over their heads from the hour when, pierced in the side by the lance, he poured out blood and water. Thus “the depths covered them”; their memory perished; “and they descended into the deep like a stone,” pressed down by their own iniquity. For they have no right at all over those whose God this is, who glorify him, and who confess him as the God of their father. From this come praises; from this, thanksgivings.

“Your right hand, O Lord, has been magnified in strength; your right hand, O Lord, struck the enemy; and in the multitude of your glory you cast down my adversaries.”

Let this voice be especially that of our martyrs. For through them the Lord’s right hand, which founded heaven and earth, was wondrously glorified by miracles: it overthrew the temples of demons and scattered idols. Thus it “struck the enemy,” not with iron, but with the blood of martyrs; “in the multitude of his glory,” for the praise and honor of his glorious grace, O holy Church, he cast down your adversaries.

Let these victors therefore say—these warriors of faith and champions of truth: “You sent your wrath, which devoured them like stubble; and by the breath of your fury the waters were gathered together. The flowing wave stood still; the depths were gathered in the midst of the sea.” You sent your wrath, that is, your zeal, O Lord God. For you were zealous for the nations that did not know you, which, led into error, went after dumb idols as they were led (1 Cor. 12); and your wrath, or zeal, devoured the frenzied gods as fire devours stubble.

Where now is adulterous Jupiter? Where Venus the harlot? Where are the monsters of the other gods? Where are the horses of those who neighed beneath them against your martyrs—that is, the savage kings and governors who shed the martyrs’ blood for their sake? Your wrath devoured them “like stubble”; and “by the breath of your fury,” that is, by the threat of the coming judgment, “the waters were gathered together.” According to the letter, “by the breath of your fury the waters were gathered together” means that “the Lord drove them back by a mighty and scorching wind blowing all night, and they stood like a wall on the right and left.” This, indeed, brought aid to those fleeing and wrath to those pursuing.

But [Col. 0648A] according to the mystery begun, “the waters are peoples” (Rev. 17). Hence: “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters” (Isa. 32). Again: “The Lord thundered over many waters” (Ps. 28). These waters could perceive or hear the breath of fury—that is, the threat of the future judgment—because they are rational; and, out of fear of it, they were gathered together. Where were they “gathered together”? “In the midst of the sea.”

For after employing a threefold repetition, he finally specified through the trope called periphrasis, that is, circumlocution, which is usually made for the ornamentation of expression: “The waters were gathered together; the flowing wave stood still; the depths were gathered in the midst of the sea.” For, as was said above, a people is signified by the name “waters”; hence, by the designation either of depths or of flowing water, he signifies the fluid and profound misery of peoples, as it is elsewhere said concerning this persecutor: “He will swallow up a river and not be amazed” (Job 40).

But this river, or flowing wave, stood still. It stood when “the waters were gathered together,” that is, when many peoples were gathered in order to be united by faith to the one God who stands and is threefold. Elsewhere Scripture says: “The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; who shall know it?” (Jer. 17). Therefore “the depths were gathered in the midst of the sea” when perverse people flowed together, from the hidden places of darkness and the depths of vices, to the one universal baptism of Christ. For what is common, public, or universal is properly called “the midst,” which we call catholic. It is beneficial for the gathering of waters that they be gathered into the midst; for what is only in one part is not authentic. That belongs to heretics, who seek corners where stolen waters are sweeter [Col. 0648C] (Prov. 9).

“The enemy said: I will pursue and overtake; I will divide the spoils, and my soul shall be filled.” This was said by “the enemy,” that is, by the devil, who is called the enemy antonomastically—that is, as though by his proper name. What wonder that he said this, trusting that the Jordan flows into his mouth? He is false, he who said: “I will ascend into heaven” (Isa. 14), desiring to be like the Most High, and his hope has disappointed him. What wonder, I say, that, now cast out from the hearts of those reborn in Christ, he should speak and say thus—he who, cast out of heaven, still, with his angels, “opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2)?

“I will pursue,” he says, “and overtake.” I shall pursue, as far as I am allowed; for of those who entered the sea he seizes no one, except some pretender or hypocrite. In what does he trust, that he says, “I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled”? He says: “I will draw my sword; my hand shall kill them.” To draw the sword is to stir up open persecution, just as, conversely, to bend the bow is to wish to deceive secretly. The Psalmist expresses both modes of persecution: “Sinners,” he says, “have drawn the sword; they have bent their bow” (Ps. 36).

Therefore “I will draw my sword,” he says; that is, cast out from hearts, I shall employ the manifest tyranny of kings, emperors, or cruel pagans. And because I cannot reach their souls, “my hand”—my power, divine permission—shall kill them bodily. But the Lord says to blessed Job concerning him: “He who made him will apply his sword” (Job 40); that is, he will be permitted to rage or kill, not as much as he wishes, but as much as is useful.

Therefore let the victorious people of God, hastening toward the inheritance which God promised, not be afraid. For this enemy, while he pursues and kills, advances their purpose all the more, so that, as pilgrims, they may reach their homeland more quickly. Thus he is proved foolish: while he strives to act for himself against God or against God’s people, he acts rather against himself and assists God’s purpose to its fulfillment. And it is said to blessed Job concerning him: “Will you put a ring in his nostrils?” (Job 40). By this saying his foolishness is especially indicated. And immediately afterward: “Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as an everlasting servant?” (ibid.). It is understood: as I do, since by opposing my will he so cooperates with me, as though he had sworn obedience and strove to show himself my most faithful servant.

It follows: “Your spirit blew, and the sea covered them; they sank like lead in mighty waters.” Catholic faith firmly holds this: as we enter Christ’s sea, the Spirit of the Lord breathes upon us—the Spirit of grace and remission—casting down, according to the prophet, all our iniquities and throwing all our sins into the depths of the sea (Mic. 7). This is the devil’s ruin. What our head first did in himself at the time of his death—“blotting out,” as [Col. 0649C] the Apostle says, “the handwriting of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us; and he removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross; and stripping principalities and powers, he displayed them confidently, triumphing openly over them” (Col. 1)—what our head did then in himself, he does also in baptism in his members. There is the likeness of his death, to which we are united, as the same Apostle says (Rom. 6).

Therefore anyone who has ascended from this sea, reborn in Christ, may rightly say and truly sing: “The sea covered them; they sank like lead in mighty waters,” fulfilling the truth of the prophecy which says: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon, who lie in the midst of your rivers and say: The river is mine, and I made myself. And I will put a bridle in your jaws, and I will make the fish of your rivers cling to your scales; and I will draw you out from the midst of your rivers, and all your fish shall cling to your scales; and I will cast you into the wilderness, you and all the fish of your river” [Col. 0649D] (Ezek. 29).

Notice that above he compared them to a stone, on account of the weight of sin; here he compares them to lead, on account of sin’s punishment or recompense, according to the prophet Zechariah, with whom a talent of lead is cast into the mouth of that iniquity (Zech. 5).

Again, praises; again, thanksgivings. “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord? Who is like you, magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, working wonders?” This is against what that Pharaoh said: “I shall be like the Most High” [Col. 0650A] (Isa. 14). It was not enough to proclaim strength in him, saying, “Who is like you among the mighty, O Lord?”, unless he also proclaimed holiness, adding, “Who is like you, magnificent in holiness?” For in this passage strength and holiness differ from one another as judgment and mercy differ elsewhere: the strength of judgment against the proud; the holiness of mercy toward godly fugitives.

In accordance with these two he adds the titles of praise, “terrible and praiseworthy”: terrible because of the strength of judgment, praiseworthy because of the holiness of mercy. According to both, “and working wonders.” What wonders? “You stretched out your hand, and the earth devoured them.” This is the wonder of strength, on account of which you are terrible, O Lord. “The earth,” he says, “devoured them”—the earth, I say, which, according to blessed Job, is dark and covered with the gloom of death, a land of misery and darkness, where is the shadow of death, no order, but everlasting horror dwells (Job 10).

“You have been a guide in your mercy to the people whom you redeemed, and in your strength you carried them to your holy dwelling.” This is the wonder of holiness or mercy, and on this account, O Lord, you are praiseworthy. “Terrible and praiseworthy”: you have accomplished such diverse wonders; “and you carried them,” he says, “in your strength.” He uses the past tense for the present, saying “you carried” in place of “you will carry,” either because he knew with complete certainty that God would complete what he had begun, or because none could frustrate his purpose.

But what is God’s holy dwelling? Is it the land of sinners, the land [Col. 0650C] of the Canaanites? There was indeed a holy dwelling there—the holy city Jerusalem, or the temple and the Holy of Holies—but these were holy not in themselves, but because they were copies of the heavenly holy things. Therefore he calls God’s holy dwelling not so much that earthly place as the land of the living, of which that place was a shadow. He foresaw that, through the glorious majesty of God the leader, the entire people of the saints would be carried there in the strength of God, which is none other than the Son of God.

“The peoples went up and were enraged,” etc. How could he know, so as to state as though it were past what was future: “Then the princes of Edom were troubled; trembling seized the mighty men of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan grew stiff with fear”? For regarding the words, “pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia,” perhaps one may answer that the Philistine land was nearby, and that before they entered the sea they had to beware lest they attempt to pass through it, as was already said above, because their pain—that is, envy—had already become known when Israel was leaving Egypt.

But when they said to Edom, “We beg you, let us pass through your land” (Num. 20), Edom had not yet answered: “You shall not pass through me, otherwise I will meet you armed” (ibid.). Nor had the king of Moab said: “This people will destroy all who dwell within our borders, just as an ox is wont to crop grasses down to the roots” (Num. 22). Whence, then, unless by a prophetic spirit, did he know how to sing these things already?

Spiritually, moreover, Edom, that is, “earthly” or “bloodstained”; Moab, which is interpreted “from the father”—understood as the devil; Canaan also, which is interpreted “commotion”; and Philistia, which is interpreted “those falling by drink”: all these both signified by their names and prefigured by their deeds those who, after Christ had conquered and been crowned, when the heavens proclaimed his glory and the sound of his apostles went out into all the earth, undertook as though to defend the defeated devil’s cause. Inflamed by his spirit, they went up against and were enraged with all believers in Christ.

“Let dread and terror fall upon them, because of the greatness of your arm.” Dread concerns future things; terror, present things. This is justly imprecated upon those who are tormented by God’s glory: upon all enemies of the faith or of the Lord’s name, visible and invisible alike. “Let them become motionless like a stone,” so that they cannot harm those who are moving and running well toward God. “Until your people, O Lord, pass over”—understood, that people which has no abiding city here, but seeks the city to come (Heb. 13). “Until this people whom you have acquired passes over.”

The repetition of the passing people is indeed an ornament of speech or song even in the literal sense. But in the mystery it is more pleasing to understand, after the former people of the Hebrews, also the following people of the Gentiles, whom Christ the leader acquired with his own blood; as the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2).

“You will bring them in [Col. 0651C] and plant them upon the mountain of your inheritance, in your most firm dwelling, which you have made, O Lord.” This is said according to the image of a vineyard, which the Psalmist also takes up in singing to the Lord: “You transplanted a vine from Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it” (Ps. 79), etc. “Upon the mountain,” he says, “of your inheritance.” The land which the Lord gave that people was indeed mountainous, but incomparably higher is the land which may rightly be called the mountain of the Lord’s inheritance, especially since he immediately adds: “in your most firm dwelling, which you have made, O Lord; your sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands established.”

Therefore the mountain in which it is a great thing for God’s people to be planted, which is rightly called the Lord’s most firm dwelling, which he himself made, which is the Lord’s sanctuary, and which he himself established with his hands, is that Lebanon concerning which the prophet says that the apostate planting was cast out in these words: “Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches, thick with foliage, lofty in height; its top was raised among dense boughs” [Col. 0651D] (Ezek. 31). And shortly afterward: “No tree in God’s paradise was like it in its beauty, because I made it beautiful” (ibid.). And then: “To whom are you likened, O glorious and lofty one among the trees of delight? Behold, you are brought down with the trees of delight to the lowest land; you shall sleep in the midst of the uncircumcised, with those slain by the sword. This is Pharaoh and all his multitude, says the Lord” (ibid.).

On this mountain, first—and this is wonderful—he planted the thief, saying: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23).

“The Lord shall reign for ever and beyond.” This is the most brilliant and resonant conclusion of a most beautiful song.
