For what follows—“For Pharaoh entered,” etc.—returns to the beginning by way of addition and concludes the whole, as it were, with a brief epilogue: “The Lord shall reign for ever.” Everyone who knows the Lord firmly holds that “the Lord shall reign for ever.” But who can grasp what is meant by “for ever”? The meaning of this word is exceedingly vast. Our sight cannot measure its length, breadth, or height. On hearing this word, perhaps we lift up our heads, yet we do not see the whole expanse of eternity.

He added “and beyond,” as though saying: As far as you can see into the distance, the Lord will reign—and beyond what you can see; beyond what the very phrase “for ever” conveys to your mind or understanding. As though you were asking, “How do you know that the Lord will reign?”, he gives this reason: “For Pharaoh entered,” etc. Does this mean that unless Pharaoh had entered the sea and unless the Lord had brought the waters back over him, the Lord would not reign? Certainly he would reign everywhere by power; but he would not reign over that possession of human beings concerning which the prophet sighs: “Lords other than you have possessed us” (Isa. 26). Unless, I say, that spiritual Pharaoh had been crushed, the Lord would not reign in us; that is, unless the ruler of this world had been cast out, Christ the Son of God would not possess us, and the Savior of the world would not reign in us.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Miriam singing the same song with the women after the men: the mystical example which this gives us.

“Therefore Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances, and she led them in song, saying: ‘Let us sing to the Lord,’” etc.

The order of the narrative is beautiful. First Moses sings the one and same song with the men; then Miriam sings it with the women. Understanding this order spiritually, let us at least sing the same faith as women with women, since [Col. 0652D] we are weak souls. For we acknowledge that the apostles and apostolic men—all who went up armed from Egypt and are strong for battle—are men; and, being as it were women in comparison with them, we cannot at all stand in their choir or sound forth in the same tone.

It should be noted that Scripture here calls Miriam a prophetess, because, as has been foretold and partly explained, the words of this song contain prophecy of future things, though they seem to speak only of present and past things. It is beautifully said that she took a timbrel: this instrument of melody, a skin stretched upon wood, signifies the mortification of the flesh, without which no soul can show itself a worthy singer. “All the women,” he says, [Col. 0653A] “went out after her.” “Woman” is named from softness. But a faithful soul must for a little while go out from its own softness, so that it may imitate men and sing worthily to God.

# THIRD BOOK ON EXODUS.  
*(Exodus, chapters XV–XXIV.)*

[Col. 0653]

## CHAPTER I. How, according to Paul, we are warned not, like many children of Israel baptized in the cloud and sea, to lose through evil works the grace of baptism which we have received in Christ.

The Apostle does not wish us to be ignorant that the things set forth above and those which follow happened as figures of us, and were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10). How for our correction? Namely, so that we may not think that we have already attained the goal, or that this alone is sufficient for us—that we have been baptized in Christ (Gal. 3)—and, deceived by this confidence, lose anew through evil deeds the grace of baptism which we received.

Seeking to break this confidence, which is useless to us, he says: “Do you not know [Col. 0653B] that those who run in the stadium all indeed run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9). And then: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brethren, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock which followed them, and the rock was Christ. But God was not pleased with most of them, for they were struck down in the wilderness. Now these things happened as a figure of us” (1 Cor. 10), etc.

Therefore let us pursue their lusts, idolatry, fornications, temptations, and murmurings in such a way that from their bodies struck down [Col. 0653C] we may derive the benefit of the correction just mentioned; and, before all else, from figures of bodily things, let us investigate according to our purpose the spiritual mysteries of Christ, the Son of God, upon the authority of the same Apostle. For “all these things,” he says, “happened to them as a figure” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER II. How the Lord tested the people at the waters of Marah.

“Moses took the children of Israel from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur. They walked three days through the wilderness and found no water; and they came to Marah,” etc.

The wilderness of Shur lies between Kadesh and Barath, where the angel found Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant (Gen. 16). It extends as far as the sea that reaches the boundaries of Egypt. Shur is interpreted “wall” or “straight.” “They walked,” he says, “three days,” etc. Their not finding water, and their inability, upon arriving at Marah, to drink its waters “because they were bitter—whence he gave the place a fitting name, calling it Marah, that is, bitterness” [Col. 0654A]—occurred as a test. For this is what you find: “There he established judgments and commands for them, and there he tested them.”

But when tested, the people were immediately found blameworthy. For “they murmured against Moses, saying: What shall we drink?” They are rightly rebuked, not because they said, “What shall we drink?”, but because they said it in murmuring. Yet this first test was wickedness. Therefore God’s gentle patience corrects them kindly and says: “If you hear the voice of the Lord your God,” etc., “I shall not bring upon you any of the sickness which I brought upon Egypt; for I am the Lord your Savior.” It is as though he said: If you do not begin to murmur or act contentiously, I, who crushed Egypt in my wrath, shall be your leader in my mercy. But if you follow the sins of the Egyptians in rebellion, I shall bring upon you every sickness which I brought upon Egypt. Here too there is a great mystery.

## CHAPTER III. That Moses, a diligent foster-father, received the children of Israel as little children, and what the waters of Marah signify.

“Scripture says, ‘Moses took the children of Israel from the Red Sea.’” Understand this as meaning that a diligent foster-father took his little foster-children from the sacrament of new regeneration. For they had indeed been baptized only in figure, and had not, as we have, been reborn in Christ (1 Cor. 10); consequently, they too, like all human beings, still needed the future cleansing accomplished by Christ’s blood. Nevertheless, because of that same prefiguration [Col. 0654C] of baptism, in their very ascent from the Red Sea they signified those little children to whom the blessed apostle Peter says: “Therefore, laying aside all malice and all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all slanders, like newborn infants desire the rational and guileless milk, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2).

It is evident that infants of this kind ought to be carried with a nurturing affection so long as they are little, so long as they need milk rather than solid food (Heb. 5). And this is the great concern incumbent upon rulers of peoples: that they should bear such persons, as it were, upon their shoulders, according to the prophet’s saying: “Their children shall be carried upon shoulders and comforted upon knees” (Isa. 66). Thus it was well and appropriately said, “he took”: for whoever [Col. 0654D] intends rightly and according to God to bear the childish dispositions of human beings takes upon himself a great burden. Moses first experienced this in himself [p. 206] and says to the Lord: “Why have you afflicted your servant? Why do I not find favour before you? Why have you laid the burden of this whole people upon me? [Col. 0655A] Did I conceive all this multitude or give birth to it, that you should say to me: Carry them in your bosom, as a nurse is accustomed to carry a little child, and bring them into the land concerning which I swore to their fathers?” (Num. 11).

“And they came,” it says, “to Marah.” Marah, whose waters they could not drink because they were bitter, signifies the old Law, whose carnal ceremonies we, little children redeemed by Christ’s blood, could not bear. Nor indeed could the fathers themselves bear them, as the apostle Peter says: “Now therefore why do you test God by putting a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (Acts 15). Surely, did those who said these things to such little children wish to give them waters from Marah to drink—waters which they themselves could not drink because of their bitterness?

“Moses cried out to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood” [Col. 0655B]. This wood, which the Lord showed to Moses—or rather, through grace, to us also—is the wood of the holy and life-giving Cross. For to cast wood into the waters of Marah and thereby turn them to sweetness is to compare the mystery of the Lord’s Passion with the letter of the Law. How sweet this is, the person who has been granted to experience it knows; the person who drinks it tastes it.

## CHAPTER IV. What Elim, the twelve springs, and the seventy palms signify

“But they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped beside the waters.” What need was there for us to know the number of springs and the number of palms, unless a mystery worthy of knowledge lay hidden in these also? [Col. 0655C]

Elim is translated “rams.” Therefore, since we sing also in the Psalm: “You led your people like sheep by the hand of Moses and Aaron” (Ps. 76); and since in the Gospel the Shepherd says of us: “I have other sheep which are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice, and there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John 10), let us understand here, by the name Elim—that is, “of rams”—the Lord’s very sheepfold. For rams are leaders of flocks and princes of the fold.

Moreover, by the abundance of twelve springs and the multitude of seventy palms, let us understand that this fold is shown to us as exceedingly pleasant for the sheep to dwell in, and as a fitting resting-place for rearing the sons of rams, concerning whom the Psalmist says: “Bring to the Lord, [Col. 0655D] sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 28). For what ought we to understand by the fullness of the twelve springs except the totality of teachers? Since the twelve are apostles, whose chief office is teaching, all those who have advanced so far through apostolic teaching that they may sit in the rank of teachers, in the midst of the Lord’s fold—that is, in the midst of the Church—and open their mouths, are rightly designated by the number twelve.

Nor is it strange that the apostolic order, or the totality of apostolic persons, should be enclosed within such a number, namely twelve, which, as arithmeticians say, is “abundant,” because it is exceeded by the sum of its parts. Its half, plainly, is six; its third, four; [Col. 0656A] its fourth, three; its sixth, two; and its twelfth, one. Together these make sixteen, a number which exceeds twelve by four units. This, I say, is not strange, for in the Church there have also been superfluous teachers who, possessing eloquence without wisdom, made heresies and schisms; and at the beginning of the faith many were found to be apostles beyond measure—that is, false apostles.

But what do we understand by the seventy palms flourishing around those springs except devout and strong martyrs? For Scripture says of every such person: “He shall be like a tree planted by the waters, which sends forth its roots toward moisture and shall not fear when heat comes,” etc. (Jer. 17). Here, therefore, the healthful delightfulness of our fold is set before us spiritual sheep, [Col. 0656B] so that we may not fear the wolves against whom our martyrs fought; for this they are now crowned and receive palms—palms as great and of such a kind as may be understood through the number seventy, composed of seven and ten. The former number commends the grace of the sevenfold Spirit; the latter, the Decalogue of the Law.

Let us delight in frequenting the twelve springs, so that Christ may rightly pronounce concerning the sheep of his Church: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing. All bear twins, and none among them is barren” (Song 4).

## CHAPTER V. On the murmuring of the children of Israel for meat, and on the appearance of manna

[Col. 0656C] **(CHAPTER 16.)** “They set out from Elim, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt. And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness,” etc.

Scripture says that the wilderness of Sin is the same as Kadesh. Sin is translated “temptation,” Sinai, “my temptation.” This name well suits the matter, since the murmuring children of Israel said: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate flesh to the full,” etc. For the Psalmist plainly testifies that such murmuring was a temptation, saying: “They tempted God in [Col. 0656D] their hearts, seeking food for their souls. And they spoke wickedly against God and said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77).

A temptation of this kind was their sin. It was not because they asked for food, but because they said: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? For he struck the rock, and waters flowed out and torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” (ibid.)—for this reason it was reckoned to them as sin. “Therefore,” says the Psalmist, “the Lord heard and delayed, and a fire was kindled in Jacob, and wrath rose against Israel” (ibid.). As has already been said, it was not because they requested food, by which mortal flesh is necessarily sustained, but because, in asking, “they did not believe in God nor hope in his salvation” [Col. 0657A] (Ps. 77).

The history is clear: manna rained down for them to eat, and flesh like dust (ibid.), namely a flock of quails. Manna was, as it is written elsewhere, “like coriander seed” (Exod. 16), that is, the seed of the herb called *corion* in Greek; and “the colour of bdellium” (Num. 11), an aromatic tree whose nature Pliny describes most fully. In place of “quail,” however, many read *ortigometra*; others interpret *ortigometra* as quails, although it is another kind of bird, even if not entirely unlike quails. Others assert that *ortigometrae* are leaders of quails, named from the island Ortygia, where they abound.

Now, as we begin to enter into the mystery drawn from this chapter [Col. 0657B] which is celebrated throughout the whole world, according to the truthful saying in the Psalm, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77), we must first [p. 207] note, I say, how great is the guilt of the evil of murmuring. Moses says to the people: “For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against God.” Yet neither the first time, when they murmured for water, nor the second, when they now murmur for meat, were they punished; God’s patience bore with them until the third occasion. For when they murmured the third time, at the graves of craving, they were no longer rebuked with words alone but were punished with death. “For,” says Scripture, “the flesh was still in their teeth, and such food had not yet failed, when behold, the wrath of the Lord was stirred up against the people and struck them with an exceedingly great plague” [Col. 0657C] (Num. 11).

Accordingly, even now in the holy Church, patience is just: a person should be rebuked in words for any fault up to the third occasion, and only then, if he has not amended his conduct, be punished.

## CHAPTER VI. On the inverted order: whether, according to the history, bread was first given to those who asked and water afterward brought forth from the struck rock, or conversely according to the Prophet

The Prophet’s order is not the same as that in which these events are set out in the holy and truthful Scripture of the history. Here the deeds done are also narrated in their actual order: bread was first given to those requesting it, and afterward water is recalled as having been brought forth from the struck rock [Col. 0657D]. But in the Prophet the order is inverted: “He split the rock in the wilderness and gave them drink as from a great abyss; he brought forth waters as rivers” (Ps. 77), etc. After this has been stated first, there follows: “And they continued still to sin against him” (ibid.). In what way? “They said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? For he struck the rock, and waters flowed out and torrents overflowed. Can he also give bread, or prepare a table for his people?” (ibid.).

In saying this, he plainly intends that the event in which, when the rock was struck, “waters flowed and torrents overflowed” should come first, and that the later event should be that “he commanded the clouds above, opened the doors of heaven, and rained manna upon them to eat.” Why is this so? Because he speaks parabolically, as he declared at the beginning of the Psalm: “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning” [Col. 0658A] (ibid.).

Lest the explanation of these parables should be difficult, the Apostle followed up his words: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (1 Cor. 10), by immediately adding: “Now the rock was Christ” (ibid.). With this statement, as though a single ray of sunlight had been cast through a window, he dispelled the darkness of the whole house, so that we might clearly see that in the preceding parables we must understand another rock and another water flowing from the rock.

The Lord likewise, when the Jews said to him, “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: He gave them bread from heaven to eat” (John 6), immediately contradicts them in his answer: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” [Col. 0658B] (ibid.). Surely he shows that the bread referred to by the Prophet, whose testimony they had misused, was one thing, and the bread which the Jews remembered their fathers having eaten in this history was another.

Therefore, with the manifold authority of the Prophet who speaks these things in parables, with the faith of the Apostle who says that all these things happened to them in figure (1 Cor. 10), and with the truth of Christ who declares himself to be the bread, let us faithfully understand the striking of the rock, when we come to that passage, as the Lord’s Passion; and, for the present, let us understand in the abundant bread, descending with the dew above the camp, his body which we receive from the holy altar.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 0658C] Whether, in accordance with the mystical meaning, the historical order could fittingly be inverted by the Prophet

But someone says: Even if the splitting of the rock signified Christ’s Passion, and the manna Christ’s table prepared for us unto salvation on earth, still the historical events ought not to have been inverted so that the Prophet first said the rock had been struck for waters to flow and then that the clouds above had been commanded and manna rained upon them for food. For before the Lord Jesus Christ was struck by the affliction of the Cross, he himself opened the doors of heaven by his word and rained down this manna. Indeed, on the very night in which he was betrayed, he himself consecrated with his own hands the holy Eucharist, commanding us to do this.

To this I say: Our Lord did this not before his Passion but at the very moment of his Passion [Col. 0658D]. He had already been sold; he was already being betrayed; his soul was already sorrowful unto death; he was already afraid and grieved; he had entered into agony and, praying, sweated drops of blood; because of the certainty of his imminent death, he was already saying that he was no longer in the world.

This too must be noted: although elsewhere he commended the necessary eating of this bread—that is, of himself—by saying, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6), he nevertheless never showed us how this could or ought to be done except in that hour in which he was betrayed, when, as has been said, he was agonizing in the distress of his Passion. Why? Because the work, reality, and power of his Passion are the sacrament by which the substance of bread and wine is changed for us into the true reality of his body and blood. Hence the Apostle says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” [Col. 0659A] (1 Cor. 11).

Moreover, everyone knows that one must first be invited to faith in the Lord’s Passion before being admitted to participation in this bread; that is, one must first be baptized into his death before being admitted to the holy altar to communicate in his flesh and blood. The Prophet therefore rightly inverted the historical acts, saying first that the rock was split so that waters might flow, and afterward that the doors of heaven were opened so that man might be fed with the bread of angels.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0659B] When the Apostle says, “They all ate the same spiritual food,” etc., and Christ says to the Jews, “Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but the Father,” etc.: whether the figures and the realities are the same in this matter

Again, someone may say: Since the Apostle says concerning the fathers, “They all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. 10), how did Christ say, when speaking to the Jews, “Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6)?

We answer: When the Apostle says “the same food,” the wording in no way indicates that he intended us to supply “the same as we have.” Certainly great Fathers before us have supplied this relation; but, as someone said concerning another matter, although they possess great authority and the greatness of their holiness or wisdom bears weight upon us, we are guided more by the evangelical authority of Christ than by arguments of anyone’s eloquence. For reason does not allow the figure and the reality to be the same.

The Apostle said of this matter, as of the other events [p. 208], that “they happened to them in figure” [Col. 0659C] (1 Cor. 10). Therefore, when he says “all,” and subsequently makes a distinction among them all by saying, “But God was not pleased with many of them, for they were overthrown in the wilderness,” it is plain to the understanding that this is as though he said: all ate one food and all drank one spiritual drink—that is, food and drink resulting not from a natural process but from spiritual [Col. 0659D] power—yet not all entered that land of promise. They were, plainly, a figure of us: we all partake of the same sacrament of Christ’s body, yet not all of us, whether we have lived well or badly, are to be admitted together into that land of the living.

Thus, what Truth says, denying in the past tense but affirming in the present, “Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven”; and what the Apostle of truth says, “They all ate the same spiritual food and all drank the same spiritual drink,” are not incompatible or contrary, as plain reason demonstrates. Now, intending to say something about the mystery of this bread, let us return to the beginning of the reading.

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0660A] What it signifies that those murmuring against Moses said, “We sat by the pots of meat,” etc.

“They say: ‘We sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full. Why have you led us into this wilderness, to kill this whole multitude by hunger?’” This murmuring of the children of Israel is a figure of Jewish contention. For just as they, after the immolation of the lamb, the drowning of Pharaoh and all his army, and the crossing of the Red Sea, looked back with extreme ingratitude to Egypt’s pots of meat and its bread of fullness, though they had been slaves and had been brought to bitterness through much affliction, so the newly baptized Jews in Christ, after the Passion of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, and after the prince of this world had already been cast out, looked back with foolish obstinacy to the old sacrifices of bulls and rams. These sacrifices the Lord God plainly despises in the sayings of the prophets; yet they contended, saying: “Unless you are circumcised and walk in every respect according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” [Col. 0660B] (Acts 15).

Moses answers: “Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord.” The apostles could indeed have said this. Did the rejection of carnal sacrifices originate with the preachers of the Gospel themselves? Certainly not. It originated with the Lord himself—for example, when he said in the Psalm: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49), and much else like it.

Let therefore the apostolic leaders of believers, [Col. 0660C] who lead a people burdened by carnal custom to spiritual understanding through Christ’s baptism, say: “For what are we?” Clearly, because while we live in the body, we are, in your judgment, far less authoritative than any prophet, even the least, who have long since departed. Nor is this surprising: even while they were still alive, they were so despised that they were killed; and, because you are their inferiors, you build their tombs as though honouring them (Matt. 23).

Yet you confess that God, the Lord of gods, spoke through them—he who does not rebuke you concerning your sacrifices, but rather says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49). Therefore, “your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord”: that is, you are not contending against the novelty of the evangelists, but against the antiquity of your own prophets [Col. 0660D].

## CHAPTER X. Who is that bread which the Lord rained from heaven upon the children of Israel in the wilderness

“Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you. Let the people go out and gather what suffices for each day, that I may test them whether they walk in my law or not. But on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather each day.” “I shall rain for you,” he says.

In agreement with this word, the Prophet says: “He commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven, and rained manna upon them to eat” (Ps. 77). He then indicates what he intends by manna, immediately adding: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” [Col. 0661A] (ibid.). Who is this bread of heaven, this bread of angels? Do angels feed in heaven on that bread which the people gathered, like coriander, and broke with a millstone or crushed in a mortar?

Therefore the bread of heaven, the bread of angels, is he himself who says in his Gospel: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (John 6). For he is the food and life of the angelic nature, and the angels desire to look into him (1 Pet. 1). Because an angel despised to do this, he fell and became the devil. He suffers perpetual hunger for this bread; he is always pale, and death follows him.

Therefore worthy is the Prophet’s exclamation, worthy his amazement: because, with the doors of heaven opened, “man ate the bread of angels” [Col. 0661B] (Ps. 77). Whence comes this? From the fact that “he commanded the clouds above and opened the doors of heaven”: that is, he revealed beforehand to the apostles and also to the prophets, of whom it is said, “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17)—that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets. Then, through himself, he opened the doors of heaven formerly shut to humankind, dissolving in his flesh the old enmities. Thus he joined earthly things to heavenly things—that is, associated human beings with angels—so that they may feed on the same bread of heaven: the angels in heavenly places, in the manifest vision of divinity; we, still placed upon earth, in the sacrament of godliness, of which the Apostle says: “Great is the sacrament of godliness: it was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed in the world, taken up in glory” [Col. 0661C] (1 Tim. 3).

There, indeed, “bread of heaven” and “bread of angels” are said in the singular; here, however, “I shall rain breads for you” is said in the plural. Yet do not suppose there is any discrepancy, since there also it is added in the plural: “He sent them provisions in abundance” (Ps. 77). Therefore Christ is one bread, or the body of Christ is one body, in itself; nevertheless, according to local churches and according to the persons offering it or the innumerable peoples receiving it, you rightly speak in the plural of provisions or breads.

The word “rained,” which both Scriptures use—God saying in this one, “Behold, I shall rain,” and the other saying, “He rained manna upon them to eat”—signifies a supply prepared everywhere in the world for all, great and small. Thus the great Prophet says of himself: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. 22); and of us, although least: “The poor shall eat and be filled; those who seek the Lord shall praise him; their hearts shall live for ever and ever” [Col. 0661D] (Ps. 21).

## CHAPTER XI. A mystical interpretation of the words: “Let the people go out and gather what suffices for each day”

“Let the people go out,” he says, “and gather what suffices for each day.” Certainly we too must go out spiritually, so that we may gather as much as can suffice. From where shall we go out? From our former way of life, from the oldness of life. For until we have put off the old man, we are not to gather manna, nor are we to eat this bread of the Lord [Col. 0662A].

Further, if we desire to eat worthily, let us depart from every curiosity of bodily sense, so that we may judge neither by sight, taste, smell, nor touch whether what we receive is Christ’s true body or true flesh. For while these colour, smell, and taste remain, there is what suffices for faith and is enough for Catholic piety. “It is the Spirit,” he says, “who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6).

Words of faith, words of truth, spoken over the substance of bread and wine, suffice for spirit and eternal life to be breathed into inanimate creatures, although their outward appearance [Col. 0662B] is not changed. This, I say, suffices for the salvation of the believer and the life of the worthy recipient. Therefore let each person gather only so much, because only so much suffices. Let each gather what suffices: that is, let each believe the Lord’s words to be spirit and life, and that by them bread and wine, without a change in outward appearance, are transferred into the true substance of the body and blood of the living Christ. For visible change into a new appearance—this into sheep’s flesh, that into a horror of blood—profits nothing; indeed, it is faithless.

## CHAPTER XII. On the words: “That I may test him, whether he walks in my law or not”

Lastly he says: “That I may test him, whether he walks in my law or not.” Was it then just that God should test that people in such a manner, or that he should still test the Christian person today over such food and drink? It was altogether just that God should test that people, for that people was testing God. It has already been said above that the greatness of their sin lay not in asking, but in asking for food while testing God and murmuring, because, according to the Psalmist, “They tempted God in their hearts, seeking food for their souls, and spoke wickedly against God. They said: Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” [Col. 0662C] (Ps. 77).

Therefore, when God showed those who tested him what he himself could do by preparing a table for them, it was just that he in turn should test them, lest they fail to know what they themselves were. This is almost like what God says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “They [Col. 0662D] provoked me with that which was not God, and I shall provoke them with that which is not a people” (Deut. 32). For when tested, they were found not to walk in his law—that is, in his faith—because, distrusting the morrow, they gathered more than was sufficient “for each day,” as is related below.

Further, manifest reason supports the justice of our being tested through this spiritual food and drink. Man was tempted by the devil and conquered; let him be tempted by God, so that he may overcome the deceit of that tempter and, by an antidote suited to the nature of the disease, fittingly aid his life. The first human beings were tempted by the devil, who said, “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3); and they believed him more than God, who said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death” [Col. 0663A] (Gen. 3).

Therefore let man be tested by the Son of God, who says of bread and wine: “Eat; this is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26). Eat, and you shall be sons of God; and let us believe his word more than our carnal eyes, which behold only the outward appearance of bread and wine. Thus let us abolish in ourselves the wicked credulity of our parents by devout credulity.

## CHAPTER XIII. [p. 209] That on the Sabbath they did not gather, but ate manna stored up on the sixth day; and on the twofold Sabbath

“But on the sixth day let them prepare what they bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather each day.” “What they bring in,” he says, means what they store up [Col. 0663B] for the following Sabbath, on which they ought to be free from work or rest in commemoration of the Creator, who worked for six days and rested on the seventh.

But in the first part of this work we have said that those days must be understood as belonging to another order, and that God’s Sabbath—that is, God’s rest—is far other than a human being’s. Why, then, was concern shown at that time for such a Sabbath as carnal Jews still observe? Because God foresaw that it would be useful to humankind in two ways.

First, just as all things happened to them in figure, so that figurative Sabbath might be a figure of the spiritual Sabbath, and by its carnal resemblance might recall that other divine work—not only as long as it was observed, but as long as it is read or is to be read [Col. 0663C] (Exod. 6). Secondly, he provided that on one day out of seven the mercy due to the hired labourer might have relief, as the Law says elsewhere: “For six days you shall work; on the seventh you shall cease, so that your ox and your ass may rest, and that the son of your female servant and the stranger may be refreshed” (Deut. 5).

Therefore, if we have recognized God’s true Sabbath, where, while he rests and rejoices in his works, the souls of the saints—now having put off the burden of the flesh—rest with him, let us know this also: the manna given to us will not be found on the Sabbath to be gathered; rather, what has been gathered beforehand will then be eaten, when he is seen face to face. For the person who now loses baptism will not be able to find another baptism there; nor will anyone who has presumed unworthily to eat the Lord’s body and drink his blood, or has utterly despised it, find there a sacrifice to offer for sins or receive for the remission of sins.

Therefore what we prepare in this sixth age should be double what the people of God once used to gather. For they, reading the letter alone, worshipped God; but for us, because “the Word was made flesh” (John 1), Christ, God and man, is to be worshipped and adored [Col. 0663D].

## CHAPTER XIV. That Moses promises the people meat and bread although the Lord spoke only of bread; and why it is said, “In the evening you shall know … in the morning you shall see”

“And Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel: ‘In the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord. For he has heard your murmuring against the Lord. But what are we, that you have murmured against us?’ And Moses said: ‘The Lord will give you meat to eat in the evening, and bread to the full in the morning,’” etc.

It should be noted [p. 210; Col. 0664A] that although the Lord spoke only of bread—“Behold, I shall rain bread from heaven for you”—Moses, conveying the commands to the people, promises meat as though on his own initiative: “The Lord,” he says, “will give you meat to eat in the evening, and bread to the full in the morning.” Indeed, later the Lord says to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel: In the evening you shall eat meat,” etc. Nevertheless, we hear evening meat promised by Moses before we hear it from the mouth of the Lord.

What then do we understand by meat [Col. 0664B] except the old sacrifices, and by manna except the new sacrifice? For, as has already been discussed above and as the prophets testify, the Lord promised that those sacrifices would be offered; he did not command them. But this new sacrifice of his body and blood he himself handed down, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). Thus the Lord himself, and Moses afterward, rightly promised the fullness of bread.

What do we understand by evening except the old state, and by morning except the new brightness of new life? “Weeping,” says the Psalmist, “will linger in the evening, and joy comes in the morning” (Ps. 29). For because the first Adam, convicted and judged for disobedience, came into this mortality at evening, while the new Adam, having fulfilled obedience, rose in the morning into immortality and incorruption, evening is rightly understood here as the old life, in which Jews sacrificed the flesh of bulls and the blood of goats; morning, however, as the new life, in which Christians, with Christ the high priest going before them, offer sacrifice and are filled with the bread of heaven [Col. 0664C].

At that evening, weeping lingered for all descending into the lower world; but from this morning there is joy, because heaven is open and paradise has been opened. Let him therefore say: “In the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord … In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.” It is as though he said: Since you remember sitting by the pots of meat, throughout this whole evening—which precedes the dawn-bearing advent of Christ—you may be served [Col. 0664D] by carnal sacrifices, from which you cannot be torn away. Yet by these sacrifices you should know and bring to remembrance that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt—for example, through the evening sacrifice of the paschal lamb—and “in the morning you shall see the glory,” that is, the glorious resurrection of the Lord, in comparison with which the glory of being brought out of Egypt is no glory.

## CHAPTER XV. What it signifies that “the quail covered the camp, and the dew around the camp” covered the surface of the earth like hoarfrost, while the children of Israel said, “Manhu”

> “So it came to pass in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning dew lay round about the camp. [Col. 0665A] And when it had covered the surface of the ground, there appeared in the wilderness something small, like a thing pounded with a pestle, resembling hoarfrost upon the earth. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another: *Manhu*—that is, ‘What is this?’”

A splendid representation of realities and a beautiful distinction of figures. The quail covered the camp, but the dew, together with which the manna descended, lay not within the camp but around the camp: it covered, I say, not the camp, but the surface of the earth. And the small thing appeared in the wilderness, while the children of Israel said: “*Manhu*.”

The dew signifies the Holy Spirit, concerning whom we have in the Psalm (Ps. 132): “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron … like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion”; thus “it is good and pleasant [Col. 0665B] for brethren to dwell together in unity,” which comes about through the one and only Spirit of love. For Aaron, whose name is interpreted “mountainous,” is Christ; and as the beard adheres to the head, so the perfect and strong apostles who cleave to him were then moistened with the ointment of that same head, when they were filled with his Holy Spirit. The dew of that same ointment—that is, the freely bestowed gift—descended upon the mountains of Hermon and Zion, that is, upon the Church of both peoples, Gentile and Jewish: the former, namely the Gentile people, being understood through Hermon, which is interpreted “accursed,” and the latter, that is, the Jewish people, through Mount Zion.

Therefore the dew that descended with the manna signifies the Holy Spirit, by whose sanctification the body of Christ is consecrated at the priest’s invocation. The quail covered the camp, but the dew [Col. 0665C] lay around the camp, because, plainly, while the Synagogue busies itself with carnal sacrifices, it has nothing in common with this true and living bread which descends with this dew. You must leave that camp, whoever you are who strive to gather this small thing brought by this dew.

The quail covered only the camp, but the dew covered the surface of the earth, and the small thing appeared in the wilderness, because Christ gave not to one nation alone—as he gave the law concerning carnal sacrifices—but to the whole earth and to the wilderness of all nations the grace of the Holy Spirit and the true bread from heaven, that is, himself. It was “as though pounded with a pestle,” which plainly signifies Christ bruised upon the wood of the cross through his Passion. It descended “in the likeness [Col. 0665D] of hoarfrost,” because for that people, in the persons of the reprobate portion, he made a cold mist of unbelief and envy.

Hence they said to one another: “*Manhu*,” which means, “What is this?” For they began to say this when he said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven,” and “he who eats my flesh has eternal life” (John 6), and the like; they disputed and murmured, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid.). Then, I say, they began to say, “*Manhu*”; and to this day either Jews or heretics, their followers, do not cease to say it, when we tell them, “It is Christ’s flesh,” and they always reply, “How is it? How is it?”

## CHAPTER XVI. That the children of Israel, tested by the Lord, were found faithless in three matters

> “And the children of Israel did so, and gathered, one more and another less; and they measured it by the measure of a gomor. Neither did he who had gathered more have anything over, nor did he who had prepared less find less; but each gathered according to what he was able to eat,” etc.

The children of Israel, tested by the Lord, who had said, as stated above, “that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not,” fell into the test in three matters and were found faithless.

First, because, having heard the Lord’s word saying, “Let each gather from it as much as suffices for eating, a gomor for each head, according to the number of your souls,” [Col. 0666B] they gathered “one more and another less.” For the fact that “they measured it by the measure of a gomor, and neither did he who had gathered more have anything over, nor did he who had prepared less find less” was the work of divine power and operation, and belongs to a mystery of which something will be said shortly.

Second, they fell into the test concerning the same matter when, though the Lord said through Moses, “Let no one leave any of it until morning,” they did not heed him, but “some of them left some of it until morning.”

Third, when the seventh day came, some of the people went out to gather and found nothing. Thus, after a threefold transgression had been committed, “How long,” says the Lord, “will you refuse to keep my commandments?”

Now a gomor is an Attic measure containing twelve sextarii; it is a tenth part of an ephah, as you have in what follows. The ephah, therefore, like the bath, is one measure—that is, three modii.

## CHAPTER XVII. That no one receives more or less of the grace of the Holy Spirit according to the quantity of his portion of Christ’s body or blood

> “Neither did he who had gathered more have anything over, nor did he who had prepared less find less,” etc.

Concerning the power of the food and spiritual drink—that is, the body and blood of Christ—this must be known and firmly maintained: no one receives more or less of the grace of the life-giving Spirit according to the quantity of the portion which he receives by mouth under the visible form of bread and wine. Rather, each gathers according to what he is able to eat; that is, each receives, according to what he is able to believe, forgiveness of sins and eternal life. [Col. 0666D]

For just as our father, who first sinned and whose iniquity we bear, received the just sentence or condemnation not according to the quantity of his bite, or of the fruit which he bit; and it was as effective for him, toward the full accomplishment of unbelief and disobedience, to have bitten one apple as if he had devoured every fruit upon that tree: so, conversely, none of us receives grace or life according to the quantity of the little portion of life-giving bread broken for him, which he takes with his mouth or grinds with his teeth. Rather, the reception of a very small amount is as effective for him in attaining righteousness as it would be if he alone received with his own mouth all that has been offered.

Therefore the holy Church of Christ rightly prepares not very large loaves, but small and very thin wafers for the consecration of Christ’s body, and pours in not much wine but a small amount, because, as has already been said, neither does the one who gathers more have anything over, nor does the one who has prepared less find less. [Col. 0667A]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the saying, “Let no one leave any of it until morning,” and on the avaricious who do not put their hope in God

> “And the Lord said through Moses to them: Let no one leave any of it until morning.”

According to the letter, faith is required of the people: entrusting their whole care to God, they are not to be anxious about tomorrow (Matt. 6). That miracle foreshadowed a fitting punishment for their disobedience, or scanty faith: when “some of them left some of it until morning, it began to swarm with worms and rot.”

Let the faithless avaricious person, who has not put his hope in God and therefore serves Mammon by storing up riches, know that he is rebuked by this example. “The righteous,” says the Psalmist, “shall see and fear; and they shall laugh at him and say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the multitude of his riches” (Ps. 51). For the worm of cares and anxieties consumes such a person now, while he lives; and in the future the worm that does not die will consume him. [Col. 0667B]

Spiritually, moreover, that little worm swarming from the manna is he who speaks in the Psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21). As a worm springs from manna without intercourse, so Christ, the Son of God, alone was conceived and born from a virginal womb without male seed. But when this is preached to unbelieving Jews, it is a stumbling block to them; for they reckon it foul and unworthy of God that he could have been born of a woman. Thus the true manna which came down from heaven has rotted for such people; yet what is weakness to them is power and wisdom for believers.

Concerning the words, “This is what he spoke: The rest of the Sabbath has been sanctified to the Lord,” and likewise, “Gather for six days, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord; therefore it will not be found,” and the rest, enough has already been said above. Of the golden urn, which was commanded to be placed with manna before the Lord for preservation through everlasting generations, we shall speak more suitably elsewhere. [Col. 0667D]

## CHAPTER XIX. That the Jews ought not to glory in their own merits, and what the struck rock is from which water flowed

(CHAPTER XVII.)

> “Therefore the whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin, by their stages according to the word of the Lord, and encamped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. They quarrelled with Moses and said: Give us water to drink.”

And afterwards: “Why did you make us leave Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”

Wherever there are murmurings and disputes, and God’s benefits come freely, no merits precede them. Therefore that people must not glory that the Lord magnified or honoured it [Col. 0668A] on account of its merits. For they not only failed to deserve magnificence and honour, but made themselves deserving of disgrace and reproach. Let every mouth therefore be stopped, and let the whole world be made subject to God. For what distinction is there in this respect between Jew and Greek? “All have sinned and are in need of the glory of God” (Rom. 3).

Moses first says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Because of my righteousness God has brought me in to possess this land’” (Deut. 9). Again: “Know therefore that it is not because of your righteousness that the Lord your God has given it to you, since you are a people of the stiffest neck. From the day you came out of Egypt, you have continually contended against the Lord your God in the wilderness” (ibid.).

And David: “All,” he says, “have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13).—“We know,” says the Apostle, “that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law,” etc. (Rom. 3). [Col. 0668B]

Let the grace of God alone therefore be glorified: it both brought manna from heaven and water from the rock for those then murmuring against the Lord and stirring up disputes; and now it has stood so mercifully by Jews and Gentiles who blaspheme that it places at their mouths the bread of life—of which something has already been said above—and the water of everlasting salvation, while his ambassadors meanwhile entreat them and say: “We beseech you for Christ: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5).

Meeting us while we were his enemies with bread and water—with the bread, I say, of his body, and the water which the struck rock, that is, Christ himself crucified, poured forth—he beseeches us to come into reconciliation with God the Father. For what that rock was which was struck is known to all who thirst, the Apostle proclaiming: “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), as has already been said above.

Moreover, by the water flowing from the rock must be understood not only the blood of Christ the Son of God, or the visible water which ran from his opened side together with that blood, but also the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, concerning which he himself says to the Samaritan woman: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). And elsewhere: “He who believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water [Col. 0668D] shall flow from his belly.” “But this,” says the Evangelist, “he said concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7). He immediately adds: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 16).

Therefore, unless the rock had been struck, the water would not have flowed; that is, unless Christ had departed from here through his Passion, this Paraclete would not have come to us, as he himself says. Yet we shall have occasion to speak of this mystery elsewhere.

## CHAPTER XX. On Amalek’s first battle against Israel; how he was defeated while Moses prayed

> “Now Amalek came and fought against Israel at Rephidim. And Moses said to Joshua: Choose men and fight against Amalek. Tomorrow I shall stand on the [Col. 0669A] top of the hill, holding the rod of God in my hand,” etc.

In this battle of Israel against Amalek there is something at which we rightly marvel, and which no person experienced in legitimate warfare would think devoid of mystery. What then? Was this enemy Amalek greater or stronger than all Israel’s enemies, or was he alone the one against whom battle had necessarily to be waged in such a manner?

“Moses,” Scripture says, “and Aaron and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed. Now Moses’ hands were heavy,” etc.

Was it, I ask, without the purpose of a definite mystery that this enemy was defeated in such an order? The mystery itself must therefore be diligently investigated. First of all, it must be known that Amalek was the first among all nations to attack gratuitously the people of God after its departure from Egypt. Therefore Balaam says of him in his prophecy: “Amalek is the first of the nations, but his latter end shall be destruction” (Num. 24).

But the manner in which he attacked is read thus in Deuteronomy: “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way when you came out of Egypt: how he met you and struck down [Col. 0669B] the rearmost of your host, those who were weary and lagging behind” (Deut. 27). Here the Hebrews understand “the weary” to mean those unclean persons who, according to the law, remained outside the camp. The Amalekites are said to have struck them down because, as they themselves hand down, they cut off their circumcision and threw it into heaven in mockery of God.

Therefore, because Amalek thus became the first of the nations and was the first of all to fight against Israel after the Exodus from Egypt, and because the very name Amalek is interpreted “a people licking,” he is rightly judged to bear the type of all visible and invisible enemies of the people of God fleeing from this world to God. Thus battle was waged against him in such a way that the battle itself portrayed how the devil with all who are on his side must be overcome.

Amalek came—there came the “people licking,” going after its own desires, whose prince and leader is the devil. Having taken counsel with evil spirits, it has always attacked, and does not cease to attack, the people of God dwelling as strangers in this world. Against him Moses goes up the mountain, with Aaron, whose name is interpreted “mountainous” or “mountain of strength.” By Moses we understand the Law; by Aaron, [Col. 0669D] Christ; by Hur, the Holy Spirit.

For why was the Law given, except to teach a person to fight, and according to it to lift up his hands against the devil into heaven—that is, the works of righteousness? (Heb. 7). But “Moses’ hands,” it says, “were heavy,” because the Law was plainly unable to bring anything to perfection. “Therefore they took a stone and placed it under him, and he sat upon it,” because for this purpose Christ the Son of God came into the world, and for this purpose, when he had been glorified, the Holy Spirit was given: that the solid grace of the Gospel might be substituted for the Law in its weakness, and Moses might sit upon it—that is, the Law might be fulfilled in it.

“Aaron,” it says, “and Hur supported his hands on either side.” For Christ and the Paraclete whom he sent made easy and bearable for us in the life-giving Spirit the difficulty of the killing letter, which, as the apostle Peter says, “neither our fathers nor we were able to bear” (Acts 15). [Col. 0670A] Thus “it came to pass,” it says, “that his hands did not grow weary until sunset; and Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword.”

Therefore, by this example warfare is enjoined upon Christians, and the outcome of warfare is revealed by the persistence of prayer. Moses prays and prevails; he ceases and is defeated. The Christian has learned what he must do and has discovered what he must avoid; he has learned, I say, whence he is either defeated or victorious. Moses was fighting against a human being, and fighting by praying for others. No one, then, can be excused who does not wish to conquer the enemy, since he has ceased to pray. Yet in Moses it was the body that failed; his will never ceased. If, therefore, Moses could not be excused on account of frailty, how can the will in us be excused? [Col. 0670B]

## CHAPTER XXI. On the words spoken to Moses: “Write this in a book,” etc.

> “And the Lord said to Moses: Write this in a book as a memorial, and deliver it into the ears of Joshua; for I shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”

Saul is reproved for having rejected the word of the Lord, and for the sin of disobedience is cast away by God as though for the crime of idolatry, not merely because the Lord commanded him through Samuel, saying: “I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, how he opposed him on the way when he came up from Egypt. Now therefore go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that he has” (1 Sam. 15), while he himself turned to plunder and did evil in the eyes of the Lord. He is also reproved because it was said and written in this manner: “Write this in a book as a memorial, for I shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”

For when the one who wrote nothing anywhere without authority here introduces the command of him who says, “Write this,” and then adds, “For I shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven,” he surely presses the future transgressor with the great weight of judgment, lest it seem a small audacity that, when God did not spare, he dared to spare, or that, when God commanded the vengeance of justice, he himself turned toward plunder. [Col. 0670C]

Spiritually, moreover, God wills it to be written in the book of each of our hearts that he will destroy the devil, the ancient enemy of Israel, and his angels and human followers, and blot out their memory from under heaven—namely, by saying, “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). Thus, while this Scripture remains in our hearts, we may never make peace with him, nor, when commanded to fight against this Amalek, be disobedient.

For what was commanded to one person in the words, “Deliver it into the ears of Joshua,” pertains to all of us and has been handed down for all to hear. If by fighting in this way we destroy Amalek, we shall triumph more nobly than Saul, who by sparing him erected the triumphal arch of pride; and our obedience will please God more than Saul’s sacrifices. For this is indicated by what follows: “And Moses built an altar and called [Col. 0671A] its name, ‘The Lord is my exaltation,’ saying: ‘Because [there is] a hand upon the throne of the Lord [variant: the hand of the Lord alone], and the war of God shall be against Amalek from generation to generation.’”

For he who conquers has built his own soul into God’s temple, so that, standing continually, with a stone placed beneath him, his hands may not grow weary “until sunset”—that is, until the end of the present life—and so that he may say with David: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26). And afterwards: “Upon a rock he exalted me, and now he has lifted up my head above my enemies. I shall go round about and offer in his tabernacle a sacrifice of joyful shouting” (ibid.), etc.

## CHAPTER XXII. That Moses listened to the counsel of his kinsman, in accordance with the saying of the Saviour, “the children of this age are wiser,” etc.

(CHAPTER XVIII.)

> “When Jethro, priest of Midian and kinsman of Moses, heard all that the Lord had done for Moses and for Israel his people, because the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt, he took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, whom he had sent away, and her two sons.”

For what reason Moses had sent away his wife and sons has been written above: namely, because of circumcision. For she touched his feet and said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me” (Exod. 4). And she let him go after she had said, “bridegroom of blood.”

It should be noted here that to the man in whom God spoke, whom God had established as leader of his people, through whom God had performed so many wonders, counsel was given not by God but by a Gentile man: [Col. 0671C] “You will wear yourself out,” he said, “both you and this people who are with you, with foolish labour. But hear my words and counsels, and the Lord will be with you. Be for the people in matters that pertain to the Lord.” When he had heard this, Moses did everything that Jethro had suggested; and, choosing capable men from all Israel, he appointed them as rulers of the people.

Thus this passage also clearly proves true the evangelical saying of the Lord: “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16). For in the class of affairs pertaining to the Lord, Moses was wiser than all the children of light: “No prophet has arisen again in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and wonders which he sent through him” (Deut. 34). But in the class of affairs pertaining to the governance of human society, his kinsman was found wiser than he. This is also what we see today, when many children of this age are wiser than the children of light.

Knowing this, the Apostle speaks thus to the Corinthians: “If therefore you have secular lawsuits, appoint to judge those who are despised in the Church” (1 Cor. 6). He calls them “despised” in comparison with those of nobler standing, who are less capable in matters pertaining to the Lord. For in Christ’s Church all nobility is evaluated not according to fleshly lineage but according to the spiritual gifts of the grace of regeneration. Therefore, whenever children of light receive from children of this age anything worthy of hearing or imitation, this example shows that those above ought beneficially to descend to the counsels of those below. [Col. 0672A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. That Moses sacrificed to God as a sign that he had been sent by him

(CHAPTER XIX.)

> “In the third month after Israel’s departure from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. For, having departed from Rephidim and come as far as the wilderness of Sinai, they encamped in that place; there Israel pitched its tents opposite the mountain, while Moses went up to the Lord.”

When it says, “in the third month, on this day,” this is the same as if it had said, “in the third month, on the first day of the month.” Here Moses was to sacrifice, and the truth of him who had sent him was to be fulfilled, saying: “When you have brought my people out of Egypt, you shall sacrifice to God upon this mountain” (Exod. 3).

This sacrifice of Moses was a sign of the truth that God had sent him, not because he sacrificed, but because, while he was sacrificing, God gave the clearest signs of his presence. Thus the children of Israel, terrified and shaken with fear, said to Moses: “Let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. 19). And the Lord said to Moses: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven” (Exod. 20), etc. Therefore Moses’ sacrifice upon this mountain was a sign that the Lord had sent him.

Now the first day of this third month is, by lunar reckoning, the forty-seventh day from the fourteenth day of the first month, when the Lamb was sacrificed. And on this day the Lord said to Moses: “Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day.” And afterwards: “The third day had now come, and the morning had grown bright, and behold, thunders began to be heard, lightning flashes to shine, and a very thick cloud covered the mountain.”

This day is the forty-ninth from the aforesaid sacrifice of the lamb. Add one, and they make fifty: on the fiftieth day, namely Pentecost, the Lord said to Moses: “And I shall give you stone tablets, and the law and commandments which I have written, that you may teach the children of Israel” (Exod. 24). Therefore the Law and grace accord perfectly in their numerical reckoning: for on the fiftieth day after the Paschal evening, the Law, written on stone tablets by the finger of God, [Col. 0672D] “was given through Moses; but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1), written likewise on the fiftieth day after his resurrection in the hearts of the apostles, when the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the days of the Jews’ Pentecost and the apostles’ Pentecost were fulfilled together

Here the question arises how the days of the Jews’ Pentecost were completed on the Lord’s Day, on which the Holy Spirit also came upon the apostles, according to the testimony of the Gospel. For it is certain that the last of fifty days always falls on the same weekday on which the first has dawned. But who does not know that, in that year, the first day of unleavened bread fell to the Jews on the fifth weekday, on whose evening our Lord was betrayed; that on the following day of Preparation he was crucified; that he rested on the Sabbath; and that afterwards he rose on the first of the Sabbaths, that is, on the first day after the Sabbath, which from that time we call the Lord’s Day? How then did that feast, namely Pentecost, fall on the first of the Sabbaths?

In answer, it must be known that although the Law was given on the fiftieth day after the lamb’s sacrifice at Israel’s departure from Egypt, the yearly celebration of this same gift was not commanded to be observed on the fiftieth day after the lamb’s sacrifice. For it is written in Leviticus:

> “When you have entered the land which I shall give you and have reaped its crop, you shall bring sheaves; you shall bring the firstfruits sheaf of your harvest to the priest. He shall raise the sheaf before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you on the day after the Sabbath, and shall sanctify it. Therefore, from the day on which you offered the ears of firstfruits, you shall count seven full weeks, up to the day after the completion of the seventh week, and thus you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord. And you shall call this day most celebrated and most holy” (Lev. 23).

It is clear that this command of the Law requires that, whichever weekday the fourteenth day of the first month fell upon—the evening of which was to see the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb—after that sacrifice they were to await the day after the Sabbath, that is, the day following the Sabbath. On that day, after the sheaf of ears had been raised before the Lord, seven full weeks were to be counted: namely, forty-nine days; and the day after the completion of the seventh week, which is the fiftieth day, was to be called most celebrated and most holy—the day called in Greek *Pentecost*. This will be explained more fully in Leviticus. [Col. 0673C]

Thus no doubt remains, nor is there any need now for a further question, concerning how the days of the Jews’ Pentecost and the days of the apostles’ Pentecost were fulfilled together. For on the day when they were commanded to raise their sheaf, Christ the Son of God likewise rose from the dead: the bundle of the living, who put to death their members that are upon the earth. Of him the bride speaks in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall lodge between my breasts” (Song 1). And immediately she adds: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna (*cyprus*) in the vineyards of Engedi” (ibid.).

For on account of our weakness he was a bundle of myrrh while he lay dead in the tomb; but by the power of God he was raised like a cluster of henna (*cyprus*), as regards the sweetness of the resurrection. Thereafter, while the Jews counted seven weeks according to the Law in order to observe, on the day after their completion, a dead festival, Christ God, living and showing himself alive to his disciples by many proofs, ascended above all the heavens on the fortieth day; and when they were observing the fiftieth day and receiving the killing letter, he filled believers with his life-giving gifts by the descent of the Holy Spirit.

Now, as we are about to enter the darkness of the aforesaid Mount Sinai, let us carry before us the lamp of apostolic understanding, so that with it we may search, for our benefit and according to the Gospel of Christ, the things spoken there.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the things mystically enacted beside Mount Sinai

He says:

> “You have not come to a fire that can be touched and approached, nor to whirlwind, darkness, and storm, nor to the sound of a trumpet and a voice of words, which those who heard begged that no word might be spoken to them. For they could not bear what was commanded: ‘Even if a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.’ And so terrible was the sight that Moses said: ‘I am terrified and trembling.’ But you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, living Jerusalem, to the assembly of many thousands of angels, to the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, to God the judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of the New Testament, and to the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than Abel” (Heb. 12).

When he says these things, he clearly sets the matter before us by a sharp comparison and does not permit us to be careless concerning the care and reverence due to heavenly realities, after the pattern of which those visible and sensible things were spoken or done so terribly, and are now to be discussed.

First, as is customary, the Lord, in order to gain goodwill, recalls his past benefits and promises future ones: “You yourselves,” he says, “have seen what I have done to the Egyptians, how I bore you upon eagles’ wings and took you to myself. If therefore you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my own possession among all peoples,” etc.

If these things deserved to be recalled to them so that they might not be ungrateful—since he had liberated them from masters who, although proud and unjust, were still human beings—and had brought them to that tangible fire, that whirlwind and darkness: how much more must we call to mind that God, becoming man, has delivered us from our sins by a more abundant grace than was then given, borne us upon the wings of eagles—swiftly and loftily flying and strongly carrying their young—to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and taken us to himself, so that where he is, we too may be.

“If therefore,” he says, “you hear my voice and keep my covenant”—understand, the covenant which I made with Abraham, or the covenant, that is, the Law which I am presently about to give you. He did not merely say, “if you hear,” but added, “and keep my covenant,” because surely “not the hearers of the law shall be justified before God” (Rom. 2).

“You shall be,” he says, “my own possession among all peoples.” For all the earth is mine, and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. What was said then has likewise been fulfilled by the Lord today. For behold, the earth belongs to the Lord, and through Christ he himself rules the nations. But the people which is, in its elect portion, the priestly kingdom or royal priesthood of us all is that people; for from it, according to the flesh, came Christ, king and priest of all, the Holy of holies. Hence he most truly testified that “salvation is from the Jews” (John 4).

That people, therefore, is God’s peculiar people, for “we are strangers and sojourners” (Eph. 2). And although there are more priests among us, the kingdom and priesthood belong in a special sense to that people, from which comes Christ the king and priest, and whose priesthood is the very priesthood that we exercise. [Col. 0675A]

Note also that, like a householder making an agreement with day-labourers whom he is immediately to send into the work of the Law, he continues speaking until the agreement itself is approved by them, all saying: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do.” When Moses reported these words of the people to the Lord, he delayed no longer: “Go,” he says, “to the people, sanctify them today and tomorrow, let them wash their garments, and let them be ready for the third day.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the words, “Be ready for the morrow; do not approach your wives.” [Col. 0675B]

Many matters in this chapter require careful consideration. First, Moses, being commanded to sanctify the people, defines that sanctification as follows: “Be ready for the third day; do not approach your wives.” Is, then, approaching one’s wife unlawful? Certainly not. But, as another Scripture says: “Everything has its season, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed intervals. There is a time for embracing and a time for refraining from embraces” (Eccles. II). The time for refraining from embraces is when a time of sanctification is at hand. For what is it to be sanctified, except to abstain even from lawful things? He who abstains only from unlawful things has indeed escaped the punishment of sin, but has not yet attained the glory of holiness. [Col. 0675C] Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done” (Luke XVII). For, in order to attain sanctification, it is not enough to have fulfilled the commandment unless one adds the performance of counsel as well. This was being done here so that they might be holy—that is, worthy, insofar as is possible for human beings, to hear or see the present majesty of God. They are therefore rightly advised to practise continence even in a lawful matter, when it is said: “Be ready; do not approach your wives.” If this had rightly to be said to those who were approaching that visible fire, the whirlwind, darkness, storm, and sound of the trumpet, as has already been said above, how much more to us who approach [Col. 0675D] “the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,” and the assembly of many thousands of angels, and the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and God the judge of all, and the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and Jesus the mediator of the New Testament, and the blood of sprinkling, speaking better things than Abel?

The same Apostle, reflecting on this elsewhere, extends the hand of indulgence to the incontinent: “Do not deprive one another,” he says, “except perhaps by mutual consent for a time, that you may give yourselves to prayer; and return together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your incontinence” (I Cor. VII). But he urges the continent, having wives, to be as though they had none (ibid.); and to virgins he gives counsel that they should remain as they are, judging this to be good because of the impending necessity (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXVII. What it signifies that preparation for sanctification is commanded for the third day.

What further is meant by the fact that preparation for sanctification is commanded for the third day? If we ask this, the further question at once occurs: why did the Lord God himself, who gave this command, having become man, sanctify himself over three days? For when the hour of his passion was imminent, after saying, “Sanctify them in truth. Thy word is truth. As thou hast sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world” (John XVII), he immediately added: “And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also may be sanctified [Col. 0676B] in truth” (ibid.). What was this sanctification of his? Undoubtedly his sacrifice was necessary for our sanctification; he completed it on the third day by rising from the dead into the glory of immortality and incorruption, and thus, according to the prophet Zechariah, after his filthy garments had been removed, he was clothed in change of raiment (Zech. III).

Yet the answer to this is readily given: God, to whom our nature in Christ, sacrificing himself, offered satisfaction so that we might be reconciled to him—God, I say, who is our Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—therefore it was fitting that, although his Holy One was not to see corruption (Ps. XVII), the festal celebration of his resurrection should nevertheless be deferred until the third day. Thus, rightly, here already he imposed upon human beings a three-day sanctification as an example of his future sanctification, whence the authority of three-day repentance or affliction was thereafter established for sinners.

Moreover, the words, “and let them wash their garments,” are plainly not of great value for sanctification before the Lord in their literal sense; nevertheless, when this is done as a rite of sanctification, it suggests that inward purity also is pleasing to God. However these matters may stand, one must wash by repentance the garments of the soul—that is, its corruptible members. Of these holy Job says: “My garments shall abhor me” (Job IX); that is, my corruptible members shall make me abhorrent. Concerning washing them, or not defiling them, it is written elsewhere: [Col. 0676D] “Blessed is he who keeps his garments, lest he walk naked and they see his shame” (Apoc. XVI). Likewise: “Let thy garments be white at all times, and let oil”—that is, charity issuing from thy heart—“not fail from thy head” (Eccles. IX).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the words: “Everyone who touches the mountain shall surely die.”

“Everyone,” he says, “who touches the mountain shall surely die. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be crushed with stones or pierced with darts. Whether beast or man, he shall not live,” and so forth. The reason for these terrors was the present ignorance of the uncultivated people. Like an unruly adolescent who did not know how to revere a loving father, they needed a stern pedagogue. They had to be taught that the God of their fathers was not like the gods of Egypt, in whose rites—or rather sacrileges—it was customary to play and lead dances, to eat and drink, and then to defile and be defiled by every kind of fornication.

Indeed, they could not readily or easily learn this; for, after such great and terrible signs, without hesitation and as though they had seen nothing, they made a molten calf. “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play. And they said: These are thy gods, O Israel, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII).
