Thus the cause of the terrible things displayed—the blaring trumpet, thunder, flashing lightning, smoking mountain, thick cloud or darkness, and the intervening sentence, “Everyone who [Col. 0677B] touches the mountain shall surely die”—was the degraded state of the people themselves. Since they had not yet attained charity, they had to be constrained by fear. Hence, a little later Moses says: “God has come to test you, and that his terror might be in you, so that you might not sin” (Exod. XX).

But is it evil to wish to see the Lord? On the contrary: it is good, and the best of all things. Yet it is evil for one who dares seek him out of curiosity, supposing either that God is visible in his own nature or that, like a human being, he is locally divided or circumscribed by bodily members. Therefore intrusive and unworthy curiosity was rightly repelled by the insertion of the commandment. Once the commandment had been imposed, the punishment of the transgressor is just; and therefore, most justly: “Everyone,” he says, “who touches the mountain shall surely die,” and in such a way that the rest may fear. How is it that “no hand shall touch him”? Namely, the one cast away as polluted and unclean. Rather, “he shall be crushed with stones or pierced with darts.” Why shall a beast be killed? So that the beast’s master, who neglected to guard it, may grieve on its account, and that in the very thing in which his negligence lies he may be struck by the equitable measure of judgment.

## CHAPTER XXIX. How it was said, “When the trumpet begins to sound, then let them ascend the mountain,” although the contrary was said above.

“When,” he says, “the trumpet begins to sound, then let them ascend the mountain.” But above it has already been said: “Take heed that you do not ascend the mountain.” And afterward the Lord again says: “Warn the people, lest perhaps they wish to cross the boundaries in order to see the Lord, and a very great multitude of them perish.” Therefore, when it is said, “when the trumpet begins to sound, let them ascend the mountain,” this must be understood as far as the boundaries established round about.

Moreover, how eagerly Moses clings to the divine vision is suggested by this: when the Lord said to him, “Go down and warn the people, lest perhaps they wish to cross the boundaries. Let also the priests who ascend to the Lord be sanctified, lest I strike them,” Moses answered: “The multitude cannot ascend [Col. 0678A] Mount Sinai. For thou thyself hast testified and commanded, saying: Set bounds around the mountain and sanctify it.” Yet, although he wished under this pretext to make God feel secure, he did not succeed. For the Lord persisted in his decree: “Go,” he said, “descend; and thou shalt ascend, thou and Aaron with thee.”

This was said or done as an example for those who were to be placed over God’s people, like Moses. Though they desire to cling more closely to the contemplation of heavenly things, the cause or care of those subject to them sometimes becomes an impediment. By the example and command of the Saviour, who for our sake came forth from the bosom of the Father, they are sometimes compelled to set aside the sweetness of the highest contemplation and stoop to the little ones, so that they may discuss bodily matters with them. Thus Paul the Apostle, who had been caught up to the third heaven or paradise and heard “secret words which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (II Cor. XII), descended from such heights to such low matters as to lay down the rules of marriage: “Let the husband,” he says, “render to the wife her due, and likewise the wife to the husband” (I Cor. VII).

## CHAPTER XXX. What Mount Sion signifies, according to the Apostle’s teaching; and what is to be understood by the words: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be crushed with stones.”

The same Apostle has explained in the chapter written above what Mount Sinai signifies: “But you have come,” he says, “to Mount Sion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. XII). For when he contrasts these things with the fire and darkness of Mount Sinai, which Moses ascended and the people could not ascend, he plainly wishes us to understand that there was the figure and here the truth; there the shadow and here the body, or reality.

Therefore, to the one whom God has sent, and to whom he deigns, following Moses’ example, to give a sign that he himself has sent him, he opens the gates of this Mount Sion and of the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, calling him into the secrets of contemplation, where the people do not deserve to ascend because they are weighed down by carnal understanding. “And if a beast,” he says, “touches the mountain, it shall be crushed with stones.” For if one who lives beast-like dares to search out the heights of the Godhead, that glorious dignity draws darkness over itself for him, and, while the whole mountain of the Scriptures smokes, wraps unworthy eyes in blindness. Hence the Psalmist says: “He made darkness his hiding-place; around him was his tabernacle, dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII). Thus, though it is the splendid light of truth, he sees nothing but the darkness of falsehood, and is crushed by those stones which the same writer signifies in other words when he says: “He shall rain snares upon sinners; fire, sulphur, and a spirit of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. X). Thus Arius and every other heresiarch has been stoned by the heavenly majesty. And this is because he was a beast. For if, living rationally as a human being, he had first trained himself through the active life and then advanced in due order to contemplate the glory of truth, the strength of that majesty would have held back its stones from him.

Meanwhile, the one called by the Lord, caught up as far as the third heaven or paradise, and in mind surpassing even that, [Col. 0679A] traverses the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. He marvels at its walls built of every precious stone, its towers constructed of gems, its streets paved with pure gold (Apoc. XXI), and the multitude of many thousands of angels around it and within it; and with his whole heart desires never to be absent from the festival of so great a vision. But “he who hears must say, Come” (Apoc. XXII): that is, one who has tasted beforehand the heavenly sweetness must invite others to win rest, who, miserably labouring and burdened, do not yet know where peace and true refreshment are found. For the treasures of blessedness have not been opened to him so that, once he has found riches, he may dwell upon them alone.

Moses is therefore told to descend, intending to ascend again, and to take Aaron his brother with him; and he is to preach to the people that, after washing their garments, they may ascend to the Lord. There are thunderings, flashes of lightning, smoke and fire, and the blast of the trumpet, so that what is written may come to pass: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains and they smoke” (Ps. X). Likewise: “The earth was moved and trembled; the foundations of the mountains were troubled and shaken, because thou wast angry with them. Smoke went up in his wrath, and fire blazed from before him; coals were kindled by him,” and so forth (Ps. XVII). For the earth is moved and trembles, and the foundations of the mountains are troubled and smoke, when, having heard through the preacher of the future coming of the dreadful Judge, those who previously knew only earthly things examine themselves in repentance. As mountainous pride descends, smoke—that is, tearful prayer—rises from fear of the Lord’s wrath; and the fire of sorrow, blazing from before his face—that is, from the knowledge of truth—consumes sins.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The Decalogue of commandments; why, at the end, it says, “Thou shalt not covet,” although covetousness is the root of all evils; and concerning charity.

(CHAP. XX.) “And God spoke all these words: I am the Lord thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no strange gods before me. Thou shalt not make for thyself a graven image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above, or which is on earth beneath, or of those things which are in the waters under the earth; thou shalt not adore them nor serve them,” [Col. 0679D] and so forth.

This Decalogue is placed at the head of the law—that is, the number of ten commandments. The first of them is: “Thou shalt have no strange gods before me”; the last: “Thou shalt not covet.” But the Apostle says that “covetousness is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI). Why, then, is “Thou shalt not covet” not placed first here? It should be understood that, just as the upper branches of an evil tree are first cut away and one thus gradually reaches the roots, so evil deeds, being nearer to covetousness, are first gradually cut away, and finally covetousness or concupiscence itself is cut off by the voice of the prohibition.

It should indeed be noted that almost all these commandments are stated as prohibitions. Hence the Apostle most truly says: “The law is not made for the just man, but for the unjust, the ungodly, and sinners, the wicked, and the defiled” (I Tim. I). God had undertaken to heal unjust people, wholly given over to covetousness; and therefore, like a diligent farmer, his first concern was to hoe the soil occupied by evil roots, in preparation for a better planting—namely, charity, which alone is laid down for the just. For the same Apostle, before saying that the law was laid down for the unjust and unsubmissive, had said to the just man—that is, to his disciple Timothy—“The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (ibid.). Where charity is present, there is no need to say: “Thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not bear false witness.”

Accordingly, when the Lord was asked by an expert in the law, “Master, which is [Col. 0680B] the great commandment in the law?” he replied: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. And the second is like it: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII). Therefore charity itself is not commanded here at the beginning; rather, those things contrary to charity are prohibited, so that, once they have been uprooted, charity itself—the root of all good things—may at last be planted.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That four commandments concern the love of God, but six the love of one’s neighbour.

There are ten commandments. The first, as has been said, is: “Thou shalt have no strange gods before me; thou shalt not make for thyself a graven image.” The following, but final, commandment is: “Thou shalt not covet.” Of these, four serve the love of God, and six serve the love of one’s neighbour.

“Thou shalt have no strange gods before me; thou shalt not make for thyself a graven image, nor any likeness; thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” By prohibiting these four things opposed to the love of God, the word of God intends to make room for that love of God itself. For you cannot both have strange gods and love the true God. He says, therefore: “Thou shalt have no strange gods before me”; that is, you shall consider no one God except the one Creator of heaven and earth.

Likewise, to make a graven image, or any likeness of things in heaven, on earth, [Col. 0680D] or in the waters, and to think that God is like any of these, is iniquity and opposed to the love of God. “To whom,” says the prophet, “have you made God like? Or what image will you set before him?” (Isa. XL). This applies against the Anthropomorphites, who think that God is composed of human bodily members. In this way, assuredly, they fashion for themselves a great image, seated in heaven and touching the earth with its feet, though he himself says: “Heaven is my throne, and the earth my footstool” (Isa. LXVI). Thus he says: “Thou shalt not make for thyself a graven image, nor any likeness which is in heaven above,” and so forth.

Certainly, when he says here: “I am the Lord thy God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands who love me and keep my commandments,” this is to be understood in every commandment: namely, that the transgressor may fear punishment and the fulfiller of the commandment may hope for reward. At an appropriate time he also declared himself strong and one who repays the iniquity of fathers in children unto the fourth and third generation: namely, when all Mount Sinai was smoking and wholly terrifying because the Lord had descended, which was an indication of strength; and when he had repaid in the third and fourth generation the iniquity of the fathers who had sold their brother Joseph—yet not without mercy, since, with their captivity ended, they were returning from Egypt in the fourth generation.

Likewise, to take God’s name in vain—as poets do—or not to consider it worthy of reverence wherever the Lord’s name is invoked, is altogether contrary to the love of God. He says, therefore: “Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain; for the Lord will not hold him guiltless who has taken the name of the Lord his God vainly.” Likewise, to do any good not for God’s praise or in hope of eternal recompense, but in order to be seen by human beings, is contrary to the love of God. Therefore he says: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” That is, in all your works look to God’s recompense, or prepare rest for yourself in God as your reward: this is truly to sanctify the Sabbath day. The carnal Sabbath-observance of the Jews has already been discussed elsewhere.

The six commandments which follow are: “Honour thy father and thy mother. Thou shalt not kill. [Col. 0681C] Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal. Thou shalt not speak false testimony against thy neighbour. Thou shalt not covet.” They uproot all things hostile to the love of one’s neighbour and support the natural law which says: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” These things may in some measure be observed by the nations, even by the more honourable Gentiles; but without the love of God they did not profit them unto life. Since they had strange gods and did the other things forbidden in the four commandments mentioned above, they did not attain blessedness.

The arrangement of the Ten Commandments in our codices, according to the translation of blessed Jerome, is now as follows. Yet elsewhere we read that the four commandments concerning love of God are reduced to three, while conversely the last of those concerning love of one’s neighbour—namely, “Thou shalt not covet”—is divided into two: one being heard as “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife,” and the other as “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s property.” Thus three commandments concern the love of God and seven the love of one’s neighbour. We think that this was taken from the Seventy Interpreters [the Septuagint].

These are the ten strings of the singer of God, who says in the Psalm: “O God, I will sing a new song to thee; upon the ten-stringed psaltery I will sing praise to thee” (Ps. CXLIII). Likewise: “Give praise to the Lord upon the harp; upon the psaltery of ten strings sing praise to him” (Ps. XXXII). Whoever lives without these lies whenever he professes to give thanks to the Lord upon a ten-stringed psaltery.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the words: “The people saw voices and lamps,” and so forth. What an altar of earth without steps signifies.

“But all the people saw the voices and lamps, and the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain.” “They saw voices”—that is, they understood them—but they did not see God, who formed the voices. Nor did they see merely flashing lamps, but also “the smoking mountain,” because there was not in all of them integrity of faith or perfection of the fear of the Lord such as Moses possessed in perfection; and therefore he saw flame in the bush without smoke. “And terrified and shaken with fear, they stood afar off, saying to Moses: Speak thou to us, and we will hear,” and so forth. That they spoke thus praiseworthily is clear [Col. 0682B] in the book of Deuteronomy from Moses’ recollection: “When the Lord heard this, he said to me: I have heard the voice of the words of this people, which they have spoken to thee; all that they have spoken is good. Who will grant them to have such a mind, that they may fear me and keep all my commandments at all times, that it may be well with them and with their children for ever?” (Deut. V).

To this meaning pertains what the Lord further says here: “You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make silver gods, nor shall you make golden gods for yourselves. You shall make me an altar of earth.” And a little later: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar, lest your shame be uncovered.” Does he command, then, that an altar be made for him only of piled-up earth, lest even that altar rise above level ground? Certainly not. For later he says: “You shall make me an altar of setim wood, and cover it with bronze” (Exod. XXVI). Solomon too made in the Temple an altar of bronze (III Kings VIII), ten cubits high. Could one ascend to it without steps? Certainly not. Rather, one ascended by fifteen steps in that sanctuary, corresponding to the fifteen Songs of Ascents sung in David; and these expressed what those steps signified: namely, that by advances in virtue one must ascend into the heavenly Holy of Holies.

Therefore all these things are shown to have been said figuratively in reference to what they had said in humility of heart: “Let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die.” For Moses, also mindful of this passage, says again in Deuteronomy: “The Lord thy God will raise up for thee a prophet from thy nation and from thy brethren, like unto me. Him shalt thou hear, as thou didst ask of the Lord thy God in Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and thou saidst: I will hear no more the voice of the Lord my God, and I will see this great fire no more, lest I die. And the Lord said to me: All that they have spoken is good. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brethren, like unto thee” (Deut. XVIII), and so forth.

This prophet—that is, himself—is meant in this passage: “I will come to thee and bless thee.” And a little later: “Behold, I will send my angel, who will go before thee, guard thee on the way, and bring thee into the place I have prepared. Observe him and hear his voice; do not think him to be despised, for he will not forgive when thou hast sinned, and my name is in him” (Exod. [Col. 0683A] XXIII). Therefore, after Moses had said: “God has come to test you, and that his terror might be in you, so that you may not sin”—namely, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX)—the Lord, intending that prophet, that angel of great counsel, says: “You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven, saying: You shall not make silver gods, nor make golden gods for yourselves,” and you were unable to bear it. I say, therefore: “You shall make me an altar of earth”; that is, you shall humbly believe in the incarnation of that prophet whom I will raise up for you from among your brethren. “And you shall offer upon it your holocausts and your peace-offerings, sheep and oxen, in every place in which there shall be a memorial of my name.”

“From the rising of the sun even unto its setting,” says the prophet Malachi, “my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is offered, and a clean oblation is offered to my name” (Mal. I). Therefore he says that whatever anyone wishes duly to offer—sheep or ox, that is, a lesser or greater action—he will establish in the construction of that altar, that is, in faith in the Lord’s incarnation. “I will come to thee” is understood according to that altar, “and I will bless” thee with every heavenly blessing and spiritual grace.

“But if thou shalt make me an altar of stone, thou shalt not build it of hewn stones. For if thou lift thy tool upon it, it shall be polluted.” The stones are the virtues of the mind. From them we make an altar to the Lord when, having faith in his incarnation, we build them upon that foundation. But iron or a tool is arrogance, the vice by which the mind is chiefly cut off from its Creator. Therefore, if, when the altar has been built, “thou lift thy tool upon it”—that is, if thou arrogate those virtues to thyself—“it shall be polluted.”

“You shall not ascend by steps to my altar”—understand, the altar made of earth—that is, you shall not say that the incarnate Son is less than the Father, “lest thy shame be uncovered.” For nothing is more shameful than heretical shame. Or again, “you shall not ascend by steps,” that is, you shall not exalt yourself because of your spiritual advances; because of this vice shame is uncovered, since contempt of the flesh surely accompanies pride of mind.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Why judgments are rightly placed after the commandments.

(CHAP. XXI.) “These are the judgments which thou shalt set before them.” Rightly and in proper order, after the commandments have been given, judgments are set forth. For not all would observe or heed the commandments; therefore it was necessary to prescribe what judgment would make each transgressor liable. But *judgment* in the singular does not have the same meaning as *judgments* in the plural. In the singular, *judgment* often signifies condemnation; in the plural, *judgments* signify both the punishment of the guilty and the defence of the innocent.

After the ten commandments have been given, the holy, spotless, just, and good law of the Lord (Ps. XVIII; Rom. VII) sets forth the ordinances of both judgment and mercy, so that this passage seems truly to have supplied the Psalmist, singing upon the ten-stringed psaltery, with his first subject when he said: “I will sing to thee, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” [Col. 0684A] (Ps. C). The subject of the song of judgment is eminent from this place up to where it says: “He who sacrifices to gods shall be put to death, except to God alone” (Exod. XXII); while the sweet melodies of mercy are from what immediately follows, “Thou shalt not afflict a stranger” (ibid.), as far as the words: “Six days thou shalt work; on the seventh day thou shalt cease, that thine ox and ass may rest, and that the son of thy handmaid and the stranger may be refreshed” (Exod. XXIII).

The matters are obscure and slight, yet resplendent in judgment and illustrious in justice. For example: “If one man’s ox wounds another ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price, and shall divide between them the carcass of the dead one.” Do not consider here the value of the livestock, but the equity of the judgment. What concern could such majesty have for oxen? Yet admirable is the wisdom that judges concerning goring oxen, just as wondrous is the strength that fought Pharaoh through frogs and flies. These judgments of the Lord, then, are “true judgments, justified in themselves” (Ps. XVIII), which, he says, “thou shalt set before them.” They are not those judgments of which the Psalmist says: “Thy judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. XXXV), or those of which the Apostle says: “O the depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI). Rather, these are such judgments as those of which the Psalmist also says: “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of thy mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). They have manifest equity, visible to every person who reasons properly; and hence histories report that, even before Christ’s coming, they were received by the kings of the nations with the highest favour and praise. A few points about them should briefly be examined in order to demonstrate this testimony to their evident justice.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Why the judgments concerning the purchase of Hebrews are proposed first, and how they obtained that freedom.

“If thou buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve thee six years; in the seventh he shall go out free, without payment,” and so forth. “If anyone sells his daughter as a servant-woman, she shall not go out as maidservants are accustomed to go out,” and so forth. It may reasonably be asked why these are first in the order of the judgments to be set forth. To this I say: these judgments are particular to the Hebrew people; the rest should be common to all people or all nations.

Why are these particular to the Hebrews? Because their father Jacob served Laban for six years for flocks, and in the seventh went out free with his dignity preserved, choosing rather to live as a stranger with his fathers Abraham and Isaac than by longer service to gain more in the land or among the kindred of his fathers. This free spirit of their father stored up for his descendants such merit before the Lord that the law protects them: no one among them is compelled to serve beyond six years against his will.

Conversely, their mother Leah, sold through her father’s injustice as though into servitude, went out as maidservants were accustomed to go out. Hence both she and her sister Rachel complained in this way: “Have we anything remaining among the possessions and inheritance of our father’s house? Has he not reckoned us as strangers and sold us, and consumed our price?” [Col. 0685A] (Gen. XXXI). Thus, according to the letter, these are judgments particular to the Hebrews.

“If thou buy,” he says, “a Hebrew servant, he shall serve thee six years; in the seventh he shall go out free without payment”—understand, if he wishes. For he is free-born, and his father, having sold himself, went out free in the seventh year of service because he wished to do so; he did not sell himself in perpetuity. “With whatever garment”—that is, with whatever condition—“he entered, with the same let him go out,” because their father brought neither more nor less, but only what he had rightfully acquired. “If he had a wife, his wife also shall go out with him.” For their father had wives, the two sisters Leah and Rachel, whom he had acquired by agreement; when he entered into service for the flocks, he entered with them, and he left with them.

“But if the servant says: I love my master, and my wives and children; I will not go out free, let him,” says the Lord, “bring him to the gods,” and so forth. By “gods” understand priests, according to what was said to Moses: “Behold, I have made thee god to Pharaoh” (Exod. VII), namely by reason of the dignity of the divine office. “He shall be brought,” he says, “to the door and the doorposts,” so that there may be many observers and witnesses. “And he shall pierce his ear with an awl,” so that he may no longer be able to erase or conceal the memorial of the profession once made. “And he shall be his servant for ever.” We hasten past the moral sweetness of this chapter to other matters, for it must be sought in the place where it has been set forth by the holy Fathers.

“If anyone sells his daughter as a servant-woman”—understand, as Laban sold your mother Leah, whom he imposed upon Jacob and sent forth without a dowry—“she shall not go out as maidservants are accustomed to go out” (Gen. XXIX). This is on the authority of your father Jacob as an example, who did not allow her to go out like a maidservant without any dowry. For by his craft he placed poplar rods in the channels, having peeled them in part, so that at the heat of mating the sheep should look upon the rods and bring forth spotted, variegated, and diversely coloured offspring (Gen. XXX). Thus, because he could not contend in judgment against the stronger Laban for the dowry of a wife for whom he had not asked, he took prudent thought for himself by craft as well; and the man became exceedingly rich, and had many flocks, male and female servants, camels, [Col. 0685D] and asses.

Accordingly, the buyer may take care that she whom he has bought, because she is a daughter, shall not wholly lack dowry support, whether he does not wish to betroth her to himself or to his son. “If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master, to whom she has been given, he shall let her go.” Here he covertly reminds them of their own condition, or of their mother’s, because Leah was indeed displeasing—for “her eyes were weak” (Gen. XXIX)—and Jacob could rightly have dismissed her, since he had not served for her and had not pledged her marital faith. “But he has no power to sell her to a foreign people, if he has rejected her,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the different punishment of one who kills a person by ambush and one who kills his enemy.

“Whoever strikes a man with the intention of killing him shall surely die. [Col. 0686A] But whoever did not lie in wait, but God delivered him into his hands, I will appoint for you a place to which he must flee.”—“I will appoint for you a place,” he says; that is, I will set apart for you cities of refuge, to which the man must flee who did not lie in wait, but God delivered his enemy into his hands. For example: when Saul was pursuing David, and Saul had “entered a cave to relieve himself, while David and his men lay hidden in the inner part of the cave. And David’s servants said to him: Behold the day of which the Lord spoke to you: I will deliver your enemy into your hand” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 24), etc. Likewise: “David and Abishai came to the people by night, and found Saul lying asleep in the camp. And Abishai said to David: God has shut up your enemy into your hands. Now therefore [Col. 0686B] I will pin him to the ground with the spear at one stroke, and there will be no need for a second” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 26). Clearly David had not lain in wait; rather, God had delivered into his hands an enemy who had gratuitously lain in wait for him. Hence he says: “Take notice and see that there is no wickedness in me, while you lie in wait for my life” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 24). And Saul spoke in accordance with this law: “You are more righteous than I” (ibid.), because, that is, under the law’s permission you could have killed me, and would have had a lawful place of refuge until the priest of that time should die.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the statement, “If anyone deliberately…”: that a murderer is to be dragged away from the altar and handed over to death.

“If anyone deliberately kills his neighbour, and by lying in wait, you shall drag him away from my altar, that he may die.” [Col. 0686C]—“You shall drag him away from my altar, that he may die,” he says; that is, even if he flees to my altar, you shall pursue him even there, and, having torn him away, kill him. For the altar’s protection is owed nothing to one who, by deceitfully killing his neighbour, has forfeited every claim to protection.

Therefore no one rightly finds fault either with Solomon’s judgment or with Benaiah’s hand, because he killed Joab there, when Joab had fled into the tabernacle of the Lord, was holding the horn of the altar, and was saying: “I will not go out, but here I shall die” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 2). For Joab had killed two righteous men, better than himself—Abner and Amasa, commanders of the army—and had shed in peace the blood of war; that is, in the kiss of peace, saying, “Hail, my brother,” and taking his chin in his hand as if to kiss him (2 [Col. 0686D] Kings [2 Samuel] 20). I say that no one rightly finds fault with the fact that such a man was torn from the altar and killed here, since the Lord says here of such persons: “You shall drag him away from my altar, that he may die.”

The remaining matters likewise possess an evident beauty of justice, which a rational and diligent person readily discerns, so that, delighted freely by its countenance, he says: “The Lord is faithful in all his words; the Lord is righteous in all his ways” (Ps. XLIV [source citation; text Ps. 144, Vulgate 144; modern 145]). When, therefore, a Hebrew servant has performed all these works of justice, will he immediately be perfect and receive the reward of eternal life? Certainly not; for the Apostle also testified that “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). And one of the chief righteous men under the Law says in tearful confession: “All our righteousnesses are like the rag of a menstruous woman” [Col. 0687A] (Isa. 64). Rightly, then, after all these things the Lord himself does not yet promise the kingdom of heaven to the workers of this law, but says:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the saying, “Behold, I shall send my angel,” etc.

(Chapter 23.) “Behold, I shall send an angel who may go before you, guard you on the way, and bring you to the place which I have prepared. Observe him and listen to his voice; do not think him to be despised, because he will not pardon you when you sin, and my name is in him.”

This is not that angel whom the Lord promises through the prophet Malachi: “Behold,” he says, “I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face” (Mal. 3). For that one is John the Baptist, a prophet and more than a prophet, an angel—that is, a messenger—not a herald of one who was to come, but the messenger and announcer of this great Angel already present. Of him the same prophet immediately adds: “And at once the ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his temple” (ibid.).

The particular distinction of this Angel is here set forth [p. 220], [Col. 0687B] when God says: “My name is in him.” He did not say, “My name is upon him,” which could rightly be said of any of the least among the elect, whose prophetic cry is this: “But you are in us, O Lord, and your name has been invoked over us” (Jer. 14). Rather, he says, “My name is in him”; that is, by reason of natural divinity he is designated by the same name as I am. For he too is called, and is, equally with me, God, Lord, almighty, invisible, uncreated, immeasurable, eternal, and whatever else is predicated substantially of God. This alone distinguishes the name: I am called Father in relation to him, and he Son in relation to me.

“I shall send him, that he may go before you,” namely by opening for you the gates of righteousness; “and guard you on the way,” so that, what you cannot attain by your own choice, you may attain through his grace; “and bring you to the place which I have prepared,” namely, a place marked out from the world’s beginning by many dwelling-places, from which the apostate angels fell, because their foot was that of pride, and therefore “they were cast out and could not stand” (Ps. 35 [Vulgate; modern 36]).

“Observe him, and listen to his voice.” Observe him, I say, as one not speaking from himself and performing my works; [Col. 0687D] and listen to his voice, when under two witnesses—namely, word and deed—he professes that he has come in the name of God his Father. “Do not think him to be despised, because he will not pardon you when you sin”: do not think him contemptible because he is a man, because he is mortal, because he died through the weakness of human nature—for he lives through the power of God (2 Cor. 13). Having authority to execute judgment, “he will not pardon you when you sin” by hating him without cause.

“But if you listen to his voice and do all that I speak, I shall be an enemy to your enemies and shall afflict those who afflict you; and my angel shall go before you and bring you to the Amorite,” etc. It has already been said elsewhere that the enemies of Israel—that is, of all who seek the Lord and flee the Egypt of this world—are evil spirits, and that the names of the Amorites, Hivites, and the other [Col. 0688A] nations correspond to them according to their respective interpretations. Therefore, passing over the present matter, let us hasten to others.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. How he promises fruitfulness to the Church, saying: “There shall be none barren or sterile in your land.”

“There shall be none barren or sterile in your land. I shall fulfil the number of your days.” He promises the holy Church the fruitfulness of blessed seed, which the prophet Isaiah foresaw when he said: “Praise, O barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. XXXIV [probably 54]). For after that Angel went before us and, ascending into heaven, gave to men the gifts [Col. 0688B] of the Holy Spirit, there is no one in this land, which he watered with his blood, who is unfruitful in the word of God and sterile in good works. In every place Mother Church bears spiritual children and gives birth by regenerating those dead in sin into living persons destined for eternal life.

Briefly touching upon the reward of this fruitfulness, he says: “I shall fulfil the number of your days”; that is, throughout ages which cannot be numbered, I shall extend and enlarge your life. “I shall send my terror ahead of you, and shall destroy every people into whose land you enter,” etc. We know that these things happened in such a way that we may truly proclaim that they occurred as a figure of the terror by which our enemy, the evil spirits, were struck down through Christ’s cross. Hence we may confidently say to the very head of our enemies: [Col. 0688C] “O crooked serpent, you who stir up quiet hearts through a thousand winding paths and devious frauds, depart. Christ is here; Christ is here. Melt away. The sign which you yourself know condemns your host.”

But who are the hornets of whom he says: “I shall send hornets beforehand, and they shall drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite before you enter”? Who, I ask, are spiritually to be understood by the hornets, which we know are born from horse dung, and which he says he will send against the Canaanite, just as he sent flies against the Egyptians, unless they are the lowly and despised of this world? In order to confound what is noble and strong, he sent them before our sight, so that, once the pride of the age had been crushed through them, we might peacefully [Col. 0688D] enter eternal life. These hornets, who professed themselves to be, as it were, the world’s refuse and the offscouring of all things (1 Cor. 4), defeated the kites, drove away the devil, prince of this world, and swiftly trampled under their feet all his pomp.

“I shall not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land be reduced to desolation and wild beasts increase against you.” This means: I shall not destroy the vices that resist your purpose or intention without the labour of lawful conflict, lest sudden victory’s glory raise you up into pride. For it is better to fight with men than to be subjected to beasts; that is, it is more tolerable, for example, to be buffeted by the thorn of the flesh than to be laid waste by the thorn of self-exaltation. The former is a human temptation; the latter is a devilish one. Thus he says: “Little by little I shall drive them out from before me, [Col. 0689A] until you increase and possess the land.” It is as though he said: The ascents which you have set in your heart in this vale of tears, in this place into which, O man, you have fallen through your fault (Ps. 83 [Vulgate; modern 84]), you will accomplish gradually through the aid of grace that trains you. You will go from strength to strength until you see the God of gods in Zion: this is truly to increase and to possess the land of the living.

“I shall set your boundaries from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river.” Spiritually, these are the boundaries of Christianity. By the Red Sea and the desert we understand the Jewish people: the Red Sea signifies the portion of the elect, who were first cleansed by the reddening blood of Christ, and among whom the Church’s baptism was first celebrated; the desert signifies the portion of the reprobate, [Col. 0689B] who, because of unbelief, were deserted by God who dwells among men, and by Christ the man. By the sea of the Philistines and the great river—which Scripture elsewhere calls the Euphrates, a name which we in Latin render as “fruit-bearing”—we understand the multitude of the Gentiles, or the depth of the nations, to whom the boundaries of the apostles were extended, beginning from Jerusalem, where, as has been said, the Red Sea of our baptism was first hallowed.

Moreover, according to the letter, the four regions of the promised land are distinguished when it says, “from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river.” Elsewhere we read that the sea of the Philistines is called the Great Sea, since in relation to their land it lay toward the setting of the sun.

## CHAPTER XL. [Col. 0689C] That the beginning, middle, and end of God’s discourse with Moses are the same.

“I shall deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hands and drive them out from before you. You shall make no covenant with them or with their gods. Let them not dwell in your land, lest perhaps they cause you to sin against me, if you serve their gods; for this will certainly be a snare to you.”

The beginning, middle, and end of this discourse are one and the same. For at the beginning it was said: “You shall have no strange gods before me.” In the middle [p. 221], it was said that whoever sacrifices to gods shall be put to death, except when sacrifice is made to God alone. And here at the end it says: “You shall make no covenant with their gods,” etc. And rightly so, because the most diligent knowledge of the one God is the root of all good things; accordingly, the whole work of the gracious planter is especially devoted to this. Once it has been rooted and founded in the heart, whatever springs up from it puts forth leaves and flowers in grace, and bears fruit unto eternal life. Conversely, service to strange gods is the cause of destruction, producing every evil fruit and bringing everlasting death, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “For this reason God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that they dishonour their bodies among themselves; they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 1), etc.

Therefore, just as service to the creature [Col. 0690A] makes a person dishonoured even in the outward works of the flesh, so, conversely, faithful worship of the Creator makes him glorious through the ensuing fruits of the Spirit. Indeed, today we all openly profess to be worshippers of the Creator; but on the great authority of Christ and his Apostle, service of idols is understood in such an extended sense that many professed Christians are involved in that sacrilege. For by evangelical authority, if we are greedy, we serve not God but Mammon (Matt. 6; Luke 10). And the Apostle testifies that covetousness “is the service of idols” (Eph. 5; Col. 3). Thus here, as also above where it was said, “You shall not make gods of silver, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves,” the meaning for us is the same as if it were said: You shall not devote yourselves to greed; you shall not serve Mammon.

## CHAPTER XLI. [Col. 0690B] On what day the Law was given, and how, after an altar had been built at the foot of the mountain, the people said for the third time: “All the words which the Lord has spoken we shall do.”

(Chapter 24.) “Moses therefore came and told the people all the words and judgments of the Lord. And all the people answered with one voice: All the words which the Lord has spoken we shall do.”

It must be remembered that this third day of the third month, as has been said above, was not the fiftieth but the forty-ninth day from the fourteenth day of the first month, that is, from the sacrifice of the lamb. For, according to lunar reckoning, one month has thirty days and another [Col. 0690C] twenty-nine. Thus the sixteen days remaining in the first month after the fourteenth, together with the thirty days of the second month and these three days of the third month, make forty-nine days.

Then are we mistaken in saying that the Law was given on the fiftieth day, since on the forty-ninth day God spoke all these words, and “Moses came and told the people all the words and judgments of the Lord, and all the people answered with one voice: All the words which the Lord has spoken we shall do”? Certainly not. For see what follows: “Moses wrote all the words of the Lord; and rising early in the morning, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel.” That morning was the fiftieth day, [Col. 0690D] on which the Law was finally given. How? “And Scripture says that he sent young men from the sons of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed twelve calves as peace offerings to the Lord. Moses then took half of the blood and put it into basins, while he poured the remaining part upon the altar. Then, taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people. And they said: All that the Lord has spoken we shall do, and we shall be obedient.” This third repetition of their profession is now a complete and irrevocable confirmation. For on the first day of the month they said, “All that the Lord has spoken we shall do”; on the third day they said, “All the words which the Lord has spoken we shall do”; and here they say, “All that the Lord has spoken we shall do, and we shall be [Col. 0691A] obedient.”

“But Moses sprinkled the people with the blood he had taken, and said: This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.” And thereafter: “The Lord said to Moses: Come up to me on the mountain and remain there, and I shall give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written.” Here at last is the solemn and duly completed giving of the Law. For on the preceding forty-ninth day, what occurred should be called a kind of catechetical instruction. For it is one thing to say, “Behold the law under which you wish to serve: if you can keep it, enter; if you cannot, depart freely”; it is another to sign with one’s own hand the confirmed profession of the law that has been sought.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the dedication of the covenant, after the altar had been built, by the blood of twelve calves.

Recalling this passage, the Apostle, after saying, “For a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it is not yet valid while the testator lives” (Heb. 9 [OCR: 11]), immediately adds: “Therefore not even the first covenant was dedicated without blood. For when every commandment of the Law had been read by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying: This is the blood of the covenant which God has commanded for you” (ibid.).

He maintains that the first covenant was dedicated here: after the altar with the twelve pillars representing the twelve tribes had been built, the Law was recited to those professing obedience; the victims were sacrificed; Moses poured half the blood upon the altar, [Col. 0691C] and sprinkled the people with the remaining half, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant.” What, then, should we think this dedication of the covenant is, if not the acceptance of its written instrument on account of the testator’s promises: that he himself would be their God and they his people, according to the character of a marital covenant? Hence in Ezekiel, among other things, he says: “Your breasts had swelled and your hair had grown, yet you were naked and full of shame. And I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time was the time of lovers. I spread my garment over you and covered your disgrace; I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God” (Ezek. 16), etc.

Great, therefore, and worthy is the memorial of this fiftieth day, [Col. 0691D] on which that woman—the Synagogue—who had multiplied and become great in Egypt, and had now, as the same prophet says, reached the age of womanhood; who at the day of her birth had no navel cord cut, had not been washed with water for salvation, and had begun to serve many gods—was made the wife of one man, one God. She was washed with water, cleansed from her blood, clothed and shod, and received all the ornaments of righteousness, which the same prophet carefully enumerates under the names of adornments.

In the above-mentioned chapter the Apostle says: “It was necessary, therefore, for the copies of heavenly things to be cleansed by these; but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices than these” (Heb. 9). According to evangelical and apostolic faith, the heavenly things are those holy things into which [Col. 0692A] Jesus entered—namely, “heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us” (ibid.). But these holy things delivered to that people are copies of those heavenly realities, as the same Apostle says, citing the testimony of the present Scripture: “If he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the Law, [p. 222] who serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things, as Moses was instructed when he was completing the tabernacle: See, he says, that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Heb. 8). Therefore it is now pleasing to compare this present passage more carefully with the heavenly realities of which these and the things that follow are copies.

## CHAPTER XLIII. [Col. 0692B] That the blood of the calves signifies the blood of the heavenly man, Christ.

First, the blood of the calves, by which these copies were cleansed, was a figure of the blood of the heavenly man Jesus Christ, by which heavenly and earthly things alike were reconciled. The sign of the salvation which his blood truly bestowed was anticipated by the blood of goats and calves.

Moreover, the fact that Moses sent young men rather than old men from the sons of Israel to offer burnt offerings is a figure of that youth of which the Psalmist says: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 102 [Vulgate; modern 103]). For the Lord Jesus Christ was to send not old but new men, not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit: the twelve apostles, new priests and ministers of the new and true [Col. 0692C] sacrifice.

What, further, does it set forth for us that he poured half the blood upon the altar and sprinkled half upon the people, except that two heavenly realities alike derive from the one and same blood of Christ, Son of God? By one we are sprinkled in baptism for the remission of sins; by the other we receive true blood, together with true flesh, from the holy altar. Thus blood placed in basins is poured partly on the altar and sprinkled partly on the people, because the word of the Lord’s Passion, stored in the hearts of the apostles and of all Christ’s priests, is poured forth through their mouths and tongues into these sacraments, so that we may both be truly baptized into the death of Jesus Christ, sprinkled with his blood, and truly drink his blood from the holy altar.

The Apostle testifies that this figurative sprinkling was performed with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop (Heb. 9). Thus blood also flowed with water from Christ’s side (John 19); and for this reason apostolic faith rightly ordained that water should be mixed with wine in the sacrament of the holy Church. No faithful person doubts that in the celebration of holy baptism water receives, through the word of the cross and the power of the Holy Spirit, the efficacy of Christ’s blood to wash away the believer’s sins.

Hyssop, a lowly herb, signifies humble faith in the Lord’s Passion; for as hyssop relieves swelling of the lungs, so faith in Christ, by healing, brings down the pride of the heart. By the scarlet wool we understand the imitation of that same Passion proposed to us, because, as blessed Peter the Apostle says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” [Col. 0693A] (1 Pet. 2). The Apostle also asserts that the book itself was sprinkled, because Holy Scripture almost everywhere contains faith in Christ’s Passion, and cannot in any way be understood without it.

Without the sprinkling of this blood no one shall see God. For Christ says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3). Likewise: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). Therefore, before the people had been sprinkled with that figurative blood, the Lord rightly said: “Go down and solemnly warn the people, lest they wish to cross the boundaries in order to see, and a very great multitude of them perish” (Exod. 19). But now, after the sprinkling: “Moses and Aaron,” Scripture says, “and Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, went up; and they saw the God of Israel. Under his feet was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear. He did not lay his hand upon those sons of Israel who had withdrawn far off; and they saw God, and ate and drank.”

They saw the God of Israel, but not as he is. For he says: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). And long after this vision John the Evangelist says: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4). Therefore this vision too is a copy of that heavenly vision of God in which “we shall see him as he is” [Col. 0693B] (1 John 3). The words, “Under his feet was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear,” mystically indicate the firmness, purity, and loftiness of that kingdom in which he promises to be seen.

“He did not lay his hand,” it says, “upon those sons of Israel who had withdrawn far off.” It is as though it said: Before they had been sprinkled with the blood of the covenant which the Lord had made with them, he had laid his hand upon them—a fearful and terrible hand—when he said: “Everyone who touches the mountain shall surely die; he shall be crushed with stones or pierced with darts” (Exod. 19). But now, because they were covenant partners, because they had been sprinkled with the blood of the covenant, he did not lay his hand upon them. He did not prohibit them from seeing him, although in the fear described above they had withdrawn far off and had not dared to ascend the appointed boundaries.

“And they saw God,” as has already been said, “and ate and drank.” All this was a copy of that vision in which we shall eat and drink and shall be satisfied and made drunk by that very vision. For the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16 [Vulgate; modern 17]). Likewise: “They shall be made drunk with the abundance of your house, and you shall make them drink from the torrent of your delight” [Col. 0693C] (Ps. 35 [Vulgate; modern 36]).

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the saying: “Come up to me, and remain there,” and on the two stone tablets written by the finger of God.

“The Lord said to Moses: Come up to me on the mountain, and remain there; and I shall give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written, that [Col. 0694A] you may teach the children of Israel. Moses and Joshua his minister arose.”

It was said above: “Moses and Aaron and Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel went up”; but it was not said, “They went up to the Lord.” Here, however, it is said, “Come up to me,” which signifies that Moses was invited to familiar conversation; and it is added, “remain there”—understand: not for one hour or one day, but “remain there,” that is, remain there forty days and forty nights.

“And I shall give you two tablets of stone, and the law and commandments which I have written.” He did not say, “and the law which I have written,” but “the commandments which I have written.” For Moses himself wrote the law, as was also said above concerning the judgments: Moses wrote all the words of the Lord. But the finger of God wrote the commandments, as Moses himself says in Deuteronomy: “The Lord gave me two tablets of stone written by the finger of God” (Deut. 9).

This too was a copy of heavenly things. Of which heavenly things? Namely, of those accomplished through the new man Jesus Christ, who ascended to God, not upon an earthly mountain but into heaven itself, in order to receive for us not the killing letter but the life-giving Spirit (2 Cor. 3). Hence: “You ascended on high, you led captivity captive, you received gifts among men” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate; modern 68]). What gifts? “And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers” (Eph. 4). These and similar spiritual gifts he wrote for us “not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Cor. [Col. 0694B] 3). He wrote not with a pen or ink, but with the finger of God—that is, with the Holy Spirit.

For on the fiftieth day after he rose from the dead, of which this fiftieth day was also a figure, when all his disciples were gathered together, this finger of God was sent to write: this Holy Spirit, manifold, subtle, eloquent, [p. 223] sure, and discerning (Acts 2). The first proof of the writer’s work appeared in men who had previously been unlearned and without letters, in that they immediately “began to speak in tongues the mighty works of God” (ibid.). That and the works which followed were heavenly works, so that this Scripture given on stone tablets may rightly be called a copy of those heavenly things. For of such things it is said: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8).

But someone may say: These stone tablets written by the finger of God were later broken. For when Moses returned from the mountain and approached, “he saw the calf and the dances; and, greatly angered, he threw the tablets from his hand and broke them at the foot of the mountain” (Exod. 32). How did this belong to the copy of heavenly things? Clearly this also belonged to it, because that people, upon whose tablets the heavenly gifts had first been inscribed by the finger of God, was, behold, shattered and cast away through rebellion.

“Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the former ones, and I shall write upon them the words which were upon the tablets that you broke” (Exod. 34). These later tablets were not broken. For after those to whom the word of God ought first to have been spoken had been rejected (Acts 13), it was proclaimed to the Gentiles, and there the writing of the finger remains.

Certainly, according to the arrangement of the text, the commandments were divided upon those two tablets in such a way that one contained those pertaining to the love of God, the first of which is: “You shall have no strange gods before me”; the other, those pertaining to love of neighbour, the first of which is: “Honour your father and your mother.” Hence the Apostle calls this the first commandment [Col. 0695A] (Eph. 6).

## CHAPTER XLV. How Moses was able to endure forty days without food.

“When Moses had gone up, the cloud covered the mountain, and the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it with a cloud for six days.” He says that the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai because Moses experienced the great and glorious abundance of the Lord’s sweetness, which he has indeed hidden for those who fear him (Ps. 30 [Vulgate; modern 31]), but revealed to this man in no small measure, so that he feasted on it not for one day but for forty days and forty nights.

For one might ask how a human being endured so long without food and drink, when human nature cannot last more than seven days without all nourishment. “But on the seventh day,” it says, “he called him from the midst of the darkness.” It was altogether within human possibility that, through eagerness for heavenly feasting, he did not eat bread or drink water for six days. But unless the Lord had called him on the seventh day, human nature, left to itself, would soon have withered entirely. Therefore he called him from the midst of the darkness; and his voice is sweet and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. By his call he so enriched the needy nature of man that, until the fortieth day, Moses could forget not only food and drink but even the whole human condition.

Thus Moses deserved to experience in himself the truth of the saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” [Col. 0695B] (Deut. 3 [probably 8]). Likewise, when Elijah fasted for forty days and forty nights, Scripture did not leave unspoken that this was not achieved by human ability but received as a gift from God’s power. For when the Angel of the Lord touched him a second time and said, “Rise and eat” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19), after he had eaten and drunk, it immediately adds: “And he walked in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights” (ibid.). Scripture says “in the strength of that food” so that you may understand that this strength was not, and could not be, in the nature of even a very strong man practiced in fasting.

Divinity made this provision very usefully, so that it might possess an adequate testimony to Christ’s humanity. For he was to fast forty days and forty nights, so that for the gluttony of the first sinful man, this innocent second man might undergo the chastisement of a fitting satisfaction, and through fasting acquire for us who believe in him the food of eternal life which the former man lost by eating. But this, as was said, is beyond human nature; and therefore heretical perversity, which maintains that he appeared not as a true man but in a phantasm, would have brazenly seized upon so prolonged a fast in support of its madness.

Divinity therefore usefully provided for us, as has been said, that Christ’s humanity as a fasting man should have two witnesses of truth: one from the Law and one from the prophets. Indeed, if it please us, we may say that this true God-and-man, our Saviour, had not merely two but three witnesses in this matter. For Moses also fasted a second time for forty days and forty nights. Thus this word too shall stand not merely in the mouth of two, [Col. 0696A] but even of three witnesses (Deut. 19).

## CHAPTER XLVI. What it means that Moses, receiving the commandments, entered into the midst of the cloud, ascended the mountain, and remained there forty days and forty nights.

“Now the appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the summit of the mountain in the sight of the children of Israel.” This appearance too of the Lord’s glory was a copy of heavenly things. For when, on the fortieth day, as was said above, heavenly grace shone forth, there was likewise an appearance of the glory of the Lord as fire. “There appeared to them,” it says, “tongues divided as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them” (Acts 2). In both places the vitality of fire prefigured the zeal and fervour of the Spirit against sins.

“And Moses, entering into the midst of the cloud, ascended the mountain, and was there forty days and forty nights.” Some have called the cloud or darkness, which Scripture frequently mentions in these passages, inaccessible light, because the Apostle says: “No man has seen him, nor can see him, who dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6). Yet this interpretation—that the Law is meant under the designation of cloud or darkness—has not pleased many interpreters of Scripture, because it depends upon antiphrasis.

But apart from the typological interpretation, the fact that Moses enters the midst of the cloud also morally indicates that those who strive toward contemplation ought to seek quiet and purity of heart. For what does it mean that here he received God’s sublime commands, ascended to the heights, and, in order to penetrate inward things, was hidden from outward tumults, except that holy men, who are compelled by the necessity of their office to serve in outward ministries, always diligently retreat to the hidden places of the heart? There they ascend the summit of their inmost thought and receive the law, as if on a mountain, while, setting aside the tumults of temporal actions, they search out, upon the height of contemplation, the judgment of the divine will.

# FOURTH BOOK ON EXODUS. (Exodus, chapters 24–35.)

[Col. 0697]

[p. 224]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the tabernacle of Moses: that the heavenly tabernacle was its pattern.

The true tabernacle, “which God pitched, and not man” (Heb. VIII), was the pattern of the tabernacle which Moses pitched—so declares God himself, and not man. For he says: “See, and make it according to the pattern which was shown thee on the mountain” (Exod. XXV). Recalling this saying, the Apostle says: “For Jesus entered not into sanctuaries made with hands, copies of the true ones, but into heaven itself” (Heb. IX). This great authority of the divine Architect made the construction of that hand-made tabernacle visible to the whole world. Where? In this holy and truthful Scripture, which has preserved and rescued from oblivion all the measurements, numbers, and weights of that building [Col. 0697B].

All who are soldiers of the kingdom of heaven, pilgrims in this world—who pass through, have no abiding city here, and seek the city to come (Heb. XIII)—turn aside to behold it. They contemplate here the patterns of heavenly things, which they already know in part, in order that they may advance in knowledge. In their wonder they say: “How beloved are thy tabernacles, O Lord of hosts” (Ps. LXXXIII). Let us therefore, whom the straight course of our purpose has brought to this place, linger here for a little, so that, drawn by the beauty of the tabernacle, our soul may long and faint for the courts of the Lord, while heart and flesh exult in the living God, where the sparrow finds a house and the turtle-dove a nest for herself (ibid.). May God look upon the sparrow according to the heart, tending toward [Col. 0697C] that heavenly house, and upon the turtle-dove according to the flesh, labouring in the present tabernacle; and, since what we undertake is both holy and lofty, may the help of his grace go before the sparrow in right thinking and follow the turtle-dove in right action.

## CHAPTER II. Why the Apostle, reversing the expression, says that Moses’ tabernacle was a pattern of the heavenly tabernacle.

First, one wishes to ask why, in speaking of patterns, the Apostle altered the manner of the divine expression. For God says: “According to all the likeness of the tabernacle which is shown thee, and of all its vessels for its service, so shall ye make it” (Exod. XXV). Likewise: “See and make according to the pattern shown thee [Col. 0697D] on the mountain” (ibid.). Here he plainly says that the things which he commanded Moses to make were copies of those which he showed him. Conversely, the Apostle calls the things Moses made copies of those which God showed him. For he says: “If therefore he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are those who offer gifts according to the Law, who serve a copy and shadow of heavenly things” (Heb. IX) [Col. 0698A]. And immediately he adds the testimony already quoted, by which God rather declared heavenly things to be the patterns of earthly things: “As Moses was instructed: See, he says, that thou make all things according to the pattern shown thee on the mountain” (ibid.).

This, then, is what we ask; and, God granting it, we shall quickly find the answer. God was speaking to Moses and, before he made earthly things, was showing him heavenly things; before he made carnal things, spiritual things. By what vision, or of what kind, did he show them? By an inward vision, a prophetic vision. “For he spoke with him face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend” (Exod. XXXIII). How does a man speak with his friend? By not concealing his counsel from him, making him privy to his secrets [Col. 0698B]. Therefore, when he spoke to him as a man speaks with his friend, would he conceal from him the highest fruit of his friendship, namely, the future heavenly priesthood of Christ his Son? Rather, he taught him both past and future things.

Does not John, with the authority of the Mosaic Scripture, say: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God; all things were made through him, and without him was made nothing” (John I)? For the earlier writer spoke thus, since God said, “Let it be, and it was made” (Gen. I), which amounts to the same thing. For if he said, “Let it be, and it was made,” it was made through the Word. Therefore he much less concealed from his friend that the Word would become flesh; that Christ, God and man, would become the propitiation for our sins; that in his tabernacle—which is the present Church—he would set forth the table of his body and blood; and that Christ himself, the great lampstand, would illuminate that same tabernacle, shining with all the gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0698C].

Accordingly, since Moses first saw these spiritual or heavenly realities, and afterwards made the Holy of Holies in material form for that people, those heavenly things are called, and are, his patterns. But the Hebrews—for it is to them that the Apostle speaks in that Epistle—first knew the hand-made tabernacle, the ark, the mercy-seat, the table, the lampstand, and all the other hand-made things; and the Apostle moved them from likenesses of those things to reach out toward knowledge of heavenly things [Col. 0698D]. Therefore it was right to say, conversely, to them that these earthly things were copies of heavenly things (Heb. VIII), copies of the true things (Heb. IX), copies, I say, and shadows of things to come.

Now, therefore, with God as our guide and with the lampstand—which he is—shining before us, let us enter upon the structure of the tabernacle itself.

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 0699A] On the firstfruits which the Lord commanded to be taken for the construction of the tabernacle.

(CHAP. XXV.) “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take for me firstfruits.” Explaining what he meant, or what he wished to be understood by saying “firstfruits,” he immediately added: “From every man who offers willingly, ye shall receive them.” He “offers willingly” who offers something not under compelled servitude but from spontaneous charity. Therefore offerings of charity, whether great or small, are firstfruits to the Lord and contribute to the adornment of his heavenly tabernacle. Conversely, whatever is offered sadly is late fruit and cannot contribute to the beauty of the Lord’s house.

Accordingly, when the Apostle had said: “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; and he who sows in blessings shall also reap of blessings” (II Cor. IX) [Col. 0699B], he immediately added: “Each one, as he has purposed in his heart, not out of sadness or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver,” etc. (ibid.). Thus he rightly said what all helpers of God’s tabernacle—that is, Christ’s Church—should fittingly hear: “From every man who offers willingly, ye shall receive them.”

What was said of material things must likewise be said and understood of spiritual things. For whatever good we do, whether material or spiritual, if we do it “before men, that they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V), is firstfruit; and God, who receives firstfruits, commands it to be accepted [Col. 0699C]. Conversely, if anyone acts before men merely in order to be seen by them, he establishes for himself no memorial in God’s tabernacle. For in being seen by men he has received his reward.

## CHAPTER IV. Again on the same subject: why lesser gifts are sometimes dearer to God than greater ones, according to the giver’s intention.

“But these are the things which ye must receive: gold, silver, bronze, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, blue skins, and shittim wood,” etc. Therefore, for offerings to be firstfruits, it is not the quantity of the offerings but the good will of the offerers that accomplishes this. Goats’ hair differs greatly in value from gold and silver [Col. 0699D], yet both are placed under the same name of firstfruits. Nor should there be any doubt that goats’ hair and rams’ skins were sometimes of greater value than gold, silver, and precious stones before God, who searches hearts.

For the God and Lord of that same tabernacle, when he sat opposite the treasury and watched how the crowd cast bronze coins into the treasury, while many rich persons cast in much, saw one poor widow come and put in two small coins, which make a quadrans. Calling his disciples, he said to them: “Amen, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all. For they all put in from what they had in abundance; but she, from her poverty, put in all that she had, her whole livelihood” (Mark XII).

The contributions made toward spiritual building are spiritual goods. Certainly, “to whom more is entrusted, more is required” (Luke XII) [Col. 0700A], for the perfecting of the heavenly saints, of whom those things are, as has often been said, patterns for us. Hence, when the Apostle said, “And he himself gave some as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, others as teachers and pastors” (Eph. IV), he significantly added, “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (ibid.). These and similar great gifts are gold, silver, and precious stones.

We see, for we read, long ranks of blessed men and women, boys and girls, advancing to Christ’s heavenly ministry, who faithfully and devoutly offered such things in the Lord’s sanctuary [Col. 0700B]. And so we, insignificant as we are, since we cannot offer such a thing to the heavenly priest, nevertheless enter eagerly with good will to behold the sanctuary, lest we appear altogether empty before him; truthfully declaring that everything pleases us—the order of the priest, the devotion of those who minister, and the charity of those who offer.

What significance gold, silver, and the other firstfruits, which are commanded to be received when offered willingly, have, we shall say in their proper places, as the several things are employed in the work, so far as we are able. And the mysteries of the reading itself will make clear how truly it was said: “And I will dwell in the midst of them when they have made me a sanctuary.” The likeness of the tabernacle shown to Moses has already been discussed above. The beginning of the construction is the ark, which begins thus:

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 0700C] On the ark: how it signified the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, or of his body; and who are the poles by which it ought to be carried.

“Join together an ark of shittim wood, whose length shall be two and a half cubits, its breadth one and a half cubits, and likewise its height one and a half cubits; and thou shalt overlay it with the purest gold inside and outside. And thou shalt make above it a golden crown all round, and four golden rings, which thou shalt place at the four corners of the ark.” — “An ark,” he says, “of shittim wood.” Shittim wood is incorruptible and thorny, not greatly unlike the character of the white thorn.

At the beginning of the sanctuary the ark is joined together, because at the beginning of the holy Church the Holy Spirit joined together from the Virgin the members of a human body for the Son of God [Col. 0700D]. The ark is joined from shittim wood, incorruptible wood, because the Son of God was incarnate from the seed of the faithful Fathers, fragrant in everlasting memory.

“Its length,” he says, “shall be two and a half cubits; its breadth one cubit and a half; and likewise its height one cubit and a half”: that it may, with reverence preserved, be accessible and touchable by a human being inside and outside, according to the measure or stature of a man. For the length of the human body, from the sole of the foot to the neck, is three cubits. Therefore, since the ark’s height is only one and a half cubits, it is evident that it does not exceed the bent posture of the human body; and, since its length is two and a half cubits, it readily admits hands stretched right and left for every religious act [Col. 0701A]. Its breadth too, one and a half cubits, is plainly suitable for hands resting upon it.

All this mystically suggests to us that the incarnate divinity, in every way and measure—that is, according to human capacity—graciously yielded itself in love. “God, approaching, was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III). He was exposed to human eyes, set before human ears, and placed in human hands. John says: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, and which our hands have handled” (I John I).

“And thou shalt overlay it,” he says, “with the purest gold within and without,” because Christ was shown to be the Son of God through the gold of true divinity: inwardly, through inherent wisdom; outwardly, through divine works [Col. 0701B]. “And thou shalt make above it a golden crown all round.” The ark is encircled above by a golden crown because this ornament of compassion is, as it were, a diadem upon the head of the Son of God: by the grace of his goodness he willed, and by the power of his majesty he was able, to assume humanity—which he could not have done unless he were God.

For the order or nature of creatures does not permit one creature to be united substantially with another; for example, a man with an angel, or an angel with a man. Therefore, also because of this supremely mighty and wonderful humility, let him be proclaimed true and victorious God.

“And four,” he says, “golden rings, which thou shalt place at the four corners of the ark”: because, clearly, while faith in Christ’s incarnation is spread abroad through the four regions of the world, it is without doubt preached as girded by the four holy books of the Gospel [Col. 0701C]. “Thou shalt also make poles of shittim wood,” etc. Poles of shittim wood are made and inserted into those same rings for carrying, because strong and steadfast teachers, like incorruptible wood, must be sought: teachers who, always adhering to the instruction of the sacred volumes, proclaim the unity of the holy Church and carry the ark, as it were, by inserted rings.

To carry the ark on poles is for good teachers, through preaching, to lead the holy Church and the untrained minds of unbelievers. “And overlay them,” he says, “with gold”: that while they sound forth to others with the splendour of speech, they may themselves shine with the splendour of life. “They shall always be in the rings and shall never be removed,” he says; that is, they shall always keep watch in the sacred books and never depart from the study of holy reading [Col. 0701D]. For the poles are commanded always to remain in the rings so that, when need requires the ark to be carried, no delay in inserting the poles for carrying might occur; because, when a subject asks his pastor some spiritual question, it is highly disgraceful if he then seeks to learn when he ought to be resolving the question.
