“Therefore the poles shall always be in the rings,” he says, “ready to carry the ark”: that is, those who undertake the office of preaching shall always be ready to give an answer to everyone asking them “concerning the faith of Jesus Christ which is in them” (I Pet. III). “And thou shalt place in the ark the testimony which I shall give thee.” Understand: the golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod which budded, and the tablets of the covenant.

## CHAPTER VI. On the mercy-seat: how it was a sign of the Lord’s passion; and what the two cherubim mystically are, and why it is said, “From thence I will command thee.”

“And thou shalt make a mercy-seat of the purest gold. Its length shall be two cubits and a half, and its breadth one cubit and a half.” The mercy-seat has the same length and breadth as the ark, because the Son of God suffered for us with the same intention of love by which he was incarnate. For the same incarnate God is our mercy-seat, but through his passion and death. Through that God has been propitiated toward us, and through it we receive remission of sins, into which we were baptized, as the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized into the same Christ Jesus” (Rom. VI) [Col. 0702B]. Therefore, unless the incarnate God had also died, he would have remained alone.

After the ark’s construction, “thou shalt also make,” he says, “a mercy-seat.” Of what? “Of the purest gold.” Gold signifies the preciousness of Christ’s divine substance. He significantly and expressly said “purest,” because precisely in that God is most pure from every defilement, Christ the Son of God became our mercy-seat; precisely in that he could take away the sins of the world as the Lamb of God, “holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Heb. VII). The two Testaments declare this with concordant voices; the Law and the Gospel preach it in one Spirit and with the same meaning.

It follows: “Thou shalt also make two golden cherubim, beaten out, at either side of the oracle” [Col. 0702C]. According to the letter, Scripture does not state what workmanship the cherubim had, what their form was, or from what it was derived. Yet it is a representation of the angelic creature, whose strength, with a flaming and turning sword, Scripture records as set before Paradise in Genesis (Gen. III). The present Scripture gives painters warrant to depict it with wings, clearly because of the swiftness of spiritual nature. For it follows: “Let them cover either side of the mercy-seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle,” that is, the mercy-seat. It further follows: “And let them look toward one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat.”

“Let them look toward,” he says, not “look upon.” Indeed, to cover the mercy-seat with wings and turn their faces toward one another means not to look before themselves, but, turning the wing toward the head, to look at one another [Col. 0702D]. According to the aforesaid account of patterns, however, the two cherubim—whose name is interpreted “fulness of knowledge”—are the two Testaments, from which we who thirst for the knowledge of God drink, and in which nothing is lacking of what must be sought or known concerning God.

“Thou shalt make,” therefore, he says, “two golden cherubim, beaten out.” The two cherubim are two witnesses, in whose mouth stands every word concerning our propitiation. They are golden because the Old and New Testaments shine with the same true wisdom of God and are written with the same simple truth, “more desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Ps. XVIII). They are beaten out because, certainly, the holy Scripture of each Testament was composed amid blows and pressures.

They spread their wings and protect the oracle because they defend the humility of our crucified Lord Jesus Christ against Jewish and heretical blasphemies [Col. 0703A]. For the Jews thought “him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled” (Isa. LIII); but, as the two cherubim testify, “he was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we are healed” (ibid.). He died for the nation, “and not for the nation only, but that he might gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad” (John XI).

With faces turned, they look toward the mercy-seat because the two Testaments differ from each other in nothing. What one promises, the other displays; and thus they behold between themselves the Mediator of God and men. The cherubim would turn their faces away from one another if one Testament denied what the other promises.

“By which the ark is to be covered,” he says. Therefore the mercy-seat is higher than the ark, and it is said: “by which the ark is to be covered,” as though it said, “to which the ark is to be subjected.” Hence the Apostle: “And above it, cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat” (Heb. IX) [Col. 0703B]. Here, indeed, “overshadowing” is said in the neuter gender. Elsewhere, however, that *cherubim* is expressed in the masculine is clearer from this passage, “thou shalt also make two golden cherubim, beaten out,” and from many other places.

Observe how sonorously the Apostle says: “and above it, cherubim of glory.” Whoever has been anointed with the Holy Spirit’s unction knows that the two Testaments everywhere breathe the glory of the Son of God. One of them says: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honour” (Ps. VIII); the other: “And we have seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John I) [Col. 0703C]. In these sayings there is indeed the very word “glory”; but throughout the entire sequence of the Scriptures the reality of glory resounds in continually harmonious faith.

“From thence,” he says, “I will command thee and speak to thee from above the mercy-seat,” namely, from between the two cherubim which are above the ark of the testimony. What does this mean: “From thence I will command thee and speak to thee”? Can a man receive God’s answers from elsewhere? Certainly not. For unless, through the death of Christ his Son, God had broken down the wall of enmities, humankind had no access to God (Eph. II); nor had man anything else to give as the price of reconciliation [Col. 0703D]. Through the death of this Re-propitiator we have been reconciled; and accordingly we receive the Spirit of reconciliation, of whom the Propitiator himself says elsewhere: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you. But if I go away, I will send him to you” (John XVI).

Therefore, because through that Paraclete we receive him who teaches us all truth and announces to us the things that are to come (ibid.), “from thence,” he says, “I will command thee and speak to thee all things which I shall command through thee to the children of Israel.”

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 0704A] On the table: how it signified the refreshment of the same body and blood of the Lord; and on its crowns, rings, poles, vessels, and the loaves of presentation.

“Thou shalt also make a table of shittim wood, two cubits in length, one cubit in breadth, and one cubit and a half in height; and thou shalt overlay it with the purest gold.” — “It shall be,” he says, “two cubits in length.” This length is conveniently sufficient for one person alone sitting at it. “And one cubit and a half in height”: this height rises a little above the knee of a seated person. “And one cubit in breadth”: this breadth does not accommodate a guest seated opposite, whether eating separately or at a distance.

What is this table, prepared after the mercy-seat in the Lord’s tabernacle, except the table of the Lord’s body and blood, having its beginning in the passion of our same Lord Jesus Christ? For when he was distressed, already sold and immediately to be betrayed; when his soul was sorrowful unto death; when, being in agony, he prayed at greater length and his sweat ran down like blood to the ground (Matt. XXVI) [Col. 0704B], meanwhile the maker of our propitiation and redemption prepared the table: taking bread, blessing and breaking it, he gave it to his disciples, saying, “Take and eat. This is my body, which shall be delivered for you.” Likewise the cup: “This,” he said, “is the cup of my blood, which shall be shed for you” (ibid.).

This is the Lord’s table, sufficiently suited to our measure if faith alone is not lacking; yet so that one stands there for all, as the stated measurements of that hand-made table signify. For one is the Father of the table or banquet; one is our priest or high priest, Christ; and one is the table of which the Psalmist says: “Thou hast prepared before me a table against those who trouble me” (Ps. XXII) [Col. 0704C]. Likewise: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied; and they shall praise the Lord who seek him; their hearts shall live for ever and ever” (Ps. XXI).

“And thou shalt overlay it,” he says, “with the purest gold.” Why is it not wholly of molten or beaten gold, but made from shittim wood and overlaid with the purest gold? Clearly because both kinds, bread and wine, are taken from the earth: the one from the common or public granary, the other from the storehouse. But God, the Creator of substances and kinds, and the Holy Spirit, their former, come; and the gold of the incarnate Word—the gold of Christ crucified, dead and buried, and after his glorious resurrection taken up into heaven at the Father’s right hand—does not merely cover their surface, but effectively changes these into his flesh and blood, although the outward appearance remains [Col. 0704D]. Here the confession of the lips is required.

It follows: “Thou shalt make for it a golden rim all round,” that is, a projection of thin gold extending outward. And because a reward is granted to the heart believing unto righteousness and the mouth confessing unto salvation (Rom. X), so that it may understand what it believes: “And for the rim,” he says, “a chased”—that is, embossed or carved—“crown, four fingers high,” that is, a palm, by which the gift of understanding is mystically signified.

For the cubit, which the table’s breadth does not exceed, is six palms; and that number signifies activity. Hence the palm of the crown, because it is the seventh, rightly signifies the rest of contemplation by which a believer’s faith is rewarded. “And above it,” he says, “another small golden crown” [Col. 0705A]. Scripture rightly kept silence concerning the workmanship or measure of the crown above the first, because the reward by which this present rest of contemplation, or dignity of understanding itself, is to be crowned is something that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (Isa. LXIV).

“Thou shalt also prepare four golden rings and place them at the four corners of the same table, one at each foot,” etc., as was said above concerning the four golden rings placed at the four corners of the ark. For just as the ark of the Lord’s incarnation, so also the table of his body and blood is everywhere defended by the four books of the Gospel. And just as strong and steadfast teachers ought to carry—that is, to preach—the faith of the incarnation and the sacrament of this table, like poles inserted into rings, that is, always firmly adhering to the instruction of the sacred volumes [Col. 0705B].

“Thou shalt prepare dishes and bowls, censers and cups, in which libations are to be offered, of the purest gold.” A dish is a vessel weighing twelve drachmas, but a cup ten. Bowls are so called because they are of glass: for glass in Greek is called *phialin*. They have a wide mouth, whereas a cup is known to have a narrower mouth.

What, then, is signified by bowls except abundant teaching, and by cups except small and narrow knowledge? One person, full of the teaching of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers; therefore, by what he says, he offers a bowl. Another cannot explain what he perceives; nevertheless, because he announces it somehow, he certainly offers a taste by means of a cup [Col. 0705C]. Therefore, those placed in God’s tabernacle—that is, the holy Church—if they cannot offer bowls through the wisdom of teaching, ought, insofar as they are sufficient through the generosity of divinity for their neighbours, to give cups of a good word.

“And thou shalt set upon the table the loaves of presentation continually before me.” The bread of presentation is Christ himself, as the catholic faith holds, whom the holy Church continually sets before God. For that bread of presentation which was set forth as a type of this bread was long ago defiled by the wickedness of the Jews. Hence through the prophet Malachi the Lord says: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar” (Mal. I). And afterwards: “I will not accept a gift from your hand, for from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name” (ibid.) [Col. 0705D].

## CHAPTER VIII. How the lampstand signified Christ’s glory, or Christ glorified; and the branches and bowls, its seven knobs, its seven lamps, its weight, and its very position.

“Thou shalt also make a beaten lampstand of the purest gold: its shaft and branches, bowls and knobs, and lilies proceeding from it. Six branches shall come forth from its sides, three from one side and three from the other. Three bowls, as in the form of a nut, on each branch, together with knobs and lilies,” etc.

Scripture labours to present to the eyes of its readers the workmanship of the lampstand, as of the other prescribed things, so that, because all was divinely made and accomplished by the divine Spirit, while the things themselves cannot remain according to their material, the rationale of them remains and there may be an everlasting remembrance of the things themselves [Col. 0706A]. Of the knobs and lilies, only a few traces remain in the lampstands commonly made or found today. For knobs—that is, round nodes upon the shafts—and lilies upon the heads of lampstands are commonly seen. But bowls, if they were made on the authority of the present Scripture, or if they are made anywhere, would surely delight the eyes of beholders by their elaborate beauty.

But since these are patterns of heavenly things, let us contemplate from it the heavenly lampstand: namely Christ incarnate, whose seven lamps are the seven spirits of God, of which the seven lamps set upon that material lampstand were patterns, as the following words show. “Thou shalt make,” he says, “seven lamps, that they may shine opposite.”

Therefore Christ, upon whom “rested the Spirit of the Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. XI), is the lampstand of heaven, the lampstand and light of the world, ever shining with seven such inextinguishable lamps [Col. 0706B]. He who, by the ark, is represented because of the mystery of the incarnation; by the mercy-seat, because of the price of his passion and blood; by the table, because of the sacrament of his body and blood, which he gave us as food and drink; is rightly represented by the lampstand of seven lamps because of the sevenfold [Col. 0706C] Spirit who rested upon him and whom, crowned with glory and honour and sitting at the Father’s right hand, he gave to men.

Why, then, did “six branches come forth from the sides of the lampstand,” that is, from the greater shaft? Clearly because the first brightness of this our lampstand which we know comes from this: that through him God made all things in the number of six days. “Three branches came forth from one side and three from the other,” because in the first three days God unfolded the fabric of the world through his Word, while in the remaining three days he filled it with moving and sentient creatures.

Why also were there “three bowls, in the likeness of a nut, upon each branch, together with knobs and a lily”? Clearly because this too belongs to the brightness of this lampstand: that it intoxicates us with the wine of knowledge, so that we may forget the delights of the world which we love [Col. 0706D]. The knob, which rolls in every direction, signifies the mobility of the preaching we have received since this lampstand shone forth; because it can neither be held back by adversity nor raised up by prosperity, it is a knob. And lilies are suitably added to the lampstand after bowls and knobs, because after this intoxication and mobility of preaching follows that green country, which blooms for holy souls as with everlasting flowers. Thus bowls and knobs pertain to labour, lilies to reward.

Therefore, because all things were made through the Word in six days, while the seventh day, on which God rested, is the Son himself, as we said at the beginning of the present work, six branches rightly came forth from one shaft—that is, from one lampstand. And because, when the Word himself became flesh (John I), when the rod came forth from the root of Jesse and the flower rose from his root, the sevenfold Spirit of the Lord rested upon him (Isa. XI), seven lamps are likewise rightly numbered upon the lampstand [Col. 0707A].

“That they may shine,” he says, “opposite,” that is, toward the table. For he later expresses this in saying: “And thou shalt place the lampstand opposite the table, on the southern side of the tabernacle.” The table stood on the northern side (Exod. XXXVI). This mystically suggests that the light of our lampstand—that is, the evangelical grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God—shone upon us from the south, that is, from the great charity of God the Father, while we were on the northern side: that is, the side concerning which the devil says, “I will sit upon the mount of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV).

For us, I say, who were northerners—that is, cold through unbelief—the aforesaid table was set forth; and from the southern charity of God Christ, the lampstand of the heavenly sanctuary, shone forth [Col. 0707B]. “The whole weight of the lampstand, with all its vessels”—that is, with the snuffers and the receptacles where the snuffed material is extinguished—“shall be,” he says, “one talent of the purest gold.”

The greatest talent is one hundred and twenty pounds. A great weight signifies the great talent of the world, which, weighed in the balance of the cross, outweighed the scale placed against it and cast our sins into the sea. And because it is the purest [Col. 0707C] gold—that is, because Christ is God most pure from every defilement—our whole redemption was accomplished in its weight. And because, being perfect God and man, he endured the pains of suffering and thus came to the glory of resurrection, the lampstand was rightly beaten.

“See and make according to the pattern which was shown thee on the mountain.” This has already been discussed above.

## CHAPTER IX. On the division or arrangement of the second tabernacle.

(CAP. XXVI.) “The tabernacle, moreover, shall be made thus: you shall make ten curtains of fine twisted linen, and of blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, varied with embroidered work,” etc. The Apostle briefly touches upon the substance of this reading as follows: “The first tabernacle was made, in which were the lampstands, and the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. But behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, overlaid on every side with gold, in which were a vessel containing manna, Aaron’s rod which had budded, and the tablets of the covenant; and above it the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat” (Heb. IX).

It must first be understood that he calls it the first and second tabernacle not according to the order in which their construction is narrated, but according to the order of ministry or entry. Therefore, returning now in reverse order, we must say a few things about the arrangement or placement of the two tabernacles, beginning at the end of the passage, where it was said: “At the entrance of the court there shall be a curtain twenty cubits [Exod. XXVII].” The first gate of entry into the court was twenty cubits wide. It had four pillars, from which hung a veil stretched across twenty cubits and raised to five cubits, variegated in those four often-mentioned colours by needlework. One entering through this gate was received into the court. Its right and left sides extended inward for fifteen cubits each, with three pillars on each side, so as to place the door of the inner tabernacle at the midpoint of the side which they reached, just as they placed the gate of the court in the middle of the side from which they began.

In this court stood the altar of sacrifices, square in shape, five cubits long and equally wide. Between the gate and the altar was a space in which those who placed sacrifices upon the altar moved about. Further inward, between the altar and the door of the tabernacle, was the place of ashes before the altar, and beyond that the bronze basin, where priests washed their hands and feet, whether they were to minister at the altar in the court or enter the inner tabernacle. The curtains of this court, moreover, were of linen, stretched along the sides supported by three pillars for fifteen cubits, and raised five cubits high. From this court one entered the door of the tabernacle after passing the altar and the bronze basin. Upon entering by that door, one encountered the veil arranged at the entrance, variegated in those four colours, upon five pillars of shittim wood. Having passed that veil, one was received into the middle part of the tabernacle, between this veil and the other, which had been set upon four inner pillars, made from those four colours, and which separated the holy things outside from the Holy of Holies situated within.

In this middle space between the two veils stood the golden table holding the loaves of presentation, on the north side; opposite it, on the south side, stood the golden lampstand with seven lamps. Up to this point priests alone were permitted to enter. Further within, that is, in the Holy of Holies beyond the veil of four pillars, stood the gilded ark of testimony, in which were the stone tablets of the Law, Aaron’s rod, a golden vessel containing manna, and the mercy-seat. Above it stood the two cherubim, overshadowing the mercy-seat with their wings and looking upon one another and upon it. Before the ark—that is, between the ark and the veil—stood the altar of incense, which Scripture sometimes calls golden and sometimes gilded: it calls golden that which was in fact gold-plated. But no one except the high priest was permitted to enter this Holy of Holies daily to offer incense; rather, he entered once yearly with blood to purify the altar, and perhaps also when necessity required it because of the sin of a priest or of the whole synagogue, as is written in Leviticus. Now, finally, let us enter again from the beginning with a historical exposition, and pursue the arrangement according to its spiritual meaning.

## CHAPTER X. That the tabernacle was a type of the Church; what is the pattern of the curtains, and what mystery it contains.

“The tabernacle, moreover, shall be made thus.” After the construction of the ark, the mercy-seat, the table, and the lampstand, instructions are given for making the tabernacle, which is their place. For after the incarnation, passion, and participation in the body and blood of Christ the Son of God, and the sending through him of the Holy Spirit, the holy Church, which is his place, is established in heaven from the ancients and gathered upon earth from new people.

How? By what institution or order? He says: “You shall make ten curtains of fine twisted linen, and blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, varied with embroidered work.” The number ten is the second triangular unity, as arithmeticians know better. Therefore ten, the second triangular unity, signifies the one faith of the one Trinity. This number of curtains also fittingly corresponds to the Decalogue by which the same God is served. Curtains, moreover, are hangings—that is, veils—and are called *cortinae* because they were originally made of skins.

“Of fine twisted linen,” he says, “and blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet.” Fine linen is a kind of very white flax. Blue is the colour of the sky, purple of the sea, and scarlet of fire. By these four principal colours is signified all that variety of virtues of which the Psalm sings: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed round about in golden fringes with varieties” (Ps. XLIV). This weaving signifies, finally, that glory which is within, which Christ alone, the King, sees in his bride, the king’s daughter—especially because it must be covered with haircloth coverings.

“Varied with embroidered work,” he says: that is, depicted by a needle in the manner of a feather. “The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits; its breadth shall be four cubits.” This measure of breadth is one seventh of the length: for four times seven, and seven times four, make twenty-eight. The seventh part commonly signifies the rest of contemplation. Thus the very measurements of the curtains, which must be covered with haircloth coverings, confirm that those orders of the Church are signified who live in the repose of contemplation.

“Five curtains,” he says, “shall be joined one to another, and the other five shall likewise adhere by a similar joining.” How? “You shall make,” he says, “blue loops upon the sides and edges of the curtains, so that they may be joined together.” The blue loops are the heavenly bonds of brotherly love, and by brotherly love one ascends to the love of God. “You shall also make,” he says, “fifty golden rings, by which the veils of the curtains are to be joined, so that one tabernacle may be made.” The golden rings are bonds of divine love; inserted, as it were, into the blue loops of brotherly love, they make that love holy and worthy of God. Since this charity covers a multitude of sins (I Pet. IV), there are fittingly fifty loops on each side and fifty rings: by this number remission is signified and commanded by the Law. Hence the fiftieth year is called Jubilee (Lev. XXV), that is, “releasing.”

The variety and costly weaving of the curtains are beautiful; but they are not to be left bare outside, for they could not withstand the violence of rain or hail. Therefore it follows:

## CHAPTER XI. On the eleven haircloth coverings which cover these curtains, and on the red-dyed skins of rams: what we should understand mystically by these.

“You shall make eleven coverings to cover the roof of the tabernacle.” Thus the life of the saints is splendid; but unless it is carefully hidden beneath the protection of superiors, as under haircloth, the beauty of its integrity is not preserved. Therefore, so that within the tabernacle linen may shine, scarlet may gleam, and blue and purple may likewise shine with their lovely colours, skins and haircloths above bear the rain, winds, and dust.

Those, therefore, who advance in great virtues within the bosom of holy Church ought not to despise the life of their superiors when they see them occupied with outward matters. For their own secure penetration of inward things depends upon the aid of those who labour outwardly against the storms of this age. Yet by the coverings which shield linen, purple, blue, and scarlet from injury by storms, wealthy secular people in the Church may be understood: they provide from their means the necessities of life for saints, or for those serving God under a holy rule, so that they may have no necessity to wander outside—which is not expedient for their souls—and do so for the redemption of their sins.

Hence there are eleven coverings and they are of haircloth: because, as they themselves do not deny, they have transgressed the commandments of the Decalogue and thus stand, as it were, within the number eleven; but desiring to produce fruits worthy of repentance, signified by haircloth, they protect the tabernacle, as was said. The number thirty cubits in length, the number of married persons—as sixty is of widows and one hundred of virgins—also agrees well with this interpretation.

But according to the letter, or the visible construction of the tabernacle, the following words immediately explain why there are eleven coverings and why they exceed the curtains’ length by two cubits: “You shall join five separately, and six together, so that you double the sixth covering at the front of the roof.” And shortly thereafter: “What remains of the coverings prepared for the roof—namely, the one covering which is extra—you shall cover the back of the tabernacle with half of it.” Half a covering is two cubits in breadth, since its breadth is four cubits. Thus a single covering was not to be divided from top to bottom, with one part doubled at the front of the roof and the remainder covering the back of the tabernacle. Certainly not. Rather, since there are only ten curtains beneath the extended covering of eleven haircloth coverings, four cubits remain over—the breadth of one covering. Thus the extension of the joined coverings was to be arranged so that two cubits hung down at the front and, folded back, were doubled; while another two were similarly let down to protect the back of the tabernacle. Likewise, the two cubits remaining in the length of the coverings beyond the length of the curtains were distributed over each side of the tabernacle. For he says: “A cubit shall hang down on one side, and another on the other—the excess in the length of the coverings—protecting both sides of the tabernacle.”

All this is mystically referred to the interpretation stated above: the life of spiritual persons, if it is to be tranquil, as is signified by the beauty of the curtains, needs support in every direction from secular believers. Here it must not be passed over that the coverings were made from goats’ hair. Hence Scripture later says: “Bezalel therefore made eleven coverings of goats’ hair to cover the roof of the tabernacle” (Exod. XXXVI). “You shall make fifty loops in the manner of one covering,” etc., as above, except that neither the loops are called blue nor the clasps golden, but bronze. This is because believers who live in the world, or through whose support the outward life of spiritual persons is aided, are strengthened by the same love, though they do not shine with the same brilliance of heavenly wisdom.

“You shall make another covering for the roof from red-dyed rams’ skins, and over this again another covering from blue skins.” A red or blue colour belongs to rams’ skins not by nature but by craftsmanship. These fittingly signify the faithful harmony of secular persons, who do not themselves possess an abundance of virtues in action, but possess it by loving those in whom it exists. Thus, after the Psalm had said, “Pray for the things that make for the peace of Jerusalem” (Ps. CXXI), it immediately adds: “and abundance for those who love you” (ibid.). Jerusalem—that is, any holy soul that seeks its peace and sees God by contemplation—abounds in spiritual goods. But one who is not established in the same vocation, yet loves another advancing in this way, also enjoys abundance together with that same Jerusalem. And according to the literal sense, it should be noted that the cheaper or less laboriously made things are placed higher in the tabernacle and closer to the weather: after the curtains come haircloth coverings, then red-dyed rams’ skins, and then blue skins.

## CHAPTER XII. On the upright boards of the tabernacle, their joining and bases, and the bars which hold them: what these signify spiritually.

“You shall also make upright boards for the tabernacle, of shittim wood, each ten cubits long and one cubit and a half broad.” The upright boards in the tabernacle signify the prelates who hold precedence in the Church: adorned with simplicity, secure in prudence, provident in secular matters, and thoughtful in divine things. For in boards there is neither beauty joined with softness, as in curtains, nor protection joined with roughness, as in haircloth coverings. They therefore rightly signify prelates, who ought neither to neglect care for their subjects because of their love for heavenly things, nor to neglect contemplation of heavenly things because of temporal care for their subjects.

Yet their rest in contemplation is diminished by the effort of activity. Hence they rightly have ten cubits in length without diminution, but only one cubit and a half in breadth. What falls short to a half does not signify the fullness of completeness or entirety. “Two mortises shall be made in the sides of each board, by which one board is joined to another.” The joining of the boards is the bond of charity necessary for governors of churches, so that what the Apostle said may come to pass: “that you all say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you” (I Cor. I).

“There shall be twenty,” he says, “on the south side, and similarly on the second side, which faces north.” Since the boards stand upright and are each one cubit and a half broad, each row of boards is plainly thirty cubits long; it does not reach the extent of the roof stretched above, which extends forty cubits in length according to the number or spread of the ten curtains, each four cubits broad. The two bases placed under each board are the foundations of the apostles and prophets (Eph. II), upon whose faith or authority the entire fabric of the spiritual building rests. They are called silver. For what is signified by the silver bases of the boards but the prophetic words of faith? When the prophets first spoke openly of the Lord’s incarnation, we see them as bases rising from the foundation and sustaining the weight of the structure placed above them.

Thus two joined bases are set beneath each board, because when the holy prophets agree in their words concerning the incarnation of the Mediator, subsequent preachers build the Church without hesitation; and, because they do not disagree among themselves, they fix it more firmly. Nor without reason are the bases ordered to be cast from silver. The nature of silver is preserved through use; without use it turns black. Likewise, the sayings of the prophets before the coming of the Mediator remained, as it were, black, because they were not in use for spiritual understanding and could not be perceived on account of obscurity. But after the Mediator came and set them before our eyes by his incarnation, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth; he made the understanding of the fathers who went before available for use, because he expounded words by deeds.

“On the western side of the tabernacle,” he says, “you shall make six boards, and again two others which shall be raised at the corners behind the back of the tabernacle. Thus there shall be eight boards together.” By the eight boards placed on the western side we rightly understand the eight beatitudes that will follow the end of this present life for those who deserve them. “For the two boards,” he says, “which are to be placed at the corners, the same joining shall be kept,” because the first and eighth beatitudes retain the same place of glory, namely, the promise of the kingdom of heaven. Two bases are likewise placed beneath each of these boards, because the hope of these beatitudes is assured by prophetic as well as evangelical or apostolic faith.

According to the historical arrangement, however, what purpose should we suppose the two boards raised at the corners behind the back of the tabernacle serve except ornament? “You shall also make five bars of shittim wood to hold the boards on one side of the tabernacle, and five others on the other side, and the same number on the western side,” etc. The boards are supported by the double strength of bases and bars so that they may stand. Thus the rulers of the Church—the apostles or apostolic men—need support both from spiritual and from carnal persons. As the bases signify prophetic utterances, by whose authority they sow spiritual things, so the bars fittingly represent the support of the rich and powerful, from whose abundance they reap material things.

These bars are themselves clothed with gold equally with the boards, because powerful people of this world, who are inserted through golden rings into the boards, as it were, to hold them firm—by supplying necessities to preachers of the faith in communion with that same faith—are rightly believed to be rewarded with the same reward. “He who receives a prophet,” says the Lord, “in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive a righteous man’s reward” (Matt. X). The bars are rightly commanded to extend along each side, and in the same number along the western side, because carnal people, insofar as they are rich in this world, are occupied chiefly with the five bodily senses and with matters transacted through them.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the tabernacle and the veil dividing the first from the second, called the Holy of Holies; and how the Apostle says its position and rite were a parable.

“You shall make a veil of blue and purple, twice-dyed scarlet and fine twisted linen, woven in embroidered work and beautiful variety; you shall hang it before four pillars of shittim wood,” etc. Thus far the discourse has moved swiftly through the construction of the tabernacle; now at last we must return to the chapter of the Apostle mentioned above. “The first tabernacle was made,” he says, “in which were the lampstands, the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place. But behind the second veil was the tabernacle called the Holy of Holies” (Heb. IX), etc.

The veil which he mentions there is this one concerning which the Lord speaks here: “You shall make a veil,” he says, “of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, in embroidered work,” etc. The Apostle’s words, “behind the veil, the second tabernacle called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, and above it the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat,” are the same as what is said here: “You shall place the ark of testimony within the veil; it shall divide the sanctuary from the Holy of Holies. You shall place the mercy-seat upon the ark of testimony in the Holy of Holies.”

What the same Apostle says was in the first tabernacle—“the lampstands, the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place”—is what is here added: “You shall place the table outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite the table.” He continues: “You shall also make a curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle, of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, in embroidered work; and you shall overlay five pillars of shittim wood with gold, before which the curtain shall be drawn. Their tops shall be golden and their bases bronze.”

Thus the table, the setting forth of the loaves, and the lampstand stood between the two veils; but the ark and mercy-seat, with the two cherubim, stood beyond the second veil. It continues further:

(CAP. XXVII.) “You shall make an altar of shittim wood, five cubits long and equally wide—that is, square—and three cubits high.” Thus this threefold arrangement must be carefully distinguished. First, as was said above, the altar of sacrifices confronted the person entering. Then, after passing the first veil, came the first tabernacle, in which were the table and lampstand. After passing the second veil came the second tabernacle, in which were the ark and the cherubim overshadowing the mercy-seat.

Perhaps someone may ask what the mercy-seat was. Certainly, since the Lord commanded it to be made of gold, and Scripture states its length and breadth to be the same as those of the ark itself, but says nothing of its height, it should be understood as a golden slab of such dimensions that the ark could be covered by it. “When these things had thus been arranged, priests always entered the first tabernacle to perform the duties of sacrifices. But into the second the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people” (Heb. II), the Holy Spirit signifying by this that the way of the holy ones had not yet been revealed, etc. Let us therefore briefly examine, with his help, this parabolic signification of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIV. What the second tabernacle is mystically, and what the elements of its structure signify.

The second tabernacle, in which was the ark and above it the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat, mystically signifies that tabernacle into which Jesus entered: not one made by hands, not holy things that are copies of the true, but heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us (Heb. IX). For in that the high priest alone entered once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people, the Holy Spirit signified that now Christ, once at the consummation of the ages, appeared to abolish sin through his sacrifice; once offered to take away the sins of many, he will appear a second time without sin for the salvation through faith of those who await him (ibid.).

The four pillars made there, having silver bases and golden tops, prefigured the four Gospels, which harmoniously testify to the foretold entry of Christ the high priest. Because their teaching accords with prophetic truth and proclaims the true humanity and the glorious divinity of the one and same Christ, they truly have silver bases and golden tops. The veil hangs before them because we do not yet see him “as he is” (I John III). “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (II Cor. V). By faith we hold that there is the mercy-seat, Jesus Christ, “who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. VIII). Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “For with you there is propitiation” (Ps. CXXIX).

The censer also is there: namely, the most sweet remembrance of our reconciliation, in the wounds’ scars which continually appear, scars which the Son of God bore for us in our flesh. There is the true ark: namely, the substance of our flesh, taken from the Virgin and suspended on the cross, not at all consumed by the power of the resurrection, but changed only into the glory of immortality and incorruption. It contains the rod, the manna, and the tablets of the covenant. The rod is the Father’s authority over all things, concerning which he says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). The manna is the sweetness of grace: “God raised him up and exalted him as Prince and Saviour,” says the Apostle Peter, immediately adding, “to give repentance and remission of sins” (Acts V). The tablets of the covenant are the book of judgment, of which Daniel says: “The court sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII). For judgment will concern those things written in the books of the covenant, and every person’s conscience will be opened.

Nor are the two cherubim absent there, through which we understand the things preached to us through the two Testaments: mercy and judgment. For “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV). They look upon one another with faces turned toward the mercy-seat, and the whole matter rests on this: “mercy triumphs over judgment” (Jas. II). We hold all these things by faith and do not yet see them by sight; therefore the veil rightly hangs before the pillars.

## CHAPTER XV. On the first tabernacle, which signifies the present Church; what the table and lampstand signify in it, what the five pillars signify, and what the veil hanging before them signifies.

The tabernacle which is second in the description but first in the order of entry, as the Apostle says (Heb. IX), signifies the present Church. There is a table there, and opposite the table a lampstand. Indeed, in this Church—or rather, in this pilgrimage and temporal tabernacle of the Church—there is the Lord’s table, prepared for those labouring in the contest of struggle, a table of twofold refreshment. For here the bread is set forth: that is, Holy Scripture, which refreshes the mind with the great abundance of God’s word; and the bread of his body and the cup of blood, which the Christian receives from the holy altar as profitable to himself for eternal life.

Here also is the lampstand, shining for those who worthily share the feast: namely, Christ, who says, “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Once, as a testimony to his power, this lampstand visibly displayed the flame of its lamps, when, having already been assumed into heaven, he openly showed the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire, by whom he enlightened the apostles (Acts II).

It should be noted that the Lord commanded the table to stand on the north side and the lampstand on the south side of the tabernacle (Exod. XXVI). For to us, who were the northern portion—that is, the kingdom of the devil—cold in unbelief and alienated from God, the table of the Lord was extended; and God placed the southern lampstand of grace against our darkness, so that, eating and drinking and walking together in the light, we might sing: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture” (Ps. XXII). Again: “For even if I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me” (ibid.).

The five pillars at the entrance of this tabernacle are the five books of Moses, bearing testimony to the present Church. The bronze bases of the pillars signify the lowly literal learning of Mosaic Scripture. Their golden tops signify the surpassing glory of spiritual understanding. Those who are little in understanding can reach only the bronze bases—that is, they can read only the not very noble letter; but those who have become mature by progress reach the gold, that is, the tops of the pillars, when, neglecting the killing letter, they stretch out toward the life-giving Spirit (II Cor. III). The veil hanging before the pillars is the veil which has indeed been torn for us in Christ’s passion, but has been placed over the hearts of the Jews. Therefore they do not enter with us, because, hindered by the veil, they do not deserve to see the gold shining in the pillars—that is, in the books of Moses.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the altar placed outside, which signified the temporal ministry of the Jews.

The altar placed outside is the ministry of the Jews: holy indeed before Christ, who was promised through it, came; but now, since he has entered the Holy of Holies, it has been rejected together with its ministers, who do not follow him, and cast aside as unclean. It formerly had ordinances of worship and a worldly sanctuary, but it could not “make perfect in conscience the worshipper, consisting only in foods and drinks and various washings and bodily ordinances imposed until the time of correction” (Heb. IX). But now, since the time of correction has come, it not only cannot make one serving in those things perfect, but is not even the beginning of any good. Indeed, with the Apostle it must be reckoned a loss and cast aside as dung (Phil. III).

Therefore, having entered the court of the patriarchs, we confidently pass by that altar and enter beyond the veil, despising the bronze bases of the pillars and gladly beholding their golden tops: that is, leaving the killing letter of the Law and embracing the life-giving Spirit. From there we faithfully approach the Lord’s table, where neither bulls’ flesh is sacrificed nor goats’ blood drunk, but the bread of eternal life, which is Christ’s body, is set forth, and the cup of everlasting salvation, which is the blood of that same Christ, Son of God, is poured out—until at last we enter that heavenly sanctuary, to which Christ himself, our forerunner, has gone before us.

## CHAPTER XVII. Through the court of the tabernacle with its pegs, and its pillars with their bases and tops, the faith or life of the fathers before the Law is mystically understood.

The court of the tabernacle signifies the breadth and manner of life of the patriarchs and all the saints who lived before the Law, not yet constrained by the Scripture of the Law. The bronze pegs set around it signify nothing other than the faith of the patriarchs, without which neither court nor tabernacle can stand or be holy.

“One side shall extend one hundred cubits in length toward the south; likewise, on the northern side, curtains one hundred cubits long; but in breadth toward the west, fifty cubits; likewise toward the east, curtains fifty cubits wide.” The number one hundred in length is the third square unity, for ten times ten makes one hundred. It signifies the patient faith and patient hope of the patriarchs, constant everywhere, in adversity and prosperity alike, after the manner of a square stone. The Apostle measures their patience with devout reflection: “All these died according to faith,” he says, “not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” (Heb. XI). They are therefore the founders of the true tabernacle of which this is the pattern. Hence the same Apostle immediately says: “For those who say these things show that they seek a country” (ibid.). And shortly before: “They awaited,” he says, “a city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (ibid.).

Thus, since those fathers dwelt in tents or huts because of their hope for the future city, the heavenly tabernacle, compacted from virtues, of which this pattern made by Moses is an image, existed first in them. The breadth of fifty cubits is half the aforementioned length and, by that very number fifty, prefigures the coming Jubilee. For through the breadth of charity Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob received, in the promise, Jubilee—that is, remission of sins through Christ—and the blessing of all nations.

The number of sixty pillars pertains to their perfection. For there are twenty on the southern side, likewise twenty on the northern side, and ten pillars in the western width—[Note: Col. 0717D: “I think it should be added: and an equal number on the eastern side.”]—making sixty. This number, composed of six and ten, fittingly signifies the perfection of those fathers, who, though they did not possess the written Law, nevertheless laudably fulfilled the Decalogue of the Law well and perfectly through their actions.

Nevertheless, all the pillars of the court, having bronze bases and silver tops, were less distinguished than all those in the tabernacle. Yet discerning minds should not consider the ancient fathers before the Law contemptible because they committed certain acts which the Law later prohibited: for example, because Abraham, though he had Sarah as his wife, fathered a son by the concubine Hagar; or because Jacob married two sisters at once. In this respect the pillars are indeed less beautiful—for such conduct is not to be drawn into imitation—but they are sufficiently excused because none of these things had yet been prohibited by Law.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That the entrance of the tabernacle was from only one side, namely the east; whereas the holy Trinity itself, which we read of in the Apocalypse, has three gates on each of four sides.

“In the length of the court which faces east there shall be fifty cubits, of which hangings of fifteen cubits shall be assigned to one side, with three pillars and as many bases.” The literal sense is clear: from the east the entrance into the court, and thence into the tabernacle, extends through fifteen cubits and three pillars on either side. And in this the rationale of the pattern, or of the heavenly things, seems to fail. For where the Spirit speaks manifestly of heavenly things, introducing the matter thus: “And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, having the glory of God” (Rev. 21), [Col. 0718B] shortly afterwards it adds: “On the east three gates, on the north three gates, on the south three gates, and on the west three gates” (ibid.). Here, however, the entrance stands open from the east alone, through four pillars. For it continues: “At the entrance of the court there shall be a hanging of twenty cubits. It shall have four pillars with four bases.” Add to this that, when the entrance is taken from the east, the face of one entering looks toward the west, by which nothing good is signified.

Therefore, since both the altar, which is first reached through that entrance, and its whole order were to become obsolete and grow old and perish, its position inclined toward the west. Nor ought we to wonder at the differing gates: namely, that in this typical and shadowy tabernacle the entrance lay open from one side, through four [Col. 0718C] pillars, having a veil five cubits high; whereas into the heavenly holy places themselves, of which this was the pattern, the same opportunity of entering is offered from the four quarters of the world through three gates, as was said above. For that people which used this pattern presumes righteousness from works of the Law; but the calling of all the nations, which tends toward the true and heavenly holy places, seeks righteousness by faith alone, receiving the baptism of Christ who calls in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XIX. That the city of God does not need the lamp of the Scriptures; and that for this reason the lamp was commanded to burn not within, but outside, the veil.

“Command the children of Israel that they bring you oil from [Col. 0718D] olive trees, very pure and beaten with a pestle, so that a lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of testimony outside the veil which is spread before the Testimony; and Aaron and the children of Israel shall set it up, that it may give light before the Lord until morning.”

One might suppose that in that which was more sacred—the second tabernacle—the lamp ought continually to burn beside the veil in perpetual service. What, then, but a mystery is set forth in this rite also: namely, that in those holy places not made with hands, into which Jesus entered once for all, there is no need of a lamp? For John says thus in the Apocalypse concerning that holy and eternal city: “For the glory of God [Col. 0719A] shall illumine it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

Therefore let the lamp always burn outside the veil in the former tabernacle, before the Lord until morning, in perpetual service: that is, in the present Church let every believer shine with the grace of the Holy Spirit which he possesses, so that people may see their good works and thereby open their eyes to glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5). For this intention of charity is the very pure oil beaten with a pestle: that is, willingly pressed down by labours for the edification of neighbours. “Aaron and his sons,” he says, “shall set it up”: namely, those who are lawful priests of the Lord by right of succession. Indeed, to devote oneself to true charity and, in good works, to seek not one’s own glory but God’s, is precisely what it is to be a priest worthy and lawful before God. Paul admonished his beloved disciple to set up such a lamp when he said: “For this reason I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Tim. 1).—“Let it burn,” he says, “until morning”: that is, until the end of the present life. For on that day we shall not need the light of a lamp, when “as He is” (1 John 3)—“we shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XX. On priestly garments.

(CH. 28.) “Bring near to yourself Aaron your brother, with his sons, from among the children of Israel, that they may minister to me in the priesthood: Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. And you shall make a holy garment for your brother, [Col. 0719C] for glory and beauty. And you shall speak to all who are wise of heart, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they may make Aaron’s garments, in which he may minister to me when sanctified,” etc.

We come to the priestly vestments. First they must be explained simply according to the Jewish manner, and then their mystical meaning must be examined individually. They are not described here in the order in which they are put on the priest. For the linen breeches, by which the shamefulness of the flesh is first covered, are placed last in this description; while, conversely, the breastpiece, than which there was nothing holier among the garments except the golden plate to be bound upon the high priest’s forehead, is designated first. For he says: “These shall be the garments which they shall make: the breastpiece and the ephod, the linen tunic, the close-fitting tunic, the turban, [Col. 0719D] and the belt.” And after much else: “You shall also make,” he says, “linen breeches, to cover the flesh of their nakedness,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXI. How the Hebrews interpret the four colours—blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen—and on the weaving of the ephod and breastpiece.

“They shall make the ephod of gold, and blue, and purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, in embroidered work.” The Hebrews refer the four colours so often combined in this Scripture to the four elements from which all things subsist. Fine linen, they say, is assigned to earth because it grows from the earth; purple to the sea, because it is dyed from its shellfish; blue to air, because of the resemblance of its colour; scarlet to fire and ether. They recall that it is fitting that the high priest pray to the Creator not only for Israel but for the whole world. For this world consists of earth, water, air, and fire, and these elements belong to all things.

“You shall make the ephod of gold and blue and purple and twice-dyed scarlet and twisted fine linen, in embroidered work.” Let us understand that this is a garment of the high priest, called *ephod* among the Hebrews. For one must not immediately think of that ephod which Samuel, though a Levite, is written in the First Book of Kings to have worn while still a very small child (1 Sam. 2)—that is, a linen ephod—nor of the same garment which David is reported to have worn before the ark of the Lord (2 Sam. 6). For one thing is to have a garment woven from the four aforementioned colours—blue, fine linen, [Col. 0720B] purple, and scarlet—and from gold; another is to have a simple linen garment in imitation of priests.

“It shall have two joined edges at both sides of its upper parts, that they may be joined together into one; and the very weaving and all the variety of the work shall be of gold and blue,” etc. Plates of gold, he says—that is, thin leaves—are beaten into astonishing fineness; from these are cut threads, twisted beneath a covering of the three colours, blue, scarlet, and purple, together with a linen warp. Thus is made a little cloak of remarkable beauty, dazzling the eyes with its brightness like the garments called *caracallae*, but without hoods; it is to have joined edges at both sides of its upper parts, that they may come together into one.

“And you shall take twelve onyx stones and engrave upon them the names of the children of Israel: six names on one stone and [Col. 0720C] six on the other.” Thus, when the high priest enters the Holy of Holies, he bears upon his shoulders the names of the people for whom he is to pray to the Lord. This, indeed, is what follows: “And you shall set them on both sides of the ephod as a memorial for the children of Israel; and Aaron shall bear their names before the Lord upon both shoulders for remembrance. You shall also make the breastpiece of judgment in embroidered work, according to the weaving of the ephod,” etc.

The surface meaning of the text is clear; and for those wishing to know the arrangement of all the items—the ephod, the breastpiece, the blue tunic with bells and golden pomegranates, the linen tunic and belt, the tiara, and, holiest of all, the golden plate hanging over the high priest’s forehead from the tiara—the literal description is readily available. We cannot set forth a clearer description than it gives. We therefore now add the mystical explanations of the individual items as they have been handed down by the Fathers: first according to the Hebrews, then according to ecclesiastical writers.

## CHAPTER XXII. What the Hebrews have handed down mystically concerning each of the garments.

First, they say, the linen garment signifies earth; the second, blue garment signifies air, displaying this in its colour, because we are gradually raised from earthly things to lofty ones. The blue garment itself, extending from the head down to the ankles, signifies the air poured out from heaven to earth. The pomegranates and bells placed on its lower parts signify lightning and thunder; or earth and water, and the mutual harmony of all the elements, all things being so interwoven with one another that in each individual thing all the others are found.

That the aforementioned colours are interwoven with gold, they wish to signify that the colour of life and the providence of divine intelligence penetrate all things. They interpret the ephod and the two stones—whether emeralds or onyxes—which are above and cover either shoulder, as the two hemispheres, one above the earth and the other beneath the earth; or as the sun and moon, which shine above. They interpret the belt by which the priest’s breast and linen tunic—that is, the earth—are bound as the Ocean. They expound the breastpiece set in the middle as the earth, which, like a point, although [Col. 0721B] it contains all things within itself, is nevertheless surrounded by all the elements.

They interpret the twelve stones either as the circle of the zodiac or as the twelve months; and by the individual rows they bind individual seasons, assigning three months to each. Nor should this seem an exposition belonging to some pagan people. For because heavenly things and God’s ordering have been disgraced by the names of idols, God’s providence—which moves by a fixed law, proceeds, and governs all things—must not therefore be denied. For in Job we also read of Arcturus, Orion, and Mazzaroth (Job 9), that is, the circle of the zodiac, and of other names of stars; not because the same terms exist among the Hebrews, but because we cannot understand what is said except by familiar terms.

Moreover, that which is in the middle is fittingly called the breastpiece (*rationale*). For all things are full of reason, and earthly things adhere to heavenly ones; indeed, the order of earthly things and of seasons, heat and cold, and the twofold moderation between them descends from the course and rational order of heaven. Hence the breastpiece is bound more firmly to the ephod. But when it is said, “You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth,” this signifies that there is never falsehood in God’s ordering; rather, truth itself is shown to human beings by many signs and arguments and comes even to mortals. Hence it has come about that we know the order of sun and moon, year, months, seasons, and hours; likewise the conditions of calm weather and winds and of all things, receiving from God implanted wisdom, from Him who dwells in and teaches His own dwelling-place, [Col. 0721D] and who shows us knowledge of its structure.

Above all, the turban and blue band signify heaven, and the gold plate which is on the high priest’s forehead, together with the name of God inscribed upon it, signifies that all things below are governed by God’s will. We judge that the same thing is represented under other names in the cherubim and the four living creatures, which are so blended and joined that the others are found in each one; and that they go steadily forward and do not turn back. For times glide away, leaving the past behind and hastening toward the future. That they are always in motion signifies what philosophers also suppose: that the world runs in its own order and is ceaselessly turned, like a wheel, in its course (Ezek. 1). Hence there is a wheel within a wheel: that is, times within time; the year returns into itself; the wheels themselves are raised to heaven; above the crystal is a throne of sapphire; and above the throne is the likeness of one seated, whose lower parts are fiery and upper parts electrum-like, to show that lower things need fire and purification, whereas things above remain in the purity of their created condition. And just as the priest’s attire has a gold plate above, so Ezekiel places electrum in the breast and at the summit (ibid.).

It was therefore fitting, as we said above in part, that the high priest of God, bearing in his garments a type of all creatures, should indicate that all things need God’s mercy, and that when sacrifice was offered to Him, the whole creation might be expiated: so that he should pray, both in voice and in dress, not for children, parents, and kinsfolk alone, but for every creature.

[Col. 0722B] Concerning the linen breeches they are accustomed to say this: the principle of seed and generation, belonging to the flesh, is through it assigned to earth. Hence God says to Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). And the causes of this matter—how from a tiny seed and most foul beginnings such great beauty of human beings or diverse things arises—are veiled and do not lie open to human eyes.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Jesus Christ the great High Priest, and on understanding his spiritual garment mystically through Aaron’s vestments.

The Hebrews, indeed, skilled in the Law not so much by God’s Spirit as by their own spirit or ingenuity, and ignorant of the heavenly things according to whose pattern these things also were commanded to be made—as the Lord repeatedly says, “You shall make it according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain”—have set forth such an interpretation of the priestly garments. But we, who believe by faith in the heavenly things spoken of and now know them in part by knowledge, interpret these same things more deeply.

Let us behold one great High Priest, Jesus Christ, the heavenly and true High Priest, in whose heavenly attire we do not doubt that these things have been fulfilled, and whom we too must imitate, so that we may be a royal priesthood and a holy nation. The linen breeches of the great High Priest signify the beauty of the holy incarnation of Christ, the Son of God, by which our ignoble nature was adorned beforehand; and the wound of original sin, unhappily covered in Adam by fig leaves, was excluded in him. For he, unlike us, was not conceived through ulcerous lust, [Col. 0722D] but from a pure and simple virgin; he put on twisted fine linen—that is, the beauty and strength of a white and undefiled body—and thus covered the shamefulness of his body, which is the Church, namely original sin.

Of this garment John says in the Apocalypse: “He has written on his garment and on his thigh, King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19). Next, the close-fitting linen tunic—that is, the undergarment, commonly called a shirt (*camisia*)—is the new life of that same heavenly man; because, just as he was conceived and born in a new and unprecedented manner, so he lived among men with a beauty new and contrary to the old way of life. The belt about the loins is the strength of the Godhead, by which he could not be moved. Hence, after saying in the Psalm, “Moreover, even unto [Col. 0723A] night my loins rebuked me” (Ps. 15), he immediately adds: “I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved.”

For he so knew our frailty, and his loins rebuked him even to night—that is, unto the tribulation of death—that he knew by experience that, although he was never in any passible manner stirred by temptation, this was not due to the nature of the flesh itself but to the Godhead which was at his right hand. Hence the Apostle says most truly: “For we do not have a High Priest unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one tempted in all things according to our likeness, without sin” (Heb. 9). Finally, he learned from this to sympathize with our weaknesses whenever we are tempted by our loins, because he was tempted by other weaknesses as he would have been tempted by the temptation of sin, had he not been God—which we are not.

The blue tunic with bells and pomegranates is the glorious life or conduct of our same High Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ, from John’s baptism onward. From then on he began to resound with bells—that is, to sound forth through open and public preaching—with pomegranates flashing between them, that is, works of miracles accompanying almost every word. The very blue colour of the tunic expresses the heavenly dignity of those works. Hence it is said in the Song of Songs: “His hands are rounded, golden, full of blue” (Song 5). There the works are signified in his hands, here in his garment, by the blue, airy colour, as has been said, of him [Col. 0723C] who is not from earth nor speaks from earth, but comes from heaven and is above all.

And fittingly the red pomegranates hang round the lower edge of the tunic at the feet, while the bells ring at the entrance of the sanctuary, because especially at the end of his mortal life the Redeemer’s active love and teaching shone forth. “For,” says the Evangelist, “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end also” (John 13). The whole world heard the bells, that is, the precepts of love with which he resounded at that supper; and the whole world received the red pomegranates, namely the fruit of eternal life, from his entrance into the heavenly sanctuary.

The ephod of this High Priest is the obedience of charity, because Christ himself, the Son of God, placed his shoulders beneath our sins in order to bear them—indeed, to take them away—and ascended to the cross with them. For “the Lord,” says the Prophet, “placed upon him the iniquities of us all” (Ps. 53). And rightly the ephod had to be made from the four aforesaid colours, corresponding to the four elements of the world, and interwoven with gold; because “he is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John), by a charity not compelled but voluntary, which surpasses the other virtues as gold excels other metals.

The two joined edges, and the individual onyx stones on each shoulder, inscribed with the names of the twelve sons of Israel, are the two peoples, separated in time but joined in cause or sacrament, whose sins Christ bore in his body. For neither could be saved except by Christ’s grace, and each needed Christ, the one and same bearer of sins. And rightly these are onyx stones, a kind of gem or stone having the colour of a human fingernail, from which it has received its name—for the Greeks call a fingernail *onyx*. Rightly, I say, because for human beings God became human, burdened with the ephod of sins. Stones of this kind are inscribed with the names of the sons of Israel, that is, of all the elect: for he knows by name all whose sins he bore upon himself. Thus, as he drew near to the hour of his passion, he said: “I know whom I have chosen” (John 13).

“You shall engrave them,” he says, “according to the order of their birth.” Therefore all the elder sons are written on one stone, all the younger on the other. The elder sons of Israel are those enrolled before the younger ones, who were enrolled after the advent of this strong-shouldered bearer of sins. The elders, I say, are those from the Jews; the younger are those from the nations. For God speaks of that people to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4).

The breastpiece, then, is joined to the ephod because mercy and truth have met one another. Mercy is understood in the ephod; truth in the breastpiece. Hence it is called the breastpiece of judgment, and doctrine and truth are inscribed upon it. For he who redeemed in mercy will himself judge in truth (Isa. 84). Thus the names of all the sons of Israel are not inscribed upon one or two onyx stones in the breastpiece, as they are in the ephod, but individually upon individual stones. For Christ redeemed all by one grace [Col. 0724C] and bore the sins of all upon his shoulders; but in judgment “he will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2). Nor will all the elect have the same rewards, but rewards differing according to their differing merits. “For,” he says, “there are many dwelling places in my Father’s house” (John 14). The manifold and distinct arrangement of precious stones indicates the multitude of heavenly dwelling places. Indeed, in Ezekiel, against the prince of Tyre, nine orders of angels are indicated by nine names of stones (Ezek. 28).

It should be noted that on the ephod there are not only chains but also hooks to bind the breastpiece of judgment, because in the Redeemer’s mercy lie the anchors of our hope, so that mercy may always triumph over [Col. 0724D] judgment. The High Priest bears this on his breast, for in his presence he has all persons inscribed and has prepared from the beginning of the world dwelling places suited to the merits of all.

The High Priest also receives the turban upon his head, lest Cerinthus or Arius, or any other heretic, suppose that he has seen the head of Jesus Christ the Son of God—that is, his beginning. For he did not, as we do, have the beginning of his existence from flesh, according to the blasphemy of Cerinthus, who denied that he existed before Mary; rather, he conceals there the divine Head which was in the beginning and before the ages. Therefore the turban covers the High Priest’s head because the antiquity or origin of Christ’s divinity is incomprehensible.

The golden plate hanging over the forehead is the crown of glory and honour upon the Redeemer’s head. “You have crowned him,” he says, “with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8). And after the Apostle had said, “Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2), he immediately adds: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name.”

The mystery of this—the name which is above every name—lies in the fact that “Holy of the Lord” is inscribed upon the plate: that is, the Tetragrammaton name of the Lord, which they call ineffable. It is written with four letters, Joth, He, Vau, He, which cannot be gathered into a syllable or articulated sound. The secret of this writing has remained hidden until now, except insofar as it may be gathered from the interpretation of the letters, which greatly delights evangelical faith. For Joth is interpreted “beginning,” He “this one,” Vau and He “this one.” The continuous sense of the letters is: “Beginning, this one and this one.” This, I say, rightly delights us, because this one, the Father, is beginning, and this one, the Son, is beginning. Whoever sees that the Father is beginning readily agrees. The Son also asserts that he is beginning, because when the Jews asked him, “Who are you?” he said: “The Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). This name is surely above every name, because nothing can be above beginning.

Therefore the eighth adornment of the High Priest is the golden plate, bearing the inscribed ineffable name, which is called “Holy of the Lord,” because the Father gave Christ the High Priest, crowned with the glory of his eighth day—that is, his resurrection—on account of his passion and death, “the name which is above [Col. 0725C] every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

We pass over the moral adornment of Aaron’s sons, that is, of Christ’s priests, as they strive to make progress; for it is found in its proper places, as the Fathers have expounded it. And the matters subsequently commanded to Moses by the Lord, who says: “But this also you shall do, that they may be consecrated to me in the priesthood: take a bullock from the herd and two unblemished rams” (CH. 29), etc.—because they are here commanded and then recounted as performed in Leviticus—we defer for the present; for they will be more suitably discussed there.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the calf made by the children of Israel, who also exchanged the truth of God for a lie.

(CH. 32.) “When the people saw that Moses delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered against Aaron and said: Rise, make us gods to go before us; for as to this man Moses, who led us out from the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him,” etc.

The event is plain: they quickly acted—or rather, quickly fell away—by making a calf and worshipping a carved image. And what is most astonishing, they “exchanged their great glory for the likeness of a calf eating grass” (Ps. 10). The Lord himself, as though astonished at the swiftness of their falling away, says: “They have quickly departed from the way which I showed them, and have made for themselves a molten calf.”

Therefore let every mouth of the Jews be stopped no less than that of the Greeks (Rom. 2), for they too exchanged the truth of God for a lie. For they said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” By saying this, I say, they changed the truth of God into a lie and served the creature rather than the Creator—namely, with the slavery of sin. Thus Scripture says: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” In the glory of the likeness of a calf eating grass they ate and drank; and therefore they immediately vomited themselves forth into obscene games, given over to a reprobate mind to do what was unfitting, and so received in themselves the due recompense for their error.

Therefore, as the Apostle testifies, the boasting of the Jews is excluded, lest he insult the Greek (Rom. 2) because he served the creature; for, what is graver, he himself also served it in transgression. For he had the Law, and the word of God, as though gold, still glowed fresh from the fire. A little earlier Moses had read the “book of the covenant” in the hearing of the people; and they said: “All that the Lord has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient” (Exod. 24). By this act they had certainly hung golden earrings upon their inward ears. “But he sprinkled the blood which he had taken upon the people and said: This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you” (ibid.). Thus they had sworn a nuptial union to the one God, their husband, and, as has been said, had faces adorned with the earrings of his commandments.

But now they took “gold earrings from the ears of their wives and their sons and daughters,” fashioned them in cast work, and made from them “a molten calf.” With the same feet by which they had crossed the sea, they danced before such an image; and the truth they had sung, saying, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he cast into the sea” (Exod. 15), they exchanged for a lie by singing: “These are your gods, Israel, who led you out of the land of Egypt.”
