Therefore the Jew who judges the Greek fleeing to the grace of God for former sins is inexcusable (Rom. 2), for he has done the same things he judges. And whenever the rod of that tutor was withdrawn from him even a little, the foolish child returned to the same or similar crimes of idolatry.

## CHAPTER XXV. That God did not say in vain, “Let me be, that my wrath may be kindled,” etc.; and that it has now truly come to pass thus.

In this crime the foreshadowing of the present Jewish confusion and disgrace is readily recognized. For just as then they cast the beauty or ornament of their ears—the golden earrings—into the making of the calf, and, abandoning truth, worshipped falsehood, so it was to come about that they would exchange the golden truth of the Law and Prophets for the lie which they now practise, holding the sacred books in their hands and fashioning blasphemies against Christ with viperous tongues. Foreseeing this already, the Lord said to Moses: “I see that this people is stiff-necked. Let me be, that my wrath may be kindled against [Col. 0727A] them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation.”

What Moses did is briefly suggested here by the report that God said, “Let me be.” But the Psalmist expresses it more strongly: “And he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen one stood in the breach before him” (Ps. 105). By the exceeding humility of “the breach” he signifies that Moses restrained God. For a breach is the exceeding humility of heart, which alone is a strong and powerful thing before Almighty God and the Lord, the prince of all strength, so that when it is exerted God is, as it were, unable to stretch out his arm to strike: the queen of virtues acts to prevent herself from being rejected, and prevails through her own reverence.

Yet did God say in vain, “Let me be, that my wrath may be kindled against them and I may destroy them”? Did he say into the wind, “And I will make you into a great nation”? Rather, as it was said, so it has now come to pass. God broke the stiff neck of that people, but made Moses into a great nation. For he enlarged the spiritual Law of Moses into the whole Church of the nations, spread throughout the entire world. Therefore he did not say in vain, “I will destroy them, and make you into a great nation”: he spoke, and it came to pass. Yet he deferred its accomplishment, lest he do it then and there while Moses would not let him, as was said: “And the Lord was appeased,” says Scripture, “so as not to do the evil which he had spoken against the people.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. What is mystically signified by the breaking of the first tablets, the crushed calf, its dust scattered in water and given to drink.

Moses returned from the mountain carrying in his hand the two tablets of testimony, written on both sides and made by the work of God. When he approached the camp, he saw the calf and the dances; and, greatly angered, he threw the tablets from his hand and broke them at the foot of the mountain. The breaking of those stone tablets foreshadowed the breaking mentioned above, by which God today broke the stiff neck of that people. For just as those tablets were broken by Moses, so the stony hearts of the Jews were broken and rejected, Moses accusing them, as he says: “There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5).

“And seizing the calf which they had made, he burned it and [Col. 0727D] crushed it to powder; he scattered the powder in water and gave it to the children of Israel to drink.” They receive for drinking the powder of the calf which they had worshipped, in contempt of their superstition, so that they may learn to despise what they saw cast into excrement. But according to the anagogical sense, the same must be understood from this event as from that prophetic saying: “You crushed the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of Ethiopia” (Ps. 73). For behold, God through Moses crushed the heads of the dragon—or of the calf, by which the worship of the devil may be understood—and, reduced to powder, gave them to his people to drink: those who had belonged in part to the devil or to his kingdom, broken by repentance and reduced to the dust of humble conscience, he incorporated into his Church through the water of baptism.

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 0728A] On the severity of Moses in saying, “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh,” and his compassion in praying to God for them; how he is to be imitated by prelates in both respects.

“Now when Moses saw that the people had been stripped naked (for Aaron had stripped them, to the shame of their filth, and had left them naked among their enemies), he stood in the gate of the camp and said: ‘Whoever is for the Lord, join me.’” And all the sons of Levi gathered to him. To them he said: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate, and let each kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor,” and the rest.

Moses’ severity, therefore, is not novel [Col. 0728B] in accusing the Jews who fashioned the calf of falsehood and blasphemed Christ, the ark of truth, as was stated above in the testimony: “There is one who accuses you—Moses, in whom you hope.” For he did not so restrain God and repress His wrath, lest He destroy them, that he lacked good zeal or did not burn with jealousy for the Lord. Rather, he says: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh, and let each kill his brother, his neighbor, and his friend.”

Some say that he reduced the golden calf to powder and gave it to them to drink as a sign of guilt; and that, by this action, those who had instigated the crime were exposed or detected by their lips protruding with gold. Then, as the executioners went and returned from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, the culprits were not slain indiscriminately [Col. 0728C], but were punished with judgment.

It is now fitting to observe mercy joined with severity in Moses’ heart. Certainly, when he heard, “Go down: your people has sinned,” as though the divine voice were saying to him, “He who has fallen into such a sin is no longer mine,” and when the Lord further added: “Leave me, that my wrath may be kindled against them, and I will make you into a great nation,” Moses placed himself as a barrier against the onset of God’s wrath in order to appease it. Again, returning to the Lord, he said: “Either forgive them this sin; or, if you will not, blot me out of the book which you have written.” This is indeed mercy.

But rulers ought to possess, in relation to those subject to them, not only mercy that provides justly, but also discipline that rages piously. [Col. 0728D] He, therefore, who is bound by such love for the people against their sins—consider with what zeal for righteousness he must burn. For as soon as he had obtained, by his petition, pardon for their first offense, so that they would not be destroyed, he came to that same people and said: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbor. And on that day twenty-three thousand men fell.”

Behold: he who sought the life of men even at the cost of his own death also extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Within, he burned with the fires of love; without, he was inflamed with zeal for severity. His compassion was so great that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord for them. His severity was so great that, because he feared that they might be struck by God, he himself struck them with the sword of judgment. Thus he loved [Col. 0729A] those over whom he presided, that he did not spare even himself for their sake; yet he pursued the offenders whom he loved so as to strike them down, even when the Lord spared them. A strong envoy in both respects, a wonderful mediator in both respects: he bound the people’s cause before the Lord with prayers, and God’s cause before the people with swords.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Against those who sit upon the chair of Moses and do not follow his example

All who preside over the government of souls must take from this an example of how they ought to preside—or rather, how they ought to be of service: namely, that inwardly, loving, they should oppose divine wrath by prayer; outwardly, severe, they should destroy guilt by punishment. Otherwise they sit badly upon Moses’ chair. For they are like [Col. 0729B] the Scribes and Pharisees if, sitting in Moses’ place, they abandon the aforesaid office or Moses’ care.

Let such persons think that the Lord speaks of them in His Gospel: “The 238 Scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses. Therefore observe and do all things whatsoever they tell you; but do not act according to their works. For they say and do not do,” etc. (Matt. XXIII).

For this reason the holy Roman Church is accustomed, every year, on one of the Sundays, to bring before the eyes of such idle and negligent persons—and, according to the prophet Amos, those sleeping upon ivory beds and luxuriating upon their couches, after eating lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd (Amos VI)—the lamp of this aforementioned Gospel reading, which awakens sleepers. At the same time she sounds forth in a mighty chant this example of Moses, lest they fail to know what they ought to follow: namely, that Moses consecrated the altar to the Lord and, sacrificing victims, made the morning sacrifice as a sweet fragrance to the Lord God before the children of Israel; and then, rising, he ascended the mountain where God appointed him. Seeing Him, he fell down and worshipped Him, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, forgive the sins of your people; [Col. 0729C] or, if you will not, blot me out of the book which you have written.” And thereafter he prayed: “If I have found grace in your eyes, show yourself openly to me, that I may see you,” etc.

Why is this matter proclaimed in so lengthy and piercing a chant, unless because it is a great concern that those who preside should be stirred up to follow Moses’ example [Col. 0729D]: not to broaden their phylacteries or magnify their fringes, but to provide for the people, lest perhaps, stripped of God’s grace and placed naked among visible or invisible enemies because of their sins, they may be naked; and to cover them with merits and protect them with prayers. Let us now carefully run through those things that have been said and deserve examination.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Moses’ words, “Either forgive,” etc.; and on the Lord’s saying, “But on the day of vengeance I will visit this sin”

“Either forgive them this sin,” he says, “or, if you will not, blot me out of the book which you have written.” Why? Clearly because I too am a sinful man: if there is no propitiation with you, if judgment with you is without [Col. 0730A] mercy, it follows that you must blot me also from your book. “For if you observe iniquities, who shall endure?” (Ps. CXXXIX.) Therefore, if you do not forgive sins, if only the righteous remain written with you, it follows that I too shall not remain in your book which you have written.

God is said both to write and to blot out what He has written, not because He changes, like a man frequently changing his style and intending to write again what is worthy to be read; but because, through judgment on their deeds, He removes from memory many who seem to be written for Him, since they confess that they know God but deny Him by their deeds. “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XXII): that is, many are enrolled in the present Church by giving their names in the book of confession, but few—something greatly to be feared—will escape the flood of judgment.

Thus He immediately answers: “Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book”; and at once: “But you, go and lead this people whither I have spoken to you.” “But you,” He says—understand, you whom “I know by name.” For afterwards He says: “You have found grace before me, and I know you by name.”

Therefore, when, in response to the petition, “Either forgive them this sin, or, if you will not, blot me out of your book which you have written,” the Lord answers thus: “Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book; but you, go and lead this people whither I have spoken to you,” He wonderfully avoids either alternative: neither wholly forgiving this sin nor permitting His faithful servant, trembling in great humility at others’ ruin, [Col. 0730C] to be swallowed up by excessive sorrow (II Cor. II) or to draw near to despair.

For He does not forgive this sin to them when He immediately adds: “My angel shall go before you. But on the day of vengeance I will visit this sin of theirs also.” Concerning this vengeance He immediately adds, prophetically and mystically: “Therefore the Lord struck the people because of the guilt of the calf which Aaron made.” For both on account of the guilt of this material calf, which this Aaron made, and on account of the guilt of the calf—that is, the falsehood—which the chief priests made, into which they changed the truth of God, as has already been said above, by blaspheming and denying Christ the Son of God: behold, the Lord struck the Jewish people.

Hence He pointedly said, “I will visit this sin of theirs also”—“this also,” I say, implying another sin, of which this is the type or prefiguration, which they would commit.

## CHAPTER XXX. That the same Spirit spoke in these words, “If you will not, blot me out of the book,” and in the Apostle’s words, “I myself wished to be anathema for my brethren”

It should be noted that Moses did not say: “Blot me out of your book for them,” or, “I desire to be blotted out so that these may be written.” Rather, he says: “If you do not forgive them, blot me out,” which is the same as saying: “If you blot them out, blot me out with them.” We say this because the Apostle, in the same Spirit, says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that there is great sorrow for me and continual pain in my heart; for I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, who are my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. IX), etc.

For the one and the other spoke with the same love, though they differ slightly in their words. The Apostle wishes to be anathema for his brethren; Moses consents to be blotted out with them. The one wishes to redeem his brethren’s salvation by his own separation; the other, if he cannot obtain their salvation, consents to be blotted out with them from the book of the living, or to become anathema.

The words of both are weighty and exceed our powers. Great men, too, have until now turned each statement over in their minds and have not been able adequately to express the matter as it is. For this is almost ineffable, and can be perceived even in thought only by those who possess something of the Spirit of that same love: how a man intimate with God, for whatever cause or reason, can admit into his mind that he should be anathema from God or consent to be blotted from His book; and how, in this consent, he not only incurs no punishment or guilt, but even deserves greater grace before God.

This much at least glimmers for us concerning so great a matter: because God is love and God is humility, when anyone withdraws from God through humility or love, judging himself more unworthy than those for whom he intercedes, in a wonderful manner the more he humbles himself, the more he ascends; the more he condemns himself, the more he is justified; the more he seems to withdraw from God, the nearer he becomes to Him.

We who are cold and poor do not know the riches of such a soul. Therefore, when we read of that man wishing himself to be anathema for his brethren, and of this man consenting to be blotted from God’s book, we either evade their words or distort utterances of great gravity into a paltry meaning. But one touched by the same Spirit sees, at least in some measure and according to his reverence, how much such a disposition of mind avails before God. He seems to himself to see the Majesty terrible to all heavens and earth rise from His throne and approach a wounded heart, beseeching a friend who is, as it were, departing not to leave Him, and saying, for example: “I will show you all good, and I will call in the name of the Lord before me” (Exod. XXXIII).

The blessed soul, sensing this, uses its strength, because God can resist only the proud; and when God says, “Leave me, that I may be angry with your consent,” it does not heed Him, does not consent, and does not permit Him—unless at times God performs a human being’s will. Wonderfully broken in these its strengths, as was said of Moses, “He stood in the breach before Him” (Ps. CV), it is fed with ineffable sweetness and torn by an ineffable wound of love, the blood of which the Most High does not endure to behold without reverence.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That God said, “My angel shall go before you,” adding, “For I will not go up with you”

“My angel,” He says, “shall go before you. But on the day of vengeance I will visit this sin of theirs also.” And thereafter (Chapter XXXIII): “I will send before you an angel, that I may drive out [Col. 0732A] the Canaanite, and you may enter a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people,” etc.

It may seem strange how, in response to Moses’ prayer, the Lord was appeased so that He would not do the evil He had spoken against His people, and yet this same Moses, after saying, “You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each one against his son and his brother,” said on the following day to the people: “You have committed a very great sin. I will go up to the Lord, in case I may somehow be able to plead with Him for your crime.”

But it is clear that the Lord had indeed been appeased so as not to destroy them bodily at that time, Moses urging Him and, as it were, counseling Him: “Do not, I pray, let the Egyptians say: ‘He brought them out craftily in order to kill them in the mountains and wipe them away from the earth.’” Yet He had not yet been appeased to profess Himself again as their God. Thus He still speaks with an alien disposition, as He had spoken once before: “Go, and go down from this place, you and your people”—your people, I say, not mine.

Therefore, “My angel shall go before you,” He says; or, “I will send before you an angel”—understand, only so that you may enter the land of the Canaanites, not so that you may enter the land of the living. “For I am not your God. You yourselves are not my people.” For this is what He says: “For I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people, lest perhaps I destroy you on the way.” It is as though He said: Since you are a stiff-necked people, it is not expedient for you to call me your God, profess my worship, or bear my laws, being so prone and ready to transgress.

For it is much less grievous not to know God than to provoke Him when known; more tolerable to be ignorant of God’s way than, after recognizing it, to turn back. Therefore, if I go up with you, if you call me your God, I shall more justly destroy you on the way, as you provoke me with stiff neck.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How it is not contradictory that He says, “I will not go up with you,” and then adds, “Once I will go up in your midst”

“I will not go up with you,” He says, “because you are a stiff-necked people, lest perhaps I destroy you on the way.” And thereafter: “You are a stiff-necked people. Once I will go up in your midst, and I will destroy you.” These statements seem contrary or inconsistent: “I will not go up with you, lest perhaps I destroy you,” and “Once I will go up in your midst, and I will destroy you.”

But the difference in the wording must be noted. Negatively He said: “I will not go up with you”; affirmatively: “Once I will go up,” He said, “in your midst.” It differs considerably in word and sense that there He said “with you,” but here “in your midst.” For example, when a conqueror or enemy has burst into a city, he is rightly said to have gone up in the midst of the people; he is not rightly said to have gone up with the people.

Thus both what He said, “I will not go up with you, because you are a stiff-necked people, lest perhaps I destroy you,” and what He said again, “Once I will go up in your midst, and I will destroy you,” must be carefully seen by the lamp of discernment.

“I will not go up with you,” He said. Why? “Lest perhaps I destroy you.” For you are a stiff-necked people; you are a child in understanding; you are like a wanton and unteachable young bull. You are a natural man and do not receive the things of God (I Cor. II). Therefore I shall place a veil over your face (II Cor. III); therefore I shall speak to you about the height of heavenly mysteries not in the manifestation of realities, but in figures and shadows. Why? “Lest perhaps I destroy you.” For you would not endure the height of realities, but would blaspheme, rebel with stiff neck, and so provoke me to destroy you.

Nevertheless, this will happen at some time. “Once I will go up,” not indeed with you, but “in your midst, and I will destroy you”—“I will go up, I say, in your midst; for I shall be seen on earth and converse with men” (Baruch III)—“and I will destroy you,” He says, meaning: from my book which I have written.

For this refers to what was said above when Moses declared: “Either forgive them this sin, or blot me out of your book which you have written.” “Whoever has sinned against me,” He said, “I will blot him out of my book.” Nor was the threat empty. For once He went up, once He was made man, once He suffered, died, rose again, and ascended into heaven; and then at last He blotted out that stiff-necked people, intolerant beyond measure of His coming, fulfilling the prophecy which says: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and let them not be written with the righteous” (Ps. LXVIII).

He blotted them out, that is, He did not write them; and those who appeared to be written, because they called themselves sons of Abraham and possessed temple and altar, He erased like a fault of the pen, destroying with them their temple and altar. Therefore, although they say that they are Jews, they are not Jews, but are the synagogue of Satan (Rev. II). They have plainly been blotted out, God writing in their place the names of other confessors and raising up other sons of Abraham in their stead.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the words, “Now lay aside your adornment,” etc.; and on the mystical meaning of Moses’ pitching outside the camp the tent now called the Tent of the Covenant

“Now when the people heard this very evil word, they mourned, and no one wore his customary adornment. And the Lord said: ‘Now lay aside your adornment, that I may know what I shall do to you.’” [Col. 0733D]

This edifies the reader according to the historical sense: for unless the sinner walks with bowed head, God does not yet acknowledge what He will do to him. For He has no material on which to build mercy unless the bearing or habit of penitence comes first.

“Therefore the children of Israel laid aside their adornment from Mount Horeb. Moses also took the tent and pitched it far outside the camp; and he called its name the Tent of the Covenant.” We might think that these things were said or done on the single day when Moses descended from the mountain, but behold, the letter resists this: for the tent which Moses pitched outside the camp had already been made.

O great and wonderful spectacle, great and wonderful dispensation of heavenly mysteries! Meanwhile, while the tent is established, there is enmity between God and the people because of the guilt of the calf; and this enmity is not removed until the tent is first pitched, which is likewise called the Tent of the Covenant.

We have spoken above about the heavenly realities after whose pattern this very tent was made. What, then, does this mean, except that, while enmity existed between God and human beings, the true tent, “which God pitched and not man” (Heb. VIII), began to be made through the incarnation of Christ the Son of God, in order to remove that enmity?

Accordingly, one must carefully note what is said: “And all the people who had any question went out to the Tent of the Covenant outside the camp. And when Moses went out to the Tent of the Covenant, all the people rose, and each stood at the entrance of his tent. And they watched Moses’ back until he entered the tent. But when he had entered the Tent of the Covenant, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the entrance, and spoke with Moses, while they saw that the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the tent. And they stood and worshipped at the doors of their tents.”

What does it mean that the tent is pitched outside the camp, except that the heavenly holy places, of which Christ is high priest and minister, are pitched outside the carnal ceremonies of the Jews—whom the soul of the Lord hated, as Isaiah says (Isa. I)? And what does it mean that every person who had some question went out to that Tent of the Covenant, except that everyone who seeks the truth of the Scriptures must go out to these holy mysteries of Christ, through which we are reconciled to God? For the veil placed over the heart of the Jews is removed in Christ alone.

What, I say, does it mean that, when Moses entered the Tent of the Covenant, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the door of the tent in the sight of all, except that, when the law given through Moses is joined with the grace and truth made through Jesus Christ (John I), at the entrance of reconciliation stands the incarnation of that same Christ, the Son of God? Thus no one can enter the Tent of the Covenant—that is, be reconciled to God—except through this pillar of cloud, in which Wisdom placed His throne; through this flesh, in which “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II).

“He spoke with Moses while all beheld.” How did they behold? “And they watched,” he says, “Moses’ back until he entered the tent.” Therefore the Law and the Gospel have a familiar and harmonious conversation; but until all things promised in both Testaments are fulfilled, the Jews will not see. For the children of Israel saw not Moses’ face but his back.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the words, “And they too stood and worshipped at the doors of their tents”

According to the historical sense, this matter itself edifies the reader morally. For what does it mean for the people to behold the pillar of cloud and stand and worship at the doors of their tents, except that when the human mind, however imperfectly, perceives those higher and heavenly things in an enigma, it already goes beyond the barriers of bodily dwelling by uplifted thought, and humbly worships Him whose substance it cannot see, but whose power it already marvels at through the illumination of the Spirit?

And when Moses enters the tent, the people behold his back and remain at the entrances of their tents, because when any holy preacher speaks lofty things concerning God and in some measure enters the dwelling-place of the heavenly habitation, the people behold his back. Although the weak cannot fully weigh the power of his preaching, they nevertheless behold, as it were, his back, because they follow by understanding those final things which they are able to comprehend. Yet even in the least things that they are capable of receiving, they already go out, as it were, from their tents and stand at the doors, because they endeavor to leave the dwellings of the flesh and advance toward those joys of eternal life of which they hear.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the words, “The Lord spoke with Moses face to face,” etc., and His later words, “Show me your face”

“The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend.” Afterwards Moses says: “If I have found grace in your sight, show yourself openly to me, that I may see you.” Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would say, “Show me,” and not, “Show me yourself.” But if He was God with whom he was speaking face to face, why did he ask to see the One whom he saw?

This request shows that he thirsted to behold Him through the unbounded clarity of His nature, whom he had already begun to see through certain images: so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, in such a way that no created temporal image might stand between him and the vision of eternity.

Why, then, was it said: “The Lord spoke with Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend,” when unbounded light cannot be seen in its substance by those living in this mortal flesh? Clearly, because He did not conceal His counsel from Moses and made him aware of His secrets.

For how is a man accustomed to speak with his friend? Certainly by opening his counsel to him, not concealing what he intends to do, because the friend is the guardian of the mind; and from this the word *friend* [*amicus*] took its origin.

And we know that Moses was the greatest of the prophets, as the Lord bears witness concerning him when He says to Aaron and Miriam: “Hear my words. If there is among you a prophet of the Lord, I shall appear to him in a vision, or speak with him through a dream. But my servant Moses is not so, who is most faithful in all my house. For I shall speak with him mouth to mouth, openly; and he sees the Lord not through enigmas and figures” (Num. XII).

Again, Scripture says: “And no prophet arose thereafter in Israel like Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all [Col. 0736A] signs and wonders” (Deut. XXXIV). Therefore, because Moses was granted what belongs to prophets—namely, to foresee God’s counsel, which was hidden from carnal or common people under figures and shadowy ceremonies—and because this was given to Moses but not to later prophets, it was rightly said of him that “the Lord spoke with him face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The mystical meaning of Joshua’s not departing from the tent when Moses returned to the camp

“And when he returned to the camp, his servant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, did not depart from the tent.” Moses’ return to the camp is the reading of the Law or the grace of the Gospel. Above we said that the Lord’s conversation with Moses at the entrance of the tent is the harmony of Law and grace at the entrance to the true and heavenly tent. For one who enters the Tent of the Covenant—that is, who desires to be reconciled to God through the death of His Son—must receive or profess both.

Therefore Moses returns to the camp, but Joshua his servant does not depart from the tent, because the Law is indeed read in the synagogue, which does not approach the true tent; but the spirit of the Law remains with Christ’s grace in the Gospel.

Joshua, Moses’ servant, fittingly signifies the spirit of the Law also because he led the people into that land of promise which the Lord had promised to the same people through Moses. For the letter of the Law contains God’s promises; but unless by the spiritual understanding of the Law, no one can be made worthy of those promises. Let carnal Jews, therefore, read the letter that kills; for the life-giving Spirit does not depart from the tent whose high priest is Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That the Lord was appeased so as not to do evil, but not so as to be their God and go up with them

“Moses said to the Lord: ‘You command me to lead this people out, and you do not show me whom you will send with me, especially since you have said: “I know you by name, and you have found grace before me.”’”

This is what was said above: the Lord had indeed been appeased so as not to do the evil He had spoken against His people and so as to bring them into the land of the Canaanites; but He had not also been appeased so as to go up with them and be their God, which is to bring them into the land and region of the living.

Thus he says: “You command me to lead this people out”—understand, into this land of the dead or mortals—“and you do not show me whom you will send with me”—understand, who may bring this people into the land of the living—especially since you have said: “I know you by name.”

As though it follows from the fact that he himself is known to God that he can commend others who are not worthy of God’s knowledge, human compassion desires thus to bind God by the mouth of Moses. For the same Lord says through another prophet: “If these three men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in their midst, they would deliver their own souls by their righteousness” (Ezek. XIV). They alone will be delivered. They will not deliver sons or daughters, but they alone will be delivered.

“You do not show me,” he says, “whom you will send with me.” Did God then not show Moses that He would send Christ His Son, when, as stated above, He spoke with him “face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend”? But hear what follows.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That Moses longs for Christ’s coming when he says, “Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out of this place”

“If therefore I have found grace in your sight, show me your face, that I may know you and find grace before your eyes; look upon your people, this nation.” He therefore asks that this be shown to him—that is, to the people of Israel, whose person he bears, whose cause he has undertaken, and whose embassy he has discharged, using to the utmost the strength he could, thus far holding God when He said, “Leave me.” He asks, I say, that the One whom God will send be shown to the people of Israel, so that, when He comes, He may show them His face and be seen openly.

“And the Lord said to this: ‘My face shall go before you, and I will give you rest.’” This is said too little; for it can be understood as referring only to what He said above: “that I may drive out the Canaanite, the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.”

“Therefore Moses said: ‘Unless you yourself go before us, do not lead us out of this place.’” Because by “face” an angel could be understood, who would suffice to overthrow the human Canaanite, “unless you yourself go before us,” he says—the One who alone can cast out the devil, prince of the world—“do not lead us out of this place.” For what good is it for us to live and produce children unless you yourself come, who alone can regenerate to life those born for death?

He adds further: “For in what shall we be able to know, I and your people, that we have found grace in your sight, unless you walk with us, so that we may be glorified by all peoples who dwell upon the earth?”

“So that we may be glorified above all peoples,” he says. Does the most gentle man, with all the brokenness of his heart, then seek to be glorified by the slaughter of nations and victories in war? Surely this glory is vain. Rather, with a most powerful prayer, he urges that people, in the person of its elect portion, be glorified by all peoples saying: “Salvation is from the Jews” (John IV).

Accordingly the Lord immediately says: “And I will do this word which you have spoken.” “This,” He says, “I will do: that you and my people may be glorified by all peoples who dwell upon the earth, because yours ‘is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; and Christ is from you according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for the ages’” (Rom. IX). In this way all peoples now glorify that people, and thus truly make that glory their own glory.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Lord’s words, “I know you by name,” and the name by which He knows each of the elect

“For you have found grace before me, and I know you yourself by name.” God confirms here what the servant of God had shortly before recalled with groaning: “Especially since you have said: ‘I know you by name, and you have found grace before me.’”

But by what name does God know him? Is it merely by the name which Pharaoh’s daughter gave him, calling him Moses, saying, “Because I drew him out of the water”? (Exod. II). Of course, God could not fail to know him by this name, since He even deigned to call him by it from the bush, saying twice: “Moses, Moses” (Exod. III).

But what great thing is it for anyone to be known or addressed by name in that manner by God? Surely God likewise knew how to name Pharaoh, king of Egypt, addressing also in the prophet the one prefigured by him: “Behold, I am against you, Pharaoh king of Egypt, great dragon” (Ezek. XXIX); and to that same prince of pride: “I have cast you out, O Tyre” (Ezek. XXVIII). What great thing, then, is it for God to know someone thus by name? And shall we need names of this sort in His kingdom?

Therefore, when He says, “I know you yourself by name,” we must understand: by the name of God which has been invoked over you. For by this name God knows everyone written in the book of life. Thus in the Apocalypse He says of the conqueror: “And I will write upon him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem which comes down from heaven from my God, and my new name” (Rev. III).

By this name God recognizes both Moses and every elect human being. But although it is one and the same name, it is written as if in diverse letters: in one person golden writing is praised; in another, silver; in another again, purple or white. For the gifts of the Lord’s name are many, and not all are bestowed upon one person. To the extent that each person knows God, to that extent the Lord’s name shines in him.

For *name* [*nomen*] is said to derive from *knowledge* [*notio*]. There is, therefore, one name of the Lord which He has written upon us, and there are many names of ours by which He knows us. Hence He says in the plural: “Rejoice in this, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X).

## CHAPTER XL. That these three statements must be carefully distinguished: “I will show you all good”; “You cannot see my face”; “Behold, there is a place with me, and you shall stand upon the rock”

“He who said: ‘Show me your glory.’ He answered: ‘I will show you all good things, and I will call upon the name of the Lord before you; and I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me.’ And again he said: ‘You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live.’ And again: ‘Behold,’ he says, ‘there is a place by me,’” etc.

Here a double distinction must carefully be observed: “He answered: ‘I will show you all good things.’ And again he said: ‘You cannot see my face,’” spoken in the person of the Jewish people, with reference to the reprobate portion. But when he again says: “Behold, there is a place by me; you shall stand upon the rock; and when my glory passes by, I will put you in the cleft of the rock and protect you with my right hand until I pass by; then I will take away [Col. 0739A] my hand, and you shall see my back,” understand this likewise as said in the person of that same people, but with reference to the elect portion.

Indeed, mortal humanity, darkened and weakened by the sin of the first parent, cannot see God as long as it lives in this mortal body; for even the holy Daniel could not endure the sight of an angel of God. “When he came,” he says, “to me, terrified, I fell upon my face; and while he was speaking to me, I collapsed, face downward upon the ground” (Dan. VIII). And afterwards: “And I, Daniel, was weak and ill for days” (ibid.).

But here we seek mystical meanings: namely, that it is not without reason that, especially at this point, when the people had offended God, Moses is believed to have asked in such order concerning the glory of the Lord to be avoided. Therefore, when he asked and said: [Col. 0739B] “Show me your glory,” he received the answer: “I will show you all good things, and I will call upon the name of the Lord before you; and I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me.” This is said to him in his own person and relates to what he had said above: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written.” It is as though he said: “I will show you my glory; I will show you all good things—not to just anyone, nor equally to the whole people for whom you plead, but to you, whom I know by name. And I will call upon the name of the Lord before you.”

“I will call,” that is, I will show that same glory in the name of the Lord by which I know you. I will call, certainly, before you, so that you may plainly see what you now see “through a mirror and in an enigma,” and know [Col. 0739C] “in part” (I Cor. XIII). “And I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be gracious to whom it pleases me,” because I owe nothing to anyone: Adam, the father of all, sinned in me; and therefore whatever I show to you or to anyone else is a matter of grace, not of debt.

Then, after making the distinction, he says again: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live.” This is as though he said: Among this people for whom you pray, whose spokesman you are, I shall not so ascend that it may see my face, that I may show it my glory. Why? “For no human being shall see me and live.” But I shall therefore ascend, having become human among human beings, so that the human being who died in Adam may live again in me. If, therefore, I ascend not in humanity, [Col. 0739D] as hidden God but as manifest God, the benefit of the cross will be prevented, and humanity will not live because it will not be redeemed.

Nevertheless, those who have faith will not be denied an opportunity to see. This is what follows: “Behold, there is a place by me; you shall stand upon the rock. And when my glory passes by, I will put you in the cleft of the rock and protect you with my right hand until I pass by; then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back.” For this was said with reference to the elect: namely, Peter and the other apostles, or all those from the same people who believed or would believe. It did them no harm that they did not see the face—that is, the presence—of the Lord as it was. For after he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, they then understood, and thus in a certain way saw his back. [Col. 0740A]

Let him therefore say: “There is a place by me; you shall stand upon the rock.” Peter was already standing upon that rock when he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI); and for that reason he received this answer: “And I say to you: You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (ibid.). “And when my glory passes by”—that is, when I pass from this world, glorified by the great glory of resurrection and ascension—“I will put you,” that is, every Israelite who is of your faith, whomever the smoke of envy has not blinded, “I will put,” I say, “in the cleft of the rock,” that is, in faith in my passion; “and I will protect you with my right hand,” for no one will snatch him from my hand, “until I pass by,” as has been said. “And I will take away my hand,” that is, [Col. 0740B] I will raise up my power; “and you shall see my back,” as has already been said. But “my face,” that is, while I am present in the body, “you cannot see”—my majesty.

## CHAPTER XLI. On “Cut for yourself,” etc.; and on the saying of Paul: “Not again laying a foundation of repentance from dead works.”

(CH. XXXIV.) “And thereafter: ‘Cut,’ he says, ‘for yourself two tablets of stone like the former ones, and I will write upon them the words which the tablets that you broke contained,’” etc.

Here, because the transgressing nation had nullified the first faith in the casting of the calf, and the entire structure of the covenant had collapsed, it is begun again almost from another starting point when it is said: “Be ready [Col. 0740C] in the morning, that you may at once ascend Mount Sinai,” etc. “Let no one ascend with you, nor let anyone be seen throughout the whole mountain; nor may oxen and sheep graze opposite it.”

And again the divine speech joins together the commandments that it had earlier given with a similar summons: “Beware,” it says, “lest you ever form alliances with the inhabitants of that land, which would be your ruin; but destroy their altars, break their statues, and cut down their sacred groves. 243 Do not worship a foreign god,” etc. This repetition of the commandments is an everlasting reproach to carnal Jews who glory in their own righteousness, so that they may not boast and that every mouth of theirs too may be stopped, as has already been said above.

But the Apostle says: “Leaving aside,” he says, “the elementary teaching about Christ, let us be carried on [Col. 0740D] to perfection, not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God” (Heb. VI), etc. Is apostolic authority then contrary to this legal passage, since it denies that the foundation of repentance must be laid again, whereas here the tablets are cut again and the law is repeated from the beginning? Certainly not. For neither is the foundation laid again here. The foundation of the covenant is this:

“Moses therefore took half the blood and put it into bowls; but he poured the remaining part upon the altar. Taking the book of the covenant, when he had read it aloud in the hearing of the people, he sprinkled the people with the blood he had taken and said: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words’” (Exod. XXIV).

If this had been done again, it could rightly be said that the foundation had again been laid [Col. 0741A]. Since it was not done, apostolic authority plainly agrees with the law. For the Apostle did not deny that repentance should be granted to the fallen—as Novatus wrongly understood him—but the foundation of repentance, that is, baptism, in which the firmness of repentance is founded. For after saying, “the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward the Lord,” he added, “instruction concerning baptisms and also laying on of hands.” Therefore, he did not deny room for repentance; he denied that baptism should be repeated.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the words, “Lord, sovereign Lord,” etc.; and on the Lord’s answer: “I will make a covenant in the sight of all.”

“Lord, sovereign Lord God, merciful and gracious, [Col. 0741B] patient, abundant in mercy, and true.”

It should be observed that although the whole purpose is to pray for the people’s crime and to implore mercy, nevertheless, among so many names of divine praise and so many words of mercy, he did not pass over justice or truth in silence. He says: “Merciful and gracious, patient and abundant in mercy,” and finally adds: “and true.” Likewise, in explaining the grounds of these very names, after he said: “You preserve mercy unto thousands; you take away iniquity, crimes, and sins; and no one is innocent before you in himself”—all of which concerns the mercy and glory of the One who justifies—he adds: “You repay the iniquity of fathers in their children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.” This undoubtedly concerns justice and truth.

How then, you ask, does the same God say through the prophet: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. XVIII)? Clearly, the son does not bear whatever iniquity of his father he does not imitate; but the iniquity of fathers is repaid in children and grandchildren who imitate their wicked fathers. For example, we are not all Adam’s children merely according to the flesh. If, therefore, we imitate his iniquity—that is, his unbelief, by which he trusted the serpent rather than God—the iniquity of that father is justly repaid in us his children. But if, fleeing the iniquity of that old human being, we take refuge in the justice of the new human being, Jesus Christ the Son of God, we certainly shall not bear his iniquity.

Accordingly Moses’ prayer concludes beautifully: “And Moses quickly [Col. 0741D] bowed down to the ground; and worshipping, he said: ‘If I have found grace in your sight, Lord, I beseech you, go with us; for this is a stiff-necked people. Take away our iniquities and sins, and possess us.’” When he says, “Go with us,” etc., evangelical faith rejoices confidently to understand: that the Word may become flesh and dwell among us, and that we may see his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father (John I). For from Adam we were a stiff-necked people; therefore we needed the medicine of God’s humility.

To this the Lord replies: “I will make a covenant in the sight of all. I will perform signs which have never been seen upon the earth or among any nations, so that this people in whose midst you are may see the terrible work of the Lord which I shall do.” For what are the signs never seen, or what is the terrible work of the Lord which the people under Moses’ leadership is to see, if not that God became human, that he was crucified, died, was buried, and rose on the third day, with Moses’ prophecy lending its supporting testimony? For if you look at the signs that were performed among that people before this Son of God came, greater things had been seen on earth; greater signs had been wrought in the midst of Egypt. Nor did that people, under all its kings, see so terrible a work of the Lord as what the Lord had already done to Pharaoh and all his servants. [Col. 0742A]

The commandments briefly repeated here end as before: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk” (Exod. XXIII, XXXIV). By this saying we are forbidden to think carnally about Christ. For Cerinthus wished to boil the kid in its mother’s milk, since he said that Christ took his beginning from Mary. But he was God before his mother and before his mother’s forefathers—indeed, before the origin of the world; for “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I).

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the inscription of the second tablets.

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Write these words for yourself, by which I have made a covenant both with you and with Israel.’”

When the former tablets were broken, others like the former were cut, and the same words were written upon them, because, after the carnal Jews had been broken because of unbelief, tablets of fleshly heart belonging to another people, chosen from all nations, were made; and the same commandments were entrusted to them. [Col. 0742C]

It should be observed that God spoke and distinguished his words thus: “by which I have made a covenant both with you and with Israel.” “Both with you,” he says, “and with Israel”: that is, with this people and with that people which is to come afterwards. For the spiritual king changes—indeed, rejects—the carnal ceremonies; and the righteousness which is from faith in Jesus Christ neither concerns itself with them nor depends upon them. But the ten words of the law may not be changed, and the holy, just, and good law of the covenant requires their observance by both the new and the old. Hence they are elsewhere said to have been written by the work of God, elsewhere by the finger of God; and by this expression they are indicated to be eternal or unchangeable. Moses’ twice-forty-day fast has already been discussed above.

## CHAPTER XLIV. [Col. 0742D] On Moses’ horned face from fellowship with the Lord’s speech, and on his placing a veil over his face because the children of Israel were afraid to approach.

“And when Moses came down from Mount Sinai, he held the two tablets of testimony, and did not know that his face was horned through fellowship with the speech of God. But Aaron and the children of Israel, seeing Moses’ horned face, were afraid to approach.”

The horned—that is, shining 244 or radiant—face of Moses, together with the writing of the second tablets, has now openly shown the whole world what it prefigured by its miracle. For where the second tablets—that is, the hearts of the Christian people—received the written commandments of God, and the law began to be understood spiritually by them, the face—that is, the meaning—of Moses sent forth such splendor that the children of Israel, that is, the carnal Jews, unable to bear it, fled into hiding. [Col. 0743A]

“When he had finished speaking,” he says, “he put a veil over his face. When he entered before the Lord and spoke with him, he removed it until he came out. Then he spoke to the children of Israel all that had been commanded him. They saw that Moses’ face, when he came out, was horned; but he covered his face again whenever he spoke to them.”

This needs no exposition from us. For the Apostle says: “And not as Moses put a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face, which is done away; but their minds were dulled. For until this present day the same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is done away in Christ. But even to this present day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. Yet when they turn to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away” (II Cor. III).

Therefore, Moses’ putting a veil over his face, removing it when he entered before the Lord and spoke with him, and covering his face again whenever he spoke to the children of Israel, was a foreshadowing of the matter which the whole world now recognizes. For while Moses speaks to Christ—that is, to the evangelical Church in which Christ is—he takes away his veil and shows an uncovered face. For he removes the killing letter and brings forth the life-giving Spirit. But where he is read in the synagogues of the Jews, he covers his face—that is, the spiritual meaning of the law. For because of the golden calf of their blasphemies, they have lost their eyes and cannot endure the brightness [Col. 0744A] of truth. For, as the Apostle says, “the Gospel is veiled among those who perish,” in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the illumination of the Gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine upon them (II Cor. IV).

Here we bring this treatise on Exodus to an end, since everything said or done here concerning the construction of the tabernacle has been treated above as far as we were able. Yet it is not fitting to pass over what Moses says to the children of Israel: that “the Lord called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom and understanding; and also Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And he taught them both wisdom to make the works of a carpenter, embroiderer, and weaver in colors” (Exod. XXXV). [Col. 0744B]

For Bezalel is interpreted “shadow of God,” because by his name, as has been said, he signifies the work of the tabernacle itself, which made a shadow—that is, served as an image—of the heavenly tabernacle. Oholiab is likewise interpreted “my father’s protection”; by this name he signifies that those who assist God or his tabernacle should hope for his protection as their reward. Since Scripture says that “the Lord called them by name and taught them both wisdom,” who can doubt that these and all such crafts are gifts of God? Therefore, wherever such useful and lawful skills are found in a person, they ought to be valued; and skilled artisans should be admonished to employ them profitably as God’s talent, since this is not their own ability but a trust committed to them by the Creator who bestows all things, and he himself will demand an account from those to whom he has entrusted it.

# The Forty-Two Books of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, On the Trinity and Its Works: Commentaries on Leviticus

## BOOK ONE. (Leviticus, chapters I–VIII)

[Col. 0743]

### 245 CHAPTER I. [Col. 0743C] Why this book is called Leviticus, and why the ritual of sacrifices was instituted as not necessary for the time.

This book is called in Hebrew *Vayyiqra*, in Greek *Leviticus*, and in Latin *Ministerialis* (“Ministerial”), namely from its principal subject matter, because it deals with priestly ministrations. Thus the preceding book is called in Hebrew *Ellesmoth*, in Greek *Exodus*, and in Latin [Col. 0744C] *Exitus* (“Departure”), likewise from its principal subject, because the chief matter treated in it is the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

Therefore, because priestly ministrations are treated here, this book is called *Leviticus* by the Greeks—not because this word has a Greek origin, for it derives from Levi, which is Hebrew and means “added,” but because this book treats of [Col. 0745A] priestly ministrations of the Levitical tribe.

Now the sacrifices whose ritual is ordered here were established not as necessary instruments for accomplishing salvation, but as certain barriers set up because of transgressions. The law itself, the prophets, and the Apostle alike bear witness to this. For this very law of sacrifices, after first saying: “The priest shall pour the blood upon the altar of the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony and shall burn the fat as a sweet fragrance to the Lord” (Lev. XVII), immediately adds: “And the children of Israel shall no longer sacrifice their victims to demons, with whom they have committed fornication” (ibid.). And in the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says: “Add your burnt offerings to your victims and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor command [Col. 0745B] them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning the matter of burnt offerings and victims” (Jer. VII).

What then was the law? “It was set in place because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom he had promised it, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. III). Let us therefore enter upon a spiritual examination of the law of sacrifices—not for the sake of the sacrifices themselves, but because they too were arranged according to the pattern of the true and heavenly sacrifice, with the help of the Lord of heavenly things—and let us take care to refer everything to our own benefit, we who serve the heavenly tabernacle.

### CHAPTER II. The ways or kinds by which the rite of offerings or sacrifices is distinguished.

(CHAPTER I.) “And the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the [Col. 0745C] tabernacle of testimony, saying: ‘Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: A person who offers from among you a victim to the Lord—from cattle, that is, oxen and sheep—when offering sacrifices: if his offering is a burnt offering, he shall offer from the herd an unblemished male at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, that he may make the Lord favorable to himself.’”

Before examining the words themselves one by one, it is worthwhile first to make a division and briefly gather the whole law of sacrifices. Some offerings or sacrifices are called burnt offerings; others, peace offerings; others, offerings for sin. Again, among those called offerings for sin, some are for the sin of the priest together with the multitude, while others are for the sin of any person, whether ruler [Col. 0745D] or commoner.

Those for the sin of the priest alone, and those for the sin of the priest together with the multitude, seem to differ little or not at all. Both are commanded to be burned outside the camp, and this distinguishes them from the burnt offering: the burnt offering is burned on the altar, but those outside the camp. Likewise, offerings for the sin of a ruler and for the sin of a common person are brought under the same law. In both, after the memorial portion has been set apart for the food of the Lord’s fire—namely the fat that covers the vital organs and all the inner fat, the two kidneys with the fat that covers them, and the lobe of the liver with the kidneys—once these have been separated, the rest goes to the priest for food.

### 246 CHAPTER III. [Col. 0746A] Why everything is commanded to be taken only from three kinds—herd, flock, and birds—and what these signify mystically.

It should be observed that all these are commanded to be taken from three kinds: from the herd, from the flock, and from birds. From the herd, a calf; from the flock, a ram or goat; from birds, a turtledove or dove. Apart from these five kinds of animals, the law of sacrifices recognizes no other living creatures, whether clean or unclean.

Before seeking mystical reasons, let us first set forth the ordinary differences between herd, flock, and birds. The herd is useful in two ways: it both works the earth and supplies an abundance of milk. The flock—that is, a ram or goat—does no work, but supplies only the produce of milk and wool. A turtledove or dove is capable of neither and is free from every service of this kind.

Therefore, in these three kinds let us understand three orders, by whose lawful sacrifices service is rendered in the heavenly tabernacle. In the prophet Ezekiel these are denoted by the three men, Noah, Daniel, and Job: one order of rulers, another of those devoted to contemplation, and a third of those who work well and lawfully in the affairs of the world. For all who sacrifice themselves to the living God, presenting their bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, their rational service (Rom. XII), are distinguished among these three orders. At one time what is offered is a burnt offering, that is, thanksgiving; at another time, the same work of repentance is an offering for sin; at another, a peace offering—that is, prayer seeking peace from the assault of vices, as when one says with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. VII). [Col. 0746C]

### CHAPTER IV. Why Christ alone is the head of all these, from whom or in whom every sacrifice is accomplished.

Christ alone is the head of all these. For it principally belongs to him to offer burnt offerings of thanksgiving, who, according to the likeness of Noah, rescued the ark of his Church from the waves and destruction of the world. Of him one may most rightly say that he “built an altar to the Lord, offering a burnt offering upon it” (Gen. VIII). For on account of him the Lord smelled the odor [Col. 0746D] of sweetness and blessed us, saying: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. IX).

Likewise, it belongs to him alone to offer peace offerings according to the likeness of Daniel, who said: “At this time there is no prince, prophet, or leader; no burnt offering, sacrifice, oblation, incense, or place of firstfruits before you, that we may find mercy; but may we be received in a contrite soul and humble spirit, as in a burnt offering of rams and bulls, and as in thousands of fat lambs” (Dan. III). For he alone made peace between God and human beings, dissolving the ancient enmities. He had no altar or sacrifice other than himself, and in his flesh and blood he was more acceptably received than thousands of bulls, rams, [Col. 0747A] or fat lambs.

No less does it belong to him to offer sacrifices for sin—not his own but that of others—according to the likeness of Job, who rose early and offered sacrifices for each of his children, saying: “Perhaps my children have blessed God in their hearts” (Job I), and thus he sacrificed them to the Lord.

Let us now examine the individual matters more carefully.

### CHAPTER V. On the offering of a burnt offering from the herd: what its ritual is, and why, mystically, it is the offering of one who lives according to Job.

“If,” he says, “his offering is a burnt offering, he shall offer from the herd an unblemished male at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, that he may make the Lord favorable to himself.”

The offering is from the herd for one who lives [Col. 0747B] according to Job, as has been said: one who, under the yoke of marriage, governed his household well and trained his children in every piety and submission, so that, as we have already said, he offered burnt offerings for each of them, saying: “Perhaps they have sinned and blessed God in their hearts” (Job I). His offering is a burnt offering—that is, wholly burned—when, giving thanks for a good work and attributing everything wholly not to himself but to God, he offers it.

For it says: “He shall offer an unblemished male at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, that he may make the Lord favorable to himself.” To offer an unblemished male from the herd in this order is to preserve honorable marriage and, according to the Apostle, an undefiled marriage bed (Heb. XIII), so as to make the Lord favorable—the strict judge, namely, of fornicators and adulterers. By what rite? It follows: [Col. 0747C] “He shall put his hands upon the head of the victim, and it shall be accepted and avail for his expiation. And he shall sacrifice the calf before the Lord.”

To put hands upon the head of the victim and sacrifice the calf to God is, by applying the discipline of good works, to restrain one’s married flesh for the honor of the Lord, so as to be able to devote oneself to prayer. “And the sons of Aaron the priest,” it says, “shall offer its blood around the altar, at the entrance of the tabernacle.” The sons of Aaron—whose name means “mountain of strength”—the sons, I say, of Aaron the priest, are the members of the priest, or of the great High Priest who passed through the heavens, Jesus Christ: those who devote themselves to him in whatever order.

For it is said through the apostle Peter not only to those who administer Christ’s sacraments with hands and voice, [Col. 0747D] but to all believers: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II). And in the Apocalypse, the voice of all the elect who praise him says: “For you were slain and redeemed us to God in your blood, and made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (Apoc. V).

Their altar, moreover, is faith, upon which they must place whatever they offer; without it they cannot offer anything worthy or pleasing. Therefore they pour out the blood of the victim “around the altar, before the entrance of the tabernacle,” when they kill the will of flesh and blood for Christ, so that they may stand worthily in his tabernacle. For example, when, because of the saying: “If therefore you offer your gift at the altar and remember that your brother has [Col. 0748A] something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, when you come, offer your gift” (Matt. V)—when, because of this saying, a person removes anger from his heart, he has poured out the blood of his victim “around the altar,” in accordance with the Lord’s command.

“And when the skin of the victim has been removed,” he says, “they shall cut the limbs into pieces.” To remove the skin of the victim is to reject all hypocrisy, which pretenders do not do: inwardly ugly, they are handsome in a beautiful skin, such as were the scribes and Pharisees, against whom our Lord pronounces woe because they do everything for human beings. To cut the limbs into pieces is to mortify vices, according to the Apostle who says: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, impurity, lust, evil desire, and covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Col. III). [Col. 0748B]

Then finally: “They shall,” he says, “put fire upon the altar, having first arranged a pile of wood; and arranging upon it the limbs that have been cut, namely the head and all that adheres to the liver, with the entrails and feet washed in water, the priest shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet odor to the Lord.”

To arrange the limbs that have been cut is rationally to order those members which had been weapons of iniquity offered to sin, so that they become weapons of righteousness, in order that, according to the Apostle, our service may be rational (Rom. XII). For it is rightly ordered, for example, that a husband render fidelity to his wife, a wife to her husband, and both to God.

What members? “Namely, the head and all that adheres to the liver.” The head is the intention, which all the members of the whole work follow. Desire and pleasure reside in the liver, according to those who discuss natural philosophy. The entrails signify hidden thoughts; the feet, daily sins, without which human or earthly life cannot be carried on. When all these have been “washed in water”—that is, cleansed through confession and tears—“the priest,” he says, “shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet odor to the Lord.”

“Is God concerned about oxen?” (I Cor. IX). If God is not concerned about an ox alive and treading out grain, how much less about a dead ox whose skin has been removed and which has been cut into pieces. It was therefore said rather for our sake: when we have done the things stated above and have burned ourselves as a burnt offering to the Lord, attributing all to him and not to ourselves, he is concerned [Col. 0748D] for these things, and a sweet odor rises to him. Conversely, there is the stench of sinners who live for themselves rather than for God, as God testifies: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I).

### CHAPTER VI. On the offering of a burnt offering from the flock: what its ritual is, and why, mystically, it is the offering of one who lives according to Noah.

“But if the offering is from the flock, he shall offer a year-old and unblemished sheep or goat as a burnt offering. And he shall sacrifice it at the side of the altar which faces north, before the Lord,” etc.

“The offering is from the flock” for one who lives according to Noah, who, as has been said, presided over the ark amid the waters of the flood. The person, I say, who, following his example, has undertaken the administration of a household [Col. 0749A], has his offering from rams or goats. For even if he is truly a clean and wholly white ram, in his own estimation he is a goat—that is, a sinner.

“He shall offer a year-old and unblemished animal.” A year-old animal, that is, a male of one year, is already strong, able to brandish its little horn, and is now fit to lead the flock. It therefore signifies the fullness of virtues in one worthy to preside over the Lord’s sheep, such as the Apostle describes himself confidently: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (II Cor. XIII). And again, as one conscious of a strong little horn: “What do you wish?” he says. “Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV). He is unblemished when he takes care and says: “Lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” [Col. 0749B] (I Cor. IX). And he urges his disciple to present himself as “a worker without shame” (II Tim. II).

For this order, breadth of love together with the spirit of strength is especially necessary. Hence it is added: “And he shall sacrifice it at the side of the altar which faces north.” The side of the altar is the breadth of love, by which the same Apostle, enlarged in heart, says: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us” (II Cor. VI), etc. Sacrificing himself at this side of the altar, the same year-old ram, leader of the Lord’s flock, says: “Most gladly I will spend and be spent for your souls” (II Cor. XII).

“It faces north,” he says. The north signifies the devil, who said: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV). The side of love faces this north, because nothing is so contrary to the devil as the breadth of love. “And the sons of Aaron shall pour out its blood around the altar, and they shall divide its limbs,” etc. [Col. 0749C]

### CHAPTER VII. On the offering of a burnt offering from birds: what its ritual is, and why, mystically, it is the offering of one who lives according to Daniel.

“Now if the offering to the Lord is a burnt offering of birds, the priest shall offer it at the altar from turtledoves or young pigeons.” The offering is from birds for one who lives according to Daniel—that is, who leads a celibate life, concerned only with “how he may please God” [Col. 0749D] (I Cor. VII), and, free from every burden or service, is lifted to the heights on the wing of contemplation, enjoying holy leisure. “From turtledoves,” he says, “and young pigeons.” Each bird has lamentation instead of song. The difference is only that the turtledove is solitary in its roaming, while the pigeon is accustomed to lament in flocks. Thus the turtledove signifies the solitary or eremitic life, and the pigeon the cenobitic life, of those who fly by contemplation. “The priest,” he says, “shall offer it at the altar.” How? “He shall twist its head back to its neck, and, having broken it at the wound, shall cause the blood to run down upon the rim of the altar.”

The head must be turned back toward the neck or the wings—that is, the understanding toward the aims of the virtues—so that whatever one engaged in such a purpose does may tend to this end: that he may pass over to heavenly things in the continual flight of contemplation. Or the head should remain attached to the neck and not be cut off altogether, because the mind, which governs all actions as the head governs the body, must indeed be cut off from the delight of the flesh, but must not be cut off from necessary care of the flesh. For it is written: “Make not provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII). What, therefore, ought not to be provided in desires must without doubt be provided in necessity. “Having broken it at the wound,” he says, “he shall cause the blood to run down upon the rim of the altar.” Blood is poured out at the altar when, as said above, one utterly renounces one’s own will.

“But he shall cast away the crop of the throat and the feathers, near the altar on the eastern side, in the place where ashes are usually poured out.” The crop of the throat, in which the turtledove or pigeon stores the grains it has found, signifies the capacity of memory, by the good use of which the mind profitably gathers up the sayings of the Scriptures. The feathers signify the agility of mind by which it knows how to pursue sublime things and grasp the lofty meaning of utterances. Yet the educated mind in some fashion disregards this natural ability, since in the light of truth it sees that all it perceives concerning God comes not from its own powers but from a heavenly gift. “Therefore,” he says, “he shall cast away the crop of the throat and the feathers toward the eastern side”: that is, he shall despise in himself the aforesaid capacities of memory and intellect, confessing heavenly grace.

The place in which the ashes of burnt offerings are usually poured out signifies the righteous humility of a person who, lest he be exalted by the gift received or the greatness of revelations (I Cor. XII), remembers [Col. 0750C] that he is ashes and will return to ashes. Hence he further adds: “And he shall break its wings.” For a winged bird is raised aloft by its wings. Therefore he shall break the wings—that is, he shall lower strength into weakness—when, as said above, the mind does not exalt itself over the gift which God bestows. Thus it is said of Moses that “he stood in the breach before Him” (Ps. CV).—“He shall not cut it 248 nor divide it with iron,” he says. For a virtue received should not be wholly unknown; otherwise it cannot be guarded. Let it therefore be broken, but not cut or divided with iron: that is, let it be unrecognized through humility, but thoroughly known through reason, so that it may be preserved. “And he shall burn it upon the altar, on the wood with fire placed beneath,” etc.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0750D] On the offering of fine flour; why it is said, “When a soul offers”; that its offering should be fine flour; and what its rite is.

(CH. II.) “When a soul offers an oblation of sacrifice to the Lord, its offering shall be fine flour.” Although by a part you may rightly understand the whole—that is, by “soul,” the human being—yet in such a matter he has elegantly preferred to say “soul” rather than “human being.” For in a true sacrifice it is not enough that a human being be seen as bodily present, especially since the Lord of sacrifice looks not at bodily form or appearance but at the intention of the soul. “Therefore, when a soul offers an oblation of sacrifice to the Lord, its offering shall be fine flour.”

Up to this point the literal discourse concerned the offering of cattle or flesh; now it concerns the offering of flour. Indeed, it is fitting that one who seeks in every way to make an acceptable offering should offer not barley or bran, but fine flour, to God the giver of all things. Yet this is not empty of spiritual meaning. Fine flour is the inner pith of grain and wheat. What, then, is Holy Scripture but God’s grain? The pith of the wheat is the spiritual understanding of the word. Therefore, one who desires to sacrifice rightly, when reading and chanting psalms, should offer spiritual understanding in the praises of his Creator.

The Apostle sought to do this when he said: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV). To sing with the spirit is to recite the words of psalms from memory; to sing with the mind is to apprehend inwardly the life-giving sense of the words. Therefore, whoever offers praise to God should offer a profitable sense, pleasing to God, in order to make the sacrifice flourish. For example, when he says, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII), he should understand as the bread of fine flour not so much the bran of the letter as that bread of the Spirit—not the bread which Moses gave, nor that which Moses ate with the people, but that which the Father sealed and in which He gave life to the world (John VI), by which He feeds angels immortally. Since the Jews do not do this, following the killing letter and not the life-giving Spirit, what they offer is contemptible; and rightly it is said to them through the prophet: “You offer polluted bread upon my altar” (Mal. I).

“Thus,” he says, “its offering shall be fine flour.” But in such an offering it is not enough to possess right understanding alone. He therefore continues [Col. 0751C]: “And he shall pour oil upon it and put frankincense on it.” Oil signifies charity; frankincense signifies the fragrance of good repute. The divine word commands that whoever sacrifices the aforesaid fine flour of the divine word in speech or writing should do so with charity and should have a good testimony among those outside. In this manner he will offer both oil and frankincense to his God.

“And he shall bring it to the sons of Aaron the priest. One of them shall take a handful full of fine flour and oil, and all the frankincense, and shall place the memorial portion upon the altar as a most sweet fragrance to the Lord. But what remains of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and his sons, a holy of holies from the oblations of the Lord.” This one signifies either the truth of the Church or, certainly, Christ himself, the great High Priest. “He shall take,” he says [Col. 0751D], “a handful full of fine flour and oil, and all the frankincense”—that is, the intention of charity and the fragrance of good life belonging to one who labours in word and doctrine—“and shall place the memorial portion upon the altar as a most sweet fragrance to the Lord.”
