This corresponds to what the same person signifies in the Apocalypse by the angel standing beside the altar of the temple with a golden censer in his hand, to whom much incense was given so that he might offer it with the prayers of the saints upon the golden altar before the eyes of the Lord. He plainly takes this aforesaid memorial portion upon the altar, so that the one from whom it is received may be in everlasting remembrance. “But what remains,” he says, “of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and his sons,” because for those who gladly read the Scriptures—and for that reason are sons of Aaron, that is, the nearer members of Christ—whatever the holy teachers have left in their books from such sacrifice is a holy and desirable refreshment. Therefore, he says, it shall be “a holy of holies from the oblations of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER IX

That an offering of fine flour from a frying-pan must be divided into small pieces, whereas an offering from a griddle must not be crumbled; that both must be unleavened and mingled with oil; and what these things signify mystically.

“But when you offer a sacrifice baked in an oven, it shall be loaves of fine flour, namely unleavened, mingled with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil. If your offering is of fine flour from a frying-pan, mingled with oil and unleavened, you shall divide it into small pieces and pour oil upon it. But if the sacrifice is from a griddle, fine flour shall likewise be mingled with oil.”

For one who cooks the fine flour of God’s word in an oven—that is, expounds Holy Scripture in the Holy Spirit—making loaves without the leaven of any heretical perversity or vain glory and mingled, as stated above, with the oil of charity, persecution is always at hand. Either he is disparaged by false brethren among those within, or he is more openly attacked by impious and godless people outside. Therefore he says: “If your offering is of fine flour from a frying-pan, mingled with oil and unleavened”—that is, if you have inward conflicts of words with false brethren because of your zeal for Holy Scripture, which you have handled with the oil of charity and without the leaven of falsehood—“you shall divide it into small pieces”: that is, you shall examine each saying most carefully, lest anything perhaps be justly censured; “and you shall pour oil upon it.”

Upon fine flour already mingled with oil, and again divided into small pieces, you shall pour oil: that is, upon Holy Scripture illuminated by charity and again examined point by point against opponents, you shall add not the zeal of bitterness but the oil of the same charity, more ardently still, so that you may gain them. The frying-pan is a vessel named from the noise it makes, for oil sounds and crackles when it is fried in it. It therefore signifies the inward burning of fraternal rivalry: that is, the envy of false brethren sounding and clamouring within. The griddle, however, signifies the open malice of those outside, who burned holy people bodily stretched out upon fires, while they were sacrificing to God the fine flour of truth. There also oil is mingled; for when the body is roasted, charity overflows and boils up more fervently.

Therefore he says: “But if the sacrifice is from a griddle, fine flour shall likewise be mingled with oil.” Notice that if the offering is from a frying-pan, it is commanded to be divided into small pieces and then oil poured upon it; but if it is from a griddle, it is not commanded to be divided into small pieces but only mingled with oil. For against false brethren, who lie in wait for truth under the Christian name, there is need of the most careful division and subtle discrimination, because they themselves, lurking maliciously under the same terms which we use for the faith, strive against the faith. Hence our Lord says: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you 249 [Col. 0753A] in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves” (Matt. VII).

But against those who hate even the name of Christ, the conflict is not so doubtful or subtle. There, as on an open field, even the simplicity of rustic believers can recognize the enemy. For just as our Lord himself, when he was being fried, as it were, in a hissing frying-pan by seditious clamour and questions raised against him by the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees of the Jews, defended the justice of his cause by subtle recollection of the Scriptures, but when he stood before Pilate said nothing to him concerning the Scriptures; so his chosen disciples, whenever they are troubled by perverse questions from those who have knowledge of the Scriptures, must answer watchfully from the Scriptures and divide their words, as it were, into small pieces. But whenever they are harassed by those who do not receive the Scriptures or have not heard them, they should not pour out discourse about such matters.

It follows: “When offering it to the Lord, you shall deliver it into the hands of the priest,” etc., as above.

## CHAPTER X

That every offering offered to the Lord must be without leaven and honey, and seasoned with salt; and what these things signify mystically.

“Every offering which is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven. Neither any leaven nor honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord. You shall offer only their first fruits and gifts, but they shall not be placed on the altar as a pleasing fragrance.” Concerning old leaven, the leaven of malice and wickedness, something has already been said elsewhere. Honey signifies the sweetness of temporal joy, to which the delight of God’s word is constantly preferred by the wise man who says: “How sweet are thy words to my palate, above honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII). “Nothing of honey,” he says—that is, of vain and passing delight—“shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord.”

On the contrary, we are commanded to eat the lamb with wild lettuces, which are very bitter and signify the bitter lamentations of penitents; without these, our sacrifice is not sufficiently dear to God. Knowing this, the Psalmist says: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise” (Ps. L). Therefore, he says, neither anything of leaven nor of honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord, because, just as God hates the leaven of malice and wickedness, so he does not admit unsuitable merriment. For this is not now a time for laughing but for weeping (Eccl. III). “Woe to you,” he says, “who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke VI).—“You shall offer only their first fruits and gifts,” he says, namely, as dill or mint is tithed; “but they shall not be placed on the altar as a pleasing fragrance.”

“Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; you shall not take away the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt.” The threefold repetition of salt should be noted: “Whatever you offer, you shall season with salt; you shall not take away the salt of the covenant of your God; and in every offering you shall offer salt.” Under the name of salt, therefore, he impresses and repeats this more fully: do nothing without discernment. For just as what is not seasoned with salt is tasteless, and flesh denied the seasoning of salt decays more quickly, so everything we do, if it is done without discernment, is not pleasing to eternal wisdom and is worthy of rejection as though rotten or foul-smelling.

For this reason he said three times, “the salt of the covenant of your God,” because the covenant of the Lord abides in discernment; but among those who act without discernment, the covenant with God cannot remain lasting or incorrupt. Accordingly, the Lord says: “You are the salt of the earth. But if salt has become foolish, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER XI

What it means mystically to offer green ears of grain; to roast them with fire; and to pour oil and place frankincense upon them.

[Col. 0754B] “But if you offer to the Lord a gift of the first fruits of your crops, from ears still green, you shall roast them with fire and crush them in the manner of flour, and thus offer your first fruits to the Lord, pouring oil upon them and placing frankincense upon them, because it is an oblation of the Lord.” The crops are our sacred reading. We offer a gift of first fruits from ears still green when, in the service of the Lord, we set before ourselves for imitation the examples of those Fathers who lived before the Law. “For the field is the world, the seed is the word of God, and the harvest is the consummation of the age” (Matt. XIII). Therefore, when we read the examples of the Fathers and set them before ourselves for imitation—men whom the heat of the Law had not yet scorched—we offer to the Lord a gift of first fruits, as it were, from ears still green.

But certain deeds of theirs, although we read that they were performed historically, cannot in the same manner be followed or used in our defence as authoritative examples. Indeed, even after the giving of the Law there are certain deeds of saints from which we are rightly restrained according to the evangelical rule. For example, before the giving of the Law Abraham, the patriarch and friend of God, took as wife his sister, the daughter of his father but not of his mother (Gen. III); and after the Law, holy David also had several wives at the same time (I Kings III). Thus, as ears still green, they stood in the field of this world before Christ’s coming, until, with the rising of that same Sun of righteousness, as in full summer, the harvest of virtues ripened and was made firm.

Therefore, he says, if you offer to the Lord a gift of the first fruits of your crops from ears still green, “you shall roast them with fire and crush them in the manner of flour.” That is: if you set before yourself for imitation the examples of the ancient Fathers, you shall burn away with the Holy Spirit the rough chaff of the letter and, by crushing it through spiritual understanding, make it like evangelical fine flour, so that what would now be judged adultery may be referred to an evangelical mystery. For if you follow or imitate according to the letter the fact that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman, you are rightly removed from the altar of the Lord as an adulterer. But if, with the Apostle, you understand these things to have been said allegorically (Gal. IV), you roast the green ears with fire and crush them in the manner of flour, worthily bringing first fruits to the Lord [Col. 0755A] and pouring oil upon them and placing frankincense upon them: that is, considering with devout charity for the Lord’s honour that what holy and faithful persons did in an age still new, when God had not forbidden it, is not reckoned to them as sin. “And the priest shall burn, in remembrance of the gift, a portion of the crushed flour and oil, and all the frankincense.” This too should be understood as above.

## CHAPTER XII

On the peace offering: how it differs from the burnt offering; its mystical rite; and why it is not commanded to be made from birds.

(CH. III.) “But if his offering is a peace offering, and he wishes to offer it from cattle, male or female, he shall offer it without blemish before the Lord.” This is joined to the preceding reading as follows. Above he had said (Lev. I): “If his offering is a burnt offering, and from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, to make the Lord favourable to him,” etc., 250 down to the words, “and he shall break the wings of the turtledove or pigeon, and shall not cut it nor divide it with iron.” After a few intervening remarks concerning the sacrifice of flour, he now at last adds: “But if his offering is a peace offering,” etc.

The burnt offering—that is, the wholly burned offering—we have already said is the sacrifice of those giving thanks because, through the help of God’s grace, they have burned all their vices with the fire of the Holy Spirit. But the peace offering belongs to those who, according to the Apostle, delight indeed in the law of God according to the inward person, yet see another law in their members warring against the law of their mind, seek peace, and say: “Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. VII). The distinction, therefore, between this sacrifice—that is, the peace offering—and the burnt offering must be carefully considered.

The offering of a burnt offering, whether from the herd, the flocks, or birds, is commanded, in accordance with its name, to be wholly burned. But the Law now says concerning the peace offering: “And the sons of Aaron the priest shall pour the blood around the altar, and they shall offer from the peace offering an oblation to the Lord.” If it is from cattle, they shall burn “the fat covering the vital organs, and all the fat which is inside, the two kidneys with the fat that covers them, and the membrane of the liver with the kidneys, upon the altar as a burnt offering on the wood with fire laid beneath, as an oblation of a most sweet fragrance to the Lord.” “But if his offering is from sheep and he brings a lamb,” these likewise shall be separated and offered as a burnt offering to the Lord in the same manner. “But if it is a goat,” the same law of separation shall nevertheless apply: namely, “you shall eat neither fat nor blood at all,” he says. For it should be understood that “whatever remains shall belong to Aaron and his sons, a holy of holies from the oblations of the Lord” (Lev. II).

This distinction between the burnt offering and the peace offering is plain in its historical sense. But in the spiritual sense, those whose struggle is such that the other law in their members still wars against the law of their mind must weigh very carefully what is said. For what is it to burn as a burnt offering “the fat which covers the vital organs and all the fat which is inside,” except to chastise the body and reduce it to servitude? For what is the fat covering the vital organs except the other law which is in the delicate members and wars against the vital law of the mind? What, I ask, is it to burn “the two kidneys with the fat which covers them” as a burnt offering except to say to the Lord with the Psalmist: “Prove me, O Lord, and test me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. XXV)?

But it is not enough to chastise the bodily kidneys by abstinence from food unless the inward root of desire is burned up by the fire of the Holy Spirit. He says: “And the membrane of the liver with the kidneys.” According to physicians, the force of pleasure and desire resides in the liver. Therefore, not the kidneys alone, but also with the kidneys the membrane of the liver, must be burned: that is, not merely the bodily kidneys through abstinence from food and drink, but also the inward root of desire through the love of the Holy Spirit. Whether this offering—that is, the peace offering—is from cattle or sheep, whether male or female, sheep or goat, these things must likewise be separated according to the same rite and offered as a burnt offering. For whatever the rank of one in whom the other law of the members still wars against the law of the mind, it is beneficial for that person, by personal labour and invocation of the Holy Spirit, both to burn the mind’s desire and to afflict the body’s kidneys.

Then what remains of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and the sons of his priests, because it will be the concern of those who have already advanced in virtues and know how to preside over others to assist these persons’ weakness with prayers, train them by examples, and instruct them by discipline. It should be noted in this sacrifice—that is, the peace offering—that with the fat and kidneys the tail also must be offered through its blood. For he says: “And they shall offer from the peace offering a sacrifice to the Lord: the fat and the whole tail with the kidneys,” etc. The tail is the end of the body. By this name also the Spirit says to the Churches: “He who perseveres unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X).

It should likewise be noted that a sacrifice of this kind—that is, a peace offering—is taken from cattle and from flocks of sheep and goats, just as is the burnt offering; but it is not commanded to be taken from birds—that is, from turtledoves and young pigeons. Why is this? Clearly because those who already fly upwards on the wing of contemplation do not have that struggle in which, as we have said, another law in the members wars against the law of the mind. It follows.

## CHAPTER XIII

On the sin offering and how it differs from the burnt offering and the peace offering.

(CH. IV.) “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel: A soul which sins through ignorance and does something against any of the commandments of the Lord, which He commanded not to be done—if the priest who is anointed sins, causing the people to offend, he shall offer to the Lord for his sin a spotless calf, and he shall bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord, lay his hand upon its head, and immolate it to the Lord,” etc. This is the law of the offering made for sin. It is the first and universal sacrifice of all.

Its difference in the literal sense from the burnt offering and the peace offering is evident: for certain parts are not taken from it, as from the peace offering, for the priests to eat; nor is it wholly burned upon the altar like the burnt offering, but is entirely burned outside the camp. Therefore let us pursue its law more carefully, guided by apostolic authority. He says: “If the priest who is anointed sins, causing the people to offend, he shall offer for his sin a spotless calf,” etc.; and then: “But if the whole assembly of Israel has sinned through ignorance, and through inadvertence has done what is contrary to the commandment of the Lord, and afterwards has understood its sin, it shall offer a calf for sin,” etc. In both cases it is thus prescribed: “But he shall carry outside the camp the skin and all the flesh, with the head and feet and intestines and dung and the rest of the body, and shall burn them.”

Moreover, this is the Apostle’s statement: “For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through himself, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach” (Heb. XIII).

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0757C] That Adam was, in the mystical sense, the priest of whom the Law says, “If the priest sins, causing the people to offend”; and that Christ was the calf offered for his sin.

Who, then, is this priest who sins, causing the people to offend, except Adam, the first human being? He ought to have been a priest and to honour the Lord with a continual sacrifice of praise. For this end he was instructed above the cattle and beasts of the earth—that is, made in the image and likeness of God—and placed in paradise, to be increased in his children by the Creator’s blessing, so that he might give thanks to the same Creator and offer a sacrifice of praise 251. Yet when he ought to have done this, he sinned and caused all the people of his posterity to offend. For in him we all sinned, and in him we all justly died.

Therefore he says: “He shall offer to the Lord for his sin a spotless calf, and he shall bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony before the Lord, lay his hand upon its head, and immolate it to the Lord.” This was thus fulfilled. Adam—not the same Adam in person, but the same in nature—namely, the new Adam, God and man, Christ Jesus, offered a spotless calf for his sin: for his “sin,” that is, for the sin of his own people. Through his grace he made our sin his own debt. Hence he says in the Psalm: “Then I paid what I had not seized” (Ps. LXVIII).

What spotless calf did he offer? Himself: his spotless body, conceived and born without any stain of sin, from the herd of great oxen—that is, from the race of the ancient patriarchs. He brought that calf, that is, himself, and stood at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony: of the heavenly and true tabernacle, which had been closed to us, so that by his blood he might open for us the heavenly holy of holies. He laid his hand upon its head and immolated it to the Lord: that is, he rendered himself obedient and offered himself as a sacrifice to God his Father.

And it should be noted that “to the Lord” is repeated three times: “He shall offer a spotless calf to the Lord; he shall bring it before the Lord; and he shall immolate it to the Lord.” For Christ sacrificed the calf of his humanity to the ruling Trinity, satisfying for us by a death of three days. Hence he further continues: “He shall also take some of the blood of the calf and bring it into the tabernacle of testimony. And when he has dipped his finger in the blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before the Lord, toward the veil of the sanctuary; and he shall put some of the same blood upon the horn of the altar of most pleasing incense to the Lord, which is in the tabernacle of testimony.”

This too was thus fulfilled. For Christ, the calf of our propitiation, “entered once into the holy places through his own blood” (Heb. IX). This does not mean, for example, that he himself carried into those heavenly holy places the blood of his body which flowed from his side when pierced by the lance; rather, he brought before God the Father the effect of that blood—namely, the remission of sins for the whole Church, which is the tabernacle of his testimony. How? “And when he has dipped his finger,” he says, “in the blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before the Lord toward the veil of the sanctuary,” etc.

To dip the finger in the blood is to give the Holy Spirit through his blood. For the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God, as in the saying: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI), which another Evangelist expresses more plainly: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. XII). Moreover, this Holy Spirit is given to no one for the remission of sins except through Christ’s blood. Hence that saying: “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John VII).

“Therefore, when the priest has dipped his finger in the blood”—that is, when through his own blood he has obtained the Holy Spirit—“he shall sprinkle it,” he says, “seven times before the Lord toward the veil of the sanctuary.” This Holy Spirit is sevenfold. The veil of the sanctuary signifies the covering or closure of the heavenly mysteries of Christ himself, the Son of God. Thus, to sprinkle the blood seven times with the finger dipped in it is, through the sevenfold Spirit given by his passion, to open the understanding of the disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV).

“And he shall put,” he says, “some of the same blood upon the horn of the altar of incense most pleasing to the Lord, which is in the tabernacle of testimony.” The horn of the altar is the strength or exaltation of Christ himself. Hence the Psalmist says: “Keep the feast day in thick branches even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. CXVII): that is, abstain from servile works and attend to good works until you come to knowledge of Christ’s divinity, which is the exaltation of your mind. The altar is called that of incense most pleasing to the Lord because God the Father receives the incense, or fragrant offerings, of our prayers only from Christ or through Christ.

“He shall therefore put some of the same blood upon the horn of the altar of incense”: that is, raised from the dead, ascended into heaven, and seated at the right hand of God, he will preserve forever the traces of his passion—the scars of the wounds, the marks of the nails and lance—so that by this memorial of most pleasing fragrance he may always intercede for us.

## CHAPTER XV

That pouring the remaining blood at the base of the altar at the entrance of the tabernacle signifies that the nations are baptized into his death after his passion.

“But he shall pour all the remaining blood at the base of the altar of burnt offering, at the entrance of the tabernacle.” The foundation of Christian faith is baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Therefore it is rightly said, “at the entrance of the tabernacle,” because no one has entrance into the tabernacle of the Lord, which is the Church of God, except through the regeneration of baptism. He says: “But he shall pour all the remaining blood at the base of the altar.”

For after he rose from the dead he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). By this saying he surely poured the remnant of his blood at the base of the altar. For the Apostle also says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. VI), etc. Therefore, “he shall pour the remaining blood at the base of the altar at the entrance of the tabernacle”: that is, after he has cleansed through his blood all the elect of former times, he gives the remaining portion of the same grace to nations and Jews who will believe in the future through the word of the apostles, at the entrance of the true tabernacle. Thus, through baptism, all who wish to be united to his body—that is, to enter his Church and become sharers in his resurrection—may be planted together in the likeness of his death.

## CHAPTER XVI

What it means that the skin, flesh, head, feet, intestines, and dung are burned outside the camp, and the ashes poured into a clean place; that the fat of the calf is offered for sin; and that in the sacrifice of bread and wine there is the truth of flesh and blood and the whole grace of the incarnate Word.

[Col. 0759D] “And he shall offer the fat of the calf for sin: both that which covers the vital parts and all that is within; the two kidneys and the membrane above them, together with the fat of the liver and the kidneys, as it is removed from the calf of the peace-offering; and he shall burn them upon the altar of burnt-offering. But the hide, and all the flesh, with the head and feet, entrails and dung, and the rest of the body, he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place, where ashes are customarily poured out. And he shall burn it upon a pile of wood, which shall be burned in the place where the ashes are poured out.”

There can therefore be no doubt that the body of the victim which is commanded to be burned outside the camp signifies that the Lord Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the apostolic testimony confirms (Heb. XIII), cited above. What, then, does this reservation of the fat and of the other things commanded to be separated for the burnt-offering mean, except that the same calf, the same great priest, who was presently to be led out, made an evening sacrifice by changing bread and wine into his body and blood. For in this sacrifice you do not attend to the hide—that is, the visible appearance of man—or to all the dung of our mortal and wretched substance; rather, faith there grasps, and the mind of the soul perceives, whatever fatness there is—that is, whatever spiritual grace is in Christ.

Hence the holy Church, together with its same head, says: “Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII). Yet one may ask this: although it is said to be body and blood, bread is not changed into the appearance of flesh, nor [Col. 0760B] wine into the dreadful appearance of blood. That is, some common person may murmur: why does not the priest also burn the calf’s dung and hide? But these were once burned outside the gate, when the fire of the Passion consumed the hide of our mortality and corruption upon the pile of wood—that is, upon the gibbet of the cross—and finally, when he himself rose from the dead, what was mortal was swallowed up by life.

Why after his resurrection was he made invisible, and seen only when he wished and by whom he wished, so that he vanished when he wished, unless because all corruption had been swallowed up? For what is necessarily visible is without doubt also corruptible. Therefore let no scruple of unbelief trouble anyone concerning the dung and hide of the calf—that is, concerning the visible and corruptible appearance of the Lord’s body and blood.

[Col. 0760C] For Christian faith acknowledges that the whole fat, the whole richness of the calf—that is, the entire grace and truth of the incarnate Word, by which the faithful soul needs to be filled—is present there. In name, reality, and effect, it is true flesh and true blood. In name, certainly, because the priest who performs the consecrations, and who gives true names to things, said: “This is my body. This is the chalice of my blood.” In reality, because it is indeed the Holy of Holies, just as truly as this priest who sanctifies is the Holy of Holies. In effect likewise, because, just as by suffering once he effectively brought remission of sins to all in the past, so now he powerfully bestows remission of sins upon those who come to the Church through the same faith and worthily receive it.

Where the faithful soul is filled with such abundant fatness, possessing so many elements of true being, why should you be disturbed because the hide and dung—that is, the dreadful appearance of flesh and blood—do not appear? Yet the priest who is Christ’s vicar should not overlook this: together with the fat, that great Priest also offered to God his Father as a burnt-offering the two kidneys and the membrane of the liver—that is, every movement of his own will according to this spiritual law. For he did not yield to the reproaches of his kidneys; rather, before the hide and dung of his flesh were carried outside the gate to be burned in the manner described, he had burned his kidneys. For he said: “Not my will, my Father, but yours be done” (Luke XXII).

[Col. 0761A] This, I say, no priest should overlook; but from Christ’s example he too should strive to burn—that is, to mortify—his kidneys together with the liver: that is, the pleasure of the flesh or the desire which, according to natural philosophers, resides in the liver.

“They shall be burned,” it says, “in a clean place where ashes are customarily poured out.” The place where ashes are customarily poured out is the common bosom of the earth and the necessity of human burial. For there ashes are customarily poured out—that is, the bodies of all mortals, soon to be dissolved into ash. The word “clean,” however, the holy Evangelist did not pass over. After saying, “Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a tomb” (John XIX), he immediately added, “in which no one had yet been laid” (ibid.).

He thus emphatically expressed the singular purity of this unique ash, saying not merely that it was laid in a place where ashes are customarily poured out, but in a clean place. For just as no one had previously entered the womb from which he was conceived, and just as no one had previously been laid in the tomb in which he was placed, so no one’s ash had ever been poured out in that purity into which this ash was poured. Hence this holy ash, by granting them participation in itself, will be able to restore the ashes of all to their former state. Indeed, it was poured into the earth precisely because, being clean, it might raise again with itself our bodies, returned to ash because of sins.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the words, “If the whole assembly of Israel shall be ignorant,” etc.: that actual sins are to be understood through that ignorance of the multitude, and that these too, like original sin, are abolished through the mystery of Christ’s Passion.

“If the whole assembly of Israel shall be ignorant, and through inexperience shall do what is contrary to the Lord’s commandment, and afterward shall understand its sin, it shall offer a calf for sin and bring it to the door of the tabernacle; and the elders of the people shall lay their hands upon its head before the Lord,” etc., as above.

What has been said thus far could likewise have been said even if the one and only original sin had been abolished by Christ’s death. But the Apostle says: “And not as through one sin is the gift. For judgment from one offense came unto condemnation, but grace from many offenses unto justification. For if death reigned through one by the offense of one, much more those receiving the abundance of grace and of the gift and of righteousness shall reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ” (Rom. V).

Both by this testimony of the Apostle and by the whole teaching of evangelical truth, Catholic faith firmly maintains that not original sin only, but also all actual sins together, are remitted to us through the Passion of Christ, the Son of God. Well, then, after the Law speaks of the priest’s sin, it adds: “If the whole assembly of Israel shall be ignorant and through inexperience shall do what is contrary to the Lord’s commandment,” etc.

After the priest’s sin, the entire multitude also became ignorant; because after the first man sinned—he who, as was said above, ought to have been a priest in God’s paradise and to have offered sacrifices of thanksgiving and praise—the whole populous mass of humankind also fell away into ignorance of God, accumulating actual sins upon original guilt. Hence the Apostle says: “There is no one righteous, no one who understands or seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Rom. III), etc.; words taken from the testimony of the Psalm (Ps. XIII).

And in order to prove that the Jew who rests in the Law and boasts in God is not excepted from this universality of those who have turned aside and become useless, he immediately added: “But we know that whatever things the Law speaks, it speaks to those who are under the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped” (Rom. III), etc. Therefore both the sin of the priest, who caused the people to sin, and the sin of the whole assembly together are lawfully expiated by the same animal—that is, the calf—and by the same rite of sacrifice; because both original sin, contracted from Adam, and all actual sins together are abolished by the same sacrament of Christ’s Passion.

Upon the head of that irrational animal only the elders laid hands, for the whole multitude could not all lay hands upon one animal. But we, the whole multitude—whoever have been baptized into his death—laid hands upon the head of this rational calf, that is, Christ. For we imposed upon his head and strong shoulders all our sins to be borne or taken away; indeed, God did so through our hands. “Through hands,” that is, through the faith or profession of believers, he placed upon him the iniquities of us all (Isa. LIII).

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 0762C] On the sin committed after baptism, according to the Law’s words, “If a ruler sins,” etc.; on who the ruler is and what soul is meant by “one of the people of the land”; and on the ruler’s offering, that is, the offering of a prelate.

“If a ruler sins and through ignorance does one thing among many forbidden by the Lord’s Law, and afterward understands his sin, he shall offer to the Lord an unblemished he-goat from the goats, and shall lay his hand upon its head. When he has slain it in the place where the burnt-offering is customarily killed before the Lord, because it is for sin, the priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the victim for sin, touching the horns of the altar of burnt-offering and pouring the rest at its base. He shall burn the fat upon it, as is customarily done with peace-offerings.”

After the sacrament of Christ’s Passion, received in baptism, those who sin are no longer offered the same remedy or the same abundance of grace. For Christ became our victim for sin, a victim for which we once rendered a sure redemption for sins when each of us was baptized into his death. In comparison with the security which we received in baptism concerning former sins, whether as infants or as adults, redemption is exceedingly precarious if we sin again, however worthy fruits of repentance we may produce.

Although it has been said, “On whatever day a man who has turned back groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XVIII), it has not also been said: On whatever day he groans, his sins shall be forgiven him. Nor is it certain whether they are forgiven in this age or in the age to come. For it was not said lightly or doubtfully: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (I Cor. III).

Yet this statement may rightly be understood of the primary conversion by which someone turns from the error and sins of Adam, the old man, and passes with groaning to the Lord or the Son of God; thereby the son does not bear the iniquity of his father—namely, of him who first sinned.

Therefore, after the rite for sacrificing the calf has been given, the victim is made smaller when it says: “If a ruler sins and does one thing among many forbidden by the Lord’s Law, he shall offer a he-goat.” And afterward: “But if a soul from the people of the land sins through ignorance and recognizes its sin, it shall offer an unblemished she-goat,” etc.

The ruler is he who stands preeminent among many as a ram among sheep or as a he-goat among she-goats. If he sins and does one thing among many forbidden by the Lord’s Law, then by that very fact that he sins he sets a bad example before his inferiors. “But if afterward he recognizes his sin, he shall offer,” it says, “a victim to the Lord”—not again a calf, but “a he-goat.” For he shall not again be renewed unto repentance, that is, baptized again, which would be to crucify the Son of God afresh in himself and expose him to contempt (Heb. VI). Rather, “he shall offer a he-goat”: that is, through the mortification of actual repentance, he shall slaughter himself, so that he may profitably receive from the holy altar, for your sin, the sacrament of that same Passion of Christ.

For by sinning and doing one thing among many forbidden by the Lord’s Law—for example, by committing adultery or striking with a murderous horn—he himself has become a he-goat, such as will indeed be placed on the left, to whom it will be said: “Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). Therefore, if he desires to be saved, he shall slaughter the he-goat: that is, by repenting, he shall punish himself.

Where? “In the place,” it says, “where burnt-offerings are customarily slain before the Lord.” The place in which burnt-offerings are customarily slain is the Catholic Church. Outside it there is no place for a true sacrifice. Therefore he shall repent in the Catholic Church, in the confession of the true faith, and upon this foundation he shall build works worthy of repentance.

“The priest,” it says, “shall dip his finger in the blood of the victim for sin, touching the horns of the altar of burnt-offering and pouring the rest at its base.” In this sacrifice too, spiritually, the priest and the victim are the same, because he offers himself. “I beseech you,” says the Apostle, “to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, your rational service” (Rom. XI). Those who do this will rejoice, saying according to the Apocalypse: “You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (Apoc. V).

The priest therefore dips his finger in the blood of his own victim when he applies the discernment of active repentance even to the mortification of his own desire. He touches the horns of the altar when, after recovering his former dignity, he again undertakes the authority of teaching others—as did he who, after saying penitently following his guilt, “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit” (Ps. L), immediately added, “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you” (ibid.).

There is, nevertheless, some difference. A sin committed secretly and disclosed to a priest by voluntary confession is forgiven, at the priest’s intercession, with such generosity that former dignity too is recovered along with pardon. But a crime detected or publicly proven makes a person, after repentance, content with lay communion alone, according to the authority of the sacred canons.

It should also be noted that above the horns of the inner altar of incense are dipped in the blood of the calf, whereas here the horns of the outer altar of burnt-offering are dipped in the blood of the he-goat, and subsequently in that of the she-goat. For, as was said above, compared with the security received in baptism, redemption is exceedingly precarious if we sin again. But “he shall pour the remaining blood,” it says, “at its base,” when thereafter he guards against all temptations of desires, pouring them out in pure confession.

He also burns the fat as is customary in peace-offerings, when, as said above, he aims to possess the settled state of the peaceable, such as the Apostle longed for when he said: “I delight in the Law of God according to the inward man, but I see another law in my members” (Rom. VII).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the sin of the commoner, that is, the subordinate, and his offering, [Col. 0764C] and on the words, “If he sins through ignorance,” etc.

“But if a soul from the people of the land sins through ignorance, doing anything forbidden by the Lord’s Law and thus transgresses, and recognizes its sin, it shall offer an unblemished she-goat,” etc.

The law for the commoner is the same as that for the ruler, except that the ruler must offer a male he-goat and the commoner a female she-goat; and this is fitting. For as a female does not conceive from herself but receives seed from a male, so a commoner or member of the people does not discover the fire of sins from himself, but commits sin by following the prior example of a superior. The law, I say, is the same for both: for both he who supplies a bad example and he who imitates it need the same cleansing of repentance.

Finally, one must ask why the Law, assigning a certain limit to pardonable sin, says: “If he sins through ignorance.” If we suppose that sinning through ignorance means lacking discernment of good and evil, or not having read or heard the Lord’s commandments, then after sin the Law of the Lord admits no one possessing knowledge within the doors of its propitiation. But far be this! For who in this respect—that is, in knowledge of the Law—was greater than David? Yet after adultery and homicide together, he was received when penitent (II Kings XII).

We must therefore ask what the limit is, which, once the sinner has reached it, warrants the judgment that he sins not through ignorance. We say, then, that when someone has proceeded so far that, even when reproved concerning his sin, he not only does not amend but moreover wishes to defend his deeds, then at last he must be said to sin not through ignorance but knowingly, and therefore to have no excuse for his sin.

For there is an ignorance not so much of age or simplicity as of weakness: at the hour of temptation the mind is enveloped in such darkness that in a wonderful manner it does not know what it knows and does not see what it sees. Of this kind of ignorance the Apostle said: “[A high priest] can have compassion on those who are ignorant and err,” for he immediately added, “because he himself also is encompassed with weakness” (Heb. V).

This law of mercy extends a hand only to those who are of this kind, and it embraces within the compass of redemption only the sins of those who sin through ignorance. For those who approve of their sins, who love iniquity and willingly look upon it, and who, when reproved, as has just been said, uphold their sins with proud defense—for them there is no place of propitiation. Hence the Psalmist says: “If I have looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. LXV). And the Apostle says: “For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. X).

## CHAPTER XX. On the words, “But if he offers from the flock,” in accordance with the counsel of Matthew XIX in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect,” etc.

“But if he offers from the flock a victim for sin, namely an unblemished sheep, he shall lay his hand upon its head and slaughter it in the place where the victims for burnt-offerings are customarily slain,” etc., as above.

After giving a commandment, the spiritual and holy Law also provides counsel. What it has so far said about offering a he-goat or she-goat to one who recognizes his sin is a commandment. But what it now says about offering a sheep is counsel. For it does not say, “He shall offer a sheep,” but conditionally: “But if,” it says, “he offers from the flock a sheep for sin.”

Here we rightly understand the Holy Spirit to have signified what Christ’s Gospel now openly proclaims: repentance is preached as a commandment to sinners, yet the counsel of perfection is not concealed. To sinners it says by way of commandment: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV). And John, with a warning of coming wrath, says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. III). But to the righteous person it says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX).

Indeed, one who repents according to this distinction, giving some things as a fruit of repentance but retaining some for himself, sacrifices a he-goat which will not be shorn. But one who reserves nothing for himself, sells all and gives it to the poor, and thus follows Christ, sacrifices a shorn sheep. Beholding a flock of such sheep in the holy Church, the Bridegroom says in the Song: “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing” (Song IV).

But this, as stated above, is counsel rather than commandment: namely, to give all things and retain nothing. Therefore, “if,” it says, “he offers an unblemished sheep”—that is, if he leaves even a simple life and lawful manner of living, in order that he may more effectively take the kingdom of heaven by force—“he shall lay his hand upon its head,” that is, he shall profess his vow by an evident action. Thereafter he will no longer be permitted to possess anything as his own—nothing whatsoever—not even his own body under his own authority. “And he shall slaughter it in the place where the victims for burnt-offerings are customarily slain,” etc., as above.

## CHAPTER XXI. “If a soul sins and hears the voice of one swearing,” etc., to be understood in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them”; and that the touch of uncleanness is consent to sin.

(CHAPTER V.) “If a soul sins and hears the voice of one swearing, and is a witness because he himself has seen or knows of it, unless he gives judgment, he shall bear his iniquity.”

After saying, “Although they knew the righteousness of God, they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death” (Rom. I), the Apostle immediately added: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them” (ibid.). This sacred Law says the same thing harmoniously in the present passage. For until now it has spoken of those who do one thing among many forbidden by the Lord’s Law; now it plainly instructs concerning those who consent to those who act.

“If a soul sins,” it says, “and hears the voice of one swearing,” etc. Without doubt, the one who swears falsely does one thing among many forbidden by the Lord’s Law. But one who is a witness or has knowledge, who saw or heard that in which the other swore falsely, yet is silent and does not report it, unquestionably consents by his silence; by failing to report it he has made himself a participant in the perjury. And because he did not report it, he shall bear his own iniquity, because in consenting he is such as the other is in acting, as the Apostle just cited testifies.

Therefore, having spoken above of those who act, and now begun his statement about those who consent to those acting, the Law, about to show a remedy, continues: “A soul which has touched anything unclean, whether something killed by a beast, or dead of itself, or any other creeping thing, and has forgotten its uncleanness, is guilty and has sinned. And if it touches anything of human uncleanness, according to every iniquity by which one is customarily defiled, and afterward recognizes it after having forgotten, it shall be subject to guilt.”

What it signified by saying, “A soul which has touched anything unclean, whether something killed by a beast,” it nearly expressed by saying, “and if it touches anything of human uncleanness,” etc. For human uncleanness is truly a carcass, because through works of uncleanness it has driven the true life—that is, God’s Spirit—far from itself; and thus the soul, deprived of God, stinks as though dead, just as the body decays when it has lost its soul.

One touches who consents; and in touching the uncleanness of a human being, as it were a carcass, one licks it with a flattering tongue. But if one does not consent, one is not defiled by mere bodily touch, nor is the soul made guilty. Yet if the uncleanness is heretical, it must not be touched even by bodily contact or cohabitation, but must especially be avoided. For if, by the Apostle’s command, a carnal fornicator is to be avoided so completely that one ought not even to take food with such a person (I Cor. V), how much more ought one avoid him who speaks wrongly concerning God?

The Lord says: “There is no one who performs any mighty work in my name and can soon speak evil of me” (Mark IX). Therefore one who, by speaking wrongly of the Son of God, is an evil heretic cannot confer the power of baptism, although we establish that a fornicator or drunkard could baptize validly.

> [Note: [Col. 0767D] Understand this if, in the form of baptism, by heretical persuasion he has not expressly named the Son of God, as though the Son’s name were unnecessary, together [Col. 0768D] with the name of the Father and of the Holy Spirit.]

Heretical uncleanness, whose every work or mystery is a kind of corpse-like thing, must therefore especially be avoided. Its corpse—whether killed by a beast or dead of itself [Col. 0767B]—that is, whether corrupted by another’s fault or its own: whatever the uncleanness of the person and however it may be constituted, the soul which touches it, which consents to it, and still more which defends it, if after forgetting it later recognizes it, shall be subject to guilt.

Or, as said above, it shall bear its iniquity—that is, by performing worthy repentance it shall be subject, I say, to guilt: it shall bear its guilt in this age, lest it be crushed beneath it in the age to come. It must certainly be observed that it says, “and, having forgotten, afterward recognizes it.” For unless one later recognizes what one had negligently forgotten, one will not be subject to one’s guilt, will not bear it—indeed, will not carry away one’s iniquity by performing worthy repentance.

Yet, unlike the other cases, the manner or quantity of the offering is not defined in this case, because consent is not the same for all persons or at all times. For it sometimes happens by necessity that someone says that he consents. Therefore, when it says, “and, having forgotten, afterward recognizes it,” the question of what burden of repentance he is deservedly commanded to undergo is rightly left to his understanding or conscience.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the words, “A soul which swears,” etc.; on one who swore to do evil, who is guilty whether he does it or does not do it; and on how and what the one who swore should offer.

“A soul which swears and declares with its lips that it will do something either evil or good, and confirms the same by oath or speech, and afterward, having forgotten, recognizes its sin, shall do repentance for sin and offer a lamb from the flock or a she-goat.”

This passage is one of those of which it is sung in the Psalm: “He rains snares upon sinners” (Ps. X). For it ensnared many sinners: for example, Herod in John’s beheading. Having sworn to the dancing girl, he therefore seemed bound by legal necessity to kill him, lest he commit perjury (Matt. XIV). It also ensnared the forty Jews in the Acts of the Apostles, who vowed not to eat bread before killing Paul (Acts XIV). For they thought that, whatever they had sworn or vowed—whether good or evil—they would be free under the Law provided only that they fulfilled what they had sworn.

For the Law says: “A soul which swears and declares with its lips that it will do something evil or good,” etc. Was this then to be understood to mean that, whether a person had sworn to act well or ill, and had forgotten to carry it out, he should do penance for that reason? This is what those thought who were always inclined toward evil as much as toward good—indeed, more toward evil than toward good.

But according to the truth, the meaning of this present passage is as follows: one who swore to do something good is free if he carries it out; if he does not fulfill it, he is guilty. But one who swore to do something evil—for example, to remain with a prostitute—is guilty whether he carries it out or not. Thus, besieged on every side because he does not wish to leave by the lawful gate, he must leap down from the lower part of the wall—that is, sin in that matter in which the sin is lighter and can be cured by a more immediate remedy.

Yet morally it may rightly be said that the person has sworn to do evil to himself who has vowed to wear down his flesh through abstinence, a thing altogether evil and harsh to the perceptions of the flesh. Therefore, one who, after forgetting, later recognizes his oath or vow, “shall offer,” it says, “a lamb from the flock or a she-goat.” What does the lamb signify except the innocence of the active life? What does the she-goat, feeding often while hanging on the highest and outermost rocks, signify except the contemplative life?

Therefore, one who sees that he has not fulfilled his promises and resolutions should apply himself more diligently to God’s sacrifice, either through the innocence of good work or through the lofty pasture of contemplation. And fittingly a ewe-lamb from the flock is not commanded to be offered, whereas a she-goat from the flock is; for the active life belongs to many, the contemplative life to few.

“But if his hand is not able to offer an animal, he shall offer to the Lord two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and the other for a burnt-offering; and he shall give them to the priest,” etc.

According to the letter, the Law of the Lord kindly provides for the poor, being content with what can be obtained more cheaply. According to the spiritual understanding, however, it gives counsel to those whose minds are so poor that they cannot be as those who use the world as though not using it, buy as though not possessing, or have wives as though not having them (I Cor. VII).

For what is it to be unable to find a ewe-lamb or a she-goat and therefore to offer two young pigeons or two turtledoves, except to be unable in a secular manner of life to pursue either the active or the contemplative life, and therefore to transfer publicly by profession into the spiritual order, according to the Psalm: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. LIV)?

What, moreover, is signified by the two turtledoves except a twofold groaning of repentance, so that, when we do not rise to offer good works, we may pour ourselves out doubly, because we have both failed to do what was right and committed what was wrong? Hence one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt-offering. A burnt-offering is so called because it is wholly burned. Thus we offer one turtledove for sin when we groan for guilt. But we make a burnt-offering from the other when, because we have neglected good things, we wholly inflame ourselves and burn with the fire of sorrow.

And the head is rightly commanded to be bent back toward the wings, so that you may do what you say and join your mouth to works. Yet the head must not be cut off so that it is separated from the body; rather, “it shall adhere to the neck,” it says, because the mind, signified by the head, must be cut away from fleshly pleasure, but the necessary care of the flesh must not be cut away.

According to the allegorical meaning also, the head of the turtledove was cut, and yet was not severed from its body, because by undergoing death for us Christ, our head, truly joined us all together in that very death of his. Therefore the cut head of the turtledove remained attached to the body, because our Redeemer suffered for us, yet was not separated from us by his Passion.

But rare is the person who, pierced by the spirit of devotion, knows how to take wings like a dove, fly, and rest (ibid.), and so knows how to utter the groaning of a turtledove or a dove in repentance or prayer. But the law of mercy is extended still further, and adds:

## CHAPTER XXIII. On one unable to offer two turtledoves or young pigeons: what it mystically signifies to offer a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour.

“But if his hand cannot offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall offer for sin fine flour, a tenth part of an ephah. He shall not put oil into it nor place any incense upon it, because it is for sin. And he shall give it to the priest, who, taking a full handful from it, shall burn it upon the altar as a memorial of the one who offered it, praying for him and making expiation. The remaining part, however, he shall have as an offering.”

An ephah and a bath are the same measure, of three modii. In his Gospel the Lord of the Law says: “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward” (Matt. X). Let us say likewise, according to the wording of the present passage: he who feeds a priest in the name of a priest shall receive a priest’s reward.

“If his hand cannot offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons,” this means spiritually that one who cannot pray or have, as stated above, a twofold groaning in prayer should feed one whose office is always to pray, so that by sowing his carnal things he may worthily deserve to reap that person’s spiritual things (I Cor. IX).

It should therefore be observed that it says: “Taking a full handful from it, he shall burn it upon the altar as a memorial of the one who offered it, praying for him and making expiation; but the remaining part he himself shall have as an offering.” For then a priest lawfully receives the sinner’s gift, when first lifting up the person’s remembrance before the Lord with the full handful of his conscience, he burns the prayer poured out for him with the true and lawful fire of charity.

But if he does not care for such a person and, with his mouth filled by the gift, closes it against prayer, he takes another’s sin upon himself; and there is fulfilled in him what the Lord says through the prophet concerning such people: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. IV).

Likewise, one must not pass over what is said concerning this kind of offering: “He shall not put oil into it nor place any incense upon it, because it is for sin.” For it makes a great difference whether someone gives from a gratuitous vow and free charity, or from servile fear because of a crime committed. In the former case, the oil of cheerfulness shines, which God loves in the giver; in the latter, it is well if there is not present the dark eye of one wishing to sin with impunity, which God hates. There incense of devotion delights God who receives it with a sweet odor; here it is well if the gift not offered does not offend by the stench of unworthy repentance.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What it is to sin through error in things sacrificed to the Lord; and what it is to offer for this a ram bought for two shekels, and to restore the damage with the addition of a fifth part.

[Col. 0770B] “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a person, through error, transgresses the sacred ordinances by sinning in matters consecrated to the Lord, he shall offer for his offence an unblemished ram from the flock, which may be bought for two shekels, according to the sanctuary weight. And he shall restore the damage which he caused, and add a fifth part over and above, delivering it to the priest.” Sacred ordinances are the rites of sacrifice, or all sacred things, which in Greek are called *orgia* [sacred rites]. Moreover, the rites of sacrifice and our true *orgia* are all the visible sacraments of Christ the Son of God which we celebrate in the holy Church; of these baptism and the Eucharist are the greatest, having been instituted by our Lord himself, while the secondary observances are those thereafter rightly and profitably arranged concerning these matters by the holy apostles or apostolic men.

And in [Col. 0770C] these we sin and inflict loss upon the household of our Lord whenever, with wandering heart, roving eyes, ears strained and turned aside toward vanities, otherwise occupied—or rather idle—we disturb and rend the sacrifice of praise which is uttered in our mouths, and sometimes lose some portion of the holy men that has escaped us. Sometimes indeed—and this is greatly to be feared—even the most precious substance of the Lord’s body and blood is lost through such carelessness. Therefore, when this happens, the person through whose negligence it occurred should understand what is now said: “He shall offer for his offence an unblemished ram from the flock,” etc.

That is, he must offer an unblemished ram, whose whole price is two shekels: namely, the twofold commandment of love for God and neighbour, according to the weight of the heavenly sanctuary not made by hands. For it was not an earthly human being, but the God of heaven, who weighed out the two commandments of love, by which alone we redeem the soul that must be offered to God, since love alone covers a multitude of sins (1 Pet. 4). Each shekel, according to the sanctuary weight, contains twenty obols; and here they signify the two Testaments, without whose fullness neither commandment of love is established.

But to add a fifth part in restoring the loss means not only to repent in heart, but also to punish through outward penitence the five bodily senses by whose wandering the error was committed. “The priest,” that is, “shall make intercession for him by offering the ram, and it shall be forgiven him.” Then God will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, when the priest intercedes for us—namely, that priest “who died—indeed, who also rose again—who is at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us” (Rom. 8), no longer by the submission of prayers, but by presenting the case to be pleaded.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the words, “If a person sins through ignorance,” and on the fact that ignorance has different modes

“If a person sins through ignorance and does one of those things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and afterward, guilty of sin, understands his iniquity, he shall offer to the priest an unblemished ram from the flock according to the measure and valuation of the sin.”

It should be noted that, although up to this point he prescribed different remedies for those sinning through ignorance according to the character of the sins or the condition of the sinners, he now decrees, as though changing his judgment, that a person—that is, any human being whatsoever his condition—who likewise sins through ignorance shall offer one and the same animal, namely an unblemished ram. But one must understand that there is a difference between a person’s ignorance arising from an overwhelming blindness of mind, and ignorance or error arising from lack of knowledge of the law or from heedless negligence. For example, the drunken person is ignorant in one way, the sober person in another. The former errs because through vice he has lost the sound condition of his mind; the latter because he has never possessed knowledge of the matter in question.

Thus, surely, one whose eye has been darkened by desire is ignorant in one way; one who, through age or simplicity, does not know what lies between his right hand and his left is ignorant in another. [Col. 0771C] For if there were not an ignorance brought about by the madness of evil desire, David—indeed, learned in the law and accustomed to the Holy Spirit from childhood—would never have said: “Remember not the offences of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24). And of one who is ignorant in this manner you may rightly say: “The one who is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14)—unless, it is understood, he afterwards comes to understanding through repentance.

But concerning those who are ignorant through lack of knowledge, God speaks through his prophet: “You grieve over the ivy, for which you did not labour, which came into being in one night and perished in one night; and shall I not spare Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand human beings who do not know what is between their right hand and their left?” (Jon. 4). It is evident that the present passage speaks of such people. For it follows: “The priest shall pray for him concerning what he did unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him, because he sinned against the Lord through error.” Therefore it is not without reason that every person here offers an unblemished ram, whereas above one who sinned through ignorance was commanded to offer a goat for sin. For as much as an unblemished ram surpasses a lustful goat, so much nearer to pardon is the person who erred unknowingly than the one whom his own desire stupefied in order that he might be ignorant.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the words, “The person who, having despised the Lord, denies a deposit entrusted by his neighbour”

(CHAPTER VI.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If a person sins and, having despised the Lord, denies to his neighbour a deposit entrusted to his fidelity; or extorts something by violence; or commits fraud; or finds a lost object and, further denying it, swears falsely; or does any other of the many things by which people commonly sin: convicted of the offence, he shall restore in full all that he wished to obtain by deceit, and shall add a fifth part besides to the person upon whom he inflicted loss,” etc.

No one should suppose that the holy law is contrary to itself because elsewhere it says, “Whoever does this or that shall surely die, and his blood shall be upon his own head,” whereas here an offering is accepted and, through the priest’s intercession, forgiveness granted for every sin without any exception among all things forbidden by the law of the Lord. For one kind of accusation mercy pardons in sacrifices, another justice condemns in judgments. For example, suppose someone has committed adultery, has been caught by no one, and cannot be accused by any witnesses, but makes himself his own accuser: such a person is admitted under this present law, which mercy established, and by sacrifice, through the mediation of the priest, obtains remission.

Hence this law everywhere expressly sets the condition for receiving sacrifice by saying, “if he understands his sin.” But if, after committing the crime, he is caught or becomes known through another person, he is killed, stoned, and his blood is imputed to his own head. Thus the holy law is not contrary to itself; Christ’s Church observes it still today. For it gladly receives among the gates of pardon a hidden cause of sin disclosed in secret confession; but crimes discovered or made known through another person are punished without remedy not only by a civil tribunal but also by synodal severity. The former deprives the guilty of life; the latter deprives them of ecclesiastical honours. Therefore the present words, “convicted of the offence, let him restore everything,” must be understood in this sense: he is convicted by the witness of conscience so that he may accuse himself in voluntary confession.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the words, “This is the law of the holocaust,” that this is in a sense a conclusion of what has been said above, and that our sacrifice for sin is faith, the peace-offering hope, and the holocaust love

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the holocaust.” [Col. 0772D] Teachers of secular eloquence are accustomed to take great care that they conclude the end of their discourse by a recapitulation of their purpose, gathering together and recalling the matters of which they have spoken, so that the discourse may be renewed rather than begun afresh, and so that the hearer, if he has committed it to memory, may be brought back to what he himself remembers. This most ancient spokesman of the holy law has deigned to do here, gathering up what he has said thus far and recalling it in this manner: “This is the law of the holocaust; this is the law of the sin-offering; this is the law of the peace-offering.”

First, according to the spiritual and true order of sacrifice, we must set forth the most certain names of these sacrifices, lest there be doubt as to what work of our humility is the sacrifice for sin, what the peace-offering, and what the holocaust, as we have already said to the best of our ability. Our sacrifice for sin, then, is faith; the peace-offering is hope; and the holocaust is love. For although above, in an unarranged exposition, the holocaust was placed first and the sacrifice for sin last, nevertheless in the order of living and advancing the sacrifice for sin comes first—that is, faith—and the holocaust comes last—that is, love.

So too in the order of heavenly gifts by which the Son of God descended all the way to us, the spirit of wisdom comes first and the spirit of fear last. Yet, preserving the order of advancement by which we ascend to the Lord, the spirit of fear comes first, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110), while the spirit of wisdom is highest. Therefore the sacrifices here once concealed beneath the veil over Moses’ face have now been revealed in the face of Christ’s glory: faith, hope, and love. This is the law of the greatest of these—that is, of love, the great and true holocaust.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That the altar is Christ and the fire the Spirit of Christ, concerning which it says, “It shall be burned on the altar all night”; and its mystical meaning

“It shall be burned on the altar all night until morning. The fire shall be from the same altar. The priest shall be clothed in a linen tunic and linen breeches.” Our altar is Christ, of whom it is elsewhere said: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. 20), that is, you shall humbly believe in the incarnation of Christ, the Son of God. This visible altar is his sign: just as it stands above the whole temple, so Christ is head of the whole Church.

The fire from the same altar is the Holy Spirit: the fire which he came to cast upon the earth and ardently desired to be kindled (Luke 12). Our holocaust, moreover, is our heart wholly burned—that is, wholly given to divine love and, for his sake, separated from every love of the flesh. Night is the present life, however much it is illumined by the star-like gifts of this same fire, that is, of the Holy Spirit, in comparison with that day in which their God shall be seen in Zion (Ps. 83), when what we now see through a mirror in an enigma we shall see face to face (1 Cor. 13). “It shall be burned,” he says, “all night,” that is, until the end of life.

[Col. 0773D] How? “The priest,” he says, “shall be clothed in a linen tunic and breeches; and he shall take away the ashes which the devouring fire has consumed, and, placing them beside the altar, he shall put off his former garments; and, clothed in others, he shall carry them outside the camp and have them consumed to ashes in a very clean place.” The priestly linen tunic, as has already been said elsewhere, signifies the life of the new person; conversely, the tunic of skins with which Adam was clothed after sin signified the old life of the same old person.

The linen breeches signify the strict purpose of chastity with which anyone who desires bravely to devote his whole heart to the fire of divine love must gird himself, so that he does not yield even to the permitted love of the marriage bond; for such a person is divided and concerned with the things of this world, how he may please his wife (1 Cor. 7). The holocaust, I say, shall burn all night, and scarcely will anyone suffice to burn it wholly clean, burning without ceasing to the end of life.

“And he shall take away the ashes which the devouring fire has consumed.” The ashes left in the morning are impure thoughts, from which no one can be free by himself. For who, at that morning, at that dreadful end of his life, will boast that he has a chaste heart? For example, when any holy priest of this holocaust, or priestly beloved, says: “My beloved, I will take hold of you and lead you into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me” (Song 8), and in such images of a fleshly bridegroom and bride contemplates the truth of the heavenly union, where the creature hopes to enjoy the true embraces of the Creator, how can that person keep himself undefiled from every ash—that is, from thoughts of fleshly union?

“He shall therefore take away,” he says, “the ashes which the devouring fire has consumed, and place them beside the altar”: that is, he shall carry his small thoughts to Christ, who bears the whole care of our salvation. He shall do this through continual examination of his heart and frequent confession of heart and mouth. What follows? “He shall put off,” it says, “his former garments and, clothed in others, shall carry them outside the camp and have them consumed to ashes in a very clean place.” To put off the former garments means finally to lay aside the covering of the flesh; to be clothed in others means to receive the grace of eternal recompense.

Then “he shall carry them”—namely, his ashes—“outside the camp and have them consumed to ashes in a very clean place,” because outside the warfare of the present life love will indeed burn away completely the remnants of the aforesaid impurities in that most pure world. For, as Isaiah says, “This love is the fire of the Lord in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31)—that is, in the Church of this present life it is however small, but in that heavenly peace it is ineffable, such as “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the same fire which “shall always burn,” it says, “on the altar, which the priest shall nourish by placing wood upon it every morning”

“The fire on the altar shall always burn; the priest shall nourish it, placing wood upon it every morning, day by day. And when the holocaust has been laid upon it, he shall burn over it the fat of the peace-offerings. This is a perpetual fire, which shall never fail on the altar.”

The altar of God, as was said above, is faith in Christ in our heart. Upon it the fire is commanded always to burn because from it we must continually kindle toward the Lord the flame of love. The priest shall lay wood upon it each day, lest it be extinguished. For every preacher of Christ has indeed become a member of the high Priest, as the apostle Peter says to all believers: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2). And as the apostle John says: “You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (Rev. 5).

Therefore, let the priest nourishing the fire on the altar place wood upon it daily: that is, lest the flame of love fail in him, let every believer not cease to gather into his heart both the examples of those who went before and the testimonies of Holy Scripture. For it is as though one supplies fuel to the fire when, in the exercise of love, one furnishes either examples of the Fathers or commandments of the Lord. Since our inward newness itself grows old daily by the course of this life, this fire must be nourished by added wood, so that when it is weakened by the habit of our oldness, it may be revived through the testimonies and examples of the Fathers.

And it is rightly commanded that wood be gathered every morning, day by day. For these things are not done unless the night of blindness is extinguished. Or certainly, because morning is the first part of the day, every believer should set aside thoughts of the present life and consider this first: by what means he may kindle in himself the pursuit of love that is already, as it were, failing. For this fire upon the Lord’s altar—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is diligently restored by the examples of the Fathers and the Lord’s testimonies.

It is well added: “And after the holocaust has been laid upon it, he shall burn over it the fat of the peace-offerings.” For whoever kindles this fire of love also lays himself upon it as a holocaust, and burns away every vice by which he formerly lived wrongly. When he considers inwardly his thoughts and slays his reprobate life with the sword of conversion, he places himself upon the altar of his own heart and burns himself with the fire of love. The fat of this peace-offering is fragrant because the inward struggle of the new life, making peace between us and God, gives forth from us a most sweet odour.

And because this same love remains unextinguished in the hearts of the elect, it is fittingly added: “This is a perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar.” This fire indeed never fails from the altar, because even after this life the fervour of love increases in their minds. For eternal contemplation brings it about that the more almighty God is known, the more he is loved.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the law of sacrifice and libations: that it must be eaten without leaven—that is, good works must be done without the windy swelling of vainglory

“This is the law of sacrifice and libations, which the sons of Aaron shall offer before the Lord and before the altar. The priest shall take a handful of flour mingled with oil, and all the incense placed upon the flour. And he shall burn it on the altar as a memorial of a most sweet odour to the Lord. But Aaron with his sons shall eat the remainder of the flour without leaven, and shall eat it in the holy place of the tabernacle.”

It is best to make the holocaust spoken of above—the wholly burned offering—that is, to attribute wholly to God, not to oneself, a good work proved in the fire of love, and to flee the wind of popular praise, according to the command: “Beware of doing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6). Yet if you always flee a spectator, you will never have an imitator. Therefore the same Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5).
