Rightly, then, after the law of the holocaust, by which the hidden burning of love is signified, follows the law of its sacrifice and libations, a part of which Aaron and his sons eat; thereby is signified a good work done before people so that God may be glorified. “The priest,” it says, “shall take a handful of flour mingled with oil, and all that has been placed upon the flour”: that is, whoever offers God a work of righteousness shall consider the steadfastness of a most pure conscience, the intention of benefit to one’s neighbour, and the sweetly fragrant expectation of divine praise.

“And he shall burn these,” it says, “on the altar, but Aaron with his sons shall eat the remaining portion of the flour.” When one doing good has established the aforementioned things well in the root of his heart, he then rightly permits the light of his work to shine before people, so that he himself is not seen by people, but so that the Father in heaven may be glorified. Thus it shall be eaten without leaven, that is, without the windy swelling of vainglory; it shall be eaten “in the holy place of the tabernacle,” that is, the good work shall be performed for the common edification of Christ’s Church.

“It shall not be leavened,” he says, because a part of it is offered to the Lord as incense: that is, the good work will not be spoiled by the wind of empty glory, and the fact that it has been seen by people will not itself be reckoned as payment, because the whole intention of the worker is directed toward the Lord. “It shall be most holy”—even though people have seen and praised it—“as the offering for sin and for offence”; that is, where the intention is pure, it will no more be harmed by human praise than if a person guilty of transgression had paid something owed as a debt, in which every swelling of boastfulness certainly has less room.

And because not every good work should indiscriminately be made public, even as an example, “Only the males of Aaron’s stock,” it says, “shall eat of it”: that is, one will endeavour to make one’s righteousness shine only before those people of whom there may be hope that they will advance courageously by imitation. And because the whole desirable fruit of this public visibility is this: “Everyone,” it says, “who touches these things shall be sanctified,” that is, everyone who has imitated your good works shall be saved.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the offering of Aaron and his sons: that purity which is sought in others by counsel is required of priests

“This is the offering of Aaron and his sons which they must offer to the Lord on the day of their anointing. They shall offer a tenth part of an ephah of flour in a perpetual sacrifice: half of it in the morning and half in the evening. It shall be fried on a griddle, mingled with oil. The priest who succeeds his father by right shall offer it hot, as a most sweet odour before the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned upon the altar.”

The holocaust—that is, the secret sacrifice of true love, in which the faithful soul is free for contemplation of the Lord—is sought in other people by counsel, but required of priests by command. For example, that laypeople who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Cor. 7) is a matter of counsel. But that priests should be divided in such matters, neither law nor reason permits.

“This,” he says, “is the offering of Aaron and his sons on the day of their anointing.” By “on the day of their anointing” he means according to the commitment or course of their calling. For, lest you suppose that they must make this offering only on the one day upon which they were anointed, he immediately adds: “They shall offer a tenth part of an ephah in a perpetual sacrifice.” And, signifying that priests ought to devote the whole time of their lives to prayer, he says, “half of it in the morning and half in the evening.” If every morning and every evening, then at all times; for all time varies through the changing succession of morning and evening, that is, of day and night.

And because the priest’s breast ought to burn in remembrance of Christ’s passion through the compassion of love, “it shall be fried,” he says, “on a griddle mingled with oil.” And because nothing must be done lukewarmly or negligently in so great a matter, “the priest who succeeds his father by right,” he says, “shall offer it hot as an odour of sweetness to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned upon the altar,” as was said above.

And because it is unworthy for a priest to need reconciliation—for what standing or dignity is there in the priesthood if he entangles himself in secular affairs and becomes as the people, so the priest?—“Every sacrifice of priests,” it says, “shall be consumed by fire, and no one shall eat of it.” This cannot be done unless he wholly strips himself of cares of the flesh and removes his heart from this world, so that he may be free for God alone and enjoy God alone.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the law of the sin-offering, which must be eaten in a holy place, and on the garment sprinkled with its blood, which must be washed in a holy place

“This is the law of the sin-offering: in the place where the holocaust is offered, it shall be sacrificed before the Lord; it is most holy. The priest who offers it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle.”

The order set down above has here been somewhat changed in the recapitulation. There, after the holocaust, the peace-offering and then the sin-offering were arranged; here, however, the law of the sin-offering comes first and then the law of the peace-offering. Perhaps he delayed the law of the sin-offering above because he was going to say more about it. For in the present order the Psalmist also joins the holocaust and the offering for sin: “You did not require holocaust and offering for sin” (Ps. 39).

Nevertheless, as we have said, our sacrifice for sin is properly faith. For what is the redemption of sin, through which death entered into this world, except believing that the Lord Jesus suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through himself? (Heb. 13.) But above we explained, on the apostle’s testimony, that this was signified by the fact that the bodies of the animals whose blood was brought by the high priest into the holy places were burned outside the camp. Therefore faith is the spiritual sacrifice for sin; in time or in the order of the stages by which we ascend it comes first, but in dignity it is intermediate between hope and love.

One point in these distinctions should certainly not be overlooked: when it is said, “This is the law of the sin-offering,” and afterward, “This likewise is the law of the offering for offence,” and later the law of both offerings is one. It should not, I say, be overlooked that there is some difference between sin and offence. Sin is doing something forbidden by the Lord’s law; offence is neglecting something commanded. But let us now touch briefly on the words of this law itself.

“In the place,” it says, “where the holocaust is offered”—that is, in the catholic Church, outside of which there is no possessing or receiving the burning of the Holy Spirit—“it shall be sacrificed before the Lord.” Otherwise, if it is sacrificed elsewhere, in some gathering of heretics, it is not a sin-offering; it is not the body given for us; it is not the blood shed for the sins of the whole world. “Most holy,” it says: that is, beyond the other holy things performed in the aforesaid place of the holocaust, this is holy. “The priest who offers it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle.”

Therefore canonical authority rightly and lawfully decreed that a priest celebrating Mass should never dare to omit communicating himself. The holy place and the court of the tabernacle are the present Church: holy place and court of the tabernacle, namely, the heavenly one. For here is the faith of the patriarchs and prophets, through and from which one enters that heavenly temple of God. Conversely, the gatherings of Jews or heretics are impure, where, as has already been said, this holy offering neither ought nor can be sacrificed.

“Whatever touches its flesh shall be sanctified. If a garment is sprinkled with its blood, it shall be washed in a holy place.” This is usefully understood literally just as it is said. For whatever touches the body of the Lord is doubtless sanctified and reverently washed, so that it is not even lawful for a priest to return the tips of his fingers, once they have touched it, to common uses unless he has first washed them carefully. Likewise, if a garment has been sprinkled with this blood, this is deservedly regarded as a grave offence. Yet the garment itself is rightly considered consecrated by God, so that it is not only washed in a holy place set apart from all common sight, but is also stored by the more diligent as a most precious pledge.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the prophetic statement, “If a person carries consecrated flesh in the hem of his garment, shall it become consecrated?”

This should by no means seem contrary to the foregoing meaning: in the prophet Haggai, after he had asked the priests by the word of the Lord, saying: “If a person carries consecrated flesh in the hem of his garment, and touches with its edge bread, or cooked food, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it become consecrated? They answered, saying: No” (Hag. 2).

For in the words “shall it become consecrated?” one must understand: shall the person who touches something consecrated or offered to the Lord be sanctified, whether by carrying it or by consuming any food? For neither by carrying, nor by eating or drinking something holy or touched by something holy, can a person be sanctified. Rather, on the contrary, such a person will be defiled all the more if he presumptuously touches holy things while he himself is polluted in soul. For it immediately follows: “If one polluted in soul touches any of all these things, shall it be defiled? And the priests answered and said: It shall be defiled” (ibid.).

Therefore, applying this to ourselves, let us say: if an impious person marks his forehead or breast with the sign of the cross, will the devil flee from him because of that sign? Certainly not; rather, the devil will be enclosed more tightly; indeed, that person’s soul will nonetheless belong to the devil, according to the Scripture which says: “When an impious person curses the devil, he curses his own soul” (Ecclus. 21).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the “earthen vessel,” etc.; that not a woman but a male should eat its flesh; and that the sin-offering should not be eaten but burned

“But the earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken; if it is a bronze vessel, it shall be scoured and washed with water. Every male of the priestly line shall eat its flesh, because it is most holy. But the offering slain for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make atonement in the sanctuary, shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire.”

“The earthen vessel,” it says, “shall be broken,” namely, lest after sacred use it be returned to common kitchen uses. But the “bronze vessel shall be scoured and washed,” undoubtedly because it would be broken at greater loss than an earthen vessel. We, however, make the sacred offering not in an earthen, bronze, or wooden vessel, but only in one of silver or gold.

Spiritually, the earthen vessel in which the offering was cooked is broken: that is, all earthliness in the person for whom this singular offering is prepared is destroyed, according to what is said in the Psalm, where after “You shall rule them with a rod of iron” (Ps. 2), it is immediately added: “You shall break them like a potter’s vessel” (ibid.). But if it is a bronze vessel—that is, a heart strengthened in a good purpose to sin no more—“it shall be scoured and washed with water,” that is, it shall be washed by daily repentance, so that it may shine more brightly.

And because no soft or undisciplined person is worthy to eat such an offering, “every male,” it says, “of the priestly line”—that is, every strong person who, by resisting inwardly in a manful way, is worthy to be called or to be a son or kinsman of Christ the great Priest—“shall eat its flesh.” Why? “Because it is most holy.” Therefore a woman—that is, any soft or unclean soul—is unworthy of this food, because it is most holy.

It follows: “But the offering slain for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make atonement in the sanctuary, shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire.” It is as if he said: What has been said thus far concerns only that offering for sin which is not only slain for sin, but whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make atonement in the sanctuary; it shall not be eaten but burned with fire. Why?

To pursue the spiritual meaning: the visible bodily appearance in which the offering for the sins of us living persons was slain—Christ, the Son of God, whose blood, or rather the cause of his blood, was once brought into those heavenly holy places before the eyes of God the Father to atone for and propitiate the offences of the people—that appearance, I say, when it was slain in contemptibility, ought not to be eaten but burned with fire: that is, through the Holy Spirit, by the power of the resurrection, it was to be removed from every corruption of mortality or passibility, lest it seem to be taken away and lifted into heaven.

(CHAPTER VII.) “This likewise is the law of the offering for offence: it is most holy,” etc. As was said above, an offence is failure to do what has been commanded, while sin is committing what has been forbidden. The same things must be done for the offering for offence as for the sin-offering. “For the law of both offerings,” it says, “shall be one.” For the person who has not done what was commanded needs the same remedy of Christ’s sacraments as the person who has committed what was forbidden.

Yet it is added here, what had not yet been said: “The priest who offers the victim of the holocaust shall have the sheep’s skin.” This is just according to both letter and spirit. For the person who has caused another to turn from the error of his way and has brought him as far as reconciliation at the sacred altar deserves, as a victor, to receive that person’s spoils; that is, he who has sown spiritual things in that person may reap his carnal things (1 Cor. 9).

“And every sacrifice,” it says, “of flour which is baked in an oven, and whatever is prepared on a griddle or in a frying-pan, shall belong to the priest by whom it is offered.” For it is just before the Lord that whatever good work a person has done—whether in the oven of married life, on the griddle of widowhood, or in the frying-pan of virgin purpose—should belong to the glory of the one by whose prompting or admonition it was done, “whether the offering is mingled with oil or dry”: that is, whether the good work was accomplished from love or from fear. “It shall be divided in equal measure among all the sons of Aaron.”

This has hitherto been observed from the law, especially in monasteries. For there all the sons of Aaron—that is, all whose commitment or office is to pray for the sin of laypeople, and who receive their alms—live according to the apostolic rule that “they had all things in common. And distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts 4).

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the law of the peace-offering: how it is celebrated in the Church at public observances
“This is the law of the peace-offering which is offered to the Lord. If the offering is for thanksgiving, they shall offer unleavened loaves sprinkled with oil, and unleavened cakes anointed with oil, and cooked fine flour, and small cakes sprinkled with an admixture of oil, and also leavened loaves with the sacrifice of thanksgiving which is immolated for peace-offerings. From these one shall be offered to the Lord as firstfruits, and it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the victim. Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day, and nothing of it shall remain until morning.”

Peace-offerings, such as today give forth their fragrance in the Church of Christ—and of which these carnal things were shadows—are signs of hope, and are performed for every sort of advancement, both in private observances and in public assemblies. Hence the Apostle, exhorting his disciple, says: “I beseech that, first of all, supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in high station, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity” (1 Tim. 2). How the particular character of this law is to be observed privately was explained above: namely, in the person who says with the Apostle, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, but I see another law in my members” (Rom. 7), etc.

But in this renewal of the same law several things have been added, which must now be discussed in such a way that we also consider the common peace-offerings which, as was said, are customarily celebrated in the Church of Christ at public assemblies. “If,” he says, “the offering be for thanksgiving,” etc. The whole burnt-offering indeed—in which the entire inward heart is cooked in the fire of divine love—is rightly called thanksgiving. Yet it is one thing to kindle inward thanksgiving before divine things, and to burn in secret love or sorrow for the sole vision of divinity which the mind desires; it is another to render solemn words or public vows for public benefits of this present life as well—for example, for the prosperous condition of kings, under whom we may lead a quiet life.

“Unleavened cakes,” he says, “anointed with oil, and small cakes sprinkled with an admixture of oil.” [Col. 0781C] A *laganum* is bread first cooked in water and afterwards fried in oil. A *collyrida* is a square loaf likewise fried with oil. And rightly is the bread to be offered sprinkled with oil, through which the joy of charity is understood; for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9).

Nor should it trouble us that he also commands leavened loaves to be offered, although above he said: “Every offering offered to the Lord shall be without leaven” (Lev. 2). For there it was also added: “You shall offer only their firstfruits, and the gifts shall not be placed upon the altar for an odor of sweetness” (ibid.); and here it is sufficiently stated that they are not placed upon the altar but offered as firstfruits, when it says: “From these one shall be offered to the Lord as firstfruits, and [Col. 0781D] it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the victim.”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. What are the three days on whose third day it is not lawful to eat the flesh of the victim.

“Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day, and nothing of it shall remain until morning. If anyone has offered a victim by vow or freely, it shall likewise be eaten on the same day. But if anything remains on the next day, it is lawful to eat it. Whatever the third day finds, fire shall consume.”

What are these three days, on the third of which it is not lawful to eat the flesh of the victim? Surely they are the three states of human life concerning which, above, when this law of peace-offerings was first set forth, we said: namely, that the final state is when a person still sins without fear, concerning whom the Apostle says: “I once lived without the law” (Rom. 7); the intermediate state, when he now struggles against sin, of which the same Apostle subsequently says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man” (ibid.), etc.; and the best and first state, when at last he has victoriously trampled sin itself beneath his feet, concerning which, after he had said, “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid.), he at once answered himself: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (ibid.).

Therefore the flesh is eaten on the same day when the offerings of one whom the grace of God has already delivered through Jesus Christ are received by priests, so that he is no longer led captive under the law of sin. It is still lawfully eaten on the second day when the offerings of one not yet delivered are received, but who gives the priests—observers of his conscience—hope of struggle, and commends himself to their prayers. But on the third day it is not eaten: not when the offerings of one living without the law are not received, one who does not resist in order to be delivered, but perhaps even glories in the worst deeds. This is wicked.

He therefore says: “If anyone eats of the flesh of the victim of peace-offerings on the third day, the offering shall become void and shall not profit the offerer. Rather, every soul that has defiled itself with such food shall be guilty of transgression.” Thus a gift received from the ungodly not only does not benefit the giver, but also makes its recipient guilty of transgression. And rightly so: for the one sins obstinately, and the other eats his sins.

Accordingly, he repeats what he had said, that whatever the third day finds fire shall consume, saying: “Flesh that has touched anything unclean shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire. Whoever is clean shall eat of it.” [Col. 0782C] For, according to the sense stated above, the third day—that is, the final state of a sinful life—is unclean; and the flesh touches this uncleanness when an offering passes from an unrepentant sinner to a flattering priest. “It shall not be eaten,” he says, “but shall be burned with fire. Whoever is clean shall eat of it.”

Then, after it has been burned with fire, will whoever is clean finally eat of it? According to the outward shell of the letter, this cannot stand; but according to the inward marrow of the Spirit, it is certain. For after the sinner’s offering has been burned with the coals of repentance—that is, once the priest has testimony from God that, without sparing, he has heaped those same coals upon the sinner’s head, seeking not what is his but the man himself—he will indeed confidently partake of what is his.

Yet the words may be joined to the preceding statement, where it was said, “Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day”—namely, the flesh of the victim—so that, with the intervening words included, it may rightly say, “Whoever is clean shall eat of it,” understanding: of the victim. For it continues: “The defiled soul that eats of the flesh of the victim of peace-offerings which has been offered to the Lord shall perish from among his people. And whoever touches the uncleanness of a human being or of a beast, or of anything which can defile, and eats of flesh of this kind, shall perish from among his people.”

Here the Holy Spirit prescribes a wholly true and holy law for priests—or rather, not for priests, but for fat cows, such as those to whom he speaks through the prophet: “Hear this word, you fat cows who are on Mount Samaria, who oppress the needy and crush the poor, who say to your masters: Bring, and let us drink” (Amos 4), etc. “The defiled soul,” he says, “which eats of the flesh of the victim of peace-offerings.” What is it for a defiled soul to eat from the flesh of the peace-offering that has been offered to the Lord, except for a priest who seeks what is his own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2) to hunger after the offerings of sinners, so that they may be offered supposedly to the Lord, while he is rather providing for his own belly, his own god?

For when priestly dignity humbles itself in flattery before a rich sinner, and, greedily gaping for his little cakes, forgets to move its tongue, to speak and declare [Col. 0783B] that person’s sin to him, its soul is certainly defiled; and because it has perversely seized what ought in right order to be offered to the Lord, “it shall perish from among its people.” “Whoever,” he says, “touches the uncleanness of a human being”—indeed, of “a beast” rotting in its dung—“or of anything that can defile,” namely every sin, whose touch, that is, consent, is truly defilement, “and eats of flesh of this kind”: whoever flatters the sinner whom, by reason of his office, he ought to rebuke with the two-edged sword—that is, with the word of truth—according to the saying, “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep” (Eccl. 12), therefore “shall perish from among his people.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Col. 0783C] What it mystically means not to eat the fat of ox, sheep, and goat; and what it means to put the fat of an animal that died of itself to various uses.

“Speak to the children of Israel: You shall not eat the fat of ox, sheep, or goat. The fat of a carcass that died of itself, and of an animal seized by a beast, you may put to various uses.”

The sacred law continues its judgment against greedy priests. “You shall not eat,” it says, “the fat of ox, sheep, and goat.” God speaks through the prophet to the transgressors of this word: “You killed what was fat, you ate the milk, and clothed yourselves with the wool” (Ezek. 34), etc. To eat the fat of ox, sheep, and goat is to cherish the sins of those “whose iniquity came forth as from fat” (Ps. 72), and so to stroke them flatteringly, as though they had fat necks, for the sake of gain.

“You may put to various uses,” he says, “the fat of a carcass that died of itself, and of an animal seized by a beast.” Most beautifully and most holy spoken. Behold: a lawful priest sets before a rich man, wise in his own estimation and “hoping in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6), and brings vividly before his eyes by vigorous preaching, some ungodly swine from Epicurus’s herd: one who in his life ran against God with upraised neck, was loved for his fat neck, whose face was covered with fatness, and from whose sides flesh hung down toward ruin; but who at his end—great signs often appearing, as has often happened—perished as though upon a dung-heap, vomited up the riches he had devoured, and had them drawn from his belly by God.

When the priest faithfully strives so that the rich sinner still surviving may be frightened by that person’s example, what else does he do than employ for various uses the fat of a carcass that died of itself and of an animal seized by a beast—that is, by the devil—while refusing to take it as food? Having inserted this comparison, he continues with a threat: “If anyone eats the fat which ought to be offered as incense to the Lord, he shall perish from among his people.” As if he said: If anyone flatters and cherishes the vices of a rich person whom he ought to instruct, so that through repentance that person might sacrifice or burn himself to the Lord, he shall perish from the people of the saints.

“And you shall not take,” he says, “the blood of any animal as food, whether of birds or cattle. Every soul that eats blood shall perish from among his people.” The words differ, but the meaning is the same. For God also says through the prophet: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the ungodly, I will require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3 and 33). Behold the priest who, for gain, keeps silent about a person’s death: in the words of the aforesaid prophet, who says, “They gave life to their souls and profaned me among my people for a handful of oil and a morsel of bread, so that they might kill souls which do not die and give life to souls which do not live, lying to my people who believe lies” (Ezek. 13). He eats the blood of the fat ones, and therefore “shall perish from among his people.” What, then, ought to be done? He says:

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. What is meant by, “He who offers a peace-offering,” and what the breast and right shoulder, set apart for the use of priests, mean. [Col. 0784C]

“He who offers a victim of peace-offerings to the Lord shall offer with it both the sacrifice and its libations.” This the priest should preach; this he should cry aloud; this he should announce. “He who offers,” he says, “a victim of peace-offerings”—that is, the outward offering of his hand to the Lord—“shall offer with it also the true sacrifice,” that is, a contrite spirit, a crushed and humbled heart. Let him offer this to God, and provide people with a good example, which are the worthy and lawful libations of the sacred victim.

For if he offers his possession to God but keeps himself for himself, he will be compared to Cain and it will be said to him: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, is it not evil?” (Gen. 4). For Cain offered rightly in that he offered to God, to whom he ought to have offered; but he divided wrongly, because he offered to God what was of lesser value—his possession—but kept for himself what was most precious, namely himself.

Therefore, whoever prepares for God a victim from his own possession “shall offer with it both the sacrifice and its libations”: libations, I say, so that God may be glorified in him; so that what he offers may be unspoiled, whole, and complete; so that together with the outwardly offered possession God may have the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and crushed heart. These three lawful things are required in the offering of peace-offerings: that the minister of the altar may live from the altar (1 Cor. 9); that God, the indwelling Lord, may possess the offerer’s heart; and that the light of a good work, shining before people, may contribute to the glorification of God.

How shall he offer these things? “He shall hold,” it says, “in his hands the fat of the victim and the breast. And when he has consecrated both offerings [Col. 0785A] to the Lord, he shall hand them over to the priest, who shall burn the fat upon the altar; but the breast shall belong to Aaron and his sons. The right shoulder also shall be cut off from the victims of peace-offerings as the priest’s firstfruits.”

To hold the fat in one’s hands is to restrain the luxury of the flesh. To hold the breast likewise is to reveal through confession evil thoughts that come upon one’s heart. For the heart is contained in the breast, and thoughts move within the heart. “And when he has consecrated both offerings to the Lord, he shall hand them over to the priest.” For first the deeds of the flesh and the intentions of thought must be summoned inwardly to judgment before the Lord: conscience must accuse, fear bind, reason discern; and when a person has received this answer, when he has formed this resolve that henceforth he wishes to amend his life, then at last he will offer pure confession to the priest.

For the person who approaches confession while still wishing not to abandon his sins has not yet consecrated to the Lord the fat of the victim of peace-offerings and the breast; consequently, whatever he offers to the priest is offered in vain. For confession without ensuing contrition and correction cannot save; it should rather be called a profession of sinning than a confession of sin. First, therefore, he shall consecrate these things to the Lord; then he shall hand them over to the priest.

“Who shall burn the fat upon the altar; but the breast shall belong to Aaron and his sons.” The lawful priest, he says, shall not eat the fat, but “shall burn it upon the altar”: that is, he shall not deceive the penitent, content with his own advantage—as bad physicians do when they neglect to cut away decayed flesh—but shall drive the knife of judgment more deeply, provoking him to groaning and to produce fruits worthy of repentance. For this is what follows: “He shall cut off the right shoulder as the priest’s firstfruits.” By the right shoulder understand upright and strong works, which the priest should require from the penitent—for example, that he may say with the Apostle: “For as you have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now yield your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6).

“But the breast shall belong to Aaron and his sons; he shall burn the fat upon the altar.” As if he said: The works of the flesh shall openly be burned with the coals of repentance, as has been said; but sorrowful thoughts shall cry inwardly to Christ and to his holy ministers. “He of the sons of Aaron who offers the fat and blood shall himself have the right shoulder as his portion. For I have taken from the children of Israel the breast of consecration and the shoulder of separation, from their victims of peace-offerings, and have given them to Aaron and his sons by an everlasting law, from all the people of Israel.”

An equitable law. “Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that those who work in the sanctuary eat of the things which are of the sanctuary, and those who serve the altar share with the altar?” (1 Cor. 9). “Therefore he of the sons of Aaron who offers shall himself have the right shoulder”: that is, whoever among Christ’s disciples mortifies by his preaching the fattened heart and the works of flesh and blood of some person, and thus sows his spiritual goods, shall receive from that person carnal [Col. 0786A] fruit—that is, the provision necessary for life.

He called it “the breast of elevation” from the preceding words, “He shall hold in his hands the fat and the breast”; but “the shoulder of separation” from the fact that it was to be set aside as the priest’s portion. “I have taken these,” he says, “from the children of Israel and have given them to Aaron the priest and his sons,” so that they themselves may meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night in the breast, may perform God’s commandments bravely in the right shoulder, may bear concern for others in the breast, and receive in the shoulder the fruit of their labor.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning the words, “This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons by an everlasting ordinance”: this must be understood not according to the veil of the letter, but according to the brightness of spiritual understanding. [Col. 0786B]

“This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons in the ceremonies of the Lord, on the day when Moses presented them to minister in the priesthood; and these things the Lord commanded to be given them by the children of Israel, as an everlasting ordinance throughout their generations. This is the law of the burnt-offering, and of sacrifice for sin and trespass, and for consecration, and of victims of peace-offerings, which the Lord established for Moses on Mount Sinai, when he commanded the children of Israel to offer their offerings to the Lord in the wilderness of Sinai.”

Again, in a shorter conclusion, he sets forth all that he has discussed thus far, leading the reader more deeply back to the law of the Lord—to the beginning of this book of Leviticus, namely to the completion of the tabernacle, where the Lord spoke to Moses: “Bring near to yourself Aaron with his sons, that they may minister to me in the priesthood” (Exod. 28). “This,” he says, “is the anointing of Aaron and his sons, and this is the law of the burnt-offering,” etc.

He has pointed out distinctly, as with a finger, the law of priests and the law of the people. If we have rightly looked with unveiled face beyond the veil torn at Christ’s death, by which this sanctuary of the divine law was concealed, we readily perceive that all these things which have been said are worthy of the gravity of the speaker; so that the Psalmist rightly sang: “The law of the Lord is immaculate, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones. The righteousnesses of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 18).

“By an everlasting law,” he says. Everlasting indeed, yet not according to the veil of the letter, but according to the charity of spiritual understanding. Otherwise, how will the law and the prophets agree? For here the lawgiver, having said, “This is the law of the burnt-offering,” etc., immediately adds: “Which the Lord established for Moses on Mount Sinai, when he commanded the children of Israel to offer their offerings to the Lord in the wilderness of Sinai.” Yet in the prophet the same Lord says: “Add your burnt-offerings to your victims, and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them on the day when I led them out of the land of Egypt, concerning the matter of burnt-offerings and victims” (Jer. 7).

How, then, do the law and the prophets not differ or disagree, unless the Lord spoke to Moses about the spiritual and everlasting [Col. 0787A] law, while he said nothing about the carnal law of sacrifices? For the Lord established it for Moses, but Moses spoke to the people. Moses received from the Lord the brightness of the Spirit, but presented to the people the obscurity of the letter, until there should come those who believed God the Son in God the Father and, enlightened by this faith, saw the law of the Spirit in the law of the letter.

Accordingly, the distinction is rightly made: “Which the Lord established for Moses on Mount Sinai, and when he commanded [Col. 0788A] the children of Israel to offer their offerings in the wilderness of Sinai.” For he showed one thing to Moses and commanded another to that people, as the Lord himself testifies when above he says: “See, and make according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25). Therefore, when Moses spoke to the people, he placed a veil over his face; but when he spoke to the Lord, he removed it (Exod. 34).

# SECOND BOOK ON LEVITICUS  
*(Leviticus, chapters 8–27)*

[Col. 0787]

## CHAPTER I. Why, when Moses clothed his brother, no mention is made of the linen breeches alone, although these were the first garment.

*(Chapter 8.)* “Moses did as the Lord commanded. And when the whole multitude had assembled before the entrance, he said: This is the word which the Lord commanded to be done. And immediately he presented Aaron and his sons. After he had washed them, he clothed the high priest, girding him with a linen tunic, clothing him with a hyacinth-blue robe, and placing the ephod over it.”

Above, where the Lord commanded that these garments be made for the high priest’s glory and beauty, we explained, as far as we could, their mystical meanings garment by garment. One question here remains: why, although Moses clothed his brother with all the other things, does no mention occur here of the linen breeches alone, which were the first garment according to the Lord’s command? We must not suppose that this happened without purpose or by chance through forgetfulness.

We say, therefore, that the breeches covering the shamefulness of the flesh were commanded to be made as a figure of continence, which especially befits priests. But this continence, by which a person is sanctified in complete purity and, in the transformation of the new person in Jesus Christ, lives out virginal beauty—this continence or purity, I say, does not come by the precept of the Law, but by the counsel of the Gospel. Therefore, when Moses, writing the Law and prefiguring the Law in his own person, clothed his brother, Scripture rightly remained silent about this matter, that by its very silence it might acknowledge that virginity is not a commandment of the Law, but a counsel offered by grace.

Nor should we pass over the fact that the priests are not clothed in priestly glory, by the Lord’s command, until they have first been washed with water. This signifies that we become “a royal priesthood and a holy nation” only through baptism (1 Pet. 2).

## CHAPTER II. On the oil of anointing with which Aaron was anointed: it signifies the Holy Spirit, by whom Christ was anointed.

“And he took the oil of anointing, with which he anointed the tabernacle with all its furnishings,” etc. The point to note from this entire lengthy chapter is that the tabernacle with all its furnishings was anointed before Aaron, priest of the tabernacle; and that Moses offered the victim of burnt-offering, sin-offering, consecration, and peace-offering before Aaron did. Yet the manner differed. The tabernacle was consecrated by the oil of anointing alone, but Aaron by both oil and blood; Moses’s offerings were consumed by ordinary fire, but Aaron’s sacrifices by a heavenly flame.

But before we pursue these mysteries, something must briefly be said about the oil of anointing itself, which we have deferred until now. Above, the Lord spoke to Moses: “Take for yourself choice spices: five hundred shekels of principal and choice myrrh, half as much cinnamon, that is, two hundred and fifty shekels; likewise two hundred and fifty shekels of calamus; also five hundred shekels of cassia by the weight of the sanctuary; and one *hin* measure of olive oil. You shall make the holy oil of anointing, a compounded ointment, the work of a perfumer; and with it you shall anoint the tabernacle of testimony, the ark of the covenant, and the table with its vessels” (Exod. 30).

It is known to all that the oil by which our Lord, the Son of God, was anointed—whence he is called in Hebrew *Messiah* and in Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One”—is the oil of the Holy Spirit. The sign or material token of this oil was that with which kings, priests, and prophets were formerly anointed. But why was that true oil of exultation signified here in the Law not by plain oil, but by oil mixed with four substances—myrrh, cinnamon, cassia, and calamus? Clearly because it is not enough for anyone to have received the Holy Spirit in some fashion—for example, for prophecy or the working of signs—unless he also possesses the four highest virtues, which secular philosophy calls justice, prudence, temperance, and fortitude, but our theology calls faith, hope, charity, and perseverance in them.

Thus, from four substances—myrrh, cinnamon, cassia, and calamus—mixed with oil, is made the most precious royal and priestly ointment. “The flesh of a human being shall not be anointed with it,” and no other such thing shall be made according to its composition. “Whoever makes it,” he says, “shall be cut off from his people” (ibid.). For from the virtues mentioned above, together with the Holy Spirit, is made the good grace which the carnal person never enjoys and to whose transformation no sect or secular eloquence can ever attain. [Col. 0789A] Should it attempt this, “it shall without doubt,” says the Lord, “be cut off.”

## CHAPTER III. What it signifies that the tabernacle was anointed before Aaron, but without blood; that the altar was sprinkled seven times; and what the bronze basin is.

Therefore, as stated above, the tabernacle was anointed with the oil of anointing before Aaron, but without blood, because the true tabernacle—the Church—received the Holy Spirit first in its patriarchs, kings, and prophets before the Holy of Holies, the great high priest Jesus Christ, Son of God, who is mystically understood through Aaron, was anointed; but it did not possess a victim in the truth of sacrifice, that is, one by whose blood it might be anointed for the remission of sins.

“And when,” it says, “he had sprinkled the altar seven times in sanctifying it, he anointed it and all its vessels.” He anointed it by sprinkling seven times, thereby signifying that the same Holy Spirit is sevenfold. “He also sanctified the basin with its base by oil.” Concerning this basin it is written above: “He made the bronze basin from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle” (Exod. 38).

For the Lord had spoken thus: “You shall make a bronze basin with its base for washing, and place it between the tabernacle of testimony and the altar. Water having been put into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it when they are about to enter the tabernacle of testimony and when they approach the altar, in order to offer incense upon it to the Lord, lest perhaps they die. It shall be an everlasting ordinance for him and for his descendants throughout their generations” (Exod. 30).

This basin, which Moses made at the Lord’s command, signifies this very Holy Scripture, which the same Moses wrote by divine inspiration. For the mirrors of the women from which that basin was made mystically are examples of holy souls, concerning whom all this Scripture was composed: for example, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses himself, who wrote it. These souls, like beautiful women seeking God their lover, kept watch at the entrance of the heavenly tabernacle, which had not yet been opened so long as Christ, the great priest, had not yet been anointed.

For what purpose did Moses make such a basin? “For washing,” it says: “that, water having been put into it, Aaron and his sons might wash their hands and feet in it when about to enter the tabernacle of testimony.” It is surely fitting and excellent that priests about to enter the heavenly tabernacle should wash their hands and feet in those mirrors of holy souls: in the faith and obedience of Abraham, in the faith and patience of Isaac, in the faith and gentleness of Jacob, and in the most clear virtues of the rest. They should wash, I say, their hands and feet—that is, through compunction and imitation of those persons, they should cleanse the daily sins of deeds and thoughts which cling to the faculties of the mind as dust clings to feet.

Not only the sons, but “Aaron,” it says, “and his sons shall wash.” This is plain, because our Aaron, the mountain of strength, the priest or great high priest Christ, washed first and before all. For he sanctified himself for us. He washed, I say, because he fulfilled all the Scriptures, and, though his hands and feet were clean, by patiently enduring all things so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, he cleansed in himself the defilements of us all.

## CHAPTER IV. On the mystical pouring out of oil upon Aaron’s head; and what the head, beard, and edge of the garment are, upon which, according to the Psalmist, the ointment descends.

“Pouring,” it says, “the oil upon Aaron’s head, he anointed and consecrated him.” Commending the mystery of this act, the Holy Spirit in David, after saying, “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132), immediately adds: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends upon the edge of his garment” (ibid.).

Therefore the mystery of this anointing is not far from us, but near in our mouth and heart. This Psalmist sang that the pouring out of that ointment was a sign of the goodness and pleasantness of brothers dwelling together in unity. But what is “brothers dwelling together in unity,” except that all who have become children of the one Father, God, have one ruler and savior, Christ—just as the many members of one body have one head—by possessing concord through the Spirit of charity poured out in their hearts by the One?

Thus this is precisely the meaning of the words. To dwell together in unity is a goodness and pleasantness of the kind rightly signified by what is written here: that “pouring oil upon Aaron’s head, he anointed and consecrated him.” And because it was poured out in generous abundance, it first descended upon his beard and then upon the edge of his garment.

For the aforesaid goodness and pleasantness of brothers dwelling together in unity is the oil of gladness—that is, the Holy Spirit. That best ointment was poured in its entirety, with all its fullness, upon that head which is Christ—for he is the head of the body, the Church—“in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). It was so poured not merely from the time when it descended upon him in the form of a dove (Matt. 3), but from his first conception, which was accomplished by the power or operation of the Holy Spirit alone (Luke 1).

From that head it first descended upon his beard, and then upon the edge of his garment: because from the fullness of the same Holy Spirit the strong men, the Apostles, who adhered to and stood so near him as a beard does to the head, were first filled; and afterwards the Church, which is adorned by its faith and virtues, in the manner of someone dressed in precious clothing, according to the saying: “As I live, says the Lord, you shall put on all these as an ornament” (Isa. 49).

Something has already elsewhere been said about the sons of Aaron, priests of lesser rank. The differences among offerings, according to which Moses is now related to have made offerings, have likewise been discussed above. It remains now to say why the priestly anointing was performed not only with oil but also with blood.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 0791A] How, in Aaron, the old priesthood as a figure of Christ’s new priesthood was consecrated first by oil and afterwards by blood.

“When Moses,” he says, “had sacrificed the second ram in the consecration of the priests, he took some of its blood and touched the tip of Aaron’s ear, the thumb of his right hand, and likewise of his foot. He also presented Aaron’s sons. And when he had touched with the blood of the sacrificed ram the tip of their right ear and the thumb of their right hand and right foot, he poured the remainder around the altar.”

The old priesthood, a figure of the new, is first consecrated with oil and then with blood. Thus the great high priest of the true heavenly tabernacle was first sanctified by the Holy Spirit and afterwards also by his own blood [Col. 0791B]. Of the Spirit’s sanctification the Psalmist says: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Of the sanctification by his own blood, John the Evangelist records that, when he was about to shed his blood, he said: “For their sake I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17). Likewise in Luke: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12).

How, then, is the priest consecrated by blood? “Taking,” he says, “some of the blood, he touched the tip of his right ear and the thumb of his right hand, and likewise of his foot.” The touch of blood upon the tip of the high priest’s right ear is the receiving of the command which the Father gave, or the obedience of Christ the Son of God, [Col. 0791C] as the Apostle says of him: “Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). And he himself says of himself in the prophet: “The Lord God opened my ear; but I do not resist, I did not turn back” (Isa. 50).

The touch of blood upon the tip of the thumb of the right hand is the carrying out of the Father’s will, he himself saying through the Psalmist: “You held my right hand, and in your will you guided me” (Ps. 78). The touch upon the tip of the thumb of the right foot, which is the end of the body, is the completion of that same obedience. The Psalmist says concerning this: “That your foot may be dipped in blood” (Ps. 67). Aaron’s sons likewise are marked with blood [Col. 0791D], so that, by Christ’s example, the apostles too may obey, work, or contend lawfully, and persevere to the end.

“But the fat and the tail, and all the fat that covers the entrails,” etc.—since their mystical reasons have already been set forth above, we have judged it superfluous to repeat them now. For what is signified by the statement that “the consecration is completed in seven days” is clear from many places in Scripture: namely, that the whole duration of the present age runs through seven days, and is concluded by the eighth, that is, by the time of the future resurrection. This has already been fulfilled in the great high priest Christ, but is yet to be fulfilled in us, who, as sons of Aaron, labor throughout the whole time of consecration for the eighth day, not departing from the entrance of the tabernacle during all seven days [Col. 0792A]—that is, not departing during this entire time from the faith of Christ’s Church—and “by day and by night,” that is, both in prosperity and adversity, keeping “the watches, O Lord,” lest we die, according to our purpose or order.

## CHAPTER VI. How, on the eighth day of consecration, fire went forth from the Lord and consumed the burnt offering, as a type of the Holy Spirit.

(CH. IX.) It remains, therefore, to consider this: on the eighth day Moses said, “This is the word which the Lord commanded: Do it, and his glory will appear to you.” And when Aaron offered the burnt offering and prayed for himself and the people according to the rite mentioned above, “behold,” he says, “fire went forth from the Lord [Col. 0792B] and devoured the burnt offering and the fats that were upon the altar,” whereas nothing of the kind had occurred with the offerings of Moses.

What does this mean except that the Holy Spirit was given to us for the remission of sins not through the sacrifices of the Law, which were prefigured by Moses, but through the sacrifice of Christ, of whom Aaron was a type? Hence he says in the Psalm: “You did not demand burnt offering and sacrifice for sin; then I said, Behold, I come” (Ps. 39). When he came, he had no other victim to offer as a burnt offering or for sin except himself. And fire descended upon him—fire, I say, of which he said, “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12)—and devoured the burnt offering by that devouring which, following the Apostle, we rightly call transformation, since [Col. 0792C] “having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

This is that fire of which it was said above: “The fire upon the altar shall always burn; the priest shall feed it, placing wood upon it every morning” (Lev. 6). For this true fire now consumes sins in the first resurrection of souls and afterwards will devour even bodily mortality or corruption in the second resurrection. It must never fail upon the altar, that is, in the faith through which Christ dwells in our hearts. Therefore, with profound mystery, it was ordained that the visible fire which went forth from the Lord and devoured the burnt offering, while the crowds looked on, fell “upon [Col. 0792D] their faces,” and praised the Lord, should never fail, but should always burn upon the altar as the priest supplied wood. Hence Scripture immediately adds, with most orderly and wonderful providence:

## CHAPTER VII.

What is mystically prefigured in Nadab and Abihu, who died when they offered strange fire to the Lord.

(CH. X.) “Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, seized their censers, placed fire in them, and laid incense upon it, offering before the Lord strange fire, which had not been commanded them. And fire went forth from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.”

*Nadab* means “willing”; *Abihu* means “my father,” or “father himself.” They signify the Jewish people, who are willing—indeed, excessively importunate—in their carnal ceremonies. For although God says, “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49), and likewise in Isaiah, “I did not desire the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Isa. 1), [Col. 0793A] yet, while God says these things and others like them, they press them upon him as though he were asking for them, as though God required them.

They also boastfully say, “He is my father,” or “father himself.” “Abraham,” they say, “is our father; and we were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8). Therefore, when fire went forth from the Lord and devoured the burnt offerings, “Nadab and Abihu seized their censers, placed fire in them, and, laying incense upon it, offered before the Lord strange fire, [Col. 0793B] which had not been commanded them.” After the true fire of the Holy Spirit went forth from the Lord—that is, proceeded from the Father—and showed that the true burnt offering of Christ, the Son of God, was accepted, by coming down from above, that is, upon his disciples in tongues of fire (Acts 2), the Jewish people still most importunately and offensively press upon God a foreign worship and ceremonies hateful to him, though the prophets cry out against them.

What follows? “Fire,” he says, “went forth from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord.” Nothing is truer. For that people was devoured by a twofold fire: their temple was burned by the advancing Roman army, and their souls are consumed by the fire of Gehenna. Hence God, in the song of Deuteronomy, after saying, “They provoked me by that which was not God, and stirred me to anger by their abominations; and I will provoke them by that which is not a people, and I will anger them by a foolish nation” (Deut. 32), immediately adds: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell; it shall devour the earth with its increase and burn the foundations of the mountains” (ibid.).

“This,” says Moses, “is what the Lord spoke: I shall be sanctified in those who draw near to me, and I shall be glorified in the sight of all the people. Hearing this, Aaron was silent.” According to the letter, Moses indicates that by that visible occurrence Aaron might know with certainty that God is holy, that he will always defend and vindicate the dignity of his holiness against those who, unprepared, uncalled, or unauthorized, without due order and reverence, presume to thrust themselves into or immerse themselves in God’s sacred ministries [Col. 0793D]. “And this,” he says, “the Lord spoke,” namely, above, when Mount Sinai was wholly smoking, where he also said: “Let the priests also who approach the Lord sanctify themselves, lest I strike them” (Exod. 19), etc.

But according to allegory, this indicates that the punishment of the Jewish people establishes that henceforth no one should dare to glory in the flesh, but in faith in Jesus Christ alone. Aaron is silent upon hearing this: that is, the great priest Christ is silent, who once wept over the unhappy city of Jerusalem (Luke 19) in human feeling, but exercises the rational counsel of his divinity rather than follows the regard of the flesh in the death or perdition of those near to him according to the flesh [Col. 0794A].

“But Moses summoned Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Uzziel, Aaron’s uncle, and said to them: Go, and 267 remove your brothers from before the sanctuary, and carry them outside the camp.” *Mishael* means “God’s touch,” or “who has asked?”; *Elzaphan*, “God’s watchtower”; *Uzziel*, “God is my strength.” They signify the lawful sons of that people, on the side of the elect, who could truly say, “God is my strength”—for example, Moses himself, Isaiah, and the rest—who, in accordance with the names Elzaphan and Mishael, watched from afar for the coming Son of God and, touched by God, say even today: “Who asked? Who required these things from your hands?” For after the priests had been burned, as was said above, the touch of God, the Spirit of God, says this in Isaiah: “Who required [Col. 0794B] these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts?” (Isa. 1), etc.

These remove their carnal Jewish brothers from before the sanctuary and carry them outside the camp. For they accuse and condemn them, as the Lord says to them: “There is one who accuses you—Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5).

“Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his sons: Do not uncover your heads, and do not tear your garments, lest perhaps you die and wrath arise against the whole congregation.” He does not command what nature makes impossible—that a father should not grieve for the death of his sons, or brothers for the death of brothers—but what is possible: that they should not display the sorrow of the heart by a public bodily gesture. The sons of Aaron, that is, Christ’s apostles, lawfully observed this spiritually [Col. 0794C].

For although they grieve over the ruin of their people, as, for example, Paul says: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brothers, my kinsmen” (Rom. 9), etc.—although, I say, they grieve, nevertheless they do not uncover their heads or tear their garments. That is, they do not cease to honor their ministry; they defend with unbroken faith the truth of Holy Scripture against the unbelief of their nation; and in this way they do not depart from the entrance of the tabernacle, otherwise they would perish. “For woe is me,” says the same Apostle, “if I do not preach the Gospel” (1 Cor. [Col. 0794D] 9).

Therefore he says: “But you shall not depart from the entrance of the tabernacle; otherwise you shall perish. For the oil of holy anointing is upon you.” For the oil of holy anointing is upon them, which teaches them concerning all things (1 John 2): it teaches them that, because of their flesh or nation, they ought not to uncover their head—that is, their mind—of the faith and grace of Christ, tear their garment—that is, the doctrine of truth—or leave the entrance of the tabernacle—that is, cease from the order of the true sacrifice through zeal for the Jewish priesthood.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why Aaron’s sons should not drink wine or anything that could intoxicate when they enter the tabernacle, and what this means in the mystical sense.

“The Lord also said to Aaron: You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die; for it is an everlasting commandment throughout your generations, so that you may know how to distinguish between holy and profane, between unclean and clean, and may teach the children of Israel all my ordinances which the Lord spoke to them through the hand of Moses.”

According to the letter, this is plainly a command of sobriety, because wine makes even the wise fall away (Ecclus. 19). “Fornication,” says the prophet, “and wine and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. 4). And the Apostle says: “Do not be drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5). Therefore the holy Church most rightly decrees that those who are priests and continually enter the sanctuary of the true sacrifice should abstain altogether from marriage [Col. 0795B] and flee every form of debauchery. For under this law, in which the flesh of brute animals was sacrificed, priests had to abstain completely, at the time when they entered the tabernacle, not only from debauchery but even from the wine in which debauchery lies.

But, to continue the allegory begun, God—and not man—gave this command spiritually. For it is reported not that Moses but the Lord himself spoke it: namely, that at this time, when Christ has gone before us and we enter the true tabernacle, we should by no means follow the killing letter of the Law. Wine sometimes signifies the power of the Holy Spirit, as in: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). Yet when it is diminished in comparison with something better, as in: “For your breasts are better than wine” (Song 1), it signifies the severity [Col. 0795C] of the Law, than which the milky sweetness of the Gospel is undoubtedly better.

Why, then, should wine of this kind not be drunk? “So that,” he says, “you may know how to distinguish between holy and profane, between unclean and clean,” etc. Are they not, then, to drink wine in order that they may distinguish between an ox and a camel, a goat and a *choerogryllus*? For, if one follows the bare letter, this sort of distinction is set down afterwards. Therefore, so that lawful priests may distinguish true purity from true impurity, they are forbidden to drink wine—that is, to follow the severe letter of the Law.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the offered goat, which Moses sought and found burned up; and Aaron’s words, “How could I eat with a sorrowful mind?”—of what present Jewish sacrifice this was a type.

“Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his surviving sons: Take the sacrifice remaining from the offering of the Lord, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, because it is most holy.” These things concerning the commands or traditions are now repeated in writing so that the narrative may proceed in order to what follows.

Meanwhile Moses sought the goat offered for sin and found it burned up. Angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron’s surviving sons, he said: “Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy place? For it is most holy, and it was given to you, that [Col. 0796A] you might bear the iniquity of the multitude and intercede for it before the Lord—especially since none of its blood was brought into the sanctuary.”

This also is not without mystery; otherwise it would seem to have been written in vain. The goat offered for sin did not reach the priests to be eaten; when sought, it was found not merely burned, as a burnt offering, but consumed by fire. It is the sacrifice of the Jews, which was not admitted into the rite of Christ, the true priest. Hence Moses becomes angry, as a type of those zealots for the Law who, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles, wished to mingle the ceremonies of the Law with Christ’s Gospel (Acts 15).

Aaron answered: “A victim for sin and a burnt offering were offered to the Lord for me today. But what you see happened to me. How [Col. 0796B] could I eat it, or please the Lord in ceremonies with a sorrowful mind?” When Moses heard this, he accepted the explanation.

On the surface of the history, it is clear that, because his sons had died for their presumption, not merely the pleasure but even the willingness to eat was taken from their father. But according to the spiritual sense already begun, a reason is given why the great high priest Christ and his sons, namely the apostles, hate the Jewish victims.

“A victim for sin and a burnt offering,” he says, “were offered to the Lord today.” It is as if Christ himself were speaking in his apostles: In this acceptable time, in this day of salvation (2 Cor. 6), I was offered, as I foretold in the Psalm: “You did not demand burnt offering and sacrifice for sin; then I said, Behold, I come” (Ps. 39). I was offered, I say, because I willed it, and, being offered, I bore away the sins of the world (Isa. 53).

But it befell me that my sons—“alien sons,” who “lied to me and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17)—offered strange fire, refusing to receive the heavenly and true fire, namely the Holy Spirit. How then can I admit their ceremonies rather than hand over their temple and city to be burned, especially since I came “not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 5, 6)? On hearing this, “Moses accepted the explanation.” Thus those who were from among the Jews accepted the explanation, Christ speaking in James and the other apostles and judging that those who were turning to the Lord from among the Gentiles ought not to be troubled [Col. 0796D] (Acts 15). Therefore it rightly follows immediately:

## CHAPTER X. What it mystically means that, after the fire was given, the law concerning animals to be eaten was given; and what it means to divide the hoof and chew the cud.

(CH. XI.) “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Say to the children of Israel: These are the animals which you shall eat among all the animals of the earth. Every animal among cattle which has a divided hoof and chews the cud, you shall eat. But whatever chews the cud and has a hoof but does not divide it, such as the camel, you shall not eat,” etc.

The animals for which God cares are human beings. It is fitting, I say, that immediately after the fire was given from heaven and the sons of Aaron died, this law concerning animals to be eaten and not eaten was given. For after the coming of the Holy Spirit and the destruction of the Synagogue, the holy apostles too were commanded to distinguish between persons to be received and persons not to be received, or rejected. Thus, when Peter was hungry and wished to eat, there was shown to him in an ecstasy of mind “a certain vessel, like a great sheet, being let down to earth from heaven by its four corners; and in it were all four-footed animals, creeping things of the earth, and birds of heaven. And a voice came to him: Rise, Peter; kill and eat. But Peter said: Far be it from me, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common or unclean. And the voice came to him a second time: What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10) [Col. 0797A].

What must be understood under the names of quadrupeds, creeping things, birds, and creatures that swim in this holy and spiritual law is the same as what was understood in that vision. “These,” he says, “are unclean or defiled to you”—unless, that is understood, God sanctifies them. For these animals, though they are not human beings, as was said above, are such that, when God inspires them, they can change their former habit of impurity. Hence Peter, as we said, was told: “What God has cleansed, do not call common.” Let us now distinguish the causes of impurity according to the distinctions before us.

“Every animal,” he says, “that has a divided hoof and chews the cud, you shall eat.” To have a divided hoof and at the same time chew the cud is to have a discerning understanding of the holy Trinity and carefully to reconsider its remembrance in speech and deed [Col. 0797C]. “You shall eat every such one,” he says, because whoever is such should confidently be admitted into the body or communion of the Church.

“But whatever indeed chews the cud and has a hoof, yet does not divide it, you shall not eat.” One seems indeed to chew the cud but does not divide the hoof if one appears to act rightly but errs in faith, not rightly distinguishing the persons of the one Trinity. Conversely, one divides the hoof but does not chew the cud if one professes to know God but denies him by deeds. “You shall not touch their carcasses,” he says—that is, you shall not consent to dead works. The fourth kind, placed much farther below—namely, the animal which neither divides the hoof nor chews the cud—is wholly opposite to the first and therefore much more unclean: it signifies the person who honors God neither in understanding nor in action [Col. 0797D].

## CHAPTER XI. What it means for fish to have fins; for birds to be four-footed; and what a creeping thing is.

“These are the creatures born in the waters which it is lawful to eat. Everything that has fins and scales, whether in the sea, rivers, or pools, you shall eat. But whatever among the creatures that move and live in the waters does not have fins and scales shall be abominable and detestable to you.”

The unclean creatures that swim are especially the Jews: they swim in the streams of the Scriptures but have no fins, because they follow the letter alone, which kills, and do not leap up to the Spirit that gives life [Col. 0798A].

“These are the birds you shall not eat and must avoid,” etc. The unclean birds are the vain philosophers of the Gentiles. Those among them who philosophize with their mind about heavenly things—for example, the sun, moon, stars, and the rest—but live with their belly and body upon the earth and in the mud of vices, are rightly compared to birds walking upon four feet. Those who are regarded as belonging to no good or honorable profession even among men—such as gluttons, actors, evildoers, and prostitutes—are also not inappropriately likened to creeping things. According to the character or distinctive quality of every vice, different people are rightly compared with different creeping things or unclean animals, as is supported by the authorities not only of sacred but also of secular writings. Hence it is read that Circe, daughter of the Sun, transformed the companions of Ulysses into various shapes, to the astonishment of boys. [Note: [Col. 0797D] Pliny, *Natural History* XXV.2.5; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.19; Hyginus, *Fables* 125, 156, 199; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, throughout.]

“Therefore these,” he says, “are unclean; and whoever touches their carcasses shall be defiled and unclean until evening”—that is, until perfect repentance. By this statement, often repeated, every consent to iniquity is spiritually condemned. It is now pleasing briefly to survey the names and natures of the animals mentioned in this Scripture.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the properties or natures of the animals which the Law expressly decrees to be unclean.

The *choerogryllus* is a prickly beast, larger than a hedgehog. The ostrich is called by a Greek name; it is an animal which appears to have feathers like a bird but does not rise high from the ground [Col. 0798C]. It is called an owl because it flies about at night; it is also the *nycticorax*, a bird that shuns the light. The *larus* is the *gala*, which is always accustomed to remain upon waters. The *bubo*, or eagle-owl, receives its name from the sound of its cry; it is a funereal bird, laden with feathers and dwelling in caves. The *mergus* is so called from its continual diving, a black bird hostile to fish. The ibis is a bird of the Nile River which draws out its belly’s excrement with its own beak; it gladly feeds on serpent eggs. The Greeks call the *onocrotalus*—a long-beaked bird resembling a swan, but larger. The *porphyrion* is a bird of purple color, as its name seems to indicate; others say it is white and like a swan, while others identify it with the pelican. Birds like coots are of the size and color of swans [Col. 0798D], with hard, large beaks, and dwell upon rocky shores. The Latins call them *diomedeae* and the Greeks *herodii*.

The *choradrion* is a wholly white bird whose internal parts cure dim eyes. The Greeks call it the *upupa*, because it settles upon human dung and feeds on foul excrement: a most filthy bird, with projecting crests, helmeted, dwelling among graves and dung heaps. The *attacus* and *ophimachus* are unknown birds. The *bruchus* is a locust which does not yet fly. The *locusta* is so called because it has long feet like a spear. The Greeks call this, whether marine or land-dwelling, *astagon*. *Mustela* is Greek, that is, “long mouse.” The crocodile is a four-footed animal named from its saffron color; it is born in the Nile. The *migale* [Col. 0799A] is an unknown beast, said nevertheless to resemble a chameleon. The chameleon has no single color, but is covered in diverse variegation like a leopard. The little body of the chameleon changes with utmost ease to the colors which it sees. The *stellio* is a kind of lizard, named from its color: its back is marked with shining spots like stars. A lizard is a kind of creeping creature so called because it has an arm. The mole is a land animal without eyes, always digging the earth; the Greeks call it *aphalaca*. Let the discourse now return to the spiritual sense.

## CHAPTER XIII. What it means mystically to touch, carry, or eat their carcasses; to wash garments; and so forth.

[Col. 0799B] “Whoever touches their carcasses shall be defiled and shall be unclean until evening. And if it is necessary to carry any dead thing of theirs, he shall wash his garments and be unclean until sunset.”

There are three things forbidden: eating, touching, and carrying something unclean. They differ in this respect: to do evil, to consent to evil, and for a time, out of necessity, to endure evil. But the necessity for which something unclean is to be carried must be legitimate: namely, where evil either cannot be corrected at all, or cannot be removed except with greater harm to the matter.

For example, when Naaman the Syrian said to Elisha the prophet: “This alone is the matter concerning which you should pray to the Lord for your servant: when my lord enters the temple of Rimmon to worship, leaning upon my hand, if I worship in the temple of Rimmon while he worships in that same place, may the Lord forgive your servant in this matter” (4 Kings 5). It was necessary for him to carry what was unclean—to endure the evil—not indeed in order to worship Rimmon, but to worship in the temple of Rimmon, where he could worship the true God just as well as in any place. Therefore the prophet immediately says to him: “Go in peace” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, the conscience of the one carrying it is not entirely unharmed; and even if he trusts in the excuse of necessity, this cannot rightly be called security but rather rashness. “Therefore,” he says, “he shall wash his garments”—that is, he shall weep over the misery of necessity itself; yet no trustworthy account relates that anyone did this. “And he shall be unclean until sunset”—that is, he shall place his hope in the death of him who, by dying, bore the sins of the world into death [Col. 0799D].

“Whoever touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening. And whatever any part of their carcasses falls upon shall be defiled.” This is the harsh and heavy yoke of servitude, of which the Apostle Peter most truly says: “Which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear” (Acts 15). An earthen vessel is broken; every food and every liquid in a vessel is cast away as unclean; ovens and cooking-pots—earthen cooking vessels with three feet—are destroyed. Yet springs and cisterns are not condemned to impurity on this account, nor is seed defiled unless water has been poured upon it before the carcass touches it.

Therefore, since we believe the Truth who says, “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person” (Matt. 15), let us understand by these things, as we began, rather those things that proceed from a person. For “these,” he says, “are what defile a person: evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies” (ibid.). Let us guard all that is ours from these, lest it be defiled by contact with them; and let us set the most diligent guardians over those committed to us, lest they be corrupted by the wretchedness of persons of this kind, saying with the Apostle: “Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle” (Col. 2) [Col. 0800A].

If it is an earthen vessel—that is, one whom we find taking pleasure in the company or conversation of such people and who is not yet strengthened in a good purpose—let it be broken: that is, let him be rebuked most severely, even restrained by blows. If it is an oven—that is, an adolescent, whose condition of age naturally burns like an oven—or cooking-pots, of which we spoke before: if, I say, they are ovens or cooking-pots, let them be destroyed according to the character of their conduct, that is, afflicted by blows or excessive fasts, so that they may be changed for the better.

If there is any liquid in a vessel—that is, if someone is not self-directed in counsel but is governed by another’s counsel, just as a vessel holds water not innate to itself but poured in from elsewhere—and such a person converses with one unclean, do not believe that he does so with a clean conscience, since the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15) [Col. 0800B].

But if they are springs, cisterns, or any collections of waters—the one having a vein of living waters, the other yielding drinkable rain received from heaven—that is, if they are wise persons possessing “every good gift and every perfect gift from above” (Jas. 1), by which they can govern a pure mind, and if such persons are seen conversing with those who are defiled and unclean, they shall be clean. That is, they shall be believed to be discussing with unclean persons a plan of chastity and purity.
