But if, he says, a carcass touches seed, it shall not defile it: that is, if one dead to God comes into conversation with one who has received a word of wisdom or knowledge, those who see this should not immediately condemn him, for example by saying with the Pharisees: “This man receives sinners and eats with them” (Matt. 9). For it can happen—and has often happened—that from seed of this sort the carcass of impurity may blossom again into purity and recover living character and beauty [Col. 0800D].

Nevertheless, if the same person who excels in speech has previously often been caught slipping in conduct, he is not to be believed. Therefore it follows: “But if anyone has poured water upon seed, and afterwards it has been touched by carcasses, it shall immediately be defiled.” It is as though he said: But if formerly—yesterday, the day before yesterday, or whenever—someone has justly stained that gossiper with reproach, and he does not have a good testimony from those outside (1 Tim. 3), and after this he mixes himself in conversation with the carcasses of sinners, do not believe that he is fit or qualified to win them over.

## CHAPTER XIV. What is mystically meant by: “If an animal which it is lawful for you to eat has died, whoever,” etc.

[Col. 0801A] “If an animal which it is lawful for you to eat has died, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until evening.” This plainly refers to what the Apostle says: “If one called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, do not even take food with such a one” (1 Cor. 5). And further: “Remove the evil one from among yourselves” (ibid.). Likewise another says: “Do not receive him into the house, nor say ‘Greetings’ to him. For whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him shares in his evil works” (2 John 1).

“And whoever eats or drinks anything from it shall wash his garments,” etc., as above [Col. 0801B]. “And such were some of us; but we were washed, we were sanctified, we were justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6). Therefore Christ’s Church has now lawfully touched, carried, and incorporated us into itself, while God cries from heaven on behalf of us all: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” (Acts 10).

Why, then, should those things which are still unclean not be abominable to us, and why should we not defile our souls by taking them as food? He says: “For I am the Lord your God. Be holy, because I am holy.” And again: “For I am the Lord who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that I might be your God. You shall be holy, because I am holy.”

If, then, we follow the royal law, let us not be conformed to the former desires of our ignorance, to which we were enslaved in Egypt, from which God brought us out. Peter the Apostle understood these under the names of impurity, when, after first saying, “Do not be conformed to the former desires of your ignorance, but according to him who called you holy, be yourselves also holy in all manner of life” (1 Pet. 1), he immediately introduced this passage, taken from here: “For it is written: You shall be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (ibid.) [Col. 0801C].

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the woman who, having received seed, has conceived; and concerning the common cause of our impurity, namely that there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

(CAP. XII.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a woman, having received seed, bears a male child, she shall be unclean for seven days, according to the days of her menstrual separation; and on the eighth day the little boy shall be circumcised. But she herself shall remain in the blood of her purification.” The immaculate law of the Lord permits no one at all to boast as though of his own cleanness, “that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world become subject to God” (Rom. III).

For if we Gentiles were unclean creeping things and serpents—which we ourselves do not deny, while giving thanks with our Corrector—how was it otherwise with them, that the animals they had were clean, such as it was lawful to eat? Were not they too conceived from unclean seed (Job XIV)—from unclean seed, I say, which in the first human beings the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, touched and defiled with his poison? If this is not so, why does this law speak thus, “which whatever it says speaks to those who are under the law?” (Rom. III). “There is therefore no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Rom. X). For all sinned—or rather, to speak according to the present letter, all were defiled—and needed the cleansing grace of God (Rom. III).

For how slight was the cleansing of the circumcised Jew, brought with sacrifices to that handmade temple, unless Christ, the Son of God, himself had come—both sacrifice and temple not made with hands—he who takes away the sins of the world. Thus Isaiah says: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloths of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV). Therefore let us confess that we were unclean creeping things, provided that the mouths also of those who insulted us are stopped, and every mouth stopped, where their righteousnesses are compared, on the basis of their own reading, with a menstrual cloth [Col. 0802B]. And we know that no one has washed the menstrual uncleanness of those who do not believe in Christ; but God has purified these creeping things, and adorned them with a hoof well divided and a ruminating mouth. But now let us examine the very words of this law.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the same matter; why it expressly says “having received seed”; and on the cleansing of her who has borne a male and of her who has borne a female.

“If a woman,” he says, “having received seed, bears a male child, she shall be unclean for seven days,” etc. The holy prophetic Spirit carefully defined his law by saying, “if, having received seed, she bears.” For he foresaw that there would be a certain woman who would indeed give birth, but would bear a child without having received seed [Col. 0802C]. Otherwise he would have made this definition in vain. Therefore, by the necessity of the law, the one woman—the one and only mother of Christ the Son of God—was altogether free; yet she laudably underwent this same law through voluntary humility.

“If,” he says, “she bears a male child, she shall be unclean for seven days.” And afterwards: “But if she bears a female, she shall be unclean for two weeks, according to the rite of menstrual flux; and for sixty-six days she shall remain in the blood of her purification.” In the plain literal sense, it must not be passed over that a woman giving birth to a female child bears a greater penalty of weakness or uncleanness than one giving birth to a male. And rightly both the written and natural law burden the female more than the male in this respect, because, at the entrance of sin through which death entered this world, the woman stood nearer than the man to that reptilian vessel of the devil, from which he hissed forth the poison that was the beginning of our uncleanness [Col. 0802D]. For it was not through the man that the woman, but through the woman that the man, was defiled by the devil’s lie (Rom. V). Rightly, therefore, in the case of a female both the natural flow and the period imposed by the law for purification are doubled.

Nevertheless, in the remedy of cleansing grace there is no difference. “For there,” says the Apostle, “is neither male nor female” (Gal. III). Hence under this law no sacrifice other than that for a son is given for a daughter: namely, a lamb, together with a dove or a turtledove. These are properly offered when the person who approaches faithfully believes in the passion of Christ, the uncontaminated and spotless Lamb, and has groaning, so as to reign with him through suffering with him: either in a flock, like the dove, or alone, like the turtledove [Col. 0803A]. For the dove is accustomed to moan in a flock, but the turtledove wanders and moans alone; and therefore the former signifies the public assemblies of the Church, the latter the secret tears of prayers. Thus, to moan in a flock like a dove is to do penance in the public Church; but to moan alone like a turtledove is to choose laments that are hidden or even remote from other people.

“But if her hand does not find, nor is she able to offer, a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons,” etc. His hand does not find a lamb who lacks such capacity that he can comprehend the mysteries of the true Lamb, Christ the Son of God. Let him therefore offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons—that is, let him be content with the practice of the twofold love. “One for a whole burnt offering, and the other [Col. 0803B] for sin.” For love of God burns wholly within; but love of neighbour strives outwardly, through works of mercy, to redeem sin.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the law concerning the leper: that God has taken care concerning this matter for the sake of mystery.

(CAP. XIII.) “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: A man in whose flesh and skin there arises a change of colour, or a pustule, or something as it were shining—that is, a plague of leprosy—shall be brought to Aaron the priest and to any one of his sons,” etc. The letter of this law is certainly plain. But why did the Lord God speak such things to Moses? Was it so great a concern to him to observe the leprosy of the human body and the leprosy of a household wall? For what is unclean to him except sin? Is he concerned with bodily diseases rather than with vices of the soul? “God, a mighty judge, has brandished his sword; he has bent his bow and made it ready” (Ps. VII).

Therefore, the same judgment must be made in this respect concerning the law of leprosies as concerning the sacrifices of brute animals. For, as we have already said elsewhere with prophetic testimonies, God did not institute such sacrifices because he was to eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats; rather, because the children of Israel eagerly craved such things voluntarily, according to Egyptian custom, and could not be weaned from them. Therefore they were so ordered that their arrangement might at least bear the shadow or figure of the true sacrifice in which God delights [Col. 0803D].

Likewise, God does not give a law concerning the examination and avoidance of leprosy because he abhors bodily weaknesses, but because a human being’s sense—even that of a very wise person—namely the external sense of sight or touch, almost naturally recoils from such an affliction, unless true mercy or unfeigned love has taught him to suffer with or have compassion on another. Therefore he established such a law for examining and avoiding leprosy, whose shadow or spiritual figure should instruct the spiritual person concerning spiritual things.

Accordingly, because it can happen—and has often happened—that in the house of cleanness, which is the Church of God, the most unclean leprosy, heretical leprosy, should arise, rightly, after the law has mystically been given concerning uncleannesses not to be admitted, it is also given [Col. 0804A] concerning their expulsion in anyone in whom, after knowledge of the truth, apostate or heretical uncleanness is found to have sprung up.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the priest’s diligence in judging leprosy, according to the Apostle who says: “Avoid a heretical person after a first or second admonition.”

He says, therefore: “A man in whose flesh or skin there arises a change of colour,” etc. First let us connect these things with the Apostle’s command, saying: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition, knowing that one of this kind is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Tit. III). Certainly, just as in this holy, just, and good law there are occasions when a man examined by the priest ought at once to be condemned as leprous and separated at the priest’s judgment, and occasions when he ought to be shut up once and again and examined on the seventh day, so in the holy Church there are occasions when, as soon as a man has departed from the faith, he ought to be called a heretic, and occasions when he ought first to be addressed once and again with pious admonitions.

Finally, if a person who stands opposed to faith and truth is such that there is no doubt that he errs in hypocrisy not through ignorance but malice, traffics in deceitful words, and speaks lies—as Simon Magus already was when he first thrust himself upon the apostles there (Acts VIII)—sentence should not be delayed; rather, the most wicked leprosy must immediately be cast out and separated, lest the rest be corrupted. He says therefore: “When he sees leprosy in the skin, and the hairs changed to a white colour, and the appearance of the leprosy itself lower than the rest of the flesh and skin, it is a plague of leprosy, and he shall be separated at his judgment” [Col. 0804C]. And afterwards he repeats this in confirmation:

“If,” he says, “a plague of leprosy is in a man, he shall be brought to the priest, and he shall look at him. And when the colour in the skin is white and it has changed the appearance of the hair, and the living flesh itself has appeared, it shall be judged a very old leprosy, deeply embedded in the skin. Therefore the priest shall pronounce him unclean and shall not shut him up, because the uncleanness is evident.”

Then indeed the hair is changed to a white colour and the appearance itself is lower than the rest of the flesh and skin when something is done under the whiteness and humility of hypocrisy, so that the simple in faith are led into error; concerning such persons the Apostle forewarns us, saying: “Let no one deceive you, coming in humility and worship of angels, walking in things which he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding the head, from which the whole body, joined and supplied by its bonds and connections, grows with the growth of God” (Col. II) [Col. 0804D].

Then, I say, with the appearance of the hairs changed, living flesh also appears, when what has been mentioned is knowingly done or stubbornly defended; this is sinning even by touching what is holy. To be sure, the leprosy of dead flesh is the discordant speech from right faith of an ignorant person, and this can be forgiven. But the leprosy of living flesh is the blasphemy of a person who knows the truth, and this “will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. XII).

“‘It shall be judged a very old leprosy,’ he says, ‘deeply embedded in the skin; the priest shall pronounce him unclean and shall not shut him up, because the uncleanness is evident’” [Col. 0805A]. This means: he will not take pains to correct a manifest heretic, but will avoid him and pronounce him to be avoided, because he is perverted, because he is incorrigible.

“But if there is a shining whiteness in the skin, not lower than the remaining flesh, and the hairs are of their former colour, the priest shall shut him up for seven days and examine him on the seventh day. And if the leprosy has not spread further nor passed its former bounds in the skin, he shall again shut him up for another seven days; and on the seventh day he shall inspect him. If the leprosy has become dimmer and has not spread in the skin, he shall cleanse him, because it is a scab.”

The meaning is this: if he seems to have erred through ignorance, rather than to have constructed blasphemy through vain glory, craft, or hypocrisy, he shall be examined separately, with the understanding of truth, by the most faithful steward of the word through all seven days—that is, throughout all the divinely inspired Scriptures [Col. 0805B]. “And if the leprosy has not spread further, nor passed its former bounds”—that is, if he has not increased his guilt by defending his error, as all heretics do whose hearts the devil overturns—“he shall again shut him up for another seven days and inspect him on the seventh day”: that is, with good hope he shall again catechize him in all the Scriptures of catholic truth, and, when he is well established, present him to holy Mother Church, saying that it was a scab and not leprosy—that he sinned through ignorance, not malice.

“And the man shall wash his garments, and he shall be clean.” According to this spiritual meaning, ecclesiastical prudence knows what distinction ought to be observed in washing garments. For one who has been corrected from heretical leprosy and restored to the integrity of faith—whatever sort of leprosy it may have been—provided that he was baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is not given a second washing of the flesh; but, after confession has been made, he receives the spirit of reconciliation and remission of sins, by which the garments are sufficiently washed, so that such a person may be clean [Col. 0805C].

“And if, after he has been seen by the priest and restored to cleanness, the leprosy grows again, he shall be brought to him and condemned as unclean.” And this is just. For if a sinner is again estranged from the womb, wanders from the belly, and speaks falsehood (Ps. LVII), what hope can remain? How can he be excused on grounds of ignorance? Thus, just as the Apostle mentioned above says, “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Tit. III), precisely because he is inexcusable, indeed incorrigible, so now the law decrees unclean the person who, having been restored to cleanness, has again contracted leprosy.

This, plainly, is what someone does when, perhaps needing some assistance which the catholic Church could provide, he professes the right faith because he is told: “You will not be helped here unless you communicate”; and then, needing something else for which, for example, he might be helped among Arians, he again [Col. 0806A] deserts the catholic faith because the Arians say: “You will not be helped unless you communicate here.” Like chaff lightly carried by every wind, now he flies from the threshing-floor to the hedge, now he is carried back from the hedge to the threshing-floor. Therefore he will be condemned as unclean according to this law and, according to the evangelical precept of the Apostle, avoided “because he is perverted.”

## CHAPTER XIX. What if leprosy is judged very clean, and therefore the person exceedingly clean, according to the Apostle’s saying: “I wrote to you in the Epistle not to associate with fornicators.”

“But if leprosy has broken out and spread over the skin, and has covered all the flesh from head to foot—everything that falls under the sight of the eyes—the priest shall examine him and judge him to be held by a very clean leprosy, because he has wholly turned white; and therefore the person shall be clean. But whenever living flesh appears in him, then by the priest’s judgment he shall be defiled and reckoned among the unclean.”

The Apostle, in lawful harmony with the mystery of this passage, says to the Corinthians: “I wrote to you in the Epistle: Do not associate with fornicators—not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the covetous, or robbers, or idolaters; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I have written to you not to associate: if one who is called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, not even to take food with such a one. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Do you not judge those who are inside? But God will judge those who are outside. Remove the evil from among yourselves” (I Cor. III).

For what is it to be covered entirely with leprosy from head to foot except to be a fornicator or covetous person and, both in profession and deed, altogether outside? What is it for living flesh to be sprinkled with leprosy except to be called a brother and yet to be a fornicator, and to do the other works contrary to the name of brother? Therefore, for leprosy to break out and spread in the skin, covering all the flesh from head to foot, whatever falls under the eyes’ sight, and, when examined by the priest, to be judged leprosy indeed but very clean leprosy, because it has all turned white, and therefore for the person to be declared clean—this is plainly to associate freely with the fornicators of this world, the covetous, robbers, and idolaters, and to judge nothing concerning them because they are outside and God will judge them [Col. 0806D].

“Such a person shall be clean,” he says: that is, such intercourse will not defile you under ecclesiastical law, and in this way his leprosy will be very clean to you. For our Lord also associated with such people, and was reproached accordingly as a friend of sinners and tax collectors (Matt. XI). Otherwise, if such persons had to be avoided, both we and the apostles would have had to leave this world; indeed, our Lord himself would never have come into this world.

Conversely, for living flesh to appear in leprosy, or for living flesh to be sprinkled with leprosy—which is far different from, and unlike, the preceding case, and is therefore judged unclean—plainly means that the person “who has a name that he lives” (Apoc. III), who is called a brother and is inside, must be judged; and with such a one not even food is to be taken, but evil is to be removed from among yourselves (I Cor. III) [Col. 0807A].

But what if the brother is swallowed up by excessive sorrow? (II Cor. II). Is he then altogether to be abandoned, when he ought only for this reason to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord? (I Cor. V). Thus, after the statement, “for if living flesh is sprinkled with leprosy, it is unclean,” there immediately follows: “But if it has again turned to whiteness and covered the whole person, the priest shall examine him and decree him clean.”

This is as though it said: if he has been swallowed up by excessive sorrow—or even before he is wholly swallowed up—the priest shall look upon him: namely, the one who knows that he has received care of weak souls, not tyranny over healthy ones, and is therefore a lawful priest. He shall look upon him, I say, with a merciful gaze; he shall confirm love toward him, declaring him clean, so that he may judge that one who associates with him in conversation is not to incur an equal penalty of excommunication, but should instead send wise persons who may, as it were secretly, comfort the wavering brother [Col. 0807B].

## CHAPTER XX. Mystically, on the leprosy of one who has a congenital ulcer and of one burned by fire: on the distinction between a heresiarch and a heretic.

“Flesh and skin in which an ulcer has arisen and has healed, and in the place of the ulcer there appears a scar, white or reddish, the person shall be brought to the priest.” Likewise: “Flesh and skin which fire has burned, and which, when healed, has a white or reddish scar: the priest shall examine it. And behold, it has turned white, and its place is lower than the remaining skin; he shall pronounce him unclean, because a plague of leprosy has arisen in the scar.”

Up to this point the holy and mystical law has spoken indiscriminately concerning the leprosy of every kind of heresy; now it speaks distinctly, first concerning the leprosy of the heresiarch—that is, of the one from whom the heresy originated—and that of the person who has been defiled by heretical contagion not through his own fault but under another’s influence. Thus, as a congenital ulcer and a burn differ in their own causes, so the guilt of a heresiarch differs from that of the person whose soul has been burned by the deceiver. The former, ulcerated by his own fault, conceived deadly poison; the latter perhaps unwittingly, while flattering a wealthy heretic, is in some sense stretched out beside coals and is burned in the leg by sparks flying from the crackling furnace [Col. 0807D].

The law for both is the same. For there is little difference in guilt between being able to deceive and being deceived. “When,” he says, “the priest sees the place of the leprosy lower than the remaining flesh and the hairs turned white, he shall pronounce him unclean. For a plague of leprosy has arisen in the ulcer,” etc. Since this law has already been explained, let us proceed with the rest. Yet this must not be passed over: in the flesh or skin, after the congenital ulcer has healed, the plague of leprosy then arises when a vicious man, of great wealth and great, ardent talent, having been reproved by the Church for his own vice, becomes worse; and, after a single carnal vice has been healed or restrained as though it were an ulcer, he falls into heresy, makes schisms, and troubles catholic peace, inflamed by his own anger [Col. 0808A].

Such was Nicholas, the seventh man in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts VI). Rebuked on account of jealousy for his exceptionally beautiful wife, he is said to have replied that anyone who wished might take her as wife; and on this account he taught unbelievers that the apostles permitted indiscriminate and common unions with women for all.

## CHAPTER XXI. On leprosy of the head or beard, and the need cautiously to distinguish whether it is leprosy, a scab, or baldness.

“Man or woman, in whose head or beard leprosy has sprung up, the priest shall examine them. And if the place is lower than the remaining flesh, and the hair yellow and thinner than usual, he shall pronounce them unclean, because it is leprosy of the head or beard. But if he sees the place of the spot equal to the neighbouring flesh,” etc., as above.

From this passage one may learn that judgment should not rashly be pronounced concerning anyone’s practice, especially a practice which can be performed with a good intention. For leprosy has sprung up—or is thought to have sprung up—upon the head or beard, a part of the body not hidden or so covered by clothing, when someone publicly maintains in the Church a practice that has, or is believed to have, a cause of unbelief. Such cases, I say, must not be judged rashly. For it can happen [Col. 0808C] that what is thought to be ringworm or leprosy of the head because the hair falls out may be a scab or baldness: that is, what is said to depart from faithful or sound teaching may be held with a good purpose and a clean conscience.

For example, a person may favour virginity too zealously, and the opinion may arise that he condemns marriage; or he may criticize a brother who eats meat too immoderately, and thereby afford an occasion for people to suppose that, against the Apostle, he wishes to teach that God’s good creation ought to be rejected (I Tim. IV). He shall be brought, he says, to the priest, and the matter shall be carefully examined in the same order already set out above. Once the truth of the matter has been discovered, if it is leprosy the person shall be declared unclean; if it is a scab, after the garments have first been washed, he shall be cleansed; if it is baldness, he shall be clean without any further proceeding.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the separated leper: what it means to have torn garments, an uncovered head, a mouth covered with clothing, and to proclaim himself defiled and unclean.

“Therefore, whoever is marked with leprosy and separated at the priest’s judgment shall have torn garments, an uncovered head, and a mouth covered with clothing; he shall proclaim himself defiled and unclean. Throughout the whole time that he is leprous and unclean, he shall live alone outside the camp.”

This is the harsh and powerful staff of the killing letter, anathematizing the diseases of the wretched body with greater shame and ignominy than adulteries themselves, which God hates. But what the life-giving Spirit says to the Churches in this place is altogether just and reasonable. For one who is marked with heretical leprosy is indeed to be marked, because he is certainly to be avoided.

“He shall therefore,” it says, “have torn garments.” Plainly the heretic has torn garments; for in being a heretic, he has torn for himself that garment of Christ, as a type of which the soldiers refused to tear the tunic of Christ the Lord himself (John XIX). Hence he is called—and is—a schismatic, because by tearing apart the one unity of faith or the truth of Scripture, he himself is torn and rent [Col. 0809A].

He also has “an uncovered head,” for he has lost the crown of hope in the Lord; indeed, he has lost the very head whose members we are—the head, I say, of the Church, Christ, “from whom the whole body is supplied through its bond and connection and grows with the growth of God” (Col. II). Instead, he has taken for himself the devil, the head of enemies: an ulcerated head, a leprous head.

He also has “a mouth covered with clothing”: that is, a double-tongued and deceitful mouth stopped up by the spirit of pretence. “Covered with clothing,” I say. For he takes the greatest care that those who have an open nose of discernment should not detect by its stench his malignant mouth or throat, of which it is written elsewhere: “Their throat is an open grave; they acted deceitfully with their tongues; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. XIII). Nor is this without reason. For “he shall proclaim himself defiled and unclean.” When the heretic thinks that he is whispering, he is shouting; when he imagines that he is hissing with a viper’s tongue, his barking deafens every hearer [Col. 0809C]. When, I say, he slanders God the king in his chamber, the bird of heaven hears and reports it (Eccles. X); and terror and astonishment arise throughout the whole house of Christ, which is the Church. Therefore whatever the heretic says is a cry and stirs up a crowd.

What then? “Throughout the whole time,” it says, “that he is leprous and unclean, he shall live alone outside the camp.” Therefore let no one promise pardon after death to a heretic whom the camp of the catholic Church does not receive while alive. For heretical leprosy or uncleanness, which is not cleansed in this life by repentance, has no means of cure after this life. “Whatever your hand is able to do,” says Ecclesiastes, “do diligently; for there is neither work nor reasoning nor wisdom nor knowledge in the underworld, to which you are hastening” (Eccles. IX).

Therefore, throughout all time—that is, for ages of ages, without limit and without end—he shall be outside the camp of the everlasting Church: alone, although among the multitude of the lost; alone, I say, and solitary, because abandoned by God; a deserter and deserted, a defiler and unclean, if during the time in which he lives he has not been amended by the spirit of reconciliation [Col. 0809D].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the leprosy of garments; and that a leprous garment must be burned—that is, heretical writing must be wholly removed.

“A woollen or linen garment which has leprosy in its warp or weft, or indeed a skin or anything made from skin, if it is infected with a white or reddish spot, shall be reckoned leprosy and shall be shown to the priest. After examining it, he shall shut it up for seven days; and looking again on the seventh day, if he discovers that it has increased, it is persistent leprosy. He shall judge the garment and everything in which it is found unclean, and therefore it shall be burned with fire.”

A woollen or linen garment, or a garment certainly of skin—any leprous garment, I say—is a perverse writing of a heretic, woven or sewn with a coarser style, like wool, or a subtler one, like linen; or drawn from Plato and the other philosophers dead to God, like a leather garment, gathered, that is, from dead animals. Thus, if it has a white or reddish spot—that is, if anything disagrees with the entirety of the Scriptures, whether in humble or lofty speech—it shall be reckoned “leprosy,” namely heretical unbelief [Col. 0810B], by the person who reads or hears it; and it “shall be shown to the priest,” namely, to a man possessing the true sense and judgment of the Scriptures. Whoever does not show it to him shall be condemnable as though for consenting.

“Having examined it, he shall shut it up for seven days”: that is, he shall not issue a rash judgment, but shall compare it with the whole authority of the Scriptures. And if he “discovers that the leprosy has increased”—that is, that it truly is heresy—“it shall be burned with fire.” For in no way does a heretical writing perish from memory better or more quickly. The leprous garment, therefore—that is, the perverse writing—shall be burned with visible flames; but the incurable leprous writer, namely the impenitent heretic, shall be burned with unquenchable flames, eternal flames, the flames of Gehenna [Col. 0810C].

In contrast, that garment which the wise woman made—“for she sought wool and linen and worked with the counsel of her hands”—shall clothe her noble husband; “and she shall be given of the fruit of her hands, and her works shall praise her in the gates” (Prov. XXXI).

“But if he sees that it has not increased”—that is, if he judges it not to be heresy and that what sounds perverse can be understood in a good sense—“he shall command them to wash that in which the leprosy is”: that is, he shall preach or explain before all the sound or useful sense of the expression. “And when he sees that the former appearance has not returned”—that is, that his sound interpretation helps neither readers nor hearers—“he shall burn it with fire,” as has been said [Col. 0810D].

“But if the place of the leprosy has become dimmer after the garment has been washed, he shall tear it off and separate it from the whole”: that is, if error or heresy is in a single chapter, while many things are faithful or useful in the whole body of the book, he shall remove the fault and preserve the rest. Some have attempted to do this with the books of Origen.

“But if it appears further in those places which were previously unspotted, it is a flying and wandering leprosy”: that is, if disagreements arise and scandals are made even from those portions of the writings which had formerly appeared harmless, they ought to be burned with fire, because they harm the simple more than they profit the wise and discerning, when writings of approved faith are sufficient. “If it ceases”—that is, if the disagreement or disturbance among readers can be calmed by reason—“he shall wash again those things which are clean” [Col. 0811A]: that is, he shall defend or commend what is catholic by a repeated testimony, “and they shall be clean”: they shall remain authoritative.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the cleansing of the leper—that is, the heretic; that to cleanse one already cleansed is to reconcile one corrected; and what it means to offer two sparrows.

(CAP. XIV.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the rite for the leper. When he is to be cleansed, he shall be brought to the priest. The priest, going out from the camp, when he finds that the leprosy has been cleansed, shall command the person to be purified to offer for himself two live sparrows which are lawful to eat, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. He shall command one of the sparrows to be sacrificed in an earthen vessel over living waters. But he shall dip the other, alive, with the cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop, in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow; with this he shall sprinkle seven times the person who is to be cleansed, so that he may rightly be purified.”

Truly the law is “good” and holy “if anyone uses it lawfully” (I Tim. I). Truly the face of Moses is splendid if anyone looks upon it with the veil removed (II Cor. III). We have seen and understood how it casts out the leper—that is, the heretic—because he is leprous. Let us now see how it cleanses him—that is, reconciles him—when he has been cleansed and corrected in the catholic faith. For this is to cleanse one who has been cleansed: to reconcile one who has been corrected.

“Let him offer,” it says, “for himself two sparrows.” The sparrow here signifies Christ, who also says in the psalm: “I have watched, and have become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. CI): that is, I have risen and ascended into heaven, separated from human beings, like a solitary sparrow on a roof, set apart from other birds and resting in its own place [Col. 0811C]. But two sparrows must be offered: “and he shall command,” it says, “one of the sparrows to be sacrificed in an earthen vessel over living waters; but he shall dip the other alive in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow,” etc.

Why is this so, except because the person reconciled to the Church must confess Christ as crucified and dead from our weakness, and now living by the power of God? (II Cor. XIII). For in shadow or figure these two sparrows are offered, but in the truth of substance Christ is one: one and the same person, of a twofold nature; crucified in respect of one, as has been said, but in respect of the other now alive, since he “dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him” (Rom. VI) [Col. 0811D].

Therefore, when the two sparrows lawful for eating have been offered—for both of the matters mentioned must now be believed—one is sacrificed, and with the other, alive and bearing the blood of the sacrificed bird, the person to be cleansed is sprinkled seven times. For Christ was sacrificed, and he himself, restored to life, gave the sevenfold Spirit, without whom no one is duly sprinkled so as to be cleansed by the remission of sins. This is wonderfully celebrated in the sacraments of the Church, as the faithful know.

The sparrow is sacrificed “in an earthen vessel”: that is, faith is recited concerning that passion of Christ which arose from our weakness. And this is “over living waters”: that is, according to the Scriptures containing the truth of life. There are the cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop [Col. 0812A]. The incorruptible cedar wood signifies hope of the future resurrection and incorruption; the scarlet thread, love; and hyssop, a lowly herb by which swelling of the lungs is reduced, signifies faith itself, by which our hearts are purified. Without these reconciliation does not take place.

Therefore, after one sparrow has been sacrificed, the other is dipped alive in its blood, and the person to be cleansed is sprinkled seven times, that he may duly be cleansed. For the one and same Christ is wondrously both daily sacrificed here in his sacrament and lives in heaven, never to die. Having received this faith, whoever has been a heretic, “sprinkled seven times”—that is, renewed by the holy sevenfold Spirit, who is given in the catholic Church alone—“shall release the living sparrow into the field, that it may fly away,” confessing, namely, that Christ, as has been said, remains forever and will never die.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the mystical observance concerning the leper who has been cleansed, and concerning his rites and offerings.

“When a man has washed his garments, he shall shave all the hair of his body and wash himself with water. Then, being purified, he shall enter the camp—provided only that he remains outside his tent for seven days; and on the seventh day he shall shave the hair of his head, his beard, his eyebrows, and all the hair of his body. After washing again both his garments and his body, on the eighth day he shall take two unblemished lambs, and a year-old ewe without blemish, and three tenths of fine flour for a sacrifice, mixed with oil, and separately a sextary of oil. And when the priest who is purifying the man has set him and all these things before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, he shall take the lamb and offer it for guilt, together with the sextary of oil,” etc.

“And when,” he says, “the man has washed his garments,” namely with that washing of which the Prophet says in the psalm: “I shall wash my bed every night; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. VI), “he shall shave all the hair of his body,” that is, he shall cut off from himself every heretical superstition; “and he shall wash himself with water,” that is, he shall be instructed by sacred teaching. And, purified in this manner, he shall enter the camp; for from that time onward he shall be reckoned within the Catholic Church—“provided only that he remain outside his tent for seven days,” lest, still untrained, he mingle with the evil conversations of his heretical companions and be corrupted once more by their revived leprosy. [Col. 0812C]

“Let him remain,” I say, “outside his tent for seven days,” that is, until Christ is perfectly formed in him, to whom he is born anew through grace bringing him forth again. Nor is this contrary to what was previously commanded to the priests at their consecration: “You shall not go out from the entrance of the tabernacle for seven days” (Lev. VIII). For to priests the tabernacle is the Catholic Church; but to this leper, his tent was the gathering of heretics.

“And on the seventh day,” he says, “he shall shave the hair of his head, his beard, his eyebrows, and all the hair of his body.” This is the perfection of reformation in one who had been a bearded and inveterate heretic: that he return altogether to the childhood of innocence; that, putting aside philosophy and empty deceit, which is “according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world,” and not according to the Spirit (Col. II), he may flourish again in him who is the head of the body, the Church (Col. I), through a complete stripping off of the body of flesh. This is to shave the hair of the head—that is, the former dispositions of the heart—the manly beard, the eyebrows of pride, and the hairs of the whole body, so that the whole person may proceed as new.

“And after washing again his garments and body,” that is, after confession has been made again and again, “on the eighth day he shall take two unblemished lambs, a year-old ewe without blemish, and three tenths of fine flour,” etc. This offering of the leper differs from the aforementioned offerings of the priests, because there the Law commands a calf, a goat, and a lamb to be taken, while the same quantity of unleavened bread is prescribed from the basket; here, however, “he shall take,” it says, “two lambs, a year-old ewe, and three tenths of fine flour.” [Col. 0813A]

Certainly this is required of the heretic who has been cleansed from such leprosy: when the brows of all vain philosophy have been shaven away, he must embrace the simplicity of faith; and thus, with the two unblemished lambs, confess in the two Testaments the one “year-old ewe”—that is, the one Catholic faith, simply. For from a priest—that is, from one who has never strayed from the faith—such painstaking exactitude is neither required nor demanded, that he should be content with simple faith; since he has made no one anxious by attempting to comprehend God by human reasoning.

Therefore, “he shall take three tenths of fine flour for the sacrifice.” When three tenths have been taken, seven tenths remain. He shall therefore take three tenths of fine flour—that is, with a pure mind and public voice he shall confess the three Persons of the one Godhead—in order that he may receive in the Catholic mother Church the seven tenths which he did not have, namely the holy sevenfold Spirit. But it is not enough to confess the holy Trinity in the sight of the Church unless, under the leading authority of love, one works faithfully toward both God and neighbour.

“The fine flour,” he says, “shall be mixed with oil, and separately it shall have a sextary of oil”: that is, the oil of charity is mixed within, before the Lord, while outwardly there are the six works of mercy toward one’s neighbour: to give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, shelter to the stranger, clothe the naked, visit the sick, and come to the one in prison (Matt. XXV). The rest we pass over, because it is almost the same as what we have discussed above concerning the consecration of priests—or rather, at the beginning of this volume—as far as we were able.

Nor is it surprising that priests are consecrated by the same rite by which one who had been leprous is cleansed. For in the reconciliation of a heretic all the mysteries of the Christian faith must be performed, by which we have been made a kingdom and priests to our God (Rev. V), except that the washing of the flesh is not repeated for one who comes from heretics, however perverse, provided that they baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“But if he is poor and his hand cannot find the things that have been mentioned,” etc. That person is poor who, because of the smallness of his knowledge, does not penetrate the depths of the Scriptures, which are bounded by the two Testaments. “He shall therefore take,” it says, “a lamb for sin,” that is, for the correction of the heretical plague he shall take hold of the creed of apostolic faith; “and a tenth part of fine flour mixed with oil, and a sextary of oil,” that is, the one faith of the three Persons without subtle investigation—provided only that he have love toward God and neighbour, according to the sense explained above. [Col. 0813B]

“He shall also take,” it says, “two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one of which shall be for sin and the other for a burnt offering” (Lev. XII): namely, having a twofold groaning, either because he said and did things not belonging to Catholic purity, or because he did not say and do things alien to the contagion of heretical leprosy. The rest, as has already been said, we pass over; for we are not obliged to repeat the same things everywhere in all their places.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the leprosy of houses: how it is to be examined when reported to the priest—that is, how heresy among persons living together in any rank is to be investigated.

“Then the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: When you have entered the land of Canaan, which I shall give you as a possession, if there is a plague of leprosy in a house, the owner of the house shall go and report it to the priest, saying: ‘Something like a plague of leprosy seems to me to be in my house.’ But he shall command them first to remove everything before he enters it and sees whether it is leprosy, lest everything in the house be made unclean. Then he shall enter in order to inspect the leprosy of the house,” etc.

Here too the life-giving spirit of the Law, derived from what precedes, lies ready to hand. For if God’s concern and judgment are not about leprosy of the flesh but leprosy of the mind, or sin of the flesh, how much less is he concerned with the leprosy of walls or of visible, senseless stones? Therefore, reason requires that “house” here be understood in the sense in which we call individual persons parts of a house.

Nor is this yet merely spiritual. For even literally Scripture often divides a tribe into families or kindreds, a kindred into houses, and a house into men. “When, therefore,” it says, “you have entered the land of Canaan, which I shall give you as a possession, if there is a plague of leprosy in the houses,” etc. From the time when, under Christian kings and Catholic rulers, the holy Church was allowed to rule publicly in its assemblies and govern the divine dominion by heavenly laws, we have entered the land of Canaan, which means “their movement.” [Col. 0814B]

For the land of Canaan, which the Lord gave that people to possess, signifies the land of the living, from which malignant spirits have been expelled: because, according to the name Canaan, “their foot was moved” (Ps. XCIII), “they fell and could not stand” (Ps. XXXV). Yet because through the gates of the present Church we enter that land, we do not speak vainly when we say that we have already entered it; and we glory in blessed hope, since, while still pilgrims in the body, we can already have our citizenship in heaven with the Apostle (Phil. III).

“If,” it says, “there is a plague of leprosy in the houses,” that is, if heresy arises in any assemblies of the Church, monasteries, or any orders living in common, “the owner of the house shall go, reporting it to the priest”—it is understood because he cannot heal the deadly plague by himself. For then the owner of the house, the one set over Christ’s household, must seek the assistance of someone greater or superior when he cannot cure the domestic disease by himself.

“But he shall command them to remove everything from the house before he enters it and sees whether it is leprosy.” When the priest is about to enter the house in order to see whether what has been reported is leprosy or not, everything which can be removed must first be removed. That is, when a disagreement over faith or doctrines has arisen in an assembly or community of persons living together, before the matter is examined those who do not agree with the makers of scandal must declare the position in which they dissent from the others. For once clear reasoning has proved the leprosy to be heretical, judicial sentence will fall alike not only upon its authors but upon those who agree with them. [Col. 0814C]

Why, then, does he command that they remove everything? “Lest,” he says, “all that is in the house become unclean”: namely, when the evidence of convicted impurity has been brought forward. “Then he shall enter to inspect the leprosy of the house,” that is, after he has separated both parts of the schism and obtained a distinct knowledge of each.

“And when he sees in its walls depressions, disfigured by pallor or redness, and lower than the rest of the surface, he shall go out of the entrance of the house and immediately shut it up for seven days.” This means: when he hears that the propositions of the disputants differ altogether from the beauty and soundness of the holy Scriptures, he shall go out with his whole mind turned away and impose silence upon the unclean spirit—that is, heretical leprosy—for “seven days,” that is, by setting before it the authority of all truth, “that the upright may see or understand and rejoice, and all iniquity may stop its mouth” (Ps. CVI).

## CHAPTER XXVII. If after seven days he finds that the leprosy has grown, he shall command the stones to be removed: that is, if heresy persists after every admonition, he shall expel its authors; and if even so it makes no progress, he shall destroy the whole heretical house.

“And when he returns on the seventh day, he shall inspect it. If the leprosy has grown, he shall command the stones in which the leprosy is to be removed, and shall throw them outside the city into an unclean place. But he shall have the house itself scraped all around on the inside, and the dust from the scraping scattered outside the city into an unclean place; and other stones shall be put in place of those removed, and the house shall be plastered with other mortar.”

“On the seventh day,” it says—that is, after he has used every care of sound teaching—when he returns, if he finds that the heretical leprosy “has grown,” “he shall command the stones in which the leprosy is to be removed”: that is, he shall employ the iron of severance, removing and expelling those who are authors of the same impiety. “And he shall throw them outside the city”—outside, I say, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem; outside the peace of ecclesiastical communion—“into an unclean place,” into the circus or theatre of the devil, or into the evil fellowship of evil persons, among the dead, among those who are in hell. [Col. 0815D]

“But he shall scrape the house itself all around on the inside.” For the entire community of cohabitants cannot remain free from their contamination, as Scripture says: “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Ecclus. XIII). “He shall scrape it,” I say, “all around”: that is, he shall compel all, both by confession of speech and by subscription of hand, to anathematize the heretical doctrine; “and he shall scatter the dust from the scraping outside the city into an unclean place,” so that no impurity and no heretical opinions may remain in the entire house of God.

But “he shall also command other stones to be placed in place of those which have been removed,” namely, so that, when evil persons are miserably destroyed (Matt. XXI), the house may be filled with other members of the household, who may rightly be joined to the household of the Lord for the truth of faith and the establishment of Catholic peace. Finally, “he shall plaster the house with other mortar”: that is, after evil opinions have been expelled, he shall restore the whole condition of faith or Catholic peace by diligent preaching and better teaching.

“But if, after the stones have been removed, the dust taken away, and other earth plastered on, the priest enters and sees that the leprosy has returned and the walls are sprinkled with spots, it is a persistent leprosy, and the house is unclean. They shall immediately destroy it,” etc. For just as, after the first and second inspection, a leprous person is condemned as unclean, so also a house, after the first and second examination, if the leprosy increases, is rightly destroyed. That is, just as a heretical person is to be avoided after a first and second admonition, so the whole house—the Church of the wicked, the assembly of heretics—must be anathematized after the first and second visitation of an orthodox priest. [Col. 0816A]

“They shall therefore destroy,” he says, “the house, its stones, its timber, and all its dust, and throw them outside the town into an unclean place”: namely, with that prince of impurity, the devil, to whom it was said through the prophet under the name of the king of Babylon: “All the kings of the nations, all of them, slept in glory, each in his own house. But you are cast out of your tomb like a useless branch, polluted and wrapped up with those slain by the sword” (Isa. XIV).

“But if, upon entering, he sees that the leprosy has not grown in the house after it has been plastered anew, he shall purify it, its health having been restored. And for its purification he shall take two birds,” etc., as above.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning him who suffers a discharge of semen—that is, incontinence of speech—and concerning her who has a flow of blood—that is, one who slanders any brother—and concerning their mystical offering if healed.

(CH. XV.) “A man who suffers a discharge of semen shall be unclean. And then he shall be judged subject to this defect when the foul moisture has adhered to his flesh at every moment and grown upon it.” Likewise: “A woman who suffers a flow of blood when the month returns shall be separated for seven days.” And afterwards: “A woman who suffers a flow of blood for many days, not at the time of her monthly period, or who does not cease to flow with blood after menstruation, shall be unclean, as though she were at the time of menstruation, as long as she is subject to this affliction.”

In due order, after the Law concerning condemnable leprosy—that is, heretical perversity—has been given, Scripture sets forth the Law concerning a discharge of semen and menstrual blood: that is, the incontinence of a murmuring mouth and the verbosity of a slanderous tongue. What is it to suffer a discharge of semen or blood except to pour forth slanderous or even criminal words?

Certainly, one who slanders God or blasphemes God, and one who slanders his neighbour or judges his neighbour, belong together. For if someone, during this time of Catholic peace, when every heresy has been stoned or buried beneath sufficient writings of the orthodox, hates even the neighbour whom he sees, how could he, when the tares of heretics flourished, have been faithful to the God whom he does not see? Therefore this person too is unclean.

If he is established in a profession of virtue or in any eminent rank, he is a man suffering a discharge of blood. But if he belongs to the common multitude of secular persons and holds no office of ecclesiastical or civic rank, he is rightly called a woman suffering a menstrual discharge of blood, so long as he does not spare others with his slanderous tongue, so long as he does not cease to nourish scandals and create dissensions. [Col. 0816D]

And observe how cautiously this is said, how carefully defined: “Then,” it says, “he shall be judged subject to this defect when the foul moisture has adhered to his flesh at every moment and grown upon it.” This means: he shall not be judged subject to the defect of the tongue for one word; for “if anyone does not offend in word, this one is a perfect man” (Jas. III). But when the foul and wet pest of talkativeness adheres unceasingly to his mouth by habitual practice, and bread of this sort is sweet to his throat, then he too shall be unclean—yet not in the same degree as the leper, not yet in the same degree as the heretic.

For this Law does not require that he be separated and live alone outside the camp. Holy Church has excellently and lawfully learned to bear and endure such persons within her camp, though grieving and saying: “Woe is me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner. I was peaceful with those who hate peace” (Ps. CXIX). She maintains this rule of discernment: toward neighbours who hate peace, she remains peaceable as long as she can without impairing the bond of unity; but with those who hate the peace of God, who speak wrongly concerning God and are heretics, she has no peace or communion of toleration.

The cleansing of such persons is without blood. For it says: “If he who suffers such an affliction has been healed, he shall count seven days after his cleansing; and after washing his garments and his whole body in living water, he shall be clean. On the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, and shall come before the Lord to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony and give them to the priest,” etc. [Col. 0817C]

Thus, I say, the cleansing of such persons—and of those women whose blood has stopped and ceased to flow—is without blood, whereas the cleansing of the leper takes place only with the blood of a living bird. For all who are inwardly within the confession of faith, although they are chaff, when through repentance they are changed and become grain, do not require solemn reconciliation; they need only offer the groaning of the turtledove and pigeon, and they are saved. The rest, since it is obvious and has been said above in similar or partly identical terms, we pass over in our eagerness to proceed.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That a woman suffering from the defect of menstrual flow should not be prohibited from entering into holy communion.

Yet this point concerning menstrual blood should not be passed over according to the letter, because under the Gospel of Christ a woman suffering such an affliction is not unclean before God (Matt. IX). A man, however, is rendered unclean—namely, “a man who lies with her during the time of menstrual blood shall be unclean.” And by this Law a man is forbidden to have intercourse with her, a provision by which the sacred Law certainly takes much care for conceptions. For it is said that fetuses conceived in this way acquire a defect of seed, so that leprous and elephantine persons are born from such conception, and corrupted discharge produces foul bodies in either sex through deformity or abnormality of limbs.

But why should she be unclean before God on account of this affliction? For ecclesiastical authority rightly judges that a woman experiencing her monthly period ought not to be forbidden to enter church, because the superfluity of nature cannot be reckoned to her as guilt; and it is unjust that she should be deprived of entrance into the Church because she suffers it unwillingly. [Col. 0818A]

For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her infirmity departed from her (Mark V). If, then, a woman in a flow of blood could laudably touch the Lord’s garment, why should a woman suffering the superfluity of menstrual blood not be allowed to enter the Lord’s church?

But you say: illness compelled that woman, whereas custom constrains those of whom we speak. If, therefore, she who, while ill, touched the Lord’s garment acted rightly in daring to do so, why should what is granted to one sick person not be granted to all women who are afflicted by a defect of their nature? Nor should she be prohibited from receiving the mystery of holy communion on these days. If, out of great reverence, she does not presume to receive it, she is to be praised; but if she receives it, she is not to be judged.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the mystery of the two goats: one is a type of Christ, the other of Antichrist.

(CH. XVI.) “The Lord spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron, who were killed when they offered strange fire, and commanded him, saying: Speak to Aaron your brother, that he may not enter the sanctuary at every time—the place within the veil, before the mercy-seat by which the ark is covered—lest he die; for I shall appear in a cloud over the oracle, unless he first does these things. He shall offer a calf for sin and a ram for a burnt offering,” etc.

After the mystical and ordered constitution of God’s holy house set forth in this sacred writing of Leviticus, the account returns again to its head—that is, to Aaron the high priest and his sacrifice. Thus above we had, by the Lord’s command, that Aaron offered a calf and two rams: the calf for sin, one ram for a burnt offering, and then a goat. Then followed the death of Aaron’s sons; then the distinction between clean and unclean animals; then the Law concerning the leprous man and the leprous house; then concerning the man suffering a discharge of semen and the woman suffering a flow of blood. After these things, I say, the narrative returns fittingly to Aaron, when the Lord speaks these things to Moses.

But there is some difference. For it says: “After he has washed, he shall be clothed with all these things. And he shall receive from the whole multitude of the children of Israel two goats for sin and one ram for a burnt offering. And when he has offered the calf and prayed for himself and for his house, he shall make the two goats stand before the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, casting lots upon each: one lot for the Lord and the other for the goat sent away,” etc. [Col. 0818D]

This differs somewhat from the earlier account, for there no mention is made of the goat sent away. Here too there is a great mystery. After the death of Aaron’s two sons, who died when they offered strange fire, and after the mysteries have been spoken, and indeed after the destruction of the Jews, who now perish in their sin, these same things must be fulfilled in deed. Then, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the time will come when the remnant of the people of Israel shall be saved (Rom. XI).

“He shall make the two goats stand at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony”: that is, when the man of sin, the son of perdition, has been revealed—the one who is truly a foul goat on account of his own sins—Christ himself shall become known to that people. Though Christ is, because of his own innocence, the unblemished Lamb of God, he was offered like a goat, as though a sinner, for the sins of the whole world. Then lots shall be cast upon each, so that it may be plainly apparent to all which of them has come blessed in the name of the Father amid the multitude of mercy, and which has emerged accursed in his own name amid the multitude of his wrath.

For he whose lot came forth from the Lord, who was offered for our sins, “shall kill that other one with the spirit of his mouth and destroy him by the brightness of his coming” (II Thess. II). Since the rest has been stated above—namely, what it means that the high priest enters the sanctuary alone, pouring the taken blood around upon the horns of the altar, sprinkling seven times with his finger, and cleansing and sanctifying it from the impurities of the children of Israel—we must now speak of the goat sent away, which remains.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That the living goat which is sent away is Antichrist himself.

“He shall offer,” it says, “the living goat, and, placing both hands upon its head, shall confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their offenses and sins. Calling these down upon its head, he shall send it away through a prepared man into the wilderness,” etc.

This goat, as was said before, is Antichrist. It is a living goat, since he will not come as Christ came, to die for the sins of men, but is wholly contrary both to Christ’s cause and to his death. Hence he is called Antichrist—that is, one opposed to Christ. Barabbas, the robber, author of sedition and murder (Matt. XXVII), was released alive as a type of him; and even now the devil tyrannizes over them through seditions and murders. But our goat died for our sins—died, I say, once to sin, but now lives to God (Rom. VI). [Col. 0819D]

“Calling down upon his head,” it says, “all the iniquities of the children of Israel, all their offenses and sins”: for the blood of all souls shall flow back upon his head. “He shall send him away through a prepared man into the wilderness”: that is, he shall cast him down into hell, into the hands of his father the devil, certainly an evil man and a man of iniquity, of whom the master of the household says in the Gospel: “An enemy has done this” (Matt. XIII).

According to this signification, the ministry of that man who signifies the devil, who will carry his goat into the solitude of hell, is exceedingly shameful. But hear what follows afterwards: “But the one who has sent away the goat sent away shall wash his garments and his body with water, and thus enter the camp.” In this respect, because he touched that goat and for a moment bore the type of the Prince of all purity, he “shall wash his garments” before entering the camp.

Aaron himself also, because he placed both hands upon the head of that same goat, “shall wash his flesh in a holy place and put on his garments. But they shall carry outside the camp the calf and the goat which were sacrificed for sin, and whose blood was brought in to complete atonement in the sanctuary, and they shall burn them with fire,” etc. These things were explained above; but here, as said before, they are recapitulated, precisely because the remnant of Israel will be saved by no blood other than that of our one Lord Jesus Christ, who “suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood” (Heb. XIII). [Col. 0820B]

## CHAPTER XXXII. The judgment of the Law concerning not eating carrion, and why Abraham, who had his sister as wife, did not act against this Law which says: “You shall not do according to the custom of Egypt.”

(CH. XVII.) Then, after a few intervening matters, which are plain in meaning and have already been explained in various places, the recapitulation continues and states more clearly what those unclean things are from whose eating or touching the holy Law deters the holy people.

“The person,” it says, “who eats a carcass or something taken by a beast, whether native-born or foreigner, shall wash his garments and himself with water; and he shall be unclean until evening, and in this way he shall become clean.” This too had been said above, and afterwards: “These,” it says, “are the animals which you shall eat among all the living creatures of the earth” (Lev. XI), and you shall reckon these and these as unclean.

For if you ask which are the unclean things which God hates, he says (CH. XVIII): “You shall not do according to the custom of the land of Egypt in which you lived, nor shall you act according to the custom of the land of Canaan into which I shall bring you.” And afterwards: “No man shall approach one near to him by blood.” For these truly are unclean animals, carcass-like animals, which the people of God ought not to eat—that is, admit into their fellowship: all persons doing these things and committing these unclean and irrational acts, uncovering the nakedness of mother or father, revealing the shame of a sister by the father or a sister by the mother.

But if you object: “Then Abraham acted against God’s good pleasure by uncovering the nakedness of his sister; for Sarah was his sister, the daughter of his father and not of his mother.” We shall answer that he did this according to the custom of the nations, which God prohibits here. Before God brought him forth from among those peoples, his sister had already married him. He had not yet received such a command either in written Law or even in God’s spoken word. “Where there is no command, there is no transgression” (Rom. IV). [Col. 0820D]

Persons doing these things, then—uncovering blood-related nakedness in whatever way, exposing the uncleanness of a menstruating woman, lying with a neighbour’s wife, giving their seed to the idol Moloch and passing it through fire—these, and other workers of iniquity, are defiled and unclean, “to whom nothing is clean” (Tit. I). For these things proceed from the human being and, according to Gospel truth, defile the human being (Matt. XV); for “what enters the mouth,” he says, “does not defile the human being” (ibid.).

We do not linger over these in search of the depth of mysteries, because on the surface they display an evident principle of justice: preparing everlasting guilt for transgressors, but great rest of conscience for their hearers—or rather, their doers.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the three annual solemnities: which is the month of Unleavened Bread, which the month of Firstfruits, and which the month of the gathering of crops.

(CH. XXIII.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: These are the holy festivals of the Lord, which you must celebrate at their appointed times. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, is the Lord’s *phase*, or Passover—that is, the passage—and on the fifteenth day of this month is the Lord’s solemnity of Unleavened Bread,” etc.

Here the connected rationale of the three solemnities, concerning which the Lord said in Exodus, is set out more clearly: “Three times in every year,” he says, “you shall celebrate festivals for me: the solemnity of Unleavened Bread, the solemnity of the month of Firstfruits, and also the solemnity at the end of the year, when you gather all your crops from the field” (Exod. XXIII).

Concerning the solemnity of Unleavened Bread, he now says: “On the fourteenth day of the first month at evening is the Lord’s *phase*, or Passover—that is, passage.” Concerning the solemnity of the month of Firstfruits: “When,” he says, “you have entered the land which I shall give you and have harvested the crop, you shall bring sheaves of ears, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest. He shall lift up the bundle before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you on the day after the Sabbath, and he shall sanctify it.”

And afterwards: “You shall therefore count from the day after the Sabbath, on which you offered the sheaf of firstfruits, seven full weeks, up to the day after the completion of the seventh week—that is, fifty days—and then you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord,” etc. [Col. 0821C]

This is the solemnity of the month of Firstfruits, which month is called *Theseri* among the Hebrews and June among the Romans. This solemnity is called that of Firstfruits and also the feast of Weeks. It is also called in Greek *Pentecost*, that is, “the fiftieth day.”

Concerning the solemnity of gathered crops: “In the seventh month,” he says, “on the first day of the month, you shall have a memorial Sabbath with trumpet blasts, and it shall be called holy. You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning these same solemnities and the respective reasons for each. [Col. 0822B]

These three legal solemnities have very well-known reasons, and bear witness to God’s benefits, great and worthy of splendid commemoration. The reason for the solemnity of Unleavened Bread—the paschal solemnity, that is—is this: “With a mighty hand,” he says, “the Lord brought us out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage. For when Pharaoh was hardened and would not let us go, the Lord slew every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man even to the firstborn of beasts” (Exod. XIII).

The reason for the solemnity of Firstfruits, or of Weeks, is this: in the third month after their departure from the land of Egypt, the Lord made a covenant with the children of Israel and gave them the law written on tablets by the finger of God. The covenant was made not on the third, as [Col. 0822C] most people read carelessly, but on the fourth day of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the fourteenth moon, or day, of the first month. Thus it was done: “Moses took half the blood and put it into bowls; but he poured the remaining part upon the altar. Taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people. He also sprinkled the blood that had been taken upon the people and said: This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words” (Exod. XXIV).

The reason for the solemnity of the seventh month, called the feast of Tabernacles, is this: from the day of their departure from the land of Egypt they lived in tents for forty years; and, when that generation which had murmured against the Lord had at last perished, their children entered the land of promise [Col. 0822D] (Num. XIV). This reason belongs partly to sorrow and partly to joy: to sorrow, because the bodies of the fathers lay prostrate in the wilderness; to joy, because their children entered the land, as has been stated. Therefore this celebration was commanded to be observed in remembrance of both matters: first with sorrow, afterwards with joy.

For he says: “On the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a most solemn Day of Atonements, and it shall be called holy. You shall afflict your souls on it and offer a burnt offering to the Lord. Every soul which is not afflicted on that day shall perish from among its people.” This is in remembrance of the evils, because, as stated above, the bodies of the fathers lay prostrate in the wilderness for forty years because they had disparaged [Col. 0823A] the land which the scouts had examined among the children of Israel, saying: “The land which we have explored devours its inhabitants” (Num. XIII), etc.

This is “the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the tenth; it shall become for the house of Judah joy and gladness and splendid solemnities” (Zech. VIII). He says “into joy and gladness,” plainly after affliction. Hence here too he afterwards says: “From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when you have gathered all the fruits of your land, you shall celebrate the Lord’s feast for seven days. On the first day and on the eighth day there shall be a Sabbath, that is, rest; and on the first day you shall take for yourselves the fruit of the most beautiful tree, palm branches, branches of thick-leaved trees, and willows from the brook, and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God”—[Col. 0823B] namely, because, after the sin of murmuring or disparagement by which their fathers disparaged the land, and for which their bodies lay prostrate in the wilderness, joy succeeded for the children who entered the land. Therefore the first observance of this solemnity is fasting, and its final observance gladness or joy. It proclaims both matters: affliction to be observed on one day, namely the tenth, and joy to be celebrated for seven days beginning on the fifteenth day.

“The first day of the month is a Sabbath,” that is, a holy memorial feast with trumpets sounding, so that, hearing the trumpet-blast, they may be ready for the coming feasts and may rest from work on that day. For, he says, “You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. [Col. 0823C] That the solemnity of Weeks, which in Greek is called Πεντεκόστη, “Pentecost,” has the best and more divine reason; and that the law commanded seven weeks to be counted from the day after the Sabbath.

Of these three solemnities, the feast of Weeks has the best and more divine reason; as was said above, it is called in Greek Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day. For it was indeed a great benefit of God that he liberated that people from Pharaoh’s dominion, and that he brought them into the land which he had sworn to their fathers. But the greatest and best benefit was that, in the manner stated above, he made a covenant with them so that he might be their God. For those benefits were good indeed, but temporary; this benefit is good and best because it is eternal.

Hence it was most beautifully and most holily provided by the authority of the [Col. 0823D] holy law that, in the year in which the Saviour suffered, this solemnity should fall upon that day which shines more brightly and sweetly in Christ’s Gospel because of his resurrection and because of the coming of the Holy Spirit. For it says: “He shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, that it may be acceptable for you, on the day after the Sabbath, and he shall sanctify it.” And afterwards: “You shall therefore count from the day after the Sabbath, on which you offered the sheaf of firstfruits, seven full weeks, until the day after the completion of the seventh week—that is, fifty days—and then you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord.”

What was the day after the Sabbath except the day following the Sabbath, the Lord’s Day, on which Christ rose? Since, therefore, fifty days begin to be counted not [Col. 0824A] from the evening of the fourteenth paschal moon, nor from the very immolation of the lamb, but from the day after the Sabbath, wherever it may fall within the days of Passover, it is plainly evident that the Jewish day of Pentecost then fell on a Sunday. For a number of fifty days always ends on the same weekday from which it begins.

Thus it happens that we and the Jews often celebrate holy Pentecost on the same day: because we offer the paschal sacrifice not on the same day on which they slaughter their lamb, but on that day on which they offer before the Lord the sheaf of ears, the firstfruits of the harvest from the sheaves. This is truly a holy, truly a great mystery. Is God concerned with an insensible sheaf of ears? Or rather, did he command these things [Col. 0824B] because of this our sheaf, of whom the bride says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh” (Cant. I), immediately adding: “My beloved is to me a cluster of cypress” (*ibid.*). For he who is called a bundle of myrrh because of the bitterness of his passion is the same who is called a cluster of cypress because of the sweetness of his resurrection.

Did not this holy and mystical law, I ask, [280] in provision for the resurrection of this sheaf, which was to rise on the day after the Sabbath, command such a sheaf to be lifted before the Lord on the day after the Sabbath? Thus there is a present reason why the day on which the Holy Spirit was sent to the apostles is the Jews’ completion of Pentecost: according to the terms of that year, that day was already the fifty-third from the evening immolation of the lamb.
