Hence [Col. 0824C] the diligent faith, or ingenuity, of the holy Church deserves praise for having ordained that, on whatever weekday the *sanguinei* (“bloody” or “bloodthirsty”) Jews slaughter their lamb or kid, the day after the Sabbath should be awaited—the day on which they customarily, according to the law, lift the firstfruits of the harvest, namely the sheaf of ears—and only then should we lift up our life-giving sheaf, who says: “I have risen, and I am still with you” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

Therefore, of the three solemnities, the feast of Weeks has the greatest and more heavenly reason; and for this reason it pleases and delights us especially that the Lord’s Day is both its beginning and its end, so that the Jews, even while envious, have celebrated on both sides the day of Christian joy.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. [Col. 0824D] On this same “day after the Sabbath,” and how, and why, the Jews were accustomed to transfer feasts from one day to another.

As Josephus also writes in the *Antiquities*: “The day after the Sabbath must be understood as the sixteenth moon, because the fifteenth, being holy and solemn, is called Sabbath in the general sense, since no work may be done on that day. But it is certainly established that in the year of the Lord’s Passion, since, according to the Gospel, the fourteenth moon fell on Thursday, the sixteenth moon was the Sabbath. Was then one and the same day both a Sabbath in itself and, because of the preceding day of Passover, a day after the Sabbath?”

Here it is worth knowing the ancient Jewish custom [Col. 0825A], which is as follows. Their practice is, wherever they can avoid it, never to place two Sabbaths—that is, two feast-days on which work is forbidden—in succession. For, they say, many troublesome and inconvenient things would result for us; for example, in caring for the dead, who, if kept from the first evening of the earlier Sabbath, might by the fourth day produce the unpleasantness of decay. Therefore, when the paschal terminus, that is the fourteenth moon, fell on Thursday, they did indeed eat the lamb that same night, but they left the solemnity of the following day to be transferred to the Sabbath.

With this understood, no one wonders why, when [Col. 0825B] the Lord suffered, although the Jews had eaten the lamb on the preceding evening—which the Lord himself had also eaten with his disciples—the Jews nevertheless found time to conduct trials, though it was the fifteenth moon, which by the holy law ought to have been a holy and solemn day. It is therefore clear that there is no contradiction whatever in the fact that, as has already been said, on the day on which Christ rose the Jews lifted their sheaf of ears; and from that point, counting fifty days, they too celebrated their Pentecost in completion on the day on which the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles.

This is the lamb of which it is now [Col. 0825C] said mystically: “And on the same day on which the sheaf is consecrated, an unblemished lamb of one year shall be slain as a burnt offering to the Lord.” As a burnt offering, I say, to the Lord, and not for eating, as on the paschal evening. For in that form in which he gave himself to be eaten by his apostles—the form, I say, of bread and wine—the Lamb of God is sacrificed by us on the paschal evening in such a way that we also eat the same Lamb of God. But in that form in which he rose on the day after the Sabbath, we do not eat him at all; rather, we offer him wholly in burnt sacrifice to the Lord, so that, whole, entire, and unharmed, he may sit at God’s right hand.

There are other [Col. 0825C] Jewish transfers of the same feast-day which, although it would be superfluous to write of them, we shall nevertheless not pass over, as we have received them from the Jews. For they avoid celebrating the day of Passover not only on Friday but also on Monday, Wednesday, and Sunday. For if they celebrated Passover on Monday, the Day of Propitiation—that is, the tenth day of the seventh month, which is the one hundred and seventy-third day after Passover—would fall for them on Friday, on which they may do no work at all. If they celebrated Passover on Wednesday, they would have the Day of Propitiation on Sunday; and, having two Sabbaths, that is, two consecutive feast-days, on both occasions, they would suffer the inconveniences mentioned above.

Yet if you ask them for an authoritative reason from Scripture for all these things which have been said, they can produce none at all; and they admit that these traditions are not of God or Moses but of their teachers, the Scribes and Pharisees. But there is no need now to be concerned how these unhappy people act, since, having neither place nor offering, they do not observe the law, as they themselves admit; nor do they count their fifty days from the day after the Sabbath, but from the paschal evening itself.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Col. 0826A] That Christ is our feast of Unleavened Bread, the coming of the Holy Spirit our Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord our most joyful feast of gathered fruits.

For us, however, the reasons for the three solemnities of our year are wholly spiritual, wholly heavenly. For “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V), through whom we have been liberated with an eternal liberation not from Pharaoh the man but from Pharaoh the devil. Our Pentecost, that is, the feast of fifty days, is the coming of the Holy Spirit, through whom God made a gracious covenant with us Gentiles, giving the tongues of all nations to the apostles, so that there might be a means by which, or a way in which, we might hear this grace.

Our feast of [Col. 0826B] fruits gathered from the earth at the end of the year is our feast, namely the Nativity of Jesus Christ the Son of God, in which we truly gather the fruits of our earth—our earth, I say, the virginal earth—of which we have heard the Holy Spirit promise: “The Lord will give goodness, and our earth shall yield her fruit” (Ps. LXXXIV). We may indeed take wonderful delight in the fact that, according to the Roman reckoning, we have the end of the year precisely when we receive the fruit of this aforesaid earth, when in heart, mouth, and hands we bear God and man born of the Virgin. According to the Greek observance too, likewise, the end of the year is then, when the Nativity of Christ brings joy and gladness to all the people.

But the fact that this sacred law says in Exodus, as has already been stated, “You shall also observe the solemnity at the end of the year, when you have gathered all your crops from the field” (Exod. XXIII), and says here, that is, in Leviticus, that this is to be done “in the seventh month,” can stand only according to the Egyptian year, from whom they had then departed. For it is not among the Hebrews but among the Egyptians that the end or beginning of the year is about September, in their month called Thoth. Let the chronologers of the Gentiles—that is, of the Romans and Greeks—therefore take particular delight in the fact that Christ was born at the end of their year, in whom we gathered the fruits of our earth and in whom we receive the [281] truth of the holy Scriptures fulfilled.

Let us then hear [Col. 0826C] what is said: “On the first day you shall take for yourselves the fruit of the most beautiful tree, palm branches, branches of thick-leaved trees, and willows from the brook; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God.” “You shall rejoice,” he says. This indeed is what we Gentiles do at the aforesaid end of our year, receiving the fruit of the virginal womb with such exultation that we thereby clearly prove true also the oracle which says: “And he shall be the expectation of the Gentiles” (Gen. XLIX).

What night, among the whole multitude of nights in the year, has deserved such joy from every rank, from both sexes, from old men, young men, youths, boys, and girls? “I announce to you,” says the angel, “great joy, which shall be for all the people” (Luke II). And he spoke truly, for so it is, even in this mournful and miserable world. Above all, [Col. 0827A] inward spiritual religion, according to the most holy institution of the Roman Church, rejoices before the Lord its God on that day—or rather, on that night—taking the fruit of the most beautiful tree: that is, setting forth the refreshment of the holy Eucharist twice on that night. For what else? Are not the body and blood of the Son of God, which gifts we offer or receive twice on that night, the fruits of the most beautiful tree, that is, of the undefiled Virgin?

“You shall take,” he says, “palm branches, branches of thick-leaved trees, and willows from the brook.” It would be surprising if the true investigator of joy were not prompted by this passage when he ordered the offices of the aforesaid solemnity so that, after the Nativity of Christ the Son of God, Stephen the protomartyr should follow before all others—Stephen, the first martyr to meet that everlasting glory. [Col. 0827B] Then comes John, beloved of the Lord; in the third place, the host of Innocents, whom murderous Herod killed. For in that victorious protomartyr the holy Church truly raises palm branches; in this beloved of the Lord, as it were a branch of thick-leaved wood, because the dense and most sublime Scripture, beginning from the eternal beginning, here adorns and defends the right faith; but in the innocent little ones, as it were willows from the brook, because, having done nothing—just as willows bear no fruit—they suddenly sprang, by grace alone, into the verdure of the eternal homeland.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. [Col. 0827C] On the seventh-year Sabbath of the land, and on the jubilee, that is, the year of remission; and why God promises that people nothing except temporal goods if they obey, and threatens temporal evils if they do not obey.

(CH. XXV.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land which I shall give you, let the land keep a Sabbath for the Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its fruits. But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of rest for the land, a Sabbath for the Lord. You shall not sow the field or prune the vineyard. You shall not reap what the ground produces of itself, nor gather the first grapes of your vineyard as a vintage.” And afterwards: “You shall also count for yourself seven weeks of years, that is, seven times seven, which together make forty-nine years. And you shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month, [Col. 0827D] on the tenth day of the month.”

Before the Lord divides the land among his people “by the measuring-line of distribution” (Ps. LXXVII), he prescribes the law of that land and sets forth the terms on which he wishes the children of Israel to live, not as owners of the land, but as tenants of the Lord of the land, that is, their God. “You shall sanctify,” he says, “the fiftieth year, and proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of your land. For it is jubilee.” Therefore, he says, you shall proclaim remission because it is jubilee. For *jubilaeus* means “letting go” or “remitting.” Why shall you proclaim remission, and why is that year itself jubilee? He says: “A man shall return to his possession” [Col. 0828A]—understand, if necessity has compelled him to sell it—“and each one shall return to his former family, because it is jubilee and the fiftieth year. You shall not sow, nor reap what grows of itself in the field, nor gather the first fruits of the vintage.”

By what right? He says a little below: “The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, because it is mine, and you are my strangers and tenants. Therefore every region of your possession shall be sold subject to the condition of redemption.” Thus a man shall return to his possession. “And each one,” he says, “shall return to his former family”—understand, one who has sold himself under compulsion of poverty. For he says this below: “If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, he shall work for you until the year of jubilee; and afterwards he shall go out with his children and return to his kindred and to the possession of his fathers.” By what right? He says: “For they are my servants, and I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” And again: “For the children of Israel whom I brought out of the land of Egypt are my servants.”

God [Col. 0828B] beautifully acknowledges his own right, so that he may exercise it lawfully by a law of mercy. But what great thing is it for the Lord God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, sea and everything in them—what, I say, great or glorious thing is it—to declare or prescribe for himself a right over a small tract of land, which is plainly no very large corner of Syrian territory? Plainly, because those to whom he speaks are children, little ones (Gal. III), lovers of little things, desirous of insignificant possessions, greedy for earthly goods, as those who did not yet know heavenly goods.

Therefore, although this good is ever so small before the sight of the great God [Col. 0828C], he does not disdain, for the matter and for the time, to magnify its advantage; nor does the wise Father care what or how great the thing is that he gives, provided that by that gift he makes the child attentive to himself and bound to himself. This law, too, is a great and wise pedagogue; but the reward which it promises is small, in order to encourage the good disposition of the child, and the rod by which it threatens is small, in order to deter the child’s waywardness. For what does it promise, and what does it threaten?

“If,” he says, “you walk in my commandments, I shall give you rains in their seasons, and the earth shall bring forth its growth, and the trees shall be filled with fruit” (Lev. XXVI). And afterwards: “You shall eat the oldest of old stores, and cast out the old when new supplies arrive” (*ibid.*). These things and others like them it promises, and nowhere speaks openly of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0828D], because that people was a child, not yet knowing how either to hope for or to love invisible and heavenly things.

Then he says: “But if you do not listen to me and do not do all my commandments, I shall swiftly visit you with want and fever, which will consume your eyes and waste away your souls. In vain you shall sow seed, which your enemies will devour” (*ibid.*). Again: “I shall send against you the beasts of the field, which shall consume you and your cattle and reduce everything to scarcity, and your roads shall become deserted” (*ibid.*). And afterwards: “When you flee into the cities, I shall send pestilence into your midst, and you shall be delivered into the hands of enemies, after I have broken the staff of your bread, so that ten women shall bake bread in one oven and give it back by weight; you shall eat and not be satisfied” (*ibid.*).

These things and others like them it threatens [Col. 0829A], and nowhere speaks openly of the hell of unquenchable fire, where “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII), because, as has already been said, that people was a child and did not know how to fear invisible evils. Thus God, not according to his own greatness but according to their servile understanding, handles a small matter as though with vast effort—though he will nevertheless give, along with those slight goods, great and eternal rewards to the obedient, and, along with those transient evils, everlasting punishments to the disobedient.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That we ought to observe these Sabbaths of the land not carnally but spiritually.

[Col. 0829B] But we are in the fullness of time of which the great and perfect man, the Apostle, speaks: “And when we were little children, we were serving under the elements of the world. But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Gal. IV), etc.

Placed in this fullness, it is not fitting that we should turn “again to weak and needy elements” (*ibid.*), imagining, namely, that nothing else is done here than what the dry letter sounds forth when it says: “For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its fruits; but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of rest for the land, a Sabbath for the Lord,” etc. For the Romans would not think it anything great [Col. 0829C] that God gave that people a small tract of land, since their own ancestors, few in number under the leadership of Aeneas, were able to occupy Latium, and they themselves afterwards subjected the world to themselves by great and repeated victories in war.

Thus they too can be led by human reasoning to believe that the God of majesty never deigned to speak either about the goods of that land, or about the signification of better things; nor about the inconveniences of that small land, or about the figure of invisible eternal evils. Therefore, since God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII), we now also contemplate these things in the Spirit, where we rightly reject the letter in accordance with the capacity of exercised senses.

## CHAPTER XL. [Col. 0829D] What our Sabbaths are, and what is our land, whose Sabbaths concern the Holy Spirit.

“For six years,” he says, “you shall sow your field, but in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of rest for the Lord.” Suppose that the Apostle had said in counsel: “This therefore I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (I Cor. VII), etc. For what is our land, about which God or the Holy Spirit is concerned, except our flesh?

“For six years,” therefore, he says, “you shall sow your field,” that is, you shall sow in your flesh until a sufficient generation of children has been produced. For the number six is perfect; and in this place it beautifully signifies, in a spiritual sense, sufficient offspring, for whose hope alone one should devote oneself to marriage. “But in the seventh year there shall be a Sabbath of rest for the land, a Sabbath for the Lord” [Col. 0830A]—that is, after receiving children, you shall devote yourself to continence and apply yourself to chastity, in whose dwelling God should rightly delight.

“You shall not sow the field nor prune the vineyard”—that is, you shall not follow the spontaneous impulses of the flesh; rather, possessing a field or vineyard, you shall be as though not possessing one—that is, having a husband or wife, you shall be as though not having one—and in this manner: “You shall not reap what the ground produces of itself, nor gather the first grapes of your vineyard as a vintage.” That is, by indulging, as has been stated, the spontaneous motions of the flesh, you shall not practise lust as though it were a just or lawful thing. “For it is a year of rest for the land”—that is, it is time for you to be free from such bondage to corruption.

“But they shall be [Col. 0830B] food for you,” he says, “for you and your male servant, your female servant, hired worker, and stranger who dwells with you. All that grows shall provide food for your beasts and cattle.” But, he says, you shall transform the works of the flesh, works of corruption, into works of the Spirit, works of glory and honour, so that people whose imperfection or weaker faith needs strengthening by good example—whether like servants or maidservants, hired workers and strangers, or indeed even like beasts or cattle in their carnal way of life—may see and glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. V), being in some manner fed as with food supplied from your land.

## CHAPTER XLI. Who is our jubilee, that is, the year of release.

[Col. 0830C] “You shall also count for yourself seven weeks of years,” that is, seven times seven, which together make forty-nine years. “And you shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, at the time of atonement, throughout all your land. And you shall sanctify the fiftieth year, and proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of your land. For it is jubilee.” Jubilee, as was said above, means “letting go.”

But what progress have we made in the school of this holy law, in the discipline of law and Gospel, if we have not learned to remit the debts of our brothers—debts, I say, that is, the sins of our debtors? For our Lord, after proposing the parable of a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants, concluded thus: “So also my Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts” (Matt. XVIII). For Peter had said to him: “Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Up to seven times?” “I do not say to you up to seven times,” he says, “but up to seventy times seven” (*ibid.*).

“Therefore you shall sanctify,” he says [Col. 0830D], “the jubilee year”; that is, with holy and charitable remission you shall receive your brother who sins against you and repents. The sinner, I say, is not to be forgiven merely up to seven times, a number that is indivisible—for it cannot be divided into equal parts, and signifies the unforgivable sin of one who does not repent—but seven times seven, a divisible number, or seventy times seven, a number likewise divisible into equal parts, and signifying a sin which can be dissolved, because the brother who has sinned, when he does penance, can be corrected.

This is the truly holy and most beautiful [Col. 0831A] feast of jubilee, to be celebrated together while the evangelical trumpet sounds: so that a person may return to his possession and each may return to his former family; that is, with all discord removed, all may have one heart and one soul, preserve the unity of the Spirit and the unbroken bond of peace (Eph. IV), singing: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII).

[283] ## CHAPTER XLII. [Col. 0831B] On this same lawful release, according to the law of houses to be redeemed: one law for houses in walled cities, another for those in fields or villages, and on the dwellings of Levites.

But the ground of remission itself ought to be a feast. For there are many people who, most absurdly, are ready to remit an injury against God but difficult and slow in forgiving an injury against themselves. Surely the mark of a well-ordered and well-instructed mind is rather to be ready and prompt to forgive an injury against oneself, but slower in forgiving an injury against God.

Accordingly, the discerning and provident spirit of the law continues and says: “Whoever sells a house within the walls of a city shall have the right to redeem it until one year is completed. If he does not redeem it and the cycle of the year has elapsed, the buyer and his descendants shall possess it forever, and it may not be redeemed even in the jubilee. But if the house is in a village without walls [Col. 0831C], it shall be sold according to the law of fields. But if it has not been redeemed, it shall return to its owner in the jubilee.”

The sale of houses is the alienation of minds. For whenever anyone, captivated by the sweetness of sin, destroys himself, he certainly sells for nothing a house most necessary to him. Therefore the Lord says through the prophet: “You were sold for nothing” (Isa. LII). Some houses that are sold lie within the city walls, while others are in a village, because sometimes one sins against God, sometimes against one’s neighbour. Both indeed concern God, but there is a very great difference in their redemption. Hence Eli says to his sons: “If a man sins against a man, God can be appeased for him; but if a man sins against God, who shall pray for him?” [Col. 0831D] (I Sam. II).

“He who sells,” therefore, he says, “a house within the walls of a city shall have the right to redeem it until one year is completed. If he does not redeem it and the cycle of the year has elapsed, the buyer and his descendants shall possess it forever, and it may not be redeemed even in the jubilee.” This means: one “who is called a fornicator, or covetous, or serving idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard” (I Cor. V)—one, I say, who is such a person or does anything of this sort, and even wishes to defend his deeds—may, so long as the time of life remains to him, repent and amend, redeem his sin, and be absolved by the Church, if he wishes. But if he does not repent and the end of his life overtakes him unrepentant, the buyer, the devil, will possess his soul, [Col. 0832A] and because it was not lamented in this life, his sin will not be remitted in the age to come (Matt. XII).

“But if the house is in a village without walls” [Col. 0831C]—that is, if a sin against one’s neighbour has been committed, a sin not fortified by the wall of self-defence—“it shall be sold according to the law of fields,” that is, it shall be held under a pardonable condition. For “if,” he says, “it has not previously been redeemed, it shall return to its owner in the jubilee”; that is, even if it has not been compensated with worthy satisfaction before the end of life, the neighbour against whom the sin was committed will pray for the sinner, not only lawfully but even commendably, that the sin may be forgiven.

“The houses of Levites which are in cities may always be redeemed. If they have not been redeemed, they shall return to their owners in the jubilee,” etc. That seller of his house situated within the walls of a city [Col. 0832B] is a Levite who, although he has sinned against God and arrogantly despised him, nevertheless does not remain in sin until his stench exposes him unwillingly; rather, moved by God and contrite, he endeavours personally to disclose to a spiritual elder the cause of his sin, still hidden within his soul, anticipating the face of the Lord in confession (Ps. XCII). This is indeed lawful, as belonging to the Levitical order, that is, to a good and holy purpose.

Such Levites’ “houses,” he says, “can always be redeemed; and if they have not been redeemed, they shall return to their owners in the jubilee,” because, although their sins have not been redeemed in the present age by fruits of penance sufficiently worthy, they will at least not lack pardon in the future, “yet so as through fire,” namely purgatorial fire (I Cor. III).

Origen [Col. 0832C], concerning what is said here—“if he does not redeem it and the cycle of the year has elapsed, the buyer shall possess it forever, and it may not be redeemed”—meaning I know not what, says: “There is only one place of penance in the Church.” But however he may have said it, the interpretation should be chosen which harms neither the authority of the wise nor the faith of the simple.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the saying, “If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you”: how wisely one ought to heed the humble confession of penitents.

The recipient of confession must here be learned in the divine law and endowed with outstanding prudent discernment, so that [Col. 0832D] he may know by what measure and moderation to assess the price of each redemption—that is, what burdens of penance he should impose upon each person according to the nature of the offences or the capacity of those confessing. The holy law therefore continues, a law both just and good:

“If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, you shall not oppress him with the servitude of slaves; but he shall be with you as a hired servant or a resident alien. He shall work with you until the year of jubilee, and afterwards he shall depart with his children and return to his kindred and to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, and I brought them out of the land of Egypt.”

“If,” he says, “compelled by poverty”—that is, by the spirit of fear—“your brother sells himself to you,” as he plainly does when, fearing because of his guilt and contrite, he subjects himself to the judgment [Col. 0833A] of God through God’s minister, so that he may obtain pardon and salvation, prepared to do for the redemption of his soul whatever you command. For why does he subject himself to you except because poverty compels him—namely, that poverty in which the Lord places the beginning of blessedness, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V)? Unless this poverty distressed him, one who perhaps surpasses you in birth, intellect, or even civic dignity would never beg from you counsel for his salvation at the cost of shame.

“You shall not, therefore,” he says, “oppress him with the servitude of slaves”: that is, do not rely upon your own righteousness as though you yourself had no need of God’s mercy, like that Pharisee who, seeing the sinful woman weeping at the Lord’s feet, discovered with a dry heart the fountain of mercy: “If this man were a prophet,” he said, “he would know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, for she is a sinner” (Luke VII). Certainly, if this woman, compelled by the same poverty, had sold herself to such a man, he would not have received her with fatherly compassion, but would have oppressed her with the servitude of slaves—indeed, worse still, perhaps have driven her away with kicks.

“But,” he says, “he shall be as a hired servant and a resident alien”: that is, through your ministry he shall obtain the forgiveness of sins for which he serves, and, received without constraint, shall dwell with you in the grace or righteousness into which you have been enlarged. “He shall work with you until the year of jubilee,” that is, until the hoped-for remission, producing for himself the fruits worthy of repentance which you have enjoined upon him; and afterwards he shall return [Col. 0833C] to the kindred and possession of his fathers—namely, by recovering the rank of his former dignity or office. For sins disclosed in this manner do not deprive their author of his proper honour or rank; David too says, “I will teach the wicked thy ways” (Ps. L), though he had certainly committed a great crime.

“For they are my servants,” he says, “and I brought them out of the land of Egypt.” It is as though he said: Therefore you shall not oppress him, as has been stated, because he has not subjected himself to you, but to me; he has confessed what he did, not through your fear, but through mine; and I, by a hidden inspiration, called him from the darkness of his sins so that he might come to the light of your counsel.

“They shall not be sold on the terms of slaves, nor shall you afflict him by your power; but fear your God.” It is as though he said: Persons of this sort are not to be treated [Col. 0833D] as those who, persisting in slavish wickedness, have been discovered or convicted by judges. “But,” he says, “fear your God,” that is, “considering lest you too be tempted” (Gal. VI). For “let him who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (I Cor. X).

“Fear,” I say, “your God,” and mourn for yourself in another’s calamity, because perhaps you have fallen in like matters, or may fall if you have not fallen. “Let male and female slaves be for you from the nations that are around you, and from the resident aliens who dwell among you.” Oppress with strength and fear, he says, those whom their slavish condition of character exposes—those who, unless they had been sought out as though with weapons, after the manner of war by which laborious victory is won over the surrounding nations and those who were enemies or rebels are captured, would never have disclosed their guilt. Exercise more severe discipline, I say, upon those who disclosed their sin not through voluntary confession but because it became known through others.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning one who has sinned in your presence—that is, with your knowledge—and how you should temper true discipline towards him, according to the saying: “If the hand of an alien and a stranger has become strong among you.”

“If the hand of an alien and stranger becomes strong among you, and your impoverished brother sells himself to him, or to anyone of his stock, after he has been sold he may be redeemed. Whoever among his brothers wishes may redeem him,” etc.

The spiritual law extends a great hand of mercy into every circumstance of danger. For what if the sinner himself has not disclosed his offence, nor has it publicly become known through another, but you alone know it? Will you immediately make it public? Certainly not. Rather, the Lord says: “Go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone; if he hears you, you have gained your brother” (Matt. I).

“If, therefore,” he says, “the hand of an alien and stranger has become strong among you.” This stranger is the devil, who becomes strong among us when, in those who belong to us, “his portion becomes fat, as Habakkuk says, and his food is choice” (Hab. I). Nathan, sent by the Lord to David, speaks of this stranger: “There were two men in one city, one rich and the other poor” (II Kings XII). And thereafter: “But when a certain stranger had come to the rich man, sparing to take from his own sheep and cattle [Col. 0834C] to provide a feast for that stranger who had come to him, he took the poor man’s ewe” (ibid.), etc.

Therefore the stranger—an exile, indeed a fugitive, from every city of God—is the devil. David received him when he came upon him at that time, and fed the scoundrel as though with a great feast, when he committed adultery with Uriah’s wife and killed Uriah himself with the sword of the sons of Ammon.

“If, therefore,” he says, “the hand of an alien and stranger”—that is, of the devil—“has become strong among you, and your brother, having been impoverished”—that is, overcome by temptation—“has sold himself to him,” as David sold himself, “after he has been sold he may be redeemed.” For repentance must not be denied after sin. “Whoever among his brothers wishes may redeem him,” namely, by rebuking him [Col. 0834D] between himself and him alone (Matt. XVIII), thus gaining him, and also doing what the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. VI).

“But if he himself is able, he shall redeem himself”: namely, by anticipating every rebuke through voluntary confession, as was said above. He shall redeem himself, it says:

“Only calculating the years from the time of sale until the year of jubilee, and calculating the money for which he was sold according to the number of years and according to the reckoning of a hired servant. If the years remaining until the jubilee are more numerous, according to these he shall repay the price,” etc.

To calculate the years from the time of sale until the year of jubilee, and the payment according to the number of years, plainly means to disclose in pure and sincere confession whether the sin has been repeated more seldom or more frequently, [Col. 0835A] and to undertake the burden of penance according to the frequency of the sin. For if, for example, a young man sinned once with a virgin by an accidental occurrence, or committed one theft, he is not to be punished with the same degree of penance as one who has fallen into the same sin more often.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the blessings God promises and the evils he threatens as though to carnal persons, and how they should rightly be understood spiritually by us.

(CHAPTER XXVI.) “I am the Lord your God: You shall not make for yourselves an idol,” etc. God and Lord of majesty, about to confirm his commandments and immediately promise fitting rewards, declares his supreme authority. The spiritual person sees in the spirit no less than in the letter what blessings he promises and what evils he threatens.

There is no need of exposition concerning the rains he gives in their seasons to those who keep his commandments; what shoots the earth produces; with what fruit its trees are filled; how the threshing of harvest follows upon the vintage, and the vintage upon the sowing; what bread we eat to fullness; what peace we have within our borders; what the evil beasts are which God removes; what sword does not cross our boundaries; what very old provisions we eat; or what old things we cast away when new things arrive. For it is clear to us that our rains are heavenly teachings; our earth is the Church; the trees are individual persons; harvest and vintage are the common works of righteousness; our bread is the living bread [Col. 0835C] which came down from heaven; our peace is Christ; the evil beasts are malignant spirits; the sword is eternal damnation; the very old things to be eaten are the most ancient precepts of the Decalogue, to be duly fulfilled with God’s help; and the old things to be cast aside when new things arrive are the old ceremonies, to be observed in the spirit while the antiquity of the letter is set aside. All these things prosper for us by divine aid because of the merit of preceding faith.

Conversely, the evils which the Lord God threatens to those who do not obey his commandments are plain to understand both in letter and in spirit. “I will visit you swiftly,” he says, “with want and burning fever,” etc. Spiritual evils rather than carnal ones, and eternal rather than transitory evils, ought indeed to be feared; eternal rather than transitory goods should be loved. [Col. 0835D] Nevertheless, no Scripture forbids us to pray to God also for temporal goods and to seek his help against temporal evils.

## 285 CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning the saying, “A man who makes a vow,” etc., and that failure to fulfil what one has vowed is most grave.

(CHAPTER XXVII.) “A man who makes a vow, and vows, and promises his soul to God, shall give its price according to valuation. If it is a male, from the twentieth year up to the sixtieth year, he shall give fifty shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary measure. If a female, thirty; but from the fifth year up to the twentieth, a male twenty shekels, a female ten,” etc.

First, it should be noted that making a vow is not commanded, although the psalm says: “Make vows and fulfil them” (Ps. LXXV). Certainly, when it says “make vows,” it speaks not with the authority of one commanding, but from the intention of one giving counsel; but when it adds, “and fulfil them,” it speaks with the authority of one commanding. For whether someone vows or does not vow lies within his power; but once he has vowed, he then fulfils it by necessity, because he owes it.

Next, it must be understood that one who offers God what belongs to him while retaining himself for himself is not sufficiently dear to God—indeed, he is displeasing to God. For though he offered rightly in that he offered to God, to whom he owed it, he divided wrongly because he withheld from God what was better and gave what was of less worth. Hence he is likened to Cain, who offered God the fruits of the earth, but kept his heart in evil (Gen. IV).

Therefore the holy law first puts forward the vow of the soul and then adds the vow of a possessed thing, when it says: “A man who makes a vow, and vows, and promises his soul,” etc. And then: “An animal,” it says, “which may be sacrificed to the Lord, if anyone vows it, shall be holy and may not be exchanged,” etc. By periphrasis—that is, by circumlocution—and by a threefold repetition, not of words but of the same meaning, when it says, “who makes a vow and vows and promises the tenor of the vow,” it seeks to indicate how great the content of the vow ought to be.

And truly, not only under the severity of the law, but also under the sweetness of the Gospel, failure to fulfil whatever one has vowed is most grave and very dangerous. For in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter says: “Ananias, why has Satan tempted your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to withhold part of the price of the field?” (Acts V), etc. “When Ananias heard these words, he fell down and died” (ibid.).

Nevertheless, the Church under Christ’s Gospel renders this deadly letter of the vow void and rejects it: that is, it was permitted to a carnal people to vow their soul in such a manner that failure to redeem it was guilt, while fulfilment of the vow was sacrilege. Rather, the Christian should vow his soul in such a way that, once he has vowed it, he may not redeem it, and if he has not vowed it, he undoubtedly loses it. How? Namely, by dying to sin and living to righteousness (Rom. VI); by being crucified to the world, mortifying his members which are upon the earth (Col. III); and thus, by hating his soul, preserving it unto eternal life (John XII).

# THE FORTY-TWO BOOKS OF R. D. D. RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE TRINITY AND ITS WORKS. COMMENTARIES ON NUMBERS

## BOOK ONE. (Numbers, chapters I–XIV.)

[Col. 0837]

## 286 CHAPTER I. Concerning what is said in the Apocalypse: “And when I had devoured the book, my belly became bitter,” and why, for readers of this book of Numbers, the bitterness of fear is rightly found in the fact that the numbered children of Israel are cast down.

In the Apocalypse John receives an open book in order to devour it from the hand of the mighty angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth. Because he sends stronger preachers to greater dangers and lesser ones to lesser dangers, he certainly sets his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth. “And I took,” he says, “the book and devoured it; and it was in my mouth sweet as honey. And when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter” (Rev. X).

This book, which this angel also holds open in his hand, and which the Lamb, receiving it sealed in another place, looses from its seven seals (Rev. V), is Holy Scripture. The one and same Christ fulfilled it in himself, performing for us the office both of angel—that is, messenger—and, as a lamb, of one slain for our sins.

We too have attempted, with John, to receive and devour this book from the angel’s hand, though with a small mouth and teeth not sufficiently strong. In what has thus far been said it has been in our mouth sweet as honey; but now there is before us that by which our belly may be made bitter, and our inward sense rightly shaken by great fear. For this is the book of Numbers, in which all the children of Israel, commanded by the Lord, were counted by their generations, families, houses, and the names of their individual chiefs, from twenty years old and above; yet they did not enter the promised land, but their bodies were cast down in the desert.

This is what makes bitter the belly of any spiritual person who has diligently devoured the aforesaid book. For what is more bitter than that in this book those who are counted are cast down, and then the enumeration is repeated? For the Apostle testifies: “These things happened as a figure of us and were written for our correction” (I Cor. X). In what respect did they happen as a figure of us, or what did they prefigure concerning us, except that all of us have been counted according to our present profession of faith? For all of us gave our names in Christ’s baptism, and yet not all run in such a way as to attain the prize (I Cor. IX).

Therefore, while we sing, “How sweet are thy words to my palate, O Lord—more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII), let us rejoice in our calling; but, fearing the uncertainty of our course or attainment, let us be made bitter, according to the true and mystical sense of the present book into which we now enter.

## CHAPTER II. The names and interpretations of the chiefs, tribes, and houses; and that they signify the profession of those who believe in Christ.

(CHAPTER I.) These are the names of the chiefs, tribes, and houses in their kindreds: “From the tribe of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur. From Simeon, Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai. From Judah, Nahshon son of Amminadab. From Issachar, Nethanel son of Zuar. From Zebulun, Eliab son of Helon. Of the sons of Joseph: from Ephraim, Elishama son of Ammihud; from Manasseh, Gamaliel son of Pedahzur; from Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni; from Dan, Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai; from Asher, Pagiel son of Ochran; from Gad, Eliasaph son of Deuel; from Naphtali, Ahira son of Enan. These were the most noble chiefs of the multitude.”

Nearly all their names are distinguished by their own interpretations. Reuben is interpreted “seeing sons”; Elizur, “my God is strong”; Shedeur, “light of the breasts”; Simeon, “hearing sorrow”; Shelumiel, “God repays me,” or “God is my peace”; Zurishaddai, “containing my breasts,” or “my Lord is strong”; Judah, “confession”; Nahshon, “serpentine” or “divination”; Amminadab, “spontaneous of my people”; Issachar, “reward”; Nethanel, “gift of God”; Zuar, “little one”; Zebulun, “dwelling of strength”; Eliab, “God is my father”; Helon, “strength of an army”; Joseph, “increase”; Ephraim, “fruitful” or “growing”; Elishama, “my God has heard”; Ammihud, “my people are renowned”; Manasseh, “forgetfulness”; Gamaliel [printed “Samaliel”], “recompense of God”; Pedahzur, “redemption of the strong”; [287] Benjamin, “son of the right hand”; Abidan, “my father is judge”; Gideon, “temptation of iniquity,” or “encircling the womb”; Dan, “judgment” or “judging”; Ahiezer, “my brother is helper”; Ammishaddai, “my people are sufficient”; Asher, “blessed”; Pagiel, “meet me, God”; Gad, “girded”; Eliasaph, “my God has gathered”; Deuel, “let them acknowledge God”; Naphtali, “he has enlarged me”; Ahira, “friend of my brother”; Enan, “cloud.”

These names, I say, are nearly all splendid, and they signify the beautiful profession of all of us who run in the present way, who have all crossed the sea of baptism, and who have now all been baptized not in the cloud and sea, but in that which was signified through the cloud and sea; all of us eat spiritual food and drink spiritual drink from the rock (I Cor. X), which is no longer Christ in figure but in truth.

But in the Apocalypse the Spirit says to the churches: “He who conquers shall thus be clothed in white garments, and I shall not erase his name from the book of life; and I shall confess his name before my Father and before his angels” (Rev. III). When he says of the one who conquers, “I shall not erase his name, and I shall confess his name,” he surely intends the contrary to be understood concerning the one who does not conquer: that he erases his name and does not confess his name, however beautifully that name may seem written in the present Church and however highly it may be recited among the professors of Christian faith.

Indeed, these chiefs were counted by name, as were all those under them from the age of twenty and above: “Their number was six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men able to go out to war.” Yet all, I say, were cast down in the wilderness except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh. Let us also consider the order of the armies, since we believe that it too is not devoid of a figure of ourselves.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the order of the armies, or the arrangement of the camps; that it signifies the city in the Apocalypse with its threefold arrangement of gates.

“The children of Israel shall set up camp, each according to his companies or divisions and his army. But the Levites shall pitch their tents around the tabernacle, lest wrath come upon the multitude of the children of Israel; and they shall keep watch in the guards of the tabernacle of testimony.” And then:

(CHAPTER II.) “To the east Judah shall pitch tents according to the companies of his army; and the chief of his sons shall be Nahshon son of Amminadab, and the whole sum of warriors of his stock, seventy-four thousand six hundred.”

In the Song of Songs the bridegroom says: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely, like Jerusalem, terrible as an army set in order” (Song VI). Again: “I have compared you, my friend, to my cavalry in Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song III). Therefore, guided not only by reason but also by this preceding authority, let us believe that the aforesaid arrangement of the camps was set out as a figure of the holy Church.

For what is more beautiful or more reasonable, according to the life-giving Spirit, than such an ordering of the camps? On the east, three tribes of Israel; on the west, three tribes; on the south, three tribes; and on the north, three tribes shall camp. And concerning that holy city of God—which is the Church, signified, as stated above, by this ordered array of camps—it is written in the Apocalypse: “It had a great and high wall, having twelve gates; and at the gates twelve angels, and names written, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel. On the east, three gates; on the north, three gates; on the south, three gates; and on the west, three gates” (Rev. XXI).

Accordingly the distinguished and orthodox poet says:

> Whether the first sun guides boys, or excessive heat  
> Kindles youths, or the full light of life’s completed age  
> Perfects men, or whether the cold age of the north wind  
> Calls decrepit old age to holy rites,  
> The threefold Name meets them at the fourfold crossroads.

It is thus clear that such an arrangement of the tribes is a figure of the fullness of grace, by which the one catholic and apostolic faith of the Holy Trinity now receives those coming from every people and nation, every sex and age.

Moreover, it should be noted that Dan pitched camp on the northern side. For because Antichrist is believed to be coming from his stock, he rightly sits in the north, which bears an evil meaning, as the prophet says: “From the north evil shall be unleashed upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. I). Asher and Naphtali, who camped with him, certainly signify good things by their names: Asher means “blessed,” and Naphtali “breadth.” Yet Dan, Asher, and Naphtali were all born from maidservants, all from concubines.

By contrast, on the east, where the sun rises, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun—all born from the free woman Leah—pitched their tents. On the west, from which the mild and springlike west winds blow, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin—all born from the free woman Rachel—pitched theirs. On the southern side, from which the face of day is brighter but excessive heat sometimes burns, Reuben, Gad, and Simeon pitched camp; of these Gad was born from a maidservant, the rest from a free woman.

## CHAPTER IV. What it signifies mystically that the Levites were not counted among the children of Israel.

“But the Levites were not counted among the children of Israel. For thus the Lord commanded Moses.”

The Levites in the present Church of Christ are those who serve at the altar, who are consecrated by sacred honours, and who have undertaken the offices of celebrating the altar. The sacred canons command these persons to abstain from secular cares (II Tim. II). “A bishop,” they say, “or presbyter or deacon must by no means undertake secular concerns—for example, by conducting business or hunting, or by going to war. Otherwise, let him be deposed.”

The Levites, therefore, were rightly not counted among the children of Israel by the Lord’s command, because priests and ministers of the altar ought not to be as the people are.

(CHAPTER III.) Among them—that is, among the Levites—Aaron the high priest stands out, whose firstborn was Nadab, followed by Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Nadab is interpreted “spontaneous”; Abihu, “my father is,” or “my father himself”; Eleazar, “my God is helper,” or “help of my God”; Ithamar, “where bitter,” or “where a palm tree is.” In these names almost the whole condition of our priestly and Levitical order is expressed.

For many of us are too eager for the offices of the altar, according to the name Nadab, and glory too much in God, according to the name Abihu; they despise the lay people as though God were Father to themselves alone. But those who exercise the honour of their rank humbly and worthily may rightly say, according to the name Eleazar, “My God is helper,” or “help of my God,” because whatever is done by them worthily and perfectly is believed to be done by God. According to the name Ithamar, this is required of them: that through the bitter discipline of their bodies they run so as to receive the prize, lest after preaching to others they themselves should become reprobate (I Cor. IX).

“Nadab and Abihu,” it says, “died when they offered strange fire”: namely, as a type of Jews or heretics, whose sacrifices are dead.

## 288 CHAPTER V. Concerning the arrangement of the Levitical families around the tabernacle, and that Moses together with Aaron pitched camp on the east.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Count the sons of Levi by the houses of their fathers and their families, every male from one month old and upward, as above. Moses counted them as the Lord had commanded, and the sons of Levi were found according to their names: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi,” etc.

Their names, too, signify beautiful or splendid sacred mysteries. Levi means “added” or “taken up”; Gershon, “stranger”; Kohath, “patience”; Merari, “bitternesses”; Libni, “to my son”; [Col. 0841D] Shimei, “hear” or “my hearing”; Amram, “exalted people”; Izhar, “it is south” or “southern”; Hebron, “participation in strength,” or “everlasting increase”; Uzziel, “my strength is God”; Mahli, “my choir”; Mushi, “but my ruler,” or “my feeler.”

All these Levitical persons or families, as they hold an office intermediate between God and the people, likewise kept watch in a position intermediate between the tabernacle and the camps of the twelve tribes. The Gershonites were behind the tabernacle to the west; the Kohathites to the south; the Merarites to the north. Moses and Aaron with his sons were before the tabernacle of the covenant—that is, to the east.

Here it should be noted that Moses, leader of the people, and Aaron, high priest, together pitch camp to the east. Hence we sing in the psalm: “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Ps. XCVII), because in the present Church priestly holiness always has great need of the authority of leaders or magistrates and of the swords of kings or emperors. When they agree with one another, nothing is safer; but when they disagree against one another, nothing can be more destructive to the condition of Christianity in this world.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the saying, “You shall take the Levites in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel”; that the firstborn were formerly priests; and why the priesthood was transferred to the one Levitical tribe.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I have taken the Levites from the children of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel. The Levites shall be mine, for every firstborn is mine, from the day when I struck all the firstborn in the land of Egypt.” And then: “Count the firstborn males of the children of Israel from one month old and upward, and you shall have their total. And you shall take the Levites for me in place of every firstborn of the children of Israel.”

It has already been stated elsewhere that Hebrew tradition holds that, up to Aaron’s priesthood, all firstborn from Noah’s lineage were priests and offered victims to God; that Noah’s firstborn Shem himself was Melchizedek; and that this was the birthright which Esau sold to Jacob. Why, then, is all priestly dignity transferred under the law, or gathered into the one tribe of Levi, and all service of the altar restricted to that tribe alone?

Clearly because the sacrifices and ministries of that time were not commanded but permitted, as we have demonstrated above in many places by testimonies from the prophets. For the true sacrifice was to be in the Church according to the order of Melchizedek: the sacrifice belonging to the firstborn—indeed, to the one holy and immaculate firstborn, to whom “the Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

He says in another psalm: “You did not require burnt offering and sacrifice for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. XXXIX)—with the implied meaning: “I am coming to sacrifice my flesh and blood for many for the remission of all sins.” For what else did God require, or what other redemption did he will, but the flesh [Col. 0842D] and blood of the holy and immaculate one? “Will I eat the flesh of bulls,” he says, “or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. XLIX), and much else of this kind.

Therefore, before they possessed the sacrifice they were to offer, why should the firstborn approach the priesthood by command of the law? Thus, as the sacrifice to be offered at that time was not commanded but permitted, so all the priests and ministers from the tribe of Levi were not commanded but admitted: not so much priests as deputies for the absent firstborn priests, appointed to receive a wage for their support until the Firstborn should come who would not redeem himself but, as high priest of the good things to come, would offer himself for us all, being made, as stated above, “a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek.”

The evangelist Luke has this beautifully in view when, after saying of the Virgin whom he had related conceived by the Holy Spirit, “And she bore her son” (Luke II), he immediately added, “her firstborn” (ibid.). According to the foregoing account, this would plainly be superfluous unless he were attending to a great mystery according to the Scriptures. He therefore said “firstborn” so that the learned ecclesiastical man might understand that he is the one who would finally remove the Levitical priesthood, the vicarious priesthood, and that he himself, the Firstborn, together with his whole body, which is the Church, would stand in his heavenly sanctuary, exercising his priesthood.

The command that five shekels be received for the redemption of the firstborn is also fitting, because this bodily life uses the five senses—a life which this Firstborn did not redeem but offered to death for us all. Why, then, is this tribe, the Levitical tribe, admitted in place of the firstborn? Clearly because Moses and Aaron, who led the children of Israel out of Egypt, from the house of bondage, belonged to that tribe; and it was fitting that the tribe through which temporal salvation came should also furnish ministers for the temporal sacrifice.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the service of the sons of Kohath, and the mystical meaning of the saying: “That they may carry the wrapped things and not touch the vessels of the sanctuary, lest they die.”

(CHAPTER IV.) “This is the service of the sons of Kohath: Aaron and his sons shall enter the tabernacle of the covenant and the Holy of Holies when the camp is to move; they shall take down that which hangs before the doors and wrap the ark of the testimony in it, and shall cover it again with a covering of violet skins.” And then:

“When Aaron and his sons have wrapped the sanctuary and all its vessels, when the camp is moving, then the sons of Kohath shall enter to carry the wrapped things; and they shall not touch the vessels of the sanctuary, lest they die.”

Great is the reverence due to divine worship, and great and severe the discipline. “Aaron and his sons,” it says, “shall enter; they themselves shall arrange the work of each and assign what each person must carry. Let no others, out of curiosity, see what is in the sanctuary before the things are wrapped; otherwise they will die.”

According to this rule, therefore, the only legitimate priests today are those to whom God, on account of the merit of their election, has entrusted his secrets—persons such as those to whom the Saviour says in his Gospel: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Matt. XIII). They may handle with their hands the ark of testimony, the table [289] of the offering, the censers and mortars, also the cups and bowls for pouring libations, the lampstand with its lamps and tongs, snuffers and all vessels for oil, as well as the golden altar and all the vessels used in the sanctuary; and they may wrap them in violet and scarlet cloths.

But the sons of Kohath shall carry the wrapped things and not touch them, lest they die. That is, the former may behold with the free sight of the eyes of their hearts, opened for them by God, the mysteries of the incarnation, birth, passion, and resurrection of Christ the Son of God, as well as the coming of the Holy Spirit; they may treat them in sacred speech and adorn them with beautiful writings. The latter should hear them, or read what they have expounded.

Those, I say, to whom it is given to hear the kingdom of God in parables should not themselves presume to be interpreters or authors, lest they fall into heresy. Let the less learned carry, either with the sons of Kohath the sacred vessels, or with the Gershonites the curtains of the tabernacle and the covering of the covenant and all its tents, or the boards of testimony and their bars, pillars, and bases; also the pillars of the court round about with their bases, pegs, and cords. That is, if they are able, let some read mystical matters expounded ably by orthodox Fathers; if they are not able, let others read or preach the deeds of newer or older historians, and others the moral precepts of the saints, in which there is less danger for those weak in faith.

## CHAPTER VIII. That this commandment is violated when unworthy persons are admitted to the order of sacred mystery.

But now, what is most dangerous, the sons of Kohath, the sons of Gershon, and the sons of Merari—who have not attained to the dignity of Aaron and his sons—not only are not kept from seeing or touching the holy things within the sanctuary, but are even summoned and irreverently rush inside, when men are called to the most sacred mysteries of Christ’s altar whom even the lay populace might rightly despise, considering the merit of their life and the quality or quantity of their learning. Those who readily admit such men today do not heed the Lord speaking to Moses and Aaron: “Do not destroy the people of Kohath from the midst of the Levites, so that they may live and not die if they touch the holy of holies; Aaron and his sons shall enter,” etc. For truly, since all who have seized the name or tonsure of a cleric rush, once admitted, into Christ’s sanctuary and unworthily touch and handle the holy of holies, they therefore die, and are struck down swiftly not only in soul but also in body. For “therefore,” says the Apostle, “many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11).

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the command to put out of the camp every leper, everyone with a discharge of seed, and everyone defiled by contact with a dead person.

(Chapter V.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel to put out of the camp every leper, everyone with a discharge of seed, and everyone defiled by contact with a dead person. Put out both male and female from the camp, lest they defile it while they dwell with you.” Once the battle-array of the camp has been ordered—the whole holy and wholly clean, as it ought to be, according to the heavenly realities of which these things are copies, terrible to evil spirits—the spiritual law now commands that, under the names of the leper and the sufferer from a discharge of seed, all harmful and all unclean things be anathematized.

How one should proceed in such cases it had set forth more fully above in Leviticus. Yet there is some difference. There it does not command that a man suffering from a discharge of seed be cast outside the camp, because it would indeed be too harsh for holy Church immediately to cast from her assembly, as though he were a heretic, everyone who is given to much speaking and thereby defiles himself. Therefore, when it says, “Let them put out of the camp every leper,” and adds, “and everyone with a discharge of seed,” we must understand the same person: one who has such a discharge of seed that he is also a leper—that is, one whose tongue is so uncontrolled that he is also a heretic. For it immediately adds, “and everyone defiled by contact with a dead person.” Indeed, one and the same man is a leper, has a discharge of seed, and is defiled by contact with a dead person when a heretic dares to preach, being unable to keep silence and unable to speak pure things; thus he kills his hearers and is thereby defiled by the dead person. “Put out of the camp,” therefore, it says, “everyone of this kind, male and female.”

But concerning other sins the law is not equally severe. For it continues: “When a man or woman has committed any of the sins that commonly happen to human beings, and through negligence has transgressed the Lord’s commandment and incurred guilt, they shall confess their sin, restore the principal amount, and add a fifth part to the person against whom they have sinned,” etc. For every sin a remedy, or rule of redemption, is provided. But for the leper and for the one with a discharge of seed, nothing else is provided except expulsion from the camp.

Thus Christ also speaks in his Gospel consistently with this mystical law when he says: “Every sin will be forgiven to human beings; but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12). But this was discussed more fully above in Leviticus; let us now continue what we began.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the man whose wife has strayed: how he must investigate it, and what reality it mystically signifies in Christ.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: If a man’s wife has gone astray and, despising her husband, has slept with another man; and her husband has been unable to discover it, but the adultery is hidden and cannot be proved by witnesses, because she was not found in the act of fornication; if a spirit of jealousy moves the husband against his wife, whether she is defiled or is accused on false suspicion, he shall bring her to the priest and offer an offering for her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour,” etc.

According to the above-described fourfold arrangement of the camp, Christ’s evangelical Church is most praiseworthy, so that he himself rightly admires her and says: “Who is this who comes forth, or who ascends through the wilderness, like the dawn rising, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle-array?” (Song 6). This Church, I say, is praiseworthy; but what will become of the adulterous Synagogue? What will her husband, her former spouse, do—the one whom she despised by sleeping with another man? For, despising God her lover and despising God’s Son, Christ, she shamelessly went astray and slept with the devil.

Yet her husband cannot expose this; the adultery is hidden. For who can readily catch or convict the contentious Synagogue? She has indeed committed adultery, but she defends herself with so many evasions that few are sufficiently learned in the law, or sufficiently powerful in the Scriptures, to prove by argument that she belongs not to God but to “the synagogue of Satan” (Rev. 2). Thus, in a sense, the adultery is hidden and cannot be proved by witnesses: she confesses that the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is her God, and, as stated, can scarcely be convicted of denying him by her deeds; she was not found in fornication, because she visibly serves no idol, as she once served Astarte, worshipped Baal, and was initiated into Baal-peor.

What then will her husband do? “If,” it says, “a spirit of jealousy moves the husband against his wife, whether she is defiled or is accused on false suspicion, he shall bring her to the priest and offer an offering for her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour.” Clearly the spirit of jealousy—that is, spousal zeal—moved her husband, God, against that wife who truly is defiled, though in her own contentious judgment she is merely charged upon suspicion. Moved thus, he brings her to the priest, to “the great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus Christ his Son” (Heb. 4), so that she may receive judgment under him. “And he shall offer,” it says, “an offering for her, a tenth of an ephah of barley flour.”

Let this have been done, and have had to be done, literally for every woman who despised her husband; and let her have had in her offering not fine wheaten flour but barley—the food of beasts—because she followed the emission of beasts. But according to the spiritual sense now undertaken, the entire offering of the adulterous Synagogue is, as it were, barley, because she reads only the literal chaff of the Scriptures, so coarse and bristling that it is more likely to choke than nourish. “He shall not,” it says, “pour oil upon it or put incense on it.” Why? “Because it is a sacrifice of jealousy, an offering that investigates adultery.” For indeed he gave her neither the holy Spirit of love nor any fruit of pleasing fragrance, because, on account of the aforesaid adultery, he fiercely kindled the fire of anger.

“Therefore the priest shall offer her and set her before the Lord. He shall take holy water in an earthen vessel and put into it a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle. When the woman has stood in the Lord’s presence, he shall uncover her head and put the sacrifice upon her hands,” etc. The literal meaning of this examination is plain; yet it was no less plainly fulfilled in the Spirit upon that synagogue of Satan. Afterwards, when Christ had ascended into heaven and she had also scourged his apostles, killed some of them, stoned others, and persecuted them from city to city—afterwards, I say—she was set before the Lord with head uncovered, surrounded and hemmed in by the Roman army, on every side without the complete protection of God.

Then upon the hands of that evil and adulterous generation he placed the sacrifice of memorial and the offering of jealousy, so that there might come upon her “all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the prophet, whom they killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23). “But he himself shall hold the most bitter waters, in which he has compounded the curse with an imprecation”—that is, as the Prophet says: “He rains snares upon sinners; fire and sulphur and a tempestuous wind are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10). Again: “Let their table before them become a snare, a recompense, and a stumbling-block” (Ps. 68).

These curses, I say, compounded in the waters of the Scriptures, which she made most bitter for herself, were held by her former husband and placed at her mouth with that prophetic complaint: “As a woman despises her lover, so has the house of Israel despised me” (Jer. 3). Again: “You have the brow of a harlot” (ibid.). It continues: “He shall adjure her and say: If you have turned aside from your husband, have been defiled, and have lain with another man, you shall be subject to these curses: May the Lord make you a curse and an example to all his people. May he cause your thigh to waste away and your swollen womb to burst. May the cursed waters enter into your belly, so that your womb swells and your thigh wastes away. And the woman shall answer: Amen, amen.”

Behold, today it is clear and has become manifest to the whole world that that woman is cursed; that adulteress has been set up as an example to all; she limps with her thigh wasted away from all her paths, and her swollen womb has burst, so that no living offspring at all can be born from her. For when the Roman army acted, she was captured and carried captive among all nations; and thus she bears about her curse—that curse, I say, which is not from God but from herself, because she spoke thus and invoked it upon herself: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). To this day she continually confirms it, for she always answers and says, “Amen, amen.”

Therefore it is clear that she turned aside from her husband and lay with another, because she killed Christ and clung to the devil. For if it were not so, she would by no means be subject to these curses. For the law of jealousy said: “If no stranger has lain with you, and if, having abandoned your husband’s bed, you have not been defiled, these most bitter waters into which I have cast curses will not harm you.” But what is the book in which the priest wrote these curses? Surely it is the book of judgment in which are written all the curses that the sinful soul has brought upon itself since Adam first sinned.

But he blotted them out with the most bitter waters, which he himself drank from the brook on the way (Ps. 109). For he took away the sins of the whole world. Yet he gave those same bitter waters again to that adulteress to drink, because she spoke thus and chose it for herself, as said above, crying to her governor Pilate: “His blood be upon us and upon our children”; and to this she says even now, “Amen, amen,” continually cursing Christ.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the law of the Nazirites, and the Evangelist’s saying: “That what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: He shall be called a Nazarene.”

(Chapter VI.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When a man or a woman makes a vow to be sanctified and desires to consecrate himself or herself to the Lord, they shall abstain from wine and everything that can intoxicate. They shall not drink vinegar made from wine or from any other drink, nor anything pressed from grapes,” etc.

This is the law of Nazirites—that is, of holy or consecrated persons—of whom it is written in the book of Maccabees: “They roused the Nazirites who had completed their days, and they cried with a loud voice to heaven, saying: What shall we do with these men, and where shall we take them?” (1 Macc. 3). In their affliction they were beseeching God with more earnestness because they had such patrons, namely Nazirites, who had great merit before the most merciful God because they had fulfilled their days, afflicted by sacred continence and votive abstinence.

But what does this law of theirs mean, or what rationale does it have, especially where it says: “If anyone suddenly dies in his presence, the head of his consecration shall be defiled; he shall shave it immediately on that same day, so that the previous days become void, because his sanctification has been defiled”? What sense is there, I say, in being so strictly forbidden to approach a dead person, and to be defiled even at the funeral of father, mother, brother, or sister, so that if someone suddenly dies in his presence he is immediately defiled and the preceding days are counted void? Therefore, since in this killing letter we make no progress, we must necessarily seek the life-giving Spirit.

Surely this is the law under which the Son of God was made; this, I say, is the law which that Nazirite fulfilled in such a way that it is believed to have been written for him—indeed, concerning him. Knowing this, the Evangelist Matthew, after saying, “When Joseph heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of Herod his father, he was afraid to go there; and, warned in a dream, he withdrew into the regions of Galilee; and coming, he dwelt in a city called Nazareth” (Matt. 2), immediately added: “That what was spoken through the prophets might be fulfilled: He shall be called a Nazarene” (ibid.).

For if you ask where, or through which prophets, it was said that “he shall be called a Nazarene,” behold, it has already been said here in this greatest of prophets that “he shall be called a Nazarene,” provided that, with the veil of the letter removed, we lawfully behold the brightness of the Spirit. Once this is well perceived, it will also become clear why the aforesaid Evangelist used such a testimony in such a place and for such a reason: namely, because what Moses here prefigured in words, our Lord as an infant prefigured there in deeds, when, fleeing Judea because Archelaus reigned there, he came to Nazareth and dwelt there.

## CHAPTER XII. How this Nazirite—that is, our holy Lord God Jesus—spiritually fulfilled the law of the Nazirites.

“During all the time of his consecration,” it says, “he shall not approach a dead person; nor shall he be defiled at the funeral even of father, mother, brother, or sister, because the consecration of God is upon his head. All the days of his separation he shall be holy to the Lord. But if someone suddenly dies in his presence, the head of his consecration shall be defiled.” He shall shave it immediately on that same day of his purification.

The entire time of consecration of this Nazirite—that holy one who alone is truly holy, “who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2)—was the whole time of his present life, from his conception by the Holy Spirit until his resurrection from the dead. Throughout all that time he did not approach a dead person and was defiled by no one’s funeral, because he never committed even a light sin, never consented to another’s sin; indeed, even when entering this world, he brought with him no trace of original sin, through which death entered the world. For he had upon his head the consecration of his God: that is, the full outpouring of the Holy Spirit, by whom he was conceived from the Virgin’s womb.

I say, the consecration of his God, because God is his God according to the human nature which he assumed and according to which he is a Nazirite, as he says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20). This Nazirite grew his hair because he took upon himself the sins of the human race and performed penitence for all even unto death: baptized by John in penitence with tax collectors and sinners, afflicted by fasting for forty days and forty nights, so that he became “obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2).

But someone died suddenly in his presence: namely, that Jewish people, crying, “Crucify, crucify” (Matt. 32 [probably 27]), and crying, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (ibid.). There that people suddenly died; and through that corpse the head of this Nazirite was, as it were, defiled—not for himself, but for the one who died. For why did that people die except because, moved by envy when the crowds sang, “Hosanna to the Son of David. Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 12 [probably 21]), it contrived how this Nazirite might become accursed under the law which says: “Everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed by God” (Deut. 21), so that this act might prove that he was not the one of whom the Prophet sang, “Blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 117)?

Thus, by the very thing through which the Jew died, this Nazirite was defiled—that is, made subject to the curse of the law. Or rather, by the very thing through which the former was defiled, the latter died. The Nazirite immediately shaved his head, but in such a way that the preceding days became void because his sanctification was defiled. For whom but that dead man were the preceding days made void?
