Truly, woe thereby to such a dead man: because from the time he fell before this Nazirite, it profits him nothing that such a Holy of holies took flesh from his flesh, that he was seen in his land for thirty-three years and dwelt among human beings (Baruch 3), he who created all things.

Thus the preceding days of the Nazirite were made void for him—indeed, all the days of the whole age from the time when he conversed with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his fathers. From this point the covenant was made void, the giving of the law was made void, and every act of worship was made void, so much so that God’s soul now hates all things that had been holy to him, from the time he filled his hands with this blood (Isa. 1). The Nazirite shaved his head over him and cast back upon him, because he had died, his sins—the sins of the whole world which he had assumed upon himself.

He also shaved away our sins with the same razor of his Passion, but did not cast them back upon us, because he did not impute his death to us. Instead, he gave them to be scattered to every wind; and thus the Prophet says: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us” (Ps. 102).

## CHAPTER XIII. Further concerning the same: what it signifies according to the mystical law that, when his head was shaved on account of the Jewish people who fell dead before him, their former days were made void.

“He shall shave,” it says, “immediately on the same day of his purification, and again on the seventh day. But on the eighth day he shall offer two turtle-doves or two young pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant of testimony. The priest shall make one a sin-offering and the other a burnt-offering, and shall make atonement for him because he sinned concerning the dead person. He shall sanctify his head on that day and consecrate to the Lord the days of his separation, offering a year-old lamb for sin.”

Well does the Nazirite shave his head also on the seventh day and renew himself by sacrifice on the eighth, because the Passion of this holy one extended across seven days. For from the tenth day of the moon, on which he entered the city—the day on which, according to the law, the paschal lamb to be sacrificed on the evening of the fourteenth day of the moon was taken into every Jewish household—until, I say, the seventh day from that day, which was the Sabbath of his burial: on the eighth day thereafter, which is the first day of the Sabbath, he rose from the dead. Then he completed the new sacrifice which he had instituted at the time of his Passion, offering two turtle-doves or two young pigeons; that is, granting the Holy Spirit of twofold love at the entrance of the covenant of testimony, in the opening of the heavenly kingdom, which he unlocked for us that day after conquering death.

“And the priest,” it says, “shall make one a sin-offering and the other a burnt-offering,” because he gave one gift of the Holy Spirit, for the remission of sins, to love one’s neighbour; and the other, in the diverse distributions of graces, to love God. He gave one while still on earth, the other while already seated in heaven at the Father’s right hand. These two turtle-doves or young pigeons, I say, the Nazirite himself—the priest himself, or the great high priest who passed through the heavens (Heb. 4)—received in his own power in order to give them.

“And he shall make atonement,” it says, “for him”—that is, the priest himself shall make atonement for the Nazirite himself; he shall make atonement for himself, that is, for his body, for us his faithful people, whom he made fellow-members of himself. Paul bears witness when he says: “Who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8). Yet he intercedes not by praying in humble petition, but powerfully, by the right of an advocate, for us.

“And he shall sanctify his head,” it says, etc., as above. The head of this Nazirite was sanctified, because now, according to Zechariah, after the filthy garments of our mortality in which he had been clothed were removed from him, a clean turban was placed upon his head and he was clothed with changes of garments (Zech. 3), crowned, that is, with the glory of immortality and the honour of incorruption. And he so consecrated “the days of his separation” that he now dies no more and death has no further dominion over him (Rom. 6), “still offering a year-old lamb for sin”: namely, through the hands of the Church sacrificing his body and blood for the whole Catholic people in the holy, great, and ineffable mystery of the altar—yet in such a way that the former days were made void, as stated above.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the same Nazirite, Christ: when the days which he decreed by vow will be fulfilled.

“This is the law of consecration: When the days which he decreed by vow are fulfilled, he shall bring him to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant and offer his offering to the Lord: a spotless year-old lamb for sin as a burnt-offering, a spotless year-old ewe for sin, and a spotless ram as a peace-offering,” etc.

When will the days of this Nazirite, which he decreed by vow, be fulfilled? Surely when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in (Rom. 2 [probably 11]). For then it will be time for the remnant of the children of Israel to be saved (ibid.), which he decreed by vow, as he says: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Although this must be understood with reference to a temporal dispensation: for although he himself preached only to Jews, he will nevertheless come to them and regather their remnant near the end of the age.

Then he will give for them the threefold sacrifice, discussed more fully in Leviticus: the sacrifice called the sacrifice of faith for sin, the peace-offering of hope, and the burnt-offering of love. Then “the Nazirite shall be shaved before the door of the tabernacle of the covenant”: that is, by the sacrament of the same Passion by which he took away the sins of the world, he will take away their sins—he who is himself priest, himself Nazirite, himself the door of the tabernacle of the covenant, of the heavenly tabernacle.

“And he shall take his hair”—that is, the sins of the Jewish people—“and put it on the fire,” when the prophecy is fulfilled which says: “If the Lord takes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and washes the blood of Jerusalem from her midst in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4), then he will “take” from them, or receive, “the shoulder and breast” of the ram—that is, good works with confession of heart and mouth—and also “the thigh,” that is, confidence in the flesh, so that they may no longer boast, as hitherto, in the flesh, but in Abraham’s faith. After this the Nazirite may drink wine, because from then on Christ will reign for ever and beyond, when that which we do not yet see fulfilled is accomplished: “You have subjected all things under his feet” (Ps. 8; 1 Cor. 15).

## CHAPTER XV. The moral meaning of the Nazirites’ growing hair, which they cut after their vow.

In a moral sense, when we speak of avoiding superfluous thoughts, let us draw this as an example: they grow hair, which after the vow they cut off and thereafter burn in the fire of sacrifice. For what does the Nazirites’ growing hair signify except that thoughts of presumption increase through great continence of life? But what does it mean that, once the devotion has been completed, the Nazirite is commanded to shave his head and afterward to put his hair into the fire of sacrifice, except that we reach the summit of perfection when we conquer outward vices in such a way that we also cut off superfluous thoughts from the mind?

To burn these, surely, in the fire of sacrifice is to set them aflame with the flames of divine love, so that the whole heart may burn in God’s love and, burning up superfluous thoughts like a Nazirite’s hair, may consume them in the perfection of devotion.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the saying, “Thus you shall bless the children of Israel”: that “the Lord” is said three times, meaning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus you shall bless the children of Israel, and say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord show you his face and have mercy on you. May the Lord turn his countenance toward you and give you peace. They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them.”

What the Lord, speaking to Moses, concealed from them here under the veil of the letter, that aforesaid Nazirite revealed in glorious brightness when his head had been sanctified and he had put on the change of garments of resurrection. For he said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). For what other blessing than this is there by which that holy priest blesses the children of Israel? “May the Lord,” it says—understand, the Father—“bless you”; “may he also show you his face”—understand, the Son; “may he turn his countenance toward you”—understand, the Holy Spirit.

What could be more beautiful, what more delightful? Behold, in this most ancient law we see the light of new grace: the Trinity of the holy name, which the Jew hates, which the heretic Arius divides, which Sabellius confounds. Here, in the ancient book of Numbers, we recognize it lovingly united and clearly distinct. Observe also the beauty of the individual clauses. “May the Lord,” that is, the Father, “bless you”—which is to give good things—“and keep you”—which is to deliver from evils. “May the Lord,” the Son, “show you his face”—which is to give good things—“and have mercy on you”—which is to deliver from evils. “May the Lord,” the Spirit, “turn his countenance toward you”—which is to give good things—“and give you peace”—which is to deliver from evils.

For this is the twofold fruit of the divine blessing: that we may be filled with good things and lack evils; that, marked with this name of the Trinity, we may receive here in the present both remission of sins and every gift of divine grace, and in the future may be freed from the punishments of hell and from the corruption of our bodies, as we hope will happen in the glory of the resurrection. “They shall invoke,” he says, “my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them.”

Because he had said, “Aaron and his sons, thus you shall bless the children of Israel,” lest anyone suppose that the blessing lay in the name, or that anyone is blessed by a human being, he defined what he had said: “They shall invoke,” he says, “my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them.” Therefore let no one glory in the authority of a human being, so that, for example, one of us may say: “I indeed belong to Paul, another to Apollos, another to Cephas, another to Christ. Was Paul,” says the Apostle, “crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 8 [probably 1]).

Therefore, whoever invokes the Lord’s name over us, the one who blesses is the Lord God alone: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. With the Psalmist, in the sense of the present passage, we therefore say: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us” (Ps. 66).

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the erection of the tabernacle and the offerings of the leaders: that they all offered the same things.

(Chapter VII.) “It came to pass on the day when Moses completed the tabernacle and erected it, anointed and sanctified it with all its vessels, and likewise anointed and sanctified the altar and its vessels, that the leaders of Israel, the heads of the families of the individual tribes, the chiefs of those who had been counted, presented offerings before the Lord: six covered wagons with twelve oxen,” etc.

After many extensive exercises in the mysteries, we gladly return once more to the tabernacle, in order to dig hidden treasures out of it, rejoicing over these holy utterances of the law as one who finds great spoil (Ps. 118). Once the tabernacle has been completed and erected, at the Lord’s command the individual leaders offer gifts, each on his own day, at the dedication of the altar; and the gifts all offer are the same, as the Lord ordained.

Certainly the size and number of all the tribes were not equal: in some more, in others fewer, were counted by clans, houses, families, heads, and individual names, from twenty years old and upward, as the Lord had commanded Moses. For example, Judah’s number was twice—and more than twice—as great as the multitude counted from Manasseh. What, then, does it mean that the quantity of all the offerings presented by the individual leaders is the same, and that no more was required at the Lord’s command from the seventy-four thousand six hundred who belonged to Judah than from the thirty-two thousand two hundred who belonged to Manasseh?

Surely: “On the first day Nahshon son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah, offered his offering: a silver dish weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, a silver bowl containing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight, both full of fine flour mixed with oil for sacrifice; a small gold mortar of ten shekels full of incense; a bull from the herd, a ram, and a year-old lamb for a burnt-offering; a goat for sin; and, for the sacrifice of peace-offerings, two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five year-old lambs,” etc. “On the second day, Nethanel son of Zuar, leader of the tribe of Issachar,” etc. “On the third day, the leader of the children of Zebulun, Eliab son of Helon,” etc. “On the fourth day, the leader of the children of Reuben, Elizur son of Shedeur,” etc. “On the fifth day, the leader of the children of Simeon, Shelumiel son of Zurishaddai,” etc. “On the sixth day, the leader of the children of Gad, Eliasaph son of Deuel. On the seventh day, the leader of the children of Ephraim, Elishama son of Ammihud. On the eighth day, the leader of the children of Manasseh, Gamaliel son of Pedahzur. On the ninth day, the leader of the children of Benjamin, Abidan son of Gideoni. On the tenth day, the leader of the children of Dan, Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai. On the eleventh day, the leader of the children of Asher, Pagiel son of Ochran. On the twelfth day, the leader of the children of Naphtali, Ahira son of Enan.”

All offered equal things, and Moses’ pen does not weary of repeating the same things so often, in each case with the same words and almost the same syllables. What does this mean, I ask, except that the letter of the law conceals a great mystery in this passage also?

## CHAPTER XVIII. That Christ fulfilled this passage of the law when he chose the twelve apostles for himself; and that the tabernacle was erected and sanctified when he suffered and rose again, and that thereafter the leaders—that is, the apostles—offered the gifts of faith.

Therefore we now look to him “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2), who fulfilled the Law in himself, as he says: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law; I have not come to abolish it, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5). Indeed, in fulfilling this part of the Law, “he called to himself those whom he wished; and going up onto the mountain, they came to him. And he appointed twelve to be with him, and to send them out to preach; and he gave them authority [Col. 0854C] to heal infirmities and cast out demons” (Mark 3)—“And when,” Mark says, “his own people heard of it, they went out to restrain him, for they said that he had gone out of his mind” (ibid.).

But that truly and uniquely blessed man had not gone out of his mind; rather, “his delight was in the law of the Lord, and in his law he meditated day and night” (Ps. 1). For he himself was the sanctuary of the whole Law, the very word of the Law, the Word of God made flesh. He was then meditating upon fulfilling the Law: that is, according to the present mystery of this Law, appointing the leaders of the twelve spiritual camps. Looking also to this, he says elsewhere to the same apostles: “Amen, I say to you that you who have left everything and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man [Col. 0854D] sits upon the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). For Peter had said to him: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you. What then shall there be for us?” (ibid.).

He greatly honoured them; he marked out for them great honour and a great reward in answering thus. For he wishes it to be understood that he is indeed the Lord of the heavenly tabernacle, while they will be the leaders of the tribes of the Lord. After saying, “Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same [unity]” (Ps. 121), the Psalmist immediately adds: “For thither the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to give thanks to the name of the Lord” (ibid.). And what those leaders of the twelve sons of Israel were commanded to do or offer bodily was to be fulfilled spiritually by them or through them.

For when was that heavenly tabernacle—after whose pattern Moses made this tabernacle—erected, anointed, and sanctified with all its vessels, except when Jesus Christ, the Son of God, high priest of the tabernacle, poured out his own blood? By that blood he anointed and sanctified the whole Church, gathered as great as it had been from the origin of the world, by granting remission of sins. Then these leaders immediately followed, offering oxen and carts for carrying the tabernacle or the sanctuary of the tabernacle, when they undertook to preach throughout the whole world the faith of the patriarchs and prophets. In this respect they themselves are the oxen; they themselves are the carts; they themselves are the rulers; they themselves are the bearers of the Church.

Each offered a silver basin weighing one hundred and thirty shekels. This number, consisting of a hundred and thirty, rightly signifies faith in the one God and the three persons. They also possess a silver bowl holding seventy shekels. This number, composed of ten and seven, signifies the sevenfold evangelical grace of the Holy Spirit and the true knowledge of the Law, whose commandments are ten. They also offered a little golden mortar of ten golden shekels, full of incense: that is, with harmonious voice they preached Christ, the Son of God. His body, conceived of the Virgin, was golden and spotless, containing within itself all the precious incense of pure prayer; through the passion of death it was crushed for us.

These things they offered; these things each preached to the praise [Col. 0855C] and glory of God on his own day—that is, each according to the measure of grace or revelation which he received from the Lord, from the one and same Holy Spirit. Some indeed drew more, others fewer, to the faith; yet all preached by the same Spirit and with the same understanding. So too those tribal leaders had some more and some fewer thousands of their tribe under their hand, yet all offered equal things, all the same vessels.

And they indeed offered fine flour in vessels—visible fine flour mixed with visible oil. But these men preached the spirit of the Law hidden in the letter: the true and invisible fine flour, the true and life-giving food of all believing souls. They offered [Col. 0855D] “an ox, a ram, and a year-old lamb for a burnt offering, and a goat for sin; and for the sacrifice of peace offerings, two oxen, five rams, five he-goats, and five year-old lambs.” These, I say, our leaders each offered. For, while preaching to others lest they themselves should become reprobate, they afflicted themselves and exposed themselves also to sufferings (1 Cor. 9).

For they are those of whom each says in Psalm 65: “And my mouth spoke in my tribulation. I shall offer you fat burnt offerings with the incense of rams; I shall offer you oxen with goats.” That entire psalm is the voice of these leaders. It is as though each of them says, even while in tribulation: “I shall preach to others, that they too may be led to the same end by my example; and meanwhile here [Col. 0856A] I shall offer you fat burnt offerings”—that is, myself made into a fat burnt offering, wholly consumed by the inward fire of love, with rams, oxen, and goats burned: that is, with every resistance, every exaltation, every foulness of vices of flesh and spirit burned up. For this reason there are five rams, five lambs, and five goats: because in the five senses the flesh, when permitted, indulges in wantonness.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the fact that, when Moses entered the tabernacle of the covenant, he heard the voice speaking to him from the mercy-seat; and an example from the Acts of the Apostles, showing when Moses entered and when that which was prefigured there was heard and accomplished in reality.

**(CHAP. VIII.)** “And when Moses entered the tabernacle of the covenant to consult the oracle, he heard the voice [Col. 0856B] speaking to him from the mercy-seat which was over the ark of testimony, between the two cherubim; and from there it spoke to him. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and say to him: When you set up the seven lamps of the lampstand, let them be placed on the south side.”

From the time when the tabernacle was sanctified, Moses enters the tabernacle of the covenant. For, from the time when the holy Church was redeemed through Christ, man was reconciled and made familiar with God. From that time, I say, Moses, consulting the oracle, “heard the voice speaking to him from the mercy-seat, which was over the ark of testimony between the two cherubim,” because those who were Moses’ disciples then came to know God’s counsel concerning all the nations: that he wished to offer them also a way to repentance.

For what voice did he hear speaking? He says: “Speak to Aaron and say to him: When you set up the seven lamps of the lampstands, let them be set up on the south side.” And Scripture immediately continues and says: “He therefore commanded this, that the lamps should face northward, opposite the table of the loaves of presentation.” The lampstand faces the direction toward which its lamps are to give light. It is as though he said: although he commands the seven lamps of the lampstand to be set up on the south side opposite the table of the loaves of presentation, while the table itself, as is written in Exodus (Exod. 25, 37), was commanded to be placed on the north side, he therefore commanded that the lamps should face northward, directly opposite.

He wished to impress upon us strongly [Col. 0856D] that the lampstand with seven lamps—that is, Christ, in whom the seven shining Spirits rest—wished to turn the gracious gaze of his mercy toward the north, that is, toward the nations, which until then had not possessed the true sun; and there to have the table of the loaves of presentation, that is, the truth of the Scriptures or the sacrament of his body and blood. That the lampstand signifies Christ crowned with the glory of the resurrection, that the seven lamps signify the sevenfold Holy Spirit, and that the north or north wind signifies us Gentiles, has been more fully explained in Exodus (Exod. 25).

This, I say, he wished strongly to impress upon us: namely, that this had been commanded for the grace of a definite mystery, he being mindful of the pattern which the Lord had shown him [Col. 0857A] on the mountain. “When,” he says, “Moses entered the tabernacle of the covenant to consult the oracle, he heard the voice speaking to him from the mercy-seat, which was over the ark of testimony between the two cherubim, and from there it spoke to him.”

In the Acts of the Apostles we have the occasion when Moses entered the tabernacle of the covenant, consulted the oracle, and heard such a voice—the voice of so great a propitiation—between the two cherubim: that is, from the harmonious testimony of the two Testaments. “When no small dissension had arisen between Paul and Barnabas and the Gentiles to whom God had opened the door of faith, it was decided that Paul and Barnabas, and certain others from among them, should go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem concerning this question” (Acts 15). And afterwards: “When much dispute [Col. 0857B] had taken place, Peter arose and said to them: Men and brethren, hear me. You know that from ancient days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe” (ibid.), etc.

“And after they had fallen silent, James answered, saying: Men and brethren, hear me. Simon has related how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for his name; and the words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written: After these things I shall return, and I shall build again the tabernacle of David which has fallen; and I shall rebuild its ruins and raise it up, so that the rest of humankind may seek the Lord, and all the nations upon whom my name has been called, says the Lord who does these things. His work is known to the Lord from eternity” (ibid.), etc.

Therefore, when Moses entered and consulted [Col. 0857C] the oracle, the voice was heard commanding that the lampstand of seven lamps should face northward, directly opposite, and that the lamps should shine toward the direction upon which the lampstand looks. For when the question had arisen and the oracle of the Holy Spirit was consulted, this was defended by manifest authorities: that Christ is the expectation of the nations.

Even today Moses enters the tabernacle to consult the oracle whenever good rulers, recognizing that they cannot discern doubtful matters, return to the secret place of the mind as though to a certain tabernacle. Having examined the divine Law, as though the ark were set before them, they consult the Lord; and what they first hear inwardly, they afterwards make known outwardly by their deeds. For, in order to minister without offence to outward concerns, they strive unceasingly to return to the secrets [Col. 0857D] of the heart. Thus they hear God’s voice as though by hidden inspiration, while through mental meditation they are drawn away from carnal senses.

## CHAPTER XX. On the purification of the Levites: the mystical meaning of their being commanded to shave all the hair of their flesh.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the Levites from the midst of the children of Israel, and purify them according to this rite. Let them be sprinkled with water of purification, and let them shave all the hair of their flesh. And when they have washed their garments and have been cleansed, they shall take an ox from the herd,” etc.

“They shave,” he says, “all the hair of their flesh.” The hairs of the flesh are the thoughts of the old life, which we cut away from the mind in such a manner that we are troubled by no grief at their loss. The hairs of the flesh are whatever is superfluous in human corruption. For a Levite is so called because he is taken up. Therefore Levites must shave all the hair of the flesh, because one who is taken up into divine service ought to appear before God’s eyes clean of every thought of the flesh. Let the mind not bring forth unlawful thoughts and make the beautiful appearance of the soul ugly, as though by luxuriant hairs.

Yet however far the virtue of holy conduct has raised anyone, something from the oldness of life still arises in him which must be removed. Hence the Levites’ hairs were commanded to be shaved, not plucked out. When hairs are shaved, their roots remain in the flesh and grow again, to be cut again. Thus superfluous thoughts must indeed be cut off with great diligence, but they can by no means be completely cut away. For the flesh always produces superfluities, which the spirit must continually cut away with the blade of watchful care. But we discern these things within ourselves more subtly when we penetrate the heights of contemplation.

Yet no one can attain this perfection of purity or beauty unless he has first shaved from his mind, with the razor of divine love, all worldly resources. Therefore our Lord, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5), says to the rich young man, so that this Law of the Levites also may be fulfilled by those taken up by him: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). And afterwards: “And everyone [Col. 0858C] who has left house or brothers” (ibid.), etc.

Moses himself also proves that this is truly the shaving of the Levites, when in Deuteronomy he says in the blessing of Levi: “He who said to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you’; and to his brothers, ‘I am ignorant of you’: these have kept your word and preserved your covenant; they shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” (Deut. 33).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the same subject, and the meaning of the children of Israel laying hands upon the Levites, and the Levites laying their hands upon the heads of the oxen to be sacrificed.

This very Moses proves here, I say, that the sons of Levi ought to be shaved spiritually, when there he immediately adds: “They shall place incense in your wrath, and a burnt offering upon your altar” (Deut. 33); and here, [Col. 0858D] after saying, “Let them be sprinkled with water of purification, and let them shave all the hair of their flesh,” he immediately adds: “And when they have washed their garments and have been cleansed, they shall take an ox from the herd and its libation, fine flour mixed with oil. But you shall take another ox from the herd for sin, and you shall bring the Levites before the tabernacle of the covenant, after summoning the whole multitude of the children of Israel. And when the Levites are before the Lord, the children of Israel shall lay their hands upon them, and Aaron shall offer the Levites as an offering before the Lord from the children of Israel, that they may serve in his ministry. The Levites also shall lay their hands upon the heads of the oxen,” etc.

What does it mean for Levites sprinkled with water, shaved, and cleansed after washing their garments, to touch before the Lord one ox for a burnt offering and the other for sin, with their hands laid upon their heads, after the children of Israel have first laid their hands upon them, either separately or together? What is this, I say, except that men of a spiritual vocation, cleansed from their own vices and shaved of all worldly possessions and cares, should devote themselves solely to that for which they have been taken up: namely, to place incense in the Lord’s wrath and a burnt offering upon his altar—that is, to intercede for the sins of the peoples?

For the children of Israel lay their hands upon the Levites, who receive tithes from them; and the Levites lay their hands upon the heads of the oxen, of which, he says, “you shall make one for sin and the other for a burnt offering,” when men of the spiritual order take upon themselves the sins of secular people, from whose alms they live, and strive by offering the sacrifices of prayers to press those sins down before the Lord and overcome them unto their remission or pardon. Because this must be done with great earnestness, it is recalled as having been done by a threefold repetition at the end of the chapter: “And Moses and Aaron and the entire multitude of the children of Israel did concerning the Levites what the Lord had commanded Moses.” And then: “And they were purified, and they washed their garments,” etc. And then, a third time: “As the Lord had commanded Moses concerning the Levites, so it was done.”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Levites’ serving from twenty-five years of age onward, and becoming guardians of the vessels in their fiftieth year.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is [Col. 0859C] the law of the Levites: from twenty-five years old and upward they shall enter to minister in the tabernacle of the covenant. And when they have completed their fiftieth year, they shall cease to serve; they shall be ministers to their brothers in the tabernacle of the covenant, to guard what has been entrusted to them.”

What is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth arises, except the very conflicts against every vice? And what is signified by the fiftieth year, which contains the rest of jubilee, except inward rest born of the mind’s conquered warfare? And what is figured by the vessels of the tabernacle except the souls of the faithful? Therefore let the Levites serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, and from their fiftieth become guardians of the vessels, so that those who still endure the struggles of attacking vices may not presume to undertake the care of others.

For while the elect are still in temptation, they must be subject, serve, and be wearied by duties and labours. But when they have subdued the wars of temptations, so that they are now secure within themselves in deep tranquillity, let them receive the charge of souls. For in the tranquil age of the mind, when the heat of temptation has withdrawn, they are guardians of the vessels, because they become teachers or rulers of souls.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the saying: “The man who is unclean because of a human soul, or is on a distant journey, shall keep the Passover for the Lord in the second month.”

**(CHAP. IX.)** “Let the children of Israel keep the Passover at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of this month at evening, according to all its ceremonies and ordinances. And Moses commanded the children of Israel to keep the Passover. They kept it at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, on Mount Sinai. According to all that the Lord had commanded Moses, the children of Israel did.”

We know the definition and law of the great solemnity called in Hebrew *Phase*, that is, “Passover” or “passing over”; we have also treated it more fully in Exodus. Namely, Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, and by his blood we marked our doorposts once for all when we were baptized into his death. But we must always feast upon his flesh and the same blood with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5).

But let us see what follows: “Behold, certain men were unclean because of a human soul, and could not keep the Passover on that day. Coming to Moses and Aaron, they said to them: ‘We are unclean because of a human soul. Why are we deprived, so that we cannot offer the offering to the Lord at its appointed time among the children of Israel?’” By this occasion, after consultation with the Lord, what had been lacking to the Law was supplied thus: “The man,” he says, “who is unclean because of a soul, or on a distant journey among your people, shall keep the Passover for the Lord in the second month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening; they shall eat it with unleavened bread and wild lettuces,” etc.

This part of the Law is both a prophecy of Jewish uncleanness and a rule for discerning the case of each individual person. For the Jews are unclean because of a soul, because they killed Christ; and therefore blindness has come upon them, so that they do not see that Christ is the true Passover, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters into this paschal feast (Rom. 11). At last the remnant among them shall be saved (ibid.), not otherwise than by eating the same Lamb, not otherwise than by marking the doorposts of their foreheads with the blood of Christ.

This, I say, shall come to pass. Those unclean because of a soul therefore do not keep the Passover for the Lord in the first month, but will keep it in the second. That is, the Jews, defiled by Christ’s blood, do not now eat his flesh or drink his blood; but toward the end of the age those of them who remain will eat and drink. Moreover, with respect to individual persons, this is a ruling of discriminating synodal discipline: one who ought to keep the Passover for the Lord in the highest rank—that is, to celebrate the most holy mysteries of the altar—if, for example, a presbyter or deacon is unclean because of a soul, that is, has committed a crime worthy of death, should thereafter be content with lay communion. Thus, clearly, under this mystical law he is, as it were, deferred from the first month to the second, because he is cast down from a higher rank to the lowest.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the children of Israel’s setting out when the cloud was lifted, and encamping where it stood.

“And when the cloud which protected the tabernacle had been removed, then the children of Israel set out; and in [Col. 0861A] the place where the cloud had stood, there they encamped. At the command of the Lord they set out, and at his command they pitched the tabernacle,” etc.

According to the historical sense, it was indeed glorious and honourable for those leaders and armies that they set out at the Lord’s command and pitched the tabernacle at his command, remaining in the same place throughout all the days on which the cloud stood over the tabernacle. By the word of the Lord they pitched their tents, and by his word they set out; and they kept the Lord’s watch according to the command of the Lord through the hand of Moses.

But those heavenly realities, after whose pattern these things were made, are more hidden indeed, yet more glorious than these. What are they? Namely, that our fathers and our leaders, equipped for spiritual campaign, conveyed to us the Lord’s sanctuary by preaching the incarnation or birth, passion, resurrection from the dead, and ascension of Christ the Son of God. They did not set out according to their own choice, going where they themselves wished, but when, where, and how the Spirit of Jesus commanded them.

Hence we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they came to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them. And when they had passed through Mysia, they went down to Troas. During the night a vision was shown to Paul: a certain Macedonian man stood, begging him and saying, ‘Cross over into Macedonia and help us.’ When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought [Col. 0861C] to depart for Macedonia, being assured that God had called us to evangelize them” (Acts 16).

Therefore these too set out at the command of the Lord, with the cloud preceding them, which is Christ according to his human body; concerning this cloud we have spoken more fully in Exodus.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the two silver hammered trumpets, the distinction of their sound, and why only two were commanded to be made.

**(CHAP. X.)** “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Make for yourself two hammered silver trumpets, by which you may summon the multitude when the camp is to be moved. And when you sound the trumpets, the whole assembly shall gather to you at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant.”

It is almost natural for human minds to be affected by the sounds of trumpets, and according to the character of their notes either to be shaken with fear, carried away with courage, or composed in reverence. The Lord, the giver and creator of minds, deigned to recognize this, and made a careful distinction between their sounds as follows: “If you sound once, the leaders and heads of the multitude of Israel shall come to you. But if a longer and broken sound is sounded, the camps shall move. When the people are to be assembled, the trumpet sound shall be simple, and they shall not wail in broken notes.”

A long and broken trumpet sound announces the movement of the camp or departure for war; a simple—that is, unbroken—sound summons the people to assemble. Concerning a broken and wailing sound, the prophet Hosea says: “Sound the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; wail in Beth-aven behind you, Benjamin” (Hos. 5). In conformity with the character of the broken sound or wailing, the prophet appropriately breaks up his own expression also in a four-part division.

Concerning the simple—that is, unbroken—sound, however, the prophet Joel says: “Sanctify a fast; summon an assembly; gather the elders, all inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God; and cry to the Lord: Ah, ah, ah, for the day, because the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come like devastation from the Mighty One” (Joel 1). Between these stands the sounding once, sufficient to summon only the leaders or heads of the multitude of Israel.

According to the spiritual meaning, the trumpet sound is the voice of preachers. Without them, however beautiful and well ordered the battle line of the camp may be, it is not terrible. That the trumpet sound signifies preaching or the rebuke of sins is not left unspoken by the prophets; and why two rather than three or four ought to be made is likewise signified by the prophets and revealed in Christ.

For what else does the trumpet of preaching announce except the coming day of fearful judgment, as was said shortly before in the prophet Joel: “Because the day of the Lord is near” (ibid.)? Now the same Judge has not merely one but two comings: one in which he has already come to be judged, the other in which he will come to judge. Both are terrible, especially to those among whom, or against whom, prophetic Scripture chiefly sounds its trumpet; both comings, I say, are terrible to them, both are comings of judgment. For concerning the first coming he says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). Whether the second coming is terrible, it is superfluous to ask or establish by testimonies.

Therefore, because there are two comings of the fearful Judge, around which all divinely inspired Scripture—all legal, prophetic, and evangelical Scripture—expends all its labour, all its spirit, and all its effort, the Lord rightly commands Moses to make not three or four, not, I say, more or fewer, but only two trumpets. They are silver because the words of preachers shine with the brightness of light and cloud the minds of hearers with none of their own obscurity. For, as the Psalmist says, “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 12; cited here as Ps. 2). They are hammered because preachers who walk according to the truth of the Scriptures must grow through the blows of tribulations.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the saying, “If you sound once, the leaders shall come,” etc.; and the proper ordering of preaching according to these directions.

“If you sound once, the leaders and heads of the multitude of Israel shall come to you. But if a longer and broken sound is sounded,” etc.

This distinction must be observed with the utmost care by the seven angels standing before God, to whom seven trumpets were given, who prepared themselves to sound the trumpets (Rev. 8): that is, by all preachers eminent in the Church of God, whoever have been given from above the perfect gift of teaching, whoever have undertaken the office of holy preaching imposed upon them.

For in figure or signification two trumpets, as stated above, were commanded to be made; but in evangelical reality and truth, just as there are many preachers, so there are many gifts given according to the divisions of grace. Their totality is rightly understood through the number seven of the angels and trumpets. This distinction or discernment, I say, must be carefully observed: when the people are to be gathered, the trumpet sound should be simple and not brokenly wailing; when they are to go out to war, a longer and broken or wailing sound should rebuke; but when leaders or heads of the multitude are called, they should sound once.

That is: when hearers are first called to faith, the judgment to come should be announced to them terribly and solemnly. But when instruction is directed to those who already possess faith, they should be stirred with moderation to battle against the ranks of vices. When dealing with those already well instructed and living spiritually, one should hold with them a gentle, familiar conversation.

Paul, the most excellent of trumpet-sounding men, knew how to administer this mode of discernment. To the Romans, who were still so unformed in faith that they did not understand that they were saved by God’s grace and not by their own merits, and therefore contended against the Jews, he speaks with the greatest severity: “For the wrath of God is revealed against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is manifest to them” [Col. 0863C] (Rom. 1), etc. Recounting first the vices of the Gentiles, he sounds, as it were, a simple trumpet note and does not wail in broken tones, seeking thereby to gather the people and reconcile the discordant minds of the two peoples.

But in writing his Second Epistle to the Corinthians, now no longer dealing with faith or grace but with the battle against vices, he moderates his message as though breaking the trumpet sound: “And through,” he says, “the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; through glory and dishonour; through evil report and good report; as deceivers and true; as unknown and known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened and not killed; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many; as having nothing, and possessing all things” (2 Cor. 6).

Finally, after many such things, he again speaks as though with broken wailing: “I asked Titus, and sent with him a brother. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Did we not walk in the same steps? Have you long supposed that we were defending ourselves before you? Before God we speak in Christ. But all things, beloved, are for your edification. For I fear lest perhaps, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and I may be found by you such as you do not wish; lest perhaps there be among you contentions, jealousies, outbursts of anger, dissensions, detractions, scurrilities, whisperings, swellings of pride, seditions; lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who formerly sinned and have not repented” (2 Cor. 12).

But where he in a sense calls only the leaders, and in one well-instructed disciple admonishes all who are heads of the multitude of Israel, he sounds the trumpet once—that is, he speaks softly—because it is enough to have spoken once to the wise: “For this reason I remind you to rekindle the grace of God which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and sobriety. Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord” (2 Tim. 1), etc. All these things he says softly and in an almost ordinary manner.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the saying, “If you have a feast,” etc.; and how this is well fulfilled in the Church of Christ.

“The sons of Aaron the priest shall sound the trumpets, and this shall be [Col. 0864B] an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations. If you have a feast, holy days, and Kalends, you shall sound the trumpets over the burnt offerings and peace offerings, so that they may be for you a remembrance before your God.”

The holy Roman Church has excellently wished this too to be an everlasting ordinance in its generations. For whenever it has a feast, holy days, and Kalends, who does not wonder at how great a spiritual trumpet sound it resounds over its burnt offerings and peace offerings? For what is its feast but the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ? What are its holy days, what its Kalends, except the annual day of the incarnation or even birth of the same Christ, the Son of God, and, more especially, the most glorious season of his resurrection? These are its holy days, these are its Kalends; and besides these, the anniversaries of the holy apostles and blessed martyrs.

Who, I say, having ears to hear, is not shaken and astonished by its trumpet sound on these days? Who does not wonder at the order of its mind? Around the feast which God has given it, around the table of Christ who bestowed these festivals, it has summoned from the entire treasury of the holy Scriptures such great and such spiritual trumpet voices, with the beauty of musical sweetness, to be sung and read concerning burnt offerings and peace offerings, that whoever deserves to discover their rationale may truly say in his soul that saying from the Song of Songs: “The king brought me into his chamber; the king brought me into the wine cellar” [Col. 0864D] (Song 1 and 2).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Moses’ saying to his father-in-law, when the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sinai: “Do not leave us; come with us, and you shall be our guide.”

“On the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the covenant. And the children of Israel set out in their companies from the wilderness of Sinai, and the cloud came to rest in the wilderness of Paran; and they broke camp. And Moses said to Hobab, son of Raguel the Midianite, his kinsman: ‘We are setting out for the place which the Lord will give us. Come with us, that we may do you good,’” etc.

Often we can better persuade the proud toward what is useful if we say that their advancement will benefit us rather than them, if we ask that their improvement be bestowed more upon us than upon themselves. For pride is readily bent toward good when its bending is believed to benefit others also. Hence here Moses, who was making his way through the wilderness under God’s guidance, with the pillar of cloud leading him, wished to draw Hobab his kinsman away from the manner of life of his Gentile people and subject him to the rule of almighty God. He said: “We are setting out for the place which the Lord will give us; come with us, that we may do you good, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel.” When Hobab answered him, “I will not go with you, but I shall return to my own land, in which I was born,” Moses immediately added: “Do not leave us, for you know in what places we ought to encamp in the wilderness, and you shall be our guide.”

For Moses was not troubled by ignorance of the route: knowledge of the Godhead had opened him out into knowledge of prophecy; the pillar went before him outwardly; and inwardly, through his diligent intercourse with God, familiar speech instructed him concerning all things. But the prudent man, speaking to a proud hearer, asked for assistance in order that he might give it; he sought a guide on the road in order that he might become Hobab’s guide to life. Thus he brought it about that the proud hearer became all the more devoted to the voice persuading him to better things because he was thought necessary; and from the very point at which he believed himself to be preceding his exhorter, he bowed beneath the words of exhortation.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the fact that, when the ark was lifted up, Moses said, “Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered”; and on Christ’s exaltation, according to the meaning of Psalm sixty-seven. [Col. 0865C]

“And when the ark was lifted up, Moses said: ‘Arise, O Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee before your face.’ But when it was set down, he said: ‘Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the host of Israel.’”

When the cloud was lifted up and the leaders were moving the camp, Moses remained in contemplation of that pattern which the Lord had shown him on the mountain, as Scripture repeatedly testifies: “Arise, O Lord,” he says, or, “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered” (Ps. 67 [68]). For Psalm sixty-seven has its beginning, its heavenly cause or subject matter, from this: “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee before his face.”

Where, then, does God arise? Precisely there where the lifted cloud signifies that he is to arise. The prophetic Spirit in the Psalmist investigated what was meant by the lifting of the cloud and by the leaders’ setting out as they moved the camp. “You ascended on high,” he says; “you led captivity captive; you received gifts among men” (ibid.). Then, continuing in the mystical sense of the present passage, he says: “They saw your processions, O God—the processions of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary. The leaders went before, joined with those who sang psalms; in the midst were young maidens playing tambourines. There was Benjamin, the youth, in ecstasy of mind; the rulers of Judah, their leaders; the rulers of Zebulun; the rulers of Naphtali” (ibid.).

A third witness comes forward, the Apostle, and with the whole veil removed speaks more plainly with unveiled face, showing what the lifting of the cloud is, who are the leaders of the camp, what is the ascent on high, and what are the gifts among men. “To each one of us,” he says, “grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.” Therefore he says: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men. And he himself gave some as apostles, others as prophets, others as evangelists, others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for building up the Body of Christ” (Eph. 4).

Let God therefore arise—that is, let Christ ascend on high—and through these leaders, who set out to us when the cloud of his flesh has been lifted up: through the apostles, evangelists, prophets, teachers, and pastors; through these, I say, “rulers of Judah, rulers of Zebulun, rulers of Naphtali,” who are beautiful in faith, strong in hope, and enlarged in charity. Among them too is “Benjamin, the youth, in ecstasy of mind”: namely Paul, the least of the apostles, caught up to the third heaven. “Let his enemies be scattered, and let those who hate him flee before his face”: this has happened, is happening, and at the end of the age will happen until victory is complete.

“But when the ark was set down, Moses said: ‘Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the host of Israel.’” This too will surely happen when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in. For then the Lord will return to that carnal Israel, so that a remnant from them may be saved (Rom. 11).

## CHAPTER XXX. [Col. 0866C] On the murmur of the people which arose; on their longing for cucumbers and melons; and on the nature of manna.

(CH. 11.) “Meanwhile a murmur arose among the people, like that of persons grieving over their labor, against the Lord. When he heard it, he was angry. The fire of the Lord was kindled against them and devoured the outermost part of the camp. When the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire was extinguished; and he called the name of that place Burning, because the fire of the Lord had been kindled against them.”

From this point begin the causes why, as was said at the beginning of this book of Numbers, “the belly of the eater is made bitter.” All who had been numbered from twenty years old and upward now begin to be destroyed, and their bodies are laid low in the wilderness, as a figure of us—as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 10)—who all, having been made candidates by Christ’s baptism, begin to run, but do not all attain the goal; and all seem to fight, but not all are crowned.

This is the first cause: the temptation of those who lusted—temptation, I say, and the lust of those enslaved to the enticements of the belly. For they said: “Who will give us flesh to eat? We remember the fish that we ate in Egypt for nothing; cucumbers and melons come to mind, leeks and onions and garlic. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing except manna.” These things, I say, they said in lustful testing, and in testing lusted. For the Psalmist says: “They tempted God in their hearts, so that they might ask food for their souls. And they spoke wickedly against God; they said: ‘Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?’” (Ps. 77 [78]), etc.

Truly wretched and contemptible are they who, despising such bread, while they crave meat, have sunk so far in the quarrel of the belly that they turn longing eyes toward such worthless kinds of herbs. “Cucumbers and melons come to mind,” they say, “and leeks and onions and garlic.” The cucumber is cold by nature and harmful to the stomach. *Pepo* is a Greek name, and its origin is uncertain to Latin speakers; its nature is exceedingly cold. It is well known that leeks and onions are unpleasant in taste, for at times they draw tears from the one eating them. It is also certain that garlic is most unpleasant. Hence Flaccus, jesting bitterly, complains thus:

> If anyone once with impious hand  
> has broken his father’s aged throat,  
> let him eat garlic more harmful than hemlock.  
> (HORACE, *Epodes* I, ode 3.)

Accordingly, censuring them and vehemently magnifying their fault, Scripture says: “Now manna was like coriander seed, the color of bdellium. The people went about and gathered it, ground it in a mill or pounded it in a mortar, cooked it in a pot, and made cakes from it, having a taste like bread made with oil. And when dew fell upon the camp at night, manna fell with it.” In order to rebuke them, it sets forth the appearance, color, and taste of the bread received from God, together with its spontaneous abundance.

Coriander is an herb suited for medicines, called in Greek *korion* (κόριον). Bdellium is an amber-like resin flowing from the aromatic bdellium tree. Because of this kind of lust, “the fire,” it says, “kindled against them devoured the outermost part of the camp,” and the name of that place was called Burning, because the fire of the Lord had been kindled against them; or it was called Graves of Lust: “for there,” it says, “they buried the people who had desired.”

## CHAPTER XXXI. That those like them were first the Jews, and then all in the Church who, abandoning their purpose, despise God’s word or Christ’s mysteries.

Those like them—indeed, their sons in the first place—were those who, converted from the circumcision in the beginnings of evangelical faith, had set before themselves the table of the living bread which came down from heaven: the true manna, the living and true sacrifice, Christ himself, the true sacrament of his body and blood. Yet, I say, with this food set before them, they looked back to the pots of flesh—to the flesh of the former burnt offerings and sacrifices which God did not demand from the hands of their fathers, as the prophets testified (Isa. 1; Jer. 7). Contending and quarreling over these things, divided against the apostles (Acts 15), they truly returned to Egypt; they were rolled back into the darkness of ancient oldness.

In the second place, those like the murmurers mentioned above—indeed, their sons—are all who, having heard the voice saying, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11), seize the beginning of a good course but, ensnared by their former desires, do not complete the course. They despise the word of God set before them, or even the most holy office of Christ’s altar, for the sake of which they left the labors and burdens of the world, professing that holy leisure whereby they might be free to see God.

For many of these sometimes burn with desire as they remember the meats over whose pots they sat in the world, and the fish which they ate; and cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic come to their minds—the sorts of things with which at times even the burning stomach of a gorged rich man delights to cool itself, according to Flaccus:

> … when full of turnips  
> and acid, he prefers elecampane; nor has all poverty yet  
> been driven away by the banquets of kings.  
> (HORACE, *Satires* II, satire 2.)

While occupied with such desires, these men take no interest in sacred reading or in the office they have undertaken. Remembering Egypt, they surely despise heavenly manna; and thus, restless themselves and disturbing others, they grievously afflict some servant of the Lord set over them, so that he may say with this Moses to the Lord: “Why have I not found grace before you?”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the words, “Gather for me seventy men,” etc.; and how he said, “I will take of your spirit and give it to them.”

“And the Lord said to Moses: ‘Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; bring them to the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, and make them stand there with you, that I may come down and speak with you. I will take of your spirit and give it to them, that they may bear the burden of the people with you, and that you may not be burdened alone.’”

From one and the same furnace, light breaks forth for the good and fire for the evil. From one and the same kiln of tribulation, I say, the fire of the Lord was kindled against the reprobate and the Spirit of the Lord, which was in Moses, was poured out upon the elect. Why was this so, except that hope might be given to all who are afflicted after the example of Moses—who, desiring to live piously, groan under the evil habits of those whose care they have undertaken—that they might know to hope that, while they themselves are wearied by labor and almost fail, many others may advance through their virtues?

For it was not without reason that it was said: “I will take of your spirit and give it to them,” when it might have been said, “I will give them of my Spirit.” For because Moses’ patience merited that many should receive the Spirit of the Lord, so that through their progress merit might increase for him, it was rightly said: “I will take of your spirit and give it to them.”

Nor, because it says “I will take,” should we childishly imagine that a portion was divided and that therefore the grace of the Spirit of the Lord possessed by Moses was diminished. For elemental fire has such power that, although divided into parts, it knows no diminution of its borrowed light; how much more does the true and eternal fire, the Spirit of the Lord, suffer no diminution when he is imparted to many? Therefore what he said, “I will take,” is as though he had said, “I will receive.”

It should be carefully noted that, when he had said, “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel,” he added, “whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people.” For God truly seeks not old age in years but old age of soul. “For venerable old age is not that which lasts long, nor is it measured by the number of years. For the gray hairs of a human being are understanding, and an unblemished life is the age of old age” (Wis. 4). This old age, or these gray hairs, are recognized not so much by the bodily eyes as by the judgment of reason; and God plainly seeks such persons here when he specifies them in saying, “whom you know.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. [Col. 0869B] On the fact that Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses; and on the tale written concerning his Ethiopian wife.

(CH. 12.) “Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses because of his Ethiopian wife, and said: ‘Has the Lord spoken through Moses alone? Has he not spoken through us as well?’ When the Lord heard this, he was angry.”

“Because of his Ethiopian wife,” it says. Jewish writers have handed down the following tale on the occasion of this expression. Moses, the adopted son of Thesmuth, daughter of the king of Egypt, threw to the ground and broke the royal crown which she herself had placed upon his head. Egyptian seers had foretold that this was a sign that the Egyptian kingdom would be destroyed through him. Pharaoh, seeking to forestall this event, ordered without delay that the man who seemed destined to be the ruin of his kingdom should be killed. But, by his daughter’s favorable intervention, Moses was rescued from death and returned unharmed to his own people.

After many years, when the Ethiopians attacked Egypt and were nearly overcoming it, while the Egyptians were succumbing, diviners declared that Egypt would be subdued by Ethiopia unless its army, supported by an Israelite commander, went out to restrain the hostile assaults; through him alone, they said, common victory could truly be expected. Immediately, by divine providence, Moses was chosen by Pharaoh for this danger—so that, if perhaps he did not strike down the enemies, he himself might at least perish by the enemies. But God ordered things otherwise than Pharaoh hoped, for he foresaw Moses both as conqueror of the Ethiopians and as the fulfillment of the prophecy once foreshadowed in the breaking of the royal crown.

Moses therefore girded himself for war; a large body of soldiers was enrolled, and he advanced with hope of victory. But Pharaoh awaited his return at the risk of his own ruin and Egypt’s disgrace. They came to the walls of the enemy cities. The strength which God supplies to his own man—at that time an Egyptian officer, but afterward to become his soldier—attacked the enemies courageously, broke those charging against him, crushed them, and weakened all their strength, hitherto unbroken. He no longer sought a bloody victory with the loss of his own soldiers, but won a noble palm with glory and the safety of his men.

To crown his praise, he joined to himself in marriage the daughter of the Ethiopian king, first because she sought him on account of the grace of his beauty, then because he loved her on account of the alliance of the two kingdoms, which was more fully established by the union of so unexpected a marriage. Thus he returned to Pharaoh, bringing back not only a triumph but also a united disposition toward peace and concord. Yet Pharaoh would have preferred to triumph with a double joy if, after the enemy’s defeat, the victorious Moses had happened to die.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On his Ethiopian wife; how Moses, because he was a very meek man, made God his defender chiefly by keeping silence; and on the words, “But my servant Moses is not such a one.”

But this tale is readily despised because it has no authority from the Scriptures. Nor is there any need to seek outside the present Scripture why those who spoke against him called his wife Ethiopian. For since Moses had married the daughter of Jethro, priest of Midian (Exod. 2), and the land of Midian lies near the land of the Ethiopians, it is rightly understood that, because they called her a Midianite wife, they called her an Ethiopian wife. Such is the bitterness of quarrelers: they always seize upon something from nearby in order to increase contempt.

A little earlier Jethro had brought her back (Exod. 18), and they began to be indignant against their brother and leader because he had a foreign wife. The slander might have been refuted by Moses’ authority alone: namely, that a superior ought not to be reproved by subjects, especially one through whom God spoke such great and manifest things. But carnal pride prevailed stubbornly in the opposite direction, and its onward force produced spiritual pride. For they said: “Has the Lord spoken through Moses alone? Has he not spoken through us as well?”

This was because, a little earlier, the multitude of prophets had increased: the seventy elders had received from Moses himself a prophetic spirit, when the Lord said to Moses: “I will take of your spirit and give it to them” (Num. 11). Therefore, because of the multitude of prophets, the one greatest prophet seemed to diminish and to become cheap in their eyes. This frequently happens in Christ’s Church: growing disciples dare contentiously to obscure their teacher; subjects, their illustrious superior; distinguished sons, their father.

Something similar had happened to the Apostle Paul when he said to the Corinthians: “You are already filled. You have already become rich. You reign without us—and would that you did reign, that we too might reign with you” (1 Cor. 4). And then: “I write these things not to shame you, but to warn you as my dearest children. For though you have ten thousand instructors in Christ, yet you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (ibid.).

Since this first happened to Moses, an example had to be established at the outset, which later generations might fear to follow. “When the Lord heard it,” he was angry. Why? “For Moses,” it says, “was a very meek man, above all the men who dwelt upon the earth.” This is a sweet praise, an exceedingly great praise, of an outstanding virtue. Any superior who possesses it may rightly say: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 2). It shows that God rightly was angry, or ought to have been angry, because Moses was not merely meek in some measure but was the meekest above all people dwelling on earth.

He did not defend himself at all; and by this means, as if by a lawful cause, he made God his defender all the more by silence. For “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deut. 32). Yet it is too little merely to say that he was very meek, for this praise was far inferior to Moses’ merit. Therefore the Lord supplied concerning Moses what Moses had said too little about himself. He says: “Hear my words. If there be any prophet of the Lord among you, I will appear to him in a vision, or speak to him in a dream. But my servant Moses is not such a one, who is most faithful in all my house. For I speak with him mouth to mouth, openly; and he sees the Lord, not through riddles. Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?”

A great commendation; a most powerful defense. The utterance of the Judge wished its hearers to be attentive: “Hear my words,” he says, using fitting gravity. Then he distinguishes the modes of his speech, saying: “If there be any prophet of the Lord among you,” etc. Since they had said, “Has the Lord spoken through Moses alone? Has he not spoken through us as well?” they ought to have known their measure, so that, recognizing the difference between lesser and greater, they would not exalt themselves above themselves. Even among equals, one must observe the command: “Outdoing one another in honor” (Rom. 12).

“I will appear to him in a vision,” he says, “or speak to him in a dream.” Dreams present images of future things; and, if they have a prudent interpreter, they are in some degree prophecies. First images or figures of future events are perceived; then, by conjecture, the events themselves are foreseen in part. Thus Joseph in Egypt interpreted Pharaoh’s dreams (Gen. 41); thus Daniel in Babylon first heard Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams and saw his own, and then, with the Spirit revealing, prophesied concerning future things by conjecture, not uncertainly.

“But my servant Moses,” he says, “is not such a one, who is most faithful in all my house.” He does not first see figures in a dream and then infer future things; or rather, conversely, he first beholds from afar the future realities themselves and then, as the occasion requires, covers and wraps them in figures and riddles. For it has often been said to him: “See and make according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25). Therefore he says: “For I speak to him mouth to mouth, and openly; he sees the Lord not through riddles.” It is as though he said: First he sees with a clear gaze the order of future realities; and although he writes riddles and figures, he himself inwardly holds the truth of the realities. “Why then were you not afraid to speak against my servant Moses?” This questioning, which convicts the guilty, is the expression of an angry mind, and it was immediately followed by a penal sentence.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That Moses, having an Ethiopian wife, signifies Christ having the Church from the Gentiles; but Miriam’s leprosy and separation signify the sins of the Synagogue that blasphemes Christ. [Col. 0872A]

“And he departed in anger from them. The cloud also withdrew, which had been over the tabernacle. And behold, Miriam was covered with white leprosy like snow,” etc.

For the allegorical sense, the matter must be repeated from above; then it will become clear what this prophetess, made bright by grace and spat upon by God because of guilt—that is, made leprous—signifies. Here Moses, having an Ethiopian wife, mystically signifies Christ the Lord, who did not despise the Church from among the Gentiles, once sinful. Aaron and Miriam—that is, the carnal priesthood of the Jews and all their old Synagogue—bear this with extreme pain. This, I say, they cannot bear; about this they murmur; and they endure great torment of envy, for they always hate the salvation of the Gentiles.

Unable to bear this, and having the eye of their heart darkened by this beam of envy, they burst out into hatred of the Lord Christ himself; and, because he condescends to the wretched, they fight against mercy itself. For they say: “Has God spoken through Moses alone?” that is, through Christ alone, your Moses? “Has he not spoken through us as well?” that is, through our prophets?

For our law has men of power who performed signs both on earth and in heaven: they divided the Red Sea and the River Jordan; they brought down manna from heaven; they made the sun stand still in heaven or even go backward. When they spoke these and similar things in malignant envy, the Lord was angry. It is clear, manifest, that the Lord was angry with the proud Synagogue and its carnal priesthood. The Lord Father, the Lord Son, the Lord Holy Spirit, was angry with that people. For behold, it was made leprous; it was covered all over with shining leprosy. The greatly angered Father spat in its face and threw upon its countenance the dung of its festivals (Mal. 2).

As its blasphemy was more wicked than the slander of Aaron and Miriam, and as this one was considered worthy of glory much greater than Moses, so the wound of that people—the leprosy of that Synagogue—is worse. For Moses was indeed faithful in all God’s house, as he says: “But my servant Moses is not such a one, who is most faithful in all my house”—faithful, I say, or “most faithful in the house of God,” not in his own house, as a servant, as a testimony to what was to be spoken. But Christ is as a Son in his own house, whose house we are.

Therefore whatever that leprous woman touches is unclean—unclean, I say, is whatever she handles, whatever she celebrates together; and it is hateful to God. She is separated at the judgment of the high priest who has entered the heavens, Christ Jesus. She has torn garments, an uncovered head, a mouth veiled by clothing; she cries aloud that she is contaminated and unclean—concerning all of which the law of the leper was discussed above.

For all the time that she is leprous and persists in this uncleanness of her unbelief, she shall dwell alone outside the camp: alone, I say, outside the true and heavenly camp; as though dead—indeed, truly dead—and like an untimely birth cast forth from its mother’s womb. “She was estranged from the womb; she went astray from the belly; she spoke falsehood” (Ps. 35 [36]); her faithful mother, the Church of patriarchs and prophets, did not teach her.

“But Moses cries to the Lord, saying: ‘O God, I beseech you, heal her.’” Indeed, all antiquity, all the faith of the ancient Fathers, intercedes for that people. But she will not be healed; she will not be recalled to the camp until seven days have passed—that is, until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in. “If her father,” he says, “had spat in her face, ought she not at least to have been ashamed for seven days?” Surely this is a true comparison.

For if any child had so exasperated and provoked to anger the father whom he ought to honor and cherish that the father, stirred up, spat in his face—the face of his child which, under nature’s guidance, he had been accustomed to cover with kisses—how could such a child, forgetting his father’s spittle because of his own insolence, fail to blush among his fellows for at least seven days? To whom can a person be precious who has been spat upon by his own father as something vile? “If therefore her father had spat in her face,” etc.

“But I,” he says, “am your Father, who say to Pharaoh: ‘Israel is my firstborn son; let my son go’” (Exod. 4); and behold, being in some sense exasperated, I spat in this one’s face when I covered all her flesh with most white leprosy, leprosy like snow—that is, most true leprosy. Let her therefore be separated for seven days, etc., as above.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. [Col. 0873C] On the spies who disparaged the land; and on the fact that this temptation was the chief reason why the bodies of nearly all who had been numbered were laid low in the wilderness.

(CH. 13.) “Israel set out from Hazeroth and pitched tents in the wilderness of Paran. There the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Send men to survey the land of Canaan, which I shall give you; one from each tribe, chosen from the leaders.’ Moses did as the Lord commanded,” etc.

The historical account is clear: the spies who were sent surveyed the land; proceeding to the brook of the cluster, they cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole. Returning after forty days, all except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh disparaged the land which they had inspected, saying: “The land which we have surveyed devours its inhabitants,” and immediately: “The people,” they say, “whom we saw are of lofty stature.”

This statement is plainly too contrary to the preceding one. Such is the habit of slanderers: while they strive to disparage, they sometimes say things contrary to themselves, caring nothing for the direction in which their words fall, provided that they overthrow their hearers’ hearts. At last, when the whole multitude cried out and wanted to crush with stones those who followed the Lord with another spirit, the Lord’s judgment was pronounced in this sentence: “As I live,” he says, “and the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of the Lord: nevertheless, all the men who saw my majesty and the signs which I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and tempted me now ten times, and did not obey my voice, shall not see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers” (Num. 14).

This tenth temptation, the worst of the other temptations, was the chief reason why none of all those who had been numbered from twenty years old and upward, except the two just mentioned, should enter that land of promise; rather, their bodies should be laid low in the wilderness.

Moreover, the Prophet—or rather, the Holy Spirit—in the Psalm, after saying, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Ps. 94 [95]), immediately added: “As in the provocation, according to the day of temptation in the wilderness, where your fathers tempted me, tested me, and saw my works. For forty years I was offended with that generation, and I said: ‘These always err in heart, and they have not known my ways’; so I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter into my rest’” (ibid.).

Using this testimony, the Apostle immediately adds: “Take heed, brothers, lest perhaps there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God. But exhort one another each day, while it is called ‘today,’ lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. For we have become partakers of Christ, provided that we hold firm to the end the beginning of his substance, while it is said: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as in that provocation.’ For some, when they heard, provoked him; but not all who went out from Egypt through Moses.
