But with whom was he offended for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose corpses were laid low in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter into his rest, except to those who were unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief” (Heb. 3).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Mystically, that we who read the Scriptures are spies of the land of the living; and that the cluster which two men carried on a pole is Christ, whom two peoples read in the Scriptures.

Let us therefore retain the well-known allegory of the present chapter for the instruction of holy, chaste fear, so that, according to the same Apostle, “we may fear lest, while the promise of entering into his rest remains, any one of us should be thought to have fallen short. For,” he says, “the good news was proclaimed to us also, as to them” (Heb. 4).

According to the testimonies already cited from the Psalmist and the Apostle, what does that land then surveyed in this way signify except the Lord’s rest? And what is this rest of the Lord—concerning which, again determining a certain day, he says in David, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts”—and finally concludes thus: “To whom I swore in my wrath: ‘They shall not enter into my rest’”? What, I ask, is this present rest of the Lord, having its appointed day after that seventh day on which the Lord rested from his works? It is surely the resurrection of the flesh, the resurrection of Christ, the glorious rest of the Lord.

We have been sent to survey this rest, this land of the living—all of us who hold the Holy Scriptures in our hands. First the Lord says to the Jews: “Search the Scriptures, because you think that in them you have life” (John 5); then the Evangelist says also concerning the apostles that “he then opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24). For those who understand the Scriptures may rightly sing this: “The Lord brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey, so that the law of the Lord might always be in your mouth.”

Therefore by reading and understanding we ascend and survey the most excellent land. We proceeded to the brook of the cluster; the branch was cut off with its cluster of grapes, and two men carry it upon a pole. For what is the brook of the cluster except the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ? Surely the bride says concerning him in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna in the vineyards of Engaddi” (Song 1). And concerning his passion it was said through the Prophet: “He shall drink from the brook on the way” (Ps. 109 [110]).

Thus, in surveying the land, we came to the brook of the cluster: by reading the prophets, we understood that Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. But how was the branch cut off with its cluster unless, by the iron of the passion, his soul was cut off and departed from the flesh with the sweetest divinity inherent in it? For concerning this branch it was thus foretold through the Prophet: “He was cut off from the land of the living” (Isa. 53).

Therefore two men carry the cut-off branch on a pole: that is, two peoples, believing and confessing that he rose from the dead, worship Christ who suffered and died upon the cross. Yet when two men carry a cut-off branch upon a pole, the one who goes ahead and carries it does not see it, while the one who follows always has it before his eyes. Thus indeed the earlier people, which preceded the blessed times of the Lord’s passion, did not see the sweetest cluster—that is, Christ—whom it carried by faith. But we who follow see and possess the present reality of salvation, of which they had hope alone.

Therefore it is said to us with the apostles: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke 10). We also brought from that place pomegranates and figs, because we understood that the deaths or persecutions suffered by the prophets were testimonies of Christ who was to suffer.

We surveyed this for forty days. For he who admitted us to survey the resurrection of the flesh presented himself alive to us by many proofs, appearing to the disciples for forty days and speaking concerning the kingdom of God (Acts 1). One of the spies says: “What was from the beginning, what we heard, what we saw with our eyes, and what our hands touched” (1 John 1).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That the spies who disparaged the land are mystically heretics, especially those who do not believe in the true resurrection of the flesh.

Therefore, all of us who are led by the Spirit of God say with Caleb: “Let us go up and take possession of the land, for we shall be able to obtain it.” Caleb is interpreted as “heart” or “dog.” And by his very name no less than by his faith he expresses the truth or witness of those who are like the heart of Christ the Lord, as it is written: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV). For if he who separates the precious from the vile—that is, truth from falsehood—is himself the mouth of the Lord, why should he not rightly be said to be, as it were, the heart of the Lord, since he possesses the Spirit of Christ?

He is also the Lord’s dog, as it is likewise written: “The tongue of your dogs [shall have its portion] from your enemies” (Ps. LXVII), that is, the apostles are witnesses drawn from the Jews who hate you. Thus Caleb—that is, every witness of truth—preaches faithfully and cries out confidently: “Let us go up and take possession of the land,” that is, let us believe that Christ rose from the dead, and, believing, attain the glory of that resurrection.

But the others—the others, I say, who were with us—namely the heretical antichrists, who “went out from us, but were not of us” (I John II), disparage the land which they inspected. They deny faith in the resurrection, or try to weaken the truth of the flesh in which we are to rise. “The land,” they say, “which we surveyed devours its inhabitants.” What else do heretics assert when they say that the true substance of flesh will not rise? Surely, if the same flesh does not rise, if it is to be subtler than winds and air, then the land of the living which we await devours its inhabitants.

But immediately they make contradictory statements about themselves: “The people whom we saw are of very great stature” [Col. 0876C]. For heretics are divided against themselves concerning this very matter: while some deny that true flesh will rise, others, on the contrary, expect there also sexual intercourse and the procreation of children. Thus they are opposed to one another: the former do not hope for the very substance itself, while the latter expect an excessive corporeality of that same substance.

[Chapter XIV.] “But Joshua the son of Nun,” or Jesus Nave, which is interpreted “Saviour,” son of beauty, “and Caleb”—whose name has already been interpreted above—Joshua, I say, and Caleb, that is, Christ the Saviour and his apostles, together with all who profess the catholic faith, “tore their garments,” that is, they rejected from their fellowship the blasphemies of such persons. “And they spoke to the whole multitude of the children of Israel: The land which we surveyed is exceedingly good,” etc.

Why say more? “When all the multitude cried out and wished to overwhelm them with stones, the glory of the Lord appeared over the tent of the covenant,” and, declaring a fitting punishment, said: “Your corpses shall lie in the wilderness; your children shall wander in the desert for forty years, and they shall bear your fornication, until the corpses of your fathers are consumed in the desert. According to the number of the forty days in which you considered the land, a year shall be reckoned for each day, and for forty years you shall bear your iniquities.”

This example has been established for all heretics and unbelievers. “Let us therefore see,” as the apostle mentioned above says, “lest perhaps there be in any of us an evil heart of unbelief” [Col. 0877A] (Heb. III). For truly, just as those disparagers received a year for a day, so all heretics together with unbelieving Jews shall receive everlasting destruction for the guilt of temporal blasphemy.

And at that time, when the Lord said, “How long will they not believe me, despite all the signs which I performed before them? Therefore I shall strike them with pestilence and consume them”—when, I say, the Lord spoke these words—“Moses prayed, saying: Forgive, I beseech you, the sin of this people according to the greatness of your mercy.” But now he accuses both them and all heretics. For as Truth says to the Jews: “There is one who accuses you—Moses, in whom you hope” (John V), so the Church, the pillar of truth (I Tim. III), says to all heretics: There are those who accuse you: the Law and the Prophets, the Gospel and all the apostolic writings, from whose knowledge you presume.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. An enumeration of the ten temptations, concerning which he says: “And they have now tempted me ten times.”

“And they have now tempted me ten times,” he says. Let us briefly enumerate those temptations here.

Of the first temptation, Exodus reads as follows: “The people disputed with Moses and said: Give us water to drink. Moses answered them: Why do you dispute with me? Why do you tempt the Lord?” (Exod. XVII).

Of the second temptation, the Book of Numbers writes: “When the people lacked water,” etc. [Col. 0877C], up to the place where it says: “This is the water of contradiction; there the children of Israel disputed against the Lord, and he was sanctified in them” (Num. XX).

The third temptation occurred on the plain by the Red Sea. There they are said to have murmured against the Lord, because they did not believe Moses when he told them, on the Lord’s word, that the Egyptians had been destroyed; rather, they feared that the Egyptians would pursue them (Exod. XIV). Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Our fathers in Egypt did not understand your wonders; they were not mindful of your mercy, and they provoked you to anger at the Red Sea” (Ps. CV).

The fourth and fifth temptations arose over the manna. One temptation concerned the manna itself, as Exodus says: “This is the word which the Lord has commanded: Let each person gather from it as much as is sufficient for eating” [Col. 0877D] (Exod. XVI). And shortly afterward Moses said to them: “Let no one leave any of it until morning.” “But they did not heed him, and left some of it until morning” (ibid.).

The other temptation is that of which the same book says shortly afterward: “For six days it shall be gathered, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord; therefore it shall not be found. The seventh day came, and some of the people went out to gather it, but did not find it. And the Lord said to Moses: How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my law?” (ibid.).

The sixth and seventh temptations took place at the Graves of Craving: namely, the temptation concerning meat, which also includes the first temptation concerning meat. Of this Exodus says: “Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel: In the evening you shall know that the Lord has brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see his glory. For he has heard your murmuring against the Lord” [Col. 0878A] (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God. Therefore it came to pass in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp” (ibid.).

Of the seventh, Numbers says here: “Meanwhile a murmuring of the people arose, as of persons grieving over their toil, against the Lord. When the Lord heard it, he was angry; and the fire of the Lord was kindled among them and devoured the outer part of the camp” (Num. XI). And shortly afterward: “Sanctify yourselves; tomorrow you shall eat meat. For I heard you saying: Who will give us food of meat? It was well with us in Egypt” [Col. 0878B] (ibid.), etc.

The eighth temptation was the golden calf, which the children of Israel made for themselves in the wilderness while Moses delayed with the Lord on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXXII).

The ninth temptation occurred here in the wilderness of Paran, which is itself called Barne, concerning the spies: “How long,” he says, “will this people disparage me? How long will they not believe me despite all the signs which I have done before them?” And shortly after: “According to the number of the forty days in which you considered the land, for forty years you shall bear your iniquities.”

The tenth temptation consisted in this: “When Moses had spoken all the words of the Lord to all the children of Israel, the people mourned greatly. And behold, rising early in the morning, they went up to the summit of the mountain and said: We are ready to go up to the place of which the Lord spoke, because we have sinned. Moses said to them: Why do you transgress the word of the Lord? It will not turn out prosperously for you. Do not go up, for the Lord is not with you.” Again, shortly afterward: “But they, darkened in mind, went up to the summit of the mountain. Yet the ark of the covenant of the Lord and Moses did not depart from the camp” [Col. 0878C].

## CHAPTER XL. That the armed children of Israel went up while the ark of the Lord remained behind, and that in this too they were a type of heretics.

Let us now return to the sequence. After Moses had spoken to the children of Israel all the words of the Lord, saying: “Your corpses shall lie in the wilderness; your children shall wander in the desert for forty years,” they, as has already been said, went up to the summit of the mountain, while the ark of the Lord and Moses did not depart from the camp. “Then the Amalekite and the Canaanite, who lived in the mountain, came down; and striking and cutting them down, pursued them as far as Horma.”

This mountain in which the Amalekite and Canaanite are said to dwell is understood to be Mount Seir, as Deuteronomy says [p. 304]: “Therefore the Amorite, who dwelt in the mountains, came out and met you, pursued you as bees are accustomed to pursue, and struck you down from Seir as far as Horma” (Deut. I).

Amalekite is interpreted “a people that licks,” Canaanite “possessing,” Seir “hairy,” and Horma “anathema.” By these names are understood evil spirits, who, as far as Horma—that is, down to the depth of hell, which is an everlasting anathema—pursue, cutting down like conquerors, all the aforesaid disparagers of the holy land, all heretics. For the ark of the Lord’s covenant is not with them [Col. 0880A]; the law of the Lord, the law of truth, is not with them. Therefore whatever weapons they seize as though they were weapons of the word of God will not profit them. Nor does it avail them to have said, “We have sinned,” since they have by no means been reconciled to the catholic Church through worthy fruits of repentance.

# SECOND BOOK ON NUMBERS  
(Num., chapters XV–XXXIV)

[Col. 0879]

## CHAPTER I. On the saying: “The soul that has committed anything through pride shall perish from among its people.”

[Chapter XV.] “If through ignorance you pass over any of these things which the Lord spoke to Moses and commanded through him, from the day when he began to command and thereafter, and if the multitude has forgotten to perform them, it shall offer a bull from the herd, a most sweet-smelling holocaust to the Lord, with its sacrifice and libations as the ritual requires, and a goat for sin,” etc.

Here, by a fitting recapitulation, the law of sacrifices, of which fuller account was given in Leviticus, is recalled; and something is added which must be observed with the greatest diligence and utmost caution. “The soul,” he says, “which has committed anything through pride, whether he be a citizen or a stranger, since he has been rebellious against the Lord, shall perish from among his people. For he despised the word of the Lord and made void his commandment; therefore he shall be destroyed and shall bear his iniquity.”

The Prophets and the Gospel follow this law of justice. The Prophets, when Amos says: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four; for three crimes of Gaza, and for four; for three crimes of Tyre, and for four, I will not turn him back” [Col. 0879C] (Amos I). The first crime is to conceive iniquity in the mind. The second crime is to bring forth sorrow in deed. The third is to draw the work of iniquity into practice or habit. The fourth crime is to defend evil deeds through the spirit of pride. Therefore, “for four,” he says, “I will not turn him back”: that is, when the answer has been made proudly, the sin is no longer remissible.

As stated above, the Gospel confirms this when the Saviour says that there is a sin which is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come: namely, blasphemy against the Spirit, or a word against the Holy Spirit (Matt. XII). This is nothing other than the evil of pride, by which someone, defending himself against his own conscience as it convicts him of sin, crushes the Holy Spirit.

John also speaks of this in his Epistle: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (I John V). Eli also says to his sons: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased for him; but if a man sins against the Lord, who shall pray for him?” (I Kings I).

For this reason it should also be noted that our Lord is recorded to have raised only three dead persons: one lying in a house (Matt. IX), another being carried out through the gate of the city (Luke VII), and a third, four days dead and stinking, from the tomb (John XI) [Col. 0880B]. He is not recorded to have raised a fourth, for the same reason that it had already been said in the prophet: “For three crimes, and for four, I will not turn him back.”

## CHAPTER II. On the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath day: that he sinned through pride; and on Korah, Dathan, and Abiram: that their deaths are examples showing that the soul which sins through pride perishes.

By a fitting recapitulation, I say, the law of sacrifices has now been recalled; and immediately it is taught that the sin of pride has no sacrifice. At once it is added: “It came to pass, when the children of Israel were in the wilderness and found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day, that they brought him to Moses and Aaron and to the whole multitude. They confined him in prison, not knowing what they ought to do with him. And the Lord said to Moses: This man shall surely die.”

And afterwards: [Chapter XVI.] “Behold, Korah, son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On, son of Peleth, of the sons of Reuben, rose up against Moses, together with two hundred and fifty other children of Israel, men of rank in the assembly, who were called by name at the appointed time of counsel. When they had stood against Moses and Aaron, they said: Let it be enough for you, for the whole multitude is holy, and the Lord is among them” [Col. 0880D].

Therefore, with these examples immediately following, he says: “The soul which has committed anything through pride shall perish from among its people” (Num. XV), whether what it has committed, in which it has been rebellious against the Lord, is small or great. For although what Korah committed was great, and Dathan and Abiram were rebellious in it—since they shattered unity by saying, “We will not come, we will not come”—yet gathering wood was a small matter or deed. Nevertheless, he who offended by gathering wood on the Sabbath day is told: “He shall surely die; let all the people overwhelm him with stones.”

Clearly, this was because he did what seemed a small thing through pride: because he despised the word of the Lord, because he scorned the law of the Sabbath—indeed, the lawgiver himself—in his Sabbath. Therefore he had to die. God considered not what or how great the deed was, but with what mind he had done it. Thus the soul which commits anything through pride, whether it be great or small, shall surely perish.

Meanwhile, the just distribution of punishments in pride itself must be noted. Dathan and Abiram, who when summoned said mockingly, “We will not come, we will not come,” did not die the ordinary death of men. Rather, the Lord performed a new thing: the earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, and they went down alive into hell. But Korah and the assembly of two hundred and fifty men who followed him—who did not, like the others, say, “We will not come”—were indeed punished by heavenly wrath for the same pride; yet they were not swallowed up by the earth, a most extraordinary event, but were consumed by fire [Col. 0881B]. The man found gathering wood, whose contempt or pride did not rise so far as theirs, died a more ordinary human death: he was killed by men and stoned by all the people.

## CHAPTER III. By what right Moses said, “Do not regard their sacrifices,” and afterwards, “When one man sins, will your wrath rage against all?”

“Do not,” he says, “regard their sacrifices.” And afterwards: “O most mighty God of the spirits of all flesh, when one man sins, will your wrath rage against all?” Therefore one may now most truly say of these men that they are the two olive trees and the two lampstands shining before the Lord, ruler of the whole earth, and that they have power to shut heaven and open its gates (Rev. XI), because their tongues have become keys of heaven.

For those who say, “Do not regard their sacrifices,” shut not only heaven but even the eyes of the Lord himself. Again, when, by saying, “O most mighty God of the spirits of all flesh,” etc., they turn wrath away from the people, they are surely using their tongues as keys of heaven, so as to shut heaven against the proud but open it to the meek.

Yet it is not will that effects this power, but the cause. Where the cause of pride provokes wrath and exults in its own mockeries, saying, “Truly you have brought us into a land flowing with streams of milk and honey; you have given us possessions of fields and vineyards. Do you also wish to put out our eyes? We will not come”—there the man of whom it was said above, “Moses was a man most meek above all men who dwelt on earth” [Col. 0881D] (Num. XII), there, I say, this most meek man becomes very angry and speaks almost imperiously to the Lord: “Do not regard their sacrifices.”

He is angry, I say, not in his own spirit but in the Spirit of him to whom the Psalmist speaks: “You are terrible, and who shall resist you? From that moment, your wrath” (Ps. LXXV). Surely, from the moment God is resisted, from that moment God is terribly angry. And everyone who is truly meek, whose indweller is God, is angry wherever the evil of pride arises. There he uses the harsh sword of anathema: he separates from God the person already separated, to deliver him to the devil.

But where, with the aforesaid keys—the keys of heaven—they have opened by their tongues the gates of heaven in order that wrath may rain down, they do not forget mercy even amid that wrath. Falling prostrate upon their faces, they say: “O most mighty God of the spirits of all flesh, when one man sins, will your wrath rage against all?” In both respects they are strong; in both effective. Those whom they gave over, God was angry with; from those whom they forbade, present wrath was removed [Col. 0882A].

## CHAPTER IV. What mystery is contained in the fact that the evil of pride was restrained by the rod that budded.

[Chapter XVII.] By what means, at last, was the evil of pride eradicated and the complaints of the children of Israel restrained by the Lord? He says: “Speak to the children of Israel, and take from them individual rods according to their clans, from all the leaders of the children of Israel, twelve rods of the tribes; and you shall write the name of each one upon his rod. But Aaron’s name shall be on the rod of Levi. And one rod shall contain all the families separately. You shall place them in the tent of the covenant before the testimony, where I shall speak to you. The rod of the one whom I choose shall bud,” etc.

Most beautifully and most mercifully, the most mighty God, after avenging the evil of pride, as though he had laid aside the weapons of his power, employs a budding rod against the swelling pride and complaints of the children of Israel. By the rod’s budding, its buds swelling into flowers and bursting forth into fruit, he thereafter teaches them not to be proud.

What does this most beautiful order foreshadow, except that the humility of Christ, the Son of God, had to be set against the pride of the devil? Isaiah the prophet knew this when he said: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my wrath, and the staff itself: my indignation is in his hand” [Col. 0882C] (Isa. X); and afterwards: “I shall visit upon the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria, and upon the glory of the loftiness of his eyes” (ibid.). After saying these and other things enigmatically concerning the devil’s pride, he added and said concerning Christ’s humility:

“A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him. He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor hear according to the hearing of his ears; but he shall judge the poor in righteousness, and reprove with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth. He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips shall kill the wicked” (Isa. XI).

Thus according to the letter a true history is set forth; but according to the Spirit it is a recapitulation of mysteries, like the seven sections which we read in the Apocalypse of John. For what is that rod, which here neither planted nor watered buds, flowers, and produces fruit, and which, in the prophet just cited, comes forth from the root of Jesse and produces a flower upon which the sevenfold Spirit of the Lord rests? What, I ask, is this rod except the royal Virgin of Davidic stock, who, according to the faith of the Gospel, brought forth for us Christ without male seed: the true flower and the true glory of humankind, “in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” [Col. 0882D] (Col. II)?

In that rod the old stock of Eve flourished anew in beautiful newness; in the flower which she bore, the woodland of our flesh blossomed again; in that nut, crushed or broken by the wood of the cross, our soul found the kernel of life. Our hungry soul, I say, was fed from it and received life.

That rod indeed then settled the dispute and removed the complaints of the children of Israel, who murmured against Moses and Aaron, as though he had acquired the priesthood more by fraternal affection than by heavenly appointment. But this royal rod, this flower of virginity, this fruit of a virginal womb restrained Jewish pride, striking the nation down and casting down the glory of the handmade temple; and it made manifest that God’s concern is not a carnal but a spiritual priesthood, because Christ alone is priest forever—not according to the slaughter of bulls or goats, but according to the order of Melchizedek [Col. 0883B] (Ps. CIX).

## CHAPTER V. On the saying, “You and your sons shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary”: that this burden signifies Christ’s priesthood, by which he bore upon himself the sins of the world.

[Chapter XVIII.] “Therefore the Lord immediately continues, saying to Aaron: You and your sons and your father’s house with you shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary.” And again: “You and your sons together shall bear the sin of your priesthood.” And then a third time: “But you and your sons shall minister in the tent of testimony. The Levites shall keep watch according to your commands and over all the works of the tent,” etc.

The threefold repetition of the divine appointment or ordinance is a strong confirmation. As the mystery of the incarnation of Christ, Son of God, was signified in the rod flowering and bearing fruit, so in the order or office of him who bears the iniquity of the sanctuary and sustains the sins of his priesthood is mystically signified the burden or work of the same Christ, the true priest, upon whom the Lord laid the iniquities of us all, as the prophet foretold [Col. 0883C] (Isa. LIII).

What religious discipline or distinction Levites and priests ought to observe in ministry; what and what kind of offerings they should receive from the people; what discipline a victim ought to have—these things the sacred law recalls here in recapitulation. For it had already spoken more fully of them above; and therefore, omitting them here, let us proceed to other matters.

For the unblemished red heifer of full age, which has borne no yoke and is led out to be immolated—or rather burned—outside the camp, signifies here no different thing than the unblemished calf in Leviticus, which is to be offered by the same rite. Except that here the female sex signifies Christ’s maternal love, by which, becoming obedient to the Father for us, he brought forth our salvation in his distress [Col. 0883D].

## CHAPTER VI. Mystically, on expiating the touch of a human corpse, and on the saying: “If he is not sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh.”

[Chapter XIX.] “Whoever touches the corpse of a human being and is unclean on that account for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days, and so shall be cleansed. If he has not been sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh” [Col. 0884A].

This sprinkling is a shadow or figure; Christ’s sacrament is the reality and truth. For the Apostle says: “If the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself unblemished to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God?” (Heb. IX).

Therefore, the water and ashes of the heifer which are sprinkled here are the same as the blood of the calf in Leviticus: namely, the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. The touch of a dead human body signifies dead works, from which he cleansed us. For we touch a human corpse as often as we fall into a sin for which it is expedient that we be purified by the water of expiation—that is, whenever we incur a sin which must be redeemed by confession and the satisfaction of repentance.

But “if he has not been sprinkled on the third day,” he says, “he cannot be cleansed on the seventh.” This means: unless the baptized person holds the catholic faith in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he cannot be justified by any confession of sins or strictness of repentance, nor can he obtain the grace of the sevenfold Holy Spirit [Col. 0884B].

It should be noted, however, that he did not say: Everyone who touches a human corpse shall on that account be unclean for seven days. For a person is not unclean for so long no matter how or wherever he touches a human corpse. A little further down he defines it thus: “If anyone in a field touches the corpse of a slain person, or of one who died naturally, or his bone, or a tomb, he shall be unclean for seven days.”

The man who sprinkles a person from the ashes of burning and sin with living waters must distinguish this with the greatest care: whether the person touched the corpse in a field, where there is an open place of escape, or within the confined walls of a city. That is, the man who enjoins repentance upon one confessing must most carefully distinguish whether the person who did dead works, or consented to dead works, sinned voluntarily or was overtaken by some necessity and could not avoid sin. For according to the degrees of necessity or voluntary choice, he must weigh the burdens of repentance which he is to impose.

What then does it mean that the very person who carries the ashes or “sprinkles the waters” is unclean, and therefore “shall wash his garments”? Clearly, one who has undertaken the care of another’s sins shall by no means live with a clean or secure conscience unless he takes upon himself in part the burdens of the repentance which he enjoins, as the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and thus fulfill the law of Christ” [Col. 0884D] (Gal. VI).

Because of this share in uncleanness, the bride in the Song of Songs, excessively and more than rightly anxious, says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Cant. V).

Therefore, “everyone who touches the waters of expiation,” that is, whoever, having received another’s confession of sin, suggests remedies of repentance, “shall be unclean until evening”: that is, until by praying for one another he brings to perfection the love which covers a multitude of sins (I Pet. IV).

What does he mean when he meanwhile says, “A vessel which has no cover or binding over it shall be unclean”? What does he intend by this saying in such a matter, except that you ought to reveal the hidden cause of your sin to such an elder as knows both how to tend his own wounds and not to disclose or reveal another’s? For one who does not know how to keep a secret is a vessel “without a cover or binding over it,” and is unclean.

But in any matter whatsoever, anyone who is incontinent of mouth or tongue is unclean, “like a vessel having no cover or binding over it.” And wherever uncleanness has been contracted, unless it is sprinkled with the water of expiation, as has already been said, its filth shall remain upon him.

The greatest caution must be exercised lest an unclean person touch a clean one, because “whatever an unclean person touches,” he says, “he shall make unclean”—“for evil conversations corrupt good morals” [Col. 0885B] (I Cor. XV). And the prudent steward of God’s house must also take care that no one who is unclean be joined to another in any fellowship, not even in conversation. For “the soul,” he says, “which touches any of these things shall be unclean until evening,” that is, until fitting satisfaction and amendment.

## CHAPTER VII. On the temptation and dispute over water, and on Moses’ saying, “Can we bring water out of this rock?”—that in this unbelief he bore the type of the Jews and Pharisees.

[Chapter XX.] “When the people lacked water, they assembled against Moses and Aaron, and, turning to sedition, said: Would that we had perished with our brothers before the Lord! Why have you brought the Church of the Lord into the wilderness, so that both we and our beasts may die?” etc.

After many wanderings they came to the wilderness of Zin. Scripture says that this is the same as Kadesh. The event is well known: they “provoked the Lord at the waters of Contradiction” [Col. 0885C] (Ps. CV), testing and murmuring according to their custom; “and Moses was distressed because of them, because they embittered his spirit and he spoke rashly with his lips” (ibid.).

He spoke very rashly—very differently and far otherwise than he was accustomed to speak. “Listen,” he says, “you rebels and unbelievers: can we bring water out of this rock for you?” He was not accustomed to speak this way, for example when he divided the sea, or rather when he scourged Egypt with so many plagues. He did not say: Can we bring frogs out of the rivers? Can we send down hail with fire from heaven? Can we divide the Red Sea into divisions?

Here his spirit was embittered; he almost lost faith, and so he spoke rashly with his lips. Hence he immediately receives the sentence: “Because you did not believe me,” says the Lord, “so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these peoples into the land which I shall give them.”

Now that the rock was Christ in mystery or figure, the whole world has long sung together with the Apostle of Christ (I Cor. X). A little earlier, in the rod which flowered and produced the nut, we beheld his most holy incarnation; in this struck rock we understand the saving passion of the same Christ.

Moses, striker of the rock and unbelieving in this place—Moses, I say, and Aaron, unbelieving in this place—were likewise, in mystery or figure, the scribes and Pharisees. The thirsty people were the crowd eagerly listening to the Lord Jesus; hence those men, angered, said: “But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed” [Col. 0886A] (John VII).

“Can we bring water out of this rock for you?” Imagine that the scribes and Pharisees said of that rock, Christ himself: Can you hope to drink sound teaching from this deceiver? Again: “He has a demon and is mad; why do you listen to him?” (John X).

Thus they spoke rashly with their lips (Ps. CV), that is, they spoke against their own conscience. For they knew, for example, that he cast out demons by the Spirit of God, yet by the most wicked rashness of their lips they said: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons” (Matt. XII). In this unbelieving and turbulent fury they struck the rock of righteousness.

They struck twice, for with the two pieces of wood of one cross they crucified Christ: with their tongues and with the hands of the Gentiles. When this was done, “waters came forth in great abundance.” Nothing is truer: when Christ suffered, the waters of the Scriptures flowed forth and the torrents of the graces of the Holy Spirit overflowed. Previously the Scriptures were indeed read, but they were not understood; the killing letter was read, but the living and saving water of the life-giving Spirit did not flow.

Likewise, the Spirit had previously been given to some, but had not been given for the remission of sins. “For the Spirit,” says the Evangelist, “had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” [Col. 0886B] (John VII). It had therefore been given in diverse distributions of graces—for example, in prophecy, which even evil persons may possess—but not, as stated above, for reconciliation or remission of sins.

“Because you did not believe me,” he says, “so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these peoples into the land which I shall give them.” “You shall not bring them in,” I say. This is too little for the mystery. Indeed, you yourselves shall not enter. For in these persons, namely the scribes and Pharisees, we especially understand the sentence of that oath: “To whom I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. XCIV).

“Woe therefore to you, scribes and Pharisees and lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge: you yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those entering” (Luke XI). “You shall not enter into the rest of the Lord.” Rather, while you stand outside and remain idle, the office of bringing others in shall be entrusted to others.

“This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel disputed against the Lord, and he was sanctified in them” [Col. 0886D]. “This,” he says, “is the water of contradiction.” The Jews contradict; heretics contradict the water which flowed from the Lord’s side in rivers of living water, whatever streams from the belly of one who believes in him (John VII). Yet amid those very contradictions, the Holy of Holies was sanctified in them, was glorified in them; for from that very contradiction he ascended more glorious.

## CHAPTER VIII. Who, mystically, is the one who, after the flowering rod and the water brought forth from the rock, does not permit Israel to pass through.

“Moses meanwhile sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, to say: ‘Thus says your brother Israel: [Col. 0887A] You know all the hardship that has befallen us: how our fathers went down into Egypt and dwelt there for a long time; how the Egyptians afflicted us and our fathers; and how we cried to the Lord, and he heard us and sent an angel who brought us out of Egypt. Behold, we are stationed in the city of Kadesh, which is on the farthest edge of your territory. We beg you, allow us to pass through your land,’” etc.

Let us not linger over the obvious literal sense, but pursue the order of the mysteries. Who is this Edom who, after the flowering and fruit-bearing rod, after water was brought forth from the rock, answers the messengers’ request, “We beg you, allow us to pass through your land,” with: “You shall not pass,” he says, “you shall not pass; otherwise I shall meet you armed,” and immediately goes out “to meet them with an innumerable [Col. 0887B] multitude and a strong hand”? Who, I ask, according to the mystery, is this Edom? Surely he is the one against whom the prophetic complaint resounds: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation’” (Ps. 136 [137]). He is Israel in name and flesh, but Edom in reality and conduct: he who, for the red cooking—for the blood of Christ, that he might be sated with it—sold his birthright. His were the fathers, the covenant, the legislation, the worship, and the promises (Rom. 9); yet Jacob, that is, Christ’s evangelical Church, supplanted him in all these things.

To this Edom the Lord’s messengers spoke: evangelical messengers, bearing peace with beautiful feet (Isa. 52), who were the first to drink the water flowing from the aforesaid rock: “We beg you, allow us [Col. 0887C] to pass through your land”—to pass through the land of Judaea, to preach the evangelical grace in your synagogues, in your temple, around your houses. “You shall not pass through me,” he says. Moreover, he said this and, after having them beaten, charged them not to pass through him, not to speak in the name of Jesus to anyone (Acts 5). Thus he met them armed, he who gave this charge after having them beaten.

By contrast they say: “We will travel by the beaten road,” that is, we shall hold to an ancient and well-known teaching. For the beaten road is the Gospel: beaten by the faith of the patriarchs, beaten by the testimonies of the Law and the prophets. Therefore, by saying nothing new and teaching nothing not established by the authority of the Scriptures, we shall travel by the beaten road. “If,” they say, “we drink your waters,” [Col. 0887D] that is, if in preaching the Gospel we receive a modest livelihood, what great thing is this? “We will pay what is just.” Reaping material things, we shall sow spiritual things (1 Cor. 9). This, indeed, is just; for “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. 5).

That Edom persisted in saying: You shall not pass; you shall not preach the Gospel here. “Moreover, he went out to meet them with an innumerable multitude and a strong hand.” For he killed some, flogged others, stoned others, and persecuted them from city to city (Matt. 25 [probably 23:34]). Therefore Israel turned aside from him. And they said: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

## CHAPTER IX. [Col. 0888A] On the death of Aaron, and how it mystically signifies that the Jewish priesthood was to have an end.

“And when they had moved camp from Kadesh, they came to Mount Hor, which is on the borders of the land of Edom. There the Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Let Aaron,’ he says, ‘go to his people. For he shall not enter the land which I gave to the children of Israel, because he was unbelieving toward my word at the waters of contradiction.’”

Although Aaron could at times signify Christ, the great priest, by his name and office, yet by dying he cannot possibly be worthy to signify him who remains forever, who has an everlasting priesthood (Heb. 7), especially since the reason for his earlier death was that he was unbelieving [Col. 0888B] toward the word of the Lord at the waters of contradiction. Therefore, by dying because of his sin, he signifies the downfall of that priesthood whose ministers died in their sin: the Jewish priesthood, the carnal and shadowy priesthood.

But the death of Miriam, mentioned a little earlier, with no preceding or prescribed cause of sin, prefigures the end of legal observance, which was to pass away not because of the evil of error but because of the pre-eminence of a better grace. “Take,” says the Lord, “Aaron and his son with him, and lead them up Mount Hor.” Hor is interpreted “light.” Aaron therefore dies on Mount Hor. For it was to come about that, through the manifestation of truth, the shadowy priesthood of the Jews would be destroyed.

Sound and strong, he goes to death on his own feet; for the priests [Col. 0888C] of the Jews, while they consider themselves sound and righteous, die in their sin. Hence they are observed to be severely denounced in the Psalm, Christ speaking in person: “And the strong rushed upon me” (Ps. 58 [59]), like madmen striking the physician while thinking themselves healthy. He is stripped of his garments in order to die; for their temple and every sanctuary were destroyed, lest the Jews should boast, even falsely, of the life-giving power of their priesthood. Aaron dies, as is written below, in the fortieth year after the children of Israel’s departure from Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, when he was one hundred and twenty-three years old.

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 0888D] How the Canaanite king Arad, who fought against Israel, signifies the devil; and how Israel’s binding itself by a vow in order to conquer signifies the devotion of preachers.

(CHAP. XXI.) “When the Canaanite king Arad, who lived to the south, heard that Israel had come by the way of the spies, he fought against him; and, gaining the victory, took captives from him. But Israel, binding itself to the Lord by a vow, said: ‘If you deliver this people into my hand, I will utterly destroy his cities,’” etc.

In the order of spiritual matters, these historical events proceed as follows. After Christ’s passion and glorification, and after the gift of the Spirit—which were signified by the struck rock and the waters flowing from it—Edom, that is, the earthly or bloodthirsty Jewish [Col. 0889A] people, forbade Israel to pass through its land and prohibited Christ’s apostles from preaching the new grace in its synagogues. Then the Canaanite king Arad heard—that is, the ruler or possessor of this world, the devil, mystically understood through the Canaanite king Arad, perceived it. For *Chananaeus* means “possessing,” and *Arad*, “descending”; and the devil is descending and flowing downward, while “possessing” means the ruler of this world (John 14). He heard, I say, and could not fail to know the grace of evangelical preaching “by the way of the spies,” that is, by the apostles’ urgency.

While that strong, armed one possessed the nations and reigned securely in long-standing peace in his own court (Luke 11)—not a lawful king, but a tyrant who had seized power—when he heard that salvation was going forth to the nations, he fought against [Col. 0889B] that spiritual Israel and, gaining victory, took captives from it. Thus he fought by the laws and arms of kings and emperors; he stirred up persecutions, issued edicts, and, tearing apart bodies whose souls he could not touch, carried them off as if they were spoil, violently stripping away those bodies, which were in a sense garments of the souls. In this way he prevailed for a time; but, conquering outwardly, he was defeated inwardly, and made his victors—the martyrs—more glorious.

But Israel, binding itself by a vow, said: “If you deliver this people into my hand, I will destroy his cities.” By binding itself with such a vow, that Israel declared that it fought not for itself but for God; and therefore “the Lord heard his voice and delivered the Canaanite.” So indeed our preachers, bearing peace to us with beautiful feet (Isa. 52), [Col. 0889C] proposed to seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2); and therefore the Lord granted their desire, his ear heard the preparations of their hearts (Ps. 10 [11]), so that they might conquer the Canaanite, cast the malignant possessor out of his ancient seats—the devil, ruler of this world, ruler of darkness (Eph. 6).

“He destroyed him, overthrowing his cities, and called the name of that place Hormah, that is, ‘anathema,’” or “devoted to destruction.” It should be noted that where that carnal Israel first wins by fighting, the cause that produces victory is the condemnation of covetousness. In the same way spiritual Israel conquers, and its warfare makes triumphant progress, when it proclaims the word of God chastely and with the sole intention of charity, and, contending lawfully for the heavenly crown, tramples vainglory beneath its feet. Such leaders—our preachers of Christ—conquered the world and drove that Canaanite, that is, the devil, out of his kingdom.

## CHAPTER XI. On the fiery serpents which the Lord sent among the people, and on the bronze serpent which Moses raised up.

“They set out also from Mount Hor, by the road leading to the Red Sea, in order to go around the land of Edom; and the people began to grow weary of the journey and labor.” And then: “Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people. Because of the bites and deaths of many, they came to Moses and said: ‘Pray that he may take away the serpents from us.’ Moses prayed for [Col. 0890A] the people, and the Lord spoke to him: ‘Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign.’”

The light of evangelical truth has revealed, in its own splendor, the hidden mystery of the present passage. For he said: “And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3). Before this, he had said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

Therefore this too was done as a figure of us, whom serpents truly bit: as many serpents as the many gods our fathers worshiped, as many vices as have ravaged both our souls and our bodies. Therefore those through whose ministry we have been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0890B] so that we may see the kingdom of God, themselves killed that spiritual Canaanite, as was said; and when they taught us to worship the sign of Christ’s cross—or rather Christ himself crucified—they set up, as it were, a bronze serpent as a sign. When, wounded, we look upon him, we are healed; for believing in him, we do not perish but have eternal life (ibid.).

The matter is brilliant and glorious; but because it is known to almost everyone and celebrated throughout the whole world, and because we are setting out on a long journey, let it suffice for the present that we have touched on it briefly.

## CHAPTER XII. On Moab, which is interpreted “from the father,” and how heretics are figured by it.

“And moving from there, they came to the torrent Zared. [Col. 0890C] Leaving it, they encamped opposite Arnon, which is in the wilderness and projects into the borders of the Amorite. For Arnon is the boundary of Moab, dividing the Moabites and the Amorites.”

In the manifest history, after the bronze serpent had been set up as a sign for those bitten by serpents to look upon and be healed, they finally come to the borders of Moab. This is because, after the sign of the Son of God had also been visibly lifted up throughout the world, so that faithful Israel, abandoning the idols of the nations, might worship this instead, the perversity of heretics arose in opposition to the faith.

Zared is interpreted “alien”; Arnon, “their curse”; Amorite, “bitter”; Moab, “from the father.” By these names the alienation, curse, and bitterness of heretics—who are from their father the devil—are rightly understood. Hence it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord: “As he did at the Red Sea, so he will do at the torrents of Arnon. The rocks of the torrents were bent down, so that they might rest in Arnon and lie down in the borders of the Moabites.”

No reasoning compels us to suppose that material books of the Wars of the Lord existed before this writing of Moses, who speaks these things. Nor do we know of any other wars of the Lord than those in which the word of the Lord fights, through faithful human beings, against every impiety. Therefore what is said is prophecy, which this Moses saw in the heavenly book with those same eyes by which he deserved, or was able, to see all heavenly things. According to the pattern shown to him on the mountain (Exod. 25), he spoke, did, and established these ordinances of ceremonies [Col. 0891A] by which the carnal people might serve in the handmade tabernacle. Thus it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord—that is, it is known and celebrated in the faith of evangelical truth, where the true and mighty wars of the Lord are read.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the torrents of Arnon: how they signify the eloquence of heretics; how what happened at the Red Sea takes place in them; and on Israel’s song concerning the well.

“As he did,” he says, “at the Red Sea, so he will do at the torrents of Arnon.” How did he act at the Red Sea? “The Lord,” it says, “looked down upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, destroyed their army, overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were carried into the depths” (Exod. 14).

The torrents of Arnon are the streams of eloquent heretics, mounting the chariot of pride and rolling words of sin against Christ and his holy catholic people. Thus it is foretold concerning them from the Book of the Wars of the Lord—from every book of catholic truth or divine authority—that, after the likeness of Pharaoh and his armies, they too will be overthrown and hurled into the depths of hell with the devil.

“The rocks of the torrents were bent down, so that they might rest in Aran and lie down in the borders of the Moabites.” Under the metaphorical designation of bent-down rocks, he expresses the fear of the trembling Moabites at the entrance of the children of Israel and their resting in Aran—that is, placing their hope in the diviner Balaam, whom they had brought from Aran—in order that they might lie down [Col. 0891C] in the borders of the Moabites, namely, when they had driven the children of Israel away from those same borders by Balaam’s curse.

“From that place the well appeared. Concerning it the Lord spoke to Moses: ‘Gather the people, and I will give them water.’ Then Israel sang this song: ‘Rise up, O well!’ They sang together: ‘The well which the princes dug, and the leaders of the multitude prepared, in the giver of the law and with their staffs.’”

According to the history, it was not a very great or song-worthy thing that “a well appeared from that place.” Greater things had appeared to them—for example, when water flowed from the struck rock—yet Israel then sang no song. Let us therefore investigate the mystery, which is truly worthy of a joyful song.

“The rocks of the torrents,” that is, the hearers or admirers of heretics, “were bent down, so that they might rest in Aran,” when kings or emperors themselves, forgetful alike of the Christian faith and their own dignity, submitted themselves to the blessings—or rather curses—of heretics, placing their hope in them as in Balaam, delighted by the elegance of their speech, which is signified by Aran. For Aran is interpreted “ornament.” And they lay down “in the borders of the Moabites,” that is, they adhered to the communion of those who are from their father the devil, together with its defense.

“From that place,” he says, “the well appeared.” Nothing is truer; nothing more certain. For indeed, stirred by the disputes of heretics, the princes and leaders of our faith, orthodox and catholic men, searched more deeply into the profound things of Scripture [Col. 0892A] and thus “dug and prepared the well of living water with their staffs.” Yet this was not “with their staffs” independently, but “in the giver of the law,” with their staffs—as the Apostle, having said, “I labored more abundantly than all of them” (1 Cor. 15), immediately added, “yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.).

The staffs of the leaders or princes of our multitude, with which they dug the well “in the giver of the law,” were their strong and persevering minds. By fighting against the blasphemies of heretics, the teachers of the Church opened the truth of the Scriptures to us “in the giver of the law,” that is, with God’s grace cooperating. “Rise up, O well!” they sang together, etc. Who sang together? Clearly those who held—and indeed still hold—the catholic faith; those who thirst for sound teaching and gladly drink living water: the whole spiritual Israel, all true Israelites in whom there is no deceit (John 1).

“Let the well rise up,” he says. To where or from where should it rise? Let it rise from its depths to the lips of those who thirst, to the mouths and hands of little children, so that they may easily drink the living water springing up into eternal life (John 4). And this took place, because the leaders and princes dug it; because, by faithfully expounding the sacred Scriptures, they made them intelligible to us.

From where did they receive this? “From the wilderness to Mathanah; from Mathanah to Nahaliel; from Nahaliel to Bamoth. Bamoth is a valley in the region of Moab, on the summit of Pisgah, which looks toward the wilderness.” These names of the camping places of the children of Israel are not merely literal; in the spirit of prophecy they signify the merits or progress of the aforesaid leaders and princes: Mathanah, “gift”; Nahaliel, “the ascent of my God”; Bamoth, “high places”; Pisgah, “much mouth,” or “the mouth of the beloved.”

“From the wilderness,” he says, “to Mathanah”: that is, from the perfect and good gift, descending from above from the Father of lights. These leaders ascended Nahaliel, that is, “the ascent of God,” first by the virtue of the active life, then to Bamoth, that is, to the lofty grace of the contemplative life. Thereafter “there is for them a valley in the region of Moab”—which is certainly literal—“on the summit of Pisgah”; but this is also true in the spirit. For they possess outstanding humility amid great and lofty wisdom or knowledge, with the copious and beloved eloquence of the “much mouth” or “mouth of the beloved,” [Col. 0892D] “which looks toward the wilderness”: that is, which fights with all diligence against the falsehood of the devil, the deserter.

## CHAPTER XIV. Why Israel begged Sihon, king of the Amorites, to permit passage through his land, although Israel was to possess the land of Canaan.

“But Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, saying: ‘I beg you, let me pass through your land. We shall not turn aside into fields or vineyards; we shall not drink water from wells. We shall travel by the royal road until we have passed through your borders.’ But he was unwilling to allow Israel to pass through his territory,” etc.

Setting aside for the moment what Moab was—which he will relate later—he now tells what Sihon, king of the Amorites, did and received. But how does Israel send messengers to this man, begging him to grant passage through his land? Why does Israel not invade his land by right of war, when it was to possess the land of Canaan, as God had promised its fathers? Was not the Amorite, like the Jebusite, a son of Canaan? Did not Israel conquer the Amorite who dwelt beyond the Jordan? Why then does Israel now send messengers near the Jordan to Sihon, king of the Amorites, begging that passage through his land be granted?

It is because this land of the Amorites had been the land of Moab. Moses says in Deuteronomy: “We came to the road leading to the wilderness of Moab. And the Lord said to me: ‘Do not fight against the Moabites or enter into battle against [Col. 0893B] them. For I shall give you nothing of their land, because I have given Ar to the children of Lot as a possession’” (Deut. 2).

Thus, as though one might ask why Israel begs by messengers that it may pass through the Amorite’s land—“We shall not turn aside,” it says, “into fields or vineyards; we shall not drink water from wells, until we have passed through your borders”—when, in accordance with the oath which God established for Abraham, swore to Isaac, and “ordained for Jacob as an everlasting covenant” (Ps. 104 [105]), Israel ought to have hoped for the whole land of Canaan as the portion of its inheritance (ibid.), including the Amorite’s land: he immediately gives the reason, saying, “The city Heshbon belonged to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who fought against the king of Moab and took all the land that had been under his rule as far as Arnon.”

Unable to prove this by the authority of Scripture—which did not exist—he confirms it by a proverb sung in the mouth of the people down to that time: “Therefore it is said in the proverb: ‘Come to Heshbon; let the city of Sihon be built and established. Fire went out from Heshbon, a flame from the town of Sihon, and consumed Ar of the Moabites and the inhabitants of the heights of Arnon. Woe to you, Moab! You have perished, people of Chemosh,’” etc.

By this proverb, in which the defeated are mocked and the victor applauded, it is proved to Israel no less firmly than by writing that the land was not part of its allotted inheritance. Nevertheless, what was not Israel’s by hereditary right came to be its by right of war. “For he was unwilling,” it says, “to allow Israel to pass through his borders. [Col. 0893D] Rather, having gathered an army, he went out to meet Israel in the wilderness, came to Jahaz, and fought against him. He was struck by the edge of the sword, and his land was possessed from Arnon as far as Jabbok and the children of Ammon, because the boundaries of the Ammonites were held by a strong defense.”

By what defense were the boundaries of the Ammonites held? Certainly by God’s defense, as Moses likewise records God as saying in Deuteronomy: “Today you shall cross the boundaries of Moab, the city named Ar, and you shall approach the vicinity of the children of Ammon. Take care not to fight against them or provoke them to battle. For I shall give you nothing of the land of the children of Ammon, because I have given it to the children of Lot as a possession” (Deut. 2).

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 0894A] What spiritual meaning is indicated by the fact that Israel, about to cross the Jordan, already possesses cities and villages around the Jordan.

Israel, about to cross the Jordan, already possesses on this side of the Jordan cities and villages, the land of the king of the Amorites, and the land of Og, king of Bashan. Of him it is subsequently added: “Og, king of Bashan, met him to fight at Edrei.” Both were kings of the Amorites, as it is said in Deuteronomy: “At that time we took the land from the hand of the two kings of the Amorites” (Deut. 3), etc. And further: “For only Og, king of Bashan, remained of the stock of giants. His iron bed is shown in Rabbah of the children of Ammon, nine cubits long and four wide according to the measure of a man’s cubit [Col. 0894B]” (ibid.).

“Of the stock,” he says, “of giants”—not indeed those who are said to have existed before the flood, Scripture saying, “There were giants upon the earth in those days” (Gen. 6), but those who could have existed after the flood, such as the Anakim. He alone is said to have remained, perhaps because he was exceptionally proud among other great and tall men.

Thus, as said before, Israel possesses the land before it has yet crossed the Jordan. Nearly similar to this is the fact that spiritual Israel—whose portion is the Lord, whose lot and inheritance is the land of the living—already in this world, before crossing the Jordan and before being made blessed by the second resurrection, possesses the riches of wealthy secular kings and emperors, holds strongholds, and presides over cities. We speak of Christ’s holy Church; we refer to apostolic ranks, whose fathers and princes, holding the sword of the word of God, grew so strong, became so mighty in battle, that by subjecting to Christ’s yoke the souls of tyrants and powerful kings, they also seized, as excellent spoils for the use of Christ’s servants, the greater parts of kingdoms.

And indeed “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8); nor are they deprived of the eternal reward because of this temporal recompense, since “the laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke 10)—a wage which no mortal can adequately repay from material possessions to Christ’s faithful ministers, who worthily sow spiritual things (1 Cor. 9). Yet to those who are drawn by no love of eternal goods and proclaim Christ so as to gain, not the things of Jesus Christ, but their own things (Phil. 2), it is rightly and lawfully said: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6). Consequently, like the children of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, of whom something will be said later, dwelling on this side of the Jordan, they shall not have the glory of the second resurrection.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Balaam’s covetousness, and how he was the one called Elihu in the book of Job.

(CHAP. XXII.) “And they set out and camped in the plains of Moab, where Jericho lies across the Jordan. When Balak son of Zippor saw all that Israel had done to the Amorite, and that the Moabites greatly feared him and could not withstand his assault, he said to the elders of Midian: ‘This people will destroy all who dwell within [Col. 0895A] our borders, as an ox ordinarily crops grass down to its roots.’ He was then king in Moab. Therefore he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor, a diviner, who dwelt beside the river in the land of the children of Ammon,” etc.

The Hebrews maintain that this Balaam, called a *divinus* or *hariolus*—a seer or diviner—was the one called Elihu in the book of Job: first a holy man and a prophet of God, but later, through disobedience and desire for gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, called a *divinus* or *hariolus*. Indeed, plain reasoning proves that he was disobedient to God, desired gifts, and wished to curse Israel.

When summoned by the king of Moab, who said, “Behold, a people has come out of Egypt and is settled opposite me. Come therefore and curse this people, for it is stronger than I,” etc., Balaam said to the messengers, who held the price of divination in their hands: “Stay here tonight, and I will answer whatever the Lord tells me.” He did not say: “Far be it from me! I shall not curse this people; may your money perish with you.” Rather, the wicked man investigates God’s secrets once and again, in case God’s patience might perhaps permit what burning covetousness urged him to do.

So desirous was he of gifts or of cursing that, when dismissed under a condition by God, who said, “If these men have come to call you, rise and go with them, but only on this condition: that you do what I command you”—he “rose early in the morning,” that is, hurriedly, disregarding the condition. He acted like wicked servants who render eye-service: when they are sent or released to do lawful things, they presume to commit unlawful things also. Therefore “the angel of the Lord stood against him with drawn sword,” so that he might learn from present punishment how grievous it is to abuse what is permitted or to disregard the Lord’s command.

## CHAPTER XVII. How he represents those prelates for whom all things are for sale, and how they may be rebuked, as this man was rebuked by a mute beast of burden.

The kind of persons he represents is clear from apostolic writings. The Apostle Peter, after speaking of destructive and blasphemous persons, says, among other things: “Having a heart trained in covetousness, children of curse, they have forsaken [Col. 0895D] the right way and gone astray” (2 Pet. 2). He immediately adds: “They followed the way of Balaam of Bosor, who loved the wages of iniquity. Yet he had a rebuker of his madness: a mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, rebuked the prophet’s folly” (ibid.).

Jude also, in his Epistle, after saying, “But these people blaspheme whatever they do not know; and whatever they know naturally, like mute animals, by these things they are corrupted” (Jude 1), immediately adds: “Woe to them, for they have gone in the way of Cain, poured themselves out in Balaam’s error for reward, and perished in Korah’s rebellion” (ibid.).

Thus Balaam—whose name is interpreted “vain people”—bears the likeness of those who are established in the Church only in name and vain profession. Just as this man, though descended from Shem, as Abraham was, did not belong to Abraham’s faith and inheritance, so they have “eyes full of adultery and unceasing sin” (2 Pet. 2) and are “children of curse” (ibid.). Whatever curses or blessings they chant, they sell for a price, and with them everything is for sale.

Though such persons are blasphemous and corrupt, they imagine that all sacred reality rests with them alone: that whatever they give is holy; that only those whom they bless are blessed; and that all upon whom they heap curses are cursed. Likewise Balak, whose name is interpreted “licking” or “crushing,” and who also descended from Shem—for Moab was born from Lot, Abraham’s nephew—represents those who, situated in the Church and Christians only in a false name, hire such persons for a price as arbiters of blessing [Col. 0896B] and cursing. They are consequently reckoned guilty of the same crime as those who sell: wicked purchasers, to be driven from God’s temple by the cord of his wrath, who lick and crush—flattering vices and crushing, as far as they can, every work of virtue.

Where such things take place, the mouths of subjects are rightly given freedom to rebuke their prelates. For behold, this man, pursuing the wages of iniquity, “had, as has already been said, a rebuker of his madness: a mute beast of burden, speaking with a human voice, rebuked the prophet’s folly.” However much it may be a beast of burden, however much it may have received the rider’s bridle in its mouth, yet if it sees the angel of the Lord standing in the road with drawn sword—if, I say, it sees that Angel of Great Counsel on the evangelical way, driving sellers and buyers from the temple, from the Father’s house, with a terrible judgment (Matt. 21)—whom its rider, that is, its prelate, cannot see because his heart is blinded by covetousness, it will turn aside from the road and, despite the rider’s anger and even his blows, prevent him from accomplishing the wicked work of covetousness.

Let us now examine the prophetic words of this *hariolus*, or *divinus*—this diviner or seer.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Why it should not be thought strange that the Lord placed a word in his mouth, and what he prophesied in his first oracle.

(CAP. XXIII.) “Taking up his parable, he said: ‘Balak, king of the Moabites, brought me from Aram, from the mountains of the East. Come,’ he said, ‘curse Jacob; hasten, and denounce Israel. How shall I curse one whom God has not cursed [Col. 0896D]? On what ground shall I denounce one whom the Lord does not denounce? From the tops of the rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall behold him. The people shall dwell alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations. Who can count the dust of Jacob, or know the number of Israel’s offspring? Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs.’”

“The Lord,” he says, “put this word into his mouth,” lest perhaps you should wonder that a prophet so wicked, divided between Balak’s altars and God, could be admitted so that the Lord would put a word in his mouth, and would allow his own word to be imposed upon an idolater and diviner. Yet the faithful prophet Samuel, when he had said to Saul, “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening than offering the fat of rams” [Col. 0897A] (1 Sam. 15), immediately added: “For resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry” (ibid.). Yet Scripture later reports of that same man: “He too went to Ramah,” namely while pursuing David, “and came as far as the great cistern which is in Socoth; and he asked and said, ‘Where are Samuel and David?’ And it was said to him, ‘Behold, they are at Naioth in Ramah.’ And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him also, and he went on walking and prophesying until he came to Naioth in Ramah. He too stripped off his garments, and prophesied with the others before Samuel. And he sang naked all that day and night” (1 Sam. 19).

Therefore, since even to this day the Spirit speaks mysteries through unworthy persons—so that even in the Gospel the spirit of malignity says, “I know who you are, the Holy One of God” [Col. 0897B] (Mark 1)—let us listen not to who says it, but to what is said.

“Taking up,” he says, “his parable.” The figurative utterance begins with what he says: “From the tops of the rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall behold him.” For what he first stated—“How shall I curse one whom God has not cursed? On what ground shall I denounce one whom the Lord does not denounce?”—has a plain and evident sense according to the ordinary meaning of the words. No one, indeed, can effectively curse or denounce one to whom blessing has been given by the Lord, whose praise or testimony is from God.

Therefore, when he says, “From the tops of the rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall behold him,” understand the lofty fathers, the supreme patriarchs, of this people: [Col. 0897C] fathers not so much according to their flesh as according to their faith. From the height of those rocks, from the height of those hills, contemplate the dignity of that people. For you never understand better how much the Jew has beyond the Gentile than when, with the Apostle, you say that theirs “are the adoption, the covenant, the glory, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9). Certainly you have seen this people from the tops of the rocks and beheld it glorious from the hills.

What shall I see of it from the tops of the rocks? What sort of people shall I behold from the hills? “The people,” he says, “shall dwell alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations.” Abraham, he says, and his children—children, I mean, [Col. 0897D] not of his flesh but of his promise—“shall dwell alone.” They shall be the sole and distinctive worshippers of the one God, the people of one ruler, the body of one head. “They shall dwell alone,” I say: they alone shall possess as an inheritance the blessing which God promised to their father Abraham, saying, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22).

Although those who had been scattered, the children of God, are to be gathered into one from every part of the world (John 11), after their gathering, after they have received God’s blessing, they shall not be reckoned among the nations. This is like their father Abraham himself: after being called out of the nations and led out from the Chaldeans, he was no longer reckoned among the nations or counted among the Chaldeans. He dwelt alone, a pilgrim, stranger, and solitary man, having no abiding city here, but seeking the city to come [Col. 0898A] (Heb. 13). So, I say, all the people of his faith shall dwell alone in tents, because they will not build cities in the land together with the nations.

“Who can count the dust of Jacob, or know the number of Israel’s offspring?” It is as if he said: Do not suppose, because I said, “They shall dwell alone,” that the people whom I saw from the tops of the rocks are few. Do not suppose, because I said, “They shall not be reckoned among the nations,” that the one nation which I beheld from the hills numbers only a few thousands. For if anyone can count the dust of the earth (Gen. 13), he can also count the dust of Jacob; and if anyone can count the stars of heaven (Gen. 5), he will also be able to know the number of Israel’s offspring.

“Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs.” Empty sighs of one making wishes; frivolous and fleeting desires of one prophesying! He ceased to sigh and ceased to desire when, overcome by greed, he afterward gave counsel as to what Balak’s people should do to this people. Therefore his soul died the death of the wicked, and his end became like that of the Midianites. For when, by the Lord’s command, the children of Israel avenged themselves upon the Midianites, they also slew with the sword this Balaam son of Beor [Col. 0898B] (Num. 32).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the character of his speech: how, after the manner of corrupters, he sweetly flatters and adulterates the word of his God

“And Balak said: ‘Come with me to another place, from which you may see a part of Israel, though you cannot see all of it; curse them from there,’” and so forth.

When Balaam spoke the things written above [Col. 0898C], he was contemplating—as was stated there—the farthest part of the people: that is, he foresaw not merely present things but, by the prophetic Spirit, what would come about in the last days. But Balak, and whoever is like him—whoever, as has already been said, is signified by that name—cares only for the present and refuses to hear of what will happen in times far off. He therefore says: “Come with me to another place, from which you may see a part of Israel, though you cannot see all of it.” It is as though he said: Do not show me the whole; do not announce the future to me; show me only the present portion of events. Look only to how I may strike him and drive him from my land.

“Stand,” he says, “Balak, and listen. Hear, son of Zippor: [Col. 0898D] God is not like a man, that he should lie; nor like a son of man, that he should change. Has he spoken and will he not do it? Has the Lord said something and will he not fulfil it?”

In all the sayings of this troublesome prophet, his elegant loquacity should be noted. By doubling everything, he repeats each point once stated, not indeed in identical words but in the same sense, so that there is a dissimilar likeness, after the fashion of an affected and seductively pleasing song. “Stand,” he says, “Balak, and listen.” Then he immediately repeats it: “Hear, son of Zippor.” “God,” he says, “is not like a man, that he should lie”; and immediately, doubling this very statement, he says, “nor like a son of man, that he should change.” Thus, and so forth.

By this very manner of speaking he aptly represents those who adulterate the word of God: while chanting blessings, they care nothing for the force [Col. 0899A] of the words, attending more to the dance of their little voice than to the majesty of the divine meanings. The Lord most gravely forbade this to the preachers of the Gospel: “Greet no one,” he says, “on the road” (Luke 10). For those truly greet people on the road who do not desire the word of God which they chant aloud to benefit their hearers.

## CHAPTER XX. On his saying, “God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros,” and so forth: what he said in the second blessing
