“God,” he says, “is not like a man, that he should lie,” and so forth. It is as though he said: I came to another place, but did not find God changed. Once he placed a word in my mouth, and does not allow it to be changed, since every man is a liar and every son of man changeable; but God does not lie in the same way, nor does he similarly change from his purpose.

“I was brought to bless; I cannot prevent the blessing. There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel. The Lord his God is with him, and the shout of a king’s victory is with him. God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros. There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In their times it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God has done. Behold, the people shall rise up like a lioness, and shall lift itself like a lion. It shall not lie down until it devours prey and drinks the blood of the slain.”

We hear the prophet as if bound and chained, uttering word after word, against his will, the silver utterances of truth [Col. 0899C]. “I was brought,” he says, “to bless”—sent, of course, by him who alone is arbiter of all blessings. I wish to prevent “the blessing,” but I cannot prevent it. What then? I shall bless unwillingly; I shall not sing blessings voluntarily.

“There is no idol in Jacob; no image is seen in Israel.” But what is there? “The Lord his God is with him”—with him, I say, as a jealous husband is with his wife, forbidding the adultery of idols and driving far away the fornication of images. And lest, when the husband is absent, she might have adulterous intercourse with idols or images in the silence of the night: “The shout,” he says, “of a king’s victory is in him.” The shout of the king’s victory is the jealous voice which spoke from Mount Sinai amid the ever more violent sound of the trumpet: “You shall have no other gods before me; you shall not make for yourself a graven image” [Col. 0899D] (Exod. 20), and so forth.

By what right, by what due claim, does he alone wish to exercise authority, as though by marital law? “God,” he says, “brought him out of Egypt.” Certainly this is a just and lawful cause. He led this nation out of Egypt with a mighty hand and outstretched arm, and made a covenant with it by sprinkling blood over all his words. Remembering this, he himself says in the prophet Ezekiel: “Passing by you, I saw you trampled in your blood; and I said to you, when you were in your blood, ‘Live’” (Ezek. 16). And afterward: “I passed by you and saw you, and behold, your time was a time for lovers. I spread my garment over you and covered your shame; I swore to you, and [Col. 0900A] entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God. And you became mine, and I washed you with water” (ibid.), and so forth.

Therefore there is no idol in Jacob, nor may there be one; no image is seen in Israel, nor may one be seen. “There is not,” I say, nor ought there to be, “augury in Jacob or divination in Israel.” Why? Because, he says, “God brought him out of Egypt.” And immediately: “Whose strength,” he says, “is like that of a rhinoceros.”

From this brief expression a great meaning may be understood. The rhinoceros is a one-horned animal, so called in Greek because it has a horn upon its nose—that is, above the nostril on its forehead. It is of such strength that no one can conquer it, and of such fierceness that no one can touch it. Yet, according to natural philosophers, it alone admits the caresses of a virgin maiden: it is drawn by the scent of virginity; when it perceives that a maiden is present in a field, it seeks her of its own accord, lowers its head, and gladly falls asleep in her gentle lap. There it is seized and pierced by the hunter; thus skill accomplishes what no force could achieve.

Referring to this, the prophetic Spirit says: “Whose”—that is, God’s—“strength is like that of a rhinoceros.” This is altogether as true as it is devout. For God, the mightiest of spirits, like a unicorn—that is, God of singular power, incomprehensible God, God of unconquered might—after bringing that people out of Egypt, was drawn by the scent of a virginal womb, sought the Virgin, and was enclosed within the confines of virginal modesty. From her alone he could be seized and killed. Therefore “his strength is like that of a rhinoceros. In their times it shall be said to Jacob and [Col. 0900C] Israel what God has done”: that is, when the time comes, it shall be preached to true Jacob and true Israel what God signified by leading this people out of Egypt, and why it is rightly said that “his strength is like that of a rhinoceros.”

“Behold, the people shall rise up like a lioness, and shall lift itself like a lion. It shall not lie down until it devours prey and drinks the blood of the slain.” This may indeed be referred literally to the battles of that people: when Joshua led them across the Jordan, they rose like a lioness and lifted themselves like a lion; nor did they lie down in the land of promise before devouring prey and shedding the blood of their enemies. But it is better and more certainly referred to those times in which, as he now says, “it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God has done.”

For behold: after that most mighty rhinoceros was brought down from the Virgin’s lap to death on the cross, his people rose like a lioness; for their prince himself, rising from the dead, rose like a lion, according to Jacob’s prophecy: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; you have gone up to the prey, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness” [Col. 0900D] (Gen. 49), and so forth. Therefore, “it shall not lie down,” he says, “until it devours prey and drinks the blood of the slain,” expressing metaphorically, through the mighty lion, the ardent power of Christ and his apostles. They did not rest until, running throughout the whole world, they dragged from the ancient seats of the temples the devil, the prince of this world—whom Christ himself had conquered in hell like a lion—as a lioness.

## CHAPTER XXI. On what he said in the third blessing, speaking of himself: “The man whose eye is shut says,” and so forth; and what, spiritually understood, is the beauty of Israel’s tents

(CAP. XXIV.) “When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, he did not go as he had gone before to seek augury. But turning his face toward the wilderness and lifting up his eyes, he saw Israel dwelling in tents according to its tribes. And when the Spirit of God rushed upon him, he took up his parable and said: ‘Balaam son of Beor says; the man whose eye is shut says; the hearer of God’s words says; he who has beheld the vision of the Almighty says; he falls, and thus his eyes are opened.’”

“When,” he says, [Col. 0901B] “he saw”—when he had learned by experience—“that it steadily pleased the Lord to bless,” since he had said, “God is not like a man, that he should lie; nor like a son of man, that he should change,” having lost the hope for which he had gaped in his greed, “he did not go as he had gone before to seek augury.” Augury is, as it were, *augurarium*, the chatter of birds, by which frenzied persons have customarily sought to discover future events. Not that an oracle of God should be called augury, but that such a word was rightly used in contempt of such a prophet and such a greedy inquirer.

“The man,” he says, “whose eye is shut,” and so forth. It is great and excellent to be a hearer of God’s words; yet it is evil and perverse to have a shut eye. Likewise, it is beautiful and honourable to behold the vision of the Almighty, but the order of beholding must be right and lawful. He, however, presented the order in reverse when he immediately said: “He falls, and thus his eyes are opened.” Had he not said this, the two preceding statements—“whose eye is shut” and “who has beheld the vision of the Almighty”—would seem contrary or contradictory. But now it becomes clear that, by prophetic knowledge, he is indeed a hearer of God’s words and has beheld the Almighty’s vision; yet through greed he has a heart blinded, and he falls into covetousness, though he nonetheless has open eyes, so that he has no excuse for his fall or sin.

What did such a man say? “How beautiful are your tents, O Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel: like wooded valleys, like gardens watered beside rivers, like tabernacles [Col. 0901D] which the Lord has pitched, like cedars beside waters.” According to the historical arrangement of the camp described above, Jacob’s tents were beautiful; but because these are God’s words, because this is the vision of the Almighty, let us understand here the spiritual beauty of the spiritual Jacob’s tents.

The tents of the true Israel and spiritual Jacob, a pilgrim in this present world, are the devout and, according to Christ’s discipline, rightly ordered ranks of married persons, continent persons, widows, and virgins, of both sexes. Each of these tents is indeed beautiful in its own vocation. And how beautiful are the tents, how beautiful the tabernacles! “Like wooded valleys,” [Col. 0902A] he says, “like gardens watered beside rivers,” and so forth.

That this is so is evident from other passages of Scripture. In Isaiah, the Lord promises to the Gentile world once forsaken the merits of spiritual virtues as shrubs in a desert: “I will give,” he says, “in the wilderness cedar, thorn, myrtle, and olive tree. I will set in the desert fir, elm, and box tree together, that they may see, know, consider, and understand alike” (Isa. 41). Therefore, “beautiful tents, like wooded valleys.”

Likewise: “You shall be like a watered garden, and like a fountain of waters whose waters do not fail” (Isa. 58). And in the Song of Songs: “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed, a fountain of gardens, a well of living waters flowing forcefully from Lebanon” (Song 4). Behold, “beautiful tents, like gardens watered beside rivers.” [Col. 0902B]

And when the Psalmist had said, “Watering the mountains from his upper chambers” (Ps. 103), and so forth, he immediately continued: “The trees of the field,” he says, “shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted.” Therefore, “beautiful tents, like cedars beside waters”: namely, those in which birds make their nests, whose abundance, when they are wealthy persons, supplies the want of the poor.

## CHAPTER XXII. Prophecy concerning Christ from the words, “Water shall flow from his bucket”; and concerning the Kenite, “Asshur shall take you”

[Note: Rupert discusses the Kenite only below, in chapter 24 [Col. 0901].]

“Water shall flow from his bucket, and his seed shall be in many waters.” What is his bucket? Or rather, what is his water? His water, his living water, is Holy Scripture, to which he invites through the prophet, saying: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” [Col. 0902C] (Isa. 55)—that is, all who love and seek God, read the Holy Scriptures. This water is the water of the Israelite people; for to them the utterances of God were entrusted. What then is his bucket but his Christ? For water is drawn by a bucket, and Holy Scripture is opened through Christ. Or rather, through him thirst is aroused so that this water may be desired; through him understanding is opened, so that the Scriptures may be understood.

“Water,” therefore, “shall flow from his bucket”: that is, the true understanding of the Scriptures shall flow from his Christ. What follows? “And his seed,” he says, “shall be in many waters.” What the water from his bucket is, the multitude of waters from his seed is. For his seed—the seed of his father Abraham—is Christ. “His seed shall be in many waters”: that is, this seed shall pour forth many waters. By drinking, we have experienced that his seed is truly “in many waters.”

“He who believes in me,” he says, “from his belly shall flow rivers of living water” [Col. 0902D] (John 7). Likewise: “Whoever drinks of the water which I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water which I shall give him shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). By drinking his grace, I say, we have experienced this. Behold, from this bucket, which is Christ himself, we have received many gifts of the Holy Spirit in the one Church, and possess many and most abundant streams of Scripture.

“His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed.” This was fulfilled as follows. Saul, his king—that is, Israel’s king—was sought contrary to the Lord’s will, who said to Samuel: “Hear the voice of the people in all that they say to you; for they have not rejected you, but me” [Col. 0903A] (1 Sam. 8). Therefore Samuel commanded, from the Lord’s mouth: “Go and strike Amalek, and destroy all that belongs to him. Spare him not, but kill from man to woman, child and infant” (1 Sam. 15).

But Saul did indeed strike Amalek, yet spared Agag, king of Amalek. “He did not wish to destroy everything that was beautiful; whatever was worthless and rejected, that he destroyed. Then the word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: ‘I regret that I made Saul king, because he has forsaken me and has not fulfilled my words in deed’” (ibid.). And afterward: “Fill your horn with oil and come, that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for among his sons I have provided myself a king” [Col. 0903B] (1 Sam. 16).

This, I say, which this fallen man, and so forth, said with open eyes—“His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed”—must be understood not of Israel, but of its kings: that none of his descendants should reign. But why, in so great a matter, does the prophetic Spirit mention this king? Namely, in order to establish that no one but his God is rightfully his king. For this is what he immediately adds: “God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros.” The Spirit of the Lord said this in him, I say, in order to establish that no one but his God is rightfully his king.

Accordingly, when God himself said to Samuel, “They have not rejected you, but me, that I should not reign over them” (1 Sam. 8), he immediately added: “According to all their works which they have done from the day when I brought them out of Egypt to this day—how they have forsaken me and served foreign gods—so they do also to you” [Col. 0903C] (ibid.). Therefore, after saying, “His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed,” he immediately adds, in order to establish that Israel ought never to have had a king except God alone: “God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros,” in the same sense as above.

But because they abandoned their God—their most mighty king, like the rhinoceros, made graspable from the Virgin’s lap and led to death—and became his enemies, they will receive another, namely Antichrist, whom they sought in Saul’s type. “They shall devour,” he says, “the nations that are his enemies; they shall break their bones and pierce them with arrows.” For today we nations devour them as enemies of this kind, so that none of them dares lift his head, breaking their bones—that is, the arguments which they consider strong—and piercing them with the arrows of truth. For all of us who are instructed in the word of truth and ready to give an account of our faith (1 Pet. 3) are rightly called the Lord’s archers, archers of the Mighty One, whose words in us are “sharp arrows with desolating coals” [Col. 0903D] (Ps. 119).

“Lying down, he slept like a lion, and like a lioness; who will dare awaken him?” The patriarch Jacob foretold this in the same Spirit, though in a better state of mind, as was said above (Gen. 49). Slain on the wood, he lay in the tomb and slept like a roaring lion in hell; and in his apostles—indeed, in his whole Church—he plundered the whole world, “like a lioness, whom,” he says, “no one will dare awaken”: no one will be able to resist him.

“Whoever blesses you shall himself be blessed, and whoever curses you shall be reckoned under a curse.” This is clearer than daylight: whoever blesses Christ and his holy people shall share in his blessing, when he says, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” [Col. 0904A] (Matt. 25). Conversely, whoever utters blasphemies shall be cursed at his coming, when he says: “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXIII. What he meant in saying, “Yet, as I go to my people, I will give counsel concerning what your people shall do to this people,” adding, “in the last time”

“Yet, as I go to my people, I will give counsel concerning what your people shall do to this people in the last time.” What counsel this fallen man with open eyes gave, or why he said “in the last time,” will appear from the events that follow:

“The man whose eye is shut says; the hearer of God’s words says; he who knows the teaching of the Most High and sees the visions of the Almighty says; he falls, and has open eyes: ‘I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall arise from Jacob, [315] and a sceptre shall rise from Israel; it shall strike the leaders of Moab and lay waste all the sons of Seth. And Edom shall be his possession; the inheritance of Seir shall yield to its enemies, while Israel shall act mightily. From Jacob shall come one who rules and destroys the remnants of the city.’”

By repeated confession—indeed, profession—he proclaims his own folly: while inwardly hearing God’s words, he has through greed a shut eye of the heart and does not provide for his own salvation; he falls while having open eyes, as he said above. He adds statements no less great than the earlier ones: “I shall see him,” he says, “but not now.” In this parable he almost discloses whom he confesses that he will see; the whole world knows its sense well enough. “A star shall arise from Jacob,” and so forth. For it is a manifest and true prophecy of Christ’s birth: he himself is the bright morning star, and at his birth he was to be revealed through a visible star [Col. 0904D] (Matt. 2).

“A star,” therefore, he says, “shall arise from Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise from Israel”: that is, the light of truth and the heavenly rule shall proceed from the flesh of this people. This sceptre “shall strike the leaders of Moab,” that is, all the enemies of the true Israel, all of whom you may rightly call Moabites. In the present case and before the king of Moab, the whole body of his enemies is rightly designated through Moab alone.

But what does he mean by saying, “It shall lay waste all the sons of Seth”? Are all the sons of Seth his enemies? Is not the whole world, are not all human beings since the flood, descended from Seth? Certainly Noah alone with his household survived the flood, and from him the world was again filled. Who does not know that Seth was his ancestor? For Seth begot Enos; Enos begot Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel begot Jared; Jared begot Enoch; Enoch begot Methuselah; Methuselah [Col. 0905A] begot Lamech; and Lamech begot Noah (Gen. 5).

Therefore, when he says, “It shall lay waste all the sons of Seth,” it is as though he said: the sceptre of Israel, the iron sceptre—the most righteous and mighty king—shall lay waste all the nations, according also to the prophecy in which the Father speaks in the Psalm: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall rule them with an iron sceptre” (Ps. 2).

“And Edom,” he says—that is, the Church of the nations converted from earthly-mindedness—“shall be his possession,” as another prophetic oracle also declares: “I shall stretch out my shoe over Edom” (Ps. 59 and 107), that is, I shall reveal to the nations the mystery of my incarnation. “The inheritance of Seir shall yield to its enemies.” Seir means “the hairy ones”: the inheritance of the devil, which we nations once were, when we paid the tribute of sacrilegious worship to him in dumb images. We were, I say, but are no longer; for, as was said above, we were given as an inheritance to the king of Israel when he asked the Father.

Therefore, the inheritance of Seir which yields to its enemies consists of those, whether Gentiles or Jews, who still flatter the defeated devil as their lord. They shall yield to their enemies—that is, they shall be abandoned—because this is what they chose and preferred: those same masters. For those masters are themselves, most miserably, their enemies.

Israel therefore shall act mightily—Israel, I say, whoever belongs to Israel by faith, even if not Israel by flesh—shall act mightily and shall conquer the world mightily with its king. Whence comes this? “From Jacob,” he says, “shall come one who rules and destroys the remnants of the city.” One from Jacob’s flesh [Col. 0905C] shall be commander of the army and leader in war; at his first coming he shall receive dominion, kingdom, and honour, so that every people, tribe, and tongue may serve him (Rev. 5); and at his second coming, namely on the day of judgment, he shall destroy the remnants of the city which do not belong to him: the hostile city, the city of the devil.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the parable in which he said, “Amalek is the beginning of the nations; his end shall perish”

“When he saw Amalek, he took up his parable and said: ‘Amalek is the beginning of the nations; his end shall perish.’” The parable is brief, but a long vengeance is pronounced against Amalek. “Amalek,” he says, “is the beginning”: not in nationality, but in impiety against Israel. For when Israel had departed from Egypt, “Amalek came first of all the nations and fought against him at Rephidim” [Col. 0905D] (Exod. 16).

Therefore, he says, his end shall perish: namely, when, as was said above, “because of Agag his king, Israel’s king shall be taken away and his kingdom removed.” His end shall perish, I say: not merely temporally or bodily, but he shall also be condemned eternally and spiritually. Moses says: “His hand is that of the Lord alone, and God’s war shall be against Amalek from generation to generation” (ibid.).

“He also saw the Kenite.” The Kenites sprang from Jethro, or Hobab, Moses’ kinsman. Thus it is written in the book of Judges: “Heber the Kenite had formerly separated from the other Kenites, his brothers, the sons of Hobab, Moses’ kinsman” [Col. 0906A] (Judg. 4). He saw, therefore, the Kenite—understand, dwelling among Amalek, yet not opposing Israel together with him—because of the kinship of his aforesaid father Hobab with Moses, and therefore not destined to undergo the same destruction with Amalek.

Thus, when Saul was plundering Amalek, he said to the Kenite: “Go, withdraw, and depart from Amalek, lest I involve you with him. For you showed mercy to all the children of Israel when they came up from Egypt” (1 Sam. 15). The Kenite’s father showed mercy to Israel when, not only did he not oppose them like Amalek, but he also gave good advice on Israel’s behalf, saying to Moses: “What is this that you are doing among the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people wait from morning until evening?” (Exod. 18).

He saw, therefore. “And taking up his parable, he said: ‘Your dwelling is indeed strong; but if you place your nest in a rock and are chosen from the stock of Ham, how long will you be able to remain?’” “Your dwelling,” he says, “is strong,” perhaps because of the position or nature of the places. But can it stand against God, by whose hand Amalek—in whose midst you are—shall have its end destroyed? Certainly not. For unless you had withdrawn from the midst, when Saul said, “Go and withdraw from the midst of Amalek,” you would easily have been involved with him.

Therefore your dwelling is indeed strong, so that you may be safe from the attack of other nations. But how long can you remain so? “For Asshur shall take you” [Col. 0906C]—as it shall take very many nations and very many kingdoms of the earth. “Even if you place your nest in a rock and are chosen from the stock of Ham, he shall take you.” Nimrod, son of Cush, son of Ham, was chosen from the stock of Ham. For “he began to be mighty on the earth and was a mighty hunter before the Lord. Hence came the proverb, ‘Like Nimrod, a mighty hunter before the Lord.’ The beginning of his kingdom was Babylon” (Gen. 10). Therefore, “your dwelling is indeed strong,” he says; but even if you are strong like that hunter chosen from the stock of Ham, and build yourself another Babylon for a nest, “Asshur shall take you.”

## CHAPTER XXV. His prophecy: “They shall come in triremes from Italy; they shall overcome the Assyrians,” and so forth

“Taking up his parable, he spoke again: ‘Alas, who shall live when God does these things? They shall come in triremes from Italy, they shall overcome the Assyrians and lay waste the Hebrews; and at last they too shall perish.’”

This prophecy was then figurative, but now the matter is manifest: “They came in triremes from Italy”; the Roman legions came, I say, fighting not only on land but also by sea. And that beast which Daniel saw—the fourth beast, dreadful, marvellous, and exceedingly strong, with great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest under its feet [Col. 0906D] (Dan. 7)—overcame and crushed even the most powerful kingdom of the Assyrians, and, after devastating their most beautiful region, overthrew the temple of the Jews.

And at last they too perished—or rather, shall perish. For although Rome is not destroyed by the nations, it is nevertheless certain that, in the aspect under which it is called Babylon, it shall be desolated by division against itself, and house does not cease to fall upon house (Matt. 12). “Alas,” he says, “who shall live when God does these things?” Again he sighs in an exclamation of grief, calling blessed those eyes which were to see the Hebrews laid waste and the Assyrians overcome, the Roman empire flourishing, and the kingdom of heaven shining forth.

In the same manner the first prophecy too had sighed: “Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like theirs.” But the root of bitterness—covetousness, “the root of all evils” [Col. 0907B] (1 Tim. 6)—destroyed these sighs and every gift of prophecy or wisdom. For, thirsting excessively for the gifts of the wicked, he had said to Balak amid words of blessing: “Yet, as I go to my people, I will give counsel concerning what your people shall do to this people in the last time.” The following events disclose the secret of his most wicked counsel.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Israel’s initiation into Baal-peor, worshipping the gods of the sons of Moab
(Cap. XXV.) “Now at that time Israel was staying in Shittim, and the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their sacrifices. And they ate and worshipped their gods. Thus Israel was initiated into Baal-peor.” By his counsel [Col. 0907C] it came about that the beauty of the daughters of Moab was set before the lustful people, on the stipulated condition of sexual union: once desire had been aroused, the women would not yield to the men unless, first invited to the sacrifices, they ate and worshipped their gods and were initiated into Baal-peor.

That wicked prophet knew wherein lay that people’s supreme strength; fearing it, Moab said: “This people will wipe out all who dwell within our borders, just as an ox is accustomed to crop the grass down to its roots” (Num. XXII). He knew, I say, why that people would rise like a lioness and spring up like a lion, not lying down (Num. XXIV), until it had devoured its prey and drunk the blood [Col. 0907D] of the slain: namely, because the Lord its God was with it, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros. Therefore, in order to drive the lover of chastity, like a rhinoceros, away from Israel, he gave this impious counsel: that the people, enticed into fornication, might moreover be initiated against their God not into just any idol, but into Baal-peor—that is, the image of obscenity—who among the Romans of old was the same as Priapus.

But in this knowledge his eye was greatly darkened; nor was he able to foresee that by this means God would by no means withdraw from his people. Rather, through the dagger of Phinehas the priest and his excellent zeal, God’s wrath would be turned away from the children of Israel, while he himself, together with his fornicators, would be killed by the sword.

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 0908A] What is meant by his adding “at the end time,” after saying: “I will give counsel what your people shall do to this people.”

What, then, is meant by this: when he had said, “I will give counsel what your people shall do to this people,” he added, “at the end time” (Num. XXIV)? Certainly, as he spoke under the rushing influence of God’s Spirit, he beheld that final time when that people would truly receive the abomination—“the abomination, I say, of desolation” (Matt. XXIV)—namely Antichrist, who is prefigured by Baal-peor. Hence it was said with the utmost appropriateness: “Israel was initiated into Baal-peor.”

For then, when it thus committed fornication in God’s presence, “it was initiated into Baal-peor”; but when [Col. 0908B] it receives Antichrist coming in his own name, it will bring Baal-peor to completion. The middle stage of its fornication was when, before Pilate, having denied its God and delivered up its peaceable king, it demanded that Barabbas, the instigator of sedition and a type of the same Antichrist, be released to it (Matt. XXVII).

Therefore, when through the spirit of prophecy, looking far ahead from the words, “God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros” (Num. XXIV), he also saw the Romans coming in ships, by whom the Assyrians would be overcome and the Hebrews devastated, he did not yet cease. But proceeding further, he also saw the obscenity of Antichrist, which that people would fully receive in the final time; and he perceived already then that it could be initiated into such an idol, and gave counsel as to how this might be done [Col. 0908C].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That the whole generation—everyone numbered from twenty years old and upward—was consumed by seven plagues.

“The Lord said, ‘Take all the leaders of the people and hang them before the sun on gibbets, that my fury may be turned away from Israel.’” And afterward: “And behold, one of the children of Israel entered before his brethren to a Midianite prostitute, while Moses and all the multitude of the children of Israel looked on, weeping before the entrance of the tabernacle. When Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw this, he rose from the midst of the multitude; and, taking a dagger, he went in after the Israelite man into the brothel and pierced them both together—the man, that is, [Col. 0908D] and the woman in their genital parts. And the plague ceased among the children of Israel.”

Behold, that whole generation—all who had been numbered from twenty years old and upward—was consumed by seven plagues.

The first plague was at the Graves of Craving, where, while the meat was still in their teeth and that kind of food had not yet failed, “behold, the wrath of the Lord was aroused, and he struck him with an exceedingly great plague” (Num. XI).

The second plague was where Korah, Dathan, and Abiram perished by an unprecedented death of men, and God did a new thing: opening its mouth, the earth swallowed them and all that belonged to them, and they went down alive into hell (Num. XVI).

The third plague was on the same day, when fire came forth from the Lord and killed two hundred and fifty men who [Col. 0909A] were offering incense (ibid.).

The fourth plague was on the following day, upon those who murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying, “You have killed the people of the Lord”; and fourteen thousand seven hundred men were struck down, apart from those who had perished in the rebellion of Korah (ibid.).

The fifth plague was when, as they went around the land of Edom, the people began to be weary of the journey and its labor. They spoke against the Lord and Moses, and for this reason the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people (Num. XXI).

The sixth plague was this punishment of all the leaders of the people, whom the Lord commanded to be hung “before the sun on gibbets” for the crime of Baal-peor (Num. XXV).

The seventh plague was that by which Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, at last turned away the Lord’s wrath from the children of Israel: “striking the Israelite man [Col. 0909B] Zimri, namely a leader from the kindred and tribe of Simeon, together with the Midianite prostitute, namely Cozbi, daughter of Zur, a most noble chief of the Midianites” (ibid.), piercing them both together, “the man, that is, and the woman in their genital parts.”

By these seven plagues, I say, those were consumed who had been numbered in the last plagues, after the ten plagues of Egypt. In correspondence with the number of those plagues, John also describes in the Apocalypse seven last plagues: “for in them,” he says, “the wrath of God is completed” (Rev. XV). By this sevenfold number of plagues he signifies the totality of plagues by which God destroys those who, already enrolled by name in the Church, confess that they know God but deny him by their deeds (Titus I), and are unworthy to receive the land of promise, the land of the living, “in the [Col. 0909C] measuring-line of allotment” (Ps. LXXVII).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the second numbering of the children of Israel.

(Chap. XXVI.) After these things the children of Israel are again numbered, the Lord likewise commanding that all, “from twenty years old and upward, by their houses and kindreds, who were able to go forth to war,” be counted; and the total was almost restored. For in the first enumeration, “the whole number of the children of Israel,” he says, “by their houses and families, who were able to go forth to war, was six hundred and three thousand five hundred and fifty men” (Num. I). In this second enumeration likewise, “the total,” he says, “of the children of Israel who were counted is this: six hundred thousand and one thousand seven hundred and thirty.”

And afterward: “This,” he says, “is the number of the children of Israel who were enrolled by Moses and Eleazar the priest in the plains of Moab above the Jordan, opposite Jericho; among them there was none of those who had previously been numbered by Moses and Aaron in the wilderness of Sinai.” These enter the land, after vengeance has first been taken upon the Midianites. Moses says in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Arm from among yourselves men for battle, who may exact the Lord’s vengeance upon the Midianites. Let a thousand men from each tribe be chosen from Israel and sent to war” (Num. XXXI).

Not one of them fell in battle, as the victorious men rejoice in saying to Moses: “Your servants have counted the number of the warriors whom we had under our command, and not even one is missing. Therefore we offer as gifts to the Lord, each one of us, whatever gold we have been able to find in the spoil” (ibid.) [Col. 0910A].

Thus, in the present Church, the fall of many becomes the rising of others, as Scripture says in the book of Job: “He will crush many and innumerable persons, and set others in their place. For he knows their works; therefore he will bring in the night and they shall be crushed. He struck them as wicked men in the sight of beholders” (Job XXXIV), etc. Knowing this, the Apostle also said, since indeed no one ought to be secure while he remains in this life: “I do not consider that I have attained it” (Phil. III).

In the present Church there is a loss among those called whenever those who seemed to stand fall. But in that heavenly Church, beyond doubt, the number of the elect, foreknown and predestined before all ages, shall be completed and shall remain whole [Col. 0910B]. And it should be noted that not all who are here numbered a second time take vengeance upon the Midianites, but the chosen: a thousand from every tribe, that is, twelve thousand equipped for battle. For not all who are to be saved will also judge; rather, a few judges will sit upon thrones (Matt. XIX), and those who have not been judged, or who are to be judged, will not judge. The greater number, however, will be judged and saved through judgment.

The Psalm also speaks of the judges, under the likeness of combatants, according to the present passage: “The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands” (Ps. CXLIX), etc. The slaughter of the Midianites signifies the punishment of those who, having been judged, will be sent into eternal fire. Let us now pass over those things which are sufficiently plain in themselves and have already been stated elsewhere, and proceed with the rest.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the vow of a man, of a married woman, and of one still of maidenly age.

(Chap. XXX.) “This is the word which the Lord commanded. If any man makes a vow, or binds himself by an oath, he shall not make his word void, but shall fulfill everything that he promised. If a woman makes some vow and binds herself by an oath while she is in her father’s house and still of maidenly age, and if her father learns of the vow which she has promised and of the oath by which she has bound her soul, and remains silent, she shall be bound by her vow,” etc.

The Holy Spirit indeed suggests to all the counsel of salvation in the Psalm, and commands the keeping of one’s purpose, saying: “Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him” [Col. 0910D] (Ps. LXXV). Yet in this very matter, if you truly strive to please him who is “terrible, and who takes away the spirit of princes” (ibid.), the greatest discernment is necessary. For what if you yourself cannot lawfully be under your own authority? How may you fulfill what you were not permitted even to vow?

Therefore, whoever you are, devout soul, you must not lack the authority of this law. “If a woman,” he says, “makes some vow and binds herself by an oath,” etc. And afterward: “But if, as soon as he hears it, her father contradicts it, both her vows and her oaths shall be void, and she shall not be held liable for the promise, because her father contradicted it.”

Accordingly, whoever is under the governance of a superior: it is good to make a vow and to have pious devotion; but whatever you do without permission from your spiritual father will be reckoned as presumption and vain glory, not as reward. The mature judgment of the venerable Fathers did not pronounce this sentence without cause; it was drawn from this fountain of the law and flowed from the vein of this present passage.

For what is a soul living under the care of a prelate, professing under another’s authority to render to God the due service of obedience, except a daughter placed in her father’s house and still of maidenly age? “If therefore, as soon as he hears it, her father contradicts it, both her vows and her oaths shall be void.” Even if she has deemed the ground unworthy of her feet and flown into heaven, her father will hold her foot and draw her down as long as he thinks fit [Col. 0911A].

“If she has a husband and makes some vow, and a word once issued from her mouth has bound her soul by an oath, on the day when her husband hears it and does not contradict it, she shall be bound by her vow and shall fulfill whatever she promised. But if, on hearing it, he immediately contradicts it and makes her promises void, together with the words by which she bound her soul, God will be merciful to her,” etc.

Not content to state this law concerning a married woman once, Scripture repeats it a third time. Accordingly, it has such force also in carnal matters that the Apostle did not hesitate to say: “Let the husband render to the wife what is due, and likewise the wife to the husband. The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does” (I Cor. VII), etc. He declared this under the authority of the present law: namely, that if a woman has made a vow and bound herself by an oath to afflict her soul through fasting and abstinence from other things, or something of this sort, it is within her husband’s discretion whether she does or does not do it. Since such a vow does the husband no injury, still more, if she has vowed continence—which may provide the husband an occasion for adultery—it shall be within the husband’s discretion.

“But if the husband, hearing it, remains silent and postpones his decision until the next day, she shall fulfill whatever she vowed and promised, because as soon as he heard it he was silent.” Why? Clearly, because to have kept silent is to have approved. And approval is almost to have vowed. Therefore she shall fulfill it, because unquestionably both owe it.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the forty-two encampments of the children of Israel.

(Chap. XXXIII.) Finally, in the last part of this book of Numbers, which among the Hebrews is called [Col. 0911D] *Vagedaber* (“And he spoke”), it is written: “These are the encampments of the children of Israel, who departed from the land of Egypt by their companies under the hand of Moses and Aaron,” etc. This catalogue of encampments, forty-two in number from the first to the last, corresponding to the equal number of Christ’s generations—what mystery it contains has been discussed more fully by the blessed man Jerome. Therefore the subject does not require our own composition; nevertheless, we shall set down the mystical interpretations of each name according to him.

“They departed,” he says, “from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month,” etc. Rameses is interpreted by some as “turbulent agitation,” or “bitterness,” or “the agitation of a moth”; but we, he says, judge that it is more truly rendered “the thunder of joy.”

The second encampment was at Succoth, which means “booths” or “tents,” because they first pitched their tents there. The place accordingly took its name from this fact, and for this reason the solemnity of Tabernacles is on the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

The third encampment was at Etham, meaning “strength and perfection”; and David sings of it: “You broke apart the rivers of Etham” (Ps. LXXIII), that is, the strong ones.

The fourth encampment was opposite Pihahiroth, looking toward Baal-zephon before Migdol. Pihahiroth means “mouth of nobles”; Baal-zephon, “lord of the north”; Migdol, “greatness” or “tower.”

The fifth encampment was at Marah, meaning “bitterness.” The sixth was at Elim, rendered “rams and strong men.” The seventh was at the Red Sea. One asks how, after the crossing of the Red Sea, Marah, and Elim mentioned above [Col. 0912B], they came again to the Red Sea, unless perhaps, as they proceeded on their journey, they encountered an inlet of the sea beside which they encamped. For it is one thing to cross through the sea and another to pitch tents nearby.

The eighth encampment was in the wilderness of Sin, though according to the order of Exodus it is the seventh. Sin means “a thorn-bush” or “hatred,” both of which suit mystical meanings: after we have come to the place from which the Lord is to speak to us, we may deserve the great hatred of the enemy and see the bush burning yet not consumed—that is, illumined by the fire of the Holy Spirit, who gives light and does not burn up; or even be inflamed by persecutions, yet not perish, since the Lord is in it.

The ninth encampment was at Dophkah, meaning “knocking,” according to the Lord’s saying: “Knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. VII).

The tenth encampment was at Alush, which is not found in Exodus and is believed to be included within the wilderness of Sin. That same book says: “The whole multitude of the children of Israel departed from the wilderness of Sin by their encampments, according to the command of the Lord, and came to Rephidim” (Exod. XVII). From this it is clear that several encampments are indicated by the name of one region. Alush means “leaven,” namely that which “a woman took and mixed with three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matt. XIII).

The eleventh encampment was at Rephidim, meaning “weakening of the strong” or “relaxation of the hands.” There Moses went up the mountain, and while Joshua fought Amalek, he sat upon a stone so that his hands should not grow weary [Col. 0912D].

The twelfth encampment was in the wilderness of Sinai. There are described the middle part of Exodus, the entire book of Leviticus, not a few commands of Numbers, the distribution of the people tribe by tribe, and the offerings of the leaders. Sinai means “thorn-bushes”: not one, as above in the wilderness of Sin, but many. For since it is the twelfth encampment and belongs to the number of the apostles, there is a beginning there, but here perfection; there a solitary number, here a multiple one. It is one thing to possess one grace and another to possess many.

The thirteenth encampment was at the Graves of Craving, where those who murmured received quails and devoured them to nausea and vomiting.

The fourteenth encampment was at Hazeroth, rendered “courts,” [Col. 0913A] where Aaron and Miriam murmured against Moses because of his Ethiopian wife.

The fifteenth encampment was at Rithmah. It should be noted that the remaining eighteen encampments, whose catalogue is now briefly described—from Rithmah through Ezion-gaber, that is, through the thirty-second encampment—are included under the name of the wilderness of Paran. In them we recognize all the events recorded as having happened at different times. Rithmah means “sound” or “juniper.” This wood is said to preserve fire for a long time, so that if embers are covered by its ashes, they endure for as much as a year. From this we learn that after the Graves of Craving and the vestibules, we should pass to the wood which retains heat for a long time, so that we may be fervent in spirit, and with clear sound and a voice raised on high preach the Gospel of the Lord.

The sixteenth encampment was at Rimmon-perez, meaning “division of a pomegranate,” which others call a “granate apple.” The fruit of this tree is understood in Scripture in two ways: either as the bosom of the Church, which covers the whole multitude of believers with its rind; or as the diversity and harmony of virtues, in accordance with what is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). Thus the individual ranks are divided, so that all are held together in the same structure.

The seventeenth encampment was at Libnah, which we may render “brick,” namely the making of which caused the people serving in Egypt to groan. From this we learn that on the journey of this life we now grow from one state into another, now diminish; and that after the ecclesiastical order we often pass over to the work of bricks [Col. 0913C].

The eighteenth encampment was at Rissah, rendered “bridles.” For if after progress we again descend to works of mud, we must be bridled, and our wandering and headlong course directed by the nets of the Scriptures.

The nineteenth encampment was at Kehelathah, meaning “Church.” The wandering steps of those who run are drawn back with bridles to the Church, and they hasten to enter once more the doors which they had earlier left.

The twentieth encampment was at Mount Shepher, meaning “beauty.” See what benefit bridles bring: they draw us back from vices and lead us into the choirs of virtues, so that they make us dwell in Christ, the most beautiful mountain.

The twenty-first encampment was at Haradah, rendered “wonder” [Col. 0913D]. How beautiful is the order of progress, how excellent the fabric of believers! After brickwork we are bridled; after bridles we are brought into the Church; after dwelling in the Church we ascend to Christ the mountain, where, standing, we are astonished and marvel, so that our speech is surpassed in his praises.

The twenty-second encampment was at Moseroth, rendered “assemblies,” of which we may say: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. CXXXII). Likewise: God, “who makes those of one manner dwell in a house” (Ps. LXVII).

The twenty-third encampment was at Tahath, rendered “fear”—the fear urged by the Apostle: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. XI); “for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” [Col. 0914A] (I Pet. V).

The twenty-fourth encampment was at Terah. By this word, and with the same letters, Abraham’s father is designated; he is said to have obtained the name of a driver-away or repeller because he drove off crows which were devastating the grain of men. Therefore let us also imitate Terah, carefully preventing the birds of heaven, which hasten to devour the wheat sown beside the way, from doing so.

The twenty-fifth encampment was at Mithkah, rendered “sweetness,” namely that of which the Psalm says: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII).

The twenty-sixth encampment was at Hashmonah, which in our language means “haste,” by which, pressing onward to what lies ahead, we forget the things behind and stretch ourselves toward those to come.

The twenty-seventh encampment was at Moseroth, meaning “bonds” or “discipline”: bonds, I say, of the kind of which the prophet says: “And the Sabeans,” he says, “tall men, shall pass over to you and be yours; they shall walk after you, bound with manacles” (Isa. XLV). We remain in these bonds while we hasten in swift course to teachers and wear down their thresholds, occupied with precepts of virtue and the mysteries of the Scriptures [Col. 0914B].

The twenty-eighth encampment was at Bene-jaakan, rendered “sons of necessity” or “of gnashing,” such as those concerning whom you may say with Zion: “I am barren and do not bear; I have been removed and carried captive—and who has reared these? I was left bereft and alone; where were these?” (Isa. XLIX). Refer “sons of gnashing” to the sense that, through fear of punishment and of that place where there is gnashing of teeth and weeping (Matt. VIII), they forsake the devil and hasten to be born again in Christ.

The twenty-ninth encampment was at Mount Gidgad, meaning “messenger” or “expedition,” or indeed, what is truer, “cutting”: that we may not keep our sword from blood, as the prophet says: “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently, and who keeps his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII)—that is, from devouring the flesh and killing the vices of the flesh.

The thirtieth encampment was at Jotbathah, meaning “goodness,” so that, when we have come to a perfect man in the priestly rank, we may imitate him who said: “I am the good Shepherd. The good Shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X).

The thirty-first encampment was at Abronah, meaning “passing” or “passage.” By this word it is signified, if we wish to gather examples from all the Scriptures to prove it, that we do not have here an abiding city (Heb. XIII), but must pass “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, unto the house of God” [Col. 0914D] (Ps. XLI).

The thirty-second encampment was at Ezion-gaber, rendered “woods of a man,” such as we are in the hand of God our craftsman, who makes different vessels that are necessary in a great house (II Tim. II). Up to this point is the wilderness of Paran, containing eighteen encampments, which are not set out in the catalogue of the earlier journey.

The thirty-third encampment was in the wilderness of Zin: this is Kadesh. One asks why the eighth encampment is now said to be the thirty-third. But one must know that the former is written with the letter *samech* and means “thorn-bush” or “hatred,” whereas this one is written with *tsade* and means [Col. 0915A] “command.” And the word Kadesh joined to it does not mean “holy,” as most suppose, but “changed” or “transferred.” In Genesis, according to the Hebrew truth, we read that when Judah, supposing Tamar to be a prostitute, sends gifts, the messenger entrusted with the gifts asks where the *cadosa*—that is, the prostitute whose dress differed from that of other women—was (Gen. XXXVIII). We find the same thing in many places.

But if Kadesh means “holy,” it must be understood by antiphrasis, as the Fates are called *Parcae* from their least sparing, and “war” from its not being war, and a “grove” from its not shining.

The thirty-fourth encampment was at Mount Hor, which most interpret as “light.” By this name the place is shown worthy through the merits of the priest, at least according to his own person; for, according to the mysteries, his death signifies the destruction of the Jewish priesthood.

The thirty-fifth encampment was at Zalmonah, meaning “little image.” The thirty-sixth was at Punon, meaning “little mouth” (*os*, “mouth,” not *os*, “bone”). These two encampments, the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth, are not found in the historical sequence. Instead, it is written of them: “They departed from Mount Hor by the way of the Red Sea, in order to go around the land of Edom.” From this it is shown that they were situated at the borders and around the land of Edom.

According to the name Zalmonah, the passion of the Son of God—the true and express image—is preserved by contemplating it; and at Punon, what the heart believes is uttered by the mouth, as one reads in the Apostle: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” [Col. 0915C] (Rom. X).

The thirty-seventh encampment was at Oboth, rendered “magicians” or “pythons,” such as those who fought against Moses and Aaron. When we live among scorpions yet overcome their poisons, we have surely encamped at Oboth.

The thirty-eighth encampment was at Iye-abarim, meaning “heaps of stones of those passing by.” Of such stones it is written: “Holy stones are rolled over the earth” (Zech. IX). Yet there are others whom the prophet commands to be removed from the way (Jer. L), lest the feet of those walking through this world and hastening to pass on to other encampments should stumble over them.

The thirty-ninth encampment was at Dibon-gad, meaning “temptation understood strongly,” by which we understand that we ought not to raise ourselves in pride. For before destruction the heart is lifted up, and before glory it is humbled.

The fortieth encampment was at Almon-diblathaim, meaning “in contempt of wounds or reproaches.” By it we learn that every sweetness and enticement of pleasures in this world must be despised, and that we ought not to be drunk with wine, in which are the reproaches of debauchery (Eph. V) [Col. 0915D].

The forty-first encampment was in the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo. “In the mountains,” he says, “of Abarim,” meaning “of those passing over”: namely, although he may be in the mountains of virtues, the citizen of heaven still remains in need so long as he is a pilgrim here. Nebo means “ending,” namely that in which the Law comes to an end and its memory is not found. But the grace of the Gospel extends without any end.

The forty-second and final encampment was in the plains of Moab. Let us briefly recount what took place there.

## CHAPTER XXXII. A brief account of the events that occurred at the final, that is, the forty-second, encampment.

While the people was dwelling there, it was blessed by the divine Balaam, whom Balak son of Zippor had hired for payment; God’s blessing overcame the curse and turned it into praise. It heard the Lord’s voice sounding from a profane mouth: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel, and [Col. 0916A] shall strike the chiefs of Moab and lay waste all the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be his inheritance” (Num. XXIV).

It committed fornication with the daughters of Midian; and Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, zealous with the Lord’s zeal, pierced Zimri and the Midianite prostitute with a dagger (Num. XXV). Hence he also received as a reward, for everlasting remembrance, the belly of the victim. The people is numbered again, and the Levites are also numbered, so that, after the wicked have been killed, a new people of God may be enrolled (Num. XXVI).

The five sons of Zelophehad appeal and, by the Lord’s judgment, receive an inheritance, so that even the female sex may not be excluded from the Lord’s possession among their brothers (Num. XXVII). Joshua succeeds Moses on the mountain (ibid.) and learns from the Law what he ought spiritually to offer in the Church: first, what is to be offered each day; what on the Sabbath; what at the calends; what at Passover; what at Pentecost (Num. XXVIII); what at the new moon of the first month; what on the fast of the tenth day of that month; what at the Feast of Tabernacles, when the tabernacles are pitched, on the fifteenth day of the aforesaid month (Num. [Col. 0916C] XXIX).

The vows of wives and daughters made without the authorization of fathers and husbands are declared void (Num. XXX). There follow the war against the Midianites (Num. XXXI), the death of the divine Balaam, the division of the spoil, and an offering from it in the tabernacle of God (ibid.). Reuben and Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, are the first to receive a possession around the Jordan in the wilderness (Num. XXXII). For they had very many cattle and had not yet reached the point at which they could dwell with the Temple.

The people is instructed to destroy idols in the holy land and to leave none of the former inhabitants alive (ibid.). The province is formerly described by its boundaries, and the inheritance of the two and a half tribes is set apart. The leaders of the tribes who are to enter the holy land are numbered (Num. XXXIV).

The Levites receive forty-two cities with their surrounding pasturelands extending a thousand paces in every direction, equal in number to these encampments; and they receive six further cities of refuge, three on this side of the Jordan and three beyond the Jordan, making forty-eight in all. There are regulations as to who is to be received as a fugitive, who is to be put to death, and who is to be preserved until the death of the high priest (Num. XXXV, XXXVI).

Deuteronomy follows: the second law of those who meditate on the Gospel. There we learn briefly what Moses spoke to the people between Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and the places of gold, after the rejection of most faithless Judah—an eleven-day journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir as far as Kadesh-barnea. At the end he sings the song in which the Synagogue is most plainly cast off and the Church joined to the Lord. The children of Israel are blessed; and again, in Simeon, pitiable Judah is cast off [Col. 0917A].

“O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways beyond tracing out!” (Rom. XI.) “Who is wise, and shall understand these things? Who is discerning, and shall know them? For the ways of the Lord are right, and the righteous shall walk in them, but transgressors shall fall in them” (Hos. XIV).

# The Forty-Two Books of R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, On the Trinity and Its Works: On Deuteronomy

## Book One. (Deut., chapters I–XXV.)

[Col. 0917]

### CHAPTER I. On Deuteronomy and the Song of Deuteronomy, and on their being, as it were, second and third witnesses.

This book is entitled Deuteronomy, that is, “the second law.” Very briefly, moreover, in the Song of the same Deuteronomy, all things from Israel’s departure out of Egypt are counted and weighed. Why is this? Clearly because judgment is prepared for the Lord, and sufficient testimonies must be provided for those who are to stand before his tribunal and be judged by the Law—I mean, indeed, against those who do not listen to the Law when it accuses them.

For the Law itself says: “One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever the sin or crime may be; but every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. XIX). And lest you suppose that this requires no repetition of words [Col. 0917C] spoken or deeds done, but only a number of persons, the Apostle Paul, after saying, “Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you” (II Cor. XIII), immediately added: “Every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (ibid.).

Therefore Moses, about to accuse all transgressors, establishes every word in the mouth not merely of one witness but of two—indeed, of three—when, after the written Law, he writes Deuteronomy and then the Song of Deuteronomy. Two witnesses convict by reading; you, O transgressing Jews, are the third witness, convicting yourselves by taking heed, so that you may have no excuse for your sin. This Deuteronomy begins thus.

### CHAPTER II. That at the beginning of this book the ten temptations are enumerated more obscurely.

[Col. 0917D] **CHAPTER I.** These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness plain, opposite the Red Sea, between Paran and Tophel and [Col. 0918B] Laban, and Hazeroth, where there is much gold; eleven days’ journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir, as far as Kadesh-barnea. It is as though he said: These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the wilderness plain, opposite the Red Sea, between Paran and Tophel, and Laban, and Hazeroth, and the abundance of gold: an eleven-day journey from Horeb by way of Mount Seir, as far as Kadesh-barnea. These are the words by which Moses rebuked the children of Israel for the ten temptations by which they tested the Lord. Hence the Lord says in the book of Numbers: “Yet all the men who have seen my majesty and the signs which I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tested me now ten times, and have not obeyed my voice, shall not see the land concerning which I swore to their fathers” (Num. 14).

[Col. 0918C] Moses here briefly and obscurely enumerates these temptations when he says, “in the wilderness,” thereby indicating that, because of the lack of water, they tested the Lord twice. Moreover, the phrase “in the wilderness plain, opposite the Red Sea, between Paran and Tophel and Laban and Hazeroth, where there is much gold,” should be understood thus. The children of Israel are said to have murmured against the Lord in the plain opposite the Red Sea because they did not believe Moses when he told them, by the word of the Lord, that the Egyptians had been destroyed; rather, they feared that the Egyptians were pursuing them. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Our fathers in Egypt did not understand thy wonders; they did not remember the multitude of thy mercies, and they provoked thee as they went up to the Red Sea” (Ps. 105).

Now *Paran* means “wild ass”; *Tophel*, “folly”; *Laban*, [Col. 0918D] “white.” This is to be understood as follows: the children of Israel, having become like a wild ass, acted foolishly, testing the Lord twice concerning the white thing—that is, concerning [Col. 0919A] manna. Manna is called white, as in Exodus: “And the house of Israel called its name Man; it was like white coriander seed” (Exod. 16). The same ten temptations have already been discussed in Exodus.

**CHAPTER III. That the very manner of expression in this book, by deliberate purpose, invites the hearer to love.**

And Moses began to expound the law, saying: “The Lord our God spoke to us at Horeb, saying: ‘You have dwelt long enough on this mountain,’” etc. This exposition of the law is a brief and lucid recollection of nearly everything that was said or done separately and in scattered places. Everywhere it breathes the great, abundant, and attentive love of the man who was meek above all men dwelling on earth, [Col. 0919B] evidently aiming to raise the goodwill of his hearers upward toward the Lord. For, while expounding it, after recalling many great benefits, he says: “And now, Israel, hear the commandments and judgments which I teach you, that by doing them you may live and, entering in, possess the land which the Lord God of your fathers will give you” (Deut. 4). And afterwards: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God is one God. You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6).

Likewise, after some further matters: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you, except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with your whole heart and [Col. 0919C] whole soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances which I command you today, that it may be well with you? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that is in them, belong to the Lord your God; and yet the Lord clung to your fathers and loved them, and chose their seed after them—that is, you—from all nations, as is demonstrated today. Therefore circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Deut. 10), etc.

In expounding thus, he employs so great and so painstaking an art of sweetness throughout that you cannot doubt that this book is especially one of those beds of spices of which it was said in praise of the Bridegroom: “His cheeks are like beds of spices, planted by perfumers” (Cant. 5). For the learned perfumer who plants the whole bed of this Scripture strives to delight the reader by drawing him through sight and fragrance, so that, by the beauty of God’s benefits, he may invite every conscience to love him. And now, although many things may profitably be said from these passages, and many more—and higher things than we can grasp or attain—yet, because we have touched upon each matter in its proper place, let us now run briefly through a few chief points of this book, omitting the rest: namely, those in which there is a promise of Christ, the Son of God, or his coming.

**CHAPTER IV. Concerning the words, “A prophet from your nation,” etc.; and what, according to this passage, the Lord God spoke concerning himself.**

(Chapter 18.) “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brethren, like me; [Col. 0920A] you shall hear him, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and you said: ‘I shall no longer hear the voice of the Lord my God, nor see this great fire again, lest I die.’”

There is no doubt that this great prophet is Christ himself, the Son of God: the Prophet and the Lord of the prophets; for he is both man and God. Scripture does not expressly say how Israel asked for him on Mount Horeb, except that, when they saw the voices and lights, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain, terrified and shaken with fear, they stood far off and said to Moses: “Speak to us, and we will hear; let not the Lord speak to us, lest perhaps we die” (Exod. 20). Therefore God, considering not their words but their necessity, regarded that utterance itself as a request, since to ask for a Mediator was precisely to ask that God should speak in this manner.

Accordingly, when he had said, “The Lord your God will now raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brethren, like me,” he immediately added, “You shall hear him, as you asked of the Lord [Col. 0920B] God at Horeb.” That is, you will be able to hear him, as you asked that God’s speech might become audible and bearable for you; for he, having the fiery majesty of divinity covered by the cloud of flesh, will speak to you.

Further, so that those Jews—Jewish rulers and experts in the law—who did not receive him might be especially without excuse at the coming of this prophet, he offers them such a sign or test: “If you answer in silent thought, ‘How can I know the word which the Lord has not spoken?’ you shall have this sign: whatever that prophet predicts in the name of the Lord, and it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet invented it through the swelling pride of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him” (ibid.).

Knowing that this had been written concerning himself, this Prophet says in his Gospel against the calumniators among the Jews: “For the works which the Father gave me to accomplish—the very works which I do—bear testimony concerning me that the Father sent me” (John 5). And elsewhere: “The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself; but the Father abiding in me, he does the works” (John 14). It is as though he said: The subsequent works—the works of my Father, which no one else has done—bear witness to my words that I did not invent them from my own heart, as did the false prophets against whom Scripture warned us.

Your law says that this shall be [Col. 0920C] the sign of the great prophet whom, according to that same law, you must in every respect hear: “Whatever that prophet predicts in the name of the Lord and it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet invented it through the swelling pride of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him.” But concerning him “in whose mouth I place my words,” he says, “whoever refuses to hear him, I myself shall exact vengeance” (Exod. 20). Therefore, since the present testimony of works makes it clear that I am that prophet who was to be raised up according to God’s promise—since there is not in me the sign of a prophet inventing words through pride of mind—he himself will exact vengeance, because you refuse to hear.

**CHAPTER V.** [Col. 0921A] **On the setting apart of cities of refuge, and on the spiritual meaning of the death of the priest.**

(Chapter 19.) “When the Lord your God has destroyed the nations whose land he will give you, and you have possessed it and dwelt in their cities and houses, you shall set apart three cities in the midst of the land which the Lord your God will give you as a possession. Carefully preparing the road, you shall divide the entire territory of your land equally into three parts, so that whoever has fled because of homicide may have a nearby place to which he may escape.”

Here it is plainly given to understand that the one who has shed blood unwillingly must remain in the cities of refuge until the death of the priest, and return to his own land after that priest has died. Here, I say, it is given to understand that this great prophet is that great priest. What, then, is it to remain in the city of refuge until the death of this great priest, our great Prophet, except to do penance in faith in the passion of this Christ, the Son of God? For if he is found outside the boundaries of the cities assigned to exiles, he will be killed by [Col. 0921B] the avenger of blood; “for the fugitive ought to have remained in the city until the death of the high priest” (Num. 35). That is, if one departs from the present life without baptism in the name of Christ Jesus, he will be condemned, as that Prophet foretold; for he ought to have fixed the bounds of his search for salvation in his death alone.

What, then, are these three cities, equally distant from one another, except faith, hope, and love, the three principal virtues? And indeed, although there are three, “love is greater than these” (1 Cor. 13); yet they are equally distant from one another because none of them is more or less necessary for salvation.

But it immediately follows: “This shall be the law for the homicide who flees, whose life is to be preserved: one who strikes his neighbour unwittingly, and is proved to have had no hatred against him yesterday or the day before, but simply went with him into the forest to cut wood; and, while cutting wood in turn, the axe flies from his hand, and the iron slips from the handle, strikes his companion, and kills him.” We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn with any neighbour to consider our sins. We cut down wood simply when, with a devout intention, we prune the vices of those who sin. But the axe flies from the hand when rebuke carries itself into severity [Col. 0921C] beyond what is necessary. The iron leaps from the handle when an overly harsh word slips out in correction and, striking the friend, kills him: that is, when an insult uttered kills one’s hearer’s spirit of love. For the mind of the corrected person suddenly rushes into hatred if immoderate rebuke constrains it more than it ought.

But the person who imprudently strikes the wood and destroys his neighbour must flee to the three cities, so that, defended in one of them, he may live. For if, turning to penitential lamentation, he is hidden in the unity of the sacrament under faith, hope, and love, he is not held guilty of the homicide he committed; and the kinsman of the slain person, even if he finds him, does not kill him. For when the strict Judge comes—the one who joined himself to us through sharing our nature—he undoubtedly does not demand from him vengeance for the guilt of sin whom hope, faith, and love conceal beneath his pardon. Therefore a fault not committed from deliberate malice is more readily forgiven.

What then? Are only those sins which we commit unwillingly or unknowingly erased by Christ’s death? Certainly, the one who kills unwillingly is the one who does not will the very thing that he kills; he does not will, I say, and does not know what he kills, when the very thing he has killed displeases him, when what he has done displeases him. But the person to whom what he did or was does not displease, who does not perform true repentance from the heart—Christ’s death, the death of the great priest, does him no good, even though he flee to the aforesaid cities: that is, even though he says that he believes in Christ, presumes that he hopes, and confesses that he loves the Lord.

**CHAPTER VI.** [Col. 0922B] **On burying the body of one hanged on a gibbet, and on the words, “Accursed by God is he who hangs upon the wood.”**

(Chapter 21.) “When a man has sinned in a matter punishable by death, has been sentenced to death, and has been hanged on a gibbet, his corpse shall not remain on the wood, but shall be buried on the same day, because he who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God; and you shall not defile your land which the Lord your God has given you as a possession.”

Those who know that the law plainly said this—friends of the law, or rather corrupters of the law and enemies of God—cunningly hanged on a gibbet the foretold great prophet, the great priest of whom it had been sung, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21), so that it might consequently be established that he was accursed by God and therefore that this man, according to their judgment or accusation, was not from God.

But, O Jews, blinded by malice: he indeed became accursed, for the Apostle also says this. Our Lord, I say, became the curse of the law in order to redeem us from the curse (Gal. 3). Yet is hanging on the wood, according to the words of the law, the antecedent cause of the curse? Not to mention that it does not say, “When a man sentenced to death has been hanged on a gibbet,” but first states, “When a man has sinned in a matter punishable by death,” and only then adds, “and, having been sentenced to death, was hanged on a gibbet”—not to mention, I say, that this manifestly clears our Lord of the curse, since he was indeed hanged on the wood but did not sin in a matter deserving death.

Does it say, “He who hangs on the wood is accursed by God”? Does it pronounce a curse, saying “May he be accursed,” or simply “Accursed,” so that the verb “may he be” may be understood as the word of one cursing? Or does it not rather make a statement, saying, “He who hangs upon the wood is accursed by God”—not because he hangs, but he who hangs upon the wood? For the text of the Hebrew truth is not as the Seventy translated it, since they did not perfectly possess God’s meaning; they were not prophets but translators. Therefore in this matter, as in many others, they did not translate fully: “Accursed is everyone who hangs upon the wood,” whereas the Hebrew reads: “Accursed by God is he who hangs upon the wood.”

Indeed, this translation differs from the truth in three respects. For where the Hebrew says, “is accursed,” they translated the absolute “accursed,” so that “may he be” can be understood. Again, the Hebrew adds “by God,” which is absent from the Septuagint; while, conversely, the Septuagint adds “everyone,” which is not found in the Hebrew.

Why then, you ask, did the Apostle use their translation in this statement? For he says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Accursed is everyone who hangs upon the wood’” (Gal. 3). Why did he employ this quotation? Clearly because the edition of the Seventy Interpreters had been current among the Greeks to whom he wrote from the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus; and, when he asserted that the Scriptures bore witness to Christ, it would have been excessively troublesome—indeed, he would scarcely have been heard—if he had also attempted to show that the Scriptures themselves had been badly translated, since the authority of the Seventy Interpreters was held in the highest renown among them. He therefore preferred to cite the statement with a meaning that would edify rather than offend longstanding readers by correcting the Scripture.

Moreover, the intention of this same declaration of curse may better be seen from the fact that it commands him to be buried because he is “accursed by God.” Is burial not a share in blessing for the dead, and, conversely, is being deprived of burial like a donkey not a curse? Thus it was terribly said of a certain king, as he deserved: “With the burial of a donkey—that is, with no burial—he shall be buried” (Jer. 22). Did not holy and great men, the fathers and patriarchs, carefully direct that their bodies be buried, even transferred; and did they not regard burial as a great thing, not merely anywhere, but in the tombs of their fathers?

O marvellous and ancient plan of this Crucified One! So long before he came, he gave a command concerning the burial of his body in such a way that the legal command, written for himself alone, benefited all who were crucified. For while it was permitted without penalty to throw to dogs, unburied, those beheaded, stoned, or killed by some other violence, the prophetic law—written, as it were, by God’s finger—forbade burial to be denied to those crucified, on account of this one who was to be crucified.

Was not, then, the prophetic Spirit of Christ’s own crucifixion roaring with unutterable groanings in the heart of Moses as he wrote such a law, so that, while all crucified persons were buried by law, this one Crucified for the salvation of the world, accursed [Col. 0923D] by God, might not be deprived of burial? It should be noted, as has already been said, that it does not say as a curse, “May he be accursed,” but, giving the reason why he should be buried the same day, declares, “because he is accursed,” adding also “by God,” which it does nowhere among all the curses of the law. For example, when it says: “You shall be accursed in the city, accursed in the field, accursed in your entering, accursed in your going out” (Deut. 28), and similarly in the rest, it nowhere says “by God,” except only in this place.

Why is this, unless because this one alone is truly accursed by God—in that, as the prophet says, “God placed upon him the iniquities of us all” (Isa. 53)? “Therefore,” it says, “let him who hangs upon the wood be buried, because one who hangs upon the wood is to come who will be accursed by God”—by God, I say, transferring onto him the curses of the human race.
