If someone objects that curses have often been uttered by God—for example, when he says to Cain, “Now therefore you are accursed from the earth, which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand” (Gen. 4)—we reply, on the contrary, that this is not the pouring out of a curse, but the declaration of a curse already existing. This is especially clear because he does not say, “May you be accursed,” but “You are accursed”; and not “by me,” but by your sins. Cain was not accursed by God, but by his brother’s blood crying from the ground and declaring Cain’s impieties to God himself.

Therefore this one alone was accursed by God and not by his own sin: by God, I say, who placed upon him the curse of us all that was upon us—that is, all our iniquity. The law did not add without the marvellous art of the Holy Spirit: “And you shall not defile the land which the Lord [Col. 0924B] your God will give you as a possession.” It said and wrote this even though the land might instead seem defiled if it received into itself the body of one accursed.

What then? What does the writer of the law mean in this place also? Surely this: the land which God gave to the true Israel as a possession is the body of this one uniquely and for our sake accursed. Israel did not then defile the body given to it—did not allow it to be defiled—when Joseph and Nicodemus buried it on the same day, according to the common law concerning all who hung on the wood: namely, lest it should be shamefully cast away unburied and, by those dogs who had surrounded it while living, be spat upon even when lifeless. They, however, thought that their land was not defiled if the body of anyone so killed was not exposed to the eyes of the living.

If anyone further asks why the lawgiver was so greatly concerned for this, since the most holy body could have been guarded from heaven even if unburied, just as many bodies of martyrs were preserved from harm by dogs or birds, let us ask him why, when the same Lord died and the earth shook, the tombs of the saints were opened (Matt. 27). Either no adequate answer, or this answer alone, will plainly be given: it was expedient for the bodies of the dead that the body of this dead man, which brought the resurrection of the dead, should be joined with them in the tombs; and for that reason they opened themselves eagerly and with longing to receive it. For as it was fitting that the soul of the Lord Jesus should descend to the souls in [Col. 0924D] the underworld, so that he might lead them out thence, so also it was necessary that his body should come to bodies, so that it might raise them up.

**CHAPTER VII. What it means for the corpse of a man, whose killer is unknown, to be found in the land; and what it means to ascertain the nearest city, to break there the heifer’s neck, and to wash the hands.**

“When the corpse of a slain man is found in the land which the Lord your God will give you, and the perpetrator of the killing is unknown, your elders and judges shall go out and measure the distances from the place of the corpse to each of the cities round about. When they have ascertained which is nearest of all, the elders of that city shall take from the herd a heifer which has not drawn a yoke or broken the ground with a plough. They shall bring it to a rough and stony valley, which has never been ploughed nor received seed, and there they shall break the heifer’s neck,” etc.

The elders and judges of the present passage—that is, the holy Apostles—fulfilled its mystery in this way. In the land which their Lord God gave them, that is, in the fullness of the holy Scriptures, whose meaning the Lord Jesus opened to them (Luke 24), they found the corpse of a slain man: that is, they understood both the sacrilege of those who killed him and the truth and innocence of the one killed, Christ the Son of God. Yet the guilty party in the killing was in a sense unknown: both because the Jews did not themselves kill him with their own hands but handed him over to Gentiles to be killed, and because they persistently contend that they killed not Christ their king but a magician and malefactor.

What then? They went out and measured from the place of the corpse the distances of the cities round about. The place of the corpse, or place of the killing, in that land which the Lord God gave—in that holy Scripture whose understanding Christ bestowed—is any passage of Scripture that manifestly expresses the passion of the Redeemer. For example: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). Again: “After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed” (Dan. 9). Having observed such a passage, they perceived that the city—or Church—of the Gentiles was nearer to grace or salvation than the people of the Jews.

For when Isaiah had said what was just cited, “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter,” etc.—which is the place of Christ’s killing—he immediately added nearby: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; sing praise and cry aloud, you who did not bear, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband, says the Lord” (Isa. 54). Likewise, when Daniel had said, “Christ shall be killed,” as stated above, which is likewise the place of Christ’s killing, he immediately added: “And the people who will deny him shall not be his” (Dan. 9). Therefore, according to the arrangement of the land, according to the most sacred text of divine Scripture, this city is nearer than that city to the place of the corpse: the Gentile people is nearer to Christ’s grace than the Jewish people.

What, therefore, will the elders of this [Col. 0925D] city do? “They shall take,” it says, “a heifer from the herd that has not drawn a yoke or broken the ground with a plough, bring it to a rough and stony valley which has never been ploughed nor received seed, and there break the heifer’s neck.” The wanton heifer, the heifer badly free and accustomed to no yoke of divine worship, was our flesh, brutish and vicious. Therefore, in order that the blood of the slain man might not be imputed to us, it was necessary to break this heifer’s neck—that is, to mortify the pride of the flesh, the members or works of the flesh—in a rough and stony valley, that is, in humble and laborious repentance; and then to wash the hands, that is, to be baptized in the death of Christ Jesus.

Accordingly it immediately adds: “And the elders of that city shall come to the slain man and wash [Col. 0926A] their hands over the heifer, and say: ‘Our hands have not shed this blood, nor have our eyes seen it.’” But does this saying also suit those who shared in the Jews’ crime, who shouted that that man should be crucified and afterwards washed their hands? Can they too say, “Our hands have not shed this blood, nor have our eyes seen it”? Certainly they too could say it truthfully, because through washing their hands they were changed into others.

All who have been baptized in Christ Jesus, all who have been baptized into the death of Christ Jesus, have been so renewed—indeed, so changed into others—that they are no longer what they were before God. Thus the Apostle says: “We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). Again: “I have been crucified with Christ; yet I live, but no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2).

Therefore those very persons who shed Christ’s blood and afterwards repented, having been baptized in his name, after washing thus and being changed into others by that washing, rightly and truthfully say: “Our hands have not shed this blood, nor have our eyes seen it. Be merciful, O Lord, to thy people Israel, whom thou hast redeemed, and do not impute innocent blood in the midst of thy people Israel.” Nevertheless, from us also, who were far off but by the aforesaid measuring line have been made near, the guilt of blood is removed; we are strangers to the blood of the Innocent One that was shed, when we have done what the Lord commanded. But if we do not do this and do not believe in him who was killed, we consent to those who killed him, and therefore his blood will justly be required of us.

**CHAPTER VIII. What it means spiritually, when a city is under siege, not to cut down fruit-bearing trees but to construct engines from wild trees; and what it means first to offer peace to a besieged city.**

(Chapter 20.) “When you have besieged a city for a long time and surrounded it with fortifications in order to take it, you shall not cut down the trees from which food may be eaten, nor shall you devastate the region around it with axes, because it is wood and not a man, and cannot increase the number of those fighting against you. But if there are any trees which are not fruit-bearing but wild, though fit also for other uses, cut them down and construct engines until you capture the city which fights against [Col. 0926D] you.”

The substance of this chapter is that fruit-bearing trees are to be preserved, but those which bear no fruit are to be cut down. Is God, then, concerned with trees? If, according to the Apostle, he is not concerned with oxen (1 Cor. 9), how much less is he concerned with insensible trees? These woods or trees, therefore, are human beings; and according to this likeness we understand what is truly said in the Gospel: “Therefore bear fruits worthy of repentance. For now the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3).

Indeed, he who besieges a city for a long time and surrounds it with fortifications in order to take it is he who, stronger than the armed strong man guarding his court, comes upon him and does not cease until the end of the age to subdue his city, hostile to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem (Luke 11). Therefore, because his first coming was in peace and offered forgiveness of sins to all, while his second will be in terror, he will, as a stern conqueror, cast into hell those who refused to receive his peace.

In the preceding chapter—which we pass over because of haste—the same holy and spiritual law had familiarly said these same things to its own disciple, Christ the Son of God: “When you approach to take a city, you shall first offer it peace. If it receives you and opens its gates to you, all the people in it shall be saved and shall serve you under tribute. But if they refuse to make a covenant and begin war against you, you shall besiege it,” etc. For he first offered peace to the city he approached to conquer when, entering this world to conquer the devil’s kingdom, he first preached repentance and forgiveness of sins to all nations (Matt. 4). To receive him and open the gates to him is to believe with an open heart unto righteousness and to make confession with an open mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10). Those who make a covenant with him in this way will be saved; but those who refuse to receive him, being besieged and conquered, will at last be struck by the sword of judgment.

Therefore, he says, “You shall not cut down the trees from which food may be eaten”: that is, you shall not judge sinners who bear fruits worthy of repentance. Why? “Because,” he says, “it is wood, not a man, and cannot increase the number of those fighting against you.” Is, then, non-fruit-bearing wood—that is, the sinner who does not produce the fruits of repentance—a man and able to increase the number of the enemies against this warrior? Certainly: he seems to himself to be a man—that is, wise and rational—to such an extent that he considers foolish what we preach, Jesus Christ and him crucified (1 Cor. 1), who through that very cross besieges or attacks the devil. And he seems to himself able to increase Christ’s enemies to such an extent that, through disputation, he sometimes delays or impedes the running word of God.

Conversely, the one who judges that he knows nothing among such people except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2), is, by his own judgment, not a man but a piece of wood awaiting dew from heaven, so that it may blossom again and, by bearing worthy fruit, recover the state of its first origin, which it lost in Adam through the tree of desire. Such a person neither can nor wishes to increase the number of enemies against Christ, God and man. He, therefore, will be saved; but the other will be cut down as useless wood, according to what is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent” (Isa. 29; 1 Cor. 1).

Yet if useful things proceed in him or from him which may effectively be hurled against the fortifications of that opposing city, we—or rather Christ, who speaks in us—will not disdain to seize them, so as to use well things badly composed. Thus, after Scripture prudently said, “Cut them down,” it immediately added, “and construct engines, until you capture the city which fights against you.” We read that the Apostle first did this when, after saying, “In him we live and move and are,” [Col. 0928A] he immediately added: “As certain of your own poets have said, ‘For we are also his offspring’” (Acts 17). Again: “One of them, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’” (Titus 1). Likewise, it is not merely blameless but even praiseworthy whenever an ecclesiastical man brings together useful examples or testimonies from the wild trees which have been cut down—that is, from the wise of this world who have been condemned—so that the city which fights against Christ may be defeated by its own strength.

**CHAPTER IX. On the beautiful woman captured and loved in war: how she may lawfully be taken as a wife, and what she signifies mystically.**
[Col. 0928B] **(Chapter XXI.)** “If you go out to fight against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand, and you take captives, and see among the captives a beautiful woman, and love her and wish to have her as a wife, you shall bring her into your house. She shall shave her hair, pare her nails, put off the garment in which she was captured, and, sitting in your house, shall weep for her father and mother for one month. Afterward you shall go in to her and sleep with her, and she shall be your wife.”

The Hebrews relate that David did this literally with Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur (II Kings [II Sam.] III): namely, that, having captured her in battle, he cut off her hair and nails and, according to this law, took her as his wife; by her he begot Tamar and [Col. 0928C] Absalom.

But according to the mystical sense, an ecclesiastical man ought to do this as follows. The beautiful woman among the captives or enemies is Holy Scripture as found in the writings of heretics. For many heretics or founders of heresies sat in the chair of Moses—indeed, even at the summit of apostolic authority—and although they held erroneous views about the Godhead, nevertheless said many useful things concerning morals and allegorical subtlety.

“If, therefore,” it says, “you go out to fight against your enemies”—that is, if you have a holy zeal against heretics, the enemies of the Christian faith—“and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand,” so that by mighty faith and sound doctrine you obtain the palm of truth, no necessity of the law is imposed upon you requiring that you dare not love any beautiful woman found among them: that is, that you ought not read or hear any useful exposition of the Scriptures written by them. Rather, having tested all things, you may hold fast what is good and abstain from every appearance of evil (I Thess. V).

For this is what is now said: “She shall shave her hair, pare her nails, and put off the garment in which she was captured. Afterwards you shall go in to her, sleep with her, and she shall be your wife.” To shave the hair, pare the nails, and change the garment of the beautiful woman means to cut away from sacred reading everything perverse and everything superfluous; carefully and diligently to remove every appearance of evil—that is, heretical meaning—so that you may have a suitable wife, according to that saying: “I said to wisdom, You are my sister; and I called prudence [Col. 0929A] my friend” (Prov. VII).

“But if afterward she does not please you, you shall let her go free; you may not sell her for money or oppress her by force, because you have humbled her.” Literally, the equity is plain; but according to the anagogical sense, the fickleness of readers’ judgments is forbidden. Such fickleness is reproved by ecclesiastical history in Theophilus, bishop of the city of Alexandria. Since he was an enemy of John of Constantinople, called Chrysostom, he condemned, out of zeal against John, the reading of Origen, to which he had gladly devoted himself. Then, after John had been condemned, because he did not restrain himself from reading Origen, he himself again devoted himself to the reading of that same Origen.

When someone asked him how he could again embrace what he had rejected, he replied: “The books of Origen [Col. 0929B] are like a meadow full of flowers: whatever good I find in them I pluck; if I encounter anything thorny, I leave it aside, as though it might prick me.”

Therefore, “if afterwards she does not please you, you shall let her go free”: that is, if, after examination, you condemn any captured reading, however much it has been trimmed, you shall not draw it back into your school again after changing your opinion, because you have humbled it—that is, condemned it—lest you appear to have condemned it less through reason than through envy.

## Chapter X. Concerning a man who has two wives: why he may not make the son of the beloved wife the firstborn; and how Christ, possessing the Synagogue and the Church from the Gentiles, must fulfil this.

[Col. 0929C] “If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and has children by them, and the son of the hated wife is the firstborn, then when he wishes to divide his property among his sons, he may not make the son of the beloved wife the firstborn and prefer him to the son of the hated wife. Rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn and give him a double portion of all that he has. For he is the beginning of his children, and the rights of the firstborn are due to him,” and so forth.

“He may not,” it says, “make the son of the beloved wife the firstborn”—unless, implicitly, the son of the hated wife has lost the honour of the firstborn through his own fault. For because Reuben, the firstborn of the less beloved wife, went up to his father’s bed and defiled his couch (Gen. XXXV), Jacob was able to make Joseph, the son of the more beloved Rachel, firstborn, as is written in Chronicles: “Reuben was the firstborn of Israel; but because he violated his father’s bed, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph, son of Israel, and he was not reckoned as firstborn. But Judah, who was strongest among his brothers, produced rulers from his stock; the birthright, however, was reckoned to Joseph” (I Chron. V).

Spiritually, moreover, the Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, fulfilled this part of the law as well. For he is that man who had two wives: one beloved, namely the Synagogue, most dear for the sake of the fathers; the other hated, namely the Gentile people, to whom he speaks through Isaiah: “For the Lord has called you as a woman deserted and sorrowful in spirit, and as a wife rejected from her youth” (Isa. [Col. 0930A] LIV).

Yet this rejected, this hated wife bore first: for she received the first advent of her Bridegroom, the Son of God. The other, however, now remaining barren, will receive his second advent. For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, then all Israel shall be saved (Rom. XI).

Therefore the son of the hated wife is the firstborn, and by the law the man cannot make the son of the beloved wife firstborn and prefer him to the Christian people, the son of this hated wife. As he says: “I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is true” (John V). For what did this man, made of a woman and made under the law (Gal. IV)—what, I say, did this man hear when he said these things, except the law of righteousness, being a hearer and doer of the holy, just, and good law? Although he loved that beloved wife, although from natural affection he could even weep over her [Col. 0930B] (Luke XIX), he could not be so unjust as not to acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn, following the reasoning of his divinity rather than carnal affection.

He therefore gave this firstborn a double portion of what he possessed. For in that once-beloved wife, the letter alone remaining, the son of this wife who is no longer hated—namely, the Christian people—possesses Holy Scripture in such a manner that, together with the historical sense, he also holds its spiritual mysteries. For he is the beginning of his children, because he was the first to believe at Christ’s coming, and the rights of the firstborn are due to him. Hence this possessor of the firstborn rights rejoices in the Psalm and says: “He has chosen for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved” (Ps. XLVI).

“The beauty of Jacob,” he says, because, just as that Jacob, according to his name, supplanted his brother Esau, so this son [Col. 0930C] of the hated wife snatched from the son of the beloved wife the birthright of the heavenly blessing.

## Chapter XI. Concerning the bringing of a rebellious son to judgment, which Eli did not do; and how spiritual fathers in the Church ought to act.

“If a man begets a rebellious and unruly son, who does not obey the command of father and mother and, when corrected, despises obedience, they shall seize him and bring him to the elders of that city and to the gate of judgment. They shall say to them: ‘This son of ours is unruly and rebellious; he despises to heed our admonitions; he gives himself up to revelries, debauchery, and banquets.’ The people of the city shall overwhelm him with stones and he shall die; and you shall remove evil from among you, that all Israel may fear.”

The grave and mature judgment of the holy law excludes from fathers’ hearts toward their children the tender feelings of false affection, lest such feelings be entertained. For in the cause of God, the wise father does not even acknowledge his son. Since the aged Eli neglected this authority of the law, he incurred a dreadful danger to his life.

For ought he to have been satisfied merely to say gently: “Why do you do such things, which I hear are very wicked deeds among all the people? Do not do so, my sons” (I Kings [I Sam.] II)? Could not that aged priest have learned from this reading of the law what kind and degree of zealous severity he ought to exercise toward disobedient sons? Rightly, therefore, although he had said, “Do not do so, my sons,” rightly, I say, [Col. 0931A] father Eli is accused of not correcting his sons, the Lord saying: “You have honoured your sons more than me” (ibid.). Likewise it is said of him that he knew his sons behaved unworthily and did not correct them; for he did not correct them who did not correct them lawfully.

Let every spiritual father who claims rightly to preside over the house of God remember this. If this man perhaps has begotten a rebellious and unruly son who will not listen and despises obedience, he should know that the first sin of our race, for which we suffer, is disobedience; and that God’s justice has reserved no pardon for the rebellious and unruly. Rather, as it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV).

Yet he must consider that he will render an account to God of all his judgments, lest perhaps the flame of envy or zeal consume his soul. For this reason he shall not rush into his own judgment, but shall summon wise men as witnesses. The holy and orthodox Fathers rightly established this in the care of children, in accordance with the command of this preceding authority. For the present law says: “They shall seize him and bring him to the elders of that city and to the gate of judgment,” and so forth.

Thus other sins are indeed to be tolerated in the house of God; but the severity of wise Fathers overwhelms rebellious and unruly sons, in order to remove evil from its midst, under the present authority of the Lord’s law—indeed, under God’s own example, who expelled the first disobedient children, namely humankind, from Paradise.

## Chapter XII. [Col. 0931C] What it means spiritually to restore or lift up a brother’s ox, sheep, or ass, even if he is not a neighbour; and how Christ fulfils this.

**(Chapter XXI.)** “You shall not see your brother’s ox or sheep straying and pass by; rather, you shall restore it to your brother. Even if your brother is not near you and you do not know him, you shall bring it to your house, and it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it and receives it. You shall do likewise with the ass,” and so forth.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, subject in every respect to the law, showed that he fulfilled this command excellently when he rode upon an ass—the lowliest of all beasts of burden—while coming to the city of Jerusalem to suffer for the salvation of the world, according to the prophecy of Zechariah, who says to that holy city itself, indeed to the heavenly Jerusalem of which that city was a type or shadow: “Behold, your king [Col. 0931D] will come to you, righteous and a saviour; he is poor and riding upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. IX).

For what does that ass upon which the Lord sits mystically signify, except the foolish people of the Gentiles? The simpler people of the Hebrews who followed the Lord were indeed an ass, as the Pharisees said: “But this crowd which does not know the law are accursed” (John VII); yet they were the ass of a near neighbour. But this holy and spiritual law says: “Even if your brother is not near you and you do not know him, you shall bring it into your house,” and so forth.

Therefore, in order to fulfil the entire law, this our Saviour even mounted the ass of one not near to him, and brought it into his house, when he received the Gentile people, choosing the foolish things of the world to confound the wise (I Cor. I). Sitting upon the back of one obedient and saying, “Show me your ways, O Lord, and teach me your paths” [Col. 0932A] (Ps. XXIV), he led it by the way of wisdom into his heavenly house, while children came to meet him and, with praise of God, lifted up branches of victory (Matt. XXI). By these children the holy angels are rightly understood, rejoicing in the blessedness of our redemption.

The same is rightly understood of the straying sheep, as is especially proved by the parable of the hundred sheep and the one lost sheep (Luke XV). The entire arrangement of the present chapter should be noted carefully. At both its beginning and end, the lifting up of the Jewish people—who were near to the Lord according to the flesh—is commanded; but in the middle, the lifting up of the Gentile people, alien from his flesh and from God’s covenant, is commanded.

For at the beginning it says: “You shall not see your brother’s ox or sheep straying and pass by; rather, you shall restore it to your brother.” At the end it says: “If you see your brother’s ass or ox fallen while straying on the road, you shall not despise it, but shall lift it up with him.” But in the middle it says: “Even if your brother is not near you and you do not know him, you shall bring to your house”—namely, his ox or ass.

The brother of this man, who alone could fulfil the whole law, is the Jewish people: a brother or kinsman of the Lord according to the flesh of Abraham. The Saviour first sought them when they strayed at his first advent, brought some of them back to the way of salvation, and will not altogether despise them now as they lie beneath the burden of sin, but will lift them up at the end. Meanwhile, as has been said, the ass which had perished—one who was not then his neighbour or brother—is restored, because simple and lowly persons are gathered by grace from the Gentiles who do not belong to Abraham’s flesh.

## Chapter XIII. What it means spiritually that a woman should not wear a man’s garment, nor a man a woman’s garment.

[Col. 0932C] “A woman shall not wear a man’s garment, nor shall a man use a woman’s garment; for whoever does these things is abominable before God.”

Nature itself so spontaneously abhors both these things that the Apostle did not hesitate to say even of the lesser matter: “Judge for yourselves. Is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled? Does not nature itself teach us that if a man lets his hair grow, it is a disgrace to him?” [Col. 0932D] (I Cor. XI), and so forth.

Spiritually, however, a woman puts on a man’s garment when one who does not know how to govern the conduct of his own life dares to be a judge of another’s life and presumes to preside though he has not yet learned to be subject. Conversely, a man wears a woman’s garment when one who has already received spiritual gifts—namely prophecy, a word of wisdom, kinds of tongues (I Cor. XII), or anything else for which he might rightly be called a man and, as a man, preside over the house of God, which is the Church—nevertheless follows unstable vices and, through a contemptible life, deserves that whatever preaching he may have should likewise rightly be despised.

“Both,” it says, “are abominable before God who do these things”; this surely needs no support from our assertion.

## Chapter XIV. [Col. 0933A] How Christ, walking on the way of this life, found a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, took the young, and allowed the mother to depart.

“If, as you walk along the way, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting upon the young or the eggs, you shall not take her together with the children. Rather, you shall let her go, while keeping the captured children, that it may go well with you and that you may live a long time.”

Great matters are signified by small terms; and, to speak more magnificently, here too a great splendour is veiled beneath a small covering upon the face of Moses. The prophet Jeremiah, when consulted as to whose nest or eggs, and of what sort of bird, are to be understood here, explains it thus: “The partridge brooded over what it did not lay; it made riches, but not with justice. In the middle of its days it shall leave them, and at its end it shall be foolish” (Jer. XVII).

“The partridge,” he says, “brooded over what it did not lay.” For it is accustomed to steal and brood over the eggs of its fellow bird. But the chicks, when born, hear the cry of the one that laid the eggs; immediately leaving the one that stole them and brooded over stolen eggs in order to make riches and enrich its nest, and not with justice—that is, through robbery—they return to the one who is their mother and laid them first. Therefore it says: “In the middle of its days it shall leave them, and at its end it shall be foolish.” For while it foolishly desires to deceive, it is itself deceived; its cunning is defeated by nature.

This partridge is the devil, who by his craft stole the mass of the human race from the Creator in the first parents; and from that time brooded over what he did not lay—that is, he wickedly enticed them in the vices [Col. 0933C] of this world and caused those whom he did not create to be born in sin. Hence in Isaiah, boasting under the name of Asshur, he says: “Like a mighty man I brought down those sitting in high places, and my hand found the strength of peoples like a nest” (Isa. X).

Thus, like eggs from a lofty nest, he stole them from a nest not his own—the persons from whom chicks were to be born—when by deceit he led human beings out of Paradise, from whom all the already predestined children of God were to be born, the Lord saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I). And he made riches, but not with justice, because he became the prince of this world and, in a perverse order, was worshipped by human beings in temples of idols as God.

“But in the middle of his days,” it says, “he shall leave them”: this has already happened. “And at his end he shall be foolish”: this is still to come. For the whole extent of his days reaches to the last judgment. Yet before that judgment, the one who was to judge came to be judged; and by his passion he took away the riches which the devil had seized without judgment, while reserving judgment for the robber, as he says: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John XII).

At last, “at his end he shall be foolish”: that is, he shall be convicted of folly, namely when he is cast down before the eyes of all [Col. 0933D] (Job XL). Therefore this holy law speaks beautifully and reverently to you, O Christ Jesus, singular hearer and doer of the law: “If, as you walk along the way, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting upon the young or eggs,” and so forth.

The bird’s nest in the tree was the people of Israel: under the aforesaid prince of this world, indeed a child of wrath by nature like the rest, yet situated on the height of the law and in the exalted faith of Abraham. The bird’s nest on the ground was all the Gentile world, wickedly brooded over beneath the devil’s wings, sunk in every earthly desire and also in ignorance of God.

But the Son of God, walking along the way, found a nest in each place, because, entering the changeability of this present life, he looked in grace upon both groups, without distinction between Jew and Greek. “You shall not take her with the children,” it says, “but shall let her go, keeping the children captive.” You shall not keep the adulterous mother who, as stated above, brooded over what she had not laid. For the liberator’s grace did not seek the devil; it sought only the children, to regenerate them by grace. Therefore the children are kept captive in order that they may be saved; therefore such a mother is allowed to depart, so that at her end she may perish.

## Chapter XV. Mystically, concerning the same matter: how Christ did this, and how we are to do it, retaining the mystical meanings and dismissing the letter of the law.

[Col. 0934B] “You shall not take the mother with the children, but shall let her go, while keeping the captured children, that it may go well with you and that you may live a long time.”

The mother sitting over the young or eggs is the letter of the Synagogue, the letter of the law which kills; but the eggs or young themselves are the mysteries of the spirit of the law, the life-giving Spirit. But Christ did not retain that mother, that letter, as he says in the Psalm: “Because I have not known learning [*litteratura*], I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. LXX). He kept only the captured children, for he wills that the law be fulfilled spiritually by his disciples.

“You shall not take,” he says, “but shall let her go.” For what purpose? “That it may go well with you,” he says, “and that you may live a long time.”

Let us say something else which can illustrate this passage more suitably. He says in the Psalm: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest at some time my people forget” (Ps. LVIII). But what then? “Scatter them in your might” (ibid.). Behold, today we see the mother alone flown away without her children, and we know where she is: for the Synagogue, the enemy of Christ, is scattered throughout the whole world, possessing only the letter of the law. This itself benefits Christ, so that he may live a long time—that is, so that his people may never forget her.

Therefore we too, or each one of us, go along the way because we traverse the present life; and we find birds’ nests on the ground and in the tree when we read words of history to be retained either in the contemplative or the active life. For the precepts of the active life are a bird’s nest on the ground; the precepts of the contemplative life are a nest in the tree. The mother broods over the young or eggs when history itself nurtures spiritual understanding.

Let us not retain her with the children, but let her go, keeping the children captive. For in certain passages the historical narrative must be set aside, so that only the young of this mother—that is, the meanings of spiritual understanding—may come to us as food; and we may be nourished not by the mother but by the young.

For when we read that the gold and silver of the Egyptians were taken by the Israelite people through the deception of borrowing (Exod. II), and again when we read that carnal sacrifices were offered to God, what is there in this nest of words except that the mother must be dismissed and the children retained? For when we draw the alertness of intellect from secular persons into the defence of truth, and turn their eloquence to the use of righteousness, what else do we do but take gold and silver from the Egyptians, so that by it both we may be shown to have become rich and they poor, as it is written: “Bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (II Cor. X)?

And when we subdue our bodies through abstinence, what else do we do but offer spiritual sacrifices to almighty God, as Paul again says: “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Rom. XII)? Thus, dismissing the mother, we eat the young when we dismiss historical examples but retain in the mind the allegorical meanings derived from them [Col. 0935B]. Hence it is rightly added: “That it may go well with you and that you may live a long time,” because that person lives for a long time who, through spiritual understanding, lays hold of the years of eternity.

## Chapter XVI. What it means mystically to build a new house and make a wall around the roof.

“When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you be guilty when someone falls and tumbles headlong.”

This construction of houses accords with the custom of the province of Palestine, where people usually sit upon roofs. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you have said in darkness shall be spoken in the light; and what you have spoken into the ear in private rooms shall be preached upon the roofs” (Luke XII). Therefore, because people used to sit upon roofs, “you shall make,” it says, “a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you be guilty when someone falls and tumbles headlong.”

We read also in the building of the Temple: “He covered the house with cedar ceilings and built a storey over the entire house five cubits high” (III Kings [I Kgs.] VI). For their roofs were not raised into peaks in our manner, but were made flat and level.

Spiritually, he builds a house who, caring for the house of God, forms the minds of those subject to him by the word of doctrine appropriate to his office. Hence it is said: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain” (Ps. CXXVI). That is to say: unless the Lord prepares the hearts of hearers, even very wise builders vainly expend their supply of words.

Therefore, when “you build a new house”—that is, when you have laid the beginnings of doctrine in the minds of those subject to you—“you shall make a wall around the roof”: that is, you shall fortify whatever you say with sufficient arguments or testimonies from Scripture, lest you become guilty when someone falls and tumbles headlong. This happens whenever careless speech affords hearers an occasion for perverse interpretation. Therefore let whatever you say be fortified, so that no one may fall through your teaching, unless he deliberately and contentiously throws himself down.

## Chapter XVII. What it means spiritually not to sow a vineyard with another seed; and what it means literally and spiritually that the seed and what grows from the vineyard are alike consecrated.

[Col. 0936A] “You shall not sow your vineyard with another seed, lest both the seed that you have sown and what grows from the vineyard be alike consecrated.”

The practical skill of countrymen and farmers also knows this: a vineyard requires soil kept free for itself, so that not only should no seed be sown in it, but even when the ground spontaneously produces useless herbs, they must be vigorously uprooted with the hoe. Otherwise the richness of the soil, whose abundance the vineyard requires, is wasted in vain, because when it is divided among many things it has less strength in each one.

Thus both the seed and what grows from the vineyard are alike consecrated—that is, reduced to barrenness and left idle in an ungrateful rest for their cultivators—according to that passage where the Lord, warning the people who deserved it, said: “Your land shall be desolate and your cities destroyed,” and immediately added (Lev. XXVI): “Then the land shall enjoy its sabbaths throughout all the days of its desolation” (ibid.). Therefore, lest they be alike consecrated—that is, lest they be alike reduced to the sabbath of barrenness.

Spiritually, moreover, since the whole Church is the Lord’s vineyard, if it is sown with heretical seed or with Jewish ceremonies—in which that people thinks itself rich—no good fruits can be gathered from it. Yet those are especially the Lord’s vineyard whose rank and spiritual purpose are more sacred within that same Church. Concerning such persons the Lord says to the prophet: “Son of man, what shall be done with the wood of the vine, beyond all the trees of the groves which are among the trees of the forest? Shall wood be taken from it to make a work, or shall a peg be fashioned from it upon which any vessel may hang?” [Col. 0936C] (Ezek. XV).

Certainly, if those whose work was spiritual descend to secular business, what they had been is lost, and what they undertake sometimes does not prosper. Therefore in the Acts of the Apostles the Apostles themselves say: “It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables” (Acts VI). And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Therefore, if you have secular lawsuits, appoint as judges those who are of no account in the Church” (I Cor. VI).

“You shall not sow,” therefore, it says, “your vineyard with another seed, lest both the seed you have sown and what grows from the vineyard be alike consecrated”: that is, do not wrong those eminent in the Church and fruitful in heavenly doctrine by burdening them with the occupation of contemptible affairs, lest, while they are divided in both directions, they prove useful in neither, and so, as if in a consecrated sabbath, perform nothing fruitful for the kingdom of God. Hence canonical authority forbids ministers of the holy altar to become entangled in secular affairs. “No one serving God,” says the Apostle, “entangles himself in secular business” (II Tim. II).

## Chapter XVIII. What it means not to plough with an ox and an ass together; not to wear a garment woven of linen and wool; and to make cords upon the fringes.

“You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together; you shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen.”

This may be understood as spoken to teachers against association with the unlearned. “You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together” is as if it said plainly: You shall not join wise persons and fools together in preaching, lest, through one who cannot fulfil the task, you hinder the one who is able.

But what is signified by this garment except the character of hypocrites, who display kindness toward their neighbours while covering over, by the deceit of their wickedness, the things they say? A garment made of wool and linen always shows the wool on its surface and conceals the linen beneath. What, then, does wool signify except simplicity? What does linen signify except subtlety? Often a subtle and sharp person outwardly displays the simplicity of gentleness but inwardly hides the subtlety of malice. Such a person clothes himself in the garment of his conduct as though in wool and linen, when simplicity is displayed by him on the surface [Col. 0937B], while the subtlety of malice is preserved in the mind.

Therefore it immediately adds: “You shall make cords upon the fringes, at the four corners of your cloak with which you cover yourself.” The garment already described, in which the wise person walks while guarding it so as not to walk naked, is composed by the weaving together of all virtues. Its corners—that is, its principal elements—are the four virtues which even the pagans knew how to call by their proper names: temperance, justice, fortitude, and prudence. When the wise person walks adorned with these for God’s sake, not so that he himself may be seen by men but so that the Father in heaven may be glorified (Matt. VI), and perseveres to the end in this love of God and neighbour while doing good works so that he may be saved, then indeed he has made cords upon the fringes at the four corners of his cloak.

But our Lord sharply rebukes the unsuitable fringes of the aforesaid hypocrites, saying: “They broaden their phylacteries and enlarge their fringes” (Matt. XXIII). They accuse themselves greatly when, neglecting the thing signified, they enlarge before human eyes the fringes which signify it.

## Chapter XIX. Concerning the man who, hating the wife he has taken, says, “I did not find her a virgin”; and who, when her parents produce proofs of virginity, is beaten and compelled to keep her: how this is to be understood as fulfilled in Christ.

If a man takes a wife and afterwards comes to hate her, seeks occasions on which to dismiss her, and, imputing a shameful name to her, says, “I took this wife, [Col. 0937D] and when I went in to her I did not find her a virgin,” then her father and mother shall take her and bring with them the tokens of her virginity to the elders of her city who are at the gate. And the father shall say: “I gave my daughter to this man as wife. Because he hates her, he imputes a shameful name to her and says, ‘I did not find your daughter a virgin.’ And behold, these are the tokens of my daughter’s virginity.” They shall spread the garment before the elders of the city. And the elders of that city shall seize the man and beat him, fining him one hundred shekels of silver, which he shall give to the girl’s father, because he has cast a shameful name upon a virgin of Israel. He shall have her as his wife and shall not be able to dismiss her for all the days of his life.

This letter of divine justice or wisdom is most obscure to chaste minds. For what chaste mind can patiently endure even to contemplate how bloody traces of violated virginity may be preserved on a cloth? Yet in this place also let that same Wisdom of God console us, crying concerning such a death-dealing letter: “For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclus. 24). And again: “Those who make me clear shall have eternal life” (ibid.). Therefore let us draw forth from the dark cavern of this letter the bright mystery of the Spirit, and understand this law in such a way that it is not unworthy of Christ, the husband of holy Church, to have been subject to it.

“If a man,” it says, “takes a wife and afterwards comes to hate her,” etc. Spiritually, this happened as follows. The man took a wife when the Son of God assumed human nature. Hence it is written: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun, and he [Col. 0938B] is like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18). This mystery is known to the spiritual sons or friends of the same bridegroom. Thus they rejoice and say: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). And again with the Apostle: “The two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery in Christ and in the Church” (Eph. 5).

In that assumption of flesh, this husband knew his wife: namely, the whole Church of Jews and Gentiles, numerous indeed through diversity of times and places, but one according to the sacrament of faith. Yet after taking her he in some sense came to hate her and sought occasions for dismissing her. For he said to his disciples: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. 10). Again: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). And again: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs to eat” (ibid.).

Such utterances were utterances of hatred, not according to the reasoning of divinity, but according to the perception of the flesh; they did not accord with his former purpose or with the truth of the Scriptures. For before he was incarnate, he had professed love for the Church of the Gentiles in all the prophets. Thus, as though he had changed his purpose, he cast upon her a shameful name, saying: “I took this wife, and when I went in to her I did not find her a virgin.” “I did not find her a virgin,” he says, “but prostituted to thousands of many gods, as though to many husbands.” Yet this was in vain.

For in the aforesaid union—in that incarnation—the holy tokens of virginity were laid up to be seen. For that woman once prostituted acted—yes, acted—in penitence; she mortified her flesh; and moreover, beneath the swords of persecutors, she poured out her blood for him, her husband. What then? “Her father and mother,” he says, “shall take her and bring with them the tokens of her virginity to the elders of that city who are at the gate; and they shall spread the garment before the elders of the city; and they shall seize the man and beat him,” etc., as above.

Surely, by a wondrous manner and a wondrous order of love, because of the very charge for which he rebuked the Church from the Gentiles, the Son of God made man was himself beaten and fastened to the cross. And at the gate of the city, before the elders of the city—that is, in the council [Col. 0939A] of heaven, in the sight of the Father and his holy angels—she was judged to be a virgin: she who, in union with him, displayed traces of her blood; who did penance through his preaching; who poured out her blood for his faith. For even if she had previously been prostituted, after she was thus joined to him she deserves now to be called a virgin, and is one.

But who is her father, or who her mother, except the apostolic order and the primitive Church, by whose testimony she is defended in heaven and on earth? “They shall beat him,” it says, “and moreover fine him one hundred shekels of silver, which he shall give to the girl’s father, because he has cast a shameful name upon a virgin of Israel.” Finally, because he accused of sin the Church or Synagogue, whom he wished to be a virgin, this husband was beaten and moreover crucified—indeed, in order to erase the sin of her prostitution, he deigned to be beaten and crucified. And he gave one hundred shekels of silver, that is, the fullness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

“He shall have her as his wife,” it says, “and shall not be able to dismiss her all the days of his life,” namely, once the prophecy has been fulfilled which says: “The young man shall dwell with the virgin, and your sons shall dwell in you; and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so your God shall rejoice over you” (Isa. 62).

It follows: “But if what he alleges is true, and virginity is not found in the girl, they shall cast her out beyond the doors of her father’s house; and the men of that city shall stone her, and she shall die, because she committed an outrage in Israel by prostituting herself in her father’s house; and you shall remove evil from your midst.”

Meanwhile this must be understood: when the grace of God is in the woman’s power, whether the charge made by this husband is true or not depends upon her. For she who has done penance, as was said above, and has thus shown herself to be a chaste virgin—in her the shameful name has perished. But she who has not done penance, and loves Barabbas more than the Son of God, loves Antichrist more than Christ, has been defamed because she truly committed an outrage in Israel and her sin remains. Therefore, “they shall cast her out,” that is, the Synagogue, beyond the doors of her former Father, God; and the men of her city shall stone her—that is, all the judges who shall sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19)—and she shall die because she prostituted herself in her Father’s house; that is, she shall be condemned because she clung to the devil, [Col. 0939D] though she had the law and prophets of her God.

## CHAPTER XX

If a man sleeps with another’s wife, both shall die; the distinction between the woman found in the field and the one found in the city; and the fact that the adulterer is the devil, while the girl whom he oppressed in the field was the Synagogue in Egypt.

“If a man sleeps with another’s wife, both shall die,” that is, the adulterer and the adulteress, “and you shall remove evil from Israel.” This is a general judgment concerning adultery. But it makes a difference whether adultery has been committed by force or by consent.

It follows, therefore: “If a man has betrothed a virgin girl, and someone finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and they shall be stoned: the girl, because she did not cry out though she was in the city; the man, because he humbled his neighbor’s wife. And you shall remove evil from your midst. But if a man finds in the field a betrothed girl and seizes her and lies with her, the man alone shall die; the girl shall suffer nothing and is not guilty of death. For as a robber rises against his brother and kills his life, so the girl suffered. She was alone in the field; she cried out, and no one was present to save her.”

In the clear justice of this distinction there is likewise a just judgment concerning spiritual adultery. For the man who slept with another’s wife is the unclean man, the devil, who dared to corrupt the rational creature, namely man. He found in the field the virgin girl betrothed to God and lay with her when, before the giving of the Law, he subjugated to himself the Hebrew people while they were sojourning in Egypt. For there she served foreign gods, though God, the lawful husband, had betrothed her to himself in Abraham, Isaac, [Col. 0940B] and Jacob.

“The girl cried out, and no one was present to save her”—no one, I say, for there was no Law; no prophet had yet come who would call that people back from the worship of the Egyptian gods. Only her cry came to Jesus, and he alone descended to deliver his people. Therefore, as a robber rises against his brother and kills his life, so that girl—so that young nation—suffered: within, the devil corrupting her; without, Pharaoh reducing her to slavery. She was alone in that field, alone in Egypt, far removed from the city and kingdom of God.

Therefore, “that man,” it says, “shall die alone; the girl shall suffer nothing and is not guilty of death.” The devil alone will bear the punishment of such adultery, just as Pharaoh alone, with his chariots and horsemen, perished as his type; while that people crossed the sea unharmed, glorified by miracles and defended by heavenly protections (Exod. 14).

But this same adulterer found the betrothed girl in the city as often as the same people, now protected by the holy Scriptures and by angelic guardianship, prostituted itself to idolatry: initiating itself into Baal-peor, worshipping Baal, and serving Astaroth. Moreover, the corrupting devil then lay with her in the city when she demanded that Jesus Christ, the eternal bridegroom and lover of souls, the Son of God, be crucified and that a murderous man be given to her instead (Acts 3).

Therefore, “you shall bring them both out to the gate of that city, and they shall be stoned.” It is plain to the whole world that this adulteress has already been brought out; she has now been drawn not only spiritually but also bodily and visibly from the city of God, and has been overwhelmed by many calamities as by stones. Having lost the protection of angels, she now has no watchman—that is, no prophet—of the kind concerning whom God himself says: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not cease to praise the name of the Lord” (Isa. 62). The earthly city Jerusalem itself has also become deserted; the temple has been burned; and those who survived the sword of the Romans were carried captive among all nations.

## CHAPTER XXI

Concerning the words, “Both shall die”: it is to be understood that this applies if the man slept with her with the woman’s consent.

Therefore, if, it says, a man sleeps with another’s wife, “both shall die,” it is understood: if the man slept with her with the woman’s consent. For if she was violated unwillingly, if she suffered force, then, just as a robber rises against his brother and kills his life, the man alone will be the adulterer; she shall suffer nothing and is not guilty of death. Why? Clearly because the flesh alone was violated, while the mind, where the faith of marriage resides, remained uncorrupted. Only violated faith is culpable; only the loss of faith is adultery.

For where faith has not been sealed by any betrothal, if a corruptor approaches, there is indeed a fault, but adultery in neither party. For it follows: “If a man finds a virgin girl who has no bridegroom and, having seized her, lies with her, and the matter comes to judgment, he who slept with her shall give the girl’s father fifty shekels of silver and shall have [Col. 0941B] her as his wife, because he humbled her. He shall not be able to dismiss her all the days of his life.”

Thus the sanction of marriage lies not so much in the union or commingling of flesh as in the sacrament of betrothal. Therefore, lawfully and reasonably, the angel speaks to Joseph concerning the virgin who was never to be known carnally—or who had been known—when he says: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife; for what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1). “Lawfully,” I say, that is, according to the present Law, he calls her in the Gospel a wife solely because of the faith of betrothal.

The same must further be understood concerning spiritual adultery: namely, that her own husband, God, judges no soul that was unwilling or suffered force from an adulterer as an adulteress. Knowing this very well, the unconquered martyr and chaste virgin first says concerning carnal adultery: “The body is never defiled except by consent of the mind. For if you cause me to be violated against my will, my chastity will be doubled for my crown.” She also introduces testimony taken from the present passage of the Law, saying: “For God regards the violator of chastity as a serpent, as a robber, as a barbarian.” Then, concerning spiritual adultery, she likewise says: “Even if you put incense in my hand and make me cast sacrifices by my hand, God sees these things and laughs.” And giving a judgment common to both, she says: “For he judges concerning dispositions and wills.”

## CHAPTER XXII

[Col. 0941D] Concerning the statement that a eunuch shall not enter the Church of the Lord: how many kinds of eunuchs there are, and what sort of eunuch does not enter the Church of the Lord.

(CH. 23.) “A eunuch whose testicles have been crushed or cut off, and whose member has been severed, shall not enter the Church of the Lord.” In Isaiah we read: “Let not the eunuch say: Behold, I am a dry tree. For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: If they keep my sabbaths, do what I have willed, and hold fast my covenant, I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish” (Isa. 56).

Are Law and prophets therefore so opposed to one another that the Law says, “A eunuch shall not enter the Church of the Lord,” while the Lord, on the contrary, says through the prophet, “I will give eunuchs a place in my house and within my [Col. 0942A] walls”? For what is the Lord’s house, or what are his walls, except the Church of the Lord? Yet the meaning of “eunuch” here and there is certainly not the same. There it is to be understood literally; here spiritually, because it is spiritual.

Therefore let us now enumerate the kinds of eunuchs themselves. In the Gospel the Lord says: “There are eunuchs who were born so; there are eunuchs who were made so by men; and there are eunuchs who made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). This third eunuch-making, or castration, because it is done not by the cutting of iron but by a purpose of chastity, is indeed more spiritual, though not wholly so, since celibacy is visible in the flesh. And these are undoubtedly praiseworthy eunuchs, to whom, according to the prophet cited above, the Lord gives a place in his house and in his walls, and a name better than sons and daughters.

Of none of all these kinds can one truthfully say that he does not enter the Church of the Lord—except that canonical authority forbids those who have been mutilated or cut from the sacred honors of the altar. Therefore we must still inquire what sort of eunuch it is who does not enter the Church of the Lord. For those who inquire into this are also met by the saying elsewhere: “Cursed is everyone who has not produced seed in Israel.” Neither can rightly be understood without the other; for although the words differ, the meaning is the same.

Therefore the eunuch who does not enter the Church of the Lord, and the one who does not produce seed in Israel—and who ought for that reason to be accursed, because he has not produced seed in Israel—is the man who, though he can build up his neighbor by speech, goes about mute; or who, though he knows good and useful things, prefers idle and empty things. He is the opposite of the one who made himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. For just as that praiseworthy man, possessing the natural capacity to beget children, abstains from the flesh for the kingdom of heaven so that he may be free for prayer and, according to the apostolic counsel, be concerned only with the things of the Lord, so this man is detestable: entrusted with the talent of the word of God, by which he could work well and profitably trade for the edification of many, he gives himself to idleness and neglects the grace he received unworthily.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 0942D] How the statement, “If there is among you a man who has been defiled by a nocturnal dream,” is to be observed with proper discernment.

“If there is among you a man who has been defiled by a nocturnal dream, let him go outside the camp and not return before evening. Let him wash with water, and after sunset he shall return to the camp.”

Here it is rightly asked whether, after the nocturnal emission that commonly occurs in sleep, anyone may receive the body of the Lord, or whether a priest may celebrate the sacred mysteries; for the Law plainly permits entrance into the church or camp only after washing with water, and not before evening. Spiritually, indeed, this means that a person is deceived as though in a dream when, tempted by impurity, he is defiled in thought by real images. He must be washed with water, so that he may wash away the faults of thought with tears; and unless the fire of temptation has first departed, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

But, to retain now the plain literal sense, in this same dream-emission there is a very necessary discernment, by which one must carefully consider from what cause it occurs in the sleeper’s mind. Sometimes it results from overindulgence; sometimes from natural excess or illness; sometimes from thought. When it results from overindulgence, the mind incurs some guilt, though not to the point of being forbidden to receive the holy mystery or to celebrate the solemn rites of Mass, when perhaps either a feast-day requires it or necessity itself compels the celebration of the mystery because another priest is absent from the place. But when it arises from natural excess or illness, this emission need not be feared at all, because the mind is to be regarded as having suffered it rather than caused it.

But if the sleeping emission arises from an impure waking thought, the mind’s guilt is manifest. Every sin of thought is completed in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. Let him therefore see from what root that defilement proceeded: whether from suggestion, from delight, or—what is the greater sin—from consent; that is, what he thought knowingly and experienced unknowingly. Thus the person defiled by a nocturnal dream is left to the judgment of his own conscience, so that, according to the measure of the defilement, he may be washed worthily by his tears or by the satisfaction of penance before he returns to the camp of God—that is, before he participates in Christ’s sacred mysteries.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0943C] In what mystical sense the words, “You shall dig round about and cover what has been expelled with earth,” are to be understood.

“You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the necessities of nature, carrying a small spade on your belt. When you sit down, you shall dig round about and cover with the earth you have removed that by which you have been relieved. For the Lord your God walks in the midst of the camp, to deliver you and hand over your enemies to you. Therefore your camp shall be holy, and nothing filthy shall appear in it, lest he forsake you.”

“You shall dig round about,” he says, “and cover with the earth you have removed that by which you have been relieved.” Burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, certain superfluous thoughts, like a burden upon the mind, break forth from the womb of our mind. But we ought to carry a small spade beneath the belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have about us the sharp goad of compunction, which unceasingly pierces the soil of our mind with the sorrow of repentance and hides what breaks forth from us foully.

The discharge of the belly is covered by excavated earth with a spade when the superfluity of our mind, examined by subtle rebuke, is hidden from the eyes of God by the goad of compunction. The Gospel saying also accords with this meaning: “He who loves his life shall lose it; and he who hates his life in this world shall keep it unto eternal life” (John 12). For he loves his life who cherishes his present life in pleasures as much as in vices; who flatters himself; who even defends his evil life; who says with that foolish rich man: “Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years” (Luke 12). Such a man, therefore, will lose it, for in the night—that is, at a time or hour he does not know—it will be demanded of him (ibid.).

Conversely, he hates his life who abhors what he remembers his former life to have been; who, converted, groans and punishes himself by repentance, counting each of his acts, accusing himself for each one, and condemning himself by his own judgment. For he too, as though seated, digs round about and covers with earth that by which he has been relieved, according to the prophet saying: “At night I meditated with my heart; I was exercised and I searched my spirit” (Ps. 76). He does this out of reverence for the Lord his God, who walks in the midst of the camp, lest any filth appear before him and, offended, he forsake the foul place of the heart. Such a man, therefore, keeps his life unto eternal life.

## CHAPTER XXV

How Christ does what he says, “Do not hand over a slave to his master who has fled to you”—that is, he does not abandon to the devil one who has turned to him—and how the Church ought to observe this.

“Do not hand over a slave to his master who has fled to you. He shall dwell with you in the place he chooses and shall rest in one of your cities; you shall not afflict him.”

To continue for the moment with the spiritual sense, this saying of the Gospel accords with this chapter: “Everything which the Father gives me shall come to me, and the one who comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6). “The one who comes to me,” he says, whether slave or free—that is, whether Gentile or Jew—“I will not cast out.” For the Gentile people was the slave of as many masters as it was a worshipper of demons, while the Jewish people considered itself free.

Likewise, individual persons are slaves of as many masters as they have vices or sins, because “everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8), and for that reason does not remain in the house forever (ibid.). But that liberator does not cast out the one who comes to him, as has already been said: that is, he repels none who turn back from the error of their life by withholding his grace, whether Jew or Gentile, male or female, barbarian or Scythian (Gal. 3). Thus he fulfills the Law also in this way: he does not hand over to his master the slave who has turned to him, nor abandon to the devil the one who formerly served him.

Asking for this, the Psalmist says: “Do not hand me over, Lord, from my desire to the sinner” (Ps. 130). Therefore you, whoever you are, fellow-priest of him who gave the Law, whoever in his house, which is the holy Church, have undertaken the offices of holy freedom: do not hand over to his master the slave who has fled to you, that is, one confessing his sins and wishing to abandon them. Do not drive him into despair, whatever or however great a crime he has committed. “Do not afflict him”; rather, console him according to the Apostle, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow (2 Cor. 2).

“He shall dwell with you in the place he chooses and shall rest in one of your cities”; that is, in whatever vocation or order he has chosen, he shall perform his penance until the end. Moreover, according to the literal sense, the holy Church of Christ observes this command in such a way that, according to canonical authority, it ought never to return slaves of Jews or pagans who have once fled to it, regardless of any persuasions. For canonical law has decreed that if any slave of Jews or pagans flees to venerable places for the sake of faith, we must by no means allow him to suffer harm. But whether formerly a Christian or now to be baptized, he is to be protected in every way into freedom by the religious patronage of ecclesiastical mercy, without any loss to Christian poor persons.

## CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0945B] What it means spiritually to enter one’s neighbor’s vineyard, eat grapes within it, and not carry them outside.

“When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, eat grapes as much as you please, but do not carry any out with you.” Your neighbor is the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who mercifully received the wounded man when he was descending from Jericho to Jerusalem. He is called and is that man’s neighbor because he showed mercy to him (Luke 10). Hence he speaks to him through the prophet: “As with our neighbor, as with our brother, so I was well pleased” (Ps. 34).

Moreover, his vineyard is his Church, as the Spirit says in the prophet: “I shall sing to my beloved the song of my cousin concerning his vineyard. A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, a son of oil” (Isa. 5). And again: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his delightful shoot” (ibid.). You entered this vineyard when you were called to faith in Christ as a laborer by the master of the household (Matt. 20).

“Eat grapes,” therefore, he says, “as much as you please, but do not carry them outside with you”: that is, perform as many good works as you can, with a good heart and willing mind, but do nothing merely for human eyes. For the person who makes his light shine before people so that they may see his good works and glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5), truly eats grapes inside and in no way harms his neighbor; indeed, he is pleasing to his neighbor’s love. But the one who performs his righteousness before people in order to be seen by them has undoubtedly carried the grapes outside and in this has injured his friend’s favor. For concerning such persons he says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (John 6). They have received it, I say, and shall not enter the same vineyard of their neighbor in eternal fellowship.

## CHAPTER XXVII

What it means to pluck ears from a grainfield and rub them in the hand, but not harvest with a sickle.

“If you enter your friend’s grainfield, you shall pluck ears and rub them in your hand, but you shall not harvest with a sickle.” The grainfield of this same friend or neighbor is holy Scripture, woven from the words and deeds of his fathers according to the flesh. “You shall pluck an ear with your hand,” therefore, so that you may reach the hidden kernels; that is, you shall examine the death-dealing letter in order to live from the spiritual meaning hidden within. “But you shall not harvest with a sickle”: that is, you shall not condemn whatever is done or was done by the ancient fathers.

For example: Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (Gal. 4). If you rebuke or judge these and similar acts as adulteries, failing to distinguish the order of times—that is, that there was one permission before the Law, another under the Law, and another in the beauty of the Gospel—if, I say, you rebuke or condemn such things in the holy fathers, the fathers of our faith, from whose seed Christ our salvation came to us, then you have certainly harvested your friend’s grainfield with an undiscerning sickle. Therefore you shall only rub the bristling ear in your hand: that is, you shall understand that these things were spoken allegorically.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0946B] That if a man takes a wife and hates her, he is permitted to give her a bill of divorce: how this should be understood of each of us, and how Christ did this to the Synagogue.

(CH. 24.) “If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor before his eyes because of some uncleanness, he shall write a bill of divorce and give it into her hand and dismiss her from his house. When she has gone out and married another husband, and he likewise comes to hate her and gives her a bill of divorce and dismisses her from his house—or if he has certainly died—the former husband shall not be able to take her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and made abominable before the Lord, lest you cause your land to sin, which the Lord your God gives you to possess.”

It is surely clear that, according to the letter, the force of the command lacks rational grounds. Truth itself testifies to this in the Gospel: when the Pharisees objected that Moses commanded a bill of divorce to be given and a wife dismissed, he replied: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses commanded you to dismiss your wives. But from the beginning it was not so,” etc. (Matt. 19). Here too, therefore, let us rub the ear of the letter and take from it the kernel of spiritual meaning.

A man takes a wife when he undertakes the care of earthly activity. If he recognizes its uncleanness, he gives a bill of divorce and dismisses her from his house, because an earthly activity that was strongly loved before it was possessed is often recognized, once possessed, to be unclean, when it appears to be polluted by sins. Let the man therefore dismiss her from his house, casting her love out of his mind. Let her, having gone out, take another husband, because another desires the earthly activity that you abandon. But perhaps it too will someday come to be hated, so that he may usefully dismiss it.

It is well said, moreover, “he dismissed her, or certainly he died,” because every person either dismisses earthly care or dies: that is, either he does not yield to it from his heart, or because of it he wholly falls in the life of his soul. Whether, then, the husband who follows her dismisses her or dies, the former husband cannot take her as his wife because she has been defiled. Thus one who has once abandoned earthly care and the intention of this present life must never return to it, since he has already declared it polluted by his own judgment; for that was why he first abandoned it—because he recognized that it was polluted.

Moreover, according to allegory there is a higher sense: namely, that, as he testified through the prophet, God gave a bill of divorce to your mother, the Synagogue, O Jews. Nevertheless, the same God of judgment partly sets aside the letter of the command out of mercy, when he says likewise through the prophet: “It is commonly said: If a man dismisses his wife and she departs from him and takes another husband, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be defiled and contaminated? But you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you” (Jer. 3).

Thus the Synagogue has now received a bill of divorce, because, as a woman despises her lover, so she despised Christ and took the devil as another husband. Nevertheless, she will return to her former husband, and he will receive her when she returns, because “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 2).

## CHAPTER XXIX

What it means that neither the lower nor the upper millstone must be taken as a pledge.

“You shall not take as a pledge the lower and upper millstone, because he has set before you his life.” “To take” sometimes means “to take away.” Thus the Apostle Paul says: “You endure it if someone devours you, if someone takes” (2 Cor. 11), as though saying, “if someone seizes.” The pledge of a debtor is the confession of a sinner. For a pledge is taken from a debtor when confession of sin is demanded from a sinner.

The upper and lower millstones are hope and fear. Hope lifts to higher things; fear presses the heart downward. But the upper and lower millstone are so necessarily joined that either is useless without the other. Hope and fear ought to be joined in the sinner’s breast, because he hopes vainly for mercy if he does not also fear justice; and he fears justice vainly if he does not also trust in mercy.

Therefore it is forbidden to take either the upper or lower millstone as a pledge, because one who preaches to a sinner must so shape his preaching with such balance that he neither removes fear by abandoning hope nor, by removing hope, leaves him in fear alone. For the upper or lower millstone is taken away if, through the preacher’s tongue, either fear or hope is separated from the other in the sinner’s breast.

## CHAPTER XXX

What it means that, after setting forth the sentence against one who has sold his brother, it immediately added that the plague of leprosy must be avoided; and that the person who has the Gospel of Christ for sale also sells his brother and is consequently leprous, like Gehazi.

If a man is caught enticing his brother from among the children of Israel, and, having sold him, receives a price, he shall be put to death; and you shall remove evil from your midst. Plainly, even according to the literal sense, the sale of a brother is a great sacrilege, of which Jacob’s sons made themselves guilty when Joseph was sold by them into slavery (Gen. XXXVII).
