But immediately it follows: “Take diligent care not to incur the plague of leprosy, but [Col. 0948A] do whatever the priests of the Levitical race teach you, according to what I have commanded them, and fulfil it carefully.” And directly thereafter: “Remember what the Lord your God did to Miriam on the way, when you came out of Egypt.” What does this mean: that, after such a command has been set forth, it decrees that leprosy must be so diligently avoided? Or can anyone observe this, or is it within his power not to incur the plague of leprosy? Therefore something deeper must be sought here also.

For a man was caught receiving a price after selling his brother when the Jewish people shed the blood of Christ, their brother according to the flesh, and gave and received a price; for Judas the traitor received the thirty silver pieces, the price of blood (Matt. XXVII). By this deed the whole Synagogue incurred the leprosy of a curse, [Col. 0948B] of which Miriam, as has already been said in its place, was a type when a white leprosy covered her whole body (Num. XII). Therefore, whoever you are who have learned that Christ was to come from the Law and the Prophets, and have been able to read or hear of his sale in the Gospel, take diligent care not to incur the plague of leprosy: that is, lest, by consenting to the sacrileges of the Jews, you be covered with a curse, clothed in everlasting shame, and, cast out with that assembly of evildoers, dwell outside the camp of the Church making its way to heaven. Take diligent care of this, I say, and do whatever the priests of the Levitical race teach you—that is, the preachers of evangelical truth. For they can teach you how to be free from such leprosy.

Moreover, he too sells his brother who holds the Gospel [Col. 0948C] of Christ for sale. For he is your brother, as he says in the Gospel: “Go to my brothers and say to them: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father’” (John XX). And elsewhere, after he had said, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” (Matt. XII), stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said: “Behold, my mother and my brothers.” Therefore whoever sells Christ’s Gospel, especially whoever makes any sacrament of Christ a thing for sale, surely sells his brother. Such a person incurs leprosy so thoroughly that he is judged a heretic, as that magician Simon was in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts VIII), from whom sellers or buyers of Christ’s graces are called Simoniacs even to this day. Therefore, whoever has read or heard, “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. X), “take,” he says, [Col. 0948D] “diligent care not to incur the plague of leprosy”—that is understood, for such a sale of one’s brother—and so suffer in the soul what Gehazi suffered in the body. For just as Miriam’s leprosy signifies the spiritual ruin [p. 335] of those who, through pride of mind, fall into the pit of heretical teaching, so Gehazi’s leprosy expresses the disease of those who, because they make any evangelical grace a saleable thing, are cast out like lepers from the bosom of Mother Church (IV Kings V).

## CHAPTER XXXI. One who demands back something from his neighbour ought not to enter his house; that is, no one ought to be inquisitive or suspicious concerning a sinner’s conscience.

“And when you demand from your neighbour some thing which [Col. 0949A] he owes you, you shall not enter his house to take a pledge; but you shall stand outside, and he shall bring out to you what he has. But if he is poor, the pledge shall not remain with you overnight; rather, you shall return it to him immediately before sunset, so that, sleeping in his garment, he may bless you.”

On its very surface, this law of mercy is beautiful and pleasing. Yet what lies hidden within is more beautiful. Spiritually, we demand something from our neighbour whenever we rebuke a neighbour for some sin, according to that Gospel saying: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. XVIII). “You shall not enter,” he says, “his house to take a pledge.” He enters his neighbour’s house to take a pledge who scrutinizes his life inquisitively and too suspiciously, in order to find an accusation [Col. 0949B] against him. Therefore, he says, you shall not enter the house—that is, you shall not act inquisitively so that you may publicly accuse or rebuke things perhaps committed in secret.

But what then? “You shall stand outside, and he shall bring out to you what he has.” You shall stand outside, I say; you shall knock outside; you shall speak outside—so that you speak not to one person but to all, not concerning one thing but concerning everything—announcing that there is nothing covered which shall not be revealed, nothing hidden which shall not at least be known in the future judgment (Matt. X), so that, while you make all anxious, no one may remain secure. Then he will bring out to you what he has; that is, of his own accord he will confess what he has done, and you will pray for him, according to the Apostle’s command: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. V).

You, therefore, [Col. 0949C] shall immediately forgive one who confesses willingly. For this is what follows: “If he is poor, the pledge shall not remain with you overnight, but you shall return it immediately before sunset,” and so forth. You must exercise this discernment: if he is poor in spirit, if he confesses humbly, if he is contrite for his sin, forgive him immediately before sunset—that is, before he falls into the danger of despair—so that, sleeping in his garment, that is, resting in the hope of his salvation, he may bless you, because you have gained his soul, so that you may have righteousness before the Lord your God: namely, the righteousness which he wished you to understand when he said, “If he listens to you, you have gained your brother” (Matt. XVIII).

## CHAPTER XXXII. Why these statements do not appear contrary: “Fathers shall not be put to death for sons,” and “You repay the iniquity of fathers in sons and grandchildren.”

[Col. 0949D] “Fathers shall not be put to death for sons, nor sons for fathers; but each shall die in his own sin.” Elsewhere it is said: “You repay the iniquity of fathers in sons and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XXXIV). These should not appear contrary to one another. When he says, “Nor shall sons be put to death for fathers,” it must be understood: sons who do not follow their fathers’ sins. But where it is said, “You repay the iniquity of fathers in sons and grandchildren,” it must likewise be understood: those who imitate their wicked fathers.

In this distinction, although the principle of justice plainly presents itself, a great and ancient question remains concerning infants alone: why, although they have committed no actual [Col. 0950A] sin, they are held in the underworld for their fathers’ iniquity alone, that is, for original sin. Concerning them, though you may most rightly say to God, “Your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. XXXV), and may say with blessed Job speaking in the person of such as these, “You multiply my wounds even without cause” (Job IX), yet concerning all who are predestined to death this must be known: sin is the cause of their generation, or of their superfluous origin. For after Eve’s sin it was said: “I will multiply your sufferings and your conceptions” (Gen. III). Conversely, the efficient cause of the generation or origin of those predestined to life is God’s blessing, spoken before sin: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth; subdue it” (Gen. I), etc.

Certainly infants who are taken from this light before receiving Christ’s grace [Col. 0950B] reveal, by the very fact that they have been so taken away, that they arose not from the preceding blessing, but from the excess consequent upon sin. By that same justice by which it was said, “I will multiply your sufferings and your conceptions,” superfluous human beings are born and by the same justice they die. Accordingly, after still more careful definition, the sentence must be completed: “Nor shall sons die for fathers”—that is understood—if they deserve to have other fathers, namely the priests of holy Church; indeed, another father, that is, Christ the new Adam.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What is left behind after the reaping of harvest should not be gathered again; that is, good works ought not always, or altogether, to be concealed from human eyes.

“When you reap the crop in your field and forget a sheaf [Col. 0950C] and leave it behind, you shall not return to take it; but you shall allow the stranger, the orphan, and the widow to take it, that the Lord your God may bless you in every work of your hands. If you gather the fruits of olive trees, whatever remains on the trees, you shall not return to gather it, but you shall leave it for the stranger, the orphan, and the widow. Remember that you too served in Egypt.”

This surface sense of the letter is plain, and greatly builds up our minds toward humanity and godliness; nor does this part of the letter kill—indeed, it gives life no less than the spirit. It is easy now to draw the spirit from the letter, not as life from what kills, but as treasure from treasure, as honey from wax. Spiritually, the harvests of our crops, the fruits of our olive trees, [Col. 0950D] and the clusters of our vineyards are our works of righteousness. And we surely gather our crop, our olives, and our clusters without leaving any remnant when we take such care not to perform our righteousness before men that no one sees us. Yet if we always fear a spectator so greatly, we shall never have an imitator.

Therefore, he says, you shall not return to take the sheaf which you forgot and left behind; you shall not gather whatever remains among the olive trees or the remaining clusters of the vineyard. But you shall allow the stranger, the orphan, and the widow to take them; you shall leave them for the orphan, stranger, and widow; they shall pass to the use of the stranger, orphan, and widow. The stranger, orphan, and widow, because they have not sown, because they have not planted olive trees or vineyards, are the poor [Col. 0951A] of the Church: they indeed possess faith, but have not yet performed works of righteousness suited to faith. Therefore let us store up many of our works within the secret of conscience, because of the danger of wretched vainglory; yet let us leave some such works [p. 336] for orphans, strangers, and widows, that they may be stirred by our examples, so that, as our Lord says, they may see our good works and glorify our Father who is in heaven (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Why, in correcting a person, the number of stripes should not exceed forty; and concerning the Lord’s forty-day fast.

(CHAP. XXV.) “If there is a case between certain persons and they appeal to the judges, the judges shall give the palm of righteousness to the one whom they see to be just, [Col. 0951B] and condemn the impious person for impiety. But if they judge the sinner worthy of stripes, they shall lay him down and have him beaten before them. The measure of stripes shall correspond to the measure of the sin, provided only that it does not exceed the number forty, lest your brother depart shamefully lacerated before your eyes.”

We know that the remedy of the rod’s stripes is for faults which are not unto death: both that past fault may be washed away and that the desire to sin in the future may be restrained by fear after experiencing punishment. For this reason too, in ecclesiastical discipline, we ought at the very beginning of sin to restrain the wicked, hard, proud, or disobedient by blows or bodily chastisement, knowing what is written: “A fool is not corrected by words” (Prov. XXIII). And again: “Strike your son with the rod, and you shall deliver his soul [Col. 0951C] from death” (ibid.).

But why, under this law, must the quantity of stripes not exceed forty? Why, when a man has been laid low beneath so many strokes, was he not to be shamefully mangled before that people by receiving the full number of so many stripes? Clearly because all of them together had sinned in the crime of the calf which Aaron made, and Moses, prostrate for forty days and forty nights beneath the blows of fasting, made satisfaction to the Lord for their guilt. For he says: “I lay before the Lord forty days and nights” (Deut. IX), or, “I fell before the Lord, as previously, for forty days and forty nights, eating no bread and drinking no water, because of all your sins which you committed against the Lord; and the Lord heard me [Col. 0951D] this time also.”

Thus, in the very heat of judgment, the holy law rightly recalls mercy, with wondrous care allowing people, under every punishment of any individual, not to forget the universal offence; for they are bound by the law of that number through which they themselves, while another suffered punishment, obtained mercy. This mercy of the Law also gave limited aid to the Apostle Paul. For he says: “Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one” (II Cor. XI). Unjust judges, having unjustly judged and wickedly laid him down, beat him sparingly five times, lest they should seem, through pleasure in killing or delight in cruelty, to make full use of what was allowed them; for from the number forty, which they did not dare to exceed, they withheld one stripe from his already torn body.

[p. 336]

But Jesus Christ, the new man who spiritually fulfilled the whole Law, likewise obeyed this part of the Law in himself: for the gluttony of the first man, enduring the stripes of fasting, he did not exceed the number of forty days. For when they were completed, behold, angels came and ministered to him (Matt. IV). Hence even to this day it is customary, in both public and private satisfactions, to prescribe this number of days, and thus for persons voluntarily prostrate and penitent to be lawfully beaten before the Lord with the stripes of abstinence.

## CHAPTER XXXV. “You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out grain.”

“You shall not muzzle the ox treading out your grain on the threshing-floor.” It is already a well-known and celebrated authority that an ox is not to be understood here simply as an ox. [Col. 0952B] For the Apostle Paul, after saying, “Do we not have authority to eat and drink?” (I Cor. IX), immediately added: “Am I saying these things according to man? Or does not the Law also say this? For it is written in the Law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it treads out grain.’ Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he indeed say it for our sake? For it was written for our sake, because the one who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and the one who threshes, in hope of receiving the fruit” (ibid.).

Therefore, in this place the ox must be understood as the Evangelist—that is, the preacher of the Gospel—who surely separates grain from chaff on the threshing-floor when, expounding the Scriptures in the public Church, he brings forth the spiritual sense of the Law from the barren letter. God’s righteousness provides for him when it says: “You shall not muzzle the ox [Col. 0952C] treading out your grain on the threshing-floor”; that is, you shall not allow the preacher who supplies your soul’s provisions to hunger in body. You shall not deny your earthly goods, I say, to one who sows spiritual goods for you (ibid.), especially since in the Gospel Truth itself—and that same righteousness—says: “The labourer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the statement, “His brother shall take the wife of the deceased and raise up his brother’s seed”; and concerning Ruth the Moabite, by whom Obed was begotten, father of Jesse, David’s father.

“When brothers live together and one of them dies without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry another man; rather, his brother shall take her and raise up his brother’s seed. And he shall call the firstborn son from her by the name [Col. 0952D] of the deceased, so that his name may not be blotted out from Israel. But if he does not wish to take his brother’s wife, who is owed to him by the law, the woman shall go to the city gate and appeal to the elders, saying: ‘My husband’s brother refuses to raise up his brother’s seed in Israel and to take me in marriage.’ They shall immediately summon and question him. If he replies, ‘I do not wish to take her as wife,’ the woman shall come before him in the presence of the elders, take the sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and say: ‘Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother’s house.’ And his name in Israel shall be called: The House of the Unsandaled.”

According to the letter of this Law, a way was made and an entrance opened through which the Gentiles too might have a place in the lineage of Christ, who according to the flesh is from the Jews: namely, so that Boaz, by right of kinship, might take Ruth the Moabite [Col. 0953A] as wife, while the man who was nearer of kin refused to take his brother’s wife and raise up his seed (Ruth IV). Yet it should be noted that the woman did not approach him entirely according to this Law, before the elders, to take the sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and say, “Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother’s house.” Rather Boaz said to that kinsman: “Take off your sandal,” and he immediately removed it from his foot. And Boaz said to the elders and all the people of Israel: “You are witnesses today” (ibid.), etc. Perhaps because the woman was a foreigner, she did not dare to use the full liberty or permission of the Law.

By her was begotten Obed, father of Jesse, father of David, who according to the flesh is the father of our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0953B] Thus, as has already been said, after Rahab the prostitute, Ruth the Moabite was admitted, through the grace [p. 337] of this Law, into the lineage of Christ the Son of God. Concerning her the prophet Isaiah says: “Send forth the lamb, O Lord, the ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. XVI). For that rock of the desert was the woman from the midst of the Gentiles—the Gentile world, namely, which had previously been abandoned by God—from whom Christ, the Lamb of God, David’s son according to the flesh, came forth.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Mystically, the deceased man is Christ; and his brother, who is able to govern the Church of God, ought to raise up his seed.

Moreover, mystically, the deceased brother is he who, appearing after the glory of the resurrection, said: “Go, tell [Col. 0953C] my brothers” (John XX), and who died as if without children because he has not yet filled up the number of his elect. His surviving brother is commanded to receive his wife, because it is surely fitting that the care of holy Church be imposed upon one who is able to govern her well. The woman spits in the face of one unwilling to do this, because whoever does not take care to benefit others through the gifts he has received is reproached by holy Church even for his good qualities, which, as it were, casts spittle in his face. The sandal is removed from one of his feet, so that he is called the House of the Unsandaled. For it is written: “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI). Therefore, if we take care of our neighbour as we do of ourselves, we protect both feet with the sandal. But one who considers his own advantage [Col. 0953D] and neglects his neighbours loses, shamefully, the sandal of one foot.

Meanwhile the deceased man’s wife—the wife, I say, the Synagogue—who ought to have been married to the deceased, that is, to him who died for her, married another. For she preferred to have Barabbas the robber; and, despising him who came blessed in his Father’s name, she awaits another who will come accursed in his own name. Hence also that saying: “Because beside me you uncovered yourself and received an adulterer” (Isa. LVII).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. “If men have a quarrel between them,” etc.; what mystery this signifies in Christ and Satan’s Synagogue, and how the Synagogue’s hand has now been cut off.

“If men have a quarrel between them, and one begins to fight against [Col. 0954A] another, and the wife of one man, wishing to rescue her husband from the hand of the stronger man, puts out her hand and seizes his private parts, you shall cut off her hand; you shall not be moved by any pity for her.”

This is a deserved punishment for a brazen and shameless little woman, who, attacking the tender and hidden roots of nature, would afflict a strong man—though herself without strength—with both pain and shame. But why did the finger of God deign to remember such a matter, such a slight misfortune, in the written Law of righteousness? Certainly, if you suppose it written without spirit or mystical meaning, this body of the letter is trivial and ridiculous. Therefore let us seek a mystery here too, that we may everywhere pursue the woman, the enemy of the strong man.

This woman is the Synagogue. The two men who had a quarrel—or rather, a great contest—between them are [Col. 0954B], on one side, Christ and, on the other, the devil. He indeed is strong, but Christ is stronger, as he says: “When a strong man armed guards his court, all that he possesses is in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him” (Luke XVII), etc. This woman knows nothing of this stronger and strongest man except the weakness of his flesh. For just as in Noah, drunk from the vineyard which he himself planted, and with his private parts uncovered in his tent (Gen. IX), these things mystically signify the weakness of flesh—through which Christ, God and man, could be crucified by his vineyard, the house of Israel, and made drunk with vinegar and gall and all the bitterness of death—so in this place the private parts of the strong man, which the woman seizes in support of her husband, signify the human nature of the same Christ, Son of God, [Col. 0954C] according to which the Synagogue, supporting the cause of her husband—indeed, her adulterer, the devil—was able to seize and crucify him.

What then? “You shall cut off her hand,” he says, “and you shall not be moved by any pity for her.” It is plain to the whole world; the whole globe has heard and understands that the Synagogue’s hand has been cut off—cut off, I say, from the living body; cut off from the whole faith of the patriarchs and prophets—so that it can do nothing, so that all its work is dead and separated from the living God.

Moreover, men contend with each other as often as a Catholic man, strong in faith and powerful in speech, enters into public contest with a heretic for the defence of the faith. But the woman, wishing to rescue her husband from the hand of the stronger man, puts forth her hand and seizes his private parts when any supporter, ignorant of the order of disputation, breaks out into shameful or commonplace insults [Col. 0954D] and casts upon the strong man—even falsely—a stain from his past actions which he either knows or is able to invent. Therefore, he says, cut off her hand and be moved by no pity for her: that is, even if she possesses some virtue, regard it as a fault and cast it away as dung, so that you may confidently say: “Better is the wickedness of a man than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. XLII).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. “You shall not have different weights in your bag”; and how a heretic possesses these spiritually.

“You shall not have different weights in your bag, a greater and a lesser; nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure. [Col. 0955A] You shall have a just and true weight; a full and true measure shall be yours, that you may live long upon the land which the Lord God has given you. For the Lord God abominates one who does these things and detests every injustice.”

“Different weights,” he says, “a greater and a lesser; a larger and a smaller measure”: namely, a greater weight and larger measure for receiving or buying, a lesser weight and smaller measure for giving or selling. Such buyers or sellers we rightly call *mangones*, as though *mancones* (“defective persons”), because what they receive or buy they make defective—that is, less—when giving or selling. A person placed in heavenly and spiritual commerce is rightly considered like them if, when returning the precious pearls of God’s word that he has received, he mutilates them in some respect: that is, if he thinks one thing and says another concerning the same utterances of sacred Scripture.

For he receives gold, silver, grain, or even oil, as it were with a larger weight or measure and returns it with a lesser one, who, inwardly weighing God’s word by a right understanding, nevertheless outwardly perverts it by contentious exposition in perverse words. The Lord, he says, abominates the one who does these things—that is, the heretic and impious person. He abominates him, I say, so that he declares that such a sin is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. XII). For a word spoken against the Holy Spirit occurs when, though the Spirit reveals it, an evil measurer and fraudulent weigher dares to diminish the meaning of Scripture by expounding it wrongly.

[p. 338]

## CHAPTER XL. [Col. 0955C] Concerning the statement, “Remember what Amalek did to you, and you shall blot out his name from under heaven”; and how Amalek is spiritually the devil to us.

“Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, when you came out of Egypt: how he met you and struck down the rearmost of your company, those who lingered exhausted, when you were worn out by hunger and labour, and did not fear God. Therefore, when the Lord your God gives you rest and has subjected all the surrounding nations in the land which he promised you, you shall blot out his name from under heaven. Take care not to forget.”

It has already been said elsewhere that the Hebrews here [Col. 0956A] understand “the exhausted” as those unclean persons who, according to the Law, remained outside the camp, and whom the Amalekites are said to have struck down because, as they hand down, the Amalekites cut off their circumcision and threw it toward heaven in mockery of God. Most gravely is this said, most sternly commanded, against Amalek—both here, when it says, “Take care not to forget,” and in Exodus, where it says: “Write this as a memorial in a book and deliver it into the ears of Joshua. For I shall blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven” (Exod. XVII).

The task of carrying out this command fell to Saul, when the Lord said: “I have reviewed all that Amalek did to Israel, how he resisted him on the way when he came up from Egypt. Now therefore go and strike Amalek” (I Kings XV). It is therefore neither surprising nor unjust that Saul was cast away irretrievably [Col. 0956B] for such a fault, because he dared to transgress what had been commanded so solemnly from the Law once, twice, indeed three times. But both the authority of the one commanding and the punishment of the disobedient ought to establish fear in us, lest we forget what the spiritual Amalek has done to us since we came out of Egypt, since we passed through the Red Sea of Christ’s baptism: how he met us and struck down the rearmost of our company, where we lingered exhausted, when we were worn down by hunger and labour.

For this Amalek is the devil, who has relentlessly pursued each of us since, washed in Christ’s baptism, we escaped the guilt of original sin. Thus, since through faith in Christ we have come out of Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance—he seeks at least that, impeded by actual sins, we may by no means enter [Col. 0956C] the land of promise, the land of the living. Each of us knows what he has suffered from him: how he has been cut to pieces, by what or what kind of wounds he has been worn down in soul. Therefore let every one of us rise against this Amalek through repentance on his own behalf, that he may destroy his memory from under heaven; for all memory of Pharaoh and his armies—that is, of the sins which preceded baptism—has perished solely through Christ’s grace.

# SECOND BOOK ON DEUTERONOMY. (Deut., chaps. XXVI–XXXIV.)

[Col. 0955]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the statement, “When you enter the land which the Lord your God will give you,” etc.; how it pertains to us spiritually.

(CHAP. XXVI.) As we fashion the last—that is, the nineteenth—book in the Pentateuch, let us do what this holy and spiritual Law says immediately after the matters set forth above: “And when you enter the land which the Lord your God is about to give you for possession, and obtain it and dwell in it, you shall take the firstfruits of all your produce, put them in a basket, and go [Col. 0956D] to the place which the Lord your God has chosen, that his name may be invoked there. You shall approach the priest who is in those days and say to him: ‘Today I profess before the Lord your God that I have entered the land which he swore to our fathers that he would give us.’ And the priest, receiving the basket from his hand, shall set it before the altar of the Lord your God; and you shall speak before the Lord your God, before the altar: ‘A Syrian persecuted my father, who went down into Egypt,’” etc.

By the grace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have entered the land which he gave us to possess; we have obtained [Col. 0957A] it and all of us dwell in it to whom he has opened the understanding, that we might understand the Scriptures. For the field of the Scriptures is now a certain land of the living, so that, living according to them and walking in them, we rightly say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Hence the whole Church has long sung, on behalf of all believers who, after the shadow of the Law, hold the evangelical truth: “The Lord has brought you into a land flowing with milk and honey, that the Law of the Lord may always be in your mouth.”

Therefore, as we have said, with God’s help let us do what follows: “You shall take the firstfruits of all your produce and put them in a basket”—that is, in a wicker basket or a pannier—“and go to the place which the Lord your God has chosen, that his name may be invoked [Col. 0957B] there.” The firstfruits of our produce are whatever is best in our studies. The place which our Lord God has chosen for his name to be invoked is the Catholic Church; outside it he is nowhere near to those who call upon him, and outside it his name is nowhere else invoked in truth. The priest in these days is the great High Priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus Christ (Heb. IV), who, unlike the others, is not prevented by death from continuing, but has an eternal priesthood because he remains forever (Heb. VII).

Therefore let us go to this place, to this great priest, carrying the firstfruits of our produce: that is, let us bring whatever is best in our labours or studies to the building up of holy Church, to the honour [Col. 0957C] of Christ our Lord. Let all of us, each one individually, say to him: “Today I profess before the Lord your God that I have entered the land which he swore to our fathers that he would give us.” This means: I confess today—that is, in this time—that what the Lord our God promised and swore to Abraham our father has been fulfilled: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII); and that this seed is Jesus Christ, who was born in the days of King Herod and suffered under Pontius Pilate, who also rose from the dead. Thus through him it has come about that we have entered the land which he swore to our fathers to give us: the land of the living, the land of the heavenly paradise.

With this profession, [Col. 0957D] “the priest,” he says, “receiving the basket, shall set it before the altar of the Lord”—understand, before the eyes of the Lord—that your memorial may be eternal, in accordance with that saying in which the Lord himself speaks through the prophet: “My words shall not fail from your mouth, and your gifts shall be acceptable upon my altar.” And, he says, “You shall speak before the Lord your God”—understand, the reason why we had to enter, in such an order, namely through Christ’s passion, that land which he swore to our fathers to give us. That reason is as follows.

## CHAPTER II. “A Syrian persecuted,” etc. How we too, in confession and offering, must say: “A Syrian persecuted my father, who went down into Egypt.”

“A Syrian persecuted my father, who went down [Col. 0958A] into Egypt and sojourned there with a very small number. And he grew into a great, strong nation of countless multitude. And the Egyptians afflicted and persecuted us, imposing very heavy burdens. And we cried to the Lord God of our fathers, who heard us and looked upon our humility, labour, and distress, and brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand and outstretched arm, in great terror, in signs and wonders; and he brought us to this place and gave us a land flowing with milk and honey.”

“A Syrian,” he says—that is, Laban from Mesopotamian Syria—having taken his brothers, pursued my father, whom he also overtook on Mount Gilead. But in a dream he saw God saying to him: “Take care not to speak anything harsh against Jacob” [Col. 0958B] (Gen. XXXI). That father of mine, I say—that is, Jacob, who is Israel—that Syrian pursued: not my father Abraham, nor my father Isaac, but my father Jacob. For it follows: “Who went down into Egypt and sojourned there with a very small number,” etc.

Spiritually, the Syrian, whose name is interpreted “lofty,” is this world: the rejected world, the condemned world—the world, I say, in the persons of those who belong to the earthly generation—which from the beginning persecuted my father, says the faithful and Catholic man: my father, that is, the whole people of the elect, the generation of those who seek God (Ps. XXIII). For there are two generations, one of the world and one of God. From the beginning of the world, with the first brothers Cain and Abel, [Col. 0958C] they began to oppose one another, and they do not cease to be opposed to one another until the end of the age.

From the time when “the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose” (Gen. VI), my father began to go down into Egypt. From that time those belonging to the generation of God began to be entangled in the vices and errors of the opposing generation. How, according to the mystical sense of the present words, the Egyptians afflicted and persecuted them, and how the Lord spiritually delivered us from Pharaoh’s hand or service through his lamb—that is, through Christ his Son—and the other matters which follow, has been more fully explained in its proper place. That slavery was the reason why Christ the Son of God had necessarily to die, as was foretold—to die and rise again—that we might thus enter with him into this land [Col. 0958D] which he swore to our fathers.

“Therefore,” he says, “I now offer the firstfruits of the produce of the land which the Lord has given.” And you shall leave them before your Lord.

### Chapter III. On the statement: “In the third year you shall give a tithe of your fruits to the Levite and the stranger,” and on the meaning of saying: “I did not eat of them in my mourning.”

And, having worshipped the Lord your God, you shall feast upon all the good things which the Lord your God has given to you and to your household—you, the Levite, and the stranger who is with you. When you have completed the tithe of all your fruits [Col. 0959A] in the third year, the year of tithes, you shall give it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, so that they may eat within your gates and be filled.

It must be especially noted that it says, “in the third year, the year of tithes, when you have completed the tithe of all your fruits”—in the year, I say, of tithes: not in the first or second, but in the third year you shall give to the Levite and the stranger, the orphan and the widow, that they may eat within your gates and be filled. In the literal sense, this is a command of piety; but in the mystical sense, it is a representation or prophecy of the apostolic work. For the third year of tithes is the time of evangelical grace. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. Moreover, the Levite is the foster-child of the Jewish people. The stranger, or orphan, or widow is the common people of the nations. “In the third year,” he says, [Col. 0959B] “you shall give,” not to the Levite alone, but also jointly to the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, so that they may eat within your gates and be filled. That is, in the time of grace revealed, you shall distribute the nourishment of heavenly doctrine, and preach to all the word of eternal life, not to the Jew alone, as before the Law or under the Law, but without distinction both to Jew and Gentile alike.

And you shall speak before the Lord your God: “I have brought what has been sanctified from my house and have given it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow, as you commanded me. I have not transgressed your commandments or forgotten your command. I did not eat of them in my mourning; nor did I set them apart in any uncleanness; nor did I spend anything from them upon a funeral matter. I obeyed the voice of the Lord my God and did everything as you commanded me.”

Suppose that the apostle Paul spoke thus in the presence of the Lord. [Col. 0959C] For, bringing from his house what was sanctified and giving it to the Levite, the stranger, the orphan, and the widow—that is, carrying forth from the synagogue the holy grace of the Gospel and giving it, without distinction, both to Jew and Greek, as he was commanded by the Lord who said, “For I will send you far away to the nations” (Acts 22)—he did not eat anything of these things in his mourning. That is, he concealed nothing from the Gentiles because of those Jews who were his brothers and whom he mourned, saying: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness, that I have great sorrow and continual grief in my heart. For I wished that I myself might be accursed from Christ for my brothers” (Rom. 9), etc.

Indeed, if, because of this grief, [Col. 0959D] he had evaded his task and thus preached the grace of God less fully to the Gentiles, he would have eaten some of his fruits or tithes in his mourning, or spent them on a funeral matter. And since he also says, “But whatever things were gain to me, these I have counted as losses for Christ, and I count them as dung” (Phil. 3), he certainly did not set apart his fruits or tithes in any uncleanness. “Therefore,” he says, “I obeyed the voice of the Lord my God and did everything as you commanded me.”

“Look down from your sanctuary and from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven, and bless your people Israel and the land which you gave us, as you swore to our fathers, a land flowing with milk and honey,” etc. Certainly, he who has thus brought the sanctified tithes of his fruits prays with confidence in this way: that is, he who, as far as he was able, laboured in the Gospel [Col. 0960A] of Christ, both speaking and writing letters concerning perfect faith. He effectively and confidently asks that he may have some fruit from those among whom he laboured, while the Lord looks down from his sanctuary and from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven, and blesses his people. Without his regard and blessing the preacher labours in vain, because “neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

### Chapter IV. On the statement: “And you shall build an altar to the Lord from stones which iron has not touched.”

(Chapter 27.) Moses and the elders of Israel therefore commanded the people, saying: “Keep every commandment which I command you today. When you have crossed the Jordan [Col. 0960B] into the land which the Lord your God will give you, you shall set up great stones and smooth them with lime, so that you may be able to write upon them all the words of this Law, after crossing the Jordan.” And afterwards: “There you shall build an altar to the Lord your God from stones which iron has not touched.”

To set up great stones after crossing the Jordan, and to smooth them with lime so that all the words of the Lord’s Law may be written upon them, means to shake by evangelical preaching the stony minds of the nations after Christ’s passion and resurrection have been celebrated, and to inscribe upon them the utterances or arguments of saving doctrine—not by any violence, but by sweet and gentle preaching. Conversely, to wish to build an altar to the Lord out of stones touched by iron is forcibly, or by some violence, to impose the Christian Law upon unwilling hearers. But the sacred Law forbids this.

Therefore Christian religion is to be built for the Lord without iron—that is, without violence—and hard stones and worshippers of stones are to be smoothed with lime, that is, softened by gentle preaching. “And thus,” he says, “you shall write upon the stones all the words of this Law plainly and clearly,” namely, so that what was said may come to pass: “If they are silent, the stones will not be silent” (Luke 19). That is, if the Jews who possess the books deny Christ, the Gentiles, who have the Law written in their hearts (Rom. 2), will preach.

### Chapter V. On the statement: “These shall stand to bless, and those opposite shall stand to curse”: what future event is signified here.

Moses commanded the people on that day, saying: “These shall stand to bless the Lord upon Mount [Col. 0960D] Gerizim, after crossing the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. And opposite these shall stand to curse upon Mount Ebal: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.”

Since we have now proceeded as far as the end of the Law, it is fitting that we look ahead to the end of the age and establish that the final judgment is here signified from Christ’s Gospel. “When,” he says, “the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he shall sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them one from another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And he shall set the sheep indeed at his right hand, but the goats at his left. Then he shall say to those who are at his right: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; possess [Col. 0961A] the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food’” (Matt. 25), etc. And afterwards: “Then he shall also say to those who are at his left: ‘Depart from me, cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food’” (ibid.), etc.

The universal judgment which the Son of God, soon to suffer, plainly announces there in the light, Moses the servant of God here prophesies of that same one as soon to die, in shadow and beneath a veil. There are, in that passage, the King’s right and left hands, with sheep separated and divided from goats; here there are two hills facing one another, Gerizim and Ebal. Gerizim is interpreted “division”; Ebal, “failing” or “separating,” or “the ancient abyss.” There are there six works of mercy for those at the right, to bless them, [Col. 0961B] and six impious acts for those at the left, to curse them. Here likewise there are six names of Israel’s sons on Mount Gerizim for blessing, and no less six on Mount Ebal for cursing.

Nor are the twelve thrones altogether unmentioned here, concerning which he says elsewhere: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. 19). For it follows: “And the Levites shall pronounce, saying in a loud voice to all the men of Israel: ‘Cursed is the man who makes a carved image,’” etc. Twelve curses are set forth here: cursed is the man who makes a carved image; cursed is he who does not honour his father and mother; cursed is he who removes his neighbour’s boundary marks; cursed is he who causes a blind man to wander on the road; cursed is he who perverts judgment; cursed is he who lies [Col. 0961C] with his father’s wife; cursed is he who lies with any beast; cursed is he who lies with his sister; cursed is he who lies with his mother-in-law; cursed is he who secretly strikes his neighbour; cursed is he who accepts gifts to strike down the life of innocent blood; cursed is he who does not remain in the words of this Law nor fulfil them in deed.

Conversely, twelve blessings are set forth in the following order: (Chapter 28.) “And all these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you if you obey the commandments of the Lord your God. Blessed are you in the city, and blessed in the field; blessed is the fruit of your womb; blessed are your storehouses, and blessed are your remnants. You shall be blessed when going out and when coming in. The Lord shall cause your enemies who rise against you to fall before you. They shall come against you by one way and flee before you by seven. [Col. 0961D] The Lord shall send blessings upon your store-rooms; the Lord shall raise you up for himself as a holy people, as he swore to you. The Lord shall make you abound in every good thing. The Lord shall open his best treasury, heaven, to give rain to your land in its season. He shall bless all the works of your hands. The Lord shall establish you as head and not tail; and you shall always be above and not beneath.”

Thus also there are twelve thrones of judges in the Gospel, and here in the Law—as though each blessing and curse had been pronounced from an individual throne. Here are twelve blessings; there, twelve curses. Therefore, most clearly, the Gospel agrees with the Law in this also: for the judgment is one and the same, marked here in the shadow of the Law and revealed there in evangelical light [Col. 0962A].

### Chapter VI. That the following curses, thirty in number, belong specifically to the Jews; and that, on the same ground, Psalm 108 contains the same number of curses.

The blessings and curses spoken of thus far are common to all nations according to each person’s merits. For there is no distinction. Whoever has sinned under the Law—whether Jew or Gentile, since Gentiles too, by believing in Christ, have received the ten words of the Law written on tablets—shall be judged by the Law (Rom. 2). The Gospel too, cited above, testifies to this: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, then all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. 25).

But the following curses, in the saying, “If you refuse to hear the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments and ceremonies which I command you today, all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you,” belong specifically to the Jews. And behold: today they have come upon that unhappy people and manifestly overtaken it. They are thirty in number. The first is, “You shall be cursed in the city”; the last, “The stranger who lives with you in the land shall rise above you and be higher; but you shall descend and be lower. He shall be head to you, and you shall be tail.”

And deservedly they were overwhelmed by thirty curses who killed Christ the Son of God, the giver of blessing, purchased for thirty pieces of silver. [Col. 0962C] On the same ground Psalm 108 contains thirty curses, both against him who sold—namely Judas the traitor—and against those who bought. The first is: “Set a sinner over him”; the last: “Let them be clothed with their shame as with a double garment” (Ps. 108).

Leaving aside these and the other matters which follow, because they are plain and, as the foregoing matters, have been fulfilled in deed since the siege in which the Jews were miserably destroyed by the Romans in an irreparable ruin, let us now turn to the very passage of the song in which the Synagogue is manifestly rejected and the Church substituted for the praise and glory of Christ, Son of God. This Christ alone is proclaimed, defended, and extolled by the first Law, the second Law—that is, Deuteronomy, the “Second Law”—and this third testimony, the Song [Col. 0962D].

### Chapter VII. On the Song of Moses: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak.”

(Chapter 32.) “Hear, O heavens, what I shall speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.”

By metonymy the speech is addressed to the inanimate heavens and the inanimate earth; and from things which have neither ears nor any sense, the rational and wise human being seems to demand attentive hearing. It is as though he said: “Since I am a mortal man, and know that these people, or their descendants, will act wickedly after my death and quickly turn aside from the way which I have commanded them, at least you, O heavens, who will survive, and you, O earth, which will stand for ever, come to hear; stand as witnesses, so that when they act wickedly and turn aside from the way of the Lord, you, according to the curses set forth above—you heavens, I say—may be bronze above them, and you, the earth they tread, may be iron.” [Col. 0963A]

But according to the sense of inward truth, rather those heavens are summoned to hear of which the same Spirit says in the Prophet: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18); and that earth of which elsewhere he says: “The Lord shall give goodness, and our land shall give its fruit” (Ps. 84). Those heavens, I say, and that earth are summoned here to hear, concerning which another prophet also says: “Drop down, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Saviour” (Isa. 45). Thus the eloquent heavens—that is, the apostles, prophets, and all preachers—may not hesitate, having left this foolish people without counsel and without prudence, to go forth so that “their sound may go out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18), and, according to the testimony of the present song, invite the nations to praise God or to become God’s people. Thus the earth, once deserted and pathless—that is, the Church—may not hesitate to receive the saving rain from the highest heavens, that is, preaching from the mouths of the apostles, with the same hearing of faith by which the beginning of this land received it, namely the blessed Virgin, and gave its fruit by bearing Christ, God and man.

Therefore, “Hear, O heavens,” that is, O apostles; “let the earth hear,” that is, the Church to be gathered from all nations. [Col. 0963C] How, O heavens, are you to hear? How shall the words of my mouth reach the hearing of this earth? “Let my teaching thicken into rain; let my speech flow like dew, like a shower upon the grass and like drops upon the green plants.”

How does rain thicken? How does dew flow? It is known that, from below, as waters exhale a thin mist, the moisture thickens in the clouds; and from the clouds the condensed rain flows down to earth. Dew, however, condenses without clouds in the cold of night, and falls from heaven to earth in the morning calm. In this way these heavens, who have declared to us the glory of God, learned that same glory partly through the study of sacred reading and partly through God’s revelation alone. What they learned by reading and poured back to us by speaking, like moisture drawn up from below and condensed into rain, they, the gracious clouds, bestowed upon the grass. What they received by God’s revelation alone, they gathered like nocturnal dew by meditation and contemplation, and distilled it, through preaching or writing, upon the glad green plants of our faith or hope.

In both ways the perfect heaven, or firmament made firm, ought to be a fit apostle or preacher: one who does not speak from his own heart or from himself, but testifies to what he has heard, and announces and speaks what he has learned in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, among you, O heavens who hear, let my teaching thicken into rain, and through you let my speech flow like dew; that is, through the present reading of the Law and the revelation of the Holy Spirit, while you pray, the counsel of God may become known to you, and then through your mouths my speech may flow over every herb, over all the green plants flourishing throughout the whole world. [Col. 0964A]

“For,” he says, “I will call upon the name of the Lord.” Therefore, O heavens, grant goodwill to your speaker; lend a friendly ear to your singer, who asks this from the very subject at hand, because calling upon the Lord’s name is indeed a great matter. With you I shall call upon the name of the Lord: of the Lord, I say, the God whose glory you are to declare and whose works you are to announce. Therefore hear me, O heavens; therefore let the earth hear the words of my mouth.

“Give magnificence to our God. The works of God are perfect, and all his ways are judgments.” This is what I first wish you, O heavens, to hear. These are the words of my mouth which I desire you, O earth, to hear. When the Lord our God commands you, O heavens, not to rain upon this vineyard, for which he waited to produce grapes but which produced wild grapes (Isa. 5), for which he waited to produce judgment and behold [Col. 0964B] iniquity, and righteousness and behold a cry: when, I say, he commands you not to rain upon it, but rather upon the land once deserted and pathless, do not murmur and do not resist out of zeal for your people or your flesh. Rather, give magnificence to our God: follow and consider magnificent what has pleased our God. For although the cause or reason may be hidden from human beings, God’s works are nevertheless perfect—perfect, I say, and beyond reproach—and all his ways are judgments: true, just, and justified in themselves (Ps. 18). For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24).

This way by which truth migrated to the nations is mercy; this is the way by which it departed from Israel. Therefore give this magnificence to our God: believe that God’s works are perfect; confess that these ways, indeed all his ways, are judgments. What then? Because he made a covenant with Abraham, because he said, “I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations, an everlasting covenant” (Gen. 17), but has now departed from this seed of his—are his works therefore not perfect, are his ways therefore not judgments? Far from it: God is faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright—faithful, I say, in all his words; without any iniquity in all his judgments; just in all his ways; upright in all his works. [Col. 0964D]

Whence then, or for what reason, did he forget the covenant which he made with Abraham? If he is faithful, without any iniquity, just and upright, how did he disregard the oath which he swore to the fathers? Behold the answer: “They sinned against him, and they were not his children in their defilements.” They sinned—that is, they themselves made the covenant void; understand: they are his enemies and now no longer his children. They made his covenant void, as he himself, foreknowing this, said to me above: “Behold, you shall sleep with your fathers, and this people, rising up, shall commit fornication after foreign gods in the land into which it enters to dwell there. There it shall forsake me and make void the covenant which I made with it” (Deut. 31).

They sinned in defilements; in defilements they made the covenant void—not only in the defilement of the calf which Aaron made, or of Baal-peor, sins which had indeed already long been committed, but also in the defilements of Baal, Astaroth, and the other demons, and finally in the defilement of Barabbas the robber, whom they asked to have released to them. They sinned, I say—for it is certain that they sinned. Since, then, they thus sinned and were no longer his children in their defilements, and since for this reason the faithful God cast them away, say that God nevertheless remained faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright, though he cast away those with whom he had made a covenant in their fathers. For they sinned against him, and these people, now no longer his children, made that covenant void in their defilements.

Accordingly, O heavens and earth, whoever have heard these words of my mouth, do not rebuke God himself, who is faithful and without [Col. 0965B] any iniquity, but rebuke these people who are not his children and who sinned, in all your utterances and all your discourses through which you are to be heard throughout the earth and to the ends of the world. Say: “A crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people?” A crooked and perverse generation, I say—which is the same as saying, in the evangelical proclamation, “an evil and adulterous generation” (Matt. 12). It is crooked because it sprang indeed from good parents, but sprang badly, because it arose from the fathers’ flesh rather than faith alone. It is crooked and perverse because it did not imitate the faith of its fathers and was far unlike its fathers in conduct.

“Is this how you repay the Lord?” Is this, I say—that is, repaying evil for good—how you repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people? For you are foolish because, though you knew evil, you did not avoid it; you are senseless, whoever among this people do not know the good which you could have known. You are foolish when, in reading the prophets, you contentiousnessly distort the meaning of the prophets; you are senseless when you have not even read, when you refused to understand so as to act rightly (Ps. 35).

Therefore, foolish and senseless people, is this how you repay the Lord? “Is he not your father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” How great a thing it is that he is your father, as he said to Pharaoh: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4). How great a thing it is that he possessed you, made you, created you. He possessed you as Lord; he made you as potter; he created you as God. He made each person in his own individual person; he created him from one mass; he who possessed you in grace. [Col. 0965D] That he made and created you may be common to you with the other nations; but that he possessed you is a singular benefit.

As regards the propriety of the words or the distinction of their meanings, it is an act of great power that he possessed, a greater one that he made, and the greatest that he created. Conversely, it was a great grace that he created, a greater grace that he made, and the greatest grace that he possessed. Is this, then, how you repay the Lord for so many benefits: your Father, your possessor, your maker, your Creator?

“Remember the days of old; consider each generation”: namely, so that you may know that he whom you delivered up, whom you denied before Pilate (Acts 3), is your Father, who possessed, made, and created you. In order that you may know this, remember the days of old and consider each generation. For in the ancient days “all things were made through him” (John 1), and through every generation his mysteries were prefigured in words and deeds. But perhaps remembrance of ancient days and consideration of individual generations do not yet suffice for you. What then should you do? “Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will tell you.” Your Father is God himself; your elders are the Law and the prophets. Therefore ask your Father by praying; consult your elders by reading.

Ask, I say, your Father, God, with earnest prayers whether this counsel or work—whose sound has gone out into all the earth (Ps. 18)—comes from him, and he will tell you. For if he graciously heard the Gentile Cornelius praying and giving alms for this very purpose, and wonderfully showed him through his angel what he himself ought to do (Acts 10), how much more, if you ask and are willing to understand in order to act rightly, will he tell you through some revelation? Therefore, as said above, ask God your Father by prayer; consult your elders, that is, all the prophets, by reading. He will tell you, and they will say to you, that he whom you delivered up, denied, fed with gall, gave vinegar to drink, fastened with nails, and whose side you pierced with a lance, is your Father who possessed you. [Col. 0966B]

But how did he possess you, or how did he begin to possess you? He himself will plainly tell you this: “When the Most High divided the nations, when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the children of Israel.” You know that, when the sons of Adam went out from the east and found a plain in the land of Shinar, they began to make a tower whose top might reach to heaven, in order to make their name famous. There the Most High confused their language, so that no one might understand the speech of his neighbour; and so he divided them from that place into all lands (Gen. 11).

Then indeed the Most High divided the nations into discordant languages and separated the sons of Adam—that is, imitators of Adam’s pride—into all lands. He did not destroy them as he had done before by the flood, but established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the children of Israel; that is, he ordained that the human race should endure until the number of the elect should be fulfilled, all of whom are children of Israel according to faith.

“But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the measuring-line of his inheritance”—understand: in that division of nations, in that separation of Adam’s sons. For, when the languages were confused, the original language remained with the house and family of Eber. From it, through Abraham, who himself was called a Hebrew from Eber, this Hebrew people came forth as the Lord’s portion: this people of Jacob alone, I say, the measuring-line of the Lord’s inheritance; in it alone God was known, and in it alone his name was great (Ps. 75). Hence he speaks through Balaam: “The people shall dwell alone and shall not be counted among the nations” (Num. 23).

But the Lord’s portion, or the measuring-line of his inheritance, does not mean that those who are of his flesh alone, or all of them, belong to the Lord; rather, it means that those who are of his faith alone, or all of them, are the Lord’s. In this way he possessed them, and thus he began to possess them. “He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude.” [Col. 0967A] He found him in a desert land—that is, he made himself known to him in the wilderness for forty years; indeed, he first made himself known in a place of horror, that is, in the dreadful bondage of Egypt, by striking the Egyptians with ten plagues, and afterwards in the place of vast solitude, raining manna and bringing water from the rock, as has already been said, for forty years.

“He led him around, taught him, and kept him as the pupil of his eye.” He led him around, I say; for he did not lead them by the way of the Philistines’ land, which was near, but led them around by the way of the wilderness beside the Red Sea (Exod. 13). And thus, by leading them around, he kept them as the pupil of his eye, taking thought lest perhaps they should repent if they saw wars rising against them and return to Egypt (ibid.). For they were more delicate than the pupil of the eye, so that their spirit, lightly offended, often wished to return to Egypt. Therefore he led them around and taught them, not only through many experiences of good and evil, but also through the teaching of this written Law.

“As an eagle stirring her young to fly and hovering over them spreads her wings, takes them up, and carries them on her shoulders.” Thus he led them around, thus taught them, thus kept them—as an eagle does her young, according to her nature toward her offspring, neither without stern affection nor without affectionate sternness. For she is always said to test those whom she has borne, lest the shamefulness of degenerate offspring tarnish the certain royal eminence of her race among all birds. Thus it is asserted that she exposes her young to the rays of the sun and suspends the little ones in mid-air by her loving claw. But if any one, with the sunlight reflected back, preserves fearless sharpness of vision and an uninjured power of looking, that one is proved to have shown the truth of his nature by the constancy of his unclouded gaze. But if, his eyes dimmed by the sun’s rays, he turns them away, he is rejected as degenerate and unworthy of so great a parent; nor is he considered worthy of rearing who was unworthy of examination. [Col. 0967C]

Therefore, in leading them around and teaching them, he tested and proved them as an eagle tests her young. For those who murmured, tested him, and lusted in the wilderness, he struck down (Ps. 106); but those who believed and obeyed he took up, as though upon wings of grace, and carried upon his shoulders. “The Lord alone was his leader, and no foreign god was with him.”

This rebukes them: “What have you, foolish and senseless people, to do with the crowd of foreign gods? Did foreign gods lead you out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage, or help the Lord your God when he led you out?” It was not so. Rather, “the Lord alone was his leader, and no foreign god was with him”: not that horned golden calf, not most filthy Baal-peor, not Baal, nor indeed any foreign god whatever.

“He placed him upon a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields.” Him whom he found in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude, he placed upon a high land—that is, a mountainous land—that he might eat the fruits of the fields; that he might inhabit cities which he had not built and drink wine from vineyards which he had not planted; that he might possess the regions of the nations and the labours of peoples (Ps. 104). This high land, as has already been said elsewhere, is not like the land of Egypt, where, after seed is cast, waters are led for irrigation in the manner of gardens. Rather, it is mountainous and level country, awaiting rains from heaven, which the Lord God always visits and upon which his eyes rest from the beginning of the year to its end (Deut. 11). [Col. 0968A]

Therefore he placed him upon a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields, that he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone. That is, that, having become accustomed to the love of the Creator, he might at last receive the sweetness of heavenly doctrine from the rock struck by the rod of the cross and passion—namely, from Christ preaching in person with honey-flowing mouth—and oil from the hardest stone, that is, the Holy Spirit from that same Christ, made incorruptibly firm through the power of the resurrection.

“Butter from the herd, and milk from the sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, sons of Bashan, and goats, with the marrow of wheat; and they drank the most unmixed blood of the grape.” This people, whom the Lord their God found in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude, obtained all these things temporally and in actuality, so that, nourished and stirred by these bodily goods, it might gladly receive in due time spiritual butter, spiritual milk, and spiritual fat—from the spiritual herd, from the spiritual sheep and lambs or rams, sons of Bashan, that is, “fat ones”: namely, from deeds of the fathers or patriarchs to be imitated, or sayings to be followed; from the truly rich Scriptures of prophets and apostles. In accordance with this, each such person most truly says: “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22). [Col. 0968C] And they might drink the most unmixed blood of the grape, that is, the most holy blood of Christ, the Son of God.

For this reason he was established temporally upon that high land and obtained these temporal goods: that he might advance to a desire for spiritual and eternal things. But indeed...

“Jeshurun grew fat and kicked; you grew fat, sleek, and swollen. The beloved one—but ungrateful to the One who loved him; beloved, I say, yet abusing that very love proudly and fiercely—grew fat in thought, fat in deed, sleek in obstinacy, swollen in arrogance. Such a beloved one kicked, that is, he cast off with his heel the commands of the Giver. Yet this is grossness and swelling, not fullness. For one who knows true [Col. 0968D] fullness, who knows true richness, however much he abounds in butter, sheep’s milk, or the fat of lambs and rams, until he grasps God himself says: “But I am needy and poor” (Ps. 69). But he whose god is his belly, once he has filled it with the things mentioned above, having grown fat, sleek, and swollen, seems sufficient to himself in a false estimation and falsely judges that he lacks nothing.

What, then, did this beloved one do after becoming fat in this way? “He forsook God his maker and departed from God his saviour.” God is both maker and saviour. Yet it is one thing that he is maker, another that he is saviour. God is maker because he made humankind; God is saviour because he himself became human and came to save human beings. He grew fat so as to care for neither grace. [Col. 0969A] For before he came, he forsook God his maker; and after he came, he departed from God his saviour.

How did he forsake him, and how did he depart from him? “They provoked him with foreign gods, and stirred him to anger with their abominations.” Both their provoking him with foreign gods and their stirring him to anger with their abominations come to the same thing; nevertheless, they differ and have different origins. For the gods are foreign, whereas the abominations are their own; in order to commit these licentiously, they worshipped foreign gods. For example, the calf which they made (Exod. 32) and Baal-peor, to whom they were initiated (Num. 25), were foreign gods; but that, after feasting and drinking, they rose up to play (Exod. 32), and that amid sacrifices they committed fornication with the Midianite women—these were their own abominations. Thus, with foreign gods they provoked the gentle One, and with their abominations they stirred him to anger.

Likewise, in repeatedly lapsing into idolatry before he came into this world, they provoked him with foreign gods; and in blaspheming him while present, saying, “He has a demon and is mad” (John 8), and, “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matt. 12), they certainly stirred him to anger by their abominations. But with what kind of gods did they provoke him? “They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know. New and recent ones came, whom their fathers had not worshipped.” The gods whom they worshipped are not gods, but rather demons: gods only by name; new gods, because they had previously [Col. 0969C] not known them; or recent ones, because their fathers had not worshipped them.

Now therefore, heaven and earth, return to the beginning of the rebuke, and say to the crooked and perverse generation: “Is this how you repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people? You have forsaken the God who begot you and forgotten the Lord your creator.” “The God who begot you,” that is, the one who long granted to your formerly barren parents the ability, or desire, to beget you. For apart from his only Son, whom he begot from the womb before the morning star (Ps. 109), and whom he sent into this world through the Virgin’s womb, that Father begot no one from his own substance. Therefore, the one who begot you—that is, who at last gave conception to Sarah, long barren (Gen. 18), and who, at Isaac’s entreaty, granted barren Rebekah to conceive and bear Isaac’s beloved Jacob (Gen. 25), from whom or through whom the stream of your generation flowed—him, your begetter, you forsook with detestable ingratitude. And you forgot the Lord your creator—understand: him whom you had previously known through the present teaching of the Law and through the examples of those same fathers, who stored up for you the inherited knowledge of him. Hence your sin is greater than if he had never been known to you.

“The Lord saw, and was stirred to anger, because his sons and daughters provoked him.” He saw this—he from whom nothing is hidden, with eyes that never sleep and by which he sees all things. He saw, I say, your sin written with an iron stylus and a diamond point (Jer. [Col. 0970A] 17), while the Holy Spirit cries out through his prophets so that your sin may not be erased from before his face. And he was stirred to anger—not by a passible motion of his mind, for God is neither moved nor disturbed, but because the truth of judgment pursues impiety in such a way that he is now experienced not as a merciful Father but as a strict Judge. And this is because his sons and daughters provoked him, which according to every principle is less tolerable than if strangers, male or female, had provoked him.

They provoked him, namely because they sinned not through ignorance or helpless need, but knowingly and deliberately; indeed, they were skilled in fashioning sin and in seeking out falsehood. And he says: “I shall hide my face from them, and I shall consider their latter end.” [Col. 0970B] “He says,” that is, he established a sentence; for with him, to speak is to establish, so that heaven and earth—his utterance—would more easily pass away. For “God is not like a man that he should lie, nor like a son of man that he should change” (Num. 23). Therefore he says—that is, he rendered this judgment: “I shall hide my face from them,” that is, I shall blind them so that they cannot find the way of truth. I shall blind their hearts, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them (Isa. 6). And I shall say to them: “Hear indeed, but do not understand; see the vision, but do not know it.” Thus, hidden from them, I shall consider their latter end—that is, I shall await the end and completion of their sin, silently observing their astonishing audacity.

“For they are a perverse generation, unfaithful children.” The preceding causes of the condemnation of which I said, “I shall hide my face from them,” are that they are a perverse generation and unfaithful children; and the Holy Spirit likewise testifies through the prophet that they are rulers of Sodom and a people of Gomorrah (Isa. 1). Otherwise what I said above—“God is faithful and without any iniquity”—would not appear to stand. Therefore there is just judgment in this: “I gave them as a shield the toil of my heart” (Lam. 3). Although, like a bridegroom proceeding from his chamber, “I have set my tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18), they nevertheless cannot see me; indeed, it is also a scandal to them when [Col. 0970D] my tabernacle is designated as fleshly and they are told: “Behold, this is our God, our king, our saviour.”

Moreover, hear, O heavens, the just order of judgment, the equitable reciprocity of the Judge: “They provoked me with that which was not God, and irritated me with their vanities. And I shall provoke them with that which is not a people; with a foolish nation I shall irritate them.” They first provoked me, not by some slight offense or human transgression, but “with that which was not God,” that is, by treating me as though I were not God. They first irritated me with their vanities—that is, they preferred their vanities, their vain gods, to me; and finally, when given the choice, they did not hesitate to prefer Barabbas, the author of sedition, to me (Mark 15).

Therefore I shall repay them in kind: “I shall provoke them with that which is not [Col. 0971A] a people,” that is, I shall treat them as though they were not a people: as being without king, without prince, without priest, without ephod, and without teraphim (Hos. 3); as being no people at all, but already scattered among peoples and nations, and in the future annihilated with those who are nothing and assigned with those who are in hell. “And with a foolish nation I shall irritate them.” I shall irritate them, I say—that is, I shall bring them to jealousy through a non-nation, through an unwise nation; I shall send them into anger so that they see a nation reigning in their place, a wise nation whom they may envy and by whose rivalry they may be tormented.

“A fire has been kindled in my fury, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell.” I shall provoke them and irritate them; and the beginning of this provocation and irritation is that a fire has been kindled [Col. 0971B] in my fury, and, when complete, it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell. The fire kindled at present is the fire of the Romans, by which the holy city became a desolate Zion, Jerusalem became desolate, the house of their sanctification and glory was consumed by fire, all their precious things were turned into ruins, they fell by the edge of the sword, and they were carried captive among all nations. This fire of punishment, this fire of vengeance, has already been kindled; but it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell. For from this temporal vengeance they proceed to eternal torments.

Do you ask, then, whether God judges twice for the same thing, or whether double tribulation will arise? (Nah. 1). Certainly not, if in the present vengeance or tribulation you acknowledge your guilt and put an end to your sins. But because the impious will of this foolish and senseless people persists in punishment itself, he now brings upon them a day of affliction, and hereafter the fire which has been kindled shall burn to the lowest depths of hell, [Col. 0971C] as another prophet also prays: “Crush them with a double destruction, O Lord my God” (Jer. 17). At other times there is one blow, which begins here and ends there, so that one lash of correction begins temporally but is completed in eternal punishments; thus, for those who wholly refuse correction, the pursuit of present scourges becomes the beginning of following torments.

Therefore the prophetic rule is neither harmed nor bent to a wrong meaning—that it was said, “Double tribulation shall not arise” (Nah. 1), or, according to the Septuagint, “God shall not judge twice for the same thing”—even though here “a fire has been kindled in my fury,” and in the future it “shall burn to the lowest depths of hell.” “It shall devour the earth with its produce, and burn the foundations of the mountains.” It shall not, as has often happened, devour only the produce of the earth, so that there is famine in the land because of the people’s sins, but also the earth itself—those whose wrath plotted deceitful words (Ps. 34), so that they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). It shall devour the earth itself with its produce—that is, it shall take it away, so that their land is no longer theirs and they lack it, as though it had been devoured by hostile fire. And it shall burn the foundations of the mountains—that is, it shall take away the confidence of the proud: the beautiful [Col. 0972A] temple and famous city, supported by whose standing they imagine themselves firmly established in the God of their fathers’ inheritance; and they, as mountains, despise all other nations as weak valleys. The temple, I say, and the city founded upon mountains, elemental fire shall burn.
