Furthermore, it shall devour the earth—that is, their flesh; the sinful earth—that is, the people who are proud though they are earth and ashes—together with its produce, that is, with its lusts and all its evil deeds. And it shall burn the foundations of the mountains—that is, the very souls which give life—both by the fire already kindled, as has been said, and by that which shall burn in the future to the lowest depths of hell.

“I shall gather evils upon them, and I shall spend my arrows upon them.” And the Lord says this, having indeed been stirred to anger. He says it, I say, not merely secretly and inwardly, with prophets hearing, but publicly also, with apostles hearing, Jews blaspheming, and all nations throughout the world to hear through the Gospel. For when he said, “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, flog in your synagogues, and persecute from city to city” (Matt. 23), he immediately added: “So that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you: all these things shall come upon this generation” (ibid.). This is his utterance, spoken in the apostles’ hearing, concerning the gathering of evils—he who, already in Moses’ hearing, before becoming human, said: “Therefore [Col. 0972C] I shall gather evils upon them,” that is, I shall bring upon them all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth. And this justly, because by killing me and shedding my blood they shall fill up the measure of their fathers—their evil and impious fathers, who killed the righteous and shed the blood of the prophets.

“And I shall spend my arrows upon them,” because, with so many evils gathered, a few arrows or part of my arrows would not suffice to expiate them. Therefore I shall spend—that is, expend all—my arrows upon them: arrows of curse, namely those which a little earlier I stored in the quiver of a certain covenant as follows: “But if you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments and ceremonies which I command you today, all these curses shall come upon you and overtake you. Cursed shall you be in the city; cursed in the field; cursed your storehouse and your remnants; cursed the fruit of your womb” (Deut. 28), and so forth. I shall spend, I say—that is, I shall expend all these arrows of mine upon them—which I have never otherwise done, although many times I have hurled some portion of my arrows at them.

For example, when Ben-hadad, king of Syria, with his entire army was besieging Samaria, there was a great famine in Samaria; and it was besieged for so long that a donkey’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver, and a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver. One woman said to another: “Give your son so that we may eat him today, and we shall eat my son tomorrow” [Col. 0973A] (4 Kings 6). When these things occurred, I indeed shot my arrows, but did not expend them all. For meanwhile Elisha said: “Hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: At this time tomorrow a measure of fine flour shall be one shekel, and two measures of barley one shekel, at the gate of Samaria” (Jer. 7), and so it happened. But it shall not be so when I hide my face from them. But what then?

“They shall be consumed by hunger, and birds shall devour them with a most bitter bite. I shall send against them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those dragging upon the earth, and of serpents. Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within, terror: young man and virgin alike, the nursing infant together with the old man.” This indeed shall be the spending of my arrows upon them. “They shall be consumed [Col. 0973B] by hunger,” namely, when assembled at Jerusalem on the solemn day of Passover, as though driven by a certain deadly hand—three million, according to Josephus. By just judgment this time of vengeance was selected, so that those who in the days of Passover had violated their Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ, with bloodstained hands and sacrilegious cries, might, on those same days, be shut up as though in a single prison, and the whole multitude receive the destruction of the deadly punishment it deserved (Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 7, ch. 25).

Whoever wishes to know more fully by what ruinous famine they were consumed should read the fifth book of the aforesaid Josephus’s histories, from which he may learn their entire mournful tragedy. Its most dreadful event was this: a certain woman named Mary, daughter of Eleazar, noble in family and means, driven almost to insanity or madness by the extremity of the famine, slaughtered the little son at her breast, roasted him over a fire, consumed one half, and kept the other half covered. Immediately robbers burst in, drawn by the smell of the cooked flesh; for, hungry and mad with famine, they were searching the houses. When this horror was discovered by the robbers, it at once filled the whole city with dreadful news. She brought out what she had covered and said: “I have kept the best portion for you.”

Thus, he says, “they shall be consumed by hunger”—and understand, they shall not be buried, but “birds shall devour them with a most bitter bite.” Neither the multitude of the dead nor lack of strength permitted them to bury the bodies of their relatives. At first, the intolerable stench had caused an order that the dead be buried at public expense; but when the multitude of the dying began to exceed all expense, they threw the corpses down from the wall in such numbers that the valleys were filled with dead bodies and the whole land was watered with the putrefaction of human flesh. Therefore birds shall devour them with a most bitter bite—those left unburied, with a most bitter bite, because this bitterness shall be most bitter to those who survive and look on.

Nor shall birds alone devour them: “I shall send against them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those dragging them across the earth, and the teeth of serpents.” Alternatively: “I shall send against them the teeth of beasts, with the fury of those [Col. 0974A] dragging across the earth, and of serpents.” The teeth of beasts—that is, the cruelty or weapons of the Romans—I shall send against them, with the fury of those dragging the survivors mercilessly into captivity throughout the whole earth; and the teeth of serpents—that is, the cruelty of evil spirits, dragging them after the torments and deaths of their bodies to the lowest depths of hell.

For that the strong and savage Romans are rightly understood by beasts is shown, as testimony or example, by the Psalmist’s words lamenting the same calamity: “Why have you broken down her wall, so that all who pass by the way plunder her?” (Ps. 79). He immediately added: “The boar from the forest has destroyed her, and the solitary wild beast has fed upon her” (ibid.), signifying by the boar from the forest and the solitary beast the Roman emperors Titus and Vespasian. Therefore the teeth of beasts dragging across the earth are the weapons of the Romans, killing and dragging into captivity.

The aforesaid historian, gathering the total number killed by famine or sword, gives eleven hundred thousand. He reports that the remaining robbers, assassins, and plunderers perished after the city’s destruction by mutual wounds. He says that all the chosen young men, commended by bodily beauty and stature, were preserved for triumph. The rest above seventeen years of age were bound and assigned to Egypt for labor in the mines, or scattered through the other provinces: some to gladiatorial games, others to be handed over to beasts. Those found under seventeen years of age were ordered to be scattered into slavery through various [Col. 0974C] provinces. Their number reached ninety thousand. This indeed was to be dragged across the earth by the teeth of beasts, and then for souls to be led to hell was to be dragged by the teeth of serpents.

Accordingly, it was pointedly not said: “the teeth of beasts and serpents dragging across the earth with fury,” but “the teeth of beasts dragging across the earth with fury, and of serpents,” so that you should understand: teeth dragging with fury into hell. Finally, in one verse he embraced the sum of all evils: “Outside the sword shall lay them waste, and within terror: young man and virgin alike, the nursing infant together with the old man.”

For the sword outside means every outward calamity of the body; terror within means a dreadful conscience, [Col. 0974D] because, in their own knowledge, the blood of Christ, as they had invoked it upon themselves, now overflowed upon them and their children. “And I said: Where are they? I shall cause their memory to cease from among human beings.” He said these things and those already set forth; and then at last I—he to whom these future calamities, indeed all things past and future, are present—said: “Where are they?” Namely because “sinners have failed from the earth, and the wicked so that they are no more” (Ps. 103). Woe to those of whom God does not know where they are, since he himself is the place of all who exist and do not exist wickedly. Hence he says in Job: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so he who descends to hell shall not come up; he shall not return again to his house, nor shall his place know him any longer” (Job 9).

“I shall cause their memory [Col. 0975A] to cease from among human beings.” As though he said: It is too little that I, once their place, shall no longer know them; moreover, I shall cause their memory to cease even from among human beings, so that no good memory of them may remain either with God or with human beings. “But because of the wrath of their enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their adversaries should become proud and say: ‘Our high hand, and not the Lord, has done all these things.’” Thus, as foretold, I shall expend my arrows upon them so that not even one curse remains. I could have done so, and they deserved it: I could have caused their memory to cease from humanity in such a way that none of their remnant remained (Isa. 10). But perhaps their enemies would become proud and say: “It was not the Lord who did all these things, but our high hand did all these things.” Therefore I delayed and did not utterly erase all memory of them.

Indeed, I also said: “Though their number be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9). In this way their enemies do not grow proud, do not say, “Our high hand, and not the Lord, did all these things,” since remnants of them remain scattered throughout all nations, carrying books with them and the curses of the Law. Their enemies, reading these and recounting the causes of the curses, may know and say that the Lord did all these things. Moreover, their remnant further serves this end: whoever among their enemies has been converted to the faith of their fathers—since, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved (ibid.)—may not grow proud because blindness has happened to Israel while they themselves have been enlightened. The Apostle also restrains this pride when he says: “If some of the branches have been broken off, but you, though a wild olive, have been grafted among them and made a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, you do not bear the root; the root bears you” [Col. 0975C] (Rom. 11), and so forth.

Certainly this kind of restraint upon pride is a concern worthy of God: you rightly take precautions lest they say, “Our high hand, and not the Lord, did all these things.” Hence it is said in the Psalm: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: Do not kill them, lest at any time my people forget. Scatter them in your power” (Ps. 58). Now the following words of the song indicate what ought to be the disposition of the apostles and of the wise people, the Christian people, toward this same dispersion and the scattered remnants of the foolish and senseless people.

“A nation without counsel and without prudence; if only they were wise, understood, and foresaw their latter end.” What else does the Apostle desire when he says: “Speaking the truth in Christ with groaning, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers” (Rom. 9), and so forth? What, I say, does he say, what does he desire, except: “If only they were wise, understood, and foresaw their latter end”? That they might be wise about what evils, or for what causes, have been foretold for them from the Law written above; that they might understand that present events and the outcomes of present evils correspond well to the former sayings; and that they might foresee their latter end—understand, [Col. 0976A] the evils of hell which will follow these present evils for them, because they would not understand and because not even present affliction can give understanding to their hearing.

This we desire, this we wish for them—whatever of us know with upright and humble faith that these are natural olive branches, while we were a wild olive by nature, and, once those who stood naturally had been broken off, we were grafted in contrary to nature. Yet until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, this nation is without counsel and prudence: that is, it shall not be wise, understand, or foresee its latter end. Nevertheless, though we spend our words and gain none or very few of them, we say: “If only they were wise, understood, and foresaw their latter end.”

“How could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight?” Indeed, to recall the very words of the curse by which this was pronounced: How did the Lord deliver this nation to fall before its enemies? How did it go out against them by one way and flee by seven? Was it not because their God sold them and the Lord shut them in? “For our God is not as their gods, and our enemies are judges.” What then? Is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, their God, as they themselves think? Certainly not. For they themselves are among those, indeed among the foremost of those, “whose god is their belly” [Col. 0976B] (Phil. 3), and whose glory is in their shame, or private parts.

Whatever gods they worshipped, they unquestionably worshipped them because of this god, the greatest of all their gods—that is, because of their belly and private parts: namely, so that they might sit down to eat and drink and afterward rise to play (Exod. 32), a shameful, dishonourable play. Therefore their belly is their god, and it gives them cause to worship many gods. This their god sold them: this god, I say, sold them for the price of prostitution and lust. For in order to fill that god, their belly, and to indulge through the parts below the belly in lusts, they gave themselves up, betrayed their life, and destroyed their souls. Hence through the prophet they are openly called rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah (Isa. 1).

Thus the Lord shut them in after they had been sold: first, with blindness and frenzy of mind, so that they might grope at midday as a blind man gropes in darkness; [Col. 0976D] and although their life hung before their eyes, they would not believe in that very life. Then he shut them in with a hostile army, where one pursued a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight. Did they not suffer these things, therefore, because their god, as just stated, sold them, and the avenging Lord shut them in?

“For our God is not as their gods.” No, their gods are not like our God. We profess this so freely that we do not evade the common tribunal of the whole world and do not fear the judgment of any people who use reason. Even our enemies are judges. For example, Platonists, Pythagoreans, or any pagan philosophers: while they are still our enemies, while they have not yet accepted faith in Christ, they themselves are judges. [Col. 0977A] Behold, let these things be set before all: on this side our God and his cross; on that, the attendants of their god, their belly—Baal-peor, that is Priapus:

> And a red stake, thrust out from his obscene groin.  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.8.)

Let our enemies be judges between these things; let our enemies judge what is more beautiful and honorable: to worship the piety of the crucified Christ, or the erection and obscenity of Priapus. Speak now, judges who are indeed our enemies but possess the knowledge necessary for judging: what is more beautiful in your estimation—to worship the cross or adulteries? The cross, I say, unjustly fastened upon a just man, or fornications and debaucheries? What they would answer—indeed, what our enemies have answered and judged—the whole world has now heard: condemning debaucheries, they bowed pious necks beneath the cross; condemning the lusts of the belly and of what lies below the belly, [Col. 0977B] they proclaimed Christ’s glory.

But these people are still not wise and do not yet understand. Why? “Their wine is from the vineyard of Sodom and from the outskirts of Gomorrah.” For this reason their eyes have been darkened so that they do not see; for this reason they have been blinded, so that they are neither wise nor understanding and do not foresee their latter end: because their wine is from the vineyard of Sodom and from the outskirts of Gomorrah, that is, because they live in the manner of Sodom. “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster exceedingly bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps.” By vineyard understand the roots of evil thoughts; by grape and cluster, the wickedness of deeds; and by wine, evil discourse and the perverse teaching of blasphemers. Certainly, whoever shares in their evil works will be tormented with eternal bitterness; therefore he said, “a grape of gall and an exceedingly bitter cluster.” And whoever receives their fables or whisperings will be intoxicated with the everlasting drunkenness of death; therefore he said: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps.”

“Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries?” Since no repentance has erased them and the baptism of Christ, by which alone sins are remitted, has not swallowed them up, they remain stored with me and sealed in my treasuries, to be repaid in the weight and measure of the wrath which they have stored up for themselves. “Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay them [Col. 0977D] in due time, when their foot slips.” Mine, I say, is vengeance; mine is judgment; and I shall repay them, namely each according to his works, in due time, on the day of wrath, when their foot slips: that they may fall into everlasting reproach, be led down into the pit of destruction, and be cast down to the lowest depths of hell (Ps. 54).

You say: “It will happen in distant times” (Ezek. 12). But I say: “The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to come.” The day is near, even if a thousand years stand between. For “a thousand years before your eyes are as yesterday, which has passed” (Ps. 89). But suppose that a span of a thousand, indeed ten thousand or a hundred thousand years, is expected before that day. Is the day of destruction not near in a special sense for every individual sinner? For, as the Psalmist says, our years “will be considered as a spider’s web” (ibid.); the days of our years, understand, are bounded within seventy years. But if there are people of greater strength—people who, because their nature is stronger and healthier than others, live longer—if, I say, among the strong, that is, among those of healthier constitution, there are eighty years, everything beyond those eighty years is no longer life but rather labor and pain. Therefore even thus the day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to come. For fleeting years slip away, and one day is driven on by another.

Thus far the discourse has been directed against the nation without counsel and prudence, concerning those who have been blinded. Now a consoling discourse is directed to those remnants which are to be saved.

[Col. 0978B] “The Lord shall judge his people, and have mercy on his servants.” These are the two most illustrious ministries of the Lord’s throne: mercy and judgment, upon which the entire basis or matter of divine praise depends. The Psalmist also says: “I shall sing to you, O Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 84). For there is nothing in the words and works of the faithful and just Lord which is not either mercy, judgment, or both together, as the same writer says above: “Mercy and truth have met together” (ibid.). Therefore “the Lord shall judge his people”—understand, according to what has thus far been said, because he saw them provoking him and stirring him to anger with their abominations; he saw, I say, and was stirred to anger. But “he shall have mercy on his servants,” that is, on the remnants, [Col. 0978C] whom he will observe as being otherwise disposed.

“He shall see that their hand has been weakened, and that the confined too have failed, and that the remnants have been consumed.” He shall see, I say, that that hand has been weakened and has recognized its weakness—the hand which until then seemed sound and strong to itself, so that, maddened by the force of its weakness like a frenzied person, it struck the true physician, as the Psalm says: “The strong rushed upon me” (Ps. 58). For though weak and lacking the strength of true righteousness, they boasted in works of the Law, by which no one shall be justified before God, so as to stand against his Christ, saying: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Ps. 2).

He shall see that such a hand, such strength, has been weakened and humbled, and now longs for the justification that is from faith, not from works of the Law (Rom. 3). And he shall see this: that “the confined” too—the confined, I say, whom, as stated above, the Lord shut in—have failed, that is, they will no longer have any confidence in themselves; and that “the remnants,” namely those who remain from Israel, [Col. 0978D] have been consumed, in that they know themselves to be nothing and, confessing that they have been reduced to nothing, seek the aid of the Restorer and Liberator.

[Cols. 0979A–0981A]

“And they will say: ‘Where are their gods, in whom they had confidence? From whose sacrifices they ate the fat and drank the wine of the libations? Let them rise up and help you, and protect you in your need.’ See that I alone am he, and there is no other God besides me.” So greatly have they been weakened, so greatly have they failed and been consumed, that they say—or rather, they themselves no longer speak, because they have failed and been consumed; but the Lord speaks in them, and the Spirit of the Lord says in them: “Where are their gods, in whom they had confidence?” It is understood: those who were strong, who did not fail or perish—that is, who were transformed by repentance. “Where,” I say, “are their gods?” It is understood: they are nowhere, nowhere present, because they are not gods but demons.

Therefore, you remnant of Israel, see that I alone am he; I alone, I say, am he who, speaking from the midst of the bush, said: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). What I said then, I say now: this distinguishes me from all things which do not truly and simply exist, because they are mutable; and especially it distinguishes me from, or sets me apart from, all the gods who are not. Even though they may be called gods—for “there are many that are called gods, and many lords”—yet they are not gods or lords. But I so truly am that I did not cease to be even when death intervened; for although I died through the weakness of the flesh, I live through the power of God—that is, because I am the power of God. See this, and see that there is no other besides me.

“I will kill and make alive; I will strike, and I will heal; and there is none who can rescue from my hand.” See this also; know it as proved by these present effects. For I once killed the Gentile people—that is, I condemned a people given over to idolatry, worshipping foreign gods besides me—and now I, the same one, have made them alive through the Holy Spirit. Likewise, I struck my own people, the Jewish people, with blindness because they provoked and angered me; and behold, I have healed a remnant from among them.

“And there is none who can rescue from my hand”: that is, none can rescue the one who, through the rule of pride, has fallen into my dreadful hands. None, I say, can rescue from my hand, as the prophet also says: “Though these three righteous men—Noah, Daniel, and Job—were in their midst, as I live, says the Lord, they would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness; but they would not deliver sons or daughters” (Ezek. 14). For who could even touch that hand?

“I will lift up my hand to heaven, and say: ‘I live for ever.’” Who, then, can rescue from my hand—from that most high hand, raised so high to heaven that no one can touch it? My hand, which made all things, stretched out heaven, founded the earth, and poured forth the seas—even in its weakness, when clothed in flesh and seeming, as it were, bound, then too struck the proud one, and, with her acting as midwife, “the twisting serpent was brought forth” (Job 36).

How much more, after I lifted it up to heaven and said, “I live for ever,” as he also testifies who said: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6)—how much more, I say, from that time onward is there none who can rescue from this hand of mine?

“If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand takes hold of judgment, I will render vengeance to my enemies, and repay those who hate me.” What is this hand of mine which takes hold of judgment, if not the Son, who says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5)? And what is his sword, if not the division between the good and the evil, who, divided to right and left, will be separated beyond all possibility of union (Matt. 25)?

Lightning indeed flashes briefly, but strikes irrecoverably. Therefore, if I sharpen my sword like lightning—that is, if, as will undoubtedly happen, I make in a brief time, yet openly before all, the divisions of good and evil to right and left—and thus my hand takes hold of judgment, as I have already said, there will be none to rescue; but I will render vengeance to my enemies, namely the unquenchable fire of Gehenna, and there repay a fitting requital to those who hate me.

“I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.” All my arrows are sentences of judgment, here indicated by the number six: “I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink; I was a stranger and you did not take me in; naked and you did not clothe me; sick and you did not visit me; in prison and you did not come to me” (Matt. 25).

Such arrows of mine I will make drunk with blood, so that all may be expended in the effecting of vengeance. “And my sword shall devour flesh”: not because it destroys the substance of flesh itself, but because it punishes eternally those who love fleshly things and pursue the vices of the flesh—debauchees, gluttons, scoundrels, both malignant spirits and unclean human beings. Since their wickedness is shared, their punishment too is equal, according to the saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

For this is what follows: “From the blood of the slain, and from the captivity of the enemy’s bare head.” “I will make my arrows drunk with the blood of the slain,” that is, with the condemnation of ungodly human beings; “and from the captivity of the enemy’s head,” namely the devil, who is the head and prince of enemies—the head, I say, laid bare, that is, revealed. For he will be made manifest to all and cast down before the sight of all.

Let us all hear likewise the conclusion of the song: “Praise, O nations, his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants; he will repay vengeance to their enemies, and will be merciful to the land of his people.”

“Praise, O nations, his people.” Rejoice, nations, with his people; call blessed, nations, the people whose Lord is their God. For the endurance of his people, or of his servants, will not perish: he will avenge the blood of his servants and repay vengeance to their enemies, saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (ibid.), and so forth; and he will be merciful to the land of his people, saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.).

Thus today we nations offer praise. For this is our faith, this our confession: that the hand of the Lord, raised up to heaven—the Son of God, who after his resurrection was taken up into heaven—will seize judgment like lightning. In it he will avenge the blood of his servants upon ungodly persecutors and repay vengeance to their enemies, namely the devil and his angels; but to his people, his servants, he will mercifully restore the land from which he first expelled the human being on account of sin—indeed, the firm security of angelic blessedness, to which humanity would have been transferred without bodily death, had the sinner’s transgression not intervened.

Behold how far, even to the end, Moses has brought the words of the song: namely, to the Last Judgment, in which the end of all things shall be.

349

[Cols. 0981A–0981D]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the fact that Moses the lawgiver blessed the children of Israel, whereas the Psalmist said concerning a future time, “For the lawgiver will give a blessing”; and what must be understood concerning Christ.

### (Chapter XXXIII)

“This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death; and he said: ‘The Lord came from Sinai, and rose for us from Seir. He appeared from Mount Paran, and with him were thousands of saints. At his right hand was a fiery law. He loved the people.’”

Moses, he says—Moses, I say, the lawgiver—blessed the children of Israel with this blessing before his death. Yet the Prophet says: “For the lawgiver will give a blessing; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83). What are we to say to this? Certainly Scripture says of this lawgiver that he blessed; the Prophet says of another lawgiver that he will give a blessing. Having read the blessing of this former lawgiver, he prophesied the blessing of the future lawgiver.

What, then, are we to say, except that this lawgiver’s blessing belongs to those seeds of which that other lawgiver says in the Gospel: “One is he who sows and another who reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you have not laboured; others have laboured, and you have entered into their labours” (John 4)?

Thus Moses here, and the other sowers of the full field, by labouring in the Lord’s field and sowing the word of God, could place their hope in the future blessing; but that other lawgiver alone, in giving that blessing, could send his own labourers to reap into their labours.

This Moses blessed the children of Israel before his death; but the other, in his very death, obtained a blessing for all nations. Of him he afterwards says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

[Cols. 0981D–0982C]

## CHAPTER IX. What is meant, both literally and spiritually, by: “The Lord came from Sinai and rose for us from Seir,” and so forth.

“The Lord came from Sinai, and rose for us from Seir. He appeared from Mount Paran.”

According to the literal sense, he says, the Lord came to us from Sinai, rose for us from Seir, and appeared from Mount Paran, because to us Jews, to us the carnal people Israel, the Lord God became known through the things said or done in these places. Thus it was rightly sung: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). For at Sinai he gave the Law; while they journeyed around Mount Seir and remained in the wilderness of Paran, he displayed his wonders and made known his wrath and his mercy.

But according to the spiritual sense, our Saviour Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came to us Gentiles from Sinai, which is interpreted “temptation”: from Sinai, I say, that is, from his temptations. For he was “tempted in all things in like manner, apart from sin” (Heb. 4). Leaving behind his Jewish tempters after the temptation of the mountain, crowned with the glory and honour of the resurrection, he migrated to us nations.

“And he rose for us from Seir.” Seir is interpreted “hairy” or “shaggy,” a name by which the Jews, bristling with their sins, are likewise fittingly denoted. Therefore he rose for us from Seir because, according to the flesh, he arose from the Jews, and so passed to us nations, just as the birthright of Esau, Jacob’s elder brother, was transferred to the younger Jacob by supplanting (Gen. 27).

“He appeared to us also from Mount Paran,” which is interpreted “wild ass” or “their fierceness.” The wild ass is fierce and foolish—that is, the Jewish people—of whom this too is rightly understood to have been said in Job: “A vain man is lifted up into pride and thinks himself born free like a wild ass’s colt” (Job 11).

Therefore, because that colt, wishing to establish his own righteousness, refused to be subject to God’s righteousness, and because of this the Lord hid himself from them and showed himself to the nations hungering for God’s righteousness, we rightly say that he appeared to us from Mount Paran, “and with him were thousands of saints.”

For with him, incarnate from among the Jews and tested by them through the temptation of death—with him, I say—there came to us, there appeared to us, thousands of saints: that is, all the saints to whom he was promised, by whom he was awaited and prophesied. Through him, because of the same faith, we and they have been made one Church.

[Cols. 0982C–0983B]

## CHAPTER X. The mystical meaning of “At his right hand was a fiery law.”

“At his right hand was a fiery law; he loved the peoples; all the saints are in his hand. And those who draw near to his feet shall receive from his teaching. Moses commanded us the law, the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob. A king shall be with the Most Upright One.”

The fiery law at his right hand is the most ardent charity in his mightiest works, by which he loved the peoples—not, I say, one Jewish people, but all peoples. This accomplished his coming to us from Sinai, his rising for us from Seir, and his appearing to us from Mount Paran, after the likeness of that time when he appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush (Exod. 5), and delivered his people from the hand of the Egyptians with a strong hand.

Thus, with the fiery law of his right hand, with the most ardent charity of his omnipotence, he appeared to us to deliver us with a strong hand from the hand of Pharaoh and the Egyptians—that is, from the devil and his angels, the evil spirits—because he conquered the devil himself, and he, the stronger one, overcame and seized the court of that strong man.

“All the saints are in his hand”: that is, by the very fact that they are saints, they are the work of his hand. For they have not become holy by their own power, but have been sanctified by his grace (Rom. 5). Since all were born sinners from one sinner, they could be justified only through the one who alone is righteous and without sin.

Such was he who came; such was the Lord who rose and appeared to us.

“And those who draw near to his feet shall receive from his teaching”: that is, those who receive faith in his coming understand his spiritual law spiritually. For the depths of Scripture are understood only through faith in Christ.

Hence, to this day the proud Jews do not understand the Scriptures, because they do not draw near to his feet—that is, they disdain to receive the coming of his humility—and a veil is laid over their heart, which is removed in Christ (2 Cor. 3).

Therefore, when the Lord says through the prophet, “My people have been led captive because they had no knowledge” (Isa. 5), it must consequently be added: they have no knowledge because they disdained to draw near to his feet, that is, to receive the coming of his humility.

What, then, is Moses? Certainly he is not the one who gives knowledge or teaching; he merely commanded the Law, the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob. He commanded the Law, I say; he did not appear. He commanded them to hope for an inheritance, but did not himself distribute the portions of that inheritance to the multitude of Jacob.

But “a king shall be with the Most Upright One.” He, that is, the Lord, shall sit at the right hand of the most upright Lord as king. Made human, he shall sit there as king for ever, with him with whom the Word was God in the beginning. He will not command us the Law as a servant or herald, but, as a king ascending on high, leading captivity captive, he will give gifts of grace to human beings (Ps. 67).

[Cols. 0983C–0983D]

## CHAPTER XI. On the blessing of Reuben: how those who return from heresy to the catholic Church are likened to him.

“With the princes of the people gathered together, with the tribes of Israel, he said: ‘Let Reuben live and not die, though he be few in number.’”

Why should he be few in number? Because he went up to his father’s bed and defiled his couch. For this reason his father Jacob said: “You are poured out like water; do not increase” (Gen. 49).

Yet let him live and not die; let him be content with this pardon, being made spiritually unworthy of the glory of the firstborn because he went up to his father’s bed and defiled his couch—that is, because he is a heretic who corrupted the Church, Christ’s bride, by adulterating the word of God. If he returns to the Father’s grace, let him live and not die; yet let him be few in number, that is, let him not be multiplied in ecclesiastical honours, but be content with lay communion.

[Cols. 0983D–0984D]

## CHAPTER XII. On the blessing of Judah, and what is subsequently understood mystically in it.

“This is the blessing of Judah: ‘Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people. His hands shall fight for him, and his helper shall be against his adversaries.’”

In Judah, the king and prince of our confession, our Saviour Jesus Christ, the Son of God, is blessed with the same Spirit and affection with which the Prophet prays: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you” (Ps. 19), and the rest.

With the same affection, I say, and now with the same intention of the prophetic Spirit, he speaks: “Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people.”

We have all heard the voice of Judah, the voice of him who arose from Judah, by which he prayed the Father that he might be brought to his people—especially when, about to suffer, he spoke thus: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17).

And shortly after: “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me from the world. Holy Father, preserve in your name those whom you gave me, that they may be one as we also are.”

And further: “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you; that they too may be one in us, that they may be one as we are one.”

For this is the voice of Christ, the Son of God, arisen according to the flesh from Judah: the voice of Judah praying that he may be brought to his people, so that all who are his people, all his faithful ones, may be one through the same Spirit, as many members are one body, while he himself is their head.

This voice is heard throughout the Scriptures, especially in the Psalms, where the Prophet speaks in his Spirit: “O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried in the day and in the night before you” (Ps. 87); “O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Ps. 101).

Therefore, he says, “Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people”: that is, hear your Christ, whom we hope will be born from Judah; raise him from the dead, and exalt him as Prince and Saviour to give repentance and remission of sins.

But is he weak, unable to help himself? On the contrary: “His hands shall fight for him, and his helper shall be against his adversaries.”

“I have turned aside to address you, O helpers” (Acts 2), lest you think this prayer proceeds from uncertainty rather than from an eager heart and a desire leaping for joy. For he is God; he will be both God and man.

Insofar as he is God, “his hands shall fight for him”: that is, his own strength shall be in him, so that he may loose the pains of hell, because it will be impossible for him to be held by it. Insofar as he is man, “his helper shall be against his adversaries”: that is, by the help of the Godhead dwelling bodily within him, he shall accomplish all things.

This, he says, is Judah’s blessing. By a remarkable indication, he placed the title “for Judah” before what he was going to say, because in the blessings of the other tribes he used it nowhere: for that which was hoped for from Judah was a unique good, and there was no such hope concerning the other tribes.

[Cols. 0984D–0986B]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the blessing of Levi: from what he earned the blessing, and how evangelical priests should imitate him.

“Of Levi also he said: ‘Your perfection and your teaching belong to your holy man, whom you tested in temptation and judged at the waters of Contradiction. He who said to his father and mother, “I do not know you,” and to his brethren, “I do not recognize them,” and did not acknowledge his sons—these kept your word and observed your covenant. They shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel. They shall place incense in your wrath and a burnt offering upon your altar.’”

In Levi, the dignity of Phinehas the priest is blessed, as it existed at that time. At the initiation of Baal-peor, he seized a dagger, entered after an Israelite man into a brothel, and pierced them both—the man and the woman—thus causing the plague among the children of Israel to cease.

The Lord said to Moses: “Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned away my wrath from the children of Israel, because he was moved with my zeal against them, lest I should destroy the children of Israel in my zeal. Therefore say to him: Behold, I give him the peace of my covenant; and it shall be for him and for his seed a covenant of everlasting priesthood” (Num. 25).

Concerning this same man and for this same reason the Lord says again through the prophet: “My covenant was with Levi, of life and peace; and I gave him fear, and he feared me, and trembled before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. He walked with me in peace and uprightness, and turned many away from iniquity. For the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

“He walked with me,” he says, “in peace and uprightness”: it is understood, as Enoch walked, who was translated to the Lord and was not found. For the Hebrews hand down that Phinehas himself is Elijah (Gen. 5).

If this is so, it is especially fitting, because it helps us understand how God made with him a covenant of everlasting priesthood, although the legal priesthood exercised by Phinehas was not everlasting. For when he comes near the end of the age, he will certainly not lack priestly honour in the Church of Christ, whose priesthood is everlasting.

Therefore, “Your perfection, O God,” he says, “and your teaching belong to your holy man, whom you tested in temptation”—namely, as regards Phinehas, who is of Levi—“and judged at the waters of Contradiction”—namely, as regards me and Aaron, against whom you were angry at the waters of Contradiction and said: “Because you did not believe me so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I will give them” (Num. 20).

What is that perfection? “He who says to his father and mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brethren, ‘I do not recognize them,’ and did not acknowledge his sons,” and so forth, as above.

Levi at that time embraced this perfection carnally indeed, but worthily and commendably for the occasion, when Moses was angry on account of the molten calf and said: “Whoever is the Lord’s, join himself to me.” Then all the sons of Levi gathered to him. And he immediately said: “Thus says the Lord: ‘Let every man put his sword upon his thigh, and let each kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbour.’” The sons of Levi did according to Moses’ word.

“You have consecrated your hands today to the Lord, each one against his son and his brother, that a blessing may be given to you” (Exod. 32).

“These,” he says, “kept your word and observed your covenant; they shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel.” And because they there consecrated their own hands, he says: “They shall place incense in your wrath and a burnt offering upon your altar”—that is, they shall be your priests and shall stand at the time of wrath to make reconciliation.

But for an evangelical person, the life-giving Spirit must above all be followed in this passage. For where does the letter kill more?

Therefore, those who take up that sword of which the Lord of the Law, fulfilling the Law in the Gospel, says: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon earth; I came not to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to set a man against his father, and a son against his mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies shall be those of his own household. He who loves father and mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he who loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10)—those, I say, who take up that sword, the sword of the word of God, which is the Lord’s perfection and teaching, have kept your word and observed your covenant; they shall teach your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel.

And because they are perfect, therefore, O God, they shall place the incense of prayers or the burnt offerings of intercessions for your imperfect people, because they are worthy and fit to intercede for human sins.

This sword of the word of God, in the hand or upon the thigh of the apostles and evangelists, is true strength; and it will immediately be blessed thus: “Bless, O Lord, his strength, and receive the works of his hands. Strike the backs of his enemies, and let those who hate him not rise again.”

[Cols. 0986B–0987B]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the blessing of Benjamin: why he is placed after Judah and Levi, and how this blessing was especially fulfilled in the Apostle Paul.

“And of Benjamin he said: ‘The beloved of the Lord shall dwell securely in him; he shall remain as in a bridal chamber all the day, and shall rest between his shoulders.’”

It did not happen accidentally or by chance that, after Judah and Levi, he then proclaims and blesses Benjamin, neglecting the order of birth. Rather, with spiritual vision he has before him reasons which a hearer of Scripture may know more certainly than his own fingers or nails.

For it is certain that, when the kingdom of Israel was divided from the house of David because of Solomon’s sin, a lamp remained to David over Judah and Benjamin, and over the priesthood and Levitical ministry of the Temple (3 Kings 12). Therefore, under the guidance of the prophetic Spirit, he rightly blesses first the royal tribe of Judah, then the priestly or Levitical tribe, and afterwards the tribe of Benjamin, which was to be united with both in the place of David’s dwelling and kingdom.

“The beloved of the Lord,” he says, “shall dwell securely.” It is as though he said: Benjamin should consider, not without gratitude, that he is greatly loved by the Lord, because, while the calves of Samaria, or the priests of the calves, plundered the souls of the other tribes, he would dwell securely. While the other tribes worshipped what they did not know, he, with Judah and Levi, would worship what he would know.

“He shall remain in him as in a bridal chamber all the day”: in him, I say, that is, in his worship and his Law, where the soul, as in a bridal chamber, is joined to its lawful husband, God. He shall remain all the day; and “shall rest between his shoulders,” that is, between the strongest tribes, the royal and the priestly, so that vain error may not weary him with labour.

But those who look more deeply must not pass over Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin, the beloved of the Lord. Nor should one suppose that Moses, greatest of the prophets, who deserved to foresee whatever might be hoped for concerning each tribe, did not foresee so great and such a good from the stock of Benjamin; or, having foreseen it, thought it beneath him to celebrate it in the oracle of his voice.

Therefore Benjamin, the beloved of the Lord—that is, Saul, who was also Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin—by the great miracle of mercy was made, from a persecutor of the Lord, the beloved of the Lord (Acts 9). He shall dwell securely, growing stronger and stronger and confounding the Lord’s enemies.

“He shall remain in him as in a bridal chamber all the day”: that is, he shall glory in his grace at all times. And “he shall rest between his two shoulders,” between his two Testaments; he shall be nourished and glorified by the abundance of revelations.

Thus, just as in Judah the King and Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, so Benjamin, his beloved, his chosen vessel, the sanctuary of his grace, is worthily celebrated by the prophetic Spirit.

## CHAPTER XV. On the blessing of Joseph. That in Judah and in this one too Christ, the Son of God, is blessed.

Joseph also said:

“May his land be blessed by the blessing of the Lord: with the fruits of heaven and with the dew, and with the deep lying beneath; with the fruits produced by sun and moon; from the summit of the ancient mountains; with the fruits of the everlasting hills; and with the produce of the earth and its fullness.”

If you consider the literal sense, why is Joseph placed after Judah, Levi, and Benjamin, although he was next to last according to the time and order of the birth of Israel’s twelve sons? The reason is that the tribe of Ephraim, Joseph’s son, was the beginning of the kingdom of Jeroboam, who severed the ten tribes of Israel from the house of David. For King Jeroboam himself, through Ephraim, was of Joseph [Col. 0987C]. A great heap indeed of blessing is amassed because of Joseph’s merits; yet, according to the letter, whatever the present blessing proclaims is not very great, since both bad and good alike—and sometimes the bad more than the good—abound in the fruits of heaven and dew, that is, in every abundance of dew-bearing air, good and healthful climate, and the deep lying below; and likewise in the fruits of sun and moon. For, naturally, as physicists report, the fruits of the earth receive their increase from the moon and their ripening from the sun.

But according to the higher sense, worthy of the prophetic Spirit, Christ the Son of God himself is blessed in Joseph, as also in Judah: for he who was born according to the flesh from Judah is himself Joseph [Col. 0987D], Christ the Son of God, prefigured throughout the whole course of Joseph’s life. Therefore he says: “May his land be blessed by the blessing of the Lord,” etc. This blessing is divided into seven distinctions.

First: “by the blessing of the Lord, may his land be blessed.”
Second: “with the fruits of heaven and dew, and with the deep lying beneath.”
Third: “with the fruits produced by sun and moon.”
Fourth: “from the summit of the ancient mountains.”
Fifth: “with the fruits of the everlasting hills.”
Sixth: “with the produce of the earth.”
[p. 352] Seventh: “with its fullness.”

What is intended, wished, or foretold by this sevenfold blessing for Christ the Son of God—of whom Joseph, that ever-increasing son, bore the type—but that all things should be perfect and all things prosperous? For in the words, “May his land be blessed by the blessing of the Lord,” one must understand, “may it be founded or created”: his land, I mean, his earthly body, formed from earthly material, not [Col. 0988A] from male seed but from the Lord’s blessing; conceived, formed, and subjected to suffering not by mortal operation but by the working of the Holy Spirit.

In the words, “with the fruits of heaven and dew, and with the deep lying beneath,” one must understand, “may it be formed and spring up”: with the fruits, that is, of dew-bearing heaven and of the deep lying beneath—namely, through heavenly and angelic utterances, and through the moisture of virginal flesh. This accords with the other prophecy: “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Righteous One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45). For the fruit-bearing heavens dropped dew when the angel Gabriel was sent from heaven and said: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1), etc. But the deep lying beneath received the fruits of heaven—that is, the angel’s faithful words—when the faithful Virgin, opening a submissive and believing ear, said: “Behold, the handmaid of the Lord; let it be [Col. 0988B] done to me according to your word” (ibid.).

“With the fruits,” he says, “produced by sun and moon”: that is, through the truth or activity of both natures, divine and human alike. For this Son of blessing consists as one and the same God and man, not from the sun alone nor from the moon alone—that is, not from the divine nature alone nor from the human nature alone, but from both. By the sun, that is, by the divine nature, he was immutable and incapable of suffering; by the moon, that is, by human nature, he was subject to our changes and sufferings.

In the words, “from the summit of the ancient mountains and with the fruits of the everlasting hills,” one must understand, “may he proceed glorious and renowned.” The ancient mountains are the holy patriarchs; the everlasting hills are the prophets, whose testimony is stable and enduring. This ever-increasing Son was born from their flesh and has testimony from the Scriptures of the latter [Col. 0988C]. Therefore, “from the summit of the ancient mountains and with the fruits of the everlasting hills,” that is, may he come to us from the faithful seed of the patriarchs and through the faithful word of the prophets.

“With the produce of the earth,” understand: may he be richly endowed and gloriously enlarged—that is, through the many and innumerable children of the Church, spread over the whole world, born and springing up from his most holy Passion. “And with its fullness,” that is, with that glorious heavenly country, where the same earth, renewed with fullness and the blessedness of resurrection, will be filled with his good things and will enjoy an abundance of every good, both in body and in soul, in beholding him.

Finally, he says: “May the blessing of him who appeared in [Col. 0988D] the bush come upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.” This means: May that blessing be fulfilled in the head of Christ the Son of God which was then prefigured when the maker of every blessing appeared in the bush in order to deliver his people and lead them out of Egypt (Exod. 3). He is the Joseph who is to come to us, the ever-increasing Son; upon the head and crown of that Joseph, in the majesty and most exalted divinity of the Nazirite among his brothers—that is, the Holy One among all holy men and above all holy men.

May it come upon his head while he is conceived; may it come upon his crown when, now a young man, he is baptized. May the whole river of grace and blessing come, not in part but in all its fullness, upon his head or crown; and this, certainly, is none other than the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Let fire indeed come, but fire illuminating the bush without consuming it: that is, though God, the strongest of spirits, he did not dissolve the frail substance of the virginal womb, but made it a mother while preserving the virgin undefiled. May such a blessing coming from the midst of the bush free us from Pharaoh’s hand and Egypt’s mud: that is, being born from the Virgin, may it free us from the devil’s hand and the slavery of sin.

[Col. 0989A] “His beauty is like that of a firstborn bull; his horns are the horns of a rhinoceros.” It is pleasing also to consider the historical event, and how rightly that Joseph, son of Israel, is called both a Nazirite among his brothers, like a most beautiful firstborn bull, and one possessing horns resembling those of a rhinoceros. By the Law a Nazirite is commanded to let his hair grow [Col. 0989B] (Num. 6). But Joseph had grown his hair during his long confinement in prison, until he was brought out of prison at Pharaoh’s command, shaved, and clothed in a linen robe (Gen. 41). For what reason? Certainly because of his great innocence and praiseworthy righteousness: when invited and enticed by his lustful mistress, he did not at all consent to the wicked deed.

Accordingly, applauding the memorable event and cause, and alluding to his long-haired head, the patriarch Jacob also said: “May these blessings”—understand this—“be upon the head of Joseph, and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers” (Gen. 49). This lawgiver likewise says: “May the blessing come upon the head of Joseph and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.” It is clear, moreover, that Joseph was loved by his mistress because of his handsome face and comely appearance [Col. 0989C]. Therefore, “his beauty is like that of a firstborn bull,” because this handsome young man was desired by his mistress as a young bull is desired by a lascivious cow, outstanding among the rest. Alluding to the same point, the same holy Father mentioned above says: “Joseph is a son ever increasing, a son ever increasing and fair in appearance” (ibid.).

But because he strongly resisted lust, it is rightly said here: “His horns are the horns of a rhinoceros”; and above, “His bow,” he says, “rests in strength.” But, following the tropological interpretation now begun, let us refer these matters also to the Savior. His beauty is like that of a firstborn bull, because, sacrificed for the world’s salvation, he alone sufficed: the fatted calf, the firstborn calf, accepted for all as an odor of sweetness, white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands [Col. 0989D] (Song 5).

“His horns are the horns of a rhinoceros.” For he was most strong and almighty, beyond the grasp of all hunters, except that he deposited the singular horn of his omnipotence in the bosom—indeed, in the womb—of the Virgin; and from there he could be seized and killed by hunters, by the plotting Jews. Although the rhinoceros has one horn, and is therefore called the *unicornis*, nevertheless he said “horns” in the plural, because one and the same one both made all things omnipotently and restored all lost things by the same power. The nature of the rhinoceros has already been discussed elsewhere (above, ch. 20); let us now proceed to what remains.

“With them he shall thresh the nations to the ends of the earth. These are the multitudes of Ephraim, and these the thousands of Manasseh.” It is clear that in those horns he wonderfully threshed the nations to the ends of the earth in the public war. For by preaching that the Word through whom all things were made in the beginning became flesh and overcame the devil at the end of the ages, he drove the nations before him: some he put to flight and some he laid beneath his feet [Col. 0990A]. For those among them who resisted him with their swords and purpose of persecution perished; but those who received his preaching were rightly subjected beneath his feet.

Thus he threshed the nations to the ends of the earth, and in thus threshing both Gentiles and Jews he fulfilled what he had said in the Psalm: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession. You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and like [Col. 0990B] [p. 353] a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them” (Ps. 2).

The nations themselves are the multitudes of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh: that is, they have been judged and arranged as was prefigured in Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh. Ephraim was younger by birth, Manasseh firstborn; but by his blessing Father Israel set Ephraim before Manasseh (Gen. 48). So the Jewish people came before the people of the Gentiles, but through the threshing horns of this rhinoceros it came about, among other things, that this younger people stands before that former one.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the blessing of Zebulun and Issachar: that Christ’s apostles are blessed in them.

And he said to Zebulun: “Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going forth, and Issachar in your tents. They shall call peoples to the mountain [Col. 0990C]; there they shall sacrifice victims of righteousness, they who suck the abundance of the sea as milk and the hidden treasures of the sands.”

First, it should simply be said that, in the blessings or praises of Joseph, what might have been said according to the letter or historical sense is left unmentioned: namely, that Ephraim would depart from the temple of the Lord and from the kingdom or city of God, and would make golden calves. Then the best men of Zebulun and Issachar would call the peoples to the mountain—that is, to the temple in Jerusalem situated on Mount Moriah—opposing Jeroboam’s sacrilege and saying that not his calves in Bethel and Dan, but the Lord God of their fathers in Jerusalem, ought to be worshiped.

For the Hebrews say that those especially from Issachar and [Col. 0990D] Zebulun, and likewise Naphtali, devoted themselves to meditating on the Holy Scriptures day and night. They say that this is signified metaphorically in Jacob’s blessings: “Zebulun shall dwell by the shore of the sea” (Gen. 49); “Issachar, a strong ass, put his shoulder under the burden and became a servant for tribute.” This means: he submitted himself to study, laboring to learn and bringing gifts to his teachers. This accords very fully with the present statement: “They who suck the abundance of the sea as milk, and the hidden treasures of the sands.” It is as though he said: Those who receive the fullness of the Scriptures with sweetness and desire, and the hidden treasures of subtle meanings in the depth of the letters.

“There they shall sacrifice victims of righteousness”; but whatever is sacrificed to Ephraim’s calves will undoubtedly be a victim of injustice. Yet we must now advance to a higher sense. “Rejoice, Zebulun, in your going forth, and Issachar in your tents.” It is better and worthier of the prophetic Spirit if we refer this to the teaching of the Savior, who was blessed above in Joseph, since he taught especially in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali and called apostles there, as is also written in the Gospel: “Rejoice, Zebulun” (Matt. 4). Zebulun means “dwelling of strength,” and Issachar means “reward.” Rejoice, I say, apostles of the Savior: for you who have resolutely left all things and courageously endured adversities for righteousness’ sake have an abundant reward laid up in heaven. Rejoice in that going forth of yours, in those heavenly [Col. 0991B] dwellings of yours.

The prophetic discourse immediately turns its address to the hearers: “They shall call peoples to the mountain; there they shall sacrifice victims of righteousness.” They shall call peoples—not one people of Jews, but all peoples or nations—to that mountain of which, according to Isaiah, the many peoples, or all nations, who have themselves been summoned, exhort one another and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob. In the last days,” says the prophet, “the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the summit of the mountains and raised above the hills, and all nations shall flow to it” (Isa. 2), etc.

To that mountain, which is to fill the entire world, they shall call peoples; they shall call with a great voice, so that “their sound goes out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world” [Col. 0991C] (Ps. 18). “There they shall sacrifice victims of righteousness”: there alone, because apart from ascent of that mountain, apart from faith in this mountain or house of the Lord, nowhere else is it possible to sacrifice victims of righteousness. Since, at the apostles’ summons to this mountain, “the law went forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2), whatever is sacrificed anywhere—whether in Jerusalem or in the whole Synagogue—once that summons is despised, is a sacrifice of injustice and a victim of impiety.

In calling them there, he says, “they shall suck the abundance of the sea as milk”: that is, by sweet preaching they shall bring the multitude of the Gentiles into one faith, as into their own body. This agrees with the Holy and Consoling Spirit’s promise to the holy and apostolic Church in the prophet: “You shall suck the milk of the nations, and you shall be nursed at the breasts of kings” (Isa. 60) [Col. 0991D]. They shall also suck the hidden treasures of the sands: that is, with most clear perception they shall search out and, in spiritually expounding them, sweetly drink the deep mysteries of the Scriptures, of the Law and the Prophets. They shall suck treasures of sands of this kind and know by experience that “the judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the blessing of Gad: how his name, which means “girded,” suits both the historical and the spiritual sense.

And he said to Gad: “Blessed is Gad in breadth. He rested like [Col. 0992A] a lion and seized the arm and the crown of the head. And he saw his leadership, that a teacher was placed in his portion; he was with the leaders of the people, and performed the righteous deeds of the Lord and his judgment with Israel.”

“Blessed in breadth,” he says, that is, in good will, because Gad says: “We have built sheepfolds and cattle-stalls, and fortified cities for our little ones. But we ourselves, armed and girded, shall go forth to battle before the children of Israel until we bring them into their places. We shall not return to our homes until the children of Israel possess their inheritance; nor do we seek anything beyond the Jordan, because we already have our possession in its eastern region” (Num. 32).

In saying and doing this, Gad indeed saw his leadership: that is, he did not neglect [Col. 0992B] his pledge or prove false to his promise, marching as a leader in war, armed and girded according to his name, before the face of his brothers. “A teacher placed in his portion”: that is, a leader established amid dangers by his own decision, teaching by his actions going before the discipline and courage in war which the others were to follow. Thus he was with the leaders of the people: a leader in the battle-line, first in dangers; and he performed the righteous deeds of the Lord, repaying his words with deeds, and his judgment with Israel, doing what he had judged that he ought to do before, or with, all Israel.

Then “he rested like a lion and seized the arm and crown of the head.” For when he returned after fourteen years to the children whom he had left beyond the Jordan in possession, he found a great war against them from neighboring nations [Col. 0992C]. Fighting bravely, he conquered the enemies in the manner of a lion seizing an adversary’s arm and [p. 354] head, so that, having first torn away the fighting right hand, he might then drink his blood.

Spiritually, after the apostles, the successors of the apostles are instructed by this blessing. They have now received possessions on this side of the Jordan, since even here, before the estates of heaven and the land of the living, they possess resources in the Church and estates from the hand of wealthy kings, faithful rulers, or emperors. Let such men see their leadership, that teachers have been placed in their portion: that is, let them not be ignorant on what condition they have received leadership in Christ’s Church. They have been appointed not as emperors or tyrants but as teachers, within their own portion or capacity [Col. 0992D], to govern the Church which he acquired by his blood (Acts 20), for which they must render an account (Heb. 13).

Let them see this, I say, and be with the leaders of the people: that is, let them imitate the apostles, fathers and leaders of the Christian people, and after their example perform the righteous deeds of the Lord, as the circumstance requires—now with the rod, now in a spirit of gentleness—and maintain their judgment with Israel. Let them maintain, I say, their judgment or resolution, by which they professed to care for this spiritual Israel, lest the temporal reward unworthily received result in their condemnation.

Therefore Gad is blessed in breadth: namely, every preacher or prelate whose heart is enlarged through charity. Thus the Apostle, enlarged, said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” [Col. 0993A] (2 Cor. 6), etc. Certainly whoever is such a one rests like a lion and seizes the arm and crown of the head: that is, he puts on the holy Spirit of the Lion from Judah’s tribe, seizes every person who resists by the arm of the Spirit of God, and tramples down the crown of pride.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the blessing of Dan: that historically Samson, who was to arise from his tribe, but mystically Christ, whose type Samson bore, is blessed in him.

He said also to Dan: “Dan, a lion’s cub, shall flow abundantly from Bashan.” Dan—that is, Samson of the tribe of Dan—shall be as strong as a lion’s cub; for he shall easily overcome thousands of enemies as one lion overcomes many thousands of sheep. “He shall flow abundantly from Bashan”: that is, after crossing [Col. 0993B] the Jordan, once Og king of Bashan’s land has first been conquered with Israel, he shall act bravely, going up and winning his allotted inheritance in battle.

For Dan is a lion’s cub not only because of Samson but also because of the common strength in battle of the tribe. For it is written: “The children of Dan went up and fought against Leshem; they took it, struck it with the edge of the sword, possessed it, and dwelt in it, calling its name Leshem-Dan after the name of Dan their father” (Josh. 19).

But at a higher level, in Dan, because of the aforementioned Samson—whose name means “their sun”—we may understand our Sun, Christ the Sun of righteousness. This lion’s cub, that is, the Son of the most strong God, shall flow abundantly from Bashan: that is, he shall act mightily and bestow the abundance of the gifts [Col. 0993C] of the Holy Spirit, whose fullness is denoted by Bashan. Bashan indeed means “fat,” and in Christ it rightly signifies the richness of the Holy Spirit, as the Psalm says: “The mountain of God is a rich mountain” (Ps. 67).

This lion’s cub shattered the gates of hell and, rising at midnight, finally ascended into heaven. This was prefigured in Samson, also of the tribe of Dan: when besieged by enemies, he rose at midnight, carried off the city gates, and went up to the summit of a mountain (Judg. 16). The other most illustrious and mighty deeds by which he made his own tribe of Dan renowned were mysteries signifying the glory of Christ our Lord, as has long ago been expounded by the orthodox Fathers, is found expounded in writing, and is known throughout Christ’s whole Church.

## CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 0993D] On the blessing of Naphtali, and that the words, “He shall possess morning and midday,” concern the Savior’s teaching.

And he said to Naphtali: “Naphtali shall enjoy abundance, and shall be full of the Lord’s blessing; he shall possess morning and midday.” If one considers the literal sense, concerning the words “he shall possess morning and midday,” the question arises why it was not said that he would possess the west also. For it is written concerning Naphtali’s allotment: “Their border goes out as far as the Jordan, and the boundary returns toward the west at Aznoth-tabor; from there it goes out to Hukkok, passes to Zebulun on the south, to Asher on the west, and to Judah at the Jordan eastward, with fortified cities” [Col. 0994A] (Josh. 19).

It is therefore better to refer this also to the Savior’s teaching, since Naphtali truly possessed morning and midday especially where he taught, fulfilling what was said through the prophet: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9). The Evangelist also testifies to this when he says: “And leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and dwelt in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, that what was said through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and to those sitting in the region and shadow of death light has arisen’” (Matt. 4).

Therefore he shall possess morning and midday; for from there Jesus, the noonday light, began to preach. From there, I say, he shone in preaching as the same morning star and midday sun [Col. 0994B]. Thus Naphtali shall be full of the Lord’s blessing, namely, on account of the elect for whom that very morning and that very midday are pleasing, whose eyes are sound and not envious.

Universally, however, since Naphtali means “breadth,” one may understand that everyone enlarged by charity is truly full of the Lord’s blessing and possesses morning and midday here: that is, he now sees God “through a mirror, in an enigma,” but in the future face to face (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XX. On the blessing of Asher: that, according to his name, which means “blessed,” all the saints of God who are truly blessed are blessed in him.

He said also to Asher: “Blessed among sons is Asher; may he be pleasing to his brothers, and may he dip his foot in oil. Iron and bronze shall be his sandal. As are the days of your youth, so also shall be your old age. There is no other God like the God of the most upright. The ascender of heaven is your helper. By his magnificence the clouds run abroad; his dwelling is above, and beneath are everlasting arms. He shall cast out the enemy from before you and shall say, ‘Crush him.’”

That Asher was blessed among sons and begot blessed children is indicated by the fact that happy and blessed women too, possessing the spirit of prophecy, left great and long-enduring testimony of wisdom or sanctity. For the wise woman from the city [Col. 0994D] of Abel cried out and said, “Hear, hear; tell Joab” (2 Sam. 20), and afterwards: “There was a saying,” she said, “in the old proverb: ‘Let those who inquire inquire in Abel,’ and thus they obtained truth. Am I not one who answers truth in Israel? Why do you destroy the inheritance of the Lord?” (ibid.). That wise woman, I say, was, as the Hebrews relate, a daughter of this Asher [p. 355]; and for that reason she called herself a mother in Israel, because she was advanced in years. Hence it is now fittingly said of Asher her father: “Iron and bronze shall be his sandal,” by which saying length of life is beautifully signified.

Likewise, in the Gospel Anna the prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, is mentioned (Luke 2), venerable both for her long-lived sanctity and for the grace of prophecy; for she was judged worthy to recognize Christ as an infant and [Col. 0995A] to bear prophetic testimony concerning him.

But because Asher means “blessed,” let us understand that all the saints awaiting the blessed hope are blessed more broadly in this name. Thus, “Blessed among sons is Asher”: that is, blessed in good works and in virtues is that happy people whose Lord is their God. “May he be pleasing to his brothers”: that is, may he possess mutual love, just as the Lord his God loved him. “May he dip his foot in oil,” namely, by announcing peace and preaching charity. For blessed are the feet of those who proclaim peace.

“Iron and bronze shall be his sandal”: that is, as iron is strong and bronze most enduring, so may his faith be strong and persevere to the end; or, as iron is constant and bronze resounding, so may he do good steadfastly and proclaim faithfully. “As are the days of your youth, so also shall be your old age.” This is truly praiseworthy. For many, especially those who think and live carnally, are indeed wise and sharper in youth, but in old age become foolish and lapse into the folly of childhood. But you are not so.

For after King David had grown old, he at last found Abishag the Shunammite, a very beautiful young virgin [Col. 0995B] (1 Kings 1). This signifies that holy men, when they have lived many days and have grown ever colder from their former heat, then advance ever more into spiritual wisdom and toward the heavenly virgin, undefiled and incorruptible. Therefore, “as are the days of your youth, so also shall be your old age”: namely, an old age fit for the embraces of wisdom or prudence, whom you have called your beloved.

“There is no other God like the God of the most upright.” This is what those will surely say who see your foot dipped in oil and your sandal of iron or bronze. Therefore he says: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5). This, I say, they will declare; and you must therefore show your foot dipped in oil and shod with iron or bronze, not that they may see you, but that, gladdened by the pleasing light of your works, they may say: “There is no other God like the God of the Most High.”

This has often been said, and it is very well known that it benefited those who said it. For when pagans and Gentiles, marveling and rejoicing, saw Christ’s servants perfect in action and powerful in speech, they said: “That God is the true God who has such servants as you” [Col. 0995D]. When, because of you, O most upright one, God has thus been glorified, you too shall be made blessed through that same glorification of God. For they will add: “The ascender of heaven is your helper.” You are therefore, they say, most upright because he who ascended into heaven is your helper. For without his help you could do nothing.

For example, Peter is upright today; before that one ascended into heaven, Peter was not upright. At the voice of the servant-girl who kept the door, he bowed down in fear and shrank away; and, fearing to die, he denied life. But when his helper ascended above the setting—when he trampled death by rising and ascended into heaven, or, to speak according to the prophet, when “ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” [Col. 0996A] (Ps. 67)—then and from that time Peter became most upright.
