Therefore, whoever calls you most upright in glorifying God should at once add the efficient cause by which you are upright: “The ascender of heaven,” he says, “is your helper.” “By his magnificence the clouds run abroad.” It is as if he said: Why do they wonder? The help of that ascender of heaven is most mighty and effectual. For by his magnificence the clouds run abroad. By magnificence, that is, by magnificent grace, it came about that clouds run throughout the whole earth—temperate clouds, clouds full of water, watering all nations in every language and with all manner of discourse by the waters of saving teaching. These clouds are the apostles and prophets. For it was said of them: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60).

Before his magnificent ascension had granted them his help—that is, the gifts of his Spirit—these clouds did not run abroad, but rained only a little in one small place in Judea [Col. 0996B]. But what now? “His dwelling is above, and beneath are everlasting arms.” This means: He ascended into heaven and, sitting at the Father’s right hand, dwells above; from there he stretched out to us his arms, his everlasting arms, that is, the most mighty gifts of his Holy Spirit. For the same gifts of the Holy Spirit are called, in the Apocalypse, the seven horns of the Lamb (Rev. 5); so here, because of that same strength, they may rightly be called the seven everlasting arms of his dwelling.

Through the magnificence of these arms the clouds were made glorious and ran abroad: that is, the apostles, or wise and eloquent apostolic men, were distributed throughout the whole world, so that their teaching might water all the earth [Col. 0996C]. “He shall cast out the enemy from before you and shall say, ‘Crush him.’” By those arms, O Asher, O people blessed three and four times, he shall cast out from before you that enemy of whom, before the ascender of heaven stretched out his arms, he said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John 12).

Therefore first, through his Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, he shall cast the enemy out from before you, drawing all things to himself. But at the last he shall say, “Crush him”: namely, when he comes with great power and majesty, so that he may cast that enemy and all his angels into the eternal fire of Gehenna, ever burning and unquenchable [Col. 0996D] (Matt. 25). He shall say, I mean, “Crush him”: that is, he shall crush him not by hand or foot but through the word of the Almighty, which he himself is, by a great and ineffable utterance—not a passing voice, but an abiding sentence.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the universal blessing of the whole people of God, under the name of Israel and Jacob.

Israel shall dwell securely, and alone. The eye of Jacob is upon a land of grain and wine, and the heavens shall grow dark with dew. When that ascender into heaven has reigned, when he has set his dwelling-place on high by sitting at the right hand of the Father, and has stretched out beneath him the everlasting arms foretold above, then Israel—true Israel, who, with the veil removed and face unveiled, shall behold the glory of the Lord—shall dwell securely and alone. Thus another prophet also testifies:

> “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely” (Jer. 23).

What king, according to that prophet, shall reign, unless he who, according to this one, is the ascender into heaven and has set his dwelling-place on high? And by what shall he execute judgment and justice in the earth, unless by these everlasting arms—by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, who convicts the world concerning judgment and justice (John 16)?

Therefore, as both this writer and that prophet testify, true Israel shall dwell—or rather, from that time already dwells—securely and alone: securely, I say, because it has a great advocate with the Father, a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus Christ, whose confession it holds fast (Heb. 4). Alone, however, because it receives only the one catholic faith. Whoever, wherever he may be, does not think the same thing or say the same thing, is outside and beyond the boundaries of this Israel.

Meanwhile this solitary Israel does not seek to receive here the reward of its confidence. But what then? “The eye of Jacob is upon a land of grain and wine.” The eye, I say—that is, the intention—of Jacob, the mighty supplanter, is directed toward that land of the living, from which he will displace unworthy inhabitants. It is a land of grain and wine: of grain, that is, of eternal life, where the bread of angels shall be seen in its own substance; and a land of wine, where the river of love, the torrent of delight, does not fail. Toward that land the eye of Jacob is directed; there strong Jacob has placed his hope.

“And the heavens shall grow dark with dew.” While Jacob’s eye looks toward that land, so long as he is a pilgrim in this world, the heavenly homeland is hidden from the contemplating mind in a sweet darkness and a dark sweetness; so that, wonderfully and almost ineffably, the mind fails in the very effort to see it, and rejoices, filled by its own failing.

“Blessed are you, O Israel. Who is like you, O people who are saved?” Again Israel is called blessed, because truly blessed is the people whose Lord is its God. “Who,” he says, “is like you?” No one, understand: for you are saved, whereas the people to whom the ascender into heaven has not been given as a helper is destined for destruction, and is in this respect utterly and oppositely unlike you.

Yet do not reckon this to yourself or suppose that it has arisen from you. Rather: “In the Lord is the shield of your help, and the sword of your glory.” The shield of your help, by which you were able to quench the fiery darts of your enemy; and the sword of the word of God, by which you triumphed gloriously in pursuing the enemy or cutting away the vices of the flesh (Eph. 6)—these were in the Lord and not in yourself: a gift of the Lord’s grace, not a work of your own strength.

“Your enemies shall deny you, and you shall tread upon their necks.” This too belongs to the Lord’s glory: his enemies first denied him before Pilate; but he, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, trod upon their necks. And he gave you power so that, when enemies likewise deny you—those who are your enemies because of him—you too may at last tread upon their necks on the day of judgment.

## Chapter XXII. On the death of Moses: that he undoubtedly truly died, just as his brother Aaron died; and on Joshua his successor

**(Chapter XXXIV.)** “Moses, the servant of the Lord, died in the land of Moab, at the Lord’s command; and he buried him in the valley in the land of Moab, opposite Peor. And no man knew his burial-place up to the present day.”

Many maintain that Moses did not truly die in the proper sense of the word, but that the Lord hid him; and that by the name “dead” one ought to understand his concealment or translation. They take as their principal argument the fact that, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, Moses appeared speaking with him together with Elijah (Matt. 17).

But if he did not die, and is believed instead to have been translated by the Lord, like Enoch and Elijah, how could this be reckoned as the Lord’s indignation or wrath? Surely such translation is not indignation but gracious favour, not wrath but great grace. Moses himself says: “Nor is the Lord’s indignation against the people to be wondered at, when he was angry even with me and said because of you: ‘You too shall not enter; but Joshua son of Nun, your minister, shall enter in your stead’” (Deut. 1). Again: “The Lord was angry with me because of your words, and swore that I should not cross the Jordan or enter the excellent land which he is about to give you. Behold, I die in this land; I shall not cross the Jordan. You shall cross and possess that noble land” (Deut. 4).

Even now, in his wrath, the Lord says: “This is the land concerning which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I shall give it to your seed.’ You have seen it with your eyes, but you shall not cross into it.” Finally, did not Aaron at least truly die, in a genuine laying down of the body? Who could conceal even this? A little earlier the Lord says to Moses: “Go up this mountain of Abarim”—that is, “Passage”—“to Mount Nebo, and die, as your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor, because you transgressed against me at the waters of Contradiction and did not sanctify me among the children of Israel” (Deut. 32).

Therefore, whatever contrary arguments anyone may attempt, we freely affirm that, just as Aaron truly died by a real laying down of his body, so Moses did also.

“Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died.” It is as though he said: Behold, that sentence of the Lord rises against me by which, after saying universally, “My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh” (Gen. 6), he immediately pointed, as it were, an angry finger singularly against me: “His days,” he says, “shall be one hundred and twenty years” (ibid.). For he has appointed the days of a human being, which cannot be exceeded (Job 14).

“His eye was not dim, nor had his teeth moved.” He could therefore still have been fit for this life, had the Lord not, as vengeance hastened, said: “Go up this mountain and die.”

“Now Joshua son of Nun was filled with the spirit of wisdom, because Moses laid his hands upon him. And the children of Israel obeyed him and did as the Lord commanded Moses. And no prophet arose again in Israel like Moses.”

The evasive Jews, fleeing everywhere from the meaning of truth, when asked of whom Moses spoke here—“The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from among your brothers, like me; him you shall hear, as you asked of the Lord your God in Horeb” (Deut. 68 [an apparent erroneous citation])—answer that it was said of Joshua.

But observe that after saying, “Joshua was filled with the spirit of wisdom,” and so forth, Scripture immediately adds: “And no prophet arose again in Israel like Moses.” This plainly amounts to saying: Joshua was not like Moses. Therefore “no prophet arose again in Israel like Moses”—you must understand: except that one who is not only a prophet but Lord of the prophets; who according to his humanity is like Moses, that is, another lawgiver, but according to his divinity is not like Moses, but is greater than Moses.

“Whom the Lord knew face to face in all signs and wonders.” It has already been said elsewhere concerning this that the Lord knew Moses face to face beyond all others, in that he showed him heavenly mysteries, or knowledge of future things, beyond all the prophets—not through a dream or figures (Num. 12), but by certain and proper vision.

What mystery the death of Moses and the succession of Joshua contain will be disclosed by the opening passages of the following book.

## Chapter XXIII. That the Lord truly said to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me”

The Lord truly and faithfully said to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me; for he wrote concerning me” (John 5). For what else did Moses write except the things that concern him? Or upon whom other than the Son of God did that writer direct his gaze?

Truly, as was said here at the end, the Lord knew him face to face in all the signs and wonders which he sent through him to perform in the land of Egypt against Pharaoh, all his servants, and the whole of that land; and in all the mighty hand and great wonders which Moses performed before all Israel. In all these things the Lord knew him, and Moses himself knew the Lord face to face.

For while outwardly performing all these earthly things, he inwardly beheld with certain sight the heavenly pattern shown to him on the mountain. In accordance with those realities—the true realities—like an excellent painter with skilled hand, he drew imitative lines of figures upon a tablet.

This brightness of the inward countenance of Moses, now wholly unveiled in Christ before the world, accuses the fleeing Jews, who cannot endure to see in their own Moses the glory of Christ, the Son of God, in whom they do not believe. Rightly, therefore, and truthfully he says: “There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope” (ibid.), because you do not believe in him; because you spread the veil of unbelief over his most radiant face.

But we believe, and therefore we have spoken (2 Cor. 4). If we have said anything otherwise than it should have been said, anything too little or too feebly, we ask pardon from you and from the spirit of Moses, with Christ as guide or indwelling presence.

# The Forty-Two Books of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, on the Trinity and Its Works: Commentaries on the Book of Joshua

## Book One

## Chapter I. That Joshua is now the eighth mirror of Christ, the Son of God, prefigured by seven figures in the Pentateuch of Moses

In seven sections of the Pentateuch of Moses we have treated the recapitulated passion of Christ, the Son of God. Now, in the eighth, Joshua, we are about to celebrate the glory and triumph of his resurrection and entry into heaven.

The first was in the death of righteous Abel. The second was in Noah’s distresses. The third was in Isaac’s sacrifice. The fourth was in Joseph’s sale and chains. The fifth was in the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt through the sacrifice of the lamb. The sixth was in Moses striking the rock with a rod and bringing forth water for the thirsty people. The seventh was in his raising up the serpent in the wilderness, because thus the Son of Man had to be lifted up (John 3).

Now entering the eighth mirror of the same Christ, Son of God—namely, Joshua—we recognize in his battles and victories that same prince and Saviour of the world who has brought us into the land of the living. Having entered there first, rising from the dead, he dies no longer; death no longer has dominion over him (Rom. 6).

Such, I say, do we recognize him to be in the name and works of this Joshua: for Joshua brought the people by illustrious victories into that land of promise, which Moses could not do; and he died in peace, struggling through no sufferings, as a figure of the passion of that same Lord of ours.

Nevertheless, we shall not henceforth maintain, as we did in Moses, a continuous course or sequence of exposition. Rather, gathering the more splendid points wherever we can recognize the image of the eternal Sun shining from above, we shall hasten toward our intended end.

## Chapter II. What the Lord has now said to Joshua for the third time

**(Chapter I.)** “And it came to pass, after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord, that the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ minister, and said to him: ‘Moses my servant is dead. Arise and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you, into the land which I shall give to the children of Israel. Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread I shall give you, as I spoke to Moses. From the wilderness and Lebanon as far as the great river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, as far as the great sea toward the setting of the sun, shall be your boundary. No one shall be able to resist you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you; I shall not leave you or forsake you. Be strengthened and be stout-hearted. For you shall divide by lot for this people the land concerning which I swore to their fathers.’”

This has now happened for the third time: the Lord spoke to Joshua.

First, he spoke to him, or concerning him, when, as we have at the end of the book of Numbers, he said to Moses: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, and lay your hand upon him. At his word he shall go out and come in, he and all the children of Israel with him, and all the rest of the multitude” (Num. 17 [an apparent erroneous citation]), and the rest.

Second, he spoke to the same man when, as we have above, Moses wrote the song and taught it to the children of Israel, and the Lord commanded Joshua son of Nun: “Be strengthened and be stout-hearted. For you shall bring the children of Israel into the land which I promised, and I shall be with you” (Deut. 31).

Third, as was said, at the beginning of the present book he speaks to him: “Moses my servant is dead. Arise and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you,” and so forth.

Let us search out the hidden yet most luminous mysteries of the Spirit beneath the manifest letter of the history.

## Chapter III. That, at the first utterance of the Lord’s command, Moses laid his hands upon Joshua’s head; and that, at the first utterance of the sending Father, the Son of God was made under the Law

First, according to the interpretation of his proper name itself, Joshua son of Nave testifies that he bears the image of our Lord Jesus Christ. For *Josue* means “saviour of the Lord,” and *Nave* means “beauty.” Therefore Joshua son of Nave—that is, the saviour of the Lord, son of beauty—who is he except the only-begotten Saviour of God the Father, the son of virginity?

Without doubt the Lord God the Father spoke three times to this his Saviour, the Saviour sent by himself, and three times anointed him with the Holy Spirit, in a primary and singular manner.

First, he anointed him with the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb: for an incorrupt Virgin conceived him not from male seed but from the Holy Spirit. And according to the prophetic testimony of the same Holy Spirit, he thus spoke to him—or rather, thus spoke beforehand concerning him:

> “My heart has poured forth a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe” (Ps. 44).

Then, as though holding the hand of the already formed beautiful man in order to bring him out through the enclosure of the virgin womb, which no man had ever opened:

> “You are beautiful in form beyond the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one. In your splendour and your beauty, aim prosperously, proceed, and reign” (ibid.).

These and the other things indicated in what follows of that same psalm the Lord then spoke to this Joshua.

In that first utterance it was said: “Lay your hand upon him” (Num. 27). And afterwards: “Having laid his hands upon his head, he repeated all that the Lord had commanded” (ibid.). What, then, ought to be said from these things except that our Joshua, conceived and born by the first operation of the Holy Spirit, was made under the Law?

For Moses laid his hands upon Joshua’s head when our Saviour, God the Son of God, deigned to be subjected to the Law in order that he might redeem those under the Law (Gal. 4): not as a slave of the Law, but as a man obedient to the Law and at the same time God, the Lord of the Law; circumcised according to the Law; cleansed according to the Law, like a sinner, by the customary offering; and in all similar matters, until the appointed time, subjected to the Law as though to Moses’ hands.

Hence the Apostle says: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law” (ibid.).

## Chapter IV. That in the second utterance, “Be strengthened and be stout-hearted,” but of Christ it was said: “You are my beloved Son”

The second time God anointed this same Joshua—that is, our Saviour—or spoke to him, was when the Holy Spirit descended upon him, now a young man and already fit by mature age for the public office of preaching, in the form of a dove, while the paternal voice testified from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3; Luke 3).

In that second utterance of the Lord to the literal Joshua it was said: “Be strengthened and be stout-hearted.” Then Moses said: “Take this book, the book of the Law, and put it beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord our God, that it may be there as a testimony against you” (Deut. 31).

What is indicated through these things except that our Joshua, the prince of humility, who had remained hidden until his thirtieth year, was, by the aforesaid declaration of the Spirit in himself together with the testimony of the Father’s voice, commanded to be strengthened and stout-hearted? That is, he was commanded to use in preaching his sword, with which he had been girded upon his thigh; to arm himself for miracles and the casting out of demons with the finger of God; and to go forth mighty in the Spirit of God.

And what was it then for the book of the Law to be taken up and placed beside the ark as a testimony against Israel, except that from then on, through his passion, the Law was fulfilled against carnal Israel, against Judaism according to the flesh?

For the ark, as has already been said in its place, is the body of Christ God, fashioned from the mass of the human race. The most holy side of that ark—that body—was pierced by a spear; and when blood and water flowed forth from it for our redemption and sanctification, the Law was consummated and fulfilled.

Thus, while Joshua went forth strengthened and stout-hearted, the book of the Law of the Lord was placed beside the ark of the Lord’s covenant as a testimony against Israel. For while our Saviour preached strongly and cast out demons by the mighty finger of God, the Law was fulfilled through his passion and set as a testimony against the Jews, so that from then on Moses, whom they vainly—indeed foolishly—hope to have as their defender, accuses them (John 5).

## Chapter V. That the third utterance to Joshua, “Arise and cross this Jordan,” is to Christ: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery”

The third time the Lord Father spoke to our same Saviour and the third time anointed him with the Holy Spirit was when he brought his soul forth from hell, raised his flesh on the third day from the dead so that it should not see corruption, and crowned the new man, renewed, the Son of Man, with the glory of immortality and the honour of incorruption. From that time he set him over the works of his hands and subjected all things under his feet (Heb. 2).

We have heard in the psalm the Father’s voice by which he then spoke to him as he lay in the tomb—the voice itself and its words: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Pss. 56, 107). That harp of paternal praise and psaltery of his everlasting jubilation answered the Father: “I shall arise at dawn,” it said (ibid.).

Therefore, now that the Lord speaks for the third time to this Joshua, who is a type of that great and true Saviour resting, as has been said, in the tomb, it is rightly and according to the proper force of the mystery: “Arise,” he says, “and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you.”

For was that man lying in his own person, so that it might be said to him, “Arise”? Was he not rather standing in the exalted merits of righteousness? He was full of the Spirit of God, as God himself testified at first, saying: “Take Joshua son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God” (Num. 27), and so forth. Surely it belongs to such persons to stand. Thus one of them, freely professing concerning himself, says: “The Lord lives, before whose presence I stand” (3 Kings 17).

Therefore the same Spirit who says to our Saviour in the Prophet, as has been said, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Pss. 56, 107), is himself the Spirit of God who commands this Joshua as a type of him: “Arise.”

These words themselves must now be examined; and, as has been said, in this third summons of the mighty man we must contemplate the victorious glory of the unconquered and immortal Saviour.

## Chapter VI. How Moses, the servant of the Lord, truly died to the Jews; and what it means for Christ to cross the Jordan, and what the bounds or distribution of his promised land signify

“Moses,” he says, “my servant is dead. Arise and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you, into the land which I shall give to the children of Israel.”

To whom, or among whom, is Moses, the servant of the Lord, dead? Plainly, he is dead to the Jews. Moses is dead to the Jews unworthy of Moses’ life, in their crime, in the sacrilege by which they crucified the Lord of Moses.

Whatever Mosaic things they seem from that time onward to possess are dead and devoid of all life: the multitude of their sacrifices, holocausts of rams, fat of fattened beasts, blood of calves, lambs, or goats, their new moons, their Sabbath, their Kalends, and all their other feasts and solemnities. For how can these live, or how can they think that they possess Moses alive in them, when God, the life of the living, has hated them?

“My soul has hated these,” he says; “they have become burdensome to me” (Isa. 1). “I shall not endure them, I shall not hear; indeed, I shall turn away my eyes.”

Therefore Moses is dead to the Jews—to the Jews, I say, because of their sacrilege, because their hands are full of blood (ibid.)—Moses is dead (Deut. 34). Hence it was rightly said above: “No man knew his burial-place up to the present day” (ibid.). For who today can know the place of Moses, dead in the hands of the Jews? Their city, earthly Zion, has become desolate; that once noble house of their sanctification has become deserted. They have been scattered among all nations; they are known in every place, and yet they have no place. Nor can one say: Here or there is the place of the Jews where they ought to celebrate their dead Moses, their dead letter.

Thus, Moses having died, “Arise, Joshua; arise, Saviour; rise again, my salvation; and cross this Jordan.” Cross beyond all the carnal ceremonies of the Jews, all the Jewish purifications, all Jewish baptisms—the baptisms of cups, pots, bronze vessels, and beds (Mark 7; Heb. 6). Cross beyond them, I say; and by that very crossing make divisions between letter and Spirit.

“You and all the people with you.” For when you, the firstborn from the dead, rise from the dead, all the people rise with you, and the universal resurrection of the dead becomes an object of hope. And when you rise, all the people will cross with you into the land which I shall give to the children of Israel: the land of the living, the land truly flowing with milk and honey.

“Every place on which the sole of your foot shall tread I shall give to you, as I spoke to Moses.” This is plainly true; in our Saviour it is manifest. Every place, every heart, or every conscience upon which the sole of his foot has trodden—which has subjected itself to his feet, received his footsteps, or kept them—is his: it belongs to the Saviour, to everlasting salvation.

Conversely, those upon whom the sole of his foot has not trodden, who are not subjected to his feet, are not his. They have not been delivered to him, but given to the devil; they are not a people of acquisition, but children of perdition.

“From the wilderness and Lebanon as far as the great river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, as far as the great sea toward the setting of the sun, shall be your boundary.”

According to the letter, the boundaries of the land which that Joshua was to possess are defined. But according to the spiritual sense, dominion or rule over both Jews and Gentiles is promised to the Lord our Saviour.

For the wilderness and Lebanon, which is interpreted “white,” are the Jewish people: the wilderness, namely, with respect to those who, on account of their unbelief, have been deserted by this Saviour and abandoned by this salvation; Lebanon, with respect to those who have received the grace of his baptism or will receive it near the end of the world, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered.

The river Euphrates and the great sea are the Gentile peoples. The river Euphrates, interpreted “fruitful” or “increasing,” refers to those from the Gentiles who run to this Saviour with great increase of virtues and the fruit of eternal salvation. The great sea refers to those who, remaining false and bitter, did not receive the salvation or healing of life, and indeed persecuted him marvellously, but did not prevail. Of them we sing in the psalm: “Wonderful are the swellings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high” (Ps. 92).

“All the land of the Hittites,” that is, “of those who fear” or “are astonished”—such as those of whom Moses says in his song, “Let fear and dread fall upon them through the greatness of your arm” (Deut. 32)—all the land, I say, of those who fear and tremble under the torment of an evil conscience, from that wilderness to that great sea, and from that Lebanon to that great river Euphrates, shall be your boundary. Thus, by preaching the Gospel in every race and nation, you shall reveal the wrath of God to strike fear into the Hittites—that is, the impious: those who suppress the truth of God in unrighteousness and serve the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1).

“No one shall be able to resist you all the days of your life.” Let the strong and warlike Hittites oppose and resist the truth: they shall not prevail. Rather, according to the name of the Hittites, all who contradict you, O Saviour of the world, shall fear and tremble.

## Chapter VII. That “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you” is said to Christ: through you shall be accomplished whatever is prefigured in Moses

“As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you; I shall not leave you or forsake you. Be strengthened and be stout-hearted. For you shall divide by lot for this people the land concerning which I swore to their fathers that I would give it to them. Therefore be strengthened and be very stout-hearted,” and so forth.

“As I was with Moses,” he says, “so I shall be with you.” This means: As through Moses I defeated the fleshly Pharaoh, crushed the whole of Egypt, at last led out the children of Israel by his hand, and carried them through the Red Sea after Pharaoh had been drowned with his chariots and army, so through you, Christ, Saviour of the world, I have already conquered and shall in the future judge the spiritual Pharaoh—that is, the devil.

Through you, I say, I have shattered hell and conquered the world; and I shall conquer utterly, until the spiritual Pharaoh is drowned in the deep with his chariots and horsemen—that is, until the devil is cast down into hell with his angels and all his pomps.

Therefore, “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you”: that is, through you all things shall occur as they were prefigured through him, and those things which happened figuratively through Moses shall be fulfilled through you in truth.

“Be strengthened and be stout-hearted.” This encouraging declaration is repeated three times. First: “Be strengthened and be stout-hearted.” Second: “Therefore be strengthened and be very stout-hearted.” Third: “Be strengthened and be stout-hearted; do not fear and do not be afraid.”

According to the letter, the more manifold the repetition, the more forceful the inculcation of courage. But according to the mystery undertaken, the threefold work of the Saviour and his Spirit is commended. Explaining and distinguishing this himself, he says: “When the Paraclete comes, he shall convict the world concerning sin, justice, and judgment” (John 16), and so forth.

Therefore, “Be strengthened,” he says, “that you may convict the world concerning sin; be strengthened that you may convict it concerning justice; be strengthened that you may convict it concerning judgment.” Be strengthened and stout-hearted in all things, so that the constancy of the Gospel may be neither disturbed nor overthrown by flatteries or terrors, by prosperity or adversity.

## Chapter VIII. When and how Christ commands the leaders of the people, that is, the apostles, saying, “Pass through the midst of the camp”; and what it means to cross the Jordan after the third day

Joshua commanded the leaders of the people, saying: “Pass through the midst of the camp, and command the people, saying: ‘Prepare provisions for yourselves, for after the third day you shall cross the Jordan and enter to possess the land which the Lord your God is about to give you.’”

The leaders of the people are the holy apostles, concerning whom God the Father says in the psalm to this Joshua—that is, to Christ the Saviour, his Son:

> “Sons have been born to you in place of your fathers; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth. They shall remember your name” (Ps. 44).

Moreover, the camp or people of this Joshua consists of all the elect, all those who have been predestined to life. Where or when did Joshua—that is, our Saviour—command these leaders of his to pass through the midst of their camp and to issue these commands? In Galilee, on the mountain, after he had risen from the dead. There the leaders saw and worshipped him, though some doubted. For then he said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep all things that I have commanded you” (Matt. 28).

Therefore Joshua, who had heard the Lord say to him, “Arise and cross this Jordan,” immediately commanded the leaders of the people, saying, “Pass through the midst of the camp.” So our Saviour, who had heard God the Father say, “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp,” likewise commanded his apostles: “Go into the whole world” (Luke 9, 10); go and pass through the midst of the nations. Pass through, I say, girded and unencumbered; lingering nowhere, looking back nowhere, entangling yourselves in no secular business; carrying neither bag nor wallet; having no money in your belts (2 Cor. 3 [an apparent erroneous citation]). Thus, relieved of every burden and bowed under none, you may swiftly carry the good news to all.

“And command the people and say: ‘Prepare provisions for yourselves, for after the third day you shall cross the Jordan and enter to possess the land which the Lord our God is about to give you.’” Command, I say: use the authoritative freedom of the Spirit. For where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom: freedom that flatters no one’s beauty and fears no one’s ferocity.

“Prepare provisions for yourselves”: provide fruits worthy of repentance; store up faith; gather hope; lay up charity for yourselves. For these are provisions for eternal life.

“After the third day you shall cross the Jordan”: that is, according to the business or work of the third day, you shall cross from death to life, from enemy to friend, from the devil to God. I rose on the third day from the dead; therefore, you who have been baptized into my death by a threefold immersion, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, shall walk in newness of life, just as I rose from the dead through the glory of the Father (Rom. 6).

“Command these things to the people,” he says; “say these things; and in commanding and saying these things, pass swiftly onward.”

## Chapter IX. Who the Reubenites and Gadites are, to whom the Saviour commands: “But you shall cross armed before your brothers”

To the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua also said: “Remember the word which Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded you, saying: ‘The Lord your God has given you rest and all the land. Your wives, daughters, and livestock shall remain in the land which Moses gave you beyond the Jordan. But you shall cross armed before your brothers, all strong in hand, and fight for them,’” and so forth.

Some teachers wish to understand the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh in this way, as resembling the Jews: because they chose to live on this side of the Jordan—that is, not to receive Christ’s faith or baptism—and yet go before us girded and armed and fight for us, carrying with them through all lands the books of the Law and the Prophets, by whose testimony the Christian faith is everywhere demonstrated and defended.

But how the Saviour could grant or indeed command this to them, or how they could answer, “We shall do all that you have commanded us, and wherever you send us we shall go; as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we shall obey you,” does not belong to ecclesiastical exposition.

Therefore, the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh, who already received allotted possessions before crossing the Jordan, before entering the land of promise, mystically signify ecclesiastical orders. In this present world and life they receive lawful means, granted them by the Gospel, so that they may proclaim God’s word more diligently and as a duty; so that they may be free for evangelizing; so that they may delight to proclaim Christ not only for hope of future things, but also for the sake of present realities.

Therefore he says: “Remember the word which Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded you.” Remember the word; remember your profession; remember the Law and your obligation; remember your office or purpose. For woe to you if you do not fight, because you have already received the wages of battle; if you do not proclaim the Gospel, though you live by the Gospel.

“Cross armed before your brothers, all strong in hand, and fight for them”: armed, I say, in word and deed, and strong in hand, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, you yourselves should become reprobate (1 Cor. 9).

## Chapter X. That Joshua sent out spies although he was certain of God’s power; and what was prefigured by them, and by the prostitute who received and saved them
(CAP. II.) Therefore Joshua son of Nun sent secretly from Shittim two men as scouts, and said to them: “Go and inspect the land and the city of Jericho.” They went and entered the house of a harlot named Rahab, and rested there. The Lord was with Joshua, to whom He had said: “No one shall be able to withstand you all the days of your life.” Yet he himself sends scouts to inspect the land and the city of Jericho. Therefore no one, in any undertaking, should presume so greatly upon heavenly assistance [Col. 1008C] that he does not first also assist himself, watching according to the capacity of his intelligence and labouring according to the measure of his strength. For, just as it is a sign of little faith to doubt the divine promises, so it is a mark of excessive rashness or presumption to await heavenly aid by miracles while idly sitting with folded hands. It belongs to man to begin, but to God to bring to completion.

But to continue the mysteries we have begun: “They entered,” he says, “the house of a harlot named Rahab, and rested with her.” This harlot, notable for her faith and famous in memory, signifies the Church gathered and yet to be gathered from among the Gentiles—by her name and manner of life, but especially by this present deed. By her name, certainly: for *Rahab* is interpreted “breadth” or “expanse.” And it is certain that [Col. 1008D] the holy catholic Church has spread most widely throughout the whole world. By her life: for just as this harlot prostituted herself to many men, so the Gentile world, which is now the Church, was the base brothel of many gods. By her present deed: for just as she received into her house the scouts sent by Joshua, so the Church has received the apostles, or all preachers sent by the Saviour, cherished them with hospitality, and preserved them by faith.

Thus Joshua, he says, sent two scouts, saying: “Go, inspect the land and the city of Jericho.” *Jericho* is interpreted “defect” or “moon.” It signifies this world, subject to change and decay, as the Saviour Himself testified in the Gospel parable: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” [Col. 1009A] (Luke 10), and so forth. The two male scouts signify all preachers of the Gospel, walking in the two commandments of love; or those who receive the two Testaments, Old and New, and speak nothing outside them. They are rightly called scouts sent by the Saviour to explore the entire land and city of Jericho, since they went forth cautious and discerning against the wisdom—or rather the deceit and empty philosophy—of the world: cautious, I say, not with human cunning, but with the Spirit of God, the Spirit of manifold wisdom, discerning, subtle, eloquent, mobile, to destroy the wisdom of the wise and to catch the wise in their own cunning.

That harlot received such scouts, and, when they had entered her house, they rested with her. Beaten in councils, wearied in councils, suffering persecution [Col. 1009B] from city to city (2 Cor. 11), they rested with her; and she refreshed their inmost being by opening to them her door, receiving the word of salvation, and offering to the messengers of peace the open hearing of faith. Before they entered her house, before she gave rest to the feet of those entering and bringing peace, the harlot was a brothel of demons, a house of prostitution for idols. But once they had entered and she received them, she was already chaste: already the virgin bride of one husband, one beloved, one dove (Song 6), one undefiled, one perfect.

## CHAPTER XI. On the lie by which she was nevertheless justified; how the king of Jericho signifies the devil, and those whom he sent to Rahab signify persecutors of Christians; and how Christians may lawfully flee in persecution.

It was reported to the king of Jericho and said: “Behold, men from among the children of Israel entered here by night to spy out the land.” And the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying: “Bring out the men who came to you and entered your house. For they are scouts and have come to inspect the whole land.”

To those who raise the question of lying and think that this woman was not free from fault when she took the men and hid them, saying, “I confess that they came to me, but I did not know whence they were; and when the gate was shut in the darkness, they also went out together. I do not know where they went. Pursue them quickly, and you will catch them”—the first answer must be that she was justified even by this lie. For [Col. 1009D] the apostle James says: “Likewise also Rahab the harlot—was she not justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?” (James 2).

Certainly no one can doubt that no one can be justified by a lie, whose father is the devil. Yet she was justified by this lie, as has already been said. Therefore this too must be confidently maintained: that what is not contrary to God’s truth ought not to be called a lie; indeed, whatever cannot be said—even truthfully—while preserving love cannot pertain to God’s truth. But this has been discussed elsewhere.

Spiritually, it was reported to the king of Jericho that scouts sent by Joshua had come when it became evident in fact to the devil, prince of this world, that preachers of the Gospel sent by the Saviour had come against his dominion, the powers of the air, and the kingdom of darkness. [Col. 1010A] (CAP. III.) This, I say, was reported to him when he began to be cast out from human hearts and from the temples and images of the Gentiles.

Therefore this king sent—this king, I say, of the children of pride, and king of Jericho, that is, of folly. Who are, or who were, the envoys of this king? First Nero, the principal executioner of the devil-king; then Domitian; then Trajan; then all the rest: rulers indeed among men, but attendants of demons; ruling the world, but obeying the devil. Sent by their king—sent, that is, inspired by the devil—they said to Rahab, to the Church, now spread throughout the Roman world and having received Christ’s apostles in the one house of faith: “Bring out the men who came to you and [Col. 1010B] entered your house.” They said this through edicts, new laws, proscriptions, swords, and diverse kinds of torture. For when by every means of persecution and killing they sought to uproot Christ’s name and faith in His apostles, they were compelling the men to be brought out who had come to her and entered her house.

But she never consented to such demands. Rather, where she could not preserve both sides, she hid the pearl of faith and exposed her own life instead. Nor only this: according also to the historical example of this woman, wherever circumstance or reason required, she sent forth the Saviour’s messengers whom she had received, that they might flee by another way. Indeed, even the most faithful commanders of armies have not thereby incurred a stain upon their glory whenever, deceiving persecutors by stratagem, they fled from place to place.

For where the persecutor attacks Christ’s whole household and rages like a wolf or lion against the entire flock, there the shepherd must not flee after casting aside his arms; rather, he must stand as a companion in danger even unto death and lay down his life for the sheep. But where a robber or executioner seeks the shepherd alone, there he rightly seeks the protection of flight, according to Gospel authority: “When they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10). Thus at Damascus, when the governor of King Aretas guarded the city in order to seize Paul, because Paul alone was sought, the brethren lowered him [Col. 1010C] down the wall in a basket, and so he escaped his hands (2 Cor. 11; Acts 9). Where the universal persecution of raging Nero sought the life both of the shepherd himself and of the sheep, there he sought neither window, nor rope, nor basket, but gladly poured out his blood and died for the Saviour as an example to the sheep.

## CHAPTER XII. On the faith of Rahab, that is, of the Church, according to the mystery; on her house; on the meaning of her scarlet sign; and on the meaning of all her kindred.

Those who were hidden had not yet fallen asleep; and behold, the woman went up to them and said: “I know that the Lord has given you the land. For terror of you has fallen upon us, and all the inhabitants of the land have grown faint. We have heard that the Lord dried up the waters of the Red Sea at your entrance, when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were [Col. 1011A] beyond the Jordan, Sihon and Og, whom you slew,” and so forth.

So also today the wise and prudent woman speaks; so the faithful Church altogether still believes in heart and confesses with mouth. “We have heard,” she says, “and believe; therefore we also speak” (2 Cor. 4): “O holy apostles, we have heard that at your entrance, in your days, when you entered into life, He conquered the spiritual Pharaoh, that is, the devil, and drowned him in the waters of the Red Sea—by the blood and water which flowed from His side in His Passion. Thus you came forth from Egypt, thus you were called out of the darkness of his kingdom into marvellous light” (1 Pet. 2).

“Now therefore swear to me by the Lord that, as I have shown mercy to you, so you also will show it.” To this they replied: “We shall be free from this oath by which you have adjured us, if, when we enter the land, this scarlet cord shall be a sign, and you bind it in the window through which you sent us away, and gather your father and mother, brothers, and all your kindred into your house. Whoever goes out through the door of your house, his blood shall be upon his own head, and we shall be free.”

Mindful of this passage, we sing to our King; we sing wisely to our Saviour: “Her foundations are upon the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things have been spoken of you, O city of God” [Col. 1011B] (Ps. 86). For the psalm proceeds to explain what those glorious things are: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me” (ibid.).

Therefore Rahab, mystically, is Zion itself, whose gates the Lord loves; she is the city of God, of which glorious things have been spoken: the city, that is, the Church of God, worthy of God’s remembrance. Moreover, her foundations are the scouts themselves whom she received: they are bishops, apostles, whom she hid, upon whom she rests wholly as the foundations of her faith. She says: “Now therefore swear to me by the Lord that, as I have shown mercy to you, so you will also show it to me, that you may rescue my soul from death.”

That is to say: “Now therefore call over me the name of the Lord—the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so that, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of His majesty, and you too sit upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19), “you may save me from eternal condemnation; and as [Col. 1011C] I received you into my temporal dwelling, so may you receive me into your eternal dwellings” (Luke 16).

“We shall be free from this oath by which you have adjured us, if, when we enter the land, this scarlet cord is a sign,” and so forth. For she had asked for a sign, saying: “Give me a true sign that you will save my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and everything belonging to them, that you may rescue our souls from death.” This sign—the scarlet cord to be bound in the window—is the title of the Lord’s Passion, to be continually depicted before the Church’s eyes. The scarlet cord, I say, is the bloody seal of the cross, to be continually marked upon her forehead. What other sign could the Church, wisely providing for herself, rightly request?

Thus they say: “We shall be free from this oath”—that is, “we willingly bind ourselves by the oath with which you have adjured us on this condition: that if, when we enter the land—if, when the Saviour comes for judgment with all the elders of His people—this sign appears in you, we shall be bound by our oath and promise, so that our life shall be for yours unto death, and we shall be obliged to show mercy and truth toward you.” [Col. 1012A]

Meanwhile, gather your father and mother, brothers, and all your kindred into your house, so that your house may be one through faith. For whoever goes out through the door of your house—whoever cuts himself off from the unity of faith and makes heresies and schisms—his blood shall be upon his own head, and we shall be free.

These, therefore, are the glorious things spoken of the city of God, Joshua—that is, the Saviour—confirming these sayings and declaring: “I shall remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me”; with the implication that Joshua says: “Let Rahab the harlot alone live, with all who are with her in the house” (Josh. 6). But who are those kindred who are in this house? “Behold,” they say, “foreigners, and Tyre, and the people of the Ethiopians: these were there” (Ps. 86). *Tyre* is interpreted “narrowness.” Therefore all who are strangers to God’s worship, all oppressed by sins, all Ethiopians—that is, darkened by vices—become kindred and brothers by coming into the one house; and all are saved through the one scarlet cord, through the sign of Christ’s cross and Passion.

## CHAPTER XIII. [Col. 1012C] How, according to history, the saying “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you” was confirmed; and what it mystically means that “the lower waters of the Jordan went down and the upper waters stood still.”

(CAP. III.) Therefore all the people came out from their tents to cross the Jordan, and the priests carrying the ark of the covenant went before them. When they came to the Jordan and their feet were dipped in part of the water—for the Jordan had filled the banks of its channel at harvest time—the descending waters stood in one place; swelling like a mountain, they appeared from afar, from the city called Adam as far as the place Sarthan. But the waters below went down into the sea of the wilderness, now called the Dead Sea, until they wholly failed.

According to the letter, if perhaps you ask what the Lord intended when He said: “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you” (Josh. 1), and again: “Today I shall begin to exalt you before all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I am with you” (Exod. 14)—here you have it. Just as He was with Moses, so that when Moses raised his rod over the sea, the Lord removed it by a mighty wind blowing and burning through the whole night, turned it into dry land, and divided the waters; and when the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea, the water stood as a wall on their right and left—so now divine power, employing the same element for its service, divides the Jordan for the people as they proceed, while the priests carrying the ark of the Lord’s covenant stand upon dry ground. [Col. 1012D]

But according to the Spirit, here is one greater than Moses: behold, the Lord was more with Joshua than with Moses. In what respect? Namely, in that the descending waters stood in one place; while the lower waters, he says, went down into the sea of the wilderness, which is now called the Dead Sea, until they wholly failed.

The lower waters were the justifications of the Old Testament, concerning which the Apostle, after saying, “What is becoming old and growing aged is near to vanishing away” (Heb. 8), immediately added: “Indeed, the former also had ordinances of worship and an earthly sanctuary. For the first tabernacle was made” (Heb. 9), and so forth. But the descending and following waters are evangelical faith, the righteousness of God.

The lower waters went down into the sea of the wilderness, into the Dead Sea, and wholly failed, because the justifications of the flesh, the justifications of the Jews, all their carnal ceremonies—which brought no one to perfection (ibid.)—came to nothing like water running away (Ps. 57); indeed they are to be regarded as loss and reckoned as dung (Phil. 3). Thus they went down into the Dead Sea.

But the waters which follow, descending and coming from above, are living waters, the waters of heavenly grace [Col. 1013A] (James 1). Descending, I say, from above, from the Father of lights: behold, standing in one place, they swelled like a mountain, appearing from afar from the city called Adam as far as the place Sarthan. *Adam* is interpreted “red”; *Sarthan*, “their tribulation.” Adam, therefore—that is, the red one—is Jerusalem in the land itself; whence, according to the prophet (Isa. 63), this fair and true Joshua comes with garments dyed. But Sarthan—that is, “their tribulation”—is the Roman Empire, by which that Jerusalem was afflicted unto ruin, pitiably indeed, or rather deservedly.

From that Jerusalem to the Roman Empire, the descending waters of the Jordan appeared, swelling like a mountain. For beginning at Jerusalem, the gifts of the Lord—namely repentance and remission of sins—came even into the heart of the city of Rome. Therefore, as was said before, God is more with this Joshua than He was with Moses, and He exalted this leader and saviour before all Israel more highly than the other.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the twelve stones taken from the Jordan’s channel, and the other twelve placed in the midst of the Jordan: how these were a type of the prophets and apostles.

(CAP. IV.) The children of Israel did as Joshua commanded them, carrying twelve stones from the midst of the Jordan’s channel, as the Lord had commanded him, according to the number of the children of Israel, to the place where they encamped; and there they placed them. Joshua also placed another twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan’s channel, where the priests carrying the ark of the covenant stood; and they remain there to the present day.

These stones were ordered to be placed as foundations of useful remembrance. For why was this commanded by the Lord and done in this way? “When,” He says, “your children tomorrow ask you, saying, ‘What do these stones mean?’ you shall answer them: ‘The waters of the Jordan failed before the ark [Col. 1014A] of the covenant of the Lord our God when it crossed it. Therefore these stones were placed as a memorial for the children of Israel for ever.’”

Nor could those stones in the middle of the Jordan’s channel preserve or declare the memory of so great an event any less than the exceedingly hard stones laid upon dry ground; for they had been nourished beneath the waters and worn smooth by their long use. Even if they may sometimes be hidden beneath rising waters, yet the torrents, provoked by striking against them—as is natural with flowing waters—will always run there more strongly and impetuously, never allowing their obstacle to remain concealed.

Spiritually, the great apostles and prophets are for us living stones, who bear our faith as its foundation and continually bring before us, by deeds and words, the necessary remembrance of the Lord’s works. Hence the Apostle says: “You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2). The prophets, indeed, because they contain deeper or more obscure mysteries, lie hidden as though beneath the waters in the middle of the Jordan’s channel. But the apostles, because they testify to the Saviour’s works with unveiled and open face, stand openly before all eyes like stones placed at Gilgal, which is interpreted “revelation.” In both places there is great and evident testimony: good and delightful to believing Gentiles or Jews, sad and fearsome to unbelievers. [Col. 1014B]

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 1014C] On the reason for the circumcision, and on what may have prevented the people born during the forty years’ journey from being circumcised.

(CAP. V.) At that time the Lord said to Joshua: “Make yourself stone knives and circumcise the children of Israel a second time.” Joshua did as the Lord commanded, and circumcised the children of Israel at the hill of foreskins. This, moreover, is the reason for the second circumcision: all the male people who had come out of Egypt—all the men fit for war—died in the wilderness during the very long circuits of the journey, and they had all been circumcised. But the people born in the wilderness during the forty years’ journey through the vast desert remained uncircumcised until those who had not obeyed the Lord’s voice were consumed.

There is a proper question to be raised at this point. Moses surely could not have been ignorant of what he had written—namely, that God said to Abraham: “The male whose foreskin is not circumcised shall have that soul cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17). It has already been said in its place how necessary this remedy of circumcision was before Christ’s coming, and on what basis it ought to have continued until that coming, but afterwards to have ceased.

How then did he permit the people born in the wilderness to remain uncircumcised for so long—that is, for forty years—especially since countless little children could have died amid so great a multitude and thus, because they were uncircumcised, perished from their peoples? What, then, shall we say in order to excuse holy Moses, leader and prince of the people, from so harsh a neglect? Might it perhaps be permissible to affirm that, among God’s other wonders, this too could wonderfully have happened: that none of the children who succeeded their circumcised fathers died during the forty years of the vast wilderness? [Col. 1015A]

For Moses says to them: “The Lord led you forty years through the wilderness; your garments have not worn out, nor have the sandals upon your feet been consumed by age” (Deut. 29). If He deigned to take care that their garments should not wear out and their sandals should not be consumed by age, how much more ought we to believe that He took care that none of them died an untimely death? Otherwise, how will what the same man says in the Song stand: “He led him about, taught him, and guarded him as the pupil of His eye” (Deut. 32)?

Yet there was transgression even in this: that they were not circumcised at the proper time. For in the first circumcision—that is, when He first established the rite of circumcision—the Lord said: “The infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you” (Gen. 17). Whom, therefore, will Scripture seem to blame when it says: “Their sons succeeded in their fathers’ place, and Joshua circumcised them, because when they were born they were uncircumcised, and no one had circumcised them on the journey”? Perhaps it blames not Moses himself, but their fathers—the rebellious and unbelieving ones—because, tearing themselves apart in rebellious impatience on account of the forty years’ delay, and increasingly resisting the Lord’s commands, they were unwilling even to circumcise 365 their own sons.

For He says to them through the prophet: “Did you offer me victims or sacrifice in the wilderness for forty years, O house of Israel?” [Col. 1015C] (Amos 5). The implication is: No, but to your demons. For it continues: “You bore the tabernacle of your Moloch and the image of your idols, the star of your god which you made for yourselves.” Therefore, those who offered victims or sacrifices not to God but to their idols—what wonder if they did not circumcise their sons either?

Thus, where it now says, “when they were born they were uncircumcised, and no one circumcised them on the journey,” it must be understood as due not to Moses’ negligence but to the obstinacy of the rebellious fathers. “And this,” he says, “is the reason for the second circumcision,” that is, for the circumcision to be commanded or instituted a second time. For it was first given by command to Abraham; now it is commanded a second time to Joshua. This expression serves to commend circumcision, showing that it was now to be seriously observed: it had once been given by the Lord and, having lapsed, was again confirmed by His ordinance.

## CHAPTER XVI. How, spiritually, the second circumcision for us will be the resurrection of the flesh; how the first is now performed in Christ’s baptism; and how Christ is the stone knife.

But spiritually, the reason for our second circumcision is likewise this. In believing in Christ and being baptized, we have been circumcised with the first circumcision, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “In Christ you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hands, in putting off the body of flesh, in Christ’s circumcision; buried with Him in baptism, in which you also rose again through faith in the working of God, who raised Him from the dead” [Col. 1016A] (Col. 2).

He said this in Christ’s Gospel not without the testimony of the law and prophets. For the law says: “The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your seed, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and all your soul, that you may live” (Deut. 30). And the prophet says: “Be circumcised to the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Jer. 4).

We have therefore been circumcised with the first circumcision and raised in the first resurrection, buried with Christ in baptism and stripped of works of the flesh: “In which,” he says, “you also rose through faith in God.” Therefore, as stated before, this is the reason for our second circumcision. We all, the people of God’s possession, born—or rather reborn—under Christ’s grace, throughout this whole period of our journey through the vast wilderness, that is, the life of the present age, have indeed been circumcised with the first circumcision already discussed; but we have not yet been circumcised with the second circumcision. For we have indeed been renewed in the spirit of our mind, but in body or flesh we are still old and daily grow older; that is, we are still corruptible and mortal, and in living we advance daily more and more toward death.

Hence the same Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification” [Col. 1016B] (Rom. 8). Therefore the Lord says to Joshua—that is, God the Father says to our Saviour at that resurrection of which we have spoken: “Make yourself stone knives and circumcise the children of Israel a second time.” The Saviour will do what is commanded, and will circumcise the children of Israel at the hill of foreskins, that is, in the resurrection of the dead.

For at the sounding of the trumpet the dead will rise incorruptible, and, says the Apostle, “we shall be changed. For we shall all rise,” he says, “but we shall not all be changed.” Explaining what it is to be changed, he says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15). Not all shall be changed by this transformation; only the elect shall rise to impassibility.

The stone knife by which we have already once been circumcised in the first resurrection, and by which we are to be circumcised a second time in the second circumcision—that is, in the resurrection of the flesh—is the Word of God: the Word of God, I say, “living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword” [Col. 1016C] (Heb. 4). By His power we shall rise; by His efficacy we shall be stripped of all corruption. Therefore the stone knife is Christ, for Christ is the Word of God; and Christ Himself is called stone or rock.

## CHAPTER XVII. When the children of Israel entered the promised land, manna ceased: what this mystically signifies.

And the manna ceased after they had eaten of the produce of the land; the children of Israel used that food no longer, but ate of the produce of the land of Canaan in that present year.

The manna by which we are fed in the wilderness of this present age, until we come to the blessed homeland where we shall feast and exult in the sight or presence of God and delight in joy, is the Word of God, Holy Scripture. Moses briefly indicates this when, after saying, “The Lord afflicted you with want and gave you manna for food, which neither you nor your fathers knew,” he immediately adds: “That He might show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” [Col. 1017A] (Deut. 8).

In order that man might eat this manna, this bread of angels, God once opened the gates of heaven so that He might send it, made flesh, into our earth, and make it edible also for us little ones, almost toothless, though until then it had been the customary food of angels alone. Hence He says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6), and so forth.

Moreover, whenever the Holy Spirit opens the mouths of apostles, prophets, or teachers to preach the word of salvation and reveal the mysteries of Scripture, the Lord opens the gates of heaven and rains manna upon us to eat (Ps. 77). So long as we proceed through this wilderness of the present age, so long as we walk by faith and not by sight, we certainly need these foods. Our minds are fed by reading or hearing the Word of God; and our mouths are fed by eating from the Lord’s table the bread of eternal life and drinking the cup of everlasting salvation.

But when we come to that land of the living, to that blessed Zion where God of gods shall be seen in His own form (Ps. 83), we shall need neither the word of teaching nor these forms of bread and wine; but, beholding the bread of angels in its own substance, we shall eat it. Therefore, after they ate the produce of the land, manna ceased: because, when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial shall be abolished [Col. 1017B] (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XVIII. What it mystically signifies that He who appeared to Moses in the flame of fire was the same one who appeared to Joshua holding a sword.

When Joshua was in the field of the city of Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, holding a drawn sword. He went to him and said: “Are you one of us or of our adversaries?” He said: “Neither. But I am the commander of the Lord’s army, and now I have come.”

According to the historical sense, just as the crossing of the Jordan, so also this belongs to the promise which was spoken: “As I was with Moses, so I shall be with you.” And further: “Today I shall begin to exalt you before all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I am with you.”

For the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of the bush; but to Joshua He appears standing as a warrior and holding a drawn sword, showing to each figures or forms suited to the character of the events that followed. To Moses, who was to perform splendid miracles, fire appeared, as has already been said: “I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt,” He says, “and have heard their cry, and have come down to deliver them.” But to Joshua, who was soon to wage bloody wars, He appears holding a drawn sword, saying: “I am the commander [Col. 1017D] of the Lord’s army, and now I have come.”

To each He commends the great safeguard of humility, without which no one ever approaches the Lord—both to this one and to that: “Remove your sandal from your foot, for the place on which you stand is holy” (Exod. 3).

But now, to continue the mystery begun: there the first, here the second coming of our Saviour is prefigured. For after the children of Israel have been circumcised a second time, He is present holding a drawn sword as commander of the Lord’s army, because, when we are changed by the second circumcision—that is, the resurrection of bodies—the hand of the Lord will take up judgment, and Christ the Son of God will appear as judge of living and dead. Concerning this very sword He says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “If I whet my sword as lightning, and my hand takes hold of judgment, I shall render vengeance to my enemies” [Col. 1018A] (Deut. 32).

Nor will He alone be commander of the Lord’s army: the elders of His people themselves, with whom He will come to judgment, will have judicial swords in their hands. Hence the Psalmist sings: “The exaltations of God are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands” (Ps. 149). The nations upon which vengeance is to be executed, or the peoples among whom rebukes are to be made, are signified by the city of Jericho, of which he immediately goes on to speak.

## CHAPTER XIX. What it mystically means for Jericho to be shut up, to be encircled once on each day and seven times on the seventh day, and for that city to fall utterly when the trumpets sound.

(CAP. VI.) Now Jericho was shut up and fortified through fear of the children of Israel, and no one dared either to go out or to enter. And the Lord said to Joshua: “Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, together with its king and all its mighty men. March around the city, all you warriors, once each day. You shall do this for six days; but on the seventh day let the priests take seven trumpets, whose use is in the Jubilee, and go before the ark of the covenant; and you shall march around the city seven times,” etc.

Great and beautiful is this mystery; great and fearful is the judgment of this world within the mystery. “When,” he says, “the sound of the trumpet, prolonged and broken, has resounded and rebuked your ears, all the people shall cry out with a great shout, and the walls of the city shall utterly collapse.” So it happened. After the voice and sound had struck the ears of the multitude, the walls immediately fell, and each man went up by the place opposite him.

Here Jericho mystically signifies the city of the devil, [Col. 1018D] always hostile to the city of the living God, Jerusalem. Holy Scripture is accustomed also to call it Babylon, as in the Psalm mentioned above: “I will be mindful of Rahab and Babylon” (Ps. 86). That is, I will remember Rahab for good, but Babylon for evil: Rahab, that she alone may live with all who are with her in the house through faith; Babylon for evil, namely that her walls may utterly fall, and that she herself, with all that is in her, may be anathema.

Why, then, must the city be marched around once a day for six days, but seven times on the seventh day? Clearly because the city of the devil must be judged both on account of the creation of the world, by which it could have known the Creator, and on account of the coming of the Son of God, whom it does not receive. The circuit of the six days signifies judgment for the sixfold creation. For all these things were created in six days. The Apostle, after saying that what may be known of God is manifest among them, because God has made it manifest to them, immediately adds: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived through the things that have been made—his eternal power also and divinity—so that they are without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1), etc.

Therefore the hostile city is to be encircled once on each of the six days, because human ungodliness—of those who did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge—is to be judged for the creation of the world which they understood. But on the seventh day—that is, far more and in every respect more greatly—they are to be judged [Col. 1019B] for the coming of the Son of God, because they did not receive him. “Have they not heard? Indeed, their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Rom. 10), etc. They heard through the heavens declaring, and saw his tent set in the sun: “there is none who can hide himself from its heat” (Ps. 18). This was said as wonderfully as it was truly: the coming of the Son of God was no more hidden from them than this sun, which is seen by all. For this, I say, they are to be judged more severely, and for this they will be much more without excuse.

Therefore this too was rightly said and done: whereas on each of the other days the city was encircled once, on the seventh day it was encircled seven times. For the seventh day, on which God rested from all the work that he had accomplished—as we said more fully at the beginning of this work—is the Son of God himself, whose coming will be judgment for them. Thus the king of the city, the devil, will be cast down before the eyes of all, and its walls will utterly collapse amid weeping, as we have more fully in the Apocalypse; and all who committed fornication with her will mourn and say: “Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that mighty city, because in one hour your judgment has come.” And again, a second time: “Woe, woe, that great city, which was clothed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls, because in one hour such great riches have been laid waste.” And then, a third time: “Woe, woe, great city, by whose wealth all who have ships at sea became rich, because in one hour she has been made desolate” (Apoc. 18).

## CHAPTER XX. How Joshua, contemplating the divine judgment, anathematized the city and cursed him who would rebuild its walls.

At that time Joshua pronounced an oath, saying: “Cursed before the Lord be the man who raises up and builds the city of Jericho. In his firstborn let him lay its foundations, and in the last of his children let him set up its gates.”

He said two things: first, “Let this city be anathema, with all that is in it”; then, “Cursed before the Lord be the man who raises up the city of Jericho.” He said these two things, I say, not in bitter anger, nor through the motion of his own mind, but through contemplation of the divine judgment he condemned the sinful city hated by God. Indeed, [Col. 1020A] the divine testimony immediately followed his sentence in both respects.

For, not to mention that the walls fell utterly by God’s mere nod and without human hands, Achan, son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, by taking something from the anathema troubled all Israel, while the Lord cried out terribly: “The anathema is in your midst, Israel. You will not be able to stand before your enemies until the one defiled by this crime is removed from among you” (Josh. 7).

Likewise, he who raised up and built the city of Jericho, just as Joshua had cursed, laid its foundations in his firstborn and set up its gates in the last of his children. Thus we have in the Third Book of Kings: “In the days of Ahab, Hiel of Bethel built Jericho; in Abiram his firstborn he founded it, and in Segub his last son he set up its gates, according to the word of the Lord, which he had spoken through Joshua son of Nun” (3 Kings 16).

Certainly, the statement, “In his firstborn he founded it, and in his last son he set up its gates,” means the same as if it were said: when he laid its foundations, his firstborn son immediately died; then, as he continued building, all his sons died one by one according to the order of their birth, until, at the final stage of the work, when he set up its gates, his youngest son died. Such astonishing ambition sustained his obstinacy that, while he ambitiously sought the builder’s name, he utterly lost the honor of a father.

## CHAPTER XXI. How, in the vengeance carried out in Israel because of the anathema stolen by Achan, an example was established against avarice.

Why was vengeance taken upon them with such severity of heavenly judgment, except that fear might be established for future ages by their example? For it was to come about—as we see today—that the Church of God would be greatly disturbed by the avarice and ambition alike of false brethren. For what? Have not all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus anathematized Jericho—that is, this world—by renouncing the devil and all his pomps?

But behold, very many imitators of Achan from the tribe of Judah have gone out from among us. Though professing the Catholic faith—which is what it means to be, or to be called, of the tribe of Judah, since *Judah* is interpreted “confession”—they have taken from this anathema: they have stolen, lied, hidden it, and placed it among their vessels. For while, under a show of piety, they conduct themselves beautifully and religiously but pursue avarice, which is the service of idols (Eph. 5), and put every work of spiritual wickedness up for sale, what else do they do but steal the anathema, lie, and hide it among their vessels—or rather, among their consciences?

The whole Church of Christ first terribly anathematizes this root of wickedness and bitterness of gall in Simon Magus, through the mouth of the blessed Apostle Peter, and declares it to be a heretical water-jar. Therefore, says the Lord, “Israel will not be able to stand before its enemies, but will flee from them, because it has been defiled by the anathema.” For where avarice reigns among priests or those set over others, and money holds preeminence, those who are Israel—bearing the weapons of virtues against vices and wishing, as they ought, to rebuke and exhort—cannot stand against enemies in free resistance. For money protects those enemies, so that they may not even be rebuked with impunity for their vices.

Hence we retain in the Evangelist Matthew this beautiful mystery: when our Lord, having made a scourge from cords, drove sellers and buyers from the temple, only then did the blind and lame come to him in the temple, and he healed them (Matt. 21). He did not first heal the blind and lame before driving those robbers out of the den, because vices cannot be healed, nor virtues made bright, unless Mammon is first expelled from the hearts of priests—or the priests themselves, together with that god of theirs, are expelled from the temple of God.
