This, I say, was to come about; and therefore it was useful to prefigure in that one Achan what disturbance or punishment was reserved for all his imitators, according to his name, which is interpreted “tumult” or “troubler.” Rightly, then, was severe vengeance taken upon him without any pardon for such theft: all Israel stoned him, and everything belonging to him was consumed by fire. Joshua spoke beforehand, saying: “Because you have troubled us, may the Lord trouble you this day” (Josh. 7).

For although, when Joshua said, “My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel; confess and tell me what you have done; do not hide it,” he replied in confession: “Truly I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel, and I have done thus,” he nevertheless deserved no pardon, because his confession was excessively late. Israel had been troubled before he acknowledged his guilt; and the truthful lot, by God’s agency, exposed the man before he himself exposed the crime.

## CHAPTER XXII. Why it was the Lord’s judgment that all the kings should fight against Israel and fall in battle; and how that slaughter, and the day prolonged while the sun stood still, signify the long day of judgment.

(CAP. IX.) “When they heard these things, all the kings beyond the Jordan who lived in the mountains, the plains, the maritime regions, and along the shore of the great sea, together with those dwelling near Lebanon—the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite—gathered together to fight against Joshua and Israel with one mind and one purpose,” etc.

All gathered together under the leadership of their sin in order to perish, because it was the Lord’s judgment that their hearts should be hardened, that they should fight against Israel and fall, and that they should deserve no mercy. Why was this the Lord’s judgment? Clearly because they were so wicked and so sinful that the land itself deservedly vomited them out.

For after he had said, “Whoever lies with a beast or livestock shall surely die; a woman who submits herself to any beast shall be killed together with it” (Lev. 20)—after, I say, he had said these and similar things, he added: “Lest the land into which you are entering to inhabit it vomit you out also. Do not walk in the statutes of the nations whom I am about to expel before you. For they have done all these things, and I have abhorred them” (ibid.).

Justly, then, was it the Lord’s judgment that their hearts should be hardened, that they should fight, and that they should deserve no mercy, as the Lord had commanded Moses. For what had the Lord commanded Moses? “When,” he says, “you approach to besiege a city, first offer it peace. But if they refuse to make a treaty” (Deut. 20), etc. And further: “But of these cities which are given to you, you shall permit none at all to live; but you shall kill by the edge of the sword the Hittite, Amorite, Canaanite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite, as the Lord your God commanded you, lest perhaps they teach you to do all the abominations which they performed for their gods, and you sin against the Lord your God” (ibid.).

Yet for people it was too little that so great a victor, 368 who spared not even the dead, but commanded even the necks of the dead to be trodden underfoot and the dead to be hung upon gibbets, should be excused from cruelty by the stated testimony or command of the Law, unless he were also defended in the present instance by a new and unheard-of miracle of the just God.

(CAP. X.) “As they fled from the children of Israel and were on the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord sent great stones from heaven upon them as far as Azekah and Makkedah; and far more died from the stones of hail than the children of Israel struck with the sword. Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day when he delivered the Amorite before the children of Israel, and he said before them: ‘Sun, do not move opposite Gibeon; and moon, opposite the valley of Aijalon.’ So the sun stood in the midst of heaven and did not hasten to set for the space of one day. There was no day before or afterward so long, the Lord obeying the voice of a man and fighting for Israel.”

What, then, is in all these things except a figure or proof of the future universal judgment, when he who comes to be judged in the abundance of mercy will come to judge in the strength of justice, holding the drawn sword, as was signified above? Then indeed, with the sun standing still and not hastening to set, there will be a long day until the nation avenges itself upon its enemies.

“Is this not written,” he says, “in the book of the just?” In what book of the just, except in the whole body of holy and truthful Scriptures? For their entirety proclaims that day with dreadful announcements: a long day, a great day, a bitter day. “Near,” says the Prophet, “is the great day of the Lord; it is near and exceedingly swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; there the mighty man shall be distressed. That day is a day of wrath, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and alarm” (Zeph. 1). Truly it is a long day, truly a great day, whose magnitude the prophet cannot expound with so many words and such mighty proclamations.

## CHAPTER XXIII. In that, after the nations had been expelled, Joshua divided the land by lot with the measuring-line of distribution, it is signified that the dwelling places in the Father’s house are distributed by the grace of God and not by merits.

(CAP. XIII.) And the Lord said to Joshua: “You have grown old and are advanced in years, and a very broad land remains which has not yet been divided by lot,” etc.

Since it also proceeds from the Lord’s command that the promised land should be divided among the tribes of Israel not by human choice but by the hidden judgment of the lot, this too ought not to be thought devoid of mystery. For what is meant by the nations being expelled from before them, as the Psalmist also sings, “He divided the land among them by lot with the measuring-line of distribution” (Ps. 77), except that the blessed homeland, from which the apostate angels were expelled in their pride—all those dwelling places, which are many in the Father’s house (John 14)—is distributed by the grace of God and not by merits?

“For it is the gift of God, and not from ourselves,” says the Apostle, “lest anyone should boast” (Eph. 2). Rightly, then, was that land divided by lot, in which not human choice but God’s hidden providence accomplishes all things; for it is by God’s grace, which no merits preceded, that our land of the living is to be hoped for and possessed.

Let us now pass to the Book of Judges. Skipping over the plain and well-worn surface of the history, let us seek the venerable mystery only in those passages where the word of the Lord comes forth because of a matter or time, where something is said or done at his heavenly command.

# OF THE LORD DOM RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE TRINITY AND HIS WORKS: FORTY-TWO BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF JUDGES

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1023]

369

## CHAPTER I. That there are twelve judges up to Samuel, whence the book is called the Book of Judges.

(CHAPTER I.) After the death of Joshua, the children of Israel consulted the Lord, saying: “Who shall go up before us against the Canaanite and be leader of the war?” And the Lord said: “Judah shall go up. Behold, I have given the land into his hand,” etc.

This book is called the Book of Judges because it was written concerning those who judged Israel before the name of kings or royal power was sought among that people. The judges were twelve in number. First, Othniel son of Kenaz, brother of Caleb. Second, Ehud son of Gera, son of Benjamin. Third, Shamgar son of Anath. Fourth, Barak son of Abinoam, from Kedesh of Naphtali. Fifth, Gideon son of Joash. [Col. 1023C] Sixth, Jair the Gileadite. Seventh, Jephthah the Gileadite. Eighth, Ibzan of Bethlehem. Ninth, Elon the Zebulunite. Tenth, Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite. Eleventh, Samson. Twelfth, Samuel.

Of the first of these, Othniel, Scripture relates as follows: “And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord, who raised up for them a savior, namely Othniel son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb. And the Spirit of the Lord was in him, and he judged Israel” (Judg. 3). Since, therefore, he bears the name and performs the office of savior, and since the Spirit of the Lord was in him, it is right to seek in his person the spiritual mysteries of our Savior, Christ the Son of God. The history concerning him is as follows.

## CHAPTER II. On Othniel and his wife Achsah, daughter of Caleb: what her sitting on an ass and sighing signifies allegorically.

And Caleb said: “Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and lays it waste, to him I will give Achsah my daughter as wife.” When Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it, Caleb gave him his daughter as wife. As she was going on the journey, her husband urged her to ask her father for a field. And when she sighed while sitting on an ass, Caleb said to her: “What is the matter?” She replied: “Give me a blessing. Since you have given me dry land, give me land watered by springs also.” Therefore Caleb gave her the upper springs and the lower springs. These same things were stated by anticipation in the Book of Joshua (Josh. 15).

Now Othniel—or, more correctly, according to blessed Jerome, Athoniel—is interpreted “the time of God” or “the response of God.” It signifies the great Judge—indeed, the Savior of Israel, Christ the Son of God—whose type he was: the time of God in which he visited his people, and whose Gospel is surely the response of God. Achsah—or, more correctly, Achsaph—is interpreted “medicament”; for *Achsah* is rendered “furious woman.”

The sacramental meaning of this passage is twofold: allegorical as well as moral. For Othniel—that is, our Savior and Judge—then struck Kiriath-sepher, “the city of letters,” which had formerly been called Debir, “speaking” or “speech,” when, after the truth of the Gospel had been revealed, he rebuked the talkative synagogue of the scribes and Pharisees that gloried in the letter of the Law. For that synagogue was rightly called the city of letters, since the utterances of God were first entrusted to it (Rom. 3).

This Savior said to the scribes and Pharisees—he said it, I say, and fulfilled the saying by deed: “Amen I say to you, the kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 12). Thus he struck and condemned, in the city of letters, those who took away the key of knowledge, with the proposed reward that he might receive Achsah as his bride—that is, the new Church from among the Gentiles.

Her father became Caleb through faith, a name interpreted “as a heart”; namely God, who became to us as a heart by saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1). Hence he who became her husband, the Savior of the world, persuaded her to ask her father for a field. For he taught his Church to pray and ask God the Father for the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 6; Luke 11).

When she sighed while sitting on the ass, Caleb said to her: “What is the matter?” Achsah sits on the ass and sighs when the Church, converted to Christ, having already received the first grace—namely remission of sins—asks for the second grace, namely the illumination of the Holy Spirit and the desire for the heavenly kingdom. Hence she immediately adds: “Give me,” she says, “a blessing; since you have given me dry land, give me land watered by springs also.” For dry land is the first grace, the remission of sins, which we all alike receive in baptism; while land watered by springs is knowledge or desire of heavenly goods, which the one and same Spirit works differently in different persons, distributing to each as he wills.

## CHAPTER III. On the same matter morally: the teaching of blessed Gregory.

Moreover, in the moral sense Achsah sits upon the ass when the soul rules over the irrational motions of its flesh. [Col. 1025D] Sighing, she asks her Father for watered land, because from our Creator we must seek the grace of tears with great groaning.

For there are some who have already received the gift to speak freely for righteousness, protect the oppressed, give their possessions to the needy, and possess ardor of faith; yet they do not have the grace of tears. Such people have southern and dry land, but still need watered land. Though engaged in good works, in which they are great and fervent, they ought at least to lament the evils which they previously committed, whether from fear of punishment or from love of the heavenly kingdom.

And although compunction is divided into many forms when the several sins of the powerful are lamented—hence Jeremiah too says in the voice of penitents: “My eye has brought down streams of water” (Lam. 3)—nevertheless there are principally two kinds of compunction. The soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear and afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears because, recalling its evils, it greatly fears that it must endure eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by prolonged distress of sorrow, a certain truth is born from confidence, and the mind is inflamed with love for heavenly joys. The one who first wept lest he be led to punishment afterward weeps most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom.

For the mind contemplates the choirs of angels, the fellowship of holy spirits, and the majesty of God’s eternal vision; it laments more deeply because it lacks everlasting goods, whereas previously it had wept while fearing inward evils. Thus perfect compunction of fear delivers the mind over to compunction of love. This is fittingly described in figurative narration in this holy and true history.

Since, therefore, as I have said, there are two kinds of compunction, her father gave her the upper springs and the lower springs. The soul receives the upper springs when it afflicts itself with tears from desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives the lower springs when, in weeping, it fears the punishments of hell. The lower springs are indeed given first and the upper springs afterward; but because the compunction of love excels in dignity, the upper springs had to be mentioned first and the lower springs afterward.

## CHAPTER IV. On Barak and the prophetess Deborah, his wife, and on the identity of Lapidoth.

(CAP. IV.) The fourth of the judges now taken up by us is Barak. For in Ehud, who is the second, it is almost forced to seek a mystery or sacrament: he killed the king of Moab not so much guided by divine oracle as by human ingenuity—and indeed by deceit. Therefore he is to be called not so much sent by God as permitted by him to be a savior.

“The children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord after Ehud’s death, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. He had Sisera as commander of his army; he himself lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles. And the children of Israel cried out to the Lord. For he had nine hundred scythed chariots [Col. 1026D] and had grievously oppressed them for twenty years. Now Deborah was a prophetess, wife of Lapidoth, and she judged the people at that time. She sat under the palm which was called by her name, between Ramah and Bethel in Mount Ephraim. And the children of Israel went up to her for every judgment. She sent and called Barak son of Abinoam from Kedesh of Naphtali.”

Barak is held to have been the same person as Lapidoth, the husband of the prophetess Deborah. *Lapidoth* is interpreted “lightning,” and Barak likewise “thunderbolt.” He was called lightning because, before he avenged Israel against the Canaanites, he shone among the people like lightning through merits and the prerogatives of works; but after he avenged Israel against the Canaanites, he was called thunderbolt, that is, “one who strikes.”

The history is plain. Therefore, first briefly running through their song, let us then touch upon the beautiful mystery hidden within.

## CHAPTER V. A literal exposition of their song from blessed Jerome.

(CAP. V.) “Lord, when you went forth from Seir and passed through Edom, the earth was moved, and the heavens and clouds distilled water.”

The Lord is said to have gone forth from Seir and passed through Edom because, when the Idumeans refused to receive his Law, he gave the Law to Israel on Mount Sinai. “The earth was moved; the heavens and clouds distilled water.” The trembling of Mount Sinai is described. And when it says that the heavens and clouds distilled water, the heavens are said at the Lord’s presence to have distilled water as though, through a kind of fear, they were emitting sweat. “Likewise the mountains flowed at the presence of the Lord.” But in what follows—“and Sinai at the presence of the Lord God of Israel”—one must supply: “trembled and smoked.”

“In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the roads were at rest, and those who traveled walked by winding paths.” The roads are said to have been at rest because in the time of Shamgar, leader of Israel, the roads were occupied by Israel’s enemies, and the people did not dare to go freely up to the house of the Lord to pray. Those who traveled by them went up secretly and by winding paths out of fear of the enemies. It is not said that Shamgar completely delivered them from those enemies.

The phrase inserted somewhat above, “in the days of Jael,” must be understood thus: after Sisera had been killed by Jael, the roads were opened, and those who had previously traveled there by winding paths went to the house of the Lord without any fear. The fact that Jael or Deborah is named here is said to have been done by Deborah out of humility, because Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, killed Sisera.

“The mighty ceased in Israel; they were at rest until Deborah arose, until a mother arose in Israel.” Here he calls the teachers and preachers of the Law “mighty,” and says that they had ceased, that is, were absent, until Deborah arose to instruct Israel by preaching and exhortation and to free it from enemies by counsel.

The same Deborah also urges these mighty ones above to bless the Lord with her in these words: “You who willingly offered your lives from Israel to danger, bless the Lord.” These mighty ones, that is, the teachers, are said to have offered their lives to danger; that is, they subjected themselves to God’s Law and service and mortified body and soul in meditations day and night.

“The Lord chose new wars, and he overthrew the gates of the enemy.” How, or in what respect, were the wars new? He immediately continues and asks: “Did shield and spear appear among forty thousand in Israel?” The implied answer is: No. This is the truer reading and the truer sense, although in many manuscripts the little word *si* (“if”) is omitted and the phrase is customarily read affirmatively; this arose through scribal error.

By “shield and spear,” he should be understood as saying, as it were by oath, that among forty thousand men neither shield nor spear could be found. Therefore God is said to have chosen new wars and overthrown the gates of the enemy because he made the unarmed strong and victorious. That Israel had been stripped of weapons by Jabin king of Canaan is made clear above, where it says: “The children of Israel cried out to the Lord, for he had nine hundred scythed chariots and had grievously oppressed them for twenty years” (Judg. 5). He grievously oppressed them because he is said to have disarmed them, as is written in the Book of Samuel: “When the day of battle came, no sword or spear was found among all the people who were with Saul and Jonathan, except Saul and Jonathan his son” (1 Sam. 13).

“My heart loves the leaders of Israel.” It should be known that in Hebrew the reading is not “leaders” but “teachers.” Deborah speaks this in the person of God: God loves teachers devoted to the Law of God, of whom it is said in what follows, “You who willingly offered yourselves to danger among the people, bless the Lord.” The same men were also mentioned above where she said: “You who willingly offered your lives to danger, bless the Lord.”

“You who ride upon shining asses, who sit in judgment, and who walk on the way, speak.” Those who ride asses are said to be the people of Israel. The asses upon which they ride are the teachers of the tribes of Israel. The remaining people are said to have mounted, that is, rested, upon their teaching as upon asses.

These asses are called shining—that is, moving like the moon—while seated in the Law upon judgment, that is, upon the Law. They too are said to sit upon judgment, that is, upon the Law, and to walk in the way—the way of the Law being understood—because they did not depart from the path of the Law. Deborah therefore urges the people who rested upon these asses, that is, upon these teachers, to bless the Lord, and says: “Speak,” that is, praise.

And as if they had asked, “Where and when shall we praise the Lord?” she answers: “Where chariots were shattered and the army of the enemy was destroyed. There let the righteous acts of the Lord and the mercies of Israel’s Mighty One be recounted.” It is as though she said: Although God must always and everywhere be praised, yet he ought especially now to be praised and blessed by you, since he overthrew your enemies, as he did the Egyptians in the Red Sea (Exod. 14).

“Then the people of the Lord went down to the gates and gained dominion.” The people of the Lord went down to the gates, that is, to the gates of the Lord’s house, because, having blessed and praised the Lord at the place of victory, they went down to the house of the Lord to praise him there also, offering him prayers and sacrifices.

That teachers of the other tribes came from the tribe of Issachar is shown by the Book of Chronicles, where it says: “Of the sons of Issachar also were learned men, who marked each particular time in order to instruct Israel what they ought to do: two hundred leaders. And all the remaining tribes followed their counsel” (1 Chron. 12). And that these teachers are asses is shown in the Book of Genesis, where we read: “Issachar is a strong ass lying down between the boundaries. He saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant under tribute” (Gen. 49).

In Genesis, where the passage continues, the ass is called strong because of the strength of the Law, since he bore the Law upon his shoulder and supplied the other tribes with tribute, that is, instruction in the Law. But in the Book of Judges they are called female asses because they remained broken in strength, humbled, and weak, pressed down and humbled under the yoke of the Gentiles, and content only with the Law of God.

“Arise, arise, Deborah; arise, arise, speak a song.” It should be noted that the Hebrew reads “awake,” that is, awake in the spirit of prophecy. Therefore Deborah is urged by the voices of the aforementioned teachers to awake in the spirit of prophecy and praise and not cease from God’s praises. Hence follows: “Speak a song.”

“Arise, Barak, and seize your captives, son of Abinoam.” The Hebrew says: “Plunder your spoil, son of Ahionem.” By this saying Barak too is urged by the voices of these same teachers to plunder the remnant of his enemies, bring them utterly to destruction, and laudably acquire for himself the name of victory.

Then the remnant of the people was saved. This statement, for its interpretation, must be joined to the preceding statement, where it is said that the righteous acts of the Lord, the mercies of the mighty One of Israel, are to be recounted, because then the remnant of the people was saved. The Lord fought among the mighty. In Hebrew it reads: “The Lord fought among the mighty on my behalf,” and this is the voice of the whole people of Israel. For he fought on their behalf against the Egyptians and the other enemies of Israel. Hence it follows: From Ephraim he destroyed them in Amalek; that is, Joshua, being of the tribe of Ephraim, destroyed the mighty enemies of Israel in Amalek and its people by the edge of the sword, as is read in the book of Exodus: “Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword” (Exod. XVII). And that this same Joshua was of the tribe of Ephraim [Col. 1029C] is shown from the book of Numbers, where it says: “From the tribe of Ephraim, Hoshea son of Nun” (Num. XIII), whom it subsequently calls Joshua, saying: “Moses called Hoshea son of Nun Joshua” (Josh. VI). And after him, among your peoples, Amalek: after him—that is, after Joshua—Saul, being of the tribe of Benjamin, at the Lord’s command destroyed the people of Amalek. Deborah prophesied in the spirit of prophecy that this would happen through Saul; and this was said according to the figure called *prolepsis*, namely, that he himself would destroy Amalek, as you have in the book of Samuel (I Kings XV). But the words “O Amalek” are not found in Hebrew; the Latin translator added them for the sake of the sense.

[Col. 1029D] From Machir princes came down, and from Zebulun those who led the army into battle. In Hebrew it reads: “From Machir princes came down,” with “to battle” understood—that is, to overthrow Sisera the commander; and from Zebulun, “came down” is understood, those who led from the tribe of the scribes, that is, the tribe of Issachar; and “to battle” is understood—that is, to praise and entreat God—of whom it follows: The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah. In Hebrew: the princes, that is, the teachers of the Law, were [372] with Deborah in praising God. And they followed in Barak’s footsteps. This is to be understood as meaning that one part of them remained with Deborah to praise God, while another part followed Barak’s footsteps, to exhort the people and to fight against Sisera. He, as if headlong into an abyss, gave himself to danger. That is, Barak, [Col. 1030A] trusting the Lord’s words, gave himself to danger, hurling himself into the torrent Kishon, pursuing and defeating Sisera’s army. “Abyss” in this place is understood as the torrent Kishon.

When Reuben was divided, a contention of high-minded men was found. In Hebrew “against himself” is not present. For this is Deborah’s voice rebuking Reuben—that is, the tribe of Reuben—because, disobeying the Lord’s command, it did not go with its brothers to fight the enemies of the Lord; but, terrified by fear and disbelieving the Lord’s words, it separated itself from them and was found to be high-minded, that is, proud. Hence follows their rebuke in the spirit of prophecy:

Why do you dwell among the boundaries, to hear the bleating of the flocks? In Hebrew, not “two” but “among the [Col. 1030B] boundaries” is read; and the sense is: “O Reuben, why do you dwell—that is, why do you remain—within your boundaries, namely those of your neighboring tribes, in order to hear the bleating of the flocks?” As though one said: “You desire to keep the flocks in which you abound and fear to lose them; you take greater pleasure in hearing their bleating than in striving with your brothers to go forth against the enemies of Israel.” And because you do this, you proudly resist the Lord’s command; hence the same statement follows as above: “When Reuben was divided, a contention of high-minded men was found,” because he acted wrongly, despising the Lord’s command and behaving proudly.

Gilead rested beyond the Jordan. This too is said as a rebuke, because while Reuben delayed, Gilead remained with him in the same resolve. And Dan was occupied with ships, because, seeing that the tribe of Reuben and the [Col. 1030C] tribe of Gilead were not going with their brothers into battle, he was seized with fear and, keeping to the ships, took flight. Asher dwelt on the seashore and lingered in the harbors. Likewise this is set down as a rebuke, because Asher, dwelling on the seashore, remained in the harbors, intending rather to take flight than to fight beside his brothers. Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives to death in the region of Meron. In Hebrew: “upon the region of Meron.” The sense is that, when the other tribes refused to go, these two tribes gave their lives to death upon the region of Meron. For *Meron* means “the lofty one.” They are said to have offered their lives for the region of the Most High—that is, of God—and are therefore extolled with praise, while the other tribes are reproved.

[Col. 1030D] Kings came and fought. He means the kings of the land of Canaan who were subject to King Jabin. The kings of Canaan fought. He repeats the same point: at Taanach. Taanach is a district in which the torrent Kishon lies, near the waters of Megiddo. Megiddo is a city situated above the torrent Kishon. And when he says “near the waters of Megiddo,” it is to be understood as “near the torrent Kishon, by the city of Megiddo.” Yet they carried off no spoil. This is said mockingly, since they not only took no spoil, but were unable even to save their own lives. From heaven battle was fought against them. Because among forty thousand Israelites neither shield nor spear could be found, the Lord fought from heaven on their behalf against their enemies with hailstones and fire, as also in the book of Joshua (Josh. [Col. 1031A] X). The stars, remaining in their order and course, fought against Sisera. The stars are to be understood as angels, who fought from heaven against Sisera.

The torrent Kishon dragged away their corpses. Here there is an ellipsis, almost as if a question were being asked and the answer supplied: “into the torrent of Kadumim,” that is, into the Red Sea. Hence it follows: The torrent of Kadumim, the torrent Kishon. He calls the Red Sea the torrent of Kadumim. For *Kadumim* means “of the ancients,” because miracles were performed in it of old when the children of Israel crossed and the Egyptians perished. And because the Red Sea cast up the dead Egyptians, so that the Israelites saw them dead upon the seashore, and because these same corpses were carried off by fish and beasts of the sea, therefore the torrent Kishon dragged away their corpses, so that, in return for the Egyptian [Col. 1031B] corpses taken from it, the fish and beasts of that same Red Sea might eat the corpses of the Canaanites.

Trample down, O my soul, the mighty. Deborah says this in the person of all Israel, that all might with one mind trample the necks of their mighty—that is, their strongest—enemies, as in the book of Joshua concerning the five Canaanite kings (Josh. X). Hooves of horses. In Hebrew it is read thus: “Then the horses’ hooves fell, as they fled in their charge, and as the strongest of the enemy rushed headlong down.” For it is related that the horses’ hooves fell through hailstones from heaven, sent by angels, so that the sense is: if the horses’ hooves are believed to have fallen at the touch of stones, what do you suppose happened to the riders?

“Curse the land of Meroz,” said the angel of the Lord. In Hebrew it reads: [Col. 1031C] “Curse Meroz, says the angel of the Lord.” The angel of the Lord is understood by the Hebrews to be Michael, who commands through Deborah that the people of Israel should curse Meroz—that is, the angelic power which presided over the Canaanites. For *Meroz* means “secret.” It is therefore commanded to be cursed—that is, anathematized—because, while the other angels fought for Israel, he not only did not fight, but even persisted in opposition to them. “Curse its inhabitants,” that is, both Meroz and its people. And the reason why they are cursed is given: because they did not come to the Lord’s aid, to the help of his mighty ones.

Blessed among women is Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite—among women, namely Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah, and nearly all the other women. May she be blessed in [Col. 1031D] the tent—understood, the Lord’s tent—and may her memorial be there, as Judith’s also is. The reason why she should be blessed is properly given: because she acted wisely and prudently, in giving milk to one who asked for water. She gave milk so that the fleeing enemy might place greater trust in her. If it is asked why she did not give wine, the answer is that the household of Rechab drank no wine, as you have in Jeremiah the prophet (Jer. XXXV).

## CHAPTER VI. How Sisera mystically signifies the devil; Deborah, the Law; and Barak, whose name means “thunderbolt,” the strong men of the Law, who, using it lawfully, struck the devil mightily.

These things, spoken according to the letter, contain great mysteries of spirit and life. Sisera, indeed, commander of the [Col. 1032A] hostile army, signifies by his very name the enemy of the human race. For his name means “the vision of a horse.” The vision of a horse is the devil, who sees everything lofty; who, according to the proud and inconstant nature of a horse, raises the human spirit into pride and pollutes the lustful flesh as by an equine discharge. This leader of Jabin, whose name means “of intelligence,” seems to himself to be a cherub—that is, fullness of knowledge—the leader, I say, of Canaan: that is, of all whose feet have been moved by pride. For Canaan means “their motion.” He had nine hundred scythed chariots; that is, he was proud in every power, so that he seemed to himself to preside as God over all the orders of angels. [373]

“Now Deborah the prophetess, wife of Lapidoth,” it says. Deborah means “bees.” She signifies the Law, which, as honey in wax [Col. 1032B], contains in the letter the sweetness of the Spirit. She was the wife of Lapidoth, who is also called Barak. The husband of Deborah was the Jewish people, professing zeal for or knowledge of the Law. Lapidoth means “lightning,” Barak “thunderbolt.” Lightning indeed flashes, but only briefly; thunder strikes powerfully. Lapidoth, therefore—that is, lightning—was that people in the part of those who flashed only briefly, indeed vainly, with the mere speech of the literal Law; whereas thunderbolt was the part of those who, by fulfilling the Law, struck the devil mightily.

Therefore Deborah—that is, the holy, just, and good Law—sent and called Barak son of Abinoen: that same Jewish people, honoring God the Father with its lips, according to the name Abinoam. For Abinoen means “the beauty of my father.” “Go,” she says, “and lead [Col. 1032C] the army to Mount Tabor.” Tabor means “coming light,” signifying him of whom Zechariah truly sang: “The dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke I), etc. “Therefore lead the army to Mount Tabor,” she says; that is, believe in him, hope in him who was promised to Abraham and who was to come from Abraham’s seed—namely Christ, the true light, the blessing of all nations. For to lead the army to that mountain—that is, to place hope of life or righteousness in Christ—this Deborah commands Barak; this, indeed, the whole Law, this, I say, the holy Scripture of the Law and Prophets commands the Jewish people.

But he says: “If you come with me, I will go. If you do not wish to come, I shall not proceed.” That, plainly, was what that people said, [Col. 1032D] because, wishing to establish its own righteousness, it was unwilling to submit to God’s righteousness (Rom. X). This, I say, was not said by Barak but by Lapidoth—that is, by that people not in the part of the strong and perfected, who thundered mightily, but in the part of the imperfect, who flashed briefly or like lightning; having confidence in the works of the Law, they did not know that Christ’s advent or grace was for them. But by the works of the Law no flesh shall be justified before God (Rom. III).

Deborah therefore says: “I shall indeed go with you, but in this campaign victory shall not be credited to you, because Sisera will be delivered into the hand of a woman.” That is to say: the Law observed by you will indeed profit you, though it will not bring you to perfection; but when Christ comes, the Church from the Gentiles, hoping to be justified by faith in him alone, [Col. 1033A] will obtain perfection and full victory. But Heber the Kenite had formerly withdrawn from the other Kenites, his brothers, etc. The Kenites were descendants of Hobab—that is, Jethro—the kinsman of Moses, of whom something has already been said elsewhere.

Barak therefore came down from Mount Tabor, with ten thousand warriors with him. Barak came down—Barak, I say, no longer Lapidoth; that is, no longer lightning, but thunder came down from Mount Tabor: namely, the great and true Jewish apostles of Christ, inspired by the Holy Spirit and sent by Christ; and with them ten thousand warriors, namely the whole army of believers armed with faith. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: “The chariots of God are many thousands, thousands of the rejoicing; the Lord is among them in Sinai, in the sanctuary” (Ps. LXVII). They came down, I say, in condescension, because [Col. 1033B] themselves believing and enlightened, they deigned to look upon those not yet believing and still blind.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite: how she killed Sisera, and how she bore the type of the Church from the Gentiles.

“And the Lord terrified Sisera, all his chariots, and all his multitude by the edge of the sword before Barak,” so that Sisera leapt down from his chariot and fled on foot; and Barak pursued the fleeing chariots and army as far as Aroseth of the Gentiles, and all the enemy multitude fell unto destruction. “The Lord,” it says, “terrified Sisera.” For who else but our Lord, the Lord of hosts and King of glory, terrified the devil and [Col. 1033C] cast him down from the chariot of pride onto his feet, according to the Psalmist: “You have humbled the proud man as one wounded” (Ps. LXXXVIII). He terrified him before Barak, before the apostles who were from the Jewish people, to whom Deborah—as has already been said, that is, the sacred Law—was first joined. They were “the heavens declaring the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII); and while they threatened and thundered, working signs and wonders, the devil, terrified, leapt down from his chariot. For he lost the eminence of emperors and rulers of the age converted to Christ.

What follows? “Fleeing,” it says, “he came to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite. For there was peace between Jabin king of Azor and the house of Asher the Kenite.” Jael means “doe,” [Col. 1033D] or “a doe-like union.” She signifies the Church from the Gentiles, which, like a doe joined to a stag—that is, to her husband Christ—is now united through faith. This Church indeed eats the serpent, admitting the poison of sin; but repenting of this, she says individually in the person of each one, and universally in the person of all her members, who are one body, one Church, one people: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. XLI).

Cast down from the chariot and fleeing on foot, he entered her tent and was covered with her mantle, because, having lost the false title of divinity in which, as an adulterer, he boasted in the public assemblies of peoples, he secretly crept into the tent of the Church, so as covertly, as beneath [Col. 1034A] a mantle, to foment vices; since he could not obscure the name through Christ’s victories, he at least sought to corrupt the beauty of morals in Christ’s house. But what did she do? “She took,” it says, “a tent-peg, and likewise a hammer; entering secretly and silently, she placed the peg upon the temple of his head and, striking it with the hammer, drove it through his brain even to the ground. Joining sleep to death, he failed and died.”

Truly, according to another Scripture, “the strong woman girded her loins with strength and strengthened her arm” (Prov. XXXI). “She put her left hand to the peg, and her right hand to the workmen’s hammers.” Such a posture of the body plainly expresses the figure of the cross. The tent-peg is the very mark of Christ’s Passion. She took the peg who, commanded to mortify her members upon [Col. 1034B] the earth, bore her cross, crucifying her flesh with its vices and desires. This is done effectively when the affliction of the flesh is undertaken not for the vanity of human praise but for God’s glory—not, I say, out of ambition for popular applause, but in the fear of the Lord. Hence the Psalmist prays: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. CXVIII).

Rightly, then, she put her left hand to the peg and her right hand to the workmen’s hammers. The left hand, below, at the peg, is the visible practice of penitence in the eyes of human beings. The hammer in the right hand, above, is fear of the Lord in the intention of the heart. Thus it happened that she drove the [374] peg forcefully into his head, through his brain, even to the ground. Why did she seek a place for the wound in the head? Clearly because the head of sin must be struck, lest, after it has [Col. 1034C] crept into the belly, the struggle become more difficult. The head is the first suggestion of sin; the belly, the ensuing pleasure. Consent, moreover, is the tail, by which the mind is bound, as it is said of Behemoth to blessed Job: “He stiffens his tail like a cedar” (Job XL); that is, the devil holds most strongly whomever he has bound through consent. Therefore the place for the wound must be sought in the head: that is, without waiting for the tail of consent, indeed before the belly of pleasure, let the first suggestion be pierced through with the peg of the Lord’s cross and the hammer of the fear of the Lord.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the song of Deborah and Barak, and by what persons it ought rightly, according to the mystical sense, to be sung in the Church of Christ.

[Col. 1034D] **(CHAP. V.)** “And Deborah and Barak son of Abinoen sang on that day, saying: ‘You who willingly offered your lives from Israel to peril, bless the Lord.’” This song, expounded above according to the letter, must be sung continually in the Church in a spiritual sense by those who have willingly offered their lives for spiritual wars: that is, by those who, not content merely to have received a commandment, in order to fight more vigorously against the devil have also followed counsel, willingly offering their lives—willingly, I say, and by a free vow—with the possessions and estates which they have left for the Lord; and, when the cause required it, offering also their own lives. These are kings; these are princes. “Hear, O kings; give ear, O princes. [Col. 1035A] I, I am she who shall sing to the Lord; I shall make music to the God of Israel.”

“I,” says Deborah, “I,” says the divine Law, “am she who shall sing to the Lord.” However many kings, however many princes open their mouths to sing, I am she who shall sing to the Lord; for outside the divine Law, outside canonical Scripture, there is nothing that can sing to the Lord God. What, then, shall I sing? What shall I make music to the Lord God of Israel? “O Lord, when you went out from Seir and passed through the regions of Edom, the earth was shaken, and the heavens and clouds distilled waters. The mountains flowed from before the Lord, and Sinai from before the Lord God of Israel.”

Seir means “hairy”; Edom, “earthly” or “bloodstained”; Sinai, “temptation.” By these names is denoted that Jewish people, still pursuing its brother Jacob—that is, [Col. 1035B] the supplanter from among the Gentiles, the Christian people—hairy with sins, earthly through greed, bloodstained through cruelty, especially with the blood of Christ and of his prophets. But it is known and certain that he went forth from that Seir and passed through its regions: he left that people and passed over to the nations, speaking in the prophetic voice, speaking in the evangelical voice: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

Therefore: “O Lord,” it says, “when you went out from Seir and passed through the regions of Edom, the earth was shaken, and the heavens and clouds distilled waters”; that is, when you left the carnal ceremonies of the Jews and the Temple polluted by the blood of Christ your Son, while its guardian angels, as Josephus also testifies, cried, “Let us depart from these dwelling-places,” [Col. 1035C] the whole earth, upon hearing the preaching of your Gospel, was moved to repentance. The heavens of whom it is written, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII)—the heavens, I say, that is, the apostles—and likewise the clouds of whom elsewhere it is written, “I will command the clouds that they rain no rain upon my vineyard” (Isa. V), distilled everywhere waters of wisdom, waters of evangelical teaching, so that there were no speech or words whose voices were not heard, and “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). The Psalmist elsewhere sings the same thing in words slightly altered but with the same sense: “O God, when you went forth before your people, when you passed through the wilderness, the earth was shaken” (Ps. LXVII), etc. The remainder of the song, set out above in the literal exposition, we pass over in our [Col. 1035D] pursuit of progress.

## CHAPTER IX. A moral interpretation of Gideon’s seeing the angel while he threshed grain from the chaff, at whose command he cooked a kid.

**(CHAP. VI.)** “The children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord. He delivered them into the hand of Midian for seven years, and they were greatly oppressed by them. Then the angel of the Lord came and sat under the oak which was in Ophrah and belonged to Joash, the father of the family of Ezri. And when Gideon his son was threshing and cleansing grain in the winepress, so as to escape Midian, he appeared to him and said: ‘The Lord is with you, mighty man of valor,’” etc.

Here, first, the moral sense must not be passed over. Gideon, [Col. 1036A] while threshing grain from the chaff, saw the angel, at whose command he immediately cooked a kid, placed it upon a rock, and poured the broth of the meat over it. What is it to strike grain with a rod, except to separate by the rectitude of judgment the grains of virtues from the chaff of vices? But to those performing this work the angel appears; for the more zealously people cleanse themselves from outward things, the more does the Lord reveal inward things to them. He commands the kid to be killed—that is, every appetite of our flesh to be sacrificed; the flesh to be placed upon the rock; and the broth of the meat to be poured over it. Whom does the rock signify but him of whom Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X)?

We therefore place the flesh upon the rock when we afflict our body in imitation of Christ. He also pours out [Col. 1036B] the broth of the meat over it who, in the pattern of Christ’s life, empties even carnal thoughts. For broth, as liquid from meat, is poured upon the rock when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts. Yet the angel immediately touches these things with a rod, because the power of divine help by no means abandons our intention. And fire comes forth from the rock and consumes the broth and flesh, because the Spirit breathed forth by the Redeemer burns our heart with so great a flame of compunction that it consumes everything unlawful in it, both deed and thought. For the perfected mind watches diligently, so as not merely to refuse to do what is perverse, but also to cleanse away everything that shamefully flows within it through thoughts.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the twofold sign of the fleece, and what foretelling [Col. 1036C] of future things each contained.

“And Gideon said to the Lord: ‘If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said, I shall place this fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If dew is upon the fleece alone, and there is dryness upon all the ground, I shall know that by my hand, as you have said, you will deliver Israel.’ And it happened so,” etc.

According to the historical sense, it is indeed a sin and a temptation that he still asks for a sign a second and third time, after, in the preceding and first sign, he saw and recognized that it was the angel of the Lord when fire rose from the rock and consumed the flesh and unleavened cakes. Nor is it surprising that he could tempt the Lord against the Law, since after the victory he could make [375] an *Ephot* from the gold of that same victory, place it in his city Ephra, and commit fornication with it, he and all Israel [Col. 1036D] with him. Hence Gideon is interpreted “the testing of their iniquity,” although elsewhere it is also interpreted “encircling the womb.”

But according to the mystical sense, each sign of the fleece is a foretelling of future things. So long as there was dew upon the fleece, there was dryness over all the earth. And, conversely, when all the earth was wet with dew, the fleece alone was dry. Thus indeed, so long as God was known in Judaea and his name was great in Israel (Ps. LXXV), the whole world languished in dryness—that is, in ignorance of God. Conversely now, when the gifts of the Holy Spirit have been poured out throughout the whole multitude and breadth of the world, Judaea, lacking Christ, lies desolate in utter want of heavenly grace.

Looking to this, the Psalmist sings to the Lord. [Col. 1037A] To the Lord Father he says concerning his Son Christ: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece, and like drops dripping upon the earth” (Ps. LXXI); that is, he will first come to the knowledge of the Jews, and afterwards descend upon the earth—that is, into the knowledge of the Gentiles. The Jewish people is understood by the fleece because, just as a fleece is shorn from a lamb without injury or pain to the lamb, so the Jewish people, first cleaving to God, was separated from faith in Christ without harm to the Lord himself.

Yet it should rightly be understood otherwise as well. “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece”: that is, as rain descends upon a fleece without any injury or pain to the fleece itself, so that king will be born of a Virgin without any injury to the Virgin; and afterwards he shall descend “like drops dripping upon the earth,” that is, into the knowledge [Col. 1037B] of all human beings.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning his mystical battle against Midian with three hundred chosen men.

### CHAPTER XI. On his mystical battle against Midian with three hundred chosen men.

**(Chapter VII.)** And the Lord said to Gideon: “The people are still too numerous. Lead them down to the waters, and there I will test them. Of anyone of whom I say to you, ‘Let him go with you,’ he shall proceed; but whoever I forbid to go, let him return.” When the people had gone down to the waters, the Lord said to Gideon: “All those who lap the water with their tongues, as dogs are accustomed to lap, you shall set apart; but those who drink with bent knees shall be on the other side.” Now the number of those who lapped water, bringing it to their mouths with their hands, was three hundred men; and the rest.

Here too, as was sung above concerning Barak, “the Lord chose new wars” (Judges 5). For it was arranged that he should go into battle with only the three hundred men who drew water with their hands while standing, and who remained with him; and that he should arm them not with weapons, but with trumpets, lamps, and jars. For, as it is written, they put lighted lamps inside their jars, held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, and when they approached their enemies at close quarters, they sounded the trumpets, broke the jars, and displayed the lamps. Frightened on one side by the sound of the trumpets and on the other by the flashing of the lamps, the enemies turned to flight.

Of this battle the prophet says: “For you have overcome the yoke of his burden and the sceptre of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian” (Isa. 9). In rescuing the Gentile world, the Lord overcame the yoke of its burden when by his coming he freed it from the slavery of that demonic tyranny. He overcame the rod upon its shoulder when he restrained from redeemed humankind its smiter, by whom it had been grievously oppressed through perverse conduct. He overcame the sceptre of its oppressor when he destroyed in the hearts of believers the kingdom of that same devil, who had been accustomed to exact the due tribute of punishments for the deadly commission of sins.

What does it mean that such a battle is brought forward by the prophet and the victory of that contest is compared to the coming of our Redeemer? Did the prophet perhaps intend to show us that Gideon’s victory in battle signified the coming of our Redeemer against the devil? Certainly things were done there which, the more they transcend the ordinary practice of warfare, the less they depart from the mystery of prophecy. For who ever came to battle with jars and lamps? Who, coming against weapons, abandoned weapons? These things would surely have seemed ridiculous to us if they had not been terrible to the enemy. But from the testimony of this victory we learn not to make light of what was done.

Gideon, therefore, coming to battle signifies the advent of our Redeemer, of whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23 [24]). He prophesied our Redeemer not only by his deed but also by his name. For *Gideon* is interpreted “surrounding in the womb.” Our Lord, by the power of his majesty, encompasses all things; yet by the grace of his dispensation he came within the womb of the Virgin. What, then, is “surrounding in the womb,” except almighty God redeeming us through his dispensation, embracing all things in his divinity and taking humanity within the womb? In that womb he was incarnate, yet was not enclosed; for he was within the womb according to the substance of weakness, yet beyond the world through the power of majesty.

But *Midian* is interpreted “from judgment.” For the repelling or destruction of its enemies came not from a fault in the one who repelled them, but from the judgment of one judging justly. They are therefore called “from judgment,” because, being alien from the Redeemer’s grace, they bear even in the meaning of their name the desert of just condemnation.

Against these Gideon proceeds to battle with three hundred men. The number one hundred customarily signifies the fullness of perfection. What, then, is denoted by the introduction of the hundredfold number except perfect knowledge of the Trinity? For with those the Lord destroys his adversaries; with those he goes down to the battles of preaching: with those who are able to know divine things and know how to think rightly and perfectly concerning the Trinity, which is God.

It should further be noted that this number of three hundred is contained in the letter *tau*. By the letter *tau*, as we have already said, the form of the cross is shown: it has the shape of a cross, except that if the part which projects above the transverse line of a cross were added, it would no longer be merely the shape of a cross but the cross itself. Therefore, because the number three hundred is contained in the letter *tau*, Gideon’s three hundred followers fittingly signify those to whom it was said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 12 [probably Matt. 16:24]; Mark 8; Luke 9). Those who follow the Lord take up the cross all the more truly as they discipline themselves more sternly and afflict themselves with the compassion of charity toward their neighbours.

Hence Ezekiel (Ezek. 9) expressly indicates, in these three hundred who are contained in the letter *tau*, that the iron of enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross. They were led to the river to drink water. Whoever drew water with bent knees was removed from the purpose of battle. For the waters signify the teaching of wisdom, while the upright knee signifies right action. Therefore those said to have bent the knee while drinking water withdrew, excluded from their contest, because Christ goes to battle against the enemies of faith with those who, while drawing from the streams of doctrine, are not bent away from uprightness of action.

For all are reported to have drunk water, but not all to have remained standing with an upright knee. Those who bent their knees while drinking were rejected because, as the Apostle testifies, “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified” (Rom. 12 [probably Rom. 2:13]). Since, as we have said, slackness in works is signified by the very bending of the knees, Paul rightly says: “Lift up the slack hands and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. 12).

Thus those go forth to battle under Christ as their leader who show in their deeds what they proclaim with their mouths, who spiritually draw from the streams of doctrine but are not carnally bent into crooked deeds; for, as it is written, “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). The battle, then, was undertaken with trumpets, lamps, and jars; and, as we have said, this was the order of combat: they sounded the trumpets; lamps were placed inside the jars; after the jars had been broken, the lamps were displayed; and the enemy, terrified by their flashing light, turned to flight.

Thus in the trumpets is signified the cry of preaching; in the lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the jars, the frailty of bodies. Our leader brought such persons with him into the wars of preaching: persons who, despising bodily safety, would overthrow their enemies by dying, and would overcome their swords not with arms and swords but with patience. For our martyrs came armed to battle under their leader—but with trumpets, lamps, and jars. They sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when they offered their bodies, destined to be dissolved in suffering, to hostile swords. They shone with lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed forth in miracles.

Immediately the enemies turned to flight, because, when they saw the bodies of dead martyrs shining with miracles, they were broken by the light of truth and believed what they had attacked. Therefore they sounded the trumpets so that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken so that the lamps might appear; the lamps appeared so that the enemies might turn to flight. That is: the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved with him in death, so that they might shine in miracles. They shone in miracles so as to overthrow their enemies by divine light, in order that those enemies might no longer stand erect in resistance to God, but in submission fear him.

It should be observed that the enemies stood firm before the jars but fled from the lamps. For persecutors of the holy faith resisted the preachers while they still remained in the body; but after their bodies had been dissolved, when miracles appeared, they turned to flight, terrified and ceasing from persecution of the faithful. That is, when the jars of bodies had been broken through the preaching of trumpets, they saw and feared the lamps of miracles.

We should also consider what is written there: that they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left. We call “right-hand” whatever we esteem highly; “left-hand,” whatever we count as nothing. It is fittingly written, therefore, that they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left, because Christ’s martyrs prize the grace of preaching highly, but count bodily advantage as very small. Whoever values bodily advantage more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in his left hand and the jar in his right. For if the grace of preaching receives first place and bodily advantage second place, then unquestionably the trumpets are held in the right hands and the jars in the left.

### CHAPTER XII. On Jephthah the Gileadite: Abraham serves as an example of obedience to God, but Jephthah as an example warning us against rash vows; and on the character of John Chrysostom’s homily concerning him.

**[Col. 1040B] (Chapter XI.)** At that time there was Jephthah the Gileadite, a very strong man and a warrior, the son of a prostitute, born of Gilead; and the rest.

There is one matter in this Jephthah which human piety, joined with reason, may rightly condemn: namely, that he made a vow without deliberation, that he opened his mouth to God without the safeguard of discernment. What then? Should he have made a vow indiscriminately? Did not the Lord say in the Law: “In every offering of yours you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2)? Or perhaps did he make his vow with discernment, or offer salt in this offering, when he said: “If you deliver the children of Ammon into my hands, whoever first comes out from the doors of my house and meets me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I will offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord”?

Should not everyone know whether what he vows is good or evil, and know and see whether what he offers is blemished or unblemished? This, therefore, is what anyone may rightly blame; this is the one thing in Jephthah which a soul devoted to God ought wisely to avoid. Yet the fact that he fled to God and faithfully hoped for victory from God was not only beyond blame, but worthy of praise. Thus, in the epistle called that of the Apostle Paul to the Hebrews, he is enrolled in the catalogue of faithful fathers, who “through faith conquered kingdoms and accomplished promises” (Heb. 11).

Moreover, God is himself “inexcusable” [as printed] in this deed because he did not prevent Jephthah from sacrificing his daughter to him. Did he not come to sacrifice by the same path as holy Abraham (Gen. 22)? Certainly not: praiseworthy obedience led Abraham, whereas punishable rashness led Jephthah. Rightly, therefore, when Jephthah stretched out his hand and seized the sword to sacrifice his daughter, no angel of the Lord was present to cry from heaven: “Do not stretch out your hand over the girl, nor do anything to her” (ibid.).

Thus Abraham is an example of obedience to God; Jephthah, however, should be an example to us of guarding against rash vows. There survives a homily on this subject by John called Chrysostom, in which he did not hesitate to count this deed of Jephthah among those of which it was said: “All these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10).

“Each one of us,” he says, “ought to be Jephthah, who, having conquered the enemies of our desires, offers to God the one soul of our bodily pleasure, concerning which the Prophet said: ‘Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog’” (Ps. 21 [22]). Having slain in ourselves all delights of the flesh, we return victorious to God, offering him, as I have said, our soul, which is solitary and unique. But having torn apart the garments of evil temporal thoughts, which diversify the soul, let us offer it: to be put to death in evils and made alive in goods. Hence the Lord said in the Gospel: “Whoever loses his soul shall find it” (Matt. 10:16 [citation as printed]).

And further: “I still consider,” he says, “that this Jephthah is our Lord Jesus Christ, conqueror of the world, who offered his only daughter, the Church itself, in the time of persecution, to evil bishops—not lambs but wolves—he himself saying: ‘Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves’” (Luke 10; Matt. 10). “Therefore he offered the Church through the immolation of martyrs in the time of persecution; and a single victim was offered to God, so that the sacrifice might be acceptable to the Father from the gains of the Only-begotten. The only son offers the only daughter; the bridegroom, the bride; the father, the daughter.

“For what can be found stronger than the integrity and virginity of the Church? She conceives in corruption and gives birth in integrity. She is a virgin who has not known a man. Yet she mourns her virginity for sixty days—that is, for all her days. For she sends none who make progress within her to the Lord except through great tribulation, mourning, weeping, and tears. This Church promises her worshippers neither joy nor security in the present age, because in truth all joy is dangerous, all security is full of falls, and every pleasure is entangled in snares.”

Thus speaks the aforesaid John. But we, passing quickly over matters in which the majesty of the Lord who commands from above or acts is not resplendent, should hasten to those matters in which, because he himself is their author, the beauty of the mysteries shines forth more clearly.

### CHAPTER XIII. On the deeds of the exceedingly strong Samson: that they were manifestly works of God’s power, and that therefore mysteries of God are rightly sought in them.

**(Chapter XIII.)** Again the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, who delivered them into the hands of the Philistines for forty years. Now there was a certain man of Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, named Manoah, who had a barren wife; and the rest.

All the acts of this most powerful Nazarite Samson are wondrous, clearly displaying in themselves the work of divine power or strength. For they are not works of a human being, but of God: they were performed not by human strength, I say, but by the power of God who works miracles. They are seven in number.

The first act is that, through the announcement of an angelic ministry, the Nazarite of God was born from a barren woman. The second is that food came forth for him from the eater, and sweetness came forth from the strong one. The third is that, having caught three hundred foxes, he joined their tails to tails and bound torches in the middle; he set these on fire so that they might go through the crops of the Philistines. The fourth is that he struck them with a great blow, so that in stupefaction they placed calf upon thigh. The fifth is that with an ass’s jawbone—the jawbone of a young ass—he destroyed and struck down a thousand men. The sixth is that, besieged in Gaza, he slept until midnight and then rose, seized both doors of the gate with their posts and bar, placed them upon his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the mountain. The seventh is that he shook the two columns of a great house and, dying, killed far more than he had killed alive.

Therefore, because all these things, as has been said, are works of God and could not have been done except through the activity of the Spirit of God’s strength, let us search out in each case, as the truth and dignity of the events demand, the glorious mysteries of Christ the Son of God, in whom the sevenfold Holy Spirit rested.

### CHAPTER XIV. On the prediction that he would be a Nazarite, and on the continence imposed on his mother: in what sense this looks toward Christ and the Virgin his mother.

“You are barren,” he says, “and without children, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Beware that you drink neither wine nor strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, because you shall conceive and bear a son, whose head no razor shall touch. For he shall be a Nazarite of God from his infancy and from his mother’s womb; and he shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.”

From the very fact that Samson is promised to be born from a barren mother, he is comparable to the great and foremost fathers Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. All had mothers barren for a long time; all were granted, through faith’s merit and by a heavenly gift, to a failing nature; and all bore in their deeds a figure of Christ our Lord, whom nature did not bring forth in its ordinary manner, but grace—pre-eminent above all Nazarites—brought forth from a virgin womb.

The barrenness of this mother or woman is, figuratively, the virginity of blessed Mary. For what is more barren by nature than virginity? Therefore, when the angel of the Lord appears and says to this woman, “You are barren and without children, but you shall conceive and bear a son,” let the angel Gabriel of the Lord come to mind, saying to Mary: “You are a virgin and have not known a man, but behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1).

Likewise, when he says to this woman, “Beware that you drink neither wine nor strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, because you shall conceive and bear a son whose head no razor shall touch,” this is the mystical preparation which must be understood in the angel’s words to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid.).

For, indeed, when the Holy Spirit came upon the blessed Virgin, her purification consisted in not drinking wine or strong drink and not eating anything unclean. To drink wine or strong drink, or to eat anything unclean, means to love the will of the flesh and admit male embraces through lust. But the Holy Spirit coming upon her utterly excluded every appetite of this sort from the mind and body of the blessed Virgin. Therefore, she who was to bear a son drank neither wine nor strong drink and ate nothing unclean. Since that son is the Son of God, no razor ought to touch his head—that is, no blaspheming tongue ought to gnaw at it.

For whoever denies that he is the Son of God, whoever maintains that he is not both man and God but only man, surely shaves his head with sacrilegious daring and an exceedingly sharp razor. This is what the prostitute Delilah did (Judg. 16), that is, the carnal synagogue, ungrateful toward her lover.

“He shall be,” he says, “a Nazarite of God”—a Nazarite, that is, a holy one of God. Even demonic impurity confessed this: “I know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Luke 4).

Furthermore, the fact that, when sacrifice was offered to the Lord upon the rock while Manoah and his wife stood by, the flame ascended—“and when the flame of the altar ascended toward heaven, the angel of the Lord ascended with the flame”—beautifully suggests to us that, when God the Father accepted the sacrifice of virginal faith saying to the angel, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1), he immediately filled her chaste womb with the splendours of the Holy Spirit, and the angel departed from her.

### CHAPTER XV. That Samson himself prefigured Christ by name; that he tore a lion’s cub to pieces with his hands; and that, taking a honeycomb from its mouth, he ate it on the way—together with his riddle and the wife given to another, and the ways in which these things were signs of Christ.

She bore a son and called his name Samson. The very name of the Nazarite also sounds forth Christ: for *Samson* is interpreted “their sun.” And who does not know that Christ is the true sun, the sun of those who have eyes and look toward heaven? Therefore she called him Samson by the instruction of him through whose gift she had borne the son.

“The child grew, and the Lord blessed him; and the Spirit of the Lord began to be with him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.”

**(Chapter XIV.)** Samson therefore went down to Timnah; and the rest. This was an event full of power. “The Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson,” it says, “and he tore the lion apart, tearing it into pieces like a kid, having absolutely nothing in his hand.” The fierce, roaring lion’s cub that met him bore the type of the devil, who truly met our Saviour like a fierce and roaring lion when he came to receive his beloved bride—that is, when he came by his presence to teach the synagogue.

Where did the lion first meet him? In the wilderness, while he was fasting and hungry: “For after he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he afterwards hungered. And the tempter approached and said to him: ‘If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread’” (Matt. 4), and so forth. There he tore apart the lion that met him, having absolutely nothing in his hand. For he refuted the tempter on the third occasion, not by the power which he, as God, could have used against him, but by reason and the testimonies of Scripture—the means which he also willed us to use whenever we are tempted.

“And after some days,” it says, “behold, there was a swarm of bees in the lion’s mouth and a honeycomb. When he had taken it in his hands, he ate it on the way.” Samson, returning, took the swarm of bees and the honeycomb from the lion’s mouth because Christ, having overcome the tempter, returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit and chose the twelve apostles. How were they in the lion’s mouth? To say nothing of the fact that all were by nature, according to Adam, “children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2): Peter and Andrew, the first apostles, and Philip as well, were from the city of Bethsaida, which the lion, the devil, held in his mouth through unbelief. The Lord himself testified to this when he said: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11).

More fully, however, he then took the swarm of bees and the honeycomb from the lion’s mouth when, triumphing openly upon the cross over the enemy of humankind, he rescued from his power not only the apostles but all who would believe in him through their word. Thus he ate the honeycomb so taken in his hands on the way: that is, in this present life he delightfully carried out the Father’s will for their salvation, as he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4).

Meanwhile he also proposed a riddle to his companions: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness.” For the Lord spoke to the Jews in parables, in accordance with that passage in the Psalm: “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning” (Ps. 77 [78]). But he proposed such a riddle to them most particularly when he signified by what death he would die: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out. And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). For in that he drew all things to himself after the ruler of the world had been cast out, food came forth for them from the eater, and sweetness came forth from the strong one.

And they found the solution to this riddle. For they said: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains for ever. How then do you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’?” (Mark 16 [citation as printed]). Thus they found the solution, but they did so not by ploughing with another’s heifer, but by ploughing their own conscience: for they understood that he had signified what they were planning to do.

To what end, finally, was that marriage dissolved? “Being exceedingly angry,” it says, “he went up to his father’s house. But his wife took as husband one of his friends and bridal attendants.” It is certain, manifest to the whole world, that Christ, exceedingly angry with the Jews, went up to his Father’s house: he ascended, I say, into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. But his wife, the Synagogue, took as husband one of his friends and bridal attendants: one of the great patriarchs and prophets, friends of the Lord—namely Moses, Christ’s friend and bridal attendant, because Moses wrote of him. The Synagogue took him. Or rather, it appeared to itself that it had taken him, glorying in the letter of his Law and reading his Law without the grace of this one. For example, they say: “You may be his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses” (John 9).

### CHAPTER XVI. The mystery in Samson’s bringing a kid from the goats and wishing to enter the bedchamber, being prevented by the girl’s father, and saying in anger: “I will do you harm.”

**(Chapter XV.)** After a time, when the days of the wheat harvest were at hand, Samson came wishing to visit his wife and brought her a kid from the goats.

“After a time” means after he rose from the dead, ascended to heaven, and gave the Holy Spirit to his apostles. “When the days of the wheat harvest were at hand” means when the time of evangelical preaching had come, so that the Lord of the harvest might send his workers into the whole world. Christ himself came in his apostles, in whom he spoke, wishing to visit his wife and to convert the synagogue, bringing her a kid—that is, preaching repentance and forgiveness of sins.

When he wished, according to his customary practice, to enter her bedchamber, her father prevented him. The father of the Synagogue was the Pharisaic assembly, whose office or profession it was to instruct the people, with a teacher’s severity and a father’s affection. Such a father, usurping the key of knowledge, prevented Christ from entering the bedchamber of the Synagogue. For after the apostles had been beaten, they charged them not to speak to anyone in his name (Acts 5).

Samson replied to him: “From this day there shall be no blame in me against the Philistines, for I shall do you harm.” The sense is nearly the same, and the words correspond, to these: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you! How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling! Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23). He spoke these words with his own mouth concerning what he would suffer; and after he had suffered, risen, and ascended to heaven, he spoke again in his apostles. To those Philistines—to those Jews falling through drink and drunken with his blood—he spoke, shaking the dust from his feet: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but because you have rejected it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Thus from this day there is no longer blame in me against you. For what more ought I to have done that I did not do?

### CHAPTER XVII. The mystical meaning of Samson’s catching three hundred foxes, joining tail to tail and binding torches between them, and sending them into the Philistines’ crops—who burned both the woman and her father.

“He went and caught three hundred foxes, joined their tails to tails, and bound torches in the middle. Setting them on fire, he released them to run here and there; and they immediately went into the crops of the Philistines.”

Where did the true Samson go, or which foxes did he catch? He went to the Gentiles; he went forth into all the earth. Searching the caves of temples and the pits of shrines, he caught those foxes of whom the Psalmist, prophetically striking these Philistines—that is, the Jews—said: “They shall be delivered into the power of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. 99 [probably Ps. 63:10]).

These foxes are the evil spirits who lay hidden in the hearts of human beings, acting deceitfully in the idols of the Gentiles and uttering the responses of their own falsehood. He therefore caught three hundred foxes: that is, spreading his net through the three regions of the world—Asia, Europe, and Africa—he drew to judgment all the demons worshipped as gods. Now expelled from temples, they run here and there, seeking rest and not finding it; but bound at their tails, where the body ends, they bear a fire: that is, they are not ignorant of the judgment of condemnation that will come at the end of the age.

“They immediately went,” it says, “into the crops of the Philistines.” The crops of the Philistines were the works of the Jews, the pursuits of the scribes, and the traditions of the Pharisees.
