All went there, as is signified in the Gospel: “When an unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it walks through waterless places, seeking rest and finding none. Then it says: ‘I shall return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds it swept clean. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself; they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person becomes worse than the first” (Matt. 12; Luke 11).

For when the devil had been expelled from the heart of Gentile paganism, he returned with seven—that is, with all the spirits of wickedness—to that nation from which he had gone out, when the true God first called it back from the errors of Egypt to his worship. Thus the crops of the Philistines, and the crops already grown strong, were burned up, to such an extent that the flame consumed even vineyard and olive groves. That is, all the works of the Jews and all their ceremonies or rites were condemned by God’s hatred, so completely that hostile fire consumed even their city and temple.

The Philistines said: “Who has done this?” To them it was said: “Samson, son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to another, has done this.” Clearly, the Jews—both physically delivered to the sword and spiritually made portions for foxes, that is, for evil spirits—could not have been ignorant who had done this thing or for what crime they suffered so dreadful a fate. The judgment was therefore manifest in their hearts: their own conscience bore testimony against them, while their thoughts accused one another and could not mount a defence.

“And the Philistines went up and burned both the woman and her father.” The Philistines, I say, burned Philistines with the intention of avenging themselves; but Jews killed Jews, not because a desire to avenge Christ’s blood demanded it, but because a hidden cause set them armed against themselves. For while they were besieged outside by the Roman army, they were internally divided by a threefold war, as the histories report. There was war within the city, war among citizens, and war before the Temple. Eleazar occupied the inner parts and the whole circuit of the Temple. Simon held the upper parts of the city. John stood between them, fighting against both, below Eleazar and above Simon.

Therefore, after the fire first sent in through the foxes, the Philistines burned Philistines—that is, the woman who had deserted Samson together with her father—because through the evil spirits to whom power had been given, the Jews, inflamed against themselves, destroyed their own synagogue and the entire priestly and Levitical order; and finally their city and temple were visibly burned as well.

### CHAPTER XVIII. How Samson struck the Philistines so that, stupefied, they placed calf upon thigh; and what sort of reproach of the Jews this remains to the present day according to this interpretation.

Samson said to them: “Although you have done these things, I shall nevertheless yet demand vengeance from you; and then I shall rest.”

According to the letter, his meaning is this: although you have avenged my cause by burning my former wife and her father because he gave her to another husband, I shall nevertheless yet demand vengeance from you, as from my enemies, not as from those who avenged me. For you burned them not to favour me, but to seek your own revenge.

“And he struck them with a great blow, so that in stupefaction they placed calf upon thigh.” “In stupefaction,” he says—plainly, in bodily stupefaction. For it is not a stupor of the mind but of the body when, with the varicose veins cut or burned and the tendons of the knees contracted, the calf adheres to the thigh; thus, both shamefully and miserably, the buttocks cannot be raised from the ground.

“I shall therefore yet demand vengeance from you,” he says, so that the aforesaid foxes, whose tails I joined to tails with torches bound in the middle, did not shake their buttocks through your crops, driven by the fire, with greater ridicule than you yourselves will drag your buttocks across your land while creeping.

“And departing, he lived in the cave of the rock of Ethan.” *Ethan* is interpreted “of the strong.” How greatly he advanced from that rock against the enemy in accordance with this name is clear from what follows.

Indeed, the true Samson, prince of virtues, likewise said to his Jewish enemies: “Although you have done these things—although, made portions for foxes and delivered into the hands of the sword, you have nevertheless brought ruin upon yourselves through civil wars and the stubbornness of factions, in vengeance for my blood—I shall nevertheless yet demand vengeance from all of you who remain. I shall strike you with a great blow, so that in stupefaction you place calf upon thigh.” That is, just as one whose channels of blood have dried up, placing calf upon contracted thigh, cannot rise to the common upright stature of human beings, so you, taken captive among all nations and made a reproach to all, shall always be regarded as lowered in head and of the meanest condition.

“Then I shall rest”: that is, I shall not kill you utterly, as I said in the Prophet: “God shall show me concerning my enemies: do not kill them, lest my people ever forget; scatter them in your strength” (Ps. 58 [59]). He said and did these things; and, descending and departing, he dwells to this day in the cave of the rock of Ethan. For the cave of the rock of Ethan—the rock “of the strong”—is the secure and solitary conscience of ecclesiastical faith, in which he indeed dwells at rest.

### CHAPTER XIX. On the ass’s jawbone with which he struck a thousand men, and how Christ similarly confounds all strength through things contemptible and weak.

Descended therefore three thousand men of Judah to the cleft of the rock of Ethan. And they said to Samson: “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us?” And so forth. And finding the jawbone—that is, the mandible—of an ass lying there, he seized it and killed a thousand men with it.

Although they had already sufficiently experienced the strength of Samson the Nazirite—that is, had learned the omnipotence of Christ, the Son of God—the Philistines nevertheless went up; those who fall by drinking, or the Jews who would fall, went up into the land of Judah, the land of confession, against the Catholic Church, in which are faith and the confession of truth [Col. 1048A]. And three thousand men of Judah went down because of them to bind Samson: that is, throughout the three regions of the world—Asia, Europe, and Africa—although very many seemed to belong to Judah and confessed Christ, of whom the Apostle says, “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2), they became helpers of Jewish impiety. Though divided by many schisms, they nevertheless desired to seize Christ with the same spirit of malice.

But what did he do? “Finding the jawbone—that is, the mandible—of an ass lying there, he seized it and killed a thousand men with it.” The jawbone or mandible of an ass in Christ’s hand signifies those foolish and weak things of the world, those ignoble and despised things of the world, concerning which the Apostle says: “Consider your calling, brethren: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are” (1 Cor. 1) [Col. 1048B].

Therefore, by seizing the jawbone of the ass which lay there, he killed a thousand men: that is, having found those who “were not,” who were ignoble, despised by the world, and rejected, he confounded and destroyed his enemies. This has already partly happened through changing them for good; and it is partly yet to happen, through condemning those who could not be beneficially killed in the future judgment. God performed this marvelous work: Samson, the very strong one; Christ, the all-powerful one.

He knew [Col. 1048C] that a great contest and grave dispute awaited him against experts in the Law, against orators, against the philosophers of the world, against the noble and powerful—kings, emperors, tyrants. Knowing this, he did not at his first campaign call many wise, noble, or powerful persons, by whose boastful tongues, swords, or authority he might strengthen his Gospel. Rather, he called those who, as asses in comparison with lions, were despised by those wise, noble, and powerful men: namely, unlearned men, not scribes; men without letters, not those sitting in Moses’ seat; simple men, not orators; fishermen, not emperors.

And he said: “With the jawbone of an ass, with the mandible of a young ass, I destroyed them.” The former ass is the Jewish people; the young ass is the younger people of the Gentiles. Thus [Col. 1048D] the jawbone of the ass signifies the apostles chosen from the Jews, who were not especially great or illustrious according to the flesh; the mandible of the young ass signifies martyrs and teachers chosen from the Gentiles. For even if all those called from Jews and Gentiles at the beginning of the Gospel’s preaching were despised by the world as an ass or as a young ass, nevertheless those who bore the full weight of the struggle and achieved the whole victory were, as it were, the jawbone of the ass and the mandible of the young ass. They were more despised: that is, before this world, the most foolish of fools and most despised of the despised—men who preferred insults to honors and chose death for Christ rather than life.

## CHAPTER XX. That the Lord opened the ass’s molar tooth, and very abundant waters came forth; and what mystery this signifies.

When he had finished uttering these words, he threw the mandible from his hand; and, being exceedingly thirsty, he said: “Behold, I shall die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised.” Therefore the Lord opened the molar tooth in the ass’s jawbone, and waters came forth from it. When he drank them, his spirit was refreshed and he recovered his strength.

How did the true Samson, Christ the Lord, throw from his hand that jawbone or mandible through which he had accomplished so great a salvation and victory? Did he abandon or forsake those through whom he fought and conquered? Certainly he did not abandon or cast them off; yet he permitted them to be killed and overthrown, and “they seemed, in the eyes of the foolish, to die” [Col. 1049B] (Wisdom 3). Therefore he cast them from his hand, not unwillingly but voluntarily: they surrendered their bodies to punishment for God’s sake.

And he cried out and said: “Behold, I shall die of thirst,” and so forth. For this was a great concern of his—or rather, a great anxiety and fear of his Church, which is his body—that when the apostles, on whose merits and powers it rested, fell, religion might perish, faith be weakened, and the hands of the uncircumcised—that is, of unbelievers and impious persons—be strengthened to blot out the Christian name.

But what follows? “The Lord opened the molar tooth in the ass’s jawbone, and waters came forth from it.” Nothing is truer or more manifest. For when the holy apostles and martyrs had been laid low in death, their tombs poured forth living waters; their bodies shed abroad the grace of miracles [Col. 1049C]. This was sweet to all Christ’s members; it was to all his faithful who toiled in the Christian contest what rest is to one weary, or what a sweet stream of water is to a thirsty traveler hastening through the heat. From that time faith grew, hope was strengthened, and charity became ever more powerful. Thus Samson’s spirit was refreshed, and he regained his strength.

## CHAPTER XXI. That, besieged by enemies, he rose at midnight, carried away the gates, and ascended the mountain summit with them.

**(Chapter 16.)** He also went to Gaza, saw there a prostitute, and went in to her. When the Philistines heard this, and it became widely known among them that Samson had entered the city, they surrounded him. They stationed guards at the city gate and waited there silently all night, so that when morning came they might kill him as he departed [Col. 1049D].

This prostitute signifies the fornicating synagogue, to which God says through the prophet: “On every high hill and beneath every leafy tree you lay down as a prostitute” (Jer. 2). That most mighty Samson entered her when Christ lived among her people and deigned to preach and perform miracles among them.

But the Philistines surrounded him; the Jews also surrounded and besieged him, as he says in the Psalm: “For many dogs have surrounded me; the counsel of evildoers has besieged me” (Ps. 21). For what does the city of Gaza signify but hell? What is shown by the Philistines but the faithlessness of the Jews? When they saw the Lord dead and his body already placed in the tomb, they immediately appointed guards; and they rejoiced as though they had caught Samson in Gaza, imagining that he who had appeared as the author of life was held fast in the prison-house of hell [Col. 1050A].

But Samson at midnight not only went out; he also carried away the gates. Thus our Redeemer, rising before dawn, not only departed freely from hell, but also destroyed the very bars of hell; he carried away the gates and ascended the mountain summit, because by rising he removed the bars of hell, and by ascending he entered the kingdoms of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXII. That Delilah, who shaved Samson, signifies the Synagogue, which blasphemed Christ and crucified him at Calvary; and what it mystically means for Samson—that is, Christ—to be bound, and so forth.

After this he loved a woman living in the valley of Sorek, whose name was Delilah. The princes of the Philistines came to her and said: “Deceive him, and discover from him wherein his great strength lies, and how we may overcome him and bind him to afflict him. If you do this, each of us will give you eleven hundred pieces of silver.”

At last this woman prevailed by deception. She tested him first and could not succeed. She tested him a second and third time and could not succeed. The fourth time she tested him and prevailed. Historically, indeed, the persons or women were many and different; but mystically they are one and the same Synagogue, which repeatedly tested Christ and could not so much as catch him in speech [Col. 1050C]. At last, however, it tested him, as it were, by shaving his head, and prevailed, because it denied and blasphemed Christ, the Son of God and its king, and crucified him on Mount Calvary.

Delilah is interpreted “little poor woman.” By this name the same Synagogue is designated as exceedingly poor in understanding, though it boasts of possessing the great riches of the Law and Prophets and thus of dwelling in Sorek, which is interpreted “chosen” or “best.” Certainly the princes of the Philistines who came to her and asked her to deceive her lover Samson were the chief priests and elders of the people, who stirred up the whole multitude against Christ.

And although Samson, according to the historical narrative, spoke falsely when he said: “If I am bound with seven sinew cords, not yet dry and still moist, I shall become weak like other men”; likewise, “If I am bound with new ropes which have never been used for work, I shall become weak and like other men”; and then, “If you weave the seven locks of the hair of my head with a thread and fasten them with a pin driven into the ground, I shall be weak”—in Christ none of these things is false. Rather, because we are forbidden to doubt that Christ’s Spirit spoke in him, given the mighty present signs of divine power, we should not admit that what Delilah heard there was false; instead, she herself was false when she said: “Behold, you have spoken falsely” [Col. 1050D].

For what are ropes but sins, according to the saying: “Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins” (Prov. 5), and according to the Psalmist: “The cords of sinners have entwined me” (Ps. 118). Therefore the number seven of the cords signifies the multitude of sins, because universality is often signified by the number seven. Who does not know that the true Samson, Christ Jesus, was to take upon himself the bonds of all our sins and, though he was the God of spirits, mighty, was for our sake to appear a weak man—a man capable of suffering and death?

Therefore Christ’s Spirit says: “If I am bound with seven sinew cords, I shall be weak”; that is, unless I bear upon myself the sins of the world, I shall not be mortal or able to die, for in myself I have no cause for which I ought to die [Col. 1051A]. Why, then, did he repeat the sevenfold binding a third time? Clearly because of the three ages of the world: the first before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace. He was to take away the sins of all three; according to his humanity he was to become weak and die, while according to his divinity he was to break these same bonds of sins as one breaks a twisted thread of tow, or as the husk of a thread is broken when it receives the heat of fire.

The distinction between these times should be noted according to the difference of the bonds. The sins of the first period, before the Law, are compared with sinew cords not yet dry and still moist, because no law had restrained those people of that age, still undisciplined and fresh in their excesses; God had forbidden them nothing to check the flow of moist flesh. The sins of the second period are rightly represented by cords, but neither sinewy nor moist [Col. 1051C], because the sins of those under the Law were neither so vigorous nor so fluid. Such legal righteousness as they had, though it did not consume them, nevertheless somewhat softened them; though it did not burn them up, it nevertheless dried them to some degree.

The sins of the third period, now in progress, are rightly signified by the seven locks of the Nazirite woven with thread and bound about with a nail. For our sins—that is, the sins of all who believe in Christ—are set nearer to his head, interwoven with the thread of the Gospel fabric, and fastened with nails upon the cross by public confession. Thus the Nazirite, the Son of God, bore in his body all the sins of the world; and for all he became weak unto death according to the condition of the flesh. But, overcoming all things by the power of God, he could not be held by hell and did not see corruption in the tomb [Col. 1051D].

## CHAPTER XXIII. When or where Christ said, “I am a Nazirite,” and how, with his head shaved, he became weak like other men; how and for whom he failed.

Since she was troublesome to him and clung to him continually for many days, allowing him no time for rest, his soul failed and was wearied even unto death. Then, revealing the truth of the matter, he said to her: “Iron has never come upon my head, because I am a Nazirite—that is, consecrated to God from my mother’s womb. If my head is shaved, my strength will depart from me; I shall fail and be like other men.”

“The head of Christ,” says the Apostle, “is God” (1 Cor. 11). It is shaved when the sharp razor of a blaspheming tongue denies his power and divinity [Col. 1052A]. But however, or to whatever extent, it is shaved, will his strength depart from him, will he fail, and will he become like other men? Certainly he fails and is weakened for those who shave him by blaspheming: the coming of the Son of Man into this world profits them nothing, since they deny that he is true God and truly the Son of God.

“His soul failed,” it says, “and was wearied unto death.” According to the history, this happened, and divine providence beneficially permitted it to happen, so that the whole world might hear how great a shipwreck lies in love for a prostitute, and how ruinous the female cesspool is even to the cedar planks of mighty men. That is, the whole world might hear, and every wise person might have an example from which to beware, knowing that no one can be stronger than Samson or wiser than Solomon.

But, to continue the mystery begun: the soul of the Lord Jesus in some manner failed, and the spirit of his strength was wearied unto death, when, after the many temptations of Delilah—that is, of the little poor synagogue—asking, “By what authority do you do these things? Who are you? Whom do you make yourself?” (Matt. 21), he was at last adjured by that same woman saying: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, whether you are the Son of the blessed God” (John 1) [Col. 1052B].

Then, it says, his soul failed, sorrowful even unto death (John 8), exceedingly troubled by her questioning; and then he revealed to her the entire truth, that he was a Nazirite, that is, the holy Son of God. For he said: “You have said it. I am.” And he added: “Nevertheless I say to you, from now on you shall see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 26) [Col. 1052C].

## CHAPTER XXIV. How, and by what barber, the head of this Nazirite—that is, Christ—was shaved; and concerning the Philistines’ making the imprisoned Samson grind after his eyes were torn out: an example every Christian must avoid.

But she made him sleep upon her knees and rest his head in her lap. Then she called the barber, who shaved his seven locks; and she began to cast him away and drive him from herself. The barber hired by that prostitute to shave the seven locks of the sleeping Nazirite was Pilate [Col. 1052D], to whom she delivered and denied our Lord, the Holy of Holies, and whose crucifixion on Mount Calvary she demanded (John 19).

There she shaved the seven locks of the sleeping one: that is, she detested her king and repudiated all his right, while he was “like a sheep silent, like a lamb before its shearer, not opening his mouth” (Isa. 53). She began to cast him away and drive him from herself, even mocking him with nodding and shaking heads, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days, save yourself!” (Mark 15). Immediately his strength departed from him—that is, as his enemies supposed—especially when he himself said: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”

When the Philistines had seized him, they immediately tore out his eyes, led him bound in chains to Gaza [Col. 1053A], shut him in prison, and made him grind. Samson’s loss of his eyes aptly signifies the Lord’s death itself, because in death not only sight but all the other senses are taken away. The city of Gaza signifies hell, in which the impious wished to hold the Lord bound in chains; but this was impossible. For, as the Apostle says, “God raised him up, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2).

“And they shut him in prison and made him grind.” The Hebrews wish this, according to the letter, to mean that he was compelled to devote himself to women and lust for the begetting of exceptionally strong men; and they connect it with what is said to Babylon in Isaiah: “Take the millstone and grind flour” (Isa. 47), namely that, like a prostitute, she is open to everyone’s lust, especially because it immediately adds: “Uncover your shame” [Col. 1053B]. But did the Philistine enemies desire strong men from the stock of the Hebrews to multiply? Therefore this opinion is as disgraceful as it is frivolous.

Morally, every person must beware this example. One should know that sometimes the eye of understanding is first dulled, and then the captive mind wanders through outward desires, so that the blind mind does not know where it is being led and submits itself to the allurements of its flesh. At other times, the desires of the flesh first boil over, and after a long practice of unlawful conduct they close the eye of the heart. For the mind often sees rightly, yet does not boldly rise against perversity; though resisting, it is conquered, since, even while judging what it touches or does, it is overcome by the pleasure of its flesh.

That the eye of contemplation is often first lost, and then the mind is enslaved by carnal desires to the labors of this world, Samson, captured by the foreigners, attests. After he lost his eyes, he was assigned to the mill; for evil spirits, after they have gouged out within the eye of contemplation by the goads of temptations, send one outward to the labor of restless wandering [Col. 1053C].

## CHAPTER XXV. What it mystically means that the hair of our Nazirite, Christ, began to grow again; how he killed many more by dying than he had killed while living; which house he threw down, and by shaking which columns.

Now his hair had begun to grow again, and the princes of the Philistines gathered together to offer magnificent sacrifices to their god Dagon and to feast, saying: “Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands.” Seeing this, the people also praised their god and said the same. And when they were rejoicing at the feast, after already taking food, they ordered Samson to be summoned to amuse them, and so forth [Col. 1053D].

This entertainment was turned into mourning, this joy into grief, these banquets into vomiting, so that, having revelled, they vomited forth their bloody lives, crushed beneath the fall of the great house. For he killed many more by dying than he had killed alive.

The hair of Samson, the strongest, unconquered, and invincible one—that is, Christ, the Son of God—began to grow again when Peter, who had denied him, and all the other apostles, who had all fled after abandoning him, regained faith and confidence when he rose from the dead [Col. 1054A]. The princes and people of the Philistines rejoiced, saying: “That deceiver is dead” (Matt. 27), and his name has perished—the one who stirred up the whole earth, beginning from Galilee even to this place, teaching and deceiving many.

Saying these things and rejoicing thus, they offered magnificent sacrifices, not to God but to the devil; not in God’s temple, but in the temple of the devil, namely Dagon. For Dagon is interpreted “fish of sorrow,” signifying him of whom it is written in Isaiah: “On that day the Lord will visit with his hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, and Leviathan, the twisting serpent, and he will kill the sea-monster that is in the sea” (Isa. 27). To him, I say, they offered sacrifices after filling their hands with Christ’s blood; and whatever they thereafter sacrifice or offer, they offer not to the God of their fathers but to the devil [Col. 1054B].

Rejoicing amid such feasting, they ordered Samson to be summoned to amuse them, and they watched Samson at play. For the most wicked mockers beat Christ’s apostles after arresting them (Acts 5); yet those apostles rejoiced because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name. “We have become a spectacle,” they say, “to the world, to men, and to angels” (1 Cor. 4). Thus Christ was at play in his members: whatever miracles he performed and whatever sound teaching he delivered were, to his impious spectators, entertainment and vanity.

But he seized the two columns upon which the house rested, holding one in his right hand and the other in his left; and, shaking the columns violently, the house fell upon all the princes and the rest of the multitude who were there [Col. 1054C]. Who does not see, who does not know, that deserted Jerusalem, together with their desolated house of sanctification and their glory, fell upon all the princes and the rest of the multitude? For that most ancient temple was not overthrown by Roman destruction in a merely moderate way, nor, I say, as it had once been by the Babylonians, was it spared to such a degree. Rather, it fell utterly and perished with the nation itself, so that “not one stone was left upon another that was not destroyed.”

They lost their place and nation, though out of a pretended fear of losing them they judged the Lord’s death advantageous, saying: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11) [Col. 1054D]. The opposite occurred: precisely because they did not let him go on thus, all nations will believe in him, and the Romans took away both their place and nation.

Therefore it was rightly said that he killed many more by dying than he had killed while living. For much more because he died, we believe in him; and both visible and invisible enemies perished and suffered loss—indeed, were utterly ruined—than either we would have believed or they would have perished or suffered loss had they let him remain alive.

Thus, having recovered his strength, Samson seized the two columns on which the house rested; when the house was shaken, it fell with the destruction of many [Col. 1055A]. So Christ, raised from the dead and glorified with the glory which he had with the Father before the world existed, violently shook the two columns of that people—the kingdom and the ancient priesthood—and, through Roman hands, overthrew the place itself with a twofold crushing, of body and soul, for the Jews.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the history in which the tribe of Dan took Micah’s idol, and men of the tribe of Benjamin are related to have tortured a woman to death in an unbelievable frenzy of lust—a narrative that gravely defames the Israelites for the crime of a double fornication.

**(Chapter 17.)** There was at that time a man in Mount Ephraim named Micah. He said to his mother: “The eleven hundred pieces of silver which you had set apart for yourself, and concerning which you had sworn in my hearing—behold, I have them; they are with me.” And so forth. Therefore he returned them to his mother. She took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to a silversmith, that he might make from them a carved image and a molten image, and so forth [Col. 1055B].

From this passage to the end of this book, Holy Scripture labors to condemn and abhor two evils of the Israelite nation: the double fornication of the people of Israel. Because of them the Lord was so often angry with that land and people, and his hand is still stretched out. These evils were nearly continuous, restrained only from time to time by very few judges or righteous kings.

The first is the fornication of the soul, by which the creature departs from God, its lawful husband, prostitutes itself to idols, and commits adultery against the divine name by associating it with a carved and molten image [Col. 1055C]. The present reading severely strikes this adultery, this spiritual fornication, among that people. It burned so fiercely that at this time not only Micah, one man, made a carved image, but even the whole tribe of Dan stole it for its own great advantage, although it had not yet received its allotted possession among the other tribes and therefore ought to have sought all the more earnestly the help of the true God, at least for temporal goods.

For it is written thus: **(Chapter 18.)** “In those days there was no king in Israel, and the tribe of Dan was seeking for itself a possession in which to dwell. For until that day they had not received an inheritance among the other tribes.” And later: “They took the carved image, the ephod, the idols, and the molten image.” The priest said to them: “What are you doing?” They answered: “Be silent; put your finger upon your mouth, and come with us, that we may have you as father and priest” [Col. 1055D].

The ephod signifies the priestly garment, which in Exodus and Leviticus we call the shoulder-garment. *Teraphim* are properly called figures and images. This, then, is the first fornication: the people of Israel, inclined toward idols, committed fornication in soul against their God.

The other fornication is that which defiles bodies by various mockeries of lust, and it is then more destructive when Sodomite frenzy rages against nature. How great an unrestrainedness this brought upon that people the present reading declares most sharply.

**(Chapter 19.)** “There was,” it says, “a Levite living on the side of Mount Ephraim, who took a wife from Bethlehem of Judah. She left him, returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem, and remained with him four months,” and the rest. What could be more shameful, criminal, or cruel to hear? “The men of that city, sons of Belial”—that is, without a yoke—came and surrounded the old man’s house, began to strike the doors, and shouted to the master of the house: “Bring out the man who has entered your house, that we may abuse him” [Col. 1056A].

Though he pleaded, they were with difficulty turned away from committing this unnatural crime against the man. In a most wicked exchange, they abused his wife throughout the night and tortured her in an incredible frenzy of lust. Finally, she died. That city, Gibeah, was in the tribe of Benjamin. The entire tribe of Benjamin terribly declared that the stain of this crime belonged commonly to itself.

**(Chapter 20.)** When all the children of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, had gathered together—four hundred thousand fighting foot soldiers—to fight against Gibeah of Benjamin, they sent messengers to the whole tribe of Benjamin to say: “Why has so great a wickedness been found among you? Hand over the men of Gibeah who committed this outrage, that they may die and evil be removed from Israel.” But they refused to listen to the command of their brothers, the children of Israel. Instead, from all the cities belonging to their allotment, they gathered at Gibeah to bring them help and fight against the whole people of Israel [Col. 1056B].

Yet the unquestionable justice of the divine oracle seems also to have convicted of the same guilt all Israel, assembled to repay them for their crime as they deserved. For when they consulted the Lord, saying, “Who shall be the leader of battle in our army?” he answered, “Judah shall be your leader.” Yet the children of Benjamin came out from Gibeah and killed twenty-two thousand men of the children of Israel that day.

Again they consulted the Lord, saying, “Should we go on further to fight against the children of Benjamin or not?” “Go up against them,” he said, “and begin the battle.” Yet the children of Benjamin met them and raged in such slaughter among them that they struck down eighteen thousand men who drew the sword [Col. 1056C].

At last, when they consulted a third time and said, “Should we again go out to battle against the children of Benjamin, our brothers, or should we desist?” he answered, “Go up, for tomorrow I shall deliver them into your hands”; and so it happened.

Thus not only Benjamin, whose manifest crime disgraced it, but also Israel, fighting against them, was rebuked by the truth of God’s hidden judgment. Why did victory come so late and so sorrowfully to those avenging such a great crime, except because in the very matter for which they attacked others they accused themselves? Therefore, as stated above, this passage of history strongly accuses and sharply condemns the people of Israel for a double fornication, of soul and body, accomplishing what the Apostle says: “That every mouth may be stopped, and that neither Jew nor Greek may boast more of righteousness before God” (Rom. 3) [Col. 1056D].

## CHAPTER XXVII. That Holy Scripture longs for Christ, the King who was to come, when it repeatedly says: “In those days there was no king in Israel.”

Here too Scripture groans deeply, when, in the course of the narrative, it says once, twice, and a third time: “In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did what seemed right to himself” [Col. 1057A]. What king, or what kind of king, do you suppose it laments was not in Israel in those days?

Did the fornications cease when Saul was given as king? Did they cease under Ahaz? Under Manasseh? On the contrary, both these and most of the other kings increased them: they built altars to all the host of heaven, practiced divination and observed omens, made their sons pass through fire, made diviners, and multiplied soothsayers. In sum, except David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, all sinned. We shall be silent concerning David’s sin which he committed against Uriah, because the Lord took it away (Kings 11).

What king, then, does Scripture lament as absent in those days, if not him by whose coming or reign transgression would be ended, sin brought to an end, iniquity blotted out, everlasting righteousness brought in, vision and prophecy fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies anointed? (Dan. 9.) This is the king who was lacking when the Law had been given. The Law could reveal sin, but could not free from sin [Col. 1057B]. This King alone was to free by his grace from sin all who received his kingdom. Therefore, when Scripture recounts such great sins of the people of Israel, it rightly and fittingly groans, saying: “For in those days there was no king in Israel.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Ruth the Moabite: that through this foreign woman Christ’s lineage was in some manner restored; and that she was the rock of the desert of which Isaiah says: “Send forth the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert.”

**(Chapter 1, from the Book of Ruth.)** “In the days of one of the judges, when judges ruled in Israel, a famine came upon the land. A man departed from Bethlehem of Judah to live as a foreigner in the land of Moab, with his wife and two children. His name was Elimelech, his wife’s name Naomi, and of his two sons, one was Mahlon and the other Chilion, Ephrathites of Bethlehem of Judah.”

The Hebrews incorporate this book into the Book of Judges, because its history is narrated as having occurred in the days of the judges. It greatly delights the faithful mind that it is marked in the title by the name of Ruth rather than Boaz or Naomi. For it is no small glory that the line of Christ’s generation, almost extinguished in the deaths of the Israelite men and of the tribe of Judah, was restored through the faith of a foreign woman, as the sequence of the historical narrative itself relates [Col. 1057D].

Looking to this, the prophet says: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). By “the rock of the desert” he means Ruth the Moabite: a rock because of her own faith, but a rock of the desert because of the desolation of the Moabite people. That people truly was a desert precisely because it did not possess the Lord as its inhabitant, like the rest of the Gentiles. For the same reason, the prophet elsewhere likewise calls the Gentile world a desert, saying: “The desert and the trackless place shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult” (Isa. 35).

He knew that Christ would be born of the seed of David, son of Jesse, son of Obed, whom this foreign woman bore to Boaz [Col. 1058A], and whom that kindly man received according to the Law, in order to raise up seed for his kinsman. Beholding this, he says: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion,” marveling at the grace of God: that the Lamb of God, ruler of the earth, who himself is the salvation of the Gentiles from the Jews, would nevertheless first come from Gentile faith to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.

Furthermore, striking more sharply at Jewish pride, he says at the beginning of the book: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we should have been as Sodom, and like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). He immediately adds: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (ibid.). For, according to the foregoing accounts of twofold fornication, in what respect was this people, who had received the Law, more righteous than the people of Sodom or Gomorrah, who had not received it?

But the Lord left a seed, through the merit of the faith of Ruth the Moabite and through Boaz’s raising up seed for his brother according to the justice of the Law, from which Christ might be born according to the flesh. Thus the Israelite people did not remain like Sodom or Gomorrah in destruction [Col. 1058B]. Therefore, in saying this, the prophet strives to stop the Jewish mouth, so that no one may dare boast of personal merits.

And he pointedly says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed.” “Of hosts,” I say, because in the armies mentioned above—of the children of Israel against Benjamin—he moderated judgment with mercy and punished Sodomite sins in both parties. He added famine, because of which the first man of Judah departed as a foreigner with his sons; then, through Gentile faith, as already stated, he raised up the remnant of the seed from which salvation would proceed after those same men had died [Col. 1058C].

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Elimelech, his wife, and his two sons: what, or how, is written concerning them in Chronicles.

He, it says, was called Elimelech, and his wife Naomi; and of their two sons, one was Mahlon and the other Chilion, Ephrathites of Bethlehem in Judah. They were called Ephrathites, of course, from Ephrath, the wife of Caleb. This Elimelech is called Ahalai, or Oholoi, in Chronicles, and is written to have been the son of Sheshan, son of Jishi, son of Abphaim, son of Nadab, son of Shammai, son of Onan, son of Jerahmeel, son of Esrom, son of Perez, son of Judah, son of Israel [Col. 1058D]. Now where it is said there, “But Sheshan had no sons, only daughters,” this is because his sons—or rather, Elimelech’s sons, namely Mahlon and Chilion, of whom he was the grandfather—died without children. Again, it is written in Chronicles:

> And the kindreds of the house of those who worked fine linen, of the house of the oath; and he who caused the sun to stand still, and the men of Falsehood, and Secure, and Burning. These were princes in Moab, and those who returned to Lehem; but these words are ancient. These are the sons of the potter, dwelling in plantations and hedges, with the king in his works; and they remained there. (1 Chron. 4)

Tradition has it that this was Elimelech, in whose time the sun stood still because of transgressions against the Law, so that, seeing so great a miracle, they might turn back [Col. 1059A] to the Lord their God. Because they scorned to do so, famine consequently grew severe. And he, since he seemed foremost in the tribe of Judah, was driven from his homeland by the hardship of famine with his wife and sons, and moreover died with his sons during that same exile.

The “men of Falsehood” are his sons Mahlon and Chilion, who are there called Secure and Burning, and of whom it is said that they were princes in Moab because they took Moabite wives. This is stated more explicitly in Hebrew, as we have learned from scholars of that language: they are called not princes but husbands. What follows—“those who returned to Lehem”—shows that Naomi and [Col. 1060A] Ruth returned to Bethlehem, that is, to “the house of bread,” after they had heard of the abundance of bread in Bethlehem following the scarcity of famine. Since this history is written in the book of Ruth, the words therefore follow: “But these words are ancient.”

By “potters dwelling in plantations and hedges” he means the offspring propagated from Ruth. This planting is said to have dwelt among hedges and plantations when it attained royal dignity. “They remained there,” that is, in Bethlehem, with the king in his works, because King David arose from them, whose deeds are proclaimed with wondrous praises.

385. **R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, The Forty-Two Books On the Trinity and Its Works. On the Books of Kings**

## Book One. (1 Kings 1–16)

[Col. 1059]

## Chapter I. That David was the beginning of the fourth age of the world; and how this age corresponds to the fourth day of the first days of the world.

After the broad spectacle of the green and most flourishing third age, the splendid fourth age of the world at last receives us. Its radiant beauty raises the eyes of our mind, as it were, from earth to heaven, so that, after the practical ordinances of the Law, we may contemplate in part the mighty deeds and heavenly sayings of kings and of the prophets who prophesied under them.

For the plants of the earth, planted or commanded to spring up on the third day, are indeed beautiful; but more beautiful are the lights of heaven, made or set in the firmament on the fourth day. Thus the works of the holy Law, commanded during the third age of the world as a figure of things to come, are indeed beautiful and good; but more beautiful are the deeds and sayings of crowned kings and prophets, which shone forth as types of the kingdom of God and as testimony to the great and true King, Christ [Col. 1059C].

I would rightly say that this fourth age exults with the fourth day in praise of the Creator, and that, according to the works of both, the Holy Spirit is proclaimed the Spirit of strength. For on the fourth day the lights adorned the firmament in their powers and most fixed orders; and in the fourth age, through sung psalms and prophetic writings, [Col. 1060B] the word of God prevailed by royal authority, and the word of promise was enlarged.

In what respect? Namely, in that he who had hitherto been promised to Abraham the father as a man, or as the seed to be called in Isaac (Gen. 21), is now promised as king, with the oath spoken to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131). Again: “Once have I sworn by my Holy One: Shall I lie to David? His seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun before me, and as the moon perfect for ever, and as a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. 38).

This especially distinguishes this age from the preceding one: that the former was the third, while this is now counted as the fourth. Therefore, carrying through the course we have begun to the glory of Christ, Son of God, King of kings and Lord of prophets, we enter this age, with the holy Spirit of strength going before us and being gracious [Col. 1060C] to us, if he deigns to do so.

## Chapter II. That the first and second books of Kings are called Samuel among the Hebrews; and that Saul’s kingdom signified the kingdom of sin, but David’s the kingdom of Christ.

The first and second books of Kings are called Samuel among the Hebrews, because the kingdom of Saul and the kingdom of David, which these books contain, were ordered through him as a kind of mediator between God and kings. The name Samuel is interpreted “God.” By this name the Word of God is rightly signified, through whom [Col. 1061A] the kingdom of sin has indeed been destroyed and the kingdom of righteousness built up.

For Saul, whom the Lord gave in anger to the sinning people, saying to Samuel, “For they have not rejected you, but me, lest I should reign over them” (1 Kings 3), prefigured the kingdom of sin and death, which the human race, having cast off God’s yoke, most foolishly desired. Saul’s own name signifies this, for it is interpreted “request.”

But David, whom the Lord, after Saul’s rejection, chose according to his own heart, signifies the kingdom of righteousness, the kingdom of Christ, which God graciously bestowed upon the human race after destroying the kingdom of sin. Nor was it only the kingdom: the primacy of the priesthood also, transferred by this forerunner from the descendants of Eli to Zadok, was a figure of the true priesthood which was to be transferred from the Jews to the Church [Col. 1061B] of Christ. Thus the first book of Kings begins with Samuel himself, since he is the twelfth and last of the Judges.

## Chapter III. Concerning Elkanah and his wives Hannah and Peninnah; Hannah’s prayer; and Samuel’s birth.

(Chapter 1.) “There was a man at Ramathaim-zophim, of Mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, son of Jeroham, son of Elihu, son of Tohu, son of Zuph, an Ephrathite; and he had two wives. The name of one was Hannah, and the name of the other Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children.”

Ramathaim means “two heights,” and these two heights are understood as the two tribes, namely the royal and the priestly. That Elkanah’s father was from the tribe of [Col. 1061C] Levi is most fully taught by the book of Chronicles (1 Chron. 6), where the sequence of his genealogy is carried back to Levi. His mother too is shown to have been from the tribe of Judah in that he is called an Ephrathite. He was called an Ephrathite from Ephrath, wife of Caleb, who is known to have been from the tribe of Judah (1 Chron. 2).

And if anyone is troubled that he is called an Ephrathite from Ephrath rather than Ephraim, let him see later on (1 Kings 17) how David is called the son of an Ephrathite, though it is plainly evident that Jesse was not from Ephraim but from the tribe of Judah. Thus let him recognize that Elkanah likewise is called an Ephrathite from Ephrath (1 Chron. 6), not from Ephraim. Zophim means “watchers.”

“From Mount Ephraim.” He is said to have been from Mount Ephraim because his dwelling was there. For there is no doubt that Levites had dwellings within all the tribes. “And that man went up from his city on appointed days.” At the three feasts—Passover, Pentecost, and the feast of Tabernacles—he went up to the house of the Lord.

“And he gave portions to Peninnah his wife and to all her sons and daughters.” These portions are understood to be garments, which, according to the custom of that people, were distributed to wives, children, and servants at those same three festivals.

“Do not consider your handmaid to be like one of the daughters of Belial, for out of the abundance of my sorrow and grief I have spoken until now.” Belial means “without a yoke.” It should be noted that all who pursue drunkenness are called sons of Belial.

“And after he had weaned him, she brought him with her, with three calves, three measures of flour, and an amphora of wine; and she brought him into the house of the Lord at Shiloh” [Col. 1062A]. In Hebrew one reads not “three measures of flour” but “a measure of flour.” It is evident that this passage has been corrupted among Latin writers through scribal error. For if she offered three measures of flour with three calves, she acted contrary to the Law. For the Law commands:

> The first day of the seventh month shall be venerable and holy to you. You shall do no servile work; it is a day of sounding and trumpets. And you shall offer a burnt offering of sweetest fragrance to the Lord: one young bull from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished lambs; and for their sacrifice, fine flour mixed with oil, three tenths for each bull, two tenths for the ram, one tenth for [Col. 1062B] each lamb. This tenth is the tenth part of an ephah.

From this it is understood that Elkanah did not offer three measures of flour with the three calves, but nine tenths, which according to the Hebrew measure make one ephah.

Therefore holy Samuel is the fruit of prayer, obtained by the great faith and abundant tears of his mother. In his mother Hannah he has an example of virtue which our barren soul should imitate, if it desires to become a mother, if it longs to be fruitful in the Word of God and holy virtues. In what? Namely, in what was said: “and her countenance was no longer changed in different ways”; which is the same as saying: she stood firm in temptation and persevered in prayer. Let the faithful soul therefore imitate this: seeking, it will find; asking, it will receive; to one who knocks, it will be opened.

Now we shall expound the Song of this prophetess Hannah; and, to relieve weariness, we shall gather the mysteries of these matters, which have been related in straightforward narrative, as though by singing rather than reading or speaking.

## Chapter IV. That Hannah, who sang the Song and had been barren, signifies the same thing as Sarah according to the Apostle; and that Peninnah signifies the same as Hagar.

(Chapter 2.) “My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.” She who sings is a prophetess, and is herself made fruitful by the grace which she also signifies by her proper name; for Hannah means “grace.” Yet she prophesies and proclaims not her own personal present condition, but the future common blessings of the whole holy Church [Col. 1062D].

Therefore let us understand mystically the same thing in Hannah as in Sarah, the same in Peninnah as in Hagar, although this woman was free and that one a handmaid, and the same in Elkanah as in Abraham. For the events are in part alike and the names related in meaning. Abraham—that is, “father of many nations”—was first called Abram, which means “exalted father” (Gen. 18); and this man Elkanah, whose name means “God’s possession,” is written to have come from Ramathaim, that is, “the heights.”

Hagar means “turned” or “converted”; Peninnah means “conversion.” Sarah, however, means “princess”; Hannah means “grace,” and in each is to be understood the primacy of grace. For they gave birth not according to the flesh, as did Hagar and Peninnah, or according to the quality of their flesh, but [Col. 1063A] according to grace, though they had first been barren.

Thus Peninnah and Hannah are the two Testaments: one begetting into slavery according to the flesh, the other begetting into freedom by faith. For Elkanah, “God’s possession,” is the people of God itself, to which it was said: “He possessed you and made you and created you” (Deut. 32). In Abraham it received, indeed, in Abraham’s seed—which is Christ—the testament of faith, the testament of freedom; but on Mount Sinai, four hundred and thirty years later, it received the testament of flesh, the testament of slavery.

Yet the testament of flesh, as a testament of slavery, like Peninnah or Hagar, first bore many children, while the testament of faith, like Hannah or Sarah, long lamented its barrenness. For the children of the flesh first multiplied in that people, boasting in Abraham’s flesh, while his faith scarcely produced any offspring in a very few. Indeed, all those who came out of Egypt, twenty years old and above, except Joshua and Caleb son of Jephunneh, showed that they were descended from Abraham’s flesh alone, not also from his faith [Col. 1063B].

At last faith or grace, formerly barren, bore many through the Gospel; and the boasting of the flesh, which had many children, was weakened—indeed, excluded. Knowing by the prophetic Spirit that this was prefigured in herself, she exults and gives praise in the person of the Church, saying:

387. ## Chapter V. An exposition of her Song, in which, magnificently prophesying the mysteries of Christ and [Col. 1063C] the Church, she glories in the Lord and condemns the pride of the synagogue, typified by her who had many children.

“My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my horn has been exalted in my God.” Where only the flesh is fruitful, there is no ground for the heart to exult; for there is no exultation of heart except in the Lord. Therefore, when she says, “My heart has exulted in the Lord,” she indicates that she is singing the exultation of the universal Church which another prophet proclaims: “From fear of you, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth to spirit; we have not wrought salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26).

There it is not the flesh but the heart that exults, although the heart, first exulting, also lifts the flesh into fellowship with its exultation, according to David’s words: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). That exultation is strong, and its joy is not empty but most mighty. She therefore adds: “And my horn has been exalted in my God.” The prophet says likewise in the singular: “My horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn” (Ps. 91); and likewise in the plural: “The horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. 47); yet the thing is not different.

For the one horn of the Church is the one Christ, and its many horns are the many gifts of the Holy Spirit. Thus the true Lamb is written to have, as seven eyes, so also seven horns (Rev. 5). “My horn of this kind,” she says, “has been exalted in my God”—in my God, I say, and not in myself, for that would be vain confidence and deceptive strength [Col. 1064A].

Hence come both the inward exultation of the heart and outward confidence over my enemies. For this too is what follows: “My mouth has been enlarged over my enemies, because I have rejoiced in your salvation.” Let my enemies, formerly talkative—the children of flesh and not of faith—be humbled and speak from the earth. For now, by a reversal, authority to speak has been given to me, so that I no longer whisper in corners or speak with half a mouth, but may speak with enlarged mouth over my enemies, who reproach me for barrenness, in such a way that I may be heard throughout the world: “because I have rejoiced in your salvation.” God’s salvation is Christ.

Does one woman then exult only in Samuel? Or rather, in one holy mother, does the universal Church sing her true exultation in Christ? In these two verses of the song the meaning is not different, though the words are different and reversed. For “my heart has exulted in the Lord” is the same as “I have rejoiced in your salvation”; and “my horn has been exalted in my God” is the same as “my mouth has been enlarged over my enemies.”

Now let us hear what she brings forth worthy of her enlarged mouth. “There is none holy as the Lord; for there is none other besides you, and there is none strong like our God.” He rightly enlarges his mouth who proclaims not himself but the Lord. He fittingly exalts his horn who commends not his own righteousness but God’s. “There is none holy,” she says, “as the Lord.” She had said too little. Therefore she supplied the words, “for there is none other besides you,” and made an equal assertion: as though she had said, apart from him no one is clean from defilement. And “there is none strong,” she says, “like our God.”

To be sure, others are falsely strong, such as those of whom the prophet says in the psalm, “The strong rushed upon me” (Ps. 58). This one is truly strong and is the true strength of the humble. “There is none holy as the Lord; there is none strong like our God.” It is as though she says this to the sons of Hannah against the sons of Peninnah, to the children of grace against the children of the synagogue, to the children of promise against the children of flesh: Why do you boast so often, saying, “We are Abrahamites by nature, we are Israelites by nature and not sinners from among the Gentiles?” (Gal. 2).

“The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was one who understood or sought God. All turned aside; together they became useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13). The Law says this; and whatever the Law says, the Apostle says, we know that it speaks [Col. 1064D] to those who are under the Law (Rom. 3). Therefore no one is holy; there is none other besides you—none, I say, who can sanctify except you, O Christ, Holy of Holies. Even those saints before you came confessed this in their own words: “All our righteousnesses are as the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64).

And why do you glory in the strong men Moses and Aaron, in the strength of your Law and your priesthood? There is none strong like our God, like our Christ. For Moses and Aaron, your Law and your priesthood, did not conquer the spiritual Pharaoh, nor did they destroy him who had the dominion of death, that is, the devil. But this one conquered him; this one broke hell; this one, having conquered death, rose again. Therefore “there is none strong like our God,” like this our Savior. Therefore:

“Do not multiply proud speech in your boasting.” You boast greatly; you raise yourselves greatly; in empty glory you utter many lofty things. For example, saying: “Abraham is our father” (John 8); the covenant is ours, the legislation is ours, the worship is ours, the promises are ours, the glory is ours, the adoption as sons is ours (Rom. 9); Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are our fathers. Do not speak so; do not multiply such lofty speech from your magnificent mouth; do not boast so.

“Let old things depart from your mouth, because the Lord is a God of knowledge, and thoughts are prepared for him.” These lofty things which you have hitherto multiplied in speech are old things; they have now grown old and are to be cast away as things succeeding them come upon you. For this is what the Lord, the God of knowledge, says in Jeremiah—he who formerly gave you knowledge of the letter and now gives us knowledge of the Spirit, as he wills:

> Behold, days are coming, and I shall make a new covenant with the house of Israel and the house of Judah: not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers on the day when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, a covenant which they made void, though I was their master, says the Lord. But this shall be the covenant which I shall make with the house of Israel: after those days I shall put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their heart. (Jer. 31)

“And thoughts,” she says, “are prepared for him”—that is, intelligent thoughts; for, by contrast, he withdraws himself from thoughts that are without understanding (Wis. 1). Thoughts are prepared for the Lord, the God of knowledge, as an offering. If you wish to earn or obtain from him the gift of knowledge, not many offerings of rams and bulls, but holy thoughts are preparations for this gift. Hence the Psalmist says: “Your ear heard the preparations of their heart” (Ps. 9). Again: “The thought of man shall confess to you, and the remnant of thought shall keep a feast day for you” (Ps. 75).

“The remnant of thought,” he says. If the firstfruits of thought have been hostile, at least its remnant will keep a feast day for you by repentance and confession. Therefore, as I said, “let old things depart from your mouth”; let lofty things depart; let your boasting cease. Why? “The bow of the strong has been overcome, [Col. 1065D] and the weak have been girded with strength.”

This has occurred more than once. When the strength or power of the Egyptians was overcome and the Israelites were strengthened, then indeed the bow of the strong was overcome and the weak were girded with strength. So now also. For the bow—that is, the pride and strength—of Peninnah, in which she boasted because of her children, has been overcome; and I, who was weak through barrenness, have been girded with the strength of children. For this is what follows: “Until the barren woman bore many, and she who had many children became weak.”

For the inserted words, “Those who were first filled hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were filled,” are not sung according to the present setting of this history. Yet this and other such things have happened and do happen, so that whenever the ungodly person is proud, you may sing that royal proverb: “Let not the one who girds himself boast as though he were ungirded” (3 Kings 20).

In the Hebrew and in the translation of the Seventy, one reads not “many” but “seven.” The Jews understand this passage thus: when Samuel was born, the firstborn son of Peninnah died; thereafter, as each son of Hannah was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died in the order of their birth. But one must ask how this can stand, since Peninnah had seven children while Hannah had no more than five. Solving this question, the Hebrews count Samuel’s two sons among Hannah’s children.

According to the anagogical sense, “the bow of the strong”—that is, the confidence of the Jews, who say that they are Jews and are not, but lie: the confidence, I say, of Jews who presume upon their own strength and desire to establish their own righteousness and thus seek to submit themselves to God’s righteousness—this “bow has been overcome.” “The prophet says, ‘They bent their tongue like a bow of falsehood and not of truth’” (Jer. 9). Such is the bow of the strong which has been overcome, for they accomplished nothing by shooting against the truth, as is written elsewhere: “The arrows of little children became their wounds” (Ps. 67).

But “the weak,” namely those who attribute nothing to their own powers, who glory not in their own works but in faith in Christ Jesus, “have been girded with strength”—with the strength, I say, by which they can do violence to the kingdom of heaven and seize it by force (Matt. 11) [Col. 1066B].

“Those who were first filled,” she says, “hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were filled.” We Gentiles were formerly hungry; but the Jews were filled, that is, satisfied. It is certain that now the Gentiles are satisfied through the Word of God, by the Gospel of his Son Jesus Christ. The Jews, however, are hungry, following only the chaff of the letter and not possessing the life-giving Spirit.

But have they hired themselves out for bread? Do they prefer to hunger rather than eat the living bread with us? For such is the parable of the evangelical father: when he had received his hungry son, who had gone away into a far country and there squandered all his substance in living extravagantly—when, I say, he had received him upon his return and was celebrating a great feast, his elder brother was indignant and refused to enter (Luke 15).

Therefore for the present those who were once filled are hungry, while the hungry are satisfied, according to the prophet’s threat: “Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall hunger” (Isa. 65). Yet the time will come when they will not disdain to hire themselves out for bread. For when the fullness of the hungry Gentiles has entered in, a remnant from them will turn to eat the bread of life.

The bow of the strong has been overcome to no small degree, and the weak have been girded with strength; and, when the hungry have been satisfied, those who were formerly full now hunger. But what follows? “Until the barren woman bore many, and she who had many children became weak.” The change wrought by the right hand of the Most High was so great in the breaking of the strong and the girding of the weak that she who was barren bore many, while she who had many children and was proud became most completely weak. Thus was fulfilled [Col. 1067A] the prophecy sung by another:

> Praise, O barren woman who do not bear; sing praise and a hymn, you who did not give birth, says the Lord, because the children of the deserted woman are many, more than those of her who had a husband, says the Lord. Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Make your cords long and strengthen your stakes. For you shall break forth to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit nations and inhabit desolate cities. (Isa. 54)

And the rest.

What has been sung thus far considers all the Lord’s ways, namely mercy and judgment. Therefore, in praise of these same great things—mercy and judgment—she continues more sonorously and at greater length, with exultant heart and enlarged mouth, and says:

“[Col. 1067B] The Lord kills and gives life; he brings down to hell and brings back. The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and lifts up.” That the Lord kills belongs to judgment; that he gives life belongs to mercy. Likewise, that he brings down to hell belongs to judgment; that he brings back belongs to mercy. So too, that he makes poor belongs to judgment, while that he makes rich belongs to mercy. Again, that he humbles belongs to judgment, while that he lifts up belongs to mercy.

Thus, through these antitheses—that is, opposites—all the ways of the Lord are presented for contemplation by those who seek his covenant and testimonies. But toward what sort of persons is judgment or truth directed, and for what sort is mercy stored up? Toward whom, if not the proud, does he exercise judgment by killing, bringing down to hell, humbling, and making poor? Conversely, whom does he give life to, bring back [Col. 1067C] from hell, enrich, and lift up, if not the humble?

It follows: “Raising the needy from the dust, lifting the poor from the dungheap, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.” What is the needy and poor person except the one whom the Lord in his Gospel calls blessed: poor in spirit, that is, humble? (Matt. 5). The Lord raises from the dust and lifts from the dungheap the person whom he justifies and adorns with the splendor of his grace: one who wisely recognizes that he is dust and ashes and who is ashamed of the dung of his sins. He does this so that such a person may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory, with those, namely, whom he foreknew and predestined before the ages, called, justified, and glorified.

This has happened neither rarely nor only in a few. More fully and principally, however, we rejoice and continually sing that this happened in him who is truly known to have said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11). Of him too it is said: “He persecuted the poor and needy man, and the one pierced in heart, to put him to death” (Ps. 108).

For the Lord the Father truly put him to death by the command of his love, brought him down to hell, made him poor, and humbled him; and by the power and omnipotence of his divinity he gave that same one life again, brought him back from hell, enriched and exalted him. He raised him from the dust of our mortality; he lifted him from the dungheap, so that his flesh should not see the dung of corruption. And behold: with princes—indeed, above all princes—he sits at the right hand of the Father and holds the throne of glory.

That this is the proper understanding is proved by the conclusion of the Song [Col. 1068A]. For it closes as follows: “And he shall give dominion to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ. For the hinges of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them.” In Hebrew it reads: “For the afflicted of the earth are the Lord’s.” The Hebrews understand “the afflicted of the earth” as the poor in spirit, the humble in heart, and say that the Lord set the world upon them because they maintain that the earth stands through their merits.

Thus the proposition is splendid when she says, “Raising the needy from the dust,” and so forth; the still more splendid reason confirms the same point when she now says: “For the hinges”—that is, the afflicted—“of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them.” In agreement with this, Gospel truth places the poor in spirit at the foundation of blessedness when, about to enumerate the eight beatitudes, it begins: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5; Luke 5).

“[Col. 1068B] He shall keep the feet of his servants.” Those needy and poor persons—those, I say, who are the hinges and afflicted of the earth—are the Lord’s saints; and he “shall keep their feet,” that is, he who will not keep the feet of the proud. Fearing their fall and irrecoverable ruin, the Prophet says: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner move me” (Ps. 35). He immediately adds: “There have fallen those who work iniquity; they have been driven out and could not stand” (ibid.).

Therefore, “he shall keep the feet of his saints”—the feet, I say, of his servants, that is, the humble—so that they may reach the throne of glory and, indeed, may be able by steadfast merits to bear the world placed upon them. Thus far she has stated what sort the Lord gives life to, brings back from hell, enriches, and exalts; she now declares what sort he kills, brings down to hell, makes poor, and humbles. For it follows: “And the ungodly shall be silent in darkness, because man shall not be strengthened by his own strength.”

“The ungodly,” she says—that is, the proud, who now in their own day lift up their horn on high and speak iniquity against God (Ps. 74)—“shall be silent in darkness.” While the humble hold the throne of glory and praise the Lord God their possessor, they shall rest in the darkness of hell; indeed, wailing, they shall gnash their teeth and weep, for “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8).

“Because man,” she says, “shall not be strengthened by his own strength.” For how much strength will a man have there? When soon afterward his neck has been brought down into mud, then the ungodly person will confess that no one is strengthened either by a horse or by his own legs, just as another prophet says: “He shall not delight in the strength of a horse, nor shall he take pleasure in the legs of a man” (Ps. 146). “A horse is deceitful for salvation, and in the abundance of its strength it shall not be saved” (Ps. 32).

Moreover, to speak in a more spiritual sense: “man shall not be strengthened by strength,” that is, no one shall be justified before God by works of the Law, in which the sons of Peninnah—that is, the Jews—glory. Nor, indeed, shall anyone at all, whether Jew or Greek, be saved or justified in judgment if he is judged apart from mercy, or only according to his own merits.

[Col. 1069A] “His adversaries shall fear the Lord, and above them he shall thunder in the heavens.” This has at times happened visibly: the Lord thundered in the heavens over his adversaries, as in the book of Joshua: “When they fled before Israel and were on the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord sent great stones from heaven upon them as far as Azekah, and they died; far more died from the hailstones than those whom the children of Israel struck with the sword” (Josh. 10). But from that time this has taken place more magnificently: namely, the Lord thunders in the heavens over his adversaries, ever since he himself, who was put to death as needy and poor and led down to the lower regions, was restored to life, brought back from the lower regions, and exalted, so as to sit with the princely Father and possess the throne of glory. From that time he has thundered over his adversaries [Col. 1069B] with the great and dreadful thunder of the Gospel, and he will not cease to thunder until the end of the age, as the Apostle says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and injustice of men, who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness,” etc. (Rom. 1). Hence too is that which the Prophet foretold: “And the Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice: hail and coals of fire. And he sent forth his arrows and scattered them; he multiplied lightnings and troubled them” (Ps. 17), etc. The final movement of the one who thunders will strike his terrified adversaries with a great and irrevocable thunderbolt. For he will say to those at his left: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).—“The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and shall give [Col. 1069C] dominion to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ.”

It is as though it said: This distinction between the proud and the humble which I have foretold does not yet appear. For not every needy and poor person yet possesses the throne of glory; not every wicked person has been silenced in darkness; nor in this present life do all his adversaries fear the Lord. Indeed, on the contrary, the wicked now live in such security and exalt themselves over the humble that the humble person, still weak, is almost shaken. For he is the one—or the one in whose person the Prophet speaks in the Psalm—who says: “But as for me, my feet were almost moved, my steps nearly slipped, because I envied the enemies when I saw the peace of sinners,” etc. (Ps. 72). Therefore the distinction does not yet appear; but do not be troubled. For “the Lord shall judge the ends of the earth.” For the present he overlooks the vices of the earth; that is, he does not immediately judge or punish the earth’s pride where it begins, but he will certainly judge its end. For the merciful Creator both endures human evils through his patience and sometimes remits them through the conversion of some, so that they may return, even if late, and may at least be ashamed that they were awaited so long. But he will surely judge at last, at the end, on the day of wrath and revelation of his righteous judgment, the proud earth which despises the riches of his goodness and, not knowing that God’s patience awaits it, stores up wrath for itself according to its hardness and impenitent heart; on that day he will render to each according to his works (Rom. 2). “And he shall give,” she says, “dominion to his king.” To his king, I say—that is, to Christ. For it follows [Col. 1070A]: “And he shall exalt the horn of his Christ.” He will give dominion to this king and exalt his horn, namely, so that all things may be subjected beneath his feet. “That which is to come,” says the Apostle, “of which we speak—for we do not yet see,” he says, “all things subjected to him” (Heb. 2). He will give, moreover, according to humanity to him who possesses all things according to divinity; he will give, I say, to him who earned it through obedient suffering, just as, having conquered death, he now says as one who has earned his reward: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28). The Apostle, speaking with notable eloquence, declares his exalted horn: “For this reason God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and [Col. 1070B] every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

## CHAPTER VI. How Eli’s sons sinned; how, while the priestly men were sinning, the boy Samuel ministered before the Lord; and what law Eli transgressed by rebuking his sons far too gently and tenderly, saying, “Do not, my sons,” etc.

“But the boy Samuel was a minister in the sight of the Lord, before Eli the priest. Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial, knowing neither the Lord nor the priests’ duty toward the people. But whenever anyone sacrificed a victim, the priest’s servant came while the flesh was being cooked, with a three-pronged fork in his hand, and thrust it into the pan or kettle or pot or cauldron; and whatever [Col. 1070C] the fork brought up, the priest took for himself,” etc.

Scripture presents three crimes of Eli’s sons, and for these calls them sons of Belial. The first is already found in the words: “Whatever the fork brought up, the priest took for himself.” For under the law of sacrifice the priest was not entitled to take whatever he wished, but certain portions: namely, the breast and the right shoulder—the breast of the elevation-offering, I say, and the shoulder of separation—as is set out more fully in Leviticus (chs. 7, 8) and Exodus (ch. 29).

Their second sin is in what follows: “Even before they burned the fat, the priest’s servant came and said to the one sacrificing: Give me flesh, that I may cook it for the priest. For [Col. 1070D] I will not take boiled flesh from you, but raw. And the sacrificer said to him: Let the fat first be burned today according to the custom, and then take for yourself whatever your soul desires. But he answered him: By no means. For you will give it now; otherwise I shall take it by force.” The sacrificer rightly said, “Let the fat first be burned,” because by the command of the Lord’s law it was customary for the fat of the victim to be burned first (Exod. 29; Lev. 3, 7).
