Their third sin was that “they slept with the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle.” The Hebrews say that they are called to have slept with the women because, after menstruation or childbirth, before the sacrifice prescribed by the law had been completed, they persuaded these women to return to their husbands and have intercourse with them. They are therefore said to sleep with them because they caused them to sleep with [Col. 1071A] their husbands contrary to the precept of the law. Thus Eli himself says a little later: “For the report which I hear is not good: you cause the people of the Lord to transgress.” The people committed transgression because, without sacrifice being duly completed, they joined themselves to their wives. For just as they forcibly extorted flesh from the sacrificer, so too they extorted it from the offerer; and therefore, as by taking away the flesh they made people disparage the Lord’s sacrifice, so likewise, by joining with their wives, they caused God’s people to transgress.

“But Samuel,” he says, “ministered before the Lord as a boy.” It is as though it were said plainly: While the priestly men made the Lord’s sacrifice contemptible, there remained this one boy, upon whom, as upon a small peg, all hope of restoration hung; in him the Lord, who suffered wrong, suspended some remnants of his honour. In a sin so grave by his sons, their father—the chief priest, who himself also judged Israel—ought no longer to have exercised paternal affection, but, moved by zeal for God, judicial severity. For the law had commanded that, in a matter of justice, not even a father should spare his son. “If,” it says, “a man begets a stubborn and rebellious son, who does not obey the command of father and mother, and who, when corrected, despises obedience, they shall seize him and bring him to the elders of that city and to the gate of judgment, and shall say to them: This our son is stubborn and rebellious; he despises hearing our admonitions; he devotes himself to feasting, luxury, and banquets. The people of the city shall stone him, and he shall die, so that you may remove [Col. 1071C] evil from your midst, and all Israel, hearing of it, may be afraid” (Deut. 21). How much more ought a priestly man, putting aside such carnal affections, to have disowned his sons and manfully cut off this domestic evil? For Moses likewise said in blessing Levi: “He who said to his father and mother: I do not know you; and to his brothers: I do not recognize them; and they did not know their sons: these have kept your word and preserved your covenant, your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel. They shall place incense in your wrath and a whole burnt-offering upon your altar” (Deut. 33).

But Eli, displaying no stern discipline of a master, merely stammered the blandishments of an aged father: “Do not, my sons,” he says. “For the report which I hear is not good: you cause the people of the Lord to transgress.” Nor had he, through age, returned to childish foolishness; rather, through negligence he fostered their crimes, not through lack of understanding. For in the same place he uttered a weighty and mature sentence, worthy of wise hearers: “If a man sins against a man, God can be appeased for him; but if a man sins against God, who will pray for him?” He says that sinning against a man is not the same as sinning against God, because sin against a man is any ordinary sin and its remission is easier, while sinning against God—that is, departing from his worship—is the sin of impiety and its remission is harder. And because, when someone sins against a man, by appeasing that man he makes the man appeasable toward himself, but when someone sins against God, who will pray [Col. 1072A] for him? That is to say: through whom can he make God, against whom he has sinned, propitious to himself?

Therefore his case was taken up by the Lord himself, who judges rightly and fittingly; and from him a just sentence was thus pronounced both against the father and against the sons.

## CHAPTER VII. On the man of God who came to Eli, what and how great were the things he foretold to him, and on the word of the Lord to Samuel concerning Eli

“Now a man of God came to Eli and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Was I not plainly revealed to the house of your father when he was in Egypt in Pharaoh’s house, and did I not choose him from all the tribes of Israel as my priest?” etc.

The Jews say that this man of God was Phinehas, whom they also maintain to have been Elijah. The Lord is truly said to have been revealed to the house of his father, that is, Aaron, in the place where he says: “The Lord said to Aaron: Go to meet Moses in the wilderness” (Exod. 4). There the Lord is said first to have revealed himself to him. He was chosen as priest from all the tribes of Israel, as you have in *Hellesmoth* [Exodus] (chs. 28, 29) and *Vagecra* [Leviticus] (ch. 9).

But they suppose that the statement, “A certain man of God came to Eli,” and the rest that follows, was spoken before the time of Elkanah, but is inserted here for Samuel’s glory. “Behold, days are coming, and I shall cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house”—by “arm” he means the ark and the dignity of the priesthood—“so that there shall be no old man in your house.” By an old man he means a great priest. “And you shall see your rival in the temple amid all [Col. 1072C] Israel’s prosperity.” The rival of Eli’s house was the priest Zadok, who, after Solomon expelled Abiathar, received the priesthood, as is read in Kings: “And Solomon cast out Abiathar, so that he should no longer be priest of the Lord, in order that the word of the Lord which the Lord had spoken concerning the house of Eli might be fulfilled” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 2).

—“Nevertheless, I shall not utterly remove a man of yours from my altar, but so that your eyes may fail and your soul waste away.” The Lord says that he will not utterly take from Eli’s house a man from his altar so that there might always be a man of Eli’s house in God’s house who, seeing another appointed in the dignity of the priesthood and seeing himself deprived of that dignity, would have his eyes fail and his soul waste away. Hence it is said in [Col. 1072D] what follows: “Let him come that he may worship him”—that is, the high priest—“and receive from him a silver coin and a cake of bread, and say: Allow me, I beg you, to have one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.”

Then the boy Samuel came close by as another witness, proved in a wondrous and magnificent order: namely, commended by God before he was known either to himself or to others. Thus it was divinely arranged, for the commendation of the faithful prophet, that the high priest should understand before the boy himself that his calling had been made by God, as Scripture says: “Therefore Eli understood that the Lord was calling the boy, and he said to Samuel: Go and sleep; and if he calls you again, say: Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.” [Col. 1073A] And so it happened. Samuel’s word came not only to Eli but to all Israel. For his word to all Israel was that they would be struck by the Philistines because of the sins of Eli’s sons; subsequent events proved that word true. When the Philistines fought, a very great slaughter took place, and thirty thousand foot soldiers of Israel fell; the ark of God was captured. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, also died. Eli himself, their father, old and advanced in years, upon receiving the sad news, fell backward from his seat beside the gate, broke his neck, and died (1 Sam. 4). Holding to the plain history in all these things, let us seek the mysteries.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the statement, “The sons of Eli, sons of Belial, not knowing [Col. 1073B] the Lord”: that Eli signifies the old priesthood, and his two sons the two high priests of that period, Annas and Caiaphas

“The sons of Eli,” he says, “were sons of Belial, knowing neither the Lord nor the priests’ duty toward the people,” and the rest. Eli, old and advanced in years, signifies the old priesthood—indeed, a priesthood worn out and obsolete, such as it is known to have been at that time when the Lord Jesus wept over the city of Jerusalem, destined to fall together with it and with the old temple (Luke 19). Eli’s two sons signify the two high priests of that period, Annas and Caiaphas, truly “not knowing the Lord nor the priests’ duty toward the people,” yet sons of Eli, whose name is interpreted “My God.” For they indeed gloried in this name, so that they said concerning the God of their fathers, “My God, my God”; yet, honouring God with their lips, they dishonoured him in heart and works, as the Lord reproaches them in the Gospel (Matt. 15): “Why,” he says, “do you transgress God’s commandment because of your tradition? For God said: Honour father and mother; and: Whoever curses father or mother, let him die the death. But you say: Whoever says to father or mother, Whatever gift is from me shall benefit you, shall not honour his father or his mother. And you have made void God’s commandment because of your tradition.” And immediately: “Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied of you, saying [Isa. 29]: This people honours [Col. 1073C] me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. Yet in vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men.”

Now Hophni is interpreted “barefoot,” and Phinehas “his mouth rested.” By these names the vices of the aforesaid high priests, Annas and Caiaphas, are rightly denounced. With their mouth they indeed rested after the Lord, but in their works they were barefoot; that is, like sons of Eli, they gloried in God by saying with their mouths, “My God, my God,” but in their works denied him. For they did not seek that which was lawful for teachers and priests, namely, the breast of the victim and the right shoulder; rather, “whatever,” he says, “the fork brought up, the priest took for himself.” That is, they did not require anyone to reveal his way to the Lord by pure confession of heart and then produce fruits worthy of repentance—which would be first to receive the breast, and then the right shoulder, from the offerer—but devoted themselves wholly to satisfying their avarice. This was like fishing out whatever flesh they could with a fork or trident, aptly expressing the hook of greed.

Even before they burned the fat, the priest’s servant came and forcibly took flesh to cook for the priest. Clearly, they did not burn in the fire of worthy prayer the sins of the people, which are understood through the fat of the victim; nevertheless, they not only accepted payment for those sins but even forcibly extorted it as hired labourers or workers who had earned their wages. Hence the prophetic rebuke spoken by the Lord against them: “They shall eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4). But those who take care first to burn the fat rightly afterwards provide for flesh to be cooked for themselves, because those who worthily intercede for human sins justly receive their reward; and thus, lawfully serving the altar, they live from the altar.

Likewise, “they slept with the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle,” because they taught their own traditions, not God’s. This was to mingle wickedly in adulterous intercourse with souls seeking God. For one who commends himself rather than God, who sows not God’s teaching but his own (1 Cor. 9), may rightly be said to sleep with the souls keeping watch at the entrance of the heavenly tabernacle; and heavenly judgment condemns this sin as true adultery. For “if,” he says, [Col. 1074C] “a man sins against a man,” etc.

## CHAPTER IX. That the man of God who spoke to Eli mystically signifies the whole choir of prophets, which crushes the confidence of the old priesthood by a bitter confrontation

“Now a man of God came to Eli and said to him: Thus says the Lord: Was I not plainly revealed to the house of your father, when he was in Egypt in Pharaoh’s house? And did I choose him from all the tribes of Israel as my priest, to go up to my altar, burn incense for me, wear the ephod before me, and did I give to the house of your father all the sacrifices of the children of Israel?”

This one man mystically is the whole choir of prophets. For although the prophets are many, God’s word in the mouth of all is one. “Was I not plainly,” he says, “revealed to the house of your father?” And then: “Therefore,” says the Lord God of Israel, “I spoke, saying that your house and your father’s house should minister before me forever. But now the Lord says: Far be this from me! Rather, whoever honours me I shall glorify, but those who despise me shall be dishonoured.”

By a most weighty and bitter confrontation he crushes the disordered confidence of the old priesthood. It is as though he said: Look: you say, you put confidence in lying words, saying, “The Lord has said, the Lord has spoken, the Lord has promised and pledged to Aaron that his house shall minister before him forever. ‘God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change’ [Num. 23]. Therefore, has he said and shall he not do it? Has he spoken and shall he not fulfil it? Let us do as we please and live as we wish: he is unchangeable; our priesthood remains; it cannot be changed.” To this I say: Will it be lawful and fitting for you to change and transgress the law which you profess, but unlawful for me to change my judgment? Therefore I say: I indeed formerly spoke thus and thus, and thus and thus promised. But now I say, “Far be this from me!” Since you have changed, I too shall change. Since you are perverse, I too shall turn contrary. Or has Scripture said to me in vain: “With the holy you shall be holy; with the innocent man you shall be innocent; with the chosen you shall be chosen; and with the perverse you shall be perverse” (Ps. 17)?

Far be it from me, I say, that, because I spoke when I was speaking, I should therefore be obliged to glorify your father’s house forever! This is a hard, shameful, ruinous condition for me: that I should be obliged by a law of debt to glorify anyone because he belongs to your father’s house. But what is the case? “Whoever honours me I shall glorify; but those who despise me shall be [Col. 1075B] dishonoured,” whatever house or nation they may be from. Whether Jew or Greek, whoever honours me, I shall glorify with a glorious kingdom and a glorious priesthood, and I shall make them all a kingdom and priests to God and my Father. Whether Jew or Greek, whoever despises me shall be dishonoured; he can be neither king nor priest. This is my condition; this is the reciprocity I must maintain. Take it as law and say that I have made the promise void. Who are you, a human being, to answer God? Whatever I may have said formerly, this present utterance of mine shall stand, so that heaven and earth shall more easily pass away than this word of mine.

## CHAPTER X. That these days have now come upon the Jewish priesthood, concerning which it was said, “Behold, days are coming, and I shall cut off your arm”: days sad and bitter for the Jewish priesthood, but joyful and pleasant for the priesthood of Christ’s Church

“Behold, days are coming, and I shall cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there shall be no old man in your house; and you shall see your rival in the temple amid all Israel’s prosperity, and there shall be no old man in your house in all days.”

These days have already come and are now present: sad and bitter for the Jewish priesthood and the house of Aaron, but joyful and pleasant for the priesthood of the Church. The Jews’ arm has been cut off because it was flesh; the arm of Aaron’s house has been cut off because it was not the Lord’s arm, but a human arm. “Cursed,” says the prophet, “is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, so that his heart departs from the Lord” (Jer. 17). They trusted in man by glorying, not in Abraham’s end, but in Abraham’s flesh; they made flesh their arm, so that their heart departed from the Lord, through pride in Aaron’s priesthood and through crucifying him whom Aaron prefigured. “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord,” they say; but “behold,” says the Lord, “this house in which my name has been invoked in your sight has become a den of robbers” [Col. 1076A] (Jer. 7). Where now is that temple—indeed, where now is that den of robbers? Where are now the sacrifices of Aaron’s sons, the sacrifices of bulls, goats, lambs, and rams? Therefore Eli’s arm has been cut off; the arm of the old priesthood has been cut off, so that there is no longer an old man in his house, no longer a great priest or high pontiff named in Aaron’s house.

“And you shall see,” he says, “your rival in the temple amid all Israel’s prosperity.” Who is this rival, whom the old priesthood envies, if not he of whom the Prophet says: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109)? This is the great rival: since he is from the tribe of Judah, from which none had stood ready at the altar, the priesthood having been transferred, a transfer of the law too necessarily took place. The Jewish priest, now stripped of office, sees him with a most resentful eye in that temple with which the whole world is content—in that Church spread throughout the whole earth. He sees him, I say, amid all Israel’s prosperity, for all things concerning him are indeed prosperous and peaceful for Israel, as the same Prophet has foretold in another psalm: “Attend prosperously, proceed, and reign” (Ps. 44).

—“Nevertheless,” he says, “I shall not utterly remove a man of yours from my altar, but so that your eyes may fail and your soul waste away, and a great part of your house shall die when it has reached manhood.” In accordance with this the Apostle says: “Has God rejected his people? Far be it! For I too am an Israelite, of Abraham’s seed, from the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11). And then: “So therefore in this time also, a remnant has been saved according to the election of God’s grace” (ibid.).—“Nevertheless,” he says, “I shall not utterly remove a man of yours from my altar.” But what then? “So that,” he says, “your eyes may fail and your soul waste away.” Let your eyes fail, I say, as the same Apostle says: “He gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they might not see and ears that they might not hear, unto this present day” (ibid.). And David says: “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling-block and a recompense to them. Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see, and bend their back forever” [Col. 1076D] (Ps. 68). And later: “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own sight: blindness has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel might be saved” (Rom. 11).

—“And a great part,” he says, “of your house shall then die”—which is the greater misery—“when it has reached manhood”; that is, when the fullness of time has arrived. It shall die, I say, not only by the evil sword that separates the soul from God, but also by the Roman sword that separates the soul from the body. “And I shall raise up for myself,” he says, “a faithful priest, who shall do according to my heart and my soul; and I shall build him a faithful house, and [Col. 1077A] he shall walk before my Christ all his days.”

This faithful priest is understood to be Christ, who is also fittingly signified by the name Zadok, of whom we spoke above according to the letter. For the name means “righteous.” And the righteous, truly holy priest or high priest is he of whom the Apostle says: “Such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners,” etc. (Heb. 7). Therefore, “I shall raise up for myself,” he says, “a faithful priest”—faithful, I say, because he faithfully offers himself—“having no need daily, as the priests do, first to offer sacrifices for their own sins” (ibid.)—“who shall do according to my heart and my soul”; that is, he shall not enter through the blood of goats or calves, whose flesh I will not eat nor whose blood drink, but through his own blood he shall enter once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption.

The faithful house built for him is the Church, which lives by faith. It is built for him, I say, through the sacrament of blood and water which flowed from his side, just as in a figure of him a woman was formed from the man’s rib in the beginning. This house, once built, “shall walk,” he says, “before Christ all its days,” because Christ’s entire house, the whole Church, is a priestly race; and it walks before Christ all its days by advancing from strength to strength.

“But it shall come to pass that whoever remains in your house shall come to be prayed for, and shall offer a silver coin and a cake of bread, [Col. 1077C] and shall say: Allow me, I beg you, one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.” Who remains in Eli’s house, in the house of the Jewish priesthood, except one who, by the grace of election, has been or may be able to survive the destruction of that nation? For Scripture says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of it shall return” (Isa. 10; Rom. 9). Thus whoever remains—that is, whoever from this people has been foreordained to life—will come to the rival priest, not to the priesthood of the Synagogue but to that of the Church, now hateful to him, so that prayer may be made for him and he may be reconciled to God through the sacraments of that same Church. He shall offer a silver coin and a cake of bread: that is, the bright word of faith and works of love. And he shall say: “Allow me, I beg you, one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread.” Admit me, I say, to any one allotted share of evangelical grace, so that in the unity of the Church’s body I may eat a morsel of the living bread that came down from heaven, a morsel of the body of Christ, the Son of God, in whom alone is life and without whom no one lives.

## CHAPTER XI. That the boy Samuel came forward as another witness against the priest, and on the statement, “Nor could he see the lamp of God before it was extinguished”

(Chapter 3.) “But the boy Samuel ministered to the Lord before Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious in those days; there was no open vision. [Col. 1078A] It happened on a certain day that Eli lay in his bed and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished. But Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was. And the Lord called Samuel,” etc.

In confirmation of the preceding word, the boy Samuel comes forward here as another witness, so that, according to the law which God himself prescribed for the people (Deut. 19), not merely one witness but two might stand against the priest, who was sluggish and negligent rather than pious, and a lover of his own sons rather than of God. The event is plain. The Lord awakened by calling a third time the sleeping boy, who did not yet know the Lord and to whom the Lord’s word had not yet been revealed, etc. He governed the grace of his call in such a way that the one against whom he was sent should know first that he had been called by the Lord, before the person called knew it himself. Thus the one who would have feared to disclose the vision did not dare conceal it and could not keep silent.

Now the statement, “Nor could he see the lamp of God before it was extinguished,” has various meanings. Some punctuate it thus: “And his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see.” Then they add: “And before the lamp of the Lord was extinguished, the boy Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was.” They wish this to be understood as follows: He slept in the temple before God’s lamp was extinguished—that is, before daylight came, when that lamp was to be extinguished. For the Lord through Moses had commanded that this lamp should shine until morning. Thus in Leviticus: “The Lord says: Command the children of Israel to bring you the purest oil from olive trees, crushed in a mortar, so that the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of the Lord; and Aaron and his sons shall place it there so that it may shine before the Lord until morning” [Col. 1078C] (Lev. 24).

Others read: “Nor could he see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.” The sense is: He who by the merits of his own life and by the dignity of his priesthood was God’s lamp could not see before he was extinguished, deprived of God’s bright grace because of his sons’ sin—his mind darkened by disordered love for his sons, and his body likewise darkened by extreme old age, unable to see.

Others, more simply: “Nor could he see the lamp of God before it was extinguished”; that is, his eyes had become so dim that he could not see the lamp clearly burning in the temple. This indicates that the very old man had not even small remnants of sight left in his eyes. But now let us unfold the veils of the spiritual mysteries.

## CHAPTER XII. What it means mystically that “the boy Samuel slept, and the word of the Lord was precious,” that is, rare; when the Lord mystically comes; and when he called Samuel, who did not know him, a third time, but a fourth time once he knew him
“Samuel the boy was sleeping,” because, with the carnal priesthood of the Jews doomed to perish, the prophetic word had fallen silent. For many days before Christ’s coming no prophet had been seen in Israel. And the prophetic word that had long ago been sent and written was, as it were, sleeping under lock and key; for the Scribes and Pharisees had taken away the key of knowledge, neither entering themselves nor allowing those who wished to enter (Luke XI). Therefore, “Samuel the boy was sleeping, and the word of the Lord was precious,” that is, rare. For rare, indeed almost nonexistent, was anyone who spoke the word of the Lord to those wishing to hear it.

But the Lord came, stood, and called Samuel: he awakened the sleeper. When did the Lord come and stand, except when God descended from heaven in order, having become man, to stand for us? Then he called Samuel; then he awakened the prophetic word, which until then had slept. He awakened, I say, his child; in the child who was the forerunner he awakened his word—namely, in that child of whom it is gloriously sung: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you shall go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke I).

He called him a third time while he did not yet know him, and Zacharias, his father—the former minister of the old priesthood—first understood that calling. For first, the angel announced him by name. Secondly, at Mary’s greeting, while still enclosed in his mother’s womb, he stirred with exultation and joy. Thirdly, once born, through his father’s mouth he proclaimed the office of his own forerunning: “You too shall be called prophet of the Most High.” Thus Eli, the priest who was to be displaced, first understood that the boy was being called by the Lord, because Zacharias, priest of a carnal office, himself first understood and proclaimed the calling of the great prophet: righteous indeed in his own person before God and men, yet the minister of that priesthood which was immediately to be displaced, as has already been said—and still must be said—was prefigured in this priest Eli.

At last, the fourth time, Samuel the boy, now knowing his calling, answered the Lord who came and called as he had the second time: “Samuel, Samuel.” “Speak, Lord,” he said, “for your servant hears.” And the Lord said: “Behold, I will do a thing in Israel at which the ears of everyone who hears it shall ring. On that day I will raise up against Eli all that I have spoken concerning his house. I will begin and I will complete it. For I foretold to him that I would judge his house forever because of his iniquity: because he knew that his sons were acting unworthily and did not rebuke them. Therefore I swore to the house of Eli that the iniquity of his house should never be expiated by sacrifices and offerings” [Col. 1079D].

What did he do in response? He certainly did not rise up like Moses to hold God by that power by which God wishes and can be held, so that, standing in his presence and praying in contrition of heart, he might turn away his wrath from his house (Exod. XXXII; Ps. CV). Instead, he said: “He is the Lord; let him do what is good in his eyes.”

Ahab, though otherwise impious, acted somewhat better and more wisely. When he heard the words of the Lord spoken through Elijah—“Behold, I will bring evil upon you, and I will sweep away your descendants, and I will slay from Ahab everyone who urinates against the wall,” etc.—when, I say, he heard these words, “he tore his garments, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, slept in sackcloth, and walked with his head bowed” (III Kings XXI). Therefore, he did not see in his own days the evil brought upon his house; but Eli both saw it and endured it himself: for, on hearing the grievous report, he fell and died with his neck broken.

Now let us return to what preceded. “Speak, Lord,” he says, “for your servant hears,” etc. Certainly, according to this pattern, that greatest of prophets—first announced by name through an angel, then stirred with joy at the voice of Mary greeting him, thirdly declared, as stated above, by his father’s prophetic voice—at last, the fourth time, knowingly heard in the wilderness that the Lord was speaking. Indeed, while praying that the Lord would speak, he received the sign of the true and righteous priest, God adding: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John I). At the same time, by the Lord’s command, he received a word to speak against the old priesthood. “The word of God,” says Luke, “came upon John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness” (Luke III). And afterwards: “Even now the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (ibid.).

Matthew indicates more plainly that these words were spoken against that priesthood and Levitical ministry: “Seeing many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them: ‘Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?’” (Matt. I). And afterwards: “Even now the axe is laid to the root of the tree.” For the Pharisees were priests or clerics of the Jews. Thus the Lord then swore to the house of Eli that its iniquity would never be expiated by sacrifices and offerings, when through John he declared that the axe had been laid to the root of the tree—of those who did not bear fruit worthy of repentance, especially the Pharisees, who were plundering in the temple of God under the name of priesthood.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the battle badly fought against the Philistines; on the empty rashness with which they said, “Let us bring to ourselves the ark of the Lord who sits upon the Cherubim”; and on what the Stone of Help signified.

(CHAPTER IV.) “And it came to pass in those days that the Philistines assembled for battle. Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and encamped beside the Stone of Help” [Col. 1080D]. And so forth.

Before the narrative that immediately follows, it was stated (chapter III): “And the Lord continued to appear in Shiloh, because the Lord had been revealed to Samuel in Shiloh, according to the word of the Lord.” The meaning is this: since the Lord had been revealed to Samuel in Shiloh by words, he further caused himself likewise to appear in Shiloh by deeds, according to his own word, so that none of his words fell to the ground and all Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, might know that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord.

So indeed, not one word of John the prophet—and more than a prophet—fell to the ground. Let us look back to those days when not the Philistines, but the Romans, whom the Philistines here fittingly prefigure, assembled for battle. “The elders of Israel said,” it is written, “Why has the Lord struck us today before the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the Lord to ourselves from Shiloh; let it come into our midst, that it may save us from the hand of our enemies. Therefore the people sent to Shiloh and brought thence the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, who sits upon the Cherubim.”

That foolish and empty presumption, which then deceived the unwary and those ignorant of God’s justice and glory, likewise deceived them when, shut in by the besieging Roman army, they rioted and cried out in confidence—as histories relate—that God would by no means endure to be deprived of that beautiful temple, that beautiful golden sanctuary. With this emptiness in view, observe how sharply and bitterly, after the words “they brought thence the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts,” Scripture immediately adds, “who sits upon the Cherubim” [Col. 1081B]. For Scripture said this not as expressing its own view, but because of their remarkable vanity.

For what could be more foolish or empty? Did the Lord of hosts sit upon those Cherubim made by Moses—or rather, cast or fashioned by the craftsman Bezalel and his companion Oholiab—captivated by or delighting in the beauty of gold? Does he not rather sit upon human beings, or upon holy angels, who are full of the knowledge of God, according to the meaning of the name *cherubim*?

Thus they were deceived here and there by the same vanity, when, on account of golden images of the heavenly sanctuary, they arrogated to themselves divine assistance as though it were owed to them. For this reason they were false in pitching their camp beside the stone later called the Stone of Help. For then they were disappointed in their expectation, and now they did not have the help of that stone which they rejected to their own ruin, according to what Scripture says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII).

Then one household, that of the priest Eli, fell, with Eli himself also falling and dying with his neck broken. But now the whole nation was taken captive; the whole city, together with its temple, utterly perished in ashes; that priesthood also fell and bore its reproach among all nations, because it was defiled, stained—indeed cast out—by the blood of Christ in which we who believe have life, redemption, and cleansing.

## CHAPTER XIV. What it mystically signifies that the ark of God was captured by those same people by whom Israel was bound; that Dagon fell mutilated before the ark of the Lord; and that the Lord struck them in their hinder parts.

“But the ark of God was also captured.” To continue now the evangelical understanding of the Law: by the same Roman arms and the same emperors’ swords by which that people was besieged, cut to pieces, and led captive among all nations, the Church of God—which is the body of Christ (Col. I)—was also captured and suffered persecution at their hands.

Let us unfold the sails of the glorious vessel and run the course of spiritual understanding. (CHAPTER V.) “The Philistines took the ark of God and carried it from the Stone of Help to Ashdod. And the Philistines took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon and set it beside Dagon. When the Ashdodites arose early on the next day, behold, Dagon lay prostrate upon the ground before the ark of God. They took Dagon and restored him to his place. Again, when they arose on the following morning, they found Dagon lying upon his face on the ground before the ark of the Lord. But the head of Dagon and the two palms of his hands had been cut off upon the threshold; only the trunk of Dagon remained in its place” [Col. 1082A].

A great sight, a great miracle. The glory of the Lord, transferred from Israel, and the ark of the Lord, captured by the foreigners, exacted victory over its conquerors in a reversal of fortune. First the hand of the Lord bore heavily upon their god Dagon, and then upon the people themselves. For, it says, “the villages and fields in the middle of that region swarmed; mice were born, and there was great deadly confusion in the city; and he struck Ashdod and its borders in the secret part of the buttocks, and their protruding tumors rotted.”

The Psalmist magnificently sings of this: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine; and he struck his enemies in their hinder parts and gave them everlasting reproach” (Ps. LXXVII). What this foretold is clear. For when, in the manner described above, the old priesthood fell together with earthly Jerusalem and its man-made temple, then the ark of the Lord entered more victoriously into battle against the gods of the nations. This ark is Christ the Lord, according to his body formed from our flesh, sitting and abiding in his Church, which itself is his body and his fullness.

Before this ark Dagon fell—before it, I say, fell the whole mass of demons signified by that idol, by the very name Dagon. For it is interpreted “fish of sorrow,” signifying, as stated above, him who is in the sea: the great sea-monster Leviathan, the twisting bar-serpent. Such a Dagon fell before the ark of the Lord, finally mutilated in head and with hands cut off; that is, with the kings and princes of the earth removed from his worship, who had formerly stood and gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. II).

But what does it mean that he struck his enemies in their hinder parts, so that their protruding tumors rotted, except that those who refused to receive his victory—who, although understanding God’s power, “did not glorify him as God or give thanks”—were handed over to a reprobate mind? “For their women,” says the Apostle, “exchanged the natural use for that use which is against nature. Likewise the males also, abandoning the natural use of the female, burned in their desires toward one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the recompense due for their error” (Rom. I). Since the terrible judgment of the Lord subjected unbelievers to this most wicked vice, he certainly “struck his enemies in their hinder parts and gave them everlasting reproach.”

And who are those mice which swarmed and laid waste the land, except evil spirits—contemptible as mice to the righteous, but terrible as lions to sinners?

## CHAPTER XV. That the cows carrying the ark of the Lord signify faithful preachers in the Church, who go straight ahead, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

(CHAPTER VI.) By what means, then, was the entire victory accomplished? Surely by the steadfastness and patience of preachers, according to the miracle related next: “Taking two cows that were nursing calves, they yoked them to a cart and shut up their calves at home. They placed the ark of God upon the cart, together with the coffer containing the golden mice and the likenesses of lambs. The cows went straight along the road that leads to Beth-shemesh; they proceeded by one route, walking and lowing, and did not turn either to the right or to the left” [Col. 1083B].

For what do the cows signify except the faithful in the Church, who, while they keep in view the precepts of sacred discourse, carry, as it were, the ark of the Lord laid upon them? It should also be noted concerning them that they are said to have borne young, because many who are inwardly set upon the way of God are outwardly bound by carnal affections. Yet they do not turn aside from the straight path because they carry the ark of God in their mind.

Behold, the cows proceed to Beth-shemesh. Beth-shemesh is interpreted “house of the sun.” And the prophet says: “But for you who fear the Lord, the Sun of righteousness shall arise” (Mal. IV). If therefore we are tending toward the dwelling of the eternal Sun, it is surely fitting that we not turn aside from God’s path because of carnal affections.

With all our strength we must reflect upon the fact that the cows yoked beneath God’s cart proceed and groan. From their inmost parts they utter lowing, yet do not turn their steps from the path. They feel love through compassion, but they do not turn their necks backward. Such indeed ought holy preachers and all faithful persons within the holy Church to be: compassionate toward their neighbors through charity, yet not straying from God’s way through compassion. For the ark laid upon the cows proceeding toward Beth-shemesh is heavenly knowledge drawing near to the dwelling of inward light. But we truly tend toward Beth-shemesh only when, walking the path of uprightness, we do not turn aside toward the neighboring byways of error, even from affection for those dear to us.

Thus, thus must those proceed who, placed beneath the yoke of the sacred Law, now carry the ark of the Lord through inward knowledge: they must not turn aside from the path of uprightness because they grieve over the necessities of their kindred. Their need should indeed hold our mind, but should not turn it back, lest that same mind either become hard if it is untouched by affection, or become lax if, too much affected, it is bent aside.

## CHAPTER XVI. What it signifies that the men of Beth-shemesh rejoiced when they saw the ark of the Lord; that the cows were slain as a burnt offering; and that the men of Beth-shemesh were struck because they saw the ark of the Lord.

“Now the men of Beth-shemesh were reaping wheat in the valley. Raising their eyes, they saw the ark and rejoiced when they saw it. The cart came into the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite and stopped there. There was a great stone there; they chopped up the wood of the cart and placed the cows upon it as a burnt offering to the Lord” [Col. 1084A].

The Hebrews understand this stone, upon which they laid the cows as a burnt offering after chopping up the wood of the cart, to be the altar built by Abraham. This, etc. “The five lords of the Philistines saw it,” it says, “and returned to Ekron that day.”

So indeed the rulers of idolatry saw the perseverance of the preachers already described: namely, that no carnal affections could recall them, and that they even offered their own bodies to the Lord as a burnt offering by exposing them to sufferings. At last, put to shame, they ceased their persecutions.

“These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned to the Lord as a guilt offering: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, one for Ekron; and golden mice according to the number of the cities,” etc. By this number of cities which returned golden tumors and mice is signified the whole body of those who had previously abused the five senses of the body through fornication, but afterwards, fleeing the passions of disgrace described above, redeemed their earlier sins by subsequent good works.

The following words are: “And unto great Abel, upon which they placed the ark of the Lord.” Great Abel is a city on Israel’s border. It is called Great Abel, though it was previously called Beth-shemesh, either because of the mourning there over the men of Beth-shemesh, or to distinguish it from the city Abel-beth-maacah, concerning which the wise woman cried out to Joab: “Let them ask, let them ask in Abel” (III Kings X).

Thus it should be understood that “from the fortified city to the unwalled village, and unto Great Abel,” they gave the mice. “Upon which”—that is, upon the mourning place—“they placed the ark of God, which remained unto that day in the field of Joshua the Beth-shemite” [Col. 1084C]. It remained in his field until it was taken to Kiriath-jearim.

“Now he struck among the men of Beth-shemesh because they had seen the ark of the Lord; and he struck among the people seventy men and fifty thousand of the common people.” The Hebrews understand these seventy men as the seventy judges, whose worth and glory accounted for fifty thousand men, just as it is said of David: “For you alone are counted as ten thousand” (II Kings XVIII). He struck them because they had seen the ark of the Lord: because they had looked into it out of curiosity, though prohibited by the Law. For the Lord says in the book of Numbers: “Aaron and his sons shall enter, and they shall arrange the tasks of each person and assign what each must carry. The others must not curiously look upon the things in the sanctuary before they are wrapped up, lest they die” (Num. IV).

So the judgment of the Lord struck many thousands among the men of Beth-shemesh, men of the house of the sun, ecclesiastical men—many thousands of the people, many leading men—and caused them to go astray, because they had seen the ark of the Lord; because, unworthily, not from zeal for love but from the vice of presumption and curiosity, they had dared to investigate in the Scriptures the secrets of divinity. They became heresiarchs, God judging that the proud should not be admitted to the sight of divinity and truth.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the transfer of the ark of the Lord: that it is nowhere read to have been returned to Shiloh, through which the Synagogue is mystically understood; and that it remained in Kiriath-jearim, a name signifying the Church of the Gentiles.

(CHAPTER VII.) “And from the day when the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, the days multiplied—for it was now the twentieth year—and all the house of Israel rested after the Lord.”

After the twentieth year had been completed, Samuel transferred the same ark to Mizpah (II Chron. I), and Samuel and Saul transferred it from Mizpah to Gilgal. From there Saul transferred it to Nob; from Nob, to Gibeah. From Gibeah David transferred it to the house of Obed-edom; from Obed-edom’s house David transferred it to Zion (II Kings VI); and from Zion Solomon transferred it to the Holy of Holies (III Kings VIII; II Chron. V).

Nowhere thereafter is it read that it was returned to Shiloh, because God rejected and despised that place as a type of the Synagogue, in which the sanctuary of the Lord had once been. But it was rejected and despised, and every holy thing migrated elsewhere. Looking upon this, the prophet says: “He rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh, his tabernacle in which he dwelt among men” (Ps. LXXVII).

Shiloh is interpreted “rupture.” By this name the same Synagogue is severely denoted, because it stood against the Lord and against his Christ, saying: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Ps. II).

But now the ark of the Lord remains in Kiriath-jearim. Kiriath-jearim is interpreted “city of forests,” a name rightly designating the Church of the Gentiles. For it was once a great forest, inhabited by and open to savage beasts—that is, evil spirits—but now it is a city founded upon faith, fortified by the wall of divinity and the protections of angels. Here, therefore, it remains; here the ark of the Lord is to be found.

Thus, after the prophet had said, “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah” (Ps. CXXXI), he immediately added: “We found it in the fields of the forest. We will enter into his tabernacle; we will worship at the place where his feet stood. Arise, Lord, into your rest, you and the ark of your sanctification” (ibid.), etc.

He said this, indeed, overwhelmed by sweet joy; for he had vowed that he would not give sleep to his eyes, drowsiness to his eyelids, or rest to his temples until he found a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob (ibid.): that is, until, by the indication of the Holy Spirit, he should learn in what place the Lord and Savior would rest, and where the God of Jacob would deign to pitch his tabernacle.

Then, as the Spirit suddenly rushed upon him, he said: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah”—of it, I say, that is, of the ark of his sanctification, which we heard had been formed, or was to be formed, from the Virgin’s flesh in Ephrathah; this is Bethlehem. And then he adds: “We found it in the fields of the forest.” It is as though he said: It is no longer found there where we heard of it; it is no longer found among the people from whom it came forth, but among the Gentiles, who formerly were like forests possessed by beasts—that is, evil spirits—but are now, like fields enclosed by the hedges of God’s grace, cultivated and fruitful.

Therefore the ark of the Lord now remains in Kiriath-jearim, and the days multiply: the days, I say, of the saints, the days of virtues; and the multitude of the Gentiles grows toward the light until the appointed time when the remnant of Shiloh—that is, carnal Israel—also shall be saved. And thus “all the house of Israel rests after the Lord”: after the Lord, I say, who said, “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

According to the literal sense, they are said to have rested after the Lord because, casting away the filth of idols, they devoted themselves wholeheartedly to the Lord’s service. This is also said in what follows: “The children of Israel put away the Baals and the Astartes, and served the Lord alone. They assembled at Mizpah, drew water, and poured it out before the Lord.”

The Hebrews relate that curses were uttered over this water before the Lord, and that just as a jealous woman was tested by drinking water under the Law (Num. V), so idolaters were here tested by this water—namely, those who altogether denied having worshipped idols. They also relate that whoever was an idolater and tasted this water had his lips adhere so closely together that he could not separate them. By this judgment the idolater was detected and put to death.

The following words demonstrate this, where it says: “Samuel judged the children of Israel at Mizpah” [Col. 1086C]. To judge idolaters in this place must be understood as handing them over to death according to the Law. They also say that Moses tested in this way the idolaters who had made the calf for themselves, when he took the calf, burned it, ground it into powder, scattered it on the water, and gave the children of Israel drink from it (Exod. XXXII).

## CHAPTER XVIII. In what they sinned by asking for a king, although the Law given did not forbid them to appoint a king, but only a man of another nation.

(CHAPTER VIII.) Thus far let us consider the image, portrayed in mystical figures, of the priesthood’s transfer. Now, as though on another panel, let us contemplate the image of the kingship of Christ, the Son of God, which, after the destruction of the kingdom of sin, succeeded it in salvation and freedom.

“All the elders of Israel assembled and came to Samuel at Ramah, and said to him: ‘Behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint for us a king to judge us, as all the nations have.’ The saying displeased Samuel because they had said, ‘Give us a king to judge us.’ And Samuel prayed to the Lord. The Lord said to Samuel: ‘Hear the voice of the people in all that they say to you. For they have not rejected you, but me, lest I reign over them,’” etc.

First, according to the literal sense, one asks in what respect the people sinned by asking for a king. For the Law says: “When you enter the land which the Lord your God gives you, possess it, and dwell in it, and say, ‘I will appoint a king over me, as all the nations around me have,’ you shall appoint him whom the Lord your God chooses from among your brothers. You may not make a man of another nation king, who is not your brother” (Deut. XVII), etc.

By saying this, the Law forbade the appointment not of any king whatsoever, but of a foreign king. What, then, was the just ground of complaint for the Lawgiver when he said: “They have not rejected you, but me, lest I reign over them. According to all their deeds which they have done from the day when I brought them out of Egypt until this day—just as they have forsaken me and served foreign gods—so they also do to you”?

The answer to this is readily apparent: they said, “Give us a king to judge us,” at an unsuitable time, when they had a judge judging them justly and royally, not in the vanity of ambition but in the Spirit of God and the truth of the Lord’s word. They knew that he was faithful, as Scripture itself testifies above concerning him: “All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (I Kings III).

The people sinned in rejecting the word of the Lord reigning over them—indeed, God himself, their king—as Samuel himself later says in a sharp rebuke: “But today you have rejected the Lord your God, who alone saved you from all your evils and tribulations, and you said: ‘Not so; appoint a king over us.’”

Since the history is plain, let us now briefly touch upon the few matters requiring inquiry; then at last, in accordance with our purpose, let us weave in the mysteries.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Saul: how he began to reign; how he seemed so innocent as though he were a one-year-old son; and how he reigned for two years in that innocence.

(CHAPTER IX.) “Saul said to the servant: ‘Behold, we shall go. What shall we bring to the man?’” Saul did not suppose that Samuel could tell him about the donkeys otherwise than for payment for divination. Therefore he said: “What shall we bring to the man?”—“Hurry now, for today he comes into the city, because today there is a sacrifice for the people at the high place.” In this place “sacrifice” means the meal which Samuel had prepared for the people at the new moon.

“And I will send you away in the morning, and I will tell you all that is in your heart. And concerning the donkeys which you lost three days ago, do not be anxious, for they have been found.” It was in Saul’s heart, as the Hebrews relate, that he would become king, because in a vision he had seen himself placed at the top of a palm tree; this vision was a royal sign.

(CHAPTER X.) “When you depart from there and go farther on, and come to the oak of Tabor, you will find there three men going up to God at Bethel.” These men were going to Bethel for prayer, where Jacob had set up a stone (Gen. XXVIII). “After this you will come to the hill of God.” The hill of God was a place where prophets lived. “And the Spirit of the Lord will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them.” The Jews say that there he prophesied concerning the age to come, Gog and Magog, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishment of the impious.

“Therefore, when all these signs have happened to you, do whatever your hand finds to do, because God is with you.” It is as though he said: By these signs you will know that God has willed to make you king; therefore act royally in all that you must do, because God is with you.

“And you shall go down before me to Gilgal, for I will come down to you, that you may offer an offering and sacrifice peace offerings. You shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you must do.” Some think that Saul offered the burnt offering without blame, since Samuel, though awaited by him, did not come within the agreed seven days. But whoever carefully distinguishes this passage will find that Saul was not blamed without reason and was reproved for disobedience.

Among the Hebrews, the passage is punctuated thus: “And you shall go down before me to Gilgal, for I will come down to you.” Then they add: “To offer offerings and sacrifice peace offerings, you shall wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you must do.” Samuel therefore did not command Saul to wait seven days for Samuel’s own arrival; rather, he wished the offerings and peace sacrifices to be waited for seven days before being offered. Saul did not do this at all; therefore he is rightly blamed and marked by the charge of folly.

“Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel.” This is said not of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, but of Saul himself. For when he began to reign, he was as innocent as a son one year old; and he is said to have reigned for two years in that same innocence.

## CHAPTER XX. On Saul’s pride, of which the gravest sins were indications: one, that he offered sacrifice; the other, that, though commanded to strike and destroy Amalek, he scorned to obey and even defended his own sin.

A great and fertile tree very quickly grew old: retaining the grace of fruitfulness for only two years, it immediately, its root having decayed, lost both the beauty of its foliage and the honor of its fruit. What sort of worm, do you suppose, gnawed at its root within? Surely it was the worm of pride, by which that one also, concerning whom the word of the Lord says in Ezekiel, could be corrupted and rot away: [Col. 1088D] “Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in its branches and with thick foliage, lofty in height, and its top was raised among dense boughs.” And afterwards: “Because it was exalted in height, and gave its top a green and thick growth, and its heart was lifted up in its height, I delivered it into the hand of the mightiest of the nations” (Ezek. 31). Certainly one might say truthfully also of this man that, because his heart was lifted up in his height, God delivered him into the hand of the mightiest of the nations. For the Spirit of the Lord departed from him, and an evil spirit from the Lord agitated him.

The two sins preceding this punishment are indications to us of the pride already mentioned. The first is that a man not of the tribe of Levi but of the tribe of Benjamin, imagining in royal arrogance that nothing was forbidden him, [Col. 1089A] said (chap. 13): “Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings,” and offered the burnt offering. This was an exceedingly great arrogance in a king, deserving to be struck by heavenly judgment. For what comparable thing did Uzziah of David’s line, from the tribe of Judah, do? He merely entered the temple of the Lord intending to burn incense to the Lord upon the altar of incense. But heavenly vengeance immediately struck his pride at the appropriate place: leprosy arose upon his forehead in the house of the Lord before the priests. Therefore, until the day of his death, he lived as a leper, according to the law for lepers, in a separate house, full of the leprosy for which he had been expelled from the house of the Lord (2 Chron. 26). How much more ought this man to have been cast out, who usurped for himself the whole office of priest! Thus it is said to him: “Your [Col. 1089B] kingdom shall by no means continue any longer. The Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart,” etc.

The second sin was this: commanded by the word, or voice, of the Lord to go and strike Amalek, to destroy all that belonged to it, spare none, but kill from man to woman, child and nursing infant, ox and sheep, camel and ass, he did not do so. Instead, in derogation of the divine severity, he dared to spare Agag and the best flocks of sheep and herds, and garments and rams and everything beautiful; he was unwilling to destroy them. In this pride he also retained the presumptuous exercise of priesthood mentioned above. For it is subsequently written (chap. 15): “Samuel therefore came to Saul, and Saul was offering a burnt offering to the Lord from the choice things of the spoil which he had brought from Amalek.” Did Samuel not say above to him, when he offered a burnt offering because he was compelled by necessity: “Your kingdom shall by no means continue any longer”? Thus, persisting in evil, he did not change his sin but increased it, when he spared the best things and preserved Agag against the Lord’s command—not only a transgressor of the present commandment, but also a despiser of God’s ancient Scripture. For the Lord had said to Moses, when Amalek came and fought against Israel: “Write this as a memorial in a book, and deliver it into the ears of Joshua. For I shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek from beneath heaven” (Exod. 17).

Moreover—and this is most wicked—when he was rebuked by the word of the Lord, saying: “Were you not, when you were little in your own eyes, made head among the tribes of Israel? [Col. 1089D] Why therefore did you not obey the voice of the Lord, but turn to the spoil and do evil in the eyes of the Lord?” he dared to refute the Spirit of the Lord, who charged him with sin, saying in proud self-defense: “On the contrary, I did obey the voice of the Lord and went in the way upon which the Lord sent me; I brought Agag king of Amalek, and I destroyed Amalek. But the people took sheep and oxen from the spoil, the first of those things that were slain, in order to sacrifice them to the Lord their God at Gilgal,” etc.

For this is indeed most wicked: after the will to sin, which is first; after the accomplishment of the deed, which is second; and after its perverse practice, which is third; there is added the defense of the sin, which is fourth; and here there is no place for pardon. For God also says through the prophet: “For three crimes [Col. 1090A] of Damascus, and for four, I shall not turn him back” (Amos 1). Therefore Samuel, now most sharply provoked by such insulting injuries, after saying: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and hearkening than offering the fat of rams,” immediately added: “For rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusal to submit like the crime of idolatry,” etc.

Accordingly, enraged by so many contemptuous affronts (chap. 16), “the Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord agitated him.” A great punishment for the king; a great disgrace for the people who demanded a king contrary to God’s will. And even if all other examples of judgment and truth were lacking, this alone could suffice as testimony: every planting which the heavenly Father has not planted never reaches a good end to its condition; and every ordering of the house of the Lord which, without consulting his will, has been made by human will, will pay the penalties of disorder.

The kingdom of David, ordered by the will and hand of God, subsequently removed the stain of this reproach. Thus Samuel himself says above in testimony: “The Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and the Lord has commanded him to be leader over his people.” In saying this he clearly implies, by contrast, that the Lord never sought Saul according to his own heart. Therefore, when it is said that “Saul was chosen and good, and among the children of Israel there was no man better than he,” it must certainly be understood: not according to the Lord’s heart, but according to the people’s heart. For it follows: “From the shoulder upward he towered above all the people.” By this statement he strikes at the foolish judgment of the crowd, because it ascribes authority and the glory of offices to stature rather than merits.

## Chapter XXI. That precisely in being demon-possessed Saul prefigured the kingdom of sin, while David, in name and deeds, prefigured the kingdom of Christ

This mystery is now plain: the demon-possessed King Saul signifies the frenzied kingdom of sin, while David signifies the peaceful kingdom of righteousness—first in their names, then in their deeds. Saul is interpreted “request,” David “strong of hand” or “beloved.” What was humanity’s request except the request for sin, which man sought of his own will [Col. 1090D] when he was free and noble, created in the image of God? Conversely, who is “strong of hand” or “beloved” but Christ the Son of God, who, coming with a stronger hand, conquered the strong armed prince of sin guarding his courtyard; and who thereafter, victorious and seated at the Father’s right hand, is wholly beloved by the angels beholding him and by the people hoping in him?

“Death, which entered this world through sin, reigned until Moses,” says the Apostle (Rom. 5); and from then on, hearing through the Law opposition to its kingdom, the power of sin raged more violently. Hence the same Apostle says: “For I would not have known covetousness unless the Law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every covetous desire. For without [Col. 1091A] the Law sin was dead; but when the commandment came, sin revived” (Rom. 7).

Likewise, in each individual person, so long as they are not freed by Christ’s grace, sin reigns; and, like a maddened rider, it urges the subdued horse with spurs and lashes it with whips. Thus the pagan poet taunts an adulterer in these words:

> A not-light master drives the mind;  
> he applies sharp spurs to the weary  
> and turns it though it resists.

From such a kingdom Christ, the King strong of hand and beloved, has by dying once freed the whole world in the mass, and he does not cease even now to free each person in his own individual case by his active power. Let us now contemplate the grace of his kingdom, under mystical figures, in David, the father according to his flesh.

## Chapter XXII. On David’s election: how free it was from human favor; and that, as Samuel did not know David’s person, so John did not know Christ

[Col. 1091B] “And the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Fill your horn with oil and come, that I may send you to Jesse the Bethlehemite; for among his sons I have provided a king for myself.’ And Samuel said: ‘How shall I go? For Saul will hear and kill me.’ And the Lord said: ‘You shall take a calf from the herd in your hand and say: “I have come to sacrifice to the Lord,”’” etc.

Although Samuel knew the matter by the prophetic Spirit, so that he said: “The Lord has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and commanded him to be leader over his people” (1 Sam. 15); and again: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you and given it to your neighbor, who is better than you” (ibid.), [Col. 1091C] yet he did not know the person of that chosen man. Hence, “when the sons of Jesse had entered, he saw Eliab and said: ‘Is his anointed one before the Lord?’ And the Lord said to Samuel: ‘Do not regard his face or the height of his stature, for I have rejected him [399]; nor do I judge according to human sight. For man sees those things which appear, but the Lord looks upon the heart.’”

So indeed John, the Lord’s forerunner, knew by the Spirit the one whom he preceded, but did not know him according to the flesh or by his outward appearance. Thus he says: “I too did not know him; but he who sent me to baptize said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him—this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John [Col. 1091D] 1). This indeed greatly confirms the purity of true testimony: where the very person upon whom favor or grace is to be bestowed is not yet known, no suspicion whatever of human favor or partiality can be present in the choosing.

## Chapter XXIII. That David was anointed not with a flask, as Saul was, but with a full horn of oil: its mystical meaning; and that from that day the Spirit of the Lord was directed toward him

“Fill,” he says, “your horn with oil.” Here there is already a manifest difference. For of Saul it is said: “Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it upon his head” (1 Sam. 10). A *lenticula* was a small square oil-vessel, open at the side, so called from anointing. A horn of oil, however, containing a far more abundant supply, signified the royal and prophetic grace in David as enduring and permanent. For, it says, “the Spirit of the Lord was directed toward David from that day onward.” That is: when he was anointed with visible oil, invisible richness spread from the root into the branches of the good tree—from the root, I say, from him who said: “I am the stock and root of David” (Rev. 22). For he who later, through the new birth of the flesh, became David’s stock, was already, through the ancient nature of his divinity, David’s root. He supplies the true oil and true richness of the Holy Spirit, by which David might flower, put forth leaves, and bear fruit; indeed, by which he might himself become David’s father.

Therefore, as a tree receives richness from its root in order to bear fruit in its seasons, so David received from that root what would lay up testimonies for his Lord, his Son, in mystical deeds and prophetic utterances. [Col. 1092B] Let us therefore preserve this honor for the Father, of such majesty, and according to the flesh seated at the right hand of Majesty on high: though we cannot comprehend everything, let us not suppose that anything he did according to the present Scripture, anything he said or sang, lacked mystery.

For what mystery and beauty does this very fact contain inwardly, that he is anointed with a full horn of oil? By the fullness of oil with which the father was anointed is rightly understood the whole fullness of divinity, which now dwells bodily in his Son (Col. 2). For God did not give the Spirit to this one by measure; rather, the whole sevenfold Spirit rests in him. Knowing this, David himself—the future father of the Son of whom these things are said—after saying to him, “You loved righteousness [Col. 1092C] and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness,” immediately added, “above your companions” (Ps. 44), that is, above all saints and all anointed ones. For each of the saints is anointed with a distributive or partial grace; but in this one, as has already been said, all the fullness of divinity dwells.

## Chapter XXIV. That this same David was anointed three times, and that this itself was a type of the Lord and his Son Christ

Here it must be known that this prophet and father of so great a Son was anointed three times. First, by Samuel in the midst of his brothers, Saul being unaware. Second, at Hebron over the house of Judah, after Saul’s death. Third, over all Israel, after all Saul’s house had been deprived of hope of the kingdom. Truly, in this man, as in a mirror, the whole pattern of Christ’s anointing shone forth.

For Christ too was anointed three times. First, when he was conceived of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1; Matt. 1). Second, when, at his baptism, the Holy Spirit came upon him and he was shown in the form of a dove (Matt. 5 [probably Matt. 3]; Luke 3). Third, when, rising from the dead, he poured into his faithful such great grace of his anointing as this same anointed king-to-be, the father of that Son, wished to commend in these words: “Behold how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity, like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard, which descends upon the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132).

For when he rose, on that same [Col. 1093A] day, standing in the midst of his disciples and saying, “Peace be with you,” he breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20). Afterwards, seated at God’s right hand, he sent that same Spirit and again gave the Holy Spirit (Acts 1). Thus the true ointment descended from the head onto Aaron’s beard and the hem of his garment: that is, the Holy Spirit descended from Christ, who is our head, first upon those strong and perfect men, Christ’s apostles, and then, through their ministry, upon the whole Church.

## Chapter XXV. On David’s first anointing, secretly performed in his father’s house; and on the calf which, by the Lord’s command, Samuel brought to deceive Saul—how the devil was likewise deceived by Christ’s incarnation

[Col. 1093B] David’s first anointing took place secretly in his father’s house in this manner: “How,” Samuel says, “shall I go? For Saul will hear and kill me.” And the Lord said: “You shall take a calf from the herd in your hand and say: ‘I have come to sacrifice to the Lord,’” etc. The calf brought to be sacrificed could close Saul’s eyes, so that he would not be troubled or suspect anything: the apparent reason being fully disclosed, he would be unconcerned. Thus it was beautifully done in the figure, because it was thus to occur in reality.

The calf to be sacrificed signifies the passible nature of the King who was to be born of the Virgin—Christ, the Son of God. By this the devil was deceived, unable to understand the power of the one being born: namely, that the King of righteousness was coming to overthrow sin, and that his kingdom would have no end. For in his own evil designs he is indeed shrewd and cunning, but regarding the good things of God he is dull and foolish. Thus in Job, from the mouth of God, Behemoth—that is, “the beast”—is said to have a circle of foolishness in its nostrils (Job 40).

Likewise, at the beginning, when the serpent—or rather, the devil himself in the serpent—is cursed, God says: “Upon your breast you shall go” (Gen. 3). However subtle and cunning he may be in evil, however maliciously he may abuse his perversion of nature in attempting to know the counsel of hidden divinity, he is brutish and walks upon his breast, always trampling down his own purpose, so that while he wishes to harm heavenly things he is shown to benefit them.

This may readily be recognized in all malicious persons who are ruled by his spirit. However shrewdly skilled they may be in the knowledge of creation, the movements of heaven, the courses of the stars, or even magical arts, [Col. 1093D] they are so unteachable and incapable of grasping spiritual goods and heavenly mysteries that, if you call them to hear, you will find your labor entirely wasted: their soul is brutish and almost irrational. Therefore, when David is anointed, a calf from the herd is taken for sacrifice so that Saul may not hear; because, when the new King Christ is born, the whole passibility of human nature is displayed outwardly, lest the devil recognize this mystery. Thus, though frightened by surrounding miracles and at times suspecting something hostile to himself, he nevertheless does not know by what way or in what order the power which has entered the world undertakes the conquest of his kingdom.

## Chapter XXVI. On this same David: that he was young, tended sheep, and was ruddy and handsome; and that in all these things he prefigured Christ

[Col. 1094A] Jesse says: “There remains still the youngest, and he tends the sheep.” And afterwards: “So he sent and brought him; and he was ruddy, beautiful in appearance, and handsome of face.” He was young and tended sheep, clearly as a type of his already-mentioned Son, who, as truly young, says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11); and who, as the true Shepherd, feeds us, his sheep—us, I say, his people and the sheep of his pasture—whom he also acquired by his blood. Thus he says: “I am the good Shepherd. The good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10).

This was the occupation of righteous Abel and of the patriarchs with whom God spoke. But the fact that “he was ruddy” set forth the image of that Shepherd who laid down his life for his sheep. For he too is rightly called ruddy: not with another’s blood, as the devil, the great red dragon, is (Rev. 12), but ruddy with his own blood, as the prophet Zechariah also testifies: “I saw by night, and behold, a man mounted upon a red horse” (Zech. 1). The man mounted on the red horse is he himself, risen and resuming his body, suffused with his own blood, according to what the same prophet says later: “You also, by the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9).

No less does the statement that “he was beautiful in appearance and handsome of face” belong to such an image: not with that beauty or attractiveness which incites the wanton or incontinent to look, but with that which chastely delights the author of wisdom, while grace shines in the face and breathes in the mind itself. Scripture testifies accordingly that “the wisdom of the righteous shines in his face” (Prov. 17). Thus he could be recognized as beautiful in appearance by the prophet’s spiritual eyes, because he was the very one whom God’s grace, already preparing him to become king, had prepared. This, I say, belongs to the image of him, Christ the Son of God, of whom David later sang while playing the harp: “You are fairer in form than the children of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips; therefore God has blessed you forever. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one. In your splendor and your beauty strive prosperously, go forth and reign” (Ps. 44).

This beauty, this attractiveness of the one who goes forth and reigns, is an inward beauty: the beauty of divinity, so great that, by comparison with it, the human appearance was filth, as the prophet says: “He grew up like a shoot before him, and like a root out of thirsty ground. He had no beauty or comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no appearance” (Isa. 53), etc.

## Chapter XXVII. On how he was chosen and anointed without any human favor, as a type of the same Christ who says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you”

What king was ever anointed in this way and brought to the kingdom by such an order? All kings either individually aspired ambitiously to royalty by their own impulse, or advanced by hereditary succession, or relied upon the sons of men, were raised up and acclaimed by rulers, immediately clothed in purple and adorned with crowns; then immediately, sitting upon a lofty throne and holding scepters, they shone in their glory.

But this man, still a boy, when he followed after the ewes with young, while Saul was alive and reigning, could have had nothing of this kind in his heart, such that Samuel might say to him what he had previously said to Saul: “I shall tell you all that is in your heart” (1 Sam. 9). There were no rulers favoring and acclaiming him; rather, his elder brothers envied him and resented the boy. Thus his eldest brother later says angrily, when David is speaking with others: “Why have you come, and why have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart: you came down to see the battle” (1 Sam. 17).

He did not immediately sit on a throne, bearing a scepter, marked by purple, bright with diadem or glittering with a golden crown. Rather, poor, wandering, and fugitive, he first roamed in exile and drank, in every manner, the bitterness of complete misery before the nectar-like or honey-sweet pleasures of kingship among the people. What king, I ask, except the Lord alone and his Son Jesus Christ, God and man, proceeded and reigned in such an order?

For he who was once a child, now exalted, raised up, and exceedingly sublime, did not exalt or raise himself. In answer to the Jews who said, “Whom do you make [Col. 1095C] yourself?” he said: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing” (John 8). Again: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I have not come of myself, but there is one who sent me, whom you do not know” (John 7). The sons of men, the rulers or chiefs of peoples, did not choose him; rather, he himself chose his rulers. As he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15). He did not ascend to the kingdom by hereditary succession according to man, since he deigned to be born not even from the daughter of Herod or of any ruler, but from a poor virgin betrothed to a craftsman.

Though anointed King from the womb, he could not immediately be called or be king, crowned with royal glory and honor.
