Rather, in accordance with the prophecy saying, “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109), he was first embittered by every temptation and by the passion of death before lifting up his head into those delights which are at the Father’s right hand. Thus in all these things the son is like the father; indeed, this father David was ordained in the likeness of his future Son.

## Chapter XXVIII. On the mystical construction of the ten-stringed psaltery; that meanwhile the evil spirit agitated Saul; and that in all these things the wisdom of Christ’s Church and the madness of its enemy, the Jewish people, are prefigured

“The Spirit of the Lord was directed toward David from that day onward.” O how much beauty and grace this very phrase contains: “and was directed toward him”! It was not said thus, nor ought it to have been said thus, of Saul, from whom the Spirit [Col. 1096A] of the Lord was to depart; nor of anyone else whose feigned or double soul that Spirit of love never deigns to honor with a straight kiss, since, after a light touch, he is immediately to flee from its falseness.

The Lord had found this man according to his own heart; therefore, with a more ready and upright affection, he was borne toward his soul to kiss it. By what effects was it made clear that the Spirit of the Lord was directed toward him? First by prophetic grace, then by works of strength. For from that point he became the celebrated psalmist, prophesying and playing the harp of the mighty deeds of the Lord, composing psalms containing mysteries of the Son of God, his Son Christ. He was also clothed with strength, as he himself testified in saying to Saul (chap. 17): “Your servant was feeding his master’s flock. A lion or a bear came and took a ram from the midst of the flock; and I pursued them, struck them, and rescued it from their mouths. And they rose up against me, and I seized their jaws and choked and killed them. For I, your servant, have killed both lion and bear. Therefore this uncircumcised Philistine shall be like one of them, because he has dared to curse the army of the living God.”

Thus “the Spirit of the Lord was directed toward David,” making him, according to his very name, beloved in words and strong of hand in deeds; likewise a type of the same Christ, his Son, who acted powerfully and taught delightfully—truly strong of hand, truly beloved. For he preached and taught in such a way that his very opponents said in astonishment: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John 9).

The musical instrument of this psalmist expressed his teaching or preaching: it was called a psaltery, formed in the shape of a delta, hollow within, covered outwardly with the skins of dead animals, and having ten strings sounding above. Each of these things must be considered mystically in his evangelical preaching. Its inward hollowness consists in this: he empties one who seeks perfection of earthly possessions: “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go and sell all that you have, give it to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. [Col. 1096D] 19; Luke 18). The skins of dead animals with which it was covered are mortifications of vices; for he teaches us to suffer with him in order to reign with him, to die with him in order to rise again with him (Rom. 8; 2 Tim. 2). Its ten-stringed arrangement is the observance of the Law’s Decalogue. “For I have not come,” he says, “to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). The emission of sound from above is the pursuit of heavenly things alone, the love of God alone, and the upward-directed intention of one doing good. This he preaches and impresses: “Let not,” he says, “your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6), and similar things.

But this says too little. He himself who spoke thus and sang in teaching thus—he himself, I say, according to the humanity in which he taught—is the psaltery, as the heavenly voice said to him in the Psalm: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56). He immediately answers, even specifying the hour of the resurrection: “I shall arise,” he says, “at dawn” (ibid.). Therefore the melody of so great an instrument, namely evangelical teaching, awakened by the plucking of the strings and the movement of the fingers, resounds sweetly and clearly for one who has ears to hear. The sound of the strings in him is the very utterance of words; the differentiation of the fingers is the plurality of the gifts of the Holy Spirit, all of which are in him.

He likewise acted thus and acted with such strength that he choked the lion or the bear and rescued the sheep or ram from their mouths. This is known and certain to us, his people, the sheep of his pasture: he choked the great lion, the devil, and rescued us from his mouth. Meanwhile [Col. 1097B] an evil spirit from the Lord agitated Saul; that is, in those in whom sin and death reigned, zeal and envy, by the Lord’s judgment, blinded them more intensely in the presence [Col. 1098A] of the Savior, so that every former frenzy was milder and more tolerable compared with the present madness.

Signifying this, the Lord himself, when they said of him, “He has a demon and casts out demons by the prince of demons” (Matt. 12), said of them: “When an unclean spirit has gone out of a man, it walks through waterless places, seeking rest; and not finding it, says: ‘I shall return into my former house from which I came out’” (Luke 11), etc. For that man—that people, I mean—from whom it had gone out when, brought from Egypt where it had served foreign gods, it was converted to the worship of the one God, was entered by a more wicked and more powerful spirit when it began to persecute with Herod the Son of God newly born [Col. 1098B] and thereafter did not cease to blaspheme; “and the last state of that people becomes worse than the former” (ibid.).

# Second Book on the Books of Kings  
*(1 Sam. 17–2 Sam. 24)*

[Col. 1097]

## Chapter I. How signs in David preceded both the good things Christ the Son of God did and the evils he suffered

[Col. 1097C] *(1 Kings [1 Samuel], chap. 17).* The true David—that is, “beloved” or “strong of hand”—by preaching the kingdom of God and casting out demons by the finger of God, provided good things for us but stirred up adversities against himself. He immediately displayed certain mystical signs of both results in this David, as was said above concerning the Spirit of the Lord: namely, that by preaching and working wonders he gained life for his elect and stirred up against himself the agents of death.

In this David our good things are first prefigured, and then his adversities. For it immediately follows: And Saul said to his servants, “Find for me someone who plays well, and bring him to me.” And one of the youths answered and said: “Behold, I have seen a son of Jesse the Bethlehemite who knows how to play” (1 Sam. 16), etc. And afterwards: “Therefore whenever [Col. 1097D] the evil spirit from the Lord seized Saul, David took the harp and played with his hand; Saul was refreshed and felt relief, for the evil spirit departed from him” (ibid.).

That youth who answered Saul is said to have been Doeg the Edomite, David’s enemy. Everything which he appears to have said in David’s praise is said to have been spoken in hatred of him, because, out of enmity and envious malice, he wanted David to come to Saul, so that he might there be killed on some pretext. It immediately follows: “Now the Philistines, gathering their forces for battle, assembled at Socoh. From there they encamped between Socoh and Azekah, within the borders of Dommim. But Saul and the children of Israel,” etc.

## Chapter II. The mystical significance of Saul’s being refreshed while David played, and of the Philistine’s falling when David struck him

[Col. 1098B–C] What else is mystically indicated to us by the things just said except that Christ, beloved and strong of hand, caused his enemies—whether those from among us Gentiles or from among the Jews, who also, as the Apostle testifies, “were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2)—those enemies, I say, predestined for reconciliation or friendship, through the preaching of the Gospel, to rest from sins and breathe freely from under the devil’s yoke? And then he struck the proud enemy who held the power of death, that is, the devil, with the living stone—which he himself is—and humbled him like one wounded (Ps. 88).

Saul, therefore, in that David, while playing the harp, “refreshed him, gave him relief, and caused the evil spirit to depart from him,” signifies God’s enemies in respect of those among them who, hearing Christ’s most sweet preaching inviting them to repentance, are converted to faith in him and refreshed. Having laid down the burdens of sins, they are relieved, and through confession the devil departs from them.

But the Philistine whom David killed, against whom David alone prevailed alone, signifies the devil himself, whom the true David, Christ, alone could overcome; whom he conquered through his cross and, triumphant by his blood, cast outside. In Chronicles, this man and his brothers are read to have been giants from the race of Arasa (2 Sam. 21); in the book of Judges this is called Orpah, Naomi’s mother-in-law (Ruth 1). By his very name, as stated above, Goliath the Philistine signifies the devil. For *Goliath* is interpreted “uncovered,” while *Philistine* means “falling by drink.” He is “uncovered” by the Gospel of God as the prince of darkness—he who had formerly, protected by deceit, been worshipped as God in temples and adored in images. Likewise he is “falling by drink”: drunk with the poison of pride, he fell when his foot moved; he was expelled and could not stand.

## Chapter III. On the Philistine’s reproach, and that before Christ’s coming no one could strike the Philistine—that is, cast out the devil
“Standing, he cried out against Israel and said to them: ‘Why have you come prepared for battle? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not Saul’s servants? Choose from among yourselves a man to come down for single combat.’” And further: “Today I have reproached the battle-lines of Israel. Give me a man, and let him enter into single combat with me” [Col. 1099B].

The battle-lines of Israel are the battle-lines of the whole generation that seeks the Lord, that seeks the face of the God of Jacob, with whom that man, having been made upright, deserved to be called Israel. These battle-lines were already numerous before Christ, mighty of hand, triumphed over the devil; and among them there were many strong in faith, patient in hope, outstanding in love of the Creator. Yet none among them was so strong as to destroy the kingdom of sin and death, or by the weapons of his own righteousness to overcome the court of the strong man armed—strong, I say, in cruelty and pride.

Therefore, in Isaiah, after the Holy Spirit had said to all Israel, to the whole city of Jerusalem, which is God’s Church: “Awake, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath to the dregs; [Col. 1099C] you have drunk the cup of stupor and drained it to its sediment,” he immediately added: “There is none to raise her up among all the sons whom she bore, and none to take her by the hand among all the sons whom she reared” (Isa. 51).

That proud one therefore reproached the battle-lines of Israel; he reproached and insulted all God’s elect, whom he had overcome in Adam and held in the underworld by the right of a conqueror. “Why,” he says, “have you come prepared for battle? Why have you taken the tablets of the covenant and the ten precepts of the Law, as though you were going to fight bravely against my dominion? Am I not a Philistine, and are you not Saul’s servants?” That is: Am I not the prince of this world, and are you not servants of sin? “Choose from among yourselves a man, who may come down for single combat.”

For he knew that [Col. 1099D] he had ensnared them all and cast them all into God’s wrath, as is added in the same prophet after the words already quoted: “Your sons have been cast down; they slept at the head of every street like a trapped wild beast, full of the Lord’s indignation and the rebuke of your God” (ibid.). This was Israel’s reproach: those who had taken up the armour of the Law in order to resist sin had not themselves come prepared for battle, nor could they free themselves from adding some actual sins to original sin.

## CHAPTER IV. That Goliath was descended from Orpah, while this man proceeded from Ruth, Noemi’s other daughter-in-law; how Jesse is elsewhere said to have had seven, elsewhere eight sons; and that David too was sent by his father as a type of Christ.

“But David was the son of an Ephrathite man, of whom mention was made above, from Bethlehem of Judah, whose name was Jesse. He had eight sons and was, in Saul’s days, an old man, advanced in years among men.”

A most fitting encounter: Saul and all the Israelite men, hearing the Philistine’s words, were exceedingly astonished and afraid; but at that time David had already been given by God and suitably prepared, as though produced from an opposing stock. For the former, as was said above, was of Orpah’s line; this one, however, of Ruth’s line. Both had been daughters-in-law of Noemi. For Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and returned, but Ruth clung to her mother-in-law (Ruth 1). From Ruth’s root David, as it were, sprang forth, to strike down the pride of the Philistine born from Orpah [Col. 1100B]. This man is a type of Christ; that man, a type of Antichrist. Born from distinct—indeed contrary—lines, from the coming of Christ himself they do not cease to contend, with the whole world watching, until the end of the age.

“He had,” it says, “eight sons.” The question arises why he is here said to have had eight sons, whereas in Paralipomenon he is recorded as having no more than seven (1 Chron. 2). The solution is as follows: the prophet Nathan counted among the sons the son of Samaa, his own son, whom he had brought up and nourished in his son’s place. For seven of Jesse’s sons are said to have been brought before Samuel, while the eighth was in the pastures (1 Sam. 16). It is clear that Nathan was brought among them; he is also called Jonathan, and of him it is said near the end of Samuel: “Jonathan, son of Samaa, David’s brother, struck him down” (2 Sam. 21). Note that wherever he is called a prophet, he is written “Nathan,” not “Jonathan.”

“Jesse said: ‘Take to your brothers this ephah of parched grain and these ten loaves, and run to the camp to your brothers. Take these ten little cheeses to the commander; visit your brothers to see whether they are well, and learn with whom they are stationed.’ So David rose early and entrusted the flock to a keeper” (1 Chron. 20), and so forth.

David was not sent by his father to fight clothed in military armour, but to visit his brothers. Precisely so Christ too was sent by God his Father, not to fight through the works of the Law, which “brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7), but to visit his brothers wandering in this world [Col. 1100D]—to visit them, I say, although this expression is far too slight for what is required by the reality. This figure is called *tapinosis*, that is, the humbling of a great matter: the statement does not accomplish what it outwardly expresses.

Moses too, diminishing a great matter by this manner of speaking, says: “I will go and return to my brothers in Egypt, to see whether they are still alive.” Certainly this expression is far less than the matter he intended. Thus Christ came to visit his brothers—that is, to gather into one the scattered children of God (John 11)—not to fight in Saul’s camp, nor to impose upon us, his brothers, anything from the Law beyond the ten commandments, rightly signified by the ten loaves or the ten little cheeses, together with the ephah of parched grain: that is, together with the one faith of the Trinity.

## CHAPTER V. The mystical meaning of David’s inability to fight or walk in armour, though he at least tried it; the meaning of David’s staff, the five stones, and the one stone with which he struck.

“Saul clothed David with his garments, placed a bronze helmet on his head, and clothed him with a breastplate. So David, girded with Saul’s sword over his garment, began to try whether he could walk armed; for he was not accustomed to it. David said to Saul: ‘I cannot walk like this, because I have no practice in it.’ And he laid them aside.”

Saul’s clothing or armour, in which David could not walk when clothed or girded, and therefore laid aside, were the carnal works of the Law—as was said above—which Christ did indeed temporarily undergo, “made under the Law,” as the Apostle says (Gal. 4), but judged useless because, as the same Apostle testifies, the Law “brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7), nor could any flesh be justified before God by them (Rom. 3). He therefore laid them aside.

But why did he try whether, clothed or armed in this way, he could walk, when he had no practice in it? Did he not know that he lacked the practice? Or did he, in whom the Spirit of the Lord was directed, not know that he would conquer not by arms but by the Lord’s power, when he would not enter the fight except in that same Spirit of the Lord by whom he could foresee his victory? Why, then, did he try this vainly? Clearly because he could more beautifully show the king his hope by deed [Col. 1101C] than if he immediately rejected the king’s offered arms with a hasty word or speech, as though contemptuously.

In just the same way, why did Christ undergo the carnal justifications of the Law, being himself circumcised and made in every respect a minister of circumcision? Did he not know that his battle was not to be fought through the works or justifications of the Law, but through the cross alone? Why then was he made under the Law and admitted its observances into himself? Clearly because it was sweeter to teach people by reason than by force—sweeter and gentler, I say, to undergo a harmless observance of the Law than to give offence or occasion to any person.

Having therefore laid aside Saul’s garments, “he took,” it says, “his staff, which he always had in his hands; he chose for himself five very clear stones from the torrent, put them in the shepherd’s bag which he had with him, took a sling in his hand, and went forth [Col. 1101D] against the Philistine.”

The staff of our David—that is, Christ—which he carried against the Philistine and always held in his hands, is his care for rational sheep, undertaken against the devil, being always concerned for their salvation. The five very clear stones which he chose from the torrent are the five books of Moses, taken from the overflowing Jewish people. For the river flowed and was not checked by those stones: that is, the Jewish people ran freely after carnal desires and was restrained by no discipline of the Law.

He put them in the shepherd’s bag which he had with him: that is, he compared them with the Gospel which God, made man—the Word made flesh—brought with him to us [Col. 1102A]. For the bag is a shepherd’s vessel in which milk is customarily milked. It signifies the new evangelical Law brought by Christ, which indeed supplies an abundance of milk to little children.

He also took the sling in his hand: that is, through love he stretched out his hands upon the cross in order to cast one stone, so that by one faith alone, without works of the Law, he might overthrow the devil. Conversely, the bronze helmet upon the Philistine’s head, his chain-mail breastplate, shield, and spear—each of great weight and great display—are the armour of the devil’s pride. Of this the Lord says to blessed Job (Job 41): “Around his teeth is terror. His body is like cast shields, compacted with scales pressing one upon another.” And further: “The archer will not put him to flight; the stones of the sling become straw to him,” and so forth.

“The Philistine,” it says, “went on, advancing and drawing near against David, with his armour-bearer before him.” Who is his armour-bearer but want, always preceding his face? Thus it is likewise said of him to blessed Job: “Strength will dwell in his neck, and want will go before his face” (ibid.) [Col. 1102B].

## CHAPTER VI. Christ’s victory, and how and which women sing: “Saul struck a thousand,” and so forth.

“David hurried and ran to the battle against the Philistine. He put his hand into the bag, took one stone, threw it with the sling, and struck the Philistine in the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead [Col. 1102C], and he fell face-down upon the ground.”

At last the Philistine’s reproach and curse—the reproach, I say, by which he had insulted Israel’s battle-lines and cursed David by his gods, adding, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth”—was turned upon his own head. For, conversely, David gave his flesh to the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth. For he “took his sword and cut off his head”; and when he lay headless, “the Philistines,” Scripture says, “seeing that their strongest man was dead, fled.”

In accordance with this glory of omnipotence prefigured in himself, David sang: “You humbled the proud man like one wounded; by the arm of your strength you scattered your enemies” (Ps. 88 [89]). Thus Christ, mighty of hand, when he put forth his hand to the stone—that is, to fulfil the truth of the Scriptures through his passion—struck the forehead: namely, the devil’s shameless and proud confidence, for the proud have the shamelessness of the brow. He cut off that one’s head by removing original sin, through which he held dominion over the world.

Hence the Apostle says: “Blotting out the handwriting of the decree which stood against us and was contrary to us, he took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross; stripping principalities and powers, he exposed them openly, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2) [Col. 1102D].

Rightly, then, let the women come out to meet the victor from all the tribes of Israel, singing and leading dances; let them say with timbrels and joyful sistrums [Col. 1103A]; let them say and chant beforehand with one faith and harmonious voice: “Saul struck a thousand, and David ten thousands among his thousands” (1 Sam. 18).

These women are our souls. These women heard that he whom the reproachful Philistine cursed, whom the devil blasphemed through the mouths of the Jews and hanged upon the cross so that he might become the Law’s curse—for the Law says, “Cursed by God is he who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21)—he who is “blessed, who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21), cut off the head of the accursed enemy, that is, took away his dominion, and thereafter, rising from the dead, ascended victoriously into the heavenly Jerusalem. Awakened by faith at this report, our souls meet the victor, singing publicly and privately to him and leading dances of joy.

What do we sing? What do we confess? “Saul struck a thousand, and David ten thousands among his thousands.” Certainly, whatever woman does not know this song, whatever soul does not receive this praise, cannot share in David’s triumph.

Demonic Saul—that is, the Jewish people, who are under the reign of death and over whom sin rules—thought it a great matter that, possessing the Temple, priesthood, and worship of one God, it practised the justices of the Law. But what was that righteousness in comparison with Christ’s righteousness, he who “was made righteousness for us” (1 Cor. 1)? It was as though one should compare a thousand to ten thousand. That righteousness did indeed achieve something, because it placed hope of salvation in those who performed its works; but it brought nothing to perfection, because it could not cast out the prince of this world [Col. 1103C].

David, that is Christ, did this. Christ conquered the devil; Christ overthrew the devil; Christ destroyed death; Christ ascended above the setting; the Lord is his name. Therefore he struck ten thousand among his thousands: that is, he destroyed the totality of sin through his many powers—his own powers, I say, because they were not borrowed from elsewhere.

## CHAPTER VII. That whenever David conquers the Philistines, a Catholic overcomes a heretic; and concerning Saul’s madness, in which he attempted to pin David to the wall with a spear.

“On the next day an evil spirit of the Lord invaded Saul, and he prophesied in the midst of his house. But David played upon the harp with his hand, as he did day by day [Col. 1103D]. Saul held a spear and threw it, thinking that he could pin David to the wall. But David turned aside from before him a second time.”

Meanwhile, it must be understood that even now David extinguishes proud Goliath with his own weapons as often as a man full of right faith—which is customarily reckoned to the saints as righteousness—collects the very testimonies of sacred Scripture which the heretic adduces and thereby convicts the obstinacy of his error. For when he overcomes the proud man discoursing on the judgments of holy Scripture by the very words and arguments which that man produces, he has, as it were, beheaded the exalted Goliath with his own sword.

Thus far in David have been prefigured the good things which Christ bestowed upon us; henceforth, in the same David, are figured the evils which the same Christ suffered from the reprobate. Saul now signifies that portion of the devil’s kingdom which could never be softened by any song of the sweetest preaching. For above, whenever the evil spirit of the Lord seized Saul, David took the harp and struck it with his hand, and Saul was refreshed and felt easier, for the evil spirit withdrew from him (1 Sam. 16) [Col. 1104A].

But now, while David plays, that same madman prophesies and divines by an alien spirit, throwing the spear once and again, thinking that he can pin David to the wall. Therefore, since the Wisdom of God came and found no one free from the madness of sin, there he signifies those who, having heard Christ’s preaching, cast off the yoke of the furious master, namely sin; here, however, he signifies those whom the same preaching made worse, as the same singer or harpist says: “We played for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not weep” (Matt. 11; Luke 7).

He could have said more fully: We played for you, and you made us weep; we mourned for you, and with a spear you pinned us to the wall; with a spear you pierced us upon the cross. For the one suffering in figure escaped by flight and was not pinned; but he whose sufferings are prefigured was indeed pierced by spear and nails, yet escaped by rising again [Col. 1104B].

## CHAPTER VIII. That David suffered seven persecutions; that the number of heads of the red dragon in the Apocalypse signifies all the devil’s persecutions against Christ and the Church; and that Christ was tempted as many times by the Jews in his own person.

[Col. 1104C] Here the very persecutions suffered by David must now be counted. The first is where Saul, now throwing the spear to pin him to the wall, and David turned aside and fled. The second is where, after he struck the Philistines with a great slaughter, Saul again tried to pin him while he was playing; David turned aside, and the spear, having inflicted an ineffectual wound, struck the wall. The third is where, when David had fled and come to Achish king of Gath, Saul killed the priests of the Lord on his account.

The fourth is where the Ziphites gave notice, saying: “Behold, David is hiding among us,” and Saul arose and pursued David into the wilderness of Maon. When David despaired of being able to escape, a messenger came to Saul, saying: “Hurry and come, for the Philistines have poured over the land.” The fifth was in the wilderness of En-gedi, where Saul entered the cave to relieve himself, and David rose and silently cut off the edge of his cloak [Col. 1104D].

The sixth was where the Ziphites again reported: “Behold, David is hidden on the hill of Hachilah,” and David arose and went down into the wilderness of Ziph. There, while Saul was asleep, Abishai said: “God has today shut up your enemy into your hands. Now I shall pierce him to the ground with the spear once, and there will be no need for a second blow.” David said: “Do not kill him.” And further: “May the Lord be merciful to me, that I should not stretch out my hand against the Lord’s anointed. Now therefore take the spear which is at his head and the cup of water,” and so forth.

The seventh and last was where David said in his heart: “One day I shall fall into Saul’s hands. Is it not better that I flee and be saved in the land of the Philistines, so that Saul may despair and cease to seek me throughout all the borders of Israel? I shall flee from his hands.” So David arose and went, he and the six hundred men with him, to Achish son of Mahog, king of Gath [Col. 1105A].

By these seven persecutions of David are signified all the persecutions which the devil raised against Christ and his Church. For the number seven frequently denotes universality. Thus in the Apocalypse the great red dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan, is written to have seven heads, by which are signified all the kings who raised persecutions against Christ and his holy Church (Rev. 12).

Moreover, the persecutions which Christ suffered in his own person were seven. The first was when, according to Matthew, wicked Herod sought his life immediately after his birth and killed the infants on his account (Matt. 2). The second was when, according to Luke, he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up. When he was already playing the harp—that is, preaching—in order to soothe the fury of Saul, that is, so that the malignant spirit which possessed or drove the Jews, and had already begun to rage against him, might grow calm: “They rose up,” it says, “cast him out of the city, and led him to the brow of the mountain upon which their city was built, so that they might throw him down. But Jesus, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4) [Col. 1105B].

The third was where, according to John, he fled from the mocking Jews—fled, I say, by saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6). For in saying this he truly “fled and hid himself from them,” according to the title of the thirty-third Psalm, which is inscribed: “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him” (Ps. 33 [34]), “and he went away, drummed at the gates of the city, and saliva ran down into his beard, and he was carried in his hands” (1 Sam. 21).

This Abimelech is the same person who above is called Achish. Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father”; but Achish means “How is it?” He therefore signifies the Jews, whom Christ rightly first called “the kingdom of his Father,” signified by Abimelech, but now calls Achish, because they said: “How is it? How can it be?” In what did he change his countenance before them? Namely, in changing the rite of the old sacrifice into a new one.

Likewise, the saliva flowed into his beard because, when he said, “Unless you eat my flesh,” and so forth, he seemed to them to utter childish words. For it belongs to infants to emit saliva. Then too he drummed at the city gate when he preached the mystery of his passion to unwilling hearers who refused to listen, knowing that some would be opened by believing. He was also carried in his hands when, holding bread and wine in his hands, he said: “Take and eat: this is my body. This is my blood, the New Testament” (Matt. 26; Luke 22) [Col. 1105D]. Yet according to the Hebrew truth we now read: “And he was falling into their hands.”

The fourth persecution was when the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to seize him. When they returned and were asked, “Why have you not brought him?” they answered: “Never has a man spoken as this man speaks” (John 7). But they, persisting in their purpose, brought a woman caught in adultery, tempting him so that they might accuse him (John 8).

The fifth persecution was when he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am,” and they took up stones to throw at him (ibid.). The sixth was when he said: “I and the Father are one,” and the Jews took up stones to stone him (John 10). The seventh and last was when they assembled a council against him and did not cease until they crucified him [Col. 1106B].

## CHAPTER IX. That in accordance with this number of his persecutions David sang seven psalms, as may be seen from their titles, with the mystery of Christ’s passion and temptations.

Further, it must be known that this David sang seven psalms according to the number of the persecutions mentioned above: namely, Psalms 33, 51, 52, 53, 55, 56, and 58. This is easy to observe from their titles.

For the title of the first is: “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him and departed.” The title of the second: “A Psalm of David, when Doeg the Idumean went and reported to Saul, and said: David has come to the house of Abimelech” [Col. 1106C]. The title of the third: “Unto the end, for Amalek: David’s understanding.” This refers to David’s final flight, when he had taken refuge with Achish son of Mahog, king of Gath, and the Amalekites came while David was absent, struck Ziklag, and burned it with fire.

The title of the fourth: “Unto the end, in hymns: David’s understanding, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?” The title of the fifth: “Unto the end, for the people made far from the saints: David, in an inscription of the title, when the foreigners held him in Gath.” The title of the sixth: “Unto the end: Do not destroy; David, in an inscription of the title, when he fled from Saul’s face into the cave.” The title of the seventh: “Unto the end: Do not destroy; David, in an inscription of the title, when Saul sent to guard his house in order to kill him, and he departed” [Col. 1106D].

This last refers to the second persecution: when David had turned aside from Saul’s face and the spear, inflicting no wound, struck the wall, Saul sent his attendants by night to David’s house to guard him and kill him in the morning. When his wife Michal told David this, she let him down through a window; he went away, fled, and was saved.

Above we briefly treated the mystery of the first psalm’s title—how David, that is Christ, changed his countenance. In the title of the second psalm, Doeg, which means “motion”—Doeg the Idumean, that is, “earthly motion”—signifies Antichrist. For his reporting to Saul that David had come to the house of Abimelech, and Saul’s consequent killing of the priests of the Lord, prefigured that Antichrist would tear apart the Church by persecuting it unto death [Col. 1107A].

In the title of the third psalm, “unto the end, for Amalek,” this is mystically indicated: what happened historically to David, namely that his city was plundered and burned by the Amalekites, would also happen spiritually against Christ’s Church, which would be assailed by the faithless—namely Jews, pagans, and heretics—all of whom he denotes under the name Amalek. For Amalek is interpreted as “a licking people,” or “suffering and travailing,” according to the saying: “He conceived sorrow and gave birth to iniquity” (Ps. 7).

In the title of the fourth psalm, the Ziphites, who reported to Saul, saying, “Is not David hidden among us?”, signify the Jews who betrayed David to Saul—that is, handed Christ over to death. For Ziphites means “the flourishing.” By this name are denoted the Jews, who strove to flourish in temporal goods and were Christ’s kinsmen according to the flesh [Col. 1107B].

In the title of the fifth psalm, the foreigners who held David in Gath are the Jews made foreigners by their own deserts, as their name *allophyli* itself indicates. They held him in Gath, which means “winepress”: that is, amid the pressure of tribulation and death, having been made far from the saints and greatly unlike the apostles and Christ’s other faithful people.

In the title of the sixth psalm, where David is written to have fled from Saul’s face into the cave, this mystically signifies that Christ withdrew from the Jews’ knowledge because of their faithlessness and, as though hidden in a cave, concealed his divinity in human nature [Col. 1107C].

In the title of the seventh psalm, where Saul is written to have sent men to guard David’s house in order to kill him, this signifies that the Jewish people sent guards to watch Christ’s tomb (Matt. 27), in order to kill him—that is, so far as their own opinion went, to hold him in death. But they did not accomplish this. No argument could more surely establish the Lord’s resurrection than this: that he employed his own enemies as witnesses for himself.

As for the words written in some of these titles, “Do not destroy,” or “Do not corrupt,” “in an inscription of the title,” it would be superfluous to explain them now, since they bear little upon the subject; for it is not our purpose here to expound the Psalms or their titles. Yet I do not wish to pass over entirely the fact that, so far as their intention was concerned, they corrupted or destroyed the title of David himself—that is, of Christ—when they said: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said, I am King of the Jews’” (John 19) [Col. 1107D].

## CHAPTER X. How glory almost always followed each persecution as its companion, as a type of Christ himself, who overcame by his impassible divinity all that he suffered as a passible man.

It should also be noted that glory accompanies almost every persecution. When Saul first hurled the spear, thinking he could pin David to the wall, there immediately follows: “Saul therefore saw that he was exceedingly prudent, and he began to beware of him [Col. 1108A]. But all Israel and Judah loved David, for he went out and came in before them.” That is, when he went out to battle, he himself went out first before them in royal fashion, and returned.

“And Saul said to David: Behold, my elder daughter Merob; I will give her to you as wife,” etc. And thereafter: “But David loved Michol, Saul’s other daughter. And it was reported to Saul, and it pleased him. And he said: The king has no need of a bride-price, except only one hundred foreskins of the Philistines. And after a few days David arose, went to Acharon with the men who were under him, struck down two hundred Philistine men, brought their foreskins, and counted them out to the king, that he might become the king’s son-in-law.” Hence it was said: “In two matters you shall today be my son-in-law.”

He said that in two matters David would become his son-in-law: David had brought Philistine foreskins for Merob, whom Saul gave to Adriel the Melothite, and afterwards two hundred for Michol. Although it is not explicitly said that David gave Saul Philistine foreskins for Merob, whoever reads and investigates what comes before and after will find that he gave Saul Philistine foreskins twice. It may also be understood otherwise: “In two matters you shall today be my son-in-law,” because I asked you for one hundred Philistine foreskins and you offered two hundred. Or, more consistently, it may be understood thus: “In two matters you shall today be my son-in-law,” with the sense: In order to become my son-in-law, you formerly killed a Philistine; and now you will give one hundred Philistine foreskins. For lest this be doubtful to anyone, one should remember that, when the Philistine blasphemed and taunted [407], one of Israel said: “Have you seen this man who has come up? For he has come up to reproach Israel. The man who strikes him down, the king will enrich with great wealth and give him his daughter” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 17).

Therefore, he who had almost been pinned to the wall by a spear was immediately comforted by the glory that followed: he was made the king’s son-in-law in two matters, that is, through repeated victory. Again, when he had been attacked a second time with a spear and, shut in at home, escaped through a window, while Saul was still pursuing the fugitive, God gloriously protected and comforted the man who was sought.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 19.) “Saul,” he says, “sent officers to seize David.” Those sent first, second, and third prophesied when the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon them. Saul himself went. “And the Spirit of the Lord came also upon him, and he stripped himself of his garments and prophesied with the others before Samuel.” He prophesied, I say, no less by deed than by words. For by stripping off his garments he signified that he would leave the kingdom to the one whom he pursued.

Here a great question arises, since it is read earlier: “Samuel did not see Saul until the day of his death” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 15). Either he did not see him because, when Saul joined the prophetic band, Samuel hid himself so as not to be seen by him; or he did not see him clothed in royal attire, in which he was clothed when it was said, “he did not see him until the day of [Col. 1109A] his death”—with the understood qualification: clothed in royal dress. We must understand that Saul stripped himself not of all garments, but only of his royal ones.

Again, when David had fled and come to Achis, king of Geth, and Achis’s servants said, “Is not this David, king of Israel?” etc. (1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 21), he was greatly afraid, changed his manner of speech, collapsed into their hands, struck against the gateposts, and saliva ran down upon his beard. Meanwhile Saul had slain the priests of the Lord because of him; yet David soon triumphed in the glory that followed, and his bitterness was made sweet.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 23.) “They reported to David,” he says, “Behold, the Philistines are attacking Ceila.” He immediately consulted the Lord and, having received His oracle, went against the Philistine forces, fought against [Col. 1109B] them, drove off their livestock, and struck them with a great blow.

Here one must not pass over what was said: “And the vessels of the young men were holy” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21). Achimelech asked whether David and his young men, whom David said he had led to such-and-such a place, were clean. David answered enigmatically of himself in the plural, saying: “And the vessels of the young men were holy,” that is, free from marital intercourse. But when he says, “Moreover, this way is polluted” (*ibid.*), while in Hebrew it reads, “Moreover, this way is common” or “lay,” it should be understood thus: “This way is lay,” as though he said: The Law commands that a stranger not eat of them, and you ask whether the young men are clean—even though, if they were clean, they ought by no means to eat them. Therefore the way is lay, because you ask in a lay manner.

But what follows, “Yet today it shall be sanctified in the vessels” (*ibid.*), means that it is sanctified in the vessels—that is, in their minds—because David would by no means eat of them unless bodily necessity and danger to life compelled him. Nevertheless, it is not openly read that David himself ate those loaves. The Hebrews maintain that David did not eat those loaves. The Lord says otherwise in the Gospel.

Again, when the Ziphites went up to Saul and said, “Is not David hiding among us?” Saul and his companions went to seek him; and when David despaired of escaping Saul, God’s present help came to his aid with such joyful protection that, when David stood in this crisis, “a messenger came to Saul and said: Hurry and come, because the Philistines have poured themselves over the land” [Col. 1109D]. This was so glorious that they did not wish the memory of the deed or event to be lacking for posterity. “For they called that place the Rock of Division” (1 Kings [1 Samuel], chapter 24).

Again: “When Saul returned, he went to search for David even upon the steepest rocks, passable only to wild goats.” There the virtue and patience of the glorious man shone forth commendably. “Saul entered a cave to relieve himself, while David and his men were hiding in the inner part of the cave. David then arose and silently cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak,” etc. Saul, amazed at this, said: “You are more righteous than I.” And thereafter: “Swear to me by the Lord that you will not destroy my seed after me, nor remove my name from my father’s house” [Col. 1110A]. This was plainly glorious, so that here one may truly say that not the one who suffered injury, but the one who committed it, proved wretched.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 26.) Again, when “the Ziphites came once more to Saul and said: Behold, David is hidden on the hill of Achila; and Saul arose and went down into the wilderness of Ziph, with three thousand chosen men of Israel.” Observe what David did. “He and Abisai came to the people by night and found Saul lying asleep in the camp, with his spear fixed in the ground at his head.” After all that was said or done there, “Saul said: I have sinned; return, my son David,” etc. Does it not greatly contribute to the victor’s glory that, by such living patience, he heaped coals of fire upon the head of his enemy, although the stubborn root of malice persisted unburned in Saul’s heart?

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 27.) Again, when “David fled to Achis, dwelt in Geth, and Achis gave him Sicelech.” The Amalekites made an assault, struck Sicelech, and burned it with fire (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 30). But David, on his arrival, wiped away his present sorrow by the glory of the triumph that immediately followed. “For he struck the Amalekite raiders from evening until the evening of the next day, and recovered everything that they had taken. No one was missing, from small to great, whether sons or daughters; and David brought back all the spoil and whatever they had seized. He took all the flocks and herds and drove them before him, and they said: ‘This is David’s spoil.’”

Thus, as was said before, God turned all the adversities David suffered into prosperity, and the day of glory that followed immediately drove away the whole night of misery: clearly as a type of Christ, the Son of God—David, the same Son of God, God and man—who overcame by His impassible divinity everything that He suffered as passible man.

## CHAPTER XI. How mighty men joined David while he was hiding because of persecutions, whom he afterwards appointed princes and commanders; and how, in the same manner, Christ’s own Spirit brought to Christ while He was hidden in the weakness of the flesh the apostles, who were to be judges of the world, according to the number of David’s same princes.

This too was glorious: amid those very persecutions, while David was still fleeing and in hiding, the Spirit of the Lord gathered to him those mighty men whose faith and warlike courage would afterwards serve the king seated upon his throne.

For thus it is written in Chronicles: “These also came to David at Sicelech, while he was still fleeing from Saul son of Cis. They were mighty men and outstanding warriors, bending the bow and casting stones from slings with either hand: the leaders Abiezer and Joas son of Amaa the Gabathite, and the rest from Benjamin. And from Gad,” he says, “men most robust and excellent warriors. Their faces were like lions’ faces, and they were swift as gazelles upon the mountains. David went out to meet them [408] and said: If you come peaceably to me to help me, let my heart be joined to you; but if you plot against me for my adversaries, although I have no iniquity in my hands, may the God of our fathers see and judge. But the Spirit of the Lord clothed Abisai, leader among the Thirty, and he said: We are yours, O David, and with you, son of Isai: peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you. Therefore David received them and appointed them captains of a troop” (1 Chronicles 12).

Is it not indeed so with David, Christ the Son of God? While He was still hidden in the weakness of the flesh, still being tempted, still pressed by persecutions, His own Spirit brought Him leaders—that is, apostles—whose faith and patience would afterwards serve Him, reigning and seated at the Father’s right hand, throughout the whole world in the preaching of the Gospel. For of them it is said through the prophet: “In place of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm 44 [45]). And elsewhere: “The princes of the peoples have been gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Psalm 46 [47]).

For the beauty of this mystery shines more delightfully when we observe that, although very many mighty men gathered at that time to David in flight, Scripture identifies only eleven princes by name and number together: “Ezer,” it says, “the first leader; Obdias the second; Eliab the third; Masmanna the fourth; Hieremias the fifth; Hethi the sixth; Heliel the seventh; Johanna the eighth; Helzabath the ninth; Hieremias the tenth; Machabana the eleventh” (*ibid.*). Who would not delight in knowing that Christ, though He made more disciples, nevertheless chose only twelve, whom He named apostles (Luke 6), and that one of them perished, Judas, “the son of perdition” (John 17)?

Indeed, another received his episcopate or apostleship (Psalm 108 [109]), and the number of the twelve apostles was made complete (Acts 1); but this did not happen while that David was still hidden, still fleeing, still enduring persecution. By then He had conquered His enemies, overcome death, ascended into heaven, and, reigning, crowned with glory and honor, sat at the Father’s right hand. Thus the eleven princes of David while he was a fugitive and still in hiding were the eleven apostles of Christ while He was still mortal and passible. To them He therefore says: “But you are those who have remained with me in my trials. And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22).

What then, I ask, does this mean which is immediately said there concerning these princes: “The least commanded one hundred thousand, and the greatest one thousand” (1 Chronicles 12)? There would be no question at all if it had been said: “The greatest commanded one hundred thousand, and the least one thousand.” What does it mean, I ask, except that in the law or order of great David’s army, the one who is greater becomes as the lesser, and the one who goes before as the servant? (Luke 21 [cf. 22:26].) Therefore, so that the meaning may become clearer by reciprocal reversal: the one who commanded one hundred thousand was the least, and the one who commanded one thousand was the greatest. That is to say: the one among the princes of David, that is, Christ’s apostles, who abounded in more virtues was, by voluntary submission, the least of all; and the one who seemed to possess fewer virtues was judged greatest of all through the devout rivalry of humility.

## CHAPTER XII. What mystery lies in the fact that, amid persecutions, David lost one wife, Michol daughter of Saul, but gained two, Abigail and Achinoen the Jezreelite.

Likewise, we must not suppose it devoid of mystery that, amid the persecutions described above, David lost one wife, namely Michol, Saul’s daughter, but acquired two: Abigail, wife of Nabal of Carmel, and Achinoen the Jezreelite. For “Saul gave his daughter Michol, David’s wife, to Phalthi son of Lais, who was of Gallim” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 25). But he, Phalthi, as the Hebrews relate, did not know her carnally; for if he had known her, David would never afterwards have taken her back as his wife, because such intercourse is altogether forbidden in the Law.

This same Phalthi was of Gallim, that is, “of inundation.” “Inundation,” that is Gallim, signifies the Law. For he was a doctor of the Law, from Bahurim, that is, “the chosen.” When Michol is given to him by Saul, *Phalthi* is interpreted “escaping.” But when the same Michol is taken away from him, he is called *Phalthiel*, interpreted “escaping from God.” He is called “escaping from God” because God preserved him from touching her, lest he become a transgressor of the Law. “Her husband followed her, weeping, as far as Bahurim” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 3). He is said to have wept for joy, because the Lord had kept him from touching her.

Michol signifies the Synagogue, excessively carnal and watery—the name being rendered “into carnal water”—as one who did not know the wine that Christ, desirable to her, wished to offer her in His wedding feast, made from water; and who rather followed the water of the letter, which “brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7). To win her as His bride, David killed the Philistine—that is, Christ conquered the devil by His own death. But Saul, possessed—namely, the madness of sin reigning in that Synagogue—took her from Him and gave her to Phalthi, that is, to Moses. Not that she was truly given or subjected to Moses; for “if you believed Moses,” He says, “you would perhaps also believe me” (John 5). Rather, she thinks and trusts that this is so, according to the saying: “Be you his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses” (John 9).

Nevertheless, this same Phalthi, who now does not know the wife once belonging to David, will someday restore her to Him. For someday the Synagogue will recognize Christ through the reading of Moses. Again, David, who lost one wife, acquired two amid these persecutions, as was said: Abigail, wife of Nabal of Carmel, and Achinoen the Jezreelite. *Achinoen* means “the brother’s beauty”; *Jezrael*, “seed of God”; *Abigail*, “my father’s rejoicing”; and *Nabal*, “foolish.”

Thus Achinoen the Jezreelite—that is, “the brother’s beauty,” from the seed of God—is the ancient Church, which preceded Christ’s coming: the beauty, I say, that is, the honor and kingdom of the same Christ, the Son of God. For God the Father is the Father of the Church according to the Spirit, while Abraham is father according to the flesh. Thus she is Jezreelite, that is, from the seed of God. But Abigail is the new Church, following the coming of the same Christ, Son of God; formerly the wife of Nabal, that is, of the foolish. For she belonged to the discipline of foolish philosophers, whose wisdom God made foolish (1 Corinthians 1). Christ redeemed both Churches by the same sufferings and the same death.

## [409] CHAPTER XIII. How Abigail prevented that same David from avenging himself by his own hand, and what her gifts, with which she appeased David, signify mystically.

What did this Abigail do, worthy according to her name of her father’s rejoicing? “One of the servants reported to her, saying: Behold, David sent messengers from the wilderness to bless our lord, and he opposed them. Therefore Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves and two skins of wine,” etc. “And David said to Abigail: Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who sent you today to meet me; and blessed be your speech, and blessed be you, who have prevented me today from going to bloodshed and avenging myself with my own hand. Otherwise, as the Lord God of Israel lives, who kept me from doing evil to you, unless you had quickly come to meet me, there would not have remained to Nabal by the morning light anyone who urinates against a wall.” And thereafter: “When ten days had passed, the Lord struck Nabal and he died. Therefore David sent and spoke to Abigail, that he might take her as his wife.”

Clearly, in the pattern of this wise woman, the Church from the Gentiles wisely provided for herself. David’s messengers came to Nabal to bless him; the messengers of peace, I say, the preachers of salvation, came to this foolish world, which lies in the evil one (1 John 5), in order to confer upon it the grace of heavenly blessing—the grace of the Holy Spirit in the baptism of remission of sins. But Nabal—that is, every fool, all those who, “claiming to be wise, became fools” (Romans 1)—rejected them, persecuted them, and killed them.

What, conversely, did David do? What did the strong-handed one do in response? “Let each man,” he says, “gird on his sword.” And all girded on their swords. The sword of David and of his men is the power of judgment in the hand of Christ and His saints. For, “The praises of God,” he says, “are in their throat, and two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance upon the nations and rebukes upon the peoples; to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron shackles, to execute upon them the written judgment” (Psalm 149).

Fearing this, Abigail hurried; the multitude of the Gentiles hurried, bringing gifts, to anticipate and appease the Judge’s wrath, lest David avenge himself by his own hand. They believed the witnesses who say that “it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10), when our God shall come to judge and shall not be silent. “But she did not tell her husband Nabal.” For the Church did not seek the counsel of any philosopher or heed the decree of any ruler of the world. Rather, she rendered to all of them what was due: “to whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax; to whom honor, honor” (Romans 3 [cf. 13:7]). But as to how she might find the way of salvation or an escape from the wrath to come, she considered it with wisdom alone and sought counsel from the Spirit of God alone. For what could she discuss about such matters with drunken rulers, with the foolish philosophers of this world? “For Nabal,” he says, “was very drunk.”

What then are the gifts with which this Abigail hurried to our David? Not to mention the six works of mercy, which He will recount when He says: “For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink” (Matthew 25), etc.: that gift in particular, that singular offering above all, makes this woman’s prudence worthy of praise—the holy sacrifice, the spotless victim of His body and blood, which she daily offers on the holy altar. By these gifts the Church not only escaped wrath or the sword, but became the bride of great David.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the example worthy of imitation: how Abigail commendably kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, but reverently told him after the wine had been digested.

“And she did not tell him anything, small or great, until morning. But at daybreak, when Nabal had digested the wine, she told him all these things.” This example instructs both the whole Church and each individual believer. For what does Abigail indicate to us through this management of her disclosure, except that we correct angry people better if, amid the very agitation of their anger, we avoid them? For when disturbed, they do not know what they hear; but when restored to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed that they were endured so calmly. To minds drunk with rage, everything said rightly appears perverse. Therefore Abigail commendably kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, and commendably told him after his wine was digested; for he was able to recognize the evil he had done precisely because he had not heard it while drunk.

## CHAPTER XV. How and in what David is to be imitated in striking his heart because he had cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak.

Moreover, the foregoing example gives us much instruction for avoiding the vice of detraction and for showing humility, as subjects, even toward wicked rulers. Saul the persecutor had entered a cave to relieve himself [Col. 1114D], and David was there with his men (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 24), having already endured for so long the evils of Saul’s persecution. When his men urged him to strike Saul, David restrained them with his answers, because he ought not lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet he secretly arose and cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak.

What is signified by Saul but evil rulers, and by David but good subjects? Saul’s relieving his belly, then, is wicked superiors’ extending the malice conceived in the heart into deeds of foul odor, and displaying harmful thoughts held within themselves by carrying them out in external actions. David fears to strike him because pious minds of subjects, refraining from every plague of detraction, do not strike the lives of their superiors with any sword of the tongue, even when they justly criticize their imperfection. Yet if, because of weakness, they can scarcely refrain and speak humbly about certain extreme and external evils of their superiors, they silently cut, as it were, the hem of the cloak: for, while they detract, however harmlessly and secretly, from the dignity set over them, they defile, as it were, the garment of the king placed above them.

But then they return to themselves and rebuke themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of speech. Hence it is well written there: “After this David struck his heart because he had cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak.” The deeds of superiors are not to be struck with the sword of the mouth, even if they are rightly judged worthy of criticism. But if the tongue slips against them even in the smallest matters, the heart must be pressed by the affliction of repentance, so that one may return to oneself and, when one has sinned against the authority set over one, dread the judgment against oneself of Him by whom that authority has been placed over one [410]. For when we sin against those set over us, we oppose the ordinance of Him who ordained them and set them over us (Romans 13).

## CHAPTER XVI. What is mystically understood by the Egyptian servant, under whose guidance David, pursuing his Amalekite enemies, seized them.

Finally, the episode in which the Amalekites leave an Egyptian servant behind on the road, David restores him with food, makes him guide for his journey, pursues the Amalekites, finds them feasting, and utterly destroys them (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 30), spiritually displays the wondrous action of heavenly grace in the conversion of sinners.

For what is meant by the Egyptian servant’s becoming weary on the road among the Amalekites, except that the lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left weak and despised by that very age, so that he cannot run with it but, broken by adversity, languishes? But David finds him, because our Redeemer, truly strong of hand, sometimes converts to His love those whom He finds despised by worldly glory. He feeds him with food because He restores him with the knowledge of the word; He chooses him as guide of the journey because He even makes him His preacher. And he who could not follow the Amalekites becomes David’s guide, because the one whom the world abandoned as unworthy not only receives the Lord in his own mind after conversion but also, by preaching, brings Him even into other hearts. Under that guide David finds the feasting Amalekite and destroys him, because Christ, through the preaching of those whom the world disdained to have as companions, destroys the world’s joy.

## CHAPTER XVII. That Saul consulted a spirit of Python, and that it should be believed that not so much Samuel as an evil spirit appeared.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 28.) “Samuel was dead, and all Israel mourned for him and buried him in Ramatha, his city.” The question is asked: since he is already read above to have died (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 25), why is he here again said to have died? Above, indeed, he is said to have been buried “in his house at Ramatha” [Col. 1116A]. “In his house,” namely among his family and kindred. His death is repeated here, as the Hebrews wish, because of his resurrection, concerning which resurrection something will be said later.

“And the woman said to him: Whom shall I raise up for you? And he said: Raise Samuel for me,” etc. Having received no answer from God, Saul turns to pythons, as is likewise written here: “He consulted the Lord, and He did not answer him, neither through dreams, nor through priests, nor through prophets.” The Lord answered through dreams, as the Hebrews assert, because they sought a divine oracle by fasting and prayer, and God revealed to them in dreams the things that would happen; this, however, Saul is not read to have done in this place.

“But Saul,” he says, “removed magicians and diviners from the land,” and killed those who had pythons in their belly. The Hebrews maintain that this woman was the mother of Abner son of Ner, and that for Abner’s sake she was hidden and preserved, lest she be killed with the other female practitioners of Python. “Saul understood,” he says, “that it was Samuel, and he bowed himself to the ground and worshiped.”

Then did Saul understand rightly? Was the spirit of Python permitted to raise up a holy man? It strongly conflicts with this that the one who appeared said: “Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me.” Could the one whom God had cast down for pride, who in his last moments had consulted a spirit of Python and eaten from its calf, be with the righteous and prophets? Even if at that time holy and righteous people were also in the underworld awaiting the blessed hope, the wicked could not nevertheless be with them. For Abraham says to the rich man buried in hell—at a time when Abraham himself must without doubt still be believed to have been in hell: “And in all these things a great chasm has been established between us and you, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can they cross from there to us” (Luke 16).

Therefore, although we read in Ecclesiasticus that Samuel also prophesied after death (Ecclesiasticus 46), it should be believed that not so much Samuel as an evil spirit, in the phantom of Samuel, appeared. Thus, when it is repeated concerning Saul and his sons as they were about to die what was said above—“Samuel was dead, and all Israel mourned for him”—this is shown to operate more according to mystery than according to history. For it is fitting to say that Samuel died for the Jews who were to die in their sin, whose priesthood and kingdom alike were to perish with the Temple—the priesthood or kingdom rightly understood through anointed Saul. For not Samuel alone, but the whole Law and the prophets, died for them, because, reading only the killing letter and lacking the life-giving Spirit, they were handed over into the hands of enemies: in body, slain by human enemies; in soul, killed by evil spirits.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How and for what reason it was fitting that David should not be permitted to take part in the battle in which Saul and his people were to fall; and that, as David mourned the mighty men who fell, so Christ wept humanly for His nation.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 29.) What then is meant by this: when Saul, his sons, and all his men were about to die in battle, David was not permitted to take part in the war? “For the Philistine princes said to Achis: What do these Hebrews want?” And thereafter: “Let the man return and sit in the place where you have stationed him, and let him not go down with us into battle, lest he become our adversary when we begin to fight. For how could he appease his lord except with our heads? Is this not that David of whom they sang in dances, saying: Saul struck down his thousands, and David his ten-thousands?”

Thus it came about that David took part in the war neither with his people nor against his people, but, absent, mourned the mighty men who fell in battle. Did this happen by chance, rather than by God’s providence? Certainly it happened through God’s providence, so that David, the lawful king, could be judged neither a traitor nor an enemy of his country. For if, once admitted to the war, he fought against his own people, he would be an enemy of his country; if he turned to his own people after deserting the king to whom he had fled, and who had set him as a faithful guardian over his own head, he would stand disgraced by the charge of faithless treachery.

But neither should this be believed devoid of mystery. Thus the Savior withdrew His presence from the Jewish people when they were about to fall, together with their city and Temple, so that He would neither favor their enemies nor yet stretch forth a helping hand to His own kinsmen. We speak according to human feeling. Did He favor the enemies of His nation, He who, seeing the city, wept over it and amid tears foretold its coming evils? (Luke 19.) Therefore, while the Philistines fight against Israel, David is absent from both sides, because when the Romans besiege the city of Jerusalem Christ, the strong-handed one, assists neither side, since His grace is with neither side [411].

And that David weeps for Saul and both his sons when their fall is already complete; but Christ wept for the ruin of the Jews before it happened, in His own person, as has already been said, and, after it had happened, grieved in His apostle, in whom He also spoke, as the Apostle himself testifies: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart” (Romans 9), etc.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the death of Saul and his sons; and that the Hebrews say the Amalekite who reported Saul’s death was Doech.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 30.) “David,” he says, “will not listen to you in this matter. For the share of the one going down to battle and of the one remaining with the baggage shall be equal.” Whereas Latin manuscripts read that certain exhausted men remained behind with the baggage, the Hebrew has that they “were commanded to remain with the baggage.” This passage shows that the Hebrew truth must be followed here, which says that they remained with the baggage not because they were exhausted but because they had been ordered to do so. For it says: “The share of the one going down to battle and of the one remaining with the baggage shall be equal.” It does not say, “those who remained with the baggage because they were exhausted,” but simply, “those remaining with the baggage,” because those who had remained from exhaustion ought not to have been given any share of the spoil.

(1 KINGS [1 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 31.) “When the armor-bearer saw,” namely that Saul was dead, “he too fell upon his sword and died with him.” The Hebrews say that this armor-bearer was Doech the Idumean, who, seeing Saul dead, killed himself for fear of David. “Thus Saul died, and his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men.” These men should be understood as his household servants. His three sons were killed with him: Jonathan, Aminadab, also called Jesui, and Melchisna. But Isboset was asleep; he had been born in the year in which Saul was made king. He too is said to have been forty years old when he began to reign. From this it is inferred that Saul reigned forty years.

One must ask why in one place he is called Jesui and in another Aminadab. *Jesui* means “equal.” He is called equal because the sons are recorded to have been equal to their father in merit. *Aminadab* means “my father willingly.” For his father Saul, by his own will, through evil conduct brought it about that he should perish in such a manner together with his sons.

(2 KINGS [2 SAMUEL], CHAPTER 1.) “But on the third day, a man appeared, coming from Saul’s camp.” The Hebrews say that this Amalekite was the son of Doech. For Amalekite and Idumean are one, because Elifar was Esau’s firstborn son, and Amalec was Elifar’s son. They further maintain that the diadem and bracelet which he brought to David had been entrusted to him by his father Doech.

## CHAPTER XX. On David’s remarkable innocence in mourning dead Saul, and on the bow which the children of Israel ought to have learned through this kind of lament.

“David then uttered the following lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son, and commanded that they should teach the bow to the children of Judah, as it is written in the Book of the Just: ‘The illustrious men of Israel have been slain upon their mountains,’” etc. If you consider rightly who lamented, what he lamented, why he lamented, and, further, what mystical meaning this lament signifies, you will find that it is reasonable and drawn from the treasury of a wise man. For who lamented? [Col. 1118D] The anointed king, not ignorant of his own election, who knew that, through Saul’s death, the royal throne had been made vacant for him, so that he who had been an exile might now return to his own country. Wonderful innocence, therefore; wonderful restraint against ambition. It would have been a small thing merely to have restrained his hands, saying: “May the Lord be merciful to me, that I should not stretch forth my hand against the Lord’s anointed” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 24); for even while saying this he might have wished either that Saul’s day of death would come or that, going down into battle, he might perish. But behold: the open act of justice reveals the hidden disposition of his heart, when he himself mourns and, by the punishment or death of the man who brought the news, decrees that none of his followers should exult. Rightly, therefore, may the mighty David sing, sing confidently, and say: “O Lord [Col. 1119A] my God,” “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is iniquity in my hands, if I have repaid evil to those who requited me, let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Psalm 7).

But what did he lament? Namely, that Saul, though he was the Lord’s anointed, earned by his pride both to be cast away from the presence of the Lord and to cause all Israel with him to fall before its enemies, its illustrious men being slain. This indeed was something for a wise man to mourn, since he knew that in the deepest humility he himself must beware of the example of the man who, though he was the Lord’s anointed, deserved through pride to be handed over to an evil spirit, and fell so far that, after consulting a pythonic spirit and thus becoming condemnable through complete transgression, he ended his present life in a miserable end.

And why did he mourn? “That they might teach,” he says, “the children [Col. 1119B] of Judah the bow,” as it is written in the Book of the Just.” The bow is the strength of warfare; and certainly this bow, or strength in war, is nothing other than the hand or help of the Lord. The entire strength of war is rightly signified here by the bow, because Saul had especially perished by the bow, as was written above (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 31): the archers overtook him, and he was grievously wounded by the archers. This would certainly not have happened had he himself wished to hold or bend his own bow—that is, had he placed his hope in God, without whom Israel never conquered or acted bravely.

“As it is written,” he says, “in the book of the just of Israel.” Although some may understand this as a particular book which can nowhere be found today, more consistently this is understood as the book [Col. 1119C] mentioned in Numbers: “Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord: ‘As he did at the Red Sea, so he will do at the torrents of Arnon’” (Numbers 21), etc. But what is the Book of the Wars of the Lord except the whole of Holy Scripture, from which we are undoubtedly taught to wage the Lord’s wars? For before Moses, who said this, nothing of that sort had been written. Thus, he says, “that they might teach the children of Judah the bow, as it is written in the Book of the Just”; that is, because the children of Israel had fought badly through their own fault, at least the children of Judah, their fellow-tribesmen, should learn to make God their helper, as all the just have done, whose victories were accomplished through God’s wonderful cooperation. The Scriptures testify to this; though divided into many books, they were written by one Spirit, [Col. 1119D] and therefore are rightly counted as one book, according to the words: “And I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals” (Revelation 5).

But how do the children of Judah learn the aforesaid bow through such a lament as this: “The illustrious men of Israel have been slain upon your mountains. How have the mighty fallen! Swifter than eagles, stronger than lions: Jonathan has been slain upon your heights”? How, I say, do they learn the bow through such a lament? Clearly, the implied sense is this: Let all who fight learn from this example that, even if they are mighty and very illustrious, and even if they possess the swiftness of eagles and the strength of lions, they will nevertheless never [412] be able to achieve victory when God turns away from them. From this example, I say, let them learn this: behold, upon your mountains, O Saul—[Col. 1120A]upon your mountains, that is, because of your pride—the illustrious men of Israel were slain; the mighty fell with you. Jonathan too was slain upon your heights—your heights, I say, not his. For this son, worthy of a better father, died not because of his own pride but because of his father’s pride.

For this is contradicted by what is said: “Jonathan’s arrow never went backward.” Jonathan’s arrow was Jonathan’s faith, by which he made a covenant with David himself; and it never went backward, for he never made that covenant void. In saying “Jonathan’s arrow” in place of “Jonathan’s faith,” the writer fittingly looks back to the event itself. For it was written above [Col. 1120B] (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 20): “Jonathan therefore made a covenant with David, and Jonathan further made David swear.” And afterward: “And I will shoot three arrows. If I say to the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are on this side of you; take them,’ then come to me, for peace is with you,” etc. Therefore “Jonathan’s arrow never went backward”; that is, the covenant in whose sign Jonathan used the arrows he never made void.

In saying these things and uttering such a lament, David nevertheless strengthens Israel and urges it to hope for timely consolation from God. For he says: “Do not announce it in Gath, nor proclaim it in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult.” This means: Although the illustrious men of Israel have been slain, although the mighty have fallen and the weapons of war have perished, [Col. 1120C] quickly take up the bow again and strengthen your arm with good hope, so that your enemies may not suppose that they have won a complete triumph over you; so that it may be proclaimed to them that, although the mighty have fallen, you still have the most mighty God.

But why, he says, “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits be upon you”? Namely, that the mountain’s perpetual barrenness itself might remain a necessary lesson for posterity, so that future kings might always have before their eyes a reminder to beware the vice of pride, because there the shield of the mighty was cast away—the shield of Saul—so disgracefully, as though he had not been anointed with oil, as though it had never returned effective from the blood of the slain and the fat of the mighty.

“Daughters of Israel,” he says, “weep over Saul.” [Col. 1120D] For he must be wept over, because “he who clothed you in scarlet amid delights, who supplied golden ornaments for your adornment”—the sense is: from the spoils of enemies which he won—now lies naked; now he himself has become the prey of visible and invisible enemies.
