## CHAPTER XXI. How and what kind of lament for his Jewish people that lament of David signifies in Christ, and what bow the same lament, spiritually understood, ought to teach us.

What mystical meaning, finally, does this lament signify, except the lament of the true David—that is, Christ, “mighty of hand”—who wept over the ruin of his own people, the Jewish people? For he himself, seeing the city, wept [Col. 1121A] over it, saying: “For if you too had known!” (Luke 19). And through his Apostle he laments its ruin once it has occurred, in the words—in which Christ undoubtedly speaks—“I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren” (Romans 9), etc.

David, therefore, mourns Saul and those who fell, Israel’s mighty and illustrious men. Christ, mighty of hand or desirable, mourns the pride of carnal Israel and the false strength of the Israelites, concerning which he himself says in the Psalm: “The mighty rushed upon me” (Psalm 38), namely, those wishing to establish their own righteousness and glorying as though illustrious, not in God’s grace but in works [Col. 1121B] of the Law. And woe to those who did not forestall the lament of this David with the lamentations of their own repentance!

In lamenting, he also commanded “that they should teach the children of Judah the bow”; that is, that they should teach the children of his confession, namely the Christian people from among the Gentiles, not to boast as though of their own merits, but, submitting themselves to God’s grace, to hold the true and constant bow of heavenly strength. The Apostle, wisely carrying out this command to teach, says: “But if some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though you were a wild olive, have been grafted among them and made a partaker of the root and richness of the olive, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root you. Do not think highly, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either” (Romans 11). In saying these things and the rest, he certainly teaches the children of Judah the bow: that, if they wish to act bravely, they should not boast, but should humbly stand in the grace of God.

For, he says, “The illustrious men of Israel have been slain upon their mountains, and the illustrious mighty have fallen”—[Col. 1121C]those, namely, “who are Israelites according to the flesh, whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Romans 9). According to these things, therefore, they are truly illustrious; but in pride they are falsely mighty. Accordingly, they were slain; accordingly, they fell, especially [Col. 1121D] through the fault of the priests, who devoured the deceived people.

Therefore he says: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits be upon you.” For Gilboa is interpreted “devouring” or “running down.” By this name the Pharisees or those priests are not inappropriately indicated: the devourers and voracious men whom the Savior drove out with a whip while they committed robbery in his Father’s house and made spoil of the people, according to that prophetic saying: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hosea 4).

Therefore, he says, “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you, nor fields of firstfruits be upon you”; that is, while the whole valley of humble Gentiles is watered from above and made full so that it abounds with grain, so that the poor may eat and be satisfied and praise the Lord, you who are high and [Col. 1122A] proud shall receive neither dew—that is, the Holy Spirit—nor rain, that is, the word of saving doctrine. For “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon you” (Isaiah 5): my clouds, I say, that is, my apostles, I will command to withhold it from your pride and to rain upon the Gentiles the preaching of the Gospel. Therefore you shall not be fields of firstfruits: there shall be no first harvest from you to be carried at this time into that heavenly granary, until the fullness of the Gentiles comes in. Then a remnant from you will be saved (Romans 11), and there will no longer be an early harvest, but a late harvest.

Why? “Because there the shield of the mighty was cast away, the shield of Saul, as though he had not been anointed with oil.” There, I say—that is, in your pride—I was cast away, [Col. 1122B] I who alone am the shield of the mighty, who ought to have been the shield of Saul, that is, the defense or protection of this furious or possessed people. For at your urging it denied me before Pilate; it denied me, I say, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). What did it do by this denial except cast away its shield, the shield of the mighty, as though he had not been anointed with oil? There, I say, it cast me away, as though I were not the Messiah, were not the Christ, were not anointed with the Holy Spirit; as though I had no testimony from the blood of the slain and the fat of the mighty—that is, of evil spirits or impious men—as though I could take no spoil whatever from the hands of my enemies.

## CHAPTER XXII. [Col. 1122C] Concerning the oracle by which David is commanded to go up to Hebron, and what that ascent signifies mystically in Christ.

(2 Kings [2 Samuel] 2.) “Therefore after these things David consulted the Lord, saying: ‘Shall I go up into one of the cities of Judah?’ And the Lord said to him: ‘Go up.’ And David said: ‘Where shall I go up?’ And he answered him: ‘To Hebron.’”

Until now an exile and fugitive, David mourned and wept, drunk with much bitterness; but now, obediently prepared to return to his country and reign, he desires to sing and make melody in the tabernacle of his God, following the example of him in whose person he speaks: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory” (Psalm 107).

Indeed, to this man asking, “Shall I go up into one of the cities [Col. 1122D] of Judah?” the answer is, “Go up to Hebron.” And to that other, waiting in the tomb as though for the Father’s answer—for he did not come from himself but did everything obediently—he says: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp” (Psalm 56). And he immediately says: “I will awake at dawn” (ibid.). And as though commanded to go up to Hebron, gladly accepting this, he says: “I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing to you among the nations” (ibid.).

For Hebron was the city of the tomb of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the great Adam, as is written in the book of Joshua (Joshua 15). Hence it is also called Kiriath-arba: “Hebron was formerly called Kiriath-arba,” which is interpreted “four.” The great Adam [Col. 1123A] lay there among the Anakim. Thus Hebron, the beginning of David’s kingdom, signifies the Jewish people because Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were buried there; but because the great Adam likewise lay there, it signifies the whole human race. Therefore David is rightly both commanded to go up to Hebron in his own person and taught to sing in the person of Christ, saying: “I will confess you among the peoples, O Lord, and sing to you among the nations.” Yet he asks whether he should go up into only one of the cities of Judah, because Christ reigns only in the one Church of the one faith.

## CHAPTER XXIII. [Col. 1123B] Concerning Abner, who was first David’s adversary and afterward transferred the kingdom to David: how he is a figure of the Apostle Paul, from the same tribe of Benjamin; and what the contest signifies in which, while the young men from either side fought together, Abner struck the very swift Asahel in the groin with a reversed spear.

“Now Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul’s army, took Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, and led him about through the camps, and made him king over Gilead, over the Ashurites, over Jezreel, over Ephraim, and over all Israel.” Instead of “Ashurites,” the more correct reading is “Asherites,” that is, the tribe of Asher.

Since Abner was first David’s adversary and leader of the opposing party, but afterward transferred the kingdom from Saul’s house so that David’s throne might be raised over Israel and Judah, as the Lord had sworn to him, whom should we judge him to signify except Paul, of the tribe of Benjamin? For Abner is interpreted “the father’s lamp,” while Ish-bosheth means “man of confusion.” Paul was indeed the father’s lamp [Col. 1123C] in the presence of God even when he was still leading about Ish-bosheth—that is, while he was still defending Jewish confusion; yet in his present actions he was blind, as a persecutor and blaspheming enemy of David.

“And Abner the son of Ner went out, and the young men of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, from the camp to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and David’s young men went out and met them.” And afterward: “Each seized the head of his counterpart and thrust his sword into his opponent’s side, and they fell together.” And a little later: “Abner therefore struck Asahel in the groin with the back end of the spear, pierced him through, and he died.”

This conflict builds up the discerning reader’s [Col. 1123D] understanding in two ways: allegorically and according to anagogy. Allegorically, it signifies the conflict in the beginnings of evangelical faith between Jews and believing Gentiles. For the Jews said: We are God’s people, whom he loved and cherished from the beginning. We are circumcised; we descend from Abraham’s race and from the holy stock; God was known in Judah alone in former ages. But you are dogs rather than human beings; from the beginning you have served idols. And similar things.

Conversely, the Gentiles answered: The greater the benefits of God toward you that you recount, the more you demonstrate yourselves guilty of a greater crime; for you have always been ungrateful for all these things, and now at last you not only refused to receive the Lord Christ, always promised to you by the voices of the prophets, but even put him to a most shameful death. Thus, fighting one another, they thrust the swords of their tongues into opposing sides, [Col. 1124A] and fell together.

What then of Abner? “Abner,” it says, “struck Asahel in the groin with the reversed spear, pierced him through, and he died.” Asahel means “lifting up” or “exalting God.” Asahel, I say—the exceedingly swift runner—alone signifies all those who, contending in the aforesaid manner from either side, tried to raise the one common God toward one party or the other. But Abner, that is, the father’s lamp, who pierced Asahel with a reversed spear, is, as was said above, the Apostle Paul. When Jews and Gentiles so contend, he does not reproach their sins with an open assault; rather, in the Epistle to the Romans, he quietly recalls them, as it were indirectly, sparingly, and with restraint.

According to anagogy, however, [Col. 1124B] of whom was Asahel a type except those whom a violent fury seizes and drives headlong? In the same rush of fury, they must be avoided with as much care as they are madly carried away. Hence Abner, called the father’s lamp, flees, because the speech of teachers, which points out the heavenly light of God, avoids the angry and furious person and appears not to return verbal darts. But when the angry man does not cease from madness, it is necessary to utter certain things subtly, by which he may indirectly prick the furious person’s mind. Thus, when Abner stops against his pursuer, he does not pierce him with a direct spear, but with a reversed one. To strike from the point is to meet the oncoming force of open persecution. But to strike the pursuer with a reversed spear is to touch the furious person quietly [Col. 1124C] in certain matters and, as it were, to overcome him by sparing him.

Asahel immediately falls, because minds in commotion, while they feel themselves spared and yet are inwardly touched by the reasoning of answers under calmness, immediately fall away from that to which they had raised themselves. Thus those who recoil from the blow of the impulse that lifted them up in their own fury die, as it were, without iron.

[414] ## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the death of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, and what is mystically understood through it.

(2 Kings [2 Samuel] 4.) “Now there were two men, leaders of raiding bands, belonging to Saul’s son; the name of one was Baanah and the name of the other Rechab, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite. And the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and dwelt there as sojourners until that time,” etc.

These two men, the leaders, were commanders over Ish-bosheth’s expeditions. [Col. 1124D] When Abner had died, as the Hebrews relate, they took counsel with Mephibosheth to kill Ish-bosheth together and make Mephibosheth himself king; and Mephibosheth himself was to have been the informer of this plan [the text reads *exstitisset*, apparently corrupt]. Therefore this same Mephibosheth is introduced here in this way: “Now Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son lame in both feet; for he was five years old when news came from Jezreel concerning Saul and Jonathan,” etc.

But when Baanah and Rechab saw that their plan had been betrayed by Mephibosheth, terrified by fear, they fled to Gittaim and dwelt there as sojourners until that time. “That time” must be understood as the time when, having returned from there, they entered Ish-bosheth’s house in the heat of the day, carrying ears of wheat, and struck him in [Col. 1125A] the groin. They took ears of wheat, as though on account of firstfruits, so that they might appear to be bringing honor to the king and their deceit might not be detected.

From this passage a moral sweetness breathes forth. To strike in the groin is to pierce the mind’s life through carnal delight. For the female gatekeeper cleans grain when the mind’s guard, by discernment, separates virtues from vices. If she falls asleep, she admits conspirators to the death of her own lord. Nor would this Ish-bosheth, that is, the man of confusion, have succumbed to this death if he had not appointed a woman—that is, lax guardianship—to the entrance of the house, namely, to the mind’s doorway. A strong male guardian ought to be set over the doors of the heart, one whom neither the sleep of negligence overcomes nor the error of ignorance deceives.

## CHAPTER XXV. [Col. 1125B] Concerning the bringing of the ark of the Lord, and how that dancing of David the prophet and king, leaping, proceeded from great humility and wisdom.

(2 Kings [2 Samuel] 6.) “David assembled all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand, and David arose and went, together with all the people who were with him from the men of Judah; and they brought up the ark of the Lord of hosts, who sits above the cherubim upon it. And they placed the ark of God upon a new cart,” etc.

What was this festival of the prophet? Shall I call it the prophet’s, or the king’s? Rather, it was both the prophet’s and the king’s. For the Spirit of the Lord who was sent into him made him a prophet before making him king, and showed him the mysteries of the future Lord—his son, the great [Col. 1125C] King Christ—before allowing him to ascend the throne of Israel’s present earthly kingdom.

What, therefore, was that great solemnity of prophet and king in bringing up the ark of the Lord? “They went,” as is written more fully in Chronicles, “to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the house of Obed-edom with joy. And when the Lord had helped the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, seven bulls and seven rams were sacrificed. David was clothed in a linen ephod, and all Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord with shouting, with the sound of the trumpet and horns, and with cymbals, harps, and lyres resounding” (1 Chronicles 15), etc.

Were these things done in vain, or in the absence of the holy spirit of prophecy? If Elisha stirred up the holy spirit of prophecy [Col. 1125D] within his breast at the song of one harpist, as it is written: “But now bring me a harpist. And while the harpist was playing, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said: ‘Thus says the Lord: Make trenches in the bed of this torrent’” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 3), how much more ought that same Spirit, who was also in Elisha, be believed to have been awakened amid such great rejoicing, such a sound of trumpets, and such clamor of horns, cymbals, and lyres—especially since the king himself, forgetful as it were of royal dignity, played and danced before the ark of the Lord with all his strength, so that he seemed contemptible to his wife Michal? (1 Chronicles 15.) Did the great king, the king mighty of hand, play and dance thus [Col. 1126A] because of the wantonness of youthful blood, or rather because the great strength of the Spirit of God was breaking a humble heart—so great and strong precisely insofar as he was small and lowly in his own eyes?

## CHAPTER XXVI. How that bringing up of the ark of the Lord prefigured the glory of Christ’s resurrection, and how that singing of the lyre-players signified the sound and words of preachers which went forth into all the earth.

Therefore, once David’s kingdom over the people Israel had been established, the ark of the covenant of the Lord was brought up amid such dancing by the whole kingdom. This was a type of that event for which the entire world dances today: namely, that when the great King, the King mighty of hand and desirable, Christ, had risen from the dead and, crowned with glory and honor, had been set over the works of his Father’s hands, the resurrection of that victorious King was immediately proclaimed throughout the whole world.

For, as has already been [Col. 1126B] said more fully elsewhere, the marvelous ark, the ark containing within itself all the treasures of the whole divinity, is the structure of the human body which the Holy Spirit fashioned for the Son of God from the virginal womb; and that ark was a type of this body. For indeed the name of the Lord of hosts, sitting above the cherubim upon it, was invoked over this ark; rather, it is itself called the house of hosts, because of the fullness of knowledge and the whole divinity dwelling bodily within it.

Thus the people of the Lord in Israel sang, and the entire multitude of Jacob sang lawfully. David also, striking the harp with the singers, caused the sound of those singing to be heard in the whole world. For “there are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends [Col. 1126C] of the world” (Psalm 18)—the implied speakers saying: “He has set his tabernacle in the sun” (ibid.), etc.

The heavens which declare this glory of God, namely the apostles, are, according to the mystery of this passage, Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, and Ethan: that is, gatherers, leapers, robust men, and strong men—gathering spiritual things, leaping over carnal things, robust for enduring evils, strong for doing good. With all diligence they sang on harps “for the eighth,” that is, in every kind of mortification of the flesh, bearing witness to the resurrection which is called the eighth.

Literally, they sang “for the eighth” because they began with this phrase in the title of the sixth psalm. The Jews understand “for the eighth” as referring to circumcision; but we understand it as that better circumcision by which we are to be renewed, namely the resurrection of the flesh.

David stood in their midst, himself holding the psaltery and striking the harp, [Col. 1126D] leaping with all his strength. For he himself said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), etc.; and, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). With his beautiful fingers, that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he struck the breasts of the apostles, so that they would neither be silent nor fail; in a manner leaping, that is, performing through them the wonders by which they were helped and their speech was confirmed.

[415] ## CHAPTER XXVII. What the new cart is, what the house of Abinadab is, and what is signified by the contempt of Michal, Saul’s daughter, looking through the window.

“And they placed,” he says, “the ark of God upon a new cart, and brought it from the house of Abinadab.” The new cart by which this ark of the covenant of the Lord is carried [Col. 1127A] is Christ’s new Gospel, by which, as stated above, his resurrection is proclaimed throughout the whole world. For the four wheels of the cart are the four Evangelists.

The house of Abinadab, whose name means “my people’s willing one,” is the house, I say, of Abinadab—that is, of Christ, who freely gave himself to his people. It was formerly the Synagogue, but now it is the Church, which received faith in Christ’s resurrection while the Synagogue envied it.

And now, indeed, that Synagogue mocks our David as he plays and leaps, [Col. 1127B] sparing not its blasphemous mouth, just as Michal, Saul’s daughter, looked through the window, saw David leaping and playing before the Lord, and despised him in her heart. But the time will come when it says: “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Abinadab” (Song of Songs 6). “I did not know,” I say: my soul was troubled by an unexpected change of affairs, and I did not understand the Gospel chariots carrying the ark of God from the house of Abinadab.

For when the fullness of the Gentiles comes in (Romans 11), then this Michal will no longer look out through the window and despise the glorious King David; she herself too will follow, indeed will receive the ark of the Lord, the faith of Christ’s resurrection. Meanwhile, she looks out, as it were, through the window because, unwilling to take part in such great joys, she plots in secret whatever she may be able to blaspheme, whether in what manner or on what ground.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. [Col. 1127C] How the Lord struck Uzzah because he touched the ark of the Lord, as an example that the life of prelates ought not rashly to be reproved by their subjects.

“Ahio and Uzzah, sons of Abinadab, drove the new cart. But when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah stretched out his hand to the ark of God and held it, because the oxen kicked and had tilted it. And the Lord was angered with indignation against Uzzah and struck him for his rashness.”

The same Abinadab had commanded his two sons, Uzzah and Ahio, to carry the ark of the Lord upon their shoulders; and because neither they themselves carried it nor gave it to the Kohathites to carry, Uzzah was punished with death. For there was sin in not carrying it; and in holding up the ark there was already the punishment of sin. For it is reported [Col. 1127D] concerning Uzzah that his arm withered, as did the shoulder upon which the ark of the Lord ought to have been carried, and that a division was made in that place.

“He turned aside the ark of the Lord into the house of Obed-edom.” Obed-edom was a Levite, and David did not know why God’s indignation had come upon Uzzah. But after he learned the cause for which Uzzah was struck, he commanded it to be carried upon shoulders, as what follows shows.

Mystically, moreover, by this likeness we are more strongly warned not rashly to judge the humble bearers of God’s ark when we are ourselves idle or empty, if they should sometimes offend like kicking oxen. For example: “There arose a dispute among Jesus’ disciples as to which of them should seem to be greater” (Luke 22). Likewise in the Acts [Col. 1128A] of the Apostles: “There arose a disagreement between Barnabas and Saul, so that they departed from one another” (Acts 15). Where these or similar things happen, kicking oxen have indeed tilted the ark.

For Paul also says: “It is written in the Law of Moses: ‘You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain.’ Is God concerned with oxen? Or did he surely say it for us? For it was surely written for us” (1 Corinthians 9; Deuteronomy 25). Therefore, to restrain the boldness of reproach against rulers, “the Lord,” he says, “was angered against Uzzah with indignation and struck him for his rashness,” because those who look upon the weaknesses of the saints, instead of upon the fact that “out of weakness they were made strong, became mighty in war” (Hebrews 11), thereby provoke divine judgment against themselves.

Again, according to the moral sense, [Col. 1128B] what is the mind of a righteous person except the ark of the covenant? It is tilted by kicking oxen when even one who governs well is sometimes shaken by the disorder of subject peoples. But one loses life who proudly lifts up God’s ark, because no one would presume to correct the deeds of saints unless he first thought better things of himself. Hence the Levite is rightly called Uzzah, because the name is interpreted “strength of the Lord”: for presumptuous people would never judge the deeds or sayings of better persons to be weaknesses unless, in their audacious minds, they believed themselves strong in the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Laudable is David’s devotion in wishing to build a house for the Lord is praiseworthy, and how no one could build a house worthy of the Lord except Christ alone.

[Col. 1128C] (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 7.) “And it came to pass, when the king sat in his house and the Lord had given him rest on every side from all his enemies, that he said to Nathan the prophet: ‘Do you see that I dwell in a house of cedar, while the ark of God is set in the midst of skins?’” etc.

He said this worthily and praiseworthily: as one not ungrateful, as a fair weigher and assessor of God’s dignity and benefits. Nor did this thought occur to him by chance or in vain, [Col. 1128D] but by God’s prompting: so that, through this occasion, with his mind well prepared and the doors of his devout heart opened, he might worthily receive the promise of his Lord’s Son, Christ the eternal King, who alone knew and was able to build a house for the living God to dwell in.

Nathan, however, when he said, “Everything that is in your heart, go and do, for God is with you,” spoke from himself, not from God’s word. But what follows—“Thus says the Lord: ‘Will you build me a house?’”—he spoke from the Lord’s word.

Let us now, then, enter into the most sweet mystery of this passage and, in praise of Christ the Son of God, whose promise is here given, contemplate with fitting hearing of faith the mercies of the Lord which must be sung forever. First, let us understand David equally to represent all the holy or righteous persons who were from the beginning until the coming of Christ the Son of God. Since all were subject to sin, it is evident that they could not build a house for the Lord’s name.

But in Solomon we confess the same Christ, the Son [Col. 1129A] of God, who, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2), built the house: namely, the Church of the living God, from his blood which he poured out for us and from his Holy Spirit which he gave to us.

[416] ## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the words, “And when your days shall be fulfilled,” etc.; how the Church was promised to Christ according to the flesh, and how that Psalm, “I will sing for ever the mercies of the Lord,” concerns him.

“Will you,” he says, “build me a house to dwell in? For I have not dwelt in a house from the day when I brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt until this day.” As though he said: You will not be able to build me a house, because you are a man of blood and have shed much blood. Moreover, you will not be able to build me a house—that is, the Church—in which it may please me to dwell by grace, because, since you are not free from sins of your own, you cannot at all take away the sins of the people; and this is truly to build a house for God.

Conversely: “The Lord,” he says, “foretells to you that the Lord will make you a house.” Not you for him, but he for you will build a house in which you shall be a member of the household through the common faith, and through the privilege of grace shall obtain the honor of the paternal name. For behold, attend to me and listen: the Lord himself predicts this to you through me, his prophet; or rather, what you now hear through me, his messenger, he himself will afterward reveal to you through the Holy Spirit, as to an outstanding prophet. “When your days [Col. 1129C] are fulfilled and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall come forth from your womb, and I shall establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I shall establish the throne of his kingdom for ever. I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son.” And afterward: “Your house and your kingdom shall be faithful for ever before my face, and your throne shall be established continually.”

The majesty of these words and meanings altogether forbids their being understood of anyone other than Christ, the only Son of God and son of David: according to his divinity, David’s Lord; according to the flesh, David’s son. For whose throne, if not his, did God establish for ever? Or of whom else did he ever say, or ought he to have said: “I shall be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son?” Therefore, by a generous and wonderful exchange, while a poor and limited human being plans to build a handmade house for the immeasurable and incomprehensible God, God, on the contrary, declares that he will build for that same man an eternal house—something impossible for man—in which God himself may truly dwell. Thus the prophet says: “The Lord foretells to you”—that is, the Father—“that the Lord will make you a house,” namely, the Son of the Father. And truly the house of God, which is the holy Church, is itself David’s house: in it the Father of Christ is called God according to divinity, while David is called the father of Christ according to the flesh.

Hence comes that magnificent song of everlasting mercies, which the breadth of the heart, striving though unable sufficiently to express them with its narrow mouth, utters in this manner: “I shall sing the mercies of the Lord for ever; from generation to generation I shall proclaim your truth with my mouth” (Ps. 88). What mercies, O man, will you sing? What truth of mine will you proclaim with your mouth? “For you have said,” he declares, “Mercy shall be built up for ever in the heavens; your truth shall be prepared in them” (ibid.). And the remaining prophetic utterances to the end of the psalm are of such splendor and clarity, and of such precious faith, that the awakened spirit of devotion could, with its fire, melt gold in David’s breast.

For after hearing so great a promise, he sat before the Lord with his heart poured out and said: “Who am I, O Lord God, that you have brought me thus far?” etc. Certainly, what is said here—“If he does anything wicked, I shall rebuke him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men; but I shall not take away my mercy from him” [Col. 1130B]—is more readily explained in the psalm mentioned above: “But if his sons abandon my law and do not walk in my judgments, if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I shall visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with scourges; but I shall not scatter my mercy from him” (ibid.).

For that holy Son of David, the Holy of holies, was not going to commit any wickedness that needed rebuke “with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men.” But his sons, who are ourselves, are not without sin; indeed, our iniquities are many and our sins many, and they rightly must be visited with the rod and atoned for by purifying scourges, while mercy is not finally removed—provided there is not the hard and impenitent obstinacy of sinners. Yet the meaning of the two passages is one: namely, that the Father of the sons bore their sins upon himself, and that he is the head of the whole body of which we are members.

The firmness of this truth was also prefigured in that typical Solomon, builder of the handmade Temple. For he too abandoned the law of the Lord, and his sons, the kings of Judah, did not walk in the judgments of the Lord; for apart from David, Hezekiah, and Josiah, they all sinned. Yet God visited their iniquities with the rod and did not take his mercy from them, when, in accordance with God’s truth confirmed by an oath, David was born from among them, who, as has already been said, was to build mercy—or the house of mercy—in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the same promise, and on the fact that David had not previously received the promise that Christ would be born from his seed

“Who am I,” he says, “O Lord God, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far? Yet even this seemed too little in your sight, O Lord my God, unless you should also speak concerning the house of your servant for a long time to come.”

Although David, prophet though he was and renowned psalmist though he was, had already uttered the voices of the Spirit of the Lord directed toward himself from the first anointing, he had not yet received that which was the summit of his happiness: namely, that his salvation, Christ, would be born from him—his salvation and expectation, not only his own, but that of the whole world. For the Messiah was indeed expected from the tribe of Judah, but not yet from the house of faithful David. Here for the first time he heard this; and therefore, as though stunned, crying out in wonder at his blessing, he asked who he himself might be.

Nor was he content with this unless he also knew the place where that Lord his God and son of his womb would be born. Therefore he afflicted himself and humbled his soul for this purpose, praying that it might be revealed to him in what place he would be born, as he himself testifies in another psalm: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord, made a vow to the God of Jacob: ‘If I enter into the tabernacle of my house, if I ascend onto the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob’” (Ps. 131).

How strictly he afflicted himself, he has made known to us, and immediately added that he was heard. For while still in affliction, with the Spirit suddenly revealing it, he joyfully cried out: “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah; 417 we found it in the fields of the wood” (ibid.). By these words he asserted not only that in the Spirit he had heard where Christ would be born, but also where that ark of the Lord, the ark of God’s sanctification, was to be transferred—the ark in which the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in human nature (Col. 2), from the seed of David himself.

For Ephrathah itself is Bethlehem, David’s city, where Mary’s days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she bore her firstborn son [Col. 1131C] (Luke 2). The fields of the wood, however, are we Gentiles: fields of the wood, that is, fields now made cultivable and fertile in good fruits, whereas formerly we were woods, providing hidden dens within ourselves for evil spirits, which are indeed savage beasts. Therefore, when he says, “We heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the wood,” he certainly testifies that it was disclosed to him both where the ark of incarnate divinity was first to be heard of and where it was finally to be found.

## CHAPTER XXXII. What he means in saying: “This is the law of Adam”

“For this is the law of Adam, O Lord God. What more, therefore, can David add, to speak to you?” As though he said: Truly, according to your word, O Lord God, I shall not build you a dwelling-house for you to inhabit—you whom neither heaven nor the heaven of heavens can contain. Nor have you dwelt in a house since the day when you brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt. It is clear, moreover, that much more certainly you did not dwell in a house before that time. For “this is the law of Adam”: namely, the law of sin under which he begot us all. For according to him we too are all by nature “children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2). Therefore neither we nor others through us deserve to be your house, because none of us is clean from defilement, and all of us need that same grace of yours, that is, the remission of sins.

Hence another says: “Though I be washed as with snow-water and my hands shine most cleanly, yet you will plunge me into filth, and my garments will abhor me” (Job 9). What then can I answer against your judgment? Surely, as the same man says above: “If I wish to justify myself, my mouth will condemn me; if I show myself innocent, you will prove me perverse” (ibid.).—“For you know your servant, O Lord God.” You know, I say, that I, your servant, am not free from actual sins as well as original sin. “For your word’s sake, and according to your heart, you have done all these great things.”

It was too little to have said “for your word’s sake”—that is, for what you promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—unless he added, “and according to your heart,” that is, according to your grace, according to your free and unmerited mercy, bestowed in return for no preceding merits. “According to your heart,” I say. “For who has helped your Spirit in this? Or who has been your counselor and shown you?” (Isa. 40). With whom did you take counsel, that you might provide for yourself such an architect, who might make from us ourselves a house for you to inhabit?

“Therefore you have been magnified, O Lord God, because there is none like you, nor is there another besides you.” For all others deceive their unhappy worshippers by subtle fraud; but you save those who hope in you by the wonderful and unexpected wisdom of your heart. Yet he himself proves this more clearly from the effects, saying: “And what nation upon earth is like your people Israel, for whose sake God went, to redeem it for himself as a people?” He went, I say, by that way or in that course of his about which this same Prophet speaks elsewhere: “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit unto its summit” (Ps. 18).

For by that way through which he delivered his people from earthly Egypt and from the hand of fleshly Pharaoh, God did indeed go, but not through himself; he went, indeed, but not through the proper person of his only-begotten Son. Different is the grace of this journey and different its glory: by it, descending from heaven into a virgin’s womb, made man from the seed of this faithful David according to the truth of the present promise, he went through the Passion of death to the underworld, in order to redeem as a people for himself that nation which the spiritual Pharaoh, prince of darkness, had enslaved in Adam.

“Therefore,” he says, “your servant found his heart, to pray this prayer to you.” Namely, because you revealed the ear of your servant, saying, “I shall build you a house.” For he found his heart who said at the beginning of this prayer: “Who am I?” Conversely, whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing has certainly not yet found his heart, but deceives himself (Gal. 6). Therefore he finds his heart who, perceiving that he has no merit of his own, recognizes only the grace of God in his love, truly confessing that according to his merits he deserves not glory but punishment, not honor but rejection.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On his consolations: that he who had fled Saul seven times triumphed seven times over enemies, moreover knowing that he would be Christ’s father

**(2 Kings [Samuel], chapter 8.)** “And it came to pass after these things that David struck the Philistines and humbled them. And David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines.”

“This same David says: ‘According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations, O Lord, made my soul glad’” (Ps. 93). This the king, blessed in both respects—alike in temporal and eternal things—could truly sing even in accordance with his present successes. For once a fugitive and exile, now, having received the promise that he would become Christ’s father, he triumphs seven times over his enemies, he who, as we noted above, had fled Saul when he persecuted him seven times.

Above, he had struck the Philistines once and again: first at Baal-perazim, saying: “The Lord has divided my enemies before me as waters are divided, and therefore he called the name of that place Baal-perazim” (2 Kings [Samuel] 5); a second time in the valley of Rephaim, when the Lord said: “Do not go up to meet them, but circle around behind them, and come upon them opposite the pear-trees” (ibid.). Yet in the Hebrew it reads not “pear-trees” but “weeping ones,” that is, idols. They are called “weeping ones” because they deserve weeping and bring those who worship them to tears of misery. It is reported that the Philistines had an idol to which a sacrifice was prepared amid human tears. In their custom they sacrificed to it with tears, and David came upon them from the opposite direction.

Now, as has been said, David struck the Philistines a third time, humbled them, and took the bridle of tribute from the Philistines’ hand. The bridle of tribute consisted of the five cities of the Philistines, which frequently made Israel tributary to themselves; David took these from them, humbled them, and made them tributary to himself. “He struck Moab and measured them with a line, leveling them to the ground.” This is surely a great proclamation of complete victory: just as someone measures land with a line, so he distributed them according to his pleasure, commanding some to be spared and others to be killed—so unable to resist, just as the earth does not know how to struggle or say to its measurer, “Why do you measure me in this way?” Therefore it is magnificently said: “He measured two lines: one for killing, the other for preserving alive.”

Then David struck Hadadezer, son of Rehob, king of Zobah, and with him Damascus Syria, 418 which had come to bring him assistance. Syria too became David’s servant under tribute. He also stationed garrisons in Idumea, and Idumea became David’s servant. Then he struck the sons of Ammon, and with him the Syrian Sobath; and he killed from the Syrians seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen, and struck Sobath, the commander of the army. And thereafter the Syrians feared to provide aid to the sons of Ammon.

These are David’s seven victories. If we wish to refer them spiritually to Christ, we shall understand them all as the punishments likewise signified in the Apocalypse by the seven last plagues of the seven angels, concerning which a loud voice says from the Temple: “Go and pour out the seven bowls of God’s wrath upon the earth” (Rev. 16).

After so many and such great blessings for David’s soul and body, there follow just as many and equally grievous adversities of soul and body, so that the whole earlier structure, its columns collapsing, fell to the ground; and unless the Lord had put his hand beneath it, there would lie—alas!—an incomparable ruin of great virtues, as he himself says: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93).

**(2 Kings [Samuel], chapter 11.)** “It happened,” he says, “that David rose from his bed after midday and saw a woman washing herself opposite, upon her rooftop. And the woman was exceedingly beautiful,” etc.

The history of this great event is well known and celebrated: a certain traveler, namely the devil, came to this rich man and king David, in order to fatten himself there on the fatness of sin. But David, sparing to take from his own sheep, of which he had many—for he had many wives whom he could use lawfully—took the poor man’s ewe, took his neighbor’s ewe, and thus prepared food for that wandering and unstable traveler, who possessed nothing in the house or city of God. And that traveler, filled with such a dish of accomplished adultery, also demanded Uriah’s blood as a drink, and David likewise gave it. For he killed Uriah with the sword of the sons of Ammon (2 Kings [Samuel] 12).

Great was the fall of so great a tower; a great spectacle, in which each of us should see that, as long as he lives, he must never be secure regarding the firmness of his own standing. Thus a great cloud of misery almost entirely covered the glory of the king, made illustrious by present victories and enlarged by the blessed hope of his future seed through the promise written above. For because of this evil he afterward fled from the kingdom, according to the word of the Lord saying: “Behold, I shall raise up evil against you from your own house; I shall take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall sleep with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I shall do this thing in the sight of all Israel and in the sight of the sun.”

And at the time he feared lest, on account of his guilt, the Lord should repent and change his promise, by which he had sworn, saying: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131). He feared this and dreaded lest this calamity should come upon him. But he turned to the fortress of hope. He presumed upon the Spirit of counsel and strength; and, though God was offended, sinful man did not hesitate to put himself forward as his counselor. For in the prayer that he poured out for this sin, he said penitently: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50)—understood: Have mercy on me.

As though he said: What praise is there for justice if someone keeps faith in his promise to one faithful to him? But there is great and praiseworthy glory for justice where the one who made the promise, although offended and angered, remains faithful, looking only to the fact that he swore; he keeps faith and fulfills the promise. “Therefore, that you may be justified in your words”: that it may be told among the nations that not even my great iniquity made your faith void, and that all hearers of your good pleasure may proclaim: God is true, “but every man a liar” (Ps. 115); have mercy on me.

Thus it will happen “that you may prevail when you are judged,” since you freely offer yourself to judgment, saying in another prophet: “Who is there to be judged with me? Let him come; let us stand together; tell what you have, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43). For how great a victory for justice will it be when it cannot even be alleged that you at least neglected to preserve your truth toward us who are liars? Indeed, your truth will abound to no small degree in your glory amid our falsehood.

God, merciful to the sinner, accepted this counsel: “God faithful in his words and holy in all his works” [Col. 1135B] (Ps. 144). As though inclined toward indulgence, he preserved the faith of his word, in order to raise up his Christ from that very seed which was born from adulteress Bathsheba. Matthew, the writer of so great a genealogy, wished us reverently to know this: “David the king,” he says, “begot Solomon by her who had been Uriah’s” (Matt. 1).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. What mystery is contained in his fall involving Uriah’s wife, whom he killed with the sword of the sons of Ammon

Accordingly, the holy Fathers have rightly observed that even in this condemnable deed of David a great mystery lies hidden. It is so great that whenever it is rehearsed by Christian mouths, that traveler who came to David—the devil—ought deservedly to blush and be vehemently confounded, because, while wickedly seeking to devour the soul of prophet and king, who was prefiguring the sacraments, he powerfully assisted God’s wisdom.

For of whom does David, walking upon the rooftop, bear the type, if not of him of whom it is written: “He placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18)? Bathsheba, indeed, is said to mean “seventh well.” Yet Bethsabee is read more correctly, meaning “daughter of the oath,” provided the first syllable is shortened; otherwise, where it is lengthened, it always means “house.” Uriah, however, means “my light is God.”

What then is David’s bringing Bathsheba, Uriah’s wife, to himself, except joining to himself in spiritual understanding the law of the letter, which was joined to the carnal Jewish people, who glory as though in God’s light? Moreover, what is it that Uriah is sent to Joab with letters by which he was to be killed, except that the Jewish people themselves carry the law by whose convicting power they die? Thus, in this coming too, that traveler served the city of God and its king, Christ: for the event, although on the surface a cause of condemnation, is nevertheless in its mystery a prophecy of power. We condemn the deed as done, while we embrace the mystery.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That for this very deed he receives punishment by fleeing from the face of Absalom his son; and that in this very flight there is a great mystery of Christ

Moreover, when he receives punishment for this deed by fleeing from the face of his son Absalom, he beholds in that same flight a great mystery of Christ his Son, namely when, in the spirit of humility, he sings and composes this psalm: “O Lord, why have those who afflict me multiplied? Many rise up against me” (Ps. 3).

For in that same psalm he says: “I slept and was made drowsy; and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me.” Clearly he says this not in his own spirit but in Christ’s spirit. Christ, after many afflictions and with many rising up against him and saying, “There is no salvation for him in his God” (ibid.), was at last fastened to the cross; giving up the spirit, he fell asleep and was sunk in deep death (Matt. 27). But on the third day he arose, because the Lord sustained him: because that flesh was the flesh which the Lord God, the Word of God, took from the womb of the Virgin and united to himself in one and the same person. “Therefore,” he says, “I rose from the sleep of death” (Acts 2), the pains of hell having been loosed, since it was impossible for me to be held by it.

Therefore Absalom, whose name means “the father’s peace”—Absalom, I say, son and enemy, or rather not son but enemy, from whose face the father fled—is in the mystery Judas the betrayer, the false peace of father and master, whom he betrayed with the sign of a kiss of peace (Matt. 26). Judas, I say, apostle and devil—or rather, not apostle but devil—from whose face such a father truly fled. For Christ, or the Spirit of Christ, fled from his feigned heart, into which Satan entered (John 13).

And consequently his punishment is especially pleasing to one who praises justice, because, deprived of his mind by God’s judgment, he hanged himself (Matt. 27). Here no depth of mystery, but the very surface of the event itself, almost demonstrates Judas and Absalom to be alike. For this man, hanging from an oak, was abandoned when the mule on which he sat passed on; he deservedly received spears in his heart (1 Kings [Samuel] 18). And the other, hanging in a noose and abandoned by the intimacy of the chief priests, which he had wickedly ascended, immediately received worthy arrows—that is, the sentences of eternal condemnation and death—in his soul. And lest you think it a small matter that Absalom alone bore the figure of Judas alone, his counselor Ahithophel also perished by his own hanging (1 Kings [Samuel] 17).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That David killed Goliath’s brother, and concerning the remaining brothers who fell into the hands of the servants; and why David is called Adeodatus, Son of the Wood, Embroiderer, and Bethlehemite—namely, on account of the mystery of Christ

**[Col. 1136D] (2 Kings [Samuel], chapter 21.)** “There was again a battle of the Philistines against Israel, and David went down, and his servants with him, and they fought against the Philistines,” etc.

Gob means “pit.” “In it,” he says, “Adeodatus, son of Saltus [the Wood], the Polymitarius [Embroiderer], the Bethlehemite, struck Goliath the Gittite.” It is called a pit because, as one may be sent into a pit of lions, so David sent himself against Goliath. Adeodatus is David himself. He is called Adeodatus, “given by God,” because he was chosen by God for the kingdom. He is the Son of the Wood because he was brought out from the woodland where he pastured sheep. He is the Embroiderer because his mother was of the line of Bezalel. He is the Bethlehemite because Naomi and Ruth returned to Bethlehem in a time of abundance. And because Ruth became known to Boaz on account of bread, that place is therefore interpreted “house of bread.”

But why is he distinguished by these names in the present passage when he could more briefly have been expressed by his proper name? Plainly because of a great mystery. For assuredly not without a great foreshadowing of future things did these four born of Arapha in Gath—on whose account four battles are here enumerated—fall into the hands of David and his servants. Arapha is Orpah herself, Naomi’s other daughter-in-law, who returned to her own people and her own gods, while Ruth persisted in what she had begun, saying: “Your people shall be my people, and your God my God” (Ruth 1).

And from that Ruth Christ proceeded, according to that saying of Isaiah: “Send forth, O Lord, the Lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16). From that rock—that is, from the Gentile woman, yet one steadfastly faithful—came forth this David, and Christ, who was born from his seed. But from the other woman, Arapha, came Goliath and the others, Jesbi and Saph, and the tall man whose name is not given, having six fingers on his hands and feet.

For there were five, two of whom—namely Goliath the Philistine and his brother Goliath the Gittite—fell into David’s hand, while the rest fell into the hands of his servants. Did it then happen without mystery that the two daughters-in-law of Naomi, separated in the manner described above, should produce generations so opposed to one another, and that the monsters of that lineage should thus fall into the hands of this lineage?

Therefore, by these names or appellations David mystically signifies Christ; and by these battles, in which the mighty men of the hostile lineage are overthrown by the hand of David and his servants, are signified the spiritual battles of that same Christ, by which the falsehood hostile to all truth is destroyed. For he is himself Adeodatus, of whom the prophet sang: “A little child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). He is himself Son of the Wood, who, born in the woodland of this age, as Son of Man undertook the care of spiritual sheep and would suffocate the lions and bears, which are evil spirits. He is himself the Embroiderer who, with God the Father, fashioned heaven in the variegated workmanship of sun, moon, and stars; indeed, he does not cease to adorn his Church with the varied work of virtues. He is himself the Bethlehemite, by whose coming the present Church has become Bethlehem, that is, “house of bread,” as he says: “I am the living bread, who came down from heaven” (John 6).

Certainly, the words cited are confirmed by the words of the following song (chapter 22): “The Lord,” he says, “is my rock and my strength and my Savior; my God, my strong one, and I shall hope in him,” etc. For with a few words altered, this song is Psalm 17, which without doubt is sung in the person of Christ by the prophetic Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Who the first three mighty men were, who the secondary three mighty men were, and who the thirty mighty men were; and why Joab is counted neither among the three nor even among the thirty

**(2 Kings [Samuel], chapter 23.)** “These are the names of David’s mighty men. David, sitting in the chair, most wise, prince among the three. He is like the tenderest little worm of wood, who killed eight hundred in one onset,” etc.

After David’s many and very great deeds, perhaps you ask by what strength, and supported by what or how great mighty men, he performed them. And behold, the noble band of his mighty men is enumerated for you: the band, I say, of thirty mighty men, made keener by three mighty men—namely Abishai, Sobochai, and Jonathan son of Semmaa, David’s brother—and made keener still by three mighty men, that is, virtues: David’s wisdom, humility, and strength, altogether solid and iron-like. For “sitting in the chair, most wise”: behold wisdom. “He is like the tenderest little worm of wood”: behold humility. “Who killed eight hundred in one onset”: behold strength.

Thus three mighty men are counted in the one David, and Scripture took care earnestly to commend them to us when it said: “Abishai, Joab’s brother, was named among the three and was more noble among the three, and he was their chief; but he did not attain to the first three.” This is the same as saying: Although he was more noble among the three mighty men and their leader, still neither could his strength equal David’s strength, nor his wisdom David’s wisdom, nor his humility David’s humility.

Certainly, the reason why these mighty men are written to have been the mightiest among David’s mighty men is clearly shown by two causes, one preceding and the other following. The preceding reason is that these three are those servants of David concerning whom it was said above: “These four were born of Arapha in Gath, and they fell into the hand of David and his servants” (2 Kings [Samuel] 21). For since there were five, David himself killed two of them, namely Goliath the Philistine and his brother Goliath the Gittite; but each of these servants killed one: 420 Abishai killed Jesbibenob, Sobochai killed Saph, and Jonathan killed the tall man with six fingers on his hands and feet.

The other reason follows in the present account: “David,” he says, “desired water and said: ‘If only someone would give me a drink of water from the cistern which is in Bethlehem beside the gate.’ Therefore the three mighty men broke into the camp of the Philistines, drew water from the cistern of Bethlehem which was beside the gate, and brought it to David.” These three, then, were indeed mighty men, but, as has already been said, they did not attain to the first three, that is, to the three virtues which David attained.

Why, then, was Joab numbered neither among the three nor even among the thirty mighty men? Clearly because in David’s mighty men not merely bodily strength but rather virtues of mind are considered. Joab, moreover, had killed two just men better than himself: Abner, son of Ner, commander of Israel’s army, and Amasa, commander of Judah’s army; and he had shed the blood of war in peace, that is, by treachery or the pretense of peace. Rightly, therefore, he was not enrolled among David’s mighty men. Nevertheless, both crimes were expiated by his one death. Therefore it is written of him thus: “He”—namely Benaiah son of Jehoiada—“went down and struck the lion in the middle of the cistern, in days of snow.” This lion was Joab. “In the middle of the cistern,” that is, in the house of the Lord, where he held the horn of the altar. It is called a cistern because, just as the water of a cistern removes uncleanness, so also this cistern, that is, the sanctuary of the Lord, expiated sins “in days of snow,” because by death it expiated sin.

It should nevertheless be noted that, apart from the first three mighty men—that is, David’s three virtues—there are three subdivisions of mighty men. The first is that in which Abishai, Sobochai, and Jonathan are enrolled: they were with David but did not attain to the aforesaid first three. The second, in which are counted Eleazar son of David’s uncle, the Ahohite, and Shammah son of Agee of Harar, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada—who did not attain to the three—Scripture, he says, does not add to the first. The third is that in which thirty are continuously enumerated, namely: Asahel, Elhanan, Shammadech, Elichah, Eles, Hira, Abiezer, Mobommai, Selmon, Macharai, Eleph, Ithai, Banaiah, Elbai the Pharathonite, Abialbon, Azmaveth, Eliaba, Shammah of Arai, Ajam, Elipheleth, Eliam, Esrai, Farai, Gigaat, Bani, Selech, Naarai, Ira, Jareph, Uriah the Gittite.

Thus all together are read as thirty-seven, in such a way that David, who is called Adeodatus, is first. Let us consider these mighty men in the letter; let us seek other mighty men in the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. How, mystically, the Lord Jesus Christ is the one sitting in the chair, most wise; who his first mighty men are, who his secondary mighty men are, who the thirty mighty men are; and who are the two sons of Orpah whom he himself struck, and who the remaining three are whom his men strike
[Col. 1139C] “David, sitting in the seat, wisest among the three.” The Lord Christ, the son of this David, is that David most wise, sitting in the seat; he sits, I say, upon the throne of majesty, the Father saying to him: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109 [110]). Who are those three to whom none of the mighty could attain—his three mighty ones—if not the one God: the most mighty Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit? For the person of the Son alone assumed this man and alone was incarnate; nevertheless his Father is mighty, and his Holy Spirit is mighty. “The Father who abides in me, he does the works” (John 14); and, “I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Luke 11).

Thus in this man is the most wise Father, and in him also the Holy Spirit, the spirit of humility, [Col. 1139D] “like the tenderest little worm of wood,” under whose guidance he endured being crushed like a worm and not a man. In him the Word of God is united with the man in one and the same person; it is also his strength, by which he struck down eight hundred in a single onset. For, dying once, he despoiled hell; and now, sitting in the seat, he will judge all, living and dead. Which of all the mighty angels or men has attained thus far? After him came three most mighty men: namely, the apostles, the first preachers of the Trinity. Their strength is aptly expressed by the proper names of those first three ranks of mighty men. For Abishai is interpreted “sacrifice of the Father,” Sobochaeus “compacted,” and Jonathan “gift of the Lord.” Through them God the Father roared forth testimony to the resurrection of his sacrificed Son, [Col. 1140A] so that their sound went out into all the earth (Ps. 18 [19]); and they themselves, as though compacted and very strongly fortified, resisted their adversaries, confessing that all this was not from themselves but the Lord’s gift.

These three, I say, were most mighty; nevertheless no one should suppose that they attained to those first three. For “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88 [89]). Yet after the great David, the palm of victory is rightly granted first to them, because David killed two of the sons of Orpah—whose name means “his neck”—whereas these men each killed one of them. Christ killed two sons, as it were, of the stiff-necked devil: when by dying he conquered death, the devil’s firstborn, the death of our souls; and by rising again he restored the life of [Col. 1140B] our bodies. What we speak of is future, because, although those baptized into his death (Gal. 3) have already risen in the first resurrection, we shall rise in the second resurrection of the flesh into life and incorruption.

Therefore he who cast one of his five stones into Goliath’s forehead (1 Sam. 17 [18]) immediately, as it were, put forth his hand toward another stone in order to strike Goliath’s brother; but he has not yet struck him completely. For according to the flesh he indeed rose again in himself, but our death has not yet been utterly swallowed up in his victory. Meanwhile these mighty men rush upon Orpah’s other three sons and strike them down, because by the Word of God they crush every adversary of truth: namely, Jew, pagan, and heretic. Thus the entire race of the hostile party falls into the [Col. 1140C] hand of David and his servants, while Christ, both through himself as the head and through his mighty men, overcomes the whole body of the devil.

After these three most mighty men, three others immediately follow, though they do not attain to them: Eleazar, Shammah, and Benaiah. For after the apostles come the martyrs, champions of the same Trinity—mighty men indeed, so that the whole kingdom of David, that is, the whole Church of Christ, rightly glories in them, yet inferior to the apostles. After them are ranked another thirty mighty men: all the glorious confessors of that same holy and undivided Trinity, made distinguished by faithful belief and by courageously fulfilling the precepts of the Decalogue, and therefore able, through their outstanding merits, to protect us weaker common soldiers of great David. [Col. 1140D]

### 421 CHAPTER XXXIX. Why Uriah the Hittite is placed among the thirty mighty men; how and in what manner David sinned by numbering the people; and what the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite signifies mystically.

(2 Kings [2 Samuel], ch. 24.) “And the anger of the Lord again burned against Israel; and he moved David against them, saying to Joab: Go, number Israel and Judah,” etc.

Uriah the Hittite was placed last among the thirty mighty men because of what follows: “And the anger of the Lord again burned against Israel.” Vengeance had already been exacted upon David and his house; but divine vengeance had not yet been inflicted upon the people, who had not chosen to resist David when he killed Uriah the Hittite. Moreover, the mystery [Col. 1141A] contained in this passage is chiefly gathered from the fact that, on the occasion of this killing, the house of the Lord was built upon the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite—that is, of a Gentile man. For David said: “This is the house of God, and this is the altar for Israel’s burnt offering. And he commanded that all the proselytes in the land of Israel should be gathered, and appointed from among them stonecutters to cut and polish stones, that the house of the Lord might be built” (1 Chron. 22), etc.

David therefore, glorying in the multitude of his army—which, as is read in Paralipomenon, Satan prompted him to number Israel (1 Chron. 21 [XI])—typifies none other than the carnal people of Israel glorying in the works of the Law. For to suppose that one is justified by works of the Law, when Abraham was justified not by works but by faith, is precisely to trust in chariots and [Col. 1141B] horses and, as it were, to number the multitude of one’s army. The Apostle cries: “For if Abraham was justified by works of the Law, he has glory, but not before God” (Rom. 4), etc.

The obstinate Jew persists in contention and, despising faith in Jesus Christ, which alone can justify, claims for himself an abundant righteousness from works. “Therefore the Lord sent [Col. 1142A] a pestilence upon Israel from morning until the appointed time.” According to the literal sense, “the appointed time” means the time when the evening sacrifice was offered. But according to the mystery, this appointed time is the end of the age, when this pestilence, which now rages against that people, will cease. For when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

Meanwhile, seventy thousand men die from the people. This number is formed from seven and ten. Seven commonly signifies universality, and ten the Mosaic Law. Thus seventy thousand men die: that is, all who, despising Christ’s grace, glory in the works of the Law, are condemned. But upon the threshing-floor of a Gentile man the angel of the Lord is seen; [Col. 1142B] he also commands the prophet to tell David that he must go up and build an altar to the Lord there. For all prophetic Scripture testifies that in the faith of the Gentiles there is one Church of God, outside of which that Angel of great counsel, who saves the remnant of Israel, cannot be found.

## THE THIRD BOOK ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS. (3 Kings [1 Kings], I–XI.)

[Col. 1141]

### CHAPTER I. That Solomon, to whom his father entrusted the kingdom while still living, bore the type of Christ, according to the verse of Psalm 71 [72]: “O God, give your judgment to the king.”

(3 Kings [1 Kings], ch. 1.) “King David had grown old and was [Col. 1141C] advanced in days. And though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed,” etc.

As we enter upon Solomon and seek the mysteries of this section also, the psalm entitled “For Solomon,” namely the seventy-first [seventy-second], meets us as a necessary lamp. For he who acted outwardly here in making Solomon heir to his kingdom, David himself the father says there in the Spirit: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son,” etc. Certainly, in saying this, he indicates that in his own deed he foreshadowed what the whole world has now heard: that God the Father, the great King, gave his judgment and righteousness to his Son, Christ the King. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor [Col. 1141D] the Father.” And, according to the psalm just mentioned, “all kings shall worship him; all nations shall serve him,” etc. The plain surface of the text itself compels us to understand these words as truly spoken of Christ, the true Solomon, that is, the Peaceful One. Therefore King David is to be understood mystically as God the Father, while Solomon is Christ, the Son of God.

### 422 CHAPTER II. That King David, now grown old, bore the type of God the Father; how this old man was not warmed though covered with [Col. 1142B] garments; and what virgin maiden his prophets sought for him.

“King David had grown old and was [Col. 1142C] advanced in days.” Truly this David has grown old and is advanced in days—indeed, in days of eternity—as Daniel likewise says: “I looked,” he says, “until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days sat” (Dan. 7). And afterwards: “I looked therefore in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man was coming; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and honor and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him” (ibid.).

“And though that ancient David was covered with garments, he was not warmed,” he says. Clearly, his warmth is his charity or love; it is his Holy Spirit. Did this old man, or Ancient One, ever grow cold in respect of his own warmth? Certainly not in himself, but in relation to us, between whom and him, because of the sin of the first man, a wall of enmity had arisen. [Col. 1142D] For in him are eternal warmth, everlasting love, and the Holy Spirit, consubstantial and coeternal. But when the first man sinned against him, the warmth of his love justly hid itself inwardly from the human race.

He was covered with garments, honored with legal ceremonies; but “the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7), and the priesthood of the Law was in no way able to render satisfaction to God by sacrificing for human beings. Thus “though he was covered with garments, he was not warmed”: that is, when he was served by the carnal ceremonies of the former Testament, he received those serving him into grace through the Spirit of reconciliation. [Col. 1143A]

“Therefore his servants said to him: Let a virgin maiden be sought for our lord the king; let her stand before the king and cherish him; let her sleep in his bosom and warm our lord the king. So they sought a beautiful maiden in all the borders of Israel, and found Abishag the Shunammite, and brought her to the king.” These servants of David are the prophets of God. This virgin maiden is faith. Those servants saw that God was not warmed or reconciled with the human race while covered in legal ceremonies; and therefore they sought this virgin, this maiden—that is, faith.

Certainly, if you understand their meaning and discern their spirit [Col. 1143B] in their writings, you find that he scorned the sacrifices and burnt offerings of the Jews as useless garments, and most diligently sought the faith by which Abraham and the other patriarchs were justified. For “all our righteousnesses are like the garment of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64); but “the righteous person lives by faith” (Heb. 10; Hab. 2). Where did they find it? In Shunem, which is interpreted “captivity,” or “mortification,” or indeed “contempt.” Hence faith itself is called Shunammite: that is, captive, mortified, or despised. For this is the faith of those who are pilgrims in this age (2 Cor. 5), having no abiding city here but seeking the city to come (Heb. 13). For this reason they are despised by this world and are mortified all day long (Rom. 8); [Col. 1143C] their leaders or fathers according to this same faith were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who journeyed because of faith and confessed “that they are strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” (Heb. 11). In them these servants of David found this Shunammite; for they saw that they were justified not by works of the Law but by faith (Gal. 3).

“The maiden,” he says, “was exceedingly beautiful; and she slept with the king and ministered to him. But the king did not know her.” Faith was certainly beautiful and pleasing to God, and the faithful of old rested in God with blessed hope; yet they had not received the promised reality of salvation. Therefore the king did not know her: that is, he had not yet accepted her unto perfect salvation.

### 423 CHAPTER III. That Adonijah, who exalted himself saying, “I will reign,” bore the type of the Jewish people; and what it mystically means that Joab and Abiathar aided Adonijah’s party, whereas Zadok the priest, the others, and the strength of the army were not with Adonijah.

“Adonijah son of Haggith exalted himself, saying: I will reign. And he made for himself chariots and horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.” Adonijah is interpreted “the Lord is ruler”; Haggith, “meditating” or “speaking.” Thus this foolish and imprudent young man signifies the carnal Jewish people, pupils of the Mosaic Law, who honored God with their lips, saying, “The Lord is ruler, the Lord is ruler,” and volubly confessed this in their mother, the Synagogue; but their heart was far from God (Isa. [Col. 1144A] 13). For in pride, as though his father had not been consulted, he exalted himself. Seeking to establish his own righteousness, he was not, and is not, subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10): “I will reign,” he says.

Is not the kingdom the Lord’s, and is he ruler of the nations (Ps. 21 [22])? Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Indeed, of the Gentiles also. But he read that “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75 [76]); and therefore he thought that God ought never to be God except of the Judaism which is outward in the flesh. He made for himself chariots and horsemen by being proud, and fifty men to run before him; by this we understand the ostentation of ceremonies, in which he claimed for himself, as it were, a jubilee—that is, remission or justification.

“And his father [Col. 1144B] never rebuked him, saying: Why have you done this?” The wise king, plainly, tempered his serious anger with silence, intending in due time to rebuke his foolish presumption by deed in such a way that no word would be needed. “He also was very handsome, second in birth after Absalom.” Note that some read it thus: “And she bore him after Absalom”; “sin” is understood as the subject.

“And he conferred with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest, who aided Adonijah’s party.” Joab is interpreted “enemy” or “father”; Abiathar, “superfluous father.” Thus that foolish people already spoken of conferred with Joab and Abiathar—that is, with Pharisees who were enemies and plunderers of its soul, and with priests or high priests who taught superfluities. Their speech was vain and useless: the kind which [Col. 1144C] God condemns through the prophet, saying, “They built a wall, and these men plastered it with mud without straw” (Ezek. 13). And afterwards: “Therefore I shall cause a storm-wind to burst forth in my indignation, and there shall be a flooding rain in my fury, and hailstones of wrath unto destruction; and I shall destroy the wall that you plastered without tempering, and I shall level it to the ground, and its foundation shall be exposed, and it shall fall and be consumed in its midst” (ibid.), etc.

Jewish works are rightly compared to the wall of such a structure. For although they honored the Lord with their lips, their heart was far from him; and although they called God the Father their God, they dishonored the Son of God with exceedingly impious madness, while high priests and Pharisees plastered with untempered mud. [Col. 1144D] By soothing persuasions they deceived the unhappy people, saying: “Peace, peace,” when there was no peace (ibid.); for there was war instead, both from heaven and from earth. At last their wall fell; its foundation was revealed when God invisibly, and the Roman army visibly, destroyed it.

“But Zadok the priest, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and Nathan the prophet, and Shimei, and Rei, and all the strength of David’s army, were not with Adonijah.” Zadok is interpreted “righteous”; Benaiah, “mason” or “builder of the Lord”; Jehoiada, “knowledge of the Lord”; Nathan, “gift”; Shimei, “hearing me”; and Rei, “my shepherd.” [Col. 1145A] This Shimei is Nebat, Jeroboam’s father, who was Solomon’s teacher. Rei, however, is the priest of David, the Ira the Jairite—that is, the teacher.

Therefore that foolish young man had by no means strengthened his cause when he failed to summon men so great and such as these, and despised either seeking their favor or relying on their counsels. Indeed, the foolish people already mentioned had all the more annihilated itself. While claiming a kingdom for itself from the works of the Law, it did not seek—rather, it despised and rejected—the Righteous One, the Builder of the Lord, the Knowledge and Hearer of God the Father, and its Shepherd: names by all of which the one Christ is fittingly proclaimed. “For,” he says, “he did not invite Solomon his brother either.”

### CHAPTER IV. What it mystically means that, while the prophet Nathan speaks [Col. 1145B] with Bathsheba, Solomon is anointed king; what it means that the king is appointed while his father is living; what the father’s mule means; and what the multitude singing and ascending after him means.

“Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother: Have you heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king, while our lord David does not know it?” “Does not know it,” he says—that is, does not approve it. For above he was said not to have been unaware of it. But, “His father,” he says, “never rebuked him, saying: Why have you done this?” Therefore, “our lord David does not know it” means: he does not grant it, does not will it, does not approve it. Thus he adds greater confidence to the woman in undertaking the plan. “Now therefore come, receive counsel from me, and save your own life and that of your son [Col. 1145C] Solomon.”

As the prophet speaks and begins counsel with Bathsheba, and both stand before the great old man and wise king David, Solomon—whose name means “peaceful lord”—is anointed king.
