The whole multitude goes up after him; the earth resounds from the cry of people singing with trumpets and rejoicing with great joy; and the king has spoken beforehand: “I will command him to be leader over Israel and Judah.” This, surely, is the mystery: that when the judgment sits, according to Daniel, and the books are opened, one comes with the clouds of heaven like a Son of Man, comes even to the Ancient of Days, is presented before him, and receives power, honor, and a kingdom (Dan. 7).

The books were opened when the Holy [Col. 1145D] Spirit was given to human beings through Christ’s passion, by whom the mysteries of the Scriptures were opened and made intelligible. There will indeed be a future judgment, in which the books of consciences too are to be opened, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne; and books were opened. And another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged from what was written in the books according to their works” (Rev. 20). Yet judgment has already taken place: that judgment, namely, of which the Lord said when his passion was already near, “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12). At that judgment the books were opened, because [Col. 1146A] after the judgment of the world was accomplished through Christ’s death, the understanding of his disciples was opened so that they understood the Scriptures (Luke 24).

Therefore, when Bathsheba—by whom, as we said above, spiritual understanding is signified—begins counsel with the prophet, Solomon is appointed king. This is because, once the words of the prophets have been fulfilled and spiritually understood, Christ the Son of God is recognized as the peaceful King, the King of the Father’s glory, who draws all things to himself (John 12). The king is appointed while his father still lives because God the Father, who appointed this King, Christ, never dies. He appointed this King “heir of all things” (Heb. 1), and has never died and never will die. What is marvelous and unique: Christ is the heir of a Father who has never died and [Col. 1146B] never will die, while Christ himself, having died once and come to life again, will never die further.

He sits “upon the king’s mule,” indeed also upon his Father’s throne: that is, over the whole Church, which truly is the vehicle of the Most High, and over every principality and power, thrones and dominions. “He now sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Heb. 1). Accordingly, behold the whole multitude goes up after him, a people singing and rejoicing, and the earth resounds from their cry. We have heard great joy from the tongues of those declaring the glory of heaven—that is, the apostles speaking in all languages—because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18 [19]). Nor is this without mystery: the rejoicing [Col. 1146C] servants bless the Lord King and say, “May the Lord make Solomon’s name greater than your name.” For formerly God was known only in Judah (Ps. 75 [76]); but after the Son of God received the kingdom among all nations, the glory both of Father and Son is proclaimed, this prophecy having been fulfilled: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. 107 [108]).

### 424 CHAPTER V. Why Solomon killed Adonijah when he sought Abishag the Shunammite as his wife; and what similar thing occurred during Christ’s reign.

(3 Kings [1 Kings], ch. 2.) “Why,” he says, “do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask the kingdom for him also,” etc. [Col. 1146D]

The wise and provident king Solomon detected his brother’s treacherous schemes: namely, that if Abishag were given to the petitioner, he, having gained her marriage as though with a queen, would recover hope of regaining the kingdom. He detected this, I say, and hastened to cut off scandals that would arise against himself and his kingdom. “May God do this to me, and add this besides, because Adonijah has spoken this word against his own life.” And immediately: “As the Lord lives, today Adonijah shall die,” etc. Adonijah was killed, and Joab too was killed because he had turned aside after Adonijah and had not turned aside after Solomon. “Abiathar, however, was expelled so that he should not exercise the priesthood.”

(3 Kings [1 Kings], ch. 3.) When these things were accomplished, “the kingdom,” he says, “was established in Solomon’s hand.” Thus, indeed, in order that Christ’s [Col. 1147A] kingdom and faith might be established, and the word of the Gospel might run unhindered without Jewish scandal, the city of Jerusalem and all the glory of the man-made temple were given over to destruction at the hands of the Roman Empire. They fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations.

For what were those Jews who fell—and indeed those who, under the name of disciples, opposed the disciples of Christ the Christian Son, the pseudo-apostles—attempting? They wished to mingle the faith of the Gospel with the ceremonies of the Law. “Some,” Luke says in the Acts of the Apostles, “of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed rose up, saying that it was necessary to circumcise them”—understood: those converted from the Gentiles—“and to command them also to keep the Law of Moses” (Acts 14 [15]). Certainly, when they said these and similar [Col. 1147B] things, and wished to mix the faith of the Gospel with the ceremonies of the Law, Adonijah was, as it were, asking for Abishag the Shunammite: so that they might ascribe the whole dignity of righteousness not to faith in Christ but to works of the Law.

But Christ, the wise King, made provision for himself and his kingdom. By killing Adonijah and those who aided his party, he gave Jerusalem and its temple, as already stated, over to destruction, lest Abishag—that is, Christian faith—become in any way a concubine for his hope, and lest, while the glory of the man-made temple stood, anyone suppose that Jewish sacred observances possessed any efficacy. Now let us proceed to his distinguished and most noble work, the temple, in order to seek there also, according to our purpose, the sacred miracles of Christ, the Son of God.

### CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1147C] On Solomon’s temple, which was a type of Christ’s body, according to the testimony of the Apocalypse.

(3 Kings [1 Kings], ch. 6.) “And it came to pass in the four hundred and eightieth year after the children of Israel came out of the land of Egypt, in the fourth year, in the month Ziph, which is the second month, of King Solomon over Israel, that he began to build the house of the Lord.”

The Scriptural testimonies, rather than our own conjecture, must establish what this house, or temple of the Lord, was built to figure or typify. The Lord himself first, when the Jews questioned him in the temple, saying, “What sign do you show us, that you do these things?”, answered and said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” “But this,” [Col. 1147D] says the Evangelist, “he said concerning the temple of his body” (John 2). In saying this, he clearly intended us to understand that the man-made temple was a type of the temple not made by hands, that is, of his body.

The same Evangelist says in the Apocalypse: “And I saw no temple in it”—namely, in the holy city Jerusalem—“for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb” (Rev. 21). Solomon himself also signifies that for a type of whom he built that temple: “Wisdom,” he says, “has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars” (Prov. 9), etc. What else do these words teach except that Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1), [Col. 1148A] built for himself the temple of a human body, supported or adorned by seven pillars, which are all the gifts of the sevenfold Holy Spirit? Therefore that man-made temple was without doubt a type of the holy temple, the temple of the Lord’s body, from whose right side, according to Ezekiel, living and healing waters flowed; and all to whom that water came were made whole (Ezek. 47).

### CHAPTER VII. On the measurements of the same temple: their mystical meaning. [Col. 1148B]

“The house which King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits in length, twenty cubits in width, and thirty cubits in height.”

This arrangement of measurements is as beautiful as it is mystical. For the inhabitant of the aforesaid temple is God the Son of God himself, through whom God the Father created all his works in the number of six days, and through whom the same God—or the finger of God—wrote the ten commandments of the Law on the tablets upon Mount Sinai. Therefore the length of this temple is fittingly sixty cubits: a number formed from six and ten by multiplication. Thus Cerinthus, or every heretic whatsoever who has dared to assert that this temple was not longer than the Virgin Mary—that is, that Christ took his beginning from Mary—must be ashamed.

The width of twenty cubits signifies the breadth of charity dwelling and diffused in this temple. This number, twenty, is two within the limit of ten. He said that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor [Col. 1148C] (Matt. 22). Therefore this width of the man-made temple is the complete perfection of the twofold love remaining in that temple not made by hands, the Lord’s body. For he loves both the Father and us, to whom he became neighbor through the flesh, and he loved us unto death. Concerning his love for God the Father he says: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do” (John 14). Concerning the love by which he loves us, after saying, “This is my commandment, that you love one another,” he immediately adds, “as I have loved you” (John 15). And as though we should ask, “How, or how much, did you love us?”: “No one,” he says, “has greater love than [Col. 1148D] this, that one lay down his life for his friends” (ibid.). “You are my friends.”

Finally, what could be more beautiful, glorious, or magnificent than the height of thirty cubits? The number thirty is three within the limit of ten. And what believer does not know that the most beautiful structure of the Lord’s body rises to the lofty glory of the Holy Trinity? For the Lord’s man—[Note: [Col. 1147D] What is said of Christ as “the Lord’s man” must be understood with reference to his human nature, which is signified by the term *man*, not with reference to the hypostasis; see Augustine, *Retractations*, book I, ch. 29.]—is one of the three, one person, I say, in the Trinity. For although Christ is a giant of twofold substance, because he is God and man, he is not therefore also of two persons; rather, the same one is God and man, one and the same person. [Col. 1149A] Therefore the height of the temple is thirty cubits because the Lord’s manhood is in the highest glory of the Holy Trinity.

It should nevertheless be known that there were three ceilings in the temple: the first thirty cubits from the pavement; the second sixty cubits opposite the tops of the porticoes; and the third one hundred and twenty cubits up, at the summit of the whole house.

### 425 CHAPTER VIII. On the portico before the temple, twenty cubits long and ten wide: what it signified in Christ.

“And there was a portico before the temple, twenty cubits in length according to the measure of the temple’s width, and ten cubits in width.”

The portico before the temple signifies [Col. 1149B] the life or conduct of our same Lord, by which he lived and conducted himself before the mystery of his passion. For as long as he lived here, as long as he walked upon earth, his own followers, those who were with him, neither recognized nor understood him; for the Holy Spirit had not yet been given, and he had not yet opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. Without its light, one cannot enter or behold the inner things of that temple.

Thus his life or conduct among human beings was like a portico, in which he prepared those who believed in him so that, after his passion and resurrection had been accomplished, he might then at last bring them in to see what and how beautiful a temple of divinity he was. “And the portico had twenty cubits in length, according to the measure of the temple’s width,” by which [Col. 1149C] width, as we have already said, his charity is signified. For while walking among human beings, it was necessary that he should be patient and long-suffering in unconquered charity amid so many wrongs, insults, terrors, blasphemies, and finally scourges and the very bitterness of death. This perfection of long-suffering was the portico’s length according to the measure of the temple’s width, according to the abundant riches of the aforesaid charity dwelling within it: a charity by which he did not provoke others, nor suffer unwillingly, but was, as one hungry, satisfied with reproaches.

The width of the portico was ten cubits. Thus the portico was narrower in width than the temple itself. Why? Because while he was still conversing with human beings, his charity was not yet being diffused in act as it now is. [Col. 1149D] It was for a little while still restricted, so that he said: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Even before the foundation of the world, he had both the will and the power to extend himself to the Gentiles; but in actual exercise, as already said, he admitted only the sheep of Israel. Thus the width of the portico was less than the width of the temple: namely, than that width in which he said, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

Why has Scripture said nothing about the height of the portico? Truly here too there lies great beauty of mystery. For as long as he lived here, as long as he was mortal, he possessed no height in the sight of humankind. He was despised; he was the lowest of men. [Col. 1150A] Hence comes his utterance in the psalm: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21 [22]). Scripture therefore fittingly kept silence about the height of the portico, because while he served in this world under obedience to the Father, he was content, like a destitute and poor man, with exceeding humility.

### CHAPTER IX. What and of what sort were the slanting windows of that temple not made by hands: windows that do not seek light from outside, but give forth the charity of eternal light from within.

“He made slanting windows in the temple.”

It was necessary for windows to be made in the man-made temple, since without them it would be not a temple of venerable vision but a prison of darkness and gloom. But this temple not made by hands, the temple of the Lord’s [Col. 1150B] man, does not seek light from outside or ask elsewhere for the brightness of sun or day, since it is the temple of light, the temple of eternal fire.

Should we then suppose that there are no windows in this temple of God? On the contrary, it has very many windows: not in order to receive light from outside, but in order to pour forth from itself the true light to the whole holy city of which it is the temple, and to be the lamp of that city, as it is written in the Apocalypse (Rev. 21). What kind of windows are these? Slanting windows, almost hidden. For this is the meaning of what is said by the inhabitant of this temple—and by the temple itself, God and man, Christ: “The Spirit breathes where he wills; and you hear his voice, but do not know where he comes from or where he goes” (John 3).

The windows, therefore, are slanting—that is, they are the hidden ways and hidden [Col. 1150C] distributions of the grace dwelling in him, who alone knows by what measure, at what time, and to what end he distributes it to each person as he wills.

### CHAPTER X. What the upper storey of five cubits, the middle storey of six cubits, and the third storey of seven cubits signify mystically in that temple in height; what the doorway of the middle side-chamber signifies; and what it means that the wall-beams do not adhere.

> “And he built stories around the walls of the temple, round about the walls of the house, around the temple and the oracle; and he made side-chambers round about. The lowest story was five cubits broad, the middle story six cubits broad, and the third story seven cubits [Col. 1150D] broad. The entrance to the middle side-chamber was on the right-hand wall of the house; and by a winding stair they went up to the middle upper room, and from the middle to the third.” The wise architect admirably enlarged one and the same house upward in a threefold arrangement, and thus made it capable of containing a great multitude. Assuredly in this temple of the Godhead also, in this God-and-man, Christ, there are three stories; and everyone who desires to remain in Christ must faithfully take his stand in whichever of them applies to him.

What are these stories? Certainly they are three distinctions of good living, three orders of those who believe in Christ, which He Himself mystically distinguishes: “Two shall be in the field, two women grinding together, two in bed: one shall be taken and the other left” (Matt. 24). These likewise are the orders which we understand in the prophet Ezekiel [Col. 1151A] under the names Job, Noah, and Daniel (Ezek. 14).

The first, or lowest, order is that of those working in the field—that is, married persons—such as Job, who pleased God through faith and patience within marriage. This plainly is the first story in the temple of Christ’s Godhead: it has five cubits, by which measure are rightly understood the five bodily senses, occupied with outward work and labour.

The middle order is that of those grinding—that is, of those who preside well and go about, as it were grinding, by preaching the word of God—such as Noah, who, by steering the ark amid the waves, furnished an example to all rulers of the holy Church. This is the second story, having six cubits, the mystical measure of those who labour in word and doctrine. For God completed His works in the number of six [Col. 1151B] days; and therefore this breadth rightly signifies the condition of those who perform God’s work.

The third and highest order is that of those resting in bed—that is, those devoted to contemplation—such as Daniel, who, without marriage and as though sleeping alone in a most delightful bed, clearly beheld God’s visions as if face to face. This indeed is the third story of the Lord’s temple, having seven cubits. In that number is God’s sabbatical rest, signifying the repose of the soul that looks upon God, concerning which He Himself, after saying, “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart,” added, “and you shall find,” He says, “rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

In this highest story the holy soul now keeps sabbath: higher than the world, and, though it is still held within the narrow body, it already through contemplative repose enjoys heaven, walks among angels, and stands before God. Therefore, in the Lord’s temple there are three stories: they are the three lawful orders of those who remain in Christ.

“The entrance,” he says, “to the middle side-chamber was in the wall,” etc. What is the entrance to the middle side-chamber, through which one enters the first story in order to ascend to the middle, and from the middle to the third? The entrance in the side of the temple is the wound in the lance-pierced side of the Lord’s body. Apart from it there is no approach, no entrance or door by which anyone may enter, so as to stand before God in any order whatsoever. For when that side had been struck by the lance, blood and water flowed out from it (John 19); by that sacrament [Col. 1151D] the sin of the world was removed, and in it we have been baptized, as the Apostle says: “For as many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death” (Rom. 6).

Therefore there is one entrance, one baptism, through which one enters that temple of God. Once admitted into it, one may then ascend the house, either from the first level to the middle or from the middle to the third, according as each person may please in the ascent of virtues or the height of merits.

“But he placed beams in the house round about on the outside, so that they should not adhere to the walls of the temple.” To adhere to the temple walls is to consider only that Christ is man, that He was capable of suffering, that wicked men were able to pierce the wall of His body with nails and a lance in order to kill Him. But to consider only this, to look to this alone [Col. 1152A] and despise Him on this account, belongs to Jews, heretics, and pagans. Therefore the beams of the stories must not adhere to the walls of the temple: that is, the one faith of all orders in the Church must not look in Christ only to the nature of the flesh, but must tend toward the inward glory of His Godhead.

## CHAPTER XI. Why no iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built; why the temple was clothed with gold; what the oracle in the temple signifies; and why it was made complete with equal measurements in length, breadth, and height.

> “Now when the house was being built, it was built of dressed and perfected stones; and hammer, axe, and every iron tool were not heard in the house while it was being built.”

This may rightly be understood also of the whole of that holy heavenly city, Jerusalem: the living, holy stones of which it is built are dressed here; here in the world they are polished by cuttings and pressures; but there, in peace, they are fitted into their places by the hand of the craftsman, so that no hammer of persecutors, no axe of those who strike, no tool of those who saw, will ever again be heard.

But since the subject here is not the building of the city, but the temple of the city, the proper meaning is this: Christ, God and man, the Son of God, was conceived without human action or a man’s embrace. Therefore hammer, axe, and every iron tool were not heard in the house while it was being built, because no human action was present when Christ was conceived. The stones from which [Col. 1152C] this house was built were dressed outside, because the fathers, or all the righteous, were first generated according to the ordinary course of nature or by human action; and, when their faith had been gathered into the blessed Virgin, Christ was conceived. Here for any tool whatsoever to be heard is wickedness; and whoever has imagined that he heard it is a heretic.

> “And he built cedar stories, forty cubits high, in the rear part of the temple, from the floor to the upper parts; and he made the inner house of the oracle, the Holy of Holies. Now the oracle had twenty cubits in length, twenty cubits in breadth, and twenty cubits in height; and he covered it and clothed it with the purest gold. He also clothed the altar with cedar,” etc.

Not only the oracle, which was twenty cubits [Col. 1152D], but also the temple itself, which before the doors of the oracle was forty cubits long, he covered with the purest gold; and there was nothing in the temple not covered with gold. “He also,” it says, “covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.”

The great and wondrous work of the handmade temple prefigured the glory of the temple not made by hands—that is, of Christ the man—which we believe, proclaim, and longingly await the vision of. For what is the gold, or golden brightness, of that temple, except the immortality and impassibility of Him who sits at the right hand of the Father? Before He suffered, died, and rose again, the temple was indeed of stone and, as it were, panelled with cedar boards; but it was not yet covered with gold, because our nature in Him was indeed lowly, though not corruptible through any fault, yet it did not yet shine with that glory with which it was to be crowned after the passion of death.

But after He rose from the dead, there is now nothing in the temple not covered with the gold of immortality; for, having died once and living to God, “He dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over Him” (Rom. 6). The substance of the temple, more lowly than gold, is covered, not destroyed: for the glory of resurrection, or immortality, does not swallow up the nature of the flesh, but is put on over it.

What then is the oracle in this temple, called the Holy of Holies? The oracle in the temple is God in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Cor. 5). The oracle and the temple before the doors of the oracle are not two temples but one temple; likewise, we confess not two Christs, man and God in man, but one Christ [Col. 1153B].

Upon the utterances or responses of this oracle—upon the ordering of the incarnate Word dwelling in that sacred temple of the body—not only the Apostles but Christ Himself continually depended according to His humanity, so that He did nothing or judged nothing from Himself. Thus, for example, He could weep for His nation or the city of Jerusalem, destined for ruin, yet not deliver it by weeping.

The oracle was as great in length as in height, and no less in breadth, because the Godhead of Christ our Lord is as great in antiquity, which is understood through length, and as great in majesty, which is understood through height, as it is altogether great in charity, which is understood through breadth.

## CHAPTER XII. What the two cherubim are; why they were placed in the oracle; why Solomon made them of olive wood; what the extension of their wings means; what the small doors at the entrance to the oracle and then their corners mean; what the cherubim and the forms of palms in its decoration mean; and what the doors and doorposts of olive wood at the entrance to the temple mean.

> “He made in the oracle two cherubim of olive wood, ten cubits high.”

In the tabernacle of Moses, the two cherubim overshadowing the mercy-seat (Exod. 25) are mystically the two Testaments, jointly bearing witness to Christ, the mediator of God and men, because “He Himself is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2). In what Solomon made we likewise understand the same mystery. Both there, within the veil, and here, within the partition separating it [Col. 1153D] from the temple, he placed the cherubim.

Certainly, without prejudice to the mystery, he could have placed them in the temple outside the mercy-seat, since Christ the man, the temple of the Godhead, held both Testaments in memory and has true testimony from each concerning both His Godhead and His humanity. But it must necessarily be understood that these things were hidden, now within the oracle and then within the veil, lest the unstable people, excessively inclined to idolatry, should admire the beautiful images and worship them as God, thus offending the true and living God.

For it is written in this book of Kings: “Hezekiah broke in pieces the bronze serpent which Moses had made; for until that time the children of Israel burned incense to it” (4 Kings 18). If that people could worship not merely a golden calf but even a bronze serpent as God, how much more would it worship the cherubim, admiring their splendid—indeed, seemingly heavenly—forms? [Col. 1154A] Therefore these things were necessarily concealed, as was said, so that priestly maturity alone might behold them at appointed times; for the Lord said through Moses that “if any outsider approaches, he shall surely die” (Num. 1).

Yet there is also a mystical reason why both Testaments are hidden within: no uninitiated person should dare handle the mysteries of Scripture, lest, while the words of the Holy Spirit are examined by an alien spirit, he become a heretic and thus, according to the sentence of divine law, surely die.

> “He made them,” it says, “of olive wood.”

Olive wood signifies men of mercies, concerning whom it is written: “These are men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten. With their seed good things remain; their descendants are a holy inheritance, and their seed has stood firm in the covenants” (Ecclus. 44). For both Testaments were established through such men, who were, as it were, olive wood—that is, vessels of mercy—and their faith and merits are the material of both cherubim.

> “The cherubim stretched out their wings; one wing touched the wall, and the wing of the second cherub touched the other wall. Their other wings met one another in the middle of the temple; from one wall to the other they overshadowed everything in the oracle.”

The cherubim signify that everything belonging to the word of God—everything that must be known or preached concerning the incarnation and the true Godhead and humanity of the Son of God—is so contained in the two Testaments that outside them there is nothing that ought to be proclaimed or believed. The whole heavenly oracle is comprehended in them; and we must know this so firmly that outside them we may not listen either to man or angel.

> “He also covered the cherubim with gold.”

This means that all the lowliness of the letter should shine with the divine splendour of spiritual understanding.

> “And at the entrance to the oracle he made small doors of olive wood.”

The small doors, which are shut and opened, are the expositions of the holy sayings. According to the differing capacity of hearers, they must be shut to some and opened to others, as He says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8).

> “The doorposts,” it says, “were five-cornered, and the two doors were of olive wood.”

This construction expresses the form of a pentagon, especially when the small doors are closed: that is, the secrets of the heavenly oracle ought especially to be closed to those whose capacity does not exceed the ability of the five senses, so that in comparison with spiritual things they may be judged not so much human beings as beasts.

> “And he carved on them images of cherubim and forms of palms.”

On the doors and walls, together with the cherubim, forms of palms are also depicted, because victory from heaven is promised to those who faithfully receive the knowledge of God and contend for it.

> “He also made, at the entrance to the temple, square doorposts of olive wood [Col. 1155A], and two doors of fir wood, folding inward; and each door was double and opened by holding to the other.”

Thus there were four doors, because each door was double. Clearly, at the entrance to the temple not made by hands there are four doors, because we receive knowledge of the four Evangelists through their account of the Lord’s incarnation. These doors open while holding one another, because the Evangelists are in the fullest harmony, mutually supporting one another; and whoever regards them with devout insight perceives and believes that they differ from one another in nothing.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the statement, “And he built it in seven years,” although the Jews said to the Lord, “This temple was built in forty-six years”; and what mystery lies in that number.

> “In the fourth year the house of the Lord was founded, in the month Zio; and in the eleventh year, in the month Bul, which is the eighth month, the house was completed in all its work and all its furnishings. And he built it in seven years.”

The month Zio is April, which is also called Jar. For *Zio* means “face.” It is called “face” because, at the dedication of the temple, the cloud of glory—the face of the Lord—covered the temple. *Jar*, however, means “fear.” It is so called because there is fear that what the crops and lands require may be made unfruitful in this month by the inclemency of the weather.

“He built it,” it says, “in seven years.” In the Gospel, when the Lord had said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2), speaking [Col. 1155C] of the temple of His body, the Jews answered: “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you rebuild it in three days?” (ibid.). Some said this in the impatience of resentment: “This temple was built in forty-six years,” although they could have said more briefly, “Solomon built it in seven years.” Nevertheless, though ignorant, they spoke truly both according to history and according to mystery.

For, as the historical account testifies, when the children of the captivity returned from Babylon under Ezra or Nehemiah and began rebuilding, the building which then stood when these words were spoken was hindered by the hostile nations dwelling around them; and thus it came about that the building once begun was prolonged for forty-six years.

Moreover, they gave us mystical words, so that we may say concerning the temple of the Lord’s body that it was truly built in forty-six years: that is, it is true flesh from Adam’s flesh. For this number, according to Greek letters, is the numerical value of the name Adam. *Adam* is written with four letters: the first, alpha, α, signifies one; the second, delta, δ, four; the third, alpha, α, again one; and the fourth, mu, μ, forty. Thus we have seized this saying from the mouth of the ungodly and ignorant, joyfully declaring that this holy temple of God was truly built in forty-six years: that is, true flesh, the true body of Christ, was taken from the true flesh of Adam.

Again, the four letters of the name just mentioned signify the four quarters of the world, and they are the initial letters of their Greek names. For in Greek east is ἀνατολή, *anatolē*; west, λῆσις, *lēsis*; north, ἄρκτος, *arktos*; and south, μεσημβρία, *mesēmbria* [Col. 1156A]. Therefore the temple of the Lord’s body was taken from Adam’s body, dispersed through the four quarters of the world; and Jewish malice, though unaware of it, bore testimony to this.

## CHAPTER XIV. What the house of the forest of Lebanon signifies spiritually; and why, from Abraham to Christ, the house had as many columns—that is, forty-five—as there were generations, though the Evangelist omitted three.

**(3 KINGS, CHAPTER 7.)** “He also built the house of the forest of Lebanon, a hundred cubits long, fifty cubits broad, and thirty cubits [Col. 1156B] high; and four walks among cedar columns. For he had cut cedar wood into columns, and clad the entire ceiling with cedar boards. It was supported by forty-five columns.”

If the city Jerusalem spiritually signifies the holy Church, and that handmade temple signifies the temple of the Lord’s body, what does this house of Solomon, the house of the forest of Lebanon, signify except the house of the genealogy of the same Jesus Christ, son of David and son of Abraham? The cedar wood, incorruptible wood, was the fathers, from whom Christ Himself was according to the flesh; for on account of the merit of their great faith they are of incorruptible memory.

What, then, are the forty-five columns of this house except the same number of generations from Abraham to Christ? According to the Gospel they are no more than forty-two, but according to the truth of history they are forty-five. For the Gospel omitted three for the sake of a definite mystery, saying: “Joram begot Uzziah” (Matt. 1). Joram did not beget Uzziah, but Ahaziah; Ahaziah begot Joash, from whom Amaziah was born; and Amaziah begot Uzziah. The Evangelist’s purpose was to set forth three groups of fourteen in differing periods of time; and Joram had allied himself by marriage with the most wicked Jezebel. Therefore his memory is removed up to the third generation, lest it be placed in the order of the holy nativity.

Therefore the house of the forest of Lebanon is supported by forty-five columns, because the generations of the fathers from whom Christ was according to [Col. 1156D] the flesh—from Abraham to Christ—number forty-five. But, you ask, how can those who do not stand in Christ’s Gospel and have fallen from His genealogy be said to stand under this mystery in the number or order of its columns? Let us answer this. They indeed fell, but other and better columns took their place: namely, the prophets whom they killed or persecuted.

For example, Ahaziah, also called Ochozias, fell; in his place let Elisha the prophet stand, for by the word of the Lord he commanded Jehu and anointed him king over Israel, that he might destroy the house of Ahab and Jezebel, who had killed the prophets; Ahaziah was of their line, being descended from their daughter. Joash also, Ahaziah’s son, fell. Let Zechariah, the prophet son of Jehoiada, whom he killed, take his place. Amaziah fell; in his place let the prophet be counted who, when he rebuked Amaziah for worshipping the gods of Seir, heard this: “Are you the king’s counsellor? Be silent, lest I kill you” (2 Chron. 25).

Thus in the house of Christ, the peaceful king, there are, as has been said, forty-five columns. Why should the prophets mentioned not be admitted into Christ’s genealogy, where the fathers of His flesh deservedly fall, when it ends in Joseph, who, as is agreed, was not His father? For the Evangelist, spiritually minded and wise, intended to weave the genealogy of the incarnate Word according to faith rather than flesh. The true blessedness of this genealogy consists in this: that the Word Himself, whom the faithful Virgin bore and nursed according to the flesh, she first conceived according to faith and in her heart, and bore forth with her mouth, in accordance with the prophet’s great astonishment:

> “Before she travailed, she brought forth; and before her labour came, she bore a male child. Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen its like?” (Isa. 66).

And immediately:

> “Will the earth bring forth in one day, or will a nation be born at once? For Zion travailed and brought forth her children” (ibid.).

What is this Zion which bore before she travailed, which bore a male child before her labour came, and then in one day together bore the nation of her children, except that blessed generation which, before it bore Christ according to the flesh from the womb of the Virgin Mary, bore the same male child—that is, the strongest and almighty one—according to the Spirit; and then, when the Apostles preached, travailed and brought forth, as though in one day—that is, in a short time—the multitude of believers spread throughout the whole world?

For after the promise of the blessed seed made to Abraham, what was the work of Moses and the prophets in composing Holy Scripture, which is the word of God, except to conceive Christ in their hearts through the prophetic Spirit and bear Him with their mouths? Does not one of them affirm this too? “From fear of You, O Lord,” he says, “we have conceived and brought forth spirit; we have not wrought salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26). Likewise, after the Lord’s ascension, what was it to convert the nations suddenly to faith in Christ through the testimonies of Moses and the prophets, except for the nation of Zion’s children to be brought forth in one day? [Col. 1157D]

Therefore the holy Evangelist rightly and reverently wove Christ’s genealogy in such a manner as both to remove the wicked kings who killed the prophets after the example of their mother Jezebel, and to end it in the faithful man Joseph, the spouse of the guarded Virgin.

## CHAPTER XV. What the portico before the great portico and the portico of the throne, in which is the judgment-seat, mystically signify in the differing conditions of time: from Abraham to Noah, from Noah to Abel, and from Abel upward to the first creation of the world.

We have examined the forty-five columns; let us consider the rest.

> “And he made a portico of columns, fifty cubits long and thirty cubits broad; and another portico before the greater portico; and he made columns and capitals upon the columns. He also made the portico of the throne, in which is the judgment-seat, and covered it with cedar wood from the floor to the summit,” etc.

The portico of columns before the house, supported by columns, was that time from Abraham back to Noah—from Abraham, I say, to whom the promise was first made. The other portico before the greater portico was the condition of an earlier age, namely from Noah back to Abel, or to Adam, who was first created. The portico of the throne, in which is the judgment-seat, is that beginning of the fear of the Lord, that beginning of Holy Scripture, which is to be feared: there God separated light from darkness—that is, humble angels from proud angels—by an unassociable division, and expelled from paradise for transgression the first-formed man whom He had placed there [Col. 1158B]. There is the terrible throne; there is the dreadful judgment-seat.

He says, therefore: “He also made the portico of the throne, in which is the judgment-seat, and covered it with cedar wood from the floor to the summit. And the small house in which one sat to judge was in the middle of the portico, made in the same fashion.” Luke, the most eloquent narrator of the Lord’s genealogy and the articulate ox, led us from the temple of the Lord itself, which is in Jerusalem—from the Lord’s man Himself, who was born in it, which “the Most High founded” (Ps. 86 [87])—to this highest portico, to this small house in which the aforesaid throne or judgment-seat is found. He begins thus: “And Jesus Himself was beginning to be about thirty years of age, being, as was supposed, son of Joseph, who was of Heli”; and he ends thus: “who was of Seth, who was of Adam, who was of God” (Luke 3).

For immediately, to everyone who has ears to hear, there comes to mind that throne or judgment-seat of God at which Adam, by a just sentence, incurred judgment for his transgression and was sent into this exile, oppressed by a double death, of soul and body. But Matthew did not go beyond that house, the royal house of forty-five columns, because he did not proceed beyond Abraham, to whom the promise of the seed in which all nations would be blessed was first made (Matt. 1).

We must now briefly say how the portico differs from the house itself [Col. 1158D]. The succession of generations from Abraham to Christ is Solomon’s house, the house of the peaceful and most wise king, because from the time when Abraham heard that all nations would be blessed in his seed (Gen. 22), he believed; and through this faith he was justified. Through that same faith Christ dwelt in his heart and in the hearts of his children, as the Apostle says of us also: “That Christ may dwell by faith in your hearts” (Eph. 3).

Noah, however, and the righteous or elect who descended from him or came after him up to Abraham, received nothing of this kind; they had heard nothing concerning such a promise. They were proved and found faithful in the consideration of other matters, as Noah was, who believed God when He told him that the flood would come and built the ark at the Lord’s command, while the others did not believe, as Peter says in the Epistle: “Who had once been unbelieving, when the patience of God waited in the days of Noah, while the ark was being built” (1 Pet. 3).

Accordingly, Noah received a different sign of faith: not in his flesh, as Abraham did, who had faith in the blessed seed and therefore received the fitting sign of circumcision, but in the clouds, the Lord saying, “I will place my bow in the clouds of heaven” (Gen. 9), because Noah had believed that the floodgates of heaven would be opened to bring about the flood [Col. 1159A]. Thus the condition of that time was different, differing from the time and faith of Abraham as much as the preceding portico differs in dignity from the house.

Moreover, all the elect or righteous who were before Noah, prior to the flood, differed in another respect: apart from the natural law, they are not recorded as having received any commandment; but, knowing the Creator from creation, they pleased God by spontaneous faith and even by uncommanded sacrifices, like Abel and Enoch. Thus there was another condition of time, rightly understood now through the portico that stood before the front of the greater portico.

Finally, the highest portico of the throne, in which is the judgment-seat, is that fabric of the world, unfolded in six days, which, as we have already said, we behold at the summit of Holy Scripture. Hence we hear, as it were from a throne or judgment-seat, the imperious utterances of the Creator and King: “Let there be light” (Gen. 1); and His dividing light itself from darkness; “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters” (ibid.); and so forth—His speaking and, by speaking, making with sovereign authority. Therefore we sing: “For He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32 [33]).

> “He established them for ever and ever; He set a commandment, and it shall not pass away” (Ps. 148).

We should all still bear the sentence of that throne or judgment-seat—“On whatever day you eat from it, you shall surely die” (Gen. 3)—unless it had been removed through Him whom we have with the Father, the great advocate Jesus Christ, who intercedes for us (1 John 2).

## CHAPTER XVI. What and what kind of house is that which Solomon Christ made for Pharaoh’s daughter—that is, for the Church from the Gentiles.

> “He also made a house for Pharaoh’s daughter, whom Solomon had taken as wife, in the same manner as this portico.”

At last Solomon, who had taken Pharaoh’s daughter as wife, also made a house for her; for after all the matters mystically understood above [Col. 1159D], Christ also prepared for the Church from the Gentiles, whom He acquired as His bride, a good place in heaven and on earth. He made her a house, I say, in the same fashion as that highest portico.

For example, just as we mystically behold with spiritual eyes in that portico that “the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1), so in the house of this daughter of Pharaoh—in the sacraments of this Church from the Gentiles, which was once the daughter of spiritual Pharaoh, that is, of the devil—we do not doubt that the same Holy Spirit is borne over the waters of baptism, and that thereafter He has created new heavens and a new earth, and so forth: all things new, after a certain likeness of those old things. Of this we shall speak more fully elsewhere.

> “All things were of precious stones, which were sawn to a certain rule and measure both within and without, from the foundation to the top of the walls, and from within to the great court. The foundations were of precious stones, great stones, of ten or eight cubits.”

Those stones, those precious stones, and these foundations are those of which, or concerning which, the Apostle says: “Now you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2), etc.

That handmade building, like every handmade structure, had earthly foundations below and rose upward. But this spiritual building has its foundations above, as the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86 [87]). Indeed, the foundation of its foundations is Christ—of this no one doubts—since He is that most high stone. “Coming to Him,” Peter says, “a living stone, you yourselves also, as living stones, are built up” (1 Pet. 2); yet the goal is that we should be raised upon Him.

“They were sawn,” it says, “to a certain rule and measure, both within and without.” And afterwards: “They were cut to equal measure.” This must plainly be understood according to one and the same faith. For in faith all these stones—living stones, precious stones—are equal; and they are sawn both within and without because before God and before men they say and think the same things [Col. 1160C]. Therefore, being as it were sawn or cut, they can be well joined together and cohere with one another. But they differ greatly in operation or power; whence the Apostle says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as He wills” (1 Cor. 12).

And fittingly, “to a certain rule and measure.” For the one and only One who possesses without any measure “every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1) is He of whom John the Baptist says: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father has given all things into His hands” (John 3). But all of us have received from His fullness according to measure (John 1).

Likewise, he says, cedar wood is arranged with the stones or upon the stones, both in the greater court and in the inner court of the Lord’s house, or in the portico of the house. This signifies that in God’s building it is fitting that we should be like stones, stable and firm through patience, and like incorruptible cedar, should draw those outside by good examples. Let us say with the Apostle: “We are Christ’s sweet fragrance to God in every place” (2 Cor. 2).

The court of the house consists of those who, for love of those within, extend themselves to outward matters, so that by excluding every intrusive thing they may leave undisturbed the holy leisure of those more fitted for religion and holy contemplation. Solomon’s most careful work extends as far as that court, because whatever Christ works in those who stand within before Him, He provides also for those who, as stated above, faithfully labour for their sake by extending themselves to outward affairs [Col. 1161A].

## CHAPTER XVII. No one ought to think it incredible that, in the construction of the handmade temple, the mysteries of the temple not made by hands were expressed so perfectly, since Daniel also could foresee the number of years up to that same Christ.

Perhaps it may seem remarkable to some, or even incredible, that we should say that a human king was so intent upon spiritual matters in his work that he must be thought not even to have set the number of the columns without regard to mysteries; and that it consequently follows that he could also have known the number of generations from Abraham to Christ. But [Col. 1161B] would anyone rightly judge that he knew less than any of the prophets? Certainly not, since, when he asked for wisdom, the Lord said to him: “Behold, I have done according to your words, and have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that none before you has been like you, nor shall any arise after you” (3 Kings 3). And shortly afterwards Scripture likewise says: “And he was wiser than all men—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol” (3 Kings 4).

Ethan is interpreted “most steadfast”; Ezrahite, “eastern.” Ethan himself is Abraham the Easterner. Heman, which is interpreted “faithful,” is Moses. Calcol, which is interpreted “governing,” is Joseph. Darda is interpreted “generation of knowledge.” Mahol is interpreted “forgiveness.” The twelve tribes, the sons [Col. 1161C] of Mahol—that is, the sons of Jacob—are understood as the generation of knowledge.

With the same consistency one must say that Daniel too, who arose after him, was wiser. For God had said to Solomon, as has already been mentioned, that none before him had been, nor would any after him arise, like him. Yet Daniel was granted knowledge even of the number of years after whose completion Christ would come, Gabriel saying thus: “Know therefore and observe: from the issuing of the word for Jerusalem to be rebuilt until Christ the prince, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks” (Dan. 9), etc. Can it then be denied that this man was able to know the lesser matter—namely, in which generation, when Christ was born, that temple of divinity was to be built—when [Col. 1161D] he was wiser than all men both before him and to come after him?

Accordingly, even if we do not read that it was said to him as it was said to Moses, “See, and make according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25), nevertheless he himself saw the pattern according to which he made everything, so that he did not even set a column without contemplation of heavenly things; for not even Moses himself was wiser than he. These things have been said in order that it may be established that in his work he more carefully discerned and imitated the structure of the temple not made with hands—the temple of the Lord’s body and of his whole spiritual house—than anyone can attain in exposition by his own intellect. Yet the unanimous judgment of all churchmen is such that it would be impious to suspect anything else.

## CHAPTER XVIII

[Col. 1162A] How Hiram may be said to have had a Tyrian father, though he was full of wisdom, understanding, and learning, and was therefore able, in his work, to attend to mystical meanings.

“King Solomon also sent and brought Hiram from Tyre, the son of a widowed woman of the tribe of Naphtali, with a Tyrian father, a worker in bronze, full of wisdom and understanding and learning for doing every work in bronze. When he came to King Solomon, he made all his work, and fashioned two bronze columns.”

Of him it is read in Chronicles: “Therefore I have sent you a prudent and most learned man, Hiram my father, son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, whose father was a Tyrian” (2 Chron. 2). It should be noted that in Kings he is called Hiram, but in Chronicles Huram. Hiram is interpreted “sublime”; Huram, however, “God is exalted.”

In Kings Hiram is said to have been from Tyre, the son of a widowed woman of the tribe of Naphtali, with a Tyrian father. One should understand that his father belonged to the tribe of Naphtali; after his death, his wife—who is here written of as a widow—is said to have sent this same Hiram to Tyre for the sake of instruction. Because he was taught in Tyre, his father is called Tyrian. Thus he is said to have had a Tyrian father, although his father in fact belonged to the tribe of Naphtali.

What is read in Chronicles, namely that the king said of Hiram, “I have sent you a most prudent and learned man, Huram my father,” calls him “father” as a title of dignity, as is found in many places. He calls him “the son of a woman of the daughters [Col. 1162C] of Dan,” because his mother was of the tribe of Dan, from the family of Shelomith, sister of Oholiab, son of Ahisamach. Her son, this same Shelomith’s Egyptian, was stoned in the wilderness. For it is not supposed that the same Shelomith voluntarily joined herself to that Egyptian; rather, she suffered violence from him. Therefore it is said to have come about through her merits that one such as this should be born of her daughters, to work in the house of the Lord.

Some also maintain that, through the merits of Bilhah, Jacob’s concubine, after Rachel died she not only raised Joseph in the place of a son, but even interceded for his brothers, that he might forget his brothers’ injury; and that for this reason the Lord granted her that from one of her sons there should be born this same Oholiab, companion of Bezalel, who built [Col. 1162D] the house of the Lord; and that Huram, who built the house of the Lord in Jerusalem, should be born to her other son, namely Naphtali.

Scripture highly commended him by calling him “full of wisdom and understanding and learning.” It placed last what can be acquired through human agency, namely learning; but it named first those things which are gifts of God alone, namely wisdom and understanding. For no one can be full of wisdom—that is, good natural ability—except by God’s gift; and especially not of understanding, which is the special capacity of saints and prophets, by which, in his art, he knew how to attend to divine and mystical meanings. Learning, moreover, comes from human beings; when it proceeds rightly, it is accustomed, as though from a spark of inborn talent, to kindle a bright and great flame.

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 1163A] On the two bronze columns which he fashioned; why the first is called Jachin on the right and the second Boaz on the left; and on the line of twelve cubits which surrounds each.

“He fashioned,” he says, “two bronze columns, each column eighteen cubits high, and a line of twelve cubits surrounded each column.” What these columns, an outstanding and very great ornament of the house of the Lord, signify, their author himself suggests to us in the Song of Songs, when in praise of the bridegroom he says: “His legs are marble columns, founded upon bases of gold” (Cant. 5).

What are the bridegroom’s legs, if not all the ways of the Lord? The Lord’s level ways are only two: mercy and truth; or mercy and judgment; or righteousness and peace (Ps. 24). However much the names may vary, there are only two legs, only two ways of the Lord. Upon these columns almost the whole house rests; upon them the entire structure of Holy Scripture is supported. For whatever we read or hear concerning all the ways of the Lord is either mercy or truth.

Therefore the wise architect set only two columns in his work, admirable and worthy of contemplation—if you have the means to see the ways of the Lord which he knew well. One is truth, or judgment, which resists the proud (1 Pet. 5); the other is mercy, which sustains and strengthens the humble (ibid.) by the Spirit of grace and the Spirit of strength. Therefore, lest we be idle in not knowing or disregarding the glory of the certain mystery to be sought and contemplated in the columns, he himself gave them proper names, and this Scripture took care to commit those very names to everlasting remembrance. For it says: “When he had set up the right-hand column, he called it by the name Jachin,” that is, “firmness.” “Likewise he erected the second column and called its name Boaz.”

He wished his columns to be known indeed and renowned, marking them with names so great and clear. For what is firmness in the house of God but merciful grace, or the gratuitous mercy of the great king—of the great, I say, and peace-making King Christ? Asking for it, we say: “Strengthen, O God, that which you have wrought in us” (Ps. 67). Surely, whatever he has wrought in us, whatever he strengthens by the help of the Holy [Col. 1163D] Spirit, belongs to mercy, not judgment; to grace, not merit.

And in what strength does the second column stand, except judgment, by which heaven itself—how much more earth!—will be shaken by a violent storm? It should therefore be noted that the first is called “firmness,” and the second “in strength”: for mercy comes first, strengthening the humble with good hope; judgment follows, by which God, most strong against the proud, prepares his mighty arm.

“One column,” he says, “was eighteen cubits high.” This number demands jointly from all worshipping in the Lord’s temple faith and works, as though in rivalry. For there are ten commandments of the Law; Christ rose on the eighth day—on the eighth day, I say, on which the infant was also circumcised (Gen. 17; Luke 1). That circumcision was the seal of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4), which God rewarded in Abraham with his friendship.

Likewise, this number of height is contained under three and six: for three times six, or six times three, is eighteen. Three signifies faith in the Trinity; six—the number in which God completed the work of the world—signifies action. Therefore, that we may both believe rightly and do good to all (Gal. 6), the individual columns rise by these shared numbers; for we are drawn to both by hope of mercy and fear of judgment.

“And,” he says, “a line of twelve cubits surrounded each column.” Here it must also be understood that when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, when all nations are gathered before him (Matt. 25), then this column called Firmness, the column of mercy, will stand on the right; and the column called Boaz, “in strength,” the column of judgment, will stand on the left. Then indeed the line of twelve cubits will surround each column.

For behold, around the right-hand column is half the line, that is, six cubits: “I was hungry,” he says, “and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you received me. Naked, and you clothed me. Sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me” (ibid.). And behold, around the left-hand column are six cubits: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food. I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink. I was a stranger, and you did not receive me. Naked, and you did not clothe me. Sick and in prison, and you did not come to me” (ibid.).

Thus the line of twelve cubits surrounds each column, because a twelvefold recompense, distinguishing good and evil, will be divided between them. This interpretation is more spiritual. The carnal Hebrews, however, wholly turned away from the true temple of which we speak, interpret David and Boaz carnally in these columns: by Jachin, which they interpret “preparer,” David is understood; by the other column, Boaz is understood on account of the strength of chastity.

## CHAPTER XX

What the capitals of the columns are; why they are five cubits high and fashioned in a porch of four cubits; what the lattices or little chains upon the capitals are, by which the columns seem to hang from the oracle; and what the pomegranates interspersed among the little chains are.

“The capitals which were upon the tops of the columns were fashioned like lily-work in a porch, four cubits high. And again, other capitals were upon the tops of the columns above, according to the measure of the column opposite the lattices.”

In accordance with the mystery already begun, the paired capitals of the columns signify the consummation both of the Lord’s truth and of his mercy in the resurrection of the dead, when an equal recompense according to the works of all will be made, both in body and in soul. The lower capitals signify bodies; the higher, the consummated condition of souls. Hence a little before this it was said: “One capital was five cubits high, and the other capital five cubits high” (Matt. 16).

The capitals five cubits high belong to bodies, whose five senses will all be filled in eternal fellowship, whether with eternal goods or eternal evils. Those who, as was said above, will be on the right, from the abundance of mercy, will be satisfied through sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch in flesh now immortal and impassible, with eternal goods “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). Those on the left likewise, from the abundance of justice and truth, will be filled in all those same senses in their flesh with eternal evils, so that “their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66; Mark 9).

Nor is it contrary that these were fashioned like lily-work, because both the just and deserved condemnation of those on the left and the merciful and gratuitous salvation of those on the right will contribute to the beauty of divine praise. The Psalmist too bears witness when he says: “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100). It is therefore fitting that these capitals are said to have been five cubits high.

But those which were above them are read to have been neither five cubits high nor of any other stated measurement, because we know all the bodily senses in which our flesh will receive full recompense according to the merits of works; but we cannot know what receptacles, what numbers, or what conditions souls will have in that recompense, whether of good or evil.

Where were these capitals fashioned? “In a porch,” he says, “of four cubits,” that is, in the preceding exercise of the four principal virtues, which even the pagans knew and named with their own terms: prudence, temperance, courage, and justice. For according as someone has exercised himself in these, whether badly, like Epicurus, or well, like a churchman—not to say a Stoic or Peripatetic—so in that distinction of mercy and judgment he will be seen as belonging to the right or the left.

“Opposite the lattices,” he says. A little earlier he speaks more fully of these lattices: “There were lattices of seven rows on one capital, and seven lattices on the other capital. And he completed the columns, and two rows all around each lattice, to cover the capitals which were upon the top of the pomegranates,” etc. And in Chronicles: “Moreover, he made, as it were, little chains in the oracle, and placed them upon the tops of the columns. He also made one hundred pomegranates, which he interspersed among the little chains” (2 Chron. 3).

Thus we are given to understand that two chains, hanging down from the height of the oracle, were each divided into seven little chains, as though into branches, woven with golden garlands in the form of lattices, which joined those divisions together. In this way they were entwined with golden pomegranates, as though supporting the columns, so that, although they stood firmly, they yet appeared to hang from the oracle.

What do these little chains stretched down from the height of the oracle signify, except the most exalted reasons of the judgment and mercy already mentioned—having roots fixed so high in heaven and hidden so deeply in the incarnate Word, in the wisdom of God—that the human mind can neither comprehend nor investigate them? Hence, when the Apostle had discussed these matters at greater length, he suddenly exclaimed in wonder: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11).

For who can comprehend or investigate whence come these great lattices of God’s mercy or judgment: by which he sometimes mercifully draws this person to life, seemingly even against his will; shuts up that one, though running swiftly as it were toward life; and binds some with cords of sins? For example, concerning the Jews, he says through the prophet: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

But that he sent his fishers to the nations (Matt. 10), and commanded them to let down their nets to catch them (Mark 1; Luke 5), the whole sea of this world has experienced through great and long trial. Therefore the columns seem to hang from chains fixed above, because mortal intellects cannot reach or comprehend the reasons of God’s truth and mercy that come from the sublime oracle of God’s wisdom.

The pomegranates, however, are the works of those who are judged or saved: “Say to the righteous,” says the prophet, “that it is well, for they shall receive the fruit of their deeds” (Isa. 3). Likewise: “Woe to the soul of the wicked, for evils have been repaid to them” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 1166C] On the molten sea, in which the priests washed, which was a type of baptism in which sins are forgiven.

“He also made a molten sea, ten cubits from brim to brim, round in circumference. Its height was five cubits, and a cord of thirty cubits encircled it round about; and ornamentation ran around its brim, encompassing the sea by ten cubits,” etc.

This sea was a basin for the priests, as is also read in Chronicles: “Moreover, the priests washed in the sea” (2 Chron. 4). And fittingly, after the temple’s structure has been completed, there is added the wondrous construction of this sea in which the priests washed. For after the temple of the Lord’s body had been built or raised again, the sacrament of baptism is set forth, in which—as is plain and well known to Christian faith—we were washed, not because we were priests, but in order that we might be priests. Thus John in the Apocalypse, after saying, “Because you were slain and redeemed us to God by your blood” (Rev. 5), immediately added: “And you made us a kingdom and priests to our God” (ibid.).

Ezekiel too saw this sea’s water coming forth from the temple’s right side (Ezek. 47). Here too the present Scripture reports that this sea was set on the right side of the temple. For, it says, “he set the sea on the right side of the temple, toward the east, opposite the south.” By this statement it is also indicated that this temple faced east. For the right side of a temple facing east looks toward the south.

So too in that prophetic vision: “And I turned,” he says, “to the gate of the house, and behold waters came out from beneath the threshold of the house toward the east. For the front of the house faced east; and the waters descended to the right side of the temple, south of the altar.” Fittingly both here and there, that which anticipates the mystery of baptism extends toward the temple’s right side, toward the south, and the house faces east. For the grace of the Holy Spirit regenerating through baptism does not admit the setting of light or the cold regions of unbelieving hearts—which Scripture is accustomed to signify by west and north—but hastens toward the rising of light, commonly the day of noonday brightness: that is, toward those in whom Christ, the sun of righteousness, rises through faith (Mal. 4), and does not set; toward those in whose hearts the noonday light of truth burns with love, ever hostile to the devil, who is cold and sits in the sides of the north.

Undoubtedly the grace of so great a sacrament would have shone more fully and perfectly in this made temple if the wise king, had the position of the Jerusalem site permitted it, had been able to conduct living waters in such a way that, as is carefully described in the prophet’s already mentioned vision, they came out beneath the threshold of the house, descended to the right side of the temple, and likewise flowed abundantly from the right side. For thus what was to come—and now, as we believe, has come, and therefore we speak of it—would here have been more fully expressed: that from beneath the threshold of the house, from the right side of the temple of the Lord, when a soldier’s lance opened it, water flowed with blood (John 19); and, says the same prophet, all things to which this water or this torrent shall come shall live and stand, and all waters—that is, all peoples—shall be healed (Ezek. 47). Let us now return to the words themselves.

## CHAPTER XXII

How rightly he called that sea a basin; how our sea, that is baptism, is molten; and on its mystical measurements and carvings.

“He made,” he says, “a molten sea.” How small a thing this name denotes, compared with how great a thing it was! For what was it? It was a basin ten cubits from brim to brim, round in circumference. Its diameter was ten cubits; consequently, “a cord,” he says, “of thirty cubits encircled it”—that is, could encircle it. For this is a natural observation of geometrical science: the diameter of any circular extent, tripled, nearly makes up the entire measure of that circle’s circumference.

If, therefore, you consider only the literal construction, there is no reason why the wisest king should have called it a sea. But with respect to the mystery, this sacrament of baptism—this laver of regeneration, which flowed from the side of the temple of the Lord, from the wound of the crucified Lord—is a sea: a sea, I say, of such fullness and inundation that it has filled the whole world. For it first overflowed even upon those dead beneath the earth, for the remission of sins; then it has overflowed, and does not cease to overflow, upon those who were, are, or shall be above the earth.

It is therefore a sea, and “molten,” he says—molten, I say—because Christ, melted and made liquid in the great fire of love, poured out this grace upon us.

“This sea is ten cubits from brim to brim, and its circumference is thirty cubits.” This number clearly implies the faith which everyone approaching to be washed must necessarily confess. For arithmeticians or abacus-calculators know very well that, in the second limit, that is, the decimal, unity ten times three is thirty. But above all we need that faith which is catholic: that we confess unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, in which confession we were baptized in Christ Jesus.

Thus the ten cubits of breadth within a circumference of thirty cubits signify faith or confession, without which there is no baptism at all. For, as has been said, the person to be baptized necessarily confesses one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity.

Its height is five cubits, so that even those should be allowed or admitted in whom there is no power or height either of natural ability or knowledge beyond the five senses of the body: such as infants born that very day, scarcely exercising even their bodily senses. Christian faith carries them to Mother Church, running and hastening, and does not doubt at all that this great sea is accessible to them.

“And ornamentation ran around the brim, encompassing the sea by ten cubits. There were two rows of striped ornaments, cast in the same piece.” One who is to be washed in this sea must, besides confessing the Trinity, receive and venerate the Scripture of the two Testaments. Thus the ornamentation was upon the brim for ten cubits—that is, on the front part of the sea—so that it might wholly offer itself to the eyes of those approaching to wash. There were two rows of *hystriatae* ornaments, that is, standing out or projecting, for the purpose, evidently, of being seen, *apotitystorin*, which in Greek is said to mean “to see” or “to know.”

Thus, lest works be absent from the confession of faith—without which faith is rightly called dead (Jas. 2) or idle—the ornamentation is distinguished into two rows extending through ten cubits, signifying the reading of each Testament. Whoever receives this reading is reborn in Christ, provided that he reads it in such a way as to imitate the works, as well as confess the faith, of the saints.

## CHAPTER XXIII

That the twelve oxen supporting the sea are the twelve apostles, receiving from Christ the rule for baptizing; and what it means that their hind parts were hidden inwardly.

[Col. 1168D] “And they stood upon twelve oxen, three of which faced north, three west, three south, and three east; and the sea was above them, and their hind parts were hidden inwardly.”

Who are these twelve oxen, on which the sea is set, if not the twelve apostles, to whom the sacrament of baptism, newly consecrated in Christ’s death, was entrusted? For Christ suffered and died; and in that death of his this sacrament was established. “For,” says the Apostle, “all we who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Gal. 3). When he rose from the dead, he immediately placed this sea upon these oxen. For he said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

The sea, therefore, was placed upon twelve oxen, so that they might bear the Trinity to all nations, into the four quarters of the world, preaching and testifying to one God in Trinity. For this is what it means that three faced north, three west, three south, and three east.

“Their hind parts,” he says, “were hidden inwardly.” Certainly the hind parts of these oxen, these apostles of Christ, ought to be hidden inwardly, so that we may not look at what they once were, but at what they became by Christ’s grace. For example, Matthew before his calling was a publican and tax collector (*telonearius*); now after his calling he is an apostle and evangelist. This is the face revealed for contemplating Christ’s glory; those former things were his hind parts. Let us look upon this face, that through it we too may be enlightened; let those hind parts remain hidden, lest we imitate them.

Alternatively, the faces stand out openly, but the hind parts are hidden, because we indeed see the apostles’—or all fathers’ and pastors’—manifest works; but before the strict Judge we do not know what awaits them afterwards in hidden recompense.

## CHAPTER XXIV

What it mystically means that, in the bases, lions were not made without oxen nor oxen without lions; and why five bases bearing individual basins were set on the right and five on the left.

[Col. 1169C] Why, then, is it that in the carved work of the bases there are portrayed not only lions, but lions together with oxen and cherubim? For this is added: “And carvings between the joints, and between the wreaths and interlacings, lions and oxen and cherubim,” etc.

Why, I ask, are lions not made in the bases without oxen, nor oxen without lions? What else do the bases in the temple signify but priests in the Church? Since they bear the burdens of governance, they carry an imposed load, like bases. Cherubim are therefore portrayed on the bases because it is fitting that priests’ hearts should be filled with fullness of knowledge. By lions is figured the awe of severity; by oxen, the patience of gentleness.

Thus on these bases lions are not portrayed without oxen, nor oxen without lions, because from a priestly heart the virtue of gentleness must always be guarded amid the terror of severity: so that gentleness may season anger, and zeal for strictness may kindle this same gentleness lest it perhaps become lax.

There are ten in number, each bearing one basin, each resting upon four wheels. And, Scripture says, he set five of them on the right side of the temple and five on the left. This fittingly signifies to us that the sacrament of baptism is wholly of the right, and all the apostles are of the right; therefore the sea with its twelve oxen was placed on the right side of the temple. Yet not all baptizers and not all baptized persons are of the right.

For according to the Gospel parable of the ten virgins—five prudent and five foolish (Matt. 25)—it is certain that, of the whole body of souls called to this temple of the true Solomon, to the wedding of the true and peace-making King Christ, one part will be assigned to the right and one part to the left. One part, I say, will enter the wedding with the king; another will be left outside when the door is closed. Therefore not all the bases and not all the basins, though all alike rest upon four wheels, are placed on the right; five are on the left, because not all baptizers or all baptized persons, although they read or receive the four Gospels, will attain glory. One part of them is taken unto life; another, because it does not have love together with faith, is left for punishment.

## CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 1170B] That there are many useful vessels in the spiritual temple of God, in whose use or office we ought to serve; and what it mystically means that they are said to have been cast in clay ground between Succoth and Zarthan.

For us at last, who do not deserve to be either columns or bases in the temple of the great king, this must be our prayer: that at least we may be received among the lesser vessels, which are many. For according to the diversity of merits and of capacities for good and useful arts, the wise king sets and arranges some as cauldrons, others as dishes, others as ewers, others as water jars, others as forks, others as cups, others as bowls, and so forth; and thus every work in the temple of the Lord is completed.

And lest anyone despair or despise himself too greatly: “The king,” he says, “cast all the vessels in the plain of the Jordan, in clay ground, between Succoth and Zarthan.” All vessels indeed—now golden and beautiful vessels, now vessels of grace, now vessels of honor and glory, at whose sight we wonder and which we rightly venerate—our king, King Christ, “cast in clay ground.” He “cast [them] in clay ground,” I say: that is, he took them from the same mass and the same mud from which we too were fashioned.
