Provided we dwell “in the region of the Jordan, in the plain”—that is, hold firm to the end the faith in which we were baptized—and, like a lowly plain, are free from mountainous pride, it is not difficult for the great craftsman to form any one of us into a vessel of any glory and honor, with the same fingers by which he carefully formed all the saints, between Succoth and Zarthan: that is, in pilgrimage and tribulation.

For Succoth means “tents,” which belong, certainly, to pilgrims and soldiers. Zarthan is interpreted “their tribulation.” Indeed, without the hammer of persecutions or the chisel of temptations, vessels of whatever kind for the Lord’s temple, whether golden or of less precious bronze, do not attain perfection. Therefore we too, set in the lands of the Jordan because we have been baptized in Christ Jesus, journeying between Succoth and Zarthan because here we have no abiding city but seek the city to come (Heb. 13), and suffering many temptations if we wish to live devoutly (2 Tim. 3)—although we are clay ground, indeed mud or mire—let us submit ourselves as suppliants with faith and hope to the hands of our fashioner, the great craftsman. Thus, if we cannot become great vessels, let us at least become small ones; if not golden, at least of bronze, so that in his temple we may partake in some manner of the gift of honor and grace.

## CHAPTER XXVI

On the statement, “And he brought in the things which his father had sanctified and stored them,” etc.; and what it means mystically for rulers and chiefs with the elders to gather to King Solomon, and for sheep and oxen without number to be sacrificed.

What then did Solomon do after completing all the work he was doing in the house of the Lord? “And he brought in,” it says, “the silver, gold, and vessels which David his father had sanctified, and stored them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord.”

Nothing is truer than that everything which his father—the Father God—had sanctified, all gold and all silver and all vessels, was stored in the house of the Lord, in the unmade temple of the Lord’s body. What were, or are, those things that this Father had sanctified? All the sayings and deeds of the fathers and patriarchs; all proclamations of the prophets; all the treasures of the holy Scriptures. For all the Scriptures were fulfilled in him.

Therefore, because—as the Apostle says—“in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2), it is true that this Solomon, the great king and Son of God, stored in his temple all that David his father had sanctified. And immediately there follows:

(III Kings, Chapter VIII.) “Then all the elders of Israel were assembled, together with the princes of the tribes and the heads of the families [Col. 1171C] of the children of Israel, before King Solomon in Jerusalem, to carry the ark of the covenant of the Lord from the city of David, that is, from Zion.” And shortly afterward: “King Solomon and the whole multitude of Israel that had gathered to him walked with him before the ark, sacrificing sheep and oxen beyond estimation and number.”

A great festival, a great celebration. Here Solomon the king, at the dedication of the temple made by human hands, sacrificed sheep and oxen with as great a multitude of people as possible. But Christ, the Lord and King of all, at the dedication of the temple not made by hands—namely, his own body—offered the living and true sacrifice: not the flesh and blood of oxen and sheep, but his own flesh and blood. For what are we to understand as the dedication of this temple [Col. 1171D], if not his most holy Passion and glorious Resurrection? Then indeed he offered the sacrifice of his flesh and blood amid the great host of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth: first in the sacrament of bread and wine; afterward, in his own visible form, fastened to the wood of the cross, where he shed his blood for the redemption of our salvation.

Then, beyond doubt—then, I say, and from that time onward—all the elders of Israel, all its princes, and all its leaders, indeed all nations, were gathered to him. Exalted by such a dedication, he drew all things to himself (John XII). Hence the Apostle, after saying, “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II), immediately adds: “Therefore God also exalted him [Col. 1172A] and bestowed on him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (ibid.).

Therefore all Israel—all who were worthy to see God or to be guided by God, which is understood by the name Israel—all, without exception, who had been foreordained to eternal life, came together as many members to one head. But this very fact proves the blindness of that carnal Israel. Thus it follows:

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the filling of the house of the Lord with a cloud, and the priests’ inability to stand and minister because of the cloud, signified Jewish blindness.

“And it came to pass, when the priests had come out of the sanctuary, that a cloud filled the house of the Lord; and the priests could not [Col. 1172B] stand and minister because of the cloud. For the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord. Then Solomon said: The Lord said that he would dwell in the cloud.”

The words understood are those spoken to Moses on Mount Sinai: “Now I will come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you and may believe you forever” (Exod. XIX). It is clear, well known, and certain that the priests of the Jews—the Pharisees and the high priests of the murderers—went out from the sanctuary of the Lord; and by that same light through which all nations were illuminated, they, I say, were blinded as though by cloud or smoke through their envy.

In what order, or for what reason, they were blinded is signified here by deeds, and likewise in Isaiah by words and deeds, in this manner. 435 [Col. 1172C] “I saw,” he says, “the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the things beneath him filled the temple. Seraphim stood above it: six wings to the one and six wings to the other; and they cried one to another and said: Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory. And the thresholds of the hinges were shaken by the voice of the one crying, and the house was filled with smoke” (Isa. VI). And afterward: “Go and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; and see the vision, but do not perceive. Blind the heart of this people” (ibid.), etc.

Certainly this Lord seated upon the high throne is this same Solomon, the great king, the wise king, truly the peaceful one [Col. 1172D], who made peace between God and humankind as mediator. This, I say, is he of whom the Evangelist, after citing this prophetic testimony and saying, “Therefore the Jews could not believe, because Isaiah said: He blinded their eyes” (John XII), etc., immediately added: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke of him” (ibid.).

Therefore what is prefigured here by deeds is, as has been said, likewise prefigured in Isaiah both by deeds and words: namely, that when the true Solomon, Christ the truly peaceful King, had been crowned through the Passion of death with glory and honor—which was the true dedication of the temple, that is, of his body—while the seraphim cried, “Holy, holy, holy,” that is, while the apostles, inflamed with the ardor of the Holy Spirit, preached the holy Trinity, and thus the whole [Col. 1173A] earth was filled with his glory, whereas previously he had been known only in Judah (Ps. LXXV), the house of the Lord was filled with smoke and the heart of the Jewish people was blinded.

That God is proclaimed as made man; that Christ, the Son of God, is announced as crucified, dead, and buried—this is smoke to them; and this humility of God causes the proud eyes of men to stumble. “And the priests,” he says, “could not stand and minister because of the cloud.” Since they were thus blinded and turned their eyes away from Christ’s humility as from a cloud, they deservedly could neither stand nor minister. They went out; they were cast out; both their earthly and their heavenly priesthood were taken from them, when temple and city fell together before their eyes, upon their corpses.

[Col. 1173B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That Solomon, praying with both knees bent, “O Lord my God, there is none like thee,” was a type of Jesus Christ, who at the dedication of his temple prayed for all in that Passion by which his body was dedicated.

“Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord, in the sight of the assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven, and said: O Lord God of Israel, there is no God like thee,” etc. As is written below, he had fixed both knees upon the ground and spread his hands toward heaven.

Certainly the true Solomon, King Christ, at the dedication of his temple—in that Passion through which he was dedicated, the Passion of his body—stood before the altar of the Lord, before the eyes of the Father, before the altar of the cross, and prayed. Indeed, he cried out mightily, as [Col. 1173C] the Apostle says: “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him who was able to save him, he was heard because of his reverent submission” (Heb. V).

And indeed, when he already hung upon the cross, there is no doubt that he cried with a loud cry—though that cry of the heart was audible to God alone. But shortly before, he had disclosed in words what he ought to cry, and why he, the same High Priest and saving victim, should ascend the cross. For, “lifting up his eyes to heaven, he said: Holy Father, the hour has come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee” (John XVII), etc.

And though he was a king, he nevertheless had fixed both knees upon the ground. This is exceedingly rare among the Jews, [Col. 1173D] for, stiff with ancient pride, they disdain to bend their knees. But our King and Lord of all, having knelt—indeed, “falling upon his face and being in agony, prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground” (Luke XXII).

We must not pass over this point in the prayer of this Solomon: among other things he says, “Moreover, even the foreigner, who is not of thy people Israel, when he comes from a distant land because of thy name—for they shall hear of thy great name, thy strong hand, and thy outstretched arm everywhere—when he comes and prays in this place, hear thou in heaven, in the firmament of thy dwelling-place, and do all for which the foreigner calls upon thee.”

Certainly, in its inward meaning, these are the words [Col. 1174A] of our Lord in his aforementioned prayer: “Holy Father, keep in thy name those whom thou hast given me. And I pray not for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word” (John XI).

For he knew that, because of his Passion, the Father’s great name, strong hand, and outstretched arm everywhere would be heard; and that upon hearing this, we foreigners, who were not of the people of Israel, would come to him from a distant land and worship him, the holy temple, in confession of his name. For through the mouths of the prophets he had foretold this with such great praises as no tongue, however eloquent, can gather or unfold.

The Prophet heard his prayer from afar in the Spirit when he said: “May the Lord hear thee in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect thee. May he send thee help from the sanctuary, and defend thee from Zion. May he remember all thy sacrifice, and may thy burnt-offering become fat” (Ps. XIX). And in his person, fixed upon the same central purpose, he says: “O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried by day and by night before thee. Let my prayer enter into thy presence; incline thy ear to my supplication” (Ps. LXXXVII), etc.

[Col. 1174C]

## CHAPTER XXIX. That, as Solomon rose when his prayer was completed and blessed the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, so Christ rose from the dead and gave the Holy Spirit amid the great astonishment of the whole world.

“And it came to pass, when Solomon had completed all this prayer and supplication in praying to the Lord, that he rose from before the altar of the Lord—for he had fixed both knees upon the ground and spread his hands toward heaven. Then he stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel with a loud voice,” etc.

Truly, as we believe—and believing, rejoice with joy unspeakable and glorified—our Lord, our King, after he had prayed, after he had completed his prayer and supplication together with the sacrifice of his body and blood, after he had lain in the tomb for three days, rose from the dead. He had fixed both knees upon the ground: for he had sent his soul beneath the earth to hell, and his body into the earthen tomb. He had stretched out toward heaven his hands fixed with nails.

He rose, I say, and stood [Col. 1174D]: he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven. There he sits for himself; there he stands for us at God’s right hand. “I see,” says Stephen, “the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts VII). He sits as the ruler of those who reign; he stands as the helper of those who fight, the advocate and defender of penitents.

Standing there, 436 he blessed the whole assembly of Israel with a loud voice. What Israelite, what member of the Church or believer, does not know these things? On the very day on which he rose, he blessed them, but not yet with a loud voice. He blessed them, I say, by breathing upon them and saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John XX), but with doors shut and in a subdued voice.

But when he stood at the right hand of the power of God, when he ascended into heaven and sat at God’s right hand, then, after the tenth [Col. 1175A] day had passed, he blessed with a loud voice: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting, etc. And when this voice had occurred, the multitude assembled and was bewildered, because each one heard them speaking in his own language” (Acts II). This was the great voice of the one blessing.

By that blessing, those made from earth became heavens proclaiming the glory of God; by that voice it came about that their sound went out into all the earth (Ps. XVIII). “Therefore the king and all Israel with him sacrificed victims before the Lord; and Solomon slaughtered peace-offerings which he offered to the Lord: twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep. Thus the king and the children of Israel dedicated the temple of the Lord.”

There was great [Col. 1175B] slaughter of oxen and sheep, yet it was easily comprehended in numbers. But who among men could count how great a multitude of oxen and sheep our King slaughtered immediately after the blessing just mentioned, and thereafter? Not to mention the thousands of confessors—those who, with the sword of the persecutor present, freely offered themselves by mortifying their own members, in order to present, according to the Apostle, their bodies as “a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, their rational service” (Phil. IV).

Who can count the multitude of those who were struck down by persecutors’ swords like oxen or sheep for this their King? Hence they say weepingly to that same King: “For thy sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted [Col. 1175C] as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. VIII). Truly this Solomon slaughtered both these and those, because Christ and his Spirit were the cause or grace both for those who slaughtered themselves and for those slaughtered by persecutors, so that any one of them might say: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV).

Therefore even to this day the children of Israel, together with Solomon, dedicate that glorious temple by supplying in their flesh what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings [Col. 1175D], while he continually preaches and says through the Psalmist in the prophetic Spirit: “Take victims and enter into his courts” (Ps. LXXV). This is that great and famous festival which this Solomon performs and completes in his own time—the time of glory, the acceptable time—together with all true Israel.

## CHAPTER XXX. Whom this true Solomon sent as seafaring men to Ophir, which is interpreted “weakness”; what that weakness is; what that gold was; and what Queen Sheba was, who meanwhile came to hear his wisdom.

(III Kings, Chapter IX.) “Hiram sent his servants, seafaring men knowledgeable about the sea, together with Solomon’s servants. When they had come to Ophir, they took from there four hundred and twenty talents of gold and brought it to King Solomon.” (III Kings, Chapter X.) “And Queen Sheba also, having heard Solomon’s fame, came in the name of the Lord to test him with riddles.”

Solomon was not content with the things his father had stored up, but sent to Ophir in order that gold taken from there might be brought to him. [Col. 1176A] Ophir is interpreted “weakness.” Yet truly there was much gold in weakness when precious philosophical minds were held among weak and beggarly elements (Gal. IV), and the acuteness of rhetoricians and dialecticians was occupied with vain matters.

But Christ the wise King also stored up these things, not being content with the prophets or with his apostles, the fishermen. For he sent seafaring men knowledgeable about the sea, concerning whom it is written in the Psalm: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing business in great waters, they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. CVI). He sent, I say, his apostles—for example, Paul to Athens—and captured them and brought them in; and behold, such outstanding minds advance in the word of God, expounding the holy Scriptures [Col. 1176B] and contending for the faith in service of the great King. Thus gold was taken from Ophir.

This is how Queen Sheba came to this King: that is, the wealthy and illustrious Church from among the nations. Not that she had previously been a queen—for she had rather been the slave of demons—but because by coming to Christ she became a queen; by believing in Christ she was crowned with a royal diadem and adorned with garments of good works embroidered with gold and with the precious stones of every virtue, as the Holy Spirit says concerning her in the Psalm: “The queen stood at thy right hand in a garment embroidered with gold, surrounded by variety” (Ps. XLIV), etc.

This queen came to Jerusalem with a great retinue: that is, no longer with one people only, namely the Jews, as the Synagogue formerly possessed only the [Col. 1176C] Hebrews, but with the nations and diverse peoples of the whole world. She came, therefore, bringing gifts worthy of Christ—gold and precious gems—carried on camels: that is, on those coming from the Gentile people, who had formerly been twisted by the foulness of vices, bent beneath the burden of evils, and deformed by perversity.

With these gifts, I say, this queen enters to Christ, the peaceful King, bringing with her the gold of faith, precious incense of purity, and the brightness of gems: namely, the distinctions of character and adornments of virtues. “And she spoke all that she had in her heart”: that is, she opened her heart to him and disclosed the hidden things of her conscience in confession and repentance for former sins. These and the remaining [Col. 1176D] matters which follow are already familiar from many treatises of the saints. Let us proceed to the rest.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That the last of Solomon’s memorable works—the great ivory throne, very richly covered with yellow gold—prefigured the judicial majesty of Christ, the most pure man.

“King Solomon also made two hundred shields of pure gold and three hundred smaller shields of tested gold. He also made a great throne of ivory and covered it with very yellow gold. It had six steps, and the top of the throne was rounded at the back. Two arms supported the seat on either side, and two lions stood beside each arm; and twelve lion cubs stood on the six steps, on this side and on that.” [Col. 1177A]

We are prevented by the emphatic and admiring commendation of the present Scripture from supposing that this last of Solomon’s memorable works is insignificant or devoid of mystery, for it immediately follows: “No such work had been made in all kingdoms.” For so many shields and smaller shields signify the same thing as that armor of the mighty of which he says in the Song of Songs: “Thy neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements; a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty” (Cant. IV).

We rightly ask what this final one of his memorable works signifies; and in asking, we look toward the final works 437 of the great King Christ. What is this throne, so great and so wonderful, except the height of majesty on that last day of great [Col. 1177B] and terrible judgment? In a remarkable order, divine Wisdom arranged these symbolic works in that king so that this work—than which he certainly made nothing more memorable—might be a sign or figure of the great judgment, after which our King, having done his works, will rest from them.

A great throne: for we await a great judgment, to meet which, when we come in the cloud, even the powers of heaven will be shaken. A throne of ivory: for the judgment will consist in the purity of justice. Otherwise, unless—as this same Solomon testifies—his belly were ivory, unless Christ, man and God, had been conceived, born, and lived without any heat of lust (for the elephant, from which ivory comes, is said to be a most chaste animal), [Col. 1177C] how or by what right would he judge this world?

Therefore the great ivory throne covered with gold is the judicial majesty of the most pure man, in which the golden justice of divinity will certainly be revealed. It will have six steps, for judgment is carried out in six pronouncements: “For I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger and you did not receive me; I was sick and you did not visit me; I was in prison and you did not come to me” (Matt. XXV).

“Two arms on either side”: that is, two dispositions, that of judgment on one side and that of mercy on the other. “Two lions beside each arm”: that is, the truth of judgment, strong and terrible on both sides. For every wicked person on the left will be condemned, and the righteous person on the right will scarcely be saved (I Pet. IV). The twelve [Col. 1177D] lion cubs standing on the six steps will be the twelve apostles: twelve, that is, all the judges over the fitting recompenses proposed by either arm.

After this work, after this throne of Solomon—that is, of Christ the peaceful King—glory and riches will be in his house forever (Ps. CXI), in such abundance as the present Scripture cannot adequately signify. Yet in trying, it makes some progress. “There was no silver,” it says, “nor was it considered of any value in Solomon’s days.” And afterward: “He made silver as abundant in Jerusalem as stones.”

For after “the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty,” and at his judgment the wicked go [Col. 1178A] indeed into eternal punishment, “but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV), there will no longer be silver; it will be considered of no value in those days of eternity. For “whether prophecies, they shall be made void; whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be destroyed” (I Cor. XIII). Such silver will not ring there, since eloquent persons will not be sent to preach, teach, or prophesy. All will be perfect; all things will be completed. In all things, forever, the purest gold or silver of charity will abound.

## CHAPTER XXXII. That he loved many foreign women, concerning whom the Lord forbade them: “Most certainly,” he says, “they will turn away your hearts so that you follow their gods.”

(III Kings, Chapter XI.) “But King Solomon loved [Col. 1178B] many foreign women: the daughter of Pharaoh, and Moabite, Ammonite, Idumean, Sidonian, and Hittite women. He had about seven hundred wives as queens and three hundred concubines.”

Reproaching him for this, the Wise Man, after saying, “You gathered gold as though it were bronze, and you filled up silver as though it were lead” (Ecclus. XLVII), immediately added: “And you bowed your thighs to women. You had power over your body, and you gave a stain to your glory; you profaned your seed, brought wrath upon your children, and caused folly in your descendants, so that you made the kingdom divided” (ibid.).

But Solomon himself says in the Song of Songs: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number” [Col. 1178C] (Cant. VI). The queens, certainly, of Christ the bridegroom King are souls now united to him through love; the concubines are those who are still subject to him through fear; the maidens are those scarcely initiated in faith and in need of the guardianship of mother Church or the protection of discipline.

Was he, then, so foolish and so mixed folly with wisdom that, knowing the spiritual embraces of Christ and many souls were to be such, he dissipated himself in so many and such great carnal embraces of foreign women? Certainly, if he acted in such a way with this intention, and turned a heavenly mystery into an occasion for lust, he proved the most foolish of all fools. No rational person would deign to seek a divine mystery here, where he would rightly detest plain disgrace.

Thus the truth was rightly fulfilled of the Lord’s statement concerning foreign women: “You shall not go in to them, nor shall they come in to yours. For most certainly they will turn away your hearts so that you follow their gods” (Exod. XXXIV). For so it happened: “When he was old, his heart was corrupted through women so that he followed foreign gods.”

Most great teachers hold differing views concerning his repentance. But for the wise, there remains a most certain example: that they should never presume upon their own steadfastness as long as they live, since this man fell most disastrously, though no one before or after him was wiser (III Kings IV).

# RUPERT’S PROLOGUE TO THE BOOK OF PSALMS

[Col. 1179]

## 438 CHAPTER I. That the sayings of David and Solomon and of the other prophets are testimonies to Christ the Son of God, and that the adversaries of truth are swiftly overwhelmed in them.

We have beheld the splendid deeds of David and Solomon in this fourth age of kings, everywhere seeking the glory of Christ the King. Now at last the sayings of these same prophets and of those who follow them present themselves: they are testimonies to this same Christ, the Son of God. It is as though, after the solid course across the broad land—where the adversaries of truth can run with us, indeed against us—we have reached this deep sea, which must be crossed before the palm of victory can be attained.

But it cannot be crossed except by the wood of Christ, except by the vessel of the cross. [Col. 1179B] For to those who do not believe in Christ and do not receive the spirit of prophecy, the depth of the prophetic Scriptures is altogether impassable. As soon as the enemies of truth set foot in it, they are drowned by the abundance of testimonies to Christ and overwhelmed as by many waves.

For example, they think that in the flesh of Abraham, in the merits of the fathers, and especially in Moses, they possess grounds for rightful glory; but in the prophetic writings they are convicted as uncircumcised: “Thy father was an Amorite, and thy mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI). Therefore, with the same feet by which we ran through the solid field of the Law, we now enter the waters of the prophets, with faith as our companion guiding our steps, lest we be endangered.

## CHAPTER II. That David is the first of the prophets.

Certainly, the prophets deserved to be called prophets because they spoke sublimely about the kingdom of God, the kingdom of Christ, and the Church; and the first or chief among them is the patriarch David. Moses, Joshua, and Samuel, who came before him, openly said nothing in words about the kingdom of God, the punishments of hell, or the judgment by which the righteous are to be saved and the wicked condemned. This was not because they did not know these things, but because people excessively carnal and in love with the earth would not receive them.

But the prophets spoke magnificently about such matters, David being the first. For example: “For in death,” he says, “there is none who remembers thee; but in hell who shall confess thee?” (Ps. VI.) He was the first to sing the kingdom of Christ in intelligible words, and likewise used the words of Christ’s person suffering or rising again.

Therefore he is the first of the prophets, although no one doubts that blessed Job spoke openly before him about the resurrection of the flesh. [Col. 1179D] This subject itself now suitably suggests that we should ask why the Word of the Lord—the Spirit of the Lord—intending to speak of the powers of the age to come, chose for himself a king through whom to speak; indeed, why he wished the one through whom he had determined first to speak concerning the salvation of souls or eternal life to be a king.

For he did not choose him and desire to speak through him because he was a king; rather, because he had chosen him and prepared him for [Col. 1180A] this office, he wished him to be king. Why then did he act thus? Why did the Word of the Lord come in this way? Why did he first wish to be heard from tribunals? Why did he utter his first words from a royal throne?

Certainly because of our hardness, because of our vanity and pride. Let us carefully observe this and knowingly confess that the cause lies, or lay, in ourselves. The entire audience of this world had become deaf to God, and prided itself upon hearing vanity: “every living human being was wholly vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII). Devoted to the play of vanity, the populous wantonness of the flesh disdained to know, and could not hear, the serious concerns of eternal life and impending death.

We see the world now old and decrepit, still for the most part indulging in wantonness, disdaining the mature [Col. 1180B] words of evangelical preaching and finding the hearing of sound discourse burdensome, like a load or mass of sand. Preachers are sometimes publicly ridiculed unless they are cautious, as they are commanded to be when the Lord says: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. VII). How much more, when the world was still fresh and puffed up by the luxury of youth, would it have disdained to hear any person whatever preaching the Word of God?

Therefore the Word of the Lord was foreign to this world, and would have had the wealthy of the age attentive or well-disposed in no other way than by beginning its discourse through the mouth of a wealthy, great, strong-handed, and victorious king, such as David was.

## CHAPTER III. Why the punishments of hell and the kingdom of God could first be announced through a powerful royal person and sung in metrical [Col. 1180C] feet; and what the form of the Psaltery signifies mystically.

Nor was it enough that the powerful person just mentioned should lend authority to the Word of God by his power. Sweetness was needed, so that a mind alien to it might, through bodily senses, be brought into the required goodwill. This also the wondrous craftsman, the Spirit of the Lord eager for human salvation, provided. He wished the boy whom he was preparing as minister of the Word of God to be a harp-player, so that afterward, as he gradually advanced, he might duly make him a Psalmist: that he might prophesy the business of salvation of souls with the sweetness of music mingled in, singing as he prophesied and prophesying as he sang; so that, I say, both the words running in metrical feet and the clear notes of the Psaltery’s [Col. 1180D] strings resounding might gradually reach the mind through the ears and sweetly implant faith, hope, and the love of God.

His musical instrument was shaped like a delta, hollow within, covered externally with the skins of dead animals, and having ten strings that sounded from above. Each of these signifies something mystical for us. The inward hollowness signifies that we must empty ourselves of earthly possessions, as he says: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness remains forever and ever” (Ps. CXI). The hides of dead animals signify that we ourselves must be mortified with our vices and desires, according to the Apostle’s saying: [Col. 1181A] “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Col. III).

The arrangement of ten strings is the observance of the law of the Decalogue. Their sound sent forth from above is the desire for heavenly things alone and the love of God alone, as the same Apostle says: “But our citizenship,” he says, “is in heaven” (Phil. III). The sound of the strings is the utterance of voices; the distinction of the fingers is the plurality of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; and their movement is the activity of all righteous persons.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1181B] How the Psaltery itself, consisting of three sets of fifty psalms, proclaims and sings the threefold jubilee of faith, hope, and love: the first fifty psalms chiefly containing what is to be believed concerning Christ; the second, what is chiefly to be hoped; and the third, those things by which we are urged to love God.

Moreover, the Psaltery itself, with its three sets of fifty psalms, proclaims and sings the threefold jubilee of faith, hope, and love [Col. 1182A]. From these virtues, as we said in the first part of this work, humanity first fell: first losing love, then hope, and lastly faith. Without these none of his children recovers salvation, though they are acquired in the reverse order: first faith, then hope, finally love.

This faith must be possessed in relation to one man; this hope, in relation to one and the same man; this love, toward one and the same man, Christ. The first part, then—fifty psalms recapitulated in seven *periochae* [sections]—proclaims what we ought to believe. The second part, likewise fifty psalms, again returning through seven *periochae*, strengthens hope. The third part also, fifty psalms, seeks to enlarge love by sevenfold recapitulation through blessings [Col. 1182B] and praises.

That this may become clearer, let us not be reluctant to sketch the meaning of the individual psalms. The first begins thus:

# BOOK ONE OF COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS, THE FOURTH BOOK AMONG THE BOOKS OF KINGS

[Col. 1181]

## CHAPTER V. The order of the three sets of fifty psalms, together with the attached mystical significations of their titles.

“Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly.” What does this proclaim to us except that Christ is without sin—without sin, I say, a fact which must be believed and held in faith—because he was conceived and born of the Virgin Mary? Otherwise, unless you agree that this is what is proclaimed, there is no one of whom the saying can rightly be understood, since we all come from Adam, “in whom,” as the Apostle says, “all sinned” (Rom. V).

He was the first who, placed “in the counsel of the ungodly,” “walked” by consenting and departed from God; who “stood in the way of sinners” by carrying out the deed; and who “sat,” proud and wickedly supported, “in the chair of pestilence” by defending his guilt. In him all walked away; all stood wrongly and sat; for all, as has already been said, sinned in him, according to the Apostle’s testimony.

This first psalm, therefore, voices faith in Christ’s Incarnation: namely, that in him there was neither walking away, nor standing, nor sitting, because he was conceived and born of a virgin, and is therefore free from original sin. The remaining words of the psalm, [Col. 1181D] “But his will is in the law of the Lord,” etc., commend the active righteousness of that same Christ. Thus, by believing in him, we are rightly freed both from original sins and from actual sins, so that we may be righteous persons whose way the Lord knows. For “the way of the ungodly shall perish”: that is, the way of those [Col. 1182C] who remain unbelieving by contradicting this blessed man.

The second psalm accordingly proclaims faith in his Passion. “Why have the nations raged,” it says, “and the peoples devised vain things?” And then: “The Lord said to me, You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession.” In accordance with this, he himself says in the Gospel: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). For, lifted up from the earth—that is, fastened to the cross—he asked; indeed, the Passion itself was his asking, a sacrifice for the whole world, through the obedience with which he served the Father who said, “Ask of me.” Hence, “he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5), and he drew all things to himself [Col. 1182D], the Father giving him the nations for an inheritance and the ends of the earth for a possession. For this reason, says the Apostle, “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). Therefore “the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things” to no purpose, joining with kings and rulers—namely, Herod and Pontius Pilate—“against the Lord and against his Christ,” imagining that by this they could break “their bonds” and cast “their yoke” from themselves: that is, the yoke of the Lord and his Christ. On the contrary, through this his kingdom increased [Col. 1183A], which they too shall see “when his wrath has been kindled shortly,” when his judgment comes, which is soon to take place.

The third Psalm preaches faith in his Resurrection. “Lord,” it says, “why are those who afflict me multiplied?” And then: “I slept and was overcome by sleep, and I rose again, because the Lord sustained me.” It may indeed seem that it treats here of the same matter as in the preceding Psalm, for it deals with the Passion and Resurrection; but this is not so. [p. 440] Here it deals with the multiplication of enemies, and more plainly with the Resurrection. “I slept,” it says, “and was overcome by sleep,” namely by dying; “and I rose,” triumphing over death. And because, after his Resurrection, the enemies who had afflicted him and risen against him without cause were to be struck down—so that they would be blinded inwardly [Col. 1183B] and devastated outwardly by a miserable overthrow—it continues: “Arise, Lord; save me, my God, because you have struck all those who oppose me without cause; you have crushed the teeth of sinners.” Nor does it keep silence concerning the height of his Ascension, saying: “But you, Lord, are my defender, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head.” Thus, in the first three Psalms, the prophetic Spirit has borne witness in order to faith in his Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection.

In the fourth Psalm the apostolic Church glories in receiving the Holy Spirit (Acts 2), saying: “When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me.” And then: “[Col. 1183C] The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given gladness in my heart.” For enlargement in tribulation, the light of your countenance, O Lord, and gladness of heart are the gift of the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit. Having received him after Christ’s Resurrection or Ascension, those who formerly had narrow hearts through scanty faith—so that, abandoning the Lord, they all fled (Matt. 26)—were now enlarged and rejoiced in breadth of heart, “because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for his name” (Acts 5). They said: “The light of your countenance, Lord, has been marked upon us,” the implied meaning being: so that we might understand the Scriptures, you opening our understanding. At the same time, that Paraclete, “the Spirit of truth” (John 16), convicts the world in them and says: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity [Col. 1183D] and seek falsehood? Know that the Lord has made his holy one wonderful,” etc. After this it is known that persecution arose against the Church—from wicked enemies, Jews, false Christians, and especially heretics.

On account of these enemies, the fifth Psalm says: “Give ear to my words, Lord; understand my cry.” And then: “For there is no truth in their mouth; their heart is vain. Their throat is an open tomb; they dealt deceitfully with their tongues. Judge them, O God,” etc. The Lord gives ear to these words and understands this cry of the Church persevering until that morning in which it shall stand before him: that is, the day of judgment, when it shall see and say, “For you are not a God who wills iniquity.” On that morning, or day of judgment, who will glory that he has a chaste heart? [Col. 1184A]

It follows, therefore, and says in the sixth Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath.” The fury of the Lord will be when he says to the ungodly and sinners: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). But his wrath, remaining after the day of fury, is death and hell. Hence later: “For in death,” it says, “there is none who remembers you; but in hell who will confess you?” Accordingly this Psalm has the title: “Unto the end: a Psalm of David, for the eighth.” Its sense is: this Psalm is to be attributed to David, that is, to the penitent Church tending “unto the end,” that is, toward Christ [Col. 1184B], and it prays “for the eighth,” namely for eternal rest, which is called the eighth because it is to come after the course of this life, which is conducted through seven days.

In the seventh Psalm there is a return to the head, that is, to the beginning of our faith: to Christ’s Passion, as he prays in that same Passion through which we believe that we are saved. “Lord my God,” it says, “in you I have hoped,” etc. For the Prophet’s purpose in this Psalm is to introduce Christ according to his human nature, speaking and praying, with the Word united to him, that he may be delivered, not conformed to the minds of his enemies, and may be raised from death; and then to show, under a certain concession, the condemnation of the wicked and the glory of the righteous that are to arise from his Resurrection, and also the possibility of pardon for these evildoers, if they should repent [Col. 1184C].

The eighth Psalm is clearer than light in glorifying with wonder the Resurrection and exaltation of this same Christ. “Lord,” it says, “our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your magnificence has been lifted up above the heavens.” And then: “What is man, that you remember him, or the Son of Man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet.” Clearly, it says, man is something worthy inwardly, although outwardly he appears base and lowly beyond other animals; and this is evident from the fact “that you remember him” [Col. 1181D]. And whatever may be said of other human beings, he who was not the son of men but of a human being—that is, of the Virgin—was himself something supremely great. This is clear from the words, “because you visit him.” And it explains in what respect “you visit him”: “You made him a little lower than the angels,” etc.

It indicates the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, given through Christ’s exaltation, in this manner: “For I shall behold the heavens, the works of your fingers; the moon and the stars, which you founded.” These heavens are the holy Apostles, because from earthly persons they were made heavenly through the Holy Spirit. Although he is called, in the singular, the finger of God—as there: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke 11)—yet “the works of your fingers” is said here in the plural because that same Spirit is sevenfold and the divisions of his graces are many. The moon is the universal Church; the stars are the individual churches, “which you founded,” it says—that is, to each of which you gave increase. Because of these things, it says, your name, formerly known only in Judaea, is now “wonderful in all the earth.” This Psalm also bears the title: “For the wine-presses,” because, just as wine and a grape are contained in a wine-press, so in the Church are contained good and evil persons. [Col. 1185A]

The ninth is inscribed thus: “Unto the end, for the hidden things of the Son: a Psalm of David.” Its sense is: this Psalm is attributed to “David,” that is, to the perfect Church tending “unto the end,” that is, toward Christ, so as to be conformed to him, “for the hidden things of the Son,” that is, in consideration of the hidden judgments belonging to the Son, as it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). He is called the Son by antonomasia, as he himself testifies: “If the Son shall set you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8). The Prophet’s purpose in this Psalm is to introduce the perfect Church giving thanks to God in every way for his hidden judgments, and thereby instructing its lesser members.

At Christ’s first coming, some thought that he was merely human; but a few, that is, the elect, understood him to be both God and man. This happened by God’s hidden judgment: namely, that it should be revealed to some and concealed from others. Concerning the second coming, some who are unsound in their thinking doubt; but the faithful await it as certain. This likewise happens through God’s just judgment. Yet all alike are ignorant on what day or at what hour it shall occur. Why some are saved and others rejected, though all descend from one parent, happens through God’s hidden judgment, likewise unknown to all. That in the present age the wicked are exalted and the good are depressed also happens by God’s hidden and just judgment—hidden indeed to the wicked, but not to the good [p. 441] [Col. 1185C]. Moreover, that near the end of the age the son of perdition will so greatly exalt himself above the Church and afflict it with such bitter persecution occurs by God’s hidden judgment. In all these matters the nations, misunderstanding them, err and blaspheme God. But the perfect Church does not merely refrain from blaspheming God; rather, in all things it praises him attentively with all its strength, saying:

“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart; I will recount all your wonders. I shall be glad and rejoice [Col. 1185D] in you,” etc.

Therefore, after the preceding two Psalms, containing a recapitulation of faith in Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, which is necessary for eternal salvation, this Psalm rightly follows: in it the holy Church marvels, confessing the hidden judgments of that same Son, in accordance with the Apostle’s meaning when he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). For he said this concerning the blindness which “has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the nations should enter” (ibid.). That blindness, of course, happened immediately by a hidden judgment when Christ, according to the preceding Psalm, was crowned with glory and honour.

The tenth Psalm is chiefly directed against heretics [Col. 1186A], who meanwhile lay snares for the Church’s shrewd simplicity. Since they are sinners, since the fire of concupiscence and the sulphur of evil works have been the portion of their cup and have intoxicated them, the Lord rains snares upon them, so that through Holy Scripture they may be ensnared in many ways—that is, may understand wrongly and interpret wrongly. To such persons it says: “I trust in the Lord. How do you say to my soul: ‘Flee to the mountain,’” that is, to the eminence of our opinions, as a sparrow flies upward?

In the eleventh Psalm, the Church which awaited Christ’s coming prayed for that which the Church now present, though knowing it to have been fulfilled, nevertheless still prays for: that the work of salvation which he accomplished universally may be perfected in individual persons [Col. 1186B]. For it says: “Save me, Lord, for the holy one has failed,” namely Adam, created innocent and pure by you, in whose fall the whole human race fell. By saying this, we confess that all sinned in Adam and drew original sin from him. It continues concerning the multitude of actual sinners: “For truths have been diminished among the children of men; each has spoken vain things to his neighbour,” etc. Here we understand the Apostle’s meaning: “As through the offence of one there came condemnation upon all human beings, so through the righteousness of one there came justification of life upon all human beings” (Rom. 5). Concerning this one, indeed, the Psalm then speaks: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I shall arise, says the Lord; I shall set him in salvation; I shall act confidently [Col. 1186C] in him.” And because through him we are justified and regenerated unto life: “You, Lord,” it says, “will preserve us and keep us from this generation”—from the evil generation, the old generation of Adam.

The twelfth Psalm more earnestly asks this same Christ both to preserve us in the present life free from every sin and, after the end of this life, to grant that we may rejoice in himself for ever, saying: “How long, Lord, will you forget me?”

The thirteenth Psalm supplies us with words against every fool who says in his heart—whether he is a Jew or a heretic—“There is no God,” the implied meaning being: this man Jesus Christ is not God. For it deals with the perfidy of the Jews, because he whom their holy fathers—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—had ardently desired might be given to them, these men, seeing him present in the flesh, not only rejected his words and deeds but even handed him over to death. It also deals with their temporal and particular destruction, their future eternal condemnation, and the glorious and wondrous reward of the saints [Col. 1186D].

In the fourteenth Psalm, saying, “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?” etc., the Head intends to show definitively which persons shall attain glory under the name of Jacob or Israel. Since therefore, at the end of the preceding Psalm, he had said, “When the Lord has turned away the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad,” lest anyone vainly suppose that faith alone is sufficient for this blessedness, he intends definitively to show which persons, holding the meaning of these names, will attain glory. He puts this interrogatively, not because he has doubt in this matter, but in order to make his hearers certain of it. [Col. 1187A]

Beginning with the fifteenth Psalm, there is a third *perioche*, that is, a recapitulation of the foundation most necessary to faith: the mystery of Christ’s Passion. It is inscribed: “An inscription of a title, for David himself.” One must understand that in this Psalm the same thing is to be understood, although expressed in different and more ample words, which is reported to have been written in the title of the cross. “Preserve me, Lord,” it says, “for I have hoped in you.” And then: “You are the one who will restore my inheritance to me,” that is, you alone possess true being, and you will restore my inheritance to that true being which the fault of the first parent lost. And a little later: “Therefore my heart has been enlarged and my tongue has rejoiced; moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor give your holy one to see corruption.” Clearly, in these words he deals, in the Passion, with the Resurrection and eternal reward; in order to deserve to attain all of these, he prays to God the Father in the form of a servant. [Col. 1187B]

The sixteenth, inscribed “A prayer for David himself,” treats of the same matter. “Hear, Lord,” it says, “my righteousness; attend to my supplication,” etc. For in this Psalm the Head intends to pray to God the Father for himself and his own, that they may not fail. It also deals with persecution, the temporal and eternal condemnation of enemies, and the future glorious and full satisfaction together with his own. For he says to the Father, dying in obedience: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways.” And then: “My enemies have surrounded my soul; they have shut up their fat.” “Their fat,” I say—that is, they have shut up their heart, made gross, against the truth. “Their mouth has spoken pride.” “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God” (Matt. 27), and: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19), etc. These things concern his persecution.

But concerning the condemnation of his enemies: “Arise, Lord; anticipate him”—namely, the Jewish people—by taking from them their place and nation. “And cast him down” [Col. 1187D], giving him over to death, though he desires to hold me in death. But do not defer this far into the future. And what then? “Lord, divide them from the few upon earth in their life.” This means: while they are still living in the flesh, let them perish from the earth; let them be divided from the few, separated from the righteous. One should know that a little before the destruction of Jerusalem, certain Jews who had converted to the faith were warned by the Holy Spirit to leave the city and go into Agrippa’s kingdom, lest they perish with the impious.

Finally, concerning the glorious satisfaction of himself and his own, he says: “But I shall appear before your countenance in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” When he says, “I shall be satisfied,” he does not say this as though he lacked anything in himself, but with regard to his members, whose satisfaction will at last be complete in glory [Col. 1188A] “when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15), as the Apostle says: “When Christ, our life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3).

The seventeenth likewise treats of his death: “I shall love you, Lord, my strength.” Nor does it treat only of his death, but also of his Resurrection; of what benefit [p. 442] followed from it; through whom and in what manner this occurred; of the temporal and eternal recompense of the righteous; of the external and internal condemnation of the Jews; and, finally, of the obedience and salvation of the nations. Its title is: “Unto the end, for David, servant of the Lord, who spoke the words of this song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul.” David himself is Christ, truly strong of hand, truly desirable. He is the servant of the Lord, for he obeyed God the Father as a servant according to the form of a servant (Phil. 2). To him, as tending “unto the end,” that is, toward every perfection, are the words of this song to be attributed. But what is meant by “on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of his enemies and from the hand of Saul,” except in consideration of that day on which he rose from the dead, never again to die? (Rom. 6). For in raising him, the Lord delivered him from the power of his enemies, namely Jews and Gentiles, and from the power of death, which is rightly understood by Saul. For just as the people sought Saul as king against the Lord’s will, so Adam and Eve desired death against the Lord’s will. [Col. 1188B]

[Col. 1188C] Therefore, after three Psalms commending his Passion and Resurrection, which are the sum of our salvation and in which the foundation of faith consists, the immediately following eighteenth Psalm declares what then took place. “The heavens,” it says, “declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands.” For these heavens are the Apostles, who, though formerly earthly and weak, became such after his Passion, on receiving the Holy Spirit, that they are rightly called “heavens” and rightly called “the firmament.” “There are no speeches,” it says, “nor words, whose voices are not heard.” For on that day the Holy Spirit worked the miracle that every kind of language came forth in their mouths (Acts 2). The proclamation of such heavens did not remain in only one region. Rather: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” [Col. 1188D]

And what glory of God did these heavens proclaim? “He has set his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber. He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit even to its summit; and there is none who hides from his heat.” Thereupon, praising the law of Christ—the law of faith written by the finger of God, “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Cor. 3)—it says: “The law of the Lord is spotless, converting souls,” etc.

From that time, while he sits at the right hand of God and intercedes for us, in the nineteenth Psalm we say with the Prophet, we say with the ancient saints, and we do not cease to say until the end of the age: “May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.” We say this, not because we know it to be necessary, but from excessive longing. For neither do we doubt, nor did the Prophet doubt when he spoke these words, that he who endured tribulation for us would be heard. “May he remember,” it says, “every sacrifice of yours, and may your whole burnt offering be made fat.” It says “every sacrifice” because each of his sufferings was an individual sacrifice; but the whole burnt offering was his death itself. In the Law, a sacrifice was that of which part was burned and part reserved for the priests; a whole burnt offering was that which was entirely burned. Certainly, from this Psalm the fourth *perioche* has now begun. For it manifestly treats of the supreme matter of faith: his Passion. The Prophet, foreseeing it, said, not in doubt, as has already been stated, but in benevolent desire: “Lord, save the king.” And we say it in faith, because the Lord truly saved the king, namely by hastening his Resurrection. [Col. 1189A–B]

The twentieth Psalm immediately confirms this: “Lord,” it says, “the king shall rejoice in your strength.” “In your strength,” I say, in that strength by which he is God, he shall stand victorious. And then: “He asked life of you, and you gave it to him.” “Life,” I say—that is, resurrection—“he asked, and you gave him length of days for age and age of age.” For “having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). [Col. 1189B]

Far more fully and manifestly, the twenty-first Psalm sings of the same thing—namely, his Passion and Resurrection. The Lamb of God himself, who opens the seven seals of the great book (Rev. 5), revealed its meaning to us, not merely in some manner but with a living voice. For, about to yield up his spirit, he cried aloud: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27). Its title is: “Unto the end, for the morning taking-up: a Psalm of David.” Its sense is: this Psalm is to be attributed to Christ, the true David, tending toward victory, which is the end of the course of his obedience, “for the morning taking-up,” that is, for the Resurrection, which occurred “very early, while it was still dark” (John 20). This is said by comparison with the sun: just as the sun gradually gathers strength as it rises and drives away darkness, so Christ, in rising, gradually enlightened the minds of unbelievers. In his same Passion he instituted for us two sacraments: the washing of regeneration, when, after his side was opened, he poured out blood and water (John 19); and the mystery of his body and blood, when, holding bread and wine, he said: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26). [Col. 1189C–D]

Over these things the perfect Church immediately rejoices in the twenty-second Psalm and says: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture.” For, as though you were asking, “In whose place of pasture?” it immediately adds: “He has led me over the water of refreshment; he has converted my soul.” And then: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me.” What is the water of refreshment except saving baptism? “Over this water of baptism,” which is the foundation of good works, “the Lord,” says the Church, “has led me,” namely with the milk of preaching; and then—for this is the proper order of reading—“he has placed me in a place of pasture,” that is, he has caused me to devote myself to the Scriptures. There “he shepherds me,” namely lest I understand wrongly, “and I shall lack nothing” necessary to understanding. And what is the table which “you have prepared,” it says, “before me against those who afflict me,” except your body and your blood, whose sacrament you have set before my understanding under other forms, lest enemies prevail against me?

And because a twofold gift of the Holy Spirit was given after these things: “You have anointed my head with oil,” it says, “and my cup that intoxicates me—how excellent it is!” For, on the first bestowal of the Holy Spirit’s gift, the Apostles were gently anointed as with oil when he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20). But on the second they were, as it were, intoxicated with a second cup, made strong and eloquent, so that it was said: “These men are full of new wine” (Acts 2). [Col. 1190A–B]

By these sacraments that land and world were prepared for the Lord, of which the twenty-third Psalm immediately begins: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” For this land and this world—the land being the Church—are so called for a double reason: land because of stability and fruitfulness, world because of perfection. And because the visible sacraments mentioned above are not by themselves sufficient for anyone to dwell in the eternal Church, it more effectively indicates this by a question: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and clean in heart.” [Col. 1190B–C]

The twenty-fourth Psalm, appropriately in sequence—“A Psalm of David”—is the prayer of the penitent Church. “To you, [p. 443] Lord,” it says, “I have lifted up my soul; my God, I trust in you; I shall not be put to shame,” etc. For it prays to the Lord to make it persevere in good, at one time setting forth God’s grace and at another its own merit; for example: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” [Col. 1190C]

In the twenty-fifth Psalm the same Church prays to the Lord that through the Lord’s same mercy and truth it may at last be separated from the impious: “Judge me, Lord,” it says, “for I have walked in my innocence.” And so that it may deservedly be separated from the impious in the future, it separates itself in the present and says: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, nor shall I enter with those who work iniquity,” etc. [Col. 1190D]

In the twenty-sixth Psalm the same perfect Church intends to show the manner of the blessing it promised at the end of the preceding Psalm: “I shall bless you,” saying, “in the churches.” “The Lord is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear?” “Of whom” among visible or invisible enemies “shall I be afraid, when evildoers draw near against me to eat my flesh?” This saying is an exaggeration of the crime, as where it is said: “It is roasted now; turn it, and eat.” It also shows by its own example that nothing but one thing ought to be sought: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord,” etc.

Its title is: “A Psalm of David, before he was anointed.” Its sense is: this work is attributed to David, that is, to the perfect Church giving thanks for what it has received before it comes to perfect anointing. This sends us to the history of David, still a boy in his father’s house at Bethlehem, anointed by Samuel to be future king, the Holy Spirit thus foreshadowing him (1 Sam. 16). Then he was anointed at Hebron and reigned only over the tribe of Judah, after Saul’s death (2 Sam. 2). Afterwards he was anointed a third time, when he received the province of the entire Israelite people (2 Sam. 5). These anointings signify something mystical for us. For just as David was anointed three times, so every faithful person ought to partake of a threefold anointing: first in baptism, where they are renewed by the grace of the Holy Spirit; second, when through the bishop’s laying on of hands they are increased by the gifts of the same Holy Spirit; third, on the day of judgment, when they attain the perfect sweetness of that same spiritual grace. One must not believe that David composed this Psalm before he was anointed in his father’s house; but whether he composed it immediately after that anointing or after the second is uncertain. [Col. 1191A–B]

Then, beginning with the twenty-seventh Psalm, there is now a fifth *perioche*, when there is a return to the Head, to the sum of faith which we believe and know consists in Christ’s Passion and Resurrection. “To you, Lord, I shall cry, my God; do not be silent toward me,” etc. These are the words of our Head praying for his Resurrection, that he may not be like those descending into the pit, while at the same time inserting, under a concession, the condemnation of his enemies, when he says: “Give them according to their works and according to the wickedness of their devices,” etc. For what he says—“The Lord is my helper and my protector; in him my heart has hoped, and I was helped, and my flesh flourished again”—is a most certain declaration of the Resurrection after his prayer. In it his flesh flourished again: flesh which, though it had flowered from the root of Jesse, seemed to have been stripped of its flower beneath lashes and reproaches. [Col. 1191C–D]

When this cry of his has been heard, the Prophet suddenly cries out in the following Psalm, the twenty-eighth: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams,” etc. By saying this, he generally exhorts all the faithful, by imitating him, to offer themselves to God. He admonishes the perfect, like rams, to persevere and increase; and others, like the sons of rams, to advance quickly by good works to the offering of the same sacrifice. It is inscribed: “A Psalm of David at the completion of the tabernacle.” It sends us to the history: just as David, after receiving the ark taken away from the Philistines, established a tabernacle for the Lord in which he might be worshipped and sacrifices offered (2 Sam. 6), so every faithful person, after receiving the Catholic faith, ought to prepare himself as a tabernacle of sanctification in which to offer God the sacrifice of praise—namely faith, hope, and love. Here, indeed, the Prophet’s cry interrupts the words which he had begun to utter in the preceding Psalm in Christ’s person. [Col. 1192A]

But in the next Psalm, the twenty-ninth, he returns to the same subject or meaning and proceeds thus: “I shall exalt you, Lord, because you have received me and have not made my enemies rejoice over me,” etc. For the Head himself treats of his work and eternal reward. He also exhorts the faithful, by singing to the Lord and confessing after his example, to deserve to attain the same joy. It is entitled: “A Psalm of a song at the dedication of David’s house.” This title sends us to history. For just as David built the Lord’s temple with his own expenditure and equipment, and afterwards dedicated it with joy and solemn words in praise of the Lord, so Christ’s body, built without sin according to its unique birth, was dedicated through the Resurrection in the eternal glory of impassibility and immortality. These are the words of the changed and now undying human being, of the dedicated house: “Lord my God, I cried to you, and you healed me.” Again: “Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty.” And then: “You have torn my sackcloth and clothed me with gladness,” etc. [Col. 1192B]

The following thirtieth Psalm expounds the same subject more fully and extensively: “In you, Lord, I have hoped; I shall not be confounded for ever.” That these are his words he himself made heard and known to the whole world when he cried with a loud voice: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23). Therefore he is the one who, according to the form of a servant, hoped in God that he might not be confounded for ever, as his enemies wished to confound him, according to their estimation. “I have become,” he says, “like a ruined vessel, because I have heard the reproach of many”—for example, those saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God, save yourself” (Matt. 27).

This Psalm bears the title: “Unto the end: a Psalm of David, for ecstasy.” “For ecstasy,” it says: that is, for contemplation of Christ’s most profound understanding concerning the restoration of the human race, which he ordained through his death and Resurrection—an understanding surpassing every understanding of created beings. After he had said, “Into your hands I commend my spirit,” “he yielded up his spirit; one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water flowed out” (John 19). By that outpouring he cleansed from sins all the elect from the origin of the world and instituted baptism for us for the remission of sins. [Col. 1192C–D]

The thirty-first Psalm follows, declaring blessed all whom that blood and water touch through faith: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.” The title of this Psalm is: “Understanding for David.” Its sense is: understanding is to be attributed to one such as he who speaks in this Psalm, and such a person rightly ought to be called understanding. Such indeed was he, and he wished us to be such, when the Apostle wrote to the Romans: “But to the one who does not work, yet believes in him who justifies the impious, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace, as David also declares the blessedness of the human being to whom God reckons righteousness without works. [p. 444] Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven” (Rom. 4), etc. These are the righteous: formerly impious, but now justified by this faith. To them this Psalm says in conclusion: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; and glory, all you upright in heart.” [Col. 1193A]

Likewise the Psalm following it, that is, Psalm XXXII, says: “Rejoice in the Lord, O righteous; praise befits the upright” [Col. 1193B]. The first, or chief, among these righteous and upright persons, to whom praise is fitting and in whose mouth praise is lovely, were the apostles. Of them this psalm says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power.” “By the word of the Lord,” I mean, by the Son of God, by the presence of the Son of God, “these heavens were established, and all their power” was established “by the spirit of his mouth,” the spirit of that same Son, who is aptly called the mouth of the Lord, because through him God the Father spoke, as the prophet says: “For the mouth of the Lord has spoken” (Isa. I). These were the first to rejoice most greatly, truly blessed because their iniquities were forgiven and their sins covered [Col. 1193C], and their sorrow was turned into joy, according to the promise of him who said: “But I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John XVI). They were therefore established so that through them the Lord might accomplish what follows: “Gathering the waters of the sea as into a wineskin,” that is, bitter peoples into the unity of faith, and the rest to the end of the psalm.

The title of the following psalm, that is, the thirty-third, is: “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and he departed.” According to the history, David changed his countenance, pretending to be mad before Achish king of Gath, to whom he had fled in fear of Saul’s jealousy (I Sam. XXI). But when this man too envied his power, David feared him [Col. 1193D] and, as has been said, changed his countenance before him; thus dismissed, he departed. It should be known, however, that Achish was the personal name of the king to whom David fled; he was also called Abimelech, which was the common name of all the kings of that land, as Pharaoh was among the Egyptians and Caesar among the Romans. All this intimates something mystical to us.

For David’s changing his countenance before Achish signifies that Christ transformed the rite of the old sacrifice into a new one before the Jews. Achish means “What is this?” and signifies ignorance; the Jews are aptly understood by him, since darkness and ignorance flourished greatly among them. When Christ, accused by the Pharisees, chief priests, and scribes, was sought for death among those standing at the gate of the city [Col. 1194A], he “beat the drum”: that is, before the apostles already established in faith—the entrance into the heavenly Jerusalem—he brought forth a sweet sound from the drum, namely, the teaching that his flesh was to be put to death.

Or, if we say “before Abimelech,” the meaning remains the same. Abimelech means “the kingdom of my father”; by him likewise the Jews are denoted, among whom David reigned, who according to the flesh was called Christ’s father, because Christ deigned to be born from his lineage. Hence we read in the Gospel that the blind man said: “Son of David, have mercy on me” (Matt. XV). That Abimelech dismissed David and David departed signifies Christ’s passage to the Gentiles through the apostles, when the Jews dismissed him, after he preached to them the new sacrifice, saying: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood [Col. 1194B], you shall not have life in yourselves.” On hearing this, many, even among his disciples, withdrew, saying: “This saying is hard; and who can hear it?” (John VI.)

Therefore these are the voices of the righteous rejoicing in the preceding psalm—that is, of the apostles, whose mouths are full of the new sacrifice, the flesh and blood of the New Testament: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.” And then: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet; blessed is the man who hopes in him.” “Taste”: receive the sacrifice itself, and then “see,” then understand—namely, through experience of the thing itself—“that the Lord is sweet,” because the Lord is delightful food. And let all hope this, because “blessed is the man who [Col. 1194C] hopes in him.”

Psalm XXXIV follows with these words: “Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; overcome those who attack me.” Christ our head says this and the rest of the psalm concerning the condemnation of the Jews—not by praying for it, but by allowing it through divine judgment. And this psalm rightly follows in order upon those which preceded it. For when, with the Lord Jesus glorified, the righteous rejoiced after being justified by faith in his blood, and set before the Gentiles the rite of the new sacrifice entrusted to them, immediately the Jews, who harmed and attacked Christ, were judged and overcome: their temple was destroyed and their land lost. In anger concerning this land, as this psalm says, they devised deceitful words, saying: “Perhaps the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” [Col. 1194D] (John XI). Indeed, even to the present day, speaking deceitful things in anger over that same land, they are driven by excessive hatred, so that they cannot endure even to hear Christ’s name; though they deny it, they do not fail to know that they lost their land because of his blood.

Thus this psalm rightly follows: “Judge, O Lord,” it says, “those who harm me; overcome those who attack me; take hold of weapons and shield”—namely, those of the Roman emperors Titus and Vespasian—“and rise to help me,” so that they may be led away captive among all nations, lest, if place, nation, and beautiful temple remained to them, they should become a greater stumbling-block to evangelical faith.

Likewise this thirty-fifth psalm rightly follows: “The unjust man has said, that he may sin within himself; there is no fear of God before his eyes” [Col. 1195A]. That is, as though you were asking why that people was thus judged and overcome, Justice itself answers you in this psalm: because he is unjust; because he said it, premeditated it, knowingly resolved “to sin within himself.” Therefore he has no excuse for his sin (John XV), since he did not sin in ignorance but acted deceitfully before the sight of God, whose fear he cast away from his own eyes, in this way: “that his iniquity may be found unto hatred,” etc.

But toward those who confess their sins and do penance, he says: “O Lord, your mercy is in heaven, and your truth unto the clouds,” etc. There is no reason for a Christian to envy the unhappy Jews, captive in mind and body and, through God’s judging and overcoming them, scattered among all nations. Yet there are many ungodly persons, so rich and powerful that some weak person may be tempted to envy them [Col. 1195B].

Psalm XXXVI therefore follows, saying: “Do not envy evildoers, nor be jealous of those who commit iniquity.” Why? “For they shall quickly wither like grass, and shall soon fall like the green plants of the herbs.” Its inscription is: “A Psalm to David,” that is, this work is to be attributed to Christ, the true David, who in this psalm gives instruction to the faithful. By saying this and the rest of the psalm, he dissuades them from resenting the prosperity of the wicked or imitating their iniquity, since it is transient and exceedingly brief; instead, they should hope in the Lord, doing what is right. Through these things they will be protected in the present and crowned with God in the future [Col. 1195C].

The title of Psalm XXXVII is: “A Psalm of David, for the remembrance of the Sabbath.” Its meaning is: this work is attributed to David, that is, to Christ, and was made for remembrance of eternal rest, which is signified [445] by the Sabbath. For Sabbath means “rest.” In this psalm our head prays for those penitents who are to come, whether before baptism or after it, speaking with a certain affection in his own person concerning them. He also shows many reasons why prayer should be made for them: because they have sinned gravely and are deeply distressed by it; because he suffered for them; and because they are ready to become imitators of his Passion. “O Lord,” he says, “do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath. For your arrows have been fixed in me,” etc. By “me” and “to me” he means “my people” and “to my people.” For he himself is the head of the body, while all the elect are its members. In this psalm he prays for penitents, sympathizing with our weaknesses and grieving with those who are ignorant and err, since he was tempted in all things according to our likeness, yet without sin (Heb. IV) [Col. 1195D].
