In the following psalm, that is, the thirty-eighth, he commends his own example to the righteous: “I said: I will guard my ways, lest I sin with my tongue. I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me. I became mute and was humbled, and I kept silence even from good things,” etc. This example too is to be imitated by the righteous. For according to another prophet: “The work of righteousness is silence” (Isa. XXXII). If one must sometimes keep silence even from good things and edifying conversation for the sake of silence, how much more ought one to keep silence from evil things for fear of punishment! Yet lest we remain silent too stubbornly and indiscreetly, he immediately adds: “And my sorrow was renewed,” etc. It is as if he said: As formerly I sinned by speaking too much, so now I do so by keeping silence too much.

Thus the title is fitting: “Unto the end, for Idithun, a song of David.” Idithun means “one who leaps over.” This title signifies that David’s song is sung to those who have leapt from vices to virtues, even to moderation of speech; from temporal things unto that end beyond which one cannot leap—unto eternity, which is God. Whoever has attained it will seek nothing further [Col. 1196A].

Now in the sixth recapitulation, that is, in Psalm XXXIX, Christ says according to the form of a servant: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he inclined unto me.” Here the Prophet returns to the beginning of our faith, that is, to Christ’s Passion; this is particularly indicated by the verse: “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire, but you perfected ears for me. At the head of the book it is written of me: I have willed to do your will, O my God.” “You did not desire,” he says, “the sacrifice and offering” which the law commanded to be offered; “but you perfected ears for me,” that is, understanding, so that I alone might understand why you did not desire those things and what you did desire. “Then I said: Behold, I come.” Behold, I have been incarnate, ready to do your will. “As it is written at the head of the book,” that is, as it was ordained in your wisdom [Col. 1196C], personally united to me.

Likewise in the following psalm, that is, Psalm XL, he speaks of the humility of that same Passion: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man; in the evil day the Lord shall deliver him.” For who else says here: “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has greatly lifted up treachery against me. But you, O Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I shall repay them”? He himself leaves no room for doubt. Having said, at the very point of his Passion, “I know whom I have chosen” (John XIII), he immediately added: “But that the Scripture may be fulfilled: He who eats bread with me shall lift up his heel against me” (ibid.).

He therefore, “who though he was rich became needy and poor for our sake” (II Cor. VIII), says at the end of the preceding psalm: “But I am needy and poor; the Lord is concerned for me”; and here, at the beginning of the following one: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor man,” etc. Thus he shows both the condemnation and misery of those who are offended by him, judging him merely needy and poor—that is, merely human—and the blessedness of those who are not offended by him, believing him to be true man and true God [Col. 1196D].

In Psalm XLI the sons of Korah say: “As the deer longs for fountains of waters, so my soul longs for you, O God.” For its title reads: “Unto the end, understanding for the sons of Korah” [Col. 1197A]. The meaning is: understanding is to be ascribed to the following words spoken by the sons of Korah, that is, by imitators of our crucified Lord Jesus Christ, who through this very imitation press on to the end—that is, to the consummate good, beyond which nothing is to be desired. Korah means “baldness,” and is used for the very place where the Lord was crucified, called in Hebrew Golgotha, but in Latin Calvary (John XIX). Yet, because of the same interpretation, Korah was used more suitably than the name of the place itself, since Korah was also a person and had many sons.

Therefore the sons of Korah—that is, the aforesaid needy and poor imitators of the Crucified, who understand, beyond the poverty of his humanity, the riches of his divinity—say, all together and each individually: “As the deer,” having consumed a serpent, “longs” with the utmost swiftness “to come to fountains of waters,” being greatly thirsty, so with such desire and such haste does “my soul,” having drunk the devil’s poison through the many temptations of the flesh, burn to come “to you” to drink and to share in you; that it may thus be renewed, made conformable to you, who are the fountain of cold and unceasing water, in whom is all fullness of delight [Col. 1197B]. It is fitting that one who says this should first be refreshed at the fountain of baptism. For he says in what follows in the same psalm: “Therefore I shall remember you from the land of Jordan,” that is, because through baptism I have been made the land of Jordan, watered and fruitful, whereas I was formerly dry and barren.

In Psalm XLII any faithful soul says: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation,” etc. Above, those martyrs who suffered tribulations from outsiders spoke, setting forth their longing. Here, however, all the faithful pray generally—both martyrs and confessors—who are mingled in the threshing-floor with the chaff: that is, who suffer reproaches and tribulations from false Christians within the Church, and desire “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). They ask that in the future they may be separated from the mass of unbelievers with whom they are here mingled in the threshing-floor of the Church, as grain from chaff, and that here they may quickly be delivered from them [Col. 1197C].

The Apostle uses a verse of Psalm XLIII thus: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or peril, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are put to death all the day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. VIII). Therefore these words, “O God, we have heard with our ears; our fathers have declared to us the work which you performed in their days, in days of old,” are the words of perfected martyrs, or of those wondering why God does not swiftly act in their days as he acted in the days of the ancient fathers. “Your hand,” they say, “destroyed the nations, and you planted them; you afflicted peoples, and expelled them.” The dying martyrs desired precisely this: that the same hand of the Lord might swiftly scatter the nations—that is, the ungodly who lived as Gentiles—and plant the faithful, so that Christian faith might flourish peacefully throughout all lands.

But now, they say, “You have sold your people without price [Col. 1198A], and there was no multitude in exchange for them.” That is to say: you permitted your own [446] people also to be killed, and acquired no one from among them. To be sure, if you did acquire some, it was still not done by a worthy exchange, because “there was no multitude in exchange for them”: where a thousand were killed, scarcely two, or one, were converted. But did they therefore groan in vain? Did they desire uselessly? Certainly not. For when the Lord, who seemed to sleep, arose, the ungodly Gentiles were scattered with their idols, and multitudes of believers, from the planting of the martyrs, filled the world.

Thus this psalm fittingly bears the title: “Unto the end, for the sons of Korah, for understanding.” The meaning is: these words are set before the sons of Korah, tending “unto the end”—that is, imitators of the Crucified tending toward the consummate good. They are set before them, I say, “for understanding,” so that they may understand what is signified by God’s having dealt so graciously with the ancient fathers, while allowing these people, on the contrary, to suffer tribulation and every misery [Col. 1198B].

In Psalm XLIV God the Father most sweetly proclaims: “My heart has uttered a good word; I declare my works to the king.” This is now the seventh recapitulation of our faith, loftier than the others. It is the same thing that the Evangelist John, protesting against the unbelief of heretics who said that Christ took his beginning from Mary, declares: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). And then: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory” (ibid.).

The same Father, I say, speaks: “My heart has uttered a good word,” that is, my hidden essence brought forth a good Word; I essentially begot from myself the Son, God from God, good from good—good, I say, just as I am good, because “none is good but one, God” (Mark X). Concerning the incarnation of this Word, of which the Evangelist also says, “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us,” the prophetic spirit immediately says with great feeling: “You are beautiful in form above the sons of men; grace has been poured out upon your lips,” etc. This psalm has the title: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, for the sons of Korah, for understanding, a song for the Beloved” [Col. 1198C]. Its meaning is: this hidden and mystical song is set before the sons of Korah—that is, the faithful of the Crucified, whom he begot in his Passion—so that they may strive to understand the mysteries and secrets contained in this song. It also concerns “the Beloved,” that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, uniquely beloved; hence it is said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. III).

This treatise is called a Song because nothing is more fitting for rejoicing. It is an epithalamium, that is, a wedding-song, presented at a wedding for delight; in it the Father, speaking through the Prophet, commends his Son according to both his human and divine natures, and also the bride whom he foresaw would be joined to him: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, surrounded by variety.” And to her: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear” [Col. 1199A].

In the following psalm, that is, Psalm XLV, those through whom, or to whom first, the faith contained in the preceding psalm was preached offer themselves as an example to others, lest they fail amid tribulations. Though they had preached true and profitable things, they nevertheless suffered many shameful insults. “God,” they say, “is our refuge and strength, a helper in tribulations which have found us exceedingly.” Its title is: “Unto the end, for the sons of Korah, for hidden things,” namely, judgments, of which it says: “Therefore we shall not fear when the earth is troubled and mountains are moved into the heart of the sea.” For by a hidden judgment it came about that, at the preaching of the Gospel, the Jews were troubled and the apostles were transferred from that land formerly stable [Col. 1199B] into the heart of the sea—that is, into the midst of the Gentiles. Hence the Apostle also says in wonder: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Rom. III), etc.

Those mountains, that is, the apostles, were indeed first troubled and afflicted when the waters of the peoples were disturbed; but “the rush of the river,” it says, “gladdens the city of God.” “The rush of the river,” I mean, the abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, gladdens the apostles themselves.

Psalm XLVI then rightly and in beautiful order addresses all the nations: “All nations, clap your hands.” This is understood to be addressed to those nations to whom we were transferred when the earth was troubled, and to whom we turned when the Jews rejected us. “Clap your hands,” it says: work rightly with joy. “Rejoice to God with the voice of exultation.” Why? “For the Lord most high is terrible, a great king over all the earth. He has chosen for us his inheritance, the beauty of Jacob whom he loved.” For as Esau, who was the first-born, was rejected by God, so the Israelite people, formerly acceptable to God through a certain familiarity, has now been rejected; and you nations have received the blessing [Col. 1199C].

Psalm XLVII likewise follows beautifully on the preceding psalms, saying: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, in the city of our God, on his holy mountain.” In this psalm the apostles intend to praise our Lord and his city, founded from both walls, namely, Jews and Gentiles. For this is what he says: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great king.” “Mount Zion” means the Jews on account of a certain dignity; “the sides of the north” are the Gentiles, bordering upon the north—that is, the devil, who remained cold from the ardor of love. Its title is: “A psalm-song of the sons of Korah, on the second day of the Sabbath,” that is, the joy of the apostles from the time of the Lord’s resurrection until the end of the age. It is called “the second day of the Sabbath” according to the Hebrew reckoning, which counts all days from the Sabbath [Col. 1199D].

In Psalm XLVIII David speaks “for the sons of Korah”—that is, the apostles, who are like David, strong of hand—to the faithful of Christ: “Hear these things, all nations; receive with your ears, all who inhabit the world,” etc. In this treatise they intend to show parabolically to all who are in the faith, whatever their condition, who should fear on the day of judgment and why, so that, knowing these things and avoiding them through God’s help, they may then be secure [Col. 1200A].

Moreover, in the following psalm, that is, Psalm XLIX, Asaph intends to announce the fear of this same future judgment: “The God of gods, the Lord,” he says, “has spoken.” He has spoken “and called the earth”—namely, coming hidden in his first advent to call it to his faith. But in the second advent the same “God shall come openly; our God, and shall not keep silence. A fire shall blaze before him, and a mighty tempest around him.” Then he shall say to the sinner: “You have done these things and I kept silence; you wickedly thought that I would be like you,” etc.

Nothing is more beautiful than these courses and returns, by which the prophetic Spirit runs and returns seven times from the first advent to the end—that is, to the second advent—wisely leading, bringing back, and profitably exercising the hearer’s mind through many teachings of faith, as through very broad regions of the earth. Whoever has properly learned his ways cannot be deceived or led away from the faith. If the Jew, the adversary of Christian faith, thrusts himself into one’s path, he must quickly be taken; he will quickly fall, so that the curse pronounced against him may also be fulfilled in this manner: “May the Lord give you up, fallen before your enemies. By one way you shall go out against them, and by seven you shall flee” (Deut. XXVIII) [Col. 1200B].

Finally, Psalm L, which asks [447] forgiveness of sins, is most rightly placed as the jubilee of faith [Col. 1200C]. For in this psalm we ask for that for which we believe, and for which, believing in Christ, we are baptized: “Have mercy on me, O God.” And then: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me.” “In iniquities,” he says—understand, of the first parents. What he says concerning himself is to be understood of others. For in Adam we all sinned (Rom. V). “Death passed into all,” says the Apostle (ibid.).

The title of the psalm is: “Unto the end, a Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” The story is well known: David took Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and killed Uriah by the sword of the children of Ammon. For this sin he prays, and in praying also prophesies concerning the universal forgiveness of sins. “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall become whiter than snow.” Hyssop is a lowly herb and relieves swelling of the lungs. “You shall sprinkle me,” he says, that is, cleanse me in faith in the humility of Christ’s Passion.

The middle fifty psalms especially look toward that intermediate state of man of which the Apostle speaks in the person of the weak, still fighting in an uncertain contest: “I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind” (Rom. VII). For having been reborn and received, through faith in Christ, forgiveness of past sins, we are not yet secure; indeed, we who enter upon combat and conflict with the enemy [Col. 1201A]. In that state there is plainly need of hope together with fear.

Therefore we rightly observe that in this middle of the psalms we are summoned to the hope necessary for faith, and for this reason the recapitulations are made, not from Christ’s first advent as hitherto, but from his second advent. First, Psalm LI assails Antichrist and says: “Why do you glory in malice, you who are powerful in iniquity?” And then: “Therefore God shall destroy you unto the end,” etc. When he has been destroyed, the righteous shall see and each shall say: “But I, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God, have hoped in the mercy of God for ever and ever. I will confess to you for ever because you have done it, and I will wait for your name, because it is good, in the sight of your saints” [Col. 1201B].

David says these things in the person of the righteous against Doeg the Edomite, who had performed the service of Antichrist. For the title reads: “Unto the end, understanding of David, when Doeg the Edomite came and informed Saul, saying: David has come to the house of Ahimelech” (I Sam. XXII). Its meaning is: the Prophet’s understanding in this psalm is to speak of the coming of Antichrist, who, stirring many hearts, will persecute and kill Christ’s faithful. But he wished to direct us to the history in order to show that what is written historically must be understood spiritually.

The title of Psalm LII is: “Unto the end, for Amalek, understanding of David.” The well-known history is that David, fleeing Saul, came to Achish king of Gath and served under him, having placed his wives and children in the small town of Ziklag. The Amalekites came, burned the town, and carried off David’s wives and children. When David heard this, he pursued those raiders and freed the captives (I Sam. XXVII, XXX). Ziklag means “conversion” and signifies the Church; by the wives, holy souls; by the children, good works; by David, Christ is understood.

It should be known that David had the same understanding in this psalm that he had when he first composed it; but he repeated it because he understood that what happened to him historically at the hands of the Amalekites would happen spiritually in Christ and in the Church. For Amalek himself—“foolish”—is any Jew or heretic who, blaspheming Christ, says in his heart: “There is no God” [Col. 1201D] (Ps. XIII). Against him hope strengthens the soul of a certain wise man so that it may say: “When God restores the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice and Israel shall be glad,” as was foreshadowed in the deed of the David already mentioned.

The title of Psalm LIII is: “Unto the end, in hymns, understanding of David, when the Ziphites came and said to Saul: Is not David hidden among us?” (I Sam. XXIII). This history also is well known. It should be noted that there it is written: “When Saul heard this, he pursued David. Yet David despaired of being able to escape from Saul’s presence” (ibid.); nevertheless, contrary to his expectation, he escaped, “and going up from there he dwelt in the safest places” (I Sam. XXIV). With such a title prefixed, he says: “O God, save me in your name,” etc.

Therefore, by this example, whoever sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind should not despair of being able to escape from the hand of Saul—that is, of death or the devil—from the hand of the Ziphites, that is, “the flourishing ones,” understood as vices. Rather, let him pray, calling upon the Lord’s name, until he dwells in the safest places of God’s grace, delivered from the body of death [Col. 1202A].

Psalm LIV is the prayer of our head, treating of the present rejection of the Jews, their eternal condemnation, the reception of the Gentiles, and the eternal security of the faithful. Its title is: “Unto the end, in hymns, understanding for David himself.” Its meaning is: the understanding of this psalm is attributed to David, who is Christ, persevering “unto the end,” or consummation, of his obedience; and this “in hymns,” that is, in joy. Let every believer therefore receive lessons of hope from the example of him who says: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? And I waited for him who saved me from faintness of spirit and tempest.” And then: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he shall sustain you; he shall never allow the righteous to be shaken.” And again: “Men of blood and deceit shall not half complete their days; but I will hope in you, O Lord” [Col. 1202B].

Likewise, in the following psalm, that is, Psalm LV, let him say by the example of that same head: “Have mercy on me, O God, for man has trampled me.” And then: “From the height of the day,” that is, from the power given from above to those attacking me, “I shall fear; but I shall hope in you. In God I shall praise my words; in God I have hoped; I shall not fear what flesh can do to me.” Again: “In God I shall praise the word; in the Lord I shall praise the utterance; in God I have hoped; I shall not fear what man can do to me.”

The title of that same psalm is: “Unto the end, for the people who have become far from the holy ones, in the inscription of the title, for David himself, when the Philistines held him in Gath” (I Sam. XXI). In this psalm Christ acts for the people who have become far from the holy ones, that is, very unlike them, “in the inscription of the title”—namely, when they said: “Do not write, King of the Jews; but that he himself said, I am King of the Jews” (John XIX)—“when they held him in Gath,” that is, in the pressure of tribulations. They were indeed first made Philistines, a word meaning “foreigners,” but afterward, believing, they were saved [Col. 1202D].

In the title of Psalm LVI the Holy Spirit says: “Unto the end: Do not destroy; for David himself, in the inscription of the title, when he fled from Saul’s presence into the cave” (I Sam. XXII). What the inscription of the title of our David is has already been said and is known to all: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” Therefore, whoever you are who flee from the face of Saul—from the face of the devil, or death, or any vice, for example, according to the Apostle saying, “Flee fornication” (I Cor. VI)—do not corrupt this title; indeed, do not corrupt yourself by destroying in yourself that which is called “King of the Jews.” For what is “King of the Jews” except king of those who confess? [448] Confess your sins, therefore, so that you may be the kingdom of this king; and, following his example, hope in Jesus of Nazareth, that is, your holy Savior and king, and say: “Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for my soul trusts in you. And in the shadow of your wings I shall hope, until iniquity pass away” [Col. 1203A].

That is to say, according to the Apostle: I shall fight against the law which is in my members until the grace of God comes, which delivers me from this body of death. When it has come, you will say: “God sent his mercy and his truth, and delivered my soul from the midst of young lions.” Understand: just as he delivered my head, my king, from the midst of the sons of men, whose teeth were weapons and arrows.

Likewise, the title of Psalm LVII is: “Unto the end: Do not destroy David, in the inscription of the title.” As said above, do not destroy in yourself the title “King of the Jews.” But what does he say? “If indeed you truly speak justice, judge rightly, sons of men.” Do not say, “We are righteous.” “For in your heart you work iniquities; on earth your hands devise injustices.” Unless you say, “We are sinners and cannot be justified except through the one man Jesus Christ,” you have destroyed this title; nor does that which is called “King of the Jews” apply to you.

Likewise, if you say, “We are indeed sinners, but the fates did this, the stars did this,” you do not speak justice at all, nor judge rightly, sons of men. Such “sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood”—namely, while they accuse God and defend themselves. Therefore “God shall break their teeth in their mouth” [Col. 1203B].

Likewise, in the same sense is the title of Psalm LVIII: “Unto the end: Do not corrupt; for David himself, in the inscription of the title, when Saul sent to watch his house, that they might kill him” (I Sam. XI). Therefore, whenever Saul sends—whenever the devil sends—and besieges the house of your body or flesh with as many attendants as there are vices, in order to kill you, just as he sent the Jews to kill Christ, do not corrupt the oft-mentioned title by despairing. Rather say after Christ’s example: “Deliver me from my enemies, O my God, and free me from those who rise against me. Deliver me from those who work iniquity, and save me from men of blood; for behold, they have seized my soul, and the strong have rushed upon me,” etc.

For he who, by rising again, delivered the head itself from those who rushed upon him “strong,” indeed frenzied—who appeared strong to themselves in their madness, though they were weak, and struck the physician—will also deliver you from the force of attacking vices or evil spirits, so that you may say according to this psalm: “But I will sing of your strength, and in the morning I will exalt your mercy,” etc.

In the fifty-ninth Psalm there is a return once more to the summit of hope: “O God, you have cast us off and destroyed us; you have been angry, and have had mercy on us.” For we say this as those who look ahead to Christ’s coming, we who are to be changed into immortality and impassibility, according to the sense of this title: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed, in the inscription of the title, for David himself” [Col. 1204A].—“For those,” he says, “who are to be changed unto the end,” that is, into immortality and impassibility, because they have received the inscription of the often-mentioned title, which inscription was made for David himself. It continues: “For instruction, when he set Mesopotamia of Syria and Syria Sobal on fire, and Joab returned and struck Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand” (2 Kings VIII, X; 1 Chronicles XVIII). For this reason, he says, they shall be changed: because they have received his instruction; because, by living well and speaking well, they have become his imitators. And this is not from themselves but from God, who set them aflame with the fire of the Holy Spirit, making them Mesopotamia of Syria—that is, calling them and raising them on high. For Mesopotamia is interpreted “an exalted calling,” Syria “sublimity.” He did this to them when they had formerly been Syria Sobal, that is, the sublimity of vain antiquity. “And Joab,” he says, “returned.” Joab is interpreted “enemy”; such indeed we all were, but we have been changed into friends, because through Christ we have been reconciled. “And he struck,” he says, “Edom in the Valley of Salt, twelve thousand.” We too were Edom—earthly and bloodthirsty—but he struck us in the Valley of Salt, putting us to death with respect to vices by the two-edged sword of his word, in humility and the seasoning of virtues. And we are, as it were, the number twelve thousand, a number completed through the parts of seven, namely three and four; for three times four, or four times three, makes twelve. Possessing the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit throughout the four quarters of the world, we confess and preach faith in the Holy Trinity. At his first coming [Col. 1204C] he set believers aflame with the fire of repentance. But when he comes the second time, he will set unbelievers aflame with penal fire. In the better sense we say in this Psalm: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from before the bow,” etc.

Having received this sign, in the following Psalm, the sixtieth, the universal Church of those who fear God says: “Hear, O God, my supplication; attend to my prayer. From the ends of the earth I cried to you: while my heart was distressed, you lifted me up upon the rock. You led me, because you became my hope,” etc. This prayer plainly offers hope to the already-mentioned combatant, whose heart is distressed while he fights, while he sees “another law in his members, resisting the law of his mind and leading him captive under the law of sin” (Rom. [Col. 1204D] VII).—“You led me,” he says, “because you became my hope, a tower of strength from the face of the enemy”: namely, so that I may be able to avoid sins and attain virtues. What if my heart is now distressed? Why should I be surprised amid the heat of temptation, which comes only for a time? At some time “I shall dwell in your tabernacle for ever; I shall be protected in the covering of your wings,” etc. This Psalm is titled thus: “Unto the end, in hymns, a Psalm of David.” Aptly, “unto the end,” for in this conflict he awaits deliverance through God’s grace. And this is “in hymns,” since he ascribes not to his own powers but to God’s praises the fact that he fights and strives to conquer.

Moreover, in the following Psalm, the sixty-first, the same lawful combatant strengthens himself by holy hope: [Col. 1205A] “Shall not my soul,” he says, “be subject to God?” O law of sin, law of death, resisting the law of my mind, the law of my life, why do you strive to call me away from hope or expectation of God’s help? Surely in vain. “For from him is my salvation.” And further: “In God are my salvation and my glory; God is the help that sustains me, and my hope is in God. Hope in him, all assembly of the people,” etc. It has this title: “Unto the end, for Idithum, a Psalm of David.” Idithum means “one who leaps over.” For he leaps over those to whom he speaks, saying: “How long do you rush upon [me]?”

In the sixty-second Psalm, the Head himself is introduced in prayer, to show what may be of the greatest benefit to one who, as was said, is still in struggle and danger, fighting against vices. “O God, my [Col. 1205B] God,” he says, “I watch for you from the dawn.” Bodily vigils too are greatly helpful against vices, as is holy meditation, of which he says afterwards: “If I have remembered you upon my bed, in the mornings I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper. And in the covering of your wings I will rejoice,” etc. The Head himself says these things, as the title indicates: “A Psalm of David when he was in the desert of Idumaea” (1 Kings XXV). The meaning of this title is: these words are to be attributed to the true David, Christ, according to that condition in which he lived among the Jewish people, who were a desert because they abandoned God’s commandments for their own traditions, and Idumaea—that is, earthly or bloodthirsty—because they loved the earth and thirsted for blood.

Likewise, in the sixty-third Psalm he is introduced as praying for their instruction, and says: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I make supplication; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.” For if he who foreknew the future was willing to pray, how much more ought those who are uncertain to devote themselves to prayer, so that they may be delivered from fear of an invisible or visible enemy; lest they yield in the enemy’s persecution, or fall or despair in the devil’s temptation. Therefore he concludes this prayer with such faith: “The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall be praised.”

In the sixty-fourth Psalm, by a third recapitulation, there is a return to the summit of hope—that is, to the end of the age, when, our bodies restored, we are to set out for the heavenly homeland. It is titled: “Unto [Col. 1205D] the end, a Psalm of David; a song of Jeremiah and Haggai concerning the word of the pilgrimage, when they began to depart.” And the sense is: this Psalm belongs to David the prophet, who looks “unto the end,” that is, to the final age. It is his “Psalm,” I say, the song—that is, the delight and joy—of Jeremiah and Haggai and of all the faithful. Jeremiah is interpreted “exalted of the Lord”; Haggai, “solemn” or “sublime.” Both foretold the coming pilgrimage of the Jewish people and their return to their homeland, a return in which Haggai himself was also present. But both understood that this pilgrimage of the faithful, occurring in this life, and the return that will finally take place were signified by it. By these two all the faithful are designated: by Jeremiah, those of intermediate attainment; by Haggai, who was present at the return, the perfect, who not only acknowledge themselves to be pilgrims [Col. 1206A] but also, according to the Apostle, already have their citizenship in heaven (Phil. III). Still pilgrims in this hope, they say here: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion, and to you shall a vow be rendered in Jerusalem”—understood as the heavenly Jerusalem. And lest any of them be absent there, they pray in fear and hope: “Hear us, O God our savior, hope of all the ends of the earth and of those far off at sea,” etc.

The sixty-fifth Psalm has the same aim; hence it is titled: “Unto the end, a song of a Psalm of resurrection.” This is indeed a song of universal hope, that we may all rejoice because we shall rise; for this reason the Psalm speaks universally: “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing a Psalm to his name; give glory to his praise,” etc. Yet it also [Col. 1206B] teaches the often-mentioned combatant in what order he ought to hope, and in what manner he should set before himself the grace hoped for as the conqueror of his enemies. “If,” he says, “I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear,” etc. As though he said: If I, who ought to fight against the law that is in my members, have loved the iniquity of these very members and willingly regarded it in silence, the Lord will not hear me, so as to deliver me by his grace from this body of death. For he said “I have regarded” instead of “I have loved,” because we turn our eyes more frequently toward what we love. “Therefore God heard [me].” Because, as I said before, “my mouth spoke in tribulation,” etc. I confessed in my wretchedness, namely in the resistance of my flesh, and said: “I will offer you fat burnt offerings with incense of rams; I will offer you bulls with goats,” etc. By rams he means every resistance of the flesh; by bulls, exaltation; by goats, every foulness of evil deeds. He says that he offers all these when he punishes them by confession and repentance. Without doubt this pertains to the song of resurrection, because by acting thus he rises in the first resurrection, which is that of the soul.

The sixty-sixth Psalm seems, indeed, to say nothing in its literal wording about the toil of conflict or hope of victory. Yet it is altogether suitable and profitable, with the meaning of the whole Psalm willing and consenting, to direct ourselves toward this end and thus say: “May God have mercy on us,” namely by the repression [Col. 1206D] of carnal motions, that is, vices. “May he bless us,” by the progress of spiritual motions, that is, virtues. “May he make his face shine upon us,” that is, may he grant us knowledge of his Son, who is called his face because he is known from him, just as one is known from his face. Desiring this mercy or compassion for all who invoke his name, we then add: “May the peoples confess you, O God,” etc.

In the sixty-seventh Psalm the often-mentioned warrior finds many things with which to fight, strike, scourge, crush, and burn the enemy. “Let God arise,” he says, “and let his enemies be scattered; let those who hate him flee from before his face,” etc. For when these words are spoken in faith, a swift result follows; and, as though God were rising, those who hate him—malignant spirits with their suggestions—flee away, vanishing like smoke and melting like wax before fire. And lest the soldier of God perhaps despair if, acting incautiously, he has suffered something, or has been wounded by any sin, he afterwards hears the Holy Spirit saying to him: “God in his holy place, God who makes those of one manner dwell in a house; who brings out those in bonds with strength, likewise those who provoke [him], who dwell in graves.” This has indeed happened thus among all nations, so that there is no reason for one captive, even one dwelling in a grave, to despair, however rightly comparable to Lazarus, stinking and four days dead.

The sixty-eighth Psalm further serves the same purpose. In it our Head himself [Col. 1207B] is introduced praying for his outward tribulations in the manner in which he wishes each of his own to pray for inward temptations: “Save me, O God,” he says, “for the waters have entered even unto my soul. I am sunk in deep mire, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me.” By praying these and the rest, he indicates that he gives his own, endangered amid vices, an example of prayer when he says: “Let the poor see and rejoice; seek God, and your soul shall live, because the Lord has heard the poor and has not despised his prisoners.” Thus this Psalm aptly has the title: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed; a Psalm of David.” Its sense is: this Psalm [Col. 1207C] concerns those who are to be changed into conformity with Christ, so that they may go unto the end, that is, unto complete perfection.

Likewise the following Psalm, the sixty-ninth, is sung in the person of the same Head for the instruction of every believer, that he too may pray and labor in hope whenever he is worn down by diverse temptations from enemies seeking his soul. “O God,” he says, “attend to help me; O Lord, hasten to help me,” etc. Its title is: “Unto the end, a Psalm of David for a memorial, because the Lord saved him”; that is, this Psalm is attributed to “David,” that is, Christ, “for a memorial,” that is, in reflection upon the fact that the Lord saved him.

[Col. 1207D] The words of Psalm LXX are plainly the words of the often-mentioned combatant, placed in conflict, retaining hope and professing hope: “In you, O Lord,” he says, “I have hoped; let me not be confounded for ever.” And further: “For you are my patience, O Lord—O Lord, my hope from my youth.” Again: “But I will always hope, and will add to all your praise.” Indeed, in what he says, “O my God, deliver me from the hand of the sinner, and from the hand of the one acting against the law and of the unjust,” it is easy to understand the devil, at whose prompting that discord occurs whereby the law of sin, which is the law of the flesh, fights against the law of the mind. Certainly Christ himself is the leader and teacher of this prayer: the Head and captain of those who contend lawfully. He prays here that he may be delivered from the hand of the law-breaking Jewish [Col. 1208A] people and the unjust Roman empire, by that same justice or divinity through which he is able to deliver those who are tempted. Finally, its title is: “A Psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab and of the first captives.” And the sense is: this Psalm is Christ’s, because he both speaks in this Psalm and speaks of himself. It is also “of the sons of Jonadab,” because the Lord speaks here of those who were formerly captive sons. Thus it is also called “of the first captives.” Jonadab is fittingly introduced here both in respect of the subject matter and of the interpretation of his name. In respect of the subject matter: because, just as Jonadab the priest commands his sons to abstain from wine and live in tents, so our Lord forbids his faithful from temporal enjoyment, and admonishes them to regard themselves as pilgrims and strangers in this life and to seek the future [world] (Heb. XIII). In the interpretation of the name: Jonadab means “the Lord’s willing one.” This interpretation aptly belongs to our Lord, who above all others obeyed God the Father specially and uniquely, even unto death. He prays in this Psalm in order, as has already been said, to teach his children by his example to pray.

In Psalm LXXI, by a fourth recapitulation we are recalled to the summit of our hope, when it is said: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son,” etc. What it says, “give,” was already accomplished at the first coming. “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). But that judgment itself will occur at the second coming, when [Col. 1208C] this king, according to Gospel truth, “shall sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. XXV). There is fear in this, because he will judge in righteousness; but there is hope in that he will spare the poor and needy and save the souls of the poor. This Psalm has the title: “A Psalm of David, concerning Solomon.” It is David the prophet, I say, looking toward Christ, who is the true Solomon, the true peacemaker. For he established peace between God and human beings; between the angelic and human creation; and between Jews and Gentiles—of which this Psalm says: “In his days,” he says, “righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace.” Before that occurs—that is, the judgment already mentioned—the often-mentioned combatant meanwhile sometimes fails and falls a little away from his hope, seeing many sinners possess a kind of peace in evils while the righteous are worn down by adversities. But afterwards he repents of this error.

Corrected in this way, he speaks in the following Psalm, the seventy-second: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved, my steps almost poured out, because I was envious of the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners.” And further: “If I said, ‘I will speak thus,’ behold, I have rejected the nation of your children.”—“If,” he says, “I said,” or spoke thus—indeed, if I should say thus: “How does God know, and is there knowledge in the Most High?” etc.—“behold, I have rejected the nation of your children,” that is, then I shall be opposed to [Col. 1209A] the authority of all the saints. For those who say these and similar things are denoted in the foregoing title: “The praises of David, son of Jesse, have failed.” “Of Jesse’s son,” he says: that is, of those in whom David, Jesse’s son, reigned, and of all who imitate them. Indeed, through love of earthly or carnal things their praises have failed, while they speak thus, while, unless they have an abundance of temporal things, they cease to praise God. What then? “But for me,” he says, “it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God.” True praise begins to be offered by spiritual persons through love of heavenly things and contempt for earthly things.

The title of Psalm LXXIII is: “Understanding of Asaph.” Asaph, that is, all who have understanding, propose questions in this Psalm, saying: [Col. 1209B] “Why, O God, have you cast [us] off unto the end? Is your wrath kindled against the sheep of your pasture?” etc. Although they propose questions of this kind, they do not do so in doubt, but in concern for others’ salvation and instruction: so that, first made attentive by the questions and then instructed by the solutions, people may follow their example in applauding God’s just judgment, may not be saddened by the tribulation of the faithful, but may rejoice in hope, knowing that through suffering hard and harsh things they will attain glory.

Psalm LXXIV serves the same purpose especially: namely, to establish a most powerful consolation of hope. “We will confess to you, O God,” he says, “we will confess and invoke your name,” etc. Souls strengthened by good hope can say to the wicked: “Do not act wickedly”; [Col. 1209C] and to offenders: “Do not raise up the horn. Do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God. For neither from the east nor from the west nor from the desert mountains”—understood: there is an open place of escape—“for God is judge,” from whom no one can flee. Certainly these words principally belong to our Head, Christ; for no one other than he can say: “When I receive the time, I will judge justices; and I have established its pillars, and I will break all the horns of sinners.” Thus its title fittingly reads: “Unto the end, do not destroy; a Psalm of Asaph, a song.” And the sense is: O Asaph, that is, the unbelieving congregation of the Jews, “do not destroy” anything in this Psalm by interpreting it wrongly or attributing it to anyone but Christ. Yet when he says in the plural, “we will confess, we will invoke, [Col. 1209D] we will recount,” the Head acknowledges that he speaks together with his members.

Psalm LXXV, by a fifth recapitulation, looks toward the end of all things, which we fear in hoping and hope for in fearing. “God,” he says, “is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel. And his place has been made in peace.” And further: “From heaven you made judgment heard; the earth trembled and was still, when God arose in judgment, to save all the meek of the earth,” etc. He says “you made” prophetically instead of “you will make,” using the past tense for the future. Certainly, in what he says, “From heaven you made judgment heard; the earth trembled and was still,” there is cause for immense fear. It is the same as if he said: the earth—that is, the ungodly lovers of earth—will tremble and become still, because they will cease to work evil; for the great Judge will restrain them by saying: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). But in what he says, “to save all the meek of the earth,” the hope of the meek is greatly armed. It is the same as if he said: Rising in judgment, he will save the meek, who do not defend their sins but redeem them by alms, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” The title of this Psalm is: “Unto the end, in praises, a Psalm of Asaph, a song to the Assyrians.” Assyrian is interpreted “one who directs,” and here it signifies Jews who direct themselves—that is, who vainly exalt themselves on account of Abraham’s lineage or the works [Col. 1210B] of the Law, supposing it enough that they are carnal Judah and carnal Israel. Against their exaltation the Psalm says that God is known in that which is truly Judah, and his name is great in him who is true Israel. Judah signifies confession of sins. Israel, interpreted “seeing God” or “one made straight with God,” signifies the man striving against the assaults of vices, the kind of man often discussed already. Further, what follows, “And his place has been made in peace,” designates that state of which the Apostle says: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. VII). For truly there God broke powers, bow, shield, sword, [Col. 1210C] and war.

Placed between fear of that judgment and hope of salvation, the often-mentioned combatant says in the following Psalm, LXXVI: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, with my voice to God, and he attended to me. In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands.” And further: “I was exercised, and my spirit failed” in the very exercise. “My eyes anticipated the watches,” that is, I labored more than all others; and then I failed. Hence, “I was troubled,” namely, grieving over this very failure. “I did not speak.” I was not angry against God because the fruit of my labor failed or was delayed. And I said: “Will God cast [me] off for ever, or will he no longer add that he may be favorable?” By saying these things, etc., he plainly labors between fear [Col. 1210D] and hope; now he fails in fear, now he consoles that very failure with good hope. This Psalm has in its title “For Idithun,” which means “one who leaps over,” namely, for good will and right intention, because, setting aside all things, he seeks God alone: “My soul,” he says, “refused to be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted.”

The seventy-seventh Psalm sets before the same combatant the great works of God to meditate upon: “Attend, my people, to my law; incline your ear to the words of my mouth,” etc. This he does usefully, intending to strengthen hope, as he says: “The children who shall be born and arise shall tell their children.” Immediately adding: “That they may place their hope in God.” For continual meditation upon God’s works is of great power for one striving in the contest. Note, moreover, that this whole exposition is parabolic, as the Prophet himself testifies: “I will open my mouth in parables.” And what has been said in these words historically is to be understood spiritually. For the words of the whole Psalm, sounding forth past events, signified the future mysteries of Christ—Christ himself, that is, and those things now present in Christ’s Church.

Psalm LXXVIII recounts, in mournful declamation, the tribulations of the saints, in order to show that they occur for the faithful’s benefit, so that they may be strengthened and not despair in any contest of inward or outward temptations. “O God,” he says, “the nations have entered into your inheritance; they have defiled your holy temple,” etc. [Col. 1211B] Certainly, to each believer his own vices are barbarian nations, which have defiled God’s holy temple, that is, our body, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Cor. VI.) Therefore, resisting sin, as has often been said, they rightly say also according to this Psalm: “Help us, O God our savior; and for the glory of your name, O Lord, deliver us, and be merciful to our sins for your name’s sake.”

Likewise, in the following Psalm, LXXIX, the same combatant says: “Give ear, you who rule Israel, you who lead Joseph like a sheep.” And further: “O Lord God of hosts, how long will you be angry against the prayer of your servant? You will feed us with the bread of tears and give us drink in tears by measure,” etc. Yet principally and universally, in this Psalm the Prophet and the other ancient faithful implore Christ’s coming, which they foresaw would happen. They pray to God the Father not for themselves, but for those whom they foresee will in their time be changed into him, in accordance with this title of the same Psalm: “Unto the end, for those who shall be changed: a testimony of Asaph, a Psalm for the Assyrians. For those who shall be changed,” he says, that is, for Jews and Gentiles, who, upon the swift appearing of the Lord Jesus, are to be changed into him; but “for the Assyrians,” that is, for those directing themselves—namely, the faithless Jews who direct themselves, because, as the Apostle says, “seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” [Col. 1211D] (Rom. X). He prays for them that they may finally be converted, when he says: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations,” etc., unto the end of the Psalm.

The title of Psalm LXXX is: “Unto the end, for the presses, on the fifth day of the Sabbath, a Psalm of Asaph.” By the presses is signified God’s present Church, in which good and evil are mixed, just as oil and dregs, or wine and grapes, are mixed in presses, according to what occurred on the fifth day of the Sabbath, when the race produced from the waters partly flew aloft and partly remained beneath the waves. Thus in the present Church, those regenerated from the waters are partly borne to heaven and partly left below. It is said in the plural, “for the presses,” because of the different Churches from Jews and Gentiles. [Col. 1212A] In this Psalm the war-trumpet magnificently rouses lawful combatants to hope of victory, saying: “Rejoice in God our helper; make a joyful noise to the God of Jacob.” After much else it proposes this great example of faith: “He established it,” he says, “as a testimony in Joseph when he went forth from the land of Egypt: he heard a language that he did not know. He turned his back from burdens; his hands served in baskets.” By Joseph, who first served according to history, he means all the children of Israel; but according to allegory, all the elect, whom God brought out from the darkness of ignorance and whose backs he turned away from the burdens of sin. Therefore, whoever still strives in the often-mentioned contest should hope that one day it will be said also to him: “In tribulation you called upon me, and I delivered you; I heard you in the hidden place of the tempest,” that is, in the secret place of temptation. For I alone knew what you were suffering. “I tested you at the waters of contradiction,” that is, in your fluctuation, where, because of evil habit, another law which was in your members resisted the law of your mind (Rom. VII).

In Psalm LXXXI the Prophet says of Christ: “God stood in the synagogue of gods; in the midst, moreover, he judges gods.” For, foreseeing that the Jewish people would regard the Lord Jesus as a mere human being and therefore judge him to death, he says: “How long do you judge unjustly and accept the faces of sinners?” etc. But to him: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit among all nations.” As if he said: I warned them to judge justly and to deliver you, but they will not do so; rather, they will hand [Col. 1212C] you over to death. Rise, therefore, from the dead, and, having cast aside these few, receive all nations as your inheritance. Principally this Psalm chastises Christ’s visible enemies, the Jews; secondarily, the invisible enemies of Christ’s soldier, malignant spirits. And in this Head of ours is the end of this, that is, the fifth section. For it must be noted that whereas each section of the first fifty Psalms begins from Christ’s first coming and ends in his second, conversely, each section of these fifty Psalms begins with his second coming and returns as far as his first coming.

Psalm LXXXII, looking toward the judgment to come against Edomites, Ishmaelites, Moabites, Hagarites, Ammonites, Amalekites, and against [Col. 1212D] all foreigners—that is, against all enemies of the Church, false Christians, heretics, or unbelievers—says: “O God, who shall be like you? Do not be silent, nor be restrained, O God.” Understood: you who at your first coming were silent and restrained your power. And further: “As fire which burns the forest, and as flame burning the mountains, so shall you pursue them in your tempest, and trouble them in your wrath.”—“In your tempest,” he says, that is, in the judgment in which, through angelic ministry, good will be divided from evil as grain from chaff by a tempest. “Then let them blush and be troubled for ever and ever; then let them be confounded and perish, and let them know”—they who now refuse to know—“that your name is the Lord, [Col. 1213A] you alone are the Most High over all the earth.” Here is fear.

But the following Psalm, the eighty-third, sings the joys of hope: “How beloved,” he says, “are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs for and fails toward the courts of the Lord. My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God.”—“Have rejoiced,” he says, understood as in hope, not yet in reality. And further: “Blessed,” he says, “is the man whose help is from you: he has disposed ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed. For the lawgiver will give a blessing; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” And at the close of the conclusion: “O Lord,” he says, “of hosts, blessed is the person who hopes in you.” Thus the preceding [Col. 1213B] Psalm rouses the often-mentioned combatant by fear, lest he grow sluggish; this one, lest he be narrowed by fear, expands him through most joyful hope. Its title is “For the presses, for the sons of Korah,” that is, the imitators of the Crucified One. This Psalm is to be assigned “for the presses” already discussed above.

The following Psalm, LXXXIV, having in its title “Unto the end, for the sons of Korah,” says: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land; you have turned away Jacob’s captivity.” And immediately: “You have softened all your wrath.” This has surely already been accomplished, because the Lord God blessed through the incarnation of his Son the earth which had been cursed in Adam, and in him softened his wrath. He softened it, I say, but has not yet wholly turned it away. For the punishment of sin has not yet been entirely destroyed, since the misery of mortality and passibility remains. What therefore remains for the future, the sons of Korah pray for. “Convert us,” they say, “O God our savior, and turn away your wrath from us. Will you be angry with us for ever, or will you extend your wrath from generation to generation? O God, when you turn, you will give us life, and your people shall rejoice in you.”—“You will give us life,” he says, that is, you will raise us, etc.

In Psalm LXXXV the title reads: “A prayer for David himself.” It is called a “prayer” because almost the entire Psalm is a prayer, and whatever is inserted is chiefly directed to prayer. It is attributed to “David himself,” that is, Christ, truly strong of hand. For in this Psalm he prays to the Father concerning his passion, not in respect of that by which he is consubstantial and equal in power with him, but in respect of the frailty of the human condition, in which he was lower even than angels. Therefore let whoever fights lawfully in the often-mentioned conflict pray with his Head: “Incline, O Lord, your ear and hear me, for I am needy and poor. Preserve my soul, for I am holy; save your servant, O my God, who hopes in you.” And the rest that follows is plainly the language not of those already victorious, but of one still fighting in hope.

In Psalm LXXXVI the sons of Korah, that is, the imitators of the crucified Christ, rejoice that they are to be rescued from the depth of vices and placed in the glorious city, whose “foundations,” they say, “are in the holy mountains,” [Col. 1214A] that is, in the apostles and prophets. Rejoicing in hope over its glorious dwelling, they immediately add: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God.” What are those glorious things? “I will remember Rahab and Babylon,” etc. Surely this greatly gladdens the hope of the combatant whom the law of sin still confounds in his members because of evil habit: the Lord has promised that he will remember Rahab and Babylon—that is, those held in great expansiveness and confusion of vices. For Rahab means “breadth,” Babylon “confusion.”

The title prefixed to Psalm LXXXVII is: “A song of a Psalm, for the sons of Korah, unto the end, for Promelech, for answering.” Promelech means “in concord.” This Psalm is therefore proposed to the sons of Korah—that is, to the often-mentioned imitators of the Crucified One—for answering in concord, so that, just as he suffered for them, they too may not shrink from suffering for him if need be, and may do so in concord, that is, with the love with which he himself suffered. The title adds: “Understanding of Eman the Israelite.” Eman means “brother.” Surely Christ’s brother, the true Israelite, has this understanding. In this Psalm our Head intends to pray in his passion for his own constancy and resurrection: “O Lord God,” he says, “of my salvation, by day I cried, and by night before you,” etc. By his example, each of the sons of Korah needs to pray whenever he is endangered in the often-mentioned conflict, so that whenever the law in his members overcomes the law of his mind he may truly say: “For my soul is filled [Col. 1214C] with evils, and my life has drawn near to hell. I have been counted with those who go down into the pit,” etc.

In the eighty-eighth Psalm faithful David sings of the mercies of the Lord, which he is confident he will sing for ever. “The mercies of the Lord,” he says, “I will sing for ever.” For he had heard the prophet Nathan saying to him in the word of the Lord: “I announce to you that the Lord will build you a house. And when you have fulfilled your days, so that you go to your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall be from your sons, and I will establish his kingdom for ever. I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son” (2 Kings 7), etc. From this song of mercies that often-mentioned combatant conceives a great strengthening of hope, especially where it says: “But if his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments; if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but I will not scatter my mercy from him,” etc. This Psalm is entitled: “Understanding of Ethan the Israelite.” Ethan means “strong.” Thus every strong Israelite understands that in this Psalm Christ is commended as so great and terrible that none of the saints can be compared with him in power or be like him in divinity; likewise, that the aid of humankind in its restoration was laid upon him by God the Father, and that he himself was chosen and anointed with holy oil—that is, with every spiritual gift—as king and priest for ever. [Col. 1214D–1215A]

Psalm 89 is entitled thus: “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” Of Moses, I say—not of just anyone from the Jewish people, but of him who may by a certain privilege be called “the man of God.” This Psalm gives voice to the common hope of humankind. “Lord,” it says, “you have become a refuge to us from generation to generation,” that is, from the first righteous persons to the last. For the Prophet, foreseeing that the Jews would always remain in unbelief and error, intends in this Psalm to show that the human race is to be redeemed through Christ alone. “For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15).

Having therefore expressed the mortality granted to humankind as its due in these words—“In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flower and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither, because we have failed in your wrath and have been troubled in your fury,” etc.—he immediately added the common hope of resurrection: “Turn, O Lord,” he says, “how long? and be entreated for your servants.” And, as though heard: “We have been filled,” he says, “in the morning with your mercy”—“in the morning,” that is, on the day of resurrection. “We have been,” he says, in place of “we shall be,” because by a most certain faith the resurrection is, as it were, already accomplished: accomplished in Christ, and hoped for in us. [Col. 1215A–B]

The title of Psalm 90: “A praise-song of David.” What is praised, what is sung in this Psalm? “He who dwells,” it says, “in the help of the Most High shall abide under the protection of the God of heaven.” In this Psalm the hope of the Christian soldier is greatly strengthened—the hope which, as we have said, is very frequently impressed upon us in these fifty Psalms. It immediately continues: “He shall say to the Lord: You are my protector and my refuge; my God, I will hope in him.” Again: “He shall overshadow you with his shoulders, and under his wings you shall hope.” Then: “For you, Lord, are my hope.” And afterward the Most High says of him: “Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him,” etc.

Certainly, in the first verse of this Psalm the Prophet speaks in his own person. Thereafter he introduces the faithful speaking in their own persons as far as this verse: “Because he hoped in me, I will deliver him”; and from that point to the end of the Psalm, the Lord himself speaks. [Col. 1215B–D]

The title of Psalm 91: “A Psalm-song for the Sabbath day.” By this title the Psalm promises great rest to the combatant who labours in hope, upon whom the matter turns and to whom hope is intimated throughout all these fifty Psalms. In hope of that rest he now says: “It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing praise to your name, O Most High, to declare your mercy in the morning and your truth through the night.” Hearing or singing this, that oft-mentioned combatant should confess to the Lord the wounds he has suffered from the law of sin which he sees in his members; and then he should sing praise—that is, work rightly for the glory of the name of the Most High, so that people, seeing, may glorify the Father who is in heaven.

Then, strengthened by good hope, he will say: “My horn shall be exalted like that of the unicorn, and my old age shall be in abundant mercy. For my eye has looked down upon my enemies, and my ear shall hear of malignant men rising up against me. The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree,” etc. “My horn,” he says, “shall be exalted like that of the unicorn,” through the help of grace delivering “me from this body of death” (Rom. 7). That horn, I say, which is now depressed and almost broken by the law that is in my members, resisting the law of my mind (ibid.); and my old age—that is, that perfect holiness in which, once established, I shall grow cold toward every desire for earthly things, after the manner of an old man who has ceased through extreme age to be warm within himself—shall keep Sabbath in abundant mercy. And this is so because, even now, while still set in battle, “my eye has looked down upon my enemies.” My reason, I say, has looked down in hope of victory upon the evil spirits attacking me, while my ear hears within itself the good words of holy hope, words of consolation. “The righteous,” he says, “shall flourish like a palm tree”: for he who has contended lawfully shall be crowned (2 Tim. 2). [Col. 1215D–1216B]

In Psalm 92, which is the last of this sixth section, there is a return in the customary manner to the Head himself, saying: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself,” etc. “The Lord has reigned”: having cast out the prince of this world (John 12), the Lord gained the kingdom; when he was lifted up from the earth, the Lord drew all things to himself (ibid.). “The Lord has clothed himself with beauty.” The Lord was incarnate from the Virgin in the great beauty of holiness; that same flesh, crowned with thorns and laid in the tomb, he again put on as immortal and impassible strength, and he girded himself with his apostles armed with the power of the Holy Spirit.

Under this king, when vices arise and that often-mentioned combatant fluctuates between the law of the flesh and the law of the mind, let him speak with foresight; let him speak firm in hope: “Wonderful are the liftings up of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high.” The apostles said this against the commotions of protesting nations; let each person say it against the movements of resisting vices. The title of this Psalm is: “A praise-song of David, on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.” “Before the Sabbath,” he says, that is, in contemplation of the sixth age, which is followed by Sabbath—that is, rest—“when the earth was founded,” that is, the Church. It should indeed be noted that, as man was created on the sixth day, so in the sixth age and on that same day he was restored. For, as has already been said, incarnate and lifted up from the earth, the Lord reigned; and from then on his throne was made ready. [Col. 1216B–D]

In Psalm 93, the seventh section, we sing in contemplation of the future judgment: “God of avengings, the Lord; God of avengings has acted freely. Exalt yourself, you who judge the earth; render recompense to the proud,” etc. Because of the extreme certainty of the matter, the Prophet said “has acted freely,” speaking of future things as if of past things. The title of this Psalm: “A praise-song of David, on the fourth day of the Sabbath.” The fourth day of the Sabbath is the middle of the week, with three days preceding it and as many following. This middle of the week signifies the unforeseen time of judgment, as does that “middle of the night” in the Gospel: “At midnight,” it says, “a cry was made: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25); or as does that midpoint of human security, concerning which it likewise says: “And as it was in the days of Noah, and as it was in the days of Lot, so shall it be in the days of the Son of Man. They ate and drank” (Luke 17), etc.

In this Psalm the often-mentioned combatant should say: “Who will rise up for me against the malicious, or who will stand with me against the workers of iniquity?” And, considering the many perils of temptation in which he has been, he should immediately add: “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell.” Then: “And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the helper of my hope.” [Col. 1216D–1217B]

In the following Psalm, Psalm 94, he says: “Come, let us rejoice in the Lord; let us make joyful noise to God our Saviour. Let us go before his face in confession, and in psalms let us make joyful noise to him.” “In confession,” he says, “of sins, let us go before his face,” that is, let us anticipate his manifest coming. For a person is openly recognized by the face; therefore, by the face of the Lord his second coming is rightly understood. His first coming was hidden from many, but the latter will be manifest to all.

It should be noted that the Prophet speaks these words in his own person as far as: “Today, if you hear his voice.” From that point to the end of the Psalm he speaks in the person of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1217B–C]

Likewise Psalm 95 has in view the future judgment, and begins thus: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth.” “Sing,” he says, “a new song”—that is, observe the precepts of the new law so diligently that it may be pleasing to the Lord. He says “sing” three times, so that the very repetition may impress upon us the zeal of singing. Do these things, etc., which I have said in this Psalm, to the glory and honour of the Lord. Why? Because he comes: “For he comes to judge the earth. He shall judge the world in equity and the peoples in his truth.”

This Psalm bears the title: “When the house was being built after the captivity, a song of David” (1 Chron. 15). Universally, the house—that is, the Church—is now built after the captivity of the first parent; and the Prophet exhorts the greater persons and prelates, by preaching to their inferiors, to hasten the building of the Lord. Individually—that is, in each person—the house is built when someone, after the captivity of sin, makes progress in virtues by resisting vices, so as to become a house or temple. Certainly, at the beginning of this Psalm there is cause for rejoicing, when it says, “Sing to the Lord”; and at its end there is cause for fear, when it says, “He shall judge the world in equity; he shall judge the peoples in his truth.” [Col. 1217C–D]

Likewise, in the following Psalm, the ninety-sixth, there is cause to rejoice in hope when it says: “The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice; let many islands be glad.” There is cause to fear in humility when it immediately adds: “Cloud and darkness are round about him; righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne. Fire shall go before him and shall burn his enemies round about,” etc. For the fact that the Lord has reigned, that the world has been restored to its Lord, brings condemnation to the Jews and all his enemies, but salvation to the righteous—according to the title inscribed thus: “A Psalm of David, when his earth was restored to him.” [Col. 1217D–1218A]

Likewise the following Psalm, the ninety-seventh, at its beginning makes the faithful person rejoice in hope when it says: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wonders,” etc. But at its end it humbles by fear through these words: “The mountains shall rejoice before the Lord, because he comes to judge the earth. He shall judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in equity.”

But the next Psalm, Psalm 98, equally impresses hope and fear: “The Lord has reigned; let the peoples be angry; he who sits upon the cherubim—let the earth be moved.” For “the Lord has reigned” means that the Lord has conquered the devil. What it says—“let the peoples be angry, and let the earth be moved”—must be understood concessively, as though it said: There is no need for concern: let the Jews be as angry and as disturbed as they please, for they are “earth,” that is, devoted only to earthly things. For although they are angry and unwilling that he should reign over them, “the Lord has reigned, who sits upon the cherubim.”

This Psalm instils fear together with hope, especially where, having first said: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name,” etc., it immediately adds: “O God, you were gracious to them, and avenging all their devices.” For this is as though it said: You were so gracious to them that nevertheless you punished all their devices. Hope, then, is aided by the fact that he was gracious to them; fear is instilled by the fact that he did not leave unpunished all the offences even of such persons and of persons so great. [Col. 1218A–C]

Psalm 99 is “in confession,” that is, in consideration of confession; for it begins thus: “Make joyful noise to God, all the earth.” Then follows: “His people and the sheep of his pasture, enter his gates in confession.” That is, in order that you may be able to make joyful noise, “enter his gates”; first of all, approach him in confession of sins. And this Psalm also instils both hope and fear in prudent hearers. “For the Lord is sweet; his mercy is for ever.” In this one must hope. “And his truth is unto generation and generation.” Here one must fear, because he is true. For in his first coming he came sweetly in the abundance of mercy; in the second he will appear true and just. [Col. 1218C–D]

This is what he says in the following Psalm, Psalm 100: “I will sing to you, O Lord, mercy and judgment.” Not judgment first and then mercy, but mercy first and then judgment. For Christ, who says these things in the Prophet, was first to sing mercy to his own, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened” (Matt. 11); afterward judgment, saying: “Depart from me, you cursed” (Matt. 25). This is what he concludes by saying: “In the morning I was putting to death all the sinners of the earth, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all workers of iniquity.” For that will be the morning judgment, after the night of this age has passed.

Through all this middle part of the Psalms, therefore, we rightly tend in hope, according to that intermediate state of the human being in which “the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 9 [probably Gal. 5]), and the inward person indeed delights in the law of God but sees another law in the members resisting it (Rom. 7), etc. Therefore he groans and says: “Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (ibid.). And he immediately receives this answer of hope: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (ibid.). For there, as we have often said, hope is accompanied by fear. Yet he knows that when that grace comes, hope will be without fear, because “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4); and there the chaste soul will peacefully contemplate its lover.

According to that state of the person at peace, the third part of the following text—the last fifty Psalms—takes its character, since it breathes almost entirely, from beginning to end, ardent love. Hence come those blessings, those confessions, those praises, bearing *Alleluia* in their titles, through all of which voices blessed love strives to express its affection as far as it can. But when the happy person has arrived there, does he then cease to weep? On the contrary, he weeps, groans, and sighs greatly—but not as before. For previously he wept lest he be led to punishment; now he begins to weep because he is delayed from the kingdom. This part of the Psalms, therefore, rightly has tears intermingled with confessions and praises; indeed, it begins with weeping and, after praises, returns through seven sections to weeping. [Col. 1218D–1219C]

And immediately, weeping in Psalm 101, he says: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you. Do not turn your face away from me,” etc. For what does he lament in saying these things except that he is delayed from the kingdom, except that he is held in this mortality? “I have been struck down,” he says, “like grass.” Supply: by the punishment of the sin of the first parents. Then: “My days have declined like a shadow, and I have withered like grass.”

The title of this Psalm is thus: “The prayer of the poor man when he was distressed, and poured out his supplication before the Lord.” This poor man is principally Christ, but secondarily the humble people, or any servant of Christ. This is why the title is divided in this manner between different times, namely past and future. “The prayer of the poor man when he was distressed”: this is past. For the distress of the poor man has passed; the distress of Christ’s death has passed, in which he said, “I have been struck down like grass,” etc. Then, concerning his resurrection, he adds: “I watched,” that is, I rose again, “and became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof,” namely by ascending into heaven. But “when he shall have poured out his supplication before the Lord” is future in time, as though it meant, “whenever he shall have poured it out.” For this happens, and will continue to happen until the end of the age: namely, that following his example every poor person of God may pour out his supplication in such a prayer. [Col. 1219C–D]

Immediately in the following Psalm, Psalm 102, the happy person breaks forth in blessings: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses. He who forgives all your iniquities.” Then, chanting many grounds for righteous blessing, he finally repeats the blessings in conclusion: “Bless the Lord,” he says, “you his angels,” etc. Love could not speak more magnificently in blessing or more affectionately.

And it should be noted from what point he begins the blessings: “He who forgives,” he says, “all your iniquities.” Then: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us.” Clearly, the highest cause of love is the highest cause of blessing: that he has been propitiated for our iniquities. Indeed, he sent us his Son as propitiator, who knew our fashioning and deigned to become human. A secondary cause of love and blessing is that he made us and all things good. It is secondary, I say, not primary. For our being born would have profited us nothing, unless redemption had profited us. [Col. 1220A–B]

Therefore in the following Psalm, Psalm 103: “Bless the Lord, O my soul.” Immediately, by apostrophe, he adds: “O Lord my God, you have been exceedingly magnified.” And as though one asked, “In what?” he says: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment, stretching out heaven like a skin,” etc. According to the letter, these words celebrate the first creation of the world.
