For, as we said in the first part of this work, the Lord God was clothed with light as with a garment and put on confession and beauty when, after light had been divided from darkness (Gen. 1), the reprobate were signified by the waters: he was clothed or adorned with angels as with light—that is, with the blessed angels, with whom he deigned to clothe himself, as it were with a garment, by grace—and he deigned to be unceasingly adorned by their confession and beautiful praise.

At the final conclusion it returns to the Head: “Let sinners,” it says, “fail from the earth, and the wicked, so that they are no more. Bless the Lord, O my soul.” [Col. 1220B–C]

The following Psalm, Psalm 104, bears *Alleluia* in its title. And rightly so, for it is wholly in confessions, that is, praises. “Confess to the Lord,” it says, “and call upon his name,” etc. The greatest cause or subject matter of this confession and song is the promise of the blessed seed. God, promising it to Abraham, said: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). For after he said, “Remember his wonders which he has done, his prodigies and the judgments of his mouth,” he immediately added: “The seed of Abraham his servant.” The seed, I say, not so much according to flesh as according to faith—namely that seed in whom all nations are blessed. And directly afterward: “He remembered his covenant for ever.” What covenant except that same promise? For when the Apostle recalled that promise by saying, “The promises were made to Abraham and to his seed” (Gal. 3), he immediately continued: “But this I say: the covenant confirmed by God” (ibid.). Therefore this promise is the chief subject matter of this confession. [Col. 1220C–1221A]

The grounds of the following confession, namely Psalm 105, are the wonderful benefits of God by which he brought that people out from the land of Egypt and brought them into the land which he promised to their fathers.

The Psalm which follows, Psalm 106, has causes much greater and much worthier—that is, entirely spiritual ones. For this reason it has a double *Alleluia* in its title, although the first *Alleluia* is rightly thought to belong to the preceding Psalm, so that the sense may be: Since our fathers sinned so greatly and the Lord mercifully bestowed upon them so many and such great benefits, therefore praise the Lord, as I said at the beginning of the Psalm.

In this Psalm the Prophet exhorts all the faithful, whether from the Jews or the Gentiles, to praise the Lord, first because he delivered them from the peril of unbelief: “Confess to the Lord,” he says, “because he is good, because his mercy is for ever. Let those redeemed by the Lord say so,” etc. For it is said of all, both Jews and Gentiles, that bearing the sin of Adam’s transgression, “they wandered in a wilderness without water; they did not find the way to an inhabited city. And they cried to the Lord when they were afflicted by tribulation.” They cried, I say, not so much in voice or by any intention as by the magnitude of their misery. “And the Lord delivered them,” namely through knowledge of his Son, “that they might go into a city of habitation.” Therefore, he says, “let them confess to the Lord his mercies and his wonders”—supply: displayed to the children of men.

Then he admonishes them to praise the Lord because he delivered them from the weakness of perverse habit, from actual crimes committed after baptism. “Sitting in darkness,” he says, “and in the shadow of death, bound in poverty and iron,” etc. For to serve sin is to be bound in iron; to sit in darkness is to have the habit of sinning. The Lord delivered many such persons when they cried to him. “And he led them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds.” A third cause is that he delivered them from weariness in good works, of whom he says: “Their soul abhorred all food, and they drew near even to the gates of death.” This happens in many ways—for example, when they suffer weariness in prayer or sacred reading. And the Lord delivered such persons when they cried to him, though they had drawn near “to the gates of death,” that is, even to grave sins, which are the entrances to death. How did he “deliver them”? “He sent his word,” that is, he commanded—or merely willed—and healed them.

The fourth cause of confession and praise is that he delivered them from the distresses of their prelacy. “Those who go down,” he says, “to the sea in ships, doing work in great waters,” etc. “Those who go down in ships” are those who have received the helm of churches, as often happens. “They were troubled and moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up.” The Lord brought even these, when crying to him, out of their necessities. “For he made the storm of the sea into a breeze, and its waves were silent.” That is to say: he transformed their anxiety into a calming breeze by increasing the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that they might not be so afflicted by the tumult of cares, whether within or without. [Col. 1221A–1222A]

In Psalm 107, finally, the Head himself confesses, sings, and says: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody in my glory.” The title is: “A Psalm-song of David himself.” To whom, indeed, if not to David himself—that is, to Christ—should the words of this Psalm be attributed? For the Father says to him as he lies in the tomb: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp.” He immediately replies: “I will arise at dawn.” And he adds: “I will confess to you among the peoples, O Lord, and I will sing to you among the nations,” etc.

And so it came to pass. That harp—that is, the body through which the music of God the Father had sounded for thirty-three years, the harp, I say, of the divine musician, shattered on the mountain—lay in the tomb. But restored whole in the morning, it rose “at dawn”; and behold, it confesses—that is, it makes confessors and singers of praise to the Father among all peoples. [Col. 1222A–B]

In Psalm 108 there is a return to prayer, to weeping or groaning. “O God,” it says, “do not be silent concerning my praise, because the mouth of the sinner and the mouth of the deceitful have opened against me,” etc. This is the well-known and celebrated complaint concerning the most wretched Judas and the Jewish people, who bought Christ from him, expressed in thirty avenging or concessive maledictions. The first is: “Set a sinner over him.” The last: “Let them be clothed with their confusion as with a double garment.” Finally the Head himself says with the body: “I will greatly confess to the Lord with my mouth, and in the midst of many I will praise him,” etc. [Col. 1222B–C]

Then, immediately in the following Psalm, Psalm 109, he declares in this customary fashion what the whole Church ought to confess: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” etc. And this Psalm is well joined to the preceding one: there he dealt with the state of Christ’s extreme humiliation and abasement; here, on the contrary, with his glorious and ineffable exaltation.

Then in Psalm 110 comes the voice of confession, the voice of praise. “I will confess to you,” he says, “O Lord, with my whole heart, in the council of the righteous and in the congregation,” etc. And if you ask for what reason he confesses to the Lord, or why “confession and magnificence are his work,” it immediately follows: “The merciful and compassionate Lord has made a memorial of his wonders; he has given food to those who fear him.” That is, because in the preceding Psalm he said: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek,” and he then instituted that order for us in the sacrament of his body and blood, when he drank “from the torrent in the way”; and, immediately afterward, by the resurrection, with head exalted, opened the understanding of those who feared him so that they might understand the Scriptures. Thus this Psalm fittingly sings in response: “He has given food to those who fear him.” It concludes: “Good understanding to all who do it”—namely, the fear of the Lord. “His praise remains for age upon age.” [Col. 1222C–1223A]

The title of the following Psalm, Psalm 111: “Alleluia, the return of Haggai and Zechariah.” And the sense is: Praise the Lord, looking to that which was signified by the return of Haggai and Zechariah from the Babylonian captivity, who were also present at the rebuilding of the Temple. For it signified that we ought to return from the present captivity to God in the heavenly Jerusalem. The prophetic Spirit calls blessed those who will return there: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord,” he says; “he will greatly delight in his commandments. His seed shall be mighty upon earth; the generation of the upright shall be blessed. Glory and riches shall be in his house,” etc.

In Psalm 112, after *Alleluia* has been prefixed, the spirit of love extends the whole person into praise. “Praise the Lord, children,” it says; “praise the name of the Lord. Let the name of the Lord be blessed from this time forth and for ever.” These children are those who, by the grace of him whom they praise, have been purified from sins. It adds the reasons why they should praise and bless: “Who,” it says, “is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high?” etc. [Col. 1223A–B]

In Psalm 113 likewise *Alleluia* is prefixed, namely for praising the Lord for the conversion of unbelievers to faith, both Jews and Gentiles. Thus it says: “When Israel came out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people, Judah became his sanctification, Israel his dominion.” And the sense is: In that believers have departed from unbelief and the darkness of ignorance, and that combatants—signified by the name Jacob—have departed from the barbarity of demons and vices, all have become Jews, that is, all who confess, “his sanctification”; those who are Israel through faith have become “his dominion,” namely Jacob, so that henceforth no one may glory in the flesh, but in confession and in the power of the Holy Spirit.

“The sea saw this and fled; the Jordan turned backward.” By the sea the fullness of the Gentiles is to be understood; by the Jordan, the baptized. For the Gentiles fled from their former unbelief and errors; the baptized turned backward from the evil habit of sins. Then “the mountains,” that is, the apostles, “rejoiced” and confidently condemned idols. “The idols of the Gentiles,” it says, “are silver and gold, the works of human hands.” [Col. 1223B–C]

In Psalm 114 there is now the third section, namely a recapitulation of tears and groans. “I loved,” it says, “because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer. Because he inclined his ear to me, and in my days I will call upon him. The pains of death surrounded me,” etc. *Alleluia* is rightly prefixed to this Psalm as well, because loving, and suffering pain or groaning through love, belongs to the true and great praise of God. For how great a praise, do you think, is it truly to say, “I found tribulation and sorrow”? How few people are discoverers of their own tribulation and sorrow—of such things, that is, as ought rightly to be considered a discovery? Why ought this to be reckoned a discovery, except because in tribulation and sorrow there is a place suited to the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter? Therefore, after saying, “I found tribulation and sorrow,” he immediately added: “And I called upon the name of the Lord”—supply, saying: “O Lord, deliver my soul,” etc. [Col. 1223D–1224A]

In Psalm 115, likewise after *Alleluia* has been prefixed, the perfect lover of God says praiseworthily: “I believed; therefore I spoke,” that is, I believed and confessed. Then: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” And, finding nothing sufficient to render—for what can suffice for one who loves?—he says: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.” As though he said: I shall offer all my poverty; I shall offer my blood to him; or, if there is no persecutor, I shall frequently celebrate at his holy altar the memorial of his passion. I shall be ready to die for him, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” [Col. 1224A–B]

Psalm 116 is brief in verbal expression, great in meaning: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples.”

Psalm 117 is wholly a voice of confession, a voice of praise, with *Alleluia* prefixed. “Confess to the Lord,” it says, and gives the reason, “because he is good.” “Let all Israel say this; let the house of Aaron say this,” that is, the multitude of faithful prelates; let all say and confess it, all who in chaste fear “fear the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is for ever.” For what did the Lord do whereby he appeared good? “Out of tribulation,” it says, “I called upon the Lord, and he heard me in breadth.” Then: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.” Clearly, the supreme proof of his goodness lies in this. This stone came to the builders and was rejected; but we say: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Again, in conclusion he says as at the beginning: “Confess to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is for ever.” [Col. 1224B–C]

Psalm 118 is divided into twenty-two sections, with eight verses counted in each section. Moreover, each section has as its title one of the letters of the Hebrew alphabet. And we ask what such a heading signifies. We find, then, what is especially to be noted: that this entire psalm shines on its surface with heavenly pearls; [Col. 1224D] that it is, I say, wholly woven together with names of the Word of God, like gleaming gems. For what little verse is there in the whole extended treatment of this psalm in which some term does not resound that is rightly predicated of the Word of God, the Wisdom of God, the Son of God? For example: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way.” Plainly, our way is the Son of God. For he says: “I am the way” (John V).—“Who walk in the law of the Lord.” And what is the law of the Lord but the Word of the Lord? “Blessed are they who search his testimonies.” What are testimonies but words? And what are the many words of God but the one Word of God, the one Wisdom of God? So also in the rest. For one will scarcely find a little verse in which you do not have either ways, commandments, justifications, judgments, sayings, or utterances of the Lord, [Col. 1225A] or something equivalent in force. What, then, does this mean: that, although the psalm is of this kind, its individual sections are entitled by individual letters of the alphabet? Did the spirit of the Prophet, after so many psalms, wish to make us beginners in the ABCs of the Word of God? Certainly we understand this usefully, and truly confess it: however wise we may be, so long as we are in the body we are like little children learning the alphabet in relation to that wisdom of God; and it goes well with us if we attain even its first elements. “For we see through a mirror in an enigma,” says the Apostle (I Cor. XIII). Accordingly, let this psalm of the fourth period be for us both beginning and end.

It is divided, as has already been said, into twenty-two sections. This [Col. 1225B] number consists of three sevens, with one added beyond them, by which an octave is completed from the third seven. Through this we understand that in the eighth age of the world the fullness of the wisdom of God—signified by the words already mentioned in this psalm—will be completed for us; and what the Apostle says will come to pass: “But when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial shall be done away” (ibid.). Therefore let us, as little children, faithfully chant the eight verses of the individual sections, until, by his gift, we attain the eight Beatitudes of the Gospel.

Now let us set down below the interpretation and meaning of these same letters: Aleph, doctrine; Beth, house; Gimel, fullness; Daleth, of tablets; He, this; Vau and Zai, these; Cheth, life; Teth, good; Jod, beginning; Caph, hand; Lamed, [Col. 1225C] of the heart; Mem, from these themselves; Nun, eternal; Samech, help; Ain, fountain; Pe, of the mouth; Zadi, of righteousness; Cuph, calling; Resch, of the head; Schin, of teeth; Thau, signs. The doctrine of the house of God, Israel, is the fullness of the tablets—that is, of the law which was written on tablets. This fullness of the law is charity (Rom. XIII). This doctrine and this fullness, and such a life, are a good beginning of hand and heart—that is, of good intention and good action. For from these comes eternal help, by which we are aided toward eternal life. And this is the fountain of the mouth of righteousness, that is, the source of the doctrine preached by Christ, through which he teaches us to fulfill all righteousness, namely charity, or the doctrine of the house of God. “This is the greatest and first [Col. 1225D] commandment” (Matt. XXII). And this is the calling of the head, that is, of Christ, because all have been called to this: that they may receive this doctrine. In this doctrine there also appear the signs of the teeth, that is, of the apostles and teachers, who are in a sense the teeth of the Church, while they explain obscure and difficult commandments to the weaker members. What could be fairer or more delightful than this alphabet? Behold, all the doctrine of spiritual life is contained here.

In Psalm 119, the fifth period now returns to groaning: the groaning of the perfected, the groaning of a mind that loves and longs. “To the Lord, when I was troubled, I cried, and he heard me.” And then: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged!” etc. Plainly, this is the groaning of the perfect person, who, from the very confidence [Col. 1226A] of perfection, desires “to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I). Yet such a conscience requires humility, and presumption must be guarded against. Thus the title also bears “a song of ascents.” It signifies that one ascending to heaven ought to ascend humbly, lest, while wishing to fly to heaven out of weariness with pilgrimage, one fall into hell.

Accordingly, he goes on and says in Psalm 120: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.” As though he said: I place my confidence not in myself, but in the help of God and all his saints, whose faith I hold and upon whose merits I rely. Then, in prayer, he says to his soul: “May he not give your foot to be moved,” etc. This is [Col. 1226B] to say, according to another psalm: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me” (Ps. XXXV).

Again, in Psalm 121, there are words of confidence, when he says: “I rejoiced in the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord. Our feet were standing in your courts, Jerusalem,” etc. As though he were already there, he said, “our feet were standing,” namely with that conscience with which the Apostle also says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Immediately, in order that he may have confidence in humility, he places his foot upon a higher step of humility.

When in the following Psalm 122 he says: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, you who dwell in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands [Col. 1226C] of her mistress.” He greatly humbles himself when he compares himself to a little maidservant being beaten, with her eyes fixed upon her mistress’s hands until she commands, even by a mere gesture, that she be spared.

Likewise in Psalm 123 he speaks in great and perfect words, words of great rejoicing: “Unless the Lord had been in us, let Israel now say,” etc. Surely it is as though one already victorious says: “Our soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken,” etc.

Then follows Psalm 124, in which those advancing cautiously in humility say: “Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion,” etc. For those who say these things ascribe to God, not to themselves, [Col. 1226D] the fact that they have conquered and escaped.

In the following Psalm 125, they likewise rejoice magnificently and say: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are consoled.” And then: “The Lord has magnified his work with us; we became joyful,” etc.

Psalm 126 follows immediately, and, tempering this joy by salutarily advanced humility, says: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have labored in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain.” Its title is: “A song of ascents for Solomon.” This is right and fitting. For in whom could it be better made known that “unless the Lord builds the house, those who [Col. 1227A] build it have labored in vain”? For he built a house for the Lord, and yet could not himself remain standing, although among human beings he was of singular wisdom. Therefore, having been thoroughly taught by this experience that you cannot build the house without the Lord’s help, receive what I say: “It is vain for you to rise before the light.” Vain, I say, and foolish is the purpose of making yourselves secure before the day of judgment. But “rise after you have sat down”; that is, know yourselves to be secure only when you have laid aside the misery of mortality and passibility.

In Psalm 127 the manner, or tenor, of the song changes in these songs of ascents. For until now the psalms alternated in pairs in such a way that strength sang on high in the first, and fear answered in low tones in the following one. From this point the reverse occurs: in the first of the two, fear sings in low tones, and strength answers in high ones. “Blessed,” he says, “are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways.” And the sense is: Blessed are all who, in the very fact that they walk in the ways of the Lord, are always timid and afraid. And then: “Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed.”

Psalm 128 raises the strong words of one rejoicing as though already victorious. “Often,” he says, “have they attacked me from my youth; let Israel now say: often have they attacked me from my youth, yet they could not prevail against me.” Surely it belongs to a victorious conscience to say, “they could not prevail against me.”

[Col. 1227C] Again, in Psalm 129, he greatly abases himself in humility: “Out of the depths,” he says, “I have cried to you, Lord; Lord, hear my voice.” And then: “If you observe iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall endure?” The answer is understood: no one; because in truth no one will appear righteous in judgment on the basis of his own merits.

In the following Psalm 130, he rejoices, conscious of great virtue and great self-restraint: “Lord, my heart has not been lifted up, nor have my eyes been raised; nor have I walked in great matters, nor in wonders beyond me.” Truly, it belongs to a perfect person to have in his heart such and so great a testimony to preserved humility. “I have not,” he says, “walked in great matters.” But what then? [Col. 1227D] “If I did not think humbly,” etc.

Then, in Psalm 131, he showed us how much, and why, he had humbled himself, saying: “Remember, Lord, David and all his meekness: how he swore to the Lord, made a vow,” etc., as far as “until I find a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob.” That is, because he knew that Christ the Lord would be born from his seed, he desired also to know the place of his birth. Therefore he sat meek and humble; therefore he watched; therefore he prayed. The humility of the meek man was heard, and suddenly he exclaimed: “Behold,” he says, “we have heard of it”—that is, of his birth—“in Ephrathah.” For this Ephrathah is Bethlehem. But from there it is also found “in the fields [Col. 1228A] of the forest,” that is, in the breadth of the Church among the Gentiles, once the narrow confines of Judea have been left behind.

Immediately Psalm 132 is a goodly boast of strength: “Behold,” he says, “how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.” For although they are humble, they know themselves to be Aaron’s beard—that is, strong and perfect—having received from Christ their head the anointing of the Holy Spirit. What, finally, is the meaning of these alternations of strength and fear, of fear and strength? Surely it is what a man of God ought not to fail to know: that there is a time for acting manfully and a time for resting humbly. Thus, when the invisible enemy suggests to a servant of God that he has an excessive contempt for himself, then is the time to act bravely and steadfastly—that is, to remember the gifts or benefits of God which he has received. But when, conversely, that wily deceiver suggests exalted thoughts concerning one’s virtues, as though to a veteran soldier, then is the time to rest—that is, to reflect that he is dust and ashes, who, like a dog, has scarcely received from the Lord’s table a few small crumbs of mercy. Therefore, through the twice seven songs of ascents, the enemy has been overcome seven times from this side, that is, by fear, and seven times from that side, that is, by strength.

And he says in the following psalm, that is, Psalm 133: “Behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord,” etc. As though he said: You who stand, who do not lie down but stand in the house of the Lord, now, without [Col. 1228C] delay and without interruption, bless the Lord, ascribing to him rather than to yourselves the fact that, after ascending so many steps, you stand in his house or courts. To one who thus blesses the Lord, the reward of blessing is returned in this conclusion: “May the Lord bless you from Zion”—that is, proceeding from Zion—he who, before man proceeded from Zion, the same God “made heaven and earth.”

In the following Psalm 134, the blessings continue: for it begins with praises and ends with blessings. After the prefatory Alleluia: “Praise,” he says, “the name of the Lord; praise the Lord, you servants.” And after giving many reasons why we should praise, he reaches this conclusion: “Blessed is the Lord from Zion”—that is, [Col. 1228D] God and man who comes, who both before and after “dwells” in the heavenly “Jerusalem.” Again: “Alleluia. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Psalm 135 runs from beginning to end in wholly sweet-sounding praises and ringing thanksgivings.

The title of Psalm 136 is “A Psalm of David concerning Jeremiah.” From this psalm the sixth period is now woven in a shorter course. For there is a return to the tears of those who love, to the sighs of those who long, “concerning Jeremiah,” that is, according to Jeremiah’s meaning. For just as Jeremiah historically wrote of the captivity of the children of Israel brought about by Nebuchadnezzar, yet understood that something else was signified there, [Col. 1229A] so these men, although they utter the words of history, indicate that something else must nevertheless be understood beneath these same words. “Upon the rivers,” they say, “of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion.”—“As long as we are in the body,” says the Apostle, “we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (I Cor. V). And indeed we are captives in the captivity of sin which Adam brought about. All of us who are children of Zion groan and weep over this captivity, sitting beside the rivers of Babylon, beside the flowing vices of the present age: seeing many immersed in them, and fearing lest we ourselves fall in and be submerged. These, etc., are the psalm’s tears of those who love God, the sighs of those who desire to see the God of gods in Zion.

In the following Psalm 137, again thanksgivings, [Col. 1229B] again praises: “I will give thanks to you, Lord, with my whole heart, because you have heard the words of my mouth.” And then: “May all the kings of the earth give thanks to you, Lord, and sing in the ways of the Lord,” etc. These praises or thanksgivings are not only for benefits bestowed individually upon each person, but also for all those bestowed in common upon the human race.

In Psalm 138, Christ himself, the leader of these thanksgivings and praises, sings, speaking to the Father concerning himself: “Lord, you have tested me and known me.” Throughout this entire psalm he sets forth his perfect righteousness according to his humanity and his sublimity according to his divinity, in order to instruct the faithful in faith and righteousness, so that they may believe him to be both true God and true man, and, led by his example, may not shrink from being troubled [Col. 1229C] and trampled down.

In Psalm 139, from which the final, that is, seventh period begins, all the righteous and perfect pray and give thanks together in one voice, as though from one body: “Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man; deliver me from the unjust man.” By saying these things, etc., they pray that the Lord may preserve in them the perfection of faith and may deliver them from the perversity and perfidy of heretics—indeed, from encounters with malignant spirits, who lie in wait at the end of this life and sharpen their tongues to accuse and convict. For since this is the final period, we rightly look from here to our own end, when the prince of this world comes and seeks in each of us something of his own. Therefore each person, anxious concerning that day and watchful for that imminent hour, [Col. 1229D] says: “Keep me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner.” And then: “Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, you have overshadowed my head in the day of battle.” And immediately: “Do not hand me over, Lord, from my desire to the sinner,” etc.

And immediately in the following psalm, Psalm 140: “Lord, I have cried to you; hear me; attend to my voice when I cry to you.” For who would not need to cry out in the hour of death? “Set, Lord, a guard upon my mouth and a door of enclosure about my lips.” Whoever justifies himself, whoever trusts that he himself will appear righteous before the Lord, has neither such a guard nor such a door. But the one who said had them: “If he should wish to contend [Col. 1230A] with me, I could not answer him one thing out of a thousand” (Job IX). And then: “If I should wish to justify myself, my own mouth would condemn me” (ibid.). Again: “Even if I had anything righteous, I would not answer, but would entreat my judge” (ibid.). For this is what is said here also: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of the sinner shall not anoint my head.” Namely, lest in that necessity, when my lamp has gone out, I go in vain to buy oil, therefore, while I live, let the righteous correct me, but let the flatterer not deceive me.

Likewise, in the following Psalm 141: “With my voice,” he says, “I cried to the Lord; with my voice I made supplication to the Lord.” It is understood: desiring to be dissolved and to be with Christ (Phil. I). What, then, did I cry? What did I ask? What prayer do I pour out in his presence? “Lead my soul out of prison, that it may give thanks to your name.” “Out of prison,” he says, out of the dungeon of this captivity, where I cannot see my God, because of the guilt of the first parent, who, expelled from the light of paradise, begot all of us here as though in a prison. To this belongs the title of the psalm: “A contemplation of David when he was in the cave.” Primarily, indeed, it refers to Christ while he was still in the cave—namely, in mortal and passible flesh—with Saul, that is, death, pursuing him; but secondarily it refers to every faithful person who desires to be brought out of this miserable life as though out of prison. He desires this because he fears it, and fears it because he desires it.

[Col. 1230C] Hence immediately, in Psalm 142, he says: “Lord, hear my prayer; with your ears receive my supplication in your truth; hear me in your righteousness. And do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no living person shall be justified in your sight.” For if the matter concerns merits alone, no one will be justified. Therefore he likewise says: “For your name’s sake, Lord, you will give me life in your righteousness.” That is, so that everything may be of grace. Again: “Cause me to hear your mercy in the morning.” Your mercy, I say, which triumphs over judgment, when in the morning—that is, on the day of judgment—you say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV). Accordingly, this psalm fittingly bears the title: “A Psalm of David when his son was pursuing him.” For apart from the one Christ, there was not, [Col. 1230D] is not, and will not be any David so strong-handed that he has begotten a son whom he does not suffer as an enemy, who has not contracted sin by which he is pressed down if God enters into judgment with a human being. From here to the end are unbroken blessings, most fervent thanksgivings, and songs of praise, which faith suggests, hope conceives, and charity pours forth.

The following Psalm 143: “Blessed,” he says, “is the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle,” etc. These are the words of one who knows well in his conscience that he has with him a true friend who fights alongside him. In contemplation of that hour, in which he will have to contend with the prince of this world, who will without doubt come against him, he says to him: “You who delivered David [Col. 1231A] your servant from the evil sword, deliver me.” And so that I may be able to escape that sword in that hour, meanwhile, he says, “rescue me from the hand of foreign children,” that is, heretics or all the ungodly, “whose mouth has spoken vanity,” etc. Thus its title fittingly reads: “A Psalm of David against Goliath.” For one who, while living, conquered Goliath—that is, the devil—in his own members, and trusts that when dying he will be delivered from his evil sword, blesses the Lord God in this psalm.

The title of the following Psalm 144 is “Praise for David himself,” namely, praise sung from the mouth of one who loves to Christ, the true David. “I will exalt you,” he says, “Lord my God, my king, and I will bless your name forever and ever.” It begins with blessings, runs through blessings, and ends in everlasting blessings.

Then in Psalm 145, after the prefatory Alleluia, with how much feeling and how much love he directs praise is shown when he addresses his soul and says: “Praise the Lord, my soul.” And it answers: “I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I am.” From what source shall I praise? From what source shall I sing? From power and from mercy. From power, because “he made heaven and earth, the sea, and all things that are in them.” From mercy, because “he frees those in bonds,” because “he enlightens the blind,” etc.

Not content with his praise alone, in the following Psalm 146 he exhorts others also to praise: “Praise,” he says, [Col. 1231C] “the Lord, for the psalm is good.” And indeed the psalm is good, since these three things cooperate in it: the strings, the sound, and the movement of the fingers. By the strings we understand the drying up of the flesh; by the sound, virtues; by the movement of the fingers, good works. When these are brought to it, our praise is truly pleasing and beautiful to God. He immediately adds the reasons why we should praise: “The Lord,” he says, “building Jerusalem, will gather together the dispersions of Israel,” etc.

From that gathering of Israel, from the salvation of those broken ones, and from the calling or numbering of those stars, one city comes into being: the heavenly Jerusalem. Psalm 147 accordingly invites it to praise and says: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion,” etc. . . At last, as though choirs had been arranged for praise and a multitude had begun to sound forth, universal praise is begun: all creatures exult together with their own voice, and an unbroken harmony extends its cry without interruption or interval throughout the remaining three psalms.

First, in Psalm 148, the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of charity, says, as though immediately commanded by the word Alleluia: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights.” The choir of heavenly beings praises; all angels praise; all powers praise; all heavenly things, visible and invisible, praise. Why? “Because he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created.” Then earth and all earthly things praise. Why? Because he visited the earth which he had created and caused his praise to be not only above heaven but also [Col. 1232A] above earth. Therefore the subject of praise in this psalm is that he both created all things and redeemed the human race.

In the following Psalm 149, likewise the Holy Spirit says: “Alleluia. Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise in the assembly of the saints.” Why? “Because the Lord has been well pleased with his people,” because “the saints shall rejoice in glory,” because “the exaltations of God are in their throats,” because “two-edged swords are in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations, that they may execute upon them the written judgment.” Therefore the subject of song or praise in this psalm is that he will judge the world and glorify his saints in judgment.

In the final Psalm 150, the holy [Col. 1232B] Spirit of charity likewise says: “Alleluia. Praise the Lord in his saints.” Ten times he says “praise,” and adds or inserts no reason why they should praise; and so he concludes at the end: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.” Therefore the subject of praise in this psalm is that ineffable blessedness of the age to come—how great or what kind it is cannot be spoken or estimated—which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man (Isa. LXIV; I Cor. II).

## CHAPTER VI. How Solomon, by the same path, commends faith, hope, and charity: faith in Proverbs, hope in Ecclesiastes, charity in the Song of Songs

The same understanding of faith, hope, and charity [Col. 1232C] which we have followed in David, behold, we also see quite clearly in Solomon, with the door standing open. For he wrote three books: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. The first book, that of Proverbs, calls us to faith. The second, Ecclesiastes, invites us to hope. The third, the Song of Songs, unquestionably draws us to charity. We do not undertake to traverse this depth; rather, hastening on to other matters, we shall touch upon it only in passing.

He calls us to faith in Proverbs when, in the person of Wisdom, who is Christ, he says: “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. From eternity I was ordained, and from ancient times, before the earth was made. The abysses did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the fountains of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood in their massive weight; before the hills I was brought forth” (Prov. VIII). And then: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven columns. She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table” (ibid.). For what Wisdom says here, “The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways,” etc., the Evangelist confirms: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; this was in the beginning with God” (John I). And what it says here, “When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he enclosed the abysses by a fixed law,” etc., “I was with him arranging all things,” is what the same Evangelist expresses: “All things,” he says, “were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid.). [Col. 1233A] Likewise, what it says here, “And I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the world of the earth, and my delights were to be with the children of men” (Prov. VIII), is what the same one mentioned above says: “What was made in him was life” (John I).

Then what it says here, “Wisdom built herself a house,” is what the same Evangelist says: “And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.). And what it further says, “She hewed out seven columns; she sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and to the walls of the city,” means that he distributed the gifts of the Holy Spirit and chose the weak things of the world in order to overcome the strong (I Cor. I), and to call people to faith in the Gospel. For indeed he hewed seven columns, as it were, from the rock, when, from the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in himself, he never ceases to distribute to those who believe in him the gifts of the sevenfold [Col. 1233B] Holy Spirit.

Likewise he says: “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well. Let your fountains flow abroad, and distribute your waters in the streets” (Prov. V). What does this mean but that, by believing in Christ, one receives the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that one may offer saving doctrine to others? For incarnate Wisdom itself intended this to be understood when it said: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII). Therefore what it later says, “That he may keep you from an evil woman and from the flattering tongue of a stranger. Let not your heart desire her beauty, lest you be captured by her glances” (Prov. VI), is rightly understood as spoken concerning the avoidance of heretical teaching.

Since these matters stand thus, why does he exhort, at the beginning of Proverbs, to avoid the shedding of blood, unless he has in view Christ’s passion, which is the summit of our salvation and upon which our faith chiefly depends? Since it is the summit of human salvation, he rightly began his proverbial discourses with it. “My son,” he says, “if sinners entice you, do not consent to them. If they say: Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood, let us secretly lay snares against the innocent without cause, and let us swallow him alive like hell” (Prov. I), etc. Surely the Pharisees and chief priests, who thus spoke, were sinners; and by saying this they enticed the wretched people, and it consented to them. Yet Wisdom preached publicly, gave her voice in the streets, and cried aloud at the head of the crowds. At last, not heard, it said: “I also will laugh at your destruction and mock when what you feared [Col. 1234A] comes upon you” (ibid.). What you feared, he says, is understood from their words: “Lest perhaps the Romans come and take away our place and nation” (John XI).

Who doubts that Ecclesiastes instructs us toward hope in future things when it says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. I)? Why is everything vanity unless everything is transitory? And why does it say these things, why does it charge with vanity all things that are under heaven, unless in order that, by hope in future things—which are solid—and hope in invisible things—which are eternal—it may teach that these present and visible things ought to be despised? It runs through all things, judges all things, condemns as vanity everything in the world, every desire of the flesh, every desire of the eyes. And at first it approves certain things, for example when it says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” [Col. 1234B] (Eccles. IX). But afterward, taking up the judgment of reason again: “Youth,” it says, “and pleasure are vanity.” Thus it is called Ecclesiastes, which is interpreted “preacher,” because it first puts forward an unsound opinion on individual matters, then itself immediately, as though singing in concert, refutes it with firm reasons before everyone. Finally, at the end of the book it clearly shows its aim: “Let us all hear together the end of the discourse: Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccles. XI). “For this is the whole duty of man.—And God will bring into judgment all things that are done, for every error, whether it be good or evil” (ibid.).

In the Song of Songs, the universal Church—or individually any faithful soul that has now advanced as far as [Col. 1234C] love of God—utters this first word: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I). Plainly, the Church obtained the kiss of the mouth when the Son of God was incarnate, when, in the bridal chamber of the virgin’s womb, divine nature was joined to human nature in one person. Likewise, every soul that loves God receives a kiss when it merits to taste the sweetness of divinity through hidden inspiration. Yet this contact passes so swiftly that it is rightly compared to the whisper of a gentle breeze. But it will receive a fuller kiss and complete union when, after laying aside the body, it is brought to behold the very face of its beloved. There is no need to linger; for we have no need either to teach or to be taught that charity is signified throughout all the utterances of this book. Let us therefore pass on to other matters.

# THE FIFTH BOOK ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS  
*(III Kings XI; IV Kings XIII)*

[Col. 1233]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the Lord’s statement to Solomon, “Because you have kept this with yourself”: what it means for someone to keep his sin with himself; and why the Lord consequently foretold that his kingdom would be torn away

*(III KINGS, CHAPTER XI)*

“Therefore the Lord said to Solomon: [Col. 1234D] ‘Because you have kept this with yourself, and have not kept my covenant and my commandments which I commanded you, I will rend your kingdom apart and give it to your servant.’”—“Because,” he says, “you have kept this with yourself.” It is clear that the one to whom this is said has not yet confessed his sin. For he keeps with himself what he has done when it does not displease him. But if it displeases him, he must be said to hold it not with himself but against himself. For he does not conceal it but declares it; he does not defend it but accuses it. “For,” he says, “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always against me” (Ps. L). Again: “For I will declare my iniquity” (Ps. XXXVII).

Therefore, he says, “I will rend your kingdom apart”—that is, the thing which almost happened to your father, except that he declared his iniquity and was troubled over his sin. “For Sheba son of Bichri sounded the trumpet, saying: ‘We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse.’ And all Israel separated itself from David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah remained attached to their king” (II Kings XX). Neither Absalom could take the kingdom from him, nor Sheba tear it apart, because, indeed, what you have kept with yourself, he did not keep with himself. He had sinned less, and he shook off the sin from himself, accused it, and declared it.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the words, “And you have not kept my covenant”; how Solomon is rightly reproved for having asked for wisdom, although this pleased the Lord; and concerning what he received in a dream by night, though he was not to persevere
“And you did not keep my covenant,” he says. “For I had made a covenant with you in these words: ‘If you walk in my ways and keep my commandments, as your father walked, I will lengthen your days’ (3 Kings 3).” You did not walk in my ways, but “[Col. 1235C] kept this within yourself.” Therefore I am not bound to “lengthen your days.”

Here it is rightly asked why, when making the covenant, he made the lengthening of Solomon’s days conditional. Clearly, because Solomon is rightly reproved for this: when the Lord gave him the choice in that night through a dream, saying, “Ask what you wish me to give you” (ibid.), he did not ask for what would have been best—long days, eternal days—but asked for wisdom to discern judgment and for an understanding heart to judge the people (ibid.). “How then,” you ask, “is it written: ‘The saying pleased the Lord, because Solomon had asked for such a thing’?” (ibid.). To this I say: it pleased him, not as the highest or perfect good, but [Col. 1235D] as a good in comparison with worse things. Therefore he says: “Because you did not ask for many days for yourself, nor riches, nor the life of your enemies, but asked wisdom for yourself, behold, I have given it to you” (ibid.).

Certainly riches, many days of this present life, or vengeance upon enemies are indeed certain goods, but very low ones. To possess favor in the eyes of the Lord and the days of eternity is the true, highest, and perfect good. But to possess wisdom for discerning judgment is indeed a good, yet a middling good. Therefore it did indeed please the Lord that Solomon asked for such a thing; nevertheless he is blameworthy in that, when the Lord’s generosity so readily offered him a choice, he did not ask for that good which is true and supreme. Thus he is rightly censured because he received wisdom [Col. 1236A] in the night and through a dream, and was not to persevere in it.

## CHAPTER III. That in this judgment God handed over to Jeroboam the rending of the kingdom, and what sins of the people had preceded it.

“Now it came to pass at that time that Jeroboam went out from Jerusalem, and Ahijah the Shilonite prophet, wrapped in a new cloak, found him on the road. They alone were in the field. And Ahijah took hold of his new cloak with which he was wrapped, tore it into twelve pieces, and said to Jeroboam: ‘Take ten pieces for yourself. For thus says the Lord God of Israel: Behold, I shall tear the kingdom from Solomon’s hand, and I shall give you ten tribes.’”

The meaning is plain and appropriate to the matter itself. In the prophet [Col. 1236B] the Lord speaks; and the people who adhere to him are a certain cloak, or as it were a garment, of the Lord. But did the Lord not know what sort of man Jeroboam was, or what he was going to do, when so many pieces of the cloak—so many tribes of the people—were assigned to him? Did he not know, I say, that when he received the people torn away from the house of David, he would himself tear them away from God, by making a golden calf for them to worship as God? Why, then, did he procure such a king for his people?

Certainly he did this reasonably and in judgment, and with the same justice by which he gave Saul to those who demanded a king—a king whose future character he could not have failed to know. For then too they rejected Samuel—or rather, God in Samuel—as he himself said: “For they have not rejected you, but me” (1 Kings 8). And now they resented David’s reigning, or [Col. 1236C] having reigned, over them.

This is evident from the very sequence of events. At the beginning of David’s reign they withdrew from him for the whole seven years, neither following nor approving the Lord’s choice; David reigned at Hebron only over the tribe of Judah. Thereafter they were always wavering, always faithless toward David. What rebel against him would they not raise up, when they set Absalom his son over themselves as king against his father? After Absalom perished, they immediately followed Sheba son of Bichri when he dared to sound the trumpet, saying: “We have no share in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (2 Kings 20). Now also they revealed their envy by seeking occasions against Rehoboam and saying: “Your father imposed a most grievous yoke upon us” (3 Kings 12), although through Solomon’s wisdom they had become rich and renowned.

Therefore, as a judge, he handed the guilty over to such a king: one who would, with their own consent, tear them away from the house of David; with their own consent, I say, tear them away from the city of David; divide them from the temple of God, from the worship of the one and only true God; and make them serve idols which they had desired.

## CHAPTER IV. Why the prophet made so many pieces of his cloak, and that from that time the kingdom of Israel was rent ten times.

There is still this to ask: why did the prophet make pieces? Why did he tear his cloak into twelve pieces? Surely, if he meant to signify nothing but the division of one kingdom into two kingdoms, he could have torn one cloak into two unequal [Col. 1237A] pieces, unequal by the same measure in which one tribe was smaller than ten tribes in number. Why then did this manner rather please the prophet—or rather, the Spirit of the Lord in the prophet—and why did he make so many pieces?

Plainly, here too there is the consistency of true reason. For that kingdom of Israel, torn away from the house of David, was afterwards divided against itself ten times; and thus at last it was desolated, so that house fell upon house (Luke 11), when the king of Assyria transferred Israel beside the river Gozan into the cities of the Medes. It is easy to trace these divisions.

Baasha struck down Nadab, the son of this Jeroboam: this was the second rending of Israel’s kingdom. Zimri killed Elah, Baasha’s son, and reigned in his place. Zimri burned himself in the palace when Omri besieged him; Omri then reigned in his place [Col. 1237B] (3 Kings 15, 16, 22). After him Ahab reigned; after Ahab, his son Ahaziah; and after him, his brother Joram (4 Kings 9, 10, 15). But Jehu killed Joram and reigned in his place, down to the fourth generation. Shallum struck down the fifth after him and reigned in his place. Menahem likewise struck Shallum down and reigned in his place. Pekah son of Remaliah also struck down Pekahiah, Menahem’s son, and reigned in his place. Hoshea conspired against Pekah, struck him down, killed him, and reigned in his place. Against Hoshea the king of Assyria came up and transferred Israel among the Assyrians.

This was the tenth rending. For in Jeroboam was the first, in Baasha the second, in Zimri the third, in Omri the fourth, in Jehu the fifth, in Shallum the sixth, in Menahem the seventh, in Pekah son of Remaliah the eighth, in Hoshea the ninth, and in the king of Assyria the tenth [Col. 1237C]. He divided those already divided from God and David their king, even by transferring them in place into Assyria. Thus the count is rightly made. Well, therefore, when the prophet cut one kingdom into two kingdoms, he nevertheless gave Jeroboam ten pieces as the sign of division, because he foresaw that the kingdom would be divided ten times and so desolated.

## CHAPTER V. That this is an example of heretics, who tear themselves away from the house of David, from the Church of Christ; and why it is rightly said, “One tribe shall remain to Solomon,” although two may be named, Judah and Benjamin.

This is an example of heretics. In this way they too have been torn from the Church and divided against themselves; and [Col. 1237D] thus their kingdom has been desolated, and house has fallen upon house. The tribe of Judah, whose name means “confession,” and the city of David are the Catholic Church, holding the true confession of the one faith. Heretics went out from this Church through their divisions, as it is said: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

The brother of this Catholic Church is the Lord Jesus Christ, who, incarnate, says: “You have wounded my heart, my friend, my sister, bride” (Song 4). Again: “A garden enclosed, my sister, bride” (ibid.). This brother is rightly represented here by this prophet; for Ahijah means “my brother.” Before heretics went out from us, they were with us one cloak of this our brother, through harmony in the same religion and agreement in the same confession. But they went out from us and followed their errors [Col. 1238A]. Thus, as they went out, the cloak was torn and the pieces were handed to Jeroboam.

Jeroboam means “judging the people.” He signifies some heresiarch who, through the breath of his pride, so judges the Christian people as the wind in the threshing-floor judges chaff and grain. Arius, or any other heresiarch, blew; and by his breath he drove wherever he wished those who were vain and carnal, who, even while they still professed that they knew God with us, denied him by their deeds (Titus 1). In this manner the authors of heresies have often usefully judged the people. For “there must,” says the Apostle, “be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 1).

Here it must not be overlooked that, after the prophet had said [Col. 1238B], “Take ten pieces for yourself,” he added: “But one tribe shall remain to Solomon for the sake of David my servant.” Certainly one tribe and ten make eleven. Were there not twelve tribes of Israel? Why, then, did he say that only one tribe remained? Did not Rehoboam reign over Judah and Benjamin? Indeed, he also had very many from the other tribes under his rule. For it is later written: “Rehoboam reigned over all the children of Israel who dwelt in the cities of Judah” (3 Kings 12). Therefore this must be understood mystically: when heretics who were not of us go out from us, all who remain in the Church’s peace are rightly called one tribe, because we are not divided by schisms.

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1238C] That the devising of the calves mystically represents every invention of heretics; and how greatly their fellowship must be avoided is shown by the fact that the lion found and killed the man of God because, deceived, he ate bread there.

(3 Kings, chapter 12.) “And after Jeroboam had devised a plan, he made two golden calves and said to the people: ‘Do not go up any longer to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,’” etc.

“After he had devised a plan,” it says. O thought without understanding, and counsel without prudence! Could he, by thinking thus and counselling himself thus, reign more securely than by placing his hope in the Lord? He could indeed call the people away so that they would not go up to sacrifice in the house of the Lord; but he could not receive from this utterly evil root the fruit of a lasting kingdom for which he hoped. He reigned twenty-two years. Rather, as a slave of sin, he served [Col. 1238D] golden calves and was deprived both of kingdom and life; and he left to his son Nadab, as an inheritance, the punishment for the sin which he had stored up.

For Baasha of the house of Issachar plotted against Nadab and struck him down; and thus Jeroboam was destroyed, according to the answer and harsh message of the prophet already mentioned: “as dung is customarily swept away until it is clean” (3 Kings 14). Every plan of heretics was like this. For they too made golden calves so that the people might not go up to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the Lord. What is a heretical discourse, polished and carefully composed, but a golden calf? A golden calf [Col. 1239A] is beautiful outwardly, but inwardly empty and without sense. So every doctrine of heretics possesses outwardly the elegance of speech to charm the ears, but inwardly has no power. Therefore all who, because of beauty of speech, follow heretics who are vain and devoid of virtue worship golden calves.

“And Jeroboam went up upon the altar to burn incense.” It was not said, “he approached the altar” or “went up to the altar,” but “he went up upon the altar.” In accordance with the meaning already given, this is said elegantly and properly. For heretics climb upon their own altars because they seek not God’s glory but their own, because they preach themselves and not the Lord Jesus Christ.

How greatly their fellowship must be avoided is immediately indicated by the example which follows. The man of God who [Col. 1239B] had come from Judah at the Lord’s word, while Jeroboam stood upon the altar, and who had cried out against the altar, was found on the road by a lion and killed. For he had been commanded by the word of the Lord: “Do not eat bread, nor drink water, nor return by the way by which you came” (3 Kings 13). But a false prophet deceived him, led him back with him, and he ate bread in his house and drank water. Therefore, as had been foretold, the lion killed him on the road.

Thus we are taught to avoid the fellowship of heretics who have made calves of falsehood, and not even to take food with such persons, lest the lion find us on the road and a punishment like that of heretics come upon us. Meanwhile, it should be noted that this prophet, deceived in himself, received his punishment; but Jeroboam himself [Col. 1239C] slept with his fathers, whereas his son perished, struck by an enemy’s sword. For one who perhaps through imprudence is deceived into fellowship with heretics is, as it were, punished in himself when he is presently visited with a temporal punishment. But one who maliciously constructs a heresy receives sentence, as it were, in his son, when in his soul after this life he incurs everlasting death.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Elijah: whom he prefigured when he brought drought because of Ahab and Jezebel; why ravens fed him; and why he was sent to the widow of Zarephath.

(3 Kings, chapter 17.) After these things impiety increased in [Col. 1239D] Israel when Baal was added to Jeroboam’s calves. For Ahab son of Omri took Jezebel, daughter of Methbaal king of the Sidonians, as his wife; and he went and served Baal and worshipped him. Then Elijah the prophet, one of the inhabitants of Gilead, arose and by the word of the Lord restrained heaven, so that it did not rain upon the earth for three years and six months.

“As the Lord God of Israel lives,” he said, “before whom I stand, there shall be neither dew nor rain in these years except according to the word of my mouth. And the word of the Lord came to him, saying: ‘Arise, go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and remain there; for I have commanded a widow woman there to feed you,’” etc.

The lamp of the Gospel here shows us the light of spiritual understanding. For after the Lord had said [Col. 1240A]: “Surely you will say to me this proverb: ‘Physician, heal yourself; the things we have heard were done in Capernaum, do here also in your own country’” (Luke 4), he immediately added: “Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country. Truly I say to you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months and a great famine came upon the whole land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to Zarephath of Sidon, to a widow woman” (ibid.).

By saying this, he certainly intended it to be understood that he himself would not be accepted in his own country; and that, just as Elijah went over to the widow of Zarephath, leaving drought in Israel, so he would pass over to the Church from the Gentiles, leaving in Israel a famine of the word of God. Therefore he prefaced this so solemnly by saying [Col. 1240B], “Truly I say to you,” an expression which clearly sounds a great threat of approaching wrath.

Mystically, therefore, Elijah, whose name means “God the Lord,” is the Son of God himself, God and Lord of heaven and earth. Ahab, whose name means “brother of the father,” is the Jewish people, persecutor and killer of this same God and Lord: brother, I say, of the father—that is, co-heir with the devil, their father. This Elijah, this God and Lord, proves it when he says: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). Jezebel, whose name means “flow of blood,” is the synagogue of that same people; since it spoke thus, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27), it has not ceased to flow with blood until now.

Under her figure the Apocalypse speaks against the Jewish sect and every sect opposed to evangelical [Col. 1240C] faith: “But I have a few things against you, because you permit the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce my servants, to commit fornication and to eat things sacrificed to idols” (Revelation 2), etc.

What then does it mean that Elijah shuts heaven so that it may not rain and withdraws, except that Christ shut the mouths of the apostles against the sinful synagogue and the people who rejected him; and, leaving them drought and a famine of hearing or understanding the Word of God, withdrew? “Withdraw,” says the Lord, “and hide yourself; and I have commanded ravens to feed you.” The ravens first fed God the Lord, hidden from the Jews, whom they cannot find because the veil of malice has been placed over their [Col. 1240D] heart (2 Corinthians 3). For sinners, imitating the blackness of ravens through humble conscience, first received him with faith and charity. Foreseeing this, he himself said in one place to the scribes and Pharisees: “Amen, I say to you, tax collectors and prostitutes shall go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 21).

These ravens first fed Elijah at the torrent, because tax collectors and sinners first received Christ and his apostles in Judaea. “After some days the torrent dried up,” because in a short time those believers who were from the Jews suffered the plundering of their possessions (Hebrews 10) at the hands of their fellow-countrymen, so that, when all things failed, they themselves were in need. “For it had not rained upon the land.” Indeed, that land did not receive the saving rain of truth.

“Then the word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: ‘Arise and go to Zarephath of the Sidonians,’” etc. Zarephath was a small town of the Sidonians, situated on the public road. Now Sidon means [Col. 1241A] “useless hunting.” And what were we Gentiles but useless prey, the devil’s prey? Therefore, “Go,” he says, “to Zarephath of the Sidonians”—that is, go to the Gentiles, proclaim the Gospel publicly, preach throughout the whole world. “You shall remain there; for I have commanded a widow woman there to feed you.”

“I have commanded: I have laid down a command which shall not pass away. Through the predestination of grace I have gone beforehand to the widow woman”—that is, to the Gentile world, once unhappily married to the devil, an evil husband, but now a widow because he has been cast out—“that she may feed you,” that she may believe in you. “You shall remain there”: you shall be with her until the consummation of the age.

“He arose and went to Zarephath.” Christ arose and [Col. 1241B] went, I say, in the apostles, in whom he spoke: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

“And when he came to the gates of the city, a widow woman appeared to him, gathering sticks.” Christ now comes to the city gate when the Gentile world first receives the word of God with open hearing. Then the widow woman appeared; believing quickly, she offered herself, and the Church stood before the face of him who called her.

“I have no bread,” she says, “except as much flour as a handful can hold in a jar, and a little oil in a flask. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and prepare it for myself and my son, that we may eat and die.” The true Catholic [Col. 1241C] Church knows that it is in great poverty. It is not proud, does not exalt itself, and does not consider itself rich or self-sufficient as long as it is a widow, as long as it is a pilgrim. Whatever in the meantime it receives from the word of God and the knowledge of God is little: like only as much flour as a handful can hold. Whatever anointing it has from the Holy Spirit is like a little oil in a flask. For what is that which we now see through a mirror in an enigma (1 Corinthians 13), compared with the perfection for which we wait?

Therefore, “I have only a little flour and a little oil,” she says. “Behold, I gather two sticks”: behold, I console my poverty by embracing the wood of the cross, “that I may prepare it for myself and my son,” that from the little I have I may prepare good discourse for a hearer [Col. 1241D] newly initiated into the faith, “that we may eat and die.” For we do not yet reckon that we have attained. We work for food that does not perish (John 6); we work, as far as we can, the bread of life. Baked upon the holy altar with the two pieces of wood, marked by Christ’s cross and passion, we receive and give it “that we may eat and die.” For we confess that we do this unworthily, and therefore deserve to die if we are judged without mercy.

“Do not fear,” he says, “but go and do as you have said. Yet first make for me from that little flour a small cake baked under ashes, and bring it to me. Afterwards you shall make for yourself and your son.”

“Do not fear, but go,” having the hope of life [Col. 1242A], “and do as you have said,” believing this promise: “Whoever eats of this bread shall live for ever” (ibid.). Yet, in order that you may not fear, that you may deservedly have hope, that you may live for ever, “from that little flour”—from that faith of yours, from that evangelical tradition—“first make for me a small cake baked under ashes.” Humble your soul in fasting and offer a worthy sacrifice of repentance; then at last “you shall make for yourself and your son,” that is, you shall worthily offer and worthily receive.

“For thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘The jar of flour shall not fail, nor shall the flask of oil diminish, until the day on which the Lord gives rain upon the face of the earth.’” “It shall not fail,” he says, but shall have the effect of life “until he gives rain upon the face of the earth,” until the fullness of eternal refreshment comes. Where does the Lord God of Israel say this? In his Gospel, in his Apostle [Col. 1242B]: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup,” says the Apostle, “you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Corinthians 2).

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the son of the mistress of the household whom Elijah raised, who is said to have been Jonah; and what his death mystically signifies.

“Now it came to pass after these words that the son of the mistress of the household became ill; and his illness was very severe, so that no breath remained in him. Therefore she said to Elijah: ‘What have I to do with you, man of God?’” etc.

The Hebrews affirm that the son of this widow woman, whom Elijah raised, was the holy Jonah, who is called the son of Amittai at the beginning of his own book. They also say that for this reason the boy was called the son of Amittai, because [Col. 1242C] his mother said: “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that the word of the Lord in your mouth is true.” For *Amittai* means “truth” in our language. Because Elijah spoke truth, he who was raised is called the son of truth. And fittingly the dove is born from truth; for Jonah means “dove.”

Mystically, in the widow’s son we understand the same thing as in Lazarus, brother of Martha and Mary, in the Gospel (John 11). For the Church is rightly prefigured both by this woman’s house and by theirs. In this house Elijah, whose name means “God the Lord,” was in some way supported; in that house service was rendered in temporal things to God the Lord Jesus Christ. Thus both the widow’s son here and Lazarus there signify a sinner who [Col. 1242D] is a son of the Church and who, after receiving faith, has died in soul by committing a sin worthy of death.

Yet there is this difference: this one is raised in the house, while the other, dead four days, is recalled from the tomb (ibid.). Accordingly, this one signifies a sinner in recent fall, while the other signifies one made foul by an evil habit. The widow woman says, therefore; Mother Church says to the Lord God: “What have I to do with you, man of God?” Why does the man—or human being—contend with me in judgment (Jeremiah 2), he who is at once God and man, Son of God? “Have you entered to me to bring my iniquities to remembrance, to kill my son?”

Certainly Mother Church is so moved by loving devotion for her sinful son that, when one of her own dies through sin, she attributes it to her own iniquities. Strong in this piety, she prays so as to rebuke, rebukes so as to pray, and prevails. For Elijah says [Col. 1243A]: “Give me your son.” The Lord God says: Give me your sinner. Give him to me: come, exhort him to be present through humble confession. Then it says: “Taking him, he placed him upon his own bed.”

Elijah’s bed, the bed of God the Lord, is the holy altar and the pure, devout assembly of the holy Church. There he stretches himself out and measures himself over the boy three times. For he condescends to the penitent sinner; and when confession and satisfaction have been received, faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—which had been dead—revives and is restored. This is true restoration, and true proof of the saying: “Behold, your son lives.”

## CHAPTER IX. What Elijah’s return and showing himself to Ahab mystically [Col. 1243B] signifies; what the prophets of Baal signify when they cry out and cut themselves until bloody; what the fire invoked by Elijah and falling from heaven upon the burnt offering signifies; and what is meant by the rain being given and Elijah, girding his loins, running before Ahab.

(3 Kings, chapter 18.) “After many days the Word of the Lord came to Elijah in the third year, saying: ‘Go and show yourself to Ahab, that I may give rain upon the face of the earth,’” etc. He went and was sent for this purpose, to show himself so that rain might be given upon the face of the earth. And this came to pass. “He prayed again, and behold, the heavens became dark, and cloud and wind came, and there was heavy rain.”

Thus it shall be: the drought and famine of hearing the word of God which came upon Israel will be turned into every fullness in the last days, when Enoch and Elijah come and preach. But what does this mean: that Elijah meanwhile hastens forward as though angry; that he does not use words of warning, but acts in judgment and contends as in a quarrel?

“Elijah,” he says, “go to Obadiah, and say to your lord: [Col. 1243C] ‘Elijah is here.’” Then: “Ahab came to meet Elijah, and when he saw him, said: ‘Are you that man who troubles Israel?’ And he said: ‘I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house, because you have forsaken the commandments of the Lord and followed the Baals. Yet now send and gather to me all Israel upon Mount Carmel, and four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and four hundred prophets of the groves, who eat at Jezebel’s table.’”

So it was done. They came, and in the contest the Lord appeared superior [Col. 1243D] by answering through fire. “And all the people said: ‘The Lord himself is God; the Lord himself is God.’” Immediately it follows: “And Elijah said to them: ‘Seize the prophets of Baal; let not even one of them escape.’ When they had seized them, Elijah brought them down to the brook Kishon and killed them there.”

What, I ask, does this mean: that when the Lord was about to give rain upon the face of the earth, Elijah first came armed with such zeal? Surely it is what the true Elijah, the true God and Lord, foretells in his Gospel: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near” (Luke 21). And afterward: “For there shall be great distress upon the [Col. 1244A] earth and wrath against this people. They shall fall by the edge of the sword and shall be led captive into all nations” (ibid.).

Certainly Elijah—that is, God the Lord—came angry against Baal’s priests when, by the will of that same God and Lord, the Roman army surrounded the city of Jerusalem. For, as no believer doubts, Annas and Caiaphas, the remaining priests, all the elders, all the scribes and Pharisees who cried out against the Lord were priests of Baal—or rather, priests of Barabbas the robber. They contended for Barabbas; they took their stand in the contest for a robber. “They persuaded the people to ask that Barabbas should be released to them and that Jesus should be destroyed” (Matthew 27). There they cried out loudly: “Away, away; crucify, crucify” (John 19); and according to their custom they cut themselves [Col. 1244B] with knives and lances until they were covered with blood. According to their custom, I say; for it was always their practice to shed blood and be bloodied. And now they were covered with blood still more, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

But behold: while those priests led the sacrifice of their Barabbas, God the Father answered our Elijah, our God and Lord, through fire; for through him he gave us the Holy Spirit. How? “The waters ran around the altar,” it says, “and the trench of the water-channel was filled,” etc. Certainly, when the soldier’s spear opened the side of the crucified Lord, water ran with blood (John 29 [as printed]). Then fire fell from heaven [Col. 1244C]—the fire, I say, of which he himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it be kindled?” (Luke 12). That fire fell immediately after the burnt offering, namely upon the apostles, when divided tongues as of fire appeared to them (Acts 4 [as printed]), etc.

Moreover, Obadiah, whom Elijah met and to whom he said, “Go and say to your lord: ‘Elijah is here,’” is the very one reckoned fourth in the order of the prophets. Obadiah means “servant of the Lord.” He is rightly called by this name, for he acted as a servant of the Lord ought to act. “Your servant,” he says, “has feared the Lord from his youth. Has it not been reported to you, my lord, what I did when Jezebel killed the prophets of the Lord: that I hid a hundred men of them, fifty and fifty, and fed them with bread and water?” Because he had saved one hundred prophets, he received prophetic grace; and from being a leader [Col. 1244D] of an army he became a leader of the Church. Then he fed a small flock in Samaria; now he feeds Christ’s Churches throughout the whole world.

The following statement, concerning rain being given—“And the hand of the Lord came upon Elijah, and, having girded his loins, he ran before Ahab”—was a sign of the time when he will come running before that people, in order to turn “the hearts of fathers to their children and the heart of children to their fathers” (Matthew 4; Luke 1 [as printed]).

According to the historical surface, he teaches us by his example to persevere in prayer. For when he said to his servant [Col. 1245A], “Go up and look toward the sea,” and the servant, having looked, answered, “There is nothing,” Elijah himself, bent down to the ground, persevered with his face placed between his knees: “Return,” he said, “seven times.” “And at the seventh time, behold, a small cloud like the footprint of a man was rising from the sea.” Therefore the Apostle James, after saying, “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another that you may be saved” (James 5), put forward this example: “Elijah was a man like us, subject to suffering” (ibid.), etc.; and thus concluded: “For the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER X. Concerning his flight: how, fearing death, he wished to die; what he himself, the juniper tree, and the food by whose strength he fasted for so many days prefigure.

(III KINGS, CHAPTER XIX.) “And Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying: ‘May the gods do these things to me, and add these things besides, unless by this time tomorrow I make your life [Col. 1245B] like the life of one of them.’ Elijah therefore was afraid, and rising, went wherever his will carried him.”

A little earlier Elijah had been so strong that he kept heaven shut, and, after so many prophets of Baal had been slain, opened heaven again; but now he was so weak that, distressed by the threats of the woman Jezebel, he fled, and in terror did not know where he was going. By his open example he showed that no human being is strong in himself. Yet such weakness is not rightly blamed.
