For in the Gospel the Lord speaks by way of permission: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. 10).

But why is it that, fleeing death, he desires to die? For it follows: “And when he had come and sat beneath a juniper tree, he asked for his life that he might die. And he said: ‘It is enough for me, Lord; take [Col. 1245C] my life,’” etc. He said, “It is enough for me,” for he had lived a long time. Indeed, he himself was Phinehas, son of Eleazar, as the Hebrews relate. This might seem plausible, were it not that Phinehas was of the tribe of Levi, whereas Elijah is reported, as is read above, to have been from the inhabitants of Gilead. For Gilead is a city named from Mount Gilead, on which it was founded; Gilead, son of Machir son of Manasseh, also took it from the hand of the Amorites. The sons of Aaron possessed no city from Manasseh, from whose son Eleazar Phinehas sprang; but they had fourteen cities from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin.

But let us return to the matter at hand. Why does he fear death in such a way that he desires death? Equally worthy of inquiry is what follows. “And he cast himself down,” says Scripture, “and slept in the shade of the juniper,” etc. He slept once; then, rising, he ate and drank; he slept again; and rising once more, he ate [466] and drank. “And he walked in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights, as far as Horeb, the mountain of God.” Did these things happen by chance? Certainly not: they are full of prophetic mysteries.

Elijah, who above, by acting in the spirit of strength, bore, according to his name, the type of God and Lord, here bears in his weakness the figure of the human race. There is the mystery of the Head; here, that of the members. Jezebel, who threatens Elijah with death, is eternal death, which entered this world through sin. Whoever flees this death sits beneath the juniper tree, [Col. 1246A] that is, takes refuge in the holy and life-giving wood of the Lord’s cross. He runs to baptism; he seeks the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion. There he embraces death; there he hastens to die with Christ, lest Jezebel kill him; to be conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death, lest he be held in eternal death. Therefore he casts himself down in the juniper’s shade and falls asleep: that is, he submits himself to Christ’s cross and dies with him. “All of us,” says the Apostle, “who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6).

Then, rising, he is invited by the angel of the Lord to a meal; that is, through the priest he receives the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. He eats and drinks it, and nevertheless falls asleep again. For although the Christian, having died with Christ, has escaped eternal death, he will nonetheless die the temporal [Col. 1246B] death of the body. But the angel of the Lord returns again and invites him a second time to eat and drink. For everyone who sleeps will rise when Christ comes, at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God (1 Thess. 4); and thereafter he will eat only once, and forever, the true bread, the bread of angels, seeing God face to face. “In the strength of that food he will walk to the mountain of God forty days and forty nights”: that is, he will endure in co-eternity with God through all days—indeed, without end—with the angelic spirits.

## CHAPTER XI. On his intercession against Israel, the divine answer made to him, and what is signified by the great and mighty wind [Col. 1246C] overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks, by the earthquake, by the fire, and by the whisper of a gentle breeze.

“And when he had come there, he remained in a cave. And behold, the word of the Lord came to him. And he said to him: ‘What are you doing here, Elijah?’ But he answered: ‘I have been very zealous for the Lord God of hosts, because the children of Israel have abandoned the Lord’s covenant. They have destroyed your altars and slain your prophets with the sword, and I alone remain,’” etc.

The Apostle explains what this likeness or sign meant, taking testimony from this passage: “Do you not know what Scripture says concerning Elijah, how he intercedes with God against Israel? ‘Lord, they have killed your prophets, destroyed your altars, and I alone remain, and they seek [Col. 1246D] my life.’ But what does the divine answer say to him? ‘I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee before Baal.’ Thus, then, at this present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. 11).

Therefore, as we said above, those who bowed the knee before Baal are, mystically, to be understood as the Jews who chose Barabbas for themselves. For by the seven thousand men who did not bow their knees before Baal, the Apostle means himself and the others from among the Jews who believed. Further, what does Elijah intend when he cries out thus and intercedes against Israel, thinking himself the only one left who had not bowed the knee before Baal? Clearly, he longs for the coming of him through whom, as a prophet, he knew that the worship of God would be restored entire. He desired the Messiah—that is, Christ—to come now; as all were perishing and turning aside to evil, he cried out, more with the voice of his heart than with that of his lips, that it was time for him to come.

In answer to this the Lord says: “Go out and stand on the mountain before the Lord. And behold, the Lord passes by; and a great and mighty wind, overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake. The Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, fire. The Lord was not in the fire. And after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze; and the Lord was there.”

By the great and mighty wind overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks, he signifies the future captivity of the ten tribes of Israel, which took place under Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, during the reign of Hoshea (4 Kings 17). “The Lord is not in [Col. 1247B] the wind,” he says: that is, the end has not yet come; the Messiah, the awaited Lord, will not yet come. By the earthquake he denotes the first deportation of the tribe of Judah, when Jehoiakim, king of Judah, was to be handed over to Babylon with forty thousand men, no one being left except the poor. “The Lord is not in the earthquake”: that is, the end has not yet come; the Lord will not yet come.

By the fire he means the second captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, when Zedekiah rebelled and the king of Babylon came again; Nebuzaradan, commander of the army, burned the house of the Lord and the king’s house, burned every house with fire, and destroyed the walls of Jerusalem all around (4 Kings 25). “The Lord is not in the fire”: that is, even after the Temple has been burned and the city destroyed, the time of the Lord’s coming will not yet be at hand. “And after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze, and the Lord was there.” The whisper of a gentle breeze was the hidden and secret coming of the Lord, whom the Virgin Mary conceived, as it were from a gentle breeze—that is, from the Holy Spirit.

From the aforesaid wind to the earthquake—that is, from the captivity of the ten tribes to the first deportation of the children of Israel—there were about one hundred and twenty-seven years, calculated as follows. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, the king of Assyria deported Israel to Assyria. Hezekiah himself reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. Thus twenty-four years of his reign remained. Adding these to the fifty-five years of his son Manasseh, the two years of his son Amon, the thirty-one years of Josiah, then the eleven years of Eliakim, [Col. 1247D] who was called Jehoiakim, and finally the three years of his son Jehoiachin, makes one hundred and twenty-seven years. From that earthquake to the fire—that is, from the first deportation to the burning of the Temple and city—there were the eleven years of Zedekiah’s reign.

How many years lay between that fire or captivity and the whisper of the gentle breeze—that is, Christ’s coming—was revealed to Daniel in these words: “Seventy weeks have been shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, that transgression may be brought to an end, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be removed, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. 9), etc. Elijah’s aim, clearly, was that iniquity might be removed by Christ’s coming and everlasting righteousness brought in, while now, as iniquity abounded, he believed that he alone had been left.

## CHAPTER XII. In the anagogical sense, what that wind, that earthquake, that fire, that whisper, and Elijah himself signify when he covers his face with his cloak.

In the anagogical sense, the wind before the Lord overturns mountains and crushes rocks because the fear that rushes upon us from his coming casts down the height of our heart and melts its hardness. But the Lord is said not to be in the wind, earthquake, and fire, while he is not denied to be in the whisper of a gentle breeze, because when the mind is raised to the height of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to behold is not God. [Col. 1248B] But when it beholds something subtle, this is what it hears of the incomprehensible substance of eternity. For we perceive, as it were, the whisper of a gentle breeze when, in sudden contemplation, we delicately taste the savor of unbounded truth. Thus what we know of God is true when we feel that we cannot fully know anything about him.

Hence it is fittingly added: “When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak; and, going out, stood at the entrance of the cave,” etc. After the whisper of the gentle breeze, the prophet covered his face, because in that most subtle contemplation of truth he recognizes how great is the ignorance in which man is veiled. To draw a cloak over the face is to veil the mind, from consideration of its own weakness, so that it may not dare to seek higher things, nor rashly open the eyes of its understanding beyond itself, but reverently close them to that which it cannot grasp.

## CHAPTER XIII. How, at the Lord’s command, Elijah anointed Elisha as prophet, and Elisha anointed Jehu king over Israel; and how Ahab acted against the Lord’s decree by sparing Ben-hadad, so that the Lord said: “Your life shall be for his life,” etc.

“And the Lord said to him: ‘Go and return by your way through the wilderness to Damascus. When you arrive there, you shall anoint Hazael king over Syria; and you shall anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel. But Elisha son of Shaphat, who is from Abel-meholah, you shall anoint prophet in your place. And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes [Col. 1248D] the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill.’”

Of these commands, Scripture records Elijah as having immediately carried out only one. “Therefore, departing from there, he found Elisha son of Shaphat ploughing with twelve yokes of oxen, and he cast his cloak over him. He immediately left the oxen and ran after Elijah.” This alone, I say, Elijah did; Elisha did the rest after Elijah was taken up.

Elisha did not indeed anoint Hazael; rather, as Hazael stood before him, Elisha was troubled until his face was flushed, and he wept. “And Hazael said to him: ‘Why does my lord weep?’ And he answered: ‘Because I know what evils you will do to the children of Israel’” (4 Kings 8). And afterwards: “The Lord has shown me that you will be king of Syria” (ibid.). At that time Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was ill. Scripture immediately continues: “When he had departed from Elisha”—that is, Hazael—“he came to his master. The next day he took a coverlet, soaked it with water, and spread it over his face. When Ben-hadad had died, Hazael reigned in his place” (ibid.).

Jehu son of Nimshi he anointed later. “He called one of the sons of the prophets and said to him: ‘Gird your loins, take this little flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead. When you have come there, you will see Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi’” (4 Kings 9), etc.

Who thus altered the Lord’s decree? Ahab did so, permitted by the Lord’s judgment. Ahab did not do what the Lord had willed; he did not follow the judgment which the Lord had pronounced upon Ben-hadad. Let us see the following course of the history.

(III KINGS, CHAPTER XX.) “Ben-hadad, [Col. 1249B] king of Syria, gathered all his army, with thirty-two kings, horses, and chariots; and he went up, fought against Samaria, and besieged it.” And afterwards: “Behold, a prophet came up to Ahab king of Israel and said: ‘Thus says the Lord: Have you certainly seen all this very great multitude? Behold, I will deliver it into your hand today, that you may know that I am the Lord.’” When Ahab asked, “By whom?” he replied: “By the foot-soldiers of the provincial commanders; and you shall begin the battle.” So it happened. When battle was joined, the Syrians fled; Israel pursued them and inflicted a great slaughter upon Syria.

After a year had passed, Ben-hadad mustered the Syrians and went up to Aphek to fight Israel. For his servants said: “Their gods are gods of the mountains; therefore they overcame us. But it is better that we fight them on the plains, and we shall overcome them.” But the Lord said: “Because they have said, ‘The Lord is a God of the mountains and not a God of the valleys,’ I will give this entire great multitude into your hand.” So it happened. “The children of Israel struck down one hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in one day; and upon the twenty-seven thousand men who remained” and had fled to the city of Aphek, its wall fell. Afterwards Ben-hadad surrendered himself; Ahab lifted him into his chariot, made a covenant with him, and dismissed him.

But the Lord said: “Because you have let a man worthy of death go from your hand, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people.” It is clear, therefore, [Col. 1249D] that the Lord had judged Ben-hadad worthy of death and had therefore ordered Hazael to be anointed in his place, being about to deliver Ben-hadad into Ahab’s hand. But Ahab, proud and vain, spared him, and consequently he justly incurred the judgment of Saul, who spared Agag, king of Amalek, contrary to the Lord’s command.

The sentence, “Your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people,” was fulfilled in this way: “In the third year Jehoshaphat king of Judah went down to the king of Israel. And the king of Israel said to his servants: ‘Do you not know that Ramoth-gilead is ours, and yet we neglect to take it from the hand of the king of Syria?’” (3 Kings 22). Therefore the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead. When battle was joined, “one man drew [Col. 1250A] a bow at random and by chance struck the king of Israel between the lungs and the stomach. The blood of the wound ran into the hollow of the chariot.” “They buried the king in Samaria; they washed his chariot in the pool of Samaria; the dogs licked his blood, and they washed the reins” (ibid.).

Thus, because he had spared Ben-hadad, his life was for Ben-hadad’s life. Nor was this so merely because he had spared that impious man worthy of death. He had also killed and possessed—killed, I say—Naboth the Jezreelite, and possessed his vineyard, which Naboth had refused to sell (2 Kings 21). Ahab was so wicked that he released from his hand a man worthy of death and killed a just man through his own greed. Rightly, therefore, and in the most fitting order of judgment, his life was for that man’s life: he was killed because of the man whom he had spared; and dogs licked his blood, whose flesh they too ought to have eaten, according to the word of the Lord spoken through his servant Elijah: “If Ahab dies in the city, dogs shall eat him; but if he dies in the field, the birds of heaven shall eat him” (3 Kings 21).

But Ahab humbled himself before the Lord: he tore his garment, covered his flesh with sackcloth, fasted, [468] slept in sackcloth, and walked with bowed head. Therefore the Lord said: “I will not bring evil in his days, but in the days of his son I will bring evil upon his house” (ibid.).

Further, his people were for Ben-hadad’s people in this manner. “While Joram his son reigned, Ben-hadad gathered his whole army, went up, [Col. 1250C] and besieged Samaria. There was a great famine in Samaria, and it remained besieged until an ass’s head was sold for eighty pieces of silver and a fourth part of a cab of dove’s dung for five pieces of silver. And as the king of Israel passed along the wall, a woman cried out to him: ‘Save me, my lord king.’ He said: ‘No; let the Lord save you. From where can I save you—from the threshing floor or from the winepress?’ And the king said to her: ‘What do you want?’ She answered: ‘This woman said to me: “Give your son, that we may eat him today, and tomorrow we shall eat my son.” Therefore we cooked my son and ate him’” (4 Kings 6), etc.

Thus the Lord had commanded Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Syria, and had delivered Ben-hadad into Ahab’s hands; but Ahab, by the Lord’s permission, was the reason why Elijah did not fulfill this command, and this was turned to evil for Ahab and his house. Yet the Lord’s will could not be frustrated: Ben-hadad, a man deserving death, had to die, and Hazael had to reign—except that he was not anointed. For it was not fitting that one who would kill his master should be anointed through a prophet.

How, then, was fulfilled what the Lord said: “Whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall kill”? (3 Kings 19). Clearly, “whoever from Ahab’s house escapes the sword of Hazael,” who was prince of Syria and destined by the Lord to become its king, “Jehu shall kill”; for Jehu destroyed Ahab’s entire house.

But who escaped Jehu’s sword except Syria? Surely, if Jehu had walked perfectly in the Lord’s way, and, just as he removed Baal from Israel, had likewise forsaken and destroyed the many calves which Jeroboam had made, just as he struck the house of Ahab, he would also have deserved to strike Syria. But he did not turn away from Jeroboam’s sins, and through this Syria escaped his sword.

Yet Elisha struck it. How? It is written below: “Elisha was sick with the illness of which he died; and Joash king of Israel came down to him, wept before him, and said: ‘My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!’ And Elisha said to him: ‘Bring a bow and arrows.’ When he had brought him bow and arrows, he said to the king of Israel: ‘Put your hand upon the bow.’ When he had placed [Col. 1251B] his hand upon it, Elisha placed his own hands over the king’s hands and said: ‘Open the eastern window.’ When he had opened it, Elisha said: ‘Shoot an arrow.’ And he shot. And Elisha said: ‘An arrow of the Lord’s deliverance, an arrow of deliverance against Syria. You shall strike Syria at Aphek until you have consumed it.’ And he said: ‘Take the arrows.’ When he had taken them again, Elisha said to him: ‘Strike the ground with the arrow.’ When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God was angry with him and said: ‘If you had struck five or six or seven times, you would have struck Syria until its destruction. But now you will strike it three times’” (4 Kings 13).

This Joash was Jehu’s grandson, that is, the son of his son Jehoahaz. Therefore, the one who escaped Jehu’s sword Elisha killed: that is, Elisha struck Syria—which Jehu and his descendants had not deserved to overcome and strike—not with his hand, but through his merits.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the death of Naboth the Jezreelite: how he too, by dying, was a herald of Christ’s innocence; and what his vineyard, Ahab’s greed, and impious Jezebel prefigured.

(III KINGS, CHAPTER XXI.) Having briefly given, as far as we were able, the divine causes of military events, we now wish at last to return to the prophetic grace of Elijah and Elisha. But behold, we hear Naboth’s blood crying from the field of Jezreel, so that we must not pass it over in silence amid the mysteries of Christ the Lord. For the authority of the saints holds that, just as the house of Ahab was destroyed because of his blood shed at Jezreel, so that Elijah’s prophecy might be fulfilled, so the kingdom of the Jews was destroyed because of the blood of the true Jezreel—that is, the seed of God. Therefore, although hastening to what remains, let us turn aside to this herald of Christ’s innocence.

“Ahab spoke to Naboth, saying: ‘Give me your vineyard, that I may make it a vegetable garden, because it is adjoining and near my house. I will give you a better vineyard in exchange; or, if you think it more convenient, I will give you its worth in silver.’ Naboth answered him: ‘May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.’”

Naboth is interpreted “conspicuous” or “seat,” or indeed “exclusion.” The name of seat or exclusion fittingly belongs to Christ, because of the humiliation of his Passion and his exclusion outside the city for crucifixion. Further, he became conspicuous through resurrection and ascension, thereafter possessing the name above every name. This Naboth was a Jezreelite—fittingly, a Jezreelite. For Jezreel means “seed of God,” which is surely none other than the Son of God. He had a vineyard, namely that vineyard of which the Gospel parable speaks: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard and put a hedge around it” (Matt. 21), etc.

“Give me your vineyard,” says Ahab, “that I may make it a vegetable garden.” By Ahab, whose name means “brother of the father,” we said above that the Jewish people is signified: brother, that is, co-heir with their father the devil, after they crucified the Son of God, the Father of all. “Give me your vineyard,” he says, “that I may make it a vegetable garden.” This means: Allow us, for our own pleasures, the faith and hope of the patriarchs, also the Law and covenant, so that in earthly delights we may squander the honor or merits of the holy Fathers.

To this Naboth replies: “May the Lord be gracious to me, that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers.” Far be it, far be it, he says, that I should allow such men to be called or to be the seed of Abraham, sons of God, heirs of God’s kingdom. Rather, “If you are children of Abraham, then do the works of Abraham” (John 8); produce the fruits of my vineyard, the vineyard of my Father.

“Then Ahab came into his house, indignant and gnashing his teeth. He threw himself upon his bed, turned his face toward the wall, and would not eat [Col. 1252C] bread. But Jezebel his wife came in to him and said: ‘What is this?’” etc. We marvel, as we read, at how indignant and how enraged the Jews were; according to the aforesaid Gospel parable, they first seized the servants sent by the householder, beat one, killed another, and stoned another. They did this once and again. Finally, when the son was sent to them, the father saying, “They will respect my son,” they saw him and said: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21).

This most wicked counsel was forged by impious Jezebel—by the impious Synagogue, the impious scribes and Pharisees, the elders of the people, and the chief priests: “Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours; let us kill him, and the Romans will not come and take away our place and nation” (John 11).

“Proclaim a fast,” Jezebel says, “and make Naboth sit among the chief men of the people; and set two men, sons of Belial, against him, and let them give false testimony, saying: ‘He has cursed God and the king’; then take him out and stone him, so that he may die.” O hypocrisy hateful to God, even on the plain surface of the letter! “Proclaim a fast.” For what reason? Because of a great crime, a monstrous sacrilege: because Naboth cursed God; because Naboth blasphemed God and also the king, when the Law says: “You shall not curse the ruler of your people” (Exod. 22); and, “Whoever blasphemes God shall surely die” (Lev. 14 [perhaps OCR for Lev. 24]). Therefore proclaim [Col. 1253A] a fast and say: Let us all fast; let us all humble ourselves, because in our days we have heard so great an abomination, lest perhaps we be swallowed up by the earth together with the blasphemer.

Plainly this resembles what happened when the chief priest said: “I adjure you by the living God to tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God”; and, when he answered, “You have said it,” that great and mighty champion of God tore his garments and said: “He has blasphemed.” Why do we still need witnesses? Behold, now you have heard the blasphemy. What do you think?” And they said: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26). It resembles that, I say.

Why, moreover, did they make Naboth sit among the chief men of the people and only then set witnesses against him? Clearly, because Naboth was among the chief men of the people, and so that the entire order of the trial might seem fair. First he sat in his rank; then, after the witnesses had spoken, he was deprived of honor, and finally of life. Thus the last hypocrisy proceeded, handsomely cloaked in a wicked manner.

What more need be said? “They led him outside the city and killed him with stones.” Rather, they led the Lord outside the city and crucified him. But the Lord says: “You have killed, and moreover possessed” (3 Kings 21). And after this he added: “In this place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth, they shall lick your blood also” (ibid.). And afterwards: “Dogs shall eat Jezebel in the field of Jezreel” (ibid.), etc.

According to the history, these things happened thus. “When Jehu entered, Jezebel looked out through the window, her eyes painted with antimony and her head adorned; and she said: ‘Can there be peace for Zimri, who killed his master?’” (4 Kings 9). Clearly, so far as the moment allowed, she spoke thus in order to rebuke her killer and restrain him from killing her by the nearby alarming example; and, so that she might meanwhile please him, she adorned her eyes and head. “But he said to the eunuchs: ‘Throw her down.’ And they threw her down” (ibid.). Later, when burial was sought for her, because she was a king’s daughter, “they found nothing except the skull, the feet, and the palms of the hands; for dogs had eaten the rest” (ibid.).

This vengeance for Naboth’s blood was a portent of the vengeance for Christ’s blood. Jezebel’s fall foreshadowed that fall which Jeremiah, foreseeing it, laments under the image of the then-present Babylonian captivity: “The Lord has cast down all the beautiful things of Jacob; in his fury he has destroyed the strongholds of the virgin of Judah and cast them down to the ground. He has defiled the kingdom and its princes” (Lam. 2). Again: the Lord cast down Israel; he cast down all its walls; he filled the daughter of Judah with the humbled man and the humbled woman.

That fall was heard throughout the whole world. Where, then, is that Synagogue which killed Christ? Certainly, whatever seems to remain is such or so much as remained of Jezebel’s body for the dogs. All its kingdom and priesthood are dead; dogs—that is, evil spirits—devour whatever religious service they suppose themselves to offer God by sabbath observance or sacrifice. Let us now return to what came before.

## CHAPTER XV. On Elijah and Elisha: what is mystically signified by Elijah’s placing his cloak upon him, and by Elisha’s leaving the oxen and running after him.

“When Elijah came to Elisha, he cast his cloak over him. Elisha immediately left the oxen and ran after Elijah” (3 Kings 19). In Elijah, God and the Lord Christ are rightly understood; in Elisha, the choir of his apostles. Elijah, about to be taken up, placed his cloak upon Elisha because God and the Lord Christ, about to pass from this world to the Father, gave his office and Spirit together to the apostles. “What was mine,” Elijah says, “I have done for you.” [Col. 1254B] Indeed, God and the Lord Christ did for the apostles what was his own, saying to them at last: “As the Father sent me, so I also send you” (John 20).

“Elisha, leaving the oxen, ran after Elijah”: that is, leaving every occupation, the apostles, unencumbered and ready, carried out the dispensation of the Gospel entrusted to them.

Thereafter the historical sequence runs as follows (4 KINGS, CHAPTER I): “Ahaziah sent to him a captain of fifty and the fifty who were under him,” namely, to seize him. For Elijah had said: “Is there no God in Israel, that you have sent to consult Baalzebub, god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed upon which you have gone up, but you shall surely die.” “The captain of fifty went up to him and said to him, as he sat on the summit of the mountain: ‘Man of God, the king commands you to come down.’ ‘If I am a man of God,’ he said, ‘let fire come down from heaven and devour you and your fifty.’” This happened once and again. “When the third captain of fifty came, he bent his knees before Elijah and entreated for his life and the lives of those with him.” Then it follows (4 KINGS, CHAPTER II): “And it came to pass, when the Lord wished to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah and Elisha went from Gilgal.”

## CHAPTER XVI. What is prefigured in the mystery by Elijah’s being taken up into heaven; by the first and second captains of fifty, who were consumed by heavenly fire; and by the third, who was saved through humbling himself.

The plain history is woven in the necessary order in which the events occurred. But the things figured in it must be investigated in reverse order. For in the mystery, Elijah’s being taken up into heaven comes first, and the devouring by fire descending from heaven of his first and second executors comes later. Thus God, the Lord Christ, first ascended into heaven; afterwards Beelzebub sent his first and second executors, whom everlasting fire will finally devour on the day of judgment.

The first captain of fifty was Nero, the first to draft laws and promulgate edicts against the Christian name. The fifty belonging to this captain of fifty were all those who afterwards followed his example and, raging against the martyrs, wished to extirpate Christ’s name. Beelzebub, whom Ahaziah had sent to consult, is also called in the Gospel the prince of demons. Therefore Beelzebub—that is, the devil—also sent Nero.

The second captain of fifty will be Antichrist, and his fifty will be all the impious who, at his coming, will be armed for the slaughter of the saints. The third captain of fifty, and the fifty who were with him, signify those persecutors who repent and recover their senses from cruelty and wicked purpose through repentance. This is signified by his bending his knees, praying, and saying: “Man of God, do not despise my life and the lives of your servants who are with me” (4 Kings 1), etc.

He did not say, like the first captain of fifty to Elijah sitting on the mountain summit, “Man of God, the king commands you to come down” (ibid.); nor like the second, “Thus says the king: Hurry, come down” (ibid.). For to say to Elijah, “The king commands you to come down from the mountain summit,” or “Hurry, come down,” is to desire to bring Christ down from heaven, so that no one may dare confess that God, the Lord Christ, ascended into heaven. Therefore fire will devour these and those—that is, the first and second—at the final judgment; but God the Lord will save the third and all his fifty, all who have repented, at that coming of his.

## CHAPTER XVII. What is mystically signified by Elijah’s striking and dividing the waters of the Jordan with his cloak when he was about to be taken up into heaven; and by Elisha, who, though permitted three times to remain behind, refused to remain and went with him perseveringly.

[Col. 1255C] “So the two went on together, and fifty men of the sons of the prophets followed. They stood at a distance opposite them, while the two stood by the Jordan. Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the waters; they divided to either side, and the two crossed over on dry ground.”

Elisha, though for the third time permitted to remain behind, refused to stay; rather, he chose to go on together with Elijah. The first time Elijah had said, “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me as far as Bethel.” The second time he had said, “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me to Jericho.” The third time he had said, “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me as far as the Jordan.” But Elisha persisted and gave one and the same reply to all this: “As the Lord lives, [Col. 1255D] and as your soul lives, I will not leave you.”

Clearly, by this good of perseverance he signifies the blessed apostles, who steadfastly followed their Elijah, their God and Lord—not content merely to have fulfilled the commandment, unless they advanced also to the completion of the counsel. For when Elijah said, “Stay here,” he spoke not by commanding but by permitting; and Elisha, out of love for his master, was unwilling to avail himself of what was permitted. Thus, indeed, the apostles and apostolic men, after they had fulfilled the commandments—for example, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery”—were unwilling, for Christ’s love, to avail themselves of permitted things, namely marriage or family property. For this reason Christ says: “You are those who have remained with me in my trials” (Luke 22).

Therefore, Scripture says, “the two went on together and stood [Col. 1256A] by the Jordan.” It is agreed that the Jordan signifies the sacrament of baptism. Moreover, baptism itself was plainly instituted in Christ’s death: “For all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6). Thus the apostles followed their Lord Christ as far as the Jordan, as far as the point of the Passion. And although, struck by fear, they fled for a time in body, yet in mind they remained with him.

“Elijah took his cloak and struck the waters”: that is, Christ gave up his body; and when his side was opened, he consecrated for us the saving waters of baptism through the blood and water that flowed forth. “The waters were divided, and both crossed over on dry ground.” For death was undone, Christ rose [Col. 1256B] from the dead, and the apostles were redeemed through that same death.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the words, “Ask what you wish me to give you,” etc.; and how the same occurred to the apostles in Christ’s ascension

“And when they had crossed over, Elijah said to Elisha: Ask what you wish me to do for you before I am taken away from you. Elisha said: I beg that your spirit may be doubled in me. He answered: You have asked a difficult thing. Yet if you see me when I am taken away from you, what you have asked shall be yours; but if you do not see, it shall not be.”

“Ask,” he says, “what you wish me to do for you.” Elijah said this “when they had crossed over”; but our Lord said the same thing to his apostles in the very passage, within [Col. 1256C] the very agony of the Passion, “knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13): “Amen, amen, I say to you: if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you shall receive” (John 16).

Elisha indeed knew how to ask, saying, “I beg that your spirit may be doubled in me.” But the apostles did not know how to ask. Yet the ready kindness of the Giver intervened; and before they asked, he promised them, as it were, a double spirit, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father” (John 14). For in a sense, to do greater works is to possess a doubled [Col. 1256D] spirit of Christ.

But how did Christ’s disciples do works greater than Christ’s? What works could be greater? To pass over the rest: Christ preached the message of saving doctrine only among one people, and that not a very large one; in only one language, namely Hebrew; and he converted very few of them. But the apostles, after receiving the Holy Spirit, spoke the word of heavenly wisdom in every language to all nations. Though they were unlearned and illiterate men, by fruitful labor they won an innumerable multitude from all nations (Acts 2).

Likewise, Christ, sent by the Father, came only in a spirit of gentleness; but the apostles and the successors of the apostles, sent by Christ, came to us with the rod and with a spirit of gentleness. The rod is the power of discipline, [Col. 1257A] because Christ compelled no one. The spirit of gentleness is the mild speech of exhortation, which alone he employed; for he did not hold such a rank of preeminence as would allow him to rebuke anyone by right of office. Thus Elijah’s spirit is doubled in Elisha: doubled, I say, is in some sense the office or effect in Christ’s apostles.

Certainly, in the literal sense, Elijah’s spirit may plainly be understood as doubled in Elisha because Elisha performed more—that is, twice as many—signs as Elijah. “You have asked,” he says, “a difficult thing. Yet if you see me when I am taken away from you, what you have asked shall be yours; but if you do not see, it shall not be.” In a manner, he touched upon Elisha’s merit indirectly: because he had persevered with him, although he had so often been told, “Stay here,” he deserved to receive, as though by hereditary right, his master’s spirit in a [Col. 1257B] double measure.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the fiery chariot by which he was taken up; and that no one before or after Christ ascended, or can ascend, into heaven as Christ did

“And while they were going on and conversing as they walked, behold, a fiery chariot and fiery horses separated them both. And Elijah went up in a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha saw it and cried out: My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its 471 driver! And he saw him no more.”

The chariot, in which kings and princes customarily rode, signifies the dignity of the blessed man who is truly worthy and receives the honor which God has decreed to confer upon him. Its appearing fiery indicates the merit of his most ardent zeal, by which he was more zealous than others for the Lord God of hosts. “He saw him no more.” In praise of him the wise man says: “We live only in our life; but after death our name will not be such. Elijah indeed was carried in a whirlwind” (Ecclus. 48). And immediately he adds: “And his spirit was fulfilled in Elisha” (ibid.).

How was it fulfilled? Namely, so that Elisha himself became what he confessed his master to be: “the chariot of Israel and its driver.” Thus the king of Israel also said to Elisha when he was sick with the illness from which he died: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its driver” (4 Kings 13). He was a chariot by bearing Israel through his merits, and a driver by governing Israel through prophetic answers.

And Elijah, because he was a human being and not God, needed a chariot [Col. 1257D] by which to be lifted into heaven—not, I say, the ethereal heaven, but the aerial heaven: he was to be placed in some hidden region of the earth, and near the end of the age was to return in order to pay the debt of death. But Christ, truly according to Elijah’s name, “God and Lord,” ascended into heaven without a chariot, without any vehicle or angelic ministry: into the ethereal heaven, where he sits eternally at the Father’s right hand. No one before him ascended thus, nor will anyone ascend afterward. As he says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3). We indeed cannot ascend into heaven; but because he is our head and we are members, we are raised and carried by his divine power.

## CHAPTER XX. The mystical meaning of Elisha’s tearing his garments; of his striking the waters first with Elijah’s cloak and their not dividing, and striking them a second time and their dividing

[Col. 1258A] “He took hold of his own garments and tore them into two pieces. Then he picked up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him. He returned and stood upon the bank of the Jordan. With Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him, he struck the waters, and they were not divided. And he said: Where now is the God of Elijah? He struck the waters, and they divided here and there, and Elisha crossed over.”

The apostles’ old garments were the carnal ceremonies of the Jews. Christ’s cloak, however, is the holy Gospel. Thus Elisha took hold of his garments and tore them, and picked up Elijah’s cloak which had fallen to him, because the apostles, instructed [Col. 1258B] by the Holy Spirit, cast off carnal things from themselves, reckoning the institutions of the Law as loss and considering them dung; but they received Christ’s Gospel, which he had delivered and left to them.

They came to the waters of the Jordan, and Elisha struck the waters with that cloak. For the apostles immediately began to preach Christ’s Gospel in Judaea; they began to preach the grace of baptism. “And the waters were not divided,” it says. Certainly they were not divided and did not offer Elisha a passage. For the Jews did not yield to the apostles’ preaching and did not receive Christ’s grace. Having invoked the God of Elijah, “he struck the waters, and they divided, and Elisha crossed over.” The waters were divided at the repeated blow: that is, the grace of baptism, sent to others—that is, to the Gentiles—was received through the preaching of the Gospel. Then Elisha crossed over; then, I say, the salvation of the Lord found a way, as the apostles preached and carried it abroad publicly, and not without great fruit. For Elisha means “the salvation of my God.”

## CHAPTER XXI. The mystical meaning of Elisha’s dwelling in Jericho and healing the barren waters and evil land by putting salt into a new vessel

“Elisha dwelt in Jericho. The men of that city said to Elisha: Behold, as you yourself, my lord, see, the situation of this city is excellent; but the waters are bad and the land barren. He said: Bring me a new vessel and put [Col. 1258D] salt into it. When they had brought it, he went out to the spring of the waters, put salt into it, and said: Thus says the Lord: I have healed these waters; there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them.”

“Elisha,” it says, “dwelt in Jericho.” When the people of Jerusalem—that is, the Jews, to whom the word of God had first to be spoken—rejected it and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life (Acts 13), Elisha dwelt in Jericho. That is, the salvation of God dwelt among a Gentile people formerly destroyed and devoted to destruction, as that city Jericho was in Joshua’s days (Josh. 6). Yet by dwelling there he caused what was Jericho—that is, “defect” or “failure”—now to become Zion, holy through unfailing faith.

The Jerichoites say, “The situation of this city is excellent, but the waters are bad and the land barren.” [Col. 1259A] They could rightly and truthfully say this, since the very bad and bitter waters of the Law were being offered them. As we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the apostles had come and gathered the Church together, they reported all that God had done with them, and that he had opened to the Gentiles a door of faith” (Acts 14). “And certain men who came down from Judaea taught the brothers: Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15). And afterward: “But some believers from the sect of the Pharisees rose up, saying that they must be circumcised and commanded to keep the Law of Moses” (ibid.).

Surely the words addressed to those people are these: “Behold, the situation of this city is excellent, but the waters are bad and the land is barren.” That is to say: To believe in Christ is excellent, but the observances of the Law are burdensome and the labor useless. The apostle Peter immediately confirms this, saying: “Now therefore why do you test God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (ibid.).

“Elisha says, ‘Bring me a new vessel and put salt into it.’” This was indeed immediately done when, after all had fallen silent, James answered and concluded his speech thus: “Therefore I judge that those who turn to the Lord from among the Gentiles should not be troubled, but that we should write to them to abstain from the pollutions of idols, from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood” (ibid.). To abstain from such things is to bring a new vessel, for those things belonged to the old [Col. 1259C] vessel, to the old human being. But to put salt into the new vessel is, by acting with discernment, not to trouble those renewed in the spirit of their mind over the laborious and useless observance of the Law.

When this has been done, the Lord may truly say: “I have healed these waters; there shall no longer be death or barrenness in them.” How did he heal these waters? Certainly by giving spiritual understanding; for to understand the Law carnally was death, whereas to understand it spiritually is health and life. For the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3).

## CHAPTER XXII. That when Elisha was going up the road, boys mocked him and were therefore torn apart by two bears that came out of the forest; this was a portent of the remarkable destruction of Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian because they mocked Christ

472 [Col. 1259D] “Then he went up from there to Bethel. As he was going up the road, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead. When he turned and saw them, he cursed them in the name of the Lord. And two bears came out of the forest and tore apart forty-two of the boys.”

After the things recounted above, this event follows in a remarkable and mystical order. For what else was it but a portent of the miserable destruction of the people of Jerusalem, which, after the Lord’s ascension prefigured in Elijah, and after the apostles’ passage to the Gentiles, signified by Elisha’s dwelling in Jericho, plainly came to pass? For two bears came out of the forest and tore the boys apart because two emperors, Vespasian [Col. 1260A] the father and Titus the son, came from the city of Rome and killed the Jews.

For what reason? Because the boys mocked Elisha: because foolish Jews and their rulers, “children a hundred years old” (Isa. 65), and therefore accursed, mocked our Lord. They spat upon him, covered his face, struck him with their fists, clothed him in purple, crowned him with thorns, scourged him, and finally said: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead.” Where? Go up to the place of Calvary; go up upon the cross.

Why would so great a man curse boys in the Lord’s name unless he understood their mockery by the prophetic Spirit? That he did understand it is suggested by the wording itself: “When he turned,” it says, “he saw them and cursed them.” He clearly saw them and understood them: he understood that there would be in them future boys, malicious boys of whom mention has already been made. This curse, therefore, came not from the bitterness of anger, but from the judgment of one who foresaw.

This was now Elisha’s third sign. For the signs must be counted, so that it may plainly appear that what he asked for came to pass: namely, that Elijah’s spirit became doubled in him. The first sign was his striking the waters with Elijah’s cloak and their dividing; the second, his healing the bad waters; the third, his so effective cursing of the boys.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That when the psalmist sang, the hand of the Lord came upon Elisha: clear evidence that the Holy Spirit was not always present with the prophets; and that, together with words of divine praise, the sound of sweet music greatly aids the invocation of the Holy Spirit

(4 Kings, chapter 3.) “Now Mesha king of Moab possessed [Col. 1260C] many flocks and paid the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and one hundred thousand rams with their fleeces. But when Ahab had died, he broke the covenant,” etc.

This narrative contains the fourth work of power: “The king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom went,” it says, “and went around by a route of seven days; and there was no water for the army or for the animals following them.” And afterward: “Now bring me a psalmist,” Elisha says. “And when the psalmist sang, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said: Make trench after trench in the bed of this torrent. For thus says the Lord: You shall see neither wind nor rain, yet this bed shall be filled with water. Moreover, Moab also shall be delivered into your hand.” And so it happened.

From this one miracle of the man of God we derive a twofold fruit of instruction. First, we learn that the Spirit was not always present with the prophets, except with the one prophet, the Lord, the great one among prophets, from whom the Spirit never departed. This was his distinctive sign: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1). For one who says, “Now bring me a psalmist,” plainly does not have the grace of prophecy abiding in himself, since he prepares himself to receive its invoked coming through the psalmist’s song.

Second, we learn from this how much the sound of sweet music, joined to words of divine praise, helps to invoke the Holy Spirit. “When the psalmist sang,” it says, “the hand of the Lord came upon him.” For music inwardly moves the human spirit by a certain natural force and power; and when it is fittingly joined to the word or thought of divine praise, it shakes the inner chambers of the heart and rekindles in a person the grace of God’s Spirit which he has received. The renowned first psalmist knew this well by experience and says: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118 [119]).

## CHAPTER XXIV. The mystery in the woman’s pouring the little oil she possessed into empty vessels, which were all filled to the brim

(4 Kings, chapter 4.) “A certain woman of the wives of the prophets cried to Elisha, saying: Your servant, my husband, is dead, and you know that your servant was a man fearing God. And behold, the creditor [Col. 1261B] has come to take my two sons into servitude for himself. Elisha said to her: What do you wish me to do for you? Tell me, what do you have in your house? She answered: Your maidservant has nothing at all in my house except a little oil with which I anoint myself,” etc.

The woman obeyed the prophet’s words; and from the little oil she possessed, she poured into the empty vessels, which were all filled to the brim. By their fullness the woman was released from her debt to the creditor. What does this woman signify except the holy Church, mother, as it were, of two peoples—the Jewish and the Gentile—like two sons? Previously, through perverse action and at the persuasion of the crafty spirit, she had received from the creditor certain coins of sin, as it were, and feared to lose the two whom she had begotten in faith.

But obeying the prophet’s words—that is, the precepts of Holy Scripture—she pours into empty vessels from the little oil she has. That is, when the empty minds of many hear from the mouth of one teacher a little teaching concerning love for the Godhead, through overflowing grace they are filled to the brim with the ointment of divine love. Even now, many little vessels that had formerly been empty are full of the ointment of the Spirit, though they seemed to have received only a scant pouring of oil. And while this is given to one person after another and faith is received by the hearers, the woman—that is, the holy Church—is rescued and no longer held under her creditor’s debt. This was the fifth miracle of God’s Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXV. The mystery in the fact that Elisha’s servant, sent with a staff, did not raise the Shunammite’s son

The sixth follows immediately. “And it came to pass on a certain day that Elisha was passing through the city of Shunem. There was a great woman there,” etc.

Along with the miracle, there is also a mystery 473 in the fact that Elisha’s servant, sent with the staff, did not raise this Shunammite’s son. But Elisha himself came, stretched himself upon the dead boy, conformed himself to his limbs, walked back and forth, and breathed seven times into the dead boy’s mouth; through the ministry of compassion he immediately restored him to the light of life.

For God, the author of the human race, grieved over us as over a dead child when, in mercy, he looked upon us slain by the sting of iniquity. And because through Moses he set forth the terror of the Law, he sent the staff as though through a servant. For God held the staff through the Law when he said: “If anyone does this or that, let him die the death.” Fear, therefore, was unable to raise from the death of sin; but the grace of gentleness breathed into us raised us to the state of life.

The servant with the staff could not raise the dead boy because, as Paul testifies, “the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). But he himself came in person and humbly stretched himself over the corpse, to make himself equal to the dead limbs, and conformed himself to it, because “though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2).

He walks back and forth because he calls both Judaea and the nations near at hand and far away. He breathes seven times upon the dead because, through the opening of the divine gift, he breathes the sevenfold Spirit upon those lying in the death of sin. Immediately the living child rises, because the one whom the staff of terror could not raise returns to life through the spirit of love.

## CHAPTER XXVI. The mystical meaning of Elisha’s giving that same son—the one he raised—to the same woman by God’s power

We say that this was Elisha’s seventh miracle. But why did he give to that woman, by God’s power, the same son whom he later raised? For the event occurred thus: “He said to Gehazi his servant: Speak to this Shunammite woman: Behold, you have diligently ministered to us in every way; what would you like me to do for you? Gehazi said: She has no son, and her husband is old. Therefore he commanded that she be called. When she stood [Col. 1262C] at the door, he said to her: At this time and at this same hour, if life is your companion, you shall have a son in your womb.”

Was there not, then, a twofold miracle in this Shunammite? There certainly was, and it is no less a great one pertaining to the divine mystery. For just as Elisha himself obtained the child whom he would raise, so the Son of God caused the human race, which he gave life in the manner described above, to be conceived and born by his own blessing. For God said to the first human beings after forming them: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1), and in saying this he blessed them.

But fallen nature, with the just wrath of God permitting it, spontaneously produces the corrupt multitude of a vicious crop that has grown beyond measure and does not belong to Christ’s life-giving redemption. This is so after sin, when God says to the woman: “I will multiply your miseries and your conceptions” (Gen. 3). Thus, in the one child there are together the sixth and seventh miracles of the prophetic Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the colocynth, whose exceedingly bitter taste Elisha sweetened; and that it resembles the teaching of heretics

The eighth follows immediately: “There was a famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets dwelt before him. He said to one of his servants: Set on the large pot and cook a stew for the sons of the prophets,” etc. “There is death in the pot, man of God,” they say.

Spiritually, too, death is in the pot whenever heretical bitterness is mixed into the exposition of the Scriptures, by which we are refreshed as by a great pot. For the wild vine, which is not what it appears to be, or the colocynth, which similarly to a gourd sends out tendrils across the ground but is exceedingly bitter, signifies the pretenses of heretics, who possess “an appearance of godliness but deny its power” (2 Tim. 3). Therefore, whenever a Catholic man corrects death of this kind with sound teaching, Elisha—that is, Christ who speaks in him—casts flour into the pot, so that no bitterness remains.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That he satisfied a crowd of people with a few loaves, and its likeness in Christ

The ninth miracle consisted in satisfying a crowd of people with a few loaves, namely as a type [Col. 1263B] of him who himself satisfied many thousands bodily with a few loaves (Matt. 14; John 6), and who even now spiritually refreshes the whole Church from the few books of the prophets and apostles. “They shall eat,” he says, “and there shall be some left over.” Certainly this is what we do and what happens: by reading and expounding, we consume as much as we can, and much remains which we are unable to convey into the stomach of our understanding or memory.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian, healed by washing seven times in the Jordan: that in this event was prefigured the grace of baptism by which a Gentile is cleansed from the leprosy of sin through the working of the sevenfold Holy Spirit

(4 Kings, chapter 5.) The tenth miracle was the healing of Naaman [Col. 1263C] the Syrian. What we should understand mystically in this miracle is indicated when, to those saying to him, “Do here in your own country the things we have heard were done at Capernaum,” he replied: “Amen, I say to you, no prophet is accepted in his own country. Truly I say to you, there were many lepers in Israel in the time of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was healed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4).

Therefore, following the meaning intended by the Lord, let us rightly understand ourselves—that is, the Gentiles—in Naaman, who was not from that country, since we were strangers to Israel according to the flesh and aliens from God’s covenant. Here we should especially understand the Roman Empire. For Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Syria. Syria means “sublimity.” Therefore the king of Syria is the prince of this world; for this world was lofty and proud. Yet it is certain that under that prince the Roman Empire ruled the world. Therefore we rightly understand it in Naaman’s person.

That he was a great man, strong and rich, but leprous, plainly serves this interpretation. For the Roman [Col. 1264A] Empire truly was great, powerful, and very wealthy, but leprous: a great leper, covered by the great leprosy of innumerable errors. Now raiders had gone out from Syria and carried off captive from the land of Israel a little girl who was in the service of Naaman’s wives. This girl was Holy Scripture. The raiders were Pythagoras, Socrates, Plato, and the other philosophers, who truly, as though by brigandage, had carried this girl captive from Israel’s land: stealthily reading some portion of Holy Scripture and forcibly twisting it to their erroneous meanings, they made it serve as a handmaid to Naaman’s wife, namely their various philosophy.

“She said to her mistress: If only my master were with the prophet in Samaria, he would surely heal him of the leprosy he has!” The girl rightly says, “If only my master were with the prophet.” But the king of Syria sent him with letters to Joram, king of Israel. Thus the prince of this world twisted into heretical perversity many who wished to enter or remain on the way of truth. The king of Israel typified this perversity, as we said above: separated from David’s house and serving golden calves.

Finally, “Naaman came with horses, horsemen, and chariots, and stood at Elisha’s house door. Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying: Go, wash seven times in the Jordan; your flesh shall receive health, and you shall be cleansed. He went down and washed seven times in the Jordan; his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was cleansed.”

It is known that Elisha, of whom we speak, did not come in person to this leper, but sent to him. For Christ did not preach to the Gentiles in person; once taken up into heaven, he sent his preachers to them. “Go and wash,” he says: that is, confess faith in Christ and be baptized. “Wash seven times”: that is, be reborn not only through water but also through the sevenfold Spirit. “He went down and washed”: that is, the world humbled itself under God’s mighty hand and received baptism for the remission [Col. 1264C] of sins. “His flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child”: that is, he received his original innocence, being made one body with the little child Christ—that is, the humble and innocent Christ. For the Apostle says: “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3).

## CHAPTER XXX. Naaman’s words, “May God forgive me in this matter, if my king leans upon my hand,” etc.; and how this does not contradict the Apostle, who does not even permit reclining in an idol’s temple

“Naaman said: I beg you, grant to your servant that I may take away a load of earth carried by two pack animals. For your servant will no longer offer burnt offerings or sacrifices to foreign gods, but only to the Lord. Only in this matter may the Lord forgive your servant: when my lord enters the temple of Rimmon to worship, and leans upon my hand, if I worship in the temple of Rimmon while he is worshiping there in the same place, may the Lord forgive your servant in this matter. He said to him: Go in peace. And he departed from him at a chosen time.”

He said, “Go in peace,” and by these words reassured a man of good will. But the Apostle says: “If anyone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not the conscience of the weak person be encouraged to eat things sacrificed to idols? And through your knowledge the weak brother for whom Christ died will perish” (1 Cor. 8).

Are the apostle and the prophet then opposed to each other, since the one does not allow even reclining there, while the other permits even worship in an idol’s temple? The prophet does not permit worshiping Rimmon in Rimmon’s temple, but worshiping God in Rimmon’s temple; for God, being everywhere, could also be worshiped in Rimmon’s temple. Yet worshiping in an idol’s temple seems more serious than reclining there. Are they opposed in this difference? Not at all. In both cases, truth, which is not discordant, requires the power of discernment.

We both are distinguished and make distinctions in this respect: when we do or suffer such things, we must determine, with conscience as witness, whether we cannot escape what we encounter without a more serious loss. By this discernment the Apostle himself is defended from being judged inconsistent with himself, since he both circumcised Timothy (Acts 16) and nevertheless wrote to the Galatians: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5). For by his own judgment Christ would have profited Timothy nothing if he had circumcised his disciple without compelling necessity.

Likewise, God’s soul hates the Jews’ sacrifices, incense, and all their festivals, as he says through Isaiah, since their hands were defiled by Christ’s blood (Isa. 1). For this reason the Apostle mentioned above treats these things as loss for Christ’s sake and considers them dung (Phil. 3). Yet what did he do when necessity pressed? Having taken certain men, he paid their expenses so that they might shave their heads; and on the following day, purified with them, he entered the temple, announcing the fulfillment of the days of purification until an offering should be made for each one of them (Acts 21).

Therefore the sayings and examples of prophets and apostles—indeed, even of one and the same Apostle—are not mutually contrary. Rather, they usefully instruct a prudent person employing the virtue of discernment, so that he may know when he ought patiently to endure communion or association with evils and when he ought wisely to avoid it. Those who have not attained this help of discernment act far too rashly, sometimes cause scandals, and foster divisions in the Church. Of them one may rightly say that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge (Rom. 10).

Certainly, when that Syrian said, “Grant to your servant that I may take a load of earth carried by two pack animals for building an altar to the Lord God of Israel,” he made this request anxiously. A *burdo* is a more load-bearing animal, being born from a horse and a she-ass. “He departed from him at a chosen time,” that is, in springtime, when everything bursts into flower and the season of the year is choice; or when travelers along the road pluck and select from neighboring fields whatever comes to hand, invited by diverse flowers.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Whom or what sort of persons Gehazi represented in the Church, upon whom Naaman’s leprosy clung because of the fault of greed

“Gehazi, servant of the man of God, said: My master spared this Naaman the Syrian by not receiving from him what he brought. As the Lord lives, I will run after him and receive something from him,” etc.

This is Elisha’s eleventh miracle. Truly remarkable in prophetic grace is the fact that, though absent in body, he says: “My heart [Col. 1266A] was present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you”; and that he could pronounce so effective a sentence: “Naaman’s leprosy also shall cling to you.” “And he went out from him leprous as snow.”

The miracle upon the sinner is aptly placed eleventh, while the tenth was the miracle in which justification is signified through the Syrian’s cleansing. For every sin is an “eleven,” because in acting perversely it transgresses the commandments of the Decalogue. To continue the mystical meaning, we must consider this example of Gehazi, set forth in this citadel of Scripture against sellers of God’s grace. Everyone who gives freely because he received freely (Matt. 10), who in preaching seeks not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2), is Elisha. But whoever seeks profit from the Gospel—or, worse still, from the laying on of hands—is Gehazi. He transfers to himself the sins which he seems to cleanse; he takes upon himself the leprosy of as many people as the crafty man has drained of a talent through that detestable commerce.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the miracle by which iron that had slipped from its handle returned and floated upon the water, and what it typified
(IV KINGS, CHAP. VI.) “Now the sons of the prophets said to Elisha: ‘Behold, the place in which we dwell before you is too cramped for us. Let us go as far as the Jordan, and let each take from the forest a single beam, so that we may build ourselves there a house to live in,’” etc. This is the twelfth miracle. For it was indeed wonderful that the iron of an axe, having slipped from its handle into the depths of the Jordan [Col. 1266C], rose again and floated upon the water. Mystically, by this deed an example was given concerning the preservation of the gift of understanding. For the iron in the handle is the gift of understanding in the heart. But to cut with the wood means to rebuke those acting wickedly. Sometimes, when this is done carelessly, when a lapse into vain glory is not avoided in the very knowledge received, the iron is lost in the water, because through slack conduct understanding becomes foolish.

We know, indeed, that this understanding is given to the elect for this purpose: that they should restore it before the eyes of the Giver by good action. Hence rightly he who had lost the iron cried out: “Alas, alas, alas, my lord, and this very thing I had borrowed.” For it is characteristic of the elect that, if at any time the stealthy fault of vain glory creeps upon them in their conscience [Col. 1266D], they quickly return to their heart, and whatever they find in themselves worthy of condemnation before the eyes of the strict Judge, they pursue with tears. In weeping, they not only cautiously consider what evils they have committed, but also, from the gift received, what good things they ought to have rendered; because they feel themselves to be sinners all the more insofar as they are held debtors for the neglected goods which they could have done.

Rightly, therefore, he who lost the iron cried: “Alas, alas, alas, and this very thing I had borrowed.” As though he said: “Through the laxity of negligence I lost that which I received from the grace of the creditor, in order to repay it through good works.” But God never abandons the mind which truly recognizes itself in its sins. Thus Elisha, coming at once, casts down wood and raises the iron to the surface [Col. 1267A]; for our Redeemer, looking upon us mercifully, humbles the heart of sinners and restores to it the understanding which it had lost. He submerges the wood and raises up the iron, because he afflicts the heart and repairs knowledge.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the miracle by which he struck the Syrians with blindness and then restored their sight; and how this also shows us that more are with us than with the enemies of our salvation, and that he showed them perfect charity.

“The king of Syria was waging war against Israel. And he took counsel with his servants, saying: ‘In such-and-such a place let us lay ambushes.’ Therefore the man of God sent to the king of Israel, saying: ‘Take care not to pass through that place, because the Syrians are there in ambush,’” etc. This was the thirteenth miracle.

When the servant of the man of God [Col. 1267B] saw the chariots, horses, and army sent by the king of Syria surrounding the city, he said: “Alas, alas, alas, my lord! What shall we do?” He answered: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them.” And when Elisha had prayed, the Lord opened the boy’s eyes, and he saw; and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire surrounding Elisha.

Again he prayed, and struck the enemies with blindness. He prayed a third time, and, their eyes being opened again, “they saw that they were in the midst of Samaria.” Let us also say, whenever we are surrounded by the visible or invisible enemies of Christ—let us say it, I say, having faith, retaining hope, drawing near to God in charity: “Do not fear, O soul; do not fear, O Church, for there are more with us than with them.” Certainly, if the struggle is against evil spirits in the invisible realm [Col. 1267C], the Lord is with us; the army of angels is with us; the prince of spiritual battle and maker of victory, the Holy Spirit, is with us. But if the visible contest against heretics is proposed, nonetheless the Lord is with us; the choir of apostles is with us; the multitude of patriarchs and prophets is with us; the white-robed army of martyrs is with us; with all holy Scripture, the holy Spirit of truth is with us.

Plainly, according to the historical account, the prophet showed himself worthy of such a miracle in that place when the king of Israel said: “Shall I strike them, my father?” “You shall not strike them,” he replied. And immediately: “Set bread and water before them,” he said, “that they may eat and [Col. 1267D] drink and go to their lord.” Therefore, if by his example we desire the protection of horses and fiery chariots always to stand ready around us, let us likewise by his example heap coals of fire upon the heads of our enemies. For when Scripture had said: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (Rom. XII), it immediately added: “For in doing this, you will heap coals of fire upon his head” (ibid.), so that, conquered by your kindness, he may be pierced with compunction unto repentance.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the siege of Samaria, in which, according to Elisha’s word, a measure of fine flour was sold for one stater and two measures of barley for one stater at the gate of Samaria.

“Now it came to pass after these things that Ben-hadad [Col. 1268A], king of Syria, gathered his entire army, went up, and besieged Samaria. And there was a great famine in Samaria,” etc. This evil remained by reason of the judgment of the Lord, which he had spoken through Elijah against King Ahab on account of Ben-hadad: “Because you have let slip from your hand a man worthy of death, your life shall be for his life, and your people for his people” (III Kings XX).

His life had long since been for the life of the other: for, fighting against him at Ramoth-gilead, he was struck by an arrow and died. This then remained: and for the people of Ben-hadad there would be the people of Ahab. So long “was Samaria besieged that an ass’s head was sold for eighty silver pieces, and a fourth part of a cab of doves’ dung for five silver pieces.” Their women made a pitiable agreement: “Give your son, that we may eat him today, and tomorrow let us eat my son.” Here Elisha became a participant in the persecution of the saints. For the king said: “May the Lord do this to me and add this besides, if the head of Elisha son of Shaphat remains upon him today.”

Here too he feared, like Elijah; yet he did not flee, but said: “Do you know that the son of a murderer has sent here to cut off my head? 476 Therefore see, when the messenger comes, shut the door and do not let him enter.” The furious messenger came and said: “Behold, so great an evil is from the Lord. Why should I wait any longer for the Lord?” Thus spoke one both blasphemous and despairing.

(IV KINGS, CHAP. VII.) But Elisha said: “At this time tomorrow, a measure of fine flour shall be one stater, and two measures of barley one stater, at the gate of Samaria.” [Col. 1268C] To this one of the captains, being unbelieving, deserved to hear: “You shall see it with your eyes, but you shall not eat of it.” So it came to pass. And the miracle of Elisha’s spirit was the fourteenth. “For the Lord caused the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army to be heard in the camp of Syria. The Syrians fled. And the people went out and plundered the camp of Syria.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. On what he said to Joash king of Israel: “Strike the ground with an arrow”; and afterward: “Now, however, you shall strike it,” namely Syria, “three times.”

(IV KINGS, CHAP. XIII.) The fifteenth work of prophetic grace was this. “When Elisha was sick with the illness [Col. 1268D] of which he died, Joash king of Israel came down to him and wept before him. And Elisha said: ‘Bring a bow and arrows.’” And afterward: “Strike the ground with an arrow.” When he had struck three times and stopped, Elisha said: “If you had struck five or six or seven times, you would have struck Syria unto its complete destruction. But now you shall strike it three times.”

This is rightly reckoned in its place among Elisha’s mighty deeds, because it is to be believed that not Joash king of Israel but Elisha, by his merits and with God as author, struck Syria. For God had said: “And whoever escapes the sword of Hazael, Jehu shall kill; and whoever escapes the sword of Jehu, Elisha shall slay” (III Kings XIX). Now how Syria escaped the sword of Jehu has already been said above.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. [Col. 1269A] On how, when a dead man touched Elisha’s bones, he came to life; and what mystery of Christ this signifies.

The sixteenth and final miracle immediately follows. “Elisha died. Also, bands of Moabites came into the land that same year. But some men burying a man saw the bandits and cast the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When they had cast it in, it touched Elisha’s bones; and the man came to life and stood upon his feet.”

It is a great miracle on the surface of the history; in the spirit it signifies an incomparably greater divine work. Elisha dead is, mystically, Christ suffering for us. The Moabite bandits are evil spirits and the sins of the world. The men who saw the bandits and [Col. 1269B] cast their dead man into Elisha’s tomb were the apostles, who provided for the salvation of the world against demons and sins, and placed the dead human race in Christ’s tomb—that is, in the waters of baptism. For the water of baptism is Christ’s tomb, since in it we are immersed three times because Christ was in the tomb for three days and three nights. Hence the Apostle says: “For we have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. VI).

That the dead man touched Elisha’s bones, came to life, and stood upon his feet means what the Apostle immediately adds: “That as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Col. II).

## CHAPTER XXXVII. [Col. 1269C] It is proved from Elisha’s works that Elijah’s spirit became double in him; and that, in saying with pious and sincere intention, “I beseech you, let your spirit become double in me,” he was a Jew.

Therefore Elisha received, as he himself requested, Elijah’s spirit made double in him. For he performed double miracles here. Elijah’s were eight; Elisha’s mighty works are sixteen.

The first was that he prayed that it might not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months (III Kings XVII; Jas. V). The second was that ravens fed him at the Lord’s command until the brook dried up (III Kings XVII). The third was that the jar of flour did not fail and the flask was not diminished until the day on which the Lord gave rain [Col. 1269D] upon the face of the earth, according to his word (ibid.). The fourth was that he raised the son of the mistress of the house (ibid.). The fifth was that, when he prayed, fire fell from heaven and consumed the burnt offering, the wood, and the stones, even licking up the dust and the water which was in the water-channel (III Kings XVIII). The sixth was that, when he prayed again, the heavens became dark with clouds and wind, and there was a great rain (ibid.). The seventh was that at his word fire came down from heaven and devoured two captains of fifty and the fifty men who were with them (IV Kings I). The eighth was that, as the two went together—Elijah and Elisha—Elijah took his mantle, rolled it up, and struck the waters, which divided to either side (IV Kings II).

What was Elijah’s last miracle was conversely [Col. 1270A] Elisha’s first. It is therefore clear with what pious and sincere intention he said: “I beseech you, let your spirit become double in me” (IV Kings II). It needs no commentary of ours when God commends it by such a result attending it. It is clear, I say, that he sought not his own glory but God’s; that he did not wish to magnify himself through his works, but to glorify God; that he sought not his own exaltation but the visitation of a wretched people, whom Jeroboam had deceived, Omri had torn apart, Ahab had taken captive, and Jezebel had defiled.

Nor, because the kings persisted in perversity, should it be supposed that these two men of mercies (Ecclus. XLIV) labored in vain by striving that the name of the Lord might not be consigned to oblivion amid that abundance of iniquities. For Elijah, thinking that he labored in vain [Col. 1270B], interceded with the Lord; but the divine word rebuked him, saying that seven thousand men remained who had not bent their knees before Baal (III Kings XIX).
