Thus it is also a great evidence of divine mercy that the Godhead attended a people fallen into so many evils through such men, whose righteousness did not fall into oblivion. “Good things remain with their seed; their descendants are a holy inheritance; and their seed has stood in the covenants, and their children remain for their sake unto eternity” (Ecclus. XLIV).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Athaliah, daughter of Jezebel, who had married Joram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah: how she exercised her mother’s madness in Jerusalem and throughout Judah; and for that reason how the seed of that same Joram is removed from the Gospel genealogy down to the fourth generation.

Meanwhile, the flow of blood, in accordance with the name Jezebel, began to flow from her into Judah and Jerusalem, even into the inner parts of the temple of the Lord. For the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel was the wife of Joram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah; and he killed all his brothers with the sword, as well as certain of the princes. He walked in the ways of the kings of 477 Israel, as the house of Ahab had done. For Ahab’s daughter, as has already been said, was his wife (IV Kings VIII).

For this reason his seed is removed from the genealogy of Christ the Son of God down to the fourth generation, when it is said: “Joram begot Uzziah” (Matt. I), three persons—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—being removed from the middle. For as Jezebel had raged in Samaria, so her daughter [Col. 1270D], Athaliah, raged in Jerusalem and throughout Judah. She herself urged her son Ahaziah to act impiously. When he was killed by the hand of Jehu king of Israel, “Athaliah arose and killed all the royal offspring of the house of Joram.”

But Jehosheba, the king’s daughter and wife of Jehoiada the high priest, took Joash, son of Ahaziah, and stole him away from among the king’s sons as they were being killed; she hid him with his nurse in the bedchamber (II Chron. XXII), the Lord providing that the lamp of his servant David should not be extinguished. In the seventh year the high priest Jehoiada brought out this Joash, with princes and centurions holding arms at the king’s right and left around him; “they put a diadem upon him, gave him the law to hold in his hand, and made him king” [Col. 1271A] (ibid.). Athaliah, however, was killed by the sword (ibid.).

But this Joash returned evil for good. For while Jehoiada lived, he did what was good before the Lord; but after his death he abandoned the Lord God of his fathers and served sacred groves and carved images (II Chron. XXIV). “Then the Spirit of the Lord clothed Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, and he stood before the people and said to them: ‘Thus says the Lord: Why do you transgress the commandment of the Lord, which shall not profit you? You have forsaken the Lord, so that he may forsake you.’ They gathered against him and cast stones at him, by the king’s command, in the courts of the house [Col. 1272A] of the Lord. And King Joash did not remember the mercy which his father had shown him, but killed his son” (ibid.).

Amaziah also, his son, abandoned the Lord, contemptuously rejected his word, and did not fear to stop up the mouths of the prophets. For when the Lord sent him a prophet who said, “Why have you worshiped gods who did not deliver their people from your hand?” he answered: “Are you the king’s counselor? Be silent, lest I kill you” (I Chron. XXV). His son Uzziah succeeded him, under whom Isaiah began to prophesy.

# THE FORTY-TWO BOOKS OF RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE TRINITY AND ITS WORKS: COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET ISAIAH

## BOOK ONE. (Isaiah I–VI)

[Col. 1271]

### 478 CHAPTER ONE. Praise of the prophet Isaiah, because he treats all the mysteries of Christ and the Church so fully that he should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist; and why he interweaves spiritual realities beneath the names or images of earthly things.

Every soul that loves Christ gladly lends its ear to the prophet Isaiah, and approaches his feet with so much greater submission as it has more faithfully understood Christ speaking in him. For Christian piety rightly judges of him that he should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist; for he sets forth all the mysteries of Christ and the Church so clearly that one would think not that he is prophesying about the future, but composing a history of the past.

And although he sometimes looks to present history and signifies the people’s return to Judea after the Babylonian [Col. 1271C] captivity, yet all his concern in this is for the calling of the Gentiles and the coming of Christ. It was fitting, both in him and in the other prophets, that heavenly mysteries should be concealed under the names of earthly Jerusalem and Babylon, and of earthly things and others, so that on this account holy Scripture might be delivered from contempt and, in its proper time, be preserved in honor for the benefit of those to come.

For the Jews were excessively devoted to present and earthly things, so much so that throughout the whole Law the finger of God never deigned to invite them to do good by a promise of heavenly things, nor to frighten them from evil by a threat of infernal punishments [Col. 1272B]. Everywhere he promises good land and fertile years if they act well; if they act wickedly, he threatens famine and oppression by men. Would heavenly mysteries now have been believed by such people in plain speech? Therefore heavenly things are indeed proclaimed more openly in the prophets; yet the divine speech, like a fugitive, whenever it touches upon any of them, immediately hides itself again and again, and very often, under earthly names.

Therefore, when we have lingered over the others, we shall not be reluctant to spend some further time especially upon this prophet, desiring that the Holy Spirit, his teacher, may be entreated to reveal to us, in the same sense in which he spoke through him, the testimonies concerning Christ the Son of God which we are to gather.

### CHAPTER II. That he recapitulates the coming of Christ, around which all his intention revolves, in seven sections; and that he mystically designates all opposing parties under the nine names of the kingdoms or provinces of Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Dumah, Arabia, the Valley of Vision, Tyre, and the beasts of the south, signifying the punishments of the ungodly by the term “burden.”

(CHAP. I.) First, to sketch out its subject as though in a brief [Col. 1273A] table, it should be said that he recapitulates Christ’s coming in seven sections, around which all prophetic intention revolves; for this is he whom Isaiah awaited, whom all the saints from the beginning of the world awaited.

The first is that in which he vehemently assails Christ’s murderers with the zeal of righteous sorrow, saying most sharply: “Woe to the sinful nation, a people weighed down by iniquity.” And then: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.” The second begins where he says: “I will sing to my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard” (Isa. V). The third begins where he says: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up, and the things beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. VI). The fourth begins where he says: “At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened, and at the last time the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, was burdened” (Isa. IX). The fifth begins where he says: “And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI).

From this point nine burdens follow in succession: the burden of Babylon, the burden of Moab, the burden of Damascus, the burden of Egypt, the burden of Dumah, the burden in Arabia, the burden of the Valley of Vision, the burden of Tyre, and the burden of the beasts of the south. Under these names all adversaries of Christ and of his heavenly city Jerusalem are condemned, and upon each is laid the burden of judgment and the most grievous talent 479 of their iniquity. For the Church which they attack is the tenth. Under the same figure it happened and was said in the Gospel: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? No one was found who returned and gave glory to God except this foreigner” (Luke XVII).

This one, who is also the tenth, is the Church of one faith. For, as mathematicians know better, the number ten is a second unity. But the number nine is a multitude, a crowd opposed to unity. If one is added to it, it immediately becomes unity, because, as has already been said, ten is a second unity. Thus, if one faith is brought to many and diverse adversaries, they become one Church.

For the instruction of this one Church the prophet afterward says many things, and finally makes a sixth recapitulation, saying: “Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord” (Isa. LI). The seventh begins thus: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you” (Isa. LX). Now, with the lampstand of eternal light himself, upon whom we fix our attention, going before us, we enter the temple of this Scripture, searching not all the historical or all the moral matters contained in it, but only the testimonies of faith concerning Christ, as we have proposed throughout this work.

### CHAPTER III. That the prophet’s vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem looks to the future, when the Jews would reject and crucify the Savior as he came; and that this generation is already called a sinful nation, a people weighed down by iniquity, wicked seed, and criminal children.

“The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.” “Concerning Judah,” he says, “and Jerusalem”—that is, concerning carnal Judah and earthly [Col. 1274A] Jerusalem unto evil. But concerning spiritual Judah and heavenly Jerusalem, still partly a pilgrim in the world, this vision is revealed unto good: a vision formerly closed and sealed, but now opened and proclaimed to public understanding.

“Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken.” It is as though he said: This is the complaint of a great orator, a great preacher—of that orator, I say, whose speech is the Word of God and whose congregation is the whole Church of angels in heaven and of human beings on earth. Therefore: “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth,” so that, when you have heard what the Lord has spoken, what the Lord has complained of, you may become instruments of vengeance: you, O heavens, iron above; and you, O earth, bronze beneath.

For what has the Lord spoken? What has the Lord complained of? What injuries has one so great and such as he endured? He says: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me.” I nourished children in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, blessing and multiplying them; I exalted them in Moses, Joshua, and David, wonderfully bringing them out of Egypt, dividing the land for them by the measuring-line of distribution (Ps. LXXVII), adorning them with royal victories, and also with the royal city of David and the one temple of my name. Yet they despised me when I came to them through the proclamations of the prophets.

It is too little that they despised me. It is too little that, choosing Caesar before me, they said that they had no king other than him (John XIX). Moreover, choosing Barabbas the robber before me, they crucified me (Matt. XXVII). At this, O heavens astonished by the hearing and earth stupefied, be indignant in reverence and reverence in indignation; for it is no small indignity that I, your Lord, did all good things and received all evil things. This is so great that you, O heavens, ought rightly to be broken by humble grief, and you, O earth, ought wholly to be shaken by devout sobbing.

Let one of such children say: “What wonder if we despised you? We did not recognize you. You came too hidden, whereas according to the promises of the Fathers and prophets you ought to have walked before our eyes as a great and glorious king.” To this I say: “The ox knew its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand.” The ox is a clean animal; the ass is unclean; yet both are brute animals. Therefore the ox signifies a simple Jew, such as Peter or Andrew was—both fishermen, neither scribes nor experts in the Law. The ass signifies a simple Gentile, such as Cornelius was.

“You say,” he says, “that I came too hidden. How then did the ox know me as its owner, and the ass my manger? How, I say, unless because each was delighted by the food of the good word which I set before him, and perceived my good works done among them? But you, Israel—you, my people of Jerusalem—who sat around the temple, glorying in the Law with the Pharisees and high priests, did not love such things. Therefore you did not understand; thus Israel did not know me and my people did not understand me—that is, they refused to know and understand.

“Therefore answer, O heavens; speak, O earth; and say: ‘Woe to the sinful nation, a people weighed down by iniquity, a wicked seed, criminal children’” [Col. 1275A]. “Woe,” I say, means eternal judgment and everlasting punishment. And why this? “They have forsaken the Lord; they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel.” Before he came, they forsook the Lord by choosing Baal and the like—monstrous manifestations of demons; and when he came, they blasphemed that same Holy One of Israel, saying: “He has a demon” (John X), and “He is a carpenter, not the Son of God” (Mark VI). “They have become estranged backward.” How? First, the right and decree of their king ought to have been laid before them; but they hated him and sent an embassy after him, saying: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke XIX). Thus, estranged backward, behold: instead of the Lord they expect the devil; instead of the Holy One of Israel they expect the man of sin, the son of perdition.

### CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1275B] That their sin arose not from ignorance but from pride and envy; therefore they do not deserve pardon; and that this is the meaning of: “Every head is sick and every heart is sorrowful,” etc.

“Where shall I strike you further, as you add transgression? Every head is sick and every heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it.” It is as if he said: You have not sinned from weakness; you have not erred from ignorance. If it were so, I would know where I ought to strike you; I would find what blow I could use to correct you. But now, in what shall I strike you further, as you add transgression—adding, I say, to sin the defense of sin?

“Every head is sick and every heart is sorrowful.” In the sick head is signified the outward moth of wicked action; in the sorrowful heart, inward envy. He repeats the same thing in other words: “From the sole of the foot,” he says, “to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it.” By the sole of the foot, outward work is understood; by the crown, the dignity of inward reason. Therefore, when someone sins maliciously—as those men did when they said: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke XI), while they knew that he cast out demons by the finger of God (ibid.)—you rightly say that from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in him.

Therefore, where shall I strike you? Such madness, surely, is not forgiven either in this 480 age or in the age to come. “A wound,” he says, “a bruise, and a swollen sore.” A wound is evil; a bruise is worse; a swollen sore is worst. It is evil to be wounded by sin, even for an hour; worse to grow bruised by evil habit; worst to defend fault with the swelling of pride. Such is your madness. “It has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” I wished to bind it up and restrain you unto repentance, saying in my own person: “Repent” (Matt. IV); but you refused to receive the bonds of the Gospel. From my side I poured forth blood and water (John XIX), the medicine of eternal salvation, and you refused to draw near. I gave oil—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—to those believing in me, so that unlearned men spoke in every language (Acts II); and you refused to hear.

What then shall finally happen? “Your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire; before your eyes strangers devour your region, and it shall be desolated as in an enemy’s devastation.” For the present, take this as the beginning of sorrows. For elsewhere you shall have, as I have foretold, eternal woe. “And the daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field.” How is one or the other left? Plainly, when the crops have been taken away and the keeper departs because he has nothing further to guard, the shelter remains empty and the hut neglected—the hut which he had made for himself against the burning heat and rays of the sun, and in order to drive away from there people or little beasts that are accustomed to lie in wait for the growing vines. So the daughter of Zion shall be left, when the guarding powers of the temple depart; and she shall be “like a city which is devastated”—that is, she shall truly be devastated.

I shall say more. “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah.” Do not say: “This wrath is too great; the multitude of evils exceeds our deserts.” For unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed—unless he had predestined that a remnant from us should be saved—we would not be surrounded by the siege of men, slain by Roman swords, and led captive among all nations; but as the Lord rained sulphur and fire from the Lord upon Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. XIX), so the Son, Lord from the Father who is Lord, would most justly have rained sulphur and fire upon us in vengeance for his blood. But if he had done this, no remnant from us would remain to be saved after the fullness of the Gentiles had entered in (Rom. II).

### CHAPTER V. In what way their sin was like the sin of the Sodomites and Gomorrahites, so that, foreseeing it, he rightly said: “Hear the word of the Lord,” etc.

“Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; receive with your ears the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.” Do not say: “Why should we have been like Sodom and like Gomorrah in punishment?” For behold, I say and testify that you high priests and Pharisees are rulers of Sodom, and you people of Jerusalem are people of Gomorrah. Why? Surely because as they acted, so have you acted.

Once the Lord came—he came, I say, in his two angels—to Sodom in the evening, while Lot sat at the gate of the city. Lot strongly urged them to turn aside to him. When they entered the house, he made a feast, baked unleavened bread, and they ate. But before they went to bed [Col. 1276D], the men of the city surrounded the house, from boy to old man, all the people together; and they called Lot and said to him: “Where are the men who came in to you by night? Bring them out to us, that we may know them” (Gen. XIX).

Surely you have done something similar—indeed, something worse. The Lord came, no longer in angels but in his own person. He came, I say, into your city; and when evening came, having been received as a guest in a certain house, he ate the Passover. You came and sent officers with lanterns, torches, and weapons; you surrounded him and demanded him for mockery, being drunken, intoxicated, and vomiting, like those Sodomites already mentioned, when they surrounded Lot’s house. For they had full bellies in the evening, Scripture testifying that this was the sin [Col. 1277A] of the Sodomites: abundance of bread and idleness (Ezek. XVI).

So too, on that festival, that Passover evening, filled and drunken, you surrounded the Lord to mock, spit upon, scourge, and crucify him—joyful, like victors because you had seized him. Hence his Spirit, uttering complaint in the psalm, says: “Those who drank wine sang songs against me” (Ps. LXVIII).

But what befell that most wicked crowd of Sodomites? “The men shut the door, and struck those who were outside with blindness, from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door” (Gen. XIX). So it befell you also, O rulers of Sodom. The door of the Scriptures has been closed to you; you have been struck with blindness; wandering outside, you go about and cannot find him who said: “I am the door” [Col. 1277B] (John X). Therefore, O rulers of Sodom, hear the word of the Lord. Therefore, O people of Gomorrah, receive with your ears the law of our God. What that word of the Lord is, he says:

### CHAPTER VI. That all the sacrifices and feasts of the Jews are hateful to God, and that baptism alone pleases him.

What is the multitude of your victims to me? I am full. I have not desired whole burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened beasts, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats, etc. Still, he says, although you are public Sodomites, do you offer sacrifice to me? Do you still suppose that I can be enticed by the multitude of your victims? What are these to me? What will the blood of calves, lambs, and goats contribute to me? [Col. 1277C] I am full. I have received a great and true sacrifice, and in it I have been filled: that is, the obedience of holy Israel, whom you blasphemed, whom you killed, and with whose blood your hands are full. He filled me. That priest satisfied me. Therefore, being full, why should I admit the multitude of your victims? I do not wish—indeed, I did not wish it—when you came before my presence. The fact that Moses appointed sacrifices of this sort for you, he did not do by my will but by my permission; namely, because you, accustomed in Egypt to serve foreign gods with such sacrifices, could not be restrained from the habit.

Therefore I say: Who required these things at your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Offer sacrifice no longer in vain. Beyond the sacrifice of my priest, [Col. 1277D] to whom I swore and shall not repent, saying, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109), beyond this sacrifice, I say, do not offer your foul-smelling sacrifice. Incense is an abomination to me. New moon, Sabbath, and other festivals I will not endure. Your assemblies are iniquitous; my soul has hated your calends and your solemnities. Formerly I did not desire them, yet I bore them. But now I shall bear them no longer, for my soul has hated these things with a profound hatred. They have become burdensome to me. Yet, from the time they became burdensome to me, I endured them for forty years. I did not immediately send Titus and Vespasian to take away both your place and your nation, to destroy city and temple so that no stone should remain upon another; rather, I endured for forty years.

[Col. 1278A] I laboured in enduring. That I endured so long was labour to me. I abhorred your incense; I hated your new moon and Sabbath; my soul hated your assemblies and the filth of your solemnities. I did violence, as it were, to my own soul, that it might endure for at least forty years what it hated; and in doing so I laboured. Let the Romans finally come and remove this labour from me. And when you stretch out your hands—understand: while surrounded outside by weapons and afflicted and cut down within by famine and seditions—I will turn my eyes away from you, lest I be compelled to grieve and have pity. And when you multiply prayer by vying in offering sacrifices, staining the Temple with blood in the sight of enemies who marvel at your obstinacy, I will not hear. For your hands are full of blood. [Col. 1278B] You filled them for yourselves when you said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

This is the word of the Lord. What, then, is the law of our God? “Wash yourselves; be clean.” If perhaps some of you, struck with compunction, should say to Peter and to the rest of my apostles, “What shall we do, brethren?” (Acts 2), behold, I say to you: “Wash yourselves.” That is to say: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord” (ibid.). Therefore wash yourselves; be clean—that is, be baptized—and do not again lose the cleanness of baptism through evil works. And behold, hear seven elements of diligence to be applied: “Remove the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes; cease to do perversely; learn to do good. Seek justice; aid the oppressed; judge for the orphan; defend the widow.” Therefore strive to remain clean by these seven [Col. 1278C] ways—seven, I say, that is, by every means; for universality is signified by the number seven. And when you have done so, “Come, and argue with me.” For I shall not disdain to enter into judgment with you, I the Lord. Set forth your cases; demand rewards. For, once baptized and cleansed, you have a great advocate with me, by whose blood you washed yourselves and by faith in whom you were purified. “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow. And though they be red as the crimson worm, they shall become like white wool.”

Scarlet is a fiery colour; crimson worm is the colour of blood. Thus in scarlet are understood the sins of lust, and in crimson worm the crime of murder. “Though your sins,” he says, “the sins of Sodom, be as scarlet, since you are princes of Sodom, they shall be made white as snow,” [Col. 1278D] in accordance with that passage in the Psalm: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). “Though your sins,” the sins of murderers, “be as the crimson worm,” since you killed Christ, “they shall become like white wool,” so that his blood may no longer appear upon you, but rather the shining garment of grace.

This is the law of our God, O people of Gomorrah. “My soul has hated,” he says, “all the multitude of your victims, all your solemnities.” This alone is what I desire: wash yourselves. “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land.” If, I say, you are willing to receive this law with your ears, so as to hear it, wash yourselves, and be clean, you shall eat the good things of the land of the living. But if you refuse and provoke me to [Col. 1279A] anger, the sword shall devour you. The sword, I say, shall devour you: now, in the present time, the sword of the Romans, which separates souls from bodies; and elsewhere the malignant sword that divides souls from God and from every lot of the righteous—if you provoke me to anger; if among those whom I send to you, prophets, wise men, and scribes, you kill, scourge, crucify, stone, and persecute from city to city. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

What has the mouth of the Lord spoken? Certainly that the sword shall devour you, so that upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar (Matt. 23). This the mouth of the Lord has spoken, and confirmed it by interposing truth. “Amen, I say to you,” he says, [Col. 1279B] “all these things shall come upon that generation” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VII. That this sin belonged especially to the priests, scribes, and Pharisees, who, because of their own traditions, abandoned the traditions of God; and hence the saying: “Your silver has become dross,” etc.

I know beforehand, O princes of Sodom, that you will not hear this word of the Lord; I know, O people of Gomorrah, that you will not receive this law of our God with your ears. Therefore I say: “How has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a harlot? Righteousness dwelt in her, but now murderers.” How has the city once faithful—the faithful city of David—become a harlot? [Col. 1279C] How? In order that she might be free to prostitute herself, she killed her lawful husband. Righteousness once dwelt in her: that is, the name of the Lord; righteousness, I say, which is faith, through which alone Abraham was justified and called the friend of God. But now murderers dwell in her: killers of that same God and Lord in whom Abraham believed.

O harlot, “your silver has become dross; your wine has been mixed with water.” For you abandoned the traditions of God because of the traditions of men (Matt. 15; Mark 7). The traditions of God are silver; they are wine: “You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall love the Lord your God” (Exod. 20). The traditions of the Pharisees are dross and water, saying, “Wash the dish; baptize the jug,” while abandoning justice and faith (Mark 7; Matt. [Col. 1279D] 23). You have lost God’s silver because of the dross of the Pharisees; you have corrupted God’s wine with muddy water.

“Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves.” Faithless, I say, and for that reason not sons of Abraham, whose sons are believers alone. Companions of thieves: for they made the house of the Father a den of robbers (Matt. 21). “All love gifts; they pursue recompense.” I do not say that they accept gifts, which is common to many, but that they love gifts, which belongs to murderers. For this was especially why they killed the Lord: because he disputed against their avarice. “They pursue recompense”: they follow it, I say; they do not go before it.

This is shown in what follows: “They do not judge for the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not enter to them.” If they judged for the orphan and defended the widow’s cause, and then received something from persons freely offering it to them as worthy judges or deserving defenders, [Col. 1280A] recompenses would precede; and this would not be so blameworthy. But now they follow recompenses: that is, they receive from the violent man contending against orphan and widow, and for what they receive they overturn the orphan’s judgment and exclude the widow’s cause by closing their doors. This is not to go before, but to follow, recompenses.

For this reason the Lord of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel, says: “Alas! I will take consolation over my enemies and avenge myself upon my foes.” Namely, so that the sword may devour them, as I said above. It is no slight thing that the Lord of hosts says, “Alas!” It is not a matter of small weight that the Mighty One of Israel says, “Alas!” Great is the cause, great the grief by which this Mighty One, this Lord of hosts, is afflicted when he says, “Alas!” Nor does he receive consolation otherwise [Col. 1280B] than by being avenged, unless the sword devours his enemies.

## CHAPTER VIII. That he speaks on behalf of the apostles or believers in part: “I will smelt your dross clean away and remove all your tin”; but on behalf of unbelievers: “You shall be ashamed when you are like an oak shedding its leaves,” etc.

Now he turns to the city itself and, on behalf of the few who received the law with their ears, having said, “Wash yourselves; be clean,” says: “I will turn my hand toward you, and I will smelt your dross clean away, remove all your tin, restore your judges as at the first, and your counsellors as in ancient times. After this you shall be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city. Zion shall be redeemed in judgment, and they shall bring her back in [Col. 1280C] righteousness.”

Toward you, O Zion, I will turn my hand: I will stretch out my power to work your salvation. For the murderers dwelling in you will not be able to turn away my hand by killing me. Toward you, I say, even in my death I will turn my hand, by smelting your dross clean away and removing all your tin: namely, by giving you remission of sins through my blood. Then I will restore your judges—that is, my apostles upon twelve seats to judge (Matt. 19)—as they were at first. How were they at first? They were justified not by the multitude of victims, new moons and Sabbaths, calends, or any ceremonies of the Law, but by faith. For Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—your judges, indeed your fathers and counsellors—were justified by nothing other [Col. 1280D] than faith. To this state I shall now restore your judges and counsellors: that is, my apostles, now your counsellors, that is, your preachers, but afterwards to be judges. I shall judge them not through the Law but through faith.

“After this you shall be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city.” For, when the Holy Spirit has been sent from heaven, you shall be built up in strength, enlarged among all nations, multiply children for yourself through faith, and be called by a new name: the city of the righteous one, who “committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2) and by dying bore your sins (ibid.). You shall, I say, be called the faithful city—that is, justified not by works of the Law, but through faith in that same Jesus Christ (Rom. 3).

“Zion shall be redeemed in judgment.” Hear, ends of the earth; hear this edict of grace. Zion, [Col. 1281A] which had been sold without judgment, which had been taken captive through the devil’s lie—behold, she shall be redeemed in judgment: in the judgment of the world, by which “the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12), from the possession seized without judgment. “And they shall bring her back in righteousness.” Where will they bring her back? Into the kingdom of God, from which she had formerly been expelled in the first parents. In what righteousness will she be brought back there? In the righteousness of faith, in the regeneration of water and the Holy Spirit, without which no one, unless born again, can see the kingdom of God (John 3). Her judges and counsellors, restored as at first and as in ancient times, shall bring her back there.

“And he shall crush the wicked and sinners together, and those who have forsaken the Lord shall be consumed. For they shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed, and you shall be ashamed of the gardens which you chose, when you are [Col. 1281B] like an oak shedding its leaves and like a garden without water.” “Together,” he says, “he shall crush the wicked and sinners”: together, the rulers and the people, the princes of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah. Who will crush them but that stone of which he himself spoke in the Gospel, when he had put forward the parable of the householder’s vineyard: “Have you never read,” he says, “The stone rejected by the builders has become the head of the corner?” (Matt. 21). For immediately he says: “Whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but the one upon whom it falls, it shall crush” (ibid.).

These wicked men, these sinners, are the evil cultivators who first killed the servants and then the son of the householder. For that vineyard is Zion. Therefore those who forsook the Lord of the vineyard shall be confounded; this stone shall crush the wicked and sinners [Col. 1281C] who rejected him; and the vineyard, Zion, the kingdom of God, shall be given to a nation producing its fruits (ibid.). They shall be confounded by the idols to which they sacrificed—namely, by their idol Baal-peor, to whom they sacrificed themselves through passive lust, since indeed they are princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah; not to mention for the moment that, bodily as well, whenever opportunity permitted, they always lapsed into idols.

“And you shall be ashamed,” he says, by apostrophe, “of the gardens which you chose”: that is, of all the pleasures in which you indulged in luxury. You chose not to work in the aforesaid householder’s vineyard, but to abandon yourselves in gardens of vices. For this reason too you killed his son, saying, “The inheritance shall be ours” (Mark 12), so that you might turn the vineyard into gardens, just as Ahab, as a type of you, killed Naboth in order to make his vineyard into a vegetable garden for himself (3 Kings 21). “You shall be ashamed,” I say, “when you are like an oak shedding its leaves and like a garden without water”: that is, as unlike blessed Zion, redeemed in judgment and righteousness, as a dry oak is unlike a beautiful vineyard, and as a garden without water is unlike the Lord’s paradise.

## CHAPTER IX. On the mountain of the house of the Lord: that it is Christ himself; that, while Jews remain, all nations flow to him; that they exhort one another, saying, “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord”; and when the Law goes forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

**(Chapter II.)** The word which Isaiah son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem: “And in the last days [Col. 1282A] the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,’” etc.

I said to you: “Wash yourselves; be clean,” because your hands are full of blood, and because it was necessary that this word be spoken to you first (Acts 13). But behold, foreknowing, I now know that you will reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life. Therefore hear the word Isaiah saw: “The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you” (Matt. 21)—from you Jews, from you earthly Judah, from you bloodstained Jerusalem—and shall be given to a nation, indeed to nations, producing its fruits (ibid.). For this is what he says: “And in the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains and raised above the hills, and all nations shall flow [Col. 1282B] to it.”

“In the last days,” that is, until the very last days, until the consummation of the age, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared: the mountain of holy Zion redeemed, as I said above; the mountain of the Church, the faithful city and city of the righteous. It shall not be a small stone such as could be rejected by the builders, but one which afterwards became the head of the corner (Ps. 117). For Daniel says: “The stone which struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. 2). This mountain shall be prepared on the summit of mountains and raised above hills: on the summit, I say, of mountains and hills that long desired him, just as one of those mountains, when he had said while blessing his son, “The blessings of your father have been strengthened” (Gen. 49), added, “until [Col. 1282C] the desire of the everlasting hills should come” (ibid.).

The great mountains are the great patriarchs, prophets, and apostles; the lesser hills are the righteous, the elect of middling rank. This mountain shall be prepared and raised upon the summit of those mountains or hills; and it shall therefore be called mountain of mountains, just as foundation of foundations. Thus the house of the Lord does not have its foundation below; rather, its summit is its foundation. How shall it be prepared? How shall all nations flow to it? Raised up from the earth, it shall draw all things to itself (John 12), and it shall say: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me; go, teach all nations” (Matt. 28). This shall be the way: thereafter all nations shall flow abundantly, and many peoples shall go by a level path. Nor shall they be content merely to go; they shall also exhort one another and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.”

For to go is to believe; to say “come” is to invite others also to believe. Therefore, as they go, they shall say “come”; believers shall not cease to invite others to the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob, that is, to Christ, the highest Son of God, and to the Church of God, which approves supplanting, signified in Jacob. For just as he supplanted his brother (Gen. 27), so these nations and peoples shall supplant the Jewish people.

With what hope, with what fruit, shall we go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of God? “And he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths.” He will teach us his ways; we shall walk in his paths. That belongs to the perfect. For the ways are the Lord’s commandments; the paths are the Lord’s counsels. He will teach us his ways, saying, “You shall not kill; you shall not steal” (Exod. 20), and the like. But we, not content to walk by his ways, shall follow the paths of his counsel—for example, when he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). Therefore he will indeed teach us his ways, but we shall walk in his paths: that is, we shall accept his commandments so fully that we shall not reject his counsels. Thus shall all nations flow, and thus shall many peoples go.

“For the Law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem,” etc. The word and Law of the Lord shall not then, as hitherto, be confined within the narrow limits of one city and one Jewish people; rather, it shall go forth from the city of Zion or Jerusalem—indeed, from the faith and unity of the holy patriarchs and prophets—and shall go to all nations. For this is what follows: “And he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples.” When this was now to take place, opening a way for his Law and word, the Lord himself said: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24). To preach repentance is plainly to judge nations and rebuke many peoples for their sins. And for this to begin from Jerusalem is precisely for the word of the Lord to go forth from Jerusalem.

“And they shall forge their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles.” All nations indeed shall do this, but not all [Col. 1283C] human beings. For not all human beings shall flow and go in the way described; rather, all nations—that is, from every nation many and innumerable persons. Which among them shall go? Those, namely, who go up to the house of the Lord: they shall forge their swords into ploughshares and their spears into sickles. That is, they shall live innocently, maintaining peace with all people, if possible, so far as it depends on them (Rom. 12); indeed, very many shall abstain even from lawful wars, freely lay aside the belt even of just military service, and prefer wildernesses and monasteries to cities and fortresses. “Nation shall not lift sword against nation, nor shall they train for war any longer.”

Not to mention others, the companies and legions of martyrs shall do this as well. Holding arms and prepared to fight against the enemies of their country, they shall not fight for themselves; rather, they shall burn with such desire to ascend the mountain of the Lord and the house of the God of Jacob that, having cast away their swords, they shall gladly submit their necks to the blows of persecutors.

“House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord our God,” etc. This shall be the good part of their speech. As they ascend, all nations shall say to one another, “Come, let us go up”; nevertheless, they shall say the same to their Jewish enemies, from whom their salvation originated, who refuse to ascend together in the shared faith because of hatred for them: “O house of Jacob, O Jews, from whom salvation came to us, why do you remain below in darkness on our account? Why has blindness happened among you on our account? [Col. 1284A] Come, come; let us walk together in the light of the Lord our God.”

## CHAPTER X. Why the Lord cast off the Jews, as he says here, “For you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob”; and what evil he predicts for that house of Jacob because it will not ascend this mountain.

“For you have cast off your people, the house of Jacob, because they are filled as of old, and have had diviners like the Philistines, and have clung to foreign children. Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end of its treasures. Their land is filled with horses and its chariots are innumerable. Their land is filled with idols. They worshipped the work of their hands, what their fingers made; man bowed himself and the man was humbled. Therefore do not forgive them.”

All nations and many peoples ascending to the mountain of the Lord shall say—shall say, I repeat, insistently—to the house of Jacob: “Come, let us walk in the light of the Lord our God.” But that house of Jacob shall stop its ears so as not to hear, shut its eyes so as not to see, detest this mountain, and curse this light. Why? “You have cast off this people once your own; you have cast off this house of Jacob.” Why, Lord God, have you cast them off? “Because they are filled as of old.” That is: because, just as of old, when they made the calf at Horeb, worshipped the carved image, ate and drank and rose up to play (Ps. 105; Exod. 32), so now they are filled with a double fornication. For, like the Philistines—that is, foreigners—they had diviners through almost [Col. 1284C] every age, and they clung to foreign boys, fornicating against nature as princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah.

Because of these sins, beginning from the time when they made the calf, you have now cast them off and hardened their heart. For you said: “But on the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs” (Exod. 32). If you were going to visit that sin in which they then made the calf, it is no wonder that afterwards they had so many diviners, served idols so often, were so often filled with gold and silver and sold justice while thirsting for it, so often grew proud in horses and chariots, and so often worshipped the work of their hands; certainly, from the time of Jeroboam, they worshipped not one but two golden calves, [Col. 1284D] and, beyond that, Baal and the other monstrosities called gods. “Therefore do not forgive them”: this must indeed be granted to your righteous judgments.

What then, O wretched house of Jacob, since you do not wish to ascend the righteous mountain of the Lord? “Enter into the rock; hide yourself in a pit in the earth from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty”—namely, when the terrible army of the Romans surrounds you. Indeed, he himself confirms that I am a true prophet in this, saying: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me; rather weep over yourselves and over your children. For behold, days are coming in which they shall say, ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs which have not borne, and the breasts which have not suckled.’ Then they shall begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” [Col. 1285A] (Luke 23).

Therefore enter into the rock; hide yourself in a pit in the earth. That is, wish that the rocks may be split and the earth gape open, so that you may hide from the face of the terror of the Lord and the glory of his majesty, when, now victorious and crowned with glory and honour, he seeks you in wrath by sending visible and invisible officers: visible ones, namely Romans, to kill bodies; invisible ones, namely malignant spirits, to carry souls away, to be dragged down to the lowest depths of hell.

“The eyes of lofty man have been humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down. But the Lord alone shall be exalted in that day, because the day of the Lord of hosts is upon every proud man, and he shall be humbled,” etc. For who is this lofty man, who this proud, high, arrogant man, except you who say, “We are Abraham’s seed; we were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8), and, “We are Moses’ disciples” (John 9)? Surely to speak these and similar things in contempt of the aforesaid mountain of the Lord is great loftiness, astonishing pride, astonishing exaltation, astonishing arrogance.

Therefore every person of this kind who is arrogant shall be humbled: every lofty and erect cedar of Lebanon, that is, every priest and person who trusts in that Lebanon, that is, the beautiful Temple, to which elsewhere it is said, “Open your gates, O Lebanon” (Zech. 11). Therefore every oak of Bashan, every high mountain, every raised hill, every lofty tower, and every fortified wall shall be humbled: that is, everyone, whether commoner or ruler, who, though human by nature, is nevertheless rightly denoted by such names because of pride. All ships of Tarshish shall also be humbled: that is, all wealthy merchants whose riches are in their hands, because, growing proud in wealth, they crucified Christ the Son of God, poor and needy. For upon this, and upon everything beautiful to behold, shall come that day of the Lord, that revelation of the wrath of the Lord; and the loftiness of human beings shall be bowed down, etc.

## CHAPTER XI. On the saying, “Cease from the man whose spirit,” etc.: that Christ is the Most High, and that he truly rose, if his spirit is in his nostrils.

“Therefore cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils. For he is accounted high.” Therefore, I say, since they are thus to be humbled and bowed down, cease from [Col. 1285D] the man whose spirit is in his nostrils. Who is that but the one whom you killed, whose spirit you drove out from his nostrils—although he, when he willed, emitted his spirit from his own nostrils? Cease from him; for behold, his spirit is in his nostrils. His spirit has risen; it has been restored to his nostrils. He has ascended into heaven and is accounted high—that is, most high—for behold, he sits at the right hand of God the Father. Cease; restrain your mouth; do not let your tongue go forth; do not blaspheme.

But if you say, “Cease from the man whose spirit is in his nostrils,” that is, do not believe in him who breathes as other people do, you speak against your own intention, unhappy men. For if his spirit is in his nostrils, [Col. 1286A] he has risen, as was said, and therefore is accounted high. Therefore cease willingly, otherwise you shall cease unwillingly.

**(Chapter III.)** “For behold, the ruler, the Lord God of hosts, shall take away from Jerusalem and Judah the strong man and the mighty man, every support of bread and every support of water, the strong man and the warrior, judge and prophet, diviner and elder, captain of fifty, and honourable man of countenance,” etc. Those who wish may read the tragedy of your calamity, and shall prove that I am a true prophet in all these things.

## CHAPTER XII. That the one of whom he says, “A man shall seize his brother, one of his father’s household,” is Moses, of whom they say, “We are Moses’ disciples”; and how he says on the contrary, “I am not a physician, and there is no bread in my house,” etc.

[Col. 1286B] “For a man shall seize his brother, one of his father’s household, and say: ‘You have clothing; be our prince, and let this ruin be under your hand.’ He shall answer in that day, saying: ‘I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor clothing. Do not appoint me ruler of the people.’” For there shall be such a scarcity of people and, above all, such a want of every kind of resource, that one who has food and clothing will be thought powerful, rich, and illustrious, and will seem able through his own power to sustain and protect the common misery and calamity.

But in the deeper sense, which seems more pertinent to the matter, the man—that is, the Jewish people, who dared to crucify its Lord—shall seize its brother, one of its father’s household: that is, Moses, not God or Lord but its brother and equal, a member of the household, and not even the Lord of its father Abraham. [Col. 1286C] It shall seize him and hope in him, but shall do so in vain, saying, “We are Moses’ disciples” (John 9). In vain, I say, it shall seize him and hope in him. For it has been said: “There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope” (John 5).

Therefore he shall answer: “This is not so. I am not a physician; in my house there is neither bread nor clothing. Go away, troublesome flatterers. Do not flatter me by saying, ‘We are Moses’ disciples,’ while crucifying the Lord and teacher of Moses. Go away, ruined men. I shall not be your ruler; your ruin shall not be under my hand. I am not the physician who can heal the ruin by which you have fallen outwardly and by which you have fallen inwardly. He was—indeed, he is—the physician whom you blaspheme, whom you killed, you violently strong madmen. Why do you say, ‘You have clothing’? Is it because the legislation was entrusted to me? Certainly there is no clothing, indeed neither bread nor clothing, in my house. Clothing is in the house of him by whose finger the Law was woven. Bread is in the house of him whose food is the vision of angels.”

Why will he answer in this way and say, “Do not appoint me ruler of the people”? Certainly because of the crime of that same people. For Jerusalem has fallen and Judah has collapsed because their tongue and their devices were against the Lord, so as to provoke the eyes of his majesty. Jerusalem has fallen and Judah has collapsed because they blasphemed against the Lord and said, “Away, away! Crucify, crucify [Col. 1287A] such a one! We have no king but Caesar” (John 19), and with the fury of their tongue provoked the most merciful God to bitterness.

“The recognition of their face shall answer against them, and they proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they did not hide it.” What is “the recognition of their face” but the blindness of their mind? Truly it shall answer against them: that is, it happened to them deservedly. Why? Because “they proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they did not hide it.” Just as the Sodomites, sinning with common licence and feeling no shame whatsoever in their crime, said to Lot, “Bring out the men, that we may abuse them” (Gen. 19), so they too publicly proclaimed their sin and had no shame at all in blaspheming. Therefore, just as the recognition of their face [Col. 1287B] answered against those men, so that, struck with blindness from least to greatest, they could not find the door (ibid.), so the recognition of their own face answered against these men, so that, having a veil of wickedness over their hearts, they could not find him who says, “I am the door” (John 10).

“Woe to their soul, because evils have been repaid to them. Say to the righteous that it is well, for he shall eat the fruit of his devices.” You who hear and understand these things, praise God’s judgment, because he has justly repaid evils to them. Favour the righteous one whom they unjustly blasphemed and condemned, and say that he has done all things well, because he shall eat the fruit of his devices. Say this to the righteous, so that he in turn may favour you, and so that, while he eats, you also may eat and drink [Col. 1287C] at his table in his kingdom (Luke 22).

Conversely: “Woe to the ungodly unto evil, for the recompense of his hands shall be made to him. The extortioners of my people have despoiled them, and women have ruled over them.” Who are these extortioners and these women? Extortioners because of rapacity; women because of passive, Sodomitic lust. These extortioners, these women, were the scribes and Pharisees, who, for the sake of shameful gain—so that they might receive tithes and first-fruits with which to satisfy their lusts—persuaded the people to crucify the Son of God. In doing this they stripped the people of all glory and set it naked among enemies. Yet they call the captive people blessed, promising Antichrist in place of Christ. Therefore it follows: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way [Col. 1287D] of your steps.” Therefore he immediately says:

## CHAPTER XIII. That the Lord of whom he says, “He stands to judge,” is Christ Jesus, of whom Stephen says, “Behold, I see the heavens opened,” etc.; and that an act of his judgment has already occurred, by which the crown of the daughters of Zion was made bald when the Romans devastated them.

The Lord stands to judge, and he stands to judge the peoples. The Lord who ascended into heaven, who sits at the right hand of God—he himself stands to judge. For the protomartyr Stephen also bears witness to this when he says: “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). When he said these things, the Lord was already standing to judge, and judgment was hanging over that council of evildoers. Hence it further follows: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and its rulers” [Col. 1288A], that is, against the elders of his people and its rulers. Why? “For you,” he says, “have devoured my vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your house.” Therefore I bring a charge against you on this account; on this account I exact judgment.

O elders of my people, O rulers of my people: you have devoured my vineyard; and, what is more, you have carried the plunder of the poor into your house. Does not the Law say: “When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, eat as many grapes as you please, but do not carry any away with you” (Deut. 23)? But you entered my vineyard and killed my servants, whom I had sent to cultivate it and bear fruit (Matt. 21), so that you alone might devour my vineyard. This was too little: I sent to you my only Son, needy and poor, and you said: “This [Col. 1288B] is the heir; let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (ibid.). Therefore the plunder of the poor is in your house; for you killed the poor man so that the inheritance might be yours.

“Why do you crush my people and grind the faces of the poor?” says the Lord of hosts (Isa. 3), etc. O hard-hearted vintners, how do you devour my vineyard? By crushing and grinding the faces of the poor. Plainly, unless they put something into your mouths, you consecrate war against them. You publicly rebuke and shame poor sinners; but against the rich, though they sin more grievously, you do nothing at all. Therefore you killed the poor man so that you might usurp his vineyard, so that you might use the spoils of the poor with such cruelty.

Therefore now hear the Lord’s sentence, O women who rule his people, as he said above [Col. 1288C]. For he does not deem you worthy to be counted as men, but as women, because you flow away in pleasures and, in order to satisfy your pleasures, plunder so greedily that nothing could be more intolerable. Hear, therefore, you ruling women, women alike overflowing in luxury and blood:

“And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion were lifted up, and walked with outstretched neck, and went with the motions of their eyes and clapped, walking along, and advanced with a measured step of their feet, the Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will lay bare their hair,” etc.

For what, O hearers, O senators of the whole world, could be more shameless than these daughters of Zion—daughters, I say, that is, not men, as they ought to have been, but effeminate women? They are exalted while sitting [Col. 1288D] on Moses’ seat; they walk with outstretched necks, receiving greetings in the marketplace and loving to be called Rabbi by men; they go with motions of the eyes and clap, ever lusting after adultery and incest. As rulers of Sodom, they walk and advance with measured step; hypocrites, enlarging their phylacteries and magnifying their fringes. Thus we rightly say to them: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and all uncleanness” (Matt. 23). “So you also outwardly appear righteous to men, but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.”

Would we not, then, most justly make bald the crown and lay bare the hair of such daughters, such little women? [Col. 1289A] How will they be made bald? So that the moth [tinea] of the hypocrites may be apparent to the whole world: we shall take from them their beautiful Temple; the powers that preside over the Temple will depart; and we shall set them naked amid Roman swords.

“On that day the Lord will take away the ornament of their footwear, and the crescents, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, turbans, headbands, anklets, chains, scent-bottles, earrings, rings, gems hanging on the forehead, changes of apparel, cloaks, linen garments, ribbons, mirrors, fine linen, fillets, and veils.” For what do these things, laid over the bodies of little women, accomplish except to cast the snares of desire upon men through the windows of their eyes? So indeed whatever the scribes and Pharisees do concerning themselves and the splendid worship of the Temple [Col. 1289B] serves no other purpose than the ruin of those who look upon it. The Lord will therefore take away those things which are rightly signified by the aforesaid ornaments of women, lest they cause a scandal to beholders any longer.

For truly, if daughters of Zion of this kind had remained with all the adornment of the city and Temple, no small scandal would have arisen among many believers in Christ. Therefore, once they have been made bald and stripped naked, “there shall be stench instead of sweet perfume, and instead of a belt, a rope,” etc. For as sweet as the Synagogue’s reputation was formerly, so much the more does it now stink, since the whole earth perceives its most foul odor. Instead of the belt, or sacred girdle, of Aaron the high priest, it has received upon its head the long rope of captivity. Finally he concludes thus: “And she shall sit desolate upon the ground” [Col. 1289C]—so that the adulterous Synagogue, which formerly acted as it did, may no longer entice anyone into desiring it.

## CHAPTER XIV. That those seven women are the gifts of the Holy Spirit resting upon the one Christ.

*(Chapter 4.)* “And seven women shall take hold of one man on that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach.’”

The seven women are understood as the seven graces of the Spirit of the Lord: namely, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). They will take hold of the one man, the Lord Jesus [Col. 1289D] Christ, whom they had desired for a long time, because they could find no other in whom they might rest with everlasting steadfastness.

But this interpretation fails in part. For how can the seven spirits of God say: “We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments”? Another interpretation: “Seven women shall take hold of one man,” as above. That is to say: the daughters of Zion—those women previously described, who despoiled my people and ruled over them—killed the Lord of the vineyard in order that they might devour his vineyard more freely. Therefore they shall be made bald; therefore they shall be stripped naked; and seven women shall rise in judgment against them, that is, all the nations of all the churches among the Gentiles, whose totality is also understood in the Apocalypse under the number seven (Rev. [Col. 1290A] 2, 3, 13). They shall rise, I say, in judgment against that evil and adulterous generation of the children of Zion, and shall condemn it (Luke 11; Matt. 12).

How? By taking hold of one man—no other man than the very one whom those women killed, whom they cast out of his vineyard and murdered. They shall take hold of this man, left in his blood, and love him all the more. “We shall eat bread,” they say, etc. As though they said: The daughters of this harlot, to whom you gave your bread, whom you clothed with your garments, killed you and still do not cease to blaspheme. Come to us, and deign only that your name be invoked over us. We do not seek your bread, nor do we demand clothing from you. That harlot had no bread and needed garments. For she possessed no lands; [Col. 1290B] she was enslaved in Egypt and subject to the lust of demons and Egyptians. You redeemed her; you liberated her through the mighty deeds of your power; you fed her with manna; then you gave her land, the regions of the nations, and the labors of peoples, from which she might receive bread and clothing. When you had done these things, she cast you out; she killed you. She repaid evil to you for good.

By contrast, we shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments. We do not ask that those nations be killed for our sake, so that we may obtain their excellent land, a land flowing with milk and honey. But what do we ask? Only let your name be invoked over us, so that we may be called and may be your wives and your Churches; and thus take away our reproach [Col. 1290C], so that we may no longer be called, or be, what we were called and were: namely, “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope and without God in this world” (Eph. 2).

## CHAPTER XV. That from then on sins are remitted to all believers by the grace of the Holy Spirit, as he says: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion,” etc.

“On that day the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be sublime, and a rejoicing for those who have been saved from Israel.”

“The Branch of the Lord,” he says, “shall be magnificent and glorious,” through that gracious and unified union of the seven women, through the single faith of many Churches throughout the whole world. “And the fruit of the earth shall be sublime”: that is, men of such great perfection [Col. 1290D] that, though they are still earth by the condition of mortality, they are heaven by the greatness of heavenly wisdom, and their citizenship is already in heaven (Phil. 3). “And there shall be rejoicing for those who have been saved from Israel”; for the apostles shall rejoice when they see how greatly God has worked through them among the Gentiles (Acts 4).

“And it shall be: everyone who is left in Zion and who remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy—everyone who is written for life in Jerusalem”; understand, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, for only then shall the remnant be saved (Rom. 11). “Everyone,” he says, “who is written for life in Jerusalem”: that is, all who have been ordained beforehand to eternal life. But how shall he be called, or become, holy? He says: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanse her blood from her midst, in the spirit [Col. 1291A] of judgment and the spirit of burning.”

This indeed is a single rule of interpretation. Accordingly I said above: “Wash yourselves; be clean,” after first declaring that “your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1). That blood cannot otherwise be cleansed except by the Lord’s washing in the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning: that is, in the fire of the Holy Spirit together with the washing of visible water. That one and same Spirit is the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning. He is the spirit of judgment—that is, of discernment—because, distinguishing the faithful from the unfaithful, he grants remission of sins through faith. He is the spirit of burning because, after cleansing a human being from sins, he then kindles that person with the fire of good zeal.

“And the Lord shall create over every place of Mount Zion, and where he is invoked, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night.” Then the people will receive again [Col. 1291B] their former blessedness, which they once possessed in the wilderness, when the Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exod. 13), so that they may never be troubled either in prosperity or adversity, in accordance with what is said in the Psalm: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120).

This smoke, however, does not signify error or ignorance; for the text continues: “and the brightness of flaming fire.” Therefore the smoke which it befitted God to create will be the tearful compunction of penitents mourning their sins; in due sequence there follows the bright desire for the kingdom of God. “For over all glory there shall be a protection and a tabernacle for shade by day from the heat, for security and concealment from storm and rain” [Col. 1291C]. Whoever has deserved, after the smoke of tearful penitence, to attain the creation of flaming fire—that is, radiant desire—so that the contemplation of the joys of the heavenly homeland delights him, such a one has this glorious promise: “There shall be a protection and a tabernacle over all glory.”

For truly, one who has tasted, in contemplation, the blessedness of the world to come reckons all the glory of this world empty, 487 and is hidden in secret from the heat, storm, and rain of the present age, so that he may say with the Psalmist: “For he hid me in his tabernacle; in the day of evils he protected me in the hiding-place of his tabernacle” (Ps. 29). And in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch” (Song 5). Indeed, one who thus sleeps in concealment has been glorified above all the glory of kings, since he may say: [Col. 1291D] “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

## CHAPTER XVI. That this song is the second section concerning Christ’s Passion, and that in accordance with this song the Lord spoke the parable: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard.”

*(Chapter 5.)* “I will sing to my beloved a song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard. A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil. And he fenced it,” etc.

This song is the beginning of the second section. What he said at the beginning—“I begot and exalted children, but they despised me” (Isa. 1)—this song expounds more fully in the parable of the vineyard. It is called, however, a song by contraries, for it is in truth the same thing as the “woe” likewise pronounced at the beginning: “Woe to the sinful nation.”

“I will sing,” he says, “to my beloved,” that is, to Christ, the true beloved of my soul. For who does not know that your soul, O singer, loved and loves Christ, the supremely desirable one? Indeed, he testifies that the song was sung for Christ or concerning his work, since Christ, drawing a parable from it, says to the chief priests and Pharisees: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, and leased it to husbandmen” (Matt. 21), etc.

This song distinctly indicates whose woe it is when it says: “A song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard.” For who was the prophet’s kinsman except those husbandmen already mentioned, namely the Levitical and priestly order? Since the prophet himself was from the tribe of Judah, Levi was in a manner his uncle. His kinsmen, however, were the entire Levitical and priestly order. Moreover [Col. 1292B], the vineyard of the beloved was the people. Therefore: “I will sing to my beloved a song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard”; that is, I shall speak to Christ, so that he may announce to the husbandmen and to his vineyard—that is, to his priests and people—a lamentable song.

“A vineyard was made for my beloved.” What this vineyard is, the singer himself makes clear at the end of the conclusion: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts,” he says, “is the house of Israel.” It was made as an acquisition for my beloved, not through gold or silver, but through the many wonders which he performed in the land of Egypt. Hence it is written: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. 79). It was made “on a horn,” that is, by the same power by which he brought it out, just as Balaam, after saying of the same people, “God brought him out of Egypt,” immediately added: “His strength is like that of a rhinoceros” [Col. 1292C] (Num. 24).

This vineyard was made, as I have said, for my beloved, the “son of oil,” that is, the son of God’s charity. For it was made for him so that, when he came, he might possess it prepared for himself and sanctify it through his blood. And this he did. For through his blood he brought out of hell all those whose portion is the good vineyard. From its root, moreover, he took the apostles, from whom, or through whom, the entire world was filled with good vines. Or “for the son of oil” means “in a fertile place,” because truly nothing is more fertile than the land of promise.

“And he fenced it”: that is, he enclosed it with the protection of angels. “And he chose stones out of it”: that is, he repeatedly removed from it, with diligent care, idols or whatever could hinder the worship of God. “And he planted it as a chosen [vine],” that is, as the best vine, deeply rooted in the faith of the chosen Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. “And he built a tower in its midst,” that is, a Temple in the midst of its royal city. “And he built a winepress in it,” that is, an altar which yields profit to priests just as a winepress does to husbandmen. “And I expected,” he says, “that it would produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes”: that is, I expected it to do good, but it performed evil works.

“Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard.” Did he not, then, sing this song to the beloved of his soul? Finally, he arranged the parable later spoken in the Gospel according to the meaning of this song, so that he plainly intends it to be understood as sung to himself; and at last he asks, in nearly the same words: “When, therefore,” he says, “the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those husbandmen?” (Matt. 21). The only difference is that here he calls for judgment between the lord of the vineyard and the vineyard itself, while there it is between the lord of the vineyard and the husbandmen.

What he intends here by “wild grapes,” he discloses more plainly there, breaking out in these words: “And the husbandmen, having seized his servants, beat one, killed another” (ibid.). “And now,” he says, “I will show you what I shall do to my vineyard.” O inhabitants of Jerusalem, O men of Judah: I asked you to judge between me and my vineyard; and because you will not answer what I ask, I shall answer myself: “I will take away its hedge,” that is, I shall remove the help of angels, “and it shall be plundered. I shall tear down its wall, and it shall be trampled down; and I shall make it desolate. It shall not be watered or dug.” The meaning is: I shall destroy its walls, when the Roman army surrounds it [Col. 1293B], so that it may never be rebuilt.

Nor will it suffer under the Romans as it suffered under the Babylonians. For it follows: “And I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.” For Jeremiah, after the city had been captured, is reported to have prophesied among the people; and Ezekiel, Daniel, and the three youths either prophesied or even performed miraculous signs in captivity; later Haggai and Zechariah spoke of future things to comfort the people in bondage. But now I shall command clouds of this sort not to rain upon it: that is, that they may no longer have apostles or prophets to kill. Therefore in Leviticus he says: “I shall make your heaven iron and your earth bronze” (Lev. 26).

Why shall I command this to my clouds? “Because I expected it to produce judgment, and behold, iniquity” [Col. 1293C]. For how great was the iniquity, and how great the outcry, when they killed the servants of the householder and, seeing his Son, concerning whom he had said, “They will reverence my Son” (Matt. 21), cried: “Crucify, crucify” (Luke 25 [materially uncertain citation; presumably Luke 23]).

## CHAPTER XVII. How that invective of the Lord, in which, after reciting that parable, he reproached the scribes and Pharisees with eight woes, accords with the prophetic sense of this passage; for after this song he pronounces eight woes upon them, saying: “Woe to those who join house,” etc.

“Woe to those who join house to house and add field to field, even to the boundary of the place,” etc.

Six times in this passage the Holy Spirit cries “Woe” through this minister of his word:

“Woe to those who join house to house!”
“Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness!”
“Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity!”
“Woe to those who call evil good and good evil!”
“Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes!”
“Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine and strong men to mix drunkenness!”

Two further woes must be understood in these two sentences of wrath: “Who say: Let his work hasten; let it come quickly, so that we may see it”; and “Who justify [Col. 1293D] the wicked for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him.” Clearly all these things belong to the song which he proposed to sing to his beloved, and which he also sings to the evil husbandmen—that is, to the scribes and Pharisees, the murderers of that same beloved.

The beloved himself bears witness to this: he repeats the same number of woes sung to him by this prophet, namely eight, when after setting forth the parable of the vineyard he says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men! Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour widows’ houses, praying long prayers! Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte! Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the Temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the Temple is bound! Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and have left aside the weightier matters of the law! Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of cup and dish, but within are full of plunder and uncleanness! Woe to you, [Col. 1294B] scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every uncleanness! Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the dead and adorn the monuments of the righteous” (Matt. 23).

Does not the singer, therefore, in singing such a song, aim at the same end as his beloved to whom he sang it, who, in repeating it, inveighs against them in the same number of pronouncements?

## CHAPTER XVIII. That by the first woe he prophetically strikes at the intolerable avarice of the scribes and Pharisees, and predicts that because of it the city will be destroyed.

First, then, this woe strikes at the intolerable avarice of the scribes and Pharisees: “Woe,” he says, “to those [Col. 1294C] who join house to house and add field to field, even to the boundary of the place! Shall you dwell alone in the midst of the land? These things are in my ears, says the Lord of hosts.”

He immediately adds what punishment follows the evil of this same avarice: “Unless many houses, great and beautiful, shall become desolate and without inhabitant. For ten yokes of vineyard shall yield one small jar, and thirty measures of seed shall yield three measures.”

Clearly here he foresees and predicts that, because of the avarice of the priests, the city will be destroyed. This is confirmed by the beloved often mentioned, to whom he sang. For when he saw the city, he wept over it, saying: “If only you too had known ... that days will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart and will not leave in you one stone upon another.” Then immediately, after entering the Temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in it, saying to them: “It is written, ‘My house is a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of thieves” (Luke 19).
