The distinctive force of the expression should be noted, where through an ellipsis he most sharply signifies a greater measure of vengeance or wrath. “Unless,” he says, “many houses, great and beautiful, become desolate and without inhabitant”—understand: the woe which I have foretold to you is false. But that ten yokes of vineyard should yield one small jar and thirty measures of seed three measures means that those who had been rich perished by hunger and thirst in the Roman siege, as the narrative of that unhappy history sufficiently shows.

## CHAPTER XIX. That by the second woe he rebukes their drunkenness, in which, already drunk, they seized the Lord on that Passover evening.

“Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they are inflamed with wine! Lyre and harp, drum and flute, and wine are at your banquets; but you do not regard the work of the Lord or consider the works of his hands.”

This woe reproves the same husbandmen for excessive drunkenness. “Until evening,” he says. Plainly, in the Spirit, the future day was already present to him: that day when, intoxicated and stupefied with festive drunkenness, they seized the Lord of the vineyard, the Son of God, when it was the Passover evening. Therefore, woe to you, drunkards, he says—those drunk with vomiting, debauchery, and filth—who, inflamed with wine [Col. 1295B], seized the sober Son of God.

“Lyre and harp, drum and flute, and wine are at your banquets.” The prophet Amos, vigorously pursuing this same matter, after saying, “You who eat the lamb from the flock and the calf from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery,” turns most fittingly to these persons and says: “They imagined that they possessed instruments of song like David; drinking wine in bowls and anointed with the finest ointment, they suffered nothing over the affliction of Joseph” (Amos 6).

What this passage says, “You do not regard the work of the Lord or consider the works of his hands,” Amos expresses with great elegance when he says, “They suffered nothing over the affliction of Joseph.” For the affliction of Joseph—that is, the Passion of the Lord, which is customarily understood through Joseph’s sale—is the work of the Lord, the work of his hands, the work of our redemption. These drunkards did not regard this work of the Lord, for they suffered nothing over the affliction of Joseph while anointed with the finest ointment. How true it is that they suffered nothing over the affliction of Joseph, who were moved to excessive laughter and loud mockery over him.

What then? “Therefore my people have been led captive because they had no knowledge.” Therefore, I say, because they had no knowledge of the work of the Lord just mentioned, because they did not know how to sympathize with Joseph’s affliction, they were led captive among all nations. “And its nobles perished by hunger, and its multitude dried up with thirst.” This was so true that, in that siege, a noblewoman named Mary ate her own son.

But the vengeance is slight unless, as was foretold through Moses [Col. 1295D], “a kindled fire burns to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32). It therefore follows: “Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit. And its mighty men, its people, its lofty and glorious ones shall descend to it,” etc.

By contrast, the meek and humble will abound in the Lord’s good things; hence he finally adds: “And lambs shall feed according to their order, and strangers shall eat the deserts turned into abundance.” When the Lord has been exalted in judgment and the Holy One sanctified in his righteousness, so that the evil husbandmen perish evilly, then those who belong to the number of lambs, not goats, shall feed in the meadows of the Church; and strangers—that is, the people of the Gentiles—shall eat what was left desolate by the Jews and turned into abundance.

## CHAPTER XX. [Col. 1296A] Concerning the third woe, in which he says: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity,” because in killing Christ they fulfilled the measure of their fathers.

“Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a cart-rope.”

This woe accords with that in which the Lord says: “Woe to you who build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous” (Matt. 23). And immediately after: “Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who killed the prophets. You too, then, fill up the measure of your fathers” (ibid.).

Indeed, to fill up the measure of impious fathers in such a way that, because the fathers killed the prophets, the sons, not degenerating from them, kill the Lord of the prophets—this is precisely to draw iniquity [Col. 1296B] with cords of vanity and sin as though with a cart-rope. Therefore woe to you, because you will also draw out a long cord of punishments! For “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar, all these things shall come upon this generation” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the fourth woe of those who said: “Let it hasten; let the time come quickly,” etc.; namely, when they said: “If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross.”

“Who say: ‘Let his work hasten; let it come quickly, so that we may see it; and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, so that we may know it.’”

“Who say, ‘Let it hasten’—woe to you.” Why? Did not the work of the Holy One of Israel hasten greatly and come quickly? Did he not quickly [Col. 1296C] rise after three days? Do you not know it? Did not the guards of the tomb announce it to you—those who, when a great earthquake occurred, were terrified and, through fear of the angel descending from heaven, became like dead men? (Matt. 28). What more haste did you desire when you said: “If he is king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him”? (Matt. 27). How quickly did you desire his work to come when you said: “He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he desires him”? (ibid.). Indeed, what a most wicked demand for haste it was: you wished to question him through insult and torture whether he was the Son of God. Therefore woe to you!

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the fifth woe, because they called good evil; namely, in reserving Barabbas and condemning [Col. 1296D] Christ.

“Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter!”

Why do you so insolently pervert judgment? You call the good Son of God evil; you called the evil robber Barabbas good. You make his darkness—that is, Barabbas’s murders and seditions—your light; but his light—that is, Christ’s teaching and truth—you make darkness, that is, deception. For you say: “He is evil, and he has stirred up the people, teaching throughout all Judea” (Luke 23). Therefore woe to you who rejected his sweetness as though it were bitterness, and drank down Barabbas’s bitterness, so that you might possess his seditions as an inheritance!

## CHAPTER XXIII. [Col. 1297A] Concerning the sixth woe, against those who, wise in their own eyes, took away the key of knowledge from them.

“Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent before themselves!”

Why did you take away the key of knowledge? You yourselves did not enter, and you prevented those entering. You shut the kingdom of heaven before men, sitting on Moses’ seat, loving the chief seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23). Therefore woe to you also for this!

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the seventh woe, against those who are mighty men at mixing drunkenness.

“Woe to those who are mighty to drink wine and strong men [Col. 1297B] at mixing drunkenness!”

You drank mightily; you mixed intoxicants strongly—strong men, frenzied men. For this is why you struck the true physician. You drank the worst wine, the wine of error, and the spirit of dizziness. Hence Moses says: “Their wine is from the vineyard of Sodom and from the suburbs of Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32).

And, physically drunk on that evening mentioned above, you seized the Son of God; thereafter you have not ceased boldly—indeed obstinately—to mix the wine of wicked teaching, in defense of your homicide, to multiply blasphemies against the one whom you killed, and continually to administer hatred of him to your children. Therefore woe [Col. 1297C] to you!

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the eighth woe, against those who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous.

“Woe to you who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!”

Why did you take from him the righteousness of the righteous one, who came blessed in the name of the Lord, except because he brought you no gifts of gold and silver, but came poor and humble? “Behold,” says the prophet Zechariah, “daughter of Zion; behold, O daughter of Jerusalem: your king shall come to you, righteous and a savior; he himself is poor, riding upon a she-ass and upon a colt, the foal of a she-ass” (Zech. 9). Because he came not only righteous but also poor, as this passage says [Col. 1297D], you took his righteousness from him.

By contrast, if that other wicked rich man comes in his own name, you will receive him; for gifts you will justify him, as though you would at once gain victory over all nations, as though you would dwell in an earthly Jerusalem of gold and gems. Therefore woe to you!

## CHAPTER XXVI. That because of these evils the Roman army had to come, and how, even beyond that vengeance, the hand of the Lord is still stretched out.

“Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of flame consumes it, so their root shall be as ashes and their shoot shall rise like dust,” etc.

The whole world has heard that these things happened to them under Roman rule. “In all these things his anger has not been turned away, [Col. 1298A] but his hand is still stretched out.” This distinction indicates what no one doubts: for God’s enemies, bodily death, however horrible, is not the final punishment or the end of evils. Therefore there is no objection to understanding what follows as concerning the second coming of Christ, when he will come to judge.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the words, “And behold, he shall come swiftly,” and concerning the Day of Judgment, when he shall roar like a lion’s cub, saying to those on the left: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire.”

And he will raise a standard among the nations afar off, and whistle for him from the ends of the earth; and behold, he will come swiftly and speedily. He is neither failing nor weary; he will not slumber or sleep; the belt of his loins will not be loosened, nor the strap of his sandal broken. [Col. 1298B] His arrows are sharp, and all his bows drawn.

For when the Jews who rejected him have been scattered, he himself, he says, will raise the sign of his cross among the nations afar off, and will whistle—that is, by a hidden inspiration he will bring the nations to himself from the ends of the earth—and behold, he will come swiftly and speedily. For although his coming, which has not yet occurred, may seem delayed, there is nevertheless no delay when the greatness of the matter is considered. Hence the Wise Man says: “He will appear to us terribly and swiftly” (Wis. 6). He is neither failing nor weary: that is, at that coming he will not be mortal as before, nor weak as before. None will slumber or sleep: that is, our God will come not hidden as formerly, but manifestly. The belt of his loins will not be loosened, nor the strap of his sandal broken—namely, as once happened when he hung unbelted on the cross and, in dying, the strap of flesh was broken, because God had come shod.

But what follows? His arrows are sharp, and all his bows drawn. For he will deliver judgments that are discriminating and sharp, by the drawn bow of keen judgment, while many judges hold individual bows—that is, the authority to judge. The hoofs of his horses are like flint, and his wheel like the onset of a storm. His horses and chariots are thrones and dominions, and all the powers of heaven, which will be shaken at his coming (Luke 21); and “a mighty storm will be round about him” (Ps. 49). These horses are said to have hoofs like flints because they are eternal and are not wearied by any weakness.

His roaring is like that of a lion; [Col. 1298D] he will roar like a lion’s cub, and gnash his teeth, and seize the prey, and clasp it, and there will be none to rescue it. Truly, his roar is like that of a lion, at which the astonished earth will tremble and the dead, awakened, will leap up. He will roar like a lion’s cub, saying: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). He will gnash his teeth and seize the prey and clasp it; for he will hold those on the right as his prey, because concerning them it was prophetically said to this lion: “You have gone up to the prey, my son” (Gen. 49). There will be none to rescue it—certainly none will snatch it from his hand.

“And in that day it will sound over him like the sound of the sea.” “Over him,” he says, namely over the devil, whom, with a great sound and in the sight of all, he will cast down. “We shall look upon the land, and behold darkness of tribulation; and the light is darkened in its gloom.” “We shall look,” he says. Who are “we”? Surely we holy prophets and great patriarchs. Then will there be darkness of tribulation even for such as these? Certainly there will be, when we look upon the earth and see Tartarus gaping open. There will, I say, be darkness of tribulation so immense that, if we could in any way die, the distress caused by that sight alone would suffice to deprive us of life through the excess of fear and trembling. For “the righteous man will scarcely be saved” (1 Pet. 4 [the citation is printed as II Peter]); therefore we too shall look upon the darkness of tribulation, where that monstrous beast will be cast down, and even our light—that is, our holiness—will be darkened with terror in its gloom.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What it means for the Lord to sit upon a lofty throne; what those things beneath him that fill the temple are; what the Seraphim are; what the Lord’s face and feet are; and what is meant by their cry: “Holy, holy.”

**(CH. 6.)** “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne lofty and exalted; and the things beneath him filled the temple.”

This third section especially requires an alert interpreter, because it is particularly closed to those whom the Holy Spirit judged unworthy of the knowledge of truth, as Scripture itself plainly indicates. For at its beginning it is said: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes” (Isa. 8), and so forth. And near the end of the same section: “Bind up the testimony,” he says; “seal the law among my disciples” (ibid.).

Therefore, lest we suffer anything from their smoke—on account of whom the testimony of this vision has been bound and sealed—may the Holy Spirit illumine our hearts by the brightness of his light. Under his guidance, let us first bring forward the lamp of evangelical truth. After the Evangelist John had said, “Therefore the Jews could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them,’” he immediately added: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke concerning him” (John 12). Who, then, can doubt that the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed here, and that the prophet speaks here concerning him?

“I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne lofty and exalted”: [Col. 1299D] that is, I saw in the Spirit; I saw with the prophetic eye the Lord of all, Jesus Christ, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, exalted above all the heavens, and received into the session at the Father’s right hand. Truly that throne is lofty, and far exalted above the human lowliness in which he deigned to suffer.

Why, however, he now prefaced this with “in the year in which King Uzziah died,” but afterwards says, “And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, son of Uzziah king of Judah,” and so forth, must not be passed over in its proper place.

“And the things,” he says, “that were beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. 7). After the Lord, ascending into heaven, sat upon that lofty and exalted throne of paternal majesty, the things which are beneath him are, plainly, the gifts that he gave to human beings: the gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1300A] that he gave to the apostles and to the rest who believed in him. These fill the temple—that is, they build and complete the Church of God throughout the whole world.

“The Seraphim stood above it.” *Seraphim* is interpreted “burning” or “kindling.” Who, then, are the Seraphim but the apostles, whom the Holy Spirit made burning and kindling on the tenth day after his ascension? For divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them, and one sat upon each of them; “and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2). These stood above that temple, for these fathers and judges preside over the Church of God.

“Six wings to one, and six wings to the other.” The number six is full and perfect, because it is formed from its parts. For it has its half, namely three; its third, namely two; [Col. 1300B] and its sixth, namely one. When these are added together, they make six. And in the number of six days God completed this world. Therefore, the six wings of each Seraph signify the full and perfect knowledge of truth which the Holy Spirit taught the apostles, according to the promise of him who said: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16).

“With two wings they covered his face, and with two they covered his feet.” The face of the Lord is Christ’s divinity, concerning which it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). The feet of the Lord are Christ’s humanity, concerning which it is likewise written: “And the Word became flesh” (ibid.). They covered both—that is, they preached both and, for a time, concealed them from the unworthy; [Col. 1300C] nor did they cast their pearls before swine (Matt. 7).

“With two wings they covered”: that is, they preached both. For what does it mean that they covered the face with as many wings as the feet, and flew with the same number, except that with equal purpose they proclaimed both Christ’s divinity and his humanity, according to time or place? And to what end did they fly? What follows is: “And they cried one to another and said: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts. The whole earth is full of his glory.’”

Therefore they flew—that is, they preached the faith of the Holy Trinity, hitherto unknown—according to the rule of him who said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). This thrice “Holy” is one Lord; one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For he is the Lord God of hosts, especially from the time when the Seraphim began thus to cry to one another—that is, with concordant faith and mutual comparison of the Scriptures. For from that time especially the hosts of believers increased and multiplied. Hence it is immediately added: “The whole earth is full of his glory”—that is, whereas previously he was known only in Judaea. For the fact that here he is seen sitting upon a lofty and exalted throne and then that the whole earth is said to be full of his glory is what the Psalmist indicates in one verse: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. 107).

## CHAPTER XXIX. What is meant by the shaking of the thresholds; by the smoke filling the Lord’s house; by the lips with which the people were defiled; in whose midst the prophet laments that he dwells; and by one of the Seraphim flying to him.

“And the thresholds of the house were shaken by the voice of the one crying, and the house was filled with smoke.” As the Seraphim cried out and preached the mystery of the Trinity throughout the whole earth, immediately the thresholds of the temple were shaken and all its hinges fell, fulfilling the Savior’s threat: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23).

Otherwise: the thresholds were shaken—that is, the chief priests, Annas and Caiaphas, and all those who held pre-eminence in the Synagogue, were roused by zeal. These thresholds, I say, were shaken at the glory of the Trinity which they had heard, [Col. 1301B] and they laid hands on the crying Seraphim, in order to shut their mouths—that is, in order to forbid the apostles to speak in the Lord’s name. “Strictly,” they said, “we commanded you not to teach in this name, and behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching” (Acts 5), and so forth.

Thus the thresholds were shaken, and the house, no longer the Lord’s house, was filled with the smoke of envy; and from that same matter by which the whole earth shone with the Lord’s glory, blindness befell Israel.

“And he said: ‘Woe is me, because I was silent, because I am a man of defiled lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having defiled lips! And I saw the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.’” This is what we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “When they heard these things, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles: ‘What shall we do, brethren?’” (Acts 2). “Woe is me,” then, he says, [Col. 1301C] “because I was silent.” Indeed, not merely because “I was silent,” but, what is worse, “because I am a man of defiled lips”—which the events themselves agree may rightly be said in their person. For they cried: “Away, away, crucify, crucify!” (John 19). They truly recognized that their lips had thereby become defiled; but they had been deceived and, through ignorance, had defiled their lips by such a cry.

It follows: “And I dwell in the midst of a people having defiled lips.” For many of them did not cry out from envy, but followed the crowd. “And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said: ‘Behold, I have touched your lips, and your iniquity will be taken away and your sin cleansed.’”

This one of the Seraphim [Col. 1301D] was the apostle Peter, who, flying on the wings of grace, said: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of your sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2). “In his hand was a small stone,” he says. The small stone is the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which the sins of those who believe in Christ are burned away. It was in the Seraph’s hand—that is, in the power of the apostle Peter above the rest. For Christ specially entrusted to him the keys of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 16). “Which he had taken from the altar with tongs”: that is, which he had obtained from Christ through the firm consistency of faith. For he was the first to say: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Therefore the first has in his hand the small stone—that is, the gift of the Holy Spirit—in the power or ministry of conferring the remission of sins.

## CHAPTER XXX. What is meant by saying, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” and by “Here am I, send me”; how Stephen the first martyr offered himself; and how, according to the sense of this passage, while standing in the council he announced harsh things to that people.

“And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?’ And I said: ‘Here am I; send me.’ And he said: ‘Go and say to this people: Hear continually, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not perceive. Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them.’”

“Whom,” he says, “shall I send, and who will go for us?” As though he said: Since they allow none of those whom we send to live, and have killed me myself, whom shall I find of such courage that I may send him? Who will go, or who will dare to go for us and say to them: “I, the Son of Man whom they killed, sit upon a throne lofty and exalted; I sit or stand at the right hand of God”?

“And I said: ‘Here am I; send me.’ And he said: ‘Go,’” and so forth. Above we said that the prophet spoke in the person of those who, pierced in heart by what the apostle Peter said, declared: “What shall we do?”—“Woe is me, because I was silent,” and so forth. He now says, in the person of the same one: “Here am I; send me.” In whose person, I say, but that of Stephen the first martyr, who, full of grace and strength, did not fear to go?

Surely he, as though unbidden, offered himself voluntarily and said, “Here am I; send me.” For we do not read that he received a commission from any of the apostles, [Col. 1302C] but that, while bearing public witness to the Son of God, though merely a deacon, he performed wonders and signs of apostolic power (Acts 6). Did not this man plainly bring the very embassy of which we speak? For, standing in the council and full of the Holy Spirit, he looked intently into heaven, saw the glory of God, and said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7).

“Go,” says the Lord, “and say to this people: ‘Hear continually, and do not understand,’” and so forth. He plainly also bore this part of the embassy, for he did not conceal the causes of so great a wrath. For he said: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed [Col. 1302D] those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers” (ibid.).

Certainly, what was said—“You will hear with your ears and not understand”—was at once shown to be true. For when he said, “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God,” they cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed upon him with one accord (ibid.).

“Blind the heart of this people,” he says. “And I said: ‘How long, Lord?’ And he said: ‘Until the cities are desolated without inhabitant,’” and so forth. The sense is: They will neither hear nor see, and their heart will remain blinded, until the cities of Judaea are utterly overthrown while Vespasian and Titus wage war, so completely that not even their former name remains; and such houses as remain are without inhabitants; and the land is reduced to desolation; and the Jewish people are scattered throughout the whole world by either flight or captivity. No longer in Judaea as formerly, but among all nations, the Jewish people will multiply.

For this is what follows: “And that which had been left will multiply in the midst of the land; and still in it there will be a tenth, and it will return.” As though he said: But why do I say “it will multiply”? The misery of the remnant people will be so great that, compared with the former multitude, scarcely a tenth part will remain. “It will return,” he says, “and will be for a display, like a terebinth and like an oak which spreads its branches. The holy seed will be that which remains in it.”

“And it will be for plundering,” when, about fifty years afterwards, Hadrian comes and utterly plunders the land of Judaea, so that it is compared to a terebinth and an oak that has lost its acorns. Finally, after the final devastation, even public laws were posted, and Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been expelled. But if anyone believes in Christ, and that is fulfilled which we read above—“Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1)—then, when according to the Apostle the remnant are saved (Rom. 9), this will be the holy seed, and all the Churches will put forth shoots from the stock of the apostles.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Why he joined to that vision an event occurring in the days of Ahaz; and how he fulfilled the command stated at the beginning of the vision: “Blind the heart of this people,” and again at its end: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.”

**(CH. 7.)** “And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz son of Jotham, son of Uzziah king of Judah, that Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to wage war against it, but they could not overcome it. And they reported to the house of David, saying: ‘Syria has rested upon Ephraim.’ And his heart and the heart of his people were shaken, as the trees of a forest are shaken by the wind.”

After relating the vision, he immediately and in continuous connection adds the account of an event that took place long afterwards, saying: “And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz.” This is particularly to be noted. For it should not now escape our memory that, when he began to relate the vision, he stated its time, saying: “In the year in which King Uzziah died” (Isa. 6). Indeed, between Uzziah and this Ahaz there were sixteen years during which Uzziah’s son Jotham reigned.

Why, then, in linking together an event performed so much later with the earlier vision, did he use this connective expression, saying, “And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz”? What are we to suppose except that in the days of Ahaz he finally did what had then been commanded him? And what had been commanded? Namely, that he should blind the people’s heart—that is, that he should relate this same vision in such a way that the people, because they did not deserve it, would not understand.

For he who then said, “Blind the heart of this people,” would later say: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8). And the prophet answers: “I will wait for the Lord, who hides his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him” (ibid.). Therefore, whatever in this place seems to hinder the Jews from understanding—or rather, whatever is thought to assist their impiety against the things thereafter prophesied concerning Christ—is a binding and a seal of prophetic testimony. Indeed, they are the evangelical laws proclaimed through this prophet, who says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” and so forth. But in Christ it is revealed to us through him who opened the sealed book and loosed both these seals and its other seals.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the fact that, when it was announced to the house of David that Syria had rested upon Ephraim, the Virgin’s conception and birth are announced; why he is called Emmanuel; and likewise, “Hasten to strip the spoils; hurry to plunder.”

“They reported,” he says, “to the house of David, saying: [Col. 1304B] ‘Syria has rested upon Ephraim.’ And his heart was shaken,” and so forth. Why was the heart of David and the heart of his people shaken, as trees of a forest are shaken by the wind? Plainly because, as was subsequently stated, Syria and Ephraim and the son of Remaliah had devised an evil plan against Judah, saying: “Let us go up against Judah, tear it away for ourselves, and set in its midst the son of Tabeel as king.” For this reason the heart of the house of David was shaken—namely, lest royal honour should perish from David’s house.

“It shall not stand,” says the Lord, “and it shall not be so,” and so forth. Then comes the promise: “Unless you believe, you shall not remain.” Immediately follows: “And the Lord added to speak to Ahaz, saying: ‘Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell or in the height above.’ And Ahaz said: ‘I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord.’ And he said: ‘Hear then, house of David: Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good.’”

And thereafter: “And the Lord said to me: ‘Take for yourself a large book and write in it with a man’s stylus: Swiftly strip the spoils; quickly plunder. And I took for myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Barachiah. And I approached the prophetess; she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: “Call his name: Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder; for before the child knows how to call his father [Col. 1304D] and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be carried away before the king of the Assyrians”’” (Isa. 8).

We know and confess that this prophecy truly concerns Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Conversely, the Jews say: “What has it to do with your Christ, born so many ages later, that Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, then killed Rezin king of Syria and destroyed the great plan of Rezin, that is, of Rezin and Pekah son of Remaliah?” (4 Kings 18). “Likewise, what has it to do with your Christ that, while Hezekiah reigned, the angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians?” (4 Kings 19). “Was he born then? Rather, it was Hezekiah—who did what was good before the Lord, according to all that David his father had done, and therefore the Lord was with him—who is called Emmanuel by the prophet, since Emmanuel means ‘God with us’; he was born not of a virgin, that is, a *betulah*, but of a young woman, that is, an *‘almah*.”

To this we say: Our Emmanuel had not yet indeed come in the flesh, but nevertheless he existed before Hezekiah and Ahaz—indeed, before Abraham. Not only was the great plan of Rezin and Pekah son of Remaliah overthrown, and Sennacherib’s army struck by him or for his sake; but whatever evil Israel and its fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob ever escaped, or whatever good they attained, was brought about by the work of this Emmanuel (4 Kings 15). For who or what healed Abraham except faith in this Emmanuel? From the time when Abraham believed God speaking to him, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” [Col. 1305B] (Gen. 22), whatever good he obtained either in himself or thereafter for his descendants, he accomplished or merited by faith in this his seed, this our Emmanuel.

Let us therefore now enter the treasures of this truth, saying: “Unless you believe, you shall not remain.” This means: For the present, by the help of the future Emmanuel, you will escape Rezin king of Syria, the son of Remaliah, and also Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, and you will remain in your land; but when he comes, if you do not believe, you shall not remain, because the Romans will come and take away both your place and your nation (John 11).

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Ahaz’s impiety; concerning this same Emmanuel; in what sense the saying “He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know,” and so forth, is rightly understood; and why one who is to be born after so long a time is now promised.

“And the Lord added to speak to Ahaz, saying: ‘Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, in the depth of hell or in the height above.’ And Ahaz said: ‘I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord.’”

His refusal to ask a sign from the Lord God arose not from humility but from pride. For although it is written in Deuteronomy, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. 6; Matt. 4), and the Savior used this testimony against the devil, still, when commanded to ask, he ought to have fulfilled the command through obedience—especially since Gideon and Manoah asked for and received a sign (Judg. 6, 13). For the impious king knew that, if he asked for a sign, he would receive it and God would be glorified.

Therefore, like an idolater, who had set up altars at every street-corner and on mountains and in wooded places, and regarded fanatics as Levites, he would not ask for the sign that had been commanded. And he said: “Hear then, house of David: Is it too little for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?” Who is this who said, “Hear then, house of David”? It is not God, who above had said to Ahaz, “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God,” but the prophet, as the following words prove: “that you are troublesome also to my God.”

The sense is this: Because you not only persecute the prophets and despise their sayings, but resist the judgment of God present and commanding, so that you weary him who says elsewhere, “I have laboured in enduring” (Isa. 1), the Lord will therefore do what follows. And it should be noted that, since the supremely impious King Ahaz was unwilling to ask for a sign, the prophetic discourse turns to the house of David—that is, to the royal tribe—of which we read above: “They reported these things to the house of David, saying: ‘Syria and Ephraim have agreed.’”

“Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good.” Therefore, he says, because you are troublesome not only to men but also to my God, killing his prophets and rejecting his worship, the Lord himself will give you a sign. The Lord himself, I say, will give you a great sign, worthy of himself. For behold, a virgin shall conceive, and so forth.

This sign will be terrible to you in this respect: this Emmanuel, conceived and born of a virgin, will eat butter and honey, that he may know to reject evil and choose good. What then? Did this Emmanuel, whose name means “God with us,” come for this purpose and eat butter and honey for this purpose, that he might know to reject evil and choose good? Yes, certainly. For you are “rulers of Sodom and people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). Therefore he now speaks within himself: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18).

Therefore he will eat butter and honey: that is, having become human, he will live among human beings in every fellowship and mode of life, in the full reality of human nature, so that he may know—not merely by knowledge but also by experience—how to reject your evil, the evil of Sodom, and choose good, when you, according to the fury of the Sodomites, surround him, seeking to mock, scourge, and crucify him. Having suffered these things, he will thereafter know how to reject evil and choose good, possessing authority to execute judgment (John 5), in which without doubt he will reject evil and choose good.

“For before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be carried away before the king of the Assyrians” (Isa. 8). One might ask: Why, in view of the present danger, is the sign of Emmanuel, who is to be born so many ages later, promised to us? Plainly because before he knows, in the manner stated above, to reject evil [Col. 1306D] and choose good, before he becomes human, this same God, now with God the Father, will bring it about that the land which you abhor will be abandoned by its two kings.

“The Lord will bring upon you, upon your people, and upon your father’s house days that have not come since Ephraim was separated from Judah—with the king of the Assyrians.” “With the king of the Assyrians,” he says, “the Lord will bring upon you days such as you have never had”: namely, that, after the Assyrians have conquered the ten tribes, you may be delivered in the presence of Emmanuel.

“And in that day the Lord will whistle for the fly that is at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria,” and so forth. He calls the Egyptians flies because of the filth of idolatry and their unwarlike people, and Assyria a bee because at that time its kingdom was most powerful and most ready for war; or because nearly the entire region of Assyria and Persia then used arrows.

Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find that the holy King Josiah was slain by the Egyptians, and the people of Israel subjected to Egyptian power, so that the Egyptian king appointed a king for them. And after much time Nebuchadnezzar came with an innumerable multitude of soldiers and, after Jerusalem had been taken and the other cities of Judaea destroyed, burned the temple and placed Assyrian inhabitants in Judaea (4 Kings 23; 2 Chron. 34; 4 Kings 15; 2 Chron. 36).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. What is meant by the words, “Take for yourself a large book”; who the witnesses are; who the prophetess is whom he approached; and concerning her son.

[Col. 1307B] (CHAP. VIII.) And the Lord said to me: Take for yourself a large book, and write in it with a man’s stylus: “Swiftly strip the spoils; quickly plunder.” And I took for myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Berechiah. And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: Call his name: “Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder,” because before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be carried away before the king of the Assyrians.

Again, under another figure, the virgin birth is described. For the prudent reader receives here not the obscurity of the letter but the clarity of the Spirit. Otherwise, if someone accepts according to the letter that the prophet begot a son from the conception of a prophetess, he will consequently maintain that the prophet Hosea truly had a prostitute for his wife [Col. 1307C]. Therefore this prophetess, whom the prophet is commanded to approach, is holy Mary, in whose womb the prophecy of all the holy prophets was fulfilled. Nor could she, who conceived in the flesh, have been ignorant in mind. To this prophetess this prophet—indeed, all the holy prophets—approached; for the Holy One of all, and the Word of all, came toward her womb.

Accordingly, if we judge ourselves to know nothing except Christ Jesus, and him crucified (I Cor. II), let us seek him alone here and everywhere, because indeed whatever else we may think is not worthy of the majesty of holy Scripture.

He says: “And the Lord said to me.” To what does this connective phrase, “and he said,” refer, unless to the prophet’s inward cries, desiring to have a portion and inheritance in that blessed generation of Emmanuel? “Take for yourself a large book.” For what purpose large? How much, after all, was he going to write? “Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder.” It is indeed a great name, but it can be written very fully in a very small space. What, then, is this large book except the whole page of God’s sacred word, which Moses first, and after Moses the rest, wrote? Take it, he says—that is, be one of the fellow-servants of the Word of God, one of the harpists playing their harps before God’s throne, one of the witnesses of the virgin conception, one of the fathers in the genealogy of the Son of God.

“And write in it with a man’s stylus: ‘Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder.’” Write with a man’s stylus—that is, comprehend God’s mysteries in the manner in which men customarily write [Col. 1308A]. Or certainly, “with a man’s stylus” means: comprehend as much of God as human frailty can grasp. For you, being a human being, cannot comprehend the whole of that which Emmanuel is. For no one knows the Son fully except the Father (Matt. XI); and conversely, no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (ibid.).

“Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder”: that is, do not suffer the devil to reign any longer; do not suffer the strong armed man to keep in peace any longer the things he possesses. “And I took for myself faithful witnesses, Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Berechiah, and I approached the prophetess.” Faithful understanding holds as certain that Isaiah truly approached that prophetess whom we mentioned above at the moment when, at the voice of the angel greeting her and announcing that she would conceive and bear a son, the Holy Spirit came upon her (Luke I)—at that moment, I say, when complete knowledge of this Scripture also was poured into her along with the whole abundance of the word of God.

And immediately, with the angel’s word proclaiming the virginal conception, he spoke to her memory, telling her that this was the thing which he had said above: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” Thus he approached that prophetess here and took for himself faithful witnesses. How many? Two: Uriah the priest and Zechariah son of Berechiah. It is evident throughout all his Scripture, throughout the whole extent of his volume, that he took two faithful witnesses, two peoples possessing faith in Christ: one from the Jews, the other from the Gentiles. Uriah, whose name is interpreted “God is my light,” is the Jewish people, among whom God first deigned to shine [Col. 1308B]. By Zechariah, whose name is interpreted “mindful of the Lord,” we Gentiles are signified: we did not possess knowledge of that Emmanuel who was to come, but we hold a faith mindful of him who has come.

Moreover, we are sons of Berechiah, that is, sons blessed by the Lord; for before he came we had no good thing, as the Jewish people did, but we have it from his coming, to whom the Psalmist says: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXVII). Behold, we are the two faithful witnesses, confirming the truth of these things: that this good and most excellent co-worker in the divine generation approached that prophetess; and we confess as true whatever he foretold concerning the birth of the blessed Virgin and whatever he foretold concerning us.

Why, then, shall I now call him, “Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder”? “Because before the child knows how to call his father and mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria will be carried away before the king of the Assyrians.” At present, while he is with God—God the Word not yet made flesh—he knows only how to call upon his Father. But when, as I said above, the virgin has conceived and borne, then at last he will know how to call both father and mother. He will therefore hasten greatly, he will hurry greatly, who, before he is born from his mother, before he ought to have father on this side and mother on that, removes the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria by striking down from the Assyrian king’s army one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in a single night.

Clearly, he will do something greater when he knows how to call father and mother [Col. 1309A], that is, when he who was born from the Father before everlasting ages has been born from a mother in time. For then he will overcome the spiritual enemies—that is, the devil and all his forces.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the words: “Because this people has rejected the waters of Shiloah, and therefore the king of the Assyrians will be brought upon that people.”

And the Lord continued to speak to me, saying: “Because this people has rejected the waters of Shiloah, which flow quietly, and has rather embraced Rezin and the son of Remaliah, therefore behold, the Lord will bring upon them the strong and many waters of the river, the king of the Assyrians,” etc.

By a metaphor he speaks of the springs of Shiloah at Jerusalem and of the most violent Assyrian river, which floods the whole land of Israel with its waters [Col. 1309B] and overflows the banks of its channel. It is borne with such force that, after occupying the land of the ten tribes, it reaches Judah and, passing through, comes even up to the neck: by this he signifies the captivity close at hand. For Judah was not captured at that time; but after all the cities of the two tribes had been subdued, Jerusalem alone remained, and was delivered by the incredible mercy of God.

Thus he had described the power of Assyria and its innumerable army as a lofty flood; now he shows the same thing by another metaphor: with its wings—that is, its leaders and innumerable multitude—it covered the land of Emmanuel, that is, of God who defends it, yet did not possess it.

Mystically, by the waters of Shiloah, which is interpreted “Sent,” and which that people despised, we understand the grace of baptism, rejected by the Jewish people. For we read in the Gospel that the Lord sent to the waters of Shiloah the man blind from birth, whose eyes he had washed with mud made from his own saliva. When the blind man washed away the mud in those waters, his blindness was removed and he received the clear light of sight (John IX). This indicates, after the greatness of the sign, that the blindness of the Jews and of every unbeliever cannot otherwise be healed than by Christ’s teaching of the waters, which flows gently without the noise and clamor of words, driving away the darkness of former error.

Therefore, because the people of the ten tribes rejected the waters of Shiloah—that is, separated from Jerusalem and from the house of David—the Lord brought upon them the king of the Assyrians, a name interpreted “of those who direct.” So too, because the Jewish people rejected the grace of God and faith in Christ, the Lord brings upon them the devil, the king of the proud, and likewise the army of the Romans; and they were made captive in a double sense [Col. 1309C].

Conversely, just as the king of the Assyrians went through Judah like a flood and spread out his wings, filling the breadth of the land, yet did not prevail because you protected it, O Emmanuel, so the devil rose up through Judah—that is, against the Church of catholic confession—with many persecutions, yet did not prevail because you protected it, O Emmanuel, because you defended it, O God-with-us.

Let us therefore say—and let us all say—the words that follow to our enemies, Christ’s enemies: our persecutors, Jews, pagans, and heretics: “Gather yourselves together, peoples, and be defeated.” Again: “Form a plan, and it shall be brought to nothing. Speak a word, and it shall not come to pass.” And again, encouraging one another, let us say to our own people: “Do not call it a conspiracy”; that is, do not marvel as though something new had happened whenever the impious people address blasphemies to Christ. For everything this people says is conspiracy. “Do not fear their fear, nor be terrified. Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself. Let him be your dread and let him be your terror; and he shall be for you a sanctification, but a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence to the two houses of Israel, a snare and a ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and many among them shall stumble and fall and be broken and be caught in the snare and be taken.” That is, because they did not receive Emmanuel, but he became to them a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence. Therefore they shall be broken and led away captive.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the words: “Bind up the testimony,” and what condemnation, according to what follows, awaits those who receive not the law and testimony but false prophets—falsehood in place of truth, Antichrist in place of Christ.

“Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.” He who had said above, “Blind the heart of this people,” now commends this very event as done by his judgment, saying: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples.” It is as if he said: You have done well in binding up the testimony and sealing the law of this vision among my disciples, until my disciples come—those whom evangelical faith will make worthy, so that I may open their understanding and they may understand the Scriptures (Luke XXIV).

Immediately he answers: “I will wait for the Lord, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob, and I will look for him.” “I have bound and sealed,” he says, “and although I have great sorrow for my brothers, the Israelites, I will patiently wait for the Lord, who has hidden his face from them and has passed over to the Gentiles.” When he whom they awaited has at length returned, once the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in (Rom. II), he says to the remnant of Israel: “Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me are for a sign and a wonder in Israel from the Lord of hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.”

The children whom he displays upon his return are the multitude of the Gentiles, who entered in as a sign and wonder to Israel. Israel will indeed marvel when, having returned to its remnant from the Gentiles, he presents so many children—indeed, such a multitude of sons received from the Church of the Gentiles. “Behold, I,” he says. “And when they say to you: ‘Seek out the mediums and diviners who chirp with their incantations,’ should not a people seek a vision from its God for the living and the dead? Rather, seek the law and the testimony.”

This sense agrees with his saying in the Gospel: “And they will say to you”—that is, false apostles and false christs—“‘Behold, Christ is here,’ or ‘Behold, he is there.’ Do not go; do not follow them” (Luke XVII). For false prophets are indeed like mediums and diviners, who chirp with their incantations. Do not go, I say, but say to such mediums: “Should not the people seek a vision from their God for the living and the dead?” The meaning is: If we are God’s people, ought we not to heed his word, whether for the living or for the dead, rather than you mediums and diviners? Therefore, “rather seek the law and testimony” means that we ought to look to these rather than to your deception [Col. 1311A]. For we have his law and testimony, to which we do well to give heed as to a lamp shining in a dark place (II Pet. I).

“But if they do not speak according to this word, they shall have no morning light.” That is, if they do not answer the false prophets, the heralds of Antichrist, in this manner, they will be led into error and will not behold the eternal light. “And he shall pass through it and fall and hunger.” Whoever does not speak thus shall pass through it—that is, through the light—with blind eyes; he shall fall into the snare of condemnation and hunger for eternal glory. And when he has hungered, he shall be angry; he shall curse his king and his god. He will indeed be angry and quarrel; for there will be neither place nor time there for confession or supplication. He will curse his king, Antichrist, and his god, the devil, whom he followed after abandoning the true God. For even in hell they will not lack the bitterness of quarrels.

“And he shall look upward and gaze upon the earth, and behold distress and darkness and dissolution, anguish and pursuing gloom; and he shall not be able to fly away from his distress.” He ended the preceding section, as also this one, with a terrible conclusion, though differently. There he said, “We shall look upon the earth, and behold the darkness of tribulation” (Isa. V). Here, however, he says in the third person: “He shall look upward and gaze upon the earth, and behold distress.” There he speaks of himself together with all the elect, who, however just they may be, will be shaken by some fear on that day of judgment. Here, however, he speaks only of the portion of the condemned, for whom God above will be angry and Tartarus below will stand open. Thus he rightly ends here by saying, “And he shall not be able to fly away [Col. 1312B] from his distress,” which he did not say there.

# THE SECOND BOOK ON ISAIAH  
*(Isa. IX–XLVI)*

[Col. 1311]

## 496. CHAPTER I. That the fourth section begins with the words, “In the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened,” and why the Evangelist, taking testimony from this passage, omitted “in the former time,” etc.

(CHAP. IX.) The whole world sees the bright meaning and beautiful appearance of the fourth section, whose beginning is this: “In the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened, and in the latter time the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, was made heavy.”

The Evangelist Matthew opens for us the first entrances into its meaning when he says: “When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving the city of Nazareth, he came and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the borders of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light; and to those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light arose.’ From that time Jesus began to preach and say: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’” (Matt. IV).

Certainly, in saying these things, he wishes us to understand by the vision or rising of the great light the bright preaching of the Savior, the bright Gospel of the kingdom of God, which the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali first of all heard from his mouth [Col. 1311C]. For before John had been handed over, he never preached publicly or chose apostles, although he had disciples, before whom, while John had not yet been handed over, he changed water into wine, which was the beginning of his signs (John II).

But why did he not write the testimony taken from this passage in its entirety? For the text of the prophetic reading stands thus: “In the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened, and in the latter time the way of the sea,” etc. But the Gospel quotes it thus: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea,” etc. It omits the two principal parts of the prophecy: “In the former time it was lightened,” and “in the latter time it was made heavy.” Why, I ask, did he cite the testimony incompletely and omit these parts?

Plainly because what is to be understood here—“in the former time it was lightened, and in the latter time it was made heavy”—had not yet been fulfilled at the time when the Lord Jesus began to preach. He wished us meanwhile to understand this: that the preaching of the Lord and Savior, first heard in the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, is the vision of the great light foretold through this prophet. Now, therefore, having entered through this doorway of understanding into the expanse of the present chapter, let us traverse it, aided by however much of that same light.

## CHAPTER II. How Judaea “was lightened in the former time but made heavy in the latter,” when the Gentile people began, by believing in Christ, to see a great light; and how the devil, the violent taskmaster, was overcome.

[Col. 1312D] “In the former time,” he says, “the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened, and in the latter time the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles, was made heavy.”

The Evangelist mentioned above calls the land of Zebulun and Naphtali “the way of the sea,” because it lies beside the Sea of Galilee—that is, beside Lake Gennesaret, formed by the flowing Jordan—on whose shore stood Capernaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, and Chorazin. Here the land of the two tribes signifies the whole Israelite people. This is fitting, because he who was sent to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. XV), and who before his passion said to his disciples, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X), first preached in that land; for there he began to preach.

Thus in the former time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was lightened, but in the latter time it was made heavy: that is, Judaea heard the preaching of the present Lord and saw his wonders, but after he had been taken up into heaven, it rejected the word and judged itself unworthy of eternal life [Col. 1313A]. It was necessary to speak to them first, and last to go or send to the Gentiles, because Judaea made its heart heavy (Acts XIII).

Again: “The people of the Gentiles, who walk in darkness, saw a great light.” The phrase “in the former time” must be supplied: that is, the Jewish people was lightened in respect of the portion of the elect; in the latter time the Gentile people was lightened, when the Jewish people was made heavy in unbelief. “For those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light arose for them.” Death and the shadow of death differ in this: death belongs to those who descend to the lower regions with dead works, for “the soul that sins shall die” (Ezek. XVIII); but the shadow of death belongs to those who, though they sin, have not yet departed from this life. For they may repent, if they wish.

“You have multiplied the nation; you have not increased the joy.” O light, he says, which has risen upon those walking in darkness and dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, you have multiplied the nation of your children; for from that time onward a great nation of children of light was born. But you have not increased the joy. Whose joy? That of the apostles, who first in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali saw you, the true light, and themselves became the light of the world. You did not multiply their joy [Col. 1313B], because you mingled with the joy they had from the illumination of the Gentiles great sorrow for the blinding of their own—that is, the Jewish—people.

Yet neither did you increase the joy of the nation itself which you multiplied. For these are your words, words of the light that rose for them: “Repent, for the kingdom of God has drawn near” (Matt. IV). Certainly, for those repenting it is not yet the time of great joy. “Going forth,” says the Psalmist, “they went and wept, scattering their seed” (Ps. CXXV). But what follows? “Coming,” he says, “they shall come with exultation, bearing their sheaves” (ibid.). This is what immediately follows: “They shall rejoice before you as those rejoice in harvest, as conquerors exult over captured plunder when they divide the spoils” (ibid.).

This, then, is the somewhat increased joy, in hope, both of the apostles and of the nation; but it will be magnified in reality, when, like harvesters, they come bearing their sheaves, and like victors divide the spoils—those of the conquered one, namely the devil. “For you have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his taskmaster, as in the day of Midian. For every violent plundering with tumult, and every garment mixed with blood, shall be for burning and fuel for fire.”

For you, Lord and Savior, removed from their shoulders the yoke of his burden—that is, of the devil, who previously exulted in the world, ruled all nations, pressed everyone’s neck beneath the most grievous yoke of slavery, and with the rod that struck all compelled them to render sins to him as though tribute [Col. 1314A]. You freed them and made them serve you without any army, without the shedding of blood, by a hidden hand, just as once under Gideon you granted the people of Israel victory over the Midianites (Judg. VII).

For just as a garment stained with human blood cannot be washed but is burned in the fire while still infected by blood, so that the stains of foul gore may perish along with the garment, so the devil’s violent plundering and the tumult and crowds by which he had subjected the human race to himself have been consigned to the fires of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER III. On the birth of the little child or son who overcame him, and on his names, or the order of his names—the first being Emmanuel, the eighth Prince of Peace—and on whose zeal of the Lord of hosts accomplished this.

[Col. 1314B] “For a little child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us; and dominion has been placed upon his shoulder. And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and justice from now until eternity. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this.”

Therefore, he says, the devil and all the violent plundering by which he oppressed the human race and mingled blood with blood shall be for burning and fuel for eternal fire, because a little child has been born to us—that is, the humble Son of God—whose dominion will be upon his own shoulder, so that, being God, he can suffice by his own strength to hold his own dominion. Through the humility of his passion he exercises judgment upon the world, and through the majesty of his dominion he condemns the devil on the day of judgment.

Above he was first called Emmanuel; then his name was called, “Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder”; now he will be called by six other names: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. Observe how beautiful is the order of the names. First, Emmanuel—that is, God with us—because this is first in order: God dwelt among us, having become human. Second, “Hasten, strip the spoils; hurry to plunder,” because by dying he overcame the armed strong one, the devil, and distributed his spoils (Luke XI). Third, Wonderful, because he rose from the dead and, ascending to heaven, crowned with glory and honor, sits at God’s right hand [Col. 1314C]. Fourth, Counselor, because in giving the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, to his apostles, he took counsel with that same Spirit of counsel concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. Fifth, God, because from then on he is truly worshiped by the whole world as God. Sixth, Mighty, because he will appear mighty indeed in the judgment for which he is awaited. Seventh, Father of the age to come, because when judgment has been completed he will reign no longer as lord of servants but as father of children. Eighth, Prince of Peace, because he will truly be praised forever and will receive thanks as the author of the peace by which we, who were enemies, have been reconciled to God through his death.

Why are you amazed? “The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this.” Truly and faithfully. Who, then, is this zeal of the Lord, who will cause such a little child to be born to us and so great a son to be given to us? Who, I ask, is this good zeal of the Lord except the good Spirit of the Lord? Certainly, not by male seed but by this Spirit will such a little child be born to us and so great a son be given to us. Thus the angel Gabriel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore also the holy thing born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I).

Why, then, is the Holy Spirit in the present passage called “the zeal of the Lord”? Plainly because he is moved with zeal against the tyrant who usurps God’s kingdom, and employs his power so that the one who is born to us as a little child, the one given to us as a son, may be stronger than that strong armed one (Luke XI). Therefore this same little child declares that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God (ibid.) [Col. 1315A]. Thus, after the prince of this world has been cast out, “his dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace,” etc. His dominion, I say, shall be multiplied so that he may be ruler not only of the Jews over whom David ruled, but also of all nations, from now until eternity.

## CHAPTER IV. On the words: “The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel,” and how the heretics, signified by Ephraim, said or say: “The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones.”

“The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel.” Truly the Lord sent this Word, the good Word, the Word made flesh, into Jacob; for he willed it to be incarnate and made human from Jacob. But why was it not said, “into Isaac,” or at least “into Abraham,” to whom the promise was first made? Plainly in order to show the privilege of one most ungrateful nation. For Abraham is not, even according to the flesh, the father of only one nation; nor is Isaac the father of only one nation. For it was said to his wife Rebecca: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly” (Gen. XXV), one from Jacob and the other from Esau. But Jacob is the father of one people, which is Israel. Therefore, “The Lord sent the Word into Jacob,” that is, into that particular people, so that it might be incarnate from Jacob’s seed.

And—O wonderful ingratitude!—the Word itself fell upon Israel, so that it would be shattered by the fall of that Israel. For upon Israel came the sentence of the same Word: “Whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it shall crush him” (Matt. XXI). “And all the people of Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria shall know, who say in pride and greatness of heart: ‘The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones. The sycamores have been cut down, but we shall replace them with cedars.’”

The people of Ephraim are rightly understood as all upon whom this stone fell, all whom this Word crushed in a terrible fall: Jews as well as heretics. Why? Because when this prophecy was written, Ephraim had been torn away from the house of David and worshiped golden calves, having abandoned the Lord’s temple. Furthermore, under the name Ephraim the ten tribes are understood, because Jeroboam, who received the ten torn pieces and fashioned those calves, was from the tribe of Ephraim [Col. 1315B]. All who revolt from Christ’s kingdom imitate him, whether Jews or heretics.

Therefore all the people of Ephraim shall know—everyone who has torn himself away from Christ’s kingdom—that it is evil for them that this Word, which the Lord sent, has fallen upon them because of their pride and greatness of heart, by which they say, “The bricks have fallen; the sycamores have been cut down.” In contempt, Jews call those who believe in Christ, and all heretics call Catholics who do not belong to their sect, bricks or sycamores, which are worthless timber. “We,” they say, “shall build with the squared stone of knowledge; in place of those sycamores we shall set cedars which do not decay, because we hold an invincible doctrine.”

“And the Lord shall raise up the enemies of Rezin against him, and shall stir up his enemies into tumult.” Truly the Lord raised up Rezin—that is, worldly wisdom, whose aid that person had employed—against everyone upon whom this Word has fallen, for this Word stands only in the one who loves Christ. “And he shall stir up his enemies into tumult.” For the adversaries of God’s Word trust in worldly wisdom, but the opposite happens to them: through that same wisdom they are destroyed in tumultuous conflict. For although they fight in harmony against Christ, yet, divided among themselves into conflicting sects, they maintain irreconcilable discord.

Hence it is afterwards said: “Each one shall devour the flesh of his own arm: Manasseh Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they are against Judah” [Col. 1316A]. Finally, these words, etc., which are spoken in this passage, are to be understood in three ways. Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find civil wars in Samaria, while some fight for one king and others for another, and how, after their own kings have been killed, they unite in attacking Judah. Again, let us read of the wretched destruction of Jerusalem, and we shall find, with the Roman army surrounding it, a threefold discord within, while factions fight one another and, rushing stubbornly into rebellion, jointly provoke Roman anger, so that, with God angered, they deserve no human mercy. Again, let us read ecclesiastical histories, and we shall find the endless quarrels of heretics against one another; yet while they tear themselves apart by holding contrary opinions, they rage against the catholic Church with a united spirit of malice.

Thus in a threefold sense it was truly said: “Each one shall devour the flesh of his own arm: Manasseh Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they are against Judah.” Furthermore, the words, “A man shall not spare his brother; he shall turn to the right and hunger, and eat on the left and not be satisfied,” have this meaning: Each will be so cruel as not even to spare the most beloved name of kinship; abandoning and despising the right hand, he will be filled with things belonging to the left, while suffering hunger for pleasures and evils and always desiring to add worse evils to evil.

## CHAPTER V. On Assyria, to whom “Woe” is said, and “the rod of my anger” and “the staff itself”; that it signifies the devil; how the Lord sends him against a deceitful nation; and how he boasts against God and is to be brought low by eternal condemnation.

(CAP. X.) The devil is the incitement to all evils and likewise their penal scourge; against him, at length, opposition is made under the figure of Assyria: “Woe to Assyria! The rod of my anger, and the staff itself in his hand is my indignation. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and against the people of my wrath I will command him, that he may take spoils and seize plunder, and make them a trampling-place, like the mire of the streets.” For a little later it continues thus: “And it shall come to pass in that day that the remnant of Israel, and those who have escaped from the house of Jacob, shall no longer rely upon him who strikes them, but shall rely in truth upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. A remnant shall return, the remnant, I say, of Jacob, to the mighty God. For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant of it shall return.”

Therefore this Assyria is the devil, whose captivity is here plainly contradicted. For where the authority of the Apostle takes the lead, every other interpretation must cease: “Isaiah,” he says, “cries out concerning Israel: Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. IX). And immediately he adds: “For he is completing the word and shortening it in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (ibid.). And indeed, if we read Josephus and consider how great was the multitude of people in Jerusalem and Judaea when the Lord suffered, we understand that scarcely a few Jews were saved among the apostles and apostolic men.

The evangelical word is shortened and perfected: in place of all the elaborate ceremonies of the Law, it gave the very brief commandment of love and faith—that we should not do to another what we would not wish done to ourselves. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII).

It should finally be noted how orderly a likeness of the devil’s tyranny and condemnation was first set forth in this Assyria. First, as the rod of the Lord’s anger and the staff of his indignation, he was sent against a deceitful nation—against the nation of the ten tribes of Israel, deceitfully worshipping the monstrous inventions of gods, golden calves, Baal, and the rest. And against that people of his wrath the Lord commanded him to take spoils and seize plunder. He did so and prospered. For he carried Israel away and placed them in Halah and Habor, by the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes. The Lord had sent him; he had come by the Lord’s judgment, power having been given him to do everything according to his own will.

But he did not think so, nor did his heart judge thus; rather, he applauded himself, as though an axe should boast against him who cuts with it, or a saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn; as though a rod should raise itself against one who lifts it, or a staff—which is certainly wood—exalt itself. Therefore the Lord God sent leanness upon his fat ones, and beneath his glory a burning blazed as a fire burns.

[Col. 1318A] In the reign of Hezekiah this came to pass. Sennacherib king of the Assyrians went up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And he said to Hezekiah king of Judah: “Let not your God, in whom you trust, deceive you. Did the gods of the nations each one deliver those whom my fathers laid waste?” But in that night the angel of the Lord came and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians (IV Kings XIX).

Thus, undoubtedly, the devil is signified even by the name Assyria [499]: for it is interpreted “directing,” because the devil directs himself and trusts in himself. The Lord, I say, sent the devil against a deceitful nation, “that whoever is filthy may become filthier still” (Rev. XXII); indeed, that whoever knowingly deceives may be deceived still further. The Lord sends him, I say; for, as he himself testifies when speaking through blessed Job to God, he is an everlasting servant (Job XL).

But he does not think thus, nor does his heart judge thus. For he does not serve so as to desire to cooperate with God; nor does he make the rebels against truth captives in eternal death with the intention of accomplishing God’s justice. And for the present he acts and prospers, taking every deceitful nation captive, because he is permitted to do so. But it will come to pass that he shall receive his deserved punishments: because he dared to attack Judah and Jerusalem also; because he attempted to overthrow the Church of the catholic confession also; because he boasted arrogantly against God himself.

The angel of the Lord shall go forth and strike his camp—he shall go forth, I say, coming for judgment, the Angel of Great Counsel—and shall cast him and his angels into eternal fire. For this is what is finally introduced under a metaphor: “Behold, the sovereign Lord of hosts shall break the bottle with terror; the tall in stature shall be cut down, the lofty shall be humbled, the dense thickets of the forest shall be overthrown with iron, and Lebanon with its lofty ones shall fall.”

Yet there are differing opinions concerning the breaking of the bottle. Some maintain that Christ’s passion is signified by it: that, by God’s will, and for that reason, his flesh was delivered to death, in order that the loftiness of the Jews might be destroyed, that those once high might fall to the ground, and that Lebanon with its cedars might be cut down. Of these we read in Zechariah: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire consume your cedars” (Zech. XI). Others maintain that this passage still speaks of the Assyrian: that once he has been broken, all the surrounding nations subject to his rule are cut down and humbled, and the densest forest is overthrown. By these things they wish the people and their rulers to be understood metaphorically. Lebanon also, with its lofty ones, falls, so that absolutely nothing remains to Assyrian power.

## CHAPTER VI

The beginning of the fifth section, from the words, “And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse”; that this rod is the rod of the Lord’s anger, Assyria; and that no grace of the Holy Spirit was lacking, is lacking, or ever shall be lacking to Christ, the most beautiful flower.
