(CAP. XI.) What follows, both we confess to have been written concerning Christ, and the Circumcision does not deny. Whichever of the aforementioned opinions about the bottle is preferable, the fifth section begins here; and all this prophecy, down to the beginning of the vision or burden of Babylon, concerns Christ.

“And a rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.”

By the rod from Jesse’s root we understand the holy Virgin Mary, who had no shoot joined to her; concerning her we also read above: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII). By the flower we understand the Lord and Saviour, who says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II).

And what a beautiful contrast! Above that spiritual Assyria was shown, the rod of the Lord’s anger, with the staff of his indignation in his hand (Isa. X). But behold the rod of grace, the rod of the Lord’s rest, and in it the flower in whom dwells and upon whom rests all the fullness of divinity.

This is a notable and celebrated description of Christian faith: the sevenfold Holy Spirit. Something proper must briefly be said concerning each of the spirits: truly, none of these was lacking, is lacking, or ever shall be lacking to Christ, the most beautiful flower.

For the spirit of wisdom rested fully upon him, who, as though seated beside overflowing streams, always attended to the divinity inherent in himself, and brought all the devil’s temptations in the wilderness to an end by a wise answer (Matt. IV). The spirit of understanding rested upon him; for he knew to whom he should open the mysteries of God’s kingdom and to whom he should speak in parables. Discerning all things with the sound palate of his heart, he neither allowed demons confessing that he was the Son of God (Mark I), [Col. 1319C] nor spoke God’s mysteries to the unworthy; indeed, he forbade what is holy to be given to dogs and pearls to be cast before swine (Matt. VII).

The spirit of counsel also rested upon him; hence he hid these things from the wise and prudent in order to reveal them to little ones (Matt. XI). The spirit of strength likewise rested upon him, conscious of which he said: “No one can snatch from the hand of my Father” (John X). And again: “I know my sheep, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (ibid.). The spirit of knowledge rested upon him, since from all Scripture he brought forth sayings appropriate to the occasion or subject, so that his astonished adversaries said: “How does this man know letters, since he has not learned?” (John IX).

The spirit of piety rested upon him, since he was always intent upon giving life to the dead and, possessing gentle patience, returned good for evil. “For,” he says, “the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke IX). The spirit of the fear of the Lord rested upon him: that is, he found delight in being filled, in accordance with the Father’s will, with reproaches, saying from the beginning of his incarnation in all things—saying, I mean, not only in words but in deeds—“Father, not my will, but yours be done” (Luke XXII).

Therefore the Spirit of the Lord, who until then had found no rest in the great forest of humankind, at length rests upon this flower. Remaining in him in an eternal abiding, it never endured any repulse caused by any fault.

## CHAPTER VII

Why he preferred to say “from the root of Jesse” rather than “from the root of David”; and that everything said of this flower is contrary to the sayings of arrogant Assyria.

“He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of his ears; but he shall judge the poor in righteousness, and rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth.”

Before we proceed, we must ask why the prophet preferred here to name Jesse rather than David—to say “from the root of Jesse” rather than “from the root of David”—when the promise of this flower was made not to Jesse the father, but to his son David.

We say that David, because of his royal majesty, was an exalted person, whereas Jesse, who was also called Isai, was much humbler in rank or station. Indeed, not once but many times David, already king, was reproachfully mocked by enemies as the son of Isai. But the discourse now stood against the pride of Assyria, that is, the devil; and, as an antidote, healing grace promised humility. Therefore he rightly passed over David’s royal person: “A rod,” he says, “shall come forth from the root of Jesse,” though he could have said, “from the root of David.”

Everything said about this rod or its flower is contrary to the sayings of arrogant Assyria. He said: “Are not my princes at the same time kings?” (Isa. X). But concerning this one the Holy Spirit says: “He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of his ears.”

This has been said most truly. For did our Lord, the flower of the virginal rod, judge according to the sight of his eyes [500], and select certain leading persons according to their outward appearance, making them senators of heaven and giving them the keys of his kingdom? Did he rebuke according to the hearing of his ears, choosing eloquent men to make them advocates of truth, and rejecting others because they were uneducated and without letters? Certainly not; rather, “he shall judge the poor in righteousness.”

In what righteousness? In the righteousness of faith, which is true and ancient righteousness, by which Abraham also was justified. “For,” Scripture says, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV). How or where did he judge the poor in this righteousness? For example, Peter was poor—poor, I say, that is, humble. When he was asked, “But who do you say that I am?” he answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI). This is faith; this is the righteousness of faith. In this righteousness of faith he immediately judged the poor man and said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.), and so forth.

Truly, therefore, he “shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes,” but “shall judge the poor in righteousness.” And immediately he added: “And he shall rebuke with equity on behalf of the meek of the earth.” This he shall most plainly do on the day of final judgment. For in anger and wrath he shall say in rebuke: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me no drink” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

To rebuke these is truly to do so on behalf of the meek—that is, on behalf of the least, as he says: “Inasmuch as you did not do it to one of my least ones, neither did you do it to me” (ibid.). These least ones are the meek of the earth, because the holy angels too are meek, but not meek of the earth, since on earth they have never suffered any want.

“And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the impious one.” From the time this flower came forth from the rod or root of Jesse, he continually strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth. For he alone is our teacher; and he strikes with his word those who are subject to his discipleship, restraining them from the love of earthly things. But what follows shall come to pass: “and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the impious one,” that is, the man of sin, the son of perdition. For the Apostle says: “The Lord Jesus shall slay him with the spirit of his mouth” (II Thess. II).

“And righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins.” What he had said—“Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins”—he repeated in saying, “and faith the girdle of his reins.” For Christ’s righteousness is Christ’s faith, not that by which he himself is justified, but that by which we are justified in him. Nor did he himself need to use, as in conflict, a belt for his loins or a girdle for his reins; but Scripture, in its customary manner, speaks of the head so as immediately to look to the body, of which he is the head. Therefore righteousness is the belt of his loins and faith the girdle of his reins, because we, his members, who have been born from lust, need great faith in order to be strong against lust.

## CHAPTER VIII

How the following things have been fulfilled from that time to the present day in the Church of Christ; and what is the knowledge of the Lord which brought them about.

“The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid. The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall remain together, and a little child shall lead them.”

It should be noted that he did not say, “The lamb shall dwell with the wolf, and the kid shall lie down with the leopard,” but “the leopard shall lie down with the kid, and the wolf shall dwell with the lamb.” We say this, lest it slip from memory, because this entire passage resounds with humility opposed to the pride of Assyria.

For the wolf, that is, any persecutor, shall dwell with the lamb. For example, Paul, who at first persecuted and ravaged the Church, of whom it was said, “Benjamin is a ravening wolf” (Gen. XLIX), dwelt with Ananias, the lamb of Christian simplicity, by whom he was baptized (Acts IX); or with Peter the Apostle, to whom it was said, “Feed my lambs” (John XXI). And the leopard, which formerly did not change its spots, washed in Christ’s font, lay down with the kid—not the one at the left hand, but the one sacrificed in the Lord’s Passover.

The lion also, formerly most savage, and the sheep and calf shall remain together. Every day we see in the Church rich and poor, powerful and humble, kings and private persons living together, and governed by little children, whom we understand to be the apostles: unskilled in speech, but not in knowledge.

“The calf and the bear shall feed together; their young shall rest together; and the lion, like an ox, shall eat straw.” For when those of whom it has already been spoken are united among themselves by the Lord’s discipline, then the young of calves and bears shall rest together: that is, households following the faith of their masters, jointly taking upon themselves the Lord’s yoke, shall find rest for their souls (Matt. XI).

What, then, is the straw which the lion shall eat like an ox, if not the simple words in the Holy Scriptures? For it frequently happens that worldly people, ignorant of mystical meanings, are fed by the simple reading of the Scriptures.

“And the infant at the breast shall delight over the hole of the asp, and the one weaned from the breast shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk.” The infant, who is little in malice, shall put his hand into the asp’s hole—that is, he shall drive demons from the bodies of possessed people. But the one who is weaned and no longer nourished by the milk of infancy, but already eats solid food, shall put his hand into the basilisk’s den—that is, into Satan’s own dwelling-place—and shall draw him out from it.

“They shall neither hurt nor kill on all my holy mountain.” All these things that have been foretold have been so changed that you may rightly say: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI). “They shall not hurt on my holy mountain,” that is, in the Church, concerning which he himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V).

“Because the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as waters cover the sea.” You asked how this came about among lions and bears, wolves and leopards: behold, he gives the effective cause, saying that the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord. But what is this knowledge of the Lord, which accomplishes such wonders, if not the Lord’s humility? For when he had said to lions and bears, wolves and leopards, “Take my yoke upon you,” he immediately added, “and learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

So great a teacher declares that this alone is what he teaches: that he is meek and humble in heart. And he desires us to have minds ready to learn this one thing. Therefore the knowledge of the Lord is the Lord’s humility, just as, conversely, the folly of Assyria—that is, the devil—is the devil’s pride. With this knowledge of the Lord the earth has been filled, as waters cover the sea. How, or in what order? It immediately follows:

## CHAPTER IX

How the root of Jesse is a sign for the peoples and his tomb is glorious; and how the Lord has again stretched out his hand to possess the remnant of his people and gather the exiles of Israel.

“In that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples—the nations themselves shall entreat him, and his tomb shall be glorious.” From the time the root of Jesse stood as a sign for the peoples, the earth has been filled [501] with the knowledge of the Lord, as waters cover the sea. For what was it for the root of Jesse to stand as a sign for the peoples, if not for the Son of Man to be lifted up from the earth and draw all things to himself? (John XII). From that time, certainly, the Spirit was given, after Jesus had been glorified by that exaltation (John VII).

Concerning that Spirit which was given, the Evangelist testifies that he said: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (ibid.). Therefore the waters of the knowledge of the Lord—covering waters, with “sins” understood—the divisions of the graces of the Holy Spirit, by which the wolf dwelt with the lamb, the leopard with the kid, and the lion ate straw like an ox: “the nations themselves,” he says, “shall entreat him, and his tomb shall be glorious.”

Behold, today the nations entreat him and glory in his tomb—that is, in his death. For in what else do they profess to glory? “But far be it from me,” says the Apostle, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). The nations also speak the same thing with the Apostle in a certain act, continually tracing the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. To do this is glorious even for kings.

Why, however, was it more pleasing to say or write that his tomb, rather than his sign or his falling asleep, is glorious? Doubtless because “all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. VI). Having said this, the Apostle immediately added: “For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (ibid.).

It would have been too little for the glory of that root if it had been lifted up on the cross only for the sake of dry wood, and had fallen asleep in the sleep of death, unless, planted in the earth’s tomb, it had gloriously flowered again in resurrection. So also it would surely be too little for all who glory in that sign if only the sign of the cross were traced on their foreheads—which we do when we catechize someone—unless they too were planted in the tomb of elementary water by a threefold immersion, corresponding to his three-day burial, in order thereafter to rise as new persons and be counted among the members of the new man.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that the same flower which above was said to come forth from the root of Jesse is now, conversely, called the root of Jesse. Why is this, unless because Jesse is the root of Christ’s flesh, and Christ is the root of Jesse’s faith? Christ came forth from Jesse’s flesh; Jesse is to be raised through Christ’s Spirit.

It follows: “And it shall be in that day: the Lord shall again stretch out his hand to possess the remnant of his people which shall remain from the Assyrians, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Ethiopia, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea. And he shall raise a sign among the nations, and shall gather the exiles of Israel and assemble the scattered of Judah from the four quarters of the earth.”

The prophet speaks these things continuously after saying that the tomb would be glorious. What else, then, is prophesied to us than what is proclaimed by John in the Gospel, when he says that Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but in order to gather into one the children of God who were scattered abroad? (John XI). For behold, the Lord shall raise among the nations the sign for the peoples, of which it has already been spoken. Truly he raised and exalted it, as the serpent was raised in the wilderness, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life (John III).

The exiles of Israel are gathered; the scattered of Judah are assembled from the four quarters of the earth. For by their very gathering and assembling, whatever peoples and nations they may be become Israel and become Judah.

What, moreover, does he mean when he says: “The Lord shall again stretch out his hand to possess the remnant of his people”? What, I say, except that long ago he had already stretched out his hand to possess it, but there was still room? Certainly, with a strong hand he led the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt and, through his passion, brought them into his house; but he saw “that there is still room” (Luke XIV), because the number of the elect had not yet been completed. Therefore he stretched out his hand a second time, namely by raising that sign not only among Israel but also among the nations, as has already been said.

Nevertheless, this too must be observed attentively: when he had said, “to possess the remnant of his people,” he added, “which shall remain from the Assyrians, and from Egypt, and from Pathros,” and so forth. For what is it to remain from the Assyrians and the other nations, or the islands of the sea, except to be despised and rejected by this proud world? Certainly this is what the Apostle says: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and those that are not, to destroy those that are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence” (I Cor. I).

Thus in this too there is a great commendation of Christ’s humility, set against the pride of Assyria, of which we have already spoken.

## CHAPTER X

How, through preaching, the enemies of Judah perished and the Church was raised up from all nations; and how the Lord desolated the tongue of the Egyptian sea, that is, made foolish the wisdom of this age.

“And the jealousy of Ephraim shall be removed, and the enemies of Judah shall perish. Ephraim shall not envy Judah, and Judah shall not fight against Ephraim. And they shall fly upon the shoulder of the Philistines over the sea; together they shall plunder the children of the East. Edom and Moab shall be subject to their hand, and the children of Ammon shall be obedient.”

At that time, Isaiah says, Ephraim and Judah, now in my prophetic time divided from one another by hostile hatred, shall no longer be enemies. Rather, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, two rods shall be joined into one rod (Ezek. XXXVII), and those formerly separated shall be joined in Christ’s Church. Thus they shall labor together among the nations and fly with swift course upon the shoulder of the Philistines over the sea: that is, they shall first preach to maritime Palestine and then hasten over the sea to the other nations.

We understand this from the example of the one Apostle Paul, who was carried in foreign ships through Pamphylia, Asia, Macedonia, Achaia, diverse islands and provinces, and even to Italy and Spain, as he himself writes (Acts XIV, XVI, and XXVII; Rom. XV).

“Edom,” he says, “and Moab shall be subject to their hand, and the children of Ammon shall be obedient.” In the time when Isaiah was prophesying, these peoples were hostile to the Jewish people. Therefore he now says that, after the root of Jesse rose to reign among the nations and the banner of the cross was raised for the salvation of the whole world, then Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon—that is, the entire multitude of Arabia—also shall give their hands to the apostles, and Churches of Christ shall be raised up in places of idolatry.

“And the Lord shall desolate the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and shall raise his hand over the river in the strength of his Spirit, and strike it into seven streams, so that they may cross it wearing shoes.”

In the reign of Caesar Augustus, when the flower ascended from Jesse’s root and the first census was made in the city of Rome (Luke II), the previously most powerful kingdom of the Egyptians, which had endured through many ages, was destroyed by Cleopatra’s death. And the Egyptian river was struck into seven streams, so that it, formerly impassable as it flowed in a single channel, might be divided and cut apart into seven streams and crossed on shod feet.

But what was this in comparison with the majesty or strength of the Lord’s Spirit? Therefore this also, and the things already mentioned, must be understood spiritually, because the Spirit of the Lord is promised as the one who will accomplish them [502].

“And the Lord shall desolate the tongue of the Egyptian sea”: that is, the Lord shall make foolish, as the Apostle says, “the wisdom of this age” (I Cor. I). “And he shall raise his hand over the river”: that is, he shall declare his truth over the talkative vanity of the philosophers. And this he shall do in the strength of his Spirit—namely, the Spirit whom, sent from heaven after he ascended and sat at the right hand of God, made strong his apostles who had previously been weak.

For then they understood the Scriptures with opened understanding (Luke XXIV) and spoke in all languages (Acts II). Thus they desolated the tongue of the Egyptian sea and dried up all its light; and they struck it into seven streams, so that they might pass over, shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace, with beautiful and comely feet.

“And there shall be a way for the remnant of my people which remains from the Assyrians, as when it came up from the land of Egypt.” For as, when they fled, God divided the Red Sea and Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen, they passed through singing the song of heavenly victory (Exod. XIV), so, when these flee from the devil, he shall open for them the sacrament of saving baptism; and once the devil and all his pomps have been drowned, they shall pass over into eternal life, singing such a song.

## CHAPTER XI

On the prophet’s song, “I will confess to you, O Lord,” and so forth: where and in what God was angry with humankind; when his anger was turned into grace; what waters we have drawn from the fountains of the Saviour; and what works of his invention ought to be made known among the peoples and proclaimed throughout the whole earth.

(CAP. XII.) “I will confess to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me; your anger has turned, and you have comforted me.” “And you shall say,” he says, “in that day: ‘I will confess to you, O Lord,’” and so forth.

Each one of us has truly said, and says, this in this acceptable time, in this day of salvation (II Cor. VI). Everyone who wishes to be saved must say it; he must necessarily make this confession. For what is expressed by this confession except what we must believe? “You were angry with me,” he says—understand, in Adam, in whom all sinned. Through sin your anger, that is, death, entered into the world and thus passed to all, both Jews and Greeks (Rom. V), as the Apostle testifies to the Jews when he says: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. II).

“Your anger has turned, and you have comforted me.” You were justly angry; but mercifully your anger was turned into grace—namely, when the aforesaid rod came forth from Jesse’s root and the flower rose from his root. For in whom have you comforted me except in your Spirit resting upon him? Hence that same Spirit is called Paraclete, that is, Comforter.

For this I shall confess to you, and say: “Behold, God is my Saviour; I shall act confidently and shall not fear.” As though pointing with my finger, neither limping to the right nor to the left, I shall say: “Behold this flower, white and ruddy, which in the time of Caesar Augustus came forth from the virginal rod of Jesse’s root, and under Pontius Pilate was lifted up on the wood of the cross and torn by thorns and nails—this one, I say, and no other, is my God and my Saviour.”

Let it not be said to me that this or that other person is the Messiah, that is, Christ, and that he has not yet come but is yet to come. For this is he, and no other. Whoever else says that he himself is Christ is not my God but the devil; he is not my Saviour but the enemy and son of perdition.

“I shall act confidently and shall not fear,” not because I trust in myself, but because “the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.” Therefore I shall act confidently because that strong one is my strength, of whom it was said above: “He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the spirit of his lips he shall slay the impious one” (Isa. XI).

This flower is not only my strength but also my praise—that is, my beauty: the adornment of humankind, the glory of our flesh. How, moreover, has he become my salvation except by assuming what he was not, namely humanity, in order to save me by the ancient and timeless power of his divinity?

“You shall draw waters with joy from the fountains of the Saviour.” All who shall have spoken thus in that day, all who shall have made this confession, shall, because of the confession of the same faith, draw waters with a joy that no one shall take from you (John XVI), from the fountain—that is, from the fullness—of the Saviour.

What waters shall you draw, if not the many gifts of the Holy Spirit? For he himself also cries out in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” “Now this,” says the Evangelist, “he said concerning the Spirit whom those believing in him were to receive” (John VII).

“And you shall say in that day: ‘Confess to the Lord and call upon his name.’” In this day or present time, the prophet says, there is silence; but in that day, when you have drawn waters from the fountains of the Saviour, you shall speak and say, with the whole earth hearing: “Confess your sins to the Lord, repent, and call upon his name, in which alone sins are forgiven.”

“Make known among the peoples his inventions”—so that all peoples may marvel. For what kind, or how great, are his inventions? Good inventions, wonderful inventions, which no one would have devised except he alone. Of these he himself speaks to blessed Job: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or bind his tongue with a cord? Can you put a ring in his nostrils, or pierce his jaw with a bracelet? Will you play with him as with a bird, or bind him with your little snares?” (Job XL), and so forth.

Make known among the peoples these inventions of his, which he devised by deep counsel, in order to catch the crafty devil in his own craftiness. “Remember that his name is exalted.” Whose name? The name of God the Saviour, seated at the right hand of majesty on high. For God gave him a name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of beings in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth (Phil. II).

Remember these things, and make them known everywhere by preaching, he himself working with you and confirming the word by the signs that follow (Mark XVI). “Sing to the Lord, because he has done magnificent things.” “Sing,” he says: that is, proclaim willingly rather than unwillingly the magnificent things he has done. For you have drawn waters with joy; therefore let this Gospel be the song of your joy. “Proclaim this in all the earth”—not in Judaea alone, but throughout all the earth.

“Exult and praise, O inhabitant of Zion, because the Holy One of Israel is great in your midst.” O Zion, O watchtower, O Church placed on high, exult and praise—understand, in that day, when you say these things—because the Holy One of Israel is great in your midst: holy, I say, and the flower of holiness, upon whom, as was said above, the sevenfold Spirit of the Lord shall rest.

Thus far the prophecy concerning Christ is plain.

## CHAPTER XII

That it is neither within our ability nor part of our present purpose to pursue all the burdens which follow—among them the burden of the desert of the sea and the rest—which are enumerated in order.

(CAP. XIII.) The burdens follow, concerning which it was said at the beginning of this prophet—indeed, this evangelist (Isa. IX): “The burden of Babylon, the burden of Moab, the burden of Damascus, the burden of Egypt, the burden of the desert of the sea, the burden of Dumah, the burden in Arabia, the burden of the Valley of Vision, the burden of Tyre, [Col. 1327C] the burden of the beasts of the south.” There are in fact ten, but at the outset we counted nine, since the burden of the desert of the sea is nothing other than the burden of Babylon. This would be doubtful, were it not that, after the heading “The burden of the desert of the sea,” we read later in the same chapter: “Beloved Babylon has been made a wonder to me” (Isa. XXI). And again: “Babylon has fallen, and all the graven images of her gods have been shattered to the ground” (ibid.). And above: “Go up, Elam; besiege, Media” (ibid.). It is called a sea because of the multitude of its inhabitants. Under these names all the parties opposing the name of Christ and his holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem, are condemned, as we said at the outset. These parties—or rather, divisions—are, as it were, nine, [Col. 1327D] and attack the Catholic Church, the tenth, of one faith; for they are many, and therefore are to be understood by the number nine. If one is added to it, a second unity, or ten—that is, the number ten—comes into being.

The burden of the Valley of Vision is the burden of Jerusalem, which itself in many passages of Scripture is reckoned among the nations, because it has opposed the heavenly Jerusalem not a little—indeed, it killed both the prophets sent to it and the Lord of the prophets himself. Therefore it is now called a valley, because it is not that city of which it is written: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI); but it is the Valley of Vision because it was a nursery of seers, that is, of prophets. To pursue these matters is neither within our capacity nor our purpose. We have proposed only to distinguish seven sections and to run through them briefly, in which, by recapitulation, [Col. 1328A] evangelical faith is not so much prophesied as preached as Gospel. Five of these we have completed; now, under the Holy Spirit’s guidance, we enter upon the sixth.

## CHAPTER XIII. The sixth section begins with the words, “Awake, awake, put on strength,” etc.; by these words it is understood that the holy prophet ardently desired the Savior’s coming.

(CAP. LI.) “Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord. Awake, as in the days of old, in the generations of ages. Was it not you who struck down the proud one and wounded the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty deep, who made the depth of the sea a way, that the delivered might pass through?”

Here the Holy Spirit already intercedes through the prophet [Col. 1328B] for us “with unutterable groanings” (Rom. VIII), that the deliverer of souls may come, without whom salvation could belong to none. We must feel this with deepest affection: this holy prophet, whom we rightly call an evangelist, roared mightily from his heart’s groaning when he uttered these words and those that follow. For example: “And he grew up like a shrub before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. Truly he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. LIII). But let us now pursue the words set forth in their order.

“Awake,” he says, “awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord.” What is the arm of the Lord but the Word of the Lord, the only-begotten Son of God? For “all things were made through the Word of the Lord, and without him nothing was made” (John I). “Awake,” therefore, he says; and he repeats this very word a third time, [Col. 1328C] as though saying: “How long do you restrain yourself in the bosom of the Father, O arm of the Lord, O right hand of the Lord? Why, while you rest, shall the strong man armed, the prince of this world, prevail so long? Awake, and put on strength: put on the beautiful and mighty love, the beautiful and mighty charity of obedience. Awake thus, as in the days of old, in the generations of ages.”

Then, as though the arm of the Lord were answering him, “How did I awake in the days of old?”, he immediately adds: “Was it not you who struck down the proud one and wounded the dragon?” etc. The sense is: Was it not you who struck down proud Pharaoh and wounded one who bore the type of the proud man, displaying the image of the dragon, the devil? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty deep, as a type of the saving washing [Col. 1328D] which you purposed to pour forth for us from your side? Are you not he who made a way through the depth of the sea, that the delivered might pass through (Exod. XIV), as a type of your future sacrament, through which we were to pass in order to be called delivered, in order to be delivered from the hand of death? Did you not perform these good things, signifying, O arm of the Lord, that you would do greater things?

“And now those redeemed by the Lord shall return and come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads. They shall possess joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning shall flee away.” And now, he says, O arm of the Lord, you will do as you did in the days of old; you will awake as you awoke in the days of old. At your awakening they shall return and come to Zion with praise. Who shall return and who shall come? Those redeemed by the Lord. Who are redeemed by the Lord? Surely not all the sons of Adam, but all who had been foreordained to eternal life before Adam transgressed. They shall return [Col. 1329A] to the country they lost when they were sold in Adam. This is Zion; this is the city of all the blessed. They shall return in praise, they shall come in praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads—that is, in their hearts. Sorrow and groaning shall flee. “The former things have passed away”; there shall no longer be anything for which they suffer or groan. They shall possess joy and gladness, which no joyful or glad persons here can retain. For the gladness of this world is fleeting, and its joy is fleeting.

## CHAPTER XIV. What consolation—or what Comforter—God promises when he says, “I, even I, will comfort you”; and why he immediately says, “Who are you, that you should fear mortal man?” etc.: because, as soon as the Holy Spirit the Comforter came, he reproved, for example, Peter, so that he would not fear Nero, though he had formerly feared the maidservant who kept the door.

“I, even I, will comfort you. Who are you, that you should fear mortal man, and the son of man, who will wither like grass, and have forgotten the Lord your maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth, and have feared continually all day because of the face of the fury of him who afflicted you and prepared to destroy you? Where now is the fury of the afflicter?” etc.

“I,” he says, “who struck down the proud one, who dried up the sea, who made the depth of the sea a way—I, I say, shall myself comfort you.” No envoy or angel will come; rather, I myself shall comfort [Col. 1329C] you, with a consolation by which no one else could comfort you. I have the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter; I shall give you the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit. “Who are you, that you should fear mortal man and the son of man?” etc.

No one doubts that the Paraclete—that is, the Holy Spirit the Comforter—speaks these things in the ear of the one to whom he is given. For all of us who are strong in Christ have received strength from that Comforter. The Holy Spirit himself spoke these words to Peter, prince of the apostles: “Who are you, that you should fear mortal man and the son of man?” Or rather: who are you, that you should fear a little woman, a maidservant who kept the door? For it is certain that the apostle Peter feared such a person, and forgot the Lord his maker: he denied him (Matt. XXVI; Luke XXII) [Col. 1329D] whom he had confessed to be the Son of Man, the Son of the living God (Matt. XVI). But when this Comforter was given, he so corrected him that he who had feared the tongue of a doorkeeper no longer feared the might of the Roman Empire. Thus all the others too were strengthened, each according to his share, by the power of this Comforter, so that they did not fear those “who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. X).

“Where,” he says, “is now the fury of the afflicter? He who walks shall quickly come to open, and he shall not kill unto utter destruction, nor shall his bread fail.” Who will come to open, except him of whom the Apostle says: “The Lord will come and illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV)? This indeed pertains to the consolation of those whose judgment is overthrown in the present, [Col. 1330A] so that they may believe themselves blessed when people hate them, reproach them, and cast out their name as evil (Luke VI). “He shall not kill unto utter destruction, nor shall his bread fail”: that is, he does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live; and, desiring this, he will always set before penitents the bread of life-giving doctrine, and before those hungering for righteousness.

“I,” he says, “am the Lord your God, who troubles the sea and its waves swell; the Lord of hosts is my name. I have put my words in your mouth, and sheltered you in the shadow of my hand, that you may plant the heavens and found the earth, and say to Zion: You are my people.” The Lord God who troubles the sea and makes its waves swell—so that the onrush of persecutors may swell against his servants and their pride, with his aid, may again be calmed—[Col. 1330B] addresses the Son, whom he promises will come quickly, saying: “I have put my words in your mouth,” that is, I have given you a command to obey for the consolation of my servants. “And I have sheltered you in the shadow of my hand,” so that, when you have become obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. II), you may not be abandoned in hell, nor may your flesh see corruption (Ps. XX), in order that you may plant the heavens—that is, strengthen the apostles in faith—and found the earth, namely the new Church, and say to Zion, “You are my people.” For I asked my Father, and he gave me the nations as an inheritance (Ps. II): since the nations are my inheritance, they are called, and are, Zion.

## CHAPTER XV. How, as this prophet testifies, among all the holy or righteous persons there was none before Christ or apart from Christ who could raise up the Church—here indicated by Jerusalem—which lay fallen beneath Adam’s transgression.

Having received this answer, the prophet who above had said, “Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the Lord,” etc., at once brings glad tidings and joyfully cries: “Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath; you have drunk to the bottom the cup of stupor, and drained it even to the dregs. There is none to raise her up among all the sons she bore.”

What is this Jerusalem, to which such magnificent consolation is proclaimed, except the entire Church of the elect, however great its number, gathered from the beginning to the end of the world according to the foreknowledge and predestination [Col. 1330D] of God? It lay prostrate through the fault of the first transgression, and among all its children there was no one, however righteous, able to raise up or restore its universal ruin, except this one alone, who, as we have said, is above promised as the Comforter.

Therefore, O Jerusalem, he says, O whole Church of God, whose consolation I have heard: lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise—from the fall into which you fell in Adam—you who, in Eve’s transgression, drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath. “You have drunk to the bottom the cup of stupor, and drained it even to the dregs.” Nothing was left of that most bitter draught. Within was the death of the soul, which separated you from God; without was the death of the flesh, which separates the soul from the body.

Having said this, he addresses us, that we may be diligent [Col. 1331A] to understand, and says: “There is none to raise her up among all the sons she bore, and there is none to take her hand among all the sons she nourished.” Here the understanding of faith is needed, so that we may know how necessary the advent of Christ, the Son of God, was for the world. This Jerusalem bore many sons and nourished many. Before the Law she bore Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Under the Law she nourished Moses, Samuel, and David. Yet all of these sinned. Although they had whatever small actual righteousness they possessed, they were not free from original sin. For, as the Apostle says, all sinned in Adam (Rom. VI). How, then, could any one of them take her hand and raise her up?

“Two things,” he says, “have befallen you.” What are these two things? “Desolation and destruction, famine and sword.” Desolation signifies the death of the soul; destruction, the death of the body. Likewise famine signifies the death of the soul, which had lost God, the food of angels; the sword signifies the death of the flesh, which separates the soul from the body. These are the two things that have befallen you because of the fault of the first transgression. “Who will grieve over you? Who will comfort you?” Who, I say, will grieve over you—that is, who, undertaking penance for you, will make satisfaction for you, since none, however righteous, can make satisfaction even for himself alone? Who will comfort you—namely, after reconciliation has been obtained, peace gained, and remission of sins secured for you?

“Your sons have been cast down; they have slept at the head of all the ways, like an ensnared beast, full of the Lord’s indignation and the rebuke of your God.” [Col. 1331C] Therefore, just as an ensnared beast can only cry out but cannot escape the snare by itself, so your sons, cast down and disinherited because of the sin of their first parents, could only call aloud with great faith for a deliverer; but they could not loose the snare of their own sins, still less that of the sins of others. “They have slept at the head of all the ways”: they have died; they die daily according to the common condition of all living beings, full of the Lord’s indignation, who said: “On the day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II); full of the rebuke of your God, reproving human pride and saying: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. III).

“Therefore hear this, poor little one, drunken, but not with wine. Thus says your ruler, the Lord and your God, who has fought for [Col. 1331D] his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation; I shall not add that you should drink it any more.” Therefore, he says, because none of your sons exists who can raise you up, behold, I myself, the Lord your God, have taken—that is, undoubtedly shall take—that cup from your hand, myself dying to destroy your death, so that you may drink no more, so that you may not die eternally, once the cup has been removed and you have been raised from the double death. Hear and believe this, O poor little one: drunken not with the wine of eternal life, with which you ought to have been intoxicated, but with the wormwood of death. For thus says your ruler, who once fought for his people in order to bring them out of Egypt, and will fight again for his people in order to rescue them from hell.

“And I shall put it,” he says, “into the hand of those who humbled you and said to your soul: Bow down, [Col. 1332A] that we may pass over.” For indeed, because they humbled and bent you down in order to pass over, the devil and his angels will drink a fuller damnation; although they did not bend you unwilling but willing, and passed over you. This is what follows: “And you laid your body upon the ground, and as a road for those passing by.” The sense is: as the earth, because it is inanimate, and a road, because it is trodden, do not resist those passing over them, so you did not resist the wicked spirits seeking your soul.

## CHAPTER XVI. A repetition of the exhortation because of the greatness of the consolation, from “Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion,” and then, “For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed,” [Col. 1332B] as far as, “I who spoke, behold, I am present.”

(CAP. LII.) “Awake, awake, put on your strength, O Zion; put on the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, holy city, for the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you.” Because no small matter, no slight consolation, is promised, behold, I have said it so often, and now say it so often: awake, awake. And what are you to do by awakening, or by doing what are you to awaken? “Put on your strength; put on the garments of your glory.” Just as a noble and distinguished young woman, when her wedding day is at hand, prepares herself with all the strength she can and with all the splendour of garments she can, so as worthily to please, so you, once captive but now free, prepare yourself for the coming of your ruler, your bridegroom and lover, so that by a worthy adornment of charity you may deserve to enter his bridal chamber [Col. 1332C] in beauty. Thus awake and act confidently, for the devil, uncircumcised in heart and unclean in deed, shall no longer pass through you.

“Shake yourself from the dust; arise, sit down, Jerusalem; loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion.” Shake off the dust of sins; arise to work well; sit in reigning; and, by receiving and granting the remission of sins, loose the bonds of your neck.

“For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed.” A brief saying, but worthy of the Lord’s mouth. “You were sold for nothing,” he says. Truly for nothing: the buyer, the devil, cheated you of the entire price of the sale. “Eat,” he said, “and you shall be like gods” (Gen. III). He spoke a lie; for he did not make gods out of human beings. Therefore you were sold for nothing—and not merely for nothing, but to your ruin—because, although you could have avoided death, you have now become dead in soul and at the same time mortal in flesh.

“And without silver,” he says, “you shall be redeemed.” Truly without silver, but not without a price. “Not with corruptible gold and silver,” says the apostle Peter, “but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless and undefiled Lamb, you were redeemed” (I Pet. I). “For thus says the Lord: My people went down into Egypt at the beginning to sojourn there.” Did they come out from there redeemed by silver? Were they not rather delivered through the sacrifice of a lamb, when their doorposts and lintels had been marked with its blood? (Exod. XII.) So, he says, you too will now be redeemed without silver, [Col. 1333A] yet not without a price, but with the precious blood of the true Lamb, Christ the Son of God.

For this world is Egypt to those whom he predestined to eternal life, and the entire people of the elect came down into it in those first parents. “And Assur,” that is, the devil, “has falsely accused him without any cause.” “And now what have I here?” says the Lord. “For my people has been taken away for nothing; their rulers deal unjustly,” says the Lord, “and my name is continually blasphemed. Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I myself who spoke, behold, am present.”

Because, he says, my people was taken away for nothing, as I said above; but, on the contrary, its rulers—that is, its teachers, the scribes and Pharisees—act unjustly, and moreover by them or because of them my name is continually blasphemed: therefore, I say, my people shall know my name through myself, because I myself who spoke to Abraham, who spoke to Moses, who spoke in the prophets and psalms—behold, am present. “What have I here?” What else, I ask, remains for me? My Father “did not require whole burnt offering and sin offering”; therefore I said, “Behold, I come” (Ps. XXXIX); therefore, behold, I am present.

## CHAPTER XVII. How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the one announcing this good news; what these feet and mountains are; who the watchmen are; and how all the ends of the earth see the salvation of the God of Israel.

“How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace, announcing good, preaching [Col. 1333C] salvation, saying to Zion: Your God shall reign!”

“I am present,” he said, and by coming he shows his feet to this hearer, who both sees and hears in the Holy Spirit. What feet, except his ways? And what are his ways except mercy and truth? For it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV). On these two feet, he who now says, “Behold, I am present,” came into this world, namely, as he says, “that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John XV). For causing those who do not see to see belongs to mercy; causing those who see to become blind belongs to truth. This foot crushed the Jews; that foot raised up the nations. “How beautiful,” he says, “how lovely are the feet!” Truly, the feet are beautiful, for he is blameless in both respects.

“How beautiful are the feet upon the mountains!” Upon what mountains, except the apostles, eminent in faith and lofty in merits? These mountains first received those feet: one of them was cast down through the judgment of truth; eleven grew through mercy unto heaven. “Of one announcing and preaching peace.” What peace, except the reconciliation of the human race? “Announcing good.” What good, except the glory of God’s children? “Preaching salvation.” What salvation, except the blessed immortality of souls and bodies? “Saying to Zion: Your God shall reign.” What does “shall reign” mean, except that, when the prince of this world has been cast out, your God has taken possession of the kingdom which the tyrant had held? Therefore the feet are beautiful, because the announcement is beautiful, because this preaching is pleasing.

“The voice of your watchmen: [Col. 1334A] they have raised their voice; together they shall praise, because they shall see eye to eye when the Lord restores Zion.” O Zion, the voice of your watchmen has been heard—of the watchmen, I mean, the apostles, who observed that peace for you, preached that good to you, and announced that salvation to you. These watchmen raised their voice. Truly they raised it, for “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world” (Ps. XVIII). “Together they shall praise,” namely by thinking the same thing and teaching the same thing. “For they shall see eye to eye when the Lord restores Zion.”

They are indeed blessed above all others because they shall see eye to eye, as he says: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I tell you that many prophets and righteous persons desired [Col. 1334B] to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X). Therefore they will be reliable witnesses, and for that reason they will praise not separately but together; they will preach not discordant but harmonious things. They shall see, I say, eye to eye, when the Lord restores Zion. For when he restored Zion by redeeming it through his passion, they saw him with their eyes; and after he restored Zion, having despoiled hell, they saw him alive again with their eyes and touched him with their hands.

“Rejoice and praise together, desolate places of Jerusalem, because the Lord has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.” O you desolate places of Jerusalem, O you nations once forsaken but now Jerusalem through receiving [Col. 1334C] the remission of sins, rejoice and praise together with that Zion, with that Church of patriarchs, prophets, and all the elect who are of the circumcision. For the Lord has comforted his people by giving them the Paraclete, that is, the Holy Spirit the Comforter; he has redeemed Jerusalem—redeemed all whom he foreknew and predestined to belong to that heavenly Jerusalem. He redeemed them, I say, not with gold or silver but with his own blood (I Pet. I).

Therefore you also rejoice and praise, because he prepares his arm, that is, his Son, in the sight of all nations, according to Jacob’s prophecy: “He himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). “And all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.” For those will come from the ends of the earth who will see the glory of their God and Savior, while the children of the kingdom are cast into outer darkness (Matt. VIII). For what does the Lord say?

## CHAPTER XVIII. What it is to withdraw, to go out, not to touch what is unclean, or to be cleansed when bearing the vessels of the Lord; and in what sense the Lord Christ Jesus, who understands these things and knows how to judge, is a servant and in what sense exalted; how his appearance was glorious, whereas kings now keep silent concerning him.

“Withdraw, withdraw; go out from there; do not touch what is unclean; go out from its midst. Be cleansed, you who bear the vessels of the Lord, for you shall not go out in tumult, nor depart in flight. For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you.”

“Withdraw,” he says, from that earthly Jerusalem; withdraw from the blaspheming Jews, against whose destruction the Roman army is being prepared. Go out from there and do not touch what is unclean: no longer touch the Jewish rite, rendered unclean by Christ’s blood; go out from all their ceremonies, which the Lord’s soul hates. Go out from its midst in this manner; be cleansed—that is, be baptized in the Holy Spirit—and baptize all nations in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matt. XXVIII), that they may become vessels of the Lord.

“For you shall not go out in tumult, nor depart in flight”: this belongs to those who are defeated; rather, you shall go out as conquerors, preaching the Gospel of Christ’s victory. For the Lord will go before you, cooperating and confirming your word with the signs that follow (Mark XVI). And the God of Israel will gather you, because through you and with you he will bring in one flock from the dispersion of the nations.

“Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.” My servant is the same one who above was called my arm and my Son. Although he is Son by nature, because he “emptied himself” (Phil. II), he is my voluntary servant. Behold, he understands; behold, he knows how to render judgment—he who was judged as though he did not understand, and was silent and patient. Very soon he will be exalted and lifted up. Once he drank from the torrent (Ps. CIX): by rising he will be exalted; by ascending to heaven he will be lifted up; by sitting at the Father’s right hand he will be very high.

“As many were astonished at you, so inglorious shall his appearance be among men, and his form among the sons of men.” A remarkable form of speech, a remarkable swiftness of changes in address. The expression flees from the third person to the second, and immediately from the second to the third. Having said, “Behold, my servant shall understand,” etc., he addresses him by adding, “As many were astonished at you.” And indeed he fittingly and affectionately turns to him of whom he was speaking. But when he adds, “So inglorious shall his appearance be,” he did not wish to say “your appearance,” but said “his appearance.” Piety showed reverence to the Lord, because in truth his appearance was not inglorious in itself, but was inglorious to people who saw badly. Therefore he fittingly turns back at once to human beings, as though sparing his mouth, and completes for his hearers the statement he had begun to address to him.

The sense is this: when you performed wondrous deeds, giving sight to the eyes of the blind and raising the dead, and, further, doing what an innumerable army could not have done—driving sellers and buyers from the temple with a small whip—when, I say, you did such things, many were astonished at you. Yet, as greatly as they were astonished, so inglorious—so greatly inglorious—shall his appearance or his form be among men: among men, I say, that is, beyond all men, before whom his appearance seemed inglorious or contemptible to the proud.

When shall his appearance be so inglorious? When, having been seized, he gives his body to those striking him, his cheeks to those plucking them, and does not turn his face from those reproaching and spitting upon him; when he gives his cheek to the one striking him and is filled with these and similar insults (Isa. L). For what purpose will he suffer these things? With what result will his appearance be so inglorious? He says: “He shall sprinkle many nations.” As though he said: This one shall therefore be inglorious, [Col. 1336A] so that many nations may be sprinkled with his blood unto remission of sins.

“Kings shall keep their mouths shut concerning him. For those to whom no account was given of him shall see, and those who had not heard shall contemplate.” In a short time, for a little while, his appearance shall be inglorious; and immediately there will be so great a change in that same appearance that kings shall keep their mouths shut concerning him—the one whom the obscure and contemptible servants of the high priests reviled with insolent mouths, spat upon, mocked, and blasphemed. When, after three days, he rose from the dead, was taken into heaven, and gave the Holy Spirit, kings too will learn this discipline: they will keep their mouths shut concerning him; they will not speak blasphemy but confess his glory; compared with him they will forget royal pomp and kingly pride; and with their mouths pressed beneath his feet, they will offer humble prayer.

Why is this so? Because “those to whom no account was given of him shall see, and those who had not heard shall contemplate.” Who are those to whom no account was given, or who had not heard, except the nations who had not received the Law and had no prophets? Behold, they saw; behold, they contemplated his appearance, no longer despised but beautiful. Therefore they sing with the Psalmist: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV).

## CHAPTER XIX. How the prophet, in a more extended lamenting voice, proclaims what he had said, “His appearance shall be inglorious among men,” beginning with “Who has believed our report?” and ending with “And he was reckoned with the wicked.”

(CAP. LIII.) Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the [Col. 1336C] Lord been revealed? And he grew up like a shrub before him, and like a root out of thirsty ground. He had neither form nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no comeliness, and we desired him: despised, and the last of men, a man of sorrows, 507 and acquainted with infirmity. And as though his face were hidden and despised, we did not even esteem him.

This is what he said above: “His appearance shall be inglorious beyond that of men.” The venerable prophet, with his wounded heart and with his voice raised on high, proclaims this more fully in lamenting tones; he is rightly compared with those to whom, when he himself was already inglorious, he spoke thus: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow, because her hour has come. And you likewise now indeed have sorrow” (John XVI), etc. For truly, as are the groans of a woman in labor, so these [Col. 1336D] words sound forth the pain of a compassionate soul.

“Who,” I say, “has believed our report?”—that is, from the Jewish people. “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”—namely, when the humble Son of God, in a contemptible form, rose up against the proud devil. For although he is the arm—that is, the strength—of the Lord, his appearance was inglorious in the sight of men; and as a shrub grows, or as a root from thirsty ground, namely with dry bark and withered leaf because it has no force of moisture, so this arm of the Lord grew up before him from the cursed ground of Jewish dryness, which possessed no moisture of faith.

And indeed in their eyes he was like such a shrub or such a root; but in the eyes of the Lord, and likewise in the eyes of everyone who has faith, he was and is like a tree planted [Col. 1337A] not in thirsty ground, but “beside streams of waters” (Ps. I), of the fullness of the Holy Spirit, by whom he was also conceived and came forth. “He had neither form nor beauty”: namely, when he was spat upon, struck with blows, mocked in a white garment, crowned with thorns, and finally fixed to a cross and reckoned among criminals. Meanwhile, neither the form of divine power nor the beauty of most pure and holy humility seemed to be in him. “And we saw him, and there was no comeliness.” These words, and the rest, must be read as having human estimation understood.

For immediately the prophetic Spirit, most certain of the truth of the matter, adds: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities, and carried our sorrows. And we esteemed him as a leper, and struck by God, and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised [Col. 1337B] for our crimes. The chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we have been healed. All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way, and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth.”

The things said before this—those things, I say—were seen only by the eyes of fools, who are at the ends of the earth, who do not look inward, because they are not in the head, that is, in the heart. Yet, because of the greatness of his grief and the immensity of his righteous compassion, the prophet numbered himself among such persons, saying: “We saw him; we desired him, despised and the last of men; therefore we did not even esteem him.”

But he said these things according to the judgment of true reason, or established truth, because he truly bore not his own infirmities but ours; not his own sorrows but ours; he was wounded not for his own but for our iniquities; bruised not for his own but for our crimes. “And we,” he says, “thought him like a leper.” Who are “we” who so thought? Surely not the prophets, one of whom I am? Certainly not; but we—the unhappy Judaism, the mutilated circumcision, the hard uncircumcision—of whom we were according to the mass, but from whom we are distinguished by faith.

“We thought him like a leper.” Indeed, we wished him to be thought a leper, struck by God with leprosy and humbled, so that we said that everyone who followed him or believed in him was contaminated, just as, according to the Law, one who touches a leper is defiled. Therefore we condemned him, cast [Col. 1337D] outside the gate; we crucified him, so that thereafter no one might doubt that he was accursed by God, according to the Law which says: “Accursed by God is he who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. XXI). There, mocking him—that is, when he had been cast outside the gate of the city—we thought that we had fulfilled the Law which commands that a leper be cast outside the gate (Lev. XIII; Num. V).

What follows? “The chastisement of our peace was upon him”: that is, we were reconciled and made at peace with God through him, who was so harshly chastised, so atrociously beaten with scourges, so cruelly wounded by nails and spear. By that bruise of his body we were healed both in body and in soul. All of us, like irrational sheep, wandered; but the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all, so that he alone might suffer the punishment [Col. 1338A] which we all had deserved by wandering.

How, or by what right, did one bear the iniquity of all? Clearly because we are brute sheep, whereas he is the rational shepherd. In the balance of reason, as one shepherd outweighs a hundred sheep by the dignity of rationality, so he outweighs all of us by the power of divinity. Therefore let not the wolf howl in complaint, saying: “I seized less and paid out more.” For that one man, whom he seized though owing him nothing, is better than all of us whom he gave back—as those once, as it were, justly possessed on account of the debt of sin.

Rightly, therefore, did the Lord lay upon him the iniquity of us all; and rightly did he, foreknowing the aforesaid fruit, “offer himself because he himself willed it, and not open his mouth.” Rightly “was he led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before one shearing him he was silent and did not open [Col. 1338B] his mouth,” so that he might not only redeem us by his blood but also cover us with his wool, in order to warm with a garment those chilled by their unbelief.

What then? “From distress,” he says, “and from judgment he was taken up.” For, “the pains of hell having been loosed, God raised him up,” since it was impossible that he should be held by it (Acts II). And behold, he is a lion and roars mightily—he who was silent as a lamb before one shearing him. “Who shall declare his generation? For he has been cut off from the land of the living.”

From that time, indeed, from when he was taken up from distress and judgment by rising from the dead, “so that he dies no more and death has no more dominion over him” (Rom. VI)—from that time, I say, he is preached as the Son of God and the Son of the Virgin. But who shall recount either generation? For both are wondrous and both ineffable. For it is ineffable that, in the divine generation, the Father says in the Psalm: “My heart has uttered a good Word” (Ps. XLIV). Likewise it is ineffable what is rightly understood here concerning his generation according to the flesh, by which he “was cut off from the land of the living.”

From the land, I say—not of those dying, nor of those dead by the death of sin, by which all died in Adam—but from the land of the living, that is, from virginal ground made living through the Holy Spirit, he was cut off. “Cut off,” I say, with “without hands” understood, as Daniel also says: “A stone was cut from the mountain without hands, and struck the statue upon its feet” (Dan. II).

“For the crime of my people I struck him”: with “I, God the Father, struck this Son, Christ,” understood. Hence the Apostle: “He who did not spare even his own Son [Col. 1338D] but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. VIII).

After the Father has spoken these words, the prophet who follows completes the sentence: “And he shall give the impious for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he did no iniquity, nor was deceit in his mouth; and the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity.” The impious and the rich, I say, who, with outstretched neck, shook their heads at him when his appearance was inglorious to them, he shall give for his burial and death—that is, into the hands of the Romans and into the power of wicked spirits—according to that saying of David: “They shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII). For he was not, as they slandered him, an evildoer; rather, “he did no iniquity, nor was 508 deceit found in his mouth.”

“And the Lord,” he says, [Col. 1339A] “willed to crush him in infirmity.” What advantage, Lord, will there at last be in such a will of his? It follows: “If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand.” The meaning is: if he pays by dying the debt of Adam to the eternal Father, he will become the Father of eternal regeneration; and “as all die in Adam, so in him all shall be made alive” (I Cor. XV). For this is the will of the Lord which shall be directed in his hand.

This new Adam shall see a long-lived seed, which that true Adam had made short-lived. For the latter caused us all to return to the dust from which we were taken; this one shall cause us all to rise again and to be long-lived—that is, now immortal. “Because his soul has labored, he shall see and be satisfied.” His soul labored—namely, in death—and for this he shall see that long-lived seed, and his love shall be satisfied, for our salvation is delicious food to him.

“By his knowledge the righteous one himself shall justify many of my servants.” This is what the Apostle strongly commends in the Epistle to the Romans: that “as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one man many shall be made righteous” (Rom. V). For what is his knowledge except his obedience? “Although he was the Son of God,” says the same Apostle, “he learned obedience from the things which he suffered, and, having been made perfect, became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him” (Heb. V). Therefore, “by his knowledge,” that is, by his obedience, says God the Father, [Col. 1339C] “the righteous one himself shall justify many of my servants.” And immediately he adds: “And he himself shall bear their iniquities.” He shall bear them, he says, as both high priest and sacrifice, because he was offered for the justification of sinners.

“Therefore I shall distribute many to him, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong, because he delivered his soul to death and was reckoned with criminals; and he bore the sins of many and prayed for transgressors.” Because, he says, “he bore their iniquity,” therefore “I shall distribute many to him,” so that, distributed through many dwelling places, they may enjoy one kingdom; and he shall divide the spoils of the strong—that is, of wicked spirits, who were strong before he assumed a human body and, after the strong armed man had been overcome, he who was stronger plundered his house (Luke XI).

“He prayed for transgressors,” he says. Not only did he pray for transgressors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII); but his entire passion was a prayer for transgressors, namely for us, since in Adam we all sinned, we all transgressed. And he prayed indeed for transgressors, but not for all; and he bore not the sins of all, but the sins of many. This is manifest in the two criminals among whom he was reckoned: he left one, bore the sins of the other, and received him with himself into Paradise.

## CHAPTER XX

That the two criminals, one of whom confessed while the other persevered in blasphemy, were figures of the two peoples; and that therefore the prophet immediately says, “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear,” as though to the penitent and confessing thief, but of the other people, as though of the impenitent thief: “All beasts of the field, come to devour.”

(CAP. LIV.) With the same balance of judgment, he next distinguished likewise the two criminals, namely the Gentile and Jewish peoples. The blasphemer dies in his sin; to the other the paradise of faith and confession is opened. After so clear a proclamation of the Lord’s passion, the Holy Spirit in this prophet expresses both things in plain words.

First he adds the salvation of the Gentiles in these words: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; sing aloud praise and a hymn, you who did not bear; for many are the children of the desolate, more than of her who has a husband, says the Lord. Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Make your cords long and strengthen your stakes. For you shall penetrate to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations and inhabit the deserted cities.”

And after some intervening words: “Behold, I created the smith blowing coals in the fire and bringing forth a vessel for his work, and I created the destroyer to lay waste. Every weapon fashioned against you shall not prosper, and every tongue resisting you, in judgment you shall judge.”

By these words he indicates the persecutions which the Church was to endure for the evangelical faith. For the smith blowing coals is the devil, the craftsman of all evils, who by his blowing kindles the fires of persecutions, bringing out against her vessels of wrath containing iniquity and blasphemy; and this Church shall without doubt judge them.

Immediately he adds: “This is the inheritance of the servants of God, and their righteousness is from me, says the Lord.”

(CAP. LV.) “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy and eat. Come, buy without silver and without any exchange, wine and milk,” etc. This public invitation is manifestly addressed to the same Church from among the Gentiles, so that those who formerly did not possess the silver of the Scriptures may now hasten and, at the price of faith alone, purchase for themselves waters to drink—waters springing up into eternal life (John VII); let them buy wine and drink, if they are strong; let them buy and eat milk, if they are little ones.

All these things, I say, are set before the Church of the Gentiles. For soon afterward follows: “Behold, I gave him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and teacher to the nations. Behold, you shall call a nation which you did not know,” etc. For these and the following words are spoken as though to the thief on the right, penitent and confessing—that is, to the Gentile people receiving with humble faith Christ crucified for its salvation—down to the place where it says: “All beasts of the field, come to devour” (Isa. LVI).

And the order of the promises and the distinction of the consolations should be noted. After he said: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; sing aloud praise and a hymn,” namely because of the greatness of joy, after the likeness of a horse neighing at victory, “for the children of the desolate are more than of her who has a husband,” etc., he first promised the crowns of martyrs. “Behold,” he says, “I created the smith blowing coals in the fire,” signifying the devil, who at the very beginnings of evangelical faith kindled by his blowing the fires of persecutions, in which the golden faith of the martyrs was refined and proved.

Then, by saying, “All you who thirst, come to the waters,” he signifies the abundance of divine knowledge, which, after peace had in some measure been restored to the Church, was multiplied by many teachers who zealously drew from and expounded the Scriptures.

Finally, by saying: “And let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree,’ for thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: If they keep my Sabbaths, choose what I have willed, and hold fast my covenant, I shall give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters”—by saying these things, I say, he draws us with wonderful elegance to the beauty of ecclesiastical chastity, so that it may delight us to be eunuchs, that is, continent even through a chaste virginal resolve, and thus “make ourselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XII).

(CAP. LVI.) After these things the discourse now turns to the thief on the left—that is, to the Jewish people persisting in blasphemy—in this manner: “All beasts of the field,” that is, all the forces 509 of the Roman Empire, “come to devour” the great body of this thief, grown fat, made sleek, enlarged, and thence “kicking back,” that is, continually blaspheming (Deut. XXXII).

And in a remarkable way, before convicting the people itself by setting forth the causes of its impending evils, he invites all the beasts to devour it. For afterward he begins to speak to it thus: “But you, come near here, children of the sorceress, seed of the adulteress and prostitute. At whom have you mocked? Against whom have you opened your mouth wide and thrust out your tongue?”

First, I say, he cries aloud to all the beasts of the field, all the beasts of the wilderness, and invites them [Col. 1341C] to devour. And because the guilt was chiefly that of the priests, the prophetic discourse first accuses them after that summons of the beasts, in these words: “His watchmen are all blind; they all knew nothing. Dumb dogs, unable to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping, and loving dreams; and most shameless dogs, who knew not fullness. The shepherds themselves knew no understanding. All turned aside into their own way, each to his own greed, from the greatest to the least. Come, let us take wine and be filled with drunkenness; and tomorrow shall be as today, and much more abundant.”

Since it is evident that all these words refer to the scribes and Pharisees who persuaded the crowds to crucify the Lord, and since they are clear in meaning, the following must be joined to the foregoing:

(CAP. LVII.) “The righteous man perishes, and no one considers it in his heart; and men of mercy are gathered, because there is no one who understands. For the righteous man has been taken away from the face of evil. Let peace come, and let him rest in his bed, because he walked in his uprightness. But you, come near here, children of the sorceress.”

Between the words above, spoken in consolation to the Gentiles being gathered in, and those afterward spoken in judgment to the Synagogue being cast away, this passage is set: “The righteous man perishes, and no one considers,” so that the prophetic Spirit may strive to impress and repeat to us what we have already said: namely, that the Lord Jesus, the righteous one, perished between two thieves, so that he received one through mercy and cast away the other through judgment, as a figure of the Gentile and Jewish peoples, of whom likewise he would receive one through mercy and cast away the other through judgment.

Thus the present words are joined to the earlier ones: “You barren woman who do not bear, rejoice; sing aloud praise and a hymn,” as I have said; but “you, come near here, children of the sorceress,” for whom the righteous man perishes and among whom there is no one who considers. Nor does that righteous man alone perish, but “men of mercy are gathered,” namely his apostles, whom you persecute from city to city. You, I say, come near here for an evil day—not for the good day and day of peace of which I have just said, “Let peace come and let him rest in his bed,” by which peace he reconciled us to God and his Father—but for a day of war, that you may fall by the sword and be devoured by the beasts of the field whom I summoned a little before.

## CHAPTER XXI
