[Col. 1342B] That from the words, “But you, come near here, children of the sorceress,” down to, “The wind shall carry them all away, the breeze shall take them,” there is a recollection of sins coming upon the same generation which crucified the Lord, and that it was therefore rightly delivered visibly to the Romans and invisibly to the devil.

As in the first section, after openly announcing the calling of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews, he gave the ancient causes, saying: “For you have cast off your people, because they have been filled as in former times and have had diviners like the Philistines” (Isa. II), so now he foretells the sins of former generations as coming upon this generation which crucified the Lord: “But you,” he says, “come near here, children of the sorceress, seed of the adulteress and prostitute.”

Whose sorceress, whose adulteress or prostitute? Clearly, the Synagogue’s: she practiced divination by following her own inventions; she committed adultery and prostitution because, having abandoned God, she prostituted herself to the devil. By the Synagogue, whose children the Jews are, we mean the assembly of scribes and Pharisees, elders, priests, and high priests. These are the aforesaid blind watchmen, who do not see the Lord when he comes—indeed, when he is present—though they ought to be the first to see him by virtue of their office; they are like dumb dogs, most shameless dogs, who know no fullness, so devoted to gluttony and sleep that they cannot bark.

You ruined children of such a wicked Synagogue, come near and answer the questions set before you: “At whom have you mocked? Against whom have you opened your mouth wide and thrust out your tongue?” At whom, I say, did you mock, by spitting upon his face and plucking out his beard? Against whom did you open your mouth wide and thrust out your tongue, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the Temple and rebuild it in three days!” (Matt. XXVII).

“Are you not children of wickedness, a false seed?” You say, “Our father is Abraham” (John VIII); you say, “We have one Father, God” (ibid.). Are you not rather children of the devil, lying children of him who is both a liar and the father of lying? “You who take comfort in gods beneath every leafy tree, sacrificing children in the torrents beneath lofty rocks.” Are you not these people? Did you not practice this crime habitually? O divining and prostituted Synagogue, have you only now, recently or for the first time, raged against me with insolence? “Your portion is in the divisions of the torrent; this is your lot. To them you poured out a libation; you offered a sacrifice. Shall I not be angry over these things? Upon a high and lofty mountain you placed your bed, and you went up there to offer sacrifices. And behind the door and behind the doorpost you placed your memorial.”

The history of Kings and Chronicles tells of such crimes of yours. Indeed, before the history of Kings you committed sacrileges of this kind. For the Psalmist says: “They mingled among the nations and learned their works; they served their carved images, and these became a snare to them. They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons, and shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and daughters, whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan; and the land was polluted with blood” (Ps. CV). All these things shall come upon you in this generation. Why? “Because beside me you uncovered yourself and received an adulterer. You enlarged your bed [Col. 1343B] and made a covenant with them.”

“Beside me,” he says, “you uncovered yourself and received an adulterer.” Which adulterer? Formerly Baal, but now Barabbas. Baal beside me in the Temple; Barabbas against me in the praetorium. “You loved their bed with open hand.” But you hated me and condemned me by public outcry. “You made a covenant with them,” but denied me. With whom did you make a covenant, having denied me? Formerly, as I have said, with Baal and with the golden calves; now with Barabbas and Caesar. For you said: “Not this man, but Barabbas” (John XIX). Again: “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid.).

“You adorned yourself with royal ointment and multiplied your perfumes.” You acted after the manner of a prostitute who despises a modest husband and courts wealthy adulterers. You anointed yourself with royal ointment. Formerly you anointed yourself for an idol—for example, Moloch, who is also called Melchom, which means “their king”—namely by sacrificing; but now you anointed yourself for Caesar, namely by flattering him. “You sent your messengers far away and humbled yourself even to hell.” Formerly you sent your messengers far away to summon adulterers, the Babylonian and Egyptian gods; now you sent them to gather against me the ministers of the Roman Empire, 510 and in this way you humbled yourself even to hell, so that there you might be joined to those adulterers, not now in a bed of pleasure but in the fire of Gehenna’s punishments.

“You labored in the multitude of your ways and did not say, ‘I shall rest.’” For there is one royal way, and whoever walks in it does not labor but rests and lives; but there are many left-hand and adulterous ways, and because you have walked in them, you have always labored and never rested.

What then? “You found the life of your hand; therefore you did not ask me.” The meaning is: because you abounded in all things and overflowed with riches which you sought with all your hand, you therefore neglected the Lord, as did Sodom, which, because it was filled with bread, as Ezekiel says, therefore became proud (Ezek. XVI).

And now hear: “For whom were you anxiously afraid, that you lied and did not remember me, nor consider me in your heart? Because I was silent and as though not seeing, you forgot me. I shall declare your righteousness, and your works shall not profit you. When you cry out, let those whom you have gathered deliver you.”

“For whom,” he says, “were you anxiously afraid?”—with the words understood: “Lest perhaps the Romans come and take away both our place and our nation” (John XI). I shall bring that very thing upon you. Why? Because you lied, because you fabricated for yourself a false fear, because you deceitfully trembled there with fear “where there was no fear” (Ps. LII), and did not remember me. For you made no mention whatever of me at the time of fear which you set before yourselves. Who, indeed, said in that council: “Let us restrain our hands from this murder, for our place and nation may be preserved for us by God’s help”? Thus you did not remember me; for you did not fear with true fear, but, hastening to murder, you willingly feigned a fear that did not exist.

Therefore I shall declare your righteousness; I shall openly show to the whole world your most wicked hypocrisy. For this is your laughable “righteousness”—righteousness ironically, for truly it is unrighteousness. “Your works shall not profit you”: that is, they shall greatly harm you. “When you cry out,” namely when Roman forces surround you on every side, “let those whom you have gathered deliver you”—whatever persons or things you have gathered for your own ruin, from the blood of righteous Abel onward. For those whom you have gathered are idolatries, shed blood, blasphemies, and cries against the prophets and against the Lord of the prophets himself; all these things you have gathered for yourself to this day, for your evil.

But how shall these gathered things deliver you? “The wind shall carry them all away; the breeze shall take them.” Therefore this expression is hostile mockery, because they shall not be delivered but shall fall by the sword, and those who survive shall be led captive into all nations, as though carried off by wind or breeze.

“But he who has confidence in me shall inherit the land and possess my holy mountain.” The rest which follows—partly good on behalf of the elect, partly evil on behalf of the reprobate—down to the words, “My Spirit which is in you, and my words which I have put in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, says the Lord, from now and forever” (Isa. LIX)—we pass over in our eagerness to proceed. For we have undertaken not to traverse the whole depth of this prophet, but to seek the chief testimonies to Christ. Therefore we now conclude this, the sixth section, and immediately begin the seventh and final section with the following chapter.

## CHAPTER XXII

The seventh section, in which, because of the coming of Christ the Savior, the whole Church, lying under sin in darkness, is told: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come,” etc., down to, “And I shall glorify the house [Col. 1344D] of my majesty.”

(CAP. LX.) “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you. For behold, darkness shall cover the earth and gloom the peoples; but the Lord shall rise upon you, and his glory shall be seen in you.”

What he now says, “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem,” is the same as what he said above: “Lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem.” For this good word of consolation is addressed to the entire multitude of saints, which is one city of one King, the one true Jerusalem. She lay prostrate under the sin of the first transgression, and did not see God, her light, because a wall of enmities stood between; until Christ came, the Sun of righteousness, light from light, brightness from brightness, God from God, Son from the Father.

Therefore he says [Col. 1345A] to this Jerusalem: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem.” The command of the prophetic Spirit is a good, certain, and undoubted proclamation of the good to come. “Arise and be enlightened,” he says—that is, you shall now truly arise and be enlightened. Why? He says: “For your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen upon you.”

Your light, I say, of which you were deprived through the serpent’s deception of the first parents, to whom he said: “Eat, and your eyes shall be opened” (Gen. III)—behold, it has come; behold, it descended into the Virgin’s womb; behold, it is placed in the earthen vessel of flesh, that it may be a lamp by which you are sought and enlightened. Thus your light has come; and at his birth the glory of the Lord rose upon you, in order to cleanse you, darkened by the shame of ancient transgression.

Why do I expressly say, “upon you”? Because “behold, darkness shall cover the earth and gloom the peoples. But the Lord shall rise upon you, and his glory shall be seen in you.” Therefore “upon you,” because gloom and darkness shall cover the superfluous peoples, the peoples not belonging to you, who are not of faith, and the earth—that is, every nation intent upon earthly things and unconcerned for heavenly things; for as they are, so they shall remain covered in gloom and darkness. But upon you, who have had faith in him who was to come, the Lord shall rise, and his glory shall be seen in you.

But when that your light has come, it shall be placed not in hiding nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may be seen by the whole world (Matt. V). This is what follows: “And the nations shall walk in your light, and kings in the brightness of your rising.” For now, before that Lord rises, his name is confined within the narrow bounds of Judaea; but then, when it has been placed like a lamp upon a lampstand, the nations that were in profound darkness shall walk in that your light, and kings too shall raise their suppliant eyes to the brightness of the light which has risen for you.

Then you shall not have few children, nor Jews alone. But what? “Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise at your side.” “Sons,” he says, that is, sons illuminated by your light and purified by the baptism of your light, “shall come from afar”—from afar, I say, from every race and nation, from east and west, south and north. Until then it was not so: they came only from near at hand, only from the flesh of Abraham.

Nor shall only your sons come, but your daughters also; and as long as your daughters are little and cannot eat solid food, they draw milk of simple teaching from their side. “Then you shall see and overflow; and your heart shall marvel and be enlarged, when the multitude 511 of the sea has turned to you and the strength of the nations has come to you.”

“Then,” he says, “you shall see and rejoice and, like rivers, be flooded with sudden waters; and your heart shall marvel and be astonished—indeed, it shall be enlarged by the enlargement of love, which receives all and undergoes no constraint in bearing so many children. A flood of camels shall cover you, dromedaries of Midian and Ephah,” etc.

Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, fertile in camels, and the entire province is called Sheba. Kedar, however, is a region of the Saracens, who in the Scriptures are called Ishmaelites; and Nebaioth is one of Ishmael’s sons, from whose names the desert is called—a land poor in crops but full of livestock. Therefore, through the familiar names of barbarian peoples neighboring Israel, understand the conversion of the whole world to be proclaimed; and let this be the meaning: herds of camels, released from the bonds of iniquity and pouring out their souls to God, shall cover you, Jerusalem, with their offered gifts; and all shall come from captivity and conversion, bringing the gold of faith and incense of sacrifice.

For Midian in this place means “iniquity”; Ephah, “released” or “pouring forth”; Sheba, “conversion” or “captivity”; Kedar, “darkness”; Nebaioth, “prophecies.” Therefore the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah and all from Sheba shall come; all the livestock of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you, bringing, as has already been said, the gold of faith and the incense of sacrifice. And because they are not content with their own [Col. 1346B] salvation, they also proclaim praise to the Lord, that is, they preach God’s salvation to others as well.

“These,” he says, “shall be offered upon my acceptable altar, and I shall glorify the house of my majesty.” The house of the Lord’s majesty is the holy Church of catholic faith; his acceptable altar is Christ himself. For as this visible altar stands preeminent over the handmade temple, so the Lord Jesus Christ stands preeminent over the Lord God’s temple—that is, the Church—which we are. Therefore “upon my acceptable altar,” that is, in that Son, my Lord Jesus Christ, in whom I am appeased, these gifts shall be offered and accepted; and for the sake of that altar I shall glorify the house of my majesty—for the sake of Christ my Son, I shall glorify the Church, whose head he is (Col. I), as the resting place of my majesty.

## CHAPTER XXIII

[Col. 1346C] That those through whose ministry these promised things are accomplished are mystically signified or shown in the question: “Who are these who fly like clouds,” etc.

Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows? It is as though that blessed Jerusalem were asking how, or through whom, what she had heard would come to pass: “Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise at your side,” etc. The prophet, looking up as it were toward heaven, says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” It is a striking question, intended to make his hearers as attentive as possible. For he might have said plainly: “The apostles of the Savior, Jerusalem, enlightened by your light of which I have already spoken, and themselves made the light of the world, will go into the whole world and, through the word of preaching together with works of charity, will beget for you sons who come to you from afar, from every race and nation.” But he wished, as was fitting, both to conceal more carefully a matter to be known in its own time and, by concealing it, to signify it as far as possible through a fitting and worthy mystery, expressed by this declamatory question. He therefore says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” To this, he who sent them answers thus: “For the islands await me, and the ships of the sea from the beginning, that I may bring your sons from afar—their silver and their gold with them—for the name of the Lord your God and for the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.”

As though he said: “They are my apostles, to whom I said: ‘You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain’” (John 15). They themselves are clouds, never resting in idle leisure, but, driven by the Holy Spirit, carrying the rain of saving doctrine to all nations. They are like simple doves, yet possessing the cunning or prudence of the serpent (Matt. 10). Those individual doves stand at their own windows: that is, they exercise the distinct gifts of the Holy Spirit which they have received; always flying like clouds by preaching, always looking up toward heaven through those windows of theirs in contemplation, groaning in meditation and meditating in groaning.

To what end do they fly? “For the islands,” he says, “await me”: that is, the future churches, which are surrounded by the world as by a deep sea, await me, longing in their need; nor am I mistaken that they will gladly receive the rain of these clouds. “The islands,” I say, “and the ships of the sea await from the beginning,” namely, that they may be “the head and not the tail” (Deut. 28), according to that saying in the Psalm: “Envoys shall come from Egypt; Ethiopia shall hasten her hands to God” (Ps. 67 [68]). Just as ships arriving from afar lie ready in harbor for those who are to disembark from them and work upon many waters, so hearers will be ready for my messengers, to receive and assist them by their works, that in the deep nations they may build churches by preaching that glory of the Lord which has risen upon you. In this way I shall bring your sons from afar.

“Their silver and their gold with them, for the name of the Lord your God and for the Holy One of Israel”: that is, for the honor of the name of the Lord and of the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you—namely, as was said above, by rising over you and displaying in you his glory to be seen. What is their gold but their faith? What is their silver but the eloquence of their speech? These will come with them, so that, splendid in golden faith and bright and clear in silvery speech, they may destroy every error and every heretical perversity, for the honor of the Lord’s name.

“And the sons of foreigners shall build your walls, and their kings shall minister to you.” The foreigners—that is, the peoples of the nations, who had formerly been strangers to the covenants of promise and without hope—will themselves build you up so greatly that even their kings will minister to you: either by physically building churches at public expense and enacting laws against the persecutions of the nations and the snares of heretics, or spiritually, as kings ruling the soul and subjugating the flesh; for this truly is to minister to you and to build your walls.

## CHAPTER XXIV

That he who was promised is now present, and that the words are those of him who says, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” etc.; what that anointing is, what the proclamation of the acceptable year is, who the mourners are, what consolation is meant, and what restoration of desolate places and ruined cities.

**(CHAP. LXI.)** After promises of this sort have been set forth, he himself who was promised is present and says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me. He sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the broken-hearted, and to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those shut up, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance for our God.”

Just as in the preceding 512th section, after similar promises had been made, he himself, confirming the truth of the promises, says: “Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who was speaking—behold, I am present” (Isa. 52); so here too, after the proclamations of his coming have been set forth, he suddenly cries out, as though already present, in his own voice: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” etc. For he himself, beginning now to preach in the Gospel, confirms this in gracious speech: “The book of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him; and when he unrolled the book, he found what he wished—he found this passage, he found this writing” (Luke 4 [OCR: XLV]). “And he began to say to them: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing’” (ibid.).

Therefore, he says, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me.” As though he said: “Because the Lord anointed me, I said—and now say—that the Spirit of the Lord is upon me.” But where or when did the Lord anoint me? When I was conceived—or rather, in order that I might be conceived in my mother’s womb, the Lord anointed me. For it was not a woman by male seed, but a virgin through the anointing of the Holy Spirit, who conceived me. There the Lord anointed me king; there, I say, the Lord anointed me both king and priest. Again, in the river Jordan he designated me by the same Spirit by whom, as I have said, the Lord anointed me.

Therefore, the Spirit of the Lord is upon me: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). For the Spirit of the Lord is not upon me in part; the whole Spirit of the Lord, with all his gifts, is upon me, just as the whole and undivided dove came upon me with all its members. Why, then, is the Spirit of the Lord thus upon me? “He sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the broken-hearted.” Thus it was fitting that, like a dove, he came upon me (Matt. 3), for the dove is indeed a gentle bird and customarily gives forth groaning instead of song. He sent me, meek one, to announce good news to the meek; he sent me to heal those who groan and are broken in heart. For he sent me as physician not for the healthy and proud, but for the sick and broken-hearted; he made me not for the righteous but for sinners, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity, meek and humble of heart.

“To proclaim pardon to captives, and opening to those shut up; and to announce the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance for our God.” To which captives, or captives of what captivity, was I to proclaim pardon? To which persons shut up, and where, was I to preach opening? “To captives of sin,” he says, “pardon; to those shut up in hell, opening.” For since through one man sin entered this world, and death through sin (Rom. 5), all human beings became captives of sin; all human beings were shut up in death. But do not all captives desire pardon, nor do all those shut up love opening. What then? “That I may announce,” he says, “the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance for our God”: first the acceptable year of the Lord, then the day of vengeance.

For this acceptable year of the Lord is my first coming, which I shall announce to you by saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,” because he anointed me once in the virgin’s womb and again in the waters of the Jordan. The day of vengeance, however, will be my second coming: the day, I say, of vengeance for our God upon those who do not seek pardon and opening, but who love the slavery of sin and run toward the prison-bars of death, contemptuously closing deaf ears to the voice warning behind them and saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of God is drawing near” (Matt. 4).

“To comfort all who mourn, and to give strength to those who mourn in Zion, and to give them a crown instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning, and a mantle of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.” “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “did not send me so that I might amuse the scoffers of this world, but that I might comfort all who mourn in Zion”: that is, those who mourn because, weaned and cast away from their heavenly mother Zion on account of sin, they say with the Psalmist: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136 [137]), etc. For this purpose, I say, he sent me: to comfort mourners such as these, to give these mourners strength, and to give them these three things: a crown instead of ashes, oil instead of mourning, and a mantle of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.

That is, a crown of glory instead of the ashes of repentance; oil of joy, the consolation of the Holy Spirit, instead of mourning for the present state of bereavement and exile; and a mantle of praise—that is, the glory of resurrection—instead of a spirit of sorrow, instead of the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, which God desires and does not despise. “And in her they shall be called strong ones of righteousness, a planting of the Lord for glorification. And they shall build up the deserts of old, raise up ancient ruins, and restore cities desolate and ruined from generation to generation. And foreigners shall stand and pasture your flocks, and sons of strangers shall be your farmers and vinedressers.”

They shall be called in Zion “strong ones of righteousness”: strong ones, I say, of righteousness, those who are prepared not only to do righteousness but also to suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake (Matt. 5), possessing the holy spirit of strength. They shall be called: indeed, the names of all who love righteousness are written in the heavenly Zion; but those who steadfastly endure persecution for that righteousness will there be far more renowned and illustrious, in contrast to the strong ones of injustice, of whom the Psalmist says: “Their tents are from generation to generation; they have called their lands by their own names” (Ps. 48 [49]). These strong ones of righteousness shall be called in her “a planting of the Lord, for glorification,” evidently in contrast to the adulterate planting of which it is rightly said: “Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15).

For this planting of the Lord consists of the apostles and apostolic men, planted to glorify God, so that they too may have glory with God. But the planting on account of which that saying was uttered consisted of the scribes and Pharisees, who brought forth the thorns of insult and the thistles of blasphemy. “These shall build up the deserts of old, raise up ancient ruins, and restore cities desolate and ruined”—that building or restoring of which one of them says, one of the strong ones of righteousness, one planted by the Lord, one of the builders of the great city: “We are God’s fellow-workers; you are God’s field, God’s building. According to the grace given to me, as a wise architect I laid a foundation; but no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3).

## CHAPTER XXV

Concerning the apostles and apostolic men, preachers of the word of God, and how they ought now to reap carnal things from those among whom they sow spiritual things, and in the future to hope for double goods—that is, the goods alike of soul and body.

“And foreigners shall stand and pasture your flocks, and sons of strangers shall be your farmers and vinedressers. But you shall be called priests of the Lord; you shall be named ministers of our God. You shall eat the strength of the nations, and in their glory you shall boast.”

O strong ones of righteousness, O planting of the Lord—holy apostles and apostolic men—foreigners, who were not of your race; foreigners, I say, sons of strangers, that is, Gentiles, who were not, like you, of Abraham’s flesh, shall stand in devoted faith at your service. They shall pasture your flocks and gather your harvests, so that from those among whom you have sown spiritual things you may worthily reap their carnal things (1 Cor. 9). But you, as priests—indeed, truly priests of the Lord—shall devote yourselves to the word of God, enjoying holy leisure, in order that you may be what you are: ministers of the Lord, administering spiritual things, so that carnal things may rightly be administered to you. By this title of free birth you shall be called; this name of nobility shall be given you. “You shall eat the strength of the nations, and in their glory you shall boast.”

What is truer than this? Those yet to come will see, at the memory of your ashes, the strength—that is, the labors—of nations being brought together, and the crowns of glorious kings laid in the dust at your name. Thus you shall boast, with a holy and noble pride, when, loftier than the proud age, you shall tread underfoot in true glory the necks of all the proud. This is because, when I said, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me,” you meekly heard my proclamation and believed; and, leaving all things, you followed me, poor in possessions and poor in spirit. Therefore the world hates you, and for this reason you too will lay down your lives for me.

Yet you do not aim at this; you do not await that end, namely, that, as I said, you may “eat the strength of the nations and boast in their glory.” But what then? “For your double shame and disgrace, they shall praise their portion.” This is what you hope for; this is what you labor for: afflicted with double shame and double disgrace, the disgrace of poverty and death, that they may praise their portion—that they may have such a portion as they rightly praise; that is, that they may have eternal life, which is nothing other than to know God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17). This is the portion of the righteous; hence he joyfully says: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72 [73]).

This will be your blessedness: that, from the very things for which you are ashamed with a double disgrace—namely, living in poverty and dying in distress—the nations may come to have God as their portion, praising such a portion of their own, judging such a possession better than the trade in gold and silver. “Therefore in their land they shall possess double things, and everlasting joy shall be theirs. For I the Lord love judgment and hate robbery in a burnt offering; and I shall give their work in truth, and make an everlasting covenant with them. Their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of peoples. All who see them shall recognize them, because they are the seed which the Lord has blessed.”

He turns in address to us, whom he wishes to be imitators of these priests and ministers of his, so that we may know what they received and what we too ought to hope for if we imitate them. “Therefore,” he says, “because they left all things and followed me” (Matt. 19)—these strong ones of righteousness, builders, priests, and my ministers—“therefore in their land they shall possess double things.” For since they left few and transitory goods of the body, they shall possess many and eternal goods both of soul and body; and everlasting joy shall be theirs in both.

“For I the Lord love judgment and hate robbery in a burnt offering.” Truly, I love judgment in giving what is due, and I hate robbery in withholding a debt. I would not love judgment if I withheld the reward; I would have robbery in a burnt offering if I did not repay what was offered. But, “Amen, I say to you: there is no one who has left house, brothers, sisters, father, mother, wife, children, or fields for my sake and for the Gospel, who shall not receive a hundredfold now in this time, and in the age to come eternal life” (Mark 10). Therefore, certain of judgment and secure of recompense, let all the devout prefer, following such examples, to be put to shame with double shame or disgrace; for I, the Lord who love judgment, also regard it as hateful not to repay them whatever I receive from them in a burnt offering.

“And I shall give their work in truth, and make an everlasting covenant with them.” I shall give their work in truth, that their fruit or work may remain in truth. In contrast, it is said of the work of the reprobate: “Behold, you are from nothing, and your work is from that which is not” (Isa. 41). Again: “Behold, all the unjust are nothing, and their works are vain; their idols are wind and emptiness” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “They trust in nothing and speak vanity. They conceived toil and gave birth to iniquity. They hatched the eggs of asps and wove spiders’ webs” (Isa. 59).

Not so these priests and ministers of mine, but I shall give their work in truth: I shall give their work, I say, in the Spirit of truth, and make an everlasting covenant with them, so that they may be sons and not servants, made friends out of enemies, reconciled through my death. “And their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of peoples.” Their seed—that is, the word of their preaching—shall be known among the nations; for when those to whom it was first necessary to speak reject it, they themselves will turn to the nations (Acts 13). But their offspring also shall be known in the midst of peoples, because, though struck down by death and laid in tombs, they will sprout again: from their dead bodies living works of virtue will increase, strengthening the faith of the living.

“All who see them shall recognize them, because they are the seed which the Lord has blessed.” Truly, only those who see them will recognize them; those who shut their eyes so as not to see will not recognize them. For to see them belongs to goodwill and to a more attentive and teachable soul. Thus those who see them will recognize from their works that they are the seed which the Lord has blessed; and they will pronounce them blessed, saying that the Lord gave them, in a wonderful and unprecedented manner, the holy Spirit of blessing.

## CHAPTER XXVI

How the Church of God rejoices in this when she says, “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord,” etc.; what the garment of salvation and joy is with which Christ clothed and encircled her; and concerning the unity of the body of Christ and the Church.

[Col. 1352B] “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of joy, like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride decked with her jewels. For as the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden causes its seed to sprout, so the Lord God shall cause righteousness and praise to sprout before all nations.”

This coming, or presence, of the Savior, of which this prophetic discourse speaks, is that kiss for which the bride longed when she said in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1). For the Church, the faithful bride, born in the patriarchs and betrothed in Moses and the prophets, sighed with most eager desire of heart that her beloved himself might come and, by assuming flesh, kiss her with the kiss of his mouth. Now, delighted after this has happened, she says joyfully: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord,” etc.

That distinguished friend of the bridegroom, fellow-priest of bridegroom and bride and confidant of their mutual love, spoke as a participant in this joy: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. This joy of mine, therefore, is fulfilled” (John 3). Nor is there any doubt that this forerunner of the nativity, who also became the forerunner of the Passion, descended into hell and brought good news there to the Church that awaited him.

Therefore, since the prophet will afterward speak of his Passion—“Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 58 [OCR; cf. 63])—and since shortly before, in the person of the same one announcing and preaching, he said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me,” these words are rightly and appropriately understood as those of the Church, already in hell, exulting at his coming to meet her: “Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God.”

What is the cause of my joy, the reason for my exultation? “Because he clothed me with the garment of salvation and surrounded me with the robe of joy.” I had been stripped naked in Adam; I had covered my shame with fig leaves; wretchedly clad in garments of skin, I had been driven from paradise. But this Lord and my God clothed me, in place of leaves, as with the first robe of baptism and remission of sins—the garment of salvation; and in place of the garment of mortality’s skin, he surrounded me with the second robe, the garment of resurrection and immortality.

“Like a bridegroom adorned with a crown and like a bride decked with her jewels.” Like a bridegroom, I say, and like a bride. For we are one body: head and members, bridegroom and bride, Christ and the Church (1 Cor. 12; Rom. 12). Already in Christ, my bridegroom and head, who has suffered a little, the crown of victory shall shine forever; and in me, the bride, glittering jewels of virtues and graces shall be set. “For as the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden causes its seed to sprout, so the Lord God shall cause righteousness and praise to sprout before all nations.”

He is the bridegroom and I the bride, because he is Lord God and I am his earth or garden; because he is the cultivator and I his field (1 Cor. 3). He is one and the same: because he is Creator, he is Lord and God; and because he became man, he is my cultivator (John 15). Just as, when the cultivator plants and waters and God gives the increase (1 Cor. 3), the earth brings forth its shoot and the garden causes its seed to sprout, so, when he who is man plants and waters by evangelizing, and he who is God gives increase through his Spirit, I shall bring forth and sprout the righteousness of faith and the praise of God, not before the Jewish nation alone but before all nations: so that they may see my good works, by reading the words and deeds of the patriarchs and prophets, by hearing the voice and seeing the light of the apostles, and by seeing and believing may glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

## CHAPTER XXVII

How God the Father confirms the words of the faithful bride, saying: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent.”

**(CHAP. LXII.)** “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth as brightness and her Savior is kindled as a lamp. And the nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your glory.”

What the bride had said—“Thus the Lord God shall cause righteousness and praise to sprout before all nations”—God, the Father of the bridegroom, confirms by saying: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest,” etc. “For Zion’s sake,” he says, “and for Jerusalem’s sake, to whom I swore in Abraham, to whom I swore in David, that righteousness and praise should sprout before all nations.” In Abraham, when I swore by myself, saying: “I shall bless you and multiply your seed, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22). In David, as he himself says: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not turn from it: ‘Of the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne,’ because the Lord chose Zion” (Ps. 131 [132]).

Therefore, since I am a debtor and bound by a gratuitous oath, for Zion’s sake I shall not be silent but shall speak; and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest but shall work, until her righteous one goes forth through the afflictions of Judaea, through the winepresses of the Passion, as brightness, and her Savior is kindled as a lamp to enlighten the nations; so that the nations may see your righteous one, O Zion, and all kings your glory, O Jerusalem.

“And a new name shall be called for you, which the mouth of the Lord has named.” Surely, I say, you shall be called by a new name—that is, the Christian name; your sons, who until now were called servants, indeed enemies and children of wrath because of the fault of the first transgression of their father Adam, shall be called by a new name: the name of friends, the name of sons of God. “Which the mouth of the Lord has named.” Without doubt, whatever name the mouth of the Lord has named is eternal. Therefore, when he says, “which the mouth of the Lord has named,” it is the same as saying, “a name which shall remain for you forever.”

“And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.” The Apostle says: “For you are our glory, as we also are yours in the day of the Lord” (2 Cor. 1). If each one of us is their glory because they gained us through preaching or instruction, how much more truly are we the glory of him who gained both us and our preachers through his blood? Therefore you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God: that is, to him who redeemed you, the love of redemption will be glory, just as a crown or diadem is glory to the head of a king who has earned it. Signifying this, the same Apostle says: “It was fitting for him, for whom and through whom are all things, who had brought many sons into glory, to perfect through suffering the author of their salvation” (Heb. 2).

“You shall no longer be called Forsaken, nor shall your land any longer be called Desolate.” These were the names of your old condition, inherited from your father Adam: Forsaken, Desolate. You shall no longer be called so, nor shall I remember these names of yours with my lips. But you shall be called “My delight is in her,” and your land “Inhabited.” Until your parents’ disobedience is erased, you cannot be called “My delight is in her”; but through the obedience of your father, the man Jesus Christ, you shall rightly be called “My delight is in her,” and your land “Inhabited.”

Repeating this, I say again: “Because the Lord has taken pleasure in you, and your land shall be inhabited.” How shall your land be inhabited? By a holy habitation, an angelic habitation. For “the young man shall dwell with the virgin, and your sons shall dwell in you.” For those who are counted worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor are given in marriage, for they can no longer die; for they are equal to angels and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection (Matt. 22).

“And the bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, and your God shall rejoice over you”: that is, just as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God shall rejoice over you, because fullness of delight shall be poured into you substantially, according to that saying: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. 35 [36]).

Meanwhile, until the time of those nuptials comes, you shall be guarded against the adulterer, the devil; and I shall not sleep as I slept until I rose at the breeze after midday (Gen. 3), after the serpent, the corrupting adulterer, had committed his adultery. This is what follows: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall never be silent. You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

Who are the watchmen upon the walls of Jerusalem, who are not silent all day and all night, if not the apostles and apostolic men, rulers and priests? While spiritual adulteries must be avoided, they are set in the governance of the holy Church so that neither in prosperity nor adversity may they cease to praise the Lord’s name, to preach the beauty, nobility, riches, and strength of the rightful bridegroom, for whom one must wait a little and who will come quickly. Since they ought to help not only by the word of preaching but also by devoted prayer, the address is directed to these same persons when it says: “O you who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence”—do not allow him leisure to sleep, as he once slept so long that the adultery of the serpent-devil with human nature was accomplished. Scripture indicates this when it says: “And when they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the breeze after midday” (Gen. 3), etc.

The first human beings allowed him to sleep throughout the whole midday, since they troubled him with no praise and no prayer. But you, give him no silence until he establishes and makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth: that is, until he brings his Church to that praiseworthy condition in which neither thief nor adulterer can any longer approach.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

On the words, “The Lord swore by his right hand,” and how the Lord himself states in the Gospel the meaning of this oath: “Amen, I say to you, the kingdom of God shall be taken from you.”

“The Lord swore by his right hand and by the arm of his strength: ‘If I shall ever again give your grain as food to your enemies, or if sons of strangers shall drink your wine, for which you have labored. For those who gather it shall eat it and praise the Lord; and those who bring it together shall drink it in my holy courts.’”

After the mutual discourse of bridegroom and bride, the prophetic speech now breathes toward the Passion by which the bride is redeemed, saying: “The Lord swore.” For when did the Lord swear these things by his right hand and by the arm of his strength, except when the Son of God himself—truly the Lord’s right hand and arm of strength—said: “Amen, I say to you, the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 23)?

Finally, those evil and doomed husbandmen to whom he swore this were enemies and sons of strangers, eating the grain and drinking the wine for which the holy Church of the patriarchs and prophets had labored, and not rendering the fruit of the vineyard at harvest-time. The Lord swore, I say, that this would no longer be so. But what then? “Those who gather it shall eat it and praise the Lord”: that is, the nations producing its fruits shall possess the kingdom of God taken from them (ibid.), so that they may first gather for the Lord and then eat; first bring together and then drink in his courts, in his kingdom.

“Pass through, pass through the gates; prepare the way for the people; make the path level and choose out the stones.” The watchmen of Jerusalem’s walls—that is, the apostles—are commanded to pass through the gates, to proceed to the truth of the Gospel according to the Scriptures, and thus prepare the way for the Christian people, making the path level and removing the stones, so that there may be no stumbling-blocks or scandals by which Christian faith may stumble or fall. They indeed did this as far as they could; but because the way would have been less level, Roman arms were providentially supplied, so that neither city might remain nor Jewish temple stand. So long as that stood, the simplicity of Christians would, as it were, stumble excessively against great stones.

“And,” he says, “raise a sign to the peoples. Behold, the Lord has made it heard from the ends of the earth.” Lest the Jews imagine that the words, “Prepare the way for the people,” were spoken of themselves, he says, “Raise a sign among the nations and to the peoples of the Gentiles,” so that it is not merely the narrow territory of Judaea that is summoned to salvation, but the message is made heard at the ends of the earth, that the whole world may hear of the Passion of the Creator.

It is almost unspeakable how much wonder and expectation is contained in the statement: “Behold, the Lord has made it heard from the ends of the earth.” Say, say to those dying and despairing in the middle of the earth that the Lord has made it heard from the ends of the earth: from humble persons who, because they seemed contemptible, were in a sense the ends of the earth. “Say to the daughter of Zion: ‘Behold, your Savior comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his work before him.’”

“Say,” he says, “and testify to the daughter of Zion”: that is, to the Church of the patriarchs and prophets, to whom, by believing, power is given to become a daughter of God. What will you say to her? “Behold, this one—not another, but this one who, according to another prophet, is poor and rides upon an ass and a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. 2)—is your Savior. Behold, he comes to redeem you and save you. Behold, his reward, by which he redeems you, is with him; and his work, by which he saves you, is before him. For he does not possess outside himself the price of your redemption, but within himself: it is nothing other than his own blood. Likewise, his work, by which he gives life to you after redeeming you, is not far away but before him. For as soon as he redeems you by the price of his blood, he will give you the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of life and salvation, whom all who receive this Savior and believe in him shall receive.

“And they shall call them: ‘The holy people, redeemed by the Lord.’ But you shall be called ‘A city sought out, not forsaken.’” The name of those who believe shall be “the holy people, redeemed by the Lord,” and by this name the apostles and apostolic men shall call them. But you, O faithful Zion, mother of cities, who until now were exiled in hell, forsaken and not sought, shall henceforth be called “Sought out” and “Not forsaken.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

That the prophet wishes his Passion to be judged worthy of wonder when he says: “Who is this who comes from Edom?”

(CAP. LXIII.) “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe, advancing in the abundance of his strength.” The proclamations of his victorious Passion, which he will not repeat hereafter, he now declares more excellently in a tone of amazement, adding joy for the triumphant glory of his resurrection and ascension. “Who,” he says, “is this who comes from Edom? Who is this who comes with dyed garments from Bozrah? Who is that beautiful one in his robe, advancing in the abundance of his strength?” Edom means earthly and bloody. Bozrah, the name of a city in Moab, is interpreted “strong and fortified.” [Col. 1357A] Now the Jewish people was earthly and bloody; Jerusalem had been strong and fortified, previously surrounded by very mighty walls; or else it means hell, in which the souls of the dead were held shut up by the strongest guards. From there comes this one who is truly beautiful and, according to Psalm 44, “fair in form beyond the sons of men”: beautiful, I say, in his robe, or in dyed garments—that is, white and ruddy: white in the most spotless virginity of his flesh, and ruddy in his most holy Passion—and thus advancing to the summit of heaven in the abundance of his strength.

The angels who meet him therefore ask and say, “Who is this? Who is this?” terrified by the novelty of the event. For the mystery of Christ’s Passion and resurrection had been unknown to all preceding generations. He replies to those questioning him: “I who speak righteousness, and am mighty to save” [Col. 1357B]. “I,” he says, “am he who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in my mouth” (1 Pet. II); or, he who repays evils to the wicked and good things to the good. “I am he who came to fight against hostile powers and to free those bound from prison, so that both the adversaries may experience punishment and the captives freedom.”

Again the angels inquire and say: “Why, then, is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one treading in a winepress?” If, they say, you are he who speaks righteousness and have admitted no sin, ought not your clothing—the clothing, I mean, of your body—to have remained white just as it was when taken from the virginal womb? Why then is it now red with blood? Why are your garments like those of one treading in a winepress? For both your hands, both your feet, are [Col. 1357C] as though fastened with nails; and one of your sides is as though wounded by a spear. All these are signs of death, as though you too had trodden the winepress of death—or rather, had been trodden in the winepress of death. For in the winepress from which this comparison is drawn, one thing is trodden and another is the one who treads. But in the Passion of death, of which this discourse speaks, he who treads and he who is trodden are the same.

For he trod, in that he gave himself up for us; he was trodden like a cluster of grapes which, under the pressure of the cross, sent forth from the berry of his body wine—that is, his spirit. Likewise, he trod the winepress because, just as in a winepress the expressed wine is taken up while the grapes are left behind, so in that same Passion [Col. 1357D], by redeeming the good he took them up, while by judging the evil he left them behind.

He therefore answers those who question him: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me. I trod them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath. And their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all my clothing.” Therefore, he says, my clothing is red, and my garments are like those of one treading in a winepress, because I truly trod the winepress. But I trod it alone, for I had no helper. No angel, archangel, throne, dominion, or any of the heavenly spirits suffered for humankind; nor did I have any human helper, so much so that even Peter, who had been most confident, fled in terror—indeed, denied me.

Thus I trod the winepress alone [Col. 1358A]—understand: for the salvation of the aforesaid daughter Zion, for the salvation of all believers. What of those who do not believe? “I trod them,” he says, “in my fury and trampled them in my wrath.” I crushed them with a twofold crushing: I condemned them by my present fury and my future wrath. By present fury, namely, so that, when the Romans took away both their place and their nation, they might perish (John XI); by future wrath, so that they might descend to the lowest depths of hell. “And their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all my clothing.” Finally, my blood became their inherited blood, because they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

There their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I defiled all my clothing: whatever they had been accustomed to do for my worship or religion [Col. 1358B]—their burnt offerings, their new moons and sabbaths, and all their other festivals—from that time I hated, and judging all things polluted with blood, I turned away my eyes (Isa. I). “For the day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my recompense has come.” What day of vengeance, what day or year of recompense? Surely that which, foreseeing already because of the guilt of the calf which they had made, he said to Moses: “But in the day of vengeance I shall visit this sin of theirs also” (Exod. XXXII). That day or year of my recompense was in my heart, and now it has come; and whatever their fathers did thereafter—indeed, all the blood that was shed upon the earth from the blood of righteous Abel—behold, it comes upon this generation (Matt. XXIII).

What, finally, did I accomplish for myself? “I looked around [Col. 1358C], and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist. But my arm saved me, and my indignation itself aided me.” It was little to say, “there was no helper, and there was none to assist.” For it is known from the Gospel that not only was there no helper and none to assist, when he looked around from on high—that is, lifted up upon the cross—but, on the contrary, all who saw me mocked me; “they spoke with their lips and shook their heads” (Ps. XXI), saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days—save yourself!” (Matt. XXVII).

This manner of expression is called *tapinosis*, that is, the understatement of a great thing: the statement does not intend what it outwardly seems to show. Therefore, he says: [Col. 1358D] “I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist”; or, according to another prophet: “I waited for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for one to console me, and I found none” (Ps. LXVIII). “But my arm saved me, and my indignation itself aided me.” In what way did my arm save me? In what way did my indignation itself aid me? Namely in this: when I had become “a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII), I loosed the pains of hell, so that it should not even be possible for me to be held by it (Acts II).

And as a very strong lion is aided by his roar in crushing lesser beasts, so my indignation aided me in overthrowing all the princes of hell. Hence Jacob the patriarch says very elegantly in the Spirit: “Judah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion, and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. XLIX). Thereupon I exacted punishments from my enemies, the Jews who murdered and mocked me, so that they fell by the edge of the sword, were led captive into all nations, and their city together with the temple was razed to the ground. This is what follows: “And I trampled peoples in my fury, and made them drunk with my indignation, and brought down their crown to the earth” [Col. 1359A].

## CHAPTER XXX

A lament for the Jewish people in the person of the prophet, together with confession of the preceding evil which they deserved, and praise of the Lord’s justice, upon all that the Lord has rendered to us, down to: “So will I do for the sake of my words, that I may not destroy it all.”

“I will remember the mercies of the Lord, the praise of the Lord [Col. 1359B] for all that the Lord has rendered to us, and for the multitude of good things bestowed upon the house of Israel, which he granted them according to his compassion and according to the multitude of his mercies. And he said: ‘Surely you are my people, children who do not deny.’ And he became their Savior.”

After the final recapitulation of the Lord’s Passion, the prophet most affectionately laments the rejection of his own people—that is, the Jewish people. Yet in this same lament he is wise: tempering the force of pain with admitted reason, he begins his tearful words of prayer with true praise of God, lest, because of the adversities which follow, he seem ungrateful for God’s earlier benefits. “I will remember,” he says, “the mercies of the Lord”—understand, the ancient mercies—even amid the wrath which he brings after those mercies. As though he said: Although after so many mercies he brings wrath, he has nevertheless not changed, nor should he be accused of changeableness.

[Col. 1359C] For he bestowed a multitude of good things upon the house of Israel, according to his compassion and according to the multitude of his mercies; and meanwhile he said—I mean, in Moses, in the prophets, and in the Psalms—“Surely you are my people, children who do not deny.” That is to say: I indeed chose Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and it was truly said: “The seed of Abraham his servant, the children of Jacob his chosen” (Ps. CIV). Yet not all who are from Israel are Israelites, but only children who do not deny are reckoned in the seed. He said these things, and, his purpose remaining unchanged, became Savior only to them.

“In all their tribulation he was not distressed” [Col. 1359D]. In whose every tribulation was he not distressed? In that of the children who do not deny, the faithful children. All their tribulation, all their misery, all their sin, and all their iniquity, he himself bore without distress: not unwillingly, but in voluntary love. For this is what follows: “And the angel of his presence saved them in his love.” For if the Apostle was not distressed in the tribulation of his own people, but with an enlarged heart said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not constrained in us” (2 Cor. VI), how much more was the angel of the Lord’s presence, the angel of great counsel—whose face is the face of the Lord—not confined by any tribulation? [Col. 1359D]

“He saved them,” he says, “in his love, and in his compassion [Col. 1360A] he himself redeemed them. And he bore them and lifted them up all the days of the age.” All these are offices of the sweetest and broadest love. But they themselves provoked him to wrath and afflicted his Holy Spirit. Who were “they”? Surely the denying children: “a sinful nation, a people laden with iniquity, an evil seed, criminal children” (Isa. I). Whose holy Spirit did they provoke to wrath and afflict? The Spirit of the Holy of Holies, the angel of his presence, whom they blasphemed, denied, and killed.

What followed? “And he turned to them as an enemy, and he himself fought against them.” It is plain to the whole world that he fought against them, conquered them, killed them by the edge of the sword, and led them captive into all nations—not as a father striking with the rod of discipline, but as an enemy pursuing them even to the lowest depths of hell [Col. 1360B]. “And he remembered the days of old, Moses and his people.” He remembered the days of old, remembered Moses, remembered his people, namely in order to bring upon them all the righteous blood which had been shed over all the earth from the days of old (Luke XI); in order to take vengeance upon them because they so often embittered the spirit of Moses (Ps. CV), because they so often, through tumult, disturbed the peace of his people.

Having set forth this praise and remembrance of the Lord’s mercies, he at last enters upon a tearful lament for his people with so loud a cry of voice and roar of heart that we may rightly say that in him the Holy Spirit prays with unutterable groanings for Israel (Rom. VIII), so that at least a remnant may be saved from it (Rom. IX). “Where,” he says, “is he who brought them up from the sea [Col. 1360C] with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who placed in its midst the Spirit of his Holy One?” And shortly afterward: “Look down from heaven and see from your holy habitation and your glory. Where are your zeal and your strength? The multitude of your inward compassions and mercies has restrained itself from me. For you are our Father, and Abraham has not known us, and Israel has ignored us. You, Lord, are our Father; our Redeemer: from everlasting is your name. Why have you made us wander, Lord, from your ways? Why have you hardened our heart, so that we might not fear you?” etc. (CH. LXV).

To such lament over the blindness which befell Israel (Rom. XI), God finally replies: “They sought me who did not previously ask; they found me who did not seek me.” Immediately the Son, whose person these utterances represent, addresses the Father himself in these words: [Col. 1360D] “And I said: ‘Here I am, here I am,’ to a nation which did not call upon your name.” Why? “I spread out,” he says, “my hands all day to an unbelieving people, who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts,” etc. He speaks these things against Israel, to which blindness had happened, concerning the fullness of the Gentiles which was to enter in. Without delay he promises that a remnant from it will be saved, saying: “As when a grain is found in a cluster and one says, ‘Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,’ so will I do for the sake of my words, that I may not destroy it all,” etc.

I am not unaware that very many passages, plainly pertaining to this same faith of Christ and also to the calling of the Gentiles, have been passed over here and there. But, according to my purpose, it was fitting to select only seven portions of this prophet, in which the whole Christian faith, the evangelical faith, is contained in summary—not partially, but almost wholly complete—with face unveiled and in orderly sequence [Col. 1361A]. Here indeed we could make an end and pass to another prophet; but one point occurs, exceptionally beautiful and outstanding, which devotion to the faith does not at all permit us to pass by untouched.

## CHAPTER XXXI

On the words, “Before she travailed, she gave birth,” etc.; and how, according to these words also, what the Jews and certain heretics said—that Christ did not exist before Mary—is false.

(CH. LXVI.) “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before her labor came, she bore a male child. Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? [Col. 1361B] Shall the earth travail in one day, or shall a nation be born all at once, because Zion travailed and bore her children? Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth, says the Lord? Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren, says the Lord your God?”

These are four statements, one of which intimates to us the grace of our regeneration, while the other three intimate, through a threefold mystery most lofty and almost ineffable, the generation of the only Word of God. For when he says, “Shall the earth travail in one day, or shall a nation be born all at once, because Zion travailed and bore her children?”, he marvels at the sudden generation of those who believe in Christ: after the coming of the Holy Spirit, holy Zion—that is, the apostolic Church—regenerated a great multitude of Jews and Gentiles by the word of preaching and by saving baptism, with a miracle as great as if an entire nation were born in one day from a single womb [Col. 1361C]. This is one of the four statements just mentioned.

Of the other three, the first is that she travailed; the second, that before she travailed she gave birth; the third, that the Lord himself asserts, in a most lofty declaration, that he who causes others to give birth is not barren, but has himself also begotten. As has already been said, these three are great and wonderful evidences of Christ’s generation.

For when did Zion travail and bear a male child? Surely when the Virgin Mary—an eminent part of the holy city Zion, an eminent part and royal chamber of the holy Church, which is the watchtower in which we now watch, and in which afterward we shall see the God of gods face to face—bore Christ, a male son: a most strong son, [Col. 1361D] able to overcome the strong man armed, who, fearing no one, guarded his court and held the world as though in peace for himself (Luke XI). When that blessed Virgin bore Christ the Son, Zion surely bore a male child. For Mary did not bring Christ forth for herself alone, but for the whole Church.

But let neither Jew nor heretic now say that this same Christ began to exist from Mary. For “before she travailed, she gave birth” [Col. 1362A]. Before she travailed there, before the time came for her to bring forth from the Virgin’s womb the visible Son, holy Zion gave birth and became mother of the same Word. For she conceived in her heart and gave birth to the Word of God with her mouth. As often as the word of God came to one of the prophets or patriarchs, so often Zion gave birth to the word of the Lord: none other than that which the blessed Virgin conceived and, made flesh, brought forth.

Hence Isaiah himself, one of them, says: “By fear of you, O Lord, we have conceived and given birth; we have produced the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI). This truth is known and celebrated among holy souls: God truly joins himself to a faithful soul who loves him as a bridegroom to a bride; and when, through the spirit of love, it has received seed from him and been made pregnant, it becomes mother of the Word of God by speaking, prophesying, and—what is more—[Col. 1362B] writing the knowledge of God. Thus all legal and prophetic Scripture was composed before God gathered the entirety of all Scripture, his whole Word, into the Virgin’s womb.

The Virgin herself conceived first in mind rather than flesh; she gave birth first through her mouth in prophesying rather than through her womb in travail. Therefore it is false that Christ did not exist before Mary. Before she bore his flesh, blessed Zion bore with the mouths of the prophets the one and same Christ, the one and same Word of God. Nor is even this sufficient yet. For lest perhaps you suppose that this Word of the Lord did not exist before the prophets spoke, behold God himself says: [Col. 1362C] “Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth? Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” As though he said: Shall I, who gave others the utterance of a good word, not first have poured forth a good word from my own heart? (Ps. XLIV).

There is a solecism in the tenses of the verbs, when he says, “Shall I not give birth?” and “Shall I be barren?” instead of saying, “Did I not give birth?” and “Was I barren?” Elsewhere, however, he uses the correct—that is, past—tense, saying: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX). Yet neither because there he says, “From the womb I begot you,” nor because here he says, “Shall I not give birth?” or “Shall I be barren?”, should God therefore be thought to possess a womb or vulva. Rather, in order to signify more expressly the substantial reality of himself and of his Son or Word, God has deigned appropriately to use such expressions.

Therefore let all impiety be silent: [Col. 1362D] for that Word whom the Virgin Mary brought forth incarnate, having conceived him by faith, the souls of patriarchs and prophets had earlier brought forth in speech and writing; nonetheless God the Father himself brought him forth from the womb—that is, begot him from his own profound substance—before all ages of ages. So far is this God of ours from being a recent God (Ps. LXXX).

# THE FORTY-TWO BOOKS OF R. D. D. RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ, ON THE TRINITY AND ITS WORKS. COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 1363]

519

## CHAPTER I

Jeremiah’s prophecy marks the beginning of the fifth age; and in this age Christ’s priesthood was prefigured by deeds and signified by prophetic utterances.

The prophecy of Jeremiah is the twilight of the fifth age of the world, foretelling the Babylonian captivity, and likewise the ruin and burning of the city and temple, in such a way that he himself saw all these things with his own eyes. Here it is rightly asked what the world received at the time when, as if by a fixed boundary, the fifth age could rightly be named or reckoned after the completion of the fourth age. For the principle concerning the preceding ages stands thus: in the first age, before the Flood, humankind, like an infant left to itself, was without hearing the word of God. In the second, like a child, it received the first elements of instruction [Col. 1363B] in the covenant which God made with Noah. In the third, now like an adolescent, it received the promise of the blessed seed in Abraham and the discipline of the Law in Moses. In the fourth, like a young man, it heard in David the promise of Christ’s kingdom.

What further, then, did it hear or receive at this time, so that it may rightly be reckoned, as it were, the fifth age of a full and perfect man? It received, surely, the promise of Christ’s priesthood. For he who was promised as man in Abraham, and as king in David, was promised as priest in the prophets of this age. His priesthood is here prefigured by deeds and signified by prophetic utterances. In the preceding age it was said to him: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX); and it was said to Eli the priest, as a type of the ruined priesthood of the Jews, which the faithful priesthood of Christ and the Church was to succeed: “Behold, days are coming, and I shall cut off your arm and the arm of your father’s house, so that there shall not be an old man in your house” (1 Sam. I) [Col. 1363C].

But here, much more fully and much more sacredly, both the cause and the effect of Christ’s priesthood are figured, and the times of his coming are defined. For the Babylonian captivity of a single nation signifies the common cause for which so great a priest was necessary for the human race [Col. 1364A]; while the return of the captives under Jesus the high priest signifies the forgiveness of sins by which we are freed, under the leadership and liberation of our great high priest Jesus Christ. Moreover, the times of his coming are defined in this way: “But you, Daniel, attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks are shortened concerning your people and concerning your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. IX), etc.

At the boundary of this final age, the whole promise of this priest is magnificently fulfilled when the angel says to Joseph, Mary’s husband: “She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he himself shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I) [Col. 1364B]. For it is clear from this that this priest is God, who alone can save from sins, “having no daily need, as the priests formerly had, to offer sacrifices first for their own sins and then for those of the people” (Heb. VII).

Evangelical authority indeed established these boundaries of the ages, saying in the book of the generation of Jesus Christ: “Thus all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; and from David to the Babylonian migration, fourteen generations; and from the Babylonian migration to Christ, fourteen generations” (Matt. I). This is rightly understood to have been said with reference only to the generation of Jesus Christ, who, according to the promise made to Abraham, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII), is true man; according to that made to David, “From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne” (Ps. CXXXI), is certainly king; and according to that made to Joseph, Mary’s husband, “He himself shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. I), is by office priest and by power God [Col. 1364C].

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1365A] How this fifth age resembles the fifth day of the creation of the world, and why at that time the most precious temple was permitted to be consumed by Babylonian fire.

The beginning of the fifth age, then, contains the visible works of God, just as does the fifth day of the creation of the world, according to the spirit of counsel, which is indeed the fifth upward from the spirit of the fear of the Lord. For it belongs to divine counsel that the beautiful and noble temple of God—at that time the one and only temple in the whole world, exceedingly rich in gold, marvelous in workmanship, renowned in region—and the royal city of David and Solomon, should have been permitted to be consumed by Babylonian fire, plundered, profaned, and filled with the blood of the slain.

For the world, hitherto a self-indulgent youth, had to be taught not to think that God, the inhabitant of heaven, delights in the gold of a handmade temple or in a city’s wealth, but rather in the faith and good works of human beings, by which a temple is prepared for him within the soul. In this temple alone he delights; there he is worshipped; in it he deigns to be seen and acknowledged as present. Without it he is sought in vain outwardly by lamps or by the gold of a handmade temple [Col. 1365B].

This fifth age also has something similar to the fifth day of the world’s creation. For just as not every kind of creature that arose from the waters was then raised into the air, so not all the captives could say: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. CXXXVI). This belonged to those who remembered Zion, where the holy temple of the Lord’s name had stood, where they had been permitted, without hindrance from the Babylonian king, to worship the one and only true God. Such persons, surely, were not swallowed beneath the waters of the Babylonian river, but sat above them like the little birds which the waters produced at God’s command, ready to fly as soon as they heard the edict of King Cyrus, who permitted them to do so.

But those who remained occupied with Babylonian pleasures and with the embraces of Babylonian wives, forbidden by the Law, and preferred their captivity to the freedom that had been granted, were like little fish, whose entire pleasure lies sunk beneath the waters and who did not know how to fly away [Col. 1365C]. We must now proceed to the matter itself.

## CHAPTER III

How Jeremiah, by his proper name, by his sanctification from the womb, by the office of preaching performed seven times to Jerusalem, by reporting that the word of the Lord came to him before the siege—though he survived its destruction—and by summoning it to repentance in a determined number and order, bore the type of that same Lord whose prophet he was. [Col. 1365D]

(CHAPTER I.) First, Jeremiah, whose name is interpreted “the Lord is exalted,” bears in the whole order of his prophecy the type of the exalted Lord whose prophet he is. Surely, as a type of him who, before he was conceived as man in the Virgin’s womb, was God with God, this man is sanctified in his mother’s womb and is told: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you,” etc.

Likewise, as a type of that same Lord of ours who preached to that people, summoned to repentance those unwilling to listen, foretold the destruction of city and temple, and, though killed, nevertheless survived that destruction, and afterward, leaving the Jews in blindness, preached the Gospel to the Gentiles: this prophet prophesied against Jerusalem, calling to repentance a city perversely turned away in contentious rebellion; he foretold the coming Babylonian army and the future burning of temple and city; and, though he suffered much, he nevertheless survived that burning. After King Zedekiah was captured and deprived of his eyes, Jeremiah himself afterward prophesied to foreign nations [Col. 1366A].

Let us now count how many times the word of the Lord came to him before the siege of the city; and, according to these occasions, let us follow the order of prophecy, the order of the evangelical discourse, which is clear and well known.

First it is written thus: [Col. 1366B] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you, and I gave you as a prophet among the nations.’” Then, secondly: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘What do you see, Jeremiah?’ And I said: ‘I see a waking rod.’” Again: “What do you see? And I said: ‘I see a boiling pot, and its face is from the north.’” These two are rightly regarded as one word of the Lord, because the one and same Word is a watchful rod of correction to those who receive the discipline of repentance, and a boiling pot—that is, the judgment of eternal condemnation—to the unrepentant.

Then, in the third place: [Col. 1366C] “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying: Thus says the Lord: I have remembered you, pitying your youth and the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown’” (Jer. II), and the many further words by which he recounts Jerusalem’s sins at length and invites her to repentance.
