After these, in the fourth place: “The word which came from the Lord to Jeremiah, saying: ‘Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and preach this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah, who enter through these gates to worship the Lord. Thus says the Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel: Make your ways and your pursuits good, and I will dwell with you in this place. Do not trust in lying words, saying: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this”’” (Jer. VII) [Col. 1366D].

Then, in the fifth place: “The word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: ‘Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And say to them: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Cursed is the man who does not hear the words of this covenant which I commanded your fathers’” (Jer. XI). And after some intervening words: “The house of Israel and the house of Judah have made void my covenant which I made with their fathers” (ibid.).

Then, in the sixth place: “The word of the Lord which came to Jeremiah concerning the words of drought: ‘Judah mourned, and her gates fell, and they were darkened upon the earth, and the cry of Jerusalem went up. The great sent their lesser ones for water; they came to draw and found no water; they brought back their vessels empty’” (Jer. XIV) [Col. 1367A].

After these, in the seventh place: “The word which came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: ‘Rise and go down to the house of the potter, and there you will hear my words.’ And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the wheel. And the vessel which he was making of clay with his hands was ruined. And he turned and made it into another vessel, as seemed good in his eyes to make. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Shall I not be able to do to you, house of Israel, as this potter does? says the Lord. Behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel’” (Jer. XVIII).

After this, almost the whole prophecy concerns the imminent destruction of that city and temple.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 1367B] On the words first spoken to him: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you,” etc.; and how they proclaim the anointing of the Holy of Holies, and his obedience and glorification.

Let us now see how this prophecy, in turn, is like the Gospel of Christ. To begin with, what is said—and said according to the capacity of a holy man—is this: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the belly, I sanctified you, and gave you as a prophet among the nations. And the Lord stretched out His hand and touched my mouth. And the Lord said to me: Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, today I have set you over nations and kingdoms, that you may root up, destroy, ruin, and scatter, and build and plant,” etc. It is evident that all this speaks both of the anointing of the Holy of holies [Col. 1367C], and of his obedience and glorification. For who is there, apart from and besides him, whom God the Father knew before he was formed in the womb, sanctified before he came forth from the belly, and gave as a prophet among the nations? For of all, and of every one, of Adam’s children, that true utterance holds: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50).

Moreover, the term “sanctification” is equivocal. One thing is said to be sanctified when it is not held by the contagion of sin; and no one is sanctified by that sanctification except through the grace of Christ. Another is sanctified when it is separated from common and ordinary use for the uses or ministry of holiness. [Col. 1367D] This latter kind of sanctification extends so widely that even the firstborn of a beast is called holy to the Lord, because it is legally set apart for the use or right of the holy ministers of the altar.

Likewise, the knowledge of God, by which he now says, “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you,” is also equivocal. For he knew his only-begotten Son before he was formed in the womb in one way, and each of his elect before he was formed in the womb in another way. He knew the former through an essence co-eternal with himself; he knew each one of us through steadfast and most certain foreknowledge. Therefore, he knew the prophet before he was formed in the womb, and sanctified him before he came forth from the belly; but the one of whom this man here bears the type—the Prophet and prophesied Lord, his only-begotten Son [Col. 1368A]—he alone knew and sanctified in a singular manner, before he was formed in the womb, before he came forth from the belly, having become man. Of his being known by him, the Son himself says: “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11). And as to his having sanctified him before he came forth from the belly, the single, assured faith of all the devout and rightly believing is that he was conceived not from male seed, but from the Holy Spirit; and that he was sent as a prophet among the nations—that is, not only to the Jews, but also for the salvation of the nations.

“Behold,” he says, “I have put my words in your mouth”: namely, the words that you, in obedience, are to speak and proclaim in the world. For this is what the Son himself says elsewhere: “For I have not spoken on my own authority; but the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment as to what I should say [Col. 1368B] and what I should speak” (John 12).—“Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms.” You, I say, made obedient unto death—even death on a cross (Phil. 2)—I will set over nations and kingdoms, according to what the Psalmist sings of you: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour and set him over the works of your hands; you subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8).—“That you may root up and destroy”: “root up,” I say, things badly rooted; “destroy,” things badly built—such especially as the assemblies of the Scribes and Pharisees, having the root of avarice fixed deep in the earth, and likewise resembling tombs of the dead, which outwardly appear beautiful to men but inwardly are full of dead men’s bones (Matt. 23).

But how will you [Col. 1368C] “root up and destroy” them? When your avengers, the Romans, come and remove both their place and their nation (John 11); and then, when they have been handed over to the material sword, their souls, torn from their bodies, become portions for foxes—that is, for malignant spirits (Ps. 62). “And ruin and scatter.” Not merely “root them up” in such a way as to allow them at least to be transported together into one place of captivity; rather, “ruin” them among all nations, scatter them into roads and into small fragments of villages or cities. “And build and plant.” Whom? Not them, but others in their place: namely, build the nations hitherto abandoned; plant in the land of the living the nations which hitherto had held no place in God’s covenant.

## CHAPTER V. [Col. 1368D]

On what he says here in the second vision: first, “I see a wakeful rod”; secondly, “I see a kindled pot”; and how, in accordance with these likenesses, Christ’s first coming is a rod of correction for the penitent, while his second coming is a judgment of eternal condemnation for the impenitent.

Next, it must be understood that this Holy of holies came in such a manner that his first coming is a fatherly rod of correction for all who receive him and thereby become children of God; but his second coming will be a judgment of condemnation for the ungodly and unbelieving. He therefore says: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And I said: “I see a wakeful rod.” And the Lord said to me: “You have seen well, because I will watch over my word to perform it. What do you see?” And I said: [Col. 1369A] “I see a kindled pot, and its face is from the face of the north.”

Certainly, even when these words were spoken, evils were being prepared to be poured out upon all the inhabitants of the land of Judah from the direction of the north—that is, from Babylon, which lies north of that land. Nor is it doubtful that this one and same evil of captivity was a rod to some and a kindled pot to others. For that captivity did not come upon Daniel and his companions to the same end as it did upon everyone else. Yet, in a far higher and more momentous sense, this exalted Lord, the Holy of holies, Christ, saw a wakeful rod for us who believe, and saw “a kindled pot from the direction of the north” for the ungodly and the despisers.

He saw, I say, for us “a wakeful rod”: that is, the fear of the judgment to come and of the pains of hell. As Daniel and his companions were held in the same captivity with those against whom God had been angered because of the crimes of idolatry, so all of us—believers with unbelievers, the faithful with the ungodly—are held in one and the same captivity on account of Adam’s guilt; and all alike die, all are mortal. But for the devout and faithful, this captivity and mortality are a rod by which we are struck for a time, so that we may be trained in the discipline of humility, because we fell through pride. Therefore he says at the beginning of his preaching: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 4).

Moreover, the discipline of actual repentance is sometimes burdensome, sometimes sweet and voluntary. Of that which is imposed painfully it is written: “But if his children forsake my law and do not walk in my judgments, [Col. 1369C] I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88). For it is burdensome to be visited by the rod of any adversity or infirmity, as it is also written elsewhere: “For whom the Lord loves he corrects; moreover, he scourges 522 every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12). Yet this very burden becomes, through patience, fruitful discipline—that is, it will not lack the fruit of repentance.

Voluntary repentance, moreover, is sometimes universal and sometimes particular. It is universal when, confessing our sins, we are once baptized into the death of Christ Jesus (Gal. 3). It is particular when each of us puts to death his members that are upon the earth, as the Apostle says (Col. 3). Therefore the exalted Lord saw a wakeful rod [Col. 1369D] for the devout and faithful: wakeful, I say, that is, hastening and stirring them up to every good work. But he saw “a kindled pot” when, for example, he said through John concerning the impenitent: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3). Likewise he testifies that he himself will say: “Depart, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER VI

How, in the third place, recalling Jerusalem’s sins in order to stir her to repentance, he finally says, “Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth; make for yourself the mourning of an only-begotten son”; and how this resembles the Lord, who, after he had been unable by many means to turn Jerusalem to repentance, finally “wept over her,” announcing the evils that were to come upon her.

(CHAP. 2.) In the third place it is said: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying: Thus says the Lord: I have remembered you, taking pity on your youth and on the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown.” This, I say, and the rest that follows everywhere resound with the meaning of the Gospel of the same Lord our Lord, from the time when John had already been handed over and he himself entered upon the public work of preaching. See how strongly this discourse supports the truth of the Gospel, for which the Apostle contending says: “For there is no respect of persons with God. For as many as [Col. 1370B] sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and as many as sinned in the law will be judged through the law” (Rom. 2). Again: “For there is no distinction”—understand, of Jew and Greek—“for all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely through his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 3).

“Israel,” he says, “is holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his produce.” “The firstfruits of his produce,” he says. This is true with respect to the portion who believe or act well. For “glory and honour and peace [belong] to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 2). But see what follows afterwards: “The children of Memphis and Tahpanhes have violated you even to the crown of your head.” And then: “From of old you broke my yoke; you burst my bonds and said: ‘I will not serve.’ For upon every high hill and under every leafy tree you lay down as a harlot. How can you say, ‘I am not defiled; I have not gone after the Baals’? Look at your ways in the valleys; know what you have done.” And after some things (CHAP. 3): “But you have committed fornication with many lovers; nevertheless return to me, says the Lord, and I will receive you. Lift up your eyes straight ahead and see where you have not prostituted yourself. You sat in the roads waiting for them, like a robber in the wilderness, and you defiled the land with your fornications and your wickednesses. You have acquired the brow of a harlot; you refused to be ashamed. Therefore, at least from now on, call upon me: ‘My Father, guide of my virginity.’”

In this manner almost the whole [Col. 1370D] prophetic discourse continues: recalling dreadful sins, summoning to repentance, and finally ending in mourning and lamentation when it says (CHAP. 6): “Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and sprinkle yourself with ashes. Make for yourself the mourning of an only-begotten son, a bitter lamentation, for suddenly the destroyer will come upon you,” etc. Thus the whole preaching of the Lord likewise rebukes Jerusalem for sins and calls her to repentance: “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of God is at hand” (Matt. 4); and finally he laments her ruin, being moved by compassion for her impenitence. For, “seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: ‘For if you also had known, indeed in this your day, the things that make for your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and your enemies will cast up a rampart [Col. 1371A] around you, surround you and hem you in on every side, and dash you and your children within you to the ground’” (Luke 19), etc.

Therefore this prophetic discourse greatly supports the truth of the Gospel against Jewish boasting, when Jews puff themselves up against him preaching repentance, or against his apostles, who would have no distinction made between Jew and Greek, since all have sinned and therefore all lack the glory of God (Rom. 3); and neither can be saved or justified otherwise than through the grace of God, through faith in Jesus Christ. For, along with original sin, in which all sinned in Adam (Rom. 5), behold, the Jews also have many actual sins, and exceedingly grave ones.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 1371B]

How, in the fourth place, standing in the gate of the house of the Lord, he says among other things, “This house has become a den of robbers”; and how this refers to the fact that the Lord, entering the temple, began to cast out, saying to them the words from Isaiah, “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” and adding from this prophet, “But you have made it a den of robbers.”

(CHAP. 7.) After he ended the preceding discourse in mourning, this word of the Lord now follows in the fourth place: “Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord and preach this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah, who enter through these gates to worship the Lord,” etc. Thus, indeed, the Lord Jesus, after—as has already been said—he saw the city and wept over it, stood “in the gate of the house of the Lord” and preached this word, saying: “Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is.’” And then: “And behold, you trust in lying words, which will not profit you.” And soon after: “Behold, this house in which my name is invoked has become a den of robbers in your eyes. I, I myself, have seen it, says the Lord. Go to my place at Shiloh, where my name dwelt from the beginning, and see what I did to them.”

“I will do,” he says, “to this house in which you place your trust as I did to Shiloh, and I will cast you away from my face.” How did our Lord say these things? How did he show that in this passage of the prophet he was prefigured, and that the prophecy concerned his own cause? Namely, after he wept over the city, [Col. 1371D] immediately entering the temple he began to cast out those selling and buying in it, saying to them: “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer.’ But you have made it a den of robbers.” “And he was teaching daily in the temple” (Mark 11; Matt. 21; Luke 19).

Then, indeed, he stood with great and marvellous steadfastness in the gate of the house of the Lord; and by a great and terrible act he forbade them to trust in lying words, saying, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord it is,” casting them away from his face along with their burnt offerings, which he had never desired. As he testifies in this same prophet, saying: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices 523 [Col. 1372A] and eat the flesh; for I did not speak with your fathers, nor command them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this word I commanded them, saying: Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people. And walk in every way that I command you, that it may be well with you,” etc.

He signified this very thing by his action: namely, that he had cast away both them and their sacrifices from his face, when, making a whip of cords, he drove sellers and buyers and all the avarice of the priests out of the temple. Certainly, what he said while driving them out—“My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations, but you have made it a den of robbers”—was testimony taken partly from this prophet and partly from Isaiah. For in Isaiah it is written: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, says the Lord God” (Isa. 65). But in this prophet: “Therefore this house, in which my name is invoked, is a den of robbers.”

The continuation of this word or discourse most especially declares in a tearful denunciation that casting-away of them which was signified by the whip already mentioned: that casting-away, I say, by which, handed over to the swords of the Romans and suffering the irrecoverable destruction of city and temple, they were afterwards able to say (CHAP. 8): “Why do we sit still? Gather together, and let us enter the fortified city and be silent there, because the Lord our God has made us silent and has given us gall-water to drink.”

## CHAPTER VIII

How, in the fifth place, teaching by the word of the Lord, “Hear [Col. 1372C] the words of this covenant,” etc., he goes on to convict them of having made void the Lord’s covenant, so that we may know how reasonable it is that the Church of Christ despises whatever the Jews sacrifice.

(CHAP. 11.) The Jews, cast away and captive, scattered and dispersed, and the bloodthirsty priests of the Jews, still persist; they persist contentiously, adding their burnt offerings to their sacrifices and, as it were, eating flesh, saying: Why not today as yesterday and the day before? Why should we not at this time offer burnt offerings as of old? Is not this the covenant which God made with our fathers? Why should God be changeable and make his covenant void?

Against the contention of such sacrificers, behold: in the fifth place the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah and speaks in sequence concerning that covenant; and here the righteous and blameless Lord God clears and justifies himself of fault. “Hear,” he says, “the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Cursed is the man who does not hear the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace.” And then: “Cry aloud all these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this covenant and do them; for, protesting, I have protested to your fathers, from the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt even to this day.” And soon after: “A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers, who refused [Col. 1373A] to hear my words. They too have gone after foreign gods, to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have made void my covenant with their fathers,” etc.

Without doubt, the words of the covenant which God made with their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and with Moses, were promises of the blessed seed which is Christ—God’s promises, I say—and the corresponding faith of those same fathers, by which they were justified; and, together with that faith, the works also of the Ten Commandments, written by God’s finger through Moses on tablets of stone. But burnt offerings and sacrifices were not words of the covenant, as we have read a little above that God affirmed; rather, they were applied as certain keys and bonds for the more diligent keeping of that same covenant: not commanded, but permitted; not sought, but for a time admitted.

Yet they made void the covenant already mentioned—the covenant of faith and good works—by going after foreign gods and committing many crimes in the house of God, as the continuation of the present word or prophecy shows; and, after all else, what is worst of all, they killed Christ, in whom the whole covenant stood, and by faith in whose coming the fathers were justified. Why then do they now add sacrifices to burnt offerings and eat flesh? Why do they divide so wickedly? Why have they stolen away the better part of the covenant, that is, faith and all righteousness, while they thrust upon an unwilling—indeed rejecting—God the more contemptible part, that is, the flesh of bulls and the foul blood of goats? Have they not made void everything they offer? Are not their sacrifices the sacrifices [Col. 1373C] of Cain, who, because he divided wickedly, was the reason God did not look upon his gifts? (Gen. 4.)

For in this same chapter of this prophet our Abel’s blood—that is, Christ’s blood, whom they killed—cries out against them. In killing him, as has already been said, they most especially made the entire covenant void. “But you, O Lord, showed me, and I knew; you showed me their designs. And I was like a gentle lamb carried to the sacrifice, and I did not know that they had devised schemes against me, saying: ‘Let us put wood into his bread, and let us cut him off from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more.’ But you, O Lord Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts, let me see your vengeance upon them; for to you I have revealed my cause.”

Therefore let every mouth of the ungodly be stopped, because God is righteous but they are unrighteous; and God justly rejects their burnt offerings, by which they falsely suppose that he established the covenant, because they most unjustly rejected faith and righteousness—by which the covenant was established—through many crimes and finally through bloodstained hands raised against Christ.

## CHAPTER IX

How the sixth word of the Lord, concerning the words of drought, is rightly understood as referring to the fact that neither prophetic grace nor any visitation of the Holy Spirit remains for them, so that when they come to draw the waters of the Scriptures, they carry back empty vessels.

Since the covenant has thus been made void, prophecy is no longer given to the Jews, nor any spiritual grace whatsoever; no knowledge, no wisdom, nor any true understanding is found in their leaders, rulers, teachers, or priests. This is the true, truly great, and exceedingly ruinous drought which the Lord threatens against that same Judah in Isaiah: “And I will command the clouds,” he says, “not to rain rain upon her” (Isa. 5). Rightly, therefore, in this sixth place follows the word of the Lord which came to him concerning the words of drought. (CHAP. 14.) “Judah mourned and her gates fell; they were darkened upon the earth, and the cry of Jerusalem went up. The great sent their little ones for water; they came to draw, and did not find water; they carried back their vessels empty. They were confounded and afflicted, and covered 524 [Col. 1374B] their heads because of the devastation of the land, because rain did not come upon the land.”

Behold, we see Judah’s devastation; we see her desolation, because upon her there has not come the rain of knowledge or wisdom, which, following faith in its entirety, migrated to the Church of the nations, according to the Psalmist’s words: “You will set apart a voluntary rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. 67). And we see that the little ones come to draw water from their most obscure old men, do not find it, and carry back empty the vessels of their souls. But does Judah mourn for this? Does Jerusalem’s cry rise for this reason, as it rose to the Lord when Pharaoh died, and he sent them his clouds, Moses and Aaron? (Exod. 5.) Certainly not now. They do mourn, indeed, but not knowingly; they cry out, indeed, but their cry is brutish and without understanding. For they do not mourn that which is truly the cause of drought, their own iniquity; nor do they cry out in such a way as to say, after the example of their fathers: “Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord our God” (ibid.).

Therefore their cry does rise, but not to the Lord. For because it is not a rational cry, as this prophet himself laments in one place, “He has set a cloud before him, so that prayer may not pass through” (Lam. 3). It should indeed be believed that in those days a physical drought befell the Jews; but, just as other evils are signs of greater evils, so that drought was a portent of a worse drought. “The farmers were confounded and covered their heads. For the doe also gave birth in the field and abandoned [her young], because there was no grass; and the wild asses stood upon the rocks, [Col. 1374D] drew in the wind like dragons, and their eyes failed because there was no grass.”

Why were the farmers “confounded,” unless because they killed the lord and heir of the vineyard entrusted to them? What or what kind of “doe abandoned in the field that which she bore because there was no grass,” unless it is the faithful Church of the patriarchs, which indeed bore according to the flesh but abandoned this people because there is no knowledge? We see these things, and what follows: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks, drew in the wind like dragons, and their eyes failed because there was no grass.” Wild asses and the young of wild asses are the Jews today; for another Scripture also speaks mystically concerning that people: “The vain man is lifted up in pride and thinks himself born free like a colt of a wild ass” (Job 11).

These wild asses stand upon the rocks [Col. 1375A] of their pride and prefer to perish from thirst and hunger rather than come with a tameable neck to Christ’s mangers, rather than come in humility of spirit to the sheepfolds of Christ. They draw in “wind like dragons”: for, hot like dragons and burning excessively with the flame of envy, just as dragons in their thirst draw in wind to cool the heat of their nature, so these men, perishing of true thirst, draw in empty fables and windy genealogies in place of the true waters of knowledge, to console their want. “Their eyes failed because there was no grass”: that is, “their wickedness blinded them, because they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 2).

The prophet then prays for this people, now perishing of thirst, that it may at some time receive saving rain from heaven and that a remnant from it may be saved. “If,” he says, [Col. 1375B] “our iniquities contend against us, O Lord, deliver us. We beg you, act for the sake of your name, for our apostasies are many.” And after some things: “Let my eyes shed tears by day and by night; let them not be silent,” etc. The cause of that drought was that he shed innocent blood exceedingly abundantly, until Jerusalem was filled to the brim, apart from his sins by which he caused Judah to sin, so as to do evil before the Lord. For he says shortly afterward (CHAP. 15): “And I will give them over to rage [or: burning] among all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh, son of Hezekiah king of Judah, for all that he did in Jerusalem.”

But the cause of this drought, by which Judah now withers, is the universal blood that has been poured out upon the earth from the foundation of the world, and above all the blood of the Lord himself, from whom all saving water proceeds (Luke 11). Therefore shortly afterward he says (CHAP. 17): “O Lord, all who forsake you shall be confounded; those who depart from you shall be written in the earth, because they have forsaken the fountain of living waters, the Lord.” For because they have forsaken him—indeed, have also killed him—they are confounded; they are consumed by a double hunger, dried up by a double thirst, and destroyed by a double destruction of body and soul, according to the imprecation that follows: “Let those who persecute me be confounded, but let me not be confounded. Let them be terrified, but let me not be terrified. Bring upon them a day of affliction, and crush them with a double destruction.”

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 1375D]

How, in the seventh place, by the potter’s making a work upon the wheel, and the vessel which he made from clay with his hands being ruined, and his turning and making another vessel as pleased him to make, the dispersion of the rebellious Jews and the gathering of the nations are signified; and how in all these things God’s judgment is beyond reproach.

(CHAP. 18.) The judgments of God are just, incomprehensible, and his ways unsearchable; therefore it is fitting that a human being should not answer back to God but humbly restrain his mouth. Accordingly, the seventh word of the Lord which now follows is this: “Arise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear my words. And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the wheel. And the vessel which he was making from clay with his hands was ruined. And he turned and made that [Col. 1376A] vessel another, as it pleased him in his sight to make. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘Shall I not be able to do to you, house of Israel, as this potter does?’ says the Lord. ‘Behold, as clay is in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.’”

This is a great lesson in reverence, and a great and fitting instrument for silence and restraint of the tongue. God is our maker; but we are clay. We all, I say, Jews as well as nations, are one lump, one clay. Therefore let us not boldly investigate God’s judgments; let us not find fault with the fingers of our potter. The Apostle—the vessel of election and the pleasing work of the eternal potter—urges this upon us with vehement rebuke, and sends us here, that with this prophet we may behold the present example of divine power.

For when he had groaned over the rejection of his Israelite brethren, he said: “What then shall we say? Is there unrighteousness with God? By no means! For he says to Moses: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy’” (Rom. 9). And shortly after: “Why then is there still complaint? For who resists his will? O man, who are you to answer back to God? Can the thing formed say to him who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” (ibid.)

Certainly, in order to say these things, he too had gone down in humble mind to the potter’s house in this prophet, and had seen that the house of Israel was clay just as all the mire of the nations was clay; and that God, the potter of all, not from anything due but from grace alone, took Abraham while he was Chaldean clay and from him and from the clayey lump of his seed made such vessels of mercy, vessels of honour and grace, as he willed. What more did he owe him than to the whole 525 clay [Col. 1376C] of Adam’s race? This wise and humble man—and therefore truly wise because humble—had seen and humbly understood that rebellious clay had been ruined in the potter’s hand, not because of the potter’s incompetence but because of incomprehensible justice.

Therefore he groaned with devout feeling: “I speak the truth, I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness to me in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren” (Rom. 9), etc. But he consoled his same sorrow with discerning and prudent hope, saying shortly afterward: “But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved’” (ibid.). Again: “For blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter; and so all Israel would be saved” (Rom. 11).

Indeed, he had also seen this in this prophet: because “the potter turned and made that vessel another, as it pleased him in his sight to make,” and said: “Shall I not be able to do to you, house of Israel, as this potter does?” Moreover, we who are from the nations and believe in Christ are another vessel from the same clay. For after the same Apostle said, “But if God, willing to make known [Col. 1377A] his power, endured in much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, so that he might show the riches of his goodness upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9), he immediately added: “Whom he also called, not only from the Jews but also from the nations, as he says in Hosea: ‘I will call that which was not my people, my people; and her that had not obtained mercy, one who has obtained mercy; and it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” it shall be said to them, “Sons of the living God”’” (ibid.).

But, to return to contemplating the potter’s likeness, let us now say this: when that potter knew our fashioning by taking up our dust, then “he was making a work from clay with his hands upon the wheel,” applying his fingers—that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit—so that, now perfected in the fullness of time, the vessels might receive treasures [Col. 1377B] of mercy and honour. But unhappy clay dared to blaspheme the fingers of its potter, saying: “He has a demon” (John 8); saying: “By Beelzebub, prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Luke 12).

What then? Surely, most justly, when the potter withdrew his fingers outwardly and struck with his whole hand, “the vessel was ruined”: ruined with mighty destruction, the temple of the lost people also being demolished and the city overthrown. The prophet, allowing this destruction, says shortly afterward: “Therefore give their children over to disgrace, and hand them over to the sword. Let their wives become childless and widows, and let their husbands be killed by death. Let their young men be pierced by the sword in battle. Let a cry be heard from their houses. For you will suddenly bring a robber upon them, because they dug a pit to catch me and hid snares for my feet. But you, O Lord, know all their counsel against me unto death: do not be merciful to their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before your face. Let them fall before you; in the time of your wrath, deal with them.”

## CHAPTER XI

How, amid the evils which were announced in reply to the king’s inquiry while the city was under siege, the prophecy is confirmed that the oath of the Lord saying to David, “His seed shall remain for ever,” will not be made void, when meanwhile he says: “Behold, days shall come, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch.”

(CAP. XXI.) We have distinguished only the seven principal divisions of this prophet [Col. 1377D], and have perceived that, as it were in a shadow cast far in advance, the body of evangelical truth was prefigured. What follows pertains especially to the condition of that time, to that siege of the city; and in the first discourse it is written thus: “King Zedekiah says, ‘Inquire of the Lord for us, because Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon is fighting against us,’” etc. A favourable answer was indeed given to me, one capable of helping that time or that situation; yet, nonetheless, amid those evils, future goods also were foretold here and there.

For when, among other things, He had said against Zedekiah (CAP. XXII): “Write this man down as childless, a man who shall not prosper in his days; for there shall not be of his seed a man who [Col. 1378A] sits upon the throne of David and has authority any longer in Judah”—it was as though someone were asking: What then will become of the Lord’s oath spoken to David: “Once I have sworn by my holy one: Shall I lie to David? His seed shall remain for ever, and his throne as the sun before me, as the moon perfect for ever, and as a faithful witness in heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII)? He then added these words concerning the future (CAP. XXIII): “Behold, days shall come, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. In those days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell securely; and this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness.”

Those days have come, and behold, they are already here. For the Lord God has already raised David’s “righteous [Col. 1378B] Branch” from the dead; and behold, he reigns, crowned with glory and honour, and is “a king and wise,” so that his folly is wiser than human beings. He has performed, and will yet perform, “judgment and justice in the earth.” For he carried out the judgment of the world through his passion, casting out the prince of this world (John XII); he will carry out judgment on the last day, coming with the clouds of heaven in great power (Matt. XXIV). He performed the justice of faith by justifying everyone who is of faith, granting forgiveness of sins; he will perform justice by rendering to each according to his works (Rom. II).

Having said these things, he subsequently anticipated in his own sufferings the sufferings of the Righteous One. As has already been said above, he served as a type of him who, having conquered death by dying, and after the temple had been destroyed and the city exterminated, was to teach the nations. This man likewise, surviving the temple and city and not dead, although he suffered much, wove prophecy for foreign nations. But since we have neither the capacity nor the intention to pursue everything, passing over the broad field of his history and the great forest of his prophecy, let us turn to the section on his Lamentations.

526 CHAPTER XII. On the Lamentations: why their individual sentences are marked by individual letters of the alphabet; and why the alphabetic order itself is fourfold, because the prophet had a fourfold cause for lamenting.

We judge the Lamentations of this holy and wise prophet to be true knowledge, and to concern matters in whose understanding we are children or infants. For we know how to weep only for temporal misery and the loss of temporal things; and if temporal pleasantness smiles upon us, we forget the captivity in which we were born. This is beautifully signified to us by the fact that each little sentence of these Lamentations is marked with one letter of the alphabet. What else is suggested to us by this than that we should judge ourselves little ones in humble consciousness, so that we may be deemed worthy to be enlightened by the exposition of these sayings? For it is written: “The unfolding of your words gives light and gives understanding to little ones” (Ps. CXVIII).

Therefore, let us be arranged, like children learning their ABCs, according to this alphabet distinguished in fourfold order, not doubting that beneath these words is contained [Col. 1379A] the knowledge hidden from the wise and prudent (Matt. XI), so that they do not know even the first elements. For the mourning of which it was truly said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V), is the first doorway of understanding. May David open it for us who are shut out, and we shall see that this man had a fourfold serious cause or subject for lamentation.

The first cause was the universal captivity of the human race, by which all the children of God were cast out and scattered, sold freely into bondage in their first parents according to the flesh (Isa. LII), and subjected to condemnation. The second cause was the Babylonian captivity of God’s people, which he had seen with his own eyes, and for which it would have been harsh and unjust not to lament—especially when the Church of God was deprived of the temple and altar of the Lord’s name and compelled to venerate the monstrous gods of barbarians. The third cause for this holy man was the humility of his own conscience: the more righteous he was, the more truly, beyond the common captivity of all God’s children, he recognized the exile of his own condition. The fourth cause was that most dreadful captivity into which, as has now occurred, he foresaw that the Jews would fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations. For he could not foresee that captivity without compassionate feeling—indeed, the Lord himself, foreseeing that miserable captivity, wept over it with true tears (Luke XIX). With these matters set forth, we must now proceed to the subject.

CHAPTER XIII. In what sense that one city of the elect is rightly called full of people, mistress of nations, and ruler of provinces; and why or how she sat alone or was made tributary.

(LAM., CHAP. I.) ALEPH, that is, teaching. “How does the city sit alone, once full of people? The mistress of nations has become like a widow; the ruler of provinces has been made tributary.” Aleph is interpreted “teaching,” and, as you see, it is the first element among the Hebrews. What, then, is contained beneath it? Understand attentively, in accordance with that first and universal captivity which we mentioned above; and then at last be confident that you have grasped the first foundation of heavenly teaching.

What is “the city full of people, mistress of nations, ruler of provinces”? Surely it is that holy city Jerusalem, the mother of us all (Gal. IV), whose citizens, fellow-countrymen, or burgesses are all of us who believe. Before the foundation of the world this city was already full of people in God’s foreknowledge or predestination: those who are or will be from his holy, elect people were numbered with him. She is “mistress of nations and ruler of provinces,” because, as human nature surpasses beasts by the dignity of reason, so she surpasses nations and provinces by the dignity of faith and by knowledge or love of her Creator.

How did it happen that she sat “alone,” became “like a widow,” and paid tribute? Surely through transgression—namely, through the sin of one human being, the first human being. For in him [Col. 1380A] the whole multitude of his descendants sinned and underwent condemnation. Hence it happened that she sat “alone,” sat as a “widow”: the holy city, the Church made holy by faith, did not possess God as her husband; cast out of paradise, she lived as an exile and stranger in this world, dying and paying penal tribute to an evil master—that is, sin. This is truly the beginning of teaching: that we should believe and confess that we all sinned in Adam, so that consequently we may be justified through Christ in whom we believe (Rom. III).

CHAPTER XIV. In what night she wept while weeping, and upon what cheeks her tears were.

[Col. 1380B] BETH, that is, house. “Weeping, she wept in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks. There is none to comfort her among all her beloved ones; all her friends have despised her and have become her enemies.” Truly, “weeping, she wept in the night,” and we have heard her weeping, if we have not slept in that same night. Thus, for example, holy Job says in her person: “Let the day perish in which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A human being has been conceived.’ Let a dark tempest possess that night; let it not be counted among the days of the year nor numbered among the months. Let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise” (Job III).

That night is the devil, prince of darkness: by pretence and a lying transformation he is day, but in truth night. In that night the human being was wickedly born and became the child of that night, by yielding to its evil counsels and being cast out from the hidden rest of paradise, as from a womb, into this misery of mortality. In that night—that is, in consideration of that night—that mistress of nations, that ruler of provinces, “weeping, wept.” But do all who were or are from that holy city know how to weep this weeping? Certainly not. Rather, this weeping belongs to few; this weeping belongs to the perfect.

Therefore, after saying, “weeping, she wept in the night,” he at once adds, “and her tears are upon her cheeks.” The cheeks of this mistress were outstanding men—namely, the patriarchs and prophets. Like cheeks always exposed on the face, and not covered with cloths as most bodily members are, they too, because of the excellence of grace bestowed upon them, deserved not to be hidden in God’s holy Church. On these cheeks of the mistress are her tears: for these men wept, confessing that they were strangers and sojourners upon the earth (Heb. XI). And we see what tears of theirs we should imitate, so that we may judge laughter to be error and say to joy, “Why are you deceived in vain?”

As she thus weeps, “there is,” he says, “none to comfort her among all her beloved ones”; indeed, “all her friends despised her and became her enemies.” For those who now laugh, lovers of the world, hate such weeping. Though they may be beloved ones or friends—that is, kinsfolk or relatives—they separate themselves from her and flee far away because their thoughts are contrary.

CHAPTER XV. That the whole body of the elect is Judah, and into what affliction or servitude it fell when it migrated.

[Col. 1381A] GIMEL, that is, fullness. “Judah migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude; she dwelt among the nations and found no rest. All her persecutors overtook her in narrow straits.” Judah is interpreted “confession,” a name by which that city is rightly signified whose entire work or office is confession. Hence, when the Psalmist has said, “For there the tribes ascended, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel,” he immediately adds, as though you asked why they ascended there or what they were to do there, “to confess the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI).

To where, then, or from where did she “migrate”? From light to darkness, from rest to labour, from kingdom to captivity, from father to enemy, from life to death. Why? “Because of affliction and the multitude of servitude.” A remarkable thing! Did she desire affliction and a multitude of servitude, and therefore migrate? Certainly not; rather, she thought she was acquiring self-sufficiency and freedom for herself. But whatever it was that she sought in this fashion and found apart from God is affliction and a multitude of servitude. Therefore the Lord himself says to all: “Come to me, all who labour and are burdened” (Matt. XII). And holy Job says: “Why have you set me as your opponent, so that I have become burdensome to myself?” (Job VII).

What remarkable and pitiable deception of one migrating: while she migrates in hope of the divinity promised by the deceitful serpent, she finds nothing but [Col. 1381C] “affliction and a multitude of servitude”—the affliction, namely, of mortality, by which she is burdensome to herself, and the multitude of slavery to sin. For she serves as many masters as she has vices. Thus she “migrated” from a great good to a great evil, and “dwelt among the nations and found no rest.” Among her other evils, this worst evil was added: that she “dwelt among the nations,” like that righteous man who, dwelling among the Sodomites, surely found no rest, as it is written of him: “And he delivered righteous Lot, oppressed by the lawless and licentious conduct of the wicked; for that righteous man, dwelling among them, tortured his righteous soul day by day by seeing and hearing their wicked deeds” (II Pet. II).

Listen further: “Her persecutors overtook her in narrow straits.” It was too little that, dwelling among the nations, she should be tormented by seeing wicked deeds, unless she were also compelled by persecutions to consent to evils. Hence the Psalmist says with groaning: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged! I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has been a long time a sojourner. With those who hate peace I was peaceable; when I spoke to them, they attacked me without cause” (Ps. CXIX).

CHAPTER XVI. What roads mourn because there are none who come to the feast; what that feast is; what the destruction of the gates is; and whence come the groaning of the priests and the squalor of the virgins.

DELETH, that is, tablets. “The ways of Zion mourn because there are none who come to the solemn feast. All her gates are destroyed; her priests groan; her virgins are squalid; and she herself is oppressed with bitterness.” There is one principal way of Zion, Christ, who says, “I am the way” (John XIV); he is likewise the one principal gate and the one supreme priest of Zion. Yet everyone who, by his example, whether through the word of preaching or the example of a good work, offers others guidance toward life, is a way of Zion and one of her gates and priests.

Why do these ways mourn, these gates stand destroyed, and these priests groan? “Because,” he says, “there are none who come to the solemn feast.” This mourning or groaning is one of great charity: to grieve because there are none—or rather, very few—who come to the feast of truth [Col. 1382B] and life, to which they desire to lead many, gladly suffering their own destruction if only many might come to that feast through the occasion of their destruction. Such persons say in the Psalm: “You gave us up like sheep for food and scattered us among the nations. You sold your people without a price, and there was no multitude in exchange for them” (Ps. XLIII). This is said by comparison with someone who sells his own property and receives no price, or only a small price, from it. “You sold,” they say—that is, you allowed your people to be killed—“without a price”; and if you received some in return for them, “there was no multitude in exchange for them”: compared with those killed, you gained not many, because perhaps where a thousand were slain, scarcely two or three were converted.

For this reason the aforesaid ways or gates of Zion mourn, her priests groan, her virgins are squalid—that is, those living a celibate life are contemptible to this world—and “she herself” is therefore “oppressed with bitterness.” Yet this very bitterness bears the fruit of eternal sweetness.

Here the four letters placed before these words must now be joined together. For they complete a full meaning through their interpretations: Aleph is “teaching,” beth “house,” gimel “fullness,” and deleth “tablets.” Now the house of God is the Church, and the sacred law was inscribed upon tablets. Thus the meaning is: The teaching of God’s Church is the fullness of the law, namely charity; and this lamentation is the lamentation of that perfect charity.

CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 1382D] How enemies became chief and adversaries were enriched, and how her little ones were led into captivity.

HE, that is, “this.” “Her enemies have become chief; her adversaries have been enriched, because the Lord has spoken against her because of the multitude of her iniquities. Her little ones have been led into captivity before the face of the oppressor.” This too adds to the heap of miseries: those who are enemies or adversaries of the Church rule in this world, are heads of peoples, become wealthy and rich, and thus are more powerful for persecution and stronger for killing. Thus Cain is higher in this world than Abel; Esau richer than Jacob. So too with almost all others until the end of the age.

This is so “because the Lord has spoken against her because of the multitude [Col. 1383A] of her iniquities,” so that, while Cain kills and Esau persecutes, she may receive in this present age what she deserves and not be punished with them in the future. But more grievous, and almost beyond consolation, is the fact that it sometimes happens that her little ones are led “into captivity before the face of tribulation”: that is, her weak and imperfect children are corrupted by examples, deceived by persuasions, terrified by threats, and thus yield as prey to adversaries.

CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning prelates, and how or when rams without pasture go away “without strength before the face of the pursuer.”

VAU, that is, “and.” “All her splendour has gone forth from the daughter of Zion. Her princes have become like rams finding no pasture, and have gone away without strength before the face of the pursuer.” These words are rightly understood as referring to the weaker part of Zion. For Zion which is true and truly strong has all splendour within and all glory within, according to the saying: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. XLIV). But of that Zion which glories in the eyes of all for the sake of outward religious display, you may rightly say that “all her splendour has gone forth from the daughter of Zion.”

Likewise, you may rightly say that “her princes have become like rams finding no pasture and have gone away without strength before the face of the pursuer,” whenever prelates live as though they were ignorant of the commandments, as though they had not read the Scriptures, surrendering—with no strength of soul—to sins and to the vices that drive them onward.

CHAPTER XIX. [Col. 1383C] That it is truly lamentable that we do not remember our sojourning or pilgrimage except when evils oppress us.

ZAI, that is, “this.” “Jerusalem remembered the days of her affliction and her transgression, all her desirable things which she had had from ancient days, when her people fell into the hand of the enemy and there was no helper. Her enemies saw her and mocked her sabbaths.” The days of Jerusalem’s affliction are the days of this present life. For this life is affliction, pilgrimage, and captivity. Her desirable things, “which she had had from ancient days,” are the sayings or judgments of the Lord which she received in ancient days, “more desirable than much gold and precious stone, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XVIII).

Transgression immediately accompanied the reception of these desirable things. For they made a calf at Horeb while the tablets were still being written on Mount Sinai (Exod. XXXII; Deut. IV), and from that time they did not cease to transgress. Jerusalem remembered this affliction of hers, as we have said, and this transgression, and these desirable things of hers. But when did she remember? “When her people fell into the hand of the enemy and there was no helper,” when enemies had leisure to see her, insult her religion, and mock her Sabbaths.

This is truly lamentable: she could not otherwise remember her own sojourning and pilgrimage unless she was oppressed by evils, trampled by enemies, and delivered into the hands of the nations. “I would have preferred,” he says, “that she should remember of her own accord; I would have preferred that she should abound even in prosperity and never be deceived by prosperity; that she should use transitory things and never forget eternal things.”

CHAPTER XX. That, when the sin of pride has gone before, the soul becomes unstable and falls from vice into vice; and the meaning of these four elements: HE, VAU, ZAI, HETH.

HETH, that is, life. “Jerusalem committed sin; therefore she has become unstable. All who glorified her have despised her, because they saw her disgrace. But she herself, groaning, turned backward.” “Therefore,” he says, “she has become unstable [Col. 1384B] and falls from vice into vice, because she ‘committed sin.’” Let her not therefore accuse God because of her instability. For she did not “commit sin” because God created her with an unstable nature; rather, she “became unstable” because she “committed sin.”

What sin? The sin of pride, which also made demons out of angels. Hence, after the Psalmist said, “Let not the foot of pride come against me,” he immediately added: “There those who work iniquity have fallen; they have been cast out and could not stand” (Ps. XXXV). The whole of Jerusalem first committed this sin in Adam; hence she became so unstable, both through vanity of mind and mortality of body, that she could never be restored except through Christ’s grace alone.

Then also each individual soul which has not deserved to stand manfully, having fallen from its former condition, so that those who previously glorified it now, by a reversal, despise it when they see its disgrace—such a soul, I say, groaning and turned backward, should look at itself and will find that a hidden sin of pride went before and that because of it she became unstable and fell from vice into vice.

Again let us join the four letters: he, vau, zai, heth. He means “this,” vau and zai mean “and this,” and heth means “life.” The meaning is: “This and this are life.” That is, these things and whatever are of this sort, when committed to meditation and memory, lead toward life.

CHAPTER XXI. That it is truly lamentable to have filth upon one’s feet.

THET, that is, good. “Her filth is upon [Col. 1384D] her feet, and she did not remember her end. She has been brought down exceedingly, having no comforter. See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile.” “Her filth,” he says, “is upon her feet.” Whose? The renowned mistress of nations and ruler of provinces, who ought to have remembered her end, so as not to touch filthy earth with her feet or seek earthly things with the desire of greed, but, though exiled here in body, to dwell in heaven in mind.

She did not do so; she did not thus remember her end. Rather, she “has been brought down” exceedingly by loving the earth and consigning the height of heaven to forgetfulness, “having no comforter”—indeed, neither seeking nor keeping before her eyes her husband, who is in heaven, as comforter, while she seeks vain consolation upon earth. Let her at least now, when warned as “her people fall into the hand of the enemy,” say—let her, the transgressor, at least now, returning to her heart, say: “See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile.”

529 CHAPTER XXII. What meaning is contained under the interpretation of these elements, THET and JOD; and that confession is a good beginning of righteousness.

JOD, that is, beginning. “The enemy stretched out his hand to all her desirable things, because she saw nations entering her sanctuary, concerning whom you had commanded that they should not enter your assembly.” Therefore let her confess and truly say, “See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile,” because the enemy, the devil, “stretched out his hand” and defiled “all her desirable things”; and because she saw “nations”—that is, all the ranks of vices—“entering the sanctuary” of her own breast, concerning whom, O God, you commanded that they should not enter “your assembly.”

Let us join these two elements, theth and jod. Theth means “good,” jod “beginning.” The meaning is: This confession is a good beginning when it says, “See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile,” for such reasons; “for the righteous person is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. XVIII).

CHAPTER XXIII. How the earlier saints gave all their precious things for food to refresh the soul: that is, how they obtained not yet the reality but the hope of the promise which they had heard.

CAPH, that is, hand. “All her people groan [Col. 1385C] and seek bread; they gave all their precious things for food, to refresh the soul. See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile.” “All her people,” I say, in the better part constituted by the perfect, are “groaning and seeking bread.” For all the people, Lord, have reason of this kind to groan and need bread; nevertheless, not all understand their hunger, and not all know how to seek their bread.

What bread, except that which the first parent lost because of the forbidden fruit? This mistress did not possess the true bread (John VI), which is the food of angels; and therefore her people were wasting away from hunger. At last, as “all groaning and seeking” this bread, they waited hungry in the underworld for this bread to descend from heaven, to give life to the world, restore the vision of God, and break down the wall of enmity.

Meanwhile, before this living bread descended, “they gave all their precious things to refresh the soul.” For the holy fathers and great patriarchs possessed precious faith and precious love of God; they gave these for the food of hope, by which to refresh their souls, but they did not restore or satisfy them. For a long time they sustained their souls by the blessed hope of the promise which they had heard; and they were blessed because, through their faith, love, and obedience, they had deserved to possess such a hope.

“See,” she says, “O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile.” In what respect “vile”? In that, for the vile food of the forbidden tree, I lost the living bread, and all my people wasted away in hunger.

CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the words, “See whether there is any sorrow,” etc.; that every sorrow occurring for any other perishable thing is vain; and what meaning the two joined elements CAPH and LAMECH have.

LAMECH, that is, heart. “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow. For he has gathered me as a vintage, as the Lord spoke in the day of his anger.” You, he says, who pass by the way, who know and confess that you are strangers and sojourners upon the earth, having no abiding city here but seeking the one to come (Heb. XIII)—“all of you attend and see whether there is [Col. 1386B] any sorrow like my sorrow,” whether there is any cause for which a person may rightly grieve outside the cause for which my sorrow exists.

Certainly every sorrow which is not mine is light and vain, because it concerns vain and perishable things; just as, conversely, every joy which is not mine is vain, because it depends upon the vanity of temporal things. For from where does my sorrow come? From this: “He has gathered me as a vintage, as the Lord spoke in the day of his anger.” That day of anger was the day of which he said to the first human beings: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. II).

They ate, and the day on which they ate was a day of anger; and that anger brought just death upon souls and just mortality upon bodies. Then the Lord said that I was dust and would return to dust. As he then spoke, so from that time he “has gathered me as a vintage” and does not cease gathering me until the end: daily cutting my clusters from the vine, daily taking away my children through death of the flesh.

When these two elements are joined—caph, “hand,” and lamech, “heart”—their combined meaning requires the hand of the heart: that is, the works of faith which are in the heart. Otherwise, what good will faith do, since without works it is dead? (Jas. II).

CHAPTER XXV. That God made the bodily condition mortal in order to humble the soul, and permits the soul itself to be afflicted by many sufferings.

MEM, that is, “from them.” “From on high he sent fire into [Col. 1386D] my bones and instructed me; he spread a net for my feet, turned me backward, and made me desolate, consumed with sorrow all day long.” “He sent fire,” he says, “into my bones, from on high,” from the throne of his judgment: a lamentable fire, not shining but consuming, drying up, devouring. This fire is the mortal condition by which vigorous youth, gradually dried out, is drawn together and wrinkled into dry old age, and at last, when all moisture has been consumed, dissolves and disperses into ashes and cinders.

Yet by this fire he instructed me, that I might learn not to be proud, know how to walk with bowed head, and understand what Adam refused to understand: namely, that I am not God, but dust. Further, that he might instruct me, “he spread a net for my feet”—that is, he gave me the law. For what is the law but a net spread for my feet? Certainly the law is not a net of sin; rather, “I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known coveting unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of coveting” (Rom. VII).

Therefore, when he gave me the law and delayed grace, he in a certain manner “spread a net for my feet,” and in this way “turned me backward.” For “when the commandment came, sin, which had been dead without the law, revived” (ibid.). But I died, and the commandment which was for life was found to be for me unto death. Thus “he made me desolate, consumed with sorrow all day long,” so that in sorrow I may say: “Wretched human being that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid.).

CHAPTER XXVI. That in doing evil a human being is the slave of sin and can be freed only through God’s grace.

[Col. 1387B] NUN, that is, eternal. “The yoke of my iniquities has kept watch; in his hand they are entwined and laid upon my neck. My strength has been weakened; the Lord gave me into a hand from which I cannot rise.” “The yoke,” he says, “of my iniquities has kept watch.” For everyone who does iniquity is the slave of iniquity (John VIII), as though sin were keeping watch lest its slave, having broken his fetter, should escape by night. The slave of sin sometimes wishes to escape, but though he wills it negligently and often sleeps very deeply, sin does not sleep.

My iniquities “are entwined in his hand,” like a net or bonds, “and laid upon my neck”—the neck of the human being, upon which pride sat, whence he gladly heard the saying: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. II). I struggle and wish to resist, but “my strength has been weakened,” because liberating grace has not yet come. “The Lord gave me into a hand from which I cannot rise”—that is, unless his grace comes and frees me.

CHAPTER XXVII. That salvation could not be in any of the fathers or patriarchs, since they too were mortal; and what the three joined elements MEM, NUN, and SAMECH signify.

SAMECH, that is, help. “The Lord has taken away all my mighty ones from my midst; he summoned against me a time to crush my chosen ones. The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah.” My mighty ones, my chosen ones, were the patriarchs: great, indeed, righteous, and holy; yet I could glory in none of them, for salvation was in none of them. He “took them away from my midst,” because they died, and none of them could rescue his own soul from the hand of the underworld.

“He summoned against me a time” to crush those “chosen ones of mine,” establishing the limits which they cannot pass beyond. And this is against me, so that I may not be permitted to glory in a human being. In this way “the Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah”—that is, for me, the daughter of his confession, who ought to be a virgin, that is, to look upon none besides my Creator. “He trod the winepress for me,” I say, in order to intoxicate me with bitterness, which is the fruit of sin.

Let the three letters already mentioned be joined: mem, “from them”; nun, “eternal”; and samech, “help.” The meaning is: “From these, eternal help.” From which “these”? Namely, from those things signified by the preceding four elements: theth, jod, caph, and lamech—that is, from the good beginning of confession and the hand of the heart, by which the works of faith are understood.

CHAPTER XXVIII. That the true ancient Church had reason to weep because the Comforter was far from her.

AIN, that is, fountain. “Therefore I weep, and my eye pours down water, because the comforter who would restore my soul is far from me. My children have become lost, because the enemy has prevailed.” “Therefore,” I say, because “the Lord sent fire into my bones from on high,” because “the yoke of my iniquities kept watch,” because “he took away all my mighty ones from my midst”; and, further, because he is far from me and has not yet come—the Comforter, Christ the Lord, who is to come and restore “my soul to his rest and freedom.” In the meantime “my children become lost,” for they descend to the underworld, “because the enemy has prevailed,” guarding his courtyard like a strong man armed (Luke XI). “Therefore I weep,” and therefore “my eye pours down the water” of tears.

CHAPTER XXIX. [Col. 1388C] That Zion could not console herself by stretching out her hands.

PHE, that is, mouth. “Zion stretched out her hands; there is none to comfort her. The Lord commanded Jacob’s enemies against him round about him. Jerusalem has become among them like one defiled by menstruation.” Zion “stretched out her hands”—that is, the works of the law and the righteousnesses of the flesh—but through those works “there is none to comfort her,” for the Lord does not justify her through them. But what then? If, with hands thus outstretched, she supposes herself justified, “the Lord commanded her enemies”—that is, her sins—“against her round about”; and her sins are far more numerous, indeed incomparably more numerous, than her thousand justifications, “as if” she were “defiled by menstruation.” Another prophet likewise bears witness when he says: “We have all become as unclean persons, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. LXIV).

CHAPTER XXX. That we provoked the mouth of the Lord to anger—namely, by defending our fault in Adam—and what the three letters AIN, PHE, and ZADI together signify.

ZADI, that is, “righteousness.” “The Lord is righteous, for I provoked his mouth to anger. Hear, I beseech you, all peoples, and behold my sorrow. My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity.” The prophet says: No, Zion does not accuse God in all these things; for “the Lord is righteous,” and his judgment is upright (Ps. 118 [119]); rather, she accuses herself, “because she provoked the mouth of the Lord” to anger—understand, in Adam, in whom she also sinned. And how did she provoke the Lord’s mouth to anger? Certainly because she defended her sin; for the defense of sin became the cause of righteous wrath. “Hear,” he says, “I beseech you, all peoples”: for this must also be proclaimed to you, so that you may hear and behold my sorrow, because “my virgins and my young men have gone into captivity”—indeed, they were even born in captivity. As for “my virgins and my young men,” that is, all who belong to me, small and great, weak and strong: this is not their place, this is not their kingdom, but a sojourning and an exile. Hear this, all you peoples, and hasten together toward the true and abiding city. The three letters joined together—ain, that is “fountain”; phe, interpreted “mouth”; zadi, that is “righteousness”—together signify this meaning: “the fountain of the mouth of righteousness.” For such lamentation and such confession are the fountain of a mouth beneath which runs the vein of righteousness, supplying truth, so that it may accuse not God but itself.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Whenever the Church appoints priests for herself, they have deceived her; this is to be understood of those who feed themselves and seek what is their own.

COPH, that is, “calling.” “I called my friends, and they deceived me. My priests and my elders perished in the city; they sought food for themselves, that they might revive their souls.” “Whom,” you ask, “did I call my friends? My priests, my elders?” Whenever I appointed priests for myself, whenever I set elders over myself, then I “called my friends” to myself, that they might behold my sorrow, console me, and alleviate my distress. But “they also deceived me”; for they were friends of the table, seeking what was their own and not seeking the salvation of my children. For how many such friends ever yielded the true fruit of friendship? Aaron himself scarcely performed his office as befitted a friend. Almost all “perished in the city,” that is, in my cause they were as though they did not exist: they fell silent, because “they sought food for themselves, that they might revive their souls”; they sought gain for themselves, and, according to the prophet, though called shepherds, they fed not the flock but themselves (Ezek. 34).

## CHAPTER XXXII. How, in him in whom we all sinned, our belly was disturbed and our heart overturned—that is, our body was made mortal; and what these two elements, COPH and RES, signify when joined.

RES, that is, “head.” “See, O Lord, that I am distressed; my belly is troubled, my heart is overturned within me, because I am full of bitterness. Outside the sword has slain; within, there is death like it.” Since “I called my friends, and they deceived me,” you, “O Lord,” who alone behold labor and sorrow, “see that I am distressed, that my belly is troubled and my heart overturned”—that is, because the whole human being has died by a twofold death. “My belly,” that is, the outward part of the human being, is mortal, and therefore already dead, because it will most certainly die. But “my heart,” that is, the inward part of the human being, has long since been dead, namely from the moment sin was committed. Thus, outwardly and inwardly, “I am full of bitterness.”

What she meant by “my belly is troubled and my heart overturned,” she almost explained by adding: “Outside the sword has slain, and within there is death like it.” For “outside,” as it were in the belly, “the sword has slain,” when by the righteous sentence of death the soul is separated from the body; but “within,” that is, in the heart, “there is death like it,” when, just as the body dies by the separation of the soul, so the soul is dead by separation from God. Let us join these two elements, coph, interpreted “calling,” and res, interpreted “head,” so that we may understand “the calling of the Head,” that is, of Christ, who is the head of the Church (Eph. 5). For because, she says, “I called my friends, and they deceived me,” she now calls upon her Head, Christ, saying, “See, O Lord, that I am distressed,” hoping that through him she will be restored both from the disturbance of the belly and the overturning of the heart—that is, that she will rise again by the resurrection both of body and soul.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How the enemies—that is, evil spirits—rejoiced in the evil of the human race; and how, in return, the Church will rejoice over them on the Day of Judgment.

SIN, that is, “teeth.” “They heard that I groan, and there is none to console me. All my enemies heard of my evil. They rejoiced, because you did it. You have brought the day of consolation, and they shall become like me.” Who are those “enemies of mine” who heard of my evil and “rejoiced”? That great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, and his angels, “heard that I groan,” and mockingly say, “There is none to console her.” These “enemies of mine,” I say, “heard of my evil,” and, conducting a triumph as for victory, “rejoiced,” driving before the chariot of their pride, in insult, the whole captivity which they captured in the first man.

But what then? “You have brought me the day of consolation”—you have brought it, I say, for it is as certain as if you had already brought it. For you promised Abraham, O God who do not lie (Num. 23; Titus 1), “the day of consolation,” the day of Christ, before the eyes of my enemies, who now rejoice because you, in righteous anger, “did” my evil. And when you have brought “the day of consolation, they shall become like me.” How “like me”? Certainly in this: that I, in reverse, shall hear—indeed, shall see—their evil on the day of wrath and revelation of your righteous judgment.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How they are to be thoroughly gathered as a vintage, with an irrecoverable vintage and irrevocable condemnation, while the Church has a day of consolation; and what the final two elements, SIN and THAU, signify when joined.

THAU, that is, “signs.” “Let all their evil enter before you, and thoroughly gather them as a vintage, as you thoroughly gathered me because of all my iniquities. For my groans are many, and my heart is grieving.” “Let all their evil,” he says, “enter before you, and thoroughly gather them as a vintage.” For their evil has indeed already entered before you, but not “all” of it. And you have already “gathered them as a vintage,” but have not “thoroughly gathered them.” Long ago, indeed, “their evil”—that is, the pride by which they swelled above the other angels, their prince the devil saying, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14)—this, I say, “their evil entered before you,” and for it you “gathered them as a vintage,” that is, judged them: for you cast them from heaven and hurled them down into this dark air.

But that other evil, by which they deceived me, your creature, through the serpent, has not yet entered before you; it has not yet been examined by your judgment. What evil came from me did enter before you, for you examined it, first saying to the man Adam: “Where are you? For who told you that you were naked, unless you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” Then you said to the woman: “Why have you done this?” (Gen. 3). Thus what evil came from me entered before you, and for it you “gathered me as a vintage,” first saying to the woman: “I will multiply your hardships and your conceptions; in pain you shall bear children”; then saying to both man and woman: “Because you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid.).

But at that time, what evil came from the devil did not enter before you in this way; for you did not examine it or impose punishment for the fact that, having entered the serpent, he deceived the human being. Therefore let “all their evil,” all the evil of the devil and his angels, “enter before you” on the final day of the great judgment; and you who have already “gathered me as a vintage,” do “thoroughly gather them” with an irrecoverable vintage, with endless condemnation. For they should not only marvel at being gathered as a vintage—which has already happened to them, when you cast them out of heaven—but they also deserve to be thoroughly gathered, so that they may be taken away into eternal fire and not be sought again through all ages of ages.

But for me, as I have already said, you will bring “the day of consolation.” Why? By what judgment? By a judgment of mercy: “for my groans are many, and my heart grieving,” which are marks of repentance.
