Let us join these two final elements, sin, interpreted “teeth,” and thau, that is, “sign,” and say: “the signs of teeth.” By the signs of teeth all Holy Scripture is understood, because every utterance is formed by the teeth. What has this to do with the present matter? Clearly, that we may understand the very beautiful point: the matters contained beneath these two letters are those which all divinely inspired Scripture teaches us. For what else does it proclaim except that, after that evil of deceived humanity over which “all the enemies rejoiced,” there was to be brought to the Church “the day of consolation,” that is, the first coming of Christ, the Son of God; and that afterward judgment will come, in which the devil and his angels, and with them all the ungodly, are to be thoroughly gathered as a vintage and cast into eternal fire? (Matt. 25.) This lamentation having therefore ended, what bearing the following one has upon the matter has been briefly said above and must still be stated.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That, in the following alphabet, a lamentation is set forth concerning that time when Nebuzaradan burned Jerusalem with fire and, together with it, burned the house of the Lord.

(THREN. CH. II.) We shall understand the entire lamentation set forth in the following alphabet as concerning that earthly Jerusalem which, at that time, Nebuzaradan, commander of the army and servant of the king of Babylon, set on fire and burned, together with the house of the Lord and the king’s house. Having also destroyed the walls of Jerusalem round about, he carried the remnant of the people into Babylon, leaving only vine-dressers and farmers from among the poor of the land (4 Kings 25; Jer. 39). This was truly lamentable to the holy and wise man, not only because of the very magnitude of the slaughter and conflagration, but also because of the hardness of the sinful nation: so great evils would not have been inflicted on his people by God, who is by nature compassionate and merciful (Ps. 110 [111]), for slight sins.

All who today also trust in lying words ought to be directed to the lamentation of this alphabet, just as those to whom this lamenter previously said: “Do not trust in lying words, saying, ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord’” (Jer. 7). For even today there are many childish people who imagine that God, who is spirit, delights in gold or silver, marble veneers, and the beautiful walls of a handmade temple; and they do not consider what sort of persons they themselves are, or that they ought themselves to be the holy temple of God, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3). Let this alphabet therefore be set before such persons.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. In what respect Jerusalem is called the footstool of the Lord’s feet, and how the Lord cast her down from heaven to earth.

ALEPH. “How the Lord, in his wrath, covered the daughter of Zion with darkness; he cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth and did not remember the footstool of his feet in the day of his wrath.” He calls the city of Jerusalem the footstool of the Lord’s feet, on that account on which Holy Scripture is accustomed to name that city: namely, because of the worship of the divine religion and the temple of the Lord’s name, which, according to the conditions of that time, was first celebrated in that city with whatever rite was then observed. For the same reason, throughout all Holy Scripture it bears the type of Christ’s Church, in which the Lord’s name is now invoked in the true rite throughout all the earth.

And then, because the Lord’s name was invoked in that city alone, it alone deserved to be called the footstool of the Lord’s feet. But now, because the Lord’s name is invoked throughout all the earth and the whole earth is full of the churches of Christ, the whole earth rightly deserves to be called his footstool. Hence comes that prophetic saying, that is, a saying concerning the future: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). And when the Lord said in the Gospel, “Do not swear by heaven, because it is the throne of God,” he immediately added, “nor by the earth, because it is the footstool of his feet” (Matt. 5). For the time was already at hand when what the Psalmist had sung would come to pass: “Be exalted,” he says, “above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” (Ps. 107 [108]).

Now observe how elegantly, with what a magnificent comparison, he expressed the tumult of a wretched city falling, when he said, “and he did not remember the footstool of his feet in the day of his wrath.” He sets before the eyes a king, or some majestic father, sitting upon a high seat with a footstool beneath his feet, so aroused in fury and stirred in wrath that, with his feet no longer steady, he hurls his footstool far away, unaware—because anger prevents him from noticing—how much harm this will do to his dangling feet. With such an onset, he says, he “cast the daughter of Zion and the glory of Israel from heaven to earth,” from every dignity to every disgrace, and wrapped her, as she fell, in the darkness of madness.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That pride was the fault for which Jerusalem and the temple had to be cast down.

BETH. “The Lord cast down without sparing all the beautiful things of Jacob; in his wrath he destroyed the strongholds of the virgin of Judah and cast them down to earth. He defiled the kingdom and its princes.” What he had said, “he cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth,” he repeated again when he said, “he cast down without sparing.” And a third time: he “cast the virgin of Judah down to earth.” By all these expressions he indicated the character of the fault and showed that it was the fault of pride for which Jerusalem was destroyed. Pride is indeed a great evil, for which he must be believed neither to have spared virgins nor ever to spare them.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That the cause of that ruin was that God broke the horn of Israel.

GIMEL. “In the wrath of his fury he broke every horn of Israel; he drew back his right hand before the enemy, and he burned in Jacob like a consuming fiery flame round about.” Here he expressed pride more fully by a related term, saying: “He broke the horns of Israel”; for it is usual and common to call the proud “horned.” Therefore God not without reason “drew back his right hand,” so as not to help Israel or make it stand before the enemy—not because he despised his own work, but because he could not bear the indignity of human beings being horned.

Why, then, did he not say, “He kindled a fire,” but “he burned in Jacob like a consuming fiery flame round about”? Was not the fire truly kindled by which Nebuzaradan, servant of the king of Babylon, burned the city and the temple? Therefore he means that the city itself, fanning, as it were, a fire with the wind of its pride, stirred up against itself the hatred of the nations; and that this was the consuming fiery flame round about, which, as an efficient cause, was followed by the elemental fire.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. That God is hostile to the proud, and therefore said thus: “He bent his bow.”

DALETH. “He bent his bow like an enemy; he strengthened his right hand like an adversary, and slew everything lovely to the sight in the tent of the daughter of Zion. He poured out his indignation as it were.” Because the horn of pride was the cause, and God resists the proud (Jas. 4), he did not take up the rod as a father, but “like an enemy he bent his bow, and like an adversary he strengthened his right hand”: that he might shoot forth his arrow forcefully through her heart, and drive his firmly thrust sword down to the vital parts, as an enemy or adversary does.

For he did not, as often happened, hand over his people into the hands of nations so that, remaining in their land, they endured the rule of their conquerors; rather, “he slew everything lovely to the sight in the tent of the daughter of Zion”—that is, everything that pleased, and by which wanton young Zion thought God was pleased. And “he poured out his indignation as it were like fire,” so that in anger he might take everything away, as fire devours all stubble.

## CHAPTER XL. That he did not say, “The Lord became an enemy,” but “like an enemy,” because neither the reality nor the name of enemy applies to God.

HE. “The Lord became like an enemy; he cast down Israel, he cast down all its walls, he destroyed all its strongholds, and filled the daughter of Judah with humiliation and the humiliated.” The Lord, he says, who said to Pharaoh, “Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you: Let my son go” (Exod. 4)—that Father and Lord “became like an enemy.” It must be carefully noted that he did not say, “He became an enemy,” but “He became like an enemy.” For neither the thing nor the term “enemy” applies to God. An enemy is one who violates rights, removes or denies what is just, and from whose side the fruit of friendship, peace, fails or perishes.

The Lord, therefore, did not become an enemy but “became like an enemy” by removing or slaying everything lovely to the sight in Zion; by casting down Israel, casting down all its walls, destroying its strongholds, and filling the daughter of Judah with humiliation and the humiliated—since his enmity was not against human beings, but against pride.

## CHAPTER XLI. How he calls that city and temple the tent of the Lord.

VAU. “He destroyed his tent like a garden; he demolished his tabernacle. The Lord gave over to oblivion in Zion the feast and the sabbath; and, in the reproach and indignation of his wrath, the king and priest.” That most august temple was the tent or tabernacle of the Lord; for in it, as in a tent customarily pitched only for a time, faith did military service for the Lord’s name among those who were pilgrims, who had no abiding city here but sought the future one (Heb. 13). He “destroyed it like a garden” and valued the holy place of his name no more highly than a worthless vegetable garden (3 Kings 27). He gave “feast and sabbath,” which were certainly lovely to behold, “over to oblivion,” and gave over “king and priest to the indignation of his wrath and to reproach.”

Finally, this must not be passed over: he cast down the king with such disgrace that the king of Babylon, after first killing his sons before his eyes, then tore out his eyes (4 Kings 25).

## CHAPTER XLII. What is meant by, “They raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.”

ZADI. “The Lord rejected his altar, cursed his sanctuary, gave the walls of its towers into the hand of the enemy; they raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.” You asked what he had said above: “He did not remember the footstool of his feet in the day of his wrath.” See: he made it plain by saying, “He rejected his altar, cursed his sanctuary.” Moreover, how powerfully he expressed the greatness of the sorrow and the tumult of misery when he said: “They raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.” It is as if he said: Never had they sung more loudly in the joy of a feast day than they now cried out in their distress and pain.

## CHAPTER XLIII. How he stretched over Zion the measuring-line of a seventy-year captivity.

HETH. “The Lord planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out his line and did not withdraw his hand from destruction. And the outer wall mourned, and the wall was destroyed together with it.” These things did not happen by chance: the Lord planned them; the Lord acted with deliberation, as the principle of usefulness required. As he considered and weighed the whole matter in the balance of reason, it pleased him that the wall of the daughter of Zion should be destroyed, so that her vanity might receive some instruction from adversity. And he himself stretched over her his measuring-line of seventy years’ duration; and he resolved not to withdraw “his hand from destruction,” that is, not to end the captivity before those years were completed. Nor will the outer wall and the wall, which were destroyed together, be rebuilt earlier.

## CHAPTER XLIV. What her gates and bars are which the Lord broke, so that her prophets found no vision from the Lord.

THET. “Her gates sank into the earth; he destroyed and broke her bars; her king and her princes are among the nations; there is no law, and her prophets have found no vision from the Lord.” The height of the gates and the strength of the bars are likewise counted among the things lovely to behold; and these gates of the city, with their bars broken and destroyed, sank into the earth, for the reason over which another prophet laments: “Judgment has been turned backward and righteousness stands far off, because truth has fallen in the street and equity could not enter” (Isa. 59).

Yet he intends king and princes, law and prophets metaphorically. For, as though you asked, “What gates did he sink into the earth? What bars did he destroy and break?” he says: “Her king and her princes are among the nations; there is no law, and her prophets found no vision from the Lord.” The transformation is very fitting. Where there is no king or prince, where a law that is absent among the nations does not exercise its authority, where heavenly oracles are closed to prophets and visions of God withdrawn, the people are like a city lying open without gates and bars.

## CHAPTER XLV. How the elders sat upon the ground and were silent, and the virgins sprinkled their heads with ashes.

JOD. “The elders of the daughter of Zion sat upon the ground and were silent; they sprinkled their heads with ashes. The elders of Jerusalem put on sackcloth; the virgins of Judah cast their heads to the ground.” Formerly upright and much-speaking, the elders of the daughter of Zion now, cast down and maimed by the breaking of pride’s horn, sat silently upon the ground—cast down from their former confidence in the temple of the Lord as far as earth is distant from heaven. The virgins of Jerusalem, the virgins of Judah, sprinkled their heads with “ashes,” the emblem of sorrow; and, having no bridegrooms for whom to prepare themselves, they “cast their heads to the ground.” Thus was fulfilled what another prophet had foretold: “Therefore the Lord will not rejoice over her young men, nor have mercy on her fatherless and widows” (Isa. 9).

## CHAPTER XLVI. Why he now says, “My eyes failed through tears,” though earlier he had said, “Therefore give their children to famine,” and so forth.

CAPH. “My eyes failed through tears; my inward parts were troubled; my liver was poured out upon the ground because of the ruin of the daughter of my people, when child and nursing infant failed in the streets of the city.” “When,” he says, “child and nursing infant failed,” then “my eyes failed through tears and my inward parts”—indeed, they “were troubled” by the tumult of compassion—and “my liver,” the source of blood, “was poured out upon the ground.” What then? Could the natural affection of flesh and blood, following the judgment of reason, remain at the height of zeal?

Before these things happened I said: “Therefore give their children to famine and deliver them into the hands of the sword. Let their wives become childless and widows, and let their men be slain by death” (Jer. 8). These things, I say, and others like them I uttered, agreeing through the Spirit with your judgment and justice. But when the evils themselves came, and the event was set before my eyes, compassion prevailed, and nature, falling back from the heavenly judgments into itself, fell wounded.

## CHAPTER XLVII. How infants hanging at their mothers’ breasts, tortured by hunger, breathed out their souls.

LAMECH. “They said to their mothers: Where is grain and wine?—as they failed like the wounded in the streets of the city, as they breathed out their souls in their mothers’ bosoms.” How meanwhile could the eyes restrain their tears? With the simplicity of childhood mingled with distress—or distress mingled with simplicity—the little ones said to their mothers, pale and wasting with hunger: “Where is grain? Where is wine?” Being of an age unable to distinguish whether their mothers were accustomed to obtain grain and wine through labor or to bring them forth from their own nature; and, saying these things amid their very wailing, they failed “like the wounded”—indeed, truly transfixed by the sting of hunger—and, a sight intolerable to human feeling, slipping from dry breasts, “breathed out their souls” in their mothers’ bosoms.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. How Jerusalem, because of her impenitence, could be compared with no one, and therefore says, “Who will heal you?”

MEM. “To what shall I compare you, or to what shall I liken you, daughter Jerusalem? To what shall I make you equal and console you, virgin daughter Zion? For your ruin is great as the sea: who will heal you?” Shall I compare you, he says, with the Ninevites? Certainly not, for at Jonah’s preaching they repented (Jonah 3). Shall I make you equal to Tyre or Sidon? Certainly not; for the things done and said in you were not done and said in them. If they had been done in them, they would long ago have repented in ashes and sackcloth (Matt. 11). Who, then, will heal you? Surely not even the physician of physicians himself, should he come down from heaven. “Your ruin is great as the sea,” and whoever approaches to heal you suffers in you shipwreck through persecutions and death itself.

## CHAPTER XLIX. How he rebukes both the false prophets and Jerusalem herself because she listened to them.

NUN. “Your prophets saw for you false and foolish things; they did not expose your iniquity, so as to call you to repentance, but they saw for you false exaltations and banishments.” Where now is that prophet of yours, Hananiah son of Azzur, who took the chain from my neck and broke it, saying: “Thus says the Lord: Shall I break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations after two years of days?” (Jer. 28.) And where are your other prophets, who said: “You shall not see the sword, and there shall be no famine among you, but the Lord will give you peace in this place” (Jer. 14)?

I said: “These prophets falsely prophesy to you a lying vision, a deceitful divination, and the deception of their own heart; and you did not hear me” (ibid.). Behold, the event itself proves that “they saw for you false and foolish things” and “did not expose your iniquity,” physicians as unskilled as they were unfaithful, “so as to call you to repentance.”

## CHAPTER L. That, to complete the sum of miseries, passers-by also clapped their hands over her in mockery.

SAMECH. “All who passed by on the road clapped their hands over you; they hissed and shook their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem. ‘Is this,’ they said, ‘the city of perfect beauty, the joy of all the earth?’” “Is this it?” they say. O what a change of circumstances! “The city of perfect beauty, the joy of all the earth,” to which gold was brought from the whole world; which had no silver, nor considered it of any value, because her fleets went by sea bringing gold, and she possessed silver in as great abundance as stones (3 Kings 10). Is this that city? Saying these things, they “clapped their hands,” “hissed” with their mouths, and “shook their heads” over you.

## CHAPTER LI. How truly they mocked her, since, even after seventy years, when her bondage was released, they vigorously opposed the rebuilding of the city.

PHE. “All your enemies opened their mouth over you; they hissed and gnashed their teeth and said: ‘We shall devour her. Behold, this is the day we awaited; we found it, we saw it.’” A grievous reproach! A lamentable insult! For how greatly, think you, did they mock; with what willing minds did they behold the long-awaited day of your desolation, they who, even after seventy years, not yet satisfied by so long a spectacle of your sufferings, when the captivity had been released and a decree had gone forth that the city should be rebuilt, opposed it with all their might—writing letters to King Artaxerxes that he should change the decree, and moreover preparing arms to obstruct the work (1 Esdr. 4).

## CHAPTER LII. How this happened not so much through Nebuzaradan as by the judgment of the Lord, who had also foretold such things through Moses.

AIN. “The Lord did what he planned; he fulfilled his word, which he commanded from ancient days; he destroyed and did not spare; he made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted the horn of your adversaries over you.” It was not Nebuzaradan, he says, nor Nebuchadnezzar himself, king of Babylon, who did these things to you. The Lord himself planned them and himself did them. What then? Did he plan something new? Was not his doing these things to you the fulfillment of “the word which he commanded from ancient days”? Did he not long ago command Moses that “if you will not hear the voice of the Lord your God,” these and these things “shall come upon you, and the Lord will bring you and the king whom you appoint over yourself to a nation which neither you nor your fathers know, and you shall serve other gods”? (Deut. 28.)

## CHAPTER LIII. What was cried by the heart of the prophets who foretold these things and were not heard as they cried over the walls of the daughter of Zion.

SADE. “Their heart cried to the Lord over the walls of the daughter of Zion: Let tears run down like a torrent day and night; give yourself no rest, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent.” “Their heart cried.” Whose “heart”? Was it the heart of the enemies, whose horn he exalted over you, or of the adversaries whom he made rejoice over you? Rather, it was the heart of those to whom, or through whom, that word of the Lord was given, “which he commanded from ancient days” and now fulfilled. “Their”—that is, Moses’ and the prophets’—“heart cried to the Lord over the walls of the daughter of Zion.” As watchmen appointed to give warning, they cried out that you might turn from your ungodliness; and by crying out they saved their own souls. But you, O daughter Zion, because you did not hear their cry, behold, you have died in your iniquity.

Why was it not said, “Their mouth cried,” but “their heart cried”? Clearly because they did not cry carelessly; they did not offer words in the manner of a greeting, but they cried, announced, and prophesied with willing mind, with all the affection of their heart, and with the deep feeling of charity, wishing to help, so that the evil of swiftly approaching danger might by no means seize you sleeping. Why was it not said, “Their heart cried to Zion,” but “cried to the Lord”? Because, together with the cry of proclamation by which they wished to summon Zion, they also cried to the Lord in prayer; and concerning the very fact that they had cried to Zion, though unheard, they made the Lord their witness.

They said to you: “Let tears run down like a torrent day and night,” that you may extinguish the impending fire of wrath and fury; “give yourself no rest,” lest the wrath of the Lord seize you like a thief; “and let not the pupil of your eye be silent,” because the Most High hears the cry of tears rather than that of lips.

## CHAPTER LIV. What is meant by their cry: “Arise, praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches.”

COPH. “Arise, praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches; pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord. Lift up your hands to him for the lives of your little ones, who failed from hunger at the head of every street.” “Arise,” I say, and take up your weapons: weapons of praises, weapons of vigils, weapons of tears—which is to pour out “your heart like water”—and do this “before the presence of the Lord,” so that by ordered strength you may hold the most strong Lord and bend him, inclined to mercy, by devotion.

Meanwhile remember to lift up your hands to him; for there is little strength in praise, vigils, and the pouring out of tears, unless, by extending alms and so forth, by performing works of mercy, you lift up to God—lift up even to heaven—your hands for the life of your little ones. Crying these things to you, they said:

## CHAPTER LV. What they cry when they say: “See, O Lord, whom you have gathered as a vintage.”

RES. “See, O Lord, and consider whom you have thus gathered as a vintage. Shall women then eat their own fruit, little children the measure of a handbreadth? Shall priest and prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord?” This is what their heart cried for you to the Lord, while crying also to you over your walls, daughter Zion. They still cry: “See, O Lord,” they say. Why do you turn away your face? If you turn here the eyes of your mercy, and yourself behold what you are doing, you will be wounded by your own sight and judge that enough punishment has been exacted. “Shall women then eat their own fruit, little children the measure of a handbreadth,” and will you, who are merciful, be able to endure the sight? “Shall priest and prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord,” and will your inward compassion restrain itself as it beholds this?

See both this and that—that is, famine and sword. “See,” I say, “what people,” what place, “you have thus gathered as a vintage.” For it is not a distant people or an unknown place, but your own nation and holy city.

## CHAPTER LVI. That the divine nature is drawn to mercy much more than human nature.

SIN. “The old man and the child lie on the ground outside; my virgins and young men have fallen by the sword. You slew them in the day of your wrath; you struck and had no pity.” See this: “child and old man lie outside on the ground.” Is not human nature itself drawn to mercy by these ages of children and old persons? Therefore see how they lie, how greatly you have struck them, and how you have not spared. For the divine nature is drawn to mercy much more than human nature; and doubtless, when you see what you have done, you will have mercy.

## CHAPTER LVII. How he attributes what happened, as it were, to God.

[Col. 1400B] THAU. “You summoned, as though to a solemn day, those who would terrify from every side; and on the day of the Lord’s wrath there was none who escaped or remained. Those whom I had brought forth and nourished, my enemy consumed.” See and consider all these things—what you have done; and, your mind wounded together with them by the sight, you will doubtless consider those who remain and call back your captives.

## CHAPTER LVIII. That in the third alphabet the prophet laments his own particular cause; and why here the individual letters are now repeated three times, whereas in the others they occur singly.

*(Lam. chap. III.)* After the universal lamentation of the human race, after the common lamentation of one nation, the prophet at last, in this third place, laments his own particular captivity in personal lamentations. The particular and individual captivity of each person is the measure of his own sin, the weight of his own tribulation. Once this has been noticed, the other question which might be raised readily presents itself: namely, why, whereas a single alphabet is assigned to each of the other Lamentations, a triple alphabet is assigned to this one alone. For this man had a threefold cause for lamenting: first, because he himself, like all human beings, was taken captive in Adam; second, because while he lived and watched, although the possessions of the enemy were preserved unharmed, his own possessions were burned and his nation taken captive; third, because he knew his own frailty and had been afflicted by his own calamities and by every kind of suffering among his people and at their hands. Let us therefore prepare ourselves as teachable little children for this alphabet; and, taught by this lamenter, each of us shall know, both from a cause that is personal and from one that is universal, what is truly lamentable.

## CHAPTER LIX. What that poverty is, what the darkness is, and what are those hands of which he speaks.

ALEPH. “I am a man seeing my poverty under the rod of his indignation.”  
ALEPH. “He led me and brought me into darkness, and not into light.”  
ALEPH. “He has only turned and turned again his hand against me all day long.”

“I,” he says, “am a man seeing my poverty.” He did not say, “I am a poor man,” for he would have said little enough: indeed, every human being is truly poor. Every human being is poor in the first parent, stripped of his own glory and laid bare of the glory of God. But not every human being sees, not every human being understands, this very poverty of his own. Therefore he preferred to say what was sufficient and worthy of imitation: [Col. 1401A] “I am a man seeing my poverty,” seeing it, I say, “under the rod of his indignation”—that is, admonished to see by the punishment of corruption and mortality, by which all of us human beings have been struck so that we die; and because we have been struck, all of us fall ill, and at last dust returns to dust.

ALEPH. “He led me and brought me into darkness, and not into light.” This second evil was added for me to the common poverty: that “he led me and brought me, not into light but into darkness,” so that I might see the darkness of my nation—the dense and tangled darkness of miseries—over which, lamenting with them, he said above: “How in his wrath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with a cloud of darkness” *(Lam. II)*, and so forth.

ALEPH. “He has only turned and turned again his hand [Col. 1401B] against me all day long.” What, he says, shall I say of my own particular case, of the misery of my individual conscience? Others live; the others whom I see are human beings; and whatever may be true of them, I know “only” this concerning myself: that he has “turned his hand against me,” and has turned his hand against me not for an hour but “all day long.” As many wounds of sin as are in my soul, so many wounds from his hand are in me. As many adversities as beset my mind and body, so many scourges of his hand rage against me.

## CHAPTER LX. How he laments that he was made mortal in Adam, fed with gall in the burning of Jerusalem, and darkened by his own faults.

BETH. “He has made my skin and my flesh old; he has crushed my bones.” Because of old Adam, [Col. 1401C] he has made my skin old, he has made my flesh old. In what respect “has he made my skin old”? In the condition of mortality. In what respect “has he made my flesh old”? In concupiscence and the passion of desire. In what respect “has he crushed my bones”? In that “I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do” *(Rom. VII).* Reason is bone in me; and bone, that is, good will, by which I delight in the law of God according to the inward human being. But he has “crushed these very bones of mine” by the warring law of sin which is in my members *(ibid.)*, justly laid upon me.

BETH. “He has built round about me, and surrounded me with gall and toil.” Because of that oldness and crushing laid upon the whole human race, he “built” a structure of calamity [Col. 1401D] “round about me”: in my people he summoned famine, sword, and fire, and made them stand around me. “And he surrounded me with gall and toil”: with the gall of bitterness and sorrow in the mind, with the toil of prison and hunger in the flesh. For I heard the reproaches of many and terror on every side: “Persecute him, and let us persecute him” *(Jer. XX).* They even beat me and put me into prison; they cast me into the pit in which there was no water, so that I might die there of hunger *(Jer. XXXVII, XXXVIII).*

BETH. “He has placed me in dark places, like the dead of old.” Moreover, he has “placed me in the dark places” of my own conscience. For he does not permit me to be certain concerning my own salvation, so as to think that I have already attained it *(Phil. III).* I am always under suspicion in the fear of the judgment to come, so that I presume concerning salvation no more than the everlasting dead can presume—those whom consciousness of guilt consigns daily to everlasting death. For I am in no respect more righteous except through the grace of God, except through the gratuitous mercy of him who calls and justifies whom he wills *(Rom. VIII).*

## CHAPTER LXI. That, fallen into God’s enmity in Adam, he was laid waste by the city’s present evils and, in his own passions, was struck as though by arrows.

GIMEL. “He has built against me all around, so that I cannot go out; he has made my fetter heavy.” What has he “built all around against me”? Surely, the wall of enmity because of Adam, who aspired to God’s divinity. For according to him, I and my fathers are by nature children of wrath, as are the rest *(Eph. II).* I cannot “go out” through [Col. 1402B] this wall, “for he has made my fetter heavy”; nor can I do so except that “in my God I shall pass over the wall” *(Ps. XVII).*

GIMEL. “But even when I cry out and plead, he shuts out my prayer.” Not only do I have that common source of grief; this grief also is recent, while I see the captivity of my nation, for which indeed I can cry out and plead. “But when I cry out,” he will not hear, until the number of seventy years is fulfilled; until that limit, he has shut out my prayer.

GIMEL. “He has blocked my ways with square stones; he has overthrown my paths.” Beyond the things external to me, at home “he has blocked my ways”; in my own conscience “he has overthrown my paths.” I wish, while placed in the body on earth, to live in heaven in my mind; I desire more fully to grasp the fullness of the Lord which I have tasted. But he, by allowing temptations and permitting waves of thoughts, has hemmed me in—or rather, that I may accuse myself, he lays my own sins as square stones upon my sinful conscience. Thus “he has blocked my ways and overthrown my paths,” so that I cannot run to contemplate his glory.

## CHAPTER LXII. How God became an ambushing bear to the transgressing human being, and how for that reason he overthrew paths inclined toward evil.

DALETH. “He has become to me an ambushing bear, a lion in hiding.” Wonderful is the bitterness of the grief; wonderful the harshness of the lament. Who, then, has become to you “an ambushing bear,” who “a lion in hiding”? How has God, the most mighty God of spirits, the God who knows all things, become a bear or a lion to you? Where or when did he lie in wait? In paradise, where the serpent spoke with me—that is, with my father Adam—where the devil, who had entered the serpent, sent Eve to Adam *(Gen. III).* He kept silent while that one spoke; he was silent while the human being assented to him; and once the sacrilege had been committed, angry like a bear, he came forth from ambushes, like a lion from hiding, and said: “Adam, where are you?” *(ibid.)*, and so forth. Does not Scripture suggest his ambush by the image of a midday sleep? For it says: “And when he had heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise at the breeze after midday” *(ibid.).* Did he, then, act unjustly—he who, as though sleeping through the whole midday, kept silent, and, once [Col. 1403A] the crime had been committed, as though only then first awakened, came out from his hiding places to question him? Certainly not. For he had warned them beforehand, saying: “On whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” *(Gen. II).*

DALETH. “He has overthrown my paths and broken me; he has made me desolate.” Because of that universal evil, behold, today he has “overthrown my paths”—that is, the paths of my nation, crooked paths, paths inclined toward evil—and in the hand of the king of Babylon he has “broken me” with sword, famine, and fire. “He has made me desolate,” namely through a captivity of seventy years. When he says “desolate” in the person of Jerusalem, he plainly laments the present evil of captivity.

DALETH. “He has stretched out his bow and set me like a target for the arrow.” This he says of his own person; this he bewails concerning his own conscience. For outwardly also he had bodily been exposed to such sufferings that he rightly laments that he has been set like a target for the arrow; and inwardly, in his soul, though he was righteous, there was much that lay open to the arrows of temptations. Hence the Psalmist says: “For your arrows have been fixed in me” *(Ps. XXXVII).*

## CHAPTER LXIII. How, wounded in Adam by the arrows of lusts, he was mocked by his own people while prophesying the imminent captivity, and was embittered by prisons and hunger.

HE. “He sent into my kidneys the daughters of his quiver.” The authority of the catholic faith holds it as certain that, unless the guilt of transgression had been committed, bestial pleasure would not have been introduced into the flesh of the rational human being. The human being had been so made that the spirit would rule the flesh, [Col. 1403C] provided that the spirit itself remained subject to God, its ruler; and consequently the human being would be led to beget offspring not by lust but by reason. But the spirit refused to be subject to God; therefore it was made subject to the flesh. And so “man was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” *(Ps. XLVIII).* Therefore let him say in the person of the human race: “He sent into my kidneys the daughters of his quiver,” that is, he exposed me to passions of concupiscence by the inescapable judgments of his justice.

HE. “I became a mockery to all my people, their song all day long.” That is, while I say, “Thus says the Lord: The Chaldeans will come; Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon will come” *(Jer. XXXII)*, they mocked me, singing against me all day long the truth of the prophecy, as though mocking words of madness, error, and insanity.

HE. “He filled me with bitterness; he made me drunk with wormwood.” Indeed, it contributed to the increase of the public evil for them to laugh when they had done wrong and to sing amid the worst things; but he also “filled me with bitterness” from beatings, prison, and hunger, and “made me drunk with wormwood” from fear, pain, and sorrow.

## CHAPTER LXIV. How, in the bite of the first human being, he lost his teeth; how, during the city’s siege, while speaking for it in the Lord’s presence, his soul was rejected; and how in his own conscience he feared concerning his merits.

VAU. “He broke my teeth by number; he fed me with ashes.” It is known that God broke the human being’s teeth because of sin; for they become loose [Col. 1404A] and fall out in bent and withered old people. And even if in some persons they remain stronger until the end of life, as in Moses, of whom it is written that “his teeth were not moved” *(Deut. XXXIV)*, nevertheless they are broken in the grave, where decay has consumed even the bones. But did God thus break only the human being’s teeth? Did he not break all the limbs and all the bones, and reduce them to dust? Why, then, did he speak of the teeth alone? Surely because the human being committed the first sin with his teeth, when he bit the fruit of the forbidden tree. Therefore, he says, “he broke my teeth by number and fed me with ashes,” because, on account of the bite, he broke the human race by death and commanded it to return to ashes.

VAU. “My soul has been rejected; I have forgotten good things.” Beyond that universal evil, behold, at the present time, while the city is besieged and the children of my people perish and are endangered amid famine and sword, while I stood in his presence to speak good things for them, “my soul has been rejected”: my prayer has not been heard. He bestowed many good things on our fathers, but because of the multitude of present evils, “I have forgotten the good things” of the past.

VAU. “And I said: My end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.” To those common evils is added for me the fear of God’s judgment and justice; for, if I am judged without mercy, “my end has perished, and my hope from the Lord.” This I said, agreeing with the Psalmist who says: “For no living person shall be justified in your sight” *(Ps. CXLII).*

## CHAPTER LXV. How he asks God to remember the first transgression and the punishments which followed from it, and what future good he hopes from it for himself because he receives present evils.

ZADI. “Remember my poverty and transgression, the wormwood and gall.” After you have been angry, he says, with the human being who sinned, remember mercy; for, on account of one human being’s sin, there is much punishment, much poverty, wormwood, and gall. Poverty is the mortality of the body. Wormwood and gall are the death of the soul. If you remember these things, mercy will judge that much punishment has been exacted. Knowing this, another says: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and my calamity were weighed in a balance. This would appear heavier than the sand of the sea” *(Job XXXI).*

ZADI. “In remembrance I shall remember, and my soul will waste away within me.” I shall remember the evils that I saw—the evils of the city and people, famine, sword, and fire—so that no consolation may erase this remembrance; and with unceasing grief, through the continual punishment of sorrow, my soul will waste away within me.

ZADI. “Recalling these things in my heart.” It is understood: I shall be tormented by divine affliction; and therefore I shall “hope” for consolation in that heavenly country, because I receive evils in my life.

## CHAPTER LXVI. That he rejoices that the human being was not, like the devil, abandoned because of sin; and that after the night of Babylonian captivity there will be a morning of freedom.

ETH. “The mercies of the Lord—that we have not been consumed, [Col. 1405A] because his compassions have not failed.” Since, he says, both angel and human being sinned, the angel who became the devil and his associate angels were consumed; for they are not to be sought again unto eternity, and all the Lord’s compassions toward them have failed, for God will never have mercy on them. We human beings, however, have not thus been consumed; rather, in his wrath God will remember his mercy toward us. Thanks, then, be to the mercies of the Lord, because mercy has exalted itself over judgment in our case.

ETH. “New in the morning; great is your faithfulness.” “His compassions,” I say, “have not failed,” but like the new morning they will arise after the present night of darkness has passed. For what reason? “Great is your faithfulness”: that is, there are many whose faith deserves that, after this darkness in which you have been covered in the wrath of the Lord, O daughter Zion, the morning of new compassions should arise for you.

ETH. “The Lord is my portion, my soul has said; therefore I will wait for him.” Now, he says, I return to myself, to whom the word of the Lord came, saying: “You shall not take a wife, and you shall not have sons and daughters in this place” *(Jer. XVI)*, and so forth. Hearing these things, “my soul said: The Lord is my portion; therefore I will wait for him.” That is, let others who wish be anxious and troubled about many things; for me, one thing is necessary *(Luke X).* Therefore I shall wait for the one Lord, rejecting concern for earthly things, which are many.

## CHAPTER LXVII. How he who is just in exercising severity upon Adam is good to those who hope in him; and how it is good for Babylon’s captives not to murmur but to await the Lord’s salvation in silence.

TETH. “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.” Do not despair, whoever you are, judging the Lord to be excessively severe because he was so greatly angered with the first human beings over a small or trifling matter, that is, over the not-large fruit of a forbidden tree. For “the Lord is good to those who hope in him,” and who in hoping confess their guilt—which those first human beings did not do. “The Lord,” I say, “is good to the soul that seeks him,” whom they did not seek; rather, fleeing from his face, they hid themselves among the trees of paradise *(Gen. III).* But what is he to those who hope in him, who do not seek him but flee him? Is he not good even to them? Rather, he is just. And although he is just and good, nevertheless he works one thing insofar as he is good, another insofar as he is just. For being good, through mercy he saves those who hope in and seek him; being just, through judgment he condemns those who despair and flee from him. “Therefore hope in the Lord, and do goodness” *(Ps. XXXVI)*, because “the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.”

TETH. “It is good to await in silence the salvation of the Lord.” O captives, who according to the present history will sit and weep for seventy years by the rivers of Babylon when you remember Zion *(Ps. CXXXVI)*, because “it is good to await [Col. 1406A] in silence the salvation of the Lord,” do not murmur because this captivity too has been added to you after that universal captivity of the human race. Rather, with silence and humility await the salvation of the Lord, Christ God, who, before he comes in the flesh, will free you from Babylonian captivity; and when he has come in the flesh, will transform the captivity of this whole world into the freedom of the glory of the children of God *(Rom. VIII).*

TETH. “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth.” What I say universally concerning the whole human race, journeying in this world—what I say commonly concerning the present captivity of our Zion—I shall also say particularly of each man: that “it is good” for him “when he has borne the yoke from his youth,” that is, when he has humbled himself in all things, not reproaching God’s judgments. In many other cases, and most particularly in these divisions, the individual statements correspond in their very wording to their own headings. For *Teth* is interpreted “good,” and each statement proclaims what is truly good.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. How the person who sits alone and raises himself above himself differs from the first human being; and how, in that captivity, one must be silent, if perhaps there is hope that she who was led into Babylon may be restored.

JOD. “He shall sit alone and be silent, because he shall raise himself above himself.” Such a person will surely belong to the new human being, not to that old one who refused to sit alone and be silent, entering into counsel with that whisperer, deceiver, the ancient serpent. For did he sit alone or silently, and raise himself [Col. 1406C] above himself to God—he whose whole mind was fixed upon him who was above him? Certainly not: rather, he inclined himself toward the whisper of the little beast creeping upon the earth.

JOD. “He shall put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope.” Not in heaven, but “in the dust he shall put his mouth,” hearing his good Master say to him: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” *(Matt. XI).* In doing this he will humbly wait “if perhaps there may be hope.” For he will say: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” *(Joel II).* Surely this is I. I shall put “my mouth in the dust,” saying: “You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is right” *(Ps. CXVIII)*—“if perhaps there may be hope,” if perhaps the captivity now led into Babylon may be restored, plucked like a firebrand from the fire.

JOD. “He shall give his cheek to the one who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches.” “To the one who strikes him,” I say, “he shall give his cheek,” not to one who strikes his nation; he shall be filled with his own reproaches, not those of others. For in the one case patience is praiseworthy; in the other, hardness of mind is blameworthy. Whoever has borne “the yoke from his youth” will act in this way. But what human being bore the yoke more readily than that man who, “being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as plunder, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness” of human beings “and found in appearance as a human being? He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death upon a cross” *(Phil. II).* Therefore he, supreme in patience, “will give his cheek to the one who strikes him,” [Col. 1407A] or rather, according to another prophet, “will give his body to those who strike it, and his cheeks to those who pluck them; he will not turn his face away from those who rebuke and spit upon him” *(Isa. L)*; and he will “be filled with reproaches” of this sort, not unwillingly, but because of his exceedingly great love for us, accepting them as the bread of fullness. Let each of us also, when suffering persecution for righteousness, give his cheek to the one striking him and be filled with reproaches, willingly accepting present evils, so that we may be filled with future goods.

## CHAPTER LXIX. How he who sent Adam out of paradise will not reject him forever, but will again have mercy and bring him back from Babylonian captivity; and how he who humbles each person has not wholly cast him away, but, on the contrary, loves the one he corrects and receives the one he scourges.

CAPH. “For the Lord will not reject forever.” I said above that “the Lord is good to those who hope in him”; and if you ask in what respect I said it, behold, I now say: “because he will not reject forever.” He rejected for a time, saying: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil; see lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever” *(Gen. III)*; but he will not reject forever. He will yet seek out his creature and draw all things to himself *(John XII).* The repelling sword, the flaming sword which he placed before paradise, he will someday turn aside and give us freely to eat from the tree of life.

CAPH. “For if he has cast off, he will also have mercy according to the multitude of his mercies.” I said, and I said truly, that “it is good to await in silence the salvation of the Lord,” because, even if he has cast off, even if he has rejected his altar, he will nevertheless “have mercy,” so that, when captivity is ended, Jerusalem may be rebuilt and the temple restored.

CAPH. “For he has not humbled and cast off the children of men from his whole heart.” I said, I say, and said truly, that “it is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth.” For even if he has humbled individual children of humankind, of whom I am first in number, he has not humbled them “from his whole heart”: not everything by which he humbled or cast off proceeded from anger, but he instructs us usefully through labors, as it is written: “For whom the Lord loves he corrects; moreover, he scourges every son whom he receives” *(Heb. XII).*

## CHAPTER LXX. How the Lord does not know how to crush the righteous together with the impious, to turn aside a person’s judgment, or to pervert a human being in judgment.

LAMED. “To crush beneath his feet all the bound of the earth;”  
LAMED. “To turn aside the judgment of a man before the face of the Most High;”  
LAMED. “To pervert a human being in his judgment—the Lord does not know.”

For this reason I said: the Lord is good, because he does not know how to do these things. O praiseworthy ignorance! O pure simplicity, and simple purity of divinity! He does not know how to crush indiscriminately beneath his feet all those bound upon earth. For example, he does not treat Cain and Abel, Jacob and Esau alike, but knows how to save some through grace and crush others through justice. He does not know how to turn aside “the judgment of a man before [Col. 1408A] the face of the Most High,” and as a wise judge he knows how to preserve the three boys unharmed in the furnace of fire *(Dan. III).* He does not know how to pervert a human being in his judgment—that is, to make the upright perverse—and he knows how to make the perverse upright and just.

## CHAPTER LXXI. How blameworthy it is if someone says that anything comes to pass without the Lord’s command; if he says that neither good nor evil proceeds from the mouth of the Most High, murmuring about sins and imputing them to fatal necessity.

MEM. “Who is this who spoke, so that it came to pass, when the Lord did not command?”  
MEM. “Will neither good things nor evil things proceed from the mouth of the Most High?”  
MEM. “Why has a living man murmured, a man concerning his sins?”

Since the Lord is so good, “who is this” who sets a table for Fortune [*fortuna*] and says, “This or that will happen,” “when the Lord did not command”? For when he says that these or those things happen by chance or accident, or even ascribes the causes of human death or life to the stars, does he suppose that any of these things happen without the Lord’s command? “Who is this?” In short, he is absolutely nobody, as though he ought not to be known. When he says that “neither good nor evil proceeds from the mouth of the Most High,” but that all things happen by chance, who would deem him worthy of knowing, who ought to count him as known? For it belongs to no sense or reason to suppose that the Most High does not care for human affairs, especially on the ground that at this time so beautiful a temple has been destroyed and a city of such great name made desolate. Further, “why has a human being murmured,” why has “a living man murmured concerning [Col. 1408C] his sins,” saying that he is compelled to sin by fatal necessity?

## CHAPTER LXXII. That one should rather return to the discrimination of the heart, and make confession of sins together with good works.

NUN. “Let us examine our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord.” Let us anathematize this most wicked sect of the despairing person, and instead “examine our ways”—that is, the holy Scriptures—and, believing them when they testify that God cares for us, “seek and return to the Lord,” because, as I said above, “the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.”

NUN. “Let us raise our hearts with our hands to the Lord in heaven.” Let us not, I say, despair, but “raise our hearts with our hands”: that is, let us have faith joined with good works. Thus it will come to pass that “from the mouth of the Most High,” from the mouth of the Lord who is in heaven, after the evils which we deserved, his good things will proceed; he will turn the captivity of Zion, and we shall be like those consoled, and our mouth will be filled with joy from the good things of his mouth *(Ps. CXXV).*

NUN. “We have acted wickedly and provoked you to anger; therefore you are inexorable.” Let none of us say: “Fate binds me; the necessity fixed in the stars compelled me.” For God’s creature is not evil; rather, “we have acted wickedly,” and each person has voluntarily brought the lord of sin upon his own neck. Thus we “provoked you, God, to anger; therefore you are inexorable,” so that you would not immediately free those wishing to be freed and fighting against sin.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. [Col. 1409A] How in the first human being God struck the human race, and did not hear those handed over to enemies.

SAMECH. “You covered us in wrath and struck us; you killed and did not spare.” It is not as that unknown man said: “Neither good nor evil shall proceed from the mouth of the Most High.” Rather, just judgments have proceeded from your mouth; and for a definite cause or reason, in wrath on account of Adam’s sin, you “covered us and struck us, killed us and did not spare”—that is, with a wall of enmity set before us, with just death in the soul and the punishment of mortality in the body, you “struck us.” Thus “you killed and did not spare.”

SAMECH. “You placed a cloud before us, so that prayer may not pass through.” Behold, even in the present affliction you have placed before yourself the cloud of our sins, set the density of our crimes before your face; and therefore, when people perished by famine or sword and, after the Babylonian fire, went into captivity, you did not hear their cry or prayer.

SAMECH. “You have made me an uprooting and a rejection among the peoples.” Beyond those universal or common evils, this was added to me: that me—to whom you had said, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of the womb I sanctified you” *(Jer. I)*—you “made among the peoples” like “an uprooting and a rejection,” like corrupt or poisonous grass which is uprooted and cast away lest it corrupt even the soil itself. Thus people hated me, reproached me, and cast out my name as evil *(Luke VI).*

## CHAPTER LXXIV. [Col. 1409C] That from the beginning enemies have never been lacking to the elect, and that prophecy itself was a cause of tribulation to the prophets.

PHE. “All enemies opened their mouths against us.” From the beginning of the age, the devil and his angels have been invisible enemies to us; Cain and all his followers, visible enemies. “All” of them on every side “opened their mouth against us”; often they attacked us, often they built upon our back *(Ps. CXXVIII).*

PHE. “Terror and a snare have become to us prophecy and crushing.” This too is a lamentable evil of the present time: while we prophesy, “Thus says the Lord,” and, “These words the Lord commanded,” and, “Thus says the Lord: I will give Zedekiah king [Col. 1409D] of Judah, his servants, and his people into the hand of the king of Babylon” *(Jer. XXI)*, because of such prophecy we are afraid, ensnared, beaten, put in stocks, and crushed by every evil.

PHE. “My eye has brought down streams of water over the crushing of the daughter of my people.” Thus evils are everywhere: evils outside and within. Outside there are terror, snare, and crushing because of prophecy; within there are grief and groaning because of the prophecy’s fulfillment and truth, because of the crushing of the daughter of my people.

## CHAPTER LXXV. That he wept over the universal ruin of the human race, into which it fell through Adam; over his nation’s present captivity; and over his own frailty.

AIN. “My eye has been afflicted and has not been silent, because there was no rest.” “My eye”—the eye of the inward human being, the eye of the heart, which was created to see God—seeing its pain, “has been afflicted and has not been silent.” For it has a great voice and the eloquent tongue of reason. Why has it been afflicted? “Because there was no rest,” because through the fault of the first transgression it was born for labor.

AIN. “Until the Lord should look down and see from heaven.” This same eye of mine did not fall silent “until the Lord should look down and see from heaven”; his looking and seeing are both the release of the ancient captivity and the consolation of the present captives who were led into Babylon.

AIN. “My eye has plundered my soul among all the daughters of my city.” This is a most evident lament of personal grief. For what is “my eye” that “has plundered my soul,” if not the eye of concupiscence? For by adding “among all the daughters of my city,” he sufficiently expressed the eye of concupiscence—the wandering eye, the captive eye, and the captor of the unhappy soul. For since we have five windows through which death enters—that is, the five bodily senses through which death enters the soul within like a thief or robber—of them all sight is most effective for the work of that same death. It should be noted that two letters here, *phe* and *ain*, occur in reverse order. *Ain* should properly have come first, and *phe* later, in the order of the alphabet. Nor was this done without reason: for *ain* is interpreted “spring” or “eye,” and therefore this element more suitably fits “my eye has been afflicted; my eye has plundered [Col. 1410C] my soul.”

## CHAPTER LXXVI. That the devil caught the first human being as a bird by hunting, and that besides this he endured many waves of temptation inwardly in his mind.

ZADI. “My enemies caught me in hunting like a bird, without cause.” My enemies, the devil and his angels, hating me without cause, caught me and the entire human race in one human being by hunting, with the trap of the tree of concupiscence.

ZADI. “My life has fallen into a pit, and they placed a stone upon me.” Beyond that universal capture of the world, my life fell into a pit: for they lowered me with ropes into the pit in which there was no water but mud; and I went down into the mire; and, insofar as lay in their power, they placed a stone upon me, with the settled intent that I should die there of hunger *(Jer. XXXVIII).*

ZADI. “Waters overflowed above my head; I said: I have perished.” Beyond the things that I suffered outwardly, “waters” and waves of temptations “overflowed” inwardly in my mind; and, almost falling away from hope, “I said: I have perished,” just as another also says: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?” *(Rom. VII).*

## CHAPTER LXXVII. How, not despairing, he called upon God; how he does not cease praying for those led captive; and what consolation he received by the divine answer.

COPH. “I called upon your name, O Lord, from the lowest [Col. 1411A] pit.” To say, “I have perished,” and yet “I called upon the name” of the Lord, truly belongs not to one despairing but to one struggling between hope and fear. Indeed, the lowest pit is original sin, because whoever is held by it is undoubtedly separated from God and enclosed in certain condemnation. Both this speaker and all human beings before Christ’s coming were held in that pit; and therefore he rightly declares that he calls upon the Lord’s name “from the lowest pit.”

COPH. “You heard my voice; do not turn away your ear from my sobbing and cries.” You “heard,” I say, but to have heard already is not the same as to have answered immediately. For you heard by knowledge penetrating all things; in order that you may hear by grace, you must be entreated. Be open to entreaty, most high Creator, concerning our captivity, cast down and almost buried.

COPH. [Col. 1411B] “You drew near on the day when I called upon you; you said: Do not fear.” For it belongs to you to draw near in proportion to the matter, to the full magnitude of calamity and misery; hence another says: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” *(Ps. XXXIII).* “You said,” wounded by profound compassion, you said, I say, “Do not fear”—a consoling voice of fatherly or motherly tenderness.

## Chapter LXXVIII. How he asks for judgment though he is conscious that he has not deserved the evils he suffered

**RESCH.** “Thou hast judged, O Lord, the cause of my soul; the redeemer of my life.” — Thou hast indeed judged the cause of my soul with merciful judgment; and that judgment is the redemption of my life. Hence the Psalmist: “Judge me, O God, and discern my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. XLVII).

**RESCH.** “Thou hast seen, O Lord, their iniquity against me: judge my judgment.” [Col. 1411C] Thou hast seen with those eyes by which Thou seest all things; no information needs to be supplied to Thee. Thou hast seen and knowest “their iniquity against me,” those for whom I stood in Thy presence to speak good things on their behalf. Therefore “judge my judgment,” and do not allow my labour to perish without fruit.

**RESCH.** “Thou hast seen all their fury, all their thoughts against me.” That I may now speak not only of outward pressures: Thou hast seen “all the fury” of those against whom I seek judgment, and “all the thoughts” of my visible and invisible enemies “against me.” For Thou alone considerest toil and sorrow, as the Psalmist says [Col. 1411D] (Ps. X). Therefore “judge my judgment; discern my cause.”

## Chapter LXXIX. Against those devoted to evil and hostile to innocence

**SCHIN.** “Thou hast heard their reproaches, O Lord, all their evil thoughts against me.” From the time when the blood of righteous Abel first sent forth from the earth its voice of crying to Thee, Thou hast heard the reproaches of the continuing generation of the wicked against the generation of Thy elect; nor is there need that anyone should teach Thee, who knowest all things.

**SCHIN.** “Thou hast heard the lips of those rising up, and their thoughts against me all day long.” Thou hast heard not only lips which a human being could hear, but also [Col. 1412A] their thoughts—indeed, Thou hast seen them, O Lord—according to that saying: Man sees the face, but God sees the heart (1 Sam. XVI). They rose up all day long: “all day,” I say, that is, not for an hour, but continually they thought and spoke against me.

**SCHIN.** “See their sitting down and their rising up: I am their song.” “See,” I say, their “sitting down and rising up,” a spectacle worth beholding—how different, how unlike the sitting down of the godly and the rising up of the righteous. For the godly or righteous sit well, that they may rise well: that is, they humble themselves that they may be exalted, according to the words, “Rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow” (Ps. CXXVI). But these men abase themselves in a most wicked sitting down, in hypocrisy, in order to deceive; and when they have achieved this, they rise [Col. 1412B] cruelly and exult, as though victorious in utterly evil deeds. For when they have thus risen, “I am their song.” Hence the Head of us all says: “Those who sat in the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang of me” (Ps. LXVIII).

## Chapter LXXX. How he says, “Render to them their recompense,” not in cursing but in conceding

**THAU.** “Render to them their recompense, O Lord, according to the work of their hands.” I say “render,” not in a spirit of imprecation but of concession, knowing the constancy of Thy justice, of which the Psalmist also says: “For Thou wilt render to each one according to his works” (Ps. LXI; Matt. XVI).

**THAU.** “Thou shalt give them a shield for the heart—Thy labour.” [Col. 1412C] This will be the first recompense: that Thou darken and shut the eyes of their heart, lest they know Thee, whom to know is the reward of the godly. Thou Thyself shalt labour, Thou who didst send us to labour; Thou shalt labour, I say, even unto death in their sins. And this shall be “a shield for their heart”: that they may not believe in Thee because they have heard that Thou didst labour so greatly.

**THAU.** “Thou shalt pursue them in wrath and crush them beneath the heavens, O Lord.” This will be the second recompense, by which Thou shalt pursue and crush them with eternal crushing on the last day of the great judgment.

## Chapter LXXXI. How the Jews who killed Christ were the most cruel and most ruined of all who persecuted the prophets and righteous; and how, for this reason, they were darkened and scattered

[Col. 1412D] **(Lamentations, Chapter IV.)** Of all those who persecuted the prophets and all the saints, and who, by persecuting them, increased the continual sorrow of their sojourn in this world—of all these, I say—the Jews proved the most cruel and the most ruined. They persecuted the Son of God as He sojourned in this world, poor and sorrowful; and Him whom the Father had struck with the wound of most obedient love, they struck with a most wicked death. As He Himself, voicing a just complaint through the Prophet, says: “For they persecuted him whom Thou hast struck, and they added to the sorrow of my wounds” (Ps. LXVIII).

This lamenter had just conceded their condemnation in justice, saying: “Render to them their recompense, [Col. 1413A] O Lord, according to the work of their hands; Thou shalt give them a shield for the heart—Thy labour; Thou shalt pursue them in wrath and crush them beneath the heavens, O Lord.” Now, by the natural affection of pity, he laments, beginning thus:

**ALEPH.** “How has the gold become dim; how the finest colour has changed; the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street.” It belongs alike to one grieving and wondering to say, “How has the gold become dim? How has the finest colour changed?” The Jews were gold of the finest colour, from whom salvation comes. Hence the Apostle: “According to the Gospel, indeed, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, most beloved for the fathers’ sake” (Rom. XI).

How did this gold become dim when its colour changed? How did blindness happen to them? How were [Col. 1413B] their eyes darkened, so that they might not see? Moreover, when they were still “stones of the sanctuary,” and the house of the Lord had begun to be built from among them, how were they “scattered at the head of every street”? For they lost both their place and their nation; spiritually cast out from the sanctuary of the Lord, so that they are “scattered at the head of every street”—that is, leaders of wanderers, or of those who seek earthly things, and the most covetous of all the covetous. Bodily also they were scattered among all nations and, captives in individual cities, secured for themselves small streets in which to live.

## Chapter LXXXII. How the Jews were formerly illustrious, with what gold they were clothed, and how they are now earthen vessels

[Col. 1413C] **BETH.** “The illustrious sons of Zion, clothed with the finest gold—how have they been accounted earthen vessels, the work of a potter’s hands?” The “sons of Zion,” I say, were “illustrious and clothed with the finest gold.” How, or how illustrious? Very illustrious, as the Apostle says: “Whose is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. IX).

They were therefore very illustrious. How were they “clothed with the finest gold”? Surely because “the oracles of God were first entrusted to them” (Rom. III). Thus the finest gold is the Law and the Prophets, [543] with which they were clothed only outwardly. For they possessed it not in love of heart but in display of speech. Behold, then, they “were accounted [Col. 1413D] as earthen vessels, the work of a potter’s hands,” shattered by the iron rod of the king established by God the Father, because they would not hear that same king proclaiming the command of the Lord (Ps. II).

## Chapter LXXXIII. On the cruelty of the *lamia*, that is, of that people, compared with the *lamia*, because it killed its own children in saying, “His blood be upon us and upon …”

**GIMEL.** “Even the *lamiae* have bared the breast and nursed their young; the daughter of my people is cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness.” A *lamia* is a monstrous creature, so called from tearing (*laniando*). Yet it has a natural affection for its offspring. Therefore he now says: “Even the *lamiae* have bared the breast and nursed [Col. 1414A] their young.” The meaning is: all natures of living creatures—all cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth—even the *lamiae*, which are not so much beasts as monsters, have a natural affection for their offspring.

But “the daughter of my people” is exceedingly “cruel”; she did not so much as bare her breast to her most unhappy young. To what, then, can she be compared? There is one creature, the ostrich, which has feathers in the likeness of a bird, yet is not raised high above the earth. It is of such great and forgetful cruelty that it leaves behind its eggs, cast out in the dust. Like this is the daughter of my people: possessing indeed an appearance of virtue, yet not possessing the power to fly on high; with cruel mind forgetting in the dust of destruction the simple common people whom she should have cherished for eternal salvation.

Too little has been said for the comparison; but there was no other monster or creature that could display a likeness of all her cruelty. For the daughter of my people not only leaves her descendants as the ostrich leaves its eggs, but moreover kills them, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII).

**DALETH.** “The tongue of the nursing child clung to its palate in thirst. Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them.”

**PHE.** “Those who feasted delicately perished in the streets; those who were reared in scarlet embraced dung.” These things befell the wretched Jews both bodily and spiritually. Before they were born, as was said above, the blood of Christ was left to them as an inheritance by their cruel mother, the Synagogue. Let us read of the destruction of wretched Jerusalem, and [Col. 1414C] we shall see that too little is said here for the magnitude of the famine and thirst.

Spiritually, moreover, from that time until today the tongue of the nursing child clings “to its palate in thirst,” and there is no one to break bread for the little ones who ask. For they suffer excessive hunger and thirst for hearing the word of God—not because they desire the word of God, but because they prefer to perish rather than break for themselves the bread of the Scriptures and live from the marrow of spiritual understanding. Formerly “they feasted delicately and were reared in scarlet,” as sons of the kingdom and beloved for the faith of the fathers; but now they perish in the ways, opposed by evil spirits, while they embrace dung—that is, put their trust in fleshly ceremonies, which the Apostle also calls loss and reckons as dung (Phil. III).

## Chapter LXXXIV. How the iniquity of that people became greater than the sin of the Sodomites; and how it is said, “They did not lay hands upon her”

[Col. 1414D] **VAU.** “The iniquity of the daughter of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and no hands were laid upon her.” It plainly became greater: greater in guilt and greater in punishment. For how far did the iniquity of the Sodomites proceed? “And no hands,” he says, “were laid upon her.” We read that, while the Lord was lodging with righteous Lot, they surrounded the house, from youth to old age, the whole people together, and said: “Bring out the men here, that we may know them” (Gen. XIX). Great iniquity indeed; but [Col. 1415A] “they did not lay hands upon her”—that is, the crime did not proceed to the accomplishment of the deed.

But how far did the iniquity of the people of my city proceed? When the Lord was lodging there and had celebrated the Passover, they surrounded Him, coming out with swords and clubs (Matt. XXVI), and laid hands upon Him. That is, they seized Him whom the hands in Sodom did not seize: they seized Him, I say; apprehended Him, mocked Him, scourged Him, killed Him. Therefore “the iniquity of my people is greater than the sin of the Sodomites,” and consequently its punishment is greater also. For Sodom was overthrown in a moment without hands, but my people, tortured for a long time, were at last overthrown by both their own hands and those of the Romans.

## Chapter LXXXV. How the Nazarites of that nation were whiter than snow and brighter than milk, and whose faces have now been blackened

**ZAIN.** “Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than old ivory, fairer than sapphire.”

**CHETH.** “Their face has become blacker than coals, and they are not recognized in the streets; their skin has clung to their bones, it has dried up and become like wood.” Truly, therefore, “the finest colour has changed.” For how great, how beautiful were the Nazarites of this people? “Nazarites,” that is, its holy ones, were Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Samuel, and David, and all the other saints “who through faith conquered kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises” (Heb. XI).

These Nazarites “were whiter than snow, brighter than milk.” In snow there is only the beauty of whiteness; [Col. 1415C] in milk, together with brightness, there is also sweetness of taste. It was too little, then, that they were whiter than snow unless they were also brighter than milk: that is, it would have been too little for them to be white in their own purity, unless through their teaching they offered those coming to them a taste of eternal sweetness.

But though they were white and bright, by sufferings added thereto they acquired a certain purple redness. For they endured mockeries and beatings, and also chains and prisons. “They were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, slain by the sword.” Therefore they were “redder than old ivory”—the bone, of course, of a chaste creature, which, when it is white, possesses a greater beauty through redness. Finally, they were “fairer than sapphire,” that is, not unworthy of heavenly dwellings. For sapphire has the appearance of a clear sky, [Col. 1415D] and by that very appearance aptly signifies heavenly dwellings.

But now “their face has been blackened beyond coal.” Whose? Namely, the children who, though born from Nazarite fathers, ought themselves by faith to have been Nazarites. They have become blacker than coals, that is, having lost every grace by which they once lived, extinguished and blackened by the dark blindness of the mind. “And they are not,” he says, “recognized in the streets.” For who would deign to recognize them as the seed of Abraham? In the streets, at the crossways, this is sung against them: “You are the seed of Canaan and not of Judah; your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. XVI).

“Their skin has clung to their bones,” that is, they have been given over to the senses of the flesh. For the skin—that is, [Col. 1416A] outward religion—which ought to be white as snow and bright as milk, has dried up and become like wood, having lost the loveliness of its fruits and the beauty of its leaves having fallen away.

**TETH.** “It was better for those slain by the sword than for those killed by hunger, because these wasted away, consumed by the barrenness of the land.”

## Chapter LXXXVI. On the dreadful hunger during the Jewish siege, when “the hands of compassionate women,” he says, “cooked their own children”

**JOD.** “The hands of compassionate women cooked their own children; they became their food in the crushing of the daughter of my people.” Clearly and without hesitation, it “was better,” that is, easier, “for those slain by the sword than for those killed by hunger.” Not only because they suffered death more quickly, but because they escaped the necessity of multiplying their crimes. For what a horror it was that, while they gradually wasted away from hunger, during the very delays of that dreadful consumption, “the hands of compassionate women cooked their own children, and they became their food”! For we read that a certain woman did this, named Mary, noble in family and wealth, who was found at Jerusalem with the rest of the multitude and endured with all the common disaster of the siege [Col. 1416B].

It is a lamentable irony, fitting for mourning, by which he calls compassionate women of this sort who were brutally driven into madness by hunger.

**CAPH.** “The Lord has fulfilled His fury; He has poured out the wrath of His indignation; He has kindled a fire in Zion, and it has devoured her foundations.” Where did the Lord utter these things according to His fury? In Moses, among the many dreadful curses which He threatened with prophetic truth: “The man who is delicate in life and exceedingly luxurious,” he says, “shall look grudgingly upon his brother, and upon the wife who lies in his bosom, lest he give them of the flesh of his children which he will eat, because he has nothing else in the siege and distress with which your enemies shall lay you waste within all your gates” (Deut. XXVIII), etc.
