## Chapter LXXXVII. How they did not believe the prediction that these evils would come upon them; how they cried to His apostles, “Depart, depart, go away”; and how the apostles turned to the nations

**LAMED.** “The kings of the earth and all the inhabitants of the city did not believe that an adversary and enemy would enter through the gates of Jerusalem.”

**MEM.** “Because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in her midst the blood of the righteous.”

**NUN.** “The blind wandered in the streets; they were defiled with blood. And since they could not enter, they held their fringes.” [Col. 1416D] “The kings of the earth” and the rulers who stood and assembled against the Lord and against His Christ (Ps. II)—indeed, “the inhabitants of the city also did not believe”—that because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, who shed in her midst the blood of the righteous, “an adversary and enemy would enter through the gates of Jerusalem.”

They did not believe, I say, when they heard Him preach to them: “That upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel unto the blood of Zacharias, son of Barachias, whom you killed between the temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you, all these things shall come upon this generation” (Matt. XXIII). Again, when they heard that He had wept over the city and said: “For days shall come upon thee, and thine enemies shall surround thee with a rampart” (Luke XIX), etc., they did not believe.

It is too little to say that they did not believe: they also killed Him, and by killing Him filled up the measure of their fathers. Therefore they wandered, blind, in the streets, so that, after the example of the Sodomites, they could not find the door (Gen. XIX), because they were defiled by the blood of Him who says: “I am the door” (John X). And since they could not, it is understood, seize Him, they held their fringes: that is, since they did not grasp [Col. 1417B] true righteousness, they followed empty ceremonies, vain and ragged righteousnesses of the flesh.

**SAMECH.** “Depart, you defiled ones, they cried to them; depart, go away, do not touch. For they quarrelled and were moved, and they said: He shall no longer dwell among them.” Therefore they wandered blind in the streets, defiled with blood, because after they had shed the blood of the prophets and of the Lord of the prophets Himself, they cried out against the prophets, sages, and scribes whom He sent to them (Matt. XXIII). They cried out, I say, while persecuting them from city to city; and they quarrelled and were stirred up, raising seditions against Christ’s apostles, and said: “Depart, you defiled ones; depart, go away, do not touch; do not speak to us in this name.”

They said this among the nations; and by saying it they caused them to go to the nations [Col. 1417C] and to say to them: “To you it was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken; but since you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts XIII). Therefore, he says, He shall no longer dwell among them, so that, as He departs, He says: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

## Chapter LXXXVIII. How the face of the Lord divided them during the siege because of internal discord, since they had chosen Barabbas, the author of sedition, for themselves and crucified Christ; whom at last the remnant of Israel, recognizing Him, will say: “They made our steps slippery; Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, was taken in our sins”

[Col. 1417D] **PHE.** “The face of the Lord has divided them; He will no longer regard them. They did not reverence the faces of the priests, nor have pity upon the elders.” Because of these things “the face of the Lord”—the angry face, such as, according to the Psalmist, is the countenance of the Lord against those who do evil (Ps. XXXV)—“divided them”; divided them, I say, by manifold division against themselves.

Before the Roman enemy entered through the gates of Jerusalem, while they were still shut in, they tore themselves apart within by a threefold war, as Josephus relates. To one who reads that miserable tragedy, it is quite clear how truly this was said: “They did not reverence the faces of the priests, nor have pity upon the elders.” “He will no longer,” he says—God is understood—“regard them,” but will permit [Col. 1418A] them, divided by their own seditions, to perish. And rightly so: for, when the choice was given to them, they requested that Barabbas, the author of sedition, should be released to them, while they killed their peaceful king.

**AIN.** “While we still stood, our eyes failed, looking for our vain help, when we watched attentively for a nation that could not save us.”

**ZADI.** “They made our steps slippery in the way of our streets; our end drew near, our days were fulfilled, because our end came.” Let at least the remnant of Israel say this; let them say it, that they may be converted and saved. What wonder if, after we fell by killing Christ the Lord, “the face of the Lord divided us” thus? Indeed, even “while we still stood,” before we had accomplished our ruin in His death, “our eyes” often failed us, having turned away from the Lord our God “toward our vain help,” watching attentively “for a nation that could not save us.”

For example, we hoped in Egypt, putting confidence in horses and riders; we also worshipped Baal and calves as God. In this way “they made our steps slippery,” and we limped between two sides “in the way of our streets,” that is, in licentious idolatry full of crimes. For streets are broad ways and signify the wandering and licentious rite of idolatry. Therefore our end drew near; therefore our days were fulfilled; and the Lord is righteous, who did these things to us.

**COPH.** “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven; they pursued us upon the mountains, they lay in wait for us in the wilderness.” “Our end,” I say, came—and it came swiftly [Col. 1418C]; this did not happen after a long time. “For what were our persecutors swifter than, if not our sins?” Moreover, God speaks to Cain concerning the swiftness of pursuing sin: “If thou doest well, shalt thou not receive? But if thou doest ill, sin will immediately be present at the door” (Gen. IV).

Thus “our persecutors,” that is, our sins, “were swifter than the eagles of heaven,” because when they had been committed, they were immediately present at the door, so that no escape was open anywhere. “They pursued us upon the mountains; they lay in wait for us in the wilderness.” Therefore the Psalmist says: “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains” (Ps. LXXIV)—the place of escape is understood—“for God is judge” (ibid.). By mountains he metaphorically signifies the pride of sinners; by the wilderness, abandonment by God, according to His own words: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

**RESCH.** “Christ the Lord, the breath of our mouth, was taken in our sins; to whom we said: In thy shadow we shall live among the nations.” What, finally, is the sum of our swift persecutors, of our sins swiftly pursuing us? Surely the death of Christ the Lord: for He was taken in our sins, because through our crime He was led to death. And Him to whom we said, before He came, “In Thy shadow we shall live among the nations”—that is, in Thy grace we shall be saved and distinguished from every unholy nation, for we read this and things like it concerning Him in the Scriptures—Him, I say, we seized in our sins and handed over to death.

By doing this we killed ourselves. For Christ the Lord Himself is the breath of our mouth: the Breath, I say, without whom there is nowhere life, nowhere salvation, and without whom whatever we read or suppose that we know from the Law or the Prophets is dead and without soul.

## Chapter LXXXIX. How he concludes all the Lamentations with the good hope of consolation, saying ironically, “Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom; thy iniquity is completed,” etc.; by Edom signifying all earthly people who inflict persecution, and by Zion all the elect who endure it

**SCHIN.** “Rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom, who dwellest in the land of Uz. The cup shall come to thee also; thou shalt be drunken and made naked.”

**THAU.** “Thy iniquity is completed, O daughter of Zion; He shall no longer cause thee to be carried away. He has visited thy iniquity, O daughter of Edom; He has uncovered thy sins.” [Col. 1419B]

The conclusion of the Lamentations refreshes the lamenter with the good hope of consolation: both through the impending and wholly certain vengeance upon the enemies, and through the visitation and eternal liberation of holy Zion, which had been captive.

“Rejoice,” he says, “and be glad, O daughter of Edom, who dwellest in the land of Uz.” By the name Edom, which means “earthly” or “bloody,” he signifies all enemies of heavenly Jerusalem, because they are truly earthly. Thus the Psalmist, lamenting in the same Spirit as this writer: “By the rivers [Col. 1420A] of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion” (Ps. CXXXVI), etc., signifies the enemies of that same Zion by this same name, saying to the Lord: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: Empty her, empty her, even to her foundation” (ibid.).

“Rejoice,” he says, “and be glad, O daughter of Edom, who dwellest in the land of Uz”; that is, you who have an earthly foundation, who receive your consolation here. For Uz means “comforter.” This is grave irony. For why should you rejoice and be glad, O daughter of Edom? Because “the cup of the wrath of God shall also come to thee, by which thou shalt be made drunken and naked.” For thou shalt drink the gall of everlasting bitterness and shalt be dishonoured in eternal shame.

“But thy iniquity is completed, O daughter of Zion”: that is, thy punishment or captivity [Col. 1420B] is temporal; “He shall no longer cause thee to be carried away,” this present-worldly deportation or captivity having ended. “He has visited thy iniquity”—namely, God—O “daughter of Edom; He has uncovered thy sins.” The repetition confirms the condemnation and disgrace of Edom.

Here the prophet designates the enemies of the heavenly Jerusalem once and again by Edom, whereas, if he attended only to the historical narrative, he should rather have named Babylon. The Psalmist, however, first signifies those same enemies of Jerusalem by Edom, saying: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom”; then by Babylon, saying: “Blessed is he who shall repay thee thy repayment” (ibid.).

# The Forty-Two Books of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, On the Trinity and Its Works: Commentaries on the Prophet Ezekiel

## Book One. Ezekiel I–XII

[Col. 1419]

[546] ## Chapter I. How, amid the affliction of the city, consoling visions of the future kingdom of God increased among the holy prophets

In this fifth age of the world, which we entered in the preceding volume, prophetic visions of the kingdom of God become more frequent among the saints captive in Babylon. Their brightness announces that it will come more swiftly, just as, when dawn whitens, no one can doubt that the sun is near. For the Holy Spirit no longer speaks into the ears of the prophets only by words, as before; He also paints beforehand with the finger of God—which He Himself is—certain images by which He may more familiarly instruct the eyes of those who see.

For example: before this captivity, where was the Son of Man seen coming in the clouds of heaven, so that kingdom and honour might be given to Him, and all peoples, tribes, and languages might serve Him? O venerable order of the kingdom of God! O reasonable and seasonable consolation of God the King!

This kingdom does not come with haste, as does the kingdom of this world, of which it has most rightly been said: “An inheritance hurried after at the beginning shall lack blessing in its latter end” (Prov. XX). Cain, seeker of the earth, hastened to build a city and call its name after his son Enoch, after killing his brother Abel (Gen. IV). From that time the children of this age hastened to reign, until the flood came and destroyed them all.

After this Nimrod arose, mighty on the earth and a strong hunter before the Lord; and he reigned in haste. The beginning of his kingdom was this very place of which we now speak: Babylon (Gen. X). In it there was kingship, and now the Lord had placed the iron yoke of its king Nebuchadnezzar upon the neck of all nations (Jer. XI). But meanwhile the kingdom of God was coming slowly; and its citizens, in hope of it, departed from their land and kindred, “not having received the promises, but beholding them afar off and greeting them, and confessing that they are strangers and pilgrims upon the earth” (Heb. XI).

Now, when the kingdom of the world was especially strengthened, the citizens of the kingdom of God were strangers and pilgrims—indeed captives—and, reminded by the present place of their captivity, they said: “By the waters of Babylon we sat there and wept, when we remembered Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. CXXXVI), etc.

## Chapter II. That the prophet Ezekiel is difficult, and that in the first vision one should rightly inquire how the four living creatures are one living creature

Therefore, receiving the revelations of the kingdom of God with due reverence, let us approach the prophet Ezekiel, whose difficulty, as blessed Jerome says, is attested by the tradition of the Hebrews. For among them, unless someone has reached the age of priestly ministry—that is, completed his thirtieth year—he is not permitted to read either the beginning of Genesis, or the Song of Songs, or the beginning and end of this volume, so that the full maturity of human nature may attain to perfect knowledge and mystical understandings.

Jerome likewise says: “We have spoken more fully concerning this vision, because it is obscure and is variously expounded by many.” Blessed Pope Gregory also, according to the fullness of the grace granted to him, spoke most fully on the prophecy from the stated—that is, thirtieth—year down to the passage: “And thou, take for thyself an iron pan and set it as an iron wall between thee and the city” (Ezek. IV).

Since such great men have spoken concerning this vision, and before them it was variously expounded by many, and since—as they themselves confess—it contains much obscurity, what shall we do? We are held by the delight of our undertaking, so that even in this most difficult prophet we are not weary of lingering, as though before a hardship, while seeking testimonies to the glory of Christ, the Son of God. For we confess that no small part of obscurity remains, which still requires more diligent elucidation.

What is that? Surely, the likeness of the four living creatures. In what respect does this likeness still contain any obscurity or difficulty? Namely, in this: they are called both four living creatures and one living creature. For thus, after many things, we read in the prophecy of the sixth year: “This is the living creature which I saw by the river Chebar. And when the Cherubim walked, the wheels also went beside them” (Ezek. X). And afterwards: “This is the living creature which I saw beneath the God of Israel by the river Chebar, and I understood that they were Cherubim. Each had four faces, and each four wings, and beneath their wings the likeness of a human hand; and the likeness of their faces was the same faces [547] which I had seen by the river Chebar” (ibid.).

Therefore we desire, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, to seek these living creatures, which are both four and one, fearing nothing if, in a vision variously expounded by many because of its own obscurity, we increase the variety or number of interpretations. For the very living creature whom we seek, once found, is such and so great that by its name alone, or by its authority, it can defend our littleness, if need be, against the contempt or indignation of all who shall see these things.

## Chapter III. Concerning the prophet himself: how he bore the type of the Son of God whose vision he saw; what the whirlwind is, what the great cloud is, what the enfolding fire is, and what the other accompanying things are
[Col. 1422C] **(CHAPTER I.)** “And I saw, and behold, a storm-wind was coming from the north, and a great cloud, and enfolding fire, and brightness around it. And from its midst something like the appearance of electrum—that is, from the midst of the fire—and from their midst the likeness of four living creatures; and this was their appearance: the likeness of a man was in them; and each had four faces, and each four wings; and their legs were straight legs, and the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot, and sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.”

This seer, who now says in his own, or first, person, “And I saw,” had previously spoken of himself in the third person: “And the hand of the Lord came upon him there.” Yet before this he had also said in the first person: “The heavens were opened, and I saw [Col. 1422D] visions of God.” Thus he preserves truth joined with humility: in humility he says, “the hand of the Lord came upon him,” while for the necessary truth of the matter he says, “and I saw visions of God.”

Moreover, when he says “visions of God,” we rightly and fittingly understand the Son, God from God; for nothing more readily presents itself to the mind than that these visions pertain to the very person of the Son of God, whom he also signifies by name. For *Ezekiel* is interpreted “strength of God.” And *Buzi* is interpreted “despised” or “rejected.” Rightly, therefore, the Son of God is designated through Ezekiel, the priest, son of Buzi: for although he is the strength of God, “a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109 [Vulgate]), according to the flesh he is the son of a contemptible people—the Jewish people—held in contempt because it despised its own Son. [Col. 1423A]

These visions of God, therefore, are revelations of the coming of Christ, the Son of God. In this prophet he is most fittingly called in one place one living creature, in another four living creatures, namely because of the four mysteries of his Gospel necessary for us, each of which must later be recognized in its proper form. For one who is to behold the coming of this Son of God, the reason why it was necessary for him to come to us is fittingly set forth beforehand. “And behold,” he says, “a storm-wind was coming from the north,” and so forth.

The storm-wind came from the north when the devil, cold toward the love of God, blew forth and by the whirlwind of temptation cast down the human race, in its first parents, from the state of blessedness. Then came “a great cloud,” that is, the blindness of the same human race, [Col. 1423B] in which man, enveloped and made God’s enemy, fell away from the vision of his face. After this came “enfolding fire,” that is, the condemnation which receives sinners after this life and envelops them in everlasting horror.

Nevertheless, “there was brightness around it,” he says, because, indeed, even in that justly inflicted wrath, the Godhead did not cease to shine, pursuing its creature and calling it back to knowledge of himself through many warnings and signs. For these reasons the Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2), God and man, Jesus Christ, had necessarily to come to us.

Accordingly there follows: “But from its midst something like the appearance of electrum,” that is, from the midst of the fire. Electrum, a most precious substance composed of gold and silver, is the one and same person of the aforesaid Mediator between God and men: in him the precious [Col. 1423C] Godhead is as gold, while our humanity in him is like the purest silver. Such is the appearance of electrum “from the midst of the fire,” because the Mediator between God and men, condemned and dead on our account, rose victorious from hell in this form.

“And from their midst”—namely, from the wind or whirlwind, the cloud and fire, and the brightness flashing round about—came “the likeness of four living creatures.” O beholder of God’s visions: if, as you yourself will say later after much discourse, the living creature is one, how do you count four? He says: “And this was their appearance: the likeness of a man was in them; and each had four faces, and each four wings.” It is as though he said: The likeness of a man—Jesus Christ, the Son of God—was indeed one; a likeness, I say, and not yet the reality, for he was not yet by nature the Son of Man. But this “one” had “four [Col. 1423D] faces and four wings”—faces and wings which no one hoping for the vision of God may fail to know.

What, then, are these? The first is the incarnation or birth of the same man, Jesus Christ the Son of God; the second, his passion; the third, his resurrection; the fourth, his ascension or session at the right hand of the Father. We may not fail to see these faces, as the apostolic Creed of the catholic confession teaches:

“I believe,” it says, “in God the Father almighty, creator of heaven and earth.” There immediately follows: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” This is the one living creature; this is the one man of whom he now says, “the likeness of a man was in them.”—“Who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary.” [Col. 1424A] This is the first face. “He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried; he descended into hell.” This is the second face. “On the third day he rose from the dead.” This is the third face. “He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” This is the fourth face.

So many faces, and just as many wings, belong to this one. Yet the faces and the wings are the same things. They are faces because they can be known through faith and must be known; they are wings because they cannot be comprehended by human reason. “Their legs were straight legs,” because their course is the righteousness of God, and avails unto righteousness for everyone who believes. For what could be straighter or more just than that Christ was obedient to the Father in all these things? Therefore he immediately adds: [Col. 1424B] “And the sole of their feet was like the sole of a calf’s foot.” By the command of the Law, a calf used to be offered for the sin of the people, or of the priest and the people together. Thus the sole of their foot, like “the sole of a calf’s foot,” that is, their final benefit, is the remission of the sins of the whole world.

“And sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze.” Let us recall that after our Redeemer was incarnate and suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, he made magnificent gifts sparkle forth for humankind, when “suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where the apostles were sitting; and divided tongues, as of fire, appeared to them” (Acts 2). Let us recall this, I say, and we shall know what he meant by “sparks like the appearance [Col. 1424C] of glowing bronze.” For those gifts were “sparks like the appearance of glowing bronze,” since with the heat of fiery love they gave forth the far-audible ringing sound of evangelical preaching.

548 **CHAPTER IV. What it means for the faces and wings to be in four parts, for the wings themselves to be joined to one another, and for it to say: “They did not turn back when they went.”**

“And the hands of a man were under their wings, in their four parts. And they had faces and wings in four parts; and their wings were joined one to another. They did not turn back when they went, but each went straight before its face.”

We now know their faces in part; we follow their wings by hope. For we hope that what we now see through a glass, in an enigma, we shall at last see face to face. We touch the hands through the intimacy of love; by these hands we are also drawn, so that through faith and hope, with that same love as the worker, we may run after the faces and wings. “Under the wings,” he says, “were the hands of a man in four parts,” because in the four mysteries of the Gospel already mentioned, we could not behold by faith the height of the divine counsel unless love, bending down to us, caressed us by a familiar touch. [Col. 1424D]

“And their wings were joined one to another,” because these things are so joined and associated with one another that it profits nothing to have faith in one unless you also believe the other. For example: what does it profit to believe that Christ suffered for the salvation of the human race unless one also believes that he was born of the incorrupt Virgin?

“They did not turn back,” he says, “when they went, but each went straight before its face.” It is true, and must be believed with sound faith, that after they have proceeded once, they will not return again. For what the most impious heresy has dared to rave cannot occur: that Christ should be born again, suffer again, rise again, and ascend into heaven again. Rather, as the Apostle says: “Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6). Again:

“Nor [does he offer] himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy places every year with blood not his own; otherwise he would have had to suffer frequently from the foundation of the world. But now once, at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the destruction of sin through his sacrifice. And as it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this judgment, so also Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many; a second time, without sin, he will appear to those who await him in faith for salvation” (Heb. 9). [Col. 1425A–B]

Therefore each went straight before its face and did not turn back, because each of the things we have mentioned happened once and shall not be repeated.

**CHAPTER V. What the face of a man, the face of a lion, [Col. 1425C] the face of a calf, and the face of a flying eagle signify in the one Christ; why the lion’s face is on the right, the calf’s face on the left, and the eagle’s face above.**

“Now the likeness of their faces was the face of a man, and the face of a lion on the right of all four; but the face of an ox was on the left of all four, and the face of an eagle above all four. And their faces and their wings were stretched out above.”

This is what we said a little earlier: when we have believed—and therefore also spoken (Ps. 115 [Vulgate])—that Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, was conceived of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary, then we behold the face of a true man: conceived and born not in phantasm, but in the reality of flesh without sin.

When likewise we believe and confess that he suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, was buried, and descended into hell, we undoubtedly contemplate the face of the calf: an immaculate calf, not such as we understand according to the letter, but according to the spirit of the Law. The Lord says to Moses: “If the anointed priest sins, causing the people to offend, he shall offer to the Lord for his sin an immaculate calf” (Lev. 4), and so forth—matters of which we have spoken more fully elsewhere, as far as we were able. [Col. 1425D]

When, no less, we believe and confess that on the third day he rose from the dead, we surely grasp, with trembling faith and faithful trembling, the face of the most mighty lion, of whom the patriarch Jacob says: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness. Who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49).

Finally, when we believe and confess [Col. 1426A] that “he ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead,” behold: this is for us “the face of the eagle,” whom a cloud received from human sight, as he himself said: “And no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3).

Meanwhile, it should be noted that he beholds the lion’s face on the right and the ox’s face on the left of all four—that is, of the one Mediator between God and men, in whom these four are said to be. For the right hand commonly signifies prosperity and the left adversity. “The face of the lion, therefore, is on the right,” because the happiness of his resurrection is great; “but the face of the ox is on the left,” because the humility of his passion was harsh and laborious for him, as he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26); and: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (ibid.). [Col. 1426B]

The face of the eagle is above because we joyfully see that he ascended into heaven, as the Apostle says: “We see the Lord Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour” (Heb. 2), and so forth. Moreover, his coming from there to judge the living and the dead pertains to the eagle’s face, which, as natural philosophers report, is accustomed to judge its young. It exposes each to the rays of the sun; the one that gazes freely upon the sun it recognizes as of its own kind, while the one that cannot endure the sun with eyes dazzled and groping, it condemns and rejects as the adulterous blemish of its own stock.

So this one who ascended into heaven, when he comes from there to judge the living and the dead, will examine each and every one of us, brought before that terrible tribunal of his own or his Father’s majesty. Whoever the glory of the Godhead shall strike back according to his conscience, he will deliver to unquenchable fire; but whoever that glory judges worthy of its gaze, it will place among that glorious and blessed company of the children of God. [Col. 1426C]

**CHAPTER VI. Why the order of the living creatures is not the same in the Apocalypse; from what point of view John there set the lion’s face first, while the prophet here set the face of a man first; and in what sense this prophet says that each had four wings, while John says that the individual living creatures had six wings.**

[Col. 1426D] Here it is rightly asked why the order of these four living creatures is not the same in the Apocalypse. For that Scripture says: “And the first living creature was like a lion; and the second living creature was like a calf; and the third living creature had a face like that of a man; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” (Rev. 4). It is therefore asked what such a different order means.

First we say that there is nothing contradictory in its saying “the first, second, and third living creature.” For 549 this prophet adds nothing of that kind of designation, but only says: “The likeness of their faces was the face of a man and the face of a lion on the right,” and so forth. Yet since he first places the likeness of a man, let it be understood as having the same force as if he said, “the first face was that of a man, and the second the face of a lion or calf.”

Both orders are valid, and neither is contrary to the other, though they proceed from different points of view: John’s from the perspective of the Old Testament, this prophet’s from the perspective of the event to be accomplished. For in the writings of Moses the lawgiver, the one and same Mediator between God and men is called first a lion, then a man. First, I say, he is called a lion, then a calf, then a man, then an eagle through Moses. [Col. 1427A]

For in Genesis the patriarch Jacob says: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. Resting, you lay down like a lion and like a lioness” (Gen. 49). In Leviticus, however, he is undoubtedly figured by the calf that is commanded to be sacrificed for sin and carried outside the camp and burned (Lev. 9). In Deuteronomy, the man is promised in the truth of flesh and of the whole human nature, when Moses himself says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me; him you shall hear, as you asked of the Lord your God at Horeb” (Deut. 18).

For one who considers the grounds of that request truly understands clearly from Exodus that this saying and promise mean that God would become man, so that man might speak with him. Finally, in the Song of Deuteronomy he is compared to an eagle: “As an eagle provokes its young to fly and hovers over them, it spread its wings and took them up and bore them upon its shoulders” (Deut. 32). This is rightly understood so that, when he says, “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3), [Col. 1427B–C] we understand that it benefits us if he does for us what an eagle does, “provoking its young to fly and hovering over them”: that he carry us upon his shoulders to the place where we cannot ascend, and carry us upon the wings of his Godhead.

Therefore he who said, “the first living creature was like a lion,” spoke truly, because thus the event had been foretold; and this prophet, who placed the face of a man first, acted no less rightly, because thus the event was to be fulfilled. If you weigh the matter properly, there is a beautiful rivalry, as though two persons were outdoing one another in honour: John, writing of the New Testament, preserves the sacred order of Old Testament Scripture, while this prophet, writing of the Old Testament, observes the most sacred accomplishment and order of evangelical newness.

It is also asked how this prophet can say, “each had four faces and four wings,” whereas John says that the four individual living creatures each had six wings. The brief answer is that the individual faces each have individual wings, and, in the same sense, six wings: because in each mystery of Christ the Son of God there is one and the same excellence, one flight, one Spirit, one Godhead, one Word through whom all things were made in six days. [Col. 1427D]

**CHAPTER VII. Why holy Church rightly chose to receive no more than four Evangelists, and which face most suitably corresponds to each Evangelist.**

Therefore, as we proposed to investigate above, we think that we have found that there is both one living creature and four living creatures: that is, there is one Christ and four principal mysteries of Christ, whose faces no Christian may be ignorant of, even though one cannot comprehend their flight. Hence the zeal and diligence of holy Church, worthy indeed of praise and reverence, which refused to have more Evangelists than this number.

For many besides these wrote Gospels, as Luke himself testifies, saying: “Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the events fulfilled among us, as those who from the beginning themselves saw them and were ministers [Col. 1428A] delivered them to us, it seemed good also to me, having carefully traced all things from the beginning, to write them to you in order, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the truth of the words in which you have been instructed” (Luke 1).

Thus, lest a crowd of writers composing upon so majestic a subject according to their own—that is, human—understanding should make it cheap, and lest the multitude of sayings or events should burden the minds and ears of humankind to the point of weariness by filling them up, the discriminating wisdom of the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the Church, set a limit. It judged the four-horse chariot of the Evangelists sufficient for the Gospel word of Christ—God and man, priest and king—which was to run through the world.

For it was not human appointment but God’s calling that prepared these men, and, as though in mirrors of grace, impressed in them the four faces of this prophetic truth. Thus, in Matthew the face of a man is recognized; in Mark, the face of a lion; in Luke, the face of a calf; in John, the face of a flying eagle. This is known to almost everyone, although great teachers have said different things concerning Matthew and Mark: some assign the face of a man to Matthew and the face of a lion to Mark, whereas others, conversely, assign the lion’s face to Matthew and the face of a man to Mark. [Col. 1428B–C]

Not only the Evangelists, but every one of the faithful according to his measure, can imitate these faces by pursuing with faith prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. For a Christian to be prudent—that is, to have the face of Christ the man—to be temperate, crucifying his flesh with its vices and desires—that plainly is to have the face of a calf—to be strong in adversities, that is to have the face of a lion; and to keep justice, that is to have the face of a flying eagle.

**CHAPTER VIII. How the faces and wings of the living creatures are stretched out above; what the two wings are and how they are joined; how they cover their bodies; and how the living creatures themselves are said to have gone, or to go, wherever the impulse of the spirit was, and not to turn back.**

“And their faces and their wings were stretched out above. Two wings of each were joined together, and two covered their bodies.” The faces and wings of the living creatures are stretched out above because they are neither from the earth nor speak of the earth, but are from above and tend upward. They call the mind of the rational human being upward, that it may despise whatever is below and say: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). [Col. 1428D]

The two wings of each that are joined, and the two that cover their bodies, are the same: all the lofty-sounding Scriptures of the divine Testaments that bear witness to evangelical faith. All these are joined together and sound in harmony for the opening of faith to believers. Yet they are also joined for covering and closing it to unbelievers, as the Apostle says: “And even if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, lest the illumination of the Gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine forth” (2 Cor. 4). [Col. 1429A]

“And each of them walked straight before its face. Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went; nor did they turn back when they walked.” Above he also said that they did not turn back 550 when they went, but that each went straight before its face. We might suppose that the repetition was made only to confirm the point, were it not for the inserted phrase—which we do not think idle—“wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went.”

The phrase describes, surely, a certain sharpness in those who advance, steadfastness in those who fight, and the triumphant glory of those who conquer. For who does not know that the mysteries of the Gospel began to advance through the world under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, and that the heralds of the Gospel could advance only “wherever the impulse of the spirit was”? Otherwise, unless they were borne onward by the most mighty impulse of the Spirit, the obstacles raised by opponents were so great that they would have advanced in vain and returned empty from their walking.

But he who is himself man and God, priest and king, says to his four-horse chariots, to his living creatures: “When they bring you before synagogues and magistrates and authorities, do not be anxious how or what you shall answer, or what you shall say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that hour what you ought to say” (Luke 12). Again: “For it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). [Col. 1429B–C]

Therefore, “wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went, and they did not turn back when they walked”: that is, with the Holy Spirit as the leader and commander in war, when they fought against the devil, the prince of the world, they did not return without the result of victory. Indeed, this is what God says through another prophet, speaking of his word: “It shall not return to me empty, but shall do whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things for which I sent it” (Isa. 5 [citation as printed]).

**CHAPTER IX. How the appearance of the living creatures is like the appearance of burning coals of fire; what that fire is; and how lightning went out from the fire.**

“And the likeness of the living creatures: their appearance was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps. This was a vision moving back and forth in the midst of the living creatures: the brightness of fire, and lightning going forth from the fire.”

The likeness of the living creatures is good, having a good effect in both respects: on one side burning like the appearance of glowing coals, on the other illuminating like the appearance of lamps. Nothing is truer, nothing more certain and firm in the Christian faith. For what do we attain by directing ourselves toward the appearance of such living creatures? What do we receive by believing in the one Jesus Christ, Son of God, conceived and born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary; then suffering, crucified, dead and buried; then raised from the dead on the third day by his own power; then raised above the heavens to sit with the Father’s majesty? [Col. 1429D–1430A]

What, I say, do we attain or receive by beholding these faces, believing and confessing these things? Surely the twofold gift of the Holy Spirit: the first is remission of sins; the second is the distribution of diverse graces. At the first beholding of these faces—that is, at the first confession of Christ—when we are baptized, we receive remission of sins; and there the appearance of the living creatures is for us “like burning coals of fire,” for all the stains of earlier offences are burned and consumed there.

Then, at the second beholding of the same faces, when we receive the laying on of hands, a grace apportioned among individuals is bestowed as the Holy Spirit wills; and there they are for us “like the appearance of lamps.” For each one of us shines in the grace he has received: one in faith, another in a word of wisdom or knowledge, another in the working of miracles (1 Cor. 12). The “likeness of the appearance of the living creatures” is therefore good and effective.

But what, or in what manner, was—or rather, what is—“this vision moving back and forth in the midst of the four living creatures: the brightness of fire, and lightning going forth from the fire”? Brightness brings the serene beauty of light; lightning going forth brings troublesome fear. Therefore, “the brightness of fire” is the radiant serenity of love, while “the lightning going forth” is the severity of the fear of God. In order or in action, love comes first and fear afterward. [Col. 1430B–C]

Thus, because from the one and same contemplation of these living creatures the fire of love shines and the punitive lightning of fear goes forth—which perfect love casts out (1 John 4)—it was rightly said: “This was a vision moving back and forth in the midst of the four living creatures.” For as long as we are in this mortal body, such a vision moves back and forth in every one of us: the soul, contemplating God and heavenly glory, is now expanded by love, now constrained by fear, from the one and same fire of heavenly desire.

For although it has greatly progressed in love, which when perfect casts out servile fear, it is nevertheless not without that fear of which it is written: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever” (Ps. 18 [Vulgate]). This fear makes a person loving, reverent, and devout; no longer indeed a slave in fear, but rejoicing with trembling. For although one loves and rejoices in loving, still no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred (Eccl. 9). And even if he knows, according to the saying, “The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8), he nevertheless does not presume that he knows; but, knowing, in a certain manner does not know, and not knowing, in some manner knows. [Col. 1430D]

**CHAPTER X. When the living creatures return in the likeness of flashing lightning, although it was said above that “they did not return.”**

“And the living creatures went and returned in the likeness of flashing lightning.”—“They returned,” he says. Yet above he said once and again that “they did not return.” Does he affirm the very thing he denied? Certainly not; rather, there are different kinds of returning. We have spoken above of two ways in which they do not return; now we must say in what way, or ways, they do return.

First, no believer is unaware that these living creatures will then return in the likeness of flashing lightning, when he comes with great power and majesty to judge the world, as he says: “For as lightning goes forth from the east and appears as far as the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be” (Luke 11; Matt. 24). [Col. 1431A]

Then, I say, these living creatures will return. For then, to convict the ungodly and gladden the godly, it will become manifest to all how truly the one and same Mediator between God and men, Christ, is man, calf, lion, and eagle: that is, how truly, although he was God, he assumed flesh, suffered for the whole world, rose again, and ascended into heaven.

Further, it should be known that when we are baptized, or baptize, in the name of Christ Jesus, and likewise when we celebrate on the holy altar the most sacred mystery of his body and blood, these living creatures undoubtedly return to us in invisible presence. For the Apostle speaks of their return according to the sacrament of baptism: “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). [Col. 1431B–C]

And concerning their return according to the sacrament of his body and blood, the same Apostle says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11). 551 Thus these living creatures also return: their return or presence is invisible, but their act or sacrament is visible. Hence he says: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

**CHAPTER XI. What is the one wheel appearing beside the living creatures; what its four faces are; what is meant by “like the appearance of the sea”; how the four have one likeness; and how there is a wheel within a wheel.**
> “And as I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures, having four faces; [Col. 1431D] and the appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the appearance of the sea. And the four had one likeness, and their appearance and works were as though a wheel were within a wheel.”
>
> The one wheel in this place is the whole holy Scripture of the Old Testament, of which one may truly say with the Psalmist: “The sound of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 76). For indeed God thunders from it, testifying to the whole world and not permitting the authority of the four living creatures to remain hidden. Therefore, “as I looked,” he says, “at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures.” Nothing is truer. For when we truly look upon these living creatures—that is, when we faithfully believe the four mysteries of evangelical faith already mentioned—the Scripture of the holy Law and Prophets becomes manifest and intelligible, [Col. 1432A] wholly perfected in the form of a wheel, as when one brings a very bright lamp near some obscure object.
>
> For the more closely, in wishing to understand the Law and Prophets, you apply these faces—the faces of Christ—the more beautiful and perfect you will find this wheel in contemplating it, and in admiring it you will rejoice. Conversely, the more negligently or sluggishly you look upon these living creatures, the more dull and lifeless you will suppose this wheel to be. Thus the Jews, because they do not look upon these living creatures, make this wheel seem to themselves almost dead and ignoble—not because it is so, but because the life within it can be seen or found only in Christ, according to these living creatures. Hence the Apostle says: “Even to this day the same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is removed in Christ” (1 Cor. 3).
>
> Thus, when he says here, “as I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared,” it is as if he said: Unless I had looked at the living creatures, that wheel would not have appeared to me. It appeared upon the earth beside the living creatures, as though saying: No one will look upon me unless he looks upon these living creatures; I shall appear to no one unless these living creatures have appeared to him. Why, moreover, was “upon the earth” added, unless because they had formerly lain hidden, and still, wherever these living creatures are not looked upon, they lie hidden beneath the earth, beneath Jewish earthliness?
>
> Or “upon the earth” means that the wheel now appears over all the earth, whereas formerly, so that it might not run abroad, it was restrained within Judaea alone. Thus is fulfilled what the Psalmist said: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and let your glory be over all the earth” [Col. 1432C] (Ps. 107). “Having,” he says, “four faces.” These are the four faces of the living creatures—or rather, as was said above, of the one living creature—and they are precisely, and not otherwise, the four faces of the one wheel. He does not here set out their particular properties in the wheel, but they are the same faces.
>
> For all holy Scripture, the ancient Scripture, both legal and prophetic, is marked out by these four faces—namely, the man, the calf, the lion, and the flying eagle—because whatever it says that is useful for teaching, instructing, and educating every person tends toward this and has this in view: that it may testify to and defend, according to the faith of the Gospel, that Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and human beings, is truly human (1 Tim. 2), truly suffered and died, truly rose from the dead, and truly ascended into heaven.
>
> “And,” he says, [Col. 1432D] “the appearance of the wheels and their workmanship was like the appearance of the sea.” What sort of vision or appearance of the sea do you suppose this is? To those inexperienced and timid of heart it is fearful and hopeless; but to those experienced and steadfast of mind it is so manageable that they do not hesitate to entrust themselves to frail timber in order to overcome the height of the waves and the violence of the mighty deep. Then, if a gentle breeze blows, they are swiftly and pleasantly borne to their desired homeland; but if they follow a contrary wind and wandering stars, they do not reach harbor, but lose both their goods and their lives in the waves.
>
> Such, indeed, is the appearance of the wheels, or of the wheel having four faces. To the idle and to those who lack the true strength of faith, it is fearful and inaccessible; but to the diligent and those who have good hope it is so manageable that they do not hesitate to entrust themselves to the little vessel of the Church and to the tree of the Cross, in order to cross the depth of the sayings and meanings, which are manifold in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. Then, if the grace of the Holy Spirit breathes upon them, they speed in this as in a delightful voyage toward that heavenly homeland; but if they follow the spirit of error and heretical vanity, they perish more grievously in this deep than if, confessing their own poverty, they had never dared to undertake the voyage.
>
> “And,” he says, “the four had one likeness.” Truly one likeness: for if someone errs regarding one face, he will never retain knowledge of the truth in the others. For example, one who does not rightly perceive that the face of the lion consists in Christ’s having risen [Col. 1433B] from the dead—as this wheel testifies in that passage: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up. You have lain down in rest as a lion, and as a lioness: who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49)—will never perceive the face of the flying eagle in Christ’s ascent into heaven, where, according to the testimony of this wheel, he may carry us—his young—upon his shoulders.
>
> Likewise, one who does not perceive the face of the man, so as to believe that he is God and human, has no basis for knowing how he could redeem the world by his Passion. Thus “the four have one likeness,” so that whoever is mistaken concerning one face is consequently mistaken concerning them all. “And their appearance and works were as though a wheel were within a wheel.” This is shown better by drawing than by writing, and better by doing than by speaking: namely, how a wheel is drawn through the middle, as it were through the center, of another wheel; and how, to the extent that one contains the other, it is itself contained by the other.
>
> But according to the spiritual or mystical sense, “a wheel is within a wheel”: that is, the spiritual meaning is within the letter. For when we receive both—the truth of the history and the understanding of allegory—we truly possess “a wheel within a wheel.”

## Chapter XII. How the wheels go by their four sides; how, or to whom, their appearance is terrible; and how their whole body is full of eyes

> “Going by their four sides they went, and they did not turn back when they went. There was also stature in the wheels, and height, and a terrible appearance, and [Col. 1433D] their whole body was full of eyes round about, all four of them.”

How, I ask, it could or can happen that bodily or visible wheels should proceed by their four sides and not turn back when they have gone—especially when their appearance and workmanship are such as though “a wheel were within a wheel”—let whoever can see it. But since this is a vision, it may be understood that all at once the same wheels departed in four different directions and did not turn back as they went.

In the thing signified, there is no doubt how this occurred or occurs: holy Scripture, having the four faces often mentioned, went forth through its four faces—that is, containing the fourfold meaning of the incarnation, Passion, resurrection, and ascension [Col. 1434A] of Christ the Son of God, it occupied the four regions of the world. That “they did not turn back when they went” must be understood as above.

But how, or to whom, is the stature and height of the wheels, or their appearance, terrible? It is terrible to those who see wrongly, and to the envious Jews, because they did not look upon, and would not look upon, these living creatures beside which these wheels stood. Therefore the height or appearance of the wheels is terrible to them, especially because their whole body is full of eyes. Thus Moses, once horned—that is, radiant—from communion with the word of God, was terrible to them, though he ought rather to have been sweet and worthy of reverence; and they were afraid to come near him.

What the rays of the shining face signified in Moses, the many eyes in the body [Col. 1434B] of the wheels signify in this vision. Whatever Moses says when the veil is removed is splendid; whatever the wheel of holy Scripture contains is lofty and luminous to those who believe in Christ. But for Jews who do not receive Christ and refuse to admit that the Scriptures speak of him, whatever is set before them from it is, the loftier it is, the more terrible; and the more luminous it is, the more intolerable. They flee as they once fled Moses, and stubbornly bind over their bleary eyes with the veil of unbelief.

## Chapter XIII. How the wheels go with the living creatures when they go, are raised when they are raised, follow the Spirit, and have the spirit of life in them

> “When the living creatures went, the wheels also went beside them; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were lifted up together. Wherever the spirit went, there they went, following the spirit; and the wheels were lifted up together. For the spirit of life was in the wheels.”

For the living creatures to walk is for Christ’s Gospel to pass from place to place and from nation to nation; and for them to be lifted up from the earth is to be understood sublimely, because it is written: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2 [the text prints Isa. I]). Finally, when repentance and remission of sins began to be preached in Christ’s name from Jerusalem, these living creatures began from that time to walk; from that time they were lifted “from the earth,” that is, understood sublimely, and held by the whole world in such great reverence that the world worships no less the face of the man or calf, according to the foregoing explanation, than God the Father, creator of man and calf; and no less the lion or flying eagle than the Trinity, creator of the whole world.

As the living creatures thus go and are thus raised, the wheels likewise go and are likewise raised, because wherever Christ’s Gospel proceeds, the Law and Prophets accompany it. Neither, indeed, is granted to anyone apart from the other; and however lowly the husk of the letter may be, the Law is honored and glorified with majesty equal to that of the Gospel in one and the same Spirit. Why? “For the spirit of life was in the wheels.” It is as though he said: The rough letter of the Law outwardly kills, but the life-giving Spirit within is gentle and sweet.

It is therefore true that “wherever [Col. 1435A] the spirit went, there the wheels were lifted up together, following it.” That is to say: Wherever the Holy Spirit is present, there, as the Holy Spirit opens the understanding to comprehend the Scriptures, the Scriptures themselves are held in great honor; they are revered and received with majesty as great as that of Christ’s Gospel. For who, worthily receiving the saying concerning the Word of God, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1), would not immediately, understanding it, receive with the same reverence the saying from the Psalm: “For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148)? And likewise the saying from Moses: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Gen. 1); God said, “Let this or that be,” and it was so.

Therefore, when they went, the wheels went; when they stood, the wheels stood; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels followed them and were raised together, because “the spirit of life was in the wheels.” Therefore let the Jews not suppose that, when they caused these living creatures to depart and go to the nations, the Law and Prophets remained with them; or that, when these living creatures stand outside their synagogue, the Law and Prophets are within. For if this is their true prophet, then when the living creatures departed, the wheels departed with them; and when our living creatures stand outside, these wheels have left that synagogue and stand outside. Outside, I say, stands the spirit of life which is in the wheels; within the synagogue lies hidden only the letter which kills.

## Chapter XIV. [Col. 1435C] What the likeness of the firmament above the heads of the living creatures is, like the terrible appearance of crystal; what the wings stretched out beneath the firmament, one toward another, are; and how each covers its body

> “And above the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of a firmament, like the terrible appearance of crystal, stretched out above their heads. But beneath the firmament their wings were straight, one toward another. Each covered its body with two wings, and the other was likewise covered.”

The likeness of the firmament above the heads of the living creatures is the kingdom of immortality, prepared as a reward for those who proclaim and receive Christ’s Gospel. This firmament is “like the terrible appearance of crystal,” because crystal is indeed very hard, but is formed from water. Thus the kingdom is rightly understood through crystal: there the angelic nature, made immutable out of mutable, has been so hardened that it can no longer dissolve or fall into sin, because, when the apostate angels voluntarily fell, that portion humbly guarded against falling and refused to move its foot with the proud.

Human nature also is to be rewarded in the same way: after the resurrection it will be made firm, so that it can thereafter neither die nor sin. Crystal is called terrible and extended above the heads of the living creatures because those angelic powers which stand before the presence of almighty God are terrible and fearsome to us who are still placed in this corruption. Hence Daniel, when he had seen certain images of that kingdom, said: “My spirit was troubled. I, Daniel, was exceedingly terrified, and [Col. 1436A] the visions of my head disturbed me” (Dan. 7).

Under this firmament, he says, “their wings were straight, one toward another”; nevertheless, “each covered its body with two wings.” For as long as we remain in this mortal body, in which the wings of heavenly graces open themselves to us, whatever resounds as right and reasonable throughout the Gospel of the holy living creatures is in the highest harmony, one with another. For they agree and fit together well: that Christ is not merely human but also truly God; and consequently that, being truly God, one human being could worthily redeem the whole world by his Passion; and likewise that, because he is God, he could rise from the dead and ascend into heaven.

Yet these very things are now partly veiled from us, nor can we know them fully, as the Apostle says: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13). But for unbelievers all is more fully veiled: as was said above, because they are unbelievers, God has blinded their minds.

Therefore, “beneath the firmament their wings are indeed straight, one toward another, but each covers its body with two wings,” because as long as life is lived in this mortality, what we believe is itself hidden from us to no small extent. “And the other,” he says, “was likewise covered.” “Likewise,” I say, because insofar as any one of the things we have believed is hidden from each of us, the other is veiled in the same measure; nor can anyone deserve to comprehend the mystery of the most holy Incarnation in a greater measure than that of the Passion or Resurrection.

## Chapter XV. What it is to hear the sound of wings like the sound of many waters; in what sense it is like the sound of the most high God; what the sound of an army camp is; and what it is for their wings to be lowered when they stand

> “And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters, like the sound of the most high God. When they went, it was like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of an army camp. And when they stood, their wings were lowered. For when a voice came from above the firmament that was over their heads, they stood and lowered their wings.”

When “there suddenly came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where the apostles were sitting” (Acts 2), from that point the sound of the wings of the heavenly living creatures began to be heard, so that “when this sound had arisen, the multitude came together and was bewildered, because each heard them speaking in his own language” (ibid.). Then, I say, the sound of their wings began to be heard like the sound of many waters.

For many heavenly graces, many gifts of charisms, then flowed together; many streams of living water began to flow from the belly of believers, in many utterances, many languages, and the tongues of every nation. Thus was fulfilled: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45). Likewise: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. Day pours forth speech to day, and night makes known knowledge to night. There are no utterances or words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” [Col. 1437A] (Ps. 18).

Therefore, “I heard,” he says, “the sound of wings like the sound of many waters.” This sound was made greater by the movement of other waters, the movement of opposing waters, according to the testimony of another Psalm: “The rivers have lifted up, O Lord, the rivers have lifted up their voice; the rivers have lifted up their waves at the voices of many waters. Wonderful are the swellings of the sea; wonderful is the Lord on high” (Ps. 92). Whose miracle was this, if not that of the wonderful Lord? For they had been unlearned and unlettered people, to whom was now given a mouth and wisdom which none of their adversaries could resist or contradict (Luke 21).

Accordingly, after saying “like the sound of many waters,” he immediately added, “like the sound of the most high God.” They themselves confess this when they say, “that the surpassing greatness of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2 Cor. 4). For they truly did not receive such a sound, or such great voices, from a human being or through a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ—namely, the most high God, seated upon a lofty throne at the Father’s right hand.

“When they went,” he says, “it was like the sound of a multitude, like the sound of army camps.” “When they went,” that is, when they preached. For in response to the sound of preaching there arose the sound of contradiction, according to what was said before: “The rivers have lifted up their waves at the voices of many waters”; and from this came something like the sound of a multitude and of army camps.

“And when they stood, their wings were lowered.” When they stood, that is, when they did not preach. For at times they stood because God prevented them from proceeding and the Holy Spirit forbade them, according to that passage in Acts: “Passing through Phrygia and the region of Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them” [Col. 1437D] (Acts 16).

Therefore, when a voice came from above the firmament, when they heard the command of the most high God or of the Holy Spirit forbidding them—the command that hung over their heads, to which they were subject and ready to obey—they “stood,” that is, they did not preach; and then “their wings were lowered.” Nor was there anything like the sound of a multitude or of army camps, because there was no contradiction or warfare except in response to the sound of preaching that came from them.

## Chapter XVI. What the likeness of a throne above the firmament is, and what the appearance of a man seated upon the throne is

> “And above the firmament, which was over their heads, was as it were the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne; and upon the likeness of the throne was the likeness as it were of the appearance of a man above. And I saw as it were the appearance of electrum, like the appearance of fire within it round about, from his loins upward; and from his loins downward I saw as it were the appearance of shining fire round about, like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day. This was the appearance of brightness round about. This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.”

That, above the firmament in that kingdom of immortality, above every principality, power, and might, there is not merely the likeness but the reality of a throne; and that not merely “the likeness as it were of the appearance of a man,” but the true appearance of the true man Jesus Christ sits above it—this requires no assertion on our part. For the catholic faith holds it certain, and it is sacrilege for anyone to doubt that what was then shown in an image has since been fulfilled in the reality of the thing, from the time when, “as the apostles looked on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their sight” (Acts 1), “and he sits [Col. 1438B] at the right hand of God” (Mark 16), according to the saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, ‘Sit at my right hand’” (Ps. 109).

His seat signifies stability and glory, when it says, “like the appearance of a sapphire stone.” For in stone there is stability, and in sapphire the beauty of a serene sky. But why does he see only “the appearance of a man” in that likeness of a throne, when until now he has enumerated four faces: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of a calf, and the face of a flying eagle? Clearly because the one who sits is called lion, calf, and eagle only by likeness or figurative transference; but he is a human being, and remains so in the truth of his nature.

“And,” he says, “I saw this man as it were the appearance of electrum.” For just as electrum consists not of one kind alone but of two kinds, gold and silver, so that man consists not of one nature alone but of two: God from his own substance, or that of God the Father; human from our substance, which he assumed. And he says not only “as it were the appearance of electrum,” but “like the appearance of fire within it, round about, from his loins upward.” The fire within is the fiery power of his divinity, which dwells within, clothed in flesh. “For our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. 12).

From “his loins,” I say, upward there is only fire; for “from his loins downward I saw,” he says, “as it were the appearance of shining fire round about, and also like the appearance of a rainbow when it is in a cloud on a rainy day.” What does this mean except that before the assumption of flesh, which is rightly expressed by the loins, God, angry with the human race, was only consuming fire; but after he assumed flesh, he became not only fire but also an inclination toward propitiation for us? For the rainbow on a rainy day is the sign of covenant and peace, as God himself promised Noah (Gen. 9).

Therefore, “from his loins downward,” there are together the appearance of fire and the appearance of a rainbow, which is the sign of propitiation; because, after he became human, he tempered the fire of his justice or judgment with the gentle breeze of mercy, so that this fire shall judge no one who now, meanwhile, wishes through faith to flee to his mercy. Such is this appearance: a brightness so moderated all around, prepared for all who are around him, who believe in him, and who look to him.

(Chapter II.) [Col. 1439A] “This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord”: that is, it presented a worthy and fitting likeness of what is now the glory of the Lord, the glory of the Son of God—indeed, the glory and honor of that Son of Man, crowned and set over the works of the Father’s hands.

## Chapter XVII. Whom the prophet prefigured when he said, “And I saw and fell upon my face,” etc.; and how he was sent to apostate nations

> “And I saw, and I fell upon my face. And I heard the voice of one speaking, who said to me: Son of man, stand upon your feet, and I will speak with you. And after he had spoken to me, the spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet.”

After the glory of Christ’s Gospel had been revealed, the prophetic vision now begins to show what thereafter followed or follows. Its speech is indeed veiled, but its order of speech or revelation is such that, when compared with events subsequently enacted, it is almost a historical narrative. After the prophet had fully seen the astonishing figures or images of the Gospel, he now bears the type of a preacher of the same Gospel—that is, of the apostles or disciples of Christ.

“And I saw,” he says, “and I fell upon my face.” He did not fall upon his face as soon as he saw the likeness of the four living creatures or the other things that followed; but after he saw the likeness of the throne, and above it the likeness as it were of the appearance of a man, “I fell,” he says, “upon my face.” Thus the apostles did not immediately, when they began to follow Christ the Lord and see the glory of his Gospel, know or believe in him so as to worship him; but after he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, they worshiped him and preached that he ought to be worshiped.

“And,” he says, “I heard the voice of one speaking, who said to me: Son of man, stand upon your feet.” By calling him “son of man,” he reminded him of his own condition, lest he fail to know that his admission to the heavenly vision was a matter of grace rather than merit. In a certain sense, the apostles too were told: “Stand upon your feet.” And the Spirit truly entered into them and set them upon their feet when those formerly weak and timid were clothed with power from on high and strengthened by the Holy Spirit. Thus, for example, Peter, who had been afraid to confess Christ, his Lord and Master, before a single servant-girl guarding the door, no longer hesitated to confess him in the full synagogue—indeed, before all Rome, mistress of the world, armed with so many bundles of rods, so many authorities, and so many swords.

> “And I heard one speaking to me and saying: Son of man, I send you to the children of Israel, to apostate nations that have departed from me. Their fathers have transgressed my covenant unto this day, and the children are hard of face and indomitable of heart.”

What else do we think was said to the apostles, except that, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, they should go to the children of Israel—now no longer God’s people, but, in the plural, “nations,” apostate nations that had departed from the Lord; worse than any nations, whose fathers had transgressed the Lord’s covenant unto that day, and who themselves, the most wicked children of evil fathers, [Col. 1440A] were hard of face and indomitable of heart? Nor would Stephen the protomartyr have said to them at that time without scriptural authority: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7).

> “And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Perhaps they themselves will hear, and perhaps they will cease, for they are a provoking house. And they shall know that a prophet has been among them.”

The Lord God did not fail to know that they would neither hear nor cease, just as their fathers had neither heard nor ceased; but the word of God had first to be spoken to them (Acts 13), so that they might be without excuse in refusing to know that the prophet of whom Moses had foretold (Deut. 18) had been among them.

## Chapter XVIII. [Col. 1440B] What it means that a scroll was spread before him, rolled up and written within and without; and what it means that lamentations, a song, and woe were written in it

> “Open your mouth and eat whatever I give you. And I looked, and behold, a hand was sent to me, in which was a rolled-up scroll. And he spread it before me; it was written within and without. And in it were written lamentations, and a song, and woe.”

This rolled-up scroll is the same one mentioned in the Apocalypse as sealed with seven seals (Rev. 5). It is “written within and without”: within, that is, by allegory; without, by history. Within, by spiritual understanding; without, by the simple sense [Col. 1440C] of the letter. This scroll, then, is the whole Scripture of the sanctuary. The hand sent forth spread it before the apostles when the Son of God, the Father’s right hand, gave them understanding of the Scriptures, as Luke says: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

Lamentations, a song, and woe are written in this scroll. First lamentations, then song, because those who sow in tears shall reap in joy (Ps. 125); but woe to those who now refuse to lament—that is, to repent—because they shall be sent into eternal fire. What else does the whole scroll contain? What else, I say, does all sacred Scripture contain?

And it is rightly said, “Open your mouth and eat whatever I give you,” because we must dispose ourselves, in devout eagerness and submission, to eat the food of God’s word, according to what is said in the Psalm: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80 [the text prints Ps. XXC]). For to eat is to understand Scripture, and this is God’s gift; for this reason he says, “Eat whatever I give you.” Thus it belongs to us to open our mouths—that is, to seek the understanding of Scripture—but to God to fill them—that is, to disclose Scripture’s true meaning.

(Chapter III.) Unless the hand sent forth had spread this scroll, we would not read it today: that is, unless Christ the Son of God had fulfilled it in the work of his own person, we would not understand holy Scripture. “And I ate it, and it became sweet as honey in my mouth.” Whoever has experienced it knows how truly sweet is the food of the Scriptures, that is, their spiritual meaning. Therefore he says: “How sweet are your sayings to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” [Col. 1441A] (Ps. 118).

> “And he said to me: Son of man, go to the house of Israel, and speak my words to them. For you are not sent to a people of deep speech and an unknown language, whose words you cannot understand. And if you were sent to them, they would hear you; but the house of Israel would not hear you, because they will not hear me.”

How truly these things were said, the outcome proved. “If,” he says, “you were sent to many peoples of deep speech and unknown language, they would hear you”—and this came to pass. “But the house of Israel would not hear you”—and this too came to pass. For we are the many peoples of deep speech: Greeks and Latins. We heard the apostles of Christ sent to us, but the house of Israel refused to hear them.

We pass quickly over what is plain—indeed, we skip some matters—because now that the door has been opened, if you continually look to apostolic times, there is almost nothing that delays the steps of understanding. [Col. 1441B]

## Chapter XIX. How the apostles of Christ, whom this Spirit took up, heard behind them the voice of a great commotion: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place.”

“And the Spirit took me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion: ‘Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place’; and the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another, and the sound of the wheels following the living creatures, and the sound of a great commotion.”

This first saying certainly suits the apostolic order. “The Spirit took me up,” he says—understood: for his work or ministry. For thus the same Holy Spirit says in the Acts of the Apostles: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13).

But what is meant by this: when the Spirit took him up, “I heard,” he says, “behind me the sound of a great commotion: ‘Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place’”?
