Certainly, though many things may rightly and profitably be said on this subject, let us confidently affirm, on the authority of Scripture, that “to everyone who has, more shall be given” (Luke 15): that is, for every evangelist, in proportion to the grace of knowledge or wisdom he has received, it shall be increased more and more.

Therefore, “the Spirit took me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great commotion, and the sound of the wings of the living creatures striking one against another, and the sound of the wheels following the living creatures,” is as though he said:

When, at the command of the Holy Spirit, I obediently undertook the ministry of the Gospel and began to expend the talent entrusted to me, I began to grow richer and richer in understanding; I began to have ears to hear; and by inward hearing I heard the sound of a great commotion—the voice and lamentation of the heavenly homeland and of the whole angelic court. Though I was still bodily a pilgrim on earth, my mind was lifted up and conversed in heaven. I came more clearly to understand the wings of the Gospel mysteries striking one against another—that is, rendering harmonious testimonies to the truth. Likewise I understood the sound of the wheels following the living creatures—that is, the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, harmonizing with Christ’s Gospel.

I heard all these things “behind me,” that is, I recollected them from what had gone before. For example, Peter did not hear before him: he did not understand the deeds or sayings of the Lord who was present. Therefore it was said to him: “What I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward” (John 13). And elsewhere, both to Peter and to the others: “Are you still without understanding?” (Matthew 15). Nor is this surprising. For they were unlearned and illiterate men.

But when the promised Spirit took him up—of whom the Lord himself had said: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16)—Peter recollected the past Gospel of Christ in understanding and intelligence; he heard inwardly the voices of the Prophets from the past and proclaimed them outwardly. For he said: “Men of Judaea, and all you who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you: these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. But this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel: ‘And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy’” (Acts 2), and so forth.

And soon after: “For David says concerning him: ‘I kept the Lord always before my eyes, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be shaken. Therefore my heart rejoiced and my tongue exulted; moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope, because you will not abandon my soul in hell, nor give your Holy One to see corruption’” (ibid.).

Thus he who formerly could not even hear before him the sound of the wings of the living creatures, once taken up by the Spirit heard behind him, with a great commotion, not only the voice of the living creatures but also that of the wheels following them. That is: while I had God present before me, I could not even understand the reason for his incarnation, the benefit of his passion, the truth of his resurrection, or the glory of his ascension. But now that the Holy Spirit has been sent from heaven, I have been able to apprehend not only these things but also, from what had gone before, the mysteries of the Law and the Prophets, with great certainty of hearing.

And, as though you were asking what kind of voice he heard—or lest you doubt whether the voice heard in that great commotion was articulate or inarticulate—he fittingly says: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his holy place.” Not because this was the only voice, but because it was the first voice of praise heard in the commotion of the living creatures. For when the first face of the man moved its wing—that is, when God first appeared as man in the flesh—this same voice of angelic praise was heard: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2).

Therefore, if you ask from what holy place the glory of the Lord was blessed, behold his place: the exalted throne of the Father’s majesty, at whose right hand the glorious conqueror sat down. Desiring and at the same time foretelling this, they said: “Glory to God in the highest.”

## CHAPTER XX

How the apostles of Christ, after receiving the Holy Spirit, became bitter and indignant; and how they came to the heap of new produce, sat down, and remained mourning.

“The Spirit also lifted me up and took me up; and I went away bitter, in the indignation of my spirit. For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me.”

Appropriately and fittingly. For it would have been too little for the holy apostles, through being taken up by the Spirit, to hear behind them—that is, to understand past events and the ancient Scriptures—unless, raised by that same Spirit and made lofty with fitting confidence, they dared to proceed bitter and indignant, in spiritual indignation and stern bitterness. The Holy Spirit signified that he would impart to them precisely such indignation and bitterness when he chose to appear in fire. For “there appeared to them divided tongues, as of fire” (Acts 2).

Therefore, as though you were asking how he was bitter, or with what indignation, he immediately adds: “For the hand of the Lord was with me, strengthening me.” Thus the strength of zeal by which the apostles were made strong is itself the bitterness opposed to the sweetness of vices; it is that indignation which, for God’s cause, does not hesitate to despise even the highly placed.

“And I came to the captivity, to the heap of new produce, to those who dwelt by the river Chobar; and I sat where they sat, and remained seven days mourning in their midst.”

In a wonderful manner this prophetic Scripture also indicates the time at which the grace of the Holy Spirit sent Christ’s apostles, armed with power, to preach, by saying: “And I came to the captivity, to the heap of new produce.” For the two loaves of firstfruits, which by the Law were commanded to be offered at the solemnity of Pentecost, testify at what season of the year heaps of new produce stand in those lands.

Thus it is not without reason that he says he came to a heap of new produce: spiritually, according to the season, he calls “new produce” those who were gathered to Christ through the apostles’ preaching on the very day of the Holy Spirit’s coming. Spiritually, I say, he calls them “captivity”; spiritually, “a heap of new produce”; spiritually, he says that they dwell beside the river Chobar.

They are “captivity,” because, by believing in Christ, they confessed themselves captives and exiles in Adam from that heavenly Jerusalem. They are “a heap of new produce,” because, having been buried with the grain of wheat, Christ, through baptism into death (Colossians 2), they thereafter began to walk in newness of life (Romans 6). They dwelt “beside the river Chobar,” which in our language means “heavy,” because all who truly remembered the heavenly Jerusalem held before their sorrowful eyes the burden of wretched mortality and wept, according to that saying of David: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, O Zion” (Psalm 136 [137]).

“I sat,” he says, “where they sat, and remained seven days mourning in their midst.” The apostles, certainly, sat mourning in the midst of those previously mentioned—mourning, I say, not only because they were captives in the Babylon of this world, but also because they could bring exceedingly few of their Jewish kinsmen back to remembrance of the heavenly Jerusalem; moreover, because they endured many persecutions inflicted by them.

The seven days during which he is said to have sat in their midst, before afterward going out into the plain at the Lord’s command, signify the whole period during which the apostles did not leave Judaea: namely, nearly twice seven years, until the fourth year of Claudius, when Paul and Barnabas were sent by the Holy Spirit to preach to the Gentiles and Peter entered Rome.

## CHAPTER XXI

How great is the necessity of evangelizing for those entrusted with a stewardship, according to the words, “I have appointed you a watchman over the house of Israel”; and how, by these things, the destruction of Jerusalem is foretold—a destruction which followed the Lord’s passion and the apostles’ preaching.

“When seven days had passed, the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, I have appointed you a watchman over the house of Israel. You shall hear a word from my mouth and announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not announce it to him or speak to turn him from his evil way, so that he may live, that wicked man shall die in his wickedness; but I shall require his blood from your hand.”

Great and terrible is the obligation of watchmen of this kind. Knowing it, Paul, one of them, says: “For if I preach the Gospel, I have no ground for glorying; for necessity is laid upon me. Woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me” (1 Corinthians 9).

Great likewise, and just, was the condemnation of Judaea, which refused, as far as it could, to heed the wakeful cry of the watchmen; indeed, it persecuted them and drove them far away. For it follows: “But if you announce it to the wicked, and he is not converted from his wickedness and from his wicked way, he shall die in his iniquity; but you have delivered your own soul.”

The Lord himself had previously taught the apostles in the Gospel how they should recognize and declare such deliverance: “And whoever does not receive you, as you depart from that place, shake the dust off your feet as a testimony against them” (Matthew 10; Mark 6; Luke 9). Scripture in the Acts of the Apostles does not conceal that they did this: wearied by Jewish seditions, they passed over to the Gentiles with consciences set free.

This passage then follows concerning that transition: “And the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he said to me: Rise and go out into the plain, and there I shall speak with you. And I rose and went out into the plain.” Mystically, the plain is the breadth of the Gentiles. “There,” he says, “I shall speak with you”—understood: with much greater fruit among hearers.

“Behold, there the glory of the Lord stood, like the glory that I had seen beside the river Chobar.” The meaning is this: in the plain, in the breadth of the Gentiles, the glory of the Gospel shone no less, in every grace, wonder, mighty work, and sign, than it had in the Church of those Jews who believed. It first shone from that time when Peter was speaking to those coming from the Gentiles and the Holy Spirit fell upon those hearing the word, and they spoke in tongues and magnified God (Acts 10).

Hence Peter says: “If then God gave them the same grace as he gave to us who believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?” (Acts 11). And elsewhere: “God, who knows hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as to us; and he made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15).

Therefore the glory of the Lord which stood beside the river Chobar afterward stood in the plain, because, as Paul also says, “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Romans 10); and through unmerited grace the same glory of the Lord revealed itself first to the Jew and afterward to the Greek, that it might justify both through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 2).

“And I fell upon my face, and the Spirit entered into me and set me upon my feet.” Why is this said concerning the prophet in the plain, as earlier beside the river Chobar, unless it is specially indicated that the Holy Spirit was also to be given to the elect among the Gentiles—a Spirit who would first cast down those whom he took up from the standing of their pride, and afterward establish them “upon their feet,” that is, upon their good works?

And now the glory of the Lord, removed from the Israelite people, has been scattered abroad among the exalted Gentiles; but at the end of the world it will return to them, as it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved” (Romans 11).

It follows, therefore: “And he spoke to me and said to me: Go in and shut yourself up in the midst of your house.” He is commanded to shut himself up in the midst of his house, because in the time of Antichrist the hardened Jewish people, converted from those Gentiles who have remained in unbelief, will be pressed by persecutions.

Hence it is further added: “And you, son of man, behold, bonds are laid upon you; they shall bind you with them, and you shall not go out into their midst. And I shall make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you shall be mute, not like a man rebuking, because they are a rebellious house.” The prophet receives bonds and is bound in his house because, when Judaea believes in the last times, it will suffer the most grievous persecutions of Antichrist. And he shall not go out into their midst because preaching does not reach the hearts of the wicked while the tongue of the good is silent, bound by tribulations.

## CHAPTER XXII

Concerning the siege of the city: how it was a portent that the prophet was commanded to lie upon his left side and bear the iniquities of the house of Israel for three hundred and ninety days, and to lie upon his right side and bear the iniquities of the house of Judah for forty days.

**(Chapter 4.)** “And you, son of man, take for yourself a brick and draw upon it the city of Jerusalem, and set a siege against it,” etc.

According to the order of events and the prophetic meaning of things which were then to happen but have now happened, this chapter of prophecy ought to be joined to the place where he said a little earlier: “And I rose and went out into the plain, and behold, the glory of the Lord stood like the glory which I had seen beside the river Chobar.”

For after the glory of the Lord went out from the Jews to the Gentiles, the overthrow of the wretched city of Jerusalem followed—an event known throughout the world, which we do not doubt is prophetically foreshown here. For it follows: “And you shall lie upon your left side and place upon it the iniquities of the house of Israel. According to the number of days that you lie upon it, you shall bear their iniquities. And I have given you the years of their iniquity, according to the number of days: three hundred and ninety days; and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel. And when you have completed these, you shall lie a second time upon your right side and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days. I have given you a day for a year, a day, I say, for a year.”

After he had said, “You shall lie upon your right side a second time and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days,” only then did he add: “I have given you a day for a year.” Notice that when he said, “But I have given you the years of their iniquity, according to the number of days: three hundred and ninety days; and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel,” he did not similarly add: “I have given you a day for a year.”

We say this in order to avoid the very long extent of years, beginning long before this prophecy, and to approach more freely the point toward which we are moving, according to the sure outcome of historical events. For from Pekah king of Israel, under whom Shalmaneser devastated many thousands of the Israelite people, until the fortieth year of Ahasuerus, we may indeed calculate three hundred and ninety years, when all persecution of the Jewish people was mitigated (4 Kings 17; 1 Ezra 4). But this calculation, and the other interpretations proposed by various writers concerning this place, are troublesome and, in our judgment, less suitable to the matter now under discussion.

Therefore, since the present letter of the text does not compel us to accept in both cases—that is, in the lying upon the left as well as the right side—that a day is given for a year, let us now approach the final destruction of Jerusalem, of which we began to speak above. When historical truth has been examined, we shall see how rightly the prophet was bound and constrained as a sign of it and commanded to lie thus.

## CHAPTER XXIII

Concerning the wretched siege of Jerusalem, which took place in the forty-first year after Christ’s passion, under the emperors Titus and Vespasian.

In the first year of Vespasian’s accession to the empire—the forty-first year from the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ—Titus, chosen to execute his father’s triumph, was sent to Jerusalem with a picked force, after three years of the campaign already undertaken; for this was its fourth year.

For Vespasian the father, as Titus his victorious son afterward recounts, though he could have fallen unexpectedly upon an unprepared enemy, went around Galilee and burned its outlying districts, in order, he says, that you might lay aside your insolence and ask pardon. He showed his strength; and though he terrified everyone, he went to Egypt to grant time for repentance. “Our absence made you more insolent, because you supposed us occupied,” and so forth.

Thus, in the fourth year of the campaign and, as already stated, the first of Vespasian’s reign, after the military ranks had been filled within a few days from those forces of which a picked body had been sent into Italy, they came to the city, reported to be oppressed by the arms of brigands and hemmed in by the supports of factions. For a third tyrant, Eleazar, had entered it, having occupied the inner parts of the Temple and its entire circuit, stationing armed men even above the doors in the front of the vestibule itself.

Simon, whom the people had introduced as their tyrant, held the upper city, and the lower parts were likewise filled by his people. Between the three was John: inferior to Eleazar, superior to Simon, yet better supplied than the others with engines and every kind of weapon, and thus able to match them in war.

The Passover feast was at hand; and, as Moses had sung long before, “outside the sword was laying them waste, and inside terror” (Deuteronomy 32). When the battle outside first began and then ceased for a little, internal conflict followed. For, as already said, under cover of the Passover celebration, John, having bribed many, approached the Temple supposedly for worship. The factional leaders had indeed then urged one another to unite their efforts in defending their country, lest their discord give the Romans a bloodless victory. Thus, granted entry as though to allies, he carried out his deception. Those who entered in civilian guise but armed underneath, casting off their outer garments, raised their swords, their breasts armored and their bodies equipped for battle.

After these beginnings of evil, the whole year passed in misery. It was plain to the wretched people that Barabbas, author of sedition, was then alive among them, while Jesus, prince of peace, was dead to them (Matthew 27; Luke 23; John 18). The enemy outside the wall offered peace; the authors of sedition fought inside the wall. Hunger forced men out, for whom death by the sword was a benefit compared with fasting.

Simon raged inside; John raged; through their agents they laid snares for individuals. If anyone tried to flee, he was dragged over the ground and torn apart. The relatives of those who had gone away were also slaughtered, or the bodies of many fixed to crosses were displayed to those of their own people who had escaped.

The famine raged so far that a woman named Mary, from one of the wealthiest districts of Peraea, killed with a sword the infant whom she had borne, put him to the fire, and, her natural motherly affection obliterated, ate him. Why say more? In the fifth month of the returning year, on the tenth day of the month, the Temple, whose bare structure had long remained, was burned—on the very day on which it had once been set on fire when the Babylonians attacked.

Yet even before this, when the walls were demolished, an exit had been opened for those shut in to flee to the Romans. They were so wasted by hunger that, when food was set before them, many, after swallowing some softer nourishment, were choked because the passages of their throats were already closed.

Who, therefore, does not see that the history of so dreadful a tragedy agrees with the number of days of this prophetic lying on the left side? Even if the days of the wretched siege seem somewhat more than three hundred and ninety, until the opportunity was made for those shut in to flee to the Romans—a point difficult to establish—nevertheless, for the prophet’s labor in place of the entire part of the second year, however small it may have been, twenty-five days suffice. Let us now return to the words of the prophecy itself.

## CHAPTER XXIV

How the passion and imprisonment of the Gospel’s preachers, and also their rejection, were foreshadowed in this prophet; and how the most evil and terrible famine among the besieged is signified by the kind of bread which the prophet is commanded to bake for himself on dung and eat.

After the glory of the Lord went out into the plain, signifying that Gospel preaching would go out to the Gentiles after the Jews had been left behind, the Spirit says to the prophet: “Go in and shut yourself up in the midst of your house. And you, son of man, behold, bonds are laid upon you; they shall bind you with them, and you shall not go out from their midst. And I shall make your tongue cleave to your palate, and you shall be mute, not like a man rebuking, because they are a rebellious house” (Ezekiel 3).

By this portent it is signified that the preachers of the Gospel will suffer bonds and prisons from their own household and fellow tribesmen, and will for this reason close their mouths to them, until preaching is again restored to them near the end of the age and at least a remnant among them is converted. For it follows: “But when I have spoken to you, I shall open your mouth, and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord God: He who hears, let him hear; and he who is silent, let him be silent; because they are a rebellious house.”

The Lord says to those who had killed the prophets and, as the aforementioned bonds signify, were about to persecute the apostles: “That upon you may come all righteous blood shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar. Amen, I say to you: all these things shall come upon this generation” (Matthew 23).

It follows, therefore: “And you, son of man, take for yourself a brick and set it before you; draw upon it the city of Jerusalem; set a siege against it; build fortifications; heap up an embankment; set camps against it; and place battering rams around it.” This is the Roman siege, foreseeing which the Lord wept over Jerusalem, saying: “Because, if you too had known …” (Luke 19).

“And you, take for yourself an iron pan and place it as an iron wall between yourself and the city; set your face firmly against it, and it shall be under siege, and you shall surround it.” This is a sign to the house of Israel. This is the wrath of God, of which the same Lord says above: “For there shall be great distress upon the earth and wrath upon this people” (Luke 21).

For the iron pan, which is also an iron wall, signifies the exceeding greatness of heavenly wrath, whose severity mercy cannot pass through in order to reach those shut in or besieged. And, so that the prophet may know how long the siege will last: “And you,” he says, “shall lie upon your left side, and place upon it the iniquities of the house of Israel; according to the number of days that you lie upon it, you shall bear their iniquity. But I have given you the years of their iniquity, according to the number of days: three hundred and ninety days; and you shall bear the iniquity of the house of Israel.”

“Years,” he says: plainly more than one, but fewer than two. Likewise, in order that he may know how much time would pass from the perpetrated sacrilege of the Lord’s death to that same siege: “And when,” he says, “you have completed these things, you shall lie a second time upon your right side and bear the iniquity of the house of Judah for forty days. I have given you a day for a year, a day, I say, for a year.”

Finally, from the Lord’s passion to the siege of the city—which, as stated above, began in the fourth year of the campaign—there were forty years. Rightly, therefore, because it would have been too great and unbearable a burden for the prophet to lie for so long upon one side, “I have given you,” he says, “a day for a year.”

Then, lest he should be ignorant how evil and terrible the fury of famine would be in that siege: “And you,” he says, “take for yourself wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and vetch; put them in one vessel; and make for yourself breads according to the number of days that you lie on one side: for three hundred and ninety days you shall eat it. Your food which you eat shall be by weight, twenty staters a day; from time to time you shall eat it. And you shall drink water by measure, the sixth part of a hin; from time to time you shall drink it. And you shall eat it as a barley ash-cake, and you shall cover it before their eyes with dung that comes forth from a human being.” And the Lord said: “Thus shall the children of Israel eat their polluted bread among the nations to which I shall drive them.”

“Among the nations,” that is, among the besieging Romans, “to which I shall drive them,” he says, when famine prevails and subdues them. And he rightly called it “polluted bread.” For what bread was more polluted than that which, in order to eat it, they defiled with parricidal blood? They laid snares for one another, each seeking to snatch from the other. Wherever there was a suspicion of food, there was war among members of the same household. They fought for food; their dearest relatives were killed; the dead were searched, lest some food might be concealed in their garments.

Some were thought to pretend to be dead so that people would not suspect that, while alive, they possessed food. Yet they could neither perform the function of the living nor pretend death; rather, with open mouths, like rabid dogs catching the currents of air, they wandered here and there. They watched beasts when they emptied their bellies, and searched old cattle dung, so that—horrible even to see—it became food for the hungry.

Therefore he rightly says: “You shall cover it with dung that comes forth from a human being,” because people were to pollute their food with one another’s blood. Yet, when the prophet recoiled from this, a milder concession was granted: he was to use cattle dung instead of human excrement.

It should certainly be noticed that he says nothing at all about bread during the forty days of lying upon the right side. For during the forty years already mentioned, the Jews were not punished with bloodshed or famine for their crimes; rather, they abounded in luxuries, as the apostle James testifies in an indignant spirit when addressing them: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl over the miseries that shall come upon you” (James 5). And shortly afterward: “You have feasted upon the earth and nourished your hearts in luxuries. On the day of slaughter you have led [them] on; you have killed the righteous one, and he did not resist you” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXV

How the remaining Jews, like the hairs of the head or beard, were shaved off with a very sharp sword; how Jerusalem was utterly destroyed by three most cruel tyrants.

**(Chapter 5.)** “And you, son of man, take for yourself a sharp sword, a razor for shaving hair; take it and pass it over your head and your beard. Take for yourself scales for weighing and divide them. A third part you shall burn with fire in the midst of the city when the days of the siege are completed. A third part you shall take and strike with the sword around it. Another third you shall scatter to the wind, and I shall draw the sword after them. And from them you shall take a small number and bind them in the edge of your garment. From these you shall again take some, throw them into the midst of the fire, and burn them with fire. From them a fire shall go out into the whole house of Israel.”

This is a recapitulation and brief summary of the miseries of the aforementioned siege and of Jerusalem’s destruction. “Take for yourself,” he says, “a sharp sword, a razor for shaving hairs.” The sharp sword shaving hairs is the severe avenging judgment upon crimes, destined to exterminate the superfluous Jews.

For just as the hairs of the head or beard adhere to the body but are neither parts nor members of the body, so the Jews of whom, or against whom, the discourse speaks adhered to the God of their fathers in name or profession, but did not belong to him through any fear of truth or affection of love. Hence the saying: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29; Matthew 15).

“You shall take it,” he says, “and pass it over your head and beard, and divide them by the scales of weighing,” so that they may fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations, according to the measure and weight of their sins.

For “a third part you shall burn with fire in the midst of the city, when the days of the siege are completed.” These are those whom the discordant sword of the three brigands—John, Simon, and Eleazar—slaughtered within the city, along with the unceasing famine that destroyed the people in such multitudes that, since they could not be buried, the remains of the dead were thrown from the wall into deep ravines.

Finally, when Titus saw the steep hollows filled with corpses and the gore floating upon the torn entrails, he groaned deeply and, raising his hands to heaven, testified that this should not be attributed to him. He had wished to grant pardon if surrender went forward; he had waited for them to ask for peace; he was ready to preserve them unharmed if they laid down their arms.

“And you shall take a third part and strike them with the sword around it.” These are those whom the Roman sword cut down in battles joined outside the city. “Another third you shall scatter to the wind.” These are those who, sold and made captive, were led away among all nations. Very many were for sale, but few buyers were found, because even the Romans disdained to keep Jews as slaves.

“And I shall draw the sword after them.” These are those who, while Titus proceeded through the individual cities and celebrated the spectacle of victory, were killed in the arena wherever they went, and, torn apart by beasts, paid the due penalty of rebellion.

“And from them you shall take a small number and bind them in the edge of your garment.” These are those preserved alive, who until now live a life bound beneath the yoke of extreme slavery, legal condition, and tribute. But do they escape vengeance for Christ’s blood? Certainly not. For because they are unbelieving and remain in unbelief, “from them,” he says, “you shall again take some and cast them into the midst of the fire and burn them with fire.”

“And from them,” I say—not all of them, for some among them will be converted, and at the end a remnant will be saved, whom the fire of Gehenna will not receive. “From them a fire shall go out into the house of Israel,” for indeed in the time of Antichrist persecution will arise from them against all who shall truly be the house of Israel.

## CHAPTER XXVI

How all the evils which befell Jerusalem came chiefly through the fault of the priests, scribes, and Pharisees; and why it is consequently said: “Thus says the Lord to the mountains and valleys: Behold, I shall bring the sword upon you.”

**(Chapter 6.)** “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them. Say: Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God to the mountains, hills, rocks, and valleys: Behold, I shall bring the sword upon you; I shall destroy your high places, demolish your altars, break your images, and cast your slain before your idols,” etc.

The chief responsibility for all the evils spoken of here rests upon the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees. Therefore, after the Lord wept over the city and foretold all these evils that would come upon it, he immediately entered the Temple and began to cast out those selling and buying there, rebuking the priests because they had made the house of prayer a den of brigands (Luke 19). This prophetic discourse likewise attacks those same priests under the metaphorical names of mountains, hills, rocks, and valleys.

There were three orders prominent in the world: priests, scribes, and Pharisees. All of them, indeed, through their own self-estimation or their ranks, were like mountains, hills, and rocks; but in reality, through hypocrisy and profound greed, they were all low valleys, all drawing in the sewerage of avarice. Thus the Lord in the Gospel once and again—indeed six or seven times—rebukes them with sharp invective, as they deserved: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe mint and dill while leaving aside the weightier matters of the Law; woe to you, hypocrites,” who do this and that (Matthew 23).

And, to their shame, he fittingly does not say: Behold, I shall destroy my Temple because of you, and the altar, and the holy of holies, upon which your greed eagerly fastens. Rather: “I shall destroy,” he says, “your high places, demolish your altars, break your images, and cast your slain before your idols,” calling his own Temple, because of them, by the infamous names of high places, images, and idols, and likewise his altar; for they did not worship him in that Temple so much as shameful gain, or Mammon, the god of shameful gain.

Nevertheless, all these evils came upon that generation also because of the former high places, images, and idols worshipped by their fathers, and because of which they shed the blood of the Prophets. For by killing the Lord of the Prophets and persecuting his apostles, they filled up the measure of their fathers.

## CHAPTER XXVII

Concerning the terror and greatness of the day of judgment, on which the wicked shall receive evils greater than all past evils; and how this is what was said: “The end has come; the end has come upon the four quarters of the earth.”

(CAP. VII.) “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: And thou, son of man, thus saith the Lord God to the land of Israel: The end is come; the end is come upon the four quarters of the earth. Now is the end upon thee, and I will send my fury upon thee, and I will judge thee according to thy ways, and I will set all thine abominations against thee. And mine eye shall not spare thee, neither will I have pity; but I will lay thy ways upon thee, and thine abominations shall be in the midst of thee, and ye shall know that I am the Lord. Thus saith the Lord God: One affliction—behold, affliction cometh; the end is come, the end is come; it hath awakened against thee, behold, it cometh. Destruction cometh upon thee that dwellest in the [Col. 1452B] land. The time cometh; the day of slaughter is near, and not the glory of the mountains.”

And if to those upon whom Babylonian captivity then hung it seemed that that end, that affliction, and that day of slaughter were being pointed out, as it were, with a finger, yet to us who still read these things that end and that day of affliction, that day of slaughter, is undoubtedly proclaimed: the day which shall come, no longer, as then, upon one nation, but “upon the four quarters of the earth” and upon every inhabitant of the earth—a true end, a true day of affliction, truly “a day of slaughter,” whose magnitude neither this present discourse nor any discourse whatsoever is sufficient to express.

For, to complete the course of exposition now begun, this is the day of the universal judgment, which truly “will be a time of slaughter, and not of the glory of the mountains,” that is, of the proud. So another prophet, though he seems to speak only of the Babylonian captivity foretold, in a similar proclamation spoke of that last day: “The great day of the Lord is near, near and exceeding swift. The voice of the day of the Lord is bitter; the mighty man shall be troubled there” (Zeph. I), and so forth.

For since this is the end of evangelical faith—that he who for our sake became man and suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, is believed to be coming thence to judge the living and the dead—rightly, as at the beginning of this prophecy, in the fifth year of the captivity, we understand through the four faces of the living creatures the fourfold Gospel of Christ, so at the end, that is, from this place up to that which he later says, “I will deal with them according to [Col. 1452D] their way, and judge them according to their judgments,” we understand the future universal judgment to be announced.

And let not the evil servant say in his heart, “This will happen in times far off,” or, “My lord delayeth his coming,” and, made more secure by this presumption, begin “to beat his fellow-servants, and to eat and drink with the drunken” (Luke XII). For truly, even if he does not believe that that judgment is so near that it can be pointed out with a finger, saying, “Behold the end; behold the affliction; behold the day of slaughter; behold, the end comes; now the end comes”; or, according to the other prophet, “The day of the Lord is near, near, and exceedingly swift” (Zeph. I)—at least he cannot conceal from himself that he will soon die by his own individual death and then be judged in respect of his soul. “The lord of that servant shall come in a day when he expecteth him not, and at an hour that he knoweth not, and shall divide him, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites” (Luke XII).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

That the vision of the sixth year concerns the same mysteries of Christ the Son of God: namely, that through the four increasing abominations the reasons are given why the Lord forsook the Jews and went forth into the field of the Gentiles.

(CAP. VIII.) After the prophecy of the one—that is, the fifth—year of the captivity, we judge that that of the following, namely the sixth, year also ought not to be passed over. For indeed, up to the words, “He said, and the Spirit lifted me up and brought me into Chaldea, to the captivity, in a vision of the Spirit of God; and the vision which I had seen was taken up from me” [Col. 1453B] (Ezek. XI), it looks to the same mystery of Christ and to the same sacraments of the Gospel of Christ the Son of God.

“And it came to pass in the sixth year, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month, as I sat in my house and the elders of Judah sat before me, that the hand of the Lord God fell upon me there. And I looked, and behold, a likeness as the appearance of fire: from the appearance of his loins downward, fire; and from his loins upward, as the appearance of brightness, like the appearance of electrum. And the likeness of a hand was put forth and seized me by the lock of my head, and the Spirit lifted me between earth and heaven and brought me in visions of God to Jerusalem, beside the inner gate which faced north, where the idol of jealousy stood, provoking jealousy. And behold, there was the glory of the God of Israel, according to the vision [Col. 1453C] which I had seen in the plain.”

We read that the preceding vision came to the prophet in the fifth year of Jeconiah’s captivity, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month (Ezek. I). But this vision, which we now intend to expound, is recorded as having occurred in the sixth year of the same king, in the sixth month, on the fifth day of the month. It is therefore clear that these things written took place after one year and two months; and either that prophecy was interrupted for a year and two months, or that the matters which the preceding discourse relates occurred throughout the whole fourteen months.

“And he said to me: Son of man, lift up thine eyes toward the way of the north. And I lifted up mine eyes toward the way of the north, and behold, on the north side of the altar, at the very entrance, was the idol of jealousy,” and so forth.

The four successive increases of abominations shown to the prophet in this vision must be carefully considered. For if you were asking, as it were, for the grounds of justice—why, according to the prophecy of the preceding year, the glory of the Lord went out into the field of the Gentiles after forsaking the Jews, while the Jews themselves were afterwards besieged, perished by famine, fell by the sword, and were led captive among all nations—behold, he goes back more deeply. By displaying four abominations of the nation, progressively worsening, he then represents and confirms, under almost the same image, the destruction of that same nation, beginning thus: “The visitations of the city have drawn near” (Ezek. IX). And afterwards: “And I looked, and behold, four wheels beside the cherubim: one wheel beside one cherub, and another wheel beside another cherub; and their appearance and likeness [Col. 1454A] were one for all four, as if a wheel were in the midst of the earth,” and so forth (ibid.).

Concerning him whose “likeness was as the appearance of fire, from the appearance of his loins downward fire, and from his loins upward as the appearance of brightness, like the appearance of electrum,” has already been said above. Nor is there any doubt that he is Christ the Son of God, the same also Son of Man, in whom is the likeness of electrum, compounded of gold and silver; who also at the end will judge the world by fire. This is signified, as it were, by the fiery lower parts of the body, when it is said, “From the appearance of his loins downward, fire.”

This is the first abomination: “And I lifted up mine eyes toward the way of the north, and behold, 561 on the north side of the altar, at the very entrance, the idol of jealousy. Again he said, Thou shalt see greater abominations” [Col. 1454B] (Ezek. VIII).

These are the greater abominations: “When I had broken through the wall, one door appeared. And when I entered, I saw, and behold, every likeness of creeping things and abominable beasts, and all the idols of the house of Israel were painted on the wall all around. And seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel stood before the pictures, with Jeconiah son of Saphan standing in their midst; and every one had a censer in his hand, and a cloud of incense-smoke rose up.”

These are greater abominations, because there was only “the idol of jealousy at the very entrance” there; but here there were not only idols, but also “seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel standing, and Jeconiah in their midst, and every one of them holding a censer in his hand, while a cloud of incense-smoke [Col. 1454C] rose up.”

“Again,” he says, “thou shalt see greater abominations.” What are those greater ones? “He brought me through the gate of the house of the Lord facing north; and behold, women sat there mourning Adonis.”

According to the Gentile fable, in the month of July Adonis, Venus’s beloved and a most beautiful youth, was killed and afterwards was said to have returned to life. Therefore they called the same month July by his name and celebrated an annual rite for him, in which he was mourned by women as if dead, and afterwards was sung of and praised as if restored to life.

These are greater abominations, because men were standing there, whereas here women also sat. For it is worse in abominations to have sat than to have stood: that is, it is a greater injury to have made sin habitual than merely to have committed sin. But more on this below.

“Again,” he says, “thou shalt see greater abominations.” What are these greater abominations? “And he brought me into the inner court of the house of the Lord, and behold, at the entrance of the temple of the Lord, between the porch and the altar, about twenty-five men, with their backs toward the temple of the Lord and their faces toward the east, worshipped the rising sun. And behold,” he says, “they apply the branch to their nostrils.”

To worship the rising sun, which is certainly a creature, is plainly to err; but to have one’s back toward the temple of the Lord and to apply a branch to one’s nostrils is plainly to despise the Lord who rebukes them and to delight in one’s own evils.

## CHAPTER XXIX

That by these four stages of increase the same thing ought to be understood as by the prophetic expression: “For three transgressions of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, and the rest, and for four I will not turn him back.”

As we are to consider these increases of sin more carefully, let us recall another prophet, through whom God speaks: “For three transgressions of Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, or Edom, or the children of Ammon, or indeed Moab, or Israel”—by whose number of seven all nations are signified—“for three transgressions,” I say, “of any one of them, and for four I will not turn him back” (Amos I–II).

The first transgression is to entertain evil in desire; the second, to perpetrate it in deed; the third, to have it as a habit; the fourth, to defend evil deeds and to take pleasure in oneself in them.

The first of these is signified by “the idol of jealousy at the very entrance on the north side.” For what is it to have the idol of jealousy at the entrance, except to entertain an evil desire—which is the entrance of perversity—before the eyes of the Lord? Therefore he says: “Put away the evil of your thoughts from before mine eyes” (Isa. I).

But what is it for each person to stand before an idol with a censer in his hand, so that a cloud of incense-smoke rises, except to carry out in deed a premeditated crime, so that the effect of sin bursts forth even to the outward senses? What then is it for women to sit in mourning for Adonis, except for effeminate souls to have become putrid in the habit of sin?

The first verse of the Psalter briefly embraces these three things: “Blessed is the man who hath not gone in the counsel of the ungodly” [Col. 1455C] (Ps. I), that is, who has not conceived an evil desire—the thing signified by having within “the idol of jealousy on the north side,” that is, from the devil’s suggestion. “And hath not stood in the way of sinners” (ibid.), that is, who has not come to the actual effect of sin—the thing signified by standing before an idol and producing from the censer in one’s hand a cloud of vapour. And, “He hath not sat in the seat of pestilence” (ibid.), that is, one who does not corrupt his neighbours by the stench of evil habit—the thing signified by women sitting and mourning Adonis. For, in truth, like women with seductive gestures, they sing while mourning and mourn while singing: they mourn Adonis as dead and sing of him as though restored to life; they grieve over pleasures lost and rejoice in pleasures regained, to the overthrow of those who hear them.

The prophet already mentioned, looking to these three and saying, “For three transgressions,” as it were checked himself. For it is possible, and it has sometimes happened, that the Lord converts one who has reached even evil habit. Hence in his Gospel he raised not only the girl lying dead in the house, and the young man already being carried to the tomb (Luke VII), but also Lazarus, dead four days and already stinking (John XI).

Thus, when the prophet Amos had said, “For three transgressions,” he did not at once complete the expression by saying, “I will not turn him back.” For although it happens more rarely, it is nevertheless clear that the Lord converts, or has converted, one of this kind. He therefore preferred to say, “And for four I will not turn him back” [Col. 1456A].

For the fourth transgression, according to this passage, is, while worshipping the sun, to turn one’s back toward the temple of the Lord and apply a branch to one’s nostrils: that is, amid the very habit of sin, proudly to despise the voice of the Lord calling one back, to employ brazen self-defence, and meanwhile to rejoice in evil deeds and exult in most wicked things as though in the sweet scent of a little branch (Prov. I).

All the offspring of the human race also inherited this from the corrupt root of the first parent. For after he had conceived in his heart the secret ambition to be divine, bitten the forbidden tree, and hidden himself from the face of the Lord, he also lifted up his neck in the fourth transgression, saying: “The woman whom thou gavest me as a companion gave me, and I ate” (Gen. III).

But now let us return to the very nation, or city, against which this discourse is first directed, and number these four increases of its sin, on account of which it was justly cast away at the coming of the Saviour.

## CHAPTER XXX

What it was for that people to have the idol of jealousy; what it was to stand before idols with a censer; what it was for women sitting to mourn Adonis; and what it was to worship the rising sun while applying a branch to their nostrils.

“And I lifted up mine eyes toward the way of the north, and behold, on the north side of the altar, at the very [Col. 1456C] entrance, was the idol of jealousy.”

To lift up the eyes is to recall earlier times to memory: namely, the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, when they set out and crossed the sea by a mighty hand and an outstretched arm (Exod. XII). Was not the idol of jealousy at the very entrance, when they were first being admitted to the worship of the God of their fathers? Certainly they carried Egypt with them in their minds; they bore Egypt and the idols of Egypt with them in an unchanged mind, though they did not yet betray this in action.

They came to greater abominations when the wall was pierced—that is, when occasion was given: they murmured, wailed for Egypt and for Egypt’s pots of meat (Exod. XVI), and made and worshipped the head of a calf according to the monstrous rite of Egypt (Exod. XXXII). Therefore there was only the idol of jealousy; but here men stood before idols with censers and incense-smoke: that is, there, when they departed from Egypt, idolatry lay hidden in a mind badly formed; here, however, it broke forth openly in deed.

From this they also came to greater abominations, namely women sitting and mourning Adonis. For the greed for filth of this kind became habitual, as it is written in the book of the prophets: “Did ye offer unto me victims or sacrifices forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel? And ye took up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, images which ye made for yourselves to worship them” (Amos V; Acts VII).

They came as far as women sitting—that is, so far that, because of sacrilegious crimes of this sort, the effeminate nation slew the prophets of the Lord in the settledness, that is, ingrained habit, of such conduct. Jezebel first did this, and after her, her daughter Athaliah. Jezebel raged in Samaria; Athaliah in Jerusalem. The former brought Baal into Israel and killed the prophets of the Lord (III Kings XIX); the latter likewise introduced Baal into the temple of the Lord at Jerusalem and killed the kings—indeed, she killed all the royal seed, lest anyone remain to reign from the house of David [Col. 1457A] (IV Kings XI).

The final and worst thing of all remained for that nation: to turn their faces toward the east and their backs against the temple of the Lord. And this it did. For it despised Christ, the Son of God, the true and holy temple of divinity. Nor was it enough that, having turned its back toward it, it rejected the oracles of truth proceeding from it; it also dared to destroy it with sacrilegious hands and tongues. “For their faces were toward the east, and they worshipped the rising sun”: that is, they sought brightness and the light of this present age, in despair of the age to come.

Therefore he said to them: “How can ye believe, who receive glory one from another, and seek not the glory which is from God alone?” (John V). In so great a crime they also applied the branch to their nostrils: that is, they pleased themselves, as though they had fulfilled the law, from whose fruit they did not eat, while they handled only with ostentation the sweet-smelling leaves of its words. “Therefore upon that generation came all the righteous blood shed upon the earth from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXIII). This is what follows.

## CHAPTER XXXI

That for these things it was cried, “The visitations of the city have drawn near”; who the six men coming were; what the vessel in the hand of each was; who the man in their midst clothed in linen was; and what the writer’s ink-horn at his loins was.

(CAP. IX.) “And he cried in mine ears with a loud voice, saying: The visitations of the city have drawn near, and every man hath a vessel of slaughter in his hand. And behold, six men came from the way of the upper gate which faces north, and each had his inner vessel in his hand. One man also was in their midst, clothed in linen, with a writer’s ink-horn at his loins.”

“The visitations of the city have drawn near”: namely, those which, because of the aforesaid abominations—the abominations of the calf—as soon as they had made it, the Lord threatened, saying: “But in the day of vengeance I will visit this sin of theirs also” [Col. 1457D] (Exod. XXXII).

“And every man hath a vessel of slaughter in his hand,” because in that evil and adulterous generation, beyond the sins of the fathers, each also had his own sins in his hand, or in his vessel—that is, in his own conscience—by which they filled up the measure of their fathers, especially by persecuting Christ and his apostles, or his wise men. Of these they killed, stoned, crucified, scourged, and persecuted from city to city (Matt. XXIII).

And who are the six men coming with their individual vessels in hand, unless the six ages of the world, whose sins, from the blood of righteous Abel, were all to be poured back upon that generation? “But the one man in their midst, clothed in linen and with a writer’s ink-horn at his loins” [Col. 1458A] is Christ the Son of God, who, clothed in the linen of our flesh, came into this world in order to enroll in the book of life his elect, who were to be exempted from the vengeance mentioned.

A sign of this was that, immediately when he was to be born, “an edict went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled” (Luke II). “And they entered,” he says, “and stood beside the brazen altar.” They stood ready, I say, to perform the command: the one man to fulfil the command of mercy, the others to execute the sentence of justice.

The brazen altar was outside, beyond the veil; for the golden altar was within the veil, together with the table, the mercy-seat, the ark of the covenant, and the two cherubim: this was called the Holy of Holies. That altar outside was a sign of the present Church; the altar within, of the Church above or heavenly. This man stood outside, for by his own blood he was to enter within.

“And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from the cherubim” which was over him, to the threshold of the house. “And he called the man clothed in linen, who had the writer’s ink-horn at his loins.” Then the glory of the Lord was lifted up to the threshold of the house and called this man when, at the Jordan, at his baptism, the glory of the Father bore witness by manifest signs: the Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, and at the same time there came down a voice saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Col. 1458C] (Matt. III).

Then, I say, he called this man and sent him to preach the Gospel to the poor (Luke IV). For until then he had not preached the Gospel; from then he began to preach and to exercise his priesthood, of which the linen clothing seen here was a sign.

## CHAPTER XXXII

What it is to mark tau upon the foreheads of the men who sigh; what it is that all who are not marked with this sign should be struck; and what it is to begin at the sanctuary of the Lord.

“And the Lord said to him: Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark tau upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and grieve over all the abominations done in its midst. And to the others he said: Hear me: pass through the city after him and strike. Let not your eye spare, neither have pity. Slay old man, youth and virgin, little child and women, unto utter destruction. But do not slay any upon whom ye see tau; and begin at my sanctuary.”

In the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans use even to this day, the final letter, tau, has the likeness of a cross, which is depicted upon Christians’ foreheads and marked by the frequent signing of the hand. It should therefore be noted that it is said: “Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark tau upon the foreheads of the men who sigh and grieve over all the abominations done in its midst.”

For this is what our Lord, when he was about to pass from this world to the Father and to inscribe the sign of his cross upon our foreheads—not with ink, but with his blood and the Holy Spirit—first began to preach, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” [Col. 1459A] (Matt. IV). For this sign is inscribed not on just anyone, but on those who sigh and grieve over their former evils, that is, those who repent. For we are not baptized for the remission of sins otherwise than by renouncing the devil and his pomps; and this is to receive the seal of Christ’s cross.

This man consecrated this sign by his passion for the elect both dead and living. And even today, although he sits in heaven and is bodily absent, however many ministers he may have of this marking, he himself is the one who marks; for he himself is the one who baptizes. “Pass through the city after him,” he says, “and strike”—understand, everyone upon whom you do not see the sign of tau. But do not slay anyone upon whom you see it.

So once in Egypt the children of Israel were commanded: “Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood, and sprinkle the lintel and both doorposts with it; for the Lord will pass through, striking the Egyptians. And when he sees the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, he will pass over the door and will not permit the destroyer to enter and strike” (Exod. XII).

Here there is no distinction between Israelite and Egyptian except the blood of the lamb on the posts and lintels of the houses; likewise here there is no distinction between righteous and sinner except the sign of tau—the sign of the cross of Christ the Son of God—upon their foreheads.

“And begin at my sanctuary,” he says. Why? Because the people whose sanctuary is mine thinks that it has no need of the seal of the cross, the seal of God’s righteousness, since it wishes to establish its own righteousness and therefore is not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. X). Therefore, lest it think the righteousness of faith and the seal of Christ’s cross unnecessary for itself, or suppose that the prophecy of this slaughter does not concern it, pour out all these vessels upon this generation, as many as have been filled from the blood of righteous Abel; and, pouring out and striking, begin at my sanctuary, so that not one stone may be left upon another in this beautiful temple [Col. 1459C] (Matt. XXIII–XXIV): in this great city defile the house, fill the courts with the slain, and go out.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

What it is for the man clothed in linen to say, “I have done as thou commandedst me”; and what it is that he is told, “Enter into the midst of the wheels, fill thine hand with coals of fire, and scatter them over the city.”

“And behold, the man clothed in linen, who had the ink-horn at his back, answered, saying: I have done as thou commandedst me. (CAP. X.) And I looked, and behold, in the firmament over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire stone, like the appearance of the likeness of a throne. And he said to the man clothed in linen: Enter into the midst of the wheels beneath the cherubim, fill thine hand with coals of fire which are between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city.”

“I have done,” he says, “as thou [Col. 1460A] commandedst me.” As though he said: I became obedient to thee unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. II); and by doing so I marked the foreheads. I consecrated the sign by which the foreheads of those who sigh and grieve, repent, and seek remission of sins are marked. There remains for me the reward of obedience: give me the name which is above every name, that at my name every knee may bow, of things in heaven, things on earth, and things under the earth (ibid.).

For this is what the Psalmist says in his person (Ps. CVII): “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready”—understand, to obey thee. Let that which remains now take place: let me rise from the dead, and then at last “I will sing and make melody in my glory.” But God, namely the Father, immediately replies: “Awake, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp.” And he says, “I will arise at dawn.” Then God the Father says to God the Son: “Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and let thy glory be over all the earth.”

Of that exaltation this is said here: “And I looked, and behold, in the firmament over the heads of the cherubim there appeared above them something like a sapphire stone, like the appearance of the likeness of a throne.” For in the preceding vision also it was said that there was a throne of sapphire stone in the firmament over the heads of the cherubim, or, as it is written there, “which was above the heads of the living creatures” (Ezek. II): the session at the Father’s right hand, concerning which David too says in the Spirit, “The Lord said unto my Lord” (Ps. CIX), and so forth. Here likewise, in the same Spirit, he reports that the same Father said: “Enter into the midst of the wheels beneath the cherubim, fill thine hand with coals of fire which are between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city” [Col. 1460C].

For when Christ the Son of God rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, sitting at the right hand of God, by that same resurrection, ascension, and session he entered “into the midst of the wheels”: namely, in order to illuminate or open the mysteries of the Scriptures which had previously been closed. These, as was said above, are signified by the likeness of the wheels, which are said also to be beneath the cherubim because all the heavenly creatures mentioned there look into them, as we explained more fully in that place.

And what is meant when he is told upon entering, “Fill thine hand with coals of fire which are between the cherubim, and scatter them over the city,” except: receive authority to execute judgment because thou art the Son of Man (John V), to judge the sinful city, indeed the whole world, by fire? This fire is among the cherubim: that is, it is proclaimed throughout the Scriptures among those things which are written concerning the often-mentioned living creatures.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

What it is for the cherubim to stand on the right when the man enters; for the inner court to be filled with cloud and the outer court with the brightness of glory; and what it is for a cherub to stretch forth a hand to the fire and give it to the man clothed in linen.

“And he entered in my sight; and the cherubim stood on the right side of the house when the man entered, and the cloud filled the inner court. And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the cherubim to the threshold of the house, and the house [Col. 1461A] was filled with cloud, and the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the Lord; and the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court, like the voice of God Almighty speaking.”

He rightly says, “in my sight,” for “while the apostles looked on, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts I). Likewise rightly, “the cherubim stood on the right side of the house when he entered”: for whatever was written, or existed, according to the living creatures of which we have spoken, began openly to bear witness to his glory when he had been taken up.

“And the cloud,” he says, “filled the inner court”: that is, the Jewish people, which was inside and had until then been near to God, was darkened through unbelief. “And the glory of the Lord was lifted up from above the cherubim to the threshold of the house”: namely, that glory of the Lord of which the Psalmist says, “Be thou exalted above the heavens, O God, and let thy glory be over all the earth” (Ps. CVII), became openly known to all according to the truth of the Scriptures, as the apostles preached.

“And the house was filled with cloud”—understand, when the glory of the Lord lifted itself to the threshold of the house. For the chief priests and the Levitical order, and likewise the scribes and Pharisees, whose office was the service of the house, were first struck with blindness, while the glory of the resurrection appeared outside. “And the court was filled with the brightness of the glory of the Lord,” for very many of the people believed at the beginning of the evangelical preaching, enlightened by the Holy Spirit. “And the sound of the wings of the cherubim was heard as far as the outer court,” for the sound of the apostles preaching quickly reached us Gentiles, who were outside.

What was that sound? “Like the voice of God Almighty speaking,” truly. For it was not they who spoke, but the Holy Spirit; nor did the men speak from themselves, but Christ spoke in them, and God the Father worked with men who had formerly been unlearned and without letters, confirming their word by the signs which followed [Col. 1461C] (Mark XVI).

“And the cherub stretched forth a hand from the midst of the cherubim to the fire which was among the cherubim, and took it and gave it into the hand of him who was clothed in linen. And he, having received it, went out.”

Who does not know for what purpose that man went out after receiving the fire, what he did, or what he will do? For that city afterwards burned with hostile fire, and finally he will judge the whole world by fire. But how is the cherub said to have stretched out his hand and given fire to this man? And who is this cherub? Surely he who is signified by the man himself: in both the cherub and the man, Christ is one and the same God and man.

He himself, I say, is cherub in that he is the wisdom of God; for *cherub* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” This was what that infamous prince of Tyre aspired to be, and therefore this prophet speaks to him in rebuke and irony: “Thou art the extended and protecting cherub” (Ezek. XXVIII). He is likewise the man because, though he was God, he became man. Thus the one and the same both gives and receives: in that he is God, he gives to the inferior nature of man; in that he is man, he receives from the higher divinity.

Hence the Psalmist says: “Thou hast ascended on high; thou hast taken captivity captive; thou hast received gifts in men” [Col. 1462A] (Ps. LXVII). Whether one says, according to the Hebrew truth, “Thou hast received gifts in men,” or, according to the Apostle, “He gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV), in the Septuagint the understanding is guided by faith through the distinction already stated. “And there appeared in the cherubim the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings. And I saw, and behold, four wheels beside the cherubim, one wheel beside one cherub and another wheel beside another cherub. The appearance of the wheels was like the vision of a chrysolite stone. And their appearance was one likeness for all four, as though a wheel were in the midst of a wheel.”

And a little later: “This is the living creature which I saw by the river Chebar.” And afterwards: “This is the living creature which I saw above the God of Israel by the river Chebar. And I understood that they were four cherubim, each with four faces, each with four wings, and the likeness of a human hand beneath their wings,” and so forth.

We necessarily mentioned these matters above, where it was necessary to discern how these living creatures are both four and one. Therefore we pass them over in the present place, especially since their more extended treatment has once for all compelled us, in the interest of moving forward, to avoid repeating what has already been said.

Yet this should be noted: formerly the appearance of the wheels was “as the appearance of the sea,” but now it is “as the appearance of a chrysolite stone,” or carbuncle, so that the likeness of the punishments by fire, which is delivered by the cherub, may be shown.

## CHAPTER XXXV

When he says, “The vision which I had seen was taken up from me,” it must be understood as referring to that man, and as extending until the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, when he saw the same appearance of the man.

(CAP. XI.) The prophet took care to conclude the account of the present vision thus: “And the spirit lifted me up and brought me into Chaldea, to the exiles, in a vision—in the vision, in the Spirit of God—and the vision which I had seen was taken up from me.” When he says that the vision of the glory of the Lord was taken up from him, it may be understood as remaining so until the twenty-fifth year of the exile. For the vision which he saw in this year and the preceding one—namely, the appearance of the glorious and desirable man and the likeness of the heavenly living creatures, a vision of “the likeness of the glory of the Lord” (Ezek. II)—is not thereafter recorded as seen [Col. 1462D] until the twenty-fifth year of the exile, when he says: “The hand of the Lord came upon me, and behold, a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, and a linen cord was in his hand” (Ezek. XL). Again: “And I saw a vision according to the appearance which I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and an appearance according to the sight which I had seen by the river Chebar” (Ezek. XLIII).

This vision, like the two which we previously touched upon, namely those of the fifth and sixth years of the exile, concerns the very person and evangelical glory of Christ, the Son of God. But the intervening passages are prophecies of other, or at least impending, events. For example, after, “the vision which I had seen was taken up from me”—a vision surely concerning things to come long afterwards—he immediately adds something [Col. 1463A] near at hand, that is, concerning the impending Babylonian captivity (CAP. XII): “Therefore, son of man, prepare for yourself the equipment of exile, and you shall go into exile before their eyes.” And further: “This burden concerns the prince who is in Jerusalem. I shall spread my net over him, and he shall be taken in my dragnet; and I shall bring him into Babylon, into the land of the Chaldeans, and he shall not see it, [Col. 1464A] and there he shall die.” He means Prince Zedekiah, whose face was to be covered so that, being blind, he should not see the land of Babylon (4 Kings XXV).

Therefore let us also here make an end of the present volume; and from the glory of the Lord now repeated for the third time—that is, from the vision of the twenty-fifth year—let us take the beginning of the following book.

## 565. SECOND BOOK ON EZEKIEL  
*(Ezek. XL–XLVIII)*

[Col. 1463]

## CHAPTER I

Concerning the final vision: that it is exceedingly closed, and therefore must above all be brought near to the lampstand which is Christ, so that it may in some measure be understood.

Since we wish to follow the heavenly living creatures of which we spoke above, and since it is written of them, “Each one went straight forward” (Ezek. I), let us likewise, according to our measure, go straight forward—that is, let us keep faithfully in mind the purpose of our undertaking—so that we may be able to see and understand, at least in some part, a vision which is exceedingly closed, not to say obscure.

Now our purpose in this work is, as we proposed at the beginning, to seek the glory of the holy Trinity, the faith of Christ, and the glory of his kingdom. What lampstand is brighter than this? Or in what other light shall we be able to see this light, except in that light of which the Scriptures unquestionably speak? Let us therefore draw nearer and unfold the volume of this vision by its light; for truly, the more nearly and attentively we look upon his own proper person, the more fully the meaning of this Scripture, which is closed, will be opened to us.

## CHAPTER II

That this vision concerns Christ’s glory or divinity more deeply than the earlier ones; and what is the city into whose building that man led the prophet.

(CAP. XL.) “In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month, in the fourteenth year after the city was struck down, on that very day the hand of the Lord came upon me, and he brought me there in visions of God. He brought me into the land of Israel and set me upon a mountain [Col. 1463D] exceedingly high, upon which there was something like the structure of a city facing south. And he brought me there, and behold, there was a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, with a linen cord in his hand and a measuring reed in his hand. And he stood in the gate.”

In the first two years of his prophecy, this man had indeed once and again seen the great glory, or likeness of the glory, of the Lord: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of a calf, and the face of a flying eagle; and then something like the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne; and above the likeness of the throne, the likeness as it were of the [Col. 1464A] appearance of a man (Ezek. I). But is Christ the Son of God only all this, and no more? Is there nothing further to know or believe concerning him beyond what these faces signify—namely, that he was born a man of the Virgin, suffered, rose again, ascended into heaven, and will come from that seat of paternal majesty to judge the living and the dead? Does not the rule of faith also demand, as most necessary to our salvation, that we believe and know that he was God, “and all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I)?

Rightly, then, after the prophet had seen the things mentioned above, he is led by the hand of the Lord into the land of Israel and “set upon a mountain exceedingly high”: namely, into that land and upon that exceedingly high mountain where “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (ibid.), so that he may see that all things were made through him, and [Col. 1464C] that, before the Word became flesh, all received from his fullness that very thing by which they were filled (ibid.). There was, as it were, the structure of the city facing south: the city of Jerusalem, concerning which the Psalm says: “Jerusalem,” it says, “which is built as a city, whose participation is in the same” [*in idipsum*] (Ps. CXXI).

For it is still being built from human beings, though it was long ago built from blessed spirits. Their whole fellowship detests the cold north—that is, the proud devil—and in humility turns southward, that is, toward the Holy Spirit, loving and praising its Creator. “And he brought me there,” he says—understand, in the Spirit—that I might contemplate the work which God wrought from the beginning, he who at the end of the ages deigned to become man. For he immediately goes on to speak of him: “And behold, a man [Col. 1464D] whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, with a linen cord in his hand and a measuring reed in his hand.”

## CHAPTER III

Why the man’s appearance was like bronze, and why a cord and a measuring reed were in his hand.

“Behold,” he says, “a man.” A man, not yet in actual essence, but in foreknowledge and fixed ordination; yet God then as now in eternal and unchangeable essence. “Whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” For he is the sounding Word of the Father, whose sound has today gone forth so greatly into all the earth that he was rightly prefigured by bronze, a metal of great resonance. “And a linen cord in his hand, and a measuring reed in his hand.”

The cord belongs to architects or builders, while the reed belongs to writers. And rightly both were—indeed, are—in the hand of this Word: for he is the architect and maker of the world; and he himself, before becoming man, composed the holy legal and prophetic Scripture. And rightly the cord is called simply a cord, whereas the reed is called a measuring reed. For he made the fabric of the world, whose workmanship the cord signified, by himself alone; he did not receive the power of that work or structure by measure. But he set forth Holy Scripture through human beings, to whom he gave, not all things to all alike, but to each one according to the measure he willed.

“And he stood in the gate.” Truly he stood, and still stands, in the gate, because no one truly enters either into true knowledge of the making of the world or into sound understanding of Holy Scripture except through him. Nor does he merely stand in the gate: he himself is also the gate—gate, I say, and gatekeeper; door and doorkeeper. He is the gate or door inasmuch as he is man; the gatekeeper or doorkeeper inasmuch as he is God. “I,” he says, “am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John X). And nevertheless he says of himself: “To him the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER IV

How fittingly he says to one to whom he is about to show lofty things, “Son of man”; and that it is fitting for one who sees to proclaim.

“And the same man spoke to me: Son of man, see with your eyes, hear with your ears, and set your heart upon all that I shall show you, because you have been brought here in order that these things may be shown you. Proclaim all that you see to the house of Israel.” — “Son of man,” he says. It is a fitting reminder of weakness, as if he said: O seer, do not be lifted up by the greatness of the revelations when you see visions of God, for you are a son of man, a worm. Let this not escape you; hold it in memory.

With your head thus humbled, “see with your eyes and hear with your ears”—with the eyes of the heart and the ears of the inner man—“and set your heart upon all that I shall show you.” Do not be like those whose heart is so turned away that they refuse to understand. For this is fitting: be present with a willing heart, and do not be ungrateful, “because you have been brought here in order that these things may be shown you,” so that you may meet with all the saints “in the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV); so that you may no longer be a child like those who, hearing that the Messiah is to come, think—or will think—that he is only man, and not also God before becoming man or a man.
