And because, just as “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, so with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X), proclaim all that you see to the house of Israel. Although this proclamation must for the present, because of the time and the mystery’s concealment, remain closed—for the house of Israel now, if you proclaim it in bare words, neither wishes nor is able to bear it—nevertheless proclaim what you see: not only to the present house, indeed not so much to the present as to the future house of Israel, not so much to the fleshly as to the spiritual house. First, for yourself, now in the present, deposit in the treasuries of truth the gold of confession which, though hidden, has been entrusted to you; then it will also benefit the future house of Israel, seeing and knowing in part, and nevertheless reverencing what it cannot see or know, until, when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part is done away (1 Cor. XIII).

## CHAPTER V

Why, although both the cord and the reed are in the man’s hand, nothing is said to the prophet about the cord; that by the reed of six cubits and a handbreadth is understood the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit; and what is the wall outside round about the house.

“And behold, there was a wall outside round about the house on every side, and in the man’s hand a measuring reed of six cubits and a handbreadth; and he measured the breadth of the building, one reed, and likewise its height, one reed.” First it should be noted that, although both the linen cord and the measuring reed are in the man’s hand, the cord is passed over in silence: nothing is shown by means of it, while everything takes place before the prophet’s eyes by means of the measuring reed. Why is this? Clearly because the prophet, or anyone else, is not brought here to learn how God made the fabric of the world, which is understood through the architect’s cord, but only to see what Scripture says about it, Scripture expressed by the reed; and to believe, according to its [Col. 1466C] testimony, that the one and only God made heaven and earth and all that is in them through his Word—through his Word, I say, which also became flesh, whose glory, says the Evangelist, “we saw” (John I).

But what is this reed in the man’s hand except that of which the Father says in David: “My tongue is the reed of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. XLIV)? What, I ask, is this measuring reed of six cubits and a handbreadth except the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit? For one cubit of this reed is fear, one cubit piety, one cubit fortitude, one cubit counsel, one cubit understanding; while the handbreadth is wisdom. The other gifts are, indeed, weapons or instruments of those who act in time, but wisdom is the reward of those at rest; abiding happily in that life, it completes the handbreadth.

Therefore, “there was a wall outside round about the house on every side, and in the man’s hand a measuring reed,” because before this man distributed by his hand the measures of the reed—that is, of the Holy Spirit—to his prophets, what was in the hidden and ineffable house with God lay concealed from all men. Even now we can know nothing further except what he deigned to declare through their mind and mouth, by his reed—that is, the Holy Spirit. “And he measured,” he says, “the breadth of the building, one reed, and likewise its height, one reed.” The breadth of the building is the literal sense of Scripture, while its height is the spiritual sense of that same Scripture. He measured both by one reed, because both have been handed down to us by one and the same author, the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER VI

What is meant by the eastern gate to which the man came; what by the ascending steps; and what by the chamber.

“And he came to the gate which faced the eastern way, and he went up by its steps; and he measured the threshold of the gate, one reed—that is, one threshold, one reed in breadth. And the chamber, one reed in length and one reed in breadth; and between the chambers, five cubits; and the threshold of the gate beside the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed; and he measured the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed.”

The gate which faces the eastern way is the first origin of the world. This man came to that gate; for already, indeed long before, he was in the bosom of the Father. Thus he is and will be the Wisdom of God, who says in Proverbs: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before the earth was made. I was with him, arranging all things, and I delighted day by day,” etc. (Prov. VIII). “And he went up,” he says, “by its steps.” By steps, I say, he went up to the gate of the eastern way: for by stages and through certain ascents he ordered his works—for example, he first created the inanimate earth; then living trees; then living and sentient animals of the earth; then man, living, sentient, and rational.

“And he measured the threshold of the gate, or the breadth of the threshold, one reed; that is, one threshold, one reed in breadth.” The threshold of the gate is the entrance to the building. Hence the threshold rightly signifies the ordering of the whole work, concerning which the Evangelist says: “That which was made in him was life” (John I). Therefore he measured the threshold of the gate—or the breadth of the threshold—by one reed: that is, he purposed to enlarge his works in one Spirit, according to that Spirit’s breadth and magnificence; so that, because he is sevenfold, he might make six forms of most beautiful work and, completing his work on the seventh day, rest from all work.

That rest is immediately signified by the name “chamber”: “And the chamber,” he says, “one reed in length and one reed in breadth.” The chamber’s position was square, signifying the full eternity and eternal fullness of the Lord’s rest, measured by one reed—that is, made perfect in the Holy Spirit, who is true love. “And between the chambers, five cubits.” There the Creator is truly joined to the creature like a bridegroom to a bride in the chamber of marriage. This is indeed a customary comparison in Holy Scripture (Ps. XVIII); but there are five cubits between those chambers—that is, those chambers are wholly unlike these which man knows only through the five senses. For no one perceives the delight of that chamber through the five senses of the flesh, Scripture bearing witness: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared in that chamber for those who love him” (Isa. LXIV; 1 Cor. II). Why both one chamber and several chambers are rightly spoken of, we shall not pass over later.

“And the threshold [Col. 1468A] of the gate beside the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed; and he measured the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed.” The order of the words is: “And he measured the threshold of the gate according to the measure of the vestibule which was within, namely one reed.” For when the prophet says, “The threshold of the gate beside the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed; and he measured the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed,” it is plainly shown that the threshold previously described was outside.

Now the outer threshold is the letter; the inner threshold in Holy Scripture is allegory. Because we proceed through the letter to allegory, we come, as it were, from the threshold that is outside to that which is within. Rightly both are measured by one reed, because the truth of both—the letter and the allegory alike—is commended by the same author, the Spirit. Or rather, because, as we said above, the Evangelist testifies, “That which was made in him was life” (John I), we rightly understand there to be an inner threshold and here an inner vestibule, so that both there and here we understand “that which was made in him was life”; and only then do we proceed, according to the order of Scripture and in keeping with our purpose, with “that which was made.” For it follows:

## CHAPTER VII

What it means that he first measured with the reed and then every measurement is made in cubits; and that the vestibule of the gate is described as eight cubits, with two cubits at its front.

“And he measured the vestibule of the gate: eight cubits, and its front: two cubits; but the vestibule of the gate was within. Moreover, the chambers of the gate toward the eastern way were three on this side and three on that side; the measure of the three was one, and the measure of the fronts was one on either side.”

It should be noted that here the reckoning of measurement changes from the reed to cubits. While the man measures the outer court, the inner court—each with its three gates—the temple also, and the treasury chambers, no mention is made of the reed; every measurement is made in cubits. This ought not to pass unremarked, because what has been said so far is to be understood according to “what was made in him was life,” whereas what the discourse now begins to recount should be understood according to “that which was made,” in the same order in which Scripture proceeds, beginning thus: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. I).

For what does it mean that, after saying, “And he measured the inner vestibule of the gate, one reed”—that is, six cubits and a handbreadth—he immediately adds: “And he measured the vestibule of the gate: eight cubits; but the vestibule of the gate was within”? What, I ask, does it mean that one and the same inner vestibule, measured by one reed, is immediately said to be eight cubits, unless it means that where the work of the creature was immutably life, there also its end was fixed, so that after a mutable course it might be perfected in the eighth age?

For the number seven, contained in the reed of six cubits and a handbreadth, is indivisible; hence among philosophers it is called male. But eight is female because it is divisible and is cut into equal parts down to the final unit. Thus, by the former is understood the immutable life which, according to the Evangelist, was in the Word; by the latter, the mutable course of the rational creature, which, as has already been said, is perfected in the eighth age of the world.

With these things having been set forth according to, as has often been said, “what was made in him was life,” we now at last enter into the outward work of the creature, “that which was made,” to the praise and glory of this glorious man and most faithful measurer. For, as everywhere in all the Scriptures, so especially in this vision, he testifies that he is the ancient architect of the world, who deigned to become man within it; and, as the Psalm also confesses concerning the glorious city of God, whose foundations are in the holy mountains: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI).

## CHAPTER VIII

What are the three chambers on this side and three on that; how there is one measure for the three; and in what respect one measure belongs to angels and elect human beings.

“And he measured its front, two cubits. The chambers of the gate also toward the eastern way were three on this side and three on that side. The measure of the three was one, and the measure of the fronts was one on either side.”

The front of the vestibule is the beginning and first utterance of Scripture, by which the world’s first making is described. The measure of this front is two cubits. For it says: “In the beginning God created heaven [Col. 1469C] and earth” (Gen. I). One cubit is heaven, that is, all invisible things; likewise one cubit is earth, that is, all visible things. Great indeed are both that creature and this creature; yet, considered in relation to the greatness of this immeasurable man, either scarcely deserves to be called a cubit. For, according to another prophet, he weighed the heavens in his palm and suspended the mass of the earth on three fingers (Isa. XL).

Why, then, were there six chambers, three on this side and three on that, toward the eastern way, unless because the maker of the world worked on twice three days and only then entered into his rest? His rest is indeed one; but because one craftsman set forth six kinds of work, there are rightly six chambers, while nevertheless one rest is signified. By saying “on this side and on that,” moreover, he briefly distinguishes the chambers of heaven and earth, the chambers of angelic and human creatures. The angelic creature, precisely because it does not have an earthly body, is in comparison with humanity like heaven; yet both the human and angelic creatures have been admitted, by the Creator’s gracious condescension, to the chambers of blessed rest.

“The measure,” he says, “of the three was one.” He did not say, “the measure of all,” that is, of the six chambers—although this too is true in some respect. For elect human beings shall be like the angels of God (Matt. XXII), and in the Apocalypse we read: “the measure of a man, which is that of an angel” (Apoc. XXI). But he said, “the measure of the three was one,” namely of the three on this side and the three on that: on this side, the angels, apart from whom no rational creature was made on the first three days, on which the fabric of the world was set forth; on that side, human beings, apart from whom likewise no rational creature was made on the remaining three days, on which that same fabric was adorned with moving creatures.

Thus the one measure of the three on this side is when it was said: “Let light be made; and light was made; and God saw the light, that it was good” (Gen. I); for this is the angelic creature. The one measure of the three is again when it was said: “Therefore the Lord God formed man from the slime of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. II). This is the one and common measure of human nature. Moreover, the measure of the fronts is one on either side, for the image and likeness of God shine forth in each creature’s front—that is, in its mind. Although on this side, namely on our side, we read: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. I), nevertheless the same thing must be understood on the other side, though it is not expressed in the same words. For when it says, “Let light be made,” the brightness of God’s image and likeness is expressed in the angelic creature more briefly indeed, but no less truly. Finally, conversely, when man has been made and perfected in the image and likeness of God—that is, because he is rational and an imitator of divine goodness—both creatures are regarded as distinguished.

## CHAPTER IX

What is the breadth of the gate of ten cubits, and its length of thirteen.

“And he measured the breadth of the threshold of the gate: ten cubits; and the length of the gate: thirteen cubits.” This gate is not the same as the one above. It is to be understood, not as opening from the building mentioned before, but conversely, opening into the middle of the chambers. This gate is the law or condition by the observance of which we enter into that rest of God in the eternal chambers. “For,” says the Apostle, “we who have believed enter into rest, as he said: ‘If they shall enter into my rest’” (Heb. IV). Again: “For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his labours, as God rested from his works” (ibid.).

“And the length of the gate,” he says, “thirteen cubits.” Here the length of the gate means its height, just as we call a person whom we see to be tall “of long stature.” For the gate’s length cannot be understood transversely, since its breadth is shown by ten cubits. It is a great gate—broad and spacious enough, by the measure of man, if you look at the small body. Yet the Lord says: “How narrow the gate and strait the way that leads to life, and few there are who find it” (Matt. VII).

But there is a certain grossness or vastness for which this gate, ten cubits broad and thirteen long, is indeed exceedingly narrow and strait. This is the vastness of desires; this is the grossness of riches. For he says also: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIX). The breadth of ten cubits is the ten commandments of the law. And since one of them is, “You shall not covet” (Exod. XX), how could one enter through this gate who is broader than its breadth by as much as greed has heaped more desires around him?

That breadth indeed belonged to the former people, who received the ten commandments of the law. But ours, from the Gospel, is a length of thirteen cubits: upon those same commandments is given faith in the holy Trinity, by which we are required to confess one God alone in such a way that we make certain the distinction of the persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER X

What is the one-cubit ledge before the chambers; what are the six-cubit chambers; and what is the breadth of twenty-five cubits from roof to roof.

“And a ledge before the chambers, one cubit; and one cubit was the boundary on either side. But the chambers were six cubits on this side and on that.” By the “ledge before the chambers” we understand the projection of the roof extending beyond the wall. This was “one cubit”: by that cubit Christ, the mediator between God and men, is understood, as though projecting beyond the walls of the chambers, while outwardly, in the human form which he assumed, he always presents to all elect angels and human beings the blessed vision.

Within, in the inner person, is the delight which is understood by the chambers, because divinity is ineffably united to the creature that loves it. Yet beyond this, he also always appears outwardly in that place and is at hand: that desirable appearance of the Son of Man, into which angels desire to look (1 Pet. I), and by whose same vision humanity too is undoubtedly always gladdened—ever desired, ever present; those who love do not fail, and those who fail do not suffer.

“The chambers were six cubits on this side and on that”—understand, and one handbreadth, as was said above. But he repeated it so that he might immediately add: “And he measured the gate from the roof of one chamber to the roof of the other: a breadth of twenty-five cubits, door opposite door.” This number is formed by multiplying the number five by itself. And since we are endowed with the five bodily senses, this square number, produced by multiplying five by five, signifies their likeness; and although they are less spiritual, they are nevertheless multiplied outwardly in good works through progress.

Therefore, lest we doubt that only spiritual persons or those of virginal purpose enter into that rest and rest with God resting from his works, he says: “He measured the breadth from the roof of one chamber to the roof of the other: twenty-five cubits.” We read something nearly like this in the Song of Songs, where, after it had been said: “King Solomon made himself a litter of the woods of Lebanon; its pillars he made of silver, its back of gold, its ascent of purple” (Song III), it immediately adds: “Its midst he paved with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” (ibid.).

By “door opposite door,” understand the doors of the chambers, the three on this side and the three on that. It signifies the reciprocal harmony and patience, always in the praise of God, of the hearts and voices together of angels and human beings.

## CHAPTER XI

How he made fronts of sixty cubits and fifty cubits before the face of the gate; what the slanting windows are; and what the carved representation of palms round about is.

“And he made the fronts sixty cubits, and from the front [Col. 1472A] of the court of the gate all around. And before the face of the gate, which extended to the face of the inner vestibule, fifty cubits.” He measured at sixty cubits the length of the open-air space whose breadth was twenty-five cubits. This was the space of the court between the fronts of the aforesaid court. But because the inner vestibule of the gate, coming opposite the gate, occupied eight cubits and moreover had two cubits in its front, it admitted sixty cubits at its sides; yet in front of itself, or in front of the gate of the court, it made fifty out of the sixty cubits—that is, ten fewer. This is why, after saying, “He made the fronts sixty cubits,” he immediately added: “And before the face of the gate which extended to the face of the inner vestibule of the gate, fifty cubits.”

Now by the sixty cubits, a number composed of six and ten—for six times ten, or ten times six, makes sixty—are signified the works of those entering; by fifty, however, the grace of mercy coming to meet them. For this number is sanctified by the Law, since in the fiftieth year every possession after sale is commanded to return to its owner; hence that same year of remission is called Jubilee, that is, “letting go” (Lev. XXV). Certainly we need both, whoever we are, if we desire to enter into those chambers, into that rest of the Lord in which that former one rested from his works. For which of angels or human beings could enter there through merits alone, unless received by grace? Or how great are the works of any one of us, that we should enter into the same rest as God by the mere due of righteousness?

We shall speak later about the gates of the court which were all around. “And there were slanting windows in the chambers and in their fronts that were within the gate all around. Likewise there were windows in the vestibules, all around within, and before the fronts a carved representation of palms.” The windows are called slanting like arrows, because, like arrows, they admit a narrow beam of light into houses and widen within. But if the chambers are the rest of God of which we are speaking, and God is light, these windows differ from ours in that our windows receive light from outside, whereas these send it out from within.

The carving or representation of palms is also shown to us so that, having gained victory over the world, we may be made worthy, after the toil of battle, to enter that rest with the palm of virtues.

## CHAPTER XII

What is the outer court, concerning which he says, “And he brought me out into the outer court,” etc.; what is meant by the thirty treasury chambers; and what by the gates, or by the length of one hundred cubits.

«And he brought me out to the outer court; and behold, chambers and a pavement laid with stone in the court all round about. Thirty chambers were around the pavement. And the pavement in front of the gates, corresponding to the length of the gates, was lower. And he measured [Col. 1473A] the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court outside: one hundred cubits, toward the east and toward the north.»

After the measurement of the former structure and of the chambers, the prophet is brought out to the outer court. For, having entered Holy Scripture, after the account of the making of the world has been completed and after we have read that God rested from his works, we proceed to the subsequent history of events which were done, or are done, outside the secret place of that rest. It begins thus: “Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. 2), and so forth. All this history is, as it were, the outer court down to Abraham. But from Abraham—whom Christ, to be born from his seed, was first promised (Gen. 12)—there is an inner court down to [Col. 1473B] the establishment of the true temple, which this prophecy measures after that court: that is, down to the incarnation of Christ himself, in whose temple God, made man, was reconciled to the human race.

Therefore, “He brought me,” he says, “to the outer court; and behold, chambers and a pavement laid with stone in the court all around”: that is, after he had enabled me to understand how God rested on the seventh day when his work was completed, he opened my understanding so that I might grasp what is subsequently read. And behold, the letter appeared exceedingly rich and laborious, because it contains the treasure of spiritual understanding and, as it were, the variegated beauty of marble. “Thirty chambers,” he says, “were around the pavement.” The number thirty of the chambers signifies the chastity of marriage, which God established and consecrated in the first human beings. Whatever chaste and God-worthy married couples are read of in that Scripture after that union were, or are, chambers preserving a treasure of spiritual meanings and much gold of Christ’s mysteries. For example: “The Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled up flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam” (Gen. 2), and so forth. [Col. 1473C] This is truly a great chamber, a repository of the truest treasure. For this is “a great mystery” which that letter preserves: “But I,” says the Apostle, “speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 3).

And just as a varied and beautiful pavement is spread upon the earth in marble, so in this passage and in the others, whoever has eyes to see beholds, above the lowly letter, the adornment of spiritual understanding. “And the pavement,” he says, “in front of the gates, corresponding to the length of the gates, was lower.” Truly it was “according to the length of the gates,” for insofar as the holy Fathers—who were for us gates of the Word of God or of the Christ to come—were distant in their own times from the aforementioned temple of God, that is, from Christ’s incarnation, their mystical marriages and deeds are venerable in interpretation.

“And he measured the breadth from the front of the lower gate to the front of the inner court, within, one hundred cubits, toward the east and toward the north.” The measure of one hundred cubits is the recompense of eternal goods, [Col. 1474A] whose fullness the Lord also signifies in the Gospel: “He shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.” That is, he shall receive eternal things for temporal ones—a recompense as profitable as the number one hundred is in comparison with a small number. He measured such a breadth from the front of the lower gate, that is, from the first Adam, who was most distant in time from the temple of God so often mentioned. For to this first man the command was given: “From every tree of paradise eat; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat” (Gen. 2). If he had indeed kept that command, he would have received, as it were, the hundred cubits of recompense. For, in exchange for the one tree forbidden him, he would at some time have eaten from the tree of life and would have been immortal in both body and soul; at some time [Col. 1474B] he would have passed, without bodily death, into blessed immortality and the immortal blessedness of the angels.

“And he measured,” he says, “toward the east and toward the north”: that is, he promised recompense to all who deserve it, whether amid the prosperity of peace or amid the adversity of temptation.

## CHAPTER XIII. What the gate facing the northern way is; what is meant by the measure of fifty cubits in length and twenty-five in breadth; what the windows are; what the vestibule is; and what the ascent of seven steps is

“He also measured the gate of the outer court which faced the northern way; and he measured from gate to gate toward the southern way, both in length and in breadth; and its chambers, three on this side and three [Col. 1474C] on that; and its front and its vestibule, according to the measure of the former gate: its length fifty cubits and its breadth twenty-five cubits.”

After the eastern gate, through which prosperous and good things are usually announced, one comes to the gate facing the northern way, through which adverse things are undoubtedly signified. For after the reading concerning the Creator of the world and the happiness granted to the first human being, there follows the history of misery and great unhappiness. Man, deceived by the devil, was cast out of paradise, dead in spirit and mortal in flesh; and he carried to all his descendants the inheritance of that same twofold death. Then, when human beings had multiplied and all flesh had become corrupt, that world [Col. 1474D] perished, overwhelmed by the flood (Gen. 7).

Yet even there the diligence and benevolence of this most careful measurer did not cease. Rather, “according to the measure of the former gate, he measured both in length and in breadth,” and so forth: that is, he spoke to humankind and disclosed his works to them, so that, according to their capacity, they might act well after his example and themselves deserve to enter the chambers of his rest. “He measured the length fifty cubits and the breadth twenty-five cubits”: for he set before them the hope of forgiveness, which they might obtain through the length of faith and through the breadth of charity exercised in the good works of the five senses.

“He measured,” I say, “from the gate of the northern way to the gate in the southern way”: that is, so that he might repay evils to the wicked in the aforesaid flood according to their deserts, while reserving good things for the good, in order that the world might be restored from their seed. Their chambers were the hidden places of a good conscience: three on this side and three on that side. Three on this side, that is, in the present—in faith, hope, and charity; and three on that side, that is, in the future, in the blessed vision of the Trinity.

“But its windows and its vestibule and its carvings were according to the measure of the gate facing east; and its ascent had seven steps, and the vestibule was before it. And the gate of the inner court was opposite the northern and eastern gates; and he measured from gate to gate one hundred cubits.” By the windows and vestibule, which were according to the measure of the gate facing east, this is subtly indicated: that those established at the entrance of the virtues and looking toward their author—whose work was the creation of the world and rest in the kingdom of immortality—would come to his vision. [Col. 1475B]

The seven steps by which its ascent was made are these: the first, fear; the second, piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, fortitude; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; the seventh, wisdom. Isaiah, enumerating these same steps in our very Head, numbered them descending rather than ascending, saying: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11). And rightly so: because he spoke from heavenly things to those below, he began with wisdom and descended to fear. Here, however, because the discourse concerns earthly human beings tending upward from below, the same steps are rightly numbered in ascending order. For since it is written, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1), it is beyond doubt that one ascends from fear to wisdom, not returns from wisdom to fear. For wisdom has perfect charity.

Concerning the one hundred cubits, or the mystery of this number, enough has been said above.

## CHAPTER XIV. What the southern way, or gate facing south, is; and why, according to the order of times, the first gate of the outer court is called eastern, the second northern, and the third southern

“And he brought me to the southern way; and behold, a gate faced toward the south. And he measured its front and its vestibule according to the measures above, [Col. 1475D] and its windows and the vestibules all around,” and so forth, as above.

After the northern gate one goes out to the southern way or gate, through which good things are signified. For after the adversity of the preceding age and the destruction of impious human beings, prosperous things immediately meet us as we follow the order of Scripture. For example, when God speaks to Noah: “Behold, I establish my covenant with you and with your seed after you, and with every living creature that is with you, both birds and cattle and beasts of the earth, all that came forth from the ark, and every beast of the earth. I establish my covenant with you, and all flesh shall never again be destroyed by the waters of a flood, nor shall there henceforth be a flood to devastate the earth” (Gen. 9), and so forth.

The same understanding is to be applied to all the measures [Col. 1476A] of this gate and to the steps by which one ascends to it, for they are altogether the same as above. Here, indeed, is the end of the measurements of the court, or of the gates of the outer court. It should be noted that here the gates are arranged in the following order: the eastern first, the northern second, and the southern third—plainly according to the sequence or order of the times or events which Scripture has recalled up to this point.

The order is not the same for the gates of the inner court. Rather, the gate which there will be last by name, namely the southern, here comes first, as the text says.

## CHAPTER XV. Why, in a different order, the first gate of the inner court is called southern, the second eastern, and the third northern; what they signify; and why in the vestibule of the northern gate there are sixteen tables, four larger and twelve [Col. 1476B] smaller

“And he brought me into the inner court by the southern gate, and he measured the gate according to the measures above: its chamber, its front, and its vestibule by the same measures,” and so forth.

The first gate of this inner court is called southern; the second, eastern; and the third, northern. This is plainly according to the sequence or order of the times or events which took place. For this inner court is that succession of fathers contained in the Book of the Generation of Jesus Christ in Matthew (Matt. 1). These are the fathers from whom Christ according to the flesh came: the true temple of God, a temple not made by hands. The southern gate there is Abraham; the eastern, David; the northern, the Babylonian captivity.

In this one respect the chronological order fails, though the quality of the events demands it: namely, that the first, as has been said, is called southern and the second eastern. For since Abraham was earlier in time and the promise of the blessed seed, which is Christ, was first made to him (Gen. 12; 22), this gate, placed first, might rightly seem to have been called eastern. Yet although David was later in time and the promise of God was made later to him—God saying, “From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon your throne” (Ps. 119 [120])—there is another, not insignificant aspect of dignity because of which he more properly deserves here to be called the eastern gate. He deserved to receive a promise equal to Abraham’s; and he sang, with sacred heart and prophetic mouth, the mysteries of Christ, the Son of God. Abraham did not do this. [Col. 1476D]

David, wiser than all who taught him and more understanding than the elders (Ps. 118 [119]), was the first in the whole genealogy of Jesus Christ to sing with wonderful elegance the mysteries of Christ: the mysteries of his birth, passion, resurrection, ascension, and kingdom. In words almost bare—so far as the circumstances of the time permitted, or the hardness of the people of that age could bear—he went before under royal authority in daring to speak of the kingdom of God, the judgment to come, and the powers of the age to come; things about which Moses wrote nothing except through figures and enigmas.

He is therefore rightly called here the eastern gate by a twofold grace: because he was the father of Christ, the Son of God; further, because he himself received the promise; and further, because, born many ages later, he conceived its mysteries with a faithful heart [Col. 1477A] and uttered them with a holy mouth. [The printed text calls this a “twofold” grace while listing these three grounds.] If we duly weigh these matters, we shall take greater delight in the fact that the evangelist Matthew named him both before and after Abraham in that genealogy: first saying, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matt. 1), and afterward saying, “Jesse begot David” (ibid.).

That the northern gate should be written here as third was also required by the sequence or quality of events. For, as Jeremiah foretold, “From the north every evil shall be opened upon the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. 1); the Babylonian captivity was wholly northern—that is, exceedingly adverse. Yet that same captivity should be called a gate because at that time prophetic grace was poured out more abundantly upon the people of God, or the court of God’s temple: Jeremiah, this very Ezekiel, Daniel, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi prophesied. Indeed, nearly all the other prophets, in almost everything they say, are occupied with that Babylonian captivity—not because they threaten that captivity alone to the sinful people, but because it was a type of the captivity in which all human beings universally live in exile in the Babylon of this world under the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar. From this we can be delivered only through the repentance which all the prophets unanimously preach, and through the grace of Christ.

Therefore, rightly, in the vestibule of this northern gate sixteen tables are seen on either side. They are the writings of the sixteen prophets: some prophesied before, some after, and some during that captivity. Since everything that we offer worthy of God rests upon their faith or testimonies, it is rightly said: “Upon which they slaughtered, and upon which they placed the vessels in which the burnt offering and sacrifice are offered.”—

“And outside the inner gate were chambers of singers in the inner court, which was at the side of the gate facing north; and their faces were toward the southern way. One was at the side of the eastern gate, which faced the northern way.” The singers of this court are the Law and the Prophets: that is, all the twenty-four books of Old Testament Scripture, whom John in the Apocalypse presents under the number of the twenty-four elders, worshipping the Lamb and offering their crowns with faces cast down, while standing before the four living creatures full of eyes [Col. 1477D] before and behind—that is, looking both to the past and to the future—and crying with unwearying voice: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come” (Apoc. 6).

The chambers of these singers are indeed outside the inner gate: that is, their whole reward is laid up outside the present life. Their faces—their one face, that is, their harmonious intention—are turned toward the southern way from the side of the eastern gate. For their intention tends toward the true fullness of light, toward the coming of the true East, Christ the Son of God. This gate, indeed, “faced the northern way,” so that it might call back those whom the north wind—the devil—had carried away and caused to wander from the East of the true and eternal Sun.

Yet this should not be passed over: the vestibules of each of the gates of this inner court are said to face the outer court, so that it may be understood that the holy and righteous persons before the Law and those under the Law had one faith and one expectation or hope.

## CHAPTER XVI. The mystical meaning of the difference in the number of steps for ascending the gates of the inner court: namely, that there are seven there and eight here

Nor should this be passed over: the ascents of the gates of this inner court and those of the outer court differ in the number of steps. For those were ascended by seven steps, but these by eight. Before Abraham, whom we said was the first and southern gate of this court, there is no mention of the eighth, which signifies the resurrection. [Col. 1478B] Rather, the end was in the seventh, in which God rested from his works.

The first mention of the eighth occurs with Abraham, when God says: “An infant eight days old shall be circumcised among you” (Gen. 17). By the circumcision of the infant, faith in his seed, which is Christ, was marked; and by the eighth day, the resurrection which was to be granted through Christ himself in the eighth age of the world was prefigured.

Moreover, in the Gospel Christ himself first establishes Abraham’s faith in the resurrection, when he says to the Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection: “Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22). [Col. 1478C] And the Apostle said of Abraham: “By faith he offered Isaac when he was tested, and he who had received the promises was offering his only-begotten son, to whom it had been said, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called,’ reasoning that God is able even to raise from the dead” (Heb. 11).

Therefore, where an increase of faith is found according to the Scriptures, the steps of ascent also rightly increase, and after seven the ascent is completed in the eighth. This signifies the progress of those who believed or hoped so to enter into God’s rest and to keep sabbath with him from their works that they also believed or expected the resurrection of the flesh to be celebrated in the eighth age of the world. As a sign of this faith, they received circumcision on the eighth day.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 1478D] On the chamber of the priests who keep watch in the guard-duties of the temple, the chamber of the priests who keep watch for the ministry of the altar, why it is said, “These are the sons of Zadok,” and what the altar before the face of the temple is

“And he said to me: This is the chamber which faces the southern way; it shall belong to the priests who keep watch in the guard-duties of the temple. But the chamber which faces the northern way shall belong to the priests who keep watch for the ministry of the altar.”

It should be observed that the priests to whom the guard-duties of the temple are assigned dwell in the chamber facing the southern way, where the light is fullest. But those who keep watch for the ministry of the altar, on which sacrifices for sin are offered, are in the chamber [Col. 1479A] facing the northern way, desiring to receive and save those who come from the north and offer sacrifices for their sins.

Without doubt, the chamber on both sides is one Holy Scripture, in which our treasure lies, if we are truly rich—if we know how to possess, within the case of the letter, the gold of the Spirit and of Christ’s mysteries, precious stones. Such a chamber stands open both toward the south and toward the north, because, if one attends to Scripture, especially prophetic Scripture, it possesses the riches of salvation no less for Jews than for Gentiles.

But who are these priests? He says: “These are the sons of Zadok, who come near from the sons of Levi to the Lord in order to minister to him.” Zadok is interpreted “righteous.” Now faith is the beginning of righteousness, by which Abraham was justified even before circumcision. “For Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness” (Gen. 15). Therefore he rightly did not say, “These are the sons of Abraham,” or “the sons of Israel,” or even “the sons of Levi,” but “These are the sons of Zadok.” “For not all those who are from Israel are Israelites; nor because they are Abraham’s seed are they all children. But, ‘In Isaac shall your seed be called’: that is, not the children of the flesh are God’s children, but the children of the promise are reckoned as the seed” (Rom. 9).

Therefore those whose chambers these are, who rightly keep watch in the guard-duties of the temple or in the ministry of the altar—these, I say, are the sons of Zadok, sons of the righteous God, or of Christ the Son of God, and thereby truly sons of Abraham, because they are sons of righteousness.

“And he measured the court, one hundred cubits in length and one hundred [Col. 1479C] cubits in breadth.” Here the one hundred cubits are to be understood in the same sense as in the outer court. For the faithful fathers according to the flesh of Christ—of whose flesh the temple of his body was constructed, and therefore we call them the inner court—received a hundredfold because of the pilgrimage by which they dwelt as strangers in a foreign land for the sake of the promise. For, according to the Apostle, looking toward the recompense, they were in no way disappointed in their expectation (Heb. 11).

“And the altar before the face of the temple.” “The altar before the face of the temple” was the faith of those same fathers, which went before the building of that temple—that is, Christ’s incarnation—with a worthy meeting, and which is immediately designated in this prophet by mystical measures, beginning thus:

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 1479D] On the glory of God: how it was prefigured through the mystery of the temple in the same way as in the first visions by the four faces of a human being, lion, calf, and eagle

“And he brought me into the vestibule of the temple, and measured the vestibule five cubits on this side and five cubits on that, and the breadth of the gate three cubits on this side and three cubits on that.”

The prophetic Spirit superimposed upon the matters hitherto said or signified the visions of the two years in which this prophet began to prophesy. There he expressed Christ’s glorious humanity through the four faces of a human being, lion, calf, and flying eagle; here he signified his eternal divinity—and that divinity far more ancient than the same humanity—by wondrous and very hidden modes. At last, the glory which he had seen there once and again he now recounts here for the third time, strengthening the assertion of his faith with sufficient testimonies: namely, that he who appeared as a human being on earth, suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven is the very one who created all things with the Father.

For after some matters he says: “And he led me to the gate facing the eastern way; and behold, the glory of the God of Israel entered by the eastern way, and his voice was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his majesty. And I saw a vision according to the appearance which they had seen when he came to destroy the city, and appearances according to the vision which I had seen beside the river Chebar; and I fell upon my face” (Ezek. 43). Therefore, rejoicing and confessing with this prophet and with the beloved evangelist that “we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1), let us follow, so far as we can, where this venerable man leads his fellow-initiate (*symmistēs*).

## CHAPTER XIX. What the vestibule of five cubits on this side and five on that is; what the gate three cubits wide on this side and three on that is; and what the columns in the fronts, one on this side and the other on that, are

“And he brought me,” he says, “into the vestibule of the temple.” To be brought into the vestibule of the temple is to be instructed in the word of faith: to learn the necessary reasons for the coming of Christ, the Son of God; why God built for himself the temple of a human body; and for whom he came—whether for certain persons or, without distinction of persons, for all human beings.

Now observe what he has done. “He measured the vestibule five cubits on this side and five cubits on that, and the breadth of the gate three cubits on this side and three cubits on that.” The ten cubits, five on this side and five on that, have in their midst a gate three cubits broad on this side and three on that. This is the Decalogue of the Law, which “brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). Therefore it was necessary that Christ, the gate of righteousness, should offer himself in its midst and, as it were, supply with either hand the deficiency of the weak and powerless Law.

Hence the Apostle says: “For what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and concerning sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom. 8). Therefore, in order that the justification of the Law might be fulfilled, Christ, the gate of righteousness, came; and, as though sustaining us on right and left, he caused the Law of the ten commandments to have power to accomplish something.

Whence did that man have this power or capacity? Plainly because he is not merely human, but God himself—the one who made all things in six days. Otherwise, not even he could do it. He therefore says: “He measured the breadth of the gate three cubits on this side and three on that,” making six cubits. Scripture bears witness to this breadth: for in six days, as has already been said, God said, “Let it be,” and everything whatever among created things was made (Gen. 1). If he spoke and it was made, it was made through the Word; and Christ is the Word of God. Therefore he was able [Col. 1481A] to bring the imperfect Law to perfection.

And he came not only for the salvation of the Jews, but also for that of the Gentiles; indeed, he came to call not the righteous but sinners (Matt. 9). Therefore it follows: “But the length of the vestibule was twenty cubits and the breadth eleven cubits.” This number, twenty, is twice ten. “Therefore the length of the vestibule, twenty cubits,” signifies the extension of Christ’s grace, whose coming reaches not only to the Jews but also to the salvation of the Gentiles. The number eleven, moreover, is a type of sinners. For every sin is elevenfold, because whenever anyone speaks perversely, he transgresses the commandments of the Decalogue. Great, therefore, if you look to the mystery, is the breadth of the vestibule: great and broad is the grace of the righteous God, which receives the whole world, bent beneath the burden of sin, into its bosom.

“And one ascended to it by eight steps.” The eight steps have already been discussed above and need not be repeated, unless perhaps we take the same steps from the Gospel under other names, calling them the eight beatitudes. The first is, “Blessed are the poor in spirit”; the eighth: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

“And there were columns in the fronts, one on this side and another on that.” The two columns in the fronts are one on this side, called mercy, and the other on that side, called judgment. The column of mercy stands on one side, that of judgment on the other. For at his first coming the Lord Christ came mercifully to redeem; at his second he will come [Col. 1481C] to judge. This is the entire introduction into the vestibule of the temple, because the person who desires to enter the temple—that is, to be united through baptism to Christ’s body—must believe and confess all these things.

## CHAPTER XX. On the words, “And he brought me into the temple”; and on the six cubits of breadth of the fronts on this side and six on that, and the five cubits of breadth of the gate on this side and five on that

(Chapter 41.) “And he brought me into the temple, and measured the fronts six cubits in breadth on this side and six cubits in breadth on that. The breadth of the tabernacle and the breadth of the gate were ten cubits; and the sides of the gate were five cubits on this side and five cubits on that.”

After the station in the vestibule, to be brought into the temple itself is, after making one’s confession, to be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For from that point each person has entered into the temple of the Lord’s body in such a manner as to have put on Christ, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3).

“Six cubits,” he says, “of breadth on this side and six cubits of breadth on that.” This is the breadth of confession which whoever deserves to enter this temple must know. The Apostle confesses six cubits on this side—by the number of days in which the one Creator expounded the multitude of creatures—when he says: “For in him all things in heaven and on earth were created, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things consist in him” (Col. 1). [Col. 1482A] He likewise confesses six cubits on that side when he immediately adds: “And he is the head of the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that in all things he might hold the preeminence; because it pleased God that all fullness should dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth” (ibid.).

These are the fronts of the temple, this its beautiful appearance, a great and luminous spectacle in the eyes of the confessing soul. Yet this very beauty of confession requires works. It follows therefore: “The breadth of the gate was ten cubits, and the sides of the gate were five cubits on this side and five cubits on that.” By “tabernacle” he means the inner house. Around it were the sides, that is, the twice thirty-three boards, as the following discourse describes. The breadth of the gate, moreover, was the entrance to that tabernacle: ten cubits wide, with sides of five cubits on each side, together making twenty cubits, which was the breadth of the tabernacle. For he immediately adds: “And he measured its length forty cubits and its breadth twenty cubits.”

Therefore, after the matters already stated, the gate’s breadth of ten cubits is the progress of good works running in the breadth of charity, upon which the whole Decalogue of the Law is known to depend. For faith works through love (Gal. 5), and therefore immediately after the six cubits of the fronts the gate of this breadth is opened before us.

## CHAPTER XXI. [Col. 1482C] On the arrangement of the oracle, and the meaning of the measure of two cubits in the front of the gate

“And having entered within, he measured two cubits at the front of the gate, and the gate six cubits, and the breadth of the gate seven cubits. And he measured its length twenty cubits and its breadth twenty cubits before the face of the temple. And he said to me: This is the Holy of Holies.”

The oracle, or Holy of Holies, in the temple is God in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). The oracle and the temple before the doors of the oracle are not two temples but one temple; likewise, we confess not two Christs—one human and God in the human—but one Christ.

Not only the apostles, but Christ himself continually depended, according to his humanity, upon the utterances or responses of that oracle and upon the ordering of the incarnate Word inhabiting the temple of the sacred body, so that he did and judged nothing of himself. Thus, for example, he could weep for his nation or for the city of Jerusalem that was about to fall, yet by weeping did not free it.

That oracle was as great in breadth and height as it was in length, because the divinity of Christ our Lord is as great in antiquity, which is understood through length, and in majesty, which is understood through height, as it is altogether in charity, which is understood through breadth. The temple’s length of forty cubits, moreover—a number always associated with toil—signifies the labours of the present life, which the Lord, as man, endured patiently in his body. All this is briefly [Col. 1483A] signified by the two cubits at the front of the gate, when we confess that the one and same Christ is God and human being. This is the sum of Catholic confession.

## CHAPTER XXII. What the twice thirty-three sides signify; what is meant by the side’s length of six cubits and breadth of four cubits; and why these sides did not touch the wall of the temple
“And he measured the wall of the house: six cubits; and the width of the side-chamber: four cubits, all around the house. And the side-chambers, side by side, were twice thirty-three; and there were projections entering into the wall of the house in the side-chambers round about, so that they might be supported and yet not touch the wall of the temple.”

By saying “twice thirty-three” side-chambers, when he might have said sixty-six, the meaning is more pleasing to the understanding [Col. 1483B]. For during thirty-three years the Son of God the Father, God of majesty, endured to dwell as a stranger in this world in the temple of the Lord’s body; and therefore the side-chambers are rightly distinguished as twice thirty-three, since through all those years both natures of Christ—divine and human—served the Father in obedience.

“Now the length of the side-chamber was six cubits, and its width four cubits.” By the former, that is, the number six, is signified the perfection of the divine works which he wrought wondrously, as he says: “If I had not done among them the works which no one else has done” (John 15). By the latter, that is, the number four, are signified the four elements of this world, under which he served, having emptied himself in the form of a servant, “made in the likeness of men, [Col. 1483C] and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2).

These side-chambers did not touch the wall of the temple, because he assumed the labours of this present life not as enduring but as temporary—labours wholly to be removed by the glory of the resurrection. The Apostle bears witness when he says: “But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the removal of sin through his sacrifice; and as it is appointed for human beings once to die, and after this judgment, so also Christ, having been offered once to take away the sins of many, shall appear a second time, without sin, for salvation to those who await him in faith” (Heb. 9).

## CHAPTER XXIII. What, mystically, the three stories—that is, the three upper chambers—mean in this temple; what it means to ascend through the door to the upper and middle levels [Col. 1483D]; and what that door is.

“And there was a passage winding upward in a spiral, and it led around into the upper chamber of the temple; therefore the temple was broader in the upper parts, and thus one ascended from the lower parts to the upper, into the middle.”

What he said, “to the upper parts into the middle,” is the same as saying, “into the middle and upper chamber.” For there were three stories, concerning which, in connection with Solomon’s temple, we have spoken according to the mystery; and now we say that in this temple of divinity—in Christ, God and man—there are three floors (1 Kings 6), and whoever desires to remain in Christ must faithfully stand in whichever of them applies.

What are these floors? Surely, three distinctions of good living; three orders of those who believe in Christ [Col. 1484A], which he himself also mystically distinguishes: “Two,” he says, “shall be in the field; two women grinding at one mill; two in one bed: one shall be taken and one left” (Matt. 24). Likewise, these are the orders which, in this prophet, we understand under the names Job, Noah, Daniel, and so forth, as may be read there (Ezek. 14).

Let us say something further. When, from the life which we live on earth, we arrive at rest of spirit in the world to come, we are, as it were, making for the upper level of the house. And when, released from the flesh, we ascend to rest of spirit, we await the restoration of our flesh on the day of resurrection as an ascent to the highest upper chamber.

As for the statement that “there was a passage winding upward in a spiral and leading around into the upper chamber of the temple, and therefore the temple was broader in the upper parts, and thus from the [Col. 1484B] lower parts one ascended to the upper and into the middle,” I think it clear to the reader that what lies below is always narrower, and that, little by little, as we strive toward the heights, a broader way opens before us, and is fulfilled what is written: “In tribulation you made room for me” (Ps. 4).

By the circular passage and spiral we ascend to the temple’s upper chamber. This form, among all figures, is judged most beautiful even by the philosophers of this world: heaven, sun, moon, and the other stars; the point of the earth; and, in human bodies, the eyes as though other stars, the form of the head—which is the receptacle of all the senses—and the rounded fingers, thighs, and arms all display this circular form.

“And the door,” he says, [Col. 1484C] “of the side-chamber was toward the east.” Concerning this door it is written also in the description of Solomon’s temple: “The door of the middle side-chamber was in the right-hand wall of the house; and by a spiral stair they went up into the middle chamber, and from the middle into the third” (1 Kings 6).

We have said this about it: the door of the side of the temple is the wound in the pierced side of the Lord’s body. Apart from it there is no entrance, no door or gate through which anyone may enter so as to stand before God in any order. For from that side, when it was struck by the spear, blood and water flowed forth (John 19). By this sacrament the sin of the world was destroyed; in it we too were baptized into Christ Jesus, as the Apostle says: “For all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6).

Therefore there is one door, one [Col. 1484D] baptism (Eph. 4), through which, upon entering that temple of God, once a person has been admitted, he may then ascend either from the first level to the middle, or from the middle to the third, according as the ascent of virtues or loftiness of merits pleases each. We pass rapidly over matters that are clearer, in order to linger over those that are more difficult and more useful.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How the house had the first ceiling after thirty cubits, the second after sixty, and the third after one hundred and twenty; and how the words “And I saw a height all round about in the house,” etc., are to be understood mystically.

“And I saw in the house a height all round about: the foundations of the side-chambers, according to the measure of a reed, six cubits in extent. And the width of the outer wall of the side-chamber [Col. 1485A] was five cubits, and the interior of the house was in the side-chambers of the house.”

These side-chambers are to be understood as those of which Scripture says, in the description of Solomon’s temple in the Book of Kings: “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings” (1 Kings 6). Ceilings are floors fastened with nails beneath beams; their painted ornament commonly presents a marvellous sight to those who look upon them.

Now there were three ceilings in the temple: the first thirty cubits above the pavement; the second at sixty cubits, opposite the tops of the porticoes; the third at one hundred and twenty cubits, at the summit of the whole house. For in Palestine, unlike Egypt, houses do not have peaked roofs; rather, their roofs are built flat, suitable for sitting or walking upon. [Col. 1485B] Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “What you hear in the ear shall be proclaimed upon the housetops” (Luke 19).

But spiritually, having entered this temple through faith, we also see “a height all around, the foundations of the side-chambers, according to the measure of a reed, six cubits in extent,” and “the width of the outer wall of the side-chamber, five cubits.” What are these elevated side-chambers all around, unless they are the lofty and perfect mysteries of spiritual understanding hidden in that temple of the Lord’s humanity? Thus they are rightly said to be founded “according to the measure of a reed, six cubits,” because all things have been written firmly and with steadfast faith according to the measure which God allotted to each of the prophets and apostles.

The external [Col. 1485C] width of five cubits—the number more appropriate to those who are carnal because of the five bodily senses—is the moderate level of the literal or historical sense of Scripture, which must be set before those incapable of beholding the lofty mysteries of heaven according to their capacity. The interior of the house, in the side-chambers of the house, of which we spoke above, is properly the evangelical teaching. In this temple we especially see both a height according to the measure of a reed of six cubits and likewise a measure of five cubits, so that, as has already been said, both the more perfect, signified by six, and those of moderate capacity, signified by five, may have a measure by which they may profitably raise the sight of their inward eyes.

“And between the treasuries, a width of twenty cubits all around the house on every side”—“I saw” is to be understood. These treasuries are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in this temple, that is, in Christ. But the twenty cubits’ width between them, a number consisting of two tens, signifies the most excellent way of the twofold love of God and neighbour, without which, the Apostle declares, all other gifts avail nothing (1 Cor. 12).

## CHAPTER XXV. What benefit accrued to us from the God of majesty building for himself the temple of a human body, according to the words, “the building which was separated,” etc.

What benefit accrued to us from the God of majesty building for himself, according to the prophetic vision, the temple of a human body? None other than that of which [Col. 1486A] the Apostle speaks: “In him it pleased all fullness to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things on earth or things in heaven” (Col. 1).

It follows: “And the building which was separated, facing the way looking toward the sea, was seventy cubits broad. But the wall of the building was five cubits broad all around, and its length ninety cubits. And he measured the house, one hundred cubits in length; and the separated building and its wall were one hundred cubits in length.” — “And the building,” he says, “which was separated.” What was that building? Surely, the blessed fellowship of the holy angels, between whom and ourselves there was a great separation, a great estrangement. Therefore it is said: “The building was separated.”

Immediately it adds: “Facing the way looking toward the sea.” The way looking toward the sea was our God Christ, who through his prophets foretold that in the fullness of time he would deign to come down to us and suffer, in our sea, the shipwreck of death and, after the example of Jonah, a three-day burial. That separated building was turned toward this way: the loving fellowship of the holy angels, separated from us, awaited his grace—awaited, I say, the time when he would make peace and join us to them through his blood.

That building had a width of seventy cubits. This number is seven in tens; therefore, in a wider limit, this breadth signifies the most spacious repose of love, [Col. 1486C] because even then the angelic fellowship rested in its God without us. Yet much was lacking to its perfection or completion, because the hundredth sheep had perished and the tenth coin was lost (Luke 15).

Thus he says: “But the wall of the building was five cubits broad all around, and its length ninety cubits.” Five, which is half of the second unit—that is, of ten—signifies that the knowledge of God’s manifold wisdom was not yet full or perfect. For the blessed angels already knew how great God’s power was, but they had not yet learned by experience how great his mercy was. They were to learn this through the wonderful work of our restoration. Hence the Apostle says: [Col. 1486D] “To enlighten all concerning the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (Eph. 3).

Thus the wall was, as it were, half-full—that is, five cubits—and had not yet attained the whole signified by the second unit, that is, by ten. Likewise, “its length was ninety cubits” and had not reached one hundred. For the number was diminished by the loss of the hundredth sheep. But what did he do? “He measured the house, one hundred cubits in length; and the separated building, and its walls, one hundred cubits in length.” — “Now the breadth before the face of the house, and of that which was separated toward the east, was [Col. 1487A] one hundred cubits.”

This measurement is square. Its meaning is: he restored the hundredth sheep to the fold and made the number of his sheep complete (Luke 15). And as the number one hundred is square—for ten times ten makes one hundred—so he wholly restored and filled his fold, once maimed in great part, as though by a square.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What is signified by the words, “And he measured the length of the building,” etc.

“And he measured the length of the building opposite its face, which was separated toward the rear, and the *ethecae* on either side, one hundred cubits; and the inner temple, and the vestibules of the court, thresholds and slanting windows, and the *ethecae* around on three sides, opposite the threshold of each one, and timbered round about in a circle. From the ground up to the windows—and the windows were closed—above the doors, and up to the inner house; and outside, around the whole wall, within and without, according to measurements; and cherubim and palm trees were carved: a palm tree between cherub and cherub.”

When the aforesaid temple was built—or rather, when it was destroyed by Jewish impiety and raised by divine power on the third day—the separated building immediately became perfect and advanced from ninety to one hundred cubits. That is, the blessed fellowship of angels was made complete by the finding of the tenth coin that had been lost and the hundredth sheep that had perished (Luke 15).

For all the elect, from the beginning of the world, who had awaited Christ’s grace then entered when the gates of that building were opened; and at the finding of the sheep which the gracious shepherd bore back upon his own shoulders, all that rejoicing fold of heavenly sheep was gladdened, and there was a common joy among the rejoicing friends.

Yet there was still room, for the predetermined number of the elect had not been filled entirely by those who had preceded the coming of this grace. Therefore, “he measured,” he says, “the length of the building toward the rear.” What is “toward the rear,” except after his departure? Thus, after that venerable man had departed, “he measured the length of one hundred cubits, the length of the building opposite its face, which was separated.” That is, after he ascended into heaven, he gave gifts to human beings [Col. 1487D] in full abundance (Eph. 4), as if with a hundredfold perfection, for the sake of those who were still enemies by not believing in, or not knowing, Christ the Son of God.

The vestibules of the court, thresholds, slanting windows, and *ethecae*—that is, projections on either side—signify the various ministries of the holy apostles, prophets, evangelists, teachers, and pastors, whom he appointed or gave “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ” (ibid.), that is, of the Church. The Church too is the temple [Col. 1488A] of God; it is here called the inner temple, which that often-mentioned man measured toward the rear—that is, after his ascension—as we have said.

At Rome, *ethecae* are called projecting balconies or battlements extending from the walls of upper rooms, named after their first inventor. Everything was carved or artistically made, from the pavement to the windows; and the windows were closed, etc. For nothing in God’s temple was made by God without reason and measure: from the pavement—that is, from the weakest elect person—up to the windows, that is, the most illustrious preachers through whom the brightness of truth shone upon God’s house.

But why are even the closed windows said to be carved or artistically wrought? Surely this is what we today joyfully marvel at, and marvelling joyfully observe, throughout the whole world: after the mouths of Christ’s blessed apostles were closed by death—those windows through which the world had been enlightened while they were still open and still exercised the office of speech in preaching—after those windows were closed, they were carved and fashioned more beautifully and splendidly: carved by virtues, fashioned by miracles.

There are “cherubim and palms”: that is, the abundance of knowledge which we daily investigate in their writings, and the victories of martyrdom, not won without blood, which we venerate in their deeds. There is “the face of a man beside the palm on this side, and the face of a lion beside the palm on the other side.” For all their teaching sets forth these two things to us: he who came at his first advent as a gentle man in the abundance of mercy will come at his second advent as a terrible lion in the great strength of judgment.

## CHAPTER XXVII. The words, “This is the measure before the Lord”: namely, the wooden altar signifying the mystery of the cross and the sacrament of the body and blood; and what its height of three cubits and length of two cubits signify.

“The wooden altar was three cubits high and two cubits long; and its corners, its length, and its sides were of wood. And he said to me: This is the table before the Lord.”

Surely that man also measured this toward the rear. For the wooden altar is the mystery of the cross, the mystery or sacrament of Christ’s passion. “When his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13), in that very passage looking “toward the rear”—that is, toward us who would believe after that same passage—“he measured the wooden altar,” that is, the already mentioned sacrament of his cross or passion. Taking the substance of bread and wine in his hands, he said after the blessing: “This is my body; this is my blood” (Matt. 26; Mark 14; Luke 22; 1 Cor. II).

The “height of this altar, three cubits; its length, two cubits.” The height of three cubits is faith in the holy Trinity, without which there is nowhere an altar of God. The length of two cubits is the extension of the twofold love of God and neighbour, without which nothing worthy of God can be offered and which anyone approaching this altar to sacrifice a living victim greatly needs.

Its corners, length, and sides are wooden: for the entire sacrament of Christ’s altar consists in the wood of the life-giving cross, because the sum of the whole sacrifice is the passion of him who [Col. 1489A] sacrificed himself upon the wood of the cross for the whole world. “And this,” he says, “is the table before the Lord”—understand, the sole and only one. For the Jewish table of sacrifice is no longer before the Lord. “Do not,” he says, “continue to offer sacrifice in vain. Incense is an abomination to me” (Isa. 1). Again: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats?” (ibid.)—understand, no. But what then? “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49), and many similar things.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. What the two doors in the temple or sanctuary signify, and what the two little doors on either side mean.

“And there were two doors in the temple and in the sanctuary. And in the two doors on either side were two little doors which folded back upon one another; for there were two doors on either side of the doors.”

The two doors of temple and sanctuary are the two Testaments. Their keeper is he whose temple it is: “the holy and true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3).

In these two doors are two little doors on either side, folding back upon one another; this is clear according to the letter. For in larger dining rooms it is customary for two doors to adjoin and be joined together, so that the larger entrance may be closed or opened not merely with two great doors but with four smaller ones.

According to the spiritual sense, “there were two little doors on either side, folding back upon one another,” so that you may have spiritual understanding in history and historical truth in tropology [Col. 1489C]. Each needs the other, and if one is lacking, knowledge is not complete.

“And cherubim and carvings of palms were carved upon the doors of the temple, as they were represented also upon the walls. Therefore there were thicker timbers on the outside of the front of the vestibule.” — “Cherubim and carvings of palms,” he says, “were carved upon the doors.” For what does the sacred Scripture of the two Testaments contain, if not a multitude of knowledge and the emblems of victory? From it we know God, and to know him is the summit of knowledge. From it we take the weapons by using which “not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6), we may happily arrive, with the palm of righteousness, at the crown of victory.

Therefore, he says, “the timbers were thicker on the outside of the vestibule of the gate,” so that they might have firmness and be able to receive carving. And, according to spiritual understanding, the doors are fittingly strong and carved, so that they may possess both strength and beauty, lest anyone like Uzziah should break into the Holy of Holies and arrogate the priesthood to himself (2 Chron. 26).

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the Church of the Gentiles received nothing less, and that God made no distinction between Jew and Greek; rightly understood in the words, “on the front, the length of the door was one hundred cubits,” etc.

(Chapter 42.) “And he brought me out into the outer court by the way leading northward, and brought me into the chamber which was opposite the separated building and opposite the temple facing north. On the front, the length of the north door was one hundred cubits, and the width fifty cubits, opposite the twenty cubits of the inner court and opposite the stone-paved floor of the outer court, where portico joined portico in three stories.”

That man chiefly measured these parts “toward the rear.” For this is the Church from among the Gentiles, whose measures are described here. Lying under the north, cold, it had received no benefit of divine colour or light. After that man who ascended into heaven came, as it were, to its rear—whose face, that is, bodily presence, it had not seen—and believing in him already taken up, it received evangelical measures of hundreds and fifties, just as that woman suffering from an issue of blood, coming up from behind and touching the hem of his garment, deserved to be saved through her faith (Matt. 9; Luke 8).

“He brought me out,” he says, “into the outer court, by the way leading northward,” namely, when the Jews, who were as though in the south, rejected and blasphemed, and the apostles acted by the authority of the Holy Spirit in saying: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). For the Lord thus commanded us: “I have set you as a salvation for the Gentiles, that you may be salvation [Col. 1490C] to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49).
