Thus, in commanding, the Lord led the prophet and the company of apostles “into the chamber which was opposite the separated building and opposite the temple facing north.” For he opened to them the treasury of truth, so that from the Scriptures they might understand the calling of the Gentiles: that God was not God of the Jews alone but also of the Gentiles, from whom that repeatedly mentioned heavenly building had until then been separated.

“On the front he measured the length of the north door, one hundred cubits, and the width, fifty cubits.” For what did the Church of the Gentiles receive less, or what distinction did God make between Jew and Greek? (Rom. 3). The width of fifty cubits is the most ample forgiveness of sins. Arguing that this comes through faith rather than works of the law, the Apostle adduces as his chief proof that Abraham was justified by faith, not through circumcision but before circumcision.

The length of one hundred cubits is the full and perfect recompense of things to come, laid up no less for Greek than Jew, according to the same Apostle: “For glory,” he says, “and honour and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 2).

“Where portico joined portico in three stories.” “In three stories,” that is, having three ceilings. For he adds later: “For there were three stories, and they had no columns, such as were the columns of the courts.” This is an affirmation of the Gentiles’ faith and admiration of their readiness, because they were swift to believe. Portico joined portico in three stories; indeed, there were three stories, and although they had no columns “such as were the columns of the courts,” that is, although they did not possess the patriarchs or prophets who had been pillars of the Jews, their hearing or understanding quickly joined the apostolic faith and swiftly embraced the confession of the holy and undivided Trinity.

## CHAPTER XXX. How the measurements of five hundred reeds all around, or toward the four parts of the world, signify the knowledge of Scripture, spread through the four parts of the world by Christ after the reconciliation of humankind.

“And when he had completed the measurements of the inner house, he brought me out by the way of the gate facing the eastern way, and measured it all around. He measured toward the east wind, by the measuring reed, five hundred reeds by the measuring reed all around. And he measured toward the north wind five hundred reeds by the measuring reed round about. And toward the south wind he measured five hundred reeds by the measuring reed all around. And toward the west wind he measured five hundred reeds by the measuring reed. By the four winds he measured its wall.”

Since, as far as we could, we have followed in this vision the prophet—or rather, the prophet’s guide, the wondrous man and wise architect—and have confessed with willing faith both that all things were made through him and that all things were restored through him, which especially concerned the purpose of our work, henceforth, omitting much for brevity’s sake, we shall draw from this vision only the more important matters.

First, according to the literal description, it must be said that this wall altogether had two thousand reeds. But if the reed was six cubits and a palm—the palm being the sixth part of a cubit—it is clear that the outer wall all around had two thousand reeds, amounting to twelve thousand three hundred and thirty-three and one third cubits, with a third of two thousand. Let the prudent and diligent reader read the Book of Joshua son of Nun, and he will find how this measurement is observed in the suburban lands.

But, to return to the mystical sense: after the divisions of the temple courts [Col. 1491D] and buildings, what does such a great multiplicity of reeds signify except the reconciliation of humankind accomplished through Christ after his incarnation, and the knowledge of the Scriptures spread through the four regions of the world? Previously God was known only in Judah (Ps. 75), and sacred Scripture, signified by the reed, was confined there within narrow limits. But now, since Christ ascended into heaven, his Church has been extended toward east, north, south, and west as if by five hundred reeds: that is, it possesses manifold knowledge of God. From the few books of the Law, Prophets, and Gospels, the world has filled its libraries by exposition and commentary.

That this multitude produced twelve thousand with three hundred and thirty-three [Col. 1492A], and in addition one third of two thousand, contains this mystery: a thousand is assigned to each apostle, yet no one attains the measure of the fullness and perfection of Christ unless three hundred and thirty-three cubits are added, by which the mystery of the holy and undivided Trinity is shown.

Moreover, the number five hundred, being twenty times fifty, pertains to the forgiveness of all sins, as both the Old Scripture and the Saviour’s words in the Gospel show. He says: “There were two debtors to a certain moneylender; one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both” (Luke 7).

“And the wall separates between the sanctuary and the place of the people.” From this we understand that the whole foregoing description of the temple has been assigned to the ministries of the priests who are the sons of Zadok; for this number, extended through so great a space and encompassing everything, separates the sanctuary from the place of the people.

## CHAPTER XXXI. The words, “I saw the vision according to the appearance which I had seen when he came to destroy,” etc.

(Chapter 43.) “And he led me to the gate facing the eastern way; and behold, the glory of the God of Israel entered by the eastern way, and his voice was like the sound of many waters, and the earth shone with his majesty. And I saw a vision according to the appearance which I had seen when he came to destroy the city, [Col. 1492C] and appearances according to the vision which I had seen by the river Chebar; and I fell upon my face.”

At last the necessary order of faith is here completed. After reviewing from a great distance all the preceding divisions, he says: “And I saw a vision according to the appearance which I had seen when he came to destroy the city, and appearances according to the vision which I had seen by the river Chebar”—understand, in the fifth year and likewise the sixth year of the captivity of King Jehoiachin.

What was that appearance, or what were those forms? Surely, the appearance of a man, the appearance of a lion, the appearance of a calf, and the appearance of a flying eagle. In those appearances or forms were signified the true humanity, true passion, resurrection, and ascension [Col. 1492D] of Christ, the Son of God. All these things must be believed in the heart unto righteousness and confessed with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 1).

This is evangelical doctrine: sweeter to hear as nourishment of milk for little children and healthful to taste for the soul. Yet it is not enough for perfection of faith unless, after the draught of milk, one advances to solid food and believes and confesses that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and all things were made through him” (John 1); and that the latter thing, which a person could grasp earlier, came after this—namely, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.)—and that according to those faces of man, calf, lion, and flying eagle, he displayed his glory to us.

Thus in the earlier years [Col. 1493A] of his prophecy he received or wrote what little children can more readily grasp; and at last, in this final vision, having senses trained for more mature matters, he received—or wrote for those whose senses are perfected—what Christ, the Son of God, was before those faces. Then at last he falls upon his face: that is, the true worshipper, worshipping in spirit and truth, worships with perfect adoration (John 4).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the words, “And he turned me to the way of the gate of the sanctuary,” etc.; how in these words too the prophetic vision designates the virgin birth.

Nevertheless, however deeply we dig into the hidden treasure of this vision, we have not yet brought forth all that Christian truth compels us to believe or confess concerning Christ our God and Lord. Nor has the text anywhere yet answered for us that which shines most brightly in the full beauty of the Catholic confession: that the face of the man, of which he has often spoken, was conceived and brought forth by the Virgin Mother. Let us therefore follow in the footsteps of the holy Fathers who investigated these passages; let us also investigate, hear, and rejoice in understanding that we have found that this holy prophet did not forget to confess, as he had been taught by the Holy Spirit, the venerable birth from the virginal womb. He says further on (Chapter XLIV):

“And he brought me back to the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary, which faced east, and it was shut. And the Lord said to me: This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord, the God of Israel, has entered through it; and it shall be shut for the prince. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord; he shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate, and shall go out by its way.”

By saying these things he plainly declares himself instructed, under an apt figure, that the man who was God entered this world through the Virgin’s womb. “He brought me back,” he says, “to the way of the outer gate of the sanctuary.” What is the gate of the sanctuary except the Virgin, through whom the gate of the outer sanctuary—the heavenly sanctuary, which was outside us, outside which we ourselves were—was first opened? Moreover, the way of this gate is the line of descent woven in the Gospel from Abraham down to “Joseph her husband, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ” (Matt. 1).

This gate, facing east and receiving in herself the true sun of righteousness—as we truly believe and confess—was shut. For no man had opened her in order that she might conceive or give birth. And the Lord said to me: “This gate shall be shut”—that is, as it now is. It was shut while she conceived; while she gives birth it will nonetheless remain shut. “It shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it.” Shut before childbirth, it will remain shut after childbirth.

For from the time when the angel spoke, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee; and that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1), and when he was born, she remained an everlasting virgin, to confound those who suppose that after the Savior’s birth she had children by Joseph, on account of the brethren mentioned in the Gospel (Matt. 12; Mark 3).

Beautifully, after saying, “And no man shall pass through it,” he immediately added, “Because the Lord, the God of Israel, has entered through it.” It is as though he said: Do not wonder that no man passes through it, and yet she shall bear a son; for the son whom she shall bear is the Lord God of Israel. If he whom she bears were merely a man and not God, it would have been necessary for a man to pass through her before childbirth—indeed, before conception. But now it is the Lord God of Israel who, coming from elsewhere, entered this world through her; and therefore it is no wonder that such a son could preserve the shut gate—that is, his mother—incorrupt.

“And it shall be shut for the prince,” that is, for the work or honor of the prince. This prince of the great dominion, who is in the form of God, “shall himself sit in it”: he shall humble himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2), “that he may eat bread before the Lord,” that is, that he may obey God his Father; for this is for him to eat bread, as he himself testifies when he says: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4). “He shall enter by the way of the vestibule of the gate, and shall go out by its way.”

The distinction between the entrance and exit of this prince must be carefully noted. For all of us, who are born with open gates—that is, with corrupted members—enter by the way through which the propagating seed enters, and by the same way we go out; hence we are lowborn and altogether common. But this noble prince “shall enter,” he says, “by the way of the vestibule of the gate,” that is, he shall be conceived through the faith of the believing Virgin; so that he may go out not now by the way of the vestibule of the gate, but “by its way,” that is, through unimpaired virginity: true flesh from flesh, a true man from his mother, he shall be born.

## Chapter XXXIII. How he promulgates certain legal ordinances for the correction of transgressors of the law, issuing them by the authority of the Lord who says “Thus says the Lord,” and how this legislation is to be understood spiritually because of the number seven.

After this certain legal ordinances follow, for the correction of transgressors of the law, and the discourse begins thus:

“And he brought me by the way of the north gate before the house, and I looked, and behold, the glory of the Lord filled the house of the Lord, and I fell upon my face. And the Lord said to me: Son of man, set thy heart, and see with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears all that I say to thee concerning all the ceremonies of the house of the Lord and all its laws; and set thy heart upon the ways of the temple, through all the exits of the sanctuary.”

Thus, entering upon a new legislation, as though superseding the law of Moses now blotted out, he introduces seven pronouncements bearing the authority of the speaking Lord God:

“Thus says the Lord God: Let all your abominations suffice you, O house of Israel, because you bring in foreign sons, uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh, to be in my sanctuary.”

“Thus says the Lord God: No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and uncircumcised in flesh shall enter my sanctuary—no foreign son who is among the children of Israel.”

(Chapter XLVI.) “Thus says the Lord God: Let it suffice you, princes of Israel. Put away iniquity and plundering; do judgment and justice; remove your boundaries from my people, says the Lord.”

“Thus says the Lord God: In the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall take an unblemished calf from the herd, and you shall expiate the sanctuary.”

(Chapter XLVI.) “Thus says the Lord God: The gate of the inner court, which faces east, shall be shut during the six days on which work is done; but on the Sabbath day it shall be opened, and it shall also be opened on the day of the new moon.”

“Thus says the Lord God: If the prince gives a house to one of his sons, it shall be the inheritance of his sons; they shall possess it by inheritance.”

(Chapter XLVII.) “Thus says the Lord God: This is the boundary within which you shall possess the land among the twelve tribes of Israel, because Joseph has a double portion.”

Reading these things and counting the intervening instances of divine authority, we ask what they mean; and this number immediately answers that a spiritual law is here proposed to spiritual persons, because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. At the same time we recall the saying of Moses the lawgiver: “The Lord thy God shall raise up for thee a prophet from thy nation and from thy brethren, like unto me; him thou shalt hear, as me” (Deut. 18). It is as if he said: As I, a man, am an old lawgiver for thee, the carnal people Israel, so he, the true man, will be a new lawgiver for the spiritual people.

Therefore, while we ask what this legislation means in this prophet, all things answer us that the prince who, according to the preceding passage, goes out through the shut gate brings a better law for his principality: a new law, a law of life and spirit, able to free the whole human being from the law of sin and death. Accordingly, we also observe that the prophet’s statement at the beginning is by no means devoid of mystery: “And he brought me by the way of the north gate” (Ezek. 44). For this man, this new lawgiver, according to the prophecy of the patriarch Jacob, “is the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49), who had been turned toward the north—that is, toward the devil, signified by the cold north—whom they had followed through long-standing and ancient errors; and, when the Jews rejected the law of this man, those nations too were to receive it.

## Chapter XXXIV. Concerning the waters coming forth and descending from the right side: that they signify the gifts proceeding from the unmade temple of Christ’s body.

It must next be noted that at the seventh pronouncement the land is divided, when he says: “This is the boundary within which you shall possess the land.” The health of the land and waters having been previously stated or anticipated, so that we should rightly understand the land of the living in this distribution, the prophet describes in this way the source from which the health of the land proceeded:

“And he brought me back to the gate of the house, and behold, waters were coming in from beneath the threshold of the house toward the east; for the front of the house faced east, but the waters descended to the right side of the temple, south of the altar. And he brought me out by the way of the north gate, and led me around by the outer way to the outer gate, the way that faced east; and behold, waters flowing abundantly from the right side. When the man went out eastward, having a measuring line in his hand, he measured a thousand cubits and led me through the water up to the ankles. Again he measured a thousand and led me through the water up to the knees. And he measured a thousand and led me through the water up to the loins. And he measured a thousand: a torrent which I could not cross, because the waters had swollen deep—a torrent that cannot be forded. And he said to me: Surely thou hast seen, son of man. And he led me out and brought me back to the bank of the torrent. And when I had returned, behold, on the bank of the torrent there were very many trees on either side. And he said to me: These waters that go forth toward the eastern mounds of sand and descend to the plains of the desert shall enter the sea, and shall go out, and the waters shall be healed.”

If we attend rightly, this world was a dead sea. Why, then, was the side of the Lord’s temple—the temple not made with hands—pierced by a lance, and water with blood ran from that wound, except that the death of this world might be removed and the waters of the human race healed? Nor did merely visible water flow visibly from the visible body or side for the accomplishment of healing; but from the invisible divinity invisible water also proceeded: the water of saving wisdom, water—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit (John 19). Therefore it is most rightly said: “Behold, waters flowing abundantly from the right side,” from the divine side.

But this must be distinguished cautiously and carefully: he first said, “The waters descended to the right side of the temple, south of the altar,” and then, “Behold, waters flowing abundantly from the right side.” Since this temple is God’s own temple, “in which all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2), how or from where did these waters, which are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, descend into it? Thus this statement does not permit us to forget that God and man are one and the same Christ, and that in him human nature received what divine nature in Christ could nevertheless give.

Now let us see in what order, and by what increase of overflowing grace, this living water healed our dead waters. Yet first let it not pass unnoticed that, having said, “The waters descended to the right side of the temple, south of the altar,” in order then to say, “And behold, waters flowing abundantly from the right side,” he inserted: “And he brought me out by the way of the north gate.” What does it mean that the prophet is led out by way of the cold north gate to behold the outflow of living waters, except that the grace of the Holy Spirit was to be poured out upon the nations? Now let us return to what was proposed.

## Chapter XXXV. What it signifies that at the first measurement the water reaches the ankles, at the second to the knees, at the third to the loins, while at the fourth it cannot be crossed; and what it means that all waters are healed and great fish multiply, and why the city is named “The Lord is there.”

“And he measured a thousand cubits, and led me through the water up to the ankles.” The thousand cubits of this measurer signify the fullness of the grace-giver, who at the first measurement bore away all the sins of the world, by which he led the prophet through up to the ankles. For by ankles wet by the water of the first measurement is signified the destruction of original sin, because on account of it God said to the serpent concerning the woman: “She shall crush thy head, and thou shalt lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. 2).

For especially on account of original sin the devil, the ancient serpent, lay in wait for the heel of the woman and her seed—that is, for its final end—so far as to dare, as a plotter, to approach Christ himself, the Son of God; yet he could do no harm, as Christ himself testifies: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” (John 12).

“Again he measured a thousand, and led me through the water up to the knees.” By the ankles are signified the apostles alone, concerning whom the prophet says: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who proclaims peace!” (Isa. 52). By the knees are signified all worshippers of the same Christ, Son of God. The water of the second measurement reached as far as these knees when, having said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20).

For concerning all who bend the knee to Christ he said: “He measured a thousand a third time, and led me through the water up to the loins.” Then indeed he measured a third time and “led his own, of whom this prophet here bears the type, through the water up to the loins,” when, already seated at the right hand of God, he sent the Holy Spirit and clothed with power, girded with strength, those who until then had been carnal and weak.

He will measure a fourth time and make a torrent “which,” says the prophet, “I could not cross,” namely in the resurrection; for neither eye could see nor ear hear, nor could the estimation of it ascend into the heart of man (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2). Then our waters will be fully healed, and every soul wherever this torrent comes will live; and there will be very many fish—namely, all the elect—whom the Lord signified in the catch of one hundred and fifty-three fish after his resurrection (John 21).

Yet not all waters will be healed. For the Apostle also says: “We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore it rightly follows here as well: “But its shores and marshes shall not be healed, because they shall be given over to saltworks.” The shores and marshes of this sea are hard human hearts: hard, I say, like shore-stones through the hardness of unbelief; likewise marshy—that is, muddy through the clotted foulness of every vice. These “shall not be healed, because they shall be given over to saltworks”: that is, even if they rise again, they shall not rise to the healing of incorruption, but shall rise to the suffering of eternal death.

“And above the torrent, upon its banks on either side, every fruit-bearing tree shall arise, bearing firstfruits every month.” These things, and so forth, because nearly the same are read in the Apocalypse (Rev. 22), and because we are pressing on to other matters and wish to be brief, we here end this exposition. We pray the glorious man, the measurer or architect of the great city and his temple, and its prince, to grant us some share in the estates of this city, which he measured at five hundred and four thousand on every side.

Without doubt, there a hundredfold return is laid up for the saints who leave behind here whatever is theirs for that prince. It is evident, moreover, that while earthly things are left behind, the five senses of the body are deprived of their pleasures. Therefore the five hundred thousand are rightly distinguished, so that, according to the number of senses restrained here in hope of things to come, that same hundredfold reward may be multiplied five times.

But above every blessedness this is to be embraced, with which the passage is finally concluded (Chapter XLVIII): “And the name of the city from that day shall be: The Lord is there.” For what we now know in part, what we now see through a mirror in obscurity, then we shall know as we are known; then we shall see face to face (1 Cor. 13), we shall see him as he is (1 John 3), we shall see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83).

# R. D. D. Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, *On the Trinity and Its Works*: Commentaries on the Prophet Daniel

## Book One

[Col. 1499]

### Chapter I. On Daniel’s visions: how the kingdom of God was shown sevenfold, for the consolation of its citizens living under the Babylonian yoke.

As Christ opens it, whose works and mysteries we seek in this, we now look into the book of Daniel. Although we desire to finish our undertaken course sooner, we cannot bear to pass over this part of Scripture untouched. For we are held there by a great spectacle. What is that spectacle? An imaginal single combat of the kingdom of God against the kingdom of the devil, shown sevenfold for the consolation of captive pilgrims under the Babylonian yoke, citizens of the kingdom of God.

The first form is that in which a single stone flashing from a mountain, without hands, breaks and crushes a great and exceedingly terrible statue (Dan. 2).

The second is that in which fire neither touches nor afflicts the three youths sent by the king into the burning furnace, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God (Dan. 3).

The third is that in which a great and powerful king, admiring his great Babylon which he had built, is driven mad by a voice falling from heaven, is cast out from among men, eats grass like an ox, and is compelled by this experience to confess that the Most High lives forever, “and his kingdom is from generation to generation; and there is none who can resist his hand or say to him: Why hast thou done this?” (Dan. 4).

The fourth is that in which the kingdom of Babylon itself is conquered by God the king and given to the Medes and Persians, when Belshazzar the Chaldean is killed and Darius the Mede succeeds him (Dan. 5).

The fifth is that in which God’s advocate defeats the malicious petitioners of a mortal human king: “My God,” he says, “sent his angel and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did me no harm, because righteousness was found in me before him” (Dan. 6). The king, declaring this, says: “The God of Daniel, he is the living God and everlasting for ages; and his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his dominion is unto eternity” (ibid.).

The sixth is that in which, when the four winds of heaven contend and four beasts arise from the sea, after them at last “with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of man came, and came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and honor and kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him” (Dan. 7).

The seventh is that in which, by an oracle of this kind, it is taught more clearly that the kingdom of sin is to be destroyed by the coming of the kingdom of God’s righteousness: “Seventy weeks are shortened upon thy people and upon thy holy city, that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may receive an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of holies may be anointed” (Dan. 9).

Let us linger here briefly and, though repeating familiar things, proclaim without weariness the praise and glory of Christ the King.

### Chapter II. On Nebuchadnezzar: how, by attacking and taking Jerusalem captive once and again, he bore the type of the devil, enemy of Christ’s Church.

First, as for the king of Babylon, conqueror and lord of many nations: present evils as well as forewarnings of the future do not permit him to count the glory of his victories safe or secure. He bears the type of the devil precisely in this: by attacking Jerusalem once and again, he trampled it down and led the people of God captive from it.

Once, namely, when, as it is written here, in the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim, he besieged it, removed King Jehoiakim, carried off part of the vessels of the house of the Lord, brought them into the house of his own god, and led captive all the strong men and warriors, appointing as king Zedekiah, Jehoiakim’s uncle (4 Kings 24).

And again, when that same Zedekiah rebelled in the ninth year of his reign: he himself and all his army came to Jerusalem; the city was breached; he seized Zedekiah, put out his eyes, bound him in chains, and led him to Babylon. Nebuzaradan, commander of his army and his servant, also destroyed Jerusalem, burned the house of the Lord, carried the remaining portion of the people into Babylon, and took all the remaining vessels with which they ministered to the Lord (4 Kings 25).

In both instances, as has already been said, this king of Babylon bears the type of the devil. Thus the devil attacked the holy city, the heavenly Jerusalem of the living God, once and again. Once, when in pride he rose against the Most High and drew with him into confusion the angels, companions of his pride, who became demons (Isa. 14). Again, when he led the first man, deceived together with his whole race, into this region of confusion—indeed, into a double captivity of body and soul (Gen. 3).

Hence it should be noted that in the first deportation Nebuchadnezzar transferred only part of the people and part of the vessels (4 Kings 24); but in the second he took both the remaining part of the people and the remaining vessels; he also destroyed Jerusalem’s walls and burned the house of the Lord with fire (4 Kings 25). Thus, in the first invasion of the heavenly city Jerusalem, he destroyed a part—that is, some angels; but in the second, he destroyed not some but all human beings, whose multitude, as the part of the elect, is holy Jerusalem. All, I say, he destroyed in the one parent, and set them ablaze with the hellish fire of sin.

Therefore the carnal Nebuchadnezzar, who counts wickedness as glory as though it were victory, sees visions of another kingdom, the kingdom of God, by whose coming he cannot be ignorant that not only his Babylon but the whole world will perish. So also the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar, the devil, devastator of the heavenly Jerusalem, was never so secure in his kingdom—the kingdom of sin and death—as not in some way to dream of the salvation that he did not wish to know, Scripture testifying that a kingdom would someday rise against him. For the great King and foundation of the kingdom of God says in his Gospel: “When a strong man armed guards his court, all that he possesses is in peace; but if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he will take away all his weapons” (Luke 11).

“In peace,” he says, “are the things that he possesses.” Thus this man too, bearing the type, as we have said, of that same strong man, said in vain swelling pride, after he had already heard explained that the holy watcher was crying out against him: “Is not this Babylon, which I have built into the house of my kingdom by the strength of my might and for the glory of my splendor?” (Dan. 4). Therefore Christ did not say of him, “The things that he possesses are in peace,” because he could ever truly be secure, but because he was a swollen robber who, in frenzied pride, falsely claimed for himself a peace that did not exist.

### Chapter III. What things Daniel desired, and of what kind, so as to merit being called a man of desires: his resolving in his heart not to defile himself with the king’s table.

Now let us recall that this holy Daniel was called by heavenly testimony “a man of desires” (Dan. 9). For of what sort of desires was he a man, except such as we may infer from revelations of this kind? Let us say, then, that since the one God is the one desire of the saints, two things are to be desired by them for his sake: first, that the kingdom of sin may be removed, which has already happened and is happening through Christ’s first advent; second, that every voice of insult may be taken away from God’s enemies, which is to be done through Christ’s second advent.

The circumstances of that time undoubtedly greatly increased the flame of these desires in this holy man. For he loved God, and necessarily, for the sake of him whom he loved, he was zealous against the kingdom of sin, hostile to God’s kingdom, and against sinful human beings, enemies of his kingdom, so that he might say with David: “How long shall sinners, O Lord, how long shall sinners glory?” (Ps. 93), and similar words. He saw himself an exile, born into this world because of original sin; he heard the nations say, on account of the actual sins for which God’s people had been taken captive: “Where is their God?” (Ps. 113). On one side he saw the tyranny of the devil; on the other, the pride of man in words. Surely he hated friendship with both, because he desired the true glory of God alone.

Thus he obtained consolations suited to the matter and the time, in accordance with the preparations by which he prepared his heart, as the Psalmist says: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; thy ear has heard the preparations of their heart” (Ps. 9). This Scripture at once indicates, in the first place, the sorrowful preparations of this man:

“But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not be defiled by the king’s table, nor by the wine of his drinking; and he asked the chief of the eunuchs that he might not be contaminated.”

And afterwards: “To these youths God gave knowledge and learning in every book and wisdom; but to Daniel, understanding of all visions and dreams.” Therefore, because he was such a man of desires, and manfully desired the judgment of God, it is clear that he deserved to be so named by divine foreknowledge. For Daniel means “judgment of God.”

### Chapter IV. That it was brought about by God’s providence that not Daniel himself, but Nebuchadnezzar, dreamed the mystery of God’s kingdom; and why it is not surprising that God revealed his secrets to an impious man.

The diligent providence of God the consoler must be carefully noted. “Nebuchadnezzar,” says Scripture (Chapter 2), “saw a dream, and his spirit was troubled, and the dream fled from him. Therefore the king commanded that the diviners, magicians, sorcerers, and Chaldeans be summoned, to declare to the king his dreams,” and so forth.

Daniel himself did not see the dream; rather, Nebuchadnezzar saw what Daniel was to interpret, and could not retain the vision in memory. To what end was God working, he who is accustomed to reveal his secrets not to the proud but to the humble, indeed not to his enemies but to his friends? Surely it was that even then he might give his captives mercy in the sight of him who had taken them captive (Ps. 105). And this happened: for on the occasion of the revelations, that first king “raised Daniel to high rank, gave him many great gifts, appointed him ruler over all the provinces of Babylon and chief over all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel, however, asked the king, and he appointed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego over the administration of the province of Babylon. But Daniel himself was at the king’s gate.”

Nor should it be surprising that an impious king was admitted to heavenly mysteries for this reason, so that he might say: “Behold, I see four men, unbound and walking in the midst of the fire; there is no harm in them, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God.” For the Holy Spirit did not disdain, for this same reason, to prophesy the victories of Cyrus, king of the Persians: “Who says to Cyrus: Thou art my shepherd, and thou shalt fulfill all my will; who says to Jerusalem: Thou shalt be built; and to the temple: Thou shalt be founded. Thus says the Lord to Cyrus my anointed, whose right hand I have grasped, that I may subject nations before his face and turn the backs of kings.” And afterwards: “I have called thee by my name, I have made thee like me, and thou hast not known me. I am the Lord, and there is none else. Apart from me there is no God. I have girded thee, and thou hast not known me” (Isa. 44–45).

Therefore, because that captivity was not like the wrath now brought to completion against the Jews—of which Moses says in the Song: “A fire is kindled in my anger, and it shall burn even to the lowest hell” (Deut. 32)—but was the rod of paternal correction, this also must not be omitted in praise of God’s mercy: while he corrects, scourges, and strikes, he simultaneously opens the gates of his mercy, so much so that, in order through his goodwill to make provision for his captives, he admitted some barbarian, pagan kings to revelations of his secrets, while others, before they were born, he made illustrious by the prophetic trumpet, promising and proclaiming their future victories.

### Chapter V. That Daniel was sought in order that he might perish with his companions; and on the song, “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat,” and so forth, which David sang in their person.

“And the decree having gone forth, the wise men were being slain; and Daniel and his companions were sought that they might perish.” O harsh interrogation! Therefore long before, in the prophetic spirit, David said in the person of these and of others like them:

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered thee, O Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.”

Why did we weep there?

“Because there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who carried us away said: Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion. How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136).

Surely this weeping and this most sorrowful lament applied first to Daniel and his companions for such a reason. For the sacrament of the vision which Nebuchadnezzar had seen was a word of song; it was “a hymn from the songs of Zion,” it was “a song of the Lord.” Yet they were in a foreign land, not only because they were captives in that Babylon, but also because they were exiles in this world, made captives in Adam from their heavenly mother Jerusalem. “How then,” they say, “shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?”

O king, the song you demand, the mystery of the vision you seek by a harsh demand—this, I say, and so forth: we cannot here sing or know the secrets of heaven and the songs of the blessed archangels, except for the very few among us who are prophets, to whom God reveals them, not because of their merits but by his grace.

“When Arioch had made the matter known to Daniel, Daniel went in and asked the king to give him time to declare the interpretation to the king.” Even had he not been sought to be killed with his companions, yet because he was a man of desires, as we have already said above, and desired the glory of God, he would certainly have judged the present business not to be neglected, since God could be glorified through it.

For the Chaldeans had said to their king: “The matter which thou, O king, demandest is difficult, and no one will be found who can declare it in the king’s presence, except gods whose dwelling is not with men.” But, O servants, not of gods but of demons—who have no intercourse with human beings regarding the mysteries of heaven—no one will be found who can declare this matter except the one true God, whose fellowship with pious human beings is familiar, as he says: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6).

Thus Daniel entered his house, not merely that he and the other wise men of Babylon might not perish, but also that the matter might advance to the praise of God. He told the matter to his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, that they might seek mercy from the face of the God of heaven concerning this mystery. “Then the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision by night, and Daniel blessed the God of heaven,” and so forth.

It was rightly revealed then and at the proper time. God had long intended to reveal it thus, but by delaying he awaited the time and place. For, remembering mercy in wrath, he now intended to commend and honor his captives. He was silent, therefore, until “the decree had gone forth and the wise men were being slain,” so that help might come more gratefully, because it came in greater danger.

And, to return to the question from the Psalm mentioned above, where those who weep under a harsh demand say, “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” first the king himself and the whole kingdom of Babylon were stirred; and by this disturbance, as though all peoples and nations had assembled, a common audience was prepared. Thus, when these singers began to sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land, granted to them by mercy, the people might stand listening—not only attentive and favorably disposed, but most eager hearers, reverent fellow-praisers, and admirers. It would have happened otherwise if the prophetic Spirit, by an excessively spontaneous song, had sung to those willows: surely the grim and brutish filth of swine would have trampled underfoot the pearls of the songs of Zion.

### Chapter VI. On the interpretation of the dream Nebuchadnezzar saw, the succession of kingdoms, and how Christ, according to that dream, the stone, crushes every kingdom.

“You, O king, began to ponder on your bed what would happen after these things, and he who reveals mysteries showed you what is to come,” etc. “The dream,” he says, “is true.” Behold, we see that “the dream is true, and its interpretation trustworthy,” because, in accordance with these things, through the childbirth of the incorrupt Virgin the God of heaven will raise up a kingdom which shall never be destroyed; and his kingdom shall not be given to another people. It has crushed and consumes all these kingdoms: the golden kingdom of the Babylonians, which was exceedingly rich; the silver kingdom of the Persians and Medes, that is, less wealthy; [Col. 1505B] the bronze kingdom of the Macedonians, that is, resounding with much eloquence; and the iron kingdom of the Romans, that is, the strongest, for iron crushes and subdues all things.

This kingdom, I say, crushes all these kingdoms, and it itself, of which we speak, shall stand forever to come. For just as the Apostle, having prefaced that saying of David, “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. VIII), says concerning him of whom we speak: “For we do not yet see all things subjected to him; but we see the Lord Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Heb. II), so here also, after setting forth what is most certain—that “the stone was cut out from the mountain without hands,” that is, [Col. 1505C] Christ was born of the Virgin without a man’s embrace—and became a great mountain after striking the statue of the kingdoms of this world. Let us say that this is yet to come, although it has already partly occurred.

For we do not yet see all kingdoms crushed and consumed; but we see that he who crushed them by his first coming, the stone, has filled the whole earth. Yet at his second coming he shall crush and consume them all utterly, and his kingdom shall stand forever.

## CHAPTER VII. How the sending of the three into the fiery furnace prefigured Christ’s martyrs; how “the appearance of the fourth,” he says, “was like the Son of God”; and how he, on seeing this and blessing God, bore the type of the kingdom of this world that has been converted to Christ.

**(Chapter III.)** “King Nebuchadnezzar made a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six cubits broad, and set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. Then King Nebuchadnezzar sent for the satraps, magistrates, judges, commanders, tyrants, prefects, and all the rulers of the regions, that they might come to the dedication of the statue which King Nebuchadnezzar had set up.”

By the preceding revelation it had been sufficiently shown that wisdom and might belong to the Lord; that he changes times and seasons, transfers and establishes kingdoms; and that he crushes and consumes all these things by one stone—that is, by the solid power of Christ his Son. But who there asked or understood what kinds of things, or how great, this crushing or consuming was, is, and will be, through [Col. 1506A] the wars of the martyrs, even to the end of the age?

The narrative therefore proceeds in fitting and truly mystical order, setting forth in this vision a wondrous prefiguration of Christ’s martyrs, whose faith is indeed a stone. For Christ is in them, and none can doubt that Christ fights in them. In what more venerable way could their conflict, to be waged against the kingdom of the world and against the kingdom of the devil, have been prefigured?

“King Nebuchadnezzar,” he says, “made a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six cubits broad.” Doubtless this is brute idolatry, erected by the king of Babylon—by the most foul Nero, the disgrace of the Roman Empire. Rome, that is, was a second Babylon, as the apostle Peter testifies when he says: “The Church which is gathered in Babylon greets you” [Col. 1506B] (I Pet. V).

He erected it, I say, not because idolatry had not existed before, but because, rebelling against the stone which, as stated above, had struck the kingdoms of the world, he raised that same idolatry higher, and was the first to issue decrees. He wrote to magistrates, judges, commanders, tyrants, prefects, and all the rulers of kingdoms, that they should assemble for the dedication of the statue, should conspire to defend the ancient error against the new teaching of Christian faith.

Its height was sixty cubits, its breadth six cubits. The number six in the units place and in the tens place signifies the totality of creation, because all things were created in six days. And significantly he extended his statue by this number in both dimensions; though he did not know it, this signified what the Apostle says: “They served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. I).

Why say more? Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who did not worship the gods of the king of Babylon and did not adore the statue he had erected, were bound and cast into the midst of the blazing furnace. And they walked in the midst of the flame, praising the Lord and singing a hymn to the Lord. Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished, rose quickly, and said to his nobles: “Did we not cast three men into the midst of the fire? Behold, I see four men, unbound, walking in the midst of the fire; they have suffered no harm, and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God.”

Shadrach means “my adornment”; Meshach, “who is laughter”; Abednego, “serving in silence.” Likewise, Hananiah means “the grace of the Lord”; [Col. 1506D] Azariah, “the help of the Lord”; Mishael, “who is the salvation of God.” These three, alike by their number and their names, their cause and their sufferings, signify all the soldiers and warriors of the kingdom of God: confessors of the Trinity—adorned, rejoicing, and serving in silence—that is, innocent in life, “rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. XII). In them is the grace of the Lord; with them in their very sufferings is the help of the Lord; and theirs is the salvation of the Lord—Christ himself, for whose sake they suffered, and of whom this man, in an understanding born of wonder, says: “The appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God.”

For he himself says elsewhere through the prophet to the single love of his martyrs: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name: you are mine. When you pass through the waters, I shall be with you, and the rivers shall not overwhelm you. When [Col. 1507A] you walk through fire, you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not blaze upon you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior” (Isa. XLIII).

But this same Nebuchadnezzar says: “Blessed is their God, who sent his angel and delivered his servants.” Does he then weaken or destroy his earlier statement by calling an angel him of whom he had foretold, “The appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God”? Certainly not. For he who is by nature the Son of God became for us, by office, the Angel of the Lord, the Angel of great counsel.

“They looked upon these men,” he says, “because the fire had exercised no power over their bodies; the hair of their heads had not been scorched, their garments had not been altered, and the smell of fire had not passed over them.” Let us truly proclaim all these things concerning our martyrs, the witnesses of Christ the Son of God: so long as Christ’s faith remained in them uncorrupted and unconquered, the punishments and death had no power over them; nothing harmed them; and although they seemed to the eyes of the foolish to die (Wis. III), they are not dead. For they live to their God, who said: “Not a hair of your head shall perish” (Luke XXI).

“Blessed,” says Nebuchadnezzar, “is their God—namely, the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego,” the very man who had cast them into the fire—“because he sent his angel and delivered his servants.” “Therefore this decree is established by me: that every people, tribe, and language which speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall perish, and its house shall be laid waste.”

Behold, today the Roman Empire itself, which killed Christ’s martyrs, speaks and proclaims thus. Truly God is wonderful even in evils, which he knows how to use so beneficially for good. This man, evil and useless to himself, see what good and useful prophecies he uttered for the whole world. From the same opening he poured forth waters both sweet and bitter: sweet to us, bitter to himself. A little earlier, falling upon his face and worshiping the God of Daniel, he had said, “Truly your God is God of gods and Lord of kings,” and so forth—pouring out, as it were, cups of sweetness. Afterwards he said these bitter words to the worshipers of that same God and Lord: “And who is the god that will deliver you from my hand?” Now, however, he speaks sweet words again: “Therefore this decree is established by me,” and so forth.

Yet he was not to persist in that sweetness. For, as has already been said, he bore the type of this kingdom of the world, which, though one and the same, would through some persons of royal dignity utter sweet proclamations, and through others bitter blasphemies against the majesty of God’s kingdom. Let us therefore follow the order of the narrative, to see by what image the victory of that same kingdom of God is finally marked out as to be accomplished.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Nebuchadnezzar was driven out from among men and ate grass like an ox; how this prefigured the Apostle’s statement, “God has made foolish the wisdom of this world through the Gospel of Christ”; and concerning the victory of God’s kingdom, whose power he confessed after his understanding had been restored.

**(Chapter IV.)** “I, Nebuchadnezzar, was at ease in my house and flourishing in my palace. I saw a dream which terrified me, and my thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me. And a decree was issued by me that all the wise men of Babylon should be brought before me, and that they should reveal to me the interpretation of the dream,” etc.

Behold, for the third time the proud weakness of the human king, contending with the strength of God, is overcome. For he spoke—or rather, answered—the interpretation of the dream that he had heard against himself: the great and strong tree was to be cut down, its branches lopped off and its leaves shaken away, until it was stripped bare. He answered, I say, and said:

“Is this not great Babylon which I have built as the house of my kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” It was as though he said: And who is that watcher and holy one, at whose command or cry I, strong and mighty, I, the glorious and splendid builder of great Babylon, can be driven from among men in such a manner?

Thus, though already once and twice defeated, and though an inglorious confessor of the heavenly victory, he now lifted up his neck a third time in uttering these words. But immediately the wanton and ungovernable ox perceives that it is exceedingly hard to kick against the goad. “While the word was still in the king’s mouth,” Scripture says, “a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has departed from you,’” etc. That same hour the word was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar. He was driven out from among men and ate grass like an ox.

We therefore ask in what way this event also signifies a part of the victory—the victory of the King who is God, the victory of the kingdom of Christ the Son of God. At once there comes to mind what the Apostle says: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (I Cor. I). Again: “God chose the foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame, and God chose the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame” (ibid.).

Surely the madness of so great, so mighty, and so proud a king offered a beautiful and fitting image of the wisdom of this world which is to be rejected, especially in that he ate grass like an ox. For concerning that enormous fool, of whom this man is a type, the Lord says to blessed Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he eats grass like an ox” (Job XL).

What is the grass that serves as fodder for this ox, if not the multitude of carnal persons, green in the morning, quickly flowering, and likewise quickly withering once their flower has been lost? “For all flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The sun has risen, the grass has dried up, and its flower has fallen” (Isa. XL).

Therefore, Nebuchadnezzar, driven from among men when the holy watcher descended and at his cry, ate grass like an ox; because, when Christ, the power and wisdom of God, descended into this world, at his preaching the wisdom of this world—the wisdom of the rulers of this age—was made foolish (I Cor. I), and, driven out from men who received divine reason, could devour only grass: that is, superfluous people, sprouting beyond measure through the defect of the flesh.

But after these things the text continues:

“Therefore, at the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted up my eyes to heaven, and my understanding was restored [Col. 1509A] to me, and I blessed the Most High,” etc.

Does it therefore follow, as some supposed—men whom the Church of God proved truly foolish when they imagined themselves wise—that the aforementioned Behemoth must open his brutish mouth and breast in repentance or penitence, to utter praises and blessings of the Most High? Certainly not. For eternal fire has been prepared for him and his angels, as the truth of the Gospel declares (Matt. XXV).

But, while the same truth of Christ is preserved and remains, it may be understood much more soundly that a great part of his body—that is, many of the wise of this age, such as the wisdom of God has made foolish (I Cor. III)—have come to their senses and daily come to their senses until the end of the age. Thus the Lord says concerning this same Behemoth to the aforesaid blessed Job through other comparisons: “His friends shall cut him in pieces, and merchants shall divide him” (Job XL). And immediately afterward: “Will you fill a net with his skin, or a fishers’ hut with his head?” (ibid.).

For it is understood as though he said: I, who, calling fishermen, make them fishers of men (Matt. IV), first fill my net with his skin, gathering those at the farthest limits and without number; and afterwards, subduing wise adversaries to myself, fill a fishers’ hut, as it were, with his head.

Let it suffice to have said these things for our purpose: namely, that in this king of Babylon, now conquered for the third time, we might understand the perfect victory of the King of heaven to be signified, when he himself confesses it, saying in his third confession: “For his power is an everlasting power, and his kingdom from generation to generation; and all the inhabitants of the earth are reckoned as nothing before him.”

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the overthrow of Babylon by the Medes and Persians, and how through it is signified the future destruction, on the day of judgment, of the entire city of the devil.

It shall come to pass that the entire city of the devil shall be destroyed and perish beneath heaven: that city which has opposed the city of the living God from the beginning and does not cease to oppose it until the end of the age. The narrative therefore proceeds in a fittingly mystical order to that overthrow of Babylon by the Medes and Persians—the Babylon which, with its king, destroyed that earthly Jerusalem in which the name of the living God was invoked, and led his people captive.

**(Chapter V.)** “King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and each drank according to his age,” etc.

Here we fix the eye especially upon our subject and purpose, where, he says, “fingers appeared, like the hand of a man writing opposite the lampstand upon the surface of the wall of the royal hall; and the king watched the joints of the writing hand. Then the king’s countenance changed, his thoughts troubled him, the joints of his loins were loosened, and his knees struck against one another.”

What does that hand indicate? Surely the same Son of God—designated in the first chapter by the stone cut from the mountain without hands, in the second by his own name, and in the third by the name “watcher and holy one”—is designated in the fourth chapter by the writing hand. For the hand, that is, the right hand of the Father, employs itself in judging the impiety of spiritual Babylon and in destroying the kingdom of the world, its enemy; writing—or rather, having long since written down—all the evils which this Babylon has inflicted upon his saints.

And it should be noted that the hand appeared in the midst of the banquet on that night, and powerfully shook the security of the drunken king and his nobles by its dreadful vision. Thus that day shall come suddenly and unexpectedly upon the secure and the despisers of God, as he himself testifies when he says: “And as it happened in the days of Noah, so shall it be in the days of the Son of Man. They ate and drank, married wives and were given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered into the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all” (Matt. XXIV).

Therefore, when King Belshazzar had made a great feast, and each drank according to his age; when he himself and his nobles, his wives and concubines, were drinking wine and praising their gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stone: in that same hour fingers appeared, like the hand of a man writing opposite the lampstand upon the surface of the wall—writing, I say, the sin, judgment, and wrath corresponding to the sins of Babylon’s pride. For so it shall be on the day when the Son of Man is revealed, and Babylon, the city of the devil, the city of confusion, the harlot drunk with the blood of the saints, shall be exposed by that same revelation.

The kingdom of that Babylon was numbered and completed, weighed in the balance and divided, and given to the Medes and Persians. But the kingdom of this Babylon, likewise counted through its individual murders and other crimes, weighed in a just balance and divided by a terrible sentence, shall be given not to human beings but to demons; not to Medes or Persians, but to evil spirits; not to Darius, but to the devil and his angels.

Foreseeing this, Isaiah says: “Come down, sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit upon the ground” (Isa. XLVII). “There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans”—that is, of the strong ones, namely the evil spirits, of whom she is rightly called the daughter because she has imitated their fierce pride. And afterwards: “And now hear this, you delicate one who dwell securely, who say in your heart: ‘I am, and besides me there is no other. I shall not sit as a widow, nor know barrenness.’ These two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day: barrenness and widowhood” (ibid.), etc.

In the Apocalypse also, he who is here figured by the writing hand—he himself, I say, the angel descending from heaven with great authority, by whose glory the earth was illuminated—cries in a mighty voice: “Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen, and has become a habitation of demons, a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean bird, because all nations have drunk of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth have committed fornication with her” (Apoc. XVIII).

## CHAPTER X. Concerning Belshazzar’s death and the giving of his kingdom to the Medes and Persians; and how, through the envy endured by Daniel, greater glory accrued to him.

“That same night Belshazzar, king of the Chaldeans, was slain, [Col. 1511A] and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, being sixty-two years old.”

In this manner was fulfilled the truth of the prophecy which had long before been spoken to King Nebuchadnezzar: “You are the golden head; and after you another kingdom, inferior to you, shall arise” (Dan. II). By that prophecy of the kingdom then still to come, the prophetic spirit of grace gained the goodwill of the captives; and still more by this prophecy, spoken most recently—namely, on that very night—“Your kingdom has been divided and given to the Medes and Persians.”

By the preceding merits of this prophetic proclamation, Daniel was able to become beloved and welcome to the new government, as a consolation to the captives. The following words immediately show this clearly.

**(Chapter VI.)** “It pleased Darius, and he appointed over the kingdom one hundred and twenty satraps, and over them three presidents, of whom Daniel was one, so that the satraps might render account to them and the king might suffer no inconvenience.”

But what pleased the wise king burned up the satraps by this splendid man’s own splendor. His distinguished virtue stirred them all to envy of him. “They sought,” he says, “an occasion against Daniel from the king’s side, but they could find no cause or ground for suspicion, because he was faithful and no fault or suspicion could be found in him,” etc.

Since the literal history of this marvelous event lies plain and open to all, it is fitting that in this herald also we should contemplate the glory of Christ, Lord and King. For Daniel endured envy because of the glorious temporal favor of earthly rulers; but he had attained that same glory by receiving the grace of the prophetic Spirit, for the glory of the true God. Therefore, in his suffering let us contemplate the truth of Christ’s passion; and in his victory let us proclaim the figure of Christ’s victory.

## CHAPTER XI. How, in being cast into the pit through the envy of the rulers and remaining unharmed, Daniel signified the passion and victory of Christ, whom the Jews killed through envy.

“The presidents and satraps sought an occasion against Daniel from the king’s side.”

Daniel, whose very name means “judgment of God,” here bears the type of Christ the Son of God, whose judgment is indeed God’s judgment, because the Father gave all judgment to him (John V). Who does not know that the rulers, priests, and elders of the Jews repeatedly and excessively sought an occasion against him from the king’s side? For they had Caesar as their king, and out of envy of him they said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX).

They sought, I say, an occasion against him from the king’s side, so that they might perhaps say: “He made himself a king; he forbade tribute to be paid to Caesar” (Luke XXIII). But, he says, “they could find no cause or ground for suspicion, because he was faithful and no fault or suspicion could be found in him.” Truly he was faithful and true, and righteousness fought and judged in him. For he said: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. XXII).

Nevertheless these rulers prevailed and extorted from their unwilling king a sentence that Daniel should be cast into the lions’ pit. This occurred because of that pretext: because Daniel prayed to his God; because he did not obey the slanderous decree secretly obtained from the king of the Persians and Medes; because, although he rendered to the king what belonged to the king, he nevertheless took care to render to God what belonged to God.

Thus indeed the chief priests, by persuading the crowds with tumultuous shouting, extorted the condemnation of our Lord Jesus Christ under Roman law. Not that we judge Pilate, the governor and servant of the Roman Empire, to have been altogether excusable, as though he had truly been forced against his own will; rather, we do not doubt that he wished to appear forced, so that afterwards he might incur no accusation for a man unjustly condemned (Matt. XXVII; Mark XV).

But by whatever servant, and with whatever disposition of the agent who served it, they inflicted the power of the Roman Empire as they wished; and they cast innocent Christ, the Son of God, into the lions’ pit—that is, they killed him, so that he descended into hell.

“But,” Daniel says, “my God sent his angel, and shut the mouths of the lions, and they did me no harm, because righteousness was found in me before him.” Rather, he saved his own arm, as he says: “My arm saved for me, and my indignation itself assisted me” (Isa. LXIII). So completely did he save his own arm, shutting the mouths of the spiritual lions, that he raised him “from the dead, the pains of hell having been loosed, because it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts II).

The king rejoiced greatly at this. For at last the Roman Empire heard—heard this, I say, patiently—and wisely recognized that God had raised Jesus from the dead; and when the emperors themselves believed, the Roman world rejoiced greatly.

“And he commanded,” he says, “that Daniel be brought up from the pit.” The majesty of the Roman Empire altered its laws and changed its decrees; and it commanded that the Lord Jesus Christ, who had been reckoned among those descending into the pit, should be proclaimed as one drawn up from the pit of death: that God and man, Christ, having died once, had risen and was henceforth immortal forever (Rom. VI). This is sufficiently and clearly prefigured in the present decree:

“Peace be multiplied to you,” says Darius. “A decree is established by me that, throughout all my empire and kingdom, men should tremble and fear the God of Daniel. For he is the living God, eternal for ages; his kingdom shall not be destroyed, and his power endures forever.”

Those who accused Daniel were themselves cast into the lions’ pit and immediately consumed, because those who confined Christ in death and brought his life down to the pit of death themselves thereby came into death; they themselves descended to hell. Thus was fulfilled the prophecy of the Psalmist: “They dug a pit before my face, and fell into it” (Ps. LVI). Again: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole which he made” (Ps. VII).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the battle of the four winds of heaven; the Ancient of Days sitting; the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven; and the judgment of the world.

**(Chapter VII.)** “In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel saw a dream. The vision of his head was upon his bed; and, writing down the dream, he set it forth in a brief account, touching on it summarily. He said: ‘I saw in my vision by night, and behold, the four winds of heaven were contending upon the great sea, and four great beasts, diverse from one another, were rising out of the sea.’”

This vision is a great and manifest testimony concerning Christ, the Son of God and likewise Son of Man; a great and broad spectacle of revelation, which the simple eyes of believers can behold with nothing more willingly, and the kindly ears of those who love God the most ancient Father and the Son of God the Father—new indeed as man, but nevertheless ancient as God—can hear with nothing more sweetly.

“The four winds of heaven,” he says, “were contending upon the great sea, and four great beasts were rising up.” What the beasts signified, one of those standing by sufficiently explained: “These four great beasts,” he says, “are four kingdoms which shall arise from the earth.” But why winds, and why beasts? Surely winds because of vanity, beasts because of ferocity. “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes, “and all is vanity” (Eccl. I).

The great sea is this age. Therefore the four winds of heaven contended upon this great sea, because the four kingdoms of this age, failing to consider the brevity of their own duration, blew vainly: the Babylonian kingdom, likened to a lioness with wings because of pride and luxury; the kingdom of the Persians and Medes, to a bear because of ferocity; the Greek kingdom, to a leopard because of the frivolous variety of sects; and the Roman kingdom, to a terrible and wondrous beast with iron teeth because of its invincible strength.

What else were these bestial kingdoms but winds? They were winds, I say, and winds of heaven; yet they did not possess heaven, which through pride they imagined they could attain. Nor could they hold even the sea for long, which they troubled for a moment and then passed over.

After they had therefore passed away with their windy vanity, “I watched,” he says, “until thrones were set up and the Ancient of Days sat.” Surely this was the sweet image of God’s kingdom which, as has already been said above, the very man who saw these things awaited: a citizen of heaven, a pilgrim in this age, a captive of that Babylon. Therefore he desired God’s kingdom all the more ardently, so that he deserved to be called a man of desires and, for the consolation of his soul, to behold such great and wondrous visions of that same kingdom of God.

For what could he have wished to see more sweetly, or more profitably for consolation? “The Ancient of Days,” he says, “sat.” But formerly he had no seat in the human race, because through the transgression of the first man the kingdom of sin and death had entered this world. Therefore he sat: that is, he established judgment against the devil, the persuader of his kingdom’s overthrow. For it follows: “The court sat, and the books were opened.”

This is indeed understood of the future judgment, because concerning Antichrist, the final king of the devil’s kingdom, it was first said: “I considered the horns, and behold, another little horn arose in their midst; and three of the first horns were torn up before it; and behold, in this horn were eyes like the eyes of a man, and a mouth speaking great things.”

But immediately afterwards it follows: “I watched in the vision of the night, and behold, one like the Son of Man came with the clouds of heaven, and came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him, and he gave him power, honor, and a kingdom, and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him.”

Christian faith holds it certain that this was accomplished at his first coming. The Son of Man has already come even to the Ancient of Days; we have already presented him before him—every one of us who believes and confesses that he was offered for our sins, and who daily celebrates upon the holy altar the sacred mystery of his offering. He has already given him power, honor, and a kingdom. For because of the suffering of death he has already crowned him with glory and honor, and appointed him over the works of his hands (Heb. II). For this is what he said after rising from the dead: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

And then all peoples, tribes, and languages serve him, being baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in accordance with his command. What then if some still resist his service? They assuredly owe service and shall receive punishment from him, because of their slavish fear and stiff-necked rebellion: “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX). And immediately: “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (ibid.).

Therefore the words, “I watched until thrones were set up and the Ancient of Days sat,” and likewise, “The court sat and the books were opened,” speak indeed of the majesty of the future judgment and the second coming. Yet they do so in such a way that some consideration is also given to the first coming, in which that same judgment began to be enacted, as the Judge himself testifies when he says: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John XII).

Therefore, for the praise of God and the glory of God’s kingdom, which is now within us, I gladly refer these things to the first coming of Christ the Son of God, so that we may confess that what is to be consummated at the second coming was begun at the first.

## CHAPTER XIII. What the thrones that were set up are; what his throne is; what the flame of fire and its wheels of burning fire are; what the fiery stream proceeding from before him is; and what the sitting judgment is.

“Aspiciebam,” he says, “until thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat.” I watched, I say, longing and sighing with the longing and sighing common to all the righteous: they knew that in Adam they had fallen away from the kingdom of God, and they awaited its recovery in us—the glory of his own kingdom. And so it came to pass: “Thrones were set in place, and the Ancient of Days took his seat.” The one throne and the many thrones are the one Church and the many saints, in whose hearts that Ancient of Days took his seat; for God was not new to them. His throne is Abraham; his throne is David; his throne is each of the saints, [Col. 1515A] in whose hearts he sat through faith, those thrones having been set in place—that is, prepared by long expectation for the coming of his kingdom.

How did he sit? “His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool.” These are the glorious insignia of his kingdom. Snow signifies the forgiveness of sins, and wool the covering of our nakedness. Hence the Psalmist: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). Likewise: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31).

“His throne was a flame of fire; its wheels, burning fire. A fiery and swift stream went forth from before him.” Although fire may here be understood as wrath, and flame as future vengeance, nevertheless the fiery stream deserves a gentler interpretation, especially because it is said to have gone forth from before him. For what that is not sweet or lovable goes forth or proceeds from before him? Therefore, not without reason and not by forced interpretation, we say that the fiery stream is the Holy Spirit, of whom the Psalmist says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45). And in Isaiah the same Holy Spirit says: “Behold, I will turn toward them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent, the glory of the nations” (Isa. 66). This stream undoubtedly went forth from before him; hence the Holy Spirit is said to proceed. It is fiery and swift because it makes minds fiery and renders tongues eloquent and alive. He both testified to this and demonstrated it by its effect when he appeared over the disciples as fire, and they began to speak in diverse tongues [Col. 1515C] (Acts 2)—with swift tongues, so that no power of the age could impose silence upon them.

From that time onward his throne—that is, his Church—is a flame of fire, and the wheels of his Gospels are burning fire. “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him.” This may rightly be understood of angelic spirits, of whose innumerable thousands some minister to him and some stand before him (Rev. 5). But because the matter concerns the human race, from which God in his graciousness acquired thousands for his kingdom, it is helpful to continue the interpretation thus. When the fiery and swift stream went forth from before him, “thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him”; that is, when the Holy Spirit who proceeds from him was given, innumerable people who formerly were not his, reborn through water and that same [Col. 1515D] Spirit, began in their allotted ranks to serve his majesty: some ministering through the active life, others standing before him through the contemplative life. More minister in the active life; fewer stand before him in contemplation. Appropriately, then, an indefinite quantity is given: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him”; but a definite one: “And ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him. The court sat, and the books were opened.”

This is, as it were, the boundary between the two judgments; it bears upon each judgment in a fitting sense. For the judgment has already sat, as was foretold, so that the ruler of this world might be cast out (John 12); but it will sit again, so that that same ruler together with his angels—that same ruler, I say, as a head with all [Col. 1516A] his body—may receive the punishments he deserves. Hence follows: “I watched because of the sound of the great words which that horn was speaking. And I saw that the beast had been slain, its body destroyed, and given over to the fire to be burned,” etc.

Likewise, “the books have already been opened,” when the Lamb opened the great book sealed with seven seals, and when he opened the understanding of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). The books, I say, were opened through the first judgment, so that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might become blind (John 9). But the books—the books of consciences—will be opened, so that each may be judged from the things written therein.

## CHAPTER XIV. [Col. 1516B] Concerning the coming Son of Man: how he comes even to the Ancient of Days, and how authority, honor, and a kingdom are given to him.

Thus far the divine judgment has plainly been described, but it has not been stated by whose hand or person it is to be carried out. For the Ancient of Days will not judge in person, because “the Father judges no one” (John 5). And if thrones have been set in place for him, it does not follow that he is to sit in judgment, so that this Ancient of Days is to be expected to sit visibly and locally in order to pronounce sentence, clothed in a snowy or white garment and with a grey head. Thus it has not yet been said what person, or what kind of person, is to carry out the judgment.
