But what follows? “I watched therefore in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven [Col. 1516C] one like a Son of Man was coming; and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him; and he gave him authority, honor, and a kingdom, and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His authority is an eternal authority, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed.”

Thus the saying proclaimed by the Son of Man himself in the Gospel—“The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid.)—is very clearly supported by the testimony of this prophetic vision. What reason, moreover, is there that the Son of Man rather than the Father should execute judgment, except that he is the Son of Man? Thus he himself, after saying, “He gave him authority to execute judgment,” immediately, as though you were asking by what right or by what order of justice the Son judges rather than the Father, adds: “Because,” [Col. 1516D] he says, “he is the Son of Man” (ibid.).

It is as if he said: Because the person of the Son devoted himself more laboriously to the restoration of the world, even to the point of becoming the Son of Man. For this person alone was incarnate and suffered for the salvation of the world. He therefore rightly has authority to execute judgment, so that the person who alone redeemed may alone judge—that is, so that in the judgment the person of the Son alone may be seen, according to the visible form, the form of a servant, in which he alone emptied himself.

But since we are hastening to other matters, and these points, together with the rest, have been treated by the most learned Fathers, let us now proceed to the seventh proclamation of this prophet, by which he was permitted to declare both the kingdom of God for which he waited and its appointed time.

## 589. CHAPTER XV. [Col. 1517A] How the seventy weeks are to be calculated, of which it is said to the prophet: “Seventy weeks are shortened upon your people, that transgression may be brought to completion,” etc., “and the Holy of Holies may be anointed.”

(CHAPTER 9.) “In the first year of Darius son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, who ruled over the kingdom of the Chaldeans, while,” Daniel says, “I was speaking and praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people Israel, in order to lay my supplications before my God for the holy mountain of my God—while I was speaking in prayer, behold, the man Gabriel, whom I had seen in the vision at the beginning, flying swiftly, touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice. And he instructed me and spoke with me and said: Daniel, I have now gone forth [Col. 1517B] to instruct you and enable you to understand. At the beginning of your supplications the word went forth, and I have come to tell you, because you are a man of desires. Therefore attend to the word and understand the vision: Seventy weeks are shortened upon your people and upon your holy city, that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. Know therefore, and observe: From the issuing of the word that Jerusalem is to be rebuilt, until Christ the leader, there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; and the street and walls shall again be built in the distress of times.”

From Ezra’s narrative we have learned that Nehemiah, when he was cupbearer to King Artaxerxes, in the twentieth year of his reign and in the month Nisan obtained from him permission to restore the walls of Jerusalem (2 Esdras 1), although the temple had long before been allowed to be constructed. The work itself, as stated, he completed amid distress of time: namely, he was so attacked by neighboring peoples that the builders are said to have fought with one hand, their sword girded to their loins, and restored the wall with the other (2 Esdras 4).

From this time, therefore, calculate seventy weeks until Christ the leader—that is, 490 years of twelve lunar months, which are 475 solar years. For the Persians reigned 116 years from the aforesaid twentieth year of King Artaxerxes to the death of Darius; then the Macedonians for 300 years until the death of Cleopatra; and thereafter the Romans held the monarchy for fifty-nine years until the seventeenth year of Tiberius Caesar. Together these make, as we have said, 475 years, and they are contained in twenty-five nineteen-year cycles; for twenty-five times nineteen makes 475.

And since seven intercalary months accrue in each cycle, multiply twenty-five by seven: 175. These are the intercalary months in 475 years. If, then, you wish to know how many lunar years they make, divide 175 by twelve. Twelve times fourteen makes 168. They therefore make fourteen years, with seven months remaining. Add these to the 475 years written above, and the total becomes 489. Add also the seven surplus [Col. 1518A] months and the part of the eighteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar in which the Lord suffered, and you will find, from the appointed time to his passion, seventy shortened weeks—that is, 490 lunar years.

But at his baptism, when the Holy of Holies was anointed by the Holy Spirit descending upon him like a dove, not only had the seven and sixty-two weeks been completed, but part of the seventieth week had already begun. “And after,” he says, “seventy-two weeks Christ shall be slain, and his people, who are to deny him, shall not be his.” Christ was not slain immediately after the sixty-two weeks, but at the end of the seventieth. This week, so far as we can infer, he separated from the others because he was going to say more about it. For Christ was crucified in it by the faithless people, who denied him not only in his passion but continuously from the time he began to be proclaimed by John.

What follows—“And the people with the coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary; and its end shall be desolation, and after the end of war desolation is decreed”—does not belong to the seventy weeks. For it had been foretold that those weeks would extend as far as Christ’s leadership. But Scripture, after announcing his coming and passion, shows what would also happen afterward to the people who refused to receive him. By the coming leader it means Titus, who in the fortieth year after the Lord’s passion would so destroy the city and sanctuary with the Roman people that one stone would not remain upon another (Luke 19).

But after setting out these matters by anticipation, it immediately returned to explain the outcome of the week it had omitted. “One week shall confirm the covenant with many.” This is the last week itself, in which John the Baptist, or the Lord and the apostles, by preaching converted many to faith. “And in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall fail.” The middle of this seventieth week was the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when, after Christ’s baptism had begun, the purification effected by sacrificial victims began gradually to seem worthless to believers. Likewise, what follows—“And in the temple shall be an abomination of desolation, and desolation shall endure until consummation and the end”—looks to subsequent times.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Daniel’s prayer: how an answer was given him in accordance with it, although he seems to have prayed for the ending of the Babylonian captivity then existing, whereas, seemingly to the contrary, a greater devastation of the Jews is announced to him.

The outcome attests the truth of this prophecy, both in the history of ancient times and in that of our own day. But if you attend to the letter alone, did Daniel’s prayer request answers of this kind? For he had said: “I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet, that seventy years of the desolation of Jerusalem should be completed.” And then, praying, he said: “Turn away, I beseech you, your anger and fury from your city Jerusalem and from your holy mountain. For because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and your people are a reproach [Col. 1519A] to all around us. Now therefore hear, O Lord our God, the prayer of your servant and his supplications, and show your face upon your sanctuary, which lies desolate. For your own sake, incline your ear, O my God, and hear; open your eyes and see our desolation and the city upon which your name has been invoked.”

Thus, if you attend to the letter alone, you find nothing besides that Babylonian captivity of seventy years, nothing besides the ashes of the city and temple made with hands, which he laments or desires to recover. But if this was so—if this alone was his desire—did he receive consolation suited to his request? Did he not rather hear things contrary to his wishes? For he was not told: Jerusalem shall be rebuilt, the temple shall be renewed, and the whole ceremonial worship restored. Instead, what is said is wholly contrary: “Christ,” he says, “shall be slain; and his people, who are to deny him, shall not be his; and the people with the coming leader shall destroy city and sanctuary; its end shall be desolation; after the end of war desolation is decreed; sacrifice and offering shall fail; an abomination of desolation shall be in the temple; and desolation shall endure until consummation and the end.”

Therefore, when he says, “I, Daniel, understood from the books the number of years concerning which the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet, that seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation should be completed,” he intimates to the attentive reader that he understood through the prophetic Spirit what the Church of Christ now sees with unveiled face: namely, that the captivity of the one Jewish people [Col. 1519C] was an image of that other great captivity which befell the whole human race when the one Adam sinned, and that the seventy years of captivity signified the whole time during which the people of God are pilgrims in this age. For what great thing was it to understand what Jeremiah’s prophetic words plainly declared to everyone?

Therefore, when he prays, “Hear, O Lord our God, the prayer of your servant and his supplications, and show your face upon your sanctuary, which lies desolate,” etc., when, I say, he says these things, he intends greater matters beneath these words. He thus desires that captivity to be ended while being concerned for the greater captivity; he will bear lightly the greater destruction of temple or city, the cessation also of sacrifice and offering, and the perpetual desolation [Col. 1519D] of the temple—an abominable thing—provided that what was necessary should be done: namely, that “transgression may be brought to completion, sin may come to an end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed.”

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the seventy years of captivity: when, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, they were completed, and how Josephus wrote contradictory things about them.

Moreover, since that captivity of the Jewish people signifies the captivity of sin which, as has been said, befell the whole human race, its release consequently signifies the salvation of the world. To speak in the language of this Scripture, it was a type of the bringing of transgression to completion, the ending of sin, the blotting out of iniquity, the bringing in of everlasting righteousness, the fulfillment of vision and prophecy, and the anointing of the Holy of Holies—who is himself the true temple, the temple not made with hands, the king and founder of the city in which he deigned to be born as man.

Therefore, intending to say a few things concerning the release from captivity and the rebuilding of the temple, in keeping with the course of our undertaking, let us first speak according to the letter concerning the seventy years themselves. “When,” Jeremiah says, “seventy years have begun to be fulfilled in Babylon, I will visit you and fulfill my good word upon you, and bring you back to this place, says the Lord” (Jer. 29). “But in the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, to fulfill the word of the Lord which he had spoken [Col. 1520B] by the mouth of Jeremiah, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians, and he sent forth a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, even in writing, saying: Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judaea” (1 Esdras 1), etc.

But, the Samaritans hindering it, the work was interrupted until the second year of Darius. In that year the seventieth year of the captivity of Jerusalem was completed (Jer. 25, 29), according to Eusebius, who adduces the prophet Zechariah as a witness. In the second year of Darius, the Angel speaks in Zechariah: “O Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry?” (Zech. 1). This is the seventieth year. Likewise, in the fourth year of Darius, the same prophet says: “When you fasted and mourned through these seventy years, did you fast a fast for me?” (Zech. 7).

In the sixth year of Darius the building of the temple was completed, on the third day of the month Adar; this was the forty-sixth year from the laying of its foundations under Cyrus. Hence the Jews say in the Gospel: “This temple was built in forty-six years” (John 2). They began to build in the second year of Darius, in the sixth month, on the twenty-fourth day; and in the sixth year (Hag. 2), as stated, they completed it in the twelfth month, on the third day. It is clear from this that the work on the temple had already been carried out to no small extent before then.

Josephus agrees here in the *Antiquities*, writing that the temple, Jerusalem, and all Judaea remained desolate for seventy years. Yet, in reckoning the kings of Babylon, if indeed he wrote it thus and the faulty manuscript does not deceive us, he gathers a different total from the destruction of Jerusalem to the overthrow of the Chaldean kingdom. For he writes that after Nebuchadnezzar, who according to Holy Scripture lived twenty-five years after Jerusalem’s destruction, his son Evilmerodach reigned eighteen years; after him his son Egesar reigned forty years; then Jasordach succeeded him for nine months; and, after his death, the empire passed to Belshazzar, who was called Naboon. In Belshazzar’s seventeenth year Babylon was captured by Kings Cyrus and Darius. This Darius took the prophet Daniel with him into Media and honored him greatly.

According to Josephus, if indeed he wrote this and it is not a faulty manuscript that deceives us, the total is one hundred years and nine additional months. The Hebrews, as blessed Jerome says, relate the following tale. After the seventieth year, in which Jeremiah had said that the captivity of the Jewish people would be ended—and of which Zechariah also speaks at the beginning of his book—Belshazzar, thinking God’s promise void and false, turned to rejoicing, held a great banquet, and in some manner mocked the hope of the Jews and the vessels of God’s temple. But vengeance followed immediately. Let us now return to what we had begun.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning King Cyrus: how, according to the prophecy of Isaiah, he was likened to Christ, especially because he freed God’s people and sent them back to their homeland.

According to mystical interpretations, King Cyrus signifies the Lord Savior both in his name and in his deeds. We say this not from our own conjecture, but from the clear words of Isaiah, in which the Lord says: “I have likened you, and you did not know me” (Isa. 45). For God likened him to his Son, although Cyrus himself by no means knew God as the one who likened him.

But you ask: In what did he liken him? First, in that he deigned to call Cyrus his Christ, saying: “Thus says the Lord to Cyrus my Christ, whose right hand I have taken hold of, that I may subject nations before his face,” etc. (ibid.). Secondly, he ordained long before Cyrus was born that he should be called Cyrus, a name interpreted as “heir.” For this title fittingly belongs to him to whom God the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). The Apostle also says of him: “Whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages” (Heb. 1). And when he appeared in the flesh, his persecuting enemies said: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21; Mark 12).

The Lord God therefore likened Cyrus to his only-begotten Son, God and our Lord Jesus Christ. For just as Cyrus, after overthrowing the Chaldean kingdom, freed God’s people and sent them back to their homeland, commanded that the temple burned in Jerusalem should be rebuilt, and took care to publish this decree in writing so that the words of the prophet Jeremiah—who had foretold that this would happen—might be fulfilled; so the mediator between God and human beings (1 Tim. 2), after overthrowing throughout the world the kingdom of the devil, gathers into his own heavenly city the true Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace—his elect who had been scattered and recalled from the devil’s tyranny. He also makes this known in writing, by sending the holy Scriptures throughout the whole world, through which he proclaims faith in his name and hope of salvation to all who belong to his kingdom, that is, to all the elect.

Likewise, what Cyrus said in his decree, “The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth” (1 Esdras 1), truly belongs to the majesty of him alone who said: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). Yet it seems less true when Cyrus says that all earthly kingdoms had been handed over to him by God—unless perhaps it should be understood that, at the time when he wrote this, he had no kingdom hostile to his own; or at least that, having conquered, destroyed, and exhausted so mighty and ancient an empire as that of the Chaldeans, he believed that no power throughout the whole world could resist his kingdom.

It should especially be believed, from Isaiah’s prophecy, that this King Cyrus loved the children of Israel, released them from captivity, sent them home, and commanded the rebuilding of the temple of the Lord their God. For he had heard that both Isaiah and Jeremiah, their prophets, had through the Spirit of God foretold his kingdom and the destruction of the Babylonians (Isa. 45; Jer. 44). Indeed those prophets had also described in spiritual terms the very method of conquest by which he took Babylon. Isaiah says: “I say to the deep: Be desolate, and I will dry up your rivers” (Isa. 44). Jeremiah says: “The very broad wall of Babylon shall be undermined by digging, and her lofty gates shall be burned with fire” (Jer. 51).

For histories relate that the enemy entered the city through the dried and desolated bed of the Euphrates, which flowed through the middle of Babylon, after its waters had been divided and drained through many channels. We do not deny that everything contained in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah concerning the building of this city or temple is full of spiritual mysteries; but the length of the course we have undertaken calls us away, lest we linger too long upon individual passages. We shall therefore touch upon a few points according to the proclamations of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who at that time prophesied with great spirit.

For these prophets had great spirit, since, against the decree of so great a king and against the Samaritans and all the surrounding nations who hindered the building of the Lord’s temple, they commanded that the temple be built, as it is written. “Therefore the copy of the decree of King Artaxerxes was read before Rehum, Beelt[e]em, Samsai the scribe, and their counselors; and they went hurriedly to Jerusalem to the Jews and stopped them by force and power” (1 Esdras 4). “Then the work of the house of God in Jerusalem was interrupted, and it was not carried on until the second year of Darius king of the Persians. But Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Addo prophesied to the Jews who were in Judaea and Jerusalem, in the name of the God of Israel. Then Zerubbabel son of Salathiel and Joshua son of Josedec arose and began to build the temple of God in Jerusalem, and the prophets of God were with them, helping them” (1 Esdras 4–5).

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the prophecy of Haggai the prophet, who at the time when the temple was being rebuilt prophesied the glory of the Lord’s spiritual house and foretold that the Desired One of all nations would come.

The first of them, Haggai, says:

> “And now, be strong, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and be strong, Jesus son of Josedec, great priest; and be strong, all you people of the land, says the Lord of hosts, and act. For I am with you, says the Lord of hosts, according to the word which I covenanted with you when you came out [Col. 1523A] from the land of Egypt; and my Spirit shall be in your midst. Do not fear. For thus says the Lord of hosts: Yet one little while, and I will shake heaven and earth, the sea and dry land; I will shake all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come; and I will fill this house with glory, says the Lord of hosts. Mine is the silver, and mine is the gold, says the Lord of hosts. The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says the Lord of hosts; and in this place I will give peace, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. 2).

Even this alone which he says, “the Desired One of all nations shall come,” can strike the hearer so that he opens sleeping eyes and is lifted from earth to heaven, and does not suppose that the words, “I will fill this house with glory, and the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former,” were spoken of that inanimate house of stone.

First, therefore, behold the mystery of the Trinity. “I,” he says, “am with you, and my Spirit, and the word in which I established the covenant with you when you came out of Egypt.” And when he says, “in your midst,” this should be understood in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: “There stands in your midst one whom you do not know, who comes after me” (John 1).

Thus says the Lord of hosts to you who see the former house as though it were nothing. I shook heaven when my voice was heard from heaven: “You yourselves saw that I spoke with you from heaven” (Exod. 20). I shook the earth when I delivered my covenant to the former people, and darkness, tempest, and gloom were seen at my hearing. [Col. 1523C] I shook the Red Sea when I provided a way for the people as they passed through. I shook the dry land—either Egypt, stripping it of its devotion to God through plagues, or the wilderness through which the people wandered forty years. These things I shall shake once more.

For at the time of the Lord’s passion, when the sun fled away, heaven was shaken and darkness fell over all the earth until the ninth hour (Mark 15). Truly, after that Desired One of all nations came, all nations were shaken and the glory of the Lord’s house was fulfilled. And as the Lord surpasses the servant, so much better is this house over which the Lord presides than the former house over which a servant presided. For the Church becomes more illustrious than the Synagogue once was.

Nevertheless, I should like to adhere more closely to the interpretation we began to maintain above. We said that the description of the former house—that is, the Babylonian captivity, Jerusalem’s destroyed city, and the temple set on fire—was a type of the universal captivity in which the entire human race was made captive in Adam by the king of Babylon, the ruler of this world, the devil, king of confusion. Let us therefore speak—or rather, let us listen to the Lord speaking—on this: “The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.” In order that this may happen, “the Desired One of all nations shall come.”

Plainly, behold: we see, believe, and confess that human nature has been restored through the coming of this Desired One to a dignity higher than its original state. If the Lord’s house—which, we ask, are we ourselves—had not been consumed by the fire of diabolical confusion in Adam, the Son of God would not have assumed our nature, to be crowned with glory and honor because of his suffering of death. If God had not assumed our—that is, human—nature, then our nature would not have ascended above angelic dignity. But now our flesh has so surpassed every creature that, confessing the glory of the holy Trinity and marveling at humanity in its exaltation, we reverently regard human nature. For we confess and worship in the one person of the Son both the substance of God and that of man.

Therefore, “the latter glory of this house is greater than the former.” For the blessedness of our congregation is now far greater, gathered as we are under so great a leader and so glorious a prince, than it would have been had the flame of diabolical envy never consumed us in our first parent. In this sense, what was the point of saying, “Mine is the silver, and mine is the gold”? To answer this, we first ask what silver, and what or what kind of gold, belongs to God. Here we hear the Psalmist proclaiming: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11). Likewise: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Ps. 18).

Thus, wishing to declare the riches by which he would make his house glorious, he says, “Mine is the gold, and mine is the silver,” signifying his gifts which he was going to give to human beings. Scripture speaks of this same Desired One: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. [Col. 1524C] 67; Eph. 4).

This Desired One has indeed already come; but at his first coming heaven, earth, sea, and dry land were not shaken to such an extent, nor has the great glory of his house yet appeared or been fulfilled. “Now,” John says, “we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 5). Nor was he yet desired by all nations, since they did not know him.

Therefore, the words stated beforehand—“For I am with you, the word which I covenanted with you when you came out of the land of Egypt, and my Spirit shall be in your midst”—in which, as we have said, the mystery of the Trinity is briefly expressed, belong to the first coming of this Desired One. Through it we spiritually came out of the land of Egypt, baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Once this is observed, what follows requires no further inquiry: “Yet one little while, and I will shake heaven and earth and sea and dry land”—namely, with that shaking expressed in the Gospel in these words:

> “There shall be signs in the sun, moon, and stars; and upon the earth distress of nations through confusion at the sound of the sea and the waves, while people wither away from fear and expectation of what is coming upon the whole world. For the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Luke 21).

Thus he who first came hidden will come manifestly at his second coming (Ps. 49), with heaven, earth, sea, [Col. 1525A] and dry land shaken, and all nations shaken; as is immediately said in the same place: “And then they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with great power and majesty” (Luke 21). Then, I say, the Desired One will come to all nations—that is, to his faithful elect gathered from all nations. Then the glory of this house promised here will appear, and concerning it the passage immediately continues: “But when these things begin to happen, look up and lift up your heads, because your redemption draws near” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the prophecy of Zechariah at the same time: how he says, “The Lord showed me Jesus the priest,” etc., and how God the Father rebuked Satan on behalf of Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1525B] After him—namely, Haggai, somewhat his junior, beginning to prophesy two months later—Zechariah son of Barachiah, “mindful of the Lord” according to his own name and “blessed of the Lord” according to his father’s name, likewise joins with Haggai (whose name means “great feast”) in urging, in hope and faith in the Lord, that the city of Jerusalem be rebuilt, whether king or nations oppose it. In this manner he is mindful of Jesus the great priest:

“And the Lord showed me Jesus the great priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to Satan: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; may the Lord rebuke you, he who chose Jerusalem’” (Zech. 3), etc.

We do not greatly value the way the Hebrews expound that passage, since the entire understanding of the Jews is fleshly, clinging carnally to the letter alone. We understand that Jesus is here designated by his own name, that is, our Savior. For he is the one whom, before he came, many righteous persons and prophets—of whom this Zechariah is one—desired to see, and did not see (Luke 10). Yet it was much that they saw him, indeed foresaw him, under some image.

Therefore this prophet joyfully says: “And he showed me Jesus the great priest,” namely in a prophetic vision, as God was accustomed, for great consolation, to show him to holy prophets mourning their own sins or those of the people. It would not have sufficed to say “priest” unless he had added “great,” since he is not one among many priests, who are prevented by death from remaining; rather, above all of them he possesses an eternal priesthood, because he remains for ever, he to whom it was said: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109).

He also said “standing,” that is, established in an unshaken rank—indeed, standing before the countenance of God on our behalf, and ready to obey him even unto death—“before the angel of the Lord,” that is, in accordance with the good pleasure of the Word, the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily within him. This is the Angel of Great Counsel; not that he is one thing in one respect and another in another, or that we admit two persons in the Son, but because the same one Christ Jesus both, as God, commands the humanity he has assumed, and, as man, obeys the divinity of the Word united to himself.

“And Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him”—it is understood: but he did not prevail. “For the ruler of this world comes,” he says, “and has nothing in me” (John 14). He came and stood and opposed him as far as causing him to be put to death; but all this was at his right hand, that is, for the increase of his glory. For this reason God both rebuked Satan and exalted him, giving him the name that is above every name (Phil. 2).

I say that the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—rebuked him. Therefore it is beautifully said: “And the Lord said to Satan.” The Lord spoke concerning the Lord, and surely spoke for the Lord, the great priest. But what did the Lord Father, the Lord Holy Spirit, do in rebuking Satan for the Lord Son? He cast him out, according to the saying: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12).

For in rebuking him, the Lord who chose Jerusalem cast him out through Christ’s passion, as an enemy—indeed, as a thief—from his kingdom, as an adulterer from his bridal chamber. For Jerusalem is that intellectual city and bride of God which Satan had plundered like a thief and, in the first man, defiled through the serpent like an adulterer.

“Is not this,” he says, “a brand plucked from the fire?” (Zech. 3). It is as though Satan said: “By what right does the Lord rebuke me? By what right does he cast me out?” Most impure Satan, is not this man, whom you dared to approach and oppose, one who died though he had committed no sin, descended to hell, and shook himself free just as a brand is plucked from the fire, “when the pains of hell had been loosed, since it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2)?

## CHAPTER XXI. How Jesus was clothed in filthy garments—not with his own filth, but with that of others—and how the filthy garments were taken from him, and a clean turban placed upon his head.

“And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the face of the angel. He answered and said to those standing before him: ‘Take the filthy garments from him.’ And he said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and have clothed you with change of garments.’ And he said: ‘Put a clean turban upon his head.’ And they put a clean turban upon his head and clothed him with change of garments” (Zech. 3).

How was this Jesus clothed in filthy garments? Certainly in the manner spoken of also by another prophet:

“He came up like a shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has neither form nor beauty. And we saw him, and there was no appearance in him; we considered him despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity. Truly he bore our sicknesses and carried our pains. And we considered him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled” (Isa. 53), etc.

Thus, that is, “clothed in filthy garments, Jesus stood before the face of the angel,” namely in the agony of his passion. Here there is nothing to prevent us—indeed, it is more pleasing, in accordance with the truth of the Gospel—from understanding “angel” in its customary sense. For when, being in agony, he prayed at greater length, and his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground—wherein, beyond doubt, he appeared clothed in the filthy garments of weakness—an angel from heaven appeared to strengthen him (Luke 22).

Nor is this surprising. For the Psalmist says: “You made him a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8), namely in that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2). But, he says, “Take the filthy garments from him.” The angel said this in the person of God, adding also: “Put a clean turban upon his head.”

Let us say, then, that this has already been done: through the passion of death Jesus the great priest laid aside the filthy garments—that is, he put off the condition of mortality together with the sins and iniquities of all of us, which he had taken upon himself. But in rising from the dead he was clothed with change of garments, and a clean turban was placed upon his head. Hence we sing with the Psalmist: “You have crowned him with glory and honor” (Ps. 8); and with the Apostle: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the saying: “Behold, I will bring my servant, the East,” etc.

Moreover, even daily the filthy garments of this great Priest are removed and he is clothed in change of garments whenever the sins of his body, which is the Church, are washed away and works of righteousness are put on. Yet, according to this reasoning—that he is the head and the Church the body, that he, I say, is the head and we are the members—we should understand what has been said hitherto concerning this great Priest as referring to the head, and what follows as referring to the body.

“Hear, Jesus the great priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, for they are men of portent. For behold, I will bring my servant, the East; for behold, the stone which I have set before Jesus: upon one stone are seven eyes” (Zech. 3). And after some intervening words: “He shall bring forth the chief stone, and shall make grace equal to his grace” (Zech. 4).

“Hear,” he says, “Jesus the great priest”—indeed, hear, Church, body of Jesus the great Priest, royal and priestly race; and let the friends who dwell before you hear, that is, the apostles and prophets, truly friends, ready to lay down their lives for you and therefore dwelling before you: that they may fight by dying and die while fighting for you. Hence they are “men of portent,” that is, authors of great examples or great heralds of things to come.

“Behold, I will bring my servant, the East”: that is, Christ my Son, my servant according to the form of a servant assumed, “the East” according to the light of eternal divinity. “For behold, the stone which I have set before Jesus: upon one stone are seven eyes.” I called him “the East” for this reason: because with seven eyes he illumines the whole world. For he is servant because of the human nature assumed; he is East because of the sevenfold fullness of divinity dwelling bodily within him; he is stone because of the present mystery, that is, because of the building of the heavenly city or temple, of which that city was beginning to be built as a type when the prophet saw this vision.

Since these things are so, it is clear why he then says: “And he shall bring forth the chief stone.” For all of us who are built upon the foundation are called living stones; but he is called not merely a living stone, but also the chief stone, for this reason: that he is transparent with seven eyes, and that he who became man in order to be set beneath us as a foundation was the same God in the beginning.

Then follows: “He shall make grace equal to its grace.” Shall we therefore be equal to him? Certainly not, because we are adopted, whereas he is the natural Son of God. Nor is it said, “He shall make grace equal to his nature,” but “He shall make grace equal to his grace,” so that Israelites who believe and the people of the nations may receive equal grace and an equal gift. For these are the walls which this cornerstone, this chief stone, joins together in himself.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the lampstand, concerning which he likewise says, “Behold, a lampstand wholly of gold,” etc.; on its lamps upon it, and how it is Christ; and on the two olive trees, one at its right and one at its left.

“And he said to me: ‘What do you see?’ And I said: ‘I saw, and behold, a lampstand wholly of gold, and its lamp upon its top, and its seven lamps upon it, and seven pouring-vessels for the lamps which were upon its top, and two olive trees above it, one at the right of the lamp and one at its left’” (Zech. 4).

He who shortly before was signified by the stone of seven eyes is now signified by the golden lampstand, wholly furnished with seven lamps: namely Christ, who, shining with the seven spirits, illumines the entire house of his Church. We spoke more fully of this lampstand in Exodus, where the Lord commands it to be made through Moses with the same number of lamps (Exod. 15).

Therefore, hastening now to other matters, we desire only to recognize the two olive trees above it, “one at the right of the lamp and one at its left.” Some interpret these as Moses and Elijah, who spoke with the Lord on the mountain—that is, the Law and the Prophets, harmoniously proclaiming his passion. Others interpret them as the Law and the Gospel, so that the Gospel is on the right and the Law on the left.

Accordingly, not moving far from this interpretation, but desiring to distinguish the two olive trees more clearly, we ask by what two things standing on either side so great and brilliant a lampstand, or lamp of the lampstand, is fittingly adorned. The Apostle, writing to the Colossians of this lampstand—that is, Christ—speaks thus:

“He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; for in him all things were created in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers: all things were created through him and in him. And he is before all things, and all things subsist in him” (Col. 1).

Whoever faithfully understands these things concerning him surely beholds the fruitful olive tree standing at the right of the lampstand or lamp, because God the Father truly created all these things because of his goodness, through his good Word. The Apostle immediately continues:

“And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, that he might hold the first place in all things. For it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell in him, and through him to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth” (ibid.).

Whoever likewise receives these things concerning him with grateful faith surely sees the beautiful olive tree on the left—on the left, I say, because these things were accomplished amid the adversity of tribulation, through the benevolence of love by which, obeying the Father, he condescended to our misery.

How could a great mountain—that is, the prince of darkness—stand before a lampstand of such greatness and brightness? Therefore it is rebuked by a sudden command, that it should remove and cast itself into the sea: “Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel? Become a plain” (Zech. 4). Zerubbabel too signifies Christ, the great leader, born according to the flesh in this Babylon; for he too received this name because he had been born in Babylon.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the saying: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion: behold, your king shall come to you, righteous.”

“Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, Jerusalem: behold, your king shall come to you, righteous and Savior, himself poor and riding upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass. And I will destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem; the bow of war shall be broken, and he shall speak peace to the nations. His power shall be from sea to sea and from the rivers to the ends of the earth. You also, in the blood of your covenant, have brought forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9).

What was shown to Daniel—after gold and silver, bronze also and iron, and likewise after four great beasts ascending from the sea, which are the four kingdoms of the world (Dan. 7)—namely the kingdom of God after those same kingdoms of this proud world, the kingdom of Christ’s humility, this prophet also proclaims.

For above he had said: “And I turned and lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots coming forth from between two mountains, and the mountains were mountains of bronze. In the first chariot were red horses; in the second chariot black horses; in the third chariot white horses; and in the fourth chariot strong dappled horses” (Zech. 6).

These, indeed, were the four kingdoms of the world coming forth as though from between two mountains, which were bronze—that is, invincible and exceedingly strong, and such as no passage of age, it was thought, could consume. “In the first chariot were red horses”: they were bloody and bloodthirsty, dreadful in the Babylonian captivity and cruelty. “In the second chariot black horses”: the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, which, riding and issuing forth in a two-horse chariot through King Ahasuerus’s decree, announced with grievous tidings the death of all the Jews. “In the third chariot white horses”: the Macedonians, under whose king Antiochus we read of the victory of the Maccabees. “In the fourth chariot strong dappled horses”: for we know that some Roman rulers were merciful toward the Jewish nation, such as Gaius Caesar Augustus and Claudius, while others were persecutors and terrible, such as Gaius Caligula, Nero, Vespasian, and Hadrian.

But now, proclaiming the kingdom of God, after saying, “Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and Savior,” he immediately adds: “Himself poor and riding upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass.” It is as though he said: “These are in chariots, and those on horses, but this one comes to us blessed in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 19).

For when, according to the literal sense of this prophecy, he came into the city of Jerusalem seated upon a colt of an ass in order to receive the kingdom—that is, through his passion to draw all things to himself—the crowds cried aloud to him: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. 21); blessed is the kingdom that comes, of David our father.

He then makes clear, by adding, wherein the effect or office of this kingdom consists: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9). This is understood as follows: By the blood of your passion, you in your mercy liberated those who were held bound in the prison of hell, in which there is no mercy at all.

Immediately, joyfully addressing them, he says: “Return to the stronghold, prisoners of hope” (ibid.). The sense is: You who are now bound, who hope for release from your bonds in Christ’s coming, return to the stronghold—which we must understand as none other than the dwelling-place of paradise, into which the thief first entered with the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXV. What the house of David is, and what Jerusalem, of which he says: “And I will pour out upon the house of David,” etc.

“And I will pour out upon the house of David and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem the spirit of grace and prayers; and they shall look upon me whom they pierced. And they shall mourn for him as for an only-begotten son, and grieve over him as one grieves at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. 12). And afterward: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13).

This spirit of grace and this fountain of the house of David are the Spirit and the water of which our Savior, in the Gospel, speaks—the Savior of all the holy Scriptures: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

Moreover, Jerusalem, upon which this Spirit is poured, is itself the menstruous woman, for whose washing that fountain of the house of David was opened; that is, the side of the Son of God, the son of David, was opened by the lance, whence the water of saving washing flowed together with the sacred blood of our redemption (John 19).

And lest anyone suppose that only the Church from among the nations should be understood as the menstruous woman because of the filth of idolatry with which it was polluted, Isaiah, the holy prophet, one of the elect of the former people, says: “We have all become as one unclean, and all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. 64).

Therefore the whole Church, from the first elect person to the last, is Jerusalem—at the time when the prophets spoke these things, still menstruous, that is, polluted by the blood of original sin. It could become the city or kingdom of the God who is Holy of Holies only if the Lord poured upon it the spirit of grace and prayers, that is, the Spirit of remission of sins; only if the fountain of the house of David were opened for its washing, that is, only if, from the side of the crucified Savior, blood were poured out together with water and the saving sacrament of baptism instituted.

Certainly, one first approaches the visible sacrament of the font and only afterward receives the Spirit for the remission of sins. But because the Spirit is the governor of that same washing, and the whole benefit of the visible font depends on him, it is rightly said first, “I will pour out the spirit of grace and prayers,” and afterward, “There shall be an open fountain of the house of David.” Thus the true David did not say anything new, but spoke in agreement with the truthful testimonies of this and the other Scriptures: “Unless one is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3).

But because that earthly Jerusalem was not going to receive this Spirit or fountain, therefore “on that day,” he says, “there shall be great mourning in Jerusalem” (Zech. 12), etc. That mourning, begun with the Roman siege, continues unto the end, as Moses says in the song: “A fire has been kindled in my anger, and it shall burn to the lowest hell” (Deut. 32).

And we should note—indeed, it is remarkable—that he said: “They shall mourn for him as for an only-begotten son, and grieve over him as one grieves at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. 12). What then? O Jews, Christ the Son of God did not please you because he was such, because he came in such a manner, because he acted thus and thus, because he spoke thus and thus. He did not please you at all; he did not suit your mind. You want another; you await another. But he, namely God the Father who sent this Son, has no other. This Son is to him both firstborn and only-begotten. He has no other, I say: he is his first and his last; he will send no other.

What then will you do, left desolate? Certainly, as he himself says: “Then you shall look upon him whom you pierced.” As he says, now does his Spirit speak with grave truth and true gravity: “You shall mourn for him as for an only-begotten son, and grieve as one grieves at the death of a firstborn.” For this firstborn is dead to you, because you yourselves killed the only-begotten for yourselves; henceforth you will have neither this Savior nor another, because he alone is, he is the firstborn, he is the only-begotten.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the prophecy in which it is said: “Behold, I send my angel,” etc.; how here also, through a parable taken from the temple, he prophesies of the new temple and Christ’s new priesthood.

After Zechariah, Malachi, the last in the order of the twelve prophets—whom the Hebrews themselves maintain was Ezra the priest—says:

“Behold, I will send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face; and immediately the Ruler whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire. Behold, he comes, says the Lord. And who shall stand to see him? For he is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers’ herb. He shall sit, refining and cleansing silver; and he shall purify the sons of Levi. He shall strain them as gold and as silver, and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness” (Mal. 3), etc.

Here too, taking his parable from the temple then being rebuilt, he prophesies of the new temple and the new priesthood of Christ. For shortly before he speaks thus of the rejected worship of that temple: “Behold, I will cast your arm away, and scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemn feasts” (Mal. 2). Likewise: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not receive an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts; and you have polluted it” (Mal. 1).

Therefore, “behold, he comes,” or “immediately he shall come to his temple”: we understand this to mean that he shall come to his Church, to the holy sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the womb of the incorrupt Virgin, in order from it to build for himself the true temple, as another Scripture says: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9).

And in the Gospel he himself is the Ruler, the Lord, and here he is likewise the angel of the covenant: “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and after three days I will raise it up”—speaking of the temple of his body (John 2). This has occurred, and he has already come.

But, O Jews, you who say, “He will come at the end of time; he has not yet come”: how does the outcome of events not teach you the truth? For what temple will the Ruler find as his own? It has been destroyed down to its foundations. Or if it must be built by another before Christ comes, what further will their Christ do, when everything has been restored by another?

Thus the Ruler, the Lord whom you seek, and the Angel of the Covenant whom you desire, has already come—but not such as you seek, not such as you desire. For you seek a ruler of cities, a wielder of the scepter of earthly empire, a giver of gold and silver, one who will satisfy your greed and your luxuries for a thousand ages of years. But he is not such, nor ought he to have come for that purpose. Rather, he came in order, like a refiner’s fire and fullers’ herb, to sit refining and cleansing silver and purifying the sons of Levi; and this he has already done and does not cease to do until the end of the age.

For he sits at the right hand of God, henceforth the fiery and immortal Lord of judgment. Without delay, after he ascended there, he sent his fire—he sent the Holy Spirit as fire—and cleansed and purified the sons of Levi, that is, his apostles, the lawful successors of his priesthood. He strained them as gold, namely melted by his love, with which they were ineffably set ablaze, so that each of them could truly say: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5).

From that time “the sacrifice of Judah and Jerusalem,” that is, of confession and peace, is pleasing and shall be pleasing to God: the body and blood of Christ his Son. Concerning this sacrifice the Psalmist, rejecting the flesh of bulls and the blood of goats, says: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 49).

This sacrifice is so pleasing “as the days of the age and as the ancient years,” that is, as the holy angels, who are bright days of immortal eternity and everlasting years. For through this unique sacrifice we are made equal to the angels of God. He immediately adds concerning the second coming: “And I will come near to you in judgment, and I will be a swift witness against evildoers, adulterers, and perjurers” (Mal. 3).

## CHAPTER XXVII. How these words may also profitably be understood of the man-made temple, to which “they brought him, as it is written in the law of the Lord, because every male opening the womb,” etc.; and how the priesthood was formerly that of the firstborn, and how he is the firstborn.

Nevertheless, it is valid and greatly relevant that, when he says, “Immediately he shall come to his temple” (Mal. 3), we understand the temple as made by hands, and recall that in the Gospel according to Luke it is written:

“And when the days of Mary’s purification were completed according to the law of Moses, they brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: ‘Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord’” (Luke 2).

Nor should we overlook this: although, under the same commandment of the law, every firstborn was redeemed for five shekels of silver (Lev. 27), this firstborn of a virgin was not redeemed. They merely offered the sacrifice prescribed in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons. This was not the redemption of a firstborn but an offering for the woman who had given birth, that she might be cleansed from the flow of blood—not because she had borne a firstborn, but simply because she had borne, whether a male or a female (Lev. 12).

Why do we say these things? Because in ancient times the priesthood belonged to the firstborn, and these were the birthrights which Esau sold to his brother Jacob for a dish of lentils (Gen. 25). But because, through the leaders of the tribe of Levi, namely Moses and Aaron, some small measure of salvation was accomplished, so that the children of Israel were led out of the land of Egypt, out of that house of bondage, while the true sacrifice did not yet exist, the lawgiver—indeed, God, author and giver of the law—did not take great care that the firstborn should retain his right in that fleshly sacrifice, until this Son of God should come, possessing the true sacrifice, the firstborn and likewise the only-begotten of the Virgin.

Aware of this, the divine Evangelist, when he had said, “And she bore her son,” immediately added “her firstborn” (Luke 2), so that the prudent reader or hearer might understand that he was the one to whom the priesthood belonged; and that, after the vicarious priesthood of the Levitical tribe was removed, he, unredeemed, would stand before God the Father offering himself—henceforth a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. 109).

Therefore, he says, he will come to his temple: that is, he will receive his priesthood, offered to God and his Father, Holy of Holies, Priest of priests; “and he shall purify the sons of Levi,” that is, he will make new priests, not by lot but by faith, not according to Levi’s flesh but according to the grace of the Holy Spirit.

For lest anyone suppose that the person of Levi too was rejected when the priesthood was rejected, he had said shortly before:

“And you shall know that I have sent this commandment to you, that my covenant might be with Levi, says the Lord of hosts. My covenant with him was of life and peace, and I gave him fear, and he feared me; and he trembled before my name. The law of truth was in his mouth, and iniquity was not found on his lips. In peace and equity he walked with me, and turned many from iniquity. For the lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2).

Thus he indeed exercised the honor of the priesthood in his descendants for a time. But now this Ruler, the Lord and Angel of the Covenant, coming to his temple, in anger and severity drove out his descendants, the chief priests and Pharisees, with a scourge made—while preparing to refine and purify for himself other priests, like gold and silver, by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore he says: “But you have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the law; you have made void the covenant of Levi” (ibid.), etc. A faithful soul, formed by learned devotion, does not fail to know that what follows—“Will a man crucify God? For you have crucified me in tithes and firstfruits, and you, the whole nation, have crucified me” (Mal. 3)—refers to the fact that the chief priests and Pharisees crucified this Ruler, the Lord and Angel of the Covenant, because of their greed. Therefore he said, “In tithes and firstfruits you crucify me.”

He himself testifies to this in the Psalm, when he says: “For zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68). That is to say: “Because I was zealous for your house, driving out those who bought and sold, and saying: ‘It is written, My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves’” (Matt. 21), “I therefore suffered all these things, the sum of which is that they crucified me.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How, as we hasten toward the end, we could not dwell upon every prophet in order to examine the gifts of confession which each brought to the temple of God not made by hands.

Having followed thus far the holy choir of patriarchs and prophets, we have come to the temple in which Christ, the Holy of Holies and high priest, arrayed in the white robe of piety, “not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood,” stood before God the Father for the reconciliation of humankind (Heb. 9). We have observed what gold of his own confession and beauty each of them offered, according to his zeal, ardent desire, and devotion, hastening to have a share in his sacrifice, according to Psalm 95, which bears the title: “When the house was being built after the captivity: a song of David.”

For there it is written: “Confession and beauty are before him; holiness and magnificence are in his sanctuary.” And we know that the house being built after the captivity is the house of our hope, the house of Wisdom, which she built for herself: the house of flesh or body which the Word of God assumed for himself from the Virgin, in which the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily, after the captivity in which we were made captives in Adam. The temple made by hands was built after the Babylonian captivity as a type of this house.

Thus far we have followed the venerable heaven of the saints of old and contemplated what confession and beauty, what holiness and magnificence, each offered. And even if we have not examined everything, we should nevertheless rejoice that, as in the dim light of night, in which sight is not yet clear, we have been admitted to their blessed vision.

But this greatly grieves our smallness: as we hasten on, we have not been allowed to know each individual countenance of all of them or to weigh the gifts of confession offered by each. For we have passed over nine of them: namely Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah; and holy Job, who was not indeed born from the same line of Abraham’s seed, but who in every respect strives with these men to testify to the glory of Christ, king and priest.

Let us therefore hope that all of them are well disposed toward us, since we judged neither their faith nor their dignity to be negligible; but, avoiding weariness from excessive abundance—or rather confessing our own sluggishness—weary, we have turned aside to rest, as it were at the horn of the altar, thus bringing this fifth age to its end and restoring our impoverished spirit by a little refreshment for the course of the sixth.

# Forty-Two Books of Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, On the Trinity and Its Works, in a Volume of Commentaries on the Four Evangelists

## Book One

### 597. CHAPTER I. On the sixth age of the world, in which, after all the heralds had been sent beforehand, he himself came who had been speaking: king and priest.

In the sixth age of the world Christ, the Son of God, is born from the Virgin; and, all heralds having long since been sent beforehand, at last he himself who had been speaking is present. From that time onward, behold, the kingdom of God is within us (Luke 17); for the king goes before us—the king, I say, and priest, who goes before us and enters on our behalf. He also speaks in the Psalm: “But I have been established king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment” (Ps. 2).

Therefore from that time we have been made a kingdom and priests to the Lord our God. Since this one is bone of our bones and flesh of our flesh, he consoles our ancient ignobility by so great an honor of nobility. For we were all servants, since all of us were born from a servant—that is, from Adam, who committed sin and therefore was the servant of sin (John 8). But this one is noble: nobly created from his Virgin mother, more nobly born from God the Father. Thus a person worthy to rule the human race was given when, as has already been said, Christ the Son of God was born from the Virgin.

## CHAPTER II. How this sixth age corresponds to the sixth day of the world’s first creation.

The sixth age of the world therefore corresponds to the sixth day of creation [Col. 1536B] according to the spirit of understanding, which is in turn sixth from the spirit of the fear of the Lord. For there you have: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), “and let him have dominion over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, every creature, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth.” Here, however, you have the man who was made, who is himself “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature; for in him all things in heaven and on earth were created, visible and invisible” (Col. 1).

That man was made such that, by the dignity of reason, he presides over the fishes of the sea and the other living creatures; this man was born such that he might surpass human beings by the majesty of divinity, or by the primacy of spiritual understanding. In both cases, as has been said, understanding—the sixth spirit from fear—works: there, because he surpasses the other animals through understanding [Col. 1536C] and gives them names; here, because he opens human minds to understand the Scriptures, those whose names he has written in heaven. That man is lofty and upright in stature above every kind of animal; this one is “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44 [45]). That man is the cultivator of paradise; this one is the Lord—indeed, also the planter—of paradise.

But matters of this sort must be discussed in the third part of this work, which our design has dedicated to the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the holy Trinity. Let us now pursue what concerns the present place: that is, let us proclaim the kingdom of this King according to the Gospel proclamations.

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 1537A] How great is the nobility of this King, according to the beginnings of the four Gospels of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.

The first evangelist, Matthew, says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1). After him Mark begins thus: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God” (Mark 1). Then, in Luke, the angel Gabriel answers Mary when she asks, “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?”: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore also the holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). Then John, returning to a yet higher beginning, says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” And: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

Once these things have been seen, faith—which knows how to test faces of free birth and distinguish them from the common-born—recognizes the splendid nobility of its King, and [p. 598] believes and confesses, with grateful praises, that this man alone is the noble man for the human race, the one who alone is worthy to reign, and whose servitude every human being’s true and only freedom consists in professing.

For what is the appearance of this King of ours according to what has been set down? Surely, when it says, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,” the hearing of faith proves that he is a true human being, since he was born from the seed of David and Abraham, human beings. Yet they were not especially noble: they were conceived in iniquities, and each was conceived by his mother in sins [Col. 1537C]. How then does the generation of this Jesus Christ, uniquely noble and illustrious, surpass what was ignoble in them? Surely because his mother conceived him not from a man’s seed but by the working of the Holy Spirit, as the same faith heard in Luke when the angel said: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.”

Therefore this son of David, son of Abraham, is far nobler than all his fathers, even according to the form of a servant. For he was never a servant; he was not even a servant in the mass, because he did not commit sin even in Adam, “in whom,” as the Apostle says, “all sinned” (Rom. 5). Mark and John proclaim more highly that which is nobler than this nobility of humanity. Mark, in saying, “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son [Col. 1537D] of God,” confesses that nobility which derives not from a mother but from the Father, not from flesh but from divinity.

Yet he defined it less fully against the slavish blasphemies of heretical baseness. For many are called and read of as sons of God—whether humans or angels—sons, that is, of God by the grace of adoption, not by the property of nature. John, perceiving this, settled the entire dispute by defining what kind of Son of God he is, and how unlike in nature are all those who are called and are sons of God. For, he says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Behold the face of free birth of our King: Son of Man without sin, Son of God by nature, not by gift.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1538A] On the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham: how it is above all spiritual; hence the line reaches Joseph, who did not beget him according to the flesh; and Jezebel’s descendants were rooted out to the fourth generation because she killed the prophets, heralds of the true God.

Let him now open for us the book of his generation, that we may see what kind of generation it is, on what principle it was written, and why it should be called a book of generation. In Genesis we read: “This is the book of the generation of Adam. In the day when God created man, he made him in the image of God; male and female he created them. And he blessed them and called their name Adam, in the day when they were created” (Gen. 5).

“This,” he says, “is the book of Adam’s generation”: an earthly book, a book of earthly generation, a book of a generation written in the earth, according to the saying: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17). For man had departed from God, and by departing had deserved to be written in the earth, God saying: “Until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for dust you are, and into dust you shall return” (Gen. 3).

But this man Jesus Christ, the noble King, the great King, the heavenly man, the new man, was therefore born and therefore given as King: that he might enroll his subjects in the book of life and make known the names of his citizens in the heavenly court. Thus this is the book of an elect generation, of the Christian generation enrolled in heaven; and the book of Adam’s generation is wholly unlike it. For in that book the generation of the sons of men and of the sons of God is confused, because “the sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful” [Col. 1538C] (Gen. 6), “took wives for themselves from among all whom they chose.” But this book admits the single generation of the sons of God, brothers and co-heirs of Jesus Christ.

Otherwise, what reason is there for the line of generation to reach Joseph, who did not beget Jesus Christ? Or why did it remove from the midst of this generation these three—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah? The divine evangelist, therefore, in a manner suited to evangelical dignity, gave less attention to Christ’s generation according to the flesh, which belonged to few and was not by itself sufficient for their salvation. Rather, he directed his attention to the generation of grace, which belongs, or can belong, to many and can by itself suffice for their salvation.

The one whose book of generation this is commended this by his own authority. When a certain woman, raising her voice from the crowd, said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11), he corrected this confession of imperfect understanding and said: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (ibid.). This is what the blessed womb that bore you, O Christ, did: it believed God’s word; it believed the angel announcing God’s omnipotence; and it gave the prompt reply of its faith: “Be it done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). Therefore she is blessed, and this is the principal cause of her blessedness.

This Abraham did: though he had a barren wife, he believed God saying, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 13); and, hoping in that faith and secure regarding the promised reward, he entered upon perpetual pilgrimage. Therefore he too is blessed by the testimony of evangelical praise written here at the head of the book: “Jesus Christ, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1) [Col. 1539A].

Jezebel did not do this. On the contrary, she killed the prophets of the Lord, heralds of this generation. Therefore she is not blessed; rather, her offspring were rooted out from this book of the generation of Jesus Christ to the fourth generation. For those descendants of hers already named—Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah—following her example, killed the prophets of the Lord or forbade them to prophesy.

## CHAPTER V. Why the younger David is placed before Abraham, saying “son of David, son of Abraham”; and how David merited to become father of the Word of God, who is Christ, before he became father of Christ according to the flesh.

[Col. 1539B] Why, then, is the younger David placed before his father Abraham in this book of generation, saying, “son of David, son of Abraham”? Surely the evangelist did this in accordance with his purpose. For if you observe carefully, while he proclaims Christ’s kingdom, he records the royal insignia of this King more fully than the other evangelists; nor will the capacity of our own study pass this over in silence.

David had been a king, and the royal promise was made to him: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131 [132]). Moreover, by deeds he prefigured, and by words he sang, the mysteries of the kingdom of Christ his Son. Of his mystical deeds or figurative sufferings we have spoken, as far as we could, in their proper place. The whole Church sings his utterances, and in singing them confesses Christ’s kingdom.

For example, in that king David this King Christ speaks: “But I have been established King by him upon Sion, his holy mountain, proclaiming his commandment” (Ps. 2). Again, in the same psalm, the person of the Father speaks concerning this Son of his, our King: “My heart has uttered a good word; I declare my works to the King” (Ps. 44 [45]). And to the King himself he says: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one, in your splendor and beauty. Press on, proceed prosperously, and reign.” And shortly afterward: “Peoples shall fall beneath you into the hearts of the King’s enemies; your throne, O God, is for ever and ever. The rod of rectitude is the rod of your kingdom” (ibid.), and so forth to the end of the psalm.

The prophet himself likewise says to the Father concerning him: “O God, give your judgment to the King, and your justice to the King’s Son” (Ps. 71 [72]). Why say more? Everything that David spoke to the Lord or sang is a mystery of this King, Christ, Son of God and his Son. Thus the woman who to this day raises her voice from the whole crowd of Jews, pagans, and heretics—namely, the Catholic Church—rightly blesses his soul and says: “Blessed is the soul of King David, which heard the word of God and kept it; which, admitted to the chaste union of God the Father, received the good Word from his heart or mouth, and merited to be father first of the Word, who is Christ, and only afterward father of Christ’s flesh.”

Therefore this evangelist rightly placed, in the book of generation, the King’s royal father before the father whom Scripture declares to be father only of the seed, that is, of the human being, saying: “Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” [Col. 1539D].

## CHAPTER VI. [Col. 1540A] That these three—Abraham, David, and Joseph—are especially eminent in this generation; and that the promise of Christ was made to them in three ascending stages.

Then, in his proper place and order, he is named when it is said: “Jesse begot David the king” (Matt. 1); finally, for the third time he is recalled in Joseph by the notable designation of the angelic proclamation: “Joseph, son of David, do not fear” (ibid.). Yet this magnificent designation belongs particularly to blessed Joseph, who merited, by the most fitting title, to be called father because he was the spouse and guardian of the blessed Virgin and of the King, the Son of God, son of David, born from her.

Behold: in this book of generation these three are the distinguished fathers of Jesus Christ—man, King, and God. Correspondingly, we perceive that the promise of Christ, spiritually made to Abraham, David, and Joseph, has a threefold progression [Col. 1540B]. For he is understood as merely man in the promise made to Abraham in this way: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). But he is proclaimed as King in the promise made to David: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131 [132]). To blessed Joseph, however, he is promised as God when it is said: “She shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1).

For to save from sins belongs to God, and none but God alone can do this. Thus, when it says, “For he shall save his people from their sins,” it is equivalent in meaning to saying: “For he is God; and therefore you shall call him Jesus,” that is, Savior [Col. 1540C].

## CHAPTER VII. How the three Magi, in accordance with these same stages, offered myrrh, gold, and incense.

In a wondrous manner, through a wondrous and venerable gift of grace, the birth or coming of this King poured back upon the Gentiles all at once the treasures of this faith which the aforementioned fathers of Jesus Christ had stored up separately. The evangelist of the kingdom of God immediately recounts this as follows: “When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king, behold, Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east, and have come to worship him” (Matt. 2).

These Gentiles at once confessed Jesus to be man, King, and God in words, and attested it by gifts. By saying, “Where is he who has been born?” they confessed him man; by saying, “King of the Jews,” King; by saying, “We saw his star,” they confessed him God. Likewise, opening their vessels and offering gifts to him, they attested by gold that he was King, by incense that he was God, and by myrrh that he was a mortal man [Col. 1540D].

This, I say, was granted to the Gentiles by one inspiration, through a wondrous and venerable gift of grace: what had been prepared for the fathers of the Jewish people through the threefold progression of promise described above. From the good treasure of their hearts, they brought forth the whole sum of Christian faith, both in speech and in gifts.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 1541A] On Herod’s disturbance, by which he himself and all Jerusalem with him were disturbed.

“When King Herod heard this, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him” (Matt. 2). Herod’s and Jerusalem’s disturbance proceeded from the deep of limitless error, from blindness of mind and the darkness of inexcusable ignorance. For such ignorance—namely, ignorance of the kingdom of God, the kingdom of this King—is a sin, indeed a punishment for sin, as Wisdom says: “They thought these things and went astray; for their wickedness blinded them, and they did not know the mysteries of God” (Wis. 2).

This error, this ignorance, descending from the head—that is, from the elders who seemed to govern the people—involved simple and unlearned people without malice. Thus even the apostles, who believed and rejoiced that their teacher, the Lord Jesus Christ, the King of the Jews promised in the Law and Prophets, had come, nevertheless erred by thinking too carnally about his kingdom: not maliciously, as has been said, but simply, until Jesus himself had been glorified and they had received his Spirit, so that they might know that his kingdom is not of this world.

But the ignorance of the scribes and Pharisees, who continually read the Law and the Prophets, was malicious and a condemnable blindness. Reading of the Messiah to come—that is, Christ—they wished, or were able, to understand not a kingdom of righteousness but a kingdom of sin and covetousness; meanwhile, under a show of religion, they pursued their own desires. Therefore this judgment of the King strikes them fiercely: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, because you shut the kingdom of heaven before men: for you do not enter yourselves, nor do you permit those entering to enter” (Matt. 23) [Col. 1541C].

Thus, when the King of heaven was born, Herod, king of earth, was disturbed.
