Blind as he was, and possessed of a penal ignorance of this kingdom, he supposed that he would be cast down from his own kingdom by that King—although he was neither a bearer of the scepter from Judah’s tribe nor a ruler from Judah’s thigh. For he had heard the prophetic writing: “The scepter shall not be removed from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49).

## CHAPTER IX. How vainly Herod feared, although the prophet said, “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah,” etc.; for the same prophet proclaims that Christ’s kingdom, by heavenly power, would injure no earthly kingdom.

[Col. 1541D] “And gathering together all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he asked them where Christ should be born. But they said to him: In Bethlehem of Judea. For thus it has been written through the prophet: ‘And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader who shall rule my people Israel’” (Matt. 2).

As has been said, he had heard that Christ was to be born, and that neither the scepter would be removed from Judah nor the ruler from his thigh until that one came. But while he himself was king, the scepter from Judah and the ruler from its thigh had been removed; for he was born of an Idumean father and an Arabian mother. Therefore he asked where Christ would be born in order to devise treachery.

The scribes and chief priests did indeed draw their judgment truthfully from the prophetic Scripture. But had the prophet said only this—that Christ the King would be born in Bethlehem? Had not the Holy Spirit through that same prophet said that the birth of this King would harm neither Herod nor any mortal at all? Certainly, before identifying the place of his birth, he took care to proclaim the marvelous innocence of his kingdom. For he had said: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the top of the mountains, and exalted above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten to it. They shall beat their swords into ploughshares and their spears into pruning-hooks. Nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any more” (Mic. 4), and so forth.

Therefore blind men were giving evil guidance to a blind man, and so both were falling into the pit. Herod asked where Christ would be born, without knowing to ask what kind of kingdom his would be; and they, showing the place of his birth, did not see in that same Scripture the peace and innocence of his kingdom [Col. 1542B]. For what could be truer than what it says: “Nation shall not take up sword against nation, nor shall they learn war any more”?

For the nation of this King—the nation converted to this King—is wholly a nation of little children: it will by no means take up the sword or wage war against the nation of Herod or the Roman Empire. Rather, when the opposing nation strikes it with the sword, it will always proclaim peace, even in death. Just as the little children whom you immediately murdered, O disastrous Herod, did not defend themselves and did not strike you back, so the entire nation of this King, when killed, will not raise the sword and will not wage war against a murderous nation like you.

Nor is the following statement of the Spirit, consoling the city of this King, Sion, through the same prophet contrary to this: “Arise and thresh, daughter of Sion; for I will make your horn iron and your hoofs brass, and you shall crush many peoples, and shall devote their plunder to the Lord and their strength to the Lord of all the earth” (ibid.). The horn is entirely different, and the slaying unlike. This horn is raised not against human beings but against the devil; this slaying is not of people but of vices. This horn was given from heaven, as this King said to his own: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). This slaying is that of which Peter was told: “Arise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10) [Col. 1542D]. Therefore, O Herod, robber and murderer of your own sons, you trembled with fear where there was no fear.

## CHAPTER X. On the saying in Hosea, “Out of Egypt I called my Son”: how truly it pertains to Christ, and how impiously Julian accused the evangelist of mocking the simplicity of the Gentiles.

“He arose, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew into Egypt. And he remained there until Herod’s death, that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Out of Egypt I called my Son’” (Matt. 2). The prophet through whom this was said is Hosea. The text, or passage, from which this brief testimony is taken reads as follows: “As the morning passes, the king of Israel has passed away; because Israel is a child, and I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my Son” (Hos. 11).

Therefore, led—and indeed compelled—by the authority of this evangelist, let us truly say that the king of Israel who passed away like the morning is Herod, the foreign king who passes away; but the child Israel is the Savior, then an infant, the child whom the Father loved and of whom he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3) [Col. 1543A].

Herod, I say, was the king of Israel of that time, a foreigner who was to pass away like the morning—that is, a temporal ruler soon to perish. Thus when the angel says to Joseph, “Arise, take the child and his mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell you” (Matt. 2)—that is, until Herod’s death—then, after Herod’s death, was fulfilled what the Lord had said through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.”

The prophetic words contained in the text around this testimony are likewise the words of the same angel; and he says: “As the morning passes, the king of Israel has passed away; because Israel is a child, and I loved him,” says the Lord. The sense is this: “This king of Israel, who sought the child in order to destroy him—behold, he is dead, and in dying he passes away, as the morning passes. For morning passes quickly, although it returns again; but this man shall return no more. Therefore, as the morning passes, so he has passed away; indeed, because he will never return, whereas morning returns, he has passed away, because this child Israel is my child, whom he sought to destroy, and I loved him.”

For according to another prophet: “Behold my child; I will receive him; my chosen one, in whom my soul has taken pleasure” (Isa. 43 [42]). Thus the kings of Israel acted in former times: “They called them; thus they went away from before them. They sacrificed to the Baals and offered sacrifice to images” (Hos. 11). It is to be understood: killing the prophets in defense of idols, just as now they sought to kill the child, the Lord of the prophets, departing from the presence of their king Herod, who summoned them to kill so many infants on his account.

And what follows—“I was like a foster-father to Ephraim; I carried them in my arms, and they did not know that I healed them” (ibid.)—is likewise to be understood of the present time. For just as then, when they had sinned and made calves for themselves, I gave opportunity for repentance, and they did not know that I healed them, so that, once the wound of idolatry had been closed, they might recover their former health; so now, when I had come as the merciful shepherd to carry upon my shoulders the sick sheep that had strayed, they did not know that I healed them. Indeed, they would not know or understand that I had come to save them [Col. 1543D].

What follows? “He shall not return into the land of Egypt; Asshur himself shall be his king, because they would not be converted. And the sword began in his cities; it shall consume his chosen men and devour their heads; and my people shall hang in suspense at my return. But a yoke shall be imposed upon him together, which shall not be removed” (ibid.). It is entirely so now as well. For just as then, because they would not be converted, the sword began in their cities and the yoke of captivity was imposed upon them by Asshur, so now, much more, because they would not be converted, they fell by the edge of the sword and were led captive among all nations [Col. 1544A].

The present place does not permit us to pursue the remainder. Let us be content to have observed this alone: Julian Augustus impiously accused this evangelist, in the work he vomited forth against the Christians, saying that he transferred to Christ what had been written of Israel in order to mock the simplicity of those who had believed from among the Gentiles. In truth, however, the evangelist mocked no one; rather, being a witness of truth, he faithfully illuminated for those who have the eyes of faith a broad passage of obscure prophecy by a brief verse.

## CHAPTER XI. How rightly the evangelist, intending to say, “Out of Egypt I called my Son,” prefaced it with “As the morning passes, the king of Israel has passed away”; this can be said more broadly of every kingdom of the world, because it rose in the morning and quickly passed away.

Let us return to the matter, for we were speaking of the kingdom of this King, to whom we have also dedicated the present volume, at whose birth King Herod was troubled and asked the place of his birth. Returning therefore to the subject of this kingdom, we ought greatly to delight in what was said of its first adversary: “As the morning passes, the king of Israel has passed away” (Hos. 11).

Let us say more broadly, to the glory and praise of the kingdom of God: “As the morning passes, the kingdom of this world has passed away.” For it rose in the morning—“morning,” that is, it was hastily built by the children of this age. The first of them was Cain, who, after killing his brother, hastened to build a city and name it after his firstborn son [Col. 1544C]. From then onward, by their successive lines, the rulers of that generation all ruled contentiously—men all of the morning, all hasty. And behold, in the time of which we speak, their kingdom was exceedingly strong: like “a terrible and very strong beast, having iron teeth, devouring and breaking in pieces and trampling the residue under its feet” (Dan. 7).

It had already devoured and broken in pieces; the whole world lay already crushed beneath its feet. Then, in this humble King born of a Virgin, the kingdom of God silently rose, as it were, in the evening—that is, near the end of the age. All the children of the other generation, suffering persecution from the generation of Cain, as though laboring throughout the whole day and bearing the burden and heat of the day, had awaited this evening kingdom of God. They had no continuing city here but sought the city to come, confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth (Heb. 11).

Distinguishing those from these, the Spirit of this King says in the psalm: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down, you who eat the bread of sorrow. When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold: the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward is the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126 [127]) [Col. 1544D].

The King himself acted in every respect in this way. He did not wish to rise before the light, because that was vain. Rather, after he had sat down—humbled unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2)—after he had eaten the bread of sorrow, enduring his Passion while doing the Father’s will (John 4), which at that time was food to him, only then did he rise into the light; only then did he enter into his glory. He did not wish to rise before the light; indeed, when he knew that they were coming to seize him and make him king, “he fled again to the mountain, himself alone” (John 6).

Thus not King Herod alone but every kingdom of this world, like the morning, has passed away, according to the saying: “An inheritance hastily acquired in the beginning shall lack blessing in the end” (Prov. 20); but the kingdom of God, built through patience, shall remain forever [Col. 1545A].

## CHAPTER XII. That the kings of the earth feared in vain, because John did not say, “Take up arms against kings because of Christ,” but “Repent,” etc.

“In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea and saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand’” (Matt. 3), and so forth. Surely the kings of the earth feared in vain and were disturbed without cause. See what kind of commander-in-chief this King has, what kind of standard-bearer, what kind of chief officer of the first legion: clothed in camel’s hair and girded with a leather belt.

He does not say, “Take up arms, for the kingdom of the Jews is at hand,” but: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” He does not say, “Sons of kings and patriarchs, I show you how to undertake courageous wars,” but: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” He does not say, “Do not pay tribute to Caesar,” but: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” He does not say, “The yoke of emperors has now been broken,” but: “For now the axe has been laid to the roots of the trees.” He does not say, “The Jewish olive-groves will be preserved and the Roman orchards cut down,” but, without distinction between gardens or groves: “Every tree,” he says, “that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and thrown into the fire” [Col. 1545C].

Leaving the rest aside, it is most relevant to the present inquiry to explain this one statement: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” What is the kingdom of heaven? It is the kingdom of the saints, or of those who shall reign in heaven. For the saints whose kingdom is in heaven are themselves called, and are, heavens, according to the saying: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands. There are no speeches or words whose voices are not heard” (Ps. 18 [19]).

The kingdom of these heavens had until then been far away, because they did not yet possess their King but awaited the one promised. “All these,” says the Apostle, “died according to faith, not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth” (Heb. 11). “For those who say such things make it clear that they seek a homeland.” Therefore it had formerly been far off; but now, he says, “the kingdom of heaven is at hand.”

When, or how, will it be at hand? When this King has been lifted up from the earth. By that very lifting up he will destroy the kingdom of sin and death, which, as the same Apostle says, “reigned from Adam until Moses” (Rom. 3 [5]). This does not mean that the kingdom was destroyed through the Law of Moses, but that from Moses onward sin, hearing the contradiction of the written Law directed against it, began, like an angered tyrant, to rage more fiercely against those subject to it [Col. 1546A].

This King, lifted up from the earth, will destroy the kingdom of sin and draw all things to himself. Rising from the dead, he will enter into his glory as King of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, he says, repent, because those who repent are to be cleansed from slavery to sin, raised up by the King’s blood, and admitted into the kingdom of heaven.

And do not wish to say, “We have Abraham as father,” because this is not the kingdom of those who have Abraham as father, but of those who repent. Indeed, those who do not glory in the flesh but repent can truly say: “We have Abraham as father.” For this is what follows: “For I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise up children to Abraham”—that is, if only they know, or are willing, to repent [Col. 1546B]. For the Gentiles were worshipers of stones.

## CHAPTER XIII. [p. 602] What reason there was why he who had committed no sin came to the baptism of John, who baptized unto repentance.

“Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him. But John forbade him, saying: ‘I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?’ Jesus answered him: ‘Permit it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.’ Then he allowed him” (Matt. 3; John 1).

The entire court of royal Christian faith holds as certain that this King was a free man, that he committed no sin and therefore was not a servant of sin, and consequently did not need repentance. But John baptized unto repentance: “I indeed baptize you in water unto repentance; but he who is to come after me is stronger than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He shall baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.”

Why, therefore, did he come to receive such a baptism? Surely because the cause required it and the rule of justice demanded it. There were two reasons. The first was that he might undertake repentance to be performed for all, which he immediately did. For after he was baptized, he fasted forty days and forty nights, and then was continually afflicted by temptations, persecutions, insults, reproaches, scourges, and the torment of final death.

The second reason was that no one might think himself righteous and therefore not in need of repentance or baptism; so that no one, considering himself righteous, might refuse to receive the Lord’s baptism, when the Lord himself had received the servant’s baptism. For whoever thought in this way could neither be called nor be a soldier of this King, nor enter the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1546D].

## CHAPTER XIV. Why this King saw the Spirit like a dove at his first coming, but shall be revealed in fire at his second; that this King was anointed a second time; and concerning the saying, “In you I am well pleased.”

Baptized, Jesus immediately came up from the water. And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him. Behold, a voice from heaven said: “This is my beloved Son, [Col. 1547A] in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III; Mark I; Luke I; John I). Why, at his first coming, did this king see the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him? Surely because he then came to us in gentleness, in the abundance of mercy; because he came in the spirit of compassion, not to condemn sinners but to invite them to repentance. When he comes the second time, a dove will not then appear over him; rather, he will be revealed in fire: “A fire shall burn before him” (I Cor. III; Ps. XLIX).

At this second time our king, our God in assumed humanity, was anointed with the oil of gladness. For he had already been anointed once in the womb of the Virgin, since he was conceived not from a man’s seed but through the working of the Holy Spirit. Therefore this Holy One was anointed a second time in baptism, before his companions, [Col. 1547B] that is, before all the saints whom he made his companions, so that what he is by nature, they might be by grace—namely, sons of God. But of this elsewhere. Let us now pursue the matter at hand.

“This,” he says, “is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” When or how was I well pleased in this one? Certainly when, in this one, I created heaven and earth in the beginning; when in this one I made all things. Then, I say, I was well pleased in him, as Scripture testifies when it says: “God said, Let there be light, and there was light; and God saw that the light was good.” God said, “Let this or that be,” and it was so; and God saw that it was good. Likewise: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. I). Thus I was well pleased in this one, approving by my own judgment that I was a good and [Col. 1547C] useful worker and architect.

The Father said this fittingly, lest the kindly hearer doubt that this beloved Son is that Word through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John I). Yet the good God could also truly be well pleased in him when he willed that he, who was God, should become man because of his love, and should suffer for humankind. For he never performed any work more worthy of the praise of goodness.

## CHAPTER XV. On the three temptations in which this king conquered victoriously, while all others had been slaves of sin; and on the words, “the angels came and ministered to him.”

Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry. Then the tempter came [Col. 1547D] and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become bread” (Matt. IV; Mark I; Luke IV), etc.

Because this Son was a king, and it is the duty of a lawful king to meet the enemy in the front line and to furnish in his own person examples of courage to the wavering soldier, so that, after acting thus, he may then exhort his army with greater authority: fittingly, therefore, when he was about to teach, he first admitted our temptations into himself and conquered them; and by conquering he willed that his soldiers too should conquer.

But why did he will to endure the threefold temptation of the deceitful enemy? Let us consider each one and examine what kind it is; and the depth of the reason will now show itself in the humility of the temptation.

“If you are the Son of God, command that these stones [Col. 1548A] become bread.” This temptation is exceedingly ancient: it is gluttony itself, through which the first human being was tempted and enticed. “Man,” he says, “does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII). Such, plainly, ought then to have been the answer of the rational human being: “Humanity does not live by every tree, or by the tree alone, in Paradise, but by faithfully keeping the command set before it by God.” He did not answer thus, but opened his mouth rather for the bite than for such a reply. Therefore he became the slave of him by whom he was conquered. But this one, pursuing the royal law, went forth free—he of whom it is said in the Psalm: “Go forth prosperously; proceed and reign” (Ps. XLIV).

“If you are the Son of God,” he says, “cast yourself down. For it is written that God commanded his angels concerning you” (Ps. XC), etc. This temptation belongs to Jewish [Col. 1548B] curiosity. For “the Jews seek signs” (I Cor. I). They indeed tempted God in their hearts by demanding food for their souls; and they spoke wickedly against God, saying: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Exod. XVII; Ps. LXXVII), and so forth. They also said: “Is God among us, or not?” But this one, accepting the command given to humanity, says: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deut. VI).

“All these things I will give you,” he says, “if, falling down, you worship me.” This temptation belongs to pagan madness. For pagans, or Gentiles, worshipped the devil in images for the kingdoms of the world and their glory; and, in order to be exalted outwardly, they fell inwardly. But this one, standing in his proper rank, with knee erect and the neck of royal freedom unbent, says: “It is written”—understood as addressed to humanity—[Col. 1548C] “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (ibid.).

Therefore, O most beautiful in form beyond the children of men, it is fitting that you alone should reign and possess the kingdom alike of Jews and Gentiles, because, tempted in every respect according to likeness, you conquered; and without sin you passed beyond the temptations of Jews and Gentiles, by which they were universally tempted and all conquered in Adam, and individually tempted and all conquered in themselves—except one—as it is written: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, no, not even one” (Ps. XIII, LII).

And because service is due to a victorious king from his rejoicing ministers, the Evangelist says: “Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and ministered to him.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On the preaching of our Lord and King, which he began after John had been handed over; and on the prophetic testimony in which, among other things, it was said: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.”

When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee, and so forth, as far as “teaching in their synagogues and preaching the Gospel of the kingdom” (Matt. IV). As though hastening toward the royal insignia, this Evangelist here passed over one and the same first year of the Gospel, about which John writes very much. He fittingly begins here with John’s being handed over, since from that time this King and Lord began publicly to preach in the exercise of his own authority. For, he says, “he was teaching them as one having authority, and not as [Col. 1549A] their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. VII).

Nor do we believe that only what he here drew from the prophet as testimony was fulfilled: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali” (Isa. IX), and so forth, as far as “a light has risen upon them.” But the remaining words of the same prophetic chapter also were fulfilled. Because of their length, this scribe of the great King suppresses them, leaving them to be understood as though a doorway had been opened, so that you may know that this is he of whom it is there written: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace. Upon the throne of David and over his kingdom he shall sit, to establish it and strengthen it in judgment and justice from now and forever” (ibid.).

“Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” He acted in accordance with the testimony set forth by the prophet, so that his dominion, which is the kingdom of heaven, might be multiplied: inviting sinners to repentance and then calling Simon Peter, Andrew his brother, and the other apostles. For if you ask how his dominion was to be multiplied, he says: “I will make you fishers of men.” And so it came to pass. The few who then followed their king became fishers of men; and from that time the dominion of Christ the great King is multiplied by the multitude of the Gentiles. When adversaries and hostile death have been removed, there shall be peace, and there shall be no end of peace.

## CHAPTER XVII. That Jesus, when the crowds had been called, taught his disciples what those who serve in God’s kingdom ought to be like.

[Col. 1549C] Seeing the crowds, he went up the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. Opening his mouth, he taught them, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” etc.

Let our King and Lord now speak to us the laws of his kingdom: no longer as one ascending a small mountain, but as the ascender of heaven itself; seated not upon the summit of an earthly mountain but at the right hand of Majesty on high (Heb. I); opening, in the majesty of his dominion, not his mouth in a bodily manner, but invisibly his treasure, in which the riches of salvation—that is, wisdom and knowledge—are stored.

For, desiring to speak of the glory of his kingdom and its power according to this Evangelist, who speaks of almost all things concerning him in royal terms, we have hastened thus far, to the point where, seeing the crowds, he went up the mountain and opened his royal mouth, [Col. 1549D] so that the King might himself speak by his own mouth—he who had formerly spoken through the mouths of his heralds. He spoke, I say, judgments worthy of the opening of his mouth; and he taught what men ought to be, and what sort they ought to be, who serve in God’s kingdom; by what order of battle and with what weapons they must win the eternal pay of that kingdom.

For the carnal children of the kingdom, who had heard that it had been promised to their fathers that, in the time when the Messiah reigned, they would be rich and prosperous and free to take pride in riches, supposed that, when earthly kings and princes heard the name of this King—as Herod did—the soldiers of God’s kingdom would have to shed their blood and seize cities and revenues for themselves.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What kind of laws and edicts belong to this King of God’s kingdom, so that Herod and the other kings of the world need not fear him, when he thus declares to the soldiers of his kingdom: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V; Luke VI). O beloved kingdom of God! O compassionate and venerable condition proposed to those who seek the kingdom of God! “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit”; blessed are those who possess the spirit of the fear of the Lord, because, although they may be rich in this age, as Abraham was, although they walk clothed in royal purple and celebrate frequent triumphs over enemies, as David did, they walk with a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, knowing themselves to be poor in spiritual goods, continually begging and seeking alms with suppliant [Col. 1550B] groaning from the one and only rich King of God’s kingdom.

That perverse angel in heaven did not do this, thinking himself sufficient for himself; and the angel fell and became the devil (Isa. XIV). Nor did Adam, that first father of our race, do this in Paradise, thinking he could adorn himself by his own riches with likeness to God; and therefore he fell from Paradise and fell into hell. Thus all the proud with their swollen spirit are miserable, but the poor in spirit are blessed, because by begging in this manner they will receive a great alms—namely, the kingdom of heaven—from the hand of the King.

For this is what the Psalmist says concerning this King, this Son of the King, or his judgment: “He shall judge the poor of the people and save the children of the poor.” Again: “He shall spare the poor and needy, and shall save the souls of the poor” (Ps. LXXI). He himself is the example of the poverty to be commanded, as befits a king. For in the prophet this distinction is given concerning him: “Behold, your king shall come to you, righteous and a saviour; he is poor and riding upon a she-ass, and upon a colt, the foal of a she-ass” (Zech. IX). Again, this complaint is uttered concerning him against Judas, or the Jewish people: “He persecuted a needy and poor man, and one pierced in heart, to put him to death” (Ps. CVIII).

“Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.” The meek are those who have the spirit of compassion: gentle and teachable, not defending their own deeds but confessing their sins to the truth. These are blessed, because they shall [Col. 1550C] possess the earth, which Adam, harsh and unteachable, lost through the contrary spirit. For when God questioned him and said, “Why have you done this?”, the thorny hedgehog exacerbated matters by his harsh answer: the woman said, “The serpent deceived me; I ate”; the man said, “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me, and I ate” (Gen. III). These harsh persons defended themselves thus, and therefore they are miserable, because they lost the land of the living.

But blessed are the meek, who neither criticize God’s judgments or commandments nor defend themselves; for they shall possess the earth—not this land of the dead and dying, which harsh kings subject to themselves with bloody arms and yet cannot possess, but the land of the living, in which is the tree of life, which truly flows with milk and honey. Moreover, the King himself elsewhere persuades his soldiers by his own example concerning what he preaches here, when he truly says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Blessed, I say, are those who have so progressed in the spirit of knowledge that they know this time to be a time of mourning; who know how to mourn their dead—that is, themselves. For all died in Adam; and from him there is no house in which there is not a dead person, since, along with the universal death of original sin, each person draws along the proper deadly consequence of actual sin as well. Those who mourn in this knowledge—that is, who repent—are surely blessed, because they shall be comforted. For they are those to whom the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, is promised and given, announcing to them that the cause of this mourning, death, has been destroyed for them in the one man, in this their King, Christ [Col. 1551B] the Lord Jesus. He says these things here and speaks elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me. He sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those shut up; to comfort all who mourn and to bestow strength upon those who mourn in Zion, and to give them a crown instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow” (Isa. LXI).

Indeed, the King did not lack an example of this part either. Before he said these things, he first mourned and gave his soldiers an example of mourning, namely when, mourning the death caused by our sin, he fasted forty days and forty nights (Luke IV).

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” These are strong and therefore blessed, for they have the holy spirit [Col. 1551C] of strength, while, fortified by faith and hope in their aforesaid mourning, they thirst and eagerly produce fruits worthy of repentance. Blessed, I say, because they shall be filled and satisfied precisely with that for which they hunger and thirst: that is, they shall be justified through their one righteous King, Jesus Christ.

The King himself, who teaches this virtue of hungering and thirsting for righteousness, also supplied its example in deed, saying: “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III). He certainly said this as one hungering and thirsting, as he testifies elsewhere: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (John IV).

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” They act truly and justly in a blessed manner who, with the spirit of counsel, mercifully pardon those who sin against them when they are able to harm them, because of that agreement which the King himself established between God and human beings: that they may say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI; Luke XI). Blessed, I say, are these persons, because, without justice opposing it, they shall obtain mercy, so that God may forgive them the sins they have committed against him.

Conversely, the unmerciful are not blessed, because they shall not obtain mercy. This is especially proved by that Gospel parable concerning the justice of the King, who wished to settle accounts with his servants. “And when he began to settle accounts, one who owed ten thousand talents was brought before him.” For the conclusion is entirely just: “So also my Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother [Col. 1552A] from your hearts” (Matt. XVIII).

Plainly, this King did not need such reciprocity, since he committed no sin that might be forgiven him. Nevertheless, he did what he taught. For he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII). And so it came to pass: those who believed were forgiven.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Pure in heart is the person whom the purity of love, through works of mercy, has cleansed, so that he may have the simple eye of the heart, free from hatred, and may be clean from every dust of desire and every disturbance of anger.

But behold, we read that holy Moses prayed to the Lord his God for the people with exceeding compassion when he had said: “Leave me, that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation” [Col. 1552B] (Exod. XXXII). His heart was so free of all desire or ambition that he cared nothing for the promise, “I will make you into a great nation,” but stood in the breach, with a broken heart, before him, in order to turn away his anger. Yet although he was conscious of having so pure a heart, he said: “If therefore I have found grace in your sight, show me your face.” “You cannot,” says the Lord, “see my face. For no human being shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXIII).

What then shall we say? Surely Moses too was pure in heart; yet nonetheless the sentence of truth is true. For he did not say: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they see God,” or “have seen God,” but “for they shall see God”—understood: afterward, once the wall of enmity has been removed. While that wall stood between them, ever since the first human being through sin set God’s hostile wrath against himself, neither Moses nor any human being ever saw God (John I).

This King himself, who speaks these things, testifies that the power to grant this vision of God rests with himself—namely, that he grants the vision of God to whom he wills—when elsewhere he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. XI). To the pure in heart he gives the spirit of understanding through a mirror, in an enigma, so that they may understand the Scriptures, which are indeed clear mirrors of the divine vision.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Peacemakers are those who, first and chiefly, zealously seek peace between themselves and God, and, so far as they can, between all human beings and God; secondly, they endeavor to settle disputes between person and person and to bind together the concord of love. Surely these are blessed, because they shall be called sons of God: sons, I say, not by nature but by grace; brothers and co-heirs of the only-begotten Son, the Prince of Peace, who through his blood dissolved enmities between God and human beings and restored peace.

These, in the seventh spirit—the spirit of wisdom—already begin to keep sabbath, while still placed in this mortal body; and they are, as has already been said, sons of God, sons of wisdom.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” This had already been the reward of the first rank: “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” What, then, is added in the eighth, when it is said: “Blessed are those who [Col. 1553A] suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”? For it is indeed a great thing to be poor in spirit and to attain the remaining degrees of righteousness; but the greatest and best thing is to endure persecution for that righteousness. How then can the reward be one and the same for an inferior and the highest merit—that is, for the first and the eighth?

But let us observe that all the things hitherto set forth—that is, from the first through the seventh degree—are common merits or rewards of all the hosts of this King, namely angels and human beings; whereas this—suffering persecution for righteousness’ sake—is peculiar to human beings, who consist of soul and body. Therefore both angels and human beings are blessed when poor in spirit, meek, mourning or suffering with others, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful or compassionate, pure in heart, and peacemakers; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven, in which they shall possess the land of the living, be comforted and satisfied, obtain mercy, see God, and be called sons of God.

Furthermore, human beings are blessed who alone suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake in their bodies: the kingdom of heaven, which they already possess with the blessed angels in respect of the soul, they shall possess also in respect of the body in the eighth—that is, in the resurrection.

But it would have been insufficient merely to say, “those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake,” since this today belongs visibly to few persons—unless perhaps it may be affirmed that all who desire to live godly in Christ (II Tim. III), even though they have outward peace, nevertheless suffer inward assault from spiritual or carnal vices [Col. 1553C] for the righteousness of that same godliness.

Therefore, when he had said, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” he continued: “Blessed are you when they revile you,” etc. In saying this, he undoubtedly reached even us, the latest, whom Jews still today revile in their synagogues under the name Nazarenes.

Certainly, although our King has supplied examples in himself of everything he has said thus far, he gave so great and such an example of this patience—that is, of enduring persecution for righteousness’ sake—that it cannot be unknown; indeed, it would be wicked and impious to forget it. For he suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake even unto death, death upon [Col. 1553D] a cross (Phil. II), and therefore the kingdom of heaven is his. “For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (ibid.).

Why then, O kings and princes of the earth, are you disturbed with wicked anxiety on hearing the name of Christ the King or of his kingdom? Be at ease: by law the soldiers of this King, or the citizens of this kingdom, are forbidden to be like you—proud, harsh, scoffers, weary of righteousness, unmerciful, impure, and restless—but are to be altogether such that they prefer to suffer injustice rather than commit it, to be exiles rather than reign, and to be slain rather than slay.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the following parts of his discourse, and how he flatters or curries favor with no one by preaching harsh and severe things: “Enter through the narrow gate”; and that, following this example, all helpers of God’s kingdom ought not so delight in the number of disciples that they fail to preach to them the hard things by which one goes to God.

After these great and lawful matters, and in the great court of the whole Church, whose ears are prepared to hear, the eloquent speaker enters upon a discourse worthy of himself in this way: “You are the salt of the earth. But if salt has lost its savor, by what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing further except to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by people. You are the light of the world” (Matt. V), etc.

The King of God’s kingdom speaks these words to his chief men, or first officers—that is, the apostles. By a brief comparison he expresses sufficiently the great difference between them and earthly leaders or princes, and all who serve an earthly kingdom: namely, that they are not like those who devote themselves to wars and dissensions, but that they should season with the salt of heavenly doctrine a tasteless world possessing ignorance of God; that in teaching they should deserve their hearers’ goodwill by speaking good words, while at the same time bringing forth the light of good works.

But what does this great and vehement severity of royal authority mean, proposing at the very beginning of his kingdom judgments so formidable to his subjects in such stern terms? “Do not think,” he says, “that I came to abolish the law or the prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.” And soon after: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.” After this, and other such things, which are surely narrow [Col. 1554C] indeed, and are more perfect than the precepts of the law in proportion as they are narrower, he says: “Enter through the narrow gate, for broad is the gate and wide the way that leads to destruction, and many enter through it. How narrow the gate and constricted the way that leads to life, and few find it” (Matt. VII).

What, I ask, does it mean that this wise King, at the beginning of his kingdom—indeed, before he was yet seated upon the throne of his kingdom—proclaims such hard and severe things? Did he still not know what he afterward said, speaking of his distinguished soldier, when, after saying, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A man clothed in soft garments?” he immediately added: “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. XI)? Indeed, he had long before known the reason why the kingdom of Israel had been torn away from the house of David: namely, because the new king had said, “My little finger is thicker than my father’s back; and now my father laid a heavy yoke upon you, but I will add to your yoke.” On hearing this, the people said: “What share have we in David, or what inheritance in the son of Jesse? Return to your tents, O Israel. Now see to your own house, David.” And Israel went away to its tents. But over the children of Israel who dwelt in the cities of Judah, the house of David reigned (III Kings XII).

He knew, I say, that this had happened and that something like it would happen to himself. For if the holy Fathers found in David’s adultery and homicide a sacred example of a heavenly mystery, why should it not help us to find in the folly of the boy king an image of the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God? For it is established by the sure and true testimony of those same Fathers that the fact that the kingdom of Israel was torn from the house of David, while the tribe of Judah clung to its king, is like or parallel to what befell the true David, Christ: when the rebellious multitude was torn away from his faith through many and much-speaking heresies, while only the Church of true confession, as they fashioned calves of falsehood, held the truth and clung to its King and to the temple of its God.

Accordingly, what this King now says—this new King, not yet crowned through the passion of death with glory and honor—“You have heard that it was said to the ancients; but I say to you,” and in all things showing the way of his kingdom to be narrower than it had previously been (Matt. V), is almost the same as though he said: [Col. 1555B] “My Father laid a heavy yoke upon you, but I will add to your yoke.”

For God the Father imposed a heavy yoke upon people inclined to bloodshed, saying: “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX); a heavy yoke upon the wanton and lustful, saying: “You shall not commit adultery” (Deut. V); a heavy yoke upon those who swear, saying: “You shall not swear falsely” (Lev. XIX); a heavy yoke upon the angry and those eager for private vengeance, saying: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. XXI). But this Son of the same God added to their yoke, [606] saying: “Everyone who is angry shall be liable”; “everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery”; “do not swear at all; let your word be Yes, yes; No, no”; and, “But I say to you, do not resist evil” (Deut. XIX).

What does this mean, then, except that this King is God and Lord of judgment, and that what is ordinarily harmful to an earthly kingdom benefits his heavenly kingdom? Earthly kings, after all, are made by human beings; they need tributes and taxes, and kings who are needy and poor relieve their panting want through the revenues of men. But to this heavenly Lord and King the wise king of the earth truly says: “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV).

Therefore earthly persons, in order to become kings and dwell in royal houses, wear soft garments—that is, they speak pleasing things. But this King, who truly says to people, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John XV)—this King, I say, one and only, made neither by human beings nor through human beings—flatters no one. Rather, his words are straight like goads and like nails driven deeply, so that he may judge and test those who are deemed worthy of his kingdom.

All the helpers of his kingdom must do likewise in accordance with his example: they must flatter no one because they delight in the number of disciples, but must preach to them the hard and severe things through which one goes to God. Nor is there anything here which a prudent commander of soldiers either does fear or ought to fear. For one who truly comes seeking God and desires sincerely to serve in God’s kingdom is frightened by no austerity of military law, knowing that the King who has set forth these hard things says at the end of his discourse: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine and does them shall be likened to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew [Col. 1556A] and rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon a rock” (Matt. VII).

Those who do not heed these things, as the Apostle says, “all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. II), are like the scribes and Pharisees whom the Evangelist immediately marks out when he says: “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. VII). For those who receive something from someone deprive themselves of authority: they judge to be a good soldier the one who gives something into their mouths; but against those who give them nothing they sanctify war. This King did not do this. Therefore it is said: “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as the scribes and Pharisees”—that is, unlike them, he did not make the authority of teaching contemptible by seeking his own interests.

## CHAPTER XX. How it was truly said, “He was teaching them as one having authority,” according to the signs he performed.

Furthermore, “He was teaching them as one having authority, and not as their scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. VII)—whether good or bad is understood. For among them there were good scribes, namely those of whom Moses and Ezra were the best; and there were good Pharisees, namely Aaron and his sons—indeed, all who belonged to priestly or Levitical descent. For the clergy of that people are called Pharisees.

Let us take the comparison from the best. This one was not teaching as Moses and Aaron did, but as one having authority. For example: “The Lord said to [Col. 1556C] Moses, ‘Why do you cry to me? Speak to the children of Israel, that they may go forward. But lift up your rod and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the children of Israel may walk in the midst of the sea on dry ground’” (Exod. XIV). In this way, and in all else that he did, Moses did not possess authority in himself, since he was human and not God; and therefore he necessarily cried out to God, who possessed authority.

But this one accomplished all things as one having authority, since he was not merely human but God and human. Let us therefore consider how he performed his works as one having authority. When he came down from the mountain and great crowds followed him, “behold,” it says, “a leper came and worshipped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me’” (Matt. VIII). He did not say, “If you cry to God, you can obtain cleansing for me,” but, what is a mark of great faith, he said: “If you will, you can cleanse me.”

But he, truly possessing authority, so that he might signify that same authority even through the gesture of his body, stretched out his hand and touched him, saying: “I will it; be cleansed.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

Then the centurion approached and confessed with extraordinary faith that he had authority, as indeed he truly did: “Only speak the word, and my servant will be healed. For I too am a man under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it” (Mark I; Luke V).

Finally, after proposing this comparison, this man of admirable faith intended the following to be understood, as though he said: “You, a human being who are also God, have all sufferings [Col. 1557A] and every infirmity serving under your authority and judgments. You say to this one, ‘Go,’ and it goes; you say, I mean, to this spirit of infirmity, ‘Depart,’ and it departs. Likewise you say to another, when cause and reason require, ‘Come,’ and it comes, so that the person whom you wish to be scourged may be scourged—you who know how to make good use of evil services.”

Thus he confessed his authority and received the response proper to one possessing authority, according to the merit of his faith: “Go, and let it be done to you as you have believed.” So too, whatever else he did, he worked as one possessing authority and not as the scribes and Pharisees—indeed, not as the highest leaders Moses and Aaron, who needed crying out and prayer in order to accomplish anything. Therefore the crowds were rightly astonished at his teaching.

## CHAPTER XXI. That it also belonged to royal authority to grant others the power to cast out unclean spirits and heal every infirmity; and whether the signs of the ancient saints or of the apostles were greater.

Because we have begun to speak of power, and ought to recognize the royal power of our Lord, let us not pass over what bears most directly on this matter. “And having called his twelve disciples, he gave them power over unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal every disease and every infirmity. Now the names of the twelve apostles are these: first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James of Zebedee, and John his brother; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James of Alphaeus and Thaddaeus; Simon the Canaanite [Col. 1557C], and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed him” (Matt. 10).

Behold one who possesses power truly royal, power rightfully divine. Nor does he merely possess power: he is able to give power to human beings. What more, I ask, did God, in the form of God, confer upon human beings than God now does in the form of a man, the Lord in the form of a servant? Let us compare the power which God in the form of God gave to Moses with the power which God in the form of a servant gave here to the apostles.

What was that power which this mighty one had given Moses? It was in casting down the rod before Pharaoh so that it became a serpent and devoured 607 the rods of the magicians; in bringing forth frogs and gnats, also dog-flies, and death upon all the cattle of the Egyptians; in scattering ashes into the sky, so that sores came upon people; in stretching out [Col. 1557D] his hands to heaven so that the Lord rained fire and hail, so that locusts came upon all the borders of Egypt, so that darkness covered the whole land of Egypt for three days, and so that, after the Lord had struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, he raised his rod over the sea and, when it was divided, the people crossed over.

These are indeed great works of great power; yet it must wisely be considered that that power did not work so directly for human salvation. For all those things were done outside the very substance of the human being. Here, however, the Lord of power himself works upon the very substance of the human being, and gives to those upon whom he bestows power precisely power over unclean spirits, to cast them out and to heal every disease and every infirmity. [Col. 1558A] Where the grace of mercy is greater, there without doubt is the greater dignity of venerable power. These works belong both to power and to grace; they are nearer to human salvation and therefore were rightly reserved for the advent of the Saviour, whose power they properly are, and through whom grace came.

Nevertheless, the most eminent prophets, Elijah and Elisha, performed certain works of this sort. Elijah raised the dead (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17); Elisha too restored life to a dead person and showed a leper the washing by which he might be cleansed (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4–5). But these things were done so as to prefigure the sacraments of life and salvation to be accomplished through this mighty one, as he himself intimates in the Gospel, saying: “Truly I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years [Col. 1558B] and six months and a great famine came over the whole land; yet Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath of Sidon. And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (Luke 4).

## CHAPTER XXII

How, according to the prophecy that says, “Hear, my servant Jacob, and Israel whom I have chosen,” etc., this one is the true Jacob and the true Israel; and because the former physically begot twelve sons, while this one spiritually begot twelve apostles, to whom he gave this power.

The first to whom this mighty one gave this power were the twelve apostles, of whom Mark also says: “He made twelve to be with him, and to send them out to preach; and he gave them power to heal infirmities and to cast out demons” (Mark 3). [Col. 1558C] It is especially pleasing that this heavenly man, the true Jacob and spiritual Israel, at the beginning of his people or generation begot twelve spiritual sons, thereby proving that Jacob, or Israel, who physically begot twelve sons—the patriarchs, fathers, and rulers of a future people—had preceded as a type of himself.

For he is truly that Jacob and that Israel to whom the Father says in Isaiah: “And now hear, my servant Jacob, and Israel whom I have chosen. For I will pour waters upon the thirsty land, and streams upon the dry ground. I will pour out my Spirit upon your seed and my blessing upon your offspring” (Isa. 54 [apparently 44]), etc. What could be truer, if you look to this man—what, I say, truer or more certain than his saying, “I will pour out my Spirit upon your seed and my blessing upon your offspring”? For he poured out [Col. 1558D] his Holy Spirit upon this seed and upon this first offspring of his, and, in that same Spirit, his blessing, when divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, rested upon each one of them, and they began to speak in diverse languages as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2).

What follows? “They shall spring up among the grass like willows beside flowing waters. One shall say, ‘I am the Lord’s’; another shall be called by the name of Jacob; another shall write with his hand, ‘For the Lord,’ and shall take the name of the God of Israel” (Isa. 44). This is so true that it needs no assertion from us—indeed, that it must not be unknown: after the Holy Spirit of blessing was poured out, those who had been few immediately sprang up [Col. 1559A] like willows; that is, they were rapidly multiplied as they summoned and converted all nations. Each one, in his own measure, professed what he was or what he was able to do, according to the grace he received through the will of the Lord and God who distributes it.

Therefore, as that Jacob or Israel begot twelve sons (Gen. 33), so this true Jacob and true Israel spiritually begot, as the beginning of his people, twelve apostles. And the former says of his physical children, “They are the little ones whom God has given me” (Isa. 8); while this one says of his spiritual children, “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Heb. 2).

## CHAPTER XXIII

Why, among such sons and rulers of the kingdom of God, he who knew all things also admitted Judas, who did not belong to that kingdom.

[Col. 1559B] But among the king’s sons and the rulers of God’s kingdom, what place had that Judas, who was to become the betrayer of the king himself and of the king’s sons? The king did not choose him in ignorance, for elsewhere he says: “I know whom I have chosen” (John 13). Why then did he choose such a man and give this sort of man power along with the others? As though we had already asked him, he himself answered: “That the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘He who eats my bread shall lift up his heel against me’” (ibid.).

But would he not have chosen such a man unless Scripture had foretold it? On the contrary, unless he was going to choose such a man, Scripture would not have said this. We do not improperly use the word “choice,” since he himself says: “Have not I chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” (John 6).

Why then, knowing him to be evil, did he admit him among the good? Clearly, in order that he might first do what he afterwards taught ought to be done in the parables which he first spoke to us. For when he had expounded the parable of the sower, which he had spoken first, he immediately proposed this other: “The kingdom of heaven has become like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went away” (Matt. 13), etc.

Clearly, the householder, the sower of good seed, who says, “Lest perhaps, while gathering the tares, you uproot the wheat with them; let both grow until the harvest” (ibid.), is the king of the kingdom of heaven—that is, of the present Church, or congregation of saints. In it, tares are mingled with the good seed; that is, the children of wickedness, whom the enemy, the devil, has oversown among the children of the kingdom, remain mixed until the harvest, that is, until the consummation of the age. [Col. 1559D]

He commands that they be tolerated when he says, “Let both grow until the harvest,” since they often bloom earlier and grow higher, so that they attain the highest honours in ecclesiastical ranks. The mixture of the evil does no harm to the good, who unwillingly endure them for a time because they cannot correct them. Therefore, what he was going to command, he himself rightly did first, as became a teacher: he admitted Judas into that number of saints to whom he gave power to cast out unclean spirits and to heal every disease and infirmity, so that you may know that God’s gifts reach 608 [Col. 1560A] those who receive them with faith, even if the one through whom they receive them is like Judas.

Yet it must be known that, after—as Luke writes—Satan entered into him and he went and spoke with the chief priests and magistrates about how he might betray him to them, and they rejoiced, agreed to give him money, and he promised (Luke 22), he no longer exercised that apostolic power either in casting out unclean spirits or in healing diseases and infirmities. For on the following day, while they were at supper, he was marked out as the betrayer by the dipped morsel; he immediately went out, and before the Jews crucified the man whom he had betrayed, he hanged himself with a noose (Matt. 27).

Nor should we suppose that Christ’s true apostles were so sluggish in patience that, after he had been identified, they could, had he not gone out, have continued to share communion with him as before. We say this so that we may not suppose that the tares which the hostile man has oversown among the good seed must be tolerated without discernment of circumstances or times, or that communion with such persons does no harm. While Judas was still a hidden thief and God-Christ alone knew it, his fellowship and apostolic power did no harm to the good apostles. But once his utterly wicked iniquity came to light in action—when he entered into an agreement for betrayal and murder with the enemies of his Lord and teacher—once Christ the man made this known to human beings, does reason allow that thereafter faithful people could join themselves without fault in any fellowship with that devil? [Col. 1560B]

[Col. 1560C] So indeed, as long as any children of wickedness, however great the scandals they cause in Christ’s kingdom, still act so as to conceal themselves under the Christian name, and God alone knows what they are, they must be tolerated. But when Christ, who speaks in the Church, publicly identifies them by a deed as bearing the name they deserve, then neither reason nor the rule of truth permits us even to eat with such persons (1 Cor. 5).

## CHAPTER XXIV

Concerning the enemies of God’s kingdom who said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons,” to whom he said: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.”

[Col. 1560D] The first power of this king was in casting out demons; it stirred his enemies, scorched by the flame of envy, in this way: “A demon-possessed man, blind and mute, was brought to him; and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw. And all the crowds were amazed and said, ‘Can this be the Son of David?’ But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, ‘This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebub, prince of demons’” (Matt. 12).

We inquire and desire to know what these enemies of God’s kingdom were inwardly, when outwardly they appeared thus: men who breathed out through the open gates of mouth and tongue such a great and dreadful stench of blasphemy, raging against their own conscience and against truth, which was not unknown to them. For they knew that the Lord cast out demons by the finger of God; they knew it, I say, guided by the same reasoning by which the magicians before Pharaoh could know and say, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 7 [apparently 8]).

We inquire, then: from where can we know this? [Col. 1561A] He says: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand. And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then shall his kingdom stand?” (Matt. 12). This is indeed a powerful argument, and none more forceful, true, or consistent is found among secular rhetoricians or dialecticians. But what does it establish? Surely this: that Satan’s kingdom cannot stand. For he concluded thus: “How then shall his kingdom stand?” Was that, then, the question—whether his kingdom stood? Had these adversaries of God’s kingdom affirmed this? If they had not affirmed it, he refutes them in vain. In vain—far be it!—does the wise king of God’s kingdom argue so forcefully against them.

[Col. 1561B] We are therefore compelled to say that these most wicked and perverse adversaries, in his hearing, if not with the sound of their voices then with the cry of a settled thought, said that Satan’s kingdom stood. But how can we prove so great a matter? It may seem little to someone that we merely state it. Unless Satan himself, who ruled them, had affirmed this in their hearts, our Lord would not have argued in this way from its contrary.

Let us therefore have recourse to the authority of holy and truthful Scripture. In Isaiah the Holy Spirit speaks, having undoubtedly long before heard the blasphemies which he was to receive from these mockers: “Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men who rule over my people in Jerusalem. For you have said, ‘We have made a covenant with [Col. 1561C] death, and with hell we have made an agreement. When the overflowing scourge passes through, it shall not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and in falsehood we have taken refuge.’ Therefore thus says the Lord God: ‘Behold, I will lay in the foundations of Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, firmly founded. Whoever believes shall not hasten. And I will make judgment by weight and righteousness by measure. Hail shall sweep away the hope of falsehood, and waters shall overflow the refuge. Your covenant with death shall be annulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand. When the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trampled under foot. Whenever it passes through, it shall take you away’” (Isa. 28).

Led by such testimony of prophetic truth, we do not hesitate to say [Col. 1561D] that they were so utterly lost that, all hope before God having been destroyed, they turned aside to the devil and made a pact with him through secret exchanges of sorcery. They would do whatever pleased such a master, even to the killing of the great king God himself, provided only that they did not lose the wealth of the Temple and their customary plundering of the people. For this is what is said in a certain parable: “Let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. 21).

Yet, although they had most miserably made falsehood their hope and hoped to be protected by falsehood, they acted greatly against that very hope when they said, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons.” For in saying this they confessed that among demons there is no faith, no concord, no binding force of compact, no keeping of a sworn covenant. [Col. 1562A] Jesus, therefore, knowing their thoughts, aptly said: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste,” etc.

“He knew their thoughts.” What thoughts? Surely not the statement, “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, prince of demons,” for these were spoken words. Rather, knowing their thoughts—that they hoped Satan’s kingdom would stand, for which reason they had made a covenant with death and an agreement with hell—and hearing their words, by which they admitted that Satan’s kingdom was divided, he deigned to construct such a syllogism, in order to convict them from their own mouths that, deceived and ruined, they had made falsehood their hope: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste, and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand. If Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then shall his kingdom stand?”

[Col. 1562B] Then immediately: “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out?” (Matt. 12). For their sons too, by the apostolic power already handed over to them, as stated above, could already cast—or had begun to cast—demons out of possessed bodies. It was also to come about that they would cast them out from the souls of the nations and drive them from temples, altars, and images, while these same adversaries looked on with envy; yet they would be unable to say that this was done by Beelzebub, because Beelzebub could not act against himself in the matter in which his kingdom would be destroyed above all—namely, the worship of idols.

[Col. 1562C] “What then,” he says, “will you say?” You will indeed have nothing to say, and nevertheless you will continue to persecute. What follows? “Therefore they shall be your judges” (ibid.). For they shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel (Matt. 19), because, when they have done what they ought to do first—that is, spoken God’s word first to you—you will not believe. Therefore, being about to judge you, and already judging you, they will turn to the Gentiles.

“But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.” As if he said: If you restrain your mouths, flowing with blasphemies, and correct mind and tongue so that you say what is worthy and true—that I cast out demons by the Spirit of God—then the kingdom of God has come upon you, so that, freed from the slavery of sin, you may become the seats and houses [Col. 1562D] of God’s kingdom.

But you speak thus not through ignorance but through envy, not through error but through hatred of truth. Therefore I say to you: “Every word and blasphemy shall be forgiven to human beings, but blasphemies against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).

Finally, the person who speaks a word against the Spirit is one who, knowing the truth from the Scriptures—which are surely the words of the Holy Spirit—holds that same truth down in unrighteousness or falsehood, in the frenzy of envy or hatred uttering another’s words against the conscience of his own heart. Such a person will indeed not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come—not because any sin is truly unforgivable for those who repent, but because such a person is never judged worthy by God to aspire to the humility of true repentance, the Holy Spirit himself, against whom he sinned, passing judgment. [Col. 1563A]

## CHAPTER XXV

Concerning the primacy of the apostle Peter among those rulers of God’s kingdom; and how, though he still did not know what God’s kingdom itself would be, when he said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you,” he received the power of God’s kingdom.

The aforesaid twelve apostles had received power, as has been said, to cast out unclean spirits and, by preaching the kingdom of God, to heal every disease and every infirmity. They all received it indeed; but among them all Peter, through his firstborn faith, had deserved this distinction. [Col. 1563B] He was the first to say, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” so that he might receive the keys of that same kingdom of God, the king himself saying to him, in praise of his proven faith: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church. And the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.”

[Col. 1563C] A share in heavenly jurisdiction and in the senatorial dignity contained in these words—“Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16; Mark 8; Luke 9)—was entrusted jointly to the other apostles as well. For elsewhere he says: “Truly I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. 18). And again elsewhere: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20).

Thus the power is common to all, but the one and singular privilege belongs to Peter alone: to him it was first and individually said, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” They received power in God’s kingdom, but they did not possess knowledge of that kingdom—what sort of kingdom it was, and by what way or order one ascends into it. Peter, their leader, as well as the others, did not know.

Therefore, when the king himself said that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, and be killed and rise again on the third day—which was, certainly, to enter into the kingdom—[Col. 1563D] Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying: “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall not happen to you.” He immediately deserved to hear: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling block to me, for you do not savour the things of God but those of men” (Matt. 16; Mark 8).

He was Satan—that is, an adversary—in an excessively straightforward sense, and through an excessively simple intention he opposed the common good. The others too erred greatly through the same ignorance. James and John, the sons of Zebedee, said: “Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask.” He said to them: “What do you want me to do for you?” They said: “Grant us to sit, one at your right hand and the other at your left, in your glory” (Mark 10).

Thus, though they had been called to preach the glory of God’s kingdom to the whole world, [Col. 1564A] how unformed, untaught, little, and infant-like they were. Therefore the king himself, who was also the teacher of little ones, deigned to become their instructor; and because they were little ones who needed milk and not solid food (Heb. 5), he spoke to them in parables, so that through familiar likenesses of things he might gradually lead us into the unknown mysteries of the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXVI

Concerning the parables of the same king, which introduce the knowledge of the mysteries of God’s kingdom; and concerning his saying, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables,” adding, “because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear.”

[Col. 1564B] What is especially delightful in the arrangement of this evangelist is that there are as many introductory parables as there are apostles: twelve. The first is the parable of the sower: while he sows, “some,” he says, “fell beside the road, and birds came and ate them” (Matt. 13), and the rest.

Certainly, when he says to them in, or concerning, that parable, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to them it has not been given,” or, more clearly in Luke, “But to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Luke 8), this must not be understood of the time at which these words were spoken, but of the time when the Holy Spirit would come and teach them all truth. With this in view, he himself, being about to suffer, immediately says to them: [Col. 1564C] “I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I shall no longer speak to you in figures of speech” (John 16).

The second parable is of the man who sowed good seed in his field: “But while people slept, his enemy came and sowed tares in the midst of the wheat, and went away” (Matt. 13). The third is that which he proposed, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which indeed is the smallest of all seeds; but when it has grown, it is greater than all vegetables and becomes 610 a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches” (Luke 13). The fourth is this: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened” (Matt. 13). [Col. 1564D] The fifth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides” (ibid.). The sixth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls” (ibid.). The seventh: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind” (ibid.). The eighth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants. And when he began to settle accounts, one who owed him ten thousand talents was brought before him” (Matt. 18). The ninth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire labourers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20). The tenth: “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. 22).

[Col. 1565A] For we omit from this number two parables which he spoke not so much to his disciples as to the chief priests, his enemies. One is: “A man had two sons; and approaching the first, he said, ‘Son, go today and work in my vineyard’” (Matt. 21). The other: “There was a householder who planted a vineyard, put a hedge around it, and dug a winepress in it” (ibid.), etc.

The eleventh is: “Then the kingdom of heaven shall be like ten virgins, who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride” (Matt. 25). The twelfth: “A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and entrusted his goods to them. And to one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one” (ibid.).

In these parables he spoke to them with the purpose of introducing them, sometimes to them alone and sometimes while crowds also stood by and listened. [Col. 1565B] Clearly, when in the first he said, “To you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven,” or of God’s kingdom, “but to them it has not been given,” or “but to the rest in parables” (Matt. 13; Luke 8), as we had begun to say above, this was fulfilled when these rulers received the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of truth, and all began to know the mystery of God’s kingdom which had been hidden in the Law and the Prophets.
