We, however, the common people or laity, to whom such great grace has not been given, began, with faith going before us, gradually to perceive through these Gospel parables the same mysteries of God’s kingdom.

But what does he mean when he adds: “Therefore I speak to them in parables, that the prophecy of Isaiah the prophet may be fulfilled in them, saying: ‘By hearing you shall hear and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see and shall not see’” (Matt. 3 [apparently 13])? Did he then speak in parables so that those of whom this had been prophesied might not perceive the mysteries of God’s kingdom?

The very text or sequence of the passage compels us to understand it in this way. For the disciples had said, while the crowds stood on the shore: “Why do you speak to them in parables?” (ibid.). The answer to that question—indeed, I might say, to that aim or desire, because they did not yet know the true way to advance toward the manifestation of God’s kingdom—[Col. 1565C] would have been for him to show himself openly, not in parables but in the deed itself and with power visible to all, to be the king of God’s kingdom.

But the king of God’s kingdom was to proceed in such an order that the humble, enlightened, should be admitted within, while the proud were left outside to wander, blind, in the streets. Therefore, after he said, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of God’s kingdom,” he added, terribly and fittingly for the occasion: [Col. 1565D] “because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

Concerning his mighty works, or miracles: that they are such that from them the power and mercy of the king of God may alike be made manifest.

This evangelist has interwoven the works of miracles, signifying the same thing as the aforesaid parables concerning God’s kingdom, so that both royal power and merciful grace appear in all of them to those who attend carefully. There are eighteen in number, performed at definite places and upon definite persons.

The first is when, as he came down from the mountain and crowds followed him, “behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying, ‘Lord, if you will, you are able to cleanse me.’ And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying, [Col. 1566A] ‘I will; be cleansed’” (Matt. 8).

The second is when, to the centurion who said, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only speak a word, and my servant shall be healed,” he marvelled at his faith and said with royal command: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done to you” (ibid.).

The third is when he touched Peter’s mother-in-law’s hand, fever left her, and she rose and served them (ibid.).

The fourth is when, after a great disturbance had arisen on the sea, he who slept—the king of heaven, earth, and sea—rose and commanded the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm (ibid.).

The fifth is when demons begged that same king who had power, saying, “If you cast us out, send us into the herd of swine.” He did not deem such beings worthy of a lengthy or familiar reply, but said: “Go” (ibid.).

The sixth is when he saw a paralytic lying on a bed and the faith of those presenting him. He said: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you.” [Col. 1566B] Because certain scribes murmured at this, saying, “He blasphemes,” he said, “that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins,” and then said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Matt. 9).

The seventh is when the woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years came up behind him and touched the fringe of his garment. But he turned, saw her, and said with his customary authority: “Take courage, daughter; your faith has made you whole” (ibid.).

The eighth is when the Lord of life and death said: “Go away, for the girl is not dead but asleep.” After the crowd had been put out, he took her hand and she rose (ibid.).

[Col. 1566C] The ninth is when two blind men cried out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” Approving their confession of his royal name, he said: “According to your faith, let it be done to you” (ibid.).

The tenth is when they brought him a mute man who had a demon; and after the demon was cast out, the mute man spoke (ibid.).

The eleventh is when the Lord of the Sabbath, having convicted his adversaries that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, said to the man with a withered hand: “Stretch out your hand.” And he stretched it out (Mark 3).

The twelfth is when a blind and mute demon-possessed man was brought to him and he healed him, so that he spoke and saw (Matt. 12). Because the Pharisees envied and blasphemed on account of this, he defended his right: that he was the king of God’s kingdom, who had come to bind the strong armed man, while they, servants of the same tyrant, were to be caught up in the downfall of his divided kingdom (ibid.).

[Col. 1566D] The thirteenth is when he fed five thousand men, apart from women and children, with five barley loaves and two fish (Matt. 14), on account of which, according to another evangelist, they wished to seize him and make him their king (Mark 6).

The fourteenth is when, as the disciples were in danger in the middle of the sea, “in the fourth watch of the night he came to them walking upon the sea.” When Peter said, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters,” he said: “Come” (Matt. 14).

The fifteenth is when he said to the Canaanite woman—the king and noble father of freeborn sons—“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” She replied, “Yes, Lord; for even the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” He immediately turned the severity of his rule or judgment into mercy, saying: [Col. 1567A] “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you will” (Matt. 15).

The sixteenth is when, having compassion on the crowd because they had nothing to eat and would faint on the way if he dismissed them fasting, he fed four thousand people, apart from women and children, with seven loaves and a few small fish (Matt. 15).

The seventeenth is when he took Peter, James, and John his brother up a high mountain, was transfigured before them, his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white like snow. “And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared to them, speaking with him” (Matt. 17). In this he prefigured the present glory of his kingdom, Moses and Elijah—that is, the Law and the Prophets—bearing witness that the king himself now reigns forever in flesh made immortal, in the splendour of divinity. [Col. 1567B]

The eighteenth is when a man fell on his knees before him and said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he is lunatic and suffers grievously.” He answered: “O unbelieving and perverse generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I endure you? Bring him to me.” He rebuked him, and the demon went out of him. “And this kind,” he says, “is not cast out except through prayer and fasting” (ibid.), though he himself, possessing power, had cast it out not through prayer nor through fasting.

After these great works of his mighty mercy, or merciful power, through which he spiritually prefigured greater inward goods for all who serve his kingdom, one dreadful work is set forth, [Col. 1567C] by which he signified to the enemies of that kingdom the magnitude of the wrath and vengeance now upon them: “He entered,” it says, “into the Temple of God, and cast out all who sold and bought in the Temple; and he overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those who sold doves” (Matt. 21; John 2).

Finally, this point concerning the power of the king deserves serious attention: with one whip made of cords, a man then despised—and so despised that he was afterwards crucified—did what an innumerable army could not have done. That uproar by which they were so thrown into confusion, that cord by which they were thus expelled from the Temple, prefigured the storm by which, entwined in the long cords of their sins from the blood of righteous Abel onward, they were cast out of God’s kingdom. The Romans took away both their place and their nation; the whole world heard the tumult of that event.

## CHAPTER XXVIII [Col. 1567D]

How, at the end, all scandals are to be taken away from God’s kingdom; and why Father Augustine does not vainly wish Matthew to be understood in the face of the lion.

Almost no one is unaware, and absolutely no one ought to be unaware, that all these things and the other daily deeds and sayings of Christ, as they have been expounded by the holy Fathers, contain mysteries of the kingdom of God, that is, of the present Church. This kingdom, until the end of the age, mingled from good and evil, is alike instructed and perfected in all patience according to the command and example of the King. Finally, how all scandals are to be removed from this kingdom—a matter signified by many parables in this Evangelist—is declared by this terrible final pronouncement of the King before his Passion:

[Col. 1568A] “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on his left” (Matt. 25), etc.

It has often been said, and must often be said, that this Evangelist has spoken almost everywhere in such a way that the majesty of the kingdom of heaven, the royal person, and the royal power of our Lord Jesus Christ are set before us for contemplation alike in his words and in their meanings. Having observed this, Father Augustine (*On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, I.6; *Tractates on John*, 36), where he proposes the four Gospel faces for contemplation, both in the Apostle and in the prophet, judges not without reason—or wishes it to be understood—that Matthew is the face of the lion and Mark the face of the man, although many others have handed down the reverse: that Matthew is to be recognized in the man and Mark in the lion.

[Col. 1568B] As we bring our treatment of this sixth age to its end, let us say briefly something of the seventh, so that, according to our purpose, we may at last, though weary, arrive at the praise and adoration of the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the seventh age of the world: why it is truly called and is the Sabbath, that is, rest; and what that rest is

The seventh age of the world is not called or designated an age according to time or the sequence of times. For it does not succeed this sixth age temporally as the fifth succeeds the fourth and the sixth the fifth; rather, joined to it as though at its side, it runs with it until the end of the age, until the day of the universal resurrection.

[Col. 1568C] It is the hidden reality of another age, in which the souls of the elect, having laid aside their bodies, rest with God in a blessed sabbath-keeping; they who, through the six ages of the world, by differing merits of works, have deserved to enter differing dwelling-places indeed, but the same rest.

This itself is called and is Sabbath, that is, rest, because there they do no work; rather, having received the reward of their works, they henceforth keep holiday in peaceful leisure. It is rightly understood that the legal Sabbath given to circumcision was a type of this sabbath-keeping, so that whatever the letter of the Law says concerning that carnal Sabbath, the rational person, skilled in the spirit of the Law and instructed in its truth, may understand spiritually concerning this one.

[Col. 1568D] For example, the Lord says: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20). This commandment is the fourth in the Decalogue, written on tablets by the finger of God. You understand it truly only when you understand it in a manner worthy of the finger of God who wrote it: namely, when you perceive that to sanctify the Sabbath day means as though it had been said: “Remember that whatever good you do, do it not for any transient and vain thing, but for eternal recompense.”

Thus the present life is the time for doing what is good, and has its proper reason and opportunity; but the whole duration of that age belongs to those who rest, and possesses the fixed and unchangeable law of Sabbath. God first entered that rest, as Scripture also testifies when it says:

[Col. 1569A] “God completed on the seventh day the work that he had made, and rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had accomplished” (Gen. 2). The Apostle says: “For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his. Let us therefore hasten to enter into that rest” (Heb. 4), etc.

## CHAPTER XXX. That Christ truly kept Sabbath there after the labor of his Passion; and, rising from the dead, had already entered the eighth

Moreover, after the labor of his Passion and death, God rested in that Sabbath of his. For God was in Christ; and because, on account of the unity of person, God is fittingly said to have labored where Christ labored and was wearied even unto death, God is beautifully said to have rested where the soul, separated from the body by the cross, kept Sabbath—a soul from which the Word, God, once assumed, never departed.

[Col. 1569B] Therefore God rested in his Sabbath from his works when Christ, God and man, rested according to his soul in the secret place of divinity and according to his body in the tomb of the earth. That divine ordering delights greatly: six days of laboring in the sweat of the Passion, and on the seventh resting after laying aside the flesh.

For, as the Gospel history faithfully relates, on the first of the days—that is, on the Lord’s Day—he entered Jerusalem to suffer; on the second and third, the gentle Lamb endured constant snares among the most cruel butchers; on the fourth, he was betrayed by his disciple; on the fifth, writing a testament for his children, he bequeathed the inheritance of his body and blood;

[Col. 1569C] on the sixth, in dying, he completed all his work with sharp labor; on the seventh, he rested in the tomb and, in that age which we call the seventh, kept Sabbath with the blessed spirits until the first day of the week. Then, rising from the dead, he was already in the eighth, that is, in the glory of immortality and incorruption.

Therefore, looking especially to him, let us say with the Apostle: “He who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his” (Heb. 4). For by that labor of his and that rest of his, God and our Lord Jesus Christ obtained rest for us,

[Col. 1570A] so that, having laid aside the flesh, we may immediately rest in the seventh, until, after the resurrection of the flesh has been accomplished, we reign in the eighth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That he invites us to this sabbath-keeping by saying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you”

This seventh age, therefore, corresponds to the seventh day of the world’s creation, the Sabbath, that is, the Lord’s rest; and, corresponding to the seventh gift—the spirit of the fear of the Lord—it possesses the Spirit of wisdom, which itself is rest for her children. The children of wisdom hasten to it with every desire; and although they still labor here under the condition of mortality, transferred thither in mind, they make haste to rest as much as they can.

For mother Wisdom continually invites them, saying:

[Col. 1570B] “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11).

While she cries these things aloud outside, giving her voice in the streets, she nevertheless teaches inwardly by the Holy Spirit, inwardly persuading the heart, so that those suffering weariness from the cares and anxieties of this age may delight in the sweetness of holy contemplation.

They therefore come to the school of wisdom, in accordance also with that counsel which the Spirit of the same Wisdom offers in the Psalm: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45 [46]).

[Col. 1570C] In this school, the better and more effectively each has studied, the nearer and better prepared he becomes for this seventh age, that is, rest. And when he departs from the schools, the more practiced he is in the word of God, the more honorably he stands before the King’s face, and receives from him a higher rank in that eternal choir of the blessed, as the prophet testifies:

“Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who have instructed many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 2).

Thus the active life is indeed truly blessed, but the contemplative life is more blessed, according also to the testimony of the Lord, who, without condemning the former, praises the latter: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10).

End of the second part of this book *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, concerning the works of the Son, the second person of the same Trinity.

# The Forty-Two Books of Lord Rupert, Abbot of Deutz, on the Trinity and Its Works: On the Works of the Holy Spirit

## BOOK I

[Col. 1571]

## CHAPTER I. On the twofold resurrection of the dead: one by which we now rise in soul by receiving the Holy Spirit; the other by which our mortal bodies also will be made alive because of that same Holy Spirit dwelling in us

The Psalmist, confessing in brief praise both the wrath and the grace of the Almighty, says: “When you turn away your face, they shall be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they shall fail and return to their dust. Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103 [104]).

For what must be held in memory and confessed in supplication is that, because of the sin of one man, God turned away his face, and we were troubled; he took away our spirit and we failed, and we return to our dust.

[Col. 1571B] Here the punishment of a twofold death is to be understood as the vengeance of wrath. For on the day when they ate from the forbidden tree, God turned away his face, and the transgressors were troubled—that is, they died in soul. Besides that death, he took away their spirit, saying to man: “For dust you are, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3).

What must likewise be believed faithfully and recalled with every giving of thanks is that, because of the righteousness of the one man Jesus Christ, God sent forth his Spirit, and we were created, and he renewed the face of the earth.

[Col. 1571C] Here the pardon of a twofold grace, the twofold glory of life or vivification, must be recognized. For on the day or hour when a person believes in Christ and receives the sacrament of his baptism, God sends forth his Spirit and that person is created, so that, with every oldness of sin abolished, he is now a new creature according to the soul. Besides this, the face of the earth—that is, the earthly body, which has grown old and died because of sin—will be renewed on the last day in the resurrection.

This twofold grace, the resurrection of souls and the renewal of bodies, this twofold resurrection of the dead, must now be pondered and treated by us in praise and glory of that same Holy Spirit,

[Col. 1572A] our God and Lord, whose sending through Christ has already made our souls live and will make our bodies alive. For the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the Spirit lives because of justification. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also make alive your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8).

## CHAPTER II. That the new man Christ is the first and principal work of the Holy Spirit, and therefore the discussion of the works of the same Holy Spirit should rightly begin from the conception of that man

But the straight path and lawful order for contemplating this grace will then at last be observed by us if we first know the Prince and Giver of grace, the mediator of God and human beings (1 Tim. 2), the man Jesus Christ (1 John 2). He is, according to his humanity, the first and principal work of the Holy Spirit, than which neither God nor this Spirit of God ever made anything more beautiful or more precious. This is the new man, this the new creation.

Perhaps you say: If Christ is a new creation, if—as the Apostle says—“we too in Christ are a new creation” (2 Cor. 5; Gal. 6), how did Scripture speak truly when it says that God rested or ceased on the seventh day from all his work which he had accomplished? How had he ceased if he was going to make this new creation?

[Col. 1572B] To this, I say, we must first know that the person whom that Scripture describes as having created the old creation is God the Father. The person who spoke and by speaking made is the Father of the Word, by whom the heavens were established (Ps. 32 [33]); he is the Father generating the Word, through whom all things were made (John 1).

The letter likewise requires us to understand of this person that he rested and ceased. Does it therefore follow, because God the Father ceased, that his Spirit ceased? Certainly not. For even if the Father ceased, whose proper work was to create the nature of things, the Holy Spirit did not cease, whose proper work is to make nature better.

[Col. 1572C] Thus let us rightly distinguish God the Father and God the Holy Spirit: the Father created, while the Holy Spirit refashioned whatever creature he willed; and each person worked through the third, or middle, person—that is, through the Son. But the Father worked through the Son as God alone; the Holy Spirit, through the Son now made man. For as no creature was made except through the Son as God, so none was refashioned except through the same Son of God made man.

Therefore, as we had begun to say, the new man Jesus Christ is the first and principal work of the Holy Spirit, since he was conceived from the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1573A] Accordingly, so that we may have a great and evident doorway into discourse concerning the Creator, the Holy Spirit who renews the face of the earth, we shall take our beginning from that sending of him concerning which the angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

We shall do this if first we deserve briefly to anticipate the countenance of that same Holy Spirit in the confession of the true faith.

## CHAPTER III. That the Holy Spirit is God and Lord consubstantial with the Father and the Son, and that this person is properly the love of God: the angel who does not possess it is a devil; the human being who does not possess it is condemned with the angel who lacks it

[Col. 1573C] We believe and confess that the Holy Spirit is true God and Lord, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son: that is, in every respect the same in substance as the Father and the Son, though not the same in person as the Father and the Son. For as the person of the Father differs from that of the Son, so likewise the person of the Holy Spirit differs; but the divinity, glory, and majesty of the Holy Spirit are nevertheless the same as those of the Father and the Son.

And, that we may distinguish the properties of the person of the Son and of this Holy Spirit by other names also: just as we call the Son the Word or Reason of the Father—not an affective word, nor an artificial reason, but the substantial Word and Reason living eternally and substantially—

[Col. 1573D] so we call the Holy Spirit the charity or love of the Father and the Son: not accidental charity or an adventitious love, but substantial charity and love of eternal constancy.

That we may deserve in some measure to contemplate how great is the force—or rather, how great is the majesty—of this love, let us now compare, within the same genus or species, a creature that shares in it with a creature that does not.

Certainly, if among the angelic order you compare two, one is the devil and the other perhaps holy Gabriel or glorious Michael. If from the human race, for example, you take from the apostolic company, one is the blessed apostle Peter and the other is Judas the devil.

[Col. 1574A] Yet this alone makes the difference: this human being or this angel shares in this love, while that human being or angel does not share in it. Each, through the majesty of the Word by whom he was made, has rationality; they differ only in this, as was said: one has communion in this love, and the other does not.

Thus, even in this, the characteristic operation of the Holy Spirit is clear: namely, that through the Word of the Father the rational creature receives being, but through the Holy Spirit it receives well-being.

## CHAPTER IV. That the Holy Spirit proceeds; and that the Son is rightly said to have proceeded from God, while this one is said to proceed from God

This God, this Holy Spirit, is at times said to be sent or sent forth—as we recalled above: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created” (Ps. 103 [104])—and at other times is said to proceed.

[Col. 1574B] It was too little for his majesty or glory that he should be said to be sent unless he were also said to proceed. For an inferior person is often said to be sent, and one who is sent may go or come against his own will. But the Holy Spirit, Lord in his own person, is not less than the one sending him, and when sent he deigned to come by his own grace.

Therefore he is rightly called “proceeding” or “who proceeds,” so that the very word may indicate together both the dignity and the will of the ruling person.

That this one is proceeding, or proceeds, was first said not by any author, angel, or prophet, but by God and our Lord Jesus Christ himself, in his own words: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15).

[Col. 1574C] Notice that in speaking of himself he used the past tense of this verb: “For I,” he says, “proceeded from God and came” (John 8). Again, elsewhere: “I went forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). But concerning this Spirit he said not in the past but in the present tense: “who proceeds from the Father.”

For he himself proceeded from God in one way: by being born before the ages from the hidden substance of the Father, in order to create the world—something done once; or by assuming flesh, so that he who was invisible might become visible—again something done once.

This Spirit proceeds in another way when he bestows grace upon the subject creature, which occurs as often as he gives life to things that were dead and fills things that had been empty.

[Col. 1574D] Moreover, and more abundantly, in that blessed life for which we hope, he proceeds from the divine majesty by an eternal procession, as heat from the substance of fire; because, as has already been said, he himself is love—indeed, the torrent of delight—which never fails there.

## CHAPTER V. That the Son proceeded from the Father alone by being born, but the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; and that there is some difference of expression when the Son sometimes says simply “Father” and sometimes “my Father”

There is also this difference: the Son proceeded from the Father alone, namely by being born, as has already been said; but this Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

[Col. 1575A] For because the Son of God said, “the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15), it does not follow that he does not also proceed from the Son himself, since he first said: “whom I shall send to you from the Father.” It is much better to understand that he intended this distinction: “whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15).

For it must be understood that by the name Father, sometimes one of the three persons is meant, while at other times God or divinity is meant without distinction of persons. The force of this distinction is readily apparent if you carefully weigh the Gospel words.

For the Son of God sometimes says simply “Father,” and sometimes “my Father,” “Father of mine,” or “of my Father,” with a possessive pronoun. Where he names the Father in this latter way, he undoubtedly distinguishes the persons of Father and Son, and what he says of himself there far surpasses the form of a servant.

[Col. 1575B] For example: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). Again: “I have come in the name of my Father” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John 20).

But where he says simply “Father,” he wishes one divinity to be understood—not one person, but together the divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. What he says of himself there is more humble and does not rise above the form of a servant.

For example: “For the prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me; but that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14). Again: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11).

[Col. 1575C] Once this is observed, it causes no difficulty—indeed, it greatly assists faith—that he spoke thus: “When the Paraclete comes” (John 14), etc. For what does it mean that, after he had said “whom I shall send to you,” he added “from the Father,” except that you may understand that the Son of God sends the Holy Spirit not from the poverty of human nature but from the sufficiency of divine nature?

And what does it mean that he said “proceeds from my Father,” except that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the divine majesty not from one person alone, but without distinction of persons?

## CHAPTER VI. On the procession of the Holy Spirit: that he does not proceed from the Father alone, but proceeds from the Father and the Son

Therefore the Son proceeded from the Father alone by an ineffable generation; but this Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son by a likewise ineffable procession. Yet in the poverty of our pilgrimage we have certain first fruits of understanding by which we may know that he proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son.

[Col. 1575D] For behold, we read Holy Scripture. But what do we believe Holy Scripture to be except the Word of God? Certainly many words are arranged by the pen of the prophets, yet the whole body of the Scriptures is one Word of God: one Word, I say, which faithful souls conceived, as seed, from their lawful husband, God, and, bringing it forth through eloquent mouths, handed down in certain signs—that is, letters—so that it might be made known to us.

When, therefore, we read Holy Scripture, we handle the Word of God and hold before our eyes, through a mirror and in an enigma, the Son of God. And truly, if we are kindly readers, if we attend reading as kindly hearers, by reading or hearing we are kindled; by reading or hearing we advance toward love of God.

[Col. 1576A] Does not, then, the love of God proceed to us from Holy Scripture? And what is the love of God except, as we have already said above, the Spirit of God? The gift proceeds from the Father, so that through Scripture understood we may know the Son of the Father; love proceeds to us from the understanding of Scripture, so that we may love the Father of the Son and cherish the Son of the Father. Does not the Holy Spirit then proceed to us in this manner too from the Father and the Son?

Therefore, since while we live we cannot see that sun shining in its own brightness, at least from this mirror we may infer that this Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Having said these things briefly, according to time and subject, about the adorable majesty of the Holy Spirit, we must now go forward under his guidance in contemplating his beautiful work.

## CHAPTER VII. That the blessed Mary, bride of God the Father, was the sanctuary of this Holy Spirit; and that from her came all the fruit for whose sake God the Father declares himself to have been husband to the ancient Church

[Col. 1576B] First, it must be known that the blessed Virgin Mary, temple and sanctuary of this God and our Lord the Holy Spirit, was, or is, the bride of God the Father; and that in her was fulfilled the reason why that same God the Father testifies in so many passages of Scripture that he loved the Synagogue—that is, the Church of the former people—and took her in marriage.

For example, when he says in Ezekiel:

[Col. 1576C] “When you were born, on the day of your birth, your navel was not cut, and you were not washed with water for cleansing, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling-clothes. My eye did not spare you, that I might do for you one of these things out of pity for you; but you were cast out upon the face of the earth in the rejection of your life, on the day when you were born.

“But passing by you, I saw you trampled in your blood, and I said to you, when you were in your blood, ‘Live.’ I said to you, I say, when you were in your blood, ‘Live.’ I made you multiply like a shoot of the field; and you multiplied and became great, and came in and attained to womanly maturity.

[Col. 1576D] “Your breasts swelled and your hair grew, and you were naked and full of shame. And I passed by you and saw you, and behold, your time was the time of lovers. And I spread my garment over you and covered your disgrace; and I swore to you and entered into a covenant with you, says the Lord God, and you became mine.

“And I washed you with water and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil; and I clothed you in garments of various colors, and shod you with violet-colored leather, and girded you with fine linen, and clothed you with delicate fabrics; and adorned you with ornaments, and put bracelets on your hands and a necklace around your neck, and put an ornament upon your mouth, and rings in your ears, and a crown of beauty upon your head.

“And you were adorned with gold and silver, and clothed with fine linen and embroidery and many colors” (Ezek. 16).

In saying these things, he plainly declares himself to have become husband to the Synagogue, which he led forth from Egypt, trampled in the blood of sin and of fanatical error, by which she had served the Egyptian gods; and he declares that on Mount Sinai he entered into a covenant with her and gave her the ornaments of the legal Scripture.

[Col. 1577A] For that he entered into a covenant with her there is clear from the following account of Scripture: “But he sprinkled the blood which he had taken upon the people, and said: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you’” (Exod. 24).

There are many such passages in the prophetic Scriptures, in many places, where God declares that he is the husband or spouse of the Church or Synagogue. Was the Father of all wisdom, God, whose love is great and immeasurable—this God, this Holy Spirit—speaking these things in exultant or playful frivolity, rather than with the weight of a certain reality? Far be it!

[Col. 1577B] For in act he intended to be the husband of rational human nature: that is, to generate from her a Son for himself. He was already beginning to do this when he said these and such things, when he sent Moses and the prophets.

God the husband spiritually received into his chaste embraces the chosen souls from that people, souls of tested faith; and in the force of this his love, this Holy Spirit, he implanted in them his seed from his secret depths, his Word from the depth of his heart. The Word of truth received in the faithful soul opened bodies’ mouths, assuming a voice so that they might prophesy, and demanded faith from their hearers.

Thus such souls say in Isaiah: “From your fear, Lord, we conceived and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26).

[Col. 1577C] Let not suspicion of an artificially contrived likeness diminish the reality of the truth. For truly, whatever holy and truthful Scripture says to us concerning the love of God or God as lover is so true and so steadfast that these earthly matters of ours from which comparisons are drawn are rather certain shadows or passing images of that abiding truth.

But because we who are from the earth first came to know these earthly things, these are thought to be realities and those likenesses of realities; whereas in truth those are realities, and these are likenesses of realities, which pass away while those remain.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the blessedness of the Virgin Mary, and why the earlier Church should rightly be understood and called the bride of God the Father, and the later Church the bride of the Son of God

Therefore, as we had begun to say, the blessed Virgin Mary was the bride of God the Father; and in her he intended to accomplish the reason for which he called the Church of that people his spouse in the Scriptures: namely, that his Word, which in the manner already described he had made vocal through the hearts and mouths of the prophets, should become flesh through the womb of this blessed Virgin, as he had purposed before all ages.

[Col. 1577D] Once this had been done, the Word himself made flesh (John 1), God the Son of God himself made man, was to be called and to be the bridegroom; and the whole Church was to assemble for receiving the marriage writings of his union, without abandoning the Father, whom alone she had formerly been accustomed to call her husband.

Thus the blessed Virgin deserved to be both the bride of God the Father, as the best part of the earlier Church, and the model of the younger Church, the bride of the Son of God, her son.

For the Holy Spirit, who worked in her womb or from her womb the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God, was also to work from the womb or through the womb of the Church, through the life-giving washing of his grace, the regeneration of many children of God. This must be discussed by us more fully in its proper place.

[Col. 1578A] Nor do we without reason distinguish matters in this way, calling the preceding Church the bride of the Father and the following Church the bride of the Son. For the Synagogue could not be called, or be, the wife of one whom she did not know as husband.

But it is evident that the Church of that time did not know the Son of God: except insofar as he was revealed through the spirit of prophecy to very few, God was otherwise hidden. Therefore, because he did not appear in the public assembly or in the solemn worship of that religion, and because God the King had not yet made a marriage-feast for this his Son, the Son of God was not yet in act bridegroom or husband.

But God the Father, whom alone—and scarcely even him—the Synagogue knew, was her husband; and he demanded with vehement zeal that he be regarded as her lawful husband.

[Col. 1578B] For example: “At least now call me: ‘My husband; you are the guide of my virginity’” (Jer. 3). And there are many similar sayings. He, then, was the husband.

But how all the advantage of such a husband, all the fruit, all affection, all love, all power, and the entire power of begetting came, when the fullness of time arrived, to the Virgin just mentioned (Gal. 4), she who experienced it knows better; but we have heard only words committed to everlasting remembrance—the words of the archangel Gabriel, saying:

## CHAPTER IX. On the conception of the blessed Virgin Mary through this love, that is, the Holy Spirit, as the angel says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” etc.

“ The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1).

[Col. 1578C] These words, I say, we have heard only; but she both first heard them and, believing what she heard, immediately deserved to experience what she had heard. For when, with sound faith, she opened her mind and her mouth to say, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.), immediately, according to the angel’s saying, this Holy Spirit came upon her and poured himself into her through the open gates of faith.

But into what did he pour himself? Certainly, first into the sanctuary of her chaste breast, then into the temple of her sacred and incorrupt womb: into the dwelling of her breast, that he might make her a prophetess; into her womb, that he might make her a mother.

[Col. 1578D] For she is the prophetess of whom the holy prophet Isaiah speaks joyfully: “And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son” (Isa. 8).

Do we suppose that Isaiah alone approached this prophetess, or do we wonder how he could have approached her? Rather, we do not doubt that all the holy prophets, and Moses first of all, approached this prophetess. All without exception came together to her: the divided graces and particular prophecies of every one of them all came together in this prophetess; they all converged at once when the Holy Spirit came upon her.

Isaiah counted himself blessed—and indeed all the holy prophets rightly counted themselves blessed—because they knew that they would approach this prophetess in this manner: because they knew that they would bring some good Word to this temple of God, this sanctuary of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1579A] For this blessed Virgin did not receive, like each one of them, a particular grace of the Word; rather, when this Holy Spirit came upon her, she received from him the whole substance of the Word of God. She became the unique prophetess, receiving the full grace of the Holy Spirit and receiving the whole Word of God, true God, first in mind and then in womb.

Rightly considering this, that messenger had first uttered a greeting such as had never been heard in all ages: “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1).

[Col. 1579B] To explain the greatness of her grace, it would have been too little to say, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” unless he had added: “and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you.”

For in a wondrous and ineffable manner, so that she might be able to bear the strength of her conception, the power of the Most High overshadowed her: the power, I say, of the Most High—that is, this same Holy Spirit, the Spirit of love—overshadowed her.

For what did a frail girl, frail not only in sex but also by the condition of mortality, receive or conceive except the mighty Word, God; the mighty substance of the Word, from the most excellent substance of God the Father, before whom angels tremble?

Indeed, no creature can endure even his sight unless it has first been prepared by this Spirit of love, as Scripture testifies when it says: “As wax melts before the face of fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Ps. 67 [68]).

But this Virgin was not merely presented to his gaze; from the Father’s secret depths the whole Word of God, God the Word, entered into her. Accordingly, the power of the Most High fittingly overshadowed her: a power mighty in miracles and able to reconcile feminine substance with God the Word.

## CHAPTER X. That the Holy Spirit did not come upon her in such a way as to serve as seed, nor should he who was conceived be called the son of the Holy Spirit

[Col. 1579C]

Therefore, he says, “and the holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). Because “the Holy Spirit shall come upon thee, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (ibid.), and in this way that which thou shalt conceive and bear as a son shall come to pass (ibid.), although thou knowest not a man, therefore the holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God. Shall He then be called, or be, the son of the Holy Spirit? Certainly not. For the Holy Spirit will not so come upon thee as to serve as seed, nor so that the flesh of the Word, or of the Son whom thou conceivest, should be from His substance. For thou shalt indeed conceive by the Holy Spirit, but not through the Holy Spirit as begetter. [Col. 1579D] This conception by the Holy Spirit is not generation but operation. The flesh will be from the flesh of the Virgin, not from the substance of the Holy Spirit Himself.

And it should be noted that He did not say, “the holy thing shall be called or shall be,” nor did He say, “shall be,” but “that which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.” For what the Virgin conceived already existed long before. In His ancient essence He was holy; He was the Son of God. It remained only that He should be called what He was, and that, in being called the Son of God, the name of God should be made known—the name not yet known, not that by which He is called God, but that by which He is called Father of the Son. “It shall be called,” I say, “the Son of God,” which it already is: not by adoption of grace, but by the property of nature.

Likewise this should be noted: He did not say, “he who shall be born of thee, holy,” but “that which shall be born of thee, holy.” For many are indeed called holy [Col. 1580A] or sanctified, but there is one Holy Thing—that is, holiness—by which all holy persons are sanctified. This Holy Thing is this Holy of holies, whom no holiness subsequently bestowed sanctified as conceived or born in the fault of Adam’s transgression, but whom the incorrupt Virgin conceived as essentially holy by the Holy Spirit. Thus it was said better and more excellently, as it ought to have been said: “that which shall be born of thee, holy, shall be called the Son of God.”

Nor is it without significance that the archangel varied the placing of the word. For a little earlier: “and thou shalt call his name Jesus” (Matthew 2); but here he says, “and he shall be called the Son of God.” There, “thou shalt call”; here, “he shall be called.” Nevertheless, to blessed Joseph also He says: “and thou shalt call his name Jesus.” For the name Jesus, which several persons bore alike, could freely be given by her or by Joseph. But that He should be called the Son of God or Son of the Most High was to be reserved for evangelical preaching. He shall therefore be called—that is, invoked throughout all ages—by this name, Son of God, Son of the Most High.

Behold, this is that new creature, that new man of whom the Apostle says: “The first man,” he says, “is of the earth, earthly; the second man, of heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 13). Again: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; but the last, a life-giving spirit” (ibid.). Let us therefore return to what was said above; and, in praise of God the Father, who fashioned the first man by His omnipotence, and in praise of the Holy Spirit, who composed this last man with beautiful fingers, let us compare these two men and bring forth things new and old from His treasure [Col. 1580C] (Matthew 13).

## CHAPTER XI. On the fashioning of the first, earthly man and the conception of this second, heavenly Man; and on how much worthier and more perfect this conception is than that formation

The Father says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, every creature, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth” (Genesis 1). Then Scripture continues and says: “Therefore the Lord formed man of the slime of the earth, and breathed into his face the breath of life; and man became a living soul” (Genesis 2).

Comparing that earthly man with this heavenly Man, we first perceive this lack in the making of the former: God did not bless the earth itself [Col. 1580D] from whose slime He was to form him. But behold, in this new making of the heavenly Man, the archangel says—or rather, the Holy Spirit speaking in the archangel says—“Blessed art thou among women” (Luke 1). And the Psalmist, led hither by prophetic grace, sings in response: “Thou hast blessed thy land, O Lord” (Psalm 84). Moreover, this earth excels even in this, that it is the Lord’s land. For Scripture did not there say, “Therefore God formed man from the slime of His own earth,” but only “from the slime of the earth”; whereas here it says not merely, “Thou hast blessed, O Lord, the earth,” but “Thou hast blessed, O Lord, Thy land,” and so forth.

For what was that earth, and what is this earth? That earth was in no way capable of receiving the seed of God, being irrational, insensible, inanimate, and immobile. But this earth is animate, [Col. 1581A] sentient, rational, and—what is best—faithful; and because of faith, capable of receiving the Holy Spirit and the seed of God. The Holy Spirit, then, is not a better or wiser craftsman than God the Father, although this new Adam, conceived through the operation of the Holy Spirit, is better and worthier than that old Adam whom the Father made; rather, better earth, better matter and nearer to the divine reason, was taken by the Holy Spirit.

Furthermore, the intention of the two potters was not the same here and there. There the Father’s intention was to establish nature; here the Holy Spirit’s intention was to create grace. Thus, as we began to say, the Father says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Elsewhere we have already said that the Trinity plainly speaks in saying, “Let us make.” Yet making was the proper work of the Father, redeeming the proper work of the Son, and enlightening and bringing man to the likeness of God the proper work of the Holy Spirit.

“Let us make man,” therefore, He says. He said this and immediately made man; yet the subsequent narrative does not explain the making of man as having occurred exactly as He proposed when He said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” For it says: “And God created man in His image; in the image of God He created him.” It did not say: “And God created man in His image and likeness”; it did not say, “in the image and likeness of God He created him,” but only that He created him in His image, in the image of God. Thus the same Scripture does not narrate that man was made altogether as God had proposed to make him. And rightly [Col. 1581C] and providently so; for on that occasion, at that time, man did not attain that perfection. He was made in the image of God because he was made rational; he did not attain the likeness of God because he did not imitate God’s gift.

But should his fault, by which he withdrew farther from God’s likeness, frustrate God’s ancient counsel or purpose? Mindful, therefore, of that purpose, the Holy Spirit comes to perform His own part, to perfect the making of man, so that He might bring man to the likeness of God, which man does not attain save by participation in Him—that is, the Holy Spirit. The likeness itself came, I say; the invisible image of God came, and in that blessed Virgin they met one another; [Col. 1581D] in that dwelling of the chaste breast they kissed one another. For, as the Apostle says, the image of God is the Son of God Himself (2 Corinthians 4); but the likeness of both is here the one Spirit of Father and Son.

For this reason it should also be noted that it was not said, “Let us make man in our likeness and image,” but “in our image and likeness.” For as the Son is not the Son of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, but of the Father alone, so He is not the image of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, but of the Father alone. Therefore we would not rightly reverse the order into “in our likeness and image”—“our image,” that is, the image of the Father and the Holy Spirit. But as the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, so He is also the likeness of the Father and the Son. Therefore we affirm that it was rightly said [Col. 1582A]: “in our image and likeness”—“our likeness,” that is, the likeness of the Father and the Son.

The likeness and the invisible image of God thus came together in the blessed Virgin; and, as we sing in the Psalm: “Mercy and truth have met one another; justice and peace have kissed” (Psalm 84). For truth and justice, according to the authority of the Scriptures, are true names of this image, that is, the Son of God; mercy and peace are devout names of this likeness, that is, the Holy Spirit. Thus the saying, “Mercy and truth have met one another,” is repeated in the words, “Justice and peace have kissed.” Then, in saying, “Truth has sprung from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (ibid.), he removes the impiety of the blasphemy which says that Jesus took His beginning from Mary. [Col. 1582B] For the one and same Son of God did indeed spring from the earth according to the flesh, but according to His divinity had previously looked down from heaven.

## CHAPTER XII. On the consideration of this work of the Holy Spirit, with the prophetic testimony in which God the Father says: “My heart hath uttered a good word,” etc.

But how did this Holy Spirit and that Son of God come together in that sanctuary unless the Father sent them, as He says in David: “My heart hath uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly” (Psalm 44)? Nor is this to be understood only of the creation of the world, where the Father uttered a good word in creating something and saying, “Let it be” (Genesis [Col. 1582C] 1), especially since He immediately adds in this passage: “Thou art fairer in beauty than the sons of men; grace is poured out upon thy lips” (Psalm 44), and so forth.

Here also, then—or rather, here most of all—the heart of the Father uttered the good Word into the Virgin’s womb, and He spoke His works to the king. How? “My tongue,” He says—that is, My Spirit—is truly the pen of a scribe writing swiftly; it swiftly inscribed My Word, the good Word, upon human nature, and thus I spoke My works to the king: so that the assumed man might be ignorant of none of all the things I made, and might know how to do all things which I knew how to do. Therefore He who formerly said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” here makes by His Spirit the new man, whom we truly confess to be the very image, and in whom we do not doubt that the fullness of God’s likeness is present.

And there indeed He said: “And let him rule over the fishes of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, every creature, and every creeping thing that moves upon the earth” (Genesis 1). But here He says: “Peoples shall fall beneath thee into the hearts of the king’s enemies. Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the rod of righteousness is the rod of thy kingdom” (Psalm 44). He commanded the former to rule fishes, birds, and beasts, namely by the dignity of reason; but this Man, peoples, namely by the authority of divine majesty. For when He had said, “Peoples shall fall beneath thee into the hearts of the king’s enemies”—although this means the same as, “The peoples who had been enemies will adore thee with true adoration of heart”—lest anything be lacking, even in the precise wording, He immediately added: “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” He plainly called this One God, who [Col. 1583A] ought to rule peoples by so much more than the former ruled fishes, birds, and beasts.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the saying, “Male and female He created them,” and the saying here, “He himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber”; and on how He blessed them and Him

There also it was said: “Male and female He created them; and God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1). “Male and female,” He says, “He created them.” Here, much more honorably, after He had said, “I speak my works to the king; thou art fairer in beauty than the sons of men; grace is poured out upon thy lips,” He then prepares marriage for Him: “The queen stood at thy right hand” (Psalm 44). Yet we must know that, still more secretly, in the lodging of the virginal [Col. 1583B] womb something was done far more beautiful and sweeter than what was there done and said: “Male and female He created them.” For elsewhere it is written also of this Man: “And He himself as a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm 18). From what chamber did this bridegroom proceed, if not from the sacred womb of the undefiled Virgin?

We must know, then, concerning Christ, God and man, that this Holy Spirit did not create them male and female, but in the one Christ, of one and the same person, joined created human nature to the created Word of God. “And He blessed them and said.” Assuredly God blessed this God and man, anointed Him with the oil of blessing—or rather, poured upon His lips the grace of every blessing—as He says: “Grace is poured out upon thy lips; therefore God hath blessed thee for ever.” And immediately: “God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy fellows” (Psalm 44).

“Above thy fellows,” I say. For unlike thy fellows, who, after being conceived in offences or sins, each afterward receives by the grace of the merciful One apportioned gifts of blessing, thou dost not receive thus; rather, in thy very conception thou possessest the fullness of all blessing, so that all thy fellows or partakers may receive from thy fullness. And for what did He bless them? Assuredly that they might increase and multiply; for thus He said: “Increase and multiply.” That blessing, indeed, could not be rendered void on God’s part; but on man’s part [Col. 1583D] it was almost rendered void, so that it would have been better for us had we not been born, had men not increased and multiplied, unless the author of blessing had come to their aid by renewing the blessing.

But for what did God bless this Man? For what did He anoint Him with the oil of gladness above His partakers? Assuredly that He too might increase and multiply: increase in His own person, because He was made a little lower than the angels, and advance to the right hand of Majesty on high, with all things subjected to Him (Hebrews 1; Psalm 8); and multiply in His sons—or rather, His brothers [619] and co-heirs, sons of God, sons of adoption. For this He blessed Him with royal blessing, with priestly blessing. For all who have increased and multiplied through His blessing are kings, are priests; whence, giving thanks, they say: “And thou hast made us a kingdom and priests to our God, and we shall reign upon the earth” (Revelation 5). In them the ordinance of blessing which follows truly remains confirmed: “And fill the earth and subdue it.” For they subject their earthliness and rule over beasts—that is, the bestial vices of themselves and of the men subject to them.

## CHAPTER XIV. On how each man, both the first and this second, was formed from the slime of the earth; what in this Man is not only more venerable but also more marvellous; and why neither the Word nor the Holy Spirit should shrink from a woman’s womb

“Therefore the Lord God formed man from the slime of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life,” [Col. 1584B] “and man”—the first man is understood—“became a living soul” (Genesis 2); but this last man became a life-giving spirit. It is indeed truly proclaimed of both this last and that first man alike that the Lord God formed both the one and the other from the slime of the earth. But among the multitude of the sons of men there has not been, is not, nor will be anyone else of whom this can in the same manner truly be proclaimed. For all men are indeed formed from the slime of the earth, but in a very different manner and order: not by a new work, but by the course of nature.

The Lord God formed both these men from the slime of the earth: the former, indeed, from the slime of insensible and inanimate earth; but the Holy Spirit formed this Man from the slime of earth that was animate—that is, from the moisture of virginal flesh—by His own operation. [Col. 1584C] He formed the former without father and mother; this Man from a mother without a father. Both formations are marvellous. Yet, against those who in heretical rashness argue, “How could a man be formed or born from a virgin?” but do not say, “How could the first man be formed from the slime of the earth?”, we do not hesitate to call the former marvellous but the latter more marvellous. For it is more marvellous that a man should be made from inanimate earth than that a man should be conceived or born from a woman’s flesh, though virginal. Thus this formation is more venerable, but that one more marvellous.

But if thou considerest the greatness of the condescension, among all things made either in heaven or on earth nothing is more marvellous than that God deigned [Col. 1584D] to be conceived or born of a woman. For we do not so greatly marvel that the Almighty could grant conception or childbirth to a virgin; rather, we ought much more to marvel and at the same time to venerate that so great a One willed this: that God, the Son of God, the Spirit of God did not shrink from a woman’s womb. The Word of God, God the Word, did not shrink, I say, from mingling Himself with the moisture of womanly flesh as though a coagulating agent; the Spirit of God, God the Spirit, did not shrink from applying all His fingers and, as a diligent potter, completing from that substance the little vessel of a human body.

Yet if thou attend to reason, what cause was there for divinity to shrink from its own creature? Whoever thou art that shrinkest from such a thing, weigh thine own horror: whether it arises from sensation or from reason. [Col. 1585A] For it differs whether the horror by which thou art affected by something proceeds from sensation or reason. Indeed, in many cases sensation shrinks more from what surpasses it in the judgment of reason. For example, thou shrinkest more from touching a serpent than a stone; yet in judgment thou dost not hesitate to prefer a serpent to a stone, plainly because a stone is an insensible and inanimate thing while a serpent is an animate and sentient body. But God makes use of no senses: God the Son of God acts not by sensation but by reason—indeed, He Himself is everlasting reason.

But if thou weighest the matter rightly, thy horror regarding female nature proceeds more from sensation than from reason. There was therefore nothing for which the Son of God should shrink from His creature—that is, female nature—especially when the Holy Spirit of God, who, as has already been said, is wholly in reason and is the impassible God subject to no senses, had prepared it for Him and preserved it free from every corruption [Col. 1585B].

## CHAPTER XV. On the saying, “Fairer in beauty than the sons of men,” and on why the first man is rightly said only to be formed, while this Man is rightly said to be both form and formed

At last we distinguish this formed Man from that formed man not only in that the Holy Spirit formed this Man from virginal flesh whereas the Lord God formed the other from the slime of the earth, but also by the very term “formation.” For we say that the former is merely formed, whereas this Man is both formed and Form itself [Col. 1585C]. To make this clearer, we must define what a formed thing is and what form alone is. A formed thing is that which consists jointly of matter and form; but form simply speaking is form lacking matter. Nothing such exists except the one God. For He alone is form without matter. He consists of no matter whatsoever, since He was neither created nor made; hence He is subject to no accidents and is unchangeable. All other things are formed, that is, consist of matter and form—as, for example, a statue. For it consists of material, perhaps bronze or stone, and of whatever form the craftsman has chosen: that of a human being, a horse, or anything else whatsoever. Yet bronze itself is not simply form, for it consists of its own matter, namely earth. Earth too is formed, and not simply form. For earth is said to be heavy and dry.

Thus formed thing and form differ in this: simple form is God alone, who is not formed; all else is formed, and among formed things man is without doubt the strongest. For no one doubts that he is formed and that his matter is earth. But that first Adam was man only; this second is both God and man. Therefore the former, as we proposed above, is merely formed; this latter is both formed and Form itself. Hence He is rightly called beautiful or fair: “fairer in beauty than the sons of men” (Psalm 44). This is a most beautiful and devout work of the Holy Spirit: that through the intervention of eternal love, which He Himself is, He joined the Form of the Lord to formed man, by an everlasting and indissoluble union, so that Form and formed thing are one beautiful being, one fair God and man, Jesus Christ, of a single person.

## CHAPTER XVI. On this further difference: God breathed the breath of life into the face of that first man, whereas in this Man the whole Spirit of life, the Spirit of grace, rests

“And He breathed into his face the breath of life” (Genesis 2). This is to be understood simply concerning that man: when the body had been formed from the slime of the earth, God then breathed into his face the breath of life—that is, He implanted in him the created substance of a living soul. [Col. 1586B] For Scripture establishes this when it immediately adds: “And man became a living soul.”

But concerning this Man it must be understood more worthily and divinely: He breathed into His face the breath of life—that is, the Holy Spirit, His maker and the worker of His purity, breathed into His face the Spirit of life, that He might rest in Him and remain there in everlasting abiding. For this was His flower, His rest, which He promised Himself in prophetic truth, Isaiah saying: “And there shall come forth a rod from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11).

But into what face did He breathe this breath of life? Plainly, into the substance of the rational soul. For no one may doubt that the Holy Spirit made the whole man—that is, body and soul—and that the Word of God, God the Word, assumed the whole man. Not, as some heretics maintain, was the Word in the flesh in place of a soul; nor, as others, exceedingly brutish, maintain, did He assume an irrational and brute soul. Rather, true God assumed true flesh and a rational soul, the whole true man, because man had wholly perished in soul and body, and therefore the whole man—that is, soul and body—had to be assumed by the Redeemer.

Into that face, into that rational faculty of the glorious soul, this whole Spirit breathed; and by His fullness He made the creature worthy of the Creator, the created substance worthy of the uncreated God: [Col. 1586D] mature in wisdom, enlarged in understanding, provident in counsel, steadfast in strength, eloquent in knowledge, gentle in piety, humble in holy fear. For God the Word did not need to be filled with the Holy Spirit, since that same Holy Spirit proceeds from Him no less than from God the Father. But the created soul of our needy nature, with its flesh, needed to receive this Spirit; and it received Him not by measure, as John testifies: “For God giveth not the Spirit by measure” (John 3), but received, as already said, the entire sevenfold grace of the Spirit. Hence man “became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15).

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 1587A] On comparison of the expressions, “The first man became a living soul; the last, a life-giving spirit”

Let us compare also this part of the apostolic definition—“a life-giving spirit”—with the older phrase, “a living soul.” In the latter there is truly the scantness of poverty; in the former, the fullness of riches. For when he says, “a living soul,” it must be understood, “and not able to give life.” For our first parent was indeed made a living man, so that he could naturally transmit seed for the propagation of offspring; yet he did not have the power either to give a living soul to his own seed or to confer spiritual grace upon the already living soul of his offspring.

But this Man, prior to His forerunner John and therefore undoubtedly older than he in His own flesh, was so made that, though He was to generate nothing according to the animal man, He might give life in the Spirit to those generated in the flesh before or after Him. His own forerunner testifies to this, saying: “And of his fullness we have all received” (John 1). For the prophets received prophetic grace from His fullness before He became man; and after He became man, they received in this same Spirit the remission of sins. Therefore “a living soul” is far less; “a life-giving spirit” far higher.

Although after Him the apostles and apostolic men, Catholic bishops and orthodox presbyters give life by preaching and baptizing, yet this Man alone and only He was made “a life-giving spirit.” For neither we nor our forebears received from the fullness of the apostles, but from this fullness of His, from which the apostles and prophets received. For they could do nothing, either for us or for themselves, without Him.

Let us follow the order of the operation of the Holy Spirit in this heavenly Man, looking at His pattern in that earthly man, which the Apostle briefly indicated in saying, “who is the figure of him that was to come” (Romans 5).

## CHAPTER XVIII. On how God placed that man in the paradise of delight; whereas, more marvellously, the Holy Spirit bestowed a kind of paradise upon this Man and brought forth from it the river of evangelical teaching

[Col. 1587D] “Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which He placed the man whom He had formed; and the Lord God brought forth from the ground every tree beautiful to behold and sweet for food, the tree of life also in the midst of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And a river issued from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it divides into four heads” (Genesis 2).

Indeed, before this flower had risen from the rod of Jesse’s stock, the same Lord, the same God, the Holy Spirit, had planted a spiritual paradise of delight, and in it every tree beautiful to behold and sweet for food; but He had been able to rest upon none of all the trees. For the Church was the paradise of the holy patriarchs and prophets of old; and in it Abraham was a beautiful tree, Isaac a beautiful tree, Jacob a beautiful tree, and the other holy and righteous fathers beautiful and pleasant trees, whose fruits of faith are even today very sweet for those who read them to eat—that is, to imitate. The Spirit of the Lord sometimes alighted upon the flowers of such trees; but, as has been said, He could rest upon none of them.

The Lord planted such a paradise of delight from the beginning—that is, from the first chosen person. For the first chosen person was the first planting of this paradise. The Lord God placed that man in a local paradise; but the Holy Spirit placed this spiritual paradise, marvellously, in this Man. Yet to whom will this seem marvellous, if he rightly considers the greatness of His soul? For a soul in which the fullness of divinity dwells is not of small capacity [Col. 1588B] (Colossians 2).

Therefore—and more truly I may say—such a soul itself became the paradise of God’s delights, containing within itself the whole planted paradise of the Scriptures: the tree of life also in the midst of paradise, that is, the very substance of the eternal Word in its midst; and likewise the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, that is, the temptations arising from the weakness which He assumed from us. For because the first man was tempted and overcome through that tree, human weakness is rightly understood by it; and through this weakness this Man was tempted and found faithful—tempted, I say, “in all things according to the likeness, without sin” (Hebrews 4)—so that He who already knew our formation by knowledge might know it also by experience, and, having experienced it, might know how to reject evil and choose good (Isaiah 7).

Yet in a certain manner this Man too was placed in paradise, namely as “a minister of the circumcision” (Romans 15), that He might work the works of the Spirit in the garden of the paternal law. The river which issues for us from this paradise is evangelical teaching. The river of this teaching is divided for us into four heads, that is, the four Gospels; or into the four chief mysteries of Christ: His incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension. By faith in and confession of these, the whole world is watered through baptism.

## CHAPTER XIX. On how the Holy Spirit placed this Man a second time in paradise, and how this tempted Man conquered the tempter who had conquered the first man

“Therefore the Lord took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight, to work and keep it.” It had already been said that the Lord God planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which He had placed the man whom He had formed. Was that earthly man therefore placed twice in that paradise? Certainly not. That earthly man was not placed there twice; but this heavenly Man was placed twice in the spiritual paradise by the Holy Spirit.

For after He had already placed Him there by the placement of incarnation which we have described, the same Spirit placed Him by the placement of the preaching enjoined upon Him. The manner of this second placement is as follows: “And it came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and Jesus, being baptized and praying, that heaven was opened; and the Holy Spirit descended in bodily form as a dove upon him” [Col. 1589A] (Luke 3). And afterward: “But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit into the desert” (Luke 4).

This manner of placement differs from the former, both according to the wording already set down and according to the present matter. For it was said first that He placed in paradise the man whom He had formed, and nothing was added. But afterward, when it had first been said, “Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight,” there is added, “to work and keep it.” Thus, in the first placement by which this Holy Spirit placed this heavenly Man in His paradise—the first placement, I say, of incarnation—until His thirtieth year no exercise of any work is mentioned. But in this repeated placement He Himself acted and spoke thus: “He returned in the power of the Spirit into Galilee, and came to Nazareth, and entered the synagogue on the Sabbath day according to his custom, and stood up to read. And the book of Isaiah the prophet was delivered to him. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, wherefore he hath anointed me; he hath sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, to heal the broken of heart, and to preach deliverance to captives, sight to the blind, to send the bruised away in deliverance, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.’ And when he had folded the book, he returned it to the minister and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed upon him. And he began to say to them: ‘This Scripture is fulfilled today in your hearing’” (Luke 4; Isaiah 61).

Therefore the Lord God truly took His man—the Lord and God, the Holy Spirit, took His heavenly and new Man—and placed Him in the paradise of His delight, in the paradise of the Church: no ordinary paradise now, but the paradise of His delightful dwelling-place. From that time He placed Him there to work and keep it: to work, I say, according to the dovelike simplicity of the Holy Spirit Himself, and to keep it against the serpent-like cunning of the devil.

For this is especially an answering contrast: the devil was sent to that earthly man in a serpent, whereas this Holy Spirit was sent upon this heavenly Man in the form of a dove. Thus the former fell into temptation through the serpent; this Man, through the dove—that is, through this Spirit of piety—conquered the tempter. For when this man, driven by this Spirit into the desert, had fasted forty days and forty nights and eaten nothing, and was suffering the natural hunger of that man’s appetite, the devil, that ancient serpent, said to Him: “If thou art the Son of God, command this stone that it become bread.” He answered with what this gentle dove, this Holy Spirit, suggested, what the dovelike Scripture had forewarned in holy speech: “Man liveth not by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God” (Luke 4).

Thus He clothed the disgrace of incontinent appetite with the beauty of self-control; and thus the dove, in a marvellous contest with the serpent, outwitted the malicious one by simplicity, thereafter gradually leading man onward to perfection, until by perfect obedience He utterly trampled down and crushed the head and [Col. 1590A] body of the serpent. But now let our discourse chiefly attend to the dove itself, to which this particular part of our little work is especially dedicated.

## CHAPTER XX. Why this Spirit came upon Him a second time, and why He chose to signify Him by a dove rather than by another form
First we ask what was the reason that the Holy Spirit should come upon this man of his, not in just any manner, but as a dove; and from whom might we ask more fittingly than from him who saw it and, having seen it, bore witness that this is the Son of God? For he says: “And I did not know him. But that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing with water” (John 1). Again: “And I did not know him. But he who sent me to baptize with water [Col. 1590B] said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (ibid.).

Therefore John was seeking him and wished to know the one whom he did not know by appearance; and, desiring to know, he struck heaven with the deep sighs of profound longing, so that the one whom he knew to have come in the Spirit, yet did not recognize in appearance, might be revealed to him. For he was not thrusting himself forward by seeking testimony. He remained hidden in himself; he did not glorify himself, offering to all an example of humility which the Apostle profitably preached to his own, saying: “No one takes the honor to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was.” So Christ also “did not glorify himself, that he might become a High Priest,” but he who said to him: “You are my Son” (Heb. 4), [Col. 1590C] etc.

Accordingly, it was not in order that he might become Christ—that is, not that he might then first be anointed, he who at the very beginning of his conception had been fully anointed—but in order that it might be made manifest in Israel who was Christ, that his anointing came upon the Anointed One: his own Spirit came upon Christ in a visible form. Yet the same Spirit could likewise have manifested him through another form. Why then did he appear over him as a dove rather than as fire or flame?
