The answer is that by this or some similar sign, anyone moderately anointed could fittingly have been revealed—that is, one in whom not a princely but an ordinary, not a universal but a particular grace was signified as given, and not the whole fullness of grace itself as dwelling. But here the one to be revealed was he “in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily” [Col. 1590D] (Col. 2). Therefore such a sign had to be given for his manifestation as it had never been fitting to use before or after for any saint. For what is a dove? Surely, something whole: head and limbs, an entire body.

Thus it signified that in this uniquely anointed one the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily—“bodily,” I say, 622 that is, just as the dove appeared over him and remained in him with an entire body, no part of the dove’s body mutilated, so it signifies that no grace of the sevenfold Spirit is lacking to this great Priest. Hence he is the Father of adoption, the supreme prince of all the children of God, and the great High Priest.

Finally, Matthew is chiefly concerned with his kingship, Luke especially with his priesthood. [Col. 1591A] The sacred generation and conception of this great Priest, celebrated as effected by the Holy Spirit, concerning which we have spoken according to our ability, the eloquent calf recounts with holy utterance. Therefore this too must be noted: what Matthew did not do, Luke does here in writing the genealogy—he ascends upward, weaving together the entire genealogy of adoption, which belongs to priestly ministry. For this priest was not to beget according to the flesh, but to sanctify according to the Spirit.

Thus, although Matthew traced the generation of the flesh by descending almost directly, Luke, ascending, did not touch even one step of carnal generation with the word, but began thus: “As was supposed, the son of Joseph,” and immediately added: “who was of Heli” (Luke 3)—that is, understood as an adoptive son. For according to the flesh, not Heli [Col. 1591B] but Jacob was his father. After this beginning, he nowhere uses the word employed by Matthew, namely “begot” (Matt. 1); he sufficiently shows that he intends not the carnal generation of a man but the spiritual generation of a priest.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the distinctive properties of the individual graces which he bestowed upon him all together: wisdom, understanding, and so forth

It is worthwhile to distinguish, from the acts that follow, the distinctive properties of the several graces—namely, wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear (Isa. 11).

Certainly, this especially belongs to wisdom: when, immediately after being led by the same Spirit into the wilderness, “he had fasted forty days and forty nights” (Matt. 4; Mark 1; Luke 4), he overcame the ancient deceits committed by the tempter, fleeing sin—which is the highest wisdom. Yet this passage contains something proper to knowledge as well: namely, that he takes his answers from the treasury of the Scriptures and says: “It is written: ‘Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.’ It is written: ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.’ It is written: ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test’” (ibid.).

Understanding is shown when the book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him and he found written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he anointed me; he sent me to preach good news to the poor, to heal the broken-hearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to send forth the oppressed into release”; and he says, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 3). For when he says these things, he understands—and wishes them to be understood as—spiritual healing of those spiritually broken, [Col. 1591D] spiritual release of those spiritually captive, spiritual sight of those spiritually blind, and spiritual sending forth of those spiritually oppressed.

Further, he gives certain signs of hidden counsel to those who have eyes or ears, when he says: “Truly I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when heaven was shut for three years and six months, when a great famine came over all the land; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow woman at Zarephath of the Sidonians. And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (3 Kings 17; 4 Kings 4; Luke 4). For in saying this, he truly indicates that he holds within himself that counsel: [Col. 1592A] namely, that when the heaven of mercy is shut against the proud Jews, he will cause the entire rain of legal and prophetic grace to migrate to the Gentiles; and, leaving the leprosy of the Jews’ sin uncured, he hastens to cleanse the leprosy of the Gentiles by the sevenfold washing—that is, by the complete grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

The first act of fortitude occurs when, after they had driven him out of the city and led him to the brow of the hill on which their city was built in order to throw him down, “he himself, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4). In this very act he signifies a greater work of fortitude. What is it? Surely this: when at last, after many persecutions, they wished to cast him down into hell, he himself passed from death into life, or through death into his glory; behold, he went through their midst—[Col. 1592B] through the midst of those persecuting him and not seeing him—and passed over to the believing and enlightened Gentiles.

Moreover, it was an act of fortitude that demons were tortured by his presence and confessed their torments, saying: “Leave us! What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? We know who you are: the Holy One of God.” But he rebuked them and did not allow them to speak, saying to one of them: “Be silent, and come out” (ibid.). What great fortitude this beginning or sign represented, he himself indicates sparingly in one place: “When a strong man, armed, guards his court, his possessions are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, he takes away all his armor in which he trusted and distributes his spoils” (Luke 11).

Knowledge was shown in what we have already touched on: how readily, how suitably to matter and time, he everywhere always produced testimonies drawn from all the Scriptures, so that his astonished opponents said: “How does this man know letters, when he has not learned?” (John 7).

No one can fail to know that piety is shown when he intends the meaning of parables such as these: “A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers” (Luke 10). Again: The master of the house, angry because he had prepared a great supper and all who had been invited began together to excuse themselves, said to his servant: “Go quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in here the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame” (Luke 14). Again: “Which of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness [Col. 1592D] and go after the one that was lost until he finds it? And when he finds it, he lays it on his shoulders rejoicing” (Luke 15). Again: “A certain man had two sons; and the younger of them said to his father: ‘Father, give me the portion of the property that falls to me’” (ibid.). Again: “There was a certain rich man who had a steward, and this man was accused to him as though he had squandered his goods” (Luke 16), etc.

These, finally, are the venerable marks of piety: namely, that the Samaritan, moved by compassion for the man who fell among robbers, approached him, bound his wounds, poured in oil and wine, put him upon his own beast, brought him to an inn, and took care of him (Luke 10). And likewise elsewhere: that, moved by compassion, he ran and fell upon the neck of the one who had returned through repentance—one who by his own judgment was now unworthy to be called a son—and kissed him; [Col. 1593A] and killed for him the fattened calf, saying: “Let us eat and celebrate, for this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15). That the good shepherd sought the sheep which had strayed and, having found it, joyfully laid it on his shoulders; that, following the example of the steward of unrighteousness, whom the master praised because he had acted prudently, he judged that we ought to act thus: “Make friends for yourselves from unrighteous mammon,” he says, “so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 15).

Finally, the holy and venerable fear is shown in this: he does not offer himself with boastful contempt for death, but, afraid and suffering weariness, kneels and prays: “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; take [Col. 1593B] this cup away from me”; and, greatly humbled in the same reverent fear, says: “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14). Further, the mark of true and perfect fear in him is that an angel from heaven appeared to strengthen him; and, being in agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the earth (Luke 22). Clearly it befitted him to give future martyrs a useful example, that they should not presume upon the strength of their endurance but should be anxiously afraid in the humility of patience.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the seven natural virtues of the dove: how each of them signifies a particular virtue or grace, and in what ways Christ spiritually possesses these same virtues of the dove in his acts

[Col. 1593C] Therefore the Spirit of sevenfold grace rested wholly upon him, in accordance with the sign by which this was manifested—that is, in accordance with the dove’s complete body. Accordingly, this too must not be passed over: the nature of this bird, namely the dove, exercises seven virtues of its own, by a certain likeness corresponding to the seven graces of this Holy Spirit which we have mentioned.

First, it sits above streams of water, so that, when it sees the shadow of a hawk, it may swiftly escape. Second, it eats nothing living. Third, it nourishes the young of others. Fourth, it nests in the holes of a rock. Fifth, it gathers the whiter grains. Sixth, it lacks gall. Seventh, it has a groan instead of song.

Thus, in its sitting beside streams and guarding against the hawk there is an image of wisdom; [Col. 1593D] in its rearing the young of others, of counsel; in its nesting in the holes of the rock, of fortitude; in its gathering the whiter grains, of knowledge; in its lack of gall, of piety; and in its having a groan instead of song, an image of fear.

For this Holy Spirit—or rather he in whom the Holy Spirit is, especially our Lord, the possessor of its entire fullness—sat beside the fullest streams of the Scriptures, foreseeing and powerfully avoiding all the temptations of the ancient enemy; and this belongs to wisdom. He eats nothing living: that is, he never condemned any righteous person, nor did he incorporate into himself, through respect of persons, anyone living wickedly—that is, serving desires and vices; and this is understanding. He nourishes other young: that is, after the Jews were cast off, he receives the Gentiles to be nourished, we who were strangers to God’s covenant; and this belongs to incomprehensible and unsearchable counsel. [Col. 1594A]

He nests in the rock where the serpent cannot approach: that is, he places the hope of his own in the wounds of his passion, where the devil cannot snatch it away; and this belongs to fortitude. He gathers the whiter grains: that is, in all his speech he brings together the more lucid meanings from the heap of the Scriptures; and this belongs to knowledge. He lacked gall: that is, he did not return evil for evil or curse for curse; indeed, he even prayed for his executioners, saying: “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23); and this belongs to piety. He had groaning instead of song: that is, with unutterable groanings and, as the Apostle says, “with a loud cry and many tears,” interceding for us (Heb. 5), he “became obedient [Col. 1594B] unto death” (Phil. 2); and this belongs to fear.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That the dove itself was the sign of this matter, which the Church firmly maintains: namely, that he is the one who baptizes

Of what, then, was that kind of form a sign or manifestation? It was surely the sign of our Lord, the unique Priest and sole Baptizer, in that he baptizes. For it was said: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending as a dove and remaining in him, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1). It was not said, “This is the Son of God,” or “This is the Christ,” though this too could truly have been said; rather, “This is the one who baptizes.”

Therefore John the Baptist was seeking the Baptizer; he longed for baptism—that is, he desired this effect and this benefit, for which he rejoiced that Christ had come: he thirsted to see Christ and to point him out when seen, so that he might baptize in the Holy Spirit, that is, take away the sins of the world. For the whole world was in filth; every human being was unclean and unwashed. Not the Gentile world alone was defiled by the flow of blood; the Holy Spirit also judged all the righteousnesses of the Synagogue, through the prophets, to be like a menstrual cloth (Isa. 64).

“What then,” you ask, “of Abraham? Was not he at least clean, when Scripture says: ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness’?” (Gen. 12). Certainly, he was not yet clean by reason of that righteousness; but by reason of that righteousness he merited, upon receiving the promise, to hope for this purifier. Therefore, until the one who baptizes came, Abraham and all his posterity, merely instructed by the word of promise, waited outside and did not yet participate in the heavenly Church through the vision of God. [Col. 1594D]

What of John himself, who while still in his mother’s womb was filled with the Holy Spirit? Why then did he say: “I ought to be baptized by you” (Matt. 3)? When he leapt in his mother’s womb at the voice of Mary’s greeting, could he not have been cleansed by that same joy of the Holy Spirit through which he leapt? Certainly he was not yet clean by reason of this, nor had he thereby already put off the stain of original guilt. There he received the Holy Spirit not for the remission of sins but for prophetic—indeed, more than prophetic—grace.

Therefore John the Baptist desired baptism for himself and for the whole world, [Col. 1595A] and his desire received this answer: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending as a dove and remaining in him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1). And just as the righteous Simeon, awaiting the consolation of Israel and having this Holy Spirit within him, received from the Spirit himself the answer that he would not see death before he had first seen Christ God (Luke 2), so this man—no less than Simeon or any saint in holy longing—received from the grace dwelling in him the answer that he would not finish his course of baptizing in water before he had first seen the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, granting remission of sins to the whole world.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That this one, by the grace of the one Holy Spirit, truly baptizes and has baptized all the elect; and that this must be maintained against the heresies and schisms of unbelievers

This was not said only because of the common need then existing in the human race, but also in order to preserve the guardianship of peace and charity in the future Church; and so it was said, and such a sign was given.

Indeed, it is certain, and no one may doubt, 624 that he washed all the saints who had awaited him through the past generations from the beginning of the world—all, I say, down to that chosen thief—of all sins through himself in the Holy Spirit, in the water and blood flowing from his side (Rev. 1). But he was to baptize, through the ministers of his grace, [Col. 1595C] those who would believe in this same Holy Spirit, in the sacrament of that same water and blood.

For here there were surely bound to be disputes of crows quarreling separately and baptizing separately, and saying against one another: “I baptize; I sanctify. Could that adulterer, drunkard, or fornicator baptize you? Could he sanctify you? The faith of that man or this man who baptized you was dead without works; therefore he gave you a dead baptism.” Thus, suitably and rightly, while the peace-making dove designated it, it was said: “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3).

For those who were baptized would be so prone to divisions that they would be puffed up and quarrel not only for good men against bad, but even for good men against good—as though for their own supposedly best baptizers against less good baptizers. They had already begun to do this, those to whom the Apostle, the vessel of election, said: “It has been reported to me concerning you, brothers, by those of Chloe, that there are quarrels among you. What I mean is that each of you says: ‘I belong to Paul’; ‘I belong to Apollos’; ‘I belong to Cephas’; ‘I belong to Christ.’ Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1). [Col. 1595D]

Here he had rightly understood what the gentle dove preferred—that is, this Spirit of piety, the Spirit of unity and peace—when it designated one and said: “This is the one who baptizes.” As though it said: “Whether the Church visibly employs good ministers or bad, eminent or lowly, this is the one who invisibly baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

But fuller discussion must be given later, after some intervening matters, concerning the baptism of the Lord Christ and of this Holy Spirit. For now, let this be said: this Holy Spirit declared that at last he had obtained—or rather, had made for himself—the one unique dwelling worthy of him (Matt. 3; Luke 3; John 1; Mark 1), when he appeared in such a form over this man who was properly his own and remained in him—not by measure, granting him a divisible grace as to his participants or associates, but dwelling in him bodily with his entire Godhead (Col. 2). [Col. 1596A] And by descending upon him when the heavens were opened, he testified that through his passion the heavens would be opened to those believing in him—heavens which, from the time humankind sinned, had been closed to the human race.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the statement, “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan”; and why, although it is said of the other spirits, “And the Spirit shall rest upon him,” of fear alone it is said, “And the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him”

“But Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4). “Full,” I say, “of the Holy Spirit”: for the dove itself, as we have already said, had signified this by descending upon him and remaining in him.

But was the Lord Jesus full of the Holy Spirit only from that time and not before? Was he not conceived of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin’s womb? Or, when he formed that temple of his sacred body, did the Spirit stand outside and not enter until the man had reached [Col. 1596C] his thirtieth year? Indeed, the uncircumscribed Spirit of God did not stand outside when God created the sacred body; nor, after creating it once, did grace ever depart or become absent at any hour or moment, as though growing cold.

Why then is he now first said to be full of the Holy Spirit when he returns from the Jordan? Certainly because the Holy Spirit, who had hitherto kept himself within, began here to go forth: from the banquet chamber of the mind to the functions of the body; from power to action; from inward rest to outward ministry. Thus, through teaching, he might pour grace upon the lips; through the performance of miracles, he might set his hands in motion—hands “turned like gold, full of hyacinths.”

Further, he rightly ought to be called full of the Holy Spirit from the point at which [Col. 1596D] he began to do those things which belong to the Spirit of the fear of the Lord: namely, to suffer hunger by fasting, to endure the deceits of the tempter, to travel about and preach the kingdom of God, and, in accordance with the Father’s will or command, to become “obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). For it had been written: “And the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 2).

Finally, in the entire sequence of the seven spirits it should be noted that, although it is said, “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety” (ibid.), in these spirits the verb of resting is not changed; but in the seventh, the wording or mode of expression is at last changed: “And the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” Therefore, if we are aware that the Evangelist deliberately agrees here with the Prophet, so that, because the latter had said, “And the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall rest upon him,” the former, observing the force of the earlier expression, correspondingly said, “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan,” [Col. 1597A] then a spectacle for the wonder of the whole creation is set before us: namely, that the Creator of human beings descended even to the point from which sinful humanity, rising out of infernal sins and vices, must take the beginning of its ascent. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110 [Vulgate numbering]).

The Creator descended this far when the Prophet said, after all the degrees of the spirits of the Lord: “And the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” It was not remarkable that the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety should rest upon him—not remarkable, I say, because it was magnificent: all these things declared the divine majesty by ancient dignity. But what angel or human being would not marvel that the Lord descended even to the fear of the Lord—that God and Lord, to be feared by heaven and earth, became fearful, not partially but fully, and as fully as human beings speaking in the same Holy Spirit were able to signify by the word “filling” or “fullness”? Accordingly, with fitting wonder it is said: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. That he by whom Jesus is said to be full is truly God, and that filling the soul of any human being belongs to God alone

Furthermore, since in the present work we intend not merely to recount the works of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1597C] but also to proclaim, venerate, and adore his very person, let Macedonius—or whoever else is guilty of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—hear this, he who has dared to say, “He is not God,” or, I say, concerning the words, “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit.” What then? Is he not God, he by whom the Lord Jesus, who fills all things, is full?

Indeed, leaving aside for the moment that particular man, to fill any human being of more limited capacity belongs to none but God. Let us put it more clearly: to enter substantially into the spirit of a human being belongs to none but God. A created spirit cannot be infused into a created spirit: an angelic spirit into a human spirit, or a human spirit into an angelic spirit. Neither is capable of containing the other, nor can either be contained by the other. For neither [Col. 1597D] 625 is subtler than the other. Both are creatures; both are rational and immortal. God alone, subtler by nature or substance than both, can therefore be contained by both.

But behold: not only do we read everywhere that human beings are filled with the Holy Spirit, but the Evangelist declares that the Lord Jesus himself is full of the Holy Spirit. How, then, did that aforesaid crow Macedonius fail to see that this dove, this Holy Spirit, is God?

But perhaps he would say in reply: “Is not a human being sometimes said to be, and in fact is, full of an evil spirit?” To this I say: he is indeed said to be so, but the one is filled by the Holy Spirit in one way and the other by an evil spirit in another. For an evil spirit is not substantially infused into the substance of the human spirit itself; rather, creeping in through hidden passages and received through the cavities of the body, it besieges the soul in its own seats and tortures it with infernal scourges to whatever extent it is permitted. [Col. 1598A] Thus fever, and likewise the excessive heat of drink, overturns the mind and destroys the power of reason; yet neither fever nor the wine’s intoxicating force, to be processed through the body, fills the very substance of the soul.

But this Holy Spirit enters substantially into the substance of the soul; ineffably, by expanding it he fills it, and by filling it he expands it. He dwells and walks substantially within it. This is the reward, this the glory laid up for the saints in the future. For in the present age it belongs to very few even to perceive, if only for an hour or a moment, his substantial touch—apart from this one singular man, of whom alone it was uniquely said: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining in him.”

What we have said is plainly easy to establish from the very names of this same Holy Spirit: “the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel, the spirit of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge, the spirit of piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” For where, do you suppose, do wisdom or understanding dwell, except in the soul? Where do counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, or the fear of the Lord dwell, except in the soul or mind? Therefore this uncreated Spirit alone can be substantially contained by a human or angelic spirit; and from this fact alone Macedonius and every such crow are convicted that this dove is such, this Holy Spirit so great, that he is God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That, where Jesus is said to be full, all of us are invited to draw; that there are two gifts of this Spirit; and which the ancient Fathers received first and which afterwards; likewise, what we received first and what afterwards

[Col. 1598C] Certainly, when he is here said to be full of the Holy Spirit, by that same saying we are invited to draw from him. Likewise, when that other witness of this fullness says, “And from his fullness we have all received” (John 1), we are urged to receive, urged to draw. He is the one from whom, in whom, and through whom we draw grace and truth; we have received the Spirit of grace and the Spirit of truth.

For after saying, “And from his fullness we have all received,” he immediately added: “And grace for grace, because the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (ibid.). Both we and those who say, “From his fullness we have all received”—we, I say, both those after and those before the passion of this one who is full—have drawn the same gifts, but in a reversed order.

For how many, or what, are the gifts of this Spirit except two: one for the remission of sins, the other for distributions of graces? We and they received these same things, but not in the same order. For they first received distributions of graces and afterwards remission of sins; we first received remission of sins and then distributions of graces (1 Cor. 12). For all up to John first received distributions of graces; indeed, they died before receiving remission [Col. 1599A] of sins. They received this long-awaited remission only at last in Christ’s passion. They were strong in faith, powerful in miracles, and mighty in prophetic grace; and yet they were all kept in the underworld because of original sin.

Christ’s blood was shed, and water ran with the blood from his side; and because they had possessed faith, it washed away the sins of all of them. The apostles too first received certain graces of this kind, so as to heal the sick and cast out unclean spirits; and, after Christ’s passion, they received remission of sins in order to enter the kingdom of heaven. But all of us who have come to faith after that same passion of Christ are first baptized for the remission of sins, and only then receive such graces from the same Holy Spirit, “distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

That this gift was manifestly bestowed upon Cornelius and the others who together heard the word, although they had not yet been baptized for the remission of sins—for the Holy Spirit fell upon them, and they spoke in tongues and magnified God (Acts 10)—occurred through the necessary advocacy of this Holy Spirit at that time. For those who believed from the circumcision said, and would go on saying: “Why did you enter men who have the foreskin?” (Acts 11). Therefore, so that authority for receiving into Christ’s faith those uncircumcised in the flesh should not be lacking, God suitably presented himself here as advocate—this Spirit whom the flesh would not dare to prohibit—so that, under great protection, Peter might firmly say: [Col. 1599C] “If therefore God gave them the same grace as he gave to us who believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who then was I, that I could prohibit God?” (ibid.). Apart from this, almost nowhere after the glorification of the Lord Jesus do we find that this Holy Spirit was given first in distributions of graces rather than in remission of sins.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the procession of the Holy Spirit against those who said that he proceeds from the Father alone and not from the Son; and that, in the procession through which sins are remitted, he proceeds from the person of the Son

Accordingly, since there are two persons, Father and Son, from whom this Holy Spirit proceeds, so there are, as has been said, two gifts of the same Spirit. We judge it not implausible to say that, by the procession in which he proceeds from the Father, his operation is distributed in the divisions of graces; but by the procession in which he proceeds from the Son, the same Spirit is given for the remission of sins.

For did the patriarchs and prophets confess the Son of God before human beings? Yet they received diverse gifts of charisms, not because they had known the Son or believed in him, but so that they might know him and, believing, await his coming. Their being prophets and foreknowing that the Son of God would come was received not by a prior confession of Father and Son, but of the Father alone, or of God alone.

But once the Son of God presented himself as human to human beings, and the purse full of God’s gold—that is, full of the fullness of this Holy Spirit—was torn open by the suffering of the passion, then from that point this same Holy Spirit proceeded, or began to proceed, for the remission of sins. [Col. 1600A] No one doubts it, distrusts it, or questions it except an unbeliever. He then proceeded to the dead held in the prison-enclosures of the underworld, fettered by the hereditary bond of sin from Adam; and he washed all the righteousness of the saints, hitherto comparable to a menstrual cloth, until it was pure and perfect. From then on, he proceeds to all the living who are baptized into the same death of the same Son of God, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, against the error of those who said that this Holy Spirit proceeds not from Father and Son but from the person of the Father alone, it must firmly be said that the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father is the distribution of graces, while his proceeding from the Son is the remission of sins. Which of these is the better gift, the more beneficial or happier, we have no doubt; with the Psalmist we say: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31 [Vulgate numbering]). He did not say, “Blessed are those who have prophecy,” though he himself was certainly one of them, and foremost among them; but he said, “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven”—the whole body of whom is the one Church of all the elect. Desiring or hoping to be one of them, he said elsewhere: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50 [Vulgate numbering]).

## CHAPTER XXIX. How he who is full of the Holy Spirit, in whom the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, is said not to know something; and that there is a threefold mode of knowing
One further point remains to be investigated in this theme. If Jesus is full of the Holy Spirit (Luke 4), if the whole dove remains in him, if “all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him” (Col. 2), how does he confess either that he does not know something or that he cannot do something? For he says: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Matt. 24). And in John: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5). Again: “I cannot of myself do anything. As I hear, I judge” [Col. 1600D] (ibid.).

First we inquire concerning that day: why or how did he say, “No one knows, neither the angels nor the Son, but the Father alone”? For if here we understand in “the Father alone” only one person, and consequently judge that neither the Son nor this Holy Spirit knows that day, then assuredly we do not maintain the unity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in divinity, nor their equality in majesty. And where then is that which the whole Church says to the Son through the mouth of the apostle Peter: “Lord, you know all things” (John 21)? Where is that which the apostle Paul says of this Holy Spirit: “The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. 2)?

Therefore what is said—“of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels nor the Son”—must be received more faithfully and reverently. Certainly, we faithfully say that “the Son does not know,” that is, he does not make you know [Col. 1601A] it. But this does not satisfy against Arian disputations, since neither does the Father make us know it. Therefore, that we may hold more firmly and soundly what he said, let us consider the speaker’s intention, and at the same time ask whether the mode of knowing is simple or manifold.

This immediately suggests itself: it is manifold. For we are said to know what we understand; to know what we do not disapprove; and to know what we have experienced. These modes differ greatly in God, if you observe rightly. In the first mode, the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—always knows all things. In the second mode, he always knows good things and never knows evil things. In the third mode, he sometimes knows and sometimes does not know certain good things or certain evil things: good things, for example, when he says to Abraham, “Now I know that you fear God, and have not spared your only-begotten [Col. 1601B] son for my sake” (Gen. 22). For what was in Abraham—namely, fear of the Lord—he declared that he now knew in the mode in which he had not known it before, namely by experience.

Likewise, with evils, when, for example, he says to Abraham: “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grievous. I will go down and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry which has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. 18). For he wished to know what was evil, indeed most evil, in the mode in which he had not previously known it—that is, by experience. And this occurred. For he immediately knew in that mode, because, with the same crime by which they were accustomed to rage against men, raging likewise against him, they said to Lot: “Where are the men who entered your house at night? Bring them out here, that we may know them” (Gen. [Col. 1601C] 19).

Since, therefore, there are three modes of God’s knowledge or cognition, let us ask, in order to know according to which mode he said, “Of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels in heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone,” what the speaker’s intention was. This also readily presents itself to those who seek it: plainly, he said this in order to instill in us fear of that day—of his coming and of the consummation of the age. For he had said: “Then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty. And he shall send his angels with a trumpet and a loud voice, and they shall gather his elect from the four winds, from the heights of the heavens to their bounds” (Matt. 24; Mark 13).

Therefore, in his saying, “Of that day and hour no one knows, neither [Col. 1601D] the angels nor the Son, but the Father alone,” we faithfully understand this sense, as if he had said: That day will be of such wrath, such calamity and misery, such tribulation and anguish, as no one has ever been able, can now be able, or will be able to know beforehand by experience—not the angels of heaven, in that dreadful division of light and darkness, that is, of good and evil angels; nor the Son in the whole agony of his passion or death.

For it is evident that by “the Son,” that is, himself, insofar as he is man, he set himself in place of every human being. He did not say, “Neither the angels in heaven nor men on earth,” but, “Neither the angels in heaven, nor the Son.” It follows, therefore, that when he says, “except the Father alone,” it is as though he had said: except God alone—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—especially [Col. 1602A] since he did not say “my Father,” in which one person would necessarily be understood.

And that God knows the greatness and bitterness of that day not by experience—for he is the impassible God—but holds this knowledge in himself in such a way that no creature can know otherwise than by the act itself and the actual event what anguish will be there, where, as God himself says to blessed Job: “Before the eyes of all, that beast shall be cast down” (Job 40); and: “When he is lifted up, the angels shall fear, and, terrified, shall be purified” (Job 41). Indeed, if we or the angels then were mortal, or if after the resurrection we could in any way die, the mere sight would render us lifeless: we would see hell opened and the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, into which [Col. 1602B] we too would have been hurled had we not been prevented by grace alone.

## Chapter XXX. Of how great a power it is that the Son himself says that he cannot do anything except what he sees the Father doing.

It remains to inquire concerning what he says: “The Son cannot do anything”; and, “I cannot of myself do anything” (John 5). For this likewise seemed contrary to the fullness of which he was speaking, unless it is rightly understood as befits the subject.

First, therefore, let us in this case also gather from the preceding sayings and deeds the speaker’s intention. They are as follows: “Rise, take up your pallet, and walk.” And immediately the man was made well; he took up [Col. 1602C] his pallet and walked. Now it was the Sabbath on that day. Therefore the Jews said to the man who had been healed: “It is the Sabbath; it is not lawful for you to carry your pallet.” And afterwards: “Therefore the Jews persecuted Jesus, because he did these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them: ‘My Father works until now, and I work.’” And immediately afterwards: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (ibid.), and so forth.

With what intention, do you suppose, did he say here, “My Father works until now, and I work,” except to teach that he too is Lord of the Sabbath? “My Father,” he says, “because he is Lord of the Sabbath, works even now on Sabbaths, no less than on the first or second Sabbath: giving rain [Col. 1602D] upon the earth, bringing forth grass for cattle, bringing winds out of his treasuries” (Ps. 103 [104]), “making his sun rise” (Matt. 5); and none of you says, “Why does he not keep the Sabbath?” Perhaps, if you have any reason, you judge that he is not bound by the law of the Sabbath because “he does all things well” (Mark 7) and cannot do anything wrongly. Therefore he is rightly not bound by the law of the Sabbath, because he cannot do evil.

To this, I say: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything of himself.” What is this to say except steadfastly to assert that the Son of God, equally with the Father, is the unchangeable God? For what is it for someone to do something of himself, except to do something separately, outside God, without God’s command or will? [Col. 1603A] What, I ask, is this except to commit sin or to sin? Certainly the devil first acted of himself when he first committed sin and sinned; and all who sin and act from themselves imitate him, abandoning fellowship with or authority from God.

Likewise, they act from themselves when they speak outside God—speaking falsehood, calling evil good and good evil (Isa. 5), and defending the same. “We shall magnify our tongue; our lips are our own. Who is lord over us?” (Ps. 11 [12]). “But,” he says, “the Son cannot do anything of himself.” Therefore the Son is unchangeable, although the heretic Arius said that he was changeable. For he cannot do anything of himself, and this is impossible for him by nature.

And if the holy angels [Col. 1603B] were strengthened after the fall of him who acted of himself, so that they can no longer act from themselves, they did not have this by nature but received it by grace. This Son always possessed, and possesses, it by nature. Therefore, confident in his stable right, he says: “My Father works until now, and I work,” because, just as he does, so I too unchangeably do all things well, doing nothing of myself except what I see the Father doing. Thus what he said here—that he cannot do something—is not only no contradiction to the fullness of which we were speaking, but is an even stronger proof of his fullness and power.

## Chapter XXXI. How, in accordance with the order of the graces of the same Holy Spirit, Christ works in his Church through works distinguished from his passion until the end of the age.

Now the sails of faith must be spread out upon the deep. For, breathing upon us himself, we desire to pass through the seven streams of this sevenfold Spirit—those things which have hitherto flowed from this one who is full, or from his fullness, and do not cease to flow until the end of the age—according to the order in which, from the passion of Christ the Lord to the last day of judgment, we can observe from the works themselves that the Spirit operates more especially in this universal world.

The order undertaken by us is this. In the very passion of Christ’s humility, the devil’s cunning was overcome, according to the saying: “And his wisdom struck down the proud one” (Isa. 26, 51); and in the sacraments of that same passion, by which [Col. 1603D] we are regenerated, or have been regenerated, we shall proclaim the holy Spirit of wisdom. In that, through Christ’s same passion, the veil of the temple was torn (Matt. 27)—or rather, the veil of Moses’ face, laid upon the hearts of the Jews, was removed from believing hearts [Col. 1604A] (Exod. 34; 2 Cor. 3), so that they might understand the Scriptures with unveiled understanding, especially the apostles, who were unlearned and illiterate men—we shall confess the holy Spirit of understanding.

In that blindness happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in (Rom. 11), and the temple of the old worship was given over to destruction, lest its stones, standing in the way, hinder the chariots of the Gospel as they raced onward—we must glorify for ourselves the holy Spirit of counsel. In the battles of the martyrs, through which the devil was defeated and expelled from the temples, shrines, and idols of the nations, while his adversaries were unable to withstand or contradict them—we must praise the holy Spirit of fortitude, who spoke in them.

In our holy fathers and doctors, who expounded the sacred Scriptures by faithfully treating them, so that in them that prophetic saying was truly fulfilled: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12)—we must reverence with fitting thanksgiving the holy Spirit of knowledge. In that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, the veil will then be removed (2 Cor. 3), and the remnant from Israel will be converted (Rom. 9, 11)—we must confess the holy Spirit of piety. In that he will come to judge the living and the dead, so that those who have done good may come forth to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment (John 5)—we must proclaim the holy Spirit of the fear of the Lord.

Indeed, while attending to the seven first days of creation and to the same number of subsequent ages of the world, we looked to these same spirits, because [Col. 1604C] God the Father and God the Son worked according to them. But there, as in an image; here, in the reality itself, we behold the person of God the Holy Spirit present with us. The order itself also differs. For there we ascended from fear to wisdom; here we descend from wisdom to fear, having at the end of the age that which we must always fear, however perfect we may be, although among men we may seem already to have attained it.

For who, whether wise or understanding, prudent or strong, possessing treasures of knowledge or piety, will boast that he has a pure heart there, where the powers of heaven will be shaken, where angels will fear and, terrified, be purified? Great, therefore, is the Spirit of the fear of the Lord there. Accordingly, as we are about to sail through these streams of sevenfold grace [Col. 1604D], we invoke the Holy Spirit himself as guide and helmsman, that, with him directing our course, we may deserve to reach the desired end with the fruit of joy. Amen.

# Second Book on the Works of the Holy Spirit. First Book on Wisdom.

[Col. 1605]

## Chapter I [Col. 1605A]. On the Spirit of wisdom: that through this Spirit Christ, by obeying and suffering, offered himself to God.

We call the Holy Spirit—the Spirit through whom, as the Apostle says, Christ offered himself to God as a living sacrifice, in order that by his blood he might cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb. 9)—the Spirit of wisdom: that wisdom, I say, which none of the rulers of this age knew. “For if they had known it,” says the same Apostle, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

When, however, we call or hear “the Spirit of wisdom,” we understand him as its maker or giver. And we do not hesitate to say that the definition of the wisdom which this Spirit effects, if it is converted into its proper terms, is a certain perception by which the very substance of wisdom is perceived by us—wisdom which, according to the divine nature, is Christ himself, the Son of God, the Word of God, God the Word.

Since, as has been said, he is wisdom itself according to the divine nature, according to the human nature this Spirit of wisdom is said to rest in him, and he himself is called wise, because his soul possesses, beyond all participants in wisdom, a full perception of the substantial wisdom dwelling within it. We ought to recognize or investigate this perception of wisdom especially from his obedience or suffering, from the course or fruit of his obedience or suffering. With his help we shall do so; but first let us attempt to distinguish the face of this wisdom from the face of the wisdom of the children of this age.

## Chapter II [Col. 1605C]. That the wisdom effected by this Holy Spirit and the wisdom of this world differ in contrary ways and never cease to oppose one another until the end of the age.

The wisdom effected by this Holy Spirit, whence he is called the Spirit of wisdom, differs chiefly from worldly wisdom in that the latter overturns and destroys, while the former maintains or preserves in man the right order of his original formation. For the latter recalls—indeed, never forgets—what the former disdains to know or remember: namely, that God said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness, that he may rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of heaven, the beasts, and every creeping thing” (Gen. 1). And afterwards, as the same Scripture reports: “He formed man from the clay of the earth” [Col. 1605D] (Gen. 2).

Recollecting and always retaining this, it preserves the same order of formation: it lifts the soul upward to God’s image, but humbles the body [Col. 1606A] to the earth, from whose clay God formed it, so that the human spirit may be subject to God and the body to the spirit. Conversely, the wisdom of this world, as has been said, so overturns and destroys this same order that it makes the puffed-up mind of man forgetful of God, while it values highly the body and the body’s resources, such as riches, positions of power, and nobility of birth. Thus man’s spirit rebels against God, while the inferior portion, the flesh, rules over the spirit.

The judgment of reason does not exempt even the philosophers of this world from this charge. “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”; for they served the creature rather than the Creator. Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that they dishonored their bodies among themselves (Rom. 1). That wisdom, therefore, proceeding in a very perverted order, as though walking on its hands, raises its feet upward and drags its head upon the ground; but this wisdom, walking uprightly, presses the ground with its feet and directs its face toward heaven.

With faces so diverse—indeed, contrary—peace or harmony could never arise; rather, they always oppose one another and do not cease their opposition until the end of the age. The supreme boast of the former is to have been able to surpass equals even by doing them injury; the supreme praise of the latter is not only to inflict no injury while helping equals or even inferiors, but even to endure injury with equanimity.

Their greatest conflict was displayed before the whole world in the passion of Christ, the Son of God: nowhere did this Spirit of wisdom conquer so nobly through patience, and nowhere was the wisdom of the world so ignobly exposed as foolish. Let us therefore now enter, as proposed, into this spectacle. This new Adam first exercised the strength of wisdom in that he committed no sin, from which the old Adam did not abstain; and then in that he obediently subjects himself in all things to one greater than himself, which the other did not do.

By “greater,” with respect to the assumed manhood, we mean the God who assumed it: greater, I say, in that impassible divinity than in the passible humanity, as he says: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14). Finally, when he calls the Father greater than himself but does not add “my,” we understand not merely one person but the one God, Father of all, “who is above all, and through all, and in us all” (Eph. 4): that is, [Col. 1606D] Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

To this greater one, I say, this new man—this one who is God and man in one and the same person, the one Christ—subjected himself in all obedience: namely, in that he had committed no sin [Col. 1607A] (1 Pet. 2), and therefore owed nothing to death, yet nevertheless willed to die for the command of that greater one, as he says: “For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me. But that the world may know that I love 629 the Father, and as the Father gave me commandment, so I do” (John 14).

Moreover, he did not will to die by any kind of death, but by the death of the cross. The Apostle fittingly magnifies this when, having said, “He became obedient for us unto death,” he adds, “even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2). For, as truly wise, he considered that he ought not to die without great fruit, as this same Spirit of wisdom had long before said of him, as it were according to the condition: “If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he shall see long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand. Because his soul labored, he shall see and be satisfied. By his knowledge, he himself, my righteous servant, shall justify many” (Isa. 53), and so forth.

The old man did not do this. He refused to submit himself to one greater; he refused to be obedient even to abstinence—abstinence, moreover, from a single tree. How much better is one obedient unto death, even death on a cross. This is true wisdom: an obedience greatly necessary for humankind, the patience of one who is wise and obedient, alone able to remove from us the reproaches of that folly and disobedience.

This wisdom, or this Spirit of wisdom, opened the mouths of the human race and made its tongue eloquent, so that all of us who believe in this wise Christ, the Son of God, may confidently say: “Our father, the old Adam, the father of our flesh, sinned foolishly and is no more; yet we have borne his iniquity [Col. 1607C] (Lam. 3). But likewise our Father, the Lord Christ, the new Adam, the Father of our faith, did righteousness and is now no longer in this world. Why then should we not receive the inheritance of his righteousness, when we bore from that father an inheritance of unrighteousness?”

## Chapter III. On blessed Job: that in him there went beforehand a type of this wisdom, that is, of Christ’s patience.

The subject is great and must be expressed in elevated language, yet not without the sure support of the Scriptures, nor without a reliable position among the matters previously treated, so that the more faithful discourse may stand firmly in its proper rank and not weary itself through distaste at an uncertain multitude of statements.

We now rejoice in that very matter over which, in a certain place much earlier, we grieved: namely, that when we considered in order the venerable images or figures of the future truth—that is, Christ the Son of God—in patriarchs, kings, and prophets, we passed over blessed Job as an example of patience. The venerable authority of the Fathers did not fail to declare that he went beforehand as a type of the same Lord Christ and of his Church. This, I say, now gives us joy, for remembrance of him has no small place here.

For the Spirit of wisdom, of whom we now speak, who rested fully in the patience of this wise Christ, set forth in Job’s patience and illustrious contest a figure of his own future resting. Therefore, because we are dazzled by the great majesty and splendor of the matter of which [Col. 1608A] we speak, let us hold this as a mirror before the sun, that we may more tolerably and with surer sight be able to follow this holy Spirit of wisdom at work in Christ.

## Chapter IV. How Satan, when he sought permission to test Job, the exemplar of this wisdom, was ranging over the earth and walking through it; but here, when he caused Christ to be killed, he was cast out.

The exemplar of this wisdom—which, as the Apostle says, is folly to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1), although “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (ibid.)—is found in this: Satan, having gone forth from the presence of the Lord, struck Job with a grievous sore from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head; and Job, sitting on a dungheap, scraped away the discharge with a potsherd (Job 1–2).

Certainly Satan aimed the most grievous sore at Job—that is, at the suffering Lord Jesus, understood as suffering for us—when the ungodly, whose hearts Satan possessed, said, according to the testimony of that wise man: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2). He struck Job out of envy for the simplicity and uprightness of one who was innocent and feared God; but he caused Christ to be struck because he could not endure the torments he suffered from Christ’s presence, as he confessed many times.

For example, he said through the mouth of the man into whom he had sent a whole legion: “What have I to do with you, Jesus, Son of the most high God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me” (Mark 5). Satan was pressed harder in Christ and summoned more severely to judgment and dispute in Christ than in Job. For there, when the Lord had asked him, “Whence do you come?” he had answered once and again: “I have ranged over the earth and walked through it” (Job 1). Judgment was not demanded; there was no one to say: “Now is the judgment of the world; now you shall be cast out, O Satan, ranger of the world and walker through the earth.”

There was no one, I say, to say this; and therefore he gloried that, since no stronger conqueror came against him, he was free to range over the earth and walk through it. But here was one who said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world shall be cast out” (John 12). Therefore, when this suffering one, once rich and sitting as a true king, surrounded by an army of angels, was cast outside the gate and struck with a most shameful death, reckoned as though a leper, Job truly sat on the dungheap covered in discharge. For the Lord had laid upon him the iniquities of us all (Isa. 52 [53]).

But he was to blot out those same iniquities of ours, all corruption, and even our mortality itself through the power of the resurrection. Therefore it was rightly said that Job scraped the discharge away with a potsherd. The potsherd, first soft clay and afterwards hardened by baking fire, is Christ’s flesh: first passible and mortal, as being our clay; then, through the fire of the passion, so strengthened in the resurrection that it can never again be dissolved by death or any corruption.

This took place in reality in the one of whom we speak, through the Spirit of wisdom; but to the perception, or wisdom, [Col. 1609A] of this age it appeared foolishness. Yet so it is: “Since,” says the Apostle, “the world could not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1). Indeed, unless God had descended to this supposed folly, the world, vainly wise, would not have known God.

## Chapter V. That all the elect cursed, so far as they could, the same day or night which Job cursed; but Christ alone, because he committed no sin, could curse—that is, condemn—it effectively.

After these things Job opened his mouth and cursed his day, saying: “May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived.’ May that day be turned into darkness; may God not seek it from above, and may it not be illumined with light” (Job 3).

The day of birth, or the night, which it was wise to curse, was the sin of the first man: a day, I say, ironically, but truly a night. For on that occasion, as though in daylight, the opening of our eyes was promised us by the deceiver when he said: “Eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3). But when he was believed, a wall of enmity arose between us and God, and thus we were conceived in night—that is, so as not to see God.

Job cursed that day—indeed, that night—so far as he could; and so did every other person, from the beginning of the world, who condemned that sin of the devil and longed for God’s righteousness. But none of their curses could condemn it sufficiently effectively. He subsequently gives the reasons for this impossibility: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why, after coming forth from the womb, did I not perish at once? Why was I received upon knees? Why suckled at breasts?” (Job 3).

Far be it from us to believe that so great a man, endowed with such knowledge of the Spirit and meanwhile praised by the Judge’s own testimony, wished that he had died as an abortive child. Rather, just as he is recognized through his reward, he bears within himself the witness of his own strength; the weight of his words must be weighed inwardly.

For sin is committed in the heart in four ways and consummated in deed in four ways. In the heart it is committed through suggestion, delight, consent, and the boldness of self-defense. Suggestion comes through the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the boldness of self-defense through pride. For guilt, which ought to terrify the mind, exalts it; by bringing it low, it raises it up, yet by raising it more grievously it trips it up.

Thus the ancient enemy broke the first man’s uprightness by these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve delighted; Adam consented; and, even when questioned, Adam refused through boldness to confess his fault (Gen. 3). Clearly, neither did we die in that womb, nor did we perish at once when we came forth from that womb; indeed, we were received upon the same knees and suckled at the same breasts. For, as the Apostle says, “in that Adam all sinned” (Rom. 3).

Therefore neither the aforesaid Job nor any of the elect could effectively enough curse—that is, condemn—the day or night of that sin. Apart from their actual sins, of which they were not wholly free, they all contracted from Adam that same original [Col. 1610A] sin. This one alone could effectively curse—that is, condemn—as the Apostle says: “What was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his Son, condemned sin in the flesh on account of sin” (Rom. 8).

## Chapter VI. How Christ said—or says—on behalf of the whole human race: “May the day perish on which I was born,” and so forth.

Accordingly, let this one man say—let this one say these words on behalf of the whole human race: “May the day perish on which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived’” (Job 3). But was he born on that day of sin and conceived in that night of unhappiness? Certainly he was born on that day and conceived in that night. Yet this new man and that old man were born and conceived in very different ways.

For the latter was born or conceived in the manner described above, so that, being a human being and being well, he might become a sinner and come to be in an evil condition. But the former was conceived and born in such a way that, being God, impassible and immortal, he might become human and come to be passible and mortal. Both were indeed in the day or night of sin: the one so that he might become sin, the other because sin had come to be.

The former, deceived by wicked suggestion and born—that is, degenerated—through the corruption of his own substance; the latter, conceived of the Virgin by the will of the Father and his own will, and made human by assumption of another substance. The former was born to the devil, both for guilt and punishment. The latter was born to God without guilt, for the punishment of guilt.

Here is the place of wisdom; here one must attend to what the Spirit of wisdom says or signifies. Behold: Christ the man, a righteous man, owes much to sinful people. “Let the weakened hands be strengthened, and the feeble knees of sinners be made firm” (Isa. 35), because, if they have been trained by faith and piety, if they are wise advocates or learned in law, they have grounds on which to bind their Judge.

For let him say: “I was born because of the day of your sin, conceived because of the night of your iniquity; and I, who was the immortal Lord God, became mortal man.” Let faithful sinners, penitent sinners, reply: “Although we owe you much, Christ God, because you became human, you in turn owe us much, Christ man, because you were assumed into God for our sake. For had we not been sinners, there would have been no reason why you should be assumed into God.”

Let them be strengthened, I say; for they ought not to consider only that the Lord of such great dignity suffered such injuries because of the utterly unworthy offenses of servile persons, even death—death, moreover, of the cross (Phil. 2). But they should also consider that, had the servants not sinned, their servile nature would not have been assumed into the Lord God. For that Lord received no more injury than glory on behalf of his rebellious or wicked servants. For those for whom he hung on the cross, for those same people he now sits at the right hand of God to intercede [Col. 1611A] (Rom. 8; Ps. 106 [107]).

Here, when a person has received the account of truth, from whomever he receives it—whether from Jew or Gentile—the King of God’s kingdom gladly suffers violence, so that the violent may seize the kingdom itself (Matt. 11). To them, as though overcome by argument, he opens his mouth and says: “May the day on which I was born, and the night in which it was said, ‘A man has been conceived,’ perish for you.”

That is to say: May the day of sin—which, according to the serpent’s falsehood when it said, “Eat, and your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3), was thought to be day but is in truth now night—in which day or night, that is, because of which day or night, I who was God was born as man, perish for you. How may it perish? “May God not seek it from above, and may it not be illumined with light” (Job 3).

Let this be your blessedness, which the Prophet likewise says with longing in the Psalm: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven” (Ps. 31 [32]), and so forth. For for that day not to be sought, and not to be illumined with light, is for iniquities to be forgiven and sins covered. In this generosity he then opened his mouth once, never to close it eternally, when he said: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16).

## Chapter VII. That the Jews who formerly shone were blinded in his passion, and that it is fitting for him to say against them: “Let the stars be darkened in the gloom of that night.”

“Let darkness and the shadows of death darken it; let gloom seize it, and let it be wrapped in bitterness. Let a dark whirlwind possess that night; let it not be counted among the days of the year, nor numbered among the months. Let that night be solitary and unworthy of praise. Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse Leviathan. Let its stars be darkened by its gloom” (Job 3).

“Let darkness and the shadow of death,” he says, “darken it”—understand: in the reprobate [Col. 1611C]. For in the elect that day or night has perished. Indeed, for this purpose too he opened his mouth, having been given authority to execute judgment: that he might condemn in the reprobate that same day of sin which he destroyed in the elect. Thus, when he had said, “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved,” he immediately added, “But he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16).

We pass over these things and the rest that follows, since they are many and are made clearer than light in the Expositions of the blessed Pope Gregory; we select only a few out of the multitude, according to the purpose by which we now desire to extend the mind in praises of the Spirit of wisdom. “Let its stars,” he says, “be darkened by its gloom.” The stars here must be understood as those which we likewise understand in the Apocalypse, where it is written: “The dragon’s tail [Col. 1611D] drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth” (Rev. 12). To draw stars down to earth is to entangle in the iniquity of open error those who seem by their manner of life to cling to heavenly things, through earthly love.

Such, certainly, were then the Jews: although they were thought to possess the light of the Scriptures and supposed themselves to be stars, according to the promise made to Abraham: “Look up to heaven and count the stars, if you can; so shall your seed be” (Gen. 15), they were drawn to earth, bound by the tail of the ancient dragon, when, speaking in the wrathfulness of earth, they said: “Let us kill him, lest perhaps the Romans come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11 [the text reads John 2]). Looking upon these stars, therefore, he says: “Let the stars [Col. 1612A] be darkened by its gloom.”

How did he say this? Certainly not so much by speech as by a wonderful deed, when, after he was crucified, darkness came over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth hour (Matt. 27). By this sign they were told that they would lose the light and be left in darkness, in the depth of ignorance of the truth. Hence the Apostle says: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: that a partial blindness has happened to Israel” (Rom. 11 [the text reads Rom. 2]); and immediately afterwards: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 1612B] That the cross of Christ was that balance in which the one who sighed said: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, were weighed,” etc.

These were the ways of the unsearchable wisdom of God: mercy and truth (Ps. 85 [Vulg. 84]), or mercy and judgment. In that passion of Christ the Spirit of wisdom was effecting this: that mercy might triumph over judgment (James 2), while none of the rulers of darkness or of this age, who crucified it, knew it. This, I say, the Spirit of wisdom was effecting: that, once the balance of equity had been weighed, it might appear that more punishment had been taken from the human race than guilt deserved; and thus just reason might demand that the sentence of the ancient condemnation now be changed, and reasonable justice might not deny it.

Sighing this in the blessed Job, the Spirit of that same wisdom spoke for us all: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance; this calamity would appear heavier than the sand of the sea” (Job 6). But how could this be? How could the calamity of the human race appear heavier than its sins, unless more should be condemned than guilty, more punished than the authors or heirs of sin?

This, therefore, the Spirit of wisdom accomplished by a wonderful and praiseworthy art. In Christ’s being handed over to death—he who had committed no sin—there was the cross, the Father’s balance. On one side, in the pan of judgment, lay the sins of the world; on the other, in the pan of mercy, the calamity [Col. 1612D] of the human race. The calamity outweighed the other pan in the pan of mercy; raising the pan of judgment, it hurled the sins down into the depth of the sea.

Why was this so? Plainly because more were condemned than guilty—more, I say, punished than deserved punishment. One was added to the number of the condemned; one remained over: Christ, condemned though not guilty, punished though having no cause why he should be punished. The passion of this suffering one, unjustly added to the just sufferings of the whole human race, outweighed them like a mass of sand; the calamity of the world was heavier than its sins. Accordingly, our cause—that is, the cause of those condemned—was indeed taken up mercifully, but the sentence by which we had been condemned was changed justly.

Praise, therefore, be to this Spirit of wisdom, by whose such device it came about that he justly destroyed [Col. 1613A] all enemies, when one who owed nothing to death was admitted to it.

## CHAPTER IX. How this wisdom was mocked in that man by the sons of folly, and that it was said concerning him: “He who is mocked by his friend, like me.”

Meanwhile such great wisdom is mocked—mocked, I say, by the sons of folly, applauding one another as though they had cunningly and effectively laid snares for blood, hiding traps against the innocent, and saying to one another: “Let us swallow him alive like hell, and whole, like one going down into the pit; we shall find every precious substance” (Prov. 1).

We read and have heard of their mockery: “They spat in his face, struck him with fists, and slapped his face” (Matt. 26). They also struck his head with a reed [Col. 1613B] and, kneeling, greeted him and said, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27). And when they had already crucified him, they mocked him still further, saying: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days—save yourself!” (Mark 15). Again: “He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he is King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him” (Matt. 27).

In this way the foolish sons of folly mocked him. But behold: in this man the consoling Spirit of wisdom was already saying on his behalf: “He who is mocked by his friend, like me, shall call upon God, and he will hear him. For the simplicity of the righteous is mocked; a lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time. The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, though he has given all things [Col. 1613C] into their hands. Surely ask the beasts, and they will teach you; and the birds of heaven, and they will tell you. Speak to the earth, and it will answer you; and the fish of the sea will recount it to you. Who does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things, in whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh? Does not the ear judge words, and the palate of one eating judge taste? Among the ancients is wisdom, and in length of time prudence. With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding. If he destroys, there is no one to rebuild; and if he shuts a man in, there is no one to open. If he restrains the waters, all things will dry up; and if he releases them, they will overturn the earth. With him are strength and wisdom; he knows both the deceiver and the deceived. [Col. 1613D] He brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment. He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a rope. He leads priests away dishonoured and overthrows the mighty. Changing the speech of truthful men, he takes away the teaching of the elders. He pours contempt upon princes and raises those who had been oppressed. He reveals deep things out of darkness and brings the shadow of death into light. He multiplies nations and destroys them, and restores those overthrown to wholeness. He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth and deceives them, so that they walk vainly where there is no path. They grope as in darkness and not in light, and he makes them wander like drunkards” (Job 12).

Certainly he indicates that these words are prophetic when he immediately adds: “Behold, my eye has seen all these things, my ear has heard them, and I have understood each one” (Job 13). [Col. 1614A] I say that these things are prophetic; by the spirit of prophecy he declares that what was to come was present to his eyes. For he saw as present those things that were to follow, in the presence of him to whom neither future things arrive nor past things depart.

## CHAPTER X. That, as a type of him who was to be mocked by the Jewish people akin to him, Job was mocked by his friends; and that it was truly said of Christ: “A lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time.”

Therefore, what he said—stricken and sitting upon a dung-heap (Job 2), as a type of him—was a judgment of condemnation upon those sons of folly who mocked the truly wise and supremely wise one in the manner described above: “He who is mocked by his friend,” he says, “like me” (Job 12).

For what is “like me,” except as though he said: “I, who am mocked by my friends, bear the type of the one mocked”? For I am mocked by my friends; he is mocked—that is, without doubt, he is to be mocked by his friend, by his kinsman, the Jewish people. To that people he speaks in the psalm: “For if an enemy had cursed me, I would surely have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken great things against me, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my familiar friend, who together with me took sweet food: in the house of God we walked in agreement” (Ps. 55 [Vulg. 54]).

For that people, in remarkable folly, cursed him with whom it took sweet food; that is, it mocked him hanging upon the cross, whom it prefigured in the ceremonies of sacrifices in the temple. And just as Job’s friends mocked him [Col. 1614C] sitting upon the dung-heap, though they had been accustomed to revere him sitting like a king with an army surrounding him, so the scribes and Pharisees mocked that one dying, though in reading the prophets they proclaimed him to be truly the great king, the King of kings.

But how were those friends, lifting up their eyes, unable to recognize that he was Job (Job 2), unless these people did not recognize—or rather, were unwilling to recognize—that he was Christ, who had been promised to their fathers? They were unwilling, I say, to recognize him because they lifted up—that is, held uplifted in pride—their eyes. Therefore, “he who is mocked by his friend like me shall call upon God,” he says, “and he will hear him. For the simplicity of the righteous is mocked.”

It is as though he said: “Behold, mocked by my friends, [Col. 1614D] I call upon God, and he does not yet hear me—not yet, I say, hear me so as to receive me into his heavenly kingdom because of this mockery. Another is to be mocked by his friend like me; and in the very mockery he will call upon God, and God will hear him, crowning him with glory and honour because of that very mockery” (Ps. 8).

Then he will say: “In my tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry entered into his ears in his presence” (Ps. 18 [Vulg. 17]). For just as my weakness is now mocked, so then the simplicity of that righteous one will be mocked: because, “like a sheep he is led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one shearing it, so he does not open his mouth” (Isa. 53); and this will be reckoned as folly. Yet “his foolishness is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1).

What then? “A lamp despised [Col. 1615A] in the thoughts of the rich, prepared for the appointed time.” For this righteous one, whose simplicity is mocked, is he of whom God speaks in the prophet: “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest, until her righteousness goes forth like brightness, and her Saviour is kindled like a lamp” (Isa. 62).

This lamp, shining in sayings or teachings and resplendent in miracles, was despised in the thoughts of the rich—in the pride of darkness, which could not comprehend that light. Why? Because it did not shine as they wished; it did not blaze as they wished their Messiah to blaze, namely for the present and vain glory of men. For they did not expect such a Christ as they saw in him, but one such as the Antichrist, whom they will receive, shining with malignant splendour. [Col. 1615B] Therefore this lamp was especially despised in their thoughts when, through the death of the cross, they thought that they had extinguished its light.

But it was—and is—prepared for the appointed time, in which what is written will happen to them: “Lord, let your hand be exalted, that they may not see; let them see and be confounded, those who envy your people, and let fire devour your enemies” (Isa. 26).
