Looking toward that appointed time of its own, when this lamp would be placed upon the lampstand of heaven, it endured the mockers of darkness while it was thought to be extinguished; truly a lamp of wisdom also by reason of its silence, according to the saying: “The wise man shall be silent until the time” (Prov. 2).

## CHAPTER XI. How or from what source those were rich who despised this lamp of wisdom.

[Col. 1615C] Were those, then, rich in whose thoughts this lamp was despised? Or was it the disposition of rich men, and not rather of poor men, to despise this lamp’s splendid deeds and luminous sayings? Certainly they were rich, but not from what was their own: rich by robbery, rich from another’s property. Thus, when it is said, “in the thoughts of the rich,” understand the same reproach as though it had been said, “in the thoughts of robbers.” For it follows: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, although he has given all things into their hands.”

Indeed, these were robbers of God and robbers of every neighbour. That they were robbers of God is attested by God himself, when in Hosea he brings forth a complaint concerning their Synagogue: “And she did not know that I gave her my grain in its season, [Col. 1615D] and my wine in its season, and I shall free my wool and my flax which covered her shame” (Hos. 2). Further, that they were also robbers of their neighbours is attested in Isaiah, when he says: “You have devoured my vineyard; the spoil of the poor is in your houses” (Isa. 3). Again: “Woe to those who join house to house and add field to field, even to the boundary of the place” (Isa. 5), and similar passages.

Therefore, when he had said, “in the thoughts of the rich,” as though you were asking from where or how they had become rich, he says: “The tents of robbers abound.” But why did he not say “houses,” but “tents of robbers”? Plainly, that he might strike more sharply at their ingratitude in returning evil to God for good. By this expression [Col. 1616A] he sends us back to the history of their poverty and flight: when, fleeing from the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery—where because of the sale of their brother Joseph they were slaves in a just captivity—they dwelt in tents, possessing not even a footstep of any land, except that God drove nations out before them and apportioned their land to them by lot.

“He gave them,” I say, “the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labours of peoples” (Ps. 105 [Vulg. 104]). “The tents of robbers abound,” then: that is, from tents they came to wealth, indeed by God’s gift; yet they abused those very riches as robbers of God. In what respect? “They boldly provoke God,” he says, “although he has given all things into their hands.”

And indeed, on this account he himself could have complained in his own person, saying: “My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I made you sad? Answer me. Because I brought you out of the land of Egypt; because I led you through the desert for forty years, fed you with manna, and brought you into a land exceedingly good? What more ought I to have done for you that I did not do?” (Mic. 6). [Col. 1616B] These things, I say, and others like them, he could have complained of in his own person. But, possessing silence until the appointed time—which was characteristic of the wise man—he waited until the Spirit of wisdom himself should bring forth this complaint, taken from the prophets, through the mouth of all nations, adding: “You prepared a cross for your Saviour.”

## CHAPTER XII. What beasts, birds of heaven, earth, and fish of the sea taught, indicated, and answered: that this lamp is prepared for the appointed time.

Certainly, he says: “Ask the beasts, and they will teach you; and the birds of heaven, and they will tell you. Speak to the earth, and it will answer you; and the fish of the sea will recount it to you.” Great and true is the praise of this Spirit of wisdom, because he not only, as is written elsewhere, “opened the mouth of the dumb and made the tongues of infants eloquent” (Wis. 10), but also gave beasts, birds of heaven, and fish of the sea the power to teach, indicate, and recount.

For what are these beasts, these birds of heaven, and these fish, except persons once brutish, who had no knowledge of God? Some indeed are beasts of the earth, others birds of heaven, others fish of the sea, according to their different skills or offices; but in this respect we were all mute and brutish. Now, however, the Spirit of wisdom has opened our mouths [Col. 1616D] and made our tongues eloquent, so that we may teach those rich men—or rather, robbers—who despised this lamp in their thoughts; and may indicate and recount to them that this contempt of theirs is blindness. We may recount it and convict them, if not that they may be converted, then at least that they may be put to shame and tormented by envy, according to the saying: “I shall provoke you to jealousy by a non-nation; by a foolish nation I shall move you to wrath” (Rom. 10).

“Who,” he says, “does not know that the hand of the Lord has made all these things, in whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all human flesh?” Or rather, who does not know that he whose hand made these things is the Lord? He made these things—the one who, though he was a lamp, as has already been said, was despised in the thoughts [Col. 1617A] of the rich. He made them, I say, at the appointed time for which he was prepared. For in his own time, when he had ascended above the heavens and sat at the right hand of the Father, he shone forth splendidly and sent out divided tongues like fire—or rather, truly the fire of the Holy Spirit—which also sat upon each of the disciples; the visible appearance of fire was its sign (Acts 2).

That invisible fire, blazing forth from a few apostles, illuminated the whole earth; and it so enlightened the aforementioned beasts of the earth, birds of heaven, and fish of the sea that they could know, teach, indicate, and recount the mighty works of God to men or sons of men—that is, to Jews and to Jewish teachers who gloried in being the only men, or sons of men.

Therefore this Lord, whose [Col. 1617B] hand made these things—this Lord, I say, in whose hand is the soul of every living thing and the spirit of all flesh—is wholly man, whose power is so great that he can make men out of stones (Matt. 3). Hence he says: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

But behold, those foolish men, who reproach us as beasts, say one thing and think another: “He is not the Lord,” they say, “who has done these things for you; he is not the one whose change this is, the Son or right hand of the Most High. He was great, but he was a deceiver; he was not the true Son of God.”

To this we say: All beasts of the earth, all birds of heaven, all [Col. 1617C] fish of the sea, whose ears the Spirit of wisdom has opened and whose palates he has healed—does not the ear judge words, and the palate of the eater judge taste? That is: do we not ourselves know what we have experienced? Or can we hear anything from a human being more certain than what we have learned inwardly, as though by tasting, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit? For we know that through faith in him we have received the Spirit; and we who were beasts—behold, we are men, indeed gods, and dwell in mind in the heavens. Many of us, moreover, have been so inflamed by that lamp that demons depart at their sight and flee from possessed bodies.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why, after saying, “Among the ancients is wisdom,” etc., he added, “With him are wisdom,” etc.

[Col. 1617D] “Among the ancients is wisdom, and in length of time prudence. With him are wisdom and strength; he possesses counsel and understanding.” Just as the ear judges words and the palate of those eating judges taste, so by the most certain discernment of reason these former beasts judge that this one, or that which is in him, is above all the earlier saints or righteous men: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and all the prophets.

For among those ancients, those who lived long ago, there is wisdom and prudence—namely, those from whom, or through whom, Holy Scripture was composed, containing all the treasures of wisdom and prudence. Yet wisdom is in them one way, and in this one another way. In them it is by participation; in this one it is in the whole universality of himself.

Moreover, they differ also in this: in them there is wisdom alone, but in this one wisdom together with strength. For they were unable to bring what they understood wisely into effect; but he brought wisdom into action unto victory, destroying death and restoring life. Add also that in him are counsel and understanding. By counsel he made foolish the cunning of the devil; by understanding he not only possessed or penetrated the secrets of Scripture, or all the mysteries of God, but also opened them to others whom he wished and as he wished.

Moreover, consider his terrible deeds in hidden judgments, because with him is the Spirit of wisdom and strength: “If he destroys, no one can rebuild; and if he shuts a man in, no one can open. If he restrains [Col. 1618B] the waters, everything will dry up; and if he releases them, they will overturn the earth.”

O mockers, O foolish rich men, despisers of this lamp: why do you taunt, shaking your heads and saying, “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days” (Matt. 27)? If he destroys, no one—no one can rebuild; no one can place stone upon stone again. If he shuts you in by a Roman siege, as he certainly will, no one can open a way for you to escape, whether from east or west or the deserted mountains (Ps. 75 [Vulg. 74]).

But you suppose that he has no strength because of the cross and the nails which you see in his hands. Foolish and blind men: the arms of the cross are horns in his hands; and, as wisdom, the companion of strength and likewise present in him, dictates, there his strength is hidden [Col. 1618C] (Hab. 3), hidden, I say, until the time when the spear also pierces his side and a perpetual stream of blood and water flows from it.

Why? Certainly because “if he restrains the waters, everything will dry up; and if he releases them, they will overturn the earth.” For if, with his body intact—if, with his side unopened—he had wished to escape your sacrilegious hands or tongues, and had in this way withheld the visible waters of baptism and the invisible waters of the grace of the Holy Spirit, all things would have remained dry as they were. But because he chose to die and be pierced by a spear, behold: he released those waters and overturned the earth—that is, sins.

For this reason he chose to conceal the wisdom and strength which are in him when you said, as though to one without wisdom, “Prophesy to us: who is it that struck you?” (Luke 22); and when you said, as though to one without strength, “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God!” (Mark 13; Matt. 27).

## CHAPTER XIV. In what his strength stood against Jewish pride, and in what his wisdom stood against malice; and whose belt he loosed and whose teaching he removed.

Therefore I have said, and say again: “With him are strength and wisdom.” In what is his wisdom? “He knows both the deceiver and the deceived. He brings counsellors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment.” In what is his strength? “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a rope. He leads priests away dishonoured and overthrows the mighty.”

Does he not know both your deceiving Synagogue, O scribes and [Col. 1619A] Pharisees, and the one deceived by you, the wretched people, when you fabricated for it a specious but deceitful plea, saying: “The Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John 11)? His wisdom knows it, and brought such counsellors to a foolish end. For as it is said elsewhere, “Upon those who fear the frost, snow shall fall” (Job 6): because you hypocritically feared what was vain, he made you fear what was true, so that the Romans truly came and took away your place and nation—not because you let him go, but because you did not let him go in this manner.

Thus indeed his wisdom brought counsellors to a foolish end and judges to bewilderment; thus his strength loosed the belt of kings—that is, your confidence, O proud men—and girded your loins with the rope of captivity. It led priests dishonoured, namely Annas and Caiaphas and the other priests of that kind, whose faces he covered with the dung of their solemnities; and in this way it overthrew the mighty, taking the kingdom of God away from them and giving it to a nation producing its fruits (Matt. 21).

“Changing the speech of truthful men and taking away the teaching of the elders”—understand: wisdom is with him. For because they refused to receive the truth, he mixed among them a spirit of error and dizziness, so that those who ought to have been truthful might perversely distort the Scriptures to their own desires, their speech wickedly altered; and in this way he removed from the elders—that is, from those to whom the oracles of God were first entrusted (Rom. 3)—their authority to teach.

“He pours contempt upon princes and raises those who had been oppressed”—understand: strength is with him. He made the rulers of Jewish unbelief contemptible throughout the whole world; and those oppressed by the weight of sins or by demonic slavery, namely the Gentiles, because they received his faith, he raised up in the great freedom of liberating grace.

“He reveals deep things out of darkness and brings the shadow of death into light”—understand: wisdom is with him. For this lamp did this in the very respect in which it was despised in the thoughts of the rich. Through the humility of his passion it revealed our depths from the darkness of ignorance and brought us, who sat in the shadow of death, into the light of the knowledge of God.

“He multiplies nations and destroys them, and restores those overthrown [Col. 1619D] to wholeness”—understand: strength is with him. For this too belongs to true and great strength, and to great and terrible judgment: after he had multiplied the nations, saying to the first human beings, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1), he destroyed them when those same first parents sinned. He involved all nations—all their descendants—in the same sentence of destruction.

But behold: while he suffers, while he dies, and while so splendid a lamp is despised in the thoughts of the rich as though extinguished, by that same passion or death he restores to wholeness those whom he had overthrown. “To wholeness,” I say, so that not even one may be missing from all whom he had destined for life when he said, “Increase and multiply.”

“He changes the heart of the princes of the people of the earth and deceives them, so that they walk vainly where there is no path; they grope [Col. 1620A] as in darkness and not in light, and he makes them wander like drunkards”—understand: wisdom is with him. For how did he change the heart of the rulers of the people of the earth and deceive them, except as was said in the prophet: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6)?

Therefore, that from then on they walk vainly where there is no path, that they grope as in darkness and not in light, that they wander as drunkards—all this is great material for praise of this Spirit of wisdom, of whom it is also said with astonishing truth that he deceived them and made them wander like drunkards.

## CHAPTER XV. [Col. 1620B] How, while he was despised in the thoughts of the rich, he was worthy of reverence before God the Father, saying: “You shall call me, and I shall answer you; or certainly I shall speak, and you shall answer me.”

Meanwhile, he who was despised in outward form in the thoughts of rich mockers, the Spirit of wisdom in that same form had placed before the Father as a man worthy of reverence and, because of his reverence, worthy to be heard (Heb. 5), pleading the cause of the poor—that is, of the humble—according to the words subsequently added in that same blessed Job: “Call me, and I shall answer you; or certainly you answer me. Show me how many iniquities and sins, crimes and offences I have. Why do you hide your face and consider me your enemy?” (Job 13), etc.

For when he said these things, he sighed for that calling and answering by which lost man was sought again through the obedience of Christ who suffered and died. Sought again, I say: for long before he had once been sought and called, when Scripture says: “And the Lord God called Adam and said to him, ‘Where are you?’”

But when God called, the man then did not answer; rather he said: “I heard your voice in paradise and was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself.” Again: “Who,” he says, “told you that you were naked, unless it was because you ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” And Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me as companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3).

Was this an answer to the one calling? Surely, when the Lord God said, “Where are you?” he called the man back to his heart, that he might reply penitently: “Alas! I am in transgression.” From that point it was indeed good that he should at least answer when called; but better that he himself should speak first, and that God should answer how many iniquities he had.

He did not do that: he did not speak, but allowed God, as it were, to sleep through the whole midday. Thus Scripture rebukes him, saying: “And when [Col. 1620D] they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in paradise in the breeze after midday” (ibid.), etc. Thus the man did not speak, nor did he give God the business of answering; consequently, after his ungrateful silence, God at last rose quietly, as though sated with sleep after midday, and, angry that he had not been called, himself called the man first.

Therefore, as we began to say, it was good for man to answer God when called; better if man first spoke and confessed his sins; but best of all if man had never transgressed God’s command. Thus, in the person of the human race, the holy man, desiring man to be called again and desiring that man who, when called, would answer wisely—or rather, would speak first; or certainly, what is best, would be perfectly obedient in himself and then intercede by speaking for the rest—said: “Call me, and I shall answer you; or certainly I shall speak, and you answer me how many iniquities and sins I have.”

This was now being done; to this the Spirit of wisdom had devoted the whole man whom he had taken beforehand, while he was mocked by those sons of folly like a man who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth (Ps. 38 [Vulg. 37]). He was disputing wisely and earnestly with God and therefore had, for the time being, no leisure to reply to those mockers. He was making the hope of the human race wholly true and not vain, because it had been said: “Call me, and I shall answer you; or certainly I shall speak, and you answer me.”

That first man who was called hid himself from the face of the Lord God in the midst of the trees of paradise and gave no good answer. This second man, called, stood before the face of the Lord God in the midst of the wood of the cross and answered the Father with perfect and complete obedience; indeed, he spoke so that the Father might answer him how many iniquities and sins we had, and might show him our crimes and offences.

## CHAPTER XVI. What is better: that man be called by God and answer him, or that man speak and God answer, [Col. 1621C] and show how many his iniquities and sins are.

Let us now compare the two, and see which is better: that a human being should be called by God and answer him, or that a human being should speak and God answer the human being how great his iniquities and sins are. For he said, “Call me, and I will answer you”; and immediately, most wisely correcting and improving the good proposition, he adds: “Or rather, I will speak, and you answer me.” What? “How many iniquities and sins have I?” Let us therefore ask to what end it is better, or more pertains to wisdom, that a human being speak and God answer him, than that God call a human being and the human being answer him how great his iniquities and sins are.

If we weigh the matter rightly, it is blameworthy to postpone confession of sin so long that God the Judge says: “What have you done?” (Gen. 4). Even if, when called or examined, the human being answers how great his iniquities or sins are and says, “I have sinned; have patience with me,” or, “Forgive me”—which Adam is not recorded to have done, nor did his son Cain the fratricide—even if, I say, when summoned to judgment he truthfully answers what he has done, as David did (2 Kings 12), nevertheless it is already blameworthy that a person should defer confession of sin until such a summons from God. But to anticipate the face of the Lord God, and before being called to speak with voluntary confession, is wise counsel than which no better can be found by a sinful human being. Why? Because, when a person is called to answer God, he must answer to judgment; but when God is called—or invoked—to answer, after the human being has first spoken and has first related his iniquities, there is room for God to speak mercy and to say to the questioning person, “How many iniquities and sins have I?” “None,” he says. “For I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isa. 4 [probably Isa. 44:22]). It is therefore much better that the human being speak first. And for this reason, having said, “Call me, and I will answer you,” he immediately supplies, by a swift correction, what was inferior: “Or rather,” he says, “I will speak, and you answer me.”

Behold: through Christ, who, as has already been said, was utterly unlike the one who hid himself amid the tree of paradise and, even when called, gave no wise answer, he stood openly amid the tree of the cross and voluntarily pleaded our cause. Behold, I say, through him, and instructed by that same Spirit of wisdom, we have spoken first: “How many iniquities and sins have we?” And God has answered us: “Behold, now none.” Where have we so spoken, and where has he so answered us? Certainly in the baptism of the same Christ our Lord. But of this elsewhere. Let us now pursue the argument at hand.

## Chapter XVII. How justly and how strongly the Head prayed for all the world on behalf of the members, saying, “Why do you hide your face,” etc.; and how eloquence, the handmaid of true wisdom, accompanied it

True wisdom displays itself so conspicuously in this passage that secular eloquence nowhere runs more readily to attend it. In almost all the holy Scriptures, eloquence freely serves wisdom in such a way that, while seeking truth alone, we are rightly delighted also by the beauty of the expressions and the elegance of the words. For behold what they call the most perfect and complete argumentation in this Scripture—certainly older than all Greek and Latin rhetoricians: a beautiful and pleasant discourse, set out in five parts, namely proposition, reason, confirmation of the reason, ornament, and conclusion.

For the faithful advocate proposes on behalf of us all when he says: “Why do you hide your face, and consider me your enemy? You display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue dry stubble.” Immediately he introduces the reason: “For you write bitter things against me, and wish to consume me by the sins of my youth.” He at once appends confirmation of the reason when he says: “You have put my foot in the stocks, and watched all my paths, and considered the tracks of my feet—I who am to be consumed like rottenness, and like a garment eaten by moth” (Job 13).

He immediately adds a most ambitious ornament—not an ornament decked out with verbal trappings, but one most unfruitful in the sweet truth of profound humility and in true sweetness, and therefore very powerful for winning the ears and bending justice, not for shaking his mercy, with which we had grave enmity: “A human being born of woman, living for a short time, is filled with many miseries. He comes forth like a flower and is crushed; he flees like a shadow and never remains in the same condition. And do you consider it worthy to open your eyes upon one such as this and to bring him with you into judgment? Who can make clean one conceived of unclean seed, except you alone? The days of a human being are short; the number of his months is with you. You have appointed his bounds, which cannot be passed” [Col. 1623A]. Finally, he employs an elegant conclusion when he says: “Withdraw therefore a little from him, that he may rest, until his desired day comes, like the day of a hired laborer” (Job 14).

Great and vehement is the contention of this advocate, that is, of the Spirit of wisdom; and, as far as lay in him, it was capable of compelling God to answer how many iniquities and sins humanity had. If those great ancient orators, the holy men of old whose discourse this was, had stood with untroubled countenance in the heavenly court and had not been covered or defiled with any stains of sin, this one great impediment would still have remained: justice repelled persons stained by ancient disgrace and held back the voices of mercy from God the Judge sitting there. But behold, one was present and stood for all: a human being worthy of reverence and, because of his reverence, worthy to be heard (Heb. 5), against whom God, the just Judge of our nature, could bring no complaint; indeed, God was held indebted to him by a great exchange. For he had neither contracted original sin nor committed actual sin, and yet, out of obedience to God’s command, he underwent the penalty of sin—that is, death.

He therefore said: “Answer me: how many iniquities and sins have I? Show me my crimes and offenses.” What could God answer to this? Could he answer that this man had any iniquities or sins in his own person, rather than righteousness and merits? Accordingly, it was now fitting for him to challenge God, saying: “Why do you hide your face, and consider me your enemy?” (Job 13). And if God answered, “It is not I who hide my face from you, nor do I consider you an enemy; indeed, you are my most beloved Son, as I testified by the voice that came down to you from the magnificent glory, when I said: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased’” (1 Pet. 1; Matt. 3; John 1)—this man surely had a firm claim and a lawful cause to say truthfully: “What you did to one of the least of mine—indeed, to all of mine—you did to me” (Matt. 25).

For truly all the righteous and elect who had awaited him from the beginning of the world were his; and from all of them God hid his face, with the wall of enmities placed between, considering them enemies because of the sin committed by Adam, the common father of all. For they too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest (Eph. 2). “Why then,” he says, “do you hide your face and consider me your enemy?” In what respect? “For you write bitter things against me, and wish to consume me by the sins of my youth.” For you write—indeed, you retain written before you—bitter things against me, which you pronounced to this human being of the world: “Because you listened to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground in your work. In labors you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you, and you shall eat the plants of the earth. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3).

Such bitter things you have written against me ever since; and at the same time you wish to consume me by the sins of my youth. For, both for original sin and for actual sins committed through youthful lightness—concerning which the Psalmist says, “Remember not the offenses of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. 24)—you wish hitherto to consume every person. Then: “You have put my foot in the stocks,” binding each person with the cords of his sins, so that he may not do whatever he wills: although he may sometimes delight in the law of God according to the inward man, he sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind and leading him captive under the law of sin which is in his members (Rom. 7).

## Chapter XVIII. That he was justly heard for his reverence, according as the Apostle also says: “For if many died through the offense of one, much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded unto many”

By pleading these things and the other matters already mentioned, or things like them, with inward crying—with “a loud cry and many tears,” as the Apostle says (Heb. 5)—through this Spirit of wisdom he won victory in judgment, according to the principle of equity. Considering this, the same Apostle says: “For if many died through the offense of one, much more the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded unto many” (Rom. 5). And shortly thereafter: “For if death reigned through one by the offense of one, much more those receiving the abundance of the gift of grace and righteousness shall reign in life through the one Jesus Christ” (ibid.). Again: “As through the offense of one all human beings came into condemnation, so also through the righteousness of one all human beings came into justification of life. For as through the disobedience of one human being many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many shall be made righteous” (ibid.).

What else could the equitable Father, the just God, answer or determine? For what could be fairer or more reasonable? Or should that height of supreme majesty have been less ready to grant the grace of mercy than it had been to exercise the wrath of justice? For through one human being sin entered this world, and death through sin, and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (ibid.). Such was the ready justice of the Judge that, when one sinned, all of us, who had not yet been born, received an inheritance of sin, an inheritance of death. We acknowledge that the punishment was just, that the justice was true and irreproachable. For children could rightfully possess nothing but what had been stored up by their parents.

But behold another Father of our race, not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit. Thanks be to this Spirit of wisdom—one, manifold, subtle, mobile, eloquent, certain, sweet, gracious, steadfast—because by his subtlety, mobility, and keenness he found a means by which he might regenerate us, born to that old man, to this new man. Could divinity, then, as has been said, be less generous in justifying by the grace of mercy than it had been in condemning by the wrath of justice? Therefore, without disturbing or confusing the order of the former judgment, but with the cause removed through which the judgment of death had entered, the answer of life and peace was pronounced, and the entire wall of enmity was dissolved (Eph. 2).

## Chapter XIX. On the saying in Luke 23, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”: he knew that he would rise again; and hence the saying, “If a tree is cut down, it has hope”

Then this new Adam fell asleep, and while falling asleep said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23). He said this with certainty—certain, I say, and assured that he would soon receive back his entrusted deposit with great profit, as indeed happened. For because he thus surrendered his spirit, behold, he obtained for all his sons, for all the sons of his regeneration, the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, and he himself received back his own spirit. Otherwise, unless this human being had surrendered his own spirit, the spirit of his life, the Paraclete Spirit, precisely as Paraclete—that is, in granting forgiveness of sins—would not have come. Therefore he also said: “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16).

And so, just as for that old Adam, while he slept, a rib was immediately taken from his side and built or formed into a wife for him, so that offspring might be propagated (Gen. 2), so for this new Adam, now lulled into sleep in death, the sacrament of blood and water came forth from his opened side, and immediately from it the Church was re-formed, from which many children might be born throughout the world. For what Christian faith knows best and ought to know is this: immediately the whole company of the ancient elect, gathered from the beginning of the world and awaiting its redemption in the lower regions, was cleansed by that blood and that water, regenerated, and joined to this man. Thereafter, as many as are individually baptized from all nations, so many children are born from this man and from this his wife.

Nor, when he thus fell asleep, was he ignorant how soon he would awake, or how soon he would receive again the spirit which he was entrusting to the Father’s hand, together with so great a reward of accomplished obedience. For earlier, when he had said of this his sleep: “Behold, we go up to Jerusalem, and all things written by the prophets concerning the Son of Man shall be fulfilled. For he will be handed over to the Gentiles, mocked, scourged, and spat upon; and after they have scourged him, they will kill him,” he immediately added: “And on the third day he will rise again” (Luke 18).

For this reason the holy Job mentioned above, after the matters already stated, immediately says concerning him: “A tree has hope: if it is cut down, it grows green again, and its branches sprout. If its root has grown old in the earth, and its trunk has died in the dust, at the scent of water it shall bud and put forth foliage, as when it was first planted” (Job 14). For what is this tree except he himself who, when he was being cut down, said: “For if they do these things in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke 23). Therefore, “if it is cut down, it grows green again”—understand: on the third day, through the swiftness of the resurrection. This is because he never had any dryness—that is, he was a human being without all corruption of sin; indeed, because he was not only human but also God, whose greenness never fails.

But concerning a person who is merely human and not God, who is born in the sins of the ancient transgression and for this reason cannot be compared or made equal to this most green tree, Job immediately adds: “But when a human being has died, and is stripped and consumed, where, I ask, is he?” (Job 14). “As waters recede from the sea and a river is emptied and dries up, so when a human being has slept, he shall not rise again; until heaven is altered, he shall not awake nor arise from his sleep” (ibid.). Thus this man is the tree of life, ever green through the Spirit of wisdom. In order to bear fruit for us—life for souls in the present and resurrection for bodies in the future—when heaven is worn away, he permitted himself to be cut down, not doubting that immediately after three days he would grow green again, once in himself the cutting-down of which he had borne, namely bodily death alone, had been emptied of its power.

## Chapter XX. How, while this sacrament of wisdom was being accomplished, it was hidden from the eyes of all living beings; and how the Jews, mockers of that wisdom, are inexcusable

This work of the Spirit of wisdom, this sacrament, was at that time, while it was being accomplished, hidden, so that no one might know it until the appointed time. Hence the same blessed Job says among other things in his parable: “Whence, then, does wisdom come, and where is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living beings; it is concealed even from the birds of heaven. Destruction and death said: ‘With our ears we have heard its report’” (Job 28).

“From the eyes,” he says, “of all living beings.” Truly, from the eyes of all living beings. For none of the human beings then living in the flesh knew what was being accomplished by the cross of Christ’s suffering, not even any of the apostles. Hence it is added: “It is concealed even from the birds of heaven.” In this passage, birds are to be understood in a good sense: those of whom it was said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed, which a man took and planted in his garden; it grew and became a great tree, and the birds of heaven rested in its branches” (Matt. 13). Above all birds of this kind the apostles flew more highly; yet even from them this mystery of wisdom was concealed while it was being accomplished.

“Destruction and death said: ‘With our ears we have heard its report’” (Job 28). That is, the evil spirits, who became the inventors of destruction and death, could not foresee what was being done against them, since from the beginning they had closed their eyes to the rays of wisdom and had been rebellious against its light. Yet some among those dead with the common death could know this, especially the patriarchs and prophets, the last of whom, John, had recently been taken from the company of the living. Though they had sung beforehand of this sacrament while alive, once dead they did not remain ignorant of it, but waited with great longing for its arrival. Therefore it was rightly not said merely, “It is hidden from the eyes of all,” but with the qualification, “of all living beings”—that is, of those then remaining in the flesh.

What then? Does it follow that those mockers who crucified him and mocked him when crucified were excusable because this wisdom was, by its own will, hidden from the eyes of all living beings? Certainly not. For it continues: “When he established a law for the rains and a path for the sounding storms, then he saw it, recounted it, prepared it, investigated it, and said to a human being: ‘Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, and to depart from evil is understanding’” (ibid.).

To what human being before the Jew—among whom this sacrament of wisdom was deposited, and while it was being deposited was mocked and despised—did God, I say, first establish a law for the rains and a path for the sounding storms, and say: “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself”? For to establish a law for the rains and a path for sounding storms was to command preachers to fulfill in their lives what they hastened to urge by their speech, so that preaching might not be despised, but might run by a more open way like a sounding storm. God first established this law for Moses and the prophets, then for the apostles. All this was first among the Jews; for to them first were entrusted the legal and prophetic oracles of God (Rom. 3), and to them first, as was fitting, the Gospel of Christ was preached. In both cases it was first said to them: “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself”; for both prophetic and evangelical Scripture teach this in harmony (Ps. 110; Prov. 1, 9; Ecclus. 1).

But that insolent people did not fear the Lord. From the beginning it was always rebellious against him, but especially at the time when these things were done, when they filled up the measure of their fathers by persecuting and killing Christ, whose prophets their fathers had killed without the fear of the Lord. Therefore they are not excusable. For wisdom was not hidden from their eyes because they did not fear the Lord; rather, it was hidden so that they might never find it because they did not fear the Lord. Conversely, it was revealed to those who feared the Lord. Though they were unlearned and without letters, they knew the mysteries of God, according to the confession of him who said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

## Chapter XXI. How he says that God said to a human being, “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself,” although the Spirit of wisdom and the Spirit of fear are distinct; and how, also because God said this to a human being, the Jews and all fools are inexcusable

But how does this saying, “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself,” not conflict with or differ from the well-known number and order of the seven Spirits, which we have undertaken to treat in this present work? For if the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself, how does another Scripture, of no lesser but of equal authority, saying, “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Isa. 11), etc., count the Spirit of fear as one and the Spirit of wisdom as another, and distinguish them from one another by the seventh place or degree?

For this inquiry a third Scripture comes to our aid, with a moderate expression as though mediating between the two: namely, that which says, “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). In saying this, it plainly establishes the harmony of the two trumpets, or instruments, of the Holy Spirit already mentioned: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. But the beginning of wisdom is wisdom, though not yet complete, just as dawn or daybreak is already day, though not yet full daylight. Therefore the fear of the Lord is wisdom, that is, the beginning or first degree of wisdom. Likewise piety is wisdom, that is, the second degree of wisdom; knowledge is wisdom, the third degree; fortitude is wisdom, the fourth degree; counsel is wisdom, the fifth degree; and understanding is wisdom, the sixth degree.

But when wisdom is named in the seventh degree, it is understood as full and perfect. Its office is, by ceasing from activities and giving oneself to contemplation, already to lay hold of future goods, eternal goods, according to the saying: “Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10). That part is nothing other than wisdom itself, to be beheld in its own form.

Therefore, having said that wisdom “is hidden from the eyes of all living beings,” lest anyone despair or fault its concealment, he says: “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom itself.” In saying this he as it were opened a door and showed the first step by which a little one might begin to ascend to the wisdom hidden from the proud. Those living persons who had separated themselves from fools and sinners living wickedly and crucifying the Lord had already approached that point—namely, the apostles, and also that blessed Joseph of Arimathea, a good and righteous man, of whom the Gospel reports that he had not consented to their counsel and actions (Luke 23).

For him it certainly was wisdom to fear the Lord and, at this first degree, to hear wisdom saying: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them. If they say, ‘Come with us; let us lie in wait for blood; let us secretly set snares against the innocent without cause; let us swallow him alive like hell, and whole like one going down into the pit. We shall find every precious substance; we shall fill our houses with spoils. Cast your lot with us; let there be one purse for us all’—my son, do not walk with them. Keep your foot from their paths. For their feet run to evil, and they hasten to shed blood” (Prov. 1).

Yet wisdom was still hidden from the eyes even of these living persons, namely the apostles and the blessed Joseph: they did not know the mysteries of Christ or understand what, or how great, was the benefit of his cross and death. But because, in fearing the Lord and refusing the enticements of sinners, they stood as it were at the doors of wisdom, they deserved to be called upward and to ascend to wisdom; that is, to receive this holy Spirit of wisdom of whom we speak, in order to know the sacraments of God.

## Chapter XXII. On the saying, “Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows feathers, or will the eagle rise at your command?”

Accordingly, the saying is rightly understood which the Lord, answering Job from the whirlwind, speaks after many other things concerning such birds of heaven: “Is it by your wisdom that the hawk grows feathers, spreading its wings toward the south? Or will the eagle rise at your command, and set its nest on high? It dwells on rocks and abides on steep crags and inaccessible cliffs. From there it looks out for food, and its eyes see from afar. Its young lick blood, and wherever a carcass is, it is immediately there” (Job 39).

“Is it by your wisdom,” he says, “that the hawk grows feathers, spreading its wings toward the south?” Almost no one is ignorant that each year, as new feathers grow, the hawk casts off its old plumage and continually renews its feathers. But this does not refer to the time of feathering when it is clothed in the nest, for then, being still a chick, it cannot spread its wings toward the south. Rather, it describes the annual renewal when the loosening of the old feather renews it. For domestic hawks are given small warm places so that they may feather better; but wild hawks customarily spread their wings when the south wind blows, so that the warmth of the wind may heat their limbs and loosen the old plumage. When wind is absent, they spread and expose their wings to the ray of the sun, making a warm breeze for themselves; and thus, with their pores opened, either the old feathers fall out or new ones grow.

What, then, is the hawk’s growing feathers in the south wind except that each one of the saints, touched by the breath of the Holy Spirit, is strengthened and, casting away the practice of the old way of life, assumes the form of the new human being? This happened especially to the apostles already mentioned. Though they were birds of the old order—that is, persons slower because of their carnal understanding, and for this reason hidden from this wisdom—they deserved, by fearing the Lord, to be preserved for the time when, under the blowing south wind, they might grow feathers: that is, when the Holy Spirit came upon them, raised up by the new feathers of graces, they might perceive the hidden things of heavenly wisdom.

Further, although what follows, “Will the eagle rise at your command?” and so forth, can be understood of the others, ecclesiastical authority has handed down that it is to be understood especially of John. Flying more loftily, he left earth and in mind passed above all the heavens; for by subtle understanding he penetrated, in beholding, the inward mysteries of the Word, and in writing proclaimed them with clear testimony.

## Chapter XXIII. When we say that wisdom was hidden from the eyes of all living beings in this respect, we nevertheless rightly except the blessed Mary, who was then alive; and the same wisdom which at the beginning said, “Let there be light,” now said to the apostles, “Receive the Holy Spirit”

There was therefore only one in this world who knew wisdom at that time: Christ himself, the wisdom of God. For, as has already been said, wisdom was hidden from the eyes of all living beings, and was concealed even from the birds of heaven. And just as, in that ancient beginning, when God had created heaven and earth, “the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Gen. 1), so in this new beginning of the new creation the whole world was empty and void of the knowledge of wisdom, and the darkness of ignorance was upon the face of the heart of the whole human race.

Yet we confidently except the blessed Mother of God, then living, because this wisdom had by no means hidden itself from her eyes. For she was a prophetess—a prophetess, I say, comparable to none of the prophets—into the sanctuary of whose breast the Holy Spirit had gathered together all prophecies. With this one exception, therefore, all the earth was empty and void, and darkness, as has been said, the darkness of ignorance, was upon the face of the deep, upon every soul of the whole human race.

Moreover, this wisdom in substance was that same wisdom which long ago said in Solomon: “The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning; from eternity I was established” (Prov. 8). And shortly afterward: “When he laid the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things; and I delighted day after day, playing before him at all times, playing in the world of the earth; and my delights were with the children of human beings” (ibid.).

Let all kindly spectators of both plays, therefore, take delight: for there, at the beginning of the old creation, wisdom said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, and it divided light from darkness (Gen. 1); and here, at the beginning of the new creation, it brought light into the lower regions, so that all the elect from the beginning of the world, who had hitherto sat in darkness, might see the true light, the true God—or rather, might pass from the region of darkness to the homeland of eternal brightness and there become light by beholding the substance of the true light: light, I say, divided from the darkness of the lower regions. And we who live might be light, divided from the darkness of this world, as the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). For it also brought light to the living when, after rising, it said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). From that time it fulfilled in its apostles what it had promised when it said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). In both works—the former work of the old creation and this work of the new—this wisdom played most delightfully before the Lord.

## Chapter XXIV. How the same wisdom played here and there; and how it played well before the Lord there, but better here, where it so played before God as to make sport of the devil

Which play, finally, do we human beings judge to be, or to have been, more beautiful, and in which do we more rightly take delight? Surely we approve this latter play more, and delight more in it, for it pertains more directly to us and was wholly accomplished for our sake. And, to exercise true discernment: there, in creating heaven and earth, wisdom indeed played well before the Lord; but here, in creating new heavens and a new earth, it so played before the Lord as to make sport of the devil.

Of this mockery the Lord himself said to blessed Job: “Before his eyes he shall take him as with a hook, and with stakes he shall pierce his nostrils. Can you draw out Leviathan with a hook, or bind his tongue with a cord? Can you put a ring in his nostrils, or pierce his jaw with a bracelet? Will he multiply prayers to you, or speak soft words to you? Will he make a covenant with you, and will you take him as an everlasting servant? Will you play with him like a bird, and bind him for your maidservants? Will friends cut him up, and merchants divide him? Can you fill nets with his skin and fish-baskets with his head?” (Job 40 [Vulgate numbering]). For at every point one must understand: “as I [will].”

This was plainly done for us human beings. That earlier work of wisdom, by contrast, was done as much for angels as for us human beings. For Leviathan was hostile to us; and that name signifies the devil’s same hostility. Leviathan, indeed, is said to mean “their addition.” Whose addition, if not that of human beings, upon whom he once brought the guilt of transgression and whose guilt he extends, by his daily worst suggestions, all the way to eternal death? While he multiplies their guilt at interest, he undoubtedly heaps up their punishments without ceasing.

Leviathan may also be called “addition” by way of mockery. By crafty persuasion he told the first human being that he would add divinity to him, but he took away immortality. Thus he could be called the “addition of human beings” in mockery: while promising to add to them what they were not, he deceitfully took away even what they were.

How did this Spirit of wisdom make sport of him here? “Before his eyes,” it says, “he shall take him as with a hook.” Who does not know that in a hook bait is displayed and the barb concealed? The bait draws him so that the barb may pierce. Therefore our Lord, coming for the redemption of humankind, made of himself, as it were, a hook for the devil’s death. For he assumed a body so that, in it, the devil might seek the death of the flesh as his bait; and while he unjustly sought that death in him, he lost us, whom he had held as though justly. Thus he was caught by the hook of the incarnation, because while he sought in Christ the bait of the body, he was pierced by the barb of divinity.

There was humanity there to draw the devourer to itself; there was divinity to pierce him. There was manifest weakness to provoke him; there was hidden power to pierce the throat of the ravager. He was therefore caught by the hook because he perished by the very means through which he devoured. Indeed, he knew the incarnate Son of God, but he did not know the order of our redemption. He knew that the Son of God had been incarnate for our redemption; but he did not know at all that this same Redeemer would pierce him by dying. Hence it is rightly said: “Before his eyes he shall take him as with a hook.” For we are said to have before our eyes what we see set before us.

The ancient enemy saw set before him the Redeemer of humankind; recognizing him, he confessed him, and confessing him, feared him, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Mark 1; Luke 4). Thus he was caught by the hook before his own eyes, because he both knew and bit.

## Chapter XXV. Concerning the one mocked through the mystery of Christ’s passion: how truly it was said, “Will he make a covenant with you, or will you take him as an everlasting servant?”

If the attentive observer considers these things and the rest set forth above rightly, the lucid exposition of the blessed Gregory, marked by authoritative teaching, shows that before the Lord there is nothing more beautiful than this play of wisdom, nothing more delightful than this mockery by the Spirit of wisdom. One saying there is which we gladly recall to the present spectacle [Col. 1632B], namely: “Will he make a covenant with thee, or wilt thou take him for an everlasting servant?” For this was spoken so magnificently and enacted so wonderfully that, if you are present as a sympathetic spectator, the eye is not sated with the sight nor the ear with the hearing. For when it is said, “Will he make a covenant with thee, or wilt thou take him for an everlasting servant?” it is understood: “for me”; as if it were said, “Will you use him thus as a servant sworn to you, an everlasting servant?” For in will he opposes, whence he is called by the Greek name *Satanas*, that is, “adversary”; but in deed he is an everlasting servant. He serves as though he were faithful; he cooperates and furthers good things as though he wished to assist the Spirit of the Lord; and his vigilance proceeds as though [Col. 1632C] he were eager to offer and disclose counsel to him.

But how or when did it happen that God used the devil’s activity as a sworn service, as faithful ministry? Rather, when did the devil ever do anything that did not advance God, from which praise and glory did not increase still further for the Lord God? From the time when this proud angel fell from heaven and, to the praise or glory of God the righteous Judge, became the devil, whatever he has ever done or wished to do has wholly served the obedience and honor of God, and does not cease to serve it until the end of the age. Thus, at the beginning of his ministry—laborious indeed for God, but useless and ruinous for himself—it was said to him: “Upon thy breast shalt thou go” (Gen. III). This is to say: As this creeping creature, whose cunning you employed, goes upon its breast and presses itself to the ground, so you, devil, though you are a rational spirit, will always burden your rational faculty with grievous folly; and wherever you turn, you will always crush your intention downward and press it by contrary deeds.

For example: By envying, you emptied out man’s merit; but by that deed you opened a place for the grace of God. You will envy this all the more, while man becomes so much higher than himself as the grace of God exceeds the merits of every creature. From that point to the end, while you willingly oppose God, you unwillingly cooperate with God; and thus, having a ring in your nostrils, you go upon your breast, because in a wondrous order you intend evil and do good. By persecuting, you bring about precisely that which you persecute in order to destroy; and, like a little hammer, you wickedly strike God’s ear, yet by striking you extend it unto glory.

Considering all these things most subtly, the wise man says: “There are spirits created for vengeance, and in their fury they have made firm their own torments” (Ecclus. XXXIX). As though he said: Such is their fury, from envy at the success of the good, that they cannot restrain themselves from doing what will result in greater torment for themselves. Thus if you ask why the devil acts so zealously in matters by which, once done, he suffers the more, harms his own will, and greatly advances another’s virtue, behold, you now have the answer: fury is the cause. For, concerning both him and his followers, the malignant spirits, it says: “In their fury they have made firm their own torments.” Perhaps this seems strange to you, if you have never heard that a man too has killed himself through fury.

Let us now, as we began, observe [Col. 1633B] the folly of this fury around Christ, and the praise of that Spirit of wisdom of which we speak. The Pharisees said—and as they spoke, the devil surely spoke in them: “Do you see that we accomplish nothing? Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John XII). Again: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him.” “From that day therefore they planned to kill him” (John XI). While these things were said and done, their possessor, the devil, was surely intent that the world should not go after him, that all should not believe in him; but in intending this he did the contrary: namely, that the whole world should go after him and all should believe in him.

Therefore he served as an everlasting servant; he served as the most watchful guardian of a sworn [Col. 1633C] covenant, securing a kingdom for his Lord, and by that same service securing torment for himself. God did not require a holocaust and sin-offering—that is, calves or fat lambs—but there was need of one Lamb as a sacrifice for the whole world. Nor did this evil servant fail in the task, pressing on with his necessary service. For he entered into Judas Iscariot and brought it about that this better Lamb should be handed over as a victim on that night when the lamb of the old Passover was eaten in every house (John XIII).

God, or the wisdom of God, intended to annul the sale by which the first man had sold himself, when, transgressing the commandment, he set before himself the vain hope of divinity. This wicked servant aided this good purpose too, by causing the traitor to sell this man—though he who sold him possessed no right over him. The Godhead intended to give this man a kingdom and to subject to his power all the kingdoms of the world; and this servant assisted in this also, bringing it about that, in a furious jest, he should be clothed in purple, given a sceptre—that is, a reed—crowned, and greeted by a royal title. And, what we should wonder at no less, because the Lord intended to lay upon him the iniquities of us all (Isa. LIII), the crown was of thorns, so that the mocking servant could not deny that this Lord of all had borne the thorns of our sins.

Mocking in all these ways, he offered his own tongue to be bound with a rope; nor can he say that force or injustice was done to him because this man drew the kingdoms of the world to himself. For although in a most wicked jest, [Col. 1634A] he nevertheless placed the royal insignia about him. The order of our salvation required that, because guilt had been wrought through wood, righteousness likewise should be wrought through wood. And in this too the wickedness of this evil servant served, by bringing it about that the man who had not been subject to guilt should be suspended on wood. It was fitting that the grace of the possessor should cleanse those whom the punishment of the redeemer had absolved. This servant brought it about that the side of him, now dead, should be opened by a lance, whence blood and water immediately came forth (John XIX).

Who can worthily admire this entire play, by which this Spirit of wisdom so mightily overcame, so wisely mocked, the deceiver of the human race? Who therefore can worthily estimate the magnificence of this saying, “Will he make a covenant with thee, and wilt thou take him for an everlasting servant?” O the depth of the riches of the wisdom [Col. 1634B] and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! (Rom. XI.)

## CHAPTER XXVI. How it accords with the plan of that same wisdom that the same Lord, having power over life and death, did not choose to rise from the dead before the third day

This too belongs in the highest degree to the same beautiful plan and rational beauty of wisdom: that the same Lord, having power over life and death, did not choose to rise before the third day. We attempt to say why this was done, or ought to have been done, or was decreed, although this also, like the rest, is far higher than our understanding.

The number three, esteemed even among secular philosophers because it is the first of the numbers which, besides unity, admit no other division, has among us a far more illustrious name—indeed, first and divine authority—both on account of the very essence of the holy indivisible Trinity and because our Savior rose from the dead on the third day. And surely the third day looks to this same mystery of the holy Trinity. For our Lord did not rise before the third day because it was fitting that the death of Christ’s flesh should obtain for us, over three days, the propitiation of the holy Trinity.

Otherwise, why are we baptized with a threefold immersion in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, “made one with the likeness of his death” (Rom. VI), unless because he endured that same death for three days—a death which he had formerly called his baptism [Col. 1634D] (Luke XII)—and did so himself in the name and obedience of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? For the Father, as the Son himself testifies, gave the cup of passion to the Son; and the Son himself gave his own soul to drink, under his own power (John XIX), as he says: “I have power to lay down my soul” (John X). And the Holy Spirit caused it to be given him to drink, as the Apostle says: “Christ offered himself through the Holy Spirit” (Heb. IX).

Accordingly, the Lord’s death lasted three days: it was ordained by the holy Trinity, and our nature alone endured it in him in order to obtain for the human race the propitiation of that same holy Trinity. Nor only this: the entire course of his life, by the number of its years, indicates that it rendered service to the holy Trinity [Col. 1635A] and obeyed its command. For in the thirty-three years during which he walked upon earth, the number three is repeated, with this single difference: one three rises to the decimal limit so as to make thirty, while the other, that it may remain simple, stands in the single place.

Isaac too was led for sacrifice as a figure of this. For from Gerar, where Abraham then dwelt, to Mount Moriah—that is, the site of the Temple—is a journey of three days, as Jerome says; and accordingly he arrived there on the third day, as the history relates: “And he came to the place which God had told him of on the third day” (Gen. XXII).

But to return to what I began: marvelous swiftness, marvelous course and return of saving grace! In three days he wiped away the sins of the three ages of the world: all who had been before the Law, all who had been under the Law, and all who were to come under grace, he saved together by one death of Christ, assigning individual days of that death to the individual ages. The Holy Spirit indicated such swiftness when, commanding the prophet, he said: “Call his name, Hasten, strip the spoils, hurry to plunder” (Isa. VIII). To this also belongs that in the Song of Songs: “Return; be like, my beloved, a gazelle or a fawn of stags upon the mountains of Bethel” (Cant. VIII).

For he hastened to strip the spoils of hell and hurried to plunder; and, returning like a gazelle or a fawn of stags—that is, the son of the patriarchs—he appeared most swift to save upon the mountains of Bethel: that is, he was seen by the apostles, so that he might swiftly turn their sorrow into joy. They are the mountains of Bethel, that is, of the house of God, which is the Church: its leaders, eminent in the highest virtues. He hastened, I say, to strip the spoils of hell—that is, to lead forth all the elect by the victor’s right. For what delay could there be in stripping them away, or what difficulty in distinguishing them?

He was the sun; those whom he sought were as mirrors. Their faith was a mirror, sufficiently capable of returning a ray by receiving the sun’s appearance; but until then they had not shone, because the intervening wall of enmity, namely original sin, stood in the way before the sun. But Christ, dying in his flesh, had dissolved and torn down that wall which covered in adverse shadow those mirror-like souls awaiting the true sun. What delay, then, could there be, once the wall was destroyed and the true sun [Col. 1635D] descended to hell, before those vessels fitted to receive light—that is, the souls of the elect—at once shone again? As soon as this sun descended there—that is, the all-powerful soul of Christ, shining with the divinity of the omnipotent Word innate to it—they shone brightly; and the princes of darkness were scattered like smoke and melted like wax before the face of fire (Ps. LXVII). The righteous, coming out of darkness and received into paradise, began to feast and rejoice in God’s presence, together with the thief at the feast, to whom the Lord, hanging on the cross, had said: “Today thou shalt be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII).

And throughout the whole Sabbath the Lord Christ rested from all his work (Gen. II), with them; and the beloved fed among the lilies until the third day breathed and the shadows declined. Therefore, on the third day, when the Trinity of the Godhead had been made propitious to us, he swiftly cast away from himself the death which he had tasted. He had signified this when, upon the cross, thirsting for our salvation, and therefore truly saying that he thirsted (John XIX), after he had tasted the vinegar offered him, he would not drink it (Matt. XXVII). For he tasted a little of death’s vinegar, which he was soon—that is, on the third day—to reject, and was to drink no more. “For rising from the dead, he now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI).

## CHAPTER XXVII. How it belonged to wisdom that, when he rose, he did not immediately triumph over his slayers, nor suddenly appear to those who loved him

After mocking his enemies, he looked to his friends and, after the clouds of sorrow, shed back upon them the serene and luminous ray [Col. 1636B] of his victory. He did so in the order and manner fitting to be carried out by this Spirit of wisdom. He did not at once blaze forth visibly before his slayers in triumph, nor exact the deserved penalties of vengeance—as men of less wisdom sometimes do, men who do not know how to restrain victory or keep measure in glory.

For he awaited an order worthy of the revelation of his glory, being not changed in respect of the Holy Spirit but remaining the same as he had been, the same one who had said: “I seek not my own glory; there is one who seeks and judges” (John VIII). It is not his custom or discipline, by contentious attack or triumphal insult, to snatch hastened glory of victory from enemies, unless perhaps usefulness demands this for a time: namely, for the instruction or confirmation of those who believe or will believe, so that upon certain impious persons a punishment fearful to the rest may be inflicted, and the conscience of the living may not be unaware that judgment belongs to Christ the Son of God, the victor.

This is to be done once: that wisdom may laugh at the destruction of the little ones who love folly and mock when what they feared comes upon them (Prov. I)—namely, when that universal judgment, which must necessarily take place, comes to pass. Meanwhile, let us know that it belongs to wisdom to permit them to treasure up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath (Rom. II): “I called,” it says, “and you refused; I stretched out my hand, and there was none who looked” (ibid.). Thus, wisely patient and patiently wise, he permitted his enemies, the chief priests and Pharisees, even then to conceal [Col. 1636D] what had happened and the sacrilege laid up in their conscience. He permitted them, with money given, to purchase for themselves the lie which the soldiers uttered: “His disciples came by night, while we slept, and stole him away” (Matt. XXVIII).

As has been said, his turning toward his friends was not sudden either, but proceeded gradually in the most fitting order: first he was to be presented to the eyes of their minds, then to those of their bodies. This is almost the natural manner of his manifestation: no one has ever seen, or is to see, him well and beneficially outwardly unless he has first seen him inwardly through faith or love. Therefore he brought it about that their hearts should first be stirred to behold him by the sharp darts of many recollections [Col. 1637A]; and only then did he present his revived body outwardly to their eyes, when they were more intently turning his image within their yearning souls.

First judged worthy of this good was Mary, once a sinful woman, a woman dear to our piety and of widely known love. She indeed bore in mindful memory the cross and all the marks of his punishments; desiring to see him, even such as the place of burial had received, she wept when she did not find him. And when the disciples departed, she did not depart, but stood outside weeping (John XX). Therefore she was first judged worthy to see joy with tearful eyes and to announce joy to the sorrowing apostles (ibid.).

After her came Peter, whose sorrow was surely greater than that of all the apostles—indeed, twofold. He was sorrowful because the Lord had suffered these things; he was sorrowful because he himself had denied the suffering Lord three times. Without doubt, from the time when, after the Lord looked upon him, he went out and wept bitterly (Luke XXII), he did not cease to grieve and be sorrowful. Therefore the Lord judged him worthy to show himself first to him rather than to the other apostles. For thus we have in the Gospel, where it is first said of him: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Peter” (Luke XXIV).

Immediately afterward came the double confirmation of the good news: the two disciples recounted how, as they went to Emmaus and spoke together about him, he joined them, and how they knew him in the breaking of bread (ibid.). What do you suppose the image of him might meanwhile have been in their minds, as they sat inside speaking of him, astonished by lamentation and by joy still mingled with tears, with the doors shut lest anyone should hear their words, or any of the enemies should come upon them—the Jews, almost naturally envious of the Lord Jesus? Thus, their souls being well prepared, the time had come for him to offer himself, so as to be recognized, commonly to the eyes of them all. Therefore he stood in their midst and said to them: “Peace be unto you” (John XX). Thus modestly and temperately did this wisdom lead his man—the wisdom of which it has been most truly said that “it reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII).

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Why he appeared first to the sinful woman rather than to the apostles, and first to Peter, who had denied him, rather than to John, whom Christ loved

[Col. 1637D] There is also in the present place another matter in which, rightly marveling at the beauty of his ordering, we may linger over the praises of the Spirit of wisdom. For he is truly wise, or worthy of the praise of wisdom, who, having set before himself a good purpose, so tempers and orders all things that nothing fails to conduce and be expedient to that same purpose.

What did this new man—or what did the holy Spirit of wisdom purpose in this new man—except to offer strong hope to sinners and the weak, to furnish sinners and the sick with the weapons of steadfast confidence, or confident steadfastness, by which they might presume to use force against the kingdom of heaven and seize it violently? He himself testifies that this was his purpose when he says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill; I came not to call the righteous, [Col. 1638A] but sinners” (Luke V).

Therefore, when he who had deigned to die for sinners, rising from the dead, appeared first to Mary the sinner rather than to the apostles (John XX), and first to Peter, who had denied his name, rather than to John, his beloved (Luke XXIV)—John who stood and remained with his mother beside the cross of the dying Christ (John XIX)—he truly conducted his work with the Spirit of wisdom and wisely looked to the end of his purpose. For how greatly does this serve that purpose! All sinners and all sinful women who have faith lift up their restored spirits by this example, having proved by effects beyond doubt that Leviathan’s jaw has been pierced, as the Lord promised: “Wilt thou,” he says, “pierce his jaw with a bracelet?” (Job XL).

Nor is the praise of wisdom found only in this, that to strengthen sinners’ hope he deigned first to appear to the sinful woman and the apostle who denied him; it is found also in permitting those for whom he had stored up much grace, whom he had foreknown and predestined before the ages—Mary and Peter, I mean—to be plunged into such great and diverse abysses of sins. For what great fruit and usefulness arose from this? Let us speak first of the sinful Mary.

Certainly he was to say to the Jews, for the instruction of all ages: “Amen, amen, I say unto you, the hour comes, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (John V). And soon after: “Do not marvel at this, for the hour comes in which all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice, and shall come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (ibid.). When he was to say these things of himself—being a man who said such great and magnificent things—present proofs were required, and therefore particular persons were needed to receive these proofs.

It was necessary that one of the elect should die bodily for the glory of the Lord God, so that through his resurrection the Son of God might be glorified, by calling him from the tomb and thereby proving his statement true: that all who are in the tombs shall hear his voice and come forth. Thus his friend Lazarus was permitted to die, not unto death, but, as has already been said, for the glory of God (John XI). It was likewise necessary that one of the elect should die spiritually, also for the glory [Col. 1638D] of God, so that through that person’s conversion the Son of God might be glorified, by forgiving many sins and thereby proving his statement true: that the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God and those who hear shall live.

Thus this woman, the sister of beloved Lazarus, already beloved, was permitted to die in sins and to be a notorious sinner—not unto death or eternal destruction, but, as has been said, for the glory of God, for testimony to God and man, Jesus Christ the Son of God, who is righteous and justifies us (Luke VII). This concerning Mary.

Further, concerning Peter: that he fell and was permitted to deny him is likewise pious and beautiful within the ordering of this Spirit of wisdom. For Peter had been appointed prince of the apostles, and great authority after Christ was to be given—or had already been given—especially to him, by Christ the Son of the living God, whom he had confessed, when he said: “Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed it to thee, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say unto thee, that thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI). Again: “Simon, son of John, dost thou love me more than these? Feed my lambs; feed my sheep” (John XXI).

With such great evangelical authority of truth going before, Christian emperors after many ages, and all the leaders of the Churches, decreed and confirmed by perpetual law that, as all prefects or judges are subject to the emperor, so the other bishops of the Churches should be subject to blessed Peter and to the Roman pontiff, supreme according to his dignity. [Col. 1639B] Great honor, lofty eminence. Yet the author of that very honor or eminence says: “He that is greater among you shall be as the lesser, and he that is chief as one who serves” (Luke XXII). He also earnestly instructs those greater ones, or ministers, toward mercy, as you may plainly gather from his most humble deeds and his parabolic sayings.

But when or how would a man placed in the eminence of honor, with great awareness of holiness, know how to stoop to the lowly and suffer with the wretched? God alone is humble by nature, merciful and compassionate by nature—indeed, he is humility itself and mercy itself. Any human being who is humble or merciful is so only accidentally. Therefore it was necessary that Peter the apostle, predestined and called to so great an eminence, should have a cause preceding the greatness of his honor, from which the knowledge of humility and compassion might continually arise in him.

For this reason he was permitted to fall; for this reason he was abandoned even to a threefold denial: in a beautiful and visible ordering of wisdom, so that all of us who are skilled spectators of that wisdom, all who have the open eyes of discernment, may rightly marvel. Observing this, we believe it wholly expedient for those who preside, both for themselves and for those over whom they preside, that they be trained in humility and compassion through a great and memorable experience of former weakness. Otherwise they scarcely, or not at all, know how to bear the weaknesses of their subjects.

For this reason, long ago, through the mouth of the prophetess Hannah, this same holy Spirit of wisdom sang, saying: “For the pillars of the earth are the Lord’s, and he has set the world upon them” (I Sam. I).
