But where we say “upon the pillars of the earth,” the idiom of the Hebrew language, as blessed Jerome says, has “upon the afflicted of the earth.” And who are the afflicted of the earth except the humble and contrite in heart? Clearly the Lord has placed the world upon those who are such, because upon those who, remembering their former weakness, have a humble consciousness within themselves, he has established his Church. They are able to bear that same world so much more gently and compassionately as they remember more fully that they needed the grace of the gentle and compassionate God.

Let these things also, then, be said in praise of the Spirit of wisdom: for wisdom, that is, with a view to a great generation and to the benefit of generations, Christ, the salvation of all, permitted those whom he had loved greatly—Mary and Peter, I mean—to fall into the abyss of death before he rose from the dead, and, when he rose, admitted them as the first participants in the joy of his life.

## CHAPTER XXIX. In what manner God added to this Lord, as to blessed Job, all the things that had been his, doubled

To what end, then, was such great and good devotion to wisdom rewarded in this man? After the Psalmist said, “Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels,” he immediately added: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honor, and hast set him over the works of thy hands; thou hast put all things under his feet” (Ps. VIII). The Apostle likewise, after saying, “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even the death of the cross,” immediately added: “Wherefore God also exalted him, and gave him a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

Now, with these prophetic and apostolic proclamations in view, let us say, so that our discourse may not depart from the proposed allegorical or figurative contemplation of blessed Job, that the Lord “added unto Job all that he had, doubled” (Job XLII). For what had this Job of ours—what, I say, had Christ God, and what had Christ man? Let us carefully weigh in each case his possessions before his passion; and it will not be doubtful that he received all things doubled.

What had Christ God possessed? Nine orders of angels. For, being in the form of God and not yet having emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, he possessed glory with God, was adored by divine services, and was God and king of angels. But behold: because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and suffered the things mentioned above, he is God and king alike of angels and of human beings. Therefore doubled things were restored to Christ God.

What, further, had Christ the man possessed before he suffered, or what did he lose when he suffered and died? He had one single life, that of his flesh; for his soul was not subject to death, as was the soul of every human being because of the first parent’s sin. This is too little said. For he ought not to die either in body [Col. 1640D] or in soul, since he had neither contracted original sin nor committed actual sin. Thus, owing no death at all, he expended only one life, that of his flesh. But behold: in his body, which is the Church, he received double things, that is, life of body and soul. By dying, he defeated the death of souls; and by rising, he restored to us the life of bodies.

## CHAPTER XXX. How it pertains to the mystery of Christ that Job received all things doubled, but received not a doubled number of children, only the same single number

But we must consider that, although it is plainly established concerning the other things that doubled things were restored to that blessed man, concerning his children this is neither so evident nor true. For he had as many as before, namely seven sons and three daughters. Indeed it may rightly be said and thought that his children had died not in the same way as his beasts and cattle, which perished together in flesh and spirit; and therefore children too were added to him in double number, since at the resurrection there will be twenty.

Yet here on earth, in his lifetime, when he possessed the other things doubled, he received only the same single number of children. This likewise is not without a great beauty of mystery in the Lord Christ. For by his passion he redeemed no more persons than had long been preordained to life, whom God commanded to be born when, blessing the first human beings after their creation, he said: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I). For sin was the cause of the birth of the rest. Indeed, as punishment for sin, an increase of conceptions came upon the woman, the same Lord saying: “I will multiply thy sufferings and thy conceptions” (Gen. III).

When he says, “I will multiply,” it must be understood as “beyond the number”: namely, that after sin you will conceive more than had been preordained in the blessing given before sin. Therefore Job received the other things doubled, but his children in the same single number, during his lifetime, because Christ the Lord redeemed by his passion double rewards of blessedness, as stated above, but only the single number of the elect: as many as, having been preordained to life, had perished in Adam. For this is what the Apostle says: “And as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (I Cor. XV). He says “all” and “all,” yet he intends not all human beings, but only those predestined to life.

# THE THIRD BOOK ON THE WORKS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. THE SECOND BOOK ON WISDOM.

[Col. 1641]

## 644 CHAPTER I. That in that passion this wisdom instituted for us two sacraments, one baptism, the other the life-giving table of Christ’s body and blood

Seeking to know the holy artisan, the Spirit of wisdom, from his works, and to glorify him as God, in the preceding volume we treated the passion of the new man Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Now we shall begin to speak of the sacraments through which we are renewed according to the image of that same new man, and which that same Spirit of wisdom poured forth for us from the fountain of his passion.

These are the two greatest sacraments: baptism and the life-giving table of his body and blood. Without doubt they are so necessary for our salvation that apart from them no way lies open for any human being to life or to the kingdom of God. For he says: “Amen, amen, I say unto you, unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John III). Again: “Amen, amen, I say unto you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you have not life in yourselves” (John VI).

Only one instructed by that same Spirit, or by that same wisdom, deserves to perceive how rightly these sacraments and their whole order or administration are ascribed to the Spirit of wisdom. The wise and prudent of this age did not know it; indeed, they regarded it as justice deserving ridicule (I Cor. I and III). Consequently, they themselves became foolish, and their wisdom became foolish—not a little, but greatly: so greatly that they have been likened to dogs and swine, and it is said against them to the little ones to whom these [Col. 1642B] mysteries have been revealed: “Do not give what is holy to dogs; do not cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them underfoot and, turning, tear you to pieces” (Matt. VII).

These sacraments are holy. These sacraments are our pearls. But those who have mocked or mock them, while seeming wise to themselves, are dogs; they are swine. Therefore let us be little ones, and in these very things let us glorify as God the Spirit of wisdom who reveals them to us, and give thanks. And first let us speak in this volume concerning baptism.

## CHAPTER II. On baptism, which is interpreted “immersion,” by which we who were born to sin are reborn to God

*Baptisma* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as *tinctio*, “immersion” or “dipping.” It is called *tinctio* because there the human being is changed for the better by the Spirit of grace and becomes something far different from what he was. Therefore, when we say *baptisma*, although, being Latin speakers, we could say *tinctio*, we employ a Greek word or name in order to signify the singular majesty and dignity of its meaning: namely, such an immersion as no other immersion can equal. Though the flesh alone is visibly dipped, the human spirit is dipped still more invisibly, so that, as has already been said, the whole human being is changed and becomes far different from what he was.

For he was a child of wrath and becomes a child of grace; he was a child of death and perdition and becomes a child of life and attainment; he was a child of Gehenna and becomes a child of God’s kingdom; he was God’s enemy, and is reconciled and becomes God’s child [Col. 1642D]. A great and wondrous immersion, of great and wondrous efficacy. Therefore we say *baptisma* in Greek and, by a foreign name, signify the unique excellence of this immersion and endeavor to convey it to ordinary understandings.

## CHAPTER III. What and how great is the difference between the baptism of John and that of Christ.

Yet we use that term equivocally, since we apply this name—baptism—to both John’s washing and Christ’s washing. I say equivocally, because, as we must understand, the nature or definition of each washing or baptism is not the same. John’s baptism is the baptism of a servant; Christ’s baptism is the baptism of the Lord. John’s baptism is in water; Christ’s baptism is in water and in the Holy Spirit. John’s baptism is for repentance; Christ’s baptism is for the remission of sins. [Col. 1643B] By John’s baptism Christ is made manifest; by his own baptism—that is, by his Passion—Christ is glorified. For John speaks of his baptism: “And I did not know him; but that he might be made manifest in Israel, therefore I came baptizing in water” (John 1). But Christ, baptized with John’s baptism, speaks of his own baptism: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” Finally, by John’s baptism the people were prepared for Christ’s baptism; by Christ’s baptism the people are made fit for the kingdom of God.

Beyond doubt, those baptized with John’s baptism, who were told to believe in him who was to come after John (Acts 19), and who departed this life before Christ’s Passion, were released—even from their great sins—when Christ was baptized in his Passion; [Col. 1643C] and they entered Paradise with him and saw the kingdom of God with him. But those who rejected God’s counsel concerning themselves, by not being baptized with John’s baptism, and departed from this light before the aforesaid baptism of Christ’s Passion, received no benefit from the ancient remedy of circumcision. Christ’s Passion did not benefit them, nor were they brought out of hell, because they were not among those of whom Christ said: “For their sakes I sanctify myself” (John 17).

Nevertheless, this too must be known: those who had been baptized with John’s baptism and remained in this life until, after Jesus was glorified, the Gospel of his baptism was preached—if they did not receive it, if they did not judge it necessary to be baptized with his baptism—received no benefit from having been baptized with John’s baptism. [Col. 1643D] Knowing this, the Apostle Paul, when he found certain disciples and asked them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” (Acts 19), and again, “Into what, then, were you baptized?”—the implication being: if you have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit—when they answered, “Into John’s baptism,” said: “John indeed baptized the people with water, saying that they should believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.” When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. And when Paul laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them (ibid.).

How much, and how greatly, inferior was that baptism of the servant—in which they had not even heard whether there was a Holy Spirit—to this baptism of the Lord, in which the Holy Spirit is given for the remission of sins? Therefore, the name of the two things is indeed common, for both are called baptism; but their nature is different according to the name.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Apostle’s saying: “As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death”; and on the Apostle John’s saying: “For there are three, he says, who bear witness on earth,” etc.

The nature of this sacrament—that is, of Christ’s baptism—is not to be examined by the arguments of human conjecture, but must be bound to the Scriptures of divine authority. The Apostle Paul says: “As many of us as were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, [Col. 1644B] so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). John, however, says: “For there are three who bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood. And there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5).

The authority of both statements is undoubtedly divine, since neither of these speakers received or learned what he says from a human being or through a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ. One establishes whence baptism proceeded and what it accomplishes in us; the other establishes by what and by how great witnesses the act performed in it is secured as valid. “We were baptized,” he says, “into his death; we were buried with him through baptism into death.” Surely by the revelation of Jesus Christ he had learned what could not be taught by a human being or through a human being: namely, [Col. 1644C] what the Spirit of wisdom intended in so ordering the death of Christ himself, that he should first give up the spirit, and only then, after his side was pierced, blood and water should come forth.

For thus it is written: “When they came to Jesus, however, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; but one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out” (John 19). What was being done, if not that all of us should be baptized in his death, because we were unclean? What, I say, was the Spirit—the maker of all wisdom—doing here, except constructing a device to outwit the wicked devil, the possessor of human nature, so that we might die to him and be born again to another?

For witnesses—witnesses on behalf of the Son of God against that enemy—were being assembled for us. Counting these witnesses, the other says: “There are three who bear witness on earth: [Col. 1644D] the spirit, the water, and the blood.” The spirit, certainly, which he gave up; and the water and blood which the spear-stroke drew forth: these are the three witnesses. For to what end, or for what reason, was the Holy Spirit dwelling with the human spirit or soul in the habitation of flesh driven out, so far as could be done, by the violence of death? And why was the side of the innocent one pierced with a spear, and such a stream flowed out, unless so that he might come to us with that same water and blood, by the unanswerable justice of judgment?

Therefore these are witnesses for us, because we are no longer his whose we were: we have died to him to whom we lived, once we have been sprinkled with these three effusions of this dead man, namely spirit, water, and blood.

## CHAPTER V. How we rightly employ those witnesses, so that what was said may justly be fulfilled for us: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”

Let us carefully weigh our case, so that we may know how reasonably, truly, and in what right order of judgment we employ these witnesses. For what was our case? Certainly the sin of our first parent, the old Adam. We confess that all sinned in him and that all died in him. Yet, in that same condemnation, God in the justice allied with his mercy provided a way by which, if we wished, we should not be held liable.

For if the sinful son of the old human being flees to another Father, to the new human being who did not sin, behold, it is written—and is fulfilled for him—[Col. 1645B] that “the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18). But if he remains in that old state, he shall bear the iniquity of his aged predecessor, as it is likewise written: “You repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, to the third and fourth generation” (Deut. 5).

Therefore the judgment of the just God concerning us is discriminating and just: he permits no unwilling person, no one dissenting from the ancient sinner, to be wrapped up in that sinful mass. Let him only renounce the old state, and, while he is allowed, hasten to become a new human being. But he must possess a known and evident testimony of his flight. Why? Because the devil, our adversary, possesses a known and manifest testimony against the human race. What testimony? The forbidden tree, the tree presumptuously violated. [Col. 1645C] For this is a known and cogent testimony against the human being: unless he had in a proud mind aspired to the height of divinity, he would not have bitten the forbidden tree. Unless, I say, he had been swollen within, he would not so easily have yielded when tempted without.

Therefore, whoever is a son seeking a new father and fleeing to the new human being Jesus Christ, so as not to bear the iniquity of his old father, must, as has already been said, have in God a testimony set against the devil’s testimony, or the written bond of sin. Thus, just as the first human being, by biting the forbidden thing, gave a manifest sign of his pride, so he, by receiving through water the visible remedy commanded, may give his Saviour a manifest sign of humility.

These things appeared foolish and laughable to the wise and prudent, [Col. 1645D] from whose eyes true wisdom hides itself, while by their vain reasoning they debate how it befitted God that one human being should be condemned for biting a tree and that all human beings should die in him, and how the washing with water could make a righteous person out of a sinner, a living person out of a dead one, and a child of grace out of a child of wrath. But it has been revealed to little ones that small things can be, and are, testimonies of great things.

For the bite of a tree—whether ever so small or ever so great—is truly, or was, evidence of great pride; and the washing in water—whether ever so small or ever so great, that is, whether of a small spring or a great sea—provided only that it is in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and with the sign of the cross, is evidence of great humility. Therefore, because a great matter is at issue and the devil, a great accuser, employs testimony in the case he brings against humanity, the accused human being, seeking God as advocate, must employ lawful and necessary witnesses.

## CHAPTER VI. That, against sin—the devil’s testimony against us—there are three witnesses for us on earth: Spirit, water, and blood; and three in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and, with these, the food and drink of Christ’s body and blood.

This must indeed be understood: against no human being—not even against an infant whose life on earth has lasted one day—does the devil possess fewer than one testimony. For an infant born today is certainly born in Adam and is liable to original sin. Nor is it proper or just that a son, after his father has been judged—especially one born after the condemnation of that same father—should obtain the inheritance of which his father was justly deprived. Therefore the infant born today has nothing in the kingdom of God, for the accuser has against him at least one testimony, that of one sin.

But a person already advanced in years who approaches the grace of baptism has as many and as great testimonies available to the devil against him as are the original and actual sins he has joined together—not so that he may be judged if he does not believe, for “he who does not believe has already been judged,” but so that he may pay the penalties due for each individual sin. [Col. 1646C] Conversely, one who takes refuge in Christ’s grace is defended, or can be defended, by no fewer than seven witnesses. For there are three who bear witness on earth: spirit, water, and blood. And there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. The seventh witness is the food and drink of Christ’s body and blood. It also stands in a particular opposition to the testimony of original sin, because that sin was food consumed unto destruction, while this sacrament is food given unto salvation. We shall now speak in order concerning each of these witnesses.

## CHAPTER VII. What it means to bear witness in heaven and on earth.

But first we must inquire what it is to bear witness on earth and to bear witness in heaven. For it is not without purpose that the two testimonies given are distinguished as earth and heaven. What, then, is it to bear witness on [Col. 1646D] earth, except to be commended in the present Church through unity of spirit in the bond of peace, by having one faith and one baptism?

For one whom the holy present Church receives into communion must say, “Jesus is Lord.” This is to have the testimony of the Spirit, because “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12). And, as was said in the preceding chapter, “the Spirit is the one who testifies that Christ is truth” (1 John 5); for just as no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit, so no one speaking except in the Holy Spirit can say that Christ is truth.

Then, once he has by believing in his heart received testimony from the Spirit, he must, by receiving visible baptism, receive testimony from the blood and water [Col. 1647A] which flowed from Christ’s side when it was opened by the soldier’s spear. This, in its entirety, is to have testimony on earth, because the present Church thus receives into its communion and into the unity of its body the person commended to her.

There follows at last the testimony in heaven from the three who are one: namely, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. The person whom the present Church has received after approving the former testimony, and has sent away in her peace into another age, she undoubtedly commends to the heavenly Church by the testimony of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so that he may happily behold in heaven the glory of him whose sacraments he faithfully observed on earth. Let us now proceed to our subject.

## CHAPTER VIII. How, when our Lord by dying instituted for us the sacrament of his baptism, these three—spirit, water, and blood—were present together.

When the Lord Jesus was baptized with that baptism of his of which, as we said above, he declared: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12)—when, I say, he suffered, died, and was baptized in that same Passion or death of his, he instituted for us the sacrament of his baptism, and these three were present together: spirit, water, and blood.

The Spirit by whom, as the Apostle says, he offered himself to God as a living sacrifice (Rom. 12; Heb. 9), and which he gave up together with his own soul; and water and blood, which, already dead, he poured out from his spear-pierced side beyond the nature of dead bodies (John 19). When these three witnesses met there, Tartarus trembled, [Col. 1647C] the earth shook, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep later rose together when he rose (Matt. 27).

What did that great earthquake signify, except that the earth and the wretched beings themselves felt the power of the sacrament? For the first witness came to the underworld with Christ’s soul, and at his coming all the elect who had awaited him in darkness, gathered there from the beginning of the world, received remission of sins. That blessed thief had gone before, who had said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23); and immediately, upon this remission of sins following, what the Lord had told him was fulfilled: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in Paradise” (ibid.).

For the thieves’ legs were broken before that blood or water was poured out. And because not only salvation of souls but also resurrection of bodies was being prepared, through the successive remaining witnesses, with the third cooperating, the earth was shaken and tombs were opened, so that witnesses to the future universal resurrection of the dead might rise with the Lord. [Col. 1647D] Therefore the three witnesses were present where this sacrament was instituted, and the first of them is the Spirit. Accordingly, we must speak of this first.

## CHAPTER IX. That the Spirit begins through the sacrament to bear witness that we are children of God; and how one and the same fountain becomes for us womb and tomb, and whence comes the first resurrection.

The Holy Spirit gives here on earth, and begins through this sacrament [Col. 1648A] to give, that testimony of which the Apostle says: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as children, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father.’ For the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. 8). Through this sacrament, I say, he began to give that testimony; for before it was instituted we were enemies.

And if some had been friends, such as Abraham, who was called God’s friend (2 Chron. 20), nevertheless it was by the institution of this sacrament—that is, from the Passion of Christ the Son of God—that this testimony began to be given, that we are children of God. Abraham’s own sons bear witness and say: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2). For Abraham himself was called God’s friend from no other source than faith and expectation of this sacrament. Finally, of all that he believed—and through believing was justified and made God’s friend—this was the sum: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). In accordance with this faith he received the sign of circumcision in that part of the body through which seed is transmitted, not yet to receive the promises, until he should come who would give the blessing.

Therefore, through this sacrament the Spirit begins to bear witness that we are children of God. For in this sacrament he himself brings it about that we are born again and become God’s children. He who, by his divine omnipotence, came upon Mary and overshadowed her, so that the only-begotten Son of God might be conceived and born of her, comes by that same omnipotence upon the waters and gives them fertility, so that children of God may be born again from them.

The spring of elemental water, enlivened by the coming of this Spirit, becomes the womb of the Church, the womb of grace. Therefore Christ says: “Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit” (John 3), etc. But the Apostle says: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6). Thus one and the same font is both womb and tomb to us: womb, because, as Christ says, we are born again; tomb, because, as Christ’s Apostle says, we are buried with Christ there and shall rise with Christ from there.

O wonderful craftsman, Spirit! He accomplished what the teacher of Israel did not know could be done, when he said: [Col. 1648D] “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” (John 3). The Lord Jesus replied well: he did not say, “It cannot happen; a human being cannot enter again into his mother’s womb and be born”; but he said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

He did not, I say, deny that a human being could enter again into his mother’s womb and be born, but said what kind of womb, or whose maternal womb, a human being ought to enter again and be born from. For when this Spirit comes upon the water, it becomes the womb of our mother, the heavenly Jerusalem—the womb from which the human being was cast out as an untimely birth when he sinned. That womb, infected by the serpent’s poison, could not retain him until the lawful time: that is, until, at the appointed time, he should be carried from the bounded region of Paradise, in which he had received not overly narrow restrictions of command, into the breadth of heaven, in the likeness of God’s angels.

This water, I say, becomes by the Holy Spirit the womb of that same mother, [Col. 1649A] within whose sacraments one, once received, ought to be kept until the day of a certain birth—that is, until the end of the present life, when one is born to see the kingdom of God. Conversely, concerning those who tear this same womb apart by making heresies and schisms, the Psalmist says: “Sinners have been alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood.” And because these too, like Adam, have become untimely births after being deceived through the serpent, he immediately adds: “Their fury is according to the likeness of the serpent” (Ps. 57), etc.

Thus this water is the womb from which, according to Christ’s declaration, we are born again; by the same act, according to the declaration of Christ’s Apostle, it is the tomb in which we are buried with Christ and from which we rise with Christ. For one enters that womb by dying, and the person who has entered by dying is born again by rising. How? The Spirit comes first and testifies that Christ is truth (1 John 5); the sinful and false human being approaches and accuses himself—himself, that is, the old human being, the old Adam, or the old condition contracted from Adam—condemns it and assigns it to death. For he says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50).

Then he receives on his forehead the marks of Christ’s Passion, the sign of Christ’s cross; and because he has this Spirit as his advocate, because he speaks true humility and a humility that is true, according to the Spirit, his being marked only with the seal of Christ’s cross, Passion, and death is as though he himself had been crucified, suffered, and died. [Col. 1649C] For Christ was crucified, suffered, and died not for himself but for the sinful human being, not on account of his own sins but on account of the sins of the penitent human being. Then he is immersed three times in the water, and this has the force for him of the three-day burial of Jesus Christ. He is lifted from the font, and behold: he who had been dead has risen with Christ in the first resurrection.

## CHAPTER X. On the two gifts of the Spirit; when and whence the Spirit began to be called Paraclete; and which gift is given first or is pre-eminent.

Once this mystery has been celebrated, whatever the hour of the day—whether morning, the third hour, the sixth, the ninth, or evening—that is, whatever the human age—whether childhood, adolescence, youth, old age, or decrepit age—the person is a new human being and a servant-child of the Lord, a new creature and a child of God.

Yet the one who has been born has not seen his Father; nor does he yet receive the inheritance which, with this Spirit as witness, has been made over to him by Christ’s blood. Therefore, let the Spirit who became witness in baptism also be guardian of the orphan, when the person who has been born again receives the second grace through the laying on of hands and the anointing with sacred chrism. From that point this Spirit is designated by a new name [Col. 1650A] and is called Paraclete. *Paraclete* is Greek; in Latin it means “consoler.” This is a new name: nowhere is the Holy Spirit called by this name before this sacrament was instituted.

When this sacrament was being instituted, when Christ was suffering, on the very night on which he was betrayed, he first called the Spirit by this name when promising him: “But because I have spoken these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart. Yet I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16).

It is as if he said: I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away—that is, that through the Passion of death I pass from this world to the Father—because unless I have suffered for you, [Col. 1650B] the Holy Spirit will not come to you in that coming which is consolation, that is, remission of sins. For this is the common consolation of all the elect: through faith in Christ they have received this Spirit for the remission of sins; and on this account they rightly deem themselves blessed, as the Psalmist says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31).

The Apostles indeed received this Paraclete—that is, the gift of this Spirit for remission of sins—on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, when the Lord breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). Yet they did not receive the second grace of the same Spirit until the fiftieth day. By the first gift they received remission of sins; by the second they were made strong, fervent with good zeal, knowing and wise, eloquent, and mighty in miracles.

Without doubt, the principal ground of *paraclesis*, that is, consolation or joy, lies in the first gift. For the Lord himself says: “Nevertheless, do not rejoice in this, that spirits are subject to you; but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). Finally, by the first gift of the Spirit the names of the elect are written in heaven through baptism, and this is the ground for rejoicing; by the second gift spirits are subjected, and so forth. Such charisms are given—or rather apportioned—to individuals as the Spirit wills, and one should not rejoice so greatly in them.

For before Christ’s coming the patriarchs and prophets received very many gifts of this grace, and the Apostles themselves cast out demons before Christ’s Passion; yet they had no cause for rejoicing unless it came about that, through Christ’s Passion, they received the first and chief consolation, the first and chief gift of this Paraclete: the remission of sins. When that was accomplished, their heart rightly rejoiced, according to the promise of him who said: “But I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16).

The teaching of this Paraclete made it almost natural to all his own that they should rejoice and exult in this first grace—namely, that through baptism they have put off the old state of sin—especially if they preserve that same grace by committing no new crimes. But they should not rejoice in the second grace, nor seek even ordinary gifts, except perhaps for God’s glory, so that God’s Church may be built up. [Col. 1651A] Hence scarcely anyone who wishes to be regarded as Christian or Catholic is willing to be passed over in silence—even though such silence would be praiseworthy—if he is wise or knowledgeable, or has power against demons.

Having said these things briefly concerning the first witness—the Spirit of God, the Spirit of adoption as children, bearing witness to our spirit that we are God’s children—let us consider the remaining witnesses.

## CHAPTER XI. That the second witness is blood; how great its authority or usefulness as testimony is; and how it is present in the sacrament of baptism.

After the Spirit, the second witness in Christ’s baptism is blood. John indeed says: “There are three who bear witness on earth: spirit, water, and blood.” But in the Gospel, after the giving up of the spirit, it is not said, “Water and blood came out,” but “Blood and water came out” (John 19). Therefore blood is the second witness, both in dignity and in the order of the text.

This witness gives testimony in this case as, in a testament, a great price for a precious or necessary thing is weighed out or paid before lawful arbiters and hearers. For example, that evangelical king of whom it is written, “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding-feast for his son” (Matt. 22), defends the bride named there and made a wedding-feast for his Son because that same Son acquired the bride by his blood. For this is known to all children of the wedding-feast.

The Apostle likewise says: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his blood” (Acts 20). Although that king says, “My oxen and fatlings have been killed,” and does not say, “My own Son has been killed and acquired this bride by his blood,” both might have been said; because, to acquire for the King’s Son this bride, the kingdom of God, both prophets and Apostles were killed, and the King’s Son himself was killed, though he now lives.

But this was passed over in the parable—or should have been passed over—that the king’s son was killed in making, or indeed in order to make, the wedding-feast, because this surpasses every customary practice—indeed, the very nature—of weddings. For if the man seeking a bride dies for that bride, there will no longer be one to take her or to make the wedding-feast.

Therefore blood bears witness in this sacrament as a known and great price confirms a claim in a great transaction concerning a great matter. For the blood of the Son of God is truly a great price, not merely because it is holy blood or because that man is the Holy of Holies, but because a human being possesses nothing he can give that is greater or dearer than his blood. Therefore he says: “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). And John says: “By this we have known God’s love: that he laid down his life for us” (1 John 3).

We find life set in place of blood and blood in place of life, because, as physicians also testify, the life of a human being—indeed of every animal—is in the blood. Thus it is also written in Genesis: “You shall not eat flesh with blood. For I shall require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast and from the hand of man” (Gen. 9). Yet in this case each—namely life and blood—must be understood separately.

For, wonderfully, he first laid down his life, and then, already lifeless, beyond the nature of dead bodies, poured blood from his side and, with the blood, water: blood in order to redeem us, water in order to wash us. For he did not wish to redeem us with his blood merely in order to possess unclean vessels, but in order to wash us from our sins and possess us clean in sanctification and honour. He therefore poured out blood as the price of redemption and water as the washing of sanctification.

Yet we also read that he washed us with blood. For the Apostle John says: “He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). Let us therefore faithfully say that the water which flowed from his side washed us, but that the water obtained from its accompanying blood the power by which it could wash us. For without blood, water could not benefit us; without blood, I say, the testament could not become valid, nor could the inheritance of the kingdom of God be assigned to us. Hence the Apostle says: “For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must necessarily intervene. For a testament is confirmed in the dead; otherwise it has no force while the one who made it is alive. Hence not even the first was dedicated without blood” (Heb. 9).

Blood, therefore, is the price of the water: that which makes the water fit to receive the Spirit and to confer remission of sins. Through this mediator, the higher Spirit is reconciled to the lower water. There, indeed, both blood and water were visibly present together, for “he who saw bore witness” (John 21); but neither visibly washed any dead or living person.

Here, however, when individual believers are baptized, only one thing—namely water—is visibly present, and it visibly and perceptibly washes. Blood is neither visibly present nor visibly joined to, or poured into, the element of water. Yet that blood is invisibly present to the sight of faith, [Col. 1652C] which is hindered by neither place nor antiquity nor length of time. For faith undoubtedly brings the inward human being there, to the place where that blood was poured out, when he is asked: “Do you believe in God the Father Almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, dead, and buried,” etc.

When he says “I believe” in this statement of Christ’s Passion and cross, that blood is undoubtedly present; and, invisibly, it washes both the invisible substance of the soul and the visible substance of the body, cleansing from all sins. For, as the Apostle says: “If the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon those who are defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself spotless to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9), etc.

We must now speak of the third witness, namely water.

## CHAPTER XII. On the third witness, namely water: that, just as the Spirit of God moved over the waters, so now we may truly say that the Spirit moves over the waters in order to make a new creation.

That water which flowed with the blood from the side of the dead Christ was a new creation, created so as to become a second beginning of the world’s re-creation. A second beginning, I say; for the beginning of the world’s first creation, and the first material of the forms to be created, was the primordial matter. For then the substance of the waters was confused, and all things lay hidden beneath the waters, when, at God’s word, “Let there be light,” etc., his Spirit was borne over the waters (Gen. 1). Yet this is the difference: then God created those waters from nothing; here, however, he created them not from nothing but from the body of the now-dead man Jesus Christ. Therefore that water was—and indeed is—a second beginning.

And over the waters in that first beginning the Spirit of God was borne so that he said, “Let there be light,” and light was made; this we rightly understand as the angelic creation. But over the waters in this beginning the same Spirit deigned to be borne so that he likewise said, “Let there be light,” and light was made; and this light we confess to be the vision of God restored to human beings. O truly great and praiseworthy craftsman, this Spirit of wisdom! In order that we might without any contradiction be a new creation, and consequently might not belong to the transgression of the old Adam, he discovered for us another beginning; he discovered a method of workmanship by which he might bring us back to that beginning and make the old human being new. This is the wisdom which none of the rulers of this world knew; “for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). Certainly the very cunning of the rulers of darkness could not foresee this. They knew that he was Christ, the Son of God; but they could in no way know or suppose that the wisdom of God could devise for us such another beginning, by which, in defending us, the justice of God could not be reproached.

For what is this? How great and how admirable an invention it is! This artifice, when it was established, wisely deceived the deceitful devil; and thereafter it wisely outwitted and powerfully conquered all the gods—or rather, not gods but demons—of the nations: Jupiter, Hercules, Juno, Minerva, and the other prodigies of demons; likewise all their worshippers, all the supposedly wise persons of this age made foolish, kings and emperors of the world. As Christ, in the contemptible form of a servant, concealing the hidden form of God, conquered the strong armed man in the very thing in which he was despised, and cast him out of his courtyard (Luke 11), so this water, in its lowly substance concealing the precious grace of the Holy Spirit and of Christ’s blood, destroyed the worship of demons; it converted temples of demons into temples of Christ, and worshippers and children of the devil into true worshippers and children of God.

## CHAPTER XIII. How mercifully the Spirit of wisdom provided for the poor, by making water—which is accessible to all—the gateway of the kingdom of God, etc.

And see how, while he so mocks the opposing party, the Spirit of wisdom mercifully provides for his own poor. For behold: water has been made the gateway of God’s kingdom. As accessible as the water is, so accessible is this entrance into God’s kingdom. Who is so poor in understanding that he cannot procure a vessel of this element at his own expense? Whether water be drawn from a lake, a river, the great sea, or a small spring, with this intention, this faith, and the hallowed invocation of the holy Name, it is that water which flowed from Christ’s sacred side.

Accordingly, in this mystery too that prophetic saying is rightly understood: “All who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten and eat. Come, buy without silver and without any exchange, wine and milk” (Isa. 55). For just as wine and milk are offered to all, without any exchange, from the fountain of the Scriptures, so this abundant sacrament of regenerating water is offered to all without gold or silver, without any loss of possessions whatsoever.

But perhaps, when a persecutor presses hard, some confessor of Christ, hindered by one of the devil’s agents, has neither time nor place to draw even a little water in a pitcher from the nearest river, to offer it to the minister of this salvation and to have it poured over him in confession of Christ. For many, overtaken by the crisis of persecution, were subjected to torments without water-baptism and were confirmed and brought to completion for Christ’s name. What then? Were they not baptized? Indeed, they attained a grace so much greater than those who die in the Church’s peace as, at a more grievous cost, they shared in the death and blood of Christ. For in baptism there is only the common likeness of death, as the Apostle says: “For if we have been made united to the likeness of his death, we shall also be united to his resurrection” (Rom. 6); but in martyrdom there is death itself. If martyrdom were not baptism, the Lord would never have said of his own passion, as was stated above: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12).

But except for those whom such an emergency overtakes, the Holy Spirit meets no one outside the fonts; he encloses the whole remission of sins within the waters and extends it no further.

## CHAPTER XIV. Again concerning the three witnesses—Spirit, blood, and water—and that without any one of them the testimony on earth is not valid.

These three, then—Spirit, water, and blood—are witnesses; without any one of them the testimony is not valid on earth, that is, in the present Church. For unless someone says, “Lord Jesus”—in which is spoken the witness of the Spirit, since “no one says, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12)—and unless he says, “This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ: not in water only, but in water and blood” (1 John 5), and, while saying these things, is baptized with elemental water, he is not to be received on earth; he is not to be admitted to ecclesiastical communion, since he lacks the lawful and necessary witnesses. One or two witnesses do not suffice in this matter.

Those disciples to whom Paul said, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” and who replied, “But we have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit” (Acts 19), had only one witness. They had, I say, one witness: water alone. For in John’s baptism, just as they had not heard whether there was a Holy Spirit, so they had not received the witness of blood. John could not instruct by the word of the cross, which did not yet exist, nor preach the blood which had not yet been shed. Therefore they had one witness, water alone; and unless they were baptized again, they were to be received neither on earth nor in heaven.

All who are baptized among heretics have two witnesses, water and blood, but do not have the third, the Spirit. For heretics, whoever they may be, who diminish or tear apart the faith of the Lord Jesus by some blasphemy, do not truly say, “Lord Jesus”; and therefore they do not speak in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). Thus, although they are instructed and baptized in him who was crucified for us, they appear indeed to possess the witness of water and blood, but are proved not to possess the witness of the Spirit. Nevertheless, if they have been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—for many heresies baptize in this name—the washing of the flesh is not repeated for those who flee from them to the catholic Church; rather, reconciled only through the laying on of hands, they receive the third witness, the Spirit.

Again, those who have the witness of Spirit and blood by saying, “Lord Jesus,” and believing that he shed his blood for us, should not hesitate, however righteous they may consider themselves, to seek the witness of the third witness, water. For whether a Jew, justified in the Law, or a philosopher praised in the pursuit of virtues, says, “Lord Jesus, and this one suffered for the whole world,” yet disdains to be baptized in water for the remission of sins because he considers himself righteous, he is by no means received on earth; he is in no way permitted here to enjoy ecclesiastical communion.

## CHAPTER XV. How the grace of baptism, though new in act, is nevertheless old in God’s will and purpose.

This tradition, moreover, must not be despised as though it were new; for although it is new in act, it is old in God’s will and purpose. To answer briefly the Jew, who almost naturally recoils from and hates this sacrament: does this sacrament first possess authoritative testimony only from Christ’s saying, “Unless one is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3)? Was not this righteousness testified long before by the Law and the Prophets—by the Law through mystical deeds, by the Prophets through manifest sayings?

Let us first recall the prophetic words. We should say, no longer to Nicodemus, “Are you a teacher in Israel and do not know these things?” (John 3), but to any Jewish teacher: “You are a blind guide of the blind, and do not know these things.” For behold, in Ezekiel God says: “I shall sanctify my great name among the nations, so that the nations may know that I am the Lord, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes. For I shall take you from the nations, gather you from all lands, and bring you into your own land. And I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and I shall cleanse you from all your idols. And I shall give you a new heart and place a new spirit in your midst. And I shall make you walk in my commandments, keep my judgments, and perform them. And you shall dwell in the land which I gave to your fathers” (Ezek. 36).

What else does God made man do in his Gospel than what God, who was to become man, promised in this prophet? For if you asked when the words in this prophet were fulfilled—“I shall sanctify my great name,” and “when I have been sanctified, I shall pour clean water upon you and place a new spirit in your midst”—you arrive at that baptism of which he said, “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12): that is, that he was immediately to be seized and led to his passion. He himself says, “For them I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth” (John 17). Having said this, and immediately sanctifying himself—that is, offering himself through the Holy Spirit, spotless, to the living God (Heb. 9; the source reads “1 John 9”)—he poured upon us this clean water of which we speak and placed in our midst the new Spirit, the Holy Spirit.

And, taking us from the nations—for we were nations, “going after dumb idols as we were led” (1 Cor. 12)—he removed the heart of stone from our flesh, because we were stones worshipping stone idols; and by giving us a heart of flesh he raised up children of Abraham from stones (Matt. 3). From that time we dwell in the land which he gave to our fathers, because, reborn from this water and this Spirit, we began to see the kingdom of God.

Likewise, in Isaiah, after he had rejected the justifications of the Jews, saying: “Do not continue to offer sacrifice in vain; incense is an abomination to me. New moons and Sabbath and other festivals I will not endure. Your assemblies are iniquitous; my soul has hated your calendars and solemnities; they have become burdensome to me; I am weary of bearing them. When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes from you; and when you multiply prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood”—he immediately states what he prefers: “Wash yourselves,” he says, “be clean” (Isa. 1). Again: “If the Lord washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleanses the blood of Jerusalem from her midst in a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4). And lest anyone, presuming upon righteousness, suppose that he has no need of this washing: “All our righteousnesses are like the garment of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64). And in Zechariah: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruating woman” (Zech. 13).

These are few examples among many prophetic sayings. But this righteousness was testified by the Law, both in many ways and especially in this: after the lamb had been sacrificed, when the children of Israel were fleeing, God opened the sea; Pharaoh too entered the sea with his chariots and horsemen; the Lord brought back the waters of the sea over them; but the children of Israel walked dry-shod through its midst (Exod. 14). Yet however many examples or testimonies from Scripture may be produced, these people persist in evil: not so much Jews or Israelites as Philistines, like those who were the first enemies of Israel fleeing toward the Red Sea, of whom Scripture says: “When Pharaoh had sent forth the people, God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is near, considering lest perhaps the people should repent if they saw wars rising up against them” (Exod. 13).

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the three who bear witness in heaven, and why he did not say “Father and Son,” but “Father and Word”; and how the Word bore witness to the assumed man.

Concerning the three witnesses bearing testimony on earth we have spoken as far as we were able. It remains briefly to speak of the three who bear witness in heaven. “For there are three,” he says, “who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5).

First one asks why he did not say, as is more customary, “Father and Son,” but “Father and Word and Holy Spirit.” We must answer that not only those three or these three witnesses bear witness that we are born of God, as he had proposed when he said, “Everything born of God conquers the world”; and, at the end of the chapter, “Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony of God in himself” (ibid.). But they themselves—indeed, principally they—bear witness to Jesus that he is the Christ, or that Christ is truth (ibid.).

Therefore, lest an occasion be provided for heretics to assert two sons, one the Son of God and the other the son of man, he did not wish, when offering testimonies concerning that man who hung on the cross and died, to say that the Father and the Son bear testimony to him. For he himself is, in both the divine and the human substance, the one Son of God. Rather, he says, “the Father and the Word and the Holy Spirit.” For truly it is not Son giving testimony to Son, but the Word giving testimony to the assumed man that he who was denied and rejected is himself, I say, the Christ, himself the truth. That is: it is not one person of Christ giving testimony to another person of Christ, but one substance of Christ giving this testimony to the other substance of Christ.

How does the Word give this testimony? To pass over much that exceeds our infancy: it gives testimony in this, namely, that whatever this man spoke is true and that all these things are one true Word. And this is lawful testimony. For the Law gives the sign by which a prophet and a non-prophet are known: “But if you answer in silent thought, ‘How can I know the word which the Lord has not spoken?’ you shall have this sign: what that prophet predicted in the name of the Lord, if it does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it; rather, the prophet has fabricated it through the swelling of his own mind, and therefore you shall not fear him” (Deut. 18).

This was certainly said on account of this prophet—indeed, the Lord of prophets. For he had promised, saying: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your nation and from your brothers, like me” (ibid.), etc. Thus, with this statement of the Law going before, he of whom this was proposed presents his credential to us, saying: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24). Moreover, against his Jewish enemies even this should suffice: he said of them, “They shall fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive among all nations” (Jer. 44 [probably Luke 21:24]), as indeed occurred.

Therefore, according to the testimony of the Word, Jesus is the Christ—Jesus, certainly, who was thought to be the son of Joseph (Luke 3)—and not some other Christ. How does the Father bear testimony to him? First, by saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 13 [probably Matt. 3:17]). Then by always hearing him in the performance of great works which no one else has done (John 15), and especially by raising him from the dead. For if he lied in calling himself Christ, the testimony of divine works would not accompany him, nor would the resurrection of his flesh—which is great testimony—follow.

Likewise the Holy Spirit bears testimony that he is the Christ, or that he is the Son of God. For, just as he said, “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he shall bear witness concerning me, and you shall bear witness” (John 15), so it was done, is done, and shall be done until the end of the age. These three bear witness in heaven, that is, invisibly. For the previously mentioned witnesses—the Spirit, water, and blood—gave testimony on earth, that is, visibly. The Spirit appeared visibly over him, having assumed the bodily form of a dove, affirming him to be the one whom he had commanded should be recognized by that sign; he who baptizes visibly poured out blood and water from his side when already dead. He would not have done this if he were not Christ, the Son of God. Now let us return to our subject.

## CHAPTER XVII. How it is not enough that three bear witness for us on earth unless three also bear witness in heaven; and how “these three” are not one person but “are one.”

After we who say, “Lord Jesus,” have been baptized with his baptism, we are commended by three witnesses on earth—that is, in the present Church—but this is not yet enough. For he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7). And the apostle James says: “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2).

Therefore, just as there are three who bear witness on earth so that we may be received into the communion of the Church, so there are three who bear witness in heaven so that we may enter the kingdom of heaven. These three witnesses are the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit. To what do they bear witness? Certainly, to love, through which faith works: namely, that we who have faith may also have love for this Name and thus may be deemed worthy to enter the glory of the kingdom of heaven, as it is written: “All who love your name shall glory in you” (Ps. 5). But how honorable it is to enjoy the testimony of such persons before all the powers of heaven (Luke 21), no one can know except those who have experienced it.

“And these three are one.” Not, “These three are one person,” but, “These three,” he says, “are one.” This is as though he had said: “These three persons are one substance.” Thus Christ himself, against the Jews, against the Arians, and likewise against the Patripassians, says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). For when he says “I and the Father,” he affirms two in person, which the Patripassians, that is, the Sabellians, deny; when he says “are,” he testifies to one in substance, which the Arians deny. Thus here too he says: “These three are one,” that is, these three are one in substance while distinct in persons. It remains, in accordance with our purpose, to speak of the seventh witness.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the seventh witness, the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood: that it is not merely testimony for us but the very testament of life; and that its institution had its beginning in the Lord’s passion.

The seventh witness for us in the present matter is the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. The power of this sacrament is not merely testimony in some fashion, but is the very testament of our life and salvation. For he says: “This is my body, which shall be given for you; this cup is the new testament in my blood, which shall be shed for you” (Matt. 26; Luke 22).

As we said above, this testimony is set in a certain proper opposition against the testimony which the devil held against us: against the guilt of forbidden food, it is food and drink of grace; against the serpent’s poison, it is the antidote of the Holy Spirit. This sacrament also has the source of its stream from the very passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. For it should be understood that, although he spoke much of it before his passion, he nowhere delivered its institution until he had come to that passion. For he had already been betrayed, as the Apostle says: “On the night in which he was betrayed, he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be given for you’” (1 Cor. 11), etc. Why this, except because this life-giving mystery was established from the Lord’s passion itself? Therefore the same Apostle immediately added: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (ibid.).

It is a beautiful and reasonable order of salvation: first, baptized by the sacrament of the above-mentioned witnesses—the Spirit, blood, and water—we wash away the stain of the old food; and only then receive, as the contrary of that food of death, this food and this drink of everlasting salvation.

## CHAPTER XIX. That as a type of these two sacraments the earlier people once crossed the sea and received bread from heaven and water from the rock; and how the Apostle says that they ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink.

As a type of these two sacraments, the earlier people once crossed the sea, ate bread from heaven in the wilderness, and drank water from the rock. Thus the Apostle says: “For I do not wish you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, all crossed the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock which followed them; and the rock was Christ.” And shortly afterward: “All these things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10).

When he says “in a figure,” one must necessarily understand: as a figure of those things which, revealed in their own time, grace and truth through Jesus Christ performed or gave. Consequently, when he says that they ate “the same food” and drank “the same drink,” and adds nothing—for example, “which we eat” or “which we drink”—his statement in no way disagrees with Christ speaking from the table, who says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.”

For the Jews had said: “What sign do you perform, that we may see and believe you? What do you work? Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Truth immediately denied this, saying: “Amen, amen, I say: Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6). It is as if he said: “This bread, of which the prophet says, ‘He gave them bread of heaven; man ate bread of angels’ (Ps. 72 [probably Ps. 78]), truly I say to you, Moses did not give it to you in past time, nor could he have given it; rather, my Father gives it in the present time.”

Thus, when the Apostle says, “They ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink,” and does not add, “which we receive in this time of revealed grace,” he is not contrary to Christ’s statement. Rather, just as he is aiming at something else, so he directs the pronouns *eandem* (“the same [feminine]”) and *eundem* (“the same [masculine]”) to something else. For his purpose is to remove from us presumptuous security, lest we suppose that we must be secure—as though, however we live after baptism and participation in Christ’s table, we must without doubt see the kingdom of God and possess eternal life.

With this purpose he says that what happened to them occurred as a figure of us: all crossed the sea, all ate manna, all drank water from the rock; nevertheless not all entered that land of promise. “But God was not well pleased,” he says, “with many of them; for they were struck down in the wilderness” (1 Cor. 10). So not all who eat this bread and drink this cup—of which that bread and water were figures—shall enter that land of the true promise and of the living, of which that land undoubtedly bore the figure.

Therefore, when he says “the same food” and “the same drink,” one must understand: the same food or drink for the wicked that it was for the good; without doubt, the same for Korah that it was for Caleb and Joshua, the same for Dathan and Abiram that it was for Moses and Aaron. If one asks how it was spiritual food and spiritual drink, the answer is easy: in no other manner than the rock too was spiritual, or was Christ. For just as he called the food spiritual and the drink spiritual, so he said of the spiritual rock: “And the rock was Christ.” Clearly he called it a spiritual rock, or a rock that was Christ, as though he had said: “a figurative representation of the spiritual rock, signifying Christ.” Likewise he called the food spiritual and the drink spiritual as though he had said: “food figurative of spiritual food, drink signifying spiritual drink.”

## CHAPTER XX. How this sacrament was as necessary to them as to us; how those who were dead could be or become its participants; and that this sacrament makes Christ’s death benefit us who did not yet exist.

Therefore each sacrament alike was necessary for them as for us, because they had received neither in reality but both in shadow or figure. Nor could they be more perfected or sanctified through that figure or shadow than Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob before them, or Samuel and David after them, who neither crossed that sea nor ate that manna.

We have said—and we should say it often, indeed we should always think this—that when Christ suffered or died and poured blood and water from his side, the sacrament of his baptism was instituted. Then all were cleansed by the same blood and the same water, when he was baptized or sanctified for all, as he had said: “I have a baptism with which to be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished” (Luke 12); and elsewhere: “For them I sanctify myself” (John 17).

What shall we say concerning the other sacrament? How did those who were dead become, or how could they become, participants in its food and drink? We cannot adequately marvel at so wonderful a thing. Since the dead could not come to eat this bread of angels, he himself went to them, so that the bread of angels, the life of the living, the resurrection of the dead, might be eaten by the dead insofar as it could be eaten by them. The dead were dispersed: their souls had descended to the lower regions, but their bodies had been laid away in the womb of the earth. Therefore the bread of life too willed to be dispersed: his soul, with God the Word, descended to the lower regions to their souls; but his body, not without the power of the same Word, present everywhere, descended into the womb of the earth to their bodies.

Thus, as the wise one—as the wisdom of God—he found for them such a remedy. In some way provision had to be made for the living, and for us who were yet to live, who did not yet exist, because he was not thereafter to descend to us in that manner. “For, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). He had to seek out for us—or rather, it was already necessary for us to know—how, while we live, we might receive him into our souls and bodies. For, as has already been said, after we were dead it could not happen that what was done once should be done again: namely, that he should die again, and that his soul should be joined to our souls in the lower regions and his body to our bodies in the earth.

Therefore, in another form, the same wise and merciful one—the wisdom of God—provided us with a remedy as wisely as mercifully. For he made for us a sacrament through which both his body might be infused into our bodies and the life of his body, that is, God the Word, into our souls, while he himself nevertheless remained whole and living.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Christ handed down this sacrament, and in what modes of being the body and blood of Christ are present.

How? “While they were at supper,” says the Evangelist, “he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat: this is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from it, all of you. This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins’” (Matt. 26). As he said of the blood, “which shall be shed for you,” so he said of the body—and it is also written in Luke—“which shall be given for you” (Luke 22).

“While they were at supper,” that is, while eating that typological supper by which this supper of truth had until then been prefigured, according to the rite which the Law prescribes thus: “On the tenth day of this month, let each person take a lamb according to their families and households. But if the number is too small to suffice for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor who is joined to his household, according to the number of souls who may suffice for eating the lamb” (Exod. 12), etc.

At that time the figure was to be fulfilled by the reality of truth, by the truth of the present reality. Therefore in Luke he says: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I say to you that from now on I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God” (Luke 22). In saying this he declared both that the old Passover was immediately to be fulfilled by the sacrament of the new Passover and answered their thought or expectation; for they were accustomed to ask, “When will the kingdom of God come?”—understanding the kingdom of God carnally, otherwise than the reality was.

Therefore, while they were at supper—that is, still sitting at the meal in which they had eaten the flesh of the lamb, the flesh of the old Passover—he took bread and blessed it. He took common bread, but by blessing he changed it far into something other than it had been, so that he could truly say: “This is my body, which shall be given for you” (Matt. 26; Mark 13 [probably Mark 14]; Luke 22). Likewise, he took the substance of wine; but by likewise giving thanks or blessing, he turned it into something else, so that Truth, who does not lie, could say: “This is my blood of the new testament, which shall be shed for many” (ibid.).

“This,” he says—that is, “this bread is my body,” or “my flesh.” For elsewhere he says: “And the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6). Yet the eyes of the flesh do not see, nor does the taste of the mouth perceive, that that bread has become Christ’s flesh or that that wine has been turned into blood. Indeed, if the color or taste of human flesh and blood were seen or perceived, it would bring human beings not greater salvation but the greatest horror. Thus the body or flesh and blood of Christ are present in the manner suitable to their being and use for us, and sufficient for our salvation.

In what manner, or in what modes of being? Namely, in name, reality, and effect. We understand them to be so in name from his saying, “This is my body; this is my blood.” Nowhere, and especially not here, should we take the Lord’s name in vain. For if, in all sanctifications performed by the Lord’s ministers upon invocation of his name, we do not dare to take the Lord’s name in vain, how much more in this sanctification, in which the Lord himself placed with his own mouth the name of his body and blood, ought we not take that very name in vain?

We also understand the body and blood of Christ to be so in reality from his saying that the body is to be given and the blood shed. We understand them to be so in effect because, after saying that the body would be given and the blood shed, he added, “for you, for the remission of sins.” Therefore, just as in that form in which he hung upon the cross he is the Holy of holies and effected remission of sins for all the elect who had gone before, so in this form of bread and wine he is likewise the Holy of holies; and there is no doubt that for all the elect who come to faith in him after that same passion he effects that same thing—that is, he confers remission of sins and eternal life. For elsewhere too he says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6). And immediately he adds: “And I shall raise him up on the last day” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXII. What the sacrament is and what the reality of the sacrament is; and that it is truly the body and blood of Christ.

[Col. 1663C] Therefore, as Father Augustine also says, in this sacrament which the worthy and unworthy alike receive, there is the reality of the sacrament, which only the worthy can receive—but not as his words have been understood by some. For they supposed him to say that what any unworthy person receives is not the body or blood of Christ, and that, according to the meaning of so great a doctor, what we visibly take from the Lord’s table is not the body or blood of Christ but only a figure or sign of Christ’s body and blood. He did not say this; indeed, he did not think it. For he was not accustomed to contradict Christ.

Christ speaks both in his own person, saying, “This is my body; this is my blood,” and through his Apostle—of whom “we have proof that Christ speaks in him” [Col. 1663D] (2 Cor. 13)—saying: “Therefore whoever eats the bread of the Lord and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11). He did not say: Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats ordinary or common bread and drinks wine as it was before the consecration had been celebrated. Rather, “he will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord”; and, he says, “he eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (ibid.).

Accordingly, let us seek from apostolic truth, not from anyone’s contentious disputation, the sense in which the aforesaid doctor distinguished sacrament [Col. 1664A] and the reality of the sacrament. Christ himself called the reality of the sacrament the mystery of his passion, as we have already said: holding this visible sacrament in his hands, when he had said, “This is my body,” he added, “which will be given up”; and when he had said, “This is my blood,” he added, “which will be poured out.”

654 The person who approaches unworthily does not share in Christ’s sufferings; he does not touch with the mouth of the mind what he receives with the mouth of the body—and this itself is why he is unworthy. Therefore this visible sacrament, which he receives with his mouth, is indeed Christ’s body and blood; for his unworthiness cannot nullify the dignity of so great a consecration. Yet he does not attain the reality of the sacrament, because in mind and in faith working through love he does not regard Christ’s passion. [Col. 1664B] Therefore he does not obtain the effect of that sacrament: namely, that this body was given for him and this blood poured out for him—that is, for the remission of his sins—so that he may have eternal life and be raised on the last day to the resurrection of life. Rather, he receives the contrary effect: he becomes guilty of the body and blood of the Lord, having eaten and drunk judgment upon himself.

## CHAPTER XXIII. That it is to be given to the unworthy, and that it matters greatly how, or on what grounds, a person is judged unworthy.

Accordingly, as the Apostle says, “Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of the cup” (1 Cor. 11), [Col. 1664C] because a sacrament of such dignity is not to be given to those who are unworthy and unexamined. Yet when we say these things, many are troubled; and we too have learned by grievous experience that those whom either guilt stings or Christian humility forms judge themselves unworthy of so great a mystery. But if they weigh more carefully the expression, not ours but the Apostle’s, they have no cause for alarm, as though we were rashly passing judgments against them.

For the wording or manner of this unworthiness differs, and it matters greatly how and by whom a person is considered unworthy. For one thing, a person may confess himself unworthy; another may consider or pronounce him unworthy. Now whoever truly [Col. 1664D] and fittingly considers the dignity of this sacrament commendably confesses himself unworthy. For who, if he judges rightly, will boast that he has a pure heart? On this point the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (ibid.). Conversely, anyone known for some crime and having given, before several witnesses or the whole Church, cause to be considered unworthy, is rightly judged unworthy in a condemnable way.

Therefore, when we are unworthy in our own judgment, the holy things are not thereby rightly withheld from us.
