But when others pronounce us unworthy—especially where an unquestionable cause of unworthiness is produced—we are rightly excluded, lest we eat and drink judgment upon ourselves. But let us now return to what we began.

## CHAPTER XXIV. How this food, which Christ gave from what was his own, is opposed to that which the first serpent persuaded human beings to take from what was another’s.

“Take and eat,” he says, “this is my body” (Matt. 26). And elsewhere: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6). When the Lamb of God says these things, there fittingly comes to mind what the serpent—or rather, through the serpent, the devil, the enemy of the human race—said: “Take and eat, and you shall be like gods” (Gen. 3).

Excellent and strikingly contrasted propositions. That one was a serpent; this one is the Lamb. That one, the old sinner; this one, the ancient Creator. That one crept upon the earth; this one came from heaven. That one hissed falsehood by the spirit of the devil; [Col. 1665B] this one proclaims truth by the Spirit of God. That one is the bearer of sin; this one, the teacher of righteousness. That one is the craftsman of death; this one, the maker of life. That one offered, as a thief, from a tree not his own; this one gave generously from his own body and blood. That one deceitfully promised what he did not possess, saying, “You shall be like gods.” This one faithfully gave what he possessed and always possesses by nature, so that we may be gods while he remains in us.

At last, that accursed one was believed more than God. Conversely, let this God be believed—if not more, then at least as much as that devil was believed. For it was believed that there was in that fruit what could not be seen: namely, a power to make people gods. Let it be believed that there is in this sacrament what cannot be seen: namely, the truth of flesh and blood, able to make us fellow-members in one body with the only-begotten Son of God. This [Col. 1665C] is what the principle or order of justice requires.

“Take,” therefore, he says, “and eat.” First take, then eat. To take is to believe faithfully, to love with thanksgiving, and with compassionate feeling to contemplate the giving up of this body and the shedding of this blood. This cannot be done unless what was wrongly received from that one is first rejected. Therefore, execrating that lie, receive, approve, and embrace this truth; and, in place of the food of death, eat the bread of eternal life and drink the cup of everlasting salvation.

## CHAPTER XXV. Why both are necessary for salvation: baptism first, and then participation in this sacrament.

“But why,” you ask, “after we have received baptism for the remission of sins, was it necessary to take food for the remission of sins? Or rather, once either of these sacraments has been received, why was the other necessary for salvation?” For he said, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” (Mark 16). Yet he had already said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6). In each case he stated the condition of life and salvation in such a way that he made no mention in either of the other. Had he said: “Whoever is baptized and eats my flesh and drinks my blood will be saved,” or “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood, after receiving the grace of baptism, has eternal life,” [Col. 1666A] there would be less left to investigate.

But now more remains to be asked: how he can say, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” when he had already said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (ibid.); and why, according to the character of original guilt, each remedy is necessary. Here the first question is more easily answered. For the statement, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” is like a skilled physician’s saying of a man half alive, wounded by robbers with many blows: “If he allows himself to be carried into my inn, he will be saved. For I shall give him food and drink of such power that he may at once recover complete health.”

So when he says, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” it must be understood: “For I will give him my body as food and my blood as drink,” or, “I have already prepared that by which, refreshed, he will undoubtedly be saved.” If, then, it still remains to ask why not either one but both sacraments are necessary for human salvation, the answer may be given: because human beings committed a twofold sin. One was pride; the other, gluttony. First, indeed, humanity was proud in mind, desiring [Col. 1666B] likeness to God—as is especially clear from the serpent’s promise, “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3). For it would not have promised them likeness to God as the reward of transgression unless it had first perceived that they themselves sought it. Then both succumbed to gluttony, as Scripture expresses more clearly when it says of the woman: “The woman saw that the tree was good for food, pleasing to the eyes, and delightful to behold; and she took of its fruit and ate, and gave it to her husband” (ibid.).

Therefore, because the sin was doubled, the sacrament too is rightly doubled. The evil of pride is healed by the good of humility in one sacrament; the fault of gluttony by the antidote of better food in the other. What could be more beautiful to eyes raised toward this dispensation of God’s mercy and justice together among us? God did not so pity wretched humanity as to neglect demanding from proud humanity a fitting satisfaction. Behold: the one who desired the likeness of God reigning [Col. 1666D] in heaven receives in baptism the likeness of the Son of God hanging on the tree. There he despised majesty; here he adores the cross. That was pride; this is humility.

In that pride the devil, finding humanity, offered forbidden food and said, “You shall be like gods.” In this humility God, finding humanity, offers the food and drink of his own body and blood, and says, “You shall remain in me, and I in you.” It should be noted that he did not use the deceiver’s same words, “You shall be like gods.” Nor indeed should he have said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will be like God,” or “will be like the Most High.” Rather, he says, “He remains in me, and I in him.” For who is, or can be, like God—that is, God without his help or grace? But we have spoken more fully about these matters elsewhere; therefore we refrain from saying more now.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That this is the first resurrection of souls, and that the second death has no power over those who have a share in it.

Behold, this is the first resurrection: to be baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and then to eat the body and drink the blood of the Lord. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have right to the tree of life and enter the city through its gates” (Rev. 22). Again: “This is the first resurrection. Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power” (Rev. 20). And shortly afterward: [Col. 1667B] “Hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death” (ibid.).

Therefore, just as there are two deaths, one of the soul and the other of the flesh, so there are two resurrections: the first of the soul and the second of the flesh. It must also be known that the soul’s death is second in the order of experience, as was said a little earlier: “Hell and death were cast into the lake of fire; this is the second death”; but it is first in act. For humanity died first in soul and then in flesh. God said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 3). Thus human beings died first in soul, through the death of sin, which separates the soul from God. For they died through the death which separates soul from body after nine hundred and thirty years.

This, therefore, is the first resurrection: baptism and participation in Christ’s body and blood. Thus the soul rises and now lives. But on the last day it will rise in the resurrection of the flesh. Therefore, when the Lord said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood,” he used the present tense: “has eternal life”; but concerning the future: “And I will raise him on the last day” (John 6). It must be understood: to the resurrection of life, so that in it the second death may have no power. For all will rise in the general resurrection of the flesh.

The first resurrection is clearly one of will; the second, of necessity. Therefore, speaking of the first resurrection, he said: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God,” indicating that this first resurrection lies in the will; “and those who hear,” he says, “will live” (John 5). For no one rises from the death of sin except willingly. Again, speaking of the second resurrection, he said: “Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice,” declaring that resurrection to be compulsory; “and they will come forth,” he says, “those who have done good to the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (ibid.). Finally, those who will come forth to the resurrection of judgment would prefer not to come forth or not to rise; indeed, they would altogether prefer not to exist rather than to exist.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Why we still die in the flesh, although the cause of death—our forefather’s transgression—is lamented in the sacrament.

[Col. 1668A] Now indeed we rejoice, knowing and saying with the Apostle that “the body is dead”—that is, certainly destined to die—“because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification” (Rom. 8). Yet a sure rationale of faith consoles us also concerning the body itself, dead or destined to die. Accordingly, he immediately says: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid.). He did not say, “He will raise your mortal bodies,” which could nevertheless rightly be said also of those who, at his voice, will come forth to the resurrection of judgment. Rather, he says, “will make alive together with”—understand, with Jesus Christ whom he raised from the dead—which belongs only to those who will come forth to the resurrection of life, precisely because his Spirit dwells in them.

Thus, as has already been said, we rejoice in knowing these things; but even in that joy there is cause to “fall down before God and weep before the Lord who made us” (Ps. 94 [Vulgate numbering]), because “we have failed in his wrath and been troubled in his fury” (Ps. 89). Meanwhile, while we groan under the burden of this mortal body, someone may perhaps say: “Since we have been reborn in Christ and escaped the guilt of our earthly parent, why do we still bear the punishment of that same guilt? Why do we still die? Why do we not pass to a better life without death’s affliction? Why are we stripped, rather than further clothed?” For, as the Apostle also says, “we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be further clothed” (2 Cor. 5).

To this, as we groan, we may reply: We have been reclaimed not through mercy alone but through justice, the companion of mercy. Indeed—and this must nonetheless be considered with great reverence—we were made mortal in our first parents and expelled from paradise not through justice alone, but also through mercy surrounding us. It must be understood that, although the cause was the same, we were not struck with death in the soul and subjected to mortality in the body by the same hand. The devil devised the death of our soul; the provident wisdom—or wise providence—of God imposed bodily mortality upon us.

For if after sin we had been permitted to live the life of the body and remain immortal, we would be like demons; for we too, like them, would have wretched eternity, or eternal wretchedness. [Col. 1668D] Therefore God, wisely providing for us, said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest perhaps he stretch forth his hand and take also from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3), etc. These words may perhaps seem to someone to resound with great wrath; but to those who possess discerning understanding, they breathe forth great clemency.

Likewise, what he said, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid.), is not so much a staff of wrath as a rod of discipline. Considering this rod of discipline, the Psalmist, instructed beforehand by the Holy Spirit, says in the person of the new man Jesus Christ—or rather, the new man himself, our head, says for all his members: “And your discipline corrected me unto the end, and your discipline itself will teach me” (Ps. 17 [Vulgate numbering]).

For what does this discipline of mortality correct except the pride of earth and ashes? What does it teach us except to humble ourselves under God’s mighty hand? Thus the Psalmist says by way of concession: “In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flourish and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither” (Ps. 89). The meaning is: From the moment of birth, mortal and liable to suffering, a human being, like grass green and beautiful in the morning, swiftly passes away—that is, fails. How? Placed in the morning of youth, he flourishes in vigor; then he passes from the very state of youth into the evening of old age; placed in that evening, he falls in dying; then he grows hard, that is, becomes a rigid corpse; then he withers, that is, becomes dry dust.

“I do not pray,” he says, “that a human being, from the moment of birth, become immortal and incapable of suffering; rather, I yield to the divine sentence, that he should thus pass away.” But alas, how unteachable we are in this respect: that we should be humble, that we should walk before our Creator with bowed head. Like grass we pass away in the morning, yet in that very passing we raise our necks as though we were oaks or fir trees, and presume upon lasting permanence. What would we do if we did not daily see the grass of our race falling, if the necks of our condition were not daily reduced to mud?

Therefore our Creator provided well for us in the very words which seem to express wrath: “lest he take from the tree of life and live forever” (Gen. 3). He provided lest, as said above, our misery should be eternal like that of demons, or our eternity wretched; and so that there might at least be temporal misery or a miserable temporality, so that what humanity intended—eternal blessedness or blessed eternity—might at some point come to be, or be able to come to be.

Therefore, because we were not made mortal in body by the same hand by which we are mortal in soul—for, at the devil’s instigation, humanity incurred for itself the death of the soul, whereas God imposed the discipline of bodily mortality to correct human pride—the guilt is rightly washed away through the sacrament of Christ’s grace, while this part of the punishment is nevertheless not remitted.

# BOOK FOUR OF THE WORKS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT: ON UNDERSTANDING

## CHAPTER I. On the Spirit of understanding: when, and to what kind of people, it was given; and how its operation was shown in the Apostle Peter.

After the Lord Jesus had been glorified and, in that very glorification, the sacraments of our salvation had been established—of which we spoke in the preceding volume to the praise and glory of the Spirit of wisdom—the Spirit was immediately given. And, in that gift, the one who is second after the Spirit of wisdom, the Spirit of understanding, at once shone forth first in operation. For “he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24).

To whom, and to what kind of people, did he give understanding of the Scriptures? Certainly not to orators, but to fishermen; not to scribes or Pharisees, but to unlearned and unlettered people. He opened their minds with such abundance that they knew all truth, taught not by man nor through man. We receive our first example of understanding in this: Peter said, “Men and brethren, the Scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David concerning Judas, who was the guide of those who arrested Jesus; for he was numbered among us and obtained a share [Col. 1670C] in this ministry” (Acts 1).

What Scripture? “Let their dwelling place,” he says, “be made desolate, and let no one dwell in it; and let another take his episcopate” (Pss. 68, 108 [Vulgate numbering]). He joined two testimonies: one, in the singular, from Psalm 108, “Let another take his episcopate”; the other, in the plural, from Psalm 68, “Let their dwelling place be made desolate.” Yet he had proposed only one individual in the singular: “The Scripture had to be fulfilled,” he said, “which the Holy Spirit foretold concerning Judas”; but here too he added the plural: “who was the guide of those who arrested Jesus” (Acts 1).

What, then, do we perceive from this statement except that the light of understanding had arisen in the hearts of the Apostles? For he signifies that Judas and the unhappy Jews, as implicated in the same crime, were likewise consigned to a similar punishment. How? Inasmuch as what befell Judas—that another should take his episcopate—would also befall the Jews: their episcopal dwelling would be desolated, while another people, the people of the Gentiles, would receive the true episcopate, the true and eternal priesthood.

## CHAPTER II. That although, on the very day Christ rose, he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, much was still lacking until the Holy Spirit came upon them.

657 Yet how great was their understanding of this kind in interpreting the Scriptures before the coming of the Holy Spirit whom they awaited as promised? Certainly only as great as the brightness of dawn compared with the noonday sun. For, still thinking carnally about Christ’s kingdom, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (Acts 1). As Luke himself records, he had already opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24). As John reports, he had already breathed upon them, saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them” (John 20). Yet they still did not think according to the Scriptures about Christ’s kingdom, to which they had been redeemed; and they still needed to receive the Holy Spirit, so that they might understand all things according to the Scriptures.

Therefore he said: “John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit. You shall receive,” he says, “power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you; and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1). They had received one gift of the Holy Spirit, namely for the remission of sins, as the Lord had said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive are forgiven them.” But they needed the Holy Spirit’s twofold gift in baptism, as John also foresaw: “He,” he says, “will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3).

Therefore, when he says to those to whom he had already given the Holy Spirit, “You shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1), and then, “You shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (ibid.), it is as though he said: “I baptized you with the Holy Spirit; I shall baptize you with fire”—so that every desire for an earthly kingdom, such as carnal Israel desires, may be burned out; so that you may be strong to despise the whole world set in evil, and keen to understand the mysteries of God’s kingdom: the kingdom of rest and peace, the everlasting kingdom.

## CHAPTER III. That the proper work of the Spirit of understanding is to teach a person divinely, not by human instruction; and how he taught the Apostles, who were unlearned and unlettered, on that day.

Why say more? The fiftieth day came—the day on which, formerly, the Law had been given after the sacrifice of the lamb—and on that day the same God who had given the obscurity of the letter filled them with the Spirit of understanding. Thus whatever earthly things the letter of the Law had spoken to earthly people—for example, a land flowing with milk and honey, and mountains from which metals are dug—they, having become heavenly, indeed themselves heavens (for the Psalmist foretold of them, “The heavens declare the glory of God,” Ps. 8 [as cited]), understood spiritually; and thereafter they trampled the earth beneath their feet while dwelling in heaven in mind.

He also indicated this gift of understanding through the appearance of fire, as is written: “There appeared to them divided tongues, as of fire” (Acts 2). For what is understanding or intelligence—at least in the order or numbering of the seven spirits of which we are speaking—except a capacity of grace by which divine words are heard inwardly and apprehended in their true sense without human teaching? Even if, when we hear and perceive from a human being or through a human being, we are rightly said to understand, yet it differs greatly when we are taught not by a human being or through a human being, but by hidden inspiration. This is the true and proper power of this Spirit of understanding, according to which the Psalmist says: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84 [Vulgate numbering]).

When, therefore, divided tongues appeared as of fire at the Spirit’s coming, by such an appearance the Holy Spirit indicated the grace which he was distributing among them. Nor did he merely make God’s language intelligible to human beings; with the same sign he also bestowed the languages of all nations upon their mouths, so that they might have many ways by which understanding of God’s words was given to them, and might go forth to all nations throughout the four quarters of the world that did not know God.

And what the Lord had previously promised came to pass: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” “This,” says the Evangelist, “he said concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (John 7). Indeed, the Spirit who outwardly displayed the appearance of illuminating fire was inwardly a fountain springing up to eternal life (John 4). Therefore the Psalmist, considering both powers, truly says: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35 [Vulgate numbering]).

We read concerning the planting of the earthly paradise that “a fountain rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Gen. 2); and then: “A river went out from the place of delight to water paradise, and from there it divides into four heads” (ibid.). Behold, the paradise of the new creation was planted from the shoots or roots of the one and only tree of life: that is, from the powers and faith of the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ. Commending him, the Psalmist says: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will give its fruit in its season” (Ps. 1).

This tree was planted beside streams of water because the Word of God—God the Word—ever living according to the fullness of every grace and sufficient for all things was implanted in the nature of flesh. Such a man is the beginning of the new planting, the holy shoot, the tree of life. The Apostles were the first offshoots of this tree; its planting, the paradise of its roots, consisted of those disciples, those believers, who were still few.

When this Spirit was given and filled their hearts with understanding, causing languages of every kind to arise in their mouths, then truly the fountain rose from the earth of paradise; then the river went out from paradise to water the whole surface of the earth. For just as the river going out from that paradise divides into four heads, that is, chief rivers, so from that apostolic Church went forth the knowledge of God, divided also into the four Gospels, which are the first rivers of doctrine necessary to us. But let us proceed with the events themselves and, following the course of Scripture, draw examples of this Spirit of understanding.

## CHAPTER IV. On the testimony of Joel’s prophecy, which Peter, though unlettered, brought forth with complete and timely appropriateness to the occasion and subject.

When some were astonished and wondered among themselves, saying, “Behold, are not all these who are speaking Galileans?” while others mockingly said, “These men are full of new wine,” Peter, standing with the Eleven, raised his voice and spoke: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and receive my words with your ears. For these are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is the third hour of the day. But this is what was foretold through the prophet [Col. 1673B] Joel: ‘And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord: I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy’” (Acts 2), etc.

Behold what it is, and how great it is, to be illumined by the Spirit of understanding of which we speak. A simple, unlettered man swiftly turns over in his mind the prophetic book, closed and sealed to the learned, and publicly recites before all, with assured voice and unhesitating understanding, a testimony suited to the time and the matter. Observe how powerfully and effectively he has thus far explained to those desiring to know nearly the whole prophet, formerly obscure.

For the prophet had first said: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the grub ate; and what the grub left, the mildew ate. Awake, you drunkards, and weep; howl, all who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth” (Joel 1), etc.; then he added: “And it shall be after these things: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2), etc.

Certainly, the Apostle’s speech made intelligible to us what lay hidden in these words of the prophet: namely, that after the destruction of the former people, the Holy Spirit would be poured out upon God’s male and female servants—that is, upon the one hundred and twenty believers gathered in that upper room. That number, one hundred and twenty, ascending gradually by increments from one to fifteen, makes the number of fifteen steps, which are mystically contained in the Psalter.

For the destruction of that people occurred through these four things—the caterpillar, locust, grub, and mildew—that is, through these four kingdoms: Babylonian, Persian, Macedonian, and Roman. What would happen after these things lay hidden in the same words of the prophet; but behold, the Spirit of understanding revealed the letter to Peter, and Peter openly declared it to the ears of those who marvelled. Nor was it necessary for him to explain each point individually: that is, what the Lord intended when he said through the prophet, “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions” (ibid.). This had been plainly accomplished before everyone’s eyes, and hence all were astonished: some wondering, others also mocking and saying that they were full of new wine.

## CHAPTER V. How he expounded this prophecy: “And I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on earth below: blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke.”

Some few points require treatment or exposition, namely these: “And I will give wonders in heaven above, and signs on earth below: blood, and fire, and a vapor of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). Thus wonderfully instructed, he commendably proceeds, beginning as follows: “Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you by mighty works, wonders, and signs which God performed through him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this man, delivered up according to the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you put to death by the hands of lawless men, afflicting him” [Col. 1674B] (Acts 2).

For he had then already been killed, when he had already given up his spirit; from his side, contrary to the nature of dead bodies, blood and water came forth. That blood was a wonder: to some, death unto death; to others, life unto life. So formerly, when the Lord “sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt, upon Pharaoh and all his servants” (Ps. 135), the blood of the lamb was a wonder of death to some, and of life to others. For doorposts marked with that blood were impenetrable to the destroyer when he saw the sign of that blood; but the unmarked doorposts of the Egyptians were accessible to him, so that he might rush in boldly and take the firstborn from each house [Col. 1674C] (Exod. 12).

So also now: those who receive the blood of this Lamb upon both doorposts—namely, those of body and mind—escape the hand of the destroying devil, having received remission of sins; but those who do not receive it will undoubtedly perish. “Whom,” he says, “God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, since it was impossible for him to be held by it. For David says concerning him: ‘I beheld the Lord always before my face, because he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved’” (Acts 2), etc.

How swiftly did this fisherman of men, swiftly taught and perfected in the art, flee to royal and prophetic testimony! He had scarcely uttered with his lips the assertion of the resurrection; and, because the matter was great, and because it was a great undertaking to affirm before those hearers—who had crucified him—that a man had risen [Col. 1674D], fearing perhaps that, with their ears wounded, they might turn away and cease to show goodwill, he swiftly seized upon testimony from a great personage: great and manifest, abundant and suited to the matter, which they ought neither to scorn nor belittle.

What a man, then, came down from that upper room; how greatly changed from the one who, when the Lord had formerly said, “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matt. 20), took him aside and said, “Far be it from you, Lord; this shall not happen to you.” For there he deserved to hear: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not savour the things that are of God” (ibid.); but here he both held the Psalms in memory and understood their mysteries.

And what is especially praiseworthy: by one and the same anticipatory use of testimony [Col. 1675A], he both retained the goodwill of his present hearers and opened for the whole world a path and doorway to understand that the utterances of the Psalms are spoken not in David’s own person but in the person of Christ. And lest any uncertainty remain for anyone on this point, he immediately meets it with a ready and vigorous, most secure argument:

“Men and brethren, permit me to speak boldly to you concerning the patriarch David: that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day.”

And he at once concludes: “Therefore, being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn to him by oath that one from the fruit of his loins should sit upon his throne, he foresaw and spoke concerning the resurrection of Christ: that he was neither left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2).

Wonderful art; wonderful ability in a man, as has been said, unlearned and without letters: for this fisherman, in order to catch human beings, cast out the sharp hook of a most powerful syllogism. See another: “For David,” he says, “did not ascend into heaven.” Having laid down this proposition, he immediately takes up this further premise: “But he himself says: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet’” (ibid.). Given these two points, which must unquestionably be granted, he immediately draws the conclusion and says: “Therefore let all the house of Israel know most certainly that God has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (ibid.).

Thus, wonderfully sharpened by the Spirit of understanding, and polished in speech as a rock of righteousness, this fisherman—formerly a man ignorant of letters—pierced the mouths of human beings as though of fish [Col. 1675C] with the hook of his argumentative discourse, so that they could not escape into the whirlpools of human disputation and hide their consciences from the truth. But let us continue the order we began.

## CHAPTER VI. On the wonder of fire: that he understood it to have been the advent of the Holy Spirit in fiery tongues

Of the three prophetic wonders given upon earth—namely blood, fire, and a vapor of smoke—he expounded one, the wonder of blood, when he said: “Jesus the Nazarene, a man approved by God among you—this man, delivered up according to the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you put to death by the hands of lawless men, afflicting him” (Acts 2), etc.

The second was the wonder of fire, which, in order to expound, he spoke thus [Col. 1675D]: “Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this gift which you see and hear” (Acts 2). You see it, namely, in the fiery tongues; you hear it in our speech. For whom did he pour out except the Holy Spirit? He received as man; he poured out as God. And indeed they could not see the very substance of the Holy Spirit, since his nature is invisible; but they saw fire. Human eyes were able to see tongues divided as if of fire, resting above each of them.

Therefore fire was a wonder; the division of tongues was a wonder; indeed, the whole range of languages in the mouths of the apostles was a wonder. And the very sound that suddenly came from heaven, as of a violent wind approaching, was a wonder. A wonder of what? Assuredly, of that sound which was to go out into all the earth, while those heavens whom it now came to establish declared the glory of God, and their firmament of most steadfast faith proclaimed the works of his hands with the magnificent thunder of the word and flashes of miracles [Col. 1676A] (Ps. 18).

For it was soon to happen, as this Spirit thundered through their mouths the proclamations of Christ, that the earth would be stirred and tremble, and the foundations of the mountains—that is, the hearts of the proud—would be troubled and shaken, because he is angry with them unless they repent. The appearance of fire was especially a great wonder because the substance of fire burns and gives light. By these qualities it was signified that the Holy Spirit made Christ’s apostles burning with zeal and shining with understanding [Col. 1676B]. Moreover, the forms of the divided tongues signified divisions of gifts.

The effect of this wonder was present; hence all marvelled, because, although those speaking were Galileans, “We hear,” they said, “each one our own language in which we were born; we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God” (Acts 2). A further great thing was signified by such a wonder: namely, that the Church would speak in the languages of all nations; that the faith of Christ would be spread among all nations; and that every tongue would confess him to whom one nation alone had previously confessed, since until then God had been known only in Judea (Ps. 76).

## CHAPTER VII. On the vapor of smoke, the third element in the prophet’s words [Col. 1676C], and what was prefigured therein: that in that vapor of smoke—that is, of repentance—where the Church’s baptism was first celebrated, three thousand people believed

The third wonder now had to be expounded, namely the vapor of smoke. But first it was necessary that there should occur in them what it was fitting for the vapor of smoke to signify in the prophet: namely, that they should be pierced with compunction and, with tearful prayer, seek counsel for their salvation. Therefore, while he paused briefly—or perhaps was still speaking—“they were pierced in heart,” it says, “and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles: ‘What shall we do, brethren?’” (Acts 2).

Once they had been so pierced and had spoken thus, there was no need for the meaning of this wonder—the vapor of smoke—to be expounded in words; for they were already smoking abundantly, and through experience apprehended the sense of the expression. For to smoke is to be pierced with compunction and weep over sins. The Psalmist also bears witness: after saying, “The earth was moved and trembled, and the foundations of the mountains were troubled, because he was angry with them,” he adds: “Smoke ascended in his anger” [Col. 1676D] (Ps. 18).

This very terror of smoke—that is, their compunction—was a wonder, especially in what follows: “Therefore those who received his words were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day” (Acts 2). For where the Church’s baptism was first celebrated, three thousand souls were gathered not without a great wonder: divine providence undoubtedly prefiguring that a multitude of believers would be gathered from the whole world into faith in the Trinity. Yet, just as illumination of the faithful may be understood in the fire, so in the vapor of smoke the blindness of the Jews may also be understood [Col. 1677A]: in one and the same vapor of smoke, both the compunction of the repentant and the blinding of the unrepentant may be signified.

## CHAPTER VIII. What wonders in heaven, and in what manner, he intended to be understood, when the sun was turned into darkness and the moon into blood

After the signs given on earth, it is pleasing not to leave untouched those wonders too which were given in heaven. For as the same prophet said, “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood” (Joel 2), so it happened. For at the Lord’s passion the sun was darkened (Matt. 27), although the moon, turned into blood, could not visibly appear to human beings [Col. 1677B].

And even if the letter fails, the foundation of prophetic truth nevertheless remains: for the darkening of the sun was truly a wonder, a fearful evil; and what would have been made intelligible by the blood-red appearance of the moon, had it been able visibly to appear turned into blood, befell that unhappy generation. Perhaps Peter, avoiding the exposition of this, was content to say only what suited the occasion: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation” (Acts 2).

For what did the wonder of the darkened sun signify, except that blindness of the Jews which then came about and has continued from then onward? For since they extinguished for themselves the Sun of righteousness, they rightly saw in the darkening of the sun this wonder of their own blindness. Moreover, whatever may have been the condition of the lunar globe in that darkening [Col. 1677C], for them the moon was turned into blood. The moon, I say—that is, their Passover—was entirely stained with Christ’s blood by their monstrous crime.

For they kept the Passover according to the course of the moon, on the fourteenth day toward evening, when the moon is fullest; they ate the lamb in accordance with the commandment of the Law (Exod. 12). Therefore we rightly understand the Jewish Passover by the moon. It is certain that when they celebrated that Passover, on the same evening on which they had eaten their own lamb, they seized our Lord, the true Lamb of God; after mocking him throughout the night, in the morning they handed him over to Pilate, urgently demanding that he be hung on the wood, crying, “Crucify, crucify,” and, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

Therefore, because these unhappy murderers stained their Passover, their full moon [Col. 1677D], with Christ’s blood, we rightly say that their moon was turned into blood. From that time God’s soul hated their Passover, their Sabbaths and new moons, and all their feasts, saying: “For your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

Nor is it without significance that, after the prophet had pronounced these five wonders—blood, fire, vapor of smoke, the sun to be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood—he immediately added: “before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). This has the same force as what the Lord himself says of himself in the Gospel: “For as lightning flashing from heaven shines to the regions under heaven, so shall the Son of Man be in his day. But first he must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation” [Col. 1678A] (Luke 17).

That those wonders were foretold to occur before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes is the same as saying: First he must suffer many things and be rejected by the crooked generation, before he comes in his majesty, flashing like lightning from heaven, great and terrible, to judge the living and the dead. Peter, assuredly, illuminated by the present Spirit of understanding and not ignorant of this, prudently contented himself for the time being with saying: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” The implication is: lest the sun likewise be turned into darkness for you, and the moon into blood.

## CHAPTER IX. How true, therefore, is what Truth said to Peter: “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will know”; and what was said elsewhere: “Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent, and revealed them to little ones”

Truth therefore spoke truly to Peter: “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will know” [Col. 1678B] (John 13). Supporting this truth are the matters now recalled by us, as well as the other things which Peter is subsequently recorded to have declared, contending for the faith and for testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ, before the people, rulers, and priests. He testified that in this had been fulfilled what God had spoken through the mouth of his holy prophets from the beginning of the age; that this was the prophet of whom Moses said: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like myself; you shall hear him” (Acts 7); and that this was the stone rejected by the builders: “by you,” he says, “who are building, which has become the head of the corner; and there is salvation in no one else, for no other name under heaven has been given to human beings in which we must be saved” [Col. 1678C] (Acts 4).

Concerning this same stone he speaks at greater length in his Epistle, according to Isaiah: “Coming to him, a living stone, indeed rejected by men, but chosen and honoured by God, you yourselves also, like living stones, are built up into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. Therefore Scripture contains: ‘Behold, I place in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, precious; and whoever believes in him shall not be confounded’” (1 Pet. 2), etc.

Nevertheless, the same Truth likewise said to all the other Apostles: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” [Col. 1678D] (John 14). For what we say in praise of the Holy Spirit, what we now preach in praise of the Spirit of understanding, occurred at that hour when, as was said above, divided tongues appeared to the apostles and the divine fire rested upon each of them (Acts 2). They perceived all the Scriptures and prophets by inward understanding—though they had not even learned letters through a human teacher—and penetrated those mysteries which had been closed to the Scribes and Pharisees, bearers of the key of knowledge, to the wise and learned in the Law. Thus was fulfilled what he likewise says: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” [Col. 1679A] (Matt. 11; printed “Matt. I”).

For what human being had opened to them the mysteries of the Psalms? Yet it is written of them—who, as has often been said, were unlearned—that, “having been released, Peter and John came to their own,” and “reported to them what the chief priests and elders had said to them. When they heard it, they lifted up their voice to the Lord with one accord and said: ‘Lord, you made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them; you who, by the Holy Spirit through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers assembled together against the Lord and against his Christ.” For truly in this city Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the nations and peoples of Israel, assembled against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, to do what your hand and your counsel decreed to be done’” [Col. 1679B] (Acts 4), etc.

Therefore, taught not by a human being nor through a human being, but wonderfully instructed by the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of understanding, opening to them the treasury of the Scriptures, they are rightly received and heard by us all as the mouth of God, since they were there. And it is wicked for us to doubt in any respect anything whatsoever written by those to whom that fire gave an understanding heart and a trained tongue; upon them, as also upon the patriarchs and prophets to whom the word of God came through that same Spirit with no human intermediary, we acknowledge that the foundation of our faith has been laid.

All others who were not there, or who did not learn in the same way, we read in such a manner that whatever they say we do not believe merely because they themselves thought so, but because they could establish their sayings by the testimony of these men or by some probable reason [Col. 1679C]. For these are the men to whom revelation was then given, when they could not be taught by a human being or through a human being—indeed, to whom was revealed by the Holy Spirit what human beings were unable to teach or know.

Therefore it is written in the Psalm: “Shall Zion say: ‘A man and a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’? The Lord will recount in the writings of the peoples and of these rulers who were in her” (Ps. 87). Questioning that city of God, of which glorious things are spoken, whose foundations are in the holy mountains (ibid.)—namely, these prophets and apostles—and saying, “O Zion, shall a man [say it]?” he denies it more emphatically than if he had declared, “A man shall never say it.”

Therefore let us also say by denial that truly, unless the Lord himself had recounted it in the writings of the peoples and of these rulers who were in her, a human being would never say, nor be able to say or comprehend, so wondrous and lofty a truth as is now read and known: “And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” [Col. 1679D]. This, surely, is as wondrous and lofty as the statement, “All things were made through the Word, and the Word was made flesh” (John 1), which is certainly so lofty that a human being could never have said it unless the Lord himself had recounted it in the Scriptures—unless the Lord, through himself, not through a human being but through the Holy Spirit, in composing the holy Scriptures, had said through the mouth of whomever or whichever persons pleased him: These are those Scriptures in which divine authority is found everywhere; for example, when it is said, “The Lord spoke,” or “said,” to Moses; “The Lord spoke,” or “the word of the Lord came,” to this or that prophet.

These Scriptures likewise are those of the persons of whom we were speaking, because divided tongues like fire appeared to them, the fire rested upon each of them, they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in diverse tongues as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance [Col. 1680A] (Acts 2). They are called in that Psalm “the Scriptures of the peoples” because they are not like Plato’s writings, grandiloquent in words but meagre in meaning, intelligible only to a few or whispering in corners; rather, they are set before all peoples and speak openly to the whole world concerning the salvation of all nations, which Scriptures were composed in one nation and had formerly been hidden there.

Accordingly, we believe in every respect in these Scriptures of the peoples, these Scriptures of the rulers—that is, of the prophets and apostles—so that we judge it wicked and alien to faith in Christ to doubt anything concerning them. Among the apostles whose writings are extant are Peter, John, James, Matthew, and Jude of James. Mark’s Gospel is said to have been written from the mouth of the apostle Peter, and Luke’s Gospel from the apostolic faith of Paul. Paul, indeed, was not there; for he had not yet been called when the Holy Spirit came upon Christ’s disciples. Yet he received no less through the Holy Spirit, nor had less than the chief apostles; concerning this something must be said by us in its proper place. For after our commemoration [Col. 1680C] of Peter, we shall touch upon the no less sweet remembrance of John, the beloved of Jesus Christ, the apostle.

## CHAPTER X. That the disciple whom Jesus loved was given a great grace of this Spirit of understanding; and that, like Joseph, he received one portion beyond his brethren, though Christ did not will that he should be preferred to the other apostles as Peter was

John the apostle and evangelist is known from his own words to have received no small grace of understanding, because he is prominent in the Church and speaks before all others. Hence we rightly say that “in the midst of the Church he opened his mouth, and the Lord filled him with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding” (Ecclus. 15).

In accordance with the grace by which Jesus loved him—by which he also reclined at supper upon his breast and said, “Lord, who is it that will betray you?” [Col. 1680D] (John 21)—he received a great measure of understanding and wisdom: of understanding, that he might understand the Scriptures; of wisdom, that he might compose them with wonderful ability of his own. He did not receive this gift in actual possession at the moment when he reclined upon Christ’s breast; but even then he had access, so that afterward he might receive from that breast in which “are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2).

For later, when he says, “Then that other disciple, who came first to the tomb, entered also, and saw, and believed,” he immediately adds, concerning both Peter and himself: “For they did not yet know the Scriptures, that he had to rise from the dead” (John 20). He too received his proper measure when the Holy Spirit came, when grace was given to each of the others according to the measure of Christ’s gift [Col. 1681A] (Eph. 4), according to the good pleasure of this Spirit, who distributes to each individually as he wills (1 Cor. 12).

But just as the patriarch Jacob loved his son Joseph and, not content for him to be made equal with his brethren in the allotment or measuring-line of the inheritance, said: “I give you one portion beyond your brethren, which I took from the hand of the Amorite with my sword and my bow” (Gen. 48), so the Lord Jesus, loving this disciple more closely than the others, and not content that he should be equal to the other apostles in this share of grace, namely the Spirit of understanding, again opened to him the secrets of heaven, so that he saw admirable visions, which he arranged in the book entitled the Apocalypse. In it he wrote almost as many mysteries as there are words, and wrote that lofty mystery of the Word of God, God incarnate, which cannot be narrated by human beings.

For he loved him. Yet this too must not be passed over: although he loved him with such a privilege of love, he nevertheless said specifically to Peter, not to this man: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” [Col. 1681B] (Matt. 16). Thus the father Jacob loved Joseph, his son foretold above the others, more than his other sons; nevertheless, he gave the royal blessing not to him but to Judah: “The sceptre,” he said, “shall not be removed from Judah until he comes who is to be sent” (Gen. 49), etc. Why? Clearly, because in giving blessings he ought not to enact his own will but God’s will, and it was fitting that he should follow not the affection of the flesh but the prompting of the Spirit.

This is almost like the matter at hand. For our Lord, though he loved all the disciples, and Peter especially, with the love of spirit or mind, loved John with a certain affection of heart, as a man loving a man. Yet he did not will to prefer him to the others in the apostolate, since in all things he attended to the divine will and says in one place: “Because I came down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6).

Therefore, in the rank or dignity of the apostolate, the blessed Simon Bar-Jonah—who first deserved to have revealed to him by the Father in heaven, not by flesh and blood, that he should hold the primacy and receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1681C] (Matt. 16)—holds first place. But this disciple, like the beloved Joseph, obtained beyond his brethren no small share from the treasure of the Father, from the Spirit of understanding, who truly stored up upon him delight and exultation. We have not passed over what he saw upon coming into this portion; for it belongs especially to the grace of understanding which we are now discussing.

## CHAPTER XI. On the book which he saw in the right hand of the One seated upon the throne: that, when the Lamb opened it, he there received his portion; and what it meant for him to receive the book from the angel’s hand and devour it, and to receive the reed given him to measure the temple

“I saw,” he says, “in the right hand of the One seated upon the throne a book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. And after a few words: ‘And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth. And he came and took the book from the right hand of the One seated on the throne’” [Col. 1682A] (Rev. 5).

Again, after some passages: “And the voice which I heard from heaven spoke with me again, saying: ‘Go, take the open book from the hand of the angel standing upon the sea and upon the earth.’ And I went to the angel, telling him to give me the book. And he said to me: ‘Take and devour it.’ And I took the book from the angel’s hand and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had devoured it, my belly was made bitter. And he said to me: ‘You must prophesy again concerning peoples, nations, tongues, and many kings’” (Rev. 10). “And a reed like a rod was given to me” (Rev. 11), etc.

This is what we said a little earlier: just as that son Joseph, increasing in stature, received one portion beyond his brethren, so this beloved disciple received, beyond his fellow disciples, an outstanding portion through the revelation of understanding. For what is this book in the right hand of the One seated upon the throne, written within and without and sealed with seven seals, except the same book which in Isaiah cannot be opened either by one who knows letters or by one who does not, though its opening is also there proclaimed thus: “On that day the deaf shall hear the words of the book” [Col. 1682B] (Isa. 29)?

This book is holy Scripture: a book written within and without, because its harmonious unity contains the Old Testament, as it were outwardly, and the New inwardly; a book sealed with seven seals, that is, a text either hidden by the complete fullness of mysteries or composed according to the ordering of the sevenfold Spirit. The true Lamb of God, Christ, possessing seven horns and seven eyes—that is, the sevenfold Spirit, compared to horns on account of the preeminence of power and to eyes on account of the illumination of grace—the Lamb “as though slain,” that is, who was indeed slain but now lives, appeared as the opener of this book’s seals when, rising from the dead and appearing to his disciples, he “opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures,” as we have said above (Luke 24). More fully, he did so when, having ascended into heaven, he gave gifts to human beings: he gave the Holy Spirit of understanding inwardly, while tongues of fire shone outwardly.

There, certainly, this John received his portion among his brethren; for with the mystery of the opened book and face unveiled, both he and the other apostles understood [Col. 1682C]. In the first seal they understood the splendour of the primitive Church through the white horse; in the following three horses—the red, black, and pale—the threefold war against it of pagans, false brethren, and heretics; in the fifth, the glory of those crowned under that war, crying beneath God’s altar; in the sixth, the evils that will come in the time of Antichrist; and in the seventh, through the silence that occurred as if for half an hour, the beginning of eternal rest. All these matters have been expounded more fully by our teachers.

They understood that all the Scriptures are fulfilled in Christ, and this was the common lot of all the apostles; for the Spirit of truth taught every one of them the truth, not only concerning the past, but also announced to them things to come. That he might receive a further portion beyond those brethren of his, a great portion, it was thus said to him: “Go and take the open book from the hand of the angel”; and a reed like a rod was given him. When he received the book it was said, “You must prophesy again concerning peoples and nations and tongues and many kings” [Col. 1683A] (Rev. 10); and when he received the reed it was said: “Rise and measure the temple of God.” He did this or that, as has been said.

For, after he was recalled from exile, he again preached the Gospel orally and wrote with the reed, measuring the temple of God, the altar, and those worshipping in it. That is, in the word of the Gospel, the hearts of individual persons, who through faith are God’s temple and in whom Christ himself, dwelling by that same faith, is the altar, are as it were measured and defined. There they find how much each advances and how far each conforms to the divine rule.

And it should be noted that he received and devoured the same book—sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his belly—only after he had been admonished by the voice speaking with him and saying, “Go and take the open book from the hand of the angel”; only after he went to the angel and asked him to give the book. For this was to happen, and did happen: the Church repeatedly entreated him, who was conversing with it, with many prayers that, in order to restore the truth of the Gospel, he would rise up both in living speech and in service of the pen.

For after he had been sent into exile by Domitian, the second persecutor of Christians after Nero, heretics had rushed into the Church like wolves into sheepfolds deprived of their shepherd. Marcion, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the other Antichrists, denying Christ before Mary, defiled the simplicity of evangelical faith with perverse teaching [Col. 1683C]. Therefore, compelled by almost all the bishops of Asia at that time, and having proclaimed a fast for all, he prayed to the Lord and, made drunk with the grace of the Holy Spirit, wrote his Gospel, by which, through the suddenly revealed light of truth, he dispelled every darkness of the heretics.

That he was compelled by almost all the bishops of Asia at that time was, assuredly, to hear the voice from heaven—that is, from the Church of God—speaking with him and saying, “Go and take the book.” Likewise, that he appointed a fast for all and prayed to the Lord was to say to the angel, “Give me the book,” or, “Give me the reed.”

## CHAPTER XII. How profitably for us and for the whole Church of Christ he received the reed—that is, the grace to write the mysteries of Christ—and why he was fittingly signified by the flying eagle both in Ezekiel’s vision and in his own Apocalypse

He received the book, took the reed, and with the eye of understanding both devoured the book by reading and read it by devouring, so that he tasted more deeply than all mortals the hidden nature of the eternal principle, the divine substance of the everlasting Word. He wielded the reed in writing and, through Scripture, poured forth again what he had devoured, so that with that same reed he pierced the bold eyes of all heretics.

For what heretic, or what form of heretical madness ever existed, whose wicked eye and whole darkened body the ray of truth from his Gospel does not pierce and strike [Col. 1684A]? His whole discourse is in God and wholly in the Word of God; hence the entire school of Christian faith depends upon his mouth, so that, whenever the loquacious heresy is hostile, whatever question must be investigated, he, the teacher consulted with mature reverence, may pronounce and resolve the controversy.

Accordingly, because he saw the highest things for us and fixed his eye upon the sun of divinity, it has rightly been observed that he is signified by the flying eagle both in Ezekiel’s vision and in his own Apocalypse (Ezek. 1). For where he saw the aforementioned book opened by the Lamb of God, there a little earlier he says: “And around the throne were four living creatures, full of eyes before and behind. And the first living creature was like a calf” (Rev. 4), etc. He designated himself as the last, saying: “And the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” [Col. 1684B] (ibid.), because he wrote his Gospel last.

Although it is more pleasing to understand one and the same Christ, the Son of God, as signified by these four living creatures—since he was born a human being, was sacrificed as a calf, rose as a lion, and flew above the stars as an eagle—nevertheless this man too is rightly called an eagle, because he deserved to contemplate more deeply with unblinking eyes that divinity by which Christ as man could ascend into heaven.

For it is written: “Wherever the body may be, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. 24). If, then, he called eagles those who are taken up to the place where they deserve to see face to face, as it is, the brightness of divinity, how much more rightly is this man called an eagle, who, while still placed in the flesh [Col. 1684C], could fix open eyes upon that sun.

## CHAPTER XIII. On what was said to him: “And it will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.”

And it will make your stomach bitter, he says; but in your mouth it will be sweet like honey (Rev. 10). The sense is this: when you receive it, you will delight in the sweetness of the divine utterance; but you will feel bitterness when you begin to preach and to put into practice what you have understood. Why? Because not all people delight in the Word of God, although it is naturally sweet; for it treats not only of the joys of heaven, but also of the flames of Gehenna. Hence Ezekiel says of this same book what John here passed over in silence: that there were written in it “lamentations and a song and woe” (Ezek. 2). For the entire sequence of the Old and New Testament warns that repentance must be done for sins—that is, lamentation; that the kingdom of heaven must be sought—where there is song; and that the infernal weeping—where there is woe—must be fled. But people who love pleasures hate the whole book because of its Scripture of lamentations and woe, and therefore make bitter the stomach of him who has devoured it.

For this was not said to John alone, nor should it be understood of John alone, that after sweetness like honey in his mouth his stomach was made bitter. Surely whoever has received this book from the hand of this angel—the Angel of Great Counsel—and, devouring even one little page from it, has made a clear belch through the voice of preaching, has scarcely, or never, been able to escape suffering something from the encounter with the red, black, or pale horse. To state this more plainly: scarcely anyone—indeed, never anyone—who has received from the heavenly gift a true understanding of Holy Scripture, and according to that same understanding of truth has denounced false vanities and insanities, fails to suffer some bitterness either through open persecution from the enemies of God, or through the inward slander of false brethren who are Christians only in name, or through the attack of heretics, “who went out from us, but were not of us” (1 John 2).

But above all, whoever has devoured this book suffers such trouble among his own people. For he does not lie who said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: no prophet is accepted in his own country” (Luke 4). Conversely, whoever has received the spirit of this world, whomsoever the philosophy of this world has even slightly imbued, ascends on a feast-day, because his time is always ready; and he attends, as it were, to morning songs, that he may eat in the morning and be remembered among those who eat in the morning. Of the wisdom of such men Isaiah speaks under the figure of a harlot: “Take up the harp; go about the city, harlot consigned to oblivion. Sing well; repeat your song often, that you may be remembered” (Isa. 23). He assigned the harlot a very meagre reward, and that with reproach, in saying, “that you may be remembered.” For she is a harlot, and is consigned to oblivion, precisely because she sings not that God may be remembered, but that she herself may be remembered.

For the present, indeed, this song is sweet as honey both in her mouth and in her stomach—for “the lips of a harlot drip honeycomb”—but afterwards it will be turned for her into the gall of asps. But the understanding of the often-mentioned book, though now sweet in the mouth like honey because of the hope of everlasting joy, nevertheless makes the stomach bitter because of the reality of present exile, even if the bitterness of persecution is absent. Hence he says: “My stomach hurts; my stomach hurts” (Jer. 4). Again: “My secret is for myself; my secret is for myself. Woe is me!” (Isa. 24).

## CHAPTER XIV. On Matthew the publican: how, himself fed with the bread of life and understanding, he still makes a great feast for Christ in his own house.

After John, in the order of writing, though not also first in the excellence of evangelical Scripture, Matthew the publican likewise feeds upon the bread of life and understanding; and with that same understanding he makes a great feast for the Lord Jesus in his own house, being indeed endowed with great grace according to his name (Matt. 9). That divinely provided foretokening of this feast was fulfilled when, as Luke says more explicitly, having been called while sitting at the tax-office and following the Lord, he made Him a great feast in his house (Luke 5).

He therefore made Him a feast, and indeed a great one, as though it were the feast of a king. For, as we have already said more fully elsewhere, in this evangelist Christ is shown to be king both by lineage and by deeds. From his very beginning he says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” [Col. 1686A] (Matt. 1); then he describes the newborn King of the Jews as immediately adored by the Magi; and, weaving the whole texture of his narrative with royal acts and kingly parables, he concludes at last by having this king, now crowned with the glory of resurrection, say: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28). If you duly consider the whole course of his composition, you will recognize it as breathing the mysteries of the kingdom of God.

Nor is this surprising. He had been a publican, called from the public service of the kingdom of sin to the freedom of the kingdom of God, the kingdom of righteousness. Rightly, therefore, lest he be ungrateful to the great king of his liberation, he served that king’s laws, directing attention to what His kingdom is like, although carnal Jews expected it carnally. Observing this, Father Augustine prefers to understand Mark, in both the prophetic and evangelical vision of the four living creatures, by the face of a man; but this man—Matthew—by the face of a lion. For concerning Luke, that he is signified by the face of a calf, and John, that he is signified by the face of a flying eagle, there is one undivided judgment among all teachers. Concerning these chariots of our Aminadab—interpreted as “the willing one of my people”—for whose sake his soul troubled the unknowing Synagogue, we said much far above, namely in connection with the prophet Ezekiel. Let us therefore now proceed to what remains.

## CHAPTER XV. On James, the Lord’s brother: that he too dipped his pen in this Spirit of understanding.

James, the brother of the Lord, who because of his outstanding holiness was also called “the Just” by men, likewise dipped his pen in this Spirit of understanding. For he wrote the first of the seven Catholic Epistles. Of this James the apostle Paul said: “James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hands of fellowship to me and Barnabas, that we should go to the Gentiles, but they to the circumcision” (Gal. 2). Since he had been appointed an Apostle to the circumcision, he cared for those of the circumcision: as he taught those present by conversation, so he consoled, instructed, reproved, and corrected those absent by letter.

He wrote an Epistle to the dispersed—those who had suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake, when, after Stephen had been killed by the Jews, a great persecution arose in the Church that was at Jerusalem [Col. 1686D]—but not only to them. He wrote also to those who had not yet taken care to fulfil in works the precepts of faith in Christ, and also to those who persisted without faith and who strove, insofar as they could, to persecute and trouble that faith in believers. Thus in him was fulfilled, not a little praiseworthily, what Truth said of this Spirit: “When He has come, He will convict the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment: of sin indeed, because they did not believe in me” (John 10), etc.

For, being near at hand as bishop of Jerusalem, he reproved not only by word but also in writing those rich persons whose iniquity had issued from their fatness, so that they killed the Lord, when he says: “Come now, you rich, weep and howl in the miseries that shall come upon you. You have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days. You have feasted upon the earth, and nourished your hearts in luxuries. In the day of slaughter you have brought forth; you have killed the Just One, and He did not resist you” [Col. 1687A] (James 5). Then he turns again to those oppressed by the wickedness of such men, exhorting them to patience: “Be patient therefore, brethren,” he says, “until the coming of the Lord” (ibid.), etc.

Nor should one pass over that he very suitably argues concerning faith and works, saying: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2), or idle. For because the apostle Paul, preaching that a person is justified through faith without works (Rom. 4), was not rightly understood by those who received his statement so as to suppose that, if they had once believed in Christ, they would be saved by faith even if they acted wickedly and lived criminally and shamefully, James explained how Paul’s meaning ought to be understood. Therefore he especially employed the example of Abraham to show that faith is empty if it does not work well, since the apostle Paul too employed Abraham’s example in order to prove that a person is justified without works.

For when James recalls Abraham’s good works, which accompanied his faith, he sufficiently shows that Paul does not teach through Abraham that a person is justified by faith without works in such a way that, once a person believes, doing good no longer concerns him; rather, Paul teaches this so that no one may suppose that he arrived at the gift of justification, which is in faith, by the merits of previous good works.

## CHAPTER XVI. [Col. 1687C] On Jude, James’s brother: that he embraces a great power of understanding in a brief pen.

The apostle Jude, brother of James, whom Matthew and Mark call Thaddaeus in the Gospel, writes against the same corrupters of the faith whom Peter and John condemn in their Epistles. He too, with a brief pen, embraces a great power of understanding; for example, when he says: “Woe to them, for they have walked in the way of Cain, and have been poured out in the error of Balaam for reward, and have perished in the contradiction of Korah” (Jude 11).

In saying this, he asserts briefly but clearly that Cain was an example of all who, because of envy of better persons, assume for themselves the title of teachers, by which they may be honored. Balaam, however, is an example of those who, for love of earthly advantages, attack the truth that they themselves know. Korah, who went down alive into hell, is an example of all who, from a desire for unlawful primacy, separate themselves from the unity of the holy Church and, knowing and foreseeing how great the evil they are doing is, nevertheless descend to the hell of crimes.

But this same Epistle contains uncertain testimonies taken from apocrypha. For when it says: “When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, contended concerning the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy, but said: ‘May the Lord rebuke you’” (Jude 9), we have no certainty when, I say, Michael had a contention with the devil concerning the body of Moses. Likewise, when it says: “But Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied concerning these, saying: ‘Behold, the Lord comes with His holy thousands, to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly’” [Col. 1688A] (Jude 14), this is written from an apocryphal book.

Accordingly, in the earliest times this Epistle was rejected by many; but through the authority it acquired by antiquity and use, it deserved to be counted among the holy Scriptures—especially because Jude took from the apocrypha such a testimony as was not apocryphal or doubtful, but manifest in the true light and bright truth. For what believer does not know, or doubt, that the Lord will come with His holy thousands to execute judgment against all and to convict all the ungodly of all their impious works which they have wickedly done, and of all the harsh words which all the ungodly have spoken against Him? (Jude 15).

Moreover, when it says, “When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, contended concerning the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a judgment of blasphemy,” if this may appear to have been borrowed, it is like that passage used by the Apostle when, endeavoring to convict the Corinthians who had been drawn away from faith in the resurrection by their own, though foolish, practice, he says: “Otherwise what shall those do who are baptized for the dead, if the dead do not rise at all? Why then are they baptized for them?” (1 Cor. 15). For because he used such an argument against them, it does not follow that the Apostle approved the baptism of living persons for the dead. Rather, in order to place before their eyes their thoughtless inconsistency—by which they did not realize that they were being carried about by every wind of doctrine—he adopted a practice by which they themselves refuted their own words: while saying that there was no resurrection of the dead, they baptized living persons for the dead.

Likewise here, because he says, “When Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil, contended,” etc., it does not follow that he approved an opinion lacking the authority of Scripture. Rather, he wished out of their own mouth to conclude that they ought not to pour out blasphemy or undisciplined offense against anyone, and especially against God. For if, as they held, Michael the archangel did not wish to utter blasphemy against the devil opposing him, but restrained him with restrained speech, much more must every blasphemy be avoided by human beings, especially—as has been said—lest they offend the majesty of the Creator with undisciplined speech.

## CHAPTER XVII. [Col. 1688D] On the apostle Paul: how and with what intention he defends his rank—namely, that although he was not there, he nevertheless received the apostolic grace of understanding.

Paul, the chosen vessel, great and illustrious advocate of truth, vindicates for himself, with great struggle, a name and place in this order or office, continually standing and pleading in every assembly, every Church, every court of heaven and earth. For example, he says to the Corinthians: “Would that you could bear with a little of my foolishness—but do bear with me”; and shortly afterwards: “For if he who comes preaches another Christ, whom we have not preached, or if you receive another Christ, whom you have not received, or another Gospel, which you have not received, you would rightly endure it. For I think that I have done nothing less than the great apostles” (2 Cor. 11).

And after the most forceful course of a most vehement speech, he finally says with the utmost propriety, as though catching his breath: “I have become foolish”—that is, by recounting my merits—“you compelled me. For I ought to have been commended by you. For I have done nothing less than those who are apostles beyond measure, although I am nothing. Yet the signs of my apostleship were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, wonders, and powers. For what is there in which you were inferior to the other Churches?” [Col. 1689A] (2 Cor. 12).

Likewise, to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised Him from the dead.” And shortly afterwards: “For I make known to you, brethren, that the Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. For neither did I receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1). Having entered in this manner, he most forcefully confirms throughout the whole course of his conversion and mission both that he received the Gospel neither from man nor through man, and that the earlier apostles could contribute nothing to him for the correction or supplementation of the same Gospel: “For those who seemed to be something contributed nothing to me” (Gal. 2). And shortly afterwards: “But when Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (ibid.), etc.

Thus, both in many places in his letters and especially in their titles or superscriptions, he defends his apostleship, so that there is scarcely any of his Epistles at the beginning of which the authority of the apostolic name does not shine—except the one which he wrote to the Hebrews, whose apostle he was not. It is not so in the letters of the other apostles. For, apart from the apostle Peter, none even makes mention of this name at the beginning.

Why is this? Clearly because all the others were apostles in such a manner that they did not need to defend their apostleship.
