They had been called apostles by the Lord Himself while He dwelt among men; each had been designated by name; the Holy Spirit had come upon them on the day of Pentecost; and from them, or through them, evangelical preaching had begun. Paul was not there—not in that upper room when the Holy Spirit came—but in the synagogue of Satan, since he persecuted as many persons of this Way as he could.

Knowing this, jealous men and corrupters of evangelical truth, false apostles, disparaged his authority and the wise architect, in order to overthrow the foundation that had been well laid. They said: “He is not an apostle; he did not see the Lord; he must not be heard.” By saying these things, they unsettled many of those whom he had converted. Paul grieved not at the diminution of his own reputation, but at the overthrow of believers. Therefore he sometimes speaks as though indignant and, making a lawful defense, says: “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord? And if I am not an apostle to others, yet at least I am to you. For you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord” (1 Cor. 9) [Col. 1690A], and similar things.

At other times, however, from his own conscience he confesses with sufficient humility what he does not think worthy of being agitated by hostile disparagement. For he says: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, He appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am; and His grace in me was not empty, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15).

Again: “I who was formerly a blasphemer,” he says, “and a persecutor and injurious; but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief. And the grace of our Lord superabounded with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.” And immediately: “This saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance: that Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I obtained mercy: that in me first Jesus Christ might show all patience, for the strengthening of those who will believe unto eternal life” [Col. 1690B] (1 Tim. 1).

Since these things are so—concerning the truth of his apostleship, by which he declares himself endowed through the worthiness of God’s grace and confesses himself undeserving because of the unbelief that preceded it—let us judge the greatest and chief of all the things said to be that which the apostle Paul says of this same apostleship to the Galatians: “Not from men nor through a man.” And shortly afterwards: “For I make known to you, brethren, that the Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man. For neither did I receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1).

## CHAPTER XVIII. He was not unlettered. For he had been instructed in the letter of the Law at the feet of Gamaliel; but he received neither the spiritual sense of the Law nor the Gospel of Christ “from man” or “through a man,” but “through the revelation of Jesus Christ.”

For this is what we marvel at in the first apostles, unlearned and unlettered men: that we ascribe it to this Holy Spirit, the Spirit of understanding. Likewise, in Moses and the prophets we venerate, to the praise of the same Spirit, the fact that they at once learned by the revelation of God alone the knowledge of truth which they had neither learned nor could have learned from men or through a man.

This man, however, was not unlearned or unlettered. Rather, as he himself says: “I am a Jewish man, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, brought up in this city of Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, instructed according to the truth of the law of the fathers, zealous for the law, as you all are today” [Col. 1690D] (Acts 22). Thus there was some difference: they were unlearned and unlettered men, while he had been instructed at the feet of Gamaliel, a wise and learned man, according to the truth of the law of the fathers.

But what could he have been taught at the feet of that man according to the truth of the law of the fathers? Surely according to the Old Testament; according to the truth, not of the life-giving Spirit but of the killing letter. For example, he could have been taught that it was written: “Abraham had two sons, one by a bondwoman and one by a free woman; but he who was of the bondwoman was born according to the flesh, while he who was of the free woman was by promise.” But that these are two covenants, one indeed from Mount Sinai, bearing children unto slavery, which is Hagar, while the other is from the Jerusalem above, free, which is the mother of us all (Gal. 3)—this, I say, he could not have been taught at the feet of that man.

Let us therefore, as persons who know and are teachable, and as persons of good will, believe this Apostle of the Gentiles, our Apostle, when he says: “The Gospel which was preached by me is not according to man; for neither did I receive it from man, nor did I learn it, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ.” It must be noted that he did not say, “The letter or learning of the Law, which I did not receive or learn from man”; rather, he says: “The Gospel which was preached by me, I did not receive from man, nor did I learn.”

For he had received and learned from a man—that is, at the feet of Gamaliel—the letter of the Law, as has already been said, the killing letter. By it he was to be killed, just as Uriah the Hittite was killed by the letter of David which he carried (2 Sam. 11), unless the grace of the life-giving Spirit alone had come beforehand to meet him on that very road. For, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, he had approached the high priest and requested letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that, if he found any men or women belonging to this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. And as he made his journey (Acts 9), the whole world has heard what the grace of God did to him [Col. 1691C]; the nations and kings have heard, before whom this chosen vessel bore the name of Jesus.

He himself, bearing and recounting this same matter before a certain king, says: “At midday, O king, on the road I saw from heaven a light above the brightness of the sun shine round about me and those who were with me. And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice speaking to me in the Hebrew language: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad’” (Acts 26). Meanwhile, from what man, or through what man, did he receive or learn the Gospel? For it was not said, “He was reading the Gospel”; rather, “He was for three days and three nights without sight” (Acts 9). Ananias did not say: “The Lord Jesus sent me that I might instruct you in the Gospel”; rather, he said: “The Lord sent me that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

Nor was it said: “He read with the disciples who were at Damascus for a long time”; rather, it was said: “He was with the disciples who were at Damascus for some days; and immediately, entering the synagogues, he preached Jesus, that He is the Son of God.” All who heard were astonished and said: “Is not this the man who attacked at Jerusalem those who invoked this name, and who came here for this purpose, that he might bring them bound to the chief priests?” But he grew much stronger and confounded the Jews who dwelt at Damascus, affirming that this is the Christ [Col. 1691D] (ibid.).

Certainly such strengthening of a novice of the Gospel, and such confounding of the Jews, could by no means take place without most keen faith or great fullness of knowledge and truth. Nor did this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High occur to him without a great and fitting sign. For when Ananias said, “The Lord sent me that you may see and be filled with the Holy Spirit,” immediately there fell from his eyes something like scales, and he received his sight (ibid.).

What those scales falling from his eyes signified was understood by him who said: “And not as Moses placed a veil over his face, so that the children of Israel might not gaze upon his face, which is being done away; but their understandings were dulled. For until this day the same veil remains unrevealed in the reading of the Old Testament, because it is done away in Christ. But even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart. But we all, beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory into glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3).

Surely the veil of unbelief placed over his heart—that is, the faithlessness of Jewish blindness—when the Lord Jesus cried out from heaven, passed outwardly to his eyes; and from there it fell away, along with the scales that signified that veil. Thus the man rose resplendent, illumined both outwardly in body and inwardly in heart. There was light in his mind; the brilliance of light shone in his mouth. He had removed from his eyes the veil of the killing letter and poured forth the splendor of the life-giving Spirit. The children of Israel could not bear this; carnal Jews could not endure it. For they were confounded while he grew strong with unveiled face. Hence Scripture says: “They formed a plan to kill him, but their plot was made known to Saul” [Col. 1692C] (Acts 9).

## CHAPTER XIX. That Benjamin the young man is fittingly here, namely in the rank or privilege of apostolic primacy, and rightly says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

There, then, is “Benjamin the young man” (Ps. 67), that is, Paul of the tribe of Benjamin (Phil. 3), as he himself testifies in his Epistle; and he is a young man because he was called last, because by his own confession he is the least of the apostles (1 Cor. 15). Where? Surely in that order, measure, and apostolic privilege where Christ, ascending on high and leading captivity captive, “gave gifts to men” [Col. 1692D] (Eph. 4); where the princes went before, namely the apostles already mentioned, joined with those who sing psalms—that is, who confess in heart, voice, and work—and with young women of the new life beating timbrels in joy and thus blessing the Lord in the Churches; where the fountains of Israel appeared, fountains and rivers of living water, that is, the charisms of the Holy Spirit which was given (Ps. 67).

There, I say—in that primacy or among those fountains—is Benjamin the young man: an Apostle not doubtful or uncertain, though young, though last. Nor is he there in any ordinary manner, but “in an ecstasy of mind” (ibid.): either in the astonishment of mind of all those saying, “Is not this the man who came here for this purpose, to attack this name?”; or in the astonishment of his own mind when, struck down by the Lord on the road, he was made senseless (Acts 9); or later, when he was caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a person to utter (2 Cor. 12).

There he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15). Beautiful and fitting is this confession of the young man; sweet and glorious is this profession of the last, or least, of the apostles. Would not the first apostles, or the firstborn among the apostles, seem able to say the same thing truthfully? For which apostle, or saint or chosen person of any rank, is what he is from any source other than the grace of God? Why then did he say, in self-abasement or diminution: “By the grace of God I am what I am”?

For he had first said: “Last of all, as to one untimely born, He appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.” Having said this, he immediately added: “But by the grace of God I am what I am” [Col. 1693B] (ibid.). We say, therefore, that the earlier apostles also are what they are by the grace of God, but this man is what he is by grace in a different manner. For the calling of the other apostles differs from his calling.

The other apostles believed and followed the Lord Jesus who called them, leaving all things, when He was a man despised by men, indeed so despised that He was later crucified. But when the Lord Jesus called this man, He was already shining in heaven, seated at the right hand of Majesty on high, with such brilliance of majesty that He made blind the man whom He called and extinguished by His brightness the bodily light of a weak person unable to bear the power of the true Light.

Add to this that when, or before, the others were called, most of them were engaged in innocent and simple occupations, namely casting nets into the sea to catch fish (Matt. 4). We read that only Matthew was a publican, called from the tax-office (Matt. 9). But this man was a persecutor, a blasphemer, and an injurious person; and when he was called, he had received the letters he had requested from the high priest and was proceeding to Damascus to bring the disciples of the Lord bound (Acts 9). Why say more? With his whole soul and spirit, threatening and savage, he persecuted the Lord Jesus. And by that same force, by that same cry of the Lord rebuking him, by which Saul was cast down in order that Paul might rise, if it had pleased the Victor to strike His enemy down into eternal death, no one could rightly have reproached Him [Col. 1693D].

For the law of war and the law of victory permit the stronger victor to exact vengeance upon his enemy. But by the wonderful grace of the Victor he was preserved for life, that he might live and, living, serve, though—as has been said—he could justly have been utterly killed. He may therefore truthfully say: “By the grace of God I am what I am,” because in truth he is what he is by God’s grace not simply, not in the common manner of all saints, but in a very different way.

Never unmindful of this fact throughout his whole life, he also briefly touches upon it at the very beginning of the Epistle which he wrote to the Romans, when he says: “Paul, servant of Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1). He calls himself a servant because he knew that, conquered in war, he had been preserved by the grace of the victor. For a servant is properly one who, defeated in war, though he may lawfully be killed, is preserved solely at the victor’s will and consequently belongs as the property of the one by whom he has been granted life.

## CHAPTER XX. That truly the grace of God in him was not empty, as we especially discover by reading his Epistle to the Romans, which, in accordance with the custom of those to whom he speaks, he divided, as it were, into five acts.

“And His grace,” he says, “was not empty in me, but I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15). Let us also truly say, for we have experienced and daily experience in reading, that His grace, O holy Paul, was not empty in you [Col. 1694B]. At present we speak not so much of the abundance of your labors, by which you labored in that grace, but, considering your understanding, we say that His grace was not empty in you in this gift.

We could gather much from the treasure of wisdom and understanding which the Holy Spirit of the Lord Jesus Christ stored up in this chosen vessel of His; but that would be far too long. And much earlier, when we spoke of the Law or the Old Testament, we did this very thing to the extent of our ability, though scatteredly. Now, to say a little concerning this part of grace, let us take only the Epistle written to the Romans, a truly rich casket of wisdom and understanding; and according to its understanding let us also strive to understand the grace of truth and the truth of God’s grace.

First, we must recognize that this same Epistle, or its argument, is divided into five acts, according to the law or custom of the wise persons to whom he spoke. For among them it had been established, even in the trifles of the secular world, that any work by which morals were instructed or even reproved should not exceed five acts. Hence we read in Flaccus:

> Let no play that would be demanded and seen  
> be shorter or longer than five acts.
>
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 189–190.)

The first act, then, is the equalization of Jew and Greek: namely, that all have sinned and need the glory of God [Col. 1694D]. The second is the commendation of grace, or of faith in Christ: namely, that all ought rightly to be justified through one man. The third is the struggle: that, having been freed from the law of sin and death, we ought not to sin again. The fourth is the demonstration of what the Law could or could not accomplish before the manifestation of grace. The fifth is the admonition to the Gentiles: that they ought not to insult the Jews; that the branches of the wild olive grafted into the good olive tree ought not to boast against the natural branches because they were broken off (Rom. 3–11). For afterwards, in the remainder of the Epistle, he treats of common matters, that is, of morals. Let us now therefore enter, guided by the same Spirit of understanding, and distinguish these same acts more carefully.

## CHAPTER XXI. [Col. 1695A] On the first act, in which he equates Jew and Greek, because all have sinned and need the glory of God.

With the magnificent salutation of the grace and peace of God our Father prefixed to all God’s beloved in Rome, called to be saints, and their goodwill secured, he enters, with attention, from the words, “First indeed I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ for all of you,” as far as the words, “But the righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1). At once, first, how wisely and how sharply he strikes at the sins of the Gentiles; then he encloses the scant righteousness of the Jews under sin.

For the case indeed demanded that he should first accuse the Jew [Col. 1695B] and set him before his own face, because the whole controversy arose from the Jew. For, glorying in the flesh of Abraham, he challenged the Gentile, as though bringing a case to court, and judged him unworthy of evangelical grace, unless God’s pious and provident generosity, mercifully receiving him into the household or sojourn of the Israelite race, should do so. The converted Jew claimed Christ’s Gospel as given to himself and as his own; and he was, as has already been said, the originator of the dispute.

Therefore, although the case, as has been said, required him first to show that the Jew was under sin, he nevertheless preferred first to strike the Gentile with a severe and very dreadful enumeration of his sins, saying: “For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God [Col. 1695C] or give thanks to him, but became vain in their reasonings and their foolish heart was darkened. For while claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things. Therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonoured their bodies” (ibid.), and so forth.

Why this? If the controversy had been initiated by the Jew who hated the salvation of the Gentiles and said, “We are God’s people; we are circumcised, descended from Abraham; Christ was promised to us, and he himself testified that he came to us, saying, ‘I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel’” (Matt. 15)—when he called you dogs rather than human beings—why did he touch the Gentile rather than the Jew so sharply, [Col. 1695D] and set his former manner of life, so bespattered with foulness, before his face?

Plainly because the Gentile was more patient in hearing these things, since he voluntarily confessed his sins and, by confessing, fled to Christ’s grace. But the Jew, glorying in the flesh of righteous patriarchs and presuming upon his own fleshly righteousness, was impatient of an accusation of unrighteousness or a confession of sin. Thus, like a wise orator, he first rebukes with great force the hearer who is more patient; then he draws tight the bonds of a reasoned argument around the one who is impatient, to bind and enclose him, and ties him in the same knot.

How? “Although they knew the righteousness of God,” he says, “they did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death—not only those [Col. 1696A] who do them, but also those who approve of those who do them” (Rom. 1). For the Jew was bound to concede—and willingly conceded, as against an adversary—all that he had previously said, including this final assertion: that those who do evil things and those who approve their doers are worthy of death. But he wisely and cautiously said universally, without distinguishing Jew and Greek, that those who do such things are worthy of death; and immediately added: “Therefore you are without excuse, every human being who judges; for in judging another, you condemn yourself. For you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. 2).

As if he said: Since neither Jews nor Greeks, but those who do such things, are worthy of death—since, I say, each person is worthy of death not because he is Jew or Greek but because he does such things—therefore you are without excuse, every human being, even you, O Jew, who judge; for you do the same things that you judge. And immediately: “For we know,” he says, “that God’s judgment is according to truth against those who do such things” (ibid.). “According to truth,” that is, not according to partiality. For to show partiality whether toward Jews or Greeks is not to judge according to truth.

Nor could the Jew escape himself so as not to concede to the one who said, “You do the same things that you judge”; for he could judge nothing against the Gentile [Col. 1696B] other than what he saw in himself, conscience bearing witness. If he should wish contentiously to defend himself against his own conscience, he would be convicted by as many witnesses as there were prophets among him, and by Moses himself. For among them are read the same sins of the Jews that are found among the Gentiles. The Gentiles served the creature rather than the Creator and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man (Rom. 1); and the Jews too served works made by an artisan’s hands and exchanged his glory for the likeness of a calf eating grass (Ps. 105).

Nor could the Apostle himself know on more certain authorities concerning the Gentile than concerning the Jew that the Jew had been given over to the desires of his heart, to impurity, so as to change natural use into that which is against nature. For Isaiah says: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of my God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). Moreover, another Scripture testifies that the very best of the young men [Col. 1696C] among those Jews were placed in brothels (2 Macc. 4). He could have assembled many scriptural testimonies against them, but judged one sufficient. “For it is written,” he says, “There is no one righteous; no one understands; no one seeks God. All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one” (Rom. 3), and so forth.

And lest the Jew fail to understand that these words were spoken to or concerning himself: “But we know,” he says, “that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become subject to God; because by works of the law no flesh shall be justified before him” (ibid.).

## Chapter XXII

[Col. 1697A] On the second act, in which he says that all people ought truly to be justified through one man, and from no other source than the faith by which Abraham was justified while still a Gentile.

Thus the first act has established that all Jews and Greeks are under sin, and the Jew’s boasting has been excluded (Rom. 3). In the following act it is argued that all, both Jews and Greeks, are justified through faith in Jesus Christ, and from no other source; and that Father Abraham himself was justified by the same faith while he was a Gentile—justified, I say, by faith without works of the law, indeed even before that work which was greatest among the works of the law, the work of circumcision.

“For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” [Col. 1697B] (Rom. 4). What do you suppose he believed, except that all nations would be blessed in his seed? (Gen. 22). And what is that seed except Christ? Therefore the faith reckoned to Abraham as righteousness is faith in Christ. “How,” you ask, “was it reckoned? In circumcision or in uncircumcision?” Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. “And he received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness of faith which he had in uncircumcision” (Rom. 4).

He received, plainly, a fitting seal corresponding to the subject of his faith: because he had believed concerning seed, he had the sign of circumcision in no other bodily part than that through which seed passes. This sign was efficacious unto righteousness until the reality came—that is, the seed itself, in whose promised coming the father of the faithful had believed and been sealed. Thus the sole difference is this: he believed that he would come; we believe that he has now come. Therefore it is evident and beyond doubt that we, as they, are justified by the same faith.

Accordingly he says: “Therefore, having been justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5). And lest anyone doubt that all ought rightly to be justified through one man, after much relevant to the reasoning of this proposition he finally concludes thus: “Therefore, as through one man’s transgression condemnation came upon all human beings, so also through one man’s righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings. For as through one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so through one man’s obedience many shall be made righteous” (ibid.). It is therefore not unjustly, but justly, that the strong man armed is cast out and his goods are plundered (Luke 11); for if it was just that many should be made sinners through one man’s disobedience, it is no less just that many should be made righteous through one man’s obedience.

## Chapter XXIII

On the third act, in which he maintains that, though free, we ought not to sin again, because Christ has freed us from the law of sin and death.

In the third act, the point is made that we must now know not to sin, lest we suppose that Christ’s faith alone, or confession of the mouth, suffices for us, however we may live. “For if we have died to sin,” he says, “how shall we live in it?” (Rom. 6). And observe by what a beautiful and powerful comparison he restrains us from that servile life—indeed, from that dead servitude. “Do you not know,” [Col. 1698A] he says, “that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead, we too might walk in newness of life” (ibid.).

For the likeness of the Lord’s death, as we have recalled elsewhere, is the sacrament of baptism. In it, through the wondrous workmanship of regenerating grace, the old person dies to his former lord, that is, to sin; and, rising with the new person, Christ, receives the titles of freedom and righteousness, so that he is no longer the one whose possession he had been, and is no longer himself what he had been. Hence he immediately says: “For our old person was crucified once, in order that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we should no longer serve sin” (ibid.).

It is therefore foolish—indeed faithless—after we have died to sin to live in it again. For this is to abandon the Redeemer and Lord of one’s freedom and to flee back, for a trifling wage, to the tyrant of former captivity. Nor, even if they wish, can they again be redeemed by the certain redemption—that is, rebaptized. Hence in the Epistle to the Hebrews, after saying, “Therefore, leaving the elementary teaching about Christ, let us proceed to perfection,” he adds: “Not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and faith toward God, teaching about baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, who have also tasted the heavenly gift and become partakers of the Holy Spirit, who have likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, [Col. 1698C] to be renewed again unto repentance, since they again crucify the Son of God for themselves and expose him to public shame” (Heb. 6).

For by “to be renewed unto repentance” and “again to crucify the Son of God for themselves,” he means to become new through repentance and to be baptized again. Those who wish to be baptized again, insofar as lies in them, crucify the Son of God again and expose him to public shame. In this sense also is understood what he likewise says: “For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of truth, no sacrifice for sins remains” (Heb. 10).

But here too, after saying, “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus,” and so forth, he says: “Knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. [Col. 1698D] So you also must reckon yourselves dead indeed to sin, but alive to God” (Rom. 6). In saying all this, he frightens us so that we may fear falling back into vices after baptism, because we cannot be rebaptized. He excludes not repentance or remission of sins, but a second baptism.

This is the issue on which he stands and contends, saying: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (ibid.), and so forth, until the words: “But now we have been released from the law of death in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom. 7). It is therefore evident that he did not earlier say, “For we reckon that a person is justified by faith apart from works” (Rom. 3), in the sense that, once we believe in Christ, we should consider ourselves saved however we may live. [Col. 1699A]

## Chapter XXIV

On the fourth act, in which he strives to show what the law contributed before Christ’s advent, and what it could not contribute.

In the fourth act he intends to show what the law contributed and what it could not contribute. “What then shall we say?” he asks. “Is the law sin? Certainly not” (Rom. 7). For he had said: “When we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, worked in our members.” And again: “But now we have been released from the law of death in which we were held” (ibid.). By “the law of death,” the law through which sinful passions existed, he means no other than the Law of Moses, which brought death, through which sinful passions became known [Col. 1699B] and increased, since what is forbidden by law tends to be desired more ardently.

Therefore, lest he seem to have provided an opening for slander as an adversary of the law: “What,” he says, “shall we say? Shall we say, or appear to have said, that the law is sin? Certainly not! But what shall we say, or what did we say? Precisely this: ‘I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known coveting unless the law said, “You shall not covet.” But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, worked in me every kind of coveting. For apart from the law sin was dead’” (ibid.).

This is what it meant for the law to be, or to be called, the law of death: that through the law sin was known, and through the commandment sin took occasion to work every kind of coveting in me and increased my guilt of transgression through the knowledge of itself. For the law itself could not free from slavery to sin those very persons whom it forbade from sinning.

Because the reader perceives this only slowly in the whole human race, each person, considering himself with the Apostle as an example, says: “But I once lived apart from the law”—understand, “and then sin was dead in me.” Indeed, each one of us lived without the law as long as, either through age or ignorance, he was free from the fear of the Lord. Then sin was dead, because no opponent rose against it, just as water sometimes flows more sluggishly over level ground where no resistance from any obstacle stands in its way. “But when the commandment came,” he says, “sin revived” (ibid.). [Col. 1699D]

This is truly experienced by every soldier of God who, taking up the weapons of the Lord’s legal commandments, is found fighting against sin, so that he may say, “When the commandment came, sin revived.” For how few are there who, turning from their former way of life, immediately had peace and did not endure the conflict of sin, as though an insane tyrant were protesting? Therefore he rightly says meanwhile: “For I do not understand what I do”—that is, I do not approve of it. “For I do not do the good that I wish; but the evil that I hate, that I do.” And immediately: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person; but I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members.”

Such a combatant, labouring in hope and hoping amid labour, [Col. 1700A] says: “Wretched human being that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” And immediately answers himself: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

From this example, therefore, it is clear what the law contributed and what it could not contribute. For what is true in one human being is also true in the whole human race. Such as I was when I once lived without law or the fear of the Lord, such was the state of the world before the written law had yet been given. Again, such as I now am when “I delight in the law of God according to the inward person, but see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind,” and so forth—such was the world after receiving the law: it was weakened and, although it fought and resisted, was held by sin as victor, and through Adam.

Again, just as a person enjoys a certain peace and rest in himself, delivered by the aiding grace of God from the assault of vices, so that he no longer lives in the flesh—that is, in fleshly passions—such is this third state of the world, in which the Son of God destroyed sin’s dominion. Hence the same Apostle later says: “For what was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God accomplished by sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh: concerning sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. 8).

Yet this is fulfilled in few people: namely, in those who, though living in the flesh, are nevertheless outside the flesh by walking according to the Spirit; those who, after the example of the apostles, renounce not only unlawful things but even things which they could lawfully possess or do. [Col. 1700C] Although the whole penalty of sin has not yet been removed, nevertheless through Christ’s advent sin has been condemned and sin’s kingdom destroyed; and what remains of sin’s penalty will most certainly be destroyed at his second advent.

This is what he immediately goes on to say: “But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead”—that is, most certainly destined to die—“because of sin; but the spirit lives because of justification. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (ibid.), and so forth.

Until this occurs, patience is needed in the meantime, aided by the consolation which he later provides: “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us. For the eager expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the glory of the children of God,” and the rest, down to the words: “Neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, nor power, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (ibid.). [Col. 1700D]

## Chapter XXV

On the fifth act, in which he teaches that the wild olive ought not to glory or exalt itself against the broken natural branches of the olive—that is, the Gentiles against the Jew.

Finally, in the fifth act he returns to the principal case and teaches the Gentile—whose cause against the Jew he chiefly defends, as he says, “As long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will magnify my ministry” (Rom. 1)—not to exalt himself against the Jew but rather to humble himself and show compassion, first offering his own example. He says: “I speak the truth in Christ, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and unceasing pain in my heart. For I was wishing that I myself might be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites; theirs is the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the law, and worship, and the promises; from their stock is Christ according to the flesh, who is blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9). [Col. 1701A]

Certainly, his saying, “I was wishing that I myself might be accursed from Christ for my brothers,” has the same weight as Moses’ saying: “I beseech you, Lord, this people has committed a great sin and made gods of gold for themselves. Either forgive them this offence, or, if you do not, blot me out of the book which you have written” (Exod. 32).

It should be noted that he says not “I wish,” but “I was wishing,” because every excess of a vow or of any good thing ought promptly to be corrected. Thus Moses, mentioned above, said once, “Either forgive them this offence, or blot me out of your book which you have written”; but, since God did not approve and said, “Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book; but you, go and lead this people of whom I spoke to you,” he is not found ever again to have spoken thus.

So, as he enters the matter, the Apostle now commends the height of God’s dreadful judgment, for example when he says: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9); and then: “But what if God, willing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory, whom he also called—not only from Jews, but also from Gentiles?” (ibid.). But now he strikes those same called from the Gentiles with a salutary fear so that they may humble themselves, saying: “But if some of the branches were broken off, while you, although a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer in the root and richness of the olive tree, do not glory against the branches. But if you glory, you do not bear the root, but the root bears you. Do not think proudly, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps he will not spare you either” (Rom. 11), and so forth. [Col. 1701D]

This act concludes thus: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For from him, through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory and dominion for ages of ages” (ibid.). What remains of the Epistle instructs conduct and sets in order the adornment of holy religion: “I beseech you, brothers,” he says, “through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your rational service” (Rom. 12).

## Chapter XXVI

That these few matters out of many suffice to demonstrate that the vessel of election was filled with great grace of understanding; and that, although the same Spirit taught prophets and apostles, there is nevertheless some difference.

It was not the purpose of the present discussion to search out all the treasures of this great and most divine Epistle, but to test from its character that this Apostle is truly a vessel of election and that the Holy Spirit has truly stored up in him or upon him the delight of wisdom and the exultation of understanding of which I was speaking. Yet this must not be passed over: although the same Spirit of understanding taught both prophets and apostles—for both alike were taught not by a human being nor through a human being, but by the illumination of the Holy Spirit—there is nevertheless a great difference between them, not in the quality of their meanings but in their expression or language.

For of the former it is truly said: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17), because they wrote obscurely and shut up their writings as though beneath a seal, as it was said to one of them: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8). But Truth says to the latter: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). For how are they the light of the world except by illuminating it, so that the world might know what had been obscure—that is, what had been closed up in the law and the prophets? Although he added, “So let your light shine before human beings, that they may see your good works,” he nonetheless said, “You are the light of the world,” because of the light of doctrine; and so forth: “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house.”

For when he had said, “So let your light shine before human beings, that they may see your good works [Col. 1702C] and glorify your Father who is in heaven,” he immediately added: “Do not think that I came to abolish the law or the prophets. I did not come to abolish but to fulfil” (ibid.). How do we know how he fulfilled them except from those to whom he said, “You are the light of the world”? For this is the chief part of that light and the better effect of this light: that the dark water in the clouds of the air is illuminated—that is, the hidden knowledge contained in the law and the prophets.

All those to whom he said, “You are the light of the world,” do this; and, by way of example, so does the Apostle Paul here, when in the action described above he says: “Did Israel not know? Moses first says: ‘I will provoke you to jealousy through a non-nation; through a foolish nation I will provoke you to anger’” (Rom. 10). For in saying this he illuminates with his light almost the whole Song of Deuteronomy, showing what Christ fulfilled by coming, where it is written: “And I will provoke them through that which is not a people; through a foolish nation I will stir them to anger. A fire has been kindled in my wrath and shall burn to the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. 32).

And immediately follows: “Isaiah dares and says, ‘I was found by those who did not seek me; I openly appeared to those who did not ask for me.’ But to Israel he says, ‘All day long I stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe and contradicted me’” (Rom. 10). By saying these things he illuminates a broad passage of prophecy and shows what the prophet lamented: “But they provoked him to anger and afflicted the Spirit of his holiness,” down to the words, “Your holy city has become a wilderness; Zion has become desolate; Jerusalem is desolation; the house of our sanctification and of our glory, where our fathers praised you, has become a burning of fire, and all our precious things have been turned into ruins” (Isa. 63–64). [Col. 1703A]

This, then, is no small difference: they indeed understood; but these both understood the great mystery of godliness and opened the understanding of those others. They understood, I say, but did not also proclaim; these, however, “proclaimed the works of God and understood his deeds” (Ps. 63).

# Book Five on the Works of the Holy Spirit: On Counsel

[Col. 1703]

## Chapter I

On the Spirit of counsel: that, according to the Psalmist, God is truly terrible in counsels over the children of men.

The third Spirit after the Spirit of wisdom, the Spirit of counsel, must now be approached with our whole mind and renewed attention. For the very name signifies secrecy and depth, which the Apostle greatly admired when, after saying, “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” he immediately added: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11).

He was dealing with a mystery: the mystery of Israel’s great blindness, so that he said: “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in yourselves: that a partial blindness has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel might be saved, as it is written: ‘There shall come from Zion one who delivers, and he shall turn captivity away from Jacob’” (ibid.), and so forth. Therefore he rightly cried out in admiration of this, because it truly proceeded from the wonderful and hidden counsel of awe-inspiring divinity.

For before him, the prophet also, greatly admiring the same mystery in the Psalm, after saying, “How terrible are your works, O Lord! In the multitude of your power your enemies shall lie to you. All the earth shall worship you and sing psalms to you; it shall sing a psalm to your name,” suddenly breaks out in this cry: “Come and see the works of God; terrible in counsels over the children of men.” In this, plainly, your works are terrible, O Lord: that those who were formerly your peculiar people, abandoned by the Spirit of truth and made your enemies, lied to you [Col. 1703D] (Ps. 80). Yet this did not harm you but advanced your honour: they lied, I say, amid the multitude of your power (Ps. 65), that is, amid your many miracles, saying, “By the prince of demons he casts out demons” (Luke 11), and, “His body was taken away by night by his disciples” (Matt. 28). And, in contrast to their lies: “All the earth shall worship you, O God” (Ps. 65). Let all nations speak truth to you, O God.

## Chapter II

On the secrecy of this same counsel of God: that it is discreetly hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones.

Therefore, invited by the cry of him who says, “Come and see the works of God; terrible in counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 65), we know how we must come: namely, with a submissive heart and humble spirit. For counsel, according to the custom of counsel, is communicated not indiscriminately to everyone but to particular persons, so that, with ear applied, they may perceive something of those things which God—terrible in his work over the children of men—has separately and secretly arranged, whether publicly done or yet to be done.

For the Angel of Counsel himself, who fulfilled and fulfils in action what was determined in that counsel, said: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them [Col. 1704C] to little ones” (Matt. 11). Why? Clearly because the wise and prudent who are wise in themselves and prudent in their own eyes are malicious, restless, and contentious, and are therefore incapable of being taught. We know well that no wise person admits malicious and contentious people to his counsel.

By contrast, little ones—that is, the humble—because they are humble readily acquiesce in the Lord their God, and in everything he says they offer goodwill joined with silence, considering it the greatest crime to interrupt or to criticize a better judgment, as it is written: “For resistance is like the sin of divination, and unwillingness to acquiesce is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). God therefore rationally hides his secrets from such wise and prudent persons, judging them no more worthy to receive his mysteries than swine are to receive pearls; but he reveals them to these others. Let us therefore conform ourselves to their littleness and desire to hear and understand what matters constitute the counsel of the Lord.

## Chapter III

That, according to the Scriptures, a twofold distinction must be made: God uses counsel in one way for human beings, while human beings use it in another way for God.

Here it is necessary to know that counsel, whose tenor or use we receive from Holy Scripture, must be distinguished in two ways; according to either distinction we truly call the Holy Spirit the Spirit of counsel. The first is that by which God himself deigns to employ counsel for human beings, unto his glory. The second is that by which human beings wisely employ counsel for God, unto his glory and their own salvation.

God uses counsel for human beings when, according to the requirements of the time, he abandons things formerly ordained, such as the former decrees of the Mosaic law—for example, circumcision of the flesh, Sabbath observance, and other such matters. For God formerly received these from human beings, and holy people rightly offered them to God; but now God receives them no longer from human beings, nor does any sensible or faithful person any longer offer them to God.

In due course, with his help and to the extent of our ability, we shall have to say how God both formerly admitted these things with counsel and nevertheless now rejects those same things with counsel. Human beings use counsel for God’s glory when, not content merely to abstain from unlawful things, they reject lawful things as well, so that they may attend to God more readily. For example, as the Apostle said: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment from the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has received mercy from God to be faithful. Therefore I judge this to be good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a human being to remain thus” (1 Cor. 7). Likewise: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. 19). We shall speak of this too in its proper place. Now let us approach the former and chief part: that by which the Jews are abandoned with their Sabbaths and all their ceremonies, and the Gentiles, with their faith, are wonderfully received into grace. [Col. 1705C]

## Chapter IV

On that greatest part of counsel by which the Jews, together with their ceremonies, were abandoned, and the Gentiles, with their faith, were received.

Just as you, says the Apostle, once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so these too have now not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all. Having said this, he cried out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable [Col. 1705D] his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. XII).

He cried out greatly, and that cry was heard throughout the whole world. And why did he cry out in this way? Why did he not rather continue what he had begun to say in plain speech? But what had he begun to say? That God, by this counsel or purpose, had shut up all in unbelief, that he might have mercy on all; and that this explains why formerly, when the Jews believed, we Gentiles did not believe, whereas now, when we believe, the Jews have not believed in our mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. This too is signified by a beautiful and venerable mystery in the Gospel narrative.

“There came,” it says, “one of the rulers of the synagogue, named Jairus; and seeing him, he fell at his feet, and [Col. 1706A] begged him earnestly, saying: ‘My daughter is at the point of death; come, lay your hand upon her, that she may be saved and live’” (Mark V), etc. This girl, when she died, was twelve years old (ibid.); and that woman who came up behind him as he went and touched the fringe of his garment had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years (ibid.). Thus, when this girl was born, that woman began to flow with her blood; and when that woman was healed of her flow of blood, this girl died, to be raised by the hand of the Lord.

By this mystery, I say, the event was signified. For when the Synagogue was born, or called, in Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, then the Gentile world began, as it were, to flow with its own blood amid the filth of idolatry. And when that same Gentile world was converted to Christ, then the Synagogue died with the death of unbelief; yet at the end of the age, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in, it too shall be saved. This is what the Apostle says in the passage cited above: “For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so these too have now not believed in your mercy, that they too may obtain mercy. For God has shut up all in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all.”

It is a great matter, a high and profound matter, greater than can sufficiently be grasped or explained in words. Therefore he immediately cried out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” By that very cry he wished to awaken those who sleep, so that, awake and opening our eyes to [Col. 1706C] the light of the Holy Spirit, we may seek, each according to our ability, that which is found by few and cannot be comprehended wholly, as it is, by anyone: why God has taken such pains to establish mercy in us, and has willed that no one be saved except through attaining mercy.

## CHAPTER V. On the same subject; and that nearly the whole force of the divine counsel tends to this end: that every occasion for pride may be removed from us, and that the thing fashioned may not dare say to him who fashioned it, “Why have you made me thus?”

What does it mean that God has shut up all in unbelief in order to have mercy on all, except that God has provided that no one may be saved otherwise than through mercy, [Col. 1706D] and that thus all may be delivered from the evil sword of pride? For this was fitting for our wretched condition: that every occasion for pride should be removed from us. For through pride an angel fell and became the devil; through pride likewise man, created in the image of God, fell and became the devil’s servant.

Therefore God, providing beforehand for the future and wishing to stop every mouth so that no flesh may glory before him (Rom. I), rejected the people who gloried in Abraham’s flesh—yet not his people whom he foreknew. For the Apostle says: “Has God rejected his people? By no means! For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew.” And after setting forth the divine reply, which says, “I have left for myself [Col. 1707A] seven thousand men who have not bent the knee before Baal,” he adds: “So then, at this present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI).

Let us say something further, something more wonderful, than what we were saying: that God, acting with counsel, rejected Israel glorying in Abraham’s flesh, because he permitted a people to be born from Abraham’s flesh such as he might justly reject and, according to the prophet, call “not my people” (Rom. IX)—that is, not belonging to that blessing by which, blessing the first human beings, he said, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I), but to that sentence of avenging wrath by which, after sin, he said to the woman: “I will multiply your afflictions and your conceptions” (Gen. III).

Did those who did not belong to the number of his people whom God foreknew and predestined first begin to be born from Abraham’s flesh only at the time when Christ came? Does not the same Apostle say: “When Rebecca had conceived by one intercourse with Isaac our father—when they had not yet been born or done anything good or evil, that the purpose according to the election of grace might remain, not by works but by him who calls—it was said: ‘The greater shall serve the lesser’; as it is written: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’” (Rom. IX)?

673 So soon after Abraham, from Abraham’s only-begotten son by Sarah, who had been born through promise (Gal. IV), from that same Abraham’s seed, so recent and so new, there was born one who did not belong to that people of his own which God foreknew (Rom. XI); and although that great man begot only two, he was by no means able to beget both chosen or beloved. [Col. 1707C]

Therefore it was not for the first time when Christ came that God adopted a new counsel, permitting persons to be born from Abraham’s flesh who did not belong to the number of the elect. Rather, this was his ancient counsel: a provision for the future, guarding his elect by every means against ever again falling into the devil’s judgment. But in this age that same counsel has been more fully revealed. For, conversely, he causes his people whom he foreknew to be born from every people, and raises up children of Abraham from these stones (Matt. III).

This counsel, I say, has been revealed. For although it cannot be comprehended, it cannot be wholly unknown, as the same Apostle says: “For I do not wish you to be ignorant, brethren, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own eyes: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI).

In both cases he makes use of his own power without injustice, as owing nothing to anyone, because in Adam we all sinned. If therefore you examine this irreverently, saying, “Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?”—because he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills—and if you would imply that no causes exist, the Holy Spirit deigns to reveal nothing to you of his counsel, but immediately says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing fashioned say to him who fashioned it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. IX). [Col. 1708A]

Thus, setting aside the wise and prudent, from whom these things are deservedly hidden because of pride, he bends down to the little one: “Wishing,” he says, “to show his wrath and make known his power, God endured with much patience vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction,” etc.

## CHAPTER VI. On the fact that, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles, “it was not counsel, nor did it seem good to the Holy Spirit, to impose upon the Gentiles the most burdensome yoke of the law’s ceremonies.”

Therefore, as the fullness of the Gentiles entered, or began to enter, it was not counsel; it did not please the Holy Spirit to impose the most burdensome yoke of the ceremonies that formerly belonged to the law, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “And certain persons coming down from Judaea taught [Col. 1708B] the brethren: ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved’” (Acts XV). Likewise: “Certain men of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed rose up and said: ‘They must be circumcised and commanded also to keep the law of Moses.’ And the apostles and elders assembled to consider this matter. When much disputation had arisen, Peter stood up and said to them: ‘Men and brethren, you know that in former days God chose among us that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the Gospel and believe. And God, who knows hearts, bore witness to them, giving them the Holy Spirit just as to us; and he made no distinction between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith’” (ibid.), etc.

The Holy Spirit was present at that assembly, and he himself, counselling us well, brought that great dispute to its conclusion. Therefore the same assembly splendidly expressed the authority of that Spirit in these words: “For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose upon you no further burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what is strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these things, you will do well. Farewell” (ibid.).

We have therefore been set free by the authority of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of counsel, so that that yoke should not be laid upon our necks. Why? Clearly because it was most burdensome, as Peter says in the same place: “Now therefore why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?” (ibid.).

Yet this would contribute little to the case—that the yoke was unbearable—unless you add what they likewise say: that it “brought nothing to perfection” [Col. 1708D] (Heb. VII), and what the Apostle says elsewhere: “Gifts and sacrifices that were offered could not make perfect, according to conscience, the one who performed the service, consisting only in foods and drinks and various washings and regulations of the flesh, imposed until the time of reformation” (Heb. IX).

But it is insufficient to know that they could not, or cannot, make perfect, unless you add also that no one can even have the beginning of perfection if he thinks that he can attain the perfection of righteousness without them. For concerning that which was then considered holiest of all—the sign of circumcision—Paul himself cries out terribly: “Stand firm, and do not again be held under a yoke of slavery. Behold, I Paul say to you: if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing. And I testify again to every man who has himself circumcised that he is bound to keep the whole law. You have been cut off from Christ, you who are justified in the law; you have fallen from grace” (Gal. V). [Col. 1709A]

We gladly concede, and firmly believe without hesitation, that Christ speaks in Paul and that the Holy Spirit spoke in the aforesaid assembly of the apostles. Indeed, the authority of the speaker in this case and in that alone suffices; nevertheless, since reason also gives delight, we shall not pass over a reasoned demonstration that the law of circumcision and of all ceremonies ought to have ceased with the coming of grace. And we shall speak first about circumcision, although elsewhere we have already spoken more fully of it.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 1709B] That, with the coming of the grace of the Gospel, the law of circumcision and of all carnal ceremonies ought reasonably to have ceased.

The basis of circumcision was faith in the seed to come, which is Christ. For what did Abraham believe, having no heir and a wife barren even into both her and his old age, except that in his seed all nations would be blessed, and that his seed would be as the stars of heaven? He believed God saying this, not considering his own body as dead when he was nearly a hundred years old, nor Sarah’s womb as dead; and he received circumcision as the sign of this faith. The Apostle confirms this very point: “He received the sign, the seal of the righteousness of faith” (Rom. IV).

Therefore the basis of circumcision was faith in the future seed, that is, Christ. For to be circumcised was to profess expectation of Christ to come. It served this end: that when Christ came, through the faith of which it was the sign, they might recover that possession of Paradise which we all lost in Adam—provided, however, that they kept the law of the commandments which the finger of God wrote on tablets. Thus the aforesaid Apostle says to the Jew of that time: “Circumcision indeed profits if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision” (Rom. II). [Col. 1709C]

But behold: the awaited seed, that is, Christ, has come; and every spirit that is of God confesses this, that he came in the flesh. No one, however stubbornly he may wish, can conceal this. For “he set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII), so that he cannot be hidden, just as the visible sun at the height of heaven cannot be concealed; for “the heavens also have declared,” and “there are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard; their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (ibid.).

Therefore circumcision in the flesh—the sign by which they professed expectation of the Coming One—ought to have ceased at his advent. For from that time onward, whoever is circumcised denies by the very mark of circumcision that promised seed of Abraham to have come, and thus denies him who came blessed in the name of the Lord (Matt. XXI), who was born of the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod (Matt. II), who suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, and was buried, and rose on the third day. Apart from him there is salvation in no other; “for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts V). [Col. 1710A]

Thus the Apostle most truly says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V), because whoever is circumcised has denied Christ. By circumcising themselves, the Jews deny him who came in his Father’s name; another will come in his own name, and him they will receive. Accordingly, following the authority of the Holy Spirit, who, as we said above, judged that no burden whatever should be imposed upon us—not even the burden of circumcision—we also maintain on rational grounds that we ought not to be circumcised.

## CHAPTER VIII. That the soul of the Lord hates the Sabbaths and the other Jewish feasts, as he says in prophecy, and that it was therefore right for the Holy Spirit to judge that they should not be imposed.

Moreover, concerning the burden of the Sabbath and other festivals, this cause alone sufficiently explains why it seemed good to the Holy Spirit that they should not be imposed upon us: the soul of the Lord had long since hated them with just hatred. Thus he says in Isaiah: “New moons and Sabbath and other festivals I will not endure. Your assemblies are iniquitous. Your calends and your solemnities my soul has hated; they have become burdensome to me.” Why? “For,” he says, “your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I).

Therefore, lest we too, together with those Sabbaths and solemnities, should incur the hatred of the soul of the Lord, it rightly seemed good to the Holy Spirit—and we approve his counsel—that we should reject such refuse, or ornaments, which were formerly gain, before they were defiled by the blood [Col. 1710C] of Christ, with which that assembly filled its wicked hands.

“But,” they say, “ought not that which God established to stand, and the command which he gave to remain unalterable?” We confess that it ought; for God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change (Num. XXIII). To this those friends of the letter reply: “It is written,” they say, “that God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made, and rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished. And he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased” (Gen. II). They therefore seek to constrain us to admit that their Sabbath ought to remain and always be lawful.

Yet meanwhile they cannot deny that the God of whom Moses relates this—that he blessed the seventh day and sanctified it—is the very one who says in Isaiah: “New moons and Sabbath and other festivals I will not endure. Your calends and your solemnities my soul has hated.” What then follows except that there are different Sabbaths: one pleasing to God, the other hateful to the soul of God? Clearly they must either admit this, or admit what they charged us with: that God, who is unchangeable, has changed and become contrary to himself.

But they do not dare say this, and they cannot bear to see that there are two Sabbaths: one carnal, which God imposed for a time, or until the time of reformation; and one spiritual, which he established forever and ever, whose command he also placed on tablets of stone and which shall not pass away (Ps. CXLVIII). Therefore they turn away and flee, having that affliction which was signified when they fled in fear from the unveiled brightness of Moses’ face (Exod. XXXIV). [Col. 1711A]

For whatever we set before them concerning the splendor of the Spirit burns and torments the eyes of an envious people; only the letter pleases them, especially wherever it can veil Christ’s glory. But just as we have learned from the law and the prophets that there are two Sabbaths, so we must know why he concealed the spiritual Sabbath from them under the figure of the carnal Sabbath, and why from us he requires one Sabbath only, and that a spiritual one.

## CHAPTER IX. That God had one arrangement with the Jews and another with us Gentiles; and that almost all their festivals had earthly causes.

Let us say, then, that God clearly had one arrangement with the Jews and another with us Gentiles. For when Christ, the Son of God, came into this world and invited us Gentiles to his faith, he did not set before us earthly rewards. He did not give lands we had not possessed; he gave nothing at all carnal, but set forth and bestowed wholly spiritual goods.

To them, who had no land of their own—indeed, who were enslaved in Egypt and, because of the sin by which they sold their brother Joseph, were unworthy to receive the promises made to their fathers—God gave a very good land, a localized land, an earthly place. He gave them, I say, the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labors of peoples (Ps. CIV). Nor were they such as could be drawn to righteousness by spiritual and invisible goods, or deterred from unrighteousness by spiritual and invisible evils. [Col. 1711C]

Therefore, throughout the law written for them as they departed Egypt, nowhere are promises of Paradise or threats of hell heard. Rather, there are beautiful and melodious promises of a most excellent land, a land flowing with milk and honey; and there are harsh and terrifying threats suited to the flesh—of wars, famine, evil beasts, and captivity (Deut. XXXVIII).

To us—indeed, both to us and to all whom the true Lamb of God redeemed by his blood and called to his faith—he has set before us only heavenly or spiritual goods. For he gave, or commanded those who follow him to await, not earth but heaven. Therefore he has shown that we owe him no carnal festivals, but only spiritual ones; no earthly Sabbaths, but only heavenly ones. The Holy Spirit, the Spirit of counsel, testifies to this: he counselled us well in that assembly of the apostles mentioned above (Acts XV).

Carnal festivals and carnal Sabbaths belonged to carnal Jews, to whom God, when the law was written, set before them carnal goods and earthly rewards for observing it. They aimed at the riches of this age, at possessions of fields and vineyards, and at all the resources of this world. Thus they were rightly instructed to look to the literal feast of the world’s creation and to keep Sabbath on the seventh day, because God rested on the seventh day, blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it.

They departed from Egypt at the full moon when the yoke of slavery had been broken; they were freed not from the slavery of sin but from that of a man, not from the devil but from the fleshly Pharaoh. Therefore it was fitting that the moon should be festive and solemn for them in tribute-like celebration, [Col. 1712A] because “they sounded the trumpet at the new moon” (Ps. LXXX), and this was reckoned among the notable days of their solemnity.

They lived in tents after being led out of that house of bondage; and therefore in the seventh month they had the great Feast of Tabernacles, dwelling in booths and, in that observance, recalling and celebrating benefits of God that were indeed great, but earthly and temporal. But, as has already been said, Christ’s Gospel has bestowed upon us nothing of this kind, but wholly heavenly goods. Therefore we owe to the Savior’s grace heavenly festivals and spiritual Sabbaths: he freed us from the spiritual Pharaoh, redeemed us from the slavery of sin, introduced us through his passion and cross into the land of the living, and granted us the estates of heaven. [Col. 1712B]

Therefore, because he has persuaded us to rejoice not in the figure of this world which passes away, but in the hope of the resurrection, of which he himself is the prince, we ought not, like lovers of the world who carnally imagine that God rested, to lie idle with them on the seventh day. Rather, on the first day—which is also the eighth—on which he rose for our hope and salvation, we should devote ourselves to prayer and to hearing the word of God, taking the utmost care that on that day and on all other days we may always rest from the servile work of sin.

## CHAPTER X. That, apart from the feast of Pentecost, all their festivals had earthly causes, whereas the grounds or promises of our Gospel are heavenly.

There was one festival of that people—one, I say, of the three greater solemnities—called Pentecost, that is, the Fiftieth Day. It is also called the Feast of Weeks, because, when the seventh week from the sacrifice of the lamb was completed, it was celebrated on the following day, which was the fiftieth. It must rightly be granted that this feast had a more sacred, more spiritual, and more divine basis.

For it was indeed a great benefit of God that he delivered that people from Pharaoh’s rule and brought them into the land concerning which he had sworn to their fathers. But the greatest and best benefit was that he made a covenant with them, to be their God, and gave them the law written by the finger of God on tablets. The other benefits were good, but earthly and passing; this was good and best, because everlasting.

Yet even in this good it shines less brightly and, in comparison with perfection, is somewhat obscure, because on that same mountain they professed not the life-giving Spirit, but only the killing letter of the written law. Nor did God there require, or ought he to have required, from them the profession of that Spirit, since he set before them not spiritual goods but only earthly ones, not the kingdom of heaven but the land of Canaan as the reward for entering the covenant or receiving the law. [Col. 1712D]

Therefore, as already said, the feast of Pentecost alone had, in some measure, the basis of a true good; all the others derived a more ignoble origin from earth and in every way testified that this people, childish in understanding, loved the world. Among the disciples of evangelical grace, it is wholly unlawful to rejoice or keep a feast on account of temporal successes. Since Christian discipline consists in despising present things and loving future things, and in lifting up our heads—that is, making our hearts glad—amid the breaking up of the world, how could it follow that we should accept Jewish festivals, which look only to the present joys of temporal goods?

Accordingly, confident in the aforesaid counsel of the Holy Spirit, who judged in that assembly of the apostles that none of these things should be imposed on us, we despise them as a yoke of slavery, since we are free and sons by adoption. As the Apostle says: “You have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII). Likewise: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a servant, though he is lord of all, but he is under guardians and stewards until the time appointed by his father; so we also, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of the world” (Gal. IV). And again, shortly afterward: “Stand firm, therefore, and do not again be held under a yoke of slavery” (Gal. V). [Col. 1713B]

## CHAPTER XI. That we ought much more not to serve the legal sacrifices, since God testifies through the prophets that he neither sought nor commanded them at any time.

What, then, shall we say concerning sacrifices and offerings, except what is true: that we ought much more not to serve them? For the tradition of circumcision and feast days was once venerable: God gave circumcision to Abraham and his seed, and Holy Scripture does not fail to say that he himself kept a kind of Sabbath-rest, saying that he rested on the seventh day (Gen. II).

But concerning the slaughtered flesh of bulls and the blood of goats and rams, what glory has there ever been, or could there be, among the wise, when God denies that these began by his will or command? For he speaks in Jeremiah: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat the flesh. For I did not speak with your fathers or command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this word I commanded them, saying: ‘Hear my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in every way that I command you, that it may be well with you’” (Jer. VII). [Col. 1713D]

God truly said this in that passage. For in Exodus it is written thus: “For the Lord spoke all these words: ‘I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. You shall have no strange gods before me,’” etc., as far as the words, “If you serve their gods, they will certainly be a snare to you” (Exod. XX, XXIII). But Moses built an altar at the foot of the mountain, sent young men from the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings—indeed, they sacrificed peace-offerings to the Lord, twelve calves (Exod. XXIV)—and it is not written that the Lord spoke or commanded this.

Likewise, in Isaiah the same Lord says: “I have not desired the burnt offering of rams, the fat of fatlings, and the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands?” (Isa. I). Further, in David, whom both prophetic grace and royal authority strengthened for speech, the same God rejects the same sacrifices: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.” And shortly afterwards: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. XLIX). [Col. 1714A]

Therefore those burnt offerings or sacrifices were not so much commanded as permitted; and consequently we more readily reject them, especially because it thus seemed good to the Holy Spirit, as we have already said above. Nor do we merely say or understand that the Holy Spirit removed them from us by counsel; indeed, we do not hesitate to say what is more: that God once permitted them to be offered to himself by such counsels, lest the carnal and unstable people, if wholly kept from the sacrifices customary in Egypt, should weep like a child deprived of every game under an excessively strict pedagogue, and should either flee back more quickly into Egypt or seek gods to whom they might lawfully offer the flesh to which they were accustomed.

But when we read in Moses that God made some disposition concerning such sacrifices, this does not contradict what he says in the prophets just quoted.
