For it is one thing to have required those things from their hands, and another to have regulated the rite of what they were accustomed to sacrifice, so that those who did not yet have, and could not have, the true priest or sacrifice might at least bear the shadow of it—a rite signifying what was to come. [Col. 1714C]

## CHAPTER XII. That the Holy Spirit rightly judged that we should not be troubled about such things, provided only that we abstain from pollutions, or things sacrificed to idols, and from fornication, strangled things, and blood.

Therefore, not wholly ignorant of the reason why it seemed good to the Holy Spirit to act thus, and why he forbade us circumcision and the carnal observance of Moses’ law, we embrace the liberal exception made by the apostles, who had been well counselled by him and counselled us well. They said and judged that those Gentiles who turn to the Lord should not be troubled, [Col. 1714D] and wrote to them that they should only abstain from pollutions—or, as it is written below, from things sacrificed to idols—from fornication, from strangled things, and from blood (Acts XV).

This was said and written concerning that part of the question which had been proposed in these words: “They must be circumcised,” or, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (ibid.). But concerning the other part that had been raised, as it is written—“and they must also be commanded to keep the law of Moses”—they judged it unnecessary to decide or write. “For Moses,” they say, “from ancient times has in every city those who preach him in the synagogues, where he is read every Sabbath” (ibid.).

It is as though they said: “Concerning circumcision, which was given before Moses to our fathers, let us necessarily judge and write. For once this has been rightly judged, rightly perceived, or demonstrated—what true circumcision is—it will be evident to them how they should observe the law of Moses given later.” Directing their attention to true Judaism and perfect circumcision, which exists not outwardly, or in the flesh, but in the spirit, they say: “Let them abstain from pollutions of idols, from fornication, from strangled things, and from blood.” [Col. 1715A]

Those who say this plainly affirm that circumcision in the flesh was a sign not only of the righteousness of faith, as the Apostle Paul says (Rom. IV), but also of moral righteousness. Before the promised seed came—that is, Christ—it was necessary, as we said above, to be circumcised in flesh, so that by the sign of the seed to come they might profess their faith; yet they were also not to lack circumcision in the spirit. That is, they were neither spiritually to commit fornication away from God, nor carnally to commit fornication in their bodies, according to the Apostle already cited: “Circumcision,” he says, “profits if you keep the law” (Rom. II).

It is as if he said: Circumcision, the sign of chastity and faith, profits only if you do not commit fornication—the fornication of a spirit departing from God, or the fornication of a body corrupting flesh. But when that seed came, we are circumcised, and ought to be circumcised, only in the spirit: that is, to abstain from fornications; for “circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments” (I Cor. VII). [Col. 1715B]

Therefore, preaching and prescribing the true circumcision, without which we truly cannot be saved, they rightly judged that we must abstain from things sacrificed to idols. This is to be circumcised in spirit: namely, that our soul, joined to the true God by faith, may no longer commit fornication after idols. Likewise, we must abstain from fornication of the flesh, by which the body is corrupted and is deservedly judged, as it were, uncircumcised and unclean.

The cause of both kinds of fornication, or uncircumcision, is usually excessive and filthy greediness. With this in view, they say: “from strangled things and blood.” To drink blood is plainly an abomination of excessive greediness and most filthy gluttony. Likewise, to strangle cattle for eating is the practice of beasts and wild animals, which the madness of the belly drives disorderly and irrationally to attack and devour.

Thus they concisely but pointedly circumcised gluttony, or the greediness of the belly—from which both fornications are usually born—as it is written: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. XXXII; I Cor. X), by saying, “from strangled things and blood”: that is, from every shameful and disordered manner of devouring. [Col. 1715D]

## CHAPTER XIII. With what severity, elsewhere in each of their writings, they denounce fornication and things sacrificed to idols.

Gently, indeed, and in a spirit of meekness, did this saying or writing proceed from that counsel of the Holy Spirit—or from that Holy Spirit of counsel—that we should not commit fornication and should abstain from things sacrificed to idols. Yet for those who do not obey this meekness, the rod is ready. For one apostle from that assembly, distinguished for charity and meekness, says: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, nor give him greeting. For whoever gives him greeting shares in his evil works” (2 John 10–11).

Likewise, after another had said, “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity and a spirit of meekness?” (1 Cor. 4), immediately, because the matter required it, drawing forth the rod, he says: “It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles: that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that he who has done this deed might be removed from among you.” Having first delivered this rebuke, he immediately strikes by speaking, and speaks by striking: “Though absent in body, yet present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, him who has so acted, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you and my spirit are gathered together with the power of the Lord Jesus, to hand such a one over to Satan” (1 Cor. 5).

And, sufficiently indicating that this very blow of the rod proceeds not from fury but from counsel, he immediately added after “to hand such a one over to Satan”: “for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.). For this too belongs to the ancient counsel of Wisdom, which says: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (Prov. 23). Wishing by the example of his own chastisement to show the severity of discipline to be holy, he says: “I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators.” Explaining what he had said and specifying of which fornicators he had written, he immediately says [Col. 1716C]: “Not at all the fornicators of this world; but if anyone called a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber—with such a person, do not even take food” (1 Cor. 5).

Therefore, what was so gently said or written in that assembly, in that counsel of the Holy Spirit, is not to be taken lightly. For not only those who commit such acts, but also those among whom they have been committed, are struck by the apostolic rod if they do not separate themselves, if they too do not mourn, and do not subject fornicators to most severe penance. Concerning fornication, indeed, there is one and the same judgment among all: because it defiles, it can by no means be admitted along with a clean conscience.

But a diversity of judgments regarding things sacrificed to idols had raised a question for the same Apostle, so that he said: “We know that an idol is nothing in the world” (1 Cor. 8). Again: “We know that we all have knowledge. But knowledge puffs up, whereas charity builds up” (ibid.). And again, after much else: “What then? Do I say that what is sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? But the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Cor. 10). Finally, decisively settling that same question or dispute, he says: “If one of the unbelievers invites you and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question for conscience’ sake. But if anyone says, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat, for the sake of the one who informed you and for conscience’ sake. Now I mean not your conscience, but the other’s” (ibid.) [Col. 1717A]—namely, lest he be led into error. For although your conscience is free from devotion to the idol, you must nevertheless take care lest another suppose that you eat food sacrificed to idols for the sake of veneration.

For this was his concern, and in order to instruct them in this caution he had said above: “For if anyone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be emboldened to eat things sacrificed to idols? And through your knowledge shall the weak brother perish, for whom Christ died?” (1 Cor. 8). Immediately afterward, offering sound and salutary counsel, quite temperately, with his own example, he says: “Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat flesh, lest I cause my brother to stumble” (ibid.).

## Chapter XIV. [Col. 1717B] How Peter, as though by counsel, indicated or feigned that Jewish ceremonies ought to be observed; how Paul, by truer counsel, opposed him to his face; and yet how Paul was not contrary to himself when he circumcised Timothy and, purified according to Jewish custom, entered the Temple with offerings.

Meanwhile, while this counsel of the Holy Spirit—that the Jewish ceremonies of the dead, themselves dead, should not be observed—had only recently become known, devout men, namely the apostles, endeavoured to join or intermingle their own counsel with that same counsel of God. So far did this go that Peter, who before the others, or on behalf of all of them, had spoken the things stated above (Acts 15), was led into dissimulation, not daring openly in deed to follow what he had himself said had seemed good to the Holy Spirit.

But the same Spirit of counsel rebuked him through the mouth of another: through the humble strength and strong humility of the novice apostle, Paul, the least of the apostles. Thus he himself writes to the Galatians: “But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he was blameworthy. For before certain persons came from James, he ate with the Gentiles; but when they came, he withdrew and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision. And the rest of the Jews joined with him in his dissimulation, so that even Barnabas was carried away by them into the same dissimulation. But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Cephas before them all: ‘If you, though a Jew, live in Gentile fashion and not Jewish fashion, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?’” [Col. 1717D] (Gal. 2).

Thus the last of the apostles opposed the prince of the apostles to his face, using great freedom of the Spirit of the Lord, to confirm that counsel of the same Spirit of which I have hitherto been speaking. Yet he himself also circumcised Timothy—“because of the Jews,” Scripture says, “who were in those places; for they all knew that his father was a Gentile” (Acts 16). Likewise, after taking the men for whom he had incurred expense, so that they might shave their heads, on the following day he was purified with them and entered the Temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification until an offering should be made for each of them (Acts 21).

Did he then himself do what he rebuked in Peter? Or ought he to have rebuked in a greater man what he himself would do? Certainly not. He neither did what he rebuked in Peter, for he did not compel the Gentiles to Judaize—the sole, or at least principal, thing he rebuked in Peter. For he said: “If you, though a Jew, live in Gentile fashion and not Jewish fashion, how do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. 2). He did not compel Gentiles to Judaize; rather, in his own person he endured Judaism for the sake of necessity, becoming “as a Jew to the Jews, in order that he might gain the Jews” (1 Cor. 9). Indeed, as he testifies elsewhere, he wished himself to be anathema from Christ for these same brethren of his (Rom. 9).

He did not, I say, compel the Gentiles to Judaize, which was what he rebuked when it was done in Peter. For those who had said to him, “We have four men who have a vow upon them; take these men, purify yourself with them,” and so forth, immediately added: “But concerning those from among the Gentiles who have believed, we have written our judgment that they should abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and blood, and what is strangled, and fornication” [Col. 1718B] (Acts 21). Therefore his rebuke, by which he censured Peter’s dissimulation and thus contributed greatly to confirming God’s counsel, was true and just.

## Chapter XV. On the destruction of Jerusalem, the overthrow of the Temple, and the dispersion of the Jews, and how these were accomplished by God’s counsel.

But how slight was that confirmation in comparison with the greater one! For a greater and more extensive confirmation followed. What was it? The destruction of the wretched city; the overthrow and burning of the most august Temple; a destruction of city and Temple so great and so ruinous that “there should not be left one stone upon another which should not be destroyed” (Luke 21); such a disaster for the whole country and slaughter of the entire nation that they should “fall by the edge of the sword and be led captive into all nations.”

Let whoever wishes read Josephus’s account of the pitiable tragedy of that destruction, and he will be able to know that the pride of Jewish glory fell through no author but God, in order to confirm and uphold the grace of evangelical humility. For if that city had continued in its former glory, if that nation had been allowed to persist in its Temple with its customary sacrifices, how great, do you suppose, would have been the scandal to those believing in Christ?

Therefore, just as it is truly said, “They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark 16), so we too may, with a slight alteration concerning a related matter—or rather the greater part of the same matter—say without hesitation [Col. 1718D]: Truly it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and the apostles contributed the true counsel of the Holy Spirit for the consolation of the Gentiles, with the Lord Jesus and that same Spirit cooperating and confirming the counsel, while the destruction of the city and Temple and the dispersion of the Jews followed.

For this too truly pertains to the same counsel: not all the Jews perished from Roman famine and sword in that famous siege and dreadful destruction. Some survived, and as captives among all nations, through that same captivity or dispersion, bore throughout the whole world a splendid testimony to evangelical truth, according to the verse of Psalm 58: “God showed me concerning my enemies: do not slay them, lest my peoples ever forget; scatter them in your power” [Col. 1719A].

For Christ prays that psalm; in that psalm Christ speaks—the true David, that is, “strong of hand” or “beloved”—whom Saul, that is, that envious people, pursued even to death, according to the title of the same psalm: “For the end: Do not destroy; to David himself, for an inscription of the title, when Saul sent to guard his house in order to kill him.”

And the sense of the aforesaid verse is this: God showed me, as I considered my Jewish enemies, that I should pray for them thus: “Lord, do not slay them,” that is, do not utterly root them out from the earth. Why? Namely, lest peoples converted to confession should ever forget me: that I was born and given over to suffering for them, and thus redeemed them. This is the same as saying: Therefore let the Jews be permitted to live by your grace, so that the faith of my people may be made more certain even through their testimony. Otherwise, the Psalms and the whole Old Testament would appear to many as fictions.

“Do not therefore slay them.” But what then? “Scatter them”—understood, throughout all lands—“in your power,” that is, in your might. It should therefore be noted that the dispersion of the Jews occurred by the dispensation of divine counsel, so that they might confirm the faith of the Gentiles not only in one place but throughout every land: while they asserted that he had been crucified by their ancestors and did not deny that they possessed the Scriptures in which he had been promised to us; indeed, like our book-carriers, they carried those same Scriptures about for our use.

## Chapter XVI. [Col. 1719C] That for us to employ counsel for God’s sake is to do something beyond what he has commanded; and that those who do not do so rightly say: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.”

We have said briefly, in praise of the Spirit of counsel, that God deigned to employ counsel for the sake of human beings. It remains, according to our purpose, to say how lovers of perfection do, or ought to, employ counsel for God’s sake. To employ counsel, we say, is this: not being content to do what is commanded, they extend themselves beyond it to that which is greater and more ample than the commandment. Such conduct plainly has greater grace and a more abundant reward.

For the mere fulfilment of a command belongs to servants [Col. 1719D] and merits no great favour, according to that evangelical saying of the Lord: “Does he thank that servant because he did what he commanded him? I think not. So you also, when you have done all that is commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17).

What sort of servant was he contemplating when he said, “Does he thank that servant because he did what he commanded him?” Clearly, a servant ploughing or feeding, to whom, after returning from the field, his master would not immediately say, “Come, recline at table,” but rather, “Prepare something for me to eat; gird yourself and serve me until I eat and drink; and afterward you shall eat and drink” (ibid.). That servant was certainly the Jewish people, which had received the spirit of servitude in fear, ploughing in the field and feeding—that is, occupied with marriage—and, before itself eating or drinking, preparing for its Lord what he might eat: namely, giving tithes of everything and offering firstfruits as the Law commanded.

“Does he then thank that servant,” he says, “because he did what he commanded him? I think not.” For the servant was a debtor: he had received the command as a servant, as a tenant of land which his Lord had acquired, as he says: “The land is mine, and you are my tenants” (Lev. 25). Therefore, having employed this comparison, he immediately added: “So you also, when you have done all that is commanded you”—understood, and no more—“say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.’”

When, he says, you have done everything commanded you and nothing more, O disciples of this age and hearers of the Gospel—if you remain in the field, that is, in the world, devoted or bound to marriage, selling and buying, possessing and using this world—then, however much you do the commandments, by not committing adultery, not stealing, and not doing such things, you have indeed escaped punishment, but have not yet merited grace. For you are unprofitable, because you are unwilling to add anything beyond the debt of servitude for love or favour of our Lord. You plainly testify that, unless you feared torture and fetters, you would not even do what is commanded.

Therefore, as we began to say, to employ counsel for God’s sake belongs to friends: those who, not content to do what is commanded, extend themselves to another thing greater and more ample than the commandment, loving the grace of their Lord and preferring before all goods to see the cheerful and serene face of their Lord [Col. 1720C].

There are ten commandments, which a truer translation has distinguished thus: “You shall have no strange gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above, or in earth below, or of those things that are in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not worship or serve them. You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. Honour your father and your mother. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbour. You shall not covet” (Exod. 20).

Now we shall speak, as far as we are able, concerning the tenor of each commandment and the liberality of counsel to be added above it.

## Chapter XVII. [Col. 1720D] On the first commandment and the counsel to be added above it.

“You shall not,” he says, “have strange gods before me” (Exod. 20). According to this commandment, the whole righteousness of a servant is not to have worshipped Baal or served Astaroth, not to have been initiated into Beelphegor, or into anyone of that kind contrary to the true divinity, and not to have set such a thing in God’s Temple.

But one who desires to surpass the servile condition attends not only to the signification of these words, “strange gods,” but also to the etymology of the name “God,” so that he may not merely, according to the commandment, have no strange gods before his God, but may fear no one besides the one true God. For in Greek God is called *Theos*, which is interpreted “fear.” The Creator is called by such a name because he is to be feared; and it is rightly required of every rational creature that he be feared.

Therefore counsel beyond this commandment is accepted when the good servant, worthy of love or favour, sets before himself God alone as the one to be feared, judging no other God or Lord worthy of his fear. Even if compelled by the punishment of death to fear another, he is not turned from righteousness, remaining steadfast for the sake of the true God and Lord, by reason of friendship. Thus he speaks to his own: “But I say to you, my friends: do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after this have nothing further that they can do. Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I say to you, fear him” [Col. 1721A] (Luke 12).

## Chapter XVIII. [Col. 1721B] On the second commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“You shall not make a carved image, nor any likeness that is in heaven above or in earth below, nor of those things that are in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not worship or serve them” (Exod. 20). By this commandment the servant is required to believe that there exists no likeness, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the sea, of that one and only God before whom he must have no strange gods.

This, I say, is required of him: that he know that the true God is not circumscribed by any form. Yet those who thought him human-shaped said that God, like a human being, was circumscribed or bounded in his members according to human shape, painting for themselves in their minds a great idol; or, according to Daniel’s vision, a venerable old man, the Ancient of Days (Dan. 7). How great, do you suppose, was the image imagined in their heart or error when they heard him say: “Heaven is my throne, and earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66)? If they were asked concerning what is written, “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighed the heavens with his palm?” (Isa. 40), what, in keeping with the same fantasy, could they answer or paint anew in their minds?

Therefore, as has been said, the servant is required by the commandment to confess that God is without place and uncircumscribed, and to suppose that no creature is or can become like God, lest he experience against himself the saying which follows: “For I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquities of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” [Col. 1721D] (Exod. 20), and so forth.

For whoever has painted such an idol for himself stores up great wrath from the strong and jealous God, since he consequently thinks wrongly concerning the Son of God—as, for example, Arius did. Unable to bear that the Son of God, God, should be called or believed consubstantial with the Father, he said, looking to the likeness of a creature and wishing the uncreated Creator to be similar to a creature: “Consubstantial means what is from something else—either by participation, by derivation, or by planting. By planting, as a shoot from a root; by derivation, as branches; by participation, as two or three rings from a mass of gold. But in none of these ways,” he says, “is the Son of God.” Therefore he said that one ought not assent to the faith of consubstantiality.

Lest the servant receive a grievous blow along with this man, he must make no creature like the Creator. But if he wishes to be a friend, after this commandment he also extends his whole mind toward counsel: that, not content merely not to think such things about God, he should strive, as far as he can, for the salvation of others, showing by sound doctrine that “consubstantial” is not said according to bodily passions, division, or some cutting-off; for an intelligible and incorporeal nature cannot undergo a bodily passion. Rather, it must be understood in certain sacred and ineffable ways.

## Chapter XIX. [Col. 1722B] On the third commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” (Exod. 20). The servant necessarily hears and obeys this if he does not wish to be cruelly tortured by servile stripes or destroyed. For what is it to take the name of the Lord one’s God in vain, except to swear falsely by the name of the Lord one’s God, or to parade before trivial or playful matters that name revered by heaven and earth?

Therefore, not to take the name of the Lord God in vain is a necessary and lawful commandment. The servant who keeps it escapes punishment, so far as can be understood under this meaning. “For the Lord will not hold guiltless him who takes the name of the Lord God in vain” (ibid.). But if he desires the freedom of a friend, the counsel is never to swear at all. For the Lord and Angel of Great Counsel says in his Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not swear falsely; but you shall fulfil your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you: do not swear at all, neither by heaven, for it is God’s throne; nor by earth, for it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great king. Nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. But let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes’; ‘No, no.’ What is beyond these is from evil” [Col. 1722C] (Matt. 5).

We are compelled to acknowledge that this is not a commandment, but that what is above the commandment—namely, counsel drawn from it—is so, because we do not think that the holy, just, and good Law is contrary to the Gospel, or the Gospel to the Law; rather, we avoid even suspecting this as sacrilege.

For the Law said: “If someone entrusts money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping, and these are stolen from the one who received them, if the thief is found, he shall repay double. If the master of the house does not know, he shall be brought before the gods and shall swear that he has not put his hand to his neighbour’s property in order to commit fraud” (Exod. 22). Again: “If someone entrusts to his neighbour for safekeeping a donkey, ox, sheep, or any beast of burden, and it dies, is injured, or is taken by enemies, and no one sees it, an oath shall be between them that he has not put his hand to his neighbour’s property; the owner shall accept the oath, and the other shall not be compelled to make restitution” (ibid.).

Therefore, since we have begun to discuss commandment and counsel, and since we must by every means take care not to suppose the Gospel contrary to the Law, this third matter has presented itself to us as permitted. Let us carefully weigh these three statements: “You shall not swear falsely”; “Do not swear at all”; and “he shall be brought before the gods and shall swear,” or “an oath shall be between them that he has not put his hand to his neighbour’s property.” We shall find that not swearing falsely is a commandment; never swearing is counsel; and swearing, or making a truthful oath, is permitted.

Accordingly, one who swears falsely does evil; but one who never swears does good, choosing rather to repay what he had received on loan and which was later taken away than to offer an oath, because of the saying, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. 5; Col. 4). But one who swears and makes a truthful oath does neither good nor evil: that is, he gains neither punishment because he swore nor grace because he swore truthfully [Col. 1723B]. To summarize briefly the distinctions among these three: one who swears falsely merits punishment; one who swears truthfully merits pardon; one who does not swear at all merits grace and glory.

## Chapter XX. On the fourth commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20). This commandment is lawful, and it is lawfully kept in this: that when the servant works well, he seeks not his own glory but the glory of his Lord; that he does not seek present praise for himself from the lips of his fellow-servants or propose to establish vain glory for his own name, but attends to the Scripture saying: “Let them see your good works, not that you may be seen, but that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” [Col. 1723C] (Matt. 5).

This is truly to remember the sanctifying of the Sabbath: that the servant should aim, by working well, to merit entry into the rest of his Lord. But to remember that Sabbath which the Jew remembers even today we no longer hold to be according to the commandment; indeed, we confess it to be against the commandment and against the Lord’s will. For that Sabbath was polluted, from that great Sabbath day on which they crucified the Lord, by wicked servants with the blood of their Lord; and, as we have already said elsewhere, Isaiah testifies that from then onward the Lord’s soul hates with profound hatred every Sabbath and every feast of theirs (Isa. 1).

This, then, is the commandment: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day”—that is, in working well, place the whole end of your work where rest is holy and true. But the counsel is that you should even now keep Sabbath: that is, passing beyond the active life, you should devote yourself to contemplation. This part is so much better as the sweet friendship of a faithful servant excels, as he himself testifies when he says: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things. But one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” [Col. 1723D] (Luke 10).

He did not condemn Martha’s service, but preferred Mary’s part, as what is best to what is good. Inviting the more perfect to this Sabbath-rest also in the Psalm, he says: “Be still, and see that I am God” (Ps. 45). If he had said this as a commandment rather than as counsel, it would follow that no one who failed to do it could be loved by the Lord. But now it is written: “Jesus, looking upon him, loved him.” Whom? Clearly, the rich young man, to whom he immediately said: “One thing is lacking to you: go, sell whatever you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me.” Saddened by the word, he went away grieving, for he had many possessions (Mark 10).

Therefore it is not a commandment but counsel, for which reason Matthew records it as stated conditionally and left to his choice or will: “If you wish to be perfect” (Matt. 19). For if he does not wish to aspire to this perfection, he does not indeed deserve to be loved as a friend or son—as is one who accepts the counsel—but he is nevertheless loved in his own rank as a faithful servant who, while rightly using the world in action, has fulfilled the commandment [Col. 1724B].

## Chapter XXI. On the fifth commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. 20). This is a great commandment, worthy of great observance and of recompense with a great and beautiful reward. The saying immediately sets this reward before the attentive hearer: “that you may be long-lived upon the land which the Lord your God will give you” (ibid.).

Above this commandment there is a greater and more excellent counsel: not to have father or mother for God’s sake. The majesty of the Gospel openly proclaims this counsel; but neither has the humility of the Law wholly kept silent about it. For it says: “He who said to his father and his mother, ‘I do not know you,’ and to his brethren, ‘I am ignorant of you,’ and who did not know his sons—these kept your word and observed your covenant, your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel” [Col. 1724C] (Deut. 33).

But the Pharisees, adulterating the pure truth of good counsel, taught children to dishonour father and mother by plundering their parents’ property. They taught that it was lawful for each child to say to father and mother, “I do not know you,” and, against their will, to heap the altar of God with gifts and fill the treasury—something that benefited their own greed.

He rebuked such hypocrites, who peddled the counsel of the holy Law—that is, corrupted it as though mixing good wine with water—when he said: “Why do you also transgress God’s commandment for the sake of your tradition? For God said: ‘Honour father and mother’; and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall die the death.’ But you say: ‘Whoever says to father or mother, “Whatever gift is from me will profit you”’”—understood: he has honoured the true Father, God, and his true mother, the priestly and Levitical synagogue; and so, by bringing the plunder of father and mother into the Lord’s house for you, he has dishonoured his father and mother and deprived them of their due honour. Therefore he immediately adds: “And he has not honoured his father and mother. And you have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition” [Col. 1724D] (Matt. 15).

Therefore the commandment is to honour father and mother; but the counsel is not to know father and mother—not in the contrary way by which father and mother are dishonoured, but in a reasonable and just way, by which God, surpassing all affections, is rightly preferred to father and mother. Parents are not dishonoured where the Creator alone is preferred before them.

God himself shows by his own example how this is done, having deigned to have human parents. For while he was speaking to the crowds, when someone said to him, “Behold, your mother and your brethren stand outside, seeking to speak with you,” he replied: “Who is my mother, and who are my brethren?” Stretching out his hand toward the disciples, he said: “Behold my mother and my brethren” (Matt. 12), and so forth. For in saying this he was proclaiming the Gospel, about to command that the lover of perfection should leave father and mother for the Gospel’s sake and renounce all that he possesses.

To do this is counsel, as we have already said; but when time or circumstance requires it, it must be carried out as a commandment owing by duty. Thus father or mother must be disregarded when one cannot both obey father and mother and be a Christian [Col. 1725B]. For in such a case he speaks not so much by counsel as by an authoritative commandment: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon earth. I came not to bring peace, but a sword. For I came to separate a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies are those of his own household. Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10).

It should be noted that, though he named the other relations—son against father, daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law—he did not say husband against wife or wife against husband, lest evangelical purity appear to provide an occasion or authorization for adulteries. Hence the Apostle says: “To those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife should not depart from her husband. But if she departs, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And the husband should not put away his wife” (1 Cor. 7).

But he immediately goes on: “To the rest I say, not the Lord.” To what “rest”? Clearly, to believers joined with unbelievers. What does “I say, not the Lord” mean? “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him”—understood, without detracting from the Christian name—“let him not put her away. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put away her husband” (ibid.). Therefore this is not so much the Lord’s commandment as the Apostle’s counsel. “For this,” he says, “I say, not the Lord.”

Moreover, that it is counsel is clear from what follows: “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for the brother or sister is not subject to servitude in such cases” [Col. 1725D] (ibid.). He certainly would not have said this if remaining together, believer with unbeliever, had been the Lord’s commandment.

But to return to the point: not to know unbelieving parents is a commandment; not to know believing parents out of love for perfection is counsel; but sometimes to know them is permitted. For the Law says: “If a woman knows anything and binds herself by an oath, while she is in her father’s house and still of youthful age, and her father learns of the vow she has promised and the oath by which she has bound her soul, and remains silent, she shall be bound by her vow. Whatever she has promised or sworn, she shall fulfil in deed. But if, as soon as he hears it, her father objects, both her vows and her oaths shall be void, and she shall not be held liable for her promise, because her father objected” (Num. 30).

Thus it is permitted to regard a vow as void because of the father’s objection. For we judge it better, even when the father objects, to maintain one’s purpose and strive toward perfection—especially since, if she treats what she vowed as void because her father objected, she can hope for no other reward than that she shall not be bound by her promise [Col. 1726A].

## Chapter XXII. On the sixth commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“You shall not kill” (Exod. 20). The commandment needs an implied qualification, so that a judge or governing authority that bears the sword may not be thought a transgressor when it kills one who was lawfully to be killed, nor the kinsman of the slain when he exacts vengeance by permission of the Law.

Therefore, when it is said, “You shall not kill,” one must understand: by taking up a sword not given to you. For the Lord Christ says: “All who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26), namely that sword of which the Psalmist says: “Deliver me from the evil sword” (Ps. 143).

But beyond this commandment is the counsel of perfection: “Do not resist evil.” “But if anyone,” he says, “strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5). Again: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke 6).

For the saying, “You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy” (Lev. 19), and likewise, “An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. 21), is neither commandment nor counsel but merely permitted. But true and genuinely Christian innocence so abhors blood that it receives and proclaims not resisting evil and even loving one’s enemy as a commandment.

## Chapter XXIII. On the seventh commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20). The permission of the Law had formerly made this commandment more lax; now the severity of the Gospel binds it more strongly and more strictly. For Moses commanded that a bill of divorce be given (Deut. 24). But Christ says: “I say to you that whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery; and he who marries a dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). And when they asked, “Why then did Moses command that a bill of divorce be given?” he said: “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses permitted you to dismiss your wives. But from the beginning it was not so” (Matt. 19). Therefore, it is a commandment not to commit adultery; but the counsel above this commandment is to abstain altogether from marriage, as when the disciples, speaking of the difficulty or exigency of marriage, said: “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” He replied: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given.” And immediately after saying: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven,” he added: “He who is able to receive it, let him receive it” (ibid.). Knowing this, the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful” (1 Cor. 7).

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the eighth commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“You shall not steal” (Exod. 20). In accordance with this commandment, after the Apostle had said, “Let him who stole steal no longer,” he immediately added the counsel: “Rather, let him labour, working with his own hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need” (Eph. 4). Yet this counsel differs little from the force of the commandment. For when he says, “Let him labour, working with his hands what is good,” he intends this to be understood: if he wishes to eat. For elsewhere he says: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3). Likewise, in saying, “Let him give to one suffering need,” he intends this to be understood: if he wishes also to be helped in his own necessities. For “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

Truly great and useful in practice is this counsel of mercy. When it has been bestowed upon those near at hand, it extends even to strangers, and, what is greater, even to enemies, according to the saying of the Wise Man: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (Prov. 25). For when he has done this, it is certain that he will obtain mercy. For if one who has mercy upon the poor lends to the Lord, how much more does one who feeds his enemy and gives him drink, and thus overcomes evil with good.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the ninth commandment and the addition of counsel above it.

“You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbour” [Col. 1727C] (Exod. 20). Above this commandment it is great and praiseworthy, according to the time and circumstance, to endure falsehood when one can refute the testimony, following the example of our Lord. “At last two false witnesses came and said: ‘This man said, I can destroy the temple of God and rebuild it after three days.’ When they said these things, and the chief priest also rose and pressed him, saying, ‘Do you answer nothing to these things which these men testify against you?’ Jesus,” says the Evangelist, “was silent” (Matt. 26). Likewise, when he was accused by the chief priests and elders, and Pilate urged him, saying, “Do you not hear how many testimonies they bring against you?” he answered him not a word, so that the governor marvelled greatly (Matt. 27). Why? Because, he says, “If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I ask you, you will not answer me, nor let me go” (Luke 22).

Therefore, whoever approves this example of enduring the rashness of false testimony should also approve the consideration underlying it: namely, that if there is hope that falsehood can be corrected by a true answer, he should answer, and by answering gain over the souls of those speaking against him—if not all of them, at least some among those who heard—lest they should be brought to shed blood, not knowingly or deliberately, but through false testimony. Thus Jeremiah, when priests and prophets testified against him before the princes and all the people, saying: “This man deserves the judgment of death, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your ears,” did not remain silent, but said: “The Lord sent me to prophesy” [Col. 1728A] (Jer. 26). And shortly thereafter: “Yet know and understand that, if you kill me, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its inhabitants. For in truth the Lord sent me” (ibid.).

On the other hand, Naboth the Jezreelite, because he was accused—or judged—not through error or a sudden disturbance of mind, but through the malicious deliberation of Jezebel and the nobles, or elders, with wicked men introduced as witnesses, is read to have remained silent and answered nothing; and rightly and wisely so (3 Kings [1 Kings] 21). For he would have poured out speech in vain where there was no hearing. Thus, whoever not only keeps the commandment, so as not to speak false testimony, but also approves the counsel, so as to embrace patience when attacked by false testimony, should know, from the Lord’s example, when to remain silent: lest by his silence he permit those who might perhaps sin through error against his own blood to be deceived.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the tenth commandment, the addition of counsel above it, and how difficult it is to add anything to this commandment.

“You shall not covet your neighbour’s house; nor shall you desire his wife, his servant, his maidservant, his ox, his ass, or anything that is his” (Exod. 20). By this tenth commandment, as by a certain iron axe, the root of all transgressions is cut off or uprooted: for “the root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. 6). And it should be noted that all covetousness is struck by seven, as it were, blows—by a number which commonly signifies universality—while it is restrained by a sevenfold prohibition. For although it might have sufficed to say, “You shall not covet,” even if nothing had been added, he preferred to make the prohibition sevenfold. First: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s house”; second: “You shall not desire his wife”; third: “his servant”; fourth: “his maidservant”; fifth: “his ox”; sixth: “his ass”; seventh: “or anything that is his.”

Therefore, love of all things that are in the world is condemned, because, as the Apostle John says, “All that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). Whoever has in his will the intention to commit adultery, steal, or perpetrate any such transgression is already then convicted as a transgressor of this commandment, even if he cannot carry that will into effect.

And what shall we say about adding counsel above it, when scarcely anyone—or almost no one—is found perfect in fulfilling this commandment? “Who shall boast that he has a chaste heart?” (Prov. 20). I boldly say that there are, or have been, more who have embraced the counsel than who have perfectly fulfilled the commandment. For we do not doubt that more—that is, at least some—have said, or can say: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1); but no one, or the rarest person, can boast that he has a chaste heart. Let it therefore suffice to say this: the commandment is not to covet; the counsel is to desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Col. 1729A] How truly Truth said: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it.”

Truth therefore spoke truly; Christ spoke as truly as he spoke weightily: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish, but to fulfil” (Matt. 5). Truly, I say, he uttered a word weighed with mature gravity, being aware in himself of this Holy Spirit, the Spirit of counsel, whom he was about to give; through him, as we have said—and far better and more abundantly than we have been able to express—he was to fulfil the Law.

But to whom, and why, did he say this and speak in this way? He spoke, certainly, to his disciples who were present, believing and rejoicing that Christ—or, in their own language, Messiah—had come and that this man was he; and he spoke to his adversaries, the scribes and Pharisees, who would soon hear it and would lay snares and fabricate a slander against him as an adversary of the Law. The former expected Christ’s kingdom to be earthly in a carnal sense; the latter, tormented by the spirit of envy on account of that same king, would vainly seek some means of slandering his teaching as though justly.

With regard to the latter, it is evident how truly and decisively they were forestalled by this promise, especially because he fulfilled his words in reality: he taught no one to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but taught rather that, by the voluntary choice of their own counsel, they should add what the weak Law had commanded less fully. But regarding his disciples, who supposed that his kingdom would be earthly, what else can we say except that they thought he intended to abolish the Law and the Prophets? For when they supposed that in his kingdom it would be lawful to kill, strip the nations of their spoils, and build a golden and jewel-adorned Jerusalem, what else did they expect [Col. 1730B] than to live without law and, under the name of God’s kingdom, to establish a kingdom of covetousness? He found them such, and called them such, but by giving this Holy Spirit, the Spirit of counsel, he made them altogether different.

# THE SIXTH BOOK ON THE WORKS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT: ON FORTITUDE

[Col. 1729]

## 683 CHAPTER I. On the Spirit of fortitude: how beautifully he is placed in the middle of the seven Spirits, and how the others are more concerned with repose, while this one is more concerned with action.

The fourth, and likewise the middle, of the seven Spirits of God—the Spirit of fortitude—is proclaimed as seated, as it were, in a certain position of command. And rightly so. For among the other works of the Holy Spirit, the work of fortitude is great and wonderful. Thus the victorious Lamb of God, having seven horns and seven eyes, is likened, on account of this most powerful horn, to the lion, the strongest and king of beasts, when in the Apocalypse it is said of the one whom John saw as a Lamb in the midst of the throne: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Rev. 5). And in the most ancient prophecy the same Spirit says for the same reason: “Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up” [Col. 1729D] (Gen. 49).

Beautifully, therefore, the Spirit of fortitude is placed in the middle of the Spirits, so that by this very place or rank he may with equal right receive praise together with the first, namely the Spirit of wisdom. For blessed Job says: “With him are wisdom and strength” (Job 12). Indeed, by “wisdom” in that passage all the other Spirits are rightly understood, except the Spirit of fortitude: because the Spirit of understanding, the Spirit of counsel, the Spirit of knowledge, of piety, and of the fear of the Lord cooperate more closely with the Spirit of wisdom, so that he may be exercised sufficiently and more fully within, and in repose. But the Spirit of fortitude is more concerned with action [Col. 1730C] and works or fights outwardly; by fighting, he establishes for them their holy repose.

## CHAPTER II. On considering the Spirit of fortitude first in Christ, then in the apostles and holy preachers, and then in the governors of the Church, according to Solomon’s saying: “There are three things which go well: the strongest lion among beasts, the cock,” etc.

Let us therefore consider the great deeds of this Spirit—that is, the Spirit of fortitude—which we are to proclaim: first in Christ himself; then in the apostles, or apostolic men, preachers of Christ; and then also in the holy rulers of Christ’s Church, according to that saying of the wisest Solomon: “There are three things which go well, and a fourth which proceeds happily: the lion, strongest among beasts, who will fear no encounter; the cock, girded about the loins; and the ram; and there is no king who can withstand him. There is one who appeared foolish after being lifted on high; for if he had understood, he would have put his hand over his mouth” (Prov. 30).

The lion, strongest among beasts, is God—the strongest among spirits—God, I say, and man, Christ, of whom it was most truly said: “He will fear no encounter.” For when, by his own power and not through an imposed necessity, he was laying down his life, he said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). And before this, fearing nothing of the encounter that awaited him, he said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12).

The cock, which distinguishes and by its crowing announces the hours of night—the cock, I say, girded about the loins—is the preacher who, through the night of the present age, does not allow us to sleep in the profound slumber of security, but announces that the laborious light is drawing near, that is, the day of judgment. Meanwhile he chastises his own body and reduces it to slavery, “lest perhaps,” he says, “after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). Such is his song: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light; let us walk honourably as in the day” [Col. 1731A] (Rom. 13), and other such words.

The ram, moreover, is every prelate: one who does not preach outwardly but presides inwardly over rational sheep, leading them to and bringing them back to the folds. “There is no king,” it says, “who can withstand him.” For he does not fear the swords of kings so as to forget his purpose; indeed, even if a king resists and strikes him with the sword, he lives more nobly and leads those sheep more effectively by his living example.

But the one who appeared foolish when lifted on high will be Antichrist. He proceeds successfully indeed, but not well as those other things do. For he will act and prosper, but he will not prosper to a good end; and therefore he will not go well. How greatly did this Spirit of fortitude shine in that strongest lion, in that girded cock, and in that horned ram! That lion both conquered the lion-devil by himself, and, through that cock and ram—or together with that cock and ram—overcame the beast Daniel saw: “a beast terrible and wonderful and exceedingly strong, having great iron teeth, devouring and crushing, and trampling the rest beneath its feet” [Col. 1731C] (Dan. 7).

For it is no small marvel that, when the Roman empire was not youthful but already fully grown and strengthened, while it lay still and the whole world trembled beneath it, this Spirit—the Spirit of fortitude—sent against its laws a crowing cock and a ram bearing no weapons except the two horns of twin charity; he overcame its rage, irrationally and without measure raging, and laid beneath their feet to be trampled the beast that had trampled the world. These are the great deeds of the Spirit of fortitude. With his help, as we are about to say something concerning them, let us first speak of the aforesaid lion: what he did to make so great a matter possible for the cock and the ram.

## 684 CHAPTER III. On the lion, who is also the lamb: how, according to John’s Apocalypse, he first conquered and bound the devil by dying; and after him the girded cock and the aforesaid ram—that is, Christ’s apostles and martyrs, of whom Stephen is the first.

The lion, who is also the lamb, attacked and bound by dying the devil, the rider and mover of the aforesaid beast, according to what John says in the Apocalypse: “And I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years. And he cast him into the abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him, so that he might deceive the nations no longer, until the thousand years were ended. After these things he must be released for a short time” (Rev. 20).

We understand the angel descending from heaven as the Lord Jesus Christ, who is called the Angel of Great Counsel. Visiting the region of mortals, he, being stronger, chose to bind the strong one, in order to make vessels of mercy from his vessels, which had long been vessels of wrath. He accomplished by deed what he had earlier promised by preaching: “No one can enter the strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man”—that is, the devil (Mark 3). For what was this strong man’s house or courtyard, if not the world, and especially the Roman empire? Surrounded by its armed retainers and supported by its obedience, he lay in human hearts and was defended in the shrines of the nations.

The key of the abyss is the depth of the divine judgments. For “the judgments of God are a great abyss” (Ps. 37 [36]). Thus that strong angel bound him—the devil—with chains, in that he restrained and checked his power to deceive those human beings who had been foreordained to life. The thousand years may be understood as all the years of this age, so that in the perfect number the fullness of time itself is implied. For the number one thousand is the solid square of the number ten. Ten multiplied ten times makes one hundred, which is already a square figure, but not yet full. But in order to rise in height and become solid, one hundred is again multiplied tenfold, becoming one thousand.

Nor can the Psalm’s words be better understood otherwise: “He has remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded for a thousand generations” [Col. 1732C] (Ps. 104 [105]), than as meaning: for all generations. “And he cast him,” it says, “into the abyss.” He cast the devil into the abyss, a name signifying the innumerable multitude of the ungodly, whose hearts are profoundly deep in their malice against the Church of God. This does not mean that the devil was not there before; he is said to have been cast there because, excluded from believers, he began more fully to possess the ungodly. For one is possessed more fully by the devil who is not only estranged from God but also hates, without cause, those who serve God.

He is also said to have shut and sealed over him, because, after the temples of idols had been shut—or rather destroyed—he restrained the responses of that devil’s deception, and converted many temples in which he had been worshipped into churches, sealed and sanctified by the cross and by the invocation of his name, which is invoked over us. Therefore, once the devil, the rider, had been captured and bound by this prince of fortitude, the army of his warriors—his apostles and martyrs, who were the aforesaid cock and ram—immediately rushed upon the beast we have described, which was his mount or seat. Since we are to speak of them, from whom could we more rightly begin than from the protomartyr?

He was called Stephen by a truly wonderful and venerable presage of divinity: in the hidden counsel of this fortitude he had been predestined by blessed lot to be its standard-bearer. For *Stephen* means “crowned.” Yet he was not to be crowned alone, but first; for all the righteous souls that follow him continually receive the name which, as we have said, by divine presage belonged particularly to him [Col. 1733A]. Let us therefore speak.

## CHAPTER IV. On blessed Stephen, called “full of grace and fortitude,” who, freely using that fortitude among the people, put into action the prophetic saying: “Behold, I am here; send me.”

“Stephen, full of grace and fortitude, performed great signs and wonders among the people. But some rose up from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and those from Cilicia and Asia, disputing with Stephen; and they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6).

True is what Truth said, what Christ spoke in his agony, when he was about to be handed over—indeed, while he was being handed over to be reckoned among criminals: “When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 16). Already, I believe, O blessed Stephen, standard-bearer of the blessed, when he said these things he was listening to your voice; he was already hearing the voice of the Spirit of fortitude and grace which was to fill you. For you were the first to convict the world; through you the Spirit of truth first convicted the world. He heard the voices and had already counted the stones you were to receive; and on that very night he was meditating upon your blood, when, having entered into agony, he prayed more earnestly, and his sweat became like drops of blood running down to the ground (Luke 22).

Could you have been absent from his awareness or foreknowledge when he said: “Behold, I send to you prophets, wise men, and scribes; and some of them you will kill and crucify, and some of them you will scourge in your synagogues” [Col. 1733C] (Matt. 23)? And shortly afterward: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (ibid.). Indeed, to go back still further: when, while the prophet saw and heard, he said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” and the prophet replied, “Behold, I am here; send me,” you were in the Lord’s preparation, before the One seated upon the throne; and his Spirit—the Spirit of fortitude and grace which was to be in you—stirred up the prophet to say: “Behold, I am here; send me” (Isa. 6).

For by what human being, or through what human being, did God command you to go and so courageously convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment? We read that the apostles said: “It is not fitting for us to leave the word of God and serve tables”; and then it is written that they chose Stephen, “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6). But we do not read that the apostles sent Stephen to testify among the people with apostolic grace or fortitude. What then? “Stephen,” Scripture says, “full of grace and fortitude, performed great signs and wonders among the people.” Therefore, blessed man, while the Lord sat upon a throne high and lifted up—that is, while the Son of Man, crowned because of his suffering of death, was exalted to sit at the Father’s right hand—and said, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” as though he complained and said, “They kill them all and allow none of those whom we have sent from the beginning of the world to live,” you in some manner said: “Behold, I am here; send me.” For freely and unbidden, you did not hesitate to bear witness to the Lord Jesus, seated [Col. 1734A] or standing at the right hand of God’s power.

## 685 CHAPTER V. On the fortitude, wisdom, and Spirit by which he spoke, whom those disputing with him could not withstand; and how he wisely defeated his accusers who said that they had heard words of blasphemy against Moses, God, and the holy place.

With what grace, then, with what fortitude was Stephen filled? Certainly with the grace of wisdom and the fortitude of the Spirit, or the Spirit of fortitude. For the text immediately adds: “They could not withstand the wisdom and Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6). Indeed, all that he said or did belongs to wisdom and fortitude. Let us consider the order of events or actions.

Then, Scripture says, “they suborned men who said that they had heard him speaking blasphemous words against Moses and God”—false witnesses, certainly, as is added below, who said: “This man does not cease speaking words against the holy place and the Law.” But he, while all looked on, having a face like the face of an angel, and being asked by the chief priest whether these things were so, spoke thus: “Men, brethren, and fathers, listen: the God of glory appeared to our father Abraham when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Haran, and said to him: ‘Leave your land and your kindred, and come into the land that I shall show you’” (Acts 7).

Thus, beginning with great grace of wisdom, he first refuted the false witnesses brought against him, who had said that they heard him speak blasphemous words against Moses and God; then, with no less great an onset of fortitude, he crushed that entire vain council, the assembly of the wicked, which had been gathered against him. For what is the force of his beginning, “The God of glory appeared,” employing a testimony hitherto unusual, though wholly true, when he could have said, “God appeared to our father Abraham”? In a manner both brief and wise, then, he dismissed the accusation of blasphemy by calling the God who appeared to Abraham “the God of glory.” For they had accused him not only concerning Moses but also concerning God. The greater portion of the blasphemy appeared to bear upon God; and therefore he first dispelled that charge, confessing that he who appeared to Abraham was the God of glory, and then adding the benefits that marked his all-powerful divinity [Col. 1734D] and divine truth: namely, that he promised to give Abraham for a possession the land “in which you now dwell,” and to his seed after him, although he had no son, and so forth.

The other part of the compound accusation of blasphemy, which concerned Moses, he at once destroys by a glorious testimony to the truth and to his own defence: “At that time Moses was born and was pleasing to God,” and so on, as far as the words: “This is the Moses who said to the children of Israel: ‘God will raise up for you from your brethren a prophet like me; him you shall hear.’ This is he who was in the Church in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai, and with our fathers, who received living words to give to us” (ibid.).

All that he says concerning Moses defends his clear conscience against the false witnesses and reveals him, as is fitting, to think rightly of God’s holy servant. And see with what force of wisdom he throws back upon that brood of vipers the stain cast upon himself. For when he had said, “who received living words to give to you,” he immediately added: “Whom our fathers would not obey, but rejected, and in their hearts turned back to Egypt,” and so forth, to that prophetic testimony: “Did you offer victims or sacrifices to me for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel? And you took up the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, the images which you made in order to worship them; and I will carry you away beyond Babylon” (Acts 7).

Having said these things, by which the aforesaid slander of blasphemy against both God and Moses was refuted, it remained for him to say something also concerning the allegation added by the false witnesses, their accusation against the holy place: “For we heard him,” they say, “declaring that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place and change the traditions which Moses handed down to us” [Col. 1735B] (Acts 6). If he had said this, he would have said what was true, and he would have spoken with that Truth which had foretold: “Not one stone shall remain upon another” (Matt. 24)—a truth which, even if he were silent, these stones themselves were ready to cry out (Luke 19). But what blasphemy would it have been to say anything of this kind about those holy stones?

He therefore says: “The tabernacle of testimony was with our fathers in the wilderness,” and so forth, to the words: “But the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands, as the prophet says: ‘Heaven is my throne and earth the footstool of my feet. What house will you build for me, says the Lord, or what is the place of my rest? Has not my hand made all these things?’” (Acts 7). It is as though he said: “What blasphemy is there in saying that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place, when God does not dwell in it, as the prophet testifies that the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands?” For nothing can rightly be called blasphemy except what is spoken against the Most High, or against that in which the Most High dwells.

“But Solomon,” you say, “built this house for him.” “Has not my hand,” he says through the prophet, “made all these things?” If heaven and earth shall pass away, along with all these things made by my hand, how much more this house which Solomon’s hand built, especially since it had long ago been consumed by Babylonian fire?

Furthermore, it should be noted that, after he had said, “The tabernacle of testimony was with our fathers in the wilderness,” he immediately added: “As he directed Moses when he spoke to him, that he should make it according to the pattern which he had seen” [Col. 1735D] (ibid.). For by this statement he addresses that part of the slander in which, after they had said, “We heard him declaring that this Jesus the Nazarene will destroy this place,” they had added, “and change the traditions which Moses handed down to us” (Acts 6). And truly, by the wonderful art of the wisdom or grace with which he was filled, he not only did not deny that he had said—or ought to have said—that Jesus the Nazarene would change the traditions handed down by Moses; he almost gave the reason why those traditions had to be changed. It was this: those traditions, handed down by Moses, were not God’s traditions, but had been handed down according to the pattern or figure of the future traditions of God, which Moses saw, God showing them beforehand, with the intellectual eye, the prophetic eye.

Nor did he say this without authority, but upon the authority of Moses himself—indeed, of God, who said to Moses: “See and make according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. 25). Therefore, he either did say, or ought to have said—what he did not deny having said—that Jesus the Nazarene would change the traditions handed down by Moses; that is, the patterns or shadows of heavenly things would now have to cease, once the heavenly realities themselves had been disclosed through Jesus the Nazarene.

## 686 CHAPTER VI. With what fortitude he rebukes the unbelievers, saying, “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears,” [Col. 1736B] and the rest; though dying for them in unconquered charity, he prayed.

Having set forth what belonged to wisdom, which no one could withstand, or to the grace with which he was filled—having defended himself from the charge of blasphemy brought against him, and having properly made use of lawful defence—let us now hear what belonged to fortitude, with which sacred authority likewise declares that he was full: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you,” continuing to: “You who received the Law by the ordinances of angels and did not keep it” (Acts 7).

This is the mark of true fortitude—true, I say—not of rash impatience or ill-considered fury, but of righteous zeal and of fortitude that is zealous justly and rationally. For in this very saying he does not follow an impulse of his own heart, but the true testimony of the divine voice. For the Lord himself first says: “You are a stiff-necked people; if I go up in your midst even once, I will destroy you” (Exod. 33). Then Moses also says: “Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and stiffen your neck no longer” (Deut. 10). And in the prophet the Lord says: “Their fathers have transgressed my covenant to this day, and the children are hard of face and unyielding of heart” (Ezek. 2). Likewise: “For the whole house of Israel is of a rubbed forehead and a hard heart” (Ezek. 3).

Therefore, when false witnesses attacked him, he defended himself with wonderful wisdom; yet with equally wonderful fortitude he attacked the guilty, laying upon them a charge for which he did not cease to bring necessary testimony: “Stiff-necked,” he says, “and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did, so do you.” Always, I say—that is, from the time when, as you came out of Egypt and the tablets were being written by the finger of God, the Spirit of God, you said to Aaron: “Make us gods to go before us; for we do not know what has happened to this Moses who brought us out of the land of Egypt” (Acts 7).

But true fortitude is never without charity; and then action is truly performed in the Spirit of fortitude when fortitude itself is surrounded by the fellowship of strongest charity. Therefore, when they became more wicked through his rebuke, were cut to the heart, and gnashed their teeth at him, as they cast him out of the city and stoned him, he knelt down and cried with a loud voice: “Lord, do not lay this sin against them” (ibid.). O truly strong man, who rose not against human beings but against human malice! Truly steadfast and strong, whom so many stones could not drive from the citadel of charity, in which “love is strong as death” (Song 8)—indeed, stronger than death. For at the very moment of his dying, the fortitude of love prevailed in his soul more than the fortitude of death.

At least he might have said, “May God see and judge” (Exod. 5), or some such thing which he could have said with justice; but kneeling down, he said—indeed, he cried with a loud voice—“Lord, do not lay this sin against them.” The former would have been the due of justice; the latter was the voluntary office of charity. Strong, therefore, in both respects: strong and gentle in each part. There, fiercely rebuking with fortitude; here, enduring death with fortitude. Thus, in the end, a twofold praise is securely sung to the victor [Col. 1737B]: he first returned to the Saviour the death which the Saviour deigned to suffer for all, and he first offered to the Saviour, for those stoning him, the prayer which the Saviour had offered for those crucifying him. All righteous souls follow him, professing the same warfare and seeking the crown of the same victory.

## CHAPTER VII. On the apostle Peter: what manner of man this Spirit of fortitude found, and what manner of man it made him; how before the Lord’s Passion he walked upon the waters and, becoming afraid, began to sink; but after the Resurrection, girded with his tunic, he threw himself into the sea and came to him; and what these things foreshadowed.

We spoke of the recruit whom the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of strength, plainly armed [Col. 1737C]. What shall we say of the masters of the soldiery, Peter and Paul, whom that same Spirit of strength armed against the very head of the beast mentioned above? For, to speak first of Peter, we know what sort of man this Spirit found, and what sort it made him. Before this Spirit was given, when the Lord Jesus had been glorified, Peter had not even recognized the name of military service; he was not yet able either to bear, or even to touch, or to look upon with his own eyes the military standards of Christ. The threefold denial bears witness: there Peter was found a liar, and Christ the truth, when—not some important person, but a maidservant who kept the door—said, “Are you too one of this man’s disciples?” Peter denied it (John 18); and yet no sword or spear appeared in that maidservant’s hand [Col. 1737D]. A little earlier, however, contending with the Lord, he had said: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26). Thus he who had said, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the cock will not crow until you have denied me three times” (ibid.), was victor in the contest and won the palm of truth. Afterwards, as though alluding to that premature confidence, he says to the same Peter: “Amen, amen, I say to you, when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.” The Evangelist says that he said this to signify by what death Peter was to glorify God (John 21).

For when was Peter younger, and girding himself? Surely when, inexperienced and untrained in arduous conflicts, he presumed too greatly upon his own conscience or strength, saying, “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22); and, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you” (Matt. 26); when he drew the sword and, striking boldly, cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant (ibid.). Then Peter was younger, for he had not yet advanced far in wisdom. Not knowing that it belongs to God alone to gird a soldier, he girded himself when he made such great and bold promises about himself. But he grew old when, having received this Holy Spirit, the Spirit of strength, he became wise. From then on he stretched out his hands to him who knows how to gird; aware and experienced of his own weakness, he was girded by another. For this Holy Spirit made him strong [Col. 1738A–B] and led him where he did not wish to be led: namely, to the passion of death, which the feeling of the flesh recoils from with natural horror, however willing the spirit may be.

When the Lord said these things to Peter, he had already signified both conditions in him. Long before, when the little boat in which the disciples were was being tossed by waves in the middle of the sea—for the wind was contrary—and he himself came to them in the fourth watch of the night, walking upon the sea, and said to them, as they were troubled and crying out in fear, “It is I; do not be afraid,” Peter answered: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you upon the waters.” He said, “Come”; and the rest follows, up to the words addressed to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14). Surely, in that little faith by which he doubted and therefore began to sink, the weakness by which he was to deny the Lord was prefigured [Col. 1738B–C].

For that contrary wind, over which the Lord walked unafraid, prefigured the assault of the prince of this world. The same Lord, confident that this prince had nothing in him, was to overcome his tribulations and the Jewish disturbances. Peter likewise walked upon the waters, but saw the strong wind and was afraid, and therefore began to sink; for so it was to be that, presuming upon his faith and saying, “Why can I not follow you now? I lay down my life for you,” he would immediately fear at the voice of one little woman and deny him—which indeed was to sink into the depths of the sea (ibid.). But Jesus, stretching out his hand, caught him as he began to sink (Luke [Col. 1738D] 22), because, as the Evangelist testifies, looking upon him, he summoned to tears one greatly endangered by that same denial.

But when the Savior had overcome those same waters and, by rising again from the dead, had calmed every storm for himself, Peter threw himself into the sea, girded with his tunic, and was in no danger. For it is written: “When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded himself with his tunic—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea.
