But the other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land, but about two hundred cubits away, dragging the net of fish” (John 21). Immediately follows what we cited shortly before: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished” (ibid.), and so forth. Therefore the very truth confirmed in his own words what had been prefigured at sea: namely, that Peter, who in presuming on his own strength had in some sense girded himself by saying, “I lay down my life for you,” and who at once, by denying him, was almost entirely submerged, would, when girded by another—that is, when the Holy Spirit strengthened his mind—overcome all the waters of every tribulation [Col. 1739A].

## CHAPTER VIII. Of the apostle Paul: how weak—indeed, how frenzied—he was, and what sort of man this Spirit of strength made him.

But Paul had been not merely weak in some ordinary fashion, but foremost among the gravely ill—that is, the frenzied—of whom the physician, sharply struck in the Psalm, says: “The strong rushed upon me,” that is, those truly weak [Col. 1739B] and falsely strong, who presumed upon the health of their own righteousness, and struck and crucified the true physician (Ps. 58). He had been one of such weak and frenzied persons when he persecuted the same physician in his members, whom he could not touch in the head seated in heaven. For “he ravaged the Church, entering house after house and dragging off men and women, delivering them to prison” (Acts 8).

But he changed his strength—indeed, his frenzy of cruelty—into the true health of genuine strength. Who could recount all the works which this Spirit of strength accomplished through him? When Saul was cast to the ground and Paul rose again, and, having received food there, was strengthened, he immediately entered the synagogues and preached Jesus. While all marveled at his sudden change [Col. 1739C], he grew ever stronger and confounded the Jews living at Damascus, proving that this was the Christ (Acts 9). From then on he acted boldly everywhere and conquered everywhere: “I give thanks,” he says, “to him who strengthened me” (1 Tim. 1).

It has therefore rightly been observed that the Lord’s words to blessed Job should be understood of him: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you, or remain at your manger? Will you bind the rhinoceros with your cord for ploughing, or will he break up the clods of the valleys after you? Will you trust in his great strength and leave your labours to him? Will you believe that he will return your seed to you and gather your threshing-floor?” (Job 39). This rhinoceros may indeed be understood to represent the people of singular pride, concerning whom the Lord says through the Prophet: “Deliver me from the mouth of the lion, and my humility from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps. 21). Yet this is more clearly evident when one man is drawn from that people into the midst: Saul, formerly foremost in pride, but afterward Paul, pre-eminent in humility [Col. 1739D].

He bore a horn in his nostril when he believed that he would please God by cruelty. Every hunter feared this rhinoceros, because every preacher dreaded his savagery. But, to capture him, a virgin opened her bosom: for when he was on his way to Damascus, the incarnate Wisdom of God manifested herself to him. For the rhinoceros, which is also called the *monoceros* (“one-horned creature”), is said to possess strength so great and so untamable that it cannot be captured in any way by the power of hunters. But a virgin girl is set before it; when she opens her bosom, the beast, wondrously abandoning all its ferocity, lays down its head, and thus, deceived, it is suddenly found as though enfeebled and is captured [Col. 1740A].

“Will the rhinoceros,” therefore, he says, “be willing to serve you?”—understand: as he is willing to serve me. “Or remain at your manger?” Namely, as this man was bound by me through Ananias to the sacrament of baptism. “Will you bind him with your cord for ploughing?” That is, will you constrain him by your command to preach, so that he says: “Woe is me if I do not preach the Gospel!” (1 Cor. 9). “Or will he break up the clods of the valleys after you?” That is, the impediments of the humble—understand: as he does after me. For example, when he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5). For he who, by rebuking the harshness of the Law, shattered it in the humble mind of believers—what else did he do but break up clods in the valley after me?

“Will you trust in his great strength?” Understand: as I do, who send him far away among the Gentiles, that he may bear my name before kings and Gentiles (Acts 9). “And will you leave your labours to him?” Understand: as I do, who act thus so that he may say, “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ” (Col. 5), having been afflicted seven times, as he himself says: “Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I suffered shipwreck” (2 Cor. 11). “Will you believe that he will return your seed to you?” That is, fruitful preaching; “and gather your threshing-floor?” That is, enlarge the breadth of the Church into one faith. Understand: you will not believe it. For Ananias too said: “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints” (Acts 9), and so forth [Col. 1740B–C]. For he did not believe that the man who had hitherto scattered the Lord’s threshing-floor with the horn of pride would gather it.

## CHAPTER IX. Of those two most valiant leaders: how, in concord, they approached Rome—called a beast because of its cruelty and an ass because of its error—and brought it, against the inherited discord of the brothers Romulus and Remus, into the concord of one faith.

Great, then, was this change wrought by the right hand of the Most High in this man; great and marvelous in both Peter and Paul was the proof of this Spirit of strength. It healed one who was falsely strong and the other who was truly fearful, both genuinely weak; and it armed them with its strength so that they went to that Rome, mistress of the world, figuratively called Babylon—the great and terrible beast that, as has already been said, devoured with iron teeth, crushed, and trampled what remained under its feet (Dan. 7) [Col. 1740D].

Yet, with regard to those among its people who were to believe, wandering through foolish simplicity or simple foolishness, let us truthfully call it an ass. Then the Lord Jesus sent two disciples to untie that ass, or the head of the ass—that is, the ruler of paganism—when he sent these preachers of truth to Rome. For it was bound by the chain of diabolical slavery, and those who abused its service were to say: “What are you doing, untying the ass?” (Mark 11). But the Lord says: “If anyone says anything to you, say: ‘Because the Lord has need of it’” (Matt. 21).

These two came with the purpose that, although Rome might say to them with swords and various punishments, “What are you doing?”, they would not cease or desist: strong—most strong—unfasteners of the bond, saying, “The Lord has need of this; it is necessary to the Lord” (Mark 11) [Col. 1741A]. What could be more beautiful than this counterposition of two spiritual brothers against the two brothers who founded that city? For the brothers Romulus and Remus founded it under an evil omen, so that civil discord might never fail within it and new civil wars might always revive. For, as our author says:

> “The first walls were moistened with fraternal blood.”  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book 1, verse 95)

Romulus indeed killed Remus because he could not endure a partner. Hence the same poet says:

> “[Lacuna] and all power  
> will be intolerant of a partner [lacuna].”  
> (Lucan, ibid., vv. 92–93)

Therefore, in a fine spectacle, against the discordant blood brothers there were sent these two brothers in the Spirit, united in spiritual brotherhood. Upon the old foundations of discord they might lay Christ, the new foundation of concord, and might build a new city for the great king, God, through the shedding of their own blood. On account of the great steadfastness of its apostolic faith, this city truly deserved to be called the seat of righteousness, the house of faith, and the court of modesty—though it had formerly been the throne of pride, the abyss of greed, the whirlpool of blood, and the pit of murders [Col. 1741B].

## CHAPTER X. Of Nero, the attendant of diabolical cruelty; and how it did Satan, his rider, no good that he killed these men on one and the same day—though, as some say, with one year intervening.

These leaders of Christian devotion had already overcome a multitude of Gentiles, inscribing upon those they had rightly cast down the trophies of Christ’s victory. At last they attacked that famous citadel, with Nero presiding: a peculiar attendant of every kind of cruelty. Since the whole world already knew both his cruelty and his unprecedented impurity, a certain wise man, still marveling and indignant that such a man had been powerful, lamented thus:

> “We know what ruin he wrought—  
> the city burned and fathers slain—  
> he who, savage after killing his brother,  
> was drenched in his mother’s shed blood,  
> and, roaming over her body stiff with death,  
> did not wet his face with tears, but could be  
> censor of the dead woman’s beauty.  
>
> Yet he ruled with his sceptre those peoples  
> whom Phoebus sees, descending his rays beneath the waves  
> as he comes from the furthest east;  
> those whom the seven cold Bears press upon;  
> those whom the violent South Wind scorches with dry heat,  
> baking again the burning sands.  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> [lacuna]  
>
> Alas for the grievous lot, whenever an unjust  
> sword is added to savage poison.”  
> (Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, book 2, metre C)

Likewise:

> “Though proud Nero adorned himself  
> with Tyrian purple and snow-white gems,  
> he nevertheless flourished, hateful to all,  
> in his raging luxury.”  
> (Boethius, ibid., book 3, metre 4)

Many histories report how raging was his luxury and how great the crimes and outrages of impurity and cruelty that he committed. But for the present purpose it is enough to say that Christians may glory in having such a persecutor: not just any man, nor a man of ordinary sort, but the illegitimate master of every obscenity, who by persecuting this name testified that it was opposed to the unclean spirit dwelling in him [Col. 1742A–B].

Thus, while such a contemptible man ruled the Roman world, these leaders of the apostles brought the standard of devotion into the great city. What could that dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, do or accomplish? At that time he lay in that city and rested upon the unclean neck of such an emperor. For, as said above, that angel who came down from heaven, holding the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand, had bound him (Rev. 20). Therefore he prevailed nothing against their protector, the Spirit of strength. But Nero, raging on Satan’s behalf, as one filled wholly with the spirit of wickedness, killed only their bodies.

But what benefit did this bring Satan? Could that immortal Spirit be extinguished by their death? Certainly not: rather, grace abounded more widely among many. Christ was not crucified anew in Peter, nor was he who spoke in Paul so cut down by the sword that he could speak no longer. On the contrary, the word of God grew stronger when it was thought to have been extinguished with their death [Col. 1742C].

Thus Samson, most strong, when he had thrown from his hand the jawbone of an ass with which he had struck down a thousand men, did indeed thirst, but he did not fail. For the Lord opened a hollow tooth in the jaw, and waters came forth from it. Having drunk them, he refreshed his spirit and recovered his strength (Judg. 15). Did the true Samson, Christ the Lord, then abandon these men as they died, or cast them away at the moment of death, so as to abandon them dead—those through whom he fought and conquered while they lived? For they were like the jawbone of an ass: not greatly noble or illustrious according to the flesh, especially Peter, who was no emperor or senator but a fisherman. Certainly he did not abandon or cast them away. Nevertheless, he allowed them to be killed and struck down; but when they had been struck down, their tombs poured forth living waters, their bodies poured out the grace of miracles, and this refreshed Christ’s faith so that it did not fail, and made it abound in larger multitudes of believers [Col. 1742D].

One of them indeed hung fastened to a cross; the other fell by the sword. Peter, about to be fastened to the cross, humbly strong and strongly humble, said: “Because my Lord Jesus Christ descended from heaven to earth, he was raised upon an upright cross. Turn my cross around, because I am not worthy to be crucified as my Lord was.” They therefore turned the cross, placed his feet upward, and fastened his hands downward [Col. 1743A]. Concerning this, a faithful and praiseworthy man in the faith sang in verse:

> “Thus his hand is fixed below; his sole is turned toward the summit.  
> Greater in thought because lesser in bodily form,  
> he knew that heaven is more swiftly reached by humility:  
> he lowers his face, about to yield up his spirit.”  
> (Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 12)

Paul, about to be struck by the sword and awaiting that hour, says, strengthened by the same Spirit: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4). And immediately afterward: “The Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through my preaching the message might be fully accomplished and all the Gentiles might hear; and I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (ibid.) [Col. 1743B].

It is believed that both adorned heaven with their illustrious martyrdom on one and the same day of one and the same year. Yet some think that, though they completed martyrdom on the same day, they did not do so in the same year. Hence the poet quoted above says:

> “One day, though renewed after a full year,  
> saw both men crowned by proud death with the laurel.”

And immediately afterward:

> “When the wheel of the revolving year had run its circuit  
> and the rising sun had brought back the same day,  
> Nero poured his burning fury upon Paul’s throat  
> and ordered the teacher of the Gentiles to be struck down.”  
> (Prudentius, ibid.)

## CHAPTER XI. That the same Spirit of strength must be proclaimed in the remaining apostles.

The same change wrought by the right hand of the Most High took place also in the other apostles, and the same work of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of strength, must be proclaimed. All were weak before his coming, and through his coming were made strong. For when the officers seized Jesus, all left him and fled, just as he had foretold (Matt. 26). “Do you now believe?” he says. “Behold, the hour is coming, and has now come, when you will be scattered, each to his own place, and will leave me alone” (John 16). Therefore they were weak and needed this Strengthener.

For this reason, immediately before ascending to heaven, he said: “I will send upon you the promise of my Father. But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24) [Col. 1743C–D]. This power came and clothed them, making them so strong that no one could strike terror into them. For it is written: “Having summoned the apostles, they beat them and charged them not to speak at all in the name of Jesus, and let them go. They indeed went from the presence of the council rejoicing because they had been deemed worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5).

They were therefore clothed with true power: rejoicing in strength and strong in joy, concerning which he had likewise said to them: “I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you” (John 16). Long beforehand the Prophet foresaw this strength, or steadfastness, conferred on them by this Spirit of strength: “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God, and the firmament announces the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). He called “heavens” those who had formerly been earth; he called “firmament” those who had formerly been weak. And rightly so. For, strengthened in this way, they made the whole earth astonished by thundering with preaching and flashing with miracles. For, as follows: “Their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (ibid.) [Col. 1744A].

Andrew invaded Achaia, Matthew Ethiopia, Thomas and Bartholomew India, and the remaining apostles the remaining regions of the world, to wage war under the banner of the cross. Bringing the trophies of the victorious Christ into the regions of the defeated devil, they willingly added their own blood and planted the Church everywhere on earth with their blood.

## CHAPTER XII. Of the apostle John: that he too drank the Lord’s cup, although he ended his life in peace.

After Nero, Domitian stirred up the second persecution against Christians. Under him John, beloved of the Lord Jesus, was thrown into a vessel of boiling oil; but protected by his lover’s grace, he emerged unharmed, so that he might end his life in peace, according to the truth of him who said: “Thus I will have him remain until I come” (John 21) [Col. 1744B].

But the same Lord Jesus had long before said to him and to his brother James: “You will indeed drink my cup; but to sit with me is not mine to give you” (Mark 10). Did Wisdom then forget its own pronouncement when it said, “Thus I will have him remain until I come,” and, holding this will fixed, preserved him so that he might end his present life in peace? James indeed, his brother, was able to drink his cup and was the first of all the apostles in Judaea to drink it, being killed by the sword of faithless Herod (Acts 12). But John, after all the apostles, fell asleep in peace, giving thanks and saying: “Invited to your banquet, I come giving thanks, because you have deigned, Lord Jesus Christ, to invite me to your feast, knowing that I desired you with all my heart.”

He had descended into a pit in order to say this prayer, and afterward that pit was found full, containing nothing but manna. Did the Lord, then, as has been said, forget his own declaration, “You will drink my cup”? Certainly not. For this man also drank the Lord’s cup: not only because he was thrown into a vessel of boiling oil and, on account of his unwavering constancy in preaching the Gospel, was banished to the island of Patmos, but also because—what must especially be proclaimed and is worthy of the highest praise—where the soul of the blessed Virgin and Mother of God was pierced by a sword, there the soul of this beloved disciple too was wounded [Col. 1744C–D].

For while the other disciples scattered in flight, he stood with that mother beside the Lord’s cross and saw with his own eyes Jesus drink the cup of suffering. If it pleased the Father, who gave his Son that cup, and if it so seemed good to the Son, who drank that cup, to judge that John had drunk his cup precisely because he stood near at such an hour, who can condemn this? For no one can be so unfeeling as to make little of what Simeon said to his mother: “And a sword will pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2), because she was to see all her inward parts, in that son of hers, crucified. As has been said, this beloved disciple likewise stood with her beside the cross (John 19), and, if you believe it, he too was wounded in mind. Therefore, as we now believe, he is by no means without the great honor of this glorious proclamation: that he too drank the Lord’s cup [Col. 1745A].

## CHAPTER XIII. Of the glorious martyrs, their battles and victories: that Abel and Cain never fought with so great or such a conflict, though they had always been opposed even before Christ’s coming.

After the remarkable triumphs of the commanders—that is, of the apostles—follow the victorious battles of the martyrs: great was the devil’s wrath, great the strength of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1745B], great the slaughter of bodies, great the glorification of souls. Never had Abel on one side and Cain on the other, the city of God on one side and the city of the devil on the other, holy Jerusalem on one side and Babylon the harlot on the other, come together upon the battlefield to fight with spirits so great, with arms so great and of such a kind.

Certainly they had formerly fought also in ancient enmities and had made many memorable assaults upon one another; but they used another kind of weapons, fought for other causes, and won victories of another character. For when Abraham, father of the blessed seed and father of believers, with his three hundred and eighteen household servants pursued and conquered the four victorious kings (Gen. 14); when Moses, leader of the Lord’s people, killed Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan, and avenged the children of Israel upon the Midianites (Num. 12, 13); when Joshua killed so many nations and so many kings of the Canaanites; when so many judges fought against the nations and so often delivered the children of Israel (Josh. 10, 11, 15); when David struck down the Philistine (1 Sam. 17) and afterward crushed Israel’s enemies in such great wars: then too the city of God fought against the city of the devil, and the generation of faith against the generation of sin, but with other weapons, as has been said, another kind of warfare, and another form of triumph [Col. 1745B–C].

Here the Lord chose new wars. When he himself, the leader, was ascending to battle to cast out the strong armed man, the prince of this world, the devil, he said to Peter: “Put your sword back into its sheath” (Matt. 26). Peter thought he must fight according to that old custom of which we have already spoken, and therefore that the same Lord had shortly before said: “But now, whoever has a purse, let him take it, and likewise a bag; and whoever has none, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword” (Luke 22). Still occupied by an earthly understanding, when they heard this they said: “Lord, behold, here are two swords.” But he was not seeking such a sword, and therefore immediately said to them: “It is enough” (ibid.).

As though saying: “It has been enough to fight with such a sword under the Law, or by the Law’s permission, until now. Now put that sword back into its sheath; and let whoever does not have the other sword—the word of God, of which it is written, ‘Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one’ (Ps. 44)—buy it by selling his tunic,” that is, by setting aside every earthly possession, so that he may, free and unencumbered, be able to draw with a strong hand the great sword, not against human beings but against human vices [Col. 1745D–1746A].

With what voice, with what speech, can we describe these battles, so marvelous and magnificent? This warfare is above us; this kind of war is too lofty for our speech to attain. Let us instead hear what the Spirit says of such a battle.

## CHAPTER XIV. Of the persecutions of the martyrs, according to that passage of the Apocalypse: “And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had given birth, he might devour her child.”

“And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and a crown of twelve stars upon her head; she was with child, and cried out in labour and anguish to give birth. And another sign appeared in heaven. And behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns” (Rev. 12), and so forth [Col. 1746A–B].

This woman is the holy Church: once naked with that nakedness which Holy Scripture indicates befell our first parents through sin, but now clothed—not with any ordinary garment, but clothed with the sun, that is, Christ, the true sun, the sun of righteousness. For the Apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). The moon is beneath her feet: that is, the mutability of temporal goods is held in contempt by her. It had not been so until then. For the sake of temporal goods, for the land not of the living but of the dying—that is, the land of Canaan—the Church had hitherto fought with the material sword. Therefore the moon had not previously been beneath her feet.

But now, that she may become perfect, she is commanded to renounce the entire world, indeed even to hate her own body or soul. And behold, the moon is under her feet, and on her head is a crown of twelve stars. On her head—that is, at her beginning—the crown of twelve stars is the glory of the twelve apostles. Whether you understand Christ, or the very beginning of the nascent Church, as denoted by the term “head,” its head was adorned with the number twelve of the apostles [Col. 1746B–C].

“She was with child, and cried out in labour and anguish to give birth.” Her cry certainly aroused the war against her that follows. Indeed, to cry out was truly to fight and provoke the enemy. For what was it for the woman to be with child, to cry out in labour, and to be in anguish to give birth, except to have in her heart the good word of God, conceived from the Spirit of God’s love; to preach with a great affection of charity; and to be intensely concerned for the begetting of spiritual children? Paul alone could not say this: “My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4). The intention and affection of the entire order of preachers whom the Holy Spirit has sent—which order is truly the mother Church—is such that they may give birth to spiritual children and form Christ in their hearers. Therefore, because they could not be silent while Christ’s charity compelled them, just as a woman with child cannot be silent when she suffers the pains of childbirth, the devil was angry and rose up against her in war.

It follows: “And behold, a great red dragon, having seven heads and ten horns, and upon his heads seven diadems; and his tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven and cast them to earth. And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had given birth, he might devour her child” (Rev. 12) [Col. 1746D–1747A].

For the devil, bloody in savagery and deceitful in malice, armed himself against the Church with the power of earthly rule. In his seven heads we understand all his kings; in his ten horns, all the kingdoms of the world, of which he proudly boasts as though they were his horns. For in the Gospel he even dares address the Son of God himself, showing him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, and saying: “I will give you all this power and their glory, for they have been delivered to me, and I give them to whomever I wish. Therefore, if you worship me, all shall be yours” (Matt. 4; Luke 4).

His tail drew a third part of the stars of heaven because, by deceitful fraud, he cast down an innumerable portion of angels or human beings, as though by his tail. His tail is the blind part, the unclean part, concealing unclean things beneath its own covering lest they be exposed. “He stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had given birth, he might devour her child.” The devil lay in wait for mother Church even then, when these mysteries were seen, striving to extinguish Christ—that is, faith in Christ, which she preached—in the hearts of believers [Col. 1747A–B].

“But she gave birth to a male child.” For the Church always gave birth to Christ, though the dragon opposed her. She gives birth, I say, to a male—that is, to one strong enough to conquer the devil who had conquered the woman. For what other son, what other male, rules the nations with a rod of iron—that is, with inflexible justice, governing the good and breaking the evil like a potter’s vessel? (Ps. 2). The dragon, wishing to devour such a son of the blessed woman so that his memory or faith might never exist, stood before her. But what happened? “Her child,” it says, “was caught up to God and to his throne.” Truly, it greatly frustrates the perverse will of the angry dragon that this male child of the woman did not remain among the dead, nor did his flesh see corruption (Ps. 15), but he quickly rose and ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God. Had this not happened, this red dragon—that is, the devil, the murderer—could have erased his memory, so great as it now is among us [Col. 1747B–C].

Therefore he himself, hastening to rise in the Psalm, after saying, “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead,” and so forth, immediately adds: “Will you perform wonders for the dead? Or will physicians raise them up, and will they confess you? Will anyone declare your mercy in the grave, and your truth in destruction?” (Ps. 87). As though saying: “By my resurrection you will perform wonders for the dead, raising them spiritually through your physicians and bringing them to knowledge of you and justifying them. This would not happen if I remained in the grave and in destruction, as my enemies desire.”

This is what he said under those questions. Thus, as though it were asked why the dragon, who stood ready to devour, did not devour this woman’s son, the reason is added: because her child was caught up to God and to his throne—that is, because Christ rose from the dead, ascended to the Father, and sits at his right hand. Afterwards it adds [Col. 1747D–1748A]: “And the dragon was angry with the woman, and went away to make war upon the rest of her seed” (Rev. 12). This is the war that we now contemplate, which in the present passage we intend to proclaim in praise and glory of the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of strength.

## CHAPTER XV. Of the battles of the martyrs according to the mystical likeness of Gideon’s war, and of what follows in the Apocalypse: “And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon.”

O praiseworthy army of those remaining, who are or were of the seed of this woman. They fought by preaching, conquered by suffering, and triumphed by dying. Outwardly the dragon fought; inwardly he was overcome. Outwardly he shattered earthen vessels; inwardly victory shone like gold. By bodily death they seemed to be defeated; spiritually, as conquerors, they were crowned. Such things were once prefigured when Gideon, as leader, fought wondrously against the hosts of the Midianites. He divided the three hundred men into three companies, and gave them trumpets in their hands, and empty jars, with lamps in the midst of the jars (Judg. XIX). They went to battle; when the jars were broken, the lamps flashed forth, and at the gleaming of their light the enemies were terrified and turned to flight (ibid.). In the trumpets was the cry of preaching; in the lamps, the brilliance of miracles; in the jars was signified the frailty of bodies. They sounded the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when, for God’s sake, they gave their bodies over to torments; they shone with lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they flashed forth in miracles [Col. 1748C]. Thus the whole battle is heavenly; the whole victory spiritual.

Therefore, immediately after the woman’s flight into the wilderness, it is added: “And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon. And the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any more in heaven” (Rev. XII). For since the victory over the devil is spiritually accomplished in heaven—that is, in the Church—through ministering spirits, Michael, whose name is interpreted “Who is like God?”, and his angels are said to fight. But because the battle itself belongs to the holy martyrs, for whose sake the holy ministering or assisting angels are sent, it is immediately added: “And they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb, and through the word of their testimony; and they did not love their lives unto death” (ibid.). Thus, while these—namely, the blessed martyrs—were visibly dying before the eyes of the foolish, and those—namely, the blessed angels—were invisibly defending them, a place was made free in heaven. A place and a religion were prepared in the Church for the living and true God, so that sacrifice was now offered to the true God in more temples than sacrifice had formerly been offered to the devil in shrines.

He therefore says: “And that great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world, was cast down to the earth; and his angels were sent down with him” (ibid.). Certainly, his being said here to be cast down to earth belongs to that saying of the very King of martyrs, who was shortly to suffer: “Now shall the prince of this world be cast out” (John XVI). For where He suffered, by His power He at once cast out the prince of this world, or this dragon, from all the saints or elect whom He foreknew and predestined from the foundation of the world. Yet in actual fact He then cast him out only from those whom He had believing in Himself, whether dead or living, at the time of His Passion [Col. 1749A]. From them he was cast out in such a way that he could no longer even fight against them. But concerning those who had indeed already been predestined, though not yet called, he still dared to hope that he would conquer, so that they might not follow when called; and in this hope he fought in fury and with great wrath.

Hence it is immediately said: “Woe to the earth and the sea, because the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has but a short time” (Rev. XII). For great woe threatens those whom the most wicked enemy possesses in wrath: devouring and trampling them as earth, troubling them as sea, and taking vengeance upon those whom he more closely encloses for the wrath he feels because he has been expelled from the spiritual realm [Col. 1749B]. For this earth is that of which it was once said to the serpent: “You shall eat earth all the days” (Gen. III). While Michael and his angels fight upon this earth, as has already been said, and while the holy martyrs die and conquer by dying, he is crushed beneath their feet, as it is written: “You shall tread upon the asp and basilisk” (Ps. XC), and so forth.

## CHAPTER XVI. On these same innumerable conquerors, according to the saying: “After these things I saw a great multitude which no one could number.”

[Col. 1749C] Who can number the multitude of these conquerors? For it is written: “After these things I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands. And they cried with a loud voice, saying: Salvation belongs to our God, who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb” (Rev. VII).

Finally, these victors, so strong and so illustrious, having palms in their hands and clothed in white robes—although all the elect are rightly understood as clothed with robes through baptism and adorned with palms through the triumph of the cross—are especially those concerning whom it was already said in the passage mentioned above: “And they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb, and through the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives unto death” (Rev. XII) [Col. 1749D]. Likewise, elsewhere: “These are they who came out of great tribulation; they washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. VII).

For we judge that, besides that first robe which we all receive in baptism—which is one universal robe belonging to all who are regenerated—there are also individual robes belonging to each person, in accordance also with another passage of Scripture concerning fine linen: “Fine linen,” it says, “is the righteous deeds of the saints” (Rev. XIX). Such robes these fighters, coming out of great tribulation, washed in the blood of the Lamb: all who, after the fine linen of righteous deeds, after the beautiful adornment of good works, deserved to shed their own blood in testimony to the same Lamb, Christ the Son of God [Col. 1750A].

Yet very many, not yet adorned with such robes, hastened to confess the holy Name; shining with the freshness of baptism, not yet embellished with any adornments of works, they put on the glory of martyrdom. Of the faith of such persons one poet sang thus:

> First, amid the uncertain chance of combat, faith enters the field,  
> ready to fight, wild in rustic dress,  
> bare in the shoulders, with unshorn hair and bared arms.  
> For a sudden heat of praise, burning for new battles,  
> remembers neither weapons nor defensive covering.  
> But trusting in a strong heart and with limbs uncovered,  
> it challenges the perils of mad warfare to be broken.  
> (Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, vv. 21–27.)

Therefore all who attain the kingdom of God are conquerors, and palms are in their hands, because no one reaches that kingdom except by conquering its enemy. But far above the rest stand these, who conquered in a double manner: both by resisting sins, or the suggestions of the ancient serpent—which is the common victory of all the elect—and by not loving their lives unto death, which is the special triumph of the blessed martyrs [Col. 1750B].

For there remains for these that song, still sung today in heaven—that is, in the Church—by those who say with a loud voice: “Now have come salvation and strength and the kingdom of our God and the power of His Christ, because the accuser of our brethren has been cast down, he who accused them before our God day and night” (Rev. XII). For it follows: “And they conquered him through the blood of the Lamb, and through the word of their testimony, and they did not love their lives unto death” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XVII. On these same saints who will come with their Lord and King, and on blessed Lawrence, whom we cannot allow ourselves to pass over.

[Col. 1750C] Behold, we now celebrate the triumphant joy of these fighters, though we do not yet see the glory of their triumph itself. But behold, the Lord whom we await will appear; and though He delays, we who await Him do not fail, for He will indeed come, and with Him thousands of these saints, having written upon His thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. XIX).

He will come with the pageantry of His triumph, while the heavens tremble and all the powers of heaven are shaken; the insignia of this warfare and military arms will go before Him; and these soldiers, now unbelted after the labor they endured throughout the campaign of war, will advance—not without a great spectacle for heaven and earth [Col. 1750D]. Above all the victorious insignia of triumph, the cross of their King will appear.

We cannot note the faces of all or reverently name each one individually, for they are many and innumerable to us. We invoke the King Himself, the Lord Jesus, leader of all might, that, as He advances in this His triumph while we look on, He may deign to pause briefly; and that by the same hand by which He grants rewards to these victors, He may not deny us pardon for the sake of this very Name which we utter: Lord Jesus.

Yet we cannot allow one unknown or unseen leader among these to pass by: namely, him who stands nearest at His side, wondrous in appearance, venerable in bearing, fiery and ruddy, lofty in stature, serene in shining countenance—one taken, as it were, from a furnace of fire, and such as gold tested by fire [Col. 1751A]. Such a one, we believe, looks upon us and does not disdain to regard those who love and diligently proclaim the praises of his King.

If you ask his name, it is Lawrence; and it is especially delightful to hear that name from the mouth of his own King and Lord, because it is sweet and heartfelt for such a King to name and commend such a soldier. If He Himself who wrote in His book should utter this very name to us through His inward lips, and impress it upon our heart by the utterance of His tongue—that is, His Spirit—so that we may be able, even briefly, to say something worthily and perceptibly concerning him, there is no doubt that he will answer; and with that love by which, strong in death and stronger than death, he could not be overcome by flames, he will cheerfully smile upon us little ones with a holy kiss [Col. 1751B].

## CHAPTER XVIII. On his extraordinary death, how it was heard as a most mighty trumpet through the whole world, and on his foreknowledge of it when he said to Hippolytus: “Afterward, when I cry out, listen and come.”

It has been said before our time:

> Ancient mother of shrines,  
> now Rome, devoted to Christ,  
> under the victorious leadership of Lawrence  
> you triumph over barbarous rites.  
>   
> You had conquered proud kings  
> and curbed peoples with the reins [Col. 1751C];  
> now you impose the yoke of empire  
> upon monstrous idols.  
>   
> Not through the turbulent forces  
> of Cossus, Camillus, or Caesar,  
> but in the not bloodless battle  
> of the martyr Lawrence,  
> faith fought armed,  
> lavish with its own blood.  
> (Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn 2, vv. 1–15.)

Indeed, this could have been said of all the martyrs of the holy Roman Church, under whose leadership Rome triumphed over barbarous rites; but he is the chief leader of that triumph. For his unusual or unprecedented death was like the greatest trumpet of the whole war, heard throughout the world and sounding without ceasing.

Foreseeing that the novelty of his death would be admired through all ages, he himself told his recruit Hippolytus in words sufficiently solemn and weighty: “Hide Christ more deeply in the secret places of the inner man; afterward, when I cry out, listen and come” [Col. 1751D]. For Hippolytus had said: “Why do I not also cry aloud, since I am a Christian and recline with you?” He was, of course, rightly emulating the Roman who, in that same place, merely professed Christian soldiery and, crying, “I am a Christian,” immediately received the reward of eternal life together with the palm of martyrdom.

He therefore said, “When I cry out, listen and come,” comparing the great miracle of his Passion to a small thing, namely a vocal cry; for this manner of speech is called *tapeinosis*, that is, the humbling of a great thing, where the meaning does not intend what the expression appears to indicate. Yet in another sense he did not at all diminish the great thing, but rather magnified it: by saying, “when I cry out,” he signified that his death would be a tremendous cry, in the sense in which we read that the blood of Abel, the first martyr, cries from the earth to God (Gen. IV) [Col. 1752A].

“Listen to this cry,” he says, “and come”: that is, as an eager and resolute soldier, aroused and stirred by the signal of a great commander, by the sound of a mighty trumpet, rushes to battle. Therefore, after the leaders of the apostles, who came from the earlier Church of the Jews, from the flesh of the patriarchs and prophets, this man is the greatest leader of the Church of the Gentiles, the Roman Church, mother of Churches. Under this leader, says the poet, “O victorious Rome, you triumph over barbarous rites,” which you could not do through the turbulent forces of Cossus, Camillus, or Caesar. For those men, on the contrary, while conquering human beings in order to make you mistress of peoples, made you the slave of barbarous rites and captive of many demons [Col. 1752B].

## CHAPTER XIX. That this martyr is, in a certain likeness, another Abel.

Here we observe something worthy and beautiful: that this man is another Abel by a particular likeness, beyond the general distinction or opposition of good and evil, according to which all good people are customarily called Abel and all evil people Cain.

For what was Rome, on the side of the ungodly—as it had been until then—if not the city, dedication, or possession of fratricidal Cain? We do not say this because anything relevant to this mystery is contained in the fact that Romulus, founder of the City, killed his brother and fellow-worker Remus, or because, as someone says:

> The first walls were drenched with fraternal blood.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, I.95.)

For both were Cain, just as later Sulla and Marius, or Caesar and the great Pompey, were Cain. But we say this because Cain and his city were the whole of Rome, and all who founded it, advanced it by wars, and filled it with the blood of nations [Col. 1752C].

But Abel are and were all who, in Rome or from Rome, were begotten according to the flesh from the same father, Romulus, or the same mother, Rome, but regenerated according to the spirit from Christ and His holy Church. So too, all who from the beginning to the end of the age, in whatever part of the world and from whatever nation they are born according to the flesh, have been or are regenerated to God through faith, are all Abel; and all who do not belong to them are, on the contrary, Cain. Beyond this general or universal opposition, as already said, of the two generations of good and evil, this blessed martyr among us Gentiles is Abel by a particular likeness, and Decius Caesar, the most impious man who killed him, was Cain [Col. 1752D].

## CHAPTER XX. What likeness he had or enacted, so that we may rightly call him another Abel; and concerning his cry, by which he does not cease even now to cry out in the holy Church.

First, no one is unable to know or perceive that, just as Abel “offered a sacrifice, and God looked upon him and upon his gifts” (Gen. IV), and that was the cause of his death, so this man offered to God a great and famous sacrifice by giving the treasures of the Church to the poor; and this was likewise the first cause of his death [Col. 1753A].

That Cain was angry, and his countenance fell (Gen. IV), when he saw that the Lord had looked upon Abel and his gifts. And this possessor—or possession—of death, this tyrant of profound avarice, was angry when he saw the poor whose hands carried away the resources he sought and conveyed them into heavenly treasures. He was angry, I say, and his countenance fell. For he was unable to look upon or give attention to the loftiness and brightness of what was said in this manner: “These are eternal treasures, which never diminish or decrease; they are scattered among individuals and found in all.”

For we see that poor Christians are truly eternal treasures, since talents of graces have been distributed among them. “For to one,” says the Apostle, “through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit” (1 Cor. XII), together with the other gifts of grace. These are, indeed, for the most part granted more readily and abundantly by the steward or Lord of heavenly riches, the Holy Spirit, to the faithful poor, so that in their pilgrimage within their wretched body they may have a means of consoling their poverty, low estate, or weakness [Col. 1753B].

These gifts, scattered from the Lord’s treasures among individuals, are found in all; for charity makes common to all what is bestowed separately upon each one, just as the function performed by each individual member is common to all the members of one body. Such treasures never decrease or diminish, for no one loses a spiritual gift when he shares it for the benefit of his neighbors.

Therefore he was angry, and his countenance fell, as was said of those like him by the Psalmist: “They have fixed their eyes to bend down toward the earth” (Ps. XVI) [Col. 1753C]. This is said by comparison with judges or tyrants of any kind: whenever they wish someone to be cruelly punished, they do not wish to look upon the blows, but look at the ground, lest, seeing the sufferers’ blood, they be bent toward mercy. Thus it is said of this man that his countenance fell toward the earth: his purpose was to have no eyes of humility toward an innocent man.

And Cain said to his brother, in order to kill him: “Let us go out.” But this man shut the martyr inside the palace at night. The retreat was different, but the intention the same. Both this man and that intended to have leisure to perpetrate their crime without witnesses. For what would it be to roast a living man? Or how could it be done in public, in the sight of the sun, before so great and extensive a city? Although Rome was a beast, or a woman drunk with the blood of the saints, nevertheless, even through that bestial drunkenness, she had not so lost the face or eyes of a human being that every sex and age within her could endure such a spectacle with cruel indifference [Col. 1754A].

Therefore, at night and in the palace, with a few persons who themselves marvelled, that robber of cruelty ordered him to be roasted alive until the flesh to be devoured was fully cooked. The soul remained wondrously so long within the body, through that Spirit of might of whom we speak and whose glory we now proclaim, so that, if he had been a ram or at least a fish, he could have been eaten, and nothing that was still as it were raw might disagree unpleasantly with that malignant cook’s palate. Therefore he said: “Look, wretch, you have roasted one side; turn the other, and eat.”

Thus both that Cain said to Abel, “Let us go out,” and this Cain, after many blows in the daytime contest, ordered this Abel to be brought to him at night within the palace, with the same intention: namely, that he might safely, fearing no judgment from any man, even a silent one, feed upon the dainties of cruelty in a horrible crime [Col. 1754B].

This is his cry, which all of us have heard, concerning which he had said: “Afterward, when I cry out, listen and come.” The one to whom he said this heard it and, because of this cry, ran to the contest of the same confession. But this cry does not cease even today in the holy Roman Church; it leaps forth also into all the earth, taking up this proclamation or declamation from holy and prophetic Scripture: “You have proved my heart, O Lord, and visited me in the night; you have examined me by fire, and no iniquity has been found in me” (Ps. XVI).

For we truly say that, after Him of whom the Apostle speaks—“But you have come,” he says, “to Jesus the mediator of the New Testament, and to the sprinkling of blood speaking better things than Abel. See that you do not refuse Him who speaks” (Heb. XII)—this declamation fits the person of no blessed martyr known to us so well as it fits this man, who was thus visited and tested in the temporal night, or in the nighttime, and examined by material fire [Col. 1754C].

## CHAPTER XXI. On his saying: “I offered myself as a sacrifice to God for an odor of sweetness, because a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.”

Nor is it enough, for the devout veneration of this martyr, merely to hear or recite this cry of his, unless we perceive in our inmost sense the devout and sweet odor belonging to it. For he said: “I offered myself as a sacrifice to God for an odor of sweetness, because a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” [Col. 1754D].

But who knows what a contrite spirit is? Who knows this? Who is wise and understands it? Truly, no one except one who receives it. Contrition of spirit is a hidden treasure and is not easily found by just anyone. It is wholly hidden from the wise and great; only at last, and with difficulty, is it revealed to the little ones. Whoever finally finds it rightly rejoices and says: “I found tribulation and sorrow” (Ps. CXIV). For it is no small or slight discovery. It makes a place sure and fitting for invoking the name of the Lord.

Therefore, after saying, “I found tribulation and sorrow,” he immediately added, “and I called upon the name of the Lord”; understand that then it ought fittingly to have been invoked, since the same Spirit testifies elsewhere that “the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. XXXIII) [Col. 1755A]. Thus finding tribulation and sorrow creates the opportunity and the fitting time for invoking the Lord’s name as a good and not contemptible sacrifice. Therefore, after saying, “I offered myself as a sacrifice to God for an odor of sweetness,” he immediately added, “because a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.” This is the same as saying: “Because I found tribulation and sorrow.”

Therefore, if we who have heard this cry and exalt it in admiration also perceive the odor of the sacrifice that was burned—that is, of the contrite spirit—then at last we worthily praise this most valiant conqueror, the consul of heaven, heir of paradise, ornament of the Roman Empire; and worthily we weigh the gold of God, the jewel of the Son of God, the workmanship of the Holy Spirit, in whom You are most rightly glorified, You whom we proclaim, O Spirit of might [Col. 1756A].

# THE SEVENTH BOOK ON THE WORKS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT: ON KNOWLEDGE

[Col. 1755]

## CHAPTER I. On the holy Spirit of knowledge: how and why He was especially necessary in the Gospel of Christ.

After the battles of the martyrs, of which we spoke in the preceding volume, there followed in the Church of Christ the pursuits of holy and true philosophers—that is, learned teachers. After the Spirit of might, the holy Spirit of knowledge is set down next in descending order. This was necessary for evangelical faith because the devil, who had hitherto fought openly against it, is not only a lion but also a dragon: a lion because he rages openly, a dragon because he deceives secretly.

So long as he raged roaring through open persecution by Nero and others like him, compelling his satellites to deny the Christian name, he acted as a lion [Col. 1755C]. And so long as this was the case, even simple people without much knowledge could recognize that he was the devil and could avoid or fight him, not as one striking at random; for combat against him there was need almost solely of the Spirit of might.

But when the rulers of the age, in whom he trusted as in his weapons, had now inclined to the faith of Christ, and that strong one had been cast out from the temples or shrines of idols, he turned wholly to deceits under the Christian name, deceiving Christians through the phantasms of heresies. Then he began especially to act as a dragon does; and such a one could easily be recognized or refuted as the devil only by the prudent and those possessing knowledge—the one who had previously roared as a lion now hissing as a dragon. It was therefore expedient for evangelical faith that, after the Spirit of might, the Spirit of knowledge should come to aid it in its dangers in due order [Col. 1755D].

## CHAPTER II. What is the difference between knowledge and wisdom, since one Spirit is counted as the Spirit of knowledge and another as the Spirit of wisdom.

Here it must now be clearly distinguished what knowledge is and what wisdom is, and how they differ from each other. For there is evidently some difference, both from this enumeration of spirits, in which one is proclaimed the Spirit of wisdom and another the Spirit of knowledge [Col. 1756B], and from other passages of Scripture: for example, where it is said, “The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge” (Isa. XXXIII); and where the Apostle says of Christ: “In Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II).

We say, therefore, that knowledge is acquaintance with all good and lawful arts; but wisdom is love or reverence, not without holy fear, for one thing only—namely, God—if indeed He may be called a thing. A certain pagan also says that the first wisdom is to be free from folly.

We further say that those who possess knowledge of things however extensive, yet do not hold God in their knowledge, are improperly called wise, because they are in truth foolish. Thus the Apostle says of those who, philosophizing about the creation, knew the Creator but did not glorify Him: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I) [Col. 1756C].

Accordingly, if a man is wise, he is also knowing; but the converse does not follow: if he is knowing, he is also wise. Just as, if something is rational, it is also animal, but the converse does not follow, that if it is animal, it is rational. For truly, just as whatever remains when rationality is removed from an animal is brute, so whatever remains when wisdom—which is knowledge of God—is removed from knowledge is foolish. To make this clearer, let us now use divisions and show that chaste wisdom is contained within the very broad meaning of this word “knowledge.”

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 1756D] How the general name of knowledge is subdivided down to philosophy, and how one philosophy is empty while another is true and sound.

Knowledge is either literary or non-literary. Literary knowledge is learned through letters: such are all the arts contained in books. Non-literary knowledge is not learned through letters: such are sculpture or craftsmanship, and anything of this kind, which is rightly called knowledge but is not acquired by reading [Col. 1757A].

Again, literary knowledge is either liberal or illiberal. The art of medicine is literary and illiberal, an art which philosophers do not profess, although physicians attribute very great liberality to their art. They say that it is not numbered among the seven liberal arts because it consists of all of them or operates through all of them: that is, no one can truly be called or be a physician unless he is skilled in all the liberal arts.

But literary and liberal learning is called philosophy. It has three parts in logic, namely grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric; and four parts in physics: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy. Thus far secular masters of the arts have led the classification of knowledge through subdivisions.

But churchmen have further subdivided philosophy—which is the best and most excellent object of knowledge—calling one philosophy empty, that is, not according to God, and another sound and true, that is, according to God [Col. 1757B]. For the Apostle says to the Colossians: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ” (Col. II).

What he had said, “through philosophy,” he repeated by saying, “empty deceit”; and he explained why he had so described philosophy, or empty deceit, by adding: “according to the tradition of men, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ.” Therefore there is another philosophy opposed to this, which is not according to the tradition of men but according to Christ; not empty or deceitful, but weighty and true.

How philosophy according to Christ is undertaken or practiced is taught by apostolic and evangelical writings—indeed, by prophetic writings also. Whoever truly possesses knowledge for the service of the truth that is Christ finds in them whatever is useful from the seven liberal arts, distributed with the utmost gravity and fitness [Col. 1757C]. Therefore philosophy—that is, literary and liberal knowledge—is one thing when practiced according to the elements of the world or the tradition of men, and another when practiced according to Christ. In the former manner it is rightly called empty or deceitful philosophy; in the latter manner, it is called simply knowledge or philosophy, or—with an addition—sound philosophy or knowledge of God.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1757D] On the measured term “philosophy,” why it was adopted or approved; on vain philosophers who, “professing themselves to be wise, became fools”; and on the saying: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.”

Philosophy is interpreted as “love of wisdom.” The more prudent rightly preferred to give this name to knowledge of the liberal arts. For some wished to call that discipline wisdom, and themselves wise. But more careful thinkers judged that many people possessing knowledge of such arts nevertheless lived in such a way that even in the judgment of human beings they rightly appeared unworthy of the name of wise persons, since they did not know true and heavenly wisdom.

Therefore they did not wish to call it wisdom, because this knowledge does not make all who attain it wise—that is, free from folly. At the same time, it seemed close to arrogance for them to call themselves wise, a vice alien to wise persons [Col. 1758A]. Yet if they called it knowledge, their study would not, under that name, be honored more than the capacities of the other arts which are not liberal, though these too, as was said above, must be held under the generic name of knowledge.

Thus, using a moderated term, they preferred well to call such knowledge philosophy, that is, love of wisdom, and themselves philosophers, that is, lovers of wisdom. Yet even in doing this, they did indeed speak more honorably, but nonetheless called themselves wise, because they wished to be regarded as wise; and, says the Apostle, “professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I) [Col. 1758B].

Why? Because they did not care, by the path of such philosophy or knowledge, to reach the abode of true wisdom—that is, to glorify God and give thanks to God. Rebuking them for this, the same Apostle says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those human beings who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because that which is known of God is manifest in them. For God revealed it to them. For His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood through the things that have been made and are seen” (ibid.), and so forth.

Therefore he does not condemn studies, or the schools of grammarians, dialecticians, rhetoricians, arithmeticians, geometers, musicians, and astronomers. Rather, he reproves in them this: that they did not seek from these studies the fruit of wisdom for which these arts were given by God—namely, to have God in their knowledge and glorify Him as God [Col. 1758C].

Further, one should know that in many places “wisdom” is written or spoken in place of “knowledge” in common usage. For example, in the Acts of the Apostles Stephen says: “Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts VII). And the Apostle speaks to the Corinthians: “For it is written: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.” And then: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of preaching to save those who believe.” And shortly afterward: “But God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. I).

Yet in speaking thus, he does not call wisdom or men wise according to his own sense or judgment—for he says to the Romans, “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools”—but he strikes more sharply at their haughty self-estimation, by which they seemed wise to themselves [Col. 1758D].

## CHAPTER V. That everything to which the term knowledge is rightly applied is a gift of God, and that therefore the Holy Spirit is rightly called the Spirit of knowledge.

Knowledge and wisdom thus differ as greater and lesser, because we signify more things by the term “knowledge” than by the term “wisdom,” and “knowledge” is the more general name. That all things which we distinguished under this genus, knowledge, by dividing it, are gifts of God—and that therefore the Holy Spirit is rightly proclaimed the Spirit of knowledge—is more than sufficiently established by examples. Nevertheless, let us briefly give particular examples of each.

We are taught that non-literary and illiberal knowledge is a gift of God when we read in Exodus: “Behold, the Lord called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom and understanding and knowledge in every kind of instruction, to devise and make work in gold and silver and bronze, in carving stones, and in carpentry” (Exod. XXXI) [Col. 1759A]. Whatever can be invented by craftsmanship, He gave into his heart. “And Oholiab also, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan” (ibid.). “He instructed both of them with wisdom, that they might make the works of the carpenter, the embroiderer, and the needleworker, in blue and purple, scarlet twice dyed, and fine linen.”

Here both wisdom and knowledge are mentioned, as also understanding: namely, because Bezalel, filled with the Spirit of God, inwardly perceived the divine meanings of those works which he outwardly made through artistic knowledge.

Likewise, that literary and illiberal knowledge, such as the art of medicine, is a gift of God is taught by that saying of the Wise Man: “Honor the physician” (Ecclus. XXXVIII), for medicine is not except from God. That literary and liberal knowledge, which is philosophy, is a gift of God is evident also from what is written in Daniel: “But to these youths, namely Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, God gave knowledge and learning in every book and wisdom; but to Daniel He gave understanding of all visions and dreams. And they stood before the king, and in every matter of wisdom and understanding about which the king questioned them, he found them tenfold superior to all the diviners and magicians who were in his whole kingdom” (Dan. I) [Col. 1759C].

## Chapter VI. How the Apostle’s saying, “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up,” makes the name of knowledge suspect to those who misunderstand it

This great and beautiful grace of the Holy Spirit is even today suspect to simpler people, chiefly because the Apostle, speaking to the Corinthians, says of it: “Now concerning things sacrificed to idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8). They have heard almost this alone, and remember this alone—that he said, “Knowledge puffs up”—without asking, or knowing how to ask, either what he said or why he added, “but charity builds up.” As though knowledge and charity were opposites and could not coexist; and as though, by setting them in opposition, he had said, “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up.” Thus knowledge seems to them to be neglected—indeed, despised—and only when they have turned their whole minds away from the pursuit of knowledge do they think they can truly say: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; neither have I walked in great matters” (Ps. 130). “For,” they say, “the Apostle of Christ says, ‘Knowledge puffs up.’”

But he did not say this in that sense; he did not wish his saying to be understood in that way. Nor did he wish to oppose charity to knowledge, but to join it to knowledge. For knowledge—understand, without charity—puffs up; but charity—understand, together with knowledge—builds up. Thus charity and knowledge are rightly joined, and walk together in Holy Scripture, just as wisdom and knowledge do. For charity itself is true wisdom. Charity indeed builds up somewhat even without knowledge; with knowledge it builds up greatly. But knowledge without charity puffs up.

Otherwise, he who says these things would be declaring himself to be puffed up—which is absurd. For before saying, “Knowledge puffs up,” he had prefaced it: “We know that we all have knowledge.” His purpose, therefore, is that the wise Corinthians, who possess knowledge, should also possess charity: that is, that they should not scandalize weaker brethren by eating food sacrificed to idols and arguing that what has been offered is nothing, because an idol is nothing. For nothing substantial has been added to wood, stone, or bronze to make it an idol; rather, by the craftsman’s hand an image has been formed as an accident. Such knowledge indeed puffs up when, lacking charity, it takes no concern that the conscience of brethren is defiled because it is weak. [Col. 1760B]

Therefore, the saying, “Knowledge puffs up,” ought not to make knowledge suspect or contemptible in the judgment of an ecclesiastical man. Rather, it should be judged honourable, as it truly is: first because the Holy Spirit numbers it among His seven principal gifts; then because divine authority commends it thus in Daniel: “Those who have been learned shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, as stars for everlasting eternities” (Dan. 12).

## Chapter VII. Why knowledge was especially necessary in the Gospel of Christ, when the serpent cast down to earth sent water from his mouth after the woman like a river, to cause her to be swept away by the river; and concerning the doctrine of the impious Arius

Therefore, as we said above, after the battles of the martyrs had been celebrated by the Spirit of fortitude, the holy Spirit of knowledge fittingly succeeded to His work. For that dragon, the ancient serpent, who had been cast down from heaven—where he had presumptuously claimed divinity—to earth by those who fought, so that he might no longer be worshipped in temples or receive sacrifice in public cults, through the mouths of evil men such as Arius, began to hiss blasphemies against the Son of God, so as likewise to draw the simple people after himself. They were unable, or did not know how, to avoid the poison of death concealed in the beauty of his speech.

This is what had been magnificently foreshown in the Apocalypse by that truly great, truly wondrous sign: “And when the dragon saw that he had been cast down to earth, he persecuted the woman who had borne the male child” (Rev. 12). And immediately after: “And the serpent sent water from his mouth after the woman like a river, that he might cause her to be swept away by the river” (ibid.). What was that most evil river, sent forth from the dragon’s mouth after Michael and his angels had fought and he had been cast down to earth, if not the teaching of talkative heretics, flowing in their fluency? They began especially then to flow, when the supreme emperors, converted to the faith of Christ, fighting with the holy angels and the Church of God by laws and edicts, had driven the devil from his former seats—from the old temples and altars.

Certainly the aforesaid Arius was the dragon’s mouth, from which, as we read in ecclesiastical histories, that foul river burst forth in this kind of flow: “Some say that the Son is an eructation; others, an emanation; others, co-unbegotten. These impieties we cannot even hear, though heretics threaten us with innumerable deaths. But because we say, think, have taught, and teach that the Son is neither unbegotten nor in any way a part of the Unbegotten, nor derived from another substrate, but subsists by will and counsel before times and before ages as full God, only-begotten, mutable; and that before He was begotten or created, predestined or founded, He was not—for He was not unbegotten—we suffer persecution, because he said: ‘The Son has a beginning, but God is without beginning.’ And because we said, ‘He is from things not existing’—and we said this in the sense that He is neither a part of God nor from any substrate—for that reason we suffer persecution.” [Col. 1761A–B]

This heresy was foul water, and not yet a great river, when it flowed from its own source, from that mouth of the dragon. But just as we see any river first flow from its source in a narrow channel, then grow as it proceeds, and, with many waters or little streams running into it, swell boundlessly; so the strength of that most impious heresy gradually increased as it crept onward, and grew beyond measure. Many tongues of many people converged upon it: tongues loud in speech, flowing with abundance of eloquence, and arguing against the simplicity of evangelical faith, until that great, shipwrecking river overflowed nearly the whole world. There could be no doubt that it had been sent forth from the mouth of the ancient dragon.

“But the earth,” he says, “helped the woman; and the earth opened its mouth and swallowed the river which the dragon sent from his mouth” (ibid.). How did the earth help the woman, or how did it swallow the river? Certainly, by letters of the Christian Empire, that holy and most renowned Council of Nicaea—of three hundred and eighteen bishops—was assembled to help that woman, to aid the Catholic Church in danger. With them, as leaders and commanders in the Lord’s wars, gathered very many good and excellent men from diverse nations: some exceptionally fitted to understand and speak, trained in every sort of knowledge or learning that it befitted this holy Spirit of knowledge to suggest or bestow, and at the same time distinguished by virtue of life. Through them Christ raised the dead, healed the living, and worked countless other miracles. [Col. 1761C–D]

There indeed the earth helped the woman; there it swallowed that river. For it condemned Arius’s impious doctrine and the other plagues of heresies which sprang up with or from that doctrine. The ages still marvel that the Holy Spirit fought there for the truth with the same number of bishops as that with which Father Abraham once, leading out the armed servants born in his own household against victorious kings, triumphed in his faith.

But what followed? “And the dragon,” he says, “was angry with the woman, and went to make war with the rest of her seed, who keep the commandments of God and have the testimony of Jesus” (ibid.). For the dragon, the devil, did not rest after that heretical river had been swallowed up in this way, and after Arius had perished in a destruction he deserved. Rather, he most bitterly restored his strength through the fickleness of Constantius, and cruelly availed himself of the pride of the utterly impious Valens. Armed with their powers, angry with the woman, he proceeded to make war with the rest of her seed. Through them he raged no less than he had raged through Decius or Nero in open and public persecutions. [Col. 1762A]

## Chapter VIII. On the thirst of the saints who helped that woman, and on the prophetic invitation: “All you who thirst, come to the waters”

Worn out and breathless from this conflict, all who belonged to her seed began to burn and, with good desire, to thirst for the living springs of knowledge. At once they perceived that the Holy Spirit had spoken through the prophet especially for them and in such a matter: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy and eat. Come, buy wine and milk without silver and without any exchange” (Isa. 55).

Thus the thirsty came; coming, they thirsted; and they sat beside the fullest streams of the Scriptures, like doves washed with milk—that is, possessing a simple and kindly eye, which is of great value for attaining the truth of the Scriptures and understanding the meaning in which the Scriptures speak of God. By contrast, the contentious heretics seized words and misunderstood the sense of Scripture because they possessed the malicious eye of envy and sought their own glory rather than God’s. Swollen, quarrelsome, verbose, and arrogant, they breathed a devilish pride against God and neighbour in the loftiness of their speech. [Col. 1762B–C]

For this reason they produced heresies and schisms: puffed up in spirit, exceedingly false and deceptive, they imagined that they could bind the words of truth in the chains of dialectical—indeed sophistical—vanity. In truth, however, the art of dialectic does not pursue truth or bind the word of God; rather, if anyone uses it lawfully, it follows truth and confirms the true word of God by faithful arguments. Let one who is both studious and well disposed toward dialectic and rhetoric carefully observe the course of Holy Scripture, and he will see that these handmaids attend it as their mistress.

Accordingly, all who belonged to the seed of this woman and considered with what affection children ought to defend the chastity of their mother, the Church, approached the waters. Therefore they usefully understood Holy Scripture, precisely because they sought not their own glory but God’s, and desired to defend their mother both by their life and by their death. For this is the path, rule, or condition of learning. In the previously mentioned chapter of the prophet, God Himself, the Lord of knowledge, sets it forth: “Hearken, listening to me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in abundance. Incline your ear and come to me; hear, and your soul shall live” (Isa. 55).

In saying, “Hearken, listening to me,” He had not yet expressed the necessary manner of hearing; and therefore He added: “Incline your ear and come to me.” Then He immediately repeated what He had prefaced: “Hearken, listening to me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in abundance,” saying: “Hear me, and your soul shall live.” Finally, “incline your ear” means “humble your mind.” For the one who bends in humility is worthy to be taught, according to the saying: “Those who draw near to His feet shall receive of His teaching” (Deut. 33). [Col. 1763A]

## Chapter IX. How Jesus, then wearied, sat upon the well and gave living water to the thirsty

Therefore these thirsty persons came to the waters while the Lord Jesus had long been sitting upon the well and asking the Samaritan woman to give Him something to drink, because He was weary (John 4). And who had wearied Him? First, the Jew who had crucified Him; then the heretic who had now blasphemed Him. From the weariness of the cross or death He had indeed already recovered in Himself, because He had risen again; but from the weariness of blasphemy He still laboured in certain of His members, in certain of His faithful who were being troubled.

Weary, therefore, He sat upon the well of lower water, upon the depth of worldly knowledge. He desired to drink, intending in grateful exchange to give the living water of His own knowledge; He invited to the water those who thirsted for it. For this was a grateful exchange: that believers who possessed the resources of the liberal arts should, by using them well against heretics who used the same arts badly, defend the truth. This was to give drink to Jesus, weary and thirsty; and to those who did this, He gave living water by opening their understanding ever more fully to comprehend the truth of the Scriptures. [Col. 1763B–C]

Thus there came about a friendly and beautiful commerce. They offered to the Lord who asked the water which they had drawn from the wells of philosophy, of which He Himself said: “Everyone who drinks of this water shall thirst again.” And they received from Him, as already stated, living water, of which the same Lord says: “Whoever drinks shall never thirst” (ibid.). Yet “who has first given to Him, and it shall be repaid to him?” (Rom. 11). Certainly no one. For, as was said above, prophetic knowledge and every lawful kind of knowledge are His gift; but He is accustomed to give greater gifts to those who use His good gifts well.

Moreover, this too must not later be passed over: those whom He deigned to have as defenders of ecclesiastical faith, whose tongue He Himself made effective against heretics or for the instruction of His Church, He Himself provided that they should first be trained in the liberal arts. Before descending into the perils of the sea to fight, they were, as it were, trained first near the shore in lighter exercises.
