Thus they received and drank living water, so that a fountain might arise in them and their fountains might be distributed abroad, and they might distribute their waters in the streets: that is, they might not merely read and understand the writings of others, but themselves write what others could profitably read. [Col. 1763C–D]

## Chapter X. How the seven liberal arts then especially entered the ecclesiastical dining-hall of their mistress, Wisdom, and how greatly it matters whether words adorn things or things adorn words

The seven liberal arts entered, therefore, like handmaids into the sacred and reverend dining-hall of their mistress, Wisdom. They were arranged and commanded to sit there, as though brought from licentious crossroads into the strict and stern teaching of the word of God. For previously they had wandered about: wanton, chattering, wordy little girls, doing nothing but busying themselves with curiosity. They seemed more active as they ran about investigating creation, while neglecting the Creator Himself.

They were therefore set to work, so that they might no longer tell superfluous tales about the creation of the world, but might seriously and faithfully speak what was fitting about the Creator, and might labour to weave a good discourse to His honour with splendid workmanship: that is, so that things might no longer be adorned by words, but words by things. [Col. 1764A]

For this is the difference between discourse concerning creation and the vain, and sometimes false, matters disputed by men, and discourse treating of the Creator or eternal life: there poor and meagre things are adorned with verbal cosmetics sought from every quarter; here words, however resonant and brilliant, are surpassed and adorned by the majesty of the things or meanings themselves. Hence to that school the prophet says tropologically: “Take up the harp, go about the city, O harlot given over to forgetfulness. Sing well, repeat the song often, that remembrance of you may endure” (Isa. 23). But Christ Himself says in the Song of Songs: “Your lips distil a honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song 4). Again: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears” (Song 2).

And rightly is that one called a harlot, while this one is called the friend of the wise. The former strives to please spectators or hearers everywhere and to commend herself; the latter seeks to show not herself, nor any beautiful or desirable creature, but God alone as beautiful and worthy of every desire. She seeks entirely not her own glory, but God’s. [Col. 1764B–C]

But why do we say that these arts were then admitted into that school? It would be truer to say that, although they had previously been unknown to have entered, from that time they appeared within it. For those who searched the Scriptures intelligently found this to be so, experienced it to be so, and were greatly astonished not merely that the arts were there, but that they lay so hidden beneath the light and majesty of their mistress, Wisdom, that it was not easy to perceive that they were there. It is almost as when the sun shines upon the earth: the new moon, the waning moon, and the stars in the same region of the sky are hidden, and the common observer does not see that they are there. For the moon and stars shine in one hemisphere when the sun is absent and circles through the other; but they cannot shine in the same hemisphere with the sun.

In much the same way, although the arts of liberal learning are present together with the wisdom of God in Holy Scripture, they cannot ordinarily appear brilliant there, though in other inquiries they are accustomed to show themselves and shine greatly on their own. They especially do not appear, though they are there, because Holy Scripture uses them in such a way as not to state how they should be used. Let us not be reluctant to go through the individual arts and establish what has been said by a few examples.

## Chapter XI. On the first of them, grammar and its parts: how Holy Scripture uses them so as not to pass over even fable; and how it possessed beforehand what Greek authors boast of having discovered

The first of the liberal arts, grammar—that is, skill in speaking—is so present, and was first present, in Holy Scripture, or the wisdom of God, that there can be no doubt that the Hebrews received, with the law of the Lord through Moses, the rudiments of this art itself: namely, the common letters followed by copyists, the study of which is like a certain infancy of grammatical art.

It is not the business of the present undertaking to describe and distinguish the divisions of grammatical art, which some number as thirty: the eight parts of speech; articulated sound; syllable; metrical feet; accents; punctuation; notation; orthography; analogy; etymology; gloss; distinction; barbarism; solecism; faults; metaplasm; figures; tropes; prose; metres; fables; and history. Yet it is so true that these are contained or observed in Scripture that it does not even omit fable. Grammarians named fables from *fari*, “to speak,” because they are not events that happened but things invented only in speech. They were introduced so that, by a fictional conversation among dumb animals, or even among things without life, some image of human life might be discerned. [Col. 1765A–B]

The son of Jerubbaal uses it thus in the book of Judges: “Hear me, men of Shechem, so that God may hear you. The trees went to anoint a king over themselves. And they said to the olive tree: ‘Rule over us.’ It answered: ‘Can I abandon my fatness, by which gods and men make use of me, and come to be set over the trees?’ And the trees said to the fig tree: ‘Come and receive kingship over us’” (Judg. 9), etc.

And in Chronicles, when Amaziah king of Judah had sent to the king of Israel saying, “Come, let us look one another in the face,” the latter sent messengers back, saying: “The thistle that is in Lebanon sent to the cedar of Lebanon, saying: ‘Give your daughter to my son as a wife.’ And behold, the beasts that were in the forest passed by and trampled the thistle” (2 Chron. 25).

Figures also—whose Greek name, *schemata*, we rightly render “attire,” “form,” or “figure,” because through them speech is in some fashion clothed and adorned—may plainly be recognized as occurring everywhere in Holy Scripture. Thus in the Psalm: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Ps. 86). This figure is called *prolepsis*, that is, anticipation or presupposition, when matters that ought to follow are placed first. For he first puts “its,” saying, “Its foundations,” and afterward adds whose they are—namely, the Lord’s—by saying, “The Lord loves.” Thus the remaining figures, or kinds of figure, are found scattered through Holy Scripture. [Col. 1765C–D]

The Greeks indeed boast that they discovered such figures and tropes. But since Holy Scripture surpasses every other scripture not only in authority, because it is divine, or in usefulness, because it leads to eternal life, but also in antiquity, their boasting is not merely empty but false. Likewise, Scripture has not been ignorant of metres, so called because they are bounded by fixed measures and intervals of feet. Lyric metres composed the Psalter; and almost the whole book of holy Job consists of hexameter verses, running with dactyl and spondee. [Col. 1766A]

## Chapter XII. On rhetoric, or the parts of rhetoric: how sacred Scripture uses all these well, as matter and occasion require

Whoever has ever somewhere beheld rhetoric—that is, the art of speaking well—with open eyes, so as to recognize its face truly, will not be mistaken, upon approaching the Scripture of which we speak, unless perhaps he is asleep or blinded by the cloud of ill will, in saying that it is especially present there.

Let us briefly collect examples here of its first part, invention. For rhetoric has five parts: invention, arrangement, style, memory, and delivery. Considering invention, then, let us first say that the invention of these true rhetoricians of whom we now speak—those who, in writing Holy Scripture, plead God’s cases with humankind—is surpassing and most true. For what they found to say or declare, they found not, like rhetoricians engaged in forensic or civic practice, from their own heart or talent, but from the Holy Spirit. As the Apostle Peter also says: “Understanding this first: that no prophetic Scripture comes by one’s own interpretation. For prophecy was not brought at any time by human will, but holy men of God spoke while inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1). [Col. 1766B–C]

Rhetoricians say that this invention is exercised or expended in six parts: introduction, narration, division, confirmation, refutation, and conclusion. “Introduction,” they say, “is the beginning of a speech by which the mind of the hearer or judge is established or prepared for hearing. Narration is an account of things done, or said to have been done. Division is that by which we make clear what is agreed concerning the matter in controversy, and by which we set forth the matters of which we shall speak. Confirmation is the presentation of our arguments with assertion. Refutation is the discussion of opposing arguments. Conclusion is the artful end of a speech.”

They divide the first of these parts, the introduction, into two: the direct opening and insinuation. The direct opening, they say, occurs when we immediately, by overt arguments, make the hearer’s mind fit to listen to us—that is, attentive, teachable, and well disposed. Insinuation occurs when, recognizing that the hearer’s mind has been alienated from us by the nature of the case, we secretly and by dissimulation accomplish all this, so that in the work of speaking we may attain the same advantage. [Col. 1766C–D]

Again, they say that if the kind of cause is honourable, one may use or not use a direct opening. But what dishonourable cause does the holy Spirit, author of Holy Scripture, undertake or wish to be heard in? Therefore those rhetoricians ought not rightly to criticize Him: He may use or not use direct openings. For Moses did not use a direct opening but began the statement with narration, saying: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). Neither Joshua, nor the books of Judges or Kings, used direct openings; but they likewise began with narration.

This was not by chance or ignorance. For where it seemed expedient, no one knew or could use a direct opening better than Moses, not merely so as to make men attentive, but even to make the heavens themselves attentive, and the earth herself eager to hear, when he says: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deut. 32). The patriarch Jacob also knew fittingly how to do the same when he said: “Gather together and hear, sons of Jacob; hear, Israel, your father. Gather together, that I may declare to you what shall come upon you in the last days” (Gen. 49). This plainly is a direct opening by one eager to make his sons attentive, teachable, and well disposed to hear. [Col. 1767A–B]

At other times too, throughout nearly every chapter of the law and the prophets, the same kind of direct opening is effective, as in: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying,” or “Thus says the Lord of hosts” (Exod. 32). But the woman of Tekoa uses insinuation—the other species of introduction, which they say should be employed when the hearer’s mind has been alienated, offended, or wearied by listening—before King David. His mind had been alienated from his son Absalom by the dreadful nature of the case. She speaks thus: “Alas! I am a widow; my husband is dead, and your handmaid had two sons. They quarrelled with one another in the field, and there was no one who could restrain them. One struck the other and killed him. And behold, the whole kindred rises up against your handmaid, saying: ‘Hand over him who struck his brother, that we may kill him for the life of his brother whom he killed, and destroy his inheritance’” (2 Sam. 14), etc. [Col. 1767B–C]

But why seek examples here or there, when Wisdom incarnate herself deigned to use this method with her own mouth? For He said: “Simon, I have something to say to you.” And he said: “Master, speak.” “Two debtors owed a certain lender: one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them, then, loves him more?” (Luke 7), etc. There are many other examples according to the same method, with an introduction prefaced or not prefaced, as the speaker wills.

How brief and how clear is every narration in Holy Scripture! We judge—and certainly do not judge wrongly—that every narration by secular writers, however carefully composed, is loose, ragged, and miserably obscure in comparison with it. It is so brief and so lucid that in a wonderful and almost ineffable manner it always delights the hearer and always holds him in fresh interest. What is no less remarkable, it is so easy that anyone may trust himself capable of imitating it, yet so weighty that no one can attain its measure. Thus you may most rightly say with Flaccus:

> So that anyone  
> May hope to do the same, sweat much, and labour in vain  
> When daring to do the same.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica*, 240–242)

And elsewhere:

> He will scratch his head before he writes, and gnaw his living nails.  
> Turn your stylus often, if you are to write what is worthy of being read.  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.10.70–73) [Col. 1768A]

By what division the holy Spirit, the Author of Scripture, makes use of it—although we could give many splendid examples—we shall set forth only one, taken from the previously mentioned passage of the Gospel. Simon had said within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman it is who touches him, because she is a sinner” (Luke 7). On this, certainly, Simon and the Lord were agreed: she was a sinner. For the Lord willingly allowed himself to be touched; Simon silently reproved that touch. He therefore employed division, because, leaving aside the point that she was a sinner, he undertook to defend the fact that she touched him. “Do you see this woman?” he says. “I entered your house: you gave me no water for my feet; but she has watered my feet with tears and wiped them with her hair” (ibid.), and so forth.

Defence is effected through confirmation and refutation: through the confirmation, namely, of one’s own side, and the refutation of the opposing side. Let us take examples of these, so as not to go farther afield, from the same passage. For, by continually juxtaposing three pairs of propositions in opposition, he confirms on the one hand the true righteousness of the penitent woman, which arises from faith and love, and on the other hand refutes false righteousness by rebuking it. “You gave me no water for my feet, but she has watered my feet with tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss; but she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased to kiss my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil; but she has anointed my feet with ointment” (ibid.). Finally, how gently and temperately does the fourth contrast avoid aggravating the odium of rebuke? For he says: “Therefore I say to you: many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much. But he to whom less is forgiven loves less” (ibid.). In short, it is as if he said: “But you, who, as you suppose, have less to be forgiven, love less.” The sense is: to this woman, who loves much, many sins are forgiven by a great remission; but to you, who love less, your sins are forgiven less.

At last, in the conclusion—which is the artistic ending of a discourse—he proceeds not so much artfully as wisely and justly, when he says: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (ibid.). In confirmation and refutation, rhetoricians consider it a great matter to employ arguments; and they judge it very difficult to polish and deliver fluently what they have discovered. “This,” they say, “prevents us from lingering longer than necessary on the same points, from repeatedly returning to the same thing, from abandoning an argument once begun, or from passing awkwardly to another.” They call that argument most complete and perfect which is divided into five parts: proposition, reason, confirmation of the reason, embellishment, and conclusion.

The Spirit of God neither failed to know nor disdained this in his Scripture. If you attend carefully, it shines forth in no few examples. Indeed, the clearer examples are more numerous; but we wish now briefly to give some examples from a place where this faculty is perhaps less apparent. The proposition is that verse of the eighth Psalm: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” (Psalm 8). In it the Prophet briefly indicates what he intends to prove. The reason is what he appends in the following two verses:

“Because your magnificence is exalted above the heavens. Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise because of your enemies, that you might destroy the enemy and the avenger” (ibid.).

By these words he demonstrates the truth of what he intends: namely, that the Lord’s name is wonderful because Christ was magnificently exalted and ascended into heaven; and then, out of the mouth of the apostles, who were like infants—that is, unlearned and illiterate men (Acts 4)—he perfected the praise of evangelical faith or preaching.

The confirmation of the reason is what he adds: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you have founded” (Psalm 8). This verse briefly confirms the point he had set forth: namely, that it is not so astonishing or incredible that the Lord should perfect praise out of the mouths of infants, since those who had been infants or nursing children became, upon receiving the Holy Spirit, heavens, upon whose faith the moon and stars—that is, the Church and all the elect—could be founded.

The embellishment is contained in the following verses:

“What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you visit him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, moreover also the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea” (ibid.).

By these verses he notably dignified and enriched the matter with the abundant adornment of piety, marvelling at the greatness of God’s condescension: how he sought so greatly after man, cast down so far from eternity by the envy of the devil.

The conclusion is the repetition of the first verse: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth!” For by this conclusion he briefly gathers up the parts of the argument. This, then, is a complete five-part argument of confirmation: it confirms that the Lord’s name is wonderful in all the earth.

In the following Psalm, however, from the verse which says, “Arise, O Lord, let not man prevail,” to that which says, “Arise, O Lord God, let your hand be exalted” (Psalm 9), there is likewise, if you consider it rightly, a complete five-part argument of refutation. For it refutes the hostile man of sin, the son of perdition, of whom the Apostle says: “who exalts himself above everything that is called God or is worshipped” (2 Thessalonians 2).

There are, moreover, occasions when shorter arguments are made by omitting one or two parts: namely, when the matter to be stated is briefer and easily entrusted to memory. Then embellishment should be omitted if the subject appears insufficiently rich for enlargement and adornment. But if the matter is both slight and lowly, then both embellishment and conclusion should be omitted. Such arguments occur in such abundance in our Scriptures that I consider it superfluous to give examples, especially since, in accordance with our purpose, enough has been said and we must hasten on to other matters.

Moreover, our orators or discoverers have also admitted the three kinds of causes: demonstrative, deliberative, and judicial. For they deal not briefly with the praise or blame of some particular person—indeed, of very many definite persons—which are the parts of the demonstrative kind; for example, when God is praised or the devil blamed. Likewise, persuasion and dissuasion, the parts of the deliberative kind, sound forth neither rarely nor lightly: they commend good and dissuade from evil. Likewise, they very frequently handle accusation and defence, which are parts of the judicial kind: accusing the unjust and defending the just. Thus, for example, in the Apostle, the injustice of one man, through which many were made sinners, is accused; and the righteousness of one man, through which many are made righteous, is defended (Romans 5).

No secular writer has ever handled, or could handle, as justly and wisely as they are handled in the holy Scriptures of which we speak, the issues which they call conjectural, legal, and juridical. A conjectural issue occurs when there is controversy about a fact, as follows: someone entrusted to his neighbour for safekeeping an ass, ox, sheep, or any beast of burden, and perhaps it died, was injured, or was captured by enemies, but no one saw it. What then shall be done? “An oath,” Scripture says, “shall be between them, that he has not laid his hand upon his neighbour’s property; and the Lord shall accept the oath, and he shall not be compelled to make restitution” (Exodus 22). And there are many similar cases.

A legal issue occurs when a controversy arises from a written text or texts, as follows. The Jews thought that they were faithfully fulfilling the divine Scripture of the holy Law by offering incense and eating the flesh of sacrifice. But what does Scripture say? “Add your burnt offerings to your victims and eat the flesh. For I did not speak to your fathers or command them, on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and victims. But I commanded them this word, saying: Hear my voice, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people” (Jeremiah 7), and so forth.

But above all, the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews (chapter 7), stands upon this issue, comparing the will of the writer—indeed, of God—with the writing or letter on which the Jew alone relies, or preferring that will to the letter; and he explains sufficiently intelligibly and convincingly the intention of the aforementioned writer.

A juridical issue occurs when the deed is agreed upon—that is, it is not denied that it was done—but the question is whether it was done lawfully or unlawfully. It has two parts, one called absolute and the other assumptive. The absolute part is wholly condemned in the judgments of the Lord. It is called absolute when the very deed that was done is said to have been done rightly, so that nothing external is introduced. But before the Lord, nothing which has been rightly done is questioned as though it had not been done rightly. Therefore this part is blameworthy before him and deserves no pardon. Such is the following:

“What is this,” Samuel says, “the sound of sheep which resounds in my ears, and of herds which I hear?” (1 Samuel 15). And afterward: “Why, then, did you not obey the voice of the Lord, but turned to plunder and did evil in the eyes of the Lord?” Saul said: “Indeed, I obeyed the voice of the Lord, and went on the way on which the Lord sent me; I brought Agag, king of Amalek, and destroyed Amalek” (ibid.), and so forth.

The other part is assumptive, which in God’s judgments is partly admitted and partly condemned. Its four parts are concession, removal of the charge, transfer of the charge, and comparison. Concession of guilt is not merely admitted by God: it is almost the only thing, or at least the chief thing, which is admitted. For concession occurs when the accused asks to be forgiven. Indeed, we are all guilty before him; this is the whole path of our peace; and that person is most righteous who most fully acknowledges guilt and most earnestly asks forgiveness for himself, according to the saying: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Proverbs 18).

This concession has two parts: supplication and exculpation. Supplication occurs when the accused confesses both that he acted deliberately and that he sinned, yet asks for mercy; for example, David: “Against you alone,” he says, “have I sinned, and done evil before you” (Psalm 50). Exculpation occurs when the accused denies that he acted deliberately: that is, he acted through ignorance, chance—or what we more correctly call an event—or necessity.

Through ignorance, as follows: “God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: ‘Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken; for she has a husband.’ But Abimelech had not touched her. And he said: ‘Lord, will you destroy a righteous and ignorant nation?’” (Genesis 20).

Through chance or occurrence—which rhetoricians call fortune—as follows: Moses, angered against the remaining sons of Aaron, said: “Why did you not eat the sin-offering in the holy place, since it is most holy?” Aaron replied: “Today the sin-offering and the burnt-offering have been offered before the Lord; but what you see has happened to me. How could I eat it, or please the Lord in the ceremonies, with a grieving mind?” (Leviticus 10).

Through necessity, as follows: “Why have you torn your garments, Jephthah?” “Alas, my daughter,” he says, “you have deceived me, and you yourself have been deceived. For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I shall not be able to do otherwise” (Judges 11). For through the necessity of his vow—because he had opened his mouth, saying, “Whoever first comes out of the doors of my house and meets me as I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I shall offer him as a burnt offering to the Lord” (ibid.)—through the necessity, I say, of the vow, he who kills his daughter by offering her is exculpated and excused, and deserves to be numbered in the catalogue of saints who “through faith conquered kingdoms” (Hebrews 11).

Likewise David received and ate the consecrated bread, given by the priest Abimelech; and because he did this from necessity, he is exculpated and excused, when the Lord says: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the loaves of offering, which it was not lawful for him or those with him to eat, but for priests alone?” (Matthew 12). And immediately afterward: “But if you knew what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent” (ibid.). Thus concession and its parts, supplication and exculpation, are admitted in the judgments of God.

Comparison of guilt is likewise found in this manner: “You, Paul, who said, ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing’ (Galatians 5), why did you circumcise Timothy (Acts 16)? And why, having taken men with you and purified yourself with them, did you enter the Temple, announcing the completion of the days of purification until an offering was made for each of them?” (Acts 21). “In order to avoid,” he says, “the danger of a greater offence”: namely, because they had heard concerning me that I taught apostasy from Moses (ibid.). This was false, for I am with Moses in spirit and truth; but this could not be demonstrated by argument, and so I demonstrated it, not without some resemblance of guilt.

Transfer and removal of guilt, two of the four parts of the assumptive issue—the latter branch of the juridical issue—must everywhere be avoided by the wise in the judgment of God, because from them arise the origin or increase of sin. God said to Adam: “Who told you that you were naked, unless you have eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?” And he said: “The woman whom you gave to be my companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3). In saying this, he wished to transfer the guilt from himself. For transfer of guilt occurs when we do not deny that we acted, but say that we were compelled by the sins of others.

Likewise, “The Lord God said to the woman: ‘Why have you done this?’ She replied: ‘The serpent deceived me, and I ate’” (ibid.). In saying this, she wished not to remove the charge from herself, but to remove the blame itself—that is, the cause of the charge. For removal of guilt is said to occur when we remove not the charge but its cause from ourselves, transferring it either to a person or assigning it to some thing. But to what kind of person did the woman transfer the guilt, if indeed it deserves to be called a person? To the serpent, whether spiritual—that is, the devil—or earthly—that is, a snake. To what thing? To the serpent’s deception.

But this transfer does not cleanse; it defiles. It does not acquit; it entangles. For what was the serpent’s promise when it deceived them? “You shall by no means die; for God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods” (ibid.). Let the woman say that the serpent not only urged her, but also showed such a reason why she ought to eat. Does not the guilt increase through such a removal of guilt? Rightly, therefore, may we say that transfer or removal of guilt is never sought from holy Scripture or established between ourselves and God; comparison is scarcely admitted; but concession is always admitted, and especially supplication, which is the better of the two parts of concession.

## Chapter XIII. [Col. 1773A] On Dialectic: that it too is present in Holy Scripture, especially at the beginning of Genesis, where genera and species are expressed by the very names, and difference, accidents, and syllogistic force are not neglected.

Was dialectic to be displayed, or more freely uttered, before God’s wisdom, the author of the Holy Scriptures? Yet it is there also; and, carrying out the parts of its assigned work before its mistress, it sits more watchfully at her side and investigates truth. Does any pupil of the art of dialectic, having entered the walls—or even the first doorway—of Holy Scripture, doubt this?

First, one may assert that genus and difference, species, property, and accident—matters which the sages of the age consider great and difficult—are like the first elements of this Scripture at its beginning. For it is written: “Let the earth bring forth green grass, making seed, and fruit-bearing wood making fruit according to its kind” (Genesis 1). Again: “The earth brought forth green grass, bearing seed according to its kind, and wood making fruit, each having seed according to its species” (ibid.). And below: “God created the great sea-creatures, and every living and moving soul which the waters had brought forth according to their species, and every winged thing according to its kind” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “Let the earth bring forth the living soul in its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their species.” And God made “the beasts of the earth according to their species, cattle, and every creeping thing according to its kind” (ibid.).

These are undoubtedly the genera and species of which philosophers speak. In defining genus, they say that genus is what is predicated, as to what a thing is, of several things differing in species. In defining species, they say that species is what is placed under an assigned genus, and of which the genus is predicated as to what it is. Or thus: species is what is predicated, as to what a thing is, of several things differing in number. “But this definition,” they say, “is of the most specific species,” and so forth.

Let us then say what, in the very letter of Holy Scripture, both delights the simple and exercises the learned or philosophers. For we judge it no less necessary for this Scripture than for Aristotle’s teaching on the Categories to know what genus and difference are, what species and property are, and what accident is. When it says, “fruit-bearing wood making fruit according to its kind, each having seed according to its species,” it certainly establishes wood as the genus; and when it says “fruit-bearing,” or “making fruit,” it supplies the difference which, added to the genus—namely, wood—constitutes a species of wood, that is, a tree.

For it divides wood, as a genus, by opposing differences, saying “fruit-bearing,” or “making fruit,” and adding, “each having seed,” or “whose seed is in itself.” For it is one thing to make fruit and another merely to have seed. The Psalmist uses the same division in the praises of God: “Fruit-bearing trees and all cedars” (Psalm 148), except that he placed a species in place of a difference—that is, cedar in place of non-fruit-bearing wood. Thus only fruit-bearing wood is a tree; non-fruit-bearing wood is not customarily called a tree.

Hence a man of our times, of celebrated memory and outstanding intelligence, is said to have played very elegantly with the matter while lying in bed. He said:

> The bed is wooden, yet cut from no tree.  
> Whoever can solve this, let him solve it, and it shall be his.

For he spoke truly: the little bed was indeed made of wood, but not of fruit-bearing wood; and therefore it was truly cut from no tree, since, as has already been said, not every sort of wood, but fruit-bearing wood, is a tree.

Wood, then, is a genus, for it is predicated of several things differing in species: namely, fruit-bearing wood, or wood making fruit, and unfruitful wood, or wood not bearing fruit but only seed. This is an animate body, indeed, but not yet a sentient body—or so it is called. Then the differences and species of animate and sentient body alike—that is, of animal or living soul—are distinguished when it is said: “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with a living soul, and winged creatures above the earth” (Genesis 1), and so forth.

For when it first says, “Let the waters bring forth creeping things with a living soul,” and afterwards adds, “Let the earth bring forth the living soul” (ibid.), genera and species or differences are subordinated far better and more correctly according to this most worthy Scripture than Porphyry arranged them. For, when by subdivision he had reached the constitution of animal, he immediately subdivided animal by the differences rational and irrational, and likewise mortal and immortal.

But this most sacred sequence of the reading divides things so that one kind of animal is produced by water and another by land. First, it subdivides that which water produces into three differences, or establishes three species, by subdividing or saying, “winged creature above the earth, under the firmament of heaven”; “God created the great sea-creatures”; and “every living and moving soul which the waters had produced” (ibid.). For winged creatures differ from the other things produced by water in that they came forth above the earth and now fly beneath the firmament of heaven. But the great sea-creatures, while remaining in the waters, differ in that they come by live birth; for very many come by egg.

With regard to this third difference, those which come by egg, when it says “according to their species,” subordinate species must be understood—species which cannot, of course, be enumerated. Then, concerning the living soul which the earth produces, when it says, “Let the earth bring forth the living soul in its kind: cattle, creeping things, and beasts of the earth according to their species,” and then, “Let us make man,” God says, “in our image and likeness” (ibid.), there is the division of animal by which Porphyry divides it. For of terrestrial animal, one is rational and another irrational, according to the truth or most powerful efficacy of this utterance of God.

For man’s rationality lies in the statement: “Let us make man in our image,” or “God created man in his image” (Genesis 1). But this Scripture has not handed down the subdivision of rational into mortal and immortal. For it neither customarily calls angels, who are immortal, animals, nor believed or granted that the sun, moon, and stars are immortal animals, or are animals in any way, or possess souls.

I should now like, following the sequence of this sacred reading, to proceed from the most general genus, substance, to the most specific species, man, in the order in which Scripture itself leads us. “Substance,” they say, “is a certain thing and is itself a genus; under it is body.” But, according to the words of this Scripture, we say that under substance are, on the one side, earth and, on the other, heaven: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (ibid.).

Earth is every corporeal substance, that is, every body visible to bodily eyes. For heaven is the homeland of spirits; although we hope that our bodies will be transferred there—for Christ, with his flesh, has gone before us—yet it is not body, because it is not seen by the bodily eyes of mortals. Therefore, under substance is body; under body, tangible body; under tangible body, solid or immovable body; under solid body, animate body; under animate body, animal; under animal, earthly or terrestrial animal; under terrestrial animal, rational animal.

Solid and immovable body is placed under tangible body, for water too is a tangible body, but is not solid or immovable. This solid body is dry land, which is now properly called earth, God saying: “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear” (ibid.). And immediately: “And it was so. And God called the dry land earth” (ibid.).

We have proceeded as far as this Scripture has led us: namely, as far as rational animal, that is, man. We leave aside the division of rational animal, because, as was said above, it is not handed down by this Scripture, and is therefore rightly left aside by its readers. Thus man is a species of terrestrial animal, and his difference is notably expressed when it says: “God created man in his image; in the image of God he created him” (ibid.).

Moreover, when it says, “Therefore the Lord God, having formed from the ground all the animals of the earth and all the birds of heaven, brought them to Adam” (Genesis 2), and immediately afterward, “But for Adam no helper like him was found” (ibid.), not only the difference but also the property of man must fittingly be set forth. For the writer ought to know, in saying this, what is man’s property, by which he is most especially distinguished and for which no like helper was found.

We therefore say here, as occasion requires, that man alone is capable of receiving instruction; he alone is bipedal, so that, with head raised and upright posture, he looks toward heaven; he alone is capable of laughter; and, as we rightly say according to the authority of this Scripture, among all animals he alone possesses not merely a rational mind but also a tongue for speech.

The last of the things they set forth is accident. But the greatest accident for man, and that concerning which the Holy Spirit, the holy author of Scripture, takes the greatest and most worthy care, is sin and death, the penalty of sin. For all divinely inspired Scripture strives most earnestly concerning this: it testifies that sin truly is an accident, that “God made man upright” (Ecclesiastes 7), and that “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1).

Truth defends this from the passage of Scripture which we have just touched upon, when it says: “Both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2). And immediately afterward: “The woman therefore saw that the tree was good for eating, pleasing to the eyes, and delightful in appearance; she took of its fruit and ate, and gave to her husband, who ate. And the eyes of both were opened. When they knew that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves and made loincloths for themselves” (Genesis 3). And below: “I shall multiply,” he says, “your hardships and your conceptions.” And to the man: “In the sweat of your face,” he says, “you shall eat bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return” (ibid.).

Accordingly, if you attend not to the fables of pagans or heretics but to the truth of Scripture, evil arises not from some substantial essence but from accident; that is, there neither were nor are two principles, of good and evil, so that good things subsist from a good ruler and evil things from an evil ruler. For it is clear especially from this or these passages that every evil befell man after the preceding greatest accident, namely sin: both the death of the soul, of which it was said, “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Genesis 2); the death of the body; all pains, the first of which is that of which it is said, “In pain you shall bear your children”; and the final punishment or pain of the body, that is, its death, of which he said, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Genesis 3).

For substance had first been created; first, I say, the Lord God had formed man from the mud of the earth, breathed the breath of life into his face, and placed him in the paradise of delight which he had planted. And both were naked, Adam and his wife, and were not ashamed, because the cause for shame had not yet arisen. Evil, therefore, is not something substantial, but accidental or actual; and there is absolutely no creature, visible or invisible, that can be understood as evil by nature.

This is truly a great and arduous accident, concerning which, or on account of which, everyone who is truly wise studies and labours; no one is free from examining it except the foolish. This is the whole end of wisdom which is from God: to study and strive so that an accident of this kind may be absent from its subject. For this reason the Wisdom of God came down from heaven, was incarnate, and earnestly established in this world the great school—that is, the holy Church.

But to deal with or dispute about very slight accidents—for example, sleepiness, raven-black or Ethiopian blackness, or any colour whatsoever—is not the concern of a mind occupied and anxious about life’s necessary business; nor has that holy philosophy which came from heaven leisure to descend to such matters. It leaves them to the wise of this world, who are foolish before God. Since they disdained to know that great accident, sin or the punishment of sin, with the same contempt by which, “when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Romans 1), they gave such a poor and narrow definition of accident: “Accident,” they say, “is what is present or absent without destruction of the subject.”

By such a definition they did not at all comprehend that accident which wholly corrupts—or rather destroys—the subject, namely man, so that he returns to dust and, as the Psalmist admits while lamenting, and laments while admitting: “In the morning he passes away like grass; in the morning he flourishes and passes away; in the evening he falls, hardens, and withers” (Psalm 89).

Certainly, Holy Scripture—or rather the Creator himself—removes from himself the whole multitude of all accidents when he says to Moses: “I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exodus 3). Therefore, when human beings, subject to accidental miseries and thus not truly being because they change and never remain in the same state (Job 14), discuss accidents, let them never presume to bind the Creator within their terms, even though they hear many things said or preached of him in Holy Scripture that signify quantity, quality, relation, place, time, position, possession, action, and passion.

For God is called great or immeasurable, not because he was ever small or of some measure; and good, not because he could have been anything other than good; Father of the Son or Son of the Father, not because at any time the one was not Father or the other was not Son. He is said to be in a place, not because he passes from place to place, since he is uncircumscribed. He is said to have begotten “today,” although there was never a time when the one was not Father or the other was not Son. He is said to sit, not because, as the Anthropomorphites suppose, he has a form capable of being stretched out or folded together. He is said to be clothed in a garment, though, since he has no body, he is certainly not bound by cloth. He is written to rest or to have rested, though he always was and is at rest; to be patient, though he is subject to no passions. Rather, he is always what he always was and is never changed, since he has not been formed but is merely matter lacking form; and therefore he is subject to no accidents.

The usefulness and power of this art are wholly displayed in syllogisms, whose conclusion greatly assists the reader in investigating truth, provided that there is no error of deceiving an opponent by sophistries of false conclusions. But which of all secular writers has known—or could know—how to weave or bind a difficult syllogism as strongly and sweetly as this Holy Scripture does?

So as not to go farther afield, the proposition in this chapter of the book is: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1). Here God is undoubtedly the subject; “created heaven and earth” is the predicate. A proposition must be granted when it is evident that the predicate belongs to the subject. Faith therefore grants it, for the discourse of this Scripture is addressed not to unbelievers but to believers, and against unbelievers.

The assumption immediately follows when it says: “But the earth was empty and void, and darkness was upon the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (ibid.), and so forth. What could be more impressive than this assumption, in which the writer presents the point to be assumed in such a way as also to show the matter itself: namely, how the Creator, who had created from nothing, took up for his work that assumption of formless matter in order to make and distinguish forms? For it follows: “And God said: Let light be made,” and so forth. At last he concludes: “Therefore the heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed” (ibid.). The page of divine Scripture is full of such perfect syllogisms, whose brevity gives rhetoricians particular pleasure.

## Chapter XIV. [Col. 1778B] On Arithmetic: that it is present there, and that many mysteries are inferred by the rationale of numbers.

Arithmetic, that is, the theory of numbers, reveals in many places of Holy Scripture how much mystery it contains. For it was not said without reason in the praises of God: “You have made all things in measure, number, and weight” (Wisdom 11). The number six, which is perfect in its divisors, signifies the perfection of the world by a certain meaning of its number. Likewise, the forty days during which Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted cannot be understood without knowledge of numbers. So too there are other numbers in the sacred Scriptures whose figures we can explain only if we are skilled in this art and science.

It is also given to us, in some measure, to stand under the discipline of numbers when we learn the hours by it, when we discuss the course of the months, and when we recognize the span of the returning year. By number, indeed, we are instructed so that we may not be confused. Take number away from all things, and all things perish. Remove computation from the world, and blind ignorance embraces everything. One who does not know the art of calculation cannot differ from the other animals.

## Chapter XV. On Geometry: that many things according to that discipline are found in the Scriptures.

Geometrical science has many terms in the Holy Scriptures: namely, finger, palm, cubit, foot, pace, stadion, mile, and other such terms. Yet this science is for the most part marked by the fault of curiosity [Col. 1778D], and in that respect is nowhere admitted into the sacred accounts of God’s word. For it is said to have been discovered first by the Egyptians, because, when the Nile overflowed and all their properties were covered with mud, the need to divide the land by lines and measurements gave the art its name. Afterwards the keener intellects of the wise advanced further and measured the spaces of sea, heaven, and air. For, prompted by zeal, after measuring the earth they began also to investigate the spaces of heaven: at what distance the moon stands from the earth, the sun itself from the moon, and by what measure it extends as far as the summit of heaven. Thus they distinguished the intervals of heaven itself and the circuit of the sphere by a plausible calculation of stadia. But because this discipline began with the measurement of the earth, it retained from its origin [Col. 1779A] both its name and character. For *geometria* is named from earth and measurement: earth is called *ge* in Greek, and measurement *metra*.

But what bearing has this upon true usefulness? What profit is it for us to know or conjecture by how many stadia the globe of the moon or of the sun is raised above the earth; how much the size of the sun exceeds the size of the earth; or through how many stadia the earth itself extends? Thus this branch of concern or study was not worthy of true wisdom. Yet, in another respect, this same discipline was acceptable in Scripture: namely, for constructing something in accordance with a command, by suitable and rational measurements. For example: “Make yourself an ark,” it says, “of smoothed wood; you shall make compartments in the ark and coat it inside and out with pitch; and thus shall you make it. The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits [Col. 1779B], its breadth fifty cubits, and its height thirty cubits” (Gen. 6).

This is indeed a rational proportion, apart from the deeper mysteries that escape us: its breadth is one sixth of its length, and its height one tenth of that same length. For fifty is the sixth part of three hundred, and thirty the tenth part of three hundred. This figure also bears a certain resemblance to the human body, since a man’s body when laid out, either prone or supine, has a length six times its breadth and ten times its height. Likewise, many matters in the arrangement of the tabernacle and many in the construction of the temple are usefully considered; beyond the rational design of the structure itself, they signify something by which the attentive reader’s mind may be more beneficially edified [Col. 1779C].

## CHAPTER XVI. On music: that it too is very closely connected with Holy Scripture.

Is music, then, foreign to the Holy Scripture of which we speak? On the contrary, it is very much at home in it: native to it and, as it were, consecrated together with it; more official than the other arts and more necessary. Moses says that its inventor was Tubal, of Cain’s lineage before the Flood (Gen. 4). But for the service of wisdom, as an aid or co-worker in heavenly teaching, the Holy Spirit introduced it through David, the chief of the prophets.

For a great undertaking and contest had been entrusted to the word of God: to frighten and restrain with fear of hell the youthful wantonness of the world in its revelry [Col. 1779D], and to awaken the excessively carnal lovers of this present age to the love of God’s kingdom. This had to be done in plain speech and with direct names, which Moses, the writer of the Law, did not do. For nowhere did the Law openly promise God’s kingdom in words, nor threaten the punishments of hell—except only where it says in the Song of Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest parts of hell” (Deut. 23). Rather, it threatened transgressors with famine, sword, pestilence, and evil beasts; but to the obedient it promised a land flowing with milk and honey, a land from whose mountains metals of bronze might be dug.

Through the mouth of this Prophet and King, the Holy Spirit first began to pray with inexpressible groanings (Rom. 8), expressing matters in clear speech [Col. 1780A], so that man might be delivered from hell and attain the kingdom of God. Therefore, to make hearers—hitherto untaught—attentive, receptive, and well disposed toward so great and necessary a matter, he employed sounding instruments together with the melody of hymn-singing voices: the sound of the trumpet, psaltery and harp, strings and organ, well-sounding cymbals; singing mercy and judgment to the Lord. Nor was he ignorant of number itself, wherein the power of music consists, and which Pythagoras among the Greeks is said later to have discovered from the sound of hammers.

Nor is it surprising, since long before David Abraham, by a wondrous and venerable method, sang to the Lord both mercy and judgment—not with instrumental voice or instruments, but solely by proportional numbers, in which musical power consists. For the Lord had said: “If I find fifty righteous persons in Sodom, in the midst of the city, I shall spare the whole place for their sake” (Gen. 18). Then Abraham entered into discourse and, trusting in the greatness of his humility, said: “What if five be lacking from the fifty righteous? Will you destroy the whole city for the sake of forty-five?” And then: “But if forty are found, what will you do? What if thirty are found there? What if twenty are found there? What if ten are found there?” And the Lord, answering each question, said: “I shall not destroy it if I find forty-five there; I shall not strike it down for forty; I shall not do it if I find thirty there; I shall not destroy it for twenty; I shall not destroy it for ten” (ibid.) [Col. 1780B].

Did Abraham reduce the numbers in this way by chance? Or rather, was he teaching his children to sing mercy and judgment to the Lord? For he divided and diminished them proportionally in such a way as to omit none of those proportions that produce musical sounds. Thus forty-five compared with forty make an *epogdoon*, that is, a sesquioctave ratio, and produce a tone; forty compared with thirty make an *epitriton*, that is, a sesquitertian ratio, and yield the fourth (*diatessaron*); thirty compared with twenty make an *ennolion*, that is, a sesquialter ratio, and yield the sound of the fifth (*diapente*); twenty compared with ten are double, and produce the greatest consonance, the octave (*diapason*); thirty compared with ten are triple, and yield an octave with a fifth; while forty compared with ten are quadruple, and produce a double octave [Col. 1780C].

Since, therefore, no musical proportion is absent from these numbers, we must not suppose that so great a man, especially while speaking with God, picked them out by chance and without reason, just as they came to his lips [Col. 1780D]. Much more might be said on this subject, but it does not belong to our present purpose, and we are approaching the end.

## CHAPTER XVII. On astronomy: that it too is present there, and what is the difference between astronomy and astrology.

It is clear that Holy Scripture also does not lack knowledge of astronomy, especially since at the very beginning it says: “And God said: Let lights be made in the firmament, and let them divide day and night, and let them be for signs, seasons, days, and years” (Gen. 1). Ecclesiastes likewise says: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there, rising again, it turns through the south and bends toward the north” (Eccles. 1).

We say knowledge or study of astronomy, not astrology; for there is some difference [Col. 1781A] between the two. Astronomy considers the revolution of heaven and includes the risings, settings, and movements of the stars, and the reasons why they are so called. Astrology, however, is partly natural and partly superstitious. It is natural when it traces the courses of sun and moon, or the fixed seasonal positions of the stars. But its superstitious form is that followed by the astrologers, who make predictions from the stars; they also distribute the twelve signs of heaven among the individual limbs of soul or body, and seek to foretell human births and characters from the course of the stars.

Accordingly, we derive astronomical calculation from Holy Scripture, especially concerning the course of the moon, because of the lawful date for observing Passover: that is, the fourteenth day of the first month. For the Hebrews know and observe from the Law only lunar [Col. 1781B] months. In accordance with the moon’s natural course, they complete the twelve months of ordinary years with months of thirty and twenty-nine days; and in the third or second year, as calculation requires, they add at the end of the year an intercalary thirteenth month of thirty days. But enough has been said about these matters. Let us now return to what was above.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On blessed Jerome, a man of great learning, and how he wrote a catalogue of many illustrious men endowed with grace.

Therefore, when we say that the liberal arts were introduced to cooperate with Holy Scripture when our teachers, stirred by good zeal toward the Catholic faith, applied themselves more fervently to the study of Holy Scripture, we recognize that it is more correct and true to say that they were then to be found there. They had not previously appeared in contrast with the brightness of wisdom, chiefly because dust from earthly wisdom had fallen into their weak eyes.

Blessed Jerome, one of their foremost number, acknowledges this when he says:

> Many years ago, when I had cut myself off, for the kingdom of heaven, from home, parents, sister, relatives, and—what was greater than these—from the habit of more plentiful food, and was making my way to Jerusalem to serve as a soldier, I could not do without the library which I had assembled at Rome with the utmost zeal and labour. Thus, wretched man that I was, I fasted in order to read Cicero; and after nightly vigils, after tears which the recollection of my former sins drew from the depths of my being, Plato was taken into my hands. But whenever, returning to myself, I attempted to read the prophets, their uncultivated speech horrified me; and because with blind eyes I could not see the light, I attributed this not to the fault of my eyes but to that of the sun.  
> [Note: [Col. 1781D] St Jerome, Epistle I class., Ep. 22, to Eustochium, *On the Guarding of Virginity*, ed. Migne.]

But thanks be to the true and highest Light, because, once those eyes had quickly been enlightened and healed, he was able to perceive the sun—that is, the luminous discourse of Holy Scripture. Having long before been sufficiently taught by secular masters—as he himself says, “Victorinus and Donatus the grammarian, my teacher and instructor, are held in renown at Rome” [Note: [Col. 1782D] St Jerome, *Chronicle*, A.D. 358.]—he attained, Christ willing and through strenuous spiritual study, to the truth of all the books of the Old Testament [Col. 1782A].

Learned in Greek, Latin, and Hebrew letters, he translated into Latin from the true edition, and also commented upon, all the Hebrew books contained in the canon of the Old Testament. He has benefited us so greatly in translating the Lord’s Scripture that we have no need to go to the Hebrew source, since he is known to have abundantly satisfied us by the great clarity of his eloquence. Moreover, among the other works of his studies, all marked with his own prefaces, he began with blessed Peter and arranged in order the lives of one hundred and thirty-five illustrious men down to the fourteenth year of Theodosius. He briefly described all those who had consigned anything concerning Holy Scripture to record, imitating Tranquillus and the Greek Apollonius, and placing himself too at the end of the volume, as one untimely born [Col. 1782B] and the least of all Christians.

## CHAPTER XIX. On blessed Augustine: that in him this holy Spirit of knowledge is truly praiseworthy, and how humbly he confesses that he received so great a gift of grace.

There is indeed much in these men for which this holy Spirit of knowledge may justly be praised. But as we hasten to the end, we touch upon only one of them, in whom this Spirit plainly worked: a man whom it deemed worthy for its praise, for the defence of its Church and the Catholic faith, and for a perpetual fortification. This is Augustine, pillar and ground of the truth, and truly a pillar of cloud, in which the wisdom of God placed its throne. From his mouth the saving rain did not cease to distil—indeed, a river’s torrent flowed against [Col. 1782C] that river of heretics which, as we said above, the devil-dragon sent from his mouth after the woman, that is, the Church (Rev. 12).

Before calling him into His marvellous light, God’s providence allowed him in youth to wander in the darkness of the Manicheans. Yet, even in that error and without his knowing it, this Spirit surrounded him by wondrous grace, suggesting the great gift of knowledge which he would later use well for the benefit of Christ’s Church in its proper time. Augustine himself judges how great a gift of intellect he had received, when, among other things, he says to the Lord in humble confession:

> And what did it profit me that, when I was nearly twenty years old, certain Aristotelian works called the Ten Categories came into my hands? When my Carthaginian teacher, a rhetorician, mentioned their names with cheeks puffed up in pride, and when others who were considered learned spoke of them, I hung upon their words in eager expectation, as though they meant some great and divine thing. Yet I read them alone and understood them. When I compared them with those who said they had scarcely understood them even when the most learned teachers explained them not only in speech but by drawing many figures in the dust, they could tell me nothing more than I had discovered by reading alone to myself.  
> [Note: [Col. 1782D] St Augustine, *Confessions*, Book V, ch. 16.]

And afterwards:

> And what did it profit me that I, then the most wretched slave of my desires, read by myself and understood every book of the arts called liberal which I was able to read? I rejoiced in them, yet did not know whence came whatever truth and certainty was in them [Col. 1783A]. For my back was turned toward the light and toward those things which illuminate the face; therefore my own face, by which I saw things when illumined, was not illumined. Whatever I understood without great difficulty, with no human being teaching me, concerning the art of speaking or reasoning, divisions of figures, music, or numbers—you know, Lord my God, that swiftness of understanding and sharpness of discernment are your gifts. Yet I did not sacrifice them to you. Thus they had power over me not for use but rather for destruction, because I strove to hold so good a portion of my substance under my own control, and did not preserve my strength for you (Ps. 58); rather, I went away from you into a far country, to squander it upon the desires of harlots (Luke 15). For what did a good thing profit me [Col. 1784A] when I did not use it well? I did not realize that even diligent and intelligent students understood those arts only with the greatest difficulty, unless I tried to explain those same things to them. And the most excellent among them was the one who did not follow my explanation too slowly. But what did this avail me when I thought that you, Lord God, Truth, were a luminous and immense body, and that I was a fragment of that body? Excessive perversity!  
> [Note: [Col. 1783A] St Augustine, *Confessions*, Book V, ch. 26], etc.

This, then, is why we rightly praise the holy Spirit of knowledge: it made ready such a man outwardly, and inwardly deigned to employ him in such a way that, battling throughout his life against every heresy by speech and writing, he wrote as much as no one has sufficient life to read. Hence someone is said, not idly, to have remarked:

> He lies who professes to have read you in your entirety.

# BOOK EIGHT OF *ON THE WORKS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT*: ON PIETY.

[Col. 1783]

## CHAPTER I. [Col. 1783B] On the holy Spirit of piety: how rightly we ascribe to it all that we are and all that we live; and how it is often signified in Scripture by the name of oil. Oil, moreover, flowed throughout an entire day from the *taberna meritoria* at Rome as a sign of this grace when Christ the Son of God was born.

We, most poor and needy, worship with humble mind the holy Spirit of piety, which follows next in order. We confess to it that, though we were neither wise nor understanding, neither prudent nor counsellors, neither strong nor possessed of much knowledge, we now live from this abundance of the grace of the Spirit of piety. This agrees with what that peculiar dwelling-place of all grace and all mercy says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed [Col. 1783C] me. He has sent me to bring good news to the meek, to heal those broken in heart” (Isa. 61; Luke 4), etc.

For this is that grace which, now that God’s house has been filled with a multitude of those called from diverse conditions and ranks, presses upon the eyes of the same God and Father, so that he may not see what we were or remember whence we came. And behold: we who were foolish walk among the wise; we who were dull dwell among the understanding; we who were unwise sit among counsellors of salvation; we who were weak walk among the strong; we who were unlearned glory among the knowledgeable; we who were altogether ugly—behold, we are seen among the saints, flourishing in the beauty of righteousness.

This is that piety, and these are those works of piety, for which Holy Scripture often designates this Holy Spirit [Col. 1783D] under the name of oil [Col. 1784B]. “You have made my head rich with oil” (Ps. 22). Again: “That he may make the face glad with oil” (Ps. 103). And elsewhere: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Isa. 10).

Thus fittingly and venerably, when the Lord Jesus Christ was born of the blessed Virgin at Bethlehem of Judah—anointed with the oil of gladness above all the saints, whence he is called Christ—at Rome in those days, as histories relate, a most abundant fountain of oil flowed from the *taberna meritoria* throughout the entire day. What sign could more clearly declare that, at Christ’s birth, an abundance of piety and compassion for sinners flowed from heaven? For the oil flowing throughout an entire day at Rome from the *taberna meritoria* signified that, from the guest-house Church, which had been as though prostituted to many gods, there would be given to penitents throughout the whole duration of the Roman Empire the sweetness of heavenly consolation for the remission of sins; and that where shamelessness of depravity had reigned, the gentleness of religion would abound still more [Col. 1784C].

But now, following our order, let us say how, after—or together with—that abundance of knowledge of which we spoke in the preceding book, the Spirit of piety worked more visibly in His Church; and first, what piety itself is.

## CHAPTER II. On the fact that true piety is religion and the worship of God, whom the Greeks call εὐσεβής (*eusebēs*), “pious.”

Piety, by which human beings are called pious according to their measure insofar as they imitate God, who alone is truly and uniquely pious, is true religion and the worship of God. For, blessed Augustine says, piety is commonly understood as the worship of God, which the Greeks call εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*). Yet it is also said to be shown dutifully toward parents [Col. 1784D]. In popular usage, however, this name is frequently applied to works of mercy. I think this occurred because God commands these works to be done and testifies that they please Him even before sacrifices. From this custom of speech it has come about that God Himself is called pious (2 Chron. 30; Ecclus. 11; Judith 7). The Greeks, indeed, never call Him εὐσεβής (*eusebēs*) in any usage of their language, although common usage among them also employs εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*) in the sense of mercy. Therefore, in certain passages of Scripture, so that the distinction might appear more clearly, they preferred to say not εὐσέβεια (*eusebeia*), a word formed from good worship, but θεοσέβεια (*theosebeia*), a compound meaning worship of God [Note: [Col. 1785D] Augustine, *The City of God*, Book X, ch. 1.].

Likewise: “This, however, is the end: to cling to God” (Ps. 72). Therefore, when a person knows how to love himself and is commanded to love his neighbour as himself, what else is commanded except that he should, as far as he can, commend to the neighbour the love of God? This is the worship of God; this is true religion; this is right piety; this is the service owed to God alone [Col. 1785B] [Note: [Col. 1786D] Augustine, *ibid.*, ch. 3.].

## CHAPTER III. On piety: that it makes a person meek—that is, one who does not defend his own sins, but is humble and penitent.

Therefore piety is true worship of God and true religion. Those who have wandered farthest from it are, first, the Jews, of whom the Apostle says that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10); and then Jews or Greeks alike who are not meek because they are not pious—that is, because they presume upon their works or merits, put too much trust in their own judgment, and, what is most destructive [Col. 1785C], do not think themselves in every respect to need God’s glory, nor to be able to be anything except by God’s grace.

For it is truly characteristic of piety to make a person meek: that is, not defending or justifying himself, accusing not God but himself, and not contradicting Holy Scripture, whether understood or not yet understood, because of the slowness of his own understanding—as he himself admits. Of such meek and gentle persons the Lord Himself says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). Insofar as they are made gentle by piety, they make room for the pious God and provide an entrance, so that He may know what to do with them. Thus He says to His people, defiled by the crime of the calf: “Now put off your ornament, that I may know [Col. 1785D] what to do with you” (Exod. 33).

Indeed, so long as the sinner walks erect and splendid, with the brow of a harlot, divine piety in some sense does not know what to do with him. But when he begins, recognizing himself, to walk with head bowed, it immediately knows what to do, and knowing it, comes to meet him. This is indicated by the parable of the prodigal and debauched son, who came to himself and said: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you; I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15). What then did the father know to do, and what did he do? “He was moved with compassion, and, running to meet him, fell upon his neck and kissed him” (ibid.).

And all that was done—that the son who had been lost was found because he found himself [Col. 1786A] and was received by his good father; that the fatted calf was killed for his recovery; that a feast was made and the father feasted with him—all this, I say, was done through this Spirit of piety. But our present place and order require us to consider not that the Gentile world returned to God by universal grace, cleansed through baptism from the filth of idols, but that each sinner, personally pierced with compunction, returns to repentance. For that prophet—the great prophet and Lord of prophets—when he spoke that parable, prophesied that the nations would return and be received in this manner, while at the same time showing that repentance must not be denied to any sinner returning after a fall.

Nor, when we set out to speak of piety or the Spirit of piety, and establish this as true religion, do we depart anywhere from our purpose by entering upon the subject of the remedy of penitence. For, as we shall not fail to say later, no religion is dearer to God than penitential humility. For He says: “I tell you that there shall be joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance” (ibid.) [Col. 1786B]. Only the proud seem to themselves not to need repentance; only humble persons truthfully confess that they are sinners. Therefore these are the meek who shall possess the earth, while the others are not meek and shall not possess the earth.

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1786C] That, with God’s piety, no sin except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable; and what it truly means to speak against the Holy Spirit.

First, then, we say that there is no sin, except the sin of blasphemy against the Spirit—or blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—for which repentance or forgiveness is rightly denied in Christ’s Church. The Lord Himself testifies to this—indeed, He is its author—when He says: “Amen I say to you: all sins and blasphemies by which the children of men have blasphemed shall be forgiven them. But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness for ever, but shall be guilty of an eternal sin” (Mark 3).

The Evangelist adds the reason why He said this: “For,” he says, “they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’”; or, as he had stated earlier, “He has Beelzebub, and by the prince of demons [Col. 1786D] he casts out demons” (ibid.). It is thus to be understood: the person who plainly understands the works of God, yet, because he cannot deny their power, is goaded by envy into slander and says that Christ, the Word of God, and the works of the Holy Spirit are Beelzebub—such a person will not be forgiven, either in this present age or in the age to come.

This is not because we deny that he could be forgiven by Him “who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth” (1 Tim. 2), if he wished to repent. Rather, believing the Judge and Giver of pardon—who says both that He will always receive repentance and that this blasphemy is nowhere to be forgiven—we believe that such a blasphemer, as his deserts require, will no more attain the fruits of worthy repentance than he will attain forgiveness. This accords with what John the Evangelist most truthfully wrote of some who had been blinded in merited punishment for their blasphemy: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes [Col. 1787A] and understand with their heart and be converted, and I should heal them’” (John 12).

Thus only blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—whereby someone, in the likeness of the devil and his angels, does not tremble to attack against his own conscience the majesty of the Godhead—has no forgiveness, but makes a person guilty of an eternal sin. Apart from this one sin, as has already been said above, all things are forgivable.

## CHAPTER V. On the heresy of the presbyter Novatus, who denied that those fallen during persecution could receive forgiveness from the Church; and how or which apostolic statement he misunderstood.

Now Novatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, stripped of this spirit of piety and swollen with a certain pride, utterly took away the hope of salvation even from those who had fallen away from the faith during persecution, though they had repented worthily. From him arose the heresy of the Novatians, who said that repentance was indeed not denied to persons who had thus fallen, but that forgiveness could not be given by the Church and must be reserved solely for God’s judgment [Col. 1787B].

Against this cruelty and harshness, a saying of the Emperor Constantine of blessed memory was no less memorable than the synodal decrees of bishops. When he questioned Acesius, bishop of the Novatians, and heard from him the doctrines stated above, he said: “O Acesius, set up a ladder and climb to heaven alone, if you can.”

Yet the following apostolic statement seemed to support their sect: “For it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, have also tasted the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. 6). But by this statement the Apostle did not at all attack repentance or forgiveness of sins, nor shut off hope of pardon. Rather, he denied that baptism could be repeated. The very text of the passage shows that this was undoubtedly his intention. For he had said beforehand: “Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us be carried on to perfection; not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we shall do, if God permits” (ibid.) [Col. 1787C–D].

For what does “not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms,” mean except not returning once more to the beginning of the Christian rule—that is, not being catechized again and baptized again? But concerning the reception of repentance and the granting of forgiveness, he testifies that the Church possesses this authority by Christ’s institution. He says to the Corinthians: “To whom you have forgiven anything, I forgive also; for I too, if I have forgiven anything, have forgiven it for your sakes in the person of Christ” (2 Cor. 2) [Col. 1788A].

And lest you suppose that he spoke only of the sin of fornication, he does not say, “to whom you have forgiven, who had his father’s wife”; rather, he says, “to whom you have forgiven anything,” intending the same certainty of forgiveness in whatever matter of sin, according to that evangelical promise of the Lord: “Amen I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18).

## CHAPTER VI. On the Apostle’s statement and how it should properly be understood: “For it is impossible for those who have once …,” etc.

In another sense it truly is impossible for them to be renewed; nevertheless, we must not depart from the interpretation which we have stated above of the words: “Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness for ever, but shall be guilty of an eternal sin” (Mark 3). For the person whom we said plainly understands God’s works, and then, under the goad of envy, denies what he understands, may be the same person who has once been enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, been made partaker of the Holy Spirit, and likewise tasted the good Word of God and the powers of the age to come, and then fallen away [Col. 1788B].

If an adversary perhaps presses you very strongly, you may most properly have recourse to this harmony or agreement between Christ and His Apostle. For the same Apostle says in the same Epistle to the Hebrews: “For if we sin wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10). What does “wilfully” mean except, as though he had said, “with deliberation”? And what is it to sin with deliberation except, above all, to will—when God’s works are understood, as has been said—to deny them under the goad of envy?
