Therefore, after saying, “For if we sin wilfully,” etc., he immediately adds: “But a certain fearful expectation of judgment and zeal of fire which shall consume the adversaries” (ibid.). He calls those persons adversaries who sin wilfully; and this cannot properly be said of those who sin through weakness or ignorance. Therefore, to sin wilfully is the same as to speak a word against the Holy Spirit: that is, to deny manifest works of God through envy [Col. 1788C].

Why does no sacrifice for sins remain for those who so sin after receiving the knowledge of the truth? Plainly because it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, when they have fallen away, to be renewed. Why is it impossible for them to be renewed? Certainly because whoever is such a person will not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come, but will be guilty of an eternal sin. Why will he not be forgiven either in this age or in the age to come? Certainly because, even if he should do penance, he does not deserve to be visited by the Holy Spirit, but by God’s just judgment receives that impenitent heart.

Thus the statement, “It is impossible for them to be renewed again unto repentance,” either means—as the context requires—that they ought not to be baptized again; or, if Novatus does not allow this, it is said of a sin of that kind, so that Christ’s Apostle may not disagree with Christ, who says: “He shall not be forgiven, but shall be guilty of an eternal sin” [Col. 1788D–1789A].

For it must be understood that Paul, in saying these things, a Hebrew was speaking to Hebrews. Accordingly, when he said, “if we sin wilfully,” he expressed this fittingly and significantly by adding “we”; that is, we Hebrews, who possess the testimony of the Law and have no excuse for sin. Therefore we must observe how he begins, so that it may not be uncertain or doubtful what kind of sin he means, and whom he calls fallen persons unable to be renewed. “See to it, brethren,” he says, “lest there be in any of you an evil heart of unbelief, departing from the living God. But exhort one another every day while it is called today, lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (Heb. 3).

Therefore, as we have said, we must know that a Hebrew was speaking to Hebrews, and that, with pious concern, he feared this outcome for his own people—what we see has happened today: namely, that the Jews are unbelieving through envy, and through envy deny Him whom their fathers delivered up through envy, denied through envy, and crucified [Col. 1789B].

## CHAPTER VII. On the house of piety, in which the prodigal son is received by his pious father through repentance; and how the sacred canons decree that those fallen persons who have performed penance for crimes should remain content with lay communion.

Accordingly, the house of mercy, which at the Savior’s coming stood open to the prodigal son as he returned in repentance from feeding swine, after debauchery and gluttony, remains open today to every penitent. The merciful Father looks out from afar to see whether anyone is returning from a distance, and runs to meet each person making this confession of the sinner: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15).

But how can that saying apply to one of this kind: “Quickly bring out the best robe and put it on him; put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet” (ibid.)? For, without prejudice to the higher interpretation by which we understand the best robe as the grace of holy baptism, the best robe is priestly glory, or the dignity of any ministry by which Christ is served at the holy altar. Yet the sacred canons decree that, after repentance has been performed for crimes, such persons are by no means to be promoted to this ministry, but must remain content with lay communion alone. How, then, shall we grant those of this sort the reception of the best robe, lest we seem, with the Novatians, to deny repentance to anyone?

Here, certainly, discrimination is needed: “one of this kind.” Concerning those whose crimes have been exposed without their own confession, or through legal or canonical conviction, the sacred canons and decrees of the pontiffs of the Roman See openly and expressly determine that they are not to enter ecclesiastical ranks, remain in ecclesiastical ranks, or return to ecclesiastical ranks. For, they say, the Apostle warns us of this when he says: “Have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness” (Eph. 5). Again: “Rebuke those who sin before all, that the rest also may fear” (1 Tim. 5) [Col. 1790A]. Thus Peter condemned Simon, though he nevertheless invited him to repentance (Acts 8). Thus Paul rebuked the fornicator, whom he delivered to Satan, yet so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Cor. 5).

Indeed, holy David performed repentance for deadly crimes (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 12), yet remained in his office; and blessed Peter, when he shed most bitter tears, surely repented of having denied the Lord (Matt. 26), yet remained an apostle. But for that reason the later precaution must not be thought empty: where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, so that salvation might be guarded more safely—having, I think, experienced the feigned repentances of some, prompted by their affected pursuit of honors. For the experience of many diseases compels the discovery of many remedies.

But concerning those who have not been exposed or publicly denounced, this is the sound and reasonable ruling of those same sacred canons and holy Fathers: “Divine punishment ceases if human conversion comes first.” Beginning therefore with the head and proceeding down to the fourth minister of the altar, we know that this rule is to be observed: because the lesser precedes the greater, in honor as also in crime; and the greater the guilt that follows a person, the greater the punishment to be borne—and, after repentance, it is believed to be fruitful. For what use is it to sow wheat and not gather its fruit? After worthy satisfaction, we believe that one may return to office, the prophet saying: “Will one who falls not rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?” (Jer. 8) [Col. 1790C]. Again the prophet says: “On whatever day you turn back and groan, then you shall be saved” (Ezek. 33).

Hence also the Psalmist: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50 [51]). For when he asked not to be cast away by God, the king and prophet, fallen through sin, trembled because he had seized another man’s wife; when the prophet judged his crime and he performed repentance, he added: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit” (ibid.). For if he had not made himself worthy of God through repentance, he would by no means have preached to others. For he says: “I shall teach transgressors your ways, and the ungodly shall turn to you” (ibid.).

Thus ecclesiastical concern has rightly employed discrimination; and the sum of this discrimination is that those whose crimes have been exposed do not receive the robe of holy ministry of which I was speaking, while those whose sins are hidden, or secretly committed, have incurred public infamy, are clothed in it again after worthy repentance [Col. 1790D].

## CHAPTER VIII. How the most merciful Father clothes the returning son in the best robe, if canonical authority denies him priestly glory; and how one converted possesses the best robe in the monastic habit.

What, then, will the most merciful Father do for the son who returns, if he has not only to say, “I have sinned against heaven and before you,” but has also sinned before men (Luke 15), and among men has been exposed and disgraced because of his sin [Col. 1791A]? For it may happen—and often has happened—that one publicly known in a crime is no less pierced by repentance than one who has indeed sinned against heaven and before the Father, but has remained hidden from men. Whence, then, will the Father receive a robe with which he can clothe him, when the Spirit of mercy pricks and shakes his inmost parts?

O the Father’s providence! O God’s workmanship! O riches of goodness! He has found a means of comforting the sorrowful; he has discovered a means of raising up the cast-down; he has provided for himself a means of adorning the ignoble with brilliant nobility. We mean the monastic order and habit, which the holy Fathers did not hesitate to call a second baptism.

Blessed Gregory says: “A bishop ought to celebrate Mass at the ordination of a presbyter, and an abbot at the consecration of a monk, and to say four prayers over his head, so that, as he is instructed through the four Gospels, so he may be consecrated through four prayers. And until the third day he shall keep his head veiled, in deepest silence and due reverence, bearing the figure of the Lord’s Passion. But on the third day the abbot shall remove the hood from his head, so that, having put aside the sorrow of his former sin, he may with unveiled face behold the glory of the Lord. Therefore he has been baptized a second time and cleansed from all sins.”

And immediately afterward: “For three days they remain silent, after the example of the Apostles, who, for fear of the Jews, sat in the upper room until, on the third day, the Lord, rising again, said to them: ‘Peace be with you’” (John 20). Thus the abbot shall give peace to the monk and remove the hood from his head.

Moreover, Pope Boniface of holy memory says, after some further remarks, concerning the monk’s very habit: “We believe that the office of binding and loosing is worthily administered by priests, provided that they have worthily attained elevation to this ministry.” Anyone who considers the state and habit of monks clearly affirms this. For *angelus* in Greek is called *nuntius*, “messenger,” in Latin. Therefore priests, monks, and canons who proclaim God’s commandments are called angels. But each angelic order, the nearer it contemplates God, is established in proportionately higher dignity.

Are not the cherubim veiled with six wings? Two are plainly represented in the hood by which the head is covered. That which is spread out by the arms we call two wings; and that in which the body is enclosed, two wings. Thus the number of six wings is certainly made up [Col. 1791C].

Therefore, however cast down and disgraced the prodigal son may be when he returns, the most merciful Father has and knows whence he may bring out the best robe, or nearly the best robe: namely, the habit of holy conduct, the monk’s habit—reverent and wholly penitential, and therefore reverent because penitential. For who would not reverence this habit because it is penitential, except one who thinks that he needs no repentance? But whoever thinks he has no need of repentance should know that the most merciful Lord, the Son of the most merciful Father, did not come for him, as he himself testified elsewhere: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9).

This habit, then, is a robe, not a contemptible one, which this Spirit—the Spirit of this Father, the Spirit of mercy—devised through men very well known and orthodox, among whom he undoubtedly dwelt [Col. 1792A].

## CHAPTER IX. That not only the guilty have customarily desired a robe of this kind—that is, monastic life—and that one who despises this life as a confinement for sinners, thinking himself righteous, acts wrongly.

We do not say that this Father has reserved such a robe only for sinners—that is, only for those who have lost the grace of baptism through the greatness of their crimes—and that no righteous person ought to desire or seek it. For that would be the same as saying that repentance is unnecessary for the righteous. But if we say that we have no need of repentance, however righteous we may be, we—or those on whose behalf, or with whom, we say this—are lying; we act against the truth, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1) [Col. 1792B].

For the most righteous of all mortals cannot humble himself sufficiently or repent adequately of his sins. We do not say, therefore, that this penitential order is appointed only for sinners, but also for the righteous. For when a sinner—that is, a criminal—receives this oft-mentioned robe, it is pardon and grace; when a righteous person receives it, as though by descending, it is grace and glory.

We know very many righteous persons and pillars of righteousness standing in that house of repentance, in which penitents are received under the same habit and the banquet of joy is celebrated: such as Martin of Pannonia; blessed Gregory, bishop of the Apostolic See; Augustine, likewise the disciple of that most holy Gregory; and very many other most holy men, radiant in righteousness and holiness, who nevertheless did not disdain the shining habit of monastic humility because of their precious righteousness.

Of persons such as these, the same golden-mouthed Gregory says: “It should be known that there are many righteous persons in whose life there is such joy that no repentance for sins can possibly be preferred to it. For many are conscious of no evil in themselves, and yet subject themselves to an affliction of such ardor as if they were distressed by every sin,” etc.

Let us say, therefore, that when a sinner, though criminal, receives the penitential robe of this order, he does well; and one who is righteous and has a perfect testimony of righteousness before God and men, yet nevertheless receives it, does exceedingly well. But one who, because he is righteous—or thinks himself righteous—despises this humility, saying that it is penitential and is merely a sort of confinement owed to guilty persons, acts wrongly [Col. 1792D]. But let us now leave these matters, which have something of controversy about them, and return more quickly to that house of mercy, hastening to complete the discourse we began from it.

## CHAPTER X. On the most merciful Father: why it is said, “running, he fell upon his neck”; and how the Father truly falls upon the neck of one who walks humbly because of sins.

Above we said that mercy is true religion. This true and unfeigned religion first takes root inwardly in the heart, then extends outward through speech and habit; for “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12), and “a person’s dress and gait declare what he is” (Ecclus. 19:27; cited here as IX) [Col. 1793A].

This passage most beautifully and most holily indicates to the careful reader the effective cause of this religion or mercy, where it says: “And running, he fell upon his neck” (Luke 15). For truly, whenever you see or perceive someone groaning with a broken heart and walking with bowed head according to the teaching of the true Master, who says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11), you may rightly say that the Father has fallen upon his neck. By his weight he has broken and crushed the neck of that person’s heart, so that he cannot walk upright, and at times cannot even lift his eyes to heaven, but, with his eyes fixed upon the ground, looks at the earth, remembering to himself: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3).

Promising to do this same thing in other words, the Lord says in Hosea: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing, and I went up upon the beauty of her neck; I shall mount Ephraim; Judah shall plough; Jacob shall break up his furrows. Sow for yourselves righteousness in truth, and reap in the mouth of mercy” (Hos. 10) [Col. 1793B].

For what is “Ephraim, a heifer trained to love threshing,” except a wanton soul accustomed to bear the labors of this world and miserable slavery for the sake of satisfying its lust? Such, surely, was this son who had learned to feed swine and bear an unworthy servitude, until he returned to himself and said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I perish here with hunger?” (Luke 15).

“But I,” he says, “went up upon the beauty of her neck; I shall mount Ephraim.” How he did or does this, he himself reverently indicates here when he speaks of the householder—whom no one doubts to be himself—because, seeing his son return, “he was moved with compassion; and running, he fell upon his neck and kissed him” (ibid.). For, as we have already said, to fall upon the neck is to humble the sinner’s mind greatly.

What follows? “Judah shall plough,” he says—that is, he shall confess. He is now worthy, because of his confession itself, to be called Judah; he shall plough, I say, by confessing—that is, he shall open the earth of his heart, saying: “I have sinned against heaven and before you” (ibid.). “Jacob also shall break up his furrows”: that is, the supplanter of his former vices shall say in the breaking of his heart: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (ibid.) [Col. 1793D]. Then he will do what follows: he will sow righteousness for himself in truth, and reap in the mouth of mercy which says: “Quickly bring out the best robe” (ibid.). He will reap the same robe: either the robe of righteousness, or the righteousness of the robe.

## CHAPTER XI. That the Father truly fell upon Saul’s neck, who, now Paul, walked humbly and devoutly and instructed his disciple: “Exercise yourself unto godliness.”

The Apostle Paul, magnificently experiencing in himself what we are now saying—for this Father wondrously fell upon his neck, not because he was returning, but in order that he might return, since through ignorance he had turned away—more and more instructs his beloved disciple in that mercy by which one must live in the house of the most merciful Father. He says: “Exercise yourself unto godliness. For bodily exercise profits for a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4) [Col. 1794A].

These words of one truly wise are words of great weight, worthy to be weighed in a balance. To do this more briefly, let us recall the example of two men, Jacob and Esau. One of them, Esau, exercised himself in bodily exercise, as it is written: “Esau became a man skilled in hunting, a man of the field” (Gen. 25); while the other exercised himself in godliness, as is added: “But Jacob, a simple man, dwelt in tents” (ibid.).

And indeed bodily exercise profited Esau only a little. In what little way? Scripture says: “Isaac loved Esau because he ate of his hunting” (ibid.). It was truly a small thing that Isaac loved him; for he did not attain thereby to the greatest benefit, but to a very slight one, as it is written: “When he wept with a loud cry, Isaac, moved, said: ‘Your blessing shall be in the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above’” (Gen. 27) [Col. 1794B].

We do not say that he came to be hated by God for that bodily exercise, concerning whom it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1; Rom. 9). For he earned that hatred by hatred of his brother, whom he planned to kill, and by contempt for his father and mother, whereby he mingled with foreigners and took foreign wives. But we say that bodily exercise, and his father’s love for him on account of that exercise, profited him little.

Conversely, godliness profited Jacob in all things—the Jacob who dwelt simply in tents and whom Rebecca loved for that reason—having the promise of the present life and the future. For consequently, at his mother’s desire, he received his father’s blessing and deserved to be blessed, or to receive promises of blessing, both for the present and for the future. For the present, when his father said, “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed,” he immediately began thus: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, abundance of grain, wine, and oil” (Gen. 27) [Col. 1794D].

But with respect to the future, or future life, and what benefits life, he immediately added: “Let peoples serve you and tribes bow down to you. Be lord over your brothers, and let your mother’s sons bow down before you. Cursed be everyone who curses you, and let everyone who blesses you be filled with blessings” (ibid.). In these words he received the promise of future life: that is, the promise of Christ, that Christ should be born from his seed—Christ who is future life itself, eternal life.

With this example of the two men understood beforehand, we more readily understand what the Apostle said, and how truly he said it: “Bodily exercise profits for a little, but godliness is profitable for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” [Col. 1795A]. For what was prefigured in those two is shown to endure throughout humanity: those who devote themselves to bodily or temporal matters gain from them little benefit, or almost none; but those who pursue godliness and live simply provide for themselves in all things, so that they lack nothing needed by soul and body. As Truth says in the Gospel: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6; Luke 12).

For he himself more clearly expresses that this is his meaning when he says a little later: “Godliness with sufficiency is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and without doubt we can carry nothing out. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these. For those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (1 Tim. 6) [Col. 1795B]. And immediately afterward: “But you, O man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, patience, gentleness” (ibid.).

Moreover, he teaches how godliness ought to be exercised among one another, both by prelates toward subjects and by subjects toward prelates, when he says: “Take heed to yourself and to the teaching; persist in these. For by doing this you shall save both yourself and those who hear you” (1 Tim. 4). “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all chastity” (1 Tim. 5; cited here as IV), etc. This truly is the prelates’ exercise of godliness toward subjects.

Afterward he says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be held worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching. For Scripture says: ‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing’; and: ‘The laborer is worthy of his wages.’ Do not receive an accusation against a presbyter except on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (1 Tim. 5) [Col. 1795C]. And by doing this, subjects exercise themselves in godliness toward their prelates.

Finally, he does not keep silent about how the rich of this age ought, according to their condition, to exercise themselves in godliness, when he says: “Charge the rich of this age not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living and true God, who provides us abundantly with all things for enjoyment: to do good, to become rich in good works, to give readily, to share, laying up for themselves a good foundation for the future, that they may lay hold on true life” (1 Tim. 6) [Col. 1795D].

## CHAPTER XII. On the words of paternal mercy: “Let us eat and feast, because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.”

Meanwhile, note by what and how great a reason mercy proceeds in this very haste. For when he had said: “Quickly bring out the best robe and put it on him; put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet; bring the calf and kill it; and let us eat and feast” (Luke 15), he immediately, as though someone asked the reason for so great and prompt a generosity, gave this answer: “Because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (ibid.) [Col. 1796A].

This is indeed a great reason, worthy to be heard and imitated, and long ago made known to the entire house of this Father. No member of his holy Church may be ignorant of it. Unless the one who was dead has first come to life, unless the one who was lost has been found, he may not be adorned with the ring—that is, reconciled to the Church of the faithful; he may not be shod with sandals in preparation for the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6); he may not be invited or admitted to the feast of the fatted calf—that is, to participation in the body and blood of the Lord.

Nor has the Church’s prudence overlooked the question of how one is to know that he has come to life and been found. And what is it? Surely the voice of confession, such as is heard here when the returning man says: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15) [Col. 1796B]. It is also mystically implied in another reading, where it is narrated how and in what order the Lord raised Lazarus, dead four days and already stinking. The Lord cried with a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth.” Immediately the one who had been dead came out, his hands and feet bound with bands; and only then: “Untie him,” he said, “and let him go” (John 11).

Thus, as this sinner first confesses and says, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you,” and only then is it said, “Quickly bring out the best robe,” etc.; so there the man who had been dead first came out, and only then was he commanded to be untied. In both events the same reason applies: he ought to be received into the communion of the Church because he has confessed and offered worthy repentance [Col. 1796C].

## CHAPTER XIII. That eating, feasting, and rejoicing because one has come to life or been found are not the whole work of mercy; one must also fast, pray, and weep so that the lost may be found and the dead restored to life.

Nor is it the whole or complete office of mercy to eat, feast, and rejoice because one who was dead has come to life and one who was lost has been found. Indeed, before one dead returns to life or one lost is found, fasting, prayer, and weeping that he may return to life and be found are especially the work of mercy.

A mystical example of this is the widow in the Gospel, whose only son had died and was being carried out through the city gate. Moved with compassion for her, the Lord said: “Do not weep.” He approached and touched the bier; those carrying it stood still. And he said: “Young man, I say to you: arise.” The man who had been dead sat up and began to speak, and he gave him to his mother (Luke 7) [Col. 1796D].

The widowed mother is the holy Church: widowed, I say, because her husband was crucified before her and died. Though he rose again and now lives, he is not bodily present here, but has ascended into heaven and sits at the Father’s right hand. Her son is every believer reborn to Christ through the sacraments of this same Church. But the son dies and is carried out through the city gate whenever he commits a deadly crime, to the completion of the deed—that is, a manifest act.

Here mercy is needed; here the mother must weep and pray over her dead son. For the death of sin is a bloody and dreadful death. Here holy Scripture—or the Spirit of holy Scripture, the creating Spirit—labors to enable us somehow to feel the magnitude of the danger and the terrible kind of death by which a human being dies through sinning. For it says: “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet, and a crown of twelve stars upon her head. Being with child, she cried out in labor and was tormented to give birth” (Rev. 12) [Col. 1797A]. And immediately afterward: “The dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that, when she had borne, he might devour her son” (ibid.).

Although, according to one higher interpretation, this happened once and does not cease happening until the end of the age: it happened once when the entire Church of patriarchs, prophets, and all the elect bore Christ in the flesh through the Virgin Mary, who is a part of that same Church, with the great cry of great longing and long expectation. Then the dragon stood before the woman in order, once she had borne, immediately to devour her son. He was, indeed, immediately in Herod, seeking the child in order to destroy him; and from then on he persecuted him until he was crucified, saying: “When shall he die and his name perish?” (Ps. 40 [41]).

But that male son was the same mighty God, and therefore was caught up to God and to his throne [Col. 1797C]; for he rose and ascended into heaven to the Father’s throne, to rule the nations with an iron rod (Rev. 12), that is, with inflexible justice. Then, I say, this happened once: the dragon stood before the woman giving birth, desiring to devour her son, so that his name might perish (ibid.). But now, as has already been said, it happens and does not cease happening: he stands before the woman in order to devour one of her sons who believes in Christ.

For if to win anyone for Christ, or to form Christ in anyone, were not to give birth, the Apostle would not say: “My little children, whom I labor to bear again until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4; cited here as V). Therefore this holy Spirit of mercy labors to impress upon us the perception and show us the face of this cruel and dreadful death, the death of sin: because a human being is separated from the living God and incorporated into the devil, the prince of death. He does so by displaying such images as a woman in labor and a great red dragon with seven heads, standing before her and ready to devour her child [Col. 1797D].

Oh, how many and how horrific were the gaping jaws of his mouth and throat, how bloody his teeth, how deep the hell of his belly, which the aforementioned Apostle saw in this same Spirit of mercy when he said: “For I fear lest perhaps, when I come, I may not find you such as I wish, and I may be found by you such as you do not wish; lest perhaps there be among you strife, envy, angers, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, swellings of pride, seditions; lest, when I come again, God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the impurity, fornication, and indecency which they committed” (2 Cor. 12) [Col. 1798A].

This, then, as we have said, is the true and perfect work of mercy: to weep and mourn over those who are dead in their death and lost in their perdition; and only then to eat, feast, and rejoice when they have returned to life and been found.

## CHAPTER XIV. That today there should indeed be rejoicing in the Father’s house because the son who had been dead has come to life; but also sorrow because the elder brother stands outside and refuses to enter.

By the grace of so great a Father, behold, today we take part in such a banquet and such joys, and we feast in true mercy only if we rejoice in the Lord over a sinner’s conversion. Yet this too belongs to the office of mercy: that our joy be diminished for a while because of the hardness of our brother who is outside, standing stubbornly in anger and refusing to enter. For it is written of him: “When he came and drew near to the house, he heard music and dancing. He called one of the servants and asked what these things were. And he said to him: ‘Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fatted calf because he has received him safe and sound.’ But he became angry and would not enter” (Luke 15) [Col. 1798B].

That brother is the Jewish people: specifically, the brother of the people of the Gentiles, because God is one God of Jews and Gentiles, because the one Adam whom he formed is the father of all. He is called the elder brother because he came first to the worship of the one God. He is also said to have been in the field because, in performing the just requirements of the Law, he pursued agricultural—that is, earthly—rewards.

We must carefully consider what is said: “Angry, he would not enter.” He did not remain outside through ignorance, but knowingly recognized that the Father was at home and rejoiced over the one who had been lost and found. For he called one of the servants and, asking what these things were that he heard, was informed and learned from him what was true. Let us not suppose, then, that the Jews stand outside through ignorance and refuse to enter the evangelical house—especially those who are able to call and ask one of the servants, that is, to hear the voices of the prophets read every Sabbath and to grasp their meaning in some measure [Col. 1798D].

For if they were ignorant or did not understand, rather than being unwilling to understand; if, I say, they stood outside through ignorance rather than envy, hating the salvation of the Gentiles, such a narrative of the parable would not be fitting. First music and dancing are heard; then, by calling one servant, what is taking place inside is more certainly learned.

The music is the harmonious and concordant proclamation of evangelical grace; the dance is thanksgiving and the voice of praise, heard throughout every land and among all lands—even bodily by the Jews, dispersed among all nations. They hear it and, scattered in every direction, behold in our streets, cities, and city squares our feasts by day and night, outside and inside; they perceive by sight and hearing the choirs by which we praise God and his Christ with the Holy Spirit [Col. 1799A].

Moreover, the one servant whom he was able to call and ask is the unity and single truth of all the Scriptures of the Old Testament which the Jew accepts. There are two servants from whom he might have inquired, because there are two Testaments, Old and New, from which the Jew, if he wished, could have been fully taught. But he called only one, and that one declared what was sufficient, setting forth the whole truth. For where does the Old Testament fail to speak of the younger brother’s return and of the slaughter of the fatted calf—that is, of the conversion of the Gentiles and the Passion of Christ, the Son of God?

For example, at the beginning of the discourse in which God speaks to Abraham, there is such a rationale and such a ground as affords advocacy for receiving the Gentiles and strikes down the Jews’ arrogance, by which they suppose that the Gentiles cannot be saved without them: “Go,” he says, “from your land, your kindred, and your father’s house, and go into the land which I shall show you. I shall make you into a great nation, bless you, magnify your name, and you shall be blessed. I shall bless those who bless you, and in you all the kindreds of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 12) [Col. 1799B].

Likewise, in the promise: “By myself,” says the Lord, “I have sworn, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son: I shall bless you and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand upon the shore of the sea. Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in your seed all nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22).

O Jew, even if you as a whole were such as Abraham was, and obeyed in every respect as he obeyed the Lord’s voice, what else can or will you demand as your reward than what God promised—or promised again—to Abraham? Did he promise that he would give heaven or paradise to Abraham, or to the seed of his flesh alone, if it obeyed his voice? Certainly not. Rather, he promised only a certain seed, a seed of blessing, in which not the Jew alone but all nations would be blessed.

What that seed is, and what is the manner of the blessing, the entire prophetic order attests: it is Christ and the forgiveness of sins granted through his blood. Therefore the elder brother acts impiously because he hates outside salvation; but the one who has been found and has come to life within is taught mercy: not to return evil for evil, but to love the one who hates him, to grieve with the envious person, and, if he is not yet so perfect, at least not to insult the one left outside [Col. 1799D].

For this is what the Apostle says to him: “If some of the branches have been broken off, and you, though a wild olive, have been grafted in among them and made a partaker of the root and richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you boast, it is not you who bear the root, but the root you. You will say then: ‘The branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ Well: they were broken off because of unbelief, while you stand by faith. Do not be high-minded, but fear. For if God did not spare the natural branches, perhaps neither will he spare you. See, then, the goodness and severity of God: severity indeed toward those who fell, but God’s goodness toward you, if you continue in goodness” (Rom. 11) [Col. 1800A].

To hear this and act thus is merciful. This is confirmed by the example of the one who teaches it; for he who urges it shows above that he himself does what he teaches: “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit, that I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart. For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers” (Rom. 9), etc.

## CHAPTER XV. That what was said, “Therefore his father came out and began to entreat him,” is yet to take place; and in what sense it may be said to him, “Son, you are always with me.”

What follows, then, is yet to come to pass: “Therefore his father came out and began to entreat him” (Luke 15). For this is what the Apostle says in the passage mentioned above: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter; and so all Israel shall be saved, as it is written” (Isa. 59): “There shall come from Zion one who delivers, and turns impiety away from Jacob” (Rom. 11).

For Israel’s having suffered blindness is the same as the indignant brother’s unwillingness to enter. And the coming from Zion of one who delivers and turns impiety away from Jacob is the father’s going out and entreating the envious man to put aside impiety and enter the feast of piety. The very words by which the Father will turn away impiety are these mystical words: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours. But it was right to feast and rejoice, because this your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15).

The meaning of the latter verse is plain; that of the preceding statement partly needs inquiry and partly is clear. For when he says, “All that is mine is yours,” this is likewise what the Apostle says: “To them belong the adoption as sons, and the glory, and the covenant, and the giving of the Law, and the worship, and the promises; theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 9). Thus this is plain.

But the words “you are always with me” (Luke 15) require inquiry, because, so long as that son stands outside and refuses to enter, he is plainly not with the father. Yet before this younger brother returned, before this feast was celebrated—that is, before Christ suffered, whose flesh we now eat and whose blood we drink in our feast—the elder son was not always with him. Anyone who reads the sacred histories clearly recognizes this: they relate that this elder son, repeatedly fleeing from his father’s presence and house, ran after the husks of swine, worshipping idols, sacrificing to Baal-peor, and serving the demons of neighboring nations (Num. 25; Ps. 105).

Therefore, when he says, “You are always with me,” he either speaks with reference to that portion of the people—however few—who remain without abandoning the God of their fathers, as when it was said to Elijah: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal” (3 Kings 19; Rom. 11); or else, with a most weighty rebuke, he gives the reason why the father had never made a feast for that son to dine with his friends. If this latter interpretation pleases, then when he says, “You are always with me,” it is as though he said: “You claim for yourself that you are righteous. But I did not come to make such a feast for a righteous man, but for a sinner.”

For he had said: “Behold, for so many years I serve you, and I have never transgressed your command; but this son of yours has squandered his substance by living extravagantly with prostitutes.” Thus the words “you are always with me” may be understood as spoken not because this is so, but because he arrogates it to himself. For even today, though he remains outside, that people boasts that it alone is the people of God; and though it is dying from envy and unbelief, it presumes upon its own righteousness, as the Apostle says: “Seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10).

## CHAPTER XVI. What is to be understood by the words, “You never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends.”

Before this impiety is turned away from Jacob, before that elder son hears or receives from the father’s mouth the rule of piety, what does he say to his father? Having first said, “Behold, for so many years I serve you, and I have never transgressed your command,” he immediately added indignantly and with a murmuring heart: “And you never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends. But when this son of yours, who devoured his substance with prostitutes, came, you killed for him the fatted calf” (Luke 15).

For it had indeed already been said that his father came out and began to entreat him; but before the words of entreaty themselves come these words spoken by the son. Only then do the former follow, when he says: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours; but it was right to feast and rejoice” (ibid.), and so forth.

Thus these words of the brother express the present envy of the Jewish people and its wicked expectation, by which it desires the one who will come in his own name—namely, Antichrist. Hence it must be noted that he says, “You never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends.” He did not say “a lamb” or “a calf,” but “a kid”; he said, “You did not give it to me”; he did not say, “that I might feast with you,” but “with my friends.”

For the Antichrist whom that people expects and will receive when he comes in his own name will not be a lamb, like him of whom it is written: “Like a lamb before the one who shears it he shall be silent, and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). Rather, he will be their greatest kid, one of those to be set at the left hand when the King sits upon the throne of his majesty. As his type, by the Lord’s command through Moses, the scapegoat was cursed, spat upon, and sent out into the wilderness (Lev. 16).

For if Christ too is sometimes understood by a kid, this is known to occur for an external reason: namely, because he who is called a lamb on account of innocence is called a kid because he bore upon himself the sins of many. Therefore, when that brother says, “You never gave me a kid,” the weariness of the Jewish people is implied, sighing because it has not yet received Antichrist.

Yet it calls the one whom it expects and will receive not Antichrist, but Christ. Why, then, does this parable charge it with murmuring over a kid, and call the one in whom it wishes to feast a kid? Clearly, in order to expose that people’s desire and earthly disposition: though in speech and with its lips it calls him Christ, in thought and intention it professes that it awaits Antichrist. For it does not await one who gives life to the dead, but one who kills the living; not one who makes peace, but one who stirs up wars and sheds human blood.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the kid: that it is Antichrist, at whose coming that people desires to feast.

Concerning that false lamb and true kid, false Christ and true Antichrist, after the dragon—which, as we said in the preceding book, persecuted the woman and sent a flood from its mouth after her—it is written as follows: “And I stood upon the sand of the sea” (Rev. 12). “And I saw a beast rising from the sea, having nine heads [the Vulgate: seven] and ten horns” (Rev. 13). And immediately afterward: “And one of its heads, as though slain unto death, and the wound of its death was healed. And the whole earth marveled after the beast. And they worshipped the dragon which gave authority to the beast, and they worshipped the beast, saying: Who is like the beast, and who can fight with it? And there was given to it a mouth speaking great things and blasphemy; and authority was given to it to act for forty-two months” (ibid.), and so forth.

The beast rising from the sea signifies the entire body of which that dragon—that is, the devil—is the head: namely, the whole multitude of the impious. Its seven heads and ten horns are the same thing, that is, all the power of the earthly kingdom; for by the seven heads all its kings are represented, and by the ten horns its whole kingdom. The names of blasphemy are upon its heads because its kings have been called gods.

The one of its heads, as though slain, whose mortal wound was healed, signifies Antichrist, belonging to the heads of the earthly kingdom. In imitation of our true Head, he dares to present himself as one who has risen from the dead, as though slain, and as one to be received in place of Christ, who truly accomplished this. The deceitful anticipation of this fiction is said to have appeared in Simon Magus.

Thus, in the estimation of his deceivers and by his own pretense, he will be a lamb; but in truth he will be a kid—indeed, a beast or a horn of the beast. In his pride and cruelty that envious brother, who will deservedly be condemned because he did not believe the truth but will receive a lie, feasts or wishes to feast; yet, as has already been said through the prophet and recalled by the Apostle, a remnant will be saved.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the persecution of this same Antichrist: that it will be great.

Concerning his persecution, namely Antichrist’s, that it will truly be great, the Lord declares with a most grave pronouncement when he says in Matthew: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days. Pray that your flight may not occur in winter or on a Sabbath. For then there will be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning of the world until now, nor ever shall be. And unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved; but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened. Then if anyone says to you, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or ‘There,’ do not believe it. For false Christs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Matt. 24).

The same thing is expressed in other words in the Apocalypse: “And it was given to him to make war upon the saints and to overcome them; and authority was given to him over every tribe and people and tongue and nation. And all who dwell on the earth shall worship him, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Rev. 13). And immediately afterward: “And he performed great signs, so that he even made fire come down from heaven to earth before men. And he deceives those who dwell on the earth through the signs which were given him to perform” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the abundance of piety by which at last that brother—that is, all Israel—will be saved.

After such an abundance of impiety, the Spirit of piety will work mightily, as the father says to that elder brother: “But it was right to feast and rejoice, because this your brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15). For he will hear this in the remnant of that people who will be converted and saved, and the prophetic saying recalled by the Apostle will be fulfilled: “There shall come from Zion,” he says, “one who delivers and turns impiety away from Jacob” (Rom. 8).

Then at last that elder brother will feast with the younger brother and with the father in the house of Christ, having learned that it profited him nothing—indeed, that what he had said was false: “Behold, for so many years I serve you, and I have never transgressed your command” (Luke 15). He will have learned, I say, that it availed him nothing to have trusted that he was always with the father or that all that belonged to the father was his. Yet this can in some respect be true, so much so that Salvation himself, the Savior, testifies in his own mouth: “For salvation is from the Jews” (John 4).

Indeed, he will learn that all things are to be counted as loss and regarded as dung wherever they are or have been outside that feast, outside the true delights of piety. Once this has happened, they will fulfil what was mystically prefigured in Joseph, when the lord of the land, the prince of Egypt, was recognized by his brothers, and they feasted with him at noon, and he drank and became drunk with them (Gen. 43). And he said to the same men who had sold him: “You intended evil against me, but God turned it to good” (Gen. 50). He will say this to them not in reproach, but with forgiveness and grace, setting before them the miracle of that most high purpose of his.

## CHAPTER XX. That meanwhile, while we are trained in piety, we must beware of being deceived by a false image of piety.

Meanwhile, while we pursue piety and are commanded to be trained in piety, truth is also necessary, so that piety may be true and truth may be true, lest at any time we be deceived by a false likeness of piety. For there is a leniency which wishes to appear piety, but is certainly far from the spirit of piety, since by forgiving it loosens restraints, by sparing it hates, and through its own indolence and softness permits vices that ought to have been cut away to be nourished.

The saints do not so preach piety as to neglect the dignity of severity. One eminent among them, exempting himself from this suspicion, said that one must act prudently in correction and do nothing excessively, lest, while one desires too greatly to scrape off the rust, the vessel be broken. He added that one should remain ever mindful of one’s own fragility and remember that it is written that a bruised reed is not to be broken (Matt. 12). Immediately he continued: “In these matters we do not say that one should permit vices to be nourished, but that one should cut them away prudently and with charity, as one sees expedient for each person.”

If examples are sought, who was gentler or more pious than Moses? For it is written: “Moses was a man most meek above all men who dwelt on earth” (Num. 12). Yet, when the occasion required, he knew how to be severe. Standing at the gate of the camp, he said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, join himself to me.” And all the sons of Levi gathered to him. To them he said: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let every man put his sword upon his thigh. Go to and fro from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each one kill his brother, friend, and neighbor” (Exod. 32).

He did this as one severe and rigid with good zeal (Isa. 42). Yet in the very rigor of his severity, because he was most meek, he was by no means forgetful of his gentleness. For what follows is this: “On the following day Moses spoke to the people: ‘You have sinned a great sin. I will go up to the Lord, if perhaps I may be able to entreat him for your crime.’ And, returning to the Lord, he said: ‘I beseech you, this people has sinned a great sin and has made gods of gold for themselves. Either forgive them this offence, or, if you will not, blot me out of your book which you have written’” (ibid.).

Therefore, the companion of true piety or true gentleness is, always as occasion and circumstance require, reasonable discernment—namely, when a fault is made known by someone other than its author. In Moses a salutary example of both courses has shone before us.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Gospel example of the steward who says, “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg; I know what I shall do,” and so forth; and how it is to be imitated in the exercise of piety.

But there are times when, likewise as circumstance and occasion require, piety ought to proceed alone without the rod of severity: namely, when humility of confession voluntarily reveals in secret what was secretly committed. The one in whom the Spirit of piety wholly and perpetually dwells gives us an example of this, praising the prudence of that steward who provided for himself in this manner: “What shall I do,” he says, “because my master is taking the stewardship away from me? I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg” (Luke 16). And immediately, having found a good plan, he says: “I know what I shall do, so that, when I have been removed from the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.”

Therefore, summoning each debtor of his master, he said: “How much do you owe my master?” The man said: “A hundred measures of oil.” And he said to him: “Take your note, sit down, and quickly write fifty” (ibid.), and so forth.

Finally, just as the preceding parable of the prodigal son and his elder brother, who envied him when he returned to life and was found, contains the mystery of the Gentile people and the Jewish people, so this following parable represents a prelate and a sinful subject of his—only a subject whose sins are known to no judge except God and his own conscience.

For whoever presides over souls is indeed the steward of the highest Lord. If he possesses true and truly humble prudence, if he has any real beginning of righteousness, he judges himself daily in his conscience or thought, according to the saying: “The thoughts of the righteous are judgments” (Prov. 12). He sets before his mind the tribunal of his master; and, while conscience accuses him—for “the righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. 18)—confession judges him and fear binds him. There he hears, or seems to himself to hear, his master saying: “What is this that I hear concerning you? Render an account of your stewardship; for you can no longer be steward.”

For he who guards—or ought to have guarded—souls recognizes that he has squandered much and great substance of his Lord, if he rightly considers how he ought to have preserved it. Considering this, he truly confesses that he should be removed, that he should deservedly be cast out, if judgment were conducted with him according to justice alone.

Providing for himself, therefore, that he may find mercy, he himself becomes merciful to his subjects, calling each one of them separately and saying: “How much do you owe my Lord?” For this is to be concerned for each subject or person entrusted to him: by private and secret admonition to ask him to disclose how much he owes God—that is, not to conceal his sins or the evil thoughts coming into his heart—according to the saying: “I said: I will confess against myself my injustices to the Lord” (Ps. 31).

If he immediately says, “A hundred measures of oil,” or “a hundred cors of wheat”—that is, if he simply opens his voice in confession and enumerates his sins, or does not conceal that they are great and many—the steward employs his prudence and skill: “Sit down,” he says, “quickly write fifty; sit down, quickly write eighty.” Yet he prescribes to each himself, saying: “Take your note.” This means: “Only take care yourself that henceforth you make lighter the due severity of penance. For example, you who would have owed a penance of seven or twelve years if you had been brought before the public tribunals of the Church, repent for one year, or for forty days, or, after the example of the Ninevites, for three days; and I will render an account for you to my Lord on the day of judgment.”

So greatly ought this likeness of the steward to please us. He was indeed an unjust and wasteful steward to his master, but he acted prudently for himself and wisely provided for himself. So greatly, I say, ought the example of a worldly steward to prevail among spiritual people that they may deservedly rebuke themselves and say: “The children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16).

For Truth himself said this, and it must be understood thus: worldly people provide more prudently, more watchfully, and more eagerly for their timely interests and transitory safety than men of spiritual purpose apply concern and zeal for piety to their eternal welfare. Let us at least imitate them in matters relating to God; let us at least be stirred by their example in matters pertaining to eternal life.

# BOOK NINE: ON THE WORKS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. ON THE FEAR OF THE LORD.

## CHAPTER I. On the spirit of the fear of the Lord: that expectation of the universal judgment is its greatest instrument.

Of all the things handed down to us from holy and truthful Scripture for belief and confession, the end is the universal judgment. It is truly the greatest and chief instrument of that Spirit of the Lord who is placed after the spirit of piety in the descent. For there fear is no small thing; there one must tremble with no slight fear. We may truly say again and again that there is fear, and that whoever does not tremble with fear there is not wise.

“For then the angels will fear,” says the Lord, “and, terrified, will be purified” (Job 41). “For the righteous man will scarcely be saved” (1 Pet. 4), even if, by reason of his righteousness, he is such a one as may rightly be called an angel, whose lips have preserved knowledge and who, for those seeking the Law from his mouth, has become the angel—that is, messenger—of the Lord of hosts (Mal. 2).

Thus the Spirit of the fear of the Lord is rightly so called because, by first breathing upon us, who are senseless and proud—and therefore senseless because proud—he makes us believe those things which we shall see and hear there, so that, believing and reflecting, we may fear; fearing, we may leave folly behind and flee to wisdom.

## CHAPTER II. On that great day of judgment, and how it resembles the first of the days of the world.

That day, the day of the great judgment, will be the last of the days of the world. Let us now look back to that day which holy Scripture placed first in number at its beginning, when God divided light and darkness, called the light day and the darkness night, and, it says, “there was evening and morning, one day” (Gen. 1).

It is first in number because, as we said there as far as we were able, another day is first by nature, while this one is first only in number or in the order of creation. For the day which is truly first is not temporal but eternal, not lighted by a creature but the light that illumines creation. Knowing this, the writer did not wish to say, “There was evening and morning, the first day,” but said, “There was evening and morning, one day.”

Let us look, I say, to that day and consider the wonderful ordering of God’s works. He set the same, as it were, terrible guardian at the entrance and exit of Scripture, or of his works, so that whoever enters to know God may find at the entrance why he ought to fear greatly, and at the exit may hear why he ought to tremble all the more. For when it is said, “He divided light and darkness, and called the light day and the darkness night,” we understand that the angels were judged and that the social and immutable division of good and evil spirits was made; and here we have heard in the clear words of Scripture that an immutable judgment of angels and human beings alike is to take place.

There, apostate angels were cast out of heaven into this darksome air; here, we know that those same angels and the impious people who follow them will be cast into eternal fire.

## CHAPTER III. On the seven spirits of the Lord: that he who was first in this work is also its end, namely the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

Therefore let us give thanks to this Spirit of the Lord: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. For he has willed that we should abound beyond what we ourselves could prepare or foresee, and has made us experience in truth what he deigns to promise to Israel, an infant crying and hungry: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80).

Through so long a course he has led us and brought us back by the straight path, so that the beginning is the same as the end. Going and returning, we have seen and see that the foundation of the fear of the Lord is necessary for all who ascend and have now been set on high. We now know, and dare to know, that we acted advisedly, and that by his goodness this Spirit—who is goodness itself—has cared for our smallness.

In what respect? Namely in this: when we proposed to write about the holy Trinity and its works, we kept the seven Spirits of God before our eyes—that is, in our intention—not doubting that the good God had done, and does, whatever he had done or does according to the sevenfold power in this age of the goodness of his own good and holy Spirit.

With this intention, as with a truly single eye and a lamp truly leading the way, we see that in the work of the Lord who creates all things visible and invisible the stages of the seven days were arranged according to this sevenfold Spirit, from fear to wisdom. Thus Scripture rightly said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Job 28; Ps. 110; Prov. 8). After humanity’s fall, there again followed, in the same order, the stages and advances of the seven ages according to the same seven Spirits of the Lord; and after the Lord’s Passion, with the order reversed, the same stages extended from wisdom to the fear of the Lord. Thus, according to these same Spirits, the Lord’s works are everywhere great, sought out, and wonderfully ordered (Ps. 110).

Let us sit here upon this foundation of necessary solitude and complete in the fear of the Lord what remains of this very lengthy discourse.

## CHAPTER IV. On distinguishing the meaning of fear.

First, it must be said that the meaning of good fear is divided in two ways: not indeed from different sources, but according to the different conditions of those who fear, the fear by which God is feared is one thing in one case and another in another. There is servile fear and liberal fear.

Servile fear, or the fear of servants, is that by which the punishment of sin is feared. Liberal fear, or the fear of sons, is that by which the loss of grace is guarded against. Let us try to distinguish each more clearly from the other.

Servile fear, which has punishment, belongs to beginners—that is, to those who are now beginning for the first time to look toward God, to remember the fire of Gehenna, and through that remembrance to strive against sin. This is not yet wisdom but only the beginning of wisdom; not yet altogether the fear of the Lord, but the fear of death; nor is it yet properly called holy fear, but only fear, or at least penal or anxious fear.

Liberal fear belongs to the perfect, or to those tending toward perfection—that is, to those who, after experiencing the consciousness of higher graces, voluntarily humble themselves to fear as a safeguard. This differs greatly from the former in many ways, especially in this: perfect charity casts out that servile and penal fear (1 John 4), whereas this liberal and holy fear remains for ever and ever (Ps. 18).

Yet both have this in common: each pierces the soul and sends tears, as though the soul’s blood, through the eyes, though different causes are at work. In the former, the cause is the distress of an anxious mind lest it be sent to Gehenna; in the latter, the effective cause is the soul’s longing because it is in exile and delayed from the kingdom. The subject now required by our place and purpose is the fear of beginners, also called servile or penal fear.

## CHAPTER V. That there are four fears of which the human soul is capable: two evil and two good.

This fear, or disturbance of soul, comes from faith and the Spirit of God. There are four fears of which the human soul is capable; and therefore, since we propose to discuss one of them, a definition is needed. Two fears are evil and two good.

One evil fear is a kind of passion or disturbance of mind, coming neither from faith nor from the Spirit of God. Even secular philosophers disapprove it; among them one reads, often enough, of four passions of the soul—joy, fear, hope, and sorrow—and, correspondingly, four virtues: temperance, courage, prudence, and justice. That fear is evil because it disturbs the mind over things concerning which it ought not to be disturbed: the loss of worldly wealth or the approach of adversities which, for the sake of what is beneficial, ought to have been borne bravely.

Another fear is evil though it comes from faith, because it does not come from the Spirit of God: it sometimes disturbs the mind, but does not correct it. Someone may perhaps ask how something can come from faith but not from the Spirit of God, when faith itself is a gift of the Spirit of God. To this the Apostle James says: “You believe that God is one; you do well. The demons also believe and tremble. But do you wish to know, vain man, that faith without works is idle?” (Jas. 2). Earlier he had also said: “Faith, if it does not have works, is dead in itself” (ibid.).

Therefore there is an evil fear arising from faith but not from the Spirit of God, because it does not arise from faith working through love (Gal. 5), but from idle and therefore dead faith. All demons always have this fear, because they believe and tremble. Wicked human beings do not all have it, but many who are desperate do—as did the man of whom the Acts of the Apostles relates this:

“After some days Felix came with Drusilla his wife, who was a Jewess; he summoned Paul and heard from him concerning faith in Jesus Christ. But as Paul reasoned concerning righteousness, chastity, and the judgment to come, Felix became terrified and replied: ‘For the present, go away; at a convenient time I will summon you.’ At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul; therefore he summoned him frequently and conversed with him. But after two years had passed, Felix received Portius Festus as his successor. And Felix, wishing to do the Jews a favor, left Paul bound” (Acts 24).

Felix was terrified but did not correct himself: he who, in such a manner, did the Jews a favor and left the teacher of correction in chains. But why do we seek examples of this fear so far away? The first human being feared with this fear: “I heard your voice, Lord,” he says, “and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself” (Gen. 3). For he did not fear rightly, since he hid himself and refused to confess his fault.

We have spoken above of the distinctions between the good fears: one is servile and the other liberal; one belongs to beginners and the other to the perfect; one fears punishment, the other guards against the loss of grace. But they differ also in this: one is a passion or disturbance, whereas the other is peace and rest of mind.

The former says: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger. Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord, for my bones are troubled, and my soul is greatly troubled” (Ps. 6). And shortly afterward: “My eye has been troubled because of wrath” (ibid.). The latter, however, is so tranquil, quiet, and free from all disturbance that a certain wise man truly says of it: “Whoever fears the Lord will not tremble or be afraid, for he himself is that person’s hope. Blessed is the soul of the one who fears the Lord. To whom does he look, and who is his strength? A support of power, a shelter from heat, and shade at noon; a deliverance from stumbling and help from falling; raising up the soul and illuminating the eyes, giving health, life, and blessing” (Ecclus. 34).

Therefore the true and sufficient definition of good fear, though not yet the perfect and best fear—the fear that has punishment and which perfect charity casts out—is the one we have given: it is a passion or disturbance of mind coming from faith and from the Spirit of God.

## CHAPTER VI. On good but not yet perfect fear: how it divides a person against himself by contrary wills.

The first useful effect of this fear is that it divides one and the same human being against himself, so that he is as though two persons divided against one another by contrary wills, as the Apostle says: “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. For these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things that you wish” (Gal. 5).

This was not said so that it should be thought to give any support to that heresy which maintained that the human soul has a portion of God, whereas the body is a fabric made by an evil God; and therefore that flesh rejoices and soul grieves in contrary and distinct substances, and that in the things in which the soul exults the flesh is afflicted.

This is not the meaning of the words “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” Rather, the flesh is the whole person before the breathing in of the fear of God: flesh, that is, carnal. But when the Spirit of the fear of God breathes upon him and enters his soul, he is now partly flesh and partly spirit, and these two fight against one another with contrary pleasures.

The Apostle expresses this conflict more fully elsewhere, speaking in the person of every weak and imperfect person: “But I once lived without the law” (Rom. 7). What does “I once lived without the law” mean except “I did what I wished without fear”? For the one who lives without the law is one who acts without regard for the fear of God’s judgment, rejoices when he has done evil, and exults in the worst deeds (Prov. 2).

“But when the commandment came,” he says, “sin revived” (Rom. 7). Behold the origin of the war and the beginning of the dissension of which he said, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” For the commandment comes when this spirit of fear breathes upon a person and makes the soul mindful of the commandment and mindful of the coming judgment. Then, without doubt, sin revives, which had previously been as though dead; for the ardor of sin, having burned more sluggishly and negligently, presses more fiercely and tyrannizes, as it were, when it hears that this Spirit, bearer of the commandment, has risen in opposition to it in the court of the same soul.

Thus there is a great conflict between spirit and flesh—that is, between commandment and sin, or good fear and evil desire. A person so divided afterward says: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7).

This is the conflict or dissension of flesh and spirit, which a person can know in no other way than by experiencing it. Moreover, from what he immediately says—“Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (ibid.)—it is evident that one and the same human being is divided against himself, so that the fear of God, or fear of death, recommends one thing, while weakness or habit of the flesh recommends another.

Meanwhile the fear of God increases and gains strength, so that the sin dwelling in the flesh is cast out. Then at last what remains within is holy fear, and, in the place of the sin it has expelled, it finally enjoys the companionship of charity. Longing for this amid the conflict, he says: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

How this fear grows and reaches the holiness of peace, the Lord himself shows by this parable in the Gospel: “So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the earth and sleep, and rise by day and night, and the seed should sprout and grow, while he does not know it. For the earth of itself brings forth fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4).

## CHAPTER VII. On the terrible judgment of God, which is truly the great substance or cause of this fear.

What, then, is it by which this fear lays claim to the soul and summons it to assent to itself? Surely it is the dreadful judgment of God, which all divinely inspired Scripture continually proclaims as to come on the last day. [Col. 1811C] This is indeed a great power and ample matter by which that fear, if it was small or weak, may daily be nourished and strengthened. For, to leave aside or defer the rest for the present, the chief consideration of that judgment is that a person should know or reflect that, after this life—and especially after that universal judgment—no repentance remains for the sinner and the ungodly any more than for the devil.

Does not everyone who considers it perceive the devil to be most miserable, in that he has already received, as the due reward of his wickedness, this: because, when he was able, he was unwilling to advance, he can now neither be willing nor able to advance; and on that day of judgment he will receive the punishments of eternal fire, which have no end? For all the angels were created with free choice, and so established in goodness that they had the capacity to advance to what is better. Those who wished to do so advanced: those who had a good will. Those fell away and became apostates who preferred to please themselves rather than their Creator. Thereafter their judgment took place; and those who, though able to sin, refused to sin and firmly fixed their footing in love of the Creator, received this as their reward: that they can no longer sin, nor die through sinning. “For by the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and all their power by the breath of his mouth” (Ps. 32).

Conversely, the devil and all his angels, who committed wickedness with him, fell and were expelled by the movement of pride’s foot in such a way that they can no longer stand. They received precisely such a recompense [Col. 1812A] that they can never be restored, and will without doubt still receive on that day the recompense of eternal fire. Does not everyone, I say, who notices this perceive it to be most miserable?

Certainly, in whatever state a human being may be, he faces the same danger and stands in a similar condition before the same Judge, God. For he too was created good with free choice, so that, if he wished, he could advance to what is better; and because he neglected to advance and despised God, he was cast out of Paradise. Yet now, by the grace of the Redeemer, we have been restored to this same possibility, and are called and transferred from all nations into the Church of the present age for this purpose: that we may advance toward recovering the likeness of our Creator and the eternal life which we lost in Adam. Those among us who wish to do so have advanced and do advance [Col. 1812B], so that they have become, and may become, children of God.

Whoever now advances willingly in this way will receive on that day of judgment such a reward for this good will that he can no longer fall away, and will be eternally a child of the eternal God. Conversely, whoever among us now neglects or despises advancement will likewise receive on that day such a recompense that he can no longer advance, and will be a companion and fellow sharer of the devil and his angels in the flame of eternal fire. Thus that great judgment is truly a great ground and material of the fear of God in the human soul.

## Chapter VIII. On the coming of the awe-inspiring Judge, and how he will sit upon the throne of his majesty

[Col. 1812C] A great spectacle! For the King himself, the King’s Son, to whom God the Father has given judgment, says: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He shall place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left” (Matt. 25), and so forth.

The Son of Man will come; the Son of Man will appear. He will come from there in the manner in which he ascended from here. For the angels said: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1). How had they seen him? What kind of one had they seen ascending into heaven? They had seen the form of a servant ascending; [Col. 1812D] they had seen the marks of the nails in his hands and feet; they had seen his side wounded by the lance; and a cloud received such a one from their sight.

Great and sweet was the joy of those who beheld him, because he was taken up in this manner; and great will be the fear and trembling of those who await him, because he will come in this manner and so. For the cloud received him, and he will come in a cloud. “Then,” he says, “they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud, with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24). Therefore the Psalm truly says: “God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord at the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. 46). For the Apostles rejoiced, as it is written: “And they, worshipping him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke 24). Yet they also received the trumpet’s sound and made it heard by us, when it was said: “He will come in the same way as you saw [Col. 1813A] him go into heaven.”

For this proclamation is full of fear, like the sound of a trumpet announcing a great and terrible war. The Apostle, sharing this same thought, says: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thess. 4). “With a command,” that is, with the decree of majesty; “with the voice of an archangel,” that is, with the proclamation of angelic power announcing that the Judge is present; “with the trumpet of God,” that is, with thunder and terror such as God alone can produce. For then this same God of ours, who is also the Son of Man, “will come openly and will not keep silence” (Ps. 49).

Great, therefore, is the spectacle in which he will come with clouds, and every eye will see him, including those who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him (Rev. 1). All the angels will also come with him. And, as he himself testifies in another evangelist, when he comes “the powers of heaven shall be shaken” (Luke 21). What is more fearful still: he who first came in a spirit of gentleness, as the appearance of the dove that appeared above him showed (Matt. 3), will then come in a flame of fire. “He will be revealed from heaven with the angels of his power in a flame of fire,” says the Apostle, “taking vengeance on those who do not know God and who do not obey the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Thess. 1).

By that fire the heavens will be dissolved; the sea will be dried up, as some of the Fathers suppose, and perhaps for this reason John says in the Apocalypse: “And the sea is no more” (Rev. 21).
