Apostolic Scripture has not been silent that the heavens will be dissolved by heat: “The heavens which now are, and the earth, have by the same word been stored up, reserved for fire unto the day of judgment [Col. 1813C] and destruction of ungodly men” (2 Pet. 3). Again: “The day of the Lord will come as a thief, in which the heavens will pass away with a great rushing sound, and the elements will be dissolved by heat” (ibid.).

Then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty. He will not sit, like a deputy or envoy, upon another’s throne for an hour or a time; rather, as the rightful King and monarch of heaven, he will sit upon his own throne in his own majesty.

## Chapter IX. How all nations are to be gathered before him at the sounding of the last trumpet

“And all nations shall be gathered before him” (Matt. 25). How will they be gathered, and from where? They will be gathered by rising again; [Col. 1813D] they will be gathered by leaping forth from their tombs. The Apostle says: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

Such will be the speed of the gathering, or resurrection, that those found alive will not meet the Lord sooner than the dead. For, confirming this, he says: “For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep” (ibid.). We shall not precede them, but shall be caught up together. By “we who are alive,” he spoke as if he meant: those who will then be found in the body in the condition in which we who live today are found.

And by speaking thus he truly greatly magnifies the miracle [Col. 1814A] of the most swift resurrection, in which those found alive will be unable to be quicker in meeting the Lord than those who have long since returned to dust, whom the earth has consumed, the sea swallowed, or fire devoured. Hence elsewhere he says: “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Cor. 15). You ask: How can those scattered and consumed in so many different ways and into so many different places be found so quickly? Indeed, as quickly as you, a human being, cannot see what you hold enclosed in your palm. Have not the ashes of the dead been scattered in every direction? Does not all flesh return to the earth from which it was taken? And has it not truly been said to God: “You enclose the earth in your palm” (Isa. 40)? Therefore God will find as quickly what the earth has consumed as you find what you hold enclosed in your palm—namely, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.

How will they leap forth so quickly from so many tombs, from so many hidden depths of water and earth? At the sounding of the last trumpet: with the most almighty majesty thundering and shaking all things. “For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible” (1 Cor. 15). How did Lazarus, dead four days, rise again? (John 11.) This ought indeed to suffice as an experience of the truth and as evidence that the resurrection will be accomplished swiftly and powerfully. For Christ raised him bodily in this manner in order to establish faith in his promise when he had said: “Do not marvel at this, for the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God and shall come forth” (John 5). Likewise, he raised Lazarus’s sister Mary spiritually in order to establish faith in what he had similarly said: [Col. 1814C] “Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead—that is, sinners—shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (ibid.).

How then did he raise Lazarus? He merely cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth.” And at once he who had been dead came out, bound hand and foot with strips of cloth, and his face was bound with a napkin (John 11). A wonderful thing! How did he come out when his hands and feet were bound with strips, so that he could use neither hands nor feet to come out? How did he see where or by what route to go, when his face was bound with a napkin? Therefore his coming out was not his own doing, any more than was his return to life; rather, the one and same cry of the caller which imparted life to the body shook the body out of the tomb.

Let us therefore believe that, when the last trumpet—the trumpet of God—sounds, the dead will leap forth in the same manner as that dead man came out at the cry. For that cry foreshadowed the last trumpet. Thus, by rising and rushing forth from the tombs, all nations will be gathered before him, unable to hide. Indeed, if they could hide, they would wish to hide—not only the nations, but also the kings and rulers of the nations, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “The kings of the earth, the rulers, the commanders, the rich, the mighty, and every slave and free person hid themselves in caves and in the rocks of the mountains. And they say to the mountains and rocks: ‘Fall upon us, and hide us from the face of him who sits upon the throne and from the wrath of the Lamb. For the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?’” (Rev. 6).

## Chapter X. [Col. 1815A] How the Apostle’s saying is to be understood: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them.”

We must understand not only the speed of the resurrection, but also the excessive terror in the sound of the last trumpet, when the Apostle says in the passage cited above: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first” (1 Thess. 4). For this permits us to understand that, by one and the same rush or thunder of the great sounding trumpet, at one and the same crash of the archangelic voice and command of dreadful majesty, the dead, as though sleeping, will be shaken awake from the sleep of death; and those found alive will at once fall, stunned into death, [Col. 1815B] and immediately spring back from death.

For the words “we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds” must not be understood, nor ought they to be understood, as meaning that those found alive will not see death. Rather, as has already been said, those found alive will die, and by the same shock through which they die they will immediately be raised again to life. It is great and wonderful that the dead will be shaken alive out of their tombs; but greater and more wonderful that the living will be deprived of life by fear and restored to life and consciousness by the same terror.

Even the earth itself, which has neither soul nor sense, will tremble in the presence of that majesty as though it sensed wrath and suffered consciously. If such terror, or such force of terror, is in the voice or sounding of the heralding trumpet, what, or how great, do you suppose will be the experience of present wrath or vengeance in the very act of judgment? Truly, unless after the moment of resurrection we were already immortal, if we could die in any way, we would perish merely at the sight of open Tartarus and the eternal fire prepared for the ungodly. But then we shall no longer be able to die, and, whether willing or unwilling, we must live. Hence it is said most truly: “People shall desire to die, and death shall flee from them” (Rev. 9). Thus from that time onward the wicked will have, if it can be said, a death always living and a life always dying.

## Chapter XI. On his further saying: “All indeed shall rise, but not all shall be changed”

[Col. 1815D] The same Apostle says: “All indeed shall rise, but not all shall be changed.” Again: “The dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed” (1 Cor. 15). This is the hope, consolation, and confidence of the saints—of those possessing perfect charity. “All,” he says, that is, both reprobate and elect, shall rise; but not all shall be changed: only we, namely the elect, shall be changed.

What does “we shall be changed” mean? We shall become incapable of suffering; we shall take up bodies incapable of suffering. We do not hope or expect that on that day we need not see fire, or be present at the fire itself or among those burning in that fire. Rather, we have been promised, and ought to hope, that by rising we shall be so changed that, passing through the fire, we shall not feel the fire. So great will be the power of the truth of our faith and love, and so greatly will the justice of judgment favor truth, that fire will be unable to harm or grieve those with whom truth and justice abide.

This is what the same Apostle says: “Each person’s work shall be made manifest; for the day of the Lord shall declare it, because it is revealed in fire. And the fire shall test what sort each person’s work is” (1 Cor. 3). Here is cause for fear; here one must tremble in fear. For who can presume of himself that he belongs to the lot or number of those who are thus to be changed? Who among those to be found alive then can boast that his heart is so pure that neither wood, hay, nor straw, but only gold, silver, and precious stones will be found in his work—things which the fire cannot consume?

For many of those [Col. 1816B] who have died or are dying in the peace of the Church now need a long burning in purgatorial fire, because they have built upon the foundation of Christian faith not only hay or straw—that is, lighter sins—but also wood—that is, graver sins. Therefore, even among those elect, especially those who will then be found alive, very many will be judged while burning and purified while burning in judgment. Very few will be such that the mere fear of what they will see and hear will purify them, and they will immediately be changed into impassibility.

## Chapter XII. On the separation of the sheep from the goats, and on the four divisions of humankind that will exist in that judgment

When all nations have been gathered before him, “he shall separate them,” he says, “from one another, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He shall place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left” (Matt. 25). All nations will be gathered before him; yet not all people will stand there to be judged, nor will those already judged—that is, those who do not believe—receive a sentence before his sight. For the Apostle says: “As many as have sinned without the law shall perish without the law; and as many as have sinned under the law shall be judged by the law” (Rom. 2).

Nor should we pass over the promise which our Lord made to those who followed him: “Amen, I say to you that you who have left all things and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, shall also sit upon [Col. 1816D] twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). By the number twelve is signified the entire multitude of judges, on account of the two parts of the number seven, by which universality is often signified. For three times four, or four times three, makes twelve.

There will therefore be four divisions or ranks of people in that judgment. One rank will be that of the perfect, who will not be judged but will judge. Another will be that of those without God, who will not be judged but are already judged, who will perish without the law because they did not receive the law. The remaining two ranks will be those who received the law. Some of these kept the law they received and therefore will be judged by the law and saved; others did not keep the law they received and therefore will be judged [Col. 1817A] by the law and perish.

Clearly, because they received the law, they will be gathered like a flock before the shepherd; and because these kept the law whereas those did not, they will be separated, as he says, “as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.” Those who kept the law and loved the shepherd’s care are the sheep; those who did not keep it and did not love it are the goats. They will therefore be separated from one another, so that the wanton, butting goats may not enter the same blessed sheepfolds as the gentle lambs and sheep.

Here, meanwhile, while they are in the pastures, while they graze outside in the field of this world, goats walk mingled among sheep and indulge themselves among the simple lambs. At times they even gore and tear apart some of the weaker ones, while themselves stronger, with their raised and playful horns. [Col. 1817B] But when those sheepfolds are reached, they will be separated by the shepherd’s care, in accordance with the parable of the weeds in the field, where it was said: “The Son of Man shall send his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all stumbling blocks” (Matt. 13).

Moreover, understand the words, “He shall place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left,” in light of what we read elsewhere: “The heart of the wise is at God’s right hand, and the heart of the fool at his left” (Ecclus. 10). And earlier in this same Gospel: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 5). The sheep are commanded to stand at the right, in the portion of the righteous; the goats—that is, sinners—at the left, since goats are always offered under the law for sin. He did not say female goats, which can bear offspring and “come up from the washing, all bearing twins, and none barren among them” (Song 4), but a male goat: a wanton and unruly animal, always ardent for mating.

## Chapter XIII. On what the King will say to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father”

Then the King will say to those at his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink; I was a stranger and you took me in; naked and you clothed me; sick and you visited me; I was in prison and you came to me” (Matt. 25).

Truly good, and the hearing of a great good, is this: “Come, blessed of my Father.” Great and true is the good which he brings when he says, “Possess [Col. 1817D] the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” Here we ask: in what way was that kingdom prepared for these blessed persons? We have heard when, or from what point, it was prepared: namely, from the foundation of the world. He does not say “before the foundation of the world,” but “from the foundation of the world.”

Now Holy Scripture, which teaches us all things and answers us concerning all things, begins from the foundation of the world—that is, it first narrates the creation of the world. There, then, we inquire and quickly find how that kingdom was prepared for God’s blessed ones: “God completed on the seventh day the work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished. And God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had ceased from all his work which God created in order to make” (Gen. 2).

The Apostle testifies that it was prepared from then on, saying: “To whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest, except to those who were unbelieving? And we see that they could not enter because of unbelief” (Heb. 3). And shortly afterward: “Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again sets a certain day, ‘Today,’ saying in David, after so long a time, as has been said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward have spoken of another day. Therefore there remains a sabbatism for the people of God. For whoever has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his” (Heb. 4).

Now, since we desire to discover, and rejoice whenever we are granted to discover even a little, the intention of the Holy Spirit in his Scriptures, [Col. 1818B] let us count the works which he mentions. This King enumerates to those whom he has placed at his right, so that we may know firmly, according to that royal and apostolic Scripture, that the *sabbatism* to which he calls them in saying, “Come, blessed of my Father,” is lawful. First: “I was hungry and you gave me food.” Second: “I was thirsty and you gave me drink.” Third: “I was a stranger and you took me in.” Fourth: “I was naked and you clothed me.” Fifth: “I was sick and you visited me.” Sixth: “I was in prison and you came to me.”

Thus there are six works of mercy, after which and because of which he says: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom,” just as there are six days of work—that is, six kinds of God’s works—after the completion of which God rested. Therefore that kingdom is the *sabbatism*, and the seventh day on which God rested; and from that time the kingdom was prepared for those blessed persons, when God completed his work and blessed and sanctified the seventh day on which he rested.

For this reason the Apostle rightly said: “Whoever has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his” (Heb. 4). But who is that seventh day whom God blessed and sanctified, if not the Word and Wisdom, the Son of God? For this Son, this Word, this Wisdom in whom God made all things, is truly rest, delight, and pleasure to God, as Wisdom herself says in one passage: “I was with him arranging all things, and I was delighted day by day, playing before him at all times, playing in the inhabited world; and my delights were with the children of men” (Prov. 8).

And that God truly blessed and sanctified this day of brightness, the Day himself made known plainly by his own mouth, his radiant mouth: “If he called those gods to whom the word of God came, and Scripture cannot be broken, do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (John 10). Thus, I say, that kingdom is the Word and Wisdom, or the fullness of God’s Word and Wisdom, which the Apostle awaits when he says: “Now we know in part and prophesy in part; but when what is perfect comes, what is partial will be done away with” (1 Cor. 13). Again: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to [Col. 1819A] face. Now I know in part; then I shall know as I also have been known” (ibid.).

## Chapter XIV. That those to whom he will say, “I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth, do not here attain such perfection that they possess nothing

At the same time, from this it is clear that those placed at the right and addressed in these words are those who, not attaining to that perfection of which it was said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. 19), devote themselves to the active life. They have indeed incurred sins, but have endeavored to redeem them by almsgiving.

For those devoted to the contemplative life are not to be judged but to judge. Indeed, just as it is not theirs to possess anything in this world but to have left all things for Christ, [Col. 1819B] so it is not theirs to feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, take in the stranger, clothe the naked, or visit the sick and imprisoned. “Martha, Martha,” says the Lord, “you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10).

Therefore those who, serving with Martha, are anxious and troubled about many things are first called to possess the kingdom when they are judged and saved, because by serving well they have redeemed their sins by almsgiving. But those who, sitting with Mary at the Lord’s feet, hear his word (ibid.)—that is, those who possess the contemplative life—already reign in part, for they already in some way possess their portion. For to reign, or already to make a beginning of reigning, is to devote oneself to the Word of God and, on its account, to flee not only sins but also riches and even the lawful concerns [Col. 1819C] of the world.

It should therefore be noted that where he says, “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom,” he does not add such a reason as, “because you left all things for me and followed me”; nor does he add these: “because you did not kill, commit adultery, theft, or robbery, or covet.” Instead he says, “For I was hungry and you gave me food,” and so forth. Thus we understand that those who have sinned while entangled in secular affairs, but have redeemed their sins by almsgiving as already said, are to be judged and will be in the greatest fear; while those who have left all things and followed the Lord will judge.

## Chapter XV. How great is the generosity of the recompense: that, for such works, a human being enters with God into the sabbatism

This generosity of the reward is supremely worthy of admiration: that, because of works of this kind, a human being enters with God into one and the same *sabbatism*, that is, his rest. For how great are these little works—not of righteous persons, but of penitent persons? How great, I say, are these: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, and so forth, in comparison with God’s works? He created and made blessed the holy angels; fashioned the structure of this world; balanced the firmament in the midst [Col. 1820A] of the waters; enclosed the seas within their boundaries; clothed the earth with every kind of fruit; planted Paradise; made the sun and moon to rule day and night; placed the stars in the firmament; by his command brought forth from the waters living creatures of so many different kinds and species; brought forth cattle and beasts from the earth; and formed the human being.

Yet, because of those six works, he brings people into the same *sabbatism* in which he himself rests, he who performed such six kinds of works. Add to this that, although so great and good a maker could rightly have kept sabbath, he took the form of a servant and sought the human being who had perished, not by any ordinary work, but through the toil and pain of death. What is the reason that a human being should become the companion and fellow sharer of such a working God because of such very small works?

But lest we wonder, the ingenious charity of God found how this could rightly, rationally, and lawfully occur. For he says: “Amen, I say to you: as long as you did it to one of these least ones of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25). Elsewhere he said: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” And immediately: “Whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person shall receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matt. 10).

Therefore, correspondingly, whoever receives the Creator and Savior of the world, in whom he undoubtedly receives his Father also, shall receive the glory of the same Father and Son; so that where he rests or keeps sabbath by right, because he made all things very good, there the other may rest by grace, because he did such good as he was able to do with charity.

## Chapter XVI. [Col. 1820C] Who those least ones are, and that they belong to another rank, of whom he says: “As long as you did it to one of these least ones of mine, you did it to me”

And who are the least ones whom, as it were pointing with his finger, he indicates: “As long as you did it to one of these least ones of mine, you did it to me”? Who are they, and where are they, since he says these things to all those placed at the right? They belong, therefore, to another rank: namely, the rank of those who, as we said above, are not judged but judge, according to the promise which says: “Because you left all things and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty,” and so forth.

These are truly Christ’s least ones: least by a truly precious and praiseworthy smallness. Although they were already great and mature men, knowing and able to strike back against one who struck them, to be angry with those who were angry, and knowing and able to demand eye for eye and tooth for tooth, they freely turned themselves about and became like little children. Thus, from one who took their tunic, they withheld not even their cloak; to one striking their cheek, they offered the other also (Matt. 5).

Such least ones are truly great, because their smallness proceeds from greatness of virtue: that is, from the spirit of humility, humbling themselves here so that they may deserve to be exalted with God. For the Master, gentle and humble in heart, taught them thus: “Whoever among you wishes to be first shall be your servant, just as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20). Therefore, because for God’s sake they became least ones or poor, [Col. 1821A] it is said with very just judgment: “As long as you did it to one of these least brothers of mine, you did it to me.” For whatever is bestowed on such least ones assists the Word of God and advances the Word of God, who is himself the Son of God, so that they may be free and unencumbered to devote themselves to the Word of God—which, as he himself testifies, was revealed to them when he said: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

Nevertheless, those who are not voluntarily least or poor, such as Lazarus was, are not excluded from the care of so great a Judge. For, in the broadest intention of charity, it is enough that his name has been invoked over them; and for this reason they are rightly called, and are, his least ones. Whatever is bestowed upon such persons because they belong to Christ is bestowed upon Christ. Therefore, even if they appear to commit certain blameworthy acts, they must not be despised, nor must we despair of them. Perhaps those whom the excess of their very slight littleness defiles are purified by the furnaces of poverty; and poverty, their teacher, afflicts their life until it leads them to uprightness of life.

Everyone is especially required to reflect on this by the sentence in which, after it was said, “Child, remember that you received good things in your life,” there is immediately added, “and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16).

## Chapter XVII. That at judgment there must be weighed not only what, but also how long, anyone has done for these least ones

Moreover, it should be noted that judgment weighs not only what a person does for these least ones, but also how long he does it. For we must attentively observe that he did not say, “what you did to one of my least ones,” but, “as long as you did it.” The difference is plainly very great, so great that even little grammar-school children can judge it by the syllables; and if they delay in judging, or waveringly render an uncertain decision, they immediately deserve the master’s rod. For, they say, *quod* (“what”) is a noun having the declension of a pronoun, whereas *quamdiu* (“how long,” “for as long as”) is an adverb signifying time.

Therefore, justly and as befits a just judge, he will say, “As long as you did it,” weighing, that is, not only what was done, but also how long it was done. For example, a wealthy person feasting splendidly may daily give a certain Lazarus lying at his door crumbs or leftovers (Luke 16), or, if he is more devout, the first portions of his table; and while he lives he remembers the poor, never ceasing to do something of this sort from his abundance. Another, however, possessing much property, perhaps also gold or silver stored within, builds monasteries or hostels, establishing annual revenues so that not only during his life but for a thousand generations some of these least ones—whether twenty, thirty, or even a hundred—may be well provided for and live in common. Will it not, then, as has been said, also pertain at that judgment to remember this in determining the reward, so that the one who ministered longer may receive a greater recompense?

## Chapter XVIII. How they will ask and learn what they have done, how long they have done it, and why they have done it
But it is also rightly asked how they will then first [Col. 1822A] ask and learn what, or for how long, they have done, and to whom they have done it, when the time for learning or teaching is now, and doing comes later than being taught what ought to be done. Indeed, this difficult question might be answered if we supposed that there they will ask and answer in the same way as we ask and answer here. If we thought so, we should make ourselves a laughing-stock to the wise, who would say that it follows that one man appearing in the clouds, seated in his majesty as a great king, would make such a vast elementary utterance with his great mouth that all nations gathered in the whole world, or from the whole world, could hear and understand it.

But now we know, and ought to know, that the entire judgment will be accomplished not by words or by an articulated voice, but by thoughts that cannot remain hidden and that converge with absolute certainty. [Col. 1822B] The Apostle bears witness when he says: “They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing them witness, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or even defending one another, on the day when God will judge the hidden things of men through Jesus Christ according to my Gospel” (Rom. 2).

Therefore that question of those who say, “Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink?” (Matt. 25), and so forth, will be a thought, and a conscience exulting in the openness of the heart, astonished and amazed at what it sees and hears. For, however firmly someone may now be able to know or learn the truth of the matter by singing and reading, then it will be something altogether new that that Majesty deigned to care so greatly for his least ones when hungry and thirsty [Col. 1822C] that he was hungry and thirsty in them; and not only this, but he truly, in his own passible (suffering-capable) nature, hungered and thirsted, was a stranger, was stripped of his garments by soldiers, was made infirm—indeed, even died—and descended into the prison of hell.

## CHAPTER XIX. On what he will say also to those who are at his left: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire.”

Then he will say also to those who are at his left: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). This is the hearing, truly and incomparably evil, of which the Psalmist says: “The righteous man shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear an evil [Col. 1822D] hearing” (Ps. III). For what could be worse to hear? What name more dreadful? The Blessed One, and the very blessing of the upright, calls them cursed, and says: “Depart into eternal fire.”

This is not said out of bitterness or from an excessive agitation of a mind stirred to anger, but from the most tranquil reasoning of judgment, from the true maturity—or mature truth—of the judge, who expresses the matter or merit as it is, with the authority of the Scriptures, beyond which even the Judge will say nothing. For in truth, both his calling those on the right “blessed”—saying, “Come, blessed of my Father”—and his saying to those on the left, “Depart, you cursed,” will be done according to Scripture of most ancient and divine authority.

For long ago all who were predestined to life, and who will therefore be placed at the right [Col. 1823A], were blessed, as Scripture says: “And God created man in his own image; male and female he created them. And God blessed them and said: ‘Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it’” (Gen. 1), and so forth. For by blessing them then he commanded only the elect to be born; whence they are children of the blessed or of blessing, before the admission of that sin on account of which all are born or come to be born whom God’s blessing does not know. Thus the same God says to the woman after sin: “I will multiply your sorrows and your conceptions” (Gen. 3).

Since that blessing neither ought nor could be made void, he did not say to the woman, “You are cursed,” nor to the man, “You are cursed upon the earth,” but said only: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (ibid.), as we have explained more fully in its place. Had he said, “You are cursed upon the earth,” he would have declared the whole mass cursed, and with changeable intent would have nullified the whole sentence of the former blessing.

But to Cain, from whose party all and only the reprobate come, who are to be placed at the left, he did not say, “Cursed is the earth in your work”; rather, he said, “You are cursed upon the earth” (Gen. 4). In that one declaration he announced that all who imitate him would be cursed; and these are those to whom the Judge will say: “Depart from me, you cursed.” Therefore, as has already been said, he will not speak some new thing as an angry or disturbed person, but then also he will take everything from the Scriptures and judge as he has heard.

## CHAPTER XX. Why, or on what grounds, he will say to those who sinned while living temporally: “Depart into eternal fire.”

[Col. 1823C] But why, or on what grounds, will he say to those who lived for a time and sinned for a time, “Depart into eternal fire,” repaying temporal sins with the punishment of eternal fire, and adding, “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels”? For he says: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food. I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink. I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me” (Matt. 25).

This is indeed a great and compelling reason, and therefore a just and irreproachable sentence. It is the same as though he said: Because, like the devil, you too had an unrepentant heart. For it must be known and remembered that he did not say, “For you are murderers,” or “thieves,” or “adulterers”; but, “I was hungry,” [Col. 1823D] he says, “and you did not give me food,” and so forth—that is, you refused to redeem your sins by alms.

In what respect does the devil sin otherwise than these persons, whose repentance is nonexistent? This reason justly consigns a human being to equality with the devil: just as he does not repent—although no one has ever preached, or ever will preach, repentance to him—so this person is unrepentant and scorns to produce fruits of repentance, though God has preached repentance to him not only through his servants but also through himself, this man who says these words: “Because you did not give food to me when hungry, nor drink to me when thirsty; because you did not receive me as a stranger, nor cover me when naked; because you did not visit me when sick, nor come to me when I was placed in prison; because,” I say, “[Col. 1824A] you left the six days of these works empty, you shall by no means keep Sabbath with God on the seventh day, which the Father blessed and sanctified and prepared for his blessed ones. Rather, depart, you cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

For it is certain that, if it were always permitted, they would always delight in sinning; and therefore your fire will justly burn forever—justly, I say, you will burn forever with the devil and his angels. Your fire will not be quenched, your worm will not die, and, as the prophet foretold, you will be “an object of satiated sight to all flesh” (Isa. 66). Then they too will answer him, saying: “Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and not minister to you?” (Matt. 25).

As we have said above [Col. 1824B], this inquiry of those on the left, and the Judge’s answer that follows it, will be the testimony of their own conscience and of their thoughts mutually accusing or even defending one another. For their consciences will be like opened books, and the manifestation of the Judge’s justice will be like a great book which, by its exceedingly clear reading, will show each person’s merits, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “And books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life. And the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books, according to their works” (Rev. 20).

## CHAPTER XXI. Whence the fire is so strong, or the devil and his angels so weak, that fire has been prepared for their punishment.

[Col. 1824C] But whence is the fire so strong, or the devil and his angels so weak, that they are tortured by fire and fire has been prepared for their punishment? At the same time it must be asked: from when has that eternal fire been prepared for them? In asking these things we rightly tremble, because God who made him is truly wonderful, and God who judges him is truly strong.

Yet nothing is more foolish than his proud malice, or malicious pride, in which the prudent and wise God who created him caught him. When it is said, “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels,” we rightly understand “from the foundation of the world,” which was said above concerning the kingdom for those on the right (Matt. 25). It may also be understood, “before the foundation of the world,” because before this world was established or divided into its parts, fire was created. For when it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1), while the earth, or dry land, was still hidden beneath the waters, fire was already in the caverns of the earth or concealed in veins of flint.

We should therefore observe more carefully that, whereas above he says, “Possess the kingdom prepared for you,” here he does not speak simply of fire “which has been prepared,” but “which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” For what is “prepared” except “made ready beforehand”? That is, before the devil himself was created.

Whence then is the devil himself so weak that he is tortured by material fire? Assuredly, from his nature, from his condition. For, as the great Fathers did not hesitate to affirm, he has an aerial body—that is, one made from air. When darkness was upon the face of the abyss [Col. 1825A] and God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made (Gen. 1), then the angelic creature is understood to have been made from that darkness, that is, from dark and moist air, which had not yet been illuminated by the sun or by any lights.

But a part of that same creature, subject through humility to the true Light, God, deserved through his grace to become, or to remain, light. The devil, however, and his angels, because they became rebels against the Light, fell from that grace and became darkness, not light. Just as man, because of sin, heard: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3), so the devil, because of his pride, was cast down into this murky air from which he was taken, and, as the Apostle says, is kept with the chains of hell for that judgment of which we speak, to be tormented with his angels [Col. 1825B] (2 Pet. 2).

Angels, then, are spirits in comparison with us; their bodies are as much subtler than our bodies as this air is subtler than earth. But in comparison with the Creator, who alone is an uncircumscribed spirit, they are bodies or corporeal; and, as has already been said, they were made from this air. Now it is evident that air is corrupted by fire; and, being moist and unable to endure the extreme dryness of fire, it is sometimes shattered into contrary parts and violently disturbed by mighty storms—that is, by crashes of thunder and the torrents’ assaults—up to the danger of living beings.

Therefore, from his own nature or condition, the devil and his angels have this: that they are consumed by material fire [Col. 1825C]. Then they will be convicted of real weakness, when a fire stronger than the devil, their prince, is found—the devil who exalts himself against God, the Prince of strength—and he will not be like fire—the one who imagined that he could be like God.

“I,” the truly wonderful and truly terrible God, the most mighty God of spirits, so made him that one so proud may be humbled so easily: not by hand or spear, without any kind of laborious contest in which either the Judge himself or any rational creature among his ministers must toil, but by the ministry of fire alone, sufficiently fit, sufficiently powerful, and sufficient, standing by to serve the Judge himself as though knowingly and willingly. For “fire shall burn in his sight, and a mighty tempest round about him” (Ps. 49[50]:3). The fire will move in anger and heat, but our God will be gentle and tranquil in judging and [Col. 1825D] ordering.

Then that senseless one, with fire fighting for God, overcome by pain, will be humbled and entreat; but, he says, “I will not spare him for his mighty words and pleas composed for supplication” (Job 41).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the saying: “And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

“And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25). The same thing is said in the Apocalypse in these words: “And each was judged according to his works. And hell and death were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death. And whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire. And I saw a new heaven and a [Col. 1826A] new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and the sea is no more. And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared like a bride adorned for her husband” (Rev. 20–21), and so forth.

By “death” and “hell” he means the devil and those who belong to him; by “the book of life,” God’s foreknowledge, which cannot be mistaken concerning those to whom eternal life will be given. To be found written in it is to have been predestined to glory; not to be found written is to have been predestined to eternal punishment. “This,” he says, “is the second death”: namely, to go into eternal punishment.

If there is a second death, there is also a first death, in relation to which it is called the second death. And indeed there is. For as there is a first resurrection and a second resurrection, so there is a first death and a second death. But what is the first resurrection, and what is the second resurrection? The first resurrection is the conversion by which, in the present life, through repentance, we rise from the death of sin to Christ’s grace. The second resurrection [Col. 1826B] is that by which they shall rise: these indeed to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life.

The first resurrection, by preceding it, brings it about that in that second resurrection we may rise to the glory and honor of immortality. Therefore he says: “Blessed and holy is he who has a part in the first resurrection. Over these the second death has no power; but they shall be priests of God and of Christ” (Rev. 20).

The devil and his angels died the first death when, falling from heaven, they were extinguished in this murky air and lost the light of angelic dignity, as the Lord says: “[Col. 1826C] I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). For lightning shines as it falls, and falls as it shines; and immediately—indeed, even while it falls—the light itself disappears. If the devil, to whom it is said, “How you have fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, you who rose in the morning” (Isa. 14), fell while shining, then in falling he lost his light.

He will die the second death when he is dragged away to punishment, when he is confined so that he may no longer be free to wander, and is hurled down before the sight of all (Job 40). It is likewise certain concerning humankind that, by the first death, every person is born dead in Adam; and whoever is not freed from that death through Christ’s grace—which is to rise by the first resurrection—will die the second death, descending into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How these and those will go—not on foot, certainly, but by an ineffable movement through the power of the very word which they will hear.

[Col. 1826D] How then will these go into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life? Will they walk on foot and advance step by step, or perhaps, with holy angels dragging or pushing them and with some delay, will they, unwillingly going, be led bound in chains to the places of punishment? Certainly not. Rather, by the ineffable and invisible power of the word, those who hear, “Depart, you cursed,” will at once tumble down [Col. 1827A] into Tartarus together with the devil and his angels, more swiftly than falling rain or hail, or as swiftly as lightning falls from heaven according to the Lord’s ancient vision (Luke 10).

Conversely, the righteous who hear, “Come, blessed of my Father,” will at once be snatched upward and borne upward by the power of the same word of which the Apostle says: “Upholding all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1). Knowing this, the same Apostle did not say, “We shall ascend,” although it is written in the Apocalypse, “Come up here” (Rev. 11); nor did he say, “We shall be lifted up,” which might seem possible by chariots such as those in which Elijah was lifted up (4 Kgs. 2), or by any vehicles whatever, or indeed by any ministry of angels. Rather, he says, “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

## CHAPTER XXIV. What that eternal life is into which the righteous will go.

[Col. 1827B] What then is that eternal life into which the righteous will go? Undoubtedly, that life is the same thing as the kingdom of which we spoke above. There, living is not one thing [Col. 1828A] and reigning another; indeed, there being is not one thing and living or reigning another. What, then, is that life, except the manifest glory of the divine vision, full and perfect in knowledge? “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

But the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). “Now I know in part; then I shall know as I also have been known.” That life, therefore, begins here with the aforesaid first resurrection, because we now live to the degree that we know the blessed Trinity. But there, in the second resurrection, it will be perfected, when—or from the time when—we shall see face to face God the Father and the Father’s Word in his heart and in our flesh, and the Holy [Col. 1828B] Spirit of both in both. To him be glory and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1827] End of the third part of this book, *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, concerning the works of the Spirit, the third person of that same Trinity.

# ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

**RUPERT, ABBOT OF DEUTZ.**

Prolegomena, 9. Apology for Rupert, by Gabriel Gerberon, 24. Synopsis of the Apology, 29. First part, 43. Second part, 99. Rupert’s letter to Cuno, abbot of Siegburg, 193. Rupert’s prologue to the books *On the Holy Trinity and Its Works*, 197.

# FORTY-TWO BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON THE WORKS OF THE HOLY TRINITY

## BOOK I: GENESIS

Chapter I.—That the Holy Trinity had no model outside itself by which to create these three things: heaven, earth, and all their adornment, 199.

Chapter II.—Why it is called *Genesis*, 201.

Chapter III.—That the Son, or Word, through whom heaven and earth were created, is the Beginning, 202.

Chapter IV.—Why God did not say, “Let heaven be made,” and “Let earth be made,” as He said, “Let light be made,” 203.

Chapter V.—That God’s making the world is not to be attributed to mutability, against those who say that the world is coeternal with God, 203.

Chapter VI.—Why heaven must be understood in that Beginning, 204.

Chapter VII.—How “the earth was empty and void,” and what sort of darkness was upon the face of the abyss, 204.

Chapter VIII.—How “the Spirit of God was borne over the waters,” 205.

Chapter IX.—That the Trinity is foreshown at the beginning of the book, 206.

Chapter X.—That the light which was made is the angelic creature, 206.

Chapter XI.—That the angelic creature is called light not metaphorically but in reality, 207.

Chapter XII.—That this light confesses its Creator, according to the verse of Psalm 103: “You have put on confession and beauty, clothed with light as with a garment,” 209.

Chapter XIII.—That this light was called “good,” not as it was said of the other works, “and God saw that it was good,” 210.

Chapter XIV.—That the angelic creature, just as it had a beginning, also had progress, 211.

Chapter XV.—That by the Creator’s will a certain part of that creature was corrupted, 211.

Chapter XVI.—On the devil’s envy or pride, 212.

Chapter XVII.—That the good and merciful Creator nevertheless justly made the one whom He foreknew would be evil; and on his fall, 213.

Chapter XVIII.—On the naming of day and night, and what that day is and what that night is, 215.

Chapter XIX.—Likewise, how God gave those names, 216.

Chapter XX.—Why it was not said, “Darkness and night were made, the first day,” but, “There came to be evening and morning, one day,” 217.

Chapter XXI.—Who and what that “one day” is, 218.

Chapter XXII.—On God’s saying, “Let there be a firmament,” 218.

Chapter XXIII.—What those waters “above the firmament” are, 219.

Chapter XXIV.—What kind or nature those waters ought to be considered to have, 220.

Chapter XXV.—Likewise, on the not-impossible placing of waters “above the firmament,” 221.

Chapter XXVI.—On what is written in the aforementioned psalm: “Who makes the cloud Your ascent,” 221.

Chapter XXVII.—Likewise, on burning fire, thunder, and lightning, 222.

Chapter XXVIII.—On the statement: “And He called the firmament heaven,” 223.

Chapter XXIX.—Likewise, why He called the firmament heaven, 224.

Chapter XXX.—That there came to be evening and morning, the second day; and what the second day is, 225.

Chapter XXXI.—On the third day, and why it was there said: “God saw [Col. 1870] that it was good,” 226.

Chapter XXXII.—How the words, “Let the waters be gathered into one place,” are to be understood, 226.

Chapter XXXIII.—Likewise, on the gathering of the waters and the dry land, and on what was said in the same psalm: “You founded the earth upon its stability,” 227.

Chapter XXXIV.—What need there was for the dry land, in order that mountains should rise and plains descend, 228.

Chapter XXXV.—On the statement, “Let the earth bring forth green grass,” and on the threefold repetition of each expression, 229.

Chapter XXXVI.—Likewise, on green grass, grass bearing seed, the fruit-bearing tree, and the tree whose seed alone is within itself, 230.

Chapter XXXVII.—On the planting of paradise, and on the statement: “He who lives forever created all things together,” 230.

Chapter XXXVIII.—Likewise, on the statement, “Each according to its kind,” and on the Son’s consubstantiality with God the Father, 231.

Chapter XXXIX.—Likewise, on the third day, 232.

**CHAPTER XIII.—**Concerning the statement, “And he built it in seven years,” when the Jews said to the Lord, “This Temple was built in forty-six years”; and what mystery lies in that number. 1155

**CHAPTER XV.—**What the porch in front of the greater porch, and the porch of the throne in which the tribunal stood, signify mystically, according to the different states of the times: from Abraham to Noah, from Noah to Abel, and from him upward to the first creation of the world. 1157

**CHAPTER XVI.—**What and of what kind is the house which Solomon Christ made for Pharaoh’s daughter, that is, for the Church from the Gentiles. 1159

**CHAPTER XVII.—**That no one ought to think it incredible that, in the construction of the Temple made by hands, he expressed so perfectly the mysteries of the Temple not made by hands, since Daniel too could have foreknown the number of years until that same Christ. 1161

**CHAPTER XVIII.—**How Hiram is said to have been of a Tyrian father, though he was full of wisdom and instruction and was therefore able to attend to mystical causes in performing his works. 1162

**CHAPTER XIX.—**Concerning the two bronze columns which he fashioned; why the first, on the right, is called Jachin, and the second, on the left, Boaz; and concerning the line of twelve cubits which encircles each. 1163

**CHAPTER XX.—**What the capitals of the columns are; why they are five cubits high and fashioned four cubits high in the porch; what the nets or little chains on the capitals mean, by which the columns seem to hang from the oracle; and what the pomegranates interspersed among the chains mean. 1164

**CHAPTER XXI.—**Concerning the molten sea in which the priests washed: a type of baptism, in which sins are forgiven. 1166

**CHAPTER XXII.—**How fittingly he called that sea a basin; how our sea, that is, baptism, is molten; and concerning its mystical measurements and carvings. 1167

**CHAPTER XXIII.—**That the twelve oxen bearing the sea are the twelve apostles, receiving from Christ the rule for baptizing; and what it means that their hind parts were concealed inwardly. 1168

**CHAPTER XXIV.—**What it means mystically that, on the bases, lions were not made without oxen, nor oxen without lions; and that five bases were set on the right and five on the left, each bearing a basin. 1169

**CHAPTER XXV.—**That there are many useful vessels in the spiritual Temple of God, whose use or ministry we ought to perform; and what it means mystically that they are said to have been cast in clayey ground, between Succoth and Zarthan. 1170

**CHAPTER XXVI.—**Concerning the statement, “And he brought in the things which his father had sanctified and deposited them,” etc.; and what it means mystically that princes and leaders, together with the elders, are gathered to King Solomon, and that sheep and oxen without number are sacrificed. 1171

**CHAPTER XXVII.—**That it was a sign of Jewish blindness that a cloud filled the house of the Lord, and that the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud. 1172

**CHAPTER XXVIII.—**That Solomon, praying with both knees bent, “O Lord my God,” etc., was a type of Jesus Christ, who, at the dedication of his Temple, in that passion of his body by which it was dedicated, prayed for all. 1173

**CHAPTER XXIX.—**That, as Solomon rose when his prayer was completed and blessed the assembly of Israel with a loud voice, so Christ rose from the dead and gave the Holy Spirit, amid the great amazement of the whole world. 1174

**CHAPTER XXX.—**That this true Solomon sent seafaring men to Ophir; who the queen of Sheba was, who meanwhile came to hear his wisdom. 1175

**CHAPTER XXXI.—**That the last of the memorable works which Solomon made—namely, the great ivory throne, exceedingly overlaid with pure gold—prefigured the judicial majesty of Christ, the most pure man. 1176

**CHAPTER XXXII.—**That he loved many foreign women, concerning whom the Lord, in forbidding this, said: “They will most certainly turn away your hearts, so that you follow their gods.” 1178

### BOOK IV

**CHAPTER I.—**That the sayings of David and Solomon and of the other prophets are testimonies to Christ, the Son of God, and that in them the opponents of truth are swiftly overwhelmed. 1179

**CHAPTER II.—**That David is the first of the prophets. 1179

**CHAPTER III.—**Why it was possible first to announce the punishments of hell and the kingdom of God through a mighty and royal person, and to sing them in metrical feet; and what the shape of the psaltery signifies mystically. 1180

**CHAPTER IV.—**How the psaltery itself, by its threefold set of fifty psalms, proclaims the threefold jubilee of faith, hope, and charity: the first fifty psalms chiefly containing what must be believed concerning Christ; the second chiefly what must be hoped for; and the third chiefly those things by which we are stirred to love God. 1181

### ONE BOOK OF COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS, THE FOURTH AMONG THE BOOKS OF KINGS

**CHAPTER V.—**The arrangement of the three sets of fifty psalms, together with the mystical meanings attached to their titles. 1181

**CHAPTER VI.—**How Solomon, in the same manner, commends faith, hope, and charity: faith in Proverbs, hope in Ecclesiastes, and charity in the Canticles. 1232

### BOOK V

**CHAPTER I.—**Concerning the Lord’s words to Solomon: “Because thou hast had this within thyself”; what it means for anyone to have his sin within himself; and that for this reason He foretold that his kingdom would be cut off. 1233

**CHAPTER II.—**Concerning the statement, “And thou hast not kept my covenant”; and in what respect Solomon, who asked for wisdom—although this pleased the Lord—and received it in a dream by night, is rightly reproved because he would not persevere. 1235

**CHAPTER IV.—**Why the prophet made so many divisions of his cloak, and that from then on Israel was divided tenfold. 1236

**CHAPTER VIII.—**Concerning the son of the mistress of the household whom Elijah raised, who is said to have been Jonah; and what his death designates mystically. 1242

**CHAPTER IX.—**What Elijah’s return, when he showed himself to Ahab, signifies mystically; what the prophets of Baal mean when they cried out and cut themselves so that they bled; what the fire means which fell from heaven upon the burnt offering at Elijah’s invocation; what the granting of rain means; and what it means that Elijah ran before Ahab. 1243

**CHAPTER X.—**Concerning his flight, in which, fearing death, he desired to die; and of what he himself, the juniper tree, and the food in whose strength he fasted for so many days were types. 1245

**CHAPTER XI.—**Concerning his complaint against Israel, the divine answer to him, and what is signified by the great and mighty wind overthrowing mountains and shattering rocks, by the earthquake, by the fire, etc. 1246

**CHAPTER XIII.—**How Elijah, at the Lord’s command, anointed Elisha as prophet, and Elisha anointed Jehu as king over Israel; and that Ahab acted against the Lord’s decree by sparing Ben-hadad. 1248

**CHAPTER XV.—**Concerning Elijah and Elisha: what it means mystically that Elijah placed his cloak upon Elisha and that Elisha, leaving the oxen, ran after him. 1254

**CHAPTER XVI.—**What is signified in mystery by Elijah’s being taken up into heaven; what the first and second groups of fifty, consumed by heavenly fire, mean; and what the third means, who was saved by humbling himself. 1254

**CHAPTER XVII.—**What it means mystically that Elijah, about to be taken into heaven, struck and divided the waters of the Jordan with his cloak; and that Elisha, though permitted three times to remain behind, refused to remain, but perseveringly went with him. 1255

**CHAPTER XVIII.—**Concerning the words, “Ask what thou wilt that I should give thee,” etc., and how the same was done to the apostles at Christ’s ascension. 1255

**CHAPTER XIX.—**Concerning the fiery chariot by which he was taken up; and that no one before or after Christ ascended, or can ascend, into heaven as Christ did. 1257

**CHAPTER XX.—**What it means mystically that Elisha tore his garments, and that when he first struck the waters with Elijah’s cloak they were not divided, but when he struck them a second time they were divided. 1258

**CHAPTER XXI.—**What it means mystically that Elisha lived in Jericho and healed its barren waters and utterly bad ground by putting salt into a new vessel. 1258

[Col. 1900]

**CHAPTER XXIII.—**That when the psalm-singer sang, the hand of the Lord came upon Elisha: an evident proof that the Holy Spirit was not always present with the prophets, and that, in invoking the Holy Spirit together with words of divine praise, the sound of sweet music has great power. 1260

**CHAPTER XXIV.—**What mystery lies in the fact that the woman poured out the little oil which she had into empty vessels, all of which were filled to the brim. 1261

**CHAPTER XXV.—**What mystery lies in the fact that the boy sent by Elisha did not raise the Shunammite’s son. 1261

**CHAPTER XXVI.—**What it means mystically that Elisha restored to the same woman, by God’s power, the son whom he had raised. 1262

**CHAPTER XXVII.—**Concerning the colocynth, whose very bitter taste Elisha sweetened: that the teaching of heretics is like it. 1262

**CHAPTER XXVIII.—**That he satisfied a crowd of people from a few loaves, and what corresponds to this in Christ. 1263

**CHAPTER XXIX.—**Concerning the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian, which was cured by washing seven times in the Jordan: that the grace of baptism was prefigured in that deed. 1263

**CHAPTER XXXI.—**Whose, or what sort of persons’, type in the Church Gehazi bore, to whom Naaman’s leprosy adhered because of the fault of covetousness. 1265

**CHAPTER XXXII.—**Concerning the miracle in which iron that had slipped from its handle floated upon the water: of what it was a type. 1266

**CHAPTER XXXIII.—**Concerning the miracle by which he struck the Syrians with blindness and then made them see again: that this also shows us that there are more with us than with the enemies of our salvation, and that he displayed perfect charity toward them. 1267

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.—**Concerning Athaliah, daughter of Jezebel, who had married Joram, king of Judah and son of Jehoshaphat: how she exercised her mother’s madness in Jerusalem and throughout Judah; and that therefore the seed of that same Joram is removed from Gospel remembrance down to the fourth generation. 1270

### FIRST BOOK ON ISAIAH

**CHAPTER I.—**Praise of Isaiah the prophet, because he treats all the mysteries of Christ and likewise of the Church so fully that he should be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist; and why he interweaves spiritual realities under the names or images of earthly things. 1271

**CHAPTER II.—**That he recapitulates the advent of Christ, around which his entire purpose turns, in seven sections; and mystically designates all hostile parties under the names of nine kingdoms—Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, Dumah, Arabia, the Valley of Vision, Tyre, and the beasts of the south—signifying the punishments of the wicked by the name “burden.” 1272

**CHAPTER III.—**That the prophet’s vision concerning Judah and Jerusalem concerns the future, when the Jews would reject and crucify the coming Saviour; and that this generation is already called a sinful nation, a people burdened with iniquity, an evil seed, and wicked children. 1273

**CHAPTER XIII.—**That the Lord of whom he says, “He stands to judge,” is Christ Jesus, of whom Stephen says: “Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened,” etc.; and that an act of his judgment had already occurred when the crown of the daughters of Zion was made bald by the Romans laying waste the land. 1287

**CHAPTER XV.—**That from then on sins are forgiven to all believers through the grace of the Holy Spirit, as he says: “If the Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion,” etc. 1290

**CHAPTER XXII.—**Concerning the fifth “Woe,” because they called evil good—namely, by preserving Barabbas and condemning Christ. 1296

**CHAPTER XXIII.—**Concerning the sixth “Woe” upon those who were wise in their own eyes and took away from others the key of knowledge. 1297

**CHAPTER XXIV.—**Concerning the seventh “Woe” upon those who are mighty men for mixing strong drink. 1297

**CHAPTER XXV.—**Concerning the eighth “Woe” upon those who justify the wicked for gifts and take away the justice of the righteous. 1297

**CHAPTER XXII.—**The seventh section, in which the whole Church, lying in darkness under sin, is told because of the advent of Christ the Saviour: “Arise, be enlightened, O Jerusalem, for thy light has come,” etc., as far as: “And I will glorify the house of my majesty.” 1344
