**CHAPTER XXXI.—**Concerning the words, “Before she travailed, she brought forth,” etc.; how, according to these words also, what the Jews and certain heretics said—that Christ did not exist before Mary—is false. 1361

### BOOK ON JEREMIAH
## BOOK ON JEREMIAH

**CHAPTER I.**—That Jeremiah’s prophecy marks the beginning of the fifth age, and that in this age Christ’s priesthood was prefigured in deeds and signified in prophetic utterances. 1363

**CHAPTER II.**—How this fifth age resembles the fifth day of the world’s creation, and why at that time the most precious Temple was allowed to be consumed by fire. 1365

**CHAPTER III.**—That Jeremiah bore the type of that same Lord whose prophet he was: by his own name, by his sanctification from the womb, by the office of preaching performed seven times at Jerusalem; recounting that the word of the Lord came to him before its siege, when he survived its destruction, and summoning it to repentance in a determinate number or order. 1365

**CHAPTER IV.**—Concerning what is first said to him: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you,” etc.; how it gives utterance to the anointing of the Holy of holies, and to His obedience and glorification. 1367

**CHAPTER V.**—Concerning the second vision, in which he says first, “I see a wakeful rod”; but second, “I see a boiling pot”; and how, in accordance with these likenesses, Christ’s first coming is the rod of correction for the penitent, while His second is the judgment of eternal condemnation for the impenitent. 1368

**CHAPTER VI.**—That, recalling Jerusalem’s sins for a third time in order to stir it to repentance, he finally says: “Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth; make for yourself the mourning of an only son”; and that this resembles the Lord’s action when, after He had been unable by many means to turn Jerusalem to repentance, He at last wept [Col. 1904] over it, announcing the evils to come upon it. 1369

**CHAPTER VII.**—That, standing in the gate of the house of the Lord for the fourth time, he says among other things: “Behold, this house has become a den of robbers”; and that this refers to the fact that the Lord, entering the Temple, began to cast them out, saying to them the words from Isaiah: “My house shall be called a house of prayer,” and adding from this prophet, “But you,” etc. 1371

**CHAPTER VIII.**—That, teaching for the fifth time in the word of the Lord, “Hear the words of this covenant,” etc., he proceeds to convict them of having made the Lord’s covenant void, so that we may know how reasonable it is that the Church of Christ despises whatever the Jews sacrifice. 1372

**CHAPTER IX.**—That the word of the Lord follows in the sixth place, concerning the words of drought and visitation; and that it is rightly understood to mean that neither prophetic grace nor any visitation of the Holy Spirit was granted them, so that when they come to draw the waters of the Scriptures, they carry away empty vessels. 1373

**CHAPTER X.**—That, in the seventh place, by the potter’s making a work upon the wheel, and the vessel which he was making from clay with his hands being spoiled, and his turning and making another vessel as seemed good in his eyes to make, is signified the scattering of the rebellious Jews and the gathering of the Gentiles; and that in all things God’s judgment is beyond reproach. 1375

**CHAPTER XI.**—How, among the evils predicted to the king seeking counsel in the besieged city, the prophecy is confirmed that the oath of the Lord will not be made void, He having said concerning David: “His seed shall remain for ever”; while meanwhile He says: “Behold, days shall come, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous Branch.” 1377

**CHAPTER XII.**—On the Lamentations: why individual statements are marked by individual letters of the alphabet; and why the alphabetic sequence itself is fourfold—because the prophet had a fourfold cause for lamenting. 1378

**CHAPTER XIII.**—In what sense that one city of the elect is rightly called full of people, mistress of nations, and princess of provinces; and why or how she sat alone or was made tributary. ALEPH, that is, “teaching.” 1379

**CHAPTER XIV.**—During what night she wept while weeping, and upon what cheeks her tears were shed. BETH, that is, “house.” 1380

**CHAPTER XV.**—That the whole body of the elect is Judah, and into what affliction or servitude it fell when it migrated. GIMEL, that is, “fulness.” 1381

**CHAPTER XVI.**—Which ways mourn because there are none who come to the solemn feast; what that solemn feast is; what is meant by the destruction of the gates; whence the groaning of the priests and the desolation of the virgins. DALETH, that is, “tablets.” 1381

**CHAPTER XVII.**—How the enemies became head and the adversaries were enriched, and how her little ones were led away captive. HE, that is, “this.” 1382

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—Concerning prelates, and how or when rams without pastures go away without strength before the face of the pursuer. VAU, that is, “is.” 1383

**CHAPTER XIX.**—That it is truly lamentable that we do not remember our sojourning or pilgrimage except when evils press upon us. ZAI, that is, “these.” 1383

**CHAPTER XX.**—That, when the sin of pride has gone before, the soul is unstable and falls from vice into vice; and what is the meaning of these four letters: HE, VAU, ZAI, HETH. HETH, that is, “life.” 1384

**CHAPTER XXI.**—That it is truly lamentable to have filth upon one’s feet. THETH, that is, “good.” 1384

**CHAPTER XXII.**—What meaning lies beneath the interpretation of these letters, THETH and JOD; and that confession is the good beginning of righteousness. JOD, that is, “beginning.” 1385

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—How the earlier saints gave all precious things for food to restore the soul; that is, they obtained not yet the reality but the hope of the promise which they had heard. CAPH, that is, “hand.” 1385

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—Concerning the words, “See if there is any sorrow,” etc.; that every sorrow which arises from any other perishable thing is vain; and what meaning these two conjoined letters, CAPH and LAMECH, possess. LAMECH, that is, “heart.” 1386

**CHAPTER XXV.**—That, in order to humble the soul, God made the condition of the body mortal and allows the soul to be afflicted by many sufferings. MEM, that is, “from themselves.” 1386

**CHAPTER XXVI.**—That a person doing evil is a slave of sin and can be freed only through God’s grace. NUN, that is, “eternal.” 1387

**CHAPTER XXVII.**—That salvation could not reside in any of the fathers or patriarchs, and that they too were mortal; and what these three conjoined letters, MEM, NUN, SAMECH, signify. 1387

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**—That the ancient Church had cause to weep because the Comforter had become distant. 1388

**CHAPTER XXIX.**—That Zion could not console herself by stretching out her hands. 1388

**CHAPTER XXX.**—That we provoked the mouth of the Lord to anger, namely by defending guilt in Adam; and what these three letters together, AIN, PHE, ZADI, signify. 1388

**CHAPTER XXXI.**—That whenever the Church appoints priests for herself, they have deceived her; this is to be understood of those who feed themselves and seek their own interests. 1389

**CHAPTER XXXII.**—How, in him in whom all sinned, our belly was troubled and our heart overthrown—that is, the body was made mortal; and what these two conjoined letters, COPH and RES, signify. 1389

**CHAPTER XXXIII.**—How the enemies, that is, evil spirits, rejoiced in the evil of the human race; and how the Church will rejoice over them on the day of judgment. 1390

**CHAPTER XXXIV.**—How they are to be gathered in that irrecoverable vintage, with irrevocable condemnation, while the Church has the day of consolation; and what the two final letters, SIN and THAU, joined together signify. 1390

**CHAPTER XXXV.**—That beneath the following alphabet is woven the lamentation of that time when Nebuzaradan set Jerusalem on fire and burned the house of the Lord with it. 1391

**CHAPTER XXXVI.**—In what respect Jerusalem was called the footstool of the Lord’s feet, and how the Lord cast it down from heaven to earth. 1392

**CHAPTER XXXVII.**—That pride was the fault for which Jerusalem or the Temple had to be cast down. 1393

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.**—That the cause of its ruin was that God broke the horn of Israel. 1393

**CHAPTER XXXIX.**—That God is the enemy of the proud, and therefore said: “He has bent His bow.” 1393

**CHAPTER XL.**—That He did not say, “The Lord became an enemy,” but “like an enemy”; and that neither the reality nor the name of enemy applies to God. 1394

**CHAPTER XLI.**—How He called that city, or Temple, the Lord’s tent. 1394

**CHAPTER XLII.**—What is meant by: “They raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.” 1395

**CHAPTER XLIII.**—How He stretched over that Zion the measuring-line of the seventy years’ captivity. 1395

**CHAPTER XLIV.**—What were its gates and the bars which the Lord shattered, so that its prophets could find no vision from the Lord. 1395

**CHAPTER XLV.**—How the elders sat upon the ground and kept silence, and the virgins sprinkled their heads with ashes. 1396

**CHAPTER XLVI.**—Why he now says, “My eyes fail because of tears,” when he had earlier said, “Therefore give their children over to famine,” etc. 1396

**CHAPTER XLVII.**—How infants hanging upon their mothers’ breasts, tortured by hunger, breathed out their souls. 1396

**CHAPTER XLVIII.**—How Jerusalem, in its penitence, could be compared with no one, and therefore says, “Who shall heal you?” 1397

**CHAPTER XLIX.**—How he rebukes the false prophets and Jerusalem itself because it listened to them. 1397

**CHAPTER L.**—That this too was added to the height of its miseries: passers-by clapped their hands over it in derision. 1397

**CHAPTER LI.**—How truly they derided it, since after seventy years, when its servitude had been ended, they fiercely resisted the rebuilding of the city. 1398

**CHAPTER LII.**—How this was done not so much through Nebuzaradan as by the Lord’s judgment, who had also foretold such things through Moses. 1398

**CHAPTER LIII.**—What the heart of the prophets who foretold these things cried out, and how they were not heard while crying over the walls of the daughter of Zion. 1398

**CHAPTER LIV.**—What is meant by their cry: “Arise, give praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches.” 1399

**CHAPTER LV.**—What it cries in saying: “See, O Lord, whom You have gathered as a vintage.” 1399

**CHAPTER LVI.**—That divine nature is drawn much more toward mercy than human nature. 1400

**CHAPTER LVII.**—How it attributes to God, as it were, what happened. 1400

**CHAPTER LVIII.**—That in the third alphabet the prophet laments his own cause; and why here each letter is already repeated three times, whereas in the others they occur singly. 1400

**CHAPTER LIX.**—What that poverty is, what those darknesses are, and what are the hands of which he speaks. 1400

**CHAPTER LX.**—How, made mortal in Adam, he laments that in the burning of Jerusalem he has been fed with gall and, through his own faults, darkened. 1401

**CHAPTER LXI.**—That, having fallen into God’s enmity in Adam, he was desolated amid the present evils of the city and, in his own sufferings, as though struck by arrows. 1402

**CHAPTER LXII.**—How God became an ambushing bear to transgressing man, and therefore overthrew his paths, which were inclined toward evil. 1402

**CHAPTER LXIII.**—How, wounded in Adam by the arrows of lusts [Col. 1906], mocked by his own people while prophesying their captivity, he was made bitter by prisons and hunger. 1403

**CHAPTER LXIV.**—How, in the bite of the first man, he lost his teeth; how, in the siege of the city, while speaking for it before the Lord, his soul was cast off; and how, in his own conscience, he feared on account of his deserts. 1403

**CHAPTER LXV.**—How he asks God to remember the first transgression, what punishments arose from it, and why from receiving present evils he hopes for future good. 1404

**CHAPTER LXVI.**—That he rejoices that man, unlike the devil, was not equally abandoned because of his sin; and that after the night of Babylonian captivity there will be a morning of freedom. 1404

**CHAPTER LXVII.**—How He who is righteous in exercising severity upon Adam is good to those who hope in Him; and how it is good for Babylonian captives not to murmur but silently to await the salvation of the Lord. 1405

**CHAPTER LXVIII.**—How the one who sits alone and raises himself above himself differs from the first man; and how in that captivity silence is required, if perhaps there is hope that she who was led to Babylon may be brought back. 1406

**CHAPTER LXIX.**—How He who expelled Adam from Paradise will not reject him for ever, but will again have mercy and bring him back from Babylonian captivity; and how He who humbles anyone has not cast him off altogether, but rather loves whom He corrects and receives whom He scourges. 1407

**CHAPTER LXX.**—How the Lord does not know how to crush the righteous with the wicked, to turn aside a man’s judgment, or to pervert a person in judgment. 1407

**CHAPTER LXXI.**—How blameworthy it is if someone says that anything occurs without the Lord’s command; if he says that neither good nor evil proceeds from the mouth of the Most High, murmuring over sins and attributing them to fatal necessity. 1408

**CHAPTER LXXII.**—That one ought rather to return to the discernment of the heart, and that confession of sins should be made together with good works. 1408

**CHAPTER LXXIII.**—How God struck the human race in the first man and did not hear those delivered into the hand of enemies. 1409

**CHAPTER LXXIV.**—That enemies have never been absent from the elect from the beginning, and that prophecy itself was a cause of tribulation for the prophets. 1409

**CHAPTER LXXV.**—That he mourned the universal ruin of the human race into which it fell through Adam, the present captivity of his people, and his own frailty. 1409

**CHAPTER LXXVI.**—That the devil caught the first man as a bird by hunting, and that he further endured many waves of temptations inwardly in his mind. 1410

**CHAPTER LXXVII.**—How, without despairing, he invoked God; how he does not cease to pray for the captives; and what consolation he received in the divine answer. 1410

**CHAPTER LXXVIII.**—How one who is not conscious of deserving the evils he has suffered asks for judgment. 1411

**CHAPTER LXXIX.**—Against those who pursue evil and are enemies of innocence. 1411

**CHAPTER LXXX.**—That he says, “Repay them in kind,” not by imprecating, but by conceding. 1412

**CHAPTER LXXXI.**—How the Jews who killed Christ were the cruelest and most utterly ruined of all those who persecuted prophets and righteous people; and how for this reason they were darkened and scattered. 1412

**CHAPTER LXXXII.**—How the Jews were formerly illustrious, and with what gold they were clothed, but now are earthen vessels. 1413

**CHAPTER LXXXIII.**—On the cruelty of the *lamia*, that is, of that nation, in comparison with a *lamia*, because it killed its own children, saying: “His blood be upon us, and upon …,” etc. 1413

**CHAPTER LXXXIV.**—How the iniquity of that people became greater than the sin of the Sodomites, and how the words are to be understood: “And hands did not lay hold upon her.” 1414

**CHAPTER LXXXV.**—How the Nazarites of that nation were whiter than snow, more shining than milk, and so forth; and whose faces are now blackened. 1415

**CHAPTER LXXXVI.**—On the dreadful famine of the Jewish siege: “where,” he says, “the hands of compassionate women cooked their children.” 1415

**CHAPTER LXXXVII.**—How they did not believe the one who foretold that these evils would come upon them, and cried to His apostles, “Depart, depart, go away”; and how they turned to the Gentiles. 1416

**CHAPTER LXXXIX.**—How he concludes all the Lamentations with the good hope of consolation, saying ironically [Col. 1907]: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Edom; it is completed,” etc.; by Edom signifying all earthly people who inflict persecution, and by Zion all the elect who endure it. 1419

## BOOK I ON EZEKIEL

**CHAPTER I.**—How, amid the affliction of the city, consoling visions of God’s future kingdom became abundant among the prophets. 1419

**CHAPTER II.**—That the prophet Ezekiel is difficult, and that in the first vision one should rightly inquire how the four living creatures are one living creature. 1421

**CHAPTER III.**—How the prophet himself bore the type of the Son of God whose vision he saw; what the stormy wind is, what the great cloud is, what the enfolding fire is, and what the other appended details are. 1422

**CHAPTER VII.**—That the holy Church rightly chose to receive only the four evangelists, and which face is most fitting for each evangelist. 1427

**CHAPTER IX.**—How the appearance of the living creatures is like the appearance of burning coals of fire; who that fire is; and that lightning came forth from the fire. 1429

**CHAPTER X.**—How the living creatures return in the likeness of flashing lightning, although it was said above that they did not return. 1430

**CHAPTER XI.**—What is the one wheel appearing beside the living creatures; what its four faces are; what is meant by the words “like the appearance of the sea”; how their likeness is one although they are four; and how there is a wheel within a wheel. 1431

**CHAPTER XII.**—How they go in four directions; how, or to whom, their appearance is terrifying; and how the whole body is full of eyes. 1433

**CHAPTER XIII.**—How the wheels walk when the creatures walk, and are raised when they are raised; and how they follow the spirit, or have the spirit of life in them. 1434

**CHAPTER XIV.**—What is the likeness of the firmament above the heads of the living creatures, like the terrible appearance of crystal; what are the wings stretched out beneath the firmament, one toward another; and how each covers its own body. 1435

**CHAPTER XV.**—What is meant by hearing the sound of the wings like the sound of many waters, and in what sense it is like the sound of the Most High God; what the sound of an army is; and what it means for their wings to be lowered when they stand. 1436

**CHAPTER XVI.**—What is the likeness of the throne above the firmament, and what is the appearance of the man seated upon the throne. 1437

**CHAPTER XVII.**—Whom this prophet typified when he said, “And I saw and fell upon my face”; and how he was sent to apostate nations. 1439

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—What it means for a scroll to be spread before him, rolled up and written within and without; and what it means for lamentations, a song, and woe to be written in it. 1440

**CHAPTER XIX.**—How Christ’s apostles, taken up by this Spirit, heard behind them a voice of great commotion: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord,” etc. 1441

**CHAPTER XX.**—How the apostles, having received the Holy Spirit, became bitter and indignant; to what heap of new produce they came; and how they remained grieving. 1442

**CHAPTER XXII.**—On the siege of the city: how its portent was that the prophet was commanded to lie upon his left side and bear the iniquities of the house of Israel for three hundred and ninety days, and to lie upon his right side and bear the iniquities of the house of Judah for forty days. 1445

### CHAPTER I.—On the Spirit of strength: how beautifully it occupies the middle place among the seven spirits; and that the others are more concerned with rest, whereas this one is more concerned with action. 1729

### CHAPTER II.—On considering the Spirit of strength first in Christ, then in the apostles and holy preachers, and then in the rulers of the Church, according to Solomon’s words: “There are three things which walk well: a lion, strongest of beasts; a cock,” etc. 1730

### CHAPTER III.—On the Lion who is also the Lamb: how, according to John’s Apocalypse, he first conquered and bound the devil by dying; and after him comes the girded cock and the already-mentioned ram, namely Christ’s apostles and his martyrs, of whom Stephen is first. 1731

### CHAPTER IV.—On blessed Stephen, who was called full of grace and strength, and who, freely exercising that same strength among the people, said in deed that prophetic saying: “Behold me; send me.” 1733

### CHAPTER V.—On that strength—or wisdom and Spirit—which spoke, and which those disputing with him could not resist; and how he wisely defeated the accusers who said that they had heard words of blasphemy against Moses, God, and the holy place. 1734

### CHAPTER VI.—With what strength he rebukes the unbelieving, saying, “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in hearts and ears,” and the rest—for which, nevertheless, dying in unconquered love, he prayed. 1736

### CHAPTER VII.—On Peter the apostle: what sort of man this Spirit of strength found him and what sort it made him; how before the Lord’s passion he walked upon the waters and, becoming afraid, began to sink; but after Christ’s resurrection, girded with his tunic, cast himself into the sea to reach him; and what these things foreshadowed. [Col. 1918] 1737

### CHAPTER VIII.—On Paul the apostle: how weak—or rather how frenzied—he was, and what sort of man this Spirit of strength made him. 1739

### CHAPTER IX.—On those two most courageous leaders: how together they approached Rome, a beast because of its cruelty and a she-ass because of its error, in opposition to the hereditary discord of the brothers Romulus and Remus; and brought it to the concord of one faith. 1740

### CHAPTER X.—On Nero, servant of diabolical cruelty; and that it profited his rider Satan nothing that he killed these men on one and the same day, though, as some say, a year intervened. 1741

### CHAPTER XI.—That the same Spirit of strength is to be preached in the other apostles. 1743

### CHAPTER XII.—On John the apostle: that he too drank the Lord’s cup, although he ended his life in peace. 1744

### CHAPTER XIII.—On the glorious martyrs and the battles and victories of martyrs: that Abel and Cain never fought in such a great or such a conflict, although they had always been at variance even before Christ’s coming. 1745

### CHAPTER XIV.—On the persecutions of martyrs according to the saying from the Apocalypse: “And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she had given birth he might devour her child.” 1746

### CHAPTER XV.—On the battles of martyrs according to the mystical likeness of Gideon’s war; and on the subsequent words in the Apocalypse: “And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon.” 1748

### CHAPTER XVI.—On the same innumerable conquerors, according to the words: “After these things I saw a great multitude, which no one could number.” 1749

### CHAPTER XVII.—On the same persons who will come with their Lord and King; and on blessed Lawrence. 1750

### CHAPTER XVIII.—On his extraordinary death: how it was heard, like a very great trumpet, throughout the whole world; and that, foreknowing this, he said to Hippolytus, “Afterward, when I cry out, listen and come.” 1751

### CHAPTER XIX.—That this martyr is in a certain likeness another Abel. 1752

### CHAPTER XX.—What he had or did that was similar, so that we may rightly say that he is another Abel; and on his cry—what he says, and what he does not cease to cry even today in the holy Church. 1752

### CHAPTER XXI.—On his saying: “I offered myself as a sacrifice to God for an odor of sweetness, because a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God.” 1754

# BOOK VII
Chapter I.—On the Spirit of knowledge: how, and for what reason, it was especially necessary in the Gospel of Christ. 1755

Chapter II.—What distinction there is between knowledge and wisdom, since one Spirit is numbered as that of knowledge and another as that of wisdom. 1755

Chapter III.—How the general term “knowledge” is subdivided as far as philosophy; and that there is one philosophy which is empty, and another which is true and sound. 1756

Chapter IV.—On the modest designation “philosophy”: why it was adopted or approved; on the vain philosophers who, professing themselves wise, became fools; and on the saying: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise.” 1757

Chapter V.—That all things of which right praise is given are gifts of God, and therefore belong to the Holy Spirit. 1758

Chapter VI.—That the Apostle’s saying, “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up,” makes the name of knowledge suspect to those who understand it wrongly. 1759

Chapter VII.—That knowledge was therefore especially necessary in the Gospel of Christ, because the serpent, cast down to earth, sent water from his mouth after the woman like a river, so that he might cause her to be swept away by the river; and on the doctrine of the impious Arius. 1760

Chapter VIII.—On the thirst of the saints who assist that woman, and on the prophetic invitation: “All you who thirst, come to the waters.” 1763

Chapter IX.—How Jesus, then wearied, sat upon the well and gave living water to those who thirsted. 1762

Chapter X.—That at that time the seven liberal arts also entered the banqueting hall of their mistress, the Church; and that it matters greatly whether words are adorned by things, or things by words. 1764

Chapter XI.—On the first of these, grammar, and its parts: that Holy Scripture uses them in such a way as not even to pass over a fable; and that it possessed beforehand those things which Greek authors boast of having discovered. 1765

[Col. 1919]

Chapter XII.—On rhetoric, or the parts of rhetoric: that Sacred Scripture makes good use of all these according to circumstance and time. 1766

Chapter XIII.—On dialectic: that it too is found in Holy Scripture, especially at the beginning of Genesis, where genera and species are expressed by the very names, as are differences and accidents; nor is syllogistic force neglected. 1773

Chapter XIV.—On arithmetic: that it is found there, and that many mysteries are gathered by means of numerical reasoning. 1778

Chapter XV.—On geometry: that many matters according to that discipline are found in the Scriptures. 1778

Chapter XVI.—On music: that it too is very familiar to Holy Scripture. 1779

Chapter XVII.—On astronomy: that it too is found there, and what distinction there is between astronomy and astrology. 1780

Chapter XVIII.—On blessed Jerome, a great man of learning, and on the catalogue he wrote of many distinguished men renowned for grace. 1781

Chapter XIX.—On blessed Augustine: that in him this holy Spirit of knowledge is truly praiseworthy, and how humbly he confesses that he has received the gift of this grace. 1782

## BOOK VIII

Chapter I.—On the holy Spirit of piety: how rightly we ascribe to Him all that we are and all that we live; and that this Spirit is frequently signified in the Scriptures by the name “oil.” Moreover, as a sign of this grace, oil flowed throughout the whole day from the Taberna Meritoria at Rome when Christ was born. 1783

Chapter II.—That true piety is the religion and worship of God, which the Greeks call *euseben*, that is, “pious.” 1784

Chapter III.—On piety: that it makes a person meek—that is, one who does not defend one’s own sins, but is humble and repentant. 1785

Chapter IV.—That with God’s piety no sin is unforgivable except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit; and what it truly is to speak against the Holy Spirit. 1786

Chapter V.—On the heresy of the presbyter Novatus, who, during persecution, denied that those who had fallen could receive forgiveness from the Church; and how, or which saying of the Apostle, he misunderstood. 1787

Chapter VI.—On that saying of the Apostle, and how it ought soundly to be understood: “For it is impossible for those who once …,” etc. 1788

Chapter VII.—On the house of piety, in which the prodigal son is received in repentance by his pious father; and that the sacred canons decree concerning those who have fallen after they have done penance for crimes, that they are to remain content with lay communion. 1789

Chapter VIII.—How the most merciful Father clothes the returning son with the first robe, although canonical authority denies him priestly glory; and that one converted to the monastic habit possesses the first robe. 1790

Chapter IX.—That not only criminals have been accustomed to desire such a robe—that is, monastic life—and that one who despises this life as though it were the confinement of a sinner, considering oneself righteous, acts wrongly. 1792

Chapter X.—On the most merciful Father: why it is thus said, “and running to him, he fell upon his neck”; and that the Father truly fell upon the neck of one who walks humbly on account of sins. 1792

Chapter XI.—That the Father truly fell upon Saul’s neck when he, now Paul, walked humbly and piously and instructed his disciple: “But train yourself,” he says, “for piety.” 1793

Chapter XII.—On the utterances of paternal piety, saying: “Let us eat and celebrate, because this my son was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found.” 1795

Chapter XIII.—That the whole duty of piety does not consist in eating, celebrating, or rejoicing because one has returned to life or has been found, but also in fasting, praying, and weeping, so that one who is lost may be found and one who is dead may come to life. 1796

Chapter XIV.—That today one ought indeed to rejoice not only in the Father’s house because the son who was dead has come to life, but also to grieve because the elder brother stands outside and refuses to enter. 1798

Chapter XV.—That what is said will come to pass: “Therefore his father went out and began to entreat him”; and how it is fitting to say to him: “Son, you are always with me.” 1800

[Col. 1920]

Chapter XVI.—What is to be understood in his saying: “And you never gave me a kid, that I might feast with my friends.” 1801

Chapter XVII.—On the kid: that it is Antichrist, at whose coming that people desire to feast. 1802

Chapter XVIII.—On the persecution by that same Antichrist: that it will be great. 1802

Chapter XIX.—On the abundance of piety by which at last that brother—that is, all Israel—will be saved. 1803

Chapter XX.—That meanwhile, while we are trained in piety, we must beware lest we be deceived by a false appearance of piety. 1803

Chapter XXI.—On the Gospel example of the steward, saying: “I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg; I know what I shall do,” etc.; and how it should be imitated in the exercise of piety. 1804

## BOOK IX

Chapter I.—On the Spirit of the fear of the Lord: that expectation of the universal judgment is its greatest instrument. 1805

Chapter II.—On the great day of that judgment, and how it resembles the first of the days of the world. 1806

Chapter III.—On the seven Spirits of the Lord: that He who was first in this work is also its end, namely the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. 1807

Chapter IV.—On distinguishing the meaning of fear. 1808

Chapter V.—That there are four fears perceptible to the human soul, two evil and two good. 1808

Chapter VI.—On good yet not perfected fear: how it divides a person against oneself by contrary desires. 1810

Chapter VII.—On the terrible judgment of God: that it is truly the great substance or cause of this fear. 1811

Chapter VIII.—On the coming of the dreadful Judge: how He will sit upon the throne of His majesty. 1812

Chapter IX.—How all nations are to be gathered before Him, when the last trumpet sounds. 1813

Chapter X.—How the Apostle’s saying is to be understood: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first; then we who are living, who remain, shall be caught up together with them.” 1815

Chapter XI.—On the further saying of the same Apostle: “We shall indeed all rise, but we shall not all be changed.” 1815

Chapter XII.—On the separation of the sheep from the goats; and that four divisions of people will exist at that judgment. 1816

Chapter XIII.—On what the King will say to those at His right hand: “Come, blessed of my Father.” 1817

Chapter XIV.—That those to whom He will say, “I was hungry and you gave me food,” etc., do not attain here to the perfection of possessing nothing. 1819

Chapter XV.—How great is the generosity of the reward: that through such works a human being enters with God into the sabbatical rest. 1819

Chapter XVI.—Who those “least ones” are, and that they are of another order, concerning whom He says: “As long as you did it to one of these least ones of mine, you did it to me.” 1820

Chapter XVII.—That at the judgment not only what a person has done for these least ones, but also how long one has done it, ought to be weighed. 1821

Chapter XVIII.—How they will ask and learn what they did, how long they did it, and why they did it. 1821

Chapter XIX.—On what He will also say to those at His left hand: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” 1821

Chapter XX.—Why, or on what ground, He says to those who sinned while living temporally: “Depart into eternal fire.” 1823

Chapter XXI.—Whence the devil and his angels are so strong, or so weak, that fire should be prepared for their punishment. 1824

Chapter XXII.—On His saying: “And these shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” 1825

Chapter XXIII.—How these or those will go—not, certainly, on foot, but by an ineffable motion through the power of that same Word whom they will hear. 1826

Chapter XXIV.—What that eternal life is into which the righteous will go. 1827

Index of subjects and words. 1829

**End of the one hundred and sixty-seventh volume.**
